index.title: Approach to the Patient With Common Symptoms
index.keyPoints:
• A thorough and appropriately directed history generates the highest diagnostic yield—up to 75% in some studies—with physical examination contributing an additional 10% to 15%.
  • Normal diagnostic test results do not necessarily reassure patients and should not be ordered for reassurance when the clinical probability of disease is low.
  • In evaluating a symptomatic patient, a clinical approach that prioritizes understanding a patient's fears and beliefs about serious illnesses may be as crucial as collecting symptoms.

index.title: Cough
index.keyPoints:
• Chest radiography is not indicated in the evaluation of acute cough for pneumonia in the absence of abnormal vital signs, concerning lung examination findings, or altered mental status.
  • Treatment of acute cough is primarily symptomatic; antibiotics are not recommended in immunocompetent patients with upper respiratory tract infection or acute bronchitis.
  • Common causes of chronic cough include smoking, ACE inhibitor use, upper airway cough syndrome (UACS), gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), asthma, and nonasthmatic eosinophilic bronchitis.
  • Chest radiography should be obtained in all patients with chronic cough.
  • A stepwise approach to chronic cough includes sequential empiric treatment for UACS followed by evaluation for asthma, nonasthmatic eosinophilic bronchitis, and GERD.
  • Patients with unexplained chronic cough may have improved symptoms with multimodality speech pathology therapy, antitussives, and gabapentin.

index.title: Dyspnea
index.keyPoints:
• Dyspnea has a broad differential diagnosis, and more than one cause is often present in an individual patient.
  • In the absence of an obvious cause, the initial evaluation of patients with dyspnea should include measurement of oxygen saturation and hemoglobin, ECG, and chest radiography.
  • A normal B-type natriuretic peptide or N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide level is strong evidence against the presence of heart failure.
  • High-resolution CT of the chest is the test of choice for suspected diffuse parenchymal lung disease, whereas CT angiography of the chest is indicated in patients with an intermediate or high likelihood of pulmonary embolism.
  • Cardiopulmonary exercise testing can be helpful in the evaluation of dyspnea if the initial evaluation is unrevealing, deconditioning is a possibility, or multiple problems are thought to be contributing to dyspnea.
  • In patients with significant dyspnea despite maximal medical therapy directed at the underlying cause, other nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic strategies can reduce dyspnea severity, including handheld fans, pursed lip breathing, pulmonary rehabilitation, and opioids.

index.title: Chest Pain
index.keyPoints:
• Chest pain should be characterized as cardiac, possibly cardiac, or noncardiac based on patient factors, history and physical examination, and clinical setting.
  • The initial evaluation of patients with acute chest pain should focus on consideration of the six most common life-threating causes: acute coronary syndrome, acute aortic syndrome, pericardial tamponade, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, and pneumonia.
  • Despite the many potentially serious clinical conditions in the differential diagnosis for acute chest pain, most episodes have non–life-threatening causes or are of unclear cause.
  • Adult patients with acute chest pain require a history, physical examination, 12-lead ECG, and, in most patients seen in the emergency department, chest radiography; if acute coronary syndrome is suspected, cardiac troponin should be measured.
  • Diagnostic testing in patients presenting with acute chest pain should be individualized based on the clinical suspicion of specific diseases on the differential diagnosis.
  • The reproduction of chest pain on palpation is not specific enough to rule out a cardiac cause in patients with a significant likelihood of cardiac disease.
  • Diagnostic testing in patients with possible pulmonary embolism is guided by pretest probability; imaging, usually with CT angiography, is appropriate in those with an intermediate to high probability, whereas D-dimer is the best first test in patients with low pretest probability and selected patients with intermediate probability.
  • Pulmonary hypertension in the absence of cardiac disease can cause exertional chest discomfort.

index.title: Dizziness
index.keyPoints:
• Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is characterized by sudden-onset, recurrent, and brief (usually <1 minute) symptoms that are provoked and worsened with positional changes of the head; the diagnostic test of choice is the Dix-Hallpike maneuver.
  • First-line therapy for BPPV is canalith repositioning with the Epley maneuver, which is 80% to 90% effective and may be repeated if the initial attempt is unsuccessful.
  • Vestibular neuronitis is characterized by persistent (hours to days) vertigo, often with nausea and vomiting; labyrinthitis has a presentation similar to that of vestibular neuronitis, with the additional symptom of hearing loss.
  • Patients with central vertigo often display focal neurologic findings, but 20% of patients with vertebrobasilar stroke present with isolated vertigo.
  • Evaluation of patients with vertigo includes an in-depth neurologic assessment and, in the case of acute persistent vertigo, the HINTS (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, and Test of Skew) oculomotor assessment; the HINTS examination has higher sensitivity than advanced imaging, such as MRI and CT, in early stroke and should be performed on patients with central vertigo in the differential diagnosis.
  • Treatment options for disequilibrium include visual and auditory corrective measures, medication changes, mobility aids, physical therapy, weight-bearing and resistance exercises, and fall prevention counseling.

index.title: Syncope
index.keyPoints:
• Neurally mediated (reflex) syncope is the most common form of syncope; vasovagal syncope is often preceded by nausea and diaphoresis, with fatigue and generalized weakness typically being present afterward.
  • Cardiovascular syncopal events often occur suddenly and usually without a significant prodrome, particularly when due to arrhythmia.
  • Neurologic events rarely cause syncope, although seizures can be confused with syncope; auras, witnessed abnormal posturing, involuntary head turning, tongue laceration, and prolonged postepisode confusion favor seizure over syncope.
  • An ECG should be obtained in all patients with syncope.
  • Echocardiography should be performed in patients with syncope and suspected valvular heart disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or reduced left ventricular function.
  • Exercise cardiac stress testing is indicated in patients with exertional syncope without an obvious cause.
  • In patients with syncope, tilt-table testing is reserved for those with suspected recurrent vasovagal syncope or delayed orthostatic hypotension when the initial evaluation is not diagnostic.
  • Brain imaging is not indicated in cases of syncope unless focal neurologic findings are present; carotid duplex ultrasonography plays no role in the evaluation of syncope.
  • Factors that suggest a higher risk of cardiac syncope include older age (>60 years), male sex, known cardiac disease, a brief or absent prodrome, exertional syncope, syncope in the supine position, abnormal cardiac examination, and a family history of inheritable conditions or premature sudden cardiac death.
  • Neurally mediated syncope is treated with reassurance and avoidance of provoking measures; physical counterpressure techniques can be useful in patients with a prolonged prodrome.
  • Orthostatic syncope may be treated with volume expansion (with salt liberalization, if appropriate), reconsideration of contributing medications, compression stockings, and education on postural changes.

index.title: Abdominal and Pelvic Pain
index.keyPoints:
• Triage is key in the evaluation of abdominal and pelvic pain because some causes may be life-threatening.
  • Careful history-taking focused on the localization of symptoms can help determine the cause of abdominal and pelvic pain and inform the differential diagnosis.
  • Management of abdominal or pelvic pain involves consideration of whether the symptoms warrant emergent medical attention and whether the patient is at high risk for complications.
  • If there is high suspicion for an emergent condition, prompt referral for emergency department evaluation for expedited laboratory investigation and imaging is essential.

index.title: Low Back Pain
index.keyPoints:
• Historical red flag findings that suggest a serious underlying disorder in back pain include fever, immunosuppression, chronic glucocorticoid use, recent injection drug use, pain in the supine position, cancer or weight loss, recent trauma, and neurologic symptoms.
  • Routine imaging is not indicated within the first 6 weeks of symptoms in patients with nonspecific low back pain without red flags.
  • MRI is the preferred test for back pain and suspected spinal infection, cancer, cord compression, or cauda equina syndrome and should be obtained emergently if myelopathy is suspected.
  • Nonurgent imaging with MRI may be considered in patients with back pain persisting for longer than 6 weeks in the absence of red flags; persistent or progressive symptoms despite conservative therapies; or neurologic symptoms, such as neurogenic claudication.
  • Patient education for low back pain includes providing information on the expected course and common misperceptions, centering on functional therapeutic goals, promoting self-management, addressing psychosocial factors, and encouraging physical activity as appropriate.
  • Nonpharmacologic therapies are the preferred initial treatment for acute and chronic low back pain; clinicians and patients should engage in shared decision making guided by patient values and priorities when considering the different nonpharmacologic treatment modalities.
  • NSAIDs (topical or oral) are considered first-line pharmacologic therapy for acute and chronic low back pain and should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration needed; opioid therapy should be avoided.
  • Acetaminophen and bed rest are ineffective in the treatment of acute back pain.
  • Immediate surgery is indicated for patients with suspected cord compression or cauda equina syndrome, as the strongest determinant of neurologic outcome with surgery is degree of functioning at the time of surgery.
  • The majority of patients with low back pain do not require surgery.

index.title: Scoliosis
index.keyPoints:
• Scoliosis is diagnosed with full-length posteroanterior and lateral radiography of the spine and measurement of the degree of spinal curvature (Cobb angle).
  • Although scoliosis may cause back pain, radicular symptoms, and neurogenic claudication, most patients will not develop significant clinical symptoms.
  • Treatment of scoliosis includes physical therapy, analgesics, and epidural or nerve root injections; surgical referral should be considered in patients with refractory or severe symptoms or significant spinal curvature.

index.title: Neck Pain
index.keyPoints:
• Red flags in patients with neck pain include recent trauma, unrelenting headache, significant neurologic findings, fever/chills, injection drug use, immunosuppression, and cancer or unexplained weight loss.
  • Most patients with neck pain do not require imaging studies unless red flag symptoms or risk factors for atlanto-occipital instability are present.
  • MRI is the imaging test of choice in patients with neck pain and progressive neurologic symptoms or a suspicion for cancer, infection, or myelopathy.
  • The majority of patients with musculoskeletal neck pain will have resolution or near resolution of their symptoms within 6 to 12 weeks with conservative measures, including range-of-motion exercise, physical therapy, ice or heat application, and analgesic agents.
  • Oral and topical NSAIDs are considered first-line pharmacologic therapy for musculoskeletal neck pain.
  • Patients with cervical radiculopathy with nonprogressive paresthesia and numbness without myelopathy should be treated conservatively for 6 to 8 weeks; surgery is reserved for patients with either progressive motor weakness or persistent radicular pain.

index.title: Upper Extremity Musculoskeletal Pain
index.keyPoints:
• Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) results from compression of the brachial plexus; symptoms include arm paresthesia, pain, and weakness that worsen with repetitive arm use, especially overhead activities.
  • Initial treatment of neurogenic TOS includes improving posture and physical therapy to strengthen shoulder girdle musculature; surgical decompression is reserved for progressive or disabling symptoms.
  • Diagnosis of venous and arterial TOS is usually initially accomplished with ultrasonography; treatment entails thrombolysis/embolectomy (if thrombus present), followed by decompressive surgery.
  • Rotator cuff disease encompasses all symptomatic rotator cuff disorders, including rotator cuff tendinopathy, partial- and full-thickness rotator cuff tears, subacromial bursitis, and impingement syndrome; historical clues include overuse (repetitive overhead work), anterolateral shoulder pain, and nonpositional night pain.
  • Most patients with rotator cuff disease in the absence of a suspected acute full tear do not require immediate imaging studies; treatment may include physical therapy, education, avoidance or modification of aggravating activities, and acetaminophen or NSAIDs.
  • Patients with suspected acute full-thickness rotator cuff tears may undergo expedited imaging with ultrasound or MRI; surgical repair may be indicated depending on the degree of pain, loss of function, and occupation.
  • Adhesive capsulitis is characterized by anterolateral shoulder pain and stiffness that is often worse at night; examination typically shows progressive loss of abduction or external rotation and decreased passive and active range of motion.
  • Treatment of adhesive capsulitis focuses on pain control and improved range of motion; combining intra-articular glucocorticoid injections and physical therapy may be more effective than either treatment alone.
  • Acromioclavicular joint degeneration is characterized by poorly localized pain on the superior shoulder and lateral clavicle; pain on crossed-arm adduction test and shoulder abduction beyond 120 degrees is suggestive.
  • Medial and lateral epicondylitis is diagnosed clinically, and imaging is usually not necessary; treatment includes NSAIDs, counterforce braces, physical therapy, and avoidance of pain-inducing activities.
  • Olecranon bursitis is characterized by posterior elbow swelling and tenderness with normal elbow range of motion; pain on elbow extension and reduced range of motion suggest infection or active inflammation.
  • A structured clinical evaluation is usually sufficient to diagnose carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS).
  • Indications for electrodiagnostic studies in CTS include diagnostic uncertainty and findings suggestive of moderate to severe disease (muscle weakness, thenar atrophy, sensory loss).
  • Initial treatment of mild CTS includes activity modification and nocturnal wrist-neutral splinting; glucocorticoid injection may provide symptomatic improvement.
  • Surgery should be considered in CTS in moderate or severe disease as suggested by motor loss, sensory loss, or thenar atrophy and concordant findings on electrodiagnostic testing.

index.title: Lower Extremity Musculoskeletal Pain
index.keyPoints:
• Anterior hip pain is often caused by intra-articular conditions such as osteoarthritis, avascular necrosis, femoroacetabular impingement, and labral tear.
  • Anterior hip pain in older adults that starts insidiously and worsens with standing and activity suggests osteoarthritis.
  • Lateral hip pain is most commonly secondary to greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS) and meralgia paresthetica.
  • GTPS causes lateral hip pain that worsens with lying on the affected side; tenderness to palpation of the greater trochanter is usually present.
  • Posterior hip pain is commonly caused by lumbar radiculopathy, vascular claudication, sacroiliac joint dysfunction, and gluteal tendinopathy.
  • In patients with intra-articular causes of hip pain, pain or restricted range of motion is present with internal rotation of the hip, the FADIR (Flexion, ADduction, and Internal Rotation) test, and the log roll test.
  • The FABER (Flexion, ABduction, and External Rotation) test may cause posterior hip pain in the presence of sacroiliac joint dysfunction and groin pain with an intra-articular or iliopsoas cause.
  • Hip radiography with anteroposterior pelvic and frog-leg lateral views should be performed in patients with hip pain and a suspicion for fracture, dislocation, or intra-articular cause.
  • In patients with hip pain following trauma, additional imaging with CT or MRI should be pursued if there is a high suspicion of fracture and initial radiographs are negative, especially in patients with osteoporosis.
  • MR arthrography is the preferred test in patients with a suspected labral tear of the hip.
  • Acute anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears usually result from noncontact twisting injuries and may be accompanied by an audible pop; patients often cannot bear weight immediately and develop large effusions within several hours.
  • ACL tears often require surgical reconstruction, whereas most medial collateral ligament and posterior cruciate ligament tears can be managed conservatively with rest and physical therapy.
  • For degenerative meniscal tears of the knee, nonoperative management and physical therapy are as effective as partial meniscectomy in relieving pain and improving function.
  • Patellofemoral pain syndrome is characterized by anterior knee discomfort with prolonged sitting, squatting, navigating stairs, and running; the most effective treatment is physical therapy focused on muscle strengthening.
  • All patients with prepatellar bursitis regardless of duration should undergo fluid aspiration and analysis.
  • Medial tibial stress syndrome presents as pain in the posteromedial border of the tibias in the mid to distal shins accompanied by tenderness spanning at least 5 cm; the diagnosis is clinical, and imaging is not necessary.
  • Iliotibial band syndrome is characterized by lateral knee and distal thigh pain at the end of exercise involving knee flexion and extension; treatment focuses on gradual return to activity, stretching, and strengthening.
  • No treatment is necessary for asymptomatic popliteal (Baker) cysts; joint aspiration and intra-articular or intra-cystic glucocorticoid injection may provide relief for those with symptoms.
  • Treatment of acute ankle sprain includes intermittent cryotherapy, a lace-up support or air stirrup brace combined with elastic compression wrapping, early mobilization with weight bearing as tolerated, and analgesics.
  • Patients with high ankle sprains (distal tibiofibular syndesmosis ligament injuries) should be referred for specialty consultation.
  • Stress fracture most commonly occurs in the metatarsals, tarsals, and calcaneus and is suggested by pain with percussion or pain with hopping on a single leg; plain radiography is usually diagnostic, but MRI should be completed if clinical probability is high and initial films are unrevealing.
  • Plantar fasciitis classically causes sharp, medial-inferior heel pain with the first morning steps and after prolonged rest; the medial calcaneal tubercle is frequently tender.
  • Treatment of plantar fasciitis includes plantar fascia stretches, activity modification, and foot orthoses; most patients improve, but recovery may take up to 12 months.
  • Plantar Morton neuroma (interdigital neuralgia) causes pain between the metatarsal heads and the sensation of walking on a pebble; diagnosis is clinical, and first-line therapy includes footwear modification and padding.

index.title: Lower Extremity Edema and Ulcers
index.keyPoints:
• The most common causes of lower extremity edema include venous obstruction or insufficiency, heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, and medications.
  • Conservative measures, including exercise, leg elevation, lifestyle changes, and compression stockings, are first-line therapies for chronic venous insufficiency; symptomatic patients should also be referred to a vascular specialist for consideration of endovascular intervention.
  • Venous ulcer treatment includes compression therapy, which improves venous flow, reduces edema, and promotes fibrinolysis, and early referral to a vascular specialist for consideration of venous intervention.
  • Antibiotics are not recommended for treating venous stasis ulcers in the absence of infection.

index.title: Approach to the Patient With Pain
index.keyPoints:
• In patients with pain, determination of pain onset, location, duration, character, severity, temporal nature, and responsiveness to treatment is crucial in identifying the pain generator and tailoring the diagnostic and therapeutic approaches.
  • In patients with chronic noncancer pain, additional testing and imaging are unlikely to be helpful absent the presence of a red flag (such as weight loss or fever in a patient with chronic back pain) or a substantial change in the pain pattern.
  • In patients with a history of cancer and chronic cancer-related or cancer treatment–related pain, including those in survivorship, new or worsening pain should prompt a detailed diagnostic assessment.
  • Nonpharmacologic strategies are the cornerstone of pain management; pharmacologic therapy, including nonopioid and opioid therapies, should be viewed as adjunctive to nonpharmacologic approaches.
  • Physical therapy can improve both pain and function in patients with debility due to chronic pain; exercise programs also improve pain and function in patients with chronic pain.
  • In patients with chronic pain, cognitive behavioral techniques, including cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness-based stress reduction, and biofeedback, can reduce pain and improve overall function and mood.
  • In patients with chronic pain, aggressive treatment of depression with cognitive behavioral therapy and pharmacologic therapy can lead to substantial improvement in both chronic pain and depressive symptoms.
  • Musculoskeletal or inflammatory nociceptive pain may be treated initially with trials of acetaminophen or NSAIDs; topical NSAIDs have few systemic adverse effects and may be effective for some patients.
  • In patients with chronic pain, pharmacologic therapy may be used as adjunctive treatment when nonpharmacologic therapies have not achieved their desired effect; clinicians should emphasize that pharmacologic therapies have limited efficacy in the long-term management of pain and are intended to improve function and quality of life, not pain scores.
  • Gabapentinoids, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, and tricyclic antidepressants are first-line therapies for chronic neuropathic pain; gabapentinoids should be used with caution in patients with COPD.
  • Tricyclic antidepressants can be effective for neuropathic and nociplastic pain syndromes, although their use is often limited by adverse effects and drug-drug interactions.
  • Opioid therapy in inpatients should be limited to those with moderate to severe pain.
  • Opioid therapy in inpatients should consist of immediate-release opioids prescribed at the lowest effective dose for the shortest period of time on an as-needed rather than scheduled basis.
  • Long-term opioid use is associated with poorer overall functional status, worse quality of life, and worse pain.
  • When opioids are prescribed in the outpatient setting, the lowest possible dose of an immediate-release formulation should be used.
  • A risk assessment should be completed in all patients being considered for opioid therapy, including consideration of risk factors for opioid-related harms, such as substance use, the presence of kidney or liver disease, sleep-disordered breathing, and pregnancy; the Opioid Risk Tool is a commonly used risk assessment instrument.
  • The dosage of opioid therapy in treating chronic noncancer pain should not typically exceed 50 morphine milligram equivalents per day.
  • Patients initiated on opioid therapy in the outpatient setting should be reevaluated within 1 to 4 weeks and then at least every 3 months subsequently.
  • Clinicians should offer naloxone to all patients taking opioids and especially to patients at increased risk for overdose, such as those receiving dosages of 50 morphine milligram equivalents per day or more, those concurrently taking a benzodiazepine, or those with a history of substance use disorder, a mental health disorder, or a respiratory disorder.
  • Urine drug screening and surveillance of state prescription drug monitoring programs are important risk-mitigation strategies for patients receiving opioids.
  • All patients taking scheduled opioids should receive a stimulant laxative, such as senna or bisacodyl.

index.title: Fatigue and Systemic Exertion Intolerance Disease
index.keyPoints:
• In patients with fatigue without a clear cause, it is reasonable to obtain a complete blood count, electrolyte panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone level, fasting glucose level, and kidney and liver chemistry tests.
  • “Red flag” signs or symptoms (fever, involuntary weight loss, persistent lymphadenopathy, muscle atrophy, and synovitis) should prompt evaluation for an alternative diagnosis to systemic exertion intolerance disease.
  • Patients with systemic exertion intolerance disease benefit most from a structured, multimodal approach that includes regularly scheduled office visits; no medications have shown consistent, reproducible benefit.

index.title: Insomnia
index.keyPoints:
• Routine diagnostic testing, such as polysomnography, is not recommended when evaluating insomnia unless the clinical presentation suggests a sleep disorder.
  • First-line therapy for insomnia is cognitive behavioral therapy, which includes cognitive therapy, education on sleep hygiene, and behavioral interventions.
  • Pharmacologic therapies for insomnia are associated with adverse effects and should be initiated on a short-term basis only in patients with insomnia refractory to nonpharmacologic interventions.
  • The evidence supporting the use of over-the-counter medications (e.g., anticholinergics, antihistamines, and melatonin) and several commonly used antidepressant and antipsychotic medications (e.g., trazadone, mirtazapine, and quetiapine) for insomnia is limited and they should generally not be used for this indication.

index.title: In-Flight Medical Events
index.keyPoints:
• The physician's role in in-flight events involves assessing the patient, establishing a diagnosis when possible, administering basic medical treatments, providing reassurance as appropriate, and recommending flight diversion if necessary.
  • When in-flight medical emergencies occur, physicians act as part of a collaborative team involving the flight crew and ground-based physicians; the ultimate decision of the operation of the aircraft (e.g., diversion) is made by the flight captain.
  • In the United States, physicians are not legally mandated to assist in the event of an in-flight emergency; however, physicians have an ethical obligation to provide assistance as able.

index.title: Medically Unexplained Symptoms
index.keyPoints:
• Central sensitization plays a role in many medically unexplained symptoms (MUS) as well as in some common chronic pain syndromes, such as fibromyalgia and temporomandibular disorders.
  • In patients with MUS, clinicians should limit diagnostic testing to those tests deemed medically necessary; unrevealing studies provide negligible reassurance, pose iatrogenic risks, and result in additional patient anxiety.
  • The goals of management in patients with MUS are maintaining an effective relationship with the patient, restoration of function, decreased symptom focus, and acquisition of coping mechanisms rather than abatement of symptoms.

index.title: Epidemiology and Risk Factors
index.keyPoints:
• Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death in the United States; almost 50% of adults have some form of CVD.
  • There are significant disparities in the diagnosis and treatment of CVD and many groups have been underrepresented in clinical treatment trials, making it challenging to generalize treatment decisions.
  • Beyond age and sex, risk for cardiovascular disease is strongly attributed to modifiable risk factors, including dyslipidemia, tobacco use, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity, inadequate exercise, poor sleep, and poor diet.
  • Tobacco use is the leading preventable cause of disease, disability, and death in the United States, and prioritizing smoking cessation is crucial.
  • Hypertension is a significant contributor to cardiovascular disease; the population attributable risk of hypertension for stroke is 48%, and 32% for heart failure.
  • Diabetes markedly increases the risk for cardiovascular disease, and 68% of individuals with diabetes eventually die of heart disease.
  • Obesity leads to multiple cardiovascular disease risk factors at earlier ages.
  • Obstetric complications such as preeclampsia, gestational hypertension or diabetes, and preterm or low-birth-weight delivery increase cardiovascular risk in women.
  • Validated risk prediction tools, such as the Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE) and the Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease Events (PREVENT) score, can be used to identify persons at risk for cardiovascular disease (CVD) who would benefit from preventive measures, including statin therapy.
  • The PCE is a tool to predict 10-year risk in U.S. adults aged 40 to 75 years and is recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) and other organizations to assess atherosclerotic CVD risk.
  • Nontraditional risk factors such as chronic kidney disease, selected testing (e.g., high-sensitivity C-reactive protein level, ankle-brachial index), and family history of premature coronary artery disease may help refine the degree of CVD risk in some patients.
  • The inclusion of race in cardiovascular risk calculators such as the PCE recommended by the USPSTF is problematic, and use of risk scores that better reflect individualized risk such as the PREVENT score is likely to grow.
  • Chronic kidney disease is associated with a higher incidence of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and worse cardiovascular outcomes.
  • Systemic inflammatory diseases increase cardiovascular risk; the risk for coronary artery disease is nearly 60% higher in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and is nearly doubled in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus.
  • HIV-related risk-enhancing factors for CVD include prolonged HIV viremia/delay in antiretroviral therapy; low current/nadir CD4 cell count; HIV treatment failure; and the effects of antiretroviral therapy, including metabolic syndrome and lipodystrophy/lipoatrophy.

index.title: Dyslipidemia
index.keyPoints:
• The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends universal lipid screening in adults aged 40 to 75 years to assess for dyslipidemia and to calculate the 10-year risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).
  • The primary utility of LDL cholesterol measurement is to identify patients without known ASCVD who will benefit from interventions to lower risk and to assess response to therapy.
  • Secondary causes of an elevated LDL cholesterol level, including hypothyroidism, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, nephrotic syndrome, and medications (e.g., glucocorticoids, diuretics, amiodarone), should be considered in all patients.
  • Genetic testing for familial hypercholesterolemia may be considered in patients with an LDL cholesterol level greater than 250 mg/dL (6.48 mmol/L) and in those who have an LDL cholesterol level greater than 190 mg/dL (4.92 mmol/L) and a first-degree relative with similar hypercholesterolemia or premature coronary artery disease.
  • Triglyceride levels greater than 500 to 1000 mg/dL (5.65-11.30 mmol/L) may cause acute pancreatitis.
  • All patients should be counseled regarding therapeutic lifestyle changes, including dietary modification, regular physical activity, achievement of optimal body weight, and smoking cessation.
  • Patients should adhere to a diet that focuses on consumption of fruits, vegetables, fiber, and monounsaturated fats and minimizes intake of saturated and trans fats, simple carbohydrates, and red meats.
  • High-intensity statin therapy includes atorvastatin at 40 to 80 mg/d and rosuvastatin at 20 to 40 mg/d.
  • For primary prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), the American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) recommend that patients aged 40 to 75 years with a 10-year ASCVD risk of 20% or patients of any age with an LDL cholesterol level of 190 mg/dL or higher (≥4.92 mmol/L) receive high-intensity statin therapy.
  • For primary prevention of ASCVD, the AHA/ACC recommend that patients aged 40 to 75 years with a 10-year ASCVD risk of 7.5% to less than 20% and risk-enhancing factors be treated with at least moderate-intensity statin therapy; it can also be considered in patients with a risk of 5% to less than 7.5%.
  • At least moderate-intensity statin therapy is indicated in all patients with diabetes; high-intensity statin therapy should be considered in patients with diabetes with other risk factors for ASCVD.
  • Nonstatin drugs to lower LDL cholesterol, including ezetimibe and proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) monoclonal antibodies, may be considered for primary prevention of ASCVD in patients at high risk who are either intolerant of or do not adequately respond to statin therapy despite maximum tolerated dose.
  • Patients with familial hypercholesterolemia are considered high ASCVD risk and should also be considered for nonstatin drug therapy if they are intolerant of or do not adequately respond to statin therapy.
  • The American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology recommend that all patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) aged 75 years and younger be treated with high-intensity statin therapy with an LDL cholesterol goal of less than 70 mg/dL (1.81 mmol/L).
  • In patients with ASCVD and an LDL cholesterol level that is not reduced by at least 50% or is still 70 mg/dL (1.81 mmol/L) or greater despite maximally tolerated statin therapy, nonstatin drug therapy (ezetimibe/proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 [PCSK9] monoclonal antibodies/siRNA PCSK9 inhibitors, or bempedoic acid) may be appropriate.
  • In patients with ASCVD and very high risk for recurrent events, nonstatin therapy should be considered if high-intensity statin therapy does not reduce the LDL cholesterol level by at least 50% or to less than 55 mg/dL (1.42 mmol/L).
  • A lipid panel should be obtained 4 to 12 weeks after statin therapy initiation to determine treatment adherence and response to therapy.
  • Statins are generally safe and well tolerated; liver injury occurs in less than 0.001% of patients, and the incidence of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis is less than 0.1%.
  • Baseline liver chemistry tests should be obtained when initiating statin therapy; otherwise, liver chemistry and muscle enzyme studies should not be routinely obtained in patients receiving statin therapy in the absence of symptoms of liver dysfunction or myopathy.
  • Statins are subject to several drug-drug interactions that may increase the plasma concentrations of statins and increase the risk for myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.
  • Therapeutic lifestyle changes including dietary changes, weight loss, and cessation of alcohol use are the cornerstone of management of hypertriglyceridemia as many cases of hypertriglyceridemia are due to secondary causes.
  • In adults without atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) or diabetes with a 10-year ASCVD risk of 7.5% or higher and moderate or severe hypertriglyceridemia despite lifestyle interventions and addressing reversible factors, initiating or intensifying statin therapy may be considered.
  • Icosapent ethyl may decrease the risk for cardiovascular events when used in patients older than 50 years with either established cardiovascular disease or diabetes and at least one other ASCVD risk factor who have persistently elevated triglyceride levels despite statin therapy.
  • In patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia (≥500 mg/dL [5.65 mmol/L] and especially ≥1000 mg/dL [11.30 mmol/L]), fibrates are indicated to prevent acute pancreatitis.
  • If there is an indication, anti-obesity medications, such as glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists, can help manage triglycerides in patients with obesity or diabetes.

index.title: Diagnostic Testing in Cardiology
index.keyPoints:
• In evaluating possible coronary artery disease (CAD), cardiac stress testing is best used in symptomatic patients with an intermediate pretest probability of CAD.
  • If possible, exercise should be incorporated into cardiac stress testing because exercise capacity is a powerful predictor of outcomes; individuals unable to achieve 5 metabolic equivalents of task have higher all-cause mortality.
  • Exercise ECG is a reasonable diagnostic test in patients who can exercise and have normal findings on a baseline ECG because of its ease of performance, favorable cost, and widespread availability.
  • Stress testing with imaging is an effective first-line diagnostic test for symptoms and is preferred in patients with an inability to exercise, baseline ECG abnormalities that limit interpretation of the exercise ECG, or indeterminate findings on the exercise ECG.
  • In patients undergoing cardiac stress testing with a left bundle branch block or paced rhythm on baseline ECG, exercise stress echocardiography or vasodilator myocardial perfusion imaging is preferred.
  • Cardiac single-photon emission CT myocardial perfusion imaging can quantify the extent and severity of CAD as well as prognostic information; the presence of multiple regions of hypoperfusion, unchanged or decreased post-stress ejection fraction, and transient cavity dilatation portend a worse prognosis.
  • Cardiac PET provides data on myocardial perfusion, function, and viability and gives the best perfusion images in patients with increased BMI; however, there is no PET exercise protocol.
  • Coronary angiography and coronary CT angiography (CCTA) provide anatomic information regarding the extent and severity of coronary artery disease (CAD).
  • In select symptomatic patients, particularly those younger than 65 years or those in whom less obstructive disease is suspected, CCTA is an effective initial testing option for diagnosing CAD.
  • CCTA is a reasonable test for intermediate-risk patients with acute chest pain with no known CAD and a negative or inconclusive evaluation for acute coronary syndrome (ACS).
  • Invasive coronary angiography should be considered in patients with symptoms and a high likelihood of CAD, those with high-risk findings on noninvasive testing, those with ACS, and those with CAD and ischemic symptoms refractory to medical therapy.
  • Fractional flow reserve may be added to invasive angiography or CCTA; it measures the hemodynamic significance of a lesion and helps determine the need for intervention.
  • Coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring by CT scan provides information regarding the presence and burden of coronary artery disease, but it cannot determine the degree of obstruction.
  • In asymptomatic patients, CAC scoring by CT scan should be limited to those at intermediate cardiovascular risk (and some patients at borderline risk) in whom results may influence primary prevention therapy.
  • The absence of coronary artery calcification is associated with a low risk for cardiovascular events; however, this is also dependent on age at the time of the test as younger populations can develop calcification over time.
  • The risk for myocardial infarction or death with exercise stress testing is very small (1/2500 patients).
  • Vasodilator stress testing is contraindicated in patients with reactive airways disease with active wheezing, systolic blood pressure of less than 90 mm Hg, sick sinus syndrome, or high-degree atrioventricular block.
  • Adverse effects of vasodilator agents used in cardiac stress testing include atrioventricular block, bronchospasm, chest pain, headache, and flushing; theophylline may attenuate some of these effects.
  • Femoral artery access may be complicated by retroperitoneal hemorrhage, which should be suspected in patients with hypotension, flank pain, and/or a drop in hemoglobin.
  • The mainstay of noninvasive imaging for structural heart abnormalities, including valvular abnormalities, congenital heart disease, pericardial disease, and ventricular dysfunction, is transthoracic echocardiography.
  • Common indications for transesophageal echocardiography include assessment of infective endocarditis, valvular disease when intervention is planned or when prosthetic heart valves are present, aortic abnormalities, and left atrial thrombus before cardioversion, as well as for patients with poor transthoracic imaging.
  • Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is useful in evaluating myocardial and pericardial disease, including inflammatory or infiltrative processes; it is particularly useful in diagnosing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
  • 99m-Technetium pyrophosphate scintigraphy has a high specificity for ATTR amyloidosis in the absence of a monoclonal protein.
  • The initial study in patients with palpitations, presyncope, or syncope when an arrhythmia is suspected should be 12-lead resting ECG.
  • Diagnostic studies in the evaluation of possible arrhythmias are selected on the basis of symptom frequency and the duration and timing capabilities of the recording monitor.
  • Exercise stress testing frequently is used in patients with suspected arrhythmia to evaluate for chronotropic incompetence, ischemia, and exercise-induced arrhythmias.
  • Individuals being considered for genetic testing for cardiac disease should undergo pre- and posttest genetic counseling with a qualified professional to discuss the benefits and limitations of testing.
  • Identification of a pathogenic variant in clinically affected patients with cardiac disease can inform treatment decisions and timing of intervention for selected cardiovascular conditions if used in conjunction with clinical risk features; it may also inform familial screening and testing.

index.title: Coronary Artery Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Stable angina is characterized by reproducible chest discomfort precipitated by exertion or emotional stress without appreciable worsening over a period of at least 2 months.
  • Unstable angina is new-onset angina or angina that occurs at a relatively low level of exertion or at rest, or is accelerating in frequency or severity.
  • Determining the pretest likelihood of coronary artery disease (CAD) on the basis of the history, clinical examination, and ECG results is the crucial first step in evaluating a patient with stable chest pain; coronary artery calcium scoring can help refine this likelihood.
  • Stress testing is most useful in patients with an intermediate probability of CAD; however, if the pretest probability of CAD is high, noninvasive testing may still provide prognostic information.
  • In patients younger than 65 years or those with a lower suspicion of obstructive CAD, coronary CT angiography is the preferred test for CAD; in patients aged 65 years and older or those with a high suspicion of obstructive CAD, stress testing is preferred.
  • All patients with angina or a history of an ischemic event should receive guideline-directed medical therapy comprising risk factor modification, cardioprotective medications to prevent thrombosis and limit atherosclerotic progression, and antianginal medications to improve functional capacity.
  • In patients with stable angina, antiplatelet therapy with low-dose aspirin is indicated in all those without a contraindication; in aspirin-intolerant patients, clopidogrel is an acceptable alternative.
  • High-intensity statin therapy is a cornerstone of therapy for patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) because it reduces the progression of underlying disease and the risk for myocardial infarction, death, and stroke.
  • In patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and stable CAD, a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor or glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist is preferred for the treatment of diabetes.
  • ACE inhibitor therapy is indicated for stable angina in patients with concomitant diabetes, chronic kidney disease, left ventricular dysfunction (ejection fraction ≤40%), or heart failure.
  • β-Blockers, calcium channel blockers, and nitrates are effective first-line antianginal medications in patients with stable chronic angina.
  • Ranolazine decreases angina without affecting blood pressure; it may be useful in patients with persistent anginal chest pain despite optimized management with β-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and/or nitrates.
  • In patients with refractory angina who are not candidates for revascularization, external enhanced counterpulsation may be considered for symptom relief.
  • The primary goals of revascularization in stable syndromes are to lessen angina and improve quality of life; in patients with high-risk anatomic or clinical features (left main coronary artery disease [CAD], large ischemic burden, and/or heart failure), revascularization is indicated to prevent future events and improve survival.
  • Indications for revascularization with coronary artery bypass grafting in patients with stable CAD include left main disease; triple-vessel disease; multivessel disease with severe left ventricular dysfunction; and, in patients with diabetes, multivessel disease including the left anterior descending artery.
  • Antiplatelet therapy is recommended indefinitely after percutaneous coronary revascularization; a period of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin and a P2Y~12 inhibitor is also indicated to reduce the risk for stent thrombosis and remote ischemic events.
  • In patients with stable angina who undergo percutaneous coronary intervention, DAPT is indicated for at least 1 month after bare metal stent placement and 6 months after drug-eluting stent placement.
  • In patients requiring oral anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, an oral anticoagulant plus DAPT with clopidogrel and aspirin (triple therapy) is given for 1 to 4 weeks after the procedure, followed by 6 to 12 months of clopidogrel, and then monotherapy with the oral anticoagulant.
  • Acute coronary syndromes (ACS) include ST-elevation myocardial infarction (MI) and non–ST-elevation ACS, the latter of which encompasses non–ST-elevation MI and unstable angina.
  • Chest pain is the most common presenting symptom among patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS), although other associated symptoms, such as dyspnea, fatigue, and weakness, may be more prominent in women, older adults, and patients with diabetes.
  • In patients presenting with possible ACS, an ECG performed within 10 minutes of presentation provides both diagnostic and prognostic information; ECGs should be repeated every 15 to 30 minutes as necessary to clarify the diagnosis.
  • In patients with possible ACS, the HEART score and serial troponin measurements incorporated into the HEART Clinical Decision Pathway can identify patients at very low risk for subsequent events and for whom additional inpatient evaluation is unnecessary.
  • The hallmark ECG features of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (MI) are ST-segment elevation of at least 1 mm in two or more contiguous limb or chest leads; ST-segment elevation in leads V~2 and V~3 must be at least 2 mm in men and at least 1.5 mm in women.
  • New left bundle branch block; “hyperacute” or tall, symmetric T waves (DeWinter sign); and deep anterior T-wave inversion (Wellens sign) may all indicate high-risk acute coronary syndromes (ACS).
  • Many cases of an elevated high-sensitivity troponin level are the result of myocardial injury rather than ACS; common causes include left ventricular hypertrophy, stable coronary artery disease, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease.
  • Any elevation in serum troponin is associated with myocardial injury and an elevated risk for adverse outcome, even if it is not secondary to ACS.
  • Type 2 MI is the result of nonatherothrombotic supply-demand mismatch rather than plaque rupture; causes include hypotension, severe hypertension, severe anemia, and atrial arrhythmia with rapid ventricular rate.
  • Patients with a rise and fall of troponin levels without concomitant signs of ischemia (e.g., ischemic symptoms, ECG changes, wall motion abnormalities) have acute myocardial injury, and management should focus on the underlying condition.
  • Aspirin should be administered at presentation to all patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS).
  • The choice of anticoagulant during ACS depends on the reperfusion strategy; patients proceeding to the catheterization laboratory are treated at least until revascularization, whereas in medically treated patients, it is recommended for at least 48 hours.
  • ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers are indicated in ACS in patients with impaired left ventricular function, heart failure, anterior wall infarction, or diabetes.
  • Eplerenone is indicated in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction with an ejection fraction of 40% or less and either heart failure or diabetes, especially if initiated within 1 week of presentation.
  • β-Blockers improve long-term survival in patients with ACS and should be administered orally (not intravenously) within 24 hours of presentation to all patients without contraindications.
  • High-intensity statin therapy reduces mortality and adverse clinical event rates after ACS and should be given to all patients.
  • Oxygen therapy in ACS should be reserved for patients with hypoxemia.
  • Prompt reperfusion with primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PPCI) or thrombolytic therapy is indicated in all patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI); shorter times to reperfusion are correlated with improved outcome regardless of reperfusion strategy.
  • PPCI is preferred to thrombolytic therapy for the treatment of STEMI; the goal time from first medical contact until PPCI is 90 minutes or less.
  • If PPCI is not available within 120 minutes of first medical contact, patients with STEMI should receive thrombolytic therapy and be transferred urgently to a PCI-capable center.
  • After thrombolytic therapy for STEMI, the ECG should be monitored at 60 to 90 minutes to confirm reperfusion; rescue PCI should be performed emergently in patients who do not achieve reperfusion.
  • In hemodynamically stable patients with STEMI and multivessel disease, PCI of a significant noninfarct artery stenosis after successful PPCI of the infarct vessel is recommended to reduce the risk for death or myocardial infarction.
  • Thrombolytic therapy has no benefit in patients with non–ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS) and is not recommended.
  • Patients with NSTE-ACS who have hemodynamic instability, refractory chest pain, new heart failure, or ventricular arrhythmias require emergent coronary angiography and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI).
  • In high-risk patients with NSTE-ACS (GRACE score >140, elevated troponin, new ST-segment depression), an early invasive strategy with cardiac catheterization within 24 hours of presentation should be pursued.
  • In patients with NSTE-ACS and intermediate risk, including those with intermediate risk scores (GRACE score of 109-140), a delayed invasive strategy with coronary angiography within 72 hours of presentation is appropriate.
  • Left ventricular (LV) wall rupture and acquired ventricular septal defect may complicate acute coronary syndrome, usually within 5 days of presentation; immediate surgery is usually indicated.
  • Right ventricular infarction presents as hypotension, elevated central venous pressure, clear lungs, and shock secondary to inadequate LV filling; volume resuscitation is the mainstay of therapy.
  • Anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction may be complicated by LV apical thrombus in up to 20% of cases; anticoagulation is generally recommended for at least 3 months to reduce the risk for systemic embolization.
  • All patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) should continue aspirin, preferably 81 mg/d, indefinitely; dual antiplatelet therapy is recommended in most patients for at least 1 year.
  • β-Blockers should be continued long term in patients with other indications, such as a reduced ejection fraction or angina; discontinuation of long-term β-blocker therapy may be considered in patients without other indications for use.
  • ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers should be continued indefinitely after ACS in patients with left ventricular (LV) dysfunction and may be beneficial in patients with preserved LV function, especially those with diabetes.
  • In patients at risk for sudden cardiac death after ACS, placement of an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for primary prevention of sudden death should not occur within 40 days of infarction or within 3 months of revascularization because of lack of benefit.
  • Patients with ACS should be referred for cardiac rehabilitation, a medically observed exercise program that reduces mortality while improving functional capacity, medication adherence, and risk factor profiles.
  • Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is an increasingly recognized cause of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) primarily affecting young women and those who present in the peripartum period; even if associated with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction, SCAD is often managed conservatively because vascular manipulation may lead to extension of underlying hematoma and dissection, worsening coronary flow and symptoms.
  • Coronary vasospasm is sudden coronary artery constriction occurring spontaneously or after use of prescribed or nonprescribed drugs; it is usually treated with calcium channel blockers and/or nitrates.
  • Stress cardiomyopathy presents as an ACS with ECG changes and elevated cardiac enzyme levels, often following a psychological or physical stressor; imaging often reveals systolic mid and apical ballooning with sparing of the base of the heart.
  • Stress cardiomyopathy is treated medically with β-blockers and ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, along with risk factor modification; left ventricular function usually recovers within months.
  • Stress testing is not routinely recommended in asymptomatic patients with diabetes to detect subclinical coronary artery disease.
  • In patients with type 2 diabetes and clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (CVD), a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor or glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist with demonstrated CVD benefit should be initiated as part of a glycemic control regimen.
  • Coronary artery bypass grafting is associated with improved outcomes, including lower rates of repeat revascularization and the composite of death, myocardial infarction, or stroke, in patients with diabetes undergoing revascularization.

index.title: Heart Failure
index.keyPoints:
• Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is characterized by a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 40% or less; an LVEF between 40% and 50% in symptomatic patients is termed heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction.
  • Common causes of HFrEF include coronary artery disease (CAD), hypertension, obesity, diabetes mellitus, and valvular heart disease.
  • Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is characterized by heart failure with an LVEF of 50% or greater.
  • Hypertension is the most common cause of HFpEF; aging, obesity, diabetes mellitus, atrial fibrillation, CAD, and cardiac amyloidosis may also be causative.
  • A normal B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) measurement makes heart failure an unlikely diagnosis.
  • In addition to heart failure, kidney disease, older age, sepsis, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor use, and female sex may cause an elevation in BNP levels; an increased BMI may cause a reduction in BNP levels.
  • Echocardiography is the primary diagnostic modality for evaluation of heart failure; it provides information on chamber size and thickness, systolic and diastolic function, valvular pathology, and regional wall motion abnormalities.
  • The diagnosis of heart failure is established by the measured ejection fraction along with evidence of increased left ventricular filling pressures, as demonstrated by increased central venous pressure, elevated BNP or N-terminal pro-BNP levels, echocardiographic criteria, or invasive hemodynamic assessment.
  • Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is useful in assessing possible myocarditis, infiltrative processes (hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis), and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; routine CMR imaging is not indicated in most patients with heart failure.
  • Evaluation for coronary artery disease (CAD) with stress testing or coronary angiography should be considered in all patients with heart failure; testing decisions depend on the presence of CAD risk factors and symptoms as well as findings on ECG and echocardiography.
  • Patients with symptomatic heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction are treated similarly to those with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), although the data supporting this practice are not as strong.
  • Treatment of stage B (asymptomatic) HFrEF entails an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker and β-blockade.
  • The goal treatment regimen for mortality reduction in patients with symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) comprises an angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor, a β-blocker, an aldosterone antagonist, and a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor.
  • In patients with new-onset symptomatic HFrEF, valsartan-sacubitril should be started instead of an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB); it should also replace ACE inhibitors/ARBs in those with chronic symptomatic HFrEF.
  • In patients with HFrEF, three specific β-blockers—metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol, and carvedilol—prolong survival and should be used in all patients but should not be initiated in patients with acutely decompensated heart failure.
  • SGLT2 inhibitors reduce the risk for worsening heart failure and cardiovascular death in patients with HFrEF with or without type 2 diabetes.
  • Aldosterone antagonists reduce mortality and heart failure hospitalizations in patients with symptomatic HFrEF but are underused.
  • Loop diuretics, which are the mainstay for acute management of volume overload in patients with heart failure, should be reduced in dosage or discontinued once the patient is euvolemic and able to maintain an appropriate salt-restricted diet.
  • In patients with HFrEF, digoxin reduces the risk for heart failure hospitalization but does not reduce mortality; it may be useful for rate control if concomitant atrial fibrillation is present, as well as for symptoms refractory to optimal therapy.
  • Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) placement is recommended in patients with heart failure who have an ejection fraction (EF) of 35% or less and New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class II or III symptoms while receiving guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT).
  • In patients with new-onset congestive heart failure who are starting GDMT, ICD placement should be delayed (40 days after acute myocardial infarction, 3 months in others) because these patients may have a substantial improvement in EF.
  • Cardiac resynchronization therapy is indicated in patients with an EF of 35% or less, NYHA functional class II to IV symptoms despite GDMT, sinus rhythm, and left bundle branch block with a QRS complex of 150 milliseconds or longer.
  • Current guidelines recommend against routine surveillance echocardiography in patients with chronic heart failure in the absence of a change in clinical status or planned intervention.
  • Serial B-type natriuretic peptide measurements should not be used to guide care of patients with chronic heart failure.
  • Sleep apnea is underdiagnosed in patients with heart failure, and a formal sleep assessment should be obtained in patients with symptomatic heart failure and excessive daytime sleepiness or suspected sleep-disordered breathing.
  • Cardiac rehabilitation and exercise training are recommended for all patients with symptomatic heart failure because it is associated with improvements in functional capacity, exercise duration, and quality of life.
  • Primary therapies for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) are diuretics to control symptoms of volume overload and antihypertensive agents to target a systolic blood pressure of less than 130 mm Hg.
  • Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors, aldosterone antagonists, and angiotensin receptor blockers are indicated for use in patients with HFpEF.
  • In patients with HFpEF with either elevated B-type natriuretic peptide or heart failure hospitalization within the past year, aldosterone antagonists may decrease subsequent hospitalizations.
  • Management of patients with acute decompensated heart failure focuses on identifying the cause of the heart failure exacerbation, determining the patient's physiologic state, treating fluid overload, and optimizing medical therapy before discharge.
  • In patients with decompensated heart failure with fluid overload, effective diuresis with loop diuretics is the principal therapy; high-dose diuretics (2.5 times the outpatient oral daily dosage) are associated with increased diuresis.
  • Low-dose dopamine does not improve outcomes in patients with decompensated heart failure with fluid overload.
  • Cardiorenal syndrome is a frequent complication of decompensated heart failure, and continued diuresis with higher diuretic doses is often required despite worsening kidney function; temporarily withholding ACE inhibitors and aldosterone antagonists may be necessary.
  • Cardiogenic shock is characterized by low cardiac output with hypotension accompanied by end-organ hypoperfusion evidenced by decreased mentation, cool extremities, low urine output, or elevated lactate levels.
  • In patients hospitalized with acute heart failure, early follow-up with home nurse visits and a prompt physician appointment (within 7 days) to review the medication list, assess volume status and adherence to diet and medications, and reinforce patient education reduce the risk for heart failure readmission.
  • Patients with severe heart failure symptoms despite maximal medical therapy are candidates for advanced treatment, including placement of a left ventricular assist device and heart transplantation.
  • Patients who undergo heart transplantation have a median survival of 11 years and, typically, a normal quality of life.
  • In cardiac transplant recipients, cytomegalovirus infection (within the first year) and rejection (within the first 6 months) are important complications.
  • Endomyocardial biopsy or gene expression profiling should be performed routinely after heart transplantation to diagnose early asymptomatic rejection.
  • In most patients with myocarditis, neither anti-inflammatory nor immunosuppressive therapy adds to the efficacy of guideline-based congestive heart failure management.
  • Patients with clinical features of and/or biopsy-confirmed giant cell myocarditis are at high risk for precipitous deterioration and should be treated with immunosuppressive medication and promptly transferred to a facility capable of providing mechanical cardiac support.
  • Among patients with possible cardiac sarcoidosis, confirmatory PET or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging may obviate the need for endomyocardial biopsy in those with imaging findings consistent with myocardial involvement and pathologically confirmed sarcoid at extracardiac sites.
  • Tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy represents a reversible cause of heart failure as rate or rhythm control improves cardiac function in these patients.
  • Stress-induced cardiomyopathy is a clinical syndrome associated with reduced LVEF, elevated cardiac enzyme levels, and signs of ischemia on ECG; it typically occurs in older women and may be precipitated by a stressful physical or emotional event.

index.title: Arrhythmias
index.keyPoints:
• Class IC agents such as flecainide and propafenone are contraindicated in patients with ischemic or structural heart disease because of the risk for ventricular arrhythmias and death.
  • The initiation of class III antiarrhythmic therapy, such as with dofetilide, is typically performed in an inpatient setting because of the potential for prolongation of the QT interval.
  • Amiodarone is associated with thyroid, liver, lung, and eye toxicities; regular screening for toxicity is necessary with chronic therapy.
  • Isolated asymptomatic bradyarrhythmias during sleep are unlikely to require a permanent pacemaker, but sleep apnea should be considered as a potential cause.
  • Although asymptomatic, first-degree atrioventricular (AV) block has been associated with an increased risk for atrial fibrillation and all-cause mortality.
  • In hemodynamically stable patients with bradycardia, reversible and extrinsic causes should always be addressed before more invasive measures, such as permanent pacing, are considered.
  • Mobitz type 1 second-degree (Wenckebach) AV block has a lower risk for progression to complete heart block than Mobitz type 2 second-degree AV block.
  • Permanent pacing is indicated for symptomatic bradycardia without reversible cause.
  • Patients who have AV and infranodal conduction disturbances with a high risk for progression to complete heart block, such as alternating bundle branch block, high-degree AV block, or Mobitz type 2 second-degree AV block, should receive a permanent pacemaker.
  • Sinus tachycardia is the most common tachycardia and is typically the result of physiologic demand or distress, including exercise, pain, hypovolemia, drug intoxication/withdrawal, or an acute cardiopulmonary event.
  • Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is characterized by an elevated resting heart rate, with exaggerated increases in heart rate with light activity but decreases during sleep; first-line therapy is removal of aggravating factors and exercise therapy.
  • Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome is a form of dysautonomia characterized by orthostatic intolerance and tachycardia, particularly with standing; initial treatment includes behavioral modification, compression stockings, exercise training, and increased fluid intake.
  • In patients with supraventricular tachycardia, vagal maneuvers, including the Valsalva maneuver or carotid sinus massage, are first-line therapy to acutely restore sinus rhythm.
  • Atrioventricular (AV) nodal blockers (β-blockers or calcium channel blockers) are used to prevent recurrent AV nodal reentrant tachycardia; catheter ablation should be considered in patients with recurrent arrhythmia and those who are intolerant of or prefer to avoid long-term medical therapy.
  • In patients with Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome, risk stratification for sudden cardiac death should be performed with exercise testing or electrophysiology testing.
  • First-line therapy for patients with WPW syndrome is catheter ablation; antiarrhythmic drugs are second-line therapy.
  • Symptomatic premature atrial contractions are typically treated with β-blockers or calcium channel blockers.
  • Atrial fibrillation (AF) is usually the result of long-standing risk factors, such as diabetes mellitus, smoking, significant alcohol consumption, obesity, hypertension, coronary artery disease, heart failure, and obstructive sleep apnea.
  • AF may lead to hemodynamic compromise, especially in patients with advanced diastolic dysfunction or restrictive cardiomyopathy.
  • All patients with AF should undergo echocardiography to evaluate for underlying structural heart disease and thyroid function testing; patients with risk factors for or symptoms suggestive of sleep apnea should undergo testing for sleep-disordered breathing.
  • Urgent cardioversion to sinus rhythm is indicated in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) who have hypotension, acute myocardial ischemia, or decompensated heart failure, regardless of AF duration.
  • In patients undergoing cardioversion for AF, if AF duration is clearly less than 48 hours, pre- and postprocedure anticoagulation should be provided to men with a CHA~2DS~2-VASc score of 2 or greater and for women with a score of 3 or greater.
  • In patients undergoing cardioversion for AF, if AF duration is 48 hours or longer or is unknown, anticoagulation therapy for 3 weeks before cardioversion and continued for at least 4 weeks is appropriate.
  • In patients with AF of 48 hours or longer or of unknown duration, transesophageal echocardiography, contrast CT, or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging can exclude the presence of left atrial appendage thrombus and facilitate urgent cardioversion.
  • The CHA~2DS~2-VASc score is used for primary stroke risk stratification in most patients with atrial fibrillation (AF); patients with valvular AF (a mechanical prosthetic valve or moderate/severe mitral stenosis) or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and AF should receive anticoagulation regardless of CHA~2DS~2-VASc score.
  • Men with a CHA~2DS~2-VASc score of 2 or greater and women with a score of 3 or greater should be treated with oral anticoagulation to prevent stroke; patients with lower scores may be treated in certain circumstances.
  • Direct oral anticoagulants are recommended in preference to warfarin in patients with AF, excluding those with valvular AF (moderate to severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve prosthesis).
  • Rhythm control options in AF include cardioversion, antiarrhythmic therapy, and catheter ablation.
  • In patients with AF, rate plus rhythm control offers superior symptom management compared with rate control alone; rhythm control should be considered for patients with AF and systolic heart failure.
  • In patients with AF, rhythm control is reasonable in younger patients because the long-term effects of rate-only control are unknown and rhythm control may improve long-term clinical outcomes.
  • An early rhythm control strategy may be pursued in patients with AF at high risk for adverse cardiovascular events, including those aged 75 years and older and those with a previous ischemic neurologic event or multiple risk factors for cardiovascular events.
  • In patients with AF and at least a moderate risk for stroke (CHA~2DS~2-VASc score ≥3), percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) may be considered to prevent stroke and systemic thromboembolism; LAAO requires that the patient be able to tolerate short-term oral anticoagulation while the device endothelializes.
  • A rhythm control strategy for atrial fibrillation (AF) should be considered in patients with heart failure; catheter ablation of AF in patients with underlying heart failure with reduced ejection fraction prolongs survival.
  • Management of anticoagulation in the setting of chronic atrial flutter is similar to that for atrial fibrillation; however, a rhythm control strategy is favored in atrial flutter because rate control may be difficult and often requires high doses of more than one atrioventricular nodal blocker.
  • Catheter ablation is the definitive treatment for typical atrial flutter, with a high success rate (>95%) and low risk for complications.
  • Premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) without high-risk features (syncope, family history of premature sudden cardiac death, structural heart disease) are managed with reassurance; treatment is reserved for bothersome symptoms or frequent PVCs.
  • In adult patients with known structural heart disease, 95% of wide-complex tachycardias are ventricular tachycardia (VT), and it is often unnecessary to assess additional ECG or clinical criteria.
  • If the origin of a wide-complex tachycardia is in question, VT should be assumed.
  • Idiopathic VT occurs in patients without structural heart disease and is unlikely to cause syncope or sudden cardiac death (SCD); β-blockers and calcium channel blockers are first-line therapy.
  • In patients with structural heart disease and sustained VT, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement is indicated for secondary prevention of SCD after exclusion of reversible causes.
  • Acute treatment of polymorphic VT includes defibrillation and administration of magnesium.
  • Unexplained premature death or sudden death in a first-degree family member younger than 40 years should raise suspicion for an inherited arrhythmia syndrome and prompt referral to a cardiovascular specialist.
  • Although genetic long QT syndrome is the most common inherited arrhythmia, the presence of a prolonged QT interval alone is insufficient for diagnosis because acquired QT interval prolongation secondary to structural heart disease, medication, and electrolyte abnormalities is common.
  • In addition to avoidance of QT-prolonging medications, treatment of genetic long QT syndrome includes β-blockers and, for select patients, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement, surgical sympathectomy, and/or exercise restriction.
  • Brugada syndrome is characterized by ST-segment coving in leads V~1 to V~3 with or without right bundle branch block in association with ventricular tachyarrhythmias and sudden cardiac death.
  • Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) placement is recommended for the primary prevention of sudden cardiac death (SCD) in patients with ischemic or nonischemic cardiomyopathy, ejection fraction less than or equal to 35%, and New York Heart Association functional class II or III heart failure.
  • ICD placement is recommended for the secondary prevention of SCD in patients with sustained ventricular arrhythmias (>30 seconds) or cardiac arrest without a reversible cause.
  • Infection of cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) may present insidiously and requires a high index of suspicion for diagnosis.
  • Any patient suspected of having a CIED infection should be referred urgently for specialist evaluation; blood cultures must be drawn before administration of antibiotics, and aspiration of the device pocket is never indicated.
  • Treatment of CIED infection, even when limited to the generator pocket, includes complete extraction of all hardware, debridement of the pocket, and prolonged antibiotic therapy.

index.title: Valvular Heart Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Many heart valve lesions progress slowly, causing patients to limit their activity unconsciously in response; therefore, a careful history and detailed physical examination are essential.
  • Medical therapy, although often effective for symptom palliation, has not been shown to prevent disease progression or improve long-term survival in patients with valvular heart disease (VHD).
  • Formal risk calculators, derived from national databases, may be useful in assessing surgical risk but often do not include frailty and other important patient and procedural considerations.
  • For all patients with VHD in whom surgical or interventional therapy is being considered, a multidisciplinary approach with a heart team consisting of a cardiologist, a surgeon, and an interventional cardiologist is recommended.
  • The characteristic clinical findings of severe aortic stenosis include a late-peaking systolic murmur, a diminished or absent aortic component of the S~2, and a weak and delayed carotid upstroke.
  • Echocardiography is accurate for defining the severity of aortic stenosis in most patients; when there is a discrepancy between the clinical and echocardiographic findings, aortic valve calcium scoring and cardiac catheterization should be considered in patients who are candidates for intervention.
  • Patients with low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis have a small valve area but low gradient due to left ventricular (LV) dysfunction (LV ejection fraction [LVEF] <50%) and low stroke volume (stroke volume index ≤35 mL/m^2); patients with pseudostenosis have similar characteristics, but response to dobutamine echocardiography or dobutamine cardiac catheterization can distinguish the two.
  • Patients with paradoxical low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis have a small valve area with normal LVEF (≥50%) but low flow (stroke volume index ≤35 mL/m^2) due to a combination of small LV size and high aortic impedance to flow (e.g., hypertension) or other causes of low cardiac output (e.g., atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension).
  • Aortic valve replacement prolongs life in patients with symptomatic severe aortic stenosis; surgical risk and patient age determine whether valve replacement is performed using open surgery or a transcatheter approach.
  • Aortic valve surgery is reasonable in asymptomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis and left ventricular systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction <50%), very severe aortic stenosis and low surgical risk, a B-type natriuretic peptide level more than three times normal, or abnormal results on exercise testing.
  • Among symptomatic patients with aortic stenosis who have an indication for surgery, transcatheter aortic valve implantation is recommended for those older than 80 years or for younger patients with a life expectancy less than 10 years, whereas surgical aortic valve replacement is recommended for patients younger than 65 years and those with a life expectancy greater than 20 years.
  • Characteristic clinical findings of chronic aortic regurgitation include bounding peripheral pulses, displacement of the left ventricular apex, and a diastolic decrescendo murmur heard along the right or left sternal border.
  • In chronic aortic regurgitation, surgery with traditional surgical aortic valve replacement is advised for patients with symptoms and in asymptomatic patients with left ventricular dysfunction not attributable to another cause or a dilated left ventricle.
  • Medical therapy with dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, or ARBs is recommended for patients with chronic aortic regurgitation and concomitant hypertension.
  • Emergent surgery is indicated for patients with acute aortic regurgitation due to aortic dissection.
  • Bicuspid aortic valve morphology predisposes to early valve degeneration and stenosis in most patients; associated aortic abnormalities often occur and are independent of the severity of valve dysfunction.
  • Patients with a bicuspid aortic valve typically present with an incidental systolic ejection murmur in adolescence/young adulthood and gradually progress to severe disease in the fifth or sixth decade of life.
