  • Transcatheter aortic valve implantation outcomes in carefully selected patients with bicuspid aortic valve disease are similar to those in patients with tricuspid aortic valve disease.
  • In patients with a bicuspid aortic valve, the ascending aorta and aortic arch should be examined for aortopathy by use of transthoracic echocardiography.
  • Bicuspid aortic valve is a heritable abnormality, and first-degree relatives of patients with a bicuspid aortic valve with or without aortopathy may be considered for screening with echocardiography.
  • In patients with mitral stenosis, transthoracic echocardiography is highly accurate for assessing disease severity, pulmonary pressures, and right ventricular function as well as identifying concomitant valvular lesions.
  • In patients with mitral stenosis and a discrepancy between the clinical and echocardiographic findings, exercise echocardiography or exercise testing during cardiac catheterization is indicated.
  • Heart failure is the cause of death in approximately 60% of patients with mitral stenosis, with thromboembolism causing most others.
  • Patients with mitral stenosis and a history of atrial fibrillation (AF), left atrial (LA) thrombus, or systemic embolization should receive anticoagulation with a vitamin K antagonist such as warfarin; CHA~2DS~2-VASc scoring is not used in patients with mitral stenosis.
  • Unlike with other patients with AF, patients with mitral stenosis should receive anticoagulation therapy with a vitamin K antagonist and not a direct oral anticoagulant.
  • Percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy (PBMC) is indicated for patients with symptomatic severe mitral stenosis and favorable valve morphology; contraindications to PBMC include severe valve calcification, LA thrombus, and moderate to severe mitral regurgitation.
  • Mitral valve surgery is indicated in patients with severe mitral stenosis, New York Heart Association functional class III or IV symptoms, and a nonpliable valve.
  • Primary mitral regurgitation is predominantly caused by mitral valve prolapse (also known as myxomatous or degenerative mitral valve disease), which affects approximately 2% of the general population in the United States.
  • Because of the rapid equalization of left atrial and left ventricular pressures in acute mitral regurgitation, some of the findings typical of severe chronic mitral regurgitation, such as murmur intensity and color flow imaging on echocardiography, may be less evident in acute disease.
  • In acute severe mitral regurgitation, intravenous vasodilators and intra-aortic balloon pumps can be used to treat decompensated heart failure or cardiogenic shock, but prompt surgical correction should be considered in all patients.
  • Surgery for chronic severe primary mitral regurgitation is indicated in symptomatic patients and in asymptomatic patients with left ventricular dysfunction (ejection fraction ≤60%) and/or dilation (end-systolic dimension ≥40 mm).
  • Surgical repair is preferred over replacement in patients with chronic primary mitral regurgitation.
  • In patients with chronic severe primary mitral regurgitation who are at high surgical risk, transcatheter mitral valve repair with a clip device may be considered.
  • Patients with chronic secondary mitral regurgitation should be treated with guideline-directed medical and device therapy for ventricular dysfunction; surgical intervention may be considered for those undergoing concomitant cardiac surgery.
  • Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair is FDA approved for chronic secondary mitral regurgitation with refractory symptoms despite optimal medical therapy for heart failure, but the effect on mortality is unclear.
  • In tricuspid regurgitation, loop diuretics and aldosterone antagonists may alleviate symptoms of right-sided congestion but incur the risk for causing a low-flow state with impaired cardiac output.
  • In patients with severe tricuspid regurgitation, surgery is recommended for those undergoing left-sided valve surgery; isolated tricuspid valve surgery may be considered in patients with severe symptomatic primary tricuspid regurgitation or severe symptomatic secondary tricuspid regurgitation refractory to medical therapy.
  • In patients with severe tricuspid regurgitation and elevated surgical risk, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair or transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement can be considered for select patients with a goal of symptomatic improvement.
  • In choosing a valve for patients undergoing heart valve replacement surgery, a shared decision-making process should focus on the durability of the prosthesis, the surgical risk of reoperation, and the need for lifelong anticoagulation with warfarin.
  • For aortic valve replacement, a mechanical valve is reasonable in patients younger than 50 years, a bioprosthesis is reasonable in patients older than 65 years, and either is reasonable in patients aged 50 to 65 years.
  • For mitral valve replacement, a mitral valve bioprosthesis is reasonable in patients older than 65 years, whereas a mechanical valve prosthesis is reasonable in patients younger than 65 years.
  • All patients undergoing heart valve replacement should undergo echocardiography after implantation to document baseline performance of the valve; repeat echocardiography is indicated for evidence of possible valve dysfunction (e.g., new dyspnea or heart failure, louder murmur or new murmur, thromboembolism, hemolytic anemia).
  • Echocardiography is recommended for all asymptomatic patients with a surgical bioprosthetic heart valve at baseline after implantation, at 5 and 10 years, and annually thereafter.
  • Echocardiography is recommended for all patients with a transcatheter heart valve bioprosthesis at baseline and annually thereafter.
  • Lifelong warfarin anticoagulation is recommended in all patients with a mechanical heart valve prosthesis; therapy should target a specific INR value rather than a range.
  • Direct oral anticoagulants should not be used for anticoagulation in patients with a mechanical heart valve.
  • Low-dose aspirin is reasonable for all patients with a bioprosthetic heart valve without a separate indication for anticoagulation.
  • Endocarditis prophylaxis is indicated for patients at increased risk for dental procedures involving manipulation of the gingival tissue, manipulation of the periapical regions of teeth, or perforation of the oral mucosa.
  • Amoxicillin is standard antimicrobial prophylaxis for endocarditis when indicated; ampicillin, cefazolin, or ceftriaxone is appropriate for patients who are unable to take oral medications.

index.title: Myocardial Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Although some patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) are asymptomatic, potential complications of the disease include heart failure, arrhythmias, left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction, and sudden cardiac death.
  • Heart failure symptoms in HCM are caused by diastolic dysfunction and dynamic LVOT obstruction; LVOT obstruction is present in 70% of patients and is best detected by Doppler echocardiography.
  • In patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) and a resting left ventricular outflow tract gradient less than 50 mm Hg, echocardiography with provocative maneuvers (Valsalva, exercise) is recommended to differentiate obstructive from nonobstructive disease.
  • On initial diagnosis of HCM, 24- to 48-hour ambulatory ECG monitoring should be performed to evaluate for atrial and ventricular arrhythmias.
  • Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) who have experienced sudden cardiac death (SCD) or sustained ventricular tachycardia or who have major risk factors should receive an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for SCD prevention.
  • Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging of the heart and assessment of late gadolinium enhancement can help with risk stratification for SCD in patients with HCM.
  • In patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) who have symptoms of left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction, nonvasodilating β-blockers such as metoprolol are first-line therapy.
  • In patients with symptomatic HCM in whom β-blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated, verapamil or diltiazem may be used.
  • In patients with HCM with an LVOT obstruction gradient of 50 mm Hg or greater and symptoms refractory to medical therapy, additional treatment may include cardiac myosin inhibitors, disopyramide, and surgical septal myectomy or catheter-based alcohol septal ablation to alleviate outflow obstruction.
  • In patients with HCM and atrial fibrillation, the risk for stroke is elevated independent of CHA~2DS~2-VASc score, and all patients without contraindication should receive anticoagulation.
  • Asymptomatic patients with HCM should undergo 24- to 48-hour ambulatory ECG monitoring and transthoracic echocardiography every 1 to 2 years.
  • Genetic testing is not indicated in unaffected first-degree relatives of patients with HCM unless a pathogenic genetic variant is identified in the index patient.
  • First-degree relatives of patients with HCM should undergo screening with ECG and echocardiography unless they are genotype-negative relatives in families with a known pathogenic variant.
  • Light-chain (AL) amyloidosis is a multisystem disease manifesting as cardiomyopathy, nephrotic syndrome, macroglossia, and neuropathy in the setting of a monoclonal gammopathy; treatment is directed toward underlying plasma cell dyscrasia.
  • Transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis is characterized by cardiomyopathy, carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, and neuropathy.
  • Cardiac amyloidosis is suggested by heart failure with restrictive physiology, increased left ventricular wall thickness, and low ECG voltage.
  • Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is highly sensitive and specific for cardiac amyloidosis; testing for monoclonal light chains (AL amyloidosis) and 99m-technetium pyrophosphate scintigraphy (ATTR amyloidosis) distinguishes between amyloidosis types.
  • Treatment of both hereditary and wild-type ATTR cardiac amyloidosis reduces mortality and cardiovascular hospitalization.
  • Restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM) should be suspected if echocardiography reveals biatrial enlargement and severe diastolic dysfunction in the setting of normal ventricular size, wall thickness, and systolic function.
  • Patients with RCM should be evaluated for infiltrative disease, such as hemochromatosis or amyloidosis, which is also characterized by restrictive physiology and may respond to specific therapy.
  • Differentiating between RCM and constrictive pericarditis is essential because surgical pericardiectomy may relieve symptoms and prolong life in patients with constriction.
  • Loop diuretics are usually necessary to relieve congestive symptoms in restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM), but patients with RCM require relatively high filling pressures to maintain cardiac output, and balancing relief of congestion with adequate cardiac output is challenging.
  • Atrial myxomas may present with constitutional symptoms related to interleukin production, embolic phenomena from tumor fragmentation, or symptoms referable to intracardiac obstruction (dyspnea, syncope).
  • Atrial myxomas should be removed surgically to prevent embolic events; a risk for recurrence mandates subsequent surveillance echocardiography.
  • Cardiac papillary fibroelastomas have a heterogeneous globular shape or a mobile frond-like appearance on echocardiography; if a fibroelastoma is associated with stroke, surgical removal is indicated.

index.title: Pericardial Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Acute pericarditis is diagnosed by the presence of chest pain typical for pericarditis plus at least one of five criteria: a pericardial friction rub, new ECG changes, inflammatory biomarker elevation, a new pericardial effusion, or imaging indicative of pericardial inflammation.
  • First-line therapy for acute idiopathic pericarditis is high-dose aspirin or NSAID therapy plus adjuvant colchicine therapy.
  • For acute idiopathic pericarditis that does not respond to initial therapy, treatment is determined by disease phenotype; for an inflammatory phenotype, an anti–interleukin-1 agent (rilonacept, anakinra) is second-line therapy, whereas a noninflammatory phenotype is treated with glucocorticoid therapy.
  • Peri-infarct pericarditis may occur 1 to 2 days after myocardial infarction; acetaminophen and daily aspirin are the preferred treatment, whereas other NSAIDs and glucocorticoids should be avoided.
  • Clinical features of cardiac tamponade include tachycardia, hypotension, muffled heart sounds, elevated central venous pressure, and pulsus paradoxus.
  • Normal or even elevated blood pressure is seen early in cardiac tamponade and does not preclude the diagnosis.
  • Echocardiographic findings of cardiac tamponade include early diastolic collapse of the right ventricle, late diastolic collapse of the right atrium, abnormal interventricular septal motion, and a decrease in mitral inflow velocity of more than 25% with inspiration.
  • Cardiac tamponade requires urgent drainage of pericardial fluid with either pericardiocentesis or surgery.
  • Constrictive pericarditis is characterized by pericardial thickening, fibrosis, and sometimes calcification that impair diastolic filling and limit total cardiac volume.
  • Constrictive pericarditis most commonly presents as indolent progression of right-sided heart failure symptoms, including exertional dyspnea, fatigue, peripheral edema, and abdominal swelling.
  • Transthoracic echocardiography is the initial diagnostic test for evaluating constrictive pericarditis, and Doppler echocardiography may differentiate constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy; chest radiography or CT may demonstrate partial or circumferential pericardial calcification.
  • Right heart catheterization in constrictive pericarditis may show a prominent y descent in the right atrial waveform and a right ventricular dip-and-plateau waveform (square root sign); simultaneous right and left heart catheterization may demonstrate the more specific finding of ventricular interdependence.
  • In patients with acute constrictive pericarditis with inflammation, anti-inflammatory therapy for 2 to 3 months is reasonable before surgical pericardiectomy is considered.
  • Patients with chronic pericardial constriction should be referred for surgical pericardial stripping (pericardiectomy performed via median sternotomy).

index.title: Adult Congenital Heart Disease
index.keyPoints:
• No treatment or follow-up is needed in asymptomatic patients with a patent foramen ovale (PFO).
  • In patients younger than 60 years with a PFO with high-risk features and embolic stroke of undetermined source, PFO closure is recommended after a discussion of potential benefits and risks.
  • Data are lacking regarding the benefit of closure of a PFO in patients older than 60 years.
  • Clinical findings in patients with an atrial septal defect are often subtle and may include a parasternal impulse, fixed splitting of the S~2, and a pulmonary outflow murmur.
  • The main indications for atrial septal defect (ASD) closure include right-sided cardiac chamber enlargement and functional impairment.
  • Asymptomatic, small ASDs without right heart enlargement can be monitored with clinical and echocardiographic surveillance.
  • A small ventricular septal defect without pulmonary arterial hypertension presents with a loud holosystolic murmur located at the left sternal border that obliterates the S~2.
  • Ventricular septal defect (VSD) closure is indicated when the pulmonary-to-systemic blood flow ratio is 1.5 or greater with evidence of left ventricular volume overload in the absence of pulmonary arterial hypertension.
  • VSD closure is not indicated for patients with a small left-to-right shunt and no chamber enlargement or valve disease.
  • A continuous “machinery” murmur heard beneath the left clavicle that makes the S~2 inaudible is typical for a patent ductus arteriosus.
  • Patent ductus arteriosus closure is indicated for left-sided cardiac chamber enlargement if the pulmonary artery systolic pressure is less than 50% of the systemic pressure.
  • Auscultation findings in pulmonary stenosis include an early systolic ejection click followed by a crescendo-decrescendo murmur.
  • Pulmonary balloon valvuloplasty is the preferred treatment for valvular pulmonary stenosis.
  • Findings in aortic coarctation include upper extremity hypertension, reduced blood pressure in the lower extremities, and a systolic or continuous murmur heard in the left infraclavicular region or over the back.
  • Intervention in aortic coarctation is indicated in patients with upper extremity hypertension, hemodynamic features of significant aortic coarctation, and radiologic evidence of severe coarctation with collateral flow.
  • Among patients with repaired coarctation of the aorta, hypertension most commonly occurs in those who underwent repair after the age of 1 year; when present, hypertension should be treated and the patient evaluated for recoarctation.
  • Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cyanotic congenital cardiac lesion and is characterized by a large subaortic ventricular septal defect, infundibular and/or valvular pulmonary stenosis, aortic override, and right ventricular hypertrophy.
  • Late complications after repair of tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) include right heart failure related to pulmonary valve regurgitation and, less commonly, pulmonary stenosis and left heart failure; most patients will require pulmonary valve replacement.
  • The onset of atrial or ventricular arrhythmias in patients who have undergone TOF repair should prompt evaluation of pulmonary valve and ventricular function.
  • Most patients with repaired or unrepaired congenital heart disease (CHD) require lifelong care; late complications in an adult with CHD should be managed in conjunction with a congenital cardiologist.
  • Late multiorgan system complications in patients with CHD may be related to the congenital heart defect, the type of repair, residual lesions, and related physiology.
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures is effective in reducing infective endocarditis in high-risk patients, such as those with cyanosis, residual shunts, or prosthetic valves.
  • Patients with right-to-left shunt are at increased risk for brain abscess and may develop paradoxical air embolism during intravenous therapy; the latter may be prevented by using an in-line air filter.

index.title: Diseases of the Aorta
index.keyPoints:
• Risk factors for thoracic aortic aneurysm include connective tissue disorders (Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), Turner syndrome, a bicuspid aortic valve, hypertension, smoking, and advanced age.
  • Asymptomatic patients with a bicuspid aortic valve or a genetic condition that predisposes to aortic aneurysm and/or dissection should undergo imaging to screen for abnormalities of the thoracic aorta.
  • All first-degree relatives of patients with thoracic aortic aneurysm or aortic dissection should undergo genetic testing if a pathologic variant has been identified; otherwise, screening aortic imaging is indicated.
  • Screening echocardiography might be considered in first-degree relatives of patients with a bicuspid valve.
  • Screening for aortic imaging can be accomplished with transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), with CT angiography or magnetic resonance angiography reserved for cases in which the aorta is not adequately visualized on TTE.
  • Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAAs) with a diameter smaller than 5.0 cm usually can be managed with medical therapy, including statin therapy and aggressive blood pressure control, preferably with a β-blocker, to a blood pressure less than 130/80 mm Hg.
  • In patients with Marfan syndrome and TAA, the combination of β-blockers and losartan reduces the rate of aneurysm growth.
  • Surgical repair is indicated when an ascending aortic aneurysm due to degenerative disease exceeds 5.5 cm in diameter or has rapid growth (≥0.5 cm/year or ≥0.3 cm/year over 2 years).
  • In patients with Marfan syndrome or other genetic disorders, surgical repair of an ascending aortic aneurysm exceeding 5.0 cm is indicated, depending on the underlying condition.
  • In patients with nonsyndromic hereditary TAA, the threshold for surgical repair may be 4.5 cm, depending on the family history.
  • In patients with a descending aortic aneurysm, surgical repair is indicated if the diameter is greater than 5.5 cm; thoracic endovascular aortic repair with stent grafting is usually the preferred treatment.
  • The most frequent complication of aortic atheroma is systemic thromboembolism resulting in transient ischemic attack or stroke.
  • Aortic atheroma is a coronary artery risk equivalent, and patients with an atheroma should be treated with antiplatelet and statin therapies to reduce cardiovascular risk.
  • Acute aortic dissection classically presents with the sudden onset of severe tearing pain in the chest, back, or abdomen.
  • Clinical examination findings that increase the index of suspicion for an acute aortic syndrome include asymmetric blood pressures in the upper extremities and asymmetric pulses along with a murmur of aortic insufficiency and pulsus paradoxus.
  • CT angiography is the imaging modality of choice in patients in whom acute thoracic aortic disease is suspected.
  • Intravenous β-blockers are first-line treatment to promptly (within 1 hour) reduce systolic blood pressure to less than 120 mm Hg in patients with acute aortic dissection without cardiogenic shock.
  • Emergency surgery should be considered for acute aortic dissection complicated by shock and type A acute aortic syndromes, including aortic dissection, intramural hematoma, and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer.
  • Patients with uncomplicated type B aortic syndromes usually are first treated with medical therapy; aortic repair, often with thoracic endovascular aortic repair, is indicated in the presence of complications (refractory chest/back pain or hypertension, rapid aortic expansion, or organ malperfusion).
  • Risk factors for abdominal aortic aneurysm include male sex, advanced age, smoking, atherosclerosis, hypertension, and family history.
  • One-time screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm with duplex ultrasonography is recommended in men aged 65 to 75 years who have smoked at least 100 cigarettes during their lifetime; selective screening is recommended for men in this age group who have never smoked.
  • Aortic repair should be performed in men with an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) diameter of 5.5 cm or larger and women with an AAA diameter of 5.0 cm or larger; patients with a rapid expansion in AAA size; and those with symptoms resulting from AAA (abdominal or back pain).
  • When feasible, endovascular aneurysm repair of an AAA is a reasonable alternative to open surgery; it decreases short-term mortality but incurs a higher risk for reintervention, endoleak, device failure, and postimplantation syndrome.

index.title: Peripheral Artery Disease
index.keyPoints:
• The primary risk factors for peripheral artery disease (PAD) include smoking, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and advanced age.
  • PAD is considered a coronary artery disease equivalent that warrants appropriate risk factor modification and medications for secondary prevention.
  • Peripheral artery disease (PAD) may be asymptomatic or present as intermittent claudication, atypical exertional leg pain, or more rarely, acute or chronic limb-threatening ischemia.
  • Patients with PAD have reduced exercise capacity and an elevated risk for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.
  • Most patients with intermittent claudication have stable symptoms; however, symptoms worsen in approximately 25% of patients, and up to 20% of patients will undergo lower extremity revascularization procedures over a 5-year period.
  • Peripheral artery disease is characterized by diminished, absent, or asymmetric pulses, and bruits; the presence of a cool extremity, hair loss, dependent rubor, and tissue ulceration suggests chronic limb-threatening ischemia.
  • Arterial ulcers are usually painful, located in the distal extremities (distal toes, plantar foot, anterior portion of the lower leg), and sharply demarcated with a dry base.
  • Ankle-brachial index (ABI) testing is the initial test of choice for peripheral vascular disease in most patients presenting with possible peripheral artery disease (PAD).
  • An ABI of 0.90 or less is diagnostic of PAD.
  • Patients with a high pretest probability of PAD and a normal ABI should have repeat ABI measurement after exercise.
  • An ABI greater than 1.40 indicates the presence of noncompressible arteries in the lower extremities and is considered uninterpretable; a toe-brachial index is used for diagnosis of PAD in these patients.
  • In patients with PAD, imaging with CT angiography or magnetic resonance angiography is useful in identifying the location and severity of stenosis and planning for endovascular or surgical revascularization.
  • Smoking cessation is essential to reducing cardiovascular risk in patients with peripheral artery disease.
  • Antiplatelet monotherapy, typically low-dose aspirin or clopidogrel, reduces risk for myocardial infarction, stroke, and peripheral arterial events, including chronic limb-threatening ischemia, in patients with peripheral artery disease.
  • Supervised exercise training is the most effective treatment for improving functional status in patients with peripheral artery disease (PAD).
  • Cilostazol is recommended for patients with intermittent claudication but is contraindicated in those with heart failure.
  • Pentoxifylline is ineffective in treating PAD and should not be used.
  • Semaglutide may be considered in patients with diabetes who have PAD to improve symptoms, walking distance, and quality of life.
  • In patients with life-limiting claudication and inadequate response to exercise and pharmacologic therapy, endovascular or surgical revascularization is indicated.
  • Patients with chronic limb-threatening ischemia should be considered for urgent revascularization.
  • Acute limb ischemia is characterized by at least one of the “6 P's”: paresthesia, pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia (coolness), and paralysis.
  • Patients with acute limb ischemia should receive emergent anticoagulation therapy and diagnostic angiography in preparation for endovascular or surgical revascularization.
  • Careful monitoring after limb reperfusion in acute limb ischemia is required because of frequent reocclusion, limb edema, and the possibility of compartment syndrome.

index.title: Cardiovascular Disease in Cancer Survivors
index.keyPoints:
• Thoracic irradiation damages all cells, including those of the pericardium, myocardium, valves, coronary and peripheral vasculature, and conduction system, with clinical disease usually presenting two to three decades after treatment.
  • In patients with a history of chest irradiation, traditional cardiovascular risk factors, such as smoking, dyslipidemia, and hypertension, should be aggressively managed because of the increased risk for coronary artery disease.
  • Restrictive cardiomyopathy and constrictive pericarditis are both more common after radiation therapy; although sharing some clinical features, they are important to differentiate, because management varies significantly, with pericardiectomy beneficial in constrictive pericarditis and ineffective in restrictive cardiomyopathy.
  • Traditional cardiovascular risk factors increase the cardiotoxic risk of chemotherapy and should be managed aggressively.
  • Echocardiographic measurement of global longitudinal strain, longitudinal myocardial shortening expressed as a percentage, may be a sensitive and early sign of left ventricular (LV) dysfunction in patients receiving cardiotoxic chemotherapy.
  • Chronic anthracycline toxicity usually presents as irreversible dilated cardiomyopathy, typically more than 1 year, and sometimes more than a decade, after the completion of therapy.
  • Cardiotoxicity from trastuzumab manifests as reversible LV systolic dysfunction during therapy.

index.title: Pregnancy and Cardiovascular Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Patients who have cardiovascular disease and are anticipating pregnancy should undergo multidisciplinary prepregnancy evaluation with a cardio-obstetrics team; exercise testing may be helpful for risk stratification.
  • Conditions conferring significant cardiovascular risk in pregnancy, such as untreated hypertension, significant structural heart disease, or aortopathy, should be corrected before pregnancy if feasible.
  • Cardiovascular conditions that confer a high risk for pregnancy-related complications include pulmonary hypertension, left ventricular dysfunction, severe aortic or mitral stenosis, the presence of a mechanical valve, aortic coarctation with residual gradient, and marked ascending aorta dilatation.
  • Although patients with peripartum cardiomyopathy may present with exercise intolerance and dyspnea, nonspecific symptoms, such as fatigue, cough, or wheezing, are common presentations.
  • During pregnancy, patients with peripartum cardiomyopathy should receive guideline-directed medical therapy, including β-blockers, digoxin, hydralazine, and nitrates; ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and aldosterone antagonists are teratogenic and should be avoided until after delivery.
  • In patients with peripartum cardiomyopathy, anticoagulation should be considered in the setting of acute heart failure and a left ventricular ejection fraction less than 30%; anticoagulation should be continued 6 to 8 weeks postpartum.
  • Peripartum cardiomyopathy may recur or worsen with subsequent pregnancy, and all patients should receive risk counseling, especially those with persistent left ventricular dysfunction.
  • β-Blocker use during pregnancy or lactation requires periodic fetal and newborn heart rate monitoring; labetalol is the preferred β-blocker for hypertension management, and metoprolol is the preferred β-blocker for managing heart failure and/or arrhythmias.
  • Statins are generally contraindicated during pregnancy and should be discontinued at least 6 weeks and preferably 12 weeks before planned conception.
  • Warfarin use during the first trimester of pregnancy may cause warfarin embryopathy; the risk is increased when the daily dose is greater than 5 mg, and alternate means of anticoagulation should be used.
  • In patients with mechanical heart valves, warfarin is the preferred anticoagulant, but dosages greater than 5 mg/d during the first trimester are associated with higher teratogenic risk, requiring the use of low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) monitored with anti-Xa levels or unfractionated heparin with monitoring of activated partial thromboplastin time.
  • Data on the safety of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) during pregnancy are limited; patients who become pregnant while receiving a DOAC should have their therapy switched to an appropriate alternative anticoagulant (heparin or warfarin).
  • In pregnant patients with venous thromboembolism, the preferred anticoagulant regimens are weight-based LMWH or unfractionated heparin with monitoring of partial thromboplastin time.

index.title: Approach to the Patient With Dermatologic Disease
Therapeutic Principles in Dermatology
index.keyPoints:
• For topical medications, ointments have a higher potency than creams, which have a higher potency than solutions or suspensions.
  • There is a generic equivalent in each class of topical glucocorticoids, allowing for a cost-effective approach.
  • Topical glucocorticoid therapy can avoid the adverse effects of systemic glucocorticoid therapy but may cause striae, easy bruising, atrophy, and telangiectasia.
  • Combined topical glucocorticoids and antifungal agents should be avoided because they can worsen some tinea infections and, when used in the intertriginous areas, have a high risk of causing striae.

index.title: Dermatitis
index.keyPoints:
• The primary treatment for atopic dermatitis is the use of fragrance-free, synthetic detergent and non–soap-based cleansers and moisturizers.
  • Topical glucocorticoids are first-line anti-inflammatory agents for the treatment of atopic dermatitis; steroid-sparing agents such as topical calcineurin inhibitors are useful in areas at risk for glucocorticoid-induced skin atrophy, such as face and skin folds.
  • Systemic glucocorticoids should be avoided in the treatment of atopic dermatitis because disease may flare following discontinuation.
  • Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction; a detailed history may reveal the cause, but epicutaneous patch testing may also be necessary.
  • Nickel is a frequent cause of allergic contact dermatitis and is a common component of jewelry, zippers, and cell phones.
  • Treatment of allergic contact dermatitis is topical glucocorticoids, although severe eruptions may require a 2- to 3-week taper of systemic glucocorticoids; shorter courses of systemic glucocorticoids are not recommended secondary to the risk of rebound dermatitis.
  • Hand dermatitis is characterized by pruritic, erythematous plaques on the hands and results from a combination of causes, such as excessive hand washing, contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, or dyshidrotic eczema.
  • Dyshidrotic eczema is characterized by vesicles on the palms and sides of the fingers.
  • Low-cost, effective treatment of seborrheic dermatitis includes over-the-counter medications, such as selenium sulfide or zinc pyrithione shampoos.
  • Intertrigo is dermatitis involving adjacent skin folds and is characterized by erythematous, macerated plaques; treatment includes using drying powder to reduce moisture and, if necessary, short courses of low-potency topical glucocorticoids for associated inflammation.
  • Secondary Candida infection of intertrigo is suggested by the presence of multiple small red papules and pustules surrounding the primary rash; treatment is topical antifungal agents.
  • Venous stasis dermatitis may be pruritic and erythematous; additional characteristics include findings of chronic venous stasis, such as dependent edema, hyperpigmentation, telangiectasias, and venous ulcers.
  • Venous stasis dermatitis may be misdiagnosed as cellulitis; however, cellulitis is usually unilateral, more acute in onset, and often associated with pain, leukocytosis, and occasionally fever.

index.title: Cutaneous Drug Reactions
index.keyPoints:
• Exanthematous (morbilliform) drug eruptions are the most common drug reactions and are characterized by erythematous pale pink to red papules and macules that coalesce symmetrically to form plaques starting on the trunk and spreading distally to the limbs.
  • Treatment of exanthematous drug reactions involves cessation of the causative agent and the use of systemic and/or topical glucocorticoids and oral H~1 antihistamines.
  • Fixed drug eruptions recur at the same sites with each exposure and consist of pink to purple circinate plaques with central dusky discoloration or vesiculation, most commonly on the lips, face, fingers, and genitals.
  • Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis is the rapid onset of a diffuse dense eruption of pustules accompanied by erythema and fever; most cases are caused by antibiotics.
  • Drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome (DIHS) (also known as drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms [DRESS]) develops 2 to 6 weeks after drug exposure; fever, flu-like symptoms, burning skin pain, and a morbilliform exanthem that starts on the face and upper trunk and spreads distally is characteristic.
  • Treatment of DIHS includes immediate discontinuation of the causative drug and systemic glucocorticoids tapered over weeks to months.
  • Key cutaneous features of Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) include full-thickness epidermal necrosis; truncal red or purple dusky macules that progress to vesicles, erosions, and ulceration; atypical targetoid macules with one- or two-colored rings; and painful oral, ocular, and genital erosions.
  • Involvement of the trunk and atypical targetoid macules with one- or two-colored rings rather than three-colored rings helps differentiate SJS and TEN from erythema multiforme.
  • Common systemic manifestations in SJS and TEN include fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy, elevated hepatocellular enzyme levels, and cytopenias.

index.title: Pruritus
index.keyPoints:
• When pruritus occurs in the absence of skin findings, medications and systemic disease (including kidney or liver disease, thyroid disease, or HIV infection) should be considered.
  • Common medications that may cause pruritus include opioids, calcium channel blockers, hydrochlorothiazide, and NSAIDs.
  • Topical glucocorticoids and emollients are appropriate treatment for pruritus associated with inflammatory skin conditions.

index.title: Acneiform Eruptions
index.keyPoints:
• Treatment of comedonal and inflammatory acne includes topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, and topical antibiotics; because of increased antibiotic resistance, topical antibiotics should not be used as monotherapy.
  • Topical retinoids, such as tretinoin, are first-line treatment for all types of acne, including both comedonal and inflammatory acne; all topical retinoids are contraindicated in pregnancy.
  • Topical antibiotics, such as clindamycin and erythromycin, are effective treatment for inflammatory acne, but they should always be prescribed with another topical antimicrobial agent, such as benzoyl peroxide, to prevent development of antibiotic resistance.
  • Oral antibiotics, such as doxycycline, are frequently used for moderate to severe inflammatory acne and acne resistant to topical treatment alone; courses of oral antibiotics should be limited to 3 months to decrease the risk of antibiotic resistance.
  • Isotretinoin is indicated for severe nodulocystic and recalcitrant acne; it is associated with severe birth defects and must be administered through the iPLEDGE Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy program.
  • Rosacea is characterized by chronic inflammation of the pilosebaceous units and increased vascular reactivity; clinical presentations include the erythrotelangiectatic, papulopustular, phymatous, and ocular rosacea subtypes.
  • Characteristics that differentiate rosacea from acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus include older age of onset, presence of telangiectasias, pink to bright red appearance, and susceptibility to triggers other than just sunlight.
  • Treatment for papulopustular rosacea includes topical metronidazole, azelaic acid, and topical ivermectin; oral antibiotics such as doxycycline are also useful in papulopustular as well as ocular rosacea.
  • Hidradenitis suppurativa is an inflammatory skin disorder of the apocrine glands characterized by comedones, painful nodules, abscesses, draining sinuses, and scarring in the intertriginous areas, such as the axillae, groin, and underneath the breasts.

index.title: Pigment Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• Vitiligo is an acquired autoimmune condition that causes loss of melanocytes and subsequent depigmentation of the skin; it can be associated with other autoimmune conditions such as type 1 diabetes mellitus and thyroid disease.
  • Vitiligo appears as completely depigmented, well-demarcated symmetric macules or patches with no scale that appear bright white and sharply delineated when examined with a Wood lamp.
  • Treatment of vitiligo is difficult, and there is no definitive cure; options include topical therapies, such as high-potency glucocorticoids or immunomodulators, and phototherapy with ultraviolet light for widespread involvement.
  • Melasma presents as reticulated hyperpigmented patches of the face; extrafacial involvement of the neck and forearms is less common.
  • Risk factors include pregnancy, use of oral contraceptives, and sun and heat exposure.
  • Treatment includes strict sun protection, avoidance or discontinuation of causative factors, and lightening agents.
  • Xeroderma pigmentosa is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by increased susceptibility to skin damage from ultraviolet light, including all forms of skin cancer.

index.title: Autoimmune Bullous Diseases
index.keyPoints:
• Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune bullous disease that can affect mucosal surfaces and the skin. Flaccid bullae that easily rupture, widespread erosions, and positive Nikolsky sign are hallmark findings.
  • Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by variably pruritic urticarial and eczematous plaques that progress to tense bullae; only 20% of patients have mucosal involvement.

index.title: Photo- or Light-Induced Dermatoses
index.keyPoints:
• Porphyria cutanea tarda is the most prevalent type of porphyria and presents with skin fragility and bullae or erosions on sun-exposed areas, most frequently the dorsal hands; it is often associated with alcohol use and hepatitis C virus infection.
  • Treatment of porphyria cutanea tarda includes treating the underlying condition and phlebotomy; twice-weekly hydroxychloroquine is an effective alternative to phlebotomy.
  • Photosensitivity disorders are characterized by an abnormal skin response after exposure to ultraviolet radiation; phototoxic disorders present as rapid exaggerated sunburn-like reactions, whereas photoallergic reactions present as pruritic, eczematous eruptions occurring 24 to 48 hours after sun exposure.
  • Polymorphous light eruption is characterized by a rash (most commonly pruritic erythematous papules) after sun exposure that persists for weeks and resolves without scarring.

index.title: Superficial Skin Infections
index.keyPoints:
• Bullous impetigo is caused by exfoliative toxin-producing strains of Staphylococcus aureus and presents as small vesicles or flaccid blisters that rupture easily, leaving a collarette of scale and honey-colored crusted erosions.
  • Nonbullous impetigo can be caused by either Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. It is characterized by erythematous papules or plaques with honey-colored crust.
  • Ecthyma is a deep variant of staphylococcal or streptococcal impetigo characterized by papules, pustules, or nodules that progress to punched-out ulcers with overlying eschar; it typically occurs on the legs, feet, or buttocks in children.
  • Treatment of uncomplicated impetigo includes topical antibiotics such as mupirocin or retapamulin; systemic therapy is reserved for multiple sites of infection, disease outbreaks, and ecthyma.
  • Ecthyma gangrenosum is a well-defined purpuric plaque or hemorrhagic bulla that quickly progresses to a necrotic ulceration; it most commonly occurs in the setting of Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia.
  • Tinea presents as annular scaly patches with central clearing and varying degrees of inflammation; diagnosis is made by demonstration of branching hyphae on microscopic examination of scrapings using a potassium hydroxide preparation.
  • Tinea pedis classically presents as mildly pruritic scaly patches involving the plantar surfaces of the feet in a “moccasin” distribution; a more acute bullous form with 1- to 2-mm intensely pruritic vesiculopustules can also occur.
  • Tinea incognito refers to tinea that has been erroneously treated with topical glucocorticoids, leading to an atypical clinical presentation with minimal erythema and scale.
  • Most dermatophytoses can be treated with topical antifungals; allylamines (terbinafine, butenafine, naftinine) are fungicidal and generally more effective than imidazoles.
  • For dermatophytoses involving hair-bearing skin or if there is extensive or recurrent involvement, oral terbinafine, fluconazole, or itraconazole can be used.
  • Most cases of intertrigo are not complicated by candidal infection, but, when present, candidal intertrigo presents as erythematous macerated patches with satellite pustules.
  • Pityriasis versicolor, also known as tinea versicolor, is characterized by asymptomatic, oval-to-round, minimally scaly, hyper- or hypopigmented macules that can coalesce into patches on the trunk and upper extremities.
  • Pityriasis versicolor is treated with topical ketoconazole 2% shampoo/cream or selenium sulfide suspension; recurrences are common, and weekly topical treatments can be preventive. Extensive cases can be treated with oral fluconazole.
  • Pityriasis rosea characteristically begins as a single annular patch or thin plaque with fine scaling (the herald patch), typically on the trunk, followed by numerous smaller, skin-colored to pink papules and plaques erupting along skin cleavage lines.

index.title: Ectoparasites
index.keyPoints:
• Body lice cause excoriations that result in crusted papules or linear petechiae on the trunk, neck, and proximal arms, and can transmit trench fever, louse-borne relapsing fever, and epidemic typhus.
  • Scabies infestation is characterized by intensely pruritic, crusted papules, nodules, and burrows that develop in the interdigital spaces, wrists, ankles, breasts, periumbilical area, and genitals.
  • Pruritus resulting from scabies infestation may persist for weeks after treatment and often does not represent resistance or reinfection necessitating retreatment.
  • Bedbug bites are characteristically linearly arranged urticarial papules (“breakfast, lunch, and dinner” bites) on exposed skin and are painless but pruritic.

index.title: Alopecia
index.keyPoints:
• Scarring alopecia results in permanent hair loss, whereas nonscarring alopecia may be reversible.
  • Alopecia areata, a nonscarring alopecia, is treated with intralesional or topical glucocorticoids for limited disease; in refractory or extensive disease, treatment with systemic agents such as glucocorticoids or Janus kinase inhibitors may be considered.
  • First-line treatment of androgenic alopecia is topical minoxidil, which is FDA approved for both men and women; oral finasteride is FDA approved for men only; spironolactone and finasteride can be used off-label for women; and low-dose oral minoxidil can be used off-label for men and women.

index.title: Nail Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• Onychomycosis is a dermatophytosis of the nail plate, which becomes discolored (yellow, white, or brown) and thickened with accumulation of subungual debris.
  • Treatment of onychomycosis is not necessary in most cases; indications for treatment include discomfort, recurrent associated cellulitis of the involved digit, and the presence of risk factors for cellulitis.
  • Acute paronychia is a painful swelling of the nail fold and usually affects one nail; Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause.
  • Chronic paronychia is most frequently seen in those with frequent hand immersion in water, has an insidious onset, and typically involves multiple fingers.

index.title: Benign Skin Growths
index.keyPoints:
• Seborrheic keratoses are “stuck-on” papules and plaques that most commonly occur on the trunk and spare the palms, soles, and mucous membranes; although typically brown, they range in color from tan to black.
  • Warts are usually self-limited and do not require specific treatment; however, in severe cases, including those with a protracted course or immunocompromise, destructive treatments can be used.
  • Dysplastic nevi can display one or more of the identifying characteristics of melanoma; excisional biopsy is indicated for lesions that display features suggestive of melanoma, are changing in size and color, are symptomatic, or stand out from the patient's other nevi (“ugly duckling sign”).
  • Patients with multiple dysplastic nevi are at increased risk for melanoma and should be monitored closely.
  • Solar lentigines that are larger than 1 cm in diameter or irregular in shape or color should be considered for biopsy to rule out lentigo maligna.

index.title: Premalignant and Malignant Tumors
index.keyPoints:
• Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma presents as pink, scaly indurated plaques, papules, or nodules that can ulcerate and bleed; they can be locally invasive and can metastasize.
  • First-line treatment for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is surgical excision, including Mohs micrographic surgery.
  • Keratoacanthoma is a specific type of low-grade squamous cell carcinoma characterized by a rapidly growing, round pink nodule with a central, keratin-filled crater, giving it a “volcaniform” appearance.
  • Although some keratoacanthomas can spontaneously involute, surgical treatment is recommended for the majority of cases due to inability to reliably distinguish from other types of well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.
  • Nodular basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common type of BCC, typically presenting as a pearly or translucent nodule or papule with arborizing telangiectasias; it often has a central depression or ulceration with a rolled waxy border.
  • Superficial basal cell carcinoma appears as a pink-red patch with or without scale, sometimes with a slight threadlike pearly rolled border; it is easily mistaken for actinic keratosis, psoriasis, or nummular dermatitis.
  • Identifying characteristics of melanoma are the ABCDEs: Asymmetry, irregular Border, multiple Colors, Diameter greater than 6 mm, and Evolution or change over time.
  • All suspicious pigmented lesions must be biopsied; the preferred method is an excisional biopsy with a 1- to 2-mm margin to remove the lesion in its entirety.
  • Shallow tangential biopsies should be avoided in most pigmented lesions due to risk of transection and inability to complete accurate staging in cases of melanoma.

index.title: Inflammatory Dermatoses
index.keyPoints:
• Plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris) is the most common presentation of psoriasis and is characterized by well-demarcated, erythematous, plaques with adherent silvery scale; the scalp, elbows, knees, and gluteal cleft are commonly affected.
  • Inverse psoriasis often presents without scale in the intertriginous and flexural areas; it is frequently misdiagnosed as tinea or intertrigo.
  • Psoriasis is a systemic disease, and cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death among patients with severe psoriasis.
  • Topical glucocorticoids are the mainstay of treatment for localized psoriasis.
  • In patients with extensive skin disease, psoriatic arthritis, psoriasis recalcitrant to topical treatments, or special site involvement (nails, palms/soles, scalp, or groin), systemic treatment should be considered.
  • Lichen planus is characterized by pruritic, flat-topped, violaceous papules on the flexural surfaces of the extremities (wrists and ankles) and mucous membranes.
  • Lichen planus tends to resolve over 1 to 2 years, and treatment with potent topical glucocorticoids is usually successful.
  • Erythema multiforme is a self-limited hypersensitivity reaction associated with an infectious trigger in more than 90% of cases, most commonly herpes simplex virus.
  • Erythema multiforme (EM) minor is characterized by classic targetoid plaques that appear on the face and acral sites; EM major additionally has significant mucosal involvement and systemic symptoms that can mimic Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis.
  • Treatment for erythema multiforme is mostly supportive and includes antihistamines and topical glucocorticoids; systemic glucocorticoids are highly effective for more severe disease, including painful mucosal involvement.
  • Erythema nodosum appears as tender red or violaceous subcutaneous nodules, usually on the shins bilaterally; common associated conditions include inflammatory bowel disease, sarcoidosis, pregnancy, and streptococcal infection.
  • Management of erythroderma involves treatment of infection and managing fluid and electrolyte imbalance; emollients help to restore the skin barrier, and topical glucocorticoids and systemic antihistamines can be used for management of pruritus.

index.title: Obesity and Metabolic Syndrome
index.keyPoints:
• Obesity increases risk for mortality, type 2 diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnea, mental health disorders, liver disease, and many cancers.
  • Waist circumference measurements above 102 cm (40 in) in men and 88 cm (35 in) in women are associated with increased risk for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and all-cause mortality.
  • Adults should be screened annually for obesity using BMI and waist circumference measurements.
  • Clinicians should take a comprehensive history for patients with obesity, including diet, activity, behaviors that affect their weight and health, a thorough medication history, and symptoms of obesity-related conditions.
  • Physical examination of patients with obesity should include measurements of height, weight, waist circumference, heart rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation and cardiorespiratory, thyroid, and skin examinations.
  • Laboratory evaluation of patients with obesity should include thyroid testing, lipid levels, and diabetes mellitus screening; further testing is based on patient-specific signs, symptoms, and risk factors.
  • Lifestyle modifications that are effective for treating obesity include a calorie deficit of at least 500 kcal/d, at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity physical activity per week, and the use of trained interventionists (nutritionists, behavioral therapists, or physical/exercise therapists).
  • Pharmacologic therapy for obesity and overweight may be used as an adjunct to lifestyle modifications in patients with a BMI of 30 or greater and in patients with a BMI of 27 or greater who have overweight- or obesity-associated comorbid conditions.
  • Systematic reviews show little evidence that over-the-counter weight loss supplements are effective.
  • Bariatric surgery should be reserved for patients with a BMI of 35 or greater and for those with a BMI between 30 and 34.9 who do not achieve weight loss goals or comorbidity improvement with nonsurgical treatments; for patients who identify as Asian, bariatric surgery should be considered at a lower BMI threshold of 27.5 or greater.
  • Long-term postsurgical care for bariatric surgery focuses on preventing nutritional deficiencies, managing adherence to lifestyle modifications, and monitoring for behaviors that lead to weight regain.
  • Physical activity is a mainstay for maintaining weight loss, with 200 to 300 minutes of moderate- to vigorous-intensity exercise recommended per week.
  • A diagnosis of metabolic syndrome consists of the presence of any three of the following: increased waist circumference, elevated triglyceride level, low HDL cholesterol level, elevated blood pressure, and elevated fasting glucose levels.
  • Lifestyle modifications, particularly weight loss and exercise, are the most important treatment interventions for metabolic syndrome; routine pharmacologic therapy is not recommended in patients who do not meet treatment criteria for the individual risk factors.
  • For patients aged 40 to 75 years with a single metabolic risk factor, the Endocrine Society recommends screening for all five metabolic syndrome risk factors every 3 years with a fasting lipid panel and measurement of fasting plasma glucose levels, blood pressure, and waist circumference.
  • The 10-year cardiovascular disease risk should be calculated for patients with metabolic syndrome.

index.title: Disorders of Glucose Metabolism
index.keyPoints:
• Diabetes mellitus can be diagnosed with the following screening tests: hemoglobin A~1c, fasting plasma glucose, and an oral glucose tolerance test.
  • Two abnormal diagnostic tests are required to diagnose diabetes in asymptomatic persons; this may be done by performing two different tests on the same sample or by testing two samples taken at different points in time.
  • A single random plasma glucose measurement of 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or greater plus symptoms of hyperglycemia is diagnostic of diabetes.
  • Measurement of glutamic acid decarboxylase autoantibodies is the recommended initial test for newly diagnosed immune-mediated type 1 diabetes mellitus to confirm the cause.
  • Patients with type 1 diabetes have an increased risk for other autoimmune disorders; patients should be evaluated for autoimmune thyroid disease and celiac disease.
  • Hyperglycemia accompanied by insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency defines type 2 diabetes mellitus.
  • Lifestyle modifications, including weight loss, a healthy diet, and exercise, reduce the incidence of type 2 diabetes in persons with prediabetes.
  • Metformin is recommended for type 2 diabetes prevention in persons with prediabetes, particularly those aged 25 to 59 years with a BMI of 35 or greater, those with higher fasting plasma glucose (≥110 mg/dL [6.11 mmol/L]), and those with hemoglobin A~1c values of 6% or greater, as well as in patients with a history of gestational diabetes.
  • Gestational diabetes mellitus is defined as hyperglycemia during the second or third trimester in patients without a prepregnancy diagnosis of type 1 or type 2 diabetes; hyperglycemia identified before 15 weeks' gestation is classified as type 2 (or occasionally type 1) diabetes.
  • The American Diabetes Association recommends screening pregnant patients for gestational diabetes between 24 and 28 weeks' gestation; the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends screening at 24 weeks or later.
  • Glycemic control should be assessed at least every 3 months in patients with diabetes mellitus who are not meeting treatment goals, with subsequent adjustments to therapeutic agents until the glycemic target is achieved, and every 6 months if at goal.
  • Most clinical practice guidelines recommend target hemoglobin A~1c thresholds based on a patient's health status.
  • The American Diabetes Association recommends continuous glucose monitoring for diabetes management in adults requiring insulin.
  • Lifestyle changes, including changes to diet and physical activity, are essential for the long-term management of diabetes mellitus and prevention of complications.
  • Nutrition for patients with diabetes should focus on nonstarchy vegetables, whole fruits, legumes, lean proteins, nuts and seeds, whole grains, and low-fat dairy products; red meat, sugar-sweetened beverages, sweets, and processed foods should be minimized.
  • Physical activity recommendations for patients with diabetes include moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic activity for 150 minutes/week, vigorous-intensity aerobic activity for 75 minutes/week, or a combination of both.
  • Patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus should be prescribed an intensive insulin regimen of multiple daily doses of insulin, including basal coverage to maintain glycemic control while fasting and between meals, prandial coverage, and supplemental insulin to correct hyperglycemia.
  • The American Diabetes Association recommends considering automated insulin delivery systems for patients with type 1 diabetes.
  • When choosing pharmacologic therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus, effects on mortality, cardiovascular and kidney comorbidities, effect on weight, hypoglycemia risk, adverse effects, cost, and patient values and preferences should be considered.
  • The American College of Physicians recommends metformin as first-line pharmacologic therapy for most patients with type 2 diabetes; in the setting of inadequate glycemic control, adding a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor or glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) is recommended.
  • The American Diabetes Association (ADA) recommends a GLP-1 RA and/or an SGLT2 inhibitor for patients with type 2 diabetes and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; an SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended for patients with heart failure.
  • For patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease, the ADA recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor or a GLP-1 RA.
  • In patients with type 2 diabetes who need the greater glucose-lowering effect of an injectable medication, GLP-1 RAs or dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1 RAs are preferred to insulin.
  • In patients who require insulin, the ADA recommends combination therapy with a GLP-1 RA or a dual GIP/GLP-1 RA.
  • Patients with gestational diabetes mellitus who do not achieve glycemic targets with lifestyle interventions should receive pharmacologic therapy with insulin.
  • Tight inpatient glycemic control (80-110 mg/dL [4.4-6.1 mmol/L]) is not consistently associated with improved outcomes and may increase mortality.
  • All inpatients with a known history of diabetes mellitus or hyperglycemia should have a hemoglobin A~1c test if one has not been performed within the past 3 months.
  • Treatment with insulin is preferred for inpatient management of hyperglycemia 180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L) and higher.
  • Critically ill patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus require intravenous insulin therapy with dosing based on a validated algorithm incorporating point-of-care monitoring every 30 minutes to 2 hours.
  • Noncritically ill hospitalized persons with type 1 diabetes require continuous insulin therapy, as basal insulin is needed to avoid diabetic ketoacidosis; persons with type 2 diabetes with glucose values of 180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L) or higher should also receive insulin therapy.
  • The sole use of correction insulin (“sliding-scale insulin”) in hospitalized patients with diabetes is not recommended because it is a reactive, nonphysiologic approach that leads to large glucose fluctuations.
  • Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar syndrome (HHS) must be treated early and aggressively to avoid life-threatening consequences from dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities.
  • Inciting factors for DKA and HHS development include infection, myocardial infarction, nonadherence to diabetes mellitus therapy, stress, trauma, and confounding medications.
  • Treatment of DKA and HHS requires hyperglycemia correction with intravenous insulin, intravenous hydration, electrolyte repletion, and identification and treatment of inciting factors.
  • For persons with diabetes mellitus, a blood pressure treatment target of 130/80 mm Hg or lower is generally recommended.
  • Patients aged 40 to 75 years with diabetes should be started on a moderate-intensity statin; a high-intensity statin is reasonable if one or more atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk factors is present.
  • Antiplatelet therapy with aspirin (75-162 mg/d) is recommended for secondary prevention in persons with diabetes and ASCVD.
  • Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus should have a dilated and comprehensive eye examination at the time of diagnosis and annually thereafter; patients with type 1 diabetes should begin annual eye examinations within 5 years after diagnosis.
  • Optimal control of blood pressure, glucose, and lipid parameters can prevent and delay the progression of diabetic retinopathy.
  • Panretinal laser photocoagulation can treat high-risk proliferative diabetic retinopathy and severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy.
  • Estimated glomerular filtration rate measurement and albuminuria screening are recommended to detect kidney disease early in persons with diabetes mellitus.
  • An ACE inhibitor or an angiotensin receptor blocker is recommended as first-line therapy to slow progression of diabetic kidney disease and prevent cardiovascular disease in nonpregnant persons with diabetes, hypertension, and albuminuria and/or a reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR).
  • A sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor is recommended in patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (CKD) with an eGFR of 20 mL/min/1.73 m^2 or greater to reduce kidney disease progression and cardiovascular events.
  • A glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist with demonstrated benefit reduces cardiovascular risk and kidney disease progression in persons with type 2 diabetes and CKD.
  • Glycemic control may prevent peripheral neuropathy and cardiac autonomic neuropathy in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus and can delay neuropathy progression in patients with type 2 diabetes.
  • Diabetic peripheral neuropathy typically presents with a “stocking and glove” distribution; symptoms include pain, burning, and tingling.
  • Pregabalin and duloxetine are FDA approved for treating diabetic neuropathy, and the capsaicin (8%) patch is approved to treat painful diabetic neuropathy of the feet.
  • Opioids, tramadol, or tapentadol are not recommended for treating diabetic neuropathy.
  • The American Diabetes Association recommends performing a comprehensive foot evaluation at least annually in patients with diabetes to identify risk factors for foot ulcers.
  • Patients with diabetes mellitus should be regularly assessed for neuropsychological complications, as these conditions can adversely affect glycemic control.
  • Level 1 hypoglycemia is defined as a glucose value less than 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L), and level 2 hypoglycemia is defined as less than 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L); level 3 hypoglycemia is a severe event with altered mental and/or physical status that requires assistance for hypoglycemia treatment.
  • Initial treatment of hypoglycemia in patients with diabetes mellitus depends on severity and requires oral consumption of carbohydrates or administration of glucagon or intravenous dextrose with a goal of increasing the glucose level to greater than 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L).
  • Treatment of hypoglycemia unawareness in patients with diabetes involves relaxing glycemic targets and modifying diabetes therapies to avoid continued hypoglycemia; avoiding hypoglycemia for several weeks may result in the return of adrenergic symptoms with glucose levels less than 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L).
  • In the absence of concomitant diabetes mellitus, a hypoglycemia evaluation should be performed if the criteria for the Whipple triad are met: neuroglycopenic symptoms, hypoglycemia at or below 55 mg/dL (3.1 mmol/L), and resolution of symptoms with glucose ingestion.
  • Imaging studies for pancreatogenous insulinoma or noninsulinoma should only occur after endogenous hyperinsulinism is confirmed.
  • To evaluate fasting hypoglycemia, plasma glucose should be drawn every 6 hours during a 72 hour fast; if the plasma glucose is less than 60 mg/dL (3.3 mmol/L), C-peptide, insulin, proinsulin, and β-hydroxybutyrate should be measured.
  • To evaluate postprandial hypoglycemia, baseline laboratory studies, including plasma glucose, serum C-peptide, serum insulin, and plasma proinsulin, are obtained before meal consumption; plasma glucose should be repeated every 30 minutes for 5 hours, and if it is less than 60 mg/dL (3.3 mmol/L), the other three tests should be obtained.
  • Treatment of postprandial hypoglycemia includes small frequent mixed meals with a balance of protein, fat, and carbohydrates.

index.title: Disorders of the Pituitary Gland
index.keyPoints:
• Incidental pituitary lesions discovered on imaging (pituitary incidentalomas) require hormonal testing and follow-up imaging.
  • Most incidentally discovered pituitary masses are benign, nonfunctional pituitary adenomas.
  • Patients with a pituitary incidentaloma should undergo a dedicated pituitary MRI.
  • Pituitary hypersecretion should be ruled out in all patients with pituitary incidentalomas by measuring serum prolactin and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) levels; Cushing disease also should be ruled out if suspected clinically.
  • Hypopituitarism should be assessed in patients with pituitary tumors by measuring serum follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, morning cortisol, adrenocorticotropic hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, IGF-1, and, in men, morning total testosterone; a menstrual history can assess for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in premenopausal women.
  • Mass effects of pituitary tumors most commonly include pituitary gland compression, which may cause hormone deficiencies, or optic chiasm compression, which may cause bitemporal hemianopsia.
  • A rapidly growing pituitary tumor or pituitary apoplexy may result in sudden, severe headache; bitemporal hemianopsia or blindness; or cranial nerve palsies.
  • All patients with pituitary tumors that abut or compress the optic chiasm or who have visual symptoms should be evaluated by an ophthalmologist; any abnormality on visual examination is an indication for surgery, unless the tumor is a prolactinoma.
  • Patients with a nonfunctioning pituitary adenoma should be referred for neurosurgical evaluation if visual deficits are present, the mass abuts or compresses the optic chiasm or optic nerves, or pituitary apoplexy with visual disturbance is present.
  • Macroadenomas may enlarge during pregnancy; if not resected before pregnancy, visual field testing should be performed during each trimester and MRI should be performed for any change in vision or headaches.
  • Acute or chronic traumatic brain injury and subarachnoid hemorrhage can cause varying degrees of hypopituitarism, most commonly GH deficiency.
  • Opioid effects on pituitary function may result in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, increased prolactin levels, and secondary adrenal insufficiency.
  • Patients with pituitary deficiencies related to use of immune checkpoint inhibitors can be treated with pituitary hormone replacement; immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy can be continued in patients with mild symptoms or resumed in patients with severe symptoms after those symptoms resolve.
  • Empty sella is diagnosed when the sella turcica is enlarged and not entirely filled with pituitary tissue; all patients with empty sella should undergo pituitary hormone assessment.
  • Patients with panhypopituitarism require daily replacement of thyroxine and cortisol; replacement of sex hormones, arginine vasopressin, and growth hormone is individualized.
  • The most common cause of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) deficiency is the administration of exogenous glucocorticoids with resultant suppression of corticotropin-releasing hormone and ACTH production.
  • Secondary adrenal insufficiency should be treated with hydrocortisone, 15 to 25 mg/d, usually in two divided doses; dosing must be adjusted in the setting of physiologic stress or acute illness.
  • Glucocorticoids prescribed in greater than physiologic doses for more than 3 to 4 weeks should be tapered to allow recovery of the pituitary-adrenal axis; a morning serum cortisol level can be obtained to assess recovery of the pituitary-adrenal axis.
  • Diagnosing thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) deficiency requires a low free thyroxine level and a low or inappropriately normal TSH level.
  • Treatment of TSH deficiency is daily levothyroxine; only free thyroxine levels should be used to monitor dose adequacy.
  • Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is treated by sex hormone replacement (in patients who do not desire fertility) or gonadotropin replacement (in patients who desire fertility).
  • Only adults with a history of hypothalamic or pituitary disease, surgery or irradiation to these areas, head trauma, other pituitary hormone deficiencies, or childhood-onset growth hormone deficiency should be evaluated for growth hormone deficiency.
  • An inappropriately low urine osmolality in the setting of an elevated serum osmolality and hypernatremia in a patient with polyuria (>50 mL/kg/24 h) is diagnostic of an arginine vasopressin disorder.
  • Arginine vasopressin deficiency (central diabetes insipidus) is treated with desmopressin.
  • The most common cause of hyperprolactinemia is physiologic, related to pregnancy or lactation.
  • A common cause of pathologic non–tumor-related hyperprolactinemia is medication.
  • A pituitary MRI is indicated in all patients with unexplained hyperprolactinemia.
  • For patients with macroprolactinomas, dopamine agonist therapy is recommended to decrease serum prolactin levels, reduce tumor size, and restore gonadal function.
  • Surgery should only be considered for symptomatic prolactinomas in patients who cannot tolerate dopamine agonist therapy or whose tumors do not respond to dopamine agonist therapy.
  • Patients with macroprolactinomas may require surgical tumor debulking before pregnancy or continued dopamine agonist therapy throughout pregnancy; these patients should also be monitored with visual field testing each trimester.
  • An insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) level should be obtained to evaluate for suspected acromegaly; in patients with an IGF-1 level greater than 1.3 times the upper limit of normal, a pituitary MRI should be obtained.
  • Transsphenoidal resection of the growth hormone–secreting pituitary tumor is the mainstay of therapy for patients with acromegaly.
  • Transsphenoidal resection is the treatment of choice for thyroid-stimulating hormone–secreting tumors; somatostatin analogues can be used to control hyperthyroidism before or after surgery.
  • The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion is most commonly caused by central nervous system disorders, drugs, pulmonary disease, and pituitary surgery.
  • The diagnosis of endogenous Cushing syndrome is made by first excluding exogenous glucocorticoid administration and establishing evidence of hypercortisolism; after adrenocorticotropic hormone–dependent Cushing syndrome is established, a pituitary MRI should be performed.
  • The treatment of choice for Cushing disease is transsphenoidal resection of the pituitary adenoma.

index.title: Disorders of the Adrenal Glands
index.keyPoints:
• Evaluation for Cushing syndrome should be limited to patients with a significant clinical suspicion of disease, including specific signs of Cushing syndrome or an adrenal mass.
  • Morning or random serum cortisol measurements are not reliable for diagnosing or ruling out Cushing syndrome.
  • Initial tests for Cushing syndrome have similar diagnostic accuracy and include serial 24-hour urine free cortisol measurements, serial late-night salivary cortisol measurements, and the overnight low-dose (1-mg) dexamethasone suppression test.
  • Once the diagnosis of endogenous Cushing syndrome is confirmed, the next step is adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) measurement; if ACTH is suppressed (<5 pg/mL [1.1 pmol/L]), an ACTH-independent cause is likely, and dedicated adrenal CT or MRI is indicated.
  • Surgical resection is the definitive treatment for benign and malignant cortisol-secreting adrenal tumors.
  • Testing for primary aldosteronism includes measurement of plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC) and plasma renin activity (PRA) in a morning seated sample.
  • Multiple antihypertensive medications may affect primary aldosteronism screening results but generally do not need to be withdrawn before testing; the strongest confounding medications are mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists.
  • Medical therapy with an aldosterone receptor antagonist is the treatment of choice for idiopathic hyperaldosteronism and in patients with aldosterone-producing adenomas who decline or are not candidates for surgery.
  • The localization study of choice for primary aldosteronism is dedicated adrenal CT, but the inability of CT to visualize smaller aldosterone-producing adenomas and the frequent presence of nonfunctioning incidental adrenal masses limits its use; therefore, most patients who are surgical candidates should undergo adrenal vein sampling to confirm the source.
  • Initial tests for pheochromocytoma include measuring plasma fractionated metanephrines levels or 24-hour urine fractionated metanephrine and catecholamine levels.
  • Tumor localization in suspected pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma should only be attempted after establishing the biochemical diagnosis of catecholamine excess to avoid misdiagnosing an incidental nonfunctioning adrenal mass as a pheochromocytoma.
  • The definitive treatment for pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma is surgical resection; preoperative α-blockade is essential to prevent hypertensive crises during surgery.
  • For patients with pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma, a β-blocker should never be started before adequate α-blockade because unopposed α-adrenergic vasoconstriction can result in a hypertensive crisis.
  • As many as 40% of pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas are associated with a germline variant; therefore, all patients with pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas should be offered genetic counseling.
  • Adrenocortical carcinoma is a rare, aggressive tumor that often secretes excess hormones (usually cortisol or both cortisol and androgens); patients may present with rapid onset of Cushing syndrome, with or without virilization, or symptoms from mass effect.
  • For localized adrenocortical carcinoma, first-line therapy includes open resection.
  • The most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency (AI) is autoimmune adrenalitis leading to progressive mineralocorticoid, glucocorticoid, and adrenal androgen deficiency.
  • Evaluation of primary AI includes measuring 8 am serum total cortisol and response to adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulation; primary AI is confirmed by the combination of low serum cortisol and elevated serum ACTH levels.
  • Glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid therapy are required to treat primary AI.
  • Patients with AI require instruction in “sick day” rules to increase glucocorticoid doses during illness to prevent adrenal crisis.
  • All patients with an adrenal incidentaloma should undergo testing for mild autonomous cortisol secretion.
  • Patients with an adrenal incidentaloma should undergo testing for pheochromocytoma if the unenhanced CT attenuation of the adrenal mass is greater than 10 Hounsfield units.
  • Patients with an adrenal incidentaloma and hypertension or hypokalemia require testing for primary aldosteronism.

index.title: Disorders of the Thyroid Gland
index.keyPoints:
• Patients with thyroid nodules should be evaluated with thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) measurement and ultrasound; those with a suppressed TSH level will also require thyroid scintigraphy to determine whether the nodule is hyperfunctioning.
  • The characteristics and size of nonfunctioning thyroid nodules determine the need for fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB).
  • FNAB is not recommended for subcentimeter thyroid nodules unless associated with symptoms, pathologic lymphadenopathy, extrathyroidal extension, history of childhood radiation exposure, or a familial thyroid cancer syndrome.
  • Clinical monitoring for thyroid dysfunction, including TSH measurement, is indicated for patients with thyroid nodules.
  • Patients with goiter should be questioned about iodine intake, rate of change in size, and thyroid cancer risk factors; assessed for signs and symptoms of compression; and evaluated for clinical manifestations of thyroid hormone excess or deficiency.
  • Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) measurement is the first laboratory step in assessing goiter.
  • If the TSH level is low in a patient with goiter, free thyroxine and total triiodothyronine should be measured and thyroid scintigraphy performed.
