  • If the TSH level is normal or elevated in a patient with goiter, thyroid ultrasonography is indicated in patients at risk for thyroid cancer or if palpable thyroid nodules, gland asymmetry, large goiter, rapid growth, or compressive symptoms are present.
  • Patients with goiter and signs or symptoms of compression require additional testing and potentially surgery.
  • Routine screening for thyroid cancer in persons at low risk is not recommended.
  • Surgery is the mainstay of thyroid cancer treatment; patients with differentiated thyroid cancer and high recurrence risk should also receive radioactive iodine therapy and thyroid-stimulating hormone suppression with levothyroxine.
  • After initial cancer treatment with total thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine ablation, serum thyroglobulin (Tg) levels and Tg antibody (TgAb) titers are monitored; persistent Tg levels or increasing TgAb titers suggest persistent or recurrent disease.
  • Thyroid ultrasonography is repeated in routine thyroid cancer surveillance, 6 to 12 months after the initial cancer treatment.
  • Thyroid-stimulating hormone is the most sensitive test of thyroid function and is sufficient as an initial test in patients with normal pituitary function.
  • Total triiodothyronine (T~3) measurement in the setting of hypothyroidism is not necessary or recommended; normal levels are maintained unless hypothyroidism is severe.
  • Total T~3 measurement in hyperthyroidism is recommended to identify isolated T~3 toxicosis, assess hyperthyroidism severity and therapeutic response, and differentiate hyperthyroidism from destructive thyroiditis.
  • The diagnosis of thyrotoxicosis is based on biochemical testing demonstrating a low thyroid-stimulating hormone level and elevated concentrations of free thyroxine and/or total triiodothyronine.
  • Thyroid scintigraphy with determination of radioactive iodine uptake can verify the cause of thyrotoxicosis.
  • In patients with thyrotoxicosis, radioactive iodine uptake is high (>30%) or inappropriately normal in hyperthyroidism and low (<10%) in other causes of thyrotoxicosis, such as destructive thyroiditis or exogenous thyroid hormone ingestion.
  • In Graves disease, the thyroid is diffusely enlarged, may have a bruit, and has a firm, smooth texture on examination; cervical lymphadenopathy may also occur.
  • Clinical manifestations of thyroid eye disease (Graves ophthalmopathy) may include periorbital edema, chemosis (conjunctival edema), conjunctival hyperemia, exophthalmos (protrusion of the globe), diplopia (due to oculomotor paresis), and vision loss.
  • Thyroid eye disease does not respond to the treatment of hyperthyroidism and should prompt evaluation by an ophthalmologist; moderate to severe thyroid eye disease may require immunomodulatory treatment or surgery.
  • Most patients with thyrotoxicosis benefit from β-blockers to reduce adrenergic symptoms.
  • Three treatment modalities for hyperthyroidism are thionamides (methimazole and propylthiouracil), radioactive iodine ablative therapy, and thyroidectomy; the treatment chosen depends on the cause of the hyperthyroidism, patient factors, and patient preference.
  • Thionamides are often used in the initial treatment of Graves disease, as up to 50% of patients have spontaneous remission of hyperthyroidism within 24 months; if hyperthyroidism recurs, definitive treatment with radioactive iodine therapy or thyroidectomy is recommended.
  • Agranulocytosis and liver dysfunction are rare but serious adverse effects of thionamides.
  • Thyroidectomy in Graves hyperthyroidism is most appropriate for patients with large goiters that cause compressive symptoms, moderate to severe thyroid eye disease, or coexistent thyroid cancer or primary hyperparathyroidism.
  • Because of the transient nature of thyroiditis, thionamides, radioactive iodine therapy, and thyroid surgery have no role in treatment; patients should receive supportive care.
  • Subclinical hyperthyroidism is diagnosed on the basis of persistent suppression of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) but normal thyroxine and triiodothyronine levels.
  • TSH levels normalize after 6 weeks in more than 25% of patients with subclinical hyperthyroidism; observing and rechecking thyroid function before treatment is reasonable unless the risk for complications is high.
  • Treatment of subclinical hyperthyroidism is recommended for patients with TSH levels less than 0.1 μU/mL (0.1 mU/L) and age 65 years and older, cardiac risk factors, heart disease, osteoporosis or high risk for osteoporosis, or symptoms.
  • The diagnosis of primary hypothyroidism is made by measuring the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level, and, if it is elevated, measuring the free thyroxine level.
  • TSH is elevated in overt and subclinical hypothyroidism, but free thyroxine is low in overt hypothyroidism and normal in subclinical hypothyroidism.
  • Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are present in most patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis, but measurement is unnecessary unless the diagnosis is unclear.
  • The most common cause of thyroid hormone deficiency in the United States is Hashimoto thyroiditis (chronic autoimmune thyroiditis); iodine deficiency is the most common cause globally.
  • Subclinical hypothyroidism is typically asymptomatic and diagnosed by a high thyroid-stimulating hormone level and a normal free thyroxine level.
  • Levothyroxine is the treatment of choice for thyroid hormone deficiency; it should be taken on an empty stomach 60 minutes before consuming breakfast or coffee.
  • Triiodothyronine-containing compounds are not recommended to treat hypothyroidism because of their short half-life, which causes spikes in triiodothyronine levels.
  • Treatment for subclinical hypothyroidism with a thyroid-stimulating hormone level less than 10 μU/mL (10 mU/L) should be considered only in younger patients, in pregnant patients or those attempting to become pregnant, or if significant symptoms are present.
  • Amiodarone causes transient thyroid-stimulating hormone increases in all patients, with normalization after 3 to 6 months; free and serum total thyroxine levels transiently increase, and the serum total triiodothyronine level transiently decreases.
  • Type 1 and type 2 amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT) must be distinguished from each other because the former is treated with thionamides, whereas the latter is treated with glucocorticoids; thyroid ultrasound with Doppler studies helps to distinguish these types by showing increased vascularity with type 1 and decreased vascularity with type 2.
  • Certain medications, such as lithium, interferons, interleukin-2, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and immune checkpoint inhibitors, can cause transient thyroid dysfunction or overt hypothyroidism or thyrotoxicosis, and patients taking these medications should undergo periodic thyroid function monitoring.
  • The American Thyroid Association recommends a daily oral supplement containing 150 μg of iodine for pregnant and lactating patients.
  • Patients with moderate to severe hyperthyroidism in early pregnancy should be treated with propylthiouracil during the first trimester because it is less teratogenic than methimazole; propylthiouracil can be transitioned to methimazole in the second trimester.
  • Hypothyroidism in pregnancy increases the risk for miscarriage, premature birth, and low birth weight and is associated with decreased infant neurocognitive function; levothyroxine is the recommended treatment.
  • For patients with preexisting hypothyroidism who are euthyroid taking levothyroxine before becoming pregnant, levothyroxine dosing can be empirically increased by 30% when pregnancy is confirmed.
  • Nonthyroidal illness syndrome (NTIS) commonly occurs in patients who are hospitalized and critically ill; up to 75% of hospitalized patients have physiologic thyroid function test abnormalities.
  • Treating NTIS is not recommended because of a lack of significant clinical benefit.
  • Thyroid function should not be assessed in hospitalized patients unless there is a strong clinical suspicion of thyroid dysfunction.
  • Thyroid storm is a rare disorder with high mortality (up to 30%) characterized by severe thyrotoxicosis and life-threating complications.
  • Thyroid storm often occurs with discontinuation of antithyroid drug therapy, systemic illness, labor and delivery, surgery, exposure to iodinated contrast media, or trauma.
  • ICU-level care; treatment of any precipitating illness; and β-blockers, thionamides, intravenous high-dose glucocorticoids, and potassium iodide are all used to manage thyroid storm.
  • Definitive treatment with thyroidectomy or radioactive iodine therapy is indicated in patients who survive thyroid storm.
  • Myxedema coma is a life-threatening presentation of severe hypothyroidism with hemodynamic compromise; it most often occurs when a systemic illness is superimposed on previously undiagnosed or untreated hypothyroidism.
  • Myxedema coma treatment includes aggressive supportive measures; glucocorticoids are administered empirically before thyroid hormone is initiated to treat possible concomitant adrenal insufficiency.

index.title: Reproductive Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• In women younger than 40 years, menstrual cycles shorter than 25 days or longer than 35 days are likely anovulatory.
  • Primary amenorrhea is defined as absence of menses by age 15 years in the presence of normal growth and secondary sexual characteristics or absence of menses by age 13 years in the absence of normal growth and secondary sexual characteristics.
  • The most common cause of primary amenorrhea is gonadal dysgenesis, most often Turner syndrome (45,X0).
  • Secondary amenorrhea is defined as the absence of menses for more than 3 months in women who previously had regular menstrual cycles or for 6 months in women who have irregular menses.
  • Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea may occur because of stress, weight loss, eating disorders (e.g., anorexia nervosa), or exercise and, after pregnancy, is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea.
  • After ruling out pregnancy, initial laboratory testing in primary and secondary amenorrhea should include measurement of serum follicle-stimulating hormone, estradiol, thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, and prolactin levels.
  • Estrogen-progestin therapy is used to treat patients with Turner syndrome or primary ovarian insufficiency until the usual age of menopause, about age 50 to 55 years.
  • Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea is treated with lifestyle changes related to the underlying cause, treatment of associated conditions, and sometimes short-term estrogen-progestin therapy.
  • Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is the most common cause of hirsutism and androgen excess in women and is the most common cause of anovulatory infertility.
  • The Rotterdam criteria require the presence of two of the following to diagnose PCOS: ovulatory dysfunction, androgen excess (clinical or biochemical), and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound.
  • PCOS is a diagnosis of exclusion; other conditions must be considered, including nonclassical congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hyperprolactinemia, Cushing syndrome, androgen-secreting tumors, ovarian hyperthecosis, and thyroid dysfunction.
  • Weight loss is a first-line intervention in patients with PCOS and a BMI of 25 or greater.
  • Combined oral contraceptive agents are first-line drug therapy for hirsutism and menstrual dysfunction in patients with PCOS unless fertility is desired.
  • Patients with PCOS should be screened for prediabetes/diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, obesity, hypertension, and obstructive sleep apnea.
  • Infertility evaluation is appropriate after 1 year of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse in women younger than 35 years and after 6 months in women aged 35 years or older.
  • Both partners should be evaluated concurrently for infertility, as multiple factors are often present.
  • Assessment of ovulatory function is the first step in evaluating female infertility.
  • Primary male hypogonadism is caused by testicular abnormalities; secondary hypogonadism reflects hypothalamic or pituitary dysfunction.
  • The most common medications that cause secondary hypogonadism are opioids, anabolic steroids, glucocorticoids, and gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogues.
  • Screening for hypogonadism in men with nonspecific symptoms is not recommended.
  • Male hypogonadism is diagnosed with two low (<264 ng/dL [9.2 nmol/L]) morning fasting serum total testosterone measurements.
  • Once male hypogonadism is confirmed, serum luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels should be measured; further evaluation is determined based on whether the LH and FSH levels are elevated (primary hypogonadism) or low or inappropriately normal (secondary hypogonadism).
  • In male hypogonadism, a dedicated pituitary MRI should be performed if hyperprolactinemia is present, other pituitary hormone abnormalities are identified, the serum total testosterone level is less than 150 ng/dL (5.2 nmol/L), or signs or symptoms of mass effect are present.
  • In men with biochemically proven hypogonadism, testosterone therapy can be initiated after the cause is determined, with a goal of achieving a serum total testosterone measurement in the midnormal range.
  • Testosterone therapy should be avoided in men who are planning for fertility because it impairs spermatogenesis.
  • Testosterone therapy should not be routinely prescribed in men with age-related low testosterone.
  • In men aged 65 years and older who have clear signs and symptoms of hypogonadism and unequivocally low testosterone levels, testosterone therapy should be individualized after discussing the risks and benefits.
  • Initial laboratory evaluation of male infertility is a morning fasting serum total testosterone level and semen analysis.
  • Gynecomastia is typically bilateral and is diagnosed with physical examination; palpation of subareolar glandular tissue greater than 0.5 cm in diameter is consistent with the diagnosis.
  • Treatment of a specific cause of gynecomastia during the active proliferative phase may result in regression; in longstanding gynecomastia, regression is unlikely and referral for plastic surgery may be the best option for cosmetic improvement.
  • Anabolic steroid use should be suspected in a patient who exhibits abrupt changes in behavior, such as depression, irritability, or aggression, or in men who develop a rapid increase in muscle strength along with gynecomastia, acne, small testes, and low sperm counts.
  • Laboratory evidence suggestive of anabolic steroid use includes an elevated hematocrit level, undetectable or low serum luteinizing hormone level, and low sex hormone–binding globulin level; testosterone levels may be either low or elevated, depending on the type of anabolic steroid.
  • Patients taking anabolic steroids should be encouraged to stop and counseled on the potential for short- or long-term hypogonadism after cessation.

index.title: Transgender Hormone Therapy
index.keyPoints:
• For gender-affirming treatment, feminizing hormone therapy includes estrogen (estradiol formulations are preferred over conjugated estrogens) in combination with an androgen blocker (both used off label); masculinizing hormone therapy is achieved by administering testosterone (off-label use).
  • Estrogen for gender-affirming therapy increases the risk for venous thromboembolism, infertility, hypertriglyceridemia, and weight gain.
  • Risks of testosterone therapy for gender-affirming treatment include polycythemia, infertility, acne, androgenic alopecia, hypertension, sleep apnea, weight gain, decreased HDL cholesterol, and increased LDL cholesterol.
  • Patients taking gender-affirming hormone therapy should be evaluated every 3 months in the first year and then every 6 to 12 months thereafter to monitor for appropriate response to therapy and adverse reactions.
  • Screening and preventive medicine in transgender patients should be based on the person's anatomy and risk factors.
  • Practice guidelines for gender confirmation surgery recommend that persons have been stable taking gender-affirming hormone therapy for a minimum of 6 months (unless therapy is not desired or contraindicated) and that procedures be performed by an experienced surgeon in conjunction with a multidisciplinary team.

index.title: Calcium and Metabolic Bone Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• The primary effect of vitamin D is enhancing intestinal calcium absorption, whereas the effects of parathyroid hormone are primarily mediated through regulating calcium retention and excretion in the kidney and bone resorption.
  • Ionized calcium measurement is the most accurate assessment of calcium status when abnormal serum albumin or acute acid-base disorders are present; however, measurement of total serum calcium alone may be sufficient when hypocalcemia and hypercalcemia are mild, transient, or unlikely to affect clinical decision-making.
  • 25-Hydroxyvitamin D measurement is the most appropriate test for vitamin D sufficiency.
  • Manifestations of hypercalcemia are variable but may include polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia, fatigue, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, constipation, and mental status changes; acute kidney injury, nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, and skeletal changes may also occur.
  • Initial diagnostic testing for confirmed hypercalcemia requires simultaneous serum calcium and parathyroid hormone (PTH) measurement, which allows classification as PTH-mediated or non–PTH-mediated disease.
  • Patients with primary hyperparathyroidism who are symptomatic or younger than 50 years should undergo surgical management; in asymptomatic older patients, serum calcium level, skeletal complications, and kidney involvement determine whether surgical management is indicated.
  • Medical management of primary hyperparathyroidism includes maintaining hydration, adjusting dietary calcium intake to approximately 1000 mg per day, and cautious correction of vitamin D deficiency.
  • Patients with primary hyperparathyroidism who are ineligible for or who refuse surgery should be monitored with serum calcium and creatinine measurement each year and bone mineral density assessment every 2 years; spine imaging should be considered in patients with significant height loss or back pain.
  • Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) is an autosomal dominant condition and the most common type of familial hypercalcemia.
  • Features suggestive of FHH include mild hypercalcemia since childhood, an inappropriately normal or elevated parathyroid hormone level, low 24-hour urine calcium excretion, and family history of parathyroidectomy without resolution of hypercalcemia.
  • Parathyroidectomy is not indicated for patients with FHH because hypercalcemia will not resolve with surgery.
  • Non–parathyroid hormone–mediated hypercalcemia may be related to malignancy, excess vitamin D, excessive calcium ingestion, endocrine disorders, or acute prolonged immobilization.
  • Mild hypercalcemia may be sufficiently managed by treating the underlying disorder and avoiding factors that can exacerbate hypercalcemia.
  • Initial treatment of severe hypercalcemia is aggressive hydration with 0.9% saline to replete volume loss and increase kidney excretion of calcium.
  • Loop diuretics are not recommended in hypercalcemia in the absence of kidney failure or volume overload.
  • Laryngospasm, seizure, myocardial dysfunction, and QT interval prolongation leading to sudden cardiac death caused by severe hypocalcemia can occur without prodromal paresthesia or muscle cramping.
  • The laboratory evaluation of confirmed hypocalcemia includes simultaneous measurement of serum calcium, phosphorus, creatinine, and parathyroid hormone levels.
  • Hypoparathyroidism is most commonly caused by inadvertent injury during anterior neck surgery and may present within a few hours of surgery.
  • Hypomagnesemia causes reversible functional parathyroid hypofunction and must be excluded before a low or inappropriately normal serum parathyroid hormone level is attributed to hypoparathyroidism.
  • Potent antiresorptive drugs can cause severe and protracted hypocalcemia in patients with vitamin D deficiency or chronic kidney disease; it is important to assess vitamin D levels and correct deficiency before beginning treatment with an antiresorptive drug.
  • Severe hypocalcemia necessitates urgent treatment with intravenous calcium.
  • Mild or chronic hypocalcemia may be normalized or sufficiently treated with vitamin D supplementation and oral calcium carbonate or calcium citrate.
  • The goal of therapy for most patients with chronic hypoparathyroidism is a serum calcium concentration at or just below the normal range without hypercalciuria.
  • Fragility fractures (those occurring with the equivalent of a fall from a standing height or less) after age 50 years indicate low bone strength and can be used to define clinical osteoporosis, particularly with hip and spine fractures.
  • Glucocorticoids are a well-recognized cause of bone loss and increased fracture risk; patients anticipated to be receiving long-term glucocorticoid treatment (≥2.5 mg/d for >3 months) should be assessed for fracture risk as soon as possible after therapy initiation.
  • Guidelines recommend screening for osteoporosis with bone mineral density (BMD) measurement in postmenopausal women with average risk beginning at age 65 years; screening recommendations for men vary by organization.
  • BMD testing is indicated earlier than standard screening recommendations in patients with fragility fractures, risk factors for low bone mass or osteoporosis, height loss of 4 cm (1.5 in) or more, or kyphosis.
  • In postmenopausal women and men aged 50 years and older, osteoporosis can be diagnosed clinically based on fragility fractures or a bone mineral density (BMD) T-score of −2.5 or less.
  • In premenopausal women and men younger than 50 years, osteoporosis can be diagnosed when recurrent low-energy fractures are associated with a BMD Z-score of −2 or less on dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry.
  • Osteomalacia is most commonly caused by severe and prolonged vitamin D deficiency and is treated with vitamin D supplementation.
  • A low bone mineral density Z-score (≤−2), low or low-normal serum calcium and phosphorus levels, a very low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level (<10 ng/mL [25 nmol/L]), secondary hyperparathyroidism, and an elevated alkaline phosphatase level help distinguish osteomalacia from osteoporosis.
  • Routine screening for vitamin D deficiency is not recommended in healthy populations.
  • Exercise involving weight-bearing, resistance, and balance is important for bone health and may reduce fracture risk.
  • The National Academy of Medicine recommends a calcium intake of 1000 to 1200 mg/d, ideally from dietary sources.
  • Pharmacologic treatment is recommended for patients with an osteoporosis-related hip or spine fracture; osteoporosis on bone mineral density testing; or low bone mass (osteopenia) with a 10-year risk for hip fracture of 3% or greater or risk for major osteoporosis-related fracture of 20% or greater as estimated by the Fracture Risk Assessment Tool.
  • Bisphosphonates are generally the first-line treatment of osteoporosis; alendronate and risedronate (oral) and zoledronate (intravenous) reduce the risk for spine, hip, and nonvertebral fractures.
  • Bisphosphonates are not recommended in patients with reduced kidney function (creatinine clearance <35 mL/min).
  • A drug holiday can be considered in most patients who are not at high fracture risk after 3 years (intravenous) to 5 years (oral) of bisphosphonate treatment.
  • Denosumab therapy for primary osteoporosis may be considered in patients who have contraindications to (e.g., chronic kidney disease) or experience adverse effects from bisphosphonates.
  • The effects of denosumab for the treatment of osteoporosis are not sustained when treatment is stopped, so bisphosphonate therapy should be initiated 6 months after the last treatment with denosumab.
  • Routine serial dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry bone mineral density measurements are not indicated for follow-up of patients at low risk for fractures.
  • Although Paget disease of bone may present with localized symptoms, diagnosis is most common in asymptomatic older patients presenting with elevated serum alkaline phosphatase levels or incidental radiographic findings.
  • Indications for treatment of Paget disease include bone pain; risk for fracture and progressive deformity that may compromise bone, joint, or neurologic function; and possibly, elevated serum alkaline phosphatase concentrations.
  • A single dose of intravenous zoledronate often achieves the treatment goal of reducing pain and normalizing serum alkaline phosphatase levels in patients with Paget disease of bone.
  • Serum alkaline phosphatase levels should be monitored annually in patients with Paget disease of bone; if levels or symptoms increase significantly, imaging is required.

index.title: High Value Care in Internal Medicine
index.keyPoints: • High value care is individualized care that delivers proven benefits while minimizing risks and unnecessary costs.

index.title: Clinical Decision Making and Interpreting the Medical Literature
index.keyPoints:
• Diagnostic errors are usually multifactorial in etiology, with flaws in the individual clinician's cognitive processes and systems-level issues contributing to most errors.
  • Levels of evidence describe the strength and quality of study results and can aid in clinical decision making; systematic reviews provide the highest level of evidence.
  • Experimental studies systematically expose some or all of the individuals in the study to a potential causative or protective factor; the strongest experimental design is the randomized controlled trial.
  • In observational studies, researchers observe naturally occurring events in individuals who have or have not been exposed to a risk factor or treatment; relationships between risk factors and disease may be explored, but the ability to assess for causality is limited.
  • Sensitivity is the ability of the test to accurately detect those who truly have a disease; specificity is the ability of the test to correctly identify those without the disease.
  • Likelihood ratios provide a measure of the strength of association between a clinical finding and a specific disease.
  • The number needed to treat represents the number of patients who must receive a treatment to cause one additional patient to benefit.

index.title: Medical Ethics and Professionalism
index.keyPoints:
• Physicians should be guided in their practice by the four basic principles of medical ethics: beneficence, nonmaleficence, respect for patient autonomy, and justice.
  • Appropriate boundaries between the physician and patient must always be maintained.
  • The benefits of increased access to care through telemedicine must always be balanced with the risks associated with lack of a physical encounter, such as misdiagnosis, inappropriate care, and loss of communication nuances conveyed with body language.
  • When a clinician encounters a perceived discriminatory request by a patient, the clinician must determine whether to negotiate, accommodate, offer transfer, or limit unacceptable conduct.
  • Patient abandonment, or withdrawing from an established relationship without giving reasonable notice or providing a competent replacement, is unethical and may be a cause for legal action.
  • With few exceptions, disclosure of medical information outside of the patient-physician relationship requires patient consent.
  • Physicians must frequently determine the patient's decision-making capacity, including the patient's ability to understand relevant information, appreciate the risks and benefits of treatment options, and communicate a choice consistent with the information given and the individual's values.
  • The presence of depression or early dementia does not necessarily preclude the presence of decision-making capacity but may complicate the evaluation.
  • Informed consent requires that the patient be informed of the nature of the underlying condition; the goals of treatment; and the risks of, benefits of, and alternatives to treatment, including the option to forgo treatment.
  • Surrogates and physicians are required to act in accordance with the patient's preferences for medical care, and if preferences are not known, they should serve the patient's best interests.
  • Advance care planning should include written documentation of the patient's preferences (advance directives) and should be available in the medical record.
  • If a patient requests diagnostic or therapeutic interventions for which there is no evidence of clinical benefit, physicians are not obligated to provide these interventions.
  • Physicians must be truthful with patients or surrogates when a medical error occurs.
  • Medical error disclosure may benefit physicians by alleviating distress, improving patient-physician communication, and reducing litigation.
  • The American College of Physicians does not support legalization of medical aid in dying and instead emphasizes the need to provide palliative care, relief of suffering, and compassionate biopsychosocial support to the patient and family members during the end of life.
  • Physicians are obligated to recognize, disclose, and manage all conflicts of interest; disclosure of conflicts may not be an adequate safeguard against bias, and potential conflicts should be removed if possible.
  • Physicians have a responsibility to safeguard patients from impaired physicians and to assist impaired colleagues.
  • Systems-based initiatives focusing on improving work-life balance, increasing work efficiency, and supporting sustainable workloads may decrease physician burnout.

index.title: Health Equity
index.keyPoints:
• Health inequities are largely determined by social drivers of health (e.g., economic stability, living environment, education, social and community networks, and health care access and quality) and by bias and discrimination.
  • Biases, stigma, and discrimination disproportionately affect marginalized groups and adversely impact health outcomes.
  • Health care workers should seek awareness of their own implicit biases and should use nonpejorative and person-first language.
  • Systemic policies that address and mitigate bias, stigma, and discrimination are critical to attaining health equity.
  • Race is a social construct rather than a proxy for genetics.
  • Use of race as a variable in clinical equations may perpetuate disparities; physicians should use caution when interpreting results of race-based algorithms.
  • The foundation of cross-cultural care is an understanding that many factors contribute to each patient's unique health care experience.
  • Patients who perceive their physicians to have high levels of cultural humility have higher levels of satisfaction with their health care experience, rate their physicians more highly, and are more likely to follow their physician's medical advice.
  • Health care organizations are required to provide interpreter services for patients with a non-English language preference, and use of trained medical interpreters can enhance culturally sensitive care, reduce adverse events, and improve treatment outcomes.
  • Low health literacy is associated with poorer health outcomes and decreased use of care.
  • Clinicians can improve patient understanding by using simple sentences, repeating information, asking the patient for their questions, and supplying the patient with educational materials written in plain language.

index.title: Effective Communication in Clinical Practice
index.keyPoints:
• Patient-centered care is respectful of and responsive to patient preferences, needs, and values.
  • Collaborative goal setting can help patients identify and prioritize their goals and enhance self-efficacy.
  • The use of motivational interviewing in behavioral counseling is most effective in situations in which a patient's ambivalence is high or when the importance of, desire to, or confidence to change is low.
  • Results should be disclosed to patients confidentially, in understandable language, with the intention to adequately support patients' emotions, and with collaborative planning for next steps.
  • Shared decision making can reduce decisional conflict, increase patients' knowledge of their options, and help patients reach decisions consistent with their values.
  • In teach-back, patients explain information conveyed to them in their own words, with the clinician clarifying any misunderstandings, to ensure that the patient accurately understands the information provided.
  • Strategies aimed at standardizing and improving handoffs, such as I-PASS, provide a framework for the transfer of important information and promote consistency of practice.
  • The potential for medical errors is particularly high at the time of handoffs and hospital discharge, underscoring the importance of accurate information transfer between sites of care.
  • Surgical comanagement is associated with improved pain control; decreased length of hospital stay, complications, readmissions, mortality, and cost; and high levels of satisfaction among the care team.

index.title: Genetics, Genomics, and Precision Medicine
index.keyPoints:
• Obtaining a family history can increase the proportion of patients identified as needing screening, genetic testing, or preventive treatment for some conditions.
  • Diagnostic genetic testing is performed in patients with clinical features that suggest a genetic disease or disorders with a suspected genetic basis; predictive genetic testing is performed in asymptomatic patients, such as those with a strong family history of a disease for which early intervention would alter the clinical course, or as part of prenatal counseling.
  • Patients for whom genetic testing is being considered, especially those undergoing predictive testing, should receive genetic counseling.
  • Although predictive pharmacogenomic testing is mostly investigational, testing is recommended when certain medications (e.g., allopurinol, abacavir, carbamazepine) are prescribed in routine practice, focusing on situations in which serious adverse effects or treatment failures may occur.
  • Direct-to-consumer (DTC) testing is approved only to provide health information; DTC tests are not diagnostic tests.

index.title: Patient Safety and Quality Improvement
index.keyPoints:
• Medication errors are the most common type of medical error and are preventable.
  • Effective communication among health care team members and between providers and patients is critical for successful handoffs and transitions of care.
  • Use of a standardized communication tool, such as SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation/Request) or I-PASS (Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness and contingency planning, Synthesis), can assist in effectively and consistently transferring information during handoffs.
  • Medication reconciliation is a critical aspect of medical error prevention and refers to the process of verifying the medications that a patient is taking to identify and resolve discrepancies.
  • Wrong-site, wrong-procedure, wrong-patient errors are considered never events and can be prevented by adhering to safety checklists; using structured, closed-loop communication; marking the procedure site; and using timeouts.
  • The Model for Improvement, Lean, Six Sigma, and Operational Excellence are examples of quality improvement models that can be used in the health care setting.

index.title: Routine Care of the Adult Patient
index.keyPoints:
• The periodic health examination may help maintain a strong patient-provider relationship and improve surrogate outcomes, such as reduction in cardiovascular risk factors and increased receipt of preventive services; however, the periodic health examination has not been shown to reduce morbidity, hospitalizations, or mortality.
  • The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force and the Canadian Task Force on the Periodic Health Examination recommend against performing general health checks that include a comprehensive examination and routine laboratory testing for asymptomatic adults.
  • The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends one-time abdominal ultrasonography to screen for abdominal aortic aneurysm in men aged 65 to 75 years who have smoked 100 cigarettes or more in their lifetime.
  • Screening for coronary artery disease with ECG is not recommended in asymptomatic patients at low risk.
  • The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends that all adults be screened for depression and that adults aged 19 to 64 years be screened for anxiety.
  • Adults aged 35 to 70 years who have overweight or obesity should be screened for diabetes mellitus, according to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force.
  • Lipid screening is indicated in adults aged 40 to 75 years for the purposes of calculating 10-year risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and guiding initiation of statin therapy for primary prevention.
  • Adults aged 18 years and older should be screened for hypertension.
  • Screening for osteoporosis is recommended for women aged 65 years or older and in postmenopausal women younger than 65 years who are at increased risk for osteoporosis, as determined by clinical risk assessment.
  • The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends screening for chlamydia and gonorrhea in all sexually active women aged 24 years or younger.
  • The CDC recommends one-time screening for hepatitis B virus infection in adults aged 18 years and older.
  • All persons 18 to 79 years should receive one-time hepatitis C screening.
  • The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends that all persons aged 15 to 65 years receive one-time HIV screening.
  • The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force supports routine screening for tobacco use, unhealthy alcohol use, and drug use; patients with positive screening results should be provided with behavioral counseling and treatment as appropriate.
  • The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends screening for intimate partner violence in women of reproductive age with referral to appropriate support services if the screening result is positive.
  • Recommended vaccine schedules should be closely adhered to; if a vaccination series is interrupted, it can be resumed at the point of interruption.
  • When appropriate, multiple vaccines should be given simultaneously to improve vaccination rates.
  • Vaccines can be administered safely to patients with mild acute febrile illness, those who are convalescing from illness, and those who have previously developed low- or moderate-grade fever or local reactions with vaccination.
  • Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for all individuals 6 months and older.
  • The live attenuated influenza vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy and in patients with immunocompromise.
  • Persons with a history of egg allergy of any severity can receive any influenza vaccine formulation, and patients do not require additional safety measures for egg allergy alone.
  • After primary immunization and receipt of the tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine, adults should receive one booster dose of the Td or Tdap vaccine every 10 years.
  • Pregnant persons should receive at least one dose of the Tdap vaccine between 27 and 36 weeks' gestation with every pregnancy to prevent neonatal tetanus.
  • All adults aged 50 years or older should receive the recombinant herpes zoster vaccine; vaccination is also indicated in patients aged 19 years or older with immunocompromise.
  • Pneumococcal vaccination is recommended in all adults aged 50 years or older and in adults aged 19 to 49 years with high-risk conditions.
  • Adults born in 1957 or later without documented evidence of receiving one or more doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine or laboratory-confirmed immunity against all three diseases should receive at least one MMR dose.
  • Hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for all adults aged 19 to 59 years and for patients aged 60 years and older who are at high risk for infection.
  • The respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine is recommended for pregnant persons at 32 to 36 weeks' gestation from September to January in most of the continental United States, all adults aged 75 years and older, and adults aged 60 to 74 years who are at increased risk for severe RSV disease.
  • According to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, the decision to initiate low-dose aspirin for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease in patients aged 40 to 59 years with increased cardiovascular risk should be individualized; the American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association recommend that low-dose aspirin be used infrequently in routine primary prevention of cardiovascular disease but may be considered for primary prevention in adults aged 40 to 70 years who are at higher atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk but not at increased bleeding risk.
  • After age 70 years, the benefit of aspirin decreases and bleeding risks are higher; major guidelines do not recommend aspirin for primary prevention in this age group.
  • The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends behavioral counseling interventions to promote a healthy diet and physical activity for adults with cardiovascular risk factors.
  • Adults should be advised to obtain most calories from nutrient-dense foods while monitoring portion sizes to stay within calorie limits, and food and beverage choices should reflect personal preferences, cultural traditions, and budgetary considerations.
  • Physical activity goals for adults include at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week as well as muscle-strengthening activities at least 2 days per week.
  • Medication nonadherence is associated with increased health care use, worse health outcomes, and increased costs.
  • The factors most strongly associated with medication adherence include strong provider-patient relationships and a patient's understanding of their medical conditions.
  • Given the prevalence of use and potential for harm, physicians should make inquiring about supplement use a routine component of the medication history.
  • Multivitamins should not be used in the absence of a specific indication and are not effective in compensating for a poor diet.
  • The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends against the use of β-carotene or vitamin E supplements for the prevention of cardiovascular disease or cancer.
  • Women of reproductive age are advised to take 0.4 to 0.8 mg (400-800 µg) of folic acid daily to prevent fetal neural tube defects.

index.title: Perioperative Medicine
index.keyPoints:
• Preoperative routine laboratory panels are not recommended and may lead to unnecessary additional testing; laboratory testing should be tailored to the nature of the surgery, comorbid conditions, and history and examination findings.
  • Preoperative testing is discouraged for patients undergoing ambulatory or low-risk surgery (e.g., cataract, hernia repair) because there is minimal evidence of its usefulness.
  • Patients, surgeons, and inpatient clinicians should be given clear instructions on which medications to withhold preoperatively and guidance for when the patient can safely resume taking them.
  • Early removal of indwelling catheters and voiding trials are recommended postoperatively, with ongoing close monitoring of urine output to assess for urinary retention.
  • Treatment of postoperative ileus includes minimization of postoperative opioids, adequate hydration, bowel rest, electrolyte repletion, and postoperative ambulation.
  • New perioperative atrial fibrillation, even if transient, is associated with increased short- and long-term mortality and incidence of stroke; further evaluation is indicated, and rate/rhythm control and anticoagulation should be considered in at-risk patients.
  • Patients with low cardiovascular risk (<1% risk for perioperative major adverse cardiac events [MACE]) and no risk modifiers may proceed to surgery, whereas patients with elevated risk (≥1% risk for perioperative MACE) or presence of risk modifiers should undergo an objective assessment of functional capacity.
  • Preoperative ECG is reasonable in patients with known cardiovascular disease, arrhythmia, structural heart disease, or symptoms of cardiovascular disease who are undergoing elevated-risk surgeries; it may also be considered for other asymptomatic patients undergoing elevated-risk procedures.
  • Preoperative ECG is not recommended for patients undergoing low-risk procedures.
  • Patients with coronary artery disease should not undergo routine coronary angiography or revascularization before surgery exclusively to reduce perioperative events.
  • Treating triggers (e.g., anemia, sepsis, pain), maintaining euvolemia, optimizing pain management, and continuing baseline rate control medications can reduce the risk for postoperative rapid ventricular response in patients with atrial fibrillation.
  • Patients with hypertension undergoing surgery do not require urgent blood pressure lowering preoperatively unless there is evidence of end-organ dysfunction.
  • All patients undergoing surgery should be screened for obstructive sleep apnea, which is associated with adverse perioperative outcomes.
  • Preoperative chest radiography is indicated only in patients with signs or symptoms of pulmonary illness or in those with underlying cardiac or pulmonary disease and new or unstable symptoms.
  • Spirometry should not be routinely performed preoperatively except in patients undergoing lung resection.
  • Risk for perioperative pulmonary complications can be mitigated with good oral hygiene, early mobilization, regional or neuraxial anesthesia and analgesia, prophylactic respiratory physiotherapy, and postoperative continuous positive pressure ventilation, as appropriate.
  • Atelectasis is the most common cause of postoperative hypoxia and usually occurs within the first 48 hours after surgery; in addition to hypoxia, clinical features include tachypnea and shallow breathing.
  • Treatment of atelectasis includes supplemental oxygen, lung expansion maneuvers, ambulation, and pain control.
  • Hip fracture surgery, total knee arthroplasty, and total hip arthroplasty pose a very high risk for VTE, and both mechanical and pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis is recommended.
  • The minimum recommended duration of pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis in patients undergoing orthopedic surgery is 10 to 14 days; however, in patients without increased bleeding risk, extended-duration postoperative prophylaxis (up to 35 days) is preferred.
  • Newer guidelines recommend against perioperative bridging anticoagulation in most scenarios; bridging with a parenteral agent should be considered in patients receiving vitamin K antagonists who are at high risk for thrombosis.
  • In patients treated with percutaneous coronary intervention undergoing elective noncardiac surgery, dual antiplatelet therapy should ideally be continued uninterrupted for 30 days after bare metal stent placement and 6 months after drug-eluting stent placement; the time frame should be extended to 12 months after an acute coronary syndrome.
  • In most stable patients undergoing surgery, a restrictive transfusion threshold (hemoglobin level of 7 g/dL [70 g/L]) is recommended; a threshold of 7.5 g/dL (75 g/L) may be considered for patients undergoing cardiac surgery, and a threshold of 8 g/dL (80 g/L) can be selected for those undergoing orthopedic surgery or who have underlying cardiovascular disease.
  • In patients with diabetes mellitus undergoing elective surgery, a preoperative hemoglobin A~1c of less than 8% and a blood glucose concentration of 100 to 180 mg/dL (5.6-10.0 mmol/L) should be targeted within 1 to 4 hours before surgery; if a preoperative hemoglobin A~1c of less than 8% is not feasible, a blood glucose concentration of 100 to 180 mg/dL (5.6-10.0 mmol/L) should still be targeted within 1 to 4 hours before surgery.
  • In patients with diabetes mellitus, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors should be withheld beginning 3 to 4 days before surgery to avoid euglycemic ketoacidosis.
  • For patients on insulin regimens who are undergoing surgery, basal insulin should be continued perioperatively; while fasting, patients should typically receive 50% of their usual intermediate-acting insulin dose, 75% to 80% of their long-acting analogue dose, or adjustment of their pump basal insulin rate.
  • Patients with untreated, subclinical hypothyroidism may proceed to surgery without further testing or treatment.
  • Elective surgery should be deferred in patients with uncontrolled hypo- or hyperthyroidism.
  • For patients with adrenal insufficiency or at high risk for hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis suppression who are undergoing surgery, perioperative glucocorticoid dosing recommendations are tailored to the stress of the planned procedure.
  • Perioperative acute kidney injury increases the risk for long-term kidney function decline and progression to end-stage kidney disease.
  • The two most important means of mitigating the risk for acute kidney injury in the perioperative period are maintenance of renal blood flow and avoidance of insults to the kidneys.
  • Patients with compensated cirrhosis who have Model for End-stage Liver Disease (MELD) scores of 6 to 9 or a Child-Turcotte-Pugh score of 5 to 6 and no evidence of clinically significant portal hypertension have limited excess perioperative risk.
  • Patients with a MELD score greater than 15 or a VOCAL-Penn Score predicting greater than 15% mortality at 90 days should be referred for transplant evaluation before surgery.
  • Patients with Parkinson disease who are undergoing surgery should continue anti-Parkinson agents perioperatively, and surgery should be scheduled for as early in the day as possible to minimize missed doses.
  • For patients with rheumatic disease who are undergoing surgery, traditional oral disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (methotrexate, leflunomide, hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine) and apremilast should be continued through the perioperative period.
  • Frailty is associated with worse postoperative outcomes; preoperative multimodal interventions for patients with frailty include physical therapy, nutritional interventions, and stress reduction techniques.
  • Patients with features of severe malnutrition who are undergoing surgery warrant preoperative nutritional interventions with high-protein, high-calorie oral supplementation.
  • In patients who are pregnant, elective surgery should be delayed until after pregnancy; for surgeries that cannot be delayed until after pregnancy, performing surgery during the second trimester is preferred.
  • Pregnant patients who require surgery should undergo the same preoperative medical evaluation as nonpregnant patients; additional diagnostic testing is unnecessary.

index.title: Geriatric Medicine
index.keyPoints:
• Comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) is a multidisciplinary diagnostic process to ascertain the physical, cognitive, psychological, environmental, and functional capabilities of older persons, with the objective of developing a holistic plan for maximizing function and quality of life.
  • Patients with symptoms of hearing loss should be referred to an otologist or audiologist for formal testing and hearing aid placement, if appropriate.
  • All older adults should be screened for depression.
  • Cognitive impairment is a risk factor for falls, loss of independence, and poor control of chronic diseases; clinicians should inquire about symptoms and perform further evaluation if symptoms are present.
  • Interventions shown to reduce fall risk in older adults include exercises that emphasize gait/balance training and lower extremity strength, discontinuing or decreasing the dose of centrally acting medications, and assessing and modifying the home environment.
  • Evidence of neglect or abuse of an older adult must be reported to Adult Protective Services.
  • Frailty measurement is not recommended as part of routine geriatric assessment; however, it can be assessed as part of a CGA and incorporated into preintervention assessment for many surgical, procedural, and medical treatments.
  • Hip fracture should be suspected in a patient who presents after a fall with groin pain, inability to bear weight, and an affected leg that appears externally rotated and shortened; diagnosis is confirmed with plain radiography.
  • Early operative management is the preferred treatment for most hip fractures.
  • Patients who have experienced a hip fracture should be treated for osteoporosis regardless of the results of bone mineral density testing.
  • For patients with long-term daily care needs that include requiring help with activities of daily living or medical management, nursing homes provide 24-hour nursing care.
  • Acute rehabilitation requires that the patient be able to participate in 3 hours of therapy at least 5 days per week; subacute rehabilitation is appropriate for patients who cannot tolerate this level of therapy.
  • Adverse effects from polypharmacy can be minimized with frequent review of the patient's current medications, discontinuation of drugs that are unnecessary or should be avoided, and adjustment of drug dosages as appropriate.
  • The first-line treatment for insomnia in older adults is cognitive behavioral therapy.
  • Pressure redistribution is paramount in the prevention of pressure injuries and can be facilitated by use of advanced static mattresses or overlays.
  • Hydrocolloid or occlusive dressings are effective in the treatment of stage 2 pressure injuries; more advanced pressure injuries require interdisciplinary wound care management.

index.title: Palliative Medicine
index.keyPoints:
• Specialty palliative medicine improves overall quality of life, physical symptom burden, mood, and caregiver satisfaction with patient care in the setting of serious illness.
  • Multiple guidelines recommend early initiation of palliative care services in patients with advanced cardiac, pulmonary, or kidney disease; advanced dementia; critical illness; or cancer.
  • Timely and effective end-of-life communication can help establish realistic and meaningful goals of care, reduce utilization of aggressive medical care, improve quality of life, and increase care satisfaction.
  • Structured conversations about serious illness are associated with improved goal-concordant care and reduced patient anxiety.
  • Opioids are the first line of treatment for moderate or severe chronic pain in patients living with cancer; those with inadequate response may benefit from addition of nonopioid analgesics such as acetaminophen, NSAIDs, glucocorticoids, topical therapies, neuropathic agents, and/or antidepressants with analgesic properties.
  • Opioids should be prescribed with careful attention to dosing, frequency, and side effect profile.
  • Nonpharmacologic interventions for dyspnea at the end of life include fans directed toward the patient's cheek (trigeminal nerve) or supplemental oxygen if the patient has hypoxia; although not FDA-approved for dyspnea, opioids are the pharmacologic treatment of choice for refractory dyspnea.
  • Pharmacologic therapy for constipation in patients with serious illness includes osmotic laxatives, such as polyethylene glycol, often in combination with a stimulant laxative, such as senna or bisacodyl.
  • Enteral or parenteral artificial nutritional support at the end of life does not improve survival, is invasive, and may cause increased respiratory secretions and uncomfortable edema.
  • Clinical depression is common at the end of life and should be treated if present; the choice of pharmacologic therapy must take into consideration the patient's estimated prognosis and medication's onset of action.
  • Hospice care is appropriate for patients with a life expectancy of 6 months or less if the disease takes its natural course.

index.title: Disorders of the Esophagus
index.keyPoints:
• Oropharyngeal dysphagia occurs when the patient cannot transfer the food bolus from the mouth into the upper esophagus by swallowing; it should be evaluated with a modified barium swallow with video fluoroscopy.
  • Esophageal dysphagia with solids alone suggests a mechanical obstruction, whereas dysphagia with liquids alone or with liquids and solids favors a motility disorder.
  • Upper endoscopy can be diagnostic and may be therapeutic for causes of structural esophageal dysphagia.
  • Esophageal diverticula are characterized by an outpouching of the esophageal mucosa; barium esophagram is the diagnostic test of choice.
  • Esophageal rings, webs, and strictures can be diagnosed with barium esophagram or upper endoscopy.
  • Esophageal stricture is an abnormal narrowing of the esophagus and commonly presents with progressive dysphagia.
  • High-resolution esophageal manometry is the gold standard test to evaluate and diagnose esophageal motility disorders.
  • Patients with achalasia commonly have dysphagia with solids and liquids along with regurgitation of undigested food.
  • Characteristic esophageal manometry findings of achalasia include abnormal and incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter and failed peristalsis in all swallows.
  • Treatments for achalasia include surgical or endoscopic esophagomyotomy, pneumatic dilation, and botulinum toxin injection; botulinum toxin injection is temporary and may be reserved for poor surgical candidates.
  • Medical management of esophageal spasm or hypercontractile esophagus includes antispasmodics (such as hyoscyamine), calcium channel blockers or nitrates, phosphodiesterase inhibitors (sildenafil), and botulinum toxin.
  • Typical symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease are heartburn and regurgitation; atypical symptoms include chronic cough, asthma symptoms, chest pain, sore throat, hoarseness, globus sensation, nausea, dysphagia, and odynophagia.
  • Patients with gastroesophageal reflux disease and alarm features, such as dysphagia, weight loss, hematemesis, or melena, should undergo endoscopic examination.
  • In patients with classic symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) but without alarm features, an 8-week empiric trial of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) is the initial management.
  • Considering the potential adverse effects of PPI therapy, the lowest dose required to control GERD symptoms should be used, therapy should be discontinued if an appropriate indication is lacking, and stopping or reducing long-term PPI therapy should be attempted once yearly for patients with uncomplicated GERD.
  • Indications for surgical treatment of gastroesophageal reflux disease include failure of optimal proton pump inhibitor therapy, a desire to stop the medication, and intolerable medication adverse effects; patients should undergo pH monitoring and esophageal manometry before surgery.
  • The diagnostic criteria for eosinophilic esophagitis are symptoms of esophageal dysfunction (e.g., dysphagia, food impaction, and reflux), esophageal biopsy specimens showing eosinophil counts of 15 or more per high-power field, and exclusion of other causes of eosinophilia.
  • Treatments for eosinophilic esophagitis include an empiric elimination diet, proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), and swallowed topical glucocorticoids; biologic agents, such as dupilumab, may also be considered in patients who do not respond to PPI therapy.
  • Candida esophagitis can be diagnosed clinically based on compatible symptoms, such as dysphagia and the presence of oral candidiasis; it is treated with oral fluconazole.
  • Herpes simplex virus and cytomegalovirus esophagitis are seen in immunodeficient or immunosuppressed persons, and endoscopy with biopsy is needed to confirm the diagnosis.
  • Common medications associated with pill-induced esophagitis and stricture formation include antibiotics (especially tetracyclines), bisphosphonates, NSAIDs, ferrous sulfate, and potassium chloride.
  • Strategies to prevent pill-induced esophagitis include drinking sufficient water with medications and remaining upright for 30 minutes after pill ingestion.
  • Barrett esophagus (BE) is a precursor cancer lesion caused by long-standing gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).
  • Screening for BE should be considered in individuals with chronic GERD and three or more risk factors (male sex, age >50 years, White race, tobacco smoking, obesity, and family history of BE or esophageal adenocarcinoma in a first-degree relative).
  • Patients with Barrett esophagus should receive proton pump inhibitor therapy; endoscopy-based eradication therapies are recommended for confirmed dysplasia.
  • Dysphagia with solid foods is the most common presenting symptom of esophageal carcinoma; upper endoscopy with biopsy is the gold-standard diagnostic test.
  • Superficial esophageal tumors that are limited to the mucosal lining (T1a), show no evidence of lymph node metastasis, and have low-risk features in terms of differentiation and lymphovascular invasion may be treated with endoscopic resection in an organ-sparing manner.

index.title: Disorders of the Stomach and Duodenum
index.keyPoints:
• For patients with dyspepsia, routine upper endoscopy to exclude malignancy should be reserved for patients age 60 years and older.
  • Upper endoscopy is not necessary in most patients with dyspepsia younger than 60 years, even in the presence of alarm symptoms.
  • Patients younger than 60 years with dyspepsia symptoms should be tested and, if results are positive, treated for Helicobacter pylori infection.
  • Patients with dyspepsia who are negative for H. pylori or do not have improvement after H. pylori eradication may be treated with an empiric trial of a proton pump inhibitor.
  • NSAIDs and Helicobacter pylori infection are the most common causes of peptic ulcer disease.
  • NSAIDs should be discontinued in patients with NSAID-induced bleeding peptic ulcer disease (PUD); if there is no effective alternative to NSAIDs, a selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitor plus a once-daily proton pump inhibitor (PPI) should be used.
  • PPI therapy can be discontinued after confirmation of Helicobacter pylori eradication in patients with H. pylori–associated bleeding PUD.
  • Patients with idiopathic peptic ulcers that have bled should receive once-daily PPI therapy indefinitely because of the substantial risk for rebleeding.
  • For bleeding PUD related to aspirin use for secondary cardiovascular prevention, aspirin should generally not be withheld; if aspirin therapy is interrupted, it should be restarted immediately after hemostasis is endoscopically confirmed.
  • Repeat upper endoscopy to verify peptic ulcer resolution is reserved for patients who have persistent symptoms after 8 to 12 weeks of therapy, gastric ulcer greater than 2 cm, an ulcer of unknown cause, or who did not undergo gastric ulcer biopsy during initial upper endoscopy.
  • Upper gastrointestinal complications, such as bleeding, are common with use of NSAIDs, including low-dose aspirin.
  • Proton pump inhibitors are the preferred agent for preventing and treating NSAID-related (including aspirin-related) upper gastrointestinal complications.
  • In individuals with high risk for gastrointestinal complications, including those with previous NSAID-induced gastrointestinal bleeding, a selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitor combined with a proton pump inhibitor provides the best gastrointestinal protection if avoidance of NSAIDs is not possible.
  • Indications for Helicobacter pylori testing include peptic ulcer disease, mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma, dyspepsia, adult household members of those who have H. pylori infection, before initiating long-term low-dose aspirin or in those taking long-term NSAIDs, unexplained iron deficiency anemia, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, and prevention of gastric adenocarcinoma in high-risk groups.
  • Gastric biopsies during upper endoscopy or noninvasive testing methods, including ^13C-urea breath and stool antigen tests, can confirm active Helicobacter pylori infection; negative serologic results can exclude infection, but a positive serologic result may require confirmation.
  • Treatment regimens for Helicobacter pylori should consist of at least one antimicrobial agent and one antisecretory agent; treatment duration is 14 days.
  • Helicobacter pylori eradication is evaluated with a ^13C-urea breath test, fecal antigen test, or gastric biopsy performed during upper endoscopy at least 4 weeks after completion of eradication therapy and 2 weeks after proton pump inhibitor therapy cessation.
  • After gastric outlet obstruction is excluded by upper endoscopy, patients suspected of having gastroparesis should undergo an objective test of gastric emptying, typically gastric scintigraphy.
  • Initial management of gastroparesis includes correcting dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities; nutritional support; small, frequent meals that are low in fat and soluble fiber; and, in patients with diabetes mellitus, improved glycemic control.
  • Metoclopramide is a prokinetic drug that improves gastric emptying in patients with gastroparesis but is associated with dystonia, tardive dyskinesia, and parkinsonism; the lowest effective dose should be used.
  • Adenomas of any size in the stomach should be resected, and endoscopic surveillance should be performed within 1 year of resection.
  • Environmental metaplastic atrophic gastritis results from Helicobacter pylori infection and may improve after H. pylori eradication.
  • Autoimmune atrophic gastritis is associated with pernicious anemia, iron deficiency, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, and gastric neuroendocrine tumors.
  • Management of autoimmune atrophic gastritis includes preventing pernicious anemia and iron deficiency using vitamin B~12 supplementation and iron replacement, along with surveillance for neoplasms.
  • Gastric intestinal metaplasia is a preneoplastic gastropathy frequently associated with Helicobacter pylori infection; patients with gastric intestinal metaplasia should be tested for H. pylori and treated if results are positive.
  • The primary nongenetic risk factor for gastric cancer is Helicobacter pylori infection.
  • In countries with a low incidence of gastric cancer, such as the United States, routine screening for gastric cancer is not recommended in the general population and should be reserved for those at high risk.
  • Upper endoscopy with biopsy is the diagnostic test of choice for gastric cancer.
  • Gastrointestinal stromal tumors should be evaluated with endoscopic ultrasonography and excised if symptoms or high-risk features are present.
  • Neuroendocrine tumors are usually sporadic but can be seen in the setting of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and atrophic gastritis.
  • Patients who undergo partial gastrectomy for malignancy require lifelong surveillance for cancer recurrence; patients who have undergone partial gastrectomy for benign disease also have an increased risk for gastric cancer.
  • Dumping syndrome results from rapid gastric emptying after gastric surgery; first-line treatment is smaller, more frequent meals with liquids taken following meals.

index.title: Disorders of the Pancreas
index.keyPoints:
• Biliary disease (gallstones, biliary sludge, or microlithiasis) is the most common cause of acute pancreatitis.
  • Diagnosis of acute pancreatitis requires two of three criteria: (1) acute-onset upper abdominal pain, (2) serum lipase or amylase levels elevated to at least three times the upper limit of normal, and (3) characteristic findings on imaging.
  • Patients with acute pancreatitis should undergo transabdominal ultrasonography rather than CT for evaluation of biliary disease.
  • Moderate, judicious fluid resuscitation (preferably with lactated Ringer solution) should be pursued in patients with acute pancreatitis, with careful monitoring for fluid overload.
  • In mild acute pancreatitis, oral feedings can be started as soon as nausea and vomiting are controlled and clinical symptoms are alleviated; enteral feeding should begin within 72 hours if oral feeding is not tolerated.
  • Pancreatic pseudocysts do not require drainage unless they cause significant symptoms or are infected, regardless of size.
  • Abdominal pain, which may occur as intermittent episodes or as ongoing daily pain, is the most common symptom of chronic pancreatitis.
  • CT or MRI is the initial diagnostic test of choice for chronic pancreatitis.
  • Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography is no longer used in the diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis.
  • Symptomatic management is the cornerstone of treatment for chronic pancreatitis, including in patients with refractory pain.
  • Patients with chronic pancreatitis should be counseled to avoid alcohol and tobacco use.
  • Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis is characterized by elevated numbers of IgG4-positive cells in pancreatic tissue; type 2 autoimmune pancreatitis is characterized by idiopathic duct-centric neutrophil infiltration and no or few IgG4-positive cells.
  • The HISORt criteria can assist in the diagnosis of type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis; they include diagnostic Histology; suggestive Imaging (e.g., narrowed main pancreatic duct and parenchymal “sausage-shaped” swelling); Serology with elevated serum IgG4 level; Other organ involvement; and Response to therapy with glucocorticoids.
  • Types 1 and 2 autoimmune pancreatitis are treated with glucocorticoids, but up to 60% of patients may relapse.
  • Pancreatic cancer surveillance is recommended for persons with pathogenic germline variants in BRCA1/2, ATM, or PALB2 or those with Lynch syndrome; it is also recommended in persons with a family history of pancreatic cancer.
  • Symptoms of pancreatic cancer include abdominal pain, back pain, weight loss, jaundice; new-onset type 2 diabetes mellitus is also associated with pancreatic cancer.
  • Pancreatic-protocol CT or MRI helps support the diagnosis of pancreatic cancer and delineates the extent of disease.
  • Endoscopic ultrasonography–guided fine-needle aspiration or biopsy of the pancreas is recommended for histologic confirmation of pancreatic cancer.
  • Most incidental pancreatic cysts have a very low rate of malignant transformation; intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms involving the main pancreatic duct have the highest risk for malignant transformation.
  • High-risk cysts are managed with surgical resection.
  • At least 50% of patients with familial adenomatous polyposis syndrome develop adenomas in the periampullary region, which may progress to adenocarcinoma.

index.title: Colorectal Neoplasia
index.keyPoints:
• The number of colorectal cancer cases in patients younger than 50 years is increasing.
  • Nonmodifiable risk factors for colorectal cancer include age (≥45 years), male sex, and personal or family history of colorectal cancer.
  • Modifiable risk factors for colorectal cancer include diets high in red and processed meat; low intake of fruits, vegetables, fiber, and dairy; use of alcohol and tobacco; type 2 diabetes mellitus; sedentary lifestyle; and obesity.
  • The potential benefit of aspirin and NSAIDs in preventing colorectal cancer must be weighed against the potential harms of such therapy, especially gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • For patients with a first-degree relative diagnosed with colorectal cancer or advanced polyp before age 60 years or with two or more first-degree relatives affected at any age, screening colonoscopy is recommended to begin at age 40 years or 10 years earlier than the age of the youngest first-degree relative at diagnosis, whichever comes first.
  • For patients with a first-degree relative diagnosed with colorectal cancer or advanced polyp at age 60 years or older, screening for colorectal cancer is recommended to begin at age 40 years.
  • Colonoscopy is the preferred method of screening in persons at increased risk for colorectal cancer.
  • Colorectal cancer is usually diagnosed by colonoscopy with biopsy.
  • Cross-sectional imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis should be used for staging in the initial evaluation after diagnosis.
  • Lynch syndrome carries a lifetime risk for colorectal cancer of 50% to 80%.
  • Lynch syndrome should be suspected in patients with synchronous or metachronous colorectal cancers, colorectal cancer before 50 years of age, and personal or family history of several Lynch syndrome–associated cancers.
  • Genetic counseling and testing should be offered to patients with a personal or family history consistent with Lynch syndrome, as well as to patients whose tumor shows evidence of microsatellite instability or loss of mismatch repair protein expression.
  • Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is an inherited disorder characterized by many (usually ≥100) adenomatous colon polyps; an attenuated form of FAP (AFAP) causes fewer polyps (<100).
  • In patients with classic FAP, sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy should begin at age 10 to 15 years and be repeated annually, whereas colonoscopy in patients with AFAP can be delayed until age 18 to 20 years.
  • For patients with FAP and AFAP, upper endoscopy should begin at age 20 to 25 years.
  • Adenoma and cancer develop in 100% of classic FAP cases if surgery is not performed; colectomy is the treatment of choice for classic FAP.
  • Hamartomas in the gastrointestinal tract are associated with three primary syndromes: juvenile polyposis syndrome, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS), and PTEN hamartoma syndrome.
  • A diagnosis of PJS is based on the presence of two of the following three criteria: two or more PJS-type hamartomatous polyps in the gastrointestinal tract; multiple melanotic macules in the mouth, buccal mucosa, nose, eyes, genitalia, or fingers; and family history of PJS.
  • Serrated polyposis syndrome is characterized by numerous serrated polyps in the colon; colonoscopy is recommended every 1 to 3 years.

index.title: Gastrointestinal Bleeding
index.keyPoints:
• The most common causes of upper gastrointestinal bleeding include peptic ulcer disease, gastroesophageal varices, and Mallory-Weiss tears.
  • Tachycardia (pulse rate >100/min), hypotension (systolic blood pressure <100 mm Hg), age older than 60 years, and major comorbid medical conditions are associated with increased risk for rebleeding and death in patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • A restrictive transfusion strategy is recommended in patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding who are hemodynamically stable and are without preexisting cardiovascular disease when the hemoglobin level is below 7 g/dL (70 g/L).
  • Vasoactive therapy should be initiated if variceal hemorrhage is suspected, and initiation of antibiotics is recommended for all patients with cirrhosis and upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB).
  • Aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease should be discontinued and not restarted in patients with UGIB; aspirin for secondary prevention should be discontinued only if necessary.
  • Reversal of warfarin and direct oral anticoagulants is not routinely necessary in patients with UGIB and should be considered only if the level of anticoagulation is substantially supratherapeutic, there is life-threatening bleeding, or a massive blood transfusion is undesirable.
  • Patients with UGIB and a Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score of 1 or less may be considered for early discharge or outpatient treatment.
  • For patients hospitalized with upper gastrointestinal bleeding, endoscopy should be performed within 24 hours of resuscitation; in those with rapid bleeding or suspected variceal hemorrhage, it should be performed within 12 hours of presentation.
  • The most effective approach for control of acute esophageal variceal hemorrhage is combined therapy with a vasoactive agent and endoscopic treatment.
  • Patients with peptic ulcer disease and low-risk stigmata can resume oral diet after recovery from endoscopy, receive once-daily oral proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy, and be discharged from the hospital.
  • Patients with high-risk peptic ulcer lesions requiring endoscopic treatment should receive high-dose PPI therapy for at least 72 hours; thereafter, they should continue receiving twice-daily PPI therapy for 2 weeks.
  • Nonselective β-blocker therapy (preferably carvedilol) should be initiated in addition to endoscopic band ligation for secondary prophylaxis of variceal hemorrhage.
  • Endoscopic therapy should be repeated if bleeding recurs, but routine second-look endoscopy is not recommended in patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • The three most common causes of acute hematochezia requiring hospitalization are diverticulosis, colonic ischemia, and upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • CT angiography is the initial diagnostic test in patients who have lower gastrointestinal bleeding (LGIB), are hemodynamically unstable, or have rapid ongoing bleeding, followed by immediate upper endoscopy if CT angiography does not reveal a source of bleeding.
  • Catheter-based angiography with embolization should be performed as soon as possible if active bleeding is noted on CT angiography.
  • In hemodynamically stable patients with LGIB but no evidence of rapid bleeding, colonoscopy is the first study of choice.
  • If small-bowel bleeding is suspected, second-look upper endoscopy and colonoscopy or push enteroscopy should be considered before small-bowel evaluation, especially if previous endoscopic studies were low quality.
  • Video capsule endoscopy is preferred for evaluating stable patients for suspected small-bowel bleeding following nondiagnostic endoscopy and colonoscopy.
  • CT angiography is the diagnostic test of choice for hemodynamically unstable patients or for patients with suspected brisk small-bowel bleeding.

index.title: Diarrhea, Constipation, and Irritable Bowel Syndrome
index.keyPoints:
• Acute diarrhea (<2 weeks' duration) is usually infectious; chronic diarrhea (>4 weeks' duration) is commonly noninfectious.
  • Maintaining hydration is the primary goal in treating acute diarrhea.
  • The primary causes of chronic diarrhea are irritable bowel syndrome with predominant diarrhea, functional causes, and medications.
  • The most common cause of secondary constipation is medication.
  • The cornerstone of identifying most causes of secondary constipation is a careful history and physical examination.
  • Constipation treatments include dietary and lifestyle modification, addressing causes of secondary constipation, and various pharmacologic agents.
  • Irritable bowel syndrome is defined as recurrent abdominal pain at least 1 day per week for 3 months along with at least two other criteria (defecation-related pain, change in stool frequency, or change in stool consistency).
