  • In patients with irritable bowel syndrome with predominant diarrhea, stool testing for giardiasis, testing for celiac disease, and fecal calprotectin testing to differentiate from inflammatory bowel disease are recommended.
  • Initial irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) treatment includes water-soluble fiber supplements, avoiding trigger foods, and exercise.
  • In patients with IBS, pharmacotherapy should target predominant symptoms and be used if conservative treatment is not effective.

index.title: Malabsorption
index.keyPoints:
• Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) is characterized by gastrointestinal symptoms caused by excessive bacteria in the small bowel as the result of altered structure, function, or motility of the gastrointestinal tract.
  • In patients with a high probability of SIBO and lack of access for diagnostic testing, empiric antibiotic therapy is reasonable.
  • Short bowel syndrome is defined by loss of functional small bowel, with resultant loss of absorptive area that leads to maldigestion, malabsorption, and malnutrition.
  • Lactose maldigestion is common; symptoms occur when lactose is ingested and subside when lactose is eliminated from the diet.
  • The preferred initial test for celiac disease is measurement of IgA tissue transglutaminase antibodies in combination with a total IgA level while the patient is consuming gluten.
  • Antibody testing for celiac disease is less sensitive in patients adhering to a gluten-free diet, so these patients should undergo genetic testing for HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 heterodimers; genetic testing can exclude but does not confirm disease.
  • Celiac disease is treated by lifelong avoidance of wheat, rye, and barley.
  • The most common cause of ongoing symptoms related to celiac disease is continued gluten exposure.
  • Dermatitis herpetiformis presents with intensely pruritic papules and vesicles that rapidly break and occurs most commonly on the elbows, knees, scalp, and lower back; most patients have laboratory evidence of celiac disease.
  • A gluten-free diet is the preferred long-term management of both the skin and bowel disease associated with dermatitis herpetiformis.

index.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Predominant symptoms in ulcerative colitis are bloody diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, and tenesmus; the rectum is almost always involved, and mucosal inflammation can extend contiguously to the colon.
  • Crohn disease typically involves the ileum, ileocolon, or colon, although any part of the gastrointestinal tract may be affected; inflammation is transmural and can result in fistulas, abscesses, and strictures.
  • Extraintestinal manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease may include peripheral arthritis; dermatologic conditions, such as erythema nodosum and pyoderma gangrenosum; ocular manifestations, such as episcleritis and uveitis; and primary sclerosing cholangitis.
  • Infections, particularly with Clostridioides difficile and Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli, should be excluded in patients suspected of having inflammatory bowel disease, especially if symptoms are acute.
  • Ileocolonoscopy with biopsy is needed to diagnose inflammatory bowel disease.
  • A “skip lesion” (affected areas separated by normal mucosa) is a characteristic endoscopic feature of Crohn disease.
  • 5-Aminosalicylates (5-ASAs) are the mainstay of treatment for mild to moderate ulcerative colitis; patients with proctitis should receive rectal 5-ASA, patients with left-sided disease should receive 5-ASA enemas and oral 5-ASA, and patients with extensive disease should receive oral 5-ASA therapy.
  • Glucocorticoids are commonly used to treat flares of inflammatory bowel disease and can induce remission; however, they are not effective for maintenance therapy.
  • Azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine can be used in inflammatory bowel disease after corticosteroid induction of remission; methotrexate can be used for maintaining remission in Crohn disease.
  • The anti–tumor necrosis factor agents can induce and maintain remission in moderate to severe inflammatory bowel disease; before starting this therapy, patients should undergo testing for latent tuberculosis and chronic hepatitis B virus infection.
  • Patients hospitalized for ulcerative colitis who do not respond to intravenous glucocorticoids within 3 days should be considered for colectomy or a trial of infliximab or intravenous cyclosporine.
  • In individuals planning pregnancy, clinical and endoscopic remission of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) should be achieved before conception.
  • Most medications used to treat IBD are safe in pregnancy; however, methotrexate, etrasimod, and ozanimod must be stopped at least 3 months before conception, and Janus kinase inhibitors should be avoided.
  • Patients with inflammatory bowel disease may safely receive inactivated vaccines; live vaccines should ideally be administered 4 weeks before starting immunosuppressive therapy.
  • Patients with inflammatory bowel disease have increased risk for colorectal, cervical, and skin cancers; therefore, colonoscopy, Pap testing, and skin cancer screening should be routinely performed.
  • Microscopic colitis presents with watery, nonbloody diarrhea that has a relapsing-remitting course and is sometimes accompanied by mild weight loss and abdominal pain.
  • In patients with microscopic colitis, colonoscopy reveals normal-appearing mucosa, and the diagnosis relies on histologic examination of biopsy specimens.
  • For moderate to severe microscopic colitis, first-line treatment is budesonide.

index.title: Ischemic Bowel Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI) presents with severe periumbilical abdominal pain followed by the urge to defecate and loose, nonbloody stools.
  • Acute abdominal pain out of proportion to physical examination findings should raise suspicion for early AMI.
  • CT angiography is the recommended test for diagnosing acute mesenteric ischemia.
  • Patients with acute mesenteric ischemia require emergent surgery if imaging findings signify mesenteric infarction; otherwise, endovascular intervention may be performed.
  • Chronic mesenteric ischemia should be suspected in the setting of recurrent postprandial abdominal pain.
  • The diagnosis of chronic mesenteric ischemia requires exclusion of alternative causes and compatible imaging; CT or magnetic resonance angiography findings include severe stenosis of two of the three mesenteric arteries.
  • Treatment of chronic mesenteric ischemia includes percutaneous endovascular stenting or surgical revascularization.
  • Colonic ischemia presents with the abrupt onset of lower abdominal discomfort that is mild to moderate and cramping, followed within 24 hours by diarrhea and hematochezia.
  • In suspected colonic ischemia, abdominal CT may show bowel-wall thickening and pericolonic fat stranding; colonoscopy with biopsy confirms the diagnosis.
  • Most cases of colonic ischemia spontaneously resolve; patients with more severe disease require hospitalization, and those with risk factors for poor outcome should receive broad-spectrum antibiotics.

index.title: Diverticular Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Diverticulitis can be classified as uncomplicated or complicated; complicated diverticulitis is marked by abscess, fistula, obstruction, or perforation.
  • Symptoms of uncomplicated diverticulitis include colicky abdominal pain relieved with flatus or a bowel movement, fever, and altered bowel habits.
  • CT of the abdomen and pelvis with oral and intravenous contrast is recommended to confirm acute diverticulitis in patients without a previous imaging-confirmed diagnosis and to evaluate for complicated disease.
  • Acute uncomplicated left-sided diverticulitis can initially be managed with close observation alone without antibiotics in select immunocompetent patients.
  • Intravenous antibiotics and hospitalization are required in patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis who cannot tolerate an oral diet; patients with severe comorbidities, advanced age, or immunosuppression; and patients for whom oral antibiotics have been ineffective.
  • Unless performed recently, colonoscopy should be completed in all patients with an episode of diverticulitis 6 to 8 weeks after symptoms resolve to rule out concomitant malignancy.

index.title: Appendicitis
index.keyPoints:
• Appendicitis should be suspected in patients with right-lower-quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia; the diagnosis should be confirmed by imaging, typically CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast.
  • Appendectomy is the definitive treatment of acute appendicitis; in select uncomplicated cases, nonoperative treatment may be considered.

index.title: Anorectal Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• Colonoscopy is indicated for patients with perianal symptoms and alarm features, such as age older than 45 years, altered bowel habits, anemia, inflammatory bowel disease, unexplained weight loss, or family history of colorectal cancer.
  • First-line therapy for hemorrhoids includes increased fiber and fluid intake and avoidance of straining; patients with internal hemorrhoids unresponsive to medical therapy should be referred for banding.
  • Treatment for anal fissures includes sitz baths and bulking agents; associated rectal spasm is treated with topical calcium channel blockers or nitrates.
  • Initial management of fecal incontinence is directed at reversible factors, such as diarrhea, constipation, and offending medications; conservative management includes fiber supplementation and pelvic floor exercises.
  • Presenting symptoms of anal cancer may include bleeding, pain, or pruritus; however, 25% of patients present without any anorectal symptoms.
  • Human papillomavirus infection is strongly linked with anal cancer; risk is increased in men who have sex with men and in patients with HIV infection, history of condylomata, or kidney or liver transplantation.

index.title: Ileus and Bowel Obstruction
index.keyPoints:
• Ileus is a slowing or lack of passage of luminal intestinal contents in the absence of a mechanical cause and is treated with supportive care and by addressing the underlying precipitant.
  • The most common cause of small-bowel obstruction in the United States is adhesive disease from previous surgery.
  • CT imaging is the test of choice for diagnosing small-bowel obstruction and can demonstrate the location and cause.
  • Most cases of adhesive small-bowel obstruction resolve spontaneously with conservative management, which includes bowel rest, intravenous fluids, and nasogastric decompression.
  • The three most common causes of large bowel obstruction are adenocarcinoma, colonic volvulus, and benign stricture from diverticular disease.
  • CT imaging is the diagnostic test of choice for determining the cause of large bowel obstruction.
  • Most patients with large bowel obstruction require surgical intervention.

index.title: Gastrointestinal Perforation
index.keyPoints:
• In patients with a gastrointestinal perforation, plain radiographs may demonstrate free air; however, CT is more diagnostically sensitive and can localize the injury.
  • Surgical consultation should be obtained urgently for all patients with a gastrointestinal perforation.

index.title: Approach to Nonmalignant Leukopenia and Leukocytosis
index.keyPoints:
• Duffy-null associated neutrophil count results in a chronically low absolute neutrophil count without significant clinical consequences; it is protective against malaria and is more common in those of sub-Saharan African or Middle Eastern descent.
  • Medication-induced neutropenia occurs most often in patients older than 50 years during the first 3 months of drug treatment; symptoms usually improve within 1 to 3 weeks of stopping the medication.
  • Common causes of drug-related agranulocytosis include cytotoxic chemotherapeutics, clozapine, methimazole, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
  • Cigarette smoking is a common cause of chronic neutrophilia; the neutrophilia may persist for a prolonged period (sometimes for years) after smoking cessation.
  • A leukocyte count greater than 50,000/µL (50 × 10^9/L) owing to a nonmalignant cause is termed a leukemoid reaction; it is commonly associated with Clostridioides difficile infection and other infections with severe sepsis.
  • Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis is characterized by a monoclonal population of B lymphocytes (<5000/μL [5.00 × 10^9/L]) in asymptomatic patients who lack other criteria for a diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

index.title: Hematopoietic Stem Cells and Their Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• Aplastic anemia is caused by a decrease in hematopoietic stem cells due to autoimmunity, toxins, infections, medications, or inherited syndromes.
  • Although labeled as an anemia, aplastic anemia is characterized by pancytopenia; the severity of disease is classified according to the reticulocyte count and degree of thrombocytopenia and neutropenia.
  • Asymptomatic patients with moderate (nonsevere) aplastic anemia can be closely monitored without immediate treatment.
  • Younger patients with severe or very severe aplastic anemia with a suitable donor are treated upfront with allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT); older patients and those without an HSCT donor are treated with immunosuppression.
  • Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is characterized by the loss of complement-stabilizing proteins (CD55, CD59) on the erythrocyte surface resulting in intravascular hemolysis and increased risk of arterial and venous thrombosis.
  • PNH is associated with venous thrombosis at unusual sites, including the mesenteric and cerebral vessels.
  • Eculizumab and ravulizumab decrease hemolysis and thrombotic risk in patients with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.
  • Idiopathic pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is characterized by a selective decrease in erythrocyte precursors on bone marrow examination and the absence of a secondary cause such as parvovirus B19 infection, thymoma, and large granular lymphocyte leukemia.
  • Idiopathic PRCA is commonly immunologically mediated and treated with immunosuppression.
  • Parvovirus B19 is cytotoxic to erythrocyte precursors in the bone marrow and can cause significant anemia in patients who are chronically dependent on increased erythrocyte production, such as in sickle cell disease.
  • Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are suspected in patients with one or more cytopenias and dysplastic findings on peripheral blood smear; bone marrow biopsy is required for diagnosis and risk stratification.
  • The primary goals of MDS treatment are managing symptomatic cytopenias and decreasing progression to acute myeloid leukemia; allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only cure, but it is not feasible in most patients.
  • Asymptomatic low-risk MDS can be monitored; symptomatic anemia is treated with transfusions, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, and hypomethylating agents (azacitidine and decitabine).
  • Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is defined by the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, a reciprocal translocation of the ABL1 gene on chromosome 9 to the BCR gene on chromosome 22; the translocation can be demonstrated on peripheral blood and bone marrow testing.
  • CML may present with an asymptomatic increased granulocyte count or with symptoms of weight loss, abdominal fullness secondary to splenomegaly, fatigue, or fever.
  • All patients with CML require treatment at diagnosis with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as imatinib to manage symptoms and prevent disease progression.
  • The JAK2 mutation is present in almost all patients with polycythemia vera (PV); erythrocytosis without the JAK2 mutation should prompt evaluation for secondary causes.
  • An elevated hematocrit level should raise suspicion for PV but secondary causes of erythrocytosis are much more common; evaluation for secondary causes may include a sleep study, echocardiography, measurement of the erythropoietin level, and kidney imaging.
  • Patients with PV and the JAK2 mutation are at increased risk of splanchnic vein thrombosis, which may be the presenting feature preceding hematologic manifestations.
  • All patients with PV should be treated with low-dose aspirin and phlebotomy to target a hematocrit level less than 45%.
  • Cytoreductive therapy is indicated in patients with PV at high risk for complications, including those older than 60 years and those with a history of arterial or venous thrombosis.
  • Mutations in JAK2 are seen in approximately 60% of patients with essential thrombocythemia; other driving alterations include mutations in CALR (20%-25%) and MPL (5%).
  • Secondary causes of thrombocytosis, including iron deficiency, bleeding, infection, inflammatory conditions, and as a sequela of splenectomy, are more common than essential thrombocythemia.
  • Patients with low-risk essential thrombocythemia (age <60 years, JAK2 negative, no venous or arterial thrombosis) can be monitored without therapy.
  • Aspirin is indicated in all patients with essential thrombocythemia who are JAK2 positive and those older than 60 years; cytoreductive therapy with hydroxyurea is indicated in high-risk patients, including those older than 60 years and those with a history of thrombosis.
  • Primary myelofibrosis is characterized by bone marrow fibrosis and extramedullary hematopoiesis; massive splenomegaly, leukocytosis, anemia, and thrombocytopenia are often present.
  • Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only potentially curative treatment option for patients with primary myelofibrosis but is limited to otherwise healthy patients with poor short-term survival.
  • In patients with primary myelofibrosis, Janus kinase inhibitors such as ruxolitinib improve constitutional symptoms and reduce spleen volume.
  • Hypereosinophilic syndrome is defined by a persistent eosinophil count greater than 1500/μL (1.5 × 10^9/L), with end-organ damage secondary to eosinophilic infiltration.
  • Glucocorticoids are effective treatment for hypereosinophilic syndrome, but active Strongyloides stercoralis infection must be treated or ruled out before glucocorticoid administration.
  • Systemic mastocytosis is typified by mast cell proliferation with end-organ infiltration; most patients have KIT gene mutations.
  • Manifestations of systemic mastocytosis are often related to mast cell mediator release and include anaphylaxis.
  • Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) typically manifests with anemia, thrombocytopenia, or functional neutropenia secondary to bone marrow replacement with abnormal myeloblasts.
  • Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is characterized by coagulopathy and chromosomal translocation t(15;17), leading to the fusion transcript PML::RARA; treatment with all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide cures most patients.
  • Treatment of AML (other than APL) includes induction with an anthracycline and infusional cytarabine, followed by consolidation with additional chemotherapy or allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
  • Although acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in children is often curable, survival in adults remains inferior despite the adoption of pediatric treatment regimens in appropriate patients.
  • All patients with ALL should undergo lumbar puncture with examination of cerebrospinal fluid at the time of diagnosis along with testicular examination in male patients; other staging tests such as PET/CT and scrotal ultrasonography are not necessary in the absence of specific local symptoms or findings.
  • Adult survivors of childhood cancers face higher risks of secondary cancer, cardiovascular disease, and the metabolic syndrome.

index.title: Multiple Myeloma and Related Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• Tests necessary for the evaluation of monoclonal gammopathies include serum and urine protein electrophoresis, serum and urine immunofixation, serum free light chain assay, complete blood count with differential, serum chemistries, β~2-microglobulin measurement, lactate dehydrogenase level, and quantitative immunoglobulins.
  • Axial imaging (i.e., MRI, low-dose CT, or preferably PET/CT) is more sensitive than plain radiography of the bones (skeletal surveys) to assess for osteolytic lesions in patients with a monoclonal gammopathy.
  • Bone marrow evaluation and skeletal imaging are unnecessary in patients with a monoclonal gammopathy with low-risk features and no end-organ damage.
  • Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) is characterized by an M protein level less than 3 g/dL (30 g/L), clonal plasma cells comprising less than 10% of the bone marrow cellularity, and the absence of end-organ damage.
  • Only 1% of MGUS progresses to multiple myeloma per year; treatment is not indicated, but patients should undergo surveillance based on the risk of progression.
  • Patients diagnosed with monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance require myeloma-like therapy to prevent progressive and irreversible kidney injury.
  • Hypercalcemia, kidney disease, anemia, and bone disease are classic sites of end-organ damage in multiple myeloma; immunosuppression may also be present secondary to decreased levels of normal immunoglobulins (i.e., hypogammaglobulinemia).
  • The two main causes of kidney disease in multiple myeloma are elevated free light chains, which cause tubulointerstitial damage in distal tubules, and hypercalcemia.
  • Diagnostic criteria for multiple myeloma (MM) include the SLIM criteria (≥60% bone marrow clonal plasma cells or a serum free light chain ratio of less than 0.01 or 100 or greater, or one or more focal bone lesions on imaging), or the combination of at least 10% bone marrow clonal plasma cells and at least one of the CRAB criteria (hyperCalcemia, Renal failure, Anemia, Bone disease).
  • Smoldering MM is defined by the presence of bone marrow clonal plasma cells between 10% to 59% combined with an M spike greater than 3 g/dL (30 g/L) and/or kappa or lambda urine free light chain M protein ≥500 mg/24 h in the absence of symptoms or other criteria for MM.
  • Smoldering MM has a risk of conversion to MM requiring therapy of approximately 10% per year for the first 5 years; most patients are closely followed and only treated after meeting criteria for MM requiring therapy.
  • Patients with multiple myeloma (MM) should be evaluated for autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) eligibility; autologous HSCT is not curative but does improve progression-free and overall survival.
  • In patients with MM who undergo autologous HSCT, maintenance lenalidomide improves overall survival; patients who do not undergo autologous HSCT often receive continuous treatment tailored to prognostic factors and patient characteristics.
  • Lenalidomide increases thrombotic risk in patients with MM; patients receiving lenalidomide should take low-dose aspirin if they do not have additional thrombotic risk factors, whereas those with additional risk factors may require anticoagulation.
  • Bisphosphonates, such as zoledronic acid and pamidronate, or the RANK ligand inhibitor denosumab may be used adjunctively to prevent skeletal events in patients with MM.
  • Diagnosis of immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloidosis requires biopsy of the affected tissue showing characteristic pathologic findings of apple-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy with Congo red staining.
  • Patients with AL amyloidosis should undergo analysis for a clonal plasma cell disorder with serum and urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation, serum free light chain measurement, bone marrow biopsy, and skeletal imaging.
  • Autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) improves organ function and survival in patients with AL amyloidosis and is first-line treatment in eligible patients.
  • Patients with AL amyloidosis who are ineligible for autologous HSCT should receive treatment with agents used in multiple myeloma.
  • Hyperviscosity syndrome is associated with Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM) and is characterized by diverse central nervous system symptoms (e.g., altered mental status) and mucosal bleeding; dilated retinal veins may be present on funduscopic examination.
  • Patients with WM with hyperviscosity syndrome require emergent therapeutic apheresis to remove excess IgM; concomitant therapy to decrease IgM production should also be initiated.
  • Type I cryoglobulinemia is characterized by a monoclonal immunoglobulin (usually IgM) and is associated with plasma cell dyscrasias; patients are typically asymptomatic.
  • Types II and III mixed cryoglobulinemias are composed of a mixture of polyclonal IgG and monoclonal or polyclonal IgM and are usually seen in association with hepatitis C virus infection, connective tissue disorders, or lymphoproliferative disorders.

index.title: Erythrocyte Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• Symptoms from anemia are related to its severity and how rapidly it occurs, as well as whether underlying organ or vascular disease is present.
  • Anemia can arise from blood loss, erythrocyte underproduction, erythrocyte destruction (hemolysis), or a combination of these factors.
  • Defining anemia as microcytic, macrocytic, or normocytic as well as by reticulocyte response can help refine the differential diagnosis.
  • Anemia is not a final diagnosis; the underlying cause should be investigated to inform prognosis and treatment options.
  • A low mean corpuscular volume and mean corpuscular hemoglobin, elevated red cell distribution width, and peripheral blood smear showing microcytosis and anisopoikilocytosis are virtually diagnostic of iron deficiency.
  • Iron indices consistent with iron deficiency are a low serum iron level, an elevated total iron-binding capacity, a low transferrin saturation, and a low serum ferritin level; a low serum iron level, however, may occur with other causes of anemia and alone is not diagnostic of iron deficiency.
  • A serum ferritin level less than 30 ng/mL (30 μg/L) is considered highly specific (>97%) but relatively insensitive (35% in men, 54% in women) for iron deficiency.
  • Men and postmenopausal women with iron deficiency should be evaluated for a source of occult gastrointestinal blood loss.
  • Iron deficiency is typically treated with oral iron salts, optimally dosed once daily or every other day; oral ferrous sulfate is the preferred preparation because of its tolerability, efficacy, and cost.
  • Iron replacement in iron deficiency usually results in reticulocytosis within days and an increase in hemoglobin level by 1 g/dL (10 g/L) per week; oral iron replacement should continue for at least 3 months after the hemoglobin level normalizes to replace iron stores.
  • Anemia of inflammation (AOI) is characterized by a peripheral blood smear showing a normochromic, normocytic (or mildly microcytic) anemia; a hemoglobin level of 8 to 10 g/dL (80-100 g/L); a reduced serum iron level and total iron-binding capacity; and an elevated serum ferritin level.
  • Common causes of AOI include chronic infections, autoimmune and rheumatic disease, and malignancy; diabetes mellitus or heart failure can also have an increase in inflammatory cytokines with resultant AOI.
  • Treatment of anemia of inflammation centers on treating the underlying cause; blood transfusion is seldom necessary, iron replacement is ineffective, and although supplemental erythropoietin improves anemia, it is associated with multiple complications and is infrequently used.
  • Lead intoxication, frequently from occupational exposure, is a cause of microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling and multiple symptoms, including neurocognitive changes; chelation therapy is an effective treatment.
  • The clinical presentation of thalassemia is highly variable; suggestive findings on peripheral blood smear include uniformly microcytic erythrocytes, nucleated erythrocytes, and target cells.
  • Iron overload–related heart failure and arrhythmias are the major causes of death in patients with thalassemia; serial measurement of serum ferritin levels and periodic assessment of cardiac iron loading with MRI can determine the need for chelation therapy.
  • Patients with thalassemia should receive supplemental folate and be offered genetic counseling; iron supplementation should be avoided because of the risk of iron overload.
  • Treatment options for patients with transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia include luspatercept and allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
  • Patients with anemia of kidney disease not requiring dialysis and who have a hemoglobin level greater than 10 g/dL (100 g/L) should not receive erythropoiesis-stimulating agents.
  • For patients undergoing hemodialysis who have confirmed adequate iron stores, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents should be initiated for hemoglobin levels less than 10 g/dL (100 g/L); the target hemoglobin level should not exceed 11.5 g/dL (115 g/L) to avoid complications, including hypertension, volume overload, and thrombotic disease.
  • The anemia of vitamin B~12 deficiency is characterized by macrocytic erythrocytes and the presence of hypersegmented neutrophils; markers of hemolysis and, in severe cases, pancytopenia may also be present.
  • The serum vitamin B~12 level is 95% sensitive in diagnosing vitamin B~12 deficiency; a level less than 200 pg/mL (148 pmol/L) strongly suggests deficiency, whereas a level greater than 300 pg/mL (221 pmol/L) effectively excludes the diagnosis.
  • An elevated serum methylmalonic acid level reflects inadequate tissue vitamin B~12 stores and confirms deficiency in patients with borderline or low-normal serum vitamin B~12 levels.
  • Treatment for vitamin B~12 deficiency can often be accomplished with oral vitamin B~12; parenteral therapy is usually used for initial treatment of patients with severe disease or neurologic symptoms.
  • An elevated serum homocysteine level is more than 90% sensitive in diagnosing folate deficiency and is the preferred test when deficiency is suspected despite a normal serum folate level.
  • Vitamin B~12 deficiency should be excluded before patients with folate deficiency receive folate supplementation; although the hematologic abnormalities of concomitant vitamin B~12 deficiency may improve with folate supplementation, the neurologic complications continue to progress.
  • Laboratory findings suggestive of hemolysis include increased serum indirect bilirubin, elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase, and low serum haptoglobin levels; increased plasma free hemoglobin and urobilinogen excretion can also be seen.
  • In the absence of other conditions that impair erythropoiesis, such as iron deficiency, hemolytic anemia is typically associated with an increased reticulocyte response.
  • Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency typically presents with hemolysis several days after exposure to oxidative stress, such as infection or specific medications such as sulfonamides, dapsone, and nitrofurantoin.
  • Testing for G6PD deficiency should not be performed during an acute hemolytic episode because of high false-negative results.
  • Acute painful vaso-occlusive events are the hallmark of sickle cell disease (SCD) and should be recognized and treated immediately, generally with opioid analgesics.
  • Patients with SCD and chronic pain should avoid opioids, relying instead on NSAIDs, relaxation techniques, massage, and biofeedback.
  • Hydroxyurea decreases pain events, reduces the risk of acute chest syndrome or stroke, and prolongs survival in patients with SCD; other options that reduce the frequency of acute pain episodes are L-glutamine and crizanlizumab.
  • Acute chest syndrome in SCD is characterized by fever, tachypnea, hypoxemia, dyspnea, and pulmonary infiltrates; treatment includes empiric antibiotics, intravenous fluids, supplemental oxygen, and simple erythrocyte or exchange transfusions.
  • Erythrocyte transfusions should be used judiciously in SCD to avoid risks of alloimmunization, iron overload, and transfusion-transmitted infections.
  • Transfusion therapy is indicated in SCD for symptomatic, worsening anemia, acute chest syndrome, stroke, and before surgical procedures.
  • Treatment of symptomatic warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia includes glucocorticoids, rituximab, or other immunosuppression; splenectomy is also effective in nearly 70% of patients.
  • Treatment of cold agglutinin disease is primarily directed at avoidance of cold exposure, including warming of all infusates; symptomatic patients with significant anemia respond to rituximab-based or anticomplement regimens.
  • Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, characterized by schistocytes on peripheral blood smear, has a broad differential diagnosis, and treatment is directed at a specific underlying cause.
  • Hemolysis can result from Clostridium toxins or other intraerythrocytic parasitic infections such as malaria, babesiosis, and bartonellosis.

index.title: Iron Overload Syndromes
index.keyPoints:
• Homozygosity for the HFE C282Y alteration is the most common cause of hereditary hemochromatosis (HH); phenotypic penetrance is relatively low, and most patients with these alterations do not develop clinical disease.
  • Elevated transferrin saturation (≥45%) and serum ferritin level are suggestive of HH and should prompt HFE gene testing.
  • Adult first-degree relatives of patients with HH should be screened for the disease.
  • Phlebotomy is the mainstay of treatment for HH and is indicated in symptomatic patients with evidence of end-organ injury and in asymptomatic patients with an elevated serum ferritin level and transferrin saturation.
  • A goal serum ferritin level of 50 to 100 ng/mL (50-100 μg/L) is suggested in patients with HH.
  • Iron chelation therapy is recommended in most cases of secondary iron overload because phlebotomy is contraindicated in patients with anemia.
  • Indications for iron chelation therapy in patients with secondary iron overload include a serum ferritin level over 1000 ng/mL (1000 μg/L), transfusion of over 10 to 12 units of blood, or evidence of cardiac or hepatic deposition on MRI.

index.title: Platelet Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• The diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is based on the combination of severe thrombocytopenia, a normal hemoglobin level and leukocyte count, and no alternative explanation for the low platelet count.
  • Antiplatelet antibody testing and bone marrow examination are not required for the diagnosis of ITP.
  • Patients with ITP and a platelet count greater than 30,000/μL (30 × 10^9/L) who are asymptomatic or have only mild mucocutaneous bleeding can be observed without treatment.
  • Patients with ITP and a platelet count less than 30,000/μL (30 × 10^9/L) who are asymptomatic or have only minor mucocutaneous bleeding should be treated with glucocorticoids.
  • Severe bleeding in ITP should be treated with intravenous immune globulin and glucocorticoids.
  • Patients with ITP who relapse with tapering of the glucocorticoids or have refractory ITP require second-line treatments, such as rituximab, thrombopoietin receptor agonists, and splenectomy.
  • Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) should be suspected in any patient treated with heparin whose platelet count decreases by greater than 50% from baseline or to less than 150,000/μL (150 × 10^9/L).
  • The typical onset of HIT is 5 to 10 days after heparin exposure, but it can occur more rapidly if there has been heparin exposure in the previous 90 days.
  • The 4T scoring algorithm is used to stratify the likelihood of HIT; heparin should be discontinued, and an alternate nonheparin anticoagulant started for patients with intermediate or high risk for disease while awaiting confirmatory test results.
  • Diagnosis of HIT requires an intermediate or high clinical probability and a positive confirmatory test (serotonin release assay or heparin-induced platelet aggregation assay).
  • Patients with HIT should receive anticoagulation with a nonheparin anticoagulant for at least 4 weeks in the absence of thrombosis and 3 months if thrombosis was present.
  • All patients with acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) have microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) and thrombocytopenia; few patients have the classic pentad of MAHA, thrombocytopenia, fever, kidney injury, and neurologic symptoms.
  • The mortality rate associated with TTP is high, so treatment with therapeutic plasma exchange should be started without awaiting laboratory results confirming ADAMTS13 deficiency.
  • Treatment of TTP includes immediate therapeutic plasma exchange, glucocorticoids, rituximab, and, in some patients, caplacizumab.
  • Shiga toxin–mediated hemolytic uremic syndrome is usually caused by enterotoxin-producing Escherichia coli and presents with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and kidney injury; antibiotics are ineffective, and management is supportive.
  • Complement-mediated hemolytic uremic syndrome presents with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and kidney injury; treatment is with the anti-complement monoclonal antibody eculizumab.
  • Patients presenting with mucocutaneous bleeding and normal platelet count, prothrombin time, and activated partial thromboplastin time should be evaluated for von Willebrand disease or acquired platelet dysfunction.
  • The platelet function analyzer is a useful screening test for assessing qualitative platelet disorders.

index.title: Bleeding Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• The clinical history and bleeding symptoms are the most important predictive factors to guide management for patients with a suspected bleeding disorder; laboratory testing alone is insufficient to predict bleeding risk.
  • Basic laboratory tests, including the complete blood count, prothrombin time, and activated partial thromboplastin time, help guide additional diagnostic testing of a potential bleeding disorder.
  • Mixing studies are used to differentiate between factor deficiencies and inhibitors when the prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, or thrombin time is abnormal.
  • Patients with hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) or B (factor IX deficiency) have a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal prothrombin time and complete blood count.
  • Some patients with mild hemophilia A may be treated with desmopressin to stimulate the release of preformed factor VIII from stores in endothelial cells; a desmopressin challenge test should be done before procedures to document response.
  • Factor replacement infusions (factor concentrates or recombinant factor) can help prevent and control bleeding in patients with moderate or severe hemophilia A or B.
  • Inhibitors to replacement recombinant factors develop in up to 25% of patients with hemophilia A and 5% of patients with hemophilia B; an inhibitor should be suspected when bleeding increases in frequency and severity despite adequate factor replacement.
  • Patients with hemophilia A or B with inhibitors may require treatment with activated factor VII, which bypasses the inhibitor by directly activating factor X.
  • von Willebrand factor (vWF) deficiency or dysfunction leads to mucocutaneous bleeding that mimics thrombocytopenia, including bleeding gums, epistaxis, menorrhagia, and easy bruising.
  • Desmopressin, which stimulates release of preformed vWF and factor VIII, is used to treat minor bleeding in some patients with type 1 and type 2A von Willebrand disease (vWD); it can be given prophylactically before surgery or procedures.
  • vWF concentrates are used for major bleeding in all types of vWD and to treat patients with rare subtypes 2B and 3.
  • The coagulopathy of liver disease may be distinguished from disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) by comparing factor VIII (elevated in liver disease but consumed in DIC) and factor IX (decreased in liver disease and DIC) levels.
  • Active bleeding in patients with coagulopathy of liver disease should be managed with cryoprecipitate to maintain plasma fibrinogen levels greater than 100 mg/dL (1 g/L) and platelet transfusions to achieve a platelet count greater than 50,000/μL (50 × 10^9/L).
  • Fresh frozen plasma can be administered to patients with coagulopathy of liver disease, active bleeding, and an INR greater than 2, but the short half-life of plasma coagulation factors and risk of volume overload limit its effectiveness; it should not be routinely used in acute variceal bleeding.
  • Because of their cost and association with prothrombotic complications, prothrombin complex concentrates should not be routinely used to manage the coagulopathy of liver disease.
  • In patients with liver disease who are undergoing paracentesis, thoracentesis, or routine upper endoscopy, correction of modest thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy is unnecessary.
  • Classic laboratory findings of disseminated intravascular coagulation include thrombocytopenia, prolonged prothrombin and activated partial thromboplastin times, hypofibrinogenemia, and elevated D-dimer levels.
  • Management of disseminated intravascular coagulation is directed primarily at the underlying cause; platelet transfusions, cryoprecipitate, and fresh frozen plasma may be used as needed.
  • Oral vitamin K supplements safely and effectively correct vitamin K deficiency; critically ill patients and those unable to tolerate oral intake should receive vitamin K by slow intravenous infusion.
  • Acquired hemophilia from an autoantibody directed against a clotting factor (usually factor VIII) should be considered when a patient presents with a new bleeding diathesis, prolongation of the activated partial thromboplastin time, and a low level of an isolated clotting factor.
  • Factor VIII concentrates are ineffective in patients with acquired hemophilia because of the presence of an inhibitor; instead, patients should receive activated prothrombin complex concentrates, recombinant activated factor VII, or recombinant porcine factor VIII for management of acute bleeding.

index.title: Transfusion Medicine
index.keyPoints:
• In the United States, donated whole blood is screened for hepatitis B and C viruses, HIV, human T-cell lymphotropic virus I/II, syphilis, Trypanosoma cruzi, and West Nile virus; in select regions of the country, blood is also tested for Babesia.
  • For procedures in which blood transfusion is not invariably needed, a type and screen showing no unexpected antibodies eliminates the need for routine preprocedure cross-matching of individual units.
  • Persons of childbearing age or younger who are Rh negative and patients previously sensitized to Rh antigens should never receive Rh-positive blood.
  • Transfusion of one unit of packed red blood cells raises the hematocrit by 3% and the hemoglobin level by 1 g/dL (10 g/L) in an average-sized, nonbleeding adult.
  • Cryoprecipitate contains fibrinogen and is used to treat hypofibrinogenemia and uremic bleeding if desmopressin and platelet transfusion are ineffective.
  • Platelet transfusion is not generally indicated in nonbleeding, stable patients with chronic thrombocytopenia until the platelet count decreases to less than 10,000/µL (10 × 10^9/L).
  • Platelets should generally not be used to treat patients with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
  • Fresh frozen plasma is indicated for use in plasma exchange, as treatment of coagulopathy associated with massive transfusion, and for bleeding associated with multiple acquired clotting factor deficiencies such as in disseminated intravascular coagulation.
  • Recombinant factor concentrates (not containing donor plasma) are standard care for many patients with hemophilia A and B.
  • Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate contains factors II, VII, IX, and X and is the preferred product for patients experiencing life-threatening bleeding while taking warfarin.
  • Activated factor VII is used to manage factor VII deficiency, hemophilia in patients with high inhibitor titers, and acquired hemophilia in some patients, but carries significant prothrombotic risk.
  • A restrictive transfusion threshold (hemoglobin level <7 g/dL [70 g/L]) provides equivalent outcomes as a more liberal threshold in most patients; those with acute coronary syndrome, acute stroke, acute symptomatic anemia, or acute blood loss might require transfusion at a higher hemoglobin level.
  • Acute hemolytic transfusion reactions manifest with fever and flank pain, which can progress to hypotension, diffuse bleeding, and hemoglobinuria; discontinuing the transfusion is the most important step in treatment.
  • A delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction results from the presence of antibodies to non-ABO blood group antigens; the reactions occur 7 to 14 days after transfusion and are associated with a positive direct antiglobulin test.
  • Transfusion-associated circulatory overload is the most common serious complication of blood product transfusion and is characterized by onset of respiratory distress within 12 hours of transfusion, clinical evidence of volume overload, and radiographic findings of pulmonary edema.
  • Transfusion-related acute lung injury is caused by HLA- or neutrophil-specific donor antibodies that bind to and activate recipient leukocytes in the pulmonary vasculature; it begins within 6 hours of transfusion and is similar in presentation to acute respiratory distress syndrome.
  • Febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reactions are mediated by proinflammatory cytokines elaborated by donor leukocytes and present as fever, chills, or rigors within 4 hours of transfusion; treatment is supportive.
  • No evidence supports the routine use of antihistamine or glucocorticoid prophylaxis in patients with a history of mild allergic transfusion reactions.
  • Manifestations of anaphylactic or anaphylactoid transfusion reactions include angioedema, stridor, abdominal symptoms, and hypotension.
  • Patients with severe IgA deficiency and anti-IgA antibodies undergoing transfusion should receive only washed cellular blood components or plasma components from IgA-deficient donors.
  • Patients who have undergone hematopoietic stem cell or solid organ transplantation typically require irradiated blood products to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease.
  • As patients requiring massive transfusion are resuscitated, they must be monitored for volume overload and electrolyte disturbances such as hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia or hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis.
  • Patients with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia have autoantibodies that may make cross-match–compatible units impossible to find; if life-threatening anemia is present, transfusion with ABO and Rh type-specific, cross-match–incompatible blood is indicated.

index.title: Thrombotic Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• Thrombophilia testing is less accurate during episodes of acute venous thromboembolism, and results rarely affect acute management; if thrombophilia testing is indicated, it should be deferred until anticoagulation has been discontinued, unless antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is suspected.
  • Thrombophilia testing may be considered in patients with thromboses at unusual sites, patients with recurrent idiopathic thrombosis, patients younger than 45 years with unprovoked thrombosis or with a first-degree relative younger than 45 years with thrombosis, patients with a history of recurrent fetal loss, and patients with warfarin-induced skin necrosis.
  • The acute management of patients with venous thromboembolism (VTE) does not differ based on the presence of an inherited thrombophilia.
  • The duration of anticoagulation in a patient with VTE is typically determined by whether the event was provoked by a reversible risk factor rather than the presence of an inherited thrombophilia, such as factor V Leiden or the prothrombin G20210A gene variant.
  • Although the risk of VTE is increased in patients who are heterozygous for factor V Leiden or the prothrombin G20210A gene variant, most patients do not develop thrombosis, and testing results do not influence management.
  • For patients in whom heparin is initiated and titration to a therapeutic range is difficult, antithrombin III deficiency should be considered.
  • Deficiencies of the vitamin K–dependent factors protein C and S are rare; testing for these conditions should not be performed during an acute thrombotic event or during anticoagulation with warfarin.
  • Testing for methylene tetrahydrofolate reductase alterations or measuring homocysteine levels, factor VIII levels, or plasminogen activator inhibitor activity should not be part of the standard thrombophilia evaluation.
  • Approximately half of all new venous thromboembolisms (VTE) are associated with a recent hospitalization or surgical procedure.
  • Patients with cancer undergoing general surgery and patients undergoing knee arthroplasty, hip fracture repair, or hip replacement are at especially high risk for postoperative venous thromboembolism.
  • Medications that increase the risk of VTE disease include oral contraceptives, menopausal hormone replacement therapy, tamoxifen, and some cancer therapeutics, such as lenalidomide, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, antiangiogenic therapies, and immunotherapies.
  • The diagnosis of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is based on the clinical criteria of thrombotic disease or pregnancy morbidity along with laboratory findings of medium- or high-titer antiphospholipid antibodies present on two or more occasions at least 12 weeks apart.
  • In patients with splanchnic vein thrombosis (portal vein, splenic vein, hepatic vein, or mesenteric vein thrombosis), evaluation for an underlying myeloproliferative disorder or paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria should be considered.
  • Patients with a low-probability or unlikely Wells criteria score for deep venous thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE) should undergo D-dimer testing; if the results are normal, no imaging is necessary.
  • Patients with a Wells criteria score indicating likely or moderate-probability DVT should usually undergo lower extremity ultrasonography as the first test; D-dimer testing can also be used as the first test in select patients with moderate probability of DVT.
  • Patients with a very low probability of PE and a Pulmonary Embolism Rule-Out Criteria score of zero do not require further testing with D-dimer or imaging.
  • Patients with a likely, intermediate, or high Wells score for PE should undergo imaging; D-dimer testing may also be appropriate in select patients with an intermediate probability of PE.
  • Patients with established PE can undergo echocardiography and biomarker testing with serum troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide measurements for risk stratification.
  • Most patients with deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and those with pulmonary embolism (PE) who have a good prognosis (defined as age <80 years, no significant comorbidity, and stable vital signs) and reliable home support can be safely managed without hospitalization.
  • In most patients with acute venous thromboembolism, the preferred anticoagulant is a direct oral anticoagulant.
  • Thrombolytic therapy is not routinely used for treatment of PE, but systemic thrombolysis is indicated in patients with hypotension.
  • Catheter-based thrombectomy is an option in patients with PE who have hypotension but have a contraindication to thrombolysis or with clinical deterioration despite thrombolysis.
  • Initial treatment of PE with unfractionated heparin should be avoided except in patients who are unstable and may require thrombolysis and in those in need of emergent surgery.
  • Patients with acute venous thromboembolism should receive 3 to 6 months of anticoagulation; extended duration of full- or reduced-dose anticoagulation should be considered in those without transient thrombotic risk factors.
  • Patients with asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic distal DVTs do not usually require anticoagulation in the absence of risk factors for progression but should undergo follow-up lower extremity ultrasonography weekly for 2 weeks.
  • Patients with lower extremity superficial vein thrombosis managed with supportive care require follow-up evaluation after 1 week; repeat ultrasonography is indicated for symptoms that persist or worsen.
  • In patients with lower extremity superficial vein thrombosis of at least 5 cm in length, close to the deep venous system, or with other thrombophilic risk factors, including cancer or previous venous thromboembolism, short-term anticoagulation is recommended.
  • Most arterial thrombosis is related to atherosclerotic disease or cardioembolic disease rather than thrombophilia; treatment is usually with antiplatelet therapy when related to atherosclerosis or with anticoagulation when related to cardioembolic disease.
  • Catheter-related upper extremity deep venous thrombosis (DVT) is treated with anticoagulation for a minimum of 3 months if the catheter is removed or at least the duration that the catheter remains in place.
  • Catheter-related upper extremity DVT should not result in catheter removal as long as the catheter is functioning, well positioned, and noninfected.
  • A weight-based nomogram is usually used to determine the initial dose of intravenous unfractionated heparin, and algorithms are used to calculate subsequent dose modifications based on the activated partial thromboplastin time.
  • Protamine sulfate can be administered to reverse the anticoagulant effects of unfractionated heparin.
  • Variations in bioavailability of unfractionated heparin lead to an increased likelihood of delay in achieving a steady-state therapeutic dose compared with low-molecular-weight heparin.
  • Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) has a predictable effect and typically does not require laboratory monitoring; it is preferred over unfractionated heparin in most patients.
  • Patients with obesity or creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/min who are treated with LMWH do not require anti–factor Xa level monitoring; doses should be adjusted based on kidney function or actual body weight.
  • Fondaparinux is cleared through the kidney and should be avoided in patients with creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/min.
  • When used for the treatment of acute venous thromboembolism, warfarin must be administered concomitantly with a parenteral anticoagulant (usually low-molecular-weight heparin [LMWH]) for at least 5 days and until the INR has been in the therapeutic range for at least 24 hours.
  • Warfarin therapy is preferred to direct oral anticoagulants for anticoagulation in patients with mechanical heart valves and those with high-risk antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, among others.
  • Bridging therapy, which uses unfractionated heparin or LMWH during warfarin discontinuation before an invasive procedure, is not indicated in most patients.
  • Dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban have a rapid onset of activity, no need for laboratory monitoring, and a therapeutic effect that is less likely than warfarin to be influenced by changes in diet or medications.
  • Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are as effective as warfarin in preventing and treating venous thromboembolism; although the overall rate of bleeding is comparable, patients taking a DOAC have less central nervous system bleeding and less fatal bleeding.
  • DOACs should not be used in patients with valvular heart disease, pregnancy, or high-risk antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.
  • Factor Xa inhibitors are as effective as low-molecular-weight heparin in managing venous thromboembolism in patients with cancer.

index.title: Hematologic Issues in Pregnancy
index.keyPoints:
• Physiologic anemia occurs in all pregnant patients; if the hemoglobin level drops below 10.5 g/dL (105 g/L), evaluation, including measurement of iron stores and serum vitamin B~12 and folate levels, is warranted.
  • Iron deficiency in pregnancy is treated with oral iron in the first trimester because no safety data are available regarding intravenous iron.
  • Pregnant patients with sickle cell disease (SCD) should be treated with a higher dose of folate supplementation than other pregnant patients.
  • Some medications used to control SCD and its complications, such as ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and iron chelating agents, must be discontinued during pregnancy.
  • Transfusions should be administered to pregnant patients with SCD who have symptomatic anemia, acute chest syndrome, or stroke.
  • The risk of venous thromboembolism is increased in pregnant patients with SCD; thromboprophylaxis should be administered in hospitalized patients and considered for 6 weeks postpartum.
  • Gestational thrombocytopenia affects up to 5% of pregnant patients but is not associated with adverse outcomes and resolves following delivery; evaluation for other causes of thrombocytopenia is necessary for platelet counts less than 100,000/μL (100 × 10^9/L).
  • Features suggesting immune thrombocytopenic purpura versus gestational thrombocytopenia in pregnant patients include earlier presentation (first trimester), lower platelet count nadir (<70,000/μL [70 × 10^9/L]), and a history of thrombocytopenia before pregnancy.
  • Pregnant persons should receive intravenous immune globulin or glucocorticoids to treat immune thrombocytopenic purpura if the platelet count decreases to less than 30,000/μL (30 × 10^9/L) at any time during the pregnancy as well as 1 week before delivery to achieve a platelet count of at least 50,000/μL (50 × 10^9/L) for delivery or 70,000/μL (70 × 10^9/L) if neuraxial anesthesia is anticipated.
  • HELLP (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) syndrome, pre-eclampsia, and acute fatty liver of pregnancy manifest with microangiopathic hemolysis and, usually, thrombocytopenia; although distinguishing among these disorders may be difficult, the management of each is supportive and involves early delivery.
  • Patients may develop thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy during pregnancy and often require more specific therapy, such as plasma exchange.
  • Pregnant patients with a history of unprovoked venous thromboembolism (VTE), VTE associated with previous pregnancy or oral contraceptives, or thrombophilia associated with a high thrombotic risk require prophylactic antenatal and postpartum anticoagulation continuing for 6 weeks after delivery.
  • Diagnosis of pulmonary embolism in pregnancy requires balancing the risk of radiation exposure to the fetus with the need for diagnosis; combining D-dimer testing and the YEARS criteria can help limit imaging.
  • Low-molecular-weight heparin is the treatment of choice for pregnant patients with venous thromboembolism; it should be stopped at least 24 hours before delivery, during which time unfractionated heparin can be used until the time of delivery or as caesarean section nears.

index.title: Approach to the Patient With Abnormal Liver Chemistry Studies
index.keyPoints:
• Elevated aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels represent hepatocellular injury; ALT levels are more specific for hepatocellular injury.
  • Elevated alkaline phosphatase levels represent a cholestatic pattern and may result from biliary abnormalities.
  • Prothrombin time and serum albumin levels reflect liver synthetic function.
  • The AST-to-platelet ratio index and Fibrosis-4 score are noninvasive biomarkers for liver fibrosis; elastography is a noninvasive imaging technique that assesses liver stiffness as a measure of fibrosis.

index.title: Disorders of the Gallbladder and Bile Ducts
index.keyPoints:
• Asymptomatic gallstones discovered incidentally do not require cholecystectomy except in the setting of a high risk for gallbladder cancer (gallstones >3 cm, porcelain gallbladder, or gallbladder polyps >1 cm).
  • Biliary colic pain is typically acute, lasts 30 minutes to 6 hours, is severe and steady, and is located in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium.
  • Patients with typical biliary colic symptoms and gallstones on imaging should undergo cholecystectomy.
  • Cholecystitis can be diagnosed by suggestive clinical findings and ultrasound showing gallbladder-wall thickening or edema and sonographic Murphy sign.
  • Treatment of acute cholecystitis includes analgesia, intravenous antibiotics with gram-negative and anaerobic coverage, and cholecystectomy during initial hospitalization; percutaneous cholecystostomy tube drainage or endoscopic drainage can be pursued in patients with high surgical risk.
  • Acalculous cholecystitis typically occurs in critically ill patients and results from gallbladder ischemia; alert patients present with pain whereas sedated or mechanically ventilated patients may present with leukocytosis, jaundice, or sepsis.
  • Treatment of acalculous cholecystitis includes intravenous antibiotics to cover enteric bacteria and cholecystectomy; a percutaneous cholecystostomy tube may be needed for unstable patients or poor surgical candidates.
  • Symptoms of cholangitis include fever, jaundice, and right-upper-quadrant pain.
  • Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography is the preferred method for relieving obstruction caused by a common bile duct stone.
  • Cholangitis is potentially life-threatening; antibiotics targeting gram-negative Enterobacteriaceae should be administered immediately, and identified common bile duct stones should be removed urgently.
  • Gallbladder polyps 1 cm or greater and those associated with gallbladder stones or primary sclerosing cholangitis are more likely to be neoplastic and should prompt consideration of cholecystectomy.
  • Symptoms of cholangiocarcinoma may include jaundice, right-upper-quadrant pain, and constitutional symptoms; however, symptoms typically develop only with advanced stage disease.
  • First-line treatment for perihilar cholangiocarcinoma is resection.
  • Screening for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma should include liver ultrasonography at 6- month intervals in patients with cirrhosis and annual MRCP plus measurement of CA 19-9 level in those with primary sclerosing cholangitis.

index.title: Cholestatic Liver Diseases
index.keyPoints:
• Clinical manifestations of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) include fatigue, pruritus, and elevated serum alkaline phosphatase level.
  • Diagnosis of PBC does not require liver biopsy when the alkaline phosphatase level is at least 1.5 times the upper limit of normal and an antimitochondrial antibody titer is positive.
  • For PBC, ursodeoxycholic acid treatment results in histologic improvement, better survival rates, and diminished need for liver transplantation.
  • Patients presenting with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) may be asymptomatic or have pruritus; liver enzyme abnormalities demonstrate a cholestatic pattern.
  • PSC is associated with inflammatory bowel disease in more than 70% of cases; these patients are at increased risk for colon cancer and require surveillance colonoscopy at diagnosis and annually thereafter.
  • Patients with PSC have a 15% lifetime risk for cholangiocarcinoma; annual magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography, with or without measurement of CA 19-9, is recommended for cholangiocarcinoma surveillance.

index.title: Metabolic Liver Diseases
index.keyPoints:
• Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is the most common cause of liver disease in the world, and the primary pathogenesis is insulin resistance.
  • Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is definitively diagnosed with biopsy; however, the diagnosis is presumed if the following criteria are met: elevated aminotransferase levels, exclusion of other causes of liver disease, lack of significant alcohol intake, clinical features of metabolic syndrome, and imaging findings consistent with steatosis.
  • The NAFLD Fibrosis score and Fibrosis-4 score are used to risk-stratify patients for advanced liver fibrosis; patients with low scores are managed conservatively, patients with indeterminate scores should undergo liver stiffness measurement, and patients with elevated scores should be referred to a hepatologist.
  • Lifestyle modifications are the mainstay of treatment for MASLD.
  • Gilbert syndrome is a common benign disorder of bilirubin metabolism characterized by asymptomatic transient episodes of mild jaundice and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
  • Hereditary hemochromatosis is characterized by excessive iron absorption that results in accumulation of iron in the liver and cirrhosis.
  • α~1-Antitrypsin deficiency is an autosomal codominant genetic disorder that can result in accumulation of misfolded protein in the liver; homozygosity can result in liver injury and cirrhosis.
  • Wilson disease is a rare autosomal recessive disorder that causes accumulation of copper in the liver; it typically presents in young patients (<40 years) with liver and/or neuropsychiatric manifestations, including acute liver failure.

index.title: Hepatitis
index.keyPoints:
• All adults age 18 to 79 years should be screened for hepatitis C virus (HCV), followed by HCV RNA testing if the results are positive.
  • All patients with HCV infection, except those with a short life expectancy, should be considered for treatment.
  • All adults age 18 years and older should be screened at least once in a lifetime for chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) with hepatitis B surface antigen, antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen, and antibody to hepatitis B core antigen.
  • Patients with chronic HBV infection or resolved HBV infection who receive immunosuppression may require antiviral prophylaxis to prevent reactivation.
  • Treatment of hepatitis A virus infection is supportive, and 90% or more of patients recover fully within 3 to 6 months of infection.
  • Hepatitis E virus infection should be considered in patients with an unknown cause of acute hepatitis and in immunocompromised patients with chronic hepatitis.
  • Diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis is based on elevated aminotransferase levels, positivity for one or more autoantibodies, elevated levels of IgG, exclusion of other diagnoses, and often liver histology.
  • Treatment of autoimmune hepatitis includes a combination of prednisone and azathioprine for most patients.

index.title: Drug-Induced Liver Injury
index.keyPoints:
• Patients suspected of having drug-induced liver injury (DILI) should be questioned about all prescription and nonprescription medications, including supplements.
  • Acetaminophen, antibiotics, and antiepileptics are the most common causes of DILI.
  • Diagnosis of DILI is usually based on the following: exposure to a likely offending agent, elevated liver test results, exclusion of other causes of liver injury, and improvement or resolution of liver injury following drug discontinuation.

index.title: Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Manifestations of alcoholic hepatitis (AH) may include jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, and abdominal distention from ascites.
  • Severity of AH is determined by the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score; patients with a MELD score greater than 20 are classified as having severe AH and should be considered for prednisolone therapy.
  • Intravenous N-acetylcysteine is recommended as an adjuvant to glucocorticoids in patients with severe AH.
  • All patients with advanced alcohol-associated liver disease should be referred to hepatology for further management and consideration of liver transplantation, regardless of duration of alcohol abstinence.

index.title: Vascular Diseases of the Liver
index.keyPoints:
• Portal vein thrombosis is common in patients with decompensated cirrhosis and is a consequence of reduced portal flow, hypercoagulability, and endothelial dysfunction.
  • Patients with acute portal vein thrombosis should generally receive anticoagulation with direct oral anticoagulants, vitamin K antagonists, or low-molecular-weight heparin.
  • Characteristic symptoms of Budd-Chiari syndrome include hepatomegaly, ascites, and right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain.
  • Long-term anticoagulation is required in patients with Budd-Chiari syndrome, although bleeding risks can be significant in the setting of liver disease, portal hypertension, and esophageal varices.

index.title: Advanced Chronic Liver Disease and Liver Failure
index.keyPoints:
• The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) 3.0 formula accurately predicts 3-month mortality and is used for liver transplant allocation.
  • In patients with cirrhosis who are not receiving nonselective β-blocker therapy, upper endoscopy should be performed to assess for esophageal varices; primary prophylaxis to prevent bleeding includes nonselective β-blocker therapy (carvedilol is preferred) or endoscopic variceal ligation.
  • Ultrasonography is the most effective means of identifying ascites; the serum–ascites albumin gradient and total protein levels in ascitic fluid help determine the cause of ascites.
  • Management of ascites involves a sodium-restricted diet and diuretic therapy.
  • If more than 5 L of ascitic fluid is removed at one time, supplemental albumin should be administered to prevent circulatory dysfunction after paracentesis.
  • An ascitic-fluid neutrophil count of 250/µL (0.25 × 10^9/L) or greater confirms the diagnosis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; initial treatment in community-acquired cases is with a third-generation cephalosporin.
  • Precipitating causes of hepatic encephalopathy may include infection, sedating medications, volume depletion, or gastrointestinal bleeding; treatment involves addressing the precipitating cause and administering lactulose or rifaximin.
  • Hepatopulmonary syndrome should be suspected in patients with portal hypertension who have dyspnea and hypoxemia; the diagnosis is confirmed by intrapulmonary shunting with agitated saline administration during echocardiography.
  • Patients with chronic liver disease should be vaccinated against hepatitis A and B viruses and should receive pneumococcal, COVID-19, and annual influenza vaccinations.
  • Patients with cirrhosis should avoid alcohol; sedating drugs, including opioids; and raw shellfish.
  • Patients with cirrhosis should be screened for osteoporosis; confirmed osteoporosis should be treated with antiresorptive agents.
  • Acute liver failure (ALF) is defined as the combination of hepatic encephalopathy and liver synthetic dysfunction in the setting of acute liver injury (illness duration <26 weeks) in a patient without underlying chronic liver disease.
  • Acetaminophen overdose is the most common cause of ALF in the United States.
  • All patients suspected of having acetaminophen-related ALF or with ALF of unknown cause should immediately receive intravenous N-acetylcysteine.
  • Diagnosis of ALF requires immediate referral to a liver transplantation center.
  • Referral to a transplant center is indicated for patients with acute liver failure or patients with cirrhosis with a Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score of 15 or greater, evidence of decompensated cirrhosis, or hepatocellular carcinoma.

index.title: Solid and Cystic Liver Lesions
index.keyPoints:
• Asymptomatic simple hepatic cysts are benign and require no follow-up.
  • Women with hepatic adenomas who are taking exogenous hormones should discontinue those medications; adenomas that remain 5 cm or greater in size after medication discontinuation should be resected, whereas adenomas that are smaller than 5 cm can be monitored with serial imaging.
  • Men with hepatic adenomas of any size are at increased risk for malignant transformation, and resection is recommended.
  • Focal nodular hyperplasia does not have malignant potential or pose a risk for bleeding, and asymptomatic patients do not require follow-up.
  • Hepatic angiomas are common and do not have potential for malignancy; conservative management is appropriate for asymptomatic patients.
  • Diagnosis of pyogenic liver abscess (PLA) includes contrast-based CT and radiologically guided aspiration with culture.
  • Small (≤5 cm) PLAs are treated with parenteral antibiotics and needle aspiration with or without a drainage catheter; large (>5 cm) PLAs are treated with parenteral antibiotics and percutaneous catheter drainage.
  • Treatment of amebic liver abscesses includes metronidazole or tinidazole followed by a luminal agent, such as paromomycin.
  • Hepatic granulomas are focal inflammatory lesions that can be due to infections, inflammatory disorders, medications, or malignancy; treatment depends on the cause.
  • Patients with cirrhosis and high-risk patients with hepatitis B virus infection require hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance using liver ultrasonography and α-fetoprotein measurement every 6 months.

index.title: Central Nervous System Infections
index.keyPoints:
• Enteroviruses are the most common cause of viral meningitis, usually presenting with symptoms of headache, fever, nuchal rigidity, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, myalgia, pharyngitis, maculopapular rash, and cough between May and November in North America; treatment is supportive.
  • Herpesviruses can cause meningitis throughout the year; herpes simplex virus type 2 is the most common cause and generally does not require acyclovir therapy.
  • Neuroinvasive West Nile virus may present with acute flaccid paralysis, which may lead to persistent weakness or death.
  • Bacterial meningitis usually presents with fever, acute meningeal signs (meningismus or nuchal rigidity) and altered mental status; Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired bacterial meningitis.
  • Patients with suspected community-acquired bacterial meningitis should promptly undergo blood cultures and lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement and cerebrospinal fluid analysis (cell count, glucose and protein levels, Gram stain and culture); polymerase chain reaction assays can rapidly detect common pathogens.
  • If a head CT is indicated before lumbar puncture (focal neurologic findings, altered mental status, papilledema, new seizure, history of central nervous system disease, or immunocompromise) in a patient with suspected bacterial meningitis, imaging should not delay empiric antibiotic therapy, which should be started after promptly obtaining blood cultures.
  • Empiric intravenous antibiotic therapy and dexamethasone should be started as soon as possible when community-acquired bacterial meningitis is suspected; ceftriaxone plus vancomycin is indicated for patients 50 years or younger and ampicillin, ceftriaxone, and vancomycin is indicated for patients older than 50 years or with altered cell-mediated immunity.
  • Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces morbidity and mortality in adults with community-acquired bacterial meningitis in developed countries.
  • Staphylococcus species and gram-negative bacilli (including Pseudomonas aeruginosa) are the most common causes of health care–associated meningitis and ventriculitis, but culture results can be negative.
  • Empiric intravenous therapy for health care–associated meningitis and ventriculitis is vancomycin plus either ceftazidime, cefepime, or meropenem; infected devices should be surgically removed.
  • Freshwater exposure in summertime is a key historical clue in suspected primary amebic meningoencephalitis caused by Naegleria fowleri.
  • Tuberculous meningitis classically presents as basilar meningitis with cranial neuropathies, mental status changes, and hyponatremia; it should be treated with antituberculous therapy for 1 year with initial adjunctive glucocorticoids.
  • Medications such as NSAIDS, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and intravenous immune globulin can occasionally cause aseptic meningitis.
  • Herpes simplex virus type 1 is the most common cause of sporadic encephalitis in the United States, presenting with fever, seizures, altered mental status, and focal neurologic deficits; prompt identification and treatment with intravenous acyclovir improves outcomes.
  • Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) encephalitis, which is treated with acyclovir, may present without vesicular rash, so VZV polymerase chain reaction of the cerebrospinal fluid should be ordered in all patients with encephalitis; VZV IgG antibodies should also be obtained in patients with a clinical presentation concerning for VZV vasculopathy.
  • West Nile virus is the most common cause of epidemic viral encephalitis in the United States, occurs between June and October, and may present with acute flaccid paralysis or parkinsonism; treatment is supportive.
  • Brain abscesses in immunocompetent patients are initially treated empirically based on the likely predisposing factor, with surgical or stereotactic drainage of abscesses larger than 2.5 cm.
  • If the predisposing condition is unknown, empiric intravenous treatment of a brain abscess should include vancomycin plus metronidazole and a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin.
  • In cranial epidural and subdural abscess, pathogen identification is best achieved by culture of the abscess obtained during surgical drainage.
  • MRI with contrast is the imaging modality of choice to identify location and extent of a spinal epidural abscess, and blood cultures should be obtained before starting antibiotic therapy.
  • Treatment of spinal epidural abscess includes at least 6 weeks of effective antimicrobial therapy; surgical drainage is indicated in patients with neurologic symptoms or signs.
  • Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is a demyelinating central nervous system disorder caused by the reactivation of the John Cunningham virus in immunocompromised individuals.
  • Diagnostic criteria for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy are based on clinical, radiographic, and virologic evidence; radiographic findings include white matter lesions seen as hyperintense lesions on T2-weighted images and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images.

index.title: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections
index.keyPoints:
• Patients with mild cellulitis or erysipelas without systemic signs or symptoms should receive empiric oral antibiotic therapy primarily directed against streptococci (penicillin, cephalexin, dicloxacillin, or clindamycin).
  • Patients with moderate nonpurulent cellulitis or erysipelas with systemic signs should receive empiric intravenous antibiotics (penicillin, ceftriaxone, cefazolin, clindamycin).
  • Patients with evidence of deeper necrotizing soft tissue infection such as bullae and desquamation (severe infection) should receive urgent surgical evaluation for debridement and empiric vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem like imipenem.
  • Surgical exploration can confirm the diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis and should not be delayed when the diagnosis is strongly suspected; early surgical management can reduce mortality.
  • Empiric antibiotic treatment for necrotizing fasciitis includes broad-spectrum coverage for aerobic and anaerobic gram-negative and gram-positive organisms (including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) such as a carbapenem or piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin or daptomycin.
  • Clostridial myonecrosis management includes prompt surgical exploration and debridement in addition to parenteral high-dose penicillin plus clindamycin.
