  • Primary treatment for abscesses, furuncles, and carbuncles is incision and drainage; however, some experts recommend careful consideration of adjunctive antibiotics for mild uncomplicated abscesses based on recent studies that show improved cure rates compared with incision and drainage alone.
  • For moderate and severe purulent skin infections associated with systemic symptoms, Gram stain and culture should be performed on the purulent drainage followed by empiric oral antibiotic treatment for moderate infections (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or doxycycline) and empiric intravenous antibiotics for severe infections (vancomycin, daptomycin, linezolid, telavancin, or ceftaroline).
  • Acute lymphangitis presents as tender, erythematous streaks overlying the lymphatic vessels draining the initial site of infection.
  • Acute lymphangitis or lymphadenitis is typically treated empirically with antibiotics targeting Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species.
  • Bite wound management includes irrigation with sterile normal saline; except for facial wounds, primary closure is not generally pursued.
  • Assessment for tetanus and rabies prophylaxis is essential in patients with animal bite wounds.
  • Pre-emptive amoxicillin-clavulanate is recommended for animal bite wounds in patients who are immunosuppressed and for wounds with associated edema or lymphatic or venous insufficiency; crush injury; joint or bone involvement; deep punctures; or moderate to severe injuries, especially involving the face, genitalia, or hand.
  • After debridement and cultures are obtained, mildly infected animal bite wounds can be treated with oral amoxicillin-clavulanate, whereas severe infections should be treated with intravenous antibiotic therapy (β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations, carbapenems, or ceftriaxone or a fluoroquinolone plus clindamycin or metronidazole); empiric coverage for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) can be included for patients with severe infections or MRSA risk factors.
  • Short-course prophylactic antibiotic therapy with amoxicillin-clavulanate is recommended for human bites that perforate the skin.
  • In addition to assessment for tetanus prophylaxis, evaluation of human bites for potential exposure to hepatitis B and C viruses, HIV, and other bodily fluid–transmitted pathogens is warranted.
  • Diabetic foot infection is diagnosed when pus or two or more inflammatory signs (warmth, induration, erythema, pain, and tenderness) are present.
  • Plain imaging is recommended for all patients with diabetic foot infections; additional imaging with ultrasonography or MRI may be needed when abscess or bone involvement is suspected, respectively.
  • Uninfected diabetic foot wounds should not be cultured or treated with antibiotics.
  • Mild diabetic foot infections can be treated empirically with 7 to 14 days of oral antibiotics (cephalexin, dicloxacillin, clindamycin, levofloxacin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, or doxycycline); if pus or methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) risk factors exist, a regimen active against MRSA should be prescribed.
  • For moderate and severe diabetic foot infections, polymicrobial coverage of staphylococci (including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, if risk factors are present), streptococci, and aerobic gram-negative bacilli is recommended.
  • Source control for toxic shock syndrome typically requires surgical debridement.
  • Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome is treated with penicillin and clindamycin.
  • Toxic shock syndrome caused by methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus is treated with nafcillin or cefazolin and clindamycin; vancomycin plus clindamycin is preferred for infection with methicillin-resistant S. aureus.

index.title: Osteomyelitis
index.keyPoints:
• Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen in osteomyelitis.
  • Chronic osteomyelitis frequently presents as subacute to chronic pain over the affected region of bone; fever and other systemic manifestations of infection are uncommon.
  • Underlying osteomyelitis should be considered when chronic wounds, such as pressure ulcers, do not respond to appropriate therapy.
  • In the setting of a chronic wound, a positive probe-to-bone test has high sensitivity and specificity for osteomyelitis.
  • An elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein level increases the probability of osteomyelitis and is useful in monitoring therapeutic response; however, normal inflammatory markers do not exclude the diagnosis.
  • Because of its low cost and specificity, plain radiography is recommended as an initial imaging test for suspected osteomyelitis; if radiography is negative, MRI, with and without intravenous contrast, should be obtained.
  • Obtaining biopsy material for culture and pathologic examination is important when managing suspected osteomyelitis because cultures of swabs, sinus tracts, or superficial wounds have a poor correlation with bone biopsy specimens; confirming the presence of a pathogen often enables tailoring therapy to a narrower spectrum.
  • A bone biopsy is generally not required in persons with hematogenous osteomyelitis and positive blood culture results.
  • Unless systemic signs of sepsis or concomitant soft tissue infection or bacteremia are present, empiric antibiotics should be withheld in suspected osteomyelitis until a bone biopsy is obtained.
  • Surgical debridement is indicated for osteomyelitis if bone necrosis is extensive.
  • A 4- to 6-week course of antibiotic therapy is usually sufficient for acute osteomyelitis following debridement; longer courses are required for chronic infections.
  • Osteomyelitis should be considered when a diabetic foot ulcer is deep (presence of exposed bone), large (surface area >2 cm^2), or chronic (nonhealing after 6 weeks of standard care).
  • Bone samples for diagnosis and guidance of antimicrobial therapy should be obtained in patients with osteomyelitis.
  • If infected but viable bone is present in patients with diabetes mellitus–associated osteomyelitis, a 3- to 6-week course of antibiotic therapy is recommended; therapy is extended in patients who have not undergone debridement or nonviable bone persists.
  • Indications for amputation in osteomyelitis include persistent sepsis, inability to tolerate antibiotic therapy, progressive bone destruction despite appropriate therapy, or bone destruction that compromises the mechanical integrity of the foot.
  • New-onset back or neck pain or progressive worsening of chronic pain that is unresponsive to conservative management should raise concern for vertebral osteomyelitis, especially when accompanied by elevated inflammatory markers, neurologic findings, bacteremia, or unexplained fever.
  • The diagnostic evaluation of vertebral osteomyelitis should include MRI with and without contrast and blood cultures, which should be performed before initiating antibiotics; image-guided percutaneous biopsy and aspiration should be performed in patients with negative blood culture results.
  • Parenteral antibiotic therapy, based on culture results, is recommended for uncomplicated vertebral osteomyelitis, although oral agents with high bioavailability and good bone penetration can be used for selected organisms; treatment duration is typically at least 6 weeks.

index.title: Infectious Arthritis
index.keyPoints:
• Infectious arthritis typically presents with pain, swelling, warmth, and erythema of the affected joint, accompanied by fever and constitutional symptoms.
  • Acute monoarthritis, including in a patient with well-controlled inflammatory arthritis, should prompt evaluation for infection.
  • Staphylococcus aureus is the most frequently isolated microorganism in septic arthritis.
  • Disseminated gonococcal infection may present as the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome (tenosynovitis, dermatitis, and polyarthralgia) or as purulent arthritis that presents with mono- or oligoarthritis but usually without skin lesions or fever.
  • Lyme arthritis is a late-disseminated disease manifestation and is typically monoarticular (most commonly in the knee); diagnosis should be suspected in patients who may have had untreated or incompletely treated Lyme disease.
  • Hepatitis B virus infection can cause a self-limited, sudden, severe, polyarthritis during the prodromal stage before jaundice occurs; hand and knee joints are most often involved.
  • Arthritis associated with parvovirus B19 infection presents acutely, is symmetric and polyarticular, and usually involves the small joints of the hand.
  • Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid evaluation by Gram stain, culture, and leukocyte count confirms the diagnosis of infectious arthritis; crystal analysis may be performed to exclude gout or calcium pyrophosphate deposition, but the presence of crystals does not exclude infection.
  • In patients with bacterial arthritis, empiric antibiotic therapy often includes vancomycin combined with a second agent active against gram-negative organisms (e.g., ceftriaxone; cefepime or ceftazidime if at risk for P. aeruginosa infection); infected joints should also undergo drainage.
  • Early and late prosthetic joint infections usually present with pain, warmth, joint effusion, and fever; delayed infections may be more difficult to recognize because they are often caused by less virulent microorganisms, and symptoms may be less severe.
  • Testing for prosthetic joint infection includes serum inflammatory markers, plain radiographs, blood cultures, and arthrocentesis for synovial fluid assessment.
  • Empiric antibiotics are not routinely recommended in patients with suspected prosthetic joint infection who are clinically stable until after culture or surgery is performed.
  • Many patients with prosthetic joint infections require orthopedic device removal as part of a two-stage procedure, with a new device implanted after an appropriate course of intravenous antibiotics.

index.title: Community-Acquired Bacteremia and Endocarditis
index.keyPoints:
• Bacteremia with organisms that normally colonize the skin, including coagulase-negative staphylococci, Bacillus species (other than Bacillus anthracis), Corynebacterium species, Cutibacterium acnes, or Micrococcus may result from a nonsterile blood draw representing contamination.
  • Isolation of Staphylococcus aureus in a blood culture is always considered significant and requires evaluation to differentiate uncomplicated from complicated infection.
  • Methicillin-sensitive S. aureus bacteremia is treated with high-dose cefazolin or a penicillinase-resistant semisynthetic penicillin such as nafcillin or oxacillin; alternative agents, such as vancomycin and daptomycin, are reserved for patients with serious allergies to β-lactam antibiotics.
  • For methicillin-resistant S. aureus bacteremia, vancomycin or daptomycin is the preferred antibiotic.
  • Patients with uncomplicated enterococcal bacteremia can be treated with 2 weeks of directed therapy with penicillin or ampicillin; for patients with resistant bacteria or allergies to first-line therapies, vancomycin, daptomycin, or linezolid can be used.
  • Because Streptococcus gallolyticus is part of the normal enteric flora and bloodstream infection has been associated with gastrointestinal malignancy, colonoscopy is indicated when this organism is identified.
  • Cardiac involvement is uncommon with gram-negative bacteremia; therefore, obtaining surveillance blood cultures is not typically necessary for patients with rapid clinical improvement and has been associated with increased costs and excess length of hospital stay.
  • Initial diagnostic tests for suspected infective endocarditis (IE) include blood cultures and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE); transesophageal echocardiography following TTE is indicated with intermediate or high suspicion for IE when TTE is not diagnostic.
  • The specific agents and treatment duration for streptococcal endocarditis vary based on the penicillin minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of the organism; because the MICs for Abiotrophia, Gemella, and Granulicatella are often inaccurate, endocarditis caused by these pathogens should be treated with the same regimen as endocarditis caused by viridans group streptococci with high-level penicillin resistance.
  • Left-sided Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis is associated with poorer outcomes than right-sided disease, and at least 6 weeks of antibiotic treatment is recommended for these infections.
  • Although aminoglycosides and cephalosporins are not active against enterococci, they work synergistically when given in combination with a primary antibiotic; the reduced toxicity of ceftriaxone compared with aminoglycosides makes it particularly appealing for combination therapy in patients with enterococcus endocarditis.
  • Treatment for endocarditis caused by HACEK organisms is guided by sensitivity testing; recommended regimens are 4 weeks of ceftriaxone, ampicillin, or ciprofloxacin.
  • Initial therapy for Candida endocarditis is liposomal amphotericin B (with or without 5-flucytosine) or an echinocandin such as micafungin, caspofungin, or anidulafungin; fluconazole is not recommended for initial treatment.
  • The most common reason for culture-negative endocarditis is previous antibiotic administration.
  • Culture-negative endocarditis may represent a fastidious organism not readily isolated on routine culture media; therefore, a thorough evaluation should include potential exposures and comorbidities that may suggest further targeted testing.
  • Early surgery is indicated for patients with acute infective endocarditis (IE) presenting with severe valvular dysfunction resulting in heart failure; IE caused by fungal or other highly resistant organisms; complications such as heart block, annular or aortic abscess, and destructive penetrating lesion; persistent bacteremia; recurrent emboli after more than 5 days of treatment; or vegetations larger than 10 mm.

index.title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
index.keyPoints:
• Streptococcus pneumoniae accounts for only 5% to 15% of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) infections requiring hospitalization, whereas rates of CAP caused by Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacteriaceae are rising, even among patients without identifiable health care exposure.
  • The significance of viral detection in CAP is unclear; however, an antecedent mild respiratory viral infection may increase the risk for a secondary bacterial infection.
  • Legionella pneumophila infection is associated with water exposure, including hot tubs, contaminated water towers, and air conditioning units; several features should raise suspicion for Legionella pneumonia, including gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatremia, and elevated aminotransferase levels.
  • CAP caused by anaerobic bacteria is uncommon; however, anaerobes remain important pathogens in patients with lung abscess or empyema.
  • Mycobacterial or fungal causes of CAP should be considered in patients with immunocompromising conditions, epidemiologic risk factors for infection, or subacute presentations and in those who do not respond to conventional antibacterial treatment.
  • Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) should be suspected and chest radiography performed in any patient presenting with fever associated with cough, dyspnea, or chest pain.
  • Diagnostic studies to identify a causative organism are not routinely indicated in outpatients with CAP, but should be considered in non-ICU hospitalized patients when this information would change management; diagnostic studies should be performed in all patients admitted to the ICU with CAP.
  • Procalcitonin level is insufficiently sensitive or specific to guide decision making regarding initiation of antimicrobial therapy in patients with CAP.
  • Blood cultures should be obtained routinely in patients with severe pneumonia and those treated empirically for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
  • Urinary antigen tests should be reserved for use in patients with moderate to severe CAP who require hospitalization, are immunocompromised, or have a known or possible exposure to Legionella (e.g., during an outbreak).
  • A clinical prediction model (the Pneumonia Severity Index or Infectious Diseases Society of America/American Thoracic Society criteria) can be used to identify patients with community-acquired pneumonia who may require hospital or ICU admission.
  • Outpatient empiric therapy for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in otherwise healthy patients includes monotherapy with doxycycline or amoxicillin.
  • Recommended empiric regimens for hospitalized non-ICU patients with CAP include a parenteral β-lactam agent (a third-generation cephalosporin or ampicillin-sulbactam) plus a macrolide or monotherapy with a respiratory fluoroquinolone.
  • Treatment regimens for patients with CAP requiring ICU care include coadministration of a parenteral β-lactam active against Streptococcus pneumoniae and a second agent active against Legionella species.
  • Patients with CAP caused by influenza should be treated with an antiviral agent regardless of illness duration before diagnosis; because identifying a viral organism does not rule out bacterial coinfection, antibiotics should also be prescribed when a viral pathogen is identified.
  • Standard treatment duration for uncomplicated CAP is usually 5 days; however, staphylococcal, pseudomonal, fungal, and mycobacterial pneumonia require more prolonged courses of antibiotics.
  • Lack of response to antimicrobials in patients with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) raises consideration of a resistant or atypical organism, loculated infection, or an infection mimic.
  • Patients hospitalized with CAP experience significant morbidity and are at high risk for readmission.
  • In adults with community-acquired pneumonia whose symptoms have resolved within 5 to 7 days, routine follow-up chest imaging is usually not necessary.

index.title: Tick-Borne Diseases
index.keyPoints:
• The causative spirochete of Lyme disease may be transmitted when an infected Ixodes scapularis tick attaches for at least 36 hours.
  • Early localized Lyme disease usually presents within 4 weeks of infection and is characterized by erythema migrans at the site of tick attachment.
  • Confirmatory laboratory testing is not required or recommended in patients with erythema migrans and a compatible history because antibodies may not have formed yet in the setting of early localized disease; patients should receive oral doxycycline.
  • Early disseminated Lyme disease can affect the cardiovascular and neurologic systems; the diagnosis should be confirmed through an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay followed by confirmatory testing, with antibiotic treatment indicated depending on disease severity.
  • For Lyme carditis, hospitalization is indicated for symptomatic patients or asymptomatic patients with first-degree (or higher) atrioventricular block and a PR interval of 300 milliseconds or greater.
  • Post–Lyme disease syndrome (fatigue, arthralgia, myalgia, and impairment of memory or cognition) can last for years, even after appropriate treatment; prolonged antibiotics are not effective in treating this condition.
  • Babesiosis presents with clinical findings ranging from a mild febrile illness to fatal infection; symptoms are usually nonspecific, but hemolytic anemia is a hallmark of disease.
  • Babesiosis is diagnosed by direct visualization of the organism on blood smear or polymerase chain reaction.
  • Treatment for babesiosis is atovaquone plus azithromycin, with extended treatment duration recommended for severely immunocompromised patients.
  • Southern tick–associated rash illness may be clinically indistinguishable from early-stage Lyme disease, so treatment with doxycycline is often offered.
  • Ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis often present as a nonspecific febrile illness 1 to 2 weeks after a tick bite; rash is uncommon, and frequent laboratory findings include leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver function tests.
  • Antibody levels are often negative at the time of presentation in ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis but usually become positive within 4 weeks of illness; polymerase chain reaction of whole blood at the time of acute illness may be diagnostic.
  • Doxycycline is recommended for ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis; empiric therapy should be started without awaiting results of confirmatory testing.
  • Spotted fever rickettsiosis, including Rocky Mountain spotted fever, presents with nonspecific signs and symptoms such as fever, headache, malaise, myalgia, arthralgia, with a rash developing 3 to 5 days after presentation.
  • Doxycycline should be given empirically when spotted fever rickettsiosis is clinically suspected.

index.title: Urinary Tract Infections
index.keyPoints:
• An uncomplicated urinary tract infection (UTI) refers to infections in nonpregnant women without structural or neurologic abnormalities or comorbidities.
  • UTIs in men, pregnant persons, and persons with foreign bodies; kidney disease; immunocompromise; obstruction; or urinary retention from neurologic disorders are considered complicated.
  • Designating a UTI as complicated influences the choice and duration of antimicrobial therapy and extent of investigation.
  • Most ascending UTIs are caused by a single bacterial species, specifically gram-negative aerobic bacilli.
  • Diagnosis of a urinary tract infection (UTI) is based on clinical features, the anatomic location of the infection, and the presence of pyuria and bacteriuria.
  • Urine culture is not recommended in patients with uncomplicated cystitis but is indicated in pyelonephritis, complicated cystitis, recurrent UTIs, patients with multiple antibiotic allergies, and in patients with a suspected resistant organism.
  • Imaging studies may be indicated for patients with suspected UTIs when the diagnosis is unclear; when a structural abnormality or complication is suspected; or in patients with severe illness, immunocompromise, or lack of response to appropriate therapy.
  • Preferred agents for uncomplicated cystitis in nonpregnant persons include nitrofurantoin (5 days), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (3 days), and fosfomycin (1 dose, but least preferred); fluoroquinolones should not be used as first-line therapy in cystitis.
  • Urine culture with susceptibility testing is required in acute pyelonephritis; follow-up urine cultures are only indicated in pregnant individuals.
  • Ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin are recommended for empiric outpatient treatment of pyelonephritis.
  • Avoid choosing a fluoroquinolone in severely ill patients with pyelonephritis because of the increasing potential for resistance.
  • Imaging studies are only necessary in patients with pyelonephritis and fever for more than 72 hours, persistent bacteremia, sepsis, known nephrolithiasis, or when complications are suspected.
  • Relapsed urinary tract infection (UTI) occurs with the same organism within 2 weeks of completing antimicrobial therapy and can be treated with 7 to 10 days of the same antibiotic that was initially prescribed.
  • Reinfection, the most common type of recurrent UTI, is generally caused by bacteria separate from the original infection, presents more than 2 weeks after treatment of the previous infection, and is treated with standard first-line antimicrobial agents.
  • Daily prophylactic antimicrobial therapy is an option in women who have had three or more UTIs in the previous 12 months or two or more in the previous 6 months; other options include postcoital antimicrobial prophylaxis with one self-administered dose of nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, or cephalexin.
  • Pyuria accompanying asymptomatic bacteriuria is not an indication for urine culture or antimicrobial treatment.
  • Treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria is indicated in pregnant persons and in patients scheduled to undergo an invasive procedure involving the urinary tract.

index.title: Mycobacterium tuberculosis Infection
index.keyPoints:
• Most Mycobacterium tuberculosis infections in the United States occur in foreign-born persons; however, others at high risk include those with alcohol use disorder, socioeconomically disadvantaged persons, persons without housing, persons who inject drugs, persons who are incarcerated, persons living in shelters, persons with HIV, and older adults.
  • Most persons infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis have latent infection and are asymptomatic and not contagious.
  • Clinical manifestations of active tuberculosis include fever, night sweats, weight loss, productive cough (occasionally blood tinged), anorexia, malaise, and pleuritic chest pain.
  • In patients who are immunosuppressed, tuberculosis infection may spread hematogenously, resulting in widely disseminated progressive tuberculosis, which can result in a systemic inflammatory response syndrome, septic shock, and ultimately death if not treated early.
  • Screening for latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) is recommended in persons born in or with previous residence in countries with high tuberculosis prevalence, persons who have lived in congregate settings, immunocompromised patients, patients receiving tumor necrosis factor α inhibitor medications, and patients with a known tuberculosis exposure.
  • An interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) is preferred to tuberculin skin testing (TST) for Mycobacterium tuberculosis for those with a low or intermediate risk of disease progression, with a history of bacille Calmette-Guérin vaccination, or who are unlikely to return to have their TST result interpreted.
  • LTBI is diagnosed when an asymptomatic patient has a positive TST or IGRA result with no clinical or radiographic manifestations of active tuberculosis.
  • Neither IGRA nor TST should be used to diagnose active tuberculosis; these tests can be negative in patients with active tuberculosis.
  • The classic radiographic finding in pulmonary tuberculosis is upper lobe disease with air space disease and cavities; however, any radiographic pattern can be seen.
  • Patients suspected of having active pulmonary tuberculosis should have acid-fast bacilli smear microscopy of three serial respiratory specimens obtained at least 8 hours apart, with one sample being an early morning specimen.
  • The gold standard for the diagnosis of active Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection remains the mycobacterial culture.
  • Patients with suspected active tuberculosis should undergo diagnostic nucleic acid amplification testing.
  • If signs of extrapulmonary tuberculosis infection are present, samples from those areas should be obtained and sent for acid-fast bacilli staining, mycobacterial culture, and histopathology.
  • All patients with latent tuberculosis should be screened for HIV infection.
  • Preferred treatment regimens for latent tuberculosis infection include isoniazid plus rifapentine once weekly for 3 months, rifampin daily for 4 months, or isoniazid plus rifampin daily for 3 months.
  • Pyridoxine is recommended in patients who will receive isoniazid and are at risk for peripheral neuropathy.
  • For patients with drug-susceptible active pulmonary tuberculosis, guidelines recommend a 6-month daily treatment course (four-drug regimen for 2 months, then a continuation phase of isoniazid plus rifampin, usually for 4 months) or a 4-month daily regimen (four drugs for 8 weeks followed by three drugs for 9 weeks, including moxifloxacin) in select patients.
  • Before initiating treatment with a biologic agent or Janus kinase inhibitor, all patients should be screened for active or latent tuberculosis; those diagnosed should receive tuberculosis treatment to reduce the risk of reactivation and death from disseminated disease.
  • Guidelines for determining a patient with tuberculosis is no longer contagious include appropriate antimicrobial therapy for at least 2 weeks, clinical improvement, and three negative sputum smears collected at least 8 hours apart.

index.title: Nontuberculous Mycobacterial Infections
index.keyPoints:
• Pulmonary disease caused by nontuberculous mycobacteria is most often diagnosed in older adults; the most common species are Mycobacterium avium complex, Mycobacterium kansasii, and Mycobacterium abscessus.
  • Diagnosis of nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease requires fulfillment of clinical, radiologic, and microbiologic criteria; treatment consists of multiple antibiotics administered for at least 1 year.
  • Skin and soft tissue infections caused by nontuberculous mycobacteria, such as Mycobacterium chelonae, Mycobacterium fortuitum, and M. abscessus, usually result from trauma.
  • Mycobacterium marinum is widely found in aquatic environments, and skin infections are associated with exposure to contaminated fish tanks or swimming pools.

index.title: Fungal Infections
index.keyPoints:
• Only approximately 40% to 70% of patients with invasive candidal infection have positive blood culture results; therefore, recognizing risk factors of candidiasis is essential to avoid delays in initiating effective antifungal therapy.
  • The isolation of Candida in blood cultures should never be considered a contaminant; however, Candida species isolated from the respiratory or urinary tract usually represents colonization.
  • Initial empiric management of candidemia and invasive candidiasis should include an echinocandin and intravascular device removal (if possible); patients with central nervous system and eye infections should be treated with an amphotericin B preparation or an azole, if susceptible.
  • The most common manifestation of invasive aspergillosis is pulmonary infection, but sinusitis, brain abscess, and disseminated infection may also occur.
  • Tissue biopsy is frequently necessary to establish a definitive diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis; however, chest CT, serum galactomannan and 1,3 β-d-glucan assays; serum polymerase chain reaction; and galactomannan assay and polymerase chain reaction of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid results suggest the diagnosis in patients at high risk for infection.
  • First-line treatment of invasive aspergillosis is either a mold-active triazole, such as voriconazole, or combination therapy with a mold-active triazole plus an echinocandin.
  • Cryptococcal infection most commonly manifests as subacute meningitis.
  • Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis and documentation of the CSF opening pressure are necessary in suspected cryptococcal meningitis; CSF and serum cryptococcal antigen are highly sensitive for identifying infection.
  • Amphotericin B plus flucytosine is effective induction therapy in most patients with cryptococcal meningitis and should be followed by fluconazole consolidation and maintenance therapy.
  • Cryptococcal meningitis often causes elevated intracranial pressure, and CSF removal reduces morbidity and mortality.
  • Serial cryptococcal antigen testing is not recommended for determining microbiologic cure or duration of treatment in patients with cryptococcal meningitis.
  • Acute pulmonary histoplasmosis may initially be mistaken for community-acquired pneumonia but does not respond to antibiotic therapy.
  • In immunocompetent patients, mild histoplasmosis often resolves without treatment, but antifungal therapy should be considered for immunocompromised patients and those with prolonged symptoms; treatment is recommended in severe or disseminated disease.
  • Itraconazole is the antifungal agent of choice for most patients with histoplasmosis; liposomal amphotericin B should be used initially for patients with severe respiratory and disseminated infection.
  • Coccidioidomycosis should be suspected in endemic areas; the most common symptomatic clinical presentation is pneumonia.
  • Serologic testing for Coccidioides antibodies is recommended for initial evaluation in patients with suspected coccidioidomycosis, but results may be negative in early infection.
  • Immunocompetent patients with mild to moderate Coccidioides pulmonary infection generally do not require treatment; fluconazole is first-line treatment for disseminated or severe coccidioidomycosis.
  • Pneumonia is the most common clinical presentation of blastomycosis, which is endemic along the Mississippi and Ohio River valleys.
  • The preferred treatment for mild to moderate blastomycosis is itraconazole, with liposomal amphotericin B used for central nervous system, severe pulmonary, and disseminated infections.
  • Sporotrichosis is an infection of cutaneous and lymphocutaneous tissues usually caused by direct contact with plants; extracutaneous infection can occur in immunocompromised persons.
  • Itraconazole is the preferred treatment for cutaneous and lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis.
  • Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical manifestation of mucormycosis.
  • Diagnosing mucormycosis relies on a high index of suspicion in a host with appropriate risk factors and evidence of tissue invasion.
  • Treatment of mucormycosis requires urgent, extensive surgical removal of affected tissue, reversal of any predisposing conditions, and liposomal amphotericin B.

index.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections
index.keyPoints:
• Strategies to decrease the risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) include behavioral risk reduction strategies, HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis when appropriate, and doxycycline postexposure prophylaxis when appropriate.
  • Doxycycline postexposure prophylaxis is recommended for men who have sex with men and for transgender women who have had at least one bacterial STI in the preceding 12 months.
  • Screening for Chlamydia trachomatis infection is recommended for women younger than 25 years and for women 25 years and older with risk factors.
  • Men who have sex with men should be screened at least yearly for urethral and rectal C. trachomatis infection if those sites of contact are exposed.
  • Nucleic acid amplification testing is the preferred screening and diagnostic method for C. trachomatis infection.
  • The preferred treatment of C. trachomatis cervicitis, urethritis, and proctitis is doxycycline; pregnant patients should receive azithromycin.
  • Test of cure is not recommended in patients with C. trachomatis infection except in pregnancy, when treatment nonadherence is a concern, with persistent symptoms, and when alternative regimens are used; however, because reinfection is common, patients should be retested for reinfection 3 months after treatment or at their next medical visit.
  • Screening for Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection is recommended for women younger than 25 years and for women 25 years and older with risk factors.
  • Pharyngeal, urethral, and rectal sites should be tested for N. gonorrhoeae infection at least yearly in men who have sex with men if those sites of contact are exposed.
  • Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) is the preferred screening and diagnostic test for N. gonorrhoeae infection.
  • Parenteral ceftriaxone is the preferred treatment of uncomplicated N. gonorrhoeae infection.
  • Test of cure with NAAT and culture is recommended 2 weeks after therapy in patients with N. gonorrhoeae pharyngeal infection; if NAAT is positive, confirmatory culture should be performed, if possible, before retreatment.
  • Testing for Mycoplasma genitalium infection should be performed with nucleic acid amplification testing in men with recurrent nongonococcal urethritis and in women with recurrent cervicitis or with pelvic inflammatory disease.
  • Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are the primary causative organisms in cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), urethritis, and anorectal infections, although other organisms may also be implicated.
  • The two major diagnostic criteria of cervicitis are visualization of mucopurulent discharge from the cervical os or on a swab obtained from the endocervical canal or eliciting bleeding by passing a swab into the cervical os.
  • Uterine tenderness, adnexal tenderness, or cervical motion tenderness is sufficient to make a clinical diagnosis of PID, especially if accompanied by mucopurulent cervical discharge.
  • N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis are likely causes of epididymitis in younger, sexually active men; epididymitis in older men or men who practice insertive anal intercourse may also be caused by enteric gram-negative organisms such as Escherichia coli.
  • Most states have provisions for providing empiric antibiotic therapy prescriptions for sexual partners (expedited partner therapy).
  • In primary infection, herpes simplex virus and its subtype should be confirmed by nucleic acid amplification testing using a swab obtained from the ulcer or lesion.
  • Natural disease history, mode of transmission, perinatal transmission risk, and strategies to reduce viral shedding, and therefore transmission to a seronegative sexual partner, should be discussed with all patients with genital herpes simplex virus infections.
  • Primary syphilis presents as a painless genital ulcer (chancre) with a raised regular border that demonstrates firm induration on palpation; lesions heal spontaneously in 3 to 6 weeks even without treatment.
  • The most common manifestation of secondary syphilis is rash, with characteristic involvement of the palms and soles; in intertriginous areas, papules may coalesce to form condyloma lata, and mucous patches may occur in the oral cavity and moist genital regions and are highly infectious.
  • Secondary and tertiary syphilis diagnosis relies on serologic testing; patients with a positive enzyme immunoassay result and positive rapid plasma reagin or Venereal Disease Research Lab test result, or with a reactive additional specific treponemal test if the rapid plasma reagin test is negative, and no history of syphilis treatment should be offered treatment for syphilis of unknown duration.
  • Nononcogenic types of human papillomavirus are responsible for most genital warts, which often resolve without therapy.

index.title: Fever of Unknown Origin
index.keyPoints:
• Fever of unknown origin (FUO) is categorized as classic, health care–associated, immunodeficiency-related, and travel-associated.
  • In patients with FUO, a careful history and physical examination should be performed, including past procedures or surgeries, presence of foreign bodies or implants, immunosuppression, travel, animal or other exposures, dietary habits, and medications.
  • A definitive diagnosis is lacking in up to 50% of patients with FUO despite extensive evaluation, but duration of more than 1 year is unlikely to be caused by infection or malignancy.

index.title: Bioterrorism
index.keyPoints:
• Any case of inhalational anthrax should be considered potential bioterrorism.
  • Patients with inhalational anthrax infection experience malaise, myalgia, fever, cough, dyspnea, and substernal chest discomfort; radiographic imaging reveals a widened mediastinum.
  • Treatment of anthrax is based on the presence or absence of systemic disease, with or without meningitis; postexposure prophylaxis includes a fluoroquinolone or doxycycline in addition to vaccination.
  • Smallpox viremia results in fever and systemic symptoms, followed by lesions on the oral mucosa and face, and then spreading to the extremities and, to a lesser extent, the trunk; lesions evolve synchronously.
  • Smallpox treatment includes supportive care and tecovirimat; vaccination should be provided to close contacts.
  • Primary pneumonic plague occurs after Yersinia pestis exposure through infectious aerosols and person-to-person transmission through respiratory droplets, which are likely scenarios for bioterrorism.
  • Asymptomatic persons exposed to aerosolized Y. pestis and close contacts of infected patients warrant postexposure prophylaxis with ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, or doxycycline.
  • Botulism features include cranial nerve palsies and symmetric descending flaccid paralysis with prominent bulbar signs (diplopia, dysarthria, dysphonia, and dysphagia), which may progress to respiratory failure.
  • Botulism treatment includes supportive care and early administration of antitoxin, although treatment will not reverse existent paralysis.
  • Patients with tularemia experience abrupt onset of fever and respiratory symptoms, and chest radiographs demonstrate infiltrates, hilar lymphadenopathy, and pleural effusions.
  • Tularemia is treated with streptomycin or gentamicin for 7 to 14 days for severe disease or doxycycline or ciprofloxacin for 14 days for nonsevere disease.
  • Symptoms of viral hemorrhagic fever include fever, headache, myalgia, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and unexplained bleeding and bruising appearing 2 to 21 days after exposure; disease progression results in hemorrhagic diathesis, shock, and multiorgan failure.

index.title: Travel Medicine
index.keyPoints:
• Malaria is the most common cause of febrile illness in returning travelers; symptoms include fever, headache, myalgia, and gastrointestinal symptoms.
  • Malarial symptom onset shortly after returning from travel to endemic zones and a high level of parasitemia should raise suspicion for Plasmodium falciparum infection, which can result in severe disease.
  • Identification of malarial parasites on the peripheral blood smear is diagnostic.
  • Malarial chemoprophylaxis and treatment depend on drug resistance patterns and individual contraindications to specific medications.
  • Enteric fever commonly presents with fever, headache, arthralgia, myalgia, pharyngitis, anorexia, abdominal pain with diarrhea or constipation, and pulse-temperature dissociation; patients may have blanching, salmon-colored macules (rose spots).
  • Fluoroquinolones should not be used as empiric therapy for enteric fever because of resistance; ceftriaxone, azithromycin, or a carbapenem are appropriate, depending on the region where the infection was acquired.
  • Antimicrobial prophylaxis for travelers' diarrhea is generally not recommended.
  • Fluid replacement is the mainstay of treatment for travelers' diarrhea; antimicrobial therapy (e.g., azithromycin, rifaximin, or rifamycin) is recommended only in severe disease; rifamycin and rifaximin should not be used if fever or bloody diarrhea is present.
  • Dengue fever typically presents with acute febrile illness, frontal headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, and arthralgia, with or without spontaneous bleeding; gastrointestinal or respiratory symptoms may predominate, and severe lumbosacral pain is characteristic.
  • Symptoms of chikungunya resemble dengue fever, including abrupt fever and severe bilateral and symmetrical polyarthralgia, often involving the hands and feet; a maculopapular rash on the limbs and trunk is common.
  • Of most concern in Zika virus infection is the risk to fetal development in infected pregnant persons; those who are pregnant or planning to conceive should consult the CDC website when considering travel.
  • Treatment of dengue fever, chikungunya, and Zika virus infections is supportive.
  • Hepatitis A immunity develops within 4 weeks of vaccination; vaccination is recommended for persons traveling to countries with high or intermediate endemicity and those who are not already immune.
  • Hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for all unvaccinated persons younger than 60 years (regardless of travel plans) and for those 60 years of age and older traveling to areas where hepatitis B virus is prevalent or who are at high risk for infection.
  • Rickettsial infections occur worldwide, with clinical presentation including fever, headache, malaise, conjunctivitis, and pharyngitis often accompanied by a maculopapular, vesicular, or petechial rash.
  • The treatment of choice for all rickettsial infections is doxycycline for at least 5 to 7 days.
  • Symptoms of brucellosis include fever, myalgia, arthralgia, fatigue, headache, and night sweats; focal infection may involve the central nervous system and osteoarticular, cardiovascular, and genitourinary systems.
  • The treatment of choice for uncomplicated brucellosis is doxycycline plus either rifampin or gentamicin; neurobrucellosis treatment requires several months of combined ceftriaxone, doxycycline, and rifampin.
  • Japanese encephalitis is the most prevalent cause of vaccine-preventable infectious encephalitis throughout most of Asia and parts of the western Pacific; a two-dose inactivated vaccine is recommended for travelers to endemic areas.
  • Tick-borne encephalitis is transmitted by the Ixodes tick; persons traveling to endemic areas between April and November who will be engaging in recreational activities in woodland habitats or whose occupation puts them at high risk for exposure should consider vaccination.
  • Vaccination with the live-attenuated yellow fever vaccine is recommended for travelers to endemic areas of Africa and South America.

index.title: Infectious Gastrointestinal Syndromes
index.keyPoints:
• Patients with dysentery (mucoid or bloody diarrhea, fever, abdominal cramping, tenesmus) or suspected sepsis and those who are immunocompromised or require hospitalization should have microbiologic assessment of their stool to guide antimicrobial use.
  • Most healthy patients with watery diarrhea of less than 3 days' duration can be treated with supportive care and no diagnostic assessment; when the illness is debilitating and associated with travel, antibiotic therapy with a fluoroquinolone, azithromycin, rifamycin, or rifaximin is recommended.
  • Patients with dysentery should undergo microbiologic assessment; those with severe, debilitating dysentery and fever should also receive empiric azithromycin treatment.
  • Antimotility agents, such as loperamide, are generally discouraged in patients with inflammatory diarrhea or Clostridioides difficile–associated infection.
  • Campylobacter-associated diarrhea usually resolves spontaneously; azithromycin is generally the preferred empiric treatment for those who have severe disease or are immunocompromised.
  • In patients with Shigella infection, treatment with an antibiotic agent, such as ciprofloxacin, azithromycin, or ceftriaxone, is recommended for persons with severe illness and those who are immunocompromised; antibiotic susceptibilities should be obtained.
  • Nontyphoidal Salmonella serotypes are the most common bacterial cause of foodborne illness in the United States; diagnosis is made by stool culture or molecular testing, and the illness is usually self-limited, although bacteremia with extraintestinal infection may occur.
  • Most uncomplicated Salmonella infections in adults younger than 50 years are self-limited and require only supportive care; when empiric treatment is indicated for those with more severe or invasive disease, fluoroquinolones (such as ciprofloxacin) are most often used.
  • Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli infection is usually a self-limiting illness that resolves without treatment after approximately 4 days; hydration and empiric antibiotic therapy with fluoroquinolones, azithromycin, or rifaximin are recommended in travelers when symptoms restrict activities.
  • Enterohemorrhagic E. coli strains produce a Shiga toxin that can cause hemorrhagic colitis; treatment is primarily supportive because antibiotics and antimotility agents may increase the risk of developing hemolytic uremic syndrome and do not appear to shorten infection duration.
  • Yersinia enterocolitica is the most common pathogen causing Yersinia-related diarrheal illness, usually after ingestion of contaminated food, particularly undercooked pork; the diagnosis is confirmed by molecular testing of stool or by culture of stool, blood, a throat swab, or infected tissue.
  • When treatment of Yersinia-related gastrointestinal illness is indicated, a fluoroquinolone (such as ciprofloxacin) is recommended; if disease is severe, intravenous ceftriaxone plus gentamicin is used.
  • Vibrio parahaemolyticus can cause septicemia and necrotizing skin infections in patients who have chronic liver disease, iron overload states, or diabetes.
  • Severe noninvasive V. parahaemolyticus gastrointestinal illness is usually treated with doxycycline; patients with septicemia require combination therapy, typically with doxycycline plus ceftriaxone.
  • Clostridioides difficile is the leading cause of hospital-acquired infectious diarrhea; antibiotic stewardship is paramount in reducing incidence of infection, and handwashing with soap and water is important to eliminate spores.
  • Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) for C. difficile toxin genes is rapid, sensitive, and specific if strict stool submission criteria are met; enzyme immunoassay for glutamate dehydrogenase plus toxin (discordant results require NAAT) or NAAT plus toxin should be performed in those institutional settings not adherent to the specified criteria for stool submission.
  • Treatment of an initial C. difficile infection is dictated by disease severity, with nonsevere and severe disease treated with oral fidaxomicin (preferred) or vancomycin and fulminant disease treated with higher-dose oral or nasogastric vancomycin, intravenous metronidazole, and, when ileus is present, vancomycin enema; patients with fulminant disease warrant surgical evaluation.
  • Noroviruses are the most common cause of gastroenteritis in the United States; viral shedding persists up to 2 weeks after symptom resolution, which contributes to high infectivity.
  • Patients infected with norovirus usually have self-limited watery diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and fever; treatment is supportive.
  • Immunoassays for antigen detection and molecular testing of stool are more sensitive than stool microscopy for confirming Giardia duodenalis infection.
  • In symptomatic patients infected with G. duodenalis, treatment with tinidazole, nitazoxanide, or metronidazole is recommended.
  • Postinfection lactose intolerance or irritable bowel syndrome may be mistaken for recurrent or resistant Giardia infection.
  • Municipal water supplies and swimming pools can be a source of Cryptosporidium infection.
  • Microscopic visualization of oocysts in stool using modified acid-fast staining, enzyme immunoassay or direct immunofluorescent antibody testing, or molecular testing can provide a diagnosis of Cryptosporidium infection.
  • Treatment of Cryptosporidium infection consists of supportive care for most immunocompetent persons or nitazoxanide for severe or prolonged infection; antiretroviral therapy to restore immune function is most effective in resolving infection in HIV-infected patients.
  • Treatment is recommended for all patients with amebiasis; for symptomatic patients, metronidazole or tinidazole is recommended initially for parasitic clearance followed by an intraluminal amebicide (paromomycin) for cyst clearance, and for asymptomatic patients, an intraluminal agent for eradication of cysts is recommended.
  • Cyclospora infection is typically diagnosed microscopically by visualization of oocysts with modified acid-fast staining, microscopy with ultraviolet fluorescence, or molecular testing.
  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is recommended for treatment of symptomatic Cyclospora infection.

index.title: Infections in Transplant Recipients
index.keyPoints:
• Glucocorticoid-sparing or minimizing regimens (with tacrolimus, cyclosporine, or sirolimus) are increasingly used for transplant recipients to avoid long-term glucocorticoid therapy toxicity; drug interactions are common with these agents, and monitoring is important to balance immunosuppression with toxicity.
  • Infection may occur at any time after transplantation but is most likely to occur during periods of highest immunosuppression; the risk for specific organisms varies depending on the time after transplantation.
  • Cytomegalovirus is the most significant viral infection after transplantation and may present with fever and cytopenias or with organ disease, including pneumonitis, encephalitis, hepatitis, esophagitis, and colitis.
  • Epstein-Barr virus is strongly associated with posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder, which should be suspected in any patient in the middle or late posttransplant period presenting with lymphadenopathy or an extranodal mass, often with fever.
  • Bacterial infections are common in the early period after solid organ transplantation and following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT); encapsulated bacterial infections such as Streptococcus pneumoniae remain common even late after HSCT because of impaired humoral immunity.
  • Without prophylaxis, transplant recipients are at high risk for Pneumocystis pneumonia, which presents as an acute and severe pneumonitis.
  • Prophylaxis and immunization are essential in decreasing the risk of posttransplant infections; however, live virus vaccines should be avoided after solid organ transplantation and for at least 2 years after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

index.title: Health Care–Associated Infections
index.keyPoints:
• Hand hygiene is the foundation of infection prevention; the World Health Organization has identified five key hand hygiene moments (before touching a patient, before clean or aseptic procedures, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching patient surroundings).
  • Standard precautions should be practiced universally to protect HCP from exposure to pathogens.
  • After needlestick injury, the source patient should be assessed for hepatitis B and C and HIV, and exposed health care personnel should seek immediate baseline testing and potential treatment for HIV and hepatitis B and C depending on their immune status.
  • Key prevention strategies for CAUTI include limiting urinary catheter use to appropriate indications and considering other options associated with lower infection risk when urine collection is necessary.
  • Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) is diagnosed in patients with an indwelling urethral or suprapubic catheter (or catheter removal within 48 hours before symptom onset) or with intermittent catheterization who have signs and symptoms compatible with urinary tract infection, one or more bacterial species in a urine specimen (≥10^3 colony-forming units/mL), and no other identifiable infection source.
  • Catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria is common and generally does not require treatment.
  • CAUTI management includes catheter removal, with replacement only if the catheter is still necessary, and antimicrobial treatment.
  • Candiduria in a patient with a catheter frequently represents colonization and rarely requires treatment.
  • Most surgical site infections (SSIs) occur within 30 days after surgery or within 90 days after surgery with implants.
  • Optimizing modifiable risk factors before surgery (e.g., hyperglycemia control, immunosuppressive agent reduction, tobacco cessation, weight loss) can help prevent SSIs.
  • Infected tissue or drainage should be obtained for culture in SSIs; deep-tissue or operative cultures are preferred to superficial wound swab cultures, which are likely to reflect skin or wound colonization rather than the causative pathogen.
  • SSI treatment requires debridement of necrotic tissue, drainage of abscesses or infected fluid, and specific antimicrobial therapy for organ or deep-space and deep incisional infections; superficial incisional infections can usually be managed with oral antibiotics without tissue debridement.
  • A central line–associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) should be suspected when a patient with a central venous catheter has bacteremia not resulting from infection at another site.
  • In patients with a CLABSI, infected central venous catheters should be removed and guidewire exchange should be avoided.
  • Antimicrobial therapy duration in most uncomplicated non–Staphylococcus aureus central line–associated bloodstream infections is 7 to 14 days; S. aureus infection is usually treated for at least 4 weeks, but shorter course therapy may be considered in select patients.
  • In patients receiving mechanical ventilation, the head of the bed should be elevated 30° to 45°; a supine position, particularly in patients receiving enteral nutrition, increases the risk for developing VAP
  • The diagnoses of hospital-acquired (HAP) and ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) are suggested by a new lung infiltrate on imaging plus clinical findings, including new-onset fever, leukocytosis or leukopenia, purulent sputum, and decline in oxygenation.
  • Empiric HAP and VAP regimens should include coverage for Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and other gram-negative bacilli; an agent active against methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) should be included for patients with MRSA risk factors or where MRSA prevalence exceeds 10% (or is unknown) unless a MRSA nasal swab is negative.
  • Multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs) are most prevalent in health care settings (highest incidence in long-term acute care hospitals) but are also observed in the community.
  • Limiting emergence and transmission of MDROs in health care settings requires full adherence to hand hygiene protocols, contact precautions, cleaning and disinfecting of the environment and equipment, and judicious use of antimicrobial agents.

index.title: HIV/AIDS
index.keyPoints:
• It is recommended that all adults younger than 65 years be tested for HIV infection at least once; persons with higher risk of HIV exposure should undergo repeat testing at least annually.
  • The fourth-generation HIV antigen/antibody test can identify HIV as early as 2 weeks after infection.
  • All persons with HIV should receive the COVID-19 vaccine (multiple doses may be required), pneumococcal vaccine(s), hepatitis A and B vaccine series (in those not already infected or immune), and quadrivalent meningococcal vaccine; the recombinant zoster vaccine should be given to individuals 19 years and older.
  • Influenza, tetanus-diphtheria-pertussis, and human papillomavirus vaccines are indicated in patients with HIV as they are for the general population.
  • Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccines can be given to patients with HIV infection as long as the CD4 cell count is at least 200/µL and 15% or more.
  • Opportunistic infection prophylaxis, including that against Pneumocystis jirovecii and Toxoplasma gondii, depends on the CD4 cell count in patients with HIV infection.
  • All persons with HIV infection should receive antiretroviral therapy (ART) regardless of CD4 cell count; ART should be started as soon as possible, ideally within 1 week of diagnosis.
  • Recommended initial antiretroviral regimens for persons with HIV include the use of two or three drugs from two different classes, preferably including an integrase strand transfer inhibitor.
  • Viral resistance testing should be performed at HIV diagnosis to ensure selection of a fully active regimen but should not delay three-drug ART initiation; testing should be repeated if the viral load increases during therapy.
  • Pregnant patients should promptly initiate or continue receiving HIV treatment without interruption.
  • Glucose and lipid profile should be checked at entry into HIV care and after initiating or changing antiretroviral therapy (ART); hemoglobin A~1c should not be used for the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus in patients taking ART.
  • Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) is associated with increased risks of nephrotoxicity and worsening of bone mineral density; tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) should be used preferentially over TDF in patients with or at risk for bone or kidney disease.
  • Persons coinfected with HIV and hepatitis B virus should be treated with an antiretroviral regimen that includes TDF or TAF plus emtricitabine or lamivudine; persons with HIV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) should receive HCV direct-acting antiviral treatment.
  • Rates of cardiovascular disease, including myocardial infarction and stroke, are higher in persons with HIV infection.
  • Statin therapy should be initiated in persons aged 40 to 75 years with HIV infection, particularly in patients with a 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk estimate of 5% or more.
  • HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders may manifest as impaired memory, attention, executive function, and information processing speed; antiretroviral therapy is the main treatment for HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders.
  • Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome is caused by an inflammatory response to a pre-existing infectious process; it usually occurs within 1 week to a few months of initiating effective antiretroviral therapy and presents with various infections and noninfectious complications.
  • Oral candidiasis usually presents as thrush and can be treated with a 1- to 2-week course of oral fluconazole; retrosternal burning or odynophagia suggests esophageal disease, which requires 2 to 3 weeks of systemic treatment.
  • Tuberculosis treatment in patients with HIV infection may be complicated by immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, and antiretroviral therapy initiation should be delayed to prevent this occurrence.
  • Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia usually presents as a subacute illness with fever, dyspnea, and dry cough; although chest radiographs may show bilateral interstitial infiltrates, a normal chest radiograph does not exclude the diagnosis.
  • Cryptococcus infection presents as subacute meningitis; treatment in patients with HIV includes antifungal therapy and attention to increased intracranial pressure.
  • Toxoplasma gondii infection manifests as a focal encephalitis; MRI is more sensitive than CT in revealing characteristic ring-enhancing lesions.
  • Mycobacterium avium complex infection often presents as disseminated disease in patients with CD4 cell counts less than 50/µL; symptoms and signs include fever, night sweats, weight loss, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and cytopenias.
  • Retinitis is the most common cytomegalovirus-associated end-organ disease in persons with HIV.
  • AIDS-associated malignancies are often linked to coinfection with other oncogenic viruses, including non-Hodgkin lymphoma (associated with Epstein-Barr virus), Kaposi sarcoma (associated with human herpesvirus type 8), and invasive cervical carcinoma (associated with human papillomavirus).
  • Human papillomavirus–related malignancies are significantly increased in patients infected with HIV, including cervical and anal cancers, and regular guideline-based screening is important.
  • In patients with a hematologic abnormality as the initial sign of HIV infection, antiretroviral therapy often reverses the cytopenia.
  • Reducing viral load to an undetectable level reduces the rate of HIV transmission from a sexual partner to close to zero; “Undetectable = Untransmissible” (“U = U”).
  • Postexposure prophylaxis with a three-drug regimen (tenofovir disoproxil fumarate [TDF] or tenofovir alafenamide [TAF] plus emtricitabine or lamivudine plus bictegravir or dolutegravir) should be started as soon as possible after HIV exposure; it is not recommended if more than 72 hours have passed.
  • Pre-exposure prophylaxis with oral tenofovir (TDF or TAF) and emtricitabine is recommended in persons at high risk for exposure to HIV to reduce the risk of infection; parenteral long-acting cabotegravir or lenacapavir are options for prevention of HIV acquisition from sexual transmission.

index.title: Viral Infections
index.keyPoints:
• Older adults, pregnant and postpartum persons, and patients with chronic medical conditions (especially chronic lung disease, immunocompromise, and BMI ≥40) are at higher risk for severe primary influenza, superimposed bacterial pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus, and death.
  • The Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends using polymerase chain reaction testing over rapid antigen tests for the diagnosis of influenza if testing is likely to change management.
  • Widespread influenza vaccination is the most important preventive intervention; all persons aged 6 months or older without contraindications and all health care personnel should be vaccinated.
  • Antiviral therapy should be initiated as soon as possible for adults with documented or suspected influenza who are hospitalized and for outpatients with severe or progressive illness regardless of illness duration; treatment should be initiated as soon as possible for all other patients at high risk of influenza-related complications.
  • Vaccination, masking, handwashing, and physical and social distancing are effective preventive tools for COVID-19.
  • Patients with suspected COVID-19 should be tested; nucleic acid amplification testing has superior sensitivity, but antigen tests are more convenient, less costly, and have a shorter turnaround time.
  • The mainstay of therapy for inpatients with COVID-19 who are not critically ill is intravenous remdesivir for 5 days; patients requiring oxygen therapy should also receive glucocorticoids.
  • In outpatients with COVID-19 with risk factors for progression to severe disease, nirmatrelvir-ritonavir combination therapy is a recommended treatment.
  • Respiratory syncytial virus can cause severe lower respiratory tract infection in adults older than 60 years and those who are immunocompromised.
  • Pregnant individuals, adults aged 75 years or older, and adults aged 60 to 74 years who are at risk for severe disease are eligible for the respiratory syncytial virus vaccine.
  • Herpes simplex virus (HSV) type 1 infection typically causes painful, small vesicles on an erythematous base, transitioning to pustules and subsequent crusting of the lesions; HSV-2 is sexually transmitted and typically causes genital and rectal ulcers with or without proctitis.
  • HSV-1 and HSV-2 infections can be treated and suppressed with oral nucleoside analogues (acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir); intravenous acyclovir is used for severe mucocutaneous herpes, disseminated infections in immunosuppressed persons, esophagitis, and suspected HSV encephalitis.
  • The rash of primary varicella infection (chickenpox) commonly begins on the face and trunk, then spreads to the extremities and presents in various stages of development on any one part of the body (macules, papules, vesicles, and scabs).
  • Herpes zoster typically causes a painful vesicular rash that follows a dermatomal distribution that does not cross the midline; in immunosuppressed patients, herpes zoster can affect multiple dermatomes or present with disseminated disease.
  • Young patients with herpes zoster should be tested for HIV.
  • Antiviral therapy speeds recovery and decreases the severity and duration of neuropathic pain if begun within 72 hours of varicella-zoster rash onset.
  • Postexposure varicella vaccination is appropriate in immunocompetent persons, and varicella-zoster immune globulin should be used in immunocompromised adults and pregnant persons.
  • Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection, the primary cause of infectious mononucleosis, presents with fever, severe fatigue, exudative pharyngitis, cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly.
  • Heterophile antibodies have limited sensitivity (especially in the first week of illness) and specificity for EBV infection.
  • New or recent EBV infection is strongly suggested by the presence of anti-viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgM with or without anti-VCA IgG.
  • Reactivation of latent cytomegalovirus infection is more common in immunosuppressed persons; because cytomegalovirus can present in numerous ways, a high index of clinical suspicion is important.
  • Cytomegalovirus serologic assays have limited diagnostic utility because most adults are seropositive; however, they have a role in diagnosis of acute infection and are performed routinely in pretransplant evaluations to assess the risk of cytomegalovirus reactivation following transplantation and to determine appropriate prophylaxis.
  • Diagnosis of cytomegalovirus is confirmed with molecular tests of infected fluids, by demonstrating typical cytopathic “owl's-eye” intracellular inclusions on biopsy specimens, or by cytomegalovirus immunostaining of pathologic samples.
  • In immunocompromised patients, or in immunocompetent patients with severe cytomegalovirus infection, treatment involves intravenous ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir.
  • Mpox is transmitted by respiratory secretions, skin-to-skin contact, and fomites, so prevention focuses on avoiding skin-to-skin contact with infected persons; live-virus vaccines are available for persons at high risk.
  • Mpox usually presents with painful vesicular lesions that can sometimes become umbilicated; they commonly start in the anogenital region but can spread throughout the body.

index.title: Stewardship and Emerging Resistance
index.keyPoints:
• Avoiding unnecessary antibiotic use, simplifying unnecessary combination therapy, avoiding double anaerobic coverage, converting intravenous to oral agents, streamlining de-escalation, and minimizing therapy duration are important components of antimicrobial stewardship programs.
  • Minocycline has activity against multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia.
  • Oral fosfomycin achieves high concentrations in the urine, making it useful for treating uncomplicated cystitis caused by extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli.
  • Nephrotoxicity occurs in up to 50% of patients treated with colistin, although it is usually reversible.
  • Bone and joint infections are the primary infections treated with outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy (OPAT); other potentially OPAT-treatable infections include endocarditis, cardiac device infections, abdominal infections, skin and soft tissue infections, central nervous system infections, and antibiotic-resistant infections for which parenteral antibiotics are the only option (such as urinary tract infection).

index.title: Allergy and Immunology
index.keyPoints:
• All patients with anaphylaxis require referral to an allergist for identification of the cause and prevention of future episodes.
  • A tryptase level greater than 8 ng/mL that was not measured during or immediately after an episode of anaphylaxis should prompt evaluation for hereditary or clonal mast cell diseases.
  • In patients with anaphylaxis, medications and substances that may interfere with treatment (e.g., β-blockers, ACE inhibitors) or exacerbate anaphylaxis severity through direct mast cell activation (e.g., opioids, NSAIDs, alcohol) should be modified or discontinued if possible.
  • All patients with a history of anaphylaxis should be prescribed epinephrine and educated on its use.
  • Urticaria (also called hives) are characterized by well-demarcated, erythematous, pruritic plaques that appear rapidly and resolve within hours.
  • If urticarial lesions last longer than 24 hours or are accompanied by systemic symptoms (e.g., joint pain, fever), urticarial vasculitis should be considered.
  • In most cases of urticaria, the cause is never determined, and diagnostic evaluation is not recommended unless the history suggests a specific cause.
  • Nonsedating, long-acting antihistamines are the treatment of choice for urticaria; topical antihistamines are not effective and may cause allergic contact dermatitis.
  • Angioedema occurs through two main pathways: mast cell–mediated (presenting in isolation, with urticaria, or as part of the systemic reaction in anaphylaxis) and bradykinin-mediated (presenting in isolation without evidence of mast cell activation or urticaria).
  • ACE inhibitor–induced angioedema should be suspected in anyone with angioedema taking an ACE inhibitor, regardless of when the medication was started; ACE inhibitor–induced angioedema can recur for several months after discontinuation.
  • Food allergies are diagnosed through a detailed history and physical examination, skin prick testing, specific serum IgE levels, and (in some cases) a food elimination trial and/or food challenge.
  • A tick bite, usually from from Amblyomma americanum (the Lone Star tick), may cause sensitization to galactose-α-1,3-galactose (α-gal), which is found in mammalian meat; meat ingestion can subsequently result in anaphylaxis.
  • Extensive IgE or IgG immunoassays in the evaluation of a food allergy are not recommended and may result in inappropriate diagnoses.
  • In patients with food allergies, avoiding allergens is the mainstay of treatment.
  • Patients with a systemic allergic reaction to a Hymenoptera sting (anaphylaxis or widespread urticaria without anaphylaxis) should be supplied with epinephrine for autoinjection and be considered for venom immunotherapy.
  • Serum sickness and serum sickness–like reactions are associated with fever, arthralgia, and rash within 1 to 2 weeks of administration of an inciting medication, vaccine, or exposure; kidney dysfunction occurs in serum sickness but not serum sickness–like reactions.
  • The mainstay of treatment for serum sickness and serum sickness–like reaction is avoiding the offending agent; symptoms are self-limited and often resolve within a few weeks.
  • Patients with selective IgA deficiency may be asymptomatic, present with sinopulmonary or gastrointestinal tract infections, or rarely experience anaphylaxis to transfused blood products.
  • Patients with common variable immunodeficiency can experience recurrent infections and are at increased risk for noninfectious complications, including autoimmune disease, inflammatory bowel disease, granulomatous disease, bronchiectasis, and malignancy.
  • Live vaccines should be avoided in patients with common variable immunodeficiency.
  • Early component complement deficiency is associated with an increased rate of systemic lupus erythematosus and risk for infection with encapsulated organisms; terminal complement defects can result in recurrent Neisseria infections.
  • Any defect in the classical complement pathway will result in low total hemolytic complement (CH~50) level.

index.title: Ear, Nose, Mouth, and Throat Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• Evaluation of hearing loss includes otoscopic examination, Weber and Rinne tests, and referral for audiometry; laboratory testing and imaging are rarely required.
  • Presbycusis is the most common cause of sensorineural hearing loss.
  • Medications that can cause hearing loss include antibiotics (aminoglycosides, erythromycin, vancomycin), chemotherapeutic agents (cisplatin, carboplatin), loop diuretics, and NSAIDs.
  • Sudden sensorineural hearing loss requires urgent audiometry, MRI of the retrocochlear structures, and consideration of oral glucocorticoids.
  • Acoustic neuroma is characterized by progressive, unilateral, high-frequency, sensorineural hearing loss sometimes with concomitant unilateral tinnitus and disequilibrium; MRI is the diagnostic test of choice.
  • Most cases of tinnitus are caused by hearing loss.
  • Imaging is not needed in nonpulsatile bilateral tinnitus unless it is associated with focal neurologic findings or hearing loss that is asymmetric or sudden.
  • Acute otitis media is much less common in adults than children, and management may include initial observation for uncomplicated cases; if antibiotics are prescribed, amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanic acid is appropriate.
  • Otitis media with effusion (OME) is often mistaken for acute otitis media; OME is characterized by the presence of fluid in the middle ear without acute inflammation or signs of systemic illness.
  • Acute otitis externa (AOE) is diffuse inflammation of the external ear and is caused by a bacterial infection, most commonly Pseudomonas or Staphylococcus aureus.
  • In uncomplicated AOE, topical treatments including antibiotics, glucocorticoids, antiseptics (acetic acid), and combination therapies are first-line management.
  • Malignant otitis externa is characterized by severe otalgia with ear discharge, headache, and facial pain; imaging demonstrates bony involvement, and systemic antipseudomonal antibiotic therapy is required.
  • Anterior epistaxis can be managed with compression of the alae (lower one third of the nose) for at least 15 minutes.
  • If anterior epistaxis persists despite adequate compression, anterior rhinoscopy with nasal cautery or application of a topical agent (tranexamic acid or a vasoconstrictor such as oxymetazoline) to the bleeding site is indicated.
  • Posterior epistaxis may cause substantial blood loss; patients with persistent or recurrent bleeding not controlled by local measures and anterior packing should be evaluated by an otolaryngologist for consideration of arterial ligation or endovascular embolization.
  • Pertussis (whooping cough) is suggested by cough persisting for more than 2 weeks (often with posttussive emesis), severe cough paroxysms, or an inspiratory whooping sound.
  • Acute rhinosinusitis is usually caused by viruses, allergies, or irritants; antibiotics are ineffective and should not be used in most patients.
  • Diagnosis of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS) includes cardinal symptoms for at least 10 days or double worsening. After diagnosis of ABRS, a 3- to 5-day period of watchful waiting is recommended before starting antibiotics.
  • Chronic sinusitis is characterized by at least 12 weeks of nasal congestion with purulent drainage, diminished sense of smell, or facial pain or pressure; documentation of mucosal involvement by nasal endoscopy or imaging is necessary for diagnosis.
  • First-line treatment of allergic and nonallergic rhinitis consists of avoiding precipitating factors and intranasal glucocorticoids; intranasal ipratropium is useful in patients with rhinorrhea as their main symptom.
  • Patients with acute pharyngitis and fewer than three Centor criteria generally do not require testing or treatment for streptococcal pharyngitis.
  • Patients with acute pharyngitis and a Centor score of 3 or greater should be tested with a rapid streptococcal antigen detection test; those with a positive test result should be treated with penicillin or amoxicillin.
  • Throat culture for streptococcal pharyngitis is necessary only in patients at high risk for complications (e.g., immunocompromised state) with a high clinical suspicion but a negative rapid streptococcal antigen detection test result.
  • Suppurative complications of bacterial pharyngitis include peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess, and septic jugular thrombophlebitis; CT of the neck should be obtained immediately if these complications are suspected.
  • The revised Jones criteria assist in diagnosing acute rheumatic fever and encompass major criteria (carditis, arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules) and minor criteria (prolonged PR interval, arthralgia, fever, and elevated inflammatory markers).
  • Treatment of rheumatic fever includes elimination of group A streptococcal infection, supportive treatment of joint pain, and treatment of rheumatic heart disease.
  • All patients with rheumatic fever or rheumatic heart disease should receive secondary prophylaxis against recurrent infection; the duration of prophylaxis depends on patient age and disease severity.
  • Rheumatic heart disease is a long-term complication of acute rheumatic fever and most commonly affects the mitral and aortic valves.
