  • Treatment of epiglottitis consists of immediate parenteral antibiotic therapy and hospital admission with regular airway assessment.
  • Management of sialadenitis and sialolithiasis includes stimulating saliva production with warm compresses, sialagogues (sour candies or vitamin C lozenges), salivary gland massage, increased fluid intake, and proper oral hygiene.
  • Acute bacterial sialadenitis is characterized by acute pain and swelling of the affected salivary gland, fever, and purulent drainage from the salivary ducts; initial empiric antibiotics should include coverage for Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobes.
  • Nearly half of U.S. adults have periodontal disease, which is associated with increased risk for diabetes and cardiovascular disease; gingivitis is reversible with routine prevention (e.g., brushing teeth, flossing), periodic dental visits, and cleanings.
  • Necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis, formerly called Vincent angina, is characterized by halitosis, oral pain, and ulcerated and necrotic areas of the tonsils and gingiva that bleed if scraped; treatment includes oral antibiotics, twice-daily chlorhexidine rinses for 2 weeks, and debridement if severe.
  • Dental fractures are considered an emergency because a tooth becomes nonviable 1 hour after fracture; patients should seek immediate care from a dental professional.

index.title: Eye Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• Orbital cellulitis is characterized by pain, eyelid swelling, and erythema; it can be differentiated from preseptal cellulitis by the additional presence of proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and pain with eye movement as well as CT findings of orbital involvement.
  • Viral conjunctivitis is characterized by bilateral ocular irritation, watery discharge, crusting, and other symptoms of viral infection; treatment is supportive.
  • Most patients with bacterial conjunctivitis improve without antibiotics; however, antimicrobial therapy may be considered for immunocompromised individuals or those working in health care facilities and should be provided to contact lens wearers.
  • Patients with suspected bacterial conjunctivitis who wear contact lenses should be treated with a topical antibiotic with pseudomonal activity, such as a fluoroquinolone.
  • Allergic conjunctivitis is treated by removing the offending agent (if possible) and using topical antihistamines or mast cell inhibitors.
  • Keratitis is characterized by diminished vision and severe eye discomfort; corneal stromal infiltrates and ciliary flush may be present on examination.
  • Episcleritis is a self-limited inflammation of the episclera, whereas scleritis is a painful inflammatory disorder of the sclera that can threaten vision and is often associated with underlying inflammatory disorders, such as rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Endophthalmitis is an infection within the eye (including the aqueous humor, vitreous humor, retina, and optic nerve) that requires immediate referral to an ophthalmologist.
  • Blepharitis is eyelid inflammation; treatment involves eyelid hygiene (warm compresses, eyelid washing, and massage) and artificial tears.
  • Dry eye treatment includes artificial tears and lifestyle changes; punctal plugs and topical cyclosporine are sometimes necessary.
  • Patients with a corneal abrasion in the setting of contact lens use should be treated with topical antibiotics with antipseudomonal activity.
  • Vision loss in a patient with a corneal abrasion requires immediate ophthalmology referral.
  • Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is characterized by decreased aqueous flow with a normal iridocorneal angle; peripheral visual field loss is often the earliest symptom of POAG.
  • Patients with acute-onset angle-closure glaucoma present with severe eye pain, headache, nausea/vomiting, and visualizing halos around lights; iridotomy should be performed within 1 hour of symptom presentation.
  • Age-related macular degeneration is characterized by painless central vision loss, including difficulty with facial recognition, and by central scotoma; vision difficulties may be particularly evident in low-light settings.
  • Smoking is the most significant modifiable risk factor for age-related macular degeneration.
  • Optic neuritis, a demyelinating inflammation of the optic nerve that is most commonly due to multiple sclerosis, manifests as painful acute monocular vision loss that develops over hours to days.
  • First-line therapy for optic neuritis is high-dose intravenous glucocorticoids.
  • Retinal detachment presents as acute onset of unilateral flashing lights and floaters; it is an ocular emergency requiring immediate referral to an ophthalmologist.
  • Central retinal artery occlusion is an ocular emergency characterized by sudden, painless severe monocular vision loss, most commonly due to carotid artery atherosclerosis; management includes urgent ophthalmology referral and evaluation for causes of stroke.
  • Patients with central retinal vein occlusion typically present with painless, blurred monocular vision, whereas those with branch retinal vein occlusion may be asymptomatic or present with scotoma or visual field defects.

index.title: Urologic Conditions
index.keyPoints:
• Erectile dysfunction (ED) is a significant independent risk factor for coronary artery disease, and its presence should prompt cardiovascular risk assessment.
  • Laboratory evaluation of ED should include a morning total testosterone level and, if hypothyroidism is suspected, a serum thyroid-stimulating hormone test.
  • Nonpharmacologic treatment options for ED include lifestyle modifications, such as smoking cessation, exercise, and weight optimization; psychological counseling should be considered in patients with psychogenic ED.
  • Oral phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors are first-line medical therapy for ED but are contraindicated in patients taking nitrates.
  • First-line pharmacotherapy for premature ejaculation includes a daily selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, on-demand clomipramine, and topical penile anesthetics.
  • Patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) should undergo a comprehensive medication assessment and be asked about previous sexually transmitted infections, urethral trauma, urologic procedures, and lifestyle factors that can contribute to lower urinary tract symptoms.
  • The International Prostate Symptom Score is useful to objectively assess the severity of BPH symptoms and gauge the response to treatment.
  • BPH causing mild symptoms can be managed with lifestyle modifications and active surveillance.
  • Pharmacotherapy is recommended in patients with BPH who have bothersome moderate to severe symptoms; surgical treatment is indicated in those unresponsive to pharmacotherapy or who develop complications, such as urinary retention or gross hematuria.
  • α-Blockers are first-line pharmacotherapy for BPH; combination therapy with a 5α-reductase inhibitor may be more effective than either agent alone in patients with enlarged prostates.
  • α-Blockers such as tamsulosin should be withheld before cataract surgery to avoid floppy iris syndrome.
  • Testicular torsion presents as acute, unilateral, severe scrotal pain and swelling with an elevated testis on examination and absent cremasteric reflex; it is a surgical emergency.
  • Epididymitis and epididymo-orchitis present as unilateral scrotal pain of gradual onset over days; pain may be relieved with scrotal elevation and the normal cremasteric reflex is usually present.
  • Epididymitis and epididymo-orchitis are treated with ceftriaxone and doxycycline in patients with risk factors for sexually transmitted infections; otherwise, coverage for enteric gram-negative organisms is usually sufficient.
  • Viral orchitis occurs in 20% of men with mumps; it is characterized by bilateral testicular pain and swelling with accompanying parotitis and fever.
  • Asymptomatic hydroceles require no intervention; patients with bothersome symptoms may benefit from surgical excision of the hydrocele sac.
  • Varicoceles are usually treated with conservative measures (such as NSAIDs and scrotal support); surgical treatment is indicated for bothersome symptoms or testicular atrophy in patients who desire fertility.
  • Patients with suspected acute bacterial prostatitis should not undergo prostate massage because it may lead to bacteremia.
  • Oral ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are options for treating acute bacterial prostatitis; severely ill patients and those with suspected sepsis should be hospitalized and initially treated with parenteral antibiotics.
  • Antibiotic therapy for chronic bacterial prostatitis should be guided by urine culture results and continued for 4 to 6 weeks.
  • Although no clearly established first-line treatment exists for chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome without evidence of infection, α-blockers, NSAIDs, and daily tadalafil are recommended.
  • Inguinal hernias are most common among men, but femoral hernias, which incur a greater risk for strangulation, are more common among women.
  • In men, small, asymptomatic, or minimally symptomatic indirect and direct inguinal hernias may be observed or undergo surgical repair; significantly symptomatic inguinal hernias in men and all indirect and direct inguinal hernias in women should undergo surgical repair.
  • All femoral hernias should be surgically repaired.
  • Strangulation of a nonreducible hernia is a surgical emergency and should be suspected if a hernia is accompanied by significant tenderness, overlying erythema, or nausea and vomiting.
  • Urinary incontinence is a common condition affecting adults of all ages, including 33% of community-dwelling adults older than 65 years and 66% of nursing home residents.
  • Urinary incontinence is associated with reduced health-related quality of life, loss of independence, social isolation, and increased risk for falls and depression, especially among older patients.
  • Most causes of urinary incontinence can be diagnosed clinically without laboratory testing or imaging other than a urinalysis and postvoid residual testing in selected patients; urodynamic studies are required only for complex cases in which neurologic disease is suspected, and surgical intervention is being considered.
  • Nonpharmacologic therapy, including lifestyle modification and behavioral therapy, is the preferred treatment for all types of urinary incontinence.
  • Indwelling urinary catheters are not recommended for any type of incontinence.
  • First-line behavioral therapy for stress and mixed urinary incontinence is pelvic floor muscle training (Kegel exercises).
  • In patients with stress urinary incontinence, vaginal estrogen increases continence, but transdermal patches, implants, and systemic estrogens are not helpful.
  • Urge and mixed urinary incontinence may be treated with pharmacologic therapy, including anticholinergic and antimuscarinic agents, when symptoms persist despite behavioral therapy.
  • Acute urinary retention is more common in men, with benign prostatic hyperplasia the most common cause; acute urinary retention in women is rare.
  • Medications that may cause urinary retention include anticholinergics, α-adrenergic agonists, and opioids.
  • Acute urinary retention requires immediate management with catheterization to decompress the bladder.
  • Balanitis is often the result of poor hygiene and presents with pain, irritation, and erythema of the glans penis.
  • Complications of balanitis can include phimosis (inability to retract the foreskin) and paraphimosis (when the foreskin becomes stuck behind the glans penis, resulting in vascular and lymphatic constriction); inability to reduce paraphimosis is a urologic emergency.

index.title: Breast and Gynecologic Conditions
index.keyPoints:
• Mammography is the first test performed for a breast mass or suspected pathologic nipple discharge in most women aged 30 years or older and men aged 25 years or older.
  • Ultrasonography is the preferred method of evaluation of a breast mass or suspected pathologic nipple discharge in women younger than 30 years and men younger than 25 years.
  • In patients with a breast mass, imaging results are categorized using the Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System; biopsy is recommended for category 4 and 5 breast findings.
  • A suspicious breast mass should be evaluated with a biopsy even if imaging results are negative.
  • Cyclic breast pain tends to be diffuse and bilateral, often occurs in the premenstrual phase, and frequently resolves with onset of menstruation and conservative management.
  • Noncyclic breast pain is often caused by medication use, underlying breast disease, or stretching of the Cooper ligaments; patients with noncyclic focal breast pain should be evaluated with age-appropriate imaging.
  • Lactational mastitis is secondary to milk stasis and presents with pain, redness, warmth, and swelling of the breast; treatment includes NSAIDs, cold compresses, and, most importantly, complete breast emptying.
  • Initial evaluation of all premenopausal patients with abnormal uterine bleeding includes a detailed history, physical and pelvic examinations, pregnancy testing, complete blood count, and ferritin measurement.
  • Young women with severe uterine bleeding should be screened for bleeding disorders, specifically von Willebrand disease.
  • Premenopausal patients younger than age 45 years with abnormal uterine bleeding and risk factors for endometrial cancer, including tobacco use, a history of unopposed estrogen (polycystic ovary syndrome, obesity), tamoxifen use, Lynch or Cowden syndrome, or reproductive factors (e.g., early menarche or nulliparity), should undergo endometrial biopsy.
  • Premenopausal patients aged 45 years or older with abnormal uterine bleeding should undergo endometrial biopsy.
  • Premenopausal patients aged 45 years or older with abnormal uterine bleeding should undergo endometrial biopsy.
  • In acute and severe uterine bleeding, gonadotropin-releasing hormone or intravenous administration of high-dose estrogens may be used.
  • In premenopausal patients with anovulatory abnormal uterine bleeding who are not planning pregnancy, reasonable options include oral contraceptive pills containing estrogen and progesterone, a progestin-containing intrauterine device, and depot medroxyprogesterone.
  • All postmenopausal patients with uterine bleeding should undergo endometrial biopsy unless a transvaginal ultrasound reveals an endometrial stripe 4 mm thick or less.
  • Primary dysmenorrhea can be treated with NSAIDs or estrogen-progesterone or progesterone-only methods of contraception.
  • Routine laboratory testing for the diagnosis of menopause after age 45 years is not recommended.
  • Patients with possible primary ovarian insufficiency (menopause with age of onset <40 years) should have pregnancy ruled out and undergo measurement of follicle-stimulating hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and prolactin levels.
  • In the perimenopausal period, pregnancy is possible even if menstrual cycles are irregular, and contraception should be discussed if pregnancy is not desired.
  • Systemic estrogen is the most effective therapy for vasomotor symptoms of menopause; in patients without contraindications, it is safe for most women before age 60 years or when initiated within 10 years of menopause.
  • Contraindications to hormone therapy for vasomotor symptoms of menopause include pregnancy, unexplained vaginal bleeding, liver disease, coronary artery disease, stroke, thromboembolic disease, breast cancer, and endometrial cancer.
  • Nonhormonal options for vasomotor symptoms of menopause include selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, gabapentin, and fezolinetant as well as cognitive behavioral therapy and clinical hypnosis.
  • Treatment for genitourinary syndrome of menopause includes topical low-dose vaginal estrogen therapy, vaginal moisturizers, and/or as-needed vaginal lubricants.
  • Critical diagnoses in women presenting with acute pelvic pain include ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease, ruptured ovarian cyst, ovarian torsion, and appendicitis; a pregnancy test should be obtained for all women of reproductive age presenting with acute pelvic pain.
  • Transvaginal ultrasonography is the preferred imaging test in suspected ectopic pregnancy, ruptured ovarian cyst, ovarian torsion, and tubo-ovarian abscess.
  • Risk factors for chronic pelvic pain include physical, sexual, and/or emotional abuse; pelvic inflammatory disease; history of abdominopelvic surgery; chronic pain syndromes; and psychological conditions, such as anxiety or depression.
  • Uterine fibroids are the most common pelvic tumor in women and may present with pelvic pain, urinary or bowel symptoms from mass effect, or heavy vaginal bleeding, particularly if the fibroid is submucosal.
  • Treatment of heavy menstrual bleeding from submucosal fibroids may include a combined oral contraceptive or a progestin-based intrauterine device.
  • Endometriosis is characterized by cyclic pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and dysmenorrhea; symptoms are often responsive to menstrual suppression with continuous combined oral contraceptives or progestins alone.
  • Female sexual interest/arousal disorder is characterized by a lack of or significant decrease in sexual activity, including sexual interest, thoughts, excitement, and pleasure; this is especially common in menopausal and perimenopausal women.
  • Female orgasmic disorder is characterized by a significant delay in, infrequency of, or absence of orgasm, or significantly decreased intensity of orgasm during sexual activity.
  • Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder is characterized by persistent or recurrent difficulty having sexual intercourse, vulvovaginal or pelvic pain during intercourse, fear or anxiety about vulvovaginal or pelvic pain, and/or tensing or tightening of pelvic floor muscles during attempted vaginal penetration.
  • Female sexual dysfunction requires a through history and physical examination along with a comprehensive approach to treatment addressing physical, psychological, and behavioral aspects.
  • Clinical findings do not sufficiently distinguish between the common causes of vaginitis, and laboratory testing is necessary to establish a diagnosis.
  • Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) and antigen testing have greater than 90% sensitivity and specificity for bacterial vaginosis, vulvovaginal candidiasis, and trichomoniasis; NAAT is the preferred diagnostic test for trichomoniasis.
  • Characteristic findings of bacterial vaginosis include a thin vaginal discharge, vaginal pH greater than 4.5, a positive whiff test result (application of 10% potassium hydroxide to vaginal secretions results in a fishy odor), and the presence of clue cells.
  • Diagnostic testing for vulvovaginal candidiasis involves 10% potassium hydroxide wet mount showing yeast, hyphae, or pseudohyphae.
  • There is substantial overlap in the clinical presentation of vulvar cancer, vulvar lichen planus, vulvar lichen simplex, and vulvar lichen sclerosus, and biopsy may be necessary for diagnosis.
  • Lichen sclerosus is characterized by white vulvar papules or plaques with ecchymosis or purpura and is often limited to the anogenital skin, whereas lichen planus is seen as flat-topped purple papules with overlying fine, white, lacy streaks not limited to the vulva.
  • Lichen simplex, lichen sclerosis, and lichen planus are all treated with topical glucocorticoids.

index.title: Reproductive Health
index.keyPoints:
• Any primary care visit for a woman of reproductive age is an opportunity to ask if pregnancy is desired and to offer preconception counseling.
  • For women planning pregnancy, perform a comprehensive risk assessment for adverse pregnancy outcomes and begin folic acid supplementation.
  • Women considering pregnancy who are not immune to varicella and rubella should be vaccinated and advised to avoid pregnancy for at least 4 weeks afterward.
  • Contraception should be offered to all patients of reproductive potential who do not wish to conceive, particularly those with medical conditions that increase pregnancy risk.
  • Contraindications to combination estrogen-progestin contraceptives include breast cancer, venous thromboembolism, uncontrolled hypertension, liver disease, migraine with aura, and smoking more than 15 cigarettes a day for women older than 35 years.
  • Long-acting reversible contraceptive methods are highly effective and include copper and levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine devices as well as a progestin implant.
  • Medication abortion is recommended through 10 weeks' gestation; the two medications used in combination are mifepristone, which blocks the effects of progesterone, and misoprostol, which results in uterine contractions and expulsion of products of conception.
  • All patients presenting for abortion care should be assessed for ongoing contraceptive needs.
  • Women in the postpartum period should have a complete evaluation, with attention paid to long-term risk for gestational diabetes and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
  • Women with gestational diabetes require screening with a 2-hour, 75-g oral glucose tolerance test between 4 and 12 weeks postpartum and then screening every 1 to 3 years with a hemoglobin A~1c level, fasting blood glucose level, or oral glucose tolerance test.

index.title: Mental and Behavioral Health
index.keyPoints:
• Clinicians should ask all patients about tobacco use, recommend cessation, and provide behavioral interventions and approved pharmacotherapy to patients who use tobacco.
  • Combining behavioral counseling with pharmacotherapy is more effective than either modality alone for smoking cessation.
  • Varenicline is superior to other pharmacologic treatments for smoking cessation; combining varenicline with nicotine replacement therapy is the most effective strategy.
  • All adults should be screened for alcohol use disorder (AUD).
  • Patients diagnosed with AUD often require both psychotherapeutic and pharmacologic approaches to ensure safety and minimize relapse.
  • Naltrexone is the preferred first-line pharmacologic therapy for moderate to severe AUD, with acamprosate as an alternative; notably, naltrexone can be initiated in patients who are still drinking.
  • Naltrexone for AUD is contraindicated in patients with decompensated liver disease; acamprosate is the preferred agent in this setting.
  • Long-acting benzodiazepines, such as diazepam or chlordiazepoxide, are the preferred treatment for alcohol withdrawal; phenobarbital, propofol, and dexmedetomidine may be useful in refractory cases.
  • Opioid use disorder should be treated with pharmacotherapy and adjunct psychosocial treatment; the preferred pharmacologic agents are methadone (an opioid agonist) and buprenorphine (a partial agonist).
  • Naloxone and overdose prevention education should be offered to all patients receiving opioid therapy and especially to patients at increased risk for overdose; naloxone is available without a prescription in the United States.
  • Risk factors for opioid overdose include receiving doses of greater than 50 morphine milligram equivalents per day, concurrent benzodiazepine use, and comorbidities such as COPD, obstructive sleep apnea, other substance use disorders, and mental health conditions.
  • Treatment of opioid withdrawal is supportive and may include benzodiazepines, α-adrenergic agonists, antiemetics, and long-acting opioid agonists such as methadone or buprenorphine.
  • The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force advises screening all patients for depression; the PHQ-2 and the two-question depression screen are appropriate screening instruments.
  • A key component in assessing possible depression is evaluating for secondary causes, including other psychiatric conditions, medications such as interferon and glucocorticoids, and substance use.
  • For initial acute treatment of major depressive disorder, options include cognitive behavioral therapy or second-generation antidepressants after consideration of patient-specific characteristics and adverse effects; combination therapy is a reasonable option, especially in moderate to severe disease.
  • In treating depression, antidepressants should be started at a low dosage and gradually titrated to achieve a clinical response, which can be objectively monitored using the PHQ-9.
  • If a partial response occurs in the treatment of depression, increasing the dosage of the chosen medication or adding psychotherapy (if not already used) may be appropriate; if no response is seen, switching to another second-generation antidepressant or augmenting with a second agent with or without psychotherapy is indicated.
  • In patients who respond to acute therapy for a major depressive episode, treatment should continue for 4 to 12 months after symptom resolution.
  • Patients with three or more previous major depressive episodes, persistent depressive disorder, or residual depressive symptoms should receive long-term maintenance pharmacologic therapy, ranging from 1 to 3 years or indefinitely.
  • Peripartum depression may occur during pregnancy or up to 1 year after delivery; treatment is similar to that for other forms of depression but with close attention to drug safety in pregnancy.
  • Referral to a psychiatrist is indicated for patients with severe depression, failure of initial therapy, complex psychiatric comorbidities, or a high risk for suicide.
  • Clinicians must assess patients with depression for any history of elevated mood suggestive of bipolar disorder; prescribing antidepressant monotherapy to a patient with bipolar disorder may precipitate mania.
  • The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends screening for anxiety in adults aged 19 to 64 years, including those who are pregnant or in the postpartum period.
  • Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and pharmacotherapy are equally effective in the treatment of generalized anxiety disorder; patients with comorbid mood disorders are best treated with a medication that targets their concomitant illnesses.
  • Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), buspirone, and tricyclic antidepressants are effective in the treatment of generalized anxiety disorder; SSRIs and SNRIs are preferred because they have fewer adverse effects and can treat comorbid mood disorders.
  • CBT and pharmacotherapy with SSRIs and SNRIs are effective for treating social anxiety disorder and panic disorder.
  • A specific phobia is diagnosed when there is unreasonable fear and avoidance of a situation or object that persists for 6 months or more and causes distress or impairment; CBT with exposure therapy is the mainstay of treatment.
  • Psychotherapy is the first-line treatment for posttraumatic stress disorder; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors are alternative first-line options.
  • First-line treatment for obsessive compulsive disorder is cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT); selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors may be helpful in patients with severe symptoms or inadequate response to CBT.
  • When treating patients with somatic symptom disorder and related disorders, clinicians should acknowledge the patient's symptoms, focus on improving coping mechanisms, and establish a regular appointment schedule that is not predicated on the presence of symptoms.
  • Patients with somatic symptom disorder may respond to cognitive behavioral therapy.
  • Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder) is characterized by symptoms of neurologic dysfunction (abnormal sensation or motor function) that are unexplained by a medical condition and not consistent with examination findings; disease education is the primary treatment.
  • Somatic symptom disorder and related disorders must be differentiated from factitious disorder (the intentional fabrication of symptoms or injury without clear external benefit) and malingering (the feigning of medical problems for gain).
  • Clues to the presence of an eating disorder on physical examination include muscle wasting, xerosis, lanugo, erosion of dental enamel, parotid gland enlargement, and scarring or calluses on the dorsum of the hand.
  • Medical complications of anorexia nervosa may include a hypometabolic state, electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypophosphatemia), arrhythmias, refeeding syndrome, osteopenia, and osteoporosis.
  • A multidisciplinary approach, including psychotherapy, family therapy, and monitored dietary intake, is the primary treatment for anorexia nervosa; antidepressant therapy is not effective.
  • Cognitive behavioral therapy is the most effective intervention for bulimia nervosa and binge eating disorder; antidepressant therapy may also be beneficial.
  • Mortality is significantly increased in patients with schizophrenia because of concomitant cardiovascular disease, behavioral disorders, and substance use; approximately 5% of these patients die by suicide.
  • Antipsychotic medications are effective at controlling positive symptoms of schizophrenia, but some negative symptoms usually persist; choice of therapy is based primarily on patient comorbidities and adverse effect profile.
  • Stimulants should not be prescribed to patients with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and a history of substance use disorder; atomoxetine may be preferred in such patients.

index.title: Clinical Evaluation of Kidney Function
index.keyPoints:
• Serum creatinine changes nonlinearly with glomerular filtration rate (GFR), and significant losses in kidney function at higher GFR may cause only small changes in serum creatinine.
  • To estimate GFR, the National Kidney Foundation and the American Society of Nephrology recommend using the 2021 Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology (CKD-EPI) creatinine equation, which has been refitted to estimate kidney function without a race variable.
  • Three or more erythrocytes result in a positive dipstick test for blood; a positive test in the absence of erythrocytes in the urine sediment may indicate myoglobinuria or hemoglobinuria.
  • Because moderately increased albuminuria may go undetected by dipstick, direct quantification using a random (spot) protein-creatinine ratio or albumin-creatinine ratio or a 24-hour urine collection is required in high-risk patients.
  • Urine dipstick detects acetone and acetoacetate, but not β-hydroxybutyrate; therefore, in diabetic ketoacidosis and alcoholic ketoacidosis in which β-hydroxybutyrate is the primary ketone, the dipstick underestimates ketone excretion.
  • The presence of both leukocyte esterase and nitrites on urine dipstick is highly predictive of a urinary tract infection; conversely, the absence of both has a high negative predictive value for a urinary tract infection.
  • Isomorphic erythrocytes suggest a nonglomerular origin of blood; acanthocytes, a type of dysmorphic erythrocyte, suggest a glomerular origin.
  • Pyuria is most commonly caused by a urinary tract infection (UTI); sterile pyuria is the presence of urine leukocytes in the setting of a negative urine culture, and causes include vaginitis and cervicitis, prostatitis, acute interstitial nephritis, kidney stones, kidney transplant rejection, and, less commonly, UTIs caused by organisms that do not grow by standard culture techniques.
  • Erythrocyte casts are highly suggestive of glomerulonephritis.
  • Leukocyte casts may be present in acute interstitial nephritis and infections, and granular (muddy brown) casts may be present in acute tubular necrosis.
  • The random (spot) urine protein-creatinine ratio and albumin-creatinine ratio correlate with 24-hour urine collections and are sufficiently accurate for screening and monitoring proteinuria.
  • High urine albumin levels indicate glomerular injury; the absence of albuminuria excludes most glomerular diseases.
  • Patients with diabetes mellitus should undergo yearly urine albumin-creatinine ratio assessment, beginning at diagnosis for patients with type 2 diabetes and 5 years after diagnosis for patients with type 1 diabetes.
  • Screening for proteinuria or chronic kidney disease in asymptomatic adults without risk factors is not recommended.
  • Urinalysis should not be used for urothelial cancer screening in asymptomatic adults.
  • Evaluation of hematuria should be pursued even in patients with bleeding diatheses or those taking antiplatelet or anticoagulation therapy.
  • If the cause of hematuria is thought to be due to infection, menstruation, or another benign cause, the urinalysis should be repeated to ensure resolution.
  • Evaluation of hematuria is based on the patient's underlying risk for urothelial malignancy and ranges from repeat urinalysis in 6 months for low-/negligible-risk patients to cystoscopy and CT urography for high-risk patients.
  • Ultrasonography is the most commonly used imaging modality in the evaluation of the kidneys and upper urinary tract because of its safety, cost-effectiveness, and availability.
  • CT urography allows characterization of renal tumors and cysts; noncontrast helical CT is the gold standard for diagnosing nephrolithiasis; and CT with contrast is valuable in imaging the renal vasculature.
  • Indications for kidney biopsy include glomerular hematuria, severely increased albuminuria, kidney disease of unclear cause, and kidney transplant dysfunction or monitoring.

index.title: Electrolyte Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• Isotonic hyponatremia is a laboratory artifact, and hypertonic hyponatremia results from an increased concentration of effective osmotic solute (usually glucose); hypotonic hyponatremia is further classified based on the patient's volume status.
  • The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone is most often caused by medications such as antidepressants and thiazide diuretics.
  • Treatment of acute, symptomatic, hypotonic hyponatremia consists of a 100-mL bolus of 3% saline to increase the serum sodium by 2.0 to 3.0 mEq/L (2.0-3.0 mmol/L).
  • Overly aggressive treatment of chronic isovolemic hypotonic hyponatremia can result in osmotic demyelination.
  • The therapeutic goal for chronic, symptomatic, isovolemic hypotonic hyponatremia is an increase in serum sodium by 4.0 to 6.0 mEq/L (4.0-6.0 mmol/L) in 24 hours; in patients with significant neurologic impairment, sodium can be acutely increased 2.0 to 4.0 mEq/L (2.0-4.0 mmol/L), but no greater than 6 mEq/L (6 mmol/L) in 24 hours.
  • The most common cause of hypernatremia is loss of hypotonic body fluids with inadequate water replacement due to lack of access or thirst.
  • Treatment of hypernatremia is directed at free water replacement and correction of the underlying mechanism.
  • In the presence of hypernatremia due to intravascular volume depletion, replacement fluid should be isotonic saline; otherwise, a hypotonic solution (half [0.45%] normal saline) can be used.
  • Most cases of hypokalemia are due to gastrointestinal losses or diuretics.
  • ECG manifestations of hypokalemia include ST-segment depression, decreased T-wave amplitude, and increased U-wave amplitude.
  • In patients with hypokalemia and neuromuscular or cardiac symptoms, intravenous potassium (20 mEq/h [20 mmol/h]) can be used to increase the potassium promptly.
  • Initial ECG manifestations of hyperkalemia include peaked precordial T waves and a shortened QT interval; with hyperkalemia progression there may be lengthening of the PR interval, loss of the P wave, widening of the QRS complex, a sine wave pattern, and asystole.
  • Intravenous administration of calcium gluconate quickly antagonizes the effects of hyperkalemia on the cardiac membrane.
  • Definitive treatment of severe hyperkalemia must include removal of potassium from the body; patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate can increase gastrointestinal excretion, loop diuretics can be effective in patients without severe kidney disease, and hemodialysis is the treatment of choice in patients with severe hyperkalemia and oliguric kidney disease.
  • Severe hypophosphatemia (<1.0 mg/dL [0.32 mmol/L]) is associated with life-threatening symptoms, including delirium, seizures, coma, heart failure, respiratory failure, rhabdomyolysis, and hemolysis.
  • Mild hypophosphatemia can be treated with oral sodium or potassium phosphate; levels <2.0 mg/dL (0.65 mmol/L) should be treated with intravenous sodium phosphate.
  • Causes of hyperphosphatemia include cellular lysis with release of phosphate, excessive intake, and/or decreased renal excretion from decreased glomerular filtration rate or increased tubular reabsorption (hypoparathyroidism).
  • If kidney function is adequate in patients with hyperphosphatemia, serum phosphate levels should normalize in 12 to 24 hours; if necessary, phosphate excretion can be increased with intravenous saline, and dialysis can be initiated for those with impaired kidney function.
  • Significant symptoms of hypomagnesemia usually develop when the serum magnesium level is <1.2 mg/dL (0.5 mmol/L); these include tremors, fasciculations, muscle weakness, carpopedal spasm, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, seizures, and cardiac arrhythmias.
  • Treatment of significant symptoms of hypomagnesemia includes magnesium sulfate infusions; less severe symptoms can be treated with slow-release oral magnesium.
  • Early symptoms of hypermagnesemia include loss of deep tendon reflexes, progressing to flaccid paralysis at higher levels.
  • For patients with hypermagnesemia, all magnesium-containing medications should be discontinued, and magnesium excretion can be enhanced with saline diuresis; for more severe symptoms, intravenous calcium will antagonize the effects of magnesium.

index.title: Acid-Base Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• Primary metabolic acidosis is defined by low pH and low serum bicarbonate; primary metabolic alkalosis is defined by elevated pH and elevated serum bicarbonate.
  • In primary respiratory acidosis, pH is low and arterial Pco~2 is elevated; in primary respiratory alkalosis, pH is elevated and Pco~2 is low.
  • The serum anion gap assesses whether metabolic acidosis is due to an unmeasured organic anion (increased anion gap metabolic acidosis) or to a loss of bicarbonate (normal anion gap metabolic acidosis).
  • In the presence of an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis, adding the Δ anion gap to the bicarbonate corresponds with what the bicarbonate would be if there were not an anion gap; a value >28 confirms a concomitant metabolic alkalosis.
  • Lactic acidosis is the most common cause of increased anion gap metabolic acidosis.
  • Ethylene glycol, propylene glycol, or methanol ingestion results in an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis associated with an elevated plasma osmolal gap >10 mOsm/kg H~2O.
  • In normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, a negative urine anion gap identifies a nonrenal cause or type 2 (proximal) renal tubular acidosis, whereas a positive urine anion gap is associated with distal renal tubular acidoses.
  • In type 2 (proximal) renal tubular acidosis, failure of the proximal tubule to adequately absorb filtered bicarbonate causes bicarbonate loss; treatment consists of alkali replacement.
  • Type 1 (hypokalemic distal) renal tubular acidosis occurs due to impaired distal hydrogen ion excretion resulting in a positive urine anion gap, hypokalemia, and elevated urine pH; treatment includes alkali therapy with potassium citrate or potassium bicarbonate.
  • In type 4 (hyperkalemic distal) renal tubular acidosis, aldosterone deficiency or resistance causes hyperkalemia and decreased NH~4^+ excretion, resulting in a positive urine anion gap; treatment includes correction of the underlying cause and treatment of hyperkalemia.
  • The most common causes of metabolic alkalosis are associated with low urine chloride (vomiting, nasogastric suction, and diuretic use).
  • In patients with saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis (low urine chloride, normal-low intravascular volume, and normal-low extracellular volume), treatment includes saline administration, potassium repletion, and addressing the primary cause.
  • Patients with metabolic alkalosis, volume overload, normal-low intravascular volume, and low urine chloride (cirrhosis, heart failure) are treated with diuresis.
  • Metabolic alkalosis from mineralocorticoid excess presents with hypertension, hypokalemia, euvolemia, and elevated urine chloride.
  • Respiratory acidosis is characterized by CO~2 retention and is commonly caused by pulmonary conditions associated with increased dead space or hypoventilation.
  • Treatment of respiratory acidosis includes treating the underlying disorder and may require mechanical ventilation to reduce CO~2.
  • Respiratory alkalosis is characterized by a reduction in arterial Pco~2 due to increased ventilation.
  • Early salicylate intoxication manifests with respiratory alkalosis, an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis, and mental status changes; treatment includes forced diuresis, urine alkalinization, or hemodialysis.

index.title: Kidney Stones
index.keyPoints:
• Kidney stones typically present with waxing and waning “colicky” flank pain that radiates to the groin; nausea, vomiting, and dysuria may also be present.
  • Hematuria is usually present in patients with kidney stones, although the absence of hematuria does not exclude the diagnosis.
  • Noncontrast helical CT is the gold standard modality to diagnose nephrolithiasis; kidney ultrasonography can be used in pregnant patients or when CT is unavailable, although it may miss smaller stones.
  • Eighty percent of kidney stones contain calcium; most are composed of calcium oxalate, which is associated with hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, and hypocitraturia.
  • Struvite staghorn calculi are the result of infection by urea-splitting bacteria such as Proteus, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Ureaplasma, or Staphylococcus species and can lead to both sepsis and end-stage kidney disease.
  • Uric acid stones are radiolucent and are associated with low urine pH (<5.5), chronic diarrhea, metabolic syndrome, and gout.
  • Cystine stones result from cystinuria, an autosomal recessive disease that presents at a young age.
  • Acute management of symptomatic nephrolithiasis includes pain management and facilitation of stone passage.
  • Patients should strain their urine to collect stone fragments for chemical analysis if stone composition is unknown; a 24-hour urine collection for measurement of volume, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, and sodium should be obtained from all patients with recurrent stones.
  • Urologic intervention is required in patients with kidney stones who have evidence of infection, acute kidney injury, intractable pain, and stones that fail to pass.
  • Increased fluid intake to a target urine output of >2 to 2.5 L/24 h is the most important intervention to prevent recurrent kidney stones, regardless of stone composition.

index.title: Hypertension
index.keyPoints:
• Either acute (hypertensive emergency) or chronic elevation of blood pressure can lead to significant injury in multiple organs, including the eyes, blood vessels, brain, heart, and kidneys.
  • The American Heart Association recommends a validated, automated office blood pressure (BP) device for evaluating office BP.
  • Ambulatory BP monitoring is a better predictor of cardiovascular outcomes, including left ventricular hypertrophy and cardiac death, compared with office-based BP measurements.
  • Normal BP by ambulatory blood pressure measurement includes a 24-hour average BP <115/75 mm Hg, daytime average BP <120/80 mm Hg, and nighttime average BP <100/65 mm Hg.
  • Home BP monitoring is an acceptable alternative if ambulatory BP monitoring is not available or tolerable by the patient.
  • A diagnosis of hypertension (blood pressure [BP] ≥130/80 mm Hg) should be based on an average of two or more elevated systolic and/or diastolic BP measurements obtained on two or more occasions; obtaining measurements outside of the clinical setting for diagnostic confirmation is recommended before starting treatment.
  • The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends screening for hypertension in adults ≥18 years of age to identify those at increased risk for cardiovascular disease from hypertension and to begin early interventions to decrease this risk.
  • The American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association recommend that adults receiving initial nonpharmacologic therapy for elevated BP or low-risk stage 1 hypertension should undergo repeat BP measurement within 3 to 6 months; if systolic BP remains ≥130 mm Hg or diastolic BP remains ≥80 mm Hg, pharmacologic therapy should be initiated.
  • Initial evaluation of patients with newly diagnosed hypertension includes a complete history, physical examination, and screening laboratory studies to assess for a familial pattern, secondary causes, other cardiovascular risk factors, end-organ damage, and modifiable lifestyle factors.
  • Most patients with hypertension have primary (essential) hypertension, in which no secondary underlying cause is identified.
  • Habitual high sodium intake along with low potassium intake is a critical factor contributing to the worldwide high prevalence of hypertension.
  • The 2025 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association blood pressure (BP) guideline recommends a BP goal of <130/80 mm Hg.
  • Lifestyle modifications and cardiovascular risk factors should be addressed in all patients with elevated blood pressure and hypertension.
  • In addition to lifestyle modification, pharmacologic therapy should be initiated in patients with stage 1 hypertension and clinical cardiovascular disease, previous stroke, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or a 10-year cardiovascular risk ≥7.5% and in all patients with stage 2 hypertension.
  • Combination therapy with two first-line antihypertensive drugs of different classes is recommended for adults with stage 2 hypertension.
  • Thiazide diuretics, calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, or angiotensin receptor blockers are first-line treatment options for hypertension.
  • Suboptimal BP control is frequently the result of not including a diuretic, which ensures that extracellular volume expansion is prevented or treated.
  • Dry cough is an adverse effect of ACE inhibitors but is uncommon with angiotensin receptor blockers.
  • Combined use of renin-angiotensin system agents (ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and direct renin inhibitors) is not recommended due to increased adverse events.
  • White coat hypertension is characterized by elevated in-office blood pressure (BP) readings but normal out-of-office BP measurements.
  • Lifestyle modifications and careful monitoring should be considered for patients with white coat hypertension because of increased risk for future development of hypertension and slightly higher cardiovascular risk compared with normotensive patients.
  • Masked hypertension is defined as blood pressure that is normal in the office but elevated in the ambulatory setting.
  • Masked hypertension is associated with an increased risk for sustained hypertension and cardiovascular disease; after a 3-month trial of lifestyle modifications, antihypertensive medication should be initiated if daytime ambulatory or home blood pressure is still ≥130/80 mm Hg.
  • Resistant hypertension is defined as blood pressure (BP) that remains above goal despite the concurrent use of three antihypertensive agents of different classes at maximally tolerated doses, or BP at goal but requiring four or more medications; one of the medications must be a diuretic.
  • Management of resistant hypertension includes confirming accurate out-of-office BP measurement, excluding secondary causes, addressing behaviors that contribute to high BP, avoiding drugs that exacerbate hypertension, reducing dietary sodium, and ensuring appropriate diuretic dose and frequency.
  • Common causes of secondary hypertension include primary aldosteronism, kidney disease, renovascular disease, and obstructive sleep apnea.
  • The Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guideline suggests a target systolic blood pressure (BP) of <120 mm Hg in patients with hypertension and chronic kidney disease (CKD), if tolerated, using standardized office BP measurement; the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association recommends a BP target of <130/80 mm Hg.
  • An ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker is recommended as first-line antihypertensive therapy for patients with albuminuria; treatment also includes dietary sodium restriction to <2000 mg/d and addition of a diuretic as needed to control intravascular volume.
  • Medical therapy for renovascular disease, including treatment of underlying cardiovascular risk factors and use of an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker, may be as beneficial as invasive procedures.
  • Primary aldosteronism is a common cause of secondary hypertension in middle-aged adults and an important cause of resistant hypertension; paired plasma aldosterone concentration and plasma renin activity measurements are used for screening.
  • Severe hypertension, formerly known as hypertensive urgency, is defined as severely elevated blood pressure—a systolic BP >180 mm Hg and/or diastolic BP >120 mm Hg—in a patient without obvious signs or symptoms of new or worsening target-organ damage.
  • Hypertensive emergency refers to significantly elevated blood pressure (BP, typically >180/120 mm Hg) causing acute organ damage or dysfunction (e.g., stroke, encephalopathy, acute kidney injury, retinopathy, preeclampsia/eclampsia, acute myocardial infarction, aortic dissection, or acute heart failure).
  • For adults with a hypertensive emergency and intracerebral hemorrhage, systolic BP should be reduced to <140 mm Hg during the first hour, and for individuals with aortic dissection, it should be reduced to <120 mm Hg; in patients without these conditions, BP should be reduced by a maximum of 25% over the first hour, then to 160/100 mm Hg over the next 2 to 6 hours, and then cautiously to 130-140 mm Hg during the next 24 to 48 hours.

index.title: Acute Kidney Injury
index.keyPoints:
• The Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes Acute Kidney Injury Work Group defines acute kidney injury by any of the following: increase in serum creatinine by ≥0.3 mg/dL (26.5 μmol/L) within 48 hours; increase in serum creatinine to ≥1.5 times baseline over 7 days; or urine volume <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours.
  • Acute kidney injury (AKI) can be divided into prerenal, intrinsic, and postrenal causes; prerenal AKI and acute tubular necrosis account for the majority of AKI cases in hospitalized patients.
  • Patients with acute kidney injury (AKI) can be asymptomatic until extreme loss of kidney function occurs; severe AKI can lead to symptoms caused by volume overload, electrolyte abnormalities, and uremia.
  • In patients with suspected acute kidney injury (AKI), physical examination focuses on blood pressure, heart rate, signs of volume status, and bladder percussion/palpation.
  • In patients with oliguria, the fractional excretion of sodium (FE~Na) or urea (FE~Urea) may be helpful in distinguishing between prerenal AKI and acute tubular necrosis.
  • Ultrasonography of the kidneys and bladder should be obtained for suspected urinary tract obstruction or to exclude obstruction when the underlying cause of AKI is unclear.
  • Prerenal acute kidney injury is caused by hypoperfusion of the kidney with a subsequent decrease in glomerular filtration rate, which is reversible with discontinuing nephrotoxins and treating the underlying cause in a timely manner.
  • Renal hypoperfusion can occur due to intravascular volume depletion, decreased effective arterial circulation, renal vasoconstriction, and/or medications.
  • Acute tubular necrosis due to ischemia, nephrotoxins, and/or sepsis is the most common cause of acute kidney injury in hospitalized patients; a history of sepsis, documented protracted hypotension, or nephrotoxin exposure, along with hemodynamic and volume status assessment, can aid in the diagnosis.
  • Prevention and management of rhabdomyolysis-induced acute kidney injury involves treating the underlying cause and aggressive intravenous isotonic fluid infusion aimed at maintaining urine output >200 to 300 mL/h.
  • Urine eosinophils are neither sensitive nor specific in the diagnosis of acute interstitial nephritis (AIN), and testing is not recommended.
  • Drug-induced AIN is associated with a gradual increase in serum creatinine 7 to 10 days after drug exposure but can occur sooner after repeat exposure; renal recovery is usually complete if the drug is stopped immediately after the onset of kidney injury.
  • In atheroemboli-induced acute kidney injury (AKI), plaque rupture, especially following a vascular procedure, causes cholesterol embolization resulting in ischemia with AKI and multisystem involvement; treatment is supportive.
  • Physical findings of atheroembolic disease include livedo reticularis, ischemia of the toes, and yellow refractile bodies (Hollenhorst plaques) on funduscopic examination.
  • AKI due to thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) occurs in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, hemolytic uremic syndrome, HELLP (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets) syndrome, hypertensive emergency, scleroderma renal crisis, and complement-mediated TMA (atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome).
  • Intratubular obstruction causes of acute kidney injury include monoclonal light chain deposition in multiple myeloma; calcium oxalate deposition from ethylene glycol ingestion, orlistat, and high doses of vitamin C; crystals from drugs; and uric acid or calcium phosphate crystal deposition from tumor lysis syndrome.
  • Postrenal acute kidney injury (AKI) can occur from obstruction anywhere from the renal pelvis to the external urethral meatus; diagnosis can be made through ultrasonography or noncontrast CT, with generally good renal recovery if the obstruction is relieved within 1 to 2 weeks.
  • In patients with postrenal AKI, the presence of normal urine output or polyuria does not exclude the possibility of obstructive uropathy.
  • Preventive strategies for patients at high risk for contrast-associated acute kidney injury include minimizing the amount of contrast, avoiding concomitant nephrotoxins, and administering intravenous isotonic fluids.
  • Cardiorenal syndrome is characterized by the triad of concomitant decreased kidney function, diuretic-resistant heart failure with congestion, and worsening kidney function during heart failure therapy.
  • General management of hepatorenal syndrome includes discontinuing diuretics, restricting sodium, and treatment with vasoconstrictors in combination with albumin infusion.
  • Treatment of established tumor lysis syndrome includes intravenous volume expansion, rasburicase, management of hyperkalemia and hyperphosphatemia, and kidney replacement therapy in refractory cases.
  • Abdominal compartment syndrome is characterized by a sustained elevated intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) associated with new organ dysfunction; IAP can be measured with a transvesical pressure transducer through an indwelling Foley catheter.
  • In most cases of acute kidney injury (AKI), treatment of the underlying medical condition and discontinuation of nephrotoxic medications lead to improvement in kidney function.
  • Patients with AKI should be evaluated in follow-up to monitor for complete recovery of kidney function and/or emergence or worsening of chronic kidney disease.
  • Kidney replacement therapy (KRT) is used to manage the urgent complications of severe acute kidney injury, including hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, volume overload refractory to diuretics, uremic manifestations, and dialyzable toxins.
  • There is no proven benefit to early administration of KRT versus timing based on usual clinical criteria in critically ill patients and those with sepsis.

index.title: Chronic Tubulointerstitial Nephritis
index.keyPoints:
• Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (CTIN) is characterized by interstitial scarring, fibrosis, and tubular atrophy and results in a slow decline in kidney function over months and years.
  • Tubular dysfunction, including glucosuria and other features of Fanconi syndrome, normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, or hyperkalemia, may occur in CTIN.
  • Features of chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis may include polyuria and nocturia due to renal-concentrating defects, hypertension, and a urinalysis that is normal or demonstrates pyuria and/or proteinuria <1500 mg/24 h.
  • Causes of chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (CTIN) include various systemic diseases, infections, malignancy, medications, drugs of abuse, heavy metals, and obstructive uropathy.
  • More recently recognized manifestations of CTIN include chronic interstitial nephritis in agricultural communities, affecting young to middle-aged male agricultural workers, and aristolochic acid nephropathy caused by exposure to aristolochic acid.
  • Management of CTIN includes discontinuing the offending agent and treating the underlying cause; in patients with chronic kidney disease, management is supportive.

index.title: Glomerular Diseases
index.keyPoints:
• The hallmark features of the nephrotic syndrome include a urine protein excretion >3500 mg/24 h or a urine protein-creatinine ratio >3500 mg/g, hypoalbuminemia, hypercholesterolemia, and edema.
  • Because the nephrotic syndrome is a hypercoagulable state, patients are at increased risk for thrombosis.
  • Common features of the nephritic syndrome are hematuria (with dysmorphic erythrocytes or erythrocyte casts) and proteinuria; hypertension, edema, and kidney dysfunction may also occur.
  • The American Diabetes Association recommends yearly assessment of estimated glomerular filtration rate and albuminuria in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus beginning at the time of diabetes diagnosis and yearly assessment after 5 years of disease in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus.
  • An ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker, titrated to the maximum tolerated dose, is recommended for patients with diabetic kidney disease (DKD) to control blood pressure and reduce proteinuria.
  • In the treatment of DKD, combining any two renin-angiotensin system drugs (ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, or direct renin inhibitors) is not recommended, because adverse effects are increased and there is no additional clinical benefit.
  • A sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor is recommended for all patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (regardless of urine albumin-creatinine ratio) when the estimated glomerular filtration rate is ≥20 mL/min/1.73 m^2.
  • Finerenone is recommended for patients with DKD and normal potassium levels who have persistent albuminuria despite maximum renin-angiotensin system inhibition.
  • For all patients with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), conservative therapy includes dietary sodium restriction, renin-angiotensin system–blocking drugs to control proteinuria, statin therapy, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, and edema management.
  • Initial treatment of primary FSGS with nephrotic-range proteinuria is high-dose glucocorticoids.
  • Anti–phospholipase A2 receptor antibodies are detected in approximately 75% of primary cases of membranous nephropathy and are rarely found in secondary forms; the distinction is important because secondary forms typically remit with treatment of the underlying cause.
  • Patients with membranous nephropathy are particularly prone to thrombotic complications, including lower extremity, pulmonary, and renal vein thromboses (RVTs); bilateral RVT should be suspected in patients with newly diagnosed membranous nephropathy with acute kidney injury.
  • Primary membranous nephropathy is typically treated with 6 to 12 months of conservative therapy, to allow for the possibility of spontaneous remission, before initiating immunosuppression for patients with persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria.
  • The classic presentation of minimal change glomerulopathy is sudden-onset nephrotic syndrome.
  • Minimal change glomerulopathy is initially treated with glucocorticoids.
  • Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is characterized by at least a 50% decline in glomerular filtration rate over a short period, with histologic findings of extensive glomerular crescents.
  • RPGN typically presents with oliguria, rising serum creatinine, hematuria, erythrocyte casts, and varying ranges of proteinuria; patients may rapidly progress to kidney failure.
  • The most common causes of RPGN are ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, and anti–glomerular basement membrane glomerulonephritis.
  • More than 50% of patients with anti–glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease have lung involvement, manifesting as hemoptysis, shortness of breath, or cough.
  • Treatment of anti–GBM disease includes plasmapheresis, glucocorticoids, and cyclophosphamide.
  • Most cases of ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis are idiopathic, but some may be drug induced; the most common inciting agents are hydralazine, minocycline, and antithyroid drugs.
  • Symptoms of ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis include malaise, arthralgia, myalgia, dark urine, and lung and sinus involvement.
  • Typical induction therapy for ANCA-associated vasculitis includes glucocorticoids combined with either rituximab or cyclophosphamide.
  • Common presentations of IgA nephropathy (IgAN) include asymptomatic microscopic hematuria (with or without proteinuria) or episodic gross hematuria coincident with an upper respiratory infection; however, more aggressive presentations are also possible.
  • Treatment of IgAN includes antiproteinuric therapy using an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker as well as a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
  • Kidney biopsy is required to diagnose and classify lupus nephritis (LN), which guides therapy.
  • Treatment of classes I and II LN includes conservative therapy with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker; classes III, IV, and V LN require immunosuppressive therapy; and patients with class VI LN may require consideration for kidney replacement therapy.
  • Infection-related glomerulonephritis (IRGN) results from a recently resolved infection or an infection that is ongoing at the time of development of glomerulonephritis; in industrialized countries, clinical disease is seen more often in adults and is associated with Staphylococcus aureus and gram-negative bacteria.
  • Treatment of IRGN is usually supportive and aimed at the infectious cause.
  • Treatment of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis includes immunosuppression (e.g., glucocorticoids) when nephrotic-range proteinuria and/or kidney dysfunction is present.

index.title: Kidney Manifestations of Deposition Diseases
index.keyPoints:
• Patients with myeloma cast nephropathy present with acute or slowly progressive kidney injury and have elevated serum free light chains.
  • Patients with a monoclonal immunoglobulin who do not meet diagnostic criteria for a hematologic cancer (e.g., multiple myeloma) may develop monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance that can present with proteinuria, hematuria, and elevated serum creatinine; kidney biopsy is necessary to make the diagnosis.
  • Kidney disease in amyloidosis is most commonly caused by AL amyloid composed of monoclonal gamma or kappa light chains or AA amyloid formed by serum amyloid A protein; patients frequently present with nephrotic-range proteinuria, and treatment is aimed at the underlying disorder.
  • Kidney involvement in cryoglobulinemia occurs most frequently with type II (mixed) cryoglobulins; treatment is directed at the underlying cause (e.g., eradication of hepatitis C virus).

index.title: Genetic Disorders and Kidney Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is characterized by large kidneys with multiple kidney cysts and is associated with hypertension; hematuria; abdominal, flank, or back pain; urinary tract infection; and kidney stones.
  • Patients with ADPKD and a personal or family history of subarachnoid hemorrhage, or with a family history of intracranial hemorrhage or unexplained sudden death, should be screened for intracranial aneurysms with MR angiography.
  • Tolvaptan slows kidney function decline in adults at risk for rapidly progressive ADPKD.
  • Kidney manifestations of tuberous sclerosis complex include renal angiomyolipomas, renal cell carcinoma, and cysts.
  • Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease should be suspected in patients with slowly progressive chronic kidney disease (CKD), a bland urine sediment, small kidneys, and a family history of end-stage kidney disease.
  • Hereditary nephritis (Alport syndrome) is a glomerular disease associated with sensorineural hearing loss and characteristic ocular findings.
  • Thin basement membrane nephropathy (benign familial hematuria) results in hematuria without significant proteinuria or ensuing glomerulosclerosis, with rare progression to CKD in the absence of known risk factors.
  • High-risk APOL1 genotype confers increased risk for CKD and is more common in persons of African descent.

index.title: Chronic Kidney Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is defined as abnormal kidney structure or function present for at least 3 months.
  • Staging of CKD is based on estimated glomerular filtration rate and degree of albuminuria.
  • Diagnosis of chronic kidney disease (CKD) requires an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <60 mL/min/1.73 m^2 confirmed at least 3 months after initial assessment or persistent proteinuria, albuminuria, or structural kidney disease regardless of eGFR.
  • Acute kidney injury is a substantial risk factor for subsequent CKD.
  • The Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes guidelines recommend treatment with a statin in all patients with non-dialysis–dependent chronic kidney disease (CKD) who are age 50 years or older; in adults 18 to 49 years of age with non-dialysis–dependent CKD and any of the following: coronary artery disease, prior ischemic stroke, or a >10% estimated risk for coronary death or nonfatal myocardial infarction; and in adult kidney transplant recipients.
  • Chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder is characterized by alterations of calcium, phosphorus, and regulatory hormone blood levels; abnormalities in bone turnover and mineralization; and pathologic calcification.
  • Management of chronic kidney disease-mineral bone disorder (CKD-MBD) focuses upon normalizing serum phosphorus, avoiding hypercalcemia, and addressing modifiable factors.
  • Use of calcitriol and vitamin D analogues to lower parathyroid hormone should be avoided in patients with CKD who are not on dialysis unless they have severe and progressive hyperparathyroidism.
  • Noncalcium-based phosphate binders should be used preferentially over calcium-based options in patients with CKD-MBD.
  • Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents should be considered only for patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) who have hemoglobin concentrations <10 g/dL (100 g/L); there is an increased risk for serious cardiovascular events and stroke when administered to patients with CKD and hemoglobin levels >11 g/dL (110 g/L).
  • A low-potassium diet, oral bicarbonate, and potassium binders may allow patients to continue using kidney-protective agents (e.g., ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers) by correcting hyperkalemia, which would otherwise mandate their cessation.
  • ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers decrease proteinuria and slow progression of proteinuric kidney diseases, but use of both drug classes in combination results in more adverse events without additional cardiovascular or renal benefits.
  • Routine care for patients with chronic kidney disease should include avoidance of medications such as NSAIDs and proton pump inhibitors as well as dose adjustment of medications cleared by renal excretion, including antibiotics and direct oral anticoagulants.
  • Patients with chronic kidney disease and increased proteinuria benefit from renoprotective actions of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors.
  • Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) an estimated glomerular filtration rate <30 mL/min/1.73 m^2 who require iodinated contrast should receive intravenous hydration with 0.9% saline before and after receiving contrast unless a contraindication exists.
  • For patients with advanced CKD who require MRI with gadolinium-based contrast media (GBCM), risk for nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is reduced by using group II GBCM at the lowest volume of contrast possible and timing proximate to the next scheduled hemodialysis for dialysis-dependent patients.
  • In patients with CKD, peripherally inserted central venous catheters and subclavian venous catheters should be avoided to maintain central vein patency for future dialysis vascular access.
  • Patients with advanced CKD who choose hemodialysis for kidney replacement therapy should be referred to an experienced surgeon for arteriovenous fistula placement months before the anticipated need for dialysis.
  • In patients with CKD who require opioid-based pain medications, oxycodone, hydromorphone, or tramadol are preferred because of their shorter half-life and hepatic elimination.
  • Kidney transplantation is the preferred treatment for end-stage kidney disease because of improved mortality, quality of life, and decreased health care cost.
  • Patients should be referred to a kidney transplant center for evaluation when the estimated glomerular filtration rate is 15 to 20 mL/min/1.73 m^2 or when the risk for kidney replacement therapy exceeds 40% over 2 years.
  • Preemptive kidney transplants are associated with improved clinical outcomes compared with transplantation after starting dialysis.
  • Blood pressure and kidney function of donors should be monitored as part of routine medical follow-up.
  • Potential drug-drug interactions with calcineurin inhibitors should be checked before adding or adjusting medications to avoid potential nontherapeutic or toxic drug levels.
  • Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death for kidney transplant recipients, and kidney transplantation should be treated as a cardiovascular disease equivalent.
  • Within the first month after transplantation, the most common infectious complications are similar to other surgeries and include urinary tract infections and wound infections; afterward, opportunistic infections become more prevalent.
  • Polyoma BK virus infection uniquely affects kidney transplant recipients.
  • Immunosuppression of kidney transplant recipients increases the risk for several malignancies, including nonmelanoma skin cancers, Kaposi sarcoma, and posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders; regular screening for skin cancer and other age- and sex-specific cancers is recommended.
  • Posttransplantation diabetes mellitus is common and increases cardiovascular risk.
  • Acute rejection should always be considered in the setting of acute kidney injury in a kidney transplant recipient; early recognition and treatment are associated with improved outcomes.
  • Secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism can persist for several months in patients who have received a kidney transplant; continuation of calcimimetics may be warranted in the setting of hypercalcemia.
  • Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in kidney transplant recipients.
  • Clinical outcomes are similar for patients on peritoneal dialysis compared with hemodialysis.
  • Conservative kidney care focuses on symptom management and quality of life without kidney replacement therapy in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease.
  • Complications of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) include cardiovascular disease, infection, acquired cystic kidney disease, calciphylaxis, and mood disorders.
  • Patients with ESKD often have symptoms that impair quality of life such as pruritus and sleep disturbance, including restless legs syndrome and obstructive sleep apnea.

index.title: The Kidney in Pregnancy
index.keyPoints:
• Pregnancy is associated with increased glomerular filtration rate with decreased serum creatinine and increased proteinuria.
  • Screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria at least once in early pregnancy is recommended, and, if present, treatment is indicated.
  • Mild hyponatremia from a reset in antidiuretic hormone response to hypo-osmolality occurs normally during pregnancy and requires no management.
  • Chronic hypertension is defined as hypertension that precedes pregnancy, is present before 20 weeks' gestation, or persists longer than 12 weeks postpartum.
  • The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends treating chronic hypertension in pregnant individuals to a goal blood pressure of <140/90 mm Hg.
  • Renin-angiotensin system agents (ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and direct renin inhibitors) are contraindicated in pregnancy because of teratogenicity and should be discontinued before conception in those planning pregnancy.
  • First-line therapy of chronic hypertension in pregnancy includes long-acting nifedipine and labetalol.
  • Aspirin should be initiated between 12 weeks and 28 weeks of gestation (preferably before 16 weeks) for pregnant individuals with chronic hypertension to prevent preeclampsia.
  • Gestational hypertension is defined as hypertension that presents after 20 weeks of pregnancy without proteinuria or other end-organ damage and resolves within 12 weeks of delivery.
  • Preeclampsia is defined by new-onset hypertension and proteinuria that occur after 20 weeks of pregnancy.
  • Low-dose aspirin initiated after 12 weeks of pregnancy reduces rates of preeclampsia in high-risk individuals.
  • Definitive treatment of preeclampsia is delivery.
  • Acute-onset severe hypertension in pregnancy is defined as systolic blood pressure ≥160 mm Hg and/or diastolic blood pressure ≥110 mm Hg.
  • Pregnant individuals with acute-onset severe hypertension that persists >15 minutes require emergent therapy with intravenous labetalol or hydralazine, or immediate-release oral nifedipine.
  • Pregnant individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD) have a greater risk for preeclampsia, acute kidney injury, progression of CKD, end-stage kidney disease, preterm delivery, gestational hypertension, intrauterine growth retardation, and fetal loss.
  • Patients with kidney transplants should wait at least 1 to 2 years after transplantation with a stable allograft and stable immunosuppression before attempting conception.
  • The immunosuppressants mycophenolate mofetil and sirolimus are teratogenic and must be discontinued before attempting conception.

index.title: Headache and Facial Pain
index.keyPoints:
• Head CT is indicated to assess acute headaches in the setting of trauma or suspected vascular origin; brain MRI is more appropriate for subacute or chronic headaches with new or progressive features.
  • Patients with a stable pattern of migraine or tension-type headache and a normal examination do not require neuroimaging.
  • Imaging is not indicated for tension-type headache.
  • Acetaminophen, aspirin, NSAIDs, and caffeine-containing compounds are effective immediate treatments for tension-type headache; amitriptyline is the only preventive agent shown to be effective in controlled trials.
  • Muscle relaxants, benzodiazepines, opioids, and onabotulinum toxin A have no role in managing tension-type headache.
  • The POUND mnemonic (Pulsatile quality of headache, One-day duration, Unilateral location, Nausea or vomiting, Disabling intensity) is helpful for recalling the symptoms typically associated with migraine.
  • In the presence of a stable clinical pattern of migraine and a normal neurologic examination, brain imaging is not indicated.
  • Because of an associated increased risk for stroke, estrogen-containing oral contraceptives should be avoided in migraine with aura of all subtypes.
  • In treating migraine, the use of triptans, ergot alkaloids, opioids, or combination analgesics should be limited to fewer than 8 to 10 days per month to prevent medication overuse headache.
  • Strong evidence supports the effectiveness of several NSAIDs in treating acute migraine.
  • Triptans are migraine-specific agents that are useful in moderate to severe migraine that has not responded to NSAID therapy; combining an NSAID with a triptan has superior efficacy to monotherapy with either agent.
  • Triptans are contraindicated in the presence of coronary, cerebral, or peripheral vascular disease; uncontrolled hypertension; or migraine with brainstem or hemiplegic auras.
  • Newer migraine-specific acute agents, including ditans and gepants, have favorable safety and tolerability profiles but are more expensive and slightly less effective than triptans; they are especially useful when triptans are contraindicated.
  • Migraine prevention requires nonpharmacologic measures, including trigger identification and avoidance, stress management, sleep management, dietary changes, and exercise.
  • Pharmacologic prophylaxis of episodic migraine should be considered in patients with high headache frequency (≥4 days/month) or debilitating headaches despite adequate acute treatment.
  • Topiramate is first-line pharmacologic prophylaxis for chronic migraine.
  • Initial options for episodic migraine prophylaxis include propranolol, metoprolol, amitriptyline, venlafaxine, and valproate.
  • One or two adequate but unsuccessful trials of traditional nonspecific preventive medications should be completed before using migraine-specific agents or onabotulinum toxin A for migraine prevention.
  • Cluster headache and the other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias are the most severe and stereotypic primary headache disorders and are characterized by pain in the periorbital or temporal areas with ipsilateral cranial autonomic features.
  • Cluster headache is treated with oxygen inhalation and subcutaneous sumatriptan.
  • Chronic paroxysmal hemicrania is characterized by short (2- to 30-minute) headaches occurring at least five times daily that respond to indomethacin.
  • Hemicrania continua is a persistent, side-locked headache that responds to indomethacin.
  • Thunderclap headache is a medical emergency that warrants immediate diagnostic evaluation; noncontrast head CT should be performed without delay.
  • Sensitivity of head CT for subarachnoid hemorrhage within 6 hours of onset of pain in patients without a new neurologic deficit is excellent but decreases to approximately 95% at 12 hours and to 50% at 1 week.
  • Lumbar puncture in subarachnoid hemorrhage typically reveals a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) erythrocyte count greater than 10,000/μL (10,000 × 10^6/L) and an elevated protein level; CSF xanthochromia may take 4 hours or more to develop but is nearly 100% sensitive between 12 hours and 7 days.
