  • Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) is the second most frequent cause of thunderclap headache; it is characterized by recurrent thunderclap headache and multifocal constriction of intracranial vessels normalizing within 3 months of onset.
  • Glucocorticoids may worsen the clinical course of RCVS and should be avoided when RCVS is a diagnostic consideration.
  • Headache in cerebral venous thrombosis is typically unremitting from onset and may worsen with the Valsalva maneuver; papilledema and abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI) palsy may be present secondary to increased intracranial pressure.
  • Cavernous sinus thrombosis manifests as acute-onset headache, proptosis, periorbital edema, and ophthalmoplegia; it usually involves extension of dental or sinus bacterial infections and requires immediate administration of antibiotics and, frequently, surgical drainage.
  • Dissections of the cervical arterial vessels often present with acute pain in the head and neck and are a common cause of stroke in patients younger than 50 years; anticoagulation is not superior to aspirin treatment.
  • Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) is suggested by the presence of headache, visual symptoms, and pulsatile tinnitus; a cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure greater than 250 mm H~2O in the absence of another cause of increased pressure with normal cerebrospinal fluid composition confirms the diagnosis.
  • IIH treatment is aimed primarily at preserving vision; weight loss in patients with an elevated BMI and acetazolamide are the treatments of choice.
  • Intracranial hypotension presents as a postural headache, typically worsening within 20 seconds of sitting or standing, and is sometimes accompanied by tinnitus, diplopia, neck pain, nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia.
  • Treatment of persistent headache associated with intracranial hypotension caused by cerebrospinal fluid leakage after a lumbar puncture begins with bed rest and oral caffeine; an autologous epidural blood patch should be considered in patients with refractory headaches and those with severe neurologic symptoms.
  • Spontaneous intracranial hypotension is often associated with a spinal leak, which may be detected in 50% of patients by spinal MRI or CT myelography.
  • Medication overuse headache (MOH) can result from frequent use of simple analgesics, triptans, ergot alkaloids, opioids, or combination analgesics; MOH has not been demonstrated with the use of ditans or gepants.
  • Treatment of MOH includes discontinuing the overused medication and using appropriate preventive medication directed at the primary headache disorder.
  • Opioids and butalbital compounds are associated with an increased risk for headache progression and should be avoided in patients with recurrent primary headache disorders.
  • Acetaminophen, low-dose aspirin, diphenhydramine, and metoclopramide are considered relatively safe options for acute headache treatment in pregnant patients, and triptans may be reasonable for patients with more severe migraine; however, NSAIDs are not recommended after 20 weeks' gestation.
  • Contrast-enhanced brain MRI with magnetic resonance angiography is the initial imaging test indicated for patients with trigeminal neuralgia.
  • Trigeminal neuralgia is initially managed with carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine; if medical therapy is unsuccessful, percutaneous radiofrequency coagulation, glycerol injection, focused stereotactic (gamma knife) radiosurgery, or posterior fossa microvascular decompression may be effective.
  • Occipital neuralgia treatments include conservative measures, such as massage or cool compresses, and occipital nerve injection.

index.title: Head Injury
index.keyPoints:
• When indicated, noncontrast CT is the imaging modality of choice for evaluating traumatic brain injury because of its wide availability, low expense, ability to rapidly diagnose hemorrhage, and high sensitivity for bony injuries.
  • CDC indications for using head CT to evaluate patients with mild traumatic brain injury (TBI) have nearly 100% sensitivity (but low specificity) for identifying patients with clinically important findings.
  • Patients with mild TBI, a normal neurologic examination, and (when necessary) a normal head CT scan may be safely followed as outpatients.
  • The symptoms of mild TBI, which usually involves brief or no loss of consciousness, typically resolve spontaneously within 7 to 10 days.
  • Posttraumatic headaches usually have the characteristics of migraine and tension-type headaches, and treatment is matched to the headache phenotype; opioids and butalbital products should be avoided.
  • Medical management of severe traumatic brain injury includes normalization of blood oxygenation and pressure, control of fever and blood glucose, thromboprophylaxis for deep venous thrombosis, seizure prophylaxis, and treatment of infections and gastrointestinal complications; glucocorticoids should be avoided.
  • Patients with an epidural hematoma may have a “lucid interval” followed by rapid neurologic compromise; headache, vomiting, and declining mental status may occur early.
  • In patients with epidural hematoma, urgent surgical evacuation is recommended for those with a Glasgow Coma Scale score lower than 9, anisocoria, or a hematoma greater than 30 mL in volume.
  • Subacute and chronic subdural hematomas may be associated with nonspecific symptoms, including headache, altered mental status, or somnolence, in addition to focal neurologic findings.
  • Hematoma thickness greater than 10 mm, a Glasgow Coma Scale score lower than 9, and pupillary asymmetry or fixation are indications for surgical treatment of acute subdural hematoma.
  • Hematoma thickness greater than 10 mm, midline shift greater than 5 mm, and progressive neurologic symptoms are indications for surgical treatment of chronic subdural hematoma.
  • Any athlete suspected of sustaining a mild traumatic brain injury (TBI) should be immediately removed from play and assessed by a clinician trained in evaluating and managing concussion.
  • Full return to play should occur only after symptoms related to mild TBI resolve and the patient returns to a preinjury neurocognitive state, has no symptoms with physical or cognitive exertion or stress, and successfully completes an individualized return-to-play protocol.
  • The prevalence of posttraumatic stress disorder is higher in military personnel with mild traumatic brain injury (TBI) than in civilians with mild TBI; both groups are at increased risk for suicide.
  • In patients receiving anticoagulation who experience traumatic brain injury (TBI), immediate reversal of anticoagulants is indicated.
  • The optimal time to resume anticoagulation after TBI requires balancing the risks for bleeding and thrombosis; resuming anticoagulation within 6 days increases the risk for intracranial hemorrhage, while delaying treatment beyond 13 days increases thrombotic complications.

index.title: Seizures and Epilepsy
index.keyPoints:
• Epilepsy is defined as at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or one unprovoked seizure with a risk for further seizures that is similar to the risk after two unprovoked seizures (≥60%).
  • Although both may present as staring episodes, focal impaired consciousness seizures can be distinguished from absence seizures by their longer duration, lower frequency, and the presence of aura and postictal confusion.
  • Myoclonic seizures are a single quick jerk of a limb or the entire body lasting less than a second; they can occur repetitively and result in falls.
  • Atonic seizures present with sudden loss of muscle tone, whereas tonic seizures present as increased muscle tone, which may be limited to the arms and head or involve the entire body.
  • Temporal lobe epilepsy is the most common adult-onset focal epilepsy; typical symptoms include aura, loss of awareness, staring, behavioral arrest, and amnesia.
  • In temporal lobe epilepsy, MRI may show mesial temporal sclerosis with hippocampal atrophy, T2 hyperintensity, and loss of internal architecture.
  • In most adults with focal epilepsy, brain MRI is normal and the cause is unknown.
  • The presence of myoclonic seizures is required for the diagnosis of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME); JME often is not diagnosed, however, until the first generalized tonic-clonic seizure (GTCS) occurs because myoclonic seizures often remain unrecognized.
  • Most patients with JME have GTCS, and approximately 30% of patients have absence seizures.
  • Lifelong antiseizure medication therapy is typically recommended for patients with JME.
  • Eliciting a history of previous staring events or myoclonus may help identify epilepsy.
  • Provoking factors can cause seizures in patients with or without epilepsy; medications and alcohol withdrawal are common provoking factors.
  • Seizure triggers lead to seizures in patients with preexisting epilepsy but do not cause epilepsy; common triggers include sleep deprivation, fever, and infection.
  • In differentiating seizures from stroke, seizures have positive symptoms, such as jerking, tingling, and visual flashes, whereas strokes have negative symptoms, such as weakness, numbness, and other neurologic losses of function.
  • Psychogenic nonepileptic spells/events, or functional seizures, are most often related to posttraumatic stress disorder or conversion disorder, and factitious disorder and malingering are rare; management should emphasize early diagnosis with video electroencephalographic monitoring.
  • Psychogenic nonepileptic spells/events may be characterized by nonstereotypical features, atypical postures, asynchronous limb flailing, side-to-side head shaking, and normal mental status.
  • MRI and electroencephalography are recommended for all patients with a first seizure; lumbar puncture is recommended only if an infectious cause is suspected.
  • A single routine electroencephalogram is only 40% to 50% sensitive in diagnosing epilepsy, so clinical judgment based on history is critical to diagnosis.
  • Continuous video electroencephalography is the only method of diagnosing nonconvulsive status epilepticus, but diagnosis often requires clinical correlation.
  • After a single unprovoked seizure in a patient with normal MRI and electroencephalographic (EEG) findings and with no risk factors for epilepsy, the 2-year recurrence risk is approximately 20% to 30%, and treatment is typically withheld.
  • In the setting of two unprovoked seizures or one unprovoked seizure with significant EEG or MRI abnormalities, the recurrence risk is at least 60%, and treatment is recommended.
  • Empiric treatment with antiseizure medication (ASM) generally is not recommended unless the patient's history and evaluation are strongly suggestive of epilepsy; exceptions include convulsive status epilepticus and critically ill patients.
  • Alcohol- or benzodiazepine-withdrawal seizures, which usually occur within 48 hours of cessation of use, typically are not treated with ASMs.
  • Newer ASMs, although not more effective in controlling seizures than older ASMs, are often preferred because they have fewer adverse effects, fewer drug interactions, and a reduced need for laboratory monitoring.
  • Epilepsy treatment usually is guided by the seizure type rather than drug mechanism or epilepsy cause.
  • Enzyme-inducing ASMs increase statin clearance and necessitate higher doses or alternative options; because these ASMs and valproate can increase bone catabolism, bone density testing and supplemental calcium and vitamin D are recommended with long-term use.
  • Lamotrigine is a first-line, broad-spectrum ASM with an overall excellent safety and efficacy profile but must be titrated slowly; rapid titration has been associated with Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome (also known as drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms [DRESS]), and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.
  • All ASMs carry a warning about worsening depression and suicidality, and all patients must be screened and monitored for these symptoms.
  • In adults who are seizure-free for at least 2 years, the American Academy of Neurology recommends discussing the risks and benefits of ASM withdrawal with the patient; risks include higher seizure recurrence and a small chance that they will no longer respond to medications.
  • The risk for sudden unexpected death in epilepsy is approximately 1 in 1000 and increases to approximately 1 in 100 in patients with drug-resistant seizures, especially those with uncontrolled generalized tonic-clonic seizures and those taking multiple antiseizure medications.
  • Any patient who does not achieve seizure freedom after treatment with two adequately dosed, appropriately chosen antiseizure medications is considered to have drug-resistant epilepsy and should be referred to an epilepsy center to confirm the diagnosis and determine surgical candidacy.
  • In patients with drug-resistant epilepsy, the efficacy of three or more antiseizure medications is less than 10%; surgical resection can lead to seizure freedom in 60% to 70% of appropriately chosen patients with temporal lobe epilepsy.
  • In older patients, levetiracetam, lamotrigine, and gabapentin are better tolerated and as effective as older antiseizure medications; valproate should be used cautiously because it can cause (reversible) parkinsonism and cognitive dysfunction.
  • Treatment of catamenial seizures focuses on the best antiseizure medication (ASM) regimen for the patient's epilepsy syndrome; in patients whose seizures are uncontrolled by ASMs, adding progestin-containing oral contraceptives or acetazolamide may be helpful.
  • In women with epilepsy of childbearing potential, levetiracetam, lamotrigine, and oxcarbazepine have minimal evidence of teratogenicity and are the preferred treatment options.
  • Pregnancy alone is not reason enough to stop ASMs in women with epilepsy whose disease is well controlled; physicians must balance the risk for teratogenicity with that for uncontrolled seizures, particularly generalized tonic-clonic seizures, which can result in fetal anoxia and death.
  • Valproate, phenobarbital, phenytoin, topiramate, carbamazepine, and ASM polypharmacy are associated with major congenital malformations and, if possible, should be avoided in pregnant patients with epilepsy.
  • In patients with likely convulsive status epilepticus (CSE), empiric therapy is indicated without awaiting results of electroencephalography, imaging, serum studies, or lumbar puncture because a longer duration of CSE is strongly linked to worse outcomes.
  • First-line treatment of CSE is an intravenous benzodiazepine (or intramuscular midazolam), typically followed by an intravenous antiseizure medication to avoid seizure recurrence.
  • If CSE does not cease, intubation is typically required, and patients are placed in an anesthetically induced coma for 24 to 48 hours using propofol, midazolam, or pentobarbital.
  • Nonconvulsive status epilepticus should be suspected and immediate continuous electroencephalographic monitoring initiated when a patient has altered mental status with an unclear cause, including patients in medical or surgical ICUs, even those without a known neurologic history.

index.title: Stroke
index.keyPoints:
• Determining whether a stroke is ischemic or hemorrhagic has important implications for immediate therapeutics, prevention strategies, and prognosis.
  • Hemorrhagic strokes may be intracerebral (intraparenchymal or intraventricular) or subarachnoid.
  • Neuroimaging, preferably noncontrast head CT, is required before initiating treatment for stroke.
  • Although MRI is more sensitive than CT for diagnosing acute infarction, it is not the initial test of choice to exclude hemorrhagic stroke or to make treatment decisions about thrombolysis for ischemic stroke because of its longer acquisition time.
  • In acute stroke, CT angiography of the head and neck and CT perfusion scanning may be performed emergently if endovascular therapy is being considered.
  • Duplex ultrasonography is the initial test of choice for evaluating internal carotid artery (ICA) stenosis because of its wide availability, low cost, and low risk; if high-grade ICA stenosis is detected and the patient is a candidate for surgery or stenting, confirmatory testing is required before intervention.
  • Atrial fibrillation is the most common cause of cardioembolic stroke, and indicated testing includes telemetry in patients with ischemic stroke in whom the cause has not been identified and prolonged outpatient cardiac monitoring in embolic stroke of undetermined source (ESUS).
  • The use of transesophageal echocardiography to evaluate for an intracardiac source of stroke is not routinely indicated in patients who are older, given the low yield for findings that require anticoagulation or surgery.
  • Lacunar infarcts resulting in isolated motor or sensory syndromes are caused by infarcts in deep locations, such as the internal capsule, thalamus, or pons; the main risk factor for lacunar infarcts is hypertension.
  • Patients with an ESUS have similar imaging characteristics as patients with cardioembolic stroke but have unrevealing cardiac testing and vascular imaging.
  • Patients with stenosis of the extracranial ICA greater than 70% who have a transient ischemic attack (TIA) in a downstream neurologic territory have the highest risk for stroke within 2 weeks.
  • Expedited vascular imaging of the ICA to identify surgical candidates and evaluation for atrial fibrillation are required for all patients with TIA.
  • Treatment with intravenous thrombolytics (alteplase or tenecteplase) within 3 hours of ischemic stroke onset is associated with reduced neurologic disability at 3 months after stroke; immediate MRI can be used to identify patients who can benefit from intravenous thrombolysis when time of onset is unknown (off-label use).
  • Endovascular therapy within 24 hours of stroke onset can be considered for select patients with a clinically suspected large vessel occlusion.
  • When administered within 48 hours of ischemic stroke in patients ineligible for thrombolysis or endovascular therapy, aspirin reduces the short-term risk for recurrent stroke.
  • In high-risk transient ischemic attack or minor noncardioembolic ischemic stroke, short-term dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel reduces the risk for recurrent stroke when initiated within 72 hours.
  • Emergent administration of systemic anticoagulation for ischemic stroke (whether related to atrial fibrillation or not) does not reduce the short-term risk for recurrent stroke and increases the risk for hemorrhagic conversion.
  • The optimal timing for starting systemic anticoagulation after cardioembolic stroke depends on stroke size; initiation of a direct oral anticoagulant may be considered at 2 to 4 days in patients with mild to moderate stroke and at 6 to 7 days for those with severe stroke.
  • Management of acute hypertension in ischemic stroke differs when thrombolysis is not involved; if not required by acute comorbid conditions, early blood pressure lowering, especially in patients with blood pressure lower than 220/120 mm Hg, is not recommended.
  • Internal carotid artery revascularization for primary prevention of ischemic stroke is not routinely indicated; shared decision making should be used to decide whether revascularization should be added to medical management.
  • Patients with asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis and high-risk features, such as rapid progression or high-grade stenosis, may be considered for revascularization based on perioperative risk analysis.
  • Chronic antiplatelet agents are indicated for patients with noncardioembolic ischemic stroke and transient ischemic attack (TIA); the underlying stroke subtype drives the choice of medication.
  • Chronic antiplatelet agents in noncardioembolic stroke may include aspirin, clopidogrel, or aspirin-dipyridamole; clopidogrel and aspirin-dipyridamole may be slightly superior to aspirin, but cost and ease of use make aspirin an appropriate alternative.
  • Prasugrel should be avoided in patients with a previous stroke.
  • Patients with nondisabling stroke or TIA due to stenosis of the internal carotid artery (ICA) greater than 70% and some patients with stenosis of 50% to 69% may benefit from early revascularization; in patients with complete symptomatic occlusion of the ICA, however, revascularization is not indicated.
  • Symptomatic intracranial artery stenosis greater than 70% is associated with a high risk for recurrent stroke and should be treated with a high-intensity statin, aggressive blood pressure control, and long-term aspirin use with consideration of clopidogrel for the first 90 days; stenting the affected artery is associated with a high risk for procedural stroke and should be avoided.
  • Patients with ischemic stroke may develop worsening deficits from hemorrhagic conversion of the infarct, usually within 48 hours; antiplatelet agents should be held in most patients with large hemorrhagic conversion for at least 1 week and for a shorter period in patients with petechial pattern hemorrhagic conversion with stable imaging.
  • Patients with significant symptomatic cerebral edema and increased intracranial pressure after an ischemic stroke have a survival advantage with decompressive hemicraniectomy, although neurologic compromise may be significant.
  • The most common cause of intracerebral hemorrhage that affects deep structures of the brain (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum) is hypertension.
  • Causes of lobar intracerebral hemorrhage near the cortical surface include hypertension, hemorrhagic tumors, arteriovenous malformations, cortical vein thrombosis, and, in patients older than 50 years, cerebral amyloid angiopathy.
  • Routine use of platelet transfusion in patients with intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) caused by antiplatelet agents is not indicated.
  • Blood pressure treatment is recommended for patients with ICH, with a treatment target between 130 and less than 140 mm Hg; intravenous nitrates should be avoided.
  • Early withdrawal of blood pressure control is associated with increased mortality in ICH; guidelines caution against terminating care in the first 48 hours.
  • Osmotherapy with mannitol or hypertonic saline may temporarily reduce intracranial pressure in patients with ICH; glucocorticoids are ineffective and should not be routinely administered.
  • Anticoagulation should be initiated if ICH is caused by cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.
  • In patients with cerebellar hemorrhage greater than 3 cm in diameter or volume greater than 15 mL, prophylactic decompression is recommended; surgical decompression for cerebral hemorrhages is considered on a case-by-case basis depending on locations and signs of elevated intracranial pressure.
  • The most common cause of subarachnoid hemorrhage is saccular (berry) aneurysm rupture, which has the highest morbidity and mortality among causes of hemorrhagic stroke.
  • Saccular cerebral aneurysms can often be visualized with CT angiography or magnetic resonance angiography, although the resolution is insufficient to detect smaller aneurysms; catheter-based angiography is necessary to definitively diagnose aneurysms and other causes of subarachnoid hemorrhage.
  • Within the first 48 hours of a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), aneurysmal rebleeding is a major cause of morbidity; early surgical treatment of the ruptured aneurysm and maintenance of a systolic blood pressure below 160 mm Hg are required.
  • In aneurysmal SAH, cerebral vasospasm with resultant delayed cerebral ischemia and neurologic worsening may develop beginning near day 5, and frequent monitoring with transcranial Doppler imaging (or CT angiography and perfusion studies) is recommended in all patients.
  • All patients with aneurysmal SAH should be treated as soon as possible with prophylactic nimodipine to reduce the risk for cerebral vasospasm.
  • Patients with SAH are at high risk for cardiac and pulmonary complications from a large sympathetic surge and typically require care in a specialized ICU with experience in treating SAH.
  • Hypertension management significantly reduces the risk for all hemorrhagic stroke subtypes.
  • In patients with cerebral amyloid angiopathy, long-term anticoagulation should be avoided given the annual risk for bleeding of up to 10% for first, and recurrent, intracerebral hemorrhage.
  • Cerebral aneurysms smaller than 7 mm in diameter have a low risk for rupture and can often be managed conservatively with annual noninvasive neuroimaging in the absence of multiple risk factors for rupture.
  • Pulmonary embolism is a leading cause of mortality in patients with stroke, and pharmacologic prophylaxis should be started for all patients.
  • In patients with ischemic stroke, prophylaxis against pulmonary embolism should start on admission except in patients treated with thrombolysis, in whom a 24-hour neuroimage showing no hemorrhage is required first.
  • In patients with hemorrhagic stroke, subcutaneous heparin or enoxaparin should be started 24 hours after intracerebral hemorrhage if imaging shows no evidence of expansion and in subarachnoid hemorrhage upon securing the aneurysm.
  • Patients undergoing cardiac surgery involving cardiopulmonary bypass, particularly multivalve procedures, are at highest risk for stroke in the postoperative setting, most commonly from atrial fibrillation.
  • Surgery within 90 days of stroke, regardless of cause, increases the risk for perioperative stroke; elective surgeries should be avoided within this time.
  • Most patients with stroke exhibit neurologic impairment and disability 1 year after stroke and beyond; depression is highly prevalent in patients with stroke and is one of the leading modifiable risk factors for long-term disability.
  • Patients with poststroke fatigue should be screened for poststroke sleep-disordered breathing with polysomnography; screening questionnaires for sleep-disordered breathing may not be as effective in patients with stroke.

index.title: Cognitive Impairment
index.keyPoints:
• Cognitive impairment may affect any or all of the five major domains of cognitive function: memory, executive function, attention and concentration, language, and visuospatial perception; highlighting the initial and predominant domains of impairment is helpful in making the diagnosis.
  • Subjective cognitive impairment describes a syndrome of persistent self-perceived cognitive decline that cannot be detected with cognitive testing tools; patients with subjective cognitive impairment are at heightened risk for developing mild cognitive impairment (MCI).
  • MCI is defined as cognitive decline (based on history and objective cognitive testing) with preservation of normal day-to-day function.
  • Dementia is diagnosed when cognitive impairment is associated with a decline in the patient's ability to perform basic or instrumental activities of daily living.
  • The Mini–Mental State Examination and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) are the most frequently used screening tools for cognitive impairment; the MoCA includes more tasks regarding the executive and visuospatial domains and is more applicable for patients with such impairments.
  • Evaluation of a patient with established cognitive impairment focuses on determining the underlying cause, including whether a neurodegenerative process is present; nondegenerative causes of cognitive impairment are often reversible and must be recognized and addressed early in the clinical course.
  • In patients with cognitive impairment, the cognitive examination should be followed by a neurologic examination to detect any deficits that may be attributable to cerebrovascular disease or motor evidence of neurodegenerative disease, such as parkinsonism.
  • Evaluation of a patient with cognitive impairment should include a complete blood count, a comprehensive metabolic profile, and measurement of thyroid-stimulating hormone, serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and serum vitamin B~12 levels.
  • When evaluating cognitive impairment, testing for syphilis is indicated only if suspected from the history; the treponemal antibody test is preferred over the rapid plasma reagin test.
  • Behavioral and mental health issues, including mood disorders, personality changes, altered eating habits, obsessions, social isolation, and sleep impairment, may be a cause of cognitive impairment or may be seen in some forms of dementia.
  • Safety must be assessed in patients with cognitive impairment by asking about falls, wandering, leaving the stove on, difficulty driving, and firearms.
  • Normal-pressure hydrocephalus is a clinical syndrome of cognitive impairment, gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and ventriculomegaly on brain MRI.
  • Early diagnosis of normal-pressure hydrocephalus is imperative for benefit from ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement; documented improvement in gait after high-volume lumbar puncture can help confirm the diagnosis and select patients for referral for ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement.
  • Vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) is the second most common cause of mild cognitive impairment and dementia after Alzheimer disease; it is divided into four subtypes: subcortical ischemic cognitive impairment, poststroke cognitive impairment, multi-infarct cognitive impairment, and mixed cognitive impairment.
  • In subcortical vascular (ischemic) cognitive impairment, disruption of the frontal-subcortical circuits most prominently results in executive and attention impairment.
  • Pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic treatment of modifiable cardiovascular risk factors, including hypertension, dyslipidemia, and diabetes mellitus, are recommended for managing VCI.
  • Recommended lifestyle changes for patients with VCI include 150 minutes per week of physical activity divided into three to five sessions, cognitive and social stimulation, and healthy dietary habits.
  • Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, such as donepezil or galantamine, are used to treat mild to moderate stages of VCI, whereas combination therapy with memantine has utility in moderate to severe disease (all used off label).
  • Typical Alzheimer disease usually occurs in patients older than 65 years and presents with an amnesic clinical profile with progressive impairments in episodic memory.
  • Brain MRI showing atrophy of the mesial temporal structures and parietal lobe supports a diagnosis of Alzheimer disease.
  • Patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia who are candidates for disease-modifying therapy in the appropriate clinical setting require biomarker testing such as amyloid PET scanning and cerebrospinal fluid analysis for Alzheimer disease to confirm eligibility.
  • Mild to moderate Alzheimer disease may be treated with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors; in patients with moderate to severe disease, memantine (N-methyl-d-aspartate antagonist) may be added or used alone.
  • Pharmacologic management of the atypical Alzheimer disease variants is the same as that for typical Alzheimer disease; however, additional targeted management is used for behavioral and visuospatial impairments.
  • Dysexecutive Alzheimer disease typically presents before age 65 years with predominant executive impairment, including difficulty in decision making, planning, and multitasking.
  • Posterior cortical atrophy presents as visual impairments due to deficits in visuospatial perception, including simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, and oculomotor apraxia.
  • Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) accounts for 10% of dementias diagnosed in patients younger than 65 years; behavioral variant FTD (bvFTD) is the most common form.
  • Early behavioral changes characterize bvFTD; significant impairment in executive functioning, hyperorality, compulsive behaviors, and loss of empathy are common.
  • Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first-line therapy for behavioral symptoms in bvFTD (off-label use).
  • Primary progressive aphasia (PPA) is characterized by dementia with predominant language impairment; three variants exist and are differentiated on the basis of the specific language deficit present.
  • Treatment for PPA includes speech therapy, management of neurobehavioral symptoms, and treatment of cognitive deficits with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and/or N-methyl-d-aspartate antagonists in appropriate patients.
  • Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is characterized by cognitive fluctuations, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder.
  • Parkinson disease dementia differs from DLB in the appearance of parkinsonian signs substantially before the onset of cognitive symptoms.
  • Treatment of Parkinson disease dementia and DLB includes acetylcholinesterase inhibitors; management of parkinsonian features differs between the diseases, as antiparkinsonian medications can worsen hallucinations in patients with DLB.
  • Many patients with DLB are extremely sensitive to neuroleptic medications, particularly first-generation agents, and are at high risk for severe worsening of symptoms resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome when exposed to these drugs.
  • Traumatic encephalopathy syndrome (TES) is a clinical syndrome of progressive neurodegenerative cognitive impairment following repetitive head trauma; it is associated with increased irritability, aggressiveness, personality changes, depression, and suicidality.
  • Therapeutic management of the behavioral, motor, and social symptoms of TES often requires a multidisciplinary team of clinicians, social workers, physical therapists, and occupational therapists.
  • Patients with rapidly progressive dementia must be assessed for reversible or treatable causes.
  • Wernicke encephalopathy is a common reversible clinical syndrome characterized by cognitive impairment, oculomotor dysfunction, and gait ataxia; it arises from thiamine (vitamin B~1) deficiency.
  • Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is characterized by rapidly progressive cognitive impairment variably accompanied by akinetic mutism, myoclonus, extrapyramidal signs, visual changes, and cerebellar dysfunction.
  • The real-time quaking-induced conversion (also called the RT-QuIC) assay for abnormal prion protein in cerebrospinal fluid is highly suggestive of CJD, with sensitivity exceeding 90% and specificity approaching 100%.
  • Delirium manifests as acute waxing and waning confusion that lasts for hours to days and involves multiple cognitive domains, most typically with attention and concentration, executive, and behavioral changes.
  • In delirium management, the underlying medical condition should be treated and nonpharmacologic behavioral interventions reinforced; physical and chemical restraints should be avoided when possible.
  • Nonpharmacologic methods of managing delirium should be prioritized and include engagement and empowerment of family members, calm redirection, adequate pain management, and promotion of early mobility.
  • In treating patients who have dementia with superimposed delirium, use of typical and atypical antipsychotics has been associated with increased morbidity and mortality and should be avoided.
  • Sundowning should be considered after common medical causes of delirium have been ruled out and collateral history from an informant supports the diagnosis; it is managed with nonpharmacologic behavioral interventions.
  • Anxiety and depression are common in patients with neurocognitive syndromes; nonpharmacologic interventions such as sleep hygiene, improved diet, exercise, and social and cognitive stimulation are preferred as first-line treatment.
  • Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and trazodone may be useful for managing irritability, including verbal aggression, agitation, and depressive symptoms, in patients with dementia if nonpharmacologic interventions are ineffective.
  • Typical and atypical antipsychotics have an FDA boxed warning for possible increased risk for morbidity and mortality in patients with dementia; patients and caregivers should be informed of this risk before this class of medication is prescribed.
  • Quetiapine is commonly used for patients with dementia and psychotic features because of its lower risk for extrapyramidal adverse effects; risperidone has the greatest evidence for managing neurobehavioral and psychotic symptoms in patients with dementia but has a greater risk for extrapyramidal symptoms.

index.title: Movement Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• Parkinsonism is the most typical hypokinetic movement disorder pattern; it is characterized by paucity and slowness of movements (bradykinesia).
  • Hyperkinetic movement disorders are classified according to the rhythmicity, suppressibility, randomness, and directionality of involuntary movements.
  • The diagnosis of Parkinson disease requires the presence of bradykinesia and at least one other cardinal feature of the disorder (tremor at rest, cogwheel rigidity, and gait or balance impairment) and the absence of red flags for atypical forms of parkinsonism.
  • MRI can rule out stroke or hydrocephalus in select patients with possible Parkinson disease but is unnecessary in patients who have classic Parkinson disease with no other neurologic symptoms or signs and a good response to levodopa.
  • In Parkinson disease, a dopamine transporter single-photon emission CT scan is unnecessary except to differentiate Parkinson disease from essential tremor or drug-induced parkinsonism if the distinction cannot be made clinically.
  • Depression and anxiety are common in Parkinson disease, and all patients with Parkinson disease should be screened annually for depression.
  • All patients with Parkinson disease should also be assessed for fall risk at each visit; a positive pull test result is the most reliable predictor of a risk for backward falls.
  • Detecting risk factors for falling and implementing a multidisciplinary management approach—including medications, therapy, supportive devices, and education—can reduce morbidity and costs related to falls in Parkinson disease.
  • Levodopa is the initial preferred therapy for most patients with the motor symptoms of early Parkinson disease; it should be started when the symptoms begin to impair the patient's quality of life.
  • Dopamine agonists may be prescribed as the initial dopaminergic therapy in Parkinson disease to improve motor symptoms in selected patients younger than 60 years who are at higher risk for dyskinesia.
  • Immediate-release formulations of levodopa, which have a rapid peak-dose effect, should be prescribed initially at the lowest effective dosage to minimize risk for dyskinesia.
  • Over time, as many as 50% of patients with Parkinson disease may develop motor fluctuations, including the “wearing-off” phenomenon, the “sudden off” state and the “early morning off” state; extended-release levodopa formulations may offer more sustained symptom control and reduce wearing off between doses.
  • Medication-induced psychosis, especially visual hallucinations, can occur with use of dopaminergic medications; addressing triggers and simplifying the medication regimen (including removing non-levodopa medications and decreasing the levodopa dosage) may result in improvement.
  • Device-assisted therapies (including deep brain stimulation [DBS], continuous levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel infusion, continuous subcutaneous levodopa infusion, and continuous subcutaneous apomorphine infusion) are indicated for patients who continue to benefit from levodopa but experience severe motor fluctuations; DBS is also indicated for medication-refractory tremor.
  • Parkinson-plus syndromes often are more rapidly progressive than Parkinson disease, have additional features that are atypical for idiopathic Parkinson disease, and are less responsive to standard antiparkinsonian therapies, particularly levodopa.
  • The three primary Parkinson-plus syndromes include progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy, and corticobasal degeneration.
  • Drug-induced parkinsonism may occur with dopamine receptor–blocking antipsychotic agents and antiemetic medications; it is symmetric, lacks nonmotor features, and is reversible after removal of the causative agent.
  • Essential tremor is the most common movement disorder and often presents with an isolated bilateral upper extremity action tremor; common features include a positive family history, slow progression, adolescent or middle-aged onset, and alleviation by alcohol.
  • Essential tremor treatment is based on symptoms; the most effective pharmacologic agents are propranolol, primidone, and topiramate.
  • Patients with refractory essential tremor often respond favorably to neurosurgical therapies.
  • Dystonia involves sustained or intermittent muscle contractions leading to stereotyped and directional twisting and posturing movements of specific body parts.
  • Treatment of generalized dystonia includes anticholinergic agents and, in patients with severe or refractory dystonia, globus pallidus interna deep brain stimulation; focal or segmental dystonia can be treated with botulinum toxin injections.
  • Patients with acute and subacute onset of chorea should be assessed for potentially reversible acquired causes, such as autoimmune, toxic, and metabolic causes.
  • Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant condition marked by symptoms of progressive generalized chorea, parkinsonism, gait impairment, impulsiveness, psychiatric disease, and dementia; it is the most common neurodegenerative cause of generalized chorea.
  • Myoclonus is a fast, shock-like, jerky movement that can be physiologic (e.g., hypnic jerks at sleep onset) or pathologic (caused by medications, toxins, or systemic or central disease).
  • Myoclonus treatment includes addressing the underlying systemic or toxic causes and administering antimyoclonic agents, such as clonazepam, levetiracetam, or valproic acid.
  • Tics are stereotyped, rapid, partially suppressible movements interrupting the flow of normal movements and may provide transient relief from premonitory uncomfortable sensations.
  • Tourette syndrome is characterized by childhood-onset motor and phonic tics with a duration of at least 1 year.
  • Treatment of Tourette syndrome includes reassurance (in mild disease), cognitive behavioral therapy, and addressing psychiatric comorbidities; pharmacotherapy is indicated when tics interfere with daily functioning, education, or work.
  • Patients with restless legs syndrome (RLS) should be screened for iron deficiency because iron supplementation in the presence of low-normal ferritin levels may resolve symptoms.
  • Nonpharmacologic management of RLS includes improving sleep hygiene, exercising, and avoiding caffeine, alcohol, and certain drugs; use of a peroneal nerve vibrational device may be helpful.
  • Gabapentin, gabapentin enacarbil, and pregabalin are first-line pharmacologic treatments for RLS.
  • Guidelines recommend against the routine use of levodopa and dopamine agonists in RLS, but these medications may offer symptom relief with short-term use at the expense of adverse effects with longer-term use.
  • Clonazepam, valproate, carbamazepine, and bupropion should not be used for RLS.
  • Periodic limb movements of sleep are diagnosed by using polysomnography; treatment is required only if the disorder causes marked sleep fragmentation.
  • Patients with rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder are at high risk for synuclein-related neurodegeneration, such as Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, or dementia with Lewy bodies.
  • Tardive dyskinesia is an extrapyramidal complication of dopamine receptor–blocking medications characterized by choreiform and dystonic craniofacial movements; symptoms can be permanent or take months to resolve.

index.title: Multiple Sclerosis
index.keyPoints:
• The most common clinical manifestations of multiple sclerosis (MS) are optic neuritis, myelitis, and brainstem/cerebellar syndromes.
  • An MS relapse is defined as new or worsening neurologic symptoms lasting more than 24 hours; symptoms typically develop over hours to days and peak in severity over days to weeks.
  • Pseudorelapses of MS are transient exacerbations of previous neurologic symptoms caused by temporary reduction in neuronal electrical conductance by systemic factors (e.g., infection, stress, and temperature elevation by internal or external factors).
  • Patients with MS may develop symptoms such as fatigue and cognitive deficits secondary to widespread cortical demyelination and nonlesional axonal pathology.
  • The McDonald criteria for diagnosing multiple sclerosis (MS) integrate symptoms of central nervous system demyelination resulting from a series of clinical relapses or progression and separated in space and time, physical examination findings, distribution of lesions on MRI, and (if necessary) the presence of cerebrospinal fluid–unique oligoclonal bands or elevated kappa free light chains.
  • In patients suspected of having MS, proper application of diagnostic criteria can prevent unnecessary neurologic testing, referrals, and misdiagnoses.
  • A standardized brain MRI protocol should be used to evaluate possible MS; spinal cord imaging also should be performed in patients with symptoms of myelitis, insufficient features on brain MRI to support the diagnosis, or an age older than 40 years and nonspecific findings on brain MRI.
  • Cerebrospinal fluid testing is not required for diagnosing MS, but the presence of oligoclonal bands or elevated kappa free light chains can support the diagnosis when the MRI criteria are not otherwise fully met.
  • Approximately 85% of patients with multiple sclerosis (MS) experience an initial relapsing-remitting course; approximately 15% have primary progressive MS at presentation.
  • Disease-modifying therapies reduce the risk for conversion from a clinically isolated syndrome to relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS) by approximately 50%.
  • In patients with clinically isolated syndrome, risk stratification can inform treatment decisions; the presence of brain lesions on MRI conveys a 10-year risk for conversion to RRMS of 90%.
  • Without treatment, half of patients with RRMS develop secondary progressive MS (SPMS) after a median of 10 to 15 years; the proportion of patients converting to SPMS has decreased since the introduction of disease-modifying therapies.
  • Studies have shown multiple benefits from both strengthening and aerobic exercise programs in patients with multiple sclerosis (MS).
  • Vitamin D deficiency is common in patients with MS and is associated with development of MS and accumulation of lesions on MRI; vitamin D supplementation may reduce fatigue symptoms and MRI activity, but reductions in relapses or disability progression have not been shown.
  • Patients with MS should receive standard immunizations, including COVID-19 and influenza; however, live vaccines are contraindicated in patients receiving immunosuppressive/immunomodulating therapies, and immunizations should be withheld during MS relapses.
  • Smoking is associated with a threefold risk for conversion from relapsing-remitting MS to secondary progressive MS and faster rates of disability accumulation.
  • The estrogenic state of pregnancy reduces disease activity in MS and may preclude the need for treatment during pregnancy, but the risk for relapse increases slightly in the first 3 months postpartum.
  • Patients with a possible relapse of multiple sclerosis (MS) should be evaluated for a pseudorelapse from the Uhthoff phenomenon, infection, metabolic disturbance, or other medical illness; appropriate pseudorelapse management focuses on treating underlying triggers and avoiding inappropriate changes to disease-modifying therapy or initiation of glucocorticoids.
  • The standard treatment for MS relapses is high-dose glucocorticoids, typically intravenous methylprednisolone; frequent or prolonged glucocorticoid treatment should be avoided to minimize the risks associated with long-term glucocorticoid use.
  • Patients with relapse of MS not benefiting from glucocorticoid treatment may respond to plasmapheresis; intravenous immune globulin has not been shown to be effective.
  • Disease-modifying therapies for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) prevent relapses and disability progression, may reduce mortality, and may prevent conversion to secondary progressive MS (SPMS).
  • All disease-modifying therapies have FDA approval for active SPMS.
  • Ocrelizumab is the only available therapy for primary progressive MS.
  • High-efficacy therapies, including ocrelizumab and ofatumumab, are increasingly used as first-line agents in RRMS because of their ability to limit long-term disease progression.
  • Although highly effective in RRMS, natalizumab and alemtuzumab are typically limited to use as second-line agents because of the risk for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and the risk for secondary autoimmunity and cytopenia, respectively.
  • Use of natalizumab and alemtuzumab in MS requires participation in a mandatory monitoring program for risk mitigation.
  • Muscle relaxants, such as baclofen, tizanidine, clonazepam, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, and intramuscular botulinum toxin, can help treat multiple sclerosis (MS)-associated spasticity (off label for MS).
  • Clinicians should be vigilant for the signs of depression in patients with MS; if present, they should assess for suicidality and have a low threshold for offering therapy and referrals to a psychiatrist.
  • Peripheral neuropathic pain in MS may be treated with gabapentin, pregabalin, and duloxetine; carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine are often used for patients with associated trigeminal neuralgia.
  • Dalfampridine, a voltage-gated potassium channel antagonist, can improve walking speed, leg strength, and gait in patients with MS and baseline gait impairment.

index.title: Disorders of the Spinal Cord
index.keyPoints:
• Corticospinal tract injury results in spastic paresis or paralysis, with weakness, hyperreflexia, muscle spasticity, and extensor plantar responses; sensation is often lost at or below the site of injury.
  • Injury to the distal spinal cord and lower roots (cauda equina syndrome) results in decreased muscle tone, areflexia, loss of perianal sensation, and bowel and bladder dysfunction.
  • Epidural abscess should be considered in patients with back pain and fever or predisposing conditions, such as bacteremia, recent back instrumentation, or a history of intravenous drug use.
  • In patients with back pain, a history of neoplasia should raise concern for metastatic disease and possible cord compression or pathologic vertebral fracture.
  • Chronic spinal stenosis due to osteoarthritic degenerative spinal disease may present with chronic myelopathic symptoms, including weakness and gait dysfunction.
  • Lumbar spinal stenosis may present as pseudoclaudication with exertional groin, thigh, or buttock pain that is relieved by sitting or lying down (especially with back flexion).
  • MRI of the spinal cord is the preferred means of diagnosing compressive myelopathy.
  • MRI of the entire spine (cervical, thoracic, and lumbar) should be performed emergently in cord compression thought to be secondary to abscess or malignancy because neurologic compromise can progress rapidly and multiple areas of the spine may be involved.
  • Glucocorticoids are not recommended to treat spinal cord compression secondary to hematoma, abscess, or trauma.
  • Spinal cord compression from metastatic disease requires emergent use of high-dose glucocorticoids and urgent surgical decompression and/or radiation therapy.
  • Spinal epidural hematoma or abscess causing cord compression usually requires surgical drainage.
  • In patients with chronic cervical or lumbar stenosis or acute disk herniation, managing symptoms is often sufficient treatment; surgical decompression is indicated for myelopathy refractory to medical management or significant or progressive neurologic deficits.
  • Evaluation of transverse myelitis (TM) centers on identifying secondary causes, especially infection and multiple sclerosis.
  • In patients with TM, complete myelitis, lack of elevated oligoclonal bands or IgG index in the cerebrospinal fluid, and lack of lesions on brain MRI are indicative of idiopathic TM (ITM) rather than other disorders, such as multiple sclerosis.
  • Treatment of ITM is intravenous methylprednisolone, sometimes combined with intravenous immune globulin or plasmapheresis.
  • The presence of a longitudinally extensive myelopathy (at least three spinal segments) should raise suspicion for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody–associated disease, or sarcoidosis-associated myelopathy.
  • Vitamin B~12 deficiency can result in subacute combined degeneration, which manifests as paresthesias, reduced vibration and position sense, and ataxia; spasticity and paraplegia may occur in severe cases.
  • In patients with symptoms suggestive of subacute combined degeneration and low-normal serum vitamin B~12 levels, serum methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels should be measured.
  • Copper deficiency and nitrous oxide use should be considered in patients with subacute combined degeneration without vitamin B~12 deficiency.

index.title: Neuromuscular Disorders
index.keyPoints:
• Laboratory evaluation for a suspected peripheral neuropathy should begin with a complete blood count, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate determination, serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chain assay, thyroid function tests, hemoglobin A~1c and fasting plasma glucose measurement, and vitamin B~12 measurement.
  • Weakness, asymmetry, proximal findings, a rapid course, or atypical features should prompt electromyography/nerve conduction study testing in a patient with a suspected peripheral neuropathy.
  • Electromyography and nerve conduction studies can differentiate neuropathy from other neuromuscular disorders and determine whether it is axonal or demyelinating.
  • Nerve biopsy should be considered only in the rare setting of diagnostic uncertainty in which a vasculitic, infectious, or infiltrative neuropathy is suspected.
  • In patients with carpal tunnel syndrome, weakness, thenar atrophy, refractory pain, or active denervation evident on electromyography/nerve conduction studies should prompt decompression surgery.
  • In patients with ulnar mononeuropathy, persistent pain, weakness, or active denervation on electromyography/nerve conduction studies should prompt decompression surgery.
  • Peroneal nerve palsy presents as foot drop and is caused by compression of the nerve at the head of the fibula, usually caused by crossing the legs, immobility, obesity, trauma, or compression of the leg against a bed railing.
  • In classic Bell palsy, brain imaging and extensive laboratory testing are not required, but testing for Lyme disease should be considered in endemic areas.
  • Treatment with a 10-day course of oral prednisone, started within 72 hours of onset, may expedite the rate and speed of full recovery in Bell palsy.
  • Antiviral monotherapy should be avoided in Bell palsy; adding antiviral therapy to prednisone may be considered in severe cases.
  • Plexopathies present with motor and sensory deficits in the territory of multiple contiguous nerves or dermatomes.
  • Diabetes mellitus, malignancy, radiation, infection, and trauma are common causes of plexopathies; imaging must be performed to rule out structural lesions and malignancy.
  • The most common form of diabetic neuropathy is a symmetric distal neuropathy involving small and large sensory fibers and, to a much lesser extent, distal motor nerves; examination shows length-dependent loss of light touch, pinprick, and vibration sensations; loss of the ankle reflex; and, in advanced disease, distal weakness.
  • Autonomic diabetic neuropathy causes orthostatic hypotension, bladder and erectile dysfunction, abnormal hidrosis, and gastroparesis.
  • Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoneuropathy (also called diabetic amyotrophy) presents as subacute painful involvement of the proximal lumbosacral plexus with subsequent bilateral but markedly asymmetric weakness with atrophy and unintentional weight loss; management includes supportive measures, physical therapy, and pain control.
  • Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) commonly presents with ascending weakness that starts in the lower extremities and spreads to the upper limbs and bulbar and respiratory muscles, reaching its nadir in less than 4 weeks.
  • Electromyography/nerve conduction studies are the confirmatory tests in GBS and show a predominantly demyelinating pattern; sensitivity is initially low but increases to 90% by week 5.
  • All patients with GBS should be hospitalized for close respiratory and cardiovascular monitoring.
  • In GBS, serial measurements of forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force are necessary to recognize the development of respiratory failure.
  • Plasmapheresis and intravenous immune globulin have equal efficacy in shortening recovery time and ventilation duration in GBS.
  • Glucocorticoids may worsen outcomes and are contraindicated in GBS.
  • Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy is an autoimmune neuropathy that presents with subacute or chronic progressive or relapsing symmetric proximal and distal weakness and sensory symptoms with diffuse areflexia.
  • Critical illness axonal polyneuropathy often coexists with critical illness myopathy and can lead to diffuse weakness, ventilator dependence, and prolonged posthospitalization weakness; electromyography/nerve conduction studies can differentiate neuropathy from myopathy.
  • No definitive treatment is available for critical illness neuropathy or critical illness myopathy, but appropriate glycemic control, early mobilization and physical therapy, and minimization of glucocorticoid use improve the prognosis.
  • Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1 presents with slowly progressive distal weakness, areflexia, and sensory loss without paresthesia; hammer toes, high arches, and distal leg atrophy are common findings.
  • Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a neurodegenerative motor neuron disease that causes progressive weakness, atrophy, fasciculations, and early death; 20% of patients with ALS will develop frontotemporal dementia.
  • The diagnosis of ALS requires clinical evidence of upper and lower motor neuron signs and electromyographic/nerve conduction study evidence of lower motor neuron signs in at least two (probable ALS) or more (definite ALS) regions.
  • Riluzole and edaravone are FDA-approved treatments for ALS, but they offer only modest benefits in terms of survival and functional decline.
  • Onset of myasthenia gravis (MG) most commonly occurs in the third decade of life in women and after age 50 years in men; ptosis, diplopia, and fluctuating, painless weakness without sensory loss are typical symptoms.
  • All patients with MG should undergo chest CT to assess for associated thymoma.
  • Symptomatic treatment of ocular and mild generalized myasthenia usually starts with the cholinesterase inhibitor pyridostigmine; in patients with more advanced disease, immunosuppressive therapy is required.
  • In patients with MG and myasthenic crisis or prominent bulbar or generalized weakness, treatment with intravenous immune globulin or plasmapheresis should precede initiation of glucocorticoids.
  • Thymectomy should be performed in all patients with MG and thymoma; it should also be considered in patients without thymoma who are aged 18 to 65 years and have acetylcholine receptor antibodies.
  • Most myopathies involve symmetric weakness of the proximal limb muscles; diagnosis is based on clinical assessment, muscle-related serum markers, electromyographic/nerve conduction study findings, muscle biopsy, and (sometimes) genetic testing.
  • The serum creatine kinase level is elevated in many forms of myopathy and can be followed to monitor disease activity and treatment response in inflammatory myopathies.
  • Statins should be discontinued in patients with elevated serum creatine kinase levels (>5-10 times the upper limit of normal), weakness, or severe pain.
  • In patients with a strong indication for statin therapy but significant muscle symptoms, retrial with a hydrophilic statin (rosuvastatin or pravastatin) should be considered after muscle symptoms resolve, with continued monitoring of the creatine kinase level.

index.title: Neuro-oncology
index.keyPoints:
• Seizures and headaches are common symptoms of intracranial tumors; papilledema and an inability to abduct the eyes secondary to a partial abducens nerve palsy indicate increased intracranial pressure.
  • Brain MRI is preferred for evaluating intracranial tumors, although head CT without contrast may be useful emergently to assess for complications such as hemorrhage or herniation.
  • Brain metastases are the most common intracranial tumors and typically appear as ring-enhancing lesions at the gray-white junction on postcontrast MRIs.
  • Most brain metastases are treated with whole-brain or more targeted radiation (stereotactic radiosurgery), but resection of a single or limited number of intracranial metastases may increase survival in younger patients with good baseline function.
  • Leptomeningeal metastasis may present with head or neck pain, neurologic deficits, and altered mental status; diagnosis rests on dural thickening with nodular enhancement on MRI and positive cerebrospinal fluid cytology or flow cytometry.
  • Meningiomas are the most common primary central nervous system tumors; they typically have a smooth, rounded shape and often a “tail” that tracks along the dura outside the brain parenchyma and exhibit homogeneous enhancement on postcontrast MRI.
  • Meningiomas are resected only if accompanied by severe headaches, drug-resistant seizures, significant neurologic deficits, or peritumoral edema.
  • Previous exposure to medical therapeutic radiation is the only consistent risk factor for gliomas, including glioblastoma.
  • Treatment of glioblastoma is usually resection, if possible, followed by radiation and chemotherapy with temozolomide.
  • Prognosis in glioblastoma is better in patients who are younger than 45 years, have an excellent functional status, have minimal residual tumor after resection, and receive chemotherapy and radiation after surgery.
  • The demonstration of lymphomatous cells in vitreous or cerebrospinal fluid samples may obviate the need for biopsy in diagnosing primary central nervous system lymphoma.
  • In suspected primary central nervous system lymphoma, empiric use of glucocorticoids should be avoided before biopsy because these agents can temporarily suppress lymphoma and prevent or delay a tissue diagnosis.
  • Gangliogliomas and dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumors provoke medication-resistant seizures in more than 90% of patients; therefore, patients with these tumors should be referred for resection, if possible.
  • In patients with central nervous system tumors without seizures, prophylactic antiseizure drugs are not recommended.
  • Emergent intervention for brain herniation, including elevation of the head of the bed, hyperventilation, infusion of hypertonic saline or mannitol, and administration of glucocorticoids, is necessary to prevent death.
  • Despite the risk for intracranial hemorrhage, therapeutic anticoagulation is generally recommended for patients with central nervous system (CNS) tumors and confirmed venous thromboembolic disease.
  • In patients with CNS tumors and venous thromboembolic disease, pre-anticoagulation neuroimaging with head CT to assess for hemorrhage is reasonable.
  • In hospitalized patients with CNS tumors undergoing resection, venous thromboembolic disease prophylaxis with low-molecular-weight heparin in combination with pneumatic compression stockings is recommended as soon as possible after resection.
  • Paraneoplastic/autoimmune limbic encephalitis presents as acute or subacute mood and behavioral changes, short-term memory problems, seizures, and cognitive dysfunction; it may present as a rapidly progressive dementia.
  • In suspected paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes, the patient should be thoroughly evaluated for an antibody-mediated process and for systemic cancer, which sometimes includes surveillance that continues for years after the primary syndrome is diagnosed.

index.title: Neuro-ophthalmology
index.keyPoints:
• Giant cell arteritis should be excluded emergently in patients aged 50 years or older who present with monocular transient or permanent vision loss; urgent treatment with high-dose glucocorticoids may limit vision loss.
  • In optic neuritis, intravenous methylprednisolone has been shown to shorten recovery time and reduce the 2-year incidences of recurrence or conversion to multiple sclerosis.
  • Glucocorticoids are not recommended in nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy or central or branch retinal artery occlusion unless giant cell arteritis is suspected.
  • Central or branch retinal artery occlusion should prompt urgent evaluation for carotid artery stenosis and cardioembolic disease.
  • In the absence of likely herniation, an oculomotor nerve palsy with pupillary involvement (a fixed, dilated pupil) should prompt immediate evaluation for posterior communicating artery aneurysm.
  • A pupil-sparing oculomotor nerve palsy is usually secondary to microvascular disease and does not require emergent neuroimaging in the absence of other neurologic deficits.
  • Horner syndrome comprises miosis, anhidrosis, and ptosis resulting from disruption of the sympathetic fibers anywhere along their course from the hypothalamus to the eye.
  • Evaluation of Horner syndrome may include MRI of the brain and cervical spine and, when an apical lung lesion is suspected, chest CT.

index.title: Issues in Oncology
index.keyPoints:
• In cancer treatment, an increase in overall survival is not synonymous with cure, and median survival is relevant to populations, not individuals.
  • The phrase significant improvement in survival refers to statistical certainty of a finding but is often misinterpreted as a substantial improvement in survival time.
  • Progression-free survival is the time from starting treatment to when that treatment is no longer controlling the cancer; it does not mean increased survival time.
  • In cancer treatment, response rate is the percentage of patients in a clinical trial whose tumors shrink to a prespecified degree; response rate has not been shown to correlate with overall survival.
  • The potential benefits of cancer treatment must be weighed and discussed along with their risks and toxicities; patients often face choices regarding aggressive therapies that are designed to prolong life but are associated with significant adverse effects.
  • The impact of financial toxicity, related to both the individual out-of-pocket costs and the societal costs of increasing insurance premiums, is an important consideration in oncologic care.
  • Palliative care should be instituted early in the management of patients with cancer and not reserved only for when they are no longer receiving cancer therapy.
  • Social determinants of health such as socioeconomic status, race, education, social isolation, and access to health insurance and medical care often detrimentally affect society's most vulnerable members when it comes to cancer screening, diagnosis, and survival.
  • Staging in a patient with cancer is generally the most accurate indicator of prognosis and largely dictates the therapeutic strategy.
  • Most solid tumors are staged using the TNM cancer staging system, in which T represents the size or extent of local invasion of the primary tumor (T1-T4), N indicates locoregional lymph node involvement (N0-N3), and M indicates the absence (M0) or presence (M1) of distant metastases.
  • Diagnostic imaging is crucial in determining the accurate stage of a tumor, but many patients with localized tumors have a low likelihood of distant metastases to certain sites and should not undergo routine imaging of such sites.
  • Patients with poor performance status may be divided into two groups: patients debilitated by chronic comorbidities who may only be able to tolerate less aggressive treatment and patients who are debilitated by the cancer but are otherwise medically fit and might benefit from aggressive treatment.
  • Most clinical trials used to determine cancer treatment safety and efficacy enrolled patients with good performance status, and results cannot be reliably extrapolated to patients with suboptimal performance statuses.
  • Age alone should not be regarded as a reason to avoid aggressive cancer treatment because older patients who are medically fit with a good performance status may tolerate aggressive therapy.
  • Most cancers that metastasize, although treatable with substantial potential for improvements in overall survival and quality of life, are still incurable.
  • Treatment with radiation therapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy (alone or in combination) in addition to definitive surgery is called neoadjuvant if administered preoperatively or adjuvant if administered postoperatively; both serve to eradicate residual microscopic disease and increase the chance for cure.
  • Neoadjuvant cancer therapy is used to eradicate micrometastases of an already resectable tumor, whereas conversion therapy seeks to convert an unresectable tumor to one that is resectable.
  • In cancer treatment, predictive assays identify the subset of patients who will benefit from an intervention, whereas prognostic assays can identify the subset of patients at higher or lower risk for a favorable or unfavorable outcome.
  • Precision medicine refers to agents that target specific aspects of a tumor cell; inclusionary markers include patients in a therapy that otherwise might not be considered, and exclusionary markers exclude patients from a treatment that might otherwise be used.
  • In targeted cancer therapy, the signaling pathways targeted in tumor cells may remain active in healthy cells, and disruption of these pathways can produce considerable adverse effects.
  • Immune checkpoints prevent the immune system from attacking healthy tissues (self); immunotherapy inhibits the checkpoints and allows the immune system to be more active and attack cancer cells.
  • Common checkpoint-directed therapies include those targeting cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen-4, PD-1 receptor, and PD-L1.
  • Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy uses genetically manipulated patient T cells to express a receptor for a tumor cell antigen, allowing the T cell to bind to the tumor cell and destroy it.

index.title: Breast Cancer
index.keyPoints:
• Breast cancer is the most common type of cancer, excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer, and the second leading cause of cancer-related death in women in the United States.
  • The estrogen, progesterone, and HER2 receptors play a key role in breast tumor biology, as well as in the prognosis and treatment of patients with breast cancer.
  • Patients with possible hereditary breast cancer syndromes should be referred to a genetic counselor for possible genetic testing for breast cancer susceptibility genes.
  • Patients diagnosed with breast cancer before age 50 years, those with triple-negative breast cancer or multiple primary breast cancers, and all men diagnosed with breast cancer should undergo genetic counseling and consider genetic testing for hereditary breast cancer syndromes.
  • Patients with increased risk for breast cancer based on risk assessment scores can be considered for enhanced screening (earlier initiation of screening or supplemental testing) and chemoprevention.
  • Chemoprevention options for breast cancer include selective estrogen receptor modifiers (e.g., tamoxifen, raloxifene) and aromatase inhibitors (e.g., exemestane, anastrozole, letrozole); only tamoxifen should be used in premenopausal patients.
  • Patients at high risk for breast cancer should be screened with annual mammography and breast MRI, including those with selected pathogenic/likely pathogenic genetic variants, a strong family history of breast cancer with a lifetime risk of 20% or higher, or a history of chest radiation therapy at a young age.
  • For patients with germline pathogenic or likely pathogenic BRCA1 or BRCA2 variants, breast cancer screening with annual breast MRI should start at age 25 years, with annual mammography added at age 30 years.
  • Surgical prophylaxis options to decrease the risk for breast cancer for BRCA1 and BRCA2 pathologic variant carriers include prophylactic bilateral mastectomy and prophylactic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.
  • In patients with breast cancer, small tumor size, low tumor grade, negative lymph nodes, and hormone receptor–positive status are associated with a more favorable prognosis.
  • In asymptomatic patients with newly diagnosed stage I to II breast cancer, staging imaging studies such as PET, CT, or bone scan are not recommended.
  • In patients with newly diagnosed stage III breast cancer or those with earlier-stage disease with signs, symptoms, or laboratory findings suggesting metastatic disease, staging with PET/CT or CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis plus bone scan is recommended.
  • Primary treatment for ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) includes either lumpectomy, often followed by radiation therapy, or mastectomy; postlumpectomy radiation therapy improves disease-free survival but not breast cancer–specific mortality and may not be used in some cases.
  • In estrogen receptor–positive DCIS, tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors decrease the risks for local recurrence and contralateral breast cancer but do not improve overall survival.
  • In patients with DCIS, adjuvant endocrine therapy is not indicated following bilateral mastectomy or for patients with hormone receptor–negative DCIS; there is no role for HER2 testing or HER2-targeted therapies in DCIS.
  • Breast-conservation therapy is effective for many women with small or medium (<5 cm) tumors, no skin involvement, and clear margins after resection; subsequent breast radiation therapy is recommended in most patients undergoing breast-conservation therapy.
  • Sentinel node biopsy may be omitted in selected postmenopausal women with breast cancers that are 2 cm or smaller, grade 1 or 2, hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative, and clinically node negative (confirmed by axillary ultrasound).
  • Postmastectomy radiation therapy is recommended for breast cancers greater than 5 cm, tumors with positive margins or skin involvement, inflammatory breast cancers, and patients with positive axillary lymph nodes who have other high-risk features.
  • In patients undergoing breast-conservation surgery who will receive chemotherapy or antiestrogen therapy and whole-breast radiation therapy, axillary dissection is not required if no more than two sentinel nodes are involved.
  • For patients with breast cancer without clinical nodal involvement but three or more positive sentinel nodes, axillary node dissection is recommended.
  • Most hormone receptor–positive early-stage invasive breast cancers are treated with initial excision followed by radiation therapy and adjuvant systemic therapy.
  • HER2-positive and triple-negative breast cancers with larger tumor size and/or lymph node involvement are treated with neoadjuvant therapies; assessing tumor response to therapy allows for tailoring adjuvant treatment.
  • Most patients with hormone receptor–positive, HER2-negative breast cancer first undergo surgery, followed by adjuvant endocrine therapy accomplished with selective estrogen receptor modulators or aromatase inhibitors.
  • Aromatase inhibitors are not as effective as adjuvant endocrine therapy in premenopausal women with breast cancer without concomitant ovarian function suppression, which is usually accomplished with a gonadotropin-releasing hormone antagonist.
  • In postmenopausal patients with hormone receptor–positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, aromatase inhibitor treatment for 5 to 10 years improves disease-free survival in those with high-risk features.
  • Patients with hormone receptor–positive, HER2-negative breast cancer and more than three involved axillary nodes benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy given before endocrine therapy; multigene assays can help determine risk in patients with zero to three positive axillary nodes and the need for adjuvant chemotherapy.
  • Acute adverse effects of adjuvant chemotherapy for breast cancer include bone marrow suppression, alopecia, allergic reactions, neuropathy, nausea, and premature menopause and infertility in premenopausal women; there is also a higher risk for cardiotoxicity in older women.
  • Patients who desire future childbearing should be referred to fertility specialists for consideration of oocyte or embryo banking before starting chemotherapy.
  • Neoadjuvant therapy consisting of chemotherapy-containing regimens in combination with trastuzumab and pertuzumab is the standard of care for patients with HER2-positive breast cancers larger than 2 cm or patients with positive lymph nodes.
  • The addition of trastuzumab to chemotherapy decreases the risk for HER2-positive breast cancer recurrence by 53% and the risk for death by 34%; the main toxicities of trastuzumab are infusion reactions, such as fever or chills, and reversible cardiomyopathy.
  • Patients with HER2-positive cancers larger than 5 mm or those with positive lymph nodes should be treated with adjuvant combination systemic chemotherapy along with either trastuzumab or the combination of trastuzumab with or without pertuzumab.
  • Adjuvant therapy for node-negative, HER2-positive breast cancers smaller than 2 cm can be treated with a single chemotherapy agent, such as paclitaxel, and trastuzumab.
  • Patients with triple-negative breast cancer and tumors 2 cm or larger or positive nodes are treated with neoadjuvant therapy with the checkpoint inhibitor pembrolizumab and combination chemotherapy.
  • In the absence of neoadjuvant therapy, adjuvant cytotoxic chemotherapy is recommended for patients with triple-negative cancers larger than 5 mm or patients with positive lymph nodes.
  • Patients with inflammatory breast cancer present with swelling, thickening, or erythema of the skin overlying the breast along with breast enlargement or swelling; it may be misdiagnosed as mastitis.
  • One third of patients with inflammatory breast cancer have distant metastases at diagnosis, and nearly all have lymph node involvement; all patients should undergo routine staging with either CT and bone scan or PET.
  • After completion of treatment for breast cancer, follow-up monitoring should be every 3 to 6 months for the first 3 years, every 6 to 12 months for the next 2 years, and then every year, with annual mammography for all survivors and breast MRI for those at high risk for recurrence.
