  • Surveillance blood tests and other imaging tests for breast cancer recurrence should not be routinely performed and should instead be guided by a patient's symptoms or findings on examination that raise concern for recurrence.
  • Patients taking tamoxifen should have yearly gynecologic examinations because of the increased risk for endometrial cancer, and those taking an aromatase inhibitor should undergo bone density studies to assess for osteoporosis.
  • Lymphedema management after axillary surgery for breast cancer includes manual lymphatic drainage, compression, exercise, skincare, and sequential pumps.
  • Metastatic breast cancer is not curable, but it can be treated with systemic therapy, with the goals of improved survival, symptom palliation, and maintaining quality of life.
  • A site of distant metastasis should be biopsied to confirm the diagnosis of metastatic breast cancer and to evaluate hormone receptor and HER2 status, which can be discordant from the status of the previous primary breast cancer.
  • Endocrine-based therapy is usually the initial treatment in patients with hormone receptor–positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer.
  • In patients with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer, treatment should include HER2-directed therapy; treatment with dual HER2-targeted therapy (trastuzumab and pertuzumab) added to docetaxel increases overall survival.
  • In patients with metastatic triple-negative breast cancer, chemotherapy is indicated; adding pembrolizumab improves overall survival for patients with a high PD-L1 score.

index.title: Gastroenterologic Malignancies
index.keyPoints:
• Patients with tumors arising on the right side of the large intestine have a different biology and substantially worse prognosis than tumors arising on the left.
  • All colorectal cancers (CRC) should be evaluated for mismatch repair enzyme deficiency/microsatellite instability, which changes therapeutic options and carries an approximate 20% risk for Lynch syndrome.
  • Current immunotherapies are ineffective in mismatch repair–proficient CRC but are highly effective in tumors that are mismatch repair deficient.
  • PET is not recommended for preoperative staging or postoperative surveillance in patients with colorectal cancer.
  • Patients with proximal rectal cancers without full-thickness penetration of the bowel wall or enlarged lymph nodes (stage I disease) may be treated with surgical resection alone.
  • Patients with full-thickness rectal tumors (stage II) or rectal tumors that involve lymph nodes (stage III) may be treated with chemotherapy with or without radiation therapy, followed by surgery.
  • An organ-preservation treatment option for patients with locoregional rectal cancer is total neoadjuvant therapy, in which all radiation therapy and chemotherapy are given preoperatively with nonoperative management and close observation if a complete response is achieved.
  • Radiation therapy in rectal cancer may include traditional long-course treatment with concurrent 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) or capecitabine or short-course treatment with higher-intensity radiation therapy without concurrent chemotherapy.
  • Chemotherapy options in rectal cancer include leucovorin, 5-FU, and oxaliplatin (FOLFOX) or capecitabine plus oxaliplatin (CAPOX).
  • Adverse effects of colorectal cancer treatment can include hand-foot syndrome (especially in those treated with capecitabine; 5-FU) and peripheral neuropathy (in those treated with oxaliplatin) that usually, but does not always, resolve fully.
  • Patients with stage II colon cancer that lacks high-risk features or is mismatch repair deficient have favorable prognoses and are unlikely to benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy.
  • Patients with stage III colon cancer should receive adjuvant chemotherapy.
  • After surgery for colon cancer, repeat colonoscopy should be done at 1 year, then in 3 years, followed by every 5 years; if full colonoscopy was not done at the time of surgery, the first colonoscopy should be 3 to 6 months after surgery.
  • All metastatic colorectal cancers (CRCs) require initial immunohistochemical and molecular analysis for mismatch repair (MMR) gene deficiency; KRAS, NRAS, and BRAF gene mutation status; and HER2 amplification status.
  • Patients with metastatic CRC with deficient MMR status should be treated with a PD-1 inhibitor with or without a CTLA4 inhibitor; response rates are high, and some patients will achieve a long-term complete response.
  • Unresectable proficient MMR metastatic CRC is treatable but not curable; cytotoxic chemotherapy combinations containing 5-fluorouracil or capecitabine are commonly used.
  • The anti–vascular endothelial growth factor monoclonal antibody bevacizumab potentiates the efficacy of cytotoxic chemotherapy in treating metastatic colon cancer; adverse effects include hypertension, arterial thrombotic events, and gastrointestinal perforation.
  • In patients with metastatic CRC with nonmutated (wild-type) KRAS, NRAS, and BRAF genes and a nonamplified HER2 gene, monoclonal antibodies to the epidermal growth factor receptors (cetuximab and panitumumab) are a treatment option; the appearance of an acneiform rash correlates with antitumor activity.
  • Metastatic colorectal cancer with a BRAF V600E mutation may be treated with the combination of a BRAF inhibitor, such as encorafenib, and an EGFR inhibitor, such as cetuximab or panitumumab.
  • Metastatic colorectal cancers with high amplification of HER2 (3+ amplification by immunohistochemistry) may be treated with combination anti-HER2 therapies or with fam-trastuzumab-deruxtecan.
  • Anal cancer, a squamous cell carcinoma linked to human papillomavirus, is often cured by combination radiation and chemotherapy, sparing the need for surgical resection and colostomy.
  • Germline testing for BRCA, PALB2, ATM, CHEK2, and other heritable variants is recommended for all patients with pancreatic cancer.
  • Patients with pancreatic cancer without metastatic disease who have clinical staging suggesting resectable or borderline resectable pancreatic cancer should undergo resection because it is the only option for cure; conversion therapy with radiation and/or chemotherapy can be used to convert locally unresectable disease to resectable disease.
  • PET has not been shown to add value and is not part of standard management for most pancreatic cancers.
  • Adjuvant chemotherapy after successful pancreatic resection for pancreatic cancer can prolong survival.
  • Smoking, obesity, and gastroesophageal reflux disease, especially with the development of Barrett esophagus, are risk factors for adenocarcinoma of the esophagus, gastroesophageal junction, and proximal stomach.
  • PET-CT is widely used as part of standard preoperative staging of gastroesophageal cancer, unlike for other gastrointestinal tumors; endoscopic ultrasonography is also routinely used to assess tumor depth and nodal involvement.
  • Surgery is the primary treatment of locoregional gastroesophageal cancer, often with neoadjuvant chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy; adjuvant immunotherapy is also standard.
  • In advanced gastroesophageal adenocarcinomas with HER2 overexpression, adding trastuzumab and pembrolizumab to chemotherapy improves survival.
  • In PD-L1–positive advanced gastroesophageal squamous cell and adenocarcinomas, the immune checkpoint inhibitors nivolumab or pembrolizumab are used in combination with cytotoxic chemotherapy.
  • Gastrointestinal neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) arise from the endocrine cells of the digestive tract, whereas pancreatic NETs arise from the islets of Langerhans cells; although histologically similar, gastrointestinal and pancreatic NETs behave and respond to treatment differently.
  • Gastrointestinal NETs can produce serotonin, which can cause the carcinoid syndrome, a condition characterized by diarrhea and facial flushing.
  • Well-differentiated NETs are often indolent and may initially require only observation and serial imaging.
  • Well-differentiated gastrointestinal NETs of the appendix may be diagnosed incidentally after appendectomy; tumors smaller than 2 cm confined to the appendix require no further surgery or follow-up imaging.

index.title: Lung Cancer
index.keyPoints:
• The two major classes of lung cancer are non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small cell lung cancer (SCLC); NSCLC accounts for 80% of lung cancers and is divided into adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma.
  • Testing for specific gene alterations (e.g., EGFR, ALK, ROS, RET, KRAS, HER2/neu) is recommended for most patients with NSCLC; this allows for individualized targeted therapy and potentially improved survival.
  • Paraneoplastic syndromes are most associated with SCLC, including the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy, inflammatory myopathies, and Cushing syndrome.
  • The definitive diagnosis of lung cancer requires tissue histopathology or cytology.
  • In patients with radiographic evidence of advanced-stage lung cancer, diagnosis and staging are best accomplished with a single invasive test at a location that will establish both the diagnosis and disease stage.
  • PET/CT is a standard component of initial staging for all patients with non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC); brain MRI is also performed except in very early-stage cancer.
  • NSCLC is staged using the TNM staging system, whereas small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is staged as either limited or extensive disease.
  • Patients with SCLC should undergo contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and MRI of the brain with contrast; use of PET/CT and brain MRI is an alternative staging approach.
  • Mediastinal node sampling, either via mediastinoscopy or endobronchial ultrasonography–guided biopsy, is indicated in most patients with NSCLC but is not usually performed in patients with SCLC.
  • Lobectomy is the preferred surgical procedure in early-stage non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
  • FEV~1 and Dlco should be measured in potential surgical candidates with early-stage NSCLC to predict their anticipated postoperative pulmonary reserve and suitability for resection.
  • Patients with early-stage NSCLC who are not surgical candidates can be treated with radiation therapy, preferably stereotactic body radiation therapy; for lymph node–positive cancers, combined chemotherapy and radiation therapy are used.
  • Adjuvant chemotherapy can be considered for high-risk patients with lymph node–negative early-stage NSCLC.
  • Cisplatin-based adjuvant chemotherapy is standard treatment of all resected stage II and III lung cancers.
  • Patients treated surgically for stage I or II lung cancer who have positive tumor margins should undergo re-resection; postoperative radiation therapy is indicated if repeat surgery is not possible.
  • For patients with resected early-stage lung tumors with certain mutations in the EGFR or ALK gene, adjuvant treatment with osimertinib or alectinib after chemotherapy improves outcomes.
  • For patients with resected early-stage lung tumors without mutations in the EGFR or ALK gene, adjuvant immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors, such as atezolizumab or pembrolizumab, after chemotherapy improves outcomes.
  • Stage III non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is extremely heterogeneous; in patients with resectable disease, treatment generally includes neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy and/or radiation treatment; immunotherapy is also added in specific situations.
  • In patients with resectable stage III NSCLC without EGFR and ALK alterations, neoadjuvant systemic therapy with chemotherapy and immunotherapy can improve outcomes and allow for more limited lung resection.
  • Patients with resected stage III NSCLC found to have certain EGFR mutations should receive adjuvant osimertinib.
  • Patients with resected stage III NSCLC with an ALK gene fusion should receive adjuvant alectinib.
  • Patients with unresectable locally advanced lung cancer, typically because of contralateral mediastinal nodes or an extensively invasive primary tumor, are treated with combined or sequential platinum-based chemotherapy and radiation therapy, followed by immunotherapy when appropriate.
  • Treatment of metastatic non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is directed by the cancer subtype, the presence of driver alterations, PD-L1 status, and patient performance status; if a relevant genomic alteration is present, targeted therapy is frequently the recommended first-line treatment.
  • For patients with metastatic NSCLC without a driver alteration, initial treatment consists of an immune checkpoint inhibitor either alone or in combination with chemotherapy and/or a second immune checkpoint inhibitor.
  • For patients with metastatic NSCLC, platinum-based chemotherapy is used in the first-line setting in combination with immunotherapy for patients without a driver alteration (or alone in these patients with a contraindication to immunotherapy) or in the subsequent-line setting after targeted therapies or immunotherapy.
  • Patients with a poor performance status due to lung cancer with a treatment-naive driver alteration should be considered for urgent initiation of targeted therapy.
  • Patients with limited-stage small cell lung cancer (SCLC) are treated with thoracic radiation therapy concurrent with platinum-based chemotherapy (cisplatin or carboplatin plus etoposide); prophylactic cranial irradiation should also be considered.
  • Prophylactic cranial irradiation reduces central nervous system metastases in patients with SCLC, although it increases the risk for neurocognitive impairment.
  • Patients with extensive SCLC are treated with combination platinum-etoposide chemotherapy and immunotherapy, continuing immunotherapy as maintenance until progression.
  • Despite initial response to chemotherapy, recurrence of SCLC is very common; patients with recurrent disease with a disease-free interval of more than 3 months can be re-treated with platinum-based doublet chemotherapy.

index.title: Head and Neck Cancer
index.keyPoints:
• Tobacco and alcohol use are important risk factors for head and neck cancer, and their combined use synergistically increases risk.
  • Human papillomavirus infection is a significant cause of oropharyngeal cancer; the prognosis is better than that of cancer not related to human papillomavirus.
  • Malignant neck masses are commonly painless, firm and/or fixed on examination and are not associated with antecedent infection; if malignancy is suspected, prompt referral to an otolaryngologist and direct laryngoscopy is imperative.
  • In staging head and neck cancer, MRI is preferred for assessing the primary tumor; PET/CT is useful to assess regional nodes and distant metastatic disease, although it is not accurate in nodes smaller than 1 cm.
  • Staging of head and neck cancer is the most important determinant of prognosis; staging is complex because each subsite uses a different staging system.
  • Patients with small head and neck tumors without lymph node metastases can be effectively treated with either surgery or radiation therapy.
  • Radiation therapy and larynx-sparing surgery, consisting of either transoral laser surgery or open partial laryngectomy, offer equivalent survival benefit to patients with early-stage laryngeal cancer.
  • For patients with head and neck cancer with an unresectable primary tumor, extensive nodal disease, or radiographic evidence of extranodal extension, initial treatment is with combined chemotherapy and radiation therapy depending on the primary tumor and sites of involvement.
  • Routine imaging for head and neck cancer after a negative posttreatment scan is not indicated unless signs and symptoms suggest recurrent disease.
  • Although patients who receive radiation therapy that includes the thyroid bed are at increased risk for thyroid cancer, screening thyroid ultrasonography is not indicated.
  • Patients with small, localized recurrent head and neck cancer after a long disease-free interval may be cured with additional surgery and adjuvant therapy.
  • Patients with advanced head and neck cancer not amenable to surgery or radiation therapy who are appropriate candidates for chemotherapy should receive a combination of platinum-based chemotherapy and pembrolizumab, or pembrolizumab alone in patients with PD-L1–positive cancer.

index.title: Genitourinary Cancer
index.keyPoints:
• Risk stratification using serum prostate-specific antigen measurement, Grade Group, and TNM cancer staging based on biopsy results and digital rectal examination determines prognosis and treatment options in localized prostate cancer.
  • In patients with newly diagnosed prostate cancer, staging imaging studies to assess regional lymph node involvement and metastatic disease need not be done in those with very low- or low-risk disease.
  • In patients with intermediate-risk, high-risk, or very-high-risk localized prostate cancer, imaging should be obtained to evaluate for regional lymph node involvement and metastatic disease; options include prostate-specific membrane antigen PET or radionuclide bone scan combined with CT or MRI.
  • Germline genetic testing, including for BRCA pathogenic variants, is recommended for all men with high-risk prostate cancer, including patients with positive lymph nodes or metastatic disease.
  • Somatic tumor mutation testing should be done in all patients with metastatic prostate cancer who are candidates for targeted systemic therapies.
  • Treatment options for men with newly diagnosed localized prostate cancer include active surveillance, radiation therapy, and radical prostatectomy.
  • Active surveillance is an option for men with low- or very low-risk prostate cancer who have a life expectancy of at least 10 years; 15-year metastasis-free survival is as high as 97% in appropriately selected patients.
  • In patients with localized prostate cancer detected through serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) screening, there is no difference in 10-year survival between active surveillance, surgery, and radiation therapy.
  • Adverse effects of radiation therapy for patients with localized prostate cancer include short-term enteritis (20%) and cystitis (50%); long-term effects include erectile dysfunction (up to 70% 2 years after surgery).
  • Adverse effects of radical prostatectomy for prostate cancer include chronic moderate to severe urinary incontinence (5%-10%) and erectile dysfunction (40% 2 years after surgery).
  • For men with intermediate- or higher-risk localized prostate cancer who are treated with radiation therapy, the addition of a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist or antagonist delays disease progression.
  • After definitive treatment of localized prostate cancer, patients are monitored for evidence of recurrence with serial serum PSA measurements every 3 to 4 months and digital rectal examination yearly.
  • Following radical prostatectomy, PSA level should rapidly become undetectable; after radiation therapy, PSA level will fall gradually and reach a nadir but may not become undetectable.
  • Treatment of prostate-specific antigen (PSA)–only recurrence of prostate cancer following treatment for localized prostate cancer without metastatic disease depends on previous treatment modalities and patient- and cancer-specific factors, such as life expectancy and PSA doubling time.
  • Observation is a reasonable consideration in patients with M0 recurrent prostate cancer if a slow PSA doubling time (>10 months) is present; in most other patients, androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) with or without local therapy is indicated.
  • Options for providing ADT include orchiectomy, gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist therapy (with or without antiandrogen therapy), and gonadotropin-releasing hormone antagonist therapy.
  • ADT results in many short-term (loss of lean body mass, fatigue, gynecomastia, hair loss, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, vasomotor symptoms) and long-term (increased risk for cardiovascular and venous thromboembolic disease, decreased bone density) effects.
  • Continuous androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT), including orchiectomy, gonadotropin-releasing hormone–agonist therapy, and gonadotropin-releasing hormone–antagonist therapy, are appropriate treatments for metastatic prostate cancer.
  • In patients with metastatic prostate cancer who are to be treated with a GnRH agonist, short-term antiandrogen therapy should precede or be started at the same time as the GnRH agonist to prevent a transient worsening of disease-related symptoms.
  • Response to ADT in prostate cancer can be assessed by serum prostate-specific antigen measurement and imaging; serum testosterone level should be less than 50 ng/dL (1.7 nmol/L) in men treated with ADT.
  • In patients with metastatic castration-naive prostate cancer, ADT can be combined with docetaxel alone or with darolutamide; abiraterone/prednisone alone or with docetaxel; enzalutamide; or apalutamide to improve survival.
  • Initial treatment options for castration-resistant prostate cancer include docetaxel with prednisone; abiraterone with prednisone; enzalutamide; and, for symptomatic bone metastases, radium-223.
  • Osteoclast inhibitors reduce bone pain and lower fracture risk in men with castration-resistant, metastatic prostate cancer and bony disease.
  • Testicular cancer is diagnosed through radical inguinal orchiectomy; needle biopsy of a testicular mass is contraindicated because of risk for tumor seeding to the scrotum and inguinal nodes.
  • Measurement of serum α-fetoprotein, β–human chorionic gonadotropin, and lactate dehydrogenase levels is important before and after inguinal orchiectomy for determining stage and prognosis of testicular cancer.
  • For pure seminoma, active surveillance is preferred after surgery for early-stage disease; adjuvant radiation therapy or chemotherapy with one to two cycles of carboplatin is also appropriate.
  • Patients with stage II seminoma can be treated with either radiation to the para-aortic lymph nodes and superior ipsilateral pelvis or chemotherapy, depending on the extent of lymph node involvement.
  • After chemotherapy for higher-stage seminoma, PET/CT can guide the need for resection; residual masses that show negative results on PET scan can be monitored, whereas biopsy should be considered for masses with positive test results.
  • Patients with early-stage nonseminomatous germ cell tumors can be managed with active surveillance (in selected patients), retroperitoneal lymph node dissection, or limited chemotherapy following orchiectomy.
  • Most patients with nonseminomatous germ cell tumors with nodal involvement are treated with chemotherapy.
  • Patients with CT findings pathognomonic for renal cell carcinoma do not need a biopsy to confirm the diagnosis.
  • Many different paraneoplastic syndromes can be seen in patients with renal cell carcinoma, including anemia, hepatic dysfunction in the absence of liver metastases, fever, hypercalcemia, erythrocytosis, AA amyloidosis, thrombocytosis, and polymyalgia rheumatica.
  • Management options for a suspicious solitary kidney mass smaller than 4 cm include active surveillance, surgery, or ablation.
  • Patients with resected high-risk stage II or III clear cell carcinoma should receive a year of adjuvant pembrolizumab.
  • In patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma, resecting or debulking the primary tumor can be considered, but whether this improves outcomes is unknown.
  • Any patient with gross hematuria should be referred for urologic evaluation, as should any patient confirmed to have microscopic hematuria in the absence of a clear benign cause; use of anticoagulants does not alter the need for urologic evaluation.
  • Superficial bladder cancer does not invade the muscle, and treatment includes transurethral resection of the bladder tumor alone for Ta tumors; for all other noninvasive disease, transurethral resection of the bladder tumor plus intravesical chemotherapy or bacillus Calmette-Guérin therapy is indicated.
  • Muscle-invasive bladder cancer is treated with cystectomy with or without neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy.

index.title: Gynecologic Cancer
index.keyPoints:
• Risk factors for ovarian cancer include increased age, pathogenic variants of ovarian cancer susceptibility genes, early menarche or late menopause, and nulliparity.
  • Genetic testing of high-risk variants, including BRCA1 and BRCA2 pathogenic variants, should be offered to all women with ovarian cancer, fallopian tube cancer, or primary peritoneal cancer.
  • There is no clear evidence that ovarian cancer screening with either transvaginal ultrasonography or serum CA-125 measurement improves cancer-related outcomes, even in patients at high risk.
  • For women with BRCA1, BRCA2, or mismatch repair gene pathogenic variants, prophylactic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is recommended; it should be done after the completion of childbearing or by age 35 to 40 years for patients with BRCA1 pathogenic variants and by age 40 to 45 years for patients with BRCA2 pathogenic variants.
  • Surgical exploration is recommended for diagnosis of early ovarian cancer because removing the cancer intact without rupture improves survival.
  • Patients with stage I ovarian cancer with favorable histology may be treated with surgery alone; all other patients should receive adjuvant platinum-taxane chemotherapy.
  • Surgical debulking of ovarian cancer, including the resection of metastatic disease, improves prognosis.
  • In patients with later-stage ovarian cancer, adding intraperitoneal chemotherapy, the angiogenesis inhibitor bevacizumab, and/or poly (adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase inhibitors to standard chemotherapy may improve outcomes.
  • Despite optimal treatment, 80% to 85% of women with stage III or IV ovarian cancer will relapse.
  • Patients who relapse more than 6 months after discontinuing platinum-based chemotherapy for ovarian cancer are considered to have platinum-sensitive disease and may be offered platinum-based combination chemotherapy again.
  • Risk factors for cervical cancer include earlier onset of sexual activity, several sexual partners or a high-risk partner, immunosuppression, HIV infection, low socioeconomic status, smoking, and oral contraceptive use.
  • Cervical cancer incidence and deaths in developed countries have decreased by more than 50%, primarily because of screening and preventive treatment.
  • Human papillomavirus is the causative agent in most patients with cervical cancer, and vaccination significantly reduces the risk.
  • Patients with early cervical cancer are frequently asymptomatic, but the most common symptoms are abnormal or heavy vaginal bleeding or vaginal discharge; advanced cervical cancer symptoms include pelvic or back pain and bowel or bladder symptoms.
  • Select patients with cervical cancer confined to the cervix can be treated with surgery that preserves fertility, such as conization (only for stage IA) or radical trachelectomy.
  • Patients with bulky or locally advanced cervical cancer are treated with cisplatin-based chemotherapy and radiation therapy instead of surgery.
  • Follow-up in patients with cervical cancer should include surveillance imaging and laboratory studies only if there are signs or symptoms suggestive of recurrence.
  • Endometrial (uterine) cancer is the most common gynecologic cancer; in addition to older age, major risk factors include obesity, tamoxifen use, and Lynch syndrome.
  • Treatment of endometrial cancer is primarily surgical for early-stage endometrial tumors, whereas patients with advanced disease are treated with surgery, systemic therapy, and radiation therapy.

index.title: Lymphoid Malignancies
index.keyPoints:
• Viral infections (including Epstein-Barr virus, hepatitis C virus, and HIV infection) and autoimmune rheumatic disorders (including Sjögren disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and rheumatoid arthritis) increase the risk of lymphoma.
  • Lymphadenopathy is the most common sign of lymphoma.
  • Diagnosis of lymphoma is generally established by excision or core-needle biopsy, with excision often preferred to better determine nodal architecture; fine-needle aspiration cytology is generally inadequate to diagnose lymphoma.
  • Lymphomas are staged as I to IV based on the number of disease sites and the presence of extranodal involvement; staging in most patients includes physical examination, CT, and PET.
  • In addition to stages I to IV, lymphoma stages are designated as A, B, or E; B findings include temperature higher than 38.0 °C (100.4 °F), drenching night sweats, or a weight loss of more than 10% of body weight over the past 6 months, whereas E denotes extranodal involvement in stage I and II disease.
  • A negative PET scan may render the need for bone marrow biopsy unnecessary in many patients with Hodgkin and large cell lymphoma.
  • Physical examination and PET/CT are used to stage patients with Hodgkin lymphoma.
  • All patients with classic Hodgkin lymphoma, regardless of stage, receive chemotherapy; the most common regimen is doxorubicin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine, along with either bleomycin, brentuximab vedotin, or nivolumab.
  • Bleomycin carries a significant risk for permanent lung injury, especially in older patients.
  • In patients with favorable early-stage Hodgkin lymphoma, treatment can consist of two courses of chemotherapy and involved-site radiation therapy; for more advanced disease, chemotherapy alone is used.
  • Patients with nodular lymphocyte–predominant Hodgkin lymphoma may present with localized disease that can be treated with radiation therapy alone, but this type of Hodgkin lymphoma is associated with a high rate of late relapse.
  • Many patients with follicular lymphoma are not symptomatic at diagnosis and may not require therapy for many years.
  • In advanced-stage follicular lymphoma, rituximab plus chemotherapy or with lenalidomide leads to remission in more than 90% of patients, although the disease will recur in most individuals.
  • Patients with histologic transformation of follicular lymphoma to a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma have a poor prognosis; it is suggested by a change in the clinical pattern of disease with new systemic symptoms, rapid progression of a localized area of disease, increasing serum lactate dehydrogenase level, or markedly higher areas of standardized uptake values on PET scans.
  • Histologic transformation of follicular lymphoma to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma must be confirmed by performing another lymph node biopsy.
  • Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphomas are usually indolent and have a low propensity for transformation to more aggressive lymphomas.
  • Early-stage Helicobacter pylori–associated gastric MALT lymphoma may be initially treated with antibiotics and proton pump inhibitors; other localized or advanced MALT lymphomas may be treated with radiation therapy or rituximab-based regimens.
  • Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and small lymphocytic lymphoma are the same disease; the former predominates in peripheral blood and bone marrow, whereas the latter predominates in lymph nodes.
  • CLL manifests as an increase in absolute lymphocytes on complete blood count; the lymphocytes are predominantly small and mature appearing, and they may form smudge cells on the peripheral smear.
  • Patients with low-stage, asymptomatic CLL can often be observed without therapy for many years.
  • Bruton kinase inhibitors and B-cell lymphoma 2 inhibitors, such as venetoclax, are common first-line therapy for CLL; venetoclax is associated with a high incidence of tumor lysis syndrome.
  • Patients with CLL/small lymphocytic lymphoma may develop autoimmune cytopenias, such as immune thrombocytopenic purpura and autoimmune hemolytic anemias.
  • Transformation to a large cell lymphoma (Richter transformation) occurs in about 5% of patients with CLL/small lymphocytic lymphoma and is associated with a poor prognosis and refractory disease.
  • Patients with hairy cell leukemia typically present with circulating lymphocytes with cytoplasmic projections (termed “hairy cells”), cytopenias, and splenomegaly but no lymphadenopathy.
  • Durable remissions of hairy cell leukemia can often be achieved with one course of a purine nucleoside agent, such as pentostatin or cladribine.
  • Aggressive B-cell lymphomas, such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, progress more quickly than indolent lymphomas but have a greater potential for cure.
  • Patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma often present with symptomatic enlarging lymphadenopathy; 40% may have extranodal disease, and one third have systemic B symptoms.
  • Patients who present with localized diffuse large B-cell lymphoma can be treated with a short course of chemotherapy with or without consolidative radiation therapy.
  • Standard therapy for patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is rituximab plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP); more aggressive regimens are required for high-risk disease.
  • The endemic form of Burkitt lymphoma occurs primarily in Africa, and young patients typically present with a rapidly growing large jaw mass; the sporadic form occurs at an older age, and patients present with abdominal or pelvic involvement.
  • Because of its rapid growth, tumor lysis syndrome may be present in patients with Burkitt lymphoma even before treatment; prophylaxis for tumor lysis syndrome should be instituted before starting chemotherapy.
  • The skin findings in mycosis fungoides, a subtype of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, range from nonspecific maculopapular eruptions or plaques, to more defined skin tumors with ulceration, to diffuse erythroderma.
  • Sézary syndrome is a more aggressive subtype of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma than mycosis fungoides; it is characterized by diffuse erythroderma and malignant T cells circulating in the blood.
  • Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified, is the most common T-cell lymphoma; it is typically found in older adults at an advanced stage, and patients generally have a worse prognosis compared with those who have B-cell lymphomas.

index.title: Cancer of Unknown Primary Site
index.keyPoints:
• In patients with a metastatic cancer of unknown primary (CUP), CT and histologic, endoscopic, and gender-specific cancer evaluations are reasonable; nonspecific tumor markers, PET, and gene expression arrays are usually not done, although they may be helpful in selected cases.
  • After reasonable attempts to identify primary cancer have failed, management of CUP should shift focus to treating the metastasis based on histology and prognostic factors because finding the primary site is unlikely to improve treatment options or clinical outcome.
  • Patients, particularly young men, with cancer of unknown primary who have poorly differentiated carcinoma predominantly in the midline, such as those with large retroperitoneal or mediastinal lymphadenopathy, are likely to have a germ cell tumor and should be treated for that possibility with platinum-based chemotherapy.
  • Women with a cancer of unknown primary (CUP) who have axillary lymphadenopathy should be treated for presumptive locally advanced breast cancer, even if a mammogram and breast MRI fail to demonstrate a breast tumor.
  • Patients with isolated or dominant cervical lymphadenopathy and CUP should be treated along a head and neck cancer paradigm with chemotherapy and radiation therapy.
  • Women with cancer of unknown primary who have adenocarcinoma with abdominal carcinomatosis and ascites should be treated for presumptive ovarian cancer.
  • Therapy for cancer of unknown primary (CUP) that does not fall into one of the favorable subgroups should be managed based on the pattern of presentation; cancer above the diaphragm should be treated as metastatic lung cancer, and cancer below the diaphragm should be treated as gastrointestinal cancer.
  • Palliative or hospice care is appropriate for patients with an unfavorable subtype of CUP who have substantial comorbidities and poor performance status.

index.title: Skin Cancer
index.keyPoints:
• Melanoma is a highly curable disease when detected and treated early with a wide local excision.
  • In melanoma, sentinel lymph node biopsy is not usually performed if the melanoma is nonulcerated and has a Breslow depth of less than 0.8 mm.
  • Patients with melanoma and positive sentinel lymph node biopsy specimens (stage III) should be considered for adjuvant systemic treatment with targeted therapy and/or immunotherapy if any nodal metastasis is greater than or equal to 1 mm.
  • Patients with clinical stage III or IV melanoma who are deemed surgical candidates should be considered for neoadjuvant pembrolizumab, an immune checkpoint inhibitor, before surgery followed by adjuvant pembrolizumab.
  • The use of immune checkpoint inhibitors has shown significant improvements in survival for patients with regional nodal and metastatic melanoma and is first-line therapy, including in those with BRAF, NRAS, or MEK mutations.
  • Approximately 40% to 50% of patients have melanoma that harbors a BRAF mutation that may respond to the combined inhibition of BRAF and MEK; starting treatment with immunotherapy and then proceeding to targeted therapy when needed, however, is the preferred approach.
  • Conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy plays a limited role in the treatment of melanoma.
  • Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer; patients usually present with localized disease, and metastatic disease is rare.
  • Squamous cell carcinoma most often involves sun-exposed areas and less often forms in the skin of the genital areas or from actinic keratoses; surgical excision is first-line therapy, and immunotherapy is a consideration if unresectable or metastatic disease is present.

index.title: Bone and Soft Tissue Tumors
index.keyPoints:
• Patients with bone sarcoma present with pain and sometimes a palpable mass at the affected site; core-needle biopsy is the preferred biopsy technique.
  • The diagnosis of soft-tissue sarcoma is most often confirmed with core-needle biopsy; the biopsy tract must be encompassed within the planned subsequent surgical resection.
  • Surgery is the primary treatment for nearly all soft-tissue sarcomas; neoadjuvant or adjuvant radiation therapy is used to treat high-grade tumors, and adjuvant chemotherapy is used depending on the sarcoma subtype.
  • Most gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) arise in the stomach, with fewer in the small bowel and fewest in the rectum; GISTs arising in the stomach have the best prognosis.
  • For patients undergoing a potentially curative resection of a localized GIST, low-risk tumors do not benefit from further treatment whereas higher-risk tumors are treated with imatinib for 3 years.

index.title: Oncologic Urgencies and Emergencies
index.keyPoints:
• Most patients with superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome do not require emergency intervention; in patients who are stable and who do not have a known diagnosis of active cancer, a biopsy should be obtained to confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment.
  • In patients with severe SVC syndrome with life-threatening complications, such as respiratory distress or cerebral edema, an SVC stent can be placed without a tissue diagnosis.
  • The presence of SVC syndrome does not worsen prognosis in patients who present with otherwise treatable malignancies.
  • Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in patients with increased intracranial pressure because of the risk for herniation; when a lumbar puncture is under consideration and there is a concern for increased intracranial pressure, central nervous system imaging should be obtained first.
  • Neoplastic epidural spinal cord compression (ESCC) often starts out as a progression of signs and symptoms over the course of weeks to months; early recognition is critical to maintain neurologic function.
  • Emergent MRI with contrast of the entire thecal sac is the preferred imaging test when neoplastic ESCC is suspected.
  • Neoplastic ESCC is initially treated with high-dose glucocorticoids; definitive treatment with surgery, radiation therapy, or both depends on whether the patient has a known cancer diagnosis, the stability of the spine, the sensitivity of the cancer to radiation or drug therapy, and the patient's overall prognosis.
  • Neurologic status at the time of treatment initiation is the most important predictor of outcome for patients with neoplastic ESCC; ambulatory patients tend to remain ambulatory with treatment, but most nonambulatory patients do not regain the ability to walk.
  • Malignant pleural effusions are most commonly caused by carcinomas of the breast, lung, gastrointestinal tract, and ovaries; lymphomas; and mesotheliomas.
  • For slowly recurring malignant pleural effusions, repeat thoracentesis is appropriate; for more rapidly recurring pleural effusions, either an indwelling pleural catheter or pleurodesis is used.
  • Malignancy accounts for 13% to 23% of pericardial effusions and may be the first sign of the disease; the most common malignancies that cause pericardial effusions are lung, breast, and esophageal cancers as well as melanoma, lymphoma, and leukemia.
  • Malignant pleural and pericardial effusions often reaccumulate, unless the patient responds to systemic therapy.
  • Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is caused when tumor cells release their contents into the bloodstream, either spontaneously or secondary to treatment, leading to hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia; TLS can lead to acute kidney injury, cardiac arrhythmias, seizures, and death.
  • Patients at intermediate risk for TLS can be managed with monitoring of laboratory values, ensuring adequate hydration, and a xanthine oxidase inhibitor such as allopurinol; those at high risk should also receive intravenous fluids before chemotherapy.
  • Patients with TLS should be treated with rasburicase and aggressive intravenous fluids if kidney function allows; patients require continuous cardiac monitoring and serial measurement of serum electrolyte, creatinine, and urate levels every 4 to 6 hours.
  • Patients with severe or symptomatic hypercalcemia of malignancy require immediate treatment with vigorous administration of intravenous saline; calcitonin, which can decrease calcium levels within several hours, should also be given.
  • Treatment for severe hypercalcemia of malignancy includes an intravenous bisphosphonate or denosumab, although the full effect may take days and other, more rapidly acting treatments should be given to patients with severe hypercalcemia.

index.title: Effects of Cancer Therapy and Survivorship
index.keyPoints:
• Most patients with neutropenic fever should be managed with monotherapy with an anti-pseudomonal β-lactam agent; vancomycin may be added for suspected catheter-associated infection, skin or soft-tissue infection, or pneumonia.
  • Prophylactic granulocyte colony-stimulating factor may be given to patients receiving regimens associated with a high risk for neutropenic fever or as secondary prophylaxis in patients with a previous episode of neutropenic fever.
  • Myeloid growth factors are not indicated to treat neutropenic fever in the absence of risk factors for complications; risk factors include severe neutropenia, expected prolonged neutropenia, age older than 65 years, hypotension or sepsis, and an uncontrolled primary tumor.
  • In patients undergoing emetogenic chemotherapy, antiemetic prophylaxis should be scheduled for the first 3 to 4 days after each cycle, and short-acting antiemetics should be provided as needed for breakthrough nausea.
  • Patients undergoing moderately emetogenic chemotherapy should receive prophylaxis with high-dose glucocorticoids and a serotonin receptor antagonist (ondansetron or palonosetron).
  • Antiemetic prophylaxis for patients receiving severe emetogenic chemotherapy drugs includes a serotonin receptor antagonist (ondansetron or palonosetron), a high-dose glucocorticoid, a neurokinin-1 receptor blocker (aprepitant, fosaprepitant, or netupitant), and possibly olanzapine.
  • Doxorubicin and other anthracyclines can cause irreversible, dose-related cardiomyopathy; trastuzumab can also induce dose-independent cardiomyopathy that is usually reversible.
  • The most common immune-related adverse effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors include rash, diarrhea/colitis, and endocrinopathies (hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, hypophysitis).
  • Immune-related adverse effects secondary to immune checkpoint inhibitors require prompt recognition and temporary or permanent cessation of therapy; moderate or severe toxicity requires treatment with glucocorticoid therapy, and high doses may be required in patients with severe symptoms.
  • Bone loss occurs in cancer survivors who have taken long-term glucocorticoids; in women who have undergone surgery-, medication-, radiation-, or chemotherapy-induced premature menopause or who are taking aromatase inhibitors for breast cancer; and in men treated for prostate cancer with androgen-deprivation therapy.
  • Fertility preservation options should be offered before cancer treatment in patients who are planning to have children in the future.
  • A survivorship plan provides the patient with recommendations regarding surveillance for cancer recurrence, lifestyle modifications to reduce the risk for a second malignancy, and strategies to prevent or reduce the late effects of cancer treatment.
  • Secondary malignancies may develop in cancer survivors owing to a preexisting genetic predisposition, a “field” effect from previous carcinogen exposure, or late effects of previous cancer treatments.
  • Mediastinal radiation therapy is associated with a marked increase in breast cancer beginning about 8 years after treatment; for women who receive chest radiation before age 30 years, annual breast cancer screening with breast MRI and mammography is recommended to begin 8 years after therapy, starting no sooner than age 25 years.

index.title: Screening for Cancer
index.keyPoints:
• The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends biennial mammography for breast cancer screening in average-risk women aged 40 to 74 years; however, recommendations from professional societies vary.
  • Screening for prostate cancer in asymptomatic, average-risk men is controversial, and recommendations vary; shared decision making is recommended before screening.
  • The American College of Physicians recommends screening for colorectal cancer in asymptomatic adults aged 50 to 75 years; in contrast, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, U.S. Multi-Society Task Force, and American Cancer Society recommend initiating screening for colorectal cancer at age 45 years.
  • The choice of modality for colorectal cancer screening should be based on discussion with patients, including consideration of likelihood of adherence and patient values and preferences.
  • The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends screening women aged 21 to 65 years every 3 years with a Pap test for cervical cancer; in women aged 30 to 65 years who want to lengthen the screening interval, primary human papillomavirus (HPV) testing or HPV cotesting every 5 years can be performed.
  • Both the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) and American Cancer Society (ACS) recommend annual lung cancer screening with low-dose CT for persons aged 50 years to 80 years with a 20-pack-year smoking history; the USPSTF recommends that screening be discontinued in patients who have not smoked for 15 years, whereas the ACS recommends screening all persons who formerly smoked and who meet these criteria regardless of when they last smoked.

index.title: Pulmonary Diagnostic Tests
index.keyPoints:
• Pulmonary function test findings are expressed as a percentage of the value predicted on the basis of patient characteristics.
  • In general, pulmonary function test results below 80% of predicted indicate pulmonary impairment.
  • Spirometry values include FEV~1, FVC, and the FEV~1/FVC ratio.
  • Spirometry correlates with home peak expiratory flow meter measurements but is more reliable and provides more data.
  • Bronchial challenge testing is a helpful diagnostic tool to use for patients whose symptoms suggest asthma in whom initial spirometry is normal.
  • A bronchial challenge test is positive if FEV~1 falls by 20% or more from baseline after inhalation of a provocative agent, such as methacholine.
  • Pulmonary function testing interpretation classifies abnormal results as either obstructive or restrictive and assesses the severity of impairment.
  • The FEV~1/FVC ratio is the primary measurement that defines obstructive disease, and total lung capacity is the primary measurement used to confirm restrictive disease.
  • Patients with mixed obstructive/restrictive patterns have a low FEV~1/FVC ratio (obstructive) and low total lung capacity (restrictive).
  • Dlco may be reduced in patients with COPD, diffuse parenchymal lung disease, lung resection, and pulmonary parenchymal and vascular disorders and may be elevated in those with pulmonary alveolar hemorrhage, left-to-right shunt, or asthma.
  • The shape of the spirometric flow-volume loop can help differentiate obstructive from restrictive patterns and suggest the anatomic location of airway obstruction.
  • Shorter distances on the 6-minute walk test correlate with increased mortality in several lung diseases, including COPD, diffuse parenchymal lung disease, and pulmonary arterial hypertension.
  • A normal hemoglobin saturation measured by pulse oximetry is 95% to 100%, and values below 90% indicate hypoxemia.
  • Erroneous readings on pulse oximetry may result from certain patient factors or substances in the blood; in these cases, alternative methods of measuring oxygenation (e.g., arterial blood gas analysis) are needed.
  • Fractional exhaled nitric oxide testing is recommended as an adjunct in asthma evaluation for patients aged 5 years and older.
  • Elevated fractional exhaled nitric oxide levels correlate modestly with blood and sputum eosinophilia.
  • Conventional chest radiography is indicated as the initial imaging procedure for most patients with significant respiratory symptoms.
  • High-resolution CT techniques are preferred for evaluation of diffuse parenchymal lung disease; conventional noncontrast CT is used to evaluate lung nodules and most other lung diseases; and CT angiography is used for detection of pulmonary embolism.
  • CT is currently the primary source of imaging radiation exposure for patients; low-dose CT is recommended for lung cancer screening in the United States.
  • Thoracic ultrasonography shows the presence, characteristics, and volume of pleural effusions more accurately than chest radiography.
  • Performing pleural drainage procedures with ultrasound guidance reduces risks for complications, including pneumothorax.
  • Thoracic ultrasonography assesses diaphragm function more accurately than fluoroscopy.
  • Bronchoscopy is used for the diagnosis of localized and diffuse pulmonary diseases and is important in the diagnostic evaluation of pulmonary infections, particularly in immunocompromised patients.
  • Endobronchial ultrasonography is the initial procedure of choice for obtaining tissue from mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes in the staging of patients with known or suspected thoracic malignancy.

index.title: Airways Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Asthma is characterized by cough, wheezing, chest tightness, dyspnea, and variable airflow obstruction; patients with severe symptoms have a more sustained course, lower pulmonary function, and increased risk for persistent airway obstruction.
  • Approximately 8% of the U.S. population has a diagnosis of asthma, and prevalence is increased among patients older than age 65 years, women, and persons living below the poverty level.
  • Type 2 inflammation with eosinophilia is a commonly recognized airway cellular inflammatory profile in allergic asthma; a profile of neutrophilic inflammation may be present in older patients.
  • Asthma may result from a genetic predisposition interacting with other factors, including exposure to allergens and tobacco smoke, occupational sensitizers and allergens, viral respiratory infections, air pollution, and obesity.
  • Asthma symptoms are intermittent and occur in response to various stimuli, including allergens, infections, dust, fumes, and exercise.
  • Confirmation of reversible airflow obstruction is the cornerstone of asthma diagnosis; airway obstruction that improves with bronchodilators, on subsequent measurements, or after 4 weeks of anti-inflammatory treatment supports the diagnosis.
  • In patients with clinical symptoms suggestive of asthma but normal spirometry, bronchial challenge testing (such as with methacholine) may be helpful to evaluate for asthma; a negative test excludes asthma, whereas a positive test requires clinical correlation.
  • If pulmonary function testing is not available, biomarker testing (fractional exhaled nitric oxide and blood eosinophil count) can identify type 2 inflammation.
  • Chest radiography is often helpful in asthma evaluation to assess the likelihood of other diagnoses, including COPD, heart failure, parenchymal lung disorders, central airway obstruction, and bronchiectasis.
  • At least half of all patients with asthma are estimated to have a systemic allergic response (type 2 airway inflammation).
  • Serum eosinophilia, high IgE levels, and an elevated fractional exhaled nitric oxide level are often present in patients with asthma and type 2 airway inflammation.
  • Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease describes asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis with sensitivity to aspirin or other NSAIDs that inhibit cyclooxygenase-1.
  • Long-term management of aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease includes usual stepped asthma care, discontinuation of all aspirin and cyclooxygenase-1 inhibitors, and use of leukotriene-receptor antagonists; aspirin desensitization is also an option.
  • Initial pharmacologic therapy for exercise-induced bronchoconstriction is either an inhaled glucocorticoid plus a short-acting β~2-agonist or low-dose inhaled glucocorticoid-formoterol as needed or before exercise.
  • A key clinical indicator of occupational asthma is symptom improvement during time away from work; spirometry before and after workplace exposures is a cost-effective way to confirm a suspected diagnosis.
  • Treatment for occupational asthma consists of reducing exposure to the offending agent and providing pharmacologic therapy; the overriding principle of treatment is prevention.
  • Patients with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis present with difficult-to-control asthma, productive cough, and expectoration of mucus plugs; radiographs may demonstrate pulmonary infiltrates or bronchiectasis.
  • Management of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis includes systemic glucocorticoids and/or antifungal agents, typically for several months; biologic therapy is an option in refractory disease.
  • Control of asthma should be assessed with the use of validated questionnaires.
  • Patients with asthma and daytime symptoms occurring less than twice weekly and nocturnal symptoms occurring less than twice monthly during the preceding 4 weeks are considered well controlled.
  • All patients with asthma should be provided with quick-relief (rescue) medication.
  • Controller medications are used as maintenance therapy in asthma and can be stepped up or down on the basis of symptom control and tolerance of asthma therapies.
  • Inhaler skills training and adherence to prescribed inhaled medications are essential for successful treatment.
  • Inhaled glucocorticoid-formoterol may be preferred to short-acting β~2-agonists (SABAs) as quick-relief (rescue) therapy in asthma; if SABAs are used, a combined inhaled glucocorticoid-SABA may be preferable as rescue therapy.
  • Inhaled glucocorticoids are the most effective class of asthma controller medications and should be prescribed to all symptomatic patients with asthma.
  • Inhaled long-acting β~2-agonists (LABAs) provide sustained airway dilation with once- or twice-daily dosing; when added to an inhaled glucocorticoid, they provide improved control and decrease the risk for exacerbation.
  • Single-agent use of LABAs is not recommended in asthma because of the increased risk for asthma-related death when used without concomitant inhaled glucocorticoids.
  • Long-acting muscarinic antagonists provide sustained airway dilation in patients with asthma and can be added to therapy in patients with asthma not controlled with inhaled glucocorticoid–LABA combination therapy.
  • In patients with severe persistent asthma despite standard therapy, biologic therapies reduce symptoms, the need for oral glucocorticoids, and exacerbations.
  • Phenotyping helps guide the choice of biologic therapy in difficult-to-control asthma; phenotype elements include clinical characteristics such as atopy and allergen sensitization and biomarkers such as IgE and eosinophil levels.
  • All patients with asthma should have a written asthma management plan that helps them recognize the symptoms of an exacerbation and begin self-treatment.
  • Patients who do not improve with self-treatment or who have signs that indicate a severe exacerbation should be evaluated in an acute care facility.
  • COPD affects more than 6% of the U.S. population and is the sixth leading cause of death in the United States.
  • In COPD, air trapping appears as an increased anteroposterior diameter of the chest and flattening of the diaphragm on chest radiographs.
  • Exposure to cigarette smoke is the most important risk factor for COPD in the United States, but COPD can also result from long-term exposure to other irritants, such as air pollution.
  • COPD is a heterogeneous condition, and patients present with variable symptoms, including cough, sputum production, and dyspnea.
  • In patients with COPD, the BODE index (BMI, airflow obstruction, dyspnea, exercise) provides better prognostic information than the FEV~1 alone and can estimate risk of hospitalization and 4-year survival.
  • The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force does not recommend spirometric screening for COPD in asymptomatic individuals.
  • In the appropriate clinical context, COPD is diagnosed by a postbronchodilator FEV~1/FVC ratio of less than 0.70 or less than the lower limit of normal.
  • After a diagnosis of COPD has been established, the initial assessment focuses on disease severity, which is determined using a combination of symptoms, degree of airflow obstruction on spirometry, history of acute exacerbations, and presence of comorbid conditions.
  • In patients with COPD, the GOLD model, which is determined by the combination of symptom severity and the history of acute exacerbations, can be used to assess disease severity and help guide treatment decisions.
  • Patients who have had two or more acute exacerbations within the past year, have ever been hospitalized for an acute exacerbation, or have an FEV~1 of less than 50% of predicted are at high risk for recurrent acute exacerbations.
  • An α~1-antitrypsin level should be obtained once in all patients with COPD to evaluate for α~1-antitrypsin deficiency.
  • Smoking cessation is essential in the management of COPD because it can slow the decline of FEV~1; clinicians should encourage all patients to quit smoking.
  • Success rates for smoking cessation are highest with the combination of counseling and medication therapy; patients who smoke should receive at least one of the pharmacologic treatments available for smoking cessation.
  • Bronchodilators are the mainstay of therapy for COPD irrespective of the severity of the disease.
  • Each time that bronchodilators or other inhalers are prescribed, the clinician should educate the patient on proper inhaler technique.
  • If short-acting bronchodilators are insufficient to control symptoms in patients with COPD, a long-acting bronchodilator can be added.
  • Both long-acting inhaled β~2-agonists and antimuscarinic agents are effective in COPD, and either can be used for initial relief of symptoms; if symptoms persist, the addition of a second long-acting agent from the alternate bronchodilator class is appropriate.
  • Inhaled glucocorticoids are typically used only in combination with a long-acting bronchodilator for treatment of COPD.
  • Inhaled glucocorticoids improve symptoms in patients with moderate to severe COPD but are associated with an increased risk for pneumonia.
  • In patients with severe COPD, triple inhaler therapy may provide additional symptom benefit, reduce exacerbations, and decrease mortality.
  • In patients with COPD, inhaled glucocorticoids can be added to long-acting bronchodilator therapy if the eosinophil count exceeds a threshold of 150 to 300/µL (0.2-0.3 × 10^9/L).
  • Oral glucocorticoids are recommended for short-duration treatment of acute exacerbations of COPD; however, long-term use should be avoided.
  • Infections are the most common trigger of acute exacerbations of COPD.
  • Routine immunizations, including annual influenza vaccination, are recommended for all patients with COPD.
  • The BODE index (BMI, airflow obstruction, dyspnea, exercise) may be used to estimate prognosis and 4-year survival rate in COPD.
  • Palliative care can help manage symptoms such as dyspnea, anxiety, and depression in patients with COPD at any stage of disease.
  • Guidelines suggest that patients with severe COPD should be considered for hospice care.
  • An acute exacerbation of COPD is a worsening of a patient's typical symptoms over the course of fewer than 14 days that is often accompanied by local or systemic inflammation.
  • The most common symptoms of COPD exacerbations are worsening dyspnea, an increase in the severity or frequency of cough, and an increase in the amount of or a change in the character of sputum produced.
  • Strategies to prevent COPD exacerbations include smoking cessation, pulmonary rehabilitation when appropriate, recommended immunizations, and proper inhaler technique and use of medications.
  • In select patients with severe COPD and a history of frequent exacerbations, long-term use of azithromycin or roflumilast may prevent future exacerbations.
  • A mild COPD exacerbation can be managed solely by short-acting bronchodilators; a moderate exacerbation requires antibiotics, glucocorticoids, or both; and a severe exacerbation requires an evaluation in the emergency department or hospitalization.
  • Patients who have COPD and respiratory distress or who are at risk for developing respiratory distress should be hospitalized and evaluated with chest radiography, ECG, and oxygen saturation; arterial blood gas measurements can determine the presence of hypercapnia.
  • Bronchiectasis is diagnosed by high-resolution chest CT; diagnostic criteria include an airway diameter greater than that of its accompanying vessel and a lack of distal airway tapering.
  • Every patient diagnosed with bronchiectasis requires evaluation for a treatable underlying cause although more than half of all cases are idiopathic.
  • Treatment of underlying causes of bronchiectasis is crucial to preventing disease progression.
  • Treatment of bronchiectasis focuses on airway clearance, treating infections, and preventing exacerbations.
  • Airway clearance techniques useful in bronchiectasis include bronchodilators, positive expiratory pressure devices, postural drainage, manual techniques, inhaled hypertonic saline, and exercise.
  • Long-term use of macrolide antibiotics in bronchiectasis may prevent future exacerbations; risk for future exacerbations should be weighed against the possibility of developing macrolide resistance.
  • Adults diagnosed with cystic fibrosis (CF) most often present with pulmonary or gastrointestinal symptoms; pulmonary manifestations often include chronic productive cough, recurrent sinusitis, and recurrent pulmonary infections.
  • Sweat chloride testing is the initial test for CF; abnormal results on repeat testing are diagnostic.
  • A negative sweat chloride test in an adult patient does not rule out CF.

index.title: Diffuse Parenchymal Lung Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Diffuse parenchymal lung diseases are classified into those with a known cause (such as medications, radiation, connective tissue disorders, and pneumoconiosis) and those that are idiopathic (such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and cryptogenic organizing pneumonia).
  • The most common presentation of a diffuse parenchymal lung disease (DPLD) is subacute to chronic exertional dyspnea and nonproductive cough.
  • Patients with a clinical suspicion of DPLD should undergo complete pulmonary function testing, including spirometry, lung volumes, and Dlco measurement; most patients will have restrictive physiology.
  • A normal chest radiograph does not rule out DPLD.
  • Noncontrast high-resolution CT of the chest is the imaging modality of choice for evaluation of diffuse parenchymal lung disease.
  • Smoking cessation is the primary management of all smoking-related diffuse parenchymal lung diseases; glucocorticoids may be considered in refractory or severe disease.
  • Removal of exposure to the offending antigen is essential in the treatment of hypersensitivity pneumonitis; glucocorticoids and other immunosuppressants may be used for patients with more severe or refractory symptoms.
  • Drugs associated with diffuse parenchymal lung disease include amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, immune checkpoint inhibitors, busulfan, and bleomycin.
  • Patients with radiation pneumonitis typically present 4 to 12 weeks after initial radiation exposure with cough, dyspnea, and a new radiographic infiltrate, often with a well-defined nonanatomic demarcation between normal and abnormal lung.
  • Glucocorticoids are used to treat severe forms of radiation pneumonitis, whereas observation may be appropriate for patients with mild disease.
  • When high-resolution CT findings are classic for usual interstitial pneumonia, lung biopsy is not necessary for diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
  • Therapy with nintedanib or pirfenidone decreases the rate of progression of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis but is not curative.
  • Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) occurs as both a common variant in connective tissue disease–related interstitial lung disease and as idiopathic NSIP.
  • Differentiation of idiopathic NSIP from idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is critical because the treatment algorithms and prognosis differ between these diseases.
  • On high-resolution CT scan, NSIP typically demonstrates bilateral lower lobe reticular changes and areas of ground-glass opacification.
  • Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP) typically presents as cough, dyspnea, fever, and malaise lasting weeks to months.
  • Diagnosis of COP may not require lung biopsy if the clinical presentation and high-resolution CT findings are consistent with COP; for cases with atypical presentation, lung biopsy is necessary.
  • COP responds well to glucocorticoids, but relapse with glucocorticoid tapering is common.
  • Acute interstitial pneumonia is clinically, radiographically, and pathologically indistinguishable from acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), but affected patients lack risk factors for ARDS; high-dose glucocorticoids are used, although supportive evidence is lacking.
  • In patients with combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema, pulmonary function studies may reveal preserved spirometry and lung volumes even when advanced architectural changes are present.
  • More than 90% of patients with sarcoidosis have lung involvement; radiographic staging can predict the probability of spontaneous resolution.
  • Patients with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy in the absence of features that suggest malignancy or infection (fevers, weight loss, or night sweats) likely have sarcoidosis and can be monitored without biopsy.
  • The diagnosis of sarcoidosis most commonly rests on biopsy revealing noncaseating granulomas and exclusion of mimicking conditions, such as tuberculosis and systemic granulomatous diseases.
  • The primary treatment of symptomatic sarcoidosis is glucocorticoids, often followed by glucocorticoid-sparing therapies.

index.title: Occupational Lung Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Diseases associated with occupational exposure include rhinitis, asthma, reactive airways dysfunction syndrome, COPD, pleural disease, diffuse parenchymal lung disease, and malignancy.
  • A careful employment history that includes occupational exposures is essential for diagnosis of occupational lung disease.
  • When an occupational lung disease is suspected, it is essential to obtain a complete history, including occupation, type and extent of exposure, temporal relationship of exposure to symptoms and disease, and other exposures at home and from hobbies.
  • The key to management of occupational lung disease is either removal of the offending agent from the workplace or preventing worker contact with the offending agent; further investigation of the workplace to ensure the identification of all affected individuals is also essential.
  • Treatment of patients with occupational lung disease varies depending on the underlying lung disease.

index.title: Pleural Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Heart failure, pneumonia, and malignancy are the most common causes of pleural effusion in the United States.
  • Chest radiography should be performed in the initial evaluation of possible pleural effusion.
  • Thoracic ultrasonography can characterize pleural effusions, quantify volume, and decrease complications when used to guide pleural procedures.
  • Thoracic ultrasonography is more sensitive than chest radiography for the diagnosis of small effusions, particularly in patients in the semirecumbent or supine position, such as those who are critically ill.
  • Indications for thoracentesis include diagnosing the cause of a pleural effusion and removing fluid in patients with significant symptoms, such as dyspnea.
  • Adenosine deaminase is elevated in most tuberculous pleural effusions, and a negative test result helps to exclude tuberculosis in countries with a low incidence of tuberculosis.
  • Cytologic examination of pleural fluid for malignancy has an average sensitivity of 60%; thoracoscopy should be considered if the suspicion for malignant disease is high after two negative cytologic evaluations.
  • Uncomplicated parapneumonic effusions are characterized by a pleural pH greater than 7.2 (often >7.4), a glucose level greater than 60 mg/dL (3.3 mmol/L), and a lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level less than 900 U/L; they typically resolve with treatment of the pneumonia.
  • Criteria for drainage of complicated parapneumonic effusions and empyema include the presence of frank pus, a positive Gram stain or culture, or a pH of less than 7.2; the combination of a pH of 7.2 to 7.4 and pleural LDH greater than 900 U/L should also prompt consideration of drainage.
  • Early drainage of complicated parapneumonic effusions and empyema improves outcomes; options include video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery and thoracostomy tube drainage, usually with concomitant intrapleural fibrinolytics.
  • Greater than 20% of pleural space infections include anaerobic bacteria, and empiric antibiotic regimens should include coverage for anaerobic coverage.
  • Chest radiography is an appropriate initial test in most patients with suspected pneumothorax; bedside ultrasonography is indicated when patients are unstable and concern is present for tension physiology.
  • Pneumothoraces that are greater than 2 cm on chest radiograph or associated with significant symptoms should undergo decompression.
  • In pneumothorax, recurrence prevention is recommended after the second episode of pneumothorax on the ipsilateral side in primary spontaneous pneumothorax and after the first occurrence of secondary spontaneous pneumothorax.

index.title: Pulmonary Vascular Disease
index.keyPoints:
• The normal resting mean pulmonary artery pressure is approximately 14 mm Hg and rarely exceeds 20 mm Hg; a pressure greater than 20 mm Hg is associated with increased mortality and is used to define the presence of pulmonary hypertension.
  • The term pulmonary hypertension describes a heterogenous group of diseases defined hemodynamically by the presence of elevated mean pulmonary artery pressures and further categorized into five groups on the basis of clinical features and mechanism of disease.
  • Pulmonary arterial hypertension refers to a rare subset of patients with group 1 pulmonary hypertension.
  • Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is classified into five groups on the basis of mechanism, histologic profile, hemodynamics, and clinical presentation.
  • If PH is suspected, initial noninvasive testing, including transthoracic echocardiography, should be performed to estimate tricuspid regurgitant velocity and assess additional echocardiographic signs of PH (e.g., abnormal right ventricular size, structure, and function).
  • Right heart catheterization (also known as pulmonary artery catheterization) is essential to confirm a diagnosis of PH because it measures mean pulmonary artery pressure and helps distinguish the primary cause of elevated pulmonary artery pressure.
  • Not all patients with PH fit exclusively into one category of disease; such patients may require expert evaluation with additional testing for multiple underlying contributors to PH.
  • Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) may be idiopathic or occur in association with connective tissue diseases, portal hypertension, congenital heart disease, HIV infection, schistosomiasis, and drug or toxin exposure.
  • Approximately 10% of patients with systemic sclerosis develop PAH; disease in these patients is often refractory to treatment and associated with poor outcomes.
  • The diagnosis of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is confirmed hemodynamically by right heart catheterization demonstrating precapillary PH not due to left-sided heart disease.
  • Pulmonary function testing in PAH characteristically shows normal spirometry; however, isolated reduction in DLCO may reflect underlying pulmonary vascular disease.
  • Genetic testing is recommended for all patients with idiopathic PAH and family history of PAH and should be considered in other select conditions (e.g., anorexigen-associated PAH, pulmonary veno-occlusive disease, and congenital heart disease–associated PAH).
  • Initial therapy for pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is guided by validated risk stratification tools with the goal to titrate therapy to achieve and maintain low-risk status during serial follow-up.
  • Optimizing combination therapy is associated with superior outcomes compared with single-agent therapy.
  • Novel activin-signaling inhibitors (sotatercept) should be considered in addition to conventional pulmonary vasodilator therapy for patients who do not achieve treatment goals.
  • Patients who demonstrate marked improvement in mean pulmonary artery pressure on vasoreactivity testing have a more favorable prognosis and can be initially treated with calcium channel blocker therapy; however, loss of vasoreactivity is common, requiring conventional PAH therapy.
  • Patients with pulmonary hypertension (PH) should be evaluated for chronic thromboembolic PH (CTEPH) with ventilation-perfusion scanning.
  • A normal ventilation-perfusion scan effectively rules out CTEPH.
  • In patients with prior pulmonary embolism, CTEPH should be considered in those who remain symptomatic or develop symptoms consistent with PH after 3 months of consistent anticoagulation.
  • Lifelong anticoagulation is essential in all patients with chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH).
  • Multidisciplinary care at an expert CTEPH center is key to define subsequent treatment, including assessment for pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), which is potentially curative in many patients.
  • In patients with inoperable CTEPH and those with persistent pulmonary hypertension after PTE, medical therapy with riociguat and/or balloon pulmonary angioplasty should be considered.
  • Most cases (60%-80%) of pulmonary hypertension (PH) are attributable to left-sided heart or lung disease.
  • PH can be seen with varying prevalence in patients with chronic lung diseases.
  • In patients with PH due to diffuse parenchymal lung disease, inhaled treprostinil may improve outcomes; pulmonary vasodilators have not been shown to improve outcomes in randomized controlled trials in patients with PH due to other chronic lung diseases, including COPD.
  • PH increases mortality risk in left-sided heart or lung disease, and early consideration should be given to heart and/or lung transplantation.
  • Guidelines suggest considering an evaluation for sleep-disordered breathing or nocturnal hypoxemia with polysomnography or a home sleep study in patients with PH.
  • Management of chronic right ventricular failure includes supplemental oxygen for hypoxemia, diuretic therapy for volume overload, and treatment of the underlying cause.

index.title: Lung Tumors
index.keyPoints:
• Principles of pulmonary nodule evaluation include reviewing imaging history, estimating the probability of malignancy, and discussing management preferences with the patient.
  • A focal pulmonary opacity larger than 3 cm is presumed malignant until proved otherwise.
  • A well-demarcated and fully or centrally calcified pulmonary nodule typically represents a previous infectious granuloma and is benign.
  • The first step in evaluating a solid pulmonary nodule larger than 8 mm is estimating the probability of malignancy; multiple models are available to determine this likelihood.
  • Solid pulmonary nodules between 8 and 30 mm with moderate or high probability of malignancy should be characterized further with PET/CT to determine management.
  • Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide.
  • Two major types of lung cancer are non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small cell lung cancer; NSCLC accounts for 80% of lung cancer cases.
  • The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends annual lung cancer screening with low-dose CT in patients aged 50 to 80 years who have at least a 20-pack-year smoking history, including those who have quit smoking within the past 15 years; in contrast, the American Cancer Society recommends screening all patients with a smoking history who meet the criteria regardless of when they last smoked.
  • Evaluation for possible lung cancer should determine the cell type and stage of the malignancy; most lung cancers present at a late stage.
  • In patients with suspected lung cancer, PET/CT can identify unsuspected mediastinal involvement and distant disease, which informs staging biopsy strategy and reduces futile (noncurative) surgery.
  • The definitive diagnosis of lung cancer requires tissue histopathology.
  • In patients with radiographic evidence of advanced-stage lung cancer, diagnosis and staging are best accomplished with a single biopsy at a location that will establish both the diagnosis and the disease stage.
