  • Pulmonary carcinoid tumors arise in the proximal airways and often present as an obstructing mass.
  • Surgical resection of pulmonary carcinoid tumors is often curative, and 10-year survival rates exceed 90%.
  • Hamartomas are the most common benign lung neoplasm; on imaging, they appear as smooth-bordered nodules, which may have “popcorn” calcification or contain fat.
  • Mesothelioma is associated with inhalational exposure to asbestos fibers and has a latency of 20 to 40 years.
  • Clinical suspicion for malignant pleural mesothelioma should arise in the setting of pleural thickening or recurrent exudative pleural effusion and a history of asbestos exposure.
  • The sensitivity of pleural fluid cytology for malignant mesothelioma is poor, and pleural biopsy is usually required for diagnosis.
  • Thymic lesions are the most common tumor in the anterior mediastinum and are associated with various paraneoplastic syndromes, such as pure red cell aplasia and myasthenia gravis.
  • Lymphadenopathy is the most common mass in the middle mediastinum and can be secondary to lymphoma, sarcoid, lung cancer, or metastatic disease.
  • Neurogenic neoplasms are the most common tumors in the posterior mediastinum and are classified on the basis of their neural origin.

index.title: Sleep Medicine
index.keyPoints:
• The initial evaluation of excessive daytime sleepiness should include a thorough history to assess sleep duration and time available for sleeping before additional testing is pursued.
  • All patients with excessive daytime sleepiness should be counseled about the dangers of drowsy driving and the need for 7 to 8 hours of sleep per night.
  • The most common cause of excessive daytime sleepiness is insufficient sleep syndrome, the functional impairment resulting from an inadequate amount of sleep.
  • Obstructive sleep apnea is defined by sleep interruption resulting from repetitive upper airway narrowing or collapse.
  • The apnea-hypopnea index is the total number of apnea and hypopnea events divided by total sleep time and can classify obstructive sleep apnea as mild (5-14 events per hour), moderate (15-30 per hour), or severe (>30 per hour).
  • Obesity is the most important risk factor for obstructive sleep apnea.
  • Home sleep apnea testing is most appropriate in patients without underlying cardiopulmonary or neuromuscular disease suspected of having at least moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea.
  • In-laboratory polysomnography is recommended for patients with suspected obstructive sleep apnea who have significant comorbid conditions, including heart failure, neuromuscular disease, and advanced pulmonary disease.
  • In patients who are overweight or obese, obstructive sleep apnea severity improves with weight loss.
  • Positive airway pressure (PAP) is the most effective therapy for preventing disordered breathing events and alleviating symptoms in patients with obstructive sleep apnea.
  • Auto-adjusting PAP and continuous PAP are considered therapeutic equivalents for reducing the apnea-hypopnea index and improving obstructive sleep apnea symptoms.
  • Surgical treatments for obstructive sleep apnea can be considered for patients who do not benefit from or tolerate airway pressure therapy; patients with a BMI less than 40 are most likely to benefit from surgery.
  • Central sleep apnea syndromes are defined by pauses in airflow caused by loss of output from the central respiratory generators in the brainstem, resulting in lack of respiratory effort.
  • Initial management of central sleep apnea should target modifiable risk factors, such as heart failure and opioid use.
  • It is unclear whether treatment of central sleep apnea improves cardiovascular outcomes.
  • Sleep-related hypoventilation syndromes are defined by impaired gas exchange during wakefulness that are further compromised with sleep; common associated conditions include advanced COPD, obesity hypoventilation syndrome, and restrictive lung diseases related to kyphoscoliosis or neuromuscular disorders.
  • The hallmark of obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) is daytime hypercapnia, defined as an arterial Pco~2 greater than 45 mm Hg (6.0 kPa).
  • Patients with OHS should undergo in-laboratory polysomnography.
  • Patients with OHS should be treated with nocturnal continuous positive airway pressure.
  • Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation devices are often prescribed to alleviate sleep-related symptoms and support blood oxygen levels in patients with neuromuscular disorders.

index.title: High Altitude–Related Illnesses
index.keyPoints:
• High altitude–related illnesses are difficult to predict and can occur at any age regardless of fitness level; risk factors include rapid ascent and medical comorbidities that impair oxygenation.
  • Gradual ascent to altitude as well as acetazolamide, dexamethasone, and nifedipine can be prophylactic in patients at high risk for high altitude–related illnesses.
  • Symptoms of acute mountain sickness are nonspecific and include headache, fatigue, nausea, and vomiting; disturbed sleep related to high-altitude periodic breathing is common.
  • Heavy exertion and dehydration tend to amplify acute mountain sickness symptoms, which typically resolve within 24 to 48 hours in absence of further ascent.
  • Gradual ascent to altitude and acetazolamide can prevent acute mountain sickness.
  • High-altitude cerebral edema tends to occur at higher elevations (>3000 m [10,000 ft]); it is characterized by altered mental status and ataxia progressing to coma.
  • Patients with high-altitude cerebral edema require immediate descent from altitude, particularly while still ambulatory.
  • Patients with high-altitude pulmonary edema should be treated with descent from altitude, supplemental oxygen, and rest.
  • Preflight evaluation with hypoxia altitude simulation testing to determine recommended oxygen use is helpful in certain patients with chronic lung disease; a resting oxygen saturation of less than 92% at sea level indicates a likely need for in-flight supplemental oxygen.
  • During air travel, adequate preparation with a portable oxygen concentrator and increasing the flow rate is typically recommended for patients who are already receiving long-term supplemental oxygen.
  • Although an existing pneumothorax has traditionally been considered a contraindication to flight, air travel may be safe in the presence of a small postoperative pneumothorax that has been radiographically stable.

index.title: Approach to the Patient With Rheumatologic Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Inflammatory signs include pain, erythema, swelling, and warmth; noninflammatory conditions typically lack these features, except for pain.
  • An accurate history and a thorough musculoskeletal physical examination are essential to differentiate inflammatory and noninflammatory symptoms and can help lead to a diagnosis and avoid unnecessary testing.
  • Chronic noninflammatory arthritis is usually caused by osteoarthritis.
  • Joint aspiration is usually the most effective means of distinguishing inflammatory from noninflammatory arthritis.
  • Isolated tendon and/or ligament involvement usually suggests noninflammatory disorders, such as mechanical injury/irritation, overuse, or degeneration.
  • Severe persistent inflammation of the enthesis (enthesitis) is a characteristic feature of spondyloarthritis.
  • Rheumatologic disease can cause constitutional symptoms and extra-articular manifestations affecting the skin, eyes, and internal organs.
  • Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels usually follow a common pattern, but CRP more rapidly responds to changes in inflammation.
  • Antinuclear antibody (ANA) testing should not be performed in a patient with nonspecific symptoms and normal findings on clinical examination; in that setting, it does not establish the diagnosis of a connective tissue disease.
  • ANA subserology testing should be reserved for patients positive for ANA and with a clinical syndrome suggesting a specific underlying connective tissue disease.
  • The presence of autoantibodies does not necessarily equate with a diagnosis of rheumatologic disease but can make a suspected rheumatologic diagnosis more likely; autoantibodies may also be present in patients with nonrheumatologic conditions, and low titers of autoantibodies are not uncommon in otherwise healthy persons.
  • Radiography is usually the first imaging test ordered in evaluating arthritis because it is readily available and inexpensive, requires only a low level of ionizing radiation, and is useful in monitoring arthritis progression.
  • CT is more sensitive for detecting bony abnormalities or erosions than radiography or MRI, and MRI is the most sensitive routine radiologic technique for detecting soft-tissue abnormalities, inflammation, and fluid collections.
  • Ultrasonography can provide real-time assessment of bone and soft-tissue abnormalities (including synovitis and tendonitis), can assist with tendon or joint injections, but is operator dependent.
  • Joint aspiration should be performed during evaluation of monoarthritis to diagnose or exclude infection, and synovial fluid should be sent for leukocyte count, Gram stain, cultures, and evaluation for crystals.
  • Patients with a synovial fluid leukocyte count greater than 50,000/μL (50 × 10^9/L) with polymorphonuclear cell predominance have a high likelihood of infection; counts less than 2000/μL (2.0 × 10^9/L) are usually associated with noninflammatory causes.
  • In patients with Raynaud phenomenon, nailfold capillary abnormalities are associated with an increased likelihood of an underlying disease and should prompt evaluation for a rheumatologic cause.
  • Tissue biopsy of involved organs can be helpful in diagnosing numerous rheumatologic conditions and in assessing disease activity in some conditions.
  • Depression screening should be performed in individuals with rheumatologic diseases and may improve outcomes.

index.title: Principles of Therapeutics
index.keyPoints:
• Because of adverse effects, glucocorticoids should be used at the lowest dose and shortest duration effective.
  • Patients anticipated to be receiving long-term glucocorticoids should have a baseline clinical risk assessment for osteoporosis.
  • Because of the increased risk for gastrointestinal bleeding and adverse cardiovascular and renal events, NSAIDs should be prescribed at the lowest dose for the shortest time possible.
  • The American College of Rheumatology conditionally recommends acetaminophen for patients with knee, hip, and hand osteoarthritis and limited pharmacologic options.
  • Traditional opioids should generally be avoided in rheumatologic treatment because of limited efficacy, high toxicity, and high potential for dependence.
  • Hydroxychloroquine decreases mortality and the likelihood of nephritis in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus.
  • Methotrexate is a first-line medication for rheumatoid arthritis.
  • All biologic agents increase the risk for infection; therefore, targeted screening is necessary before initiation.
  • Tofacitinib and possibly other Janus kinase inhibitors are associated with an increased risk for myocardial infarction or stroke, cancer, blood clots, and death.
  • Hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine are relatively safe in pregnancy and lactation.
  • Methotrexate is highly teratogenic and abortifacient; it must be discontinued at least 3 months before pregnancy.
  • Leflunomide is extremely teratogenic and must not be used before or during pregnancy; upon discontinuation, cholestyramine is required to remove the drug from the body in individuals planning pregnancy.
  • Mycophenolate mofetil is teratogenic and should be discontinued at least 6 weeks before pregnancy.
  • Whenever possible, vaccinations should be updated before initiation of immunosuppressive treatment.
  • Screening (and therapy if needed) for tuberculosis, hepatitis B and C virus infections, and HIV infection is recommended before initiation of immunosuppressive therapy.
  • Nonpharmacologic measures used in rheumatologic diseases include physical or occupational therapy, surgery, weight reduction, psychosocial support, and self-management programs.

index.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
index.keyPoints:
• Potential risk factors for rheumatoid arthritis include genetic and environmental factors, infectious agents, and hormones; genes make up 60% of the risk.
  • Smoking is an important and modifiable risk factor for rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Typical clinical manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) include pain, swelling, and prolonged morning stiffness in a symmetric pattern, particularly in the joints of the hands and feet.
  • The most useful laboratory studies to aid in the diagnosis of RA are rheumatoid factor and anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibodies; anti-CCP antibodies have a specificity of 95% for RA.
  • Plain radiography of the hands and/or feet is the standard imaging study for RA; radiographic changes include periarticular osteopenia, marginal erosions, and joint-space narrowing, although early radiographs may be normal.
  • Extra-articular manifestations and complications of rheumatoid arthritis include rheumatoid nodules, dry eye, interstitial lung disease, and anemia of inflammation.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis conveys a high risk for cardiovascular disease.
  • In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), treating to a target of remission or low disease activity reduces radiographic damage and cardiovascular risk and increases work productivity.
  • Methotrexate is the anchor drug in RA; it is used as both monotherapy and a component of combination therapy.
  • Biologic and targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) are used in RA for persistent moderate to high disease activity; tumor necrosis factor inhibitors are the most frequently used biologic DMARDs.
  • In RA, NSAIDs may help to control symptoms but are not disease modifying and do not prevent joint damage; they should be used sparingly and along with DMARDs.
  • Low-dose prednisone can be used to rapidly improve RA symptoms until long-term medications become effective, but long-term glucocorticoid use carries significant comorbid risk.

index.title: Osteoarthritis
index.keyPoints:
• Osteoarthritis is a chronic progressive disorder characterized by cartilage and meniscal degradation, subchondral bone changes, osteophyte formation, and low-grade synovitis.
  • Obesity is the most important modifiable risk factor for knee osteoarthritis.
  • In most cases, no identifiable proximal cause of osteoarthritis (OA) is recognized; this form is categorized as primary OA.
  • Erosive OA mostly affects the distal interphalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, is characterized by erythema and swelling, and is more common in women.
  • Commonly recognized causes of secondary OA include a history of joint damage; congenitally abnormal joints and/or malalignment; systemic metabolic, endocrine, microcrystalline, and neuropathic disorders; and underlying inflammatory arthritis with accompanying damage.
  • The most common symptom of osteoarthritis (OA) is joint pain exacerbated by activity and alleviated with rest; morning stiffness usually lasts less than 30 minutes.
  • Laboratory testing is not necessary to diagnose OA but is helpful if other causes of arthritis are being considered or to define the safety of proposed medical therapies.
  • Radiographic features of OA include asymmetric joint-space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes, and bone cysts; however, these changes may not be present in early disease, and symptoms may correlate poorly with imaging findings.
  • Nonpharmacologic therapy for osteoarthritis (OA) includes education, an exercise regimen, weight loss, and assistive devices as appropriate.
  • Pharmacologic therapy for OA includes oral, topical, and intra-articular medications; choice of treatment depends on individualized assessment, with particular attention to comorbidities and concomitant medications.
  • NSAIDs are the initial oral pharmacologic treatment of choice for OA; for knee and hand OA, topical NSAIDs are preferred over oral NSAIDs.
  • Arthroscopic surgery is not indicated in patients with OA unless they have joint buckling, instability, or locking or a concomitant and symptomatic mechanical disorder.
  • Total joint replacement relieves pain and improves function in patients with OA in whom conservative therapies have failed.

index.title: Fibromyalgia
index.keyPoints:
• The characteristic features of fibromyalgia are widespread chronic pain, fatigue, sleep disorders, and cognitive symptoms.
  • The diagnosis of fibromyalgia is no longer based on physical examination findings but rather on a careful characterization of symptoms using a validated tool.
  • Extensive laboratory studies should not be performed in patients suspected of having fibromyalgia unless other specific diagnoses are suspected.
  • Nonpharmacologic therapy (education, exercise, psychosocial support) remains a cornerstone of treatment for fibromyalgia, and pharmacotherapy is often warranted.
  • Choice of pharmacologic therapy for patients with fibromyalgia is based on symptom profile, comorbidities, and medication adverse effects.

index.title: Spondyloarthritis
index.keyPoints:
• Spondyloarthritis comprises arthritic disorders classified by common risk factors and clinical manifestations; the disorders include axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis and nonradiographic axial spondyloarthritis), psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, and enteropathic arthritis.
  • Inheriting HLA-B27 significantly increases the odds ratio of developing ankylosing spondylitis.
  • Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory disease affecting the axial skeleton (including sacroiliac joints), entheses, and peripheral joints.
  • Common extra-articular manifestations of ankylosing spondylitis include uveitis and inflammatory bowel disease.
  • Patients with nonradiographic axial spondyloarthritis present with similar clinical features as ankylosing spondylitis (radiographic axial spondyloarthritis) but do not have evidence of sacroiliitis on plain radiographs.
  • Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is an inflammatory joint disease associated with psoriasis, multiple possible joint patterns, enthesitis, and dactylitis.
  • PsA usually develops years after psoriasis, but 15% of patients may develop PsA concurrently with or even before psoriasis.
  • Spondyloarthritis, isolated sacroiliitis, and peripheral arthritis can occur in patients with inflammatory bowel disease.
  • The risk for inflammatory bowel disease is highest in patients with ankylosing spondylitis, and these patients should be regularly assessed for bowel symptoms.
  • Reactive arthritis can occur 2 to 3 weeks following specific gastrointestinal and genitourinary infections, most commonly Chlamydia trachomatis infection.
  • Reactive arthritis is typically pauciarticular, with involvement of larger joints; enthesitis (usually of the Achilles tendon or plantar fascia) and dactylitis commonly occur.
  • HLA-B27 antigen testing is never diagnostic for spondyloarthritis but can help determine risk for spondyloarthritis in uncertain situations.
  • Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein can help support an inflammatory process; however, these values are not always elevated in patients with spondyloarthritis, particularly in ankylosing spondylitis.
  • Radiography of the sacroiliac joints is an initial diagnostic test for patients suspected of having ankylosing spondylitis; radiographic evidence of sacroiliitis includes pseudo-widening of the joints, erosions, sclerosis, and ankylosis.
  • MRI of the sacroiliac joints is more sensitive than CT and can identify sacroiliac inflammation even in the absence of radiographic changes; however, 25% of healthy individuals can have similar MRI changes.
  • In psoriatic arthritis, radiographic findings take the form of erosions of the distal head of the proximal joint and juxta-articular new bone formation at the proximal head of the distal joint, leading to a “pencil-in-cup” appearance across the joint.
  • For ankylosing spondylitis, NSAIDs are recommended as the initial medication to relieve pain and improve stiffness; physical therapy to maintain general range of motion is essential.
  • For patients with ankylosing spondylitis and persistently high axial disease activity despite NSAIDs, a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor, interleukin-17 inhibitor, or Janus kinase inhibitor is recommended.
  • There is no role for conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (e.g., methotrexate or sulfasalazine) in ankylosing spondylitis with axial disease; however, sulfasalazine can be used for peripheral disease.
  • Treatment of nonradiographic axial spondyloarthritis is similar to that for ankylosing spondylitis.
  • Treatment of psoriatic arthritis should consider the category of musculoskeletal manifestations (e.g., peripheral arthritis, enthesitis, axial arthritis) as well as nonmusculoskeletal manifestations (e.g., skin disease, uveitis, inflammatory bowel disease) because available agents are not equally effective in different domains.
  • Enteropathic arthritis is best addressed by managing bowel inflammation.
  • IL-17 inhibitors can be associated with inflammatory bowel disease flares and are not preferred agents in patients with enteropathic arthritis.
  • Antibiotic treatment of reactive arthritis due to enteric organisms is not usually warranted; however, patients with Chlamydia trachomatis infection should receive antibiotic therapy.
  • For patients with reactive arthritis and mild arthritic disease, NSAIDs or joint injections with glucocorticoids may be sufficient; for more persistent or severe disease, sulfasalazine, methotrexate, or TNF inhibitors may be required.

index.title: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
index.keyPoints:
• Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a multisystem autoimmune disease characterized by a heterogeneous constellation of organ involvement and the presence of antinuclear antibodies and other autoantibodies, including anti–double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith antibodies, which are specific for SLE.
  • Approximately 90% of adult patients with SLE are female.
  • The facial eruption of acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (malar or butterfly rash) is characterized by erythema and edema over the cheeks and bridge of the nose, sparing the nasolabial folds.
  • Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SLE) can be drug-induced or can result from underlying SLE; features that may favor a drug-induced cause are widespread disease, bullous or erythema multiforme–like lesions, and vasculitic-appearing lesions.
  • Discoid lupus erythematosus is the most common manifestation of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus and more commonly occurs in isolation, with 5% to 25% of patients having coexisting SLE.
  • Joints are affected in up to 90% of patients with SLE, and joint involvement is usually nonerosive.
  • All patients with SLE should be regularly evaluated for kidney involvement through assessment of serum creatinine, urinary protein, and microscopic evaluation of urine.
  • The most common manifestations of neuropsychiatric SLE are headache, mild cognitive dysfunction, and mood disorder.
  • Asymptomatic pericarditis is the most frequent cardiac manifestation of acute SLE.
  • Pleural disease is the most common pulmonary manifestation of SLE.
  • Patients with SLE are at increased risk for thrombotic events; the risk is highest for those with triple positivity for lupus anticoagulant, anti–β~2-glycoprotein, and anticardiolipin antibodies.
  • Patients with SLE are at increased risk for infections and malignancy.
  • Patients with SLE have a 2- to 10-fold increased prevalence of coronary artery disease; high SLE disease activity and prednisone dosages greater than 10 mg/d are independent risk factors for coronary artery disease.
  • Initial evaluation for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) includes antinuclear antibody testing as well as routine laboratory testing to establish organ-specific involvement, including complete blood count, chemistry panel, and urinalysis with microscopy.
  • If results of antinuclear antibody testing are positive (titer ≥1:80) and the clinical context is supportive, autoantibodies specific to SLE (anti–double-stranded DNA, anti-Smith, anti–U1-ribonucleoprotein, anti-Ro/SSA, and anti-La/SSB) should be obtained to further characterize the disease.
  • With SLE activity, complement levels are typically reduced and anti–double-stranded DNA antibody levels elevated.
  • Drug-induced lupus erythematosus is usually milder than SLE, and symptoms usually resolve after discontinuation of the offending agent.
  • Almost all patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) without contraindications should receive hydroxychloroquine because it can reduce disease-associated damage, prevent disease flares, and improve kidney and overall survival.
  • Glucocorticoids are used in most patients with SLE, particularly in acute disease; after disease stabilizes, glucocorticoids should be tapered to the lowest effective dose, ideally to discontinuation.
  • For moderate or severe SLE, immunosuppressive therapy should be initiated concurrently with glucocorticoids to achieve and maintain disease control and to allow tapering of glucocorticoids.
  • Pregnancy can be considered when systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is quiescent, and conception should be planned after at least 6 months of adequate disease control.
  • SLE is associated with a five- to eightfold increased risk for miscarriage, stillbirth, premature delivery, and intrauterine growth retardation.
  • Fetuses of women who have anti-Ro/SSA or anti-La/SSB antibodies are at risk for neonatal lupus erythematosus (rash and/or congenital heart block).
  • Hydroxychloroquine and low-dose glucocorticoids for pregnant patients with SLE can be started during or continued throughout pregnancy; cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, and mycophenolate should be avoided because of risks for teratogenicity.

index.title: Sjögren Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Sjögren disease is an autoimmune exocrinopathy primarily affecting lacrimal and salivary glands.
  • The most common presentation of Sjögren disease is sicca (dryness of the eyes and/or mouth).
  • Patients with Sjögren disease are at increased risk for non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
  • A diagnosis of Sjögren disease is typically triggered by symptoms of ocular and oral dryness, increase in dental caries, or parotid swelling and requires objective confirmation of exocrinopathy, along with demonstration of autoimmunity.
  • In patients with Sjögren disease, management of sicca centers on preserving moisture and relieving symptoms; extraglandular involvement is treated with immunomodulation.

index.title: Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathies
index.keyPoints:
• Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies commonly present with symmetric proximal muscle weakness without substantial muscle pain or tenderness; creatine kinase level is frequently elevated and is a marker of muscle damage.
  • Muscle pain or tenderness should prompt consideration of infectious, endocrine (thyroid), or drug-induced myopathies.
  • In idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, proximal muscles, including the neck flexors and shoulder and hip girdle muscles, are commonly involved; muscle weakness may also cause difficulty swallowing, difficulty breathing, and heart failure.
  • Interstitial lung disease occurs in both polymyositis and dermatomyositis and is an important cause of morbidity and mortality.
  • Age- and sex-appropriate cancer screening is indicated in dermatomyositis and polymyositis because of an increased risk for malignancy.
  • Gottron and heliotrope rashes are characteristic of dermatomyositis.
  • Patients with polymyositis have proximal muscle weakness without the skin involvement of dermatomyositis.
  • Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy is characterized by severe, rapidly progressive proximal muscle weakness; an increased likelihood of muscle pain; and high serum creatine kinase levels.
  • Inclusion body myositis is an insidious condition in older adults that affects both the proximal and distal muscles.
  • Elevated serum creatine kinase levels are a sensitive indicator of muscle pathology, and levels can be used to monitor response to treatment and detect relapses in myositis.
  • Myositis-specific autoantibodies can be used to diagnose and subcategorize some idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIMs) but are not present in all patients.
  • In patients with IIMs, MRI can help locate a site for muscle biopsy and assess therapeutic efficacy.
  • In the evaluation of IIMs, electromyography is most helpful in differentiating myopathy from neuropathic causes of weakness (e.g., polyneuropathy, motor neuron disease).
  • Muscle biopsy is valuable for diagnosing IIMs and for excluding metabolic myopathies, mitochondrial disease, and infection.
  • Initial treatment of most idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIMs) consists of glucocorticoids, with additional immunomodulatory agents (most commonly methotrexate and azathioprine) used as glucocorticoid-sparing agents.
  • In patients being treated for IIM, worsening myopathy after prolonged glucocorticoid exposure, despite declining creatine kinase levels, suggests glucocorticoid-induced myopathy.
  • Physical therapy can help maintain muscle function and should be universally recommended in patients with IIMs.
  • Prolonged symptoms before treatment, greater weakness at presentation, extensive multisystem disease, co-occurrence of malignancy, and some autoantibodies (e.g., anti–signal recognition particle, anti-MDA5) confer a poorer prognosis in patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies.
  • Inclusion body myositis usually does not respond to immunosuppression and typically results in wheelchair dependence within 10 to 15 years.

index.title: Systemic Sclerosis
index.keyPoints:
• Systemic sclerosis is a multiorgan disease characterized by fibrosis and vasculopathy; the skin is the principal target, and Raynaud phenomenon is one of the earliest manifestations.
  • Systemic sclerosis is divided into three subtypes based on the extent of skin involvement: diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis, limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis, and systemic sclerosis sine scleroderma.
  • The absence of Raynaud phenomenon in a patient with skin thickening makes systemic sclerosis less likely.
  • The earliest skin manifestations of diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis are often diffusely swollen fingers/hands; with time, the skin becomes thickened, atrophic, and immobile.
  • Raynaud phenomenon is the most common early manifestation of systemic sclerosis (SSc).
  • Symptoms of esophageal dysmotility and reflux are common in all forms of SSc and may be an early disease manifestation.
  • Patients with scleroderma renal crisis characteristically present with manifestations of hypertensive emergency.
  • Lung involvement in SSc includes pleuritis, pulmonary arterial hypertension, and interstitial lung disease (ILD); ILD is the main cause of disease-associated death.
  • All patients with SSc should undergo pulmonary function testing and high-resolution CT at the time of initial SSc diagnosis to screen for ILD.
  • Treatment options for systemic sclerosis are mainly symptomatic and organ system specific.
  • ACE inhibitors (typically captopril) can be lifesaving in patients with scleroderma renal crisis and should be titrated to control blood pressure, even in the presence of a rising serum creatinine level.
  • Mycophenolate mofetil is the preferred agent for the treatment of interstitial lung disease in systemic sclerosis.
  • Pregnant patients with systemic sclerosis experience an increased risk for first-trimester miscarriage, preeclampsia, preterm delivery, and low birth weight.
  • Contraindications to pregnancy in patients with systemic sclerosis include pulmonary arterial hypertension and severe restrictive lung disease.

index.title: Mixed Connective Tissue Disease and Undifferentiated Connective Tissue Disease
index.keyPoints:
• Mixed connective tissue disease includes clinical manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus, autoimmune myositis, systemic sclerosis, and/or rheumatoid arthritis; anti–U1-ribonucleoprotein antibodies and high antinuclear antibody with a speckled pattern are typically present.
  • Treatment for mixed connective tissue disease is directed at the “parent” disease states and organ systems involved.
  • Patients who have undifferentiated connective tissue disease present with signs and symptoms that are autoimmune in nature (often including Raynaud phenomenon), but findings do not rise to the level of a specific rheumatologic condition.

index.title: Crystal Arthropathies
index.keyPoints:
• The hallmarks of a gout flare are pain, tenderness, swelling, redness, and warmth; flares typically begin at night and peak within 12 to 24 hours.
  • Early acute gout flares are typically monoarticular; if gout is not treated properly, gout flares tend to become increasingly frequent, more severe, and commonly polyarticular.
  • The gold standard for diagnosis of gout flare is identification of negatively birefringent, needle-like intracellular and extracellular monosodium urate crystals within synovial fluid.
  • Serum urate measured at the time of acute gout flare may not be helpful because levels can decrease during acute inflammation; a serum urate level 2 weeks after flare resolution more accurately measures baseline level.
  • The diagnosis of gout flare, even when confirmed by intracellular crystals in synovial fluid, does not definitively rule out concomitant infection.
  • Colchicine, NSAIDs, and glucocorticoids are commonly used for treating acute gout.
  • The American College of Rheumatology strongly recommends that patients receiving urate-lowering therapy achieve and maintain a serum urate target less than 6.0 mg/dL (0.35 mmol/L).
  • When urate-lowering therapy is indicated for gout, allopurinol is the recommended first-line medication for most patients.
  • Patients starting urate-lowering therapy for gout should receive anti-inflammatory prophylaxis to prevent flares.
  • Asymptomatic calcium pyrophosphate deposition is characterized by radiographic changes, including cartilage calcification (chondrocalcinosis).
  • Acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis (pseudogout) clinically resembles gout flare and most commonly involves the knee or wrist; however, crystals are rhomboid-shaped and exhibit weakly positive birefringence under polarized light.
  • Chronic calcium pyrophosphate crystal inflammatory arthritis often involves the wrists and metacarpophalangeal joints (“pseudo–rheumatoid arthritis”).
  • Osteoarthritis with calcium pyrophosphate deposition causes typical osteoarthritic findings involving joints not commonly associated with osteoarthritis (e.g., shoulders and metacarpophalangeal joints).
  • Basic calcium phosphate deposition can rarely cause “Milwaukee shoulder,” a destructive inflammatory arthritis and periarthritis of the shoulder; diagnosis is usually clinical.

index.title: Systemic Vasculitis
index.keyPoints:
• Giant cell arteritis (GCA) should be suspected in a patient older than 50 years with new or atypical headache, jaw claudication, or vision changes.
  • GCA is suspected on the basis of clinical presentation and should be confirmed by temporal artery biopsy, temporal artery ultrasonography, and/or imaging of the great vessels.
  • Suspected GCA should be treated immediately with prednisone to prevent vision loss.
  • Prednisone plus tocilizumab is conditionally recommended as initial therapy once GCA is diagnosed because the combination has improved efficacy compared with prednisone alone and typically permits faster glucocorticoid taper.
  • Polymyalgia rheumatica is associated with pain and stiffness of the shoulder and hip girdles; it responds dramatically to moderate-dose prednisone.
  • Takayasu arteritis predominantly occurs in women younger than 40 years and causes inflammation of the aorta and other large vessels.
  • Primary treatment of Takayasu arteritis is high-dose oral glucocorticoids with a slow taper, along with nonbiologic immunosuppressive medications.
  • Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) most commonly affects the skin, peripheral nervous system, gastrointestinal tract, and kidneys.
  • PAN is diagnosed with biopsy showing focal segmental panmural necrotizing inflammation of a medium-sized vessel or abdominal vascular imaging showing saccular microaneurysms and areas of narrowing in medium-sized vessels.
  • Intravenous pulse glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide are indicated for severe organ-threatening PAN; glucocorticoids and disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs are used for milder disease.
  • Patients with primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS) usually present with progressive headache, cognitive impairment, and neurologic deficits as well as transient ischemic attacks and strokes.
  • PACNS is treated with high-dose glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide.
  • Adults who had Kawasaki disease in childhood may have residual coronary aneurysms that require monitoring and management.
  • Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) affects the upper and lower airways, kidneys, eyes, skin, and peripheral nerves.
  • In GPA, most patients are ANCA positive, with antibodies against proteinase 3/c-ANCA, and tissue biopsy shows pauci-immune necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis.
  • Severe GPA is typically treated with glucocorticoids plus either rituximab or cyclophosphamide.
  • Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) characteristically affects the lungs and kidneys and is associated with ANCA positivity, usually directed against myeloperoxidase.
  • MPA is treated similarly to granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
  • Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is associated with asthma, rhinitis, sinusitis, atopy, peripheral and tissue eosinophilia, migratory pulmonary infiltrates, and mononeuritis multiplex.
  • Treatment of severe EGPA includes glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide (or rituximab).
  • Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis is associated with cutaneous symptoms (most commonly), peripheral neuropathy, arthralgia without arthritis, and glomerulonephritis.
  • Mixed cryoglobulinemias are usually associated with hepatitis C virus infection or autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus or Sjögren disease.
  • Cryoglobulinemia is treated by first addressing the underlying cause; severe manifestations necessitate treatment of the vasculitis itself with glucocorticoids and rituximab.
  • IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) can present with palpable purpura, arthritis and arthralgia, abdominal pain or gastrointestinal bleeding, and kidney involvement.
  • Adults suspected of having IgA vasculitis should be evaluated for kidney involvement because kidney disease confers a worse prognosis and usually requires immunosuppressive therapy.
  • The most common presentation of hypersensitivity vasculitis is palpable purpura, which develops 7 to 10 days after exposure to a triggering antigen.
  • Removal of the antigen (if identified) and supportive care are usually sufficient management for hypersensitivity vasculitis.

index.title: Miscellaneous Systemic Inflammatory Diseases
index.keyPoints:
• Multisystem inflammatory syndrome is an uncommon, severe immune-mediated disorder that follows an antecedent SARS-CoV-2 illness and, in adults, frequently results in inflammation affecting the heart, gastrointestinal tract, skin, and brain.
  • The most common manifestations of Behçet syndrome include recurrent painful oral and genital mucosal ulcerations, skin disease, and inflammatory eye disease.
  • Vascular, ophthalmologic, and central nervous system involvement in patients with Behçet syndrome requires aggressive treatment with immunosuppressive therapy.
  • Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis is a noninflammatory condition characterized by calcification and ossification of spinal ligaments and entheses; radiographs usually show confluent “flowing” ossification of at least four contiguous vertebral levels, usually on the right side of the spine.
  • Relapsing polychondritis is characterized by inflammation and damage of cartilaginous tissues; tissues most commonly affected include the cartilaginous portions of the external ear, nose, and trachea.
  • Autoinflammatory diseases are characterized by episodic and/or persistent inflammation and involve inherited or spontaneous variants of genes that encode for inflammatory responses.
  • Characteristics of adult-onset Still disease include fever with daily evening spikes, evanescent salmon-colored rash during febrile episodes, arthralgia, and leukocytosis.
  • Rheumatologic manifestations of sarcoidosis include arthritis, which can affect multiple joints and possibly lead to erosive damage, deformity, and dactylitis.
  • Treatment of symptomatic extrapulmonary sarcoidosis almost always requires high-dose glucocorticoids.
  • Löfgren syndrome is a form of systemic sarcoidosis that consists of bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, and migratory polyarthralgia, usually accompanied by fever; because the syndrome is usually self-limited, treatment is supportive.
  • IgG4-related disease is characterized by tumefactive infiltration of IgG4-bearing plasma cells and other lymphocytes, along with storiform fibrosis, into one or multiple organs, with resultant organ enlargement, fibrosis, and dysfunction.
  • Initial management of IgG4-related disease includes moderate- to high-dose glucocorticoids, tapered over 2 months.
  • Common clinical findings of genetic diseases of connective tissue include skin and joint laxity, skeletal fractures, and cardiovascular complications related to involvement of the aorta and cardiac valves.
  • Regular vascular monitoring is required for patients with Marfan syndrome and several types of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

bodies.cssec24001:
Approach to the Patient With Common Symptoms

Symptom concerns are responsible for more than 400 million outpatient encounters annually, representing more than half of all ambulatory care visits to clinicians. Although most symptoms resolve within several weeks, it can be challenging for clinicians to determine symptom significance and choose appropriate testing. After investigation, about 30% of symptoms remain unlinked to a specific clinical explanation. A thorough and appropriately directed history generates the highest diagnostic yield—up to 75% in some studies—with physical examination contributing an additional 10% to 15%.

In contrast, diagnostic tests may add as little as 0.5% to the probability of identifying a significant health condition. Importantly, normal diagnostic test results do not necessarily reassure patients or resolve their concerns and should not be ordered for reassurance when the clinical probability of disease is low. Unnecessary testing accounts for nearly 30% of healthcare costs. As such, physicians should consider the principles of high value care in the evaluation and treatment of these common disease symptoms (see High Value Care in Internal Medicine in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Exploring the timing, duration, severity, and context of symptoms, including environmental and occupational risks, is fundamental to the diagnostic process. Medical history and epidemiologic risk factors also usually provide crucial information. Clinicians should similarly consider patient comorbidities, such as diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis, or atrial fibrillation, which may provide a unifying diagnosis for vague symptoms such as ongoing dizziness or fatigue. Utilizing electronic health records to meticulously review previous tests, imaging, and specialist consultations is also a key step in ensuring accurate diagnoses and individualized treatment plans.

Identifying a specific cause of symptoms is often elusive. Approximately 25% of symptoms, such as headache and fatigue, may persist up to 5 years after initial presentation without a clear diagnosis. A clinical approach that prioritizes understanding a patient’s fears and beliefs about serious illnesses may be as crucial as collecting symptoms. It is vital to validate patient concerns, especially about serious illnesses such as cancer, show empathy, and actively engage in understanding the patient’s experience to effectively address frequent, recurring, or persistent symptoms. Patients who return with persistent unexplained symptoms are likely to express dissatisfaction with the quality of their relationship with their treating clinician and the medical care provided. A highly supportive and engaged approach may be the most important therapeutic intervention when physical and emotional symptoms and signs are present, such as with the commonly encountered SPADE symptoms (Sleep problems, Pain, Anxiety, Depression, and low Energy/fatigue).

Effective symptom management depends on collaboration, patience, and assessing symptom severity based on its impact on the patient’s functional capacity and quality of life. Instruments such as the Medical Outcomes Study 12-Item and 36-Item Short Form Health Surveys are useful tools in longitudinally assessing this impact.

References

Kroenke K. A practical and evidence-based approach to common symptoms: a narrative review. Ann Intern Med. 2014;161:579-86. PMID: 25329205

Kroenke K. Studying symptoms: sampling and measurement issues. Ann Intern Med. 2001;134:844-53. PMID: 11346320.

Kroenke K, Talib TL, Stump TE, et al. Incorporating PROMIS symptom measures into primary care practice—a randomized clinical trial. J Gen Intern Med. 2018;33:1245-1252. PMID: 29623512 doi:10.1007/s11606-018-4391-0

Landon SN, Padikkala J, Horwitz LI. Identifying drivers of health care value: a scoping review of the literature. BMC Health Serv Res. 2022;22:845. PMID: 35773663 doi:10.1186/s12913-022-08225-6

bodies.cssec24002:
Cough

Cough results in roughly 30 million physician office visits annually in the United States, costing billions of dollars. An evidence-based and cost-effective approach to managing cough centers on whether the symptoms are acute (<3 weeks), subacute (3-8 weeks), or chronic (>8 weeks) in duration.

Viral infections, including upper respiratory tract infections and bronchitis, often cause acute cough. Other common causes include allergic rhinosinusitis, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, COPD, asthma, and ACE inhibitor–induced cough.

The initial evaluation of the patient focuses on identifying potentially life-threatening illnesses. The presence of fever, dyspnea, chest pain, and abnormalities on lung or cardiovascular examination suggest severe respiratory or cardiovascular disease.

Pneumonia is a common concern, and findings that support obtaining a chest radiograph in a patient with acute cough include any of the following:

  • Abnormal vital signs: heart rate >100/min, respiration rate >24/min, oxygen saturation <95%, temperature >38.0 °C (100.4 °F)
  • Abnormal lung examination findings, such as rales, egophony, or tactile fremitus
  • Altered mental status

Viral respiratory pathogens (e.g., coronaviruses, adenoviruses, and rhinoviruses) are the most common causes of acute rhinosinusitis and acute bronchitis, both of which commonly cause cough. Treatment of acute viral rhinosinusitis includes intranasal glucocorticoids or intranasal ipratropium. Cough can be treated with dextromethorphan or honey. Limited evidence supports the effectiveness of other therapies for upper respiratory tract viral infections, including saline irrigation, antihistamines, and decongestants (see The Common Cold in Interdisciplinary Medicine). Antibiotics should not be initiated for most patients with acute rhinosinusitis or sinusitis without a specific indication (see [Table: Table: Acute Sinusitis Treatments]

). Sinus imaging is typically recommended only if spread into adjacent structures is suspected.

Allergic rhinosinusitis is best treated with intranasal glucocorticoids. Combination therapy with an intranasal glucocorticoid and an intranasal antihistamine is appropriate for more significant symptoms.

Influenza virus is a likely cause in patients presenting with sudden-onset fever and myalgia, especially during influenza season. SARS-CoV-2 infection also commonly causes cough along with systemic symptoms. See SARS-CoV-2 in Infectious Disease for additional information. Specific antiviral therapy should be considered in confirmed influenza and SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Viral infection is also the cause of most cases of acute bronchitis. The mainstays of acute bronchitis treatment are patient education and reassurance that the cough usually resolves in 2 to 3 weeks. Empiric treatment of acute bronchitis with antibiotics is ineffective; increases bacterial antibiotic resistance; and may cause multiple adverse effects, including Clostridioides difficile colitis. Limited evidence suggests that honey may decrease cough frequency and severity, but little evidence supports the use of expectorants or mucolytics. Patients suspected of having acute bronchitis should be counseled to return if symptoms do not improve; further evaluation and antibiotic therapy should be considered in patients with worsening or persistent symptoms.

Up to 20% of patients taking an ACE inhibitor develop a dry cough, usually within 1 to 2 weeks of therapy initiation. However, a small percentage of patients have delayed onset of cough by months. The cough usually subsides within days of discontinuing the offending agent but can sometimes persist for weeks. Angiotensin receptor blockers typically do not cause cough and may be substituted if ACE inhibitor therapy is not tolerated. Sitagliptin has also been variably associated with acute cough, and a trial of discontinuation is reasonable.

Subacute cough (3-8 weeks’ duration) is most often postinfectious following an acute respiratory tract infection, particularly with a viral or Mycoplasma infection. Postinfectious subacute cough is typically caused by upper airway cough syndrome (UACS) (formerly known as postnasal drip) or airway hyperreactivity. In patients with UACS, first-generation antihistamines with decongestants may be beneficial. Asthma therapies are typically effective in patients with evidence of airway hyperreactivity, such as wheezing. Patients with postinfectious cough that is not attributed to UACS or airway hyperreactivity may benefit from inhaled ipratropium. Bordetella pertussis infection should be considered in patients with subacute cough characterized by paroxysms of severe coughing and posttussive emesis.

Chronic cough (>8 weeks’ duration) is most often caused by UACS, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), asthma, smoking, and ACE inhibitor use. Nonasthmatic eosinophilic bronchitis (NAEB) is another increasingly recognized cause. Important but less common causes include chronic bronchitis, lung neoplasm, bronchiectasis, and chronic aspiration.

Evaluation of chronic cough begins with a thorough history, physical examination, and chest radiography (

). ACE inhibitor therapy and tobacco use should be discontinued. If the cause is not determined after initial evaluation, a stepwise approach is pursued, beginning with a 2-week trial of empiric treatment for UACS. Allergic rhinitis–associated UACS is optimally treated with intranasal glucocorticoids, whereas UACS resulting from nonallergic rhinitis responds best to first-generation antihistamines (chlorpheniramine, brompheniramine, diphenhydramine) and decongestants (pseudoephedrine) (see Rhinitis in Interdisciplinary Medicine).

Asthma should be considered in patients with symptoms that do not respond to empiric treatment for UACS. Cough-variant asthma is diagnosed if spirometry or bronchial provocation testing results are abnormal and symptoms improve with standard therapy for asthma, specifically inhaled glucocorticoids.

In patients in whom empiric treatment for UACS has failed and who do not have asthma, the most reasonable next step is to exclude NAEB with sputum analysis for eosinophils or fractional exhaled nitric oxide testing. If test results are abnormal, therapy with inhaled glucocorticoids should be initiated.

Cough without a clear cause that does not appear secondary to UACS, asthma, or NAEB may be treated with antireflux lifestyle changes to address possible GERD; empiric proton pump inhibitor therapy also may be considered (see Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease in Gastroenterology).

Patients with partial responses to UACS, asthma, NAEB, or GERD treatment should continue those therapies. A more advanced investigation may be necessary for some patients (see

).

A persistent cough without an identifiable cause despite comprehensive evaluation is termed unexplained chronic cough. Multimodality speech pathology therapy may provide benefits and should be offered to all patients with chronic cough of undetermined cause. Antitussives, including dextromethorphan and topical anesthetics (benzonatate), can reduce cough and improve quality of life. Gabapentin may be effective for unexplained chronic cough and should be considered if the risk for adverse effects is acceptable. Protussives, such as guaifenesin, can improve mucus clearance and cough intensity in select patients with excessive sputum production. Opioids, such as morphine and codeine, may be effective but should be used cautiously and only if other measures fail.

Immunocompromised patients require heightened suspicion for infections, particularly if immunosuppression is severe and common causes of cough have been excluded. Aside from common pathogens, other causes to consider include fungi, cytomegalovirus, varicella, herpesvirus, and Pneumocystis jirovecii. Regardless of radiographic findings, tuberculosis should be considered in the initial evaluation of patients with cough and risk factors for tuberculosis, including HIV infection, residence in regions with a high prevalence of tuberculosis, or recent incarceration. Specialized testing, often including advanced imaging and bronchoscopy, is often necessary. Clinicians should have a low threshold for initiating empiric antibiotic therapy while diagnostic testing is pursued.

Hemoptysis is the expectoration of blood from the lower respiratory tract. Acute bronchitis is a common cause of mild and self-limited hemoptysis; more severe causes include bronchiectasis, cancer, tuberculosis, pulmonary embolism, and left ventricular failure. Rare causes include anti–glomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture syndrome) and granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Hemoptysis requires urgent evaluation, beginning with an assessment to confirm the lower respiratory tract as the source of bleeding and exclude epistaxis or hematemesis. Chest radiography should be performed, but many patients require chest CT and bronchoscopy to determine the cause.

bodies.cssec24003:
Dyspnea

Dyspnea is a common symptom that increases in prevalence with age; more than one third of persons older than 65 years report dyspnea in an ambulatory setting. It is also a common reason for patients to seek care in urgent and emergent care settings and affects up to half of hospitalized patients.

Dyspnea is caused by multiple underlying neurophysiologic mechanisms, including increased work of breathing, air hunger, and airway irritation or damage. These mechanisms may be triggered by organ-specific pathology, physiologic stimuli (including hypoxia, hypercapnia, and acidemia), poor functional status, or medication adverse effects. More than one cause of dyspnea is present in many patients.

The history and physical examination are the most important components of the evaluation of dyspnea. An essential aspect of the history is the patient’s qualitative description of dyspnea, which may aid in the diagnosis. Chest tightness may be relatively specific for bronchoconstriction, whereas a sensation of smothering or suffocating at rest may suggest heart failure or obstructive sleep apnea. Air hunger and “inability to get a deep breath” are commonly associated with hyperinflation (such as that caused by COPD) or restrictive conditions (such as pulmonary fibrosis).

The onset, duration, and progression of dyspnea may suggest a cause ( [Table: Table: Causes of Dyspnea Based on Symptom Onset and Progression]

). Exercise-induced dyspnea occurs with most causes of dyspnea, and its absence may suggest a functional cause. Seasonal or diurnal dyspnea may occur with asthma, and worsening during the winter months is often associated with COPD.

Worsening of dyspnea with positional changes can provide useful clues. Orthopnea suggests heart failure, whereas breathlessness relieved by lying down (platypnea) suggests hepatopulmonary syndrome or a large patent foramen ovale. Dyspnea when lying on one side (trepopnea) has been associated with decompensated heart failure, diaphragmatic paralysis, and severe tricuspid regurgitation. Nocturnal dyspnea may suggest asthma or heart failure. The onset of dyspnea when leaning forward (bendopnea), such as when tying shoelaces, can be a symptom of heart failure.

A thorough evaluation for associated symptoms may further narrow the differential diagnosis. For example, chest tightness or pressure may signal acute coronary syndrome or pulmonary embolism. Unilateral or pleuritic chest pain suggests pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, or other pleural-based conditions (e.g., pneumothorax). A productive cough may characterize COPD and pneumonia, and a dry cough can be associated with diffuse parenchymal lung diseases and asthma. A nocturnal cough may suggest asthma or heart failure.

In the absence of an obvious cause, the initial evaluation may include measurement of oxygen saturation and hemoglobin, ECG, and chest radiography. Further testing should be pursued in the context of likelihood of specific diseases. In the correct clinical scenario, B-type natriuretic peptide or N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide levels are useful for ruling out heart failure. If COPD is suspected, spirometry can be diagnostic. In patients with a low clinical probability of pulmonary embolism, a negative D-dimer is useful for ruling out the disease. Point-of-care lung ultrasonography is an accurate means of rapidly detecting pleural effusion, interstitial syndrome (e.g., pulmonary edema, acute respiratory distress syndrome), alveolar consolidation, and pneumothorax. Echocardiography is usually indicated for the evaluation of dyspnea of suspected cardiac origin.

If the initial evaluation does not yield a specific diagnosis, advanced imaging may be indicated depending on the clinical suspicion. High-resolution CT of the chest is the test of choice for suspected diffuse parenchymal lung disease, whereas CT angiography of the chest or ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scanning is indicated in patients with an intermediate or high likelihood of pulmonary embolism. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing can be helpful if the initial evaluation is unrevealing, deconditioning is a possibility, or multiple problems may be contributing to dyspnea. Referral to a cardiologist or pulmonologist may be appropriate when the diagnosis remains elusive or when conditions require subspecialized input. Because many patients have more than one cause of dyspnea, care should additionally be taken not to cease the diagnostic evaluation prematurely once a potential cause is identified, especially if the degree of dyspnea experienced by the patient is out of proportion to the severity of the cause identified.

Initial management strategies are aimed at treating or modifying the underlying cause of the patient’s dyspnea. In patients with chronic conditions, the first step in reducing dyspnea is to maximize standard therapies, with regular assessment of symptom response.

In patients with persistent debilitating symptoms despite maximal medical therapy directed at the underlying cause, other nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic strategies can reduce dyspnea severity, each with varying levels of evidence. Of these therapies, pursed lip breathing, diaphragmatic breathing, handheld fans, and devices that enhance airflow are the least invasive and easiest to administer. Pulmonary rehabilitation provides significant benefit for patients with chronic lung disease and improves dyspnea in patients with COPD; exercise is the component primarily responsible for symptom relief.

Oxygen therapy should be provided when hypoxemia is present; for example, it improves survival and quality of life in patients with hypoxemia and COPD (see Oxygen Therapy in Pulmonary Medicine). However, provision of supplemental oxygen in patients without hypoxemia is usually limited to specific situations such as carbon monoxide poisoning.

Opioids can be an effective therapy for patients with dyspnea refractory to nonpharmacologic therapies and maximal medical management of the underlying disease. Opioids appear to exert an antidyspneic effect through modulation of sensory input in the central nervous system, similar to how they modulate pain signaling. Although opioids affect respiratory mechanics and may blunt respiratory drive, appropriately dosed opioids do not cause respiratory depression if treatment is symptom directed. Patient selection and subsequent opioid choice should be based on symptom burden, underlying disease, comorbid organ dysfunction, and overall risk for respiratory depression. Although systemic opioids have shown clear benefit in treating refractory dyspnea, inhaled opioids have not shown efficacy in several placebo-controlled trials. Other therapies found to be ineffective or lacking in sufficient data to recommend their use include anxiolytics, antidepressants, phenothiazines, indomethacin, nitrous oxide, and sodium bicarbonate.

Management of dyspnea in patients with serious illness is further discussed in Dyspnea in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

Chest Pain

Chest pain is very common, with a lifetime prevalence of up to 40%. It accounts for more than 4 million outpatient visits to primary care physicians and 5% of visits to emergency departments in the United States annually. Although few patients presenting with chest pain have true medical emergencies, prompt and accurate diagnosis is essential, as coronary artery disease remains a leading cause of death in adults. The physician must not only distinguish ischemic from nonischemic chest pain but also differentiate emergent causes of chest pain from nonemergent ones. The most likely cause of chest pain varies according to patient characteristics (e.g., age, sex, cardiac risk factors, known clinical conditions) and the presentation setting (e.g., outpatient setting versus emergency department). In the outpatient setting, musculoskeletal causes are the most common, accounting for approximately 40% of cases of chest pain, followed by gastrointestinal disease (19%). In the emergency department, although acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is more common than in outpatient settings, it still accounts for only approximately 5% of presentations. This section focuses primarily on the evaluation and management of acute chest pain.

Chest pain as a symptom should be conceptualized broadly. Terminology has shifted from characterizing chest pain as atypical or typical to likely cardiac, possibly cardiac, and noncardiac. Although classic ischemic symptoms (e.g., substernal location of pain, pressure-like quality, radiation to the jaw and left arm) increase the pretest probability of cardiac ischemia, less stereotypical symptoms (e.g., right-sided chest pain, epigastric pain) can also be due to cardiac ischemia. Additionally, some symptoms, such as unexplained dyspnea or syncope, should be considered as chest pain equivalents in at-risk patients, particularly in older patients.

The differential diagnosis for acute chest pain should initially focus on consideration of the six most common life-threating causes:

  • ACS
  • Acute aortic syndrome
  • Pericardial tamponade
  • Pulmonary embolus
  • Pneumothorax
  • Pneumonia

More broadly, the differential diagnosis of chest pain consists of cardiac, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, and musculoskeletal causes. Dermatologic (e.g., herpes zoster) and psychiatric (e.g., anxiety, panic attack) conditions can also manifest as chest pain. Despite the many potentially serious clinical conditions in the differential diagnosis for acute chest pain, most episodes have non–life-threatening causes (e.g., musculoskeletal pain) or are of unclear cause.

Cardiovascular causes of chest pain include ACS, stable angina, and noncoronary causes (e.g., aortic dissection, myocarditis, pericarditis, and aortic stenosis). For acute chest pain, the initial diagnostic approach focuses on evaluating potentially life-threatening diagnoses (both cardiac and noncardiac) with a focus on ACS. This approach relies on the history and physical examination and a 12-lead ECG. In settings in which ACS is a possible diagnosis and ECG is not available, patients should be transferred immediately to a setting where an ECG can be performed. In all patients presenting to the emergency department with acute chest pain and suspected ACS, cardiac troponin should be measured as soon as possible after presentation. Chest radiography should also be performed for most patients seen in the emergency department; it is quick, is relatively inexpensive, and can provide valuable information for both cardiac and noncardiac causes of chest pain.

Characterization of chest pain is helpful, as pain descriptors provided by the patient can increase or decrease the likelihood of ACS (see

and [Table: Table: Characteristics Associated With Chest Pain Classification]

) and provide clues to alternative diagnoses. Guidelines recommend characterizing pain as cardiac, possibly cardiac, or noncardiac based on patient factors, history and physical examination, and clinical setting. A high index of suspicion is needed in women, older patients, and patients with diabetes mellitus, who may be less likely to present with classic symptoms. Clinical decision pathways use patient data along with ECG and cardiac biomarker results (troponin) to classify patients seen in the emergency department as low, intermediate, or high risk and inform next steps in diagnosis. For information on specific anatomic and functional diagnostic testing modalities, see Diagnostic Testing in Cardiology in Cardiovascular Medicine.

For patients in whom ACS is neither suspected nor diagnosed, several noncoronary cardiovascular causes of chest pain should be considered. Acute aortic syndromes such as aortic dissection are characterized by sudden and severe pain at onset, often with a tearing, splitting, or ripping quality that radiates to the back. Asymmetric intensity of peripheral pulses (pulse deficit) is suggestive, and a chest radiograph may show a widened mediastinum; however, these features are insensitive, and testing for acute aortic syndrome, most frequently with CT angiography, must be considered in any patient with severe chest/thoracic pain. Pericarditis and myocarditis usually present with pleuritic chest pain. The pain in pericarditis is unaffected by exercise, worsens with recumbency, and is relieved with sitting forward. A pericardial rub may be present. Classic ECG findings are diffuse ST-segment elevation and PR-segment depression. Aortic stenosis may cause exertional chest pain, which may be accompanied by syncope, dyspnea, and other signs of heart failure.

Pulmonary causes of chest pain include pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pleuritis, pneumonia, pulmonary hypertension, and parenchymal pulmonary lesions. The pain associated with pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pleuritis, and pneumonia is generally pleuritic and is often accompanied by dyspnea.

In pulmonary embolism, pain may be accompanied by cough, wheezing, hemoptysis, tachypnea, and tachycardia. Risk factors include immobilization, recent hospitalization or surgery, paresis, previous venous thromboembolic disease, malignancy, obesity, tobacco use, and estrogen therapy. Diagnostic testing is guided by pretest probability. Pulmonary embolism may be ruled out in patients at very low risk using the Pulmonary Embolism Rule-Out Criteria (PERC) (see [Table: Table: PERC for Predicting Probability of PE]

). If the PERC score is zero in patients with very low probability, no further testing is necessary. Otherwise, for patients with low pretest probability and select patients with intermediate probability, a negative high-sensitivity D-dimer test is often sufficient to rule out thromboembolism. When pretest probability is intermediate to high, chest CT angiography with pulmonary embolism protocol or ventilation-perfusion scanning is usually pursued (see Diagnosis in Hematology)

Pneumothorax can be primary or secondary. A primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in a patient without known underlying lung disease, whereas a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in patients with known existing disease, such as COPD or cystic fibrosis. Lifetime recurrence rates are up to 50% in primary disease and even higher in secondary disease. Physical examination demonstrates decreased chest expansion, decreased breath sounds, and hyperresonance to percussion, all of which occur on the affected side. Diagnosis is made by chest radiography or ultrasonography. Tension pneumothorax, heralded by hypotension and tracheal deviation to the unaffected side, is a medical emergency. For more information, see Evaluation of Pneumothorax in Pulmonary Medicine.

Pulmonary hypertension includes pulmonary arterial hypertension and pulmonary hypertension secondary to other conditions, including heart, lung, and thromboembolic disease (see Pulmonary Hypertension in Pulmonary Medicine). The chest pain associated with pulmonary hypertension is not pleuritic but is usually accompanied by exertional dyspnea and fatigue. In most patients, the pain is caused by ischemia from either subendocardial hypoperfusion or compression of coronary arteries by enlarged pulmonary arteries. Commonly associated physical examination findings include elevated jugular venous pressure and a loud pulmonic component of the S~2 heart sound.

The most common gastrointestinal cause of chest pain is gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Although often described as heartburn, it can mimic angina. The pain generally worsens with the patient bending over or when lying down. If GERD is considered a likely diagnosis after evaluation for cardiac ischemia and other more serious causes of chest pain, an empiric trial of a proton pump inhibitor is reasonable. If alarm symptoms and signs (e.g., dysphagia, weight loss) are present, upper endoscopy should be considered (see Diagnosis of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease in Gastroenterology). Other, less common gastrointestinal causes of chest pain include cholecystitis, cholangitis, esophageal spasm, peptic ulcer disease, and pancreatitis. Although rare, esophageal rupture, which usually occurs in the setting of retching and alcohol use, is a life-threatening surgical emergency and early detection is essential.

Musculoskeletal chest pain is common, especially in women. Causes include costochondritis, osteoarthritis, and muscle strain. The pain is sharp, occasionally pleuritic, worsened or reproduced with movement or palpation, and relieved with NSAIDs. The reproduction of pain on palpation, however, is not specific enough to rule out a cardiac cause in patients with a significant likelihood of cardiac disease. Musculoskeletal chest pain may last for weeks. Imaging is usually not indicated or helpful.

Given the heterogeneous nature of chest pain, management varies significantly based on the diagnosis. Rapid identification, triage, and management of patients with potentially life-threatening causes of acute chest pain is essential. Interpretation of each patient’s clinical features and 12-lead ECG should be used to start the process of identifying patients with potentially serious diagnoses. If ACS is suspected or diagnosed, there are numerous functional and anatomic tests, including coronary angiography, that can be performed. See Diagnostic Testing in Cardiology in Cardiovascular Medicine for more information. Use of patient-centric clinical decision pathways within individual health care systems can help ensure that best practices are followed locally and prevent unnecessary testing and admissions. For instance, the HEART (History, ECG results, Age, Risk factors, and Troponin results) pathway accurately stratifies patients by risk and safely reduces hospitalization in patients with acute chest pain who are seen in the emergency department. Patients at low risk for death or major adverse cardiovascular events can usually be discharged home without urgent cardiac testing in the hospital.

Patient-centric clinical decision pathways are also essential for rapid evaluation of non-ACS causes of acute chest pain. Diagnostic modalities that have a potential role in the evaluation of acute chest pain include the following:

  • Chest radiography
  • CT with specific protocols in patients with suspected ACS (coronary CT angiography), pulmonary embolism, acute aortic syndrome, or pneumonia
  • Transthoracic echocardiography in patients with suspected valvular heart disease, pulmonary hypertension, or myopericarditis
  • Transesophageal echocardiography in patients with suspected acute aortic syndrome
  • Cardiac MRI in patients with suspected myocardial disease or acute aortic syndrome

The GRACE guidelines (Guidelines for Reasonable and Appropriate Care in the Emergency department) address recurrent chest pain in individuals who have previously undergone extensive evaluation. The GRACE guidelines emphasize strategies to avoid hospitalization for low-risk patients with recurrent chest pain. Recommendations include use of a single high-sensitivity cardiac troponin test to exclude ACS for patients who have had chest pain for 3 hours or longer. These guidelines also highlight when it is reasonable to pursue outpatient evaluation for recurrent chest pain and situations when referral to specialist care may be beneficial.
