bodies.cssec24005:
Dizziness

Dizziness is a common, nonspecific symptom seen in inpatient and outpatient settings. Patients often interchangeably use such terms as “dizzy,” “lightheaded,” “woozy,” “cloudy,” “faint,” or “off-balance” to describe the perception of dizziness. Owing to its subjective nature, variability in symptom description, and broad differential diagnosis (which includes posterior circulation stroke and other life-threatening disorders), dizziness is a challenging symptom to assess and treat.

A relevant history and physical examination should be performed to classify dizziness into one of four focused groupings: vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium, and nonspecific dizziness. This classification facilitates establishing a formal diagnosis and treatment strategy.

Vertigo is patient perception of false personal or environmental movement. Patients describe a spinning or whirling sensation, which is often accompanied by concomitant nausea, vomiting, and sudden-onset fatigue. Symptoms are typically episodic, brief, and often triggered by positional changes of the head but can be persistent. Vertigo is classified as peripheral or central, depending on the specific cause.

A thorough history and examination are crucial for differentiating between central and peripheral causes, especially in patients with acute vertigo concerning for vertebrobasilar ischemia and other central causes. Major causes of acute vertigo are presented in [Table: Table: Differential Diagnosis of Acute Vertigo]

. Examination should include an in-depth neurologic assessment and, in the case of acute persistent vertigo, the HINTS (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, and Test of Skew) oculomotor assessment ( [Table: Table: HINTS Examination and Interpretation]

).

Peripheral causes of vertigo account for 85% to 90% of all cases. Common causes include

  • Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
  • Vestibular neuronitis (also called vestibular neuritis)
  • Labyrinthitis
  • Meniere disease
  • Medication effects (toxicity from aminoglycoside or diuretic use)
  • Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster involving cranial nerve VII)
  • Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)

BPPV is the most common form of vertigo, with a lifetime prevalence of 2.4%. There is a female-to-male ratio of 2:1 to 3:1. BPPV is caused by displacement and migration of otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) within the semicircular canals. Up to 90% of cases of BPPV involve the posterior semicircular canal because it is the most gravity-dependent canal.

BPPV is characterized by sudden-onset, recurrent, and brief (usually <1 minute) symptoms that are provoked and worsened with positional changes of the head. Patients report dizziness, imbalance, nausea, and vomiting; however, no focal neurologic findings are present. Symptoms lead to increased risk for falls and a decline in functional status. Positive answers to the following three questions have been found to be helpful in the diagnosis of BPPV:

  • Do you have spinning or a whirling sensation of the surroundings or yourself?
  • Do you feel dizzy mostly when your head is moved?
  • Does the dizziness last less than 3 minutes?

The sensitivity, specificity, and precision of these questions is 87%, 90%, and 80%, respectively. These questions may be helpful for in-office visits and telephone triage of patients with acute-onset dizziness.

The diagnostic test of choice for BPPV is the Dix-Hallpike maneuver (

), which also can help differentiate between peripheral and central causes of vertigo ( [Table: Table: Interpretation of the Dix-Hallpike Maneuver]

). In the setting of BPPV, a positive finding includes the presence of a mixed upbeat-torsional nystagmus toward the affected side. Brain imaging is unnecessary for the diagnosis of BPPV. First-line therapy is canalith repositioning with the Epley maneuver, which is effective in up to 80% of patients with the first attempt and increases to 92% if repeated up to four times when the initial attempt is unsuccessful (

). Vitamin D levels can be checked, especially in patients with recurrent BPPV; if found to be low, replacement therapy may reduce the frequency of episodes.

Vestibular neuronitis is most often preceded by a viral infection affecting the vestibular portion of cranial nerve VIII. Symptoms are generally more severe and of longer duration than in BPPV, often taking hours to days to resolve. Nausea and vomiting are common. Labyrinthitis has a presentation similar to that of vestibular neuronitis, with the additional symptom of hearing loss. A central cause of vertigo, especially stroke, is the major alternative diagnostic consideration in patients with sustained vertigo.

Meniere disease presents with vertigo lasting less than 24 hours accompanied by tinnitus, hearing loss, or fullness in the affected ear; symptoms are episodic and recurrent and may be severe. Diuretics (most often hydrochlorothiazide or acetazolamide) and the vasodilator betahistine (not available in the United States) may reduce symptoms of Meniere disease.

Other than specific therapy for Meniere disease, pharmacologic therapy has not been shown to be significantly effective for peripheral vertigo. Rather, vestibular suppressants (antihistamines, benzodiazepines, and antiemetics) can be used in conjunction with other forms of therapy for temporary symptom relief. If vestibular suppressants are used, treatment duration must be limited because these agents impede vestibular functioning, vestibular recovery, and the central compensatory mechanism.

Vestibular and balance rehabilitation therapy (VBRT) is effective in the treatment of various forms of dizziness (vertigo, disequilibrium, and nonspecific dizziness), although the Epley maneuver is the treatment of choice for BPPV. VBRT focuses on balance training, core stabilization, and desensitization exercises. Therapy is often performed by physical and occupational therapists. Internet-based therapy may be an attractive option for patients. Clinical trials have demonstrated that both standalone internet-based vestibular rehabilitation and combined internet-based rehabilitation with face-to-face physiotherapy support are clinically effective and safe interventions to treat adults with a chronic vestibular syndrome.

Central causes of vertigo account for 10% to 15% of all cases and are a frequently missed and potentially life-threatening diagnosis. Central vertigo may be caused by vertebrobasilar stroke (posterior circulation ischemic or hemorrhagic events), migraine, central nervous system infection, trauma (concussion, traumatic brain injury), demyelinating disease (multiple sclerosis), or chronic alcohol use.

Patients with central vertigo secondary to vertebrobasilar stroke frequently display concomitant neurologic findings, such as nystagmus, dysphagia, dysarthria, diplopia, ataxia, postural instability, hemiparesis, and mental status changes. However, approximately 20% of patients with vertebrobasilar stroke present with isolated vertigo, and studies have shown that up to one third of these cases are misclassified as peripheral vertigo. Risk factors for stroke including advanced age, atrial fibrillation, diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, hypertension, and dyslipidemia are often present. On HINTS assessment, the absence of catch-up saccades on head impulse testing (the normal reaction that is compromised in peripheral vertigo but not central vertigo), direction-changing nystagmus, or skew deviation suggests a central cause (see [Table: Table: HINTS Examination and Interpretation]

). The HINTS examination has higher sensitivity than advanced imaging, such as MRI and CT, in early stroke and should be performed on patients with central vertigo in the differential diagnosis. The HINTS examination requires expertise to perform and interpret correctly and should be used by clinicians who have had training in this examination technique.

Imaging should be performed in patients with central vertigo. MRI is more sensitive than CT in detecting ischemic stroke and can detect infarction in the posterior fossa, often within minutes of symptom onset. CT provides an effective and expedited evaluation of hemorrhagic stroke, although hemorrhagic vertebrobasilar stroke accounts for a very small percentage of cases of centrally mediated vertigo.

Presyncope is a temporary reduction in global cerebral perfusion, causing symptoms of lightheadedness, dizziness, visual changes (tunnel vision), auditory changes, a sense of impending doom, warmth, nausea, and near loss of consciousness. Patients often report the sensation of “almost blacking out.” Postural tone is retained. In contrast, syncope is a transient reduction in global cerebral perfusion, leading to a true loss of consciousness and loss of postural tone. Notably, patients with presyncope do not have vertigo. The differential diagnosis for presyncope is similar to that for syncope (see Classification of Syncope in Common Symptoms).

Disequilibrium refers to a sensation of imbalance or unsteadiness that is primarily experienced during positional changes, standing, or walking and is relieved with sitting or lying down. Disequilibrium predominantly affects older adults, and its prevalence increases with age. Falls are four times more likely in patients with disequilibrium than those without disequilibrium and are in turn associated with significant morbidity, functional decline, and fear of future falls.

The cause of disequilibrium is often multifactorial and can involve visual and auditory impairment; muscle weakness or atrophy; physical deconditioning; pain; and/or impairment in proprioception, balance, and gait. Disequilibrium must be differentiated from specific causes of gait abnormalities and ataxia, such as movement disorders (Parkinson disease) (see Movement Disorders in Neurology), peripheral neuropathy (see Peripheral Neuropathies in Neurology), and cerebellar disease (mass lesions) (see Approach to Intracranial Tumors in Neurology). Brain MRI in patients with disequilibrium has shown significantly more subcortical white-matter lesions and frontal atrophy than in patients without disequilibrium, although the significance of these findings is unclear.

Given the multifactorial nature of disequilibrium, treatment should be multifaceted. Treatment options include visual and auditory corrective measures (eyeglasses, hearing aids), medication review (to mitigate adverse effects), mobility aids, physical therapy (balance and gait training), weight-bearing and resistance exercises, fall prevention counseling, and home safety evaluations.

Dizziness that remains nonspecific despite a thorough history, examination, and evaluation is referred to as persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) (formerly known as chronic subjective dizziness). PPPD is described as persistent, nonvertiginous dizziness or imbalance that worsens with personal motion, upright positioning, and movement of objects in the surrounding environment. Diagnosis requires that symptoms must be present on most days for at least 3 months. PPPD is often preceded by another vestibular process (BPPV, vestibular neuronitis, vestibular migraine, or stroke), trauma (concussion or traumatic brain injury), infection, or certain psychiatric conditions (anxiety, panic disorder, or major depression). Approximately 75% of patients with PPPD have concomitant anxiety or depressive symptoms. Diagnosis is typically made on the basis of chronic symptoms without an alternative cause after an appropriate evaluation.

Treatment options for PPPD include pharmacologic therapies (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) and ongoing VBRT.

Despite the practical utility of categorizing dizziness symptomatology into the four categories, there is considerable overlap among these presentations and some evidence suggests clinical unreliability. An alternative approach to dizziness emphasizes the difficulty in differentiating these four categories and instead focuses on identifying one of three clinical syndromes, specifically acute vestibular syndrome, triggered episodic vestibular syndrome, and spontaneous episodic vestibular syndrome. As suggested by the labels, this categorization of syndromes focuses on the acuity and persistence of symptoms as well as whether they are triggered (such as by head movement) or are spontaneous. The characteristics of each of these categories and a brief differential diagnosis of vestibular and nonvestibular causes of dizziness is presented in [Table: Table: Approach to Dizziness]

. Although not as intuitive as the commonly used process for evaluating dizziness, using this classification system has the potential to result in more accurate diagnosis.

Syncope

Syncope is complete, transient loss of consciousness and postural tone due to global cerebral hypoperfusion resulting from a decrease in cardiac output or systemic vascular resistance. The onset of syncope is sudden and abrupt, and recovery is rapid, with a complete return to the baseline level of functioning. Syncope has a reported cumulative incidence of 3% to 6% over a 10-year period and accounts for 1% to 2% of all emergency department visits. Approximately 40% of adults have experienced a syncopal event, with a significant rise in incidence in patients over the age of 70 years. Although the Framingham Heart Study found that 44% of patients who experienced a syncopal event did not seek medical care, a 2014 financial analysis showed that the diagnostic and therapeutic costs associated with syncope exceed $4.1 billion annually in the United States.

Syncope can be classified according to the specific cause of the event as neurally mediated (reflex), cardiovascular, orthostatic, neurologic, psychogenic, or idiopathic. These causes can be further subdivided according to the specific pathophysiologic mechanism. Approximately 40% of syncopal events are unexplained (idiopathic).

Neurally mediated syncope, or reflex syncope, is the most common form and is seen primarily in younger adults. The underlying syncopal mechanism, termed the neurocardiogenic or vasodepressor reflex, is a response of vasodilation, bradycardia, and systemic hypotension, which leads to transient hypoperfusion of the brain. Neurally mediated syncope includes the following:

  • Vasovagal syncope, which is provoked by noxious stimuli, fear, stress, or heat overexposure
  • Situational syncope, which is triggered by cough, micturition, defecation, or deglutition
  • Carotid sinus hypersensitivity, which is sometimes experienced during head rotation, shaving, or use of a tight-fitting neck collar

In patients with vasovagal syncope, prodromal symptoms, including nausea and diaphoresis, are classically present before the syncopal event, and fatigue and generalized weakness are typically present afterward, sometimes for an extended period of time.

Cardiovascular syncope is the second most common form of syncope and is associated with increased morbidity, mortality (including sudden death), and direct traumatic injury. Causes of cardiovascular syncope include arrhythmia (which may be due to coronary artery disease) and structural and obstructive disease, such as aortic and pulmonary valve stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, aortic dissection, and cardiac tamponade. Pulmonary embolism is an increasingly appreciated cardiovascular cause of syncope, with a prevalence as high as 17% in some studies. Historical characteristics that are associated with increased probability of cardiac versus noncardiac causes are listed in [Table: Table: Characteristics Associated With Cardiac and Noncardiac Syncope]

. Cardiovascular syncopal events often occur suddenly and without a significant prodrome, in particular when due to arrhythmia. Chest pain and palpitations may be present, especially if these symptoms are associated with the underlying cause such as aortic stenosis.

Orthostatic syncope is the third most common form of syncope and predominantly affects older adults. It classically occurs after changes in position and is typically associated with prodromal symptoms, such as lightheadedness. Orthostatic syncope is most commonly caused by hypovolemia, medications, or alcohol use. Less commonly, primary autonomic dysfunction (e.g., Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, multiple sclerosis) or secondary autonomic dysfunction (e.g., diabetes mellitus, amyloidosis, connective tissue disease, spinal cord injury) can lead to neurogenic orthostatic syncope.

Although neurologic conditions (e.g., seizure, head trauma) can cause loss of consciousness, they rarely cause syncope. Cerebrovascular events that lead to true syncope primarily involve the posterior (vertebrobasilar) circulation and usually present with concomitant symptoms of dizziness, vertigo, gait changes, and focal neurologic findings. Anterior circulation involvement rarely leads to syncope. Seizures can be confused with syncopal events, and bystander information can help distinguish between the two. A prospective study demonstrated that the features most suggestive of a seizure in patients with loss of consciousness were witnessed abnormal posturing, involuntary head turning, and tongue laceration. Auras, incontinence, and prolonged post-episode confusion also favor a seizure.

Psychogenic syncope, which has been referred to as pseudosyncope, generally occurs in younger patients with underlying anxiety, panic disorder, or depression.

The American Heart Association (AHA), American College of Cardiology (ACC), and Heart Rhythm Society (HRS) jointly conclude that the history and physical examination are the most important diagnostic tools in determining the underlying cause of a syncopal event. The history should focus on eliciting information on prodromal or postepisode symptoms, comorbid medical or psychiatric conditions, the psychosocial context of the event, and bystander information. A thorough review of the patient’s prescription and over-the-counter medications should be completed.

The physical examination should include an in-depth cardiovascular evaluation, including orthostatic (postural) blood pressure measurements, and a basic neurologic examination to evaluate for focal deficits. Carotid hypersensitivity can be assessed by using carotid sinus massage in individuals older than 40 years with syncope of unknown cause; however, this technique is contraindicated in patients with known carotid disease, transient ischemic attack/stroke within the past 3 months, or a carotid bruit (unless previous imaging studies have excluded significant carotid stenosis).

The AHA/ACC/HRS syncope guideline recommends that an ECG be obtained in all patients with syncope to identify underlying arrhythmia, myocardial ischemia, or QT prolongation. In general, additional studies have a low diagnostic yield; however, when there is a moderate to high pretest probability of a specific condition, these studies can help to identify or confirm a diagnosis. Tests to consider include the following:

  • Echocardiography to detect suspected valvular heart disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and reduced left ventricular function
  • Exercise stress testing in patients with exercise-related syncope
  • ECG monitoring in selected patients with a probable arrhythmic cause; the choice of test (e.g., an ambulatory monitor, event monitor, or implantable loop recorder) is based on the frequency and nature of the syncopal event (see Diagnostic Testing for Cardiac Arrhythmias in Cardiovascular Medicine)
  • Targeted laboratory studies, as guided by findings in the history and physical examination
  • Tilt-table testing in patients suspected of having recurrent vasovagal syncope or delayed orthostatic hypotension when the initial evaluation is not diagnostic.
  • Advanced cardiac imaging with CT or MRI when structural or infiltrative heart disease is suspected, especially if initial diagnostic tests are inconclusive
  • CT angiography in patients with a significant pretest probability of pulmonary embolism
  • Electrophysiology studies (reserved for patients suspected of having an arrhythmic cause of syncope that requires more detailed evaluation)
  • Electroencephalography (performed if seizure rather than syncope is suspected)

The American College of Physicians recommends against routinely obtaining brain imaging (CT or MRI) in cases of syncope that do not involve objective focal neurologic findings. Carotid duplex ultrasonography plays no role in the evaluation of syncope. Up to 18% of patients may not have a specific cause identified despite extensive testing.

An assessment of the patient’s short- and long-term morbidity and mortality risk is a necessary component of the evaluation of a patient with syncope. Short-term adverse events and death are primarily determined by the underlying cause and the effectiveness of the treatment. Risk scores have been developed to assist in risk stratification and to guide patient disposition; however, they generally do not outperform physician clinical judgment. The presence of factors that suggest a cardiac cause ( [Table: Table: Characteristics Associated With Cardiac and Noncardiac Syncope]

) or high-risk clinical characteristics ( [Table: Table: High-Risk Clinical Characteristics in the Patient With Syncope]

) should prompt consideration of hospitalization. Patients with likely reflex-mediated syncope who do not have serious underlying medical conditions can be managed in the outpatient setting.

Neurally mediated syncope can be managed with reassurance and education on avoiding provoking measures. Physical counterpressure techniques, such as leg crossing, squatting, or handgrip maneuvers, can be beneficial for neurally mediated syncope with a prolonged prodrome. Sitting during urination and tightening lower extremity muscles can mitigate micturition syncope.

Cardiovascular syncope management should target the specific underlying cardiac condition.

Orthostatic syncope may be treated with volume expansion (with salt liberalization, if appropriate), reconsideration of contributing medications, compression stockings, and education on postural changes. Initiation of additional vasoactive agents, such as fludrocortisone or midodrine, can be considered; however, available evidence on their efficacy is limited and conflicting.

Referral to a mental health specialist is appropriate for patients with psychogenic syncope.

The underlying cause of the syncopal event determines the prognosis. Patients with a syncopal episode are at increased risk for all-cause mortality (hazard ratio [HR], 1.3; 95% CI, 1.1-1.5) and cardiovascular events (HR, 1.3; 95% CI, 1.0-1.6). The risk for death is even greater in cases of cardiac syncope (HR, 2.0; 95% CI, 1.5-2.7). Neurally mediated and orthostatic syncope do not portend increased cardiovascular mortality. However, vasovagal syncope in older patients, especially if recurrent (>2 episodes), is associated with self-reported injury in almost 33% of cases.

Syncope of any cause, especially if recurrent, can severely affect quality of life, functional independence, and self-confidence. Clinicians should assess for any ensuing mood changes, the need for skilled assistance, and the need for possible driving restrictions (which vary per state law).

Abdominal and Pelvic Pain

Triage is key in the evaluation of abdominal and pelvic pain, as the list of potential causes is exhaustive and ranges from benign self-limiting causes to life-threatening diseases that require immediate intervention ( [Table: Table: Abdominal Pain by Predominant Location]

). In the ambulatory care setting, abdominal and pelvic pain is a common presenting symptom and usually has a benign cause; however, confirming the diagnosis in a single encounter can be challenging. Patients presenting to urgent care or emergency department settings are more likely to have an acute cause and more frequently require surgical intervention, sometimes on an emergent basis.

History-taking begins with open-ended discussion and focuses on establishing the acuity and chronology of symptoms and a baseline understanding of medical history that could predispose a patient to recurring abdominal pain. Initial assessment focuses on the following:

  • Localization of the pain and whether it radiates
  • Onset, duration, and severity of pain
  • Quality of the pain
  • Factors that make the pain better or worse

Anatomically, abdominal pain can often be categorized by considering the embryologic relationships of the foregut, midgut, and hindgut. As the embryo forms, neurons that will transmit sensory information from the mature stomach, proximal small intestine, liver, and pancreas travel alongside blood vessels to those primitive organs in the foregut region of the embryo. In adults, pain in the epigastric region is thus usually localized to these organs. Similarly, pain localized to the periumbilical region is associated with the midgut structures, specifically the remainder of the small intestine and colon to the transverse colon. Pain in the left lower quadrant and suprapubic region is linked to the hindgut structures including the distal colon as well as the bladder and pelvic genitourinary organs.

Abdominal pain may also originate from other structures within the abdomen such as the aorta and kidneys. It can occasionally be a manifestation of referred pain from nonabdominal organs such as the heart and lungs.

The physical examination can similarly help in differentiating the causes of pain. Assessment should include vital signs and a comprehensive abdominal examination, including evaluation for signs of peritonitis (percussion tenderness, rebound tenderness, rigidity, guarding, and pain with jostling the bed). The examination should also include an assessment of the heart and lungs and, when appropriate, a pelvic examination.

Throughout the evaluation of abdominal pain, a focus should always be maintained on recognizing causes that are immediately life-threatening and require expedited identification and treatment ( [Table: Table: Acute Abdominal Emergencies]

).

Early symptoms of acute visceral pain involving the abdominal organs are often vaguely localized and diffuse because initial pain impulses are transmitted by nerve fibers located on the walls and capsules of these organs. This causes diffuse, dull pain, which is often referred to the midline abdomen in multiple locations. If the disease progresses to involve the peritoneum, pain is perceived as more localized because a multitude of larger and more myelinated nerve fibers more accurately inform the central nervous system regarding the origin of the pain.

Common causes of foregut pain include the following:

  • Gastritis
  • Peptic ulcer disease
  • Complications of cholelithiasis (biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, acute cholangitis)
  • Pancreatitis

Gastritis symptoms are usually mild and of brief duration, with discomfort described as burning, sharp, frequently relieved with antacid medication, and worse after eating. In contrast, peptic ulcer often presents with more severe pain that is persistent and may radiate to the back. Risk factors for gastritis and peptic ulcer disease include NSAID use and infection with Helicobacter pylori. Differentiating gastritis from peptic ulcer disease and other more serious causes of pain can be difficult. A history of weight loss, persistent vomiting, dysphagia, symptoms that do not respond to symptomatic treatment, or risk factors for gastroesophageal cancer should prompt upper endoscopy.

Patients with biliary colic usually present with recurrent, short-duration episodes of right-upper-quadrant postprandial pain, often after consuming a heavy meal. The pain may radiate to the scapula and be accompanied by nausea and vomiting. If fever or persistent pain occurs, acute cholecystitis is more likely. The presence of jaundice in the setting of acute persistent right upper quadrant pain raises the likelihood of biliary obstruction and acute cholangitis, a surgical emergency. Evaluation of suspected biliary disease includes right upper quadrant ultrasonography with surgical referral for symptomatic cholelithiasis, acute cholecystitis, and acute cholangitis.

Acute pancreatitis is typically characterized by onset of boring epigastric discomfort that frequently radiates to the back. It most commonly occurs in patients with cholelithiasis or alcohol use. CT changes of an edematous pancreas and an elevated amylase level are diagnostic.

Common causes of periumbilical or midgut pain include the following:

  • Small bowel obstruction
  • Early appendicitis
  • Mesenteric ischemia (acute and chronic)
  • Gastroenteritis

The pain of small bowel obstruction is typically cramping or colicky in quality, with a crescendo of symptoms culminating in maximal discomfort and then gradually subsiding until the next cycle recurs in association with peristalsis. Imaging with plain radiography can be diagnostic, but CT is usually performed to confirm the diagnosis.

Early appendicitis may present as nonspecific symptoms of nausea, malaise, and anorexia; however, these symptoms are sometimes absent, and gradual migration of pain to the right lower quadrant is a hallmark. CT is indicated to make the diagnosis, although ultrasonography may also be helpful. Later-stage appendicitis will manifest as pain in the right-lower-quadrant or diffuse pain if peritonitis is present.

Mesenteric ischemia may be acute or chronic and occurs most commonly in patients with underlying cardiovascular disease. Acute mesenteric ischemia is characterized by the sudden onset of often severe periumbilical pain. The examination is less impressive than the degree of pain experienced, leading to the characterization of “pain out of proportion to the exam.” Acute mesenteric ischemia requires immediate evaluation with CT angiography because a delay in surgery of even a few hours has a significant effect on survival. Chronic mesenteric ischemia is much less common. Pain is colicky, typically occurs 15 to 30 minutes after meals and can last up to 4 hours before subsiding spontaneously. Evaluation for the patency of mesenteric arteries with CT angiography or ultrasonography is indicated.

Gastroenteritis is most often associated with viral causes and will present as acute onset of colicky or sharp diffuse pain related to profuse diarrhea, vomiting, and possible fever. The diagnosis is clinical and no testing is usually required unless an alternative diagnosis is suspected.

Lower-quadrant, suprapubic, or hindgut pain is commonly associated with conditions affecting the distal colon as well as the bladder and pelvic genitourinary organs. Such conditions include the following:

  • Diverticulitis
  • Colitis
  • Severe constipation
  • Urinary tract disease

Diverticulitis typically presents in adults as colicky pain localized to the left lower quadrant, left inguinal region, and bladder area and is associated with fever and malaise; constipation is common. CT is usually indicated to confirm the diagnosis and evaluate for evidence of complications such as abscess or fistula formation.

Colitis, including that secondary to inflammatory bowel disease and colonic ischemia, often presents with crampy left-lower-quadrant pain associated with diarrhea or hematochezia (see also Intestinal Manifestations of Ulcerative Colitis and Crohn Disease in Gastroenterology).

Persistent lower abdominal pain accompanied by abdominal distention and tympany is consistent with severe constipation, which could be accompanied or caused by an obstructive mass or motility disorder (see Constipation in Gastroenterology).

Urinary outflow obstruction and complicated urinary tract infection may also cause suprapubic and lower-quadrant pain.

Evaluation of pregnancy status is essential in patients of childbearing age owing to the concern for ectopic pregnancy. Urgent transvaginal ultrasonography is indicated to exclude ectopic pregnancy in pregnant patients. Pelvic inflammatory disease can also present as suprapubic and lower-quadrant discomfort and may or may not be accompanied by vaginal discharge. Transvaginal ultrasonography may also be indicated when ovarian torsion is suspected in patients of childbearing age with focal lower-quadrant symptoms. For further discussion of gynecologic causes of abdominal pain, see Acute Pelvic Pain in Interdisciplinary Medicine.

Testicular torsion may also be associated with colicky pain in the lower quadrant that radiates to the scrotum. Patients with possible torsion should undergo immediate testicular ultrasonography (see Acute Testicular and Scrotal Pain in Interdisciplinary Medicine).

In addition to the causes of visceral abdominal pain, diagnostic possibilities include nonvisceral infectious and vascular causes, especially in patients in distress. A leaking or ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm often presents as severe mid-abdominal pain radiating to the back. Hypotension and tachycardia are usually present. Lower lobe pneumonia may present as right- or left-upper-quadrant discomfort; associated respiratory symptoms, fever, or chills are often but not invariably present. Pulmonary embolism may be associated with referred abdominal pain. Acute inferior wall myocardial infarction may manifest as nausea or epigastric fullness, sometimes without concomitant chest symptoms. Herpes zoster is characterized by lancinating pain in a dermatomal distribution, which can be severe. The pain may precede the rash of zoster, in which case diagnostic delays are common.

Psoas abscess may present as a primary infection in the setting of hematogenous or lymphatic seeding from a distant site or a secondary infection resulting from direct spread of infection to the psoas from adjacent structures, including vertebrae, hip joint, gastrointestinal tract (as in the setting of Crohn disease), genitourinary tract, or from recent instrumentation to the region. Symptoms often include vague abdominal pain or flank pain along with a classic triad of back pain, fever, and limp. Pain on hip movement is suggestive of psoas abscess and CT or MRI may confirm the diagnosis; cultures of blood should be obtained, broad spectrum empiric antibiotic therapy initiated, and drainage performed with culture of the drained abscess fluid.

Underlying metabolic disease may also cause acute abdominal pain. Diabetic ketoacidosis may cause significant abdominal pain as well as nausea and vomiting in the absence of an underlying intra-abdominal process. Acute intermittent porphyria is associated with often severe abdominal pain that may last for days. Concurrent nausea and vomiting are frequently present, but the physical examination usually does not demonstrate findings consistent with peritoneal irritation. Autonomic dysfunction, peripheral neuropathy, psychiatric changes, and hyponatremia may accompany the episodes of pain. A high index of suspicion is necessary for diagnosis, which is established by demonstration of elevated urinary porphobilinogen and total porphyrin levels.

Spontaneous retroperitoneal hemorrhage may occur in the setting of anticoagulation or other hypocoagulable states, including hemodialysis. Pain may be located in the abdomen, back, and/or pelvis, and bleeding may result in hypotension or abdominal compartment syndrome (see Abdominal Compartment Syndrome in Nephrology). Diagnosis is confirmed with CT imaging, with angiography performed if clinical suspicion remains in the setting of a negative CT. Conservative therapy includes supportive resuscitation with fluid and blood products as well as discontinuation of anticoagulation therapy and correction of coagulopathy. Arterial embolization, percutaneous drainage, or open surgery may be necessary.

Centrally mediated abdominal pain syndrome (CAPS) results from central sensitization with disinhibition of pain signals. Abdominal pain without association with food intake or defecation is the primary symptom. The pain is typically nonlocalized and constant or frequently recurring. Extraintestinal symptoms, such as musculoskeletal pain, may be present. Initial evaluation should include a detailed medical and psychosocial history, physical examination, and limited laboratory studies to exclude gastrointestinal bleeding and inflammation.

Management of abdominal or pelvic pain involves consideration of whether the symptoms warrant emergent medical attention and whether the patient is at high risk for complications. If there is significant suspicion for an emergent condition, prompt referral for emergency department evaluation for expedited laboratory investigation and imaging is essential.

Imaging is indicated if obstruction, bowel perforation, sepsis, abscess, or vascular compromise is suspected. The choice of imaging technique is informed by the suspected diagnoses. CT scan is the most commonly ordered test in the evaluation of abdominal pain, although it is important to differentiate when CT angiography is necessary. Ultrasonography is usually the first-line test when biliary disease is suspected, whereas transvaginal ultrasonography is the imaging test of choice for many pelvic causes of abdominal pain.

Treatment depends on the identified diagnosis. Many acute conditions require surgical intervention. See [Table: Table: Acute Abdominal Emergencies]

for more information.

Treatment of CAPS focuses on setting appropriate goals and expectations. The combination of pharmacologic and/or psychological therapies may also have utility. Potentially useful medications include tricyclic antidepressants, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors. Cognitive behavioral therapy, psychodynamic-interpersonal therapy, mindfulness- and acceptance-based therapy, and hypnotherapy are all useful when combined with medical therapy.

Low Back Pain

Low back pain is one of the top five reasons for U.S. doctor office visits and a leading cause of disability and health care expenditure. Approximately 90% of patients have nonspecific low back pain for which no specific cause can be determined and which typically resolves with conservative care within days to weeks.

The most common identifiable causes of low back pain are spinal stenosis and degenerative disk disease with or without disk herniation. Less common identifiable causes include metabolic bone disease with or without compression fracture, cancer, and infection. Visceral diseases and psychosocial distress may also cause low back pain.

Evaluation of patients with low back pain includes a detailed history directed toward factors that increase the likelihood of specific causes of pain ( [Table: Table: Features Suggesting Specific Causes of Low Back Pain]

). The presence of historical red flag findings that suggest a serious underlying disorder should also be assessed, including the following:

  • Fever
  • Recent infection
  • Recent injection drug use
  • Immunosuppression
  • Chronic glucocorticoid use
  • Pain that is unrelieved with supine position
  • History of cancer or weight loss
  • Recent trauma
  • Neurologic symptoms

Classification of low back pain by duration as acute (<6 weeks), subacute (6-12 weeks), or chronic (>12 weeks) is also relevant, given that this is often linked to the expected time course of symptom improvement and impacts decision making related to the choice of diagnostic imaging and management strategy.

The presence of psychosocial distress, comorbid psychiatric conditions, somatization, and maladaptive coping strategies (e.g., avoiding work) should also be determined, as these are associated with poor clinical outcomes in patients with low back pain.

The physical examination should similarly include a search for evidence of an underlying disorder (see [Table: Table: Features Suggesting Specific Causes of Low Back Pain]

). Specific attention should be paid to the following red flag findings on examination:

  • Fever
  • Weight loss
  • Localized bony tenderness
  • Neurologic deficits

A thorough neurologic examination that includes strength, sensation, and reflex testing of the legs, in addition to performing both the ipsilateral and contralateral straight leg raise tests (

), can identify patterns of deficits that point to lesions (most commonly, disk herniation) at specific levels ( [Table: Table: Neurologic Deficits in Patients With Low Back Pain]

). Decreased anal sphincter tone and decreased perianal sensation raise concern for cauda equina syndrome. Many examination findings, however, are insensitive or nonspecific for the presence of a particular disorder.

Routine imaging is not indicated within the first 6 weeks of symptoms in patients with nonspecific low back pain without red flags. Anatomic abnormalities on imaging studies are common in asymptomatic persons and correlate poorly with pain generators in patients with nonspecific low back pain. In one study of asymptomatic individuals aged 50 years or older, CT scan and MRI of the lumbar spine showed disk degeneration and disk bulging in 80% and 60% of patients, respectively. As such, routine imaging may lead to unhelpful and costly interventions as well as increased patient anxiety.

However, imaging is indicated if there are red flags, such as progressive neurologic compromise, suspicion for a life- or function-threatening cause, or a plan for an invasive procedure such as surgery. Imaging modality should be chosen based on the suspected diagnosis. Plain radiography can be helpful for the initial evaluation of suspected fracture or sacroiliitis, although MRI should be obtained if plain radiography is unrevealing and clinical suspicion remains high. MRI is otherwise the preferred test for suspected spinal infection, cancer, cord compression, or cauda equina syndrome and should be obtained emergently if myelopathy is suspected.

Nonurgent MRI imaging may be considered in patients with pain persisting for longer than 6 weeks in the absence of red flags; persistent or progressive symptoms despite conservative therapies; or neurologic symptoms, such as neurogenic claudication. Patients who are otherwise unable to undergo invasive procedures, such as surgical laminectomy, are unlikely to benefit from imaging.

Measurement of inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein) may be considered in conjunction with imaging for suspected cancer or infection, although normal results do not rule out the presence of either. Electromyography and nerve conduction tests may be considered in patients with subacute or chronic radicular symptoms to assess the congruence of symptoms with radiographic findings.

Patient education is a key component of the treatment of low back pain regardless of pain duration. Education includes the following:

  • Providing information on the expected course and common misconceptions
  • Centering on functional therapeutic goals
  • Promoting self-management
  • Addressing psychosocial factors
  • Encouraging physical activity as appropriate

In all patients with low back pain, bed rest should be avoided and mood symptoms should be appropriately assessed and managed.

In addition to education, treatment modalities for patients with low back pain may include nonpharmacologic and/or pharmacologic therapies and, rarely, surgery. These interventions should be chosen based on the patient’s signs, symptoms, and comorbid conditions.

Nonpharmacologic therapies are the cornerstone of treatment for acute and chronic low back pain. For acute low back pain, potentially useful nonpharmacologic therapies include physical therapy, local heat, massage, and acupuncture, although the evidence supporting these approaches is generally weak. Spinal manipulation therapy has moderate evidence for modest pain reduction and improvement in function. The type of performing provider (physical therapist, physician, or chiropractor) does not affect outcomes.

Multiple nonpharmacologic options are available for chronic low back pain, including the following:

  • Physical therapy
  • Exercise therapy
  • Manual and massage therapy
  • Spinal mobilization/manipulation
  • Acupuncture
  • Core-strengthening exercises (e.g., Pilates, tai chi, and yoga)
  • Low-level laser therapy
  • Intensive interdisciplinary therapy
  • Mindfulness-based stress reduction
  • Cognitive behavioral therapy

Varying levels of predominantly weak evidence support these approaches.

Multidisciplinary approaches have produced greater magnitudes of improvement in long-term pain and disability compared with individual interventions. The 2016 National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines endorse self-management, exercise, manual therapy, psychological therapy, and return-to-work programs.

NSAIDs (topical or oral) reduce pain and disability in patients with acute low back pain. They are considered first-line pharmacologic therapy and should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration needed. Notably, acetaminophen is ineffective for acute low back pain. Second-line agents include short courses of nonbenzodiazepine muscle relaxants. Opioids and tramadol should be avoided. Evidence on oral glucocorticoids for pain management is weak.

A similar approach is appropriate in patients with chronic low back pain. NSAIDs (topical or oral) remain first-line pharmacologic therapy, and as-needed nonbenzodiazepine muscle relaxants may be used as second-line therapy. The serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor duloxetine is FDA approved to treat chronic low back pain and may be useful in select patients. Noninhaled cannabinoids can be considered for chronic pain but lack long-term efficacy data. Systemic glucocorticoids, tricyclic antidepressants, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and gabapentinoids (gabapentin and pregabalin) have not demonstrated benefit for chronic low back pain with or without radiculopathy. Clinicians and patients should engage in shared decision making guided by patient values and priorities when considering treatment modalities.

A 2018 randomized controlled trial demonstrated that opioids were not superior to nonopioid medications for improving pain-related function for chronic back pain; pain intensity was significantly improved in the nonopioid group, and adverse effects were less common. Multiple organizations, including the American College of Physicians and the CDC, recommend nonpharmacologic and nonopioid therapies over opioids.

Most patients with low back pain do not require surgery. Immediate surgery is indicated for patients with suspected cord compression or cauda equina syndrome, as the strongest determinant of neurologic outcome with surgery in these patients is the degree of functioning at the time of surgery. Nonurgent surgery may be considered in patients with neurologic deficits, progressively worsening spinal stenosis, or chronic pain with corresponding abnormalities on imaging that has been refractory to conservative measures and has the potential to respond to surgery.

Epidural glucocorticoid injections are frequently performed in patients with radiculopathy; however, available evidence suggests they offer only small, short-term benefits.

Trigger point injections for myofascial low back pain may be considered and are generally safe, but efficacy is variable and duration of pain relief is generally short term.

Scoliosis

Adult scoliosis is a radiologic diagnosis and refers to a three-dimensional abnormal curvature of the spine with a coronal deviation of greater than 10 degrees (Cobb angle) (

).

Adult scoliosis may result from progression of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, adult de novo scoliosis, or underlying medical disease. Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis affects 0.5% to 5% of U.S. adolescents. Although there is no significant difference in incidence of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis by gender, women are more likely to have severe disease with Cobb angles equal to or exceeding 30 degrees.

Adult de novo scoliosis is a more common cause of scoliosis in older adults, with a mean age of onset of 70.5 years and a prevalence of 21% to 68% in those older than 60 years of age. It is usually due to degenerative disease that results in asymmetric loading of the spinal column, most frequently the lumbar region. These changes can cause spondylolisthesis, spinal stenosis, and radiculopathy. Less commonly, adult scoliosis may be due to an underlying medical condition such as stroke, Parkinson disease, or trauma.

Many patients with scoliosis are asymptomatic; when symptoms do occur, they may include back pain as well as leg pain due to neurogenic claudication and/or radicular symptoms. Severe pain is rare, and the degree of curvature does not correlate with pain severity; significant disability is similarly rare.

Scoliosis is suspected on the basis of history, examination of the spine, and observations of posture and gait. The diagnosis is confirmed with full-length posteroanterior and lateral radiography of the spine, hip joints, and pelvis with measurement of the Cobb angle.

In the absence of advanced stenosis or severe neurogenic and radicular symptoms, first-line treatment of symptomatic patients includes scoliosis-specific physical therapy exercises (including the Schroth method) that focus on posture control, muscle endurance, spinal stability, and balance; analgesics; and epidural or nerve root injections. Bracing may have short- to medium-term benefit in slowing curve progression and reducing pain but can lead to muscle deconditioning and is not generally used unless recommended by a scoliosis specialist. Radiographic monitoring for progression is warranted in some circumstances. Indications for specialty referral include a Cobb angle greater than or equal to 40 degrees; significant symptoms, including poor physical functioning or adverse effects on respiration; or pain that is refractory to conservative treatment. Surgical management can be considered in select cases.

Neck Pain

Neck pain has an annual prevalence of up to 20% in the U.S. adult population, making it the fourth leading cause of disability. A priority in evaluating neck pain is differentiating musculoskeletal neck pain from other conditions that may cause serious complications or be amenable to therapy. Evaluation begins with a thorough history, including circumstances of the onset, presence of antecedent trauma, duration, progression, impact on daily activities, and accompanying symptoms. Specific note should be made of underlying medical conditions such as malignancy and immunosuppression that may predispose patients to serious causes of neck pain. The presence of conditions associated with increased risk of atlanto-occipital instability, including rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and trisomy 21, should also be noted. Examination includes inspection and palpation of the cervical spine and muscles; range-of-motion testing; and comprehensive neurologic assessment, including sensory, motor, and reflex testing. Red flag findings suggestive of the need for expedited evaluation, including imaging, are listed in [Table: Table: Red Flag Findings in Patients With Neck Pain]

.

The most common causes of neck pain are musculoskeletal such as cervical strain and spondylosis. Patients with musculoskeletal causes present with pain and stiffness with neck movement, along with decreased cervical range of motion and absence of neurologic abnormalities. Myofascial pain is also common and may be differentiated from other musculoskeletal causes by localized tenderness or trigger points on palpation of the neck and shoulder. Often, multiple musculoskeletal conditions occur in combination, making it difficult to determine one sole cause of pain. Some neurologic conditions (tension headache) and rheumatologic conditions (polymyalgia rheumatica, giant cell arteritis) may present with a constellation of symptoms including neck pain; these conditions are discussed in Tension-Type Headache in Neurology, Polymyalgia Rheumatica in Rheumatology, and Giant Cell Arteritis in Rheumatology, respectively.

Radiculopathy and myelopathy are the most common neurologic findings associated with neck pain. Cervical radiculopathy is caused by spinal nerve root compression, often resulting from degenerative spinal changes or disk herniation. Radiculopathy leads to neck pain accompanied by radiating arm pain, paresthesia, decreased deep tendon reflexes, and diminished strength in the affected extremity. In some cases, pain may be limited to the shoulder girdle or arm. On examination, the patient’s symptoms may be reproduced with the Spurling test (sensitivity, 30%; specificity, 94%) (Video: Spurling Test); a positive Spurling test is helpful in supporting the diagnosis, but a negative test does not rule out cervical radiculopathy. Cervical radiculopathy is also suggested if the pain is improved by holding the patient’s hand above the head (shoulder abduction test: sensitivity, 17% to 78%; specificity, 75% to 92%).

Compressive cervical myelopathy can cause neck pain with associated leg weakness, gait and coordination disturbances, and bladder and bowel dysfunction. Common causes include spondylosis, disk herniation, malignancy, and epidural abscess. Examination reveals upper motor neuron signs (increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, and clonus) in the upper and lower extremities; lower motor neuron signs (atrophy, hyporeflexia) may occur near the level of compression or after acute injury. The Lhermitte sign, an electric shock–like pain radiating from the neck to the spine or the arms, can be produced by forward flexion of the neck but is insensitive for the presence of cervical cord disease. See Presenting Symptoms and Signs of Myelopathy in Neurology for further discussion of cervical cord myelopathy.

Cancer should be considered in patients with a history of cancer or suggestive systemic symptoms, such as weight loss. Infectious causes, such as epidural abscess, diskitis, or osteomyelitis, should be considered in patients with fever and chills and in those with predisposing comorbid conditions, including diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, injection drug use, kidney or liver failure, and long-term glucocorticoid use.

In the absence of red flags ( [Table: Table: Red Flag Findings in Patients With Neck Pain]

), imaging is often not necessary for mild neck pain that does not interfere with activities of daily living. Plain radiography may be performed as the initial study in patients without red flags who have moderate discomfort or have not responded to conservative treatment. Plain radiography is also indicated as the initial test in patients at risk for atlantoaxial instability who have pain without red flags, such as those with ankylosing spondylitis, trisomy 21, or rheumatoid arthritis. MRI is the imaging test of choice when suspicion for cancer or infection is present, when myelopathy is suspected, or if progressive neurologic symptoms are present. MRI is usually not initially necessary in patients with suspected disk herniation without red flags. In patients who require advanced imaging but cannot undergo MRI, CT myelography can be considered.

Patients with serious underlying causes of neck pain such as malignancy, osteomyelitis/diskitis, and myelopathy often require urgent surgical intervention to prevent neurologic deterioration. Otherwise, the majority of patients with musculoskeletal neck pain will have resolution or near resolution of their symptoms within 6 to 12 weeks with conservative measures. Although multiple treatments exist for musculoskeletal neck pain, no one treatment or combination of treatments has demonstrated superiority. A multimodal approach tailored to the individual patient appears to work best and may include range-of-motion exercise, physical therapy, ice or heat applications, and analgesic agents. Stretching and strengthening exercises appear to provide intermediate-term relief of symptoms. Regular use of a cervical collar may delay improvement and should be discouraged.

Oral and topical NSAIDs are considered first-line pharmacologic therapy for musculoskeletal neck pain. Because of its favorable side-effect profile, acetaminophen is also frequently used; however, its effectiveness is not clearly established. Although muscle relaxants are often used for treatment of acute neck pain associated with muscle spasm, supporting data for their use are limited. Because of the potential for misuse, opioids should be avoided. No evidence supports the use of oral glucocorticoids in neck pain without radiculopathy.

Patients with cervical radiculopathy presenting with nonprogressive paresthesia and numbness should also be treated conservatively for 6 to 8 weeks as long as myelopathy is not present. Although data are limited, oral glucocorticoids are often used in acute cervical radiculopathy. Data supporting epidural glucocorticoid injections in patients with refractory symptoms are unconvincing. For patients with chronic radicular symptoms, venlafaxine and neuromodulators (e.g., gabapentin, tricyclic antidepressants) may provide some pain relief.

Surgery for cervical radiculopathy is generally reserved for patients with confirmed cervical nerve root compression and either progressive motor weakness or persistent radicular pain for more than 6 to 12 weeks.

For chronic cervical stenosis, managing symptoms may be sufficient in most patients. Surgical decompression may be required for patients with pain refractory to medical management or significant or progressive neurologic deficits.

For those with neck pain with a systemic cause, the underlying disorder should be appropriately treated.

bodies.cssec24011:
Upper Extremity Musculoskeletal Pain

Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) refers to signs and symptoms caused by compression of the upper extremity neurovascular bundle, located posterior to the clavicle above the first rib. There are three subtypes of TOS, distinguished by the affected structure ( [Table: Table: Subtypes of Thoracic Outlet Syndrome]

).

Treatment of TOS is contingent on the structures affected. First-line therapy for neurogenic TOS includes improving posture and physical therapy to strengthen shoulder girdle musculature. Surgical decompression is reserved for progressive or disabling symptoms. Treatment of both arterial and venous TOS involves catheter-directed thrombolysis or embolectomy when thrombosis is present, followed by prompt surgical decompression of the thoracic outlet.

The assessment of shoulder pain involves a detailed history with attention to the presence of antecedent trauma and relevant occupational or recreational activities. A comprehensive shoulder examination, performed with both shoulders fully exposed, includes inspection, palpation, range-of-motion assessment, and specialized maneuvers.

Shoulder pain with acute onset after trauma should be evaluated with appropriate imaging to rule out injury, such as fracture and dislocation, which may require urgent treatment. The initial step in evaluating atraumatic shoulder pain is to determine whether the pain arises from the shoulder (intrinsic) or is referred from another site (extrinsic), such as the cervical spine or gallbladder. Extrinsic pain is suggested by the inability to reproduce pain with shoulder movement, neuropathic pain, pain extending beyond the elbow, and pain exacerbated by neck movement. If cervical spine involvement is suspected, a detailed motor, sensory, and reflex examination in addition to a Spurling maneuver is warranted (see Diagnosis and Evaluation of Neck Pain in Common Symptoms).

The location of shoulder pain can help determine the underlying cause. Anterolateral shoulder pain is the most common shoulder pain and may be caused by impingement syndrome, subacromial bursitis, rotator cuff tendinopathy, adhesive capsulitis, or labral tears. Anterior shoulder pain that is aggravated by lifting and carrying suggests tendinitis of the long head of the biceps tendon. Pain localized to the lateral clavicle suggests acromioclavicular pathology.

Posterior shoulder pain may result from tendinopathy of the external rotators of the rotator cuff or may be referred pain from the spine. Pain that occurs with movement in any direction may be indicative of glenohumeral joint pathology, especially if examination results are equivocal.

Plain film radiographs should be obtained in patients with loss of range of motion, in addition to patients with recent trauma.

Rotator cuff disease, the most common cause of shoulder pain, encompasses all symptomatic rotator cuff disorders, including rotator cuff tendinopathy, partial- and full-thickness rotator cuff tears, subacromial bursitis, and impingement syndrome ( [Table: Table: Symptomatic Rotator Cuff Disorders]

). Risk factors for rotator cuff disease include increasing age and participation in activities that require repetitive overhead arm use. With the exception of acute traumatic rotator cuff tears, onset of symptoms is usually insidious and associated with overuse. Anterolateral shoulder pain and nonpositional night pain are characteristic.

Many examination maneuvers are available for rotator cuff disease assessment; they are most useful in combination ( [Table: Table: Physical Examination Maneuvers in Rotator Cuff Disease]

). The presence of weakness is an important distinction. Subacromial bursitis, tendinosis, and partial-thickness rotator cuff tears result in pain with intact strength, whereas full-thickness rotator cuff tears result in both pain and weakness in external rotation or abduction. Positive results on both the painful arc test and the drop arm test in the setting of weakness in external rotation are particularly suggestive of a rotator cuff tear.

Patients with suspected traumatic acute full-thickness tears should be considered for expedited imaging (usually with MRI), especially younger patients in whom early surgery may be indicated. Chronic or slowly progressive rotator cuff disease does not require imaging in most cases, but it may be considered if the diagnosis is in doubt or if surgical treatment is being considered. Although MRI is most commonly performed, ultrasonography is as accurate and is less expensive.

Patients with acute full-thickness rotator cuff tears can be considered for surgical repair depending on the degree of pain, loss of function, and occupation. Otherwise treatment of most rotator cuff disorders is primarily physical therapy, education about the expected course, and avoidance or modification of aggravating activities. Immobilization should be avoided to prevent development of adhesive capsulitis. Pharmacologic treatment should begin with acetaminophen and, if ineffective, progress to oral or topical NSAIDs. Subacromial glucocorticoid injections may provide short-term pain relief in patients with subacromial bursitis in whom other measures have failed but should be limited to minimize complication risk (tendon rupture or tear).

Surgery in patients with a chronic rotator cuff tear is reserved for those in whom 3 to 6 months of conservative therapy has failed or for physically active patients with functionally significant tears. Subacromial decompression surgery is ineffective for pain relief and is not indicated for patients with chronic shoulder pain attributed to rotator cuff disease.

Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) is the most likely diagnosis when anterolateral shoulder pain is associated with stiffness that is often worse at night and in cold weather. It usually occurs in patients older than 40 years. Examination reveals progressive loss of abduction or external rotation; both passive and active range of motion are also decreased. Adhesive capsulitis can be idiopathic but is also associated with prolonged immobilization, antecedent shoulder surgery or injury, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, and autoimmune disorders.

Adhesive capsulitis is often self-limiting over the course of months to years. Treatment focuses on pain control and improving range of motion with physical therapy and range-of-motion exercises. Intra-articular glucocorticoid injections appear to be more effective than physical therapy, although combining modalities may be most effective. Acetaminophen and NSAIDs can be used as an adjunct for analgesia. Surgery is reserved for patients with intolerable pain or who do not respond to conservative measures.

Acromioclavicular joint degeneration is typically characterized by poorly localized pain on the superior shoulder and lateral clavicle, although pain may be present throughout the shoulder region. On examination, pain is usually elicited with palpation of the acromioclavicular joint. The crossed-arm adduction test often reproduces the pain, as does shoulder abduction beyond 120 degrees, but neither test is specific for acromioclavicular joint disease. Plain radiography is often completed to assess for other structural disease and usually reveals degenerative changes of the acromioclavicular joint (

).

First-line therapy consists of NSAIDs and activity modification. Glucocorticoid injections may provide short-term pain relief.

Repetitive overhead stress, especially stress that puts weight on the shoulder, may produce a labral tear. Superior labrum anterior and posterior (SLAP) tears are common in athletes and laborers. Labral tears often present with deep anterolateral pain that worsens with abduction and external rotation, although pain may be generalized. Patients report a catching sensation with movement, crepitus, and instability of the joint. Labral tears may be difficult to diagnose, and early referral to an orthopedic surgeon with experience in treating shoulder injuries is recommended.

Elbow problems may be caused by pathology within the elbow joint, surrounding tissues, or nerves. Evaluation focuses on the history and physical examination.

Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow), or inflammation of the tendon at the lateral epicondyle, is caused by repetitive strain of extensor tendons, such as with computer use or tennis. Pain and tenderness are located over the lateral epicondyle and increase with resisted wrist extension. The Cozen test (more sensitive than specific) and the Mill test (more specific but not very sensitive) can be useful bedside maneuvers for the diagnosis of lateral epicondylitis (Video: Cozen and Mill Tests).

Medial epicondylitis (golfer’s elbow) is caused by repetitive flexion of the wrist. Pain occurs over the medial elbow and ventral forearm and worsens with resisted wrist flexion (Video: Examination for Medical Epicondylitis).

Diagnostic imaging is usually unnecessary if the clinical picture is consistent with medial or lateral epicondylitis.

Initial management of epicondylitis includes avoidance of pain-inducing activities and NSAIDs for analgesia. Physical therapy and counterforce braces may improve symptoms and prevent future exacerbations. Glucocorticoid injections may reduce pain in the short term but provide no long-term benefit. For lateral epicondylitis, patients should be reassured that symptoms generally resolve in 6 to 12 months without specific treatment and there is no evidence that using the elbow, despite pain, causes harm.

The radial nerve is susceptible to compression where it is in close proximity to the humerus in the spiral groove. Sustained pressure on the nerve, such as may occur with prolonged unconsciousness, results in weakness of the wrist extensors (wrist drop) and sensory loss on the dorsum of the first three fingers. Entrapment of the posterior interosseous branch of the radial nerve at the elbow (radial tunnel syndrome) should be considered in patients with lateral elbow pain initially diagnosed as tennis elbow that has not responded to conservative therapy.

Ulnar nerve impingement at the elbow (cubital tunnel syndrome) presents as elbow pain that worsens with flexion and is associated with paresthesia, numbness of the fourth and fifth fingers, and weakness of the interosseous muscles. Diagnosis is usually clinical, but electromyography/nerve conduction studies are often used for diagnostic confirmation or when considering surgical intervention.

Initial treatment consists of avoidance of elbow trauma and nocturnal splinting. NSAIDs can be beneficial for short-term pain relief. Surgery is an option when conservative measures fail in the setting of significant or progressive symptoms.

Olecranon bursitis is the most common cause of swelling at the elbow and is usually secondary to trauma or synovitis. Causes of synovitis include infection (septic arthritis) and rheumatologic conditions (rheumatoid, reactive, or psoriatic arthritis; gout) Posterior elbow swelling and tenderness with a normal elbow range of motion are typical (

). Swelling with pain on elbow extension and reduced range of motion suggest infection or active inflammation and synovitis.

Bursa or joint aspiration with culture and fluid analysis should be performed for severe pain, when there is any suspicion of infection or when crystal disease is suspected.

Noninfectious bursitis is treated with joint rest, ice, elbow protection, and as-needed NSAID therapy. Glucocorticoid injections should be avoided because evidence shows no benefit but an increased risk for infection or development of a draining sinus tract. Surgery may be necessary for refractory bursitis.

Bursitis secondary to infection is treated with antibiotics and aspiration; surgery may be needed in some cases.

Wrist and hand pain may be caused by trauma or overuse leading to musculoskeletal abnormalities and nerve compression. A thorough history and physical examination can localize the source of pain and narrow the differential diagnosis; however, plain radiography is often necessary to make a definitive diagnosis.

Acute wrist or hand pain associated with trauma suggests fracture or dislocation and requires radiography for evaluation, especially for scaphoid and hamate fractures. Both types of fracture frequently result from a fall onto an outstretched hand. Scaphoid fractures are characterized by radial pain, tenderness in the anatomic snuffbox, and pain with axial loading (pushing the thumb into the first metacarpophalangeal joint). Initial radiographs are normal in up to 20% of patients. If clinical suspicion is high and radiographs are normal, thumb splinting and repeat radiography in 1 to 2 weeks or immediate MRI or CT is recommended. Hamate fractures typically present with pain over the hypothenar eminence, and radiographs usually reveal the fracture.

Ulnar neuropathy from ulnar nerve entrapment at the wrist is characterized by wrist pain, interosseous muscle weakness, and diminished sensation in the fourth and fifth digits (Video: Cubital Tinal Test). Electrodiagnostic testing can confirm the clinical diagnosis. Conservative therapy, including activity modification and elbow protection, is first-line treatment for patients with mild to moderate symptoms. Patients with progressive symptoms or symptoms that persist for longer than 6 months should be considered for surgical intervention.

Ganglion cysts are caused by herniated synovial tissue surrounding tendon sheaths (

). The majority of ganglion cysts will resolve without intervention over the course of 12 to 18 months. Painful cysts may be aspirated; if cysts recur after aspiration, surgical resection is effective.

Trigger finger results from a mismatch in the size of the tendon and surrounding tendon sheath, which leads to mechanical obstruction during flexion or extension of the affected digit. Patients note snagging or locking of the affected fingers. Although initially painless, symptoms may progress to painful episodes with difficulty flexing or extending the digit. Initial management includes NSAIDs, splinting, and activity modification. Glucocorticoid injection is generally successful first-line treatment for more severe disease. Refractory cases should be referred to a specialist for consideration of surgical decompression.

De Quervain tendinopathy results from thickening of the thumb extensor tendons. Pain occurs at the thumb base, radiates to the distal radius, and is elicited with making a fist over the thumb and ulnar deviation of the wrist (Finkelstein test) (

). Initial management includes rest, NSAIDs, and thumb spica splinting. When conservative measures are ineffective, glucocorticoid injections provide symptomatic relief. Local anesthetic injection can be used to differentiate de Quervain tendinopathy from arthritis of the first carpometacarpal joint, which may present similarly. Surgery may benefit patients with symptoms that do not respond to glucocorticoid injections.

Osteoarthritis and inflammatory arthritis may affect the interphalangeal and carpometacarpal joints and cause hand and wrist pain (see Clinical Manifestations in Rheumatology).

Dupuytren contracture is a fibrosing disorder of the palmar fascia resulting in finger flexion contracture that typically spares the thumb and index finger (

). Functional loss is more prominent than pain, with minimal discomfort related to cord-like fibrosing tightness. Finger triggering may be present. Bilateral hand involvement is more common in patients with diabetes mellitus and poor glycemic control. Treatment options include glucocorticoid injection, needle aponeurotomy, and surgery.

Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) develops from increased pressure and compression of the median nerve under the transverse carpal ligament. The syndrome is characterized by pain, paresthesia, and weakness of the first three fingers and thenar eminence (the median nerve distribution). Symptoms are often worse at night and with repetitive wrist motion. CTS may also develop during pregnancy and often remits following delivery.

Diagnosis is based on concordant history and examination findings of hypoalgesia or decreased sensation over the median nerve distribution, thenar muscle atrophy, and weakened thumb abduction. Examination is often normal early in the disease. Provocative testing with the Phalen maneuver (flexion of hands at wrists) or Tinel test (percussion of the median nerve on top of the carpal tunnel) has only moderate sensitivity and specificity and should not be relied on alone to make or exclude the diagnosis of CTS. A scored clinical evaluation, such as CTS-6 (Six-Item Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Scale), can be used to aid in diagnosis. Electrodiagnostic studies are not necessary in mild cases when the diagnosis is clear but should be done when there is diagnostic uncertainty or when more severe findings, such as muscle weakness, thenar atrophy, or sensory loss, are present and surgery is a consideration. It can also be useful when cervical radiculopathy is a possibility. Ultrasonography of the carpal tunnel to document median nerve swelling is not required but may also be used to confirm the diagnosis.

Initial treatment includes activity modification and nocturnal wrist-neutral splinting. Glucocorticoid injection performed in the office may provide short-term symptomatic improvement and can be useful confirmatory diagnostic testing. Surgical division of the transverse carpal ligament promptly relieves dysesthesia and should be considered in moderate or severe disease as suggested by motor loss, sensory loss, or thenar atrophy and concordant findings on electrodiagnostic testing.

Complex regional pain syndrome is characterized by persistent pain, most commonly in a distal extremity. The cause is uncertain, but it usually occurs within 1 to 2 months following trauma. Musculoskeletal injury such as a fracture is the most frequent trigger, although it can occur after any injury, including surgery. The pain, which is often burning in nature, can be continuous and debilitating. Other features including swelling, limited range of motion, skin changes, sensory changes (including hyperalgesia and allodynia), and vasomotor instability are variably present. Evaluation may reveal limb temperature discrepancies, patchy bone demineralization, and abnormal findings on triple-phase bone scintigraphy, but the diagnosis is made clinically. Treatment should be individualized and may include NSAIDs, neuropathic pain medications such as gabapentin, and physical and occupational therapy.
