bodies.cssec24012:
Lower Extremity Musculoskeletal Pain

The evaluation of hip pain can be challenging because of the complexity of the joint, and a multifactorial cause of pain may be present in up to 25% of patients. The location of the pain (anterior/groin, lateral, or posterior) is helpful in focusing the evaluation ( [Table: Table: Causes of Hip Pain by Location]

).

Anterior hip pain can be caused by both intra- and extra-articular conditions. In older patients, pain that starts insidiously and worsens with standing and activity suggests osteoarthritis ( [Table: Table: Features and Likelihood of Hip Osteoarthritis]

). An insidious onset of anterior pain in a younger person raises concern for a labral tear if accompanied by painful clicking or catching. Femoroacetabular impingement, which is caused by abnormal contact of the femoral head-neck junction with the acetabular rim of the hip joint, produces gradual-onset groin pain at the extremes of movement that worsens after prolonged sitting and improves with standing. Gradual onset of anterior hip pain can also occur with avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis), which should be considered in the presence of alcohol use disorder, glucocorticoid use, systemic lupus erythematosus, or sickle cell disease. Anterior hip pain presenting in athletes has a specific differential diagnosis; the most common causes are labral tear, femoroacetabular impingement, hernia (athletic pubalgia or inguinal hernia), and adductor strain or tear.

Acute, anteriorly located hip pain that interferes with weight bearing and is accompanied by fever raises suspicion for infectious arthritis, whereas acute pain after a fall suggests fracture. Intra-abdominal processes (e.g., nephrolithiasis, inguinal hernia, ovarian pathology, or appendicitis) can also cause referred pain to the groin or anterior hip.

Lateral hip pain is most commonly caused by greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS) (formerly known as trochanteric bursitis) or meralgia paresthetica. GTPS typically causes pain that worsens with lying on the affected side; the pain may also radiate to the buttock or knee if the iliotibial band is affected. Meralgia paresthetica, entrapment neuropathy of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN), is characterized by distal anterolateral thigh paresthesia following the LFCN distribution associated with tight-fitting clothes or obesity. Less common causes of lateral hip pain include osteoarthritis, generally accompanied by anterior hip pain and difficulty bending over, and lower lumbar radiculopathies, which are typically associated with low back pain and other neurologic symptoms attributable to nerve root compression.

Posterior or buttock pain may be caused by lumbar radiculopathy, vascular claudication, sacroiliac joint dysfunction, or gluteal tendinopathy. Pain associated with radiation down the leg suggests lumbar radiculopathy, especially if back pain is present. Posterior hip pain with concomitant exertional leg pain or peripheral vascular disease suggests vascular claudication. Isolated posterior pain may be secondary to sacroiliac joint dysfunction; the presence of morning stiffness, uveitis, fever, or peripheral joint symptoms should prompt consideration of axial spondylarthritis (Axial Spondyloarthritis in Rheumatology). Osteoarthritis of the hip can present with pain that refers to the buttocks, especially with squatting, but is associated with other features typical of intra-articular pathology.

Examination of patients with hip pain includes evaluation of the hip, abdomen, and back; neurologic and vascular assessments of the legs; and gait assessment. Pain with both passive and active hip movement suggests an intra-articular cause, as does pain or restricted range of motion with internal rotation or the FADIR (Flexion, ADduction, and Internal Rotation) test (Video: FADIR test). The most specific test for hip joint pathology is the log roll test (

and Video: Log Roll Test).

The FABER (Flexion, ABduction, and External Rotation) test may cause posterior hip pain in the presence of sacroiliac joint dysfunction or groin pain with an intra-articular or iliopsoas cause (

).

The most common examination finding in GTPS is tenderness to palpation of the greater trochanter. Reproduction of the pain during the straight leg raise test (

) supports lumbar radiculopathy. A normal hip examination in a patient with groin pain suggests an extra-articular cause, such as an inguinal hernia.

Radiographs (anteroposterior pelvic view and frog-leg lateral view) should be obtained if intra-articular pathology, fracture, or dislocation is suspected. Radiographs are less sensitive for fracture in patients with osteoporosis and in those patients with trauma; additional imaging with CT or MRI should be pursued if there is a high suspicion of fracture and initial radiographs are negative. Similarly, MRI of the hip can be useful in patients with persistent pain and normal radiographs, especially in diagnosing disorders, such as osteomyelitis or avascular necrosis, that may not always be evident on plain films. If suspicion is high for a labral tear, MR arthrography should be performed. Hip aspiration is indicated if infectious arthritis is suspected.

Treatment of hip pain is determined by the underlying cause. See Management of Osteoarthritis in Rheumatology for a discussion of treatment options for osteoarthritis. Patients with advanced avascular necrosis often require hip arthroplasty.

Initial management of labral tears and femoroacetabular impingement includes muscle strengthening and activity modification, with surgery reserved for those in whom conservative measures fail.

Initial management of GTPS includes activity modification and analgesia with NSAIDs; targeted physical therapy may also play a role. Glucocorticoid injection or extracorporeal shockwave treatment can be considered for persistently symptomatic GTPS, with surgery limited to recalcitrant cases.

Primary treatment of meralgia paresthetica consists of reassurance that the condition is reversible, avoidance of tight-fitting clothes, and weight loss.

First-line therapy for sacroiliac joint dysfunction is physical therapy and treatment of the underlying disorder if present; limited evidence supports local glucocorticoid injection.

In patients with knee pain, the history should focus on timing (acute, subacute, or chronic) and pain characteristics. History of knee injury or surgery, osteoarthritis, and crystal arthropathies should also be elicited.

Knee examination, performed with both knees fully exposed, includes inspection, palpation, range-of-motion testing, and special maneuvers ( [Table: Table: Knee Examination Maneuvers]

).

Radiography should be performed if fracture, bony pathology, or osteoarthritis is suspected. MRI can be performed if internal derangements are suspected and surgery is being considered. Joint aspiration should be performed for a palpable effusion without obvious cause to exclude inflammatory or infectious arthritis.

For a discussion of knee osteoarthritis, see Osteoarthritis in Rheumatology.

Acute, traumatic onset of knee pain, especially when associated with swelling, should raise concern for ligamentous and/or meniscal tears. Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears usually involve noncontact twisting injuries. Patients may report a popping sound and often cannot bear weight immediately. Large effusions due to hemarthrosis often develop within 2 hours and may make initial examination challenging. The anterior drawer test (Video: Anterior Drawer Test) and Lachman test (Video: Lachman Test) frequently demonstrate increased ligamentous laxity, although the Lachman test may be most useful in the acute setting ( [Table: Table: Knee Examination Maneuvers]

). Standard knee radiography (anteroposterior, lateral, notch, and sunrise views) should be performed to evaluate for possible accompanying tibial avulsion fractures. Plain radiography can be followed by MRI to confirm an ACL tear and detect associated injuries, such as posterolateral tibial plateau impaction fractures, which occur in many primary ACL tears. ACL tears frequently require surgical reconstruction, especially in active patients or those with an unstable knee. A nonoperative approach may be appropriate as a 3-month trial or in older and less active patients.

Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) tears involve a posteriorly directed force applied to the proximal anterior tibia with the knee flexed. Increased PCL laxity may be detected by posterior drawer test and pushing posteriorly on the proximal tibia with the knee flexed at 90 degrees (the opposite motion of the anterior drawer test). Medial collateral ligament (MCL) tears typically involve a lateral blow to the knee causing valgus stress. Increased MCL laxity suggesting a tear may be detected by applying a medially directed force with the knee flexed at 30 degrees (valgus stress test) (Video: Valgus Stress Test). Most MCL and PCL tears can be managed conservatively with rest and physical therapy.

Meniscal tears often result from an acute twisting knee injury or can develop more insidiously as a result of chronic degeneration, especially in older patients. Symptoms of a meniscal tear include pain, locking, catching, and grinding. Patients with acute meniscal tears are usually able to bear weight immediately. On examination, effusions, if present, are generally small to moderate in size. Results of specialized tests, such as the Thessaly, medial-lateral grind, and McMurray tests may be positive, but individually these tests are neither sensitive nor specific; it is a combination of tests that is most informative diagnostically. (see [Table: Table: Knee Examination Maneuvers]

and Video: Thessaly Test). Imaging may not be necessary for diagnosis if the clinical findings are consistent unless surgery is being considered. Initial management of both acute and chronic meniscal tears is conservative and consists of rest, ice, and strengthening the quadriceps and hamstring muscles. For degenerative meniscal tears, physical therapy is as effective as partial meniscectomy in relieving pain and improving function. Surgery is usually reserved for younger athletic patients with persistent (>4 weeks) mechanical symptoms, whereas conservative therapy is generally offered to older patients, although this decision should be individualized depending on the degree of loss of function and impaired quality of life.

Patellofemoral pain syndrome is caused by disordered patellar tracking with knee movement. It is characterized by poorly localized anterior knee pain and/or stiffness with prolonged sitting (“theater sign”), climbing or descending stairs, and running or squatting. It is most commonly diagnosed in patients with jobs or who play sports that put repetitive stress on the knee such as runners and cyclists. On examination, applying pressure to the patella may reproduce pain. Patellar mobility can be assessed by medially and laterally displacing the patella, and abrupt patellar deviation may be noted during squatting and standing, although the utility of these findings is unclear.

NSAIDs may help alleviate symptoms in the acute setting but have not shown benefit in the long term. In the acute phase of injury, modification of activity and cryotherapy (ice, cold water immersion) are recommended. In the recovery phase, the most effective treatment for patellofemoral pain syndrome is physical therapy with an exercise program designed to strengthen the quadriceps, hamstring, and gluteus muscles. Core strengthening exercises may also have benefit and should be continued after pain relief. Both patellar taping and foot orthoses provide short-term benefit when combined with exercise therapy.

Prepatellar bursitis presents as acute or chronic swelling anterior to the patella. Acute cases are associated with tenderness, warmth, and erythema and are often caused by bacterial infection and less commonly by trauma and gout. Chronic prepatellar bursitis is usually caused by trauma, although gout and infection are possible causes. More than one cause of prepatellar bursitis may be present at once. For example, patients with bursitis secondary to repetitive trauma are at risk for development of septic bursitis. All patients with prepatellar bursitis regardless of duration should undergo fluid aspiration and analysis. Septic bursitis is managed with knee immobilization, systemic antibiotics, and re-aspiration if needed. Gouty bursitis is managed with appropriate gout therapy (for a discussion of gout flare management, see Treatment of Gout Flares in Rheumatology). Traumatic bursitis is managed with activity modification (avoidance of kneeling) and NSAIDs.

Pes anserine pain syndrome (pes anserine bursitis) is characterized by pain and swelling of the region overlying the proximal medial tibia several centimeters distal to the knee (

). It commonly occurs in athletes, especially runners, and in patients with knee osteoarthritis. Crossing the affected leg causes contraction of the semitendinosus, gracilis, and sartorius muscles, which insert on the pes anserinus, and reproduces the pain. First-line therapy includes quadriceps strengthening, local cryotherapy, activity modification, and NSAIDs. Glucocorticoid injections are highly effective for temporary pain relief.

Tendinopathy of the quadriceps or patellar tendon causes knee pain with movement, such as jumping, running, or squatting. Pain occurs superior to the patella (quadriceps tendinopathy) or distal to the patella (patellar tendinopathy) and can be reproduced with palpation of the affected area. Treatment involves conservative measures, including strengthening and stretching exercises and NSAIDs.

A patellar tendon tear causes acute knee pain with effusion after low-impact trauma, such as occurs with sports. It can also occur in the setting of fluoroquinolone or glucocorticoid use. Pain is located inferior to the patella, where there is often swelling and ecchymosis. Treatment frequently involves surgery.

Injury to the articular cartilage (osteochondral injury) can occur when there is significant trauma to the knee or as an overuse injury. Patients describe diffuse knee pain. Osteochondral injury is diagnosed through a combination of clinical evaluation, plain radiography, and MRI; arthroscopy may be needed for definitive diagnosis. Treatment is determined by size, depth, location, and stability and may be conservative or surgical.

Medial tibial stress syndrome (shin splints) presents as pain in the posteromedial border of the tibias in the mid to distal shins, usually after activity. Diffuse tenderness spanning at least 5 cm is often found over the affected area. Diagnosis is clinical and imaging is not necessary, although it may be required to rule out stress fracture, which typically has more focal tenderness on examination. Treatment includes avoidance of high-impact activities, physical therapy with stretching exercises, and use of shock-absorbing insoles.

Chronic exertional compartment syndrome is exertion-provoked swelling of a specific muscle bed, most commonly in the lower leg. Patients report throbbing pain during exercise, with gradual resolution after rest. Diffuse tenderness of the affected muscle bed may be present but only during exercise. Diagnosis is confirmed by measuring compartment pressures. Treatment includes modification of the exercise regimen, gait training, shoe inserts, and occasionally surgical fasciotomy.

Iliotibial band syndrome is characterized by poorly localized lateral knee and distal thigh pain. Pain is initially present at the end of exercise that involves knee flexion and extension, but it may occur earlier in exercise or with rest as the condition progresses. Running outdoors or downhill may worsen symptoms. On examination, there is often tenderness approximately 2 to 3 cm proximal to the lateral femoral condyle. Patients frequently have a positive result on the Noble test and weakness with hip abduction (see [Table: Table: Knee Examination Maneuvers]

and Video: Noble Test). Imaging is not usually required.

Initial treatment of iliotibial band syndrome involves abstaining from the inciting activity and using ice, followed by a gradual return to activity, stretching, strengthening, and local massage. NSAIDs appear to be effective when used as part of a multimodal approach. Local glucocorticoid injections may provide at least short-term relief.

A popliteal (Baker) cyst is an enlargement of the gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa behind and communicating with the knee joint. Popliteal cysts most commonly develop in the setting of knee trauma, osteoarthritis, or inflammatory arthritis. They are frequently asymptomatic but can present with posterior knee pain and swelling. Ruptured cysts may mimic deep venous thromboses and may be associated with ecchymosis from the popliteal fossa to the ankle. The “crescent sign” may be present with rupture, recognized as an ecchymotic area below the medial malleolus (

). In patients with asymptomatic popliteal cysts, no treatment is necessary. Symptomatic patients with unruptured cysts generally have pain relief with intracystic or intra-articular glucocorticoid injection, with or without cyst drainage. Ruptured cysts can be treated with rest, elevation, and NSAIDs. Surgical excision is reserved for severely symptomatic and functionally limited patients in whom conservative measures fail.

Acute ankle sprains are usually caused by excessive ankle inversion. Common examination findings include overlying ecchymosis and swelling with tenderness of involved ankle ligaments. Weight-bearing ability and bony tenderness are components of the Ottawa ankle rules, which help determine the necessity of obtaining radiographs to exclude fracture (

, Video: Ottawa Lateral Test, and Video: Ottawa Medial Test). Treatment includes intermittent cryotherapy and a lace-up support or air stirrup brace combined with elastic compression wrapping. Early mobilization should be encouraged with weight bearing as tolerated. Acetaminophen and NSAIDs can be used for pain control. Patients with persistent ligamentous laxity 4 to 6 weeks after injury should be referred for proprioceptive training and strengthening therapy.

High ankle sprains (distal tibiofibular syndesmosis ligament injuries) occur when an externally rotated force is applied to a dorsiflexed ankle. Pain may be elicited by squeezing the leg at mid calf (squeeze test) (Video: Squeeze Test) and by dorsiflexing and externally rotating the foot with the knee flexed (dorsiflexion-external rotation test) (Video: Dorsiflexion-External Rotation Stress Test). Although treatment is similar to that for other ankle sprains, recovery is usually delayed and referral to a specialist is recommended.

The metatarsals, tarsals, and calcaneus are the most common sites of stress fracture in the foot. Physical examination may reveal bony tenderness, pain with percussion, or pain with hopping on a single leg. The calcaneal squeeze test may elicit pain in patients with calcaneal fracture. Radiography is first-line diagnostic testing but may fail to reveal a fracture line. MRI has greater sensitivity and provides prognostic information about the risk for nonunion; it should be performed when plain films are unrevealing but clinical probability is high. Patients should also be screened for factors affecting bone health, including low caloric intake and menstrual dysfunction.

Management varies according to the risk for nonunion ( [Table: Table: Nonunion Risk in Foot and Ankle Stress Fractures]

). High-risk fractures can be treated with immobilization and serial imaging or surgical fixation; specialist involvement should be considered. Low-risk fractures are treated with rest, crutches, a walking boot, and/or footwear padding to achieve pain-free ambulation. Follow-up radiography 4 weeks after the injury can help document healing and may be especially helpful in high-risk fractures. Once the patient can ambulate without pain and has no pain on examination with provocative maneuvers, nonimpact activity can be resumed gradually. Most patients with low-risk injuries can resume running in 8 to 12 weeks; resumption of running in patients with high-risk injuries should be individualized.

Achilles tendinopathy typically develops in persons who initiate or abruptly increase activity. Patients report activity-related posterior heel pain and stiffness that improves with rest. On examination, there is usually tenderness and sometimes thickening of the Achilles tendon approximately 2 to 6 cm above the calcaneal insertion. Treatment includes activity modification, eccentric exercises (muscle lengthening in response to external resistance), and use of appropriate footwear. NSAIDs can be used for pain control.

Achilles tendon rupture can occur during strenuous activities, although it may occur spontaneously in older patients or rarely with fluoroquinolone use. Patients usually have heel pain and may report hearing a “pop.” On examination using the Thompson test, a lack of plantar flexion with calf squeezing suggests complete rupture (sensitivity, 93%; specificity, 96%) (

). A tendon defect may also be palpable. Treatment is controversial and consists of surgery with immobilization or immobilization alone.

Plantar fasciitis classically causes sharp, medial-inferior heel pain with the first morning steps and after prolonged rest. Pain usually improves with further walking but may persist in severe cases. On examination, the medial calcaneal tubercle is frequently tender. Passive toe dorsiflexion with standing may reproduce pain. First-line treatment includes plantar fascia stretches, activity modification, and foot orthoses. Because recovery time is 3 to 12 months, patient education is important to help patients manage expectations and persist with long-term therapy. For recalcitrant cases, extracorporeal shockwave therapy may be considered. Glucocorticoid injections are sometimes used, but the effects are temporary. Surgery is reserved for patients who do not respond to these measures.

Tarsal tunnel syndrome (posterior tibial nerve compression as it passes through the tarsal tunnel) causes posteromedial heel paresthesia that radiates distally into the plantar foot surface. On examination, pain may be reproduced with nerve tapping and with provocative measures that compress the nerve (plantar flexion-inversion and dorsiflexion-eversion tests). First-line treatment consists of activity modification, orthotics, and NSAIDs.

Pes planus (flat feet) is caused by failure of the medial longitudinal arch of the foot. Although it is often asymptomatic, it can be painful and result in gait abnormalities. Diagnosis is usually based on the examination finding of arch collapse with standing; in addition, the forefoot, including the lateral toes, may deviate laterally when viewed from behind. Imaging, including weight-bearing plain films, is only necessary in symptomatic patients to assess for underlying anatomic abnormalities. Treatment includes orthotics, activity change, weight loss (if appropriate), and analgesia. Surgery is reserved for refractory symptoms.

Morton neuroma (interdigital neuralgia) causes pain between the metatarsal heads and the sensation of walking on a pebble. Risk factors include the use of tight-fitting shoes and repetitive forefoot stresses such as running. Examination may reveal tenderness in the interdigital space and, in neuromas larger than 1 cm, a click when squeezing the metatarsals together. Imaging is not typically necessary. First-line therapy consists of footwear modification and padding. Glucocorticoid injections using a dorsal approach may provide temporary relief. Interdigital nerve resection is reserved for those who do not respond to conservative measures.

Hammertoe deformities (proximal interphalangeal joint flexion deformity with distal interphalangeal joint extension and extended or neutral position of the metatarsophalangeal joint) (

) occur with constricting footwear and increasing age. Treatment includes footwear modification, padding, and possibly surgery.

Hallux or bunion deformity (valgus deformity of the first toe) can lead to pain, osteoarthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint, and overlying bursitis. Treatment includes orthotic devices, NSAIDs, and possibly surgery.

Metatarsalgia typically presents as discomfort with weight-bearing over the plantar surfaces of the metatarsals, most commonly the second, third, and fourth metatarsal heads. Causes include anatomic abnormalities of the metatarsals and ligamentous failure of the transverse metatarsal arch. Examination may reveal pain with palpation, calluses over the metatarsal heads, and collapse of the transverse metatarsal arch. Plain radiographs may be useful to assess for underlying stress fracture. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and usually includes metatarsal pads and physical therapy; orthotics may be helpful in refractory cases.

Lower Extremity Edema and Ulcers

Lower extremity edema is a common symptom in inpatient and outpatient settings. It results from the accumulation of interstitial fluid in the most dependent part of the body and may be secondary to several different pathophysiologic mechanisms. The most common causes include the following:

  • Venous obstruction or insufficiency
  • Heart failure (including right-sided heart failure secondary to pulmonary disease)
  • Cirrhosis
  • Nephrotic syndrome
  • Adverse medication effect

The differential diagnosis of lower extremity edema is presented in [Table: Table: Differential Diagnosis of Lower Extremity Edema]

. A detailed history and physical examination will suggest the cause of lower extremity edema in most patients.

For bilateral leg edema, initial laboratory testing includes kidney and liver function testing, urinalysis (for detection of protein), and albumin measurement. These results should guide the decision to pursue further testing, including potential imaging to assess for mechanical obstruction or echocardiography for heart failure.

Unilateral lower extremity edema typically results from a mechanical obstruction to venous flow, such as deep venous thrombosis or cancer. Obstruction of the lymphatic system is a less common mechanism of unilateral edema. If of acute onset, unilateral edema is usually secondary to deep venous thrombosis or skin/soft tissue infection.

Chronic venous insufficiency is a common condition in which venous hypertension results in blood pooling in the legs. The most common cause of venous hypertension is venous valvular incompetence, but venous obstruction, such as with previous deep venous thrombosis, and congenital conditions (Klippel-Trénaunay syndrome) may also be causative. Symptoms include lower extremity aching, itching, restlessness, heaviness, swelling, and pain.

A thorough history and physical examination should be performed. Physical examination findings consistent with chronic venous insufficiency in addition to edema include the following:

  • Dilated veins (both varicosities and superficial telangiectasias)
  • Eczematous changes
  • Brown pigmentation from hemosiderin deposition
  • Lipodermatosclerosis (fibrosis of subcutaneous tissue) (

) - Atrophie blanche (pale plaques of scar tissue) (

) - Venous stasis ulcers

Physical findings are best observed in the gravity-dependent upright position. Chronic venous insufficiency is a clinical diagnosis, but venous duplex ultrasonography to confirm reflux is indicated if the diagnosis is in doubt, if there is concern for mechanical obstruction, or if intervention is a consideration.

Conservative measures, including exercise, leg elevation, lifestyle changes (weight loss if indicated), and compression therapy (>20-50 mm Hg, depending on the stage of disease), are first-line treatments. The presence of skin changes or ulceration should prompt at least 30 mm Hg of compression (see Foot and Leg Ulcers in Common Symptoms).

Skincare is a crucial part of management, and daily use of topical moisturizers may reduce skin breakdown and prevent infection. Stasis dermatitis may require the sparing use of a topical glucocorticoid. Wound care, including hydrocolloids and foam dressings, is essential to control drainage from ulcers and prevent maceration of the surrounding skin.

Patients with confirmed reflux who are candidates for therapy should be referred to a vascular specialist for consideration of venous ablation. Other interventional options include vein stripping, excision, or, in the case of stenosis and obstruction, stenting. Surgical options can be considered for those with symptoms refractory to medical and endovenous therapies. Patients with bothersome spider veins and small varicose veins can undergo sclerotherapy, thermocoagulation, or laser therapy.

Many agents, termed phlebotonics, including horse chestnut extracts and other nonprescription agents, have been studied for treatment of chronic venous insufficiency not accompanied by ulceration; however, no medications are FDA approved for this condition. Evidence suggests that phlebotonics may moderately reduce edema, but there is insufficient evidence that these medications improve quality of life.

Venous stasis ulcers, arterial insufficiency ulcers, and neuropathic ulcers are the most common ulcerations of the feet and lower extremities ( [Table: Table: Common Types of Foot and Leg Ulcers]

). Proper diagnosis is important because treatments are directed at the underlying cause. Arterial insufficiency ulcers are discussed in History and Physical Examination in Cardiovascular Medicine, and neuropathic ulcers are addressed in Diabetic Foot Ulcers in Endocrinology and Metabolism.

Venous stasis ulcers account for up to 70% of all leg ulcers. They occur on the lower extremities from the mid calf to the ankle, most commonly near the medial malleolus, and are associated with signs of chronic venous insufficiency. Venous stasis ulcers can be single or multiple, are typically irregularly shaped and shallow, and often weep serous fluid (

). The presence of fibrinous tissue is common but the ulcers are rarely necrotic. Pain may or may not be present but is usually not severe.

Like chronic venous insufficiency, the diagnosis is usually made clinically, although duplex ultrasonography can help confirm the diagnosis of underlying venous insufficiency if there is diagnostic uncertainty. The ankle-brachial index should be measured to rule out concurrent arterial disease.

Treatment consists of compression therapy (≥30 mm Hg), which improves venous flow, reduces edema, and promotes fibrinolysis. Compression therapy is best administered using high-compression, multicomponent bandaging; other options include elastic or inelastic compression bandages (compression stockings, Unna boots) or intermittent pneumonic compression devices. An absolute contraindication to compression therapy is an ankle-brachial index of 0.5 or less. Cautious use is advised for any patient with an ankle-brachial index of less than 0.8. Patients with a venous stasis ulcer should be referred to a vascular specialist for consideration of venous intervention, because early venous intervention can improve healing time.

Local wound care includes debridement of devitalized tissue. Simple nonadherent dressings appear to be as effective as other more expensive dressings. Care should be taken to control the drainage to prevent damage to the surrounding skin. The addition of topical cadexomer iodine may improve healing. When added to standard care, pentoxifylline has been shown to increase ulcer healing. Small, randomized trials also suggest that simvastatin may accelerate wound healing. Antibiotics should be reserved for patients with signs of infection, including erythema and tenderness at the ulcer site, lymphangitis, rapidly increasing ulcer size, and fever.

Approach to the Patient With Pain

Acute pain (<1 month’s duration) is the most common reason that patients seek emergent care and frequently occurs in hospitalized patients. Chronic pain (>3 months’ duration or lasting longer than is typically associated with tissue healing) affects one in five U.S. adults and has substantial negative effects on patient quality of life and physical, social, financial, and functional status.

Identifying pain as nociceptive, neuropathic, or nociplastic can be helpful in determining prognosis and tailoring approaches for some pain syndromes ( [Table: Table: Types of Pain]

). Some patients with chronic noncancer pain syndromes may experience mixed pain phenotypes.

Nociceptive pain is caused by tissue damage or potential tissue damage and can involve either visceral or somatic nociceptors. Visceral pain is often poorly localized and described as a cramping, pressure-like, or aching pain. Somatic pain, which is commonly associated with musculoskeletal pain, may be easier to localize than visceral pain and can be sharp or dull.

Neuropathic pain results from injury to peripheral nerve structures or the central nervous system. It is described as shooting, lancinating, or electrical and may involve sensory deficits. Neuropathic pain may also be associated with hyperalgesia (oversensitivity to a painful stimulus) or allodynia (pain from a normally nonpainful stimulus).

Nociplastic pain occurs in the absence of tissue or nerve damage and results from maladaptive changes to nociceptive processing/modulation that lead to increased sensitization and diminished inhibitory pathways. Nociplastic pain is often diffuse and nondermatomal, and sensory deficits may be present.

Pain induced by chronic opioid therapy is also increasingly recognized. Opioid-induced hyperalgesia is thought to result from repeated exposure to systemic opioids. Patients with this pain syndrome may experience a change in the character of their pain during the course of opioid therapy, worsening pain with increasing opioid dosages, and pain reduction when opioid dosages are decreased.

The first step in assessing any pain syndrome, regardless of time course, is a thorough history and physical examination. Open-ended questions should be used to determine pain onset, location, character, duration, severity, temporal nature, and responsiveness to treatment. These data are crucial to identifying the pain generator and tailoring diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. Numeric pain scales have commonly been utilized to measure pain intensity; however, the numbers may not directly correlate with patients’ perception of severity, tolerability, or functional impairment.

Additionally, it is critical to identify the impact of pain on the patient’s functional status, including physical functioning, ability to perform basic activities of daily living, and psychosocial-spiritual functioning. Psychological comorbidities influence and are influenced by experiences of chronic pain and affect response and adherence to a multimodal treatment strategy. Patients should be screened for mental health disorders, especially depression and anxiety (see Mood Disorders in Interdisciplinary Medicine), because patients with chronic pain are up to four times more likely to have concomitant depression.

The physical examination should include careful inspection of the painful region and a comprehensive neurologic evaluation. In patients with acute pain, additional diagnostic testing and imaging are often indicated. In most patients with chronic pain, such testing is unlikely to produce further diagnostic and therapeutic yield absent the presence of a red flag (such as weight loss or fever in a patient with chronic back pain) or a substantial change in the pain pattern.

In patients with a history of cancer and chronic cancer-related or cancer treatment–related pain, including those in survivorship, new or worsening pain should prompt a more detailed diagnostic assessment. The evaluation should include determination of significant changes in pain experience, new acute pain syndromes superimposed on chronic pain, and development of signs or symptoms that raise suspicion for infection or recurrent cancer and should trigger further investigation.

Substance-use screening is another essential part of the assessment of patients with chronic pain (see Substance Use Disorders in Interdisciplinary Medicine). Substance use disorders are more common in patients with chronic pain syndromes and increase the risk for opioid misuse.

Treatment plans should identify measurable outcomes that center around function and quality of life. In keeping with a biopsychosocial model, management should be directed to address the following:

  • Cause of the patient’s pain
  • Pain severity (as it affects functional status)
  • Medical and psychosocial comorbid conditions
  • Barriers to treatment, such as health care access and concomitant mental health disorders

A multimodal approach plays an important role in the management of all pain subtypes, including acute and chronic non–cancer-related pain, cancer-related pain, and pain at the end of life. Guidelines recommend personalized, interdisciplinary treatment informed by shared decision making.

Nonpharmacologic strategies are the cornerstone of pain management. In patients with chronic pain syndromes, developing a therapeutic relationship in which patients feel their pain is taken seriously and in which patients, family members, and social supports are active participants is important for success over time. Physical activity, engagement in work activities, and behavioral interventions should be encouraged regardless of pain score.

Pharmacologic therapy, including nonopioid and opioid therapies (when appropriate), should be viewed as adjunctive to nonpharmacologic therapy. Frequent monitoring of pain severity, associated effect on functional status, response to interventions, and quality of life should be documented.

Distraction techniques and music therapy have demonstrated benefit for patients with acute pain in both emergency department and postoperative settings. Evidence also supports the use of superficial heat, massage, spinal manipulation, and acupuncture for improving acute low back pain.

Patients with chronic pain should be referred to a structured physical therapy program for evaluation and treatment aimed at improving functional status. High-quality evidence suggests that physical therapy programs improve both pain and function in patients with debility due to pain. Continuation of physical therapy beyond 12 weeks should be based on iterative clinical assessments and documented gains. Like physical therapy, exercise programs improve pain and function in patients with chronic pain, although no specific regimen has proved superior.

Cognitive behavioral techniques, including cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), mindfulness-based stress reduction, and biofeedback, have been associated with reduced pain and improved overall function and mood. Referral to practices or specialized pain centers that provide these therapies should be explored when available.

Low- to moderate-quality evidence supports the use of complementary and integrative therapies, such as massage, spinal manipulation, and acupuncture in chronic pain management, and these interventions may be helpful adjuncts in some patients with chronic pain.

Interventional approaches may be appropriate for short-term relief of acute or chronic pain symptoms that can be anatomically targeted with injection-based therapy, such as nerve blocks and trigger point injections. Advanced therapies, such as high-frequency neurostimulation, hold promise for appropriately selected patients with chronic pain. Patients may be referred to a pain specialist for consideration of these therapies.

The incidence of depression increases as pain symptoms intensify, and depression itself may manifest as pain. Aggressive treatment of depression with CBT and pharmacologic therapy can lead to substantial improvement in both chronic pain and depressive symptoms. Iterative evaluation of depressive symptoms during chronic pain treatment is critical to ensuring that patients can sustain improvements.

Nonopioid pharmacologic therapy is frequently effective for mild or moderate acute and chronic pain ( [Table: Table: Nonopioid FDA-Approved Pharmacologic Treatments for Acute and Chronic Pain]

).

For acute musculoskeletal injuries and nociceptive pain (e.g., sprains, fractures, muscle strains), NSAIDs and acetaminophen are first-line therapies, although efficacy of these agents varies by the specific indication. Regularly scheduled and combination therapies are often required to achieve a reasonable level of pain control, and specific regimens should be tailored to the severity of pain, its expected duration, and the presence of comorbidities. Topical NSAIDs, such as diclofenac, have few systemic adverse effects, are generally well tolerated, and may be effective for treatment of musculoskeletal nociceptive conditions. Short courses of muscle relaxants may be beneficial in some patients with acute musculoskeletal pain. Suzetrigine, a nonopioid selective sodium channel blocker, can be used for moderate to severe short-term acute pain, such as fracture-associated pain or postoperative pain, but has not yet been evaluated for more than 14 days of use.

In patients with chronic pain, pharmacologic therapy may be used as adjunctive treatment when nonpharmacologic therapies have not achieved their desired effect. Clinicians should emphasize that medications have limited efficacy in the long-term management of pain and are intended to improve function and quality of life, not pain scores. Patients should be informed that drugs may take weeks to be effective and that a combination of medications with differing mechanisms may be necessary to provide optimal benefit (e.g., rational polypharmacy). When selecting pharmacologic therapy to add to a multimodal treatment regimen, attention to comorbid illnesses (particularly organ dysfunction) and potential drug-drug interactions is necessary.

Chronic musculoskeletal or inflammatory nociceptive pain may be treated initially with trials of acetaminophen or NSAIDs. These drugs are most appropriately used for periodic pain flares or potentially while opioid therapy is being tapered, but they should be avoided as long-term therapy owing to the potential for gastrointestinal, kidney, and cardiovascular adverse effects.

First-line therapies for chronic neuropathic pain are gabapentinoids (gabapentin and pregabalin), serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (duloxetine), and tricyclic antidepressants. Adverse effects of gabapentinoids include dizziness, disequilibrium, somnolence, weight gain, peripheral edema, and cognitive difficulties. In 2019, the FDA issued a warning that gabapentinoids may cause serious breathing difficulties in patients with respiratory risk factors, including opioid use and COPD. Clinicians should be aware of the limited supportive evidence and potential adverse effects when prescribing neuropathic pain agents in these settings; however, these drugs can be helpful when combined with patient-centered functional goals and shared decision making. Gabapentinoids and duloxetine are also frequently used off-label to treat acute pain in hospitalized or postoperative patients (as an opioid-sparing strategy), patients with cancer-associated pain, and patients with various chronic pain syndromes. These practices are supported by only modest-quality data, which are often extrapolated from studies of other pain syndromes.

Tricyclic antidepressants, such as amitriptyline, are also effective for neuropathic pain, although titration to effective dosages is often limited by adverse effects and drug-drug interactions. Other pharmacologic options for neuropathic pain include capsaicin and topical lidocaine if pain generators are focal and topically located; these may also reduce allodynia. The role of antiseizure medications in the treatment of chronic neuropathic pain is unclear, although carbamazepine appears to be effective in the treatment of trigeminal neuralgia.

Pharmacologic treatment of nociplastic pain varies according to the underlying cause and may include gabapentinoids, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, and tricyclic antidepressants. All three of these agents, for example, have some efficacy in treating fibromyalgia.

Medical cannabis is increasingly available to patients with chronic pain. Many states have passed laws legalizing cannabis use or allowing its use for medical conditions. Current data on the effectiveness of medical cannabis for chronic pain are characterized by significant heterogeneity in both patient populations and cannabis preparations, although recent systematic reviews have demonstrated that cannabis has some efficacy in the treatment of chronic noncancer pain.

The most robust data originate from studies of compounds available outside the United States (such as nabiximols), which contain higher ratios of cannabidiol to tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) than the existing FDA-approved synthetic THC (dronabinol). Little is known about the comparative efficacy of cannabis preparations. Furthermore, the long-term medical and psychosocial implications of medical cannabis use for patients with chronic pain are unknown. The 2025 American College of Physicians clinician guideline on cannabinoids for the management of chronic pain recommends counseling young adults, patients with current or past substance use disorder, those with serious mental illness, and frail patients and those at risk for falling that the harms of using cannabinoids for chronic noncancer pain likely outweigh benefits. The 2021 MAGIC guideline makes a weak recommendation to offer a trial of noninhaled medical cannabis or cannabinoids, in addition to standard care and management, to adult patients living with moderate to severe chronic pain, regardless of pain mechanism, as well as cancer-related chronic pain. Importantly, medical cannabis should not be used in pregnant or lactating persons, and inhaled cannabis is not recommended for pain management.

Nonopioid therapies are at least as effective as opioids for many acute pain conditions, and their use should be maximized in conjunction with nonpharmacologic therapies as appropriate. Current practice guidelines reinforce the need to limit opioid therapy in inpatients to those with moderate to severe pain and recommend the following:

  • Prescribing immediate-release opioids at the lowest effective dose for the shortest period of time on an as-needed rather than scheduled basis
  • Limiting coadministration with other central nervous system depressants
  • Limiting parenteral opioid formulations to patients who are unable to use oral medications or in whom parenteral forms are needed for rapid analgesia

Opioid delivery through patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) pumps can be an effective means of controlling acute pain; however, the patient must have a clear mental status and the ability to press the PCA button for boluses, and basal doses should not be programmed for opioid-naive patients. In addition, a bowel regimen including a stimulant laxative to prevent opioid-induced constipation should be used in all patients taking opioids.

PCA regimens can include hydromorphone, morphine, or fentanyl; medication selection depends on a variety of patient factors (i.e., liver and kidney function, side effects). In general, and particularly for opioid-naive patients, a demand dose of 0.5 to 2 mg intravenous morphine (or morphine milligram equivalents [MME]) with a lockout interval of 4 to 10 minutes is a reasonable starting place. Continuous PCA infusion should only be used in select circumstances, such as in patients who are opioid tolerant with acute or chronic pain not controlled with other modalities, for end-of-life care, or in the ICU.

When titrating PCA orders, careful attention to oversedation is paramount. Opioids should be held if patients demonstrate oversedation or respiratory depression. Attention to pain parameters, such as the ability to rest comfortably or take deep breaths, should be used to make PCA adjustments. When adjusting a PCA, only the dosing or the lockout interval should be changed, not both at the same time. For example, if a patient is not getting adequate relief from the demand dose, the dose should be increased. Conversely, if a patient is getting adequate relief from the demand dose but relief does not last until the lockout interval is over, then the lockout interval should be decreased.

At least once-daily attempts should be made to transition patients from intravenous to oral opioids. This is done by totaling the 24-hour opioid use on the PCA and then giving 50% of that as an equivalent oral dose, divided across several daily doses. The PCA is then discontinued after approximately 6 hours of oral opioid administration. If a patient was on long- and short-acting opioids before initiation of the PCA, then the 24-hour opioid total can be divided into 50% given as their basal dose, with the remaining 50% divided among short-acting opioids as needed for breakthrough pain.

Despite high prescribing rates, no evidence supports the use of long-term opioid therapy in patients with subacute and chronic noncancer pain, and nonopioid therapies are preferred. Evidence demonstrates that long-term opioid use is associated with poorer overall functional status, worse quality of life, and worse pain (possibly mediated through opioid tolerance and hyperalgesic mechanisms). In addition, these prescribing patterns lead to substantial morbidity and mortality.

Opioids may be appropriate in selected patients with chronic pain in whom multimodal analgesic therapy has not improved function and quality of life. The CDC clinical practice guideline on prescribing opioids for pain in adults in the outpatient setting includes the following recommendations. Importantly, these guidelines are not applicable to patients with postoperative pain; who have sickle cell disease or active cancer; who are receiving palliative care; or who are at the end of life:

  • Clinicians should maximize the use of nonopioid therapies as appropriate.
  • Opioid therapy should be considered within the context of a thorough assessment and robust discussion of risks and benefits, close monitoring, and use of risk-mitigation strategies ( [Table: Table: CDC Recommendations for Prescribing Opioids for Chronic Pain]

and [Table: Table: Risks of Long-term Opioid Therapy]

). - If, based on this assessment, clinicians deem that opioids are needed, the lowest effective dose of immediate-release opioids should be used with careful and frequent reevaluation of the benefits and harms of continued therapy, especially before dosage increases.

The CDC provides a checklist to assist clinicians in opioid prescribing.

When initiating or continuing opioid therapy, patient education is critical. Topics of discussion should include self-management to promote health and overall wellness, options for nonopioid and nonpharmacologic pain treatments, and situating realistic expectations and limitations of medical therapies. Additionally, clear treatment goals based on functional improvement and quality-of-life considerations should be established to manage patient expectations and provide a means for measuring the success or failure of treatment. These goals can be incorporated into a patient-physician prescribing agreement (a contract), which also can be used to communicate expectations for follow-up, monitoring, risk mitigation, and discontinuation or tapering. Sample patient agreement forms are available from the National Institute on Drug Abuse.

Clinicians should evaluate for risk factors associated with opioid-related harms, such as substance use, the presence of kidney or liver disease (which may affect drug metabolism), sleep-disordered breathing, and pregnancy. For a commonly used risk assessment instrument, see the Opioid Risk Tool.

The risk for opioid-related overdose is dose dependent, and the lowest possible dosage should be used to achieve the functional and quality-of-life goals established by the patient and prescriber. Given the risks and limited efficacy of opioid therapy in treating chronic noncancer pain, these dosages should not typically exceed 50 morphine milligram equivalents (MME)/d ( [Table: Table: MME Doses for Opioids for Pain Management]

). Dosages exceeding this should prompt reevaluation and closer follow-up intervals. Dosages higher than 90 MME/d significantly increase the risk of overdose and should be prescribed only in consultation with pain specialists. Very long-acting opioid formulations, such as transdermal fentanyl and methadone, are also associated with a higher risk for overdose, and dosages should not be increased more frequently than weekly. Coprescription of opioids and benzodiazepines is associated with an increased risk for death from overdose and should be avoided.

Patients should be reevaluated within 1 to 4 weeks of initiating opioid therapy and then at least every 3 months subsequently. During these visits, clinicians should reevaluate function, pain, adverse effects, complications, or co-occurring conditions (e.g., medical, behavioral health, and/or substance use disorders), and adherence to treatment plan. Clinicians should also pursue risk-mitigation strategies and optimize the entire treatment plan (e.g., self-management and nonopioid/nonpharmacologic modalities) (see Risk Mitigation in Common Symptoms).

For patients who previously received opioid prescriptions for chronic pain and present to a physician as a new patient, a discussion on opioid-prescribing best practices should be framed by the CDC guideline recommendations (see [Table: Table: CDC Recommendations for Prescribing Opioids for Chronic Pain]

). Persistent barriers to access to evidence-based pain treatment exist, and shared decision making informed by the patient’s values and experiences is critical. Recognizing that discontinuation of opioid therapy after extended use can be harmful if medications are tapered rapidly and/or patients do not receive adjunctive support, the 2022 CDC guideline recommends carefully weighing benefits and risks of tapering opioids along with the benefits and risks of continuing them.

Guidelines emphasize that opioid therapy should neither be discontinued abruptly nor reduced rapidly. Discussions on tapering opioid therapy, incorporating a nonopioid multimodal pain strategy, and setting appropriate goals are fundamental to these prescribing relationships. If tapering is intended, an individualized plan should include clear discussions with the patient, assessment for opioid use disorder, a reasonable rate of taper (usually 10% per month), close observation for opioid withdrawal symptoms, and involvement of behavioral health specialists when significant mental illness or suicide risk is present.

Before opioid initiation, patients and their family members should be aware of the risks and benefits of long-term opioid therapy, risks of substance use disorder and overdose, and strategies available to mitigate these risks, including naloxone rescue.

Urine drug screening and surveillance of state prescription drug monitoring programs (PDMPs) are important risk-mitigation strategies for patients receiving opioids. Although the optimal urine drug screening frequency is unclear, patients taking long-term opioid therapy should undergo screening at least yearly to assess for adherence to the prescribed agent and for the presence of substances that could increase the risk for opioid overdose. More frequent screening may be recommended based on individual patient characteristics. Concurrent use of nonprescribed substances is a reason to consider discontinuation of opioid prescriptions.

Guidelines recommend that physicians review state PDMP data before opioid prescription for acute, subacute, or chronic pain to determine whether a patient is receiving an opioid dosage or combination that increases their risk for overdose. At minimum, this should be done before initial prescription and then every 3 months (or more frequently in some circumstances) thereafter. The regulations for checking PDMPs before prescribing an opioid vary by state, and physicians should be familiar with the regulations in the states in which they practice.

Naloxone is effective in preventing opioid-related overdose death. Clinicians should strongly consider offering overdose prevention education and naloxone, which is now available without a prescription, to all patients taking opioid therapy and especially to those receiving 50 MME/d or more. Naloxone kits should also be strongly considered for patients with the following:

  • Concurrent benzodiazepine use
  • A nonopioid substance use disorder
  • A mental health disorder
  • Respiratory conditions, such as COPD or obstructive sleep apnea

Naloxone kits and overdose prevention education should also be extended to friends, family members, or caregivers of patients at high risk. More information about overdose prevention with the naloxone kit is available at the CDC.

Similar interventions are indicated for patients who are not prescribed opioids but are otherwise at high risk for overdose, such as those using nonprescribed opioids or substances that may be contaminated with opioids (methamphetamine and cocaine), those with a history of opioid misuse who have been recently released from incarceration, or those receiving treatment for opioid use disorder.

In patients receiving opioid therapy, constipation is nearly universal and tolerance to constipation does not develop over time. A bowel regimen should be started concurrently with opioid initiation rather than after symptoms of constipation develop. Pharmacologic therapy for all patients taking scheduled opioids should include a stimulant laxative, such as senna or bisacodyl. There is little evidence supporting the use of stool softeners, such as docusate. Most patients taking opioids should not receive supplemental fiber because these agents are usually ineffective in preventing or treating opioid-induced constipation and may cause increased symptoms, especially in debilitated patients with poor oral intake.

If constipation develops despite prophylactic therapy, intensifying treatment with stimulant laxatives or adding an osmotic laxative (e.g., polyethylene glycol) is appropriate. If maximal medical therapy has failed to achieve laxation, peripheral opioid antagonists (e.g., naldemedine, naloxegol, or methylnaltrexone) should be considered. These medications do not cross the blood-brain barrier and therefore do not affect analgesia; however, they are contraindicated in patients at risk for bowel obstruction.

Nausea related to opioid use is common. No one opioid is known to be less emetogenic than another. Opioid-induced nausea is usually transient, and tolerance generally develops over 2 to 7 days; therefore, opioids should not be switched too quickly. Antidopaminergic agents, such as metoclopramide or prochlorperazine, are the preferred agents to treat opioid-induced nausea. Serotonin receptor antagonists, such as ondansetron, may be used but can cause or worsen constipation.

Repeated opioid use can result in tolerance, physical dependence, and potential abuse. Factors that may indicate the need for more frequent follow-up include nonadherence to treatment plan (e.g., attendance of appointments), unexpected urine drug screening or PDMP data, and using more than prescribed doses and/or running out of opioids early. If any of these behaviors manifest, treating clinicians should consider shortening prescribing intervals, intensifying risk-mitigation strategies, and/or referring to interdisciplinary care that addresses pain and/or behavioral health problems including substance use disorder.

Prolonged use of opioids can result in neuroexcitatory adaptations that can cause myoclonus, allodynia, and/or increased predisposition to seizures. This can increase risk for complications of withdrawal if/when opioids are withheld. Cautious opioid taper or rotating to an alternate opioid can help mitigate these neuroexcitatory effects.

Opioid use disorder is characterized by use of opioids in increasing amounts or longer than intended, continued use of opioids despite social functional decline, repeated episodes of withdrawal, abandonment of important events or activities, and physical and psychological problems. For a discussion on the diagnosis and treatment of opioid use disorder, see Opioids in Interdisciplinary Medicine.

Pain is common in patients with serious illness, including cancer-related pain, and recognition and constant evaluation of pain are integral to effective management. For a discussion on the diagnosis and treatment of cancer-related pain, see Pain Management in Patients With Terminal Illness in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

CDC Recommendations for Prescribing Opioids for Chronic Pain (Excluding Sickle Cell Disease, Active Cancer, Palliative Care, and End-of-Life Care)^a

Determining When to Initiate or Continue Opioids for Chronic Pain

  1. Nonpharmacologic therapy and nonopioid pharmacologic therapy are preferred for chronic pain. Clinicians should consider opioid therapy only if expected benefits for both pain and function are anticipated to outweigh risks to the patient. If opioids are used, they should be combined with nonpharmacologic therapy and nonopioid pharmacologic therapy, as appropriate.

  2. Before prescribing opioid therapy for chronic pain, clinicians should establish treatment goals with all patients, including realistic goals for pain and function, and should consider how therapy will be discontinued if benefits do not outweigh risks. Clinicians should continue opioid therapy only if there is clinically meaningful improvement in pain and function that outweighs risks to patient safety.

  3. Before starting and periodically during opioid therapy, clinicians should discuss with patients known risks and realistic benefits of opioid therapy and patient and clinician responsibilities for managing therapy.

Opioid Selection, Dosage, Duration, Follow-up, and Discontinuation

  1. When prescribing opioid therapy for chronic pain, clinicians should prescribe immediate-release opioids instead of extended-release/long-acting opioids.

  2. When opioids are started, clinicians should prescribe the lowest effective dosage. Clinicians should use caution when prescribing opioids at any dosage, should carefully reassess evidence of individual benefits and risks when increasing dosage to ≥50 MME/d, and should avoid increasing dosage to ≥90 MME/d or carefully justify a decision to titrate dosage to ≥90 MME/d.

  3. Long-term opioid use often begins with treatment of acute pain. When opioids are used for acute pain, clinicians should prescribe the lowest effective dosage of immediate-release opioids and should prescribe no greater quantity than needed for the expected duration of pain severe enough to require opioids. Three days or less will often be sufficient; more than 7 days will rarely be needed.

  4. Clinicians should evaluate benefits and harms with patients within 1 to 4 weeks of starting opioid therapy for chronic pain or of dose escalation. Clinicians should evaluate benefits and harms of continued therapy with patients every 3 months or more frequently. If benefits do not outweigh harms of continued opioid therapy, clinicians should optimize other therapies and work with patients to taper opioids to lower dosages or to taper and discontinue opioids.

Assessing Risk and Addressing Harms of Opioid Use

  1. Before prescribing and periodically during continuation of opioid therapy, clinicians should evaluate risk factors for opioid-related harms. Clinicians should incorporate into the management plan strategies to mitigate risk, including considering offering naloxone when factors that increase risk for opioid overdose, such as history of overdose, history of substance use disorder, higher opioid dosages (≥50 MME/d), or concurrent benzodiazepine use, are present.

  2. Clinicians should review the patient’s history of controlled substance prescriptions using state PDMP data to determine whether the patient is receiving opioid dosages or dangerous combinations that put the patient at high risk for overdose. Clinicians should review PDMP data when prescribing opioid therapy for chronic pain and periodically during opioid therapy for chronic pain, ranging from every prescription to every 3 months.

  3. When prescribing opioids for chronic pain, clinicians should use urine drug testing before starting opioid therapy and consider urine drug testing at least annually to assess for prescribed medications as well as other controlled prescription drugs and nonprescribed substances.

  4. Clinicians should avoid prescribing opioids and benzodiazepines concurrently whenever possible.

  5. Clinicians should offer or arrange evidence-based treatment (usually medication-assisted treatment with buprenorphine or methadone in combination with behavioral therapies) for patients with opioid use disorder.

Fatigue and Systemic Exertion Intolerance Disease

Fatigue is a truly subjective symptom, with little to no corroborating objective measures. It can be described as tiredness, exhaustion, reduction in endurance, or lack of physical or mental energy. Fatigue may be categorized as acute (<1 month’s duration), subacute (1-6 months’ duration), or chronic (>6 months’ duration).

Fatigue occurs in one quarter to one third of patients in the primary care setting. Despite its high prevalence, the cause is often elusive, leading to prolonged delays in diagnosis and substantial functional decline. Direct and indirect economic costs are estimated to be up to $100 billion annually.

Fatigue is most often secondary to a specific underlying cause ( [Table: Table: Common Causes of Fatigue]

) or multiple factors (termed chronic multifactorial fatigue). It can also occur as a primary condition, such as in systemic exertion intolerance disease, although this diagnosis requires exclusion of other causes. The diagnostic evaluation of fatigue begins with a careful history and physical examination. Clinicians should note the duration, preceding factors, concomitant symptoms, prolonged deleterious lifestyle factors, and medication use. Symptoms suggestive of an underlying sleep disorder and the presence of “red flag” signs or symptoms that suggest a serious underlying cause (fever, involuntary weight loss, persistent lymphadenopathy, muscle atrophy, and synovitis) should be specifically assessed. Patients should also be asked whether the onset of symptoms was associated with symptomatic COVID-19 infection.

Diagnostic testing choices should be driven by the history and physical examination findings. In patients with fatigue without a clear cause, it is reasonable to obtain a complete blood count, electrolyte panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone level, fasting glucose level, and kidney and liver chemistry tests. A sleep study is indicated if symptoms such as excessive daytime sleepiness, witnessed apneas, and snoring suggest an underlying sleep disorder. Laboratory, imaging, and invasive studies without a clear indication should be avoided because most patients will have unrevealing or contradictory findings that provide little reassurance or direction to the patient or clinician.

Some patients experience progressive, debilitating fatigue with no identifiable cause despite an appropriate evaluation. In the past, this condition was termed chronic fatigue syndrome, myalgic encephalitis, or neurasthenia. Each of these diagnoses had different criteria, creating inconsistencies in diagnosis and treatment. In 2015, the Institute of Medicine issued an extensive guideline establishing evidence-based, consensus-based clinical diagnostic criteria under the consolidated term of systemic exertion intolerance disease (SEID). Diagnosis of SEID requires the presence of the following three symptoms:

  • A substantial reduction or impairment in the ability to engage in pre-illness levels of occupational, educational, social, or personal activities that persists for more than 6 months and is accompanied by fatigue, which is often profound, is of new or definite onset (not lifelong), is not the result of ongoing excessive exertion, and is not substantially alleviated by rest
  • Postexertional malaise
  • Unrefreshing sleep

In addition, the patient must have at least one of the following two manifestations:

  • Cognitive impairment
  • Orthostatic intolerance (symptoms such as lightheadedness, dizziness, and headache that worsen with upright posture and improve with recumbency)

Although the pathophysiology of SEID remains unclear, central sensitization may contribute. There is no convincing evidence that indolent chronic infection plays a role.

Comorbid conditions, such as fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, and interstitial cystitis, are common. Mood disorders occur concomitantly in up to 70% of patients with SEID, and all patients with SEID should be screened for depression and anxiety. In addition, clinicians should ensure that all age-appropriate screening has been performed. Sleep disorders can coexist with SEID and do not invalidate a diagnosis of SEID if identified.

Treatment of fatigue should focus on correcting any underlying causes.

In patients with SEID, treatment is supportive and focuses on treatment of symptoms and comorbid conditions. Patients benefit most from a structured multimodal approach that includes regularly scheduled office visits, patient education, and longitudinal reassessment. Pacing strategies, in which specific limits are placed on the degree of exertion, may help patients avoid “push-and-crash” cycles (overexertion resulting in worsening of symptoms, known as postexertional malaise). All patients should also receive instruction on effective sleep hygiene (see Nonpharmacologic Therapy in Common Symptoms for a discussion of sleep hygiene). Other modalities that may be of benefit include cognitive behavioral therapy, physical therapy, occupational therapy, biofeedback therapy, massage therapy, acupuncture, yoga, tai chi, and stress management activities. In patients with mood disorders, referral to a psychiatrist or psychologist is reasonable.

There are no FDA-approved medications for the treatment of SEID, and no medications have shown consistent, reproducible benefit. Medical therapy is therefore typically limited to the treatment of symptoms and comorbid conditions. There is no consistent evidence that stimulants (including amphetamines), opioids, glucocorticoids, pharmacologic sleep aids, prolonged antibiotics or antiviral agents, or immunotherapies (such as anakinra or rituximab) improve symptoms or disease course.

The prognosis for SEID varies, and this is often a source of frustration for both patients and physicians. Prognosis depends on many factors, including patient age, formal education level, severity and duration of symptoms, decline in functional status relative to premorbid level of functioning, presence of other symptoms, comorbid conditions, and availability of resources.
