Insomnia

Insomnia is a complex health problem manifesting as poor sleep quality, frustration with sleep quantity, difficulty initiating sleep, or inability to return to sleep after awakening. The prevalence of insomnia increases with age, and women tend to be affected more than men. Cardiopulmonary, neurodegenerative, and psychiatric disorders are often implicated in sleep disruption. Medications and other substances also commonly contribute to insomnia symptoms. Chronic insomnia may also increase risk for depression later in life.

Chronic insomnia is diagnosed by the presence of symptoms that (1) cause substantial functional distress or impairment; (2) occur at least three nights per week for at least 3 months; and (3) are not associated with other sleep, medical, or mental disorders. Although 10% of adults meet the diagnostic criteria for chronic insomnia, some studies have shown that up to 50% of adults report experiencing sleep problems.

All patients should be asked about sleep disruption problems. A thorough history and physical examination may point to underlying conditions that may disrupt sleep and potentially reversible causes of insomnia, such as sleep apnea or restless legs syndrome ( [Table: Table: Medical and Psychiatric Conditions That May Disrupt Sleep]

). Eliciting an accurate medication history is also an essential part of the diagnostic approach ( [Table: Table: Medications and Other Substances Associated With Sleep Disruption]

).

Physicians should obtain information on sleep patterns, including sleep difficulties (sleep initiation, maintenance, quality) and environmental factors (work schedule). The use of electronics should be assessed because there is increasing evidence that screen time, such as smartphone and tablet use, before bed can alter circadian patterns and worsen insomnia symptoms. A sleep diary can facilitate the collection of accurate sleep history, and obtaining a collateral history from the patient’s sleep partner may shed light on specific sleep-related disorders. The Insomnia Severity Index or the Athens Insomnia Scale can be helpful in a comprehensive sleep assessment.

Diagnostic testing, such as polysomnography, is not a first-line approach. It is useful when the clinical presentation suggests a sleep disorder, such as sleep apnea, narcolepsy, or a sleep movement disorder, including restless legs syndrome (see Sleep Medicine in Pulmonary Medicine). Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder events tend to last for seconds and occur with the patient’s eyes closed. Patients may have some recollection of a dream congruent with their sleep behavior.

Non-REM complex behaviors, such as sleepwalking, tend to last up to several minutes and occur with the patient’s eyes open. Patients typically do not recall the event. Factors predisposing to non-REM complex sleep behaviors include poor sleep quality, medications such as sedative-hypnotics, and fever.

The goals of treatment are to improve overall sleep and quality of life. Effective treatment programs are multimodal and include cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I); sleep hygiene techniques; environmental changes; and, in select cases, pharmacologic therapy.

CBT-I is recommended as first-line therapy for insomnia. This multicomponent treatment includes the following:

  • Cognitive therapy (to address maladaptive beliefs and expectations about sleep)
  • Educational interventions (such as sleep hygiene)
  • Behavioral interventions (such as sleep restriction therapy, stimulus-control therapy, and relaxation techniques)

CBT-I may be delivered in various formats, such as individual or group therapy, web-based modules, or written materials. CBT-I provides significant value over pharmacologic-driven approaches and carries little risk for adverse effects.

Brief behavioral therapy for insomnia is an abbreviated version of CBT-I, focusing only on the behavioral components of therapy including sleep restriction, stimulus control, and sleep hygiene. It is more convenient for many patients and of greater value than pharmacologic therapy.

Sleep hygiene strategies focus on optimizing environmental factors and reducing stimuli ( [Table: Table: Techniques for Good Sleep Hygiene]

). Although a component of CBT-I and brief behavioral therapy, sleep hygiene education is not effective or recommended as a standalone therapy for chronic insomnia. Patients frequently use blue light–filtering glasses or software programs, but their effectiveness has not been established. Sleep restriction therapy may also be attempted, which entails limiting time in bed to increase sleep efficiency.

Physicians should engage in a thorough shared decision-making process to decide whether to add pharmacologic therapy to CBT-I in patients with refractory insomnia. Several pharmacologic agents have been demonstrated to improve sleep latency and total sleep time ( [Table: Table: FDA-Approved Prescription Drug Treatment for Insomnia]

), but few studies have examined their overall effect on functioning and quality of life.

Pharmacologic therapy is also associated with harm, including daytime drowsiness, increased risk for falls and hip fracture, and medication-related hallucinations. Factors that should be considered before initiating pharmacologic therapy for insomnia are included in [Table: Table: Factors to Consider When Prescribing Drugs to Treat Insomnia]

. Ideally, medications should be taken in short-term trials (no more than 4-5 weeks) and selected to target the most problematic phase of sleep (onset versus maintenance). There are few choices for long-term pharmacologic treatment of chronic insomnia, although very-low-dose doxepin may be effective.

Benzodiazepines induce sedation by activating inhibitory gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptors. These drugs decrease sleep latency and have a sleep-promoting effect. The associated risk for rebound insomnia, addiction potential, and sedation make benzodiazepines poor options for treating insomnia, particularly in combination with other sedating agents (including opioids) and in geriatric populations. In older adults, benzodiazepine use has also been associated with an increased risk for falls and hip fractures and impaired mobility in activities of daily living.

Nonbenzodiazepine GABA-receptor agonists are typically more selective in their activity at the GABA receptor. These agents (zolpidem, eszopiclone, and zaleplon) have a rapid onset of action and short half-life, making them better choices for patients with difficulty initiating sleep. Long-acting formulations and formulations meant for use with middle-of-the-night awakenings are also available. There is potential for prolonged impaired driving skills, drowsiness, and amnesia with the use of zolpidem, eszopiclone, and zaleplon, and reports of severe or fatal injuries associated with complex sleep behaviors prompted the FDA to issue a boxed warning for these agents. Few data on long-term safety or efficacy are available, and long-term therapy should be avoided.

The dual orexin receptor antagonists (daridorexant, lemborexant, suvorexant) show increased sleep efficiency and improvement in Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) scores compared with placebo. Prolonged somnolence may occur, particularly with suvorexant, and care should be taken not to prescribe with other CYP3A inhibitors (such as HIV protease inhibitors and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers). However, serious adverse events were no more common than with placebo in randomized controlled trials.

The melatonin receptor agonist ramelteon can decrease sleep latency and increase total sleep time, although the effect is modest and can be measured in minutes. Adverse effects are less common with ramelteon than with GABA-receptor agonists.

Off-label use of antidepressant and antipsychotic medications (e.g., trazodone, mirtazapine, and quetiapine) for insomnia have limited evidence supporting their use and should generally not be used absent another indication for their use.

Patients frequently use over-the-counter medications for insomnia, including anticholinergics, antihistamines, and melatonin. Evidence supporting over-the-counter sleep aid use is limited. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine found insufficient evidence to recommend over-the-counter medication because of associated anticholinergic adverse effects and carryover daytime sleepiness. In addition, a growing body of evidence links long-term anticholinergic use to an increased risk for dementia. Antihistamines should be avoided in older adults, who have a greater chance of adverse effects from these medications. Over-the-counter melatonin may be effective for circadian rhythm disruptions and has a more favorable adverse effect profile than antihistamines, but data supporting its efficacy are poor.

Patients increasingly report use of cannabinoids for insomnia, but efficacy data for its use are lacking. In fact, cannabinoids may actually cause sleep disruption. Cannabinoids are not approved for use in insomnia and are not recommended for the treatment of chronic insomnia or any other sleep disorder.

In-Flight Medical Events

In-flight medical events are relatively common during air travel, occurring in an estimated 1 in 600 flights. The most common in-flight medical events are presyncope and syncope (typically vasovagal), accounting for up to one third of in-flight events. The frequency of these events is explained by the physiologic conditions in flight, including low humidity and high altitudes. Other common in-flight events include gastrointestinal disorders (diarrhea and vomiting), cardiovascular symptoms (chest pain), and respiratory symptoms (dyspnea and hyperventilation). Most aircraft cabins are pressurized to 6000 to 8000 feet, and the lower partial pressure of oxygen may cause dyspnea in those with significant underlying cardiopulmonary disease. In-flight cardiac arrest is rare (approximately 0.2% of in-flight events); however, it is responsible for the majority of in-flight deaths. Other frequently encountered issues include trauma caused by objects falling from overhead storage bins, hypoglycemia, psychiatric problems (most commonly anxiety or phobias), allergic reactions, seizures, headaches, and obstetric events.

Physicians who respond to in-flight medical events have access to medical resources and support. Airlines based in the United States are mandated to carry at least one automated external defibrillator, supplemental oxygen, and a medical kit. The supplies and equipment that airlines based in the United States are required to carry are listed in [Table: Table: Emergency Medical Equipment Required on U.S.-based Airline Carriers]

. Many U.S. airlines augment their kits with additional supplies. The Federal Aviation Administration does not mandate glucometers as a component of these kits, although some patients may carry their glucometers with them. The contents of international kits may vary. Flight crews are required to receive cardiopulmonary resuscitation training, including training on the use of automated external defibrillators, and to be familiar with first-aid equipment.

The physician’s role during in-flight medical events involves assessing the patient, establishing a diagnosis when possible, administering basic medical treatments, providing reassurance as appropriate, and recommending flight diversion if necessary. Most airlines contract with 24-hour call centers staffed with emergency medicine physicians with special training on the in-flight environment. Such support is accessed through the pilot, and direct communication between the physician providing assistance and the ground-based support physician may not be possible. Although the physician can recommend immediate diversion of the flight if the patient’s condition or time to treatment is critical (suspected myocardial infarction or stroke), the ultimate decision rests with the aircraft captain who takes many factors into consideration. Diverting a flight for an unplanned medical emergency can cost the airlines from $15,000 to $893,000.

In the United States, physicians are not legally mandated to assist with an in-flight medical event, although some countries do impose this obligation. Ethically, physicians should provide assistance as able. The Aviation Medical Assistance Act of 1998 includes a Good Samaritan provision that protects individuals who are medically qualified “from liability for rendering assistance unless that person is engaged in gross negligence or willful misconduct,” such as providing care while intoxicated. Providers should practice within their scope of training, be mindful of patient privacy, and document the patient encounter. Many airlines provide standard forms for documenting in-flight medical care, which should be completed when available.

Medically Unexplained Symptoms

Medically unexplained symptoms (MUS) are symptoms that cannot be attributed to a specific medical cause after a thorough medical evaluation. Some clinicians prefer the term persistent physical symptoms or persistent somatic symptoms, recognizing advances that have provided a better understanding of the underlying pathophysiology. The prevalence of patients with at least one unexplained symptom ranges from 40% to 49%. Patients with MUS are frequently seen in both primary and subspecialty clinics, resulting in significantly increased health care utilization. The costs associated with MUS are estimated at more than $250 billion annually.

Central sensitization has a potential role in the formation of MUS as well as in some common chronic pain syndromes, such as fibromyalgia and temporomandibular disorders ( [Table: Table: Conditions Associated With Central Sensitization]

). Central sensitization occurs when central nervous system hyperexcitability and reduced inhibitory responses lead to the following:

  • Pain, often in the absence of nociceptive stimuli
  • Sensory disturbances, such as allodynia and hyperalgesia
  • Alterations in autonomic, motor, and cognitive functions

Central desensitization is often, but not always, precipitated by a prodromal event, such as infection, physical or emotional trauma, surgery, medical illness, or prolonged stress. The National Institutes of Health has coined the term chronic overlapping pain conditions to describe the interrelatedness of many of these conditions, including those listed in [Table: Table: Conditions Associated With Central Sensitization]

.

Common symptoms in patients with MUS include fatigue, headache, abdominal pain, musculoskeletal pain (back pain, myalgia, arthralgia), dizziness, paresthesia, generalized weakness, transient edema, insomnia, dyspnea, chest pain, chronic facial pain, chronic pelvic pain, and chemical sensitivities. MUS are diagnosed more frequently in women, persons with lower levels of education, those with lower socioeconomic status, those with early adverse life experiences, and those with concomitant depression and anxiety.

There is no formal approach to the diagnostic evaluation of MUS; however, the initial evaluation should involve a thorough history and physical examination related to each symptom. Clinicians must address symptoms in a focused manner and diligently review any previous diagnostic evaluations. Laboratory and radiographic studies should be guided by the findings on the history and physical examination, and subspecialty referrals should be used judiciously. Given the high comorbidity of mood disturbances in patients with MUS, patients with features concerning for an underlying mood disorder should be evaluated accordingly.

Patients with MUS might have a coexisting somatic symptom disorder, a group of psychiatric conditions with specific diagnostic criteria (see Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders in Interdisciplinary Medicine). Although many somatic symptom disorders involve MUS, most patients with MUS do not meet the diagnostic criteria for these disorders.

If an underlying medical cause cannot be identified after an appropriately thorough evaluation, it is imperative that clinicians have an open and honest discussion with the patient, being mindful to acknowledge the patient’s concerns and frustrations. Frequently, patients will request, or even demand, additional testing and consultations that may not be clinically indicated. Although doing so may be challenging, clinicians should limit additional evaluations to those deemed medically necessary because unrevealing studies provide negligible reassurance, pose iatrogenic risks, and increase patient anxiety.

Management of MUS is challenging, but the foundation is an effective therapeutic relationship. Patients should be treated respectfully and cared for in a nonjudgmental manner. It is important not only to expect but also to accept the patient’s feelings of frustration; acknowledging these feelings early in the patient’s management course can help to build and strengthen the therapeutic alliance. Patients often fear that they will be perceived as producing factitious symptoms or malingering, and it is crucial to address these concerns directly if raised. One study demonstrated that working with physicians trained in communication techniques that validated patients’ experiences and symptoms, offered credible explanations and plausible mechanisms of symptom causes, and offered individualized control techniques (e.g., emotion regulation skills, relaxation, and breath control) reduced the frequency and severity of MUS. See [Table: Table: Explaining the Diagnosis]

for a step-by-step example of an approach to explaining MUS (and similar diagnoses).

Management of MUS requires a patient-focused, holistic, and multimodal approach. The goals of management are restoration of function, decreased symptom focus, and acquisition of coping mechanisms rather than abatement of symptoms. It should be made clear to patients that the treatment of MUS will probably not be curative and that symptoms may persist. Patients should be encouraged to develop short- and long-term goals with the recognition that many goals will change from a physical symptom focus to a psychosocial focus. Appointments should be regularly scheduled and consistent rather than on an as-needed basis. If additional symptoms arise, clinicians should respond empathically and perform an appropriately thorough investigation.

Interventions that may benefit patients with MUS include cognitive behavioral therapy, individual or group psychotherapy, social support, biofeedback therapy, graded exercise therapy, stress management activities, training in coping mechanisms, physical therapy, and occupational therapy. Patients with comorbid mood disorders should be considered for a trial of antidepressant therapy and referral to a psychiatrist or psychologist. Given the wide-ranging effects of MUS, treatment should be focused on both physical and psychosocial aspects of a patient’s symptomatology ( [Table: Table: Management of Patients With Medically Unexplained Symptoms]

).

Epidemiology and Risk Factors

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) encompasses many conditions, including coronary artery disease (CAD), stroke/transient ischemic attack (TIA), congenital heart disease, rhythm disorders, subclinical atherosclerosis, heart failure, valvular disease, venous disease, and peripheral artery disease (PAD). CVD is the leading cause of death in the United States with cardiac disease being responsible for over 21% of all deaths in 2022. Globally, a third of all deaths were attributed to CVD in 2019. However, from 2007 to 2017, the age-adjusted death rate for CVD fell by 16% and similarly, the age-adjusted death rate for coronary artery disease fell by 56% from 1990 to 2021.

Nearly 50% of U.S. adults currently have some form of CVD. There has been a 43% increase in CVD among men and a 29% increase in CVD among women from 1990 to 2023. Prevalence increases with age, and more than 75% of persons aged 60 to 79 years have CVD. There is also a rising rate of premature CVD in the United States. Additionally, an estimated 6.2 million U.S. adults older than 20 years have a diagnosis of heart failure, a condition with high rates of morbidity and mortality. The prevalence of heart failure is projected to increase by 46% between 2012 and 2030.

The financial costs of CVD are remarkable. CVD was responsible for 4.7 million U.S. hospital discharges in 2021. The estimated total cost of CVD for 2020 was approximately $627 billion, and the projected total cost of CVD between 2015 and 2035 is expected to increase sharply for adults aged 65 years and older.

There are significant disparities in CVD diagnosis and treatment. CVD remains the leading cause of death in women, resulting in more deaths than cancer, diabetes mellitus, and kidney disease combined. Approximately two thirds of women who die of myocardial infarction (MI) either have no symptoms or have symptoms that are unrecognized as cardiac in origin. Chest pain is the most common presenting anginal symptom in both men and women, but women are more likely to report symptoms such as shortness of breath, fatigue, dizziness, or abdominal pain that could be mistaken as secondary to an alternative diagnosis. In addition, after an acute coronary syndrome, women undergo fewer interventions, have more complications, and have higher unadjusted mortality. Mortality within the first year after a first MI is 23% in women versus 18% in men. Acute MI mortality is greatest among Black women. Black women also have a higher prevalence of CVD (10.5%) compared with White (8.1%) and Hispanic women (8.0%). These differences and disparities are likely driven by several components, including inequitable access to care, social factors, and biases held by institutions and individuals. Despite this illness burden, many groups have been underrepresented in clinical treatment trials, making it challenging to extrapolate treatment decisions (see Addressing Bias, Stigma, and Discrimination in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

The eight metrics of ideal cardiovascular health are optimal lipid, blood pressure, and glucose levels; healthy diet; appropriate energy intake; physical activity; avoidance of tobacco; and healthy sleep. However, very few persons meet all these metrics. Promotion of a healthy lifestyle throughout life remains the most important way to prevent atherosclerotic CVD (ASCVD).

Sedentary lifestyle, poor diet, and obesity all contribute to increased cardiovascular risk. According to the CDC, only 22.5% of adults meet aerobic and strengthening exercise recommendations. Average daily fruit and vegetable consumption in the United States is also suboptimal at less than 1 cup of fruit (recommended, 1.5-2 cups) and less than 1.5 cups of vegetables (recommended, 2-3 cups). The importance of improving these metrics was demonstrated in the Diabetes Prevention Program, which found that in persons at high risk for diabetes mellitus, interventions such as changes in diet, exercise, and weight loss of 5% to 7% reduced the risk for diabetes by 58%.

Tobacco use is the leading preventable cause of disease, disability, and death in the United States, and tobacco exposure is a significant risk factor for CVD. The prevalence of tobacco use continues to decline: 13% of men and 9% of women were current smokers in 2023. Prioritizing smoking cessation is crucial because the risk for heart failure and death for most former smokers after 15 years of tobacco cessation is similar to that of never smokers. Smoking status should be assessed at every visit, and cessation counseling and pharmacologic therapy should be offered to active smokers (see Tobacco in Interdisciplinary Medicine).

Poor sleep hygiene is also associated with increased CVD risk and can contribute to mental health disorders. It is important for adults to get at least 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night for optimal cardiovascular health.

Psychosocial factors, including depression, anger, and anxiety, are associated with worse cardiovascular outcomes, and depression has been linked to a higher risk for cardiovascular events. Psychosocial stressors also affect the course of treatment and adherence to a healthy lifestyle after a cardiovascular event. Although detecting and treating these disorders is important, no evidence exists that such detection and treatment affect cardiovascular risk itself.

Approximately 25.5% of the U.S. population has elevated serum cholesterol levels, to which over 3 million deaths globally were attributed. Elevated cholesterol levels are associated with increased cardiovascular risk, and reducing cholesterol levels has been shown to lower overall risk. Elevated LDL cholesterol and low HDL cholesterol levels also are independently associated with increased risk for CVD. Lipid-lowering therapies for primary and secondary prevention of CVD are discussed in Pharmacologic Therapy for Dyslipidemia in Cardiovascular Medicine.

Hypertension (blood pressure ≥130/80 mm Hg) affects approximately 46% of persons aged 20 years and older. Before age 45 years, the prevalence of hypertension is higher in men than in women; however, after age 65 years, the prevalence is higher in women. The population attributable risk of hypertension for stroke is 48%; it is 32% for heart failure. Treatment of hypertension reduces risk for stroke, heart failure, and kidney disease. Early recognition and effective management of hypertension could reduce CVD mortality by 30% among men and 38% among women. Hypertension is discussed more thoroughly in Hypertension.

Diabetes increases cardiovascular risk and is an independent indication for statin therapy. Sixty-eight percent of individuals with diabetes eventually die of heart disease. Diabetes increases ischemic stroke incidence at all ages, but this risk is most prominent (risk ratio >5) before age 65 years. In persons with diabetes, CAD is likely to be more extensive, and the incidence of multivessel disease is increased. Patients with diabetes also have worse outcomes when hospitalized for any CVD. Earlier and aggressive cardiovascular risk reduction strategies are essential when treating patients with diabetes. Novel agents for diabetes, including sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP1-RA), have shown significant cardiovascular benefits in patients with diabetes. Diabetes is discussed more thoroughly in Diabetes Mellitus.

From 2016 to 2018, the prevalence of obesity increased from 39.6% to 42.4% and the prevalence of class III obesity (BMI >40) increased from 7.7% to 9.2%. Obesity may increase the risk for CVD events, even in the absence of metabolic risk factors.

Metabolic syndrome, the hallmark feature of which is glucose intolerance, is characterized by the presence of at least three of the following conditions:

  • Elevated glucose level
  • Central obesity
  • Low HDL cholesterol level
  • Elevated triglyceride level
  • Elevated blood pressure

Approximately 34% of adults meet the criteria for metabolic syndrome. Metabolic syndrome is associated with increased risk for CVD and diabetes, with risk increasing as the number of component conditions increases (see Obesity and Metabolic Syndrome in Endocrinology and Metabolism).

A history of obstetric complications such as preeclampsia, gestational hypertension or diabetes, and preterm or low-birth-weight delivery increases CVD risk in women (see Other Cardiovascular Disorders in Cardiovascular Medicine). CVD risk is also increased in women with early menopause or polycystic ovary syndrome.

In addition to the risk for CVD as predicted by the traditional risk elements, inherited factors may increase CVD risk. A history of premature CAD (men younger than 55 years, women younger than 65 years) in parents doubles the risk for MI in men and increases it by 70% in women. Stroke in a first-degree relative increases the risk for stroke by 50%. A parental history of atrial fibrillation increases the odds of this condition by 80%. In addition to the shared environment (i.e., lifestyle), genetics may contribute to increased risk in family members and are often not incorporated in risk calculators (see Genetic Testing for Cardiovascular Disease in Cardiovascular Medicine).

Multiple other factors such as chronic kidney disease, chronic inflammatory disorders, and pregnancy-associated complications may also increase CV risk and impact treatment decisions (see [Table: Table: Risk-Enhancing Factors for Clinician-Patient Risk Discussion]

).

Multiple cardiovascular risk scores are available to assess an individual patient’s risk for major cardiovascular events and to identify preventive interventions. Traditionally, the Framingham risk score, which includes the data inputs of age, sex, systolic blood pressure, total cholesterol level, HDL cholesterol level, smoking status, and presence of diabetes, has been used to estimate the 10-year risk for a major coronary heart disease event (MI or coronary death). Similarly, the Reynolds risk score is a sex-specific calculator and includes family history and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein level. Another tool, the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA) risk score , uses coronary artery calcium score and traditional risk factors to calculate risk.

The American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE) is a risk assessment instrument derived from several diverse community-based cohorts. The ACC/AHA CVD risk calculator based on the PCE may be used to calculate 10-year ASCVD risk, thereby identifying persons who would benefit from preventive measures, including statin therapy. The PCE is recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) and other organizations to estimate the 10-year risk of ASCVD in U.S. adults aged 40 to 75 years.

There are significant racial and ethnic disparities in the prevalence of CVD in the United States. There are likely many reasons for these health disparities, such as structural social factors and inequitable access to care, including preventive measures (see Understanding Patient Context and Social Drivers of Health in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Many of these risk calculators, including the PCE recommended by the USPSTF, the Society of Thoracic Surgeons Adult Cardiac Surgery Risk Calculator, and the MESA risk score, include race as a variable in estimating cardiovascular risk. The inclusion of race as a predictor of risk is problematic. For this and several other reasons, the AHA developed the PREVENT (AHA Predicting Risk of CVD Events) equations. PREVENT represents sex-specific, race-free risk prediction equations that

  • Estimate short- and long-term risk
  • Incorporate kidney function into routine CVD risk assessment
  • Allow for additional consideration of cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic–focused clinical variables and social determinants of health metrics
  • Include heart failure and ASCVD in a total CVD outcome

Implementation of these guidelines is nascent and will likely evolve to better determine individualized risk and define optimal integration into CVD prevention strategies.

Risk factors for PAD largely parallel those for CAD, including tobacco use, diabetes, and dyslipidemia. More than 42% of individuals with CAD also have PAD, and conversely, the presence of PAD increases the risk for CAD and stroke by 45% and 35%, respectively. Clinically significant PAD (ankle-brachial index <0.9) is also associated with a 2.5 times greater prevalence of MI, worse outcomes after MI, and more extensive CAD.

CKD is associated with a higher incidence of CVD and worse cardiovascular outcomes. In persons with CKD versus without CKD, the incidence rate (per 1000 person-years) for CAD is 24.5 versus 8.4, and for stroke it is 13.4 versus 4.8. The risk for CVD-related death is 5 to 30 times higher in patients undergoing dialysis than in those with similar risk factors and preserved kidney function. Despite the recognized increase in CVD among patients with CKD, it is unclear whether targeted prevention strategies—beyond those suggested for more traditional age, blood pressure, lipid, and diabetes risk factors—succeed in modifying the risk.

The risk for CVD is higher in patients with systemic inflammatory conditions, such as systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis. The risk for CAD is nearly 60% higher in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and is nearly doubled in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus. In addition to traditional cardiovascular risk factors, the increased risk in these patients may be a result of the inflammatory process, a prothrombotic state, insulin resistance, or use of glucocorticoids or other immunosuppressive therapy.

Certain HIV-related risk-enhancing factors may confer a 1.5 to 2 times higher risk for CVD than the calculated risk using the ACC/AHA CVD risk calculator. HIV risk-enhancing factors include history of prolonged HIV viremia and/or delay in antiretroviral therapy initiation, low current or nadir CD4 cell count (<350/μL), and HIV treatment failure or nonadherence. Patients living with well-controlled HIV (undetectable viral load, normal CD4 cell count) may still be at increased risk, especially in the setting of hepatitis C virus coinfection or the possible effects of antiretroviral therapy, such as metabolic syndrome, lipodystrophy/lipoatrophy, and fatty liver disease. Patients with HIV risk-enhancing factors should be considered for intensive therapeutic lifestyle modifications, lipid-lowering therapy, or referral to a specialist.

Dyslipidemia

Although unanimous in endorsing screening for dyslipidemia, major guidelines differ in their recommendations regarding when to initiate screening in adults. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends universal lipid screening in adults aged 40 to 75 years to assess for dyslipidemia and to calculate the 10-year predicted risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) using the American Heart Association (AHA)/American College of Cardiology (ACC) Pooled Cohort Equations. The AHA also has developed the PREVENT (AHA Predicting Risk of CVD Events) equations, which provide sex-specific, race-free risk prediction for both 10-year and 30-year risk.

In contrast, the 2018 AHA/ACC Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol assigns a high priority to the estimation of lifetime ASCVD risk in children, adolescents, and adults and promotion of lifestyle risk reduction across the age spectrum; these guidelines do not limit screening to patients aged 40 to 75 years.

Lipid measurement also may be indicated to investigate familial hypercholesterolemia; to determine adherence to and effectiveness of therapy; and to evaluate dyslipidemia in the presence of potential complications, such as pancreatitis.

Fasting blood specimens are not necessarily needed for screening in the absence of hypertriglyceridemia.

LDL cholesterol is the most atherogenic lipoprotein, and the association between high LDL cholesterol levels and increased risk for ASCVD is widely accepted. The primary utility of LDL cholesterol measurement is therefore to identify patients without known ASCVD who will benefit from interventions to reduce risk of developing ASCVD and to assess response to therapy. Goals of therapy may be a percentage decrease in LDL cholesterol level, a specific LDL cholesterol goal, or both.

In patients with elevated LDL cholesterol levels, secondary causes, including hypothyroidism, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, nephrotic syndrome, and medications (e.g., glucocorticoids, diuretics, amiodarone), should be considered. Genetic testing for familial hypercholesterolemia in adults might be considered in the following circumstances:

  • LDL cholesterol level is above 250 mg/dL (6.48 mmol/L)
  • LDL cholesterol level is above 190 mg/dL (4.92 mmol/L) and the patient has a first-degree relative with similar hypercholesterolemia or premature CAD
  • Some patients in whom secondary causes have been ruled out

Elevated triglyceride levels (>150 mg/dL [1.69 mmol/L]) are independently associated with increased ASCVD risk. Causes of hypertriglyceridemia include

  • Diabetes
  • Excessive alcohol intake
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Medications, such as glucocorticoids, protease inhibitors, and estrogens
  • Obesity
  • Lifestyle factors, including concentrated sugar intake

Patients with triglyceride levels of 500 mg/dL or higher (≥5.65 mmol/L) without an identifiable cause should be evaluated for familial hypertriglyceridemia.

Acute pancreatitis may be induced by triglyceride levels greater than 500 to 1000 mg/dL (>5.65-11.30 mmol/L). Triglyceride levels should be measured in selected patients with pancreatitis, especially in cases of pancreatitis without a clear cause, such as cholelithiasis or alcohol use (see Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis of Acute Pancreatitis in Gastroenterology).

Chylomicronemia is also typically present in patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia (≥500 mg/dL [≥5.6 mmol/L]). Although the atherogenicity of chylomicrons is still being investigated, they may also cause acute pancreatitis.

HDL cholesterol is a protective factor against the development of ASCVD, and levels can contribute to the assessment of ASCVD risk. However, it is not as strong a predictor of ASCVD risk as LDL cholesterol. Pharmacologic treatment to raise HDL cholesterol levels has not shown benefit in randomized clinical trials and is not recommended.

The risk for cardiovascular events increases in direct proportion to the lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] cholesterol level, with more dramatic risk in patients with a level greater than 50 mg/dL (>1.3 mmol/L). Despite this recognized association, there is no guideline consensus regarding when to specifically screen for Lp(a) cholesterol. U.S. guidelines suggest evaluation of Lp(a) cholesterol to further stratify ASCVD risk in patients at intermediate risk, whereas European guidelines recommend testing at least once in a lifetime. Therapies that directly target Lp(a) are undergoing clinical trials to determine if they improve cardiovascular outcomes. Standard lipid-lowering therapy and aggressive risk factor modification are recommended for those with elevated Lp(a) cholesterol levels.

Treatment with therapeutic lifestyle changes and pharmacologic therapy may be indicated after assessment of ASCVD risk.

All patients should be counseled regarding therapeutic lifestyle changes, including dietary modification, regular physical activity, achievement of optimal body weight, and smoking cessation.

Patients should be encouraged to adhere to a diet that focuses on consumption of fruits, vegetables, fiber, and monounsaturated fats and minimizes intake of saturated and trans fats, simple carbohydrates, and red meats. Examples of heart-healthy diets include the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) and Mediterranean diets. The AHA/ACC additionally recommends reducing the percentage of calories from saturated fat (<7% of calories from saturated fat; <6% of calories from saturated fat in patients at high cardiovascular risk) and the percentage of calories from trans fats. Replacing saturated fats with polyunsaturated fats has been shown to reduce LDL cholesterol levels and cardiovascular mortality. To facilitate these changes, clinicians should provide patients with educational resources and, when appropriate, refer them to a dietitian. Behavioral support programs may increase adherence to appropriate diets, and referral should be considered.

The AHA/ACC also recommends that patients, including those with chronic medical conditions, engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate or at least 75 minutes of vigorous physical activity per week. Adults should perform muscle-strengthening exercises two to three times per week as well.

Statins are the mainstay of pharmacologic therapy for dyslipidemia and the primary and secondary prevention of ASCVD. Statin dosages for high- and moderate-intensity therapy are presented in [Table: Table: High- and Moderate-Intensity Statin Therapy]

.

Effective adjunctive nonstatin LDL cholesterol–lowering drugs include ezetimibe; proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors, including PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies and PCSK9-directed small interfering RNA; and bempedoic acid ( [Table: Table: Characteristics of Lipid-Lowering Nonstatin Drugs]

). Fibrates and niacin are not recommended as adjuncts to statin therapy to reduce LDL cholesterol levels.

Many guidelines exist for assessing and treating cholesterol and these guidelines stress the importance of patients knowing their cholesterol levels. A common theme across all primary prevention guidelines is calculating risk for an ASCVD event and determining the best strategy to lower cholesterol, either with lifestyle modifications alone, lipid-lowering therapy, or a combination of both.

The AHA/ACC recommendations for primary prevention of ASCVD are summarized in

. Regardless of risk category, physicians should engage all patients in a discussion that considers risk factors, healthy lifestyle, benefits and risks of drug therapy, and patient preferences (see Epidemiology and Risk Factors in Cardiovascular Medicine).

The AHA/ACC cholesterol management guideline identifies two major categories of higher-risk patients who benefit from primary prevention statin therapy without calculation of the 10-year ASCVD risk. Adults of any age with an LDL cholesterol level of 190 mg/dL or higher (≥4.92 mmol/L) should begin high-intensity statin therapy, and adults aged 40 to 75 years with diabetes should begin at least moderate-intensity statin therapy. In patients with diabetes and additional ASCVD risk factors, the 10-year ASCVD risk can be calculated to determine whether high-intensity statin therapy is indicated.

In the absence of diabetes or an LDL cholesterol level of 190 mg/dL or greater, adults aged 40 to 75 years without diabetes and with an LDL cholesterol level of 70 mg/dL to 189 mg/dL (1.81-4.90 mmol/L) should undergo risk assessment for the primary prevention of ASCVD using the Pooled Cohort Equations. The 10-year risk for ASCVD is categorized as follows:

  • High: ≥20%
  • Intermediate: 7.5% to <20%
  • Borderline: 5% to <7.5%
  • Low: <5%

In adults aged 40 to 75 years at high risk for ASCVD, high-intensity statin therapy should be initiated to reduce the LDL cholesterol level by 50% or more.

In adults at intermediate risk, the presence of risk-enhancing factors may justify initiation of moderate-intensity statin therapy ( [Table: Table: Risk-Enhancing Factors for Clinician-Patient Risk Discussion]

). When the decision about initiating statin therapy remains uncertain, it is reasonable to obtain a coronary artery calcium (CAC) score to guide therapeutic decisions (see Coronary Artery Calcium Scoring in Cardiovascular Medicine). If the CAC score is 0, it is appropriate to withhold statin therapy and reassess in 3 to 5 years, as long as higher-risk conditions (e.g., family history of premature ASCVD, cigarette smoking, or risk-enhancing biomarkers) are absent. If the CAC score is 1 to 99, it is reasonable to initiate moderate-intensity statin therapy. In patients with a CAC score of 100 or greater or at the 75th percentile or greater, it is reasonable to initiate moderate- to high-intensity statin therapy; ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitors may be added if LDL goals are not achieved with maximally tolerated statin therapy in this higher-risk group. Patients at borderline or low risk generally do not require statin therapy, but therapy can be discussed with patients at borderline risk when additional risk-enhancing factors are present.

Nonstatin drugs to lower LDL cholesterol should be considered alone or in combination with statins in patients who do not achieve adequate LDL cholesterol reduction with statin therapy or cannot tolerate statins, especially high-risk patients. Before nonstatin drugs are initiated, patient preferences as well as anticipated ASCVD risk reduction and adverse effects should be discussed.

The addition of ezetimibe, for example, may be considered in adults aged 40 to 75 years who have a baseline LDL cholesterol level less than 190 mg/dL (4.92 mmol/L) and an ASCVD risk of 20% or greater who do not achieve a 50% reduction in LDL cholesterol with maximally tolerated statin therapy. PCSK9 inhibitors can also be considered if the baseline ASCVD risk is high and reduction of LDL cholesterol is not adequate with ezetimibe alone. Similarly, ezetimibe and/or PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies may also be added for primary prevention of ASCVD in patients with an initial LDL cholesterol level of 190 mg/dL or greater (≥4.92 mmol/L) who do not achieve a 50% reduction in LDL cholesterol, or who have an LDL cholesterol level of 100 mg/dL or higher (≥2.59 mmol/L) while receiving maximally tolerated statin therapy.

The USPSTF recommendations for primary prevention statin therapy differ from those of the AHA/ACC. In asymptomatic adults aged 40 to 75 years without ASCVD who have at least one ASCVD risk factor (dyslipidemia, diabetes, hypertension, or smoking), the USPSTF recommends moderate-intensity statin therapy in those with a calculated 10-year ASCVD event risk of 10% or higher (grade B recommendation) and selective consideration of statin therapy in those with a calculated 10-year ASCVD event risk of 7.5% to 10% (grade C recommendation).

The American Diabetes Association (ADA) has also published recommendations for statin therapy in patients with diabetes. In patients aged 40 to 75 years without atherosclerotic disease, a moderate-intensity statin is recommended. For patients in this age range with one or more risk factors for ASCVD, a high-intensity statin is recommended to reduce LDL cholesterol by 50% or more of baseline, to a target level of less than 70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L). In those at higher cardiovascular risk whose LDL goals are not achieved with high-intensity or maximally tolerated statin therapy, the addition of ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor can be considered. For patients older than 75 years, initiation of moderate-intensity statin therapy is recommended if the benefit-risk profile is favorable.

The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs and U.S. Department of Defense, in their 2020 joint clinical practice guideline on managing dyslipidemia to reduce cardiovascular disease risk, recommend moderate-intensity statin therapy for primary prevention in patients with a 10-year cardiovascular risk of 12% or greater, an LDL cholesterol level of 190 mg/dL or greater (≥4.92 mmol/L), or diabetes. It also recommends treatment for those with a risk of 6% to 12% if the patient prefers treatment. A summary of the guideline recommendations is provided in [Table: Table: Summary of Dyslipidemia Pharmacotherapy Recommendations]

.

Patients in whom secondary prevention therapy is appropriate include those with the following:

  • Acute coronary syndrome (ACS), history of myocardial infarction (MI), or angina (stable or unstable)
  • Coronary or other arterial revascularization
  • Stroke or transient ischemic attack
  • Peripheral artery disease
  • Aortic aneurysm

According to AHA/ACC guidelines, high-intensity statin therapy should be initiated in patients aged 75 years or younger who have ASCVD to achieve a reduction in LDL cholesterol of 50% or greater. If there is less than a 50% reduction in LDL or the LDL cholesterol level remains 70 mg/dL (1.81 mmol/L) or greater with statin therapy alone, then nonstatin drugs like ezetimibe, monoclonal antibody PCSK9 inhibitors, siRNA-based PCSK9 inhibitors, or bempedoic acid should be considered. Recent reductions in the price of PCSK9 monoclonal antibody have made this a more cost-effective option. If high-intensity statin therapy is contraindicated or not tolerated, moderate-intensity statin therapy should be initiated to achieve a reduction in LDL cholesterol with the possible addition of nonstatin therapy to ensure LDL cholesterol of less than 70 mg/dL (1.81 mmol/L).

Patients with a history of multiple major ASCVD events or one major ASCVD event and multiple high-risk conditions are at very high risk. These patients may also benefit from the addition of nonstatin drug therapy to maximally tolerated statin therapy when the LDL cholesterol level is not reduced by 50% or more or if it remains at or greater than 55 mg/dL (1.42 mmol/L).

The ADA also recommends a high-intensity statin for all patients with diabetes and ASCVD. Similar to the AHA/ACC guidelines, the ADA also suggests adding ezetimibe and/or PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies if the LDL cholesterol level is not reduced by 50% or more or if it remains at or greater than 55 mg/dL (1.42 mmol/L).

For secondary prevention, the 2020 U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs and U.S. Department of Defense cholesterol guideline recommends at least moderate-intensity statin therapy and, in higher-risk patients, high-intensity statin therapy (see [Table: Table: Summary of Dyslipidemia Pharmacotherapy Recommendations]

). Higher-risk patients include those with MI or ACS in the past 12 months; recurrent ACS, MI, or stroke; or established cardiovascular disease with additional risk factors. Nonstatin therapy is also suggested in some higher-risk patients.

A lipid panel should be obtained 4 to 12 weeks after initiation of lipid-lowering therapy. Patients who do not achieve adequate reduction in LDL cholesterol should be assessed for medication adherence and intensity of lifestyle modifications. When treatment goals have been achieved, lipid levels should be measured every 3 to 12 months as indicated.

Statins are generally safe and well tolerated. They may cause asymptomatic, dose-related elevations in aminotransferase levels in approximately 1% of patients, but liver injury occurs in less than 0.001% of patients. Likewise, although observational studies have suggested higher rates, data from randomized trials show that the incidence of statin-associated muscle symptoms is no greater than 1%, and the incidence of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis is less than 0.1% (see Myopathies in Neurology). Before statin therapy is started, liver chemistry tests should be obtained at baseline; however, liver chemistry tests and muscle enzyme studies should not be obtained during therapy in the absence of symptoms.

Statin therapy also increases the risk for newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes by approximately 0.2% per year, although the increased risk appears to be restricted to patients with other risk factors for diabetes. In patients with previous cerebrovascular disease, statins may increase the risk for hemorrhagic stroke, but these drugs also reduce total stroke risk in this population.

Most statin-related adverse effects can be reversed by stopping treatment. In patients with statin intolerance, switching to another statin is reasonable. Other options include decreasing the dosage and/or dosing frequency and, less preferably, discontinuing statin therapy and initiating nonstatin drugs.

Statins are subject to several drug-drug interactions that predominantly increase the plasma concentrations of statins, thereby increasing the risk for myopathy and rhabdomyolysis (see Toxic Myopathy in Neurology). There are some interactions with common nonstatin cardiac medications (e.g., fibrates, dabigatran), and statins may potentiate the effect of warfarin, resulting in higher-than-expected INR values. All statins are contraindicated in pregnancy.

Therapeutic lifestyle changes are the cornerstone of management of elevated triglyceride levels. Dietary changes include reducing sugar, total fat, and alcohol consumption, and decreasing caloric intake to achieve a 5% to 10% weight loss. Medications that increase triglyceride levels, such as estrogens, β-blockers, and glucocorticoids, should be avoided if possible. Omega-3 fatty acids, which are found in many types of fish, reduce triglyceride levels and should be incorporated into the diet; however, omega-3 fatty acid supplements do not reduce heart disease, stroke, or death.

In most patients, the value of pharmacologic treatment of hypertriglyceridemia for preventing cardiovascular events is still being studied, but a well-established risk of pancreatitis remains. Elevated triglycerides may also be a sign or symptom of conditions that increase the risk of cardiovascular events like diabetes, metabolic syndrome, or obesity. Thus, in adults without ASCVD or diabetes who have a 10-year ASCVD risk of 7.5% or greater and moderate (fasting triglyceride level of 150-499 mg/dL [1.69-5.64 mmol/L]) or severe (fasting triglyceride level >500 mg/dL [5.65 mmol/L]) hypertriglyceridemia despite lifestyle interventions and addressing reversible factors, initiating or intensifying statin therapy may be considered.

In patients aged 50 years or older who have persistently elevated triglyceride levels despite statin therapy and either established cardiovascular disease or diabetes and one other ASCVD risk factor, adding the highly purified fish oil icosapent ethyl may decrease the risk for cardiovascular events, an effect lacking for other omega-3 fatty acids.

If there is an indication, anti-obesity medications, such as glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists, can help manage triglycerides in patients with obesity or diabetes.

Fibrates (preferably fenofibrate) are the most effective pharmacotherapy for hypertriglyceridemia, resulting in a 30% to 50% reduction in triglyceride level; these agents are indicated in patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia (≥500 mg/dL [5.65 mmol/L] and especially ≥1000 mg/dL [11.30 mmol/L]) to prevent acute pancreatitis. Icosapent ethyl or pharmacologic doses (4 g/d) of omega-3 fatty acid preparations are also effective at decreasing triglyceride levels.

Patients older than 75 years without known ASCVD and an LDL cholesterol level of 70 mg/dL to 189 mg/dL (1.81-4.90 mmol/L) can be engaged in a discussion of the potential benefits of statin therapy for primary prevention despite low inclusion of patients older than 75 years in pivotal clinical studies. If statin therapy is selected, a moderate-intensity statin is recommended to start, with reassessment of titration based on risk and LDL cholesterol response. It is important to note that the benefit in this population is less established than in other higher-risk groups. If the decision to initiate statin therapy is uncertain, measuring the CAC score can be helpful because statin therapy can be avoided if the CAC score is 0. It is reasonable to forego initiating a statin or to stop statin therapy in the face of functional decline, multiple comorbid conditions, frailty, or reduced life expectancy.

For secondary prevention of ASCVD in patients older than 75 years, it is reasonable to continue statins in those who are already tolerating therapy; moderate-intensity therapy is beneficial and is preferable to high-intensity therapy in these patients. However, the goal LDL cholesterol is still less than 70 mg/dL (1.81 mmol/L).

Initiation of statin therapy is not recommended in adults receiving dialysis for end-stage kidney disease, but it may be reasonable to continue a statin in patients already receiving therapy. Consideration of nonstatin therapies may also be beneficial.

When discussing the benefits of statin therapy and lifestyle modification with women, clinicians should specifically consider premature menopause and history of pregnancy-associated disorders (gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes), which increase ASCVD risk. The available evidence does not indicate that statins are hazardous during pregnancy, but they have not been proved safe and are not advised in general for pregnant individuals. Caution should also be taken when breastfeeding because statins can transfer through breast milk and therefore are not recommended for breastfeeding women. Patients of reproductive age should be counseled to use reliable contraception while taking a statin and to discontinue statin therapy 1 to 3 months before pregnancy is attempted.

Data continue to suggest an increased risk for CAD among patients with HIV infection, with even greater risk in those who also have metabolic syndrome, chronic hepatitis C virus infection, diabetes, or lipodystrophy. A recent trial found that among patients with HIV with low to moderate ASCVD risk (average 4.5%), moderate-intensity statin therapy with pitavastatin reduced cardiovascular events by 35% over 5 years compared with placebo.

Patients with rheumatoid arthritis, and likely those with other chronic inflammatory conditions, also have an increased cardiovascular risk. Thus, strong consideration should be given to lipid-lowering therapy in these patients.

Patients with HIV are at increased risk for ASCVD, and statin therapy is recommended by some guidelines if the 10-year ASCVD risk is 5% or greater; statin therapy should also be considered in lower risk patients. (see Cardiovascular Disease in Infectious Disease)

Xanthomas are lipid deposits in the connective tissue of the skin, tendons, or fasciae that manifest as yellow, orange, reddish, or yellow-brown papules, plaques, or nodules. They are associated with primary and secondary dyslipidemias, and the type of xanthoma correlates with the type of lipoprotein that is elevated. The most common xanthoma types are

  • Eruptive xanthoma
  • Plane xanthoma/xanthelasma
  • Tuberous xanthoma
  • Tendinous xanthoma

Eruptive xanthomas present as clusters of small erythematous papules, typically on the extensor surfaces of the arms, legs, and buttocks. Eruptive xanthomas are pathognomonic of hypertriglyceridemia, with a vast number of patients also having a diagnosis of diabetes. Definitive diagnosis is made by skin biopsy that shows lipid-laden macrophages in the dermis. However, in the setting of features suggestive of metabolic syndrome or hypertriglyceridemia (>1000 mg/dL [11.30 mmol/L]), biopsy may not be required before initiating management to reduce serum triglycerides. Lesions typically resolve with control of carbohydrate and lipid metabolism.

Plane xanthomas are yellow-to-red plaques found in the skin folds of the neck and trunk. They may be associated with familial dyslipidemias and various hematologic cancers. Xanthelasma is a type of plane xanthoma localized to the periorbital area, most commonly on the upper medial eyelid (

), and is characterized by soft, nontender, nonpruritic plaques. Xanthelasma may occur without dyslipidemia, particularly in older persons, but is often associated with familial dyslipidemias when present in a younger person. These lesions are also a classic feature of primary biliary cholangitis, a condition often associated with marked hypercholesterolemia.

Tuberous xanthomas occur over extensor surfaces and joints as waxy yellow-tinged papular lesions that may coalesce. Tendon xanthomas are subcutaneous nodules occurring on the extensor tendons, especially on the hands and the Achilles tendon; both tuberous and tendon xanthomas may be associated with familial hypercholesterolemia.
