Diagnostic Testing in Cardiology

The cornerstone of diagnosis in cardiovascular disease is the clinical history and physical examination. A careful history that includes symptom characteristics, timing, and duration; factors that exacerbate or relieve symptoms; and functional capacity is critical to ensuring a focused and appropriate diagnostic evaluation. Abnormal findings on the cardiovascular examination also may raise suspicion for specific cardiac conditions and guide test selection.

Cardiovascular testing can provide both diagnostic and prognostic information, and its use should be guided by symptoms, the pretest likelihood of disease, whether testing results will alter patient management, and shared decision making with patients.

Diagnostic testing for coronary artery disease (CAD) can be categorized as providing anatomic evidence of CAD burden and/or assessing functional ischemic burden.

Anatomic information on the degree and location of CAD is obtained from invasive angiography, coronary CT angiography (CCTA), and coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring.

Functional studies reveal the presence of ischemia, the location and severity of ischemia (single-photon emission CT [SPECT], PET, cardiac magnetic resonance [CMR] imaging), information on coronary blood flow (PET, fractional flow reserve [FFR]–CT), and development of wall motion abnormalities (echocardiography, CMR). Cardiac diagnostic testing modalities are summarized in [Table: Table: Diagnostic Testing for Coronary Artery Disease]

.

In non-acute stable patients presenting with possible CAD in whom testing is indicated, guidelines suggest CCTA is the preferred test in patients younger than 65 years and in those patients in whom less obstructive disease is suspected. Imaging-based stress testing is preferred for those aged 65 years or older and for patients in whom there is the suspicion of more obstructive disease. An exercise ECG remains a reasonable option in patients without contraindications. Otherwise, optimal diagnostic tests for CAD according to common clinical scenarios are presented in [Table: Table: Optimal Tests for Diagnosing CAD Based on Clinical Scenario]

.

Cardiac stress testing is commonly performed in patients in whom CAD is suspected or to stratify risk in patients with CAD. When performed in the evaluation of possible CAD, appropriate, cost-effective stress testing is based on the history, examination findings, and pretest probability of CAD (see Diagnosis and Evaluation of Stable Angina Pectoris in Cardiovascular Medicine). The pretest probability considers age; sex; symptoms; and, if known, CAC score. Stress testing is most effective in patients with an intermediate pretest probability of CAD (10% to 90%), in whom a positive test result significantly increases the likelihood of disease and a negative test result significantly decreases it. Stress testing in patients with a low likelihood of disease, such as young persons with atypical symptoms, often yields false-positive results, potentially resulting in unnecessary further testing, inaccurate diagnoses, and harms. In patients with a high pretest probability, invasive angiography rather than stress testing may be appropriate.

Assessment of the patient’s ability to exercise is important in determining the most appropriate stress test. Stress testing to evaluate for CAD should always be performed with exercise unless exercise is contraindicated or the patient is unable to exercise.

The decision to withhold cardiac medications such as nitrates and β-blockers before stress testing should be individualized. In patients who are undergoing exercise stress testing to diagnose CAD, cardiac medications that impair heart rate response (e.g., β-blockers) should be withheld for at least 24 hours before testing because these agents may lead to an inadequate peak heart rate. If the purpose of the stress test is to evaluate symptoms, determine efficacy of therapy, or determine prognosis in a patient with known CAD, then patients should continue their cardioactive medication regimen.

In patients with unchanged symptoms, the “warranty period” for a normal, adequate stress test is 1 year.

Exercise ECG is a reasonable diagnostic test in patients with normal findings on baseline ECG and no disabling comorbid conditions (e.g., frailty, marked obesity [BMI >40], peripheral artery disease, COPD, or orthopedic limitations). If there are baseline ECG abnormalities (e.g., ST-segment depression >1 mm, left bundle branch block [LBBB], left ventricular hypertrophy, paced rhythm, or preexcitation), exercise-induced ST-segment changes are not specific for CAD. Stress testing with adjunctive imaging or anatomic assessment with CCTA is indicated in these instances.

Exercise stress testing protocols use treadmill or bicycle ergometry to increase workload in a stepwise manner, which allows adequate time for the development of maximal metabolic demand. A standard Bruce protocol increases the speed and grade of the treadmill every 3 minutes. Achieving 85% of the age-predicted maximal heart rate is adequate to identify obstructive CAD; however, patients should exercise until limited by symptoms. Because heart rate and blood pressure are the major determinants of myocardial oxygen demand, achieving a rate pressure product (heart rate × systolic blood pressure) of at least 25,000 is considered an adequate workload. Stress testing should be terminated when the patient has exerted maximal effort, requests to stop, or experiences significant symptoms (angina or light-headedness). The test also should be stopped for exertional hypotension, significant hypertension (>200/110 mm Hg), ST-segment elevation or significant ST-segment depression, or significant arrhythmias.

Ischemia is identified on exercise ECG by the development of horizontal or downsloping ST-segment depression of at least 1 mm occurring 80 milliseconds after the J point (

). Unlike on a resting ECG, ST-segment depression cannot localize ischemia or suggest the culprit coronary artery. Exercise-induced hypotension or the absence of blood pressure augmentation may indicate significant obstructive disease.

Exercise stress testing also provides prognostic value in patients with known or suspected CAD. Exercise capacity is a powerful predictor of outcomes; individuals unable to achieve 5 metabolic equivalents of task, or the first stage of a Bruce protocol, have higher all-cause mortality. Heart rate recovery after cessation of exercise provides incremental prognostic information. A heart rate drop of less than 12/min in the first minute after exercise stops is associated with higher mortality. Information obtained from exercise stress testing also may be used in risk prediction models. The Duke Treadmill Score incorporates exercise duration, symptom development, and degree of ST-segment depression to calculate 5-year all-cause mortality in patients without known CAD.

Because of its simplicity, its lower cost, and widespread familiarity with its performance and interpretation, the standard treadmill ECG is a reasonable exercise test to select in patients with a normal resting ECG who can exercise.

In patients with obstructive CAD, reduced blood flow and myocardial ischemia result in a progression of myocardial abnormalities, termed the ischemic cascade. Initially, ischemia induces changes in perfusion, followed by diastolic and (at a later stage) systolic dysfunction, ECG changes, and lastly, angina. The addition of imaging studies to stress testing increases diagnostic sensitivity by detecting signs of ischemia earlier than those seen on ECG and localizing it.

Stress testing with imaging is an effective first-line diagnostic test for chest pain and is also indicated in patients with baseline ECG abnormalities that limit interpretation of the exercise ECG, or indeterminate findings on the exercise ECG. Depending on the modality used, stress testing with imaging compares wall motion, perfusion, and/or metabolism at baseline and after stress ( [Table: Table: Interpretation of Stress Testing With Imaging Results]

). Imaging with SPECT, PET, or CMR detects reduced myocardial perfusion as early evidence of ischemia. Systolic dysfunction, indicated by wall motion abnormalities during stress, can be detected by echocardiography or CMR imaging. Imaging choice should consider characteristics of the patient and modality as well as local availability and expertise (see [Table: Table: Diagnostic Testing for Coronary Artery Disease]

).

Exercise is preferred over pharmacologic stressors such as dobutamine and vasodilators, which are most useful when a patient is unable to exercise. Dobutamine, like exercise, increases myocardial oxygen demand and elicits ischemia because of insufficient perfusion to the affected myocardium. Vasodilators, such as dipyridamole, regadenoson, and adenosine, produce hyperemia and a flow disparity between myocardium supplied by unobstructed vessels and myocardium supplied by stenotic vessels where the ability of the distal vasculature to dilate further is impaired.

Exercise stress echocardiography provides information on ischemia, hemodynamic significance of valvular abnormalities, and pulmonary pressures during exercise. The sensitivity of stress echocardiography may be reduced in the setting of baseline wall motion abnormalities, systolic dysfunction, or single-vessel disease.

Exercise is performed with supine or upright bicycle ergometry, which allows continuous imaging, or with a treadmill protocol, which requires acquisition of post-stress images within 90 seconds. New wall motion abnormalities indicate ischemia in the visualized territory. Resting wall motion abnormalities that do not improve at peak exercise may indicate infarcted or hibernating myocardium (chronic but potentially reversible ischemic dysfunction).

With pharmacologic stress echocardiography, dobutamine is infused progressively (up to 40 μg/kg/min) to achieve 85% of age-predicted maximal heart rate. Atropine is additionally administered if the target heart rate is not achieved. In patients with LBBB or a paced rhythm, exercise is preferred over dobutamine.

Myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI), also known as nuclear stress testing, uses differences in myocardial blood flow to detect ischemia. MPI testing includes SPECT MPI and cardiac PET testing.

In SPECT MPI, a radiotracer is injected at rest and at peak exercise/vasodilation, and the radiotracer is taken up by the myocardium relative to blood flow. Rest images are compared with images obtained after stress. Perfusion defects observed only after stress indicate flow-limiting CAD (

). Regions with fixed defects (present at rest and with stress) may indicate infarcted or hibernating myocardium, and viability assessment can help distinguish between the two ( [Table: Table: Interpretation of Myocardial Viability Study Results]

). Gated images can provide an assessment of left ventricular systolic function. In patients with LBBB or paced rhythm undergoing MPI, vasodilator-induced stress is preferred to exercise.

SPECT imaging also can quantify the extent and severity of disease, providing additional prognostic information. High-risk features, such as multiple regions of hypoperfusion, reduction or lack of augmentation in post-stress ejection fraction, transient cavity dilatation, and wall motion abnormalities, are associated with a worse prognosis.

Technetium-based MPI has higher sensitivity and specificity than thallium-based studies and provides better image quality. Technetium-based agents also bind to the mitochondria, allowing for delayed imaging. In contrast, thallium uptake requires active metabolism, which may be useful in assessing myocardial viability.

Cardiac PET provides excellent diagnostic and prognostic information for patients with known or suspected CAD. PET provides better temporal and spatial resolution than does SPECT, which is helpful in patients with obesity or nondiagnostic SPECT results. CT may be used with PET to provide information on the presence of coronary artery calcification. PET radiotracers have a short half-life, resulting in lower radiation exposure and necessitating the use of vasodilators; there is no exercise PET protocol. Vasodilator stress also allows assessment of peak stress ejection fraction, quantification of absolute myocardial blood flow, and evaluation of myocardial metabolism. Cardiac PET can also assess myocardial viability in areas of scar to aid in revascularization decisions. The utility of PET in cardiac patients is limited by the availability of the technology.

CMR imaging may be used with dobutamine to assess wall motion abnormalities or with vasodilators such as adenosine to assess myocardial perfusion. It is commonly performed to evaluate the degree of infarction. Viability can be determined by evaluating the extent of myocardial fibrosis within the left ventricle, and measures of right and left ventricular function can be obtained with gating. CMR imaging is limited by operator expertise, length of time for image acquisition, and availability.

Anatomic assessment of the epicardial coronary arteries can be performed with noninvasive CCTA or invasive angiography. Both tests require administration of iodinated contrast agents and expose the patient to radiation. The ability to interpret CCTA may be limited in patients whose heart rate cannot be lowered sufficiently before scanning (e.g., less than 60 to 65/min) or who have extensive calcification and small distal arteries.

In select symptomatic patients, particularly those younger than 65 years or those in whom less obstructive disease is suspected, CCTA is an effective initial testing option for diagnosing CAD. In the PROMISE trial, 10,000 symptomatic patients in whom CAD was suspected were evaluated with an initial strategy of either anatomic testing with CCTA or functional testing. In patients with an intermediate pretest probability of CAD, the composite cardiovascular event rate was low (<1% per year) in both groups, and outcomes (death, myocardial infarction, hospitalization for unstable angina, or major procedural complication) at 2 years did not differ between groups.

CCTA also may play a role in evaluating acute chest pain in the emergency department. CCTA contributes to a reduced time to diagnosis without affecting safety (i.e., no difference in death or acute coronary syndromes [ACS] over 1 to 6 months of follow-up) compared with a standard evaluation including stress testing. CCTA is reasonable in intermediate-risk patients with acute chest pain and no known CAD with a negative or inconclusive evaluation for ACS. Careful consideration of patient factors is essential to avoid further testing, potential harms, and unnecessary costs.

Invasive coronary angiography provides two-dimensional images of the coronary vessel lumen through the injection of nonionic contrast material using long, thin catheters inserted through femoral, brachial, ulnar, or radial artery access. Invasive angiography should be considered in patients with symptoms and a high likelihood of CAD, those with high-risk findings on noninvasive testing, those with ACS, and those with CAD and ischemic symptoms refractory to medical therapy.

Fractional flow reserve (FFR) can be added to angiography or CCTA and measures the hemodynamic significance of a lesion and helps determine the need for intervention. FFR is the ratio of blood flow distal to the stenosis to blood flow proximal to the stenosis at maximal flow. It is measured during cardiac catheterization by placing a pressure wire across the stenosis and inducing conditions of maximal hyperemia, usually with adenosine. A FFR of less than 0.8 is indicative of a hemodynamically significant stenosis. Instantaneous wave-free ratio is a similar invasive functional assessment of coronary stenoses that does not use vasodilator administration. FFR-CT is performed by using computational fluid dynamics on CT-derived data sets. It is FDA approved and provides both anatomic and functional coronary data; it has higher specificity for diagnosing obstructive CAD than does CCTA alone. Limited availability of FFR-CT and potential delays in analysis affect its use in patients with acute symptoms.

Calcification of the coronary arteries indicates atherosclerosis and may be quantified with CT. Although CAC scoring provides information regarding the burden of disease, it cannot determine the degree of obstruction.

CAC scores are categorized as follows:

  • 0: no disease
  • 1 to 99: mild disease
  • 100 to 400: moderate disease
  • Greater than 400: severe disease

Normal reference values depend on age, ethnicity, and sex.

CAC measurement has been used for diagnosis and risk assessment in both symptomatic and asymptomatic patients. Assessment of CAC in asymptomatic patients should be limited to those at intermediate cardiovascular risk (and some patients at borderline risk) in whom CAC results may influence primary prevention therapy (see Primary Prevention of Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease in Cardiovascular Medicine). CAC score also is incorporated in the MESA Risk Score to predict 10-year coronary heart disease risk and increases the pretest probability of CAD. The absence of coronary artery calcification is associated with a low risk for cardiovascular events.

Cardiac diagnostic testing carries risks related to exercise; exposure to pharmacologic stress testing agents, contrast agents, or radiation; and vascular access for invasive procedures. In addition, inappropriate initial testing may lead to unnecessary downstream testing with added complications as well as emotional and financial costs.

There is a very small risk for myocardial infarction or death (1/2500 patients) with exercise stress testing. Absolute contraindications to exercise include unstable angina or acute myocardial infarction, uncontrolled arrhythmias, decompensated heart failure, acute pulmonary embolism or deep venous thrombosis, acute pericarditis or myocarditis, acute aortic dissection, and symptomatic severe aortic stenosis. Relative contraindications are left main coronary artery stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with severe obstruction, electrolyte abnormalities, high-degree atrioventricular (AV) block, and significant arrhythmias.

Adverse effects of vasodilator stress agents (most commonly, adenosine and regadenoson) include chest pain, headache, and flushing. AV block and bronchospasm also may occur. Theophylline may be given after testing to attenuate these effects. Vasodilator stress testing is contraindicated in patients with reactive airways disease with active wheezing, systolic blood pressure of less than 90 mm Hg, sick sinus syndrome, or high-degree AV block.

Contrast agents used in invasive angiography, coronary CCTA, CMR imaging, and echocardiography also pose a risk to the patient. Iodinated contrast material used in CT or angiography may result in acute kidney injury. Rarely, gadolinium contrast used in CMR imaging may cause nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in patients with end-stage kidney disease (see Imaging Contrast Agents in Nephrology). Microbubble contrast agents are used to enhance the endocardial borders in echocardiography and rarely may cause hypersensitivity reactions.

SPECT, PET, CAC scoring, CCTA, and coronary angiography all expose the patient to radiation. The level of radiation exposure depends on the procedure, equipment, choice of radiopharmaceutical agent and dose, operator technique, and patient characteristics (e.g., body size).

Coronary angiography may be complicated by vascular access problems, bleeding complications, coronary artery dissection, aortic dissection, and plaque disruption or thrombus leading to peripheral emboli, stroke, or myocardial infarction. Femoral artery access may be complicated by retroperitoneal hemorrhage, which should be suspected in patients with hypotension, back or flank pain, and/or a drop in hemoglobin level. Pseudoaneurysms at the arterial puncture sites occur more commonly with femoral artery access and may manifest as a large hematoma or new bruit at the access site. Arterial duplex ultrasonography is recommended for diagnosis of a suspected pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistula; CT imaging of the abdomen and pelvis is recommended for diagnosis of suspected retroperitoneal hemorrhage.

Diagnostic testing for structural heart disease should be considered in patients with suggestive history and physical examination findings, such as symptoms of heart failure; a grade 3/6 or higher systolic murmur; a late or holosystolic murmur; a diastolic or continuous murmur; or a murmur with accompanying symptoms, such as exertional dyspnea, light-headedness, or chest pain. Repeat imaging is indicated in patients with structural heart disease when there is a change in the clinical presentation, functional status, or examination findings; in congenital and valvular disease, routine surveillance imaging is guided by lesion severity (see Adult Congenital Heart Disease in Cardiovascular Medicine and General Principles of Valvular Heart Disease in Cardiovascular Medicine). Imaging modalities to evaluate for structural heart disease are listed in [Table: Table: Diagnostic Testing for Structural Heart Disease]

.

The mainstay of noninvasive imaging for structural heart abnormalities is transthoracic echocardiography (TTE). TTE evaluates right and left chamber size; thickness; and function, including wall motion. TTE also provides information on valvular pathology (including endocarditis), diastolic function, hemodynamics, and the pericardium. TTE can be used with intravenous agitated saline contrast, normally cleared by the pulmonary circulation, to document the presence of an intracardiac shunt. Dobutamine infusion during TTE may be used in patients with low-gradient aortic stenosis in the setting of reduced ejection fraction to help differentiate between severe aortic stenosis and pseudo-severe stenosis. Focused cardiac imaging with point-of-care ultrasound is commonly used in emergency medicine to assess gross cardiac function, chamber size, inferior vena cava size (a surrogate for volume status), and the presence of a pericardial effusion.

Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is commonly used to evaluate for infective endocarditis and its complications (e.g., abscess). TEE also may be used to better visualize valvular pathology, particularly if surgical or percutaneous intervention is planned; to evaluate specific structures that cannot be well visualized on TTE (e.g., prosthetic heart valves or implanted devices) or in patients with inclusive transthoracic imaging; to evaluate acute aortic abnormalities; to evaluate atrial septal defects and other congenital heart disease; to evaluate sources of embolic stroke; and to rule out left atrial thrombus before cardioversion (

). TEE requires moderate sedation and placement of the probe in the distal esophagus and stomach. Contraindications include esophageal strictures or active esophageal varices. Esophageal injury, including perforation and bleeding, is a rare complication.

CMR imaging may be used to evaluate myocardial and pericardial disease, including ischemic, inflammatory, or infiltrative processes. CMR is particularly useful in diagnosing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy when there is eccentric or apical hypertrophy that is difficult to visualize on echocardiography. CMR also can be used as an alternative to TEE to identify and stratify valvular pathology if TTE imaging is inadequate. Additionally, CMR can help in the evaluation of management of congenital heart disease.

Echocardiographic findings may raise suspicion for cardiac amyloidosis, but adjunctive imaging with CMR or tissue confirmation with biopsy is needed to confirm the diagnosis. 99m-Technetium pyrophosphate scintigraphy (^99mTc-PYP) has reemerged as a useful means for differentiating between amyloid subtypes, which guides patient management. ^99mTc-PYP imaging specifically identifies cardiac amyloidosis due to misfolded transthyretin proteins (ATTR), with a specificity greater than 99% in the absence of a monoclonal protein (see

).

The initial study in patients with palpitations, presyncope, or syncope when an arrhythmia is suspected should be a 12-lead resting ECG. The ECG may show evidence of preexcitation, ectopic rhythms, atrioventricular block, or intraventricular conduction delay, providing insight into the cause of the symptoms (see Arrhythmias in Cardiovascular Medicine). Echocardiography should be performed in patients in whom structural heart disease is suspected.

The intermittent and fleeting nature of arrhythmias can make diagnosis difficult. Diagnostic studies are selected on the basis of symptom frequency and the duration and timing capabilities of the recording monitor ( [Table: Table: Diagnostic Testing for Cardiac Arrhythmias]

). If symptoms occur daily, a 24- or 48-hour ambulatory ECG monitor (Holter monitor) may be used. Long-term ambulatory ECG monitors (e.g., long-term ambulatory ECG, event monitors) can be worn for up to 30 days if symptoms are less frequent. Most of these devices now can record both patient-triggered events as well as automatically detected arrhythmias based on heart rate and/or QRS morphology. In high-risk scenarios, mobile continuous outpatient telemetry can be used to provide near real-time notification of arrhythmias in the outpatient setting. An implanted loop recorder may be warranted in patients with very infrequent events.

Exercise stress testing frequently is used in patients with suspected or known arrhythmia to evaluate for chronotropic incompetence, ischemia, and exercise-induced arrhythmia.

Most patients do not require invasive electrophysiologic testing. Electrophysiology testing may be indicated in patients in whom the diagnosis remains indeterminate or in settings in which interventions may be needed to treat refractory arrhythmias (e.g., catheter ablation, permanent pacing).

Genetic testing for selected cardiovascular conditions is recommended by guidelines and expert consensus statements ( [Table: Table: Genetic Testing for Select Cardiovascular Phenotypes]

). Although internal medicine physicians should be familiar with the indications and options for cardiovascular genetic testing, genetic counseling and testing are best accomplished by referral to a specialized cardiovascular genetics team including cardiologists and genetics professionals. Evaluation for possible inherited cardiovascular conditions begins with a multigeneration family history with attention to disease phenotype, age of disease onset, and disease severity; these factors inform selection of the proband to maximize the yield of testing. Most monogenic cardiovascular diseases are transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner; however, autosomal recessive, X-linked, and mitochondrial transmission also are possible. Disease penetrance and expressivity vary widely among cardiovascular conditions.

Individuals being considered for genetic testing should undergo pre- and posttest genetic counseling with a qualified professional to discuss the benefits and limitations of testing. The counseling should address concerns such as the yield of testing, potential for discrimination based on test results, cost of testing, utility of results, and potential for psychologic distress. (For additional guidance, see Genetic Tests and Testing Strategies in Foundations of Clinical Practice.)

Test selection is based on the type of cardiovascular disease and the expected diagnostic yield, with phenotype-specific panels of genes most commonly used. The American College of Medical Genetics recommends five categories of variant classification:

  • Pathogenic
  • Likely pathogenic
  • Variant of uncertain significance
  • Likely benign
  • Benign

Identification of a pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in a clinically affected patient can inform treatment decisions and timing of intervention for selected cardiovascular conditions if used in conjunction with clinical risk features: for example, the need for a prophylactic defibrillator in genetic forms of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, the threshold for aortic surgery in patients with syndromic forms of aortopathy, and amyloid-specific treatment for patients with hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis.

In most cases, pathogenic or likely pathogenic genetic testing results are used to risk stratify family members who are at risk for developing the cardiovascular condition (

).
