Arrhythmias

This section provides an overall approach to arrhythmias and discusses the diagnosis and management of specific rhythm disorders.

Disruptions in cardiac rhythm or rate occur in seven basic patterns:

  • Early beats
  • Bigeminal beats
  • Grouped beats
  • Pauses
  • Bradycardia
  • Tachycardia
  • Chaotic rhythms

The fundamental diagnostic test for cardiac arrhythmia is the 12-lead ECG. It provides a comprehensive assessment of underlying cardiac electrical activity, but at a single point in time. Patients most commonly experience symptoms outside a health care environment and require cardiac rhythm measurement in an ambulatory setting. Therefore, ambulatory ECG (AECG) monitoring is a fundamental diagnostic modality (see [Table: Table: Diagnostic Testing for Cardiac Arrhythmias]

). AECG monitors are available in several forms, which vary primarily by the number of leads, capability of “real-time” monitoring and feedback of critical results, and potential for “full disclosure” of activity throughout the monitoring period.

The classic AECG device is the Holter monitor, typically used for 24 to 48 hours and recording three leads. Although Holter monitors do not provide real-time event alerts, they do provide full disclosure of data, including average heart rates, arrhythmia burden, ectopy counts, and trends for the entire monitoring period (up to 14 days, depending on the vendor). More recently, Holter monitors have been offered as a single-lead test to reduce the amount of inconvenience to patients with several wires. In contrast, cardiac event monitors are designed to capture specific “events” based on either automatic recognition of a potentially serious event or the patient’s trigger for a symptom (often up to 30 days). However, they usually do not provide real-time monitoring, and they do not produce full disclosure data. Finally, mobile continuous (outpatient) telemetry studies provide real-time monitoring and full disclosure data (up to 30 days); however, cost may be a limiting factor in their use.

In addition to the aforementioned clinical diagnostics, the use of consumer-based devices (e.g., “wearables”) is a rapidly evolving space for arrhythmia diagnosis and is already providing great value to patients and clinicians. Although a detailed review is beyond the scope of this text, it is important to consider the use of devices that specifically record cardiac electrical activity (e.g., smartwatches, personal ECG monitors) in contrast to pulse-reading, plethysmography-based devices. Devices that can record a single ECG essentially function as portable, consumer-based event monitors for patient-triggered events. Patients can record a one- or even six-lead ECG and send the tracing to their clinician for interpretation.

Antiarrhythmic agents have traditionally been organized according to primary mechanism of action using the Vaughan-Williams classification system ( [Table: Table: Commonly Used Antiarrhythmic Medications]

). Class I and class III agents are the most effective antiarrhythmic drugs; however, because of their membrane-active effects, they carry some paradoxical risk of inducing arrhythmia.

Flecainide and propafenone are the most commonly used class I agents (IC); they are used primarily to treat atrial arrhythmias and usually in conjunction with AV nodal blockers to prevent 1:1 atrial flutter. Toxicity can manifest as QRS widening (

and

). Class IC agents are contraindicated in patients with ischemic or structural heart disease because of the risk for promoting ventricular arrhythmias and death.

Class II agents (β-blockers) and class IV agents (nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers) are commonly used to inhibit AV conduction (to decrease rate) in patients with supraventricular or atrial arrhythmias. These medications may also be used to treat ventricular arrhythmias and several of them carry other indications such as for treatment of hypertension and heart failure.

Class III agents sotalol and dofetilide are used to treat atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. Class III antiarrhythmic therapy typically is initiated in an inpatient setting because of the potential for prolongation of the QT interval, with regular assessment of the corrected QT interval. Dofetilide is particularly notorious for common and dangerous drug-drug interactions.

Amiodarone, a multichannel blocker, is frequently used to treat patients with recurrent ventricular tachycardia or AF. Amiodarone has a low risk for proarrhythmia; however, it is associated with thyroid, liver, lung, and eye toxicities as well as neurologic adverse effects. Thyroid and liver function should be monitored every 6 months, and pulmonary surveillance (chest radiograph or pulmonary function testing) should occur at least annually, although there is some discrepancy in the recommended frequency of pulmonary screening between national guidelines and the package insert. Ophthalmologic examination should also be performed annually. Amiodarone interacts with many drugs, including warfarin, statins, and digoxin. Dronedarone, another multichannel blocker, may be used in patients with paroxysmal AF and no overt heart failure.

Digoxin and adenosine are excluded from the Vaughan-Williams classification. Digoxin is a positive inotropic agent that also increases vagal activity, leading to a lower resting heart rate. It can be used for rate control in patients with AF. Adenosine, which acts rapidly and is equally rapidly metabolized, is used in the acute treatment of arrhythmias to interrupt AV conduction and terminate supraventricular tachycardia (SVT).

Bradycardia (heart rate <50/min) may be asymptomatic or associated with light-headedness, syncope, exertional intolerance, dyspnea, or fatigue. It may be a normal finding or result from disease in the sinus node, atrioventricular (AV) node, or His-Purkinje system or from autonomic dysfunction.

Diagnostic evaluation consists of a thorough history, physical examination, focused laboratory testing (electrolyte levels, thyroid function testing), and resting 12-lead ECG. The evaluation should also include investigation for extrinsic and reversible causes of bradycardia, including ischemia, myocarditis, endocarditis, hypothyroidism, infectious diseases (e.g., Lyme disease), neurologic events, electrolyte disturbances, and medications (especially AV nodal blockers and parasympathomimetics). Although AV nodal blockers such as β-blockers frequently cause sinus bradycardia and block at or above the AV node, they are much less prone to cause infranodal block, such as complete heart block.

Echocardiography is frequently performed to exclude underlying structural abnormalities that might change management. Exercise stress testing to assess chronotropic competence, the expected increase in heart rate with exercise, as well as ambulatory ECG monitoring may be helpful. Clues from the history and physical examination (e.g., prior rash suggestive of Lyme disease) may dictate further testing. In patients with nocturnal bradycardia or conduction disturbances, sleep apnea should be considered and, if appropriate, evaluated and treated. Isolated asymptomatic bradyarrhythmias during sleep, however, are unlikely to require a permanent pacemaker.

Sinus bradycardia is defined as the presence of sinus rhythm with a heart rate below 60/min; however, some experts propose a more pragmatic definition of heart rate below 50/min because rates of 50 to 60/min are rarely symptomatic. Sinus bradycardia may be appropriate in trained athletes and during sleep. The most common extrinsic cause is medication use (most often β-blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, and donepezil) ( [Table: Table: Common Medications That Suppress the Sinoatrial Node]

). Inappropriate or pathologic sinus bradycardia is most frequently caused by sinus node dysfunction due to age-related myocardial fibrosis. Otherwise, sinus node dysfunction may result from right coronary ischemia, hypothyroidism, intracranial hypertension, postoperative scarring or fibrosis from cardiothoracic surgery, or infiltrative or inflammatory disorders (e.g., sarcoidosis).

AV block is classified as first degree, second degree, or third degree. First-degree AV block is defined by a delay in AV conduction (PR interval >200 ms). Although patients with first-degree AV block are asymptomatic, large cohort studies have demonstrated an association between first-degree AV block and an increased risk for atrial fibrillation (AF) and all-cause mortality.

In second-degree AV block, only some P waves conduct to the ventricles. Mobitz type 1 second-degree (Wenckebach) AV block is characterized electrocardiographically by a PR interval that progressively prolongs until a QRS complex is dropped, resulting in grouped beating (

). Mobitz type 2 second-degree AV block is typified by intermittent nonconducted P waves with unchanging PR intervals (

). When 2:1 block is present, the Mobitz type cannot be determined definitively. However, the distinction between types is important: Mobitz type 2 AV block usually occurs below the AV node and has a higher risk for progression to complete heart block. High-degree AV block refers to the presence of more than one successive nonconducted P wave, resulting in several consecutive P waves without QRS complexes.

In third-degree AV block, also termed complete heart block, no P waves conduct to the ventricles. AV dissociation is observed on the ECG (

).

Higher-grade AV blocks (Mobitz type 2 second and third degree) are generally a reflection of disease below the AV node (“infranodal conduction disease”). Surface ECG changes in the QRS morphology may also be a reflection of infranodal conduction disease. These include bundle branch blocks (right or left) and blocks of a portion of the left bundle (anterior and posterior fascicular blocks;

). Although typically these findings are not as ominous as those of higher-grade AV block, they may reflect significant underlying cardiac pathology, especially if progressive. Further evaluation of these findings should be guided by additional factors, including symptomatology and history of known cardiovascular disease.

Patients with hemodynamically significant bradycardia should receive atropine. Chronotropic drug infusions (e.g., dopamine or epinephrine) may be given until transcutaneous pacing or a temporary pacing wire (preferred) can be implemented. Temporary transvenous pacing is indicated for transient conditions causing hemodynamically unstable bradycardia or asystole. Cause-specific interventions also may be warranted (e.g., antidotes or reversal strategies for toxic ingestion/overdose).

In hemodynamically stable patients, reversible and extrinsic causes of bradycardia should always be addressed before more invasive measures, such as permanent pacing, are considered.

Common indications for permanent pacing include

  • Symptomatic bradycardia without reversible cause (including chronotropic incompetence)
  • Permanent AF and symptomatic bradycardia
  • Alternating bundle branch block (signifies high risk for subsequent complete heart block)
  • Mobitz type 2 second-degree AV block, high-degree AV block, or complete heart block, regardless of symptoms

Mobitz type 1 second-degree AV block commonly reflects changes in autonomic tone rather than intrinsic conduction disease; in the absence of underlying cardiac symptoms and disease, it usually does not require intervention other than addressing any underlying cause. Patients with stable left bundle branch block or right bundle branch block with or without a prolonged PR interval do not require permanent pacing because these intraventricular conduction delays have a low risk for progressing to complete heart block (1%-3% per year).

Types of implanted cardiac electronic devices, their functions, and their general indications are reviewed in [Table: Table: Cardiac Implantable Electronic Devices for Rhythm Disorders]

. Leadless pacing offers an important alternative to transvenous pacing in managing bradyarrhythmias.

shows a leadless pacemaker in the region of the right ventricle. The latest approved devices are now available, in limited release, for both atrial and ventricular implantation with clinical indications similar to those for traditional transvenous devices.

More specific approaches to pacing are emerging in which the ventricular lead is positioned in or near the specialized conduction system to mimic native conduction (“conduction system pacing”). Such approaches may improve the hemodynamics of ventricular pacing and occasionally may yield an ECG that appears indistinguishable from the patient’s underlying ventricular conduction.

Patients with tachycardia (heart rate >100/min) may be asymptomatic or experience tachypalpitations, a sensation of skipped beats, light-headedness, dizziness, chest discomfort, dyspnea, exertional intolerance, fatigue, progressive heart failure, near-syncope, or syncope. In asymptomatic patients, tachycardia may be discovered incidentally.

Documentation of tachycardia on ECG and correlation with symptoms are key. A 12-lead ECG recorded during symptoms, although often not possible to obtain, is ideal in terms of diagnostic value (see Diagnostic Testing for Cardiac Arrhythmias in Cardiovascular Medicine for strategies in selecting an appropriate monitoring device). On the basis of ECG findings, tachyarrhythmias are traditionally categorized as supraventricular or ventricular. Supraventricular arrhythmias involve conduction through the AV node and are characterized by normal-appearing QRS complexes unless complicated by an aberrant ventricular condition (e.g., bundle branch block). Ventricular arrhythmias originate below the AV node and are characterized by abnormal-appearing and widened QRS complexes.

In addition to a thorough history with medication review and physical examination, thyroid function testing and echocardiography may be considered in select patients with tachycardia.

Sinus tachycardia (sinus rhythm with a heart rate >100/min) is the most common tachycardia and is characteristically the result of physiologic demand or distress; thus, it may represent one of the most concerning rhythms in the hospitalized patient. The most common causes include pain, hypovolemia or anemia, intoxication or withdrawal (e.g., stimulants, opioids, alcohol), endocrine derangement (e.g., hyperthyroidism), or an acute cardiopulmonary event (e.g., pulmonary embolism). Attribution of sinus tachycardia to more benign causes, such as exercise, anxiety, or dysautonomia, is predicated on the exclusion of more serious causes. Treatment should focus primarily on the underlying cause, and pharmacotherapy to primarily and empirically reduce heart rate (e.g., β-blockers) is discouraged.

Inappropriate sinus tachycardia (IST) is a disorder characterized by an elevated resting heart rate, with exaggerated increases in heart rate with light activity. The sinus rate typically decreases during sleep. IST frequently presents in women in their second to fourth decade. Symptoms vary and may include palpitations, light-headedness, syncope (or near-syncope), dyspnea, and fatigue. Most important, the diagnosis of IST is based on the exclusion of secondary causes of tachycardia, such as hyperthyroidism, anemia, pheochromocytoma, and structural heart disease. First-line therapy is removal of aggravating factors and exercise therapy. In patients with bothersome and persistent symptoms, pharmacologic therapy may be considered primarily to improve symptoms, but the condition frequently improves over time.

Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is another condition that often presents with tachycardia. POTS is a form of dysautonomia characterized by orthostatic intolerance and excessive tachycardia, particularly with standing. Diagnostic criteria for POTS include an increase in heart rate of 30/min or more or an increase to greater than 120/min within 10 minutes of standing. Behavioral modification, compression stockings, exercise training, and increased fluid intake are important components of therapy. Medical therapy for POTS is multipronged and variable and may include β-blockers, ivabradine (off-label use and contraindicated in pregnancy), fludrocortisone, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (off-label use), midodrine, droxidopa (off-label use), and pyridostigmine (off-label use).

SVTs are rapid heart rhythms that arise from the atrium or require conduction through the AV node. Although AF and atrial flutter are technically SVTs, the term supraventricular tachycardia is generally not applied to AF or atrial flutter. SVTs can affect all age groups; prevalence is higher in women than in men. Patients often have repeated episodes of tachycardia and may report palpitations, a sensation of pounding in the neck, fatigue, light-headedness, chest discomfort, dyspnea, presyncope, and, less commonly, syncope.

The ECG typically demonstrates a narrow-complex tachycardia; however, wide QRS complexes (>120 ms) may be present in cases of bundle branch block, aberrancy, pacing, or anterograde accessory pathway conduction (preexcited tachycardia). SVTs usually occur independent of structural heart disease, although echocardiography should be performed to exclude underlying cardiac dysfunction or structural defects.

Vagal maneuvers, including the Valsalva maneuver or carotid sinus massage, are first-line therapy to restore sinus rhythm acutely in patients with SVT. Adenosine may be used to terminate SVT and simultaneously help diagnose its mechanism. Tachycardias that terminate with adenosine are typically AV node dependent (AV nodal reentrant tachycardia [AVNRT] and AV reciprocating tachycardia [AVRT]), whereas continued atrial activity (P waves) during induced AV block with adenosine is consistent with an atrial tachycardia.

AVNRT accounts for two thirds of all cases of SVT, not including cases of AF and atrial flutter. It is caused by a reentrant circuit within the AV node that uses both the fast and slow pathways. AVNRT is typically characterized by a short RP interval with a retrograde P wave inscribed very close to the QRS complex.

AVNRT may be terminated with vagal maneuvers or adenosine. AV nodal blockers (β-blockers or calcium channel blockers) are used to prevent recurrent AVNRT. In patients with AVNRT, catheter ablation should also be considered as first-line therapy, especially in those who do not tolerate or prefer to avoid long-term medical therapy. Catheter ablation of AVNRT has a high success rate, although it is associated with a small (<1%) risk for injury to the AV node, necessitating pacemaker implantation.

AVRT is an accessory pathway–mediated tachycardia that is often associated with preexcitation (delta wave) on ECG (

). Early ventricular activation over the accessory pathway causes shortening of the PR interval and slurring of the initial part of the QRS complex. In AVRT, conduction is anterograde over the AV node (orthodromic, narrow-complex AVRT) in 90% to 95% of cases; conduction is anterograde over the accessory pathway (antidromic, wide-complex AVRT) in the remaining cases.

Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome is defined by symptomatic AVRT with evidence of preexcitation on resting ECG. AF occurs in up to one third of patients with WPW syndrome. Rapid conduction over an accessory pathway in AF may result in ventricular fibrillation (VF) and sudden cardiac death (SCD), although this occurs in less than 1% of cases of WPW syndrome.

Risk stratification for SCD in WPW syndrome may be performed with exercise testing, although more frequently, patients are referred for electrophysiology testing for both risk stratification and curative ablation. Catheter ablation is first-line therapy for patients with WPW syndrome. The success rate for ablation is high but is dictated by the location of the accessory pathway. Antiarrhythmic therapy is second-line therapy.

In asymptomatic patients with preexcitation on ECG, management is controversial. Invasive testing is generally not required unless the patient has a high-risk occupation, such as a commercial airline pilot.

Premature atrial contractions (PACs) are early isolated beats that arise from the atria. They are exceedingly common, and their frequency increases with age. During ambulatory ECG monitoring, only 1% of persons have no PACs. High PAC burden is associated with increased risk for AF. Symptomatic PACs are typically treated with β-blockers or calcium channel blockers.

Atrial tachycardia may arise in the presence or absence of structural heart disease. It is characterized by a rate greater than 100/min and initiation from an atrial site other than the sinus node. β-Blocker or calcium channel blocker therapy is first-line treatment for symptomatic atrial tachycardia. Second-line treatment is catheter ablation or antiarrhythmic drug therapy. Ablation success rates are generally lower in patients with atrial tachycardia than in those with other SVTs.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is typified by three or more P-wave morphologies and a heart rate greater than 100/min (

). It is usually seen in patients with severe pulmonary disease.

AF is characterized by disorganized atrial activity with an irregularly irregular ventricular response on ECG (

). It is the most common sustained arrhythmia. Lifetime risk for AF is 25% in patients older than 40 years, and the incidence increases significantly with age. AF is associated with an increased risk for adverse cardiovascular events, including stroke and heart failure, as well as increased risk for dementia.

AF is usually the result of long-standing risk factors, such as diabetes mellitus, smoking, significant alcohol consumption, obesity, hypertension, coronary artery disease (CAD), heart failure, and obstructive sleep apnea. Behavioral risk factor modification, including increased activity, weight loss, smoking cessation, and abstinence from alcohol, is recommended to reduce risk. Modification of caffeine intake is unnecessary. Bariatric surgery should be considered for appropriate candidates. Blood pressure and blood glucose control and obstructive sleep apnea management also reduce risk.

AF is less commonly caused by reversible or acute physiologic insults, including pulmonary embolism, critical illness, or hyperthyroidism. When there are no identified risk factors, a predisposing genetic background is often present. AF immediately after cardiac surgery (postoperative AF) is a common phenomenon that also represents a “reversible” cause; it does not necessarily portend chronic AF, although perioperative AF is increasingly recognized as possibly warranting longer-term evaluation (see Atrial Fibrillation in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Patients with AF may be asymptomatic or experience palpitations, light-headedness, dizziness, dyspnea, exercise intolerance, fatigue, chest pain, near-syncope, or, rarely, syncope. In some cases, AF may lead to hemodynamic compromise, especially in patients with advanced diastolic dysfunction or restrictive cardiomyopathy. Patients with AF may also present with tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy or overt heart failure.

Among patients aged 55 years and older with an ischemic neurologic event (i.e., stroke or transient ischemic attack) of undetermined source, occult AF is thought to be present in up to 25% of cases, and 14- to 30-day ambulatory ECG monitoring is indicated for detection. If 14- to 30-day ambulatory monitoring is inconclusive, implantation of a cardiac monitor (loop recorder) may be reasonable to detect silent AF. Although such monitoring will increase the discovery of AF, data are lacking as to whether subsequent anticoagulation improves outcomes in patients with cryptogenic stroke and silent AF.

AF is now categorized by stages to recognize it as a disease continuum that requires a different strategy at each stage, including prevention, lifestyle and risk factor modification, screening, and therapy. When considering treatment, the duration of AF is an important factor. Paroxysmal AF stops spontaneously within 7 days of onset, whereas persistent AF lasts for 7 days or more or requires cardioversion to restore sinus rhythm. Long-standing persistent AF is continuous, with a duration of more than 1 year. Permanent AF refers to cases in which the physician and patient have abandoned attempts to maintain sinus rhythm.

On diagnosis, reversible causes must be ruled out. All patients should undergo thyroid function testing to evaluate for hyperthyroidism. Echocardiography is indicated to evaluate for underlying structural heart disease. Patients with risk factors for or symptoms suggestive of sleep apnea should undergo testing.

Urgent cardioversion (electrical or pharmacologic) is indicated in patients with AF and a rapid ventricular rate contributing to hypotension, acute myocardial ischemia, or decompensated heart failure. In patients with AF or atrial flutter of more than 48 hours’ duration or unknown duration that requires immediate cardioversion, anticoagulation should be initiated as soon as possible and continued for at least 4 weeks unless contraindicated. The decision about long-term anticoagulation should be based on the thromboembolic risk profile and bleeding risk profile (see Long-Term Management of Atrial Fibrillation in Cardiovascular Medicine).

In stable patients, the primary goals of therapy are to:

  • Prevent stroke
  • Control heart rate
  • Minimize or eliminate symptoms
  • Modify underlying risk factors

In patients who are not undergoing cardioversion, acute intravenous anticoagulation is usually unnecessary; however, oral anticoagulation should be initiated if the patient has sufficient risk factors for stroke.

If cardioversion is planned, the duration of AF guides antithrombotic therapy. AF with a known duration of less than 48 hours confers a low risk for thrombus formation and subsequent stroke. In patients who are otherwise at low risk for stroke, pre- and postprocedural anticoagulation need only be considered. Otherwise, preprocedural anticoagulation is reasonable as soon as possible before cardioversion for men with a CHA~2DS~2-VASc score of 2 or greater and for women with a score of 3 or greater, followed by at least 4 weeks of anticoagulant therapy.

In patients in whom the duration of AF is unclear or in whom AF has lasted longer than 48 hours, anticoagulation therapy for 3 weeks is recommended before cardioversion. In patients who would benefit from cardioversion sooner, transesophageal echocardiography, contrast CT, or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging may be performed to exclude the presence of left atrial appendage thrombus and facilitate urgent cardioversion. All patients with a duration of AF that is unclear or is 48 hours or longer who undergo cardioversion must receive anticoagulants for at least 4 weeks after the procedure because of a persistent increased risk for thromboembolic events.

Heart rate control is necessary in patients with rapid ventricular rates to improve cardiac function and alleviate symptoms. Acutely, the goal heart rate should be between 60/min and 110/min. Commonly used medications include AV nodal blockers, such as metoprolol or diltiazem. Intravenous or oral administration may be appropriate depending on symptoms. In patients with left ventricular (LV) dysfunction, calcium channel blockers should be avoided. Digoxin may be used as adjunctive therapy to improve rate control, especially in patients with heart failure.

Arterial thromboembolic events are the most serious complication of AF and may occur in any form of AF (paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent). In patients with nonvalvular AF (AF in the absence of a mechanical prosthetic valve or moderate/severe mitral stenosis), the presence of comorbid conditions (e.g., heart failure, hypertension, diabetes, or vascular disease) may increase the risk for thromboembolism 15- to 20-fold.

The decision to initiate oral anticoagulation for stroke prevention depends on the patient’s thromboembolic risk and the absence of obvious contraindications. Current guidelines recommend use of the CHA~2DS~2-VASc score in patients with nonvalvular AF. The CHA~2DS~2-VASc score is not used in patients with valvular AF or those with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy because these patients usually receive anticoagulation because of a heightened risk for thromboembolism absent other risk factors.

In all other patients, adjusted stroke rates and recommendations for antithrombotic therapy based on the CHA~2DS~2-VASc score are shown in [Table: Table: Recommendations for Nonvalvular Atrial Fibrillation and Flutter]

. The 2023 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association/Heart Rhythm Society focused update on AF recommends anticoagulation to prevent stroke in patients with nonvalvular AF who have a CHA~2DS~2-VASc score of 2 or greater in men or 3 or greater in women; however, greater leeway is now acknowledged to include other factors in the decision (e.g., chronic kidney disease, arrhythmia burden). The American College of Chest Physicians guideline on antithrombotic therapy for AF recommends anticoagulation for patients with one or more nonsex CHA~2DS~2-VASc stroke risk factors (score of ≥1 in men or ≥2 in women). Antiplatelet therapy is no longer recommended for stroke prevention in AF.

Oral anticoagulation in patients with nonvalvular AF can be accomplished with a vitamin K antagonist (warfarin) or direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) ( [Table: Table: Anticoagulants for Stroke Prevention in Atrial Fibrillation]

). DOACs are recommended in preference to warfarin in DOAC-eligible patients. Only warfarin, however, should be used in patients with valvular AF (moderate or severe mitral stenosis or mechanical valve prosthesis).

Dose-adjusted warfarin is an effective, low-cost therapy; however, its limitations include the need for frequent monitoring and adjustment and many food and drug interactions. The safety and efficacy of warfarin therapy depend on the time that the patient is in the therapeutic range (INR, 2-3). Management of warfarin overdose and warfarin-related bleeding is discussed in Warfarin in Hematology.

Four DOACs are approved for the prevention of stroke in AF: dabigatran, an oral direct thrombin inhibitor, and the factor Xa inhibitors rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban. All these agents have consistently been shown to be at least as safe and effective as dose-adjusted warfarin. Of note, patients receiving dabigatran and rivaroxaban have a higher risk for gastrointestinal bleeding relative to warfarin. Dabigatran may also be associated with dyspepsia.

DOACs have shorter half-lives than warfarin; however, no quick, readily available assay exists to determine their anticoagulant activity. Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate is recommended for life-threatening bleeding due to rivaroxaban, apixaban, or edoxaban. Idarucizumab is a dabigatran-reversal agent available for emergency invasive or surgical procedures or in cases of uncontrolled or life-threatening bleeding.

Kidney and liver function should be evaluated before initiation of a DOAC and reevaluated at least annually. See Direct Oral Anticoagulants in Hematology for recommendations regarding DOAC dosing in patients with chronic kidney or liver disease.

In patients with AF who have undergone percutaneous coronary intervention for acute coronary syndrome or drug-eluting stent placement, both anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapies are necessary in patients with a CHA~2DS~2-VASc score of 2 or greater. After a short course (1-4 weeks) of “triple therapy” with an oral anticoagulant, aspirin, and P2Y~12 inhibitor, “double therapy” with clopidogrel or ticagrelor plus a DOAC is recommended over triple therapy to reduce the risk for bleeding. Oral anticoagulant therapy alone may be reasonable in these patients after 1 year (see Antiplatelet and Anticoagulant Therapy After Revascularization in Cardiovascular Medicine). In patients receiving two or more antithrombotic agents, it is recommended that a proton pump inhibitor be initiated and NSAIDs be avoided to reduce the risk for gastrointestinal bleeding.

In patients with AF and stable CAD, treatment with rivaroxaban alone is noninferior to rivaroxaban plus aspirin in the prevention of the composite end point of stroke, systemic embolization, myocardial infarction (MI), need for revascularization, or death from any cause. Rivaroxaban monotherapy also is associated with significantly less bleeding.

The first priority among patients with AF is to control the ventricular rate. Rate control with a resting heart rate goal of less than 80/min is reasonable for symptomatic management of AF. A lenient rate control strategy (resting heart rate <110/min) may be reasonable for asymptomatic patients without LV dysfunction. β-Blockers, calcium channel blockers, and less often, digoxin are used to control the ventricular rate, although combination therapy may be necessary. Aside from resting heart rate assessment, evaluation of the heart rate with activity, such as with a 6-minute walk test, stress test, or 24-hour ambulatory ECG monitoring, may be performed.

A rhythm control strategy to treat AF by maintaining sinus rhythm may be pursued with shared decision making with the patient. Certain subgroups of patients with AF may have greater benefit from a rhythm control strategy, including those with heart failure (especially with reduced systolic function), symptomatic AF, or AF of less than 1 year’s duration; younger patients; and patients with fewer comorbid conditions. A rhythm control approach also may improve long-term clinical outcomes ( [Table: Table: Rhythm Versus Rate Control of Atrial Fibrillation]

). A strategy of early rhythm control (within 1 year of diagnosis) among patients at high risk for adverse cardiovascular events was tested in the randomized EAST-AFNET 4 trial. High risk was defined as age older than 75 years or a previous transient ischemic attack or stroke, or meeting two of the following criteria: age older than 65 years, female sex, heart failure, hypertension, diabetes, severe CAD, chronic kidney disease, and LV hypertrophy. Early rhythm control (drugs or ablation) reduced the primary composite end point of cardiovascular death, stroke, or hospitalization for heart failure or acute coronary syndrome compared with usual care.

Rhythm control often requires cardioversion in addition to antiarrhythmic therapy, which is guided by the patient’s comorbid conditions and safety considerations. However, catheter ablation has been shown to be more effective than antiarrhythmic drugs, with an acceptable safety profile.

Catheter ablation with pulmonary vein isolation is an effective rhythm control therapy in patients with symptomatic AF and may be considered in selected patients as first-line therapy. Catheter ablation is most effective in patients without significant left atrial enlargement and without multiple comorbid conditions. One year after the procedure, 70% to 90% of patients with paroxysmal AF are symptom-free; however, success rates vary. Complications include thromboembolism (0.5%-1% risk), tamponade, and vascular complications (e.g., insertion hematoma, pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula, retroperitoneal bleeding). Longer-term complications, such as pulmonary vein stenosis, are uncommon. In the latest guidelines, AF ablation has emerged as first-line therapy among specific patients, including younger (age <75 years), more symptomatic patients. This is in part supported by data demonstrating reduced progression of disease associated with ablation. Anticoagulation has been continued indefinitely following successful catheter ablation, as indicated by the CHA~2DS~2-VASc score; however, emerging data may change this practice. The ablation procedure and associated technology are also changing rapidly, and newer approaches using alternative energy sources appear to reduce the risk of complications. Similarly, the treatment of advanced, long-standing persistent AF remains a challenge and is the target of alternative approaches (e.g., hybrid surgical approaches).

AV node ablation is an option for patients with AF who continue to have symptomatic tachycardia despite rate and rhythm control therapy. Therapeutic ablation of the AV node requires implantation of a permanent pacemaker. These patients remain in AF and still require anticoagulation.

Approximately 10% to 25% of patients with AF have contraindications to oral anticoagulation or discontinue therapy for various reasons, including prior bleeding events or extreme bleeding risk. In patients with moderate to high risk for stroke (CHA~2DS~2-VASc score ≥3), left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) may be considered to prevent stroke and systemic thromboembolism. Occlusion of the left atrial appendage can be achieved percutaneously with an implanted self-expanding device or with surgical closure. However, appropriate patient selection remains a challenge, and most patients undergoing percutaneous LAAO require at least short-term oral anticoagulation while the device endothelializes. These patients also continue receiving long-term antiplatelet therapy. These patients may still be at risk for thromboembolism due to residual “leak” around the device and device-related thrombus. There is no standard of care for routine postprocedure imaging surveillance.

AF complicates nearly 40% of heart failure cases, and the combination of AF and heart failure dramatically worsens outcomes. Several clinical trials demonstrated that aggressive efforts to achieve rhythm control in patients with AF and concomitant heart failure decrease morbidity and mortality. Similarly, in patients who have heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, recent clinical trials showed that catheter ablation of AF is associated with a favorable effect on morbidity and mortality compared with medical therapy. Patient selection for catheter ablation remains important to balance the periprocedural risks (although they are low) versus the expected benefit (which may still be limited in patients with very advanced disease).

Subclinical AF most commonly refers to AF that is asymptomatic and brief (definitions range from 20 seconds to <24 hours). It is being increasingly recognized because of the growing prevalence of implantable cardiac devices and widespread availability of ambulatory ECG monitors (e.g., mobile continuous telemetry) and consumer devices (e.g., personal ECG monitors, smartwatches). Because episodes of subclinical AF are frequently asymptomatic and short-lived, symptom management and rate control are rarely required. Subclinical AF is associated with progression to AF; therefore, it is reasonable to consider traditional AF risk factor modification. In addition, stroke risk in patients with subclinical AF may be elevated. Recent guidelines for AF management recommend that oral anticoagulation be considered for patients who have either device-detected AF lasting 24 hours or longer and a CHA~2DS~2-VASc score of 2 or greater or device-detected AF lasting 5 minutes to 24 hours and a CHA~2DS~2-VASc score of 3 or greater. Another scenario in which the evidence is clearer is the detection of AF lasting more than 30 seconds among patients with embolic stroke of undetermined source (cryptogenic stroke); anticoagulation is routinely indicated in these patients. Implantable loop recorders to detect subclinical AF may be indicated in select patients with embolic stroke of undetermined source in whom ambulatory monitoring has failed to show AF.

Atrial flutter is an organized macro-reentrant tachycardia with discrete regular atrial activity on ECG, usually with an atrial rate of 250/min to 300/min. Typical atrial flutter, the dominant form in patients without prior cardiac disease, is the result of counterclockwise reentry around the tricuspid annulus. It is characterized electrocardiographically by a sawtooth pattern with inverted flutter waves in leads II, III, and aVF and positive flutter waves in lead V~1 (

). Atypical flutter is seen primarily among patients with prior ablation for AF or prior cardiac surgery. In atypical flutter, the circuit is usually in other locations in the right and/or left atria and treatment success may be lower owing to higher complexity of disease.

Management of anticoagulation in the setting of chronic atrial flutter is similar to that for AF; however, a rhythm control strategy is favored in atrial flutter because rate control may be difficult and often requires high doses of more than one AV nodal blocker. Catheter ablation is the definitive treatment for typical atrial flutter because of a very high success rate (>95%) and low complication rate.

Premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) occur in up to 75% of healthy persons. Symptoms include palpitations or the perception of skipped beats. Forceful beats are caused by increased cardiac filling during the pause after the PVC. PVCs occur more often in patients with hypertension, LV hypertrophy, previous MI, and other forms of structural heart disease, such as nonischemic cardiomyopathy.

In the absence of high-risk features (syncope, family history of premature SCD, structural heart disease), reassurance is often appropriate and medical therapy is unnecessary. However, PVCs require treatment if symptoms are bothersome or frequent (>10% of all beats or 10,000 PVCs per day). PVC-induced cardiomyopathy may result from frequent PVCs (generally >10%-15% of beats), although it occurs only in a minority of patients (see Tachycardia-Mediated Cardiomyopathy in Cardiovascular Medicine).

First-line treatment for PVC suppression is β-blocker or calcium channel blocker therapy. β-Blockers are preferred in patients with ventricular dysfunction. Membrane-active antiarrhythmic therapy (e.g., flecainide) may be used if PVCs persist despite β-blockade or calcium channel blockade. Catheter ablation should be considered in patients with continued frequent PVCs despite medical therapy, patients who cannot tolerate medical therapy, and patients who develop PVC-induced cardiomyopathy.

VT is a wide-complex, usually monomorphic, tachycardia (QRS complex ≥120 ms) originating from the ventricles. The development of VT is facilitated by the presence of abnormal ventricular conduction and/or myocardial scar tissue, and it usually occurs in patients with structural heart disease, including both ischemic and nonischemic cardiomyopathy. Sustained VT (≥30 seconds) may lead to hypotension, syncope, VF, and cardiac arrest. However, the absence of symptoms or hemodynamic changes does not exclude VT as a diagnosis.

VT in the absence of structural heart disease (idiopathic VT) typically arises from the ventricular outflow tracts, fascicles, or papillary muscles. Patients with idiopathic VT usually present with palpitations in the third to fifth decades of life. Episodes of syncope are uncommon. Arrhythmic events are often triggered by stress, emotion, or sleeplessness.

Clinically, VT should be distinguished from other, less common causes of wide-complex tachycardia, such as SVT with aberrant conduction, “preexcited” (antidromic) SVT, and ventricular paced rhythms. In adult patients with known structural heart disease, 95% of wide-complex tachycardias are VT, and using additional ECG or clinical criteria is often unnecessary. However, in patients without known structural heart disease, ECG features of VT, such as AV dissociation, fusion beats, and capture beats (

), can help distinguish VT from other conditions. If the origin of a wide-complex tachycardia is in question, VT should be assumed in directing arrhythmia therapy.

Patients with VT and hemodynamic instability should undergo immediate direct current cardioversion (see Acute Management of Sudden Cardiac Arrest in Cardiovascular Medicine for a discussion of advanced cardiac life support). Intravenous amiodarone should be administered if the VT persists or recurs after cardioversion. Patients with VT or VF in the setting of ST-elevation MI should undergo emergency revascularization. In patients with hemodynamically stable VT not in the setting of an acute MI, intravenous procainamide can be useful for VT termination; intravenous amiodarone or sotalol also may be considered.

Evaluation with resting ECG; cardiac imaging (to identify structural heart disease); and in some cases, exercise treadmill testing (to provoke arrhythmias) is indicated in patients with VT. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is useful in evaluating myocardial diseases that may manifest as VT, including arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, myocardial fibrosis/scarring, and infiltrative cardiomyopathies (e.g., sarcoidosis, amyloidosis).

Patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy who present with VT should be considered for angiography and revascularization, if appropriate, primarily to reduce ischemic burden rather than to treat the arrhythmia. Patients with cardiomyopathy and heart failure should receive guideline-directed medical therapy, including β-blockers, to minimize risk for ventricular arrhythmia. In patients with recurrent VT despite β-blocker therapy, alternative antiarrhythmic drug therapy or catheter ablation may be considered; contemporary evidence suggests that ablation is more effective than medical therapy. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) placement is indicated for secondary prevention of SCD in patients with structural heart disease or cardiomyopathy who have sustained VT/VF, provided that clearly reversible causes have been excluded (e.g., acute coronary ischemia, cocaine ingestion).

In patients with idiopathic VT, calcium channel blockers (especially verapamil) and β-blockers are first-line therapy. Catheter ablation may be considered if symptoms continue despite these therapies. ICD placement is generally unnecessary in idiopathic VT because of the benign prognosis and high efficacy of other therapies in these patients without structural heart disease.

Torsades de pointes is a form of polymorphic VT typically related to pathologic prolongation of the QT interval and subsequent triggering of arrhythmia by a ventricular ectopic beat (PVC) during this longer, vulnerable period (the “R-on-T” phenomenon) (

). QT prolongation is frequently acquired as the result of medication use (e.g., antidepressants, macrolide antibiotics), cardiac ischemia, or electrolyte abnormalities. A list of drugs categorized by their potential to cause QT prolongation is available online. Less commonly, QT prolongation is primarily related to an underlying genetic defect (see Inherited Syndromes Characterized by Sudden Cardiac Death in Cardiovascular Medicine).

Acute treatment of polymorphic VT typically involves defibrillation and administration of magnesium. Recurrent or refractory cases (“storm”) may require induction of sinus tachycardia using sympathomimetic agents (isoproterenol) or pacing to suppress triggering ventricular ectopy.

Chronic management requires treating the underlying predisposition: removal of offending drugs, correction of electrolytes, and/or revascularization. Chronic β-blockers may be used in cases of inherited long QT syndrome.

Patients younger than 40 years without ischemic or structural heart disease who have unexplained cardiac arrest, unexplained near drowning, syncope during exercise, or recurrent high-risk syncope should be evaluated for inherited arrhythmia and/or cardiomyopathy syndromes. Unexplained premature death (age <35 years) or sudden death (age <40 years) in a first-degree family member also should raise suspicion for an inherited arrhythmia syndrome and prompt referral to a cardiovascular specialist, with genetic counseling and testing as indicated by clinical findings (see Genetic Testing for Cardiovascular Disease in Cardiovascular Medicine). The diagnosis of inherited arrhythmia syndromes may be complex because of the variable penetrance and expressivity of these disorders. Characteristic findings and treatments for some common syndromes are reviewed in [Table: Table: Inherited Syndromes Characterized by Sudden Cardiac Death]

.

Genetic long QT syndrome is among the most common inherited arrhythmias, affecting between 1 in 1000 and 1 in 5000 persons (

). However, the presence of a prolonged QTc (>440 ms in men, >460 ms in women) alone is insufficient to diagnose long QT syndrome. The QT interval may fluctuate in length, and prolongation may have many causes, most of which are acquired, such as medication use, structural heart disease, and electrolyte abnormalities. Given great variability in QTc across populations as well as variable penetrance of and subtypes of long QT syndrome, diagnosing genetic long QT syndrome is complex and patients with possible long QT syndrome should be referred to a specialist. Treatment includes β-blockers (first line); avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs; and, for select patients, ICD implantation, surgical sympathectomy, and exercise restriction.

Brugada syndrome is characterized by right precordial ECG abnormalities, including ST-segment coving (concave or linear downsloping ST segment) in leads V~1 through V~3 with or without right bundle branch block, along with ventricular tachyarrhythmia and/or SCD (

). Brugada syndrome has an increased prevalence in persons of Asian descent. Arrhythmic events (including SCD) in patients with Brugada syndrome are more common at night during sleep. Abnormalities on ECG may be intermittent and may be elicited by fever or pharmacologic challenge with sodium channel blockade, such as procainamide infusion.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy/dysplasia (ARVC/D) may present as SCD in a young person. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and arrhythmic risk stratification are discussed in Risk Stratification in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy in Cardiovascular Medicine. ARVC/D usually appears between puberty and young adulthood; however, it also may be identified in older age. Patients with ARVC/D typically present with frequent ventricular ectopy and/or monomorphic VT, although in severe cases, patients may present with heart failure. The diagnosis is established by criteria incorporating a combination of ECG, family history, arrhythmia, and structural findings. ARVC/D is usually progressive, and patients should abstain from vigorous exercise. Patients with ARVC/D and cardiac arrest or risk factors (nonsustained VT, inducible VT) should be offered an ICD. β-Blockers are first-line therapy for ventricular arrhythmias, although antiarrhythmic therapy with sotalol or amiodarone or catheter ablation is often required for recurrent VT.

SCD is defined as a fatal event or collapse within 1 hour of symptom onset in a person without recent acute illness. In patients in whom death was unwitnessed, SCD is considered to have occurred if the patient was known to be alive and well within the past 24 hours. VT and VF are the most common causes of SCD (see also Anoxic Brain Injury in Critical Care Medicine).

In the United States, more than 350,000 episodes of SCD occur each year. The annual risk for SCD is 1:1000 in the general population. The highest incidence occurs in patients with preexisting structural heart disease, although LV function is normal in most patients who experience SCD. Specific risk factors include heart failure, diminished LV function, previous MI, unexplained syncope, LV hypertrophy, prior nonsustained ventricular arrhythmia, chronic kidney disease, and sleep apnea. When obtaining a family history of cardiac disease, it is important to distinguish between MI precipitating death and nonischemic SCD in afflicted relatives to help address the likelihood of an underlying genetic disorder (see Genetic Counseling, Testing, and Clinical Screening in Cardiovascular Medicine).

Sudden cardiac arrest is a rare complication after blunt trauma to the chest, as when baseball batters are struck by a pitch or during helmet-to-chest trauma in football. This injury, termed commotio cordis, requires emergent resuscitation, and patients should undergo subsequent evaluation to rule out underlying heart disease before attributing the cause to the impact.

Cardiac arrest necessitates immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and advanced cardiac life support (

). Interruptions in chest compressions should be minimized, and defibrillation should occur as soon as possible in patients with a shockable rhythm, because time to defibrillation is an important determinant of likelihood of survival to hospital discharge.

The presence or absence of a shockable rhythm guides management after CPR initiation. In patients with out-of-hospital arrest, early cardiac catheterization has value in providing early diagnosis of the cause of arrest, facilitating early intervention when applicable, and providing opportunities for advanced hemodynamic support (e.g., extracorporeal membrane oxygenation).

Outcomes for patients with out-of-hospital arrest are improved in communities with more widely accessible automatic external defibrillators and where more of the population is trained in basic life support.

ICDs have demonstrated efficacy in the primary and secondary prevention of SCD through their treatment, not prevention, of VT/VF with defibrillation. Patients with sustained ventricular arrhythmias (>30 seconds) or cardiac arrest without a reversible cause have a class 1 recommendation for secondary-prevention ICD placement. ICD placement is recommended for the primary prevention of SCD in patients with ischemic or nonischemic cardiomyopathy, ejection fraction less than or equal to 35%, and New York Heart Association functional class II or III heart failure (see [Table: Table: Class I Indications for ICD and CRT]

). Patients with heart failure and interventricular conduction defects (predominantly left bundle branch block) often benefit from cardiac resynchronization therapy in combination with a defibrillator (see Device Therapy for Heart Failure With Reduced Ejection Fraction in Cardiovascular Medicine).

In the past, ICDs were implanted almost exclusively via a transvenous approach. New techniques allow for implantation of defibrillators in the lateral chest at the midaxillary line adjacent to the heart with tunneling of the lead under the skin either above (anterior to) the sternum (subcutaneous ICD) or even just underneath the sternum over the heart (extravascular ICD) (

). These “extravascular” defibrillators have several advantages, including reduced risk for device infection.

ICD malfunction, such as lead failure, may result in inappropriate shocks. Application of a donut magnet over the device will disable defibrillator therapies while maintaining pacing functionality for bradycardia. Further management requires device interrogation and programming.

With the increasing prevalence of permanent intracardiac devices, cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED)-related infections have increased significantly in frequency. Up to 5% of patients with a CIED will develop an infection within 3 years of implantation. Infection may be limited to the generator pocket or involve the entire device, including the leads. Diagnosis of CIED-related infection requires a high index of suspicion because the presentation may be insidious and underwhelming. Any patient with suspected cardiac device infection should be referred urgently for specialist evaluation and have blood culture testing and echocardiography. Empiric antibiotics alone (without blood cultures) may cloud or delay diagnosis, and diagnostic aspiration of the device pocket is never indicated because of the risk for introducing infection in an uninfected pocket. Effective treatment of the infection usually includes complete extraction of all hardware, debridement of the pocket, sustained antibiotic therapy, and reimplantation at a new location after infection has been eradicated.

CIED clinical pocket/generator infection should be suspected in patients with swelling, erythema, warmth, and pain overlying the device. Purulent discharge/sinus formation, deformation of the pocket, and threatened erosion or an exposed generator or proximal leads may be present. Patients with infections limited to the pocket will have negative blood culture results and no evidence of lead wire or valve vegetation on transesophageal echocardiography. They are treated with 2 weeks of antibiotics plus removal of the entire CIED, including leads and generator.

Many patients have more extensive CIED infections that are not limited to the generator pocket. Patients require 4 to 6 weeks of antibiotic therapy and device removal if they have any of the following:

  • Blood culture results positive for organisms likely to cause endocarditis (Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium, Candida, non–group A streptococci, or enterococci)
  • Blood culture results positive for any organism in the absence of an alternative primary site of infection
  • Transesophageal echocardiography evidence of lead wire or valve vegetation
