Valvular Heart Disease

Valvular heart disease (VHD) involves cardiac dysfunction due to structural or functional valve abnormalities, resulting in failure of the valves to either competently close (regurgitation) or effectively open (stenosis). VHD affects approximately 20 million persons in the United States. Although there are congenital forms, VHD is largely age dependent, with a prevalence of 3% to 6% in persons aged 65 years and older.

Many heart valve lesions progress slowly, causing patients to limit their activity unconsciously in response; therefore, a careful history and detailed physical examination are essential. Exertional dyspnea is the most common symptom. Depending on the lesion and severity, other symptoms include angina, syncope, palpitations, lower extremity edema, and increasing girth (ascites). Typical physical examination findings for valvular and other cardiac lesions are described in [Table: Table: Valvular and Other Cardiac Lesions and Examination Findings]

. Video: Normal S2 Splitting demonstrates normal S~2 splitting. ECG, chest radiography, and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) are the essential tests used to evaluate VHD.

To facilitate the timing of monitoring and intervention, VHD is classified into four stages (A through D), which consider risk factors, presence of symptoms, lesion severity, ventricular response to the volume or pressure overload caused by the lesion, effect on the pulmonary or systemic circulation, and heart rhythm changes ( [Table: Table: Stages of Valvular Heart Disease Progression]

). Surveillance intervals for echocardiographic evaluation based on disease severity are listed in [Table: Table: Evaluation of Patients With Left-Sided Valvular Conditions]

.

Medical therapy, although often effective for symptom palliation, has not been shown to prevent VHD progression or improve long-term survival. Surgery, however, can be a lifesaving intervention in select patients, and surgical risk calculation, including age, comorbid conditions, frailty, and prior chest radiation, is a key component of the patient evaluation. Risk calculators, including the Society of Thoracic Surgeons Adult Cardiac Risk Calculator, derived from national databases, can assist in estimating risk for morbidity and mortality for surgical valve procedures. Although risk calculators contain many data inputs, frailty and some other important patient and procedural characteristics are not factored into the calculations. Therefore, a comprehensive approach is required for determining patient surgical risk and candidacy. Frailty, which is variably defined as a geriatric syndrome of decline in several physiologic systems and processes, portends an increased risk for mortality in patients undergoing surgery and can be measured preoperatively (see Frailty Assessment in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

For all patients in whom surgical or interventional therapy is being considered, a multidisciplinary approach with a heart team consisting of cardiologists (including an interventional cardiologist) and a surgeon is recommended. Evaluations in centers with specialized expertise in VHD (e.g., a Heart Valve Center of Excellence) is also advised for patients in whom intervention is being considered when there are no symptoms, multiple or complex morbidities are present, or surgical valve repair is favored over valve replacement.

Comprehensive guidelines and updates on the diagnosis and management of VHD are published regularly by the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and American Heart Association (AHA) and are available free of charge on the websites of those organizations.

Aortic stenosis may be congenital, as in persons with a bicuspid aortic valve, or acquired. The most common cause is degeneration of the valve that occurs with aging (

); severe lesions occur in approximately 3% of persons aged 65 years or older. Rheumatic heart disease may cause aortic stenosis, in which case the aortic disease is almost always accompanied by mitral valve involvement. Chest irradiation (e.g., mantle therapy for Hodgkin lymphoma) may also cause aortic stenosis, usually accompanied by aortic regurgitation.

Aortic stenosis causes chronic pressure overload of the left ventricle, leading to concentric left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy and myocardial interstitial fibrosis. Diastolic dysfunction follows, with eventual systolic heart failure and pulmonary congestion. The disease typically progresses with a decrease in the aortic valve area of approximately 0.12 cm^2 per year, but the rate depends on patient age, underlying severity of the stenosis, and comorbid conditions, such as kidney failure and hypertension.

Exertional dyspnea, syncope, and angina are the most common symptoms; however, symptoms may not appear until stenosis is severe. Among asymptomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis, 75% will die or develop symptoms within 5 years. Once symptoms occur, life expectancy is generally only 1 to 2 years. Thus, serial evaluation every 6 to 12 months is recommended for patients with severe disease (see [Table: Table: Evaluation of Patients With Left-Sided Valvular Conditions]

).

The characteristic clinical findings of severe aortic stenosis include a late-peaking systolic murmur (Video: Late-Peaking Systolic Murmur in Severe Aortic Stenosis), a diminished or absent aortic component of the S~2, and a delay in the carotid upstroke (pulsus tardus) that may be accompanied by a decreased pulse amplitude due to low cardiac output (pulsus parvus). The loudness or harshness of the murmur does not correlate with the severity of the aortic stenosis. Clinical findings that suggest severe aortic stenosis should be evaluated promptly (see [Table: Table: Valvular and Other Cardiac Lesions and Examination Findings]

).

The primary imaging modality for evaluation of aortic stenosis is TTE (

). Echocardiography can determine the cause of stenosis, stenosis severity (with gradient and valve area assessment), LV function and wall thickness, right ventricular (RV) function, pulmonary artery pressure, and the presence or absence of other valve pathology. In some patients, echocardiography may underestimate the severity of aortic stenosis. Further evaluation with cardiac catheterization, during which cardiac output and the aortic pressure gradient can be measured, is required when there are discrepancies between the clinical and echocardiographic findings in symptomatic patients being considered for intervention. Exercise stress testing is useful in asymptomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis to confirm asymptomatic status, but it should be performed under cardiologist supervision. Exercise stress testing is otherwise contraindicated in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis.

Further testing also may be necessary in patients with low transvalvular flow (as measured by the stroke volume index) to accurately judge the severity of stenosis. Severe aortic stenosis is typically defined by a small valve area (≤1.0 cm^2), high peak velocity (≥4 m/s), and/or high mean gradient (≥40 mm Hg). There are two patient subsets in which severe aortic stenosis may be present with a small valve area but either low velocity or low gradient and are differentiated by LV function: (1) patients with LV dysfunction (LV ejection fraction [LVEF] <50%) and low flow (stroke volume index ≤35 mL/m^2), known as low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis, and (2) patients with preserved LV function (LVEF ≥50%) and low flow (stroke volume index ≤35 mL/m^2), known as paradoxical low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis.

In patients with low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis, dobutamine echocardiography or dobutamine cardiac catheterization is needed to distinguish true severe aortic stenosis from pseudostenosis. Patients with low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis have a low ejection fraction (<50%) and low flow (≤35 mL/m^2) due to ventricular dysfunction and reduced opening forces on the aortic valve. In pseudostenosis, dobutamine administration increases cardiac output and the opening forces on the aortic valve cause the valve area to increase out of the severe range to the moderate range. With low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis, however, the calculated valve area remains in the severe range with dobutamine administration, and the aortic valve gradient and velocity increase with increased stroke volume.

Patients with paradoxical low-flow, low-gradient severe aortic stenosis have low stroke volume (≤35 mL/m^2) resulting from a combination of small LV size and high aortic impedance to flow (e.g., hypertension) or other causes of low cardiac output (e.g., atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension). Determination of lesion severity in paradoxical low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis requires consideration of the hemodynamics, valve morphology (e.g., degree of calcification), presence of LV hypertrophy, and clinical presentation of the patient.

In patients with both suspected low-flow, low-gradient severe aortic stenosis with reduced LVEF and normal (paradoxical) LVEF, measurement of aortic valve calcium score by CT may be reasonable to further define disease severity.

In patients with either low-flow, low-gradient severe aortic stenosis with reduced LV function or paradoxical low-flow, low-gradient severe aortic stenosis, observational studies have shown improved survival with aortic valve replacement compared with medical therapy.

Aortic valve replacement is a life-prolonging procedure in patients with severe aortic stenosis. The indications for aortic valve replacement in severe aortic stenosis are the presence of symptoms (e.g., dyspnea, angina, presyncope, syncope, or heart failure) or a concomitant cardiac surgical procedure for other indications (e.g., coronary artery bypass grafting or ascending aorta surgery). Aortic valve replacement is also reasonable in asymptomatic patients with any of the following:

  • Very severe aortic stenosis (≥5 m/s) and low surgical risk
  • LV systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction <50%)
  • A B-type natriuretic peptide level more than three times normal
  • Abnormal results on supervised exercise testing, such as poor exercise tolerance, or hypotension during testing

Recent trial data suggest that other asymptomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis may also benefit from transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI).

Aortic valve replacement can be performed with open cardiac surgery (surgical aortic valve replacement [SAVR]) or via a transcatheter approach (TAVI) (

). SAVR may involve either a bioprosthetic or mechanical prosthesis (see Prosthetic Valves in Cardiovascular Medicine). The choice between surgical and transcatheter interventions is based on the presence of symptoms; the patient’s surgical risk, as determined through comprehensive multidisciplinary assessment; and shared decision making, as outlined in freely available ACC/AHA guidelines.

In symptomatic patients, TAVI is recommended over SAVR for patients who are older than 80 years, younger patients with a life expectancy less than 10 years, and patients of any age with severe aortic stenosis and a high or prohibitive surgical risk. For symptomatic patients aged 65 to 80 years, either SAVR or TAVI is appropriate after shared decision making. For symptomatic patients younger than 65 years or with a life expectancy greater than 20 years, SAVR is recommended because of considerations for lifetime management and future valve interventions.

In asymptomatic patients with decreased LV function, the recommendations regarding type of valve replacement are the same as for symptomatic patients. For asymptomatic patients with an indication for intervention other than decreased LV function (very severe aortic stenosis and low surgical risk, elevated B-type natriuretic peptide level more than three times normal, or abnormal results on supervised exercise testing), SAVR is preferred to TAVI when appropriate.

Although the pathophysiology of aortic stenosis is known to be inflammatory, randomized trials have shown medical therapy, specifically statins, to be ineffective in slowing disease progression. For patients with coexistent hypertension or heart failure, guideline-directed medical therapy is recommended. In select cases, balloon valvuloplasty may be used to bridge unstable patients to therapy with TAVI or SAVR but has limited longer-term hemodynamic benefit.

Aortic regurgitation arises from aortic root pathology or intrinsic valve disease. Causes of chronic aortic regurgitation include ascending aortic dilatation and valve abnormalities due to bicuspid disease, calcific degeneration, rheumatic involvement, or chest irradiation. Acute aortic regurgitation may be caused by aortic dissection, endocarditis, blunt chest trauma, or iatrogenic damage (e.g., complications of balloon aortic valvuloplasty).

In chronic aortic regurgitation, volume overload causes progressive LV dilatation and eccentric hypertrophy. Chronic aortic regurgitation may be tolerated for many years but eventually leads to symptoms, including shortness of breath, fatigue, or angina. Clinical findings result from the large stroke volume and LV dilatation and include bounding peripheral pulses, displacement of the LV apex, and a diastolic decrescendo murmur (Video: Chronic Aortic Regurgitation) heard along either the right sternal border (suggesting root pathology) or left sternal border (suggesting valve pathology) (see [Table: Table: Valvular and Other Cardiac Lesions and Examination Findings]

). The large forward stroke volume also may cause an early-peaking systolic ejection murmur.

In acute regurgitation, the abrupt onset of volume overload may cause acute heart failure or even cardiogenic shock. Bounding pulses may not be present because stroke volume has not markedly increased, and murmurs may be softer or shorter in duration because of the rapid equalization of pressures between the aorta and left ventricle.

TTE is indicated for evaluation of aortic regurgitation and LV function. In patients with moderate or severe aortic regurgitation and suboptimal TTE images or a discrepancy between clinical and TTE findings, transesophageal echocardiography (TEE), cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging, or cardiac catheterization is indicated.

Criteria for severe aortic regurgitation include the following:

  • A jet width that occupies 65% or more of the LV outflow tract
  • Vena contracta (the width of the regurgitant jet at its most narrow portion) greater than 0.6 cm
  • Holodiastolic flow in the descending aorta
  • Regurgitation volume of 60 mL or more
  • Effective regurgitant orifice area of 0.3 cm^2 or greater

The left ventricle typically is dilated in chronic aortic regurgitation.

In patients in whom an aortic root abnormality is suspected, evaluation with CMR imaging, CT, or TEE is recommended. CT angiography is indicated in patients with acute aortic regurgitation and aortic dissection because it is highly accurate and usually rapidly available.

Surveillance in patients with aortic regurgitation is based on severity of regurgitation and other factors (see [Table: Table: Evaluation of Patients With Left-Sided Valvular Conditions]

).

In chronic aortic regurgitation, surgery with traditional open aortic valve replacement is advised for patients with symptoms (typically, dyspnea or angina), those with LV dysfunction (ejection fraction ≤55%) thought to result from aortic regurgitation, or those with severe aortic regurgitation who are undergoing other cardiac surgery. Surgical treatment of aortic regurgitation is reasonable in asymptomatic patients with severe aortic regurgitation and normal LV function with significant LV dilatation (end-systolic dimension >50 mm or indexed end-systolic dimension >25 mm/m^2). In patients with isolated severe aortic regurgitation who have indications for SAVR and are candidates for surgery, TAVI should not be performed.

Medical therapy, preferably with dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), is indicated in patients with chronic aortic regurgitation and concomitant hypertension. If surgery is not an option, therapy with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or valsartan-sacubitril is reasonable for patients who have severe aortic regurgitation with symptoms or LV dysfunction.

Significant acute aortic regurgitation due to aortic dissection is a surgical emergency requiring aortic dissection repair and aortic valve replacement or repair. For other acute causes, the indications for surgery depend on the regurgitation severity, presence of symptoms, and hemodynamic stability of the patient.

Bicuspid aortic valve disease affects approximately 1% to 2% of the general population. Bicuspid morphology leads to abnormal shear forces and predisposes to early degeneration of the valve, resulting in stenosis in most patients (up to 75%) (see

) and pure regurgitation in a small minority of patients (2%-10%). Patients with a bicuspid aortic valve typically present with an asymptomatic finding of a systolic ejection murmur in adolescence or young adulthood and gradually progress to severe disease in the fifth or sixth decade of life. More than one third of those older than 70 years with severe aortic stenosis have an underlying bicuspid valve.

Bicuspid valvulopathy is often accompanied by aortic abnormalities independent of the severity of aortic stenosis or regurgitation, including aortic aneurysm, dissection, or coarctation. Therefore, in patients with a bicuspid aortic valve, the ascending aorta and aortic arch should be examined for aortopathy with TTE. Further imaging (e.g., with CMR imaging or CT angiography) is indicated when echocardiographic assessment is suboptimal. Lifelong serial imaging is indicated if abnormalities are detected. The imaging modality and frequency depend on several factors, including the nature and severity of the abnormality, age of the patient, family history, and candidacy for surgery. Importantly, bicuspid aortic valve is a heritable abnormality, and first-degree relatives of patients with a bicuspid aortic valve with or without aortopathy may be considered for screening with echocardiography.

Management of bicuspid aortic valve disease is determined by the predominant lesion type (stenosis or regurgitation) and its severity. Although randomized trial data for TAVI in bicuspid aortic valve disease are lacking, observational data suggest that outcomes in carefully selected patients with bicuspid disease are similar to those in patients with tricuspid aortic disease who undergo TAVI.

In patients with a bicuspid valve undergoing surgery for severe aortic stenosis or regurgitation, surgical repair of the ascending aorta is reasonable if the aortic dimension is 4.5 cm or greater. In the absence of surgical indications for a stenotic or regurgitant aortic valve, surgical repair of the ascending aorta or aortic sinuses is recommended if the aortic dimension is greater than 5.5 cm and may be reasonable when the dimension is greater than 5.0 cm with an additional risk factor for dissection (e.g., family history, rate of progression ≥0.5 cm/year) (see Treatment of Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm in Cardiovascular Medicine).

No medical therapies slow aortic dilatation in patients with aortopathy and a bicuspid aortic valve. Blood pressure should be controlled in patients with concomitant hypertension.

The leading cause of mitral stenosis is rheumatic heart disease, which is more common in women than in men (4:1 ratio). Although relatively rare in the United States, rheumatic heart disease is frequent in populations with limited access to treatment for streptococcal pharyngitis. Rheumatic heart disease results in fusion of the mitral commissures and, in more advanced forms, calcification of the valve and abnormalities in the subvalvular apparatus (

). Other causes of mitral stenosis are parachute mitral valve, chest irradiation, and severe mitral annular calcification. Mitral annular calcification is more common in older adults and is associated with inflammatory disorders, peripheral artery disease, and chronic kidney disease.

The natural history of mitral stenosis is characterized by slow progression over decades, with gradual left atrial (LA) enlargement and preservation of LV function. Symptoms may arise from low cardiac output (fatigue), pulmonary congestion (dyspnea), and pulmonary hypertension with right-sided heart failure (lower extremity edema). Pregnancy, with the resulting increased blood volume and cardiac output, may also precipitate symptoms. Symptoms are typically exertional because exercise shortens diastolic filling time and increases the transvalvular flow and diastolic mitral gradient, leading to worsening of LA hypertension. Patients also may present with systemic embolization; atrial fibrillation; or, in severe cases, hemoptysis. Heart failure is the cause of death in approximately 60% of patients with mitral stenosis, with thromboembolism causing most others.

Clinical findings when the valve is pliable include a tapping LV impulse, a loud S~1, an increased pulmonic component of S~2, a diastolic opening snap, and a diastolic rumble or low-pitched murmur at the apex (Video: Mitral Stenosis and [Table: Table: Valvular and Other Cardiac Lesions and Examination Findings]

). Signs of pulmonary or systemic congestion may be present depending on lesion severity and the patient’s volume status.

TTE is highly accurate for assessing disease severity, pulmonary pressures, and RV function as well as for identifying concomitant valvular lesions (see [Table: Table: Evaluation of Patients With Left-Sided Valvular Conditions]

). Additional imaging studies or cardiac catheterization is rarely required for diagnosis, but TEE is performed if TTE images are suboptimal and for preintervention assessment. Severe mitral stenosis is defined by a mitral valve area of 1.5 cm^2 or less, which usually corresponds to a mean mitral gradient of more than 5 to 10 mm Hg at a normal heart rate. In patients with a discrepancy between the clinical and echocardiographic findings, exercise echocardiography or exercise testing during cardiac catheterization should be pursued to assess the response of the mitral gradient and pulmonary pressures.

Percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy (PBMC) is the procedure of choice for patients with significant rheumatic mitral stenosis if the valve is pliable and not severely calcified. PBMC is indicated for symptomatic patients with severe rheumatic mitral stenosis and favorable valve morphology and is reasonable in asymptomatic patients with severe rheumatic mitral stenosis and a pulmonary artery systolic pressure greater than 50 mm Hg. PBMC should not be performed in patients with LA thrombus or moderate or severe mitral regurgitation, both of which are optimally evaluated with TEE. In appropriately selected patients, the success rate with PBMC is 95%, and complications occur in fewer than 5% of patients. Mitral valve surgery is indicated in patients with severe mitral stenosis, New York Heart Association functional class III or IV symptoms, and a nonpliable valve and in asymptomatic patients with severe mitral stenosis who are undergoing concomitant cardiac surgery for another indication.

Nearly 50% of patients with mitral stenosis have atrial fibrillation, and without anticoagulation, these patients have a risk for thromboembolism of 20% to 25%. The CHA~2DS~2-VASc score is not used to stratify the risk for thromboembolism in patients with mitral stenosis; all patients with mitral stenosis and concomitant atrial fibrillation should receive a vitamin K antagonist, such as warfarin, with a goal INR of 2.0 to 3.0. Notably, initial clinical trials of direct oral anticoagulants in atrial fibrillation excluded patients with moderate to severe mitral stenosis; however, a recent study of patients with rheumatic heart disease and atrial fibrillation showed an increased risk for the composite end point of stroke, systemic embolism, myocardial infarction, or death from vascular or unknown causes with rivaroxaban compared with warfarin. Anticoagulation is also indicated in patients with mitral stenosis and a history of LA thrombus or systemic embolization.

Because the mitral gradient is heavily dependent on transvalvular flow, medical therapy with negative chronotropic agents, diuretics, and long-acting nitrates can be effective for symptom palliation in patients who are not candidates for interventional or surgical therapy.

Mitral regurgitation may arise from dysfunction of any portion of the complex valve apparatus (annulus, leaflets, chordae, papillary muscles, or LV free walls) and may present acutely or chronically. Causes of acute mitral regurgitation include infective endocarditis, papillary muscle ischemia or rupture, trauma (e.g., injury from PBMC or blunt force), or degenerative disease with chordal rupture and flail leaflet. Chronic mitral regurgitation is classified as primary, involving any portion of the mitral annulus, or secondary, involving causes other than the annulus (e.g., ventricular dysfunction). Primary mitral regurgitation is predominantly caused by mitral valve prolapse (also known as myxomatous or degenerative mitral valve disease), which affects approximately 2% of the general population in the United States. Other causes of primary mitral regurgitation are radiation therapy, rheumatic disease, and cleft mitral valve. In secondary mitral regurgitation, ventricular dysfunction causes mitral regurgitation through papillary muscle displacement and tethering of the mitral leaflets, which impairs coaptation. The mitral valve apparatus is normal in patients with chronic secondary mitral regurgitation (

).

Mitral regurgitation results in volume overload with LV dilatation and LA hypertension, which may progress and cause pulmonary hypertension and RV failure. In acute mitral regurgitation, heart failure symptoms often occur abruptly because of insufficient time for adaptive chamber dilatation and, in some patients, may result in cardiogenic shock. Because of the rapid equalization of LA and LV pressures in acute disease, some of the clinical and echocardiographic changes typical of severe chronic disease, such as the intensity of the murmur and color flow imaging on echocardiography, may be less evident in acute disease.

The physical examination in patients with chronic mitral regurgitation is notable for a blowing holosystolic murmur at the apex (Video: Rheumatic Mitral Regurgitation). In patients with mitral valve prolapse, one or more systolic clicks may precede the murmur (Video: Mitral Valve Prolapse), and variation in severity, preload, and afterload can lead to differences in murmur onset (holosystolic, mid systolic, or late systolic). In acute disease, the murmur may be very short. In patients with LV dilatation, the apical impulse may be displaced laterally and an S~3 may be audible, especially in patients with secondary mitral regurgitation due to LV dysfunction.

TTE readily and accurately assesses the severity of mitral regurgitation. In chronic primary mitral regurgitation, echocardiography may show a range of abnormalities, including prolapse (

), gross degeneration of one or both leaflets (Barlow syndrome), or chordal rupture with flail leaflet. Barlow syndrome is more common in young adults, whereas fibroelastic deficiency predominates in older patients and frequently results in chordal rupture.

Severe primary mitral regurgitation is defined by several parameters, the most common of which are an effective regurgitant orifice area of 0.4 cm^2 or larger, regurgitant volume of 60 mL or more, and vena contracta of 0.7 cm or larger. If TTE provides insufficient or discordant information, TEE or CMR imaging is indicated.

Appropriate follow-up of asymptomatic patients with mitral regurgitation is outlined in [Table: Table: Evaluation of Patients With Left-Sided Valvular Conditions]

.

In patients with acute severe mitral regurgitation, medical therapy and surgical intervention may be lifesaving. Vasodilator therapy with a titratable drug, such as nitroprusside, decreases aortic impedance and mitral regurgitation, thereby improving forward cardiac output. An intra-aortic balloon pump also may be used to decrease afterload and augment systemic and coronary perfusion pressures to treat decompensated heart failure or cardiogenic shock. Prompt surgical correction should be considered for all patients with acute severe mitral regurgitation.

Patients with chronic severe primary mitral regurgitation do poorly without surgery, particularly if they have significant symptoms, flail leaflet, or LV dilatation. Surgical repair of the mitral valve is indicated for chronic severe primary mitral regurgitation in symptomatic patients (regardless of LV systolic function) and asymptomatic patients with LV dysfunction (ejection fraction ≤60% and/or LV end-systolic dimension ≥40 mm). Surgical repair is also reasonable in asymptomatic patients with severe disease and preserved LV function if the expected repair success rate is greater than 95% and the operative risk is less than 1%. Surgical repair is preferred over replacement in all patients with primary disease, and patients should be referred to a surgical center with expertise to improve the chances of repair. Medical therapy with vasodilators is not beneficial in patients with primary mitral regurgitation in the absence of symptoms or LV dysfunction.

For patients who are not surgical candidates, transcatheter mitral valve repair with a clip device (transcatheter edge-to-edge repair [TEER]) improves coaptation of the mitral valve leaflets, leading to increased valve closure and a reduction in regurgitation (

). In selected patients with primary mitral regurgitation, success rates with TEER are approximately 90%, with a procedural mortality rate of approximately 2%.

In patients with chronic secondary mitral regurgitation, the primary goal of therapy is to address the underlying ventricular dysfunction with guideline-directed medical therapy and, if indicated, cardiac resynchronization therapy (see Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy in Cardiovascular Medicine). Guideline-directed medical therapy for ventricular dysfunction includes an ACE inhibitor, ARB, or angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor; a β-blocker; a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor; a diuretic; and/or an aldosterone antagonist. Benefits of valve repair or replacement in patients with secondary mitral regurgitation are less certain than in primary disease, although studies have demonstrated favorable LV remodeling after surgery. Surgery for secondary severe mitral regurgitation is reasonable for those undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting, but mitral regurgitation may recur after repair because of primary LV dysfunction. TEER has been approved by the FDA for patients with an ejection fraction of 20% to 50%, chronic secondary mitral regurgitation, and refractory symptoms despite optimal medical therapy for heart failure; however, the effect of TEER on mortality and heart failure hospitalization in this population has varied in studies.

Tricuspid regurgitation, the most common form of tricuspid valve disease, is frequently functional (secondary) and clinically asymptomatic. Causes of tricuspid regurgitation include cor pulmonale (or pulmonary hypertension) with RV failure, pacemaker or defibrillator lead placement, trauma, congenital abnormalities, and infective endocarditis. When symptomatic, patients may present with fatigue from low cardiac output as well as signs and symptoms of right-sided failure, such as elevated jugular venous pulse (a large c-v wave), a palpable RV lift, hepatic congestion with pulsatile liver, and peripheral edema. The murmur of tricuspid regurgitation is typically a holosystolic murmur heard along the left sternal border that increases during inspiration because of increased venous return.

Tricuspid regurgitation should be evaluated with TTE, which also allows assessment of RV function and estimation of pulmonary pressures. In patients with tricuspid regurgitation due to pacemaker or defibrillator lead placement, TEE may be required to determine the cause more clearly.

Medical therapy with loop diuretics and aldosterone antagonists alleviates symptoms of right-sided congestion but incurs the risk for causing a low-flow state with impaired cardiac output. Surgery is recommended for patients with severe tricuspid regurgitation who are undergoing left-sided valve surgery. Isolated tricuspid valve surgery may be considered in patients with either severe primary tricuspid regurgitation or severe secondary symptomatic tricuspid regurgitation refractory to medical therapy. Recent trials showed a reduction in tricuspid regurgitation with the use of either a transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement or tricuspid edge-to-edge repair in patients considered to be at high risk for surgery with severe, symptomatic tricuspid regurgitation. Both studies demonstrated improved quality of life and functional capacity but no change in survival.

Tricuspid stenosis is almost always caused by rheumatic disease. Other, infrequent causes include radiation therapy, carcinoid syndrome, and medications (e.g., the dopamine agonist cabergoline). Symptoms of tricuspid stenosis (fatigue, abdominal fullness) are typically overshadowed by those caused by the left-sided abnormalities of coexistent rheumatic mitral disease. Clinical findings include signs of right-sided congestion (elevated jugular venous pulse, hepatic congestion, peripheral edema) and a diastolic rumble. Surgery for tricuspid stenosis is typically performed in concert with surgery for rheumatic mitral disease.

Many factors influence the choice of prosthesis in a patient undergoing surgical valve replacement, including the patient’s age, the expected durability of the prosthesis, the surgical risk for reoperation in the event of degeneration, and the ability and willingness of the patient to take warfarin for anticoagulation. For patients of any age, a bioprosthetic valve is recommended for those who cannot or do not want to take anticoagulation therapy. This recommendation is counterbalanced by the expected durability of bioprostheses of 15 years, because in persons younger than 60 years, approximately 40% of valves have evidence of clinically severe deterioration by 15 years. Data on long-term durability of TAVI prostheses are currently limited to a follow-up of 8 to 10 years; however, thus far, valve durability is similar to that of surgical prostheses.

According to the ACC/AHA, an aortic mechanical valve is reasonable in patients younger than 50 years, a bioprosthesis is reasonable in patients older than 65 years, and either a bioprosthesis or mechanical aortic valve prosthesis is reasonable in those aged 50 to 65 years. In patients undergoing mitral valve replacement, a mitral valve bioprosthesis is reasonable for patients older than 65 years, as opposed to a mechanical valve prosthesis in patients younger than 65 years ( [Table: Table: Choice of Valve: Bioprosthetic Versus Mechanical]

). However, the final decision on valve type should be reached through shared decision making between the physician and patient. (See also Infective Endocarditis in Cardiovascular Medicine.)

Echocardiography should be performed after implantation to document the baseline hemodynamic performance of the valve and should be repeated for signs or symptoms of valve dysfunction (e.g., new dyspnea or heart failure, louder murmur or new murmur, thromboembolism, hemolytic anemia). In patients with a surgical bioprosthetic valve, TTE at 5 years and 10 years and then annually after implantation is reasonable, even in the absence of a change in clinical status. For patients with a transcatheter bioprosthetic valve, annual TTE is reasonable, even in the absence of a change in clinical status. For patients with suspected prosthetic valve malfunction in whom the TTE does not demonstrate regurgitation, transesophageal echocardiography should be performed.

Lifelong warfarin anticoagulation is indicated for all patients with a mechanical valve (see Perioperative Medicine/Prosthetic Heart Valves in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Because of the increased risk for valve thrombosis, direct oral anticoagulants should not be used for anticoagulation in patients with a mechanical valve. Warfarin therapy should target a specific INR value rather than a range. In patients with a mechanical aortic valve prosthesis (bileaflet or current-generation single-tilting disc) with no additional risk factors for thromboembolism (history of embolization, hypercoagulable disorder, LV dysfunction, atrial fibrillation), the goal INR for warfarin anticoagulation is 2.5. In patients with a mechanical aortic valve prosthesis with heightened risk factors for thromboembolism, an older-generation aortic valve prosthesis (ball-in-cage), or any mitral prosthesis, the target INR is 3.0.

Oral anticoagulation with warfarin should be considered for 3 to 6 months after implantation of a bioprosthetic mitral or aortic valve if bleeding risk is low, or for patients with symptomatic bioprosthetic valve thrombosis. An INR of 2.5 should be targeted in these patients.

Adding aspirin (75-100 mg/d) to warfarin may be considered in patients with a mechanical prosthesis who have other indications for antiplatelet therapy if the bleeding risk is low. Low-dose aspirin is also reasonable for all patients with a bioprosthesis.

Infective endocarditis is a common complication of valvular heart disease. Antimicrobial prophylaxis is indicated in patients with a high risk for endocarditis, as described below. The diagnosis and management of endocarditis are discussed in Endocarditis in Infectious Disease. Cardiac implantable electronic device–related infections are covered in Cardiac Implantable Electronic Device–Related Infections in Cardiovascular Medicine.

Endocarditis prophylaxis is recommended for a specific group of patients before dental procedures ( [Table: Table: Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis Before Dental Procedure]

). Although endocarditis prophylaxis was previously advised for a broad population, current guidelines recommend its use only for dental procedures involving manipulation of the gingival tissue, manipulation of the periapical regions of teeth, or perforation of the oral mucosa in patients with the following:

  • History of endocarditis
  • Cardiac transplantation with valve regurgitation due to a structurally abnormal valve
  • Prosthetic valve, including transcatheter-implanted prostheses and homografts
  • Prosthetic material used for cardiac valve repair, including annuloplasty rings, chords, and clips
  • Left ventricular assist device
  • Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease
  • Repaired congenital heart disease with residual defects at the site or adjacent to the site of a prosthetic patch or device
  • A congenital defect that has been repaired with prosthetic material (surgical or catheter-based) within the previous 6 months

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is also recommended before some cardiovascular surgical procedures, such as implantation of prosthetic heart valves, to reduce surgical site infection and early postsurgical endocarditis. Prophylaxis is not recommended for nondental procedures (e.g., cystoscopy, colonoscopy) in the absence of active infection.

Myocardial Disease

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is an autosomal dominant heritable disorder related to pathogenic variants predominantly in the genes that encode sarcomeric proteins. It is characterized by increased left ventricular (LV) wall thickness in the absence of hypertension or other underlying loading conditions. HCM affects at least 1 in 500 persons and may be identified in all age groups and ethnicities.

Many patients with HCM are asymptomatic and have normal life expectancy, with incidental diagnosis sometimes resulting from evaluation of a heart murmur or abnormal ECG. However, a significant subset of patients develop symptomatic disease and are at risk for cardiac complications, including heart failure, arrhythmias (atrial and ventricular), LV outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction, and sudden cardiac death (SCD). Symptomatic individuals usually present with dyspnea, exertional intolerance, fatigue, chest discomfort, dizziness, palpitations, or syncope. SCD may be the initial manifestation in a minority of patients.

Heart failure symptoms are attributable to abnormal LV filling (diastolic dysfunction) and dynamic LVOT obstruction. Diastolic dysfunction is multifactorial, involving increased chamber stiffness, progressive fibrosis, and myocardial ischemia due to mismatch of coronary flow and LV mass. Dynamic LVOT obstruction is found on echocardiography in 30% of patients at rest and in an additional 40% of patients with provocation; 30% of patients have no obstruction. The classic form of HCM is characterized by asymmetric LV hypertrophy with prominent interventricular septal thickening. During ventricular systole, anterior motion of the mitral valve results in early to mid-systolic obstruction of the LVOT and subsequent mitral regurgitation related to leaflet malcoaptation (“eject-obstruct-leak” triad) (Video: TTE Showing Obstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy). Patients with dynamic obstruction may develop dyspnea, presyncope, or syncope during periods of increased ventricular contractility (exercise) or with decreases in ventricular preload or afterload, all of which may worsen the degree of obstruction.

Atrial fibrillation is common in patients with HCM, and risk increases with age. During atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, diastolic filling periods shorten, worsening diastolic dysfunction; reduced LV filling may also exacerbate the LVOT gradient.

Physical examination findings may be normal in patients without LVOT obstruction. The most common feature related to LVOT obstruction is a cardiac murmur (Video: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy), and dynamic maneuvers during examination are helpful in differentiating HCM from fixed valvular aortic obstruction ( [Table: Table: Dynamic LVOT Obstruction vs Fixed Valvular Aortic Stenosis]

).

Twelve-lead ECG reveals abnormal findings in 75% to 95% of persons with HCM, such as increased QRS voltage, evidence of left atrial enlargement, LV conduction abnormalities, pathologic Q waves, and significant repolarization abnormalities (

); however, there is substantial variability in the degree of abnormalities.

The diagnosis of HCM is most commonly established by transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) (

). Echocardiography demonstrates the magnitude and distribution of hypertrophy (≥15 mm in any LV region or ≥13 mm in a person with a first-degree relative with HCM or genotype-positive status), reveals the presence and degree of dynamic LVOT obstruction and mitral regurgitation, and characterizes diastolic LV filling. Doppler echocardiography is the modality of choice for quantifying the LVOT gradient to differentiate obstructive from nonobstructive HCM, an important distinction in symptom management. In patients with HCM and resting LVOT gradient less than 50 mm Hg, echocardiography with provocative maneuvers (Valsalva, exercise) is recommended to establish the diagnosis. In patients with inconclusive echocardiographic findings, cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is indicated to clarify the diagnosis.

On initial diagnosis of HCM, regardless of symptoms, 24- to 48-hour ambulatory ECG monitoring should be performed to evaluate for arrhythmias. The presence of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia indicates higher risk for SCD. Exercise stress testing is also reasonable to determine functional status and provide prognostic information.

HCM must be differentiated from other conditions associated with increased ventricular wall thickness ( [Table: Table: Conditions With Increased Left Ventricular Wall Thickness]

). Particularly challenging is the differentiation of HCM from hypertensive heart disease and from the normal and compensatory changes in LV wall thickness seen in competitive athletes (athlete heart). In patients with hypertension, the likelihood of concomitant HCM is increased if LV wall thickness is greater than 18 mm and nonconcentric and if dynamic LVOT obstruction is present. In athletes, LV cavity dilatation and normal diastolic filling on echocardiography favor normal physiologic changes, whereas unusual or asymmetric patterns of hypertrophy favor HCM. A decrease in wall thickness after a brief period of deconditioning also favors athlete heart. When the diagnosis remains unclear, CMR imaging with gadolinium contrast may help with differentiation.

Patients with HCM have an annual risk for death of 1%, primarily related to fatal arrhythmia and heart failure. Most arrhythmic deaths are caused by ventricular fibrillation, and all patients with HCM, regardless of the presence of obstruction, should undergo assessment for SCD risk factors at the time of diagnosis and every 1 to 2 years. Major risk factors for SCD are listed in [Table: Table: Major Risk Factors for SCD in Patients With HCM]

.

An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is effective in preventing SCD in appropriately selected high-risk patients. Patients with previous SCD or sustained ventricular tachycardia have an annual recurrence rate of 10% and should receive an ICD for secondary prevention. Primary prevention with ICD placement is reasonable in patients with one or more established risk factors. For patients with HCM who are not otherwise identified as high risk for SCD or in whom a decision to proceed with ICD placement remains uncertain, CMR imaging is beneficial to assess for the presence of an LV apical aneurysm and to determine maximum LV wall thickness, ejection fraction, and the extent of myocardial fibrosis with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE). LGE is associated with increased risk for ventricular arrhythmias; in patients with indeterminate risk for SCD, LGE quantification of 15% or more may warrant ICD placement.

In addition to potential ICD therapy, management of HCM includes lifestyle modification and treatment of symptoms referable to LVOT obstruction, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation.

In patients with HCM who have overweight or obesity, therapeutic lifestyle interventions should be implemented to achieve weight loss and potentially decrease the risk for LVOT obstruction, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation. Patients with symptoms of sleep-disordered breathing should be formally evaluated, including with a sleep study.

Patients with HCM should be advised to avoid dehydration, excessive alcohol intake, and exposures that may cause vasodilation and decreased preload (e.g., saunas, hot tubs) because these situations may provoke LVOT obstruction. Mild- to moderate-intensity recreational exercise is safe and beneficial for most patients with HCM. Athletes with HCM should undergo a comprehensive evaluation and be engaged in shared discussion of the potential risks of sports participation.

In symptomatic patients, nonvasodilating β-blockers such as metoprolol should be titrated to effectiveness or maximum tolerance. Vasodilating β-blockers such as carvedilol, labetalol, and nebivolol should be avoided. Alternatively, verapamil or diltiazem may be used in patients in whom β-blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated. For patients with LVOT obstruction and persistent symptoms, adding a cardiac myosin inhibitor or disopyramide (a class IA antiarrhythmic drug with potent negative inotropic activity) to one of the other drugs is a recommended option. Diuretics must be used cautiously and only if symptoms of dyspnea cannot be managed with other therapy. Because of their propensity to exacerbate LVOT obstruction, nitrates and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors should not be used.

The first-in-class agent mavacamten was FDA approved in 2022 as a novel targeted therapy for symptomatic obstructive HCM. A cardiac myosin inhibitor, mavacamten decreases actin-myosin cross-bridge formation at the level of the sarcomere, attenuating hypercontractility. Several randomized studies have shown that in patients already receiving maximally tolerated medical therapy, mavacamten resulted in reduced LVOT gradient and improved functional class. Significant adverse effects, including systolic dysfunction and heart failure, prompted the FDA to place this drug in a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) program that mandates enhanced monitoring, including serial echocardiography. This drug is metabolized by the liver and interacts with several prescribed and over-the-counter medications. It is best prescribed by clinicians with expertise in managing HCM who are familiar with indications and toxicity. Similarly, a second myosin inhibitor, aficamten, was approved for use in 2025 and is also subject to a REMS program. The role of myosin inhibitors in the treatment of HCM is evolving and they are likely to play a more prominent role in the future.

Invasive treatment of obstruction with surgical septal myectomy or catheter-based alcohol septal ablation is recommended in patients with severe obstructive symptoms refractory to maximal medical therapy and a resting or provoked LVOT gradient of 50 mm Hg or greater. Both surgical myectomy and alcohol septal ablation reduce the LVOT gradient and obstructive symptoms. Surgical myectomy is associated with a higher likelihood of complete symptom resolution, greater obstruction relief, and a lower rate of repeat procedures. It is favored in younger patients or those with other cardiac disease requiring surgical intervention. Alcohol septal ablation may be preferred in patients with comorbid conditions that increase operative risk. Outcomes with either procedure are best when the procedure is performed in a center with expertise in HCM management.

Atrial fibrillation should be managed with an individualized approach. Stroke risk with atrial fibrillation in the setting of HCM is elevated independent of CHA~2DS~2-VASc score, and all patients without contraindication should receive anticoagulation. Direct oral anticoagulants are considered first-line anticoagulant therapy, with warfarin as a second-line option. Anticoagulation is also recommended in patients with an episode of subclinical atrial fibrillation of more than 24 hours’ duration detected by ambulatory monitoring. Low-molecular-weight heparin or warfarin (maximum dose <5 mg/day) is recommended for pregnant patients with HCM and atrial fibrillation. Patients with HCM and concomitant atrial fibrillation often remain symptomatic despite rate control, and rhythm control using antiarrhythmic drugs and/or catheter ablation in conjunction with anticoagulation should be considered early (see Long-Term Management of Atrial Fibrillation in Cardiovascular Medicine). Digoxin should be avoided in patients with atrial fibrillation and HCM because the positive inotropic effects may worsen the LVOT gradient.

A relatively small subset of patients have progression to end-stage HCM, manifesting as refractory heart failure with or without systolic dysfunction. For patients with HCM who develop systolic dysfunction (LV ejection fraction <50%), guideline-directed therapy is recommended (see ACE Inhibitors and Angiotensin Receptor Blockers in Cardiovascular Medicine) and an ICD is recommended for primary prevention of sudden cardiac death.

An ECG should be obtained every 1 to 2 years in asymptomatic patients with HCM to screen for changes in rhythm or conduction. Patients also should undergo 24- to 48-hour ambulatory ECG monitoring at diagnosis and every 1 to 2 years thereafter if asymptomatic or with the development of symptoms that suggest arrhythmia, such as palpitations or syncope. Ambulatory monitoring of longer duration may be considered to increase the yield of identifying arrhythmia.

Repeat TTE is recommended with any change in clinical status or new cardiac event. In asymptomatic patients, TTE is recommended every 1 to 2 years to assess for mitral regurgitation and changes in LV hypertrophy, function, and degree of obstruction. Although most patients with HCM have normal LV function, a decrease in LV systolic function is associated with worse outcomes, including death.

Patients with known or suspected HCM should undergo an evaluation of familial inheritance with a three-generation family history and receive genetic counseling. Genetic testing should be offered to patients who meet the clinical definition of HCM because identification of a pathogenic variant can help risk stratify family members. A pathogenic variant may be identified in up to 60% of patients with a family history of HCM; the incidence is lower (20%-30%) in isolated cases.

First-degree relatives of patients with HCM should undergo screening with ECG and echocardiography. In first-degree relatives who are children or adolescents, ECG and cardiac imaging should be performed every 1 to 2 years; in first-degree adult relatives, testing should be completed every 3 to 5 years or with a change in clinical status. Genetic testing should be offered to first-degree family members if a pathogenic variant is identified in the index case. Genotype-positive persons who do not express phenotypic features of HCM should be followed with clinical examinations at the same intervals described. The absence of an identified sarcomeric variant does not exclude familial HCM in the index patient, and first-degree relatives should continue clinical screening. Genotype-negative relatives in families with a known pathogenic variant identified in the index patient do not require ongoing clinical screening (see Genetic Testing for Cardiovascular Disease in Cardiovascular Medicine). Genetic testing results are not routinely used to guide decisions regarding treatment of HCM.

Cardiac amyloidosis results from deposition of misfolded proteins within the myocardium, leading to restrictive physiology. It is characterized by normal LV systolic function and cavity size with abnormal diastolic function with resultant heart failure symptoms. Cardiac amyloidosis has two major forms: light-chain (AL) amyloidosis and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis ( [Table: Table: Subtypes of Cardiac Amyloidosis]

). Cardiac amyloidosis is suggested by increased wall thickness on echocardiogram accompanied at times by a low-voltage ECG; however, these findings are not diagnostic. CMR imaging is an appropriate test if cardiac amyloidosis is suspected because it is highly sensitive and specific for the disease, although it does not distinguish between types. If cardiac amyloidosis is suspected based on the clinical presentation and CMR findings, the presence of monoclonal light chains, indicating likely AL amyloidosis, should be assessed. If a monoclonal disorder is not identified, 99m-technetium pyrophosphate scintigraphy of the heart may be diagnostic of ATTR amyloidosis (

). Cardiac amyloidosis is unlikely in the absence of a monoclonal plasma cell dyscrasia and negative 99m-technetium pyrophosphate scintigraphy findings. If clinical suspicion for amyloidosis remains high, endomyocardial biopsy can be pursued.

AL amyloidosis is a multiorgan disease associated with plasma cell dyscrasias. The overall diagnosis is based on the presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome; amyloid deposits on fat pad aspiration, bone marrow biopsy, or organ biopsy; abnormal serum immunoglobulin light chains; and monoclonal gammopathy (see Immunoglobulin Light-Chain Amyloidosis in Hematology). Endomyocardial biopsy is diagnostic but unnecessary in the presence of extracardiac amyloidosis with abnormalities on CMR imaging. Treatment is directed toward the hematologic malignancy. Cardiac transplantation may be considered selectively.

In the setting of abnormal CMR imaging results or positive 99m-technetium pyrophosphate scintigraphy, TTR gene sequencing should be performed to differentiate hereditary (h-ATTR) from wild-type (wt-ATTR) disease (also see Genetic Testing for Cardiovascular Disease in Cardiovascular Medicine). If a pathogenic variant is present, defining h-ATTR, the variant may be used to screen immediate family members for disease risk. h-ATTR is an autosomal dominant disease resulting from a pathogenic variant in the TTR gene, most commonly Val122Ile, which occurs in 3.4% of Black persons living in the United States. wt-ATTR amyloidosis, which yields negative genetic testing results, is an aging-linked process that may be responsible for up to 10% to 15% of cases of heart failure in older adults. In addition to heart failure, ATTR amyloidosis may cause sensory and autonomic neuropathy and carpal tunnel syndrome.

Establishing the diagnosis of ATTR cardiomyopathy is essential because disease-specific therapies, including tafamidis, acoramidis, and vutrisiran reduce the risk of hospitalization and mortality in patients with New York Heart Association functional class I through IV disease. Patisiran and inotersen, which reduce hepatic production of transthyretin, are indicated for ATTR polyneuropathy and may have benefit for ATTR cardiomyopathy. Liver or combined heart-liver transplantation may be considered for select patients with h-ATTR amyloidosis.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM) is a rare disorder characterized by abnormally stiff, noncompliant ventricles. RCM was once considered idiopathic; however, increasing evidence suggests that pathogenic variants in genes encoding sarcomeric proteins and abnormalities in desmin, an intermediate filament that regulates sarcomeric architecture, play an important role in familial and sporadic cases. The sarcomeric genetic variants implicated in RCM are similar to those linked to HCM, raising the possibility that these disorders represent different phenotypic expressions of the same heritable defect. Histologically, RCM is characterized by patchy interstitial fibrosis and myocyte disarray, which also are seen in HCM. With increasing interstitial fibrosis, the ventricles stiffen, resulting in increased pressure during normal diastolic filling.

Patients with RCM may present at any age, usually with dyspnea, peripheral edema, and exercise intolerance. Hepatomegaly and ascites may be present late in the disease course. RCM should be suspected if echocardiography reveals biatrial enlargement and severe diastolic dysfunction in the setting of normal ventricular size, wall thickness, and systolic function. Pulmonary hypertension is commonly present, as are tricuspid and mitral valve regurgitation.

Primary RCM must be differentiated from other conditions involving restrictive physiology. These conditions include those in which wall thickness typically is normal (radiation-induced fibrosis, eosinophilic diseases, hemochromatosis) as well as infiltrative diseases with increased wall thickness (see Cardiac Amyloidosis in Cardiovascular Medicine). A complete blood count with manual differential and assessment of serum ferritin and transferrin saturation are reasonable as part of the evaluation. CMR imaging with gadolinium contrast may help distinguish between conditions. When the diagnosis remains unclear, endomyocardial biopsy is reasonable for establishing a diagnosis.

RCM and constrictive pericarditis present with similar symptoms and echocardiographic findings. Differentiating between the two disorders is essential because surgical pericardiectomy may relieve symptoms and prolong life in patients with constriction. In patients with previous cardiac surgery, pericarditis, or chest irradiation, constrictive pericarditis should be strongly considered. For more information on constrictive pericarditis, see Constrictive Pericarditis in Cardiovascular Medicine.

On physical examination, patients with both RCM and constriction demonstrate elevated central venous pressure. Increase in the height of the jugular venous waveform during inspiration (Kussmaul sign) is more commonly associated with constriction. Both RCM and constrictive pericarditis may be associated with a diastolic sound—an S~3 gallop in RCM and a pericardial knock in constrictive pericarditis. Differentiating between these sounds may be difficult (see [Table: Table: Characteristics of the Selected Diastolic Heart Sounds]

).

A multimodal approach, including noninvasive imaging and invasive hemodynamic evaluation, may be required to distinguish RCM from constrictive pericarditis. Clues to the presence of constrictive pericarditis include pericardial calcification on chest radiography or CT, pericardial thickening on CT or CMR imaging, and a B-type natriuretic peptide level below 100 pg/mL (100 ng/L) (usually ≥400 pg/mL [400 ng/L] in RCM). A hallmark feature of constrictive pericarditis is ventricular interdependence, whereby total cardiac volume is limited by the rigid pericardium. With ventricular interdependence, increased filling of the right or left ventricle can occur only with reciprocal decreased filling of the other ventricle. Ventricular interdependence may be demonstrated by Doppler echocardiography, CMR imaging, or invasive hemodynamic evaluation in patients with constriction; however, it is not present in patients with RCM.

There are no medical therapies specifically for RCM. Loop diuretics are usually necessary for relief of congestive symptoms, especially in late-stage disease. However, patients with RCM require relatively high filling pressures to maintain cardiac output, and balancing relief of congestion with adequate cardiac output is often challenging. Volume status should be monitored carefully because even small changes in volume may lead to renal hypoperfusion.

Atrial fibrillation is common in patients with RCM and is poorly tolerated because of increased heart rate and reduced ventricular filling. Anticoagulation and rate control are indicated, and rhythm control should be considered early in symptomatic patients.

Survival is poor in patients with RCM, with a 5-year mortality rate of 36% and a 10-year mortality rate of 63%. Cardiovascular mortality is predominantly related to progressive heart failure and arrhythmias. Cardiac transplantation may be considered in select patients who remain symptomatic despite maximal therapy. There is no accepted indication for primary prevention ICD placement in patients with RCM who have preserved systolic function.

Most cardiac tumors are metastatic. Neoplasms with the highest potential for metastasis to the heart are melanoma, malignant thymoma, and germ cell tumors. Common tumors with an intermediate risk for cardiac involvement include carcinoma of the lung, stomach, and colon. Therapy focuses on systemic treatment of the underlying neoplasm, with cardiac surgery reserved for patients who have obstructive symptoms.

Primary cardiac tumors, which are exceedingly rare, are benign in two thirds of patients. Nearly 50% of primary cardiac tumors are atrial myxomas. Myxomas may occur in either atrium but are most commonly attached to the fossa ovalis within the left atrium (

and Video: Echocardiogram Showing Left Atrial Myxoma). Myxomas are usually solitary and discovered at a mean age of 50 years, often after a systemic embolic event. Patients with a myxoma may present with constitutional symptoms related to interleukin production, embolic phenomena from tumor fragmentation, or symptoms referable to intracardiac obstruction (dyspnea, syncope). When mitral valve obstruction is present, auscultatory findings are similar to those of mitral stenosis; however, findings may vary with position or be associated with an early diastolic sound, known as the tumor plop. Surgical removal is indicated to prevent embolic events, as is subsequent surveillance echocardiography for detection of recurrence.

Papillary fibroelastomas usually occur on the surface of the aortic and mitral valves and are commonly discovered in the eighth decade of life. Although most papillary fibroelastomas do not cause symptoms, they may be associated with stroke, transient ischemic attack, and, rarely, coronary embolization with infarction. On echocardiogram, these tumors often have a heterogeneous globular shape or a mobile frond-like appearance. Patients with embolic symptoms are treated surgically. There are no randomized data comparing surgical therapy with antithrombotic or antiplatelet therapy to prevent embolic events.

Angiosarcomas are the most common primary malignant tumor. Angiosarcomas typically arise in the right atrium and are often associated with pericardial effusion (

). Dyspnea and chest pain are common presenting symptoms. Angiosarcomas are highly vascular tumors, and CT or CMR imaging with contrast may help differentiate an angiosarcoma from a right atrial myxoma. Most patients die in 6 to 12 months. Even when complete surgical extirpation is possible, survival remains less than 2 years for most patients.
