Pericardial Disease

Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium, the thin, avascular fibrous sac surrounding the heart. It may be subclinical or present as sharp precordial pain of acute onset. Acute pericarditis has many causes ( [Table: Table: Causes of Pericardial Disease]

) but is most often idiopathic or presumed to be viral in origin.

Acute pericarditis is diagnosed clinically by the presence of pleuritic chest pain typical for pericarditis and at least one of five criteria: a pericardial friction rub, new ECG changes, inflammatory biomarker elevation, a new pericardial effusion, or imaging indicative of pericardial inflammation ( [Table: Table: Evaluation of Pericardial Disease]

). Chest pain attributable to acute pericarditis is typically sharp, severe, and positional. It is not exacerbated by exertion or relieved by rest or nitroglycerin, unlike anginal pain. Pain is characteristically worse in the supine position and improves with sitting up and leaning forward. These pain features may be related to tension of the pericardium at its sternal and diaphragmatic attachments.

A pericardial friction rub, although present in less than half of patients, is characteristic of acute pericarditis. The harsh, scratchy sound classically has three components corresponding to the cardiac cycle during normal sinus rhythm: atrial systole, ventricular systole, and ventricular filling (Video: Pericarditis). The three phases of the pericardial friction rub differentiate it from a pleural friction rub, which has two components linked to respiration. Less commonly, the rub of pericarditis may be monophasic or biphasic, but it is not affected by respiration. Auscultation should be performed during end-expiration with the patient in the supine position or sitting upright.

The typical ECG feature of acute pericarditis is concave ST-segment elevation in multiple leads that does not correspond to a single coronary artery distribution. PR-segment depression in lead II or reciprocal PR-segment elevation in lead aVR also may be present (

). In contrast, ECG findings of acute myocardial infarction (MI) include hyperacute T waves, ST-segment elevation consistent with a single coronary distribution, reciprocal ST-segment depression, pathologic Q waves during MI evolution, and absence of PR-segment change. ECG abnormalities associated with pericarditis tend to resolve more slowly than those seen with acute MI.

Echocardiography should be performed to evaluate for pericardial effusion; however, the absence of effusion does not exclude acute pericarditis. Both cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging and cardiac CT can be used for further diagnostic evaluation. CMR imaging with intravenous gadolinium contrast may be used to identify evidence of pericardial inflammation, characterized by pericardial thickening and late gadolinium enhancement (

). Alternatively, gated cardiac CT may demonstrate pericardial inflammation. Cardiac CT can be used to evaluate pericardial thickness and calcification as well as constrictive physiology.

Additional findings that support acute pericarditis include fever and serologic evidence of inflammation (leukocytosis, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein [CRP] level). These inflammatory markers also may be used to follow disease progression or resolution. Serum cardiac troponin levels are normal or may be slightly elevated if there is a component of myopericarditis.

Although most cases of acute pericarditis are idiopathic or viral, a search for alternative causes is appropriate (see [Table: Table: Causes of Pericardial Disease]

). Additional testing beyond the initial evaluation is based on suspicion for a specific cause. Tuberculosis should be considered in hospital workers, persons who are incarcerated or residing in chronic care facilities, and residents of or travelers to an endemic area. Peri-infarct pericarditis (PIP) is seen in the first 1 to 2 days after MI and manifests as continued chest pain after reperfusion. It is more common after fibrinolytic therapy than after mechanical reperfusion. PIP typically is self-limited and usually resolves in 3 to 10 days. Postpericardiotomy syndrome, characterized by pericardial inflammation that is likely autoimmune in nature, may occur after cardiac surgery, with a latency period of several weeks. The presentation and treatment of postpericardiotomy syndrome are similar to those of idiopathic pericarditis.

Most patients with acute pericarditis can be managed as outpatients; however, patients with accompanying high-risk features may require hospitalization for treatment and monitoring. These predictors of worse prognosis include the following:

  • Temperature higher than 38.0 °C (100.4 °F)
  • Subacute onset (days to weeks without acute chest pain at onset)
  • A large pericardial effusion (>20-mm diastolic echo-free space) or tamponade at presentation
  • Oral anticoagulation therapy
  • Lack of response (no relief in symptoms and/or inflammatory markers) after 1 week of treatment

First-line therapy for acute idiopathic pericarditis is high-dose aspirin or NSAIDs for 1 to 4 weeks. Colchicine also is recommended as adjunctive therapy to shorten symptom duration and reduce treatment failure and recurrence. Patients who respond to therapy initially but develop recurrent pericarditis after treatment completion may benefit from a longer course of standard therapy with slow tapering. CRP may be useful as a marker of treatment response, with tapering initiated after the CRP level normalizes.

Second-line therapy is determined based on the presence of an inflammatory phenotype. For patients with an inflammatory phenotype (characterized by fever, leukocytosis, elevated CRP, pericardial effusion, and/or pericardial inflammation on CMR), anti–interleukin-1 agents (rilonacept, anakinra) are the next step in treatment. For patients with a noninflammatory phenotype, glucocorticoid therapy (prednisone) should be considered as a second-line therapy at a dosage of 0.2 to 0.5 mg/kg continued for 3 months. Tapering should not be initiated until clinical remission, which should be followed by slow tapering. For very severe cases and refractory symptoms, radical pericardiectomy can be considered at an experienced surgical center.

Expert consensus opinion is that athletes should not return to competitive exercise for 3 months from initial onset of pericarditis and that nonathletes restrict strenuous activity until symptoms resolve.

Patients with PIP typically are managed conservatively with acetaminophen and aspirin once daily as part of standard therapy for MI. In patients with pain that persists after 7 to 10 days of acetaminophen, higher-dose aspirin may be used. Other NSAIDs and glucocorticoids should be avoided, and colchicine generally does not provide significant benefit.

Treatment of tuberculosis is with standard antituberculous therapy and may reduce the risk for reactive pericardial constriction from greater than 80% to less than 10%.

Pericardial effusions are often asymptomatic, with incidental discovery on chest radiograph, CT scan, or echocardiogram. In asymptomatic patients, most effusions are idiopathic; however, malignancy, infections, autoimmune disease, hypothyroidism, and iatrogenic causes (medications, anticoagulation therapy) should be considered (see [Table: Table: Causes of Pericardial Disease]

). In countries where tuberculosis is endemic, more than 60% of effusions are caused by tuberculosis.

Pericardiocentesis should be considered for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes if cancer, tuberculosis, or bacterial infection is strongly suspected. In patients with pericardial effusion of unknown cause and elevated inflammatory markers, empiric treatment of pericarditis may be reasonable. Drainage should be considered for large idiopathic effusions of more than 3 months’ duration, because one in three such patients have progression to cardiac tamponade.

Cardiac tamponade occurs when fluid accumulates within the pericardial space, compressing the heart and impeding diastolic filling. With rapid fluid accumulation, as may occur with trauma, aortic dissection, or invasive cardiac procedures, tamponade may arise with relatively small volumes of pericardial fluid. Subacute or chronic processes, such as neoplastic disease or hypothyroidism, may be associated with much larger effusions (several hundred milliliters in volume).

Clinical signs of tamponade include tachycardia, muffled heart sounds, and elevated central venous pressure (see [Table: Table: Evaluation of Pericardial Disease]

). Blood pressure may be elevated or normal early in the course as a result of adrenergic response, with ensuing hypotension as intrapericardial pressure rises and compromises diastolic filling. The y descent of the jugular venous pulse may be absent because passive filling of the ventricles is impeded by the increased intrapericardial pressure. This finding may be difficult to appreciate, especially in patients with tachycardia. Pulsus paradoxus represents exaggerated ventricular interdependence and is a key clinical feature of cardiac tamponade. It is characterized by a fall in systolic pressure of greater than 10 mm Hg during inspiration. Pulsus paradoxus is not specific for tamponade and must be interpreted in conjunction with other clinical and echocardiographic findings.

The ECG in patients with tamponade may demonstrate sinus tachycardia and features of a pericardial effusion, such as electrical alternans (related to a swinging motion of the heart within the pericardial fluid) (

) or low voltage. If fluid has accumulated slowly, the cardiac silhouette is typically enlarged on chest radiograph (

).

Echocardiography is an essential tool in the diagnosis of cardiac tamponade because it defines the presence, distribution, and relative volume of pericardial fluid (

). Early diastolic collapse of the right ventricle, late diastolic collapse of the right atrium, and abnormal interventricular septal motion are echocardiographic features associated with cardiac tamponade. Doppler evaluation may also demonstrate a decrease in mitral inflow velocity of more than 25% with inspiration, which is the echocardiographic equivalent of pulsus paradoxus (

).

Right heart catheterization rarely is necessary for diagnosis. Hemodynamic hallmarks of tamponade include blunting or loss of the y descent within the right atrial pressure waveform and elevated and equalized diastolic pressures. The latter reflects the transmitted effect of the intrapericardial pressure. Invasive arterial pressure recordings also show pulsus paradoxus.

Cardiac tamponade is life threatening, and urgent pericardial drainage is required after diagnostic confirmation. Fluid removal can be accomplished with pericardiocentesis or a surgical subxiphoid approach. Pericardiocentesis is often performed with echocardiographic or fluoroscopic guidance. Surgical therapy is indicated to drain fluid if pericardiocentesis cannot be performed safely, to obtain pericardial tissue for diagnostic purposes, or to prevent recurrent pericardial effusion by creating a pericardial window (often used in cases of malignant pericardial effusion). In hemodynamically unstable patients, intravenous normal saline is used to stabilize the patient as a temporizing measure or bridge to definitive therapy.

After pericardial drainage, hemodynamic and clinical evaluation may occasionally disclose findings of underlying pericardial constriction, termed effusive constrictive pericarditis. If clinical evaluation and imaging studies (such as CMR imaging) suggest an active inflammatory process, medical therapy for acute pericarditis may be considered, with surgery reserved for refractory cases.

Constrictive pericarditis is characterized by pericardial thickening, fibrosis, and sometimes calcification that impair diastolic filling and limit total cardiac volume. Most cases are idiopathic, although tuberculosis remains a major cause of constrictive pericarditis where the disease is endemic. Other causes include cardiac surgery, chest irradiation, autoimmune disease, and bacterial infection.

Constrictive pericarditis most commonly presents as indolent progression of right-sided heart failure symptoms, including peripheral edema and abdominal swelling (see [Table: Table: Evaluation of Pericardial Disease]

). Exertional dyspnea and fatigue also occur and are caused by increased diastolic pressures and limited ability to augment cardiac output due to the fixed stroke volume.

On physical examination, the central venous pressure is elevated in nearly all patients, with prominent x and y descents. The prominent y descent in constrictive pericarditis is distinct from the decreased y descent in tamponade. The height of the waveform does not fall or may increase during inspiration (Kussmaul sign), reflecting the fixed diastolic volume of the right heart. Early diastolic filling is unimpaired or even accentuated and is followed by sudden cessation when total acceptable volume is met, resulting in a high-frequency early diastolic sound (the pericardial knock). Characteristics that may be used to differentiate a pericardial knock from other diastolic sounds are listed in [Table: Table: Characteristics of the Selected Diastolic Heart Sounds]

. Pulsus paradoxus is less frequent in constrictive pericarditis than in cardiac tamponade. Peripheral edema, ascites, hepatomegaly, and pleural effusions are common.

An ECG is obtained as part of the initial evaluation and may reveal low voltage; however, no ECG findings are specific to constrictive pericarditis.

Diagnosis of constrictive pericarditis is made with imaging studies and hemodynamic evaluation. Transthoracic echocardiography reveals normal right and left ventricular size and systolic function despite prominent symptoms and findings that suggest heart failure. Dilatation of the inferior vena cava reflects elevated right-sided filling (right atrial) pressure. Doppler echocardiography and tissue Doppler velocity are required to differentiate constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy (see Differentiating Restrictive Cardiomyopathy From Constrictive Pericarditis in Cardiovascular Medicine). Myocardial relaxation is unimpaired or even enhanced in constrictive pericarditis, whereas relaxation is impaired in restrictive cardiomyopathy. The distinction between constrictive pericarditis and restrictive cardiomyopathy is important because management with pericardiectomy will be effective in the former and of no value in the latter (see Management of Constrictive Pericarditis in Cardiovascular Medicine).

Chest radiography or CT in constrictive pericarditis may demonstrate partial or circumferential pericardial calcification (

), and pericardial thickening (>3 mm) may be visible on CT or CMR imaging. Importantly, constriction may exist in the absence of these findings. CMR imaging also may demonstrate an inspiratory septal shift, a sign of ventricular interdependence.

Simultaneous left and right heart catheterization may be performed when constrictive pericarditis is suspected but not confirmed by echocardiography. Invasive hemodynamic findings of constrictive pericarditis include a prominent y descent in the right atrial waveform, which corresponds to the dip of the right ventricular dip-and-plateau waveform (square root sign), both of which represent unimpeded or rapid early diastolic ventricular filling. As inflow volume reaches the fixed pericardial constraint, pressure rises rapidly until maximum volume is achieved; pressure then remains constant, causing the plateau phase of the square root sign. A more specific finding is ventricular interdependence during simultaneous right and left ventricular systolic pressure measurement. During inspiration, right ventricular inflow is enhanced and right ventricular systolic pressure rises; however, these changes occur with a concomitant decrease in left ventricular filling and reduction in left ventricular stroke volume and systolic pressure (

). The converse is seen during expiration.

Counter to the usual chronic presentation, less frequently pericardial thickening and impaired distensibility may occur without fibrosis or calcification in the setting of acute or subacute inflammation. In these patients, constriction may be transient and resolve spontaneously. Patients with transient constrictive pericarditis present most commonly with symptoms of right-sided heart failure, although fever and chest pain may indicate active inflammation. Most cases are idiopathic; other causes include recent cardiac surgery, acute pericarditis, autoimmune disease, and chemotherapy. Systemic inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and CRP) may be elevated in transient constriction but are generally normal with fixed constriction. Echocardiographic features are similar to those of fixed constriction, although pericardial effusion is more likely in patients with transient constrictive pericarditis.

Treatment of transient constrictive pericarditis is the same as for acute pericarditis. Anti-inflammatory therapy for 2 to 3 months is reasonable in hemodynamically stable patients before consideration of surgical pericardiectomy. Diuretics improve symptoms by reducing volume overload and cardiac filling pressures but may have only modest benefit. Response to therapy is monitored clinically; echocardiographically; and if initial inflammatory markers are elevated, serologically.

Patients with chronic pericardial constriction should first be medically optimized with diuretic therapy. Those with ongoing symptomatic constrictive pericarditis can be referred for surgical pericardial stripping (pericardiectomy performed via median sternotomy). Prior to surgical intervention, cardiac CT can be beneficial for surgical planning. In advanced cases, adequate resection of the pericardium may be difficult, leading to incomplete resolution of symptoms. Diuretic therapy may be useful to relieve congestive symptoms in patients who are not deemed surgical candidates or in whom stripping was incomplete.

Adult Congenital Heart Disease

Congenital heart defects encompass a wide range of structural abnormalities of the heart, varying from simple lesions that may require little or no intervention to complex defects that usually necessitate one or more surgeries in childhood for survival. Advances in medical and surgical care have led to a growing population of adults living with congenital heart disease (CHD), now outnumbering children with CHD in North America. Lifelong surveillance is essential, as patients may develop cardiovascular residua, heart failure, endocarditis, arrhythmias, or end-organ dysfunction. Follow-up with clinicians experienced in adult CHD (ACHD)—typically a partnership between an internal medicine physician and an ACHD-trained cardiologist—is recommended throughout life. Specialized care is particularly important for individuals with complex congenital defects, those with symptoms or noncardiac organ involvement, and those planning pregnancy. The optimal interval for follow-up varies according to the specific diagnosis and the patient’s clinical status.

Adults with CHD have a higher prevalence of hepatitis C virus, particularly those who had open heart surgery before 1992 when screening of blood products in the United States became standard. The CDC guidelines for screening and vaccination should be followed, including universal hepatitis C screening and hepatitis B vaccination for all nonimmune patients aged 19 through 59 years. Persons who have undergone a Fontan procedure for single-ventricle palliation are at high risk for liver disease; they should be tested for immunity after vaccination for hepatitis A and B and offered repeat vaccination if nonimmune. Pneumococcal vaccination is advised for adults with CHD and those with asplenia or functional asplenia (right atrial isomerism), as with other types of chronic heart disease. Some conotruncal heart defects (pulmonary atresia, truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot) may be associated with 22q11 deletion (the DiGeorge spectrum), and similarly these patients should be offered pneumococcal vaccination.

Anxiety and depression are prevalent and underrecognized in patients with CHD, and screening for these mood disorders should be a routine aspect of care.

Patients with CHD should be offered reproductive health counseling. The use of contraceptive agents in patients with CHD must be balanced against the risks of pregnancy; however, no safety data are available on the various contraceptives to help guide choice. Estrogen-containing contraceptives may pose a risk in patients with CHD who are already at high risk for thromboembolic disease, including those with mechanical valves, cyanosis, Fontan physiology, previous thrombotic events, or pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). In pregnant patients, anticoagulation is associated with maternal and fetal risks. Prepregnancy counseling is recommended for all patients requiring long-term anticoagulation to enable them to make informed decisions and to understand the risks (see Anticoagulation Therapy During Pregnancy in Cardiovascular Medicine).

The foramen ovale is a passage in the superior portion of the fossa ovalis of the interatrial septum that allows oxygenated placental blood to transfer to the fetal circulation. It normally closes within the first weeks of life; however, in 25% to 30% of the population, it remains patent (

). A patent foramen ovale (PFO) is usually found incidentally on echocardiography or during evaluation of a cerebrovascular event.

A PFO is typically diagnosed by transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) or, less commonly, transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) or transcranial Doppler ultrasonography (to detect right-to-left shunt). Most PFOs diagnosed by echocardiography are incidental and benign findings because there is a small amount of left-to-right shunting of blood. Right-to-left shunting of blood across the PFO is demonstrated by color flow Doppler imaging or by intravenously injecting agitated saline and identifying its subsequent transfer through the PFO from the right atrium to the left atrium (Video: Transthoracic Echocardiogram Showing Patent Foramen Ovale), sometimes with the aid of a Valsalva maneuver.

Patients with a PFO and embolic stroke of undetermined source should receive antiplatelet therapy. In adult patients younger than 60 years with a PFO with high-risk features such as a right-to-left shunt and/or the presence of an atrial septal aneurysm and an embolic-appearing infarct without an alternate mechanism, current guidelines recommend PFO closure after a discussion of potential benefits and risks, including periprocedural complications and increased nonperiprocedural atrial fibrillation. The utility of PFO closure in patients younger than 60 years with stroke but without high-risk features is unclear, and data regarding the benefit of PFO closure in patients older than 60 years are lacking. Some experts recommend screening for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation in these patients with an implantable loop recorder or at least 28 days of cardiac event monitoring before PFO closure. For older patients, and for younger patients who do not select PFO closure, antiplatelet therapy or anticoagulation is reasonable. Insufficient data are available supporting PFO closure to decrease the frequency of migraine. No treatment or follow-up is needed in asymptomatic patients with an incidentally detected PFO.

Atrial septal aneurysm is characterized by mobile, redundant atrial septal tissue that is often associated with a PFO. Atrial septal aneurysm with a PFO reportedly increases the risk for stroke compared with PFO alone. Results of a randomized, open-label trial demonstrated that patients presenting with embolic stroke of undetermined source in the setting of an atrial septal aneurysm with PFO had a lower rate of stroke recurrence when treated with PFO closure combined with antiplatelet therapy than with antiplatelet therapy alone. Rarely, surgical excision and defect closure are considered solely on the basis of anatomic features.

Platypnea-orthodeoxia syndrome is a rare acquired disorder characterized by cyanosis and dyspnea in the upright position resulting from right-to-left shunting across a PFO or, less commonly, through an atrial septal defect (ASD) or pulmonary arteriovenous fistulae. Cyanosis in a patient with a PFO is an indication for evaluation by a cardiologist to determine whether it is related to the PFO. Device closure of the PFO may relieve symptoms and improve oxygen saturation.

An ASD is a defect in the atrial septum resulting in a left-to-right shunt that may go undetected in childhood, with eventual right-sided cardiac chamber dilatation in most patients. Ostium secundum defects, the most common type of ASD (75% of cases), are typically located in the mid portion of the atrial septum and are usually isolated anomalies. Ostium primum defects are located in the lowest portion of the atrial septum and are a component of endocardial cushion defects. Associated lesions include cleft mitral valve, ventricular septal defect (VSD), and subaortic stenosis. Sinus venosus defects are located near the superior vena cava or, rarely, the inferior vena cava; anomalous pulmonary venous connection occurs in essentially all patients with this defect. A coronary sinus ASD is a communication between the left atrium and the coronary sinus. These defects are commonly associated with a persistent left-sided superior vena cava or complex CHD.

ASDs may be associated with genetic syndromes such as Down syndrome (trisomy 21); the most frequent abnormalities reported in Down syndrome are atrioventricular septal defects, including ostium primum ASD and tetralogy of Fallot.

ASD size and associated defects influence the age of presentation. Presenting findings may include fatigue, exertional dyspnea, arrhythmias, and paradoxical embolism. ASDs may also be suspected in patients with unexplained right heart enlargement or atrial arrhythmias; atrial fibrillation is a common finding, particularly in older patients. Rarely, patients with PAH are found to have isolated ASDs.

Examination findings in patients with an ASD may be subtle and include a parasternal impulse, fixed splitting of the S~2, and a pulmonary outflow murmur (Video: Large Ostium Secundum Atrial Septal Defect).

ECG and radiographic findings in patients with an ASD are presented in [Table: Table: Imaging Findings and Late Complications in Adult CHD]

.

TTE is the preferred imaging modality for identifying ostium secundum and primum ASDs. TTE also evaluates for right-sided cardiac chamber enlargement, tricuspid regurgitation, and right ventricular systolic pressure elevation. Agitated saline contrast injection in a peripheral vein during TTE may help identify an atrial-level shunt. Sinus venosus and coronary sinus ASDs are diagnosed by TTE less readily in adults and often require other imaging modalities, such as TEE, cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging, or CT. CMR imaging and CT can identify anomalous pulmonary veins and quantify right ventricular volume and ejection fraction if needed.

Cardiac catheterization is the only method for accurately calculating pulmonary-to-systemic blood flow ratio (Qp:Qs), although cardiac MRI is emerging as an alternative. Cardiac catheterization may be recommended in patients with an ASD and PAH when ASD closure is being considered or if data gathered noninvasively are discordant or inconclusive.

In asymptomatic patients with a small ASD, no right heart enlargement, and no pulmonary hypertension, periodic clinical monitoring and echocardiographic imaging are recommended.

The main indications for ASD closure include functional impairment (dyspnea, fatigue, exercise intolerance) and right-sided cardiac chamber enlargement.

Percutaneous device closure is indicated for patients with an isolated ostium secundum ASD causing functional impairment and hemodynamic consequences and is also a reasonable option for asymptomatic patients with shunt-related hemodynamic consequences. When indicated, surgical ASD closure is preferred for ostium secundum ASDs that are large or have unfavorable anatomy for device closure, for other types of ASDs, and if cardiac surgery is planned for other indications.

Patients with an ASD and PAH require specialized care to identify candidates for closure and/or medical therapy.

Activity restriction is not required for patients with small ASDs. Large left-to-right shunts result in self-limited exercise restrictions. Patients with severe PAH are advised to avoid isometric or competitive exercise.

Pregnancy is generally well-tolerated in patients with an ASD in the absence of PAH. The risk for CHD transmission with a sporadic ASD is estimated to be around 5%. Genetic counseling is suggested if a syndrome is suspected.

Follow-up after surgical or percutaneous ASD closure includes TTE and clinical assessment within the first year after closure and periodically afterward. Endocarditis prophylaxis is indicated for 6 months after closure. Atrial fibrillation risk persists after closure, and frequency is higher with increased age at the time of ASD closure. Rare complications after device closure include device migration, erosion into the pericardium or aorta, and sudden death.

VSDs are defined by their location on the ventricular septum. Membranous VSDs are most common (80% of cases); they are usually isolated abnormalities and may close spontaneously in childhood. Muscular VSDs (10% of cases) may be located anywhere in the ventricular septum and often close spontaneously. Subpulmonary VSDs (also called outlet or supracristal VSDs) are associated with aortic regurgitation due to aortic cusp distortion. Inlet VSDs occur as part of the atrioventricular septal defect complex, characteristically seen in patients with Down syndrome.

VSDs are common at birth, but because many close spontaneously, the prevalence of VSD decreases by adulthood. VSDs that do not close spontaneously are typically identified in childhood and closed surgically if needed.

The presentation of an isolated VSD depends on the VSD size and pulmonary vascular resistance. A small VSD without PAH presents with a loud holosystolic murmur located at the left sternal border that obliterates the S~2 (Video: Small Ventricular Septal Defect), often with a palpable thrill. Small VSDs do not cause left heart enlargement or PAH.

A VSD with a moderate left-to-right shunt may cause left ventricular volume overload, and the patient may eventually present with heart failure symptoms. A displaced left ventricular apical impulse suggests volume overload. A holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border is noted; the pressure gradient between the ventricles determines the murmur quality and duration. Progressive elevation of right ventricular pressure results in reduced murmur intensity.

VSDs associated with large left-to-right shunts usually are detected in infancy by the presence of a murmur, heart failure, and failure to thrive. Failure to correct the shunt early in life usually causes fixed PAH with shunt reversal (Eisenmenger syndrome).

ECG and radiographic findings in patients with a VSD are presented in [Table: Table: Imaging Findings and Late Complications in Adult CHD]

.

TTE is the imaging modality of choice for identifying VSD location, size, and hemodynamic impact. Rarely, TEE, CMR imaging, or CT is needed to delineate cardiac anatomy. Cardiac catheterization is performed in select patients to delineate the Qp:Qs ratio and pulmonary pressures.

VSD closure is indicated to prevent left heart failure in the absence of PAH when the Qp:Qs ratio is 1.5 or greater with evidence of left ventricular volume overload. Most patients are treated surgically, but percutaneous device closure is an option for select VSDs. Large VSDs with shunt reversal (right-to-left shunting) and PAH (Eisenmenger syndrome) should not be closed because closure leads to clinical deterioration.

VSD closure is not indicated for patients with a small left-to-right shunt and no chamber enlargement or valve disease, but periodic clinical evaluation and imaging are recommended.

Patients with small VSDs do not require activity restrictions. If the pulmonary artery pressure is greater than 50% of systolic blood pressure, isometric and competitive exercise is discouraged.

Pregnancy in patients with small unrepaired VSDs is generally well-tolerated in the absence of PAH, although left heart failure may occur. Patients with VSDs and associated fixed PAH should be counseled to avoid pregnancy.

Lifelong care is recommended for patients with a VSD. Residual or recurrent VSD, arrhythmias, PAH, endocarditis, and valve regurgitation are recognized complications after VSD closure. Endocarditis prophylaxis should be provided for 6 months after closure. Clinical assessment and TTE are recommended within 1 year of VSD closure. Frequency of subsequent follow-up depends on clinical status.

A patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is a persistent fetal connection between the aorta and the left pulmonary artery. It may be an isolated abnormality or associated with other congenital cardiac defects. Prematurity and maternal rubella predispose to a PDA.

The typical murmur of a PDA is a continuous “machinery” murmur beneath the left clavicle that envelops the S~2, making it inaudible. A tiny PDA is generally asymptomatic and inaudible. Patients with a moderate-sized PDA may present with bounding pulses, wide arterial pulse pressure, left heart enlargement and dysfunction, and rarely, heart failure. A large unrepaired PDA may cause PAH with eventual shunt reversal (Eisenmenger syndrome) as well as clubbing and oxygen desaturation affecting the feet but not the hands (differential cyanosis).

ECG and radiographic findings in patients with a PDA are presented in [Table: Table: Imaging Findings and Late Complications in Adult CHD]

.

TTE is the imaging modality of choice for identifying a PDA. The PDA may be difficult to visualize in patients with severe PAH owing to equalization of pressures between the aorta and pulmonary artery. In patients with a PDA and PAH, cardiac catheterization is used to determine shunt size and reversibility of PAH. TEE, CT, and CMR imaging may identify a PDA but are not the primary diagnostic techniques.

PDA closure is indicated for left-sided cardiac chamber enlargement if the pulmonary artery systolic pressure is less than 50% of the systemic pressure. Percutaneous closure is usually performed; referral to a congenital cardiac center for consideration of closure options is recommended.

Patients with a small PDA without PAH do not require physical activity restrictions, and they should be able to tolerate pregnancy.

Pulmonary stenosis (PS) causes obstruction of right ventricular outflow and is usually an isolated valve lesion. PS may be associated with Noonan syndrome, a typically autosomal dominant condition associated with short stature; webbed neck; and other facial, skeletal, and cardiac abnormalities.

Mild and moderate PS is generally asymptomatic. Severe PS may cause exertional dyspnea.

On physical examination, mild PS is associated with a normal jugular venous waveform and precordial impulse. With more significant disease, right ventricular hypertrophy due to pressure overload results in a prominent a wave on the jugular venous waveform (Video: Giant a Wave) and a palpable right ventricular lift.

Auscultatory findings in PS include an early systolic ejection click, which is the only right-sided heart sound to decrease during inspiration, followed by a crescendo-decrescendo murmur. In severe PS, the systolic ejection murmur at the left sternal border increases in intensity and duration, and the pulmonary component of S~2 is delayed (causing a split S~2) then disappears. A right ventricular S~4 is often heard in severe PS.

ECG and radiographic findings in patients with PS are presented in [Table: Table: Imaging Findings and Late Complications in Adult CHD]

.

TTE is the imaging modality of choice for identifying PS. PS causes right ventricular hypertrophy rather than enlargement. The presence of right ventricular dilatation should prompt a search for an associated lesion, such as pulmonary regurgitation or an ASD. Cardiac catheterization is performed when percutaneous intervention for PS is considered.

Pulmonary balloon valvuloplasty is the preferred treatment for isolated valvular PS in symptomatic patients with moderate or severe PS. Surgical intervention is recommended for PS when associated lesions requiring operative intervention are present.

Patients with mild or moderate PS do not require exercise restriction. Those with untreated severe PS should be limited to low-intensity sports.

Pregnancy is generally well-tolerated in patients with PS; percutaneous valvotomy has been performed during pregnancy for severe symptomatic PS. Noonan syndrome should be suspected with PS recurrence in offspring.

Patients with previous PS intervention (balloon or surgical) often have severe pulmonary regurgitation; thus, long-term clinical and TTE follow-up is recommended. The frequency of follow-up depends on regurgitation severity and impact on the heart.

Aortic coarctation is a discrete narrowing of the aorta, usually located just beyond the left subclavian artery, causing secondary hypertension proximal and hypotension distal to the narrowing.

Aortic coarctation should be suspected in all patients with severe hypertension, especially young patients, and in patients whose hypertension does not respond to pharmacologic therapy. Severe aortic coarctation may present as heart failure and, rarely, claudication. On examination, upper extremity hypertension and reduced blood pressure and pulse amplitude in the lower extremities cause a radial artery–to–femoral artery pulse delay. A systolic or continuous murmur is heard in the left infraclavicular region or over the back. A murmur from collateral intercostal vessels also may be audible over the chest wall. Because 50% of patients with aortic coarctation have a bicuspid aortic valve, auscultation of the heart may reveal an ejection click, a systolic murmur at the cardiac base, or an S~4.

Turner syndrome, an abnormality resulting from partial or total loss of chromosome X, is often associated with coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve. Turner syndrome is characterized by short stature; webbed neck; broad chest; widely spaced nipples; and, usually, infertility. Aortic coarctation is also associated with other left-sided heart defects, VSD, and cerebral aneurysms.

ECG and radiographic findings in patients with aortic coarctation are presented in [Table: Table: Imaging Findings and Late Complications in Adult CHD]

.

The characteristic radiographic features of aortic coarctation include the “figure 3 sign” (

), which is caused by dilatation of the aorta above and below the area of coarctation. Dilatation of intercostal collateral arteries due to aortic obstruction may lead to the radiographic appearance of rib notching.

TTE is often the initial diagnostic test in patients in whom aortic coarctation is suspected; it usually identifies the coarctation and associated features, such as bicuspid aortic valve and left ventricular hypertrophy. CMR imaging and CT are recommended to identify the anatomy, severity, and location of the coarctation; the presence of collateral vessels; and associated abnormalities, such as aortic aneurysm. Cardiac catheterization is used primarily in patients in whom percutaneous intervention is being considered.

Severe aortic coarctation is associated with excess morbidity and mortality, including hypertension, coronary artery disease, stroke, aortic dissection, and heart failure. Repair reduces the risk for such complications and improves but does not normalize patient survival. Age at the time of coarctation repair is the most important predictor of long-term survival.

Indications for intervention in patients with coarctation include upper extremity hypertension, hemodynamic features of significant aortic coarctation (>20 mm Hg pressure gradient), and/or radiologic (CT or CMR) evidence of severe coarctation with collateral flow. The choice between percutaneous or surgical intervention depends on the length, location, and severity of coarctation and the presence of associated cardiovascular lesions.

Physical activity restriction is recommended for patients with severe postintervention residual or unrepaired coarctation, aortic stenosis, or a dilated aorta; these patients should avoid contact sports and isometric exercise.

A comprehensive preconception evaluation is warranted in all patients with coarctation who are considering pregnancy. Pregnancy is reasonable in patients with repaired aortic coarctation without significant residua. Those with mild or moderate residua or unoperated coarctation will generally tolerate pregnancy well but should undergo blood pressure monitoring and cardiovascular evaluation during pregnancy. Patients with severe unrepaired coarctation should avoid pregnancy.

Hypertension most commonly occurs in persons who had coarctation repair after the age of 1 year. Hypertension, regardless of the patient’s age at repair, should be treated and the patient evaluated for recoarctation. Additional intervention after repair may be required for bicuspid aortic valve, aortic aneurysm or dissection, recoarctation, coronary artery disease, systolic or diastolic heart failure, or intracranial aneurysm. Regular follow-up should include TTE, periodic aortic imaging by CT or CMR, and evaluation by a cardiologist specializing in CHD.

Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is characterized by a large subaortic VSD, infundibular and/or valvular PS, aortic override, and right ventricular hypertrophy (

). It is the most common cyanotic congenital cardiac lesion. Repair is usually performed early in life; adults who have not undergone an operation are rarely encountered in countries with access to pediatric cardiothoracic surgery.

TOF repair involves VSD patch closure and relief of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction with disruption of the pulmonary valve, causing severe pulmonary regurgitation. Adults typically have a diastolic murmur at the second left intercostal space that increases with inspiration as a result of pulmonary regurgitation. Severe long-standing pulmonary regurgitation causes right heart enlargement, tricuspid regurgitation, exercise limitation, and atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. Most adults will require reoperation after TOF repair to replace the pulmonary valve. Individuals with TOF may require several pulmonary valve replacements over a lifetime; subsequent procedures often can be performed by a transcatheter route. The incidence of sudden cardiac death after TOF repair is approximately 2% per decade. Annual congenital cardiology follow-up is recommended for patients with repaired TOF to determine optimal timing for intervention.

ECG and radiographic findings in patients with repaired TOF are presented in [Table: Table: Imaging Findings and Late Complications in Adult CHD]

.

Symptoms, arrhythmias, or right heart enlargement should prompt a search for severe pulmonary regurgitation. Prolongation of the QRS complex reflects the degree of right ventricular dilatation. Left ventricular dysfunction, prolonged QRS duration, and nonsustained ventricular tachycardia are risk factors for sudden cardiac death.

TTE is the imaging modality of choice for identifying valve dysfunction, residual VSD, left ventricular dysfunction, and aortic dilatation. CMR imaging or CT is preferred for assessing right ventricular size and function, which helps determine the appropriate timing for pulmonary valve replacement. Cardiac catheterization may be required if an intervention is planned.

Late complications of TOF include right heart failure related to pulmonary valve regurgitation and, less commonly, pulmonary stenosis and left heart failure. Indications for pulmonary valve replacement in patients with severe pulmonary regurgitation include symptoms, decreased exercise tolerance, moderate or greater right heart enlargement or mild or moderate right or left heart dysfunction, and arrhythmias. Tricuspid valve repair also may be needed. Pulmonary valve replacement is reasonable in asymptomatic patients with repaired TOF and ventricular enlargement or dysfunction and moderate or greater pulmonary regurgitation.

Patients with TOF also may present with atrial and/or ventricular arrhythmias. The onset of arrhythmias should prompt referral for evaluation of valve and ventricular function. Patients who have undergone pulmonary valve replacement are at risk for infective endocarditis and require endocarditis prophylaxis and evaluation of unexplained fever.

Physical activity restriction is recommended for patients with repaired TOF and residual sequelae; contact sports and heavy isometric exercise should be avoided. Patients with repaired TOF and pulmonary valve replacement without residual lesions may not require activity restrictions.

Patients with congenital heart defects, even if repaired in childhood, require lifelong care. Adults with heart defects are at risk for many late cardiac and multiorgan complications related to their native anatomy, the nature of the surgical repair(s), interventions, residual defects, and the presence of other comorbid conditions ( [Table: Table: Imaging Findings and Late Complications in Adult CHD]

and [Table: Table: Complications of Moderate to Severe Congenital Heart Disease]

).

Despite the multitude of late complications that may occur, it is not uncommon for patients, as well as their providers, to have the misperception that patients have been cured by the childhood surgery, leading to gaps in care and subsequent adverse outcomes. Late complications in an adult with CHD should be managed in conjunction with a congenital cardiologist because recognition and correction of residual cardiac lesions can prevent irreversible organ dysfunction.

Left heart failure occurs in patients with both left- and right-sided heart defects and is associated with hospitalizations and increased mortality. Guideline-directed medical therapy and treatment of residual lesions are recommended (see Management of Heart Failure in Cardiovascular Medicine).

Although rare in adults, heart defect–related cyanosis predisposes patients to several complications, including erythrocytosis, paradoxical cerebral emboli or abscess, gout, cholelithiasis, pulmonary hemorrhage or thrombus, kidney dysfunction, and pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma. Importantly, intravenous treatment in patients with cyanotic CHD requires in-line air filters to prevent paradoxical air embolism.

Erythrocytosis in patients with cyanosis is secondary and compensatory. It rarely requires phlebotomy; however, iron deficiency should be avoided. Brain abscess may present with subtle neurologic findings with or without fever and with or without endocarditis. A high index of suspicion is necessary to make the diagnosis, and cerebral imaging should be obtained in any patient with cyanosis who has new neurologic findings or unexplained fever.

Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures is effective in reducing infective endocarditis in high-risk patients, such as those with cyanosis related to their unrepaired or palliated CHD, residual shunts, and/or prosthetic valves (see Infective Endocarditis in Cardiovascular Medicine). Unexplained fever in the absence of localizing symptoms should prompt evaluation for endocarditis with blood cultures before antibiotic treatment is initiated.

Diseases of the Aorta

Diseases of the aorta comprise chronic conditions, such as thoracic and abdominal aortic aneurysms and aortic atheromas, and potentially life-threatening acute conditions, such as aortic dissection and aneurysm rupture. Appropriate treatment and surveillance of aortic disease are critical to preventing disease progression, complications, and death. Management of these conditions is often complicated, and guidelines from the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and American Heart Association (AHA) recommend that a multidisciplinary aortic team be engaged to determine the appropriate timing and type of intervention when indicated.

Thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is defined as an increase in the thoracic aortic diameter of greater than 50% of the expected aortic dimension, which is influenced by age, sex, and body type. TAAs may occur at the level of the aortic root, ascending aorta, aortic arch, or descending aorta. Most commonly, they involve the aortic root and ascending aorta, often forming at the site of aortic atherosclerosis.

Common causes of TAA are summarized in [Table: Table: Causes of Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm]

. TAAs are usually the result of cystic medial degeneration and weakening of the aortic wall due to loss of smooth muscle fibers and elastic fiber degeneration. TAAs occurring in patients younger than 50 years often are caused by connective tissue disorders, such as Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and Loeys-Dietz syndrome. Overall, approximately 20% of TAAs are related to a genetic or heritable condition. Bicuspid aortic valve morphology is an important risk factor for TAA formation, with TAA occurring in approximately 50% of patients with a bicuspid aortic valve. Other risk factors for TAA include hypertension, smoking, and advanced age.

TAAs often are asymptomatic and detected incidentally during thoracic imaging or transthoracic echocardiography performed for other indications. Infrequently, dysphagia and hoarseness occur when an aneurysm compresses surrounding structures. If the aneurysm ruptures, patients may have severe chest pain, back pain, sudden shortness of breath, or sudden death. A diastolic heart murmur, wide pulse pressure, or symptoms of heart failure may signal aortic regurgitation, which often occurs in combination with TAA. Patients may also initially present with clinical findings suggestive of inherited diseases that may involve the aorta, such as the tall stature, pectus excavatum, and ectopic lens seen in Marfan syndrome or the hypermobility of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Screening for abnormalities of the thoracic aorta with aortic imaging is indicated in asymptomatic patients with a bicuspid aortic valve and those with genetic conditions that predispose to aortic aneurysms and dissections (e.g., Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Turner syndrome).

All first-degree relatives of patients with aortic disease should undergo genetic testing or screening aortic imaging based on the initial presentation of the afflicted patient. Genetic testing should be performed in patients with TAA and/or dissection if any of the following are present:

  • Clinical features consistent with predisposing diseases
  • A family history of TAA and/or dissection, or intracranial or peripheral aneurysms
  • Onset at age less than 60 years

If genetic testing is positive (e.g., FBN1, TGFBR1, TGFBR2, COL3A1, MYH11), first-degree relatives should undergo genetic screening for the identified variant, with aortic imaging if they possess the variant (see Genetic Testing for Cardiovascular Disease in Cardiovascular Medicine). If no pathologic variant is identified, first-degree relatives should undergo aortic imaging screening.

If none of the aforementioned conditions is met (i.e., the afflicted relative has a sporadic aneurysm at age ≥60 years), then first-degree relatives should undergo aortic imaging screening.

Screening echocardiography might be considered in first-degree relatives of patients with a bicuspid valve.

Screening is not recommended in other asymptomatic persons.

If TAA is identified, the aortic cross-sectional area should be determined using noninvasive imaging ( [Table: Table: Thoracic Aortic Imaging Modalities]

). To determine the aortic diameter accurately, it must be measured perpendicular to the long axis of the aorta; the diameter often varies substantially depending on the type of imaging study used. The maximum aortic diameter at the site of aneurysm generally is included in the criteria for surveillance and treatment.

Because the leading cause of death in patients with TAA is rupture, surveillance and treatment depend on aneurysm size and subsequent rupture risk. The average expansion rate of TAA is 0.1 cm/year but is influenced by patient-specific factors. Expansion rate increases with increasing diameter of the aneurysm and is faster during pregnancy, when involving the ascending aorta, and in patients with either Marfan syndrome or bicuspid aortic valve. Recommendations for aneurysm surveillance are provided in [Table: Table: Recommendations for Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm Surveillance]

.

Aneurysms smaller than 5.0 cm are most often imaged with transthoracic echocardiography, provided an adequate image can be obtained. Other imaging modalities include CT angiography (CTA) and magnetic resonance angiography (MRA).

TAAs with a diameter smaller than 5.0 cm usually can be managed with medical therapy and active surveillance. Medical therapy includes aggressive blood pressure control with a goal below 130/80 mm Hg. β-Blockers are the preferred antihypertensive agents in patients with TAA. In patients with Marfan syndrome, β-blockers and losartan have been associated with a reduced rate of aneurysm growth. Statin therapy is also recommended in all patients.

When an ascending aortic aneurysm due to degenerative disease exceeds 5.5 cm in diameter or has rapid growth (≥0.5 cm/year or ≥0.3 cm/year over 2 years), surgical repair is warranted to prevent the morbidity and mortality associated with rupture. Surgery may also be considered for sporadic aneurysms 5.0 cm or larger in diameter. In patients with nonsyndromic hereditary TAA, surgical repair may be considered on the basis of family history (≥4.5 cm with high-risk family history or ≥5.0 cm without high-risk family history). In patients with Marfan syndrome or another genetically mediated disorder, the ACC/AHA guidelines suggest elective aortic repair if the aneurysm exceeds 5.0 cm, depending on the underlying condition.

Current guidelines recommend that all patients with a bicuspid aortic valve and ascending aortic aneurysm undergo aortic repair if the aneurysm exceeds 5.5 cm in diameter, unless an additional risk factor for dissection (family history of aortic dissection, aortic growth rate ≥0.3 cm/year, aortic coarctation, or aortic root dilatation/aneurysm) is present or the patient is at low operative risk, in which case aortic repair is reasonable at 5.0 cm.

In patients who require surgery for coronary artery disease (CAD) or valve pathology with an ascending aorta or aortic root larger than 5.0 cm in diameter, aortic repair should be performed at the time of cardiac surgery; an exception is if the surgery involves repair or replacement of an aortic valve (bicuspid or tricuspid), in which case the threshold is 4.5 cm.

Aneurysm location, aortic valve pathology, and the presence of concomitant CAD dictate the type of thoracic aortic repair performed. Open surgical repair is indicated for TAAs that involve the aortic root, ascending aorta, and aortic arch.

In patients with a descending aortic aneurysm with a diameter greater than 5.5 cm, repair should be performed, preferably with thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) with stent grafting. Patients should be considered for repair at a threshold lower than 5.5 cm if they have risk factors for rupture, such as

  • TAA with rapid growth (>0.5 cm/year)
  • Symptomatic aneurysm
  • Female sex
  • Heritable condition, such as Marfan, vascular Ehlers-Danlos, or Loeys-Dietz syndrome
  • End-organ damage

TEVAR offers the advantage of avoiding open surgery, although complications such as stroke, spinal ischemia, and aortic graft endoleaks may occur.

Aortic atheromatous plaques (atheromas) commonly occur in patients with evidence of atherosclerosis in other vascular beds. The most frequent complication of aortic atheroma is systemic thromboembolism resulting in transient ischemic attack or stroke. Aortic atheromas greater than 4 mm in diameter and those with a mobile component are more likely to be associated with thromboembolism than are smaller atheromas.

Aortic atheromas often are detected incidentally on imaging studies. Their presence represents a CAD risk equivalent, and patients should be considered for antiplatelet and statin therapies in addition to other risk factor interventions. There is no clear evidence that asymptomatic patients with aortic atheromas benefit from anticoagulation.

The most common and life-threatening acute aortic syndromes are acute aortic dissection and aortic aneurysm rupture. Other acute aortic syndromes include aortic intramural hematoma and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer.

Acute aortic dissection involves tearing of the aortic intima, leading to passage of blood from the true lumen of the aorta into a false lumen (

). Dissection of the aorta may propagate in an antegrade or retrograde fashion, mainly as a result of shear forces. Propagation of the dissection may cause cardiac tamponade, acute aortic regurgitation, compromise of arterial side branches (carotid, mesenteric, renal, or iliac arteries), and ischemia of organs such as the brain, intestines, or kidneys.

Aortic dissections are categorized according to their location of origin by the Stanford classification, which describes type A dissections as originating within the ascending aorta or aortic arch and type B dissections as originating distal to the left subclavian artery. Type A dissections require surgical intervention because of risk for rupture and death, whereas stable type B dissections often can be managed initially with medical stabilization and blood pressure control.

Intramural hematomas result from microtears in the aortic intima and rupture of the vasa vasorum (

). Penetrating atherosclerotic ulcers are caused by erosion of the internal elastic membrane of the aorta at the site of atherosclerotic plaque, leading to a blood-filled false space within the wall of the aorta (

). Both intramural hematomas and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcers are more common distal to the left subclavian artery (type B).

Acute aortic syndrome requires rapid diagnosis and treatment because of its life-threatening complications. Acute aortic dissection classically presents as severe, sudden-onset chest or back pain that has a tearing or ripping quality. Other presenting features may include syncope, stroke, hypertension, a murmur of aortic regurgitation, and heart failure. Asymmetric blood pressures in the upper extremities, asymmetric pulses, or pulsus paradoxus should also raise suspicion for acute aortic dissection, especially in a patient with chest pain.

Abnormalities may be present on chest radiography (widened mediastinum) and ECG (ST-segment depression), but these findings are not diagnostic.

In patients with a high likelihood of acute aortic dissection, diagnostic imaging should be performed immediately. CTA, MRA, and transesophageal echocardiography have similar sensitivity and specificity in diagnosing acute thoracic aortic disease; however, CTA is the imaging modality of choice because it can be performed rapidly, has widespread availability, and provides important information for procedural planning. Compared with CTA and MRA, the primary advantages of transesophageal echocardiography in patients with suspected aortic dissection include portability for an unstable patient, lack of iodinated contrast, and added detail in evaluating aortic valve structure and function. Transthoracic echocardiography often is used initially but is limited in its ability to image the distal ascending aorta, transverse aortic arch, and descending aorta. Invasive aortography rarely is indicated for the diagnosis of acute aortic disease; however, it is performed at the time of endovascular repair or when noninvasive testing is contraindicated or unavailable.

Patients with acute aortic dissection without evidence of shock should be monitored in a critical care setting and receive medical therapy to lower heart rate and blood pressure. Current guidelines recommend reducing systolic blood pressure to 120 mm Hg or less in the first hour. Intravenous β-blockers are first-line treatment. For hypertension that does not respond adequately to β-blocker therapy, an intravenous vasodilator (e.g., nitroprusside, nicardipine) should be administered. Pain control is often necessary and is best accomplished with intravenous opioids.

Emergency surgery should be considered for acute aortic dissection complicated by shock and type A dissection given the very high mortality rate associated with these conditions. Decisions regarding concomitant aortic arch reconstruction, aortic valve replacement, branch vessel repair, and/or coronary artery bypass graft surgery or coronary artery reimplantation depend on the anatomy of the dissection, involvement of the aortic valve or branch vessels, and other patient characteristics.

Patients with uncomplicated type B aortic syndromes usually are first treated with medical therapy. Compared with medical therapy, TEVAR is associated with similar clinical outcomes (overall survival) but improved aortic-specific death rates and disease progression measures at 5 years. Patients with type B dissection and refractory chest/back pain or hypertension, rapid aortic expansion, or organ malperfusion should undergo aortic repair, often via TEVAR.

In patients with an aortic intramural hematoma or penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer, treatment choices depend on the location of the hematoma or ulcer, progression to aortic dissection, and evidence of aortic enlargement. Immediate aortic repair is indicated in patients with a type A aortic intramural hematoma or penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer and in those with enlargement or progressive disease.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is abnormal dilatation of the abdominal aorta with an anteroposterior diameter greater than 3.0 cm. Risk factors include male sex (6:1 male-to-female incidence ratio), advanced age, smoking, atherosclerosis, hypertension, and a family history of AAA.

AAA most often is diagnosed incidentally by CTA or abdominal ultrasonography. Approximately 75% of patients with AAA are asymptomatic at the time of diagnosis. Because of the high mortality rate associated with aneurysm rupture, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends one-time screening with duplex ultrasonography in men aged 65 to 75 years who have smoked at least 100 cigarettes during their lifetime and selective screening for men in this same age group who have never smoked. For a more detailed discussion of AAA screening, see Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

Estimated annual risk for aortic rupture according to AAA dimension is shown in [Table: Table: Annual Rupture Risk of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm by Diameter]

. Surveillance guidelines vary based on AAA diameter; in patients with AAA diameter smaller than 4.0 cm, duplex ultrasonography is warranted, whereas CTA or duplex ultrasonography should be performed in patients with AAA diameter of 4.0 cm or larger. The timeframe for surveillance according to AAA diameter is shown in

. When the aortic diameter meets the threshold for aortic repair (≥5.5 cm in men, ≥5.0 cm in women), CTA or MRA is indicated to determine the exact location of the AAA (suprarenal, juxtarenal, or infrarenal) for planning repair.

Medical treatment of AAA involves risk factor modification to decrease risk for rupture, cardiovascular morbidity, and overall mortality. Aortic repair should be performed in patients with the following:

  • AAA diameter of 5.5 cm or larger in men
  • AAA diameter of 5.0 cm or larger in women
  • Rapid expansion in AAA size (>0.5 cm/6 months)
  • Symptoms resulting from AAA (e.g., abdominal or back pain)

In patients with an indication for aortic repair, the choice between open surgery and endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) is driven by the location of the AAA and involvement of the renal and mesenteric arteries. Suprarenal and juxtarenal aneurysms most often necessitate open surgical repair. In patients with an infrarenal AAA, patient age, comorbid conditions, and ability to tolerate open surgical repair determine which procedure is performed. EVAR is associated with lower short-term (30-day) morbidity and mortality but no significant differences in long-term mortality. In addition, EVAR is associated with greater need for repeat intervention and significantly higher rates of endoleak, device failure, and postimplantation syndrome (fever, leukocytosis, elevated serum C-reactive protein level). These complications necessitate diligent follow-up with noninvasive imaging tests (CTA or ultrasonography) annually to evaluate the stent graft.
