Peripheral Artery Disease

Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is typically characterized by narrowing or stenosis of the aortic bifurcation and arteries of the lower extremities, including the iliac, femoral, popliteal, and tibial arteries. Atherosclerosis is the most common cause. Risk factors for PAD include the following:

  • Smoking (current or past)
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Hypertension
  • Dyslipidemia
  • Older age
  • Family history of atherosclerosis

The incidence of PAD begins to increase at around age 40 years and rises to approximately 10% at age 70 years. PAD occurs at a later age in women than in men, but because women have a longer life span, the overall prevalence is higher in women.

PAD is considered a coronary heart disease risk equivalent, and asymptomatic and symptomatic patients with PAD are at increased risk for ischemic events, including myocardial infarction, stroke, and cardiovascular death. Thus, early recognition of PAD provides an opportunity to identify persons at increased cardiovascular risk and to modify risk factors. Guidelines conflict on the utility of screening asymptomatic patients for PAD. The American Heart Association (AHA)/American College of Cardiology (ACC) guidelines suggest that obtaining a screening ankle-brachial index (ABI) to identify PAD is reasonable in asymptomatic persons who are aged 65 years or older or who are younger than 65 years and have risk factors for atherosclerosis or known atherosclerotic disease in another vascular bed. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, however, concluded that evidence is insufficient to support screening asymptomatic patients for lower extremity PAD with an ABI.

Lower extremity PAD has a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations. Patients may present with exertional leg pain relieved by rest (intermittent claudication), atypical exertional leg pain, chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI; also termed critical limb ischemia), or acute limb ischemia.

Approximately 25% to 30% of patients with lower extremity PAD present with intermittent claudication. Most patients with intermittent claudication have stable symptoms; however, symptoms worsen in approximately 25% of patients, and 10% to 20% of patients will undergo lower extremity revascularization procedures over a 5-year period. Patients with intermittent claudication often have reduced exercise capacity and functional status compared with age- and sex-matched controls, and their annual risk for myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death is approximately 5% to 7%.

Less than 5% of patients with PAD present with CLTI, a more severe form of PAD. CLTI manifests as ischemic rest pain, tissue ulceration, and gangrene. Surgical or endovascular revascularization is usually necessary to salvage the foot or limb. Patients with CLTI often have reduced exercise capacity and functional status, and these patients have a 30% rate of major amputation and a 20% mortality rate within 1 year of diagnosis.

Acute limb ischemia is characterized by the abrupt onset of various combinations of the “6 P’s” (pain, pallor, poikilothermia, pulselessness, paresthesia, and paralysis), and emergent evaluation and revascularization are warranted to salvage the limb. Acute limb ischemia in patients with chronic symptoms from PAD may present abruptly or in a more subacute manner, typically defined as less than 14 days from new symptom onset.

A detailed history, review of symptoms, and physical examination are essential in the evaluation for vascular disease. Patients should be asked about walking impairment, atypical limb symptoms (leg weakness, paresthesia), intermittent claudication, and ischemic rest pain. In patients with exertional leg symptoms, intermittent claudication should be differentiated from pseudoclaudication (symptoms that arise from spinal stenosis) ( [Table: Table: Discriminating Claudication From Pseudoclaudication]

). Patients also should be questioned about skin breakdown and foot ulcers and educated on the importance of foot protection and wearing shoes (specifically, hard-soled shoes) when walking outside the home.

Components of the physical examination in patients with suspected PAD are listed in [Table: Table: Physical Examination of Patients for PAD]

. Vascular examination of patients in whom lower extremity PAD is suspected should include comprehensive pulse examination, auscultation for bruits, and inspection of the feet for skin and toenail changes. Patients with PAD may exhibit diminished, absent, or asymmetric pulses, and bruits may be heard at or near sites of arterial stenosis. Patients with CLTI may have coolness in the affected extremity, hair loss, and dependent rubor with pallor on leg elevation as well as evidence of poor wound healing or active ulceration. Arterial leg ulcers commonly occur on the distal toes, plantar aspect of the foot, anterior portion of the lower leg where minimal collateral arterial circulation is present, and sites of trauma. Arterial ulcers usually are painful and have sharply demarcated borders with a dry, pale gray or yellow wound base without evidence of granulation tissue (

). Clinicians should distinguish CLTI from chronic venous disease (typically characterized by leg edema; pigmented, brawny induration of the gaiter zone; and ulceration of the shin or ankle) because these conditions are treated differently (see Chronic Venous Insufficiency in Common Symptoms).

The most commonly used diagnostic method for identifying lower extremity PAD is measurement of the ABI, the ratio of lower extremity to upper extremity systolic blood pressures. ABI measurement is simple, inexpensive, and noninvasive, with a sensitivity and specificity approaching 90%. ABI values also have prognostic importance; low values are associated with higher rates of myocardial infarction, stroke, and death. Guidelines recommend ABI testing in all patients with history or physical examination findings suggestive of PAD.

When undergoing ABI testing, patients should rest for 10 minutes in a supine position before the physician measures the ankle pressures and brachial pressures with a Doppler machine. Blood pressures should be measured in both arms and in both legs at the locations of the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibialis pulses. To calculate the ABI for each leg, the higher ankle pressure in that leg is divided by the higher brachial artery pressure (regardless of side). In healthy persons, the ankle pressure is the same as or slightly higher than the brachial pressure; therefore, a normal resting ABI is between 1.00 and 1.40 ( [Table: Table: Interpretation of the Ankle-Brachial Index]

). In the presence of atherosclerotic narrowing of the limb arteries, the downstream blood pressure, and thus the ABI value, is lower. A resting ABI of 0.90 or less is diagnostic for PAD and correlates with abnormalities seen on imaging of the arterial tree. In general, patients with claudication have an ABI of 0.40 to 0.90, whereas patients with ischemic rest pain, ulceration, or gangrene have an ABI of less than 0.40. A resting ABI greater than 1.40 indicates the presence of noncompressible, calcified arteries in the lower extremities and is considered uninterpretable. A toe-brachial index is used for diagnosis in these patients, with a value less than 0.70 indicating PAD.

In patients with high pretest probability but ABI values between 0.91 and 1.40, further evaluation with exercise ABI testing is useful. It requires ABI measurements at rest and after treadmill walking or plantar flexion exercises. A postexercise ankle pressure decrease of 30 mm Hg or more or significant decline in the ABI (>20%) suggests PAD.

Segmental pressure measurements in a vascular laboratory may be used to localize diseased vessels. The procedure involves pulse volume recordings (measurement of the magnitude and contour of blood pulse volume in the lower extremities) and blood pressure measurements at several locations in the lower extremities (high thigh, low thigh, calf, posterior tibial artery, and dorsalis pedis artery) (

).

Other imaging studies used to delineate the anatomic location and severity of lower extremity PAD include arterial duplex ultrasonography, CT angiography, and magnetic resonance angiography ( [Table: Table: Imaging Modalities for the Diagnosis of PAD]

). These imaging modalities are most often used to plan for endovascular or surgical revascularization procedures. Invasive angiography is often preferred because endovascular revascularization procedures can be performed concurrently.

Treatment of PAD focuses on the following:

  • Reducing cardiovascular risk
  • Improving functional status and quality of life
  • Decreasing claudication symptoms
  • Preventing tissue injury and amputation

Cigarette smoking is the most important modifiable risk factor for PAD. Smoking cessation is imperative to lowering the risk for myocardial infarction and stroke and improving overall survival in patients with PAD. Smoking cessation is also associated with decreased risk for major amputation, improved patency rates after revascularization, and less disease progression.

Diabetes is also a strong risk factor for PAD; however, intensive glucose control has not been demonstrated to reduce macrovascular complications, including myocardial infarction, stroke, or amputation. Nevertheless, patients with PAD and concomitant diabetes should adhere to American Diabetes Association recommendations on diabetes management, with particular attention to foot care (see Management of Diabetes Mellitus in Endocrinology and Metabolism). Some studies of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have reported an increased risk for amputation in patients with PAD, whereas others have not. Although guidelines now suggest the use of SGLT2 inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide 1 agonists in patients with concomitant type 2 diabetes and PAD because of a decrease in cardiovascular events, patients taking SGLT2 inhibitors should be monitored closely.

Dyslipidemia has a mild effect on the development of PAD. According to AHA/ACC guidelines, patients with PAD should be treated with high-intensity statin therapy, and patients with PAD who are older than 75 years or intolerant of high-intensity statins should be treated with moderate-intensity statin therapy (see Secondary Prevention of Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease in Cardiovascular Medicine).

Blood pressure control has been associated with a reduction in cardiovascular events in patients with PAD. The AHA/ACC recommends a blood pressure target of less than 130/80 mm Hg in patients with PAD. Adults with hypertension and PAD are treated similarly to patients without PAD (see Management of Primary Hypertension in Nephrology), although some guidelines recommend the preferential use of ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers in patients with PAD.

Although older studies linked nonselective β-blockers (such as propranolol) with increased complications in patients with severe PAD, β~1-selective β-blockers seem to be better tolerated and may be used with caution if otherwise indicated for cardiovascular risk reduction. A meta-analysis showed no increased risk for symptom exacerbation in patients with mild to moderate PAD treated with selective β-blockers.

Guidelines recommend antiplatelet monotherapy (low-dose aspirin or clopidogrel) in patients with PAD to reduce the risk for myocardial infarction, stroke, and peripheral arterial events, including CLTI. No compelling evidence has been seen for the use of dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin plus clopidogrel in patients with PAD alone, although it may be appropriate in patients with revascularization. In the CHARISMA trial, patients with PAD who were treated with aspirin plus clopidogrel had a reduced rate of hospitalization for myocardial infarction and ischemic events, which was mitigated by a higher rate of bleeding.

No evidence has been seen that oral anticoagulation with a vitamin K antagonist (warfarin) is more effective than antiplatelet monotherapy in patients with PAD, and warfarin anticoagulation is associated with an increased risk for major bleeding, including intracerebral bleeding. There also is no evidence that direct oral anticoagulant therapy alone is superior to antiplatelet monotherapy in patients with PAD.

The combination of aspirin and low-dose rivaroxaban is an option in PAD treatment, especially in patients with low risk for bleeding. Evidence from the COMPASS trial demonstrated that aspirin (100 mg/d) plus rivaroxaban (2.5 mg twice daily), a direct factor Xa inhibitor, was associated with improved major adverse cardiovascular and limb end points when compared with aspirin plus placebo in patients with coronary artery disease and PAD. Major bleeding, primarily gastrointestinal bleeding, was increased in patients assigned to receive aspirin plus rivaroxaban; however, fatal or critical organ bleeding was not significantly different between the groups. Likewise, in the VOYAGER trial, patients undergoing endovascular or surgical revascularization for PAD had a significantly lower incidence of the primary efficacy outcome (a composite of acute limb ischemia, major amputation for vascular causes, myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, or death from cardiovascular causes) when assigned to rivaroxaban (2.5 mg twice daily) plus aspirin compared with aspirin alone.

Improving functional status and quality of life is of high importance for patients with PAD. In patients who can exercise, supervised exercise training has been associated with improved functional performance and is recommended for patients with intermittent claudication. Systematic reviews comparing supervised exercise with home exercise have reported improvements in maximal walking distance and initial claudication distance that favor supervised exercise; however, no statistically significant differences in quality of life were observed.

Cilostazol, a phosphodiesterase inhibitor with antiplatelet and vasodilator activity, increases pain-free walking distance and overall walking distance in patients with claudication, and clinical practice guidelines recommend that a therapeutic trial of cilostazol be considered in patients with claudication. As with other oral phosphodiesterase inhibitors (e.g., inotropes such as milrinone), the FDA has placed a black box warning on use of cilostazol in patients with heart failure. Pentoxifylline is ineffective in treating PAD and should not be used. The GLP-1 receptor antagonist semaglutide has been shown to improve symptoms of claudication, pain-free walking distance, and quality of life in patients with diabetes who have PAD and claudication. No approved pharmacotherapy is available for patients with CLTI.

Revascularization is not recommended in asymptomatic patients. Endovascular or surgical revascularization is effective in relieving symptoms and improving functional capacity and wound healing in patients with intermittent claudication or CLTI. Referral for revascularization is indicated in patients with life-limiting claudication who have had an inadequate response to exercise training, antiplatelet medication, and cilostazol. Patients with rest pain, ulceration, or gangrene also should be considered for revascularization, and some patients with CLTI (ABI <0.40, a flat waveform on pulse volume recording, and low or absent pedal flow on duplex ultrasonography) should be considered for urgent revascularization. Decisions regarding revascularization are ideally made by a multidisciplinary team including experts in vascular surgery, radiology, cardiology, and/or podiatry, depending on the setting/hospital. Revascularization decisions should be made considering the risk-benefit ratio, as determined by patient factors (age, frailty, comorbid conditions), anatomic factors (severity and burden of atherosclerotic disease, location of disease in the lower extremities), operator expertise, and type of procedure. In general, more proximal and focal lesions are better managed with endovascular technique, reserving surgery for longer and/or more distal lesions.

Endovascular revascularization use has dramatically increased in recent years because it is minimally invasive and confers a lower risk for perioperative adverse events compared with surgical revascularization. Endovascular techniques include balloon angioplasty, stenting (bare metal or drug eluting), and atherectomy (laser or various cutting options).

In patients with isolated iliac disease, endovascular revascularization is favored over surgery. Most patients undergo balloon angioplasty with stenting of the iliac arteries, which has a significantly higher long-term success rate than angioplasty alone.

In patients with femoral, popliteal, or tibial artery (infrainguinal) disease, the patency rates for endovascular revascularization are not as high as for iliac disease. Although infrainguinal disease traditionally has been treated with angioplasty alone, the use of atherectomy devices, nickel-titanium stents, and other novel devices is being evaluated.

Surgical revascularization, endarterectomy or surgical bypass, is still recommended for patients with complex anatomy that may limit percutaneous procedural success and long-term patency (e.g., long chronic total occlusions, multisegment disease). Surgery may also be preferred in CLTI.

Hybrid revascularization, which combines surgical and endovascular approaches in a single setting or finite time frame, has been used more frequently in conjunction with the rise in endovascular revascularization; however, it is not currently recommended by clinical practice guidelines.

Acute limb ischemia is an infrequent but life-threatening manifestation of PAD. Patients classically present with at least one of the “6 P’s”:

  • Paresthesia
  • Pain
  • Pallor
  • Pulselessness
  • Poikilothermia (coolness)
  • Paralysis

Many patients do not present with all of these characteristics, and a high index of suspicion is necessary to make the diagnosis. The most common cause is acute thrombosis of a lower extremity artery (usually at the site of preexisting atherosclerotic disease), stent, or bypass graft. Other causes include thromboembolism, vessel dissection (usually occurring periprocedurally), and trauma. Atheroembolic events may also occur after arterial manipulation, such as occurs with invasive angiography. In contrast to other causes of acute limb ischemia, treatment of atheroemboli is supportive and focuses on risk factor modification (see Acute Vascular Syndromes in Nephrology).

Acute limb ischemia otherwise represents a true medical emergency; 10% to 15% of patients undergo amputation during initial hospitalization, and 20% of patients die within 1 year.

Anticoagulation, typically with unfractionated heparin, should be initiated as soon as the diagnosis is suspected. Specialists with expertise in revascularization should be consulted to determine limb salvageability, and diagnostic angiography should be performed immediately to define the anatomic level of occlusion. In addition to surgical and endovascular revascularization options, catheter-directed thrombolysis improves outcomes in patients with acute limb ischemia.

Careful monitoring is required after limb reperfusion because of frequent reocclusion, limb edema, and the possibility of compartment syndrome. Signs and symptoms of compartment syndrome include severe pain, hypoesthesia, and leg weakness. If compartment syndrome occurs, surgical fasciotomy is indicated to prevent irreversible neurologic and soft tissue damage.

Cardiovascular Disease in Cancer Survivors

Radiation therapy improves survival in patients with Hodgkin lymphoma, early-stage breast cancer, and other thoracic malignancies. With higher survival rates, cardiovascular disease has emerged as the most common nonmalignant cause of death in patients treated with chest radiation therapy, accounting for 25% of deaths in survivors of Hodgkin lymphoma.

Radiation therapy causes a wide spectrum of cardiovascular diseases ( [Table: Table: Cardiovascular Diseases Related to Radiation Therapy]

). Thoracic irradiation damages all cells, including those of the pericardium, myocardium, valves, coronary and peripheral vasculature, and conduction system, with clinical disease usually presenting two to three decades after treatment. The risk for radiation-induced cardiac injury is increased further in patients receiving concomitant anthracyclines or trastuzumab. Contemporary techniques that limit total dosage and field size have decreased the risk for cardiac complications after radiation therapy.

Acute pericarditis is the most common early manifestation of radiotoxicity, affecting 2.5% of patients. The presentation, diagnosis, and treatment are similar to those of idiopathic acute pericarditis. Chronic or constrictive pericarditis develops in 10% to 20% of patients 5 to 10 years after radiation therapy. Pericardial calcification is not always present radiographically. Late constriction may occur in patients who have not had acute pericarditis.

Radiation also damages the microvasculature, causing endothelial dysfunction and ischemia that result in myocardial fibrosis, diastolic dysfunction, and restrictive physiology. Radiation-induced cardiomyopathy presents similarly to primary restrictive cardiomyopathy. Differentiating cardiomyopathy due to myocardial fibrosis from pericardial constriction is essential because the conditions have different treatments and outcomes (see Differentiating Restrictive Cardiomyopathy From Constrictive Pericarditis in Cardiovascular Medicine).

Although all cardiac valves may be affected by radiation therapy, left-sided involvement predominates. Valvular regurgitation due to tissue retraction is the most common valvular lesion in the first two decades after therapy, with later fibrosis and calcification leading to mixed regurgitation and stenosis (

). Radiation injury to the aorta with subsequent calcification may further complicate the surgical approach to aortic valve disease.

Radiation causes fibrosis of the conduction system and may lead to sinus node dysfunction, fascicular and bundle branch blocks, and complete heart block. Up to 75% of long-term survivors of mediastinal radiation demonstrate conduction abnormalities on ECG. The need for permanent pacing is more common after valve replacement surgery in patients who have received radiation therapy.

Coronary artery disease (CAD) occurs earlier and with increased incidence in patients treated with radiation therapy. Coronary artery lesions are typically ostial, long, smooth, and concentric and have higher fibrotic content than typical atherosclerotic lesions. The incidence of CAD is increased by traditional risk factors (e.g., smoking, dyslipidemia, and hypertension), and aggressive therapy to address these risk factors is indicated.

Surgical outcomes for patients with radiation-associated cardiovascular disease are significantly worse than in matched cohorts, and radiation-associated aortic stenosis is associated with worse short-term and long-term cardiovascular mortality. Recent trials have suggested that percutaneous approaches to aortic valve replacement may be preferable in this group. Prior radiation therapy is also a relevant concern favoring percutaneous coronary intervention rather than coronary artery bypass grafting in patients in whom either option is reasonable.

There is no consensus on cardiac testing after chest irradiation in asymptomatic patients. Baseline evaluation, including echocardiography, is reasonable; several organizations have recommended echocardiography every 5 years after completion of therapy. The role of serum biomarkers in surveillance is unclear, and their use is not recommended. Routine screening for ischemia is not as clear; however, reviewing chest CT scans obtained for cancer surveillance for coronary artery calcifications is reasonable.

Statins, ACE inhibitors, and aldosterone antagonists, although effective for risk factor reduction, have not been proved to prevent radiation-induced cardiovascular disease.

Chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy may cause reversible or dose-dependent, irreversible cardiac injury ( [Table: Table: Cardiovascular Toxic Effects of Chemotherapeutic Agents]

). Strategies to minimize cardiovascular risk should be considered before initiation of cancer treatment, including optimizing treatment of traditional risk factors and identifying patients with the greatest long-term risk ( [Table: Table: Factors That Increase Long-Term Cardiovascular Risk]

). Cardiotoxic therapies should be minimized if there are alternative therapies with equivalent outcomes.

In patients preparing to receive cancer treatment associated with possible left ventricular (LV) dysfunction, baseline echocardiography is recommended. Some expert consensus panels have recommended measurement of global longitudinal strain (GLS) as part of surveillance echocardiography. GLS expresses longitudinal myocardial shortening as a simple percentage and may be more sensitive than other echocardiographic techniques in detecting early myocardial dysfunction. For patients in whom echocardiography is technically difficult, multigated acquisition and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging are alternatives.

Acute anthracycline toxicity, which may present as heart block, arrhythmias, heart failure, myocarditis, or pericarditis, occurs in less than 1% of patients and may be reversible. Chronic progressive anthracycline toxicity usually presents as dilated cardiomyopathy and is typically irreversible. It is most closely linked to doxorubicin but may occur with epirubicin and idarubicin. Chronic progressive toxicity has an early onset (within 1 year of treatment) in up to 2.1% of patients and a late onset (after 1 year) in up to 5% of patients. Late-onset chronic progressive toxicity is related to total cumulative dose. Although the incidence has varied in clinical studies, patients with a cumulative anthracycline dose of 550 mg/m^2 may have an incidence of heart failure as high as 26%, and toxicity may not become clinically evident until 10 to 20 years after treatment. Dexrazoxane, an iron chelator, reduces the incidence of anthracycline cardiotoxicity and should be considered for patients at increased risk. Continuous anthracycline administration, as opposed to bolus, and liposomal formulations of doxorubicin should also be considered to reduce risk for anthracycline toxicity. The use of ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and β-blockers to prevent cardiotoxicity is an ongoing area of interest, but most larger trials have shown no benefit with the prophylactic use of these agents.

Although the frequency of surveillance of asymptomatic patients treated with anthracyclines must be based on clinical judgment, it is reasonable to repeat echocardiography at a cumulative anthracycline dose of 250 mg/m^2 and before each dose in patients with preexisting LV dysfunction or those receiving higher cumulative doses.

Acute reversible injury is more commonly associated with targeted molecular therapy, such as trastuzumab, multitargeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and anti–vascular endothelial growth factor antibodies. Trastuzumab toxicity causes LV systolic dysfunction, with symptoms of heart failure in 3% to 7% of patients. It is more common in patients older than age 50 years and with concomitant anthracycline use. The frequency of echocardiographic surveillance in patients receiving trastuzumab who are at high risk for cardiac dysfunction is based on clinical judgment. Trastuzumab is temporarily stopped if the LV ejection fraction (LVEF) decreases by more than 15% or drops 10% to below 50%. Patients with normalized LV function after discontinuation of trastuzumab may receive additional therapy, and retrospective data have shown that patients whose LVEF remains greater than 50% may continue treatment without long-term cardiac effects. A relative decline in GLS of greater than 15% is considered to be subclinical LV dysfunction and should prompt consultation with a cardiologist.

Multitargeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors also cause cardiotoxicity, although not all tyrosine kinase inhibitors carry the same risk. Sunitinib is associated with up to a 50% incidence of new or worsened hypertension and up to a 15% incidence of decreased LVEF; these effects may be reversible with early recognition. In patients receiving sunitinib, surveillance with baseline N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) measurement and LVEF assessment at baseline, 1 month, and every 3 months thereafter has been advocated.

Bevacizumab, an anti–vascular endothelial growth factor antibody, is associated with significant but reversible hypertension.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors have been associated with a rare (1%) incidence of myocarditis that incurs a high morbidity and mortality rate when it occurs. Having a high clinical suspicion for myocarditis in the right clinical setting (e.g., development of heart failure symptoms, elevated NT-proBNP and troponin levels) and promptly stopping the immune checkpoint inhibitor while starting immunosuppressive therapy with high-dose glucocorticoids is crucial. Other cardiovascular events associated with immune checkpoint inhibitors include pericarditis, acute coronary syndromes, arrhythmias, conduction blocks, and cardiac arrest.

Chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy has also been associated with adverse cardiac events in up to 16% of patients receiving this therapy, with the most common being arrhythmias. CAR-T therapy commonly (35%-93% of cases) causes cytokine release syndrome. Many of the symptoms (palpitations, dizziness, tachycardia, hypotension) mimic cardiac problems. Thus, having a low index of suspicion for cardiac issues in that setting is important.

Echocardiography may be repeated at therapy completion and at 6 to 12 months in asymptomatic patients at increased risk for LV dysfunction. Some guidelines suggest lifetime surveillance every 5 to 10 years in patients considered to be at high risk for developing cardiotoxicity. Risk factors for toxicity vary by type of therapy, and risk calculators are available to aid in determining risk and follow-up (cancercalc.com).

In patients with clinical signs or symptoms of cardiac dysfunction, measurement of cardiac biomarkers (e.g., troponin, NT-proBNP) and echocardiography including GLS are recommended in identifying early toxicity and guiding individual therapy. At present, treatment of patients with chemotherapy-induced heart failure follows standard paradigms, and decisions regarding continuation of chemotherapy must be individualized.

Pregnancy and Cardiovascular Disease

Maternal mortality in the United States has risen over the past two decades and remains significantly higher than in other high-income countries. Cardiovascular disease, including cardiomyopathy, coronary artery disease, and aortic pathology, is now the leading cause of pregnancy-related death. In addition, other cardiac conditions such as hypertensive disorders, valvular heart disease, congenital heart disease, arrhythmias, and thromboembolic disease may first present or worsen during pregnancy because of the hemodynamic stresses of pregnancy.

Knowledge of the cardiovascular changes of pregnancy is necessary to distinguish between normal and pathologic signs and symptoms in the pregnant patient ( [Table: Table: Normal Versus Pathologic Signs and Symptoms in Pregnancy]

). During a normal pregnancy, cardiac output increases through an elevation in both stroke volume and heart rate. The increase in stroke volume results from an increase in plasma volume and a decrease in systemic vascular resistance. A mild physiologic anemia of pregnancy also results from the increase in plasma volume. By the 32nd week of pregnancy, maternal cardiac output peaks at approximately 40% to 50% above the prepregnancy level. During delivery, the cardiac output may increase to as much as 80% above the prepregnancy level. The “fourth trimester” occurs in the 12 weeks after delivery, during which cardiovascular changes continue and complications may occur. The risk for postpartum cardiovascular complications and maternal death is highest in the first 6 weeks after delivery and remains elevated for 1 year.

All women with cardiovascular disease should receive pregnancy counseling. If appropriate, women should receive genetic counseling and possibly testing (see Genetic Testing for Cardiovascular Disease in Cardiovascular Medicine). Patients with significant cardiovascular disease who are anticipating pregnancy should undergo multidisciplinary evaluation with a cardiologist, a maternal-fetal medicine specialist, and an obstetric anesthesiologist to determine the risks of pregnancy and develop a management plan for labor and the postpartum period. The cardio-obstetrics team, which includes the internal medicine physician, works together to manage the patient from preconception through the postpartum period. Disease-specific risk should be assessed using the modified World Health Organization (mWHO) pregnancy risk classification, which is the most accurate system of risk assessment. Exercise testing to assess heart rate response and maximal oxygen consumption may also be considered for risk stratification.

Cardiovascular conditions that confer the highest risk for maternal mortality and morbidity or fetal complications (mWHO category IV) include the following:

  • Pulmonary hypertension
  • Previous peripartum cardiomyopathy with residual left ventricular (LV) dysfunction
  • Severe LV dysfunction (ejection fraction [EF] <30% or New York Heart Association functional class III-IV symptoms)
  • Severe mitral stenosis
  • Severe aortic stenosis
  • Mechanical valves
  • Coarctation with residual gradient
  • Marked ascending aorta dilatation
  • Fontan procedure with any complication

Care and delivery in patients with these conditions should be at an expert center for pregnancy and cardiac disease, and if possible, structural heart lesions should be addressed before pregnancy. Patients at lower but still substantial risk, including those in mWHO category III with conditions such as moderate LV impairment (EF 30%-45%), previous peripartum cardiomyopathy with a recovered EF, and a mechanical valve, should also be cared for in a specialized center. Patients with significant cardiovascular disease may require preterm delivery if they develop hemodynamic instability.

Patients with Marfan syndrome and similar conditions have an increased risk for pregnancy-related aortic dissection. Patients with an aortopathy should be referred to a cardiologist for risk assessment before becoming pregnant. (Also see Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm in Cardiovascular Medicine.) Aortic repair is recommended before pregnancy in patients who have Marfan syndrome and an aortic diameter of 4.5 cm or greater. Risk factors for dissection in pregnant patients with Marfan syndrome and an aortic diameter smaller than 4.5 cm include rapid dilatation of the aorta and a personal or family history of aortic dissection.

Otherwise, patients with certain cardiovascular disorders, including uncomplicated small patent ductus arteriosus, mild pulmonary stenosis, and mild uncomplicated mitral valve prolapse, have no increased morbidity or mortality with pregnancy. Similarly, pregnant patients with successfully repaired simple lesions (atrial or ventricular septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus, or anomalous pulmonary venous drainage) do well. These patients may be cared for and deliver in many hospitals without a cardio-obstetrics team.

A small increase in risk for maternal mortality or moderate increase in morbidity is associated with an unrepaired atrial or ventricular septal defect, repaired tetralogy of Fallot, most supraventricular arrhythmias, and other uncomplicated repaired heart defects without residual lesions. Patients with these conditions may also be cared for and deliver in many hospitals.

Hypertension that was present before pregnancy should be treated with labetalol, methyldopa, and extended-release nifedipine, which can be adjusted and continued through the pregnancy. For those with chronic hypertension, aspirin (81 mg/d) should be started at 12 weeks’ gestation to reduce the risk of preeclampsia. See Hypertension in Pregnancy in Nephrology for further information.

Patients with regurgitant valve lesions usually tolerate pregnancy well, likely because of decreased systemic vascular resistance. In contrast, patients with obstructive valvular lesions may experience symptoms during pregnancy because of the resultant increases in blood volume and cardiac output. These patients should be evaluated to determine whether cardiac intervention should be considered before pregnancy. Severe mitral stenosis is poorly tolerated in pregnancy and may require intervention during pregnancy to relieve obstruction if not corrected before conception; routine use of β-blockers is also recommended in these patients to reduce heart rate and lower transvalvular gradient. Similarly, patients with symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy should receive nonvasodilating β-blockers, generally metoprolol, with concomitant monitoring of fetal growth.

Most arrhythmias that develop during pregnancy are benign; therefore, shared decision making should consider the risks and benefits to both the mother and fetus of antiarrhythmic drugs, testing and procedures, and monitoring, as well as the risks of withholding such therapies. Most β-blockers, except for atenolol because it readily crosses the placenta, are safe to use during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

Vaginal delivery is generally preferred for patients with cardiovascular disease because it results in less blood loss, quicker recovery, and lower risk for thrombosis than does cesarean delivery. Cesarean delivery is recommended for patients with severe decompensated cardiovascular disease, and for some patients with a markedly dilated aorta. It is also recommended in patients receiving warfarin therapy to reduce the risk for fetal intracranial hemorrhage with vaginal birth because the fetus is fully anticoagulated.

Peripartum cardiomyopathy is defined as LV systolic dysfunction (EF<45%) recognized toward the end of pregnancy or up to 6 months after delivery in the absence of another identifiable cause. Risk factors for peripartum cardiomyopathy include the following:

  • Multiparity
  • Age older than 30 years
  • Multifetal pregnancy
  • Gestational hypertension
  • Preeclampsia
  • History of peripartum cardiomyopathy
  • Tocolytic therapy

Patients with peripartum cardiomyopathy may present with exercise intolerance, fatigue, shortness of breath, cough, wheezing, or other nonspecific symptoms; thus, patients with these symptoms should be evaluated for possible heart failure, particularly in the early postpartum period. Delays in diagnosis are not uncommon and may contribute to death.

During pregnancy, patients with peripartum cardiomyopathy should be comanaged by a cardiologist and promptly receive guideline-directed medical therapy, including β-blockers, digoxin, hydralazine, and nitrates. Diuretics should be used at the lowest dosage possible to minimize the risk for placental hypoperfusion (see Medical Therapy for Heart Failure With Reduced Ejection Fraction in Cardiovascular Medicine). ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and aldosterone antagonists are teratogenic and should be avoided until after delivery. Because of the high risk for thromboembolism associated with peripartum cardiomyopathy, anticoagulation should be considered for pregnant patients with acute heart failure and an LVEF less than 30%. Duration of anticoagulation is 6 to 8 weeks postpartum, although therapy can be discontinued earlier if the EF normalizes.

Patients with severe refractory heart failure should be referred to a specialty center for treatment.

Most patients who develop peripartum cardiomyopathy recover fully, as measured by improvement in EF; however, in a prospective study, 13% had persistent severe cardiomyopathy or major cardiovascular events. Studies suggest that the time frame for recovery is 6 months. Prognostic factors that portend a worse outcome include severe LV dysfunction/dilatation at presentation, older maternal age, and multiparity.

In patients with peripartum cardiomyopathy, subsequent pregnancy is often associated with recurrent or further reduction of LV function, potentially resulting in clinical deterioration or death. Accordingly, patients with a previous episode of peripartum cardiomyopathy, especially those with persistent LV dysfunction, should be counseled about the risks of future pregnancy.

Known valvular heart disease should be evaluated before pregnancy and repaired when indicated, because pregnancy increases cardiac output and heart rate and reduces systemic vascular resistance; these changes significantly worsen fixed outflow obstruction. Aortic stenosis requires close monitoring throughout pregnancy, with delivery representing the highest risk period because of autotransfusion, pain-induced tachycardia, and abrupt hemodynamic shifts that are problematic in a fixed-output state. In contrast, regurgitant lesions are generally better tolerated because the physiologic decrease in systemic vascular resistance reduces regurgitant volume.

Data have linked pregnancy complications (preeclampsia, preterm delivery, glucose intolerance, small-for-gestational-age delivery, placental abruption, and pregnancy loss) to the acquisition of cardiovascular risk factors and cardiovascular disease. Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are associated with premature mortality from both cardiovascular and noncardiovascular causes. It is unknown how this information should be used to reclassify cardiovascular risk in affected women, but a heart-healthy diet and exercise are recommended beginning in the postpartum period and throughout the lifespan.

Spontaneous coronary artery dissection is the leading cause of pregnancy-associated myocardial infarction and may occur at any time, including postpartum (see Acute Coronary Syndromes Not Associated With Obstructive Coronary Artery Disease in Cardiovascular Medicine). Conservative noninterventional therapy is preferred for most patients. Acute coronary syndrome in pregnancy also may be caused by atherosclerotic heart disease. Management is similar to that of nonpregnant patients (see Acute Coronary Syndromes in Cardiovascular Medicine).

Guidelines for the use of select cardiovascular drugs during pregnancy are outlined in [Table: Table: Safety of Cardiac Drugs in Pregnancy and Lactation]

. Most cardiovascular drugs are not FDA approved for use during pregnancy because of limited safety data. Cardiovascular medications should be used only when the desired therapeutic effect outweighs the risk and at the lowest effective dosage.

β-Blocker use during pregnancy or lactation requires periodic fetal and newborn heart rate monitoring because β-blockers may cross the placenta and are present in human breast milk. Labetalol is the preferred β-blocker for hypertension management. Metoprolol and possibly carvedilol are the preferred β-blockers for managing heart failure and/or arrythmias in pregnancy, when indicated. Atenolol has been linked to premature delivery and small-for-gestational-age neonates and thus is usually avoided during pregnancy.

Statins are generally contraindicated during pregnancy. It is recommended that statin therapy be discontinued at least 6 weeks and preferably 12 weeks before planned conception, although emerging data support the use of pravastatin in the second trimester.

Adenosine is the drug of choice for treatment of acute symptomatic supraventricular tachycardia that occurs during pregnancy and is unresponsive to vagal maneuvers. Recurrent episodes of tachycardia are often treated with β-blockers; sotalol and flecainide have also been used safely. Because of toxicity concerns, amiodarone is contraindicated.

A useful source of information on drugs to which breastfeeding mothers may be exposed, including potential adverse effects and suggested therapeutic alternatives, is the LactMed database.

Pregnancy is associated with hypercoagulability. [Table: Table: Anticoagulation Regimens During Pregnancy]

lists the indications for anticoagulation in pregnancy, recommended regimens, and monitoring parameters for therapy. Prepregnancy counseling is recommended for all women requiring long-term anticoagulation to enable them to make informed decisions regarding anticoagulant preference and to understand the maternal and fetal risks.

Warfarin, unfractionated heparin, and low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) can all be used during pregnancy. Careful monitoring and dosage adjustment to attain the therapeutic target are indicated for all anticoagulation regimens. Warfarin use during the first trimester may cause warfarin embryopathy; the risk is increased when the daily dose is greater than 5 mg. Warfarin is stopped before delivery because of the risk for fetal intracranial hemorrhage if spontaneous labor and vaginal delivery occur while the mother (and thus the fetus) is anticoagulated with warfarin.

Pregnant individuals with a mechanical valve prosthesis represent a high-risk subset of patients, with complications commonly occurring. Concerns include valve thrombosis, bleeding, and fetal morbidity and mortality. Warfarin appears to be most effective in preventing maternal prosthetic valve thrombosis; however, warfarin poses an increased fetal risk, with possible teratogenicity, miscarriage, and fetal loss, particularly if more than 5 mg/d is needed. Warfarin may be used after the first trimester and is associated with a lower risk for valve thrombosis. LMWH and unfractionated heparin may be safer for the fetus than warfarin, but these therapies may have a higher risk for mechanical prosthetic valve thrombosis. Weight-based LMWH heparin dosing in pregnant patients with a mechanical valve may not provide an adequate level of anticoagulation to prevent thromboembolism, and use of LMWH in a pregnant patient with a mechanical valve requires dose adjustment based on anti-Xa levels. Patients with mechanical valves should be counseled by a cardio-obstetrics team before conception and managed by a multidisciplinary team during pregnancy. Frequent monitoring of the anticoagulation level is recommended during pregnancy regardless of the regimen used.

Data on the safety of direct oral anticoagulants during pregnancy are limited. Patients who become pregnant while taking a direct oral anticoagulant should have their therapy switched to an appropriate alternative anticoagulant (heparin or warfarin).

Approach to the Patient With Dermatologic Disease

General internal medicine physicians are regularly called upon to evaluate dermatologic problems, and a thorough understanding of the skin and its associated structures is required (

). Additionally, skin manifestations of systemic disease processes are common (see [Table: Table: Dermatologic Manifestations of Systemic Disease]

). An understanding of the racial and gender disparities present in the diagnosis and management of skin disease is also important. Underdiagnosis and inadequate treatment for skin conditions is a significant issue among some patient groups and impacts health outcomes. Recognizing how biases based on race, gender, and other characteristics can affect clinical decisions and mitigating their effects is crucial to ensuring equitable healthcare delivery in dermatology. For more information, see Health Equity in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

A differential diagnosis should be initially developed on the basis of morphologic features of the primary rash rather than focusing on identification of specific rashes or growths and their characteristics.

Morphology of skin lesions can be categorized as primary or secondary. Primary skin lesion morphology is the appearance of a rash or growth in its initial or unaltered state. Over time, with itching or rubbing, secondary skin changes may occur. [Table: Table: Types of Skin Lesions]

lists primary and secondary morphologic descriptors.

Other important characteristics of skin lesions include color, distribution, and configuration. Dermatologic conditions can also be categorized as neoplastic or inflammatory. Neoplasms manifest as localized areas of abnormal skin, whereas inflammatory conditions are usually more widespread.

No standardized method has been developed for how to best perform a total-body skin examination, but experts agree that patients should be fully undressed. A systematic approach is recommended to decrease the possibility of overlooking any area of the body during examination. One method is to start with the head and neck, working down to the torso, upper extremities, and lower extremities. The routine skin examination may also be incorporated into the physical examination by assessing the trunk when auscultating the heart and lungs, the arms when checking blood pressure and pulse, and the legs when checking pulses and joints.

Rashes in persons with darker skin color may be more difficult to detect because the erythema may be more subtle. Areas of active inflammation may also develop hyper- or hypopigmentation; bug bites and acne, for example, often heal with hyperpigmentation.

Several dermatologic conditions constitute emergencies or warrant urgent attention and require immediate intervention or referral to a specialist ( [Table: Table: Dermatologic Urgencies and Emergencies]

). Worrisome pigmented lesions (e.g., suspected melanoma) also warrant urgent referral.

Diagnostic tests and tools that may augment the physical examination include microscopic examination of skin scrapings, examination with Wood lamp, and skin biopsy. Skin scrapings should be viewed on a microscope slide with potassium hydroxide if tinea is suspected or mineral oil if scabies is a consideration.

A Wood lamp is an inexpensive ultraviolet light that can be used to evaluate the depigmentation seen in vitiligo and the fluorescence seen in erythrasma.

The skin biopsy is the gold standard test used to diagnose many cutaneous conditions and allows correlation of histologic and clinical findings. [Table: Table: Types of Skin Biopsies]

describes the types of skin biopsies. Shave (

) and punch (

) biopsies are the most commonly used techniques.

Therapeutic Principles in Dermatology

The effectiveness of a topical medication depends largely on its ability to be absorbed through the skin. Absorption is dependent on the chemical structure, concentration, and delivery vehicle of the medication as well as skin hydration and thickness.

In general, ointments have a higher potency than creams, which in turn have a higher potency than solutions or suspensions. The various vehicles available for topical medications are listed in [Table: Table: Vehicles for Topical Dermatologic Medications]

. An occlusive vehicle, such as an ointment, increases penetration but leaves a greasy residue. The alcohol content and drying nature of creams and gels can cause burning and stinging on damaged skin. Patients of certain cultures or communities may have a strong preference for one vehicle versus another, and they should be invited to express this preference.

Categories of topical medications, including those most frequently used and their indications, are outlined in [Table: Table: Topical Dermatologic Medications]

. Of note, most topical therapies for dermatologic conditions are used off-label because they are not FDA approved for the specific condition in which they are commonly used.

Topical glucocorticoids are used for their anti-inflammatory effects. Because they are applied directly to the area of involvement, systemic adverse effects are minimized. Topical glucocorticoids are classified by their potency level. There is a generic equivalent in each class, allowing for a cost-effective approach ( [Table: Table: Potency of Topical Glucocorticoids]

).

Topical glucocorticoids may cause striae, easy bruising, atrophy, and telangiectasia. Adverse effects are most frequently seen when higher potencies are used for longer periods, when glucocorticoids are used in areas of thin skin (such as the face), or in skin folds, or when they are used under occlusion. Use of glucocorticoids around the eyes can exacerbate glaucoma and cause cataracts.

Topical antifungal agents are used for superficial fungal infections. Topical azole or allylamine antifungal agents are suitable for treatment of localized infection, whereas oral agents are used to treat recurrent, recalcitrant, or widespread disease.

Topical glucocorticoids are frequently commercially combined with topical antifungal agents (e.g., clotrimazole-betamethasone). These combinations should be avoided because they can worsen some tinea infections and, when used in intertriginous areas, have a high risk of causing striae.

Topical immunomodulators can be used in place of topical glucocorticoids for an extended period without the development of acne, atrophy, or striae. These medications are also beneficial when treating sensitive skin areas such as the face and intertriginous areas. Common topical immunomodulators used in dermatology are described in [Table: Table: Topical Immunomodulators for Dermatologic Use]

.

Topical retinoids are used frequently in the treatment of acne and psoriasis. They are vitamin A analogues that affect keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation. Use of these medications should be avoided in pregnancy owing to the risk of teratogenicity.

Topical antibiotics are commonly used to treat dermatologic conditions such as acne or rosacea. Topical clindamycin has few to no adverse effects, although bacterial resistance with monotherapy has been increasing during the past several decades. Combination with benzoyl peroxide avoids this risk. Mupirocin is a topical antibiotic ointment commonly used to treat skin infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus, such as impetigo. Over-the-counter combination antibiotics (neomycin and bacitracin) are also used frequently. The most frequent adverse effect is allergic contact dermatitis, which limits their utility. Common topical antibiotics are described in [Table: Table: Topical Antibiotics for Dermatologic Use]

.

Phototherapy with narrowband ultraviolet B (UVB) is an effective treatment option for several inflammatory skin conditions including psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, certain sclerosing disorders (e.g., morphea, systemic sclerosis), and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Despite the strong safety data and low costs associated with narrowband UVB therapy, its use appears to be decreasing as biologic therapy use increases. Phototherapy using psoralens and ultraviolet A is now rare owing to significant increases in skin cancer risk.

Dermatitis

Atopic dermatitis is a pruritic inflammatory condition that commonly presents on the face and flexural surfaces, such as the popliteal and antecubital fossae (

). Excoriations and thickening (lichenification) of the skin caused by scratching often accompany other signs of the atopic triad (allergic rhinitis, asthma, and eczema). Pathogenesis is multifactorial and related to compromised skin barrier and an underlying immune response. Treatment is directed toward improving skin barrier function and decreasing pro-inflammatory cytokines.

The use of fragrance-free, synthetic detergent and non–soap-based cleansers and moisturizers is the primary treatment. Application of moisturizers immediately after bathing is recommended to improve skin hydration. The American Academy of Dermatology 2023 guidelines for management of atopic dermatitis conditionally recommend against the use of topical antimicrobials (unless being used as treatment for a superimposed infection), topical antihistamines, and topical antiseptics.

Topical glucocorticoids are first-line anti-inflammatory medications used in addition to cleansers and moisturizers; glucocorticoid treatment is typically applied twice daily until lesions are cleared. Wet wrap therapy is an effective option to control atopic dermatitis flares. Wet wrap therapy involves applying a topical agent (typically a low- or mid-potency topical glucocorticoid) covered by a damp layer of moistened cotton, gauze, or bandages, and then application of a dry external layer. Wet wrap therapy is often applied for 1 to 2 hours, once or twice a day, for up to several weeks.

Topical calcineurin inhibitors, such as tacrolimus and pimecrolimus, are safe, steroid-sparing anti-inflammatory agents useful for areas such as the face and skin folds, where permanent atrophy caused by topical glucocorticoid use is a concern. Other steroid-sparing medications that are FDA approved for atopic dermatitis include the topical Janus kinase inhibitor ruxolitinib 1.5% cream, the topical phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitors crisaborole 2% ointment and roflumilast 0.15%, and the aryl hydrocarbon receptor agonist tapinarof 1% cream.

Systemic glucocorticoids should be avoided, if possible, owing to flares after discontinuation; these agents should only be considered in severe exacerbations or when bridging to another systemic therapy. Steroid-sparing therapies, such as cyclosporine, methotrexate, azathioprine, and mycophenolate mofetil, are traditional systemic treatment options. Targeted monoclonal antibodies and oral Janus kinase inhibitors are FDA-approved systemic treatments that target more specific cytokines than traditional treatments ( [Table: Table: Systemic Therapy for Moderate to Severe Atopic Dermatitis]

).

There are two types of contact dermatitis: allergic and irritant. Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction that results in an eczematous eruption at the site of contact. Irritant contact dermatitis is more common than allergic contact dermatitis and results from direct damage to the skin caused by chemicals, soaps, or detergents; it is not immune mediated.

Discovering the cause of contact dermatitis is essential to its treatment and prevention. A detailed history can help identify the cause, but often epicutaneous patch testing is needed to identify the source (

). Because allergies can develop over time, a lengthy history of using a skin product without a reaction does not exclude that product as a potential trigger. Common contact allergens are described in [Table: Table: Common Contact Allergens]

.

Urushiol, the allergen found in plants such as poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac, is a common cause of allergic contact dermatitis. Clinically, it presents with intensely pruritic, often linear, edematous papules, plaques, and vesicles (

). In sensitized patients, lesions can present at different locations at different times for up to 14 days after exposure. Fluid from blisters is not antigenic. After exposure, patients should remove contaminated clothing and gently wash the skin with soap and water.

Nickel is another common allergen and is found in everyday items such as jewelry, zippers, and cell phones. Eczematous dermatitis of the lower abdomen is a common presentation of a nickel allergy caused by a clothing snap or belt buckle. Patients may use a commercially available nickel test kit to identify items that contain nickel.

Neomycin and bacitracin are commonly used for wound care, but they can cause an allergic contact dermatitis that mimics a wound infection. Given the prevalence of sensitivity to these products, patients should use plain petrolatum in place of topical antibiotics to aid healing of clean wounds.

Avoidance of the causative agent is preventive and curative. Topical glucocorticoids are used while attempting to identify and eliminate the allergen source. Severe allergic contact eruptions may necessitate a 2- to 3-week taper of systemic glucocorticoids. Because of the risk of rebound dermatitis, shorter courses of systemic glucocorticoids are not recommended.

Lichen simplex chronicus is a condition caused by repetitive scratching or rubbing. Predisposing conditions include atopic dermatitis, xerosis, and psychiatric conditions such as obsessive-compulsive disorder. Lichen simplex chronicus manifests as thickened plaques with erythema and hyperpigmentation (see

). Exaggerated skin markings are seen on the surface of the skin as well. Common sites include the genitals, back of the neck, wrists, ankles, and lower legs. Lichen simplex chronicus is treated with moisturizers, high-potency and ultrapotent topical glucocorticoids, and intralesional glucocorticoid injections.

Hand dermatitis often results from a combination of causes, such as excessive hand washing (resulting in irritant contact dermatitis), contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, or dyshidrotic eczema. It is most commonly seen in patients who hold jobs involving prolonged exposure to water, chemicals, and occlusive gloves (health care, house cleaning, food preparation, hairstyling, mechanics). It is characterized by pruritic, erythematous plaques on the palmar and dorsal hands, which can lead to fissuring and lichenification over time (see

). Dyshidrotic eczema presents with tiny, deep vesicles on the palms and sides of the fingers (

).

The differential diagnosis of hand dermatitis includes tinea, psoriasis, mechanic’s hand of antisynthetase syndrome (

), and scabies. The patient’s entire body should be examined for other rashes that may help differentiate hand dermatitis from these other causes. If tinea is suspected, the feet should be examined for tinea pedis and onychomycosis (two feet-one hand syndrome).

Treatment includes topical emollients, such as petrolatum. A potent topical glucocorticoid may be necessary during flares. Triggers should be identified and avoided. Placing white-cotton glove liners inside of rubber gloves is recommended for patients when working with chemicals and water.

Seborrheic dermatitis is a common condition characterized by greasy, yellow, scaly, erythematous patches in seborrheic areas (scalp, face, ears, upper chest, axillae, and inguinal folds) (

). On the face, specific areas of involvement include the eyebrows, medial aspects of the cheeks, and nasal ala. This disease is believed to be caused by a heightened sensitivity to yeasts, such as Malassezia. It is more common in males and typically more severe in the winter. It is more prevalent in patients who are immunocompromised, such as those with HIV/AIDS or organ transplant recipients. Patients with Parkinson disease or Down syndrome also have a higher prevalence of seborrheic dermatitis. Diagnosis is made clinically on the basis of the distribution and appearance of the patches.

Treatment includes over-the-counter medications, such as selenium sulfide or zinc pyrithione shampoos. Ketoconazole shampoo and cream are also effective. Patients should apply the shampoo on the skin and allow it to sit for 5 minutes before rinsing it off. Low-potency topical glucocorticoids or topical calcineurin inhibitors can be used in combination with antifungal treatments when severe inflammation is present. Oral ketoconazole is not recommended owing to the risk of liver and adrenal toxicity, although other oral antifungal agents may be used for severe or refractory disease. If conventional therapies are not effective, other diagnoses must be considered, including rosacea, cutaneous lupus erythematosus, and contact dermatitis.

Nummular dermatitis is characterized by coin-shaped, pruritic, scaly plaques commonly found on the extremities (

). It is more common in males and older persons. The round plaques may be mistaken for other conditions, such as tinea corporis, psoriasis, or contact dermatitis. Medium- to high-potency topical glucocorticoids and emollients are the preferred treatment.

Intertrigo is dermatitis involving adjacent skin folds (axillary, inframammary, abdominal, and inguinal) (

). Predisposing conditions include obesity, friction, occlusion, and factors that interfere with immune response, such as diabetes mellitus. Intertrigo presents with erythematous, macerated plaques. Secondary infection with Candida is common and may be suspected by the presence of multiple small red papules and pustules that surround the primary rash (see

). For more information, see Approach to the Patient With Dermatologic Disease in Dermatology and Candidiasis in Dermatology.

Treatment of intertrigo consists of drying the area and using agents (such as drying powder) to reduce moisture and maceration and to prevent secondary yeast infection. Short courses of low-potency topical glucocorticoids may be added to treat the associated inflammation. If secondary Candida infection is suspected, concomitant treatment with topical antifungal agents can be added.

Venous stasis dermatitis is common in patients with chronic lower extremity edema, most commonly secondary to venous stasis (

). Venous stasis dermatitis can be very pruritic and erythematous, and symptoms are often bilateral with medial distal leg predominance. Dependent edema, hyperpigmentation due to hemosiderin deposition, dilated veins, and ulcerations are common associated findings (see Foot and Leg Ulcers in Common Symptoms). Symptoms can be managed topically with glucocorticoids and emollients, but the condition will not significantly improve until the edema is addressed with leg elevation and compression (see Chronic Venous Insufficiency in Common Symptoms). Often, a superimposed allergic contact dermatitis can be seen from topical agents used to treat the stasis dermatitis. Because of a similar clinical presentation, venous stasis dermatitis may be misdiagnosed as cellulitis; however, cellulitis is usually unilateral, more acute in onset, and often associated with pain, leukocytosis, and occasionally fever.

Miliaria (prickly heat, heat rash) is caused by the occlusion and subsequent rupture of the eccrine sweat ducts at various levels. Clinically, miliaria presents as numerous nonfollicular 1- to 3-mm clear vesicles or pustules that arise in any context that causes sweating and skin occlusion. Multiple forms of miliaria exist. Miliaria crystallina is characterized by asymptomatic tiny, clear, and fragile vesicles (see

). Miliaria pustulosa features vesicles with turbid fluid in them (see

). Miliaria rubra is characterized by multiple small pink papules; it is the most common form and usually found on the trunk, particularly the back.

Supportive therapy involves eliminating predisposing factors, such as sweating, and removing occluding agents or conditions (e.g., plastic ICU bed liners in direct contact with skin). Low-potency topical glucocorticoids can be used sparingly.

Cutaneous Drug Reactions

Drug reactions are an important consideration in the differential diagnosis for any rash because medications can produce almost any pattern of skin disease. The following are the most common types of cutaneous adverse reactions:

  • Exanthematous (morbilliform)
  • Fixed drug
  • Urticarial (see Urticaria in Interdisciplinary Medicine)
  • Photosensitivity (see Phototoxic and Photoallergic Conditions in Dermatology)
  • Hypersensitivity vasculitis
  • Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis
  • Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis)

Patterns of drug reactions are described in [Table: Table: Patterns of Drug and Chemical Reactions]

. Medications can also induce an array of specific diseases including psoriasis, bullous pemphigoid, and cutaneous lupus erythematosus. Discontinuing the causative drug is the first step in treating drug reactions.

Exanthematous, or morbilliform (measles-like), drug eruptions are the most common drug reactions, most likely representing a type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction. As such, the rash appears during the first or second week after drug exposure, although subsequent exposures can produce a reaction much more quickly. This eruption is benign and usually self-limited. Patients develop erythematous pale pink to red papules and macules that coalesce symmetrically to form plaques. As with any erythema, in patients with darker skin tones the eruption can appear more violet to purple or even hyperpigmented. The papules are often dense and monomorphic and accompanied by varying degrees of pruritus, beginning on the trunk and progressing distally across the limbs (

). Palms and soles are usually spared. This type of reaction is classically induced with the use of ampicillin or amoxicillin in patients with acute Epstein-Barr virus infection.

Treatment involves cessation of the causative agent and the use of systemic and/or topical glucocorticoids and oral H~1 antihistamines. Patients should be counseled to seek care immediately if they develop fever, skin pain, blisters, pustules, or mucous membrane involvement, which indicate a more serious and potentially life-threatening condition.

Fixed drug eruptions recur at the same sites on the skin with each exposure. Pink to purple circinate plaques with central dusky discoloration or vesiculation appear most commonly on the lips, face, fingers, and genitals (

). The first exposure typically generates one plaque that recurs in the same location with each repeated exposure. Additional plaques may develop with subsequent exposures. This benign eruption usually resolves with postinflammatory hyperpigmentation. Treatment involves cessation of the causative agent, and, if symptoms are significant, systemic and/or topical glucocorticoids and oral H~1 antihistamines.

Drugs are the most common cause of hypersensitivity vasculitis, a small-vessel vasculitis, which is discussed in Hypersensitivity Vasculitis in Rheumatology.

Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis is the rapid onset of a dense monomorphic eruption of pustules after a medication exposure in a patient without a history of pustular psoriasis. Eighty percent of cases are caused by antibiotics. Onset occurs within several days of exposure. Patients present with fever and erythema and eventually develop myriad dense nonfolliculocentric pustules, primarily in skin folds and on the trunk (

). Most cases are self-limited and resolve within 2 weeks. Treatment consists of cessation of the causative agent and supportive care; topical and systemic glucocorticoids may be helpful for symptomatic relief. The condition carries a mortality rate of less than 5%.

Drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome (DIHS) and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) are synonymous and represent a severe life-threatening medication reaction. DRESS is increasingly being referred to as DIHS to emphasize the fact that eosinophilia is not always present.

The most common medications that cause DIHS include sulfonamide antibiotics, allopurinol, and anticonvulsants, but many other medications have been implicated (see [Table: Table: Patterns of Drug and Chemical Reactions]

). Unlike other severe medication reactions, the onset of symptoms is delayed, often 2 to 6 weeks after exposure. Symptoms begin with fever and flu-like symptoms, quickly followed by burning skin pain and rash. Patients typically develop a morbilliform exanthem that starts on the face and upper trunk and spreads distally (

). Eventually the patient develops striking facial edema and redness (

), a hallmark of DIHS. Oral mucosal involvement is common but is less severe than Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis or erythema multiforme.

Systemic involvement is necessary for the diagnosis of DIHS and most commonly includes eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytosis and elevated hepatocellular enzyme levels. Hypotension, shock, and multisystem organ damage are possible. Death occurs in up to 20% of patients with DIHS, most commonly due to hepatic necrosis. Immediate discontinuation of the causative agent is mandatory, and systemic glucocorticoids tapered over weeks to months can be helpful.

Avoidance of the causative medication in the future is mandatory. DIHS caused by an aromatic antiepileptic agent may cross-react with other aromatic antiepileptics. For example, if phenytoin causes DIHS, the patient may experience cross-reaction with phenobarbital or carbamazepine. Systemic autoimmune disease, most notably thyroid disease, may develop months after resolution of rash, and close follow-up is important.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are a spectrum of severe life-threatening mucocutaneous reactions defined by the extent of affected body surface area (BSA) involved with immune-mediated cutaneous necrosis. SJS refers to patients with less than 10% BSA affected, and TEN refers to those with greater than 30% BSA affected. The term SJS/TEN overlap refers to patients with 10% to 30% BSA affected. SJS and TEN are the most severe and deadly of all cutaneous adverse drug reactions. Key features include full-thickness epidermal necrosis with involvement of mucous membranes. Essentially all cases of TEN are temporally correlated with medications (see [Table: Table: Patterns of Drug and Chemical Reactions]

), whereas approximately 25% of SJS cases are caused by infection or vaccination. HIV infection, kidney disease, and uncontrolled autoimmune disease also contribute to increased risk.

Symptoms usually begin within 1 to 3 weeks of exposure to the inciting agent. Patients may notice fever, malaise, and symptoms of upper respiratory infections followed by skin pain, grittiness of the eyes, and odynophagia. Within several days, patients develop red or purple dusky macules on the trunk that progress to vesicles, erosions, and ulceration. Painful erosions develop in the mouth, eyes, or genitals in as many as 95% of patients (

)

Differentiating SJS/TEN from erythema multiforme is critically important (see Erythema Multiforme in Dermatology). Erythema multiforme may also manifest with mucosal ulceration, malaise, and vesicular skin eruption but most commonly involves the extremities, whereas SJS and TEN develop on the trunk and face. Patients with SJS/TEN may exhibit atypical targetoid macules demonstrating one- or two-colored rings, whereas lesions with three-colored zones are characteristic of erythema multiforme. The presence of extensive epidermal sloughing (

) and a positive Nikolsky sign (gentle traction pressure on intact skin causes shearing of intact epidermis away from the dermis resulting in an erosion) further differentiate SJS/TEN from erythema multiforme major ( [Table: Table: Comparison of EM, SJS, and TEN]

).

Systemic manifestations are common in patients with SJS/TEN. All patients experience fever and malaise. Lymphadenopathy, elevated hepatocellular enzyme levels, and cytopenias are common. Pneumonitis, nephritis, hepatitis, and myocarditis may occur. Hypovolemia and electrolyte imbalances caused by loss of the skin barrier are common.

The acute phase of the disease lasts 1 to 2 weeks, and skin reepithelization may take 2 to 4 weeks. Mortality is high, with 5% to 10% of SJS cases being fatal and up to 33% of patients with TEN dying of disease complications such as secondary infection, transcutaneous fluid loss, or respiratory complications. Early identification and withdrawal of the causative medication improve outcomes. The SCORTEN scale is a validated severity-of-illness tool for TEN and SJS that can be applied early in the course of the disease and directly correlates with mortality ( [Table: Table: SCORTEN Tool Values]

).

Treatment of SJS/TEN is highly controversial. Intravenous glucocorticoids or intravenous immune globulins are probably the most commonly used treatments, but neither is supported by strong evidence. Cyclosporine and biologic agents are increasingly common choices. Supportive care in an ICU with experienced nursing staff is critical for wound care, and many patients are best cared for in a burn center. A low threshold is recommended for performing cultures and initiation of empiric antibiotics; however, use of prophylactic antibiotics is not recommended. Ophthalmologic and urologic consultations are mandatory if ocular or genital involvement is present because destructive scarring may occur in these areas.

Nutritional Disorders of the Skin

Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) plays multiple roles in the body, including facilitating collagen synthesis. It is found in many fruits and vegetables, and deficiency (scurvy) is usually the result of a restricted diet, sometimes in the setting of alcohol use disorder. Owing to its role in collagen synthesis, cutaneous manifestations are common and include perifollicular hemorrhage, follicular hyperkeratotic papules, and coiled “corkscrew” hairs (

). Other manifestations include petechiae, purpura, gingival bleeding, and splinter hemorrhages. Hemarthroses, edema, dyspnea, and death may occur in advanced cases. The diagnosis is clinical and supported by a low plasma vitamin C level. Many manifestations of vitamin C deficiency respond quickly to repletion. Patients typically have additional nutritional deficiencies when scurvy is present.

Niacin is found in a variety of foods, and deficiency is rare in the United States, except in patients with significant nutritional restriction, such as those with alcohol use disorder. It most frequently presents with erythema in sun-exposed areas, including the neck and hands, resembling a sunburn, and subsequently evolves into scaling hyperpigmented plaques. Other frequent manifestations include diarrhea and alteration in cognition ranging from insomnia to dementia. Diagnosis is usually made on the basis of clinical findings.

Vitamin A deficiency may result in conjunctival and generalized xerosis and follicular hyperkeratotic papules on the extensor surfaces (toad skin); it may progress to corneal scarring with white Bitot spots and night blindness.

Vitamin B~2 (riboflavin) deficiency is associated with oral-ocular-genital syndrome with angular stomatitis (

), glossitis, photophobia, and pruritic scrotal dermatitis with balanitis. Seborrheic dermatitis of the face may also occur.

Vitamin K deficiency may result in ecchymosis. Zinc deficiency, which may occur in patients with liver disease, those receiving parenteral nutrition, and those with inflammatory bowel disease, may manifest as a perioral and perianal dermatitis with vesicles, pustules, or plaques on an erythematous base.
