Pruritus

Pruritus is one of the most common symptoms in dermatology. It is frequently associated with a variety of skin diseases, especially inflammatory skin diseases such as atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, and urticaria. In older adults, xerotic (or dry) skin is a common cause of pruritus (see Dermatologic Conditions of Aging in Dermatology).

Pruritus may also occur independent of skin pathology secondary to medications and systemic diseases. Common medications that cause pruritus include opioids, calcium channel blockers, hydrochlorothiazide, and NSAIDs. A variety of systemic conditions are also associated with pruritus. Uremic pruritus is common in patients with advanced kidney disease. Liver disease such as cholestatic hepatobiliary diseases (

) as well as cirrhosis in the absence of cholestasis may cause pruritus. Thyroid disease and polycythemia vera might present with itching, the latter often occurring after a warm bath or shower (aquagenic pruritus). Generalized pruritus may be the presenting symptom in malignancies, such as Hodgkin lymphoma. Certain infections, such as HIV, may also present with generalized itching.

Neuropathic pruritus describes the itch that is caused by dysfunction of a peripheral or central nerve due to surgery, trauma, neuropathy, or infection (postherpetic neuralgia). Neuropathic itch is often localized; examples include the forearm (brachioradial pruritus) and mid to upper back (notalgia paresthetica) (

). Various psychiatric conditions can also manifest as itching (psychogenic itch) (

).

A complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, lactate dehydrogenase level, fasting blood glucose level, thyroid function studies, kidney function studies, and liver chemistry tests are an appropriate initial evaluation. A review of the patient’s medications should also be performed.

Treatment of pruritus is directed at the underlying cause ( [Table: Table: Systemic Treatments of Pruritus]

). The treatment of inflammatory skin conditions with topical glucocorticoids and emollients can help alleviate pruritus. Topical medications containing menthol can also be helpful. First-generation oral antihistamines may be helpful for nocturnal pruritus. For older patients with xerotic skin, dry skin care should be provided.

Ultraviolet phototherapy, gabapentinoids, antidepressants, and opioid receptor antagonists are other systemic treatment options for refractory pruritus.

bodies.dmsec24007:
Acneiform Eruptions

Acne vulgaris is a chronic inflammatory condition affecting the pilosebaceous unit (hair follicle and sebaceous gland). Although most common during adolescence, acne can affect patients at any age. The clinical features of acne are open comedones (blackheads); closed comedones (whiteheads); inflammatory papules and pustules; and nodulocystic lesions on the face, neck, chest, shoulders, and back (

and

).

Acne vulgaris must be differentiated from acneiform lesions, which are common and have a broad differential diagnosis. Variations in distribution and primary lesions may provide clues to help differentiate acne vulgaris from other diagnoses ( [Table: Table: Types of Acneiform Eruptions]

). Similarly, onset of acne combined with other signs of hyperandrogenism, such as hirsutism and oligomenorrhea, warrant consideration of polycystic ovary syndrome, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, or an underlying adrenal or ovarian tumor.

The pathogenesis of acne vulgaris is four-fold and includes abnormal keratinization within the hair follicle, excess sebum production (stimulated by androgens), colonization of the follicle by Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes), and the release of inflammatory cytokines. Treatment is directed at all four mechanisms (

).

No universally accepted schema for classifying acne exists, but a common grading system is to classify acne as mild, moderate, or severe ( [Table: Table: Common Grading System for the Classification of Acne]

). Mild acne consists of primarily comedones with few inflammatory papules and no nodules or cysts. Moderate acne involves several comedones and inflammatory papules; a few nodules may be present as well. Severe acne is characterized by large lesion counts involving comedones and inflammatory pustules along with several cysts.

Topical multimodality therapy is the cornerstone of acne management. Topical retinoids (primarily tretinoin, but also adapalene and tazarotene) are first-line treatments for all types of acne because they are effective for both comedonal and inflammatory acne. Retinoids help normalize the keratinization of the hair follicle and are comedolytic, thus reducing follicular plugging. They also decrease inflammatory cytokines that are activated by C. acnes and reduce postinflammatory hyperpigmentation. Topical retinoids may cause erythema, burning, and dryness. All topical retinoids are contraindicated in pregnancy.

Topical antibiotics, such as erythromycin or clindamycin, are helpful in inflammatory acne because they target C. acnes and have anti-inflammatory effects. Clindamycin, azelaic acid, and erythromycin are the only acne treatments that are demonstrated to be safe in pregnancy. Because of increased antibiotic resistance, topical antibiotics should not be used as monotherapy and should be combined with topical benzoyl peroxide with or without a topical retinoid for treatment of mild, moderate, or severe acne.

Topical benzoyl peroxide has bactericidal properties but is not known to promote the development of resistant bacteria. Benzoyl peroxide rarely may cause irritation and allergic contact dermatitis in patients.

Oral antibiotics are frequently used for moderate to severe inflammatory acne and acne that is resistant to topical treatment alone. Oral antibiotics inhibit C. acnes and can also decrease inflammation. Tetracycline-based antibiotics, such as doxycycline (preferred) and minocycline, are often used because they possess both of these desirable properties. When possible, courses of oral antibiotics should be limited to 3 months to decrease the risk of antibiotic resistance.

Intralesional corticosteroids can be used to treat larger papules and nodules to reduce the risk of scarring.

In severe nodulocystic or recalcitrant acne or when acne causes significant psychosocial distress, oral isotretinoin should be considered. Owing to teratogenicity, isotretinoin prescribers must be enrolled in the FDA-required iPLEDGE Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy program.

Adult acne is more common in women and is related to androgenic hormones. It typically presents along the jawline and often flares with the menstrual cycle. Although considered second-line therapy, oral contraceptives or spironolactone (aldosterone receptor blocker with antiandrogen activity) can be added to other treatments in women with moderate to severe acne. Combined estrogen-progesterone oral contraceptives are effective for inflammatory acne in women and girls older than 14 years without evidence of hyperandrogenism.

When counseling patients with acne, it is important to stress the importance of adherence to treatment and the time course for improvement, which is often several weeks to months. In addition to prescribed medications, only noncomedogenic cosmetics and moisturizers should be used.

Rosacea is an inflammatory condition appearing in the third to sixth decades of life. Rosacea is most common among patients of Irish and English descent who have light complexions. It is defined by chronic inflammation of the pilosebaceous units, with increased vascular reactivity. The pathogenesis is undetermined. There are a variety of clinical presentations of rosacea, including papulopustular, erythrotelangiectatic, phymatous, and ocular rosacea.

Both papulopustular and erythrotelangiectatic subtypes favor a central facial distribution, particularly involving the malar cheeks and nose as well as the glabella and central forehead. Most patients also have frequent flushing in response to triggers such as stress, alcohol consumption, heat, and excessive sunlight. The papulopustular variant of rosacea can be confused with acne, but rosacea does not present with comedonal lesions (

). Telangiectasias are seen in the erythrotelangiectatic subtype (

).

The sun sensitivity and malar erythema (often sparing the nasolabial fold) of rosacea overlap with the presentation of acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (ACLE or butterfly rash); for more information, see Cutaneous Involvement in Rheumatology. The presence of telangiectasias or pustules readily distinguishes rosacea from ACLE, which does not include these manifestations. In addition, rosacea is pink to bright red, whereas ACLE has a homogenous violet-pink or purple tone. Finally, rosacea is more common in older patients and occurs in response to other triggers in addition to sunlight, whereas ACLE is more common in younger patients, who almost always have underlying systemic lupus erythematosus.

In phymatous rosacea, severe sebaceous hyperplasia and chronic inflammation lead to fibrous overgrowth of the skin, creating a nodular, tumor-like deformation of the facial structures, most commonly the nose (rhinophyma) (

). Ocular rosacea may present with injected conjunctiva and a gritty sensation alone or with associated skin findings.

Treatment for rosacea is targeted toward the most prominent signs and symptoms in each patient. Treatment for papulopustular rosacea includes topical metronidazole, an azelaic acid formulation, and topical ivermectin. Topical glucocorticoids should be avoided. Oral antibiotics such as low-dose doxycycline have been shown to help control inflammation in papulopustular and ocular rosacea; use of low dosing decreases adverse effects and reduces the prevalence of bacterial resistance. Initial treatment of erythrotelangiectatic rosacea focuses primarily on behavioral modifications such as avoidance of identified triggers of flushing, proper use of sun protection, and use of gentle skin cleansers. Pulsed dye laser therapy is also effective for erythema and telangiectasias. For patients with severe rhinophyma, surgery is the treatment of choice.

Hidradenitis suppurativa is an inflammatory skin disorder of the apocrine glands. This disease occurs more commonly in women and typically begins after puberty. Risk factors include obesity, family history, and cigarette smoking. It is characterized by comedones, painful nodules, abscesses, draining sinuses, and scarring (

). It most frequently occurs in the intertriginous areas, such as the axillae, groin, and underneath the breasts.

Hidradenitis suppurativa is extremely difficult to treat. Weight loss and smoking cessation are encouraged. No single treatment has been effective for all patients; however, several options are available ( [Table: Table: Treatment Options for Hidradenitis Suppurativa]

). Decolonization with dilute bleach baths and chlorhexidine washes may be used in addition to topical clindamycin. Common systemic treatments include oral antibiotics such as tetracyclines or the combination of clindamycin and rifampin. Adalimumab (a tumor necrosis factor α inhibitor) and the interleukin-17 inhibitors secukinumab and bimekizumab are FDA-approved treatments for moderate to severe hidradenitis suppurativa, defined by the presence of multiple recurring nodules or abscesses and scarring.

bodies.dmsec24008:
Pigment Disorders

Vitiligo is a common acquired autoimmune condition characterized by the loss of function or absence of melanocytes, resulting in patchy depigmentation of the skin. Affecting both sexes equally, vitiligo can occur at any age and can have a significant impact on quality of life. Clinically, it appears as completely depigmented, well-demarcated symmetric macules or patches with no scale (

). Its onset is insidious and asymptomatic, starting as smaller macules that gradually enlarge and may result in depigmentation of associated hairs. It tends to be more visible in persons with darker skin types (

) or in sun-exposed areas, as the surrounding skin will darken with sun exposure. Extensor (dorsal hands and feet, elbows, knees), periorificial, and anogenital surfaces are most commonly affected. Lesions also favor sites of repeated trauma or friction (Koebner phenomenon). There is increased risk of comorbid autoimmune conditions such as thyroid disease (most common), type 1 diabetes mellitus, Addison disease, pernicious anemia, and alopecia areata.

Vitiligo can be diagnosed clinically using history and physical examination. A Wood lamp or ultraviolet A (UVA)–emitting black light can be used to assess the full extent and distribution of affected areas, which may be harder to appreciate in lighter skin types. Due to the complete absence of melanin, UVA is reflected more intensely off the stratum corneum and dermal collagen in vitiliginous skin, resulting in sharply delineated, bright white patches on Wood lamp examination.

It may be challenging to distinguish early vitiligo from other acquired causes of hypopigmentation (see [Table: Table: Common Causes of Acquired Hypopigmentation and Depigmentation]

). However, the characteristic sharply defined borders, complete depigmentation (as opposed to hypopigmentation), bright white fluorescence on Wood lamp examination, and lack of overlying scale seen in vitiligo are helpful diagnostic clues. If the diagnosis is in doubt, a skin biopsy may assist in ruling out other causes of dyspigmentation.

Treatment for depigmented skin can be challenging, prolonged, and suboptimal. Topical therapies include high-potency glucocorticoids or immunomodulators (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus). The topical Janus kinase inhibitor ruxolitinib is currently the only medication approved by the FDA for localized nonsegmental vitiligo. Phototherapy with ultraviolet light is also an option and can be the treatment of choice for widespread involvement. Repigmentation occurs first around hair follicles as they are thought to be the reservoirs for melanocytes. As a result, repigmented skin will initially have a speckled appearance. Depigmentation therapy of nonaffected skin with monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone can also be considered if the vitiligo is widespread (>50% body surface area).

Melasma, also known as chloasma or the mask of pregnancy, is a common acquired condition resulting in patchy hyperpigmentation of the skin on the face. It can also be seen on sun-exposed areas of the neck and upper extremities. In this condition, melanocytes overproduce melanin owing to a multitude of factors, including ultraviolet radiation and visible light exposure, genetic predisposition, and hormonal influence (pregnancy, use of oral contraceptives). Women and individuals with darker skin types, especially those of Hispanic, Asian, or South Asian ancestry, are more commonly affected. Clinically, it presents as ill-defined, tan to dark brown reticulated patches, mostly on the sun-exposed areas of the face (malar, mandibular, and centrofacial regions) (

). It worsens with sun exposure. The main differential diagnoses include postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, drug-induced hyperpigmentation, freckles, and lentigines. Melasma often fades during the postpartum period, with sun protection, and upon discontinuation of oral contraceptives. It may take months to years for pigmentation to normalize.

Treatment can be challenging. The mainstays of treatment are strict sun protection, avoidance or discontinuation of the causative factors, and use of topical lightening agents. Oral tranexamic acid may be used in severe or recalcitrant cases.

Xeroderma pigmentosa is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by defective DNA repair that results in increased susceptibility to skin damage from ultraviolet light. Clinical manifestations include frequent and profound sunburns with minimal light exposure; freckling at an early age; and a significantly increased incidence of all forms of skin cancer, including melanoma. There is also an increased risk of other cancers including central nervous system and hematologic malignancies. Treatment is supportive and includes strict measures to prevent exposure to ultraviolet light as well as close surveillance for the development of skin cancer.

bodies.dmsec24009:
Autoimmune Bullous Diseases

Autoimmune bullous diseases (ABDs) include primary cutaneous disorders and manifestations of underlying systemic disease ( [Table: Table: Characteristics of Autoimmune Blistering Diseases]

).

Pemphigus vulgaris is the most common of the intraepidermal ABDs, and its incidence increases with age. It occurs due to IgG autoantibody formation against desmosomal adhesion proteins desmoglein 1 and 3. The oral mucosa is involved in the majority of cases and is often the initial site of disease activity. The skin and other mucosal surfaces, such as the conjunctival, nasal, esophageal, and anogenital regions, are variably affected. Patients present with flaccid bullae that rupture easily, leaving behind painful erosions and denuded skin (see

and

). Application of lateral pressure near the edge of a blister or on normal-appearing skin induces epidermal separation and blister formation, a phenomenon known as the Nikolsky sign. A positive Nikolsky sign is not specific to pemphigus, as it can also be seen in Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome due to similar abnormalities in keratinocyte adhesion. Lesions heal with prominent dyspigmentation but not true scarring because disease pathology occurs above the basement membrane zone.

Diagnosis can be made by skin biopsy with both routine microscopy and direct immunofluorescence and/or by serologic testing for anti–desmoglein 3 with or without anti–desmoglein 1 autoantibodies; the latter is highly sensitive and specific for pemphigus.

Without treatment, patients with pemphigus are at high risk for infectious complications, insensible fluid loss, and malnutrition from poor oral intake. High-dose systemic corticosteroids (1 mg/kg/d prednisone equivalent) are the mainstay of treatment for rapid disease control, typically in combination with steroid-sparing immunosuppressive agents. Rituximab, a monoclonal antibody against CD20 on B cells, received FDA approval in 2018 and is now considered first-line treatment for moderate to severe disease. Other steroid-sparing options include methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, or azathioprine. Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) and plasmapheresis can be used for acute relief in cases where corticosteroids are contraindicated or ineffective.

Bullous pemphigoid is the most common of the subepidermal blistering disorders and occurs due to the formation of IgG autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal antigens BP180 (also known as BPAg2 or collagen XVII) and BP230 (also known as BPAg1). It is the most common ABD overall and predominantly affects patients older than 60 years. Individuals with underlying neurologic diseases (e.g., stroke, dementia, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis) are at higher risk, possibly due to coexpression of bullous pemphigoid antigens BP180 and BP230 by the central nervous system and subsequent cross-reactivity in the skin.

Patients classically present with intensely pruritic urticarial plaques that progress to tense bullae (

and

). Lesions may appear targetoid or violaceous, especially in darker skin (see

and

). Oral involvement is present in approximately 20% of patients. Bullae heal with pigment change but otherwise do not scar because the basement membrane zone remains mostly intact.

Bullous pemphigoid can be diagnosed histologically by biopsy with routine microscopy and direct immunofluorescence or serologically with testing for anti-BP180 and anti-BP230 autoantibodies.

The clinical course of bullous pemphigoid is protracted and characterized by periods of exacerbation and remission. First-line treatment for rapid disease control in widespread disease is systemic corticosteroids (0.5-1.0 mg/kg/d prednisone equivalent depending on severity); alternatively, IVIG and plasmapheresis can be considered in patients with steroid-refractory disease or contraindications. Steroid-sparing agents such as doxycycline with niacinamide, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, and azathioprine are used for long-term maintenance. Dupilumab, a subcutaneously administered monoclonal antibody against interleukin-4 receptor alpha, became the first medication to receive FDA approval for bullous pemphigoid in 2025. Recalcitrant cases may require off-label treatment with rituximab.

Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is a cutaneous manifestation of gluten-sensitive enteropathy that is seen in up to 25% of all patients with celiac disease. It occurs due to the formation of IgA autoantibodies against epidermal transglutaminase 3 within the dermal papillae. The condition is most commonly seen in patients of Northern European ancestry during the fourth decade of life. Following gluten ingestion, patients develop recurrent crops of grouped (“herpetiform”) fragile vesicles that are intensely pruritic and quickly turn into excoriated crusted erosions, classically on the elbows or knees. Lesions can also appear symmetrically on the forearms, lower back, buttocks, scalp, or nape of the neck. Nearly all patients with DH demonstrate evidence of celiac disease on bowel biopsy; however, only 10% to 20% have active gastrointestinal symptoms at the time of DH presentation. Comorbid autoimmune conditions such as Hashimoto thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes mellitus, and pernicious anemia are common. Iodine exposure, either topically (povidone-iodine antiseptic) or systemically (intravenous contrast, foods), can exacerbate DH due to upregulation of epidermal transglutaminase activity and enhanced immune complex deposition in the skin.

Diagnosis requires skin biopsy, which reveals dense neutrophilic infiltration of the dermal papillae and granular IgA deposits. Serologic testing results for anti-transglutaminase antibodies are usually positive.

Gluten avoidance is critical for control of both bowel and skin disease. Oral dapsone is extremely effective for skin disease due to its antineutrophilic properties but does not treat bowel manifestations.

bodies.dmsec24010:
Photo- or Light-Induced Dermatoses

Photo- and light-sensitivity conditions may be secondary to systemic diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus and porphyria cutanea tarda, or conditions limited to the skin, including phototoxic/photoallergic conditions and polymorphous light eruption. Diagnosis of the disorders limited to the skin is usually clinical, but skin biopsy is often performed to support the clinical diagnosis and rule out other dermatoses.

Porphyria cutanea tarda is the most prevalent type of porphyria and presents with skin fragility and bullae or erosions on sun-exposed areas, most frequently the dorsal hands (

). Hyperpigmentation of the skin and hypertrichosis of the forehead and temples are commonly seen.

Porphyria cutanea tarda is most commonly caused by an acquired defect of hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase enzyme, which results in an excess of circulating porphyrins. Accumulated porphyrins in the skin are photosensitizing and cause phototoxicity upon light exposure. Chronic hepatitis C virus infection is the most common cause, followed by alcohol-induced liver damage and hemochromatosis. The diagnosis is confirmed by increased plasma or urine porphyrin levels.

Treatment is aimed at decreasing iron overload. In addition to treatment of the underlying condition, phlebotomy is the mainstay of therapy. Twice-weekly hydroxychloroquine is an effective alternative to phlebotomy. Treatment of chronic hepatitis C virus infection may be effective for treatment of porphyria cutanea tarda, but the evidence is limited regarding this approach.

Photosensitivity disorders are a collection of conditions characterized by an abnormal skin response after exposure to ultraviolet radiation. Photosensitivity reactions related to exogenous agents are either phototoxic or photoallergic. Exogenous agents include systemic drugs, certain plants, or topical applications.

Phototoxicity is a result of direct tissue injury and presents as an exaggerated sunburn-like reaction less than 24 hours after sun exposure. Only exposed areas are affected, and it is more common than photoallergy. Photoallergy is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction found in previously sensitized individuals that can be elicited by small amounts of an offending agent. Photoallergic reactions occur more commonly after topical exposure of a sensitizing agent and present as pruritic, eczematous eruptions within 24 to 48 hours after sun exposure on sun-exposed body parts (

). Common causes of phototoxic and photoallergic reactions are listed in [Table: Table: Causes of Phototoxic and Photoallergic Reactions]

. Treatment of photosensitivity disorders includes avoidance of photosensitizing drugs and allergens and use of broad-spectrum sunscreen.

Polymorphous light eruption is the most common idiopathic photosensitivity disorder. It typically manifests before age 30 years and is most common in fair-skinned women, first appearing in the spring and early summer. Lesions appear on sun-exposed skin within hours of exposure. Although different types of eruptions may occur (polymorphous), the most common are pruritic erythematous papules (

). The type of lesion remains consistent in an individual with each occurrence. The rash persists for weeks and resolves without scarring even with continued sun exposure. The diagnosis is made clinically. Management focuses on avoidance of sun exposure and use of sunscreens; when significant symptoms are present, topical glucocorticoids are an option, although evidence of efficacy is lacking.

bodies.dmsec24011:
Superficial Skin Infections

Additional information about other skin infections including cellulitis and skin abscess is provided in Skin and Soft Tissue Infections in Infectious Disease.

Impetigo is a superficial infection of the epidermis usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes. Impetigo is most commonly seen in children but can present in adults. Impetigo is classified as bullous or nonbullous.

Bullous impetigo is specifically caused by strains of S. aureus that produce exfoliative toxins targeting the desmosomal adhesion molecule desmoglein-1 between keratinocytes (the same toxin responsible for the more extensive exfoliation seen in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome). This results in localized blister formation. Patients classically develop small vesicles or flaccid blisters that easily rupture, leaving behind collarettes of scale and honey-colored crusted erosions (see

).

Nonbullous impetigo accounts for the majority of cases (~70%) and is characterized by erythematous papules or plaques with honey-colored crust and satellite lesions (

). Abrasions, excoriations, or atopic skin with impaired skin barrier protection are especially prone to infection.

Ecthyma is functionally a deeper variant of impetigo characterized by papulopustules that progress to punched-out ulcers with overlying eschar (

). It typically occurs on the legs, feet, or buttocks and may be associated with lymphadenitis.

Diagnosis of impetigo and ecthyma can be made on the basis of clinical appearance, but bacterial culture can be obtained from the blister fluid or exudative crust for confirmation. Treatment begins with washing with soap and water and removing the crust. Topical antibiotic treatment with mupirocin or retapamulin is effective in most cases of localized uncomplicated impetigo. Oral antibiotics are recommended for patients with widespread infection, outbreaks involving multiple people, and ecthyma. Recommended antibiotics are cephalexin or dicloxacillin for dual coverage of Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species, unless methicillin-resistant S. aureus is suspected or confirmed. There is a small increased risk of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, but not rheumatic fever, following nonbullous impetigo.

Ecthyma gangrenosum is an expression of septic vasculitis that is classically seen in immunocompromised patients with bacteremia. It should not be confused with ecthyma (deep impetigo). Lesions begin as well-defined purpuric plaques or hemorrhagic bullae that quickly progress to necrotic ulcerations with eschar due to tissue ischemia from localized vasculitis (see

). Blood and tissue cultures are usually positive. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most commonly identified culprit in ecthyma gangrenosum, although various gram-positive and -negative bacteria have also been reported. The differential diagnosis includes other angioinvasive soft tissue infections, such as cutaneous aspergillosis, and atypical hemorrhagic pyoderma gangrenosum. Treatment is directed at control of the underlying infection and immunocompromised state. Increased number of skin lesions, diagnostic delay, and neutropenia are poor prognostic indicators.

Erythrasma is a benign superficial bacterial infection of the skin most commonly caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum. It manifests as thin, pink-brown plaques or patches with a characteristically dry rather than macerated appearance; it has a thin wrinkled texture similar to cigarette paper. It occurs in moist, warm regions such as the interdigital web spaces of the feet, axilla, and groin (see

). The toe web spaces are the most commonly affected, and erythrasma in this location is often misdiagnosed as tinea pedis. Symptoms are limited to mild pruritus. A Wood lamp examination reveals diffuse coral red fluorescence due to bacterial coproporphyrin production (see

). Clinical appearance and fluorescence are the best means of diagnosis; histopathology and skin scrapings are not helpful. Treatment with topical antibacterials such as erythromycin, clindamycin, or benzoyl peroxide is typically sufficient. See [Table: Table: Differential Diagnosis of Intertriginous Rashes]

for comparison with other skinfold rashes.

Tinea is a group of cutaneous infections caused by dermatophytes and classified according to the body site that is involved: tinea pedis (athlete’s foot), tinea manuum (hand), tinea cruris (perineum or jock itch), tinea capitis (scalp), tinea faciei (face), and tinea corporis (the body, excluding the genital area or inguinal folds). Three genera of fungi account for most dermatophytosis: Epidermophyton, Microsporum, and Trichophyton. Trichophyton rubrum is the most common causative species.

Infection is more prevalent in hot and humid climates and in patients who are immunocompromised, particularly those using long-term glucocorticoid therapy. Infection is acquired from other humans, animals, or fomites.

In tinea capitis, invasion of the hair follicle leads to small broken hairs, with the surrounding scalp showing erythematous scaly patches with varying degrees of crust and numbers of pustules. Occipital adenopathy is common. Individuals with coarse, curly hair are particularly susceptible (

).

The characteristic clinical presentation of tinea corporis (see

and

), cruris (see

), and faciei is annular scaly patches or thin plaques with central clearing and erythematous, scaly serpiginous borders. Tinea cruris spares the scrotum, in contrast to candidal intertrigo, which is in the differential diagnosis. Concomitant tinea pedis with tinea cruris and tinea pedis with onychomycosis are common due to autoinoculation.

The chronic form of tinea pedis and tinea manuum presents as mildly pruritic scaly patches involving most of the palms and soles in a “moccasin” or “glove” distribution (see

,

,

, and

). “Two feet, one hand” is a characteristic pattern of involvement in tinea. Tinea pedis can have a more acute bullous form, with 1- to 2-mm vesicles or pustules, and can be extremely pruritic (see figure (see

and

). The interdigital variant of tinea pedis shows fissures and maceration in the web spaces.

Tinea incognito refers to tinea that has been erroneously treated with topical glucocorticoids, which initially decreases pruritus and leads to a clinical presentation that is less inflammatory than typical (see

). Similarly, some patients, particularly those who are immunosuppressed or using topical glucocorticoids incorrectly, may develop an uncommon condition in which the dermatophyte invades the hair follicles and dermis, causing the development of erythematous or hyperpigmented perifollicular papules or small nodules; this is known as Majocchi granuloma (see

).

Tinea can be suspected on the basis of clinical presentation and pruritus; however, diagnosis is based on visualization of long branching hyphae on microscopic examination of scrapings using a potassium hydroxide preparation (see

). Fungal culture, which provides species identification, can confirm the diagnosis but is not typically necessary. However, culture is the preferred method for diagnosing tinea capitis; hair shafts should be included in the specimen. Tinea capitis caused by certain Microsporum species may also demonstrate yellow-green fluorescence on Wood lamp examination.

Tinea should be treated to prevent skin breakdown, which can be an entry port for bacterial infection. Dermatophytosis of non–hair-bearing skin with limited involvement can be treated topically with the use of topical allylamine (terbinafine, butenafine, naftinine) or imidazole creams (miconazole, clotrimazole, econazole, ketoconazole), applied once or twice daily for 2 to 4 weeks, ensuring that the application extends a few centimeters beyond the advancing border. Allylamines are fungicidal and have higher mycologic cure rates compared to fungistatic imidazoles, but they are more expensive. Unlike superficial fungal infections caused by Candida, dermatophytes do not respond to topical nystatin. Combined antifungals and topical glucocorticoids should be avoided because they can lead to increased recurrences and treatment failures. Dermatophytosis of hair-bearing skin, including tinea capitis, or those with recurrent or extensive skin involvement should be treated with oral antifungal agents such as terbinafine, fluconazole, or itraconazole.

Candida species, in particular Candida albicans, can cause superficial infections in moist occluded skin, such as the intertriginous areas, oropharyngeal mucosa, and genitals, as well as invasive disease in immunocompromised and hospitalized patients (see Systemic Candidiasis in Infectious Disease). Antibacterial therapy is a predisposing factor because it increases the number of colonizing yeast cells present in skin and mucous membranes.

Intertrigo is an inflammatory skin disease caused by moisture and friction of the inframammary, infra-abdominal, and inguinal folds (see

and Intertrigo in Dermatology); the neck folds and axilla are less commonly affected. Most cases of intertrigo represent an irritant dermatitis and are not complicated by candidal superinfection. Obesity, excessive sweating, and diabetes are important risk factors for secondary candidal overgrowth. When present, candidal intertrigo presents as erythematous patches with satellite pustules that are often macerated and malodorous. The satellite lesions and maceration also help distinguish candidal intertrigo from the well-defined, drier scaly plaques of inverse psoriasis. Diagnosis of candidal infection is frequently made on clinical grounds alone, but a potassium hydroxide preparation can show spores and pseudohyphae (

). For successful treatment, the area should be kept dry, and use of absorbent powders and zinc oxide barrier paste can be helpful. Topical imidazoles and nystatin are generally effective, but recurrences are common. For widespread infection, oral fluconazole can be added.

Chronic paronychia may also be associated with candidal infection (see Paronychia in Dermatology).

Pityriasis versicolor, or tinea versicolor, is caused by overgrowth of Malassezia furfur, a commensal yeast that lives in hair follicles and the stratum corneum. Pityriasis versicolor is one of the most common chronic superficial fungal infections and is typically found in young adults, particularly in warm, humid environments. It presents as asymptomatic or slightly pruritic oval-to-round, minimally scaly, hyper- or hypopigmented macules that can coalesce into patches on the trunk and upper extremities (

and

). The scale is quite subtle and often becomes visible only after gentle scraping (see

). Affected areas resolve with prolonged hypopigmentation due to azelaic acid production by Malassezia, which inhibits melanin synthesis even after yeast overgrowth has been eradicated.

The diagnosis of pityriasis versicolor can often be made by clinical presentation but may be confirmed by visualization of short rod-shaped hyphae and round yeast (“spaghetti and meatballs”) on microscopic examination of skin scrapings using a potassium hydroxide preparation (see

). Skin scraping is particularly helpful in differentiating active infection from residual hypopigmentation. Topical treatment using ketoconazole 2% shampoo or cream or selenium sulfide suspension is effective. Oral fluconazole or itraconazole can be used for patients with extensive disease or frequent recurrences. Because recurrences are frequent, weekly use of topical treatments can be preventive.

Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus infection that most commonly occurs in children through direct skin-to-skin transmission or contact with contaminated fomites. Atopic dermatitis with impaired skin barrier protection is a predisposing factor. Molluscum in adults is usually seen in the setting of sexual transmission or immunocompromise. Lesions appear as white-to-yellow, smooth, dome-shaped papules with umbilicated centers (

). Lesions may become painful and inflamed (often misdiagnosed as secondary infection) or develop a surrounding eczematous dermatitis due to activation of the host immune response. Immunocompromised patients may develop atypical lesions (see

). Similarly, in patients with AIDS, the lesions tend to be atypical and larger, and most commonly involve the face.

Diagnosis is based on clinical appearance. Molluscum contagiosum is usually self-limited and spontaneously resolves within 2 years. However, patients with severe protracted disease or immunocompromise can be offered treatment with in-office destructive modalities (cryotherapy, curettage, cantharidin) or topical at-home medications (tretinoin, podofilox, berdazimer). All of these treatments are associated with a risk of scarring and dyspigmentation.

For discussion of varicella/herpes zoster, see Varicella-Zoster Virus in Infectious Disease.

Pityriasis rosea is a common viral exanthem that may be related to reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 or 7. The rash begins as a single annular patch or plaque with fine scaling (the herald patch), typically on the trunk, followed by numerous smaller, skin-colored to pink papules and plaques erupting along skin cleavage lines (

). This distribution on the posterior thorax can resemble a “fir tree” pattern. The herald patch is present in more than 50% of patients and usually precedes the smaller plaques by several days up to 2 weeks; initial misdiagnosis as tinea corporis is common. Secondary syphilis should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pityriasis rosea due to its similar appearance, but secondary syphilis typically manifests as palmoplantar lesions and generalized lymphadenopathy.

Treatment is generally not necessary because the rash self-resolves over 4 to 8 weeks. Topical glucocorticoids can be used for temporary relief of pruritus. Oral acyclovir or valacyclovir may be considered in severe cases and has been shown to significantly shorten rash duration if given early during the disease course.

bodies.dmsec24012:
Ectoparasites

There are three types of lice that infest humans: head (Pediculus humanus capitis), body (Pediculus humanus corporis), and pubic (Pthirus pubis) lice. Head lice live on the scalp and attach eggs (nits) to the proximal hair shaft (

). Transmission occurs by close personal contact or by fomites, such as bedding, clothing, or hairbrushes.

Body lice live in the seams of clothing, not on the skin, and are associated with poor hygiene. Excoriations result in crusted papules or linear petechiae on the trunk, neck, and proximal arms. Body lice can transmit serious infections, including trench fever (Bartonella quintana), louse-borne relapsing fever (Borrelia recurrentis), and epidemic typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii).

Pubic lice (crab louse) are typically spread by sexual contact but may attach to other sites such as eyebrows or eyelashes (Pediculosis ciliaris). Screening for other sexually transmitted infections should be considered in patients diagnosed with pubic lice. Treatment for lice is outlined in [Table: Table: Treatment of Ectoparasitic Infestations]

.

Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei) infestation is characterized by intensely pruritic, crusted papules, nodules, and burrows that develop in the interdigital spaces, wrists, ankles, breasts, periumbilical area, and genitals (

). In patients who are immunocompromised, highly contagious crusted scabies occurs, with thick concrete-like scale. Scabies is transmitted by close personal contact, and diagnosis is confirmed by microscopic identification of mites, eggs, or scybala (feces) on a mineral oil preparation of skin scrapings (

). Outbreaks are common in settings such as nursing homes, prisons, and shelters. See [Table: Table: Treatment of Ectoparasitic Infestations]

for treatment. Pruritus may persist for weeks after eradication of scabies and does not necessarily represent resistance or reinfection. “Postscabetic pruritus” can be treated with antihistamines, topical glucocorticoids, and (if severe) oral glucocorticoids.

Bedbugs (Cimex lectularius) live in floorboards, walls, vents, bedding, or furniture and crawl to the host to feed overnight. They do not live on the human body. Bites are characteristically linearly arranged urticarial papules (“breakfast, lunch, and dinner” bites) on exposed skin (

). The lesions are painless but can be intensely pruritic. See [Table: Table: Treatment of Ectoparasitic Infestations]

for treatment.

Flea bites cause itchy pink edematous papules or nodules, typically on exposed skin areas on the lower legs as a dermal hypersensitivity reaction to flea saliva components (

). The cat flea (Ctenocephalides felis) is the most common culprit. There are no characteristic physical findings to distinguish flea bites from mosquito bites or other causes of dermal hypersensitivity reactions (medications, malignancy, idiopathic papular urticaria).

bodies.dmsec24013:
Burns and Frostbite

Burns are the fourth most common type of traumatic injury and can be caused by chemical, thermal, and electrical exposures as well as ultraviolet light. Thermal burns are assessed based on the amount of body surface area (BSA) involvement, depth of burn, and specific area involved. Grading of burns is described in [Table: Table: Classification of Burns by Depth of Injury]

. Estimating the BSA involved is based on the rule of nines: The head and neck represent 9%, each arm is 9%, each leg is 18%, the anterior trunk is 18%, the posterior trunk is 18%, and the genital region is 1% BSA. Treatment of burns is based on the depth of the injury. All burns benefit from first cooling the tissue, although overcooling (i.e., with ice) may lead to additional tissue damage from vasoconstriction; cool water or gauze soaked in cool water is sufficient. Minor superficial or partial-thickness (first-degree or superficial second-degree) burns with a small BSA involvement can be treated with gentle cleansing and application of a sterile dressing with petrolatum daily until healed. Antibiotics are not required for these burns. Wounds prone to developing infection, such as focal deep or full-thickness burns, which are not surgical candidates, or those in areas at high risk for infection, may be best treated with a topical antibiotic in addition to the sterile dressing.

Frostbite is a result of tissue damage caused by exposure to extreme cold. It most commonly affects the distal extremities or facial appendages, including the nose and ears. Frostbite initially presents with coldness and numbness of the affected area. Examination may reveal loss of sensation, blisters, indurated and firm skin, and loss of normal skin color. Although there is overlap, frostbite can be classified into four categories based on depth of injury and clinical findings ( [Table: Table: Classification of Frostbite]

). Evaluation of frostbite includes assessment of coexisting trauma, which may not be immediately evident. Immediate rewarming is the most important treatment. Expert wound care and tetanus prophylaxis are necessary in all patients. Thrombolytic therapy and iloprost, a vasodilatory prostacyclin, may be helpful for associated small-vessel thrombosis and vasoconstriction in select cases. Surgical debridement is often necessary.

bodies.dmsec24014:
Alopecia

Alopecia is the loss of hair and may be characterized as localized or generalized and scarring or nonscarring. Scarring alopecia results in permanent hair loss, whereas nonscarring alopecia is potentially reversible. The diagnosis of most cases can be determined by history and physical examination and confirmed with a punch biopsy. The area of the scalp with active hair loss (not scar) should be chosen for biopsy. Treatment options for alopecia are described in [Table: Table: Management of Selected Types of Alopecia]

.

Alopecia areata is characterized by well-circumscribed round patches of nonscarring acute hair loss. The scalp is smooth and scaleless (

). It affects both women and men, and onset usually occurs before the age of 30 years. An autoimmune etiology due to cytotoxic T-cell–mediated attack of unidentified follicular antigens has been postulated. There is an increased association with atopic dermatitis and autoimmune conditions, such as type 1 diabetes, vitiligo, and autoimmune thyroiditis. In some patients, there is complete loss of scalp hair (alopecia totalis) and all body hair (alopecia universalis). Patients with concurrent atopic dermatitis are at higher risk of developing more widespread or recalcitrant alopecia. Limited disease may undergo spontaneous remission, typically with initial regrowth of fine white hairs; intralesional or topical glucocorticoids can be used to hasten resolution. The oral Janus kinase inhibitors baricitinib, ritlecitinib, and deuruxolitinib are FDA approved for the treatment of severe alopecia areata in adults. Systemic glucocorticoids may be used for refractory disease, but relapse is common after discontinuing therapy. There is no definitive cure for alopecia areata.

Traction alopecia is a result of continuous pulling of the hair from tight styling techniques, such as braids, weaves, or ponytails. Hair loss typically occurs along the frontotemporal scalp and may progress to permanent scarring alopecia with repeated trauma over time. Follicularly based papules and pustules can be seen during the acute phase of traction alopecia; this is known as traction folliculitis. The retention of sparse hairs along the original hairline (“fringe sign”) can help differentiate this type of hair loss from other forms of alopecia (

). Cessation of tight hairstyles is the cornerstone of treatment. Topical and intralesional corticosteroid injections can be used for early traction alopecia before hair loss becomes permanent.

Trichotillomania is a form of traumatic alopecia resulting from compulsive hair-pulling behaviors. Children are most commonly affected, but it also occurs in adults with a female predominance. The condition presents with well-defined, geometrically shaped patches of nonscarring alopecia containing broken hairs of varying lengths. Typical sites of involvement include the scalp (most common), eyelashes, eyebrows, and pubic region. Concomitant obsessive-compulsive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder are common. Treatment is centered around behavior modification.

Androgenic alopecia is an androgen-dependent nonscarring alopecia seen in both men and women and is the most prevalent form of alopecia. Onset begins after puberty and can be gradual. In men, it presents as bitemporal hairline recession followed by vertex baldness (

). In women, it often presents as generalized thinning and is often first recognized as widening of the part width on the crown (

). First-line treatment is topical minoxidil 5% for both men and women. Oral treatment options for androgenic alopecia in men include low-dose minoxidil (off label), finasteride (FDA approved), and dutasteride (off label). Spironolactone, finasteride, dutasteride, and low-dose minoxidil have been used off-label for female-pattern hair loss. All treatments must be continued indefinitely to maintain results.

Telogen effluvium is caused by a traumatic event (emotionally or physiologically) that disrupts the natural hair cycle, resulting in diffuse hair shedding. After a traumatic event, the hairs in the anagen (growing) phase are prematurely converted into the telogen (resting) phase. Hair shedding occurs about 3 months after the inciting event. This is commonly seen in women in the postpartum period. In most cases, telogen effluvium is self-limiting, with resumption of normal hair growth after resolution of the inciting factor.

Discoid lupus erythematous on the scalp can result in localized scarring alopecia. It presents as multiple pink, scaly hypo- and hyperpigmented atrophic plaques (

). Topical/intralesional glucocorticoids and oral antimalarial agents are most commonly used for treatment. Patients should be monitored for progression to systemic lupus erythematosus, which occurs in up to 10% of discoid lupus cases.

Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA) is characterized by hair loss at the crown or vertex of the scalp (

). The cause of CCCA is unknown, but genetics, autoimmunity, and hair styling practices (heat, chemical relaxers, tight hairstyles) are thought to contribute. CCCA is difficult to treat, and early recognition is important. Topical/intralesional glucocorticoids and oral antibiotics such as doxycycline are often used, along with discussion of gentle hairstyling practices.

Lichen planopilaris (LPP) is a diffuse scarring alopecia that most commonly occurs in middle-aged postmenopausal women. The classic presentation is perifollicular erythema and scale involving the vertex or parietal scalp that progresses to loss of follicular ostia (

). Frontal fibrosing alopecia is a specific variant of LPP characterized by bandlike recession of the frontal hairline (

). Patients often report significant tenderness, burning, or itching of the affected areas. Concurrent lichen planus of the skin or nails is seen in about half of LPP cases. There are currently no FDA-approved treatments for this condition. Topical/intralesional/systemic corticosteroids, antimalarials, tetracycline antibiotics, systemic retinoids, 5-α reductase inhibitors, and systemic immunosuppressants have been used with varying success.

Nail Disorders

The nail complex is composed of the nail plate, hyponychium, proximal and lateral nail folds, cuticle, nail bed, and matrix (

). The hyponychium is the skin underneath the distal free edge of the nail plate. It seals the junction between the distal nail plate and the nail bed. The proximal nail fold protects the nail matrix and produces the cuticle. The nail bed is adherent to the bottom of the nail plate.

Nail disorders can be caused by various diseases, infections, trauma, and drugs ( [Table: Table: Nail Findings Associated With Systemic Conditions]

).

Onychomycosis is a dermatophytosis of the nail commonly seen in older adults, especially those with comorbidities such as diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, or immunosuppression. Toenails are most commonly affected. Distal subungual onychomycosis is the most common pattern. The distal nail plate becomes discolored (yellow, white, or brown) and thickened. Under the nail plate, there is an accumulation of subungual debris, resulting in separation of the nail plate from the nail bed (onycholysis) (

). Proximal subungual onychomycosis appears similar except that it starts at the proximal nail fold. This pattern is rare and can be associated with HIV and immunosuppression.

Although onychomycosis is treated mostly for cosmetic purposes, other indications for treatment include discomfort associated with the infected nail, recurrent cellulitis surrounding the infected nail, and the presence of additional risk factors for cellulitis (e.g., diabetes, venous insufficiency, lower extremity edema, immunosuppression). Confirmation of infection with potassium hydroxide preparation, staining with periodic acid-Schiff, or fungal culture should be performed before treatment to rule out psoriasis or traumatic nail changes. Topical antifungal agents are of limited efficacy; oral therapy with terbinafine or itraconazole is more effective.

Paronychia is an infection or irritation of the nail fold. Infection is caused by trauma or chronic maceration leading to an incompetent cuticle. Acute paronychia is painful swelling of the nail fold, most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus. It typically affects only one nail. Chronic paronychia tends to be more insidious and involve multiple fingers. It is a multifactorial condition with several inciting factors, including water, irritants, and possibly Candida species; it is most often seen in those with frequent hand immersion in water or chronic hand eczema. There is tender swelling in the nail folds with missing or dystrophic cuticles (

). Chronic paronychia can also cause ridging of the nail plate.

Treatment of acute paronychia includes the use of warm compresses, incision and drainage, and (in severe cases) oral antibiotics. For chronic paronychia, minimizing inciting factors is key. Treatment includes topical glucocorticoids and antifungal agents to reduce inflammation and minimizing inciting factors.

Nail involvement is seen in approximately half of psoriasis cases and rarely can occur as an isolated finding before the onset of skin or joint disease. The fingernails are more commonly affected than toenails. If the nail matrix is affected, tiny multiple irregularly distributed pits will be seen on the nail plate (

). In cases of nail bed involvement, yellow-red discoloration (“oil stains”) can occur (

). Other findings include nail plate thickening, separation of the nail plate from the nail bed, distal nail plate crumbling, and splinter hemorrhages (

). In some cases, the appearance can mimic onychomycosis. Patients with psoriatic nail involvement are often affected by psoriatic arthritis.

Lichen planus can present with nail involvement in about 10% of cases. Isolated nail disease without skin or mucosal symptoms is extremely rare. Patients develop permanent nail plate dystrophy, thinning, erythronychia (red streaks), and characteristic dorsal pterygium formation (fusion of the proximal nail fold with the nail matrix, resulting in a wing-like ridge) (

).

Onychocryptosis results from the inward growth of the nail plate into the lateral nail fold, causing an inflammatory foreign-body response. Ingrown nails of the great toe are the most common, presenting as painful swelling of the lateral nail fold (

). There may be some weeping granulation tissue.

Conservative treatment for mild to moderate ingrown toenails involves wider shoes, trimming the nail plate straight across, antiseptic application, and inserting a cotton pledget under the nail edge. For severe cases, partial or complete nail avulsion with matricectomy may be necessary.

Melanonychia is a brown-banded pigmentation of the nail plate that can be caused by increased melanin production in the nail matrix, benign hyperplasia, and melanoma (see Melanoma in Dermatology). Longitudinal melanonychia is benign (

) and is most commonly found on dark-skinned patients on multiple nails; it requires no treatment. Findings that may indicate the presence of malignant melanoma include a broad base with tapering at the free edge, disruption of the nail plate, or pigment extending onto the proximal nailfold or hyponychium (Hutchinson sign). Longitudinal, irregular melanonychia on a single nail is also concerning for melanoma. Subungual hemorrhage can have a similar appearance but will demonstrate red-brown globules on closer inspection (

).

Squamous cell carcinoma of the nail unit often presents with pain, swelling, and erythema. It commonly arises in the nail fold and appears as a hyperkeratotic papule or plaque similar to periungual warts (

). Patients presenting with recalcitrant periungual warts that do not respond to conventional therapy should undergo biopsy to rule out squamous cell carcinoma. When present in the nail, squamous cell carcinoma is strongly associated with human papillomavirus infection.

bodies.dmsec24016:
Benign Skin Growths

Seborrheic keratoses are benign pigmented neoplasms of keratinocyte origin that are common in older adults. They are “stuck-on,” waxy papules and plaques that occur anywhere on the body but are most commonly on the trunk and spare the palms, soles, and mucous membranes. Seborrheic keratoses range in size from a few millimeters to several centimeters. Usually they are brown, but they can range in color from tan to black and have irregular borders (

and

). The surface may be mamillated or cerebriform. Seborrheic keratosis can mimic melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma; skin biopsy is not usually necessary but confirms the diagnosis when uncertainty is present. Lesions may become inflamed or irritated and, when symptomatic, can be treated with cryotherapy or shave removal. The sign of Leser–Trélat is the sudden eruption of numerous seborrheic keratosis and is associated with an internal malignancy.

Warts (verruca and condyloma) are caused by human papillomavirus (HPV). HPV infection can occur at any age but is typically seen in children and young adults. Larger, more numerous lesions that are recalcitrant to treatment can be seen in persons who are immunocompromised. There are numerous HPV subtypes, but certain subtypes are associated with specific clinical lesions and are more common at specific sites ( [Table: Table: Human Papillomavirus Subtypes]

).

Verruca vulgaris (common warts) are skin-colored digitate papules with thrombosed capillaries (

). Verruca plana (flat warts) are skin-colored, flat-topped papules (

). Condyloma acuminata (genital warts) are smooth to digitate papules that are skin-colored to tan (

). Verruca plantaris (plantar warts) and verruca palmaris (palmar warts) are exophytic and endophytic papules with thrombosed capillaries manifesting as black dots when the top of the wart is pared down.

Diagnosis is clinical. Warts are usually self-limited; however, in severe cases, including those with a protracted course or in persons who are immunocompromised, destructive treatments can be used. Location of the lesions must be accounted for when selecting treatment, which can be associated with pigment change or scarring. Numerous treatments (salicylic acid, cryotherapy, tricarboxylic acid, cantharidin, podophyllin, fluorouracil, retinoids, laser) focused on destroying infected keratinocytes are available. Other treatments such as imiquimod and intralesional Candida elicit a local immune response to eliminate the warts. Biopsy of large atypical lesions that do not respond to standard treatment should be considered to rule out squamous cell carcinoma.

HPV vaccination prevents cervical and anal carcinoma; it can also serve to decrease anogenital warts. See Human Papillomavirus in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

A callus is a collection of thickened, hardened stratum corneum that presents as a flat papule or plaque at the site of repetitive trauma or under weightbearing pressure points. Sometimes the term corn is used interchangeably with callus; however, corns have more distinct edges, are more rounded, and have a central core that can be soft or hard. Corns are typically seen on the sides or tops of toes. Treatment of calluses and corns involves mechanical or chemical paring with salicylic acid, but removing the pressure from the site is necessary to prevent repeated formation.

Acrochordons (skin tags) are skin-colored or hyperpigmented pedunculated papules (

) most commonly seen on the neck and skin folds in older adults and those with obesity and diabetes mellitus. The presence of numerous lesions, particularly in the setting of obesity and acanthosis nigricans, is associated with insulin resistance. Skin tags also appear with increased frequency during the second trimester of pregnancy and may regress postpartum. Perianal skin tags are common in patients with Crohn disease.

If lesions become necrotic or crusted, they may require removal with cryotherapy or snip excision. They can be of cosmetic concern, especially when numerous.

Dermatofibromas are benign, fibrohistiocytic lesions that are thought to represent scar-like reactions to local trauma (e.g., bug bite, folliculitis). The extremities are most commonly affected, particularly the legs of young women. The lesions appear as tan to brown, discrete papules that often have a slightly darker brown ring encircling a central sclerotic area (

). Dermatofibromas characteristically demonstrate a positive “dimple sign,” wherein the lesion becomes indented upon application of lateral inward pressure (Video: Dimple Sign). Dermatofibromas are usually asymptomatic and do not require treatment.

Melanocytic nevi, commonly referred to as moles, are benign neoplasms composed of melanocytes. They occur anywhere on the body, including the palms, soles, and mucous membranes. Melanocytic nevi can appear early in childhood and increase in number until middle age. They vary in clinical appearance depending on the location of melanocytes within the skin ( [Table: Table: Types of Melanocytic Nevi]

and

). Clinically they can mimic melanoma, and biopsy may be necessary for accurate diagnosis.

Halo nevi are melanocytic nevi with an admixed chronic lymphocytic infiltrate that signifies regression of the nevus. They present as central tan-to-brown macules or papules with a surrounding halo of hypopigmented or depigmented skin (

). They most frequently present on the back of teenagers or young adults. Multiple halo nevi have been associated with melanoma and vitiligo.

Dysplastic (or atypical) nevi are melanocytic nevi that often share the same clinical features as melanoma, including asymmetric shape, irregular borders, multiple colors, and diameter greater than or equal to 6 mm (

). Because dysplastic nevi can display one or more of the identifying characteristics of melanoma, making an accurate clinical diagnosis is often difficult (see Melanoma in Dermatology). Lesions that demonstrate unusual clinical features, change in size/color, spontaneously itch/hurt/bleed, or stand out from other nevi should be biopsied to rule out melanoma. Excisional biopsies that sample the entire lesion, including a 1- to 2-mm border of normal surrounding skin, are the preferred method of sampling.

Dysplastic nevi are an overall marker of increased melanoma risk; however, each dysplastic nevus itself has a low risk of progressing to melanoma and should not be considered as a precursor lesion.

Numerous dysplastic nevi can be seen in familial atypical multiple-mole melanoma (FAMMM) syndrome, also known as dysplastic nevus syndrome. Criteria for this include a history of melanoma in one or more first- or second-degree relatives, the presence of more than 50 nevi, multiple nevi with atypical clinical features, and multiple nevi with atypical histologic features. Variants in the CDKN2A gene encoding the tumor suppressors p14 and p16 have been implicated. Patients with FAMMM are at a significantly higher risk for melanoma and should have regular skin examinations.

Cherry angiomas are benign vascular proliferations that appear as discrete bright red to violaceous papules favoring the trunk in adults (

). Increased age and family history are risk factors. Lesions that are traumatized or bleeding can be treated with shave removal or electrocautery for symptomatic relief.

Pyogenic granulomas, also known as lobular capillary hemangiomas, are fast-growing vascular proliferations that typically occur on the digits, lips, and oral cavity. The classic presentation is a friable, exophytic hemorrhagic papule with a collarette of scale in a child or young adult (

and

). The name is misleading because they are neither pyogenic nor granulomatous. Risk factors include preceding trauma, pregnancy, and certain medications (antiretroviral agents and oral retinoids). Treatment for symptomatic lesions is shave removal, electrocautery, or silver nitrate; however, recurrences are common. Biopsy should be considered for atypical lesions to rule out amelanotic melanoma.

Lipomas are benign neoplasms of mature adipocytes that present as mobile, subcutaneous nodules or tumors. Patients can have a single lesion or multiple, and they are most common on the trunk. Angiolipomas are a variant with a vascular component that is often painful and more common on the upper extremities. When symptomatic or larger, lipomas and angiolipomas can be excised.

Solar lentigines are tan or light brown, 1- to 3-cm well-defined macules or patches on sun-exposed areas of older adults, commonly referred to as “liver spots” (

). They are a marker of sun damage. Ephelides, or “freckles,” are 2- to 5-mm tan macules on sun-exposed areas that appear in childhood and darken with sun exposure. When solar lentigines or ephelides are larger than 1 cm or irregular in shape or color, biopsy should be considered to rule out lentigo maligna, a specific type of melanoma in situ arising on sun-damaged skin (see Melanoma in Oncology).

bodies.dmsec24017:
Premalignant and Malignant Tumors

Skin cancer is a major public health concern, and one in five people in the United States will develop it. Most cases are caused by excessive ultraviolet (UV) light exposure. People of all skin pigmentation can develop skin cancer, but fair-skinned persons are more susceptible to the damaging effects of UV light exposure.

According to the 2023 U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) guidelines, there is currently insufficient evidence to recommend for or against routine skin cancer screening in asymptomatic individuals without a personal or family history of skin cancer. The USPSTF does recommend counseling young adults with fair skin types about minimizing exposure to UV radiation to reduce their risk for skin cancer.

Actinic keratoses are precancerous lesions of the epidermis. Estimates of the risk for progression of actinic keratoses to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) vary from 0.1% to 20%. Although the risk that an individual lesion will develop into an SCC is low, many patients have multiple actinic keratoses, which increases their overall risk. Actinic keratoses present as ill-defined, pink, scaly papules to plaques, mostly in sun-exposed areas (

). Lesions are often easier to diagnose through feel rather than sight alone and characteristically have a gritty or sandpaper-like texture. Patients may report associated tenderness, stinging, or bleeding. Individual lesions can be treated with cryotherapy. In patients with diffuse actinic damage, field treatment with topical medications (5-fluorouracil, imiquimod, diclofenac, ingenol mebutate, tirbanibulin) or photodynamic therapy can be used. Lesions that do not resolve with cryotherapy or are more indurated will require biopsy to rule out SCC.

SCC, the second most common skin cancer, is a malignant neoplasm of keratinocytes. It presents as pink, scaly indurated plaques, papules, or nodules that can ulcerate and bleed (

and

). Risk factors are UV light exposure, ionizing radiation, chemical carcinogens (coal tar and arsenic), viruses (human papillomavirus), xeroderma pigmentosa, photosensitizing medications (voriconazole, hydrochlorothiazide), and immunosuppression (organ transplant). SCC occurs in areas of sun exposure and areas of chronic injury (burn scars, irradiated sites, discoid lupus erythematosus). Compared with lightly pigmented patients, those with skin of darker pigment more often develop SCC in regions with chronic inflammation or scarring.

SCC can be locally invasive and has the potential to metastasize. Histologically, it can range from well-differentiated SCC to the more aggressive poorly differentiated SCC. High-risk features in SCC are tumor diameter greater than 2 cm, tumor thickness greater than 2 mm, poorly differentiated subtypes, perineural invasion, and tumor location on the ear or nonglabrous lip (

).

With SCC in situ (Bowen disease), malignant keratinocytes are confined to the epidermis. It appears as scaly pink and tan plaques with well-defined borders (

).

Surgical excision, including Mohs micrographic surgery, is typically first-line treatment for high-risk SCC given its potentially aggressive behavior and risk for metastasis. If surgery is contraindicated, radiation therapy is an option. In cases of metastasis, immunotherapy can also be considered (see Squamous Cell Carcinoma in Oncology).

Keratoacanthoma is considered to be a low-grade variant of SCC by some and a benign tumor by others. Histologically, it can be indistinguishable from well-differentiated SCC. Keratoacanthoma has a distinct appearance and clinical course. It appears rapidly (within 4 to 6 weeks) as a round pink nodule with a central, keratin-filled crater, giving it a “volcaniform” appearance (

). After rapid growth, some keratoacanthomas may involute; however, treatment is generally recommended due to their unpredictable clinical course and overlap with well-differentiated SCC.

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is a malignant neoplasm arising from the basal layer of the epidermis. It is the most common type of skin cancer overall. Metastasis rarely occurs; however, without treatment, it can cause significant local tissue destruction. The most common causative factor is UV light exposure. Xeroderma pigmentosa also markedly increases risk. There are different histologic subtypes, including superficial, pigmented, sclerotic, and nodular, that result in varying clinical appearance. Patients usually present with a new papule that is bleeding or not healing, often in the setting of other signs of photodamage, such as freckles and lentigines.

Nodular BCC is the most common type of BCC. It presents as a pearly or translucent nodule or papule with arborizing telangiectasias. It may have a central depression or ulceration with a rolled waxy border (

). The term rodent ulcer is used to describe the ulceration. Nodular BCC is most commonly found on the face, especially the nose. Histologically, nodular BCC is a low-risk subtype, whereas micronodular BCC is higher risk. These two subtypes can only be distinguished by histologic assessment.

The superficial type of BCC appears as a pink-red patch with or without scale (

). It may have a slight thread-like pearly rolled border. It can be mistaken for an actinic keratosis; SCC in situ; or a patch of dermatitis, such as psoriasis or nummular dermatitis. Superficial BCC tends to be a persistent solitary patch that does not respond to topical glucocorticoids. Biopsy provides definitive diagnosis.

Pigmented BCC presents as shiny blue-black papules, nodules, or plaques that can appear translucent with blue-black speckles and a rolled border (

).

Sclerotic BCC, which includes morpheaform and infiltrative subtypes, presents as atrophic plaques or papules that can resemble a scar. Although it is the least common BCC, it is a high-risk, aggressive histologic subtype.

The diagnosis of BCC should be confirmed histologically with a shave or punch biopsy. The use of a dermatoscope to identify dermatoscopic patterns of BCCs (such as arborizing vessels) can improve the accuracy of pre-biopsy diagnosis.

Treatment of BCC should be based on patient preference and health status, location of the lesion, histologic subtype, size, and primary versus recurrent nature. Therapeutic options include surgery (standard excision, Mohs micrographic surgery); electrodesiccation and curettage; cryosurgery; topical or intralesional chemotherapy; radiation therapy; and, for metastatic or inoperable lesions, oral hedgehog pathway inhibitors (vismodegib, sonidegib).

Surgical excision is the most commonly used intervention and results in the highest cure rate. Mohs micrographic surgery is a highly specialized surgical technique that combines pathology and surgery for complete margin control and tissue conservation. It is appropriately used for cancers in the head and neck region, those that are large or recurrent, or in areas where tissue-sparing is critical for function.

shows BCC that would likely be managed with Mohs micrographic surgery.

Electrodesiccation and curettage can be used for superficial or nodular BCCs on the trunk. It should not be used for tumors 2 cm or larger, those with poorly defined borders, recurrent or high-risk histologic subtypes (including micronodular or morpheaform), or those appearing in certain anatomic locations (face, scalp, eyelids).

Cryosurgery for BCC differs from that for actinic keratosis; the margin, depth, and temperature must be monitored to achieve cure.

Topical chemotherapy with 5-fluorouracil or imiquimod can be used for superficial BCC; however, its cure rate is user dependent. The treatment course lasts for weeks and results in marked inflammation and irritation. Topical therapies are inappropriate for deep, recurrent, or sclerotic tumors.

Radiation therapy is generally reserved for inoperable tumors or patients who decline surgical treatment.

Follow-up skin examination every 6 to 12 months is recommended because the risk for another BCC is increased. Prevention with sun protection, including routine use of sunscreen with sun protection factor greater than 35, protective clothing (wide-brimmed hats, long sleeves), and avoidance of midday sun (10 am to 2 pm), is highly recommended. See Basal Cell Carcinoma in Oncology for more information.

Melanoma is a malignant neoplasm of the melanocytes. Although it is less common than BCC and SCC, it is histologically aggressive and has a much higher rate of metastasis. It is responsible for most skin cancer deaths. In the United States, the incidence of melanoma is increasing faster than any other cancer. The estimated lifetime risk for melanoma is 1 in 50, and it tends to affect a younger population.

Risk factors include UV light exposure (both chronic and intermittent blistering sunburns), genetics/family history, large number of nevi, dysplastic nevi, xeroderma pigmentosa, and fair skin. Although melanoma can arise from a prior nevus, the majority develop de novo.

In general, the ABCDEs of identifying characteristics can help diagnose melanoma: Asymmetry, irregular Border, multiple Colors, Diameter greater than 6 mm, and Evolution or change over time. Not all melanomas follow all of these characteristics, and biopsy should be considered if there is concern, such as for a lesion that is different from the patient’s other nevi.

There are four major clinical subtypes of melanoma: superficial spreading, lentigo maligna, acral lentiginous, and nodular. Superficial spreading melanoma is the most common type of melanoma (

). It can occur anywhere on the body. In men, the most common location is the back, whereas in women, it is more often found on the legs.

Lentigo maligna is a form of melanoma in situ that is more frequently found on chronically sun-damaged skin of the head and neck. It is usually found in older patients, peaking in the seventh and eighth decades of life. It presents as ill-defined, asymmetric brown or black macules or patches, often reaching a diameter of 5 to 7 cm before invasion (

). The change and darkening of the lesion can be very insidious and may be mistaken for a solar lentigo or seborrheic keratoses.

Acral lentiginous melanoma occurs on the palms, soles, and distal fingers and toes. It is an ill-defined, black macule plaque, and it more frequently occurs in patients with darker skin (

). The average time to diagnosis is 2 years, and it is often diagnosed at an advanced stage.

Nodular melanoma begins in the vertical growth phase and is more aggressive. It grows rapidly and presents as blue-black, smooth, or eroded nodules occurring anywhere on the body (

).

Melanoma of the nail matrix can occur on any nail but is most common on the nail of the thumb and great toe. It commonly presents as longitudinal melanonychia (

). Biopsy of the nail matrix should be performed if pigment extends onto the nail folds (Hutchinson sign). See Melanonychia in Dermatology for more information.

All suspicious pigmented lesions must be biopsied. The preferred biopsy method for a pigmented lesion is an excisional biopsy with a 1- to 2-mm margin to obtain the entire lesion and prevent sampling error. Shave biopsies should be avoided in most pigmented lesions because there is risk for transecting a melanoma and preventing accurate staging of the lesion. A modified shave technique for pigmented lesions is scoop biopsy, in which the deep dermis or subcutaneous tissue is removed to get underneath the lesion. In wide, ill-defined lesions, it may be impossible to remove the entire lesion and thus an incisional biopsy is acceptable. Definitive treatment cannot be determined until histologic confirmation and final staging of the tumor is completed. See Treatment of Melanoma in Oncology for more information.

Poor prognostic factors include male sex, increasing age, increased tumor thickness (Breslow depth), ulceration, increased tumor mitotic rate, and head/neck/trunk locations. Melanomas are staged with the tumor, nodal, and metastasis (TNM) system.
