Inflammatory Dermatoses

Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis, typically presenting with thick, well-demarcated red plaques with overlying silvery scale (

and

). It affects approximately 2% to 4% of the population. The incidence peaks at age 30 to 39 years and again around age 60 years. The severity of psoriasis can range drastically, from a single plaque to an erythrodermic presentation involving more than 90% body surface area (BSA).

Psoriasis has many clinical presentations, the most common being plaque psoriasis, or psoriasis vulgaris. Common sites of involvement are the bilateral extensor surfaces of the extremities (especially the elbow and knees) and the trunk and scalp. Lesions are prone to koebnerization, which is the appearance of new disease on previously unaffected skin at sites of trauma. Other less common subtypes include guttate (commonly seen in pediatric patients following streptococcal infection), erythrodermic (classically due to abrupt discontinuation of systemic steroids), generalized pustular, palmoplantar (frequently seen with pustules as the primary lesion), and inverse variants (often seen without scale in the intertriginous areas) (

). Inverse psoriasis is frequently misdiagnosed because of lack of scale, location (flexural), and resemblance to other conditions such as tinea and intertrigo (see [Table: Table: Differential Diagnosis of Intertriginous Rashes]

).

Psoriasis is a systemic disease. Approximately 30% of patients have concurrent psoriatic arthritis. Psoriasis is also associated with multiple cardiovascular risk factors, including obesity, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and the metabolic syndrome. Patients with severe psoriasis also have a greater risk for cardiovascular disease (the leading cause of death among patients with psoriasis) and chronic kidney disease. All patients should be counseled against tobacco use, particularly because of the elevated risk for cardiovascular disease.

The pharmacologic treatment of psoriasis depends on the severity of the disease and patient goals. Topical glucocorticoids are the mainstay of treatment for localized disease. Lower-potency formulations such as hydrocortisone 2.5% or desonide 0.05% ointment or cream are appropriate for episodic use on thinner-skinned areas of the face, neck, or intertriginous regions; however, thicker plaques and palmoplantar involvement typically require a high-potency class 1 glucocorticoid such as clobetasol propionate 0.05% or betamethasone dipropionate augmented 0.05%. Common practice is to limit continuous topical steroid use to 2 weeks at a time to minimize unwanted skin atrophy and tachyphylaxis. Steroid-sparing topical agents (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus, tapinarof, roflumilast, calcipotriene, tazorotene) can be used as monotherapy for mild disease or for daily maintenance between courses of topical steroids. Vitamin D analogues may also be used, often in combination with topical glucocorticoids.

Systemic therapies, including narrow-band ultraviolet B phototherapy, oral immunosuppressants (e.g., methotrexate, cyclosporine), acitretin, targeted oral small-molecule inhibitors (e.g., apremilast, deucravacitinib), and biologic therapy (tumor necrosis factor inhibitors, interleukin-17 inhibitors, interleukin-12/interleukin-23 inhibitors) should be considered in patients with skin involvement of greater than 10% BSA (severe psoriasis), concurrent psoriatic arthritis, or special site involvement (scalp, groin, palms/soles) and those who did not benefit from standard topical medications. Of note, systemic glucocorticoids are not recommended due to the risk of rebound flares and conversion to erythrodermic or generalized pustular variants.

Treatment goals should be assessed on an individual basis given the heterogeneity of disease burden. For some, this may mean complete clearance of all skin lesions due to psychosocial morbidity, whereas others simply desire symptomatic relief. Patients should be counseled that there is no definitive cure for psoriasis and treatments must be continued indefinitely to maintain response.

Lichen planus is a T-cell–mediated disease classically presenting as pruritic, flat-topped, violaceous papules, often on the flexural surfaces of the extremities (wrists and ankles) and mucous membranes (

). This disease is fairly common, with an incidence of 0.2% to 1% in adults. Other variants include nail, oral erosive, genital, bullous, atrophic, and hypertrophic lichen planus. Mucosal involvement may present as asymptomatic lacy white streaks of the buccal mucosa (Wickham striae) or painful erosions and ulcerations.

Lichen planus tends to resolve over the course of 1 to 2 years, although oral and nail variants are more persistent. Some studies have shown an increased prevalence of hepatitis C virus infection in patients with lichen planus, especially the oral erosive variant. As such, tests for hepatitis C virus infection in patients with lichen planus should be considered. Malignant transformation into squamous cell carcinoma has also been reported, typically in long-standing cases of oral erosive or hypertrophic lichen planus (

).

Potent topical glucocorticoids are effective in most patients. Systemic glucocorticoids, oral retinoids, hydroxychloroquine, immunosuppressants, and phototherapy are reserved for severe cutaneous or persistent oral disease. There are no FDA-approved treatments for lichen planus.

Granuloma annulare is an inflammatory skin condition that most commonly presents as smooth skin-colored to red-brown papules that coalesce into annular plaques. Lesions may be solitary or multiple and favor the skin over joint surfaces such as the dorsal hands, feet, wrist, or ankles. There is no overlying epidermal change or scale. It is typically asymptomatic or slightly tender.

Erythema multiforme (EM) is an immune-mediated condition that can be recognized by its classic targetoid plaques with characteristic histopathologic features. The sharply defined, circinate plaques feature three distinct concentric zones: a dusky necrotic center, a paler inner ring, and a dark red outer ring (

). These plaques typically appear first on the face and distal extremities and may progress to the proximal extremities. The palms and soles may also be involved, and lesions can become vesicular or bullous.

In EM minor, there is absent or minimal mucosal involvement and no systemic symptoms. Pain and pruritus may accompany skin lesions in some patients. Crops of lesions persist for approximately 7 days and resolve without scarring. Most cases of EM minor are caused by infections, with herpes simplex virus (HSV) types 1 and 2 being the most common, followed by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, particularly in children. Drug-induced cases of EM minor are less frequent and typically result from NSAIDs, antiseizure drugs, or sulfonamides. Treatment of EM minor is largely symptomatic with antihistamines and topical glucocorticoids. Antimicrobial therapy is helpful if M. pneumoniae is the trigger of EM.

EM major has the typical skin findings found in EM minor as well as severe mucosal involvement of two or more sites and systemic symptoms. Lesions in the mouth blister and become painful erosions. They are often polycyclic and involve the buccal mucosa and lips, where the edges may suggest the concentric rings of EM. The eyes, nasopharynx, and genitals are less commonly affected. Lesions fully evolve over a period of 72 hours and do not progress to Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN). Fever and malaise may precede rash, and joint pain and swelling have been described. Internal organ involvement, except as related to underlying disorder, is unusual and should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis. Skin biopsy can be helpful when the diagnosis is unclear, and direct immunofluorescence can be used to exclude the possibility of autoimmune bullous disease. EM major must be distinguished from SJS/TEN, which is a distinct clinical entity with a high mortality rate (see [Table: Table: Comparison of EM, SJS, and TEN]

).

In EM major, systemic glucocorticoids are highly effective for decreasing inflammation and pain, even if patients have an infectious trigger, and short courses (3-4 weeks) should be considered early in the disease.

EM can recur, most commonly in the setting of HSV infection. These patients may benefit from suppressive antiviral therapy.

Erythema nodosum is the most common form of panniculitis, or inflammation of the subcutaneous fat. It manifests as ill-defined, tender, erythematous or violaceous, bruise-like nodules, most commonly on the pretibial region bilaterally (

) in young to middle-aged women. Associated fever, malaise, and arthralgias have been reported in approximately half of patients.

Erythema nodosum is a nonspecific reaction to a systemic process. Conditions that are commonly associated with erythema nodosum are listed in [Table: Table: Conditions Associated With Erythema Nodosum]

.

Most cases of erythema nodosum resolve spontaneously over 4 to 6 weeks. Therapy is supportive and includes the use of NSAIDs and compression stockings. Systemic glucocorticoids may be necessary in severe cases.

Erythroderma is defined as diffuse erythema covering 80% to 90% BSA, often with concomitant pruritus, peripheral edema, erosions, scaling, and lymphadenopathy. Exacerbation of a preexisting rash and medication reaction are common causes, although up to 40% of cases are idiopathic ( [Table: Table: Causes of Acute and Chronic Erythroderma]

).

Erythroderma may be acute or chronic in presentation. Acute onset erythroderma is often secondary to drug reactions, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, and autoimmune bullous diseases. In addition, acute disease may occur in flares of atopic dermatitis or psoriasis after injudicious use and abrupt cessation of systemic glucocorticoids.

Alopecia, nail dystrophy, and thickening of the palms and soles are indicative of a long-standing cause, such as cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (

), graft-versus-host disease, psoriasis (

), or pityriasis rubra pilaris.

Complications may result from heat and fluid loss across the inflamed skin. Management of erythroderma involves treating infection and managing fluid and electrolyte imbalance. Emollients will help to restore the skin barrier, and topical glucocorticoids and systemic antihistamines will improve pruritus.

Sweet syndrome, also known as acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, is characterized by tender red to violaceous edematous papules and plaques, most commonly on the face, neck, and upper extremities (

and

). Lesions can also appear vesiculobullous, pustular, or targetoid. In addition to the skin eruption, patients typically have high fevers, leukocytosis with a left shift, elevated inflammatory markers, and muscle or joint pain. Biopsy reveals a dense dermal infiltrate of neutrophils and papillary dermal edema.

Most cases of Sweet syndrome typically develop after an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection or in the setting of hematologic abnormalities, particularly myelodysplastic syndrome or myelodysplastic syndrome transforming to acute myeloid leukemia ( [Table: Table: Conditions Associated With Sweet Syndrome]

). Sweet syndrome has also been associated with solid malignancies and medications (particularly neutrophil-stimulating medications such as granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and all-trans retinoic acid). Rapid response to systemic glucocorticoids is characteristic of this condition.

bodies.ensec24001:
Obesity and Metabolic Syndrome

Obesity, defined as a BMI of 30 or greater, is one of the biggest health problems in the United States and increases risk for mortality, type 2 diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease (CVD), obstructive sleep apnea, mental health disorders, liver disease, and many cancers. Additionally, obesity in midlife is consistently associated with increased risk for dementia. The United States has the highest obesity rate of any developed country, at approximately 40% of the population. An additional 32.0% of the population has overweight (BMI of 25.0-29.9). A lower BMI cutoff (overweight BMI 23.0-24.9, obese BMI ≥25) has been proposed by the World Health Organization for persons from Asia, as this population has been observed to experience obesity complications at a lower BMI compared with other populations.

While BMI has generally been used to define obesity, BMI may over- or underdiagnose obesity. Therefore, experts recommend that excess adiposity be confirmed with an anthropometric measurement, such as waist circumference. Confirmation, however, is not required in patients with a BMI greater than 40. Waist circumference is measured at the top of the iliac crests; measurements above 102 cm (40 in) in men and 88 cm (35 in) in women are correlated with visceral adiposity and increased risk for type 2 diabetes, CVD, and all-cause mortality ( [Table: Table: Classification of Overweight and Obesity by BMI]

).

Obesity can also be classified as preclinical or clinical. Preclinical obesity is excess adiposity with no current evidence of disease related to obesity, and clinical obesity is excess adiposity with obesity-related complications.

Multiple organizations, including the American College of Cardiology, American Heart Association, and The Obesity Society, recommend screening adults annually with BMI and waist circumference measurements. Clinicians should take a comprehensive history for patients with obesity, focusing on diet, activity, and behaviors that affect their weight and health ( [Table: Table: Lifestyle Modifications for Weight Loss]

). A thorough medication history is recommended to identify medications that may contribute to weight gain ( [Table: Table: Medications That Promote Weight Gain and Alternatives]

). Physicians should inquire about symptoms of obesity-related conditions, such as heart disease, obstructive sleep apnea, osteoarthritis, and erectile dysfunction.

Physical examination should include measurements of height, weight, waist circumference, heart rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation. Cardiorespiratory, thyroid, and skin examinations (to detect hirsutism, acanthosis nigricans, and striae) should also be performed. Examining patients with obesity may require adaptations, such as using a scale with an adequate weight limit and using an appropriately sized blood pressure cuff.

Laboratory evaluation should include thyroid testing, lipid levels, and diabetes screening. Because patients with obesity are at risk for comorbid metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease, liver chemistry testing is also recommended (see Metabolic Dysfunction–Associated Steatotic Liver Disease in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease). Other laboratory testing should be based on patient-specific signs, symptoms, and risk factors. Although obesity is associated with higher risk for certain cancers, recommendations for cancer screening are the same as for patients without obesity. See Screening for Cancer in Oncology for general information on screening.

In obesity management, use of nonjudgmental language is important to engage patients and build trust (see Addressing Bias, Stigma, and Discrimination in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Treatment options for obesity include lifestyle modification, pharmacologic therapy, and bariatric surgery.

Lifestyle modification is recommended for all patients with obesity, including reduced calorie intake, increased physical activity, and behavioral therapy. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends offering or referring patients with obesity to intensive, multicomponent behavioral interventions.

Pharmacologic therapy and surgery should be considered for patients who have not had success with weight loss after 3 to 6 months of lifestyle modification. Even small amounts of weight loss are beneficial; loss of 3% to 5% of initial body weight is associated with improvement in glycemic control, blood pressure, lipid levels, and symptoms associated with obesity-related conditions, such as osteoarthritis and sleep apnea.

Readiness to make lifestyle changes should be assessed. Engaging family members and other social supports may increase adherence to lifestyle changes. A weight loss goal can be set, but weight loss can be slow and unpredictable; setting a process goal, such as maintaining healthy habits, should be encouraged.

The calorie intake required to achieve a calorie deficit for a given person varies according to basal energy expenditure. Clinicians can estimate basal energy expenditure in calories using the Harris-Benedict Equation. [Table: Table: Lifestyle Modifications for Weight Loss]

includes typical dietary calorie intake ranges for weight loss.

Patients should gradually consume more guideline-advised healthy foods but choose a diet they can maintain with healthy foods they enjoy (see Nutrition in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Patients should check sugar and sodium contents in products, especially low-fat options. Evidence shows that any diet with a calorie deficit will produce weight loss. However, the physiologic effect of different types of calories likely differs; calories from sugar-sweetened sodas may not be processed in the same way as calories from leafy green vegetables. No type of diet (low carbohydrate, intermittent fasting, Mediterranean) is more effective than another for weight loss, and the choice of diet should account for patient preferences.

Very-low-calorie diets (<800 kcal/d) produce accelerated weight loss but require medical supervision. They should be reserved for situations requiring rapid weight loss, such as preparation for surgery.

Lifestyle interventions should include moderate- to vigorous-intensity physical activity and resistance training (see [Table: Table: Lifestyle Modifications for Weight Loss]

). Exercise has less impact on weight loss than reduced calorie intake does, but long-term commitment to regular physical activity is important for maintaining weight loss and improving cardiovascular health. Gradual progression of activity may be needed for deconditioned patients, and any physical activity is better than none. See Physical Activity in Foundations of Clinical Practice for more information on exercise.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services allow payment for “intensive behavioral weight loss counseling” by primary care providers. The content of this counseling in practice varies widely, as does its effectiveness. Using motivational interviewing techniques is encouraged (see Motivational Interviewing in Foundations of Clinical Practice and Behavioral Counseling in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Several behavioral interventions can help with weight loss and maintenance (see [Table: Table: Lifestyle Modifications for Weight Loss]

).

High-intensity programs (≥14 sessions over the course of ≥6 months) delivered by trained interventionists are associated with successful weight loss. Face-to-face interventions are most effective for weight loss, but electronic or telephone interventions have also had success. Frequent visits for at least 1 year after initial weight loss increase the chances of maintaining weight loss.

Pharmacologic therapy is an option for patients with a BMI of 30 or greater and patients with a BMI of 27 or greater and at least one obesity-associated comorbid condition who have not achieved weight loss goals after 3 to 6 months of lifestyle modification. Weight is typically regained if these medications are stopped; thus, they should be used alongside lifestyle modifications, including adequate protein intake and exercise, which also minimize loss of lean body mass. Pharmacologic therapy is effective, but potential weight loss benefit should be balanced against risk for adverse events and cost. Patients should be monitored regularly, and medications should be stopped if a patient does not have weight reduction after 12 weeks.

The 2022 American Gastroenterological Association guideline recommends using semaglutide, liraglutide, phentermine-topiramate, and naltrexone-bupropion in patients who have not had an adequate response to lifestyle interventions because these medications result in moderate to large weight losses and low risk for harm. Subsequently, in 2023, tirzepatide was approved for weight loss and has been shown to have substantial efficacy. The American Gastroenterological Association recommends against the use of orlistat. Phentermine and diethylpropion can also be considered, although each is only FDA approved for 12 weeks of use. Tirzepatide, semaglutide, and liraglutide are also approved for treating type 2 diabetes; regardless of indication, disruption of treatment for two or more consecutive doses requires restarting at a lower dose to avoid adverse gastrointestinal effects.

Weight loss supplements are not effective according to systematic reviews, and some may be harmful. Patients should be encouraged to discontinue diet supplements.

Guidelines recommend considering surgery for patients with a BMI of 35 or greater, regardless of comorbidities, and in patients with a BMI between 30 and 34.9 who do not achieve weight loss goals or comorbidity improvement with nonsurgical treatments. BMI thresholds are lower in the Asian population, and bariatric surgery should be considered in patients with a BMI of 27.5 or greater. Bariatric surgery reliably achieves weight loss but may also improve diabetes control, blood pressure, and lipid profiles. In severe obesity, bariatric surgery may reduce cardiovascular and overall mortality.

The risks associated with bariatric surgery exceed those associated with nonsurgical treatments. Therefore, candidates for bariatric surgery should be selected carefully. Patients should have acceptable surgical risk, understand the necessity of lifelong dietary and lifestyle measures for sustained weight loss, and be willing to adhere to lifelong follow-up. Candidates should not have psychological or psychiatric conditions that impede adherence to these requirements.

The most commonly performed bariatric surgical procedures are sleeve gastrectomy and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, with sleeve gastrectomy being the most common in the United States. Sleeve gastrectomy is accomplished by excising the part of the stomach along the greater curvature, creating an approximately 85% reduction in size (

). It results in restriction of caloric intake via a smaller stomach and hormonal (GLP-1 and related hormones) appetite suppression. The smaller gastric surface area also results in less production of ghrelin, an appetite stimulant.

Roux-en-Y gastric bypass involves detaching the proximal stomach and creating a small pouch, which is reattached to a limb of the small intestine (

). Weight loss results from decreased calorie intake because of the small size of the stomach pouch, malabsorption as a result of bypassing much of the stomach and proximal small intestines, and appetite suppression resulting from changes in GLP-1 and related hormones.

All bariatric procedures result in loss of excess weight in the short term and up to 70% of excess weight with Roux-en-Y and 60% with sleeve gastrectomy at 2 years. Long-term (5-year) data are less robust but suggest sustained weight loss.

Gastric banding involves placing a silicone fluid–filled band around the proximal stomach, creating a small stomach pouch with subsequent reduction in calorie intake. Gastric banding has greatly fallen in popularity given its modest efficacy and high rates of revision and complications.

More recently, other surgical and nonsurgical procedures have been developed. These include restrictive procedures (endoscopic suturing or stapling in a manner that replicates sleeve gastrectomy), pills that expand in the stomach, devices intended to decrease calorie absorption (duodenal-jejunal liners), and intragastric balloons. Intragastric balloons are typically placed endoscopically and are FDA indicated in patients with a BMI of 30 to 40 who have not benefited from previous attempts at weight loss with lifestyle changes. These techniques are less invasive than bariatric surgery, but they are temporary measures, and their long-term outcomes are unknown.

Rates of 30-day postoperative complications range from 1.3% to 8.7%. Complications include hemorrhage or leakage at the anastomosis (bypass procedures) or staple line (sleeve gastrectomy), venous thromboembolism, and bowel obstruction. Anastomotic leaks usually occur within the first week and may present with nonspecific findings, including low-grade fever, tachycardia, respiratory symptoms, and leukocytosis. Upper gastrointestinal series or contrast-enhanced CT can diagnose a leak; if suspicion is high and imaging is normal or in the setting of hemodynamic instability, surgical exploration is warranted.

Weight should be monitored closely in the early postoperative period. In patients with diabetes, sulfonylureas should be discontinued and insulin should be adjusted. As patients lose weight, frequent reassessment of medications is required. Patients should not become pregnant for 12 to 18 months after bariatric surgery because rapid weight loss can occur.

Long-term postsurgical care focuses on preventing and identifying nutritional deficiencies, managing adherence to lifestyle modifications, and monitoring for behaviors that lead to weight regain. Vitamin D deficiency is universal in patients after bariatric surgery, leading to reduced intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphorus with resultant secondary hyperparathyroidism. Persistent secondary hyperparathyroidism can last for years after bariatric surgery, and annual monitoring of calcium, albumin, parathyroid hormone, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels is recommended. Annual monitoring of vitamin B~12, folate, iron, and ferritin is also often recommended. Other considerations for monitoring include thiamine, vitamin A, zinc, copper, and 24-hour urinary calcium. Weight loss from lifestyle interventions usually plateaus after 6 months. Weight regain is common. Moderate- to vigorous-intensity physical activity of 200 to 300 minutes per week is most important for weight maintenance, but self-weighing and eating a lower-calorie diet should also be emphasized. Frequent contact with a specialist trained in weight management is helpful.

Metabolic syndrome, also referred to as insulin resistance syndrome, is a constellation of risk factors for developing type 2 diabetes and CVD. Risk factors include increased waist circumference, elevated triglyceride level, low HDL cholesterol level, elevated blood pressure, and elevated plasma glucose levels. The diagnostic criteria for metabolic syndrome proposed by the National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel III (with minor modifications by the American Heart Association and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute) are the most widely used ( [Table: Table: Diagnostic Criteria for Metabolic Syndrome]

).

Metabolic syndrome occurs in 20% to 35% of adults in the United States. The presence of a pathophysiologic link between the components of metabolic syndrome is controversial; however, insulin resistance and adipocyte cytokines associated with metabolic syndrome appear to play a central role in inducing inflammatory changes that contribute to CVD. Metabolic syndrome is more common with increased age, possibly related to normal aging physiology where muscle mass is replaced by fat (sarcopenia). Visceral fat also increases with age, contributing to insulin resistance.

Metabolic syndrome treatment focuses on addressing each of the component risk factors. Lifestyle modifications, particularly weight loss and exercise, are the most important treatment interventions.

Routine pharmacologic therapy is not recommended in patients who do not meet treatment criteria for the individual risk factors. In some studies, metformin has been shown to prevent progression to diabetes; however, it is inferior to lifestyle modifications, and its role in treating metabolic syndrome has not been established.

For patients aged 40 to 75 years with a single metabolic risk factor (e.g., increased waist circumference), the Endocrine Society recommends screening for all five risk factors every 3 years with a fasting lipid panel and measurement of fasting plasma glucose levels, blood pressure, and waist circumference. The 10-year CVD risk should be calculated for patients with metabolic syndrome.
