Disorders of Glucose Metabolism

Hyperglycemia results from abnormal carbohydrate metabolism secondary to insulin deficiency, peripheral resistance to insulin action, or both. Hyperglycemia that exceeds the normal glucose range but does not meet the diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus is defined as prediabetes, which increases the risk for developing diabetes.

Screening for type 2 diabetes mellitus in the general adult population is indicated for three reasons:

  • Type 2 diabetes is often preceded by a prolonged asymptomatic hyperglycemic period in which microvascular and macrovascular damage may occur
  • Lifestyle interventions and medications may delay or prevent type 2 diabetes onset in persons with prediabetes
  • Early intensive glucose control and management of hyperlipidemia and hypertension may prevent or reduce the progression of microvascular disease and macrovascular cardiovascular disease (CVD)

The American Diabetes Association (ADA) and the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) offer screening recommendations for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes ( [Table: Table: Screening Guidelines for Prediabetes or Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus]

).

Screening for type 1 diabetes in the general population is not currently recommended. Persons at high risk for type 1 diabetes may be screened for presymptomatic type 1 diabetes by detecting antibodies to insulin, glutamic acid decarboxylase, islet antigen 2, or zinc transporter 8. Persons with multiple islet antibodies should be referred to a specialized center for consideration of therapy to potentially delay the onset of symptomatic type 1 diabetes; teplizumab-mzwv is approved for this indication in selected persons.

Three tests can be used to diagnose diabetes and prediabetes ( [Table: Table: Diagnostic Criteria for Prediabetes and Diabetes Mellitus]

):

  • Hemoglobin A~1c
  • Fasting plasma glucose
  • Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)

Two abnormal diagnostic tests are required to diagnose diabetes in persons without hyperglycemic symptoms. This may be done by performing two different tests on the same sample or by testing two samples taken at different points in time. If the two abnormal screening test results are discordant (e.g., a hemoglobin A~1c result is normal and a fasting plasma glucose measurement is abnormal), the test that is above the diagnostic threshold should be repeated to confirm the diagnosis of diabetes. However, a single random plasma glucose value of 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or greater in the setting of symptomatic hyperglycemia (polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss) is diagnostic of diabetes and does not require further confirmatory testing.

Significant discordance may be seen between measured hemoglobin A~1c and the plasma glucose level in conditions such as pregnancy, hemoglobinopathies, HIV infection, recent transfusion or blood loss, erythropoietin treatment, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, or hemodialysis. In these conditions, diagnostic tests using random plasma glucose (if symptomatic), fasting plasma glucose measurement, or the OGTT are recommended.

The advantages and disadvantages of these tests must be considered when determining the best screening option for a patient ( [Table: Table: Comparison of Screening Tests for Diabetes Mellitus]

).

The underlying insulin abnormality is important for classifying the diabetes type and has treatment implications ( [Table: Table: Classification of Diabetes Mellitus]

).

Type 1 diabetes is characterized by a state of absolute insulin deficiency secondary to the destruction of the insulin-producing β cells in the pancreas and is classically caused by immune-mediated diabetes. Immune-mediated diabetes is the underlying cause of diabetes in 5% to 10% of persons who have been newly diagnosed. The mechanism of the β-cell destruction is multifactorial and likely caused by environmental factors and genetic susceptibilities. Specific HLA alleles demonstrate a strong association with type 1 diabetes. At diagnosis, one or more antibodies directed at the following targets is typically present: glutamic acid decarboxylase, tyrosine phosphatase–related islet antigen 2 (IA-2) and IA-2β, islet cells, insulin, and zinc transporter 8. Glutamic acid decarboxylase should be the first antibody measured; it has a high prevalence (70%) at the time of diagnosis and may remain detectable for years. If it is negative, other antibodies (specifically IA-2 and zinc transporter 8 antibodies) should be tested. The risk for developing type 1 diabetes increases when multiple antibodies are present, and it can develop in persons of any age.

Immune-mediated diabetes varies in presentation depending on the rate of β-cell destruction and ranges from moderate hyperglycemia to life-threatening diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Eventually, β-cell function declines to the point of little to no insulin secretion, as evidenced by a low or undetectable plasma C-peptide level. Immune-mediated diabetes has three stages:

  • Two or more antibodies are present, but patients have normoglycemia and no symptoms.
  • Dysglycemia develops, with plasma glucose values in the prediabetes range, but patients remain asymptomatic. At this stage, the risk for a clinical diagnosis of type 1 diabetes is 60% by 2 years and 75% by 5 years.
  • Patients experience hyperglycemia and symptoms.

Some patients may experience a “honeymoon” phase of type 1 diabetes, where a transient, partial recovery of endogenous insulin secretion occurs. This “honeymoon period” can last several weeks to years. Although patients may require less insulin during this variable timeframe, insulin use should be continued to decrease stress on the remaining functioning β cells and prolong their lifespan. Despite reduced insulin needs, insulin sensitivity may fluctuate, and careful monitoring of blood glucose levels is critical to avoid hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia. Insulin deficiency necessitates lifelong use of insulin therapy.

Patients with type 1 diabetes also have an increased risk for other autoimmune disorders, including celiac disease, thyroid disorders, myasthenia gravis, pernicious anemia, autoimmune hepatitis, vitiligo, and autoimmune primary adrenal insufficiency. Patients should be assessed for autoimmune thyroid disease at diagnosis and periodically thereafter. Adults should also be assessed for celiac disease in the presence of suggestive symptoms or signs, and young adults should be screened for celiac disease soon after diagnosis and periodically thereafter.

Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (also called LADA) is characterized by antibody development leading to β-cell destruction and ultimately to insulin deficiency. Typically, persons with this type of diabetes are not initially insulin dependent and are frequently misclassified as having type 2 diabetes. A slow progression toward insulin dependence occurs over the course of months to years after diagnosis in the setting of positive antibodies.

Idiopathic type 1 diabetes is characterized by variable insulin deficiency due to β-cell destruction in the absence of antibodies. Patients with idiopathic type 1 diabetes may develop episodic DKA.

Hyperglycemia accompanied by insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency defines type 2 diabetes. Insulin resistance is characterized by the ineffective use of insulin by the peripheral cells to process glucose and fatty acids. Plasma glucose levels remain in the normal range as long as the β cells can increase insulin production. Hyperglycemia results from a relative insulin deficiency when the pancreas can no longer produce sufficient insulin to overcome the peripheral resistance.

The pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes is multifactorial, influenced by both genetic and environmental factors. Type 2 diabetes is commonly present in first-degree relatives of persons diagnosed with or at high risk for type 2 diabetes (see [Table: Table: Screening Guidelines for Prediabetes or Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus]

). Obesity increases the risk for insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes development.

Type 2 diabetes typically presents in adulthood, although its incidence in children and adolescents is increasing as the rate of overweight and obesity increases in these populations. Type 2 diabetes has a gradual onset, with most affected persons remaining asymptomatic for several years. Clinical manifestations of insulin resistance, such as acanthosis nigricans (

), may be present on physical examination before diagnosis. At the time of diagnosis, patients may already have microvascular or macrovascular complications.

The development of type 2 diabetes in persons at high risk can be delayed or prevented with lifestyle modifications (i.e., diet, exercise), pharmacologic intervention, or bariatric surgery (see Bariatric Surgery in Endocrinology and Metabolism for more information); more intensive strategies should be considered in those at highest risk, including patients with a BMI of 35 or higher, higher glucose levels, and a history of gestational diabetes. The goal of these interventions is weight loss and the reduction of insulin resistance; additionally, mitigation of cardiovascular risk factors should be pursued.

In the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), lifestyle modifications reduced type 2 diabetes incidence in persons with prediabetes by 58%. Thus, the ADA recommends referral to an intensive lifestyle behavior change program to achieve (and maintain) at least a 7% weight loss and at least 150 min/week of moderate-intensity exercise to reduce the risk for diabetes. For every kilogram of weight loss, the risk for progression is reduced by 16% over 3.2 years. A diet rich in nonstarchy vegetables, lean protein, whole grains, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats, whole fruits, and nuts is recommended. The Endocrine Society suggests empiric vitamin D supplementation for persons with high-risk prediabetes because it may reduce progression to diabetes.

Metformin is currently the preferred pharmacologic agent for diabetes risk reduction; it reduced the incidence of diabetes by 31% in the DPP and has long-term safety data. The ADA recommends considering metformin for type 2 diabetes prevention in persons with prediabetes, particularly those aged 25 to 59 years with a BMI of 35 or greater, those with higher fasting plasma glucose levels (≥110 mg/dL [6.1 mmol/L]), and those with hemoglobin A~1c values of 6% or greater, as well as in patients with a history of gestational diabetes. Additionally, pharmacologic options for weight loss should be considered when appropriate (see Pharmacologic Therapy for Obesity in Endocrinology and Metabolism).

The CDC Diabetes Prevention Recognition Program also endorses technology-assisted modalities via smart phones, web-based applications, or telehealth as effective tools for DPP-based interventions.

Gestational diabetes is defined as hyperglycemia during the second or third trimester in patients without a prepregnancy diagnosis of type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes related to diabetes increase with worsening hyperglycemia. Complications include macrosomia, labor and delivery complications, preeclampsia, neonatal hypoglycemia, spontaneous abortion, and intrauterine fetal demise.

In patients who are planning pregnancy, the ADA recommends screening those with risk factors (see [Table: Table: Screening Guidelines for Prediabetes or Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus]

) and considering testing for all women. Additionally, the ADA recommends standard screening of any pregnant patient with risk factors for diabetes before 15 weeks of gestation and considering testing all patients at the initial prenatal visit. Patients with hyperglycemia identified before 15 weeks’ gestation are classified as having type 2 diabetes (or occasionally type 1 diabetes) rather than gestational diabetes.

If early screening is negative, the ADA recommends screening all pregnant patients for gestational diabetes between 24 and 28 weeks’ gestation. The USPSTF recommends screening at 24 weeks or later. Common screening methods and diagnostic criteria are described in [Table: Table: Diagnostic Criteria for Gestational Diabetes Mellitus]

; in the United States, the 2-step OGTT is the most commonly used approach.

Most patients with gestational diabetes have glucose normalization after pregnancy, but they are at increased risk for developing recurrent gestational diabetes and type 2 diabetes. The ADA recommends a 75-g OGTT 4 to 12 weeks postpartum to confirm resolution of hyperglycemia. If the results of the initial postpartum evaluation are normal, lifelong screening should continue every 1 to 3 years with annual fasting plasma glucose measurement, annual hemoglobin A~1c measurement, or triennial 75-g OGTT (see [Table: Table: Diagnostic Criteria for Prediabetes and Diabetes Mellitus]

).

Other causes of diabetes are listed in [Table: Table: Classification of Diabetes Mellitus]

.

Genetic variants impairing insulin secretion or insulin action are rare forms of diabetes. Maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) is inherited as an autosomal dominant monogenetic variant on different chromosomal loci. MODY has at least 14 known genetic variants. Although insulin action remains normal in MODY, glucose sensing and insulin secretion are altered. Antibodies are typically absent. Patients with MODY present with a clinical course that is frequently atypical of type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Symptom onset typically occurs before age 25 years, and a strong family history of atypical diabetes is often present in patients without obesity. Treatment varies according to the genetic variant; thus, genetic counseling and testing are recommended.

Excess hormone production associated with several endocrinopathies can also impair insulin secretion or action, inducing hyperglycemia.

β-Cell destruction may result from diseases affecting the pancreas, the effects of drugs (including use of immune checkpoint inhibitors and posttransplantation immunosuppressive agents), or viral infections. This type of diabetes may result in impaired insulin production or secretion. In cystic fibrosis, exocrine deficiency leads to malabsorption, whereas endocrine pancreatic insufficiency results in glucose intolerance and cystic fibrosis–related diabetes; insulin is the cornerstone of treatment.

The term “ketosis-prone diabetes” (KPD) incorporates several glycemic syndromes previously known as ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes, type 1B diabetes, and atypical diabetes. KPD presents with episodic DKA resulting from insulin deficiency but has varying periods of insulin dependence and independence. Initially, insulin therapy is required until DKA has resolved and the β cells are no longer impaired by glucose toxicity. Thereafter, patients with preserved β-cell function are often able to discontinue insulin, but treatment with metformin or injectable agents is often required. Plasma C-peptide measurement may be a useful test in these patients, as it is a marker for endogenous insulin production and residual β-cell function.

Effective diabetes management is best achieved through a patient-centered approach with individualized goals and treatment plans that consider patient preferences, lifestyle requirements, comorbidities, safety, and socioeconomic and psychosocial factors. Management should incorporate patient education, blood glucose monitoring (BGM), lifestyle modifications, and pharmacologic therapies.

Diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES) provides patients with the knowledge and skills to perform diabetes-related self-care and develop effective problem-solving strategies. The ADA recommends referral for DSMES at several critical periods in care, including at the time of diagnosis, annually and/or when treatment targets are unmet, when complicating circumstances develop, and at times of life and/or care transitions. Screening for behavioral health concerns and referral to a behavioral health professional if indicated are also recommended to improve engagement in DSMES. DSMES has been shown to improve outcomes, such as hemoglobin A~1c and quality of life. DSMES also reduces costs by decreasing use of acute care and inpatient facilities for diabetes management. The ADA suggests that telehealth and digital interventions can be effective methods for delivering DSMES.

Persons with diabetes should receive age-appropriate vaccinations as recommended by the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices guidelines (see Immunization in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Glycemic control should be assessed with hemoglobin A~1c measurement and/or appropriate continuous glucose metrics at least twice a year. It should be assessed at least every 3 months in persons who are not meeting treatment goals, have frequent or severe hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, or have changing health status. Treatment intensification should not be delayed in patients with uncontrolled diabetes.

Most clinical practice guidelines, including the ADA guidelines, recommend target hemoglobin A~1c thresholds based on a patient’s health status ( [Table: Table: Outpatient Glycemic Goals for Adults With Diabetes Mellitus]

). The ADA recommends a goal hemoglobin A~1c of less than 7% without significant hypoglycemia for healthy nonpregnant adults; less stringent glycemic goals may be appropriate for patients with limited life expectancy. The ADA recommends deintensifying therapy, within individualized glycemic goals, in patients who are at high risk for hypoglycemia or for whom the harms or burdens of treatment may outweigh the benefits.

The American College of Physicians (ACP) recommends a hemoglobin A~1c level between 7% and 8% in most patients with type 2 diabetes; clinicians should consider deintensifying pharmacologic therapy in patients who achieve hemoglobin A~1c levels less than 6.5%. The rationale for these targets is based on evidence that collectively demonstrates that treating to targets less than 7% compared with targets around 8% has not been shown to reduce death or macrovascular events over the course of 5 to 10 years of treatment but may instead result in substantial harms. More stringent targets may be appropriate for patients who have a long life expectancy and are interested in more intensive glycemic control with pharmacologic therapy despite the risk for harms, including but not limited to hypoglycemia, patient burden, and pharmacologic costs. The ACP also recommends avoiding a specific target hemoglobin A~1c level in patients with a life expectancy less than 10 years at an advanced age (80 years or older), residence in a nursing home, or chronic medical conditions because the harms outweigh the benefits.

BGM is recommended for patients with diabetes depending on patient circumstances, preferences, and treatment. BGM should be conducted to safely aim for glycemic targets; the main two options are fingerstick BGM and continuous glucose monitoring (CGM).

Fingerstick Blood Glucose Monitoring

Patients who are taking insulin and using fingerstick BGM may be instructed to check their blood glucose levels based on their insulin regimen. Glycemic goals vary according to individual patient characteristics (see [Table: Table: Outpatient Glycemic Goals for Adults With Diabetes Mellitus]

). Specific regimens for BGM are individualized and may include the following time points:

  • When fasting
  • Before or after meals
  • At bedtime
  • Before, during, and after exercise
  • When hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia is suspected
  • After treating hypoglycemia until normoglycemia is achieved
  • Before and during critical tasks, such as driving or operating machinery

BGM can be considered in motivated patients with nonintensive insulin regimens (basal insulin). Although the optimal testing frequency has not been determined, monitoring fasting glucose levels to inform dose adjustments results in a lower hemoglobin A~1c. In patients with type 2 diabetes not using insulin, routine BGM may not help reduce hemoglobin A~1c; however, it may be helpful when altering nutrition plans, exercise, or medications.

The average finger-stick blood glucose level generally correlates with the hemoglobin A~1c level ( [Table: Table: Hemoglobin A~1c Value and Estimated Plasma Glucose Level]

). Discordant results should prompt evaluation for factors that could alter erythrocyte structure or survival (see [Table: Table: Comparison of Screening Tests for Diabetes Mellitus]

).

Continuous Glucose Monitoring

Another BGM option is a CGM system. This technology reflects glycemic patterns in real time and can alert the user to retrospective and current glucose trends (Video: Continuous Glucose Monitor Insertion and Removal, Video: Continuous Glucose Monitor Reports). The goals of using a CGM system are to improve diabetes care by lowering hemoglobin A~1c and avoiding hypoglycemia, which is critical for those with hypoglycemia unawareness.

The ADA recommends real-time CGM or intermittently scanned CGM for diabetes management in adults requiring any type of insulin therapy.

Real-time CGM devices should be used as close to daily as possible for maximum benefit. Intermittently scanned CGM devices should be scanned at least every 8 hours. Data demonstrate improved glycemic control with longer duration of CGM system use.

Glycemic control is assessed by evaluating a patient’s time in range, typically with a goal of having a blood glucose level between 70 and 180 mg/dL (3.9-10.0 mmol/L) more than 70% of the time. The glucose management indicator on most reports reflects an estimate of the projected hemoglobin A~1c based on the most recent glycemic averages and can often serve as a surrogate value for hemoglobin A~1c. Additionally, the time in range and estimated hemoglobin A~1c correlate with the risk for microvascular complications, allowing for a more personalized treatment plan. CGM is also useful for detecting patterns in glycemic control over time and for identifying periods of hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia not otherwise detected by intermittent fingerstick BGM.

Some substances can cause sensor-associated CGM errors in measurement, including acetaminophen, hydroxyurea, high doses of vitamin C, alcohol, tetracycline, and mannitol.

Lifestyle changes are essential for the long-term management of diabetes and prevention of complications. Although these changes should be individualized, diet and physical activity are critical components for patients with type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

Nutrition therapy with a registered dietitian provides individualized diabetes-specific education to promote healthy diet choices to achieve glycemic and weight management goals. It has also been associated with reductions in hemoglobin A~1c in patients with type 1 and type 2 diabetes. The ADA recommends individualized meal plans that are healthy and evidence based. Evidence suggests that a decrease in overall carbohydrate intake results in improved glycemic control. The ADA recommends that when carbohydrates are consumed, nutrient-dense carbohydrate sources that are high in fiber (≥14 g fiber/1000 kcal) and minimally processed should be emphasized; eating plans should focus on nonstarchy vegetables, whole fruits, legumes, lean proteins, nuts and seeds, whole grains, and low-fat dairy products. Red meat, sugar-sweetened beverages, sweets, and processed foods should be minimized.

Physical activity recommendations include moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic activity for 150 minutes/week, vigorous-intensity aerobic activity for 75 minutes/week, or a combination of both. This level of activity has been shown to reduce hemoglobin A~1c, decrease weight, improve well-being, and improve CVD risk factors. Resistance training is recommended two or more times per week. Older adults with diabetes should engage in flexibility and balance training two to three times per week, if possible. Prolonged sedentary behavior should be interrupted at 30-minute intervals with light activity or standing.

Weight management should be considered a treatment goal, and providers should facilitate positive health behaviors to improve outcomes. In patients with overweight and obesity with type 2 diabetes, a goal of 3% to 7% weight loss is recommended and has been shown to improve glycemic control, although weight loss of 10% or more may be necessary to achieve the desired results. Interventions should include counseling with a focus on nutrition changes, physical activity, and behavioral strategies to achieve a calorie deficit of 500 to 750 kcal/d.

Weight loss medications (see Pharmacologic Therapy for Obesity in Endocrinology and Metabolism) may be considered as an adjunct to lifestyle changes in selected patients. Bariatric surgery should be considered to manage weight and glucose levels in persons with diabetes who have a BMI of 30 or greater (or ≥27.5 in Asian Americans) (see Bariatric Surgery in Endocrinology and Metabolism).

Smoking discontinuation is one of the most important aspects of treatment in patients with diabetes who smoke (see Tobacco in Interdisciplinary Medicine). Sleep disorders and mood disturbances should also be assessed and managed.

Because of β-cell destruction and subsequent insulin deficiency, persons with type 1 diabetes require lifelong insulin therapy. Ideally, an intensive insulin regimen should be prescribed, which includes multiple daily doses of insulin (MDI) to mimic the physiologic action of the pancreas. The insulin regimen should include basal coverage to maintain glycemic control while fasting and between meals, prandial coverage, and supplemental insulin to correct hyperglycemia ( [Table: Table: Pharmacokinetic Properties of Insulin Products]

). This coverage can be accomplished with subcutaneous insulin injections, inhaled insulin preparations, or continuous subcutaneous insulin infusions (CSII) with an insulin pump, such as a patch pump (Video: Insulin Patch Pump Filling and Insertion) or tubing pump (Video: Insulin Tubing Pump Insertion and Removal).

Initial total daily insulin dosing typically ranges from 0.4 to 1.0 U/kg/day in patients with type 1 diabetes. Basal insulin typically encompasses approximately 50% of the total daily dose of insulin, with prandial insulin covering the remaining 50%.

The timing and mode of prandial insulin delivery varies on the basis of patient needs, preferences, and dietary habits. MDI prandial dosing can be accomplished with fixed dosing, carbohydrate counting, or modified carbohydrate counting. Generally, 1 unit of insulin covers 10 to 20 g of carbohydrates consumed. A modified carbohydrate counting method can be used when the grams of carbohydrates consumed cannot be accurately counted. With this method, regular or analogue insulin doses can be adjusted by 50% based on the portion of food consumed. For example, the dose for the size of the meal would be as follows: small (50%), regular (100%), large (150%).

MDI should also incorporate supplemental insulin to correct hyperglycemia. A common method for calculating the correction dose of insulin is to give an additional 1 unit of regular or analogue insulin at the time of the premeal measurement for every blood glucose value 50 mg/dL (2.8 mmol/L) above the target glucose value in insulin-sensitive persons and 1 unit for every 25 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) in insulin-resistant persons.

Premixed insulin formulations combine intermediate- or long-acting basal insulin and rapid- or short-acting insulin in fixed concentrations. These formulations are typically administered twice daily and should be considered for patients who are unable or unwilling to perform more frequent daily insulin injections. Premixed formulations are nonphysiologic and can increase glycemic excursions, including hypoglycemia.

Inhaled insulin is a rapid-acting formulation for prandial dosing. The availability of inhaled insulin in cartridges with preset doses of insulin (4, 8, and 12 units) limits the flexibility of insulin dosing. Pulmonary function should be assessed at baseline and monitored because lung function may decline with use of inhaled insulin.

CSII pump therapy provides continuous delivery of basal insulin and uses a bolus calculator, programmed to achieve individual glycemic goals, to calculate prandial and bolus correction doses. Automated insulin delivery systems (e.g., CGM, insulin pump, and algorithm) have become an integral part of type 1 diabetes management; the algorithms used by these systems adjust insulin delivery based on real-time glucose levels, residual insulin action, and meal and exercise data. The ADA and the Endocrine Society recommend considering automated insulin delivery systems for all adults with type 1 diabetes. The choice of device should depend on the specific patient’s circumstances, preferences, and needs.

Hypoglycemia and weight gain are risks associated with insulin use. The risk for hypoglycemia is lower with analogue insulin compared with regular insulin because of a shorter duration of action. Hypoglycemia caused by insulin stacking occurs when insulin dosing is too frequent and overlaps with the duration of action of a previous insulin injection. This effect can be avoided by allowing at least 3 to 4 hours between sequential injections of analogue insulin.

An adjunctive therapy approved for use with insulin in type 1 diabetes is pramlintide, an amylin analogue. Pramlintide can lead to improved glycemic control, decreased insulin doses, and weight loss through delayed gastric emptying, increased satiety, and decreased glucagon secretion.

Most patients with type 2 diabetes will require pharmacotherapy. A number of therapeutic options are available, and this section describes characteristics of commonly used medications. Cardiovascular, kidney, and weight effects of these medications are summarized in [Table: Table: Glucose-Lowering Agents and Their Effects on Various Outcomes]

. Specific recommendations for pharmacotherapy are discussed in the following section, Pharmacologic Therapy for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus in Endocrinology and Metabolism.

Metformin decreases hepatic glucose production and increases insulin-mediated uptake of glucose in muscles. It has been a recommended first-line oral agent for newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes because of its known effectiveness and inability to cause hypoglycemia.

An estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) greater than 45 mL/min/1.73 m^2 is recommended for metformin initiation. Clinicians should assess benefits and risks of continuing therapy in patients whose eGFR decreases to less than 45 mL/min/1.73 m^2 during therapy. Metformin is contraindicated at an eGFR of less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m^2. Metformin should be held in situations that may result in kidney dysfunction, such as vomiting or diarrhea.

Gastrointestinal adverse effects are common and may be reduced by slowly titrating the dosage, administering with food, or using an extended-release formulation. Lactic acidosis is a rare risk associated with metformin use; risk for this effect is increased by heart failure requiring pharmacologic treatment, liver dysfunction, and kidney disease. Metformin causes reduced intestinal absorption of vitamin B~12 in up to 30% of patients, and 5% to 10% of patients develop vitamin B~12 deficiency, which can lead to anemia and neurologic abnormalities; annual serum vitamin B~12 measurement is recommended for patients who have been taking metformin for more than 4 years.

Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) (e.g., liraglutide, dulaglutide, semaglutide, exenatide) act through several mechanisms, including increased insulin secretion in response to hyperglycemia, slowed gastric emptying, and reduced glucagon secretion. Patients typically experience early satiety, which can contribute to overall reduced caloric intake and weight loss. With one exception (oral semaglutide), the GLP-1 RAs are injectable medications, typically taken once weekly. GLP-1 RAs have a low risk for hypoglycemia because of the glucose-dependent release of insulin. Certain GLP-1 RAs have demonstrated significant risk reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events, stroke, all-cause mortality, and kidney outcomes ( [Table: Table: Glucose-Lowering Agents and Their Effects on Various Outcomes]

). GLP-1 RAs have also shown potential in reducing liver fat content, particularly in persons with type 2 diabetes and metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).

The most common adverse effects are gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., diarrhea, nausea, vomiting) and injection site reactions. Adverse effects can be minimized with gradual dose escalation. The risk for hypoglycemia increases when used in combination with insulin or sulfonylureas. When GLP-1 RAs are used, the label of each agent should be referred to for renal dose adjustments.

GLP-1 RAs are associated with C-cell proliferation in thyroid cells; therefore, a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 is a contraindication to GLP-1 RA use. Pancreatitis has been described with these agents, and they are typically avoided in patients with a history of pancreatitis. An increased risk for gallbladder and biliary diseases has also been reported with GLP-1 RAs. Because these agents slow gastric emptying, gastroparesis is a relative contraindication to the use of GLP-1 RAs, and the dosage should be reduced or the medication discontinued if gastroparesis is exacerbated.

Tirzepatide is a novel synthetic peptide and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1 RA. It increases insulin release in a glucose-dependent fashion similar to GLP-1 RAs. The GIP incretin also stimulates insulin secretion and inhibits apoptosis of pancreatic β cells. Tirzepatide can significantly improve glycemic control and lead to greater weight reduction in a dose-dependent manner. It is administered as a once-weekly injection. Studies to evaluate atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and diabetic kidney disease (DKD) outcomes are ongoing. Tirzepatide may also have potential benefit in reducing metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH).

The adverse effect profile is similar to that of GLP-1 RAs. Similarly, tirzepatide should be avoided in patients with a personal or family history of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 or medullary thyroid carcinoma, and it is typically avoided in patients with a history of pancreatitis.

Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors (e.g., bexagliflozin, canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, ertugliflozin) are oral medications that promote renal glucose excretion by blocking the SGLT2 receptor in the proximal tubule. The increased glucosuria effectively lowers plasma glucose independent of insulin. SGLT2 inhibitors offer modest weight loss, in part because of their diuretic effects. Several trials have demonstrated significant ASCVD and DKD benefits of certain SGLT2 inhibitors (see [Table: Table: Glucose-Lowering Agents and Their Effects on Various Outcomes]

), with reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events, hospitalizations for heart failure, and end-stage kidney disease progression.

As a class, SGLT2 inhibitors have a low risk for hypoglycemia, but the risk increases when they are combined with insulin or sulfonylureas. Other potential adverse effects include hypotension, decreased volume status, and increased genitourinary infections, including urinary tract infections and vulvovaginal candidiasis. Perineal necrotizing fasciitis has been rarely reported. Lower limb amputation and extremity fractures have been reported with the use of canagliflozin and bexagliflozin, and consideration of risk factors for either is important before initiating this agent. Bladder cancer has been reported in patients using dapagliflozin. Both canagliflozin and dapagliflozin have been associated with acute kidney injury in postmarketing reports.

SGLT2 inhibitors can cause euglycemic DKA because of inhibited glucose reabsorption leading to decreased insulin secretion, increased glucagon secretion, lipolysis, and, ultimately, ketogenesis. Euglycemic DKA is more likely to occur in those with decreased oral intake, vomiting, dehydration, infection, or major illness. Clinicians should have a high level of suspicion for euglycemic DKA in patients presenting with nausea, vomiting, or malaise while taking SGLT2 inhibitors.

When SGLT2 inhibitors are used, the label of each agent should be referenced for renal dose adjustments. SGLT2 inhibitors should not be initiated in patients with an eGFR less than 20 mL/min/1.73 m^2.

The mechanism of action of dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors (e.g., sitagliptin, saxagliptin, alogliptin, linagliptin) includes a glucose-dependent increase in insulin secretion and glucose-dependent suppression of glucagon secretion. DPP-4 inhibitors offer modest improvements in glycemic control and have a low risk for hypoglycemia. They are weight neutral and do not provide ASCVD or DKD benefits.

This class of medications is associated with possible risk for pancreatitis, arthritis, and dermatologic reactions. Saxagliptin should not be used in patients with heart failure because of potential exacerbation of myocardial dysfunction. Linagliptin is the only drug in this class that does not need to be renally dosed.

Thiazolidinediones (e.g., pioglitazone) increase peripheral glucose uptake and increase insulin sensitivity in skeletal and adipose tissues. They have a low risk for hypoglycemia. Pioglitazone may reduce CVD and triglycerides. Pioglitazone may also reduce the risk for recurrent stroke or myocardial infarction in patients with a history of stroke and has shown potential benefit in patients with MASH.

Thiazolidinediones typically cause weight gain, in part owing to fluid retention, and they should be used with caution in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Thiazolidinediones have a boxed warning in patients with heart failure. They are associated with increased risk for fractures and a possible increased risk for bladder cancer.

Sulfonylureas (e.g., glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride) stimulate β-cell insulin secretion from the pancreas. Although sulfonylureas initially are effective and inexpensive, gradual β-cell loss causes them to lose their efficacy. They pose a higher risk for hypoglycemia compared with other agents, especially in patients with reduced oral intake. They also cause weight gain, potentially contributing to further insulin resistance. Sulfonylureas should be used with caution in patients with kidney or liver impairment.

Meglitinides (e.g., repaglinide, nateglinide) stimulate insulin release and may be used similarly to sulfonylureas, with similar clinical efficacy. Adverse effects include hypoglycemia and weight gain. Frequent dosing before each meal is required. Nateglinide should be used with caution in patients with kidney or liver impairment; repaglinide should be used with caution in patients with liver disease but can be used in patients with kidney impairment.

Insulin is the mainstay of therapy for type 1 diabetes but may be required by certain patients with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes. Insulin achieves glycemic control through several mechanisms of action, including decreasing hepatic glucose production, increasing peripheral glucose uptake, and suppressing ketogenesis. The available insulin formulations and their action profiles are summarized in [Table: Table: Pharmacokinetic Properties of Insulin Products]

.

Other less-used agents include α-glucosidase inhibitors, amylin mimetics, bile acid sequestrants, and dopamine-2 receptor agonists. They are typically not well tolerated and offer only modest glycemic benefits.

A patient-centered approach is recommended when choosing pharmacologic therapy. In addition to glucose-lowering efficacy, clinicians should consider effects on mortality, cardiovascular and kidney comorbidities, and weight when considering a medication (see [Table: Table: Glucose-Lowering Agents and Their Effects on Various Outcomes]

). Other important considerations include hypoglycemia risk, adverse effects, cost, and patient values and preferences.

The American College of Physicians (ACP) recommends metformin, in addition to lifestyle modifications, as first-line therapy in managing type 2 diabetes for most patients. When selecting additional therapy in the setting of inadequate glycemic control, the ACP recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 RA to reduce the risk for all-cause mortality and major adverse cardiovascular events. The presence of comorbidities may also inform the choice of additional treatment. SGLT2 inhibitors are used to reduce the risk for progression of chronic kidney disease and hospitalization due to heart failure, and these medications should be prioritized in patients with CKD or heart failure. Similarly, GLP-1 RAs reduce the risk for stroke and have positive effects on weight loss, and this therapeutic class should be prioritized in patients with an increased risk for stroke or for whom weight loss is a treatment goal. The ACP recommends against adding a DPP-4 inhibitor to metformin and lifestyle modifications, as there is no evidence of benefit in reducing all-cause mortality, cardiovascular events, heart failure hospitalization, kidney disease progression, or severe hypoglycemia.

In contrast, the ADA’s approach to type 2 diabetes management is outlined in

. Selection of initial and subsequent pharmacologic agents is largely based on patient comorbidities:

  • In patients with established ASCVD or high risk for ASCVD, the ADA recommends a GLP-1 RA and/or an SGLT2 inhibitor, as these agents have shown benefits in cardiovascular risk reduction.
  • In patients with heart failure, an SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended to reduce the risk for heart failure hospitalizations.
  • In patients with CKD and an eGFR of 20 mL/min/1.73 m^2 or greater, an SGLT2 inhibitor or a GLP-1 RA is recommended to reduce CKD progression and CV events.
  • In patients with MASLD and overweight or obesity, a GLP-1 RA or dual GIP/GLP-1 RA should be considered as an adjunct to lifestyle changes for weight loss. In patients with type 2 diabetes and biopsy-proven MASH or high risk for fibrosis, pioglitazone, a GLP-1 RA, or a dual GIP/GLP-1 RA is the preferred agent for glycemic management, as these agents have potential benefit in MASH.

In patients with ASCVD, heart failure, or CKD, recommended use of a GLP-1 RA or SGLT2 inhibitor by the ADA is independent of hemoglobin A~1c or background metformin use; this is in contrast to the ACP guidelines, which suggest metformin as the primary therapy in most patients. For patients without these comorbidities, medication selection should consider risk for hypoglycemia, effect on weight and other metabolic comorbidities, and cost. Additional agents should be added in stepwise progression if glycemic goals are not met, again considering the clinical characteristics of the patient (see

and [Table: Table: Glucose-Lowering Agents and Their Effects on Various Outcomes]

). Concomitant use of GLP-1 RAs or dual GIP/GLP-1 RAs with DPP-4 inhibitors does not provide additional benefit and should be avoided.

In most patients who need the greater glucose-lowering effect of an injectable medication, the ADA recommends a GLP-1 RA or dual GIP/GLP-1 RA rather than insulin. However, patients with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes may require insulin therapy to achieve glycemic targets. If insulin is used, the ADA recommends combination therapy with a GLP-1 RA or a dual GIP/GLP-1 RA for greater efficacy and durability of treatment effect. Algorithms provide guidance on the initiation and dosing of basal and prandial insulin regimens ( [Table: Table: Insulin Dosing Algorithms for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus]

). The ADA recommends initiation of insulin therapy regardless of the use of other glucose-lowering therapies in the setting of symptomatic hyperglycemia (polydipsia, polyuria), ongoing catabolism (weight loss), a hemoglobin A~1c of greater than 10%, or a plasma glucose level of 300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L) or higher. The American Association of Clinical Endocrinology recommends initiating insulin therapy with other agents if the initial hemoglobin A~1c is more than 9% in a symptomatic patient. After optimizing the basal insulin dose, prandial insulin should be added before the largest meal if hyperglycemia persists. A basal-bolus insulin regimen, with prandial insulin before two or more meals, should be used for continued hyperglycemia.

Ultra-long-acting basal analogue insulins may be advantageous compared with long-acting basal analogue insulins because of their prolonged action profile (>24 hours), peakless insulin delivery, and decreased variability in action between and within individuals. The pharmacodynamic profile may decrease hypoglycemia in patients at high risk, improve glycemic fluctuations, and allow for flexibility in dosing beyond 24-hour time periods.

In patients with type 2 diabetes not at glycemic goal despite adherence to glucose monitoring and multiple treatment modalities, CSII may be considered.

Pharmacologic therapy should be prescribed for patients with gestational diabetes to improve perinatal outcomes if lifestyle interventions do not achieve glycemic targets. Insulin is the recommended therapy. Although metformin or sulfonylurea therapy may be considered, both therapies cross the placenta, and no long-term safety data are available for their use during pregnancy. Additionally, sulfonylurea therapy has been associated with higher rates of neonatal macrosomia and hypoglycemia.

Several drugs can induce hyperglycemia through multiple mechanisms ( [Table: Table: Drug-Induced Hyperglycemia and Diabetes Mellitus]

). Persons at risk for hyperglycemia and diabetes mellitus development because of medications should be monitored periodically.

Tight inpatient glycemic control (80-110 mg/dL [4.4-6.1 mmol/L]) is not consistently associated with improved outcomes and may increase mortality. As a result, current inpatient glycemic goals strive to avoid complications from severe hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, such as electrolyte abnormalities and dehydration.

All inpatients with a known history of diabetes mellitus or hyperglycemia should have a hemoglobin A~1c test if one has not been performed within the past 3 months. Clinical status changes, especially in kidney function, may increase the risk for adverse events associated with noninsulin therapies. Similarly, several factors may predispose inpatients to hypoglycemia, including altered mental status, fasting (expected or unexpected), illness, insulin–meal timing mismatch, poor oral intake, and alterations in hyperglycemia-inducing therapies. Treatment with insulin is thus preferred for inpatient management of hyperglycemia 180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L) and higher. The ADA recommends a target glucose level between 140 and 180 mg/dL (7.8-10.0 mmol/L) for most critically ill patients, whereas the Society of Critical Care Medicine suggests a slightly higher glucose range of 140 to 200 mg/dL (7.8-11.1 mmol/L) to reduce the risk for hypoglycemia. In noncritically ill hospitalized patients, the ADA and the Endocrine Society suggest a target glucose level between 100 and 180 mg/dL (5.6-10.0 mmol/L). In contrast, the American College of Physicians does not recommend glucose values less than 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) because of increased hypoglycemia risk.

In critically ill patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, intravenous insulin therapy is recommended. Intravenous insulin dose adjustments should be based on a validated algorithm that incorporates point-of-care (POC) monitoring every 30 minutes to 2 hours.

For noncritically ill patients, subcutaneous insulin is appropriate. Persons with type 1 diabetes require continuous insulin therapy, and basal insulin must be provided to avoid DKA. Persons with type 2 diabetes with glucose values of 180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L) or higher should also receive insulin therapy. For these patients, continuation of outpatient oral or noninsulin injectable agents is typically not recommended because of the potential for hemodynamic or nutritional changes. As a patient nears hospital discharge with stable nutritional status and hemodynamics, reinitiation of these agents may be considered if organ function has returned to baseline.

If the patient is eating, ideal insulin management is a basal-bolus regimen with prandial coverage and correction boluses for premeal hyperglycemia. POC measurements and prandial insulin injections should occur before meal consumption. Postprandial insulin administration may be appropriate to allow for dose reduction for patients with decreased oral intake or those with delayed gastric emptying. Overnight POC measurements are warranted if undetected hypoglycemia is a concern; otherwise, overnight glucose checks should be avoided because of sleep disruption. The sole use of correction insulin (termed “sliding-scale insulin”) is not recommended because it is a reactive, nonphysiologic approach that leads to large glucose fluctuations. In noncritically ill hospitalized adults with insulin-treated diabetes who are at high risk for hypoglycemia, continuing their personal CGM with confirmatory POC BGM for insulin dosing adjustments is preferred to POC blood glucose testing alone if CGM is available.

Continuation of outpatient CSII therapy may be appropriate for noncritically ill patients who have an intact level of consciousness and can appropriately adjust pump settings in hospitals with personnel who have expertise in insulin pump therapy. If a hospitalized patient becomes unable to safely manage CSII therapy, it should be discontinued and replaced with either a subcutaneous insulin regimen or intravenous insulin.

Stress associated with acute illness, enteral and parenteral nutrition, and hyperglycemia-inducing medications in the inpatient setting may induce glucose abnormalities in persons without diabetes.

Hyperglycemia management should follow the same guidelines as in hospitalized patients with diabetes.

It is important to recognize that inpatient hyperglycemia (glucose level >140 mg/dL [7.8 mmol/L]) may occur in the setting of previously unrecognized diabetes. An inpatient hemoglobin A~1c measurement of 6.5% or higher is indicative of glucose abnormalities before the hospitalization, and these patients require follow-up for diagnosis of possible diabetes.

DKA and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar syndrome (HHS) occur with severe hyperglycemia and must be treated early and aggressively to avoid life-threatening consequences from dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities. Severe hyperglycemia is a consequence of insufficient insulin levels coupled with an increase in counterregulatory hormones. This condition impairs efficient glucose use and subsequently initiates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

DKA typically occurs in persons with type 1 diabetes mellitus younger than 65 years. DKA is a relative or absolute insulin deficiency state resulting in unsuppressed lipolysis. Fatty acid oxidation occurs with subsequent ketone body production and metabolic acidosis development. In type 2 diabetes, DKA can occur in the setting of extreme stress or illness, such as infection or acute coronary syndrome.

HHS typically occurs in persons with type 2 diabetes who are older than 65 years and is associated with a higher mortality rate compared with DKA. HHS is characterized as a partial insulin deficiency that is able to suppress lipolysis and prevent ketone body production but is unable to correct hyperglycemia or prevent subsequent dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities. HHS is associated with more extreme hyperglycemia compared with DKA because patients with type 1 diabetes are generally younger and have higher glomerular filtration rates and greater glucose excretion.

Inciting factors for DKA or HHS development include infection, myocardial infarction, nonadherence to diabetes therapy, stress, trauma, and confounding medications (e.g., atypical antipsychotics, glucocorticoids, and SGLT2 inhibitors). DKA or HHS may also be the initial presentation of a person with undiagnosed diabetes. Euglycemic DKA has been described in patients taking SGLT2 inhibitors, and a high level of suspicion is necessary during initial evaluation.

Symptoms from DKA typically occur within 24 hours of onset, whereas symptoms from HHS may not appear for several days. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, or shortness of breath. Extreme glucosuria causes an osmotic diuresis and severe volume depletion, which may be exacerbated by gastrointestinal losses of volume and electrolytes. Progression to lethargy, obtundation, and death may occur if the hyperglycemia, dehydration, and electrolyte abnormalities are not treated aggressively and early.

Initial evaluation includes measuring the plasma glucose level, serum electrolytes, serum ketones, blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine, plasma osmolality, complete blood count, arterial blood gases, and urine ketones and performing urinalysis. An ECG should also be reviewed. Cultures of blood, sputum, and urine and a chest radiograph may be obtained if an infection is suspected.

Multiple laboratory abnormalities are present with DKA and HHS ( [Table: Table: Laboratory Study Results in DKA and HHS]

). An increased anion gap metabolic acidosis is present in DKA secondary to the production of acetoacetic acid and β-hydroxybutyrate. Although some patients with HHS may have an increased anion gap, typically with glucose levels higher than 600 mg/dL (33.3 mmol/L), they do not develop significant ketoacidosis as seen in DKA. Hypertonic hyponatremia may occur in DKA and HHS with extreme hyperglycemia and osmotic shifts of water from intracellular to extracellular compartments. A normal or elevated serum sodium level indicates severe dehydration. Increased serum osmolality, frequently greater than 320 mOsm/kg H~2O, is often present in HHS secondary to more severe hyperglycemia and water loss from osmotic diuresis compared with DKA. Serum potassium levels may be elevated because of shifts from the intracellular to extracellular spaces caused by ketoacidosis and the absence of sufficient insulin. Normal or low serum potassium levels indicate a depletion of body stores and require supplementation before insulin therapy to avoid cardiac arrhythmias. Similarly, total body phosphorus is depleted, and the level should be checked. Stress may induce mild leukocytosis, but higher levels may indicate an infectious cause for DKA or HHS. Elevated amylase and lipase levels can also occur.

A multipronged approach is required to treat DKA and HHS ( [Table: Table: Management of Hyperglycemic Crisis]

). Intravenous hydration is necessary for volume repletion. Electrolyte deficits, such as potassium, should be repleted before insulin is administered. Hyperglycemia should be corrected with intravenous insulin and hourly plasma glucose measurements to guide dose adjustments. Frequent electrolyte measurements are necessary to guide repletion as hydration and insulin therapy continue. Most patients with DKA or HHS are treated in the ICU because of the complexity of care required. Conditions that contributed to DKA or HHS development, such as infection and myocardial infarction, should be identified and treated.

A major cause of morbidity and mortality in persons with diabetes mellitus is ASCVD. Diabetes is an independent risk factor for ASCVD, along with hypertension, dyslipidemia, tobacco use, family history, and albuminuria. Simultaneously managing CVD risk factors, including dyslipidemia and hypertension (see [Table: Table: Screening for Chronic Complications of Diabetes Mellitus]

for screening recommendations), is recommended to reduce morbidity and mortality.

Hypertension contributes to the development of macrovascular and microvascular complications. The ADA and American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association treatment goal for most patients is below 130/80 mm Hg, if this can be safely attained. ADA-recommended treatment strategies include lifestyle modifications (for blood pressure >120/80 mm Hg) and pharmacologic therapies (for blood pressure ≥130/80 mm Hg). Initial recommended antihypertensive regimens include ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, and thiazide diuretics. Multiple agents are often required to reach the blood pressure target. Underlying comorbidities should guide selection of therapeutic agents, such as using an ACE inhibitor or ARB titrated to the maximum tolerated dose in the presence of moderately increased albuminuria or coronary artery disease.

Patients aged 40 to 75 years with diabetes should be started on a moderate-intensity statin; a high-intensity statin is reasonable if one or more ASCVD risk factors is present. Further details regarding statin therapy in patients with diabetes are discussed in Primary Prevention of Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease in Cardiovascular Medicine.

In patients with type 2 diabetes with established ASCVD or multiple cardiovascular risk factors, the ADA recommends a GLP-1 RA and/or SGLT2 inhibitor. Furthermore, the ADA recommends that patients with type 2 diabetes and established heart failure receive an SGLT2 inhibitor. For more information, see Pharmacologic Therapy for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus in Endocrinology and Metabolism.

The ADA recommends antiplatelet therapy with aspirin (75-162 mg/d), or clopidogrel (75 mg/d) for patients with a documented aspirin allergy, for secondary prevention in persons with diabetes and ASCVD. Aspirin for primary prevention of ASCVD in persons with diabetes may not provide universal benefit; therefore, the ADA recommends a patient-centered care discussion on the benefits of aspirin versus increased risk for bleeding before considering therapy. Primary prevention may be considered in patients aged 50 to 70 years with diabetes and one or more major ASCVD risk factors who do not have increased bleeding risk; however, it is not recommended for patients older than 70 years because the risk outweighs the benefit. The USPSTF recommends individualizing the decision to use aspirin for primary prevention of ASCVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk, and it recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin for primary prevention of ASCVD in all adults aged 60 years or older.

Retinopathy is the leading cause of preventable blindness among persons with diabetes between ages 20 and 74 years in developed countries. Risk factors include diabetes duration, degree of hyperglycemia, hypertension, albuminuria, and dyslipidemia.

Diabetic retinopathy changes are classified as nonproliferative (occurs within the retina) or proliferative (occurs in the vitreous or retinal inner surface); macular edema may occur with either type. Nonproliferative retinopathy findings include microaneurysms, dot and blot hemorrhages, hard exudates (lipid deposition), soft exudates or cotton wool spots (ischemic superficial nerve fibers), venous bleeding, and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (

,

). Neovascularization caused by chronic ischemia characterizes proliferative retinopathy, which may cause intraocular hemorrhage, retinal detachment, and vision loss.

Given the preventive effects of therapy and the fact that patients with diabetic retinopathy or macular edema may be asymptomatic, screening guidelines were developed for early detection ( [Table: Table: Screening for Chronic Complications of Diabetes Mellitus]

).

Optimal control of blood pressure, glucose, and lipid parameters can prevent and delay the progression of retinopathy. Panretinal laser photocoagulation can treat high-risk proliferative diabetic retinopathy and severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy. Additionally, intravitreal injection with anti–vascular endothelial growth factor is not inferior to panretinal laser photocoagulation for reducing vision loss associated with proliferative retinopathy.

Retinopathy may develop or accelerate during pregnancy and with rapid glycemic improvements, requiring laser photocoagulation to decrease the risk for vision loss. Caution is also advised when initiating GLP-1 RA therapy in patients with pre-existing retinopathy, as worsening of retinopathy has been associated with this drug class; however, it is unclear whether the association is due directly to the medication or due to the acute reduction in blood glucose.

Macular edema is preferentially treated with intravitreal injections of anti–vascular endothelial growth factor to improve vision loss; monthly injections are required for at least 12 months, followed by intermittent injections to prevent recurrence.

DKD is the leading cause of end-stage kidney disease. Diabetes is typically present for 5 to 10 years before DKD develops.

eGFR measurement and albuminuria screening are recommended to detect kidney disease early (see [Table: Table: Screening for Chronic Complications of Diabetes Mellitus]

). Urinary albumin excretion can be determined from a random urine collection as the urine albumin-creatinine ratio (UACR). An elevated UACR (≥30 mg/g) should be confirmed by multiple measurements over the course of 3 to 6 months because temporary elevations may occur with biologic variability, illness, hyperglycemia, heart failure, hypertension, exercise, and menstruation. Annual measurements of eGFR and UACR may identify DKD progression and guide therapeutic decisions. More frequent assessments may be necessary with worsening kidney function, up to four times per year. A declining eGFR, progressive albuminuria despite treatment, or an eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m^2 warrants referral to a nephrologist.

Uncontrolled hypertension and hyperglycemia are risk factors for DKD; thus, treatment to attain blood pressure and glucose goals is recommended. The ADA recommends an ACE inhibitor or an ARB as first-line blood pressure therapy to slow DKD progression and prevent CVD in nonpregnant persons with diabetes and hypertension who have a reduced eGFR (<60 mL/min/1.73 m^2) and/or an elevated UACR (≥30 mg/g). For patients with type 2 diabetes and CKD with an eGFR of 20 mL/min/1.73 m^2 or greater, an SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended to reduce kidney disease progression and cardiovascular events. A GLP-1 RA with proven benefit will also reduce the risk for CKD progression and cardiovascular events in this population. DKD management is discussed further in Treatment and Prognosis of Diabetic Kidney Disease in Nephrology.

Diabetic neuropathy involves damage to nerves or nerve roots caused by hyperglycemia. Neuropathy may occur peripherally or affect the autonomic nervous system. Symptoms depend on the affected nerve or nerves and may be focal or diffuse in nature.

Glycemic control may prevent peripheral neuropathy and cardiac autonomic neuropathy in patients with type 1 diabetes and can delay neuropathic progression in patients with type 2 diabetes.

Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (distal symmetric polyneuropathy) is the most common presentation and typically has an ascending presentation with a “stocking and glove” distribution. Symptoms from small nerve fiber damage include pain, burning, and tingling. Small nerve fiber abnormalities can be detected on examination by assessing pinprick and temperature sensations. Abnormalities in position sense, vibration, and light touch are indicative of large nerve fiber damage and convey an increased risk for foot ulcerations. Large nerve fiber damage can be evaluated by assessing ankle reflexes and by using a 128-Hz tuning fork and a 10-g monofilament. Because diabetic peripheral neuropathy may be asymptomatic, screening should occur for early detection to prevent limb loss (see [Table: Table: Screening for Chronic Complications of Diabetes Mellitus]

).

Autonomic neuropathy may affect one or multiple organs. Symptoms may include hypoglycemia unawareness, gastroparesis, constipation, diarrhea, erectile dysfunction, and bladder dysfunction. Symptoms from cardiac autonomic dysfunction may include orthostatic hypotension, resting sinus tachycardia, and exercise intolerance. Cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy is an independent risk factor for sudden death.

The goal of diabetic neuropathy treatment is reducing symptoms, although it may not be possible to eliminate pain. The ADA and the American Academy of Neurology recommend gabapentinoids, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants, and certain sodium channel blockers (valproic acid, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, and lacosamide) as initial therapy for neuropathic pain. Carbamazepine may also be effective. Of the aforementioned agents, only pregabalin and duloxetine are FDA approved for treating diabetic neuropathy; the capsaicin (8%) patch is approved to treat painful diabetic neuropathy of the feet. Opioids, tramadol, or tapentadol are not recommended.

The primary treatment for orthostatic hypotension is increasing dietary salt and water intake, using compression stockings, and changing positions slowly. Medications that cause or worsen orthostatic changes should be discontinued and other agents (fludrocortisone, midodrine, or droxidopa) added for refractory symptoms. Exercise should be encouraged to avoid deconditioning and worsening symptoms.

Small and frequent low-fat, low-fiber meals may improve gastroparesis symptoms, along with removing drugs that may be exacerbating symptoms. Metoclopramide is a prokinetic agent approved by the FDA to treat gastroparesis. Given the risk for adverse effects, including dystonia, risks and benefits should be carefully assessed before prescribing (see Management of Gastroparesis in Gastroenterology).

Other types of diabetic neuropathies are described in [Table: Table: Peripheral Nerve Dysfunction in Diabetes Mellitus]

and are discussed in Neuropathies of Diabetes Mellitus and Impaired Glucose Tolerance in Neurology.

Lower-extremity ulcers are associated with significant morbidity, including amputations, and mortality (see Diabetic Foot Infections in Infectious Disease and Evaluation and Management of Osteomyelitis in Diabetic Foot Ulcers in Infectious Disease).

The ADA recommends performing a comprehensive evaluation at least annually to identify risk factors for ulcers, including the following:

  • History of foot ulcer or amputation
  • Pre-ulcerative callouses or corns
  • Peripheral artery disease
  • Peripheral neuropathy
  • Hyperglycemia
  • Foot deformity
  • Retinopathy
  • Tobacco use
  • DKD

The foot examination should include the following:

  • Skin inspection
  • Foot deformity assessment
  • Neurologic assessment by 10-g monofilament testing with at least one other assessment, such as pinprick, temperature, or vibration
  • Vascular assessment, including pulses in the legs and feet

Patients with evidence of sensory loss or previous ulceration or amputation should have their feet inspected at every visit. Ankle-brachial index measurement and further vascular assessment should be performed in persons with reduced or absent pedal pulses or symptoms that are concerning for claudication. Foot care specialists should be involved in the care of patients at high risk. Patients should be educated on the importance of daily foot inspections and properly fitting footwear.

Type 2 diabetes is a major risk factor for the development of MASLD. Recommendations for MASLD screening in patients with diabetes are outlined in [Table: Table: Screening for Chronic Complications of Diabetes Mellitus]

, and MASLD evaluation and management are discussed in Metabolic Dysfunction–Associated Steatotic Liver Disease in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease. Diabetes medications that are preferred in patients with MASLD and MASH are discussed in Pharmacologic Therapy for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus in Endocrinology and Metabolism.

Neuropsychological complications to consider and address in patients with diabetes mellitus include anxiety, depression, diabetes-related distress, and cognitive impairment. These conditions can adversely affect glycemic control directly and through challenges with patient adherence to management plans. Psychosocial care should be routinely provided to all patients with diabetes.

Screening for psychosocial issues and behavioral health conditions should occur at the time of diabetes diagnosis and at least annually thereafter (see Depression and Anxiety in Foundations of Clinical Practice). The ADA recommends referral to a behavioral health professional for patients with a behavioral health condition, disordered eating, diabetes distress, difficulty managing diabetes, fear of hypoglycemia, or cognitive dysfunction.

Patients with diabetes have an increased risk for dementia and cognitive decline. The ADA recommends lifetime monitoring of cognitive capacity, especially in older adults and those experiencing severe hypoglycemia (see Assessing Cognitive Symptoms in Neurology). If cognitive impairment is diagnosed, treatment plans should be simplified to reduce the risk for hypoglycemia.

Hypoglycemia can be stratified into levels of severity ( [Table: Table: Hypoglycemia Management in a Patient With Diabetes Mellitus]

).

Hyperadrenergic symptoms (sweating, tremors, anxiety, tachycardia) are the normal physiologic response to hypoglycemia and result from the release of counterregulatory hormones (glucagon, epinephrine, norepinephrine, cortisol, and growth hormone). Neuroglycopenic signs (altered mental status, dysarthria, confusion) are associated with severe hypoglycemia. Obtundation, seizures, and death may occur if severe hypoglycemia is not corrected rapidly.

Hypoglycemia can become a rate-limiting factor in achieving glycemic goals for many persons with diabetes mellitus. Severe recurrent hypoglycemia is associated with greater risk for cognitive impairment, dementia, and mortality. Individualized glycemic goals, patient education, modification of diet and exercise regimens, close glucose monitoring, and use of diabetes technologies are recommended to eliminate hypoglycemia.

Several factors contribute to hypoglycemia, including a mismatch of food consumption and insulin delivery, increased physical exertion, weight loss, worsening kidney impairment, abnormalities in gastrointestinal motility and absorption, and accidental or intentional insulin overdose. Hypoglycemia can also occur with the use of oral diabetes medications (especially sulfonylureas or meglitinides) because of incorrect dosages, drug-drug interactions, and intercurrent illnesses that alter drug metabolism or excretion. Quinolone antibiotics, salicylates, sulfonamides, and warfarin are associated with higher rates of hypoglycemia in patients who use a sulfonylurea.

Hypoglycemia treatment varies on the basis of the level of hypoglycemia, the patient’s mentation, and availability of intravenous access (see [Table: Table: Hypoglycemia Management in a Patient With Diabetes Mellitus]

). Close contacts and caretakers should be instructed on proper glucagon administration; supplies should be assessed frequently to ensure that products are not expired. CGM has been shown to reduce hypoglycemia in patients with diabetes, and CGM technology should be considered in patients at risk for hypoglycemia or with recurrent hypoglycemia.

Hospitalized patients with or without diabetes can experience hypoglycemia, which is often preventable. Hospitals should have standardized protocols in place for preventing, recognizing, treating, and documenting hypoglycemia.

Hypoglycemia unawareness is characterized by insufficient release of counterregulatory hormones and an inadequate autonomic response to hypoglycemia. Previous episodes of hypoglycemia increase the risk for developing hypoglycemia unawareness. Treatment involves relaxing glycemic targets and modifying diabetes therapies to avoid continued hypoglycemia. Avoiding hypoglycemia for several weeks may reverse hypoglycemia unawareness in some persons and result in the return of adrenergic symptoms with glucose levels less than 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L). CGM has been shown to reduce hypoglycemia in patients with hypoglycemia unawareness and is recommended for use in this population.

Hypoglycemia without concomitant diabetes is uncommon and warrants further assessment. A hypoglycemia evaluation should be performed if the criteria for the Whipple triad are met: neuroglycopenic symptoms, hypoglycemia at or below 55 mg/dL (3.1 mmol/L), and resolution of symptoms with glucose ingestion. Laboratory measurement of the plasma glucose level must confirm true hypoglycemia because POC glucose values are not reliable in this scenario.

Hypoglycemia in persons without diabetes may be attributable to medications, alcohol, illness, organ dysfunction (kidney or liver), hormonal deficiencies (adrenal insufficiency), malnutrition, and, rarely, pancreatogenous insulinoma or noninsulinoma (endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia that is not caused by an insulinoma). Other rare conditions are post–gastric bypass hypoglycemia (nesidioblastosis) and insulin autoimmune hypoglycemia.

Hypoglycemia typically occurs in the fasting or postprandial state. Diagnostic blood and urine studies should be obtained during a hypoglycemic episode in which the Whipple triad has been demonstrated. If a spontaneous episode is not witnessed, measures should be implemented to recreate circumstances that normally induce hypoglycemia (fasting or ingestion of a typical meal that causes symptoms for the individual). Imaging studies for tumor localization should occur only after confirmation of endogenous hyperinsulinism from the diagnostic blood and urine studies.

A prolonged fast, up to 72 hours, should be initiated if the hypoglycemia typically occurs while fasting. Consultation with an endocrinologist is strongly recommended.

Insulin antibody testing and an oral hypoglycemic agent screen should be performed at the beginning of the fast. During the fast, plasma glucose should be drawn every 6 hours and immediately sent to the laboratory. If the plasma glucose level is less than 60 mg/dL (3.3 mmol/L), four tests should be performed: C-peptide, insulin, proinsulin, and β-hydroxybutyrate. Blood specimen collection for the four tests should increase to every 1 to 2 hours when the glucose measurement is less than 60 mg/dL (3.3 mmol/L).

Testing is complete when one of the following parameters is met: a plasma glucose level of 45 mg/dL (2.5 mmol/L) or a plasma glucose level below 55 mg/dL (3.1 mmol/L) with signs or symptoms of hypoglycemia present. POC glucose values and hyperadrenergic symptoms should not be used to determine the end of the fast. Blood specimens should be collected again at the end of the 72-hour period if neither of these two criteria were met.

shows the interpretation of the diagnostic testing results.

Postprandial hypoglycemia typically occurs within 5 hours of the last meal. Altered gastrointestinal anatomy, as occurs after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery, is frequently the cause of postprandial hypoglycemia. Meals consisting of simple carbohydrates (e.g., pancakes, syrup, juice) are frequently the culprit.

A mixed-meal test consisting of the types of food that normally induce the hypoglycemia should be performed to determine the cause. Baseline laboratory studies including plasma glucose, serum C-peptide, serum insulin, and plasma proinsulin are obtained before meal consumption. Plasma glucose measurement is repeated every 30 minutes for 5 hours; if the level is less than 60 mg/dL (3.3 mmol/L), then the other three tests should be obtained. If neuroglycopenia occurs, the tests should be repeated before administering carbohydrates.

Screening for insulin antibodies and oral hypoglycemic agents should also occur if the patient experiences symptomatic hypoglycemia. Interpretation of the results is similar to that for results obtained during fasting hypoglycemia (see [Table: Table: Differential Diagnosis of Spontaneous Fasting Hypoglycemia]

).

Dietary adjustment can generally alleviate symptoms. Patients should be instructed to consume small frequent mixed meals with a balance of protein, fat, and carbohydrates.
