Disorders of the Pituitary Gland

The pituitary gland is located in the sella turcica above and posterior to the sphenoid sinus. The optic chiasm is superior to the pituitary gland, and the carotid arteries are lateral (

). The gland is composed of glandular tissue in the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) and neural tissue in the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis).

A rich portal vascular network connects the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary via the pituitary stalk. Stimulatory and inhibitory hormones secreted into the portal blood by the hypothalamus regulate the anterior pituitary. The posterior pituitary hormones are synthesized in the hypothalamus and travel through neurons in the stalk to be stored and released from the posterior pituitary gland. The carotid arteries provide blood to the pituitary through the hypophysial arteries, and venous drainage occurs by the petrosal sinuses to the jugular veins.

The anterior pituitary secretes six pituitary hormones:

  • Luteinizing hormone (LH)
  • Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
  • Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)
  • Prolactin
  • Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
  • Growth hormone (GH)

These six major hormones are regulated by hormones produced in the hypothalamus ( [Table: Table: Anterior Pituitary Hormones and Their Actions]

).

The posterior pituitary gland secretes oxytocin, which is necessary for parturition and lactation, and arginine vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone), which regulates water balance.

[Table: Table: Initial Testing for Pituitary Hormone Excess and Deficiency]

lists the pituitary hormones and initial evaluation for suspected pituitary excess or deficiency of each hormone.

Incidental pituitary lesions discovered on imaging are called “pituitary incidentalomas” and require evaluation, including hormonal testing and follow-up imaging (see Evaluation of Pituitary Tumors in Endocrinology and Metabolism). About 3% of patients undergoing a brain MRI will have an incidental pituitary mass. Most pituitary incidentalomas are benign, nonfunctional pituitary adenomas. Microadenomas (<1 cm) are most common, but macroadenomas (≥1 cm) may also be found incidentally. A small percentage of pituitary incidentalomas may be Rathke cleft cysts (benign embryologic remnants), craniopharyngiomas, or meningiomas. In patients with a history of malignancy, metastatic disease should be considered.

The evaluation and management of a pituitary adenoma is illustrated in

.

In patients with a pituitary incidentaloma, a dedicated pituitary MRI with and without contrast with dynamic cuts through the sella should be obtained. Patients with tumors that abut or compress the optic chiasm or with vision changes should undergo visual field testing.

Pituitary hypersecretion should be ruled out in all pituitary incidentalomas with serum prolactin and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) measurements; diagnosing a GH-secreting tumor when it is smaller than 1 cm increases the chance of surgical cure. Evaluation for Cushing disease should be considered in patients with signs or symptoms of cortisol excess (see [Table: Table: Initial Testing for Pituitary Hormone Excess and Deficiency]

).

Screening for hypopituitarism is recommended in all pituitary tumors, regardless of symptoms, by measuring serum FSH, LH, morning cortisol, ACTH, TSH, free thyroxine (T~4), IGF-1, and, in men, morning total testosterone. In premenopausal women, a menstrual history can assess for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Arginine vasopressin deficiency (central diabetes insipidus) is not associated with pituitary adenomas. Abnormal baseline testing may prompt further stimulatory testing to confirm hypopituitarism ( [Table: Table: Dynamic Testing for Pituitary Dysfunction]

).

If a patient does not require surgery for mass effect or pituitary hypersecretion, follow-up imaging to assess for interval growth is recommended. For macroadenomas, the pituitary MRI should be repeated in 6 to 12 months, and, if stable, imaging should then be completed in 1 to 3 years; the exact timing of imaging depends on the proximity of the adenoma to the optic chiasm. The role of ongoing surveillance imaging should be reassessed based on patient factors, and there is no clear consensus on when imaging should be stopped. Microadenomas (<1 cm) are much less likely to grow over time. An MRI should be repeated in 2 to 3 years, with additional imaging at less frequent intervals depending on the size of the microadenoma. There is no clear consensus for when imaging should be stopped in these patients. Repeat pituitary function testing should be completed every 1 to 2 years in patients with micro- and macroadenomas or earlier if symptoms or enlargement occur.

Mass effects of pituitary tumors most commonly include compression of the pituitary gland, resulting in hormone deficiencies, or compression of the optic chiasm, most commonly resulting in bitemporal hemianopsia. Other patterns of vision loss, including decreased visual acuity, may also develop.

Pituitary abnormalities related to gland compression range from an isolated hormone deficiency (gonadotropins and GH being the most prevalent), to panhypopituitarism (deficiency of all anterior pituitary hormones and arginine vasopressin). Pituitary stalk compression can lead to hyperprolactinemia through loss of the inhibitory effect of hypothalamic dopamine, which can also contribute to hypogonadism.

Pituitary tumors can have variable effects on compression of surrounding structures. A rapidly growing pituitary tumor or pituitary apoplexy (sudden hemorrhage or infarction of a pituitary adenoma) may result in the sudden onset of severe headaches; bitemporal hemianopsia or blindness, caused by optic chiasm compression; or cranial nerve palsies. Conversely, a slow-growing pituitary tumor may cause minimal or no peripheral vision loss because the optic chiasm is able to stretch slowly over the tumor.

Given the risk for visual loss, all patients with pituitary tumors that abut or compress the optic chiasm or who have visual symptoms should be evaluated by an ophthalmologist (preferably a neuro-ophthalmologist). Any abnormality observed on visual examination is an indication for surgery, unless the tumor is a prolactinoma.

Pituitary tumors can also invade the cavernous sinus but rarely cause mass effect or compression of the internal carotid artery within the cavernous sinus. Although headaches can be a symptom of pituitary tumors, they do not correlate well with tumor size and therefore are not typically an indication for surgery.

Patients with a nonfunctioning pituitary adenoma (i.e., one that does not secrete pituitary hormones in excess) should be referred for neurosurgical evaluation if visual deficits are related to the tumor, the mass abuts or compresses the optic chiasm or optic nerves on pituitary MRI, or pituitary apoplexy with visual disturbance is present.

Patients who have a macroadenoma close to the optic chiasm and are planning pregnancy may benefit from surgical decompression of the pituitary tumor because of the risk for physiologic enlargement during pregnancy; microadenomas rarely have a clinically significant increase in size during pregnancy. Patients with macroadenomas that are not resected before pregnancy should have visual field testing performed each trimester and a noncontrast MRI for any change in vision or headaches.

The most common surgical approach for pituitary tumors is transsphenoidal (through the nares or mouth).

The pituitary gland can be affected by other pathologic processes, such as trauma, medication adverse effects, autoimmune disease, infection, metastatic disease, infiltrative diseases, and infarction ( [Table: Table: Other Pituitary Abnormalities]

).

Acute or chronic traumatic brain injury (TBI) and subarachnoid hemorrhage can cause varying degrees of hypopituitarism, affecting 10% to 35% of patients, most commonly GH deficiency. Severe TBI is more likely to affect pituitary function.

Acutely, secondary adrenal insufficiency, arginine vasopressin deficiency, and the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion can be life-threatening. A morning serum cortisol level should be checked in critically ill patients with symptoms concerning for adrenal insufficiency, such as hypotension, hyponatremia, or hypoglycemia. A random cortisol measurement would be appropriate in critically ill patients, and patients in unstable condition should receive empiric glucocorticoid treatment. Arginine vasopressin deficiency should be evaluated in the appropriate clinical context, primarily polyuria or hypernatremia. Serum sodium monitoring can also be considered to assess for the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion.

Pituitary function can recover with time. Growth hormone deficiency is the most persistent deficiency in patients with TBI. The optimal timing to reassess pituitary function is unclear. Some experts suggest reassessing pituitary function (serum FSH, LH, morning cortisol, ACTH, TSH, free T~4, IGF-1, and, in men, morning total testosterone) at 3 to 6 months and then yearly for at least 3 years; in premenopausal women, a menstrual history is sufficient to assess for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. An alternative strategy may be to reassess pituitary function if symptoms develop. Patients with sports-related chronic repetitive head trauma may also benefit from screening for pituitary hormone deficiencies.

Exogenously administered hormones provide negative feedback to normal cells in the pituitary gland and suppress endogenous hormone production. Exogenous estrogen or testosterone suppresses the gonadotropins, exogenous thyroid hormone suppresses TSH, and glucocorticoids suppress ACTH.

Opioids have many effects on pituitary function. Notably, chronic opioid use suppresses gonadotroph function through altered GnRH release, resulting in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Opioids can also increase prolactin release, further inhibiting GnRH secretion. In women, this inhibition may manifest as irregular periods or amenorrhea. About 50% of men may have signs and symptoms of hypogonadism with laboratory evidence of low testosterone with low or inappropriately normal gonadotropins. Hypogonadism may have long-term consequences, including osteoporosis, muscle loss, and increased adiposity. Periodic assessment for symptoms of hypogonadism is recommended, but guidelines are unclear regarding biochemical screening for hypogonadism in patients taking chronic opioid therapy. Discontinuing opioid therapy should result in recovery of gonadal function. If patients cannot discontinue therapy, replacing estrogen in premenopausal women and testosterone in men is appropriate in the absence of contraindications.

Chronic opioid use (over 20 morphine mg equivalents) also inhibits corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), reducing ACTH release, thereby causing cortisol and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate deficiency in about 10% to 20% of persons; adrenal insufficiency has also been reported in acute opioid treatment. Routine biochemical testing is not currently recommended, but periodic assessment for symptoms should be considered. Patients with secondary adrenal insufficiency from opioids should be treated with hydrocortisone. Recovery is possible within weeks to months of tapering or discontinuing opioids. Rate of recovery is unclear.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors have been associated with pituitary abnormalities related to hypophysitis. These drugs are used to treat many cancers and include the following:

  • Anti–programmed cell death protein-1 (anti-PD-1) agents (e.g., nivolumab, pembrolizumab, dostarlimab, cemiplimab, retifanlimab)
  • Anti–programmed death-ligand 1 (anti-PD-L1) agents (e.g., atezolizumab, avelumab, and durvalumab)
  • Anti–cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein-4 (anti-CTL-4) agents (e.g., ipilimumab, tremelimumab)

Hypophysitis often presents with headache and fatigue and sometimes with compressive symptoms, including visual deficits, in patients with severe disease. It is more common with use of anti-CTL-4 agents (10% of patients) than anti-PD-1 therapy (0.5%-1%), in combination therapy (anti-CTL-4 plus anti-PD-1), in men, and in older patients.

Endocrine evaluation usually reveals ACTH, LH, and TSH deficiency, as well as low GH levels. Arginine vasopressin deficiency (central diabetes insipidus) is uncommon. Imaging demonstrates pituitary gland enhancement or enlargement with pituitary stalk thickening. Isolated ACTH deficiency resulting in secondary adrenal insufficiency can also occur, primarily with anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 therapy. This may or may not be associated with radiographic findings of hypophysitis.

Treatment includes replacing deficient pituitary hormones; importantly, cortisol deficiency must be treated before initiating thyroid hormone replacement. High-dose glucocorticoids (1-2 mg/kg/day for 1-2 weeks) should only be used in severe disease with compressive symptoms to treat the inflammatory process. Deficiencies are typically permanent. Treatment with checkpoint inhibitors can continue in patients with mild symptoms and can be resumed in patients with severe symptoms after those symptoms resolve.

The term “empty sella” describes a radiologic finding on MRI consisting of an enlarged sella turcica not entirely filled by pituitary tissue. The pituitary gland may be small or compressed, lining the enlarged sella, or may not be visualized. This finding is most often incidental and is seen in 8% to 35% of MRIs. The incidence is greater in women by a 5:1 ratio. It is associated with obesity.

Primary empty sella is caused by herniation of subarachnoid space and fluid into the sella, compressing the normal pituitary gland. This herniation is caused by sellar diaphragm incompetence, increased intracranial pressure, or volumetric changes in the pituitary gland. Secondary empty sella can be related to pituitary tumor infarction (mostly macroadenomas), infection, autoimmune disease, trauma, or radiotherapy.

Although most patients with an empty sella usually have normal pituitary function, clinical assessment for signs and symptoms of pituitary deficiencies should be performed. All patients, regardless of symptoms, should be screened with prolactin, morning cortisol, ACTH, IGF-1, TSH, free T~4, LH, FSH, and, in men, morning total testosterone measurements. A menstrual history is sufficient to evaluate hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in premenopausal women. Arginine vasopressin deficiency can occur, and testing is recommended if a patient has concerning symptoms. GH deficiency and hyperprolactinemia are the most common endocrine abnormalities. Additional testing should be based on symptoms. Patients with suspected idiopathic intracranial hypertension should be referred for ophthalmologic evaluation.

Asymptomatic patients with empty sella are unlikely to develop hormonal or radiologic changes.

Hypopituitarism is defined as one or more pituitary hormone deficiencies (see [Table: Table: Initial Testing for Pituitary Hormone Excess and Deficiency]

). It can result from tumor compression of the normal pituitary cells or as a complication of TBI, medications, cranial surgery (particularly after resection of a pituitary macroadenoma), or radiation therapy. Hypopituitarism can also occur in patients with functioning tumors (e.g., hyperprolactinemia, Cushing disease, acromegaly) regardless of tumor size. Somatotrophs and gonadotrophs are the most sensitive to injury; therefore, GH, LH, and FSH are the most common pituitary deficiencies. ACTH and TSH deficiencies are less common but more serious.

Pituitary apoplexy and Sheehan syndrome (pituitary infarction associated with postpartum hemorrhage) can cause acute life-threatening hypopituitarism due to ACTH deficiency.

[Table: Table: Causes of Hypopituitarism]

lists the causes of hypopituitarism.

Panhypopituitarism is a condition in which production of all pituitary hormones is insufficient, usually as a result of a large tumor, apoplexy, or complications of pituitary surgery. Patients require daily replacement of thyroxine and cortisol. Importantly, when treating acute panhypopituitarism, cortisol deficiency must be treated before initiating thyroid hormone replacement. Replacement of sex hormones, arginine vasopressin, and GH is individualized.

The most common cause of ACTH deficiency is exogenous glucocorticoid administration with resultant suppression of CRH and ACTH production. Oral, intra-articular, and, in some instances, inhaled and topical glucocorticoids can suppress the hypothalamus, leading to decreased CRH and ACTH production. Other drugs, including opioids and immune checkpoint inhibitors, have been shown to cause ACTH deficiency. It can also occur in the setting of damage to the pituitary gland after surgery or head trauma.

Symptoms of secondary cortisol deficiency include fatigue, weight loss, nausea, dizziness, arthralgias, and hyponatremia related to increased arginine vasopressin secretion/action. Patients with ACTH deficiency are at lower risk for hypotension and adrenal crisis and have normal serum potassium levels because of their intact renin-aldosterone systems.

The evaluation of adrenal insufficiency begins with measurement of a morning serum cortisol level (see

). Patients with serum cortisol levels between 3 and 15 μg/dL (82.8-414 nmol/L) require an ACTH stimulation test (see [Table: Table: Dynamic Testing for Pituitary Dysfunction]

); however, testing should be interpreted with care, as patients with early secondary adrenal insufficiency may have normal stimulated levels. Because the cortisol assay measures total serum cortisol (cortisol bound to corticosteroid-binding globulin and free cortisol), testing may be difficult to interpret in low-protein states or in those with high corticosteroid-binding globulin (e.g., women taking combined oral contraceptives). The diagnosis of secondary adrenal insufficiency is made in the setting of a low cortisol level with a concomitantly low or inappropriately normal ACTH level.

After diagnosis, secondary adrenal insufficiency should be treated with hydrocortisone, 15 to 25 mg/d, usually in two divided doses. In an emergency setting such as pituitary apoplexy, an immediate intravenous dose of 100 mg of hydrocortisone should be administered. Glucocorticoid dosing must be adjusted in the setting of physiologic stress or acute illness. Administering two to three times the baseline dose of cortisol replacement for 2 to 3 days is usually sufficient for home management of illness with fever, whereas 25 to 75 mg/d for 1 to 2 days is sufficient for mild to moderate surgical stress. In patients with major physiologic stress, including major surgery, critical illness, or active labor, 100 mg of hydrocortisone should be administered by intravenous injection followed by continuous infusion of 200 mg every 24 hours or a 50-mg intravenous injection every 6 to 8 hours. Patients with glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency also require stress dosing in the setting of physiologic stress or acute illness; the stress dose is individualized based on the patient’s current glucocorticoid dosing plan and degree of stress.

Patients with iatrogenic secondary adrenal insufficiency require a slow taper of glucocorticoids to allow recovery of the pituitary-adrenal axis. Although short bursts of glucocorticoids will not suppress the axis, supraphysiologic doses for more than 3 to 4 weeks will cause suppression. After the glucocorticoid dose is tapered close to the physiologic dose (equivalent of 4-6 mg of prednisone), patients who no longer require glucocorticoid therapy for their underlying condition may either continue an ongoing gradual taper with close monitoring for signs and symptoms of adrenal insufficiency or undergo testing with a morning serum cortisol measurement. A morning (sample collected within 1-2 hours of waking) serum cortisol level greater than 10 μg/dL (300 nmol/L) demonstrates pituitary-adrenal axis recovery, and glucocorticoids can be safely stopped. A cortisol level of 10 μg/dL (300 nmol/L) or lower indicates that the pituitary-adrenal axis has not recovered; these patients should be continued on physiologic dosing and a morning cortisol measurement should be repeated after a few weeks to months. Patients taking a long-acting glucocorticoid, such as dexamethasone, can be switched to an equivalent dose of a shorter-acting glucocorticoid, such as prednisone or hydrocortisone; this will allow for faster recovery of the pituitary-adrenal axis.

Glucocorticoid tapering can be associated with glucocorticoid withdrawal symptoms. The body becomes dependent on exogenous glucocorticoids over time, and lowering doses can trigger withdrawal symptoms. Patients should be counseled on glucocorticoid withdrawal symptoms before doses are tapered. Glucocorticoid withdrawal symptoms can occur at any point during tapering but are often exacerbated when prednisone is decreased below 15 mg/d. Symptoms include fatigue, nausea, muscle and joint pain, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. Adrenal insufficiency symptoms overlap with many symptoms of glucocorticoid withdrawal. Although adrenal insufficiency may be present when the glucocorticoid dose is less than physiologic replacement (<5-7.5 mg of prednisone), it would not occur at higher doses of prednisone. Prolonging the taper or even returning to a slightly higher glucocorticoid dose can moderate severe glucocorticoid withdrawal symptoms.

TSH deficiency results in the inability of the thyroid gland to produce free T~4 and triiodothyronine. The diagnosis of secondary hypothyroidism requires measurement of TSH and free T~4 levels; the combination of a low free T~4 level and a low or inappropriately normal TSH level indicates secondary hypothyroidism. The clinical symptoms of secondary hypothyroidism are the same as those of primary hypothyroidism, but goiter is typically absent (see [Table: Table: Manifestations of Thyrotoxicosis and Thyroid Hormone Deficiency]

).

Treatment is daily administration of levothyroxine. Because secondary hypothyroidism is caused by an inability to produce TSH, this hormone level cannot be used to monitor therapy and should not be measured after a diagnosis. Free T~4, measured before the morning dose of levothyroxine, should be used to monitor dose adequacy and should be maintained in the mid to upper half of the normal range. Free T~4 levels can be checked 4 to 6 weeks after a dose change to assess for adequacy in secondary hypothyroidism.

Gonadotropin deficiency can result from pituitary disease or GnRH deficiency, such as in Kallmann syndrome and hypothalamic amenorrhea. Gonadotropin deficiency results in a decrease of male and female sex hormones. The combination of low or inappropriately normal LH and FSH with low sex hormones is termed “hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.” Decreased caloric intake with low weight, excessive exercise such as vigorous athletic training, and stress are common causes of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in women, resulting in hypothalamic amenorrhea. Certain drugs, including opioids, can also suppress GnRH.

Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in patients who do not desire fertility can usually be treated by replacing sex hormones (testosterone in men, estrogen-progesterone in women). Although combined oral contraceptives may be appropriate in young women desiring contraception, other forms of estrogen and progesterone (e.g., estradiol patch with cyclic oral progesterone) are generally preferred. For persons with diet, exercise, or stress-related hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, lifestyle modifications may be recommended to achieve a healthy weight and lifestyle. In men and women who desire fertility, gonadotropin replacement is necessary to stimulate spermatogenesis in men and ovulation in women.

Because GH is necessary for linear growth, its deficiency in children causes short stature. GH also has other effects on the body, including regulating bone strength, muscle mass, fat distribution, and mood. Symptoms of adult GH deficiency are subtle and include fatigue, loss of muscle mass, and an increased ratio of fatty tissue to lean mass.

Because idiopathic GH deficiency in adults is rare, evaluation for GH deficiency in adult patients should only be considered in those with a history of hypothalamic or pituitary disease, surgery or irradiation to these areas, head trauma, other pituitary hormone deficiencies, or childhood-onset GH deficiency.

Because of the pulsatile nature of GH, its deficiency should be assessed by measuring IGF-1. An IGF-1 level below the normal range for sex and age is highly suggestive of GH deficiency, whereas a normal IGF-1 level does not rule out GH deficiency; therefore, provocative tests (see [Table: Table: Initial Testing for Pituitary Hormone Excess and Deficiency]

) may be necessary to establish the diagnosis.

Treatment benefits in patients with GH deficiency include improvement in exercise capacity, body composition, and bone density. GH is contraindicated in the setting of malignancy or an untreated pituitary tumor because of the potential to stimulate tumor growth. Additionally, caution should be used in patients with diabetes mellitus because treatment may worsen hyperglycemia. When therapy is indicated in adults, GH can be replaced with a low-dose daily or once weekly injection titrated to a normal age-adjusted IGF-1 level. Patients should be monitored for improvement in quality of life, metabolic parameters, bone density, and pituitary function; residual pituitary mass should be periodically evaluated. Thyroid and adrenal function should be monitored during GH therapy. Oral estrogen reduces IGF-1 levels; therefore, transdermal estrogen replacement is preferred in women with GH deficiency.

The inability of the posterior pituitary gland to secrete adequate arginine vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) results in arginine vasopressin deficiency (central diabetes insipidus). The lack of arginine vasopressin prevents reabsorption of water in the kidneys, resulting in polyuria and polydipsia. Although significant hypernatremia is rare in patients with an intact thirst mechanism and access to water, it can be severe if patients cannot drink or if they have high-volume nocturia because balancing water loss with intake at night can be difficult. An inappropriately low urine osmolality in the setting of an elevated serum osmolality and hypernatremia in a patient with polyuria (>50 mL/kg/24 hours) is diagnostic of an arginine vasopressin disorder (see Hypernatremia in Nephrology). A water deprivation test can be performed when the diagnosis is uncertain, and evaluating the response to desmopressin can help differentiate arginine vasopressin deficiency from arginine vasopressin resistance (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) (see [Table: Table: Dynamic Testing for Pituitary Dysfunction]

).

Arginine vasopressin deficiency is treated with desmopressin administered intranasally, orally, or subcutaneously. Despite the lower bioavailability of oral desmopressin, it is often preferred in patients with milder arginine vasopressin deficiency because intranasal absorption of desmopressin may be altered by changes in nasal mucosa. Doses are usually administered once nightly to prevent nocturia or twice daily if symptoms interfere with daily function; however, caution should be taken to avoid overreplacement, which can cause hyponatremia and volume overload. Frequent monitoring of fluid intake and urine output as well as serum sodium levels is recommended in hospitalized patients.

Pituitary adenomas are considered functional when they secrete pituitary hormones in excess ( [Table: Table: Initial Testing for Pituitary Hormone Excess and Deficiency]

). Although the most common functional pituitary tumors are prolactinomas, pituitary tumors that produce ACTH or GH are important to recognize because of their clinical consequences. TSH-secreting adenomas that cause hyperthyroidism occur rarely. Pituitary tumors that produce LH or FSH are extremely rare. Pituitary tumors can also rarely co-secrete more than one hormone; co-secretion most often occurs with GH and prolactin.

The most common cause of hyperprolactinemia is physiologic and related to pregnancy or lactation. [Table: Table: Causes of Hyperprolactinemia]

provides a comprehensive list of causes of hyperprolactinemia. Symptoms of hyperprolactinemia include breast tenderness, amenorrhea, and, in some patients, galactorrhea. Men often present later with symptoms of mass effect or hypogonadism and less commonly with gynecomastia and breast tenderness.

A common cause of non–tumor-related hyperprolactinemia is medication. More than 40% of patients taking typical antipsychotics have hyperprolactinemia caused by the dopamine antagonist effect (see [Table: Table: Causes of Hyperprolactinemia]

). Although medication-induced hyperprolactinemia most often results in serum prolactin levels of 25 to 100 ng/mL (25-100 μg/L), drugs such as metoclopramide, risperidone, paliperidone, and phenothiazines can lead to prolactin levels greater than 200 ng/mL (200 μg/L).

Confirming that hyperprolactinemia is related to medication can be challenging. If possible and in consultation with the patient’s care team, serum prolactin levels should be rechecked after the suspected medication has either been withheld for 3 days or switched to a medication less likely to cause hyperprolactinemia. If the medication cannot be withheld or switched, a pituitary-specific MRI should be performed to ensure that an adenoma is not present. Treating medication-induced hyperprolactinemia with a dopamine agonist is not recommended because it can exacerbate psychiatric symptoms. Instead, hypogonadism should be treated with estrogen or testosterone replacement to preserve bone mass.

A pituitary MRI is indicated in all patients with unexplained hyperprolactinemia. Serum prolactin levels correlate with tumor size in patients with prolactinomas. Patients with macroprolactinomas typically have prolactin levels greater than 200 ng/mL (200 μg/L); therefore, a macroadenoma with a prolactin level less than 100 ng/mL (100 μg/L) should raise suspicion of pituitary stalk compression from a nonfunctioning pituitary tumor.

In patients with macroprolactinomas, dopamine agonist therapy is recommended to lower prolactin levels, reduce tumor size, and restore gonadal function. Cabergoline is preferred over bromocriptine because of its superior efficacy in lowering prolactin levels and reducing tumor size; it is also better tolerated. Prolactin levels can be monitored 4 weeks after initiation of therapy and then every 3 to 4 months once stable. A macroadenoma should be reimaged 3 to 6 months after initiation of medical therapy. Subsequent imaging annually for 3 years is recommended in select patients. Reimaging should be performed if the prolactin level increases despite therapy or if new symptoms develop.

Patients with asymptomatic microadenomas (typically men, premenopausal women without hypogonadism, or postmenopausal women) do not require treatment. Premenopausal women desiring fertility should be treated with a dopamine agonist. Women with hypogonadism related to a microprolactinoma can be treated with sex hormone replacement or with a dopamine agonist. MRI should be repeated for a microadenoma in 1 year and then periodically if dopamine agonist therapy is not initiated.

Surgery should only be considered for symptomatic prolactinomas in patients who cannot tolerate dopamine agonist therapy or whose tumors do not shrink or even grow while taking dopamine agonist therapy. Recurrence after surgery is common.

Prolactinoma enlargement in pregnancy is a concern because of lactotroph hyperplasia. Microadenomas are unlikely to enlarge during pregnancy, and dopamine agonist therapy should be discontinued when pregnancy is confirmed. However, patients who have macroadenomas without previous surgical or radiation therapy have a significant risk for tumor growth; therefore, surgical tumor debulking before pregnancy or continuing dopamine agonist therapy (preferably bromocriptine) throughout pregnancy may be required in these patients. If surgery during pregnancy is necessary, the second trimester is the preferred time.

Patients with macroadenomas should be monitored with visual field testing each trimester; those with microadenomas can be monitored clinically. Headaches or visual field changes should prompt a noncontrast pituitary MRI to evaluate for change in tumor size.

Acromegaly is caused by excess GH secretion from a pituitary tumor in 95% of patients. Fewer than 5% of patients with GH excess have a GHRH-secreting tumor or neuroendocrine tumor. When GH-secreting pituitary tumors occur in children before puberty, the result is increased longitudinal growth that results in gigantism. Although gigantism is easily recognized in children, features of excess GH (acromegaly) can be more subtle in adults ( [Table: Table: Features of Acromegaly]

).

An IGF-1 level should be obtained to evaluate for suspected acromegaly. In patients with typical features of acromegaly, an IGF-1 level greater than 1.3 times the upper limit of normal is diagnostic. For patients with equivocal IGF-1 levels or more subtle examination findings, a repeat IGF-1 level or an oral glucose tolerance test should be considered (see [Table: Table: Dynamic Testing for Pituitary Dysfunction]

). When GH excess is demonstrated, a pituitary MRI should be obtained.

Transsphenoidal resection of the GH-secreting tumor is the mainstay of therapy. Patients who do not achieve remission can be treated with medical therapy alone or combined with stereotactic irradiation. Somatostatin analogues (e.g., octreotide and lanreotide) are the medications of choice because they decrease tumor size and lower GH levels. Pegvisomant, a GH receptor antagonist, and dopamine agonists, particularly cabergoline, may also be beneficial. After remission is achieved, MRI and IGF-1 levels are monitored annually.

Patients with uncontrolled acromegaly can have increased mortality risk because of heart disease, sleep apnea, and cancer (especially colon cancer), but this risk returns to baseline when IGF-1 levels are maintained in the normal range.

TSH-secreting pituitary tumors are extremely rare. These tumors cause signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism, and laboratory evaluation reveals elevated free T~4 and triiodothyronine levels with an inappropriately normal or elevated TSH level. After other causes of the laboratory abnormalities have been excluded (thyroid assay interference, TSH resistance, or familial dysalbuminemic hyperthyroxinemia), a pituitary MRI should be performed. Transsphenoidal resection of the TSH-producing tumor is the treatment of choice, although medical therapy with somatostatin analogues can be used to control hyperthyroidism before or after surgery (if residual disease is present).

The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) results in water retention with resultant hyponatremia. Central nervous system disorders (trauma, stroke, brain metastases, infection), drugs, pulmonary disease, and pituitary surgery (typically 3-7 days postoperatively) can result in excess release of arginine vasopressin. Because of the frequency of SIADH after pituitary surgery, routine measurement of the serum sodium level in the first 2 days after surgery and then again on postoperative day 7 is recommended. Treatment involves correcting the underlying pathology, fluid restriction, arginine vasopressin receptor antagonists, and hypertonic saline in severe hyponatremia (see Management of Hyponatremia in Nephrology).

The term “Cushing syndrome” describes hypercortisolism regardless of the cause, whereas “Cushing disease” describes hypercortisolism as a result of excess ACTH secretion from a pituitary tumor. ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome is most commonly due to an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma. Rarely, solitary neuroendocrine tumors elsewhere in the body (e.g., lung, pancreas) or metastatic neuroendocrine tumors, such as small cell carcinoma, can secrete ACTH and cause hypercortisolism, which is termed ectopic Cushing syndrome.

Symptoms and signs of Cushing syndrome are listed in [Table: Table: Symptoms and Signs of Cushing Syndrome]

;

shows examples of physical findings.

The diagnosis of endogenous Cushing syndrome is made by first excluding exogenous glucocorticoid administration and establishing evidence of hypercortisolism (see Cortisol Excess (Cushing Syndrome Caused by Adrenal Mass) in Endocrinology and Metabolism). Measuring ACTH establishes whether it is ACTH-dependent or ACTH-independent.

After the diagnosis of ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome is established, a pituitary MRI is needed. If no pituitary tumor is seen or if the tumor is smaller than 6 mm, inferior petrosal sinus sampling is recommended to confirm a pituitary versus ectopic source of ACTH excess. Other dynamic tests that may help differentiate an ectopic source of ACTH excess from Cushing disease include the high-dose (8-mg) dexamethasone suppression test, the corticotropin-releasing hormone stimulation test, and the desmopressin stimulation test.

The treatment of choice for Cushing disease is transsphenoidal resection of the pituitary adenoma. Remission is generally defined by a morning serum cortisol level less than 5 μg/dL (138 nmol/L) within 7 days of surgery. Patients require glucocorticoid replacement postoperatively until the normal corticotroph cells recover from prolonged cortisol suppression. Recovery can take up to 18 months; in some patients, corticotroph cells do not recover, necessitating lifelong cortisol replacement therapy. Glucocorticoid withdrawal symptoms are common after treatment of Cushing disease.

If remission is not achieved after surgery, irradiation with interim medical therapy may be required ( [Table: Table: Medication Management for Treatment of Cushing Syndrome]

). Rarely, bilateral adrenalectomy is required in patients who are unresponsive to all other therapies; these patients require lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement and carry a risk for pituitary tumor enlargement after adrenalectomy (Nelson syndrome) because of unrestrained stimulation of ACTH production.

Patients with Cushing disease require imaging and biochemical follow-up (urinary free cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol measurement) annually for several years and then less frequently. Recurrences are managed by repeat transsphenoidal resection, irradiation, or medical therapy.

Disorders of the Adrenal Glands

The adrenal glands have two functionally distinct regions: an outer cortex and an inner medulla. The adrenal cortex comprises three zones: the zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, and zona reticularis (

).

The zona glomerulosa produces the mineralocorticoid hormone aldosterone under the regulation of the renin-angiotensin system. Major stimuli to aldosterone secretion include hypotension, hypovolemia, and hyperkalemia; adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) is a less potent stimulus of aldosterone release. Aldosterone promotes sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion, and the resultant expansion of extracellular volume increases blood pressure. Aldosterone also has direct inflammatory and fibrotic effects on other organs that are independent of its blood pressure effects.

Cortisol production in the zona fasciculata is regulated by pituitary ACTH release. Cortisol, a glucocorticoid hormone, exhibits a distinct diurnal rhythm characterized by peak levels on awakening, decreasing to very low levels by evening. Most cortisol circulates in the blood attached to cortisol-binding protein, with only a small fraction circulating as biologically active, free hormone. Cortisol levels increase in response to physical illness and psychological stress. Cortisol actions include immune, vascular, anti-inflammatory, and metabolic effects.

Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and its sulfate (DHEAS) are weak androgens produced in the zona reticularis and peripherally converted to testosterone. Similar to cortisol, DHEA production is regulated by ACTH release. In women, the adrenal gland is a significant contributor to circulating androgen levels, and testicular production of androgens is the primary source in men.

The adrenal medulla secretes the catecholamines, norepinephrine and epinephrine, in response to hypotension, hypoglycemia, fear, acute illness, and other causes of psychological and physical stress. Catecholamines interact with α- and β-adrenergic receptors to increase pulse and blood pressure, dilate bronchioles, and increase metabolic rate. A small fraction of norepinephrine and epinephrine is excreted in the urine as free hormone; the rest is degraded in the liver to metanephrine and normetanephrine before urinary excretion.

The most common cause of hypercortisolemia is use of exogenous glucocorticoids. A pituitary adenoma producing ACTH is the most common cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome (ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome) (see Excess Adrenocorticotropic Hormone from Pituitary Source (Cushing Disease) in Endocrinology and Metabolism). Cortisol-secreting adrenal adenomas and, rarely, carcinomas account for 15% to 20% of endogenous causes of Cushing syndrome. Excess cortisol secretion from these tumors suppresses pituitary ACTH production (ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome). Although many of the symptoms and signs of Cushing syndrome are common in the general population, some, including proximal muscle weakness, facial plethora, wide (>1 cm) violaceous striae, and supraclavicular fat pads (

), are more specific to Cushing syndrome. Evaluation for Cushing syndrome should be limited to patients with significant clinical suspicion of disease, including specific signs of Cushing syndrome or an adrenal mass.

After excluding exogenous glucocorticoid use, the first step in evaluating endogenous Cushing syndrome involves initial and confirmatory testing for the presence of nonphysiologic cortisol excess (

). Measuring morning or random serum cortisol is unreliable because serum cortisol levels in Cushing syndrome can overlap with normal levels and the levels seen with mild hypercortisolism or pseudo-Cushing state (i.e., nonneoplastic hypercortisolism resulting from conditions such as alcohol use disorder, chronic kidney disease, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, neuropsychiatric disorders, polycystic ovary syndrome, physical stress, and malnutrition). Additionally, total cortisol levels are unreliable in the presence of abnormal binding proteins, such as in acute illness, liver dysfunction, low protein states, estrogen administration, and pregnancy.

Three initial tests for Cushing syndrome have similar diagnostic accuracy:

  • Serial 24-hour urine free cortisol measurements
  • Serial late-night salivary cortisol measurements
  • Overnight low-dose (1-mg) dexamethasone suppression test (LDST)

Urine free cortisol and late-night salivary cortisol levels reflect the serum free cortisol fraction and avoid the challenges of interpreting changes in cortisol-binding proteins that may occur with the LDST.

Urine free cortisol measurement requires a 24-hour urine collection. Spurious elevation of the urine free cortisol level can result from physiologic hypercortisolism not related to Cushing syndrome (e.g., acute illness, pregnancy) or when significant polyuria (>5 L/d) is present. False-negative results can occur in advanced kidney disease or in patients with variable rates of cortisol secretion.

To measure the late-night salivary cortisol level, the patient collects saliva at home between 11 pm and midnight on at least two different nights. Elevated levels suggest the loss of normal cortisol diurnal rhythm seen in Cushing syndrome. This test is not recommended in patients who do night shift work, have an inconsistent sleep pattern, or have gingivitis. Recent cigarette smoking or contamination by topical glucocorticoids can cause false-positive results.

The LDST depends on the principle that autonomous cortisol secretion is not suppressed by exogenous glucocorticoids. Oral dexamethasone is given at 11 pm, and the serum total cortisol level is measured at 8 am the following morning. A post-dexamethasone serum cortisol level of greater than 1.8 μg/dL (50 nmol/L) is considered a positive result. False-positive results may occur with concomitant use of medications (e.g., carbamazepine, phenytoin, pioglitazone) that induce hepatic cytochrome P450 3A4 enzymes and accelerate dexamethasone metabolism. Simultaneous serum dexamethasone measurement can confirm patient adherence or altered dexamethasone metabolism.

The clinical probability of Cushing syndrome should guide the testing strategy. If the index of suspicion for Cushing syndrome is low, a single negative test makes Cushing syndrome unlikely. If suspicion is high, two different negative initial tests are recommended to rule out disease. Similarly, many factors can raise cortisol levels in the absence of Cushing syndrome; positive test interpretation should incorporate the clinical probability of disease. A urine free cortisol level greater than three times the upper normal range in the setting of clinical manifestations of Cushing syndrome is highly suggestive of the diagnosis, whereas a positive test in the setting of low suspicion does not support the diagnosis alone and requires further testing. If at least one of the initial diagnostic tests is positive, further evaluation should involve consultation with an endocrinologist.

Once the diagnosis of endogenous Cushing syndrome is established, subsequent diagnostic steps include the following:

  • Measuring ACTH to determine whether the patient has ACTH-independent or ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome.
  • Localizing the source of ACTH in ACTH-dependent disease (see Excess Adrenocorticotropic Hormone from Pituitary Source (Cushing Disease) in Endocrinology and Metabolism) or confirming the presence of an adrenal mass or masses in ACTH-independent disease.

If ACTH is suppressed (<5 pg/mL [1.1 pmol/L]), an ACTH-independent cause is likely, and dedicated adrenal CT or MRI is indicated. If adrenal glands appear normal on imaging, the diagnosis of Cushing syndrome should be questioned.

Surgical resection is the definitive treatment for benign and malignant cortisol-secreting adrenal tumors. After adrenalectomy, patients require daily glucocorticoid therapy to allow the contralateral adrenal gland to recover from prolonged ACTH suppression. Recovery of adrenal function may take several years depending on the severity of disease.

Primary aldosteronism is a common cause of secondary hypertension. Some patients have hypokalemia, but most have normal potassium levels. Identifying patients with primary aldosteronism is important because aldosterone has deleterious effects on the cardiovascular system; treatment can prevent progression and can sometimes reverse changes. Higher cardiovascular morbidity and mortality have been noted in patients with primary aldosteronism compared with those with primary hypertension and similar blood pressure control.

The Endocrine Society suggests screening all patients with hypertension for primary aldosteronism. In contrast, the 2025 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association high blood pressure guideline recommends screening in select persons with high risk (see [Table: Table: Indications for Primary Aldosteronism Screening]

) and considering screening in patients with stage 2 hypertension.

Screening for primary aldosteronism involves measuring the plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC) and plasma renin activity (PRA) in a morning seated sample. Potassium should be measured from the same sample to ensure correct interpretation of the results because hypokalemia can falsely lower aldosterone levels. Primary aldosteronism is very likely if both of the following criteria are met:

  • 1: Renin is suppressed and aldosterone is inappropriately elevated:
    • PRA is less than or equal to 1 ng/mL/h

  • PAC is at least 7.5 ng/dL (208 pmol/L) by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS)

  • 2: Aldosterone-to-renin ratio is elevated:

    • PAC/PRA ratio is greater than 15

For aldosterone values measured with immunoassay, different thresholds should be used: PAC of at least 10 ng/dL (277 pmol/L) and PAC/PRA ratio greater than 20.

Multiple medications may affect results but generally do not need to be withdrawn before testing. Some medications raise renin levels and may therefore cause a false-negative result, whereas others lower renin levels and may cause a false-positive result ( [Table: Table: Effects of Medications on PAC/PRA Measurements]

). If a false-negative result is suspected in the context of high pretest probability for primary aldosteronism, the confounding medication should be withdrawn and the patient retested. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone and eplerenone), which are the strongest confounders, and diuretics should be withdrawn for 4 weeks before testing; ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are weaker confounders and may be withdrawn for 2 weeks. Conversely, if a false-positive result is suspected, interfering medications should be withdrawn for 2 weeks. Patients with abnormal test results should be referred to an endocrinologist for further evaluation and management.

Primary aldosteronism is caused by hyperplasia of both adrenal glands (idiopathic hyperaldosteronism) in approximately 60% of patients. A unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma (APA) is found in approximately 35% of patients. Patients with a higher likelihood of bilateral disease, such as those with normal potassium levels and modest aldosterone levels (PAC ≤8 ng/dL [222 pmol/L] by LC-MS/MS or ≤11 ng/dL [305 pmol/L] by immunoassay) should be treated with medical therapy. A unilateral APA is more likely in younger patients or patients with spontaneous hypokalemia, completely suppressed renin activity, or more elevated aldosterone levels. Patients who may have an APA require further specialized testing, which may include confirmatory testing and lateralization studies, as they may be candidates for surgery.

Medical therapy with an aldosterone receptor antagonist (spironolactone or eplerenone) is the treatment of choice for primary aldosteronism caused by nonlateralizing disease (idiopathic hyperaldosteronism) and in patients with APAs who are not candidates for or decline surgery. Medical therapy is also indicated for patients who do not have access to an endocrinologist or a center with adrenal vein sampling. Spironolactone is often preferred over eplerenone because it is less expensive and more potent. However, spironolactone is more likely to cause dose-dependent adverse effects of gynecomastia and erectile dysfunction in men and menstrual irregularities in women. Hypokalemia almost always resolves with treatment, but blood pressure control may require additional agents.

Laparoscopic adrenalectomy is effective for patients with a unilateral APA, as it reduces PAC and the attendant increased risk for cardiovascular disease. No randomized studies clearly show the superiority of adrenalectomy compared with medical therapy for APAs, but surgery may be more cost-effective in the long term. Before surgery, a dedicated adrenal CT scan should be completed, which may show normal adrenal glands, unilateral or bilateral adrenal adenoma(s), or hyperplasia. Small APAs may not be visualized on CT scan, and nonfunctioning incidental adrenal masses are also common. Thus, most patients will undergo adrenal vein sampling before surgery to confirm the source of aldosterone. After adrenalectomy, hypertension is improved in most patients and cured in some. Serum potassium levels should be monitored weekly for the first month postoperatively. Patients should eat a sodium-rich diet to avoid the risk for hyperkalemia from a transient reduction in aldosterone production in the remaining adrenal gland because of chronic suppression from hyperaldosteronism.

Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas are catecholamine-secreting tumors that arise from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla (80% to 85%) and extra-adrenal (mostly abdominal) sympathetic ganglia, respectively. Tumors can also arise from parasympathetic ganglia in the head and neck but are rarely secretory.

Hypertension associated with pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma can show a sustained pattern, with or without paroxysms, or occur as paroxysms only. Some patients remain normotensive. Fewer than 50% of patients have the classic triad of palpitations, headache, and diaphoresis.

Indications for testing for pheochromocytoma are shown in [Table: Table: Case Detection Indications for Pheochromocytoma/Paraganglioma]

. Initial tests include measurement of plasma fractionated metanephrines (i.e., free metanephrine and free normetanephrine) collected in a supine position or 24-hour urine fractionated metanephrine and catecholamine levels. The presence of psychological or physical stress and substances/medications can affect results ( [Table: Table: Substances Associated With Pheochromocytoma False-Positives]

); medications should be discontinued at least 2 weeks before testing if possible. Interpretation of results must consider the extent of metanephrine elevation, and mild elevations may necessitate repeat testing. Levels more than four times the upper limit of normal, in the absence of acute stress or illness, are consistent with a catecholamine-secreting tumor.

Plasma fractionated metanephrines measurement is highly sensitive (96% to 100%), with a specificity of 85% to 89%. Urine fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines have better specificity (98%) and sensitivity (up to 97%). Plasma fractionated metanephrines testing is more convenient and is often chosen if the index of suspicion is high. If suspicion is low, urine fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines may be a better option. The clinical relevance of significantly elevated metanephrine levels in hospitalized patients is often uncertain, and testing generally should be confirmed in the outpatient setting. Measurement of plasma 3-methoxytyramine, a metabolite of dopamine, may be indicated in patients with certain genetic variants; however, routine testing is not recommended.

Tumor localization should only be attempted after establishing the biochemical diagnosis of catecholamine excess to avoid misdiagnosing an incidental nonfunctioning adrenal mass as a pheochromocytoma. The imaging modality of choice is abdominal and pelvic contrast-enhanced CT because 85% of catecholamine-secreting tumors are intra-adrenal, with 95% residing in the abdomen or pelvis. Typical imaging features of pheochromocytomas are shown in [Table: Table: Typical Imaging Characteristics of Adrenal Masses]

.

If the CT scan is negative and suspicion of a catecholamine-secreting tumor is high, the next step is advanced nuclear imaging, including gallium-68 DOTATATE-PET, fluorodeoxyglucose-PET, iodine 123-metaiodobenzylguanidine, or octreotide scanning. Advanced imaging may also be indicated in patients with very large pheochromocytomas (>10 cm) to detect metastatic disease or in patients with paragangliomas to detect multifocal disease. Fluorodeoxyglucose-PET scanning is more sensitive for detecting metastatic disease, but its use is generally reserved for patients with established metastatic tumors.

The definitive treatment for pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma is surgical resection. Preoperative α-receptor blockade with phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin for 10 to 14 days before surgery is essential to prevent hypertensive crises during surgery. The dosage is progressively increased to achieve a blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg or less with a pulse rate of 60 to 70/min seated and a systolic blood pressure of 90 mm Hg or higher with a pulse rate of 70 to 80/min standing. To mitigate adverse effects of volume contraction, patients are instructed to increase salt and fluid intake while α-receptor blockade is titrated. A β-blocker is added after α-blockade is achieved to manage reflex tachycardia, but it should never be started before adequate α-blockade because unopposed α-adrenergic vasoconstriction can result in a hypertensive crisis. Postoperatively, patients can have significant hypotension, and most require fluid and vasopressor support at least briefly.

Most pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas are benign. Pathologic findings do not predict which tumors will develop metastases. Because metastases can occur decades after the initial diagnosis, patients should undergo long-term annual biochemical screening, typically with plasma fractionated metanephrines.

As many as 40% of pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas are associated with a germline variant, including multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 ( [Table: Table: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Syndromes]

), von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, and neurofibromatosis type 1. Therefore, all patients with pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas should be offered genetic counseling.

Androgen-producing adrenal tumors are rare and in women may lead to menstrual irregularities and virilization, including hirsutism, voice-deepening, increased muscle mass, increased libido, and clitoromegaly. Androgen-secreting tumors of the adrenal gland are readily visible on CT imaging, and adrenal vein sampling is rarely required to localize the tumor. The treatment of choice is resection. In women with elevated androgen levels and signs of virilization with negative adrenal imaging, an ovarian source should be suspected, and the ovaries should be imaged (see Evaluation of Hyperandrogenism in Endocrinology and Metabolism).

Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) is a rare, aggressive tumor that often secretes excess hormones. Approximately 50% of ACCs secrete cortisol alone; approximately 20% to 30% secrete several hormones, including cortisol and androgens; and fewer than 10% secrete aldosterone alone. Patients may present with rapid onset of Cushing syndrome, with or without virilization, or symptoms from mass effect, such as increased abdominal girth and lower extremity edema. Disease is often at an advanced stage when diagnosed, but some ACCs are discovered as an incidental adrenal mass (see [Table: Table: Typical Imaging Characteristics of Adrenal Masses]

).

For localized disease, first-line therapy includes open resection. Debulking surgery, radiation therapy, or chemotherapy may also be options for palliation in advanced ACC. Mitotane is an adrenolytic agent commonly used as adjuvant therapy and is associated with longer recurrence-free survival. Mitotane causes primary adrenal insufficiency (AI), and daily glucocorticoid replacement therapy is required, often in supraphysiologic doses; fludrocortisone replacement may also be required. Five-year survival rates range from 62% to 82% for patients with disease confined to the adrenal gland and 13% for those with tumors associated with distant metastases.

The most common cause of primary AI (Addison disease) is autoimmune adrenalitis, which is an autoimmune destruction of all layers of the adrenal cortex leading to progressive mineralocorticoid, glucocorticoid, and adrenal androgen deficiency. Approximately 90% of patients have 21-hydroxylase antibodies, and approximately 50% will develop another autoimmune endocrine disorder in their lifetime (primary hypothyroidism, primary ovarian insufficiency, hypoparathyroidism, or type 1 diabetes), which is termed autoimmune polyglandular syndrome. Celiac disease also occurs with increased frequency.

Primary AI can also be caused by infiltrative disorders, such as tuberculous/fungal infections, sarcoidosis, and lymphoma, and genetic disorders such as adrenoleukodystrophy (X-linked). Patients with classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia have primary AI (sometimes glucocorticoid deficiency only) and require lifelong treatment. Metastatic disease involving the adrenal glands rarely leads to AI even if both adrenal glands are involved.

Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage can present as acute AI and should be considered if unexpected hypotension develops. Risk factors include protein C deficiency, anticoagulation, disseminated intravascular coagulopathy, and sepsis.

Primary AI is a life-threatening disorder that often presents with insidious symptom onset, making diagnosis a challenge. Clinical and laboratory manifestations are described in [Table: Table: Manifestations of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency]

. Primary AI may also present as adrenal crisis, often precipitated by an acute illness or the initiation of thyroid hormone replacement in a patient with unrecognized chronic AI. ACTH levels are high because diminished adrenal cortisol production leads to decreased negative feedback to the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. Although not present in all patients, skin hyperpigmentation from stimulation of melanocytes by high levels of melanocyte-stimulating hormone (which has the same precursor molecule as ACTH) is considered a hallmark of primary AI.

Initial evaluation includes measuring 8 am serum total cortisol and response to ACTH stimulation. Measuring adrenal androgen levels with DHEAS may also aid in diagnosis; DHEAS levels are low in primary AI. An algorithm for diagnosing AI is outlined in

. Primary AI is confirmed by the combination of low serum cortisol and elevated serum ACTH levels. Additional evaluation may include assessment for autoimmune adrenalitis by measuring 21-hydroxylase antibodies; CT of the adrenal glands may be necessary if antibodies are absent.

Both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid therapy are required to treat primary AI. The preferred glucocorticoid is hydrocortisone taken two or three times daily. Adherence to several daily doses can be challenging, so once-daily prednisone can be used as an alternative ( [Table: Table: Dose Equivalence and Relative Potencies of Glucocorticoids]

). The principle of replacement is to administer a higher dose in the morning and to avoid replacement in the evening. Despite this attempt to mimic diurnal variation, patients with primary AI report decreased health-related quality of life. Avoiding glucocorticoid overreplacement is imperative to avoid the consequences of iatrogenic Cushing syndrome. Mineralocorticoid replacement is achieved with daily fludrocortisone.

Patients cannot mount an appropriate increase in cortisol with illness; therefore, instruction in “sick day” rules is essential to prevent adrenal crisis ( [Table: Table: Chronic Medical Treatment of Primary Adrenal Failure]

). Patients should be counseled to wear a medical alert identification, be prescribed an emergency kit that includes a high-dose injectable glucocorticoid, and be counseled to seek medical attention if vomiting prevents them from taking steroid medications. Patients with untreated concomitant AI and hypothyroidism should always receive glucocorticoid replacement therapy first to prevent precipitation of adrenal crisis by thyroid hormone replacement.

During times of physiologic stress, such as critical illness, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis is stimulated to produce increased levels of cortisol; this increase is necessary and part of normal physiology. High cortisol levels in this setting do not typically require further evaluation in the absence of other symptoms or signs suggesting an adrenal disorder. In some patients, the increase in cortisol secretion is thought to be suboptimal and termed relative AI or critical illness–related corticosteroid insufficiency. However, whether the entity of relative AI is a true disease is debated. Cortisol-binding globulin and albumin decrease in critical illness, lowering the measured total cortisol level. No diagnostic criteria for relative AI have been agreed on, despite the ability to measure free cortisol, calculated free cortisol, and basal and ACTH-stimulated total cortisol levels in critically ill patients. Studies do not show improved survival in patients with relative AI treated with high-dose glucocorticoids. Shock reversal, however, may be improved. Therefore, stress-dose hydrocortisone should be administered to patients with shock that is resistant to standard fluid and vasopressor therapy.

An adrenal incidentaloma is an adrenal mass larger than 1 cm in diameter that is detected on imaging performed for purposes other than investigating suspected adrenal disease (

). The prevalence of adrenal incidentaloma increases with age and is approximately 1% to 9% in adults. Most lesions are benign adenomas, but approximately 20% to 50% secrete excess hormones. Other causes of adrenal masses are metastases (increased probability with known primary malignancy), myelolipoma, cysts, and adrenocortical carcinoma.

The finding of an incidental adrenal mass prompts two questions:

  • Is the mass secreting excess hormone (aldosterone, cortisol, catecholamines, or androgens)?
  • Is the mass benign or malignant?

Biochemical testing should be completed in all patients with an incidental adrenal mass ( [Table: Table: Functional Assessment of an Incidental Adrenal Mass]

). All patients with an adrenal incidentaloma should undergo testing for hypercortisolism. Although Cushing syndrome may occur with adrenal incidentalomas, mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS; previously termed subclinical Cushing syndrome) is seen more commonly. MACS is characterized by ACTH-independent cortisol secretion that may result in metabolic (hyperglycemia and hypertension) and bone (osteoporosis) effects of hypercortisolism. However, the more specific clinical features of full Cushing syndrome, such as wide violaceous striae, supraclavicular fat pads (see

), and facial plethora, do not occur in MACS. Initial testing for MACS is achieved with an overnight LDST. A serum cortisol level of 1.8 μg/dL (50 nmol/L) or lower excludes autonomous cortisol secretion, and a level greater than 1.8 μg/dL (50 nmol/L) is evidence of a positive test. After a positive result, ACTH-independency (ACTH is suppressed) should be confirmed. The decision of whether to proceed to adrenalectomy in MACS is complex; decision-making should be shared with an endocrinologist. Hormonal testing for conditions other than MACS is dependent on clinical and radiologic features (see [Table: Table: Functional Assessment of an Incidental Adrenal Mass]

). If testing suggests that an incidental adrenal mass is functional (secretory), referral to an endocrinologist is recommended. Patients with normal biochemical testing on initial assessment do not need repeat hormone testing unless clinical signs or symptoms change.

Imaging findings can help characterize adrenal masses (see [Table: Table: Typical Imaging Characteristics of Adrenal Masses]

) as benign or malignant. An algorithm for management of adrenal incidentaloma, including monitoring of lesions that do not require adrenalectomy, is shown in

Biopsy has a very limited role in evaluating incidentalomas and is reserved for lesions suspicious for metastases, lymphoma, or an infiltrative process, including some infections. Biopsy should not be performed when a primary adrenocortical carcinoma is suspected because tumor seeding is possible, and the diagnosis cannot be made based on cytopathology alone. This diagnosis should be established by adrenalectomy. If biopsy is pursued, pheochromocytoma must be ruled out with biochemical testing before biopsy to avoid the possibility of a hypertensive crisis.
