Disorders of the Thyroid Gland

The thyroid consists of right and left lobes connected by a median isthmus that is anterior to the second to fourth tracheal rings. The parathyroids are behind the right and left thyroid lobes, two superiorly and two inferiorly. The recurrent laryngeal nerves course behind the thyroid. Because of the thyroid’s proximity to the trachea, esophagus, and recurrent laryngeal nerves, thyroid pathology may cause compressive symptoms including dyspnea, cough, dysphagia, and hoarseness.

The thyroid contains parafollicular cells (also called C cells) and follicular cells. Parafollicular cells produce calcitonin, which inhibits bone resorption, playing a minor role in bone physiology. Follicular cells produce thyroxine (T~4) and triiodothyronine (T~3)~. The hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis regulates thyroid hormone synthesis and secretion. Hypothalamic thyrotropin-releasing hormone triggers the pulsatile release of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) from the anterior pituitary (for more information on the pituitary gland and the hormones it secretes, see Hypothalamic and Pituitary Anatomy and Physiology in Endocrinology and Metabolism). TSH stimulates thyroid cell growth, iodide uptake, and thyroid hormone synthesis and secretion. T~4 and T~3 exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, further moderating hormone synthesis.

The thyroid is the exclusive source of T~4, whereas approximately 80% of T~3 is from peripheral T~4 deiodination, primarily in the liver and kidneys. Most T~4 (99.96%) and T~3 (99.6%) is bound to serum proteins, with approximately 70% of T~4 and T~3 bound to thyroxine-binding globulin. Albumin, transthyretin, and lipoproteins carry a smaller proportion. Only free T~4 and T~3 are biologically available. T~4 serves as a prohormone, and T~3 binds with high affinity to cellular nuclear receptors affecting gene transcription in target tissues. T~3 has positive cardiac inotropic and chronotropic effects, enhances myocardial adrenergic sensitivity, increases myocardial diastolic relaxation, augments intravascular volume, and lowers peripheral vascular resistance. T~3 also increases gastrointestinal motility, bone turnover, heat generation, and energy expenditure.

The thyroid is located in the neck between the sternal notch and thyroid cartilage. It attaches to the trachea posteriorly and elevates with swallowing and neck extension. Examination involves both inspection and palpation, including while the patient swallows liquid, with the neck slightly extended (Video: Thyroid Examination). With the examiner behind the patient, circumferential hand positioning allows focusing on palpation. With the examiner facing the patient, inspection of the thyroid during palpation is possible. The anterior approach is preferred for larger-diameter necks.

Palpable thyroid nodules are found in 5% of women and 1% of men (Video: Thyroid Nodule). The prevalence of thyroid nodules on ultrasonography is between 20% and 68%, with the incidence increasing with age.

Causes of thyroid nodules range from benign cysts and inflammatory nodules to malignancies, including primary thyroid cancer, lymphoma, or metastases. Nonthyroidal lesions, such as parathyroid adenomas, can also present as thyroid nodules. Primary thyroid neoplasms include follicular adenomas and thyroid cancer. Approximately 5% of thyroid nodules contain malignancy. Approximately 35% of incidental thyroid nodules identified on PET scan may be malignant. Family history suggestive of multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) 2A and 2B (i.e., pheochromocytoma, medullary thyroid cancer, primary hyperparathyroidism) increases the risk for medullary thyroid cancer.

The initial evaluation of a thyroid nodule begins with measuring the TSH level and evaluating sonographic characteristics with an ultrasound (

). TSH suppression is found with autonomously functioning or “hot” nodules, accounting for 5% to 10% of palpable thyroid nodules. Patients with thyroid nodules and a suppressed TSH level are further evaluated with thyroid scintigraphy. A radioactive isotope, preferably iodine 123 (^123I), is administered; the percentage taken up by the thyroid is calculated (radioactive iodine uptake [RAIU]), and an image is obtained (thyroid scan). Hot nodules concentrate radioactive iodine to a greater extent than normal thyroid tissue (

). Autonomous hot nodules have a very low risk for malignancy and rarely require fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB).

If the TSH level is normal or elevated, symptoms and ultrasound appearance guide the management of nonfunctioning nodules. The 2015 American Thyroid Association guidelines classify thyroid nodules into five sonographic patterns based on echogenicity; whether they are solid, cystic, or both; and features of malignancy. These characteristics and nodule size determine the need for biopsy ( [Table: Table: Sonographic Patterns and Recommendations for FNAB]

). FNAB is not recommended for subcentimeter nodules unless associated with symptoms, pathologic lymphadenopathy, extrathyroidal extension, history of childhood radiation exposure, or a familial thyroid cancer syndrome.

Another system for classifying nodules and their risk for malignancy is the American College of Radiology Thyroid Imaging, Reporting and Data System (ACR TI-RADS). Thyroid nodules are classified at levels from TR1 to TR5 based on points given for suspicious sonographic features. The higher the number of points, the higher the TR level and the likelihood of malignancy ( [Table: Table: TI-RADS Categories and Recommendations for Management]

). Patients with a TR3 nodule measuring 2.5 cm or larger, a TR4 nodule measuring 1.5 cm or larger, or TR5 nodule that is 1.0 cm or larger should undergo FNAB.

Thyroid nodule FNAB should be performed under ultrasound guidance because of improved accuracy. Thyroid cytopathology is interpreted and classified according to the 2023 Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology (also called TBSRTC):

  • Benign (risk for malignancy 2%-7%)
  • Atypia of undetermined significance (risk for malignancy 13%-30%)
  • Follicular neoplasm (risk for malignancy 23%-34%)
  • Suspicious for malignancy (risk for malignancy 67%-83%)
  • Malignant (risk for malignancy 97%-100%)
  • Nondiagnostic (risk for malignancy 5%-20%)

Approximately 60% to 70% of biopsied nodules have benign cytology, 20% are indeterminate, and 5% to 10% have evidence of malignancy. Thyroid FNAB cytology can be nondiagnostic in 5% to 10% of specimens.

Management is directed by FNAB cytopathology. For lesions with benign cytology, ultrasound should be repeated in 12 to 24 months; however, if the nodule had an American Thyroid Association “high suspicion” ultrasound pattern (see [Table: Table: Sonographic Patterns and Recommendations for FNAB]

), ultrasound and FNAB should be repeated within 12 months. For patients with atypia of undetermined significance or follicular neoplasm, repeat FNAB and molecular testing can further determine malignancy risk; otherwise, diagnostic surgery may be indicated. A suspicious pattern on molecular testing should be followed by thyroid surgery. Patients with cytopathology findings that are malignant or suspicious for malignancy should be referred for surgery. Repeat FNAB is necessary for nodules that are classified as nondiagnostic.

Clinical monitoring is indicated for all thyroid nodules not surgically removed and should include TSH measurement because of the increased risk for thyroid dysfunction (see Disorders of Thyroid Function in Endocrinology and Metabolism). The American Thyroid Association sonographic pattern and the clinical context guide follow-up timing after the initial ultrasound for benign nodules and nodules not evaluated with FNAB. Repeat ultrasonography should be performed within 12 months for all high-suspicion nodules, 12 to 24 months for intermediate- and low-suspicion nodules, and 24 months or longer for very low-suspicion nodules. Repeat FNAB is indicated for all high-suspicion nodules, nodules with concerning new sonographic findings, and intermediate- or low-suspicion nodules that increase 20% in at least two dimensions or by 50% in nodule volume. Repeat FNAB is not recommended for nodules with two benign biopsy results. ACR TI-RADS recommendations for the timing of follow-up ultrasounds for nodules that do not meet biopsy thresholds are presented in [Table: Table: TI-RADS Categories and Recommendations for Management]

.

Goiter is an enlarged thyroid (

). Goiters can be associated with normal thyroid function, hypothyroidism, or hyperthyroidism. The most common cause worldwide is iodine deficiency.

Patients with goiter should be questioned about iodine intake, rate of change in size, and thyroid cancer risk factors (see Thyroid Cancer in Endocrinology and Metabolism). Clinical history should focus on symptoms of thyroid hormone excess or deficiency and compression. Compressive symptoms include dyspnea, cough, dysphagia, and voice changes, which are evident in 10% to 20% of patients with goiter.

Examination should note the thyroid size, symmetry, and consistency as well as the presence of nodules or adenopathy and tracheal deviation. Possible venous obstruction is assessed with the patient’s arms raised above the head. The findings of jugular venous distension, facial plethora, and flushing indicate thoracic outlet obstruction with reduced venous return (

).

The first laboratory step to assess goiter is TSH measurement. If low, free T~4 and total T~3 should be measured and thyroid scintigraphy performed. If normal or elevated, thyroid ultrasonography is indicated in patients at risk for thyroid cancer or if palpable thyroid nodules, gland asymmetry, large goiter, rapid growth, or compressive symptoms are present. Patients with signs or symptoms of compression require additional testing (see Multinodular Goiter in Endocrinology and Metabolism), and surgery may be needed for symptomatic management. Treatment of hypothyroid and hyperthyroid conditions in the setting of goiter is discussed later throughout the text.

Multinodular goiter (MNG) (

) is the most common cause of thyroid enlargement in older adults in the United States. Evaluation includes TSH measurement. For patients in whom TSH is not suppressed, thyroid ultrasonography should be performed and discrete nodules evaluated (see Thyroid Nodules in Endocrinology and Metabolism). The frequency of malignancy in patients with MNG is similar to the frequency in those with solitary thyroid nodules.

Signs and symptoms of compression or suspected substernal extension require additional testing. CT or MRI of the neck and chest (when substernal goiter is suspected) can define anatomic relationships and assess for tracheal narrowing. Administration of iodinated contrast should be avoided, if possible, because of the potential to precipitate iodine-induced hyperthyroidism (Jod-Basedow phenomenon). A flow-volume loop study is indicated in patients with symptoms of airway compression or when the tracheal lumen measures less than 1 cm in diameter on CT or MRI (see Pulmonary Function Testing Interpretation in Pulmonary Medicine). Endoscopy or a swallowing study can assess for extrinsic esophageal compression in patients with cervical dysphagia. Consultation with an otolaryngologist is indicated to confirm clinically suspected vocal cord paralysis.

Surgery is indicated for significant compression or suspected malignancy.

The most common cause of diffuse goiter in the United States is autoimmune thyroid disease associated with thyroid dysfunction (more commonly Graves disease than Hashimoto thyroiditis). Rare causes of diffuse goiter are infiltrative disorders, such as Riedel (IgG4-related) thyroiditis. Diffuse goiter may also occur in euthyroid patients in the absence of predisposing inflammatory or neoplastic processes. Genetic predisposition, iodine insufficiency, and cigarette smoking are contributing factors.

Thyroid ultrasonography is indicated in euthyroid patients with diffuse goiter. Ultrasonography is also recommended for patients with Graves disease or Hashimoto thyroiditis when examination shows thyroid asymmetry or nodules. Additional testing is indicated if compressive signs or symptoms are present. Thyroid surgery is considered in the setting of significant compression.

Thyroid cancer is the most common endocrine malignancy. Thyroid cancer incidence has increased during the past four decades and now is the fifth most common cancer in women. Much of this change is attributable to increased incidental radiographic diagnosis of small, noninvasive cancers. Mortality rates have remained stable, with an overall 5-year survival rate of 98.1%, suggesting the possible overdiagnosis of clinically insignificant tumors. Routine screening for thyroid cancer in persons at low risk is not recommended.

Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and follicular thyroid carcinoma make up most of the thyroid cancer diagnoses in the United States. PTC commonly spreads to cervical lymph nodes but is associated with a low risk for distant metastases. In follicular thyroid carcinoma, lymph node spread is rare, but metastases to lung, bone, and other sites are possible.

Risk factors for thyroid cancer include a history of ionizing radiation exposure and a personal or family history of thyroid cancer. PTC is increased in those exposed to ionizing radiation, with the highest risk for patients with childhood exposures, such as childhood cancer treatment, and with nuclear accidents. Rapid nodule growth; a hard, fixed nodule; dysphagia; hoarseness; and cervical lymphadenopathy suggest malignancy. The diagnosis is confirmed by FNAB.

Surgery is the mainstay of thyroid cancer treatment, and no additional treatment is needed for low-risk papillary thyroid cancer that is completely resected. Risks of thyroid surgery include hypocalcemia from parathyroid injury or removal and difficulty breathing or voice changes from recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.

Postoperative radioactive iodine therapy (with iodine 131 [^131I]) should be considered for patients with differentiated thyroid cancer with an intermediate to high recurrence risk. After ^131I therapy, whole-body scanning can identify areas of ^131I uptake corresponding to metastatic disease (

). ^131I therapy also treats cancer recurrences not amenable to resection.

Treatment of high-risk differentiated thyroid cancer also includes TSH suppression with daily levothyroxine. Thyroid follicular cells are TSH responsive, as are most well-differentiated thyroid cancers. Levothyroxine is administered lifelong to suppress the TSH level, with the target TSH level determined by the recurrence risk.

After initial cancer treatment with total thyroidectomy and ^131I ablation, serum thyroglobulin (Tg), which is produced only by the thyroid, and Tg antibody (TgAb) titers are monitored. Persistent Tg levels suggest recurrent or persistent disease. When TgAb is present, Tg levels are uninterpretable because TgAb can falsely lower Tg. In such instances, the TgAb serves as a surrogate marker. A decreasing TgAb titer over time correlates with a favorable prognosis, whereas an increasing titer is suspicious for persistent or recurrent disease.

Thyroid ultrasonography is repeated in routine thyroid cancer surveillance, 6 to 12 months after the initial cancer treatment. In patients at high risk for recurrent disease, diagnostic ^123I or ^131I whole-body scanning with TSH-stimulated serum Tg measurement can be performed. If residual or recurrent thyroid cancer is suspected, such as when serum Tg is persistently elevated or increasing over time, but not identified by neck ultrasonography or ^131I whole-body scanning, CT, MRI, bone scan, or fluorodeoxyglucose-PET/CT scan can be useful.

Metastatic thyroid cancer is managed with active surveillance, additional surgery, or ^131I therapy, as well as external beam radiation therapy and/or chemotherapy (tyrosine kinase inhibitors).

Anaplastic thyroid cancer is a rare, aggressive thyroid malignancy occurring de novo or in patients with preexisting differentiated thyroid cancer. Anaplastic thyroid cancer presents with a rapidly enlarging neck mass and may be unresectable at the time of diagnosis. The median survival for these patients is 5 months. Treatment is palliative in most patients and includes surgery, external beam radiation therapy, and chemotherapy.

Medullary thyroid cancer arises from parafollicular cells. Germline RET oncogene variants occur with familial medullary thyroid cancer and MEN 2A and 2B. MEN should be ruled out with RET genetic testing before surgery; if present, the patient should be screened for pheochromocytoma with measurement of plasma fractionated metanephrines. Pheochromocytoma should be treated first if present. If screening for pheochromocytoma is negative, repeat screening should be performed annually, or sooner if symptoms develop. Medullary thyroid cancer is treated with total thyroidectomy and central neck lymph node dissection. Levothyroxine is indicated to treat postoperative hypothyroidism in patients with medullary thyroid cancer, with a goal TSH level within the reference range. Serum calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen measurement and neck ultrasonography are part of routine cancer surveillance.

TSH is the most sensitive thyroid function test in patients with normal pituitary function. If TSH is suppressed, free T~4 and total T~3 should be assessed to detect overt or subclinical hyperthyroidism. If TSH is elevated, free T~4 should be assessed to detect overt or subclinical hypothyroidism. Measuring TSH alone as an initial test is sufficient except in suspected central hypothyroidism, for which simultaneous free T~4 measurement is needed (see Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone Deficiency in Endocrinology and Metabolism). Thyroid function should not be assessed in hospitalized patients unless clinical suspicion of thyroid dysfunction is strong (see Nonthyroidal Illness Syndrome in Endocrinology and Metabolism).

Total and free T~4 and total T~3 concentrations can be assessed with various assays that are accurate in most patients with overt thyroid dysfunction; commercially available free T~3 assays are less reliable. More than 99% of thyroid hormone circulates bound to protein, particularly thyroxine-binding globulin. Therefore, total T~4 and T~3 levels vary based on binding protein levels and may not reflect actual thyroid function. T~4-binding protein alterations occur with physiologic changes (pregnancy), certain disease states (nephrotic syndrome), and medication effects (oral estrogen therapy). Free T~4, the unbound fraction of T~4 in serum, is measured using widely available immunometric assays. These tests are accurate in most clinical settings, including in patients with mild binding protein alterations.

Multiple medications affect thyroid function and thyroid hormone replacement ( [Table: Table: Medications That Affect the Thyroid]

). Patients taking more than 5 to 10 mg/d of biotin (recommended dietary intake of biotin is 30 μg/d), a common over-the-counter supplement, should discontinue it 2 to 5 days before thyroid function testing. Biotin interference causes falsely high free T~4, free T~3, total T~4, and total T~3 and falsely low TSH levels, mimicking thyrotoxicosis.

Total T~3 measurement in the setting of hypothyroidism is not necessary or recommended; normal levels are maintained unless hypothyroidism is severe. TSH increases first in hypothyroidism, followed by a decrease in free T~4.

Total T~3 measurement in hyperthyroidism is recommended in three settings:

  • Evaluating thyrotoxicosis to identify isolated T~3 toxicosis
  • Assessing hyperthyroidism severity and therapeutic response
  • Differentiating hyperthyroidism from destructive thyroiditis

In T~3 toxicosis, the T~3-to-T~4 ratio is often greater than 20 because of preferential secretion of T~3.

Reverse T~3 measurement is rarely recommended.

Thyrotoxicosis describes high levels of circulating thyroid hormones (T~4 and T~3) from any cause. Hyperthyroidism is thyrotoxicosis caused by excessive endogenous thyroid hormone production. The prevalence of hyperthyroidism in the United States is 1.3%. In primary hyperthyroidism, the thyroid is the anatomic site of dysfunction. Increased TSH secretion is a rare secondary cause of hyperthyroidism (see Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone–Secreting Tumors in Endocrinology and Metabolism).

[Table: Table: Manifestations of Thyrotoxicosis and Thyroid Hormone Deficiency]

lists signs and symptoms of thyrotoxicosis. In older adults, however, thyrotoxicosis may be apathetic and present with nonclassical symptoms and signs. Lid lag (eyelid retraction) can be seen in thyrotoxicosis of any cause resulting from increased adrenergic tone.

Thyrotoxicosis is diagnosed with a low TSH level and elevated free T~4 and/or total T~3 levels. Once the diagnosis of thyrotoxicosis has been established, the cause should be determined (

). The presence of a diffuse goiter and recently developed thyroid eye disease (exophthalmos, conjunctival inflammation, periorbital edema) is sufficient for a diagnosis of Graves disease. In these patients, thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) or thyrotropin (TSH) receptor antibody (TRAb) testing is not necessary for diagnosis; however, obtaining a baseline level can help to guide treatment.

If the cause of thyrotoxicosis is not definitive based on clinical presentation, additional evaluation is required. If the patient does not have a nodular goiter, measuring TSI or TRAb levels can identify Graves disease with high sensitivity and specificity. Third-generation TRAb measurement may provide a quicker and more cost-efficient diagnosis than thyroid scintigraphy in this presentation. Thyroid scintigraphy with RAIU can verify the cause of thyrotoxicosis and is especially recommended in patients with nodular thyroid disease. RAIU is high (>30%) (

) or inappropriately normal in hyperthyroidism and low (<10%) in other causes of thyrotoxicosis, such as destructive thyroiditis or exogenous thyroid hormone ingestion (

).

Additional testing may be indicated when the clinical diagnosis is unclear, when RAIU is unavailable or unreliable because of exposure to iodine (amiodarone, iodinated contrast) or lithium, or when scintigraphy is contraindicated (in pregnancy and lactation). Thyroid ultrasonography to evaluate for blood flow may be helpful to determine the cause of thyrotoxicosis. This test may show increased vascularity in Graves disease or hyperfunctioning nodules and decreased blood flow in patients with destructive thyroiditis (

).

Causes of thyrotoxicosis are listed in [Table: Table: Causes of Thyrotoxicosis]

. Graves disease, toxic MNG, and toxic adenoma are the most common causes of hyperthyroidism, and each demonstrates a distinctive pattern of RAIU on scintigraphy (

). A variety of medications can also cause thyrotoxicosis (see Medication-Induced Thyroid Dysfunction in Endocrinology and Metabolism).

Graves disease can affect the thyroid, ocular muscles, and skin. In iodine-sufficient geographic areas, this disease causes 80% of hyperthyroidism cases. Graves disease is an autoimmune thyroid disorder that occurs primarily in women, peaking among patients aged 30 to 60 years. It is more common in patients with other autoimmune disorders or a family history of thyroid autoimmunity. T lymphocytes become sensitized to thyroid antigens and stimulate B lymphocytes to produce TSI or TRAb.

The thyroid is diffusely enlarged, may have a bruit, and has a firm, smooth texture on examination; cervical lymphadenopathy may also occur. Systolic hypertension; tachycardia; hyperreflexia; and warm, moist skin are often present, although older patients may have an atypical presentation. Patients with Graves disease and thyroid asymmetry or nodules on examination should be evaluated with ultrasonography.

Thyroid eye disease (also called Graves ophthalmopathy) affects up to 40% of patients with Graves disease. Cigarette smoking is a risk factor and an aggravating factor. Clinical manifestations include periorbital edema, chemosis (conjunctival edema), conjunctival hyperemia, exophthalmos (protrusion of the globe) (

), diplopia (due to oculomotor paresis), and vision loss. Thyroid eye disease does not respond to the treatment of hyperthyroidism and should prompt evaluation by an ophthalmologist. Patients with moderate to severe disease may require glucocorticoids, surgery, rituximab, tocilizumab, or teprotumumab, a human monoclonal antibody inhibitor of the insulin-like growth factor-1 receptor.

Pretibial myxedema (

) is a rare infiltrative dermopathy of Graves disease affecting 2% to 3% of patients.

Toxic adenoma and MNG typically affect older adults. Thyroid nodules may produce thyroid hormones independent of TSH stimulation. Exposure to iodine (iodinated contrast in CT scanning or cardiac catheterization, amiodarone) may change a nontoxic adenoma to a toxic adenoma.

Destructive thyroiditis releases, in unregulated fashion, preformed thyroid hormone from inflamed, damaged thyroid follicles. Causes are listed in [Table: Table: Causes of Destructive Thyroiditis]

. Thyroiditis typically has three phases: thyrotoxic, hypothyroid, and return to euthyroidism. The first two phases can last up to 3 months each. Patients have increased risk for additional bouts of thyroiditis after the initial thyroiditis has resolved.

Most patients with thyrotoxicosis benefit from β-blockers to reduce adrenergic symptoms rapidly. Atenolol and metoprolol are preferred because of once-daily dosing and their cardioselective nature. High-dose propranolol has the added benefit of decreasing the peripheral conversion of T~4 to T~3, but it is noncardioselective and requires two- or three-times-daily dosing.

The three treatment modalities for hyperthyroidism are the following:

  • Thionamides (methimazole and propylthiouracil [PTU])
  • ^131I ablative therapy
  • Thyroidectomy

The treatment chosen depends on the cause of hyperthyroidism, patient factors, and patient preference; endocrinology referral is recommended. Short-term methimazole use is recommended to normalize thyroid function before treatment for patients undergoing ^131I therapy or thyroidectomy who have overt hyperthyroidism, are 65 years and older, or have cardiac disease or multiple comorbidities.

Thionamides are often used in the initial treatment of Graves hyperthyroidism. Up to 50% of patients have spontaneous remission of hyperthyroidism within 24 months; remission is more common in patients with small goiters requiring only low doses. Recurrent hyperthyroidism is likely if TRAb levels remain elevated when the drug is discontinued. If Graves hyperthyroidism recurs, definitive treatment with ^131I therapy or thyroidectomy is recommended.

Methimazole is the thionamide of choice because it achieves euthyroidism faster than PTU and can be dosed once daily (improving adherence). Additionally, PTU has been associated with fatal liver necrosis. PTU is preferred during the first trimester of pregnancy because of the potential teratogenic effects of methimazole. Agranulocytosis and liver dysfunction are rare but serious adverse effects of thionamides. Before treatment, baseline complete blood count with a differential and liver profile should be assessed because Graves disease itself may cause similar abnormalities. In the setting of fever or pharyngitis, agranulocytosis should be suspected and the patient’s absolute neutrophil count should be urgently assessed. Liver function should be assessed in any patient with symptoms or signs of hepatic dysfunction (e.g., jaundice, icterus).

The goal of ^131I ablative therapy in Graves disease is to cause hypothyroidism. Patients receiving ^131I therapy must avoid pregnancy for 6 to 12 months after treatment. In patients with thyroid eye disease, the acute escalation of thyroid autoantibody titers after ^131I therapy may exacerbate ocular symptoms. Pretreatment of thyroid eye disease or selection of alternative treatments depends on severity of ophthalmopathy.

Thyroidectomy in Graves hyperthyroidism is most appropriate for patients with large goiters that cause compressive symptoms, moderate to severe thyroid eye disease, or coexistent thyroid cancer or primary hyperparathyroidism.

First-line therapy for a toxic adenoma or toxic MNG is ^131I therapy, thyroid surgery, or thionamides. The choice is determined by patient preference, presence of compressive symptoms (surgery preferred), and access to a high-volume thyroid surgeon. Thionamides can be used to control thyroid hormone excess but do not lead to remission and are often used in preparation for definitive therapy. Thionamides can also be used as long-term therapy in patients for whom surgery would be unacceptably risky or who are unable to receive ^131I therapy.

Destructive thyroiditis is managed with β-blockers to control adrenergic symptoms and NSAIDs or high-dose glucocorticoids for pain control in painful thyroiditis. Because of the transient nature of thyroiditis, thionamides, ^131I therapy, and thyroid surgery have no role in treatment.

Subclinical hyperthyroidism is diagnosed by persistent TSH suppression with normal free T~4 and total T~3 levels. This disease affects 0.7% of the U.S. population. Approximately 0.5% to 7% progress to overt hyperthyroidism each year, and 5% to 12% revert to normal thyroid function. The most common cause is toxic MNG.

Subclinical hyperthyroidism increases the risk for atrial fibrillation and cardiovascular events. Patients with subclinical hyperthyroidism have a 34% higher risk for fracture compared with persons with normal thyroid function.

TSH normalizes after 6 weeks in more than 25% of patients with subclinical hyperthyroidism. Therefore, observation and rechecking thyroid function before treatment is reasonable unless the risk for complications, such as cardiac disease, is high. The risk for cardiovascular and skeletal complications is higher with TSH levels less than 0.1 μU/mL (0.1 mU/L). Treatment is recommended for patients with TSH levels less than 0.1 μU/mL (0.1 mU/L) and age 65 years and older, cardiac risk factors, heart disease, or osteoporosis or high risk for osteoporosis, regardless of symptoms. Treatment is generally recommended in all patients with symptoms.

Thyroid hormone deficiency affects more than 10 million Americans. It is 10 times more common in women than men.

Signs and symptoms of thyroid hormone deficiency are listed in [Table: Table: Manifestations of Thyrotoxicosis and Thyroid Hormone Deficiency]

. Thyroid hormone deficiency is associated with anemia, elevated LDL cholesterol level, hypertriglyceridemia, and hyponatremia.

Primary hypothyroidism is diagnosed by measuring the TSH level and, if the TSH level is elevated, measuring the free T~4 level. TSH is elevated in both overt and subclinical hypothyroidism, but free T~4 is low in overt hypothyroidism and normal in subclinical hypothyroidism. Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies are present in most patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis, but measurement is unnecessary unless the diagnosis is unclear.

Causes of thyroid hormone deficiency are listed in [Table: Table: Causes of Thyroid Hormone Deficiency]

. The most common cause in the United States is Hashimoto thyroiditis (chronic autoimmune thyroiditis); iodine deficiency is the most common cause globally. Iodine deficiency is uncommon in the United States because of food fortification (iodized salt). Central (secondary) hypothyroidism is also uncommon (see Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone Deficiency in Endocrinology and Metabolism). Several medications can cause thyroid hormone deficiency (see Medication-Induced Thyroid Dysfunction in Endocrinology and Metabolism).

Hashimoto thyroiditis (chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis) is an autoimmune thyroid disorder characterized by diffuse infiltration of the thyroid by lymphocytes and plasma cells with subsequent follicular atrophy and scarring. It is more common in patients with other autoimmune disorders (e.g., type 1 diabetes mellitus or vitiligo) or a family history of thyroid autoimmunity. Diffuse goiter is more common in younger patients. Ultrasonography is recommended for patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis when examination shows thyroid asymmetry or nodules. Most patients (90%) have TPO antibodies. The risk for developing hypothyroidism is fourfold higher in euthyroid patients with TPO antibodies.

Hypothyroidism occurs in all patients after thyroidectomy and 20% of patients after thyroid lobectomy. Postablative hypothyroidism occurs after ^131I therapy within 1 year in 90% of patients with Graves disease and in 60% of patients with toxic MNG but may be delayed for many years.

Subclinical hypothyroidism is common (5%-10%), typically asymptomatic, and diagnosed by a high TSH level and a normal free T~4 level. Repeating the measurement in 6 to 8 weeks confirms persistent TSH elevation. Of patients with subclinical hypothyroidism, 2% to 4% per year progress to overt hypothyroidism, whereas thyroid function will spontaneously revert to normal in one third of patients. The normal range for TSH increases with age, and a TSH level of up to 7.5 μU/mL (7.5 mU/L) is within the normal range for persons aged 80 years and older.

Subclinical hypothyroidism with TSH greater than 10 μU/mL (10 mU/L) may be a risk factor for coronary artery disease and heart failure. No evidence indicates that treating subclinical hypothyroidism improves quality of life, cognitive function, blood pressure, or weight, but in patients with elevated LDL cholesterol levels, normalization of the TSH level will lower LDL cholesterol levels.

Levothyroxine is the recommended treatment for thyroid hormone deficiency. Treatment goals include normalizing TSH (in primary hypothyroidism) or free T~4 (in central hypothyroidism) levels and resolving signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism. Beginning a full replacement dose (1.6 μg/kg lean body weight) is appropriate for most patients with overt hypothyroidism. Lower initial doses (25-50 μg/day) are recommended in patients older than 65 years and patients with cardiac disease. Repeating TSH measurement at least 6 weeks after dose initiation or modification allows treatment adequacy to be assessed.

T~3-containing compounds are not recommended because of their short half-life, resulting in nonphysiologic T~3 spikes. T~3 alone or in combination with T~4, including desiccated thyroid, has no clear benefit in treating hypothyroidism.

Treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism with a TSH level greater than 10 μU/mL (10 mU/L) should start with levothyroxine at 25 to 50 μg/day. Treating asymptomatic patients with TSH levels of 5 to 10 μU/mL (5-10 mU/L) has unclear benefits. Overtreatment is seen in more than one third of patients older than 65 years, increasing the risk for dysrhythmia and osteoporosis. Treatment for subclinical hypothyroidism with a TSH level less than 10 μU/mL (10 mU/L) should be considered in younger patients, in pregnant patients or those attempting to become pregnant, or if significant symptoms are present. For asymptomatic patients with subclinical hypothyroidism who are not candidates for treatment, thyroid function tests should be repeated in 6 months and then yearly.

Oral levothyroxine is absorbed in the jejunum and ileum. Ideally, it is taken on an empty stomach (60 minutes before breakfast or coffee). If adherence to morning administration is difficult, levothyroxine can be taken before bed. Younger patients can take missed doses the following day. The absorption of an orally administered dose is 70% to 80% under optimum fasting conditions.

Gastrointestinal disorders (such as celiac disease) may affect levothyroxine absorption and result in higher-than-expected dose requirements. Medications can also interfere with the absorption or metabolism of levothyroxine (see [Table: Table: Medications That Affect the Thyroid]

). For levothyroxine therapy, nonadherence with dosing, differing bioavailability of the generic options, TSH assay interference from heterophile antibodies and biotin-containing agents, decreased T~4 to T~3 conversion, incorrect drug storage, increased drug metabolism, and an increased drug requirement because of weight gain or pregnancy are other possible causes of treatment-refractory hypothyroidism.

The symptoms of Hashimoto thyroiditis, including fatigue, increased need for sleep, arthralgia, myalgia, and dry mouth and eyes, may not resolve completely with adequate levothyroxine therapy. Patients with severe symptoms and thyroid autoimmunity may improve with thyroidectomy; however, this is not routinely recommended.

Many medications can affect thyroid function (see [Table: Table: Medications That Affect the Thyroid]

). Patients taking medications that may cause thyroid dysfunction require periodic clinical and biochemical monitoring with TSH levels. [Table: Table: Medications That May Induce Thyroid Dysfunction]

outlines relevant medications and treatment of medication-induced thyroid dysfunction.

Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic drug with a high iodine content and prolonged half-life of 60 days or longer. Amiodarone causes a transient TSH level increase in all patients, with normalization after 3 to 6 months of therapy. Additionally, free and serum total T~4 levels transiently increase and the serum total T~3 level transiently decreases. As many as 20% of patients taking amiodarone develop hypothyroidism (most often with pre-existing Hashimoto thyroiditis). Approximately 60% of patients who develop hypothyroidism have normalized thyroid function 2 to 4 months after amiodarone cessation.

Of those taking amiodarone, 5% to 10% develop thyrotoxicosis, either type 1 amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT) in those with pre-existing Graves disease or toxic nodules (Jod-Basedow phenomenon) or type 2 (destructive thyroiditis). This distinction is important because patients with type 1 AIT are treated with thionamides and patients with type 2 AIT are treated with glucocorticoids. Thyroid ultrasound with Doppler studies helps distinguish these types by showing increased vascularity with type 1 and decreased vascularity with type 2. Amiodarone discontinuation depends on the patient’s cardiac condition and thyrotoxicosis type.

Lithium is used to treat patients with bipolar disorder. It has been associated with thyroid dysfunction, which can occur years after treatment initiation. Hypothyroidism is most common, but thyrotoxicosis can also occur.

Interferon alfa is an antiviral agent used to treat hepatitis B and certain proliferative disorders, such as essential thrombocytopenia and polycythemia vera. Interferon beta is used to treat multiple sclerosis. Both types of interferon have been associated with thyroid dysfunction, most commonly the development of de novo thyroid antibodies. A smaller proportion of patients develop clinical disease. Most patients recover spontaneously after completing interferon treatment.

Interleukin-2 is used in the treatment of some metastatic cancers. Patients treated with interleukin-2 are susceptible to developing thyroid dysfunction, most commonly hypothyroidism. Patients with elevated antibodies before starting interleukin-2 treatment are most at risk. Thyroid dysfunction may resolve after discontinuing treatment, but, in some patients, persistent hypothyroidism or thyrotoxicosis may necessitate medical therapy.

Patients who are taking tyrosine kinase inhibitors (particularly sorafenib, sunitinib, vandetanib, and axitinib) are at risk for developing thyroid dysfunction, mainly hypothyroidism secondary to destructive thyroiditis. They are also at risk for transient thyrotoxicosis followed by hypothyroidism.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., ipilimumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab) are used to treat patients with advanced cancer. These agents can lead to different endocrinopathies, including thyroid dysfunction. Hypothyroidism is most common and is often preceded by a short period of destructive thyroiditis. Patients in the thyrotoxicosis phase are treated with supportive care, including β-blockers. Close monitoring of thyroid function after the onset of thyroiditis is recommended, and subsequent hypothyroidism is managed with levothyroxine.

Thyroid hormones are essential for normal fetal development. The size of the maternal thyroid increases up to 40% during pregnancy, and production of T~4 and T~3 increases up to 50% to compensate for the increased thyroxine-binding globulin associated with pregnancy. Iodine requirements also increase up to 50%. The American Thyroid Association recommends counseling pregnant and lactating patients to take a daily oral supplement containing 150 μg of iodine, which is included in some, but not all, prenatal vitamins.

Universal TSH level screening in pregnant patients is not recommended. Patients who should be screened because of an increased risk for thyroid dysfunction are those aged 30 years and older and those with known hypothyroidism or a strong family history of thyroid dysfunction; previous head and neck irradiation; previous neck surgery; positive TPO antibodies, TSI, or TRAb; or other autoimmune disorders.

Changes in thyroid function tests during pregnancy are depicted in

. Placental human chorionic gonadotropin stimulates thyroid hormone secretion, and the TSH level may decrease as a result. In the late first trimester (weeks 7-12), the lower limit of the TSH reference range decreases by 0.4 μU/mL (0.4 mU/L) and the upper limit by 0.5 μU/mL (0.5 mU/L). TSH gradually returns to the nonpregnant reference range in the second and third trimesters.

Total T~4 concentrations increase by 7 weeks’ gestation until 16 weeks’ gestation, when they plateau at a level that persists through the remainder of pregnancy. After week 16, the upper limit of the total T~4 reference range can be estimated by multiplying the nonpregnant upper limit by 1.5. Free T~4 levels measured by indirect analogue immunoassays are inaccurate in pregnancy unless method- and trimester-specific reference ranges are applied.

Gestational thyrotoxicosis from high human chorionic gonadotropin levels is the most common cause of transient TSH suppression. If serum total or free T~4 remains within the trimester-specific reference range, treatment is unnecessary. Patients with moderate to severe hyperthyroidism in early pregnancy should be treated with PTU because it is less teratogenic than methimazole. After the first trimester, patients can be transitioned to methimazole. Thyroid function during treatment with thionamides should be followed closely, keeping the serum total or free T~4 at or just above the trimester-specific reference range to avoid fetal hypothyroidism.

Graves disease affects 0.2% of pregnant persons and is diagnosed by classic physical findings (see Graves Disease in Endocrinology and Metabolism) or elevated TSI or TRAb. Patients with Graves disease have high-risk pregnancies and should be followed by maternal-fetal specialists throughout the pregnancy.

Endocrinology consultation is indicated for thyrotoxicosis management during pregnancy.

Hypothyroidism in pregnancy increases the risk for miscarriage, premature birth, and low birth weight; additionally, it is associated with decreased infant neurocognitive function. Levothyroxine is the recommended treatment.

For patients with preexisting hypothyroidism who are euthyroid taking levothyroxine therapy before becoming pregnant, levothyroxine dosing can be empirically increased by 30% when pregnancy is confirmed. Patients with new overt hypothyroidism diagnosed during pregnancy should initiate treatment with levothyroxine. In patients with subclinical hypothyroidism, treatment depends on the presence of TPO antibodies. Levothyroxine may be considered in patients with positive TPO antibodies if the TSH level is greater than 2.5 μU/mL (2.5 mU/L); for pregnant patients who are TPO-negative, levothyroxine may be considered if the TSH level is above the pregnancy-specific reference range. The TSH level should be measured every 4 weeks for the first half of pregnancy and around 30 weeks in all patients with or at risk for hypothyroidism (antibody positive or history of hemithyroidectomy or ^131I therapy). A TSH level less than 2.5 μU/mL (2.5 mU/L) should be targeted in treated patients with hypothyroidism before conception and during pregnancy.

Thyroid nodules detected in pregnant patients are evaluated as in nonpregnant patients. The timing of FNAB, whether during or after pregnancy, is determined by the cancer risk and patient preference.

Nonthyroidal illness syndrome (NTIS), formerly known as euthyroid sick syndrome, commonly occurs in patients who are hospitalized and critically ill. Up to 75% of hospitalized patients have physiologic thyroid function test abnormalities. Nonthyroidal illness suppresses thyrotropin-releasing hormone, resulting in suppressed but detectable TSH. An undetectable TSH is not consistent with NTIS. Infrequently, TSH can be mildly elevated in recovery from NTIS, but a TSH level of 20 μU/mL (20 mU/L) or greater is not consistent with NTIS. Total T~4 may be normal in patients with mild illness and is often decreased in moderate to severe illness. Total T~3 decreases and reverse T~3 increases (biologically inactive) because of decreased deiodinase activity. Thyroxine-binding globulin decreases in illness, lowering total T~4 and T~3 levels. NTIS may be an adaptive response to systemic illness and macronutrient restriction.

Treating NTIS is not recommended because of unclear clinical benefit. In general, thyroid function should not be assessed in hospitalized patients unless there is a strong clinical suspicion of thyroid dysfunction. If NTIS is diagnosed, the TSH level should be rechecked approximately 6 weeks after the patient has recovered from nonthyroidal illness to assess for normalization.

Thyroid storm is a rare, serious disorder (up to 30% mortality) characterized by severe thyrotoxicosis and life-threatening complications. Serum thyroid hormone concentrations do not differentiate thyroid storm from severe thyrotoxicosis.

Presentation often follows discontinuation of antithyroid drug therapy, systemic illness, labor and delivery, surgery, exposure to iodinated contrast media, or trauma. Patients with Graves disease are at higher risk. Clinical manifestations include high fever, tachycardia, altered mental status, and cardiac and gastrointestinal/liver dysfunction. A scoring system ( [Table: Table: Diagnostic Criteria for Thyroid Storm]

) can suggest the diagnosis but is limited by poor specificity; thyroid storm is diagnosed clinically.

Management includes ICU-level care, treatment of any precipitating illness, thyrotoxicosis-directed therapy, and supportive measures. Thyrotoxicosis is treated with β-blockers (classically propranolol, which inhibits the conversion of T~4 to T~3), thionamides for hyperthyroidism (typically PTU, transitioning to methimazole when stable), intravenous high-dose glucocorticoids, and potassium iodide. Iodide should be administered at least 1 hour after thionamides to avoid increasing substrate to the gland. Glucocorticoid therapy is a potent inhibitor of peripheral T~4 to T~3 conversion. Bile acid sequestrants can be used to decrease T~4 and T~3 levels, especially in patients unable to take thionamides. Plasmapheresis or emergent thyroidectomy is used for patients responding poorly to medical therapy. Definitive treatment with thyroidectomy or ^131I therapy is indicated in patients who survive thyroid storm.

Myxedema coma is a rare but life-threatening presentation of severe hypothyroidism with hemodynamic compromise. Mortality is high (up to 40%), and ICU-level care is required. Risk factors for myxedema coma are female sex, advanced age, cold exposure, or a precipitating event (myocardial infarction, sepsis, trauma, anesthesia, or stroke) in patients with untreated hypothyroidism.

Mental status changes ranging from lethargy to coma to psychosis, coupled with hypothermia, are the most common manifestations. Bradycardia, hypotension, or decreased respiration rate with hypoxia and hypercapnia is frequently present. TSH is typically elevated; however, without an overtly low free T~4, myxedema coma is unlikely even in the presence of marked TSH elevation. Hyponatremia and hypoglycemia may be present. Cortisol measurement should be included in the initial testing to assess for concomitant cortisol deficiency.

In addition to addressing any underlying precipitants, patients should be treated with aggressive supportive measures, including fluids, vasopressors if necessary, ventilator support, and passive rather than active warming to avoid vasodilation and worsened hypotension. Glucocorticoids (100 mg intravenous hydrocortisone every 8 hours) are administered empirically before thyroid hormone replacement is initiated to treat possible concomitant adrenal insufficiency. If a random serum cortisol level is greater than 18 μg/dL (497 nmol/L), hydrocortisone can be discontinued. Thyroid hormone replacement requires considering the need to normalize thyroid hormone levels rapidly and the risk for a fatal cardiac event caused by thyroid hormone administration. Initial treatment is 200 to 400 μg intravenous levothyroxine, followed by a daily oral dose of 1.6 μg/kg. Intravenous daily dosing should be reduced to 75% of the oral dose. Lower levothyroxine doses are recommended with advanced age or cardiac disease. Concomitant treatment with T~3 may also be considered.

Treatment goals are improved mental status, metabolic parameters, and cardiopulmonary function. When the patient stabilizes, transition to oral levothyroxine is the goal.
