Reproductive Disorders

Coordinated actions of the hypothalamus, pituitary gland, and ovaries create ovulatory cycles. The pulsatile release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) drives the anterior pituitary cells to secrete follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) (

). FSH regulates estradiol production and follicle growth in the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle. A sudden midcycle rise in LH levels causes release of an ovum, signaling the start of the luteal phase. The luteal phase lasts a constant 14 days, during which progesterone from the corpus luteum maintains the endometrial lining. If a fertilized embryo does not implant during that time, decreased estrogen and progesterone levels result in endometrial sloughing (

).

Menses normally occur every 25 to 35 days; menstrual cycles shorter than 25 days or longer than 35 days in women younger than age 40 years are likely anovulatory, resulting in abnormal uterine bleeding or oligomenorrhea. After menopause, all reproductive function and most endocrine functions of the ovaries cease.

Amenorrhea can be intermittent or permanent. It may result from hypothalamic, pituitary, ovarian, uterine, or outflow tract disorders.

Primary amenorrhea is defined as the absence of menses by age 15 years in the presence of normal growth and secondary sexual characteristics or the absence of menses by age 13 years in the absence of normal growth and secondary sexual characteristics.

Primary amenorrhea is most commonly caused by a genetic (50%) or anatomic (15%) abnormality and warrants full evaluation for an underlying cause. Causes of primary amenorrhea include gonadal dysgenesis, vaginal agenesis, physiologic delay of puberty (constitutional delay, chronic systemic disease, acute illness), and polycystic ovary syndrome. Less common causes include isolated GnRH deficiency, transverse vaginal septum, weight loss, anorexia nervosa, hypopituitarism, and androgen insensitivity syndrome. Most causes of secondary amenorrhea can also present as primary amenorrhea.

The most common cause of primary amenorrhea is gonadal dysgenesis, most often Turner syndrome (45,X0). This syndrome is caused by loss of part or all of an X chromosome. It is associated with short stature, amenorrhea (90%) due to primary ovarian insufficiency (POI), and cardiovascular disease.

Secondary amenorrhea is defined as the absence of menses for more than 3 months in women who previously had regular menstrual cycles or for 6 months in women who have irregular menses. Oligomenorrhea, defined as fewer than nine menstrual cycles per year or cycle length longer than 35 days, should prompt the same evaluation as for secondary amenorrhea.

Pregnancy is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea. In the absence of pregnancy, secondary amenorrhea is caused by disruption anywhere along the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis or structural alterations to the uterine cavity.

Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (FHA) is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea after pregnancy. Disruption of the pulsatile release of hypothalamic GnRH may occur because of stress, weight loss, eating disorders (e.g., anorexia nervosa), or exercise. Other causes of secondary amenorrhea include intracranial tumors, pituitary infarction associated with postpartum hemorrhage, acute or chronic systemic illness, and infiltrative or destructive disorders affecting the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.

Hyperprolactinemia inhibits GnRH release and accounts for 10% to 20% of non–pregnancy-mediated amenorrhea. Oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea is the primary presentation of hyperprolactinemia in premenopausal women, although galactorrhea may also occur.

Thyroid disorders commonly cause menstrual dysfunction. Although hypothyroidism more typically causes heavy bleeding, secondary amenorrhea can also occur.

Hyperandrogenic disorders can cause amenorrhea, with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) being by far the most common cause (see Hirsutism and Polycystic Ovary Syndrome in Endocrinology and Metabolism).

Spontaneous POI affects 1 in 100 women. In addition to disordered menses, symptoms related to estrogen deficiency may develop. Most cases are sporadic, but a first-degree relative with POI suggests a familial cause (e.g., fragile X variant), whereas a personal history of autoimmune disorders can suggest an autoimmune polyglandular syndrome. Women with POI have increased risk for autoimmune adrenal insufficiency. Other potential causes of POI include a history of radiation or chemotherapy.

Amenorrhea can result from the development of scar tissue within the uterine cavity, preventing build-up and shedding of endometrial cells. Adhesions may develop after the use of intrauterine instrumentation, most commonly uterine curettage for pregnancy complications (Asherman syndrome). A less common cause is chronic endometritis secondary to Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Chlamydia trachomatis.

After excluding pregnancy, evaluation should include a thorough menstrual history of the patient and female family members as well as discussion of sexual activity, medication use, weight changes and exercise habits, and psychosocial stressors.

Headaches or visual changes can suggest pituitary pathology; galactorrhea suggests hyperprolactinemia; vasomotor symptoms are consistent with estrogen deficiency; and temperature intolerance, weight changes, and fatigue can suggest thyroid dysfunction.

Physical examination should include BMI measurement. A low BMI (<18.5) may suggest FHA resulting from an eating disorder, excessive exercise, or systemic illness. A high BMI (≥30) is frequently seen in women with PCOS. The presence of signs of clinical hyperandrogenism such as acne and hirsutism suggests PCOS or hypercortisolism (see Cortisol Excess (Cushing Syndrome Caused by Adrenal Mass) in Endocrinology and Metabolism). Vitiligo or other signs of autoimmune disease increase the likelihood of autoimmune POI. Evaluation of the vagina, cervix, and uterus should include assessment for anatomic abnormalities and vulvovaginal atrophy, which suggests estrogen deficiency. Breasts should be examined for development and expressible galactorrhea. Physical examination should also include evaluation for features of Turner syndrome, such as a low hairline, webbed neck, shield chest, and widely spaced nipples.

After ruling out pregnancy, initial laboratory testing in primary and secondary amenorrhea should include measuring serum FSH, serum estradiol, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), free thyroxine, and serum prolactin levels. These results guide subsequent evaluation (

).

If the TSH level is abnormal, thyroid dysfunction should be evaluated and managed (see Evaluation of Thyroid Function in Endocrinology and Metabolism).

If the prolactin level is elevated, repeat testing is needed to confirm the abnormality. A careful review of medications is essential because many drugs can cause hyperprolactinemia. Pituitary MRI may be indicated to assess for prolactinoma (see Hyperprolactinemia and Prolactinoma in Endocrinology and Metabolism).

If the FSH level is elevated and the estradiol level is low or normal, POI may be present. Karyotype analysis to evaluate for Turner syndrome may be indicated.

If the FSH level is normal or low and the estradiol level is low, hypothalamic hypogonadism is the most likely cause. If the estradiol level is normal, evaluation for hyperandrogenism should be considered, including measuring the serum total testosterone level. PCOS is the most likely cause of menstrual dysfunction in women with hyperandrogenism; however, other hyperandrogenic disorders, such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia, must be excluded before diagnosing PCOS. In the setting of normal estradiol levels without menstruation, uterine outflow obstruction should be considered.

The necessity and choice of imaging studies is driven by the results of biochemical testing. MRI of the sellar region (to evaluate for structural integrity of the pituitary), pelvic ultrasonography (to assess for anatomic abnormalities of uterus, vagina, and ovaries), and hysterosalpingography and hysteroscopy (to assess for uterine outflow obstructions) may be indicated.

Almost all women with Turner syndrome need exogenous estrogen therapy with cyclic progestin to prevent endometrial hyperplasia. Estrogen-progestin therapy is continued until age 50 to 55 years, the average age of menopause.

Treatment for FHA includes less-restrictive eating patterns, weight gain, or a reduction in strenuous exercise to restore menses. Additionally, it is important to treat other conditions associated with FHA, including eating disorders, anxiety, and mood disorders. Short-term estrogen-progestin therapy (preferably with transdermal estrogen) may be used if menses do not return after a reasonable trial of lifestyle and psychological interventions.

Amenorrhea caused by hyperprolactinemia secondary to a pituitary adenoma is usually managed with dopamine agonist therapy. If hyperprolactinemia-induced amenorrhea is related to medications that cannot be stopped, estrogen-progestin therapy may be indicated. See Hyperprolactinemia and Prolactinoma in Endocrinology and Metabolism for further discussion.

Treatment of POI includes estrogen-progestin therapy until approximately age 51 years. Psychosocial support is important because patients with POI have higher scores on depression, anxiety, and negative affect scales. Subspecialty consultation to discuss fertility options is also indicated.

Hyperandrogenism is defined as elevated serum concentrations of androgens in women; it presents variably with menstrual changes, hirsutism, acne, androgenic alopecia, and virilization. Hirsutism is the most common manifestation and is defined by the presence of excessive terminal hair in a male-pattern growth distribution (

). Hirsutism must be differentiated from hypertrichosis, which is generalized excessive hair growth.

The most common cause of hirsutism and androgen excess in women is PCOS, with a prevalence of 8% to 13% of reproductive-aged women. PCOS is also the most common cause of anovulatory infertility. This syndrome is associated with rapid GnRH pulses, excess LH, and insufficient FSH secretion that results in excessive ovarian androgen production and ovulatory dysfunction. PCOS is also accompanied by insulin resistance. Elevated insulin levels in PCOS further enhance ovarian and adrenal androgen production and increase the bioavailability of androgens related to a reduction in sex hormone–binding globulin (SHBG). PCOS is associated with increased incidence of metabolic syndrome, obesity, prediabetes, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and sleep apnea.

The diagnosis of PCOS is based on the presence of three features:

  • Ovulatory dysfunction (oligo-ovulation or anovulation)
  • Androgen excess (clinical or biochemical)
  • Polycystic ovarian morphology identified on ultrasound (high number of follicles per ovary, resulting in a “cyst-like” appearance)

Current practice guidelines favor use of the Rotterdam criteria, which require two of these three features to be present. Given the high prevalence of ovulatory dysfunction and hyperandrogenism in PCOS, ultrasound may not be needed to establish the diagnosis. Serum anti-müllerian hormone levels reflect the hyperfollicular state of PCOS and are frequently high-normal or overtly elevated; assays with age-specific reference ranges have thus been proposed as an alternative diagnostic criterion to ultrasound in adults. PCOS is a diagnosis of exclusion; other conditions must be considered, including nonclassical congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hyperprolactinemia, Cushing syndrome, androgen-secreting tumors, ovarian hyperthecosis, and thyroid dysfunction.

Virilization (voice deepening, clitoromegaly, male pattern baldness, severe acne) occurs only in severe hyperandrogenism and raises concern for ovarian hyperthecosis or an androgen-producing ovarian or adrenal tumor. Although androgen-secreting tumors are rare, they should be considered in patients with abrupt, rapidly progressive hirsutism or severe hyperandrogenism.

The history and physical examination should include details about the onset of hirsutism, menstrual history, family history of hyperandrogenism, assessment of blood pressure and weight, and a thorough skin examination to evaluate for abnormal sexual hair growth, acne, and signs of insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans and skin tags). Exposure to exogenous testosterone (topical, oral, or injected) should be assessed.

Women with hirsutism should have serum total testosterone with SHBG measured, as well as serum 8 am 17-hydroxyprogesterone to screen for congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Laboratory evaluation for causes of oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea (human chorionic gonadotropin, prolactin, FSH, TSH, and free thyroxine) is also indicated. Serum dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) measurement should be obtained in patients with recent onset of rapidly progressive hirsutism or virilization.

Markedly high DHEAS or testosterone levels are inconsistent with PCOS. Patients with total testosterone levels greater than 150 ng/dL (5.2 nmol/L) or DHEAS values greater than 700 μg/dL (18.9 μmol/L) require imaging to assess for ovarian tumors (transvaginal ultrasonography) or adrenal tumors (adrenal CT or MRI).

In PCOS, weight loss is a first-line intervention in patients with a BMI of 25 or greater. Sustained weight loss of 5% to 10% improves androgen levels, menstrual function, and possibly fertility. Combined (estrogen-progestin) oral contraceptive agents are first-line pharmacologic therapy for hirsutism and menstrual dysfunction unless fertility is desired. Although there are currently no data showing superiority for any particular oral contraceptive agent, those that include progestins with lower androgenicity and acceptable venous thromboembolic risk, such as norethindrone or norethindrone acetate, are favored. An antiandrogen agent (e.g., spironolactone, finasteride) is added after 6 months if cosmesis is suboptimal with oral contraceptive agents. If fertility is desired, clomiphene citrate or letrozole can be used to correct oligomenorrhea or anovulation. Metformin reduces hyperinsulinemia and androgen levels but has minimal impact on hirsutism and ovulation.

Patients with PCOS should be screened for prediabetes/diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, obesity, hypertension, and obstructive sleep apnea because of increased risk for these conditions. Metformin is indicated when impaired glucose tolerance, prediabetes, or type 2 diabetes does not respond adequately to lifestyle modification.

Mechanical hair removal may be adequate for cosmesis in women with idiopathic hirsutism. First-line pharmacologic management of hirsutism is a combined oral contraceptive agent; these agents suppress gonadotropin secretion and ovarian androgen production and increase SHBG levels. Antiandrogen therapy, usually spironolactone, can be added for a better cosmetic response; concomitant contraception is mandatory with antiandrogen therapy because of teratogenesis in male fetuses. Topical eflornithine is also approved for treatment of unwanted hair growth.

Infertility is defined as the inability to achieve pregnancy after 1 year of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse. Evaluation is appropriate when these conditions are met in women younger than 35 years, although evaluation may be pursued after 6 months for women aged 35 years and older. Evaluation and treatment of infertility is typically managed by a reproductive endocrinologist. It is imperative that both partners are evaluated concurrently because multiple factors often are present (see Male Infertility in Endocrinology and Metabolism). The most common causes of female infertility are ovulatory disorders, endometriosis, pelvic adhesions, tubal abnormalities, and hyperprolactinemia.

Key factors to assess are menstrual history (to determine ovulatory status), frequency of intercourse, family history of infertility, features of thyroid dysfunction, hirsutism, pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and galactorrhea. History of previous pregnancies, sexually transmitted infections, pelvic inflammatory disease, gynecologic procedures, cancer therapies, and substance use disorders should also be explored. Physical examination should include BMI, assessment of secondary sexual characteristics, signs of hyperandrogenism, and pelvic examination.

Because ovulatory disorders are the most common cause of female infertility, assessment of ovulatory function is the first step in evaluation. Women who menstruate approximately every 28 days with molimina symptoms (breast tenderness, abdominal bloating, ovulatory pain) are likely ovulating. In women without such cycles, ovulatory status can be assessed with a midluteal phase serum progesterone measurement (obtained 1 week before the expected menses); a level greater than 3 ng/mL (9.5 nmol/L) is evidence of recent ovulation. If anovulatory cycles are suspected, evaluation includes measurement of serum prolactin, FSH, TSH, and free thyroxine and assessment for PCOS.

Other appropriate diagnostic tests are assessment of ovarian reserve, hysterosalpingography, and laparoscopy. Assessment of ovarian reserve includes serum anti-müllerian hormone, FSH, and estradiol. Hysterosalpingography evaluates for fallopian tube obstruction and investigates the uterine cavity. Laparoscopy is appropriate when endometriosis or pelvic adhesions are suspected. If a treatable cause is not found, fertility treatment guided by a reproductive endocrinologist may include ovulation induction with clomiphene citrate or letrozole, intrauterine insemination, and in vitro fertilization.

The testes contain two anatomic units: the spermatogenic tubules, composed of germ cells and Sertoli cells, and the interstitium, containing Leydig cells. The hormonal actions of both are governed by the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. Pulsatile hypothalamic secretion of GnRH elicits pulsatile secretion of LH and FSH by the anterior pituitary. FSH in turn stimulates Sertoli cell spermatogenesis; inhibin B produced by the Sertoli cells is an important inhibitor of pituitary FSH secretion. LH separately stimulates testosterone synthesis in Leydig cells in a diurnal pattern with some testosterone undergoing conversion to dihydrotestosterone and estradiol; LH secretion is regulated by negative feedback of testosterone and estradiol (

).

The hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular axis is sensitive to stressors, including acute and chronic illness, fasting, and strenuous exercise, all of which can lower testosterone levels.

Male hypogonadism results from failure of the testes to produce physiologic levels of testosterone and a normal number of spermatozoa because of disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular axis.

Primary hypogonadism is caused by testicular abnormalities. Causes of acquired primary hypogonadism in adults include antineoplastic agents or toxins, irradiation, testicular trauma or torsion, mumps orchitis, and acute and chronic systemic illnesses. Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is the most common congenital cause of primary hypogonadism and is associated with tall stature, small testes, developmental delay, and socialization difficulties.

Secondary hypogonadism reflects a hypothalamic (GnRH) and/or pituitary (LH/FSH) deficiency. Rare congenital causes, such as Kallmann syndrome, are associated with anosmia. Common causes of acquired hypogonadotropic hypogonadism are hyperprolactinemia, iron overload syndromes, medications, critical illness, untreated sleep disorders, obesity, type 2 diabetes, liver and kidney disease, alcohol use disorder, cannabis use, and disordered eating. Uncommon causes include pituitary tumors or apoplexy, trauma, and infiltrative diseases that cause disruption of gonadotropin production.

The most common medications that cause secondary hypogonadism are opioids, anabolic steroids, glucocorticoids, and GnRH analogues. The incidence of hypogonadism has been reported to be as high as 63% in men using chronic opioids. Opioids have shown to inhibit GnRH release, leading to decreased FSH and LH secretion and decreased production of testicular testosterone.

The clinical features of male hypogonadism depend on the age of onset and severity of deficiency. Given that testosterone affects many tissues, lack of testosterone can cause many different signs and symptoms ( [Table: Table: Symptoms and Signs Suggestive of Androgen Deficiency in Men]

). When only nonspecific symptoms are present, hypogonadism is unlikely to be the cause, and patients should be evaluated for other medical conditions.

Screening for hypogonadism in men with nonspecific symptoms is not recommended. In men with specific signs and symptoms, measuring a fasting serum total testosterone level within 2 to 3 hours of awakening is indicated. If the testosterone level is low (<264 ng/dL [9.2 nmol/L]), a second morning fasting testosterone level is measured. The diagnosis is made with two separate low serum testosterone measurements. Measurement or calculation of free testosterone is appropriate when SHBG is suspected to be abnormal because this can lead to a misleading measured total testosterone level. Causes of low SHBG include obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism, growth hormone excess, exogenous androgens/anabolic steroids, glucocorticoids, progestins, and nephrotic syndrome. Causes of high SHBG include aging, hyperthyroidism, HIV infection, and liver disease.

Once hypogonadism is confirmed, the next step in evaluation is serum LH and FSH measurement (

). Elevated LH and FSH levels indicate primary hypogonadism, and the underlying cause should be investigated. Low or inappropriately normal LH and FSH levels indicate secondary hypogonadism. Evaluation for chronic illness, sleep disorders (commonly sleep apnea), obesity, liver and kidney disease, alcohol or cannabis use, and disordered eating and a detailed medication history should be performed. Iron studies and a serum prolactin measurement should also be performed to screen for iron overload syndromes and hyperprolactinemia, two common causes of secondary hypogonadism. If clinically indicated, other pituitary hormone levels can be evaluated. A dedicated pituitary MRI should be performed if hyperprolactinemia is present, other pituitary hormone abnormalities are identified, the serum total testosterone level is less than 150 ng/dL (5.2 nmol/L), or signs or symptoms of mass effect are present.

In men with biochemically proven hypogonadism, testosterone therapy can be initiated after the cause is determined. Weight loss is recommended for patients with overweight or obesity, and cessation of causative medications, if possible, should be attempted. Sleep apnea treatment with continuous positive airway pressure has not been consistently reported to raise testosterone levels, suggesting that low testosterone may be the result of concomitant obesity. However, untreated sleep apnea should be corrected before testosterone therapy is initiated, as therapy can worsen sleep apnea (see Treatment of OSA in Pulmonary Medicine for information on sleep apnea treatment). When cessation of opioid medications is not feasible, testosterone replacement therapy may need to be initiated. Testosterone should be replaced to the midnormal range (450-600 ng/dL [15.6-20.8 nmol/L]). Several testosterone replacement preparations are available ( [Table: Table: Testosterone Replacement Therapy for Male Hypogonadism]

).

Clinical benefits of testosterone therapy include increased libido, lean muscle mass, fat-free mass, bone density, and secondary sexual characteristics. Potential adverse effects include acne, effect on prostate tissue, obstructive sleep apnea, thrombophilia, and erythrocytosis. The effects of testosterone replacement on cardiovascular outcomes in men with hypogonadism have been unclear, but the TRAVERSE trial found that testosterone gel did not increase the risk for nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or cardiovascular death compared with placebo in men with hypogonadism. However, trials have found that testosterone therapy can increase blood pressure, regardless of the route of administration.

Testosterone therapy should be avoided in men who are planning for fertility (testosterone impairs spermatogenesis by suppressing pituitary FSH secretion) and men with breast or prostate cancer, a palpable prostate nodule or induration, a serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level greater than 4 ng/mL (4 μg/L) or greater than 3 ng/mL (3 μg/L) with high risk for prostate cancer, elevated hematocrit, untreated severe obstructive sleep apnea, thrombophilia, or recent (in the past 6 months) stroke or myocardial infarction.

Before testosterone therapy is initiated, baseline hematocrit should be measured in all patients, and PSA should be measured in men aged 55 to 69 years or 40 years and older with an increased risk for prostate cancer in the context of shared decision making. If hematocrit is greater than 50% or PSA is elevated, evaluation for polycythemia and prostate cancer should be pursued before starting testosterone therapy. Patients taking testosterone therapy should be reevaluated within 3 months after starting therapy and every 12 months thereafter for development of adverse effects.

As men age, testicular and hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction cause total and free testosterone levels to decline and SHBG levels to increase. Most men do not become hypogonadal. Sperm production does not change significantly with age. The consequences of male aging are not fully understood but may include negative effects on sexual function, muscle mass, erythropoiesis, and bone health.

Routinely prescribing testosterone to all men aged 65 years and older who have age-related low testosterone is not recommended, as there is no benefit and long-term evidence on adverse events is lacking. In men aged 65 years and older who have clear signs and symptoms of hypogonadism and unequivocally low testosterone levels, testosterone therapy should be individualized after discussing the risks and benefits. In this aging population, testosterone should be replaced to the low-normal range.

In couples with infertility, both male and female infertility should be assessed concurrently (see Female Infertility in Endocrinology and Metabolism).

The history should focus on potential causes of infertility: developmental history, chronic illness, infection, surgery, drugs and environmental exposures, sexual history, and previous fertility history. Physical examination should focus on evidence of androgen deficiency, with careful examination of the external genitals. If testicular examination is abnormal, referral to a urologist may be appropriate.

Laboratory evaluation should include assessment for hypogonadism starting with a morning fasting serum total testosterone level. Semen analysis should be obtained after 2 to 3 days of sexual abstinence. If the semen analysis is abnormal, the test should be repeated. A second abnormal result indicates the need for referral to a reproductive endocrinologist.

Gynecomastia is defined as a benign proliferation of glandular tissue in the male breast and occurs when the ratio of estrogens to androgens is increased. Physiologic gynecomastia is common in neonates, adolescents, and older men, but a thorough evaluation for underlying causes should be performed in all patients. Many drugs affect androgen or estrogen concentrations and are associated with gynecomastia. The most common are spironolactone, cimetidine, ketoconazole, estrogens, antiandrogens, 5α-reductase inhibitors, and protease inhibitors. Alcohol and cannabis use may also cause gynecomastia. Other identified causes include substance use disorder, malnutrition, cirrhosis, hypogonadism, testicular germ cell tumors, hyperthyroidism, chronic kidney disease, and nonprescription agents such as lavender oil and tea tree oil.

Gynecomastia is diagnosed with physical examination; palpation of subareolar glandular tissue greater than 0.5 cm in diameter is consistent with gynecomastia. It is imperative to differentiate gynecomastia from pseudogynecomastia, which is fat deposition typically seen in men with obesity. Gynecomastia is typically bilateral and may be tender if early in its course of development. Unilateral, nontender, or fixed breast masses should prompt an evaluation for breast cancer with mammography.

Evaluation of male gynecomastia without a clear cause includes measurement of human chorionic gonadotropin and serum LH, morning fasting total testosterone, estradiol, and prolactin levels.

Gynecomastia treatment begins with addressing any underlying causes and discontinuing offending agents; treatment of a specific cause of gynecomastia during the active proliferative phase may result in regression in size of the abnormal tissue. If no offending agent or underlying cause can be identified, medical therapy can be considered. Selective estrogen receptor modulators and androgens (for men with hypogonadism) are commonly used medications, although neither is FDA approved specifically for gynecomastia. If gynecomastia is longstanding, regression (spontaneously or with medical therapy) is unlikely because of fibrotic changes. In this scenario, referral for plastic surgery may be the best option for cosmetic improvement.

Anabolic steroid use has been reported in both men and women, with a prevalence of up to 7% in men. Potential adverse effects include labile mood, acne, excessive muscle bulk, gynecomastia (caused by peripheral conversion of testosterone to estradiol), testicular atrophy, diminished spermatogenesis and fertility, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, which may be permanent. Anabolic steroid use should be suspected in a patient who exhibits abrupt changes in behavior, such as depression, irritability, or aggression, or in men who develop a rapid increase in muscle strength along with gynecomastia, acne, small testes, and low sperm counts. Laboratory evidence suggestive of anabolic steroid use includes an elevated hematocrit level, undetectable or low serum LH level, and low SHBG level. Testosterone levels may be either low or elevated, depending on the type of anabolic steroid.

Patients who use anabolic steroids can be reluctant to disclose this information or stop use; however, patients should be encouraged to stop and counseled on the potential for short-term or long-term hypogonadism after cessation.

Transgender Hormone Therapy

Transgender medicine involves the care of persons whose gender identity differs from their gender assignment at birth. A transgender man was assigned female gender at birth but identifies as a man. A transgender woman was assigned male gender at birth but identifies as a woman. Gender incongruence is the diagnostic term currently used to focus on a person’s experienced identity and the need for gender-affirming therapy owing to that identity. This term is favored over gender dysphoria, which focuses on the distress and discomfort experienced if gender identity and designated gender are incongruent.

Gender-affirming care is the standard of care for treating gender incongruence; it includes hormonal and surgical therapies used to adapt the patient’s body to their experienced gender as well as social, psychological, and behavioral interventions. Gender-affirming hormone therapy is the most common medical intervention sought by transgender persons and does not require subspecialty care. The American College of Physicians supports access to evidence-based and clinically indicated gender-affirming care that is provided in line with the medically accepted standard of care using an informed consent model and strongly asserts that gender-affirming care is an essential component of comprehensive health care for transgender people.

Providing a respectful environment, including use of identified pronouns, is critical to ensure that transgender persons establish and continue primary and gender-affirming care (see Effective Communication in Clinical Practice in Foundations of Clinical Practice), as transgender persons may avoid seeking health care because of discriminatory or disrespectful interactions in previous health care encounters (see Bias, Stigma, and Discrimination in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Accurate collection of gender identity information is important. To avoid invisibility of transgender status, many organizations use a “two-step” method to collect these data: (1) gender identity and (2) sex listed on the original birth certificate. Before physical examination, a patient history is necessary to understand a person’s anatomic changes associated with gender-affirming treatment because secondary sex characteristics present on a wide spectrum of development in transgender patients.

Before initiating gender-affirming therapy, discussion is needed about risks, medical conditions that can be exacerbated by therapy, the time course of physical changes, and fertility preservation. Treatment must be individualized to the patient’s goals, and careful monitoring is needed.

Criteria for gender-affirming hormone therapy are as follows:

  • Assessment of physical and mental health conditions that can negatively affect treatment outcomes and discussion of risks/benefits
  • Established diagnosis of marked and sustained gender incongruence
  • Demonstrated patient capacity to consent to treatment
  • Exclusion of other possible causes of gender incongruence

Impact on reproduction should be discussed and reproductive options explored if desired.

Feminizing hormone therapy includes estrogen in combination with an androgen blocker, both used off label ( [Table: Table: Hormone Regimens in Transgender and Gender Diverse Adults]

). Estradiol formulations are preferred over conjugated estrogens (e.g., ethinyl estradiol). Estradiol is available in oral, sublingual, transdermal, and parenteral formulations. Antiandrogen medications include spironolactone, cyproterone acetate (not approved in the United States), and gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists.

Several risks are associated with estrogen-based regimens. Estrogen therapy increases the risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE), infertility, hypertriglyceridemia, and weight gain. Transdermal estrogen preparations are recommended for patients at higher risk for developing VTE (age greater than 45 years or a history of VTE). Tobacco cessation should also be encouraged. In the presence of additional risk factors, estrogen therapy likely increases the risk for cardiovascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, and cholelithiasis. Other possible risks of estrogen therapy include hypertension, erectile dysfunction, type 2 diabetes mellitus, low bone mass/osteoporosis, and hyperprolactinemia. No strong evidence indicates that estrogen increases the risk for breast and prostate cancer. Contraindications to estrogen therapy include history of venous thromboembolism, estrogen-sensitive neoplasm, and end-stage liver disease.

Spironolactone can increase the risk for hyperkalemia, and serum potassium levels should be monitored during therapy ( [Table: Table: Monitoring of Gender-Affirming Hormonal Therapy]

). Spironolactone can increase the risk for polyuria/dehydration if additional risk factors are present. Cyproterone acetate may increase the risk for meningioma.

Masculinizing hormone therapy is achieved by administering testosterone (off-label use), which is available in various preparations ( [Table: Table: Hormone Regimens in Transgender and Gender Diverse Adults]

).

Several risks are associated with testosterone therapy, including polycythemia, infertility, acne, androgenic alopecia, hypertension, sleep apnea, weight gain, decreased HDL cholesterol, and increased LDL cholesterol. Hematocrit or hemoglobin concentrations should be monitored during therapy (see [Table: Table: Monitoring of Gender-Affirming Hormonal Therapy]

). When additional risk factors are present, testosterone may increase the risk for hypertriglyceridemia and possibly type 2 diabetes. Conclusive data do not exist on risks for low bone mass/osteoporosis and malignancy, including that of the breast, cervix, ovaries, and uterus. Contraindications to testosterone therapy include pregnancy, severe hypertension, untreated sleep apnea, and polycythemia.

Once therapy is started, hormone dosages are adjusted to achieve therapeutic sex hormone levels. Hormone monitoring, evaluation for physical changes, and assessment for adverse reactions should occur every 3 months (or with dosage changes) in the first year and then once or twice a year thereafter ( [Table: Table: Monitoring of Gender-Affirming Hormonal Therapy]

). Several physical changes are expected with hormone therapy. Expected timing to onset and maximum effect of these changes should be discussed with patients ( [Table: Table: Timing of Physical Changes Resulting from Feminizing Hormones]

, [Table: Table: Timing of Physical Changes Resulting from Masculinizing Hormones]

).

Screening and preventive medicine should be based on the person’s anatomy and risk factors (see Screening Recommendations for Adults in Foundations of Clinical Practice for information on screening).

Gender confirmation surgery refers to a multitude of procedures that aim to align a person’s body with their gender identity. It is recommended that persons have been stable taking gender-affirming hormone therapy for a minimum of 6 months (unless therapy is not desired or is contraindicated) before gender confirmation surgery. Procedures should be performed by an experienced surgeon in conjunction with a multidisciplinary team.

Feminizing surgery includes augmentation mammoplasty, penectomy, orchiectomy, vaginoplasty, clitoroplasty, vulvoplasty, facial feminization, voice surgery, and thyroid cartilage reduction. Masculinizing surgery includes mastectomy, hysterectomy, oophorectomy, phalloplasty, vaginectomy, scrotoplasty, and implantation of penile/testicular prostheses.

Calcium and Metabolic Bone Disorders

Regulation of serum calcium levels depends on the actions of vitamin D and parathyroid hormone (PTH). The primary effect of vitamin D is enhancing intestinal calcium absorption, whereas the effects of PTH are mediated through regulating renal calcium retention and excretion and bone resorption (

).

Total calcium levels depend on the amount bound to albumin, which can be affected by nutrition, inflammation, liver or kidney disease, and acid-base status. Ionized calcium measurement may be required to accurately assess calcium levels. Estimation of the physiologically relevant calcium level in the blood using formulas to account for the reduction in protein-bound calcium when serum albumin concentrations are low is common. However, when compared with ionized calcium, this “albumin-adjusted calcium” or “corrected calcium” may misclassify patients as normocalcemic, especially when the albumin concentration is less than 3 g/dL (30 g/L). Although ionized calcium measurement is the most accurate assessment of calcium status when abnormal serum albumin or acute acid-base disorders are present, clinicians may opt to rely on total serum calcium alone when hypocalcemia and hypercalcemia are mild, transient, or unlikely to affect clinical decision-making. Situations in which ionized calcium testing may be indicated include the following:

  • Acute management of hypocalcemia or hypercalcemia, especially in critical illness
  • Inconsistency between total serum calcium level and the patient’s clinical status or other indicators of calcium concentrations (e.g., PTH level)
  • Suspected or known disorders of calcium homeostasis (e.g., hypo- or hyperparathyroidism)

Vitamin D is produced in the skin in response to sunlight and is also provided by dietary sources and supplements. Vitamin D activation requires hydroxylation, initially by the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D and subsequently by the kidney to the active form of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. 25-Hydroxyvitamin D is the storage form of vitamin D in the body, and its measurement is the most appropriate test to assess vitamin D sufficiency.

The initial response to a decline in serum calcium is an increase in PTH secretion, which decreases renal calcium excretion and increases calcium resorption from bone. PTH also induces renal conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, which subsequently increases intestinal calcium absorption and osteoclast activation. PTH-mediated mobilization of calcium from bone over the course of months to years in response to a chronic negative calcium balance can lead to metabolic bone disease.

In contrast to the response to hypocalcemia, bone and intestinal dynamics do not significantly contribute to correcting hypercalcemia. Instead, the kidney response predominates, with an increased filtered load and suppressed PTH secretion, leading to robust calcium excretion by the kidneys provided that the circulating volume is adequate.

In addition to a role in calcium homeostasis, bone resorption and formation also allow for continuous skeletal adaptation and repair; the entire skeleton is remodeled approximately every 10 years. Osteocytes coordinate bone remodeling, which is initiated by osteoclastic resorption and then followed by much slower osteoblastic bone formation, culminating in mineralization of a collagen-protein matrix. Rates of bone resorption and formation can be measured with biochemical markers of bone turnover (Video: Markers for Bone Turnover and Resorption). Although useful in clinical trials to better understand the mechanism of pharmacologic agents, the use of these markers in clinical practice is not well defined; they are best used in collaboration with an endocrinologist for select patients.

Asymptomatic hypercalcemia is a common incidental finding on routine blood tests. Classic symptoms of hypercalcemia include polyuria, polydipsia, and nocturia. Additional symptoms may include fatigue, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, constipation, and mental status changes. At higher calcium levels, patients may become obtunded. However, symptoms do not correlate only with serum calcium levels but also with the rapidity at which calcium levels change.

Severe hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria can lead to volume depletion and acute kidney injury, nephrolithiasis, or nephrocalcinosis. Skeletal manifestations reflect the underlying cause of hypercalcemia. Primary hyperparathyroidism may present as osteoporosis, and severe disease is associated with bone pain and osteitis fibrosa cystica (a radiographic diagnosis demonstrating widespread subperiosteal bone resorption [

]). In contrast, lytic bone lesions associated with hypercalcemia are often the result of multiple myeloma or breast cancer.

A thorough history and physical examination are essential in patients with hypercalcemia, as well as a careful review of medications, including supplements. Hypercalcemia is categorized as mild (serum calcium <12 mg/dL [3 mmol/L]), moderate (12-14 mg/dL [3-3.5 mmol/L]), or severe (>14 mg/dL [3.5 mmol/L]). When hypercalcemia is incidentally noted, repeat measurement is indicated, particularly if associated with a dehydrated or nonfasted state. If hypercalcemia is confirmed, simultaneous serum calcium and PTH measurement is the next step in categorizing PTH-mediated and non–PTH-mediated hypercalcemia (

, [Table: Table: Mechanisms and Causes of Hypercalcemic Disorders]

). Ionized calcium measurement may be necessary to accurately diagnose hypercalcemia when the serum albumin level is abnormal or acute acid-base disorders are present.

Thiazide diuretics may cause mild hypercalcemia, especially in the setting of previously unrecognized disease, such as subclinical primary hyperparathyroidism. Hypercalcemia associated with lithium therapy is caused by altered PTH secretion and may occur years after therapy is initiated. If possible, stopping the medication and monitoring serum calcium levels is the first step in management.

PTH secretion decreases abruptly in response to an increase in serum calcium concentration. Therefore, a serum PTH level that is elevated or inappropriately normal (usually in the upper half of the reference range) in a patient with hypercalcemia is diagnostic of PTH-mediated hypercalcemia (

).

Primary hyperparathyroidism is typically caused by a solitary parathyroid adenoma. Women are more often affected than men, with a peak incidence in the seventh decade of life. Hypercalcemia is usually mild (serum calcium level within 1 mg/dL [0.25 mmol/L] of the upper limit of normal) and may be intermittently normal. Hypercalciuria is present in up to 30% of patients, and calcium-creatinine clearance ratio is usually greater than 0.02. Because PTH enhances renal phosphate excretion, low or low-normal serum phosphorus concentrations support the diagnosis in patients with normal kidney function.

Management includes assessing symptoms and complications and considering surgical or medical intervention.

Symptomatic patients and those younger than 50 years typically undergo surgery. In asymptomatic older patients, evaluation should include assessing kidney function, 24-hour urine calcium levels, serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels, and bone mineral density (BMD) with dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) with imaging of the nondominant one-third radius, which can be particularly affected in patients with hyperparathyroidism. In the absence of a history of calcium nephrolithiasis, kidney imaging may be indicated to exclude occult stones if this finding would change management.

Findings that would prompt parathyroid surgery in asymptomatic older patients include the following:

  • A serum calcium level greater than 1 mg/dL (0.25 mmol/L) above the upper limit of normal
  • Changes in kidney function (estimated glomerular filtration rate <60 mL/min, urine calcium level >250 mg/24 h in women or >300 mg/24 h in men, or clinical or imaging evidence of a kidney stone)
  • A T-score of −2.5 or less at any site
  • Vertebral fracture on imaging

Although parathyroid imaging with four-dimensional CT, sestamibi scintigraphy, or neck ultrasonography may localize an adenoma and help plan surgical intervention, these modalities do not determine whether surgery is indicated.

Surgery results in a 95% cure rate; the rate of complications is less than 1% with an experienced surgeon. Preoperative correction of vitamin D deficiency is important given the risk for postoperative hypocalcemia, which results from relative hypoparathyroidism. In severe cases, postoperative hypocalcemia may occur in response to a rapid flux of calcium into bone (hungry bone syndrome). Patients with mild primary hyperparathyroidism commonly require calcium supplementation for up to 1 week after parathyroidectomy until residual parathyroid tissue normalizes serum calcium concentrations. Reassessment of BMD 1 year after parathyroidectomy may show improvement in BMD, especially at the spine.

Medical management includes maintaining hydration and adjusting dietary calcium intake to approximately 1000 mg per day. Measurement of serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels and cautious correction of vitamin D deficiency is important. Repletion is recommended for patients with levels less than 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L), with a goal of between 30 and 50 ng/mL (75-125 nmol/L).

Approximately one in three patients with asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism who initially defer surgery will develop indications for surgery over the course of 10 to 15 years of observation. In those ineligible for or who refuse surgery, management should include annual serum calcium and creatinine measurement. BMD should be obtained every 2 years, and spine imaging should be considered if the patient has significant height loss or back pain. Patients with an elevated serum PTH level but normal serum calcium, creatinine, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels (normocalcemic primary hyperparathyroidism) may be treated similarly to those with asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism.

Parathyroid carcinoma is very rare but may present with symptoms of severe hypercalcemia, with serum levels greater than 14 mg/dL (3.5 mmol/L) and markedly high serum PTH concentrations. The primary treatment is surgical resection. After surgery, 50% of patients may have residual or recurrent disease. Severe hypercalcemia that is not amenable to surgery can be treated chronically with cinacalcet.

In patients with end-stage kidney disease, poorly controlled hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia cause long-term secondary hyperparathyroidism that can result in multigland parathyroid hyperplasia. In some patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism, this chronic stimulation of the parathyroid glands can lead to autonomous PTH production by hyperplastic glands, resulting in eucalcemia and even hypercalcemia. This tertiary hyperparathyroidism is most commonly recognized after kidney transplantation. When PTH-lowering therapies fail, parathyroidectomy remains a valid treatment option.

For discussion of chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder, see Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral and Bone Disorder in Nephrology.

Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) is an autosomal dominant condition and the most common type of familial hypercalcemia. The parathyroid glands and kidney detect serum calcium concentrations through the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR). In FHH, an inactivating variant of the CaSR gene causes the parathyroid gland to perceive serum calcium concentrations as low, resulting in increased PTH secretion and a higher serum calcium level. Simultaneously, the variant CaSR in the kidney increases kidney resorption of calcium, leading to paradoxical hypocalciuria in the setting of hypercalcemia.

Features suggestive of FHH include mild hypercalcemia since childhood; an inappropriately normal or elevated PTH level; low 24-hour urine calcium excretion, especially if the calcium-creatinine clearance ratio is less than 0.01; and family history of parathyroidectomy without resolution of hypercalcemia. If clinically ambiguous, the diagnosis can usually be confirmed by CaSR genetic testing.

FHH is a benign condition because patients do not have sequelae of hypercalcemia. Parathyroidectomy is not indicated because hypercalcemia will not resolve with surgery.

Primary hyperparathyroidism in adolescents and young adults may be a manifestation of multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome (MEN), predominantly MEN1 and occasionally MEN2A syndromes. If the family history is positive for primary hyperparathyroidism, pituitary tumor, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, early-onset pancreatic neoplasm, pheochromocytoma, or medullary thyroid cancer, MEN screening should be considered. In contrast to sporadic primary hyperparathyroidism, hyperparathyroidism may recur in MEN syndromes and is best managed together with or by an endocrinologist.

The differential diagnosis of hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH is broad ( [Table: Table: Mechanisms and Causes of Hypercalcemic Disorders]

); the history, symptoms, and findings may suggest the underlying cause. Serum PTH is usually undetectable but may be very low (<20 pg/mL [20 ng/L]) if hypercalcemia is mild. Hypercalciuria can be severe and may precede hypercalcemia. In severe hypercalcemia, treatment should commence without delay while awaiting laboratory study results.

The most common cause of non–PTH-mediated hypercalcemia is malignancy, and it is typically severe (serum calcium >14 mg/dL [3.5 mmol/L]). Hypercalcemia of malignancy is frequently the result of tumor-produced PTH-related protein, which leads to extensive resorption of bone. Squamous cell cancers (lung, head, and neck), renal cell carcinoma, and breast cancer are associated with PTH-related protein hypercalcemia. In approximately 20% of patients, locally mediated osteolysis from extensive skeletal involvement, typically in multiple myeloma and breast cancer, is the cause. Patients with lymphoma may develop hypercalcemia secondary to increased 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D production. For more information, see Hypercalcemia of Malignancy in Oncology.

Vitamin D–dependent hypercalcemia is associated with normal to elevated serum phosphorus levels because vitamin D enhances intestinal absorption of phosphorus and suppressed PTH secretion reduces kidney phosphorus excretion.

Vitamin D intoxication from chronic high-dose ingestion of vitamin D (typically >1250 μg/d [50,000 IU/d] in patients without malabsorptive conditions) and increased storage in fat causes protracted hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis, impaired kidney function, and elevated serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels.

Unregulated conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D may occur in granulomatous tissue associated with fungal infection, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, and lymphoma, leading to increased intestinal absorption of calcium. These conditions are associated with an inappropriately normal or frankly elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D level and a suppressed serum PTH level.

Ingestion of large amounts of calcium, typically from antacid use (e.g., calcium carbonate), especially with coexistent chronic kidney disease, causes calcium-alkali (milk-alkali) syndrome.

Severe thyrotoxicosis occasionally causes hypercalcemia or hypercalciuria by increasing bone resorption; Addisonian crisis may also occasionally cause hypercalcemia.

Acute prolonged immobilization, as seen in spinal cord injuries, can cause a large efflux of calcium from the skeleton through uncoupled bone remodeling with decreased osteoblastic activity despite increased osteoclastic activity. Patients with primary hyperparathyroidism or skeletal metastases are predisposed to worsening hypercalcemia because of immobilization, as are young patients, in whom baseline bone remodeling is high.

Management depends on the severity of hypercalcemia. If it is mild (serum calcium <12 mg/dL [3 mmol/L]), then treating the underlying disorder is sufficient while avoiding factors that can exacerbate hypercalcemia, including poor hydration, excessive calcium intake, thiazide diuretics, vitamin D supplementation, and extended immobilization. Hospitalization may be needed in patients with acute kidney injury, mental status changes, or serum calcium levels greater than 12 mg/dL (3 mmol/L). Initial treatment of severe hypercalcemia (>14 mg/dL [3.5 mmol/L]) is aggressive hydration with 0.9% saline to replete volume loss and increase kidney excretion of calcium. Loop diuretics are not recommended in the absence of kidney failure or volume overload. For the acutely symptomatic patient, subcutaneous calcitonin can be used; however, the drug effect wanes after 48 hours. Hemodialysis is reserved for treating severe hypercalcemia in patients with severe kidney or cardiac dysfunction.

Long-term hypercalcemia management includes treating the underlying disorder and may also require intravenous bisphosphonate therapy to prevent calcium mobilization from the skeleton, but adequate kidney function is required.

Hypercalcemia of malignancy is managed with the above interventions as well as consideration of intravenous bisphosphonate therapy or denosumab (the latter is approved for patients with hypercalcemia that is refractory to bisphosphonates or in whom bisphosphonates are contraindicated). For more information, see Hypercalcemia of Malignancy in Oncology.

Glucocorticoids and restriction of calcium and vitamin D intake are uniquely beneficial in vitamin D–dependent hypercalcemia.

Most patients with hypocalcemia are asymptomatic or report intermittent paresthesia of the hands and feet or perioral numbness. Patients with severe hypocalcemia may present with neuromuscular symptoms and signs. Carpopedal spasm with characteristic hand posture (flexion at metacarpophalangeal joints and extension at interphalangeal joints) may be spontaneous or triggered by transient distal limb ischemia during blood pressure assessment. Facial nerve hyperirritability and muscle spasm can be demonstrated by percussion of the facial nerve just anterior to the ear. Importantly, laryngospasm, seizure, myocardial dysfunction, and QT interval prolongation leading to sudden cardiac death caused by severe hypocalcemia (serum calcium <7.5 mg/dL [1.9 mmol/L]) can occur without prodromal paresthesia or muscle cramping.

Hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia caused by chronic hypoparathyroidism can be associated with cataract formation, basal ganglia calcification, papilledema, and dental enamel hypoplasia.

Hypocalcemic disorders in outpatients are typically detected on routine blood tests and are mild, with serum calcium levels of 7.5 to 8.5 mg/dL (1.9-2.1 mmol/L). Hypocalcemia may also be detected during evaluation for fragility fractures or osteoporosis.

Hypocalcemia should be confirmed with a second measurement. Ionized calcium measurement may be necessary to accurately diagnose hypocalcemia when the serum albumin level is abnormal or acute acid-base disorders, typically acute alkalosis, are present. Causes may be evident based on the clinical context ( [Table: Table: Mechanisms and Causes of Hypocalcemic Disorders]

); otherwise, the next step is simultaneous measurement of serum calcium, phosphorus, creatinine, and PTH levels ( [Table: Table: Common Causes of Hypocalcemia and Associated Laboratory Values]

).

Hypoparathyroidism is most commonly caused by inadvertent injury during anterior neck surgery (thyroidectomy, parathyroidectomy, head and neck cancer) and may present within a few hours of surgery or, uncommonly, years later. Depending on the extent of injury or resection, surgical hypoparathyroidism may last days to weeks. Permanent hypoparathyroidism may be partial or complete; inappropriately normal serum PTH levels with concurrent hypocalcemia represent the former, whereas the latter is associated with undetectable serum PTH levels and a higher prevalence of hyperphosphatemia and hypercalciuria.

Other causes of hypocalcemia associated with insufficient PTH secretion include infiltrative disorders (hemochromatosis or Wilson disease), radiation, autoimmunity, and congenital disorders. Chronic hypocalcemia with inappropriately normal serum PTH levels occurring within a family may represent an activating variant of the CaSR gene. Hypomagnesemia, which may occur in malnutrition and alcohol use disorder and with use of loop diuretics and chronic proton pump inhibitor therapy, causes reversible functional parathyroid hypofunction and must be excluded before a low or inappropriately normal serum PTH level is attributed to hypoparathyroidism. PTH resistance (pseudohypoparathyroidism) is a rare genetic cause of hypocalcemia associated with hyperphosphatemia and an elevated PTH level.

Malnutrition or malabsorption of vitamin D and/or calcium may be suspected on the basis of clinical history (bariatric surgery, celiac disease) and confirmed by a low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level or low 24-hour urine calcium excretion (a proxy indicator of calcium intake and absorption). A common cause of acquired hypocalcemia is impaired production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and hyperphosphatemia caused by chronic kidney disease.

Rhabdomyolysis and tumor lysis syndrome increase serum phosphorus and calcium phosphate binding in the vascular space, causing low ionized calcium levels.

Hungry bone syndrome and widespread osteoblastic metastases (prostate cancer, breast cancer) can cause hypocalcemia, as can saponification of calcium (and magnesium) in necrotic fat in acute pancreatitis.

Potent antiresorptive drugs, such as intravenous bisphosphonates and denosumab, can cause severe and protracted hypocalcemia by impairing physiologic efflux of calcium from the skeleton in patients with vitamin D deficiency or chronic kidney disease. Therefore, it is important to assess vitamin D levels and correct deficiency before beginning treatment with an antiresorptive drug. Other medications that can cause hypocalcemia include foscarnet, cisplatin, cinacalcet, calcium chelators, carbamazepine, phenytoin, and phenobarbital.

Severe hypocalcemia (serum calcium <7.5 mg/dL [1.9 mmol/L]) necessitates urgent treatment with intravenous calcium. Slow administration through central intravenous access with ECG monitoring is preferred. In refractory disease, teriparatide, 20 μg twice daily, rapidly eliminates symptoms of hypocalcemia in acute postsurgical hypoparathyroidism (as an off-label indication).

Vitamin D supplementation, 25 to 100 μg/d (1000-4000 IU/d), and oral calcium carbonate or calcium citrate, administered as 1 to 3 g/d in divided doses taken with meals, may normalize or sufficiently treat mild or chronic hypocalcemia. Calcitriol is needed in the setting of hypoparathyroidism with an undetectable serum PTH level or kidney failure because activation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D requires both PTH and sufficient kidney function. Palopegteriparatide, a long-acting PTH analogue, is approved for the treatment of chronic hypoparathyroidism in adults and may allow reduced dosing or independence from calcium and active vitamin D treatment.

A reasonable goal for most patients with chronic hypoparathyroidism is a serum calcium concentration at or just below the normal range without hypercalciuria. Monitoring of urine calcium excretion is mandatory because hypercalciuria often limits therapy. Thiazide diuretics are commonly used because they decrease urine calcium excretion. Coexisting hypomagnesemia must also be corrected. Hyperphosphatemia is initially treated by reducing dietary phosphorus but occasionally requires the addition of oral phosphate binders if serum phosphorus exceeds the normal range.

Bone mass, mineral content, and macro- and microarchitecture determine bone strength. BMD reflects bone mass and mineral content and, in older adults, predicts microarchitecture deterioration. This relationship and epidemiologic data support the use of BMD determined by DXA to diagnose low bone mass or osteoporosis and assess fracture risk in older adults.

Fragility fractures (those occurring with the equivalent of a fall from a standing height or less) after age 50 years indicate low bone strength and can be used to define clinical osteoporosis, particularly with hip and spine fractures. Fragility fractures most commonly occur at the hip, spine, and forearm. Skull, cervical spine, ankle, feet, and hand fractures are not considered fragility fractures and do not routinely require bone health evaluation.

Decreased bone mass in adults may represent poor bone formation, bone loss, or both. Factors that can affect peak bone mass formation include genetic conditions, lifestyle factors, and poor childhood health. Net loss of bone mass can occur in adults when osteoclastic bone resorption exceeds osteoblastic bone formation.

The list of risk factors for low bone mass and osteoporosis ( [Table: Table: Risk Factors for Low Bone Mass (Osteopenia) and Osteoporosis]

and [Table: Table: Conditions Associated With Risk for Low Bone Mass and Osteoporosis]

) is extensive, and some patients have osteoporosis secondary to another disease.

Glucocorticoids are a well-recognized cause of significant bone loss, and the risk is increased in older patients, with larger dosages, and with longer therapy durations.

Guidelines recommend starting screening with BMD measurement at age 65 years for postmenopausal women with average risk. Guidelines vary in recommendations for routine osteoporosis screening in men. In premenopausal women and men aged 50 years or younger without risk factors, BMD assessment to estimate fracture risk is not recommended. See Osteoporosis in Foundations of Clinical Practice for further details on routine screening.

Patients with the following characteristics should have BMD testing earlier than standard screening recommendations:

  • Fragility fractures of the femur, vertebra (

), pelvis, humerus, or radius - Risk factors for low bone mass or osteoporosis - Height loss of 4 cm (1.5 in) or more - Kyphosis

The American College of Rheumatology recommends that patients anticipated to be receiving long-term glucocorticoid treatment (≥2.5 mg/d for >3 months) be assessed for fracture risk as soon as possible after therapy initiation. Adults younger than 40 years of age should undergo BMD testing with vertebral fracture assessment or spinal radiography. Adults aged 40 years and older should undergo assessment with the Fracture Risk Assessment Tool (FRAX) and DXA with vertebral fracture assessment or spinal radiographs.

BMD measurement may also be indicated when fracture risk is elevated based on the results of risk assessment tools such as the Simple Calculated Osteoporosis Risk Estimation, Osteoporosis Self-Assessment Tool, Osteoporosis Risk Assessment Instrument, and FRAX.
