lists recommendations for BMD testing.

Vertebral imaging recommendations from the Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation are as follows:

  • Women aged ≥70 years and men aged ≥80 years if T-score at the spine, total hip, or femoral neck is ≤−1.0
  • Women aged ≥65 years if T-score at the femoral neck is ≤−1.0
  • Men aged 70-79 years if T-score at the spine, total hip, or femoral neck is ≤−1.5
  • Postmenopausal women and men aged ≥50 years with the following risk factors:
    • Fracture during adulthood (age ≥50 years)
  • Historic height loss of 4 cm (1.5 in) or more from maximum lifetime height
  • Prospective height loss of 2 cm (0.8 in) or more
  • Recent or ongoing long-term glucocorticoid treatment
  • Hyperparathyroidism or other condition associated with bone loss

Vertebral imaging should be repeated when a new loss of height is noted or new back pain is reported.

In postmenopausal women and men aged 50 years and older, low bone mass (osteopenia) is diagnosed by BMD testing (T-score between −1 and −2.5) alone. Osteoporosis in these groups can be diagnosed by BMD testing or clinically. Without secondary causes of low BMD, osteoporosis is diagnosed when the femur neck, total hip, or composite (two or more diagnostic vertebrae) lumbar spine T-score is −2.5 or less, as defined by the World Health Organization. If the hip or spine cannot be accurately measured by BMD testing, DXA of the one-third radius can be used. The clinical diagnosis of osteoporosis is based on the presence of a fragility fracture, especially hip or vertebral compression fractures.

In premenopausal women and men younger than 50 years, osteoporosis can be diagnosed when recurrent low-energy fractures are associated with BMD on DXA that is below the range expected for the patient’s age (Z-score ≤−2).

BMD assessment by quantitative calcaneal ultrasonography or peripheral DXA may be used to screen for osteoporosis, but abnormal results require confirmation by central DXA. A quantitative CT scan provides a DXA equivalent T-score, is not hindered by degenerative changes in the lumbar spine, and is highly sensitive for detecting vertebral compression fractures; however, it is not recommended for osteoporosis screening because the cost and radiation exposure are greater.

Nonmodifiable factors are the most common cause of low bone mass and osteoporosis, but all patients should have a thorough history and physical examination and additional testing based on findings (see [Table: Table: Risk Factors for Low Bone Mass (Osteopenia) and Osteoporosis]

, [Table: Table: Conditions Associated With Risk for Low Bone Mass and Osteoporosis]

, and [Table: Table: Recommendations for BMD Measurement]

). Although BMD measurement may not be required in all patients to diagnose osteoporosis, it may be helpful to determine whether additional testing is needed and to guide treatment. [Table: Table: Diagnostic Studies for Secondary Causes of Osteoporosis]

summarizes testing for secondary causes.

Osteomalacia is most commonly caused by severe and prolonged vitamin D deficiency (see Vitamin D Deficiency in Endocrinology and Metabolism). The resultant low concentrations of calcium and phosphate in the bone prevent adequate mineralization of newly formed bone matrix. Unlike osteoporosis, osteomalacia does not result in permanent loss of bone structure. A period of months to years of disordered mineralization is required before bone strength is compromised.

Osteomalacia symptoms include diffuse bone pain, bone tenderness to palpation (tibial plateau and sternum), and proximal muscle weakness; however, early osteomalacia may present only with low BMD on DXA and can be indistinguishable from osteoporosis without further testing (

). Low BMD Z-score (≤−2), low or low-normal serum calcium and phosphorus levels, a very low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level (<10 ng/mL [25 nmol/L]), and secondary hyperparathyroidism help distinguish osteomalacia from osteoporosis. An elevated serum alkaline phosphatase level is particularly suggestive of osteomalacia, although mild elevation can be seen with recent osteoporotic fracture. In severe osteomalacia, radiographs may display an unusual fracture distribution (

). When bone pain in the setting of suspected osteomalacia is not explained by conventional radiographic findings, imaging with radionuclide bone scan or MRI may reveal fractures.

The goal of treatment is normalizing serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D, calcium, and phosphorus concentrations with vitamin D supplementation. The skeletal response to treatment is reflected by gradual normalization of the serum alkaline phosphatase level and symptom relief. Resolution may take as long as 12 months; subsequent BMD testing will show significant increases in or normalization of BMD.

The most appropriate test to assess for vitamin D deficiency is serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D measurement. An intake of 15 to 20 μg/d (600-800 IU/d) of vitamin D~3 is typically sufficient to prevent deficiency. Routine screening for vitamin D deficiency is not recommended in healthy populations; however, testing for deficiency is appropriate in groups at high risk or in patients with metabolic bone disorders, fragility fractures, hypocalcemia, or hyperparathyroidism.

Options for treating vitamin D deficiency vary by indication and underlying disease ( [Table: Table: Treatment of Vitamin D Deficiency]

). Daily dosing is preferred because larger, intermittent doses have been associated with increased risk for falls and fractures. Once vitamin D stores are repleted, maintenance may be guided by serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels obtained 3 months after treatment initiation.

A proliferation of scientific publications has associated vitamin D levels with extraskeletal health outcomes. The Endocrine Society recommends empiric vitamin D supplementation for persons aged 75 years and older to reduce mortality; pregnant persons to potentially lower the risk for preeclampsia, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and intrauterine and neonatal mortality; and persons with high-risk prediabetes to reduce progression to diabetes mellitus.

Decreased bone mass and fragility fractures in young and middle-aged adults may result from genetic disorders (see [Table: Table: Risk Factors for Low Bone Mass (Osteopenia) and Osteoporosis]

). Patients with mild (type 1) osteogenesis imperfecta may present with a history of childhood fractures that decrease in frequency in adulthood. Hypermobility raises suspicion for Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and related syndromes. Hypophosphatasia should be suspected in middle-aged patients with fractures and serum alkaline phosphatase levels well below the reference range.

Exercise involving weight-bearing, resistance, and balance is important for bone health and may reduce fracture risk at any age, but especially in patients older than 65 years (see Physical Activity in Foundations of Clinical Practice for general information on exercise). Discontinuation of smoking and alcohol use are also recommended.

Calcium and vitamin D were frequently supplemented in osteoporosis pharmacotherapy trials that sought to achieve 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels of 20 to 30 ng/mL (50-75 nmol/L). Although the measurable treatment effect may be small, the National Academy of Medicine recommends a calcium intake of 1000 to 1200 mg/d, ideally from dietary sources. A calcium supplement may be used for patients whose diets are insufficient but should not be recommended independent of dietary assessment and intervention. A vitamin D supplement of 25 μg/d (1000 IU/d) may also be appropriate in the context of osteoporosis care.

The Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation recommends pharmacologic treatment for patients with osteoporosis-related hip or spine fractures, those with a BMD T-score of −2.5 or less, and those with a BMD T-score between −1 and −2.5 and a 10-year risk for hip fracture of 3% or greater or risk for major osteoporosis-related fracture of 20% or greater as estimated by the FRAX. Some studies suggest that different thresholds for treatment initiation should be considered in other populations at risk.

Although a very low BMD result (T-score <−3.5) in a patient with fragility fractures may influence treatment decisions, BMD testing is not required before choosing between FDA-approved treatments. Lack of easily available testing should not delay treatment initiation.

Pharmacotherapy may also be used to prevent BMD loss in postmenopausal women at risk for osteoporosis and to prevent or treat glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis.

FDA-approved drugs for osteoporosis treatment and prevention are listed in [Table: Table: Medications for Osteoporosis Prevention and Treatment]

.

Bisphosphonates are first-line treatment for primary osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and men and reduce the risk for spine, hip, and nonvertebral fractures. Oral bisphosphonates include alendronate and risedronate; ibandronate has only shown efficacy in reducing vertebral fractures and is not first-line therapy. In glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis with moderate to high fracture risk, oral bisphosphonates are recommended as first-line therapy in adult men and women regardless of age.

Intravenous zoledronate once annually is an equally effective option if patients experience upper gastrointestinal symptoms or have difficulty taking oral bisphosphonates as directed. An acute-phase response reaction including pyrexia and myalgia may occur after the first administration of zoledronate in one third of patients but does not typically recur. Zoledronate administered every 18 months for 6 years reduces risk for vertebral and nonvertebral fracture in women with low bone mass (osteopenia), an effect not shown with other bisphosphonates.

Bisphosphonates are not recommended in patients with reduced kidney function (creatinine clearance <35 mL/min) and should not be given until vitamin D deficiency and hypocalcemia are treated, if present.

Rare adverse effects of antiresorptive agents are osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femur fracture. Osteonecrosis of the jaw may occur at any point in therapy, whereas the risk for atypical femur fracture increases with the duration of therapy. For most patients, the benefits in reducing osteoporotic fractures far outweigh the risk of these uncommon adverse effects.

In most patients, a drug holiday can be initiated after 3 years (intravenous) to 5 years (oral) of bisphosphonate treatment. Although the best means of selecting patients for extended therapy are uncertain, patients remaining at high risk for fracture may continue bisphosphonate treatment or switch to an alternative medication. Factors to consider in guiding the duration of the drug holiday include the risk for fracture, bisphosphonate used, and BMD upon repeat testing.

Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits osteoclast activation. When administered subcutaneously twice yearly, denosumab suppresses bone resorption, increases bone density, and reduces the incidence of osteoporotic fractures in men and women. The American College of Physicians suggests denosumab as a second-line agent to be used in postmenopausal women and in men with primary osteoporosis who have contraindications to (including chronic kidney disease) or experience adverse effects from bisphosphonate therapy.

Although the safety and antifracture efficacy of denosumab relative to placebo has been established for up to 3 years, the optimal treatment duration is uncertain. The effects of denosumab are not sustained when treatment is stopped, and bisphosphonate therapy, typically with zoledronate, should be initiated 6 months after the last treatment with denosumab.

Adverse effects include hypocalcemia, especially in older patients with vitamin D deficiency and those with advanced chronic kidney disease or chronic kidney disease-mineral bone disorder, and an increased rate of dermatitis and infection (primarily skin, urinary tract, abdominal, and ear). Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femur fracture have also been reported with denosumab.

Raloxifene and bazedoxifene have tissue-specific estrogen receptor effects, acting as agonists in bone and antagonists in breast and uterus tissue. Because these agents are less effective in fracture prevention than bisphosphonates and may increase the risk for venous thromboembolic disease and stroke, they are not first-line therapy for osteoporosis.

Raloxifene reduces the risk for invasive breast cancer and may be most useful in women at high risk for breast cancer. Bazedoxifene is available in combination with conjugated estrogens and prevents hot flashes and bone loss but has not been shown to reduce fracture risk.

The anabolic agents teriparatide and abaloparatide stimulate bone formation. Teriparatide (recombinant human PTH [1-34]) is approved for use in postmenopausal women and men or women with glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis who are at high risk for osteoporotic fracture. It is also used to improve bone mass in men with primary or hypogonadism-related osteoporosis at high risk for fracture. Abaloparatide (recombinant human PTH-related protein [1-34]) is approved for treating postmenopausal women and men with osteoporosis at high risk for fracture. Both agents require daily subcutaneous injection. Treatment is generally limited to 2 years and should be avoided in patients with unexplained elevations in bone-specific alkaline phosphatase, potential for malignancy involving the skeleton, or hyperparathyroidism with or without hypercalcemia. Improvement in BMD is most evident at the spine. To prevent the loss of newly formed bone, sequential therapy with an antiresorptive agent, preferably a bisphosphonate, must begin within 1 month of completing the course of anabolic treatment.

Sclerostin is an inhibitor of bone formation produced by osteocytes. Romosozumab is a monoclonal antibody inhibitor of sclerostin that increases bone formation and reduces bone resorption. Monthly subcutaneous injection of romosozumab for 1 year increases spine and hip bone density and reduces the risk for vertebral and nonvertebral fractures in postmenopausal women. Romosozumab may rarely cause osteonecrosis of the jaw or atypical femur fractures. A 1-year course of romosozumab must be followed by a bisphosphonate or denosumab. Because romosozumab may increase the risk for stroke, myocardial infarction, and cardiovascular death, it should not be used in patients who have had a myocardial infarction or stroke within the last year and should be used cautiously in patients with increased cardiovascular risk. As with other antiresorptive medications, hypocalcemia and vitamin D deficiency must be excluded before treatment initiation.

Routine serial DXA measurements of BMD are not indicated for follow-up of patients at low risk for fractures; subsequent testing depends on baseline BMD. Repeating after 15 years may be reasonable if the hip T-score is normal (>−1). A 3- to 5-year interval can be considered for a T-score between −1 and −2. Retesting at 2 years may be considered if the hip T-score is −2 to −2.4.

Repeating BMD testing in patients taking antiresorptive agents may be considered to detect lack of treatment response. Declining BMD, indicated by a statistically significant percentage decrease in g/cm^2 of bone (not by declining T-scores) or a fracture while undergoing treatment, raises concern for an unrecognized secondary cause, nonadherence, or an insufficient response that necessitates reevaluation. The Endocrine Society and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists suggest monitoring BMD every 1 to 3 years to assess treatment response. Conversely, the American College of Physicians recommends against monitoring BMD during treatment because data from several studies showed that women treated with antiresorptive treatment benefited from reduced fractures even if BMD did not increase. Instead, follow-up management should include reviewing indications for treatment, monitoring adherence, and reinforcing lifestyle measures to prevent fractures, minimize bone loss, and avoid frailty.

Drug holiday from bisphosphonate therapy usually involves measurement of BMD to establish a baseline and repeated measurement in 2 to 3 years. Although this approach ostensibly informs subsequent treatment decisions, it has not been validated.

Although Paget disease of bone may present with localized symptoms, it is most commonly diagnosed in asymptomatic older patients presenting with elevated serum alkaline phosphatase levels or incidental radiographic findings. Commonly affected bones include the skull, spine, sacrum, pelvis, femur, and tibia. Involvement of weight-bearing bones of the lower extremity may result in bone pain, deformity, or fracture. Involvement of a bone approximating a joint can contribute to degenerative joint disease. Expansion of pagetic bone of the upper spine or skull base may cause spinal cord or cranial nerve compression.

Diagnosis is based on radiographic findings of thickening of cortical bone, coarsened trabecular markings, and distortion and expansion of involved bone (

). Biopsy is rarely needed. Serum alkaline phosphatase, a marker of increased bone formation, is generally elevated but may be normal in long-term metabolically inactive disease. Patients with suspected Paget disease of bone require assessment of serum calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels and a whole-body radionuclide bone scan. If the bone scan reveals other skeletal sites suspicious for this disease, radiography of those sites is required for further evaluation.

Paget disease management is based on symptoms, location of involvement, and disease activity. Indications for treatment include bone pain; risk for fracture and progressive deformity that may compromise bone, joint, or neurologic function; and possibly elevated serum alkaline phosphatase concentrations. A single 5-mg dose of intravenous zoledronate often achieves the treatment goal of reducing pain and normalizing serum alkaline phosphatase levels for up to 5 years.

Serum alkaline phosphatase levels should be monitored annually. Retreatment is indicated if previously normalized serum alkaline phosphatase levels exceed normal levels. Involved areas may rarely undergo sarcomatous transformation, which is usually fatal. If serum alkaline phosphatase levels or symptoms increase significantly, imaging is required.

High Value Care in Internal Medicine

The United States spends more on health care than all other developed nations without improvement in medical care–related mortality or life expectancy. In response to this apparent paradox, health policy organizations advocate implementing a high-value approach to patient care. High value care is individualized care that delivers proven benefits while minimizing risks and unnecessary costs, eliminates wasteful health care habits, improves health outcomes, and avoids harms. Factors that improve high value care include reimbursement models that reward high-quality, efficient care; lower ratios of subspecialty care to primary care; and a health care organization culture that supports high value care.

When determining the value of interventions, benefits should be considered before cost. Focusing primarily on cost might result in continuing low-cost interventions that provide no benefit or avoiding expensive but highly beneficial interventions. For example, some costly or risky interventions, such as screening colonoscopy, are considered high value, whereas some inexpensive and low-risk interventions, such as daily laboratory testing in hospitalized patients, represent low value care. Examples of high and low value care are provided in [Table: Table: Examples of High Value and Low Value Care]

.

Perception of patients’ demands is an important potential driver of inappropriate testing and treatment. However, high value care that includes patients in decision making provides opportunities to educate them on balancing benefits with costs and to incorporate their preferences, resulting in care that places patients’ values, concerns, and outcomes at the center of clinical decision making.

Evidence-based decision support tools that consider value may assist physicians in providing high value care. Care coordination programs that focus on patients at risk for high-cost care may also facilitate the provision of high value care. Physicians should be aware of and intentionally avoid cognitive biases that might drive low quality care (see Diagnostic Error in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Such biases can be associated with diagnostic inaccuracies, which can lead to mismanagement and higher cost of care.

The American College of Physicians offers resources to help clinicians determine the value of common tests and interventions as well as a high value care curriculum for educators and residents.

Clinical Decision Making and Interpreting the Medical Literature

Clinical decision making is the application of reasoning to a clinical situation and is an essential skill in clinical practice, medical education, and research. Despite its ubiquity, experts often disagree on how to define this process. Some definitions limit decision making to the individual cognitive process of the clinician, whereas other definitions include social, environmental, and technical influences in the decision-making process. Much of the research in this area has focused on diagnostic reasoning because diagnostic error is a contributor to preventable harm. However, in practice, clinical decision making can be applied to diagnostic, therapeutic, screening, and advance care planning decisions.

Clinicians primarily use two parallel and intertwined systems when making decisions, known as dual-process theory. System 1 entails an intuitive, pattern-based approach, such as the instant recognition of a vesicular rash as herpes zoster. In contrast, system 2 uses an analytical, rule-based approach, such as hypothetico-deductive reasoning, in which each diagnostic possibility, including the concordant and discordant aspects of the clinical presentation, is specifically analyzed. System 1 processes have the advantage of efficiency but are also prone to error. Many clinical decisions involve the use of both systems, and it is difficult to ascertain which system a clinician is using. Experienced clinicians tend to use system 1 more than inexperienced clinicians and often use system 2 to check their system 1 processes.

Artificial intelligence and machine learning are increasingly used to aid clinical decision making. Because these tools are not without error and are dependent upon appropriate and accurate data inputs, clinicians should only use artificial intelligence tools to complement existing processes and not as a replacement for the logic and decision making of physicians and the health care team.

Diagnostic reasoning is a multifaceted process that involves systematically obtaining historical information, observing physical findings, evaluating diagnostic test results, and applying the information obtained to categorize the clinical syndrome accurately. The process comprises several interrelated steps (

). Using the data acquired, the clinician summarizes the important clinical features as a problem representation. This step guides hypothesis generation through matching of the problem representation to illness scripts, which are mental representations of diseases and conditions that a clinician builds over time through experience. Illness scripts drive the acquisition of more data that increase or decrease the likelihood of specific diseases. Interpreting the clinical information to arrive at the correct diagnosis requires an understanding of how specific features or test results influence the probability of a disease or condition. Therapeutic reasoning operates in a similar manner; appropriate treatment is selected by applying evidence from the medical literature to the unique characteristics and preferences of the individual patient.

Experience is the most important factor in the development and improvement of diagnostic reasoning abilities. The effectiveness of other proposed means of improvement is unclear; however, guided reflection and cognitive forcing strategies have shown promise in improving the accuracy of clinical decision making in early-career physicians. Cognitive forcing strategies are specific techniques involving self-monitoring of decision making to prevent an inappropriate pattern recognition diagnosis that leads to diagnostic error. Other interventions that may be beneficial include checklists and educational sessions.

Diagnostic error occurs when a patient is not provided with a timely and correct diagnosis or the diagnosis is not communicated to the patient. More specifically, a diagnostic error is present when there was a missed opportunity to make the correct diagnosis in a timely manner. The rate of diagnostic error is approximately 10%, and most patients will be subject to a diagnostic error at some point in their lifetime. Diagnostic errors are preventable in half or more of cases, making them the leading cause of malpractice claims against internal medicine physicians.

Diagnostic errors are usually multifactorial in etiology, with flaws in the individual clinician’s cognitive processes and systems-level issues contributing to most errors.

Examples of cognitive errors include the following:

  • Anchoring: disproportionate weighting of early data that influences interpretation of subsequent information.
  • Premature closure: accepting a diagnosis and discontinuing the diagnostic process before the data necessary to establish the diagnosis have been obtained.
  • Diagnostic momentum: a diagnosis is suggested early in the diagnostic process, and the diagnostic evaluation continues to move toward that diagnosis, even if the data do not support it.
  • Confirmation bias: the predisposition to seek evidence to confirm a suspected diagnosis without looking for evidence that disproves it.
  • Faulty knowledge or knowledge application: the clinician does not possess the underlying knowledge necessary to make the diagnosis or does not apply the knowledge properly.

Techniques that clinicians can use to reduce the risk for diagnostic error are provided in [Table: Table: Twelve Tips for Avoiding Diagnostic Errors]

.

Systems factors that contribute to diagnostic error include communication policies and practices, resource availability, and practice structure. Poor communication of crucial laboratory and imaging results (e.g., the incidental finding of a pulmonary nodule) may result in delayed diagnosis and patient harm. Similarly, lack of test availability (e.g., advanced imaging in a rural location) may delay diagnosis. Productivity pressures and administrative burden, and their effect on clinician time with patients, may also contribute to diagnostic errors. Chaos in a medical practice is associated with an increased risk for error, missed opportunities to provide preventive services, burnout, and physician turnover. It is essential for institutions to implement strategies to address systematic contributors to diagnostic error through protocols, policies, resource allocation, and quality initiatives.

Implicit and explicit biases can lead to diagnostic error through effects on diagnosis and treatment decisions and are a factor in health disparities observed in economically marginalized populations (see Addressing Bias, Stigma, and Discrimination in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Effective clinical decision making relies on an ability to analyze the available medical literature and translate the evidence base for use in individual clinical scenarios. To accomplish this, it is important to understand which study designs are best suited to answer the specific clinical question (e.g., etiology, diagnosis, treatment, prevention, or prognosis), how to interpret statistical tests for significance, and how to determine which information is useful in patient-centered clinical decision making.

Study designs can be divided into two broad categories: experimental studies and observational studies. Study design selection is guided by the population being studied and the suitability and feasibility of the design to address the clinical question. Experimental studies, especially those with random allocation of treatment, provide the strongest evidence for determining the cause of an outcome, the effectiveness of preventive measures, and the effectiveness of treatments or therapies. For studies of diagnosis or prognosis, the observational prospective cohort study often offers the strongest available evidence.

Levels of evidence describe the strength and quality of study results and can aid in clinical decision making. Systematic reviews, with or without meta-analyses, provide the highest level of evidence, followed by large, multicenter, randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled trials. Large, controlled studies generally provide a higher level of evidence than smaller studies, and experimental studies provide a higher level of evidence than observational studies. Reports of expert opinion provide the lowest acceptable level of evidence. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force and other organizations have developed grading systems to rank the relative rigor of clinical studies ( [Table: Table: USPSTF Hierarchy of Research Design]

).

Recommendations in clinical practice guidelines generally reflect the certainty of evidence as well as the class (or strength) of recommendation, which considers the balance of benefits versus risks for the intervention. A commonly used grading system for class of recommendation is presented in

.

Experimental studies systematically expose some or all individuals in the study to a potential causative or protective factor (the exposure, often a treatment). Exposed and unexposed participants are compared with respect to developing the outcome of interest. Examples of experimental study designs are provided in [Table: Table: Experimental Study Designs]

.

The process for allocating the exposure or treatment to the study participants affects the strength and validity of the study. The strongest experimental design is the randomized controlled trial. By randomly allocating the treatment, confounders (both known and unknown) are randomly distributed in the treatment and control groups. The least rigorous experimental design is a nonrandomized pre-post intervention, a type of quasi-experimental design in which all participants receive the treatment being studied. Because there is not a separate comparison or control group, the ability of the quasi-experimental design to determine cause and effect is limited.

In observational studies, no treatment is imposed on the persons being studied. Instead, researchers observe naturally occurring events in individuals who have or have not been exposed to a risk factor or treatment. The relationships between risk factors and disease may be explored, but the ability to assess for causality is limited.

Common observational study designs include ecologic, cross-sectional, case-control, and cohort studies. Case reports or case series, which describe an individual case or a series of related cases, are not true studies but have the potential to identify new or unique relationships to be studied further. Descriptions, uses, and examples of observational study designs are provided in [Table: Table: Observational Study Designs]

.

Narrative review articles authored by topic experts are a common source of information for clinicians. Although narrative reviews are a valuable learning resource, the information they contain is influenced by the experiences of the authors and is inherently biased. In contrast, systematic reviews involve a systematic search of the literature using predefined criteria to collect all studies that address the topic. Systematic reviews should have clear methods and, like other scientific studies, be reproducible. The systematic approach minimizes selection bias and increases the strength of the information presented. A systematic review may also include a meta-analysis if the results of the studies in the review are combined and included in a statistical analysis.

In general, a study with a larger sample size has greater power to discriminate small differences between groups; however, larger studies carry a higher cost and are logistically more complicated to administer. Because meta-analyses pool data from many individual studies and increase sample size and statistical power, the ability to detect a difference between the studied groups increases. Meta-analysis of high-quality randomized controlled trials is considered one of the highest levels of clinical evidence. Factors that limit the ability to combine study results meaningfully include differences in the study populations, research measures, and statistical techniques; these differences are termed heterogeneity. The quality of a systematic review can be evaluated against best practice criteria, such as the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) criteria.

Validity is the degree to which the study results reflect what is correct or true. It is distinct from reliability, a construct that measures how consistent the results are upon repeated measurement. Validity can be further categorized as internal or external. Internal validity refers to how well study error is minimized, whereas external validity is the extent to which the study results can be applied beyond the study setting, or the generalizability. Threats to validity include systematic and random error.

Systematic error is the influence of confounders and bias on study results. Confounders are factors other than the variables being studied that are associated with the studied population and may affect the end point being assessed. A cross-sectional study, for example, may unexpectedly show that adults receiving statin therapy have increased risk for cardiovascular events compared with those not taking statins. However, the presence of a powerful confounder—specifically, that patients receive statin therapy because they are at increased risk for cardiovascular events—influences the outcome of the study. The impact of confounding can be reduced by design strategies (e.g., matching of variables) and evaluation techniques (e.g., stratification of the analysis and regression techniques). The strongest protection against confounding is provided by random assignment of the study intervention. Bias refers to the presence of factors that skew study results in a specific direction. Bias may be introduced at any point in a study design, including patient recruitment and outcome measurement. Careful study design, such as the use of blinding, can decrease the likelihood of bias. Appropriate statistical analysis, such as using an intention-to-treat analysis (

) when analyzing a randomized controlled trial, can help to mitigate bias by preserving the effects of randomization. Once bias is present, however, it cannot be eliminated.

Random error is introduced into studies by random variability or chance. The presence of random error can be reduced by increasing study sample size and using precise measurement strategies. Statistical significance, which is reported using P values or confidence intervals, helps quantify the likelihood that the results of a study are the result of random error. A P value less than or equal to 0.05 (≤5% probability that chance alone accounts for the result) is often considered to indicate a statistically significant finding. However, this determination is arbitrary, and some researchers may opt for a different level.

Confidence intervals express the range of values within which the true result falls; the 95% confidence interval means that there is 95% confidence that the true value is within the confidence interval range. Narrower ranges imply greater certainty that the reported value reflects the true value.

Importantly, statistical significance is not equivalent to clinical significance. A treatment may result in a statistically significant decrease in symptoms, for example, but these changes may not be clinically significant.

Concepts rooted in evidence-based medicine, including sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios, risk reduction measures, and numbers needed to treat and harm, may be helpful in applying findings from the literature to patient care ( [Table: Table: Terms Used in Interpretation of Diagnostic Tests]

and [Table: Table: Terms Used in Interpretation of Therapeutics]

). Although useful, they are also subject to specific shortcomings ( [Table: Table: Application of Evidence-Based Medicine Concepts]

).

Sensitivity and specificity reflect the accuracy of a diagnostic or screening test (see [Table: Table: Terms Used in Interpretation of Diagnostic Tests]

). Sensitivity is the ability of the test to accurately detect disease in those who truly have it, or the probability that the test result will be positive in a patient with the disease. Specificity is the ability of the test to correctly identify those without the disease, or the probability that the test result will be negative in a patient without the disease. Therefore, sensitive tests are those with minimal rates of false-negative results, and specific tests are those with minimal rates of false-positive results.

Positive and negative predictive values (see [Table: Table: Terms Used in Interpretation of Diagnostic Tests]

) reflect the validity of a positive or negative test result for predicting the presence or absence of disease in a specific population. Predictive values are determined not only by sensitivity and specificity but also by disease prevalence.

Likelihood ratios (LRs) provide a measure of the strength of association between a clinical finding and a specific disease; in effect, they translate the impact of sensitivity and specificity on the disease probability. Each clinical finding, including symptoms, physical findings, and laboratory and imaging results, has a positive and negative LR for the diseases with which it is associated. The positive LR is used when the test result is positive, and the negative LR is used when the test result is negative.

LRs are used in conjunction with the pretest probability of disease (the probability of disease in the patient before the test result is considered). The interaction of the pretest probability and LR results in a posttest probability of disease. The posttest probability may then serve as the rationale for treating a patient for the disease (if the positive test resulted in a high posttest probability) or ruling out a diagnosis (if the negative test resulted in a very low posttest probability). Equations for converting pretest probability (a percentage) to pretest odds (a ratio), applying the LR, and converting posttest odds to posttest probability are available in [Table: Table: Terms Used in Interpretation of Diagnostic Tests]

.

For ease of clinical use, several general LR rules apply. Positive LR values of 2, 5, and 10 correspond to an increase in disease probability by 15%, 30%, and 45%, respectively; negative LR values of 0.5, 0.2, and 0.1 correspond to a decrease in disease probability by 15%, 30%, and 45%, respectively. Larger positive LRs and smaller negative LRs are more apt to affect clinical decisions.

Clinical tools for calculating LRs and their effect on probability of disease are widely available. Alternatively, nomograms may be used to extrapolate the posttest probability of disease from the pretest probability of disease on the basis of the LR (

).

Absolute risk reduction and relative risk reduction are measures commonly used to report the efficacy of an intervention (see [Table: Table: Terms Used in Interpretation of Therapeutics]

). Absolute risk reduction is the difference in the response to treatment between experimental and control groups. Absolute risk reduction is particularly relevant when the measure reported is a clinically meaningful end point (e.g., the incidence of cardiovascular events in studies of lipid-lowering therapy). Because these differences may seem small, investigators may also report the relative risk or risk ratio as well as relative risk reduction.

The difference in the magnitude of these measures can be illustrated with a study of lipid-lowering therapy in which the rate of acute coronary syndrome in 5 years is 3.6% in the treated group and 4.8% in the control group. The absolute risk reduction is 1.2%. The risk ratio is 75%, and the relative risk reduction is 25%. Although the absolute difference in rates between the two groups is small, the effect may appear substantial when relative risk reduction is reported.

The number needed to treat (NNT) or harm (NNH) (see [Table: Table: Terms Used in Interpretation of Therapeutics]

) expresses the clinical impact of an intervention. The NNT is the inverse of the absolute risk reduction. It represents the number of patients who must receive a treatment or intervention to cause one additional patient to benefit. The NNT provides a quantifiable measure of the treatment effect that is easily understood by physicians and patients. The acceptability of the NNT depends on the risks associated with the condition, the cost and side effects of the treatment, and other treatments available. The NNH can be calculated for studies measuring adverse outcomes but also needs to be considered in the context of the benefits of the treatment and the severity of the harm incurred.

Technique

Comments

  1. Understand heuristics^a

Availability heuristic: Diagnosing based on what is most easily available in the physician’s memory (e.g., because of a patient recently seen) rather than what is most probable

Anchoring heuristic: Settling on a diagnosis early in the diagnostic process despite data that refute the diagnosis or support another diagnosis (premature closure)

Representativeness heuristic: Application of pattern recognition (a patient’s presentation fits a “typical” case; therefore, it must be that case)

  1. Use “diagnostic timeouts”

Taking time to periodically review a case based on data but without assuming that the diagnosis is that which was previously reached

  1. Practice “worst-case scenario medicine”

Consider the most life-threatening diagnoses first:

Lessens chance of missing these diagnoses

Does not mandate testing for them

  1. Use a systematic approach to common problems

For example, anatomic approach to abdominal pain beginning from exterior to interior

  1. Ask why

For example, when a patient presents with diabetic ketoacidosis or a COPD exacerbation, ask what prompted this acute exacerbation of a chronic condition

  1. Use the clinical examination

Decreases reliance on a single test and decreases the chance of premature closure

  1. Use Bayes theorem

Use pretest and posttest probabilities

Helps avert premature closure based on a single test result

How does the patient make the physician feel?

Physicians may discount important data in patients with whom they have difficult encounters

  1. Look for clinical findings that do not fit the diagnosis

Encourages a comprehensive approach and incorporates healthy skepticism

Resist the temptation to lock onto common diagnoses at the risk of missing the uncommon

Difficult to do in most health care systems, which stress the economy of “getting it right the first time”

Table: Application of Evidence-Based Medicine Concepts

Application of Evidence-Based Medicine Concepts

Evidence-Based Medicine Concepts

Shortcomings and Examples

Sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values

Predictive values are often used in preference to sensitivity and specificity in clinical practice; however, if disease prevalence in the study population is different from that in the clinical population, the predictive values will change.

Example: Screening for cervical cancer with HPV testing alone in women aged 21-29 years results in a high false-positive rate compared with testing in women aged 30-65 years owing to higher rates of HPV exposure.

Likelihood ratio

Likelihood ratios are not interchangeable with odds ratios.

Positive likelihood ratios are not the reciprocals of negative likelihood ratios.

Example: Dry axillae are supportive of hypovolemia (LR+, 2.8), but their absence does not exclude hypovolemia (LR–, 0.6).

Absolute and relative risk reduction

Absolute and relative risk reduction calculations do not identify whether the difference is clinically significant. A large relative risk may distract from small absolute changes.

Example: Ezetimibe reduces stroke risk from 32/1000 to 27/1000. Relative risk reduction is 15.6%, but absolute risk reduction is 0.5%.

Number needed to treat or number needed to harm

These measures do not qualitatively compare the magnitude of the benefit or harm.

Example: An emergency department visit for a nosebleed requiring packing may have fewer significant long-term consequences than stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation.

External validity (generalizability)

Exclusion criteria or bias in recruitment may result in a study population that is not representative of the general population.

Example: The reduction in risk for myocardial infarction associated with a drug studied in a secondary prevention population cannot be applied to a primary prevention population.

Internal validity and bias

Intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses (

) can have significantly different results.

Example: A high rate of drug side effects may lead to frequent discontinuation, reducing efficacy in an intention-to-treat analysis. A per-protocol analysis would exclude patients who discontinued the drug and potentially overestimate the benefit in routine clinical practice.

Medical Ethics and Professionalism

Physicians should be guided in their practice by the four basic principles of medical ethics, which work in unison to define the duties of the physician to the patient ( [Table: Table: The Four Guiding Principles of Medical Ethics]

). In applying these principles, physicians must consider the specific clinical scenario, including cultural and patient-specific factors, to determine an appropriate course of action. At times, however, ethical principles may seem in conflict, leading to ethical dilemmas. For example, respecting the autonomy of a competent patient who is making poor decisions may seem to contradict the principles of beneficence and nonmaleficence. Ethical dilemma resolution can often be accomplished by the following:

  • Evaluating the medical situation
  • Understanding the context, including the motivations of those involved
  • Framing the ethical question or dilemma and considering all available options
  • Considering the ethical principles underpinning the question

With this information, clinicians can balance the ethical principles and individual interests to determine the range of possible ethical actions. When ethical dilemmas are difficult to resolve, physicians may obtain assistance through an ethics consultation.

Professionalism is the foundation of medicine’s relationship with society and governs the conduct of the physician community. Professionalism in medicine is specifically characterized by the following:

  • Placement of the patient’s interests above the physician’s self-interests (the fiduciary relationship)
  • Acquisition, maintenance, and expansion of specialized medical knowledge
  • Adherence to ethical principles
  • Self-regulation of members and responsibilities

The obligation of physicians to the welfare of their patients creates an ethical imperative to provide competent and compassionate care to all patients, regardless of their illness. Refusal to provide appropriate care to any group of patients for any reason, including infectivity or disease state, is unethical.

Because of the patient’s inherent vulnerability due to illness and the imbalance of expertise, knowledge, and power between the patient and physician, patients must be able to trust that the physician acts for their benefit (beneficence) and to minimize their harm (nonmaleficence). The altruism of serving the patient’s interests before the physician’s interests creates the trust that is essential to the patient-physician relationship.

The patient-physician relationship should be based on mutual agreement. Once this relationship has been established, the physician should strive to understand the patient’s health concerns, values, goals, and expectations to guide the provision of care.

Appropriate boundaries between the physician and patient must always be maintained. It is unethical for a physician to become sexually involved with a current patient, and sexual relationships with former patients should be avoided owing to concerns of continued vulnerability and dependence. Physicians also must maintain boundaries during the history, physical examination, and treatment process by communicating the planned actions in advance, using purposeful movements, and communicating the purpose of these actions. A chaperone should be offered during the examination of intimate areas.

Physicians may be asked to care for persons with whom they have an existing nonprofessional relationship, including close friends and family members. Caring for these individuals may be associated with impaired objectivity, insufficient history taking (e.g., failure to obtain an adequate sexual history), incomplete examination, and incomplete or biased assessment, potentially leading to poorer-quality care than that provided by an impartial physician. Physicians should weigh these considerations carefully and encourage alternative sources of care, except in emergencies. For the same reasons, physicians should not provide medical care to themselves if alternatives are available.

Patient-physician connections via social media and other electronic communications can lead to confusion over the boundaries between personal and professional interactions. Physicians should keep these spheres separate and behave professionally in both. Electronic communication with patients through a secure electronic health record (EHR) is preferred to email correspondence. Email communication is permissible in an established patient-physician relationship after mutual consent, but it should occur only via a secure email server and be documented in the patient’s EHR. Recommended safeguards for online physician activities are described in [Table: Table: Safeguards for Common Online Physician Activities]

.

Patient-physician relationships should generally be established based on an in-person or in-depth telemedicine professional encounter. Providing care or prescriptions based on only an online questionnaire or phone-based consultation does not meet acceptable standards for quality of care. On-call situations with patients who have an established relationship with a partner or the practice are a notable exception, as are urgent public health situations, such as the management of communicable diseases.

Telemedicine, or the use of electronic communication and technologies to provide health care to patients at a distance, may improve physician-patient collaboration, improve access to care, and reduce costs. The benefits of increased access to care through telemedicine must always be balanced against the risks associated with the lack of a physical encounter, such as misdiagnosis, inappropriate care, and loss of communication nuances conveyed with body language. The American College of Physicians (ACP) holds the position that a valid patient-physician relationship must be established for professionally responsible telemedicine services to occur; however, this relationship may be formed during a telemedicine encounter through real-time audiovisual technology. Telemedicine also may increase collaboration and communication between clinicians and expand the provision of specialized care to underserved areas, such as with telestroke systems or tele-ICU monitoring and management.

Conflicts between the physician and patient can arise for many reasons, such as patient refusal of a recommended course of treatment. Training in effective patient-physician communication skills and cultural competency can help to mitigate these conflicts (see Effective Communication in Clinical Practice in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Physicians should offer the rationale for proposed interventions and explore the patient’s reasoning. A deeper understanding of the patient’s background and rationale for decision making may allow for conflict resolution or prompt a search for more appropriate treatment alternatives. If the patient agrees to but is not adherent with the physician’s recommendation, a similar exploration of the patient’s decision making and contextual factors may be helpful in discerning the basis for the patient’s behavior (e.g., low health literacy, financial impediments, or transportation issues).

Discriminatory behavior toward the physician can distress the patient-physician relationship and compromise the health care environment. Physicians and trainees may also experience mistreatment from patients, families, and visitors through offensive remarks, violence, and unwanted sexual advances. Such mistreatment has been linked to physician and trainee burnout (see Physician Burnout and Moral Distress in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Although patients may refuse treatment from a specific clinician, patients do not have the right to demand or refuse care based on clinically irrelevant clinician characteristics, such as gender, skin color, sexual orientation, or religion, because this behavior results in unequal working conditions for clinicians. In general, when faced with a perceived discriminatory request, clinicians should do the following:

  • Ensure that the patient is stable
  • Assess decision-making capacity
  • Determine the reason for the request before deciding whether to accommodate, negotiate, offer transfer, or set limits on unacceptable behavior (

).

Clinical leadership should be engaged when appropriate. Physicians should support their colleagues and trainees who face discrimination or other mistreatment and adhere to the nondiscrimination policies of their institutions.

There are occasional circumstances in which the patient-physician relationship becomes irreparably compromised because of lack of trust, lack of mutual goals, or failure to maintain an effective working relationship despite efforts to resolve differences. In these cases, the physician can terminate the relationship so long as the patient’s health is stable enough for such a transition. The physician should provide formal, written documentation of the termination and facilitate the transition to a new clinician. Patient abandonment (withdrawing from an established relationship without giving reasonable notice or providing a competent replacement) is unethical and may be a cause for legal action.

Physicians must protect the privacy of patients’ medical information in order to respect patient autonomy, foster trust, and encourage honest disclosure of sensitive personal details, thereby improving patient care.

Disclosure of medical information outside of the patient-physician relationship requires patient consent. Physicians should be vigilant about protecting patient confidentiality in the era of EHRs, email, patient portals, and social media. Communication with and regarding patients should involve secure communication systems and storage. Discussing patients outside of a clinical or educational setting, such as in an elevator or via unencrypted texts, violates confidentiality and may compromise trust in the physician and profession. Physicians also must be knowledgeable in the relevant state and federal statutes regarding confidentiality, including the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA).

Confidentiality is not absolute. There are circumstances in which legitimate competing interests may conflict with the need for confidentiality, and disclosure becomes necessary to minimize a greater harm. Physicians are mandatory reporters of neglect or abuse of children or older adults and have a duty to report when patients may be a threat to themselves or others. Certain infectious diseases also must be reported to local, state, or federal institutions. In some states, physicians are required to report medical impairments that would lead to driver’s license suspension or revocation. In general, physicians should inform patients when they plan to make a report to a government institution and should do so in a way that heeds pertinent laws.

In extraordinary circumstances, physicians may withhold medical information from a patient if disclosure would lead to serious harm (e.g., withholding a new cancer diagnosis from an acutely suicidal patient), a practice known as therapeutic privilege. The invocation of this privilege should be done in consultation with the institutional ethics committee.

All adult patients are presumed legally competent to make informed medical decisions unless found otherwise by judicial determination. However, in routine clinical care, physicians must frequently determine the patient’s decision-making capacity, including the patient’s ability to understand relevant information, appreciate the risks and benefits of various treatment options, and communicate a choice consistent with the information given and the individual’s values ( [Table: Table: Legally Relevant Criteria for Decision-Making Capacity]

). The presence of depression or early dementia may complicate the evaluation but does not preclude the presence of decision-making capacity.

Decision-making capacity is not a global determination; reversible factors such as intoxication from drugs or alcohol, delirium, or an underlying medical condition may impair cognition and temporarily affect decision-making capacity. Frequent reassessment is necessary to confirm previous determinations. When a decision may result in serious consequences, determination of capacity is of even greater importance. Decisions are more likely valid when consistent with previously stated values, beliefs, and choices. Decisions that run counter to previously expressed preferences may be equally valid; however, when such changes occur, it must be clear that the patient has capacity and understands the consequences of the decisions. Patient expression of a wish or therapeutic goal is not sufficient to demonstrate capacity.

Informed consent and refusal is the process of engaging a patient with capacity in a meaningful dialogue about their health conditions, assessing the patient’s understanding, and respecting the patient’s autonomy to accept or refuse care. Informed consent requires that a patient be provided with all of the information necessary to determine the acceptability and appropriateness of the proposed treatment or intervention. Pertinent information includes the nature of the underlying condition; the goals of treatment; and the risks of, benefits of, and alternatives to treatment, including the option to forgo treatment. Information should be communicated in ways that are sensitive, appropriate for the patient’s literacy level and language abilities, and attentive to cultural context.

For informed consent to be considered valid, the patient must have decision-making capacity and be free from coercion. An exception to informed consent is a medical emergency in which a patient is unable to participate in the decision-making process; in such circumstances, consent for lifesaving therapies should be presumed unless available information or advance directives suggest otherwise.

Adults with decision-making capacity who have been informed of treatment options have the legal and ethical right to refuse all medical treatments. A patient’s universal right to refuse treatment, which is protected by law, is based on respect for autonomy, the right to self-determination, and protection of the patient’s liberty. Refusal of care should be explored thoughtfully and with empathy, with attention to the spectrum of reasonable choices, including time-limited trials of therapy. If the patient’s refusal violates the physician’s professional integrity, consultation with an ethics committee may be helpful. Conscientious objection by a physician must not violate the principle of patient nonabandonment.

In the absence of patient decision-making capacity, a surrogate is charged with making health care decisions. The most appropriate surrogate is the person who has been designated power of attorney for health care by the patient. If the patient has not designated a surrogate, a person who is knowledgeable about the patient’s expressed preferences should serve as decision maker. Many states have laws that provide a hierarchy of preferred surrogates based on relationship to the patient (typically in the sequence of spouse, adult child, parent, and adult sibling).

The surrogate generally should adhere to the instructions described in the living will and provide thoughtful and appropriate reasons for deviating from them. If there is no living will, the surrogate should make decisions based on knowledge of the patient’s preferences and values, also known as substituted judgment. If the surrogate does not have first-hand knowledge of the patient’s preferences or values, they should make decisions based on what they perceive to be in the patient’s best interests.

Advance care planning is the process by which a competent patient articulates preferences, goals, and values regarding their future medical care to assist surrogates and the health care team in the event that the patient can no longer make independent decisions. Advance care planning should include written documentation of the patient’s preferences (advance directives) and should be available in the medical record.

Advance directives may include a living will and durable power of attorney for health care (also referred to as health care power of attorney, medical power of attorney, or health care proxy). In a living will, the patient can outline specific preferences for treatment decisions (e.g., use of dialysis or mechanical ventilation). A durable power of attorney for health care allows the patient to designate a surrogate to be the primary medical decision maker when the patient cannot make their own decisions. Oral attestations or physician notes documenting preferences have legal standing and can serve as advance directives in the absence of more formal directives. Living wills and durable powers of attorney for health care come into effect only when a physician determines the patient is medically unable to make their own decisions.

The legal requirements for and implementation of advance directives vary by state, and physicians should be familiar with the laws pertaining to advance directives in the state in which they practice. State laws regarding the withdrawal of artificial nutrition and hydration may be particularly variable, and patients who have preferences regarding these interventions should clearly document them in a living will.

In some states, portable medical orders provide a more robust way for patients with serious illness and frailty to plan for future care. A Provider Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment (POLST) form, which is completed by a clinician, provides medical orders to all health care providers during a medical emergency. These orders can extend beyond resuscitation preferences to preferences about hospitalization or specific medical treatments.

Patients and their family members may request diagnostic or therapeutic interventions that challenge the physician’s sense of what is best for the patient (e.g., requesting antibiotic therapy for a suspected viral infection). Although the physician needs to respect patient autonomy, this duty must be weighed against the physician’s professional judgment and integrity, the potential harms of inappropriate interventions, and possible secondary effects (e.g., antimicrobial resistance caused by inappropriate antibiotic prescribing). Physicians are not obligated to provide diagnostic or therapeutic interventions they believe to be without clinical benefit.

Particularly difficult requests may occur in the setting of ambiguous or conflicting goals of care. For example, a physician may perceive that a patient with multiorgan failure will not achieve the goal of returning to their previous level of functioning and may therefore conclude that continued intensive care is inappropriate. However, family members may have the goal of extending their loved one’s life for as long as possible, regardless of the appropriateness of care. Effective communication regarding the preferences and goals of the patient and surrogates can often help adjudicate conflicts of values, clarify prognosis and uncertainties, and lead to conflict resolution. When resolution cannot be achieved, ethics consultation can be beneficial. Transfer of care to a physician who concurs with the patient’s or family’s plan and is willing to provide the requested intervention may be necessary when resolution is not possible.

The fiduciary nature of the patient-physician relationship, respect for the patient’s autonomy, and obligation to justice require physicians to be truthful with patients or surrogates when a medical error occurs. Several states mandate disclosure in the event of serious harm, and most states have instituted “apology laws,” which protect physician apologies and expressions of regret from legal consequences.

When disclosing an error and the harm or potential harm, the physician also should express compassion and concern for the patient and explain institutional efforts being taken to prevent similar harm from befalling others. Information on how the error occurred may take time to gather, and patients should be informed of such. Physicians should not rush into apology owing to feelings of guilt or distress because this may lead to inaccuracies that compound patient suffering. Disclosure should be performed thoughtfully and sensitively, accounting for the emotional effect on both the patient and clinician. Institutional and clinical leadership also should be involved in error disclosure to ensure that all available resources are used to support both clinicians and patients.

Disclosure may benefit physicians by alleviating distress, improving patient-physician communication, and reducing litigation. Strategies that focus on early communication and response after an error have been associated with fewer malpractice lawsuits and lower litigation costs, although these outcomes are not the primary goals of such initiatives.

Ethically, there is no distinction between withholding (not initiating) and withdrawing (removing) treatment. The decision to withdraw care can be fraught with guilt or concerns about suffering for family members, and the physician can play an important role in explaining the process and ameliorating concerns. An ethics committee or ethics consultation can be helpful in assisting family members struggling with these decisions.

Medical aid in dying, also referred to as physician aid in dying or physician-assisted death and formerly referred to as physician-assisted suicide, occurs when a physician provides a lethal prescription to a competent terminally ill patient who has requested a hastened means by which to end their life. The patient self-administers the drug with the intent to cause death. Medical aid in dying is different from euthanasia, in which a physician directly and intentionally administers an agent to cause death, and from interventions that are administered with the intent of relieving suffering but unintentionally hasten death (known as the principle of double effect).

Medical aid in dying raises profound legal, clinical, and social concerns. It may erode trust in the profession, cause harm to the most vulnerable patients, and hinder progress in improving end-of-life care. It fundamentally alters the physician’s role in society. The ACP does not support legalization of medical aid in dying and instead emphasizes the need to provide palliative care, relief of suffering, and compassionate biopsychosocial support to the patient and family members during the end of life. Several states, however, have legalized medical aid in dying. Physicians may be asked to participate in discussions regarding the practice but may assert a conscientious objection. In these situations, physicians should explore the reasons for the request in the context of goals of care, seek alternative solutions, and provide ongoing support, often in conjunction with other health care team members and community-based resources (see Palliative Medicine in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Physicians’ specialized knowledge creates a unique opportunity to intervene and benefit other citizens in emergency situations, and in this context, physicians may provide care outside of the clinical setting to persons who are not their patients. When physicians assist in these situations, patient consent to receive emergency treatment is usually presumed or implied. If the treatment is provided in good faith, Good Samaritan laws usually protect the physician from liability, except in cases of gross negligence. Providing medical care as a bystander is typically voluntary, with clinicians weighing their ethical obligations to provide assistance; however, state laws vary on this point, and several states have “failure to act” laws that are not specific to physicians.

Conflicts of interest are financial, professional, or other personal concerns that have the potential to compromise a physician’s objectivity with respect to clinical decision making. Real or potential conflicts threaten the physician’s ability to ensure that the patient’s welfare is the primary motivating factor in patient care and may undermine trust in the profession. Conflicts of interest exist in clinical care, philanthropic opportunities, and research. Physicians are obligated to recognize, disclose, and manage all conflicts of interest. Disclosure of conflicts, however, may not be an adequate safeguard against bias in decision making, and potential conflicts should be removed if possible.

Physician acceptance of gifts, hospitality, and other items and services of value from industry or grateful patients also can pose ethical problems. In deciding to accept a gift, physicians should consider multiple factors, such as the nature of the gift, the implications of accepting or refusing it, and the possible intention and expectations. Additional guidance to manage relationships with industry is listed in [Table: Table: Guidance for Managing Industry Relations and Gifts]

.

Physicians must be wary of personal business or economic interests taking priority over patient welfare. Self-referral, including referring patients to a facility in which the physician has invested and does not provide care, should be avoided. It is unethical—and, in some cases illegal—to receive kickbacks or commissions for patient referrals, recommendations of medical products, or prescription of medications. Sale of products (at a reasonable cost) from the physician’s office should be limited to those relevant to the patient’s care that meet an urgent need.

A physician may be the first to realize that a colleague is impaired or unable to carry out clinical responsibilities safely and effectively. Impairment may be caused by substance use, aging, or mental illness or other disease; however, the presence of such a disorder does not always signify impairment. Physicians have the responsibility to safeguard patients from impaired physicians and to assist impaired colleagues. A stepwise approach should be pursued, in which concerns are first discussed with the colleague if patient harm is unlikely, followed by report to clinical supervisors or the local or state medical society if patient harm is possible or imminent. If the appropriate action is unclear, physicians should seek advice from supervisors or designated officials. Physicians also should work collectively with institutions to develop methods for reporting, treating, and remediating impaired or disruptive colleagues. Impaired physicians should be allowed the opportunity to rehabilitate through a physician health program whenever possible. Outcomes for physicians with substance use disorders who participate in such programs are favorable, with more than two-thirds of participants maintaining abstinence and active medical licensure after 5 years.

Physician burnout is a response to chronic unresolvable occupational stress. Burnout includes features of emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and career dissatisfaction and may lead to depression and suicide. Common drivers of burnout include a high workload with substantial administrative work, lack of autonomy, poor work-life balance, and inefficient EHRs. Moral distress may exacerbate or lead to burnout. Moral distress occurs in situations in which physicians are unable to carry out what they believe to be ethically appropriate actions and feel their integrity is jeopardized. Moral distress is associated with a noncollaborative working environment and lack of empowerment or autonomy at work.

Burnout is common and can have a profound result on physicians’ lives and the lives of those around them. Studies have found that burnout is associated with shorter life expectancy, substance use, and broken relationships. Physicians experiencing depersonalization lack empathy and make errors, which may lead to patient harm.

Initiatives to decrease physician burnout must address the underlying systems and organizational factors contributing to the phenomenon. Although improving individual physician resiliency may help to some extent, systems-based initiatives focusing on improving work-life balance, increasing work efficiency (including EHR optimization), and supporting sustainable workloads are more likely to have a meaningful effect. Physicians should be vigilant in surveying themselves and their colleagues for symptoms of burnout and should seek assistance if they identify symptoms. The ACP provides resources to promote well-being and combat burnout.
