Health Equity

The World Health Organization defines health equity as the absence of unfair, preventable, or remediable differences in health among population groups, defined by social, economic, demographic, or geographic characteristics. Health inequities are prevalent in the United States as well as globally and are largely determined by conditions in which people live, termed social drivers of health, and by bias and discrimination.

Historically marginalized racial and ethnic groups; those living in poverty; those with mental health concerns or with physical or intellectual disabilities; incarcerated people; and the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or questioning (LGBTQ+) community have worse health outcomes compared with other populations. In these and other disadvantaged groups, various disparities exist in acute and chronic diseases, infant mortality, maternal health, life expectancy, and other measures of health and wellness. In addition to significant disparities in morbidity and mortality, health inequities cost the United States an estimated $451 billion annually.

Pursuit of health equity requires acknowledgment that health inequities are the result of historical and modern systemic, institutional, and individual actions and policies. According to the CDC, achieving health equity requires addressing historical and contemporary injustices; overcoming economic, social, and other obstacles to health and health care; and eliminating preventable health disparities. Health care organizations should collect data on patient outcomes to uncover health inequities. Data should include outcomes for race, ethnicity, and language status (REAL) as well as sexual orientation, gender identity, and expression (SOGIE). Health care systems and physicians must lead the pursuit of health equity through systemic and individual changes, and all health care professionals should be knowledgeable about identifying social drivers of health and approaches to treating patients whose health is affected by social drivers. The American College of Physicians (ACP) has proposed a comprehensive policy framework to understand and address disparities and discrimination in health and health care experienced by marginalized populations in the United States.

At $4 trillion per year, the U.S. health care system outspends every other country in the world. Despite these resources, the United States ranks low in health outcomes, access to care, and equity among high-income countries. It is estimated that only 10% to 20% of overall population health is attributed to health care, whereas social drivers of health, including economic stability, living environment, education, social and community networks, and health care access, account for up to 80%. Addressing these social drivers can improve patient care and health outcomes.

Socioeconomic position, including income, housing, and living environment, is likely the greatest indicator of health outcomes. Access to affordable housing affects one’s ability to achieve home ownership, which is critical for wealth generation and socioeconomic position. Physical conditions at home, such as the presence of mold or other indoor air pollutants, may activate airway diseases. Lack of access to green spaces, sidewalks, and safe neighborhoods may affect healthy lifestyle choices, such as exercise. Lack of access to fresh foods and grocery stores also negatively affects health outcomes in a community. In the United States, approximately 23.5 million people live in food deserts, defined as areas that lack access to affordable and healthy food options within a reasonable distance.

Educational attainment is also linked to health outcomes. Quality early childhood education is critical to child and adolescent development, and obtaining a college degree is associated with better health. Because local tax income funds public schools, access to quality education varies; lower-income communities often do not generate the tax income to result in well-funded school systems, resulting in education disparities across communities.

Access to health care itself is a social determinant of health and may depend on where a person lives. Marginalized groups and individuals from lower-income backgrounds are more likely to experience poor access to care, gaps in care, and financial barriers to care.

Because zip code is highly correlated with income, housing status, educational attainment, adverse childhood events, and access to care, there is a strong association between zip code and life expectancy. In some large cities, life expectancy across zip codes has been found to differ by as much as 25 to 30 years.

Supportive relationships have been linked to positive health outcomes; conversely, exposure to intimate partner violence, including physical abuse, sexual abuse, or psychological aggression, is associated with increased incidences of chronic disease, poor mental health, and risky behaviors, such as smoking and alcohol and substance use.

Childhood experiences affect health and well-being into adulthood. Child development is especially susceptible from birth through age 8 years. Having exposure to quality education and developmental support during this time is crucial. Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), such as neglect, physical or emotional abuse, witnessing substance abuse or domestic violence, having a family member who is incarcerated or has mental health crises, and parental divorce, have been tied to poor health outcomes and behaviors in adulthood. As the number of childhood ACEs increases, so does the likelihood of chronic disease, mental health disorders, and risky behaviors.

The National Institutes of Health defines implicit bias as a form of bias that occurs automatically and unintentionally but nevertheless affects judgments, decisions, and behaviors. Everyone has implicit biases, and clinicians are often unaware of their biases and the effect of their biases on care. Social stereotypes may result in stigmatized views of certain groups with resultant adverse effects on care.

Systemic racism, defined as a self-perpetuating form of bias built into systems (e.g., political, legal, health care, education), associated structures (e.g., laws, policies), and institutions, has played a major role in the development of health inequities in the United States. For example, historical “redlining” practices, in which persons from certain neighborhoods, primarily based on race and ethnicity, were kept from obtaining financial services such as home mortgages, reduced the possibility of building home equity and generational wealth in marginalized groups. This practice resulted in the concentration of poverty, pollution, and other adverse conditions in cities across the United States. Although redlining has been banned since 1968, people currently living in historically redlined neighborhoods continue to experience adverse conditions and poorer health outcomes.

Biases, stigma, and discrimination disproportionately affect marginalized groups and adversely impact health outcomes. Many examples of these outcomes exist in the medical literature. Peripheral vascular disease research shows that Black and Hispanic patients are more likely to experience a delayed diagnosis and are more likely to receive limb amputations when limb salvage therapies are more appropriate. Black patients are more likely to be undertreated for pain. Physical pain in women is more frequently attributed to psychological factors than is physical pain in men, leading to undertreatment of physical pain and overtreatment of depression and anxiety in women. Patients with obesity are less likely to be referred for preventive health screenings despite spending more contact hours with health care providers than those without obesity. Gay and bisexual men are at higher risk for sexually transmitted infections and HIV/AIDS; however, stigma and discrimination may prevent these individuals from seeking screening and preventive health care. Lesbian and bisexual women are less likely to receive cancer screenings, such as mammography and Pap testing.

Bias and discrimination may prevent patients from receiving effective and timely preventive and therapeutic medical care and may discourage individuals from seeking future care. Health care providers should seek awareness of their own implicit biases, which allows for better recognition of biased thoughts and actions. Bias recognition tests, such as the Implicit Association Test, are readily available and can help individuals determine their potential biases. In addition, word choice in medical care also may contribute to bias, stigma, and discrimination; using nonpejorative and person-first language (e.g., patient with obesity rather than obese patient, patient with a substance use disorder rather than drug abuser) are important steps in mitigating bias and improving equity. Systemic policies that confront and eliminate racism are paramount, and ACP offers policy recommendations to address and mitigate racism and discrimination.

Race has been used as a factor in many medical algorithms and calculators, often because of the results of group-level associations. However, these associations should not be inherently ascribed to biology, as social drivers of health, bias, racism, and their effects on health disparities underpin these differences.

Increasing awareness that race is a social construct rather than a proxy for genetics has resulted in the adjustment of many clinical tools. Until recently, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was calculated after applying a multiplicative factor for race based on older research suggesting that Black individuals have higher levels of serum creatinine due to greater muscle mass. For Black patients, the use of this multiplicative factor may have overestimated kidney function and delayed the diagnosis and treatment of kidney disease. To estimate glomerular filtration rate, the National Kidney Foundation and American Society of Nephrology now recommend using the 2021 CKD Epidemiology Collaboration equation, which has been refitted to estimate kidney function without a race variable (see also Estimation of Glomerular Filtration Rate in Nephrology). Similarly, the use of race as a modifying factor when interpreting pulmonary function tests has come under scrutiny because results may underestimate pulmonary disease severity in Black patients. In response, the American Thoracic Society published a statement recommending that race and ethnicity no longer be considered factors when interpreting results. The Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE), used to estimate the 10-year risk for developing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, guide decisions on preventive cholesterol-lowering therapies. Because the PCE use different coefficients for Black and non-Hispanic White patients, there are concerns that the PCE may perpetuate disparities. The 2023 Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease EVENTs (PREVENT) equations, developed by the American Heart Association, do not include a race variable and allow further individualization of risk (see Calculating Cardiovascular Risk in Cardiovascular Medicine for more information).

Many algorithms are being re-evaluated to remove or replace race-based modifiers. Physicians should use caution when interpreting results of race-based algorithms.

Cross-cultural care is a critical component of attaining health equity. The foundation of cross-cultural care is an understanding that many factors contribute to each patient’s unique health care experience. Gaining self-awareness of one’s own cultural identities and insight into areas where awareness is lacking can improve cross-cultural care. Cultural humility is an iterative process of self-reflection and learning that aims to foster trustworthy relationships and better understand and respect cultural differences. Cultural humility assumes that one could never learn all there is about other cultures. Exploring personal privilege, including an understanding of how one’s individual characteristics (such as race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, abilities, or socioeconomics), may have provided greater access to resources is helpful in developing the empathy and understanding required for cultural humility. Cultural humility has been tied to improved patient outcomes and reduced health care costs. Patients who perceive their physicians to have high levels of cultural humility have higher levels of satisfaction with their health care experience, rate their physicians more highly, and are more likely to follow their physician’s medical advice.

Patient-centered care is critical to delivering cross-cultural care (see

and Effective Communication in Clinical Practice in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Inquiring about the patient’s understanding of their disease processes, their health priorities, and shared decision making are necessary components of this approach.

Language and culture are often intertwined, and language barriers and cultural misunderstandings contribute to adverse health outcomes. Health care organizations are legally required to provide reliable and accessible interpreter services for patients with a non-English language preference. Trained medical interpreters are experienced in accurately interpreting medical information in an unbiased, culturally sensitive manner. The use of trained medical interpreters can enhance culturally sensitive care, reduce adverse events, and improve treatment outcomes. Patient educational materials should be offered in several languages; having linguistically diverse materials can contribute to improved health literacy of culturally diverse communities.

Providing high-quality care is enhanced by building health care teams comprising diverse individuals, because a team with diverse cultural experiences is better able to understand the experiences of a diverse patient population. Evidence supports that this practice has a positive impact on health outcomes.

As defined by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), health literacy is the degree to which individuals have the capacity to obtain, process, and understand the information required to make informed health decisions. Low health literacy is more common among older adults, marginalized racial and ethnic groups, persons with lower socioeconomic status, and medically underserved groups. Low health literacy may hinder a patient’s ability to describe their health concerns, complete health forms accurately, understand medical information, and manage their health conditions. Evidence shows that low health literacy is associated with poorer health outcomes and decreased use of care.

Clinicians need to be aware of health literacy and identify patients who may need assistance. Tools to assess health literacy in specific populations are available from AHRQ and include the Short Assessment of Health Literacy and the Rapid Estimate of Adult Literacy in Medicine. Another instrument is the Newest Vital Sign, which can help predict a patient’s ability to comprehend common instructions related to frequent primary care scenarios.

Clinicians can improve patient understanding by using simple sentences, repeating information, asking the patient for their questions, and supplying the patient with educational materials written in plain language. The teach-back method, wherein the clinician asks the patient to describe their understanding of the situation in their own words, can assess a patient’s perception of their health and provide insight into knowledge and health literacy (see Teach-Back Method in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Effective Communication in Clinical Practice

Effective communication involves a bidirectional conversation between the patient and clinician and requires the clear exchange of medical information as well as a trusting relationship. Rapport in the relationship is achieved by respectful listening, reflection, and demonstration of empathy.

Identified by the National Academy of Medicine as one of six domains of health care quality, patient-centered care is care that is respectful of and responsive to individual patient preferences, needs, and values, and it ensures that patient values guide all clinical decisions. Patient-centeredness is a component of relationship-centered care, which focuses on the meaningful and therapeutic relationship between patient and clinician. This approach views the relationship as a partnership in which the ideas, feelings, and values of the patient and the clinician influence the relationship. Relationship-centered communication improves the experience of care for both the patient and clinician, and it is associated with improvement in medical outcomes such as glycemic and blood pressure control, pain management, and adherence to medications and clinician recommendations; fewer malpractice suits; fewer medical errors; and higher satisfaction ratings from patients and clinicians. Relationship-centered communication is a set of skills that can be taught, practiced, and improved. It does not take more time than a traditional approach and can augment efficiency. Implementing the strategies outlined in [Table: Table: Implementing Principles of Patient and Family Partnership]

can enhance patient and family partnership with clinicians.

A patient-centered (or relationship-centered) interview includes functional and relational aspects: the clinician not only gathers data to make a diagnosis and manage symptoms and chronic diseases but concomitantly builds rapport with their patient and elicits the story of their illness experience (see

). Essential components of the patient-centered interview that facilitate building rapport and optimize data gathering and disease management are listed in [Table: Table: Essential Elements of Communication]

.

In addition to the relational aspects, expanding the medical history to gather data on the patient’s behavioral and psychosocial concerns, living environment, resources, social support, relationships, and functional status allows clinicians to manage patients’ chronic diseases more effectively.

A person’s belief in their ability to achieve a task, known as self-efficacy, contributes to the success of health behaviors. Collaborative goal setting is an evidence-based strategy that achieves desired health outcomes by enhancing self-efficacy. Patients are more likely to achieve goals if they have identified and prioritized them on their own. To facilitate this process, clinicians can use open-ended questions to help patients identify what matters most to them when creating goals. Evidence-based approaches such as Patient Priorities Care for older adults with multiple chronic conditions can also aid in guiding conversations. Clinicians should help patients increase the likelihood of achieving their goals by helping patients to make their goals SMART—specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and timely. Action plans should specify concrete steps patients will need to take to achieve their goals (see Motivational Interviewing in Foundations of Clinical Practice and Behavioral Counseling in Foundations of Clinical Practice). .

Several helpful models of behavioral counseling exist. Motivational interviewing is a versatile, patient-centered, relational, and evidence-based model shown to reduce alcohol consumption, binge drinking, and substance use and increase medication adherence and physical activity. Motivational interviewing presupposes that patients have within themselves both the reasons and answers for change, and it is particularly effective when a patient’s ambivalence is high or when their importance of, desire to, or confidence to change is low. Components of motivational interviewing include PACE:

  • Partnering and collaborating with the patient
  • Accepting and having Compassion for their situation and approaching the patient with the mindset that the clinician’s role is to help, and
  • Evoking the patient’s own reasons to change their behavior instead of imposing the provider’s reasons for change.

Skills that are core to the process of motivational interviewing can be summarized with the mnemonic OARS: Open-ended questions, Affirmations, Reflections, and Summaries (see [Table: Table: Core Skills for Motivational Interviewing]

). This method, which includes eliciting the patient’s perspective, focusing on the desired behavior, evoking the patient’s reasons for change without judgment, and planning next steps for change (see [Table: Table: Process of Motivational Interviewing]

), can be combined with other treatment methods such as cognitive behavioral therapy, diabetes education, and substance use disorder counseling.

Clinicians are obligated to provide timely and clear disclosure of results to patients. Results should be disclosed confidentially, in understandable language, with the intention to adequately support patients’ emotions, and with collaborative planning for next steps.

These fundamental principles also apply to more critical situations such as delivering bad or serious news and disclosing life-altering results. The SPIKES (Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotion, and Strategy and Summary) protocol for breaking bad news encompasses the essential communication elements and has been the most studied for efficacy. Components of the SPIKES protocol are shown in [Table: Table: SPIKES Protocol for Breaking Bad News]

.

Medical error disclosure involves similar communication principles; for more information about medical error disclosure, see Medical Error Disclosure in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

Shared decision making occurs when health care providers and patients collaborate to make health care decisions that draw on the provider’s knowledge, experience, and medical evidence in the context of the needs, preferences, desires, and values of the patient. The steps in this process, called SHARE, are outlined in [Table: Table: SHARE Steps for Shared Decision Making]

.

Shared decision making and decision aids can reduce decisional conflict, increase patients’ knowledge of their options, and help them reach decisions consistent with their values. A video on shared decision making is available from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality.

Patients receive substantial amounts of information in medical settings, and it is imperative to ensure that the essential information has been communicated clearly and effectively and that patients have a firm understanding. In teach-back, an evidence-based health literacy communication method, clinicians ask patients to explain the information conveyed to them in their own words. The clinician then clarifies any misunderstandings and checks in with the patient again for understanding, repeating this process until the patient accurately understands the information.

The teach-back method is used in routine sharing of information and is an important component of shared decision making and motivational interviewing. It is effective in many settings, improving knowledge recall and retention, self-care skills, and self-efficacy in patients with chronic disease. It also contributes to favorable outcome measures such as reducing hospital readmissions.

Multidisciplinary team–based care improves health care quality, patient safety, and overall outcomes. Team-based care and communication are critical to providing safe and effective care in both the outpatient and inpatient settings. Coordination of information among services and specialties improves consistency of messaging to patients and reduces fragmentation of care that may result in omissions, duplications, or care discrepancies. Critical elements for successful communication in multidisciplinary teams include the following:

  • Leveling hierarchy among team members
  • Clearly understanding roles and responsibilities of team members
  • Fostering psychological safety to minimize stress of the working environment
  • Building personal relationships with colleagues
  • Striving for direct, accurate, and timely communication, including giving and receiving feedback
  • Aligning goals

As a team leader, the physician must

  • Monitor and bring together different parts of the care plan
  • Incorporate input from various team members
  • Provide feedback and mediate when conflict exists
  • Ensure an environment of shared responsibility and respect
  • Appropriately delegate tasks

The patient-centered medical home in the outpatient setting, comprising many members of an interdisciplinary team (nurses, advanced practice providers, medical assistants, social workers, schedule coordinators, pharmacists), highlights the importance of interprofessional teamwork. Strategies for effective teamwork include the use of huddles (which may include family members when appropriate), debriefing, systems thinking, and conflict management.

Hospitalization and care transitions typically involve many clinicians and providers, and the risk for medical errors is high. The use of specific communication tools and techniques may improve outcomes and reduce errors ( [Table: Table: Structured Communication Strategies]

). Regular team meetings, with and without patients and families, update the team on patient care and progress and help ensure uniformity in treatment plans and care coordination. These meetings often occur in the setting of changes in a patient’s clinical course or in preparation for care transitions.

Handoffs, defined as the transfer and acceptance of responsibility of patient care between clinicians through effective communication, are high-frequency events in the hospital and may, if performed poorly, be a threat to patient safety (see Patient Safety and Quality Improvement in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Two thirds of sentinel events in the hospital occur in the setting of inadequate handoffs. Strategies aimed at standardizing and improving handoffs, such as I-PASS (Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness and contingency planning, Synthesis), provide a framework for the transfer of important information and promote consistency of practice (see [Table: Table: Structured Communication Strategies]

).

The potential for medical errors is particularly high at the time of hospital discharge, underscoring the importance of accurate information transfer between sites of care. When certain parts of care plans, including follow-up testing and treatment, are appropriate to be deferred until after discharge, the hospital provider is responsible for the handoff of this information to the appropriate accepting provider, typically the primary care team. Hospital teams most commonly communicate with primary care teams through the discharge summary, but a hospital provider may also directly contact primary care physicians at the time of discharge. Key information that should be relayed at the time of discharge includes the following:

  • Reason for admission
  • Diagnoses and any diagnostic uncertainty that exists at the time of discharge
  • Hospital course
  • Abnormal laboratory and imaging results
  • Discharge medication list
  • Pending tests
  • Postdischarge plan of care including follow-up appointments

Internal medicine clinicians are frequently asked to consult on the care of surgical, psychiatric, and nonmedical patients.

In the outpatient setting, consultations commonly occur for preoperative risk evaluations. Based on an evaluation of the patient’s medical problems, the internal medicine physician-as-consultant assesses the risks of the planned surgery and makes recommendations to the patient and surgical team about preoperative testing, optimization of comorbid conditions, modifications to medication regimens, measures to minimize perioperative risk, and postoperative care. See Perioperative Medicine in Foundations of Clinical Practice for additional information regarding perioperative management.

Likewise, hospital-based physicians are also frequently asked to consult on the care of surgical and nonmedical patients. This traditional medical consultation model addresses specific questions on medical management. The consultant’s responsibilities are to confirm the question being asked, evaluate the patient, and communicate recommendations on specific issues to the primary team. The primary team will implement the plan if in agreement with the recommendations. A consultant may continue to follow a patient if the clinical condition is evolving or when specifically asked to do so, or they may sign off when input on the case is complete. In the consultant role, clinicians do not typically write orders unless specifically asked to do so, but they maintain responsibility to review and interpret results of recommended studies.

A model of shared care known as comanagement has evolved between hospitalists and other teams. There are several styles of comanagement, depending on the institution, resources, and specific agreements among services. For example, a hospitalist may serve as the primary clinician with surgeons serving as consultants for a primary surgical problem, or a hospitalist may be an “embedded” consultant within a primary non-hospitalist team. In the latter model, a hospitalist may follow all patients and make recommendations on a broad array of medical issues, as well as write orders and follow up on study results. Comanagement is a more collaborative and proactive approach to patient care that promotes clear communication and delineation of responsibilities among services. Surgical comanagement is associated with improved pain control and decreased length of hospital stay, complications, readmissions, and mortality, as well as reduced cost. Surgical comanagement has been consistently associated with a high level of satisfaction with the care model among surgeons, nurses, and trainees.

Despite its advantages, comanagement also presents challenges. The presence of multiple care providers may result in duplication or omission of care or in care that is in conflict because of unclear division of responsibilities. A diffusion of responsibility may also result in substandard care. Carefully drafted service agreements among participants in the comanagement services that outline rules of engagement and division of responsibility are critical for the success of comanagement programs.

Process of Motivational Interviewing

Engage

Obtain a genuine understanding of the patient’s behavior in a nonjudgmental way.

Reflect back what the patient says, using slightly different wording if needed, to facilitate understanding and establish rapport.

Avoid making assumptions about the patient’s motivation.

Focus

Listen for change talk from the patient (giving positive reasons for changing the behavior) versus sustain talk (eliciting why the patient might want to sustain the status quo behavior).

Acknowledge sustain talk and gently encourage the patient to elaborate during change talk:

Elaborate: “Tell me more.” “Yes, I see.”

If patient feels unable to express goals, hopes, and/or reasons to change, offer suggestions of what other patients have done in similar situations.

Identify barriers to success and make a plan to combat these barriers in advance.

Genetics, Genomics, and Precision Medicine

Genetics is the study of single genes and their role in inheritance, whereas genomics is the study of an individual’s genetic material (the genome). Interest in the clinical application of genetic information, and with it the field of precision medicine, has grown steadily since the human genome was sequenced in the Human Genome Project. Precision medicine involves the application of individualized genetic information, along with environmental exposures and behavioral characteristics, to the treatment of patients, with a goal of improving clinical outcomes.

Genetic testing has an established role in several areas of routine clinical practice, including oncologic disease; neurologic disorders; rheumatologic disorders; and inherited cardiac, kidney, and gastrointestinal diseases. Although genetic testing is being used increasingly, it is not without limitations, including an absence of data in underrepresented populations and incomplete understanding of the clinical significance of many genetic variants. In addition, limitations inherent to specific testing methods and differences in approaches to interpretation may lead to differing results among testing laboratories.

This section provides an overview on taking a family history, identifying hereditary risk, and understanding genetic tests and testing strategies, including direct-to-consumer (DTC) testing.

Obtaining a family history is an important risk assessment strategy that can increase the proportion of patients identified as needing screening, genetic testing, or preventive treatment for some conditions. Features that suggest the presence of a genetically inherited condition are listed in [Table: Table: Red Flags Suggesting an Increased Genetic Risk]

.

Agreement on the essential components of a family history is lacking. Obtaining a complete three-generation family history is a reasonable initial approach to screening for genetically inherited disease; an increasing number of clinical practice guidelines incorporate information on first- and second-degree relatives. Documenting the history in the form of a family pedigree provides a helpful pictorial representation of the relationship between family members and the presence of medical conditions. Obtaining an appropriately complete family history is time consuming, however, and often requires investigation on the part of the patient. Self-administered online tools, such as the My Family Health Portrait tool, can streamline the acquisition of family disease patterns (

).

Genetic testing indications can be broadly categorized as diagnostic or predictive. Diagnostic testing is performed in patients with clinical features that suggest a genetic disease or disorders with a suspected genetic basis, such as hereditary hemochromatosis or cystic fibrosis. Predictive testing is typically performed in asymptomatic patients, such as those with a strong family history of a disease for which early intervention would alter the clinical course, or as part of prenatal counseling. As newer types of genetic testing measure large portions of the genome, diagnostic testing for one indication can also yield potentially predictive findings for other conditions.

Diagnostic and predictive tests may be performed as single-gene, panel, or whole exome or genome sequencing. Most clinical genetic tests are administered as panels that target specific disorders, such as hereditary cancer, or pharmacologically important genes (“pharmacogenes”). The Genetic Testing Registry of the National Center for Biotechnology Information provides a searchable index of clinical genetic tests and conditions.

Clinical context must always be considered when ordering genetic testing because certain types of genetic variation (e.g., copy number variation, in which a segment of the genome may be duplicated or deleted) may be missed by certain tests. Specialist involvement is appropriate when genetic test results are negative but clinical suspicion remains high.

Test performance characteristics should also be accounted for when ordering genetic testing. The American College of Physicians Ethics Manual recommends that physicians consider the following:

  • Analytical validity: ability of the test to accurately detect the presence or absence of a genetic variant
  • Clinical validity: ability of the test to accurately relate the variant to the specific disease
  • Clinical utility: ability of the test results to inform the diagnosis, treatment, or prevention of a disease
  • Personal utility: ability of the test results to provide patients with important personal or familial information to inform decision making

Patients for whom genetic testing is being considered, especially those undergoing predictive testing, should receive genetic counseling. The basic components of genetic counseling are education on the condition being tested, including the natural history, possible treatments, and preventive measures; the risks and benefits of testing; alternatives to testing, including the option to forgo testing; the implications for the patient and family members; and the costs, including the possibility of denial of coverage for disability, long-term care, and life insurance. Patients should be informed that the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008 protects against discrimination from obtaining employment (for companies with 15 or more employees) and health insurance; however, this protection does not extend to discrimination involving other types of insurance.

Patients who undergo genetic testing must understand the possibility of uncovering information that is incidental to the reason for testing. Such information may be of uncertain significance, producing stress and anxiety that are not easily relieved.

Pharmacogenomics is the study of how genetic composition affects the response to and metabolism of medications. Variation in response to medications can originate from genetic effects on the body’s response to drugs (pharmacokinetics), physiologic and biochemical effects of drugs on the body (pharmacodynamics), or drug hypersensitivity ( [Table: Table: Mechanisms of Pharmacogenomic Variants]

).

More than 95% of individuals carry functional variants in some of the most important pharmacogenes. Significant pharmacokinetic alterations are most commonly caused by alleles in genes affecting the cytochrome P-450 system, such as CYP2C19 or CYP2D6. Clinical phenotypes are assigned based on enzyme activity:

  • Poor metabolizer: little to no enzyme activity
  • Intermediate metabolizer: reduced enzyme activity
  • Extensive/normal metabolizer: normal enzyme activity
  • Rapid metabolizer: increased enzyme activity
  • Ultrarapid metabolizer: significantly increased enzyme activity

The effect of the phenotype on a particular medication depends on whether the medication is an active drug or a prodrug. Levels of medications that are taken in their active form, such as omeprazole, will be reduced in patients who are ultrarapid metabolizers and increased in patients who are poor metabolizers. Conversely, prodrugs, such as clopidogrel, require conversion to their active form; ultrarapid metabolizers will have increased drug levels, whereas poor metabolizers will have reduced levels. Correlating pharmacogenetic phenotypes with clinical drug effect is not always straightforward because other factors can influence drug levels and the clinical response may be nonlinear.

Guidance on the use of pharmacogenetic information in clinical practice is available from the Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC). Although predictive pharmacogenomic testing is mostly investigational, genetic testing is recommended when certain medications are prescribed in routine practice, focusing on situations in which serious adverse effects or treatment failures may occur (e.g., testing for HLA-B58:01 before prescribing allopurinol in patients at increased risk for severe cutaneous adverse reactions; see [Table: Table: Mechanisms of Pharmacogenomic Variants]*

). More broadly, however, the FDA issued a warning in November 2018 that pharmacogenomic testing companies have promulgated drug dosing recommendations using information that has yet to be evaluated by the FDA. There is an ongoing collaboration to review scientific evidence in this arena, and the regulatory landscape continues to evolve.

DTC genomic testing is a commercial service that allows patients to obtain genetic information without a physician order or prescription. Consumer-directed genomic testing is a similar process in which patients request that their physician authorize specific testing by a third-party laboratory or company. The FDA has approved DTC genomic testing for some disorders, and physicians may be asked to provide guidance to persons who have undergone testing on their own. Advocates argue that these services promote patient autonomy because patients can access information on genetic predispositions directly, without physician referral. Critics counter that DTC testing is not usually accompanied by pre- or posttest genetic counseling, potentially leading to variable interpretations and patient harm.

DTC genomic testing typically uses polygenic risk estimation, a technique in which risk for medical conditions is estimated by genotyping polymorphic nucleotides. Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that are disproportionately found in affected individuals are identified, and odds ratios for each SNP are determined. The SNPs are usually common but have low penetrance (that is, most people with an SNP do not develop the disease). Individually, SNPs contribute very little to overall disease risk; most SNPs have an odds ratio of less than 1.5. As an example, if a condition has a general population prevalence of 8%, possessing an associated SNP with an odds ratio of 1.3 would increase one’s risk for the condition to approximately 10%. The use of polygenic risk scores (weighted risk estimates created by using a combination of SNPs from across the entire genome) is an area of ongoing investigation.

Several key differences exist between DTC testing and clinical testing. Most important, DTC testing is approved only to provide health information; DTC tests are not diagnostic tests. The FDA recommends confirmation with clinical testing before using DTC test results in modification of patient care. Available DTC tests also assess for fewer genetic variants than do clinical tests, creating risk for false-negative results. For example, a currently available DTC test for breast cancer tests for only 3 of more than 1000 variants of BRCA1 and BRCA2. In addition, risk for false-negative results is increased in non-European populations, which are underrepresented in clinical studies of genetic testing. Finally, DTC testing creates unique privacy concerns if genetic data are made public or sold. Research teams have successfully identified people from anonymized genetic data and public records. It is also important to recognize that DTC tests are not substitutes for recommended health screenings and evaluation.

Epigenetics is the study of heritable alterations in gene expression that occur outside the DNA sequence. Epigenetics has been conceptualized as the process by which genetic material (nature) interacts with the environment (nurture) to create a specific phenotype or as a biomarker of this interaction. Mechanisms of epigenetic expression include DNA methylation, histone modification, and chromatin structure. Research studies have shown a potential association between epigenetic variants and presentations of cardiovascular, neurologic, and oncologic diseases. DNA methylation (the transfer of a methyl group to DNA) has demonstrated promise in diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic roles but has not yet entered routine clinical practice.

Precision medicine, also referred to as “personalized medicine,” is an emerging practice of medicine that uses an individual’s genetic information, environment, and lifestyle to direct and tailor disease management. Proteomics and metabalomics are increasingly being used in personalized medicine. Clinical decision making in precision medicine is based on identification of genetic risk factors; referral to genetic counseling services; appropriate choices in genetic testing; and a collaborative discussion with patients, genetic counselors, and specialists in test interpretation. Precision medicine has become increasingly used for a variety of conditions, including epilepsy, cardiovascular diseases, pulmonary conditions, cancer, and other diseases (see, for example, Cancer Precision Medicine in Oncology). Concerns remain regarding the high cost of such an approach.

bodies.fcsec24007:
Patient Safety and Quality Improvement

Quality improvement (QI) refers to a systematic approach to analyzing practice performance with the aim of providing optimal evidence-based care in a reproducible and reliable manner while also improving patient safety. QI also aims to improve the health care process by reducing waste and unnecessary treatments while ensuring that all patients receive equitable care regardless of race, ethnicity, or socioeconomic background. The focus on practice performance data may be at the patient level (such as screening), the system level (such as hospital readmission rates), or the population level (such as regional mortality rates). The process of QI is ideally continuous, occurring in real time with rapid-cycle improvements and iterative change. Successful QI requires participation from all health care team members as well as patients.

Safety and quality issues in health care are often multifactorial in etiology and occur due to systems factors, human factors, and patient-related factors. Well-functioning interdisciplinary teams, which are critical to providing complex medical care, can improve patient safety and quality (see Team-Based Care and Interprofessional Communication in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Adversely, substantial variability in care delivery and nonadherence to evidence-based guidelines may contribute to a lack of quality care. Common preventable threats to patient safety include the following:

  • Medication errors
  • Inadequate transitions of care
  • Procedural and surgical errors
  • Diagnostic errors (see Diagnostic Reasoning and Diagnostic Error in Foundations of Clinical Practice)
  • Health care–associated infections (see Health Care–Associated Infections in Infectious Disease)
  • Venous thromboembolism (see Surgery, Trauma, Hospitalization, and Immobility in Hematology)
  • Pressure injuries (see Pressure Injuries in Foundations of Clinical Practice)
  • Patient falls (see Fall Prevention in Foundations of Clinical Practice)

Medication errors are preventable events that may result in inappropriate use of medication or patient harm and are the most common type of medical error. They are estimated to occur at rates of 8% to 25% in hospitals and long-term care facilities; in the outpatient setting, medication errors are estimated to occur at rates of 2% to 33%. These types of errors may occur at any stage (prescribing/transcribing, dispensing, administering/taking, or monitoring) and by any person in the process (clinician, pharmacist, nurse, or patient). Errors may be those of omission, such as not prescribing an indicated medication, or commission, such as prescribing an incorrect medication or dose. Interventions to improve medication verification, clarification, and reconciliation have demonstrated reduced adverse drug events in hospitalized patients.

Prescribers form the first line of defense in preventing medication errors ( [Table: Table: Strategies to Prevent Medication Errors]

). Prescribers need to review a patient’s complete medical record, including medical history; medication list, including prescription and over-the-counter medications, herbal remedies, and supplements; allergies; and laboratory data (such as kidney and liver function) that may affect medication dosing. Prescribers must also be diligent in screening for possible medication interactions. A multidisciplinary approach including physicians, advanced care providers, nurses, and pharmacists using appropriate technologic tools can reduce adverse events and contribute to better safety.

When patients transition care between clinicians or care environments, they are at increased risk for harm. Handoffs between clinicians and teams are integral to this process and are defined as the transfer and acceptance of responsibility of patient care between clinicians through effective communication.

Factors that contribute to suboptimal transitions include poor communication among health care team members, incomplete transfer of information, and inadequate patient education. Patient factors that increase the likelihood of suboptimal transition of care include older age, multiple comorbid medical conditions, poor health literacy, language barriers, and cognitive impairment. Although useful for preventing many types of errors, health information technology itself may facilitate errors, such as those resulting from inappropriate use of charting templates and use of the copy-and-paste function in composing notes.

Effective communication among health care team members and between providers and patients is the key to successful handoffs and transitions of care. Use of a standardized communication tool, such as SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation/Request) or I-PASS (Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness and contingency planning, Synthesis), can assist in effectively and consistently transferring information during handoffs (see [Table: Table: Structured Communication Strategies]

). Transitions are also enhanced by physician involvement in a multidisciplinary team using a continuous, case-based multidisciplinary team management approach. During transitions, physicians should strive to provide clear, concise, and accurate patient records to subsequent providers. Accurate medication reconciliation is paramount because errors frequently occur; several studies have shown medication reconciliation is best performed by a pharmacist. At hospital discharge, physicians must focus on follow-up plans, including educating patients on the expected course and red flag symptoms that necessitate reevaluation.

Medication reconciliation is a critical aspect of medical error prevention and refers to the process of verifying the medications that a patient is taking, including the name of the medicine, dose, frequency, and route of administration, to identify and resolve discrepancies. To perform medication reconciliation, the health care team must first obtain a list of the patient’s medications, including prescribed and over-the-counter medications as well as vitamins and supplements. This list can be provided by the patient and/or obtained through their dispensing pharmacy, health care records, or the facility where the patient resides (if applicable). This list should be compared with new, discontinued, or changed medications, and any identified discrepancies (e.g., duplications, dosing errors, drug-drug interactions, omissions) should be resolved. Medication reconciliation is commonly done at points of transition for a patient, such as during hospital admission or discharge, but it can be done at any time deemed necessary by the health care team.

When conducting medication reconciliation during hospital discharge, it is crucial to clarify the medications the patient is taking at the time of discharge, any changes compared to before admission (and why those changes were made), and any medications that are currently being withheld but may need to be restarted at a later date by the outpatient team. Furthermore, it is imperative that the health care team clearly communicate any medication changes or discontinuations to the patient and/or their caregivers. Effective medication reconciliation has been demonstrated to decrease hospital readmission rates as well as adverse drug events.

Procedural and surgical errors may include medication errors; retained foreign objects; and wrong-site, wrong-procedure, wrong-patient errors (WSPEs). WSPEs are termed never events because they are preventable and should never occur in health care settings. Strategies to prevent these errors include adhering to safety checklists; using structured, closed-loop communication; marking the procedure site; and using timeouts. A timeout refers to a pause in care in which members of the clinical team confirm the correct patient, procedure, and site; timeouts are especially critical in preventing WSPEs. The Joint Commission National Universal Protocol for procedure safety comprises three steps: a preprocedure verification process (correct procedure, patient, and site); marking of the procedure site; and performing a timeout with active communication by team members regarding the correct patient, site, and procedure. Postoperative complications such as surgical site infections are also often preventable and can be mitigated by perioperative safety measures (see Prevention of Surgical Site Infections in Infectious Disease for additional information).

Error reporting should be based on nonpunitive and transparent systems that identify root causes and improve safety. Error reporting is a professional responsibility, and clinicians should be encouraged to disclose adverse events, errors, near-misses, and other safety concerns. Errors should be disclosed to both the health care system and the patient (see Medical Error Disclosure in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Organizational approaches that promote a culture of safety and a focus on systems-based improvements are critical to reporting, responding to, and learning from errors.

Error reporting platforms that are simple to use, accessible through various channels (e.g., telephone hotline, app, electronic health system), and confidential may facilitate reporting. Reporting forms typically include specific data (e.g., location, medical record number) and narrative descriptions. Ideally, only minimal information is needed to locate the record and understand the event to avoid overburdening individuals or deterring them from reporting. Reports should be analyzed using structured methods, such as root cause analysis, with a focus on systems-based causes rather than individual blame. The Joint Commission requires a root cause analysis within 45 days for all sentinel events. Findings from the analysis form the basis for systems-based interventions, which may include new workflows, standardized procedures, and improved communication processes.

Physicians have the potential to both recognize and mitigate threats to patient safety. QI interventions that are developed with physician input are much more likely to succeed than those developed without such consultation.

Several QI models that provide structure for implementing QI interventions on a systems level are available. The American College of Physicians (ACP) Advance curriculum provides a useful tool set and additional resources for implementing QI interventions.

Root cause analysis is a systematic method of determining contributors to an adverse event (or near miss). After an event is identified, an interdisciplinary team begins with the problem and works backwards from the event, repetitively asking “what contributed to this?” or “why?” to determine the root causes. The process ideally uncovers as many underlying contributors as possible. Various root cause analysis tools exist, including fishbone (also known as cause-and-effect or Ishikawa) diagrams or the “five whys” approach. Root cause analysis is a fundamental tool used in various QI models.

The Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle is another frequently used method in each of the models described in this section and provides structure for continuous improvement.

The Model for Improvement is the most commonly used QI model in health care. It provides a simple framework for QI interventions that relies on rapid PDSA cycles. A key underlying theme is that although not every change leads to improvement, improvement cannot occur without change. This model works best when frontline health care staff members are active participants. Users of this model begin by developing a goal by asking, “What are we trying to accomplish?” Next, to determine how to track success, users must answer, “How will we measure if a change yields an improvement?” The final step in this model is to determine what change is going to be made by asking the question, “What change can we make that will result in improvement?” Ideas and changes are tested iteratively through PDSA cycles.

Because this QI model does not help to identify causes of health care problems, it works best for problems with easily identifiable causes and evidence-based solutions. For example, a medical center may set the specific goal of increasing adherence to stroke treatment guidelines and use PDSA cycles to rapidly implement and assess the impact of changes, such as using a computerized admission order set.

The Lean model focuses on improving health care processes through two principles: waste elimination and respect for individuals. In this model, activities are classified as being either value added (directly contributing to meeting patient needs) or non–value added (requiring resources of time and space but not meeting patient needs). On average, most processes are only 5% value added and 95% non–value added. Value stream mapping is an example of a Lean model in which the steps of a process and time required for each step are graphically displayed, thereby highlighting process inefficiencies and allowing for their improvement.

The Lean model is best applied to directly observed problems and when flow, efficiency, and speed are prioritized; involvement of frontline health care staff members is crucial because they are in the best position to identify problems. Using the Lean model, results can typically be seen within weeks.

Six Sigma, which refers to six standard deviations from the mean, focuses on improvement through reducing variability in patient care. It relies on understanding and controlling processes by using quantitative tools, such as analysis of variance, control charts, and mathematical modeling. Six Sigma is a five-phase process: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, and Control (DMAIC). In the Define phase, key measures for determining success are established. In the Measure phase, past performance levels are determined to provide a baseline to measure future improvement. In the Analyze phase, causes of the current problems and improvement opportunities are identified. Finally, in the Control phase, improvement is standardized to maintain sustainability.

Six Sigma typically requires a time commitment of at least several months and substantial institutional resources to implement effectively. As such, it is best applied to complex, multistep health care problems in which an immediate cause or solution cannot be readily identified, such as catheter-related bloodstream infections.

Operational Excellence is a continuous QI model that has its roots in industry and frequently uses aspects of Lean, Six Sigma, and other QI models. It is a management system that aims for consistent and reliable operation of an institutional strategy by focusing on leadership, problem solving, and teamwork. The main focus is on patient needs, but it also aims to empower and engage all staff members. All levels of an organization must be invested in the model for it to be successful. Staff members must be empowered to identify problems and bring these problems, as well as potential solutions, to the attention of others and leadership. Leadership must value the opinions and contributions of the frontline staff and promote a no-blame culture in which there is no fear of reprisal. PDSA cycles, often centered on the ideas of frontline workers, are commonly used as a structural approach within the Operational Excellence framework to promote change. Operational Excellence can be used to improve quality by focusing on key performance indicators of quality and safety, such as timely completion of medication reconciliation.

Many organizations and payers assess quality of care as a condition of accreditation or participation. For example, The Joint Commission assesses a wide variety of quality metrics, such as timely provision of reperfusion therapy in acute myocardial infarction, the incidence of potentially preventable venous thromboembolic disease, and rates of influenza immunization.

Medicare also has a significant impact on measurement of health care quality. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services assess areas of hospital performance, such as hospital mortality and readmission rates, and areas of ambulatory care performance, such as hypertension control, prevention of diabetic kidney disease, and colorectal cancer screening. Patients are surveyed regarding the quality of their experience after hospitalization via the Hospital Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Provider and Systems Survey. Data related to hospital performance are publicly available.

ACP works to assess the validity of performance measures based on appropriateness criteria and drive change by determining if measures are evidence-based, methodologically sound, and clinically meaningful.

Models of QI have three main measures: structure, process, and outcomes. Structure measures are the physical organizational aspects of a health care system (e.g., equipment and staffing). Process measures focus on interactions between patients and the health care team (e.g., clinical procedures or care coordination). Outcome measures represent the effects of the delivered health care among a population of patients and include clinical (e.g., life expectancy or hemoglobin A~1c control among patients with diabetes) and patient-reported (e.g., patient satisfaction, perceived health status, and quality of life) measures. Patient-reported outcome measures are typically collected via surveys and are crucial to maintaining the patient voice in health care improvement and fostering trust between patients and physicians. Structure, process, and outcome measures are often used together in QI initiatives.

The ACP High Value Care initiative aims to improve health, avoid harms, and eliminate wasteful practices. This initiative addresses high value care broadly, offering learning resources for clinicians and medical educators, clinical guidelines, best practice advice, and patient resources on a wide variety of related topics. Components of the High Value Care initiative that are evident in MKSAP include the identification of High Value Care key points in the text.

The Joint Commission establishes annual National Patient Safety Goals to address important issues in health care safety. Recommended by a panel of patient safety experts and applied to various patient care settings, the National Patient Safety Goals center on interventions that have the highest impact on quality and safety. In publishing the goals, The Joint Commission also provides specific metrics for each goal to facilitate implementation. Goals are customized to the care setting, and separate goals are provided for hospitals, ambulatory health centers, and nursing care centers, among other settings. The goals are updated annually.

The patient-centered medical home is a model of providing primary health care that is coordinated by a health care team, including physicians, advanced practice practitioners, nurses, pharmacists, physical therapists, patient educators, and case managers, housed within a collaborative group practice. The functions of the patient-centered medical home include providing comprehensive health care, coordinating care across settings, improving access to services with extended clinician availability, and engaging in quality and safety improvement programs. Further information about the patient-centered medical home is available from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) and the ACP.

The concept of the patient-centered medical home has been expanded into the patient-centered medical neighborhood; this includes other clinicians and institutions (such as specialists and hospitals) involved in an individual patient’s care.

Clinical decision support tools that are integrated into electronic health record systems, such as order sets and alerts, can improve patient outcomes. Order sets are a bundle of predefined orders that pertain to a specific clinical scenario. Common examples include order sets for the treatment of sepsis, stroke, alcohol withdrawal, and delirium reduction. Order sets may improve adherence to evidence-based recommendations and efficiency and reduce medication errors. For optimum efficacy, order sets should be standardized, be complete, and reflect best practices. Clinical decision support alerts warn physicians about potentially unsafe clinical scenarios, such as drug-drug or drug-allergy interactions, abnormal readings from physiologic monitors, or contraindications to diagnostic tests. Alerts may also suggest possible high-risk diagnoses or treatments; for example, an alert may detect a patient with sepsis based on predefined physiologic and laboratory parameters, suggest an alternate medication dosage for a patient with kidney or liver dysfunction, or suggest that a vaccine is needed based on age and/or diagnoses. Alert fatigue, wherein clinicians are subjected to so many alerts they begin to ignore them, is a substantial drawback. The efficacy of alert systems may be improved by reducing clinically inconsequential alerts, grading alerts according to severity, customizing alerts for clinical relevance, and allowing only critical alerts to interrupt workflow.
