Routine Care of the Adult Patient

The periodic health examination is defined as a regular medical visit, often on an annual basis, for the purposes of screening and prevention. Patients have become accustomed to a comprehensive head-to-toe physical examination as well as recommendations for screening for disease, blood tests, and other routine testing. Although evidence suggests periodic health examinations may improve surrogate outcomes, such as reduction in cardiovascular risk factors and increased receipt of preventive services, there is no evidence that they reduce mortality or other patient-important outcomes. A 2019 Cochrane systematic review confirmed that general health checks may result in more new diagnoses but do not reduce morbidity, hospitalizations, or mortality. Overdiagnosis and overtreatment are potential drawbacks to periodic health checks. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) and the Canadian Task Force on the Periodic Health Examination recommend against performing general health checks that include a comprehensive examination and laboratory testing for asymptomatic adults. However, some countries, including the United Kingdom, Germany, and Japan, continue to recommend periodic health examinations.

Despite the recommendation to avoid the periodic health examination, the practice may offer value that is difficult to measure in clinical trials. It provides dedicated time for screening, immunizations, and healthy lifestyle counseling and may strengthen physician-patient relationships and patient adherence to physician recommendations. In 2011, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services introduced an annual wellness visit to develop or update a personalized prevention plan. Utilization of annual wellness visits continues to be low, but in high-performing systems, they have been shown to have a neutral to positive impact on health care costs and greater uptake in preventive services. In practices that do not routinely use periodic health examinations, automated reminder systems, online portals, and clinical assistants can help prompt patients, either at home or during focused visits, to receive any preventive services indicated.

Effective, patient-centered communication is a critical component of the routine history and physical examination and is discussed in Effective Communication in Clinical Practice in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

Obtaining a basic history as well as a focused history of presenting problems is essential in establishing a clinician-patient relationship and understanding the patient’s health, concerns, and expectations ( [Table: Table: Components of the History]

). Patients may be sensitive about sharing certain information, such as substance use and sexual practices; open and nonjudgmental communication can encourage sharing. Clinicians should preface these inquiries by informing the patient that these questions are asked of everyone, the information is necessary to provide the best care, and responses are confidential. A focused history of the primary reasons for the visit should also be obtained. It is often helpful to start with an open-ended question or statement, such as, “Tell me about your knee pain,” which often results in more information sharing than does directive questioning. A commonly taught mnemonic to elicit other relevant information is OLDCARTS (Onset, Location/radiation, Duration, Character, Aggravating factors, Relieving factors, Timing, Severity). It is often helpful to ask the patient, “What do you think is going on?”

A focused physical examination should address the patient’s concerns and relevant historical findings. Physicians should examine the patient in a sensitive and respectful manner. Regularly obtaining height and weight (to calculate BMI) as well as blood pressure is universally recommended. In addition, pulse palpation in individuals older than 65 years has been found effective for detection of atrial fibrillation (although the USPSTF concluded that there is insufficient evidence to assess the benefits or harms of screening for atrial fibrillation with ECG or other recording methods). In asymptomatic patients, the USPSTF recommends against routine abdominal, testicular, and bimanual pelvic examinations for cancer screening. Routine cardiac and lung auscultation, thyroid palpation, skin examination, visual acuity assessment, and hearing assessment may be appropriate as part of a comprehensive physical examination in persons at increased risk. Relatively little harm arises from these examinations save for the opportunity cost of providing another service that may be more valuable and the theoretical risk for overtesting and overdiagnosis. Routine testing in asymptomatic patients, such as screening complete blood count, urinalysis, and ECG in those at low risk for cardiovascular disease, is not recommended.

A physical examination is often required for adolescents and young adults before participation in organized sports. In conjunction with the American Academy of Family Physicians and several professional sports medicine organizations, the American Academy of Pediatrics created the Preparticipation Physical Evaluation. In addition, free templates for history, physical examination, and clearance forms are available on the American Academy of Pediatrics Web site. Mandatory components include evaluating for exertional symptoms, family history of premature or sudden cardiac death, and the presence of a heart murmur through auscultation in the supine and standing positions and, when indicated, with Valsalva maneuver.

Digital stethoscopes, point-of-care ultrasonography, smartphone applications, and other technological advances are becoming more commonplace in the physical examination. Several of these tools, particularly point-of-care ultrasonography, may improve diagnosis, although there is the potential for overdiagnosis as well.

Screening is appropriate for common conditions for which (1) early intervention can decrease morbidity and mortality and (2) safe, acceptable, widely available, and reasonably priced screening tests exist. Screening tests must also have adequate sensitivity and specificity to minimize false-positive and false-negative results. Population-based screening and case finding are often confused. Case finding is a strategy of targeted testing that relies on clinical judgment of appropriateness and potential benefit for a given patient who meets evidence-based criteria for inclusion in a high-risk group. The evidence that case finding improves morbidity or mortality is often weak or absent.

The effectiveness of screening tests in reducing morbidity and mortality is evaluated through clinical trials; however, studies of screening tests may be problematic due to three major types of bias.

  • Lead-time bias may result in overestimation of survival. It refers to the period of time between screen-detected disease and the point at which the disease would typically have been diagnosed clinically. The time between early detection and clinical diagnosis is mistakenly counted as survival time; however, only the measured time with diagnosed disease, not survival time, has increased (

). Using disease-specific mortality rates rather than survival time as the primary outcome in studies of screening tests can help minimize lead-time bias. - Length-time bias may also result in overestimation of survival. It occurs because slowly progressive disease is more likely than aggressive disease to be detected with screening. As slowly progressive disease often has a better prognosis than rapidly progressive disease, an overestimation of survival benefit in those with screen-detected disease may be perceived (

). An example of length-time bias is the detection of indolent and slow-growing prostate cancer rather than more aggressive tumors with a short asymptomatic phase, resulting in an overestimation of survival benefit. Overdiagnosis, or finding and treating illness that otherwise would not have become clinically apparent or caused harm in the patient’s lifetime, is an extreme example of length-time bias. Overdiagnosis is an increasingly recognized harm of breast and prostate cancer screening and may also occur with incidental detection of thyroid and kidney cancers on imaging studies. - Selection bias, such as volunteer bias, referral bias, and compliance bias, occurs when patients who undergo screening tests are healthier or more interested in their health than the general population. Using a randomized controlled trial design with an intention-to-treat analysis, in which patients are analyzed according to their original group assignment, can reduce selection bias.

The USPSTF and many specialty societies routinely aggregate and review available evidence to inform clinical practice guidelines for screening, counseling, and use of preventive medications. The USPSTF recommendations are available online. The Emergency Care Research Institute is designated an Evidence-based Practice Center by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality and maintains a clinical practice guideline repository. The American College of Physicians (ACP) has developed several types of clinical recommendations, including clinical practice guidelines, clinical guidance statements, best practice advice, and recommendations regarding high-value care, all of which are available online. Although there is much agreement among screening recommendations, guidelines often disagree when (1) sufficient evidence is lacking and expert opinion plays a larger role or (2) potential benefits and harms both exist and the balance depends on a person’s risk, preferences, and values.

An additional resource to help clinicians identify appropriate screening tests and preventive services is Prevention TaskForce, an electronic tool. With this tool, users can select USPSTF-recommended practices based on patient age, sex, and other characteristics (such as tobacco use or pregnancy).

Screening recommendations frequently change as supportive evidence emerges. It is important to be aware of changes in recommendations, reflect on the rationale and implications of the changes, and incorporate these changes appropriately into practice.

Screening should be based on the person’s age, anatomy, and risk factors.

The following section describes screening recommendations from the USPSTF and other organizations (for cancer screening recommendations, see Screening for Cancer in Oncology). The grading system of the USPSTF (A, B, C, or D, or I statement) is explained in [Table: Table: USPSTF Grading and Suggestions for Practice]

.

The USPSTF recommends one-time abdominal ultrasonography to screen for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) in all men aged 65 to 75 years who have ever smoked (grade B). Ever-smokers are commonly defined as persons who have smoked 100 cigarettes (five packs) or more in their lifetime. Surgical repair is commonly done once the diameter exceeds 5.5 cm or if the diameter is 4 cm or larger with rapid expansion (>0.5 cm/6 months) (see Treatment of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm in Cardiovascular Medicine). The prevalence of AAA has decreased over time because of the declining number of smokers but historically has been 1% to 7% in men older than 60 years. The number needed to screen to prevent one death from AAA in this population is 714. In men aged 65 to 75 years who have never smoked, selective screening is recommended (grade C), especially in those with a first-degree relative with a history of treated or ruptured AAA, with the greatest risk in those with a female first-degree relative (odds ratio, 4.32). The USPSTF assessed the benefits of screening for AAA in women aged 65 to 75 years who have ever smoked as uncertain and makes no recommendation regarding screening in this population (I statement). The USPSTF specifically recommends against routine screening in women who have never smoked and who have no family history of AAA (grade D). Women, however, may have a higher risk for rupture with smaller AAAs.

Cardiovascular risk assessment is performed in asymptomatic adults to evaluate a patient’s risk for future cardiac events; it does not identify preexisting disease and is therefore considered separate from screening (see Calculating Cardiovascular Risk in Cardiovascular Medicine).

The USPSTF does not recommend screening for coronary artery disease with either resting or exercise ECG in asymptomatic patients at low risk (grade D). In patients at intermediate or high risk for such events, evidence is inadequate to assess the relative benefits and harms of screening (I statement). Risk can be assessed by using the Framingham Risk Score or the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Pooled Cohort Equations. The USPSTF recommends using the Pooled Cohort Equations for risk assessment. Similarly, the ACP recommends against screening low-risk and asymptomatic adults with resting ECG or stress testing. No specialty organization recommends screening these populations with coronary calcium scoring or coronary angiography.

The USPSTF also does not recommend screening for carotid artery stenosis in the general adult population (grade D). The rationale for this recommendation is based on the very low prevalence of carotid stenosis (0.5%-1.0%) and resulting high rate of false-positive results yielded by commonly used ultrasonography. Auscultation of the neck for carotid bruits is ineffective for screening. Screening for carotid stenosis in asymptomatic patients could lead to harm as a result of complications from angiographic studies or endarterectomy.

The USPSTF assessed the benefits of screening for cognitive impairment as uncertain (I statement) owing to a lack of high-quality evidence. Various screening tests with high predictive value are available (see Cognitive Function in Foundations of Clinical Practice). However, it is uncertain whether early detection and pharmacologic treatment changes or improves clinical outcomes.

The USPSTF recommends that all adults, including pregnant and postpartum patients, be screened for depression (grade B). Most adults can be screened with the brief PHQ-2, which consists of two questions: “During the past 2 weeks, have you often been bothered by feeling down, depressed, or hopeless?” and “During the past 2 weeks, have you often been bothered by having little interest or pleasure in doing things?” Responses to each question may be scaled (0-3) or dichotomous (yes/no). A total score for both questions of 3 or greater or a single “yes” response indicates the possibility of clinically significant depression. Patients with a positive screening result should be formally assessed for depression and complete the PHQ-9, which may be used to monitor depression.

Other screening instruments may be more accurate for screening in specific patient populations; these include the Geriatric Depression Scale in older adults, the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale in postpartum and pregnant patients, and the PHQ-9 modified for adolescents (PHQ-A).

Effective interventions are available to prevent peripartum depression, but there are no validated risk assessment tools to identify patients who might benefit. The USPSTF suggests that those with increased risk can be identified by one or more of the following risk factors: a history of depression, current depressive symptoms that do not reach a diagnostic threshold, low income, adolescent or single parenthood, recent intimate partner violence, elevated anxiety symptoms, or a history of significant negative life events.

The USPSTF recommends screening for anxiety disorders in adults aged 19 to 64 years. Screening tool options include the Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale, Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale anxiety subscale, Geriatric Anxiety Scale, and Geriatric Anxiety Inventory. Patients with a positive screening test result should be further assessed for anxiety and, if an anxiety disorder is confirmed, treated.

The USPSTF recommends screening for diabetes mellitus in adults aged 35 to 70 years who have overweight or obesity (grade B). Screening can be accomplished by measuring fasting plasma glucose or hemoglobin A~1c.

In contrast to the USPSTF, the American Diabetes Association (ADA) recommends that screening be performed in adults of any age who have overweight or obesity and have one or more risk factors for diabetes (see [Table: Table: Screening Guidelines for Prediabetes or Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus]

). The ADA also recommends screening all adults beginning at age 35 years, regardless of risk factors, and repeating screening at 3-year intervals. Patients with prediabetes should be screened annually. Patients with a history of gestational diabetes should undergo lifelong screening every 1 to 3 years.

The USPSTF recommends calculating the cardiovascular disease risk in adults aged 40 to 75 years using the Pooled Cohort Equations to guide the initiation of statin therapy for primary prevention. This requires measurement of serum lipid levels to determine risk for an atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) event.

For adults 40 to 75 years of age, the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and American Heart Association (AHA) also recommend routine assessment of traditional cardiovascular risk factors and calculation of the 10-year risk for ASCVD by using the Pooled Cohort Equations. For adults aged 20 to 39 years, the ACC and AHA believe it is reasonable to assess traditional ASCVD risk factors at least every 4 to 6 years. See Evaluation of Lipid Levels in Cardiovascular Medicine for more information.

The USPSTF supports screening all adults beginning at age 18 years for hypertension (grade A). Screening should occur annually in adults aged 40 years or older and in younger adults at increased risk. Screening should otherwise occur at 3- to 5-year intervals. For more information, see Screening and Diagnosis of Hypertension in Nephrology and Blood Pressure Measurement in Nephrology.

The predictive value of screening for hypertension is improved through serial measurements in various settings. Before treatment is initiated, when possible and in the absence of severe hypertension or end-organ damage, the diagnosis should be confirmed with blood pressure measurements outside the clinical setting, such as ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring.

The ACC and AHA recommend annual evaluation of patients with normal blood pressure (<120/<80 mm Hg). Adults with elevated blood pressure (120-129/<80 mm Hg) or stage 1 hypertension (130-139 mm Hg systolic or 80-89 mm Hg diastolic) without clinical cardiovascular disease, previous stroke, diabetes, or chronic kidney disease and who have an estimated 10-year ASCVD risk less than 7.5% based on the AHA Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease EVENTs (PREVENT) online calculator should be managed with nonpharmacologic therapy and have a repeat blood pressure evaluation within 3 to 6 months. See Management of Primary Hypertension in Nephrology for more information on blood pressure management.

The USPSTF no longer recommends screening for obesity but does recommend referring or initiating weight loss interventions for adults with a BMI of 30 or higher (grade B). The ACC, the AHA, and The Obesity Society recommend annual screening with BMI and waist circumference measurements.

According to the USPSTF, evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for obstructive sleep apnea in asymptomatic adults with the currently available tools (I statement). Because obstructive sleep apnea is widely underrecognized, clinicians should have a low threshold for investigating for sleep apnea in patients who have symptoms consistent with the disease (see Clinical Features and Diagnosis of Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Pulmonary Medicine).

The USPSTF and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommend screening for osteoporosis in all women aged 65 years or older and in postmenopausal women younger than 65 years who are at increased risk for osteoporosis as estimated by clinical risk assessment. For postmenopausal women younger than 65 years, the USPSTF recommends first assessing for osteoporosis risk factors; those with one or more risk factors should be further evaluated with a clinical risk assessment tool. Commonly used risk assessment tools include the Fracture Risk Assessment (FRAX), Osteoporosis Self-Assessment Tool, and Osteoporosis Risk Assessment Instrument. Women at increased risk should undergo screening for osteoporosis. Screening can be accomplished with bone mineral density measurement, most commonly with dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry of the hip and lumbar spine. Although the USPSTF makes no recommendation on rescreening, ACOG suggests repeat osteoporosis screening after an interval of at least 2 years in postmenopausal patients with significant changes in risk profile or initial bone mineral density test results that approached the threshold to treat.

The USPSTF concludes that evidence is insufficient to recommend routine screening for osteoporosis in men to reduce the risk for fractures (I statement); however, the Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation (formerly the National Osteoporosis Foundation) recommends osteoporosis screening in men aged 70 years or older. Screening may be considered in younger men at high risk for osteoporosis on the basis of risk factors, such as low body weight, recent weight loss, physical inactivity, use of oral glucocorticoids, previous fragility fracture, alcohol use, and androgen deprivation through pharmacologic agents or orchiectomy.

Risk assessment and screening for osteoporosis are further discussed in Low Bone Mass (Osteopenia) and Osteoporosis in Endocrinology and Metabolism.

The USPSTF concludes that evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against screening for thyroid dysfunction (I statement). The American Thyroid Association and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinology, however, recommend measuring thyroid-stimulating hormone in individuals at risk for hypothyroidism (e.g., personal history of autoimmune disease, neck radiation, or thyroid surgery); they additionally recommend considering screening in adults aged 60 years or older.

[Table: Table: USPSTF Recommendations on Screening for Infectious Diseases]

presents USPSTF recommendations for infectious disease screening. The CDC sexually transmitted infections (STIs) screening recommendations for specific populations can be found on its Web site.

The USPSTF recommends screening for chlamydia and gonorrhea in all sexually active women aged 24 years or younger because of increased prevalence in this population. In the absence of studies on screening intervals, the USPSTF believes that repeat screening is reasonable in sexually active women aged 25 years or older whose sexual history reveals new or persistent risk factors. Screening for these diseases in low-risk heterosexual men of this age and demographic group is not recommended (I statement) owing to lack of evidence to support benefits of screening. The CDC recommends screening men in settings or populations with high prevalence or burden of disease (e.g., men who have sex with men, patients evaluated in STI clinics). For further information regarding chlamydia and gonorrhea testing, see Chlamydia trachomatis Infection in Infectious Disease and Neisseria gonorrhoeae Infection in Infectious Disease.

The CDC recommends that all adults aged 18 years and older undergo one-time screening for hepatitis B virus infection with hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen (anti-HBs), and antibody to hepatitis B core antigen (anti-HBc). All pregnant persons should be screened during each pregnancy, preferably within the first trimester, regardless of previous testing history or vaccination status. For additional information, see Hepatitis B in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease.

One-time screening for hepatitis C virus should be completed in all patients aged 18 to 79 years. The USPSTF does not promote screening in patients older than 79 years, although the CDC does not specify an upper age limit and studies of hepatitis C virus treatment demonstrate benefit in patients older than 80 years. Additionally, the CDC recommends that pregnant individuals be screened during each pregnancy. Patients with risk factors should be retested regardless of age. Screening is accomplished by testing for antibodies to the disease, followed by polymerase chain reaction viral load testing if results of initial testing are positive (see Hepatitis C in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease).

Routine HIV screening, regardless of risk, is recommended by the USPSTF for all persons aged 15 to 65 years and by the CDC for all persons aged 13 to 64 years. Pregnancy is an indication for repeat screening. The USPSTF suggests repeat screening of persons at increased risk for HIV including the following:

  • Men who have sex with men
  • Individuals with a sex partner living with HIV
  • Persons who engage in behaviors that increase the risk for infection (injection drug use, transactional sex, one or more new sex partners with unknown HIV status)
  • Those receiving care in a high-prevalence setting (STI clinic, tuberculosis clinic, correctional facility, homeless shelter)

However, the USPSTF does not specify the interval for repeat screening. The CDC recommends at least annual screening for men who have sex with men but notes that more frequent screening may be appropriate depending on risk factors. Combination HIV antibody immunoassay/p24 antigen testing is recommended for screening. Diagnosis of HIV is discussed in Screening and Diagnosis of HIV in Infectious Disease.

The USPSTF recommends that clinicians ask all adults about tobacco use, advise them to stop using tobacco, and provide behavioral intervention and pharmacotherapy for tobacco cessation (grade A) (see Tobacco in Interdisciplinary Medicine).

The USPSTF supports screening all adults for alcohol misuse with validated one- to three-item questionnaires and providing persons engaged in risky or hazardous drinking with brief behavioral counseling interventions to reduce alcohol misuse (grade B). Screening instruments to identify harmful drinking include the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test–Consumption (AUDIT-C) and the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism’s Single Alcohol Screening Question (SASQ). The AUDIT-C is a three-item version of the AUDIT, with similar performance characteristics for identifying alcohol misuse and well suited for use in primary care. The SASQ asks, “How many times in the past year have you had five [four for women] or more drinks in 1 day?” A positive test result, defined as any answer other than “zero,” has a sensitivity and specificity of approximately 80% for unhealthy alcohol use.

The USPSTF recommends asking adults aged 18 years or older about the use of illegal or nonprescribed psychoactive drugs if the physician is also able to offer treatment or refer the patient to treatment. Screening tools include the Drug Abuse Screening Test (DAST-10) and the CAGE questionnaire expanded to include drugs (CAGE-AID).

The USPSTF recommends screening for intimate partner violence in women of reproductive age and referring them to appropriate support services if the screening result is positive (grade B). Available screening tools include the Hurt, Insult, Threaten, Scream (HITS); Ongoing Abuse Screen/Ongoing Violence Assessment Tool (OAS/OVAT); Slapped, Threatened, and Throw (STaT); Humiliation, Afraid, Rape, Kick (HARK); and Woman Abuse Screening Tool (WAST).

The USPSTF states that evidence is insufficient to recommend universal screening for abuse and neglect in older or vulnerable adults (I statement).

The ACP encourages immunization of adults following immunization guidance from trusted sources that develop clinical guidance based on transparent, evidence-based methodologies and safeguards against conflicts of interest. Adult immunization resources and vaccination information to help clinicians increase adult immunization rates in their practices are available from the ACP.

It is important to adhere to recommended vaccine schedules as closely as possible. Administering doses at longer-than-recommended intervals does not appear to reduce immunologic response; however, doses should not be given at shorter-than-recommended intervals. If a vaccination series is interrupted, it can be resumed at the point of interruption. Whenever possible, multiple vaccines should be given simultaneously to improve vaccination rates.

Vaccines can be administered safely to patients with mild acute febrile illness, those who are convalescing from illness, and those who have previously developed low- or moderate-grade fever or local reactions with vaccination. Hospitalized patients should be offered recommended vaccinations based on their eligibility, particularly influenza vaccination and COVID-19 vaccination. When indicated, vaccine administration should take place at the earliest opportunity during hospitalization or at discharge.

Vaccines should be avoided if there is a history of anaphylaxis to the vaccine or the vaccine components. Live virus vaccines should generally be avoided in pregnant patients and in those with immunocompromise.

Influenza revaccination is necessary each year owing to frequent genetic changes in the influenza virus (antigenic drift). Annual vaccination is recommended for all individuals aged 6 months or older. In nonpregnant adults, annual vaccination by the end of October is preferred but can be given at any time during the influenza season; “early” vaccination in July and August is not suggested unless later vaccination might not be possible. In pregnant patients during the third trimester, however, vaccination may be considered soon after the vaccine becomes available.

The live attenuated influenza vaccine can be considered in patients aged 19 to 49 years and may be self-administered; it is contraindicated in pregnancy and immunocompromised patients and should be used with caution in patients with significant medical conditions, including cardiovascular, pulmonary, or liver disease; dialysis-dependent end-stage kidney disease; or diabetes. Pregnant patients and those who are immunocompromised should receive an inactivated or recombinant vaccine.

In the United States, all influenza vaccines are now trivalent. Adults aged 65 years or older should receive the high-dose inactivated influenza vaccine, recombinant influenza vaccine, or adjuvanted inactivated influenza vaccine unless unavailable, in which case any other age-appropriate influenza vaccine can be administered. For immunocompetent adults aged 19 to 64 years, no preferential recommendation is made for one influenza vaccine over another in persons for whom more than one vaccine is appropriate. For adults aged 18 to 64 years who are solid organ transplant recipients and are receiving immunosuppressive therapy, high-dose inactivated or adjuvanted influenza vaccines are acceptable options without a preference over other inactivated and recombinant influenza vaccines.

Persons with a history of egg allergy of any severity can receive any influenza vaccine formulation, and patients do not require additional safety measures for egg allergy alone. Persons with a history of Guillain-Barré syndrome related to previous influenza vaccination (within 6 weeks of vaccination) should generally not receive additional influenza vaccination.

For more information, see the ACP’s video “How to Recommend Flu Vaccines to Your Patients: A Time-Saving, Evidence-Based Approach.”

Primary vaccination against tetanus, diphtheria, and acellular pertussis consists of a five-dose vaccine series administered in childhood. Persons aged 11 to 18 years who have completed the primary series should receive a single dose of the tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine. In adults who did not receive Tdap at or after age 10 years, one dose of Tdap is recommended, followed by Td or Tdap every 10 years.

Unvaccinated adults should receive a three-dose series consisting of Td or Tdap, with at least one Tdap dose (preferably as the first dose). Adults who have received fewer than three doses of the primary series should complete the series with the Td or Tdap vaccine, ensuring that at least one dose of the Tdap vaccine is received.

Pregnant persons should receive at least one dose of the Tdap vaccine between 27 and 36 weeks’ gestation with every pregnancy to prevent neonatal tetanus.

COVID-19 vaccination is effective at preventing serious illness, hospitalization, and death. There are two types of available 2025-2026 COVID-19 vaccines, including mRNA vaccines and a monovalent protein subunit vaccine. These vaccines are FDA approved for all individuals 65 years and older and for adolescents and adults up to age 64 years who are at risk for severe COVID-19 due to an accompanying medical condition. However, multiple professional societies advocate for expanded vaccination coverage. The Infectious Disease Society of America supports broad vaccination beyond the approved indications, and the American Academy of Family Practice recommends that all adults 19 years and older receive a COVID-19 vaccine. Additionally, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists continues to recommend an updated COVID-19 vaccine for all pregnant and lactating persons.

For patients who have had COVID-19 infection, vaccination should be deferred until the individual has recovered from acute illness and has ended isolation. Deferring vaccination for three months is also reasonable.

All immunocompetent adults without evidence of varicella immunity should receive two varicella vaccine doses. Evidence of varicella immunity includes laboratory-confirmed disease or immunity, diagnosis or verification of varicella or zoster by a provider, documentation of age-appropriate varicella vaccination, or U.S. birth before 1980. In pregnant people and health care workers (who are at risk for repeated varicella exposure and spreading the disease to those at high risk for severe disease), U.S. birth before 1980 is not considered sufficient evidence of immunity. These patient groups must meet the other criteria. Although varicella vaccination is contraindicated in patients with severe immunosuppression, it can be considered on the basis of shared clinical decision making in patients with HIV infection and a CD4 percentage of 15% or greater and a CD4 cell count of 200 cells/µL or greater. Varicella vaccine is contraindicated during pregnancy. Aspirin should be avoided for 6 weeks after varicella vaccination because of the risk for Reye syndrome.

All adults aged 50 years or older should receive the recombinant (inactivated) herpes zoster vaccine to reduce the incidence of zoster and postherpetic neuralgia. The recombinant vaccine is also indicated in patients aged 19 years or older at increased risk for zoster because of immunosuppression or immunodeficiency secondary to disease or therapy. It is administered intramuscularly in two doses, with an interval of 2 to 6 months between doses. Vaccination is recommended regardless of previous zoster infection or vaccination with the live vaccine. The safety of the vaccines in pregnant individuals has not been determined. Pregnant patients may consider deferring administration until after pregnancy.

Pneumococcal vaccination is recommended in all adults aged 50 years or older and in adults aged 19 to 49 years with certain high-risk conditions [Table: Table: Indications for Pneumococcal Vaccination]

. Four pneumococcal vaccines are available: the 21-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV21), the 20-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV20), the 15-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV15), and the 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23).

Patients aged 50 years and older who have not previously received a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine or whose vaccination history is unknown should receive PCV20 alone, PCV21 alone, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23 at least 1 year later. Adults aged 19 to 49 years with high-risk conditions or other risk factors who require vaccination and have not received a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine should receive PCV20, PCV21, or the combination of PCV15 and PPSV23. In patients with immunocompromising conditions, a cochlear implant, or cerebrospinal fluid leak, the interval between PCV15 and PPSV23 may be shortened to a minimum of 8 weeks.

Eligible patients who previously received only PPSV23 should receive PCV20, PCV21, or PCV15 at least 1 year after the dose of PPSV23.

In patients who previously received only PCV13, one dose of PCV20 or PCV21 should be administered at least 1 year after the PCV13 dose.

In patients aged 50 years and older who previously received PCV13 at any age and PPSV23 before age 65 years, PCV20 or PCV21 should be administered at least 5 years after the last dose. If a patient received PCV13 and PPSV23 but PPSV23 was given at age 65 years or older, then shared decision making should be used to determine whether to administer PCV20 or PCV21 at least 5 years after the last vaccine dose.

For patients younger than 50 years in whom pneumococcal vaccination is indicated and who have previously received PCV13 and one or more doses of PPSV23, the recommended schedules are available at the CDC Web site.

HPV vaccination prevents persistent HPV infection, which may lead to cervical, anogenital, and nasopharyngeal cancers. A nine-valent HPV vaccine is approved for use in both females and males. Patients should receive a two-dose vaccine series at age 11 or 12 years, or until the age of 15 years if not given previously. Patients aged 15 to 26 years should receive a three-dose series. In unvaccinated patients aged 27 to 45 years, vaccination may be considered on the basis of risk, using a shared decision-making process. Vaccination is not recommended during pregnancy, although no harmful effects have been noted when the vaccine was inadvertently given to pregnant women. Pregnancy testing is not necessary before vaccination.

All U.S. adults born before 1957 are considered immune to measles and mumps. Adults born in 1957 or later without documented evidence of receiving one or more doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine or laboratory-confirmed immunity against all three diseases should receive at least one MMR dose. A second MMR dose should be administered to postsecondary students, household or close personal contacts of immunocompromised persons, and international travelers.

Health care workers should be considered separately. Those born in or after 1957 who lack evidence of immunity to measles, mumps, or rubella should receive a two-dose MMR series, with at least 4 weeks between doses, for protection against measles or mumps; at least a single dose should be administered for rubella immunity. The same administration schedule should be considered in health care workers born before 1957.

In patients of reproductive age, rubella immunity should be determined and nonpregnant patients who lack immunity should be vaccinated. Pregnant patients who lack immunity should be vaccinated at the time of delivery before leaving the hospital or at the time of pregnancy termination.

The MMR vaccine is a live virus vaccine and should not be administered to immunocompromised or pregnant individuals.

Meningococcal vaccines used in the adult population include the quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MenACWY), which protects against serogroups A, C, W, and Y; the meningococcal group B (MenB) vaccines, which protect against serogroup B disease; and the pentavalent vaccines, which protect against serogroups A, B, C, W, and Y.

MenACWY is recommended in adolescents. If the initial dose was administered at age 11 to 12 years (preferred), a booster dose is administered at age 16 years; if the initial dose was administered at age 13 to 15 years, a booster dose is administered at 16 to 18 years. If the first dose is administered after age 16 years, a booster dose is not required. First-year college students living in residence halls who did not previously receive MenACWY at age 16 years or older should receive one dose of the vaccine. MenACWY vaccines are interchangeable.

Routine two-dose series of MenB can be administered at age 16 to 23 years on the basis of shared clinical decision making. A booster dose is not recommended unless the patient develops increased risk for meningococcal disease. MenB vaccines are not interchangeable, and dosing schedules differ.

Meningococcal vaccination recommendations for adults at increased risk are summarized in [Table: Table: Indications for Meningococcal Vaccination]

.

If both the quadrivalent and MenB vaccines would be given on the same day, adults may receive a single dose of the pentavalent MenACWY–TT/MenB–FHbp vaccine as an alternative. Adults at average risk who received MenACWY–TT/MenB–FHbp for their first dose of MenB should receive MenB–FHbp for their second dose. For adults at higher risk of meningococcal disease, MenACWY–TT/MenB–FHbp may be used for additional MenACWY and MenB doses (including booster doses) if both vaccines would be given on the same day and if at least 6 months have passed since the previous MenACWY–TT/MenB–FHbp dose.

Vaccination against hepatitis A is recommended for all children. In addition, vaccination against hepatitis A is recommended for all persons who desire vaccination and for persons who are at increased risk for infection or complications of infection, including pregnant patients at risk. Persons at increased risk include those who work in or travel to endemic areas, men who have sex with men, individuals with chronic liver disease or HIV infection, those who use injection or noninjection nonprescribed substances, persons experiencing homelessness, persons who conduct hepatitis A–related research, household or close contacts of children adopted from endemic areas, and those who work in settings of possible exposure (group homes, nonresidential day care facilities for developmentally disabled persons, and health care programs serving individuals who use injection or noninjection drugs). Vaccination is also recommended for at-risk individuals during hepatitis A outbreaks. Immunization can be provided as a two-dose series of single-antigen hepatitis A vaccine or a three-dose series of combination hepatitis A and B vaccine.

Hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for all adults aged 19 to 59 years. Vaccination should also be administered to patients aged 60 years and older who are considered to be at high risk for infection ( [Table: Table: Populations With a Risk-Based Indication for HBV Vaccination]

) and can be offered to patients aged 60 years and older who desire vaccination. The traditional hepatitis B vaccination series is a three-dose series, with doses administered at 0, 1, and 6 months. A vaccine with a novel adjuvant requires only two doses administered at least 4 weeks apart.

Checking serum antibodies is not typically recommended after routine vaccination but is indicated in persons in whom subsequent clinical management is dependent on knowledge of serologic response (patients receiving long-term hemodialysis, persons living with HIV, health care and public safety workers, and needle-sharing partners of persons who are positive for HBsAg).

All adults aged 75 years and older and adults aged 60 to 74 years who are at increased risk for severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) disease should receive a single dose of the RSV vaccine. Conditions that increase the risk for severe RSV-associated disease include the following:

  • Chronic lung disease
  • Cardiovascular disease (not including isolated hypertension)
  • End-stage kidney disease
  • Chronic liver disease (e.g., cirrhosis)
  • Immunocompromising conditions
  • Neurologic and neuromuscular disorders causing impaired airway clearance or respiratory weakness
  • Chronic hematologic conditions
  • BMI of 40 or greater
  • Diabetes mellitus with complications or requiring insulin or sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor therapy
  • Residence in a nursing home
  • Other chronic condition or risk factor that might increase the risk for severe RSV disease

Pregnant persons should receive the RSV vaccine at 32 to 36 weeks’ gestation from September to January in most of the continental United States to prevent RSV-associated lower respiratory tract infections in infants. RSV vaccine administration in other geographic areas may require alternate timing depending on RSV seasonality. Currently, there are no recommendations for revaccination with subsequent pregnancies.

Vaccination against the mpox virus is recommended for persons who are at risk for infection using a two-dose vaccine series, with doses separated by 28 days. The recommended formulation is a live, nonreplicating combined smallpox/mpox vaccine that can safely be administered to immunocompromised individuals. Persons who are considered to be at risk for mpox infection and who should be vaccinated include gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men or a person who has sex with gay, bisexual, or other men who have sex with men who, in the past 6 months, have met one of the following criteria: (1) had a new diagnosis of at least one STI, (2) had more than one sexual partner, (3) engaged in sex in a commercial sex venue, or (4) engaged in sex in association with a large public event in a geographic area where mpox transmission is occurring. Additionally, persons who are sexual partners to anyone who has these risk factors or who anticipate meeting one of these criteria should also be vaccinated.

Adults known or suspected to be unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated against polio should complete the three-dose inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) series. Most adults born and raised in the United States can assume that they are immune to polio even if they do not possess written vaccination records, unless they have specific reason to believe otherwise. Adults who are at increased risk for exposure to poliovirus and who have completed the primary series may receive a one-time IPV booster dose. Individuals considered at increased risk include travelers to countries where polio is endemic or epidemic, health care and laboratory workers who handle specimens that might contain polioviruses, health care workers and caregivers who have close contact with patients in a community with a polio outbreak, and other individuals deemed to be at increased risk for exposure due to an outbreak.

In addition to considerations discussed in the previous section regarding hepatitis B, measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella, health care workers are at increased risk for acquiring and transmitting influenza, COVID-19, and pertussis. All health care workers, regardless of patient contact, should receive the influenza vaccine annually. In addition, all health care workers who have not previously received the Tdap vaccine should receive one dose, regardless of when they last received the Td vaccine.

Patients with anatomic or functional asplenia are at increased risk for infection from encapsulated organisms, including meningococcus (see [Table: Table: Indications for Meningococcal Vaccination]

), pneumococcus (see [Table: Table: Indications for Pneumococcal Vaccination]

), and Haemophilus influenzae type B, and should be appropriately vaccinated. Patients who have undergone hematopoietic stem cell transplantation should also receive the H. influenzae type B vaccine.

Vaccination recommendations for international travelers vary depending on the destination. For more information on vaccination in travelers, see Introduction in Infectious Disease.

Because of its low cost and efficacy in preventing cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events, aspirin has been considered for primary prevention of vascular disease. In 2018, however, three large trials, ASCEND, ARRIVE, and ASPREE, showed that primary prevention with aspirin led to no reduction in nonfatal myocardial infarction or mortality. In 2019, a meta-analysis of the use of aspirin for primary prevention was updated; it included more than 164,000 patients and showed no benefit in any mortality end point. Reductions in nonfatal myocardial infarction (relative risk [RR], 0.82; 95% CI, 0.72-0.94) and ischemic stroke (RR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.79-0.95) were offset by a significant increase in bleeding events, including major bleeding (RR, 1.5; 95% CI, 1.33-1.69), intracranial bleeding (RR, 1.32; 95% CI, 1.12-1.55), and major gastrointestinal bleeding (RR, 1.52; 95% CI, 1.34-1.73). Subsequently, the ACC and AHA recommended that aspirin be used infrequently in the routine primary prevention of ASCVD because of lack of net benefit; specifically, low-dose aspirin may be considered for primary prevention of ASCVD in adults aged 40 to 70 years who are at higher ASCVD risk but not at increased bleeding risk. Similarly, the ADA reaffirmed its recommendations that low-dose aspirin may be considered in patients aged 50 years or older who have diabetes and an increased cardiovascular risk but no increased risk for bleeding.

In 2022, the USPSTF updated its recommendation on the use of low-dose aspirin for the primary prevention of ASCVD. The USPSTF concluded with moderate certainty that low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10-year ASCVD risk of at least 10% has a small net benefit. The decision regarding aspirin as primary prevention in this population should be individualized, and patients who are not at increased risk for bleeding and are willing to take low-dose aspirin on a daily basis are more likely to benefit. The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin should be informed by the totality of ASCVD risk and bleeding risk as well as patient values and preferences. Factors that increase bleeding risk include concurrent anticoagulant or NSAID use, history of gastrointestinal ulcer, upper gastrointestinal pain, uncontrolled hypertension, male sex, and increasing age.

The USPSTF also concluded that implementing low-dose aspirin for the prevention of cardiovascular disease in adults 60 years of age and older has no net benefit and recommends against low-dose aspirin for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease in these patients (grade D). After age 70 years, the benefit of aspirin decreases and bleeding risks are higher; thus, the ACC, AHA, and ADA do not recommend aspirin for primary prevention in this age group.

There is some evidence for the use of aspirin in cancer prevention, with one trial showing a 34% to 40% reduction in colorectal cancer mortality with at least 5 to 10 years of aspirin therapy. The benefit is not apparent until 10 to 20 years after initiation of aspirin; no mortality benefit was observed in the first 10 years of follow-up.

The USPSTF also recommends low-dose aspirin for primary prevention of preeclampsia in pregnant patients at high risk (see Preeclampsia in Nephrology).

Healthy lifestyle counseling is directed at the leading preventable causes of death. Tobacco and obesity contribute significantly to the top two leading causes of death, heart disease and cancer, which account for almost 50% of all deaths in the United States. Other preventable causes of death include alcohol and drug use, infectious diseases, toxins, accidents, and firearms.

Tobacco use remains the number one cause of preventable disease, disability, and death in the United States; therefore, tobacco cessation is a high-priority intervention from a health and cost-effectiveness standpoint. Patients who smoke should be offered behavioral counseling and pharmacologic therapy if appropriate. For more information, see Tobacco in Interdisciplinary Medicine and Motivational Interviewing in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

All patients who have overweight or obesity should undergo counseling on the benefits of a healthy weight, regular exercise, and a healthy diet (see Behavioral Counseling in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Injury prevention, including seat belt use, use of safety helmets for motorcycles and bicycles, and home safety measures, should be emphasized. Patients should be counseled to use smoke alarms and carbon monoxide detectors in the home and to set water heaters to lower than 49 °C (120 °F) in households with infants or young children (see [Table: Table: Components of the History]

).

The CDC’s Healthy People 2030 initiative envisions “a society in which all people can achieve their full potential for health and well-being across the lifespan.” Recognizing that social determinants of health, systemic racism, and systemic bias contribute to health inequities, an area of priority for Healthy People 2030 is to advance health equity through societal efforts to increase health literacy and address historical and contemporary injustices and social determinants of health. The CDC plans to achieve this goal by identifying core objectives and monitoring how those objectives are being met across different population groups. In particular, the focus is on Leading Health Indicators, which are a subset of high-priority objectives that have an impact on major causes of death and disease in the United States ( [Table: Table: Leading Health Indicators for Healthy People 2030]

).

Sleep and stress reduction are also components of a healthy lifestyle. The AHA and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommend that adults sleep at least 7 hours per night for optimal health. Poor or inadequate sleep is associated with an increased risk for obesity, diabetes, heart disease, cancer, stroke, dementia, and death. Developing effective strategies for stress reduction is an important component of wellness and resilience. Meditation, mindfulness-based stress reduction, exercise, spending time in nature, strong personal relationships, volunteering, community involvement, cultivating hobbies, and spiritual activities are all associated with better health outcomes. Loneliness and social isolation have been associated with a 29% increase in coronary heart disease and a 32% increase in stroke.

Climate change may have several deleterious effects on human health, including higher rates of respiratory and heat-related illness, skin cancer, increased prevalence of vector-borne (malaria, chikungunya virus, dengue fever) and waterborne (cholera) diseases, food and water insecurity, and malnutrition. The ACP advises that physicians become educated about climate change, its effect on human health, and how to respond to future challenges.

Behavioral counseling is an integral part of helping patients optimize their health and habits. Patients look to their physicians as sources of preventive health information and for behavioral recommendations for diet, exercise, and substance use.

The USPSTF recommends behavioral counseling interventions to promote a healthy diet and physical activity for adults aged 18 years and older with cardiovascular risk factors, such as hypertension or elevated blood pressure, dyslipidemia, metabolic syndrome, or a 10-year ASCVD risk of 7.5% or higher (grade B). Behavioral counseling interventions are associated with a 20% reduction in cardiovascular events. For adults aged 18 years and older without cardiovascular disease risk factors, the USPSTF recommends an individualized approach to offering behavioral counseling interventions to promote a healthy diet and physical activity, owing to smaller benefits (grade C). The USPSTF also recommends behavioral counseling for patients who use tobacco or who engage in unhealthy alcohol use (see Screening for Substance Use Disorders in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Assessing the patient’s readiness to change their behavior may enhance the success of counseling, as individuals who are interested and ready to make behavioral changes are most likely to benefit from behavioral counseling. Behavioral counseling should consider patient goals and preferences; activity level and ability; overall health status; and environmental factors such as availability of grocery stores, parks, and sidewalks as well as safety, traffic, and crime and pollution levels. Common counseling techniques include motivational interviewing (see Motivational Interviewing in Foundations of Clinical Practice) and the “5 A’s” model for tobacco use (Ask the patient about tobacco use; Advise the patient to quit through clear, personalized messages; Assess the patient’s willingness to quit; Assist the patient with their attempt to quit; and Arrange for follow-up and support).

Behavioral counseling does not need to be complex or time consuming. Studies have shown that patients who were informed of having overweight by their physicians were more likely to report significant weight loss. Advice from clinicians to stop smoking nearly doubles cessation rates. Interventions can be delivered individually or in a group, in-person or remotely, and by a wide range of specially trained professionals.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture and U.S. Department of Health and Human Services published the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020-2025, which outlines healthy dietary patterns at every life stage. The dietary guidelines emphasize obtaining most (approximately 85%) of one’s calories from nutrient-dense foods while monitoring portion sizes to stay within calorie limits. Nutrient-dense foods provide vitamins, minerals, and other health-promoting components and have little or no added sugars (<10% of daily calories), saturated fat (<10% of daily calories), or sodium (<2300 mg/d). These foods consist of vegetables of all types, fruits (especially whole fruit), whole grains, seafood, unsalted nuts and seeds, fat-free and low-fat dairy products, and lean meats and poultry. These dietary patterns are compatible with the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) and Mediterranean diets, which are consistently associated with lower all-cause mortality. Patients should be encouraged to customize nutrient-dense food and beverage choices to reflect personal preferences, cultural traditions, and budgetary considerations.

Adults of legal drinking age should be advised to limit consumption of alcohol to no more than one drink (equivalence of 340 g [12 oz] of beer, 142 g [5 oz] of wine, or 43 g [1.5] oz of 80-proof liquor) per day for women and two drinks per day for men. Drinking less is better for health, and alcohol use should not be encouraged because of the risk for accidents, injuries, liver disease, and cancer as well as the potential for alcohol dependency.

Increased physical activity decreases the risk for most chronic diseases and cancer. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans recommend that adults perform at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week. In addition to aerobic activity, muscle-strengthening activities should be performed at least 2 days per week. However, there is no lower threshold to the benefit of physical activity; as little as 15 to 20 minutes per week of vigorous or 75 minutes per week of moderate-intensity physical activity (equivalent to approximately 11 minutes per day) has been shown to reduce mortality and cardiovascular disease and cancer risk.

Any physical activity is better than none, and adults should be encouraged to move more and sit less. Physical activity does not have to take the form of formal exercise; patients should be encouraged to discover ways to naturally and habitually incorporate physical activity into their daily lives. Moreover, exercise does not need to be spread throughout the week to be beneficial. Adults who achieve more than 50% of the 150 minutes per week goal on only 1 to 2 days per week (e.g., exercising only on weekends) have a reduced risk for cardiovascular outcomes that is similar to adults who spread their exercise throughout the week. Counseling by providers to increase physical activity is effective and can be enhanced with the use of apps, pedometers, accelerometers, telemonitoring, and modeling being physically active themselves.

Medication adherence is defined as the degree to which a patient adheres to the dosage and interval of their prescribed pharmacologic regimen. Nonadherence, typically defined as failure to take at least 80% of a prescribed medication regimen, has been associated with increased health care use, worse health outcomes, and increased costs. An estimated 20% to 30% of prescriptions are never filled, and an estimated 50% of patients with chronic medical conditions are nonadherent with their prescribed regimen.

Medication adherence is a complex behavior that is influenced by the patient, system, and provider. Patient-related and societal factors that may have a significant impact on medication adherence include a high burden of disease with complex medication regimens; financial stressors; distrust of clinicians and health care institutions; medication side effects; and lack of social support, including transportation. The factors most strongly associated with medication adherence include strong provider-patient relationships and a patient’s understanding of their medical conditions.

Physicians should inquire at each visit about medication adherence in a nonjudgmental manner and avoid negative comments if nonadherence is uncovered. Patient self-report may overestimate adherence by 200%, and physicians should attempt to clearly quantify the degree of adherence. Patients should be encouraged to bring their medications to appointments. If possible, family members should be engaged, and dispensing history from the pharmacy should be reviewed. For some patients, a visiting nurse may be needed to complete home visits to further assess adherence and reasons for nonadherence and to promote adherence.

Various methods exist to increase adherence, and multimodal approaches are more likely to be successful. Patients should be screened for unmet basic needs (food, housing, transportation) because spending less on basic needs to pay for chronic disease management is associated with poorer health outcomes; those with unmet basic needs should be referred to appropriate social programs. Clinicians should clearly discuss the purpose and value of each medication that is prescribed. Patient education (online resources, handouts) is low-cost and widely available. Simplifying a medication regimen (such as prescribing combination or extended-release pills or implementing a schedule to take pills simultaneously) is a feasible method for patients and may result in a patient taking fewer pills. However, combination or extended-release pills may be more expensive. The use of cost incentives (such as selecting medications with lowest copays or available discounts) should also be considered. Patient reminders, such as text or voice alerts, can be programmed into smartphones or other devices. Pill boxes may also be used. Consultation with a clinical pharmacist is a team-based approach that facilitates disease co-management but may not be available at all institutions. Cognitive behavioral therapy in the form of self-management strategies and motivational interviewing can also promote adherence.

Dietary supplements, including vitamins, minerals, botanicals, herbals, metabolites, and amino acids, are categorized as foods by the FDA. Therefore, manufacturers are not required to demonstrate efficacy or safety of their products unless the supplement includes ingredients that were introduced after 1994. Manufacturers are not allowed to make specific medical claims; however, the product’s intended effect on body structure or function may be described.

Given the prevalence of use and potential for harm, physicians should make inquiring about supplement use a routine component of the medication history. Patients take dietary supplements for various reasons, such as to prevent and treat illness, manage symptoms, and enhance health. In the United States, approximately 50% of adults report using vitamins or dietary supplements. Although reports show that multivitamins are the most commonly used supplement, persons eating a well-balanced diet are unlikely to benefit from a multivitamin. Multivitamins should not be used in the absence of a specific indication and are not effective in compensating for a poor diet. The USPSTF recommends against the use of β-carotene or vitamin E supplements for the prevention of cardiovascular disease or cancer and has concluded that the current evidence is insufficient to assess the use of multivitamins for the prevention of cardiovascular disease or cancer.

There are special populations, however, for which specific vitamin or supplement use is recommended. Women of reproductive age are advised to take 0.4 to 0.8 mg (400-800 µg) of folic acid daily to prevent fetal neural tube defects. Vegans, older adults, and persons taking proton pump inhibitors or metformin may consider vitamin B~12 supplementation to address dietary deficiency or malabsorption issues. Calcium and/or vitamin D may also be considered for older adults or individuals with suboptimal bone health. Calcium supplementation may increase the risk for cardiovascular disease and kidney stones; thus, eating a calcium-rich diet may be a preferable means of ensuring adequate intake. Persons with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) can take a specific formulation of vitamins, zinc, and copper to slow AMD progression. Omega-3 fatty acids in fish oils may help hypertriglyceridemia and improve cardiovascular health. Melatonin may be useful for jetlag. Probiotics may be helpful for antibiotic-associated diarrhea, Clostridioides difficile infection, ulcerative colitis, and periodontal disease.

Intravenous infusions of saline and electrolytes and high-dose vitamins are increasing in popularity. Vaping of vitamins has also been marketed to deliver higher concentrations of vitamins to the body. None of these methods has evidence supporting their use, and they carry many potential risks.

In addition to questionable efficacy, supplement use is associated with risk for direct and indirect harms ( [Table: Table: Common Herbal Supplements]

). Direct harms include side effects; interactions with other drugs; and harms related to inclusion of unadvertised additives, compounds, or toxins. Vitamin E, fish oil, and several herbal supplements may interact with anticoagulant or antiplatelet medications, potentially increasing the risk for bleeding or inadequate anticoagulation. Individuals who smoke should avoid β-carotene because evidence has linked β-carotene with increased risk for lung cancer. Pregnant persons should avoid excessive vitamin A because it has been linked to birth defects. Antioxidant supplements, such as vitamins C and E, may reduce the effectiveness of chemotherapy. Vitamin K, which is a common ingredient in several vitamin injections, may decrease the effectiveness of warfarin. Biotin may interfere with serum troponin and thyroid function testing. Harms may also occur indirectly when herbal supplement use replaces or delays standard treatments.

Informing patients of potential side effects of supplement use is important. The National Institutes of Health’s MedlinePlus directory of herbs and supplements and the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Web site are useful resources.
