Perioperative Medicine

Perioperative medicine encompasses risk assessment and optimization of comorbid conditions before surgery, intraoperative management, and postoperative care. The internal medicine physician’s role is to determine operative risk; communicate this information to patients, surgeons, and anesthesiologists; and recommend strategies to mitigate this risk. Decisions regarding the surgical approach and type of anesthesia are best deferred to the surgeon and anesthesiologist. Hospitalists are commonly involved in the postoperative management and/or comanagement of surgical patients (see Consultation and Comanagement in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Internal medicine physicians can also assist with setting patient and family expectations in the perioperative period and ensuring that expected outcomes align with their goals.

All preoperative laboratory testing should be tailored to the nature of the surgery, known comorbid conditions, and findings from the history or physical examination ( [Table: Table: Selected Indications for Preoperative Laboratory Testing]

). Routine laboratory panels are not recommended because they rarely guide management. All preoperative testing is discouraged for patients undergoing ambulatory or low-risk surgery (e.g., cataract, hernia repair) because there is minimal evidence of its usefulness.

Perioperative medication management begins with eliciting a comprehensive medication history, including herbal preparations, supplements, and over-the-counter medications. Medication reconciliation should be performed to confirm which medications and doses patients are taking, rectify any discrepancies in the electronic medical record, and prevent medication errors or omission or commission (see Medication Reconciliation in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

High-quality evidence to guide perioperative medication management is lacking. Recommendations are largely derived from theoretical drug interactions and expert consensus. Although most medications are tolerated throughout the perioperative period and may be continued, there are some important exceptions. [Table: Table: Perioperative Medication Management]

provides recommendations for medications with potential surgery-related risk. Patients, surgeons, and inpatient clinicians should be given clear instructions on which medications to withhold preoperatively and guidance for when to safely resume taking them. For antithrombotic management, collaboration with surgery, cardiology, anesthesiology, neurology, and hematology is critical.

The most common postoperative complications are surgical site infection, bleeding, pneumonia, sepsis, cardiovascular events, deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism, ileus, delirium, acute kidney injury, urinary retention, and urinary tract infection. Many strategies are used to reduce postoperative complications. In some settings, multimodal, evidence-based interventions have been standardized and bundled with preoperative and intraoperative protocols aimed at improving overall outcomes. These initiatives have been associated with reduced length of hospital stay, decreased complications, and improved functional recovery.

Performing preoperative risk stratification in all patients can inform the degree of monitoring necessary for cardiac, pulmonary, kidney, or neurologic dysfunction. Early detection of concerning changes in clinical status is the most effective way to prevent further decline. Laboratory monitoring should be driven by comorbid conditions, clinical status, and surgery type (e.g., monitoring serum creatinine levels in patients with chronic kidney disease and large intraoperative fluid shifts). Reappraisal of preoperative medications helps confirm optimal timing of resumption of antithrombotic medications, antihypertensives, diabetes medications, and other medications that may have been paused or had dose reductions preoperatively or intraoperatively.

Urinary retention is a common postoperative complication. Risk factors include

  • Type of surgery (anorectal surgery, hernia repair, joint arthroplasty)
  • Longer surgery
  • Type of anesthesia
  • Use of opioids and anticholinergic agents
  • Advanced age
  • Constipation
  • History of urinary retention
  • Neurologic disease

Reversible causes of postoperative urinary retention, including use of medications such as opioids, should be addressed. In patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia, α~2-blockers should be continued, whereas medications with associated anticholinergic effects, such as oxybutynin, should be withheld. Early removal of indwelling catheters and voiding trials are recommended, with ongoing close monitoring of urine output. In patients with low urine output after catheter removal, bladder ultrasonography should be performed to evaluate for urinary retention. Clean intermittent catheterization is indicated if a voiding trial is unsuccessful (postvoid residual >300-400 mL).

Postoperative ileus (POI) is relatively common after surgery. Abdominal distention and pain, nausea and vomiting, and inability to flatulate are hallmarks of POI. Risk factors for POI include abdominal and pelvic surgery; open surgical technique; and presence of other postoperative complications, such as pneumonia. Minimally invasive surgical approaches, multimodal analgesia techniques, prophylactic bowel regimens, and early ambulation may help prevent POI. Treatment consists of minimization of opioid use, hydration, bowel rest, electrolyte repletion, postoperative ambulation, and use of chewing gum. If POI is prolonged (lasting longer than 3-5 days), mechanical bowel obstruction should be considered.

Postoperative nausea and vomiting are common events that result in significant patient distress. Risk factors include use of general anesthesia, use of opioids, female sex, and younger age. Management includes ensuring adequate postoperative hydration, minimizing the use of opioids, and providing pharmacologic antiemetic therapy.

The occurrence of new perioperative atrial fibrillation, even if transient, is associated with increased short- and long-term mortality and incidence of stroke. When perioperative atrial fibrillation occurs, potential triggers should be treated and follow-up is indicated, including echocardiography, atrial fibrillation surveillance, and consideration of rate/rhythm control and anticoagulation in at-risk patients (see Atrial Fibrillation in Cardiovascular Medicine).

The preoperative cardiac evaluation is intended to assess patient risks for a major adverse cardiac event (MACE), such as ischemia, cardiac arrest, heart failure, and dysrhythmias, both during and after surgery. The approach to risk stratification recommended by the American Heart Association (AHA)/American College of Cardiology (ACC)/Multisociety perioperative guideline for patients undergoing noncardiac surgery is shown in

.

Risk calculators can be used to determine the risk for perioperative MACE. The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) ( [Table: Table: Revised Cardiac Risk Index and Major Cardiac Complications]

), the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program surgical risk calculator, and the Gupta Perioperative Risk for Myocardial Infarction or Cardiac Arrest calculator incorporate patient- and surgery-specific risk factors. Each calculator varies regarding the population used for validation and overall performance ( [Table: Table: Comparison of Tools for Estimating MACE Risk]

).

When assessing risk, patients should also be assessed for the presence of risk modifiers, including:

  • Severe valvular disease
  • Severe pulmonary hypertension
  • Elevated-risk congenital heart disease
  • Ischemic heart disease, including prior revascularization
  • Recent stroke
  • Presence of a cardiovascular implantable electronic device (pacemaker or implantable cardioverter-defibrillator)
  • Frailty

Patients with low calculated cardiovascular risk (<1% risk for perioperative MACE) and no risk modifiers may proceed to surgery without further assessment of functional capacity, whereas patients with elevated risk (≥1% risk for perioperative MACE) or risk modifiers should have functional capacity assessed. Metabolic equivalents (METs) represent a patient’s functional capacity based on the intensity of activity the patient can perform. The Duke Activity Status Index score ( [Table: Table: Duke Activity Status Index (DASI) Score Questionnaire]

) is a standardized and accurate means of estimating exercise capacity; an objective assessment of functional capacity is necessary, as data from the METS trial showed that clinician estimates of exercise capacity without use of a standardized tool do not correlate with actual patient performance on cardiopulmonary exercise testing or with postoperative cardiac outcomes. According to the AHA/ACC guideline, if functional capacity exceeds a DASI score of 34 or 4 METs, the asymptomatic patient may proceed to surgery without further testing. In patients with poor or unknown functional capacity, preoperative biomarkers, including B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), N-terminal pro-BNP, and cardiac troponin, may be used to accompany perioperative risk assessment in patients with known cardiovascular disease, aged 65 years or older, or aged 45 years or older with symptoms suggestive of cardiovascular disease; patients with normal biomarker levels can proceed to surgery, as these biomarkers have excellent negative predictive value for perioperative cardiac complications.

ECG rarely alters preoperative decision making but may provide a useful baseline to guide postoperative management in the event of complications. Preoperative ECG is reasonable in patients with known cardiovascular disease, arrhythmia, or structural heart disease or in those with symptoms of cardiovascular disease who are undergoing elevated-risk surgeries. Preoperative ECG also may be considered for asymptomatic patients undergoing elevated-risk procedures, but it is not indicated for those undergoing low-risk procedures.

Indications for preoperative echocardiography include the following:

  • A newly detected murmur
  • Dyspnea with suspected cardiac cause (e.g., elevated BNP level)
  • Examination findings suggestive of new heart failure or known heart failure with change in clinical status
  • Suspected new or worsening left ventricular dysfunction
  • Known or suspected moderate to severe valvular stenosis or regurgitation without echocardiographic assessment in the past year or with a change in clinical status

Preoperative stress testing may be considered in selected patients anticipating elevated-risk surgery who have poor or unknown functional capacity and an elevated calculated risk for perioperative events. However, coronary revascularization in stable patients before noncardiac surgery is of uncertain benefit.

Patients with coronary artery disease should not undergo routine coronary angiography or revascularization before surgery. These procedures should be reserved for patients with recognized indications based on clinical practice guidelines. AHA/ACC guidelines recommend that elective surgery be delayed 14 days after balloon angioplasty, 30 days after bare metal stent implantation, 6 months after drug-eluting stent placement for chronic coronary disease, and 12 months after drug-eluting stent placement for an acute coronary syndrome. However, if the risk of surgical delay outweighs the risk for ischemia and stent thrombosis, surgery may be considered 90 days after drug-eluting stent placement. Ideally, one antiplatelet medication (typically aspirin) would be continued through the perioperative period. Patients with an acute coronary syndrome not managed with coronary intervention are still at elevated risk for postoperative MACE, and elective surgery should be delayed for at least 60 days after the event.

Patients taking β-blockers, statins, and most antihypertensive medications (with the possible exceptions of diuretics and ACE inhibitors) should continue these medications perioperatively unless prohibited by hypotension (see [Table: Table: Perioperative Medication Management]

). Preoperative β-blockers may be beneficial for patients with increased cardiovascular risk and an independent, nonsurgical indication for β-blockade (e.g., coronary artery disease, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction). Statin therapy is recommended in patients undergoing vascular surgery or who have a long-term indication for a statin (e.g., known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or elevated 10-year risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease). Postoperative β-blocker administration should be guided by clinical circumstances, but dose reduction is preferred to discontinuation if hypotension develops. The AHA/ACC guideline recommends holding ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers 24 hours before surgery only in selected patients with well-controlled hypertension who are undergoing elevated-risk surgery, whereas the European Society of Cardiology recommends that providers consider holding these agents on the day of noncardiac surgery in all patients without heart failure to prevent perioperative hypotension.

The AHA/ACC perioperative guideline does not recommend routine postoperative ECG in asymptomatic patients. However, postoperative myocardial injury may be asymptomatic or present atypically. Troponin surveillance with measurements at 24 and 48 hours may be considered in patients with a history of cardiovascular disease, patients with cardiovascular disease symptoms, or patients aged 65 years or older with cardiovascular risk factors who are undergoing elevated-risk surgery. Patients with troponin elevations should be further evaluated for acute coronary syndromes and, if present, treated per guideline-directed management. The best way to manage patients with myocardial injury (i.e., troponin elevation without meeting the criteria for myocardial infarction) is unclear; however, antithrombotic therapy may be considered. Additionally, these patients should be evaluated for optimization of cardiovascular risk factors.

Medical management of decompensated heart failure should be optimized before surgery (see Acute Decompensated Heart Failure in Cardiovascular Medicine). Patients treated with sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors should stop these medications 3 to 4 days before surgery to reduce the risk for euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis. See [Table: Table: Perioperative Medication Management]

for perioperative management of other cardiovascular medications.

Risk management strategies for patients with a cardiac arrhythmia who are undergoing surgery include continuation of antiarrhythmic medications and, for some patients, continuous cardiac monitoring.

Patients with atrial fibrillation are at risk for rapid ventricular rate due to surgical stress, fluid shifts, and postoperative pain. Treating triggers (e.g., anemia, sepsis), maintaining euvolemia, optimizing pain management, and continuing baseline rate control medications can reduce this risk. Perioperative atrial fibrillation increases the risk for death and the duration of hospitalization and may warrant further evaluation, rate/rhythm control, and anticoagulation (see Atrial Fibrillation in Cardiovascular Medicine).

A cardiologist should be consulted for patients with a pacemaker or implantable cardioverter-defibrillator who are undergoing surgery to ensure normal device function and provide recommendations for perioperative management of the device. Patients in whom a device has been deactivated for surgery should undergo continuous cardiac monitoring until the device is reprogrammed.

The AHA/ACC guideline states that proceeding with low-risk noncardiac surgery in patients with severe asymptomatic aortic stenosis and normal left ventricular function may be reasonable. Similarly, asymptomatic patients with severe mitral regurgitation or aortic regurgitation, normal left ventricular function, and pulmonary artery pressure less than 50 mm Hg (in the setting of mitral regurgitation) may proceed with surgery. However, these patients are at higher risk for cardiovascular complications, necessitating awareness among surgical teams. Avoiding large volume shifts and minimizing hypotension and tachycardia are critical. Valvular intervention should be performed before elective noncardiac surgery in patients who are candidates for valvular intervention owing to symptoms or severity of disease.

Patients with pulmonary hypertension undergoing noncardiac surgery have higher rates of mortality and morbidity, including nonfatal myocardial ischemia, venous thromboembolism (VTE), cardiogenic shock, and dysrhythmias. Preoperative evaluation by a pulmonary hypertension specialist is advised for patients with the following:

  • Group 1 pulmonary hypertension (pulmonary arterial hypertension)
  • Group 3 pulmonary hypertension (pulmonary hypertension due to lung disease)
  • Group 4 pulmonary hypertension (pulmonary hypertension due to pulmonary artery obstructions)
  • Pulmonary hypertension due to other causes when the pulmonary hypertension is significant (mean pulmonary artery pressure >40 mm Hg)
  • Presence of right ventricular dysfunction

Postoperatively, maintaining preload, optimal pain control, and normal heart rate and blood pressure is important. Patients should continue receiving pulmonary vascular targeted therapies, such as phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, endothelin receptor antagonists, and prostacyclin analogues.

In patients with hypertension, urgent blood pressure lowering is not mandatory preoperatively unless there is evidence of end-organ dysfunction, in which case surgery should be delayed and blood pressure treated. Deferral of elevated-risk surgery may also be considered in patients with cardiovascular risk factors and a systolic blood pressure of 180 mm Hg or higher or diastolic blood pressure of 110 mm Hg or higher. Moderate preoperative hypertension has not been linked to adverse perioperative outcomes, although evidence is lacking regarding a specific blood pressure threshold. The perioperative use of specific antihypertensive agents is outlined in [Table: Table: Perioperative Medication Management]

.

Perioperative pulmonary complications include pneumonia, respiratory failure, and exacerbation of underlying lung disease. Pulmonary perioperative management involves pulmonary risk assessment, including screening for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), assessment of underlying lung disease and treatment optimization, and use of perioperative risk reduction strategies.

Before surgery, patients should be asked about any recent signs or symptoms of acute respiratory illness or chronic lung disease exacerbation; elective surgery should be postponed and appropriate treatment initiated for respiratory illness or exacerbation of underlying disease.

Patients with symptoms of dyspnea on exertion should undergo thorough history and physical examination and testing to evaluate the cause. Patients with a history of frequent exacerbations of COPD or asthma should have careful medication reconciliation to determine adequacy of current bronchodilator management and congruence with COPD and asthma treatment guidelines. Patients with baseline oxygen dependence should be assessed to ensure supplemental oxygen requirements are being met.

Pulmonary risk factors may be categorized as patient-related factors or procedure-related factors ( [Table: Table: Pulmonary Risk Factors]

). Risk calculators that include many of the important risk factors and other predictors may help determine postoperative risk for respiratory failure, pneumonia, and overall pulmonary complications. The ARISCAT score has been externally validated and measures risk for a wide variety of perioperative pulmonary complications. To date, ARISCAT and other available risk calculators do not incorporate OSA but are useful in estimating general pulmonary risk. However, there is controversy regarding the feasibility of obtaining sleep studies in patients with an urgent need for surgery, particularly among those undergoing lower risk surgeries.

All patients should be screened for OSA, which is associated with cardiac events, pulmonary complications, and ICU admissions. A commonly used screening tool for OSA is the STOP-BANG score. Although there is a paucity of data supporting delay of surgery in patients at high risk for OSA, the Society of Anesthesia and Sleep Medicine recommends preoperative sleep medicine evaluation in patients screened as high risk for OSA who also have evidence of hypoventilation (CO~2 retention), severe or uncontrolled comorbid conditions, or resting hypoxemia not attributable to other cardiopulmonary causes. However, there is controversy regarding the feasibility of obtaining sleep studies in patients with an urgent need for surgery, particularly among those undergoing lower risk surgeries.

Chest radiography is indicated only in patients with signs or symptoms of pulmonary illness or underlying cardiac or pulmonary disease with new or unstable symptoms. Spirometry is not useful for predicting risk and should not be routinely ordered for preoperative evaluation, including in patients with COPD. Furthermore, evidence does not support a spirometric threshold below which the risk of surgery is unacceptable. Spirometry is warranted in patients undergoing lung resection to help predict postoperative lung function.

Risk for perioperative pulmonary complications can be mitigated with selected interventions, including oral hygiene, early mobilization, use of regional or neuraxial anesthesia and analgesia, prophylactic respiratory physiotherapy (sputum clearance techniques, deep breathing exercises, and inspiratory muscle training), and postoperative continuous positive pressure ventilation. Surgery should be postponed and appropriate treatment initiated if there is concern for exacerbation of underlying disease or respiratory illness. Smoking cessation reduces pulmonary risk and should be encouraged as far in advance of surgery as possible. Prescribed inhaled medications should be continued throughout the perioperative period. Perioperative glucocorticoid stress dosing may be needed for patients who have required extended doses of oral glucocorticoids or who are on long-term high-dose inhaled glucocorticoid therapy (see [Table: Table: Glucocorticoid Stress Dosing Strategies]

). Perioperative management should also include goal-directed fluid management and consideration of lung-protective ventilation strategies.

In patients diagnosed with OSA, continuous positive airway pressure should be initiated preoperatively if possible. For patients with suspected OSA undergoing nonelective surgery, management includes postoperative monitoring with continuous pulse oximetry or capnography, nonsupine positioning, and limitation of sedating medications. Patients with known OSA should bring their continuous positive airway pressure device to the hospital for use in the perioperative period.

Postoperative hypoxia can present dramatically or insidiously in patients recovering from surgery and should be quickly addressed, as it may be the first sign of a life-threatening complication. Factors that contribute to postoperative hypoxia include preexisting cardiopulmonary conditions, hypoventilation effects from anesthesia and opioids, fluid shifts, pain-related hypoventilation, and cardiovascular, pulmonary, or hematologic complications.

Atelectasis is the most common cause of postoperative hypoxia and usually occurs within the first 48 hours after surgery. Risk factors include general anesthesia, thoracic or abdominal surgery, longer procedure duration, obesity, older age, underlying lung disease, and poor pain control. In addition to hypoxia, patients often have tachypnea and shallow breathing; low-grade fever may also be present. Crackles that improve after deep inspiration and bibasilar infiltrates or dependent linear densities on chest radiograph are suggestive of the diagnosis, but these findings are not specific. Treatment of atelectasis-related hypoxia requires supplemental oxygen and focuses on lung expansion maneuvers, including incentive spirometry, ambulation, and appropriate pain control. Some patients may require noninvasive ventilation. In patients with copious secretions, suctioning and chest physical therapy may be helpful.

Other causes of postoperative hypoxia include pulmonary edema, aspiration pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, hypoventilation/respiratory depression, and apnea. Orthopnea is highly suggestive of pulmonary edema, especially when accompanied by jugular venous distension, pulmonary crackles on auscultation, and a history of heart failure or poorly controlled hypertension. New onset pulmonary edema may result from myocardial infarction or volume overload in patients with reduced kidney function or from an exacerbation of chronic heart failure (see Acute Decompensated Heart Failure in Cardiovascular Medicine). Aspiration pneumonia is a risk in patients with chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease, frailty, or prolonged mechanical ventilation and is a risk factor for nosocomial sepsis (see Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia and Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia in Infectious Disease). Acute pulmonary embolism carries a high mortality risk; it typically occurs within 1 week postoperatively and presents with tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxia (see Diagnosis of PE in Hematology). Hypoventilation/respiratory depression can be related to residual anesthetic effects of postoperative opioids.

The American College of Chest Physicians (ACCP) and the American Society for Hematology (ASH) provide guidelines for VTE prophylaxis in orthopedic and nonorthopedic surgery populations ( [Table: Table: Postoperative VTE Prophylaxis Recommendations]

). The Caprini score, which has been validated in patients undergoing general or abdominal-pelvic surgery, can estimate risk for postoperative thrombosis.

Hip fracture surgery, total knee arthroplasty, and total hip arthroplasty pose a very high risk for VTE, and concomitant mechanical and pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis is recommended. Mechanical prophylaxis is provided with an intermittent pneumatic compression device for the duration of the hospital stay. For pharmacologic prophylaxis, direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) have largely replaced aspirin, heparin products, and warfarin in total joint arthroplasty, and low-molecular-weight heparin or low-dose unfractionated heparin are generally preferred in hip fracture repair (see [Table: Table: Postoperative VTE Prophylaxis Recommendations]

for additional details). The minimum recommended duration of pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis after these procedures is 10 to 14 days; however, provided that the bleeding risk is low, extended-duration postoperative prophylaxis (up to 35 days from the day of surgery) is preferred. If bleeding risk is especially high, mechanical prophylaxis is recommended over no prophylaxis.

The ACCP and ASH both recommend against preoperative placement of inferior vena cava filters for VTE prophylaxis and routine surveillance for VTE with venous compression ultrasonography.

Anticoagulant therapy increases the risk for perioperative hemorrhage and should be withheld in most patients before major surgery. For minor surgery, such as cataract surgery, simple skin surgery, or simple dental extractions, anticoagulation may be continued. The timing of withholding and resuming anticoagulation ( [Table: Table: Timing of Withholding and Restarting Anticoagulation]

) depends on surgical bleeding risk ( [Table: Table: Suggested Risk Stratification for Procedural Bleed Risk]

), kidney function (e.g., creatinine clearance), and the characteristics of the anticoagulant.

Bridging anticoagulation is the administration of therapeutic doses of short-acting parenteral therapy, usually heparin, when oral anticoagulant therapy is being withheld during the perioperative period. Newer guidelines recommend against bridging in most scenarios because of limited benefit and elevated bleeding risk. Bridging with a parenteral agent should be considered only in patients receiving vitamin K antagonists who are at high risk for thrombosis ( [Table: Table: Indications for Perioperative Bridging]

). Bridging is generally not indicated for DOACs because of their short half-life and rapid therapeutic onset, as well as the relatively low risk for thromboembolism with short-term interruption.

Postprocedural management of anticoagulation should be guided by thrombotic and bleeding risks and collaboration with the surgical team. If bridging is required, therapeutic anticoagulation is typically delayed until 48 to 72 hours after surgery with higher bleeding risk. Owing to the delayed effect of vitamin K antagonists, the first dose is typically administered 12 to 24 hours after surgery. Postoperative timing of DOAC reinstitution depends on postoperative kidney function, bleeding risk, and hemostasis (see [Table: Table: Timing of Withholding and Restarting Anticoagulation]

).

Because of the risk for spinal epidural hematoma, anticoagulant use with concomitant neuraxial (spinal and epidural) anesthesia should be avoided, and a longer interval off DOACs may be appropriate.

The perioperative management of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT), comprising aspirin plus a P2Y~12 inhibitor, in patients with coronary artery disease depends on the presence of a bare metal or drug-eluting coronary stent, time since stent placement, and the indication for DAPT (stable ischemic heart disease or acute coronary syndrome in the past year).

In patients with coronary stents, the AHA/ACC guideline recommends uninterrupted continuation of DAPT for at least 30 days after bare metal stent placement and 6 months after drug-eluting stent placement; the time frame should be extended to 12 months after an acute coronary syndrome. Elective surgery should be postponed during these time frames if DAPT cannot be continued safely throughout the perioperative period. However, if the risk of surgical delay exceeds the risk for stent thrombosis, discontinuation of the P2Y~12 inhibitor can be considered after a minimum of 3 months in patients with a drug-eluting stent. The timing of discontinuation for surgery depends on the agent prescribed. Aspirin (preferably low dose) should be continued if possible, and DAPT should be restarted as soon as bleeding risk has sufficiently diminished.

For most patients receiving long-term aspirin monotherapy for secondary prevention of cardiovascular events, the ACCP recommends continuing aspirin therapy in the perioperative period for those undergoing elective noncardiac surgery. The AHA/ACC guideline recommends continuing aspirin in this setting if the risk for cardiac events outweighs bleeding risk. If aspirin needs to be held because of high bleeding risk of surgery (e.g., intracranial or intraspinal procedures), the ACCP recommends holding aspirin for 7 days or less. The ACCP recommendations to continue aspirin are counter to the results of the POISE-2 trial. This study showed that perioperative aspirin use resulted in increased bleeding without a decrease in cardiac events, although a subgroup analysis of this trial showed greater benefit than harm to continuing perioperative aspirin in patients with previous percutaneous coronary intervention during any time frame.

A careful preoperative bleeding history, including a family history, should be obtained from all patients before surgery to evaluate for underlying bleeding disorders and anemia. Laboratory testing should be reserved for patients with a suggestive history. Patients with known factor deficiencies, platelet function defects, and other coagulopathies should have a preoperative consultation with a hematologist. In patients with cirrhosis and an elevated INR, preoperative vitamin K or blood products have not been shown to reduce bleeding risk.

In most hospitalized, hemodynamically stable patients, the Association for the Advancement of Blood and Biotherapies recommends a restrictive transfusion threshold (hemoglobin level of 7 g/dL [70 g/L]) because studies indicate equivalent or improved patient outcomes compared with higher transfusion thresholds. A threshold of 7.5 g/dL (75 g/L) may be considered for patients undergoing cardiac surgery, and a threshold of 8 g/dL (80 g/L) can be selected for those undergoing orthopedic surgery or who have underlying cardiovascular disease.

The accepted platelet transfusion threshold count is 50,000/µL (50 × 10^9/L) for patients undergoing major nonneurologic surgery. The American College of Gastroenterology recommends that patients with cirrhosis and platelet counts less than 50,000/µL (50 × 10^9/L) receive thrombopoietin receptor agonists to reduce the need for platelet transfusion. Postoperative thrombocytopenia may result from blood loss, platelet consumption, or drugs (especially heparin-induced thrombocytopenia). For a discussion of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, see Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia in Hematology.

Preoperative anemia and postoperative erythrocyte transfusion are associated with increased complications and mortality. When anemia is identified before elective surgery, efforts should be made to correct reversible causes and optimize red blood cell mass.

Evidence demonstrates that patients with perioperative hyperglycemia are at increased risk for postoperative complications, including infections, cardiovascular events, and death. Patients at risk for diabetes should be evaluated for diabetes before elective surgery. In patients with known diabetes who are scheduled to undergo elective surgical procedures, hemoglobin A~1c should be assessed before surgery. A preoperative hemoglobin A~1c of less than 8% and a blood glucose concentration of 100 to 180 mg/dL (5.6-10.0 mmol/L) should be targeted within 1 to 4 hours before surgery. For patients in whom it is not possible or reasonable to target a preoperative hemoglobin A~1c of less than 8%, a blood glucose concentration of 100 to 180 mg/dL (5.6-10.0 mmol/L) should still be targeted within 1 to 4 hours before surgery.

Diabetes medications require adjustment before surgery to avoid perioperative hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia. The American Diabetes Association recommends withholding metformin on the morning of surgery; however, AHA/ACC guidelines state that continued use of metformin perioperatively may be reasonable. Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have been associated with pulmonary aspiration in patients undergoing general anesthesia and procedural sedation. However, there is limited data to guide optimal management of GLP-1 RAs perioperatively. Joint guidance from the American Society of Anesthesiologists and other societies suggests that, with shared decision making, most patients may continue GLP-1 RAs before elective surgery. Patients at risk of delayed gastric emptying should follow a liquid diet in the 24 hours preceding surgery. If the decision is made to hold a GLP-1 RA before surgery, it should be held for 1 week or 1 day (depending on whether the medication is dosed weekly or daily, respectively) before surgery. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors should be withheld beginning 3 to 4 days before surgery because of the risk for euglycemic ketoacidosis. Other glucose-lowering noninsulin medications should generally be withheld the morning of surgery. For patients on insulin regimens, basal insulin should be continued perioperatively. While fasting for surgery, patients should receive 50% of their usual intermediate-acting insulin dose, 75% to 80% of their long-acting analogue dose, or adjustment of their pump basal insulin rate (if not automated) depending on the type of diabetes and individual factors. In patients with type 1 diabetes who are not prone to hypoglycemia, the normal basal insulin dose may be continued. The usual dose of short- and rapid-acting insulins can be administered before the day of surgery but should be held on the day of surgery unless required to correct hyperglycemia.

Postoperatively, if the patient is eating, the ideal insulin regimen is a basal-bolus regimen, with nutritional coverage and correction boluses for pre-meal hyperglycemia. For a discussion of the management of hyperglycemia in the hospital setting, see Inpatient Management of Hyperglycemia in Endocrinology and Metabolism. Metformin, other oral agents, and GLP-1 receptor agonists can generally be restarted postoperatively for stable patients who are eating and have had an uncomplicated hospital course. Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors may be restarted postoperatively when patients are eating and risk factors for ketoacidosis are resolved.

Preoperative screening for thyroid disease is not recommended in the absence of symptoms. In patients with symptoms suggestive of thyroid disease or in those with a recent change in levothyroxine dosage, it is reasonable to obtain a preoperative thyroid-stimulating hormone level.

In patients with hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine, therapy should continue uninterrupted. Patients with untreated, subclinical hypothyroidism may proceed to surgery because there is no apparent increase in perioperative mortality and morbidity. However, severe hypothyroidism may lead to perioperative myxedema coma, arrhythmias, hypotension, and other complications. Elective surgery in these patients should be postponed. Rarely, surgery may precipitate thyroid storm, clinically diagnosed based on manifestations of high fever, tachycardia, altered mental status, and cardiac and gastrointestinal/liver dysfunction. See Thyroid Storm in Endocrinology and Metabolism for more information on management.

In patients with well-controlled hyperthyroidism, therapy should be continued. Uncontrolled hyperthyroidism increases the risk for thyroid storm perioperatively; thus, surgery should be deferred until thyroid disease is controlled.

Consultation with an endocrinologist is advised if emergent surgery is required in patients with severe thyroid disease.

Although high-quality evidence to guide the use of perioperative supplemental glucocorticoid dosing (stress dosing) is lacking, guidelines generally recommend an aggressive approach. Stress dosing is administered perioperatively in patients who have known primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency or who have a high risk for hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (HPAA) suppression. Guidance for perioperative management of patients at risk for adrenal insufficiency is provided in [Table: Table: Glucocorticoid Stress Dosing Strategies]

.

If perioperative stress dosing is indicated because of adrenal insufficiency or suspected HPAA suppression, glucocorticoid dosing recommendations are tailored to the stress of the planned procedure. For minor surgical procedures using only local anesthesia, the Association of Anaesthetists recommends that patients with primary adrenal insufficiency take twice their usual dose of glucocorticoids on the day of surgery and for 1 to 2 days after. Patients who do not have adrenal insufficiency but are at increased risk for adrenal insufficiency can take their usual daily glucocorticoid dose on the morning of the procedure. Recommendations for nonminor surgery vary. For nonminor surgical procedures, the Association of Anaesthetists recommends giving 100 mg of intravenous hydrocortisone with induction of anesthesia followed by continuous infusion of 200 mg/d of intravenous hydrocortisone until the patient can resume oral glucocorticoids. Once oral glucocorticoids are resumed, twice the usual daily dose should be administered for 48 hours after surgery. Counter to these guidelines, many experts suggest replacing the continuous infusion with intermittent dosing of 50 mg of hydrocortisone every 6 to 8 hours until oral intake is resumed. In addition, using lower doses with induction for minor- or intermediate-stress surgeries and administering a similar dose of postoperative intravenous hydrocortisone may be an acceptable strategy.

Patients with glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency require stress dosing individualized based on the patient’s current glucocorticoid dosing plan and degree of stress. Multidisciplinary discussion involving the patient’s endocrinologist and/or rheumatologist may be required to determine optimal dosing.

In all situations, the patient’s individual characteristics (e.g., risk for hyperglycemia) and the surgical stress should be considered carefully. Furthermore, if preoperative stress dosing is not used, clinicians should ensure that patients take their usual glucocorticoid dose on the morning of the procedure and remain vigilant for signs and symptoms of adrenal insufficiency postoperatively.

Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) are at increased perioperative risk for acute kidney injury (AKI), fluid and electrolyte imbalance, cardiac events, metabolic acidosis, anemia, and bleeding. In all patients with CKD undergoing surgery, it is important to ensure the preoperative stability of kidney function, volume status, and electrolytes. Iodinated contrast dye and other nephrotoxic agents should be avoided in the perioperative period, and hypotension should be minimized to maintain renal perfusion pressure. For patients receiving hemodialysis, a nephrologist should be consulted for input on perioperative dialysate prescription, hemodialysis timing and heparin management, and adjustment of fluid removal perioperatively.

Perioperative AKI portends an increased risk for long-term decline in kidney function (including progression to end-stage kidney disease). The two most important means of mitigating risk for AKI are maintenance of renal blood flow and avoidance of further insults to the kidneys. Renal blood flow is maintained by avoiding renal hypoperfusion; effectively managing diuresis and antihypertensive medications; and treating anemia, which may impair peripheral vasodilation. Careful medication review is also warranted to ensure appropriate dosing based on renal clearance.

Liver disease increases the risk for perioperative infection, encephalopathy, bleeding, fluid retention, and acute kidney and liver decompensation. Clinically significant portal hypertension in particular is predictive of liver-related postoperative complications. Patients with chronic liver disease and unknown fibrosis status should be assessed for the presence of advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis with Fibrosis-4 and/or elastography. Patients with compensated cirrhosis in which clinically significant portal hypertension is unknown should be further assessed for such with cross-sectional imaging and/or measurement of liver stiffness and platelet count. Before surgery, complications of liver disease should be optimally managed in all patients. Patients with liver disease should be advised to abstain from alcohol consumption and tobacco to reduce the risk for postoperative complications.

Patients with chronic liver disease require careful preoperative evaluation and risk stratification with use of the MELD score, Child-Turcotte-Pugh classification, or VOCAL-Penn score, although other risk prediction models also exist. For more information, see Classification of Chronic Liver Disease Severity in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease. Patients with compensated liver disease and no evidence of clinically significant portal hypertension, including those with a low MELD score of 6 to 9 and Child-Turcotte-Pugh score of 5 to 6, have limited excess perioperative risk, particularly for low-risk elective procedures. In patients with higher perioperative risk, referral to a hepatologist is reasonable for further evaluation and to optimize management before proceeding with surgery. Those with severe liver disease are often at prohibitive risk for perioperative complications and death; patients with a MELD score greater than 15 or a VOCAL-Penn Score predicting greater than 15% mortality at 90 days should be referred for transplant evaluation before surgery.

See Perioperative Management of Anemia, Coagulopathies, and Thrombocytopenia in Foundations of Clinical Practice for management of patients with cirrhosis and thrombocytopenia.

Patients with neurologic disease are at increased perioperative risk for disease exacerbation and other complications. Antiepileptic medications should be continued uninterrupted.

Patients with Parkinson disease are predisposed to perioperative delirium, hallucinations, orthostatic hypotension, and complications related to dysphagia. Patients should maintain their regular treatment regimen. Surgery should be scheduled early in the day to minimize missed doses, and antidopaminergic antiemetics should be avoided. Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome is a potentially life-threatening complication resulting from withdrawal of or reduction in the dosage of dopamine agonists; it is characterized by rigidity, fever, altered mental status, and autonomic instability.

Perioperative stroke is associated with increased respiratory and cardiac complications and markedly increased mortality. Patients at highest risk for perioperative stroke include those with

  • A history of prior stroke or transient ischemic attack
  • Advanced age
  • Diabetes
  • Heart failure
  • Peripheral vascular disease
  • CKD
  • AKI

Elective noncardiac surgery should probably be delayed for a minimum of 3 months after stroke or transient ischemic attack to reduce the risk for recurrent stroke and major adverse cardiovascular events. For more information on in-hospital stroke considerations, see In-Hospital Stroke Considerations in Neurology.

Delirium commonly occurs in the postoperative setting, especially in older adults. Risk factors and treatment are similar to those for delirium in the general hospital setting (see Delirium in Neurology). Beyond delirium, patients also may have prolonged cognitive difficulties postoperatively, which may persist for months or longer.

Perioperative nerve injuries include compressive neuropathies, most commonly occurring at the sites of sustained pressure during surgical positioning. Numbness, paresthesia, pain, or weakness may result. Preventive measures include careful attention to positioning, including accommodation of preexisting position limitations. Management is primarily conservative; severe, progressive, or multifocal deficits may require team care.

For patients with a rheumatic condition, deferring elective surgery until the condition is under optimal control can reduce infection risk and improve outcomes. Perioperative medication management balances the risk for infection and impaired wound healing with the risk for worsening of the underlying rheumatic disease. Traditional oral disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (methotrexate, leflunomide, hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine) and apremilast should be continued through the perioperative period; this will reduce risk for postoperative disease flare with little or no effect on surgical risk. In patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) who are taking mycophenolate mofetil, mycophenolic acid, azathioprine, cyclosporine, or tacrolimus, therapy should be withheld for 1 week before surgery unless the SLE is severe, in which case these agents should be continued without interruption.

In most patients, biologic agents should be withheld for one dosing cycle preoperatively, with surgery performed just after the next dose would have been due. However, in patients with severe SLE, rituximab may be continued, with surgery being performed at the end of the dosing cycle and just before the next planned dose; belimumab should be continued without interruption. Janus kinase inhibitors, such as tofacitinib, should be withheld for at least 3 days before surgery. Patients receiving glucocorticoid therapy should continue taking their usual daily dose. Once the surgical wound shows evidence of healing (typically around 14 days) and in the absence of infection, agents that have been withheld should be resumed at the previously established dosage (see [Table: Table: Perioperative Medication Management]

).

As the U.S. population ages, the number of adults older than 65 years undergoing major surgery has been rising. Advanced age, functional dependence, cognitive impairment, and other geriatric syndromes are strong predictors of adverse postoperative outcomes, including pulmonary and cardiac complications, functional decline, and delirium. The American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program/American Geriatric Society preoperative guidelines focus on best practices to prepare geriatric patients for surgery and mitigate risk. The preoperative evaluation for older adults includes functional, nutritional, and cognitive assessments; medication screening for polypharmacy and high-risk medications; and expanded discussion between clinicians and patients regarding goals and expectations for surgery.

Frailty, defined as decreased physiologic reserves and increased vulnerability to stressors, is present in up to 20% of adults older than 65 years. A formal frailty assessment should be performed in patients scheduled for inpatient surgery. Frailty can be assessed by several tools (see Frailty Assessment in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Frailty is associated with worse postoperative outcomes and is thus a target for preoperative intervention. Preoperative multimodal interventions aimed at mitigating frailty risk have been developed. These programs are designed to improve patients’ overall health and fitness before surgery and most often include physical therapy, nutritional interventions, and stress reduction techniques.

Malnutrition is a risk factor for perioperative morbidity and may be present in up to 60% of older adults. Preoperative malnutrition screening with such tools as the Nutritional Risk Screening Tool, which incorporates age, BMI, weight loss, and illness severity (among other factors), is critical to mitigate complications such as infection and poor wound healing. Loss of 10% to 15% of total body weight in the preceding 6 months, a BMI less than 18.5, and a serum albumin level less than 3.0 g/dL (30 g/L) indicate severe malnutrition and are key predictors of poor surgical outcomes. Patients with these features warrant preoperative nutritional interventions with high-protein, high-calorie oral supplementation.

Finally, before any major surgery, geriatric patients and their families should be educated on delirium risk and prevention (see Delirium in Neurology), potential for functional and cognitive decline, and possible need for skilled nursing at discharge.

In women of reproductive age who are undergoing surgery, a menstrual history should be obtained and pregnancy testing performed if pregnancy is possible.

Although high-quality evidence is lacking and the current body of evidence suggests that surgery does not negatively affect obstetric or maternal outcomes, elective surgery should be delayed until after pregnancy. If surgery cannot be delayed until after delivery, performing surgery in the second trimester is preferred, if possible. Pregnant patients who require surgery should undergo a standard preoperative medical evaluation; additional diagnostic testing is unnecessary unless directed by the obstetrician. Modifications to surgical and anesthetic techniques may be required because of the anatomic and physiologic changes of pregnancy. Close collaboration among the obstetrician, surgeon, anesthesiologist, and internal medicine physician is essential. Notably, pregnancy is considered a hypercoagulable state, and the ACCP recommends perioperative mechanical or pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis for pregnant patients.
