Geriatric Medicine

The focus of care for older adults can be encompassed by the 5Ms: Mind/Mentation, Mobility, Medications, Multicomplexity, and what Matters most. When caring for older adults, clinicians should consider the following:

  • Mentation, dementia, delirium, and depression
  • Mobility and function, including impaired gait and balance and fall injury and prevention
  • Medications, including polypharmacy, deprescribing, optimal prescribing, and adverse medication effects
  • Multicomplexity, such as multimorbidities and complex biopsychosocial situations
  • Meaningful health care outcomes, including goals and care preferences

This framework is comprehensive, emphasizes patient-centered strategies and interdisciplinary coordination, and has been shown to improve outcomes for older adults. Assessing “what matters most” to patients should include addressing goals of care and advance care planning (see Patient Priorities and Goal Setting in Foundations of Clinical Practice and Advance Care Planning in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

CGA is a multidisciplinary diagnostic process to ascertain the physical, cognitive, psychological, environmental, and functional capabilities of older persons, with the objective of developing a holistic plan for maximizing function and quality of life. Common health issues in older adults include impaired mobility and physical function, deficits in sensory function (particularly vision and hearing), and cognitive decline. Polypharmacy, psychosocial issues, and the cumulative effects of chronic diseases may also contribute to decreased functional status and loss of independence. Identifying these issues requires systematic and multidimensional evaluation, which may be performed in the office, in the patient’s home, or on hospital admission or discharge. When evaluated in community-dwelling frail adults, no impact on death or nursing home admissions has been seen, but CGA may reduce the risk of unplanned hospital admissions. When completed in a dedicated inpatient geriatric unit, CGA may reduce mortality and the need for long-term placement.

Vaccinations in older adults are discussed in Immunization in Foundations of Clinical Practice. See Screening for Cancer in Oncology for recommendations on cancer screening in older adults.

Functional status assessment evaluates a patient’s ability to perform activities required for basic self-care (activities of daily living [ADLs]) or to live independently (instrumental ADLs [IADLs]). ADLs include bathing, grooming, dressing, toileting, feeding, walking, and transferring. IADLs comprise tasks such as managing finances, performing housework, shopping, self-administering medications, using transportation, preparing meals, and communicating by telephone. Standardized screening instruments for assessment of functional status are listed in [Table: Table: Indices to Assess Basic and Instrumental ADLs]

. Functional assessment may help determine the need for specific services and the appropriate level of care.

Older patients are at increased risk for many conditions that cause vision loss, including cataracts, macular degeneration, presbyopia, glaucoma, and disease-related retinopathy (e.g., diabetic retinopathy). Reduced visual acuity decreases functional status and quality of life while increasing risk for falls, depression, and cognitive impairment. Visual impairment may affect eligibility for a driver’s license based on state-specific requirements and may qualify the individual for disability benefits.

Screening tests and examination techniques to assess vision in the primary care setting include standardized questionnaires, the Snellen eye chart, and direct ophthalmoscopic examination; however, these tests may not detect disorders such as glaucoma and macular degeneration. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) concluded that evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for impaired visual acuity in asymptomatic adults aged 65 years or older, whereas the American Academy of Ophthalmology recommends performing a comprehensive eye examination in older adults every 1 to 2 years. Given the risks associated with decreased vision coupled with the prevalence of common treatable eye conditions in older adults, it is reasonable to ask about changes in vision and refer the patient to an eye specialist if changes are present.

Hearing loss is common in older adults, affecting more than 80% of persons by age 80 years. Hearing loss is socially isolating, perhaps more so than other sensory losses, and contributes to decreased quality of life and increased morbidity. Because of the impaired communication abilities inherent to hearing loss, it may be misdiagnosed as cognitive dysfunction.

Diagnostic tests that reliably screen for hearing loss include assessment of the patient’s ability to hear a whispered voice, fingers rubbing together, or a watch ticking. These tests and single-question screening (asking “Do you have difficulty hearing?”) perform as well as more complex questionnaires or handheld audiometry in detecting hearing loss.

The USPSTF reports that evidence is insufficient to assess the benefits and harms of screening for hearing loss in asymptomatic patients, whereas the American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery recommends that clinicians screen patients aged 50 years and older for hearing loss. Patients with symptoms should be referred to an otologist or audiologist for a formal hearing test and evaluation to determine whether hearing aids would be beneficial. Hearing aids and cochlear implants improve speech recognition and may improve quality of life in those with profound hearing loss.

The prevalence of depression in community-dwelling adults older than 60 years is as high as 15%, and rates are higher among those living in long-term care facilities and after hospitalization. Although diagnostic criteria for depression in older adults are no different from those in younger patients, some common symptoms, such as low energy and somatic symptoms, are often mistakenly attributed to aging or chronic illness. Depression in older adults also may be confused with cognitive dysfunction and is a risk factor for cognitive dysfunction. Chronic illness, grief associated with the loss of loved ones, social isolation due to decreased physical and cognitive function, and the need for institutionalization may contribute to depression in this population.

The USPSTF recommends screening for depression in all adults. The PHQ-2 has been validated as a screening instrument in older adults, with similar sensitivity and specificity to that in younger adults. Although sensitive, the PHQ-2 has a lower specificity for depression than more comprehensive screening instruments, and a positive screening result should therefore prompt further assessment. The PHQ-9 and the Geriatric Depression Scale have better sensitivity and specificity in older adults. The Geriatric Depression Scale, with its yes-or-no answer format, may be easier to administer in patients with cognitive impairment. When depression is suspected, a detailed medication review and inquiry about suicidality should be completed, because older adults are more likely to complete suicide attempts than younger individuals.

Older adults with depression are commonly treated with pharmacotherapy, and antidepressants protect against suicide attempts in this population. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are the most widely studied antidepressants and are considered first-line therapy. Nonpharmacologic treatment, including psychotherapy, exercise, and electroconvulsive therapy, have also been shown to be effective and may help limit negative consequences of polypharmacy. For the treatment of mild to moderate depression, nonpharmacologic options may be considered first in patients with medication intolerance or dementia. See Management of Depressive Disorders in Interdisciplinary Medicine for more information on treatment options.

Cognitive impairment is defined as a progressive decline in at least one cognitive domain (memory, attention, language, visual-spatial function, executive function) that negatively affects patient functioning. The strongest risk factor for cognitive impairment is increasing age, and the prevalence of dementia is nearly 10% in adults aged 75 to 84 years and nearly 30% in those older than 85 years. In the absence of symptoms, routine screening is not recommended by the USPSTF owing to a lack of evidence that it leads to effective intervention. Nevertheless, because cognitive impairment is a risk factor for falls, loss of independence, and poor control of chronic diseases, clinicians should routinely ask patients about cognitive impairment and further evaluate those with reported symptoms. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) advocates assessing cognitive function in the annual wellness visit by direct observation and input from family, friends, and caregivers.

The most widely studied instrument for evaluating cognitive function is the Mini–Mental State Examination (MMSE). The proprietary nature of the MMSE and the time required to administer the test (approximately 7 minutes) may preclude its use for routine outpatient case finding. The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) takes a similar amount of time to complete and is sensitive for detecting cognitive impairment; however, training and certification are required for its use. The Mini-Cog test has acceptable sensitivity and specificity in identifying dementia and is available to clinicians without charge, although it is copyright protected. It includes a three-item recall test and a clock-drawing test. More extensive neuropsychiatric testing is not typically required for most patients but may be considered in patients with equivocal results on preliminary testing or to distinguish dementia from a psychiatric disorder.

Evaluation and treatment of mild cognitive impairment (impaired cognition in the absence of impaired function) and dementia are further discussed in Cognitive Impairment in Neurology.

Older adults are at increased risk for malnutrition due to changes in diet, comorbid conditions, medications, social factors, and changes in metabolism and digestion that occur with aging. These factors may lead to accelerated rates of sarcopenia (decline in muscle mass), frailty, and increased morbidity and mortality. Xerostomia (dry mouth) is also more common with aging, and it may be accompanied by altered taste.

Patients aged 65 years and older can be assessed for malnutrition through anthropometrics, dietary history, assessment of comorbid conditions and medications, and laboratory investigations. Validated nutrition screening tools, such as the Mini Nutritional Assessment, can identify patients at high risk. Medications contributing to xerostomia should be reviewed for discontinuation if possible.

Treatment may require an interdisciplinary team approach with collaboration among physicians, nurses, dietitians, and occupational therapists. Comorbid diseases that may be contributing to malnutrition (such as depression and malabsorptive conditions) should be treated and optimized. Diets rich in fruits and vegetables coupled with adequate protein intake should be advised, along with regular physical activity. Oral supplements may be considered in some patients to provide adequate caloric intake; however, appetite stimulants are not recommended because of the possibility of adverse effects and a lack of sufficient evidence for benefit. Vitamin B~12 deficiency is common in older adults because of poor absorption and may result in neurologic and hematologic symptoms; oral supplementation should be advised for those with low vitamin B~12 levels. Some older adults may require vitamin D and calcium supplementation because of changes in metabolism and rates of osteoporosis.

BMI definitions of healthy weight, overweight, and obesity remain unclear in this population and may not be an accurate measure of health. Closely monitored weight loss may be indicated for some older adults, specifically those whose comorbid conditions might benefit from weight loss. Aggressive weight loss is generally not recommended because it might reduce both fat and lean body mass.

One in three adults older than 65 years and one in two adults older than 80 years fall every year, making falls the leading cause of injury in older adults. Many health conditions, physical characteristics, and behaviors increase risk for falling, but the greatest increases are associated with cognitive impairment, psychoactive medications, gait/balance problems, and decreased lower extremity strength. The presence of multiple risk factors has an additive effect on fall risk. Even fear of falling in the absence of falls decreases self-rated health and hastens functional decline.

Screening older adults for fall risk is recommended by the American Geriatrics Society (AGS) and is an element of the Medicare annual wellness visit. Despite these recommendations, only 25% of older adults report discussing falls with their physician. Patients should be asked about falls and unsteadiness with walking as well as fear of falling. Those who report falls or balance issues should be evaluated. Testing methods for assessing fall risk in older adults are explained in [Table: Table: Testing Methods for Assessing Fall Risk in Older Adults]

. These assessments do not require special equipment, and each can be completed quickly in a primary care office. Patients at risk for falling may be referred for more comprehensive assessment or formal gait and balance assessment and therapy. An algorithm for fall risk assessment and prevention is presented in

.

The USPSTF recommends exercise interventions for fall prevention for patients aged 65 years and older who are at increased risk for falls. Group exercise classes and individual physical therapy should be considered. Assessment of fall risk in the home and patient education can be included in fall prevention measures. The USPSTF acknowledges that the overall benefit of routinely offering multifactorial interventions to prevent falls is small and should consider the balance of benefits and harms based on the circumstances of previous falls, presence of comorbid medical conditions, and the patient’s values and preferences. The CDC has developed a toolkit for patients and providers that includes the online Check for Safety tool, a patient-administered home safety checklist with practical suggestions for reducing fall risk.

Interventions shown to reduce fall risk in the ambulatory setting include exercises that emphasize gait/balance training and lower extremity strength, discontinuation or decrease in the dosage of centrally acting medications, and assessment and modification of the home environment.

Vitamin D supplementation should not be used to prevent falls in community-dwelling adults aged 65 years or older who are not known to have osteoporosis or vitamin D deficiency.

Several fall prevention strategies can be used in the hospital setting. These strategies include physical and occupational therapy, bed alarms, limitation of medications that cause postural hypotension or weakness, and hospital sitter services for patients with cognitive impairment. Although no single intervention has been shown to decrease falls in hospitalized patients, various bundles of multifactorial intervention programs have been successful in reducing falls in the hospital setting.

Motor vehicle collisions (MVCs) are the second leading cause of injury-related death in older adults. However, driving is one of the most valued IADLs for older adults, and cessation of driving in this population is associated with negative health consequences, including depression and decreased quality of life.

Driving requires intact domains of vision, cognition, and motor/somatosensory function. A decrease in the patient’s visual acuity, reduced cognitive abilities, use of centrally acting medications, alcohol or substance use, conditions that increase risk for loss of consciousness, and mobility issues of the extremities or neck increase the risk for MVCs. Gradually accumulating deficits may go unrecognized by the older adult driver until a collision occurs. Fortunately, many older adults self-restrict driving, commonly discontinuing night driving and longer trips. Self-restricted driving, caregiver or family concern for driving safety, history of traffic citations, and impulsive behaviors also are associated with increased risk for collisions. Addressing modifiable risk factors (e.g., cataract removal), optimizing treatment of arthritic conditions, and discontinuing risky medications are strategies that may reduce the risks associated with driving.

The decision to advise an older driver to “retire from driving” (the preferred terminology) is qualitative, complex, and largely dependent on clinician judgment. Clinician reporting is voluntary in most states, and there is no valid criterion standard for driving competency; however, available options for assessing fitness to drive range from on-road tests alone to comprehensive clinical and on-road driving evaluations by occupational therapists. The AGS in partnership with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has developed a guideline for multidisciplinary evaluation of the older driver that includes screening instruments, resources for rehabilitating those at risk for becoming unsafe to drive, and resources for patients who must retire from driving.

Physician advice to retire from driving is often associated with older drivers appropriately stopping driving; however, given the risk for depression and social isolation associated with driving retirement, this advice should be coupled with support, suggestions for alternate forms of transportation, and follow-up assessment of mood and quality of life.

The role of the individual clinician in preventing MVCs caused by patients with cognitive impairment is unclear. Identifying cognitive impairment or dementia and subsequently targeting those patients for driving retirement might be expected to effectively reduce MVCs, although mandatory physician reporting of dementia to departments of motor vehicles has not been shown to reduce the percentage of collisions attributable to dementia. Effective strategies include requiring in-person application (which may include vision screening) for license renewal.

Older adults are at increased risk for mistreatment, including abuse, neglect, and financial exploitation, because of decreased functioning that leads to dependence on others. The prevalence of elder mistreatment is estimated to be 10%, but because of underreporting, may be as high as 20%. The most commonly encountered form in the health care setting is neglect, as either caregiver neglect (failure to meet the older person’s physical and mental health needs) or self-neglect (by choice or because of dementia or mental health issues). Victims are high utilizers of emergency services, hospital care, and nursing home care and have a higher mortality rate.

The USPSTF recognizes elder abuse and abuse of vulnerable adults as common and serious problems but finds insufficient evidence for the accuracy of screening tools and a lack of adequate intervention studies. Nevertheless, because of the potential negative health effects of mistreatment, screening should be considered in adults with vulnerability for or signs of abuse. Screening should be performed if possible after requesting to speak with the patient alone. Screening evaluations include the Elder Abuse Suspicion Index and the Emergency Department Senior Abuse Identification screening tool.

Findings suggestive of abuse or neglect, whether intentional or unintentional, must be reported to Adult Protective Services.

Frailty is a multifactorial geriatric syndrome that can be defined as a state of poor health from accumulated age-related health deficits. It is usually characterized by five phenotypic elements:

  • Low energy (first manifestation)
  • Weakness
  • Slow walking speed
  • Low activity level
  • Unintentional weight loss (later manifestation)

It has been linked to increased mortality, falls, and risk for hospitalization, as well as reduced mobility and health-related quality of life. Frailty is predictive of morbidity and mortality during or after many medical and surgical interventions, and its presence is associated with longer inpatient stays, increased likelihood of discharge to a skilled nursing facility, and increased risk for inpatient delirium. Notably, advanced age is not synonymous with frailty.

Because screening for frailty has not shown consistent benefit, frailty measurement is not recommended as part of routine geriatric assessment; however, the CGA is considered the gold standard for identifying frailty. Furthermore, frailty measurements are also being incorporated into preintervention assessment for many surgical, procedural, and medical treatments (see Geriatric Patients in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Applications include tailoring glycemic control and blood pressure targets, predicting response to and tolerance of surgical and chemotherapeutic cancer treatment, and predicting postoperative outcomes related to surgery.

More than 70 standardized frailty indices are available, and no one index is preferred. The frailty index, a comprehensive assessment of chronic conditions and functioning, has been in use longer than other indices; however, its length and complexity limit its usefulness in routine care. The five-item frailty phenotype was originally validated in the Cardiovascular Health Study of more than 5000 patients aged 65 years or older; it requires objective measurement of gait speed and grip strength (with a dynamometer), which may not be feasible in primary care. The frailty index and frailty phenotype are the most commonly used instruments in frailty research.

In addition to the more comprehensive assessments, many indices have been developed for specific preintervention screening. Most of these tools use self-reported measures, are simple to administer and score, and may be more easily incorporated into a primary care practice. These screening tests are useful in identifying patients who might require more formal CGA or preintervention rehabilitation. Examples of well-validated, brief, subjective instruments are presented in [Table: Table: Examples of Frailty Indices]

.

Of note, interventions performed in the early stages of frailty have the potential to reduce the associated risks. Strategies include muscle strengthening through exercise, protein and other nutritional supplementation, and addressing mood disorders and polypharmacy. Response to these interventions may require weeks to months; therefore, screening for frailty well in advance of planned interventions should occur whenever possible.

Hip fractures are more common in older patients and are a significant cause of morbidity and mortality. Despite aggressive treatment, the mortality rate may be as high as 30% within 1 year. Risk factors for hip fracture include the following:

  • Older age
  • Female sex
  • Osteoporosis
  • Falls
  • History of previous fracture
  • Low BMI
  • Low socioeconomic status
  • Prolonged bisphosphonate therapy

Medications such as corticosteroids, proton pump inhibitors, loop diuretics, and thyroid hormone, as well as those that may result in increased falls (e.g., benzodiazepines, sedatives, antidepressants, and opioids), have been associated with hip fractures.

Patients who experience a hip fracture often present with groin pain and the inability to bear weight on the affected leg after a fall. The affected leg may appear externally rotated and shortened. Diagnosis is confirmed by plain radiographs in most cases. If initial radiographic imaging results are negative and clinical suspicion remains high, MRI (preferred) or CT should be pursued. Hip fractures are classified as either extracapsular or intracapsular; intracapsular fractures (femoral head or femoral neck) are more likely to result in nonunion, malunion, or avascular necrosis owing to relatively lower amounts of cancellous bone and poorer blood supply of this area. Extracapsular fractures are intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric. Patients with prolonged exposure to bisphosphonate therapy may have atypical fractures along the femoral diaphysis.

Early operative management (ideally within 24-48 hours) is the mainstay of treatment for most patients and results in improved outcomes, including reduced pain, shorter inpatient stay, fewer medical complications, and decreased mortality. Patients with stable comorbid conditions generally do not require extensive preoperative evaluation (see Perioperative Medicine in Foundations of Clinical Practice); unnecessary testing and consultation result in surgical delays and poorer outcomes.

The presence of anticoagulation should not delay surgery (with reversal protocols when applicable) unless the benefits of spinal anesthesia outweigh the benefits of using general anesthesia. However, patients with active comorbid conditions (e.g., poorly controlled COPD or decompensated heart failure) may require stabilization before surgery. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guideline recommends remobilization postoperatively on the day of or day after surgery, with ADLs resuming between postoperative days 2 through 5. Prophylaxis for venous thromboembolism should continue for 21 to 35 days (see Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Patients with a hip fracture are at high risk for delirium, constipation, pressure injury, and urinary retention; to avoid these complications, delirium risk should be assessed and prevention strategies followed, stimulant or osmotic laxatives may be used, a foam or alternating pressure mattress should be provided, and indwelling catheters should be used only short term. All patients with hip fractures are treated for osteoporosis (see Pharmacologic Management of Low Bone Mass and Osteoporosis in Endocrinology and Metabolism), regardless of the results of bone mineral density testing, to reduce risk for subsequent fracture. Fall prevention strategies and nutritional optimization should be advised.

As the population ages, medical complexity and care needs also increase, necessitating a variety of care delivery models, including home-based and facility-based options.

Resources for older adults who wish to remain in their homes but need assistance include home health agency care and custodial care services. Home health agencies offer assistance with medication management, wound care, and physical therapy. These services are provided on an intermittent basis (usually no more than two to three times per week for an hour per skilled care need) and are covered by Medicare and Medicaid if the patient is homebound with a documented skilled care need. Custodial care services provide help with dressing, bathing, toileting, cooking, and other ADLs; these services are not covered by Medicare but may be paid for by Medicaid. Visiting physicians can also provide outpatient medical care.

When patients who are cared for by family members require additional resources for gaps in care, adult day care can provide part-time assistance when the patient’s primary caregiver is unavailable. If supervision is needed for a longer time, respite care is available at many senior living communities (assisted living facilities and nursing homes). Adult day care and respite care are not typically covered by Medicare or Medicaid.

When long-term daily care needs exceed those that can be provided in a patient’s home, three different levels of care are available: independent living, assisted living, and nursing home care. Independent living is suitable only for patients who can independently perform ADLs and IADLs and simply provides patients with the benefits of living in a community. Assisted living offers a home-like environment but provides varying levels of assistance with medications, ADLs, housekeeping, and meals. For patients requiring additional help with ADLs or medical management, nursing homes provide 24-hour nursing care as well as rehabilitation services for those who qualify. Memory care units, found within nursing homes and assisted living facilities, provide secure environments for patients with dementia or memory loss. Residential care homes use a smaller, home-like environment in the care of patients with similar needs (e.g., patients with chronic mental illness); however, the services provided vary, and the level of care provided may be similar to assisted living or nursing home care. Independent and assisted living are typically paid for with private funds, or “private pay.” Medicare does not usually cover long-term nursing home or residential home care. Medicaid may pay for long-term care depending on patient eligibility and state regulations.

Acute medical care is typically provided in a hospital setting. However, home hospital care is increasingly being studied, with the CMS issuing a waiver for approved hospitals to provide acute care in the home. This care model may offer a viable approach for older adults, including those who are socially vulnerable and medically complex.

Posthospitalization care is available in several forms. Safe return to a patient’s previous living situation can be facilitated with outpatient physical, occupational, and speech therapy in the home or clinic. If a patient requires functional improvement before returning home, rehabilitation can be performed in an acute rehabilitation program or skilled nursing facility (i.e., subacute rehabilitation). Acute rehabilitation is provided in a freestanding rehabilitation hospital or a designated hospital unit, and it requires that the patient be able to participate in 3 hours of therapy at least 5 days per week. Subacute rehabilitation is appropriate for patients who cannot tolerate this level of therapy. Original Medicare covers the costs of both options for up to 100 days if the patient had an inpatient hospitalization of at least 3 days and continues to make progress with goals. Some patients require longer-term, high-intensity medical care, including mechanical ventilation or multiple parenteral therapies; long-term acute care hospitals are an appropriate option for these patients.

Older patients are at significant risk for medication complications, and a comprehensive medication management strategy is critical for prevention. Specific elements of a medication management strategy include the following:

  • Obtaining an accurate medication history
  • Assessing medication adherence
  • Recognizing the effects of comorbid conditions and aging on drug metabolism
  • Screening for drug-drug interactions
  • Avoiding inappropriate medications
  • Assessing for polypharmacy

Patients should be asked to bring all medications to the visit for the purpose of medication reconciliation, especially after transitions of care. Medication adherence can be assessed with standardized questionnaires, pill counts, or review of pillboxes. Common alterations in drug metabolism in older patients, including decreased kidney and liver function, necessitate frequent assessment and adjustment of drug dosages. Medication lists should be reviewed regularly for drug-drug interactions, including at the time of care transitions. During medication review, physicians should specifically target the reduction of medications that may be unsafe in older patients, such as first-generation antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics, and benzodiazepines. The AGS Beers Criteria for Potentially Inappropriate Medication Use in Older Adults lists medications that are problematic for older patients as well as recommendations regarding drug interactions to avoid.

Older patients are particularly susceptible to adverse drug events. Adverse drug events may be the result of adding a new drug, increasing the dose of a previously well-tolerated drug, or drug-drug interactions. Over-the-counter drugs or supplements may also be responsible for an adverse drug event. The risk for adverse drug reactions can be reduced by stopping all unnecessary drugs, seeking safer alternatives for essential drugs, and considering nonpharmacologic alternatives to drug therapy. When prescribing new medications to older patients, starting with lower dosages and providing longer periods between dosage changes will reduce the risk for adverse drug events.

Drugs that may provide benefit to older patients also may be underprescribed. For example, statins are underprescribed in older adults, a group that may have the most to gain when properly selected. Anticoagulants are often inappropriately withheld from patients with atrial fibrillation after an episode of gastrointestinal bleeding and from those at risk for falls or who have fallen.

Polypharmacy is common among older adults, and rates of polypharmacy have risen over the past two decades. Nursing home patients take eight different medications on average, and medication errors occur in two thirds of such patients. Polypharmacy in older patients is associated with increased health care utilization and cost, medication nonadherence, and functional decline. Patients transitioning between levels of care are particularly vulnerable to inappropriate medication additions, omissions, and dose changes; the risk for these mistakes increases with the number of medications prescribed. Hazards of polypharmacy include overtreatment or undertreatment of disease, serious drug-drug interactions, drug-disease interactions, and adverse reactions.

Although treatment of comorbid health conditions in older adults often necessitates the use of several medications, physicians can minimize the potential for adverse effects from polypharmacy. Frequent review of patient medications to confirm their necessity, discontinuation of drugs that are unnecessary or inappropriate, and proper dosing are paramount, especially during care transitions.

Insomnia symptoms are common among older patients. Prevalence is higher in women, especially those who are caregivers. Untreated insomnia is associated with increased risk for depression and heart disease and poorer control of chronic conditions. The first-line treatment for insomnia in older adults is cognitive behavioral therapy; pharmacologic sleep aids must be used with caution in this population (see Pharmacologic Therapy in Common Symptoms). Sleep hygiene, discontinuation of sleep-disruptive medications, and treatment of comorbid and sleep-related illnesses are helpful adjuncts to cognitive behavioral therapy, and a multimodal approach is most successful. If nonpharmacologic treatment fails, doxepin may provide relief. Antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, antihistamines, and non-doxepin tricyclic antidepressants should be avoided.

Pressure injuries (or pressure ulcers) represent damage to the skin and underlying tissue caused by unrelieved pressure. Injuries may be caused by compression of the tissues leading to hypoxia, shear forces leading to tissue trauma, friction of skin folds leading to skin breakdown, and moisture leading to maceration of the skin. The most important risk factors for pressure injury are immobility, incontinence, impaired nutrition, immunosuppression or diabetes mellitus, and reduced skin perfusion.

The prevalence of pressure injuries ranges from 3% to 17% among hospitalized patients and approaches 50% in long-term ICU patients. Patients who develop pressure injuries during an acute care stay are much more likely to be discharged to a long-term care facility.

Pressure injury prevention is a cost-effective intervention that can positively affect health status. Improved understanding of ulcer pathogenesis and changes in reimbursement have increased the focus on identifying at-risk patients and allocating resources to prevention efforts. CMS has selected the development of a severe pressure ulcer as a “never event” (adverse events that are unambiguous [clearly identifiable and measurable], usually preventable, and serious [resulting in death or significant disability]) for health care facilities. CMS provides no additional payment when a stage 3 or 4 pressure ulcer is acquired after admission to a health care facility.

The first step in pressure injury prevention is a structured risk assessment, including a history and physical examination, to identify at-risk patients. Although standardized risk-assessment tools are available, clinical validation studies have found these instruments to have fairly low positive predictive values. Bedside clinical assessment of the skin remains an important part of risk evaluation.

In at-risk patients, pressure redistribution is paramount in the prevention of pressure injuries and may be accomplished with pressure-reducing equipment and proper patient positioning. Advanced static mattresses or overlays are effective for prevention in patients at increased risk, including in patients being discharged to home with a hospital bed. An advanced static mattress is made of specialized sheepskin, foam, or gel and is immobile when a patient lies on it, whereas an advanced static overlay is a pad composed of foam or gel that is secured to the top of a regular mattress.

Proper skin care, moisture reduction, management of incontinence, protein-containing supplements, and early mobilization can help prevent skin breakdown.

Pressure injuries may be classified by using a staging system ( [Table: Table: Classification of Pressure Injuries]

); advancing stages are characterized by increasing tissue loss, depth, and ulcer size. Treatment varies depending on stage. For stage 1 injury, aggressive implementation of prevention strategies may be successful. Stage 2 injuries can be managed with hydrocolloid or occlusive dressings, which have been shown to reduce ulcer size compared with gauze dressings in low-quality studies. Successful treatment of stage 3 and 4 pressure injuries requires interdisciplinary management including wound care, surgical debridement, surgical repair, vacuum-assisted closure, treatment of infection, and adequate nutrition. If necrotic tissue is present, it should be debrided. Stage 3 and 4 injuries without significant exudate may be dressed with hydrogel dressing, and calcium alginate dressing may be used for injuries with moderate exudate. High-absorbency foam dressing may be used for pressure injuries with moderate to heavy exudate and helps provide cushioning. The relative benefit of different support surfaces in the treatment of pressure injuries is unclear. Evidence is also insufficient to support the use of platelet-derived growth factor dressings, hydrotherapy, hyperbaric oxygen, or maggot therapy.

Palliative Medicine

Palliative medicine seeks to relieve suffering and maximize quality of life for patients with a serious illness. It uses a model of interdisciplinary team care with a focus on reducing pain and other physical, emotional, psychological, and spiritual symptoms associated with advanced disease.

All physicians practice some degree of palliative medicine and should learn and use basic palliative medicine skills in patient care ( [Table: Table: Skill Sets for Primary and Specialty Palliative Care]

). Specialty palliative medicine teams coordinate with referring physicians to align care with the patient’s goals, preferences, and values and address multidimensional care needs. Evidence shows that specialty palliative medicine improves overall quality of life, physical symptom burden, mood, and patient and caregiver satisfaction. Palliative care also reduces hospitalizations, emergency department use, and ICU admissions. It is associated with more advance care planning, and it increases the chances that patients will die in their preferred place. Notably, a palliative medicine team does not replace the primary physician, hospitalist, or specialist; rather, the team acts as an extra layer of support, integrating key information from the referring physician into goal-concordant care plans and attending to symptoms that affect quality of life. It remains the responsibility of the primary physician to explore psychosocial distress, provide anticipatory guidance, and perform basic symptom management before or concurrent with referral to palliative medicine specialists.

Although referral to palliative care historically occurred at the end of life, more recent evidence indicates that early initiation during a serious illness is associated with substantial advantages. Research on the benefits of subspecialty palliative care has mostly involved patients with incurable cancer. However, many guidelines highlight the need for early palliative care in patients with advanced cardiac, pulmonary, or kidney disease; advanced dementia; critical illness; or cancers with potentially curative interventions.

End-of-life conversations may be challenging for patients and clinicians. Patients/caregivers need information regarding their illness, symptom management, treatment options, and prognosis. However, they may also be fearful to engage in discussions, have misunderstandings or denial about their illness, or have misconceptions about end-of-life care. Clinicians may not want to cause distress to patients and families or may feel inadequately trained to lead these discussions. Nevertheless, timely and effective end-of-life communication can help align the wishes, needs, and preferences of patients and their families with realistic and meaningful goals of care. Studies have demonstrated that end-of-life communication can reduce utilization of aggressive and expensive medical care, improve quality of life, and increase care satisfaction.

Use of a structured conversation guide is associated with improved goal-concordant care and reduced patient anxiety. One model for skilled communication with patients facing a serious illness is outlined in [Table: Table: Serious Illness Conversation Guide]

; the Serious Illness Conversation Guide provides sample phrases that are designed to elicit a patient’s goals, preferences, and values after assessment of the patient’s understanding of their illness. It encourages shared decision making and enables physicians to help patients understand their illness and prognosis, elicit important goals, and make recommendations for care. The output of these conversations should be communicated to the patient’s family (as the patient deems appropriate), surrogate decision maker, and appropriate members of the health care team. Institutional advance directives, commercial advance directive forms or electronic applications, physician orders for life-sustaining treatment (POLST) forms, and medical orders for life-sustaining treatment (MOLST) forms should be viewed as mechanisms to record the outcomes of these discussions rather than as conversation guides. Online patient resources for advance care planning are available, and clinicians can undergo training to improve their conversations around end-of-life issues.

For further discussion of advance care planning and advance directives, see Advance Care Planning in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

Effective, proactive symptom management is critical to the success of palliative care interventions. Management of debilitating and distressing symptoms can improve a patient’s functioning, sense of hope, and overall quality of life.

Pain is common in patients with terminal illness, and recognition and frequent evaluation of pain are integral to effective management. Up to 90% of patients with advanced cancer have pain. However, cancer pain remains undertreated, with about one third of patients with cancer receiving inadequate analgesia. The incidence of pain in patients with other serious illnesses is also underappreciated, but it is estimated that 67% of patients with cardiovascular disease or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and up to 61% to 75% of patients with advanced dementia will experience moderate to severe pain at the end of their lives.

In addition to physical pain, many patients with advanced illness face complex psychosocial and spiritual issues related to their illness and may experience total pain, defined as physical, social, psychological, and spiritual suffering. Engaging interdisciplinary team members, such as nurses, psychologists, chaplains, and social workers, is important in addressing the nonphysical components of pain.

Nonpharmacologic interventions that may benefit patients with cancer pain include

  • Cognitive behavioral therapy to enhance coping techniques
  • Physical therapy to improve function in the setting of pain from metastatic lesions
  • Acupuncture and other complementary therapies (e.g., acupressure, reflexology)
  • Radiation therapy directed to the underlying lesions

Pharmacologic pain management often requires a multimodal strategy that uses both opioids and nonopioid analgesics. In cancer-associated pain and particularly in patients with advanced disease, the severity of the underlying pain dictates the use of opioids. Opioids are the first line of treatment for moderate or severe chronic pain in patients living with active cancer. Opioids are similarly essential for palliatively managing pain in terminal noncancer conditions. Those with poor or inadequate response to opioids may benefit from additional management with nonopioid analgesics such as acetaminophen, NSAIDs, glucocorticoids, topical therapies, neuropathic agents, and/or antidepressants with analgesic properties. Cannabinoids do not appear to reduce cancer pain when added to opioids.

Opioids should be prescribed with careful attention to dosing, frequency, and side effect profile. Safe prescribing practices, such as prescription drug monitoring program review, opioid risk assessment, and close monitoring, should also be used. [Table: Table: Opioids Commonly Used in Palliative Care]

outlines opioids most commonly used in palliative care and potential concerns. Weaker opioids, such as codeine and tramadol, are not first-line options in patients with advanced illness because of marginal effectiveness, drug-drug interactions, and wide variations in hepatic metabolism.

Short-acting opioids should be titrated to achieve relief of pain. In patients using short-acting opioids who require longer-lasting relief, long-acting agents are appropriate; however, long-acting opioids should not be the initial opioid prescribed in opioid-naive patients. Selection of a long-acting opioid should be based on underlying organ function and previous response to the equivalent short-acting formulation (e.g., converting oxycodone immediate-release to controlled-release formulation).

Orally administered transmucosal immediate-release fentanyl (TIRF) products are approved for the treatment of cancer-related pain. TIRF formulations are rapidly absorbed and offer immediate onset for patients who are not achieving adequate analgesia with high-dose morphine. Management of these medications is challenging because the dosing regimen, escalation, and frequency differ among brands. In addition, clinicians require specialized education and certification (TIRF Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy program) to initiate these medications. Methadone is another long-acting agent used to treat pain from a serious illness; however, its complex dosing and variable half-life restrict its general use. TIRF formulations and methadone are also associated with a higher risk for overdose. Owing to their complicated management, they should be prescribed in collaboration with an expert in pain management or a palliative medicine specialist with experience in their use.

When switching between opioids, which may be necessary due to side effects, comorbidities, or poorly responsive pain, equianalgesic dose conversion and dose reduction are necessary (see [Table: Table: MME Doses for Opioids for Pain Management]

). The total daily dose of the new opioid is typically reduced by 25% to 50% (and up to 90% for certain medications, such as methadone) of the calculated morphine milligram equivalent.

Dyspnea is a prominent and distressing symptom in patients with advanced illness that increases in prevalence and intensity as patients approach their last weeks to days of life. Management starts with treating the underlying condition (e.g., pleural effusion, infection, anemia, COPD, heart failure). Cancer-directed treatments for malignancy-related causes (e.g., malignant pleural effusion, atelectasis from pulmonary mass) should be consistent with the patient’s wishes, prognosis, and overall health status. Nonpharmacologic interventions include airflow interventions such as fans directed toward the patient’s cheek (trigeminal nerve) or supplemental oxygen if the patient has hypoxia. Time-limited therapeutic trials of high-flow oxygen via nasal cannula or noninvasive ventilation may be used if consistent with the patient’s goals of care. The final step in managing dyspnea uses pharmacologic measures. Although no opioids have FDA approval to treat dyspnea, these agents are commonly offered when nonpharmacologic interventions do not provide sufficient relief or if dyspnea is acute and severe. When used properly for chronic dyspnea, opioids are not associated with significant or clinically relevant adverse respiratory effects. In descending order of evidence for efficacy, benzodiazepines and then corticosteroids may be tried. If dyspnea is refractory to all other treatments, continuous palliative sedation may be offered. See Management of Dyspnea in Common Symptoms for further discussion of dyspnea.

Audible oropharyngeal secretions at the end of life (“death rattle”) are often distressing for families and clinicians and may occur in up to 50% of dying patients. These secretions are thought to rarely affect respiratory status or cause patient discomfort, although the actual effect on the patient is unknown. Educating family members on the dying process can ease their concerns. Treatment is often initiated in anticipation of or response to family distress. Nonpharmacologic measures, such as raising the head of the bed, positioning the patient on their side, and withdrawal of parenteral hydration may be helpful. Compared with placebo, prophylactic subcutaneous scopolamine butylbromide, administered when patients enter the dying phase, reduces the occurrence of death rattle without an apparent increase in adverse effects, although it may prolong the dying phase (by 13 hours compared with placebo). Deep suctioning by catheter should be avoided unless secretions are causing obvious respiratory distress.

Nausea and vomiting are common and debilitating symptoms in patients with serious illness, with many patients rating nausea as more distressing than unrelieved pain. Management of nausea should be tailored to address the underlying mechanism and associated neurotransmitter pathway ( [Table: Table: Treatment of Nausea in the Palliative Care Patient]

). More than one agent is frequently required for symptom relief. In hospitalized patients, parenteral agents should be administered on a scheduled basis to achieve symptom control and reduce the number of emesis events. The addition of olanzapine 5 mg daily for patients with advanced incurable cancer can significantly decrease chronic nausea as well as vomiting, fatigue, and pain, and improve appetite and well-being. Nausea prophylaxis in patients receiving chemotherapy is discussed in more detail in Nausea and Vomiting in Oncology.

Constipation is common in patients with serious illness and may result in extreme discomfort, restlessness, and delirium. Causes include opioids, dehydration, immobility, metabolic disturbances, tumor burden, and numerous nonopioid medications. Prophylaxis should be considered if constipation is likely to occur, such as with opioid initiation or if prolonged immobility is anticipated. Patients with constipation should be educated on increasing fluid intake and physical activity as much as possible. Pharmacologic therapy includes osmotic laxatives, such as polyethylene glycol, often in combination with a stimulant laxative, such as senna or bisacodyl. Docusate, alone or in combination, is no more effective than placebo for constipation in patients with serious illness. Third-line therapy consists of rectal suppositories and/or enema preparations. Phosphate- or magnesium-containing enema preparations are contraindicated in patients with serious illness owing to the potential for dangerous electrolyte shifts. Treatment strategies for opioid-induced constipation are covered in Adverse Effects in Common Symptoms.

Anorexia and weight loss frequently occur as part of the natural progression of terminal illness. Management involves addressing any reversible contributors to anorexia to ease patient and family distress. Dietary counseling to educate patients and their caregivers on safe feeding and food recommendations may be helpful. Although some medications are marketed for patients with anorexia and weight loss, they are marginally effective in a minority of patients and often have unacceptable side effects. Enteral or parenteral artificial nutritional support at the end of life does not improve survival; is invasive; and may cause side effects, including increased respiratory secretions and uncomfortable edema. Discussing common end-of-life symptoms, including anorexia and weight loss, and the lack of effective treatments for these expected changes can prepare patients and their family members and set realistic expectations.

The prevalence of depression in the palliative care population is estimated to be 24% to 70%. Clinical depression worsens quality of life and, if present, should be treated. Nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic approaches can be effective. Nonpharmacologic techniques with the most significant benefit include the following:

  • Counseling
  • Clinical hypnosis
  • Dignity therapy
  • Cognitive therapy
  • Music therapy
  • Guided imagery
  • Progressive muscle relaxation
  • Acupuncture
  • Mindful breathing

A variety of antidepressant agents have been studied; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), tricyclic antidepressants, and mirtazapine have all shown improvement and are well tolerated. Psychostimulants such as dextroamphetamine, methylphenidate, and modafinil have demonstrated a more rapid onset of action than SSRIs and tricyclic antidepressants in patients with serious medical illness and are helpful in patients with opioid-related sedation, severe psychomotor slowing, or mild cognitive impairment. Ketamine, alone or combined with an SSRI, also shows promise in inducing a rapid response and reducing symptoms in terminally ill patients.

Anxiety is a common symptom in patients receiving palliative care, often coexisting with depression. Potential triggers include existential fears, the uncertainty inherent to the dying process, difficult decisions, concern for loved ones, and financial issues. Some treatments, including disease-specific hormone antagonists, may also induce anxiety.

Management includes nonpharmacologic approaches such as social support, relaxation therapy, exercise, mindfulness meditation, and psychotherapy. Pharmacologic treatment with benzodiazepines may be appropriate, although close monitoring for adverse events, including delirium, is necessary. SSRIs may be helpful in patients with coexisting depression and anxiety.

Delirium at the end of life has many potentially reversible causes (e.g., medication side effects, inadequate analgesia, pain, urinary retention, constipation), although a single cause is often not identified. Treatment of reversible conditions and nonpharmacologic interventions, such as maintaining hydration, providing orienting stimuli, and reducing noise, remain standard care; however, for some patients, medications may be required to maintain patient and caregiver safety and to relieve suffering. An observational study found that antipsychotic medications prescribed on inpatient palliative units, most commonly haloperidol, quetiapine, and risperidone, were effective in resolving or improving delirium. In a randomized inpatient study evaluating the management of delirium not controlled with haloperidol alone, escalated doses of intravenous haloperidol, low-dose haloperidol alternating with chlorpromazine, and haloperidol combined with chlorpromazine were equally effective. The combination of benzodiazepines and antipsychotics may be more effective than antipsychotics alone in the treatment of delirium at the end of life.

Hospice is a form of palliative medicine that provides specialized interdisciplinary care to patients with life-limiting illness for whom disease-directed treatments are no longer effective or desired. Hospice care is appropriate for patients with a life expectancy of 6 months or less if the disease takes its natural course. There is no requirement that a patient sign a do-not-resuscitate order before entering hospice; hospice nurses and physicians can continue end-of-life care discussions with the patient and their family.

Hospice can be provided in several settings, including the home, skilled nursing facilities, and residential hospice homes. Hospice team members include physicians, advanced practice clinicians, nurses, social workers, pharmacists, chaplains, and other providers whose goals are to maximize quality of life for patients with advanced or terminal illness who are no longer receiving life-prolonging treatment. Hospice teams are associated with improved overall satisfaction with care for patients and caregivers.

Hospice referral should be considered for all patients with a limited life expectancy and is not restricted to those at the very end of life. In addition, hospice is not limited to patients with cancer: patients with a wide variety of underlying conditions receive benefit. Unfortunately, despite proven patient and caregiver benefits, hospice referrals often occur too late in the disease process, thus denying patients comprehensive, quality care at the end of life.
