Disorders of the Esophagus

Normal swallowing consists of three phases. The oral phase encompasses formation of a food bolus and transfer of the bolus to the back of the throat. The pharyngeal phase allows the bolus to be safely positioned in the upper throat; the soft palate elevates, the epiglottis protects the trachea, the tongue moves backward, and the pharyngeal wall moves forward. The esophageal phase starts with the bolus entering the esophagus with relaxation of the upper esophageal sphincter. Peristalsis (rhythmic contractions) propels the bolus down; primary peristalsis is initiated with the swallow, and secondary peristalsis is intended to clear residual bolus. This phase ends as the lower esophageal sphincter relaxes to allow the bolus to enter the stomach.

Dysphagia is a disruption in the swallowing mechanism, resulting in a bolus not passing from the mouth to the stomach. Determining whether the cause is oropharyngeal or esophageal is important in developing a differential diagnosis and management plan. See [Table: Table: Causes of Dysphagia]

.

Oropharyngeal dysphagia occurs when the patient cannot transfer the food bolus from the mouth into the upper esophagus. Common symptoms include choking, coughing, and nasal regurgitation of food and liquids; patients are at risk for aspiration pneumonia. Neurologic causes include stroke and Parkinson disease. Proximal structural causes, such as pharyngoesophageal (i.e., Zenker) diverticulum, should be considered when undigested food is brought up several hours after a meal.

The initial study for suspected oropharyngeal dysphagia is a video fluoroscopic swallow study, or modified barium swallow, with a range of liquid and solid consistencies. Routine upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and esophageal manometry have a limited role in the evaluation. Management includes dietary changes and a swallowing exercise program implemented with a speech pathologist.

Patients with esophageal dysphagia can initiate the swallowing process but often feel chest discomfort. The sensation is commonly described as food “hanging up” or feeling lodged or stuck during a meal. Patients also may describe a bolus as slow to go down or “sitting” in the chest. Occasionally, patients may have regurgitation of undigested food contents, which can be perceived as vomiting.

Esophageal dysphagia results from a structural or motility disorder. Dysphagia with solids alone often suggests a structural abnormality or mechanical obstruction, whereas dysphagia with liquids alone (or with liquids and solids) favors a motility problem. An urgent evaluation is indicated for complete obstruction, hematemesis, odynophagia, onset in an older patient, or dysphagia associated with weight loss. Esophageal food impaction, wherein a food bolus lodges and obstructs the passage of additional food, fluid, or saliva, is an indication for emergency endoscopy.

Mechanical esophageal obstruction may be benign or malignant, resulting from masses, strictures, esophageal rings (e.g., a Schatzki ring [see

]), or complex hiatal hernias. Strictures may occur because of chronic reflux esophagitis (peptic strictures), eosinophilic esophagitis, radiation therapy, or caustic injury. Dysphagia that progresses from occurring only with solids to occurring with both solids and liquids is concerning and warrants endoscopic evaluation.

Upper endoscopy allows for diagnosis (biopsy and inspection) and possibly therapy (dilation) for causes of structural esophageal dysphagia and is therefore the initial test of choice. A barium esophagram can evaluate for gross structural abnormalities but is not adequate for diagnosis of a motility disorder. Clinical management is based on the underlying cause.

Esophageal diverticula are an uncommon structural disorder characterized by an outpouching of the esophageal mucosa. Although esophageal diverticula can be completely asymptomatic, symptoms of dysphagia or regurgitation can be present. The most common of these is pharyngoesophageal or Zenker diverticulum, which occurs proximally in the hypopharynx as a result of increased intraluminal pressure from failure of cricopharyngeal muscle relaxation. Zenker diverticulum is most common in older adults. An epiphrenic diverticulum, however, is located in the distal esophagus and is caused by pulsion related to a motility disorder that increases lower esophageal sphincter (LES) pressure, such as achalasia. Barium esophagram is the diagnostic test of choice to assess for diverticula. Treatment includes myotomy (cricopharyngeal myotomy for Zenker diverticula and esophagomyotomy for epiphrenic diverticula) and sometimes secondary diverticulectomy.

Esophageal rings and webs are thin layers of mucosa that can partially obstruct the esophageal lumen. A ring is a concentric shelf of mucosa commonly occurring in the distal esophagus. Esophageal rings can be associated with hiatal hernia (i.e., Schatzki ring) and, in cases of eosinophilic esophagitis, can be the result of fibrostenotic remodeling of the esophagus. A web is a much thinner (<2 mm) noncircumferential membrane commonly occurring in the cervical esophagus. Esophageal webs are associated with Zenker diverticulum, dermatologic conditions (e.g., bullous pemphigoid), and graft-versus-host disease. Although most esophageal rings and webs are asymptomatic or nonobstructing, some patients may have dysphagia, and diagnosis can be made by barium esophagram or upper endoscopy. Symptomatic patients may require esophageal dilation.

Esophageal stricture is an abnormal narrowing of the esophagus and commonly presents with progressive dysphagia, but it can also present as odynophagia, chest pain, regurgitation, heartburn, avoidance of certain foods, or weight loss. Esophageal strictures can have several underlying causes, such as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) (peptic stricture from healing erosive esophagitis), eosinophilic esophagitis, malignancy, treatment for premalignant esophageal lesions (e.g., ablation or mucosal resection of dysplasia or early cancers), caustic ingestion, ischemia, postsurgical resection (i.e., anastomotic stricture after esophagectomy), and radiation to the head, neck, or chest. Stricture can be diagnosed with barium esophagogram or upper endoscopy. Specific treatment and duration are dictated by the underlying cause of the stricture.

Pseudoachalasia results from malignant tumor infiltration or other secondary causes leading to myenteric plexus damage. It can present similarly to achalasia. Three clinical features suggest cancer as a cause of pseudoachalasia:

  • Short duration of dysphagia (<1 year)
  • Weight loss (>6.8 kg [15 lb])
  • Age older than 55 years

Suspected pseudoachalasia should be evaluated with CT, endoscopy, or endoscopic ultrasonography. Therapy depends on patient factors, underlying disease, and available local expertise.

The esophagus is a muscular tube that passes a food bolus from the hypopharynx to the stomach through peristalsis. The upper one third of the esophagus is composed of skeletal muscle innervated by axons of lower motor neurons. The lower two thirds is smooth muscle innervated by the vagus nerve. High-resolution esophageal manometry is the gold standard to evaluate and diagnose esophageal motility disorders.

Achalasia is defined by inadequate relaxation of the LES and complete aperistalsis. Achalasia can be idiopathic or associated with viral, autoimmune, and neurodegenerative disorders and infection (Chagas disease). Damage to the ganglion cells and myenteric plexus in the esophageal body and LES leads to uncontested cholinergic nerve activation, which prevents LES relaxation. Achalasia affects men and women equally, with an annual incidence of 1 in 100,000 persons. It commonly occurs between 30 and 60 years of age. Patients commonly have dysphagia with solids and liquids along with regurgitation of undigested food. Additional symptoms include heartburn, weight loss, and chest pain unresponsive to acid-reducing agents.

On barium esophagram, achalasia can show dilation of the esophagus with narrowing at the gastroesophageal junction, known as a “bird’s beak” (see

). Upper endoscopy may reveal retained food and saliva, dilated esophageal lumen, mucosal stasis changes, no signs of mechanical obstruction or mass, and subjective “tightness” at the gastroesophageal junction while the endoscope is advanced into the stomach. Esophageal manometry, showing abnormal and incomplete relaxation of the LES and failed peristalsis in all swallows, remains the gold standard to diagnose achalasia.

Treatment is directed toward disrupting the LES, which may be done by surgical esophagomyotomy, peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM), pneumatic dilation, and botulinum toxin injection of the LES. Advantages of laparoscopic myotomy include the ability to address any hiatal hernia, if present, and perform a concurrent antireflux procedure. POEM entails creation of an esophageal submucosal tunnel extending to the LES followed by myotomy. Pneumatic dilation is an effective nonsurgical therapy. Dilators, ranging from 30 mm to 40 mm, are used to disrupt the circular muscle. Clinical symptom relief ranges from 50% to 90%, and the most common complication is perforation. Endoscopy with botulinum toxin injection into the LES inhibits acetylcholine release, relaxing the LES. However, after 1 year, only 40% of patients have continued symptom relief. Botulinum toxin injection can be repeated, but successive treatments are often less effective for symptom management. As such, botulinum toxin injections are generally recommended for patients in whom myotomy is considered a high-risk procedure.

Patients with achalasia for more than 10 years have increased risk for squamous cell carcinoma and may benefit from surveillance endoscopy; however, no guidelines are established for frequency of surveillance.

Spastic or hypercontractile disorders of the esophagus may present with noncardiac chest pain or dysphagia. Distal esophageal spasms are characterized by premature contractions, the esophagus has a “corkscrew” (

) or “rosary bead” appearance on esophagram, and premature or spastic contractions are present on esophageal manometry. Hypercontractile esophagus (formerly known as “jackhammer esophagus”), is defined by excessive peristaltic vigor.

Medical management of spasm or hypercontractile esophagus includes antispasmodics (such as hyoscyamine), calcium channel blockers or nitrates, phosphodiesterase inhibitors (sildenafil), and botulinum toxin; a tricyclic antidepressant may be considered in patients suspected of having visceral hypersensitivity. Because these findings can be observed with GERD, treatment with a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) is reasonable.

Absent contractility is characterized by 100% failed peristalsis in the presence of normal LES relaxation as seen on esophageal manometry. Patients may report GERD symptoms that result from decreased LES pressure or dysphagia from incomplete esophageal emptying. In most cases, the cause of absent contractility is unknown. However, secondary causes include smooth muscle relaxants, anticholinergic agents, estrogen, progesterone, connective tissue disorders (e.g., systemic sclerosis), and pregnancy.

Treatment is focused on lifestyle changes, such as eating upright and remaining upright for hours after meals, eating small meals frequently throughout the day (instead of two to three typical meals), slow eating, and possible avoidance of certain solid textures. Medical therapy includes acid-reducing agents for GERD and low-dose antidepressants to reduce chest discomfort. Prokinetic agents (e.g., metoclopramide) are not recommended.

GERD is characterized by reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus. It has a prevalence of 10% to 20% in the Western world. GERD occurs because of transient LES relaxation, loss of tonic function of the LES, or abnormalities in the normal valvular anatomy of the gastroesophageal junction. Increased pressure differences between the thoracic and abdominal cavities (e.g., pregnancy, obesity) and retention of gastric contents (e.g., gastroparesis, gastric outlet obstruction) can promote reflux. Many additional factors can also trigger reflux ( [Table: Table: Factors Associated With Reflux]

). Uncontrolled GERD can negatively affect quality of life because of poor sleep, low productivity, and work absences. Long-standing GERD can lead to complications, including reflux esophagitis, peptic stricture, Barrett esophagus, and esophageal adenocarcinoma.

The most common and typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation.

Atypical symptoms of GERD include the following:

  • Chronic cough
  • Asthma symptoms
  • Chest pain (a cardiac cause should be excluded before considering GERD)
  • Throat soreness or throat clearing
  • Hoarseness
  • Globus sensation (a sensation of a lump in the throat or throat tightness, not associated with swallowing meals)
  • Nausea
  • Dysphagia or odynophagia (pain while swallowing)

GERD is usually a clinical diagnosis based on history and response to antisecretory therapy. Clinical symptoms of heartburn and regurgitation strongly suggest GERD. Alarm features, such as dysphagia, weight loss, hematemesis, and melena, should warrant endoscopic examination. Patients with GERD symptoms but without alarm features may undergo an 8-week empiric trial of a PPI and attempt to discontinue the PPI therapy if symptoms are relieved. GERD is also confirmed by presence of acid-related mucosal injury on upper endoscopy, including Los Angeles grade B, C, or D esophagitis and/or the presence of Barrett esophagus. For steps in evaluation and treatment, see

. Patients with atypical esophageal symptoms may require additional evaluation ( [Table: Table: Other Common Esophageal Symptoms]

).

Most patients with GERD have normal findings on upper endoscopy; however, normal endoscopic findings do not exclude GERD, and the severity and frequency of symptoms may not correlate with endoscopic findings.

Although barium esophagram is sensitive for the detection of structural abnormalities, such as a stricture, esophageal dilation, or perforation, it is not a physiologic test of esophageal function or a diagnostic tool for reflux.

Ambulatory pH monitoring can quantify acid exposure in the esophagus. Testing to detect active acid reflux can be done with a 24-hour transnasal catheter or a 48-hour or 96-hour wireless capsule endoscopy. In patients in whom the diagnosis of GERD is unclear and endoscopy is unrevealing, diagnostic pH monitoring should be performed off acid-suppressive therapy. Impedance-pH testing can help differentiate between acid and nonacid reflux.

Esophageal manometry should be considered as part of the evaluation for patients with dysphagia or atypical reflux symptoms and before antireflux surgery to rule out motility disorders.

Asthma symptoms, chronic cough, and laryngitis can be associated with GERD, although they are atypical symptoms (see

). When these symptoms are present, other non-GERD causes should be eliminated. Laryngoscopy should not be used to diagnose GERD-related laryngitis, and edema and erythema as potential signs of reflux-induced laryngitis are nonspecific. A PPI trial is recommended in patients who have concomitant typical GERD symptoms. For patients with atypical symptoms only in whom non-GERD causes have been excluded, diagnostic testing (ambulatory esophageal pH monitoring off acid-suppressing therapy) should be considered before a PPI trial.

Weight loss is indicated for patients with recent weight gain, overweight, or obesity. Patients with nocturnal symptoms should elevate the head of the bed to sleep and be counseled to avoid meals within 2 to 3 hours of bedtime. Avoiding large meals and rich or fatty foods that stay in the stomach for longer, particularly during the last meal of the day, is helpful.

Additional dietary modification should focus on eliminating specific foods that trigger an individual patient’s symptoms rather than globally eliminating all common trigger foods (caffeine, chocolate, spicy foods, acidic foods such as citrus fruits, and fatty foods). Cessation of alcohol and tobacco use is recommended.

Pharmacologic therapy includes antacids, H~2-receptor blockers, PPIs, and potassium-competitive acid blockers (PCABs). A PPI once daily for 8 weeks is the therapy of choice for symptom relief and for treatment of erosive esophagitis (see

). Most PPIs should be taken once daily, 30 minutes before a meal or snack. Considering the risks and potential adverse effects of PPI therapy ( [Table: Table: Potential Adverse Effects of Proton Pump Inhibitors]

), the lowest dose required to control symptoms should be used and therapy should be discontinued if an appropriate indication is lacking. Similarly, patients requiring long-term maintenance therapy should be prescribed the lowest effective PPI dose. For patients with uncomplicated GERD, stopping or reducing long-term PPI therapy should be attempted once yearly.

Switching to a different PPI may be warranted for adverse reactions or unresponsive symptoms. PPIs are safe in patients who are pregnant.

Prokinetic agents, such as metoclopramide, should not be used to manage GERD unless gastroparesis is present.

Vonoprazan, a PCAB, is approved for treating heartburn related to erosive and nonerosive esophagitis. However, the use of PCABs should be reserved for those with acid-related reflux that does not respond to twice-daily PPI therapy.

The first step in addressing refractory GERD is to optimize PPI therapy by emphasizing the importance of taking medication 30 to 60 minutes before eating, increasing the dosage to twice daily, or switching to another PPI. PCAB therapy may also be considered for those who do not respond to PPI therapy.

If symptoms are still unresponsive, alternative causes must be considered. For typical symptoms, endoscopy is used to rule out eosinophilic esophagitis or erosive esophagitis. Adequacy of acid suppression therapy may be confirmed by esophageal impedance-pH testing while using optimized PPI therapy. For atypical symptoms, other causes should be evaluated, and referral to otorhinolaryngology, pulmonary, or allergy specialists to identify and treat the cause should be considered. In these patients, pH testing conducted while the patient is not receiving acid-suppression therapy may help confirm the diagnosis of acid reflux. If results of impedance-pH testing or pH testing are normal but symptoms persist, therapy for functional heartburn may be attempted with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, or tricyclic antidepressants.

Surgery is infrequently required; indications include failure of optimal PPI therapy, a desire to stop the medication, and intolerable medication adverse effects. Patients should undergo objective testing, such as pH monitoring and esophageal manometry, before surgery. Surgical treatments include laparoscopic fundoplication or bariatric surgery for obesity as well as magnetic sphincter augmentation (a magnetic ring is placed around the LES without surgical alteration of the stomach). Surgery is most effective in patients with severe reflux esophagitis; large hiatal hernias; or persistent, troublesome typical GERD symptoms. However, about one third of patients require PPI resumption 5 to 10 years after surgery. Postoperative complications include dysphagia, diarrhea, and inability to belch because of a tight fundoplication.

Transoral incisionless fundoplication (an endoscopic fundoplication created with full-thickness suture) is a consideration for patients with troublesome regurgitation or heartburn who do not wish to undergo antireflux surgery and who do not have severe reflux esophagitis or large hiatal hernias. Additional endoscopic therapies are based on thermal radiofrequency energy, silicone injection, suturing, and endoscopic resection, but long-term benefits are unproven.

Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic, allergen-induced, type 2 immune-mediated inflammatory disease characterized by symptoms of esophageal dysfunction (commonly dysphagia, food bolus obstruction, and reflux) and eosinophilic inflammation of the esophagus. EoE is commonly comorbid with atopic conditions, such as asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food allergies. Studies consistently demonstrate a male predominance, with a male-to-female risk ratio of 3:1. The reported U.S. prevalence is up to 163 per 100,000 persons, with a rapidly rising incidence.

The diagnostic criteria for EoE include the following:

  • Esophageal symptoms (e.g., dysphagia, food impaction, heartburn, chest pain)
  • Histologic examination of esophageal biopsy specimens (minimum of six biopsy specimens from at least two locations in the esophagus) showing 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field
  • Exclusion of other causes of eosinophilia (such as GERD, pill-induced esophagitis, inflammatory bowel disease, hypereosinophilic syndrome, achalasia, connective tissue or autoimmune diseases, and infection)

Endoscopic findings can include edema, rings, longitudinal furrows, luminal narrowing, exudates, and sometimes strictures (

and

).

Treatments for EoE include elimination diets, PPIs, and swallowed topical glucocorticoids (fluticasone propionate or budesonide). Biologic agents, such as the interleukin-4 receptor antagonist dupilumab, may also be considered in patients who do not respond to PPI therapy. Conventional allergy testing is unreliable to identify EoE food triggers. Instead, an empiric elimination diet focuses on inducing disease remission by removing the most common food triggers, systematic food reintroduction, and, ultimately, avoidance of only the specific trigger(s) to maintain long-term disease control. Most common EoE food triggers include dairy; wheat; soy; eggs; and, to a lesser extent, shellfish, seafood, and nuts or tree nuts. Food elimination diets to consider include single-food (dairy or animal milk), two-food (dairy and wheat), four-food (dairy, wheat, eggs, and soy) and six-food (dairy, wheat, eggs, soy, nuts, and seafood) protocols. Endoscopic dilation is a safe and effective way to manage fibrostenotic sequelae, such as strictures.

Infectious esophagitis can be caused by fungal, viral, bacterial (uncommon), or parasitic pathogens. It most commonly occurs in immunocompromised patients. Odynophagia or dysphagia is most often present initially. Candida esophagitis frequently causes dysphagia with or without odynophagia, whereas viral esophagitis produces odynophagia. Other organisms associated with esophagitis include Lactobacillus, β-hemolytic streptococci, Cryptosporidium species, Pneumocystis jirovecii, Mycobacterium avium complex, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Candida infection can occur in immunocompetent or immunocompromised persons. Diagnosis is usually made clinically based on compatible symptoms and the presence of oral candidiasis, although not all patients have oral involvement. Endoscopy and biopsy or brushings can be considered for patients who do not respond to empiric therapy or who have atypical symptoms. Endoscopy shows small, white, raised plaques, and esophageal brushings confirm the diagnosis (

). The most common species is Candida albicans, which is treated with oral fluconazole.

Herpes simplex virus and cytomegalovirus are seen in immunodeficient or immunosuppressed persons but rarely occur in immunocompetent patients (see Human Herpesvirus Infections in Infectious Disease).

Endoscopic findings of viral esophagitis can include esophageal ulcers or nonspecific inflammation. Biopsy is needed to confirm the diagnosis. Herpes simplex virus infection is treated with acyclovir, famciclovir, or valacyclovir; cytomegalovirus infection is treated with ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir.

Medications can cause esophageal injury that results in esophagitis. Risk factors for pill-induced esophagitis include the following:

  • Decreased salivary output
  • Esophageal dysmotility
  • Large pills
  • Medications that increase the LES tone (opioids)
  • Ingesting medications in the supine position

Common presentation includes symptoms of chest pain, dysphagia, and odynophagia several hours to days after taking the medication. Pill-induced esophagitis has occurred with the following:

  • Alendronate
  • Quinidine
  • Tetracycline
  • Doxycycline
  • Potassium chloride
  • Ferrous sulfate
  • Mexiletine

Medications associated with stricture formation include the following:

  • Alendronate
  • Ferrous sulfate
  • NSAIDs
  • Potassium chloride

Pill-induced esophagitis can be diagnosed by history alone, but upper endoscopy should be performed for severe symptoms, persistent symptoms, or atypical symptoms (such as hematemesis or abdominal pain). Preventive strategies include drinking sufficient water with medications and remaining upright for 30 minutes after pill ingestion.

Barrett esophagus (BE) is the replacement of the squamous epithelium with metaplastic columnar epithelium in the esophagus. Because of chronic GERD, even in patients without clinical symptoms, BE is a precursor lesion for esophageal cancer. Among those with GERD who undergo endoscopic evaluation, it is estimated that 5% to 12% will have BE. Risk factors associated with BE include chronic GERD (weekly symptoms for ≥5 years), age older than 50 years, male sex, tobacco use, obesity, and history of BE or esophageal adenocarcinoma in a first-degree relative.

The annual cancer risk is 0.2% to 0.5% per year for BE without dysplasia, 0.7% per year for BE with low-grade dysplasia, and 7% per year for BE with high-grade dysplasia.

Evidence does not support routine screening for BE based on GERD symptoms for the general population. However, the American College of Gastroenterology conditionally recommends screening endoscopy for individuals with chronic GERD symptoms and at least three risk factors, including the following:

  • Age older than 50 years
  • Male sex
  • White race
  • Tobacco use
  • Obesity
  • History of Barrett esophagus or esophageal adenocarcinoma in a first-degree relative

Although standard peroral endoscopy remains the gold standard for diagnosing BE, a swallowable, capsule sponge device combined with a biomarker represents a nonendoscopic alternative for screening.

BE is diagnosed based on endoscopic findings (

) with biopsy, which are then confirmed by pathology showing specialized intestinal metaplasia with acid-mucin–containing goblet cells. BE is categorized by endoscopy measurements as short-segment (<3 cm) or long-segment (≥3 cm). Long-segment BE is associated with an elevated cancer risk.

BE progresses along a continuum: intestinal metaplasia without dysplasia, low-grade dysplasia, high-grade dysplasia, and adenocarcinoma. The length of the BE and degree of dysplasia determine the time interval for endoscopic surveillance and therapy recommendations ( [Table: Table: Endoscopic Surveillance and Treatment of BE]

).

Medical therapy with a proton pump inhibitor should be used to treat reflux symptoms and to heal reflux esophagitis. Evidence does not suggest that antireflux surgery can prevent progression of BE to adenocarcinoma more effectively than medical therapy with PPIs. Patients should be counselled on tobacco cessation and, if they have overweight, weight loss.

Endoscopic eradication therapies for patients with confirmed dysplasia and intramucosal esophageal adenocarcinoma include endoscopic mucosal resection of all visible lesions followed by radiofrequency ablation or cryotherapy to completely eradicate the intestinal metaplasia and neoplasia. Prompt reassessment and optimization of reflux control should be pursued when eradication of intestinal metaplasia is incomplete.

The global incidence of esophageal carcinoma varies widely; high-prevalence areas include Asia and southern and eastern Africa. The two types of esophageal carcinoma are squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma. Worldwide, squamous cell carcinoma makes up 90% of all esophageal cancers, but the incidence has been decreasing. The incidence of adenocarcinoma, however, has been rising. Esophageal cancer occurs in the fifth to seventh decades of life and is three to four times more common in men; additional risk factors are listed in [Table: Table: Esophageal Adenocarcinoma, Squamous Cell Carcinoma Risks]

. In the United States, about 16,000 new cases are reported annually, with 15,000 deaths occurring in the same year. The overall 5-year survival rate ranges from 15% to 25%, depending on the cancer stage at initial presentation.

The most common initial presentation of esophageal carcinoma is dysphagia with solid foods, but asymptomatic persons have been diagnosed through surveillance endoscopy. Other symptoms include weight loss, anorexia, anemia (secondary to gastrointestinal bleeding), and chest pain.

Upper endoscopy with biopsy is the gold-standard diagnostic test. Adenocarcinoma is usually found in the distal esophagus, often as a mass, nodule, or abnormal mucosa. Squamous cell carcinoma is more commonly located in the proximal esophagus.

TNM staging is often done with endoscopic ultrasonography for locoregional disease and with CT and PET to identify metastatic disease. For treatment of esophageal carcinoma, see Gastroesophageal Cancer in Oncology. Superficial tumors that are limited to the mucosal lining (T1a), show no evidence of lymph node metastasis, and have low-risk features in terms of differentiation and lymphovascular invasion may be treated with endoscopic resection in an organ-sparing manner.

Dyspepsia is a term used to describe predominantly epigastric pain lasting at least 1 month; it may include associated early satiety, epigastric burning, nausea, and postprandial symptoms (pain, fullness, bloating, or belching). Heartburn may be present but is not a primary symptom; it may indicate coexisting gastroesophageal reflux. Although vomiting may be associated, recurrent vomiting should also raise concern for other conditions.

The list of possible organic causes of dyspepsia is extensive ( [Table: Table: Structural and Other Causes of Dyspepsia]

); the most common are peptic ulcer disease and gastroesophageal reflux disease (20% of patients with erosive esophagitis report dyspepsia). If no structural, organic, or metabolic causes of dyspepsia symptoms are identified after evaluation, the term functional dyspepsia applies.

Functional dyspepsia represents a heterogeneous group of gastrointestinal disorders predominated by one or more upper gastrointestinal symptoms (see [Table: Table: Rome IV Diagnostic Criteria for Functional Dyspepsia]

).

The evaluation of dyspepsia should be based on patient age, symptom severity, and gastric cancer risk. Upper endoscopy is commonly performed to exclude upper gastrointestinal neoplasia; however, it is invasive and costly. Given the low incidence of malignancy and consideration for cost-effectiveness in dyspepsia evaluation in younger adults, the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) and the Canadian Association of Gastroenterology (CAG) have jointly recommended routine use of upper endoscopy only in patients 60 years and older. The ACG/CAG guidelines recommend against routine use of upper endoscopy in patients younger than 60 years with dyspepsia, even in most patients with alarm features (weight loss, anemia, dysphagia, and vomiting) because these features poorly predict structural pathology, such as malignancy, peptic ulcer disease, or esophagitis. Endoscopy may be considered in younger patients at higher risk for malignancy, such as those with multiple or severe alarm features; those who have emigrated from regions with a high prevalence of malignancy (Asia, Russia, and South America); or those with a positive family history of gastric malignancy.

For patients younger than 60 years with dyspepsia symptoms, the ACG/CAG guidelines recommend noninvasive testing for Helicobacter pylori. Other testing, such as routine laboratory tests, screening for celiac disease, abdominal imaging, or gastric emptying, should be considered on an individual basis.

Management is directed at treating the cause. Patients who test positive for H. pylori should receive eradication therapy. If H. pylori results are negative or H. pylori eradication does not relieve the dyspepsia, an empiric trial of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) should be pursued. Patients diagnosed with functional dyspepsia can be treated with various interventions (see

).

Cyclic vomiting syndrome (CVS) is characterized by recurrent episodes of nausea and vomiting lasting for 1 to 6 days. Patients are asymptomatic between episodes. Although its pathogenesis is uncertain, CVS is associated with migraine headaches and autonomic abnormalities. All Rome IV clinical criteria must be fulfilled for clinical diagnosis:

  • Episodes of acute-onset vomiting lasting less than 1 week
  • At least 3 episodes in the previous year, with 2 episodes in the previous 6 months, occurring at least 1 week apart
  • Absence of vomiting between episodes

These criteria must have been present for the previous 3 months, with onset of symptoms at least 6 months before diagnosis. Symptoms must also not be attributable to another disorder.

Treatment is supportive; antimigraine triptans may assist in aborting acute episodes, and tricyclic medications may provide prophylactic benefit. Differential diagnosis of CVS includes cannabis hyperemesis syndrome, which typically improves with cannabis cessation.

The most frequently reported symptom of peptic ulcer disease (PUD) is epigastric pain, often described as worse during fasting and better with eating or use of antacid or antisecretory therapy. Pain may be accompanied by early satiety, abdominal bloating, nausea, belching, or heartburn. Other symptoms of PUD include nausea, vomiting, hematemesis, and melena. Symptoms may be minimal or absent in older adult patients, immunosuppressed patients, and patients receiving long-term NSAID therapy.

NSAIDs and H. pylori infection are the most common causes of PUD, although idiopathic (NSAID-negative, H. pylori–negative) PUD is increasingly seen in the United States as the incidence of H. pylori infection decreases. The causes of idiopathic PUD remain unclear; however, bisphosphonates, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, cocaine, methamphetamine, and stress have been implicated. Rare causes of PUD include the following:

  • Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome)
  • Systemic mastocytosis
  • α~1-Antitrypsin deficiency
  • COPD
  • Chronic kidney disease
  • Gastric cancer
  • Gastric lymphoma
  • Crohn disease
  • Eosinophilic gastritis
  • Herpes simplex virus
  • Behçet syndrome
  • Cytomegalovirus (in immunocompromised patients)

PUD is most often diagnosed by upper endoscopy (see

).

Complications include bleeding, perforation, and obstruction. Overt bleeding presents with melena, hematemesis, hematochezia, or a combination of these, whereas obscure bleeding may present with iron deficiency anemia or stool that is positive for occult blood. Perforation typically presents with sudden, severe epigastric pain that can become more generalized along with peritoneal findings. Abdominal CT is the diagnostic study of choice for suspected perforating PUD (sensitivity, 98%). Symptoms associated with obstruction may include vomiting, early satiety, abdominal distention, and weight loss.

Following confirmation of uncomplicated PUD, a once-daily PPI should be initiated and any agent causing PUD (such as an NSAID) should be discontinued. H. pylori infection should be treated if identified and eradication confirmed after treatment (see Helicobacter pylori Infection in Gastroenterology). When results of tests for H. pylori completed in the acute setting of upper gastrointestinal bleed are negative, testing should be repeated later.

Upper endoscopy should be performed within 24 hours in patients with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. In patients with bleeding PUD, there are factors that increase risk for recurrent bleeding and/or death (see Evaluation of Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding in Gastroenterology). Modifiable risks should be addressed before upper endoscopy. Nasogastric tube placement is not required before upper endoscopy. Use of PPIs before upper endoscopy may improve the endoscopic appearance of an ulcer and reduce the need for endoscopic therapy, but this approach lacks evidence in terms of clinical outcomes. A single infusion of erythromycin 30 to 90 minutes before endoscopy in a patient with acute gastrointestinal bleeding can improve visualization of the upper gastrointestinal tract.

For bleeding PUD related to aspirin used for secondary cardiovascular prevention, aspirin should generally not be withheld. If aspirin therapy is interrupted, it should be restarted immediately after hemostasis is endoscopically confirmed (see Postendoscopic Care in Gastroenterology). PPI therapy can be discontinued after confirmation of H. pylori eradication in patients with H. pylori–associated bleeding PUD. NSAIDs should be discontinued in patients with NSAID-induced bleeding PUD. If there is no effective alternative to NSAIDs, a selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitor plus a once-daily PPI should be used. Patients with idiopathic ulcers that have bled should receive once-daily PPI therapy indefinitely because of the substantial risk for rebleeding.

Repeat upper endoscopy to verify ulcer resolution should be reserved for patients who have persistent symptoms after 8 to 12 weeks of therapy, gastric ulcer greater than 2 cm, an ulcer of unknown cause, or who did not undergo gastric ulcer biopsy during initial upper endoscopy.

Perforated PUD is a surgical emergency, with a mortality rate of up to 30%; older age, comorbidity, and delayed surgery increase risk. Prompt identification, urgent surgical intervention, and proper preoperative and postoperative management of sepsis are essential. The cause of PUD (H. pylori or NSAIDs) should be addressed, and postoperative upper endoscopy to rule out gastric cancer should be considered.

Patients with gastric outlet obstruction from inflammation or scarring at the pylorus or proximal duodenum should have biopsy performed at diagnosis to exclude malignancy. For mild symptoms, PPI therapy, treatment of H. pylori infection (if identified), or cessation of NSAIDs may be effective (see Gastrointestinal Complications of NSAIDs in Gastroenterology). For severe or persistent symptoms, endoscopic dilation should be pursued, with surgery reserved for persistent obstruction following repeated attempts at endoscopic dilation.

Upper gastrointestinal complications can occur with short- or long-term NSAID use and are dose dependent, with a linear increase in incidence over time. Nearly 1% to 2% of patients taking long-term NSAID therapy experience a clinically significant upper gastrointestinal adverse event (bleeding ulcer, perforation, or obstruction) annually. The rate of upper gastrointestinal adverse events rises to 14% for NSAID users older than 60 years. The greatest risk factor for NSAID-related upper gastrointestinal complication is a history of gastrointestinal bleeding. See [Table: Table: Risk Factors for NSAID-Related Upper GI Complications]

.

Use of low-dose aspirin for cardioprophylaxis is associated with a twofold to fourfold increase in risk for upper gastrointestinal complications, including bleeding ulcer (see Pre-Endoscopic Care in Gastroenterology), perforation, and obstruction. Use of enteric-coated aspirin does not lower this risk, and an increase in aspirin dosage is associated with an increased risk for upper gastrointestinal complications. For a discussion of indications for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease with aspirin, see Aspirin for Primary Prevention in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

Prevention of NSAID-related upper gastrointestinal adverse events includes avoiding NSAIDs; addressing modifiable risk factors; coadministering gastroprotective agents, such as PPIs, misoprostol, or H~2-blockers; and using a selective cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibitor. PPIs are the preferred gastroprotective agent for the treatment and prophylaxis of NSAID-related (including aspirin-related) upper gastrointestinal complications and are superior to H~2-blockers for preventing PUD and bleeding related to low-dose aspirin use. Misoprostol may be used instead of PPIs in patients intolerant of or unwilling to take PPIs. Adverse effects of misoprostol, such as diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, and nausea, can be limiting, and the drug is contraindicated in pregnancy.

Selective COX-2 inhibitors are associated with decreased risk for gastrointestinal toxicity compared with NSAIDs, although the risk is still elevated. When coadministered with aspirin, however, a selective COX-2 inhibitor provides no advantage over an NSAID in preventing an upper gastrointestinal adverse event. Given the increased risk for PUD with concomitant use of an NSAID or selective COX-2 inhibitor with low-dose aspirin, persons at risk should receive gastroprotective therapy. Compared with an NSAID plus a PPI in patients at high risk, a selective COX-2 inhibitor plus a PPI offers a lower risk for adverse events.

After an NSAID-induced bleeding peptic ulcer, the safest strategy is avoidance of future NSAID use. If an NSAID must be used, a selective COX-2 inhibitor combined with a PPI provides the best gastrointestinal protection to prevent rebleeding.

Indications for H. pylori testing include:

  • PUD, either active or a history of PUD without documented cure of H. pylori infection
  • Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma
  • Dyspepsia
  • Adults residing in same household as person with H. pylori infection
  • Before initiating long-term low-dose aspirin or in those taking long-term NSAIDs
  • Unexplained iron deficiency anemia
  • Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
  • Primary and secondary prevention of gastric adenocarcinoma
    • Presence or history of gastric premalignant conditions
  • Presence of history of early gastric cancer resection
  • Presence or history of gastric adenocarcinoma
  • Presence or history of gastric adenomas or hyperplastic polyps
  • First-degree relative with gastric cancer
  • Patients at increased risk for gastric cancer (e.g., certain high-risk racial/ethnic groups, immigrants from regions with high gastric cancer incidence, those with hereditary cancer syndromes associated with gastric cancer; see Gastric Intestinal Metaplasia in Gastroenterology and Gastric Adenocarcinoma in Gastroenterology)
  • Patients with autoimmune gastritis

Routine testing for H. pylori is not indicated in patients with typical gastroesophageal reflux disease symptoms, lymphocytic gastritis, or hyperemesis gravidarum.

H. pylori infection can be diagnosed with gastric biopsies during upper endoscopy or noninvasively by ^13C-urea breath, stool antigen, or serologic testing. The ^13C-urea breath test and the monoclonal stool antigen test are preferred noninvasive tests because sensitivity and specificity exceed 95% for active infection. Serologic testing for IgG antibodies against H. pylori is the cheapest and most convenient method; however, it cannot distinguish between active and previous infection. Although the negative predictive value of serologic testing is reasonably high, a positive serologic result in a population with low prevalence of H. pylori infection, such as in the United States, may require confirmation with the ^13C-urea breath test, stool antigen test, or gastric biopsy. Conditions that lower H. pylori density, such as PPI use, recent antibiotic use, atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, or MALT lymphoma, can result in false-negative results on the noninvasive studies. Upper endoscopy to evaluate dyspepsia should include gastric biopsy for H. pylori testing.

In patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding, invasive testing with gastric biopsies for H. pylori has decreased sensitivity; a negative biopsy result in this setting does not exclude H. pylori infection and requires confirmation. The ^13C-urea breath test or stool antigen test is recommended for confirmation but should be performed 2 weeks after the patient has stopped PPI therapy in order to mitigate false-negative results. Serologic testing may be useful as an adjunct test in patients with bleeding PUD because this population has a high pretest probability of H. pylori infection.

Active H. pylori infection requires treatment with the goal of eradication. The first course of treatment offers the best chance of eradication and should be carefully chosen. Several first-line treatments are available, with the choice based on resistance patterns of H. pylori, previous antibiotic use by the patient, and antibiotic allergies. Therapy duration is 14 days. When treatment fails, salvage therapy should last for 14 days, using a new regimen different from that used for initial treatment (see [Table: Table: Treatment for Helicobacter pylori Infection]

).

At least 4 weeks after completion of eradication therapy, with PPI therapy cessation for at least 2 weeks, H. pylori eradication should be evaluated by using a ^13C-urea breath test, fecal antigen test, or gastric biopsy during indicated upper endoscopy. Serologic testing is not used to confirm H. pylori eradication because results can remain positive following successful eradication.

Erosive gastropathy can result from exposure to medications and toxins, including NSAIDs, iron, and alcohol. Ischemia and portal hypertension (e.g., gastric antral vascular ectasia) are additional causes. Although erosive gastropathy may result in gastrointestinal bleeding, it rarely causes clinically significant bleeding.

Eosinophilic gastritis is a rare gastropathy characterized by infiltration of eosinophils in the gastric mucosa. Secondary causes of eosinophilia should first be excluded, including parasitic and bacterial infections of the stomach, inflammatory bowel disease, hypereosinophilic syndrome, myeloproliferative disorders, polyarteritis nodosa, allergic vasculitis, systemic sclerosis, drug injury, and drug hypersensitivity. The cause of primary eosinophilic gastritis is unknown but is believed to be an allergic or immune-mediated process. Symptoms vary widely based on depth of eosinophilia (e.g., mucosal, muscularis, serosal) and other gastrointestinal tract involvement. Treatment includes elimination diets, glucocorticoids, and potentially novel biologic agents.

Lymphocytic gastritis is a rare gastropathy typically presenting with nonspecific dyspeptic symptoms and a normal-appearing stomach on endoscopy. On occasion, the stomach may have thickened folds covered by small nodules and aphthous ulceration. Celiac disease is the most common cause of lymphocytic gastritis. Other causes include HIV infection, Crohn disease, common variable immunodeficiency, and, rarely, H. pylori infection.

Gastroparesis is a heterogeneous clinical syndrome characterized by the presence of specific symptoms, absence of mechanical outlet obstruction, and objective evidence of delay in gastric emptying into the duodenum. The most common symptoms are nausea (90%), vomiting (84%), upper abdominal pain (72%), and early satiety (60%). Other symptoms may include abdominal fullness and bloating. Symptoms may be chronic or persistent or may occur intermittently. More severe cases may involve weight loss and evidence of malnutrition or dehydration. A viral prodrome, such as gastroenteritis or respiratory infection before symptom onset, may suggest postviral gastroparesis, a condition that can resolve over time. Gastroparesis has a variety of causes ( [Table: Table: Causes of Gastroparesis]

).

The first study to evaluate suspected gastroparesis is upper endoscopy to exclude gastric outlet obstruction. After a structural cause for symptoms has been excluded, an objective test to assess gastric emptying is performed ( [Table: Table: Diagnostic Tests Assessing Gastric Emptying]

). Gastric scintigraphy, the standard test for evaluating gastroparesis, assesses the emptying of a solid meal for at least 3 hours. Opioids, cannabinoids, prokinetics, antiemetics, and neuromodulators with potential impact on the results of the gastric emptying test should be stopped at least 48 hours before testing. When delayed emptying is objectively confirmed, additional testing may be required to determine the cause of the gastroparesis.

Symptom severity does not correlate with severity of delayed gastric emptying, particularly regarding abdominal bloating and epigastric pain. This suggests that gastroparesis is not simply a motility disorder but also a disorder of altered sensation (and may be interchangeable with functional dyspepsia). Initial management includes correcting dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities along with nutritional support, if needed. Initial dietary intervention should consist of small, frequent meals that are low in fat and soluble fiber. Referral to a dietitian may be beneficial. In diabetic gastroparesis, poor glycemic control (blood glucose level >200 mg/dL [11.1 mmol/L]) can worsen symptoms as well as gastric emptying, and tight glycemic control is the most important element of treatment.

Initial management of gastroparesis includes correction of dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities and repletion of micronutrient and vitamin deficiencies. Some patients may require hospitalization for severe symptoms, and mechanical gastric outlet obstruction should be excluded with endoscopy or CT imaging, if not previously performed. Antiemetic options for symptom control include 5-HT~3 antagonists, dopamine antagonists, and antihistamines. Medications that impair gastric emptying should be discontinued if possible.

Initial dietary intervention should consist of small, frequent meals that are low in fat and soluble fiber. Patients with more severe symptoms may require blenderized foods. Referral to a dietitian may be beneficial. If oral intake is insufficient, then enteral nutrition with a nasojejunal feeding tube should be trialed.

In diabetic gastroparesis, poor glycemic control (blood glucose level >200 mg/dL [11.1 mmol/L]) can worsen symptoms as well as gastric emptying, and tight glycemic control is the most important element of treatment.

Prokinetic therapy is used to improve gastric emptying and treat symptoms. Metoclopramide is the only prokinetic agent approved in the United States for treatment of gastroparesis. To minimize the significant risk for neurologic adverse effects (dystonia, parkinsonian movements, tardive dyskinesia), the lowest effective dose should be used. Therapy must be stopped immediately if neurologic adverse effects develop.

Erythromycin improves gastric emptying but should be limited to short-term use or treatment of flares (2-3 weeks) because of the development of tachyphylaxis. Intravenous erythromycin is an effective option for hospitalized patients with acute exacerbations.

Acupuncture, alone or in combination with a prokinetic agent, may be beneficial in the treatment of diabetic gastroparesis. Abdominal pain should be treated without the use of opioids (i.e., using central neuromodulators instead).

Interventional therapy, such as enteral feeding through jejunostomy, adjunctive venting gastrostomy tube, gastric stimulator placement, gastric peroral endoscopic myotomy, pyloroplasty, and subtotal or total gastrectomy, can be considered in patients who do not respond to dietary and pharmacologic therapy.

Polyps in the stomach include fundic gland polyps, hyperplastic polyps, and adenomas (see [Table: Table: Features of Gastric Polyps]

). All gastric polyps should be biopsied to determine polyp histology. Fundic gland polyps and hyperplastic polyps account for 70% to 90% of stomach polyps. Multiple fundic gland polyps are also found in patients with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP).

Hyperplastic polyps of the stomach are thought to have malignant potential. Risk factors for malignant potential of hyperplastic polyps include size greater than 1 cm and pedunculated morphology. Hyperplastic polyps greater than 1 cm should be considered on an individualized basis for resection.

Adenomas in the stomach can be sporadic or associated with hereditary syndromes, including FAP and Lynch syndrome, and should be resected regardless of size. Endoscopic surveillance should be performed within 1 year after resection; subsequent surveillance depends on mucosal findings.

Chronic atrophic gastritis can present as environmental metaplastic atrophic gastritis, also called multifocal atrophic gastritis, or as autoimmune atrophic gastritis. Environmental metaplastic atrophic gastritis results from H. pylori infection and may improve after H. pylori eradication. Autoimmune atrophic gastritis is caused by formation of autoantibody to parietal cell antigens and is commonly associated with pernicious anemia. The achlorhydria from chronic atrophic gastritis can lead to iron deficiency, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, and enteric infections. The hypergastrinemia associated with autoimmune atrophic gastritis can promote development of gastric neuroendocrine tumors. Goals of therapy for autoimmune atrophic gastritis include preventing pernicious anemia and iron deficiency with vitamin B~12 supplementation and iron replacement along with surveillance for gastric neoplasm. See Cobalamin Deficiency in Hematology for further discussion of pernicious anemia in the setting of autoimmune gastritis. Screening upper endoscopy with gastric biopsy is recommended for patients with pernicious anemia. Individuals with histologically confirmed moderate to severe atrophic gastritis with or without gastric intestinal metaplasia are likely to benefit from endoscopic surveillance, and it should be considered at an interval of every 3 years.

Gastric intestinal metaplasia is a preneoplastic gastropathy frequently arising from chronic inflammation associated with H. pylori infection. As such, patients with gastric intestinal metaplasia should be tested for H. pylori and then treated if the infection is identified. Other causes of chronic inflammation, including other gastric infections, chemical agents, and autoimmune diseases, may also promote progression to gastric intestinal metaplasia. No conclusive evidence shows that long-term PPI use promotes development of intestinal metaplasia. Gastric intestinal metaplasia is considered an intermediary stage in the multistage progression from chronic atrophic gastritis to gastric adenocarcinoma. If metaplasia is secondary to H. pylori infection, eradication therapy may decrease progression to gastric adenocarcinoma.

Given the rarity of gastric adenocarcinoma in the United States, guidelines recommend against the routine use of surveillance endoscopy in gastric intestinal metaplasia. With shared decision making, surveillance endoscopy every 3 years should be considered in patients with gastric intestinal metaplasia at increased risk, such as the following:

  • High-risk histology
    • Incomplete gastric intestinal metaplasia

  • Corpus extension (corpus involvement with simultaneous antrum or incisura involvement)

  • Any gastric intestinal metaplasia histology with one of the following risk factors for gastric cancer:

    • Family history of gastric cancer in a first-degree relative
  • Birth in or emigration from a high-incidence nation
  • Race or ethnicity with high risk, including East Asian, Latino, Black, and American Indian and Alaska Native

Intestinal metaplasia with any form of dysplasia should be resected.

Stomach adenocarcinoma has an overall low incidence in the United States; however, specific U.S. populations, such as individuals who have immigrated from countries with high gastric cancer incidence, have significantly higher gastric cancer incidence rates. Intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma is more common than diffuse-type gastric cancer. H. pylori is a recognized risk factor for both types and is the primary nongenetic risk factor for gastric cancer. Other risks are described in [Table: Table: Intestinal-type Gastric Adenocarcinoma Risk Factors]

.

There is no recommendation for routine population-based screening for gastric adenocarcinoma in countries with a low incidence of gastric cancer, such as the United States. However, the AGA recommends consideration of gastric cancer screening for patients aged 45 years and older with the following:

  • Emigration from areas with a moderate to high incidence of gastric cancer (e.g., Eastern Europe, Andean Latin America, and East Asia)
  • Family history of gastric cancer in a first-degree relative (screening should begin 10 years earlier than the age at diagnosis of the youngest affected relative)
  • Belonging to racial/ethnic group with a moderate to high incidence of gastric cancer (e.g., East Asian, Latino, Black, and American Indian and Alaska Native)
  • History of H. Pylori infection and one of the following

    • 20 pack-year history of tobacco smoking

  • Diet high in salt, red meat, or processed meats and foods

  • Those living in persistent poverty in the United States

  • Presence of an inherited gastric cancer syndrome (familial adenomatous polyposis, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, juvenile polyposis, MUTYH-associated polyposis, gastric adenocarcinoma, and proximal polyposis of the stomach) or hereditary cancer syndromes (Lynch syndrome, hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome, Li-Fraumeni syndrome)

Symptoms of gastric adenocarcinoma may be vague. They include poor appetite, weight loss, abdominal pain, early satiety, nausea, and vomiting. Iron deficiency anemia may be a sign of gastric adenocarcinoma. Upper endoscopy with biopsy is the diagnostic test of choice for gastric cancer.

For management of gastric cancer, see Gastroesophageal Cancer in Oncology.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) are the most common mesenchymal tumors of the stomach. GISTs may present with bleeding, obstruction, or abdominal pain but are usually found incidentally. Endoscopic ultrasonography is the best diagnostic modality for evaluation of a GIST. High-risk features on endoscopic ultrasonography include size greater than 2 cm, lobulated or irregular borders, invasion into adjacent structures, and heterogeneity. A GIST can be biopsied, but the high-risk endoscopic features are excellent predictors of malignant potential. Treatment consists of surgical or endoscopic excision if the GIST is symptomatic or high-risk features are present (

). For GISTs without high-risk features, yearly endoscopic surveillance is indicated. See Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors in Oncology for treatment of GISTs.

Neuroendocrine tumors (NETs; formerly called carcinoid tumors) are well-differentiated lesions that can be encountered throughout the gastrointestinal tract, including the stomach. These tumors are usually sporadic but can be seen in the setting of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and atrophic gastritis. They may present symptomatically or may be found incidentally. See Neuroendocrine Tumors in Oncology for management of gastrointestinal NETs.

For complications of bariatric surgery, see Postoperative Care for Bariatric Surgery in Endocrinology and Metabolism.

Partial or complete gastric resections are performed for benign and malignant disease. The extent of resection, type of reconstruction, and nature of the disease affect postoperative morbidity and mortality. Partial resection preserves some function of the stomach, but patients with malignancy require lifelong surveillance of the remaining stomach for recurrence. Patients who undergo partial gastrectomy for benign disease also have an increased risk for cancer in the gastric remnant 15 to 20 years after surgery, with reported frequency of 0.8% to 8.9%.

Dumping syndrome, which results from rapid gastric emptying after gastric surgery, can cause significant postprandial gastrointestinal and vasomotor symptoms. Clinical features of early dumping syndrome occur within 30 minutes of eating because of gastrointestinal hormone hypersecretion, autonomic dysregulation, and bowel distention. Symptoms include palpitations, flushing or pallor, diaphoresis, light-headedness, hypotension, and fatigue, followed by diarrhea, nausea, abdominal bloating, cramping, and borborygmus. Symptoms of late dumping syndrome occur 1 to 3 hours after meals because of reactive hypoglycemia and can include difficulty concentrating, faintness, and altered consciousness. In severe cases, protein-wasting malnutrition can occur.

Approximately 25% to 50% of all patients who have undergone gastric surgery experience some symptoms of dumping syndrome, but severe symptoms are persistent in only 10%. Oral glucose challenge testing is helpful, with a sensitivity of nearly 100% and a specificity of 94%.

First-line treatment for dumping syndrome is dietary, with smaller, more frequent meals and ingestion of liquids after meals. Decreasing simple carbohydrates and increasing protein, complex carbohydrate, and fiber intake may also alleviate symptoms.

Acarbose, an α-glucosidase inhibitor, can be used for late symptoms of dumping syndrome. Other pharmacologic therapies include anticholinergics to slow gastric emptying and antispasmodics. Severe cases may rarely require octreotide. If a trial of subcutaneous injections is effective, long-acting monthly intramuscular injections can be used.
