Disorders of the Pancreas

Acute pancreatitis is an inflammatory process involving the pancreas and extrapancreatic organs and is the most common gastrointestinal cause of hospitalization in the United States. Biliary disease, including gallstones, biliary sludge, and biliary crystals (microlithiasis), is the most common cause of acute pancreatitis (see [Table: Table: Causes of Acute Pancreatitis]

). Premature activation of digestive enzymes and release of cytokines cause autodigestion of the pancreas and inflammation, which may involve surrounding tissues and distant organs.

Acute pancreatitis is classified as mild, moderately severe, or severe. Mild acute pancreatitis does not involve organ failure or other complications, usually resolves within 1 week, and has a low mortality rate. Moderately severe or severe disease occurs in 20% of patients with acute pancreatitis. Moderately severe disease involves local or systemic complications, such as necrosis or organ failure lasting less than 48 hours. Severe acute pancreatitis is associated with a mortality rate as high as 50% and involves persistent organ failure (shock, kidney or respiratory failure, or gastrointestinal bleeding that lasts longer than 48 hours) or death.

The diagnosis of acute pancreatitis requires two of the following three criteria:

  • Acute-onset abdominal pain characteristic of pancreatitis (usually severe, persistent for hours to days, and epigastric or left upper quadrant in location, often radiating to the back, chest, or flanks)
  • Serum lipase or amylase levels elevated to at least three times the upper limit of normal
  • Characteristic imaging findings (see

)

High fever and leukocytosis are part of the cytokine cascade and do not necessarily indicate infection.

Patients with acute pancreatitis should undergo transabdominal ultrasonography to assess for gallstones and biliary duct obstruction. Transabdominal ultrasonography is preferred over CT because it has a higher sensitivity for detecting gallstones, avoids the risks of intravenous contrast material, and is more cost effective. Although less useful for assessing the biliary system, CT may be indicated if the diagnosis is in question, to exclude other fatal causes of abdominal pain (e.g., perforation), or if clinical symptoms do not improve within the first 48 to 72 hours. Pancreatic necrosis will not be visible until after 72 hours. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) may be considered in patients without abnormal findings on ultrasonography when concern remains for concomitant biliary disease; however, its use may be limited by availability.

A serum alanine aminotransferase level greater than 150 U/L suggests gallstone pancreatitis. Hyperbilirubinemia should raise suspicion of biliary obstruction or cholangitis.

Serum amylase and lipase levels may be elevated in conditions other than acute pancreatitis, such as the following:

  • Kidney disease
  • Acute appendicitis
  • Cholecystitis
  • Intestinal obstruction or ischemia
  • Peptic ulcer
  • Gynecologic disorders

Enzyme levels may be falsely low or normal in patients with hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis because of lipemic-serum interference with laboratory assays. Triglyceride levels should be measured in patients without a biliary cause of acute pancreatitis; a triglyceride level exceeding 1000 mg/dL (11.3 mmol/L) can be considered the cause of the acute pancreatitis.

Risk factors for severe disease include the following:

  • Age older than 55 years
  • Medical comorbidities
  • BMI greater than 30
  • SIRS
  • Signs of hypovolemia on presentation (e.g., serum blood urea nitrogen level >20 mg/dL [7.1 mmol/L] and rising, hematocrit >44%, or elevated serum creatinine level)
  • Pleural effusions or infiltrates
  • Altered mental status

A systematic review of 18 multiple-factor scoring systems, including the Ranson criteria and the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) II score, for predicting outcome in acute pancreatitis found these systems to have limited clinical value and accuracy. Scoring systems identify severe disease only as it develops, without enough lead time for intervention, and they are too cumbersome for routine use. Elevated hematocrit, elevated blood urea nitrogen levels, and the presence of SIRS are as accurate as complex scoring systems in predicting outcome, and they are easier to use.

Mainstays of initial management include fluid resuscitation, pain management, and antiemetics.

Early and moderate fluid resuscitation (1.5 mL/kg/h of intravenous normal saline or, preferably, lactated Ringer solution) should be given to patients with acute pancreatitis at presentation and is most beneficial in the first 12 to 24 hours. More rapid fluid resuscitation (boluses of 10 mL/kg) may be needed in patients with hypovolemia. Careful monitoring for fluid overload should be pursued during resuscitation. Patients with organ failure or SIRS should be admitted to an ICU or intermediary care setting, with fluid requirements reassessed every 6 hours for the first 24 to 48 hours.

Routine use of antibiotics is not warranted in acute pancreatitis unless there is evidence of extrapancreatic infection, such as ascending cholangitis, bacteremia, urinary tract infection, or pneumonia. Use of prophylactic antibiotics in patients with uninstrumented, sterile pancreatic necrosis to prevent infected necrosis is not recommended.

In mild acute pancreatitis, oral feedings can be started as soon as nausea and vomiting are controlled and clinical symptoms improve (typically within 24 to 48 hours). Enteral feeding should begin within 72 hours if oral feeding is not tolerated; it is usually required in patients with moderately severe or severe acute pancreatitis. Data suggest that nasogastric feedings are as effective and safe as feeding with a nasojejunal tube, and nasogastric feedings are therefore preferred. Enteral feeding promotes a healthy gut-mucosal barrier and may prevent translocation of bacteria into inflamed tissues. In patients with acute pancreatitis, total parenteral nutrition is associated with increased mortality, multiple organ failure, and systemic infection; therefore, oral or enteral feeding is preferred.

If a biliary cause of acute pancreatitis is suspected, serial liver chemistry tests and clinical symptoms can determine whether the biliary obstruction is ongoing or resolving. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is not indicated in patients with gallstone pancreatitis unless there is persistent biochemical evidence of biliary obstruction or choledocholithiasis is seen on imaging. Patients with cholangitis should undergo ERCP within 24 hours of admission. MRCP or endoscopic ultrasonography can be useful in patients with persistent elevation of liver chemistries without overt cholangitis or biliary obstruction. Patients with uncomplicated gallstone pancreatitis should be considered for cholecystectomy before discharge.

After the diagnosis is established, rechecking serum amylase and lipase levels has no value.

There are two overlapping phases of acute pancreatitis with two peaks in mortality. The early phase occurs in the first week of the disease because of local pancreatic injury and the cytokine cascade; SIRS, organ failure (especially kidney and respiratory failure), and profound hypocalcemia are possible. The late phase takes place after the first week and may persist for weeks to months in patients with moderate or severe acute pancreatitis. Significant risk for infection in peripancreatic fluid collections and necrotic tissue occurs in the late phase.

Proper classification of fluid collections in acute pancreatitis is important to guide management. There are four types of fluid collections:

  • Acute peripancreatic fluid collections occur in edematous interstitial pancreatitis (no necrosis) within the first 4 weeks, are thought to result from rupture of main or side-branch ducts because of inflammation, are sterile, and usually resolve spontaneously.
  • Pancreatic pseudocysts are acute peripancreatic fluid collections that have persisted for longer than 4 weeks, have developed a well-defined wall, and contain no solid debris (necrosis).
  • Acute necrotic collections (see

) are areas of necrosis in the pancreatic parenchyma or peripancreatic tissues within the first 4 weeks of acute pancreatitis. - Walled-off necrosis (see

) occurs after 4 weeks, when the body liquefies the necrosis and contains it within a well-defined wall.

Contrast-enhanced CT may not be able to distinguish solid from liquid content in fluid collections; therefore, necrotic collections are frequently misdiagnosed as pancreatic pseudocysts. Pancreatic pseudocysts do not require drainage unless they cause significant symptoms or are infected, regardless of size.

Because they contain only fluid, pseudocysts are easily drained under endoscopic or radiographic guidance. Walled-off necrosis is not as amenable to percutaneous or endoscopic drainage alone because of solid necrotic debris within the cavity and may require endoscopic or surgical debridement.

The management of suspected infected necrosis includes antibiotics (e.g., imipenem-cilastatin, meropenem, or ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole), with consideration of CT-guided fine-needle aspiration followed by Gram stain and culture. Drainage procedures or debridement should be delayed for at least 4 weeks if possible to allow encapsulation of the necrosis with a fibrous wall.

Chronic pancreatitis is thought to develop when the inflammatory response to acute pancreatitis persists and ongoing inflammation activates stellate cells, resulting in a fibro-inflammatory response. This causes distorted tissue architecture, loss of normal parenchyma, activation of pancreatic nociceptors, and loss of acinar and islet cell function. Genetic variants affecting inflammatory response, enzyme activation, and tissue repair are thought to play important roles in the pathogenesis of chronic pancreatitis. Many genes have been identified as disease modifiers, but the gene-environment interaction is not fully understood.

Alcohol use has long been described as a risk factor for chronic pancreatitis, but less than 3% of heavy alcohol users develop pancreatic disease. Patients who consume more than five drinks per day (or 35 drinks per week) seem to be more susceptible to chronic pancreatitis. In the largest study of patients with chronic pancreatitis in North America, 46% had a history of significant alcohol use. The higher prevalence of alcohol-associated pancreatitis among men could be partially explained by an X chromosome–linked genetic variant, the CLDN2 gene. Tobacco is considered an independent risk factor. See [Table: Table: Causes of Chronic Pancreatitis]

.

Abdominal pain is the most common presenting symptom of chronic pancreatitis (seen in 85% of patients). Pain patterns can vary from constant daily pain to intermittent episodes of severe pain. Pancreatic enzyme levels may not increase during attacks of pain because of fibrosis and atrophy of acinar cells and decreased enzyme production. Constant daily pain in chronic pancreatitis significantly reduces quality of life, with increased use of health care resources and disability benefits and time away from employment. Exocrine or endocrine insufficiency occurs in some patients as a result of significant tissue destruction.

Diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis remains challenging because hallmark anatomic features, such as pancreatic calcifications (

), occur in only 25% of patients, and other features of atrophy or duct dilation can occur normally with aging or other disease processes. CT or MRI is the initial test of choice. In the setting of high clinical suspicion and negative findings on imaging, endoscopic ultrasonography and secretin-enhanced MRCP may be useful as second- and third-line tests; pancreatic biopsy may rarely be necessary. ERCP is no longer used as a diagnostic tool for chronic pancreatitis. Genetic testing for cystic fibrosis and familial pancreatitis should be considered in younger patients. Pancreatic exocrine function may be assessed with fecal elastase testing, which has largely replaced fecal fat testing.

Management focuses on treating symptoms. No effective treatment exists to reverse or halt disease progression. Patients should be counseled to avoid alcohol and tobacco to prevent further damage and decrease attacks of inflammation and pain.

Intermittent attacks of severe acute pain are treated as acute pancreatitis. Possible complications of chronic pancreatitis, including pseudocyst formation, obstructing pancreatic duct stones, and malignancy, should be evaluated with imaging (e.g., pancreatic-protocol CT or MRCP) when a patient’s symptom pattern changes. ERCP is often first-line therapy for relief of ductal obstruction, although surgery may provide the best long-term relief.

Constant daily pain is more challenging to manage; treatment frequently involves medications such as tramadol, serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, gabapentinoids, and opioids. Long-term use of opioids should be avoided because of hyperesthesia and development of tolerance or addiction. Pancreatic enzymes are used to treat steatorrhea but do not effectively treat pain or prevent attacks of pancreatitis. Two large randomized trials of antioxidants to treat chronic pancreatitis pain showed conflicting results; guidelines suggest that antioxidants be considered, although it is unclear which antioxidants and doses are appropriate. Nerve blocks and neurolysis procedures are also recommended, although the response rate is low, and pain relief, if achieved, lasts only a few weeks (see [Table: Table: Surgeries for Refractory Pain in Chronic Pancreatitis]

). These procedures improve outcomes in patients at high-volume pancreas referral centers.

Pancreatic endocrine insufficiency may require specialty referral for labile diabetes management.

Autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP) is a frequent manifestation of IgG4-related disease. Other conditions and organs associated with IgG4-related disease are listed in [Table: Table: Conditions Associated With IgG4-Related Disease]

. Storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis are seen in the pancreas and biliary tract.

Type 1 AIP is the most common pancreatic manifestation of IgG4-related disease, with abundant infiltration of IgG4-positive plasma cells and lymphocytes; in contrast, type 2 AIP is characterized by no or few IgG4-positive cells. The 2011 International Consensus of Diagnostic Criteria for Autoimmune Pancreatitis endorsed the concept of type 1 and type 2 disease, but there is some debate over whether type 2 AIP should be considered an IgG4-related disease.

For more information on IgG4-related disease, see IgG4-Related Disease in Rheumatology.

Patients with both types of AIP may present with abdominal pain or obstructive jaundice with or without a mass. In patients presenting with obstructive jaundice or with a mass, pancreatic malignancy must be considered. Many patients with malignancy have a dilated upstream main pancreatic duct. In contrast, patients with AIP may have a narrowed main pancreatic duct or parenchymal swelling (“sausage-shaped” pancreas [

]). Endoscopic ultrasonography and biopsy may be required to differentiate AIP and pancreatic neoplasm. Ten percent of patients with type 1 AIP may develop chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic stone formation.

Patients with type 1 AIP have elevated numbers of IgG4-positive cells in pancreatic tissue (>10 IgG4-positive cells/hpf), and 60% to 80% of patients have associated sclerosing cholangitis, sclerosing sialadenitis, or retroperitoneal fibrosis. Fulfillment of one or more of the HISORt criteria (diagnostic Histology, suggestive Imaging, Serology with elevated serum IgG4, Other organ involvement, and Response to therapy with glucocorticoids) can be helpful in the diagnosis of type 1 AIP.

Type 2 AIP is characterized by idiopathic duct-centric neutrophil infiltration, known as a granulocytic epithelial lesion. Type 2 AIP is a pancreas-specific disease but is occasionally associated with inflammatory bowel disease.

Glucocorticoids are an effective treatment for types 1 and 2 AIP, starting with oral prednisolone at 0.6 to 1.0 mg/kg/d and tapered over 2 to 3 months. Response is determined by symptom relief and resolution of imaging features. Failure of clinical symptoms to respond to glucocorticoids suggests an incorrect diagnosis, and other causes should be investigated. Up to 60% of patients may relapse. Glucocorticoids or immunomodulators, such as 6-mercaptopurine, azathioprine, mycophenolate, or rituximab, are options to treat recurrent AIP.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma has a poor prognosis and increasing incidence. In the United States in 2022, there were approximately 62,000 cases diagnosed and nearly 50,000 deaths. It is predicted to become the second leading cause of cancer-related death in the United States over the next decade, with an overall 5-year survival rate of 11%. See [Table: Table: Risk Factors for Pancreatic Cancer]

.

Clinicians should not screen persons at average risk for pancreatic cancer; however, surveillance is recommended for select patients at elevated risk, preferably in a high-volume center. Patients with pathogenic germline variants in BRCA1/2, ATM, or PALB2 or those with Lynch syndrome and a family history of pancreatic cancer are candidates at age 50 years (or 5-10 years earlier than earliest pancreatic cancer diagnosis in the family). Surveillance is also recommended in those with a strong family history (familial pancreatic cancer) or in persons with familial atypical multiple-mole melanoma, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, or hereditary pancreatitis. Typically, endoscopic ultrasonography alternating annually with MRI with MRCP is recommended.

To identify hereditary risk, germline genetic testing is recommended for all patients with pancreatic cancer. First-degree relatives are also candidates for testing.

Symptoms of pancreatic adenocarcinoma include abdominal pain, back pain, weight loss, and jaundice (if the lesion obstructs the common bile duct). Pancreatic cancer is associated with diabetes mellitus, and two thirds of patients develop new-onset type 2 diabetes in the 36 months surrounding the diagnosis. Venous thromboembolic events and depression occur at higher rates in patients with pancreatic adenocarcinoma than in patients with other malignancies.

Pancreatic-protocol CT uses multiphasic arterial and venous phases with thin cuts (3 mm) through the abdomen to view the primary tumor’s relationship to mesenteric vasculature and to detect metastatic lesions. Some studies suggest that pancreatic-protocol MRI may be superior to CT for pancreatic disease.

Histopathologic confirmation of pancreatic adenocarcinoma is increasingly recommended before initiation of therapy. Endoscopic ultrasonography–guided fine-needle aspiration or biopsy is recommended for histologic confirmation of cancer.

Patients are considered for primary surgical resection if they have no involvement of mesenteric vasculature or metastatic disease and are healthy enough for major intra-abdominal surgery.

For staging and treatment of pancreatic cancer, see Pancreatic Cancer in Oncology.

Pancreatic cysts are found incidentally in 15% of patients undergoing abdominal imaging. The detection of a cystic lesion in the pancreas causes anxiety in patients and clinicians and is a growing driver of health care use in the United States.

Cystic neoplasms of the pancreas are subcategorized as mucin-producing and non–mucin-producing (

). Mucin-producing cysts, including intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms and mucinous cystic neoplasms, are thought to have malignant potential, but many never become malignant. Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms are the most common cystic lesions of the pancreas. Most intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms arise from a side branch of the pancreatic duct and have a low rate of malignant transformation. In contrast, the rate of malignant transformation is as high as 65% in intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms involving the main pancreatic duct (see

). Other high-risk features are presence of symptoms (jaundice, pancreatitis), cyst size greater than 3 cm, dilated main pancreatic duct, and a solid cyst component.

Mucinous cystic neoplasms are seen almost exclusively in women (>98%) and found in the pancreas body or tail in 90% of cases; they have a higher malignant potential than intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms. A thick fibrous capsule with epithelioid cells (similar to ovarian stroma) surrounds the tumor.

Serous cystadenoma, a non–mucin-producing cyst, possesses minimal risk for malignant potential and can often be identified by its characteristic imaging features. Serous cystic tumors require no further evaluation unless symptomatic. The rare non–mucin-producing solid pseudopapillary neoplasm (found most often in young women) is thought to have a moderate to high risk for malignant transformation, and surgical resection should be considered.

Differentiating mucinous cysts from serous cysts, pseudocysts, and cystic neuroendocrine tumors of the pancreas can be challenging because there is no definitive test with high sensitivity and specificity. Endoscopic ultrasonography with fine-needle aspiration is used for cyst fluid analysis in worrisome lesions; cyst fluid carcinoembryonic antigen levels are frequently elevated in patients with mucinous cysts, whereas cyst amylase levels are often elevated in patients with pseudocysts. Cytology of cyst fluid has a low sensitivity (<60%) to detect malignancy because of the low cellularity of cyst fluid.

Surgical resection of high-risk cysts, including intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms involving the main duct, is the only curative treatment option. Several guidelines on surveillance of pancreatic cystic neoplasms have been published, with differing recommendations based on target populations, clinical variables (symptomatic or asymptomatic), and initial and long-term surveillance recommendations.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) are rare, representing 3% of primary pancreatic neoplasms. About 10% to 25% of pancreatic NETs are functional and hypersecrete hormones, most commonly gastrin or insulin. Gastrinomas are usually sporadic but may be associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1. Excessive gastrin secretion by gastrinomas results in severe dyspepsia and reflux, peptic ulcer disease, and/or diarrhea responsive to proton pump inhibitor therapy. Evaluation for gastrinoma includes fasting serum gastrin level, measured after discontinuation of proton pump inhibitor or histamine type 2 receptor agonist therapy; to reduce risks for rebound gastric hypersecretion, endoscopy is performed to exclude active peptic disease before tapering off antisecretory therapy. See Neuroendocrine Tumors in Oncology for further discussion.

Adenocarcinoma of the ampulla of Vater accounts for 0.2% of gastrointestinal malignancies and usually presents with obstruction of the biliary system. Endoscopic ultrasonography with biopsy is the preferred method for staging and tissue diagnosis. At least 50% of patients with familial adenomatous polyposis syndrome develop adenomas in the periampullary region, which may progress to adenocarcinoma. Ampullary adenomas with and without dysplasia are resected by endoscopic ampullectomy. Invasive adenocarcinoma require surgical resection. See Adenomatous Polyposis Syndromes in Gastroenterology for more information.

Colorectal Neoplasia

Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer and second most common cause of cancer-related mortality among men and women in the United States. There are approximately 150,000 new cases in the United States annually, and lifetime risk for colorectal cancer is 4.1%.

The incidence and mortality for colorectal cancer have decreased over the past 30 years because of changes in risk factors (e.g., decreased smoking) and early detection. However, the number of colorectal cancer cases in patients younger than 50 years has steadily increased for unknown reasons. Survival rates exceed 90% with localized disease, underscoring the importance of early detection. Between 20% and 53% of adults older than 50 years have premalignant colonic adenomas detected on screening, and 3% to 8% of the adenomas have advanced histologic features. As of 2021, 71.8% of Americans older than 50 years were up to date with recommended testing.

Colorectal cancer develops through one of three mechanisms: chromosomal instability, microsatellite instability, and hypermethylation of tumor suppressor genes.

Chromosomal instability is the most common mechanism, accounting for approximately 85% of colorectal cancers. Chromosomal instability is characterized by abnormal cells that gain or lose whole or large fractions of chromosomes (aneuploidy) at an increased rate compared with normal cells. Stepwise accumulation of variants leads to progression from normal colon to adenoma to cancer. The most commonly mutated gene in this pathway is the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene, a multifunctional tumor suppressor gene. APC variants are implicated in the development and spread of colon cancer. Germline variants in APC lead to familial adenomatous polyposis.

Microsatellites are dozens to hundreds of repetitive nucleotide sequences seen throughout the human genome. The term microsatellite instability refers to mismatched bases at repeated DNA microsatellites. Microsatellite instability accounts for about 15% of colorectal cancers and is characterized by defective DNA mismatch repair, leading to several genetic variants, adenomas, and cancer. Defective mismatch repair can occur if there is a pathogenic germline variant in a mismatch repair gene in Lynch syndrome or as a result of sporadic methylation of the MLH1 promoter.

The third mechanism involves hypermethylation of tumor suppressor genes leading to their loss of function, and the development of serrated lesions and cancer. Serrated lesions are a heterogeneous group of lesions classified by their sawtooth appearance on microscopy. They are often found in the proximal colon and may be flat and difficult to distinguish from normal mucosa (

). Hypermethylation is a rare cause (<1%) of colorectal cancers.

Nonmodifiable risk factors for colon cancer include the following:

  • Age (≥45 years)
  • Male sex
  • Personal or family history of colon adenomas or colorectal cancer

The risk doubles with a family history of colorectal cancer in a first-degree relative.

Long-standing (≥8 years) colonic inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis) is associated with about a 2.7-fold increased risk; the risk depends on the severity and extent of bowel involvement. Patients with ureterocolic anastomoses after bladder surgery and adult survivors of childhood malignancy who received abdominal radiation are also at increased risk for colorectal cancer.

Modifiable risk factors include the following:

  • Diets high in red and processed meat
  • Low intake of fruits, vegetables, fiber, and dairy
  • Use of alcohol and tobacco
  • Type 2 diabetes mellitus
  • Sedentary lifestyle
  • Obesity

Substantial epidemiologic and experimental data suggest that aspirin prevents colorectal cancer. Cohort and case-control studies show that aspirin use is associated with a 30% decreased risk for colorectal cancer. Randomized controlled trials, however, have shown that aspirin decreases the risk for recurrent adenomas but has less clear benefit in preventing colorectal cancer. See Aspirin for Primary Prevention in Foundations of Clinical Practice for further discussion.

Studies of other NSAIDs for prevention of colon cancer and adenomas have also yielded positive results; however, benefits of aspirin and other NSAIDs must be weighed against harms, especially gastrointestinal bleeding.

Some evidence suggests that selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors prevent recurrent adenomas and decrease the incidence of advanced lesions; however, the associated increased cardiovascular risk confounds a recommendation of their use for chemoprevention.

Screening of patients at average risk is discussed in Colorectal Cancer in Oncology.

For those at increased risk, see [Table: Table: Colorectal Cancer Screening in Individuals at Elevated Risk]

.

Screening of patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis is discussed in Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease.

Because adenomas are an intermediary step in the progression from normal colonic mucosa to colon cancer, identification and management of adenomatous polyps are critical. Adenomas can be found throughout the colon. They are classified by morphology, histology, and degree of dysplasia ( [Table: Table: Classification of Colorectal Polyps]

). Adenomas with any degree of villous histology or high-grade dysplasia have greater malignant potential. Risk is also increased in polyps larger than 1 cm. Adenomas progress to carcinomas over approximately 8 to 10 years.

Key quality indicators for screening colonoscopy include the following:

  • Adequate bowel preparation
  • Preparation sufficient to identify polyps 6 mm or larger
  • Visualization of the entire colon to the cecum
  • Adenoma detection rate
  • Longer colonoscopy withdrawal time

Colorectal cancer may be asymptomatic or may present with iron deficiency anemia, gastrointestinal bleeding, altered bowel habits, abdominal pain, colonic obstruction, and weight loss in more advanced cases.

Colorectal cancer is usually diagnosed by colonoscopy with biopsy. Staging is based on tumor size and extent of invasion into local tissues, lymph node involvement, and evidence of metastasis (TNM system). Cross-sectional imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis should be used for staging in the initial evaluation after diagnosis. Management of colon cancer depends on stage; evidence of microsatellite instability; and presence of specific genetic mutations, including KRAS/NRAS and BRAF.

For staging and treatment of colorectal cancer, see Colorectal Cancer in Oncology.

Favorable characteristics include stage I to II cancer and lack of angiolymphatic involvement. Endoscopic resection of polyps can be curative, and negative margins after removal are a favorable sign. Malignant sessile or flat polyps are associated with higher risk for recurrence and local or distant spread.

Post-screening or post-polypectomy surveillance for colorectal cancer is based on baseline examination findings ( [Table: Table: Surveillance for CRC After Screening or Polypectomy]

).

Several hereditary syndromes are associated with colorectal cancer ( [Table: Table: Hereditary Colorectal Cancer Syndromes]

).

Lynch syndrome, one of the most common forms of cancer predisposition syndromes, is characterized by pathologic germline variants in the mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) or the epithelial cell adhesion molecule gene (EPCAM), leading to an increased risk for neoplasia of the colon and other organs. The previous name for this syndrome, hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, is no longer used because the syndrome is associated with colorectal polyps as well as extracolonic cancers. The syndrome follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern; approximately 1/279 of the population in the United States, Canada, and Australia are estimated to carry variants.

In persons with Lynch syndrome, the lifetime risk for colorectal cancer depends on the gene; the risk can be as high as 50% to 80%. Colorectal cancer in Lynch syndrome is more likely in the proximal colon and can display characteristic pathologic features, such as tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and medullary growth pattern. Colorectal tumors in Lynch syndrome exhibit microsatellite instability resulting from defective DNA mismatch repair; this can be assessed using polymerase chain reaction or immunohistochemistry (see Pathogenesis of Colorectal Neoplasia in Gastroenterology). All persons with colorectal cancer should be screened for Lynch syndrome.

Lynch syndrome should be suspected in patients with the following:

  • Synchronous colorectal cancer (occurring within 6 months of the primary tumor diagnosis)
  • Metachronous colorectal cancer (occurring more than 6 months after the primary tumor diagnosis)
  • Colorectal cancer before age 50 years
  • Several Lynch syndrome–associated cancers
  • Family history of several cancers associated with Lynch syndrome

Clinical criteria to evaluate for Lynch syndrome include the Amsterdam and Bethesda criteria ( [Table: Table: Criteria for Lynch Syndrome]

), as well as newer models, such as the PREdiction Model for gene Mutations 5 (PREMM~5). Given the limitations of the clinical criteria and predictive models, genetic counseling and testing should be offered to patients with a personal or family history consistent with Lynch syndrome, as well as to patients whose tumor shows evidence of microsatellite instability or loss of mismatch repair protein expression. In families in whom Lynch syndrome is suspected, genetic testing should ideally begin with the patient affected by cancer. When a variant is identified in a family, first-degree relatives should be tested and surveillance instituted.

Surveillance recommendations for colorectal cancer in patients with Lynch syndrome are described in [Table: Table: Colorectal Cancer Screening in Individuals at Elevated Risk]

. In women with Lynch syndrome, endometrial biopsy may be considered every 1 to 2 years starting at age 30 to 35 years. Risk-reducing total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy should be considered starting at age 40 to 45 years or after childbearing is completed.

Screening with upper endoscopy for stomach and small-bowel cancers can be considered starting at age 30 to 40 years and repeated every 2 to 4 years. Testing and treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection are also recommended. Aspirin should be considered to decrease future risk for colon cancer; the optimal dose and duration are under study.

Patients with a history of more than 10 cumulative colorectal adenomas, a family history of one of the adenomatous polyposis syndromes, or a personal history of familial adenomatous polyposis-type extracolonic manifestations (including duodenal/ampullary adenomas, desmoid tumors, papillary thyroid cancer, congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium, epidermal cysts, and osteomas) in addition to previous colon adenomas should undergo assessment for the adenomatous polyposis syndromes, beginning with genetic counseling.

Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is an inherited disorder characterized by many (usually ≥100) adenomatous colon polyps. FAP is caused by pathogenic germline variants in APC that are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, although de novo mutations occur in about 25% of cases. Adenomas in classic FAP are more numerous in the distal colon than in the proximal colon. Adenoma and cancer develop in 100% of classic FAP cases if surgery is not performed. The average age at colorectal cancer onset is 39 years, with a risk of 93% by age 50 years.

An attenuated form of FAP (AFAP) causes fewer polyps (<100 synchronous polyps) with more proximal colonic distribution. The risk for colon cancer in patients with AFAP is about 70% by age 80 years, with an average age at onset of 58 years.

Both FAP and AFAP are associated with extracolonic intestinal manifestations (see

). Duodenal adenomas require surveillance because the lifetime risk for duodenal adenocarcinoma is estimated at 4%. At least 50% of patients with FAP develop adenomatous changes of the periampullary region, which may progress to adenocarcinoma. Fundic gland polyps of the stomach do not have malignant potential but can mask the presence of gastric adenomas and cancer; risk for gastric cancer is less than 1%. Patients are also at risk for desmoid tumors, especially after abdominal surgery, and for papillary thyroid cancer. Nonmalignant findings include extra teeth, sebaceous or epidermoid cysts, osteomas, and congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigmented epithelium.

In patients with pathogenic variants causing classic FAP, sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy should begin at age 10 to 15 years and be repeated annually. Colonoscopy in patients with AFAP can be delayed until age 18 to 20 years and then repeated every 1 to 2 years thereafter. These recommendations for initial endoscopic screening also apply to first-degree relatives who have not undergone germline genetic testing. For patients with FAP and AFAP, upper endoscopy should begin at age 20 to 25 years and include visualization of the papilla with a duodenoscope ( [Table: Table: Colorectal Cancer Screening in Individuals at Elevated Risk]

). Fundic gland polyps in the stomach should be randomly sampled. Surveillance of the upper gastrointestinal tract is determined by duodenal findings. Annual thyroid ultrasonography is also recommended.

Colectomy is the treatment of choice for classic FAP and may be pursued in patients with AFAP. Absolute indications for surgery include cancer and significant symptoms, such as rectal bleeding. The following are relative indications for surgery:

  • Several adenomas greater than 6 mm
  • Increase in the number of polyps
  • Adenoma with high-grade dysplasia
  • Multiple diminutive polyps, which can prevent identification of adenomas

The type of surgery depends on the polyp burden in the rectum. High rectal polyp burden typically necessitates total proctocolectomy with ileostomy or ileal anal pouch; otherwise, subtotal colectomy with ileorectal anastomoses may be possible. Postsurgical surveillance is yearly sigmoidoscopy for patients with an intact rectum and ileoscopy every 2 years for those with an ileostomy.

MUTYH-associated polyposis (MAP) is an inherited syndrome characterized by fewer adenomas than classic FAP. MAP is a recessive condition caused by variants in the MUTYH gene, a component of base excision repair. Most patients have 20 to 99 adenomatous colon polyps. Some persons can develop cancer with only a few or no synchronous adenomas. Mean age at cancer onset is 52 years. In addition, patients with MAP can have other polyp types, including serrated lesions and hyperplastic polyps. Those with biallelic MUTYH variants should undergo annual colonoscopy. A first-degree relative of an affected individual who has not undergone genetic testing should have screening colonoscopy every 2 years, starting at age 20 years. Duodenal cancer risk in MAP is estimated at 4%, and surveillance with upper endoscopy is similar to that indicated in patients with FAP. Surgical management of the colon is also similar to that used for FAP.

Several recently described rare polyposis syndromes are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Polymerase proofreading–associated polyposis appears to have features of both FAP and Lynch syndrome and is caused by pathogenic variants in polymerase proofreading genes POLE and POLD1. Endometrial cancer has been described in this syndrome, and tumor testing shows microsatellite instability. Variants in GREM1 have also been associated with hereditary polyposis. Management guidelines are not established, but management of colonic polyps follows similar principles as for other adenomatous polyp syndromes.

Hamartomas are polyps caused by overgrowth of normal tissue. Three primary syndromes are associated with hamartomas in the gastrointestinal tract:

  • Juvenile polyposis syndrome (JPS)
  • Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS)
  • PTEN hamartoma syndrome (also known as Cowden syndrome)

JPS is caused by variants in the BMPR1A and SMAD4 genes. Its incidence is approximately 1 in 130,000 live births. Several juvenile polyps (>5 polyps) are found in the colon (98%), stomach (14%), and small bowel (14%) of patients with JPS (

). Sporadic juvenile polyps can be found in up to 1% of children and are not considered syndromic. The average age at JPS diagnosis is 18.5 years, and rectal bleeding is the most common symptom.

PJS is caused by variants in the STK11 (LKB1) gene. Its incidence is approximately 1 in 200,000 live births. PJS hamartomas are found primarily in the small bowel but can also develop in the stomach and colon (

). PJS is also characterized by hyperpigmented mucocutaneous macules on the lips and buccal mucosa (

). Small-bowel hamartomas develop at a young age in patients with PJS and may present with intussusception, obstruction, and bleeding. Microcytic anemia may suggest iron deficiency anemia due to polyp bleeding in PJS and JPS.

A PJS diagnosis is based on the presence of two of the following three criteria:

  • Two or more PJS-type hamartomatous polyps in the gastrointestinal tract
  • Multiple melanotic macules in the mouth, buccal mucosa, nose, eyes, genitalia, or fingers
  • Family history of PJS

PTEN hamartoma syndrome is caused by germline variants in the tumor suppressor gene PTEN. Macrocephaly and characteristic benign skin findings are common, including facial trichilemmomas, lipomas, and oral papillomas.

Serrated polyposis syndrome is characterized by numerous serrated polyps in the colon and an increased risk for colon cancer. The definition is based on having either of the following over the patient’s lifetime:

  • Five or more serrated polyps proximal to the rectum, all at least 5 mm and with two or more at least 10 mm
  • More than 20 serrated polyps throughout the colon, with at least five located proximal to the rectum

Estimates suggest that the prevalence of serrated polyposis syndrome is 0.3% to 0.6%. The genetic basis of the syndrome is unknown, although smoking appears to be a risk factor. Colonoscopy is recommended every 1 to 3 years, with removal of all polyps greater than 5 mm. Surgery may be considered if the polyps cannot be managed endoscopically. No extracolonic manifestations have been noted in serrated polyposis syndrome.

Gastrointestinal Bleeding

Gastrointestinal bleeding is a common cause of hospitalization in the United States. Upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) is defined as bleeding from the esophagus, stomach, or duodenum. The mortality rate for patients with UGIB varies from 2% to 10%, with much of the mortality occurring in patients with significant comorbid medical conditions. Lower gastrointestinal bleeding occurs in the colon or anorectum. It is less common, is typically less severe, and has a lower mortality rate than UGIB. Suspected small-bowel bleeding, in which bleeding does not appear to originate from the upper or lower gastrointestinal tract after upper and lower endoscopy, accounts for less than 10% of gastrointestinal bleeding. However, in 25% of patients suspected of having small-bowel bleeding, the upper or lower gastrointestinal source of bleeding was missed on initial endoscopy.

UGIB can present in various ways:

  • Hematemesis (vomiting of bright red blood or clots)
  • Coffee-ground emesis (vomiting of dark granular material resulting from the action of gastric acid on blood)
  • Melena (black, tarry stool with a distinctive odor)
  • Hematochezia (passage of red blood or clots from the rectum)

Common causes of UGIB include peptic ulcer disease (PUD), gastroesophageal varices, and Mallory-Weiss tears. PUD is the most common cause (50%), with most gastroduodenal ulcers caused by Helicobacter pylori or NSAID use (see Peptic Ulcer Disease in Gastroenterology). Erosive esophagitis is a common endoscopic finding but infrequently causes clinically important UGIB. Therefore, in a patient with significant UGIB and erosive esophagitis, alternative causes for the bleeding should be sought.

Bleeding gastroesophageal varices typically occur in the distal esophagus or proximal stomach in persons with cirrhosis (see Complications of Advanced Liver Disease in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease). Bleeding risk of varices increases with varix size and high-risk varix stigmata, such as cherry red spots.

A Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal disruption at the gastroesophageal junction and typically forms after repeated episodes of severe vomiting or retching.

See also [Table: Table: Less Common Causes of Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding]

.

The initial step in evaluation is risk assessment to determine severity. This assessment includes measuring vital signs and reviewing patient factors. The following are associated with increased risk for rebleeding and death:

  • Tachycardia (pulse rate >100/min)
  • Hypotension (systolic blood pressure <100 mm Hg)
  • Age older than 60 years
  • Major comorbid medical conditions

Several clinical scores (e.g., the Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score [which incorporates blood urea, hemoglobin, systolic blood pressure, pulse, melena, syncope, hepatic disease, cardiac failure] and the Rockall Score) are available to help predict risk for recurrent bleeding and death, need for medical intervention (e.g., transfusion, endoscopy, surgery), or safety of outpatient follow-up.

Findings of stigmata of chronic liver disease suggest a possible variceal source of bleeding.

Hemodynamic status should be assessed in all patients, and resuscitative measures must be initiated with the goal of hemodynamic stabilization before endoscopy. Adequate intravenous access, usually with two large-bore peripheral intravenous catheters (minimum 18-gauge), should be established. Hemoglobin levels should be measured in all patients. A restrictive transfusion strategy is recommended and initiated when the hemoglobin level is below 7 g/dL (70 g/L) in hemodynamically stable patients without preexisting cardiovascular disease. Patients with hypotension due to severe, ongoing UGIB and those with concomitant cardiovascular disease should be considered for transfusion before the hemoglobin level decreases below 7 g/dL (70 g/L) to prevent the decrease that may occur with fluid resuscitation alone. Care should be taken in patients with variceal hemorrhage because over-transfusion and increased portal pressure can precipitate variceal rebleeding. In patients with altered mental status, massive hematemesis, or increased risk for aspiration, endotracheal intubation should be considered.

Intravenous erythromycin given before endoscopy may improve gastric visualization and should be administered only when requested by the endoscopist. Nasogastric tube lavage is not required because there is no evidence of clinical benefit.

Intravenous proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy initiated before endoscopy decreases high-risk endoscopic stigmata in PUD and may reduce the need for endoscopic therapy (see

and

), but it does not influence outcomes, such as rebleeding or death.

Patients with cirrhosis who are suspected of having variceal hemorrhage should begin receiving vasoactive therapy, such as octreotide, somatostatin, or terlipressin, to decrease splanchnic blood flow and lower portal pressure. Initiation of antibiotics (typically ceftriaxone) at the time of hospitalization for gastrointestinal bleeding is recommended for all patients with cirrhosis because nearly 50% of patients with cirrhosis who are hospitalized with UGIB have a bacterial infection (e.g., pneumonia, urinary tract infection), and antibiotics reduce the rates of rebleeding and death and shorten hospitalization. For management of variceal bleeding, balloon tamponade may be necessary as a temporizing measure until more definitive interventions are available.

In patients with significant hemorrhage who are receiving warfarin, use of warfarin should be discontinued. In patients receiving direct oral anticoagulants, the anticoagulant should be discontinued on presentation. Reversal of warfarin and direct oral anticoagulants is not routinely necessary and should be considered only if the level of anticoagulation is substantially supratherapeutic, there is life-threatening bleeding, or a massive blood transfusion is undesirable.

Platelet transfusions should not be administered based on a platelet count target in patients with active variceal bleeding because there is no evidence of benefit. In patients with critical or life-threatening nonvariceal bleeding who have platelet counts less than 50,000/μL (50 × 10^9/L), platelets should be transfused. Aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease should be discontinued and not restarted because the risk for recurrent bleeding outweighs the benefit. Aspirin for secondary prevention in patients with high-risk cardiovascular disease should be discontinued only if necessary. Decisions about discontinuing dual antiplatelet therapy with a P2Y~12 receptor antagonist and aspirin in patients with a recent acute coronary syndrome or coronary stent placement should be made with a cardiologist. In patients with significant hemorrhage in whom the P2Y~12 receptor antagonist must be discontinued, aspirin should be continued.

Patients with hemodynamic instability, active bleeding (hematemesis or recurrent large-volume hematochezia), or suspected variceal hemorrhage should be admitted to an ICU. Most other patients can be admitted to a regular hospital ward. Patients at low risk with a Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score of 1 or less may be considered for early discharge or outpatient treatment.

Upper endoscopy is the primary diagnostic modality for evaluating UGIB. For patients hospitalized with UGIB, endoscopy should be performed within 24 hours of resuscitation; in those with rapid bleeding or suspected variceal hemorrhage, it should be done more emergently, within 12 hours of presentation.

Endoscopy can be used to determine the cause of bleeding and helps with risk stratification. Lesions at high risk for recurrent bleeding that require endoscopic treatment include actively bleeding peptic ulcers and ulcers with nonbleeding visible vessels (see

). The management of ulcers with adherent clots (see

) is determined on a case-by-case basis. Lesions at low risk for rebleeding (clean-based ulcers, ulcers with pigmented spots, and Mallory-Weiss tears) do not require endoscopic treatment (

). Most Mallory-Weiss tears (

) stop bleeding spontaneously. For actively bleeding tears, endoscopic techniques, such as epinephrine injection, thermal therapy, and endoclips, can be used.

The most effective approach for control of acute esophageal variceal hemorrhage (

) is combined therapy with a vasoactive agent (somatostatin, octreotide, or terlipressin) and endoscopic treatment. Vasoactive therapy should be continued for 2 to 5 days after variceal hemorrhage. Endoscopic variceal ligation within 12 hours of presentation is the endoscopic treatment of choice for hemostasis of active variceal hemorrhage, with a success rate of 90%. Initial pretherapeutic management of bleeding gastric or ectopic varices is identical to that of bleeding esophageal varices. In patients with bleeding gastric varices, transjugular intrahepatic portocaval shunting, endoscopic cyanoacrylate therapy, or retrograde transvenous variceal embolization or obliteration may be considered as first-line options. Endoscopic ultrasonography-guided coiling may be an option if expertise is available.

Aortoenteric fistula should always be considered in patients with a history of aortic graft surgery presenting with gastrointestinal bleeding because of its high mortality rate of 50%, even with surgical intervention. When there is a high degree of suspicion, CT angiography should be performed rather than endoscopy or other types of gastrointestinal evaluation.

Patients with PUD and low-risk stigmata can be fed after recovery from endoscopy, receive once-daily oral PPI therapy, and be discharged from the hospital. Patients with high-risk lesions requiring endoscopic treatment should receive high-dose intravenous PPI therapy (≥80 mg daily for at least 72 hours), either continuously through intravenous infusion or intermittently, to decrease rebleeding and mortality, and should remain hospitalized for this interval. Intermittent intravenous dosing is as efficacious as continuous infusion; choice of continuous infusion versus intermittent PPI therapy may be influenced by cost, availability, and logistics. For high-risk lesions, twice-daily oral PPI therapy should continue for 2 weeks after endoscopy. For treatment of PUD, see Management of Peptic Ulcer Disease in Gastroenterology.

Nonselective β-blocker therapy (propranolol, nadolol, or preferably carvedilol) should be initiated in addition to endoscopic band ligation for secondary prophylaxis of variceal hemorrhage. If propanol or nadolol is used, the dosage should be increased as tolerated to obtain a resting pulse rate of 55 to 60/min; carvedilol dosing is 6.25 mg to 12.5 mg daily and does not require dose titration for heart rate. Subsequent endoscopy with further band ligation as needed to obliterate varices should also be performed every 2 to 4 weeks. Patients with cirrhosis and gastrointestinal bleeding should have antibiotic therapy continued (most commonly ceftriaxone 1 g per 24 hours) even in the absence of ascites. Antibiotic therapy should be continued until stability is achieved or 5 days of antibiotic therapy is completed, whichever occurs sooner.

If aspirin for secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease was discontinued, it should be resumed on the day hemostasis is endoscopically confirmed. In patients with a recent acute coronary syndrome or coronary stent placement in whom a P2Y~12 receptor was discontinued, therapy should be reinitiated within 5 days. In patients in whom warfarin was discontinued, re-anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin or unfractionated heparin should be considered within 48 hours in patients at high thrombotic risk (e.g., mechanical prosthetic heart valve, atrial fibrillation with high CHA~2DS~2-VASc score, valvular atrial fibrillation, or recent venous thromboembolism). Timing to resumption of direct oral anticoagulants depends on the risk profile, but resumption generally should occur within 7 days.

For all causes of UGIB, endoscopic therapy should be repeated if bleeding recurs, but routine second-look endoscopy is not recommended. Interventional radiology or surgery is reserved for cases of rebleeding despite endoscopic treatment.

The three most common causes of acute hematochezia requiring hospitalization are diverticulosis, colonic ischemia, and UGIB ( [Table: Table: Causes of Severe Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding]

). Hemorrhoidal bleeding is a frequent cause of minor lower gastrointestinal bleeding (LGIB) characterized by a small volume of bright red blood; however, it can occasionally cause significant bleeding with hemodynamic instability (see Hemorrhoids in Gastroenterology). Severe LGIB with clinical instability may also be caused by the following:

  • Colonic angiodysplasia
  • Postpolypectomy hemorrhage
  • Developmental vascular malformation (Dieulafoy lesion)
  • Rectal varices
  • Malignancy

Fifteen percent of patients with hematochezia, however, are found to have an upper gastrointestinal source.

Diverticular bleeding is of arterial origin and may be massive and life-threatening. The bleeding is typically painless except for abdominal cramping due to the cathartic action of colonic blood. Diverticular bleeding stops spontaneously in 75% of cases; however, rebleeding is common. See Diverticular Disease in Gastroenterology for further discussion.

Colonic ischemia is a common cause of hematochezia in older patients. The bleeding is typically preceded by lower abdominal pain. Ischemia-related bleeding is usually not enough to cause altered hemodynamics but can be significant in patients receiving anticoagulants and those with more severe ischemia. For further discussion of colonic ischemia, see Ischemic Bowel Disease in Gastroenterology.

Angiodysplasia, also known as angioectasia or arteriovenous malformation, can occur throughout the colon but is most common in the right colon. The following patients are at highest risk:

  • Older patients
  • Patients with end-stage kidney disease
  • Patients receiving anticoagulation therapy

Patients with cardiac disease, especially valve dysfunction, and those with left ventricular assist devices may be at increased risk for gastrointestinal bleeding secondary to acquired von Willebrand factor deficiency.

Postpolypectomy bleeding can occur immediately after polyp removal or days to weeks later. Risk is increased in patients with polyps larger than 2 cm or polyps in the right colon and with resumption of antithrombotic therapy.

Diarrhea, abdominal pain, and hematochezia can occur with inflammatory bowel disease and infectious colitis; colonic ischemia may also present with these symptoms. LGIB from a colon malignancy may be painless or associated with obstructive symptoms.

Radiation proctitis is a common cause of rectal bleeding in patients who have undergone radiation for prostate cancer (see further discussion in Other Gastrointestinal Disorders in Oncology).

An initial patient assessment and hemodynamic resuscitation should be performed simultaneously. The timing and quality of any previous colonoscopy should be determined, particularly for a report of polypectomy or biopsies. A careful assessment should be performed for the following:

  • Use of antithrombotic or antiplatelet agents
  • Personal history of or risk factors for liver disease/portal hypertension
  • Other comorbidities
  • Recent illness

Special attention should be paid to the factors that suggest an upper gastrointestinal source of hematochezia:

  • Concomitant melena
  • Liver disease/portal hypertension
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Elevated blood urea nitrogen-to-creatinine ratio

As with upper gastrointestinal bleeding, immediate attention should be paid to hemodynamic status, and resuscitative measures must be initiated with the goal of hemodynamic stabilization before endoscopy. The approach to management of hemoglobin level and platelet count are the same as described previously for UGIB, as are decisions regarding discontinuation and/or reversal of anticoagulant and antiplatelet agents.

CT angiography is the initial diagnostic test in patients who are hemodynamically unstable after initial resuscitation or have rapid ongoing bleeding, followed by immediate upper endoscopy if CT angiography does not reveal a source of bleeding. Upper endoscopy may also be a reasonable first choice in patients with hematochezia at risk for a rapidly bleeding upper gastrointestinal source.

In hemodynamically stable patients without evidence of rapid bleeding, colonoscopy is the first study of choice in patients with LGIB. It should be performed nonurgently after adequate colon preparation; colonoscopy within 24 hours of presentation is not associated with improved clinical outcomes. Colonoscopy identifies a source of LGIB in two thirds of patients.

Radiographic studies should be considered in patients who cannot tolerate colonoscopy or colon preparation or in patients in whom a source of bleeding is not identified endoscopically. Techniques include CT angiography, traditional angiography, and, less frequently, tagged erythrocyte scintigraphy.

Catheter-based angiography with embolization should be performed as soon as possible if active bleeding is noted on CT angiography. Angiographic embolization is also frequently used to stop persistent or recurrent diverticular bleeding because of the limitations of endoscopic approaches. Surgical intervention is reserved for patients who do not respond to endoscopic or interventional radiologic hemostatic measures.

The risk for rebleeding is highest in patients with diverticular bleeding (9% to 47%) and angiodysplasia bleeding (37% to 64%). To prevent recurrent LGIB, nonaspirin NSAIDs should be avoided, particularly after diverticular or angiodysplasia bleeding. Management of antiplatelet and anticoagulant medications is similar to that in patients with UGIB.

Small-bowel bleeding occurs secondary to a gastrointestinal bleeding source between the ampulla of Vater and ileocecal valve. It can be overt, in which visible bleeding (melena or hematochezia) is present, or occult, which is characterized by anemia in the absence of gross signs of bleeding. Roughly 5% to 10% of gastrointestinal bleeding is due to a small-bowel source.

The causes of small-bowel bleeding vary with patient age ( [Table: Table: Causes of Small-Bowel Gastrointestinal Bleeding]

). Angiodysplasia (

) is the most common cause.

Important elements of the history include the following:

  • Assessment for NSAID use
  • Inflammatory bowel disease
  • Previous aortic aneurysm repair
  • Previous pancreatitis
  • Recent liver trauma, tumor, or biopsy

Key physical findings may include perioral pigmentation or mucocutaneous or cutaneous telangiectasias (

), which would raise suspicion of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, respectively.

If a bleeding source is not identified on initial endoscopy and colonoscopy and small-bowel bleeding is suspected, second-look upper endoscopy or colonoscopy should be done if the initial studies were low quality or other clinical factors exist ( [Table: Table: Need for Second-Look Tests for Suspected Small-Bowel Bleeds]

); missed lesions on the initial endoscopy are common. Push enteroscopy may be pursued in lieu of endoscopy to visualize the distal duodenum and proximal jejunum. Repeat colonoscopy should include intubation of the terminal ileum.

For evaluating stable patients suspected of having small-bowel bleeding, video capsule endoscopy is the preferred test after nondiagnostic upper endoscopy and colonoscopy. The diagnostic yield of video capsule endoscopy is 56% to 67%. In cases of uncomplicated, asymptomatic iron deficiency anemia with negative findings on upper endoscopy and colonoscopy, a trial of iron supplementation can be considered before capsule endoscopy is pursued. Capsule endoscopy uses a nondigestible wireless capsule camera (

) that is swallowed or placed endoscopically. Limitations include the inability to intervene therapeutically or precisely localize a lesion; lesions may also be missed because of incomplete visualization. The most common complication is capsule retention due to obstruction or stricture; if capsule retention is suspected, radiography should be performed. For suspected obstruction or altered anatomy (small-bowel Crohn disease, radiation enteritis, previous small-bowel surgery), CT enterography or magnetic resonance enterography should be performed instead. Barium-based studies are no longer recommended for suspected small-bowel bleeding given their poor diagnostic yield (3%-6%).

As in LGIB, CT angiography is the diagnostic test of choice for hemodynamically unstable patients or those with suspected brisk small-bowel bleeding. It is widely available, provides rapid testing, and has good diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, 89%; specificity, 85%). In patients with contraindications to CT, technetium-99m–labeled red blood cell or sulfur colloid nuclear scanning may be considered. The primary weakness of radioisotope-labeled scanning is the propensity to poorly localize the bleeding site.

After hemodynamic stabilization, therapy is guided by the source and location of bleeding. For active bleeding identified by CT angiography or red blood cell scanning, angiography with embolization should be performed. When a bleeding source is identified on video capsule endoscopy or CT angiography, device-assisted enteroscopy (single-balloon system, double-balloon system, or spiral enteroscopy) or push enteroscopy should be performed with one or more endoscopic methods of hemostasis. Intraoperative endoscopy during laparotomy/laparoscopy is the most invasive modality and is a last resort.

Pharmacologic therapy is possible for some underlying causes but is reserved for patients with contraindications to or no response to endoscopic or interventional radiologic intervention. The somatostatin analogue octreotide and the antiangiogenesis agent thalidomide have potential efficacy for vascular lesions. Hormonal therapy no longer has a role because of poor efficacy.

Tumors or masses require surgical intervention, and, if massive bleeding is present, embolization of the bleeding vessel may be necessary.

Anemia should be treated with blood transfusion when the hemoglobin level is below 7 g/dL (70 g/L) in hemodynamically stable patients without preexisting cardiovascular disease and iron supplementation thereafter if iron deficiency is found. If a causative agent is identified, such as an NSAID, the agent should be stopped. Patients with angiodysplasia and associated aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome) benefit from valve replacement surgery if indicated from a cardiac standpoint.
