Diarrhea, Constipation, and Irritable Bowel Syndrome

Diarrhea is marked by passage of a greater number of less-formed stools than normal. Diarrhea is considered acute if occurring for fewer than 2 weeks, persistent if occurring for 2 to less than 4 weeks, and chronic if occurring for at least 4 weeks. Acute diarrhea is usually infectious, whereas chronic diarrhea is usually noninfectious.

Causes of acute diarrhea include bacteria, viruses, and parasites. These can be divided into noninvasive and invasive causes. Noninvasive causes, leading to watery diarrhea, include the following:

  • Clostridioides difficile
  • Viruses (e.g., norovirus)
  • Escherichia coli
  • Cholera
  • Cryptosporidia
  • Giardia duodenalis

Invasive causes lead to dysentery or bloody diarrhea and include the following:

  • Campylobacter
  • Some strains of E. coli
  • Entamoeba histolytica
  • Shigella
  • Salmonella

Persistent diarrhea is usually caused by a parasite. See Infectious Gastrointestinal Syndromes in Infectious Disease for further information.

Acute diarrhea may be accompanied by abdominal cramping, hematochezia, tenesmus, flatulence, fever, nausea, and vomiting. For patients with acute diarrhea, evaluation for volume depletion is important. Stool testing for infectious causes depends on suspicion of disease outbreak, symptom severity, symptom duration (>7 days), and increased risk for infectious diarrhea (e.g., worker in health care or food preparation, previous exposure to antibiotics or to a person with infectious diarrhea) (see Overview of Infectious Gastrointestinal Syndromes in Infectious Disease for additional information).

Fluid therapy is the mainstay of treatment for acute diarrhea. Patients with severe diarrhea or travelers with cholera-like diarrhea should receive balanced electrolyte rehydration solutions. Hospitalization is usually unnecessary except for patients with severe disease, hemodynamic instability, or several medical comorbidities. Confirmed C. difficile infection should be treated according to comorbidities and clinical severity (see Clostridioides difficile Infection in Infectious Disease). In travel-associated illness, bismuth and loperamide can be used for mild, watery diarrhea but antimotility agents are not recommended in cases of dysentery; empiric antibiotics may be needed for moderate or severe symptoms (see Travelers’ Diarrhea in Infectious Disease).

Chronic diarrhea can be grouped by disease mechanism into the following six categories (with some common causes listed).

  • Osmotic: medications (laxatives) and undigested sugars (lactose, fructose, sorbitol, mannitol)
  • Secretory: medications (nonosmotic laxatives, antibiotics), endocrine causes (neuroendocrine tumors, hyperthyroidism), bile salt malabsorption (ileal resection, cholecystectomy), noninvasive infections (giardiasis, cryptosporidiosis), and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth
  • Steatorrhea: maldigestion (decreased bile salts, pancreatic dysfunction) and malabsorption (celiac disease, giardiasis, Whipple disease, chronic mesenteric ischemia, short bowel syndrome, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth)
  • Inflammatory: inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease), malignancy (colorectal cancer, lymphoma), invasive or toxin-mediated infections (Clostridioides difficile, cytomegalovirus, Entamoeba histolytica, tuberculosis), ischemia, and radiation colitis/enteritis
  • Motility: postsurgical (vagotomy, dumping syndrome), endocrine (diabetes mellitus, hyperthyroidism), systemic sclerosis
  • Miscellaneous: irritable bowel syndrome, functional diarrhea (frequent, loose, or watery stools without abdominal discomfort or other identifiable causes), factitious disorder, overflow diarrhea secondary to underlying constipation, fecal incontinence

These categories may overlap because some diseases have several mechanisms causing diarrhea. The most common causes are irritable bowel syndrome with predominant diarrhea (IBS-D) and functional causes.

Medications are also an important cause. Common medication-related causes include the following: antacids and proton pump inhibitors, chemotherapy, antibiotics, colchicine, metformin, NSAIDs, mesalamine, cholesterol-lowering drugs, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Uncommon causes include ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, β-adrenergic receptor antagonists, carbamazepine, lipase inhibitors, litihium, prostaglandin, and vitamin/mineral supplements.

Evaluation of chronic diarrhea includes a careful history and physical examination. Because IBS-D and functional causes are the most common, further diagnostic studies should be reserved for patients whose symptoms or examination findings suggest another cause.

The diarrhea pattern and stool characteristics can help determine the most likely diagnosis. Steatorrhea is suggested by greasy or bulky tools that are difficult to flush. The relation of symptoms to eating can also provide clues to the cause. Osmotic diarrhea occurs with eating and subsides with fasting, whereas secretory diarrhea does not subside with fasting. Nocturnal symptoms are often related to inflammatory conditions, such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Information about specific dietary factors that commonly cause osmotic diarrhea, such as lactose, fructose, and artificial sweeteners (sorbitol), should be obtained. The patient should be asked about new medications (prescription and nonprescription) and when they were initiated in relation to diarrhea onset. Concomitant symptoms may also suggest a diagnosis. Abdominal pain accompanying diarrhea may suggest IBS-D, especially when changes in bowel movements occur in the setting of abdominal pain. Rectal bleeding and weight loss suggest malignancy or IBD.

Epidemiologic factors may also be helpful. Conditions such as IBS and microscopic colitis are more common in women than men. IBS onset is most common in the third and fourth decades of life, microscopic colitis is most common in the seventh and eighth decades, and malignancy is suggested by onset at age 45 years and older.

Physical examination should assess for hydration and nutrition status, perineal disease suggesting Crohn disease, and sphincter defects suggesting fecal incontinence.

The decision to pursue additional testing, including celiac serologies, stool studies, imaging, and endoscopy, depends on the clinical scenario and likelihood of specific diseases. Complete blood count, iron studies (including ferritin level), thyroid-stimulating hormone level, and testing for celiac disease may be considered. Stool testing for fecal calprotectin (or fecal lactoferrin), giardiasis, C. difficile infection, and bile acid diarrhea may also be considered.

Analysis of stool may include the following:

  • Weight
  • Electrolytes
  • pH
  • Fat content
  • Elastase
  • Presence of blood and leukocytes

In watery stools, fecal electrolytes can be used to calculate the fecal osmotic gap:

290 – (2 × [stool sodium + stool potassium])

An osmotic gap less than 50 mOsm/kg (50 mmol/kg) suggests secretory diarrhea, and a gap exceeding 100 mOsm/kg (100 mmol/kg) suggests osmotic diarrhea.

Blood or leukocytes in the stool or an elevated fecal calprotectin level suggests an inflammatory cause. A positive 72-hour stool collection for fecal fat confirms steatorrhea; a random fecal fat assessment is not reliable for diagnosing steatorrhea. A reduced fecal elastase level may be useful for evaluating exocrine pancreatic function. When laxative abuse is suspected, a stool or urine laxative screen can aid in diagnosis.

For suspected small-bowel disease, small intestine evaluation may include small-bowel radiography, CT, or magnetic resonance enterography to identify conditions that could lead to bacterial overgrowth, such as small intestinal diverticular disease, inflammation, and strictures. Upper endoscopy is indicated when small-bowel mucosal disease (e.g., celiac disease or chronic infection) is suspected. Capsule endoscopy can visualize the small intestine but does not allow for sampling. Device-assisted enteroscopy can be used in selected patients who require sampling of small intestinal tissue based on abnormalities found on imaging or capsule endoscopy. Diagnostic yields for capsule endoscopy and device-assisted enteroscopy are low in patients with chronic diarrhea and normal laboratory or imaging results.

Colonoscopy is the primary diagnostic tool for evaluating colonic causes of diarrhea, such as IBD, microscopic colitis, chronic colon infections, and malignancy. Colon biopsies of the right and left colon are required to exclude microscopic colitis. Colonoscopy is especially important in patients with rectal bleeding or who are older than 45 years.

Additional testing (including Giardia and HIV testing) may be warranted in immunocompromised patients and patients with secretory diarrhea. Patients found to have a small-bowel tumor in the setting of diarrhea should be considered for additional testing, including radioimmunoassays for peptides or 24-hour urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid measurement for neuroendocrine tumors. Testing for gastrointestinal neuroendocrine tumors should be limited to patients who have chronic diarrhea with symptoms and signs consistent with a tumor syndrome, such as peptic ulcer disease suggestive of gastrinoma.

Treatment of osmotic diarrhea consists of identifying the unabsorbable particle or osmole and eliminating it from the diet, which may include following a low fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols (FODMAP) ( [Table: Table: Sources of FODMAP Carbohydrates]

) and lactose-free diet. Dietary restriction should be time limited (i.e., 4 weeks), ideally with a dietitian’s guidance, with complete resumption of a normal diet if symptoms do not improve. If improvement is seen, systematic reintroduction of food is indicated.

Treatment of secretory diarrhea is aimed at identifying the cause and careful management of hydration. Repletion of fat-soluble vitamins is important in patients with fat malabsorption.

Treatment of medication-induced diarrhea necessitates changing medications unless the benefits exceed the potential harms and the patient considers the diarrhea manageable. Immune checkpoint inhibitors can cause colitis presenting with diarrhea and hematochezia, and management often requires medication discontinuation, glucocorticoid initiation, or initiation of biologic therapy, such as with infliximab or vedolizumab.

Constipation is common, affecting 20% of the general population. Patients with constipation can have symptoms, such as infrequent, difficult, or incomplete defecation. Accompanying symptoms can include abdominal bloating and distention. It can be acute or chronic and secondary or idiopathic. Medications are the most common cause of secondary constipation; other causes include mechanical obstruction, systemic illnesses, altered physiologic states, and psychosocial conditions ( [Table: Table: Secondary Causes of Constipation]

).

Hospitalized and other severely ill patients may develop acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (ACPO) (also referred to as Ogilvie syndrome), which is characterized by colonic dilation, abdominal distention, abdominal pain, and constipation (or paradoxical diarrhea) without evidence of mechanical obstruction or toxic megacolon. In patients with uncomplicated ACPO (absence of ischemia, peritonitis, and significant abdominal pain as well as cecal diameter <12 cm, and/or significant abdominal pain), conservative management includes identification and treatment of the underlying disease (such as infection), discontinuation of predisposing factors (such as narcotics and other medications impairing colon motility), correction of fluid and electrolyte disorders, avoidance of oral feeding, ambulation, and decompression of the gastrointestinal tract with a nasogastric tube. For patients who are not candidates for conservative management and/or have symptoms persisting beyond 48 to 72 hours despite conservative measures, pharmacologic therapy (such as neostigmine) or endoscopic decompression should be considered; surgery is reserved for patients with clinical deterioration in whom other treatment options have failed.

After secondary causes have been excluded, chronic constipation is considered functional (idiopathic). Functional constipation is subcategorized as slow transit, normal transit, or dyssynergic defecation. Slow-transit constipation is the delayed passage of fecal contents through the colon based on objective transit testing (radiopaque marker study, scintigraphy, or wireless motility capsule). In normal-transit constipation, colonic transit times are adequate based on objective transit testing. Dyssynergic defecation (also termed pelvic floor dyssynergia, obstructed defecation, or outlet obstruction) is difficulty with or inability to expel stool because of abnormalities in contraction or relaxation of pelvic floor muscles during defecation. Functional constipation can result from slow-transit constipation and coexistent dyssynergic defecation.

A careful history identifies most causes of secondary constipation. The medication history should focus on the temporal relationship between medications and constipation onset. A history of pelvic floor trauma, such as delivery of pregnancy or sexual violence, increases risk for pelvic floor and anorectal dysfunction; lack of improvement with laxatives supports this diagnosis. The history should include assessment for alarm features:

  • Hematochezia
  • Acute constipation in older patients
  • Unintentional weight loss
  • Family history of colorectal cancer
  • Unexplained anemia
  • Age older than 45 years with no previous colonoscopy

Anorectal examination, including digital examination during the Valsalva maneuver, is important because it may identify anatomic or functional causes of an evacuation disorder.

Routine use of flat-plate radiography to quantify stool burden is not necessary but may be used for suspected fecal impaction and in the evaluation of bowel obstruction or volvulus. Colonoscopy is indicated in patients with a sudden change in bowel habits or with alarm features. Additional imaging or laboratory studies should be considered only if clinically indicated. Physiologic testing, including colon transit testing, anorectal manometry, balloon expulsion testing, or defecography, is reserved for patients with symptoms that do not respond to laxative therapy.

Treatment strategies that may be beneficial when lifestyle and dietary interventions, such as increased daily water intake, have been ineffective include bulking agents, stimulant laxatives, osmotic laxatives, secretagogues, and biofeedback ( [Table: Table: Treatments for Constipation]

). The evidence for effectiveness is strongest for polyethylene glycol, bisacodyl, sodium picosulfate, linaclotide, plecanatide, and prucalopride. Evidence also supports the use of psyllium, magnesium salts, senna, lubiprostone, fruit-based laxatives (kiwi, mango, prunes, and ficus), yogurt with galactooligosaccharide, or linseed oil. Fiber supplements, polyethylene glycol, magnesium, senna, docusate, and bisacodyl are available without a prescription. For refractory constipation, combination therapy should include agents with different mechanisms of action, such as an osmotic plus a stimulant laxative. An orally administered vibrating capsule is available for patients who do not respond to pharmacologic therapy. For the management of opioid-induced constipation, see Adverse Effects of Opioids in Common Symptoms.

Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a heterogeneous group of functional bowel disorders (also termed disorders of gut-brain interaction) defined by abdominal pain in association with defecation or change in bowel habits. Pain may worsen or subside with defecation. Altered bowel habits may include constipation, diarrhea, or both. Other common symptoms include abdominal bloating and abdominal distention. IBS is associated with diverse pathophysiologic mechanisms, including increased colonic transit, abnormal intestinal or colorectal sensation, increased colonic bile acid concentration, and epithelial barrier dysfunction. IBS is more common in women and adults younger than 50 years and is frequently associated with psychosocial disturbance.

Diagnosis of IBS is no longer one of exclusion but instead can reliably be made by clinical criteria when alarm features are absent. Diagnosis requires recurrent abdominal pain at least 1 day a week for 3 months along with at least two other criteria:

  • Defecation-related pain
  • Change in stool frequency
  • Change in stool consistency

IBS can be further subtyped into IBS with predominant constipation (IBS-C), IBS with predominant diarrhea (IBS-D), IBS with mixed bowel habits, or IBS unclassified. Evaluation for IBS relies on a comprehensive history and physical examination. No reliable biomarkers define IBS. Normal results of complete blood count and C-reactive protein testing support the diagnosis. In patients with IBS-D, stool testing for giardiasis, testing for celiac disease, and fecal calprotectin testing to differentiate from IBD are recommended.

IBS management includes lifestyle modification, changes in diet, probiotics, pharmacotherapy, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). Limited evidence suggests that exercise, stress management, and correction of impaired sleep can alleviate IBS symptoms. Some studies show that 20 to 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity 3 to 5 days per week improves IBS symptom scores. Evidence is mixed on the effectiveness of probiotics for IBS-D.

The most common dietary intervention is to increase fiber through diet or fiber supplements. Water-soluble fiber supplements, such as psyllium, are more effective than insoluble dietary fiber, such as bran. Dietary restrictions can include avoiding trigger foods, gluten (in the absence of celiac disease), dairy products, and FODMAPs (see [Table: Table: Sources of FODMAP Carbohydrates]

). Because these substances are poorly absorbed in the small intestine, they induce osmotic effects or are fermented in the colon, leading to decreased stool consistency and bloating.

If exercise, fiber supplementation, and diet manipulations fail to relieve symptoms, medications are used. Evidence supporting the various agents differs; few rigorous studies show long-term effectiveness.

Several peripherally acting medications are effective for treating IBS-C, including polyethylene glycol and intestinal secretagogues (see [Table: Table: Treatments for Constipation]

). The four intestinal secretagogues for IBS-C are linaclotide, lubiprostone, plecanatide, and tenapanor, and they are typically used to treat symptoms refractory to osmotic laxatives. Probiotics have uncertain benefit.

FDA-approved prescription medications for IBS–D treatment include rifaximin, eluxadoline, and alosetron. A 14-day course of rifaximin (a nonabsorbable antibiotic) relieves global symptoms, bloating, and loose stools associated with IBS-D for up to 10 weeks after treatment. Retreatment of patients with recurring IBS-D relieves abdominal bloating and improves stool consistency for 4 weeks after treatment.

Eluxadoline (a combination of a kappa- and mu-opioid receptor agonist and a delta-opioid receptor antagonist) relieves diarrhea and abdominal pain in adults with IBS-D. Adverse effects are mainly nausea and headache. Rare cases of pancreatitis and sphincter of Oddi spasm have been reported. Eluxadoline is contraindicated in the following situations:

  • Patients without a gallbladder
  • Known or suspected biliary obstruction
  • Sphincter of Oddi disease or dysfunction
  • Ingestion of three or more alcoholic beverages per day
  • History of pancreatitis or structural disease of the pancreas
  • Severe hepatic impairment
  • History of severe constipation

Alosetron (a selective 5-HT~3 antagonist) is recommended for women with refractory IBS-D; it alleviates abdominal pain and global symptoms. Because of the risk for severe constipation and colonic ischemia, physicians should complete a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy program before prescribing alosetron.

Other medications with clinical evidence for treatment of IBS-D include loperamide, antispasmodics, tricyclic antidepressants, and bile acid sequestrants. Loperamide, an opioid receptor agonist, slows colonic transit and increases fluid absorption. It reduces stool frequency and improves stool consistency in IBS-D but does not alleviate abdominal pain. Antispasmodics (e.g., dicyclomine and peppermint oil) decrease abdominal pain and global symptoms of IBS. Tricyclic antidepressants modestly relieve the abdominal pain and global symptoms of IBS-D; the mechanism of action may include reduced activation of pain centers in the brain and peripheral mechanisms that affect pain sensation. Approximately 25% of patients with IBS-D have evidence of bile acid malabsorption; bile acid binders, such as cholestyramine, colestipol, and colesevelam, can reduce stool frequency and improve stool consistency in these patients. Psychological therapies (e.g., CBT, hypnotherapy, multicomponent psychological therapy, and dynamic psychotherapy) are beneficial in the treatment of IBS.

Malabsorption

Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) is a syndrome of gastrointestinal symptoms caused by excessive bacteria in the small intestine. Risk factors for SIBO include various altered structural or motility-based conditions involving the gastrointestinal tract ( [Table: Table: Risk Factors for Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth]

).

Symptoms are often nonspecific. The most common are the following:

  • Abdominal discomfort
  • Flatulence
  • Gas
  • Distention
  • Bloating
  • Diarrhea

In severe SIBO, steatorrhea, weight loss, anemia, or deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins may be present.

Diagnosis of SIBO should be considered in patients with typical symptoms and predisposing risk factors. Carbohydrate substrate-based breath testing using glucose or lactulose is often used to diagnose SIBO; however, these tests have diagnostic limitations. The glucose breath test offers better sensitivity, and the lactulose breath test offers better specificity for diagnosing SIBO. Compared with small-bowel aspirate culture, the glucose breath test has a sensitivity of 20% to 93% and a specificity of 30% to 86%. The lactulose breath test demonstrates a sensitivity of 31% to 68% and a specificity of 44% to 100%. In patients with a high probability of SIBO and lack of access to objective testing, empiric antibiotic therapy with monitoring for symptom relief is a reasonable approach. Treatment consists of antibiotics, with courses repeated if the underlying condition promoting the SIBO cannot be resolved. Suggested antibiotics are listed in [Table: Table: Antibiotic Regimens for Treatment of SIBO]

.

Methanobrevibacter smithii is an archaeon that can cause elevated methane levels in the gut, which in turn has been associated with irritable bowel syndrome with constipation (see Irritable Bowel Syndrome in Gastroenterology). Because this organism is not a bacterium, the term intestinal methanogen overgrowth has been suggested to differentiate this syndrome from SIBO. An elevated methane level (≥10 ppm) during the carbohydrate breath test is diagnostic. Treatment includes neomycin plus rifaximin.

Short bowel syndrome is defined by loss of functional small bowel, with resultant loss of absorptive area that leads to maldigestion, malabsorption, and malnutrition. Surgery for strangulated bowel, Crohn disease, ischemia, trauma, or obesity can lead to short bowel syndrome.

Treatment focuses on ensuring adequate nutrition and depends on the degree of intestinal adaptation and whether the patient has an intact ileocecal valve and colon or an ileostomy. Patients with short bowel syndrome and an ileostomy usually require parenteral nutrition and hydration. Patients should be monitored for nutritional deficiencies, and those with extensive ileal resection should be tested for vitamin B~12 deficiency. Adjunctive therapies include antimotility agents, such as loperamide, and antisecretory drugs, such as proton pump inhibitors. Glucagon-like peptide 2 (GLP-2) and its analogue, teduglutide, may increase intestinal adaptation. This treatment is typically used in persons who cannot be weaned successfully from parenteral nutrition.

Carbohydrates can be classified as monosaccharides (glucose, fructose), disaccharides (lactose, sucrose), oligosaccharides (maltodextrose), or polyols (sorbitol, mannitol). These short-chain carbohydrates are osmotically active and can lead to increased luminal water retention and gas production through colonic fermentation. These actions can cause gastrointestinal symptoms, including gas, bloating, and diarrhea.

Lactose maldigestion commonly results from loss of the brush-border lactase enzyme in adolescence or adulthood. Fructose malabsorption can also cause gastrointestinal symptoms, such as bloating and diarrhea. Although lactose and fructose breath tests are available, testing is often not required because symptoms subside with elimination of the sugar from the diet and recur with ingestion of the sugar. Oral lactase enzyme replacement may be considered because it may be difficult to avoid lactose entirely.

Celiac disease is an immune-mediated disease that primarily affects the small intestine in response to dietary gluten. It is a common cause of malabsorption and affects only genetically predisposed persons. The immune reaction leads to destruction of the small intestinal villi, starting in the proximal duodenum. Although antibodies are produced as part of the immune reaction, their contribution to the pathogenesis of celiac disease is uncertain.

Testing should be pursued in patients with typical gastrointestinal symptoms or extraintestinal manifestations and should be considered in those at increased risk (type 1 diabetes mellitus, other autoimmune diseases, Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, IgA deficiency, or a first-degree family member with celiac disease). Gastrointestinal symptoms of celiac disease include the following:

  • Chronic diarrhea
  • Bloating
  • Weight loss
  • Constipation
  • Dyspepsia

Other manifestations include the following:

  • Iron deficiency anemia
  • Bone loss
  • Abnormal aminotransferase levels
  • Neurologic symptoms
  • Dermatitis herpetiformis

Patients may also be asymptomatic.

The best initial step is to test for IgA tissue transglutaminase antibodies. Because IgA deficiency is more common in celiac disease, it is recommended to measure total IgA levels concurrently to avoid false-negative results. In patients with IgA deficiency, testing for anti–deamidated gliadin peptide IgG antibodies or tissue transglutaminase IgG antibodies can be used. Antiendomysial IgA antibodies are highly specific; however, measurement is complex, and testing for these antibodies is generally reserved for situations in which data conflict. Antigliadin antibodies (IgA and IgG) should not be tested because of low sensitivity and specificity.

Antibody testing is less sensitive if the patient is adhering to a gluten-free diet. In such patients, genetic testing for HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 heterodimers should be pursued before a gluten challenge is attempted. Nearly all patients with celiac disease carry the HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 heterodimer. However, up to 40% of the general population carries one of these heterodimers; therefore, genetic testing can rule out but not confirm disease. For persons positive for one of these heterodimers, gluten can be reintroduced, preferably daily for 6 to 8 weeks, and serologic testing or duodenal biopsy can be performed. Genetic testing may also help rule out disease in patients who did not undergo serologic testing at diagnosis or in whom the diagnosis of celiac disease is unclear.

Although a markedly elevated (>10 times the upper limit of normal) transglutaminase IgA antibody titer has a positive predictive value for celiac disease approaching 100%, upper endoscopy with biopsies from the duodenum should be performed for confirmation. The diagnosis can be made in symptomatic adults who are unwilling or unable to undergo upper endoscopy and have an elevated transglutaminase IgA value (>10 times upper limit of normal) with positivity for antiendomysial antibody in a second blood sample. If clinical suspicion is high and results of initial testing are negative, upper endoscopy and duodenal biopsy can be pursued. There are specific recommendations for the biopsy procedure to minimize false-negative results. Celiac disease is confirmed by increased intraepithelial lymphocytosis and blunting or atrophy of the duodenal villi. If biopsy results suggesting celiac disease are obtained before serologic testing, confirmatory serologic testing should be performed.

Patients with celiac disease should be educated about a gluten-free diet by a knowledgeable registered dietitian. Celiac disease is managed through lifelong avoidance of wheat, rye, and barley, including in patients without symptoms. Patients should know about hidden sources of gluten, such as soy sauce (which may contain wheat) or certain medications in which gluten is an inactive ingredient. Dietary oats are generally safe but should be limited to those with a gluten-free label because cross-contact with gluten-containing grains is possible in some processing settings.

Monitoring includes the following:

  • Clinical assessment of symptoms and signs of celiac disease and assessment of dietary adherence
  • Confirmation of normalized antibody levels by repeat antibody testing at 6 and 12 months after diagnosis to assess response to the gluten-free diet (then annually)
  • Repeat upper endoscopy with biopsies for persons who have ongoing symptoms while adhering to a gluten-free diet
  • Follow-up biopsies for those with symptom resolution 2 years after starting a gluten-free diet to confirm intestinal healing

Assessment of bone density at diagnosis should be considered to ensure adequate bone health.

The most common cause of ongoing celiac disease–related symptoms is continued gluten exposure. When symptoms do not resolve completely with adherence to a gluten-free diet, the accuracy of the diagnosis should be reassessed. Other conditions that may explain ongoing symptoms include irritable bowel syndrome, lactose or fructose intolerance, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, microscopic colitis, and inflammatory bowel disease. Evaluation to exclude these conditions is critical before refractory celiac disease can be diagnosed.

In refractory celiac disease, symptoms of malabsorption and small intestinal inflammation persist despite adherence to a strict gluten-free diet. Refractory celiac disease may be associated with intestinal lymphoma; these patients are typically older than age 65 years and have diarrhea, weight loss, dehydration, and nutritional deficiencies. Possible medication-induced sprue, most commonly olmesartan-induced enteropathy, should be managed by discontinuing the offending medication. Patients with refractory celiac disease should be treated in a specialized celiac disease center.

Dermatitis herpetiformis is an extremely pruritic subepidermal autoimmune bullous disease. It typically presents with intensely pruritic papules and fragile vesicles that rapidly break, leaving tiny erosions (

). The elbows, knees, scalp, and lower back are the most common sites of involvement. Most patients have serologic and histologic evidence of celiac disease. Dapsone is quickly effective in inducing a clinical remission, but a gluten-free diet is the preferred long-term management of both the skin and bowel disease. Before initiating dapsone, patients should be tested for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.

Nonceliac gluten sensitivity is a clinical syndrome of unknown pathophysiology defined by gastrointestinal and extraintestinal symptoms that occur with gluten ingestion and subside with gluten avoidance. By definition, the diagnosis of celiac disease must be excluded. Clinical symptoms of celiac disease and nonceliac gluten sensitivity are indistinguishable. Because gluten-containing foods can also contain nonabsorbable carbohydrates (e.g., fructans), they can cause gastrointestinal symptoms due to osmotic mechanisms and fermentation by colonic bacteria. Other than assessing symptom response after withdrawal of gluten, no test is diagnostic for nonceliac gluten sensitivity; treatment focuses on gluten avoidance.

bodies.gisec24008:
Inflammatory Bowel Disease

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is an idiopathic chronic inflammatory condition of the gut that classically includes ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn disease. Microscopic colitis is considered a type of IBD with distinct clinical and pathologic features (see Microscopic Colitis in Gastroenterology).

IBD pathogenesis likely involves genetic predisposition and abnormal immunologic responses to endogenous gut bacteria. The primary risk factor for UC and Crohn disease is family history, with a risk of approximately 10% for first-degree relatives of affected patients. Tobacco smoking increases the risk for Crohn disease but is protective for UC. A diet high in ultra-processed foods is also associated with an increased IBD risk, with the strongest association observed for Crohn disease.

IBD has a bimodal age presentation, with an initial peak incidence in the second to fourth decades of life followed by a less prominent second peak in the seventh and eighth decades.

See also [Table: Table: Features of Ulcerative Colitis and Crohn Disease]

.

The major symptoms of UC include diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, rectal bleeding, and tenesmus; symptoms vary by disease extent and severity. Symptoms typically have an insidious onset and often have been present for weeks or months by the time the patient seeks care, although UC may present acutely and mimic infectious or colonic ischemia.

Rectal inflammation (proctitis) causes frequent defecatory urges and passage of small liquid stools containing mucus and blood. Although bloody diarrhea is considered the hallmark presentation of UC, diarrhea is not always present. Patients with proctitis or proctosigmoiditis may have constipation. Abdominal pain is usually not a prominent symptom of UC; however, most patients with active disease experience vague lower abdominal discomfort relieved with defecation. Physical examination findings in patients with mild or moderate UC are usually normal but may reveal mild lower abdominal discomfort over the affected colonic segment. Fever, nausea, vomiting, or severe abdominal pain indicates a severe attack or complication, such as superimposed infection or toxic megacolon.

The clinical presentation of Crohn disease may be subtle; it varies by location and severity of inflammation along the gut axis and the presence of intestinal complications (e.g., abscess, stricture, or fistula). Crohn disease typically involves the ileum, ileocolon, or colon, but can also affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract. Up to 25% of patients also exhibit upper gastrointestinal involvement.

Abdominal pain is more common in Crohn disease than in UC. The most common symptom of Crohn disease is diarrhea. Abdominal examination may reveal fullness or a tender mass in the right hypogastrium. Occasionally, the main presenting symptom is acute right-lower-quadrant pain, mimicking appendicitis. Pain may worsen postprandially. Tenesmus is less common in Crohn colitis than in UC because the rectum is often less inflamed than other colonic segments. Perianal fistulizing disease occurs in up to 25% of patients.

Fistulae are a manifestation of the transmural nature of Crohn disease and consist of abnormal connections between two epithelial surfaces (perianal, enteroenteric, enterocolonic, enterocutaneous, rectovaginal, enterovesical). Drainage of fecal material from fistulae may lead to passage of feces through the vagina, urethra, or skin. Intra-abdominal abscesses may form; the classic presentation is spiking fevers and focal abdominal tenderness, which may be masked by glucocorticoid use. Strictures may result from fibrosis or severe inflammatory luminal narrowing and may occur in any segment of the gastrointestinal tract, although the terminal ileum is the most common site. Patients with intestinal strictures often initially have colicky postprandial abdominal pain and bloating that may progress to complete intestinal obstruction.

Inflammatory conditions with extraintestinal involvement may occur with IBD. These manifestations are categorized as associated with active bowel disease or independent of bowel inflammation. An extraintestinal manifestation occurs in up to 30% of patients with IBD at some time during the disease course. Peripheral arthritis is the most common manifestation (see Enteropathic Arthritis in Rheumatology).

The two most common dermatologic manifestations are erythema nodosum and pyoderma gangrenosum. Erythema nodosum corresponds to underlying IBD activity, whereas pyoderma gangrenosum may either parallel disease activity or follow an independent course. Erythema nodosum most commonly presents as a single or several tender nodules on extensor surfaces of the lower extremities (

). Most cases are self-limited with resolution after treatment of active disease. Pyoderma gangrenosum typically presents with an exquisitely tender papule, pustule, or nodule that rapidly develops into an exudative ulcer with undermined and violaceous borders (

). The most frequent location is the lower leg; however, pyoderma gangrenosum is also frequently associated with a stoma site (peristomal) after ostomy placement. It is diagnosed after exclusion of other causes of ulceration. Management of pyoderma gangrenosum includes local wound care, immunosuppressants, and avoiding trauma and surgical debridement because of pathergy (i.e., it occurs at sites of trauma).

Ocular IBD manifestations include episcleritis and uveitis. Episcleritis is more common and consists of injection of the sclera and conjunctiva. It does not affect visual acuity and is associated with active bowel disease. Uveitis presents with headache, blurred vision, and photophobia. This ocular emergency threatens vision and requires immediate referral to an ophthalmologist. See Red Eye in Interdisciplinary Medicine for discussion of episcleritis and uveitis.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis is the major liver manifestation of IBD, occurring in 5% of patients. Patients most often have isolated elevations of serum alkaline phosphatase. The liver disease is typically progressive and independent of IBD outcome. See Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease for further discussion.

Diagnosis of IBD relies on integration of clinical presentation, endoscopic appearance, histologic assessment of mucosal biopsy specimens, radiologic features, and exclusion of infectious enteropathogens. IBD should be considered in any patient with chronic or bloody diarrhea. It is paramount to exclude infection, particularly with Clostridioides difficile and Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli, by stool tests, especially in patients with acute symptom onset. An elevated fecal calprotectin level may help differentiate IBD from IBS. Antibody tests (e.g., anti–Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies and p-ANCA) are available, but they have no role in diagnosis; they should not replace endoscopy or biopsy. Laboratory testing helps assess disease activity. Common findings include anemia, thrombocytosis, leukocytosis, and hypoalbuminemia. Iron deficiency anemia often develops from chronic blood loss. Persistently abnormal serum alkaline phosphatase levels should prompt investigation for primary sclerosing cholangitis.

Ileocolonoscopy with biopsy is needed to diagnose IBD and can further assess disease extent and severity. At presentation, 50% of patients with UC have disease limited to the rectum and sigmoid (proctosigmoiditis), 20% have left-sided disease (to the splenic flexure), and 30% present with pancolitis (to the cecum). Endoscopic findings range from decreased vascular pattern with erythema and edema (Video: Video of Colonoscopy in Ulcerative Pancolitis) in mild disease to large and deep ulcerations in severe disease. Histopathology shows features of chronic colitis, with distorted and branching colonic crypts along with crypt abscesses.

In contrast, patients with Crohn disease typically have ileocolonic disease, isolated small-bowel disease, or colonic disease; each occurs in approximately one third of patients. Some patients have isolated upper gastrointestinal tract or perianal disease without small-bowel or colonic inflammation. The earliest endoscopic findings of Crohn disease include aphthous ulcers, which can coalesce to form stellate ulcers and have a “cobblestone” mucosal appearance. A characteristic mucosal feature of Crohn disease is the “skip lesion,” consisting of affected areas separated by normal mucosa (Video: Video of Colonoscopy in Crohn Disease). Granulomatous inflammation is characteristic of Crohn disease but is uncommonly found on mucosal biopsy specimens. Histopathology in small intestinal Crohn disease shows chronic jejunitis or ileitis, and Crohn colitis has similar histology to that of UC, except for granulomas.

Imaging establishes the location, extent, and severity of IBD. Patients with a severe episode of IBD require plain abdominal radiography to assess for a dilated colon (indicating evolving toxic megacolon) or small-bowel obstruction (

). CT or magnetic resonance enterography provides information about location and severity of small-bowel disease and about complicating fistula, abscess, or stricture. Video capsule endoscopy is highly sensitive for detecting small inflammatory lesions of the intestine but is not commonly required.

Goals of IBD treatment based on STRIDE II recommendations are to induce and maintain remission and prevent progression of disease- and treatment-related complications. Remission is defined by endoscopic healing of bowel mucosa rather than symptom resolution alone. Long-term treatment targets also include normalized quality of life and absence of disability. A variety of biomarkers, including fecal calprotectin, fecal lactoferrin, and serum C-reactive protein level, can be used to noninvasively monitor disease remission and disease activity in IBD. Categories of drugs used for treatment include the following:

  • 5-Aminosalicylates (5-ASAs)
  • Glucocorticoids
  • Immunomodulators
  • Biologic agents
  • Small molecules

Stratification based on clinical severity and risk for disease complications is important in guiding IBD management:

  • Mild to moderate UC is defined as fewer than four to six bowel movements per day, mild to moderate rectal bleeding, no constitutional symptoms, and low overall inflammatory burden.
  • Severe UC is marked by more than six bloody stools per day plus signs of systemic toxicity (e.g., fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis).
  • Patients with mild Crohn disease are ambulatory and eat and drink normally, with weight loss less than 10% and no disease-related complications, although patients may have diarrhea and abdominal pain.
  • Patients with moderate to severe Crohn disease may have prominent symptoms, such as fever and abdominal pain, and may be cachectic, with significant weight loss, and may have disease-related complications. These patients are often hospitalized.

Treatment decisions should consider disease factors that predict a more aggressive course and risk for future surgery and complications. Poor prognostic factors in UC disease severity include the following:

  • Age younger than 40 years at diagnosis
  • Extensive colitis
  • Deep ulcerations on endoscopy
  • Hospitalization for colitis
  • Elevated C-reactive protein level
  • Low serum albumin level

Features that are associated with a high risk for complications of Crohn disease include the following:

  • Age younger than 30 years at diagnosis
  • Initial extensive small-bowel involvement (particularly proximal gut)
  • Perianal disease
  • Glucocorticoid dependence or resistance
  • Fistulizing or stenotic disease

Early treatment with biologic agents or small molecules is indicated in the setting of moderate to severe disease activity.

See [Table: Table: Medical Treatment of Inflammatory Bowel Disease]

for UC and Crohn disease pharmaceutical therapy.

The agent used to induce remission is frequently continued for maintenance, except for glucocorticoids, which are used only to induce remission and generally should not be used for more than 3 months. Response to therapy can be determined by assessing symptoms, laboratory testing, intestinal ultrasonography, and endoscopy with biopsy.

Some patients may not respond to induction therapy or may have decreased response to maintenance therapy. Such patients require reassessment for disease progression; nonadherence to medical therapy; or an alternative cause, such as superimposed infection.

Infectious diarrhea may be indistinguishable from a flare of Crohn disease or UC and may also be the trigger of a disease flare; therefore, it is critical to rule out enteric infection, particularly with C. difficile, in all patients by stool studies. Active C. difficile infection in patients with IBD is associated with increased disease severity, greater length of hospitalization, and increased likelihood of colectomy and mortality.

5-ASAs are believed to have an anti-inflammatory mechanism of action. The main therapeutic 5-ASAs are delayed- and controlled-release mesalamine, olsalazine, balsalazide, and sulfasalazine. Unconjugated 5-ASA (mesalamine) is rapidly absorbed in the jejunum, allowing only 20% of the drug to reach the ileum and colon. Oral 5-ASA (olsalazine, balsalazide) is modified to reduce upper gastrointestinal absorption and enhance drug delivery to the colon. Sulfasalazine has the most adverse effects, including fever, rash, nausea, and headache, and requires concomitant folate supplementation. Sulfasalazine is not considered first-line therapy but is a reasonable choice in patients already taking it who are in remission or have prominent arthritic symptoms.

5-ASAs are the mainstay of treatment of mild to moderate UC (

), with a dose-dependent response when used to induce remission. Patients with proctitis should receive 5-ASA suppositories. Patients with mild to moderate left-sided disease should receive 5-ASA enemas. Furthermore, combined 5-ASA therapy (oral and topical) is superior for inducing remission compared with oral therapy alone in the treatment of mild to moderate left-sided disease. Mild to moderate extensive disease should be treated with oral 5-ASA therapy. 5-ASAs are also effective in maintaining remission in mild to moderate disease.

Oral and intravenous glucocorticoids are commonly used to treat moderate to severe flares and can induce remission. However, glucocorticoids are not effective for maintenance therapy and have significant adverse effects. Budesonide is a potent glucocorticoid with high first-pass hepatic metabolism and fewer systemic adverse effects. Multimatrix budesonide is a colonic delivery system that induces remission in mild to moderate UC unresponsive to 5-ASAs. A topical budesonide foam is effective for mild to moderate active ulcerative proctosigmoiditis, with fewer adverse effects than seen with conventional glucocorticoids.

Thiopurines (azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine) are immunomodulators used as glucocorticoid-sparing agents in UC. They are effective in maintaining remission in UC, so they should be considered in patients who require glucocorticoids. This includes patients who require two courses of glucocorticoids for remission induction within 1 year and patients who require intravenous glucocorticoids for acute disease flare. They have a slow onset of action (2-3 months), and patients require a tapering glucocorticoid regimen to bridge the interval until thiopurines take effect. Thiopurines are no more effective than placebo in inducing remission. The immunomodulator methotrexate is not effective in UC.

Thiopurine methyltransferase, a key enzyme in the metabolism of azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine, exhibits a population polymorphism. Before initiation of thiopurines, testing for the TPMT genotype or phenotype (enzyme activity) is recommended to prevent bone marrow toxicity by identifying persons with low or absent TPMT enzyme activity. However, all patients taking thiopurines require monitoring with complete blood counts and liver chemistry testing because 70% of patients who develop leukopenia while taking these agents do not have TPMT variants.

Tumor necrosis factor (TNF), a proinflammatory cytokine, plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of IBD. The anti-TNF agents infliximab, adalimumab, and golimumab induce and maintain remission in moderate to severe UC, with infliximab being the preferred initial agent. Early use of biologic agents is appropriate after failure of 5-ASA treatment or in the setting of severely active disease. Infliximab is administered by intravenous infusion; adalimumab and golimumab are given subcutaneously. Combination therapy with biologic agents and immunomodulators is more effective than monotherapy with either agent in achieving glucocorticoid-free remission and mucosal healing. Before initiating anti-TNF agents, patients should undergo testing for latent tuberculosis because of an increased risk for tuberculosis reactivation during therapy. Those with latent tuberculosis should receive treatment before or simultaneously with anti-TNF therapy initiation. Patients should also be assessed for chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection before starting anti-TNF therapy and receive treatment if needed.

The anti-integrin agent vedolizumab is effective in inducing and maintaining remission of moderate to severe UC. In patients who are naive to biologic agents, infliximab or vedolizumab, rather than adalimumab, is recommended for inducing remission in moderate to severe disease.

Ustekinumab, a monoclonal antibody that blocks the biologic activity of interleukin (IL)-12 and IL-23 by inhibiting receptors for these cytokines on T cells, is effective in inducing and maintaining remission in patients with moderate to severe UC. Guidelines recommend using ustekinumab, rather than vedolizumab or adalimumab, for remission induction in patients who previously did not benefit from infliximab.

Risankizumab, mirikizumab, and guselkumab are monoclonal antibodies that block the biological activity of IL-23 by binding to the p19 subunit of its receptor and inhibiting the effect of this cytokine. Risankizumab, mirikizumab, and guselkumab are effective in inducing and maintaining remission in patients with moderate to severe UC.

The development of oral small molecules is rapidly changing disease management. The small-molecule agents tofacitinib, upadacitinib, ozanimod, and etrasimod are approved for treatment of UC. Benefits of small-molecule therapies include oral administration, rapid onset of action, and absence of antidrug antibodies.

Tofacitinib and upadacitinib are Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors. Tofacitinib is a pan-JAK inhibitor that is effective in inducing and maintaining remission in moderate to severe UC when anti-TNF agents have failed. Upadacitinib is a selective inhibitor of JAK-1 and is also effective for remission induction and maintenance in moderate to severe UC. Adverse effects include cytopenias, lipid abnormalities, liver injury, reactivation of latent tuberculosis, and exacerbation of HBV infection. Therefore, pretreatment laboratory studies for JAK inhibitors should include a complete blood count, liver chemistry panel, lipid panel, screening for latent tuberculosis, and testing for HBV infection. Because of findings from the ORAL Surveillance study, tofacitinib is indicated for use only after failure or intolerance to anti-TNF therapy. This restriction has also been applied to upadacitinib.

Ozanimod and etrasimod are sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators that limit lymphocyte migration from peripheral lymphoid organs. They are effective for treatment of moderate to severe UC. Drug-related adverse effects include bradycardia and macular edema. Both agents are contraindicated in patients with cardiovascular disorders and heart block, except those with a pacemaker. All patients should undergo ECG before starting treatment and should be monitored with periodic ECG during therapy.

Cyclosporine is an immunosuppressive agent used as an induction agent in select hospitalized patients with severe UC that is unresponsive to intravenous glucocorticoids. It acts as a potential bridge therapy to a slower-onset immunomodulatory or biologic agent.

5-ASAs are not effective in small-bowel Crohn disease, but sulfasalazine is effective for remission and maintenance therapy for mild colonic Crohn disease.

Oral and intravenous glucocorticoids are commonly used to treat moderate to severe flares of Crohn disease and are effective in inducing remission; however, glucocorticoids are not effective for maintenance therapy. Controlled-release budesonide is effective in inducing remission in mild to moderate ileocolonic Crohn disease.

Thiopurines are used in Crohn disease as glucocorticoid-sparing therapy but are not effective in inducing remission. Methotrexate should be considered for alleviating signs and symptoms of glucocorticoid-dependent Crohn disease and for maintaining remission. Adverse effects of methotrexate include hepatotoxicity and interstitial pneumonitis, which can manifest with cough and dyspnea of insidious onset; concomitant folate administration is necessary.

Increasing evidence supports biologic agents early in the disease course rather than in a step-up therapy approach.

The anti-TNF agents infliximab, adalimumab, and certolizumab pegol are recommended (infliximab and adalimumab are preferred) to treat moderate to severe disease and should be used initially for patients with high-risk disease or severe disease activity. Combination therapy with infliximab and azathioprine is more effective than monotherapy with either agent alone in achieving glucocorticoid-free remission and mucosal healing. By improving the pharmacokinetics of infliximab, the combination of infliximab and azathioprine is superior to infliximab monotherapy and is considered first-line therapy in the context of severe disease. Monotherapy is preferred in patients at increased risk for lymphoproliferative disease.

The antiadhesion agents vedolizumab and natalizumab are effective in inducing and maintaining remission of moderate to severe disease. However, guidelines recommend against using natalizumab because of risk for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (see Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy in Infectious Disease).

Ustekinumab is also effective in moderate to severe Crohn disease and in patients who did not benefit from standard therapy with immunomodulators and glucocorticoids or anti-TNF agents.

Newer therapeutic options are the IL-23 p19 inhibitors risankizumab, mirikizumab, and guselkumab. They are effective and well tolerated as induction and maintenance therapy in patients with moderately to severely active Crohn disease.

Oral small-molecule agents were first used to treat UC. However, upadacitinib, a selective JAK-1 inhibitor, was found to be effective and approved for treatment of patients with moderate to severe Crohn disease who have had an inadequate response or intolerance to anti-TNF agents.

Fistulizing Crohn disease is difficult to manage. The most appropriate therapy requires expert evaluation and coordination of care between the internal medicine physician, gastroenterologist, and surgeon. As part of multimodality therapy, guidelines provide a strong recommendation for infliximab combined with an antibiotic, such as metronidazole or ciprofloxacin, for perianal fistula without perianal abscess. Infliximab can be effective for enterocutaneous and rectovaginal fistulae. Short-term tacrolimus can be effective for perianal and cutaneous fistulae.

Total proctocolectomy with end-ileostomy or ileal pouch–anal anastomosis is performed for medically refractory disease, toxic megacolon, or carcinoma.

Approximately 50% of patients with Crohn disease undergo surgery within 10 years of their diagnosis. Indications for surgery in Crohn disease include the following:

  • Medically refractory fistula
  • Fibrotic stricture with obstructive symptoms
  • Symptoms refractory to medical therapy
  • Cancer

The guiding principle of surgery in Crohn disease is preservation of bowel length and function because disease frequently recurs after segmental resection. Patients with Crohn disease who undergo surgery require aggressive biologic therapy or immunomodulator treatment to decrease the rate of postoperative disease recurrence.

Severe, complicated Crohn disease and UC are potentially life-threatening conditions that require hospitalization and interdisciplinary care from hospitalists, gastroenterologists, interventional radiologists, and colorectal surgeons.

IBD is associated with a threefold increased risk for venous thromboembolism; therefore, all hospitalized patients with IBD should receive subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin or fondaparinux for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Rectal bleeding from severe UC is expected and is not a contraindication to prophylaxis. Only in cases of massive bleeding should nonpharmacologic thromboprophylaxis be used instead of anticoagulants.

For severe Crohn disease, patients should receive parenteral glucocorticoids. CT enterography is the imaging modality of choice to assess for intra-abdominal complications of Crohn disease, such as fibrostenotic small-bowel obstruction or fistulizing disease with intra-abdominal abscesses. MRI of the pelvis, endoscopic ultrasonography, and examination under anesthesia are methods to evaluate perianal disease. Therapy for complicated Crohn disease with antibiotics, immunosuppression, percutaneous drainage, and surgery is chosen on a case-by-case basis.

Common indications for hospitalization in UC include acute severe UC, failure of outpatient medical therapy, and toxic megacolon. The initial inpatient evaluation of hospitalized patients with acute severe UC aims to assess disease severity and identify and prevent potential complications. Initial review of medications is important, and NSAIDs, antidiarrheals, and narcotics, which may precipitate disease flares and toxic megacolon, should be discontinued. Mesalamine medications should be discontinued upon admission to the hospital because 2% to 3% of patients experience a paradoxical worsening of diarrhea due to hypersensitivity colitis from these agents that can mimic a severe flare. C-reactive protein should be measured at admission so that the level can be monitored during therapy. Enteric infections, such as with C. difficile and cytomegalovirus, that can cause a disease flare must be excluded. A plain abdominal radiograph should be obtained at admission to evaluate for colonic dilation indicating evolving toxic megacolon. Early flexible sigmoidoscopy is indicated to assess disease severity and to perform biopsy for cytomegalovirus infection.

An oral diet is recommended. Bowel rest with parenteral nutrition does not improve outcomes in acute severe UC; however, toxic megacolon would be a contraindication to a regular oral diet. Oral intake is important for appropriate assessment of response to treatment because eating less reduces bowel movement frequency.

Initial medical therapy for acute severe UC is with glucocorticoids. Because one third of patients do not respond to intravenous glucocorticoids, preparation for rescue medical therapy or surgery should be undertaken. Involving a colorectal surgeon early is critical, as is obtaining anticipatory laboratory testing for use of infliximab, with interferon-gamma release assay to test for latent tuberculosis and HBV serologies to exclude chronic HBV infection. Before treatment with cyclosporine, serum magnesium and total cholesterol levels should be checked.

Response to treatment is determined after 3 days of intravenous glucocorticoids. Glucocorticoid failure is predicted by eight or more daily bowel movements or three to eight daily bowel movements and a C-reactive protein level greater than 4.5 mg/dL (45 mg/L). Patients who do not respond to intravenous glucocorticoids in a few days should be considered for colectomy or a trial of infliximab or intravenous cyclosporine.

To improve pregnancy outcomes, clinical and endoscopic remission of IBD should be achieved before conception. Screening for active disease is recommended in all pregnant patients with IBD by checking fecal calprotectin before conception, every trimester, and postpartum.

Most medications used to treat IBD are safe in pregnancy. Biologic agents should be continued throughout pregnancy and lactation. Thiopurines are considered low risk during pregnancy and breastfeeding and should be continued to maintain disease remission. Shunting of metabolites can occur in up to 25% of patients in the second trimester, which can increase the risk for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. It is recommended to monitor thiopurine metabolites and liver enzymes in each trimester, at delivery, and postpartum. If intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is diagnosed or if transaminase levels become elevated, thiopurines should potentially be discontinued. Thiopurines should not be started after conception because of the risk for pancreatitis and bone marrow suppression, although the risk is small.

Methotrexate, etrasimod, and ozanimod must be stopped at least 3 months before conception because of teratogenic effects. As a result of limited data, JAK inhibitors should be avoided in pregnancy and lactation. See [Table: Table: Rheumatologic Medications and Reproductive Health]

for a list of biologic agents and associated risks posed in pregnancy. Medication adherence after delivery is critical to decrease postpartum disease flare.

All patients with IBD should be encouraged to stop smoking. Smoking increases Crohn disease activity and the risk for extraintestinal manifestations. Smoking cessation may temporarily worsen UC, but overall health benefits exceed this risk.

Patients with IBD are at increased risk for metabolic bone disease because of glucocorticoid use and diminished vitamin D and calcium absorption. Bone mineral density testing is recommended in patients with additional risk factors for osteopenia or osteoporosis, such as low BMI (<20 kg/m^2), more than 3 months of cumulative corticosteroid exposure, current smoking, postmenopausal status, or hypogonadism. Otherwise, patients with IBD should be screened for osteoporosis based on established guidelines for the general population (see Osteoporosis in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Depression and anxiety are more common in patients with IBD than the general population and are associated with medication nonadherence. Therefore, annual screening for depression and anxiety is recommended in patients with IBD.

Patients with IBD should avoid using NSAIDs when possible because these drugs can exacerbate disease activity.

Patients with IBD have increased risk for vaccine-preventable illnesses. Ideally, all immunizations should occur before immunosuppressive therapy begins.

Inactivated vaccines can be safely administered to all patients with IBD, regardless of immunosuppression. Patients with IBD should receive recommended adult immunizations (see Immunization in Foundations of Clinical Practice for further discussion of vaccination strategies). Family members should be up to date with age-appropriate vaccines as a form of indirect protection.

Live vaccines should not be administered to immunosuppressed patients with IBD, and it is preferable to administer them 4 weeks before starting immunosuppressive therapy to achieve a maximum immune response.

Patients with IBD have increased risk for anal, colorectal, cervical, and skin cancers. Some immunosuppressive treatments also increase the risk for cancer, although this risk is outweighed by the protective effect of mucosal healing and resultant reduced risk for cancers associated with chronic mucosal inflammation. Long-standing colorectal inflammation increases cancer risk. Initial colonoscopy screening for dysplasia should be performed 8 years after symptom onset in all persons with colonic IBD and immediately on diagnosis of primary sclerosing cholangitis. Patients should ideally have quiescent disease, because inflammation can obscure precancerous findings. If a patient has isolated ileal Crohn disease, then their risk for colorectal cancer is similar to the general population. Depending on findings on screening colonoscopy, surveillance colonoscopy should be performed every 1 to 5 years based on risk factors for colorectal cancer, including the following:

  • Current and previous burden of colonic inflammation
  • Family history of colorectal cancer
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis
  • History of colorectal dysplasia
  • Pseudopolyposis
  • Frequency and quality of previous surveillance examinations

A thorough perianal and anal examination should be performed during all colonoscopies, with a careful inspection of the anal canal in patients with perianal Crohn disease, anal stricture, human papillomavirus (HPV), HIV, and in those who engage in anoreceptive intercourse because of the increased risk for anal cancer.

Women with IBD who are taking immunosuppressants may have an increased risk for cervical dysplasia. Women with IBD should undergo age-appropriate cervical cancer screening and receive HPV vaccination according to established guidelines.

Patients with IBD also have an increased risk for melanoma and nonmelanoma skin cancers. Most of the risk is associated with specific treatments, such as anti-TNF agents (melanoma) and immunomodulators (nonmelanoma); however, evidence suggests that the increased risk for melanoma is also independent of treatment. American College of Gastroenterology guidelines recommend that patients with IBD undergo yearly total-body skin cancer screening. All patients with IBD should use sunscreen, wear protective clothing, avoid tanning beds, and undergo dermatologic surveillance.

Microscopic colitis is an inflammatory disease of the colon and a common cause of chronic watery diarrhea. It may occur in persons of all ages, although the disease primarily affects women older than 50 years. Risk factors include the following:

  • Increasing age
  • Female sex
  • Presence of other autoimmune diseases (e.g., celiac disease)
  • Tobacco smoking
  • Certain medications (NSAIDs, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and proton pump inhibitors)

It presents with abrupt or gradual onset of watery, nonbloody diarrhea that has a relapsing-remitting course over months to years, sometimes accompanied by mild weight loss and abdominal pain. Colonoscopy will reveal normal-appearing mucosa, with diagnosis relying on histologic examination of colon biopsy specimens. Subclassification into lymphocytic colitis and collagenous colitis (

) is based on predominating histologic features.

The first step in management of microscopic colitis is discontinuing any possible causative medications and symptomatic treatment with antidiarrheal agents, such as loperamide. For moderate to severe symptoms, first-line treatment is budesonide. Relapse of symptoms is common after discontinuation of budesonide; the recommended treatment is a longer-term course of low-dose budesonide (3-6 mg/d) as a maintenance regimen, which has lower clinical relapse risk. Drugs such as prednisone, bismuth subsalicylate, and cholestyramine are used as alternatives to budesonide but are less well studied. Patients with microscopic colitis have no long-term increased risk for colorectal cancer.

bodies.gisec24009:
Ischemic Bowel Disease

Ischemic bowel disease is caused by decreased blood flow to the small or large intestine that is insufficient to meet intestinal cellular metabolic function. It represents a spectrum of conditions that can be related to acute or chronic alterations of arterial or venous intestinal blood flow. Ischemic bowel disease can be broadly subcategorized into three clinical syndromes: acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI), chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI), and colonic ischemia ( [Table: Table: Gastrointestinal Ischemic Syndromes]

).

AMI is a rare condition caused by an abrupt decrease in blood flow to the small intestine that can be obstructive or nonobstructive. Obstructive causes include cardiogenic emboli or thrombosis related to underlying atherosclerotic disease. Nonobstructive AMI is most commonly caused by vasoconstriction of the mesenteric vasculature in the setting of severe sepsis or marked reduction in effective circulating volume (low-flow states). Mesenteric vein thrombosis may also cause AMI and often is associated with malignancy, hypercoagulable states, or intra-abdominal inflammatory conditions. Bowel infarction occurs with prolonged blood flow reduction; this is the most important prognostic factor for adverse outcomes.

AMI presents with abrupt onset of severe, constant periumbilical abdominal pain followed by the urge to defecate and loose, nonbloody stools. Hematochezia occurs in some cases of AMI (15%), and its presence signifies concomitant right colon ischemia. Although patients report severe abdominal pain, the abdominal examination in early disease is unimpressive and shows no peritoneal signs (pain out of proportion to physical examination findings). This should immediately raise suspicion of early AMI. With delayed or late presentation, intestinal ischemia progresses to infarction, and the mortality rate is high.

Laboratory and abdominal imaging findings in early AMI, before intestinal infarction develops, are nonspecific. Most patients have elevated leukocyte counts. A serum lactate level may be normal, and this should not exclude the diagnosis.

CT angiography is recommended for diagnosing AMI. Although magnetic resonance angiography avoids the risks of radiation and contrast exposure, it takes longer and is less sensitive for distal and nonocclusive disease. Duplex ultrasonography is an effective low-cost method for assessing the proximal mesenteric vessels, but adequate ultrasonography often cannot be performed in patients with AMI. The classic angiographic finding is an embolus or thrombus in the superior mesenteric artery.

Initial treatment consists of aggressive fluid resuscitation, abdominal decompression, pain management, and administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Emergent surgery is indicated if imaging findings signify mesenteric infarction, such as pneumatosis intestinalis (i.e., gas within the intestinal wall) or portal venous gas. Otherwise, angiography with selective catheterization of the mesenteric vessels may be performed along with endovascular intervention, if possible. Patients with AMI ischemia due to mesenteric venous thrombosis should receive systemic anticoagulation when there are no peritoneal signs or findings of bowel infarction to prevent thrombus propagation. For patients with AMI due to arterial occlusion, anticoagulation should be initiated after surgery to prevent additional thrombus formation.

CMI is an uncommon condition that involves a gradual decrease in blood flow to the small intestine over a period of months to years. It most commonly results from atherosclerotic narrowing of the mesenteric arteries.

The classic symptom triad is postprandial abdominal pain, sitophobia (fear of eating), and weight loss; however, this triad is seen in only 30% of patients with CMI. CMI should also be suspected in the setting of recurrent postprandial abdominal pain. Pain begins approximately 30 minutes after food ingestion when the fixed narrowing of the mesenteric arteries prevents blood flow from increasing and meeting the increased functional demand of the small bowel, with resultant ischemia.

The diagnosis requires exclusion of alternative causes of postprandial abdominal pain and weight loss, along with compatible imaging findings. CT or magnetic resonance angiography findings suggesting CMI include severe stenosis (>70%) of two of the three mesenteric arteries.

CMI is treated with percutaneous endovascular stenting or surgical revascularization. Periprocedural morbidity and mortality are lower with endovascular stenting; however, this method is less durable than surgical revascularization.

Colonic ischemia is the most common form of ischemic bowel disease. It usually results from a nonocclusive low-flow state in microvessels, which occurs with hypovolemia or hypotension. Risk factors include the following:

  • Age older than 60 years
  • Female sex
  • Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
  • Atrial fibrillation
  • Chronic kidney disease
  • Irritable bowel syndrome
  • Vasoconstrictive and antihypertensive medications
  • Constipation
  • Thrombophilia
  • COPD

Colonic ischemia presents with the abrupt onset of cramping and lower abdominal discomfort that is mild to moderate, followed within 24 hours by diarrhea and hematochezia. See Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding in Gastroenterology.

Physical examination most commonly reveals mild lower abdominal tenderness over the involved bowel segment without peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies may show mildly elevated leukocyte count and blood urea nitrogen level.

Abdominal CT is indicated to assess the severity, phase, and distribution of colonic ischemia. CT findings in colonic ischemia are nonspecific and include bowel-wall thickening (

) and pericolonic fat stranding (an increase in density within pericolonic fat secondary to inflammation), often in the distribution of the “watershed” areas of the colon (splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction). Infections that can mimic colonic ischemia, such as with cytomegalovirus, Clostridioides difficile, and Shiga toxin–producing Escherichia coli, must be excluded. Colonoscopy with biopsy is the test of choice to confirm the diagnosis.

Because colonic ischemia is usually caused by a nonocclusive low-flow state, dedicated imaging of the mesenteric vasculature is of low yield and generally not indicated. The exception is right-sided colonic ischemia, which can be the harbinger of AMI caused by a focal thrombus or embolus of the superior mesenteric artery. Therefore, patients with right-sided colonic ischemia require noninvasive imaging of the mesenteric vasculature to exclude an occlusive process of the superior mesenteric artery.

Most cases of colonic ischemia are mild and transient, with rapid spontaneous resolution. Patients with more severe disease require hospitalization for supportive care with bowel rest, intravascular volume restoration, antimicrobial therapy in many cases, and close observation. Patients with colonic ischemia who have several risk factors for poor outcome should receive broad-spectrum antibiotics. The American College of Gastroenterology has devised a risk stratification based on features associated with poor outcomes in those with colonic ischemia that helps guide antibiotic therapy ( [Table: Table: Colonic Ischemia Disease Severity and Use of Antibiotics]

). Only a few patients require surgical intervention for necrotic bowel or irreversible complications, such as stricture.
