bodies.gisec24010:
Diverticular Disease

A diverticulum is a herniation of the mucosa and submucosa through a weakness in the muscle wall. Diverticulosis (presence of diverticula) is the most common finding identified during colonoscopy. The mechanism is thought to involve diet, microbiota, genetics, and altered colonic motility. Diverticulosis incidence increases with age, with a reported prevalence of 60% in persons 60 years and older, of whom 5% experience complications, such as diverticulitis or diverticular bleeding (see Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding in Gastroenterology).

Diverticulitis has traditionally been considered an occlusive process resulting from a blocked diverticulum, with the trapping of bacteria and development of inflammation. However, a more recent alternative hypothesis posits that diverticulitis results from alterations in the gut microbiome, which may be influenced by genetics, diet, lifestyle, and medications. Risk factors for diverticulitis include the following:

  • Western dietary pattern (i.e., high in red meat, fat, and refined grains)
  • Obesity
  • Smoking
  • Physical inactivity
  • NSAIDs
  • Opioid analgesics
  • Glucocorticoids

Diverticulitis can be classified as uncomplicated or complicated. Complicated diverticulitis is marked by abscess, fistula, obstruction, or perforation.

The clinical presentation of uncomplicated diverticulitis is colicky abdominal pain relieved with flatus or a bowel movement; fever and altered bowel habits may occur. Patients with complicated diverticulitis may have more severe symptoms, including peritoneal signs and hemodynamic instability. Individuals with colovesical fistula may present with the following:

  • Dysuria
  • Urinary frequency
  • Pneumaturia
  • Fecaluria
  • Recurrent urinary tract infection

Patients with diverticulitis do not have gastrointestinal bleeding, and its presence should suggest an alternative diagnosis.

On physical examination, abdominal tenderness (usually in the left lower quadrant) is often present.

Acute diverticulitis is often diagnosed on clinical grounds based on fever, left-lower-quadrant abdominal pain, and leukocytosis. However, a diagnosis made by history, physical examination, and laboratory studies is correct in only 50% of patients. Therefore, CT of the abdomen and pelvis with oral and intravenous contrast is recommended to confirm the diagnosis in patients without a previous imaging-confirmed diagnosis and to evaluate for complicated disease. Abdominal ultrasonography, MRI, and plain abdominal radiography are other imaging options.

Uncomplicated diverticulitis has traditionally been treated with oral antibiotics (e.g., a fluoroquinolone and metronidazole) and a liquid diet; however, emerging evidence suggests close observation without antibiotics may be considered in immunocompetent patients with acute uncomplicated diverticulitis. Antibiotics are indicated for patients who are immunosuppressed, are pregnant, or have significant comorbid disease. Intravenous antibiotics and hospitalization are required in patients unable to tolerate an oral diet; patients with severe comorbidities, advanced age, or immunosuppression; and patients for whom oral antibiotics have been ineffective.

Treatment of complicated diverticulitis depends on illness severity and CT findings. If the CT scan shows a large abscess, CT-guided drainage may be needed. Surgery is indicated for patients who present with or develop peritonitis, perforation, obstruction, or persistent sepsis. Complications occur more commonly during the first episode of diverticulitis than after subsequent episodes; therefore, decisions regarding elective segmental resection should be based not on the number of diverticulitis episodes but rather on a case-by-case basis.

Measures to prevent recurrent diverticulitis include the following:

  • A high-fiber, plant-based diet
  • Smoking cessation
  • Physical activity
  • Avoidance of NSAIDs, glucocorticoids, and opioid analgesics

No evidence supports restricting foods, such as nuts, berries, and seeds, to prevent recurrent diverticulitis.

Unless performed recently (within the past 1-2 years), colonoscopy should be performed in all patients with an episode of diverticulitis 6 to 8 weeks after symptoms resolve to rule out concomitant malignancy.

A small percentage of patients (5%-10%) have persistent or “smoldering” diverticulitis, characterized by abdominal pain with leukocytosis, fever, or evidence of inflammation on CT. This smoldering process occurs despite antibiotic treatment. These patients require surgical consultation for segmental resection.

bodies.gisec24011:
Appendicitis

Appendicitis is a common cause of acute abdominal pain and is the most common abdominal surgical emergency in the world. Appendicitis occurs most frequently during the second and third decades of life. Vague periumbilical abdominal pain is the initial symptom, with subsequent emigration of the pain to the right lower quadrant. Commonly associated symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and anorexia.

Physical examination findings may initially be subtle; however, as inflammation progresses, patients develop more pronounced findings. Fever, rebound abdominal tenderness, and guarding may be present. Tenderness is often pronounced at the McBurney point (two thirds of the distance from the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine), which corresponds to the location of the appendix.

Laboratory findings may include leukocytosis and elevated C-reactive protein level. Clinical prediction tools, such as the Appendicitis Inflammatory Response score, Adult Appendicitis score, and Alvarado score, may help risk-stratify patients.

CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast is the most definitive imaging modality for adults presenting with right-lower-quadrant pain with suspected appendicitis (

). CT has superior diagnostic accuracy compared with ultrasonography. Ultrasonography is also commonly used in the initial assessment of appendicitis because of widespread availability and lack of radiation exposure but is limited in accuracy because it is operator dependent and associated with nonvisualization of the appendix, particularly in complicated cases. Ultrasonography is the diagnostic modality for pediatric patients and pregnant patients.

Appendicitis is classified as uncomplicated or complicated. Uncomplicated appendicitis is defined by acute appendicitis without signs of perforation (inflammatory mass, phlegmon, or abscess). Most appendicitis cases (80%) are uncomplicated. Although appendectomy is the definitive treatment of acute appendicitis, in select uncomplicated cases, nonoperative treatment may be considered; this includes analgesia, antibiotics for 7 to 10 days, and careful follow-up. However, 30% to 40% of patients who opt for nonoperative management will require appendectomy in the next 5 years, especially if an appendicolith is present.

Complicated (perforated) appendicitis requires treatment with intravenous antibiotics, possible percutaneous drainage in the case of an abscess, and emergent or interval appendectomy. At postoperative follow-up, colonoscopy should be considered in patients treated for a perforated appendix to exclude a cecal mass as a cause of acute appendicitis.

Anorectal Disorders

Perianal symptoms, including bright red blood per rectum, pain, itching, or a mass, should prompt a detailed evaluation of the anus, anal canal, and rectum that includes visual inspection of the anus and digital rectal examination. Anoscopy or proctoscopy may be required to establish the diagnosis. Colonoscopy is indicated when additional alarm features are present:

  • Age older than 45 years
  • Altered bowel habits
  • Anemia
  • Inflammatory bowel disease
  • Unexplained weight loss
  • Family history of colorectal cancer

Risk factors for symptomatic hemorrhoids include the following:

  • Ascites
  • Pregnancy
  • Excessive sitting or squatting
  • Systemic rheumatic disorders
  • Low dietary fiber intake
  • Obesity
  • Sedentary lifestyle

Recurrent straining and persistent bowel alterations (constipation or diarrhea) can lead to engorgement of hemorrhoid plexuses, causing symptoms of bleeding, prolapse, and swelling. Age-related changes can cause the hemorrhoid beds to slide back and forth during defecation, resulting in mucoid anal discharge, perianal wetness, soiling, irritation, or pruritus. Pain is not a common symptom of uncomplicated hemorrhoids and should raise suspicion for hemorrhoid complications, including thrombosis, ischemia, and incarceration from prolapse, or for an alternative diagnosis, such as anal fissure, perirectal infection, and perianal abscess. Hemorrhoids are categorized as internal if proximal to the dentate line, external if distal to the dentate line, or mixed if crossing the dentate line.

Evaluation should always include a careful perianal and digital rectal examination. Symptomatic hemorrhoids can be confused with rectal mucosal prolapse, full-thickness rectal prolapse, or a prolapsed rectal polyp. Prolapsed concentric folds indicate rectal prolapse as opposed to a prolapsed hemorrhoid or anal polyp. (See

for examples.) Further direct evaluation of the anorectum can be considered with anoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy. Colonoscopy should be pursued when there is no obvious source of rectal bleeding, alarm features are present, rectal bleeding persists after hemorrhoid treatment, or colorectal cancer screening is indicated per guidelines.

First-line therapy for hemorrhoids includes increased fiber intake, adequate liquid intake, and avoidance of straining. Various topical agents may reduce hemorrhoid symptoms but are not necessary for curative therapy. Patients with internal hemorrhoids unresponsive to medical therapy should be considered for banding, which is considered the most effective office-based procedure. Other options, including sclerotherapy and infrared coagulation, are less effective.

Thrombosed external hemorrhoids may be more effectively treated with surgical excision versus nonoperative therapy if addressed within 72 hours of symptom onset. Surgical hemorrhoidectomy should be reserved for refractory hemorrhoids, large external hemorrhoids, or combined internal and external hemorrhoids with rectal prolapse.

Anal fissures are longitudinal mucosal tears in the anal canal characterized by anorectal pain that is worsened by bowel movements and sitting (

). Rectal bleeding with bowel movements or wiping is common. Anal fissures are idiopathic or result from trauma caused by passage of hard stool, receptive anal intercourse, or insertion of a foreign body (such as an enema or endoscope). Idiopathic anal fissures are most commonly located in the posterior midline. Lateral anal fissures should raise concern for other entities:

  • Crohn disease
  • Ulcerative colitis
  • Tuberculosis
  • Syphilis
  • HIV infection
  • Psoriasis
  • Anal cancer

Anal fissures lasting more than 8 to 12 weeks are considered chronic and may be characterized by edema and fibrosis as well as a sentinel pile (appearing as a skin tag) or hypertrophied anal papilla within the anal canal.

Acute anal fissures generally resolve within a few weeks with the use of sitz baths, psyllium, and bulking agents. Topical anesthetics and anti-inflammatory agents can be considered to address pain or bleeding but are not required to promote fissure healing. Rectal spasm is the major reason for anal fissures becoming chronic and should be treated with topical calcium channel blockers or nitrates; calcium channel blockers are preferred, given their similar efficacy with fewer adverse effects. Patients with chronic fissures unresponsive to these measures should be referred for internal sphincter botulinum toxin injection or surgical internal lateral sphincterotomy.

Fecal incontinence is the recurrent, uncontrolled passage of fecal material; it does not include passage of clear mucus or flatus incontinence. Fecal incontinence is grossly underreported because of associated embarrassment; health care providers should inquire about it in patients at risk. Risk factors include the following:

  • Multiparity
  • Older age
  • Obesity
  • Diarrhea
  • Urinary incontinence
  • Obstetric complications
  • Anorectal surgery
  • Anorectal disease

Factors contributing to fecal incontinence include loose stools, impaired rectal storage capacity, altered rectal sensation, and reduced anal sphincter tone. Constipation with resultant fecal loading and overflow diarrhea can also cause fecal incontinence.

A digital rectal examination is essential in the evaluation. It can identify reduced anal sphincter tone, prolapsed hemorrhoids or rectum, or rectal stool impaction. Additional diagnostic testing is determined by the history and rectal examination. If fecal impaction is suspected, an abdominal radiograph can be diagnostic. If diarrhea is present, stool testing or colonoscopy should be considered. If weak sphincter tone is appreciated or rectal urgency is reported, evaluation may include neurologic evaluation for spinal cord disorders, anorectal manometry to assess anal sphincter pressure and rectal sensation, anal endosonography or MRI for anal sphincter defects, or defecography for structural evaluation of the pelvic floor.

Initial management should be directed at treating reversible factors, such as diarrhea, constipation, and offending medications. Effective dietary modifications include fiber supplementation and avoidance of trigger foods. Daily pelvic floor exercises should be used to strengthen pelvic floor muscles. If conservative measures produce no response, the next step is pelvic floor muscle training with physical therapists. In patients not responding to biofeedback therapy, other treatment options include minimally invasive procedures (e.g., sacral nerve stimulation), and surgery (e.g., sphincteroplasty, colostomy, or antegrade colonic enema therapy).

Anal cancer is rare; in 2023 there were 9760 new cases. The incidence is increasing and rose by 2.2% per year between 2010 and 2019. Squamous cell cancer is the most common type, representing 80% of all anal cancers). See

for an example.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and intraepithelial neoplasia are strongly linked with anal cancer. Risk is increased in men who have sex with men and in patients with HIV infection, history of condylomata, or kidney or liver transplantation. Prevention of HPV infection should include guideline-based HPV vaccination and use of male latex condoms. Presenting symptoms of anal cancer may include bleeding, pain, or pruritus; however, 25% of patients have no anorectal symptoms. Rates of anal squamous cell cancer are 1 in 100,000 in patients with inflammatory bowel disease or ulcerative colitis and 2 in 100,000 in patients with Crohn disease, largely in those with perianal disease. These statistics warrant heightened vigilance in patients with perianal disease.

For screening recommendations in high-risk patients, see Additional Cancer Screening Tests in Oncology.

Biopsy is required to diagnose anal cancer.

For treatment and follow-up of anal cancer, see Anal Cancer in Oncology.

bodies.gisec24013:
Ileus and Bowel Obstruction

Ileus is defined as slowing or lack of passage of luminal intestinal contents in the absence of a mechanical cause. Metabolic causes of ileus are common and include electrolyte derangements (particularly hypokalemia), uremia, and diabetic ketoacidosis. Neurogenic causes include nervous system disorders (e.g., multiple sclerosis, Parkinson disease, stroke, diabetic neuropathy) as well as postoperative ileus, which commonly occurs after abdominal and pelvic surgeries (see Ileus in Foundations of Clinical Practice). In addition, spinal injury and spinal or pelvic orthopedic procedures can result in ileus. Infectious causes include pneumonia, intra-abdominal infection, and sepsis. Drug-induced ileus may result from opioids, anticholinergic agents (e.g., tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics, antihistamines), and autonomic blockers.

Typical symptoms include abdominal distention, nausea and vomiting, and inability to tolerate oral intake. Physical examination may reveal distention and tympany with reduced bowel sounds.

Plain abdominal radiography may demonstrate distended air-filled small-bowel loops, often with air-fluid levels that raise concern for SBO. Abdominopelvic CT imaging can exclude mechanical obstruction and confirm unobstructed small-bowel distention.

Management includes supportive care, with bowel rest, intravenous fluids, and nasogastric tube decompression, as well as correction of the underlying precipitant.

Small-bowel obstruction (SBO) is an occlusion or narrowing of the intestinal lumen that leads to upstream accumulation of gas and fluids in the bowel proximal to the point of obstruction. Subsequently, bowel wall edema occurs, which eventually impairs venous return and leads to tissue damage.

The most common cause of SBO in the United States is adhesive disease from past surgery (75%). Other causes of SBO can be divided into three major categories:

  • Extraluminal obstruction (e.g., hernias, carcinomas, abscesses)
  • Obstruction that is intrinsic to the bowel wall (e.g., primary tumors, strictures, Crohn disease)
  • Intraluminal obstruction (e.g., gallstones, foreign bodies, bezoars, intussusception)

Clinical presentation of SBO varies depending on the degree, location, and cause of the obstruction. Cardinal features include colicky abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, abdominal distention, and obstipation. Examination findings include abdominal distention, tenderness, and abnormal bowel sounds. Patients may also exhibit signs of dehydration and/or fever, which may indicate concomitant infection or complication.

Abdominal radiography may demonstrate suggestive findings of SBO, such as dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels, and may identify a complication, such as perforation, that would require immediate surgical intervention. However, radiography is not sufficiently sensitive or specific for diagnosing SBO, so CT imaging is the diagnostic test of choice. CT is highly accurate for determining the presence of high-grade SBO and often shows the location and cause of obstruction. Features of SBO on CT include dilation of small bowel and a transition point where distal bowel is decompressed. Oral contrast should not be administered when high-grade bowel obstruction is suspected.

Up to 80% of cases of adhesive SBO will resolve spontaneously with conservative management with nasogastric decompression. Supportive therapy also includes bowel rest, intravenous fluids, and correction of electrolyte derangements. Surgery should be consulted, because it is often challenging to know whether SBO will resolve without surgery. Indications for surgical intervention include signs of bowel ischemia, perforation, clinical deterioration, or failure to improve with conservative management (typically within 48–72 hours). In patients without an immediate need for surgery, a water-soluble contrast study may assist in predicting the success of nonoperative management. Using a standardized water-soluble contrast protocol, the finding of contrast in the right colon within 24 hours has a 98% positive predictive value for successful nonoperative management.

Similar to the small bowel, obstruction of the colon may be due to an intraluminal, intramural, or extrinsic cause. The three most common causes of large bowel obstruction (LBO) are adenocarcinoma of the colon and rectum, colonic volvulus, and benign stricture from diverticular disease.

Patients with LBO often present with several days of abdominal discomfort, distention, and constipation regardless of the underlying cause. Symptoms preceding an obstructing colon cancer may include the insidious onset of fatigue, weight loss, and anemia. Patients with volvulus may have a more acute presentation than patients with other causes of LBO, with acute abdominal distention being the most common presentation of colonic volvulus.

A diagnosis of colonic volvulus can be made by plain abdominal radiography in up to 85% of cases; however, CT scan is the diagnostic test of choice for determining the cause of LBO. CT scan in patients with volvulus often shows a dilated, air-filled bowel loop with a central cleft (“coffee bean” sign) along with swirling of the mesenteric vessels of the affected segment.

Management of LBO is dictated by the underlying cause, patient stability, and presence of complications. Complete LBO is an emergency, and, unlike patients with SBO, most patients with LBO will require surgical intervention. Initial management involves fluid resuscitation, correction of electrolyte abnormalities, and nasogastric tube decompression. Emergent surgical intervention is required for ischemia or perforation. A self-expanding endoscopic stent can be placed for decompression as a bridge to surgery in patients with obstructing left-sided colon cancer. In the absence of perforation, ischemia, or sepsis, detorsion of the sigmoid volvulus should be attempted with a colonoscope, which converts an emergency case into an elective one. Following successful endoscopic detorsion, elective surgical sigmoid resection is indicated, because recurrence rates are high. Patients with cecal volvulus are usually managed surgically, because endoscopic intervention is rarely effective. Colonic resection is indicated for obstruction due to malignancy and diverticular stricture.

Gastrointestinal Perforation

Perforations can happen anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract from the esophagus to the rectum. A perforation is a full-thickness injury and results in release of gastrointestinal contents into the mediastinum, peritoneal cavity, or retroperitoneal space, depending on the anatomic location of the perforation. Causes include ulcers, trauma, instrumentation, obstruction, ischemia, neoplasm, infections, foreign body ingestion, and inflammatory conditions (see [Table: Table: Causes of Perforation Based on Location]

).

Clinical presentation varies by the extent and cause of injury and can range from subacute mild symptoms to acute severe abdominal or chest pain with or without sepsis. A perforation can lead to severe morbidity and death, so a high index of suspicion is necessary for timely diagnosis and management. Clinical evaluation includes a careful history and physical examination. Laboratory studies are nonspecific but useful to evaluate for infection, inflammation, electrolyte abnormalities, and end-organ damage. Plain radiographs are usually performed initially and may demonstrate free air. CT scans, which are more sensitive than radiographs, may be required for diagnosis and can localize the injury.

Initial management includes fluid resuscitation, bowel rest, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Surgical consultation should be obtained urgently for all perforations, as most patients will require surgical intervention. Endoscopic techniques to temporize or close the perforation may be appropriate for some patients who experience a small, iatrogenic injury during an endoscopic procedure. Nonoperative management is reserved for stable patients without sepsis and small, contained perforations.

Approach to Nonmalignant Leukopenia and Leukocytosis

Although leukopenia and leukocytosis may raise concern for an underlying hematologic malignancy, many causes are benign. Variability is expected in blood counts in the general population, with reference ranges spanning two standard deviations around the mean. Normal variation can sometimes explain aberrant leukocyte counts, with 2.5% of persons having cell counts that fall above or below standard reference ranges. Other common nonmalignant causes of quantitative abnormalities in the lymphocyte and neutrophil counts are listed in the following sections. The basic elements of evaluation include personal history and physical examination; family history; review of medication, supplement, and other drug use; complete blood count and differential; and peripheral blood smear.

A decreased absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) can occur in response to glucocorticoids, other medications, and various bacterial and viral infections ( [Table: Table: Nonmalignant Causes of Lymphopenia]

). Acute lymphopenia is common in hospitalized patients but is typically self-limited in this setting, and specific evaluation or management beyond that directed at the problems requiring hospitalization is usually not necessary. A chronically low ALC and recurrent infections should prompt evaluation for immunodeficiency and measurement of immunoglobulin levels. Lymphopenia without clinical consequences or an associated illness does not require treatment.

Neutropenia is defined as an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) less than 1500/µL (1.50 × 10^9/L). Severe neutropenia is classified as an ANC less than 500/μL (0.50 × 10^9/L), and agranulocytosis is defined as an ANC less than 200/µL (0.20 × 10^9/L). Neutropenia can result from impaired marrow production or from decreased circulation of neutrophils because of destruction, margination, or sequestration, especially to the spleen in the setting of portal hypertension. See [Table: Table: Nonmalignant Causes of Neutropenia]

for the common causes of neutropenia. The clinical effects of neutropenia depend on the degree of neutropenia, bone marrow reserve, and comorbid conditions.

Duffy-null associated neutrophil count (DANC) is characterized by a chronic, mildly low ANC, typically 1000 to 1500/μL (1.00-1.50 × 10^9/L), although it can be lower. Absence of the Duffy antigen, which is the receptor for Plasmodium vivax, provides protection against malaria. DANC is more common among persons in malarial endemic regions, including those of sub-Saharan African or Middle Eastern descent. Myeloid maturation and function are normal. However, myeloid progenitors are mildly reduced with decreased neutrophil reserve in the circulation and bone marrow. DANC does not result in increased frequency or severity of infections or other significant clinical consequences, although the leukocytosis response typically associated with acute infections may be blunted.

Many drugs can cause medication-induced neutropenia, which results from impairment of normal granulopoiesis in the bone marrow or through a drug-dependent, antibody-mediated immune destruction of circulating neutrophils. Medication-induced neutropenia most often occurs in patients older than 50 years. Cytotoxic chemotherapeutics are the most common offenders. Other medications that are classically associated with agranulocytosis from bone marrow suppression include clozapine, methimazole, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. The effects are typically seen within the first 3 months of drug initiation and are often reversible. Symptoms can include fever and oral ulcerations or may be related to superimposed infection, with complications occurring more commonly with lower ANCs. Treatment focuses on removing the offending agent, and symptoms often resolve within 1 to 3 weeks. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor can shorten recovery time and may be used in select patients with neutropenia and active infection. Patients with severe neutropenia or agranulocytosis and signs of infection, such as fever, require emergency intervention (see Neutropenia and Fever in Oncology).

Nutritional deficiencies can also cause neutropenia. Vitamin B~12 and folate deficiencies can lower the ANC, often with concomitant macrocytic anemia and sometimes thrombocytopenia. Copper deficiency is a rare cause of neutropenia and anemia. Vitamin B~12 and copper deficiencies can cause subacute combined degeneration (see Subacute Combined Degeneration in Neurology). Alcohol use can cause leukopenia (including neutropenia), with or without concomitant folate deficiency.

Autoimmune conditions, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, can also be associated with isolated neutropenia.

Neutrophilia, lymphocytosis, and monocytosis are often reactive secondary to infection or inflammation. Causes of neutrophilia are listed in [Table: Table: Nonmalignant Causes of Neutrophilia]

. Neutrophilia frequently accompanies bacterial infections and can be caused by certain medications, including lithium and glucocorticoids. Cigarette smoking is a common cause of chronic neutrophilia, although the mechanism is unknown; this effect often persists for a prolonged period after smoking cessation, sometimes for years. Obesity, especially in women, may also be associated with neutrophilia.

A leukocyte count greater than 50,000/µL (50 × 10^9/L) owing to a nonmalignant cause is termed a leukemoid reaction. It may occur in patients with Clostridioides difficile infection or other infections with severe sepsis, especially in the setting of new glucocorticoid therapy. Although leukemoid reactions may be difficult to differentiate from myeloproliferative disorders, they are marked by a predominance of mature neutrophils and resolve with treatment of the underlying condition, whereas neutrophilia from hematologic malignancies is persistent, progressive, and often accompanied by abnormalities in other cell lines.

Lymphocytosis occurs with many viral processes. Acute Epstein-Barr virus infection can present with lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and an elevated ALC; atypical lymphocytes may be mistaken for blasts. Clinical features usually help distinguish atypical lymphocytes from blasts, although flow cytometry provides definitive characterization. Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis refers to a monoclonal population of B lymphocytes (<5000/μL [5.00 × 10^9/L]) defined by flow cytometry that often has an immunophenotype similar to chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) but does not meet criteria for CLL or other lymphoproliferative malignancies. It is usually detected incidentally in asymptomatic patients with a modest sustained lymphocytosis. Approximately 1% to 2% of patients with a clone size greater than 2000/μL (2.00 × 10^9/L) evolve to meet criteria for CLL during each year of follow-up; patients with a smaller clone size have a much lower risk and normal life expectancy. No intervention is required, but patients should be monitored periodically for signs of progression. See [Table: Table: Nonmalignant Causes of Lymphocytosis]

for other causes of lymphocytosis.

Monocytosis accompanies some infections, such as tuberculosis. Patients with persistent monocytosis (for >6 months) without obvious infection, particularly when associated with cytopenias (e.g., anemia or thrombocytopenia), should be evaluated for possible hematopoietic stem cell disorders.

Hematopoietic Stem Cells and Their Disorders

Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) reside in the bone marrow. Their principal properties are self-renewal and multipotency as they differentiate into progenitor cells, which in turn produce leukocytes, erythrocytes, and platelets (

). The process of proliferation and differentiation to mature blood cells (known as hematopoiesis) is tightly regulated by the bone marrow microenvironment and hematopoietic growth factors ( [Table: Table: Growth Factors Involved in Hematopoiesis]

). Disorders of hematopoiesis can occur at the HSC or progenitor cell level and can lead to underproduction or overproduction of blood cells. Disorders developing from early precursors are usually more aggressive than those developing from differentiated cells. Disorders of HSCs can be broadly divided into bone marrow failure, myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs), and acute leukemias ( [Table: Table: Disorders of Hematopoietic Stem Cells]

).

Bone marrow failure syndromes are characterized by the failure of hematopoiesis to keep up with physiologic demands for blood cell production (ineffective hematopoiesis), leading to peripheral cytopenias. Rare inherited causes such as Fanconi anemia exist, but acquired disorders are more common and include intrinsic bone marrow disorders, such as myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), or extrinsic disorders resulting from toxins or autoimmunity, as in aplastic anemia (AA). Overlap is commonly seen between bone marrow failure disorders and MPNs (

).

Hyperproliferative disorders include myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs), which are characterized by excessive clonal proliferation of myeloid precursors or HSCs. These are often driven by deregulation of a growth signal resulting from a specific variant. Clonal genetic abnormalities, such as BCR::ABL1 translocation and mutations in the signaling gene JAK2 (most commonly JAK2 V617F), can be used for diagnosis and disease monitoring on peripheral blood or bone marrow testing.

Acute leukemias (myeloid or lymphoid) are aggressive clonal neoplasms in which cells also lose the capability to differentiate into mature cells (differentiation block). These disorders usually require emergent evaluation and treatment.

AA is an acquired HSC disorder characterized by severely decreased bone marrow cellularity and pancytopenia. Although it is classified as a type of anemia, patients usually have a combination of anemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia (pancytopenia).

AA is caused by a decrease in HSCs because of autoimmunity, toxins, and infections (such as HIV infection). Autoimmune injury to HSCs is the most common cause of AA. Medications, such as antithyroid medications (methimazole and propylthiouracil), β-lactam antibiotics, sulfonamides, NSAIDs, antiseizure medications, and gold salts, have also been associated with developing AA. Inherited genetic syndromes, such as Fanconi anemia, may rarely lead to AA.

AA must be differentiated from a hypoplastic variant of MDS (see

), which has decreased bone marrow cellularity in common with AA but also has dysplastic cell morphology and cytogenetic or molecular abnormalities (see [Table: Table: Classification of Myelodysplastic Syndromes]

).

The severity of AA is categorized by the degree of bone marrow cellularity and cytopenias. Severe AA is defined by less than 25% bone marrow cellularity with at least two of the following:

  • Platelet count less than 20,000/μL (20 × 10^9/L)
  • Absolute neutrophil count (ANC) less than 500/μL (0.50 × 10^9/L)
  • Reticulocyte count less than 60,000/μL (60 × 10^9/L)

Very severe AA has a worse prognosis; the criteria are the same except that the ANC is less than 200/μL (0.20 × 10^9/L). Patients with moderate (nonsevere) AA have decreased bone marrow cellularity but meet none of the above peripheral blood criteria.

Treatment decisions are based on the cause and severity of disease. Hematologists should be involved in transfusion decisions (see Transfusion Decisions in Hematology), which should be minimized before hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) to decrease the risk of alloimmunization and graft rejection. Blood products should be leukoreduced and irradiated.

In AA secondary to medications, discontinuing the offending medication usually improves the AA, but it can take weeks for cytopenias to resolve.

Asymptomatic patients with moderate AA can be closely monitored without immediate treatment.

Younger patients with severe or very severe AA and a suitable donor are treated upfront with allogeneic HSCT. Patients with severe or very severe AA who are older or who do not have an HSCT donor are treated by combination immunosuppression with antithymocyte globulin, cyclosporine, and eltrombopag. With advances in immunosuppression, HSCT, and supportive care, the overall survival of young patients with a good risk profile is greater than 80%.

Because of dysregulation in the marrow compartment, patients with AA can develop a clone of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) cells, which lack complement-stabilizing CD55 and CD59 proteins. Identification of a PNH clone has been associated with improved response to immunosuppressive therapy but does not change treatment decision making. Patients with AA and a PNH clone do not have other characteristics of PNH.

PNH is an acquired, intrinsic erythrocyte defect arising from somatic mutations in the PIGA gene, resulting in deficiency of glycophosphatidylinositol-anchored proteins on the erythrocyte surface. These proteins include complement decay accelerating factor (CD55) and complement inhibitor (CD59). Loss of these complement-stabilizing proteins allows for abnormal complement deposition, subsequently causing intravascular hemolysis, which leads to hemoglobinuria that characterizes PNH. Patients can additionally have thrombophilia with unusual sites of venous thrombosis, including mesenteric and cerebral vessels, and arterial thrombosis. Some patients have smooth muscle dystonia, which can manifest as abdominal pain. PNH can be isolated, or associated with other bone marrow diseases, including MDS (see Myelodysplastic Syndromes in Hematology) and AA. Flow cytometry demonstrating a population of cells with loss of CD55 and CD59 confirms the diagnosis.

Eculizumab and ravulizumab are monoclonal antibodies that bind C5 and inhibit activation of the terminal complement cascade. They have been shown to decrease hemolysis and thrombotic risk in PNH. Patients should receive meningococcal vaccination before their use because of an increased risk of infections with Neisseria and other encapsulated organisms. Patients with venous thrombosis whose disease is controlled by a complement inhibitor can safely stop anticoagulation after 3 to 6 months. Patients who develop venous thrombosis while receiving PNH-directed therapy should receive lifelong anticoagulation.

Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is characterized by normocytic or macrocytic anemia with decreased reticulocytes and absent or decreased erythrocyte precursors in the bone marrow. Leukocyte and platelet counts are normal. Primary and secondary causes have been implicated in the pathogenesis of PRCA ( [Table: Table: Causes of Pure Red Cell Aplasia]

). Bone marrow biopsy results showing decreased erythrocyte precursors are required for diagnosis. Although an underlying cause is often not identified, testing for parvovirus infection, CT imaging of the mediastinum for thymoma, and flow cytometry of the peripheral blood for large granular lymphocyte leukemia (a T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder) is usually indicated.

Idiopathic PRCA is commonly immunologically mediated and treated with immunosuppressive medications, such as prednisone, cyclosporine, and cyclophosphamide.

Parvovirus B19 is cytotoxic to the erythrocyte precursors in the bone marrow. This infection is usually transient, lasting 2 to 3 weeks, and may be asymptomatic or cause fever, myalgia, and malaise. Some patients develop asymmetrical arthritis, most prominently affecting the small joints of the hands and feet. Facial rash (erythema infectiosum) is less frequently seen in adults. Infection does not cause clinically significant anemia in healthy, immunocompetent patients. However, patients with chronic hemolysis (such as sickle cell disease) depend on increased erythrocyte production and can develop significant anemia with any decrease in reticulocyte production. Additionally, immunocompromised patients can have sustained viremia leading to prolonged anemia and may require intravenous immune globulin treatment to hasten viral clearance.

Patients with PRCA secondary to underlying occult thymoma may improve with thymectomy.

MDS is a group of clonal blood cancers characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis in the bone marrow leading to peripheral blood cytopenias in the setting of dysplastic and usually hypercellular bone marrow. MDS carries a variable risk of transformation to acute myeloid leukemia (AML) that correlates with prognosis. Most MDS cases are idiopathic and often age related; the median age of diagnosis is around 70 years. Secondary MDS can result from chemotherapy or radiation therapy, chemical exposure (e.g., benzene), and other factors.

MDS is a common cause of sideroblastic anemia, wherein distinctive perinuclear rings consisting of iron-loaded mitochondria are seen on bone marrow biopsy specimens (

). Alcohol consumption, copper deficiency, and certain medications (e.g., linezolid, isoniazid) may also cause sideroblastic changes and must be ruled out before MDS can be diagnosed. Other reversible causes of dysplasia that must be ruled out include deficiencies in vitamin B~12 and folate, medications, and infections (such as HIV).

MDS varies in presentation depending on the severity of the blood cell lineage(s) affected. It should be suspected in patients with otherwise unexplained cytopenias, especially with dysplastic findings on peripheral blood smear. The World Health Organization classification of MDS and its features are listed in [Table: Table: Classification of Myelodysplastic Syndromes]

. Macrocytic anemia is the most common cytopenia observed in patients with MDS. The peripheral blood smear shows dysplastic cells (hypogranular neutrophils and platelets), which do not function well and lead to an increased risk of infection and bleeding (

). Bone marrow biopsy is required for diagnosis and demonstrates dysplasia, cytogenetic and molecular abnormalities, and, often, hypercellularity.

The prognosis for patients with MDS is highly variable and depends on the degree of cytopenias (including transfusion dependence), the presence of excess bone marrow blasts (which correlates with the risk of AML transformation), and cytogenetic/molecular findings. Patients at low risk may have a median survival of almost 9 years, whereas those with greater than 10% blasts, severe pancytopenia, and adverse cytogenetic/molecular findings have a high risk of transformation to AML and typically survive less than 1 year after diagnosis.

The primary goals of MDS treatment are managing symptomatic cytopenias and reducing the risk of progression to AML. Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic, low-risk MDS can be monitored. Symptomatic anemia is treated with transfusions and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents; luspatercept is first line in most patients with low-risk MDS. Treatment with hypomethylating agents (azacitidine and decitabine) has been shown to decrease transfusion dependence and the risk of transformation to AML. Patients with low-risk MDS with the 5q− cytogenetic abnormality are often anemic and can have resolution of transfusion needs following treatment with the immunomodulatory drug lenalidomide.

Allogeneic HSCT is the only potentially curative option available for patients with MDS. Transplantation is usually not an option for older patients with MDS because of comorbidities increasing the risks of intensive treatment.

Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia shares some features of MDS and those of the MPNs. It has traditionally been considered a subset of MDS but is now classified as a separate entity. Patients have persistent peripheral monocytosis with an absolute monocyte count greater than 500/µL, often with splenomegaly and cytopenias; bone marrow specimens show dysplastic changes and fewer than 20% blasts, and abnormal cytogenetic/molecular findings. Prognosis and treatment are analogous to MDS with poor prognosis.

Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) describes detection of somatic clonal variations in genes recurrently altered in hematologic malignancies (e.g., DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1) in a patient without a known hematologic malignancy or other clonal disorder. The risk of CHIP progressing to MDS or AML is very low, but CHIP carriers are at increased risk of atherosclerosis, likely due to an increased inflammatory milieu.

The MPNs are a group of clonal stem cell disorders that share several similar features. They are defined by specific, acquired genetic variant alleles causing overproduction of functional, mature, differentiated myeloid elements, resulting in elevations in one or more cell lines in the peripheral blood (

).

Although each subtype has unique clinical and pathologic aspects, MPNs as a group share many symptoms, including constitutional symptoms of fever, night sweats, weight loss, and pruritus; splenomegaly is often present. Patients with MPNs are at increased risk for thrombosis, bleeding, and transformation to more aggressive myeloid malignancies, including AML. Although systemic mastocytosis is no longer an MPN per the World Health Organization classification, considering its similarities and previous MPN classification, its discussion is included in this section.

Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a clonal MPN resulting in abnormal production and proliferation of granulocytes, generally with normal differentiation. CML is defined by the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, a reciprocal translocation of the ABL gene on chromosome 9 to the BCR gene on chromosome 22. This arrangement results in constitutive tyrosine kinase activity that drives cellular production and symptoms.

Patients may be asymptomatic, with an increased granulocyte count on routine laboratory testing, but many have weight loss, abdominal fullness (secondary to splenomegaly), fatigue, or fever. The neutrophilia associated with CML is often accompanied by a left shift, with bands, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, promyelocytes, and even small numbers of myeloblasts (

). Thrombocytosis and anemia are common. A left shift with concurrent basophilia or eosinophilia without a clinical reason for a leukemoid reaction (such as severe infection) should also raise suspicion for CML. The Philadelphia chromosome can be detected with routine cytogenetics, fluorescence in situ hybridization, and molecular testing for the BCR::ABL1 transcript through reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction. Testing peripheral blood is as accurate as bone marrow samples in establishing the diagnosis and monitoring following initiation of treatment.

CML has chronic (<20% peripheral or marrow myeloblasts) and blast (≥20% myeloblasts) phases. Most patients present in the chronic phase, which is more indolent but responsive to therapy. The blast phase is technically a secondary acute leukemia (AML or ALL).

Treatment is necessary at diagnosis for all patients. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have revolutionized the treatment and outcomes of CML. A variety of TKIs have been approved since imatinib was initially shown to target the BCR::ABL1 oncoprotein and prevent downstream signaling. These agents have resulted in excellent long-term control of CML, improved survival, and decreased the need for HSCT.

The choice of TKI is based on adverse effect profile and patient prognosis. TKIs are generally well tolerated, but common adverse effects include fluid retention, rash, and QT prolongation; drug-drug interactions may also occur. They are avoided in pregnancy in favor of interferon-α. TKI resistance or evidence of disease progression despite treatment should raise suspicion for nonadherence or development of new variants. Patients who achieve a sustained clinical remission (>2 years), with normal bone marrow cellularity and blood counts with disappearance of the BCR::ABL1 transcript, may be candidates for stopping TKI therapy in lieu of careful monitoring. Some of these patients may be cured.

The blast phase is treated like an acute leukemia, though commonly with the addition of a TKI. Allogeneic HSCT is considered in the blast phase once remission occurs, or less commonly in the chronic phase if TKI treatment is ineffective or poorly tolerated.

Polycythemia vera (PV) is a clonal stem cell disorder characterized by excess erythrocyte production independent of erythropoietin level. The JAK2 V617F activating alteration is present in 97% of patients, and others harbor the JAK2 exon 12 mutation.

Although some patients may be asymptomatic, many have symptoms of fatigue, headache, or itching, particularly after a warm shower (aquagenic pruritus). Accompanying splenomegaly may cause abdominal fullness, reflux, or early satiety; some patients may have a ruddy complexion (plethora).

Patients have an elevated hemoglobin level (>16.5 g/dL [165 g/L] in men, >16 g/dL [160 g/L] in women), and thrombocytosis and neutrophilia are also common, hence the term polycythemia. Although erythropoietin levels are suppressed in most patients with PV, as many as 15% will have a normal erythropoietin level. Peripheral blood findings together with JAK2 testing usually establish the diagnosis.

Although elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit levels should raise suspicion for PV, especially with concomitant elevated leukocyte and platelet counts, secondary causes of erythrocytosis are much more common ( [Table: Table: Causes of Erythrocytosis]

). Secondary causes often arise through chronic or intermittent hypoxia with an adaptive increase in erythropoietin and erythrocyte mass or through ectopic production of erythropoietin, most commonly from a renal neoplasm. Testosterone supplementation also causes erythrocytosis; testosterone cessation or phlebotomy may be needed if the hematocrit level exceeds 54%. A careful history and physical examination often reveal an underlying process contributing to hemoglobin elevation; therefore, smoking history, sleep patterns, cardiopulmonary symptoms, and medications should be reviewed. Evaluation may also include a sleep study, echocardiography, measurement of the erythropoietin level, and kidney imaging to rule out secondary causes. An elevated erythrocyte count can be an appropriate physiologic response in some situations (e.g., chronic hypoxemia, which may be worsened by phlebotomy) and makes management of these patients complex. Diuretics can cause relative erythrocytosis because decreased plasma volume results in an increased hematocrit level despite a normal erythrocyte mass.

Patients with PV are at increased risk for venous and arterial (stroke, myocardial infarction) thrombosis. A unique feature of the JAK2 mutation is an increased risk of splanchnic (portal, hepatic) vein thrombosis, and this may be the presenting feature in PV, preceding hematologic manifestations.

Treatment is required for all patients and consists of phlebotomy to maintain a hematocrit level of less than 45% and low-dose aspirin to reduce thrombotic risk. Cytoreductive therapy with hydroxyurea or pegylated interferon is additionally indicated in patients at higher risk, including those older than 60 years and those with a history of myocardial infarction, stroke, or venous thrombosis. It can also be considered in patients who do not tolerate phlebotomy or those who have symptoms refractory to phlebotomy. The Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor ruxolitinib is used in patients with resistant PV or those who cannot tolerate first-line agents. Patients with venous thromboembolism generally require life-long anticoagulation.

In a few patients, PV will progress to secondary myelofibrosis or transform to AML. No interventions have been shown to reduce the risk of hematologic malignancy transformation.

Essential thrombocythemia (ET) is a clonal stem cell process characterized by a sustained increased platelet count. Mutations in JAK2 are present in approximately 60% of patients with ET; other driving alterations include mutations in CALR (20%-25%) and MPL (5%). Approximately 10% of patients with ET have no mutation identified.

Clinical features may overlap with other MPNs. ET is often diagnosed in patients who are asymptomatic with elevated platelet counts found incidentally on testing completed for other reasons. Otherwise, symptoms can include vasomotor manifestations, such as headaches, erythromelalgia, and visual disturbances. Complications can include venous or arterial thrombosis (stroke, myocardial infarction); these are more common in patients who are JAK2 positive. Hemorrhage can also be seen, especially with extreme thrombocytosis (platelet counts exceeding 1 million/µL [1000 × 10^9/L]), and is thought to be caused by intrinsic platelet dysfunction or development of acquired von Willebrand disease. Progression to secondary myelofibrosis or AML is also possible but less likely than in other MPNs.

Reactive or secondary causes of thrombocytosis are more common than ET and include iron deficiency, acute blood loss, splenectomy, infection, and other inflammatory conditions. All patients with sustained thrombocytosis should be evaluated for secondary causes. Extreme thrombocytosis with a platelet count greater than 1 million/µL (1000 × 10^9/L) is suggestive of ET; however, patients with multiple risk factors may rarely reach this level of secondary thrombocytosis (see Approach to the Patient With Thrombocytosis in Hematology).

Treatment depends on the individual patient and associated risk factors. Patients at low risk (age <60 years, JAK2 negative, no venous or arterial thrombosis) can be monitored without therapy. Low-dose aspirin should be used in all JAK2-positive patients and in those older than 60 years; it may also be considered in those with vasomotor symptoms, such as headache or erythromelalgia. Cytoreductive therapy with hydroxyurea is used in high-risk patients, including those older than 60 years and those with a history of thrombosis; it is not typically indicated in younger patients without a history of thrombotic events. Interferon is considered in pregnant patients and in those who cannot tolerate hydroxyurea. Patients with venous thromboembolism usually require lifelong anticoagulation.

Myelofibrosis is an MPN characterized by bone marrow fibrosis and extramedullary hematopoiesis. It can present de-novo or evolve from preexisting PV or ET (“secondary myelofibrosis”). Cytokine secretion from proliferating megakaryocytes results in fibroblast proliferation, deposition of reticulin fibrosis, and impaired hematopoiesis. A leukoerythroblastic picture is seen on blood smear (

). The JAK2, CAL-R, and MPL mutations are common among patients with myelofibrosis, and additional molecular and cytogenetic abnormalities are also commonly seen.

Constitutional symptoms are prominent and include fatigue, fever, night sweats, generalized pruritus, and weight loss. Splenomegaly is characteristic and often massive with associated abdominal fullness, pain, and early satiety; the cause is extramedullary hematopoiesis due to marrow fibrosis. Laboratory results vary considerably, but an elevated leukocyte count, anemia, and thrombocytopenia are common. Diagnosis is made by bone marrow biopsy, with specimens showing extensive fibrosis, which excludes non-hematologic causes such as miliary tuberculosis. This extensive fibrosis often precludes the ability to aspirate bone marrow (“dry tap”). Diagnosis increasingly relies on evaluation for concomitant alterations and molecular findings, which can also help determine prognosis. Several prognostic scoring systems are available to determine risk stratification. Low-risk disease has an estimated overall survival rate in the 15-year range, whereas survival is only approximately 16 months with high-risk features.

Treatment depends on symptoms, risk of disease progression, and survival. The only potentially curative option is allogeneic HSCT; however, transplantation carries significant morbidity and mortality risks, so it is only considered in those whose disease features indicate poor short-term survival and who are otherwise healthy enough to undergo transplantation.

Other treatments focus on addressing symptoms and controlling blood counts. Asymptomatic patients with low-risk disease can be monitored; however, most patients have some degree of symptomatology and may benefit from supportive medications. Ruxolitinib is a JAK inhibitor that has been shown to significantly improve constitutional symptoms in patients with myelofibrosis, reduce spleen volume, and improve survival. Other approved JAK inhibitors include fedratinib, momelotinib, and pacritinib, which provide similar outcomes and may be indicated in certain situations (e.g., pacritinib is approved for use when platelet count is less than 50,000/µL). These agents are all effective regardless of JAK2 mutation status. Splenectomy is associated with significant morbidity and mortality in patients with myelofibrosis and should be avoided, if possible.

Eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil count >500/μL [0.5 × 10^9/L]) is usually mild, transient, and secondary to an underlying process. Causes of eosinophilia are summarized in [Table: Table: Causes of Eosinophilia]

. Parasitic infection should be considered in patients who live in or have traveled to endemic areas, including the southeastern United States where strongyloidiasis is possible.

Hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is characterized by organ damage that is directly mediated by eosinophils and is associated with a persistently and significantly elevated eosinophil count (>1500/μL [1.5 × 10^9/L]). Dermatologic, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal complications are most common. Although infrequent, eosinophilic myocarditis is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in HES.

HES can be primary or secondary (usually infections or solid tumors). Primary HES is a rare, clonal MPN often associated with abnormal tyrosine kinase activation mediated by platelet-derived growth factor receptor-α or -β (PDGFR α or β).

Glucocorticoids are effective in HES; however, ruling out active Strongyloides stercoralis infection before administration is crucial because glucocorticoids can cause fatal dissemination of infection. In severe HES requiring immediate treatment with glucocorticoids where strongyloidiasis is a concern, concurrent treatment with ivermectin should be considered.

Patients with primary HES with the PDGFR-α or -β variant respond well to low-dose imatinib. Mepolizumab, a monoclonal antibody directed against interleukin-5, has also been shown to be effective in HES.

Treatment of secondary HES should additionally focus on addressing the underlying cause.

Mastocytosis shares many similar features with MPNs. It is characterized by excess mast cell proliferation and cellular accumulation in one or more organ systems. Cutaneous mastocytosis is limited to skin involvement, whereas systemic mastocytosis involves infiltration of other organs, which may or may not include the skin. Organs involved in systemic mastocytosis include the bone marrow, liver, spleen, and gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms and complications are often related to mast cell mediator release (histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins) and include vasodilation, flushing, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea; patients are also at increased risk for anaphylaxis. Most disease is indolent with normal life expectancy, although some patients may have more aggressive forms.

Diagnosis is usually dependent on demonstration of organ infiltration by mast cells. More than 95% of patients with systemic mastocytosis have KIT gene mutations, most commonly in the peripheral blood or bone marrow or gastrointestinal biopsy specimens. Many patients also have an elevated tryptase level.

Treatment includes antihistamines and antileukotriene drugs to control the symptoms of mast cell mediator release. Patients should carry epinephrine in case of anaphylaxis. The selective inhibitor of altered KIT, avapritinib, or other cytoreductive therapies are typically only used in patients with more aggressive forms.

Acute leukemia is a hematologic malignancy characterized by infiltration of the bone marrow, blood, and other tissues by uncontrolled proliferation and abnormal delayed differentiation of clonal myeloid or lymphoid precursor cells known as blasts. The diagnosis of acute leukemia typically requires a blast percentage of 20% or higher in the bone marrow and/or blood. In adults, AML is more common than acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). See Lymphoid Malignancies in Oncology.

AML typically manifests with anemia, thrombocytopenia, and/or neutropenia secondary to bone marrow replacement with abnormal myeloblasts. Symptoms of anemia vary depending on age and comorbidities but can include fatigue, chest pain, dyspnea, and lightheadedness. Petechiae, epistaxis, and other mucosal hemorrhages occur when the platelet count decreases to less than 20,000/μL (20 × 10^9/L). Although the leukocyte count is often elevated, the ANC tends to be low, with increased risk of infection. Myeloblasts are usually seen in the peripheral blood smear but may be absent despite unequivocal bone marrow infiltration.

Cytogenetic and molecular classification of AML is increasingly important. Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), a subtype that occurs in 10% to 15% of patients with AML, is characterized by immature leukocytes with distinctive primary granules that contribute to coagulopathy (

) and chromosomal translocation t(15;17), which leads to the fusion transcript PML::RARA. Most patients with APL achieve cure with non-chemotherapy agents targeting the underlying block in cell differentiation, including all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide.

In non-APL AML, a combination of molecular and cytogenetic markers is used for initial risk stratification. NPM1-altered AML is found in approximately one quarter of patients and is associated with a favorable outcome because of an increased likelihood of response to chemotherapy. In contrast, FLT3-ITD identification (found in approximately one quarter of patients with cytogenetically normal AML) is associated with a less favorable outcome and merits consideration for allogeneic HSCT in first remission.

AML is curable in 40% or more of adult patients aged 60 years or younger, but the cure rate decreases to 5% to 15% in adults older than age 60 years, in whom comorbidities often preclude the use of intensive chemotherapy or HSCT. Treatment consists of induction therapy, most commonly with an anthracycline (such as daunorubicin) and infusional cytarabine. The goal is to ablate the bone marrow and eliminate the blasts, although this transiently halts normal hematopoiesis as well. Normal cells recover after a period of aplasia, which extends for 3 to 4 weeks. During this time, the patient is supported by transfusions (erythrocytes and platelets) and prompt antibiotic treatment of neutropenic fever (see Neutropenia and Fever in Oncology). Response assessment includes a bone marrow aspirate and biopsy to evaluate for remission by morphology, immunophenotyping, and molecular/cytogenetic testing as appropriate based on characteristics identified at diagnosis. A complete response is achieved in 60% to 85% of patients younger than age 60 years. Consolidation therapy for responders consists of additional cycles of conventional chemotherapy in patients at low risk of relapse and allogeneic HSCT for patients at high risk.

Targeted therapy is often used in conjunction with traditional chemotherapy. Midostaurin, gilteritinib, and quizartinib are approved FLT3 inhibitors for first- or second-line therapy. Ivosidenib, olutasidenib, and enasidenib are isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) inhibitors used in patients with IDH1- or IDH2-altered AML.

Treatment for older or frail patients remains unsatisfactory; symptom management may include blood and platelet transfusions along with lower dose, often single-agent chemotherapy, such as oral hydroxyurea or low-dose cytarabine. Hypomethylating agents (decitabine and azacitidine) may also be combined with targeted therapies (FLT3 inhibitors, IDH inhibitors, or the BCL2 inhibitor venetoclax). These patients may survive only months, depending on comorbidities, treatment toxicity, and disease characteristics, and early involvement of palliative care is indicated.

Sweet syndrome, or acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, may develop in patients with hematologic abnormalities, particularly MDS and MDS evolving into AML. It is characterized by fever, neutrophilia, characteristic skin lesions (

), and a dense neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on histology (see Sweet Syndrome in Dermatology). Treatment generally involves glucocorticoids along with therapy targeted at the underlying hematologic malignancy.

ALL is more common in children and adolescents than in adults. Although ALL in children is often curable, survival in adults (older than age 18 years) remains inferior despite the adoption of pediatric treatment regimens in appropriate patients. Patients with ALL present with malaise, bleeding, infections, bone pain, or a combination of these symptoms, with a small subset (<10%) having symptomatic central nervous system involvement at diagnosis. In adults, 75% of ALL is of B-cell lineage; B-cell ALL can manifest as extramedullary disease, including gastrointestinal or testicular involvement. In contrast, a mediastinal mass with wheezing and stridor or skin involvement can be the presenting feature of T-cell ALL.

Similar to AML, ALL is classified by immunophenotype, cytogenetics, and molecular abnormalities. The most important cytogenetic abnormality in adult ALL is the Philadelphia chromosome, found in 20% to 30% of patients.

All patients with ALL should undergo lumbar puncture with examination of cerebrospinal fluid at the time of diagnosis along with testicular examination in male patients. Other staging tests such as PET/CT and scrotal ultrasonography are not necessary in the absence of specific local symptoms or findings.

Treatment regimens are complex. Regimen backbones include vincristine, anthracycline, glucocorticoids, and l-asparaginase. Some of these agents have unique toxicities; for example, l-asparaginase can lead to allergic reactions, hypofibrinogenemia, thrombosis, pancreatitis, and hypertriglyceridemia. Induction therapy is followed by intensification and consolidation. In patients with Philadelphia chromosome–positive ALL, the addition of oral TKIs such as imatinib, dasatinib, and ponatinib to traditional chemotherapy backbones has dramatically improved remission rates; after remission induction, these patients may receive additional intensive consolidation with allogeneic HSCT. Central nervous system prophylaxis with intrathecal chemotherapy is essential during ALL therapy.

A maintenance phase of oral mercaptopurine (daily) and methotrexate (weekly) can last up to 3 years; medication adherence can be problematic during this phase. Immunotherapies with a bispecific antibody (blinatumomab), antibody-drug conjugate (inotuzumab ozogamicin), or chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells are available if the disease relapses ( [Table: Table: Characteristics and Indications for Cellular Therapies]

).

Autologous and allogeneic HSCT are indicated in select patients with bone marrow failure or hematologic malignancies ( [Table: Table: Characteristics and Indications for Cellular Therapies]

). Typically, the allogeneic donor is most commonly an HLA-matched sibling or unrelated adult donor. The risk of graft-versus-host disease affecting the skin, gastrointestinal tract, and liver increases with the degree of donor-recipient HLA disparity. Better supportive measures and reduced-intensity regimens have provided transplant eligibility to older adults. However, allogeneic HSCT carries a significant risk of transplant-related mortality, and survivors continue to have long-term morbidity unrelated to relapse, such as susceptibility to bacterial or viral infections and delayed pulmonary toxicity. Physicians caring for patients who have undergone HSCT should evaluate these individuals early for symptoms suggesting infection and follow recommended immunization schedules that take into account their prolonged immunosuppressed state (see Immunization in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Treatment using CAR T cells has become available for certain patients with recurrent ALL, lymphoma, and multiple myeloma. CAR T cells are T lymphocytes (usually collected from the patient) genetically modified to recognize and attack cells expressing a particular tumor antigen (e.g., CD19 in B-cell malignancies such as ALL). These therapies are highly effective; however, patients, especially those with a high disease burden, may develop dangerous cytokine release syndrome (CRS) or neurotoxicity. Intensity of CRS and neurotoxicity symptoms can range from mild (fever or confusion) to severe. Severe CRS requiring ICU admission is often characterized by vascular leak, hypotension, pulmonary edema, cardiac dysfunction, kidney dysfunction, liver failure, coagulopathy, multiorgan system failure, and even death. Many tumor antigens are under investigation regarding the suitability of this novel cellular therapy approach for other hematologic malignancies and solid tumors.

Adult survivors of childhood cancers, including ALL, which is the most common childhood cancer, face higher risks of secondary cancer, cardiovascular disease, and the metabolic syndrome (high BMI, elevated waist circumference, dyslipidemia, elevated fasting glucose, and hypertension) compared with age-matched controls. Primary care physicians encountering such patients should request a treatment summary from the treating facility and encourage patient participation in a local survivorship clinic (see Cancer Survivorship Care Plan in Oncology). Screening for dyslipidemia, diabetes mellitus, and hypertension is recommended. Echocardiography to screen for left ventricular dysfunction should be performed, particularly if anthracycline exposure was high (doxorubicin or equivalent exceeding 250 mg/m^2) or if chest radiation was used (see Cardiotoxicity of Chemotherapy in Cardiovascular Medicine). Female survivors have a higher risk for myocardial dysfunction during pregnancy. High-dose glucocorticoids, typical of ALL regimens, pose a risk for osteopenia. The cumulative incidence of secondary cancer after radiation therapy for childhood ALL reaches 11% at 30 years; tumors include skin cancer, thyroid and parotid tumors, sarcomas, and brain tumors. Cranial radiation also increases the risk for stroke and neurocognitive defects. Patients should be counseled about lifestyle risk factors, age-based screening, and early reporting of persistent symptoms.

Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (which include erythropoietin and darbepoetin) are primarily used in patients with anemia secondary to chronic kidney disease. Guidelines suggest considering erythropoiesis-stimulating agents only for these patients who have hemoglobin concentrations less than 10 g/dL (100 g/L ) (see Anemia of Kidney Disease in Hematology).

Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF; various formulations, including biosimilars and a pegylated version) are used in patients receiving myelosuppressive chemotherapy who are at high risk of febrile neutropenia, such as those receiving intensive chemotherapy for high-risk breast cancer and those aged 65 years or older with aggressive lymphoma being treated with curative chemotherapy. G-CSF may also be indicated in patients receiving another course of chemotherapy that has already led to neutropenic fever. G-CSF is not indicated for most patients with neutropenia who are afebrile, as a routine adjunct to empiric antibiotics for patients presenting with febrile neutropenia, or for patients undergoing induction chemotherapy for acute leukemia (see Neutropenia and Fever in Oncology).
