Multiple Myeloma and Related Disorders

Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B cells that produce immunoglobulins. Plasma cell dyscrasias (PCDs), or monoclonal gammopathies, involve clonal expansion of plasma cells that produce a monoclonal immunoglobulin protein (M protein). This M protein can be a complete immunoglobulin, with IgG, IgA, IgD, or IgM complexed with a light chain (κ or λ), or a free light chain (FLC) without a heavy chain component. The M protein is seen as an M spike on serum or urine protein electrophoresis (SPEP/UPEP), an abnormal serum FLC ratio, or both. Various PCDs have been described ( [Table: Table: Disorders Associated With Monoclonal Gammopathies]

). An important distinction is that an M spike indicates a monoclonal protein, whereas IgM is immunoglobulin M. An M spike involving IgM can occur and can be seen in either lymphomas or PCDs.

Monoclonal gammopathies such as monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) and multiple myeloma (MM) may be identified incidentally by an elevated serum protein level or during evaluation of clinical findings associated with gammopathies, such as bone pain, anemia, hypercalcemia, neuropathy, or kidney injury ( [Table: Table: Plasma Cell Dyscrasia Testing Considerations]

).

The M protein in PCDs can often be detected by SPEP or UPEP (

). Serum and urine immunofixation are more sensitive tests that can also determine the immunoglobulin isotype. SPEP also helps differentiate an M spike from a polyclonal protein spike, which may be seen with infections, autoimmune diseases, and chronic liver disease, and does not represent a PCD.

Serum FLC assay is utilized to assess PCDs characterized by production of monoclonal light chains alone. In PCDs, plasma cells secrete more of either the kappa or lambda FLCs, leading to an abnormal kappa-to-lambda FLC ratio. In contrast, in inflammatory processes or kidney disease, kappa and lambda FLCs are increased proportionately, and the kappa-to-lambda FLC ratio remains normal.

Disorders other than MGUS and MM can also produce an M spike (see [Table: Table: Disorders Associated With Monoclonal Gammopathies]

). Other tests considered during the evaluation of a monoclonal gammopathy include complete blood count; serum chemistries, including creatinine, calcium, and albumin levels; β~2-microglobulin and lactate dehydrogenase level (markers of plasma cell growth); and quantitative immunoglobulins (which typically show reduction in uninvolved immunoglobulins).

Axial imaging (i.e., PET/CT, low-dose CT, or MRI) is more sensitive than plain radiography of the bones (skeletal surveys) to assess for osteolytic lesions; PET/CT is the preferred study. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy quantify the percentage of plasma cells and classify the PCD. Cytogenetic and molecular evaluation of the bone marrow aspirate may also reveal abnormalities that indicate higher risk for disease relapse. However, bone marrow testing and skeletal imaging are unnecessary in patients with low-risk features, such as those with an IgG gammopathy measuring less than 1.5 g/dL, a normal serum FLC assay and ratio, and no evidence of end-organ damage such as anemia, kidney injury, or bone pain.

MGUS is characterized by an M protein spike with a level less than 3 g/dL (30 g/L) (or <500 mg/24 h of urine M protein), clonal plasma cells comprising less than 10% of the bone marrow, and absence of end-organ damage ( [Table: Table: Plasma and Lymphoplasmacytic Cell Dyscrasia Criteria]

).

The prevalence of MGUS increases with age; it occurs in approximately 3% of persons older than 50 years and 5% of persons older than 70 years. Because only 1% of patients with MGUS progress to MM per year, most patients with MGUS will not develop MM. In addition to the type of M protein, factors that predict the risk of progression include the quantity of M protein and presence of an abnormal serum FLC ratio ( [Table: Table: Risk of MGUS Progression to Symptomatic PCD]

). Treatment is not indicated for MGUS, but patients should undergo surveillance with frequency of follow-up based on the risk of progression.

Although MGUS may be unlikely to progress to MM, patients with MGUS may be at increased risk for complications such as neuropathy, second malignancy, thrombosis, and osteoporosis with associated fractures; bone mineral density testing should be considered. Increasingly, some patients with MGUS are recognized to have end-organ damage, which has led to a newer term, monoclonal gammopathy of clinical significance. The best characterized is monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance, which typically presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria in a patient with MGUS. More likely causes of kidney disease (e.g., diabetes mellitus) must be excluded, and kidney biopsy is often necessary to confirm the diagnosis; treatment requires myeloma-like therapy to prevent progressive and irreversible kidney injury.

MM is a clonal plasma cell neoplasm that may present as smoldering (asymptomatic) disease, which requires close observation, or symptomatic disease, which requires treatment to limit end-organ damage. Approximately 36,000 new cases are diagnosed annually in the United States.

MM classically presents with one or more symptoms of anemia, bone lesions, hypercalcemia, or kidney disease (see [Table: Table: Plasma and Lymphoplasmacytic Cell Dyscrasia Criteria]

). Other possible manifestations include infections, fatigue, weight loss, neuropathy, easy bruising, and symptoms arising from extramedullary plasmacytomas.

Normocytic anemia is a common finding in MM and is caused by plasma cell infiltration of the bone marrow. A peripheral blood smear may show rouleaux formation related to elevated immunoglobulin.

Bone pain is a common symptom of MM. Plasma cells directly activate osteoclasts and inactivate osteoblasts, leading to lytic lesions (

) and pathologic fractures in the absence of significant trauma. The increased bone resorption can also cause hypercalcemia.

The two main causes of kidney disease in MM are hypercalcemia and elevated FLCs causing tubulointerstitial damage in distal tubules, resulting in cast nephropathy. NSAIDs, dehydration, and iodinated contrast should be avoided because cast nephropathy leads these patients to be vulnerable to additional kidney injury. Other causes of kidney dysfunction in MM include light-chain amyloidosis and cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis.

Patients can additionally be immunosuppressed from lower levels of normal immunoglobulins (i.e., hypogammaglobulinemia). Patients are at increased risk of respiratory infections, and myeloma-targeted chemotherapy can further increase this risk.

Diagnostic criteria for MM are listed in [Table: Table: Plasma and Lymphoplasmacytic Cell Dyscrasia Criteria]

. Evaluation of patients with suspected MM includes identifying the abnormal M protein or FLC, assessing for symptoms of MM, and determining whether the symptoms are attributable to MM. Identification and quantification of the M protein are accomplished with SPEP, UPEP, and serum FLC testing (see Evaluation of Monoclonal Gammopathies in Hematology). Bone marrow biopsy is performed to evaluate the plasma cell burden and to determine cytogenetics for risk stratification. Laboratory analysis includes complete blood count, serum creatinine and calcium levels, β~2-microglobulin measurement, and lactate dehydrogenase level. Fluorodeoxyglucose-PET/CT is the imaging study of choice to detect lytic bone lesions in the evaluation of suspected MM because of the false-negative rate of plain film skeletal surveys. Whole-body MRI and low-dose CT are other options.

Symptoms of organ dysfunction should not necessarily be attributed to the underlying PCD. Kidney biopsy may be performed to document myeloma kidney when it is clinically difficult to differentiate from another cause, such as diabetic nephropathy. Evaluation for alternative causes of hypercalcemia and anemia should be completed, especially when the patient has low-risk disease. Other examples of end-organ damage include hyperviscosity, recurrent infections, immunoglobulin light-chain amyloidosis, and peripheral neuropathy; these can all occur with MM but are similarly not specific to MM.

MM is staged based on the serum β~2-microglobulin, lactate dehydrogenase, and albumin levels and presence of standard or high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities.

Patients without findings of anemia, hypercalcemia, kidney disease, or bone disease who have bone marrow clonal plasma cells between 10% to 59% and an M spike greater than 3 g/dL (30 g/L) with or without a kappa or lambda urine FLC M protein ≥500 mg/24 h are considered to have smoldering MM. Smoldering MM has a risk of conversion to MM requiring therapy of approximately 10% per year for the first 5 years. The risk of progression decreases after the first 5 years. This risk is not uniform; risk factors for progression include a high M protein level, a large burden of clonal plasma cells, and an abnormal serum FLC ratio (see [Table: Table: Risk of MGUS Progression to Symptomatic PCD]

). Although ongoing studies will determine which circumstances are best to initiate therapy in smoldering disease, most patients are closely followed and treated following development of clinical signs of progression to MM requiring treatment.

Patients presenting with a solitary plasmacytoma of the bone (or, less commonly, a single extramedullary plasmacytoma) without findings of anemia, hypercalcemia, or kidney disease should undergo evaluation to detect multiple myeloma, including bone marrow biopsy and whole-body imaging. After completion of local radiotherapy for solitary plasmacytoma, patients require continued surveillance laboratory testing and imaging because of increased risk for future multiple myeloma.

Treatment of MM has been revolutionized over the last few years with the advent of new treatment options, which have significantly improved 5-year survival to more than 61%. All patients should initially be evaluated for autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) eligibility. Autologous HSCT allows for the administration of high-dose chemotherapy followed by autologous stem cell rescue (see [Table: Table: Characteristics and Indications for Cellular Therapies]

). In several trials, autologous HSCT following high-dose melphalan conditioning was not curative but improved progression-free and overall survival. Eligible patients now typically undergo induction therapy with multiagent chemotherapy followed by autologous HSCT and maintenance therapy. Induction chemotherapy directed against plasma cells involves various combinations of immunomodulatory drugs (lenalidomide), proteasome inhibitors (bortezomib), glucocorticoids (dexamethasone), alkylating agents (melphalan or cyclophosphamide), and monoclonal antibodies (daratumumab or isatuximab). Following HSCT, meta-analyses have shown that maintenance lenalidomide improves overall survival. Most patients do not benefit from a second HSCT, but it can be considered in patients at high risk, such as those with plasma cell leukemia.

Patients who are not eligible for HSCT, or those who relapse after HSCT, often undergo continuous therapy with various agents until progression. Treatment is tailored to prognostic factors and patient characteristics such as degree of frailty.

Available treatments are not curative; therefore, all patients eventually relapse or develop refractory disease. Several drugs are used when patients relapse:

  • Proteasome inhibitors (carfilzomib or ixazomib)
  • Immunomodulatory drugs (lenalidomide or pomalidomide)
  • Alkylating agents (bendamustine)
  • Monoclonal antibodies (daratumumab, isatuximab, or elotuzumab)
  • Bispecific antibodies (teclistamab, elranatamab, or talquetamab)
  • Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells (idecabtagene vicleucel or ciltacabtagene autoleucel) (see Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation and Cellular Therapies in Hematology)

Ongoing studies continue to evaluate the most effective combinations and sequencing of treatments. Recent data suggest that CAR T cell treatment shows such long-term disease control that it may be potentially curative.

Some agents used to treat MM have specific adverse effects. MM increases the risk of venous thromboembolism, and lenalidomide further increases this risk. Patients receiving lenalidomide should take low-dose aspirin if they do not have additional thrombotic risk factors; patients with additional risk factors or previous venous thromboembolism may require therapeutic anticoagulation. Bortezomib may cause peripheral neuropathy. Other medications (proteasome inhibitors, monoclonal antibodies) are associated with increased risk of herpes zoster reactivation, and antiviral prophylaxis is recommended. Daratumumab may cause a positive direct antiglobulin test, which can be challenging for patients who require erythrocyte transfusions.

Pain is a prominent symptom in patients with MM requiring therapy, and opioid treatment may be needed because NSAIDs can worsen kidney disease in these patients.

Surgical stabilization of impending fracture secondary to bone lesions is undertaken to prevent morbidity. Bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid and pamidronate) or the RANK ligand inhibitor denosumab may be used adjunctively to prevent skeletal events. Patients should notify their dentist that they are receiving these agents and have dental work done before treatment initiation, if possible, given the risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw.

Annual influenza vaccination (inactivated) and pneumococcal vaccination in accordance with guidelines should be administered to all patients with MM (see Immunization in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Select patients with recurrent infections and hypogammaglobulinemia may benefit from intravenous immune globulin infusions.

Amyloidosis refers to a varied group of disorders associated with extracellular deposition of misfolded proteins in a β-pleated sheet configuration. These abnormal proteins may deposit in specific organs and cause dysfunction. Various proteins have been implicated in amyloidosis ( [Table: Table: Types of Amyloid Disease]

). Amyloid tissue deposits have a characteristic apple-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy with Congo red staining.

Immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloidosis is the most common type of amyloidosis. It is caused by a clonal PCD and is characterized by production of amyloidogenic FLCs. These light chains can deposit in the skin, kidney, heart, liver, tongue, or other organs ( [Table: Table: Clinical Manifestations of AL Amyloidosis]

). Skin manifestations are present in 30% to 40% of patients and include a generalized waxy appearance, easy bruising with minor pressure (pinch purpura), violaceous discoloration around the eyes (“raccoon eyes”), yellow waxy papules and plaques especially in a periorbital location (

), dystrophic nails, and macroglossia (

).

Diagnosis requires biopsy of the affected organ showing characteristic pathologic findings. Abdominal fat pad or bone marrow biopsy may be preferred initially to avoid more invasive biopsies, because amyloid deposits are often detectable in these sites even without symptomatic skin involvement or cytopenias. After amyloid is confirmed in tissue, immunohistochemical stains or other techniques will determine the amyloid type, such as AL, transthyretin (TTR), or amyloid A protein. Patients with AL amyloidosis should undergo analysis for a clonal PCD with SPEP and UPEP, serum and urine immunofixation, serum FLC measurement, bone marrow biopsy, and skeletal imaging. The evaluation reflects that of a patient with newly diagnosed MM.

Cardiac involvement is common with AL amyloidosis, and evaluation includes echocardiography, electrocardiography with strain imaging, and B-type natriuretic peptide and serum troponin measurements. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is a sensitive imaging method to detect cardiac amyloid (see Cardiac Amyloidosis in Cardiovascular Medicine). Kidney involvement with AL amyloidosis usually manifests as nephrotic-range proteinuria; 24-hour urine protein and electrophoresis assist in diagnosis and monitoring (see Amyloidosis in Nephrology).

Prognosis of AL amyloidosis depends on the presence and extent of cardiac involvement; survival ranges from almost 8 years to only 6 months.

Treatment of AL amyloidosis starts with evaluating the patient for autologous HSCT, which has been shown to improve organ function and survival. Patients with advanced cardiac disease, stage 4 chronic kidney disease, or large pleural effusions are generally not eligible for transplantation. Patients ineligible for transplant should receive treatment with agents used for myeloma therapy. Supportive care to treat symptoms (such as diuretics for edema) is necessary.

The second most common type of amyloidosis is TTR amyloid (see [Table: Table: Types of Amyloid Disease]

), which deposits in the myocardium. Technetium-99-pyrophosphate scanning is specific for TTR amyloid. It is estimated that wild-type TTR amyloidosis (previously senile systemic amyloidosis) may account for 10% to 15% of patients who have heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Tafamidis is an oral agent that stabilizes TTR amyloid and reduces mortality and hospitalization for cardiovascular events (see Cardiac Amyloidosis in Cardiovascular Medicine).

Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM) is an indolent B-cell lymphoma with clonal lymphoplasmacytic cells in the bone marrow or lymph nodes that produce IgM. WM is differentiated from IgM MGUS by the presence of more than 10% clonal lymphoplasmacytic cells on tissue biopsy specimens and a mutation in MYD88 (present in up to 90% persons with WM). WM shares overlapping characteristics with MM and lymphoma.

Patients can present with classic “B symptoms” of drenching night sweats, fever, and weight loss and may have anemia and fatigue. Tissue infiltration may cause hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, gastrointestinal dysfunction, and kidney disease. Peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy is seen in 20% of patients and can be associated with antimyelin-associated glycoprotein antibodies.

Hyperviscosity syndrome may occur because of elevated circulating IgM and can manifest as diverse central nervous system symptoms, including headache, altered mental status, changes in vision and hearing, nystagmus, and ataxia. Funduscopic evaluation may reveal dilated retinal veins, papilledema, and flame hemorrhages. Hyperviscosity syndrome also impairs platelet and fibrinogen function, increasing the risk of mucosal bleeding. Symptomatic hyperviscosity requires emergent treatment with therapeutic apheresis to remove excess IgM. Therapy to decrease IgM production is simultaneously instituted.

Rituximab combined with chemotherapy, such as cyclophosphamide and bortezomib, along with glucocorticoids, is commonly used to treat symptomatic WM. Rituximab cannot be used in the setting of acute symptomatic hyperviscosity because it can lead to an initial disease flare. Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors (ibrutinib) may also be used. Patients with asymptomatic WM can be observed without therapy.

Cryoglobulinemia denotes the presence of clonal or polyclonal immunoglobulins that precipitate in the serum at temperatures less than 37.0 °C (98.6 °F) and dissolve with rewarming. In contrast, cold agglutinins, which are often confused with cryoglobulins, are antibodies against erythrocyte antigens that agglutinate erythrocytes in blood at temperatures less than 37.0 °C (98.6 °F) and can sometimes cause autoimmune hemolytic anemia (see Cold Agglutinin Disease in Hematology).

Cryoglobulinemia is classified as type I, II, or III based on the composition of the cryoglobulin. Type I involves a monoclonal immunoglobulin, usually IgM, and is associated with PCDs. Types II and III are called mixed cryoglobulinemias; they are composed of a mixture of polyclonal IgG and either monoclonal (type II) or polyclonal (type III) IgM. Mixed cryoglobulinemias are usually seen in association with infections such as hepatitis C virus, connective tissue disorders, and, rarely, lymphoproliferative disorders, and may lead to vasculitic syndromes and glomerulonephritis (see Cryoglobulinemic Vasculitis in Rheumatology).

Type I cryoglobulinemia is usually asymptomatic but can rarely cause symptoms from microvascular occlusion, including Raynaud phenomenon, digital cyanosis, ulcers, or gangrene. Large concentrations of cryoglobulins may lead to hyperviscosity syndrome, which may require therapeutic apheresis. Treatment is directed toward the underlying PCD to prevent cryoglobulin production.

Erythrocyte Disorders

Anemia is a pathologic state resulting in an insufficient number of erythrocytes to deliver oxygen to organs and tissues. Anemia can arise from blood loss, erythrocyte underproduction, erythrocyte destruction (hemolysis), or a combination of these factors. Patients with anemia may be entirely asymptomatic or experience symptoms of dyspnea, decreased exercise tolerance, palpitations, lightheadedness, or fatigue. Symptoms are related to the anemia severity and how rapidly it occurs, as well as whether underlying organ or vascular disease is present.

Blood loss causing anemia may be acute or chronic. Chronic blood loss results in anemia when the necessary increase in erythrocyte production cannot keep pace with the rate of loss, often secondary to iron deficiency.

Erythropoiesis is regulated by several factors, including erythropoietin production (synthesized in the kidney in response to hypoxia), the presence of micronutrients necessary for hemoglobin production, and bone marrow cellular function. Several pathophysiologic states affecting erythrocyte production can lead to anemia, including the following:

  • Absolute or relative erythropoietin deficiency (chronic kidney disease)
  • Micronutrient deficiency (iron, vitamin B~12, folate, copper)
  • Inflammation
  • Bone marrow abnormalities
  • Hematologic malignancies (e.g., myelodysplasia, multiple myeloma, metastatic disease)

Erythrocyte destruction secondary to hemolytic anemia can result from hereditary causes (sickle cell disease, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency) or acquired processes (autoimmune hemolytic anemia, microangiopathic anemias, mechanical heart valve).

Medications can cause anemia through multiple mechanisms:

  • Erythropoiesis suppression (resulting in a normocytic anemia)
  • Interference with DNA synthesis (antimetabolites, including methotrexate and hydroxyurea, resulting in macrocytic anemia)
  • Inducement of hemolytic anemia (penicillin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, methyldopa)

Specific considerations exist for patients with anemia who are pregnant, older, or hospitalized. Normal pregnancy is associated with a physiologic dilutional anemia resulting from an increase in plasma volume that exceeds the increase in erythrocyte mass. This adaptation allows oxygen delivery to the developing fetus at low viscosity.

Whether anemia is a normal result of aging is a subject of debate. Associated pathophysiologic states and nutritional deficiencies may contribute to anemia in older adults, along with a physiologic decline in bone marrow cellularity of approximately 1% per year.

Anemia in hospitalized patients most often results from acute blood loss, anemia of inflammation, or anemia of kidney disease, although excessive daily phlebotomy may also contribute.

The automated complete blood count (CBC) identifies the presence and severity of the anemia. The CBC includes the interrelated erythrocyte count, hematocrit (percentage of blood volume composed of erythrocytes), hemoglobin concentration, and erythrocyte indices, such as the mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and the red cell distribution width (RDW). The RDW reflects variations in erythrocyte size and/or shape.

Reticulocytes are immature erythrocytes identified by stains for ribosomal material that persist in the cytoplasm for several days following release from the marrow into circulation. Reticulocyte production may be reflected in the absolute reticulocyte count, the reticulocyte percentage, or the reticulocyte production index ( [Table: Table: Measures of Reticulocytosis]

). An elevated reticulocyte response reflects a healthy bone marrow response to hemolysis or bleeding, or successful treatment of the anemia. In contrast, a decreased reticulocyte response is seen in patients who cannot make adequate erythrocytes in response to the anemia, such as those with vitamin B~12 deficiency, folate deficiency, iron deficiency, anemia of inflammation, kidney disease, or those with marrow diseases such as myelodysplasia or aplastic anemia.

The clinical history is always the first step in assessing patients with anemia. Reviewing the CBC, MCV, and reticulocyte production along with the peripheral blood smear (PBS) can provide additional valuable diagnostic information. Defining the anemia as microcytic, macrocytic, or normocytic as well as by bone marrow response (elevated, normal, or suppressed reticulocyte production) can refine the differential diagnosis.

An algorithm for the evaluation of anemia can be found in

. Specific laboratory tests should be ordered based on suspected causes ( [Table: Table: Laboratory Approach to Anemia]

). Additionally, a bone marrow aspirate and biopsy may be helpful in evaluating anemia when the cause is unclear or if hematologic malignancy or stem cell disorders (e.g., lymphoma, multiple myeloma, aplastic anemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, or acute leukemia) are suspected, especially when more than one cytopenia is present. Anemia should never be considered a final diagnosis; the underlying cause should be investigated to inform prognosis and provide therapeutic opportunities linked to the specific cause.

Iron is an essential component of the hemoglobin molecule. In addition to its critical role in oxygen delivery, iron is also necessary for DNA synthesis and cellular transport. Most of the iron in the body is contained in erythrocytes; each cubic milliliter of erythrocytes contains approximately 1 mg of elemental iron.

Iron is derived from the diet as heme-based iron from red meat, poultry, and fish and non–heme-based iron from green leafy vegetables, lentils, beans, and peas. Vegetable iron has more limited uptake because of phytates and oxalates that form complexes with iron and limit bioavailability. The typical adult diet contains 5 mg of iron for every 1000 calories but only 10% to 20% of oral iron is absorbed, a process which takes place in the small bowel.

Iron intake, use, and loss exist in a fine balance. In a normal physiologic state, iron absorption is approximately equal to iron loss.

  • The typical adult man loses approximately 1 mg of iron daily from gastrointestinal mucosal turnover.
  • The typical woman, during reproductive years, loses approximately 1.5 mg of iron daily through mucosal turnover and menstrual blood loss.

Hepcidin is the key peptide involved in iron regulation (

). Hepcidin production occurs in the liver and is regulated by several proteins, including the homeostatic iron regulator (HFE) protein, hemojuvelin, matriptase-2, and transferrin receptor 1 and 2. These hepcidin regulatory proteins are important in the hereditary iron overload states (see Primary/Hereditary Hemochromatosis in Hematology).

Hepcidin negatively regulates iron absorption. Increased hepcidin production, as occurs with inflammation and increased iron stores, leads to decreased iron absorption and decreased iron transport from storage sites to erythroid precursors. In contrast, hepcidin levels decrease in response to hypoxia, anemia, and iron deficiency, resulting in increased iron absorption and mobilization of iron from storage sites.

Iron deficiency is one of the most common causes of anemia worldwide. Common causes of iron deficiency anemia are listed in [Table: Table: Causes of Iron Deficiency Anemia]

. Iron deficiency may be more prevalent during periods of increased demand (e.g., pregnancy and lactation), during normal growth and development, and in regions where endemic helminthic infections increase gastrointestinal blood loss. Iron deficiency is most commonly secondary to blood loss. For premenopausal women, this is typically secondary to menstrual blood loss, but for men or postmenopausal women, occult gastrointestinal blood loss should be suspected. It is especially important to rule out occult gastric or colonic neoplasm in these patients, and bidirectional endoscopy is recommended.

Iron deficiency in adults rarely occurs secondary to decreased oral intake, such as in vegetarians, but malabsorption is a more common cause. Iron is absorbed in the proximal small bowel, and patients with celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or surgical resection (including bariatric surgery) can experience iron and other nutritional deficiencies because of malabsorption. Iron malabsorption may occur without diarrhea, steatorrhea, or weight loss. Helicobacter pylori infection is also associated with iron deficiency because of impaired iron uptake (this mechanism is not well established) and increased iron loss from gastritis or peptic ulcer disease.

Patients with iron deficiency may be asymptomatic or may experience the following:

  • Fatigue
  • Lack of a sense of well-being
  • Irritability
  • Headache
  • Decreased exercise tolerance (sometimes disproportionately more severe than the degree of anemia)
  • Pica (dietary cravings for starch, ice, or clay)

Physical examination findings may be normal in patients with early anemia from iron deficiency. Conjunctival pallor is highly specific for a hemoglobin level less than 10 g/dL (100 g/L). Less common findings include the following:

  • Tachycardia
  • Glossitis
  • Stomatitis
  • Spooning of the nails (koilonychia; seen in severe deficiency) (

)

The combination of a low MCV and mean corpuscular hemoglobin, elevated RDW, and PBS showing erythrocyte microcytosis and anisopoikilocytosis (

) is virtually diagnostic of iron deficiency, especially in premenopausal women. Iron studies showing a low serum iron level, elevated total iron-binding capacity, low transferrin saturation (<15%; iron/total iron-binding capacity × 100), and low serum ferritin level are all consistent with the diagnosis of iron deficiency. However, a low serum iron level may occur with other causes of anemia and alone is not diagnostic of iron deficiency ( [Table: Table: Laboratory Characteristics of Types of Anemia]

). Thrombocytosis occurs frequently with iron deficiency caused by blood loss.

Low serum ferritin levels strongly suggest iron deficiency, although the most appropriate cutoff point is debated. A serum ferritin level less than 30 ng/mL (30 μg/L) is considered highly specific (>97%) but relatively insensitive (35% in men; 54% in women) for iron deficiency. To maximize sensitivity, the American Gastroenterological Society recommends a serum ferritin cutoff value of less than 45 ng/mL (45 μg/L) (sensitivity, 85%; specificity, 92%). Although serum ferritin is an acute phase reactant that increases with inflammation, a serum ferritin level greater than 100 ng/mL (100 μg/L) suggests against iron deficiency. With comorbidity or acute illness, however, iron deficiency defined by marrow aspirate staining may be present even with a ferritin level greater than 1000 ng/mL (1000 μg/L).

Iron deficiency is typically managed with oral iron salts. Oral absorption may be increased with supplemental vitamin C (ascorbic acid). Conversely, medications that reduce gastric acid (antacids, proton pump inhibitors) and a variety of food products, including fiber, grains, tea, cocoa, and eggs, can reduce absorption; iron replacement is best taken between meals. Frequent dosing (two or three times daily) of oral iron can lead to increased hepcidin production, which paradoxically reduces iron absorption. For this reason, oral iron sulfate dosed once daily or every other day may be the best replacement strategy. Oral ferrous sulfate is the least expensive preparation, with each 325-mg tablet containing 65 mg of elemental iron. Although oral ferrous fumarate, ferrous gluconate, and other oral iron salts are available, none has proven superior to ferrous sulfate in tolerability, efficacy, or cost. Similarly, delayed-release and slow-release preparations may be better tolerated, but they are more expensive and are associated with reduced iron absorption because they can bypass the intestinal sites where iron absorption occurs. Although oral iron is typically well tolerated, adverse effects can include gastrointestinal upset, constipation, and abdominal pain. Iron tablets do not interfere with fecal occult blood testing.

For patients undergoing dialysis who require large doses of iron or for patients with celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or oral iron intolerance or those who have undergone resection of the stomach or small bowel, oral iron may not be adequate treatment. These patients typically require parenteral iron. Newer parenteral iron preparations have better safety profiles (less anaphylaxis) and bioavailability than the historically used iron dextran. These preparations include iron sucrose, ferric gluconate, ferumoxytol, and ferric carboxymaltose. Data are inadequate to recommend one parenteral agent over another for patients requiring parenteral iron.

Iron replacement usually results in reticulocytosis within days and hemoglobin levels typically increase by approximately 1 g/dL (10 g/L) per week. Oral iron replacement typically lasts 3 to 6 months after normalization of hemoglobin to replace iron stores.

Patients with congestive heart failure who have iron deficiency can also benefit from iron replacement to improve functional capacity and quality of life (see Iron Therapy in Cardiovascular Medicine).

Anemia has long been recognized to occur in conjunction with chronic infections such as tuberculosis or osteomyelitis; with autoimmune conditions or rheumatic disease, such as rheumatoid arthritis; or with malignancy. Because these conditions are considered chronic diseases, these anemic states are often referred to as anemia of chronic disease. However, from a pathophysiologic standpoint, anemia of inflammation (AOI) is a more appropriate term because these anemias are related to increased hepcidin production in the liver in response to inflammatory mediators such as interleukin-6. Hepcidin causes internalization and proteolysis of ferroportin in the enterocyte and macrophage, leading to decreased iron absorption from the gut and decreased iron transfer from macrophages to erythroid precursors (see

). Inflammatory cytokines also blunt the erythropoietin response to anemia.

In patients with AOI, the PBS usually shows a normochromic, normocytic anemia. Over time, microcytosis can be seen. Normally, these patients have a hemoglobin level of 8 to 10 g/dL (80-100 g/L). The reticulocyte count is typically inappropriately low for the degree of anemia. The characteristic iron study pattern shows a low serum iron level, a reduced total iron-binding capacity, and an increased serum ferritin level. [Table: Table: Laboratory Characteristics of Types of Anemia]

lists characteristic laboratory features useful in distinguishing iron deficiency from AOI. Although seldom necessary, a bone marrow biopsy specimen would show adequate stainable iron stores in AOI.

Patients with diabetes mellitus or heart failure can also have an increase in inflammatory cytokines and related AOI. In some patients with findings consistent with AOI, the inflammatory state is not obvious. These patients do not require extensive evaluation for an occult neoplasm or other sources of inflammation.

AOI seldom requires treatment, and the anemia should improve with treatment of the underlying inflammatory condition, if identified. Iron replacement is ineffective, and blood transfusion is unnecessary in asymptomatic persons.

Although supplemental erythropoietin can correct anemia in inflammatory states, it can also lead to hypertension and thrombosis, particularly with overcorrection to a hemoglobin level of 10 g/dL (100 g/L) and should be used with caution. In studies of patients with cancer who experienced anemia because of chemotherapy and who received supplemental erythropoietin, patients felt better and had better blood counts, but cancer mortality was increased in some studies. Erythropoietin is approved for use during chemotherapy in symptomatic patients with a hemoglobin level less than 10 g/dL (100 g/L) who are undergoing cancer treatment that is not curative in intent, but it is infrequently used in practice.

Occupational exposure to lead is the most common cause of lead intoxication, although contaminated supplements or water supply and home exposure to lead paint may also occur. Even modestly increased lead levels in the blood can cause symptoms such as arthralgia, myalgia, headache, abdominal pain, and neurocognitive changes. At higher levels, anemia, chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (see Heavy Metals in Nephrology), peripheral neuropathy, and prominent neuropsychiatric changes can occur. The anemia of lead intoxication is microcytic; although basophilic stippling is frequently seen on PBS (

), it is not specific for lead intoxication.

A high index of suspicion is necessary to make the diagnosis. Evaluation should focus on occupational history and investigation of supplement use, food and water sources, and potential home exposures. Diagnosis is confirmed by an elevated blood lead level. Treatment involves removing potential sources of exposure and may require occupational changes. In patients with high lead levels, chelation therapy should be considered. Anemia usually resolves as levels decrease, but some clinical manifestations, including neuropsychiatric changes, may persist.

Hemoglobin A is a tetramer containing two α chains, two β chains (α2β2), and the iron-containing tetrapyrrole heme moiety. Production of α and β chains normally occurs in a balanced fashion from genes located on chromosomes 16 and 11, respectively. Thalassemia is a genetic disorder caused by an inherited alteration in one or more of the α or β genes that results in impaired production of the corresponding α or β chains and subsequent imbalance of their ratio. This leads to unpaired α or β chains that precipitate, resulting in reduced production of hemoglobin and destruction of erythrocyte precursors in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis). This manifests in variable degrees of microcytic anemia, hemolysis, extramedullary hematopoiesis, bone changes, impaired growth, and iron overload. Homozygous thalassemia manifests at an early age, whereas heterozygous disease may have minimal or no symptoms, leading to a diagnosis later in life.

The worldwide incidence of β-thalassemia is 1% to 5%; the incidence of α-thalassemia is even higher. Thalassemias are common in African and Mediterranean countries, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia.

The PBS typically shows microcytosis, nucleated erythrocytes, and target cells (

). Unlike other underproduction anemias, patients with heterozygous thalassemia typically have a preserved or even an increased erythrocyte count associated with a decreased MCV. The microcytic cells in thalassemia are uniform and the RDW is normal, distinguishing thalassemia from iron deficiency, in which there is considerable variation in cell shape and size (anisopoikilocytosis), leading to an elevated RDW. Because of ineffective erythropoiesis, thalassemia can also be associated with indices of hemolysis, including increased serum lactate dehydrogenase and unconjugated bilirubin levels and a decreased serum haptoglobin level.

Iron overload–related heart failure and arrhythmias are the major causes of death in patients with thalassemia. Baseline iron studies should be obtained, and serial measurements of serum ferritin and periodic assessment of cardiac iron loading with MRI can be used to monitor iron stores, particularly if transfusions are necessary. Significant iron overload may require chelation therapy (see Secondary Iron Overload in Hematology).

The normal human genome contains four copies of the α-globin gene (two copies on each chromosome 16) leading to several genotypes of α-thalassemia ( [Table: Table: α-Thalassemia Types]

). Patients with a single α-gene alteration are silent carriers and are healthy. A two-gene alteration results in α-thalassemia trait; diagnosis is usually achieved by excluding other causes of hypochromic microcytic anemia. Although hemoglobin electrophoresis results are normal in patients with one- and two-gene variants, select reference laboratories can establish the diagnosis through direct sequencing of the globin genes. Patients with a three-gene variant have more severe anemia and make a tetramer of β globin called hemoglobin H that can be identified on electrophoresis. A complete lack of α chains, called hemoglobin Barts, is typically fatal in utero.

Patients with α-thalassemia trait should receive supplemental folate and genetic counseling before starting a family. Patients with hemoglobin H disease typically have hemoglobin concentrations of approximately 7 to 8 g/dL (70-80 g/L) and seldom rely on transfusion, although transfusion may be necessary during times of physiologic stress. Care should be taken to avoid supplemental iron because these patients absorb iron more efficiently and are at increased risk of iron overload. Routine transfusions should also be avoided.

The normal human genome has two copies of the β-globin gene (one on each allele). More than 250 variants have been described in the β-globin gene resulting in a spectrum of diseases from mild reduction in β-chain synthesis (β^+-thalassemia) to complete absence of β-chain synthesis (β^0-thalassemia). As such, the clinical spectrum of disease in β-thalassemia includes β-thalassemia minor, β-thalassemia intermedia, and β-thalassemia major. β-Thalassemia minor (trait) is characterized by a microcytic anemia with a hemoglobin level of 10 to 12 g/dL (100-120 g/L). Unlike α-thalassemia trait, β-thalassemia minor produces an abnormal hemoglobin electrophoresis with an increase in hemoglobin A~2 (α~2δ~2) because of a substitution of delta globin for β globin. Hemoglobin F may also be increased depending on the specific variant. Patients with β-thalassemia intermedia have hemoglobin levels of 7 g/dL (70 g/L) without relying on transfusion. β-Thalassemia major presents early in life and is marked by severe transfusion-dependent anemia.

Patients with β-thalassemia trait and β-thalassemia intermedia should receive genetic counseling, and folate supplementation may be helpful if they have anemia. As with α-thalassemia, supplemental iron should be avoided.

Patients with β-thalassemia intermedia have lower hemoglobin levels but are not transfusion dependent; clinical presentations vary, but ineffective erythropoiesis often leads to iron overload with extramedullary erythropoiesis, splenomegaly, osteoporosis, hypogonadism, and bone pain. Management of β-thalassemia intermedia requires balancing intermittent transfusion to reduce extramedullary hematopoiesis with treatment for iron overload.

Patients with β-thalassemia major have severe transfusion-dependent anemia and frequently require iron chelation for iron overload due to ineffective erythropoiesis. For patients with more severe disease, luspatercept, a drug that acts by sequestering transforming growth factor-β proteins, improves erythrocyte maturation and reduces transfusion requirements. Select individuals with transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia may be cured with allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

Because erythropoietin is made in the renal cortex in response to anemia and hypoxia, patients with kidney disease often have anemia, with incidence increasing as the glomerular filtration rate declines. Anemia of kidney disease can be associated with fatigue, depression, dyspnea, and decreased exercise tolerance. Anemia is also associated with increased morbidity and mortality from heart disease and stroke in patients undergoing dialysis.

The anemia is typically normochromic and normocytic, and the reticulocyte response is typically low because of a relative erythropoietin deficiency. The PBS may show burr cells (echinocytes) (

) in patients with uremia.

Because kidney disease is also associated with platelet defects and gastrointestinal bleeding from ulcer disease or angiodysplasia, microcytosis in the setting of kidney disease should raise suspicion for concomitant iron deficiency. Although it is important to first rule out other causes of anemia, measuring the erythropoietin level can help with evaluating anemia in patients with mild kidney disease when there is diagnostic uncertainty regarding the cause of anemia.

Supplemental use of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) can improve anemia in patients with kidney disease. Treatment decisions are based on the degree of kidney dysfunction present and whether the patient is receiving hemodialysis. Guidelines recommend that ESAs be withheld in patients with chronic kidney disease not requiring dialysis who have a hemoglobin level greater than 10 g/dL (100 g/L). For patients with chronic kidney disease with a hemoglobin level less than 10 g/dL (100 g/L), ESA treatment should be individualized based on symptoms, speed of hemoglobin decline, and transfusion needs.

For patients undergoing dialysis, ESAs should be initiated to avoid hemoglobin levels less than 9 g/dL (90 g/L), usually starting therapy when the hemoglobin level is less than 10 g/dL (100 g/L). Hemoglobin concentrations should not exceed 11.5 g/dL (115 g/L) to avoid adverse effects, including worsening hypertension, volume overload, and thrombotic complications.

Although more than 95% of patients respond to ESAs, insufficient response can result from concomitant iron or folate deficiency, aluminum toxicity (which is much less common with contemporary hemodialysis techniques), blood loss, or inflammation. Regular monitoring of serum iron and ferritin levels is necessary to ensure an appropriate erythropoietic response. Because of high iron requirements in patients taking ESAs, parenteral iron is typically used in those receiving dialysis to maintain a serum ferritin level greater than 500 ng/mL (500 μg/L) and a transferrin saturation of at least 30%.

Vitamin B~12 (cobalamin) is necessary for DNA synthesis. Humans cannot synthesize cobalamin and must consume it in their diet; it is found in animal meats, shellfish, and dairy products. Dietary deficiency is an uncommon cause of vitamin B~12 deficiency because body stores are typically available for many years. Instead, vitamin B~12 deficiency is nearly always a result of malabsorption.

Vitamin B~12 absorption is facilitated by an acidic gastric environment, and deficiency may be the result of decreased bioavailability in the setting of age-related gastric achlorhydria, the use of proton pump inhibitors, or both. The presence of gastric intrinsic factor is also necessary to facilitate vitamin B~12 absorption in the terminal ileum. Pernicious anemia, characterized by autoimmune gastritis and intrinsic factor deficiency, is another cause of vitamin B~12 deficiency. Vitamin B~12 malabsorption can also occur in patients with more generalized malabsorptive states such as inflammatory bowel disease, pancreatic insufficiency, bacterial overgrowth, and metformin use.

Patients with vitamin B~12 deficiency can present with weight loss, glossitis, and “lemon-yellow” skin because of pallor and jaundice resulting from ineffective erythropoiesis. Vitamin B~12 deficiency can cause neurologic symptoms, including loss of vibratory sense, loss of proprioception, spastic ataxia, and other dorsal column symptoms. Psychiatric symptoms (megaloblastic mania) can manifest as dementia, hallucinations, and frank psychosis. Importantly, the neuropsychiatric manifestations of vitamin B~12 deficiency may occur before the development of anemia (see Subacute Combined Degeneration in Neurology).

In patients with vitamin B~12 deficiency, the PBS shows macrocytic erythrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils (

). Pancytopenia resulting from ineffective hematopoiesis can also be seen. Other laboratory findings are consistent with intramedullary hemolysis caused by ineffective erythropoiesis, including decreased serum haptoglobin level, elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase level, and indirect hyperbilirubinemia. The reticulocyte count is low in patients with vitamin B~12 deficiency. Antibodies to parietal cells are found in 90% of patients with pernicious anemia, whereas antibodies to intrinsic factor are detected in approximately 70%.

The serum vitamin B~12 level is approximately 95% sensitive in diagnosing deficiency in symptomatic patients. A level less than 200 pg/mL (147 pmol/L) strongly suggests deficiency, whereas a level greater than 300 pg/mL (221 pmol/L) effectively excludes the diagnosis. Lower levels may not adequately represent tissue vitamin B~12 levels; as such, equivocal levels of vitamin B~12 in the setting of a clinical suspicion of deficiency should prompt metabolite testing because an elevated serum methylmalonic acid concentration is a more sensitive indicator of vitamin B~12 deficiency. An important distinction is that vitamin B~12 deficiency causes increases in both homocysteine and methylmalonic acid levels, whereas folate deficiency, another cause of macrocytic anemia, leads to an elevation in serum homocysteine level with a normal methylmalonic acid level.

Although testing for antibodies to parietal cells and intrinsic factor is sometimes used to diagnose pernicious anemia, the varied sensitivity and specificity of these tests limit their utility.

Patients with vitamin B~12 deficiency can be treated with oral vitamin B~12 (1000-2000 μg/d) regardless of cause; an adequate amount of this dose will be absorbed, even if intrinsic factor is lacking or malabsorption is ongoing. Parenteral vitamin B~12 is more expensive and more cumbersome to administer; it is often limited to use as initial therapy in patients with severe disease or neurologic findings. Intranasal and oral gel preparations are also available but are not clearly superior to tablets. When vitamin B~12 is replaced, megaloblastic changes in the marrow improve within hours. Reticulocytosis appears in several days, and the hemoglobin level increases by approximately 1 g/dL (10 g/L) per week. If the response to vitamin B~12 is inadequate, an alternative diagnosis, such as myelodysplasia, should be considered. Neurologic changes may not be reversible with replacement. Patients with pernicious anemia are at an increased risk for upper gastrointestinal malignancies, and screening endoscopy should be considered at the time of initial diagnosis.

Folate is a common component of most diets in the United States and is found in green leafy vegetables and most fruits. Supplemental folate has been added to grains in the United States for many years to prevent birth defects. As such, dietary folate deficiency is uncommon except in patients with poor intake and malnutrition. Folate is poorly stored, and deficiency can develop in weeks to months in patients with insufficient folate ingestion. Persons who consume excess alcohol may have inadequate dietary folate in addition to impaired absorption. Drugs such as triamterene, phenytoin, and methotrexate can contribute to folate deficiency by inhibiting folate absorption or conversion to its active form. Finally, because folate is absorbed in the jejunum, gastric bypass and small bowel diseases such as celiac disease or inflammatory bowel disease can also impair folate absorption.

Patients with disease states characterized by rapid cell turnover, such as pregnancy, hemolysis, or desquamating skin disorders (psoriasis), also have increased folate requirements.

The PBS in folate deficiency is identical to that of vitamin B~12 deficiency. Serum folate measurement, if very low, helps establish the diagnosis; however, a normal level may be unreliable because a single meal can normalize levels. Although folate levels in erythrocytes may better reflect chronic folate balance, an elevated serum homocysteine level has a sensitivity greater than 90% in diagnosing folate deficiency and is the preferred test when deficiency is suspected despite a normal serum folate level.

Treatment of folate deficiency when concomitant vitamin B~12 deficiency is present results in improvement of the hematologic abnormalities of vitamin B~12 deficiency. However, the other sequalae of vitamin B~12 deficiency, including the neuropsychiatric manifestations, continue to progress; therefore, vitamin B~12 deficiency should be excluded in all patients with folate deficiency. Otherwise, patients with folate deficiency should receive oral folate, 1 to 5 mg/d and attention to the underlying cause.

Hemolysis occurs with accelerated erythrocyte destruction. It can be caused by intrinsic abnormalities of the erythrocyte or through external factors (

). Intrinsic causes are primarily inherited, and extrinsic causes are acquired, but exceptions exist. Cellular destruction can occur predominantly within blood vessels (intravascular hemolysis), by macrophages in the liver or spleen (extravascular hemolysis), or, in some cases, both. The typical bone marrow response to excessive erythrocyte destruction is increased erythropoiesis. The degree of anemia occurring with hemolysis depends on the rate of destruction and the ability of the marrow to compensate. If the rate of breakdown is mild and erythrocyte production can be maintained, the hemoglobin level may remain normal. However, if destruction is brisk or the marrow is unable to compensate because of concomitant problems that impair erythropoiesis (e.g., nutritional deficiency), anemia occurs.

Symptoms depend on anemia severity and the underlying cause. Patients may report the following:

  • Fatigue
  • Dyspnea
  • Lightheadedness
  • Jaundice
  • Darkened urine

Release of free hemoglobin causes decreased nitrous oxide, and symptoms such as esophageal spasm or development of pulmonary hypertension can occur in patients with chronic hemolysis; splenomegaly accompanies several causes.

Laboratory findings include increased serum indirect bilirubin, elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase, and low serum haptoglobin levels. Increased plasma free hemoglobin and urobilinogen excretion can also be seen. If no additional conditions that would impair erythropoiesis are present, increased reticulocytes and an elevated MCV are noted. The absence of increased reticulocytes does not preclude hemolysis in patients who are unable to mount an adequate bone marrow response.

Morphologic changes in erythrocytes seen on PBS can help determine the underlying cause:

  • Bite or blister cells in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency
  • Schistocytes in thrombotic microangiopathies
  • Spherocytes in hereditary spherocytosis or warm antibody autoimmune hemolysis
  • Erythrocyte agglutination in cold agglutinin disease

Interaction between the erythrocyte cytoskeleton and the lipid bilayer helps determine erythrocyte size, shape, flexibility, and survival. Deficiency or dysfunction of the membrane proteins, as occurs in hereditary spherocytosis (HS), elliptocytosis, and stomatocytosis, can alter these properties and result in hemolysis.

HS is more common in people of Northern European descent, and most cases are autosomal dominant. Alterations in α- or β-spectrin, ankyrin, band 3, or protein 4.2 result in defective interaction between the cytoskeleton and the lipid bilayer and formation of a spherocyte with a reduced surface-to-volume ratio. This results in the following:

  • Decreased erythrocyte deformability
  • Increased osmotic fragility
  • Elevated mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration
  • Varying degrees of hemolysis with anemia with reticulocytosis

The PBS shows numerous spherocytes (

), and flow cytometry showing reduced eosin-5-maleimide binding to band 3 on the erythrocyte establishes the diagnosis.

Most patients experience mild disease, are often asymptomatic, and have normal or near-normal hemoglobin levels with compensated hemolysis. Hemolysis can worsen at times of oxidative stress, including infection. Patients with severe HS have more brisk hemolysis that is not as well compensated. These patients are at increased risk for splenomegaly, development of pigmented gallstones, and aplastic crisis with parvovirus infection. All patients with HS should receive folate supplementation, and splenectomy is effective for those with severe disease.

Membrane defects can also be acquired. Acanthocytes (spur cells) (

) are identified by multiple irregular projections on the erythrocyte. They can be seen in severe liver disease, often alcohol-related cirrhosis, as a result of nonesterified cholesterol deposition on the erythrocyte. The cholesterol deposition causes decreased deformability and increased destruction, resulting in significant hemolytic anemia. When related to liver failure, this is known as Zieve syndrome. Treatment is supportive, although liver transplantation is curative.

The glycolytic pathway and the hexose-monophosphate shunt are the main pathways of glucose metabolism in erythrocytes. Among other functions, glucose catabolism is important for maintaining erythrocyte shape and deformability. Abnormalities in these pathways are often defined by specific enzyme deficiencies, resulting in hemolysis. Pyruvate kinase deficiency is the most common abnormality seen in the glycolytic pathway and is more common in people of Northern and Eastern European descent. It is usually diagnosed at a young age and is associated with varying degrees of hemolysis.

G6PD deficiency affects the hexose-monophosphate shunt with failure to generate nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH). NADPH is necessary to reduce oxidative stress in response to medications, infection, or other toxins. Without NADPH, hemoglobin is subject to oxidation, and denatured hemoglobin aggregates (Heinz bodies) form and may be visible on supravital stain. The erythrocytes become trapped and partially destroyed in the spleen, resulting in bite cells (

).

The gene for G6PD deficiency is on the X chromosome, so it primarily affects males. However, those with Turner syndrome (XO karyotype) and females (depending on inactivation of one of the two X chromosomes) can also be affected. G6PD provides a survival advantage against Plasmodium falciparum and is, therefore, more common in persons of African, Asian, Mediterranean, and Middle Eastern descent. Estimates are that more than 200 million persons are affected worldwide. The G6PD A variant produces mild, often asymptomatic, disease. G6PD Mediterranean is associated with favism, or hemolysis after eating fava beans.

Adults typically have signs of acute hemolysis 1 to 3 days after exposure to oxidative stress. Drugs that can trigger a hemolytic episode include the following:

  • Chloroquine
  • Sulfonamides
  • Rasburicase
  • Dapsone
  • Nitrofurantoin
  • Phenazopyridine

Semiquantitative assays that evaluate reduction of NADP to NADPH are used to assess G6PD function. Enzyme function should not be tested during an acute episode because older erythrocytes are preferentially destroyed, leaving younger erythrocytes with higher G6PD levels, resulting in a false-negative result.

Treatment involves primary prevention, with avoidance of known triggers. Removal of the offending agent and supportive interventions are mainstays of treating an acute episode.

Sickle cell disease (SCD) is characterized by homozygosity for a single point alteration in the β-globin gene on chromosome 11, resulting in the substitution of valine for glutamic acid and the resultant abnormal hemoglobin S that polymerizes under hypoxic conditions. This causes deformed erythrocytes that can adhere to the endothelium of capillaries throughout the circulation and cause vaso-occlusion. In addition, nitric oxide depletion occurs from the release of arginase and free hemoglobin from hemolyzed erythrocytes; arginase depletes arginine, a necessary precursor to nitric oxide, whereas free hemoglobin scavenges and inactivates nitric oxide. This depletion of nitric oxide results in vasoconstriction and platelet activation, complicating the clinical course. SCD affects nearly every organ system and causes unpredictable and extraordinarily painful vaso-occlusive events.

Hemoglobin S is more common in people from sub-Saharan Africa, India, the Middle East, the Caribbean, and Central and South America. Hemoglobin S can also be coinherited with hemoglobin C (hemoglobin SC), β-thalassemia (Sβ^+-thalassemia), or other hemoglobin types, which tend to lead to milder disease than hemoglobin SS. Characteristic electrophoretic patterns for sickling disorders are shown in [Table: Table: Sickle Cell Syndrome Characteristics]

.

Strong recommendations from expert guidelines for the treatment of SCD are listed in [Table: Table: Recommendations for SCD Management]

.

The only potential cure for SCD is allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, but the timing and appropriate population for transplantation have not been adequately determined. Similarly, in 2023, the FDA approved two cell-based gene therapies for sickle cell anemia treatment in patients older than 12 years. One therapy, the first in human treatment to utilize CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing techniques, increases the amount of hemoglobin F. The other creates a modified hemoglobin A. Although long-term safety remains unknown, each therapy reduced severe vaso-occlusion for at least 1 year after infusion. The role of these therapies in SCD remains undetermined.

The clinical course of SCD is marked by chronic hemolysis, vaso-occlusion with acute and chronic end-organ damage, nitric oxide depletion, and immune compromise from functional asplenia. Managing SCD requires establishment of preventive, acute, and chronic treatment goals ( [Table: Table: SCD Common Complications and Treatments]

). Considering the significant adverse effects on quality of life, reduced life expectancy, and multisystem organ involvement inherent to SCD, care at a comprehensive sickle cell center providing a multidisciplinary approach is encouraged.

Painful vaso-occlusive events are the hallmark of SCD. The frequency and severity of acute painful events vary considerably among patients, the reasons for which remain poorly understood. In most communities, a few patients with recurrent acute painful events account for most hospitalizations. Evaluation and management of pain are often suboptimal, leading to undertreatment. Painful events are associated with morbidity and mortality in patients with SCD, and the number of painful events is inversely related to life expectancy. For these reasons, painful events should be recognized and treated immediately. Opioids are the preferred analgesic, except for meperidine, which can cause seizures.

Optimal SCD treatment ideally results in reduced frequency and intensity of vaso-occlusive events, reduced negative organ involvement, and improved life expectancy. Therapies that may address these outcomes are listed in [Table: Table: Disease-Modifying Strategies in SCD]

. Hydroxyurea has the most long-term clinical data supporting its use in SCD. It increases fetal hemoglobin and improves nitric oxide production, allowing it to modulate many of the complications seen. In addition to reducing pain crises, hydroxyurea has also been shown to improve overall survival.

Additional approved agents for the prevention of painful events include L-glutamine and the P-selectin inhibitor crizanlizumab. Oral L-glutamine, a precursor of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD), is necessary to form the antioxidant NADH. It is believed that sickle cell crises are partially related to oxidant stress; a randomized trial showed treatment with L-glutamine resulted in a reduction in the number of sickle cell crises. Crizanlizumab also reduces painful crises, albeit through a different mechanism, specifically by preventing cellular adhesion.

The pathophysiology of chronic pain in SCD is poorly understood, and it is more difficult to treat. Chronic pain is exacerbated by emotional stress, anxiety, insomnia, and depression and is perhaps best treated with a holistic approach emphasizing nonopioid options such as NSAIDs, relaxation techniques, massage, and biofeedback. Patients may develop opioid dependence, although the prevalence is no greater than in a comparable age- and illness-matched population.

Pulmonary complications are the primary cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with SCD. Acute chest syndrome is a clinical diagnosis based on the following constellation of symptoms:

  • Cough
  • Shortness of breath
  • Fever (>38.6 °C [101.5 °F])
  • Tachypnea
  • Hypoxia
  • New pulmonary infiltrate

Acute chest syndrome can be the result of infection, in situ thrombosis, thromboembolism, fat or bone marrow embolism, or a combination of these factors. Patients with acute chest syndrome should be monitored closely and receive empiric antibiotics in addition to adequate hydration and supplemental oxygen for hypoxemia. Incentive spirometry should be encouraged, and adequate analgesia provided. Therapeutic anticoagulation has been shown to shorten duration of acute chest syndrome and reduce opioid consumption over prophylactic anticoagulation; it should be considered in severe disease. Patients with acute chest syndrome also require erythrocyte transfusion, either with packed red blood cells (PRBCs) or as exchange transfusion.

Pulmonary hypertension occurs in up to 30% of patients with SCD and is associated with increased mortality. Patients typically present with worsening right-sided heart failure. The appropriate management of pulmonary hypertension in SCD has not been determined. However, phosphodiesterase inhibitors, including sildenafil, have been associated with increased painful crises.

Stroke and other central nervous system disease remain major complications of SCD; approximately 30% of patients have silent or symptomatic ischemic strokes. Monthly transfusion begun after a stroke can reduce the incidence of subsequent stroke by 50% but carries the risk of iron overload necessitating iron chelation. Hydroxyurea may also help prevent stroke. In addition to ischemic stroke, patients with SCD can have moyamoya disease (irregular perforating vascular networks near occluded or stenotic vessels in the region corresponding to lenticulostriate and thalamoperforating arteries), predisposing them to cerebral bleeding in the third and fourth decade of life. Additionally, adults with SCD have lower cognitive function than healthy adults, perhaps secondary to silent ischemia or chronic anemia. It is unclear whether such cognitive decline can be prevented.

Transfusion management in SCD is complicated. Inappropriate transfusion can lead to alloimmunization, iron overload, and, more rarely, infectious complications (see Secondary Iron Overload in Hematology). Antibody formation can lead to hyperhemolysis, a presumed immune response leading to hemolysis of nearly all transfused blood in addition to native blood.

Simple transfusions with PRBCs are used to increase oxygen delivery but should not be used for uncomplicated pain crises or to treat chronic asymptomatic anemia. Indications for transfusion include the following:

  • Patients with severe/symptomatic anemia, particularly if hypoxemia or other evidence of end-organ damage is present
  • For patients undergoing surgical procedures requiring general anesthesia, PRBC transfusion targeting a hemoglobin level of 10 g/dL (100 g/L) to minimize risk of surgical complications
  • Monthly transfusions to reduce stroke risk in those at risk based on cranial Doppler arterial velocity and to reduce risk of recurrent stroke after a stroke has occurred
  • Exchange transfusion often used in the treatment of acute stroke, complicated acute chest syndrome, and acute retinal artery occlusion; simple transfusions an option when exchange transfusion unavailable

With any transfusion, care should be taken to keep hemoglobin concentrations at 10 g/dL (100 g/L) or less to avoid problems with blood hyperviscosity.

More than 1000 variants have been identified in the α- or β-globin gene, including hemoglobin C, hemoglobin D, and hemoglobin E. Most of these are only clinically relevant if coinherited with hemoglobin S.

Immune-mediated hemolysis is characterized by antibody binding to erythrocytes causing complement and phagocyte-mediated destruction. The broad classifications for autoimmune hemolytic anemia are related to the optimal temperature at which the antibodies bind to erythrocytes. Warm antibodies, typically IgG, bind at body temperature (37.0 °C [98.6 °F]) and comprise most autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Cold autoantibodies, also termed cold agglutinins (usually IgM), optimally bind at temperatures less than 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), but they can be active at body temperature as well.

Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA) and cold agglutinin disease can be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to underlying conditions. Prominent secondary causes include infections, rheumatologic processes, or malignancies, especially lymphoproliferative disorders. The laboratory hallmark of immune-mediated hemolysis is a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test result that detects IgG, complement (C3), or both on the erythrocyte surface (see

). Characteristics of immune-mediated hemolysis are shown in [Table: Table: WAIHA and Cold Agglutinin Disease Characteristics]

.

Drugs may cause immune-mediated hemolysis through different mechanisms, including inducing autoantibody formation through a hapten or drug bound to the erythrocyte membrane. Penicillin and cephalosporins are known to cause hapten-mediated hemolytic anemia. Many cases of drug-mediated autoimmune hemolysis are mild and resolve within days to several weeks after removing the offending agent.

In WAIHA, pathogenic IgG antibodies recognize Rh-type antigens on the erythrocyte surface. These antibodies may or may not fix complement. IgG-coated erythrocytes can be completely phagocytized by macrophages, mainly in the spleen through the Fc receptor, and cleared from the circulation. Partial phagocytosis of the erythrocyte surface area results in spherocytes seen on PBS.

Treatment involves addressing symptomatic anemia and decreasing antibody production to alleviate erythrocyte destruction. Patients who are asymptomatic and without significant cardiovascular effects from anemia do not require transfusion. However, transfusion may be required for those with severe anemia, symptoms, or significant comorbidities. The autoantibody obscures detection of alloantibodies, complicating identification of serocompatible donors (see Transfusion in Special Circumstances in Hematology). Additionally, the transfused blood will also be subject to hemolysis, shortening the duration of benefit. Glucocorticoids are first-line treatment, with an estimated two thirds of adults responding to treatment. Rituximab is also effective. Nearly 70% of patients respond to splenectomy, which is reserved for those who do not respond to, or do not tolerate, glucocorticoids or other immunosuppressive therapies.

In cold agglutinin disease, pathogenic IgM antibodies are directed against erythrocyte glycoprotein antigens (I or i antigen). The development of clinically significant manifestations depends on the maximum temperature at which the antibody binds (thermal amplitude) and the ability of the IgM to fix and activate complement that mediates hemolysis. A cold agglutinin that only binds at 0 °C (32 °F) would not be clinically significant, whereas one that binds at or close to body temperature may have greater consequences. If complement fixation occurs, C3-coated cells are cleared by hepatic Kupffer cells and destroyed in circulation. The autoantibody can span erythrocytes and cause agglutination, leading to an elevated MCV on laboratory testing (

). Rarely, in severe cases, marked agglutination in vivo results in vascular occlusion and organ ischemia.

Treatment is primarily directed at avoidance of cold exposure, including warming of all infusates. Glucocorticoids and splenectomy are seldom effective. Rituximab, combined with fludarabine or bendamustine, has demonstrated efficacy in case series. The anticomplement (anti-C1) drug sutimlimab has also been approved for treatment of hemolysis resulting from cold agglutinin disease.

Hemolysis can arise from mechanical shearing and destruction of erythrocytes as they circulate in the vasculature. This process is often referred to as microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, although not all causes ( [Table: Table: Fragmentation Hemolytic Anemia Differential Diagnoses]

) are related to issues in the microcirculation. Fragmented erythrocytes (schistocytes) are noted on PBS (

). The mechanism by which erythrocytes become sheared, leading to hemolysis, varies. Several causes are also associated with thrombocytopenia. Treatment is directed toward addressing the underlying cause.

Infections can directly cause lysis of erythrocytes through production of toxins, premature removal of erythrocytes by macrophages after parasitic invasion, or direct rupture of the infected erythrocytes.

Clostridium perfringens produces phospholipase C, which damages the erythrocyte lipid bilayer. Sepsis from clostridial infection can cause a brisk, life-threatening intravascular hemolysis that is severe enough to interfere with laboratory assays, including biochemical analyses and cross-matching, and can lead to severe kidney injury. Streptococcal and staphylococcal sepsis have also been associated with hemolysis.

Hemolysis results from parasitic infestation of erythrocytes from malaria (see Malaria in Infectious Disease), babesiosis (see Babesiosis in Infectious Disease), and bartonellosis. Plasmodium falciparum is associated with the most severe hemolysis of the malarial infections and has been called blackwater fever because of the associated hemoglobinuria. The parasite can be seen on thick Wright-Giemsa–stained blood smears. Babesiosis is transmitted by the Ixodes tick, and patients without a spleen are more likely to have symptomatic disease, which can include fever, fatigue, and evidence of intravascular hemolysis. A thin blood smear shows parasites in the erythrocytes in a characteristic Maltese cross pattern. Bartonellosis, common in South America, causes rapid and severe hemolytic anemia and, if left untreated, can be fatal. In each of these parasitic infections, effective treatments produce resolution of the hemolysis with eradication of the infection.
