Iron Overload Syndromes

Iron accumulation in tissues can cause tissue damage. Iron overload can arise from hereditary causes (hemochromatosis) or secondarily, most commonly from chronic transfusion therapy.

Hereditary hemochromatosis (HH) is an autosomal recessive disorder, with a prevalence of 1 in 300 in persons of northern European descent. Increased iron absorption results from reduced hepcidin and increased ferroportin expression on duodenal enterocytes. Most patients have an alteration in the HFE gene, with the most common HFE alterations being C282Y and H63D. Approximately 90% of patients with clinical disease have homozygosity for C282Y, and 5% have compound heterozygosity for C282Y and H63D alterations. The phenotypic penetrance is relatively low, and most patients with these alterations do not develop clinical disease. The prevalence of clinically significant disease is higher in men and in those with homozygosity for C282Y compared with other genetic combinations. Patients who are heterozygous for a single alteration do not develop clinical disease.

Patients are often identified at asymptomatic stages through laboratory evaluation of iron studies. A transferrin saturation greater than 45% with an elevated serum ferritin level raises suspicion for HH (

). Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, however, and increased levels can be seen in acute or chronic inflammatory conditions, alcoholic liver disease, infections, and malignancies.

Important manifestations of disease in untreated patients with HH include cirrhosis and cardiomyopathy. Once established, liver and cardiac damage is largely irreversible, although a subset of patients may experience regression in hepatic fibrosis with treatment. Other manifestations include small joint arthritis (especially the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints) and endocrinopathies. Endocrine manifestations include diabetes mellitus and pituitary injury with resultant hypogonadism and hypothyroidism. Iron deposition and excess melanin production can cause skin hyperpigmentation resulting in “bronze diabetes” in persons with concomitant diabetes. Patients with iron overload are also at risk for certain bacterial infections such as Vibrio vulnificus and Yersinia enterocolitica.

Diagnosis is confirmed by molecular genotyping along with elevated iron indices; secondary causes of elevated serum ferritin levels must also be ruled out. Specialized MRI (MRI T2) can quantify the degree of iron overload in the liver and heart and often eliminates the need for organ biopsy. Liver biopsy may still be necessary in some patients to stage the degree of liver disease. Screening for HH with at least iron saturation and serum ferritin levels is recommended for adult first-degree relatives of affected patients; HFE* analysis in these patients is also recommended by some guidelines.

Phlebotomy is the mainstay of treatment for removing excess iron in HH. One unit of blood (500 mL) contains 200 to 250 mg of iron. Indications for treatment initiation, frequency, and target serum ferritin level vary among guidelines. The American College of Gastroenterology recommends treatment in patients homozygous for C282Y with a transferrin saturation of 45% or greater and a serum ferritin level greater than 300 ng/mL (300 μg/L) in men and greater than 200 ng/mL (200 μg/L) in women.

Phlebotomy frequency depends on the serum ferritin level, degree of organ involvement, and hematocrit level. Symptomatic patients with evidence of organ injury and those with a more significantly elevated serum ferritin level (>1000 ng/mL [1000 μg/L]) should undergo aggressive therapeutic phlebotomy. Treatment initially occurs as often as once or twice weekly and is tapered thereafter.

Repeated phlebotomy ultimately removes parenchymal iron deposition. Many guidelines suggest maintaining a serum ferritin level of 50 to 100 ng/mL (50-100 μg/L), although data supporting an optimal target level are lacking. When this goal is reached, maintenance phlebotomy two to six times annually is often needed. Serum ferritin levels should be monitored every 3 to 6 months, and treatment should be modified to avoid iron deficiency. In addition to phlebotomy, alcohol avoidance is recommended. Patients without hepatic fibrosis or cardiomyopathy have normal life expectancy with regular monitoring. Periodic screening for hepatocellular carcinoma is recommended for those with advanced fibrosis on liver biopsy.

Secondary iron overload can occur because of chronic transfusions, increased absorption, or both, as in patients with hemoglobinopathies (thalassemias, sickle cell disease), bone marrow failure, and hematologic malignancies (e.g., myelodysplastic syndrome). End-organ involvement in these patients can be similar to that seen with HH, particularly hepatic iron deposition.

Therapeutic phlebotomy is contraindicated because of the presence of concomitant anemia in these patients. Iron chelation therapy is the mainstay of treatment; iron chelators include parenteral deferoxamine or oral alternatives, deferasirox and deferiprone. Chelation is often initiated when the serum ferritin level exceeds 1000 ng/mL (1000 μg/L), after approximately 10 to 12 units of blood have been transfused, or with evidence of cardiac or hepatic deposition on MRI. The nephrotoxicity of available chelating agents and the need for dosing adjustments make iron chelation difficult in patients with advanced kidney disease.

Secondary iron overload is uncommonly caused by porphyria cutanea tarda, which is associated with acquired abnormalities in porphyrin metabolism and underlying liver disease, especially hepatitis C virus infection. Cutaneous blisters (often on the hands) and hypertrichosis are characteristic. Patients respond well to phlebotomy (see Porphyria Cutanea Tarda in Dermatology).

Platelet Disorders

Platelets are megakaryocyte fragments that circulate in an inactive state for 8 to 10 days before being cleared. Approximately 30% of platelets are sequestered in the spleen and are released in response to stress. The hemostatic action of platelets is a three-stage process:

  • Platelet adherence at sites where the vascular endothelium is disrupted, a process mediated by von Willebrand factor (vWF).
  • Resultant platelet activation with concomitant shape change, resulting in the release of thromboxane A~2 and adenosine diphosphate (ADP). These activating mediators in turn stimulate other platelets to secrete further thromboxane A~2 and ADP and also promote binding of circulating fibrinogen to the activated platelets through the surface glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (GPIIb/IIIa).
  • Platelet aggregation, with fibrinogen bridging to GPIIb/IIIa on the surfaces of nearby platelets, creating large platelet aggregates.

These steps are targeted by antiplatelet medications. Aspirin irreversibly acetylates and inactivates cyclooxygenase-1, blocking thromboxane A~2 synthesis, whereas clopidogrel irreversibly binds to the P2Y~12 ADP receptor, blocking platelet activation and aggregation. Intravenous agents such as abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban inhibit fibrinogen binding to GPIIb/IIIa.

Platelets also provide the phospholipid membrane for activation of the coagulation cascade (see

).

Symptoms of thrombocytopenia include easy bruising and mucocutaneous bleeding, such as epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, hematuria, melena, or hematochezia. When thrombocytopenia is significant, the physical examination may reveal blood blisters in the mouth (wet purpura), petechiae, or ecchymoses. Splenomegaly or other findings that indicate the cause of thrombocytopenia may be present.

Evaluation of thrombocytopenia includes a thorough review of medication, dietary supplement, drug, and alcohol use. The presence of family history, viral infection, recent vaccination, liver disease, malignancies, pregnancy, sepsis, and autoimmune disease should also be queried.

Evaluation also requires a review of the peripheral blood smear to confirm the platelet count. Pseudothrombocytopenia due to platelet clumping in vitro occurs in patients with naturally occurring antibodies to ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), the anticoagulant used in some blood collection tubes (

). In this case, an accurate count can be obtained from blood drawn in tubes containing citrate or heparin. Inaccurate machine counts may also occur if the platelets are exceptionally large and are mistaken for erythrocytes with a resultant falsely low count, or if erythrocyte fragments (schistocytes) are counted as platelets, resulting in falsely elevated counts.

The normal platelet count is greater than 150,000/μL (150 × 10^9/L), but counts greater than 100,000/μL (100 × 10^9/L) present very low risk for bleeding. Counts greater than 50,000/μL (50 × 10^9/L) do not require treatment and are adequate for many surgical procedures, although 100,000/μL (100 × 10^9/L) is desirable for neurosurgery. Counts less than 50,000/μL (50 × 10^9/L) should be corrected before surgeries with significant bleeding risk. Counts less than 10,000/μL (10 × 10^9/L) are associated with risk of spontaneous bleeding. Concomitant use of drugs that impair platelet function or hemostasis further increases bleeding risk from thrombocytopenia.

Thrombocytopenia may result from decreased platelet production, abnormal platelet distribution, increased platelet destruction, or a combination of these mechanisms.

Disorders associated with bone marrow infiltration (myelofibrosis, metastatic tumors, granulomatous diseases) can decrease platelet production, as can nutritional deficiencies (vitamin B~12 or folate) or abnormalities in stem cells (aplastic anemia and myelodysplasia). In these cases, cytopenias in other cell lines often accompany the low platelet count. Low platelet production can also be seen after exposure to some drugs ( [Table: Table: Medications Associated With Non-Immune Thrombocytopenia]

) and in immune thrombocytopenia.

Liver disease with low thrombopoietin production can also cause isolated thrombocytopenia.

Splenomegaly, most commonly secondary to liver disease with portal hypertension, is a common cause of thrombocytopenia through increased sequestration without platelet destruction. The thrombocytopenia is usually associated with anemia and leukopenia.

In patients who have received large volumes of blood products, a dilutional thrombocytopenia may occur.

Gestational thrombocytopenia, a mild thrombocytopenia, is usually seen late in pregnancy and is thought to be due to increased plasma volume or pooling of platelets in the placenta (see Gestational Thrombocytopenia in Hematology).

Increased platelet destruction may be immune mediated (e.g., immune thrombocytopenic purpura, Type II heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) or secondary to non-immune causes such as abnormal platelet aggregation occurring in the setting of disseminated intravascular coagulation (see Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation in Hematology) or microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) (see Fragmentation Hemolysis in Hematology).

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is caused by autoantibodies to platelet surface antigens. It can be a primary diagnosis or occur secondary lymphoproliferative disorders (e.g., chronic lymphocytic leukemia), systemic lupus erythematosus, or infections such as HIV, hepatitis C virus, and Helicobacter pylori. Drugs can also induce immune platelet destruction. The combination of warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia and ITP is known as Evans syndrome.

Acute, persistent, and chronic ITP are defined as lasting less than 3 months, 3 to 12 months, and more than 12 months, respectively. Many patients are asymptomatic until the platelet count decreases to less than 10,000/μL (10 × 10^9/L). Fatigue and reduced health-related quality of life are common nonhematologic clinical manifestations of ITP. Petechiae and ecchymoses without splenomegaly are notable physical signs.

Diagnosis requires thrombocytopenia, which is usually isolated, with a platelet count of less than 100,000/μL (100 × 10^9/L). Laboratory findings are limited to the low platelet count unless a secondary cause is present. Testing for HIV and hepatitis C virus should be performed because patients may be otherwise asymptomatic. Bone marrow evaluation is not necessary unless clinical findings suggest an alternate diagnosis. Platelet autoantibody testing is not recommended because the test is neither sensitive nor specific enough to play a major role in establishing the diagnosis, and results do not correlate with clinical outcomes. Diagnosis is established by the combination of severe thrombocytopenia, a normal hemoglobin level and leukocyte count, and no alternative explanation for the low platelet count.

Patients with a platelet count greater than 30,000/μL (30 × 10^9/L) who are asymptomatic or have minor mucocutaneous bleeding can be carefully observed without treatment. In patients with a platelet count less than 30,000/μL (30 × 10^9/L) who are either asymptomatic or have minor mucocutaneous bleeding, treatment with a short course (<6 weeks) of prednisone or dexamethasone is recommended. These patients may be managed as outpatients if the platelet count is greater than 20,000/μL (20 × 10^9/L). The glucocorticoids are tapered over the ensuing 6 to 8 weeks while monitoring the platelet count. Complications from glucocorticoids include mood disorders, fluid retention, hyperglycemia, hypertension, and osteoporosis. If the underlying cause of ITP is HIV, the use of immunosuppressive treatments such as glucocorticoids should be done in consultation with an infectious disease specialist.

In patients with more severe thrombocytopenia and life-threatening bleeding, intravenous immune globulin may be used in addition to glucocorticoids because the response to immune globulin is rapid, albeit transient. Complications from intravenous immune globulin include infusion reactions (headache, chills, anaphylaxis in patients with IgA deficiency), kidney dysfunction, and thrombosis.

Patients who relapse with tapering of glucocorticoids or have ITP refractory to these treatments require second-line treatments, such as rituximab, thrombopoietin receptor agonists, and splenectomy. Thrombopoietin receptor agonists (e.g., daily oral eltrombopag or avatrombopag; weekly subcutaneous romiplostim) must be taken continuously to prevent relapse. Splenectomy is associated with long-term susceptibility to infection with encapsulated bacteria and is generally reserved for patients in whom medical management is unsatisfactory. Fostamatinib, an oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor, is also approved for treatment of ITP and is often used when avoiding surgery or immune suppression is desired. Bone marrow biopsy may again be considered in patients who do not respond to usual first line therapy to reassess the possibility of myelodysplastic syndrome or other bone marrow disorders as the cause of thrombocytopenia.

Because patients with chronic ITP may be asymptomatic, all treatment decisions must balance the risk of bleeding against treatment-related toxicities.

Type I heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) refers to a non−immune-mediated decrease in platelets occurring within the first few days of exposure to heparin. No further testing or intervention is needed, as the platelet count recovers promptly without thromboembolic complications.

Type II HIT is an immune-mediated thrombocytopenia occurring 5 to 10 days after exposure to heparin, or more rapidly if there has been heparin exposure in the previous 90 days. It is caused by antibodies against platelet factor 4 complexed to heparin that activate platelets and cause mild thrombocytopenia and potentially life-threatening thrombosis in the venous and arterial systems. The risk of developing HIT is higher with the use of unfractionated heparins than with low-molecular-weight heparin. Patients undergoing surgery are also more likely to develop HIT than medical patients.

Most patients with HIT develop platelet counts less than 150,000/μL (150 × 10^9/L), but severe thrombocytopenia is unusual. In patients with high baseline platelet counts, a decrease of greater than 50% is consistent with HIT. Skin necrosis at the site of heparin injection or progressive thromboembolic events in patients receiving heparin are additional signs of possible HIT, even if the platelet count remains normal.

In patients with possible HIT, the 4T scoring system ( [Table: Table: The 4T Scoring System]

) is useful for estimating the likelihood of disease and the need for discontinuing heparin while test results are pending. Patients with a high or moderate probability of HIT require immediate heparin discontinuation with initiation of an alternate anticoagulant (unless the patient is actively bleeding) (

). Argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, or possibly direct oral anticoagulants (such as rivaroxaban) are options. Warfarin should not be the initial alternate anticoagulant because the onset of antithrombotic effect requires 3 to 5 days of therapy, during which time declining levels of protein C increase the thrombotic risk.

The enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for platelet factor 4 antibodies is a sensitive screening test for HIT, and a negative test result rules out the diagnosis in most patients. The test, however, is not specific; positive ELISA results are usually reported as optical density, and controversy exists regarding the optical density level at which a test should be considered positive. A positive ELISA requires confirmation, and most laboratories send confirmatory testing for all patients who test positive on the ELISA assay with either the serotonin release assay or the heparin-induced platelet aggregation assay; these tests may require several days.

In patients with confirmed HIT, anticoagulation with a nonheparin anticoagulant agent should be continued for at least 4 weeks in individuals without documented thromboembolic events and for at least 3 months in those with associated thrombosis. Transitioning to warfarin is safe after thrombocytopenia resolves. Patients should generally avoid future heparin exposure, although short-term use for high thrombotic risk procedures, such as during cardiovascular surgery, may be tolerated if the ELISA is negative and HIT antibodies are no longer detectable.

Acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is caused by an antibody directed against ADAMTS13, the metalloprotease responsible for cleaving high-molecular-weight vWF multimers. Platelets adhere to these uncleaved multimers, generating platelet-rich thrombi in small vessels. These thrombi may cause end-organ injury and additionally shear erythrocytes, producing schistocytes (

). Autoantibodies to ADAMTS13 are responsible for TTP in most patients, but hereditary deficiency of ADAMTS13 causing TTP has also been observed. Drugs such as ticlopidine, quinine, cyclosporine, gemcitabine, and vascular endothelial growth factor inhibitors (such as bevacizumab) can cause drug-induced thrombotic microangiopathy, although in these cases ADAMTS13 deficiency is not present.

The clinical manifestations of TTP are described in [Table: Table: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura Characteristics]

. All patients have MAHA (evidenced by elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase level, decreased serum haptoglobin level, schistocytes on peripheral blood smear, an elevated reticulocyte count, and a negative direct antiglobulin [Coombs] test result) and thrombocytopenia with normal coagulation tests. Only 5% of patients present with the classic pentad of MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neurologic changes, kidney injury, and fever.

An ADAMTS13 level less than 10% supports the diagnosis; an ADAMTS13 level greater than 50% suggests an alternate diagnosis, and consideration should be given to other causes of fragmentation hemolysis (see Fragmentation Hemolysis in Hematology). The PLASMIC score is useful in guiding diagnosis while awaiting ADAMTS13 level results ( [Table: Table: PLASMIC Score]

). The mortality rate is high, and treatment should be initiated in most patients with suspected TTP until the ADAMTS13 testing is complete.

Initial treatment involves therapeutic plasma exchange (PLEX) to remove the high-molecular-weight vWF multimers and replace the deficient ADAMTS13. Plasma infusion, although not a definitive treatment, can be started if PLEX is delayed. Glucocorticoids are added to decrease autoantibody production. Rituximab (a monoclonal anti-CD20 B-cell antibody) is added to further suppress autoantibody production and to decrease the risk of recurrence. Caplacizumab (a monoclonal antibody against vWF) can be used to treat patients with severe hemolysis, severe thrombocytopenia, or significant end-organ injury. Caplacizumab is started on the first day of PLEX and continued until 30 days after the final treatment.

Remission is defined by platelet count normalization and is usually seen after 7 to 10 PLEX treatments. Overall, treatment of TTP is successful in 85% of patients.

Shiga toxin–mediated hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) presents after an acute diarrheal illness caused by enterotoxin-producing Escherichia coli O157:H7 (other strains have also been implicated). Although HUS is seen in adults, it more often affects children. It is characterized by thrombocytopenia and MAHA but is distinguished from TTP by more severe acute kidney injury and a lack of ADAMTS13 deficiency. It should also be differentiated from other causes of fragmentation hemolysis (see Fragmentation Hemolysis in Hematology). Diagnosis is confirmed by stool culture demonstrating Escherichia coli O157:H7 or stool polymerase chain reaction for Shiga toxin. Management is supportive with fluids and transfusions as needed. Antibiotics do not alter the disease course. Patients with Shiga toxin–mediated HUS have a 4% associated mortality rate, and long-term sequelae include hypertension and chronic kidney disease.

Atypical HUS, now called complement-mediated HUS, also presents with thrombocytopenia, MAHA, and kidney involvement but without diarrhea. It is caused by inherited complement dysregulation or acquired antibodies against complement proteins. Treatment with eculizumab, a monoclonal antibody that binds to complement C5 and prevents generation of the membrane attack unit, C5b-9, is warranted.

Thrombotic microangiopathies with kidney dysfunction may also occur secondary to drugs (see drugs listed in the TTP section previously), systemic lupus erythematosus, pregnancy, severe hypertension, or other infection (HIV, Streptococcus pneumoniae). In these cases, treatment is focused on the underlying disorder.

In severe disease or when the distinction from TTP is unclear, treatment with plasma exchange should begin immediately.

Patients presenting with mucocutaneous bleeding and normal platelet count, prothrombin time, and activated partial thromboplastin time should be evaluated for platelet dysfunction, which can result from hereditary or acquired disorders. Medications and underlying disorders, such as uremia, recent cardiopulmonary bypass, liver disease, myeloproliferative neoplasms, and dysproteinemia, frequently lead to abnormal platelet function. The characteristics and management of hereditary and acquired platelet dysfunction are outlined in [Table: Table: Causes of Platelet Dysfunction]

.

Many drugs, most commonly aspirin, P2Y~12 receptor antagonists, and NSAIDs, impair platelet function. Management of drug-induced platelet dysfunction depends on the clinical situation. Platelet transfusion may be considered; however, no evidence supports this practice. The decision to discontinue antiplatelet agents must balance the risks of thrombosis against the severity of the bleeding. For example, aspirin for primary prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease can be safely discontinued in a patient who is bleeding; however, dual antiplatelet therapy in patients with recently placed cardiac stents may be crucial to prevent potentially catastrophic acute stent thrombosis. In such cases, determining the appropriate management requires discussion with cardiologists before discontinuing the medications. In some cases, aspirin can be continued while the P2Y~12 receptor antagonist is withheld until adequate hemostasis is achieved.

Von Willebrand disease, a common inherited coagulation factor disorder, can impair platelet function (specifically platelet adhesion) and lead to mucocutaneous bleeding in the absence of an additional intrinsic platelet abnormality (see Von Willebrand Disease in Hematology).

Platelet function can be assessed by a variety of laboratory tests. A platelet function analyzer can be used as an initial screening test, replacing the traditional bleeding time. The test is run on a citrated blood sample exposed to collagen and either epinephrine or ADP. It is a sensitive test for von Willebrand disease and will detect abnormalities caused by antiplatelet medications. A modified platelet aggregometry device using a platelet activator can measure the amount of GPIIb/IIa receptor blockade by aspirin or P2Y~12 inhibitors. Classic platelet aggregometry tests platelet reactions to various agonists and captures the primary and secondary aggregation waves. It is labor intensive and requires technical expertise, so it is not available in all hospitals. Thromboelastography and rotational thromboelastometry are bedside devices that analyze platelet function, coagulation, and clot stability; these may be useful as screening tests in patients with unexplained bleeding.

Thrombocytosis refers to a platelet count exceeding 450,000/µL (450 × 10^9/L). Primary causes of thrombocytosis are uncommon and include myeloproliferative neoplasms (see Myeloproliferative Neoplasms in Hematology) and some myelodysplastic syndromes (see Myelodysplastic Syndromes in Hematology). Secondary or reactive causes of thrombocytosis are more common and include iron deficiency, blood loss, hemolysis, medications, recent splenectomy, and inflammatory processes, especially infection and malignancy.

Evaluation begins with a careful history and physical examination directed toward possible causes, especially underlying inflammatory diseases and hematologic malignancies. Initial laboratory evaluation should include iron studies and inflammatory markers. Clonal disorders are often suggested by involvement of other cell lines, and testing for JAK2, MPL, and CALR alterations may be appropriate.

Treatment focuses on addressing the underlying cause. Thrombosis rarely occurs with reactive thrombocytosis, even at very high platelet counts. Elevated platelet counts associated with hematologic malignancies, however, are associated with thrombotic and hemorrhagic events. Specific treatment of the disorder or use of drugs like hydroxyurea to lower the platelet count may be necessary in these cases, and treatment with antiplatelet agents may be needed after the platelet count is controlled.

Bleeding Disorders

Bleeding is controlled through a complex but balanced network of prothrombotic and fibrinolytic activity called hemostasis. Hemostasis begins with contraction of the transected vessel and the formation of a primary platelet plug. This process is initiated by platelet activation and adhesion to the denuded endothelium (mediated by collagen, thrombin, and von Willebrand factor [vWF]), followed by platelet aggregation (see Normal Platelet Physiology in Hematology for platelet activation and vWF activity). The platelet plug provides activated phospholipid membranes to facilitate clot propagation (secondary hemostasis phase) by activating coagulation factors leading to thrombin formation, conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin, and fibrin mesh formation. The fibrinolysis system is simultaneously activated, resulting in dynamic clot remodeling (

). Although it is now understood that the tissue factor–factor VII pathway is the primary initiator of thrombin generation, the traditional waterfall coagulation cascade (

) is still useful to understand coagulation tests and the factors that influence them.

The patient’s bleeding history is the most predictive factor in those with a potential bleeding disorder and provides valuable information to guide management for patients with active bleeding or those undergoing an invasive procedure. Laboratory testing alone is insufficient to predict bleeding risk (e.g., patients may have an elevated activated partial thromboplastin time [aPTT] secondary to a lupus anticoagulant but no increased risk of bleeding). Patients with bleeding disorders may have easy bruising, joint or soft-tissue bleeding, mucocutaneous bleeding (including epistaxis, bleeding following dental extractions, menstrual and postpartum bleeding, and gastrointestinal bleeding), or postoperative bleeding. Family bleeding history and medication use (including over-the-counter medications and supplements) must also be documented. The physical examination focuses on finding evidence of petechiae, ecchymoses, deep tissue hematomas, or joint effusions.

Laboratory tests used routinely to assess hemostasis include the complete blood count, prothrombin time (PT), customarily expressed as the INR, and aPTT. The PT is more sensitive to the effects of the vitamin K–dependent factors (II, VII, and X), whereas the aPTT is a more sensitive measurement of factors VIII, IX, XI, and XII. Specialized tests include the thrombin time (measures fibrinogen conversion to fibrin), platelet aggregation tests, specific factor level assays, tests for fibrin degradation products and D-dimers, and mixing studies.

Mixing studies are used to differentiate between factor deficiencies and inhibitors when the PT, aPTT, or thrombin time is abnormal. These studies combine equal parts of patient plasma with control plasma. The clotting test is measured immediately following the mix and again after an incubation period. Mixing studies correct when factor deficiencies are present, but the immediate mixing study will not correct in the presence of most factor inhibitors (e.g., lupus anticoagulant). However, when a factor VIII inhibitor is present, the aPTT will correct immediately following mixing but prolongs again after incubation.

Differential diagnoses for patients experiencing bleeding and abnormal findings on clotting assays are outlined in [Table: Table: Differential Diagnoses for Patients Experiencing Bleeding]

.

Hemophilia A and B (deficiency of factors VIII and IX, respectively) are X-linked hereditary bleeding disorders primarily found in men; however, heterozygous female carriers of factor VIII deficiency can have factor levels in the hemophilia range. Hemophilia A is more common than hemophilia B, but both are rare. They manifest in a similar fashion, with childhood onset of spontaneous hemarthrosis or bleeding into deep muscles or with excessive or delayed bleeding after trauma. Recurrent hemarthrosis causes arthropathy of the knees, ankles, and elbows in 50% of patients. Hemophilia is classified as mild, moderate, or severe according to the circulating factor levels (mild, 5%-40%; moderate, 1%-5%; severe, <1%). Patients with mild disease may not have symptoms until adulthood.

Diagnosis of moderate or severe hemophilia requires a prolonged aPTT that corrects in mixing studies, a normal PT, and a normal complete blood count. Patients with mild hemophilia may have normal aPTT measurement depending on the sensitivity of the assay used. Assay of individual factors (VIII and IX) confirms the diagnosis. In hemophilia A, vWF must be measured to rule out type 3 von Willebrand disease (see von Willebrand Disease in Hematology).

Management of bleeding in hemophilia A and B varies based on severity. Patients with mild hemophilia A and minor bleeding can be treated with desmopressin, which stimulates the release of preformed factor VIII from endothelial cells. A desmopressin challenge test should be done before minor procedures in these patients to document response.

Patients with moderate or severe hemophilia often require virally inactivated factor concentrates or recombinant factor replacement. Antifibrinolytic agents (such as ε-aminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid) are useful in controlling bleeding from dental procedures.

Factor inhibitors are neutralizing antibodies to infused factors that can develop in up to 25% of patients with hemophilia A and 3% to 5% of patients with hemophilia B who undergo recombinant factor replacement therapy. An inhibitor should be suspected when a patient with hemophilia receiving adequate factor replacement experiences a marked increase in bleeding frequency and severity. Patients with hemophilia A or B with inhibitors may require treatment with activated factor VII, which bypasses the inhibitor by activating factor X, which is located downstream from factors VIII and IX in the coagulation cascade.

In the perioperative setting, patients with moderate or severe hemophilia A will require factor VIII or, if an inhibitor is present, activated factor VII.

Some patients with hemophilia A are now receiving prophylaxis with emicizumab, a bispecific monoclonal antibody designed to bind factors IXa and X together to replicate the action of the deficient factor VIII. Emicizumab is not useful in acute bleeding, and patients still require factor VIII for acute bleeding or in preparation for surgery. The aPTT and standard factor-based testing are inaccurate in these patients and cannot be used for monitoring.

Other options for patients with hemophilia A or B requiring prophylaxis are concizumab and marstacimab. These monoclonal antibodies reduce the activity of tissue factor pathway inhibitor, augmenting the hemostatic contribution of the extrinsic pathway. More recently, the drug fitusiran was approved by the FDA. Fitusiran is an antisense oligonucleotide directed against antithrombin that reduces the activity of antithrombin. All these drugs work by increasing thrombin generation.

Factor XI deficiency (also known as hemophilia C) is a rare autosomal hereditary disorder seen predominantly in persons of Ashkenazi Jewish descent. Patients typically do not experience spontaneous bleeding but tend to have postsurgical bleeding, particularly from sites with high endogenous fibrinolytic activity (dental, nasal, oropharyngeal, genitourinary), or menorrhagia and postpartum hemorrhage. Treatment can be difficult because there is no correlation between factor levels and bleeding. Serious bleeding should be treated with factor replacement; planning for surgeries requires a detailed conversation with the patient about the risk and benefit of factor administration.

von Willebrand disease (vWD), the most common hereditary bleeding disorder, is caused by vWF deficiency or dysfunction. In hemostasis, vWF promotes platelet adhesion and functions as a protective carrier protein for factor VIII. Mucocutaneous bleeding symptoms that mimic thrombocytopenia are common manifestations of vWD.

Hereditary vWD is subclassified into three broad groups ( [Table: Table: Types of von Willebrand Disease]

); type 1 is the most common. It manifests as a quantitative decrease in vWF levels and patients become symptomatic when levels fall below 30%. Clinical factors also influence vWF levels, including type O blood (decreased levels) and pregnancy or oral contraceptive use (increased levels). The aPTT may be prolonged or normal. Although the 2021 American Society of Hematology guidelines suggest diagnostic testing with platelet-dependent vWF glycoprotein Ib tests (vWF:GPIbR and vWF:GPIbM), the ristocetin assay remains widely used and available ( [Table: Table: Tests Used for Diagnosis of von Willebrand Disease]

).

Management depends on the bleeding severity, the vWD subtype, and the clinical setting. Desmopressin acts by releasing preformed vWF and factor VIII from endothelial cells and is most effective in patients with type 1 vWD. It can be given intravenously before a surgical procedure or intranasally as needed in the outpatient setting. Patients with rare type 2B vWD should not receive desmopressin because it induces platelet aggregation, which may cause secondary thrombocytopenia. Desmopressin is also ineffective in patients with type 3 vWD. vWF concentrates are the preferred treatment for patients with these two subgroups.

Antifibrinolytic therapy (ε-aminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid) is useful after surgical procedures to protect against delayed bleeding and can be used to treat menorrhagia.

Liver disease results in reduced procoagulant and anticoagulant factors and in mild to moderate thrombocytopenia. The procoagulant factor reduction can result in PT and aPTT prolongation; however, these results do not correlate with bleeding risk because they do not reflect the parallel reduction in anticoagulant factors. Bleeding can occur because of portal hypertension, thrombocytopenia, or intercurrent problems that disturb the balance between procoagulant and anticoagulant factors. Thrombosis, including portal vein thrombosis and venous thromboembolic disease, may also occur.

Distinguishing between liver disease and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) may be challenging because patients sometimes have components of both disorders. The clinical management of the two is often analogous, but measuring the factor VIII level along with a liver-derived factor such as factor IX may be useful because factor VIII is often elevated in liver disease but consumed in DIC.

Asymptomatic patients do not require treatment, but vitamin K supplementation should be considered if concomitant deficiency is suspected. Patients experiencing bleeding may require blood product replacement, with cryoprecipitate to increase plasma fibrinogen levels to greater than 100 mg/dL (1 g/L) and platelet transfusions to maintain a platelet count greater than 50,000/μL (50 × 10^9/L). Fresh frozen plasma is sometimes given to correct INRs greater than 2 in bleeding patients, but the short half-life of plasma components and risk of volume overload limit the effectiveness of plasma administration; its use in this situation is not routinely recommended. Additionally, data suggest that it is associated with an increased risk for rebleeding and mortality in patients with acute variceal bleeding. Prothrombin complex concentrates are costly and associated with thrombotic complications; they should not be routinely used in managing the coagulopathy of liver disease.

Correction of modest thrombocytopenia (platelet count >75,000/μL [75 × 10^9/L]) or coagulopathy (INR <2) is unnecessary in patients with liver disease who are undergoing paracentesis, thoracentesis, or routine upper endoscopy.

DIC results from the simultaneous activation of coagulation and fibrinolysis. It is associated with the following:

  • Severe sepsis, usually with septic shock
  • Disseminated malignancy, most classically with mucin-secreting pancreatic adenocarcinoma
  • Pregnancy complications
  • Trauma

The initial pathogenesis involves widespread endothelial injury and circulating procoagulants that lead to disseminated microvascular thrombi, consumption of platelets and clotting factors, and erythrocyte shearing injury leading to hemolysis. Fibrinolysis is accelerated, resulting in dissolution of the microvascular thrombus, usually before thrombotic complications are noted.

Classic laboratory findings include thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT and aPTT, low plasma fibrinogen, and elevated D-dimer levels. Management is directed primarily at the underlying cause and supported with platelet transfusions, cryoprecipitate, and fresh frozen plasma as needed.

Vitamin K is a cofactor for carboxylation and activation of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as for the endogenous anticoagulants, protein C, and protein S. Deficiency may occur through multiple mechanisms. Although vitamin K is found in green vegetables, a significant proportion of the daily requirement comes from gut microflora, which may be destroyed by antibiotics. Absorption of vitamin K, which is fat soluble, requires biliary and pancreatic function. Accordingly, patients with inadequate oral intake while taking long courses of antibiotics and those who have fat malabsorption are especially at risk for vitamin K deficiency.

Vitamin K supplements safely and effectively correct the deficiency, and the response to supplementation occurs within hours. Vitamin K can be administered orally for patients who are able to eat and absorb vitamin K. Critically ill patients or those unable to take anything by mouth should receive vitamin K by slow intravenous infusion. Subcutaneous vitamin K is not reliably absorbed and is unlikely to be safer than intravenous vitamin K.

Acquired vWD occurs in conditions in which high circulatory shear stress (valvular heart disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, circulatory assist devices, and extracorporeal membrane-oxygenation systems) causes deformation of high-molecular-weight von Willebrand multimers and subsequent degradation by the proteolytic enzyme ADAMTS13. Acquired vWD can also occur from autoimmune factors (systemic lupus erythematosus), lymphoproliferative disease, and myeloproliferative disease, especially those characterized by marked thrombocytosis. Affected patients develop bleeding conditions similar to those in hereditary vWD. Desmopressin and vWF concentrates may be useful for management. Hydroxyurea can be used to lower platelet counts in myeloproliferative disease.

Acquired hemophilia results from an autoantibody directed against factor VIII. Patients present with severe bleeding from mucosal sites, large hematomas and ecchymoses without antecedent trauma, and sometimes postsurgical bleeding. Unlike inherited hemophilia A, hemarthroses are rare. Cases are associated with pregnancy and the postpartum state, malignancy, and autoimmune disorders as well as with medications, but in many cases a cause is not found.

Laboratory evaluation shows a normal platelet count and PT with a prolonged aPTT. Mixing studies do not correct the aPTT because of the presence of the inhibitor; in some cases, aPTT will correct immediately following mixing but prolongs again after incubation. The level of an inhibitor can be quantified with the Bethesda assay. One Bethesda unit is defined as the amount of inhibitor required to neutralize 50% of factor VIII activity in normal plasma. Factor analysis will additionally show a low factor VIII level.

Factor VIII concentrates typically do not correct the problem because the autoantibody will still block the factor VIII concentrate activity. Acute bleeding management requires plasma derivatives or recombinant coagulation factors that bypass the inhibited factor, such as activated prothrombin complex concentrates (FEIBA) or recombinant activated factor VII. Recombinant porcine factor VIII is not cross-reactive with human factor VIII and can also provide effective hemostasis, but it may be limited in availability. Immunosuppression, using glucocorticoids, usually combined with rituximab or cyclophosphamide, is required to eliminate the autoantibody and prevent continued inhibitor production. Emicizumab is a bispecific monoclonal antibody that mimics the function of activated factor VIII and is FDA approved for use in patients with congenital hemophilia A. It has recently been found to be effective in treating acquired hemophilia before the initiation of immunosuppressive therapy.

Acquired inhibitors can also occur against any of the other coagulation factors and should be considered when a patient presents with a new bleeding diathesis and an unexpectedly low factor level.

Transfusion Medicine

Blood donor screening includes questions regarding the donor’s general health, travel history, and high-risk behaviors. In the United States, blood is additionally tested for hepatitis B and C viruses, HIV, human T-cell lymphotropic virus I/II, syphilis, Trypanosoma cruzi (agent for Chagas disease), and West Nile virus. In select regions of the country, blood is also tested for Babesia. Platelet components are also screened for bacterial contamination before being released for transfusion.

A type and screen includes ABO/Rh blood group determination and a screening test for unexpected (non-ABO) antibodies. For procedures in which blood transfusion is not invariably needed, a type and screen showing no unexpected antibodies eliminates the need for immediate cross-matching to a specific unit of blood (compatibility testing); blood can be quickly cross-matched when and if the decision to transfuse is made. If unexpected antibodies are found, a specific cross-match is performed to ensure that erythrocytes in the selected unit do not express the relevant antigen(s).

It is essential to match blood for Rh status in persons of childbearing potential and in patients with anti-Rh antibodies; persons of childbearing age or younger who are Rh negative and patients previously sensitized to Rh antigens should never receive Rh-positive blood.

Blood may not be initially matched for patients requiring massive transfusion. In patients with ongoing or life-threatening bleeding, type-specific blood or type O/Rh-negative blood may be transfused without cross-matching as part of a massive transfusion protocol.

A direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test (DAT) (

) is performed to look for IgG or complement coating a patient’s erythrocytes and is part of the investigation for suspected hemolytic transfusion reactions (acute or delayed), autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and hemolytic disease of the newborn.

Packed red blood cells (PRBCs) are erythrocytes suspended in anticoagulant-preservative solution at a hematocrit level of 55% to 65%. Transfusion of one unit of PRBCs raises the hematocrit level by 3% and the hemoglobin level by 1 g/dL (10 g/L) in an average-sized, nonbleeding adult (for transfusion product modifications, see [Table: Table: Cellular Transfusion Product Modifications]

).

Plasma contains coagulation factors and all other plasma proteins. Plasma transfusion is indicated to restore coagulation factors for which specific factor concentrates are not available or in the setting of multiple acquired deficiencies, as in warfarin overdose when four-factor prothrombin complex concentrates (PCCs) are unavailable.

Cryoprecipitate is the fraction of plasma that precipitates when fresh frozen plasma is thawed at 1.0 to 4.0 °C (33.8-39.2 °F). It contains fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, factor VIII, and factor XIII and is commonly used to treat acquired hypofibrinogenemia. Cryoprecipitate is also used empirically in uremic bleeding if desmopressin is ineffective. Five or more units of cryoprecipitate are pooled before transfusion; 10 units of cryoprecipitate will increase the plasma fibrinogen level by 70 to 100 mg/dL (0.7-1 g/L).

Platelet concentrates are derived from whole blood. Donations by apheresis yield platelet products equivalent to approximately five platelet concentrates (platelets derived from whole blood donation) and increase the platelet count by approximately 20,000 to 30,000/μL (20-30 × 10^9/L).

Platelet transfusions are needed for patients with thrombocytopenia undergoing general surgery (platelet count <50,000/μL [50 × 10^9/L]) or neurosurgery (platelet count <100,000/μL [100 × 10^9/L]) or those who are actively bleeding. Platelets are also transfused in most stable, nonbleeding patients whose platelet counts are less than 10,000/μL (10 × 10^9/L). Platelets should generally not be used to treat patients with an established diagnosis of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and should be limited to managing life-threatening bleeding in patients with immune thrombocytopenia (see [Table: Table: Cellular Transfusion Product Modifications]

for platelet modifications).

Plasma pooled together from thousands of donors is fractionated into derivatives such as albumin, Rh immune globulins, or coagulation factor concentrates ( [Table: Table: Plasma-Derived Therapeutic Products]

). These plasma derivatives are processed to reduce the risk of transmission of infectious diseases.

Recombinant factor concentrates (not containing any donor plasma) have become standard care for many patients with hemophilia A and B (factor VIII and IX deficiency, respectively).

Four-factor PCC contains factors II, VII, IX, and X and is the preferred product for patients experiencing life-threatening bleeding while taking warfarin. Activated PCCs such as factor VIII inhibitor bypassing activity (FEIBA) contain factors II, IX, X, and activated factor VII and are used when an inhibitor to factor VIII is present. PCCs carry a significant thrombotic risk, and their use should be carefully considered. Some PCCs contain residual heparin or IgA; therefore, their use should be avoided in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and IgA deficiency.

Activated factor VII, which also has considerable prothrombotic risk, is used to manage factor VII deficiency, hemophilia in patients with high inhibitor titers, and acquired hemophilia in some patients.

Transfusion of blood products should achieve a clinically relevant goal rather than correcting an abnormal laboratory value. Along with transfusion, attempts should be made to correct causes of blood loss and improve hematopoiesis and synthetic function.

A restrictive transfusion threshold of a hemoglobin level less than 7 g/dL (70 g/L) has been shown to be as safe and effective as more liberal thresholds, except in patients with acute coronary syndrome or acute stroke. This restrictive threshold also does not apply to patients who are hemodynamically unstable or actively bleeding and should not be applied to symptomatic patients with rapidly decreasing hemoglobin concentrations.

In patients who do not desire transfusion, every attempt should be made to clarify under what circumstances they might accept blood products and which blood products or derivatives are acceptable. Preprocedure planning is key to good outcomes. In cases of bleeding, alternatives such as PCCs, activated factor VII, and antifibrinolytic agents may be acceptable and can be considered if local measures are not effective. Blood draws should be minimized in patients with anemia, and intravenous iron, vitamin B~12, folic acid, and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents can be used as appropriate.

Transfusion complications occur in approximately 1% of transfusions. Although fatal reactions are rare (incidence of 1:200,000-400,000 units), the leading causes of transfusion-related death are hemolysis, transfusion-related acute lung injury, and transfusion-associated circulatory overload.

Acute ABO-incompatible hemolytic transfusion reactions usually result from clerical errors at the time of specimen collection or blood administration. Electronic barcode systems enhance other stringent pretransfusion patient identification procedures and reduce such errors. Patient and specimen identification can be particularly problematic in high turnover areas. Rarely, high-titer A (or B) antibodies found in platelet units initiate hemolysis.

Acute hemolytic reactions manifest with fever and flank pain and usually occur immediately but can be delayed up to 24 hours. Complications can include hypotension, diffuse bleeding, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), hemoglobinuria, and death.

Management requires immediate transfusion termination because the degree of hemolysis is proportional to the volume transfused. Aggressive hydration and supportive care for associated complications (DIC, acute kidney injury) are required. A root cause investigation is initiated in each case.

Antibodies to non-ABO blood group antigens occur after exposure through previous transfusion, pregnancy, or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. These antibodies may not be detectable through pretransfusion blood matching performed years following initial exposure. Re-exposure leads to an anamnestic response and delayed hemolysis of the transfused antigen-positive erythrocytes, typically 7 to 14 days after transfusion. The causative association between a decreasing hematocrit and a previous transfusion is not always appreciated. Laboratory investigation reveals a positive DAT, and the blood bank can identify the target antigen. Patients should be informed regarding their alloimmunization status so they can communicate this information to other health care providers for subsequent surgery or other care. Some jurisdictions outside the United States have transfusion “antibody registries” for this purpose.

Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) is an underrecognized problem but may be the most common serious complication of blood product transfusion, affecting 1% or more of transfusion recipients ( [Table: Table: TACO and TRALI Characteristics]

). TACO is a reaction to the volume of the transfusion rather than any blood component. Risk factors include older age, pre-existing cardiovascular or kidney disease, and rapid administration rate. Signs and symptoms include respiratory distress within 12 hours of transfusion, positive fluid balance, elevated central venous pressure, an audible S~3 heart sound, elevated B-type natriuretic peptide level, and radiographic findings compatible with pulmonary edema. Therapy consists of diuretics and a slower rate of blood administration.

Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is defined as noncardiogenic pulmonary edema that occurs within 6 hours of transfusion, although the time to onset is usually within minutes of transfusion initiation (see [Table: Table: TACO and TRALI Characteristics]

). TRALI occurs in approximately 1 in 5000 transfusions and may be more common in recipients of plasma or platelet products than recipients of erythrocytes. TRALI typically occurs because of HLA- or neutrophil-specific antibodies from donors that bind to and activate recipient leukocytes in the pulmonary vasculature. Screening donors for these antibodies reduces the incidence of TRALI.

Symptoms include dyspnea, hypoxemia, fever, and hypotension without signs of volume overload. Radiographic findings usually resemble acute respiratory distress syndrome. Following transfusion discontinuation, management is supportive and includes supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation. The prognosis is better and recovery is quicker than that of typical acute respiratory distress syndrome. TRALI is unlikely to recur in subsequent transfusions.

Febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction (FNHTR) occurs in approximately 1% of transfusions and is mediated by proinflammatory cytokines elaborated by donor leukocytes during storage. Symptoms include a temperature increase of 1.0 °C (1.8 °F) to greater than 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) within 4 hours of transfusion or chills and rigors even in the absence of a fever. FNHTR is a diagnosis of exclusion, and the differential diagnosis of fever occurring in association with transfusion includes hemolysis and septic transfusion reaction. The DAT result is negative. Antipyretics are used for treatment, but routine prophylaxis with antipyretics is not warranted. Leukoreduction reduces the incidence of FNHTR.

Risk of infection with transfusion ranges from 1:300,000 for hepatitis B and West Nile viruses to 1:1 million for infections such as hepatitis C virus and HIV. In addition to these infections, bacterial contamination may occur, especially in platelets, because they must be stored at room temperature. Bacterial testing is performed before issuing the platelet unit, but the risk is still 1:50,000 units. Erythrocyte components may rarely be infected with Yersinia, which thrives in a cold, iron-rich environment. Leukoreduction decreases the risk of cytomegalovirus transmission and is necessary for transfusions in patients with hematologic malignancy undergoing chemotherapy or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (see [Table: Table: Cellular Transfusion Product Modifications]

).

Pruritus and urticaria occur in 1% to 5% of recipients during or after transfusion. Because the reaction may be donor specific, prophylaxis with antihistamines or glucocorticoids for future transfusions is unwarranted in most situations.

Anaphylactic or anaphylactoid reactions are rare. Manifestations include angioedema, stridor, abdominal symptoms, and hypotension. Patients may require epinephrine, bronchodilators, or fluid resuscitation. IgA deficiency should be ruled out; the presence of severe IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies necessitates using washed cellular blood components or plasma components from IgA-deficient donors for future transfusions.

Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease is a rare but fatal complication in which passenger donor lymphocytes in a cellular blood product (erythrocytes or platelets) engraft in an immunocompromised recipient and cause toxic effects in the bone marrow, skin, liver, and gastrointestinal tract. Patients at risk include those receiving chemotherapy for autoimmune disorders or malignancy, patients with aplastic anemia or other forms of immunodeficiency, patients who have undergone hematopoietic stem cell or solid organ transplantation, recipients of blood components from first-degree relatives, and premature infants. Prevention involves irradiation of cellular blood components. Patients who have undergone hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may require irradiated blood components indefinitely, and transfusion decisions should be made in collaboration with hematologists and blood bank specialists (see [Table: Table: Cellular Transfusion Product Modifications]

).

Massive transfusion is defined as the transfusion of one blood volume in 24 hours or 50% in 4 hours. When whole blood is lost and replaced with crystalloid and PRBCs, a dilutional coagulopathy develops that is often exacerbated by hypothermia, acidosis, and liver injury as well as concomitant DIC. Contemporary practice is to transfuse plasma and platelets concurrently with PRBCs to avoid the development of dilutional coagulopathy. In patients with a history of trauma, the ratio of transfusing 1 unit of PRBCs, 1 unit of plasma, and 1 unit of platelets has been advised, although the optimal ratio in other patients with massive bleeding is less clear. Blood products should be warmed to prevent hypothermia. During resuscitation, patients must be monitored closely for hypocalcemia (from citrate toxicity), hyperkalemia or hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and volume overload.

Warm reactive IgG erythrocyte autoantibodies in patients with warm antibody autoimmune hemolytic anemia are panagglutinins that interfere with antibody identification and cross-match procedures. Transfusions should be avoided in these patients, but if transfusion is urgently needed, ABO/Rh-matched but cross-match–incompatible blood may be issued. A fulminant acute hemolytic transfusion reaction is a risk in this scenario, but hidden alloantibodies are unlikely to exist in patients who have never been pregnant or received a previous transfusion. Collaboration among hospitalists, hematologists, and blood bank specialists is necessary in managing transfusion decisions in patients with warm antibody autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Analogous concerns complicate transfusion in patients with cold agglutinin autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Additionally, these patients usually require blood to be warmed during transfusion.

Apheresis procedures collect whole blood and separate it into components. Specific components (plasma, platelets, erythrocytes, leukocytes) can be removed as needed. Fluid is usually replaced with colloid and crystalloid. Laboratory monitoring is necessary because complications include hypocalcemia, thrombocytopenia, and hypofibrinogenemia.

Therapy for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is more appropriately characterized as therapeutic plasma exchange because fresh frozen plasma is provided as the replacement fluid rather than crystalloid or colloid solutions.

The same cell separators can be used to perform plateletpheresis, erythrocyte exchange transfusion, and other procedures in patients with specific indications ( [Table: Table: Indications for Therapeutic Apheresis]

).
