Thrombotic Disorders

The burden of venous thromboembolic disease, including superficial and deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE), is high and continues to increase despite better awareness of risk factors and prevention options. The incidence of a first episode of venous thromboembolism (VTE) is approximately 1 to 2 per 1000 person/years.

Alterations in three primary physiologic processes predispose persons to VTE. The Virchow triad includes reduced or turbulent blood flow, alterations or injury to the vessel wall, and changes in blood components that are prothrombotic or inhibit fibrinolysis (or both). VTE usually develops from the synergistic effect of multiple risk factors in these three domains.

The presence of hypercoagulability, or thrombophilia, is an important driver of thrombosis and can be inherited or acquired. Evaluation for hereditary thrombophilia may be considered in patients with the following factors:

  • Thromboses at unusual sites (e.g., the portal venous system)
  • Recurrent idiopathic thrombosis
  • Age younger than 45 years with unprovoked thrombosis
  • A clear family history of thrombosis in one or more first-degree relatives younger than 45 years
  • A history of recurrent fetal loss
  • Warfarin-induced skin necrosis

Many variables, including acute thrombosis and anticoagulant use, can affect outcomes of thrombophilia testing and may lead to false-positive test results ( [Table: Table: Conditions With Decreased Anticoagulant Factor Levels]

). Except for antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, a known thrombophilia will not change immediate management (e.g., selection of an initial anticoagulant), and testing should not be routinely pursued in the setting of an acute thrombotic event.

Inherited thrombophilias typically affect components of the coagulation cascade (see

) by causing the prothrombotic system to continue unsuppressed or by inhibiting clot lysis. All known inherited thrombophilias are autosomal dominant; therefore, most affected patients are heterozygous for the disorder. The two most common inherited thrombophilias are factor V Leiden (FVL) and the prothrombin G20210A gene variant. Antithrombin deficiency and protein C and S deficiencies are less common but are more significant risk factors for VTE ( [Table: Table: Thrombosis Risk With Inherited and Acquired Thrombophilias]

). These inherited thrombophilias do not appear to be associated with arterial thrombosis.

Failure to identify a known thrombophilia through laboratory testing does not mean one does not exist. Studies have shown that even without an identified inherited disorder, a family history of thrombosis remains an independent risk factor for VTE.

Although identification of inherited thrombophilias has advanced the understanding of VTE pathophysiology, it has little influence on clinical management. The acute management of patients with VTE does not differ based on the presence of an inherited thrombophilia. Duration of anticoagulation is typically determined by whether the VTE event was provoked by a reversible or self-limited insult rather than the presence or absence of an inherited thrombophilia. Similarly, even if an inherited thrombophilia is found in a patient with VTE, asymptomatic family members should not undergo thrombophilia testing.

FVL is the most common inherited thrombophilia. Normally, activated factor V combines with factor X to produce thrombin, which leads to clot formation. This process is regulated by activated protein C, which inactivates factor V to stop the process of ongoing clot formation. In FVL, mutated factor V is resistant to cleavage by activated protein C, leading to a prothrombotic state.

Heterozygous FVL is most common in patients of European ancestry, affecting up to 5% of this population. Although persons who are heterozygous have a fourfold to eightfold increased risk for developing a first VTE compared with otherwise healthy persons, most remain asymptomatic, and recent studies suggest that these patients are not at higher risk for recurrent thrombosis compared with healthy persons. FVL genetic testing or activated protein C resistance testing can be used to diagnose this condition.

The prothrombin G20210A gene variant causes increased production of prothrombin (factor II) through a guanine to adenine substitution at nucleotide 20210. It affects up to 3% of patients from Europe but is rare in those from elsewhere. Persons who are heterozygous for this variant are at a twofold to fourfold increased risk for developing a first VTE, although most patients with this variant do not experience VTE events. Data are unclear regarding risks with the homozygous state, which is rare.

Antithrombin III (ATIII) and proteins C and S serve as natural anticoagulants in the body. Variants leading to loss of function or production of these components increase the risk of VTE.

Hereditary ATIII deficiency, although rare with a prevalence of 1 in 3000 to 5000 persons, is a more significant thrombophilic risk factor than FVL or the prothrombin G20210A gene variant (see [Table: Table: Thrombosis Risk With Inherited and Acquired Thrombophilias]

). If ATIII deficiency is found, acquired ATIII deficiency is much more common than congenital deficiency and should be ruled out (see [Table: Table: Conditions With Decreased Anticoagulant Factor Levels]

). The main role of ATIII is to inhibit thrombin and activated factors IX and X (IXa and Xa). Thrombosis occurs in 30% of patients with heterozygous ATIII deficiency by age 30 years and in 65% of patients by age 50 years. The thrombosis risk is particularly high during pregnancy, leading to VTE-related pregnancy loss and pregnancy morbidity. Repeat testing is typically required to determine whether the deficiency is persistent.

For patients in whom heparin is initiated and titration to a therapeutic range is difficult, ATIII deficiency should be considered because heparin requires ATIII to be effective. ATIII concentrate can be used to treat this condition.

Protein C is a vitamin K–dependent protein that degrades activated factors V and VIII. Heterozygous protein C deficiency has a prevalence of 2 to 5 per 1000 persons and is often associated with pregnancy complications, a thrombotic event before age 50 years, and a strong family history of thrombosis. Patients can develop warfarin-induced skin necrosis (

) because of rapid protein C depletion with warfarin administration, which proceeds faster than depletion of the coagulation factors and results in a transient prothrombotic state. Homozygous deficiency is rare and causes neonatal purpura fulminans. If protein C deficiency is found, acquired causes should be ruled out (see [Table: Table: Conditions With Decreased Anticoagulant Factor Levels]

). Patients should not be tested during acute VTE events or while receiving warfarin because both cause depletion of protein C. Protein C functional testing is usually the first test performed to evaluate for deficiency; more complex testing is often necessary to confirm the diagnosis.

Protein S is a vitamin K–dependent protein that functions as a cofactor for protein C and degrades activated factors V and VIII. Protein S circulates in a free form and is bound to a complement-binding protein. Deficiency is uncommon and bears many similarities to protein C deficiency. Patients who are heterozygous for protein S deficiency typically experience VTE at a younger age (<50 years). Although rare case reports of functional protein S deficiency exist, immunoassay of circulating free protein S is usually sufficient for diagnosis. Protein S deficiency is likely the most difficult hereditary thrombophilia to confirm because multiple laboratory assays are available, but cutoffs between normal and deficient are imprecise.

Methylene tetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) gene polymorphisms cause mild elevations in homocysteine levels, which are associated with a slightly increased risk of cardiovascular disease. The heterozygous variant is common in those of European ancestry, but data regarding increased thrombotic risk are conflicting, and no evidence indicates that treatment influences outcomes. As such, testing for the MTHFR variant and measuring homocysteine levels, as well as other potential contributors to thrombosis, such as factor VIII levels and plasminogen activator inhibitor activity, should not be part of the standard thrombophilia evaluation.

VTE is more likely to occur in the setting of an acquired rather than an inherited thrombophilia. Many conditions predispose patients to the development of thrombosis.

Surgery, trauma, hospitalization, and immobilization are some of the most significant risk factors for VTE. VTE occurs frequently in medical and surgical patients; approximately half of all new VTEs are diagnosed during or within 3 months of a hospital stay or surgical procedure. If prophylaxis is not used, the risk of DVT in patients undergoing general surgery is 15% to 30%. Patients with cancer undergoing surgery and patients undergoing orthopedic procedures, including knee arthroplasty, hip fracture repair, or hip replacement, are at particularly high risk. Without prophylaxis, the risk of DVT after hip fracture surgery is approximately 60%. Nosocomial VTE risk is also increased for nonsurgical hospitalized patients, especially those who are immobilized, have acute neurologic illness, or are in the medical ICU.

Certain medical conditions, including inflammatory conditions, nephrotic syndrome, and inflammatory bowel disease, are associated with increased thrombotic risk. Obesity is also associated with increased thrombotic risk. Decisions regarding the best means of VTE prophylaxis in these patients can be complex; decision support aids, including the Caprini (see Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Foundations of Clinical Practice) and Padua scores, can help stratify nosocomial VTE risk (see Prevention in Hematology).

Cancer is diagnosed in 10% of patients within 1 year of an unprovoked VTE occurrence. Cancers of the ovary, pancreas, and liver are most frequently found. The only randomized controlled clinical trial in patients with thrombosis that compared routine age- and sex-indicated screening with extensive malignancy screening showed no survival benefit with extensive malignancy screening.

Numerous malignancies are associated with increased thrombotic risk, and thrombosis remains a leading cause of morbidity and death in patients with cancer. Some data show that prophylactic anticoagulation in certain patients with cancer reduces the risk of thrombosis ( [Table: Table: Khorana Score]

); however, prophylaxis is not routinely used in outpatients with cancer without a previous thromboembolic event. In most cases, hospitalized patients with cancer should receive prophylactic anticoagulation, although this may not be appropriate in patients at low risk for VTE or high risk for bleeding or in those hospitalized for palliative care indications.

Hormones used in contraceptives increase the risk of VTE. The risk in women using oral contraceptives is increased approximately threefold, but the absolute number of patients affected remains small. VTE risk is highest with combined oral contraceptives containing estrogen and progestin, whereas progestin-only contraceptives and intrauterine devices have a lower risk of VTE. Regardless of the type of contraceptive, VTE risk tends to be greater in women who have obesity and in those 39 years or older. Additionally, tobacco use increases the risk of VTE, and patients older than 35 years who smoke should not be prescribed oral hormonal contraceptives. Women with a previous VTE event should also avoid combined oral contraceptives when possible. However, routine thrombophilia screening before beginning contraceptive use is not indicated.

Similarly, VTE risk is increased approximately twofold in postmenopausal women taking conjugated estrogen-medroxyprogesterone hormone replacement therapy, but the absolute risk remains small. The VTE risk appears lower in postmenopausal women taking only estrogen and in those using transdermal hormone replacement. As with hormonal contraceptives, patients with a previous VTE should avoid estrogen replacement therapy when possible.

The antiestrogen, tamoxifen, also increases VTE risk; this risk increases further, approximately three times baseline, in patients receiving tamoxifen with systemic chemotherapy. The risk for VTE with aromatase inhibitors, such as anastrozole, is lower than with tamoxifen.

Patients with multiple myeloma receiving an immunomodulatory agent, such as lenalidomide or pomalidomide, have a significant risk for VTE that warrants prophylaxis with aspirin, low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), fixed-dose warfarin, or a factor Xa inhibitor, depending on the patient’s risk profile. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors, antiangiogenic therapies, and immunotherapies also increase VTE risk, although prophylactic therapy is not routinely indicated.

Prolonged anticoagulation is not indicated in patients with a medication-induced VTE event if the offending medication can be discontinued.

Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APLAS) is an autoimmune disorder associated with venous and arterial thrombosis as well as an increased risk of fetal demise during pregnancy.

APLAS evaluation includes anticardiolipin antibodies, anti–β~2-glycoprotein antibodies, and lupus anticoagulant. A clue to the presence of lupus anticoagulant is activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) prolongation. The diagnosis of APLAS requires the presence of an antiphospholipid antibody (confirmed at least 12 weeks after initial testing) in addition to multiple clinical and laboratory criteria ( [Table: Table: Diagnosis of Antiphospholipid Antibody Syndrome]

).

Typically, patients diagnosed with APLAS require long-term anticoagulation because of the risk of recurrent thrombosis. In patients with “triple positive” APLAS (presence of lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibody, and anti–β~2-glycoprotein antibody), a vitamin K antagonist (VKA) should be used rather than a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) (see Hematologic Involvement in Rheumatology). The data in patients with intermediate or low-risk APLAS remain unclear, although VKA use is preferred to a DOAC. VKA therapy initiation should include an overlap period with parenteral anticoagulation.

The myeloproliferative neoplasms have been found to confer an increased risk of thrombosis, including PE, DVT, portal vein thrombosis, and Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic venous outflow obstruction) (see Budd-Chiari Syndrome in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease). Evidence of a myeloproliferative neoplasm is discovered in approximately 50% of patients with Budd-Chiari syndrome, even when the complete blood count is normal. In the setting of splanchnic vein thrombosis (portal vein, splenic vein, hepatic vein, or mesenteric vein thrombosis), evaluation for evidence of a myeloproliferative neoplasm should be considered, including evaluation for the JAK2 tyrosine kinase alteration.

Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is another acquired stem cell disorder associated with hemolytic anemia, bone marrow failure, and thrombosis, including of the splanchnic veins (see Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria in Hematology).

A previous VTE is one of the most significant predictors of a subsequent VTE, regardless of whether an additional inherited or acquired thrombophilic risk factor is identified.

Patients with COVID-19 infection are at increased risk for thrombosis because of a dysregulated immune response, hemostatic abnormalities, and endothelial damage. The overall prevalence of VTE in hospitalized critically ill and noncritically ill patients with COVID-19 is 23% and 8%, respectively. Because of this elevated risk, in the absence of VTE, critically ill patients with COVID-19 are recommended to receive prophylactic anticoagulation rather than therapeutic anticoagulation, preferably with LMWH. Additionally, therapeutic rather than prophylactic dosing of LMWH should be considered for patients not in an intensive care setting, especially those who require low-flow oxygen with elevated D-dimer levels, unless a contraindication (e.g., increased bleeding risk) is present.

VTE risk is elevated in hospitalized, immobile, and acutely ill patients as well as those undergoing surgery. More than 50% of VTE events occur during or after hospitalization for acute illness or recent surgery. Patients with cancer or stroke history, or those in the ICU, have a particularly high risk for VTE. VTE is a major preventable cause of hospital morbidity and mortality, and hospitalized patients should be assessed for VTE risk and treated with prophylaxis when appropriate. Despite the well-recognized risks of VTE, the rate of appropriate prophylaxis is low in hospitalized patients.

Early ambulation, mechanical prophylaxis (such as intermittent pneumatic compression devices applied to the lower extremities), and prophylactic anticoagulants are options for VTE prevention. Generally, unless a clear contraindication to prophylaxis exists, pharmacologic treatment is preferred to mechanical prophylaxis in patients with elevated VTE risk. No benefit exists to combining pneumatic compression devices with pharmacologic prophylaxis.

Guidance on VTE prevention strategies is provided by the American Society of Hematology and American College of Chest Physicians. A nonsurgical patient’s thrombotic risk can be determined by using a validated risk assessment model, such as the Padua Prediction Score (see [Table: Table: Padua Prediction Score]

). If bleeding risk is not elevated and VTE risk is high (Padua score ≥4), the use of pharmacologic prophylaxis, preferably with daily LMWH, is recommended throughout the patient’s hospital stay or until mobility is fully recovered. Fondaparinux is an option but should be avoided in patients with creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/min and should be used with caution in those with more moderate kidney disease. Unfractionated heparin (UFH) may also be appropriate but is best reserved for patients with contraindications to LMWH or fondaparinux, such as those with severe kidney disease. Barring a contraindication, patients hospitalized with COVID-19 infection should receive pharmacologic prophylaxis, with some patients also benefiting from therapeutic dosing (see COVID-Related Thrombosis in Hematology).

In patients with an unacceptably high bleeding risk, mechanical prophylaxis with intermittent pneumatic compression may be used. However, the data supporting this approach in nonsurgical patients are limited.

Most patients do not require continued pharmacologic VTE prevention after discharge.

For information on VTE prophylaxis in patients undergoing surgical procedures, see Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

VTE causes significant morbidity and requires efficient evaluation and diagnosis. Previous VTE, positive family history, and other thrombophilia risk factors, especially cancer, should be assessed, as well as other potential causes of symptoms. For DVT and PE, determination of the clinical or pretest probability of disease should drive test selection. This can be accomplished through clinical gestalt or the use of validated risk scores such as the Wells criteria for DVT ( [Table: Table: Wells Criteria for DVT]

) and the Wells score for PE ( [Table: Table: Wells Criteria for PE]

).

The typical clinical presentation of DVT involves unilateral swelling, pain, warmth, and erythema of the extremity. Lower extremity DVT can be proximal (popliteal, femoral, or iliac veins) or distal (calf veins: peroneal, posterior, and anterior tibial).

The American Society of Hematology (ASH) recommends D-dimer measurement to exclude DVT in patients with low probability of DVT (≤10%), corresponding to a Wells score of zero to 1 (“DVT unlikely”). If the Wells score indicates that DVT is unlikely, a negative D-dimer obviates the need for further testing for DVT. Alternatively, the Wells score can be categorized as low (−2 to 0 points), moderate (1-2 points), or high probability (≥3). A negative D-dimer excludes the diagnosis of DVT in patients with a low probability and might also exclude the diagnosis in patients with moderate probability of DVT; the ASH guidelines recommend ultrasonography as the first diagnostic test in these patients, but also state that high-sensitivity D-dimer is acceptable in those at the lower range of this moderate probability.

For patients with a Wells score of “DVT likely” (2 or more points, if the dichotomous score is used), or a moderate or high probability (if the three-tiered approach is used), ultrasonography should be performed first. Ultrasonography may be with whole-leg or proximal lower extremity ultrasonography and compression with Doppler or duplex scanning; it remains unclear which modality of testing is most effective. A negative whole-leg ultrasound in patients with a likely or moderate probability of DVT rules out the diagnosis. However, a second proximal leg ultrasonography should be performed 1 week later in patients with moderate or likely probability with a negative proximal leg ultrasound if no alternative diagnosis for the leg symptoms is identified. In patients with a high probability of DVT, a negative ultrasound of either type should be followed by serial ultrasonography if no alternative cause is found.

Point-of-care compression ultrasonography performed by bedside providers may potentially supplant the need for formal ultrasonography (

, Video: Ultrasounds Showing Compressibility and Noncompressibility of Common Femoral Vein). Other testing methods, such as contrast venography and magnetic resonance venography, are rarely used to diagnose DVT.

Patients with confirmed acute DVT do not require CT angiography to assess the possibility of concomitant PE in the absence of respiratory symptoms.

Patients with PE may present with chest pain, dyspnea, and tachypnea; less common findings may include cough, fever, cyanosis, syncope, or shock. Examination often shows tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxemia.

PE may be ruled out in patients at very low risk using the Pulmonary Embolism Rule-Out Criteria (PERC) ( [Table: Table: PERC for Predicting Probability of PE]

). If the PERC score is zero in patients with very low probability, no further testing, including D-dimer testing and CT angiography, should be performed (Video: Determining Likelihood of PE and Need for Imaging). A meta-analysis of 12 studies found that if the PERC were applied to very low-risk patients, only 0.3% of PEs would have been missed, and 22% of D-dimer testing would have been safely avoided.

In patients with a PERC score of 1 or more or those without a very low probability of disease, the clinical probability as determined by clinical gestalt or a validated score (Wells or Geneva) should inform test choice. In patients with unlikely or low pretest probability, D-dimer testing should be pursued. If the result is negative, no imaging is warranted. If the result is positive, further evaluation is merited.

If a patient has a likely, intermediate, or high pretest probability, imaging studies are usually indicated. D-dimer testing may be considered in patients with intermediate pretest probability (approximately 20%), because a normal D-dimer level in that setting has a high negative predictive value and obviates the need for imaging. D-dimer testing should not be pursued in those with likely or high pretest probability because results would not change the need for imaging.

CT angiography has significantly improved the accuracy of PE evaluation, generally replacing the less specific ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan and avoiding the need for more invasive pulmonary arteriography. Although ASH guidelines suggest a V/Q scan as a first-line test, CT is usually favored because of its wide availability and rapid acquisition time.

In patients with kidney disease or in whom intravenous contrast is contraindicated, a V/Q scan can be pursued. A normal V/Q scan effectively rules out PE. A high-probability study result in a patient with a high likelihood of disease has a strong positive predictive value. Low probability or intermediate probability V/Q scan results need to be interpreted in the context of the clinical probability, with rates of PE varying from 4% to 66%.

Using MRI to diagnose PE avoids ionizing radiation and can visualize intraluminal filling defects in the pulmonary vasculature, but not as well as CT. New MRI techniques may enhance its role in VTE diagnosis, but CT is still considered the diagnostic test of choice in most patients.

Patients with a confirmed PE do not require ultrasonography of the lower extremities. Patients with established PE can undergo testing of biomarkers such as serum troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide for risk stratification; echocardiography (right ventricular strain and pulmonary hypertension) and CT (right ventricular dilation) may also demonstrate findings indicating a more significant PE with increased risk of complications.

Most patients with DVT can be efficiently and safely treated as outpatients. A subset of patients with PE with an excellent prognosis and reliable home support can also avoid inpatient care. The original Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI) is a validated prediction tool for clinical severity and outcomes of patients with PE. Using 11 clinical criteria, patients with PE are categorized into classes I through V, with class I and class II considered low risk for adverse outcomes. In a multicenter, prospective, open-label, randomized trial of patients with low-risk PE as determined by the PESI score, no difference was found between outpatient and inpatient management in recurrent VTE, major bleeding, or 90-day mortality. A simplified version of the PESI is also available to determine patients at risk for adverse outcomes ( [Table: Table: Simplified PESI]

). Patients with a simplified PESI score of zero who have good access to care and no other indications for hospitalization (e.g., significant hypoxemia) may be candidates for outpatient treatment.

For most patients with a VTE, anticoagulation with a DOAC is preferred to a VKA. Apixaban and rivaroxaban are effective as monotherapy, whereas dabigatran and edoxaban require initial concurrent parenteral heparin. Anticoagulation with warfarin also requires at least 5 days of concomitant parenteral heparin. Patients who require hospitalization should generally avoid initial treatment with UFH because of its unpredictable bioavailability compared with LMWH; however, because of its short half-life, UFH is often preferred in patients who are unstable and may require thrombolytic therapy and in those who may need emergent surgery for other indications.

Thrombolytic therapy is not routinely used for treatment of PE, but systemic thrombolysis is indicated in patients with hypotension. Systemic thrombolysis is favored over catheter-directed thrombolysis in these patients. Systemic thrombolysis should also be considered in those with clinical deterioration despite anticoagulation, even in the absence of hypotension. Catheter-based thrombectomy is also an option, although its role in therapy is poorly defined; it may be most useful in patients with clinical deterioration despite thrombolysis or who have hypotension but have a contraindication to thrombolysis. Given the complexity of these decisions, many hospitals have developed multidisciplinary PE response teams to triage and treat patients at high risk.

For acute DVT, catheter-directed thrombolysis may be considered in those with severe limb-threatening thrombosis, characterized by massive edema and other findings of lower extremity ischemia.

Duration of anticoagulation therapy varies based on the clinical scenario ( [Table: Table: Anticoagulant Therapy Duration for VTE]

). In thrombosis associated with reversible risk factors, 3 to 6 months of anticoagulation is adequate.

Extended anticoagulation therapy beyond 3 to 6 months should be considered in patients with persistent risk factors for recurrent VTE and those with no reversible provoking event. After completion of the initial course of full-dose anticoagulation, reduced dosing of apixaban or rivaroxaban can also be considered in patients with indications for extended anticoagulation and low bleeding risk. If extended therapy with either full- or reduced-dose anticoagulation is chosen, the risks, benefits, and choice of anticoagulant should be reevaluated yearly. In such patients in whom anticoagulation is discontinued, aspirin can be considered because of the decreased bleeding risk compared to anticoagulation and 30% to 40% risk reduction in recurrent VTE compared with placebo.

In patients with malignancy and VTE, initial anticoagulation with a DOAC, especially a factor Xa inhibitor, is preferred. Because of a lower bleeding risk, LMWH or apixaban may be preferred in patients with select gastrointestinal malignancies. If heparin is selected for initial anticoagulation in the setting of malignancy, LMWH is preferred to UFH in the absence of severe kidney disease. Anticoagulation should be extended beyond 6 months in select patients with active cancer, such as in those with metastatic disease or those receiving chemotherapy. Reduced-dose anticoagulation rather than therapeutic dosing may be considered for patients with cancer requiring extended therapy.

Inferior vena cava (IVC) filters have been used to prevent PE but are known to increase the risk of DVT; therefore, IVC filters are not recommended for patients receiving anticoagulation but may be considered in those with an acute proximal DVT with a contraindication to anticoagulation. If an IVC filter is placed, a temporary filter should be used and removed as soon as the indication for the filter has resolved.

Patients with a single isolated subsegmental PE, aged less than 65 years, and with low risk of recurrence do not require anticoagulation if a proximal DVT has been ruled out. For those with high risk of recurrence due to conditions such as cancer, previous VTE, or pregnancy, anticoagulation should be instituted as for other acute thromboses.

Patients with asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic distal DVTs do not usually require anticoagulation (see [Table: Table: Anticoagulant Therapy Duration for VTE]

). Patients with distal DVT who are not receiving anticoagulant therapy should undergo follow-up lower extremity ultrasonography weekly for 2 weeks to assess for progression of thrombus. Anticoagulation similar to that for proximal DVT is suggested in patients with distal DVT and moderate to severe symptoms or those with certain risk factors for extension, including a positive D-dimer test result, extensive thrombosis or proximity to proximal veins, no reversible provoking factor for DVT, active cancer, history of VTE, and inpatient status.

Patients with DVT or PE can develop long-term complications affecting function and quality of life. Approximately 25% to 40% of patients with symptomatic DVT develop aspects of postthrombotic syndrome and chronic venous insufficiency, usually within 2 years of VTE. Symptoms of postthrombotic syndrome include pain, heaviness, swelling, stasis dermatitis, and ulceration in the affected limb. Treatment includes leg exercises, avoiding dependent positions for lengthy periods, and using compression stockings. Emollients and a low-moderate potency topical glucocorticoid may be used for stasis dermatitis (see Venous Stasis Dermatitis in Dermatology).

Patients with PE can also develop chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (see Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension (Group 4) in Pulmonary Medicine), cardiopulmonary dysfunction, or decreased exercise tolerance.

Additional sites of thromboses, such as splanchnic, cerebral, and retinal vein thromboses are discussed elsewhere (see Cerebral Venous Thrombosis in Neurology; Retinal Vein Occlusion in Interdisciplinary Medicine).

Superficial thrombophlebitis describes thrombus and associated inflammation in a vein located near the skin’s surface; it is a common inflammatory-thrombotic disorder that does not usually cause significant morbidity or progress to PE. It typically occurs in the setting of cancer or an underlying hypercoagulable state. Cannulated veins of the hands and arms can thrombose after infusions or intravenous catheter placement; this condition does not require anticoagulant therapy (see [Table: Table: Anticoagulant Therapy Duration for VTE]

).

Superficial vein thrombosis often affects the lower extremities and accounts for 10% of lower extremity thromboses. When affecting the great saphenous vein (also referred to as the greater or long saphenous vein), superficial vein thrombosis may progress into the deep venous system. For patients at high risk for progression, low-dose fondaparinux or rivaroxaban is indicated (see [Table: Table: Anticoagulant Therapy Duration for VTE]

).

With few exceptions, such as APLAS, myeloproliferative disorders, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and thrombosis, or COVID-19 vaccine–induced thrombocytopenia, thrombophilias do not play a significant role in arterial thrombosis. The primary causes of arterial thrombosis are arteriosclerosis (treated with antiplatelet therapy) and atrial fibrillation with systemic arterial embolism (treated with anticoagulation). It is unknown whether patients with arterial clots in whom a strong thrombophilia is found are more effectively treated with antiplatelet therapy or anticoagulants.

Upper extremity DVT accounts for 10% of all DVT occurrences, approximately two thirds of which are associated with central venous catheter use or malignancy. ASH guidelines recommend against catheter removal because of thrombosis provided that the catheter is functioning, well positioned, and noninfected. Treatment consists of anticoagulation for a minimum of 3 months if the catheter is removed or at least the duration that the catheter remains in place.

Primary upper extremity DVT is uncommon and usually caused by anatomic abnormalities of the thoracic outlet system leading to axillosubclavian compression and thrombosis (venous thoracic outlet syndrome). Patients are usually young, and thrombus occurs with strenuous upper extremity activity. Expert recommendations vary regarding the use of thrombolysis or thoracic outlet decompression surgery in addition to anticoagulation. CHEST guidelines recommend that treatment of primary and secondary upper extremity DVT follow similar guidelines as lower extremity DVT (see Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in Common Symptoms).

summarizes the characteristics of unfractionated heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), and fondaparinux.

UFH works by binding to antithrombin, catalyzing its action with resultant inactivation of thrombin and factor Xa.

The aPTT is used in monitoring heparin therapy. In the setting of lupus anticoagulant (which prolongs the aPTT), heparin resistance, or markedly elevated factor VIII levels, anti–factor Xa monitoring can be used. Although ideal dosing is controversial, a weight-based nomogram is usually used, and most hospitals follow a specific dosing algorithm with nurse- or pharmacy-led protocols frequently being used. Typically, an initial bolus dose of 80 to 100 U/kg is given. UFH is available in intravenous and subcutaneous preparations, although the intravenous form is usually used for treatment of VTE.

The rate of heparin-associated major bleeding is approximately 3%. Failure to follow a dosage adjustment algorithm is associated with increased bleeding risk. When major bleeding occurs, protamine sulfate can be administered to reverse anticoagulation, using a dose of 1 mg of protamine per 100 units of heparin administered in the previous 2 hours. Protamine adverse effects include allergic reactions, hypotension, bradycardia, and respiratory toxicity.

Although weight-based nomograms and specific algorithms for adjusting dose based on aPTT results have enhanced the safety and efficacy of UFH, variations in bioavailability and potential delay in arriving at a therapeutic dose are still more likely than with LMWH. UFH should therefore be reserved for patients in whom a DOAC or LMWH is contraindicated or in those who require anticoagulation that can be stopped quickly, generally in anticipation of an invasive procedure or surgery.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is a severe complication of heparin that can result in a catastrophic thrombotic event (see Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia in Hematology).

Heparin is a rare cause of hyperkalemia and is presumed to be related to impaired aldosterone production.

LMWH is derived from UFH through a chemical depolymerization producing fragments that are one third the size of heparin.

LMWH does not affect the aPTT because the smaller fragment size does not bind as readily to thrombin but retains the ability to inactivate factor Xa. It is usually administered in weight-adjusted doses. Dosing is more predictable than with UFH, and laboratory testing is generally unnecessary. LMWH is cleared through the kidney, and the biological half-life is increased in patients with kidney disease. For patients with kidney dysfunction (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min) receiving LMWH therapy, ASH suggests against using anti–factor Xa concentration monitoring to guide LMWH dose adjustment; instead, ASH suggests using doses adjusted for kidney function as recommended in product labeling or switching to an alternative anticoagulant. In patients with obesity, dosing is based on actual body weight.

Protamine does not fully reverse the anti-Xa effect of LMWH but provides some benefit in restoring hemostasis and is recommended for life-threatening bleeding. It should be given at a dose of 1 mg of protamine per 1 mg of LMWH.

Fondaparinux is a parenteral factor Xa inhibitor indicated for use in VTE as well as acute coronary syndrome and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and thrombosis. As with LMWH and UFH, when fondaparinux is used as initial parenteral therapy for VTE, it and warfarin should overlap for a minimum of 5 days. Fondaparinux is cleared through the kidney and should be avoided in patients with creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/min.

Fondaparinux has no reversal agent, and caution should be used in patients at risk for bleeding because the half-life is 17 hours. Prothrombin complex concentrates (PCCs) and fresh frozen plasma have been administered with positive outcomes in patients experiencing bleeding.

Warfarin is a VKA. It inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, which leads to inhibition of gamma-carboxylation of precursor coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S. Laboratory monitoring of anticoagulant effect involves the prothrombin time and INR.

Because warfarin lowers protein C levels before inducing its anticoagulant effect, it can initially cause a prothrombotic state. For this reason, when warfarin is used to treat acute VTE, it should be administered initially with a parenteral anticoagulant (e.g., LMWH). The parenteral agent should be given for at least 5 days and continued until the INR is 2 or greater for at least 24 hours.

Although DOACs have changed the landscape of treatment for patients with VTE, warfarin remains a reasonable anticoagulant for some patients, including those with kidney disease, severe obesity, a mechanical heart valve, or high-risk APLAS—conditions for which alternate oral anticoagulants are not routinely used or are contraindicated.

Patients taking warfarin must have access to continued outpatient INR monitoring; many patients are managed by an anticoagulation clinic. INR self-testing is also an option. Common reasons for fluctuations in INR include changes in vitamin K intake, medications, and nonadherence. Studies attempting to decrease INR variability with low-dose daily vitamin K supplementation showed no benefit.

Bleeding is the most significant complication in patients treated with warfarin, occurring in 1% to 3% of patients per year. The risk is higher at warfarin initiation and during episodes of concurrent acute illness. The bleeding risk increases further in patients with an INR greater than 5. Independent of INR, bleeding risk is increased in patients older than 75 years or in those with previous stroke, gastrointestinal bleeding, or other chronic comorbidities. Concomitant antiplatelet therapy or NSAID use also increases the bleeding risk. The indication for antiplatelet agents for patients taking warfarin should be carefully reviewed, and dual antiplatelet therapy in combination with warfarin (triple therapy) should be avoided if possible. Acetaminophen should be used for pain relief instead of NSAIDs when feasible.

Patients with an asymptomatic INR elevation between 4.5 and 10 can often be managed by simply withholding warfarin. For INRs greater than 10 in patients without bleeding, oral vitamin K should be given. In patients experiencing life-threatening bleeding, in addition to intravenous vitamin K, four-factor PCC should be given. Three-factor PCCs contain proteins C and S and factors II, IX, and X; four-factor PCC also contains factor VII. In a clinical trial of VKA-related bleeding, four-factor PCC was found to be noninferior to fresh frozen plasma for hemostatic efficacy. Four-factor PCC is preferred because of its rapid reversal of INR, rapid infusion and administration, and decreased risk of volume overload. Recombinant factor VIIa is not recommended for warfarin reversal.

Bridging therapy, the practice of using heparin or LMWH when warfarin is temporarily stopped for an invasive procedure, is not necessary for most patients taking warfarin and is associated with increased bleeding complications without additional anticoagulant benefit. Exceptions to this may be patients with VTE within the past 4 weeks, history of VTE during anticoagulant interruption for surgery, or a procedure with very high VTE risk, such as orthopedic surgery. Bridging may also be indicated in patients with the following:

  • Atrial fibrillation who have had a stroke or transient ischemic attack in the preceding year
  • Multiple risk factors for stroke (CHADS~2 score of 5-6)
  • Mechanical heart valve

DOACs are safe and effective anticoagulation options and are recommended as the treatment of choice for VTE and atrial fibrillation. DOACs available for use in the United States are dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban. Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor, whereas the other agents are factor Xa inhibitors ( [Table: Table: Features of DOACs]

). Dabigatran and edoxaban require initial treatment with a parenteral agent when used for VTE, although rivaroxaban and apixaban are approved as monotherapy for patients with DVT and PE.

Advantages of DOACs include the following:

  • No need for routine monitoring
  • Rapid onset of action
  • Short half-life
  • Fixed dosing
  • Fewer drug-drug interactions
  • Less likely to be influenced by changes in diet

Routine coagulation studies do not reliably measure the degree of coagulation activity with DOACs. However, the thrombin time is sensitive to the presence of dabigatran and, if normal, indicates that the anticoagulant effect of dabigatran is no longer significant.

DOACs are as effective as warfarin in VTE with less central nervous system bleeding, fatal bleeding, and use of blood product support. Factor Xa inhibitors are also as effective as LMWH in managing VTE in patients with cancer, and guidelines now support factor Xa inhibitors as the preferred anticoagulant in this setting.

The bleeding risk is higher in patients taking concomitant aspirin or clopidogrel and is further increased in patients receiving dual antiplatelet therapy.

The utility and safety of DOACs do not extend to all patient groups or all indications for anticoagulation. Certain patient groups, including pregnant patients and those with mechanical heart valves, were excluded from the major trials of DOACs, and their use is contraindicated in these situations. Some studies also excluded patients with BMI greater than 40 or weight greater than 120 kg (264.5 lb). Growing evidence shows that DOACs may be effective in this population, but caution is advised. Warfarin is the preferred anticoagulant in patients with high-risk APLAS. In patients with low-risk APLAS, the role of DOACs remains unclear.

No head-to-head trials have been performed comparing the various DOACs, and choice depends on adverse-effect profiles and patient-specific characteristics. In patients with concern for gastrointestinal bleeding, dabigatran may not be preferred because of an increased rate of dyspepsia and gastrointestinal bleeding compared with warfarin.

All DOACs are at least partially eliminated through the kidney (see [Table: Table: Features of DOACs]

), and dose adjustment may be required in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease. Apixaban has the lowest kidney elimination rate and is approved for patients undergoing dialysis; however, caution should be used. Data from a 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis suggest that DOACs may be preferred in patients with early-stage chronic kidney disease (estimated glomerular filtration rate <60 mL/min/1.73 m^2) and atrial fibrillation. Additionally, the risk of bleeding with DOACs appears to be no worse than with VKAs. DOACs should be used with caution or avoided in patients with Child-Pugh class B or C liver disease.

Bridging therapy is not used for patients taking DOACs because of their short half-life and immediate effect. Discontinuation of the DOAC depends on the half-life of the drug, the type of procedure, and the patient’s kidney function. DOACs should be stopped 24 to 48 hours before surgery with moderate bleeding risk and 72 hours before surgery with higher bleeding risk. In patients with impaired kidney function, DOACs should be stopped earlier. For procedures with low bleeding risk, DOACs can be resumed promptly when effective hemostasis is secured. For procedures with higher rates of bleeding, reinstitution is usually delayed 2 to 3 days.

The standard approach to patients experiencing bleeding on DOACs involves hemodynamic monitoring and resuscitation with fluid and blood products. Activated charcoal can be considered if the DOAC was ingested recently (<6 hours). Hemodialysis can be considered with dabigatran therapy if new kidney disease is found.

For patients with life-threatening bleeding who are taking an oral factor Xa inhibitor, guidelines suggest stopping the oral factor Xa inhibitor and considering treatment with a four-factor PCC. Previous recommendations suggested andexanet alfa as an alternative, but this agent was removed from the U.S. market in 2025. The major adverse effects of four-factor PCCs are thrombotic events; and a careful analysis of the risks and benefits of four-factor PCC administration is necessary for each patient.

Idarucizumab is an FDA-approved monoclonal antibody fragment that binds free and thrombin-bound dabigatran and neutralizes its activity. Idarucizumab was found to be safe and effective in reversing the anticoagulant effects of dabigatran in patients who experienced serious, life-threatening bleeding determined to require a reversal agent or who required an urgent invasive procedure. Its use is recommended in the ASH 2018 guidelines on VTE treatment. If idarucizumab is not available, activated PCC is an alternative for patients with dabigatran-associated major bleeding.

There is often concern when older adults begin oral anticoagulation, because age is an important risk factor for the bleeding complications associated with anticoagulation. Oral anticoagulation may be excluded as a therapeutic option because of a perceived fall risk. However, recommendations suggest that neither age nor fall risk is reason to withhold anticoagulation from patients who meet clinical criteria. The true risk of serious bleeding related to a fall while taking an anticoagulant is unclear, and small studies have not shown an increased risk of major bleeding in patients taking oral anticoagulants who were considered at high risk for falls. Risk factors for falls should be thoroughly evaluated, and appropriate steps must be used for prevention (see Fall Prevention in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Hematologic Issues in Pregnancy

Patients should be screened for anemia during pregnancy. Physiologic anemia occurs in all pregnant patients because of a disproportionate increase in plasma volume compared to the increase in erythrocyte mass. The measured hemoglobin level typically remains greater than 10.5 g/dL (105 g/L). If the hemoglobin level decreases further, additional evaluation of the anemia is warranted, including measurement of iron stores and serum vitamin B~12 and folate levels.

Worldwide, iron deficiency during pregnancy remains a significant problem. In 2017, the World Health Organization estimated that up to 60% of pregnant persons have pathologic anemia, most commonly secondary to iron deficiency. Iron deficiency in pregnancy can lead to anemia in infants and developmental delays because of iron-dependent neurogenesis; additionally, maternal morbidity is common in patients with anemia. In the first trimester, iron deficiency is treated with oral iron because no safety data are available regarding intravenous iron. Intravenous iron can be used after the 13th week for those who are intolerant of or unresponsive to oral iron supplementation and those late in pregnancy (after 34 weeks’ gestation) with severe iron deficiency anemia (e.g., hemoglobin <10 g/dL [100 g/L]) (see Iron Deficiency in Hematology).

The physiologic stresses of pregnancy are especially challenging for patients with sickle cell disease (SCD) because of underlying hemolytic anemia and, in some cases, multiorgan dysfunction. Multidisciplinary care, including obstetricians and hematologists experienced in managing patients with SCD, is warranted. Prepregnancy counseling is recommended to discuss hereditary considerations (i.e., likelihood of a newborn with SCD), risks of pregnancy to the patient, and fertility issues because the ovary is recognized as a site of end-organ damage. Folate supplementation is recommended for all pregnant persons, but a higher dose is required in pregnant persons with SCD. Iron stores must also be monitored. Pregnant persons with SCD should be monitored closely with monthly complete blood counts.

Painful vaso-occlusive events increase during pregnancy, and careful avoidance of precipitating triggers is necessary. Pain should be managed with acetaminophen and opioid analgesics, and NSAIDs should be avoided after 30 weeks’ gestation to avoid premature closure of the fetal patent ductus arteriosus.

Some medications used to control SCD and its complications, including iron chelating agents, ACE inhibitors, and angiotensin receptor blockers, must be discontinued during pregnancy because of the risk of teratogenicity. Shared decision making is needed to determine whether to continue hydroxyurea considering the clear benefit in reducing vaso-occlusive crises (which pose a potential risk to the fetus) versus the teratogenicity seen in some animal studies.

Expert opinion varies regarding the use of prophylactic transfusions in pregnancy for patients with sickle cell anemia. A meta-analysis found reductions in maternal mortality, painful episodes, and pulmonary complications with prophylactic transfusion. However, guidelines recommend prophylactic transfusion only for patients with a high-risk pregnancy or history of severe SCD-related complications. Frequent transfusions may lead to alloimmunization, increasing the risk of hemolytic disease of the newborn. Alloantibody screening should be performed early, and, if positive, phenotypic matching should be considered to avoid delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction or hemolytic disease of the newborn (see Delayed Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction in Hematology).

Patients who have symptomatic anemia, acute chest syndrome, or stroke should undergo transfusion.

The risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) is increased; therefore, thromboprophylaxis should be administered in hospitalized patients and considered for 6 weeks postpartum because of the thrombophilic state; estrogen-containing hormonal contraceptives should be avoided in the immediate postpartum period.

The cardiopulmonary demands of pregnancy increase the risk of pulmonary hypertension, which, when present, is associated with a significant mortality risk. Suggestive clinical features (e.g., new exertional dyspnea) should be evaluated by echocardiography.

Pregnant patients with SCD are also at increased risk for complications of the pregnancy itself, including miscarriage, intrauterine growth restriction, eclampsia, preterm labor, placental abruption, and stillbirth.

Gestational thrombocytopenia affects approximately 5% of pregnant persons, usually during the second or third trimester. The cause is uncertain, but it is usually mild and self-limited. Most patients are asymptomatic, with platelet counts greater than 100,000/μL (100 × 10^9/L), although they are occasionally lower. In gestational thrombocytopenia, the fetus is unaffected, intervention is unnecessary, and platelet counts spontaneously return to normal after delivery. Evaluation for other causes of thrombocytopenia is necessary for platelet counts less than 100,000/μL (100 × 10^9/L).

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) (see Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura in Hematology) is uncommon but occurs more frequently in pregnant persons than in the general population. Differentiating ITP from gestational thrombocytopenia may be difficult, but features suggesting ITP include earlier presentation (first trimester), lower platelet count nadir (<70,000/μL [70 × 10^9/L]), and a history of thrombocytopenia before pregnancy (even if mild).

If the platelet count remains greater than 30,000/μL (30 × 10^9/L), the pregnancy is not at risk. Patients should receive intravenous immune globulin or glucocorticoids if the platelet count decreases to less than 30,000/μL (30 × 10^9/L) at any time during pregnancy. The target platelet count for delivery (vaginal or cesarean section) is 50,000/μL (50 × 10^9/L), and therapy should begin approximately 1 week before the expected delivery date to achieve that goal. Neuraxial anesthesia requirements vary, but a platelet count greater than 70,000/μL (70 × 10^9/L) is optimal.

ITP autoantibodies can cross the placenta and affect the fetus; 20% to 30% of neonates born to a pregnant person with ITP are reported to have platelet counts less than 50,000/μL (50 × 10^9/L), especially if an older sibling was born with thrombocytopenia. Neonatal platelet counts can continue to decrease for 2 to 5 days after delivery. Fetal thrombocytopenia is not influenced by maternal treatment with either glucocorticoids or intravenous immune globulin. Despite the increased likelihood of neonatal thrombocytopenia, the risk of intracerebral hemorrhage is less than 1% and is unaffected by cesarean section delivery.

The thrombotic microangiopathies of pregnancy encompass a spectrum of disorders with clinical features of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia, often occurring during the third trimester.

The distinction between HELLP (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) syndrome, pre-eclampsia, and acute fatty liver of pregnancy may be difficult, but the management for these disorders is supportive and focused on early delivery. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy (previously called atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome; see Platelet Disorders in Hematology) can also occur during pregnancy ( [Table: Table: Features of the Thrombotic Microangiopathies of Pregnancy]

) and may require additional therapy, including plasma exchange or the anticomplement agent eculizumab.

The risk of VTE in pregnancy and up to 6 weeks postpartum is higher than in the general population, but the absolute risk is still low (<1%). Nevertheless, pulmonary emboli account for about 9% of maternal deaths. The increased risk is a result of multiple pregnancy-specific factors, such as venous stasis caused by uterine compression of abdominal veins; increased venous capacitance; increased circulating procoagulant factors; and decreased circulating protein S. VTE risk increases further in the postpartum period because of endothelial injury during delivery and an additional increase in the procoagulant factors. Other risk factors for VTE include multiple births, advanced maternal age, obesity, smoking, cesarean section, and varicose veins.

The risk of VTE is further increased in patients with inherited thrombophilias. However, testing for these disorders in pregnancy is not routinely recommended.

Pregnant patients with a history of unprovoked VTE, VTE associated with previous pregnancy or oral contraceptives, or thrombophilia associated with a high thrombotic risk require prophylactic antenatal and 6-week postpartum anticoagulation. Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) should be used in the antenatal setting; warfarin is teratogenic and crosses the placenta, and the direct oral anticoagulants have not been studied in pregnancy or lactation. LMWH can be transitioned to unfractionated heparin around the time of delivery because of a shorter half-life.

Lower extremity ultrasonography is required to diagnose deep venous thrombosis, which most often occurs in the left lower extremity in pregnancy because of anatomic compression of the iliac vein.

Diagnosing pulmonary embolism in pregnancy is challenging because of the desire to limit radiation exposure. CT pulmonary angiography leads to a higher maternal exposure than ventilation-perfusion scanning. Perfusion-only imaging can also be used to decrease radiation exposure and is most useful in patients expected to have a normal ventilation scan based on a normal chest radiograph. In pregnant persons with suspected pulmonary embolism, using the combination of D-dimer testing and the YEARS criteria can help avoid imaging and thereby decrease radiation exposure ( [Table: Table: YEARS Criteria]

).

LMWH is the treatment of choice for pregnant patients with VTE. Warfarin is teratogenic and should be avoided in the first trimester, although it may be the preferred treatment in pregnant patients in a limited number of highly thromboembolic conditions such as the presence of a mechanical heart valve (see Anticoagulation Therapy During Pregnancy in Cardiovascular Medicine). However, warfarin is safe to resume after delivery and with breastfeeding. LMWH must be stopped at least 24 hours before delivery; unfractionated heparin can be used instead and discontinued as labor progresses or several hours before cesarean section. Postpartum anticoagulation is begun as soon as hemostasis is achieved and should continue for at least 6 weeks. The goal duration of treatment for uncomplicated VTE during pregnancy is a total anticoagulation period of 3 to 6 months.

Thrombolytic therapy raises the risk of maternal hemorrhage and should be reserved for life-threatening situations.

Approach to the Patient With Abnormal Liver Chemistry Studies

Liver test abnormalities can be used to categorize liver disease into hepatocellular or cholestatic patterns.

Elevations of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels reflect hepatocellular injury. Elevated ALT levels are more specific for hepatocellular injury because ALT is primarily found in the liver, whereas AST is also present in other tissues, such as muscle (cardiac and skeletal).

Elevation in alkaline phosphatase (ALP) represents a cholestatic pattern and typically results from biliary disorders. However, ALP is also produced in bone, intestine, and placenta; elevated ALP is expected in pregnancy. ALP fractionation or gamma-glutamyltransferase can help determine a hepatic source of ALP elevation.

Bilirubin has unconjugated and conjugated forms. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (elevated indirect bilirubin [total bilirubin minus direct bilirubin]) often results from hemolysis or benign disorders of bilirubin conjugation, such as Gilbert syndrome (see Gilbert Syndrome in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease). Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (elevated direct bilirubin) usually reflects a liver or biliary disorder.

Elevated prothrombin time/INR and decreased serum albumin levels may reflect diminished liver synthetic function. Albumin levels can also be decreased in the following instances:

  • Malnutrition
  • Nephrotic syndrome
  • Acute inflammation (such as severe sepsis)
  • Chronic inflammation
  • Protein-losing enteropathies

Prothrombin time/INR can be elevated in vitamin K deficiency, warfarin therapy, and inherited or acquired factor deficiency.

The relative levels and severity of AST, ALT, and ALP elevations provide clues about the cause of liver disease ( [Table: Table: Liver Chemistry Studies in Common Hepatobiliary Disorders]

). The duration of abnormal liver test results is also important in evaluating causes of liver injury (acute: <6 months; chronic: ≥6 months).

Abdominal ultrasonography is an appropriate initial imaging modality and may show increased echogenicity, consistent with liver steatosis, biliary ductal dilation in cases of biliary obstruction, or possible features of cirrhosis (liver nodularity) or portal hypertension (recanalized paraumbilical vein, splenomegaly, ascites).

When fibrosis and cirrhosis are suspected, both serologic and imaging techniques are used to detect and estimate the extent of fibrosis and potentially avoid biopsy. Blood-based noninvasive liver diseases assessments, such as the AST-to-platelet ratio index and the Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) index, should be the initial instruments used to screen for fibrosis in chronic liver disease, including chronic viral hepatitis and metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). A noninvasive imaging technique, elastography (transient, shear wave, or magnetic resonance), assesses liver stiffness as a measure of fibrosis. Ultrasound-based elastography or magnetic resonance elastography are used to assess for and stage the severity of fibrosis in chronic liver disease. High stiffness values may also occur with the following:

  • Significant liver inflammation (ALT level >100 U/L)
  • Hepatic congestion or severe steatosis
  • Infiltrative disorders
  • Bile duct obstruction

Disorders of the Gallbladder and Bile Ducts

Gallstones are characterized as cholesterol stones or pigment stones. Cholesterol stones result from supersaturation of bile with cholesterol; they account for approximately 75% of gallstones in the United States. Risk factors for cholesterol stones include the following:

  • Older age
  • Female sex (twice as likely in women as in men)
  • Native American ethnicity
  • Western diet
  • Pregnancy
  • Rapid weight loss
  • Obesity
  • Total parenteral nutrition
  • Estrogen supplementation

Predisposing factors for pigment stones include the following:

  • Chronic hemolysis
  • Ineffective erythropoiesis
  • Crohn disease
  • Cirrhosis
  • Biliary stasis
  • Bacterial biliary infections

Gallstones are commonly discovered with abdominal ultrasonography (

) and CT performed for unrelated reasons.

Incidental gallstones are typically asymptomatic, and prophylactic cholecystectomy is generally not recommended. Cholecystectomy is indicated in asymptomatic patients with characteristics posing a high risk for gallbladder cancer: gallstones larger than 3 cm, porcelain gallbladder (calcification of the gallbladder wall), or gallbladder polyps larger than 1 cm.

Biliary colic results from contraction of the gallbladder in the presence of an obstructed cystic duct, usually by a gallstone. Pain is typically of acute onset, lasts 30 minutes to 6 hours, is severe and steady, and is located in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium. Pain may radiate to the right shoulder and is associated with nausea, vomiting, and diaphoresis. Symptoms may be precipitated by meals, which cause gallbladder contraction. Constant, unremitting abdominal pain is not usually associated with biliary colic.

Patients with typical biliary colic symptoms and gallstones on imaging should undergo cholecystectomy because of an increased risk for future complications, including choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, and pancreatitis.

Acute cholecystitis is caused by cystic duct obstruction and gallbladder inflammation, often accompanied by gallbladder infection. Patients present with severe right-upper-quadrant pain or epigastric pain lasting longer than 6 hours, as well as fever and tenderness in the right upper quadrant. A positive Murphy sign (inspiratory arrest during deep inspiration upon palpation of the gallbladder fossa) may be present.

Laboratory studies may show leukocytosis; liver chemistries are often normal or minimally elevated unless complications, such as common bile duct obstruction or cholangitis, are present. Acute cholecystitis is suggested by ultrasound showing gallbladder wall thickening and/or edema and a sonographic Murphy sign (arrest of respiration with compression by the ultrasonography probe) (

). Lack of gallbladder filling on hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scanning supports this diagnosis; this test is appropriate in the setting of a high clinical likelihood of acute cholecystitis but a negative or indeterminate ultrasound finding.

Treatment includes analgesia, intravenous antibiotics with gram-negative and anaerobic coverage, and cholecystectomy. Most patients should undergo cholecystectomy during initial hospitalization. Emergency surgery is necessary for suspected gallbladder perforation or emphysematous cholecystitis (infection of the gallbladder wall with gas-forming organisms, such as Clostridium perfringens). Most patients should undergo cholecystectomy during initial hospitalization. Patients with high surgical risk who respond to antibiotics can be reassessed later to determine whether their surgical risk has decreased. In patients who are poor surgical candidates and do not respond to antibiotics, percutaneous cholecystostomy tube drainage or endoscopic drainage can be pursued.

Acalculous cholecystitis typically occurs in critically ill patients and results from gallbladder ischemia, which can be complicated by enteric bacterial infection. Risk factors include the following:

  • Cardiac surgery
  • Sepsis
  • Burns
  • Vasculitis

Alert patients typically present with pain, similar to that seen in cholecystitis. However, in sedated or mechanically ventilated patients, it may present with leukocytosis, jaundice, or sepsis. The diagnosis is made by ultrasound showing pericholecystic fluid, gallbladder distention, and pneumatosis without stones (

).

Treatment entails intravenous antibiotics to cover enteric bacteria and cholecystectomy. A percutaneous cholecystostomy tube may be needed for unstable patients or poor surgical candidates. Endoscopic gallbladder drainage can be considered. The mortality rate for untreated acalculous cholecystitis is as high as 50%.

Functional gallbladder disorder should be considered in patients with biliary pain without gallstones or structural pathology. Other causes of upper abdominal discomfort, including peptic ulcer disease and angina, should be considered. A gallbladder ejection fraction less than 40% as measured by cholecystokinin-stimulated cholescintigraphy supports the diagnosis but may not predict response to cholecystectomy.

Reassurance and antispasmodic agents may be of benefit. If no other cause of pain is found, pain recurs, and the gallbladder ejection fraction is less than 40%, then cholecystectomy can be considered.

Common bile duct stones are a leading cause of obstructive jaundice and pancreatitis. Although 20% of common duct stones pass spontaneously and less than 50% of patients develop symptoms, stone extraction should be offered to most patients. Symptoms of common bile duct stones include jaundice and abdominal pain. Common duct stones may be visualized by transabdominal ultrasonography. In the absence of visualization, an elevated serum bilirubin level and dilated common duct on ultrasonography suggest the diagnosis. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is the preferred method for stone extraction and should be performed in patients with a high likelihood of choledocholithiasis (

). In patients who are suspected of having common duct stones but have indeterminate findings on ultrasonography, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) or endoscopic ultrasonography should be performed to avoid ERCP risks. Cholecystectomy should be performed within 2 weeks of stone extraction.

Cholangitis is infection of the biliary tree, usually in the setting of biliary stasis or obstruction. Symptoms include fever, jaundice, and right-upper-quadrant pain (Charcot triad). Patients with cholangitis present with leukocytosis and elevated serum direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase levels. In more severe cases, altered mental status and septic shock may also occur; this is referred to as the Reynolds pentad and occurs in only 3.5% to 5% of patients. Cholangitis is potentially life-threatening; antibiotics targeting gram-negative Enterobacteriaceae should be administered immediately. Common bile duct stones should be removed urgently with ERCP in patients with cholangitis, after which elective cholecystectomy should be performed during initial hospitalization to reduce the risk for complications. In patients who are not surgical candidates, endoscopic sphincterotomy can facilitate passage of additional common bile duct stones.

Gallbladder polyps are usually found incidentally and can be seen on 1% to 5% of gallbladder ultrasounds. Neoplastic adenomas represent less than 0.5% of polyps. The best predictor of a malignant lesion is size, with polyps 1 cm or greater more likely to be neoplastic. Gallbladder polyps associated with gallbladder stones or primary sclerosing cholangitis are also more likely to be neoplastic. See

.

Gallbladder cancer is rare, with an incidence in the United States of 1 to 2 cases per 100,000. Risk factors include active smoking, large gallstones (>3 cm), gallbladder polyps larger than 1 cm, primary sclerosing cholangitis, biliary (ductal) cysts with an abnormal pancreaticobiliary duct junction, and obesity. The gallbladder is a reservoir for Salmonella typhi in chronically infected patients, and these patients are also at higher risk for gallbladder cancer.

Early cancers are often asymptomatic or present with biliary colic. Symptoms in advanced cancer include the following:

  • Right-upper-quadrant pain
  • Nausea
  • Vomiting
  • Weight loss
  • Jaundice

Gallbladder cancer should be suspected if a gallbladder mass is seen on CT or MRI or a palpable right-upper-quadrant mass is found on examination.

Early gallbladder cancer is commonly diagnosed incidentally when cholecystectomy is performed for biliary colic. Incidental tumors invading the lamina propria (stage T1a) do not require further treatment; more advanced lesions require more extensive surgery.

The treatment of choice for gallbladder cancer is surgery. Unresectable disease is treated with chemotherapy with or without radiation or with palliative care.

Cholangiocarcinoma is rare but has become an increasingly recognized malignancy. Affected patients are typically 50 to 70 years of age. See [Table: Table: Risk Factors for Cholangiocarcinoma]

. Symptoms, including jaundice, right-upper-quadrant pain, and constitutional symptoms, typically develop with advanced-stage disease.

There are three types of cholangiocarcinoma:

  • Perihilar: occurs at the confluence of right and left hepatic ducts
  • Distal: occurs in the extrahepatic bile duct distal to the cystic duct
  • Intrahepatic: occurs in bile ducts within the liver parenchyma

Most cases of cholangiocarcinoma are extrahepatic.

Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma can be difficult to diagnose and may require both magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). During ERCP, bile-duct brushings are obtained for cytologic examination and fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH), and possibly biliary biopsies. Serial ERCP may be required because cytologic studies have low sensitivity. First-line therapy is resection. Patients with unresectable perihilar cholangiocarcinoma smaller than 3 cm and without extrahepatic spread can be evaluated for liver transplantation. Percutaneous or transluminal biopsy excludes liver transplantation because of the risk for tumor seeding.

Distal cholangiocarcinoma is diagnosed by ultrasonography, with or without contrast, in addition to contrast-enhanced CT and MRCP. Tissue confirmation may require repeat sampling for cytology, FISH, and/or biliary biopsies. Staging requires CT, MRI, and fluorodeoxyglucose PET. The preferred treatment is pancreaticoduodenectomy; however, only a small percentage of patients are candidates, and the rate of recurrence is high. Gemcitabine-cisplatin combined with durvalumab is standard therapy for patients who cannot undergo pancreaticoduodenectomy, and palliative endoscopic procedures exist for bile duct drainage. Five-year survival for patients with distal cholangiocarcinoma, including those who undergo resection, is low (20%-30%).

Screening for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma should include liver ultrasonography at 6- month intervals in patients with cirrhosis and annual MRCP plus measurement of CA 19-9 level in those with primary sclerosing cholangitis. Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is typically diagnosed through multiphase CT or MRI of the liver along with biopsy for histologic confirmation. MRI is preferred to CT for disease staging. Those with possible resectable disease should undergo fluorodeoxyglucose PET to identify lymph node or distant metastases. This should be followed by endoscopic ultrasonography with fine-needle aspiration of suspect lymph nodes identified during staging.

Patients with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma should be considered for discussion by a multidisciplinary tumor board. If possible, patients should be considered for surgical resection followed by adjuvant capecitabine or S-1. Chemotherapy may be offered to patients who are not candidates for surgical therapy. Immune checkpoint inhibitors may be a consideration in those in whom first-line chemotherapy (gemcitabine/cisplatin) fails. Those with early-stage disease in the setting of cirrhosis may be candidates for liver transplantation.

Cholestatic Liver Diseases

Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), previously termed primary biliary cirrhosis, is an autoimmune disease affecting the small and medium bile ducts. The female-to-male predominance is 9 to 1. PBC is often asymptomatic, but the most common presenting symptoms are fatigue and/or pruritus. Liver chemistry tests usually demonstrate a cholestatic pattern of injury with elevated serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) level. Ultrasonography or magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) should be performed to exclude large bile duct obstruction.

Diagnosis of PBC does not require liver biopsy when the ALP level is at least 1.5 times the upper limit of normal and the antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) result is positive. In patients with negative AMA results (approximately 5% of patients with PBC are AMA-negative) and strong suspicion for PBC, liver biopsy is necessary. Elastography can be used for fibrosis staging.

Initial treatment is ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), which results in histologic improvement, improves survival rates, and diminishes the need for liver transplantation. There are several criteria for biochemical response to treatment that incorporate ALP and often bilirubin. Patients with normal bilirubin and albumin levels who respond to treatment have a life expectancy similar to that of persons without PBC. Options for patients who do not respond to or are intolerant of UDCA include a peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor agonist, such as elafibranor or seladelpar, or a fibrate (off-label), either added to UDCA or as monotherapy.

PBC is associated with other autoimmune conditions, particularly autoimmune thyroid disease. Thus, thyroid-stimulating hormone level should be checked yearly. In addition, patients with PBC are at increased risk for osteoporosis and should have adequate vitamin D and calcium intake. Bone mineral density should be assessed with dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry at diagnosis and every 2 years. Patients with elevated lipid levels may be at risk for cardiovascular disease and can be considered for lipid-lowering therapy. Patients should also be screened and treated for fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies. First-degree relatives of patients with PBC, especially women, should be screened by periodically checking ALP level.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is an autoimmune fibroinflammatory disease of the large bile ducts, but it can also affect the small bile ducts (small-duct PSC). It is more common in men than women, which is unique among the autoimmune liver diseases. PSC often presents without symptoms with a cholestatic pattern of liver enzyme abnormalities; pruritus may also be the presenting feature.

PSC can be diagnosed by MRCP (see

). Diagnosis does not usually require liver biopsy unless small-duct PSC is suspected.

PSC is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) in more than 70% of cases (primarily ulcerative colitis); conversely, up to 7.5% of patients with ulcerative colitis have PSC. All patients with PSC without known IBD should undergo colonoscopy at the time of PSC diagnosis. Patients with IBD and PSC have a high risk for colon cancer and should undergo surveillance colonoscopy every 1 to 2 years.

Patients with PSC have a 15% lifetime risk for cholangiocarcinoma (see Cholangiocarcinoma in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease). Yearly MRCP with or without CA 19-9 measurement is recommended for cholangiocarcinoma surveillance. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography should be considered in patients with a dominant stricture or bile duct mass on MRCP because either of these could indicate cholangiocarcinoma. The incidence of cholangiocarcinoma is highest in the first 2 years after PSC diagnosis. There is also an increased risk for gallbladder cancer in PSC; regular screening with ultrasonography should be considered. The management of gallbladder polyps is discussed in Gallbladder Polyps in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease.

There is no proven effective medical therapy for PSC; median transplant-free survival for patients with PSC is 12 years. Transplantation should be considered for patients with decompensated cirrhosis, those with recurrent bacterial cholangitis, and highly selected patients with perihilar cholangiocarcinoma.
