Metabolic Liver Diseases

Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD, formerly termed nonalcoholic fatty liver disease [NAFLD]) is the most common chronic liver disease in the world and has an estimated prevalence of 30% to 35% in the United States. MASLD encompasses a spectrum of disease, but the key underlying metabolic dysfunction is insulin resistance. Most cases do not involve liver inflammation; excess fat in the liver (steatosis) without inflammation or fibrosis is considered relatively benign. In the United States, 5% to 12% of the population has liver steatosis with inflammation (metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis [MASH], formerly known as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis [NASH]), which in turn can lead to progressive fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis. Unrecognized MASH is likely a major cause of cryptogenic cirrhosis. The mechanisms by which patients with MASLD develop MASH are not fully understood, but metabolic, genetic, and environmental factors contribute.

Most patients with MASLD are asymptomatic; some may note nonspecific symptoms, such as fatigue or vague right-upper-quadrant abdominal discomfort. Mildly elevated serum aminotransferase levels are common in MASLD, but these levels can be normal even with advanced fibrosis. Liver steatosis is most often diagnosed by imaging.

The diagnosis of inflammation (i.e., MASH) in a patient with hepatic steatosis can be challenging. Liver biopsy is the only definitive test for MASH but is impractical to perform in all patients with liver steatosis. Patients with the following criteria are presumed to have MASH:

  • Elevated aminotransferase levels
  • Negative result on serologic evaluation for alternative causes
  • No significant alcohol consumption (significant is defined as >21 standard drinks per week for men and >14 standard drinks per week for women)
  • Clinical features of the metabolic syndrome
  • Imaging findings consistent with liver steatosis

Low titers of autoantibodies (antinuclear antibody, anti–smooth muscle antibody) are present in 20% of patients with MASLD, but the clinical significance of this is unknown. Patients with MASLD and significant alcohol intake are considered to have metabolic dysfunction–associated and alcoholic liver disease (MetALD).

The American Diabetes Association recommends that patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus or prediabetes be screened for liver fibrosis, even if liver enzyme levels are normal, using the Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) score. The NAFLD Fibrosis score and FIB-4 score use clinical data to identify patients at risk for advanced fibrosis. Patients with low FIB-4 scores are classified as low risk and are managed with weight loss and lifestyle modifications. Repeat noninvasive testing in 1 to 2 years is suggested in patients with metabolic risk factors, such as prediabetes or type 2 diabetes. Patients with indeterminate FIB-4 scores should undergo liver stiffness measurement with vibration-controlled transient elastography. This test can help determine whether patients with MASH have developed significant hepatic fibrosis; patients with low liver stiffness are at low risk, but patients with measurements consistent with advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis should be evaluated by a hepatologist. Patients with a high FIB-4 score should be referred to hepatology for further evaluation and management. Liver biopsy should be considered when the diagnosis is in doubt or when the presence of hepatic fibrosis cannot otherwise be determined.

MASLD management focuses on weight loss, diet modification, and moderate exercise. A target of 7% to 10% weight loss (through lifestyle modification, pharmacotherapy, or bariatric surgery) is associated with improvement in liver histology. Minimizing refined sugars, particularly fructose, may be beneficial. Moderate exercise (150 minutes weekly) has been associated with decreased liver steatosis and aminotransferase levels, independent of weight loss. Resmetirom, a thyroid hormone receptor-β agonist, is approved for the treatment of adults with MASH and moderate to severe fibrosis (stage F2 or F3) but not cirrhosis. Potential drug interactions (e.g., clopidogrel and statins) should be reviewed, and monitoring for hepatotoxicity is recommended. Thyroid function should be evaluated before treatment. Off-label use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists or pioglitazone may be considered for persons with type 2 diabetes or obesity, and vitamin E may be considered for the treatment of MASH in persons without type 2 diabetes. All pharmacologic therapy for MASH should be prescribed in conjunction with comprehensive lifestyle modification.

Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in patients with MASH and statin therapy should be considered, even in the presence of elevated aminotransferase levels. Alcohol consumption can contribute to disease progression in MASLD. It is important to regularly assess alcohol consumption and advise abstinence in patients with significant fibrosis (fibrosis stage ≥2).

Gilbert syndrome is a common benign disorder of bilirubin metabolism arising from variants in the UGT1A1 gene promoter, which is responsible for bilirubin conjugation in the liver. Estimated population prevalence is approximately 5% to 10%. Patients typically present in adolescence with asymptomatic episodes of mild jaundice precipitated by fasting, physical exertion, or stress. Laboratory testing demonstrates unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia; total bilirubin generally does not exceed 5 mg/dL (85.5 µmol/L). Results of other liver tests are normal. The differential diagnosis includes hemolysis and drug-induced hyperbilirubinemia.

The diagnosis is typically made by demonstrating the following:

  • Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal aminotransferase and ALP levels on repeat testing
  • Exclusion of hemolysis (e.g., with a peripheral blood smear, reticulocyte count, haptoglobin and/or lactate dehydrogenase levels)
  • Exclusion of drug-induced hyperbilirubinemia

Genetic testing is performed only if there is diagnostic confusion. No therapy is required.

Hereditary hemochromatosis (HH) is an autosomal recessive condition characterized by excessive accumulation of iron in the liver due to a variant in the genes that control hepcidin synthesis, resulting in increased intestinal iron absorption. HH is most commonly associated with homozygosity of the C282Y variant of the HFE gene or, less commonly, with C282Y/H63D compound heterozygosity. However, the penetrance of these variants is low; only about 10% of persons carrying homozygous C282Y/C282Y HFE alleles develop iron overload. Other pathogenic HFE variants and non-HFE variants are rare. C282Y heterozygosity (C282Y/wild-type) is not associated with HH.

Elevated transferrin saturation and elevated serum ferritin levels suggest the possibility of HH, but genetic testing is required to confirm the diagnosis. Notably, other chronic liver diseases can be associated with elevated ferritin levels, particularly alcoholic liver disease and MASLD.

Patients with HH who have a ferritin level above 1000 ng/mL (1000 µg/L) or abnormal serum aminotransferase levels at the time of diagnosis should undergo further testing for cirrhosis. A liver biopsy for fibrosis assessment and measurement of hepatic iron content should be considered. Removal of excessive iron, usually by therapeutic phlebotomy, should be performed in all patients with HH and evidence of iron overload. Patients with cirrhosis should be screened for hepatocellular carcinoma. Liver failure from hereditary hemochromatosis is treated with liver transplantation.

First-degree relatives of patients with HH should be screened with transferrin saturation and serum ferritin level first, followed by HFE genotype testing if results of iron studies are abnormal.

See further discussion in Primary/Hereditary Hemochromatosis in Hematology.

α~1-Antitrypsin deficiency is an autosomal codominant genetic disorder that in some cases results in accumulation of a misfolded form of α~1-antitrypsin in the liver. Homozygosity for this condition may cause liver injury, hepatomegaly from retained α~1-antitrypsin protein, and eventual cirrhosis. α~1-Antitrypsin deficiency also leads to lack of inhibition of elastase in the lung, with resultant characteristic emphysema of the lower lung parenchyma. Patients heterozygous for α~1-antitrypsin deficiency may be at increased risk for liver injury in the setting of other liver diseases, including viral hepatitis and MASLD. Supplemental α~1-antitrypsin prevents progressive lung injury but does not affect cirrhosis progression. Liver transplantation is required to treat liver failure resulting from α~1-antitrypsin deficiency.

Wilson disease is a rare autosomal recessive disorder that causes copper accumulation in the liver, brain, and cornea. Liver manifestations of Wilson disease are highly variable, ranging from asymptomatic liver enzyme abnormalities to cirrhosis or acute liver failure (ALF). Unexplained liver disease in any patient younger than 40 years should prompt an investigation for Wilson disease, although a small minority of patients may present after the age of 40 years.

ALF in Wilson disease may be accompanied by Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia (secondary to sudden release of copper from hepatocytes), acute kidney injury, and normal or significantly low serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels. Neuropsychiatric disease can be seen in patients with Wilson disease (highly variable but most often dysarthria, dystonia, parkinsonism, tremor, and/or ataxia). Kayser-Fleischer rings around the corneal-sclero junction are seen on slit-lamp examination in nearly all patients with Wilson disease and associated neurologic findings and in 50% of patients without neurologic manifestations.

Laboratory evaluation is typically notable for low serum ceruloplasmin and a high 24-hour urinary copper level. Assessment for Kayser-Fleischer rings should be performed. Histologic changes on liver biopsy can be nonspecific, although hepatic copper levels are typically high. Genetic testing for ATP7B gene variants is used to confirm the clinical diagnosis.

Treatment is lifelong and involves administration of copper chelators, either d-penicillamine or trientine and/or oral zinc to decrease intestinal absorption of copper. Urgent liver transplantation is necessary in ALF secondary to Wilson disease.

Hepatitis

Worldwide, approximately 58 million persons are infected with hepatitis C virus (HCV). HCV is most commonly transmitted through injection drug use, blood transfusions before 1992, or high-risk sexual practices. All patients age 18 to 79 years should receive a one-time screening for HCV antibody, followed by HCV RNA testing if the antibody result is positive. Although guidelines from the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force suggest not screening patients older than 79 years in the absence of specific risk factors, the CDC does not specify an upper age limit. Patients with continued risk for infection ( [Table: Table: Indications for HCV Screening and Testing]

) should undergo ongoing periodic screening. Patients positive for HCV antibody and HCV RNA have active infection. The antibody result remains positive for life, but positivity does not confer immunity from infection or reinfection in those who are negative for HCV RNA.

Acute HCV infection is usually asymptomatic, but symptoms such as jaundice, nausea, and right-upper-quadrant pain can occur. A positive HCV RNA but negative HCV antibody result is consistent with acute infection. Although symptomatic acute infection is associated with higher rates of spontaneous clearance, antiviral treatment is now recommended instead of monitoring for clearance.

HCV results in chronic infection in 60% to 80% of patients; 10% to 30% progress to cirrhosis over two to three decades. Risk for hepatocellular carcinoma in patients with cirrhosis is 2% to 4% per year.

Several extrahepatic diseases are associated with chronic HCV infection, including the following:

  • Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
  • Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
  • Mixed cryoglobulinemia
  • Porphyria cutanea tarda (see Porphyria Cutanea Tarda in Dermatology)

All patients with HCV infection should be tested for HBV (see Hepatitis B in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease for further discussion) because routes of transmission may be shared and HBV can reactivate during direct-acting antiviral therapy for HCV infection. Susceptible patients should receive HBV vaccination. Patients who test positive for HBsAg with detectable HBV DNA and who do not meet standard HBV treatment criteria should undergo regular HBV DNA monitoring until 12 weeks after completion of HCV treatment, or they can receive HBV prophylaxis.

Treatment should be considered for all HCV-infected patients except those with a short life expectancy or those who are at high risk for treatment nonadherence. Active substance use disorder is not by itself a contraindication to HCV treatment, because clearance can reduce transmission in the community. Patients with decompensated cirrhosis should see a hepatologist before treatment and be considered for liver transplantation.

Patients being considered for treatment should be assessed for cirrhosis by one or more of the following methods (see Approach to the Patient With Abnormal Liver Chemistry Studies in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease):

  • Clinical evaluation (e.g., decompensation or evidence of portal hypertension)
  • FIB-4 or other serologic tests
  • Elastography

Routine liver biopsy for pretreatment fibrosis assessment is not recommended.

Currently approved treatment regimens include a combination of direct-acting antivirals with different mechanisms of action to minimize virologic resistance. In treatment-naïve persons, simplified pangenotypic regimens can be used based on the presence or absence of cirrhosis (current recommendations on HCV treatment regimens can be found at www.hcvguidelines.org). Rates of sustained virologic response (SVR), defined by undetectable HCV RNA in blood 12 weeks after treatment ends, exceed 90% to 95% in most patients. A treatment algorithm is available for patients with past treatment experience who have not achieved SVR.

HCV antibody positivity remains indefinitely and should not be rechecked. Patients can become reinfected if reexposed; HCV RNA testing is used to assess for reinfection. SVR markedly reduces risk for liver-related morbidity and mortality. Patients with advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis require ongoing surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma even after SVR.

Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a DNA virus affecting 296 million persons worldwide. See Hepatitis B in Foundations of Clinical Practice for HBV vaccination strategies. HBV can be transmitted in the following ways:

  • Perinatally
  • Sexual exposure
  • Direct contact with blood
  • Percutaneous exposure

Acute HBV infection may present as symptomatic acute hepatitis. Approximately 30% of adults may develop jaundice from acute infection, with aminotransferase levels as high as 3000 U/L and nonspecific symptoms (e.g., malaise, nausea, and right-upper-quadrant pain). Acute liver failure develops in approximately 0.5% of patients.

Chronic HBV infection is diagnosed after 6 months in patients with persistent hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) detected in serum. The risk for chronic HBV infection decreases with age at time of infection: newborns acquiring HBV have the highest risk (90%), whereas adults have an approximately 5% risk. Screening for chronic HBV infection with HBsAg, antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen (anti-HBs), and antibody to hepatitis B core antigen (HBc) should be performed in all adults age 18 years and older at least once in a lifetime and in all pregnant individuals during the first trimester of each pregnancy, regardless of vaccination status or previous HBV testing history. Rescreening is recommended in persons with risk factors and before initiation of immunosuppressive or cytotoxic therapy ( [Table: Table: Indications for HBV Screening and Testing]

).

Four phases of chronic HBV infection are differentiated based on immune response:

  • Immune tolerant
  • Immune active
  • Immune control (inactive carrier)
  • Reactivation (reactivation may be precipitated by immunosuppression even in patients with resolved infection)

(See

and [Table: Table: Interpretation of HBV Serology Test Results]

.)

Treatment with nucleoside analogues (entecavir or tenofovir) is advised for patients with acute liver failure, those in the immune-active phase or reactivation phase (generally those with viremia and elevated aminotransferase levels and/or necroinflammation on histopathology), and those with cirrhosis. Treatment is also recommended at the beginning of the third trimester in pregnant patients with viral load greater than 200,000 IU/mL. Lamivudine, adefovir, and telbivudine are no longer recommended because of resistance. Treatment of HBV infection in pregnancy is discussed in Viral Hepatitis in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease.

Treatment goals for patients in the hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg)–positive immune-active phase are HBeAg loss with anti-HBe seroconversion, which should then be followed by an additional 12 months of treatment (consolidation phase) before consideration of treatment withdrawal. Close follow-up is required to monitor for reactivation. Goals of treatment in the HBeAg-negative immune-active phase are HBV DNA suppression and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) normalization; oral antiviral agents are generally continued indefinitely in this setting. Patients with cirrhosis should continue oral antiviral medications indefinitely. HBsAg loss, with or without anti-HB surface antibody seroconversion, is considered a “functional cure” but rarely occurs with oral antiviral treatment. Although poorly tolerated, pegylated interferon for 48 weeks may be considered in selected patients without cirrhosis who have high ALT levels and low HBV DNA levels.

Management of an inactive carrier who is in the HbeAg-negative immune-control phase includes obtaining ALT and HBV DNA levels every 6 to 12 months because there is a low risk for spontaneous reactivation; this testing should be performed sooner if symptoms concerning for hepatitis develop. Assessment for fibrosis should also be performed with a Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) score, followed by elastography if indicated by the FIB-4 score. Treatment with antiviral therapy should be considered only if cirrhosis or evidence of reactivation is present.

Patients with chronic HBV infection (HBsAg-positive) or resolved HBV infection (HBsAg- negative and anti-HB core antibody–positive) may experience reactivation with significant immunosuppression, even if they are anti-HBs positive. Reactivation is characterized by a rise in HBV DNA and seroconversion to HBsAg positivity that is sometimes accompanied by IgM anti-HB core antibody positivity in previously HBsAg-negative/anti-HB core antibody (IgG)–positive patients. Reactivation may be asymptomatic, result in a hepatitis flare (evidenced by an ALT level >100 U/L and more than threefold above baseline), or result in hepatic failure (

).

Patients taking immunosuppressive medications may be categorized as high risk (>10%), moderate risk (1%-10%), or low risk (<1%) for reactivation (

). Patients at high risk should receive prophylactic oral antiviral therapy (tenofovir or entecavir). The American Gastroenterological Association suggests prophylactic antiviral therapy for patients at moderate risk as well, although monitoring at 1- to 3-month intervals could be considered as an alternative strategy. Patients at low risk do not require antiviral prophylaxis and can be monitored.

Approximately 40% of deaths in HBV-infected persons older than age 40 years are related to hepatocellular carcinoma or decompensated cirrhosis (see [Table: Table: Risk Factors for Cirrhosis or HCC in Chronic HBV Infection]

). Refer to Hepatocellular Carcinoma in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease for recommendations on hepatocellular carcinoma screening and surveillance.

Rare extrahepatic complications of HBV infection include the following, all of which should prompt oral antiviral therapy:

  • Membranous nephropathy
  • Membranoproliferative nephropathy
  • Polyarteritis nodosa
  • Cryoglobulinemia

Hepatitis D virus (HDV) is a defective RNA virus that requires concurrent infection with HBV for human infection. HDV infection is variably distributed globally, with higher prevalence in Eastern Europe, Southern Europe, the Mediterranean region, the Middle East, West and Central Africa, East Asia, and the Amazon Basin; it is relatively uncommon in North America. The outcome of simultaneous infection with HBV and HDV (coinfection) is similar to that of acute HBV infection; however, HDV superinfection in a patient with chronic HBV infection may present as severe acute hepatitis or worsening of chronic liver injury/inflammation and typically results in chronic HDV infection. Chronic HDV infection should be considered in individuals with positivity for HBsAg from endemic areas or those being treated for chronic HBV with evidence of persistent inflammation despite adequate HBV suppression. It is diagnosed through detection of total anti-HDV antibody in a person with a positive HBsAg test result.

Although the optimal treatment regimen is uncertain, HDV-infected patients with evidence of active liver disease should be considered for pegylated interferon treatment. In the setting of decompensated liver disease, liver transplantation is the only option.

Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is an RNA virus causing acute hepatitis. HAV infection is usually self-limited, but atypical forms include relapsing-remitting infection with cholestatic features and, rarely, acute liver failure. HAV transmission is fecal-oral. Risk factors include the following:

  • International travel
  • Contacts with HAV-infected household members
  • Men who have sex with men
  • Homelessness
  • Exposure to day care or institutionalized settings
  • Recreational drug use

HAV incidence declined dramatically after introduction of universal childhood HAV vaccination, but recent outbreaks have occurred in the United States among unvaccinated people, especially those reporting homelessness or drug use (see Hepatitis A in Foundations of Clinical Practice for vaccination recommendations).

The incubation period for HAV is 15 to 50 days. A prodrome of malaise, nausea, vomiting, fever, and right-upper-quadrant pain is followed approximately 1 week later by jaundice and hepatomegaly. Death is rare, but risk may be increased in patients with preexisting chronic liver disease.

Laboratory studies may show aminotransferase levels exceeding 1000 U/L and total bilirubin level of 10 mg/dL (171 µmol/L) or higher. Acute illness is diagnosed by HAV IgM antibodies, although false-positive results may occur. HAV IgG antibodies indicate previous infection or vaccination and provide immunity from reinfection.

Treatment is supportive, and at least 90% of patients recover fully within 3 to 6 months.

HAV can be transmitted during the prodrome stage and up to 1 week after development of jaundice. Persons who have recently been exposed to HAV and have not been immunized should receive postexposure prophylaxis as soon as possible (within 2 weeks of exposure). Postexposure prophylaxis consists of the following:

  • HAV vaccine in all nonvaccinated persons age 12 months or older
  • Immune globulin in patients who are immunocompromised, have HIV infection, have received an organ transplant, have chronic kidney disease, are undergoing dialysis, or have chronic liver disease; adults older than 40 years may also be considered for immune globulin

Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is an RNA virus with worldwide distribution. In developing countries, HEV is transmitted by the fecal-oral route through contaminated water; in developed countries, transmission occurs through contaminated food, mostly undercooked pork or venison. The incubation period is 2 to 5 weeks. Approximately 50% of cases are asymptomatic. Symptoms of HEV infection are similar to those of other acute viral hepatitides and include the following:

  • Jaundice
  • Malaise
  • Nausea
  • Vomiting
  • Anorexia
  • Right-upper-quadrant pain

Aminotransferase levels may be markedly elevated (>1000 U/L). Diagnosis relies on detecting HEV IgM or HEV RNA. Treatment is supportive, and recovery is expected in 4 to 6 weeks. Chronic HEV infection is typically seen only in immunocompromised patients (e.g., solid organ transplant recipients) and is treated with ribavirin. HEV infection should be considered in patients with an unknown cause of acute hepatitis and in immunocompromised patients with chronic hepatitis.

Other viruses can cause hepatitis. These viruses, along with their symptoms, laboratory findings, and treatment options, are listed in [Table: Table: Other Viral Causes of Hepatitis]

.

Autoimmune hepatitis is four times more common in women than men and can be associated with other autoimmune diseases (e.g., autoimmune thyroiditis, rheumatoid arthritis, or ulcerative colitis). It can affect persons of any age but most frequently occurs in middle-aged adults. The clinical presentation of autoimmune hepatitis varies widely from asymptomatic elevation of aminotransferase levels to acute liver failure. Patients with features of acute liver failure require urgent transfer to a transplant center. Diagnosis is based on the following:

  • Elevated serum aminotransferase levels
  • Positive results on tests for one or more autoantibodies (e.g., antinuclear, anti–smooth muscle, anti–liver kidney microsome type 1, anti–liver cytosol 1, or anti–soluble liver antigen/liver-pancreas antibodies)
  • Elevated total IgG
  • Exclusion of other diagnoses (e.g., Wilson disease, viral hepatitis, and drug-induced liver injury)
  • Liver histology

The initial goal of treatment is to induce biochemical remission, typically with glucocorticoids alone or in combination with azathioprine. Biochemical remission occurs in 80% of patients within 3 years of starting therapy, whereas histologic remission lags by several months or more. Duration of treatment should be 2 to 3 years before consideration of withdrawal. Liver biopsy is recommended to determine histologic response before consideration of drug withdrawal. High relapse rates after discontinuation of treatment underscore the need for serial monitoring of liver tests.

bodies.hpsec24006:
Drug-Induced Liver Injury

Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) encompasses a spectrum of liver injury patterns and severity. DILI can be induced by prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal/complementary and alternative medications, as well as by nutritional supplements. Thus, patients suspected of having DILI should be asked about exposure to medications in the past 6 months, both prescription and nonprescription, including supplements. The National Institutes of Health’s LiverTox tool is a useful resource to assess a given medication’s risk for hepatotoxicity.

The mechanism of action of DILI can be predictable (dose-dependent intrinsic hepatotoxicity) or idiosyncratic (unpredictable). Acetaminophen is the medication most recognized to have predictable hepatotoxicity. People who chronically drink alcohol can develop acetaminophen hepatotoxicity even when taking therapeutic doses of acetaminophen. The early recognition of acetaminophen-induced liver injury is critical so that N-acetylcysteine can be administered promptly to prevent liver failure.

Of the many agents that can cause idiosyncratic DILI, the two most common classes are antibiotics (particularly amoxicillin-clavulanate) and antiepileptics (phenytoin and valproate), representing 60% of all DILI cases. Immune checkpoint inhibitors are an increasingly common cause of DILI.

The pattern of liver test abnormalities and histologic injury varies widely. Injury may be predominantly hepatocellular (e.g., acetaminophen), cholestatic (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate), or mixed (e.g., phenytoin). It is important to consider and exclude other potential causes based on the biochemical pattern of injury. Liver biopsy is not required for the diagnosis but may be helpful when the diagnosis is uncertain; histopathologic findings are rarely pathognomonic for DILI, although features of autoimmune hepatitis can be seen in DILI-induced autoimmune hepatitis.

DILI management requires identifying and discontinuing the offending drug; resolution of liver injury supports the diagnosis. DILI with autoimmune features (e.g., associated with immune checkpoint inhibitors) is often treated with glucocorticoids. Reexposure to the drug to demonstrate recurrence is not generally advisable because of the risk for severe toxicity upon rechallenge. In most cases, resolution occurs after drug discontinuation. However, jaundice that occurs with cholestatic drug reactions can take months to resolve and may even progress to the need for liver transplantation.

bodies.hpsec24007:
Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease

Alcohol-associated liver disease takes the form of steatosis or steatohepatitis accompanied by varying degrees of fibrosis or cirrhosis. A history of alcohol use is the most important component in diagnosing alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD), although not all patients are forthcoming about alcohol use. See Alcohol in Interdisciplinary Medicine for more information about screening for alcohol use disorder. ALD is the leading cause of liver-related mortality in the United States, contributing to nearly half of cirrhosis-related hospitalizations and more than 40% of listings for liver transplantation.

Alcoholic hepatitis (AH) is a distinct clinical syndrome of severe steatohepatitis in the setting of heavy alcohol use, often presenting with jaundice, right-upper-quadrant or epigastric abdominal pain, and/or abdominal distention from ascites. Ascites is common, even in the absence of underlying cirrhosis; thus, it may be difficult to determine whether a patient with AH has underlying cirrhosis. Physical examination may show evidence of hepatomegaly and/or findings of advanced liver disease, including the following:

  • Muscle wasting
  • Jaundice
  • Spider angiomata
  • Gynecomastia
  • Testicular atrophy
  • Palmar erythema

Laboratory evaluation of AH is typically notable for elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels and an AST-to-ALT ratio greater than 2. AST or ALT levels greater than 500 U/L should raise the question of an alternative diagnosis or concurrent liver injury (e.g., from acetaminophen).

AH is most often diagnosed clinically; liver biopsy is rarely required. All patients require assessment for nutritional deficiencies, thiamine replacement, and alcohol use disorder treatment (see Alcohol in Interdisciplinary Medicine for additional information regarding alcohol use disorder treatment).

Severity of alcoholic hepatitis has historically been determined by the Maddrey discriminant function (MDF) score. However, the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score is now the preferred scoring instrument to assess severity, predict mortality, and guide glucocorticoid therapy. Nonsevere AH (MELD score ≤20) requires supportive measures. In severe AH (MELD score >20), treatment with prednisolone (which, unlike prednisone, does not require hepatic metabolism) is recommended. Contraindications to prednisolone include the following:

  • Active infection
  • Upper gastrointestinal bleeding
  • Severe kidney injury
  • Concomitant liver disease (especially hepatitis C virus or hepatitis B virus infection)
  • Multiorgan failure

Intravenous N-acetylcysteine is recommended as an adjuvant to glucocorticoids in patients with severe AH.

Pentoxifylline is no longer recommended for treatment of AH. The universal use of prophylactic antibiotics for patients hospitalized for AH is also not recommended.

Response to glucocorticoids can be assessed on day 7 (or day 4, which has been shown to have similar accuracy to measurement on day 7) with the Lille score. Because of risk for infection, prednisolone should be discontinued in patients who do not respond to treatment (Lille score >0.45); those who do respond should continue prednisolone for a total of 28 days. Select patients with severe AH may be considered for early liver transplantation.

All patients with AH should have dietary assessment, because malnutrition is common and nutritional supplementation may improve clinical outcomes.

Approximately 25% of patients who drink heavily develop cirrhosis. Alcoholic cirrhosis can be difficult to diagnose in the setting of AH; therefore, the diagnosis should be considered after resolution of an acute episode. Cirrhosis may be diagnosed on clinical and radiologic grounds in patients with portal hypertension that persists after a period of abstinence and a compatible history of alcohol intake. Elastography should not be used in the presence of significant liver inflammation (AST or ALT level >100 U/L) because it will increase liver stiffness. However, in patients who have had improvement in liver test results with continued abstinence, elastography can be considered to assess for advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis. Liver biopsy is sometimes necessary in cases with diagnostic ambiguity. Nutritional assessments and alcohol treatment are required. Adequate protein intake (1.0-1.5 g/kg body weight/day from predominantly vegetarian sources) and late evening snacks are recommended in patients with cirrhosis. Alcohol abstinence can result in significant stabilization of liver function and reversal of portal hypertension. Patients with alcohol-associated liver disease and evidence of cirrhosis with or without portal hypertension should be referred to hepatology for further management and consideration of liver transplantation, regardless of duration of alcohol abstinence.

bodies.hpsec24008:
Vascular Diseases of the Liver

Portal vein thrombosis is common in patients with decompensated cirrhosis and is due to reduced portal inflow, hypercoagulability, and endothelial dysfunction (Virchow triad). It occasionally occurs in patients without cirrhosis, including those with pancreatitis, sepsis, pregnancy, intraabdominal infection, and malignancy. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, fever, and ascites. It is typically diagnosed by abdominal Doppler ultrasonography; contrast-enhanced CT or MRI should be completed to delineate the extent of thrombosis and to assess for tumor thrombosis.

Chronic portal vein thrombosis is typically asymptomatic and does not usually require anticoagulant therapy unless thrombophilia, bowel ischemia, or progression of thrombus is present. Patients with acute portal vein thrombosis should receive anticoagulation unless risk for bleeding is prohibitive. Direct oral anticoagulants, vitamin K antagonists, or low-molecular-weight heparin are the anticoagulants of choice. Systemic thrombolytic therapy and catheter-directed thrombolysis are rarely indicated.

Budd-Chiari syndrome describes any disease process that obstructs the normal outflow of blood from the liver, usually as thrombosis of the hepatic veins. The syndrome may be associated with any of the following:

  • Myeloproliferative neoplasms
  • Pregnancy
  • Oral contraceptive use
  • Inflammatory bowel disease
  • Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
  • Inherited thrombophilias
  • Malignancy (especially hepatocellular carcinoma and renal cell carcinoma)
  • Vascular web

Characteristic symptoms include hepatomegaly, ascites, and right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain. Budd-Chiari syndrome is typically diagnosed by Doppler ultrasonography in the appropriate clinical setting. The caudate lobe of the liver is hypertrophied because caudate venous outflow is directly into the inferior vena cava rather than through the hepatic veins. Long-term anticoagulation is required in patients with Budd-Chiari syndrome, although bleeding risks can be significant in patients with acute or chronic liver disease, portal hypertension, and esophageal varices. Angioplasty of the hepatic veins and/or placement of a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt or surgical shunt can be used to reestablish adequate hepatic venous drainage. If liver failure develops, liver transplantation may be considered.

bodies.hpsec24009:
Advanced Chronic Liver Disease and Liver Failure

Classification of hepatic fibrosis from early fibrosis to cirrhosis is frequently performed through noninvasive means (see

), which often replaces the need for a liver biopsy. Blood-based noninvasive liver disease assessments and elastography are commonly used modalities.

The Child-Turcotte-Pugh (CTP) score and Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score are prognostic in patients with cirrhosis. The 1-year survival rates for CTP class A, B, and C cirrhosis are 100%, 80%, and 45%, respectively. See [Table: Table: Child-Turcotte-Pugh Score]

for details on the score components.

The MELD 3.0 formula includes patient sex; INR; and serum levels of bilirubin, sodium, albumin, and creatinine. It is accurate in predicting 3-month mortality. Patients with a MELD 3.0 score of 15 or greater should be referred for liver transplantation evaluation.

Both the CTP score and the MELD score can estimate postoperative morbidity and mortality in patients with cirrhosis.

Patients with chronic liver disease from any cause are at risk for cirrhosis. Compensated cirrhosis is uncomplicated and may be asymptomatic or associated with nonspecific symptoms. Decompensated cirrhosis is associated with complications, including ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, and variceal hemorrhage, as well as shortened median survival.

In the setting of advanced cirrhosis, portal venous hypertension results from obstruction of blood flow caused by the following:

  • Intrahepatic fibrosis
  • Regenerating liver nodules
  • Increased intrahepatic vascular resistance
  • Increased flow through the portal vein

Prehepatic causes, including portal vein thrombosis, and posthepatic causes, such as Budd-Chiari syndrome, can result in portal hypertension in the absence of cirrhosis. See Vascular Diseases of the Liver in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease for additional discussion of portal vein thrombosis and Budd-Chiari syndrome. The most common complications of portal hypertension include gastroesophageal varices, ascites, and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. These complications herald a high rate of progressive decompensation and mortality and should prompt consideration of liver transplantation.

Nonselective β-blockers (NSBBs) can reduce portal hypertension via a reduction in portal and collateral blood flow. Carvedilol, at a dose of 6.25 mg to 12.5 mg daily, is the recommended NSBB for treating clinically significant portal hypertension in cirrhosis. NSBBs should not be used in patients with asthma, advanced heart block, or bradyarrhythmia.

Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunts (TIPS) provide partial diversion of portal vein flow, with the goal of reducing the portosystemic pressure gradient to no greater than 12 mm Hg. TIPS is indicated for treatment of portal hypertension complicated by variceal hemorrhage, refractory ascites, hepatic hydrothorax, and other complications resistant to medical therapy. TIPS can be associated with increased hepatic encephalopathy due to shunting of blood that has bypassed hepatic detoxification. The altered venous return may also result in hepatic ischemia or heart failure. Following placement, careful monitoring of liver function, cardiac function, renal function, and encephalopathy are required.

Esophageal varices are dilated vessels within the lumen of the esophagus that provide extrahepatic pathways of blood flow from the portal to the systemic circulation (

).

If pressure in the lumen of a varix increases, esophageal varices enlarge and may spontaneously rupture, leading to bleeding, which may be massive. Pharmacologic treatment with a NSBB can reduce the risk for acute variceal hemorrhage and associated mortality. Upper endoscopy should be performed in all patients with cirrhosis not receiving an NSBB for clinically significant portal hypertension to assess for varices and risk-stratify for bleeding potential. Management of varices in patients with cirrhosis depends on varix size, presence of high-risk stigmata, and whether cirrhosis is compensated ( [Table: Table: Management of Screening-Detected Esophageal Varices]

).

See Management of Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding in Gastroenterology for discussion of management and secondary prophylaxis of variceal hemorrhage.

Gastric varices are seen in up to 25% of patients with cirrhosis and have a reported incidence of bleeding of 16% to 45% at 3 years. Varices that extend from the esophagus into the cardia of the stomach, along the lesser curvature of the stomach, are treated with band ligation and/or NSBB therapy. Varices of the gastric fundus or isolated varices in other parts of the stomach are generally not amenable to band ligation, although treatment with an NSBB can be considered. Bleeding varices in these areas are treated with the following:

  • Hemodynamic resuscitation
  • Antibiotic therapy
  • Octreotide, terlipressin, or somatostatin
  • Injection sclerotherapy (with cyanoacrylate glue) with or without endoscopic ultrasound-guided coiling

A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) should be considered for bleeding gastric varices. Balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration is another endovascular procedure to eradicate gastric varices through the systemic circulation. Medical therapy using an NSBB should be considered for prevention of bleeding from gastric varices. Isolated gastric varices can occur with splenic vein thrombosis and can be treated with splenectomy, splenic vein stenting, or splenic artery embolization.

Portal hypertensive gastropathy occurs in the presence of dilated mucosal gastric veins and venules and is a common endoscopic finding in patients with cirrhosis. It is rarely a cause of significant acute bleeding but may cause chronic blood loss. Treatment is focused on the underlying portal hypertension, including the use of an NSBB.

Gastric antral vascular ectasias (GAVE) consist of ectatic vessels that line the mucosa of the distal stomach (i.e., “watermelon stomach”). GAVE can be present in patients without cirrhosis, but in the setting of portal hypertension, these mucosal lesions tend to be more diffuse (

) than the classic linear pattern. These are typically treated with endoscopic therapy, such as argon plasma coagulation. Portal decompressive interventions, such as TIPS, are not effective.

Ascites occurs in 50% of patients within 10 years of cirrhosis diagnosis and is the most common symptom of decompensated cirrhosis. Physical examination maneuvers can detect ascites, although they perform poorly compared with ultrasonography, which has high sensitivity.

When ascites is first detected, diagnostic paracentesis should be performed. The initial laboratory investigation of ascitic fluid should include polymorphonuclear leukocyte count, fluid total protein, albumin, and serum albumin to calculate the serum–ascites albumin gradient, commonly referred to as the SAAG. The SAAG is measured by subtracting the level of albumin in the ascitic fluid from the serum albumin measurement:

SAAG = serum albumin – ascites albumin

The SAAG and the total protein levels in ascitic fluid help to determine the possible cause of the ascites (

).

In 85% of patients with ascites, the cause is cirrhosis. Management of ascites involves a sodium-restricted diet (<2 g/d). Diuretic therapy, typically with spironolactone and furosemide, is often required to assist with natriuresis. After ascites is adequately mobilized, attempts should be made to taper the diuretics to the lowest dose necessary to maintain minimal or no ascites. Body weight, kidney function, and electrolyte levels should be regularly checked after initiation of, or changes to, diuretic regimens.

Paracentesis can be performed if ascites does not resolve with sodium restriction and diuretic therapy, or if diuretic therapy is poorly tolerated.

Paracentesis is generally safe, but complications may occur. The most common complication is an ascitic fluid leak; this can be minimized with proper Z-track technique, which generates a nonlinear path between the ascitic fluid and skin. Most ascitic fluid leaks resolve spontaneously. Bleeding, infection, and bowel perforation are rare procedural complications. If more than 5 L of ascitic fluid is removed at one time, supplemental 25% albumin at a dose of 6 to 8 g/L of ascitic fluid removed should be administered to prevent circulatory dysfunction after paracentesis. Patients requiring large-volume paracentesis should be referred for specialist management. Indwelling drains in ascites due to portal hypertension are not recommended because of high rates of complications, although they may be considered for end-of-life palliation.

Patients with ascites should discontinue ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs to minimize perpetuation of kidney dysfunction. In the setting of refractory ascites, consideration should be given to discontinuing NSBBs to prevent circulatory dysfunction. This is especially relevant when there is coexisting hyponatremia, hypotension, and/or acute kidney injury.

Patients with ascites can develop pleural effusions (hepatic hydrothorax) because of permeability of the diaphragm and negative intrathoracic pressure. These effusions tend to be right-sided. Exclusion of other causes of pleural effusions is necessary. Management is similar to that for ascites, with dietary sodium restriction and diuretic therapy. Symptomatic hepatic hydrothorax may require thoracentesis or TIPS. Chemical pleurodesis is typically not beneficial. Indwelling chest tubes are not advised and should be avoided because of the high risk for complications.

Patients with refractory ascites and/or hepatic hydrothorax should be referred for specialty management of their liver dysfunction, including consideration for possible TIPS or liver transplantation.

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is an infection of portal hypertensive ascitic fluid. SBP can present with fever, abdominal pain, encephalopathy, and/or kidney dysfunction; it should be considered in any patient with ascites whose clinical status declines. In patients with cirrhosis and ascites, long-term prophylactic antibiotic therapy, typically with a fluoroquinolone, is recommended to prevent SBP if the ascitic fluid protein level is less than 1.5 g/dL (15 g/L) and is associated with one of the following:

  • Impaired kidney function (defined as serum creatinine level >1.2 mg/dL [106.1 µmol/L], blood urea nitrogen level >25 mg/dL [8.9 mmol/L], or serum sodium level <130 mEq/L [130 mmol/L])
  • Liver failure (CTP score >9 and bilirubin level >3 mg/dL [51.3 µmol/L])

SBP is diagnosed by an ascitic-fluid neutrophil count of 250/µL (0.25 × 10^9/L) or higher on diagnostic or therapeutic paracentesis. Bacterial culture of ascitic fluid, obtained after direct inoculation of at least 10 mL of fluid into culture bottles at the bedside, should also be performed but is often negative.

Prompt initiation of a third-generation cephalosporin is the initial treatment of community-acquired SBP. Patients with SBP should be treated with intravenous albumin (1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3) in addition to antibiotics. Patients with kidney dysfunction or significant hepatic dysfunction (defined as serum bilirubin level >5 mg/dL [85.5 μmoL]) are more likely to have a survival benefit with albumin therapy.

Follow-up paracentesis to demonstrate lessened inflammation can be performed if clinical improvement is not obvious. SBP commonly recurs, and indefinite secondary prophylactic therapy with once-daily norfloxacin or ciprofloxacin should be offered after SBP resolves. Temporarily withholding NSBB therapy, if present, should be considered if hypotension or acute kidney injury occurs. SBP has a high mortality rate, and patients who develop SBP should be considered for liver transplantation.

Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) refers to reversible brain dysfunction ranging from minimal abnormalities to frank coma, resulting from insufficient hepatic function and portosystemic shunting of blood caused by portal hypertension. HE can develop spontaneously or be precipitated by other factors, such as infection, sedating medications, volume depletion, or gastrointestinal bleeding, and it heralds worsening liver function.

Detection of minimal HE manifestations requires neuropsychiatric testing, although overt changes of HE, ranging from personality changes to frank coma, are common in advanced cirrhosis ( [Table: Table: Classification of Hepatic Encephalopathy]

). Asterixis—a flapping hand tremor (Video: Video of Asterixis)—is typically present in middle stages of HE. Asterixis is absent in subclinical HE and is lost as patients progress to later stages of HE, including coma.

Patients with severe HE should be monitored in an ICU. Diminishing consciousness should prompt consideration of intubation if airway-protective reflexes are lost.

Treatment of HE is multifaceted. Precipitating causes, such as infection or gastrointestinal bleeding, should be promptly treated, and sedating medications should be discontinued. Administration of the nonabsorbed disaccharide lactulose decreases gut absorption of nitrogenous substances that cause encephalopathy and results in improvement in most patients. If response to lactulose therapy is suboptimal, rifaximin can be given to alter bacterial flora in the intestine. Although rifaximin is better tolerated than lactulose, it is often not a first-line therapy because of its expense. Dietary supplementation with branched chain amino acids can also be considered for HE management.

Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) occurs in the setting of portal hypertension and is caused by reduced renal blood flow during simultaneous dilatation of the splanchnic vasculature. Most patients who develop HRS have cirrhosis, although alcoholic hepatitis and acute liver failure are also associated with HRS. The diagnosis and management of hepatorenal syndrome are discussed further in Hepatorenal Syndrome in Nephrology. Patients with cirrhosis and acute kidney injury should be considered for urgent liver transplantation evaluation given the high short-term mortality.

Hepatopulmonary syndrome is characterized by dilation of intrapulmonary vessels in patients with portal hypertension, resulting in right-to-left shunting of blood and hypoxemia. The dilated vessels reside in the inferior aspects of the lungs, and increased perfusion of these areas in the upright position results in orthodeoxia (worsening oxygen saturation while upright) and platypnea (worsening dyspnea when upright). The diagnosis should be suspected in patients with portal hypertension who have dyspnea and hypoxemia, with hypoxemia confirmed by arterial blood gas analysis. Findings of intrapulmonary shunting upon agitated saline administration during echocardiography confirm the diagnosis. Macroaggregated albumin perfusion studies can also aid in diagnosis. Hepatopulmonary syndrome is initially treated with supplemental oxygen, but the only effective treatment is liver transplantation.

Portopulmonary hypertension should be suspected in patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension who present with dyspnea on exertion. Although less common than hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension is a complication of advanced cirrhosis with a high mortality rate. Echocardiography demonstrates right ventricular systolic pressures greater than 50 mm Hg, which necessitates right-heart catheterization to confirm the diagnosis. Patients with preserved right ventricular function who attain a mean pulmonary artery pressure less than 35 mm Hg with vasodilator therapies can benefit from liver transplantation. Prostacyclin analogues, phosphodiesterase inhibitors, and endothelin receptor antagonists have been used to treat portopulmonary hypertension.

Patients with chronic liver disease are at risk for severe complications if they develop acute hepatitis; they should be vaccinated against hepatitis A and B viruses if they are not immune. Nonresponse to vaccinations is more common in patients with cirrhosis, and postvaccination immunity should be assessed. Patients with chronic liver disease should receive annual influenza vaccination, COVID-19 vaccination, and pneumococcal vaccinations. Other vaccinations should be given based on current recommendations (see Immunization in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Patients with cirrhosis should avoid the following:

  • Alcohol
  • Sedating medications, such as opioids and benzodiazepines (to prevent hepatic encephalopathy)
  • Raw shellfish, which can transmit Vibrio vulnificus, an organism causing potentially fatal infection in patients with cirrhosis

Metabolic bone disease is common in patients with cirrhosis, and patients should be screened for osteoporosis. The development of osteoporosis in patients with cirrhosis is multifactorial and is associated with jaundice (negatively affects osteoblast viability), hypogonadism, and decreased levels of insulin-like growth factor. Cholestasis also decreases absorption of vitamin D. Patients with osteoporosis are treated with calcium supplementation (ideally from dietary sources), vitamin D, and antiresorptive agents. Patients with esophageal varices should receive intravenous rather than oral bisphosphonates. Patients with osteopenia should be treated with calcium plus vitamin D. Weight-bearing exercises are encouraged in patients with cirrhosis. Bone mineral density should be assessed with dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry at diagnosis of cirrhosis and every 2 years thereafter.

Protein-calorie malnutrition is common in patients with cirrhosis. Protein consumption is essential to prevent the catabolic effects of chronic liver disease. Patients with cirrhosis should consume 1.0 to 1.5 g of protein/d per kg of body weight. The addition of late evening snacks can help reduce the risk for ascites and HE by improving glycogen stores and reducing the risk for sarcopenia.

Medications metabolized by the liver may require dosage adjustments depending on cirrhosis severity. Patients with advanced cirrhosis (CTP class B or C) often require dosage adjustments, whereas patients with well-compensated cirrhosis (CTP class A) may not.

Patients with advanced cirrhosis have complex analgesic prescribing needs. Narcotic analgesics can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy. NSAIDs can impair renal perfusion, worsen kidney function, and exacerbate fluid retention. Acetaminophen doses up to 2000 mg daily are generally safe in patients with cirrhosis. Alternative approaches to pain control, including nonpharmacologic options (e.g., physical therapy, behavioral therapy, and local injection therapies) as indicated, should be considered.

Acute liver failure (ALF) is defined as severe acute (illness duration <26 weeks) liver injury associated with hepatic encephalopathy and impaired liver synthetic function (usually based on an abnormally elevated INR) in a patient without preexisting liver disease. The most common cause of ALF in the United States is acetaminophen overdose. See also [Table: Table: Causes of Acute Liver Failure]

.

Early signs of hepatic encephalopathy can be subtle and include the following:

  • Disordered sleep
  • Impaired attention
  • Mood lability or other personality changes that may be apparent only to close friends and relatives

Diagnosis of ALF should prompt consideration of early referral to a liver transplant center.

Prompt identification and treatment of the underlying cause of liver failure are critical. All patients with suspected acetaminophen-related ALF or with ALF of unknown cause should immediately receive intravenous N-acetylcysteine.

Patients with ALF require monitoring of mental status because progressive hepatic encephalopathy can result in fatal cerebral edema (see Hepatic Encephalopathy in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease). Kidney injury is common and may progress to requiring kidney replacement therapy. Norepinephrine is the recommended vasopressor for hypotension that is refractory to fluid resuscitation. Patients with acute liver failure are at risk for hypoglycemia and infection; however, the routine use of prophylactic antimicrobial agents is not recommended. Routine correction of coagulopathy is also not recommended unless there is active bleeding or a high-risk procedure is planned.

Referral for liver transplantation is indicated in patients whose MELD 3.0 score is 15 or greater because transplantation provides a survival advantage in these patients. The MELD 3.0 formula includes patient sex; INR; and serum levels of bilirubin, sodium, albumin, and creatinine. Referral should also be considered for patients with decompensated cirrhosis (e.g., ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, esophageal variceal bleeding, HE, jaundice, hepatorenal syndrome) or hepatocellular carcinoma.

Patients should generally be abstinent from alcohol, although transplant centers may differ in their requirements for sobriety duration and chemical-dependency treatment. Other factors important in candidate selection include adequate social support, ability to adhere to medical treatment, and absence of significant cardiopulmonary and psychiatric comorbidities and active infectious diseases.

Appropriate candidates are placed on the national waiting list, with the highest priority given to patients with ALF and high MELD scores. MELD exception points may also be added in the presence of specific disorders, including the following conditions:

  • Hepatocellular carcinoma
  • Portopulmonary hypertension
  • Hepatopulmonary syndrome
  • Familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy
  • Primary hyperoxaluria
  • Cystic fibrosis
  • Hilar cholangiocarcinoma

After transplantation, the average 1-year survival rate is 92%; at 5 years, the survival rate is 75% to 85%. Recipients require lifelong immunosuppression, most commonly with tacrolimus or cyclosporine. Recipients are at increased risk for the following:

  • Diabetes
  • Hypertension
  • Hyperlipidemia
  • Chronic kidney disease
  • Cardiovascular disease
  • Malignancy secondary to immunosuppressive medications

Solid and Cystic Liver Lesions

Benign liver lesions are typically discovered incidentally on abdominal imaging and are asymptomatic, with the exceptions of liver abscesses and some lesions larger than 5 cm. Most liver lesions are diagnosed noninvasively with multiphasic contrast-enhanced CT or MRI. Percutaneous fine-needle aspiration of cystic lesions is performed when imaging is nondiagnostic and information obtained from aspiration will prompt a change in management. Risks of liver biopsy—including bleeding, perforation, and death—are rare but must be considered.

Hepatic cysts are a common radiologic finding. Simple cysts are smooth, with thin walls and anechoic features on ultrasonography. Patients with polycystic liver disease or autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease can present with numerous liver cysts. Asymptomatic simple hepatic cysts are benign and require no follow-up. Cysts with septations, fenestrations, calcifications, mural thickening, nodularity, heterogeneity, or presence of daughter cysts on ultrasonography should be further evaluated with CT or MRI. Large cysts rarely present with abdominal pain; these require surgical defenestration or, if surgery is contraindicated, cyst aspiration and sclerotherapy. Rarely, extensive polycystic liver disease may lead to portal hypertension (due to vascular obstruction) or malnutrition (due to gastric compression). Management options include surgical debulking, but if this is not technically feasible, liver transplantation may be indicated. Cystadenomas are distinguished from simple cysts by the presence of thick, complex walls on ultrasonography; they require surgical resection because of the risk for malignancy.

Hepatic adenomas are rare liver neoplasms. They are eight times more common in women than men. Risk factors include the following:

  • Oral contraceptives
  • Androgen treatment
  • Types 1 and 3 glycogen storage disease
  • Obesity

Although hepatic adenomas are benign, they may rupture (especially larger ones), with resultant hemorrhage, or undergo malignant transformation.

Hepatic adenomas may be incidentally found on imaging. Hepatic adenomas can be differentiated from focal nodular hyperplasia by using MRI with bile-excreted contrast material, such as gadobenate dimeglumine or gadoxetate disodium, because they typically do not have normal biliary excretion. Biopsy is indicated only when there is diagnostic uncertainty. However, biopsy may increase the risk for bleeding and should be performed only if the result will likely change management.

Treatment depends on use of oral contraceptives and adenoma size. Weight loss should be encouraged in patients with overweight or obesity. Women with adenomas less than 5 cm in size should discontinue use of exogenous hormones (e.g., oral contraceptives, hormone-impregnated devices, anabolic steroids) and undergo serial imaging every 6 months for 2 years and then annually thereafter. Women with adenomas 5 cm or greater in size should also discontinue exogenous hormones and then undergo a 6- to 12-month period of observation to evaluate for regression. Patients with adenomas that regress to less than 5 cm can be monitored with serial MRI, initially every 6 months and then less frequently. However, lesions that remain 5 cm or greater should be considered for resection because of an increased risk for hemorrhage or malignant transformation. Men with hepatic adenomas of any size are at increased risk for malignant transformation, and resection is recommended.

Pregnancy can result in adenoma growth, and resection or ablation of adenomas can be considered if pregnancy is being contemplated. In the setting of pregnancy, hepatic adenomas should be monitored closely for growth.

Focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) is the second most common benign liver tumor and a frequent incidental finding, with a female predominance. It is caused by a congenital arterial anomaly leading to a focal area of regeneration that appears as a stellate scar on CT or MRI. CT or MRI with and without contrast can confirm the diagnosis. FNH does not have malignant potential or pose a risk for bleeding, and asymptomatic cases do not require follow-up. Oral contraceptives and hormonal therapy do not have to be discontinued or avoided in a patient with confirmed FNH. Abdominal pain from FNH is rare, but intervention for painful FNH is reasonable to consider.

Hepatic hemangiomas are the most common benign liver lesion and are more frequent in women. Up to 20% of affected patients have several hemangiomas. Hepatic hemangiomas are rarely symptomatic, and, in most cases, symptoms that might be ascribed to a hemangioma are due to other causes. Hemangiomas do not have potential for malignancy, and spontaneous bleeding is rare. The diagnosis can sometimes be made with ultrasonography if the lesion is less than 2 cm and has a typical presentation and the patient does not have liver disease or risk factors for liver disease or malignancy (see

). Otherwise, the diagnosis should be confirmed by using MRI or CT with contrast, which typically shows peripheral nodular enhancement and progressive centripetal contrast enhancement. Biopsies should be avoided because of bleeding risk. There is no clear contraindication to the use of oral contraceptives or to pregnancy. Conservative management is reasonable, with follow-up reserved for rare symptomatic instances.

Pyogenic liver abscesses (PLAs) are usually caused by complications of biliary tract infections; portal venous spread of intra-abdominal infections, such as diverticulitis; or hematogenous spread from systemic infection. Patients with PLAs present with fever, right-upper-quadrant pain, and malaise. PLAs are typically polymicrobial, but an emerging cause of monomicrobial pyogenic liver abscesses is hypervirulent strains of Klebsiella pneumoniae, associated with colorectal cancer. Contrast-based CT is the most reliable imaging test (

), and the diagnosis is confirmed by radiologically guided aspiration with aspirate culture. Blood cultures should also be sent.

Small abscesses (≤5 cm) can be successfully treated with administration of parenteral antibiotics and needle aspiration, with or without leaving a drainage catheter in place. Larger abscesses (>5 cm) are treated with parenteral antibiotics and percutaneous catheter drainage until drainage is minimal. Surgical excision of pyogenic hepatic abscesses is rarely needed.

Amebic abscesses of the liver are found in developing areas of the world and in persons who have emigrated from countries where amebiasis is endemic. Intestinal infection with amebae can result in invasion of the portal vein and migration to the liver. Symptoms of amebic liver abscess may vary and typically include right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain and fever. Amebic liver abscess is diagnosed by hepatic imaging and serologic testing; aspiration is usually not required.

Treatment of the hepatic infection using metronidazole or tinidazole should be followed by a luminal agent, such as paromomycin.

Granulomas are focal inflammatory lesions that consist of mononuclear cells, lymphocytes, and fibroblasts. Hepatic granulomatous disease can be seen with infections, including the following:

  • Tuberculosis
  • Fungal infection (e.g., coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis)
  • Q fever
  • Cytomegalovirus infection
  • Epstein-Barr virus infection
  • Viral hepatitis

Granulomas also occur with inflammatory disorders (e.g., sarcoidosis), medications (e.g., allopurinol), and malignancies (e.g., lymphoma).

Symptoms of hepatic granulomas are nonspecific, and although often asymptomatic, they can include fever, malaise, and night sweats in addition to symptoms seen with the underlying disorder. Hepatic sarcoidosis may occur in patients with other systemic manifestations of sarcoidosis but can also be the only manifestation of sarcoidosis (for further discussion, see Sarcoidosis in Rheumatology). Portal hypertension can result from granulomas and cause constriction and obliteration of small portal veins; this occurs in fewer than 5% of patients. In patients with hepatic sarcoidosis, 6% to 8% progress to cirrhosis, although liver failure and the need for liver transplantation are rare.

Alkaline phosphatase and aminotransferase levels can be elevated regardless of cause. No single test can definitively diagnose hepatic sarcoidosis. Biopsy may be necessary.

Treatment of hepatic granulomas depends on the cause. Infectious causes should be treated if identified. Potential offending medications should be discontinued.

Most patients with hepatic sarcoidosis are asymptomatic and do not require treatment. Ursodeoxycholic acid or glucocorticoids may be considered if symptoms exist or liver chemistries are substantially elevated.

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common liver tumor in patients with cirrhosis, the sixth most common cause of cancer worldwide, and the third most common cause of cancer-related death worldwide and in the United States. More than 80% of patients with HCC have cirrhosis.

Patients with cirrhosis, regardless of cause, require surveillance with liver ultrasonography and α-fetoprotein (AFP) measurement every 6 months. This approach leads to early diagnosis, increased rate of curative treatment, and improved 3-year survival rates. Patients with HBV infection can develop HCC even without cirrhosis; indications for HCC surveillance in this patient population are outlined in [Table: Table: Populations Recommended for HCC Screening and Surveillance]

. Repeat ultrasonography and AFP measurement should be performed at a shorter interval (3-6 months) if a lesion less than 1 cm is seen on ultrasonography. Diagnostic multiphasic contrast-enhanced CT or MRI should be performed for any lesion larger than 1 cm on ultrasonography, AFP level of 20 ng/mL or greater (≥20 µg/L), or rising AFP level.

HCC is typically diagnosed noninvasively with multiphasic contrast-enhanced CT or MRI in patients with cirrhosis and a lesion measuring at least 1 cm (

). Biopsy may be needed for lesions that are indeterminate on imaging, or in the absence of cirrhosis or at-risk chronic HBV infection. The Barcelona clinical liver cancer staging system is recommended for tumor staging.

Patients with HCC should be discussed and managed by a multidisciplinary tumor board. Surgical resection is the treatment of choice for patients without underlying cirrhosis or those with limited tumor burden, well-compensated cirrhosis without clinically significant portal hypertension, and an adequate future liver remnant size. Surveillance for HCC recurrence should be performed after surgical resection using contrast-enhanced multiphasic CT or MRI every 3 to 6 months. Patients with solitary tumors 5 cm or smaller should be treated with curative intent using local ablative therapies if they are ineligible for or decline surgical therapy. Local ablative therapies include radiofrequency or microwave ablation for lesions 3 cm or smaller, targeted radioembolization for lesions larger than 3 cm, and transarterial chemoembolization for higher-stage HCC. Adjuvant immune checkpoint inhibitor–based systemic therapy may be considered in patients at increased risk for recurrence after liver resection or local ablation.

Liver transplantation is the treatment of choice for eligible patients with early-stage HCC and clinically significant portal hypertension and/or decompensated cirrhosis, or those with HCC that recurs within the Milan criteria after surgical resection. Milan criteria include having up to three liver lesions 3 cm or smaller or one lesion 5 cm or smaller, without apparent vascular invasion and without extrahepatic spread. Local ablative (locoregional) therapies can be used as bridging therapy in the pretransplant period for patients being evaluated or listed for liver transplantation.

Patients with preserved liver function who are not eligible for locoregional therapy or resection, who demonstrate disease progression following therapy, or who have metastatic disease should be treated with systemic therapy consisting of the immune checkpoint inhibitor atezolizumab plus the antiangiogenic agent bevacizumab, or the alternative combination of durvalumab plus tremelimumab. Those who are not candidates for either combination therapy should be offered one of the two multikinase inhibitors, lenvatinib or sorafenib. Systemic therapy should not be used in patients with poor liver function or as adjuvant therapy in those undergoing curative surgical resection or local ablation.
