Central Nervous System Infections

Central nervous system (CNS) infections can be associated with high rates of mortality and neurologic sequelae. Early empiric antimicrobial treatment and prompt identification of the pathogen are crucial to reduce adverse clinical outcomes.

Syndromes can include meningitis (infection of the meninges), encephalitis (infection/inflammation of the cerebral cortex), meningoencephalitis (infection involving the meninges and cortex), and space-occupying lesions. This syndromic classification refers to infection of specific CNS compartments but realistically exists on a spectrum; consequently, significant overlap in causative pathogens (specifically viruses that can cause meningitis and encephalitis syndromes) can occur.

Lumbar puncture is essential in the diagnosis of meningitis and encephalitis and should be performed promptly unless cranial imaging is necessary (

). Cranial imaging in suspected meningitis is of limited utility in patients without altered mental status or focal neurologic findings, but it is important in those with encephalitis or focal intracranial lesions, in whom radiographic patterns may provide clues to the underlying diagnosis. Molecular diagnostic techniques, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) for viruses, bacteria, fungi, and mycobacteria, can provide rapid and accurate diagnosis. A rapid multiplex PCR assay that can detect 14 pathogens is available. However, this panel should not be used routinely because of concerns for false-positive results (e.g., cytomegalovirus, human herpesvirus type 6) in patients without a compatible clinical disease or risk factors; this assay is instead best utilized with an infectious disease consultation.

Meningitis refers to infection or inflammation of the meninges surrounding the brain and spinal cord. This is a diverse clinical syndrome that can present acutely (e.g., acute bacterial or viral meningitis) or in a more subacute-to-chronic fashion (e.g., tuberculous or fungal meningitis). Symptoms may include fever, headache, or neck stiffness; complications related to persistent inflammation of the meninges can lead to significant neurologic morbidity.

Acute meningitis syndromes are most commonly caused by viral or bacterial pathogens and require urgent evaluation and empiric therapy to prevent neurologic sequelae. Clinical features develop over the course of hours to days and typically include fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered mentation. CSF examination can help distinguish between viral and bacterial causes ( [Table: Table: Meningitis Cerebrospinal Fluid Findings]

). Expedited evaluation (lumbar puncture, imaging, microbiologic testing) and early empiric therapy for treatable causes is warranted before diagnosis.

Enteroviruses are the most common cause of viral meningitis, usually presenting between May and November in North America, with symptoms including headache, fever, nuchal rigidity, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, myalgia, pharyngitis, maculopapular rash, and cough. A CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose and mildly elevated protein levels is typical ( [Table: Table: Meningitis Cerebrospinal Fluid Findings]

), although a neutrophil predominance may be seen early in infection. Enterovirus PCR confirms the diagnosis. Treatment is supportive, with a benign clinical course.

Herpesviruses can cause meningitis throughout the year; herpes simplex virus (HSV) types 1 and 2 and varicella-zoster virus (VZV) are the most common; cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus are less common causes. Of the herpesviruses, HSV-2 is the most common cause of viral meningitis that can sometimes recur (recurrent benign lymphocytic meningitis, also called Mollaret meningitis). The CSF findings resemble enteroviral meningitis. Outcomes for HSV-2 meningitis are generally favorable without requiring acyclovir therapy, although therapy is often administered to patients requiring hospitalization.

VZV can cause encephalitis, aseptic meningitis, myelitis, and CNS vasculitis presenting as a stroke. Vesicular lesions are a clue to the diagnosis but may be absent (zoster sine herpete). VZV may be detected in the CSF without clinical signs of meningitis or encephalitis, and patients with primary varicella or zoster do not require lumbar puncture (LP) unless they have clinical signs of CNS involvement. Immunocompromised and older adult patients are at higher risk for VZV meningitis and encephalitis. Diagnosis is confirmed by VZV PCR of the CSF or demonstration of intrathecal antibodies, and therapy is intravenous acyclovir.

Mosquito-borne viruses such as West Nile virus (WNV), St. Louis encephalitis virus, and the California serogroup viruses can cause meningitis or encephalitis between June and October in North America. Neuroinvasive WNV may present with acute flaccid paralysis, potentially leading to persistent weakness or death. The CSF formula resembles enteroviral meningitis. The diagnosis is made by serum or CSF serology (WNV IgM). Treatment is supportive.

Acute HIV infection can present as aseptic meningitis associated with a mononucleosis-like syndrome with fever, rash, and myalgia.

Less common viral causes include mumps, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, parainfluenza, adenoviruses, influenza A and B, measles, rubella, poliovirus, rotavirus, and parvovirus B19.

Bacterial meningitis usually presents with fever, acute meningeal signs (meningismus or nuchal rigidity) and altered mental status. The incidence of Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis has decreased with the availability of conjugate vaccines; however, S. pneumoniae remains the most common cause of community-acquired bacterial meningitis. N. meningitidis serogroup B accounts for a significant percentage of infections in the United States because the quadrivalent conjugate vaccine (serogroups A,C,W,Y), which is recommended for all children, does not include serogroup B. FDA-approved vaccines that target or include serogroup B are available in the United States; however, they are only indicated for patients at increased risk of meningitis (see Meningococcal Disease in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Regardless of N. meningitidis immunization status, antimicrobial prophylaxis with ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone (depending on local ciprofloxacin resistance patterns) is indicated for close contacts of persons with meningococcal disease. Listeria monocytogenes is an uncommon cause of meningitis in adults, but the risk increases in patients older than 50 years and those with altered cell-mediated immunity.

Lyme disease, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, can present with a lymphocytic meningitis in the first weeks or months after the tick bite. Common clinical features include headache, photophobia, nausea, history of erythema migrans, tick bite occurring in an endemic area, and facial paralysis, which can be unilateral or bilateral (see Early Disseminated Disease in Infectious Disease).

All patients with suspected community-acquired bacterial meningitis should promptly undergo blood cultures and LP with opening pressure measurement and CSF analysis (cell count, glucose and protein levels, Gram stain and culture); a delay is associated with a decrease in the culture yield. CSF findings characteristic of bacterial meningitis are provided in [Table: Table: Meningitis Cerebrospinal Fluid Findings]

. A negative CSF Gram stain result is more common in patients who have received antimicrobial therapy or in patients with meningitis caused by L. monocytogenes or gram-negative bacilli (sensitivity <50%). PCR tests have high sensitivity and specificity and are also available as rapid multiplex assays for the most common pathogens. If a head CT is indicated before LP (focal neurologic findings, altered mental status, papilledema, new seizure, history of CNS disease, or immunocompromise), imaging should not delay empiric antibiotic therapy, which should be started after promptly obtaining blood cultures (

).

Intravenous antibiotic therapy should be started as soon as possible. If the CSF Gram stain result is negative, initial empiric antibiotic selection is based on age, local epidemiologic patterns of pneumococcal resistance, and the necessity for ampicillin coverage for L. monocytogenes ( [Table: Table: Bacterial Meningitis Empiric Treatment]

). Despite antibiotic therapy, mortality for bacterial meningitis remains approximately 25%. Adjunctive dexamethasone, given concomitantly with or just before the first dose of antibiotic therapy, reduces morbidity and mortality in adults with bacterial meningitis in developed countries. Dexamethasone should be administered for 4 days in adult patients with confirmed S. pneumoniae meningitis; emerging data suggest that dexamethasone may be appropriate in cases of nonpneumococcal community-acquired bacterial meningitis as well.

Health care–associated meningitis and ventriculitis, or nosocomial meningitis, can occur after head trauma or a neurosurgical procedure (craniotomy, LP) or secondary to a device infection (for example, CSF shunt or drain, intrathecal pump, deep brain stimulator). CSF drains or shunts are used for the temporary or permanent management of intracranial pressure, respectively. If infected, they should be surgically removed. Abnormal CSF cell count, glucose level, and protein level do not reliably confirm or rule out infection in these patients. Staphylococcus species and gram-negative bacilli (including Pseudomonas aeruginosa) are the most common causes, but culture results can be negative. Less virulent bacterial species, particularly Cutibacterium acnes, should also be considered because CSF culture may require prolonged incubation to grow this organism. The use of β-d-glucan and galactomannan CSF assays may aid in diagnosing health care–related fungal ventriculitis and meningitis. Empiric antimicrobial therapy is outlined in [Table: Table: Bacterial Meningitis Empiric Treatment]

.

Primary amebic meningoencephalitis (caused by Naegleria fowleri) represents a highly fatal infection. Naegleria clinically resembles bacterial meningitis. Freshwater exposure during the summer is a key historical clue for Naegleria infection. Examination of a fresh CSF sample can reveal motile trophozoites, but the CDC should perform confirmatory testing by PCR. Treatment is with a combination of antimicrobials (usually including amphotericin B and miltefosine).

Subacute and chronic meningitis are defined by symptom duration between 5 and 30 days and more than 30 days, respectively. The most common infectious causes are Mycobacterium tuberculosis and fungi.

Tuberculous meningitis classically presents as basilar meningitis with cranial neuropathies (particularly of cranial nerve VI), mental status changes, and hyponatremia resulting from the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion or cerebral salt wasting. A history of tuberculosis exposure, an abnormal chest radiograph, a positive tuberculin skin test result, or a positive interferon-γ release assay result is suggestive but can be absent. CSF examination shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis (leukocyte count of 100-500/µL [100-500 × 10^6/L]), elevated protein level, and hypoglycorrhachia. CSF acid-fast bacilli smear is insensitive, and culture results are positive in only 38% to 88% of patients. Culture sensitivity increases when CSF analysis is performed serially for at least 3 days. Nucleic acid amplification testing should be performed when possible, especially when the acid-fast bacilli stain result is negative and suspicion is high, because it might increase diagnostic yield and allow expedited treatment. The four-drug regimen of rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol should be given until cultures and susceptibilities are available. Initial adjunctive dexamethasone for 6 to 8 weeks improves clinical outcomes in tuberculous meningitis. Antituberculous therapy should be administered for 1 year.

Fungal pathogens, including Cryptococcus neoformans, Coccidioides immitis, Histoplasma capsulatum, and other endemic mycoses, are a significant cause of subacute or chronic meningitis syndromes. Fungal meningitis is discussed in Fungal Infections in Infectious Disease.

Parasitic causes of eosinophilic meningitis include Angiostrongylous cantonensis, Gnathostoma spinigerum, and Baylisascaris procyonis. These are relatively uncommon helminthic infections in which the parasites migrate from the gastrointestinal tract to the CNS. Symptoms can be severe and lead to significant neurologic damage and even death. Diagnosis is suggested by CSF and blood eosinophilia with compatible exposures. Treatment often includes glucocorticoids and antiparasitic agents such as albendazole.

Noninfectious processes can occasionally produce an aseptic meningitis syndrome that mimics infection. Noninfectious causes of aseptic meningitis can include the following:

  • Medications (NSAIDs, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, intravenous immune globulin)
  • Meningeal involvement of leukemia, lymphoma, and metastatic carcinoma (CSF cytology shows atypical or immature cells and severe hypoglycorrhachia [<10 mg/dL (0.6 mmol/L)])
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus
  • Behçet syndrome
  • Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome (uveomeningoencephalitis)
  • Neurosarcoidosis

Chemical meningitis can be seen after intrathecal injections, intracranial hemorrhage, neurosurgical procedures, or spinal anesthesia.

CSF profiles differ amongst noninfectious causes. Clues to the diagnosis of drug-induced meningitis include temporal relation to the drug exposure and resolution on discontinuation. Neoplastic meningitis often shows atypical cells or lymphocytic pleocytosis (the latter in the setting of lymphomatous involvement) and can have a low glucose level; diagnosis can be challenging and is aided by repeated large-volume CSF sampling. Autoinflammatory syndromes like systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet syndrome, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome, and neurosarcoidosis may be suggested by extraneurologic markers of disease. Meningeal biopsy may occasionally be required if the diagnosis is uncertain.

Encephalitis refers to inflammation of the brain parenchyma. Probable or confirmed encephalitis is defined by the presence of one major (altered consciousness for more than 24 hours) and at least three minor criteria (fever, new-onset seizure, new-onset focal neurologic findings, CSF pleocytosis, and abnormal MRI or electroencephalographic findings) as classified by the International Encephalitis Consortium. The causative agent is unknown in 37% to 70% of infections; diagnostic yields are greater if viral PCR and arboviral serologies are performed and autoimmune causes are investigated. The most common causes are viral (HSV type 1, VZV, and WNV) and autoimmune diseases.

HSV-1 is the most common cause of sporadic encephalitis in the United States, requiring prompt identification and treatment with intravenous acyclovir. Factors associated with an adverse outcome include older age, abnormal Glasgow Coma Scale score, and delay in starting antiviral therapy. HSV-1 encephalitis commonly presents with fever, seizures, altered mental status, and focal neurologic deficits with temporal lobe edema, hemorrhage, or enhancement on imaging. The CSF formula usually shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, an elevated protein level, and a normal glucose level; however, little to no pleocytosis is occasionally seen. Diagnosis is confirmed by HSV PCR of the CSF (98% sensitivity, 94% specificity). However, false-negative results have been reported; if HSV is suspected, a repeat PCR should be obtained within 1 week while continuing acyclovir therapy. Intravenous acyclovir should be continued for 14 to 21 days. Electroencephalography can be helpful in identifying the degree of cerebral dysfunction and specific area of the brain involved and in detecting subclinical seizure activity.

VZV is a commonly underdiagnosed, treatable cause of encephalitis in adults. VZV can present with vasculopathy as a stroke, encephalitis, meningitis, radiculopathy, or myelitis. A vesicular rash may not be present, so a CSF VZV PCR should be performed in all patients with encephalitis. In addition, CSF VZV IgG antibodies should be measured in patients with a clinical presentation consistent with VZV vasculopathy because the sensitivity of CSF PCR is much lower in these patients. VZV encephalitis and vasculitis may present with a hemorrhagic CSF. Treatment with intravenous acyclovir for 10 to 14 days is recommended.

Human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) is a ubiquitous herpesvirus that can reactivate in the setting of altered immunity. It can cause severe limbic encephalitis (altered consciousness, focal neurologic signs, seizures, psychosis) in allogeneic stem cell transplant recipients. Antiviral agents are often used to treat infection in immunocompromised patients, although data supporting treatment are limited. CNS disease in immunocompetent patients has been rarely reported; positive PCR testing for HHV-6 in immunocompetent individuals most often reflects nonspecific viral reactivation or chromosomal integration rather than acute encephalitis.

Cytomegalovirus can cause encephalitis with periventricular enhancement on imaging in immunosuppressed patients (e.g., with AIDS or after transplantation). Diagnosis is by PCR of the CSF for cytomegalovirus, and treatment is ganciclovir plus foscarnet.

Epstein-Barr virus can rarely cause meningoencephalitis in young, immunocompetent patients presenting with infectious mononucleosis syndromes.

Arboviral CNS infections in the United States occur between June and October and include the following viruses:

  • West Nile
  • Eastern equine encephalitis
  • St. Louis encephalitis
  • Powassan (see Powassan Virus in Infectious Disease)
  • La Crosse

WNV is the most common cause of epidemic viral encephalitis in the United States; meningitis, acute flaccid paralysis (similar to poliomyelitis), neuropathy, and retinopathy can also occur. Older patients and those who have undergone transplantation or are immunosuppressed have a higher risk of death. WNV affects the thalamus and the basal ganglia; patients may have facial or arm tremors, parkinsonism, and myoclonus. Hypodense lesions or enhancements are variably seen in the thalamus, basal ganglia, and midbrain on brain MRI. A positive WNV IgM in the CSF confirms the diagnosis; treatment is supportive.

After being bitten or exposed to bodily fluids of a rabid animal, rabies can cause a fatal encephalitis in humans. Dog bites account for most cases worldwide. In the United States, rabies is uncommon and mostly seen after exposure to bats (even without a perceived bite or scratch), as well as raccoons, skunks, and foxes, or after a dog bite in patients with recent travel to endemic countries.

Brain abscesses can occur in any patient but are most common in men. Predisposing conditions in immunocompetent patients are listed in [Table: Table: Predisposing Conditions for Brain Abscess]

. Brain abscesses are most commonly caused by aerobic and microaerophilic streptococci, anaerobes, S. aureus, and Enterobacteriaceae with causative agents associated with predisposing conditions ( [Table: Table: Causes of Brain Abscess]

). If the predisposing condition for a community-acquired brain abscess (i.e., not neurosurgically associated) is unknown, initial empiric therapy usually includes the combination of vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and metronidazole. In patients who have recently undergone neurosurgery, cefepime should be used instead of ceftriaxone for empiric therapy. Aspiration of the brain abscess for culture is often necessary for definitive diagnosis; surgical or stereotactic drainage should be performed if the abscess is large (>2.5 cm). Antibiotic therapy should be given for 6 to 8 weeks with follow-up cranial imaging to ensure resolution of the infection.

Immunosuppressed patients (e.g., with HIV or AIDS, undergoing solid organ or bone marrow transplantation) are at risk for developing brain abscesses from several opportunistic infections. See Opportunistic Infections in Infectious Disease and Specific Posttransplantation Infections in Infectious Disease.

Cranial epidural abscess and subdural empyema can arise from underlying osteomyelitis complicating paranasal sinusitis (Pott puffy tumor) or otitis media or after neurosurgical procedures or head trauma. Rarely, they may arise as a complication of bacterial meningitis. Cranial epidural abscesses usually grow slowly, presenting with subacute to chronic symptoms of headache, localized bone pain, and focal neurologic signs. In contrast, subdural empyema is a rapidly progressive infection with high mortality that represents a neurosurgical emergency. The CSF formula in both parameningeal infections shows neutrophilic pleocytosis and a very high protein concentration, frequently with negative Gram stain and culture results. Pathogen identification is best achieved by culture of the abscess obtained during surgical drainage.

Spinal epidural abscess most commonly results from hematogenous dissemination. S. aureus accounts for approximately 50% of infections; streptococci and gram-negative bacilli such as Escherichia coli are also implicated. Predisposing factors for bacteremia include

  • Endocarditis
  • Injection drug use
  • Long-term intravenous catheters (e.g., hemodialysis catheters, central lines)
  • Urinary tract infection

Spinal epidural abscess can also occur after neurosurgical procedures (spinal fusion, epidural catheter placement) or paraspinal injection. Patients usually develop localized pain at the site of infection that later radiates down the spine.

MRI with contrast is the imaging modality of choice to identify the abscess location and extent. All patients should undergo a baseline laboratory evaluation, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Blood cultures should be obtained before starting antibiotics.

Treatment should include at least 6 weeks of effective antimicrobial therapy. Surgical drainage is indicated in patients with neurologic symptoms or signs (lower extremity weakness, numbness, bladder and bowel dysfunction).

Follow-up MRI is not routinely indicated unless the patient has persistent elevation of inflammatory markers, lack of clinical response, or new neurologic symptoms or signs. Tuberculosis (Pott disease) and brucellosis should be considered in patients with negative culture results and appropriate travel history or risk factors.

Acute flaccid myelitis presents as acute-onset limb weakness and can be caused by polio viruses (in endemic countries), nonpolio enteroviruses (such as EV-D68 and EV-71 in children), and WNV. Acute flaccid myelitis can progress rapidly and may be complicated by respiratory failure; all patients should be hospitalized initially for close monitoring. Unfortunately, no therapies are proven to improve outcomes.

Granulomatous amebic encephalitis (GAE) is caused by the free-living amebae Acanthamoeba and Balamuthia mandrillaris. GAE typically presents with solitary or multiple focal brain lesions and develops over weeks to months. Acanthamoeba typically produces infection in immunocompromised patients, whereas Balamuthia can infect immunocompetent persons. GAE is almost uniformly fatal. The optimal treatment typically involves a combination of agents, and expert consultation is advised.

Neurocysticercosis (caused by Taenia solium) (

) is endemic in Mexico, Central and South America, and Asia. It most commonly presents with seizures or hydrocephalus, and CT scan of the head shows multiple cysts or calcified lesions. Treatment includes managing seizures and increased intracranial pressure and administering adjunctive glucocorticoids and praziquantel for viable cystic lesions. Calcified lesions represent dead parasites and do not require therapy.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a demyelinating CNS disorder caused by the reactivation of the John Cunningham virus (JCV) in immunocompromised individuals (e.g., AIDS, those treated with immunomodulatory medications for malignant or autoimmune diseases). Diagnostic criteria for PML are based on three domains: clinical, radiographic, and virologic evidence (CSF JCV PCR); the presence of all three criteria provides a definitive diagnosis. Clinical criteria include the following:

  • Behavioral and cognitive abnormalities
  • Motor weakness
  • Gait abnormalities
  • Visual field deficits
  • Speech and language disturbances
  • Seizures, and lack of coordination

Radiographic findings include white matter lesions seen as hyperintense lesions on T2-weighted images and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images. Tissue diagnosis is usually not required but may be necessary if evaluation for other causes and repeat CSF PCR for JCV are negative. Management is directed at treating the underlying immunocompromised state when possible.

Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

Risk factors for skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs) include breach of the epidermis associated with trauma (injection drugs, surgery, bites, lacerations, abrasions) and nontrauma (ulcers, tinea pedis), impaired lymphatic and venous drainage (chronic venous insufficiency, lymphedema), immunocompromising conditions (diabetes mellitus, neutropenia, cirrhosis, HIV, and transplantation), peripheral arterial disease, and history of cellulitis.

Infections can be characterized by anatomic involvement (

), severity (mild, moderate, severe), and presence or absence of pus. Nonpurulent, spreading skin infections (usually caused by β-hemolytic streptococci like Streptococcus pyogenes) typically include erysipelas, cellulitis, and necrotizing SSTIs; purulent skin infections (generally caused by staphylococci, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus [MRSA]) refer to folliculitis, abscesses, furuncles, and carbuncles. [Table: Table: Risk Factors for Skin Pathogens]

includes other pathogens and their associated risk factors for less common causes of skin infection. Superficial skin infections are covered in Superficial Skin Infections in Dermatology.

Erysipelas refers to infection of the epidermis, upper dermis, and superficial lymphatics. Usually involving the face or lower extremities, this infection is brightly erythematous and tender, with distinct elevated borders and associated fever, lymphangitis, and regional lymphadenopathy (

). Cellulitis refers to infection involving the deeper dermis and subcutaneous fat tissue. Inflammatory signs of infection are similar to erysipelas, but the area of involvement is less well demarcated (

).

Although erysipelas and cellulitis are usually diagnosed clinically, approximately one third of patients are misdiagnosed. Clinical mimics (

) include contact dermatitis, venous stasis dermatitis, lymphedema, erythema nodosum, deep venous thrombosis, lipodermatosclerosis, erythromelalgia, trauma-related inflammation, pyoderma gangrenosum, and hypersensitivity reactions. Blood cultures are positive in approximately 5% of patients with cellulitis, so they are not routinely indicated; however, cultures should be performed for those with malignancy or who are immunocompromised, have severe systemic features, or have certain predisposing features (e.g., immersion injury, animal bite). Culture of skin tissue aspirate or biopsy should also be considered for these patients. Radiographic imaging is unhelpful for primary diagnosis but may be useful when a deeper necrotizing infection is suspected.

For immunocompetent patients with nonpurulent skin infection who have no systemic signs or symptoms (mild infection), empiric oral antibiotic therapy primarily directed against streptococci is recommended as outlined in [Table: Table: Treatment of Skin Infections]

. Treatment duration for uncomplicated infection can be as short as 5 days but should be extended as necessary until the infection improves. In patients with systemic signs (moderate infection), intravenous treatment is recommended (see [Table: Table: Treatment of Skin Infections]

). An antibiotic such as vancomycin with coverage against streptococci and MRSA is recommended when nonpurulent cellulitis is associated with penetrating trauma, nasal colonization or infection with MRSA elsewhere, or injection drug use. Treating predisposing factors (e.g., tinea pedis, edema, and primary skin disorders) may decrease the risk for recurrent infection. Prophylactic antibiotics, such as penicillin, can be considered in select patients with more than three episodes of nonpurulent cellulitis annually; consultation with an infectious diseases expert is suggested.

Patients who are immunocompromised, who have systemic inflammatory response syndrome and hypotension, or who have evidence of deeper necrotizing infection such as bullae and desquamation (severe infection) should receive urgent surgical evaluation for debridement. Initial empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy should be started (see [Table: Table: Treatment of Skin Infections]

); treatment may be adjusted based on culture and sensitivity results from lesion-associated specimens.

Necrotizing soft tissue infections, which involve subdermal compartments such as fascia and possibly muscle, are uncommon but potentially life threatening.

In necrotizing fasciitis (NF), infection usually spreads along the superficial fascia. These infections may be monomicrobial or polymicrobial, consisting of mixed aerobic and anaerobic bacteria, and are often associated with toxin production. In monomicrobial infection, the classically associated pathogen is S. pyogenes; other potential organisms are provided in [Table: Table: Treatment of Skin Infections]

. NF characteristically occurs in the setting of previous skin trauma or infection and most commonly affects the extremities. Risk factors include diabetes, injection drug use, alcohol use disorder, malignancy, immunosuppression, obesity, and liver disease. Patients with diabetes are at risk for NF of the perineum, a polymicrobial infection known as Fournier gangrene that usually results from antecedent genitourinary or anorectal infection or previous trauma to the genital area.

The initial presentation of NF resembles cellulitis before rapid progression with edema, severe pain, hemorrhagic bullous lesions, skin necrosis, and local crepitus. Systemic toxicity manifests with fever, hypotension, tachycardia, mental status changes, and tachypnea. A hallmark of infection is “woody” induration discovered by palpation of involved subcutaneous tissues. Necrosis of local nerves may result in anesthesia.

Although elevated serum lactate levels may assist in the diagnosis of necrotizing infection, individual laboratory study results are nonspecific. The Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) score was developed to improve diagnostic accuracy ( [Table: Table: LRINEC]

).

However, subsequent analysis of the sensitivity of the LRINEC score has shown it may not be optimal for ruling out NF, so surgical evaluation should be pursued in patients with a high index of clinical suspicion.

Plain radiographs, CT scans, and MRI may demonstrate gas and swelling in soft tissues. Surgical exploration can confirm the diagnosis of NF and should not be delayed when the diagnosis is highly suspected, particularly because early surgical management can reduce mortality. Blood culture(s) obtained before antibiotic administration or deep intraoperative specimen culture can establish the microbiologic cause.

In confirmed NF, repeated surgical debridement is typically required. Pending culture results, initial empiric antibiotic treatment includes broad-spectrum coverage for aerobic and anaerobic gram-negative and gram-positive organisms (including MRSA) such as a carbapenem or piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin or daptomycin. Some experts also recommend adding an agent that suppresses toxin production such as clindamycin or linezolid. See [Table: Table: Treatment of Skin Infections]

for treatment of NF caused by S. pyogenes, Vibrio vulnificus, Aeromonas hydrophila, or clostridial species. Antimicrobial discontinuation can be considered when the patient is afebrile, clinically stable, and surgical debridement is no longer required.

Clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene), another subtype of necrotizing soft tissue infection, refers to a life-threatening toxin-associated infection of the muscle, commonly after contamination of trauma-associated wounds (usually Clostridium perfringens) or, less commonly, from hematogenous dissemination from a gastrointestinal source, particularly colonic neoplasms (atraumatic spontaneous gas gangrene usually caused by Clostridium septicum;

). The clinical presentation typically includes the abrupt onset of severe pain; initially, pallor of the affected area is noted with subsequent bronze and then violaceous discoloration. Progression is rapid; bullae (

) and crepitus may develop as well as shock and multiple organ failure. Imaging demonstrating gas in tissues may provide a clue to diagnosis. Prompt surgical exploration and debridement is needed for source control and definitive diagnosis (i.e., demonstrating the presence of clostridial gram-positive rods in involved tissue). Antibiotic therapy consists of parenteral high-dose penicillin plus clindamycin.

Folliculitis results from superficial inflammation or infection of the hair follicle. It typically presents as pruritic perifollicular erythematous papules and pustules on the face, scalp, trunk, and thigh; however, it can appear on any hair-bearing area of skin (

). Risk factors for folliculitis are occlusive dressings or friction from clothing, increased sweating, obesity, and long-term topical glucocorticoid use. Folliculitis can be noninfectious (HIV-associated eosinophilic folliculitis) or infectious. The most frequent cause of infectious folliculitis is S. aureus. Other common infectious causes are as follows:

  • Gram-negative bacteria (Klebsiella or Enterobacter species, from prolonged antibiotic treatment for acne)
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa (associated with hot tubs;

) - Malassezia (yeast) - Viral folliculitis (from herpes simplex or varicella zoster) - Demodex folliculitis (caused by a mite)

Folliculitis is typically diagnosed from history and clinical presentation. Mild cases of staphylococcal folliculitis are usually self-limited, but topical antibiotics can be used (see [Table: Table: Treatment of Skin Infections]

). Systemic antibiotics, with coverage against S. aureus, may be required for extensive, refractory, or recurrent folliculitis. Pseudomonas folliculitis is usually self-limited, although oral ciprofloxacin can be used for immunosuppressed persons or persistent or severe infections.

Abscesses are erythematous, nodular, localized collections of pus within the dermis and subcutaneous fat (

). Furuncles (boils) are hair follicle–associated abscesses that extend into the dermis and subcutaneous tissue. These inflammatory nodules are typically seen on the face, neck, and axilla. Infection that extends subcutaneously to involve several furuncles is known as a carbuncle. This coalescence of abscesses can result in systemic signs of infection.

Primary treatment for abscesses, furuncles, and carbuncles is incision and drainage. Gram stain and culture should be obtained from the purulent drainage when antibiotic administration is planned. According to the 2014 Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guidelines, mild infections without systemic symptoms do not require antibiotic therapy after drainage. However, based on recent studies that show improved cure rates, some experts recommend careful consideration of adjunctive antibiotics for uncomplicated abscesses rather than incision and drainage alone, considering that antibiotic use carries risk for adverse events. For patients with moderate infections who have systemic signs of infection, empiric oral antibiotic treatment directed against MRSA is recommended (see [Table: Table: Treatment of Skin Infections]

). Empiric treatment with MRSA-directed parenteral therapy is recommended in immunocompromised patients or patients with hypotension and systemic inflammatory response syndrome (severe infection). Broader-spectrum coverage, including addition of cefepime or a carbapenem, is often administered pending culture and sensitivities of the purulent drainage.

If MRSA is the cause of multiple recurrences of purulent skin infection, decolonization with topical intranasal mupirocin, chlorhexidine washes, bleach baths, and decontamination of personal items such as clothes, towels, and sheets should be considered. Other diagnoses such as hidradenitis suppurativa, pilonidal cysts, or a foreign body should be considered when no microbial cause is identified.

Newer antibiotics for SSTIs caused by MRSA include tedizolid, delafloxacin, omadacycline, oritavancin, and dalbavancin. Use of these antibiotics is recommended in consultation with an infectious disease specialist.

Infectious lymphangitis refers to infection of the lymphatic vessels, usually following contiguous spread from an adjacent skin or soft tissue infection. Lymphatic spread to regional lymph nodes produces accompanying lymphadenitis or infection of the lymph node itself.

Acute lymphangitis most commonly occurs as a complication of adjacent cellulitis or erysipelas caused by β-hemolytic streptococci or Staphylococcus aureus. It presents as tender, erythematous streaks overlying the lymphatic vessels draining the initial site of infection (

). Suppurative lymphadenitis requiring drainage is an infrequent complication of this condition. Less commonly, acute lymphangitis can occur following epidemiologic exposures such as animal bites or water exposures (see [Table: Table: Risk Factors for Skin Pathogens]

).

Subacute or chronic lymphangitis is often nodular or ulcerative in nature. A variety of bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal, parasitic, and viral pathogens can cause subacute lymphangitis, including Bartonella henselae (cat scratch disease), Sporothrix schenckii (sporotrichosis; see Sporotrichosis in Infectious Disease), and Mycobacterium marinum. A careful exposure history is necessary to guide appropriate diagnostic testing.

Acute lymphangitis or lymphadenitis is typically treated empirically with antibiotics targeting Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species in the absence of specific epidemiologic exposures. Additional diagnostic testing should be pursued in patients who do not improve with empiric therapy, in infections associated with uncommon epidemiologic exposures, or in nodular or ulcerative disease. Aspiration or biopsy of a nodule can be performed for histopathologic evaluation and culture.

Bites from cats and dogs represent approximately 1% of emergency department visits in the United States; most wounds (about 80%) will not become infected. Cat bites are more likely to become infected because of deeper puncture wounds created by cats’ sharp, slender teeth. The microbiology of infection depends on the microbiota of the animal’s mouth and of the patient’s skin. Mixed aerobes and anaerobes typically compose the bacteria in bite wounds:

  • Staphylococci
  • Streptococci
  • Bacteroides species
  • Porphyromonas species
  • Fusobacterium species
  • Pasteurella species

Capnocytophaga canimorsus is a common constituent of canine microbiota and can cause severe infections, particularly in patients with asplenia. Those with alcohol use disorder, with an immunocompromising condition (e.g., cancer, diabetes, HIV), or who are taking immunosuppressive medications (e.g., chemotherapy, glucocorticoids, rituximab) may also have a higher risk of infection.

Wound management includes assessment and irrigation with sterile saline. Assessment allows for characterization of wound extent and dimensions; signs of inflammation and infection, including edema, erythema, pain, necrosis, lymphangitis, and pus; and local neurovascular involvement. Surgical evaluation is recommended for wounds with neurovascular complications; deep wounds, including those that extend to the tendons, bone, or joints; complicated facial wounds; and wounds requiring extensive debridement. Radiographs may demonstrate fracture, other bony involvement, or foreign bodies, such as teeth. Assessment for tetanus and rabies prophylaxis is essential (see Tetanus, Diphtheria, and Pertussis in Foundations of Clinical Practice and Rabies Encephalitis in Infectious Disease). Rabies postexposure prophylaxis should be administered as soon as possible to unvaccinated individuals and includes a dose of human rabies immune globulin and rabies vaccination. Except for facial wounds, primary wound closure is not generally pursued.

The severity of the wound and the immune status of the patient are deciding factors for beginning early antibiotic prophylaxis without clinical signs of infection. Because of its activity against pathogens associated with animal bite wounds, a 3- to 5-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate is recommended for patients who are immunosuppressed, including those with cirrhosis and asplenia. Pre-emptive antibiotic therapy is also recommended for wounds with associated edema or lymphatic or venous insufficiency; crush injury; joint or bone involvement; deep punctures; or moderate to severe injuries, especially involving the face, genitalia, or hand. If a patient is allergic to penicillin, combination therapy with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, a fluoroquinolone, or doxycycline plus clindamycin or metronidazole can be used.

For clinically infected bite wounds, antibiotics are recommended after debridement and tissue wound cultures (and blood cultures, if systemic signs of infection are present) are obtained. For outpatient management of mildly infected wounds, oral antibiotics such as amoxicillin-clavulanate are recommended. The duration of antibiotic therapy is usually less than 2 weeks unless bone or joint involvement dictates a more prolonged course.

Intravenous therapy is indicated for severe infections with systemic involvement, including sepsis; severe injuries, particularly those associated with tendon, nerve, vascular, or crush injuries; and hand infections. Intravenous antibiotic options include β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations (ampicillin-sulbactam, piperacillin-tazobactam), carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem), or ceftriaxone or a fluoroquinolone plus clindamycin or metronidazole. Empiric MRSA coverage can be included for patients with severe infections or risk factors for MRSA infection, as follows:

  • Nasal colonization
  • Recent hospitalization
  • Recent antibiotic use
  • Hemodialysis
  • Injection drug use
  • Close contact with MRSA infection
  • Incarceration
  • Previous MRSA infection
  • HIV
  • Contact sport participation

Antibiotics can be tailored when culture and susceptibility data are available. Surgical consultation is usually obtained.

Intentional biting of others, self-inflicted wounds such as those occurring from fingernail biting, and clenched-fist injuries after a punch to another person’s mouth are the most common causes of human bite wounds. These wounds are at risk for infection with human skin and mouth organisms:

  • Staphylococci
  • Streptococci
  • Eikenella corrodens
  • Peptostreptococcus
  • Fusobacterium
  • Prevotella species

Short-course (3-5 days) prophylactic antibiotic therapy with amoxicillin-clavulanate is recommended for human bites that perforate the skin. The management of infected wounds is similar to that for animal bites, including empiric MRSA coverage in patients at increased risk for MRSA infection. Hand involvement warrants surgical evaluation. In addition to tetanus prophylaxis assessment, evaluation for potential exposure to hepatitis B and C viruses, HIV, and other bodily fluid–transmitted pathogens is warranted.

Foot infections typically result after trauma in persons with diabetes who have vasculopathy, neuropathy (Charcot foot), suboptimal glucose control, and immunologic deficits (see Diabetic Foot Ulcers in Endocrinology and Metabolism). Additional risk factors for infection include presence of an ulcer for longer than 1 month, recurrent ulcers, toe amputation, kidney function impairment, and walking barefoot.

Infection is diagnosed when pus or two or more inflammatory signs (warmth, induration, erythema, pain, and tenderness) are present. A positive probe-to-bone test in a diabetic foot wound is consistent with a clinical diagnosis of osteomyelitis (see Evaluation and Management of Osteomyelitis in Diabetic Foot Ulcers in Infectious Disease).

Plain imaging is recommended for all patients with new foot infections to assess for soft tissue gas, foreign body, and bony involvement. Although plain radiography is an inexpensive and specific test for the presence of osteomyelitis, a negative result cannot exclude the diagnosis (see Laboratory and Imaging Studies in Infectious Disease). Additional imaging with ultrasonography (for abscess) or MRI (for bone involvement) is recommended when clinically indicated. The affected foot or limb should also be assessed for arterial ischemia, venous insufficiency, neuropathy, and biomechanical abnormalities such as Charcot arthropathy or hammer toe. Surgical consultation can evaluate the need for debridement, resection, amputation, or revascularization.

Following debridement of overlying callous or necrotic tissue, infections should be classified according to severity and extent ( [Table: Table: Diabetic Foot Infection Classifications]

). Evidence of critical ischemia makes diagnosis more challenging.

Uninfected wounds should not be cultured or treated with antibiotics.

Mild infections are typically caused by aerobic staphylococci (non-MRSA) and streptococci and can be empirically treated with a short course (7-14 days) of oral antibiotics:

  • Cephalexin or dicloxacillin
  • Clindamycin, levofloxacin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, doxycycline (β-lactam allergy)
  • Amoxicillin-clavulanate, ampicillin-sulbactam (recent antibiotic exposure)

Empiric coverage for anaerobic organisms is not necessary. For mild infections with pus or MRSA risk factors, wound cultures should be obtained by curettage or biopsy of deep tissue before initiating antibiotics. An empiric regimen active against MRSA should be prescribed.

For moderate and severe infections, polymicrobial coverage of staphylococci (including MRSA, if risk factors are present), streptococci, and aerobic gram-negative bacilli is recommended after deep-tissue cultures are obtained. Antipseudomonal therapy is indicated for macerated wounds or in patients with previous antibiotic exposure. Ischemia or necrosis may suggest an anaerobic mixed infection, and broad therapy is recommended. Moderate to severe infections are usually treated for 10 days after debridement but may require longer courses when surgery is not performed; if osteomyelitis is present, approximately 6 weeks of antibiotic therapy is administered if surgical debridement is not performed (see Evaluation and Management of Osteomyelitis in Diabetic Foot Ulcers in Infectious Disease).

Wound care, glycemic control, and off-loading areas of biomechanical stress are essential for all diabetic foot wounds and infections.

S. aureus– and S. pyogenes–associated exotoxins cause cytokine production that can result in toxic shock syndrome (TSS) ( [Table: Table: Diagnostic Criteria for TSS]

) (

). Staphylococcal TSS is associated with tampon use, nasal packings, surgical wounds, skin ulcers, burns, catheters, and injection drug use. Streptococcal TSS is associated with skin and soft tissue infection, particularly NF. Bacteremia and mortality rates are higher with streptococcal than staphylococcal TSS. Source control typically requires surgical debridement. Antibiotics for streptococcal TSS consist of penicillin plus clindamycin, the latter added to eradicate the high inoculum of bacteria present and to suppress toxin production. If methicillin-susceptible S. aureus is the cause, nafcillin or cefazolin, in combination with clindamycin, are recommended; for MRSA, vancomycin and clindamycin are recommended (for intolerance to vancomycin, daptomycin or ceftaroline may be used). Linezolid can be used if clindamycin resistance is present. Although the 2014 IDSA guidelines do not recommend routine adjunctive intravenous immune globulin use in TSS, some experts favor its administration in streptococcal TSS based on reported mortality benefits.

Although uncommon, TSS secondary to Paeniclostridium sordellii can occur following natural childbirth, spontaneous and medically induced abortions, or routine gynecologic procedures. The presentation includes lethargy, vomiting, profound edema, marked leukocytosis, and multiorgan failure; fever is often absent. Management includes supportive care, surgical debridement, and administration of penicillin plus clindamycin.

Osteomyelitis

Osteomyelitis, infection involving bone, may result from hematogenous dissemination, direct bone trauma, or contiguous spread of bacteria. Hematogenous osteomyelitis in adults most commonly affects vertebral bodies. Direct bone trauma includes penetrating wounds, fracture, or surgical instrumentation. Contiguous-spread osteomyelitis may arise from chronic wounds (e.g., pressure sores, foot ulcers) or adjacent soft tissue infection. Population-based studies suggest the incidence of osteomyelitis among adults is increasing in the United States, most likely because of the increasing prevalence of diabetes mellitus.

Staphylococcus aureus is the most prevalent and destructive species implicated in osteomyelitis. Coagulase-negative staphylococci, including Staphylococcus lugdunensis, also account for a significant proportion of events, especially through direct contamination and hardware-related infections. Polymicrobial infections are often associated with trauma or diabetic wounds of the foot.

Osteomyelitis may present as subacute or chronic pain over the affected region of bone. If osteomyelitis has resulted from direct contamination of a wound, the wound may fail to heal or may reopen after healing. Spontaneously opening wounds accompanied by drainage (sinus tracts) are a manifestation of chronic infection. Underlying osteomyelitis should be considered when chronic wounds, such as pressure ulcers, do not respond to appropriate therapy. Fever and other systemic manifestations of infection are uncommon but are more likely in patients with acute hematogenous infection. Clinical findings in patients with diabetes-associated foot ulcer osteomyelitis and vertebral osteomyelitis are discussed separately.

In the setting of a chronic wound resulting from pressure, diabetes, or other vasculopathy, a positive probe-to-bone test (sterile probe inserted into the wound base to evaluate penetration to bone or joint capsule) has high sensitivity and specificity for osteomyelitis. An elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein level increases the probability of infection and is useful in monitoring therapeutic response; however, normal inflammatory markers do not exclude the diagnosis. Anemia may be present in chronic osteomyelitis. Leukocytosis or positive blood cultures are uncommon except in acute hematogenous osteomyelitis; therefore, blood cultures should be obtained when hematogenous osteomyelitis (e.g., vertebral osteomyelitis) is suspected or in patients with systemic manifestations (e.g., fever).

Plain radiography is an inexpensive and specific test and is an appropriate initial imaging test if symptoms have been present for at least 14 days. However, a negative result cannot exclude the diagnosis because radiography lacks sufficient sensitivity. If a plain radiograph is not diagnostic, MRI with and without intravenous contrast is preferred (

). If MRI cannot be obtained, CT with intravenous contrast is an alternative. Nuclear medicine studies, although sensitive, are expensive and sometimes nonspecific for osteomyelitis but can be used when neither CT nor MRI are possible (e.g., presence of metal hardware). Considering the high sensitivity of these tests, they are mostly used to exclude the likelihood of osteomyelitis.

Obtaining biopsy material for culture and pathologic examination is important when evaluating suspected osteomyelitis because cultures of swabs, sinus tracts, or superficial wounds have a poor correlation with bone biopsy specimens, especially osteomyelitis in diabetic foot infection, decubitus ulcers, and postoperative and posttraumatic settings. Confirming the presence of a pathogen maximizes the chance that the chosen antibiotic therapy will be successful and often enables tailoring therapy to a narrower spectrum. Specimens may be obtained at surgery or by image-guided biopsy. A bone biopsy is generally not required in persons with hematogenous osteomyelitis and positive blood culture results. In culture-negative disease, additional testing of biopsy material with nucleic acid amplification techniques may yield the causative organism, although these techniques will not provide information regarding antimicrobial susceptibilities.

Antibiotic susceptibility testing from bone or blood culture isolates and knowledge of antibiotic levels achievable in bone for the selected agent should guide antibiotic therapy for osteomyelitis. Unless systemic signs of sepsis or concomitant soft tissue infection or bacteremia are present, empiric antibiotics should be withheld until a bone biopsy is obtained. Surgical debridement is indicated if bone necrosis is extensive. Involved orthopedic hardware should be removed, if possible, to increase the chance of therapeutic success. Parenteral antimicrobial agents are usually chosen initially; the efficacy of oral agents, especially those with high bioavailability, is increasingly reported. Rifampin should be considered, if the organism is sensitive, in combination with another antistaphylococcal agent to manage S. aureus infections in the setting of retained orthopedic hardware.

Little evidence is available to guide recommendations on therapy duration. When infected bone has been completely removed (e.g., through amputation), postoperative antibiotics may not be necessary; if utilized, a short course (2-5 days) will suffice. When residual infected bone remains following debridement, 4 to 6 weeks of antibiotics is considered sufficient for acute infections, whereas longer courses may be required for patients with chronic infections and those with hardware. In some circumstances, especially when hardware cannot be removed, indefinite suppressive therapy may be required. Relapse can occur many years after therapy completion.

Some patients might decline surgery or may not be appropriate candidates because of underlying comorbidities or anatomical factors that prevent adequate debridement or wound closure. In the absence of sepsis or surrounding soft tissue problems, obtaining cultures and initiating antimicrobial therapy is generally not indicated. Conservative management with wound care and monitoring is recommended.

Diabetic foot infections are among the most frequent diabetes-related complication necessitating hospitalization, cause significant morbidity (limb amputation), and are associated with increased mortality (see Diabetic Foot Infections in Infectious Disease and Diabetic Foot Ulcers in Endocrinology and Metabolism). Nonhealing ulcers are a source of infection and may spread contiguously to bone. Peripheral vascular disease contributes to infection risk and delayed healing.

Osteomyelitis should be considered when a diabetic foot ulcer is deep (presence of exposed bone), large (surface area >2 cm^2), or chronic (nonhealing after 6 weeks of standard care). Up to two thirds of affected patients do not have leukocytosis or elevated inflammatory markers. Unless a skin or soft tissue infection is also present, progression to sepsis is uncommon. A probe-to-bone test should be performed. Imaging options are as described for other causes of osteomyelitis. All patients with a new diabetic foot infection should have plain radiography to assess for bony abnormalities, soft tissue gas, and foreign bodies.

Correlation between deep wound cultures and bone biopsy samples is variable, and bone biopsy remains the recommended modality for microbiologic diagnosis. S. aureus and streptococcal species account for most osteomyelitis complicating diabetic foot ulcers; gram-negative organisms are found in as many as 25% of infections. Anaerobes are much less common and, if present, are more commonly associated with necrosis or gangrene. Infections may be polymicrobial, especially in the setting of deep, chronic wounds previously treated with antimicrobials.

If infected but viable bone is present, a 3- to 6-week course of parenteral or oral antibiotic therapy is recommended depending whether surgical resection was performed and its extent. If minor amputation is performed and bone margins have positive cultures or histology reveals residual infection, 3 to 4 weeks of antibiotics is generally recommended. If no debridement is performed or nonviable bone persists, the treatment course is typically extended to 6 weeks. Treatment with highly bioavailable oral regimens with adequate bone penetration (metronidazole, fluoroquinolones, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) may prevent the need for parenteral antibiotics.

Indications for amputation include persistent sepsis, inability to tolerate antibiotic therapy, progressive bone destruction despite appropriate therapy, or bone destruction that compromises the mechanical integrity of the foot. The patient may also choose amputation over prolonged antibiotic therapy. However, limb salvage may be possible when treatment is directed by a multidisciplinary team. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy, growth factors, and topical negative-pressure therapy have insufficient evidence of benefit to recommend their use.

Vertebral osteomyelitis is almost exclusively secondary to hematogenous dissemination; it can also be a sequela of spine surgery. Risk factors include the following:

  • Older age
  • Injection drug use
  • Immunocompromise
  • Indwelling catheters
  • Previous spinal surgery
  • Degenerative disease

Infection occurs in the intervertebral disk space and then spreads to the avascular disk as well as adjacent vertebral bodies (spondylodiskitis). The lumbar spine is most frequently involved, followed by the thoracic and then the cervical spine. Positive blood cultures may obviate the need for bone biopsy. Most infections are monomicrobial and commonly caused by S. aureus, but persistent bacteremia with coagulase-negative staphylococci (especially S. lugdunensis) and streptococci may also lead to vertebral osteomyelitis. Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (especially in persons who inject drugs), and Candida species may also cause vertebral osteomyelitis (more commonly in patients who inject drugs, those who are immunosuppressed, or following surgery).

New-onset back or neck pain or progressive worsening of chronic pain that is unresponsive to conservative management should raise concern for vertebral osteomyelitis, especially when accompanied by elevated inflammatory marker levels, focal neurologic findings, bacteremia, or unexplained fever. Neurologic findings can include sensory loss, weakness, or radiculopathy and are reported in up to one third of patients. Point tenderness is present in only one third of patients.

MRI with and without contrast is the preferred imaging modality. Blood cultures should be performed in all patients before antibiotics are started. Image-guided percutaneous biopsy and aspiration should be performed in patients with negative blood culture results (sensitivity of 38%-60%); if results from the aspirate are inconclusive, aspiration should be repeated to optimize sensitivity of the microbiologic and pathologic diagnosis. Open biopsy should be reserved for patients with a nondiagnostic aspiration or those not responding to a course of empiric antimicrobial therapy. Nucleic acid amplification performed on tissue can increase biopsy yield. Testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection and serologic tests for Brucella species are appropriate for patients at risk for these pathogens (see Mycobacterium tuberculosis Infection Diagnosis in Infectious Disease and Brucellosis in Infectious Disease). A strongly positive Brucella serologic result in the correct epidemiologic setting is considered diagnostic, and biopsy is unnecessary.

Patients with neurologic compromise or spinal instability should undergo evaluation for immediate surgical intervention. Patients with severe sepsis, progressive neurologic deficit, spinal instability, or epidural abscess (see Spinal Epidural Abscess in Infectious Disease) should receive empiric antibiotic therapy (generally vancomycin combined with a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin). Otherwise, initiation of antibiotic therapy for uncomplicated vertebral osteomyelitis is based on culture results. Parenteral therapy is generally recommended, especially for S. aureus. However, oral agents with high bioavailability and good bone penetration (such as fluoroquinolones) may be used, especially for Enterobacteriaceae. Antibiotic therapy duration is typically at least 6 weeks. Infections caused by methicillin-resistant S. aureus, those associated with undrained paravertebral or psoas abscess, and those in persons with extensive bone destruction may require longer therapy. Patients with indwelling hardware in the involved region often require prolonged suppressive oral antibiotics active against identified pathogens. Weekly monitoring of inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein) should also be performed. Repeat imaging, especially MRI, should be reserved for patients who do not respond clinically.

Infectious Arthritis

Bacterial arthritis is a medical emergency requiring immediate diagnosis and treatment. Risk factors for infectious arthritis are listed in [Table: Table: Infectious Arthritis Risk Factors]

. Infection usually occurs through hematogenous seeding to the synovium. Direct inoculation (i.e., trauma, bite) or contiguous spread (i.e., infected skin ulcer) are other potential mechanisms of infection.

Presenting symptoms include pain, swelling, warmth, and erythema of the affected joint, accompanied by fever and constitutional symptoms. Most joint infections are monoarticular; the knee joint is most commonly involved, but any joint may be affected. Acute monoarthritis, including in a patient with well-controlled inflammatory arthritis, should prompt evaluation for infection. Polyarticular infectious arthritis may occur in persons who use injection drugs, those experiencing overwhelming sepsis with bacteremia, those with systemic inflammatory disorders (such as rheumatoid arthritis), and immunosuppressed patients.

The most common cause of septic arthritis in adults is infection with gram-positive cocci. Staphylococcus aureus (including methicillin-resistant S. aureus) is the most frequent microorganism. Streptococci (including β-hemolytic groups A, B, C, and G) are the second most common.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection typically occurs in younger, sexually active patients (see Neisseria gonorrhoeae Infection in Infectious Disease). Risk factors for dissemination include terminal complement deficiencies, drugs that suppress terminal complement activation (i.e., eculizumab), pregnancy, and recent menstruation. Disseminated gonococcal infection may present in one of two ways, although overlap may occur. The first presentation is the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome, a triad of tenosynovitis, dermatitis (usually painless pustular or vesiculopustular lesions) (

), and polyarthralgia without frank arthritis. Fever, chills, and malaise are common. Inflammation of tendons of the wrists, fingers, ankles, and toes distinguishes this syndrome from other forms of infectious arthritis. The second presentation is a purulent arthritis, usually without associated skin lesions or fever. Patients have acute onset of monoarticular or oligoarticular arthritis; the knees, wrists, and ankles are most commonly involved.

Aerobic gram-negative bacilli are the predominant cause of nongonococcal gram-negative joint infections. Predisposing factors include injection drug use, advanced age, health care–associated bloodstream infections, traumatic wounds, and an immunocompromised state. Pseudomonas aeruginosa can be seen in infection related to injection drug use and immunosuppressive conditions. Patients with sickle cell anemia or systemic lupus erythematosus may develop joint infections with Salmonella species. Infection with enteric organisms such as Escherichia coli may be associated with urinary tract infections. Streptobacillus moniliformis, a filamentous gram-negative bacillus, can cause rat-bite bite fever, a febrile-rash syndrome that is associated with a polyarticular arthritis.

Although arthralgia and myalgia often occur at the earlier stages of Lyme disease, Lyme arthritis is a late-disseminated stage manifestation. It is typically monoarticular, migratory (improves even without treatment but may recur in the same or a different joint), and most commonly involves the knee (

). It should be suspected in patients with untreated or incompletely treated Lyme disease, although not all patients will have a history compatible with previous Lyme infection. See Lyme Disease in Infectious Disease for further information on Lyme disease testing and treatment.

Fungi are uncommon causes of native joint infections, usually involving large weight-bearing joints. Risk factors include immunosuppression and exposure to fungi in endemic areas. Infection may be indolent and more difficult to diagnose than other joint infections. Fungal causes include coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, cryptococcosis, candidiasis, and sporotrichosis. Fungal arthritis is usually a result of hematogenous dissemination but can occur after direct inoculation of the joint.

Arthritis or arthralgia can be a complication of viral infections ( [Table: Table: Viral Arthritis and Arthralgia]

).

Hepatitis B virus infection causes a self-limited polyarthritis in up to 25% of infected patients during a prodromal stage before the onset of jaundice (see Hepatitis B in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease). Joint involvement can be sudden and severe, with a pattern that is usually symmetric but can be migratory or additive. Hand and knee joints are most often involved; wrists, ankles, elbows, shoulders, and other large joints may be involved as well. Morning stiffness is common. Fusiform swelling of the small joints of the hand may be found on physical examination. The arthritis is not known to progress or cause joint damage. Rarely, patients with chronic hepatitis B virus infection may have polyarthralgia or polyarthritis, often in conjunction with polyarteritis nodosa (see Polyarteritis Nodosa in Rheumatology).

Up to 60% of adults, typically women, with parvovirus B19 experience arthritis. It often presents acutely, is symmetric and polyarticular, and typically involves the proximal small joints of the hands. Rash is frequently present. Parvovirus B19 arthritis should be suspected when appropriate clinical features are present in someone who has exposure to children, such as teachers and caregivers; children frequently experience parvovirus B19 infection as a fever accompanied by a facial rash (with a slapped-cheek appearance), also called fifth disease. Joint symptoms in adults may persist for weeks to months.

Zika, dengue, and chikungunya viruses are transmitted by Aedes mosquitos in tropical areas (see Dengue Fever, Chikungunya, and Zika in Infectious Disease for further details on manifestations, diagnosis, and testing). Zika infection causes arthralgia along with fever, rash, and conjunctivitis. Dengue fever causes arthralgia, fever, and rash but may be associated with severe muscle and bone pain, headache, and hemorrhagic complications. In acute chikungunya infection, polyarthralgia and inflammatory arthritis are predominant features; patients may experience synovial thickening and tenosynovitis, often involving the hands and feet, in addition to fever and rash. The musculoskeletal symptoms of Zika and dengue infections tend to subside within days to weeks, whereas symptoms of chikungunya infection usually last longer (can last months to years), resembling rheumatoid arthritis in some cases. Chronic arthritis (>3 months after infection) typically includes the same joints that were acutely involved.

Arthritis is uncommon in childhood rubella infection, but arthralgia complicates up to 60% of rubella infections in adults and occurs primarily in women. Symmetric and migratory joint involvement, usually affecting the small joints of the hands, wrists, elbows, ankles, and knees, begins with the onset of the maculopapular rash and typically resolves within 2 weeks. Immunization is effective for preventing infection.

Physical examination commonly shows loss of active and passive range of motion in addition to signs of inflammation. Careful skin examination can reveal signs suggesting gonococcal infection (pustular skin lesions) or potential portals of entry for pathogens (scratches, bites, or foreign bodies).

In patients suspected of having infectious arthritis, the most important diagnostic procedure is expeditious arthrocentesis. The synovial fluid should be evaluated with Gram stain, culture (bacterial and, when indicated, mycobacterial and fungal), leukocyte count, and crystal analysis. Synovial fluid glucose, lactate dehydrogenase, and total protein levels do not aid in diagnosis and should not be ordered. Patients with suspected Lyme arthritis should be evaluated using a two-tiered approach (see

); serologic testing is preferred to polymerase chain reaction testing for Borrelia burgdorferi DNA or culture of blood or synovial fluid. Polymerase chain reaction assay to detect mycobacteria or gonococcal DNA may be ordered if clinically indicated. Peripheral blood leukocyte count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level are often elevated but may also be elevated in inflammatory arthritis.

Synovial fluid leukocyte counts are typically greater than 50,000/μL (50 × 10^9/L) and may exceed 100,000/μL (100 × 10^9/L), with a polymorphonuclear cell predominance. Such high leukocyte counts may occur in other conditions (e.g., crystal arthropathies) but should be presumed infectious until proven otherwise (see [Table: Table: Synovial Fluid Analysis for Arthritic Conditions]

). Importantly, the presence of crystals does not exclude the possibility of concomitant infection. Synovial fluid leukocyte counts may be lower in patients with gonococcal, Lyme, mycobacterial, or fungal infections; patients who inject drugs; or those who are immunocompromised. A Gram stain positive for bacteria should be considered definitive, but a negative result does not rule out infection. Synovial fluid cultures are usually positive in bacterial infections unless antibiotics were administered before arthrocentesis. Synovial biopsy is rarely needed but may be helpful in patients with mycobacterial or fungal infection.

Blood cultures should be drawn before antibiotic administration. When gonococcal arthritis is suspected, a urine sample or swabs from genital, rectal, or pharyngeal areas should be obtained for nucleic acid amplification testing.

Plain radiographs usually appear normal early in the course, later showing nonspecific changes. Baseline radiographs are helpful to identify other diseases or contiguous osteomyelitis. In advanced or particularly virulent infection, radiographs may show periosteal reaction, marginal or central erosions, and subchondral bone destruction (

). Bony ankylosis is a late sequela. In joints that are difficult to evaluate clinically or have complex anatomic structures, ultrasonography, CT, and MRI can delineate the extent of an effusion and identify early bony changes.

Empiric antibiotic therapy should be started pending culture results. In suspected bacterial arthritis, the initial antimicrobial coverage should be broad and account for host factors, such as immunosuppression and injection drug use as well as likely causative microorganisms and regional antibiotic sensitivity data. Antibiotics should initially be given parenterally. Considering the high prevalence of methicillin-resistant S. aureus, vancomycin, often combined with a second agent active against gram-negative organisms (e.g., ceftriaxone; cefepime or ceftazidime if at risk for P. aeruginosa infection), is appropriate empiric therapy. A pathogen-directed antimicrobial regimen should be chosen when culture and sensitivity results become available ( [Table: Table: Native Joint Infectious Arthritis Treatment]

). The treatment duration depends on the causative organism and patient response and comorbidities, but bacterial arthritis usually requires 2 to 4 weeks of treatment, with longer courses in contiguous osteomyelitis. An exception is disseminated gonococcal infection, which may be treated for only 7 to 14 days when the clinical response is prompt.

An infected joint must also be adequately drained. This is typically performed surgically unless arthrocentesis can provide adequate drainage.

Antibiotic treatment is recommended for all patients with Lyme arthritis (see [Table: Table: Native Joint Infectious Arthritis Treatment]

). Most patients respond to antibiotic therapy, but those who have posttreatment Lyme arthritis should be referred to an appropriate specialist for consideration of NSAIDs, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (e.g., hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and biologic agents such as tumor necrosis factor inhibitors), intra-articular glucocorticoids, or synovectomy.

Treatment of arthritis associated with viral infections is largely supportive, although specific viral therapy is appropriate for HIV and viral hepatitis infections. Patients with chronic chikungunya arthritis should be referred to a rheumatologist to determine the need for disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs.

Bacterial infection complicates about 2% of joint replacements; rates are higher in patients with immunocompromising conditions (including diabetes mellitus and cancer), obesity, and rheumatoid arthritis. Infection with staphylococci is most common. Prosthetic joint infections (PJIs) can be divided into early (<3 months after placement), delayed (3-24 months after placement), and late onset (>24 months after placement). However, these definitions are controversial, and some sources define delayed infections as occurring 3 to 12 months after surgery.

Early and delayed infections are usually related to surgical contamination at the time of implantation, whereas late infections result from hematogenous seeding from other sites of infection. Early infections are often caused by S. aureus, anaerobes, gram-negative bacilli, or polymicrobial infection, whereas delayed infections are often caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci, enterococci, or Cutibacterium species. Late infections are usually caused by S. aureus, β-hemolytic streptococci, or gram-negative bacilli.

PJIs are unlikely to occur from dental procedures; based on guidelines from the American Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons and the American Dental Association, prophylactic antibiotics are no longer recommended for patients with prosthetic joints undergoing dental procedures. Likewise, antimicrobial prophylaxis is not generally needed for patients undergoing gastrointestinal endoscopy.

Early and late PJIs typically present with pain, warmth, effusion, and fever. Delayed infections, however, may be more difficult to recognize because symptoms are less severe, and they are often caused by less virulent microorganisms.

Although nonspecific, initial testing for PJI typically includes serum inflammatory markers, such as C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and plain radiographs. Blood cultures may be helpful in acute PJI. Assessment of synovial fluid with arthrocentesis is a cornerstone of diagnosis and should include leukocyte count and differential as well as culture, preferably with synovial fluid inoculated in blood culture bottles. Several diagnostic criteria for PJI exist and include communication of sinus tract with prosthesis or at least two positive periprosthetic cultures with the same microorganism.

Treatment of PJI is challenging and requires early surgical consultation. Orthopedic implants serve as a nidus for microorganisms, and the avascularity of the infected hardware limits antibiotic penetrance. Many patients require debridement and orthopedic device removal as part of a two-stage procedure, with a new device implanted after an appropriate course of intravenous antibiotics (usually 4-6 weeks). Other surgical options, to be considered on an individual basis, include one-stage exchange arthroplasty, debridement and retention of prosthesis, permanent resection arthroplasty, and amputation. Empiric antibiotics are not routinely recommended until after culture or surgery is performed in patients with suspected PJI who are clinically stable. Potential antibiotic choices are presented in [Table: Table: Bacterial Prosthetic Joint Infection Treatment]

, with pathogen-directed therapy finalized when susceptibility results become available. Pathogens and surgical intervention performed will dictate the choice and duration of antibiotics.
