Community-Acquired Bacteremia and Endocarditis

Primary bacteremia refers to a positive blood culture without a clear source of infection outside the bloodstream. An important subset of primary bacteremia, central line–associated bacteremia (CLABSI), is reviewed in Central Line–Associated Bloodstream Infections in Infectious Disease. Primary bacteremia is a hallmark of endocarditis, and in select cases may serve as a trigger to pursue additional evaluation for an endovascular infection. Differentiating uncomplicated bacteremia from endocarditis has important clinical implications; endocarditis treatment requires bactericidal antibiotics and necessitates a longer duration of treatment than uncomplicated bacteremia. Secondary bacteremia, which refers to seeding of the bloodstream related to a localized infection (e.g., bacteremia associated with pneumonia), is a common and potentially life-threatening complication; these types of infections are covered in the ACP MKSAP sections corresponding to the underlying condition.

Isolation of bacteria from a blood culture does not invariably represent a bloodstream infection. Bacteremia with organisms that normally colonize the skin, including coagulase-negative staphylococci, Bacillus species (other than Bacillus anthracis), Corynebacterium species, Cutibacterium acnes or Micrococcus may result from a nonsterile blood draw representing contamination. The significance of a positive culture with one of these low-virulence organisms should be interpreted in the context of the clinical presentation. Growth from a patient with a prosthetic device or implant or isolation in multiple sets of blood cultures may suggest pathogenicity.

Isolation of Staphylococcus aureus in a blood culture is always considered significant and requires evaluation to differentiate uncomplicated from complicated infection. Patients with S. aureus bacteremia require a thorough clinical evaluation to exclude sites of metastatic infection, particularly septic pulmonary emboli, septic arthritis, or spinal osteomyelitis/diskitis; the latter two sites may require surgical intervention. Source control often involves removing infected prosthetic material or draining a loculated infection. In patients with S. aureus bacteremia, infectious diseases consultation should be obtained.

The frequency of endocarditis among patients with S. aureus bacteremia is as high as 30%, making evaluation for valvular infection an essential component of management. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is the most sensitive study for confirming endocarditis; however, patients should first undergo transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) because identification of a vegetation may obviate the need for TEE. The VIRSTA score is a validated predictive tool that allows risk stratification for endocarditis in patients with S. aureus bacteremia ( [Table: Table: Prognostic Scores for Endocarditis Risk Assessment]

) and may assist in identifying patients with S. aureus bacteremia and a negative TTE who should undergo TEE. A score of 2 or less is associated with low likelihood of endocarditis, whereas TEE is warranted for those with a score of 3 or greater.

Positive blood cultures after the first 3 days of antibiotic treatment suggests a complicated infection (including endocarditis), lack of source control, or subtherapeutic drug levels. For patients with uncomplicated S. aureus bacteremia, a 14-day course of therapy is indicated; shorter courses have been associated with lower success rates and relapse.

Methicillin-sensitive S. aureus (MSSA) is optimally treated with high-dose cefazolin or a penicillinase-resistant semisynthetic penicillin such as nafcillin or oxacillin. Use of an alternative agent, such as vancomycin or daptomycin, is reserved for patients with serious allergies to β-lactam antibiotics because treatment of MSSA bacteremia with vancomycin is associated with higher rates of relapse and microbiologic failure. For patients with complicated infection involving the central nervous system (brain abscess or meningitis), a penicillinase-resistant semisynthetic penicillin should be prescribed because cefazolin does not achieve adequate levels owing to poor penetration across the blood-brain barrier.

For methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) bacteremia, vancomycin or daptomycin is the preferred antibiotic. Vancomycin monitoring by measuring the ratio of area under the curve to minimum inhibitory concentration (AUC/MIC) provides a more precise estimate of optimal dosing than trough measurement but requires pharmacist support. Daptomycin offers the advantage of once-daily dosing but does not achieve therapeutic levels in the lung because it binds to surfactant, precluding its use for associated pneumonia. Daptomycin is the preferred agent for MRSA bacteremia when the vancomycin MIC is reliably determined to be 2 µg/mL or greater. Salvage regimens for prolonged (e.g., >7 days) MRSA bacteremia include high-dose daptomycin (8-10 mg/kg/d) and combination therapy with daptomycin plus ceftaroline.

Enterococci are part of the normal gut microbiome, and enterococcal bacteremia is commonly associated with gastrointestinal or genitourinary infections. However, endocarditis is present in about 25% of patients with community-acquired enterococcal bacteremia. The DENOVA score is a predictive instrument that can identify patients with enterococcal bacteremia at low risk for endocarditis, for whom TEE can be deferred (see [Table: Table: Prognostic Scores for Endocarditis Risk Assessment]

). Patients with uncomplicated bacteremia can be treated with 2 weeks of directed therapy with penicillin or ampicillin; for patients with resistant bacteria or allergies to first-line therapies, vancomycin, daptomycin, or linezolid can be used. Synergistic treatment with an aminoglycoside or high-dose ceftriaxone is not indicated.

Endocarditis is present in only 7% of cases of streptococcal bacteremia, but the prevalence varies significantly based on species. Streptococcus pneumoniae and Streptococcus pyogenes are uncommon causes of valvular infection, whereas isolation of viridans group streptococci (a heterogeneous group consisting of normal oropharyngeal colonizers) and Streptococcus gallolyticus (previously Streptococcus bovis) from more than one set of blood cultures should prompt a diagnostic evaluation for endocarditis. S. gallolyticus is part of the normal enteric flora, and bloodstream infection has been associated with gastrointestinal malignancy; therefore, colonoscopy is indicated when this organism is identified.

Growth of viridans group streptococci from two or more blood cultures is a major microbiologic criterion in the Duke Criteria for the diagnosis of endocarditis ( [Table: Table: Endocarditis Diagnostic Criteria]

); the clinical significance of a single positive blood culture is questionable. Transient bacteremia may be seen with dental procedures or trivial trauma, such as vigorous tooth brushing, and is common in patients with cancer with mucositis. Viridans group streptococci may also colonize the skin, and a single positive blood culture may represent contamination.

Bloodstream isolation of Streptococcus anginosus, Streptococcus intermedius, or Streptococcus constellatus (collectively termed S. anginosus or Streptococcus milleri group) has special significance. These organisms are rare causes of endocarditis, but they are strongly associated with pyogenic infections. Bacteremia with one of these organisms may indicate an occult suppurative focus such as a liver or brain abscess.

Growth of enteric gram-negative bacilli (GNB) suggests an infection of the gastrointestinal or genitourinary tract, and evaluation should be directed toward these anatomic regions. Detection of GNB in a blood culture cannot be attributed to skin contamination, and positive cultures for GNB require antibiotic treatment. GNB are rare causes of endocarditis. Exceptions include the HACEK organisms (see Endocarditis Caused by HACEK Organisms in Infectious Disease) and Salmonella species, which can cause endovascular infection in older adults or those with pre-existing vascular disease. Because cardiac involvement is uncommon with GNB bacteremia, obtaining surveillance blood cultures is not typically necessary for patients with rapid clinical improvement (e.g., defervescence and resolution of leukocytosis) and has been associated with increased costs and excess length of hospital stay.

Infective endocarditis (IE) is a life-threatening bacterial or fungal infection of the endocardium involving valvular structures or implanted cardiac devices. Major risk factors are injection drug use and indwelling venous catheters; additional predisposition is seen with the following:

  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Immunosuppression
  • Congenital heart disease
  • Cardiac transplantation with valvulopathy
  • Implanted cardiac devices (e.g., cardiac valve prostheses, permanent pacemakers, implanted cardioverter-defibrillators, and prosthetic material for repair of congenital lesions)

Antibiotic prophylaxis for patients with risk factors for endocarditis is discussed in Infective Endocarditis in Cardiovascular Medicine. Also see Cardiac Implantable Electronic Device–Related Infections in Cardiovascular Medicine for discussion of cardiac implantable electronic device–related infections.

IE carries significant risk for morbidity and mortality, with high rates of in-hospital and 1-year mortality. Early diagnosis, targeted antimicrobial therapy, and recognizing the need for early surgical intervention enhance patient survival. In addition, hospitalization of patients who use injection drugs represents an opportunity for initiating treatment for substance use disorders (see Substance Use Disorders in Interdisciplinary Medicine).

Many clinical manifestations of IE are nonspecific, and a high index of suspicion is necessary to make the diagnosis. Findings that should prompt consideration of IE include fever without a clear alternate cause, a new cardiac murmur, and septic emboli. Bacterial endocarditis caused by S. pneumoniae and S. aureus can present as purulent meningitis, and patients can present with stroke symptoms secondary to embolic infarction. Physical findings can also suggest the diagnosis:

  • Splinter hemorrhages (

) - Conjunctival hemorrhage or petechiae (

) - Osler nodes (

) - Janeway lesions (

) - Roth spots (hemorrhagic lesions of the retina)

Blood cultures are positive in 90% of patients with IE; the microbiology of endocarditis is described in [Table: Table: Endocarditis Microbiology]

. Most instances of culture-negative endocarditis occur in patients who have received antibiotics before cultures. Serologic testing may identify fastidious organisms that are difficult to culture. In patients with a prosthetic valve, IE syndrome is classified according to the time from surgery as early (within 60 days), intermediate (60-365 days), and late (>365 days). Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) is characterized by infection with hospital-acquired microbes, such as S. aureus. Coagulase-negative staphylococci are the most common microbes in intermediate PVE. S. aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci are important causes of late PVE; however, the microbes in late PVE more typically resemble those of native valve endocarditis.

TTE is indicated to identify vegetations and associated hemodynamic derangements. TEE is indicated with intermediate or high suspicion for IE when TTE is not diagnostic, especially in the setting of a prosthetic valve, intracardiac device, repaired congenital disease with residual prosthetic material, or myocardial abscess, which in turn is suggested by new conduction abnormalities on ECG or persistent bacteremia despite antibiotic therapy. In patients with IE who have a change in clinical signs or symptoms, repeat echocardiography is recommended for reevaluation.

Definitive diagnosis of IE requires pathologic confirmation of microorganisms demonstrated by culture or histologic examination of a vegetation, a vegetation that has embolized, or an intracardiac abscess specimen. Much more commonly, the diagnosis is made using the Duke–International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Disease Criteria (see [Table: Table: Endocarditis Diagnostic Criteria]

). Clinical criteria for definite IE include either two major criteria, one major criterion plus three minor criteria, or five minor criteria. Possible IE requires one major criterion and one minor criterion or three minor criteria. IE is excluded when a firm alternative diagnosis is available or if no pathologic evidence of IE is found at surgery or at autopsy with antibiotic therapy for 4 days or less.

Appropriate antimicrobial therapy should be initiated promptly after cultures have been obtained. Empiric treatment should consider patient risk factors, such as intravenous drug use or the presence of an indwelling intravenous catheter, and focus on the most common causes of acute endocarditis:

  • S. aureus (MSSA and MRSA)
  • Streptococcus
  • Enterococcus

Regimens for empiric antibiotic therapy in critically ill patients with acute endocarditis are provided in [Table: Table: Endocarditis Empiric Antibiotic Therapy]

. Antimicrobials should not be administered to patients with valvular heart disease and unexplained fever before several blood cultures are drawn. Empiric antibiotic combinations can be modified when microbiologic results are available. Infectious disease consultation is warranted for advice on empiric treatment, targeted treatment, and the duration of therapy.

The specific therapeutic regimen varies based on the type of infection and presence of prosthetic material. When determining therapy duration, the date of the first negative blood culture is considered the start of treatment.

Optimal treatment of native valve endocarditis should include an antibiotic that can achieve bactericidal levels in the vegetation matrix and at sites of embolic disease.

Historically, parenteral antibiotics were required to achieve therapeutic levels inside the infected thrombus. Recent studies have suggested that early transition to step-down oral therapy in select patients is associated with similar outcomes and fewer complications; however, further data on the use of oral antibiotic therapy for IE are needed. Transition to an oral regimen may be considered in some patients with native valve endocarditis who are clinically stable after at least 10 days of parenteral therapy.

The specific agents and treatment duration for streptococcal endocarditis vary based on the penicillin MIC of the organism ( [Table: Table: Streptococcal Endocarditis Treatment]

). Three species, Abiotrophia, Gemella, and Granulicatella, previously termed nutritionally variant streptococci, merit special consideration. MIC determinations for these organisms are often inaccurate, and endocarditis caused by these pathogens should be treated the same as endocarditis caused by viridans group streptococci with high-level penicillin resistance (MIC ≥0.5).

S. aureus endocarditis is typically a fulminant infection, with mortality exceeding 20%. The clinical presentation varies depending on the involved valve. Right-sided (tricuspid) endocarditis is most commonly diagnosed in patients who inject drugs by vein or patients with long-term central venous catheters. Patients with right-sided endocarditis may have chest pain or hemoptysis related to septic pulmonary emboli. Radiographically, emboli appear as pleural-based nodular lesions, often with central cavitation (

). In some patients with uncomplicated tricuspid valve endocarditis (native valve, absence of extrapulmonary infection, intact kidney function) caused by MSSA, a 2-week course of an antistaphylococcal β-lactam antibiotic is adequate for cure. However, treatment regimens for MRSA right-sided endocarditis should mirror those for left-sided infection, because short-course (e.g., 2 weeks) vancomycin, even in this highly select population, is associated with an unacceptably high failure rate.

Left-sided S. aureus endocarditis is associated with poorer outcomes than right-sided disease, and at least 6 weeks of antibiotic treatment is recommended for these infections. Embolism occurs in up to 40% of patients with left-sided endocarditis, most devastatingly to the central nervous system. Anticoagulant initiation or continuation in patients with left-sided endocarditis (regardless of organism) carries a significant risk for intracranial bleeding, and multidisciplinary teams should be involved to determine the risk-benefit ratio.

Recommendations for antibiotic therapy for left-sided S. aureus endocarditis are listed in [Table: Table: Left-sided Staphylococcal Endocarditis Treatment]

. For MSSA endocarditis, use of a β-lactam antibiotic is strongly preferred. The median duration of bacteremia in patients with endocarditis treated with a cephalosporin or penicillinase-resistant semisynthetic penicillin is 4 days, compared with 7 days with vancomycin. Some authorities prefer a penicillinase-resistant semisynthetic penicillin such as nafcillin or oxacillin over cefazolin for the treatment of MSSA endocarditis because of the inoculum effect (an increase in the cefazolin MIC in the presence of a high concentration of bacteria), although the clinical significance of this phenomenon is uncertain. First-generation cephalosporins do not have adequate penetration to treat brain abscesses or meningitis, and a penicillinase-resistant semisynthetic penicillin (or, for patients who cannot tolerate these agents, vancomycin) is required in this setting.

Addition of an aminoglycoside for synergy is no longer recommended for the treatment of native valve staphylococcal endocarditis. Aminoglycoside therapy may decrease bacteremia duration by an average of 1 day but has not been shown to improve outcomes and is associated with an increased risk of nephrotoxicity.

Coagulase-negative staphylococci are frequent pathogens in prosthetic valve endocarditis, but rarely cause native valve endocarditis. Staphylococcus lugdunensis is the most virulent member of this class; when this organism is isolated in two or more blood cultures, evaluation for native valve endocarditis is warranted. Treatment for native or prosthetic valve endocarditis caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci is the same as that for S. aureus endocarditis (see [Table: Table: Left-sided Staphylococcal Endocarditis Treatment]

).

Enterococci are the third leading cause of native valve endocarditis. Increasing antimicrobial resistance has complicated the treatment of this condition ( [Table: Table: Enterococcal Endocarditis Treatment]

). Enterococci have some intrinsic resistance to ampicillin and vancomycin, requiring the use of a second agent to achieve bactericidal activity. Although aminoglycosides and cephalosporins are not active against enterococci, they work synergistically when given in combination with a primary antibiotic. The reduced toxicity of ceftriaxone compared with aminoglycosides makes it a particularly appealing option for combination therapy. Optimal treatment for vancomycin-resistant enterococci endocarditis has not been well defined but typically requires daptomycin or linezolid.

The HACEK organisms are a group of fastidious, gram-negative bacteria that have been associated with endocarditis; the acronym includes the first letter of each organism’s genus: Haemophilus aphrophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens, and Kingella kingae. H. aphrophilus and Actinobacillus have been recategorized as Aggregatibacter species. Historically, HACEK organisms were included as causes of culture-negative endocarditis, but with the improved sensitivity of automated blood culture systems, standard microbiology testing is diagnostic. Treatment for endocarditis caused by HACEK organisms is guided by sensitivity testing; recommended regimens are 4 weeks of ceftriaxone, ampicillin, or ciprofloxacin.

Candida endocarditis primarily occurs following cardiac valve surgery, in persons who inject drugs intravenously, or in those with chronic central venous catheters. Initial therapy is either liposomal formulation of amphotericin B (with or without 5-flucytosine) or an echinocandin such as micafungin, caspofungin, or anidulafungin. Fluconazole monotherapy is associated with high risk of relapse and increased mortality and is not recommended as initial treatment; step-down therapy to fluconazole can be considered for patients with a susceptible isolate after clearance of candidemia. Valve replacement surgery is required for curative intent along with at least 6 weeks of postoperative antifungal therapy. For patients who are not surgical candidates, lifetime fluconazole (or an alternative azole) suppression is recommended.

A hallmark of IE is high-grade bacteremia; however, blood cultures are negative in approximately 10% of cases. The most common reason for culture-negative endocarditis is previous antibiotic administration causing sterilization of blood cultures.

A second category of culture-negative endocarditis is infection with a fastidious organism not readily isolated on routine culture media. Therefore, culture-negative endocarditis warrants a thorough patient history and physical examination focused on potential exposures or comorbidities that may suggest targeted testing for these unusual causes ( [Table: Table: Culture-negative Endocarditis]

). Evaluation should include serology and, when valve replacement is performed, culture, polymerase chain reaction testing, and histopathology on valve tissue.

Noninfectious causes, such as marantic endocarditis seen with certain malignancies or Libman-Sacks endocarditis in systemic lupus erythematosus, may mimic infectious endocarditis.

Infection of prosthetic valves typically involves the suture ring rather than the leaflets. Prosthetic valve endocarditis is associated with annular and myocardial abscesses, both of which are indications for surgery.

Clearance of bacteremia from prosthetic cardiac material is challenging, requiring a more protracted course of therapy and the use of synergistic agents. For instance, the recommended treatment for staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis includes the primary antistaphylococcal agent for 6 weeks along with a synergistic aminoglycoside for 2 weeks and rifampin for 6 weeks. Rifampin should not be initiated until bloodstream clearance to reduce inducing resistance (see [Table: Table: Left-sided Staphylococcal Endocarditis Treatment]

).

The decision to pursue surgery for treatment of IE and the timing of such surgery are complex and require a multidisciplinary approach. Early surgery (during hospitalization and before completion of an antimicrobial course) is recommended for patients with any of the following:

  • Severe valvular dysfunction resulting in symptomatic heart failure
  • IE caused by fungal infections or other highly resistant organisms
  • Associated complications, such as annular or aortic abscess, destructive penetrating lesions, or heart block
  • Persistent bacteremia
  • Recurrent emboli after more than 5 days of appropriate antibiotic therapy
  • Large (>10-mm) vegetations

For patients who undergo valve replacement surgery, growth of an organism from the surgical specimen mandates resetting therapy initiation to the date of surgery regardless of how many weeks of preoperative antibiotics the patient received. Whether to transition treatment from a native valve to a prosthetic valve regimen following valve replacement surgery remains controversial.

Community-Acquired Pneumonia

Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is a leading cause of infection and hospitalization in the United States. The spectrum of illness caused by CAP ranges from mild disease, with approximately 50% of patients managed in the ambulatory setting, to fatal infections. Rates of infection, hospitalization, and death increase with advanced age; the incidence of hospitalization for CAP among adults 80 years or older is 25 times higher than in those younger than 50 years. Common comorbid conditions associated with increased incidence of CAP include COPD, diabetes mellitus, and heart failure.

Health care–associated pneumonia, previously considered a distinct entity, has been recategorized as CAP after studies confirmed that, in patients residing in long-term care facilities or who were hospitalized in the preceding 3 months, pathogens do not differ substantially from those in community-dwelling patients with similar comorbid conditions. In contrast, hospital-acquired pneumonia remains a distinct syndrome, with unique microbiology, antibiotic treatments, and outcomes (see Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia and Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia in Infectious Disease).

CAP is usually caused by infection with a viral or bacterial pathogen; fungal or mycobacterial infections occur much less frequently. The probability of infection with a specific organism varies based on age, comorbidities, seasonality, and geography. Epidemiologic risk factors and conditions associated with specific pathogens are listed in [Table: Table: CAP Pathogen Risk Factors]

.

Streptococcus pneumoniae, the leading bacterial cause of CAP, has decreased in incidence and accounts for only 5% to 15% of hospitalized cases in recent studies. This decrease at least partially results from the success of vaccination strategies in at-risk populations (see Pneumococcal Disease in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Rates of CAP caused by Staphylococcus aureus (including methicillin-resistant strains), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacteriaceae, however, are rising, even among patients without identifiable health care exposure. The CDC-EPIC trial, a multicenter study that performed prospective microbiologic and molecular testing on patients hospitalized with CAP, more frequently identified a viral rather than a bacterial pathogen (

). The significance of viral detection in CAP is unclear. The use of polymerase chain reaction has increased the detection of viral pathogens in patients hospitalized with CAP, which may lead to overestimation of their role as the cause. An antecedent mild upper respiratory viral infection may increase the risk for a secondary bacterial pneumonia. This phenomenon is well documented for postinfluenza CAP caused by S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, and Streptococcus pyogenes. More recently, the COVID-19 pandemic significantly influenced the epidemiology of CAP. Despite extensive laboratory investigation, no causative organism was identified in 62% of patients in the CDC-EPIC trial.

Atypical pneumonia refers to CAP caused by organisms not culturable on standard bacterial media, including viruses and fastidious bacteria such as Legionella species, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydia pneumoniae. Legionella pneumophila is a recognized cause of severe disease. Legionellosis is associated with water exposure, including hot tubs, contaminated water towers, and air conditioning units; however, infection may occur without an obvious source. A history of recent travel has been reported in approximately 10% of Legionella cases reported to the CDC. Several unique features should raise suspicion for Legionella pneumonia, including the presence of gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatremia, and elevated aminotransferase levels. M. pneumoniae is transmitted from person to person by respiratory droplets causing upper respiratory infection that progresses to pneumonia in up to 10% of persons. Extrapulmonary complications of M. pneumoniae can occur, including various rashes such as erythema multiforme and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

CAP caused by anaerobic bacteria is uncommon. Historically, anaerobes were considered important pathogens in aspiration pneumonia. Recent studies have questioned this role, with S. pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae isolated much more commonly than anaerobes in patients with community-acquired aspiration pneumonia. Risk factors for aspiration pneumonia include dysphagia, decreased consciousness (alcohol or substance use, seizures, stroke), poor dentition, gastroesophageal reflux, and vomiting. Anaerobes remain important pathogens in patients with lung abscess or empyema.

Patients with mycobacterial or fungal causes of CAP are often evaluated initially in the primary or urgent care setting. Typical empiric antibiotics are not effective and may delay appropriate diagnosis and treatment. Fungal or mycobacterial pathogens should be considered in patients with immunocompromising conditions, epidemiologic risk factors for infection (e.g., incarceration, certain hobbies or occupations, and pertinent regional or foreign travel), or subacute presentations and in patients who do not respond to conventional antibacterial treatment.

CAP should be suspected and chest imaging performed in any patient presenting with fever associated with cough, dyspnea, or chest pain. Symptoms may be subtle or absent in older adults or immunosuppressed patients, and clinicians should maintain a low threshold for pursuing radiographic studies in these populations. Posteroanterior and lateral chest radiography is recommended, acknowledging that, compared with chest CT, the sensitivity is less than 50%. In addition to confirming the diagnosis, radiographic patterns may provide clues to particular causes ( [Table: Table: CAP Radiographic Patterns]

), guide clinical decisions regarding appropriate site of care, and inform need for thoracentesis. When plain radiographs are normal but suspicion for CAP remains high, chest radiography may be repeated after 24 hours; for patients at high risk (febrile neutropenia or acute respiratory distress syndrome requiring intervention) with normal radiographs, chest CT should be pursued.

Routine laboratory studies are indicated to ascertain the severity of infection, determine the optimal site of care, and ensure appropriate antimicrobial dosing. HIV testing should be performed if indicated; a positive result expands the spectrum of potentially causative organisms. Procalcitonin level is insufficiently sensitive or specific to guide decision making regarding initiation of antimicrobial therapy. Rapid testing for influenza virus (see Clinical Features and Evaluation of Influenza in Infectious Disease) during influenza activity and for COVID-19 may assist in identifying patients who would benefit from oseltamivir and COVID-19 therapy, respectively, and to determine appropriate transmission-based precautions at hospital admission. A positive test result does not exclude a concomitant bacterial pathogen.

Diagnostic studies to identify a causative organism are not routinely indicated in outpatients with CAP but should be considered in hospitalized patients, particularly when they are at risk for infection with methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) or P. aeruginosa or a viral cause (e.g., influenza or SARS-CoV-2) is a concern. All patients with CAP who require admission to the ICU should undergo diagnostic evaluation to attempt to confirm a microbial cause. Interpretation of sputum Gram stain and culture is hampered by oropharyngeal colonization, and growth may reflect nonpathogenic organisms. A good-quality sputum culture obtained before antibiotic initiation is diagnostic in up to 80% of pneumococcal infections; sensitivity decreases after antibiotic therapy. Sputum Gram stain and culture are appropriate for specific patients:

  • Those admitted to the ICU (preferably an endotracheal aspirate in intubated patients)
  • Those who did not respond to outpatient antibiotic therapy
  • Those with cavitary lung lesions
  • Those with underlying structural lung disease

In these cases, mycobacterial, Nocardia, or fungal causes may also need to be considered.

Blood culture results are positive in 20% to 25% of patients with pneumococcal pneumonia, although cultures offer lower yield in patients with other bacterial causes. Blood cultures should be obtained routinely in patients with severe pneumonia and those treated empirically for MRSA or P. aeruginosa, because a negative result may allow de-escalation of antibiotic therapy (see Antimicrobial Therapy in Infectious Disease). Pneumococcal urinary antigen testing is more than 70% sensitive, and results are not affected by antibiotic administration. Legionella urinary antigen test results are positive in most patients with L. pneumophila serotype 1 infection. However, the test does not detect other serotypes, and results can remain positive for prolonged periods after infection. Urinary antigen tests should be reserved for use in patients with moderate to severe CAP who require hospitalization, are immunocompromised, or have a known or possible exposure to Legionella (e.g., during an outbreak).

To improve detection of influenza and COVID-19, rapid nucleic acid amplification tests are preferred instead of antigen diagnostic tests. Respiratory viral panel results using nucleic acid amplification are positive in up to 40% of patients hospitalized with CAP; however, a positive result may reflect viral coinfection or antecedent predisposing infection rather than current clinical illness. Although these panels are less helpful in guiding decisions about discontinuing antibiotic therapy, a positive respiratory viral panel might have significant infection control implications among patients who are hospitalized.

Additional testing is indicated in select patients based on epidemiologic risk factors (see [Table: Table: CAP Pathogen Risk Factors]

) or clinical or radiographic findings (see [Table: Table: CAP Radiographic Patterns]

). Fungal, modified acid-fast, and acid-fast bacilli stains of sputum can be performed. Enzyme immunoassay is the initial test for coccidioidomycosis, with confirmatory testing with complement fixation and immunodiffusion. Histoplasmosis and blastomycosis can be detected by urine or blood antigen testing. Serology for Coxiella burnetii, Francisella tularensis, Legionella, Mycoplasma, and Chlamydia, using acute and convalescent sera, can document seroconversion or a fourfold increase in titers, but these tests do not help make a diagnosis in the acute setting; antibiotic therapy initiation should not be delayed while awaiting results for convalescent sera.

Diagnostic thoracentesis of parapneumonic effusions should be considered to exclude concomitant empyema requiring drainage (see Indications for Thoracentesis in the Setting of Pleural Effusion in Pulmonary Medicine). Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy should be considered in patients who do not respond to empiric therapy.

Ambulatory management is adequate for many patients with CAP. Clinical prediction models are available to identify patients who can be safely managed in the outpatient setting. The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) is a validated predictor of all-cause mortality at 30 days. The initial assessment determines the presence of 11 variables associated with adverse outcomes ( [Table: Table: CAP Clinical Decision Support Scoring Systems]

). Patients with no risk factors (severity risk class I) can typically be managed as outpatients. Although the PSI may aid in site-of-care decisions, it should not supersede clinical judgment. The use of the PSI is preferred over the use of the CURB-65 (confusion, urea, respiration rate, blood pressure, age 65 years and older) because it identifies a larger proportion of patients at low risk and has greater discriminative power in predicting mortality.

Consensus guidelines by the Infectious Diseases Society of America and the American Thoracic Society (IDSA/ATS) provide criteria to identify patients with severe pneumonia who are best managed in the ICU (see [Table: Table: CAP Clinical Decision Support Scoring Systems]

). In addition to the need for mechanical ventilation or vasopressor support to maintain blood pressure, the presence of three or more minor criteria suggests a higher mortality rate, and ICU care is recommended.

IDSA/ATS guidelines for the management of CAP were updated in 2019 to address the challenges of increasingly resistant organisms causing CAP. These recommendations balance the need to effectively treat infection, often without an identified pathogen, with the competing imperative for judicious antibiotic use. Treatment recommendations are stratified by site of care, which in turn is determined by infection severity and comorbidities (see [Table: Table: CAP Clinical Decision Support Scoring Systems]

and [Table: Table: Empiric Antibiotics for CAP]

).

In otherwise healthy patients who do not require hospitalization, recommended regimens include monotherapy with doxycycline or amoxicillin (1 g three times per day). Compared with previous IDSA CAP guidelines, macrolides (azithromycin and clarithromycin) are only recommended if the regional prevalence of pneumococcal resistance to this class is known to be less than 25% (in the United States, macrolide resistance exceeds 30%).

For patients with significant comorbidities treated as outpatients, a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone or a β-lactam plus either a macrolide or doxycycline is recommended. Options for oral β-lactams include amoxicillin-clavulanate, cefuroxime, and cefpodoxime. Macrolides and fluoroquinolones may prolong the QTc interval, and alternative agents (i.e., a β-lactam plus doxycycline) should be considered in patients at risk for torsades de pointes, including those with a history of a long QT interval, taking other medications that can prolong the QT interval, and with electrolyte abnormalities. Patients who have not responded to a previous CAP regimen who still meet criteria for outpatient therapy should be retreated with an agent from an alternative class.

Patients with more severe infections requiring hospitalization may be infected with a broader spectrum of bacterial pathogens, reflecting host susceptibility and organism virulence. Hospitalized patients with CAP are most commonly infected with the organisms shown in

. Recommended empiric regimens are shown in [Table: Table: Empiric Antibiotics for CAP]

. Patients with previously isolated respiratory MRSA or P. aeruginosa are at risk for recurrent infections with these organisms; therefore, an antibiotic active against the previously cultured pathogens should be included.

The microbiology and suggested treatment regimens among patients with CAP requiring ICU care are shown in [Table: Table: Empiric Antibiotics for CAP]

. In this population, combination therapy with a macrolide has shown a survival benefit compared with combination therapy with a respiratory fluoroquinolone, making the former the preferred treatment.

MRSA is not adequately treated by the previously discussed empiric regimens, but it is increasingly recognized as causing CAP, particularly in critically ill patients. CAP caused by MRSA is associated with preceding influenza infection, hospitalization or parenteral antibiotics in the past 90 days, and injection drug use, although it may present in patients without any identifiable risk factors. Empiric therapy for MRSA should be considered in patients with one of the following risk factors:

  • MRSA growth on a previous respiratory culture
  • A suspicious Gram stain (gram-positive cocci in clusters)
  • Conventional therapy failure
  • Pleural-based lung nodules (suggesting septic pulmonary emboli;

) - Cavitary lung lesions

Optimal treatment for MRSA CAP has not been defined, but options include vancomycin and linezolid; ceftaroline is FDA approved for CAP treatment and has activity against MRSA, but it has not been specifically approved for treatment of MRSA CAP. Notably, daptomycin binds to surfactant, resulting in negligible alveolar levels, and is therefore ineffective in pulmonary infections. In patients with blood cultures, respiratory cultures, and nasal polymerase chain reaction negative for MRSA, antibiotic therapy can be de-escalated.

P. aeruginosa is another pathogen not adequately treated by standard empiric regimens. Pseudomonas should be considered in immunocompromised patients and in patients with underlying structural lung disease or medical conditions requiring repeated courses of antibiotics. Infection with this bacterium in the preceding year or hospitalization or parenteral antibiotic administration in the preceding 90 days are also recognized risk factors for infection. When clinical concern for Pseudomonas is present, treatment should include an antipseudomonal β-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, ceftazidime, aztreonam, imipenem, or meropenem) in conjunction with an agent active against atypical organisms (either a macrolide or a respiratory fluoroquinolone). Empiric treatment with a quinolone is relatively contraindicated in patients who did not respond to a previous course of a drug in this class.

Patients with CAP who test positive for influenza should also be treated with an antiviral agent regardless of duration of illness before diagnosis; however, antiviral therapy is unlikely to benefit patients with uncomplicated illnesses that began more than 48 hours before testing. Identification of a viral organism as the causative agent of CAP does not exclude a bacterial coinfection. S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, and S. pyogenes have all been associated with postinfluenza necrotizing CAP. Therefore, the IDSA/ATS guidelines recommend prescribing antibiotics for CAP even when a viral pathogen is identified.

Anaerobic infections are uncommon causes of CAP. For patients in whom a concern exists for anaerobic infection and who can be treated in the ambulatory setting, amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate are active against most oral anaerobic bacteria. In hospitalized patients with CAP, the addition of anaerobic coverage is only recommended if lung abscess or empyema is suspected. In patients with a lung abscess, ampicillin-sulbactam or a carbapenem can be used; for patients allergic to β-lactam agents, clindamycin monotherapy or levofloxacin plus metronidazole are alternatives.

For patients with severe pneumonia in the ICU who are responding to empiric therapy without culture evidence of MRSA or Pseudomonas at 48 hours, the likelihood of infection with one of these agents is low, and antibiotics can be de-escalated to a standard regimen for nonsevere CAP in hospitalized patients. For patients with uncomplicated CAP who demonstrate rapid defervescence and clinical improvement over the first 3 days, a 5-day course of therapy is adequate for cure. Exceptions include patients with cavitary disease or lung abscess, empyema, concomitant bacteremia, extrapulmonary infection, or ongoing instability, defined as persistent fever, abnormal vital signs, or hypoxia. Many authorities also recommend a longer antibiotic duration for CAP caused by S. aureus or Pseudomonas. Fungal or mycobacterial lung infections require an extended course of treatment.

Studies suggest a role for ancillary treatment with glucocorticoids. Combination therapy with an antiviral agent and glucocorticoids or interleukin-6 inhibitors have shown improved outcomes for pneumonia in severe SARS-CoV-2 infection. Glucocorticoids may also provide a survival benefit for patients with severe bacterial pneumonia (e.g., PSI risk class of IV or V, CURB-65 score ≥3, or ICU-level care required) but should be avoided when fungal or mycobacterial infection is being considered.

CAP has a mortality rate of 10% to 12% among hospitalized patients. Survivors may experience significant morbidity, including prolonged hospitalization, protracted convalescence, and high rates of hospital readmission. Related complications include localized lung inflammation, secondary spread of infection, and toxicity related to treatment ( [Table: Table: CAP Complications]

).

Lack of response to antimicrobials raises consideration of a resistant or atypical organism not being treated, loculated infection (such as empyema), or an infection mimic (tumor, vasculitis, congestive heart failure, pulmonary embolism). Patients with significant pleural fluid collections should undergo diagnostic thoracentesis; chest tube drainage is indicated for empyema. See Parapneumonic Effusion and Empyema in Pulmonary Medicine for further information.

In adults with CAP whose symptoms have resolved within 5 to 7 days, routine follow-up chest imaging is typically not necessary.

Readmission rates among hospitalized patients approach 20%. This population should have close outpatient follow-up to ensure clinical stability after therapy completion.

Tick-Borne Diseases

Lyme disease is the most common tick-borne infection in the United States, with more than 30,000 new infections reported annually. More than 95% of infections in the United States occur in the Northeast, mid-Atlantic, and upper Midwest regions (

). These areas are endemic for the vector, Ixodes scapularis (blacklegged deer tick;

). The causative spirochete, Borrelia burgdorferi, is transmitted intradermally when a tick ingests a blood meal.

In select situations, prophylaxis with a single dose (200 mg) of doxycycline may decrease the risk for Lyme disease after a tick bite. Prophylactic doxycycline is only recommended if the tick is reliably identified as a blacklegged deer tick, attachment lasted 36 hours or longer, antibiotics can be started within 72 hours after tick removal, and B. burgdorferi prevalence in ticks in the region exceeds 20%. Otherwise, observation is recommended, with treatment given if suggestive symptoms develop. Other infections spread by this tick vector, such as Powassan virus encephalitis or babesiosis, are not prevented by doxycycline prophylaxis.

The clinical manifestations, diagnostic testing, and treatment of Lyme disease vary according to the stage of infection ( [Table: Table: Lyme Disease by Stage of Infection]

). Information on uncommon pathogens and emerging infections that may be indistinguishable from Lyme disease are listed in [Table: Table: U.S. Tick-borne Pathogens in Humans]

.

Early localized disease typically presents within 4 weeks of infection. Most infected persons (70%-80%) develop erythema migrans (EM), a red, annular skin rash (

) that often, but not always, has central clearing (

). Systemic symptoms are variably present.

The EM rash is usually painless, nonpruritic, and circumferentially enlarging. Atypical presentations of EM, with confluent erythroderma, ulceration, or vesiculation, may confound the diagnosis. Local cutaneous reactions resulting from hypersensitivity to tick saliva may resemble EM but tend to occur earlier, are pruritic, and do not enlarge significantly after onset.

Confirmatory laboratory testing is not required or recommended in a patient with EM and a compatible history. In fact, antibody testing in early localized disease is insensitive because seroconversion may be delayed for several weeks after an EM rash appears. Doxycycline offers the advantage of treating incubating Anaplasma phagocytophilum, which is also spread by blacklegged ticks and can coinfect patients with Lyme disease.

Without antibiotic treatment (see [Table: Table: Lyme Disease by Stage of Infection]

), hematogenous dissemination occurs in up to 60% of patients. Symptoms of early disseminated disease present weeks to months after infection. The most common manifestation is a flu-like illness characterized by fevers, arthralgia, myalgia, and lymphadenopathy and often associated with multiple concurrent EM eruptions at sites distant from the original tick attachment.

Disseminated infection may also involve the heart and the nervous system. Lyme carditis results in injury to the conduction system and atrioventricular nodal block. Progression to complete heart block can occur rapidly despite antibiotic treatment, so hospitalization is indicated for close monitoring of symptomatic patients with cardiac involvement or asymptomatic patients with first-degree (or higher) atrioventricular block and a PR interval of 300 milliseconds or greater. Permanent pacemaker placement is not necessary because the heart block is reversible with antibiotic therapy.

Neurologic infection occurs in approximately 15% of untreated patients. Aseptic meningitis, facial palsy (unilateral or bilateral), and radiculopathy can present alone or with skin, musculoskeletal, or cardiac findings. Serum antibody testing, rather than polymerase chain reaction of cerebrospinal fluid or serum, is recommended to diagnose Lyme disease involving the peripheral or central nervous system (see Bacterial Meningitis in Infectious Disease).

As with early localized disease, laboratory confirmation is unnecessary when classic EM is present. Without diagnostic skin findings, serologic testing should be pursued through a two-tiered approach (

); the initial enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay is highly sensitive but lacks specificity, and positive or equivocal tests must be confirmed. Previously, Western blot was the recommended confirmatory test; however, an alternative option using a second sequential enzyme immunoassay has been FDA-approved for this purpose.

IgM antibody is detectable before IgG antibody in early infection; therefore, testing for both antibodies should be performed in patients presenting within 30 days of symptom onset. After this time, only IgG antibody testing is recommended because, after the first month of symptoms, an isolated IgM antibody is likely to be a false positive. Antibodies may remain detectable for years despite treatment; therefore, serial titers are not useful.

Approximately 60% of untreated patients with Lyme disease develop monoarticular or oligoarticular inflammatory arthritis as a late complication. The knee and other large joints are disproportionally affected. Even without antibiotic treatment, inflammation typically resolves over weeks to months but often has a relapsing-remitting pattern. In approximately 10% of patients with Lyme arthritis, joint symptoms are persistent (see Lyme Arthritis in Infectious Disease). Diagnosis requires laboratory confirmation at this stage. Treatment requires prolonged oral antibiotics; parenteral therapy is used when oral therapy is unsuccessful (see [Table: Table: Lyme Disease by Stage of Infection]

). Late neurologic or skin findings (acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans and borrelial lymphocytoma) are rare in the United States but more frequent in European infections.

Post–Lyme disease syndrome has been reported in approximately 10% of patients after treatment of EM. Although often erroneously called chronic Lyme disease, no microbiologic evidence of chronic or latent infection is found after appropriate treatment. Symptoms include fatigue, arthralgia, myalgia, and memory or cognitive impairment that can last for years despite treatment. Clinical trials have shown no benefit to prolonged antibiotic treatment. Evaluation for coinfection with another tick-borne pathogen or for a noninfectious cause is indicated.

Babesiosis is caused by the intraerythrocytic protozoan Babesia microti, which is spread by I. scapularis (blacklegged deer tick) and thus occurs in areas of Lyme endemicity (

). Transmission through transfusion of infected blood products may result in infections outside of endemic regions.

Approximately 20% of infections are asymptomatic, with the remainder ranging from mild illness to fatal disease (10%). Risk factors for severe disease include age older than 50 years, immunocompromise, and asplenia. Symptoms typically begin within 1 month after tick bite and within 2 months after transfusion of infected blood products. Symptoms are nonspecific and include fever (89%), fatigue (82%), chills (67%), headache (47%), myalgia (43%), and cough (28%). Physical examination may reveal jaundice, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly, which rarely progresses to splenic rupture. The hallmark of babesiosis is hemolysis, with anemia almost invariably present. Severe disease may include multiorgan involvement, including thrombocytopenia, elevated serum aminotransferase levels, acute kidney injury, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and congestive heart failure.

Visualization of B. microti on thin blood smears is diagnostic (

). With low-level parasitemia, the sensitivity of microscopy is poor. Therefore, polymerase chain reaction should be pursued if the clinical suspicion of babesiosis is high. Antibody testing does not differentiate acute from previous infection and is not recommended for diagnosis.

The first-line treatment for babesiosis is outlined in [Table: Table: Babesiosis Treatment]

. Immunocompromised patients often require a longer treatment course, typically 6 weeks, including 2 weeks after documented clearance of parasites on blood smear. Exchange transfusion may be indicated in patients with high-grade (>10%) parasitemia and those with severe disease characterized by severe hemolytic anemia or marked pulmonary, kidney, or liver manifestations.

Southern tick–associated rash illness (STARI) presents with EM identical to that seen in Lyme disease but without clinical progression or complications. STARI is associated with Amblyomma americanum, also known as the Lone Star tick, which is endemic to the southeastern, south-central, and eastern United States (see

). No infectious cause has been confirmed. Therefore, diagnosis is based on clinical and geographic features. Because skin findings for STARI and early-stage Lyme disease are indistinguishable, treatment with doxycycline is often offered; however, it is undetermined if treatment for STARI is necessary or beneficial.

Ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis are clinically similar illnesses spread by different tick vectors and caused by distinct bacterial pathogens. Ehrlichiosis is usually caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis, which is transmitted by the Lone Star tick. Anaplasmosis is caused by A. phagocytophilum, which is transmitted by Ixodes ticks, and occurs in areas of Lyme endemicity (

).

These syndromes typically begin with a nonspecific febrile illness 1 to 2 weeks after a tick bite ( [Table: Table: Features of Ehrlichiosis, Anaplasmosis, and Spotted Fever Rickettsioses]

). Rash is uncommon in adults. Leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and increased serum aminotransferase levels are often present.

Basophilic inclusion bodies (termed morulae) visualized in the cytoplasm of leukocytes (

) suggest the diagnosis but are present in few cases. Antibody tests are often negative in acute illness; a convalescent specimen 2 to 4 weeks after onset of symptoms showing a four-fold rise in titer is confirmatory. Polymerase chain reaction of whole blood at the time of acute illness is highly sensitive, particularly if performed before therapy. Doxycycline is the recommended treatment for ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis. Because delay in treatment is associated with increased mortality, empiric therapy should be started even in the absence of confirmatory testing.

Spotted fever group rickettsioses (SFR) are a group of closely related tick-borne infections that are serologically indistinguishable. The most common and most serious of the SFR in the United States is Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF), caused by Rickettsia rickettsii and transmitted by the dog tick and other vectors (see

). RMSF has been reported throughout the continental United States but occurs most frequently in a linear distribution extending from North Carolina to Oklahoma.

Clinically, RMSF presents with nonspecific symptoms similar to those of ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis (see [Table: Table: Features of Ehrlichiosis, Anaplasmosis, and Spotted Fever Rickettsioses]

). The hallmark feature is a rash; however, skin findings are typically delayed by several days after fever onset and may not be apparent at the initial clinical evaluation. The rash evolves from a macular eruption localized to the ankles or wrists, with central spread and progression to petechiae or purpura (

). Lesions are found on the palms and soles in as many as 50% of patients; the face is generally spared. Purpura fulminans may occur and result in loss of digits or limbs. Up to 30% of patients have meningoencephalitis.

Immunohistochemical analysis of skin biopsy samples may be diagnostic. Serology is insensitive during acute illness, and testing convalescent serum is often needed to confirm the diagnosis. Doxycycline should be given empirically when SFR is suspected because treatment delay is associated with more severe disease and increased mortality.

Powassan virus is an emerging tick-borne infection spread by Ixodes ticks (see [Table: Table: U.S. Tick-borne Pathogens in Humans]

). Most reported infections have presented with meningoencephalitis, with a high mortality rate (see Encephalitis Caused by Arboviruses in Infectious Disease). Diagnosis can be made by the presence of IgM and neutralizing antibody in serum and CSF as well as viral antigen and PCR in blood, tissue, or CSF; testing is coordinated with state health departments. No antiviral therapy is available, and treatment is supportive.

Urinary Tract Infections

Community-acquired urinary tract infections (UTIs) account for approximately 9 million ambulatory visits and 2 million hospitalizations annually in the United States, making UTIs one of the most common infections for which an antibiotic is prescribed. Another 1 million nosocomial UTIs are diagnosed annually, primarily urinary catheter associated, accounting for a significant proportion of health care–associated infections (see Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections in Infectious Disease). Approximately 50% of all women experience a UTI by age 30 years; sexual activity is a major risk factor. Other risk factors include structural and functional abnormalities, use of spermicidal agents and diaphragms, pregnancy, diabetes mellitus, obesity, urethral catheterization (or other urinary tract instrumentation), incontinence, immunosuppression, and genetic factors (female relative with history of UTIs).

UTIs are classified based on anatomic location as lower (cystitis), upper (pyelonephritis, perinephric abscess), or prostatitis (see Acute Prostatitis in Interdisciplinary Medicine). The term uncomplicated UTI refers to infections in nonpregnant women without structural or neurologic abnormalities or comorbidities. UTIs are referred to as complicated in the following populations and settings:

  • Men
  • Pregnant persons
  • Persons with foreign bodies (e.g., indwelling catheters or calculi)
  • Kidney disease
  • Immunocompromise
  • Obstruction
  • Urinary retention from neurologic disorders

Advanced age combined with other major comorbidities or frailty may be considered a complicating factor, although age alone does not define a complicated versus uncomplicated infection. Designating a UTI as complicated influences the choice and duration of antimicrobial therapy and extent of investigation ( [Table: Table: Risk Factors for Complicated UTI]

).

Most infections occur by the ascending route. In 95% of ascending UTIs, a single bacterial species is the cause, primarily gram-negative aerobic bacilli originating from the bowel. Uropathogenic Escherichia coli accounts for 75% to 95% of UTIs in women. Less common pathogens include other Enterobacteriaceae, streptococci (particularly Streptococcus agalactiae), enterococci, and staphylococci (most often Staphylococcus saprophyticus). UTIs occurring in health care settings frequently involve a varied group of organisms (such as Enterobacter, Providencia, Morganella, Citrobacter, Serratia, Pseudomonas, and Corynebacterium urealyticum). Staphylococcus aureus isolation in the urine may be related to instrumentation or a possible hematogenous infection (e.g., endocarditis).

Diagnosis is based on numerous clinical features, determining the anatomic location of infection (lower or upper urinary tract), and the presence of pyuria (≥10 leukocytes/µL) and bacteriuria. Pyuria can be detected by urine dipstick, which relies on the presence of leukocyte esterase. Although the sensitivity and specificity of dipstick testing are high (about 75% and 85%, respectively), pyuria may result from conditions other than infection. Leukocyte casts support a diagnosis of pyelonephritis. Microscopic or gross hematuria may occur with a UTI but may also be seen with nephrolithiasis and tumors. A positive nitrite test result signifies the presence of gram-negative bacteria capable of converting nitrates into nitrites.

Quantitative cultures of a midstream, clean-void urine sample are the most accurate way to demonstrate bacteriuria in patients with suspected UTI. Because of predictable microbiology and short treatment courses, culture is not recommended in patients with uncomplicated cystitis. Urine cultures are indicated in pyelonephritis, complicated cystitis, and recurrent UTIs; in patients with histories of multiple antibiotic allergies; and in patients with a suspected resistant organism (recent antibiotic treatment, health care–associated infection, and previous multidrug-resistant UTI). The growth of 10^5 colony-forming units (CFU)/mL or greater in urine is considered significant bacteriuria; however, lower CFU counts may support a diagnosis in those with symptoms.

In most adults, imaging studies are not required, but they may be indicated when the diagnosis is unclear, when a structural abnormality or complication is suspected, or in patients with severe illness, immunocompromise, or lack of response to appropriate therapy. Ultrasonography can detect obstruction, whereas noncontrast helical CT is recommended for visualizing kidney stones. Although less sensitive than CT, kidney ultrasonography is less expensive, has no radiation exposure, and can be used if CT is unavailable. Contrast-enhanced CT (CT urography) is recommended when intrarenal or perinephric abscess is suspected.

Without treatment, uncomplicated cystitis (urinary frequency and urgency, dysuria, and suprapubic discomfort) resolves in up to 50% of patients within 1 week. Recommended first-line antibiotic regimens should consider increased rates of E. coli antimicrobial resistance, the efficacy and advantages of short-course therapies, and the potential adverse effects of antimicrobials. Preferred agents in nonpregnant patients include the following:

  • Nitrofurantoin (5 days)
  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (3 days) (unless community rates of resistance are >20% or if used for a UTI in the previous 3 months)
  • Fosfomycin (1 dose, but expensive and possibly less effective)

Fluoroquinolones (3 days) and β-lactam agents (including amoxicillin-clavulanate, cefdinir, cefaclor, and cefpodoxime-proxetil, each 3-7 days) are considered acceptable alternative second-line therapies. β-Lactams are not preferred if other recommended agents are available because they are less effective in eradicating infection.

During pregnancy, penicillins, cephalosporins, and fosfomycin are reasonable options for susceptible organisms. Sulfonamides and nitrofurantoin can also be prescribed in the second and third trimesters; these agents can be considered in the first trimester if no other alternative agents are available and risks and benefits have been discussed. Quinolones are generally avoided in pregnancy.

Extended-spectrum β-lactamase–producing Enterobacteriaceae causing cystitis have increased in frequency, especially with recent antimicrobial or health care–facility exposure. Because of the greater risk of resistant and polymicrobial infections, urine culture and susceptibility testing are indicated in all patients with complicated cystitis. Fluoroquinolones are the preferred choice pending results, although fosfomycin, nitrofurantoin, and β-lactams are alternative options. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is used for specific susceptible pathogens. The recommended treatment duration ranges from 5 to 10 days (depending on the antibiotic utilized) rather than a 3-day regimen.

Test of cure is not indicated in patients reporting symptom resolution.

Lower urinary tract symptoms (frequency, urgency, and dysuria) often precede the fever, chills, flank pain, and sometimes nausea and vomiting that characterize acute pyelonephritis. Infection can usually be managed in the outpatient setting with oral antibiotics. Hospitalization is advised in specific circumstances:

  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Obstructive disease
  • Pregnancy
  • Complicating comorbidities
  • Pathogen resistance requiring parenteral antibiotic therapy
  • Inability to tolerate oral medications
  • Lack of reliable home supervision or clinical follow-up

Urine culture with susceptibility testing, ideally obtained before initiation of empiric therapy, is recommended to optimize therapy. Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin for 7 days or levofloxacin for 5 days) are the only oral agents recommended for empiric outpatient treatment, but an initial dose of a long-acting parenteral antibiotic (such as ceftriaxone, 1 g, or a once-daily aminoglycoside) should be given before oral fluoroquinolone courses when local resistance rates exceed 10%. When a fluoroquinolone is contraindicated, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (twice daily for 14 days) may be used after pathogen susceptibility is proven; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole should be avoided as initial empiric therapy because of the high level of E. coli resistance in the community. Oral β-lactams have lower efficacy with higher relapse rates but may be alternatives if susceptibility results are known and no other options are available.

Depending on the risk of antimicrobial resistance, inpatient parenteral antimicrobial options include a fluoroquinolone, extended-spectrum cephalosporins or extended-spectrum penicillins, or a carbapenem. Empiric fluoroquinolone therapy is avoided in severely ill patients with pyelonephritis because of the increasing potential for resistance.

Therapy can be completed with active oral agents when an adequate clinical response has been observed. Patients with bacteremia do not require longer treatment courses and may be transitioned to appropriate oral therapy when clinically stable.

Imaging studies are only necessary in patients with prolonged fever (>72 hours) or persistent bacteremia, in whom complications such as obstruction or perinephric and intrarenal abscesses must be excluded. If a renal abscess is present, management may also include percutaneous or surgical drainage, depending on the extent and location of the abscess; drainage is recommended for abscesses 5 cm or greater, whereas abscesses less than 5 cm can often be managed with antibiotic therapy alone. Perinephric abscesses 3 cm or greater typically require therapeutic drainage; smaller abscesses may also require drainage for diagnostic reasons.

Routine follow-up urine cultures are only indicated in pregnant individuals.

An estimated 25% to 30% of patients experience a second infection within 6 months of their first UTI.

Relapsed infections are those recurring with the same organism within 2 weeks of completing antimicrobial therapy (5%-10% of cases). Relapse suggests infection with a resistant bacterium, incomplete treatment, or a structural abnormality, including renal calculi. Relapsed infection requires a urine culture. Assuming the organism is sensitive, patients with relapsed infection are treated for a presumed upper UTI for 7 to 10 days with the same antibiotic as initially prescribed or an alternative agent based on susceptibility data.

Reinfection, the most common type of recurrent UTI, is generally caused by a bacterial strain separate from the original infection and presents more than 2 weeks after treatment of the previous infection. The same first-line antimicrobial agent can be given for reinfections, unless the recurrence occurs within 3 months, particularly if the original agent was trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, because of the increased chance of resistance.

Cystoscopy and imaging studies are indicated when structural abnormalities or obstruction are suspected.

Strategies to prevent infection recurrence include antimicrobial and nonantimicrobial interventions, such as topical vaginal estrogen use in postmenopausal patients without contraindications. Cranberry products have not been proven effective in controlled trials. Prophylactic daily antimicrobial agents have been found to reduce the risk of recurrences by nearly 95%; they are an option in women who have had three or more UTIs in the previous 12 months, or two or more in the previous 6 months, and have received no benefit from other prevention efforts. Prophylactic therapy may be considered in pregnant patients who have required treatment for recurrent cystitis or asymptomatic bacteriuria to prevent recurrence during pregnancy, although data regarding management in this situation are limited. Approximately 50% of patients revert to previous recurrence patterns within 6 months of prophylaxis discontinuation. Recommended daily low-dose prophylactic antibiotics in nonpregnant patients include nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and cephalexin. Fluoroquinolones are very effective but not recommended. For sexually active women with recurrent cystitis, postcoital antimicrobial prophylaxis with one self-administered dose of nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, or cephalexin can be used.

Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) is defined as the presence of at least 10^5 CFU/mL of a uropathogen from two consecutive voided urine specimens in women or one specimen in men, or at least 10^5 CFU/mL of one pathogen from a catheterized urine specimen in women or men. In all cases, local or systemic signs or symptoms of infection are absent. The prevalence of ASB ranges from 1% to 5% in healthy premenopausal women (2%-10% in pregnant women) to almost 100% in patients with long-term indwelling urinary catheters.

Accompanying pyuria is not an indication for antimicrobial treatment. Reflex cultures based on detection of more than 10 leukocytes per high-powered field in asymptomatic patients or in patients presenting with signs or symptoms unrelated to the urinary system should be avoided. ASB treatment neither decreases the frequency of symptomatic infections nor improves other outcomes. Inappropriate treatment is a major driver of antimicrobial resistance, particularly in health care facilities.

However, treatment is indicated in pregnant persons and in patients undergoing an invasive procedure involving the urinary tract ( [Table: Table: Asymptomatic Bacteriuria Screening and Treatment]

). It is not recommended to screen for or treat ASB in kidney transplant recipients more than 1 month after transplantation. Evidence is insufficient for or against screening for or treating ASB in transplant recipients 30 days or less after transplantation. For pregnant patients with asymptomatic bacteriuria, preferred treatment options include amoxicillin-clavulanate, cephalosporins (e.g., cephalexin, cefpodoxime), nitrofurantoin (in the second and third trimesters; also reasonable in the first trimester if no appropriate alternatives are available), and fosfomycin.
