Mycobacterium tuberculosis Infection

Approximately 25% of the world’s population is infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis; around 10 million new M. tuberculosis infections and 1.3 million deaths occur annually. Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) accounts for 3.5% of new infections and 20.5% of relapsed infections. Extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB) accounts for approximately 6.2% of all MDR-TB infections worldwide.

In 2022, 8300 tuberculosis infections were reported in the United States (2.5 per 100,000 persons); 73% were among persons born outside the United States. Others at high risk include those with alcohol use disorder, socioeconomically disadvantaged persons, persons without housing, persons who inject drugs, persons who are incarcerated, persons living in shelters, persons with HIV, and older adults.

Tuberculosis is classified as pulmonary, extrapulmonary, or both. Primary tuberculosis occurs soon after the initial infection, most frequently in children and immunosuppressed persons. The pulmonary lesions often heal spontaneously. Secondary or reactivation tuberculosis results from endogenous reactivation of a latent infection. Most cases of active tuberculosis are caused by reactivation of latent tuberculosis in the setting of immunosuppression. Risk factors for developing active tuberculosis are shown in [Table: Table: Active Mycobacterium tuberculosis Risk Factors]

. Of secondary infections, 75% are pulmonary, except in those infected with HIV, in whom extrapulmonary infection is more common.

Most persons infected with M. tuberculosis have latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) and are asymptomatic and noncontagious. Manifestations of active infection include fever, night sweats, weight loss, productive cough (occasionally blood tinged), anorexia, malaise, and pleuritic chest pain. Hemoptysis occurs in 10% to 20% of patients with positive acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear results. In patients who are immunosuppressed, the infection may also spread hematogenously, producing miliary (progressive, widely disseminated) tuberculosis, which can result in a systemic inflammatory response syndrome, septic shock, and ultimately death if not diagnosed and treated early. Extrapulmonary disease may result from hematogenous dissemination and may be seen in up to 30% of patients with active tuberculosis. It may involve almost any organ system, including the pleura, lymph nodes, central nervous system (see Tuberculous Meningitis in Infectious Disease), skeletal system, pericardium, larynx, peritoneum, and genitourinary system.

The goal of diagnosing and treating LTBI is to decrease the risk for reactivation tuberculosis. Screening of asymptomatic adults is recommended in populations at increased risk:

  • Patients born in or with previous residence in countries with high tuberculosis prevalence
  • Persons who have lived in congregate settings such as prisons or homeless shelters
  • Immunocompromised patients (those with HIV/AIDS or those who have previously undergone organ transplantation)
  • Patients receiving tumor necrosis factor α inhibitor medications
  • Patients with a known tuberculosis exposure

Those with a very low likelihood of LTBI should not be tested routinely because the yield is low and a false-positive result is possible.

Testing methods are interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) performed on a blood sample and tuberculin skin testing (TST). In those with a known exposure, baseline testing should be performed as soon as possible to evaluate for previous LTBI. After a negative baseline IGRA or TST, a repeat IGRA or TST should be performed 8 to 10 weeks after exposure. The IGRA or TST will be positive within 4 to 10 weeks after tuberculosis infection. LTBI is diagnosed in an asymptomatic patient who has a positive TST or IGRA result with no clinical or radiographic manifestations of active tuberculosis. Neither test is used to diagnose active tuberculosis; these tests can be negative in patients with active tuberculosis.

The CDC recommends performing an IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube and T-SPOT.TB test) rather than a TST in persons 5 years or older who are likely to have M. tuberculosis infection, have a low or intermediate risk of disease progression, have a history of bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination, or are unlikely to return to have their TST result interpreted. IGRAs have fewer false-positive results from previous BCG vaccination or infection by nontuberculous mycobacteria than TST.

TST is the alternative diagnostic test if IGRA is not feasible or available. Purified protein derivative is injected intradermally and interpreted after 48 to 72 hours by measuring the transverse diameter of induration, not erythema. The criteria for a positive TST result are based on the patient’s risk factors for tuberculosis ( [Table: Table: Tuberculin Skin Test Interpretation]

). A false-negative TST result may occur in patients with recent tuberculosis infection, overwhelming active tuberculosis infection, recent viral infections, or severe immunocompromise (e.g., AIDS) and in those younger than 6 years. Patients with remote exposure to M. tuberculosis may initially have a negative TST result that can become positive several weeks later after a second TST (“booster effect”). A second TST is recommended in health care personnel 7 to 21 days after initial testing and should be performed on the opposite forearm; it is not required if IGRA is used. The CDC no longer recommends annual tuberculosis testing for health care personnel unless a known exposure or ongoing transmission is identified in the facility.

The lifetime risk of developing active infection in immunocompetent patients with LTBI is 5% to 10%, with the highest risk of development of active tuberculosis within 2 years of the initial infection. The risk of developing active tuberculosis is higher in patients who are immunocompromised.

The classic radiographic finding in pulmonary tuberculosis is upper lobe disease with air space disease and cavities (

). However, any radiographic pattern can be seen.

All patients suspected of having active pulmonary tuberculosis should have AFB smear microscopy of respiratory specimens. Testing three specimens is highly recommended because false-negative results from a single specimen are not uncommon. False-positive results are also not uncommon resulting from infection or contamination with nontuberculous mycobacteria; thus, a positive smear result requires culture confirmation. At least 3 mL of sputum should be submitted (5-10 mL is preferred). Serial specimens must be obtained at least 8 hours apart, with one sample being an early morning specimen.

The gold standard for diagnosis of active infection remains mycobacterial culture. Whether AFB staining results are positive or negative, liquid and solid cultures should be performed for every specimen obtained. Liquid culture allows for faster growth and more rapid identification of organisms (2-4 weeks).

Patients with suspected active tuberculosis should also undergo diagnostic nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) of the initial respiratory specimen. The positive predictive value of a NAAT on a smear-positive sputum sample is 95%, and NAAT for M. tuberculosis can be used to verify the organism. Mycobacterial cultures are also recommended so in vitro susceptibilities can be obtained. Among patients with a negative AFB smear and a moderate to high suspicion of pulmonary tuberculosis, the sensitivity of NAAT is 50% to 80%. A NAAT is available that provides additional molecular identification of rifampin-resistant strains, providing optimization of empiric antituberculous therapy. A negative NAAT result cannot be used to exclude pulmonary tuberculosis.

If signs of extrapulmonary infection are present, samples from those sites are obtained and sent for AFB stain, mycobacterial culture, and histopathology. Histopathology may demonstrate caseating granulomas, which suggest but are not exclusive to or diagnostic of tuberculosis. In disseminated tuberculosis, blood cultures for mycobacteria using isolator methodology are helpful.

When suitable antimicrobial therapy is administered and taken appropriately, clinical and microbiologic cure rates are approximately 95%. Therapy depends on several factors, including the classification of infection (latent versus active), pulmonary versus extrapulmonary infection, demonstration of a drug-resistant organism, and patient adherence.

All patients with a positive IGRA or positive TST should be evaluated for active disease, with a full medical history, physical examination, and chest radiography, and be screened for HIV infection. If no sign of active infection is present, patients should be offered treatment for LTBI. The 2020 CDC guidelines include five treatment regimens ( [Table: Table: Latent Tuberculosis Treatment]

). Pyridoxine is recommended in patients who will receive isoniazid and are at risk for peripheral neuropathy (diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, malnutrition, HIV infection, and alcohol use disorder). Monitoring of liver chemistry tests is not routinely required unless patients are at risk for hepatotoxicity (HIV, chronic hepatitis B or C infections, alcohol use disorder, pregnancy, concurrent hepatotoxic drugs, or underlying liver disease).

Rifamycins are contraindicated in pregnancy. In pregnant individuals with LTBI, a 6- to 9-month regimen of isoniazid plus pyridoxine may be offered; some experts prefer to defer therapy until after delivery, unless the patient is at high risk of developing active infection owing to immunocompromise, including HIV infection.

When active tuberculosis is verified, the initial isolate should undergo in vitro susceptibility testing for first-line agents (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol). This testing is important because of the advent of MDR-TB and XDR-TB. If rifampin resistance was detected during NAAT assessment, in vitro susceptibilities to first-line and second-line agents should be performed ( [Table: Table: Antituberculous Drugs]

).

Two guideline-based recommended regimens are available for treating drug-susceptible active pulmonary tuberculosis. One option is a four-drug regimen (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) taken daily for 2 months (intensive phase) followed by isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months (continuation phase). The second option (moxifloxacin, rifapentine, isoniazid, pyrazinamide) is taken daily for 8 weeks (intensive phase) followed by moxifloxacin, rifapentine, and isoniazid for 9 weeks (continuation phase); it is equally effective in select patients ( [Table: Table: Preferred Active Tuberculosis Treatment Regimens]

).

Sputum specimens should be evaluated at 1- and 2-month intervals to assess for clearance of infection. Clinical assessment and laboratory testing (complete blood count, liver chemistry testing, hepatitis serology) should be performed before initiating therapy.

Patients should be advised of the possible adverse effects of various medications (see [Table: Table: Antituberculous Drugs]

). Approximately 15% to 25% of patients receiving the four-drug regimen experience an adverse effect. Most are mild, and therapy may be continued; up to 15% are severe enough that therapy must be discontinued temporarily. If a hypersensitivity reaction is observed, all four drugs should be discontinued with sequential rechallenging to determine the cause.

M. tuberculosis resistance to individual drugs arises by spontaneous point mutations. Depending on the specific resistance pattern, the regimen must be altered. In isoniazid-resistant tuberculosis, the recommended regimen of rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide is administered for 6 months, and adding a later generation fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin) to the regimen is recommended. For rifampin-resistant, quinolone-resistant infections, a 6-month course of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid is as effective and safe as more prolonged regimens. Similarly, for rifampin-resistant, quinolone-susceptible infections, a 6-month course of bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, and moxifloxacin, rather than a 15-month regimen, is recommended. In those with isoniazid- and rifampin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), the recommendation is to use five drugs in the intensive phase of treatment and four drugs in the continuation phase of treatment. The recommended intensive-phase duration is between 5 and 7 months after culture conversion, with the total duration between 15 and 21 months after culture conversion (see [Table: Table: Antituberculous Drugs]

).

Patients treated with biologic medications (such as tumor necrosis factor inhibitors) or Janus kinase inhibitors have an increased risk of reactivation tuberculosis and death from disseminated disease. These patients should be evaluated for active or latent tuberculosis by performing chest radiography and IGRA (preferred) or TST before beginning this therapy. All patients should receive treatment for tuberculosis (latent or active) if identified, although LTBI treatment does not completely eliminate the risk for active mycobacterial infection in this population.

The best way to prevent tuberculosis is to diagnose, isolate, and treat infection rapidly until patients are considered noncontagious and disease is cured. Airborne precautions (see [Table: Table: Transmission-Based Precautions]

) should be instituted for hospitalized patients, who should also wear a surgical mask when outside of the room to contain respiratory secretions. Airborne precautions should be discontinued only after approval by the infection prevention program.

Criteria to determine a patient is no longer contagious include appropriate antimicrobial therapy for at least 2 weeks, clinical improvement of signs and symptoms, and three negative sputum smears collected at least 8 hours apart, with one smear being an early-morning specimen. Patients with negative smear results are less contagious, although they may still have active tuberculosis.

Nontuberculous Mycobacterial Infections

Nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) comprise species other than Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex and Mycobacterium leprae. NTM are divided into slow (growth on solid media in 2-4 weeks) and rapid (growth usually in <7 days) growers ( [Table: Table: Nontuberculous Mycobacteria Classifications]

). These organisms are found in water, soil, domestic and wild animals, milk, and food products. They are responsible for a spectrum of clinical infections ( [Table: Table: Diseases Caused by Nontuberculous Mycobacteria]

).

Pulmonary disease caused by NTM is most often diagnosed in older adults with or without chronic lung disease (i.e., bronchiectasis or COPD). The most common species isolated in pulmonary infection are Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC), Mycobacterium kansasii, and Mycobacterium abscessus. In immunocompetent patients, MAC exposure has also been linked to the development of hypersensitivity pneumonitis, particularly after hot tub use (“hot tub lung”). Diagnosing pulmonary disease is challenging because a positive culture from a nonsterile site may reflect colonization rather than true infection. In patients with MAC pulmonary infection, cavitary lung disease is seen classically in middle-aged or older adult men with underlying lung disease; in women older than 50 years, nodules and bronchiectasis are typically seen on chest imaging.

Fulfillment of certain clinical, radiologic, and microbiologic criteria are required for diagnosis ( [Table: Table: Pulmonary Nontuberculous Mycobacterial Disease Criteria]

). Treatment is recommended for patients meeting diagnostic criteria, especially if sputum smears are positive for acid-fast bacilli or cavitary lung disease is present. First-line therapy for MAC pulmonary infection includes combination azithromycin, rifampin, and ethambutol; an aminoglycoside may be added for significant cavitary disease. Most pulmonary NTM infections require prolonged treatment with multiple antimicrobials for at least 12 months, and consultation with a treatment expert should be obtained.

Skin and soft tissue infections are most likely caused by rapidly growing mycobacteria such as M. chelonae, M. fortuitum, and M. abscessus (see [Table: Table: Risk Factors for Skin Pathogens]

). Infection often results from trauma, and outbreaks have been associated with pedicures (infected whirlpool and foot baths) and tattooing. Patients initially have nodular cutaneous lesions that may ultimately ulcerate. M. marinum is widely found in aquatic environments (salt and fresh water), and skin infections are associated with exposure to contaminated fish tanks or swimming pools.

MAC is the most common pathogen (80% of cases) causing NTM lymphadenitis; less common causes include M. haemophilum, M. fortuitum, and M. abscessus. Similar to scrofula (tuberculous lymphadenitis), cervical disease is most common, with infection through the oropharyngeal mucosa. Surgical excision is preferred and is often curative, whereas incision and drainage may lead to a chronic draining sinus. Antimicrobial therapies are indicated when surgery is contraindicated.

Disseminated disease caused by MAC in persons with HIV infection occurs most commonly when the CD4 cell count is less than 50/µL. The incidence has decreased in recent years because of the use of potent antiretroviral therapy (see Mycobacterium avium complex in Infectious Disease).

NTM rarely cause surgical site infections, but they have been reported in patients who have undergone cosmetic surgery without adequate infection control practices and have been associated with medical tourism. They have also been isolated as the causative agent in central catheter–related infections. Mycobacterium chimaera has been associated with hospital-acquired prosthetic valve endocarditis and disseminated infection related to contaminated heater-cooler devices used during cardiac surgery.

Fungal Infections

Fungal infections commonly encountered in North America include candidiasis, aspergillosis, pneumocystis (see Pneumocystis jirovecii in Infectious Disease), cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, and mucormycosis. Increased recognition and advances in diagnostic testing for fungal infections have led to increased incidence. Additionally, populations at risk worldwide are increasing, partly because of expanding geographic distributions of these organisms and increasing numbers of patients living with immunocompromising conditions.

Candida albicans and other Candida species are part of normal human flora. In certain circumstances, they can become pathogenic, causing a spectrum of diseases ranging from local mucocutaneous infection (see Opportunistic Infections in Infectious Disease, Infectious Esophagitis in Gastroenterology, and Vulvovaginal Candidiasis in Interdisciplinary Medicine) to invasive infection and candidemia.

Patients at the highest risk for candidemia are those who are immunocompromised, who have had recent abdominal surgery or trauma, or who are in the ICU ( [Table: Table: Systemic Candidiasis Risk Factors]

). Candidemia symptoms can range from an isolated fever to septic shock. The isolation of Candida in blood cultures should never be considered a contaminant, but when recovered from the respiratory or urinary tract, it generally represents colonization, not infection. Candida meningitis is usually associated with recent central nervous system (CNS) surgery or ventricular shunt. Endophthalmitis, septic arthritis, and endocarditis are other forms of invasive infection that generally arise as sequelae of candidemia.

Diagnosing invasive candidiasis is challenging because blood cultures are positive in only approximately 40% to 70% of patients. Having a high index of suspicion for candidiasis in patients at high risk is essential to avoid delays in initiating antifungal therapy and increased mortality. Nonculture, direct molecular diagnostic methods provide rapid (within hours) diagnosis of candidemia and can be performed after antifungal therapy initiation. The β-d-glucan assay may support the diagnosis of invasive fungal infections, including candidiasis, particularly among patients with negative blood cultures. However, this assay is not specific for Candida and can be positive with other fungal infections (e.g., Aspergillus, Pneumocystis jirovecii).

In invasive Candida infections, species identification and susceptibility testing are necessary. Several Candida species (e.g., Candida glabrata, Candida krusei, and Candida auris) have low susceptibility or intrinsic resistance to antifungal agents. C. auris is an emerging species that presents a serious global threat. Microbiologic identification is difficult, and C. auris is often resistant to azoles and polyenes and occasionally to echinocandins. It has been associated with numerous health care outbreaks.

Initial empiric treatment of candidemia and invasive candidiasis should include an echinocandin and intravascular device removal (if present/possible). However, because echinocandins have poor penetration into the CNS and the eye, patients with CNS and eye infections should be treated with an amphotericin B preparation, or an azole if the organism is found to be susceptible; treatment may also require additional agents depending on patient characteristics and disease extent. For all invasive Candida infections, prompt treatment initiation is critical, and follow-up blood cultures are required to document clearance. The Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends performing a dilated funduscopic examination in all patients with candidemia to exclude endophthalmitis; however, the American Academy of Ophthalmology only recommends this examination in patients with symptoms or signs of ocular infection. Species identification, sensitivities, and follow-up blood culture results guide therapy. Antifungal therapy duration for candidemia should be 14 days from the first negative blood culture result in patients with uncomplicated candidemia and up to 6 weeks in patients with end-organ disease.

The most common species causing aspergillosis in humans are the following:

  • Aspergillus fumigatus
  • Aspergillus flavus
  • Aspergillus niger
  • Aspergillus terreus (amphotericin resistant)

Aspergillus generally produces illness after inhalation of airborne spores (90%) in susceptible persons and occasionally by traumatic skin inoculation.

Invasive aspergillosis most often occurs in immunosuppressed patients with prolonged neutropenia or those who are recipients of a lung or hematopoietic stem cell transplant ( [Table: Table: Invasive Aspergillosis Risk Factors]

). Aspergillosis usually begins in the respiratory tract and then may enter the circulatory system (angioinvasion). The most common manifestation is pulmonary infection (60%), but sinusitis, brain abscess, and disseminated infection may also occur. Symptoms and signs are often nonspecific ( [Table: Table: Invasive Aspergillosis Features]

), and blood culture results are generally negative; however, timely diagnosis and treatment are essential to decrease morbidity and mortality. Therefore, when invasive pulmonary aspergillosis is suspected, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and tissue biopsy are recommended to establish the diagnosis (

). Chest CT; serum galactomannan and 1,3 β-d-glucan assays; serum polymerase chain reaction; and galactomannan assay and polymerase chain reaction of BAL fluid can be useful in establishing a diagnosis of invasive infection. Pulmonary nodules, often with a “halo sign” (

); thromboembolic pulmonary infarction (wedge-shaped peripheral densities); or necrosis with cavitation (air-crescent sign) are typical radiologic findings, especially in patients with neutropenia and recipients of hematopoietic stem cell transplant.

First-line treatment of invasive aspergillosis is either a mold-active triazole, such as voriconazole, or combination therapy with a mold-active triazole plus an echinocandin. Combination therapy should be considered in patients with critical illness or if concern exists for triazole resistance. Alternative agents include liposomal amphotericin B, isavuconazole, posaconazole, and other lipid formulations of amphotericin B. When possible, decreasing immunosuppression improves treatment response. Therapeutic drug monitoring is recommended for mold-active triazoles.

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis results from hypersensitivity to Aspergillus species colonizing the respiratory tract. This condition is seen primarily in patients with cystic fibrosis and asthma (see Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis in Pulmonary Medicine).

Cryptococcus is an encapsulated yeast that is ubiquitous in the environment. Patients with immunocompromising conditions such as advanced HIV infection, malignancy, cirrhosis, organ transplantation, and prolonged glucocorticoid use are most commonly affected, but infection can also occur in healthy persons. Cryptococcus neoformans is the most commonly identified species, but Cryptococcus gattii is seen with increasing frequency in the Pacific Northwest region of North America and appears to be spreading southward. The pathogenesis of cryptococcosis involves inhalation of spores into the respiratory tract, followed by dissemination into susceptible tissues, especially the CNS.

Cryptococcal infection most commonly manifests as subacute meningitis, and cryptococcosis is the most common cause of fungal CNS infection worldwide. Clinical manifestations are listed in [Table: Table: Cryptococcosis Features]

, and indicators of poor prognosis are provided in [Table: Table: Poor Prognosis in Cryptococcal Meningitis]

. Blood culture may be positive for cryptococcus, indicating disseminated disease, which should prompt evaluation for CNS disease. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis is essential to diagnose CNS involvement; classic findings include the following:

  • Increased leukocyte count (mainly lymphocytes)
  • Increased protein level
  • Low to normal glucose level
  • Yeast on Gram stain or culture
  • Presence of cryptococcal antigen

The cryptococcal antigen has greater than 95% sensitivity and specificity when performed on CSF or blood; it is more sensitive than cultures or polymerase chain reaction.

Cryptococcal meningitis often causes elevated intracranial pressure (ICP). Therefore, the opening pressure should be assessed during lumbar puncture, and, if elevated (≥200 mm H~2O), CSF should be removed until opening pressure is reduced to a normal level of 200 mm H~2O or less or to half of the original opening pressure if it was extremely high. Aggressive ICP reduction decreases early morbidity and mortality; if untreated, ICP can lead to herniation, blindness, or other neurologic deficits. Daily lumbar punctures or insertion of a ventricular shunt may be necessary to adequately control elevated ICP.

A lipid formulation of amphotericin B plus flucytosine for at least 2 weeks is recommended for induction therapy for cryptococcal meningitis and is effective in more than 90% of patients. If clinical improvement is noted and repeat CSF cultures are negative after 2 weeks of induction therapy, consolidation therapy can be initiated with fluconazole (400-800 mg/d) for 8 weeks. After the consolidation phase, patients should receive maintenance therapy with a lower dose of fluconazole (200 mg/d) for 1 year. Patients with HIV infection and cryptococcal meningitis should generally delay initiation of antiretroviral therapy until 4 to 6 weeks after starting antifungal treatment because of the risk for immune reconstitution syndrome. They also require maintenance (suppressive) therapy with fluconazole for at least 1 year and until their immunocompromised state has been reduced; this reduction includes maintaining CD4 cell counts greater than 100/µL and an undetectable viral load. Serial cryptococcal antigen testing is not a sensitive marker for microbiologic cure and is not recommended for determining treatment adequacy.

Histoplasma capsulatum, one of the most common endemic mycoses in the world, is a dimorphic organism. Acquired by inhalation of conidia, this organism primarily produces asymptomatic pulmonary infection. Its distribution includes the Mississippi River Valley (Ohio, Missouri, Indiana, Mississippi) in the United States; Central and South America; the Caribbean; and regions of Europe, Africa, Australia, and Asia (

).

Acute pulmonary histoplasmosis is the most common symptomatic infection, with cough, fever, chills, and myalgia developing 1 to 4 weeks following exposure. It may initially be mistaken for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) but does not respond to antibiotic therapy. Radiographically, infection often appears as patchy, nodular infiltrates with distribution throughout the bilateral lung fields (

). Other presentations include disseminated infections (immunosuppressed patients) (

), chronic cavitary infection (patients with underlying lung disease) (

), inflammatory pericarditis, and granulomatous or sclerosing mediastinitis.

Histoplasma antigen can be detected on urine, blood, CSF, or BAL fluid; the sensitivity increases when multiple sample types are tested, in disseminated infections, and in immunocompromised patients. Serologic testing can be helpful, especially in non-immunocompromised patients whose symptoms have been present more than 1 month. Antigen and antibody tests for Histoplasma can cross-react with Blastomyces. Fungal cultures of tissue or blood can take 4 to 6 weeks to grow; although often unhelpful for acute management, cultures may provide a later diagnosis. Because Histoplasma is dimorphic, it will grow as a mold in the clinical laboratory (colder temperature) and will appear as a yeast form on histopathology (because of warmer body temperature).

Asymptomatic and minimally symptomatic acute pulmonary histoplasmosis typically resolve without treatment. Antifungal therapy should be considered for immunocompromised patients or those with prolonged symptoms. Patients with moderate disease should receive treatment if they have prolonged illness duration, experience severe or worsening symptoms, or experience progression of pulmonary infiltrates or hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Treatment is recommended for patients with severe or disseminated disease. Itraconazole with therapeutic drug monitoring is recommended for mild to moderate infection. For acute infection, therapy duration is 6 to 12 weeks with radiographic evidence that pneumonia has resolved; for chronic cavitary pulmonary infection, the duration is at least 12 months, and therapy should not be discontinued until radiographic findings have stabilized. Serial testing of the Histoplasma antigen level is useful for determining therapy adequacy. Patients with severe respiratory or disseminated infection should receive liposomal amphotericin B initially, followed by de-escalation to oral itraconazole.

Coccidioides is a dimorphic fungus endemic to desert regions of the Western United States (

). Infection is usually acquired by inhalation of aerosolized arthroconidia; the fungus then transitions to the yeast form in the body.

Most infections have minimal or no associated symptoms. The most common clinical presentation is pneumonia with symptoms of cough, fever, and chest pain, often difficult to distinguish from bacterial CAP. Coccidioidomycosis should be considered in patients with CAP and endemic exposure, especially if symptoms do not improve with empiric antibiotics. Extrathoracic dissemination can manifest as meningitis or osteoarticular or cutaneous infection (

). Coccidioides meningitis may demonstrate an eosinophilic pleocytosis on CSF analysis. The risk for infection (and dissemination) is greater in those who are immunocompromised, pregnant, younger than 5 years, or older than 50 years.

Serologic testing for Coccidioides antibodies is recommended for initial evaluation, but results can be negative in early illness, requiring subsequent retesting. Antigen testing on serum and urine may be useful in patients who are immunocompromised or in severe disease; these assays can cross-react with Histoplasma and Blastomyces. Cultures and histopathology from affected tissue may also yield a diagnosis. The laboratory should be alerted if Coccidioides is suspected because, when grown in culture, this organism can be transmitted to laboratory personnel.

Immunocompetent patients with mild to moderate pulmonary infection generally do not require treatment. Fluconazole is first-line treatment for most nonpregnant patients with disseminated or severe infection, including meningitis; lifelong fluconazole is recommended for patients with Coccidioides meningitis because of the high risk for relapse.

Blastomyces dermatitidis is a dimorphic, round, broad-based, budding yeast. In the United States, blastomycosis is endemic along the Mississippi and Ohio River valleys (

). Infection occurs by inhalation of conidia and is often asymptomatic. Acute or chronic pneumonia is the most common clinical presentation; extrapulmonary disease occurs through hematogenous dissemination, most commonly to bones or skin (

and

). Immunocompromised patients and pregnant persons are at risk for more severe or disseminated infection.

Diagnosis can be made by histopathology or culture of affected tissue, although cultures can take up to 5 weeks to grow. Serology for Blastomyces antibodies as well as urine and serum antigen testing are frequently utilized for diagnosis but can cross-react with the other endemic fungi. Most cases of blastomycosis require treatment. The preferred treatment for mild to moderate infection is itraconazole. Liposomal amphotericin B is recommended for CNS, severe pulmonary, and disseminated infections.

Sporothrix schenckii is a dimorphic fungus found most often in soil, plants, or plant debris. Although found worldwide, most reported infections are from North and South America and Japan. Infection occurs after direct contact with plants, such as roses and sphagnum moss. Direct cutaneous inoculation of the organism results in nodular or ulcerative lesions at the site with subsequent eruption of nodular lesions proximally through lymphatic spread (

). Extracutaneous infection (osteoarticular, pulmonary, ocular, or disseminated) can occur in patients who are immunocompromised but is uncommon.

Diagnosis requires culture of the organism from affected tissues. Treatment is with itraconazole.

Mucormycosis (formerly zygomycosis) is a devasting mold infection associated with high morbidity and mortality in highly immunocompromised persons. Patients with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, hematologic malignancies, and iron overload states (including deferoxamine administration) and those who have undergone stem cell transplantation are particularly at risk. The most common organisms are Rhizopus, Rhizomucor, and Mucor species. These fungi are commonly found in the environment on decaying organic debris and soil and are generally acquired by inhalation, although inoculation through penetrating trauma does occur infrequently.

Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical manifestation of mucormycosis (

). Patients may have symptoms of acute sinusitis, although in patients with neutropenia, fever may be the only symptom. This infection can erode through tissue and bone into adjacent structures, causing tissue necrosis, and can even invade into the orbits and brain. Pulmonary mucormycosis is relatively common and can be difficult to distinguish from pulmonary aspergillosis. Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion and is generally made based on histopathology or cultures from biopsy of affected tissue; no serologic studies are available.

Treatment requires urgent, extensive surgical removal of affected tissue (especially in sinusitis), reversal of predisposing conditions, and early antifungal therapy. Initial treatment is liposomal amphotericin B; posaconazole or isavuconazole can be used as step-down or salvage therapy. Mortality rates remain as high as 60% to 80%, even with therapy.

Sexually Transmitted Infections

A detailed sexual history is crucial to understand individual risk for sexually transmitted infections (STIs). STI risk factors include a new partner, more than one current partner, a partner with an STI, a partner who has concurrent partners, and a history of an STI. Adolescents, young adults, and men who have sex with men (MSM) are among the groups who have been disproportionately affected by STIs.

Unrecognized or inadequately treated STIs are a preventable cause of infertility. The CDC provides evidence-based guidelines for diagnosis and management. Any patient diagnosed with an STI should be evaluated for other STIs, including HIV, and receive risk reduction counseling.

Transgender and gender-diverse persons may experience stigma that can negatively affect health care service utilization, and thus have missed opportunities for STI and HIV prevention, testing, or treatment. Providers should take a comprehensive medical history, including preferred pronouns and gender identity, to improve STI care.

Recommendations for STI screening and testing are often designated for “men” or “women;” however, the efficacy of screening and testing is based on anatomy rather than gender. STI screening in all populations, including transgender and gender-diverse individuals, should be based on anatomy and other risk factors for STIs.

Screening for STIs is crucial for patient health and public safety because many STIs are asymptomatic and can lead to serious complications if left untreated (see Screening for Infectious Diseases in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Strategies to decrease the risk of STIs include individualized discussion of behavioral risk reduction strategies, HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis when appropriate (see Prevention in Infectious Disease), and doxycycline postexposure prophylaxis when appropriate. To prevent chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis, doxycycline postexposure prophylaxis is recommended for men who have sex with men and for transgender women who have had at least one bacterial STI in the preceding 12 months. Patient-administered doxycycline (200 mg as a single dose) has been proven to reduce rates of chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis when taken within 72 hours of oral, vaginal, or anal sex.

Vaccines are available for human papillomavirus and hepatitis A and B viruses. See Vaccinations Recommended for Some Adults in Foundations of Clinical Practice for information on these vaccines.

Chlamydia trachomatis is the most commonly reported bacterial STI in the United States. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends screening of all sexually active women younger than 25 years, and women aged 25 years and older if they have STI risk factors ( [Table: Table: Screening for Gonorrhea and Chlamydia]

). The CDC recommends screening men in settings or populations with high prevalence or burden of disease (MSM, STI clinics).

Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) is preferred for screening and diagnosis. First-catch urine sample (for men) and vaginal or endocervical swabs (for women) can be used. Oropharyngeal and rectal infection can occur, and these extragenital sites should be evaluated using NAAT; MSM should be screened at least yearly for urethral and rectal infection, if those sites of contact are exposed, and more frequently (e.g., every 3-6 months) if they have multiple partners or ongoing risk behaviors.

Treatment of clinical syndromes caused by C. trachomatis is outlined in [Table: Table: Treatment of Common STIs]

. Test of cure is not routinely recommended, except in pregnancy, when treatment nonadherence is a concern, with persistent symptoms, and when alternative regimens are used. Because reinfection is common, patients should be retested 3 months after treatment or at their next medical appointment.

In addition to cervicitis, urethritis, pharyngitis, and rectal infection, disseminated gonococcal infection (presenting as arthritis-dermatitis syndrome) can occur (see Disseminated Gonococcal Infection in Infectious Disease).

USPSTF screening recommendations are identical to those for chlamydia (see [Table: Table: Screening for Gonorrhea and Chlamydia]

). For screening and diagnosis, NAAT is preferred, using a first-catch urine sample (men) and vaginal or endocervical swabs (women). Pharyngeal, urethral, and rectal sites should be tested at least yearly in MSM if those sites of contact are exposed, based on individual sexual practices. More frequent screening should occur (e.g., every 3-6 months) in the setting of multiple partners or ongoing risk behaviors. In patients with disseminated gonococcal infection, all N. gonorrhoeae isolates should be tested for antimicrobial susceptibility. Patients with suspected disseminated gonococcal infection should have cultures performed on the following:

  • Blood
  • Synovial fluid (if arthritis is present)
  • Purulent skin lesions (if present)
  • Cerebrospinal fluid (if meningitis is suspected)

Because culture yield is not high, NAAT from all potential sites of exposure (genital, pharyngeal, rectal) should also be obtained.

Treatment is outlined in [Table: Table: Treatment of Common STIs]

. For uncomplicated gonococcal infections of the cervix, urethra, or rectum, ceftriaxone monotherapy is recommended. In patients with a severe cephalosporin allergy, parenteral gentamicin plus oral azithromycin is an option.

Patients with N. gonorrhoeae who do not respond to treatment should have repeat testing with NAAT and culture so that susceptibility data can be obtained; expert consultation is advised.

It is not necessary to perform a test of cure in patients with uncomplicated urogenital or rectal infection. However, patients with pharyngeal infection should receive a test of cure 2 weeks after therapy; if NAAT is positive, confirmatory culture should be performed. Retesting of all patients is recommended 3 months after treatment to assess for reinfection.

Mycoplasma genitalium is an emerging STI that can cause urethritis in men; it has been reported to cause up to 20% of nongonococcal urethritis and 46% of nongonococcal/nonchlamydial urethritis. M. genitalium is also associated with cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Testing should be performed with NAAT in men with recurrent nongonococcal urethritis and in women with recurrent cervicitis; it should also be considered in women with PID. Routine screening in asymptomatic persons is not recommended. Treatment is sequential, with doxycycline for the initial regimen, followed by azithromycin (for macrolide-sensitive organisms) or moxifloxacin (macrolide resistant or resistance testing not available) (see [Table: Table: Treatment of Common STIs]

).

Patients with cervicitis may have vaginal discharge and intermenstrual bleeding, but many are asymptomatic. The major diagnostic criteria are visualizing mucopurulent discharge from the cervical os or on a swab obtained from the endocervical canal and bleeding elicited by passing a swab into the cervical os. N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis are the most common pathogens; however, the cause remains unknown in many cases. The role of M. genitalium is unclear. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is occasionally implicated. Noninfectious causes (e.g., chemical irritation from douching) should also be considered. Patients should be tested for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis with NAAT and be evaluated for bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis (see Vaginitis in Interdisciplinary Medicine).

PID describes inflammatory conditions of the upper genital tract in women. Unrecognized PID may result in infertility, chronic pelvic pain, and ectopic pregnancy, the risk of which increases with recurrent episodes. Symptoms may be mild or nonspecific and include lower abdominal pain, vaginal discharge, intermenstrual bleeding or bleeding after intercourse, and dyspareunia. Fever and other signs of systemic toxicity are uncommon.

Uterine tenderness, adnexal tenderness, or cervical motion tenderness is sufficient to make a clinical diagnosis of PID, especially if accompanied by mucopurulent cervical discharge.

PID is believed to be polymicrobial; however, testing is only indicated for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. M. genitalium has been associated with PID, and testing should be considered, but the role of treatment for this pathogen is unclear. Most infections can be managed in the ambulatory setting with oral antibiotics (see [Table: Table: Treatment of Common STIs]

). Indications for hospitalization include inability to exclude a surgical emergency (such as appendicitis), pregnancy, severe systemic toxicity, tubo-ovarian abscess, inability to tolerate oral antibiotics, and failure of initial outpatient management.

Men with urethritis can have dysuria, urethral pruritus, and mucopurulent discharge. N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and M. genitalium are common causes; Trichomonas vaginalis may also be causative. A first-catch urine sample is the specimen of choice and should be tested for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis by NAAT. A Gram stain of urethral discharge that does not show gram-negative diplococci within polymorphonuclear leukocytes supports a diagnosis of nongonococcal urethritis. NAAT testing for T. vaginalis or M. genitalium should be performed for men who have persistent or recurrent symptoms after initial empiric treatment. Microscopic examination of a urethral sample that reveals a leukocyte count greater than 2 per oil immersion field has a high positive predictive value for infectious urethritis, but the negative predictive value is poor. A positive leukocyte esterase test result or a microscopic examination of a first-void urine specimen with a leukocyte count greater than 10/hpf is also diagnostic for infectious urethritis. This testing is not required if mucoid, mucopurulent, or purulent urethral discharge is demonstrated on examination. See [Table: Table: Treatment of Common STIs]

for treatment.

Persons with epididymitis present with unilateral pain and swelling in the epididymis; the testes may also be inflamed (epididymo-orchitis). N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis are likely causes in younger, sexually active men. Enteric gram-negative organisms, such as Escherichia coli, can also be the causative agents in men who practice insertive anal sex; these organisms can also cause epididymitis from bacteriuria resulting from bladder outlet obstruction (such as in benign prostatic hyperplasia) or from instrumentation or surgery of the genitourinary tract. NAAT for STI pathogens should be performed on first-catch urine, as well as a urine culture. Empiric treatment is appropriate in sexually active men. Persistent symptoms despite treatment should be re-evaluated for complications or other causes, including noninfectious causes. See Acute Testicular and Scrotal Pain in Interdisciplinary Medicine for further information.

In addition to receptive anal intercourse, infection may occur in women because of autoinoculation from vaginal discharge. The evaluation of patients with anorectal pain, rectal discharge, or tenesmus should include a thorough sexual history. Causes include C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae, syphilis, and HSV. Infections caused by lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) serovars (L1, L2, or L3) of C. trachomatis are an increasing cause of proctitis and proctocolitis. Mpox can also cause anorectal pain and proctitis; see Mpox in Infectious Disease for further information.

Diagnostic evaluation should include NAAT for C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae, and HSV polymerase chain reaction of any anorectal lesions, as well as serologic testing for syphilis. Although NAAT can evaluate for C. trachomatis, additional molecular testing is required to identify LGV serovars; however, this testing is not yet widely available.

Treatment of these clinical syndromes is outlined in [Table: Table: Treatment of Common STIs]

. Empiric treatment based on clinical syndrome is reasonable in symptomatic patients who may not be able to return for follow up. Diagnostic testing should still be performed because many STIs are reportable, and test results will be informative if the infection fails to respond to empiric therapy as well as for partner notification and treatment.

Patients should abstain from sexual contact until 7 days after completion of therapy and all sexual partners have been treated. Sexual partners in the previous 60 days, or the most recent partner if greater than 60 days, should be referred for evaluation and treatment. Although independent evaluation and testing of sexual partners is preferred, most states have laws pertaining to the provision of empiric antibiotic therapy prescriptions to the patient for their partners (expedited partner therapy, or EPT).

In some populations, such as young heterosexual women and MSM, HSV-1 is a more common cause of symptomatic primary infection than HSV-2. HSV-1 is less likely than HSV-2 to cause symptomatic recurrent ulcers and subclinical shedding. Differentiation between the two viral subtypes is important in counseling patients regarding the natural history of their infection.

Primary infection presents as multiple painful lesions that begin as erythematous papules, progress to vesicles (

), then ulcerate (

), crust, and eventually heal within 2 to 3 weeks. Primary infection is often accompanied by significant systemic symptoms, which can include meningitis (see Viral Meningitis in Infectious Disease). Tender inguinal lymphadenopathy may be present. See Herpes Simplex Virus Types 1 and 2 in Infectious Disease for discussion of extragenital manifestations.

NAAT for HSV-1 and HSV-2 using a swab obtained from the ulcer or lesion is preferred to confirm the diagnosis. Serologic testing is not advised for diagnosing symptomatic ulcer disease. Serologic testing may be performed when evaluating the potential benefits of long-term suppressive therapy to decrease the transmission risk in serodiscordant couples or to evaluate maternal serostatus in the context of evaluating a neonate with or at risk for herpes virus infection. The CDC recommends considering HSV serologic testing in persons who present for STI evaluation, MSM with previously undiagnosed genital tract infection, and persons living with HIV who present for STI evaluation. Serologic screening in the general population is not recommended.

Antiviral therapy for primary infection has been shown to decrease time to symptom resolution, lesion healing, and viral shedding ( [Table: Table: Treatment of Genital Herpes Simplex Virus]

).

Recurrent genital HSV infections are less severe. Many patients will experience prodromal itching, burning, or tingling before ulcers appear. Atypical presentations such as fissures and excoriations may occur. Recurrent infection can be managed with either episodic self-start therapy (initiated within 24 hours of symptoms) or long-term suppressive therapy (see [Table: Table: Treatment of Genital Herpes Simplex Virus]

). Transmission, asymptomatic shedding, and risk of perinatal transmission, as well as ways to reduce transmission to a sexual partner should be discussed with all patients. Long-term suppressive therapy should be considered for persons with frequent recurrences and can decrease the risk of transmission to seronegative sexual partners. Laboratory monitoring is not required for patients undergoing long-term suppressive therapy; however, the continued need for therapy should be reviewed annually.

The incidence of primary and secondary syphilis has been increasing in the United States since 2000, and a significant increase in congenital infections has been reported. Screening is recommended for those at increased risk and for all pregnant persons at the initial prenatal visit. If a patient is not screened early in pregnancy, the USPSTF recommends screening at the first available opportunity. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists also recommends universal rescreening in the third trimester and at delivery ( [Table: Table: Screening for Syphilis]

).

Primary syphilis presents as a painless genital ulcer (chancre) with a raised regular border that demonstrates firm induration on palpation (

). Several chancres may be present and may occur in the oral cavity or other mucous membranes. Regional lymphadenopathy may be present. Serologic test results may be negative in early primary infection. Even without treatment, lesions heal spontaneously in 3 to 6 weeks.

The most common manifestation of secondary syphilis is rash. Various forms are described; involvement of the palms and soles is characteristic. In intertriginous areas, papules may coalesce to form

.

(superficial erosions on mucosal surfaces) may occur in the oral cavity and moist genital regions and are highly infectious. Prominent systemic symptoms and generalized lymphadenopathy are common. Secondary syphilis manifestations can also resolve without treatment, followed by latent infection (a positive serologic test result without clinical manifestations). If the duration of latent infection is less than 12 months, it is termed early latent; greater than 12 months is late latent. Practically, these determinations can be made only if past serology results are available. Otherwise, patients are considered to have syphilis of unknown duration.

Tertiary syphilis refers to gummas, cardiovascular syphilis, psychiatric manifestations (e.g., memory loss or personality changes), and late neurosyphilis (any involvement of the central nervous system, which can occur at any stage of syphilis). Argyll Robertson pupil is an ophthalmologic finding in late neurosyphilis characterized by small and irregular pupils that do not constrict well to light but do constrict when focused on an object nearby (light-near dissociation).

Treponema pallidum meningitis incidence is greatest within the 2 years after infection but is estimated to occur in less than 2.5% of infected patients. Headache and meningismus are common, and the cerebrospinal fluid usually shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis with an elevated protein level.

Cerebrospinal fluid should be examined in any patient with unexplained neurologic symptoms and serologic evidence of syphilis and should be considered in those who do not demonstrate an appropriate serologic response to syphilis treatment.

Secondary and tertiary syphilis diagnosis relies on serologic testing. Many laboratories use the “reverse” serologic testing strategy, starting with an automated enzyme immunoassay followed by a nonspecific test (rapid plasma reagin [RPR] or Venereal Disease Research Lab test). Patients with a positive enzyme immunoassay result but negative RPR or Venereal Disease Research Lab test result (discordant results) should have a second specific treponemal antibody test to confirm the result. Those with a confirmed positive result and no history of syphilis treatment should be offered treatment for syphilis.

In patients with a history of appropriate treatment for syphilis, nontreponemal testing, usually RPR, should be performed; results of nontreponemal testing performed after previous treatment are needed to distinguish new infection from inadequately treated previous infection and expected serologic findings after treatment. A fourfold titer increase, or a reactive result that was previously nonreactive, confirms a new syphilis infection.

Syphilis treatment is based on disease stage and is outlined in [Table: Table: Treatment of Syphilis]

. Sexual partners of persons with untreated primary, secondary, or early latent syphilis exposed in the preceding 90 days should be treated empirically, regardless of serologic results. Sexual partners of persons with a diagnosis of syphilis exposed more than 90 days before the diagnosis should be treated for early syphilis if serologic test results are not quickly available and follow-up is uncertain. If serologic tests are negative, treatment is unnecessary; if serologic tests are positive, treatment is based on clinical and laboratory evaluation and syphilis stage.

Except for proctitis or proctocolitis caused by the LGV serovars of C. trachomatis, these two STIs are rarely seen in the United States. The clinical presentation, evaluation, and treatment are outlined in [Table: Table: Chancroid and Lymphogranuloma Venereum]

.

Genital warts have a variety of appearances, including papular or pedunculated lesions (

). Most are asymptomatic; however, large lesions may cause irritation or pain depending on their location. Nononcogenic types of human papillomavirus (HPV) are responsible for most lesions. Specific testing for HPV is not recommended for diagnosis. See Human Papillomavirus in Foundations of Clinical Practice for information on HPV vaccination.

Warts often resolve without therapy, but treatment is indicated for symptomatic warts or those causing psychological distress. Patients should be counseled that successful treatment might not eliminate the risk of transmission. Patient-applied therapies include imiquimod, podofilox, and sinecatechins; provider-administered therapies include trichloroacetic or bichloroacetic acid, cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen or cryoprobe, or surgical removal. No evidence indicates any recommended modality is superior. Ulcerated or pigmented warts and those that fail to respond to or worsen after therapy should be biopsied to exclude a cancerous lesion.

Fever of Unknown Origin

Historically, the definition of fever of unknown origin (FUO) included fever (temperature ≥38.3 °C [100.9 °F]) that persists for at least 3 weeks and remains unexplained despite hospitalization and extensive evaluation. Hospital duration has shortened over time, from 1 week to 3 inpatient days, and the definition may also include failure to identify a cause despite three or more outpatient visits.

Diagnostic advances have revealed a spectrum of diseases causing FUO, with origins more rapidly identifiable for many cases. FUO generally falls into one of four categories: classic, health care–associated, immunodeficiency-related, and travel-associated ( [Table: Table: FUO Characteristics]

). Many FUO occurrences are atypical presentations of common diseases; in adults, common causes of FUO include infections, neoplasm or malignancy, rheumatologic or inflammatory disorders, and miscellaneous causes.

A careful history and physical examination should be performed and repeated often during the evaluation period. The history should include procedures, surgeries, presence of foreign bodies or implants, immunosuppression, travel, animal and other exposures (including hobbies), dietary habits, and medications (including over-the-counter medications). Temporary discontinuation of any new or potentially offending medications should be considered. The degree and pattern of fever is nonspecific and nondiagnostic in most instances.

Initial testing for classic FUO should address any focal signs and symptoms ( [Table: Table: FUO Evaluation]

). Biopsy without a laboratory or radiographic abnormality is low yield but can be helpful when leukopenia or thrombocytopenia is present. PET scan is increasingly recognized as a valuable diagnostic test for FUO, and early use is associated with improved diagnostic efficiency and reduced costs.

A definitive diagnosis is lacking in up to 50% of patients despite extensive evaluation. FUO lasting more than 1 year is unlikely to be caused by infection or malignancy and is generally associated with a benign long-term course.

Bioterrorism

Unusually severe illness, rapid increase in disease incidence, atypical clinical presentation, and uncommon geographic, temporal, or demographic clustering of disease outbreaks suggest a bioterrorism attack. Bioterrorism agents are classified ( [Table: Table: Potential Bioterrorism Agents]

) according to ease of dissemination, mortality rate, potential for social disruption, and need for public health preparedness.

Anthrax infection is caused by Bacillus anthracis spores (

; panel A and panel B). Spores may be spread by aerosolization, with infection following inhalation; any case of inhalation anthrax must be considered potential bioterrorism. Infection may also occur by cutaneous contact, with a characteristic black eschar forming at the site of inoculation (

; panel C), or by ingestion. Person-to-person transmission does not occur.

Clinical features are described in [Table: Table: Class A Bioterrorism Agents]

. Meningitis occurs in up to 50% of persons. Rapid clinical deterioration leads to shock and death. Radiographic imaging reveals a widened mediastinum (

; panel D). Diagnosis is made by culture or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of blood, tissues, or fluid samples.

Treatment is outlined in [Table: Table: Class A Bioterrorism Agents]

. Postexposure prophylaxis consists of a fluoroquinolone or doxycycline and vaccination.

Routine smallpox vaccination ceased in 1980, after the World Health Organization declared the disease eradicated, leaving much of the world’s population without immunity. Following inhalation, the virus is sequestered in regional lymph nodes, where multiplication occurs, followed by a primary viremia with dissemination to lymphoid organs.

Secondary viremia occurs 1 week later, accompanied by fever, systemic symptoms, and centrifugal rash, beginning with lesions on the oral mucosa and face before spreading to the extremities and, to a lesser extent, the trunk (

). Patients remain contagious until all scabs and crusts are shed.

Treatment is listed in [Table: Table: Class A Bioterrorism Agents]

. Vaccination should be provided to close contacts. Intravenous vaccinia immune globulin is indicated in certain vaccinia-related complications or when vaccination is contraindicated.

Primary pneumonic plague occurs after Yersinia pestis exposure through infectious aerosols and person-to-person transmission through respiratory droplets, which are likely scenarios for bioterrorism. Disease manifestations depend on the site of inoculation. Chest radiographs are nonspecific. Gram stain and cultures of sputum and blood (using the highest-level biosafety procedures) are often diagnostic (

).

Treatment is outlined in [Table: Table: Class A Bioterrorism Agents]

. Untreated, pneumonic plague is almost always fatal. Asymptomatic persons exposed to aerosolized Y. pestis and close contacts of infected patients warrant postexposure prophylaxis.

Botulism may spread in a bioterrorism attack through inhalation or ingestion of botulinum neurotoxin after aerosol release or food contamination. Clinical features are described in [Table: Table: Class A Bioterrorism Agents]

. Patients remain afebrile with normal mental status; nausea, abdominal pain, and dry mouth often accompany the paralysis. Autonomic dysfunction may also occur.

Diagnosis is clinical, and confirmation depends on identifying the toxin from serum, vomitus, stool, gastric contents, or foods. Treatment involves supportive care (see [Table: Table: Class A Bioterrorism Agents]

) and prompt administration of heptavalent antitoxin, without awaiting toxin identification; however, administration will not reverse existent paralysis. Antibiotics are not useful.

Francisella tularensis is transmitted by arthropod vectors, direct animal contact, and inhalation; person-to-person spread does not occur. Bioterrorism-associated infections most often manifest as pneumonia, with chest radiographs demonstrating infiltrates, hilar lymphadenopathy, and pleural effusions, or as the typhoidal form.

Rapid diagnosis relies on a thorough history and serologic, immunohistochemical, and PCR testing; culture of tissues and fluids is low yield and potentially dangerous to laboratory personnel. Treatment is noted in [Table: Table: Class A Bioterrorism Agents]

. Mortality is less than 4% in treated patients but reaches 30% in untreated pneumonic or typhoidal tularemia. No vaccine is available.

The Ebola and Marburg hemorrhagic viruses are the most likely to be used as biologic weapons. Aerosolization is a likely mode of terrorist dissemination. Symptoms appear 2 to 21 days after exposure (see [Table: Table: Class A Bioterrorism Agents]

). Mortality rates can reach 90%.

Depending on the stage of infection, diagnosis may be confirmed by antigen and antibody assays and PCR. Exposed persons are monitored during the incubation period, and isolated if symptoms develop. Treatment is supportive (see [Table: Table: Class A Bioterrorism Agents]

). An effective, preventative vaccine is available.
