Travel Medicine

Pretravel consultation should occur at least 4 weeks before international travel. Regularly updated information by country is available on the CDC and World Health Organization websites. Travel-related illnesses are reported in 20% to 60% of returning travelers; many of these illnesses are vaccine preventable. Pretravel immunizations are listed in [Table: Table: Immunizations for Travel]

. Potentially severe travel-associated infections are listed in [Table: Table: Travel-Associated Infections]

, the most significant of which are reviewed here.

Evaluation of a returning traveler who is ill includes a detailed travel itinerary, nature of accommodations, activities while abroad, sexual history, whether pretravel vaccines or prophylactic medications were given, and course of the illness. Initial laboratory evaluation should include the following:

  • Complete blood count
  • Metabolic panel
  • Blood cultures
  • Malaria testing (if supported by geography)

Travelers may also have infections that are not necessarily specific to their travel destination, such as acute HIV and mononucleosis, and clinical findings should guide testing for more common pathogens.

Malaria is the most common cause of febrile illness in returning travelers, particularly from sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia, and less frequently from Central and South America and some Caribbean countries. Malaria is caused by the protozoan parasite Plasmodium and is transmitted through the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. Plasmodium species vary in incidence geographically and cause a spectrum of disease from a subacute presentation to severe, life-threatening illness. Preventive measures include limiting outdoor exposure between dusk and dawn, using insecticide-impregnated bed nets and insect repellents containing 20% to 30% N-diethyl-3-methylbenzamide (DEET), and using antimalarial chemoprophylaxis.

Incubation periods range from 1 week to 3 months. Symptoms include fever, headache, myalgia, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Anemia, thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly, and elevated aminotransferase levels may be present. Severe disease occurs with hyperparasitemia caused by Plasmodium falciparum (and less commonly Plasmodium knowlesi) ( [Table: Table: Criteria for Severe Malaria]

).

Because of their potential for severe infection, identifying P. falciparum and P. knowlesi is critical. [Table: Table: Plasmodium Species Characteristics]

presents features of specific Plasmodium species. Symptom onset shortly after returning from travel to endemic zones, a high level of parasitemia, and distinctive intraerythrocytic findings (

) should raise suspicion for P. falciparum infection.

Identification of malarial parasites on the peripheral blood smear is diagnostic; testing should be repeated in patients with suspected malaria and an initial negative test. Rapid tests that detect malaria antigens are increasingly used in endemic areas. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and serologic assays are typically available through reference laboratories, but results are not often available quickly, which can delay diagnosis.

Malarial chemoprophylaxis and treatment depend on drug resistance patterns and individual contraindications to specific medications ( [Table: Table: Antimalarial Chemoprophylaxis Information]

and [Table: Table: Malaria Treatment Regimens]

). For P. vivax or P. ovale infection, acute and antirelapse treatment is required; it is necessary to treat the erythrocytic phase, which causes symptomatic disease, as well as the liver hypnozoites, which cause relapse of latent infection. A full treatment regimen should be considered for travelers to remote areas where access to medical care may not be readily available. Additional detailed information about malaria is provided in the CDC Yellow Book or by calling the CDC malaria hotline (770-488-7788).

Typhoid fever and paratyphoid fever are caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi and S. enterica serotype Paratyphi (A, B, and C), respectively, and is acquired through consumption of fecally contaminated food or water. Travel to Asia (particularly South Asia) and portions of Africa and Latin America pose the greatest risk of infection. Oral and parenteral vaccines (see [Table: Table: Immunizations for Travel]

) provide temporary immunity in 50% to 80% of recipients.

Fever with headache, arthralgia, myalgia, pharyngitis, and anorexia follows a 1- to 30-day incubation period. Abdominal pain can be accompanied by diarrhea or constipation. In untreated illness, temperature progressively increases and may remain elevated (up to 40 °C [104 °F]) for 4 to 8 weeks. A pulse-temperature dissociation (relative bradycardia) is common. Patients may have blanching, 1- to 4-mm salmon-colored macules (

) on the chest and abdomen during the second week of illness. Moderate hepatosplenomegaly, leukopenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated aminotransferase levels are common. Secondary bacteremia may cause complications such as empyema, muscle abscess, and endovascular infections. Intestinal hemorrhage or perforation may occur 2 to 3 weeks after infection onset. Encephalopathy occurs in more severe cases.

Gallbladder invasion by typhoid bacilli may result in an asymptomatic carrier state with organisms shed in the stool for more than 1 year. Persons with gallstones and chronic biliary disease are at greatest risk.

Isolation of S. enterica serotype Typhi or Paratyphi from blood, stool, urine, or bone marrow is diagnostic; isolation success declines after the first week of illness. Rapid serologic tests are available to distinguish S. enterica serotype Typhi antibodies; however, rapid antibody tests are not recommended to diagnose acute disease because of limited diagnostic accuracy.

Antibiotic treatment decreases mortality and shortens fever duration; it should be guided by travel history. More than 85% of isolates in Southeast Asia are resistant to fluoroquinolones, so these agents should not be used as empiric therapy. For patients who traveled to Iraq or Pakistan, or who did not travel internationally before symptoms started, a carbapenem is recommended for complicated disease and azithromycin is recommended for uncomplicated disease. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin are empiric options for those who have returned from other countries. Because of antibiotic resistance, all isolates should undergo susceptibility testing. Preferred treatments, after susceptibility results are available, include the following:

  • Ceftriaxone
  • Fluoroquinolones
  • Azithromycin

Although data are limited, adjunctive dexamethasone decreases mortality in severe illness, such as associated shock and encephalopathy. A prolonged antibiotic course effectively eradicates chronic carriage in most patients, although cholecystectomy may be needed if eradication is unsuccessful.

The most common travel-associated infection is diarrhea, defined by the sudden onset of three or more loose or watery stools per day with at least one of the following:

  • Fever
  • Cramps
  • Nausea
  • Abdominal pain
  • Blood in the stools

Risk is greatest for travelers to South and Southeast Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East, and Central and South America.

Travelers’ diarrhea usually occurs within the first 2 weeks of travel and is usually self-limited; however, life-threatening volume depletion or severe colitis with systemic manifestations can occur. Some travelers develop chronic diarrhea or a postinfective irritable bowel syndrome.

Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli is the most common cause (see [Table: Table: Strains of Escherichia coli]

and Escherichia coli Infection in Infectious Disease).

Pretravel advice includes avoiding consumption of tap water (through drinks, ice, or when brushing teeth), undercooked meats, unpasteurized dairy products, and fruits and vegetables that are not peeled just before eating. Water disinfection can be accomplished by boiling for 3 minutes or by using chlorine and iodine. Bottled water may also be consumed.

Antimicrobial prophylaxis is generally not recommended because of the potential for adverse effects. Prophylaxis may rarely be considered for short-term use in persons with immunocompromising conditions or significant comorbidities. Bismuth subsalicylate can be used to prevent diarrhea, but the dosage required is inconvenient and can lead to salicylate toxicity. Probiotics are not recommended.

Fluid replacement is the mainstay of treatment. Antimicrobials are recommended in severe disease and may be considered in those with moderate disease ( [Table: Table: Treatment for Travelers’ Diarrhea]

). Self-treatment with azithromycin rifaximin, or rifamycin is usually sufficient. Rifaximin and rifamycin are minimally absorbed oral antibiotic alternatives to azithromycin but are not recommended if fever or bloody diarrhea is present. Fluoroquinolones may be used but are no longer a preferred treatment due to increasing microbial resistance and adverse effects. Bismuth subsalicylate in large doses can be used in milder cases. Antimotility medications (e.g., loperamide and diphenoxylate) should not be used alone in patients with fever or bloody diarrhea because of increased risk of colitis and colonic perforation.

The dengue fever, chikungunya, and Zika arboviruses are spread by daytime-feeding Aedes species mosquitoes, and their presentations are similar ( [Table: Table: Features of Selected Arbovirus Infections]

).

Dengue fever is the most prevalent arthropod-borne viral infection in the world and a frequent cause of acute febrile illness among travelers returning from endemic areas, including tropical and subtropical areas worldwide. The incubation period is 4 to 7 days. Infection may be asymptomatic or present as an acute febrile illness associated with characteristic symptoms (see [Table: Table: Travel-Associated Infections]

). The tourniquet test can assess associated microvascular fragility (

). As the fever abates, a scarlatiniform rash, which spares the palms and soles, may appear on extensor surfaces. Fever typically lasts for 2 to 7 days; however, some patients experience a second febrile period (saddleback pattern). In patients with severe infection, life-threatening hemorrhage and shock may ensue, with liver failure, encephalopathy, and myocarditis. This syndrome appears to be related to previous infection of a different serotype and is unlikely in travelers who have not previously had dengue fever. Laboratory findings include leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated serum aminotransferase levels.

Diagnosis is confirmed by reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR), detection of viral antigen, or serology. Therapy is supportive.

Beginning in 2013, chikungunya virus emerged in the Americas, with outbreaks in Central and South America and the Caribbean. A virus-like particle vaccine is available for prevention (see [Table: Table: Immunizations for Travel]

).

Symptoms resemble dengue fever (see [Table: Table: Travel-Associated Infections]

); severe disease is uncommon. Laboratory findings include lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated aminotransferase levels. Illness typically resolves spontaneously in 7 to 10 days. However, some patients experience arthralgia or arthritis for months or years.

Definitive diagnosis relies on serologic assays or viral RNA detection by RT-PCR testing. Symptomatic treatment includes NSAIDs. However, for patients who have traveled to dengue-endemic areas, NSAIDs and aspirin should be avoided until dengue is excluded (to reduce the risk of bleeding complications).

Thousands of Zika virus infections were reported in the United States between 2015 and 2016, including some resulting from local transmission. No Zika virus transmission by mosquitoes has been reported in the continental United States since 2018. Most patients recover uneventfully after a mild illness; however, infection is associated with fetal abnormalities, including anencephaly. Pregnant persons should be advised against travel to areas where Zika outbreaks exist. Individuals who are pregnant and those who are planning to conceive should consult the CDC website for current information when considering travel. Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) is used for diagnosis in early infection, but a negative NAAT does not exclude infection. After the first week of infection, IgM antibody testing is usually positive and may remain positive for months to years. Treatment is supportive.

Hepatitis A virus infection is acquired through ingestion of food and water contaminated with human feces. Travel to parts of Africa and Asia, Central and South America, and Eastern Europe poses the greatest risk of infection. Patients initially experience malaise, nausea, vomiting, fever, and right upper quadrant pain; jaundice and hepatomegaly follow about 1 week later. Laboratory studies show elevated aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, and total bilirubin levels.

Hepatitis A vaccination is recommended for persons traveling to countries with high or intermediate endemicity and those who are not already immune (see [Table: Table: Immunizations for Travel]

). Protective antibody titers develop within 4 weeks in more than 90% of healthy recipients after the initial dose. A second dose is given 6 to 18 months after the initial injection. Serum immune globulin is indicated for those who decline vaccination or are allergic to its components. Immune globulin may also be considered in addition to vaccination if travel is scheduled within 2 weeks for adults older than 40 years, immunocompromised persons, and persons with chronic liver disease and other chronic medical conditions (for further information, see Hepatitis A in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease).

Hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for all unvaccinated persons younger than 60 years (regardless of travel plans) and for those 60 years of age and older traveling to areas where hepatitis B virus is prevalent or who are at high risk for infection (see [Table: Table: Immunizations for Travel]

).

See Hepatitis C in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease for discussion of hepatitis C virus.

Rickettsial infections occur worldwide and are transmitted by fleas, lice, mites, and ticks. Rickettsia typhi (murine typhus) is prevalent in tropical and subtropical areas but can also occur in Texas, California, and Hawaii. Rickettsia prowazekii is the only rickettsial species transmitted by human body lice and has a worldwide distribution. Rickettsia akari (rickettsialpox) occurs in urban centers worldwide, with the common house mouse serving as a reservoir.

African tick-bite fever (Rickettsia africae) is second only to malaria as the cause of febrile illness in those who have journeyed to Africa, especially South Africa. Symptoms include fever, headache, malaise, conjunctivitis, and pharyngitis often accompanied by a maculopapular, vesicular, or petechial rash. An eschar with regional lymphadenopathy develops at the site of inoculation following the bite of a tick or mite infected with R. africae, Rickettsia conorii (Mediterranean spotted fever), Orientia tsutsugamushi (scrub typhus), and R. akari. Following the initial lesion, patients with rickettsialpox develop constitutional symptoms and a papulovesicular rash. Microvascular permeability is the hallmark of rickettsial infections, with extensive vasculitic skin lesions. Severe complications may include shock, meningoencephalitis, and organ damage. Recrudescent attacks are known to occur months and even years later.

Diagnosis is confirmed by PCR or immunohistochemical analysis of skin biopsy. Confirmatory serologic assays often do not detect antibodies until the convalescent phase of illness. When clinical suspicion is high, empiric therapy is warranted. The treatment of choice for all rickettsial infections is doxycycline for at least 5 to 7 days.

Human brucellosis may follow ingestion of unpasteurized dairy products or undercooked meat, by direct contact with fluids from infected animals, or by inhalation of contaminated aerosols. The highest prevalence is found in the Mediterranean countries, Balkans, Persian Gulf, Middle East, and Central and South America.

Symptoms include fever, myalgia, arthralgia, fatigue, headache, and night sweats. Focal infection may involve the central nervous system and osteoarticular, cardiovascular, and genitourinary systems. Disease relapse and chronic infection may occur.

Diagnosis relies on cultures of blood, bone marrow, other body fluids, or tissue. An initial elevated titer of 1:160 or greater on the serum agglutination test or demonstration of a fourfold increase from acute to convalescent titers is diagnostic.

The preferred treatment for uncomplicated brucellosis is extended therapy with doxycycline plus either rifampin or gentamicin. Neurobrucellosis requires several months of combined ceftriaxone, doxycycline, and rifampin.

Japanese encephalitis virus is a flavivirus transmitted by mosquitos. It is the most prevalent cause of vaccine-preventable infectious encephalitis throughout most of Asia and parts of the western Pacific. The risk of infection for most travelers is low, and most infected persons remain asymptomatic. Encephalitis occurs in <1% of infections. The mortality rate is 20% to 30%.

Diagnosis is confirmed by the detection of virus-specific IgM antibodies in the cerebrospinal fluid. Viral RNA detection is definitive but insensitive. Treatment is supportive. In the United States, a two-dose inactivated vaccine is available and recommended for travelers to endemic areas based on risk stratification.

Tick-borne encephalitis is caused by three related subtypes of flaviviruses classified by their endemic geographic areas (European, Siberian, and Far Eastern). Most infections occur between April to November after a bite from an Ixodes tick. Persons 60 years and older have the greatest risk of severe infection. A biphasic illness occurs in about one third of infected persons after an incubation period (1-2 weeks), beginning with a nonspecific phase:

  • Fever
  • Headache
  • Malaise
  • Arthralgia

A second neuroinvasive phase may develop in the few patients who do not fully recover, manifested by the following:

  • Meningitis
  • Encephalitis
  • Altered mental status
  • Seizures
  • Cranial nerve palsies
  • Flaccid paralysis

Disease severity, case fatality, and permanent neurologic deficits increase with age and vary by geographic location (Far Eastern is most severe, followed by Siberian and European).

Diagnosis is confirmed by detection of IgM antibodies from cerebrospinal fluid or serum. Treatment is supportive.

For most U.S. travelers to endemic areas, the risk of disease is low. Persons who are traveling to an endemic area during April through November and who will be engaging in recreational activities in woodland habitats (e.g., hiking, camping, fishing, hunting) or whose occupation puts them at high risk should consider vaccination. An inactivated vaccine was approved for use in the United States in 2021.

The yellow fever flavivirus belongs to the viral hemorrhagic fever group. Infection is transmitted by mosquitoes in endemic areas of sub-Saharan Africa and tropical regions of South America. Clinical manifestations range from mild to severe life-threatening disease with a 30% to 60% mortality rate. Diagnosis is confirmed by the following:

  • Viral RNA detection (by RT-PCR)
  • Virus isolation performed early in the disease course
  • IgM antibodies

Treatment is supportive. Vaccination with the approved, live-attenuated yellow fever vaccine is recommended for travelers to endemic areas of Africa and South America. Immunity is life-long, and a booster is no longer recommended. A certificate of proof of vaccination is required for entry into several endemic countries, and travelers who have recently visited yellow fever zones are prohibited entrance to some nonendemic countries without similar documentation (www.cdc.gov/travel); a medical waiver can be given to persons with a precaution or contraindication to vaccination.

Infectious Gastrointestinal Syndromes

Diarrhea is defined as three or more unformed stools daily. Diarrhea lasting up to 2 weeks is considered acute, more than 2 weeks and less than 4 weeks is persistent, and 4 weeks or more is chronic. Acute infectious diarrheal presentations include acute gastroenteritis, with associated fever, nausea, vomiting, flatulence, tenesmus, and crampy abdominal pain. Chronic infectious diarrhea is most likely caused by parasites. Risk factors include travel, antibiotic use, contaminated food or water consumption, and ill contacts. Not all diarrheal presentations are infectious, such as inflammatory bowel disease, endocrine disorders, celiac disease, irritable bowel syndrome, food intolerance, and medication-induced diarrhea.

Generally, patients with dysentery (mucoid or bloody diarrhea, fever, abdominal cramping, tenesmus) or suspected sepsis and those who are immunocompromised or require hospitalization should have diagnostic stool assessment to guide antimicrobial use. Additional areas of concern include prolonged symptoms (>1 week) or outbreak settings where day care participants, institutional residents, health care providers, or food handlers are present. Rapid multiplex molecular gastrointestinal assays that identify common bacterial, parasitic, and viral pathogens from a stool sample are increasingly available and generally more sensitive than stool culture and microscopy with special stains. Isolates from culture, however, can provide antibiotic susceptibilities and strain-typing information in outbreak situations that are unavailable from culture-independent diagnostic assays.

Most healthy patients with mild watery diarrheal illness of less than 3 days’ duration can be treated supportively (i.e., fluid repletion and nutrition maintenance) without additional diagnostic assessment or antimicrobial therapy. When acute diarrhea is debilitating and associated with travel, antibiotic therapy with a fluoroquinolone, azithromycin, rifamycin, or rifaximin is recommended, although resistance of enteric pathogens to fluoroquinolones is increasing worldwide. If illness is not travel associated and fever of 38.3 °C (101.0 °F) or greater persists for 3 or more days, then microbiologic assessment should be considered followed by empiric azithromycin treatment. Microbiologic assessment should guide treatment of persistent and chronic diarrhea.

In patients with dysentery, stable individuals without fever (≤37.8 °C [100 °F]) should have microbiologic assessment to guide therapy; those with severe, debilitating dysentery and fever (≥38.3 °C [101 °F]) should undergo microbiologic assessment followed by empiric azithromycin treatment. For severe travel-associated dysentery, empiric azithromycin treatment is recommended. Antimotility agents, such as loperamide, are generally discouraged in patients with inflammatory diarrhea (fever, abdominal pain, bloody stools) or Clostridioides difficile–associated infection.

Campylobacter-associated gastroenteritis is usually foodborne, often secondary to undercooked poultry. The incubation period is about 3 days. [Table: Table: Characteristics of Infectious Diarrhea]

presents the clinical findings and postinfection complications. Campylobacter jejuni is the most commonly associated trigger of Guillain-Barré syndrome (see Guillain-Barré Syndrome in Neurology). Stools are occasionally visibly bloody. Stool culture and molecular testing can be used for diagnosis; blood cultures can identify extraintestinal disease.

Diarrhea usually resolves spontaneously. Patients who have severe disease (bloody stools, bacteremia, high fever, or prolonged [>1 week] symptoms) or are immunocompromised should receive antibiotic therapy. When indicated, azithromycin is preferred because of increasing fluoroquinolone resistance.

Shigella infection is most commonly spread through fecal-oral contamination. Fewer than 100 bacteria can cause infection, and the incubation period is approximately 3 days. Patients typically present with dysentery. More serious complications include bacteremia, seizures, and intestinal obstruction and perforation; postinfectious sequelae may also occur (see [Table: Table: Characteristics of Infectious Diarrhea]

). Routine stool culture and molecular testing can assist with diagnosis. Blood cultures can confirm invasive disease in patients with severe infection.

Treatment with antibiotics is recommended for persons with severe illness (those requiring hospitalization, with invasive disease, or with complications) and those who are immunocompromised. Treatment may also be recommended when outbreaks occur. Ciprofloxacin, azithromycin, and ceftriaxone have been used for treatment, but ideally antibiotic susceptibilities should be obtained because of increasing resistance. National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System data can help guide empiric decisions.

Salmonella infections can be typhoidal or nontyphoidal. Typhoidal infections cause enteric fever, a syndrome consisting of fever, abdominal pain, rash, hepatosplenomegaly, and relative bradycardia (see Typhoid (Enteric) Fever in Infectious Disease). Enteric fever is caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi and S. enterica serotype Paratyphi, which is uncommon in the United States, with most affected persons traveling to endemic areas and ingesting contaminated water or food. Nontyphoidal serotypes are the most common bacterial cause of foodborne illness in the United States.

Nontyphoidal Salmonella infection usually results from ingesting fecally contaminated water or food of animal origin, including poultry, eggs, and milk. Contact with infected animals (including pet reptiles, amphibians, and poultry) is a less common mode of transmission. The incubation period is usually less than 3 days, and symptoms typically include crampy abdominal pain, fever, diarrhea (not usually visibly bloody), headache, nausea, and vomiting. Stool culture or molecular testing can be diagnostic. Illness is usually self-limited, although bacteremia with extraintestinal infection (involving vascular endothelium, joints, or meninges) may occur. Nontyphoidal Salmonella bacteremia is considered an opportunistic infection in patients with HIV. Salmonella osteomyelitis is classically associated with sickle cell disease. Severe invasive disease is more likely in infants, older adults, patients with cell-mediated immunodeficiency, and patients with hypochlorhydria. Postinfection complications can occur (see [Table: Table: Characteristics of Infectious Diarrhea]

).

Most uncomplicated Salmonella infections in adults younger than 50 years are self-limited and require only supportive care. Antibiotics are typically reserved for patients with more serious illness (including severe diarrhea requiring hospitalization, bacteremia, high fever, or sepsis) and those at high risk for severe complicated invasive disease (including infants, patients ≥50 years with significant joint disease or valvular, endovascular, or cardiac abnormalities; immunocompromised patients; and adults ≥65 years of age). Fluoroquinolones (such as ciprofloxacin) are most often used, but potentially active agents include azithromycin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, amoxicillin, and ampicillin. An intravenous fluoroquinolone, or third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone, is often administered for patients with bacteremia and can be transitioned to an oral fluoroquinolone in those with clinical improvement. Local antibiotic susceptibilities should dictate empiric therapy.

Although Escherichia coli are normal inhabitants of the intestinal microbiome, some strains can become enteropathogenic ( [Table: Table: Strains of Escherichia coli]

).

Enterotoxigenic E. coli infection (ETEC) is the most common cause of travelers’ diarrhea. ETEC results from ingestion of water or food contaminated with stool and has an incubation period of 1 to 3 days. Enterotoxins cause watery diarrhea with abdominal cramping, nausea, and low-grade or no fever. Usually self-limiting, the illness resolves after approximately 4 days. Hydration and empiric antibiotic therapy with fluoroquinolones, azithromycin, or rifaximin are recommended in travelers with ETEC when symptoms restrict activities, although increasing resistance to fluoroquinolones and their associated adverse effects must be considered.

Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) strains, such as O157:H7, produce a Shiga toxin (i.e., Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, or STEC) that can cause hemorrhagic colitis. These bacteria are found in cow intestines and are transmitted by ingesting undercooked hamburgers or fecally contaminated food and water; fecal-oral transmission through exposure to infected animals is also possible. The incubation period is about 3 days, and patients typically have visibly bloody diarrhea, crampy abdominal pain, and no fever (a distinguishing feature from other causes of bloody diarrhea). Alerting the laboratory is recommended so that appropriate culture media and Shiga toxin assays can be performed. Hemolytic uremic syndrome develops in less than 10% of patients infected with EHEC and manifests as microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and kidney injury (see Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome and Other Thrombotic Microangiopathies in Hematology). Treatment is primarily supportive; antibiotics and antimotility agents may increase the risk of developing hemolytic uremic syndrome and do not appear to shorten infection duration.

Yersinia enterocolitica is the most common pathogen causing Yersinia-related diarrheal illness, usually after ingestion of contaminated food, particularly undercooked pork. Patients with iron overload states, including hemochromatosis, are at increased risk for infection (including bacteremia) owing to the siderophilic characteristics of Yersinia species. The incubation period is approximately 5 days, and patients typically have fever, abdominal pain, diarrhea (possibly bloody), and, in some cases, nausea and emesis. The organism replicates in lymphoid tissue (including tonsillar tissue and mesenteric lymph nodes), which results in pharyngitis or right lower-quadrant pain mimicking appendicitis. Postinfection complications may occur (see [Table: Table: Characteristics of Infectious Diarrhea]

). Gastrointestinal illness is confirmed by stool molecular testing or specialized stool culture. The organism can be cultured from infected tissue (including the throat in patients with clinical pharyngitis) or blood.

Uncomplicated gastrointestinal illness in healthy, immunocompetent adults does not require treatment. When treatment is indicated, a fluoroquinolone (such as ciprofloxacin) is recommended. If bacteremia or sepsis is present, intravenous ceftriaxone plus gentamicin is used.

In the United States, Vibrio parahaemolyticus is the most common Vibrio species to cause gastrointestinal illness, usually after consumption of undercooked oysters and other shellfish. The incubation period is about 2 days; presenting symptoms include diarrhea (can be bloody), fever, nausea or emesis, and crampy abdominal pain (see [Table: Table: Characteristics of Infectious Diarrhea]

). Wound infections, resulting from exposure to estuarine waters, are usually mild but can be severe in patients who have chronic liver disease, iron overload states, or diabetes. Septicemia can also occur, particularly in patients with underlying liver disease.

Severe noninvasive gastrointestinal illness can be treated with doxycycline; alternatives include ciprofloxacin and azithromycin. Patients with septicemia require more aggressive combination therapy, typically with doxycycline plus ceftriaxone.

C. difficile is the leading cause of hospital-acquired infectious diarrhea and results from fecal-oral transmission. Risk factors for infection include exposure to antibiotic and chemotherapeutic agents, older age, severe underlying comorbidities, presence of inflammatory bowel disease, solid organ transplantation, gastrointestinal surgery, and (possibly) gastric acid suppression with proton pump inhibitors. Antibiotic stewardship is paramount in reducing incidence of infection, and handwashing with soap and water is the gold standard for infection control; alcohol-based gels do not eliminate spores.

Asymptomatic colonization can occur; for those with pathologic infection, the incubation period can be as long as 3 months after perturbation of the intestinal flora with antibiotic agents. Community-acquired infections without previous exposure to health care settings, antibiotic agents, or both have been increasingly reported.

C. difficile produces an enterotoxin (toxin A) and a cytotoxin (toxin B) that are pathogenic. Symptomatic patients typically have watery diarrhea (rarely bloody), crampy abdominal pain, malaise, and, in some cases, nausea and fever. Abnormal laboratory study findings are nonspecific but can include marked leukocytosis, an elevated serum creatinine level, and hypoalbuminemia. Imaging, also nonspecific, should be performed in patients with clinical manifestations of severe disease or fulminant colitis and may demonstrate colonic wall thickening, mucosal edema, fat stranding, and megacolon; CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the preferred modality, and plain radiographs may be useful when CT is not readily available. Colonoscopy, although not a routine diagnostic modality, may show pseudomembranes (

).

Diagnosis is usually established by testing unformed stools from persons not taking laxatives who have unexplained new-onset diarrhea occurring three or more times daily. Although highly specific and rapid, enzyme immunoassay (EIA) testing for presence of toxin A and B lacks sensitivity. EIA testing for glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH), an antigenic protein present in all C. difficile isolates, is sensitive but lacks specificity. Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) for C. difficile toxin genes is sensitive and specific if appropriate institutional stool submission criteria are strictly met (no laxative use; more than three new-onset, unformed, and unexplained stools in 24 hours). In this setting, NAAT alone is sufficient. A multistep diagnostic approach for stool EIA toxin testing using GDH plus toxin, GDH plus toxin (with discordant results followed by NAAT), or NAAT plus toxin can also be pursued, particularly in settings not adherent to specified stool submission criteria.

In infected patients, antibiotics should be stopped, if possible. Treatment is dictated by severity of disease ( [Table: Table: Initial Clostridioides difficile Infection Treatment]

). Severe disease is defined by a leukocyte count of 15,000/µL (15 × 10^9/L) or greater or a serum creatinine level of 1.5 mg/dL (133 µmol/L) or greater. The Infectious Diseases Society of America and Society for Healthcare Epidemiology of America recommend oral fidaxomicin (preferred) or oral vancomycin for 10 days for severe and nonsevere disease. If neither of these agents is available, oral metronidazole can be used for nonsevere disease. Fulminant disease includes associated shock, hypotension, toxic megacolon, or ileus. Higher-dose oral or nasogastric vancomycin, intravenous metronidazole, and (possibly) vancomycin enema (when ileus is present) are recommended. Patients with fulminant disease warrant surgical evaluation.

Recurrent infection is reported in as many as 25% of patients, and treatment recommendations are provided in [Table: Table: Recurrent Clostridioides difficile Infection Treatment]

. Fecal microbiota products (oral capsules or rectal suspension) are available for use in patients with recurrent infections to prevent further recurrences. Retesting stool for C. difficile after treatment for evidence of cure in patients who have no symptoms is not recommended.

Viruses are the most common cause of acute gastroenteritis. Rotavirus infects young children, and noroviruses, which are the most common cause of gastroenteritis in the United States, affect all ages. Norovirus outbreaks on cruise ships and in schools and other institutionalized settings are well documented. Norovirus transmission from person to person is primarily fecal-oral. Infection can develop after ingestion of fewer than 100 viral particles. The incubation period is typically less than 2 days, and infected patients usually have self-limited watery diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and fever (see [Table: Table: Characteristics of Infectious Diarrhea]

).

Diagnostic molecular testing is available and may be helpful in outbreak investigations. Viral shedding persists for as long as 2 weeks after symptom resolution, which contributes to its high infectivity. Because norovirus is not killed by alcohol, hand hygiene should consist of handwashing with soap and water rather than use of alcohol-based hand disinfection. Treatment is supportive.

Parasitic infection should be considered in patients with chronic diarrhea. Immunosuppressed persons are at increased risk for chronic and severe infection.

Giardia duodenalis (previously G. lamblia) is the most common parasitic pathogen in the United States. Cysts from infected animals are excreted in stool into reservoirs of fresh water, and subsequent ingestion of contaminated water (or food) containing as few as 10 cysts can lead to human infection. Person-to-person transmission is also possible. Persons at risk for infection include outdoor travelers, children in day care centers, immunocompromised hosts (particularly those with humoral immunodeficiency), and persons engaged in sexual activity that includes oral-anal contact. The incubation period is about 1 to 2 weeks. More than half of infected patients are asymptomatic; however, if present, symptoms, can last for several weeks until spontaneously resolving (see [Table: Table: Characteristics of Infectious Diarrhea]

). Chronic infection may develop, particularly in persons with hypogammaglobulinemia. Immunoassays for antigen detection and molecular testing of stool are more sensitive than stool microscopy for confirming the diagnosis.

Treatment is recommended for symptomatic patients; tinidazole, nitazoxanide, or metronidazole can be used. Postinfection lactose intolerance or irritable bowel syndrome may be mistaken for recurrent or resistant Giardia infection.

Cryptosporidium species can infect humans and other mammals. Infection occurs after consumption of fecally contaminated water or food or through close person-to-person or animal-to-person transmission. Municipal water supplies and swimming pools are potential sources of infection because the thick-walled oocysts are chlorine resistant and might evade filtration. Highly infectious, ingestion of fewer than 50 oocysts may result in infection. The incubation period is 7 days. Clinical findings are described in [Table: Table: Characteristics of Infectious Diarrhea]

. Symptoms usually last less than 2 weeks before spontaneously resolving in immunocompetent persons. Immunocompromised patients, in particular patients with advanced HIV, can develop serious and prolonged infection. Diagnosis from stool can be pursued microscopically by visualization of oocysts with modified acid-fast staining, EIA or direct immunofluorescent antibody testing, or molecular testing.

Treatment for immunocompetent patients usually consists of supportive care. When antimicrobial agents are considered for severe or prolonged infection, nitazoxanide is recommended. In HIV-infected patients, antiretroviral therapy to restore immune function is most effective in resolving infection.

Entamoeba histolytica is responsible for amebiasis. In the United States, most infections are diagnosed in travelers returning from tropical countries, persons who have emigrated from these areas, persons in institutionalized settings, or those who practice oral-anal sex. Amebiasis is highly infectious, with ingestion of only a small number of cysts needed for infection. The incubation period is 2 to 4 weeks. Clinical findings are described in [Table: Table: Characteristics of Infectious Diarrhea]

. Immunodeficiency is a risk factor for severe infection. Microscopic visualization of cysts or trophozoites by specialized experts, stool antigen immunoassay testing, stool molecular testing, and serologic antibody testing can provide a diagnosis, although the latter does not distinguish current from remote infection.

Treatment is recommended for all infected patients. In symptomatic patients, treatment with metronidazole or tinidazole is recommended initially for parasitic clearance followed by an intraluminal amebicide, such as paromomycin, diloxanide furoate, or iodoquinol for cyst clearance. In asymptomatic infections, an intraluminal agent for eradication of cysts is recommended.

Cyclospora infections are typically acquired after consumption of food or water that is fecally contaminated with Cyclospora oocysts. In the United States, many of these infections have been traced to imported fresh produce from tropical and subtropical areas or have occurred in travelers to endemic areas. The incubation period is approximately 1 week. Symptoms can last for several weeks and may be more pronounced in patients with HIV infection. Cyclospora infection is typically diagnosed microscopically (see [Table: Table: Characteristics of Infectious Diarrhea]

), and symptomatic patients should be treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

Staphylococcus aureus and Bacillus cereus can each cause food poisoning characterized by rapid onset of gastrointestinal symptoms. Symptoms may begin within 30 minutes to several hours after exposure resulting from ingestion of heat-stable preformed toxin. S. aureus enterotoxin-mediated gastroenteritis causes nausea and vomiting accompanied by abdominal cramping; diarrhea is also common. B. cereus illness can be emetic or diarrheal. Management of S. aureus and B. cereus foodborne illness is supportive.

Infections in Transplant Recipients

Rates of solid organ transplantation (SOT) and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) procedures continue to increase, as does long-term survival in transplant recipients. With more patients living longer after transplantation, awareness of principles involved in recognizing and preventing infection in transplant recipients remains important for all physicians.

Despite improvements in immunosuppression and antimicrobial therapy, infection remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality after SOT and HSCT. Infection is among the highest causes of morbidity and mortality in the first year after transplantation. Additionally, the degree of immunosuppression and its duration is directly associated with risk for infection.

Successful transplantation depends on modulating the immune system to prevent organ rejection in SOT and to minimize graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) in allogeneic HSCT. Immunosuppressive regimens involve multiple agents ( [Table: Table: Immunosuppressive Agents Used in Transplantation]

), with different mechanisms of action, that are chosen to minimize overlapping toxicities. After SOT, induction and maintenance strategies are applied; immunosuppression is most intensive in the first several months after transplantation and often includes lymphocyte depletion therapy. Immunosuppression may require intensification during episodes of rejection, with associated increased risk of infection.

Glucocorticoid-sparing or minimizing regimens are increasingly used to avoid the toxicities of long-term glucocorticoid therapy. Tacrolimus, cyclosporine, and sirolimus are the cornerstones, usually combined with mycophenolate or, less commonly, azathioprine. Drug interactions are common with these agents, and many drugs can affect antirejection medication levels. Monitoring is important to balance adequate immunosuppression with toxicity.

Infection may occur at any time after transplantation, but the highest likelihood of infection is in periods of highest immunosuppression, usually within the first few months after transplantation. The infection source may be donor derived (transmitted with the allograft), latent or colonizing organism in recipients, or de novo exposures. Risk for infection is also affected by pre-existing conditions (e.g., diabetes mellitus, cirrhosis, and neutropenia) and antimicrobial prophylaxis regimens.

The specific infection risk varies depending on the timing after transplantation. [Table: Table: Common Infections after SOT]

and

list the typical timeline of risk for specific infections after SOT and HSCT, respectively. However, the timelines are extended if immunosuppression is augmented to treat rejection or GVHD.

Infections within the first month after SOT are similar to those occurring among hospitalized postsurgical patients and most commonly include surgical site, catheter-related, and other nosocomial infections. The middle period (months 1-6) is associated with the highest risk for opportunistic infections because of the prolonged exposure to intensive cellular immunosuppression, with significant risk for viral and fungal infection. Reduction in immunosuppression in patients who are stable 6 to 12 months or more after transplantation leads to decreased risk for opportunistic infections, but patients remain at increased risk for infection because of the need for lifelong immunosuppression.

Infections in the first 2 to 4 weeks following HSCT are primarily related to the profound neutropenia and mucosal barrier disruption caused by cytotoxic chemotherapy conditioning regimens (see Neutropenia and Fever in Oncology). During the pre-engraftment period, recipients are at high risk for bacterial, Candida, and mold infections as well as reactivation of herpes simplex virus and varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infections. Pre-engraftment is followed by an extended period of impaired cell-mediated and humoral immunity owing to the time needed for recovery of lymphocytes and immunosuppression to reduce GVHD. GVHD treatment dramatically increases the risk for opportunistic infections.

Risk for certain infections depends on previous donor and recipient infections, exposures, and immunity. Standard donor and recipient pretransplant testing includes testing for latent tuberculosis (interferon-γ release assay or tuberculin skin test); serologies for cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), VZV, HIV, hepatitis B and C viruses, syphilis, and toxoplasmosis; and, if from an endemic region, serologies for Strongyloides, Leishmania, and Trypanosoma cruzi. Immunosuppressive drugs and altered anatomy after transplantation also contribute to atypical presentations, making diagnosis of common infections challenging. Noninfectious complications such as rejection, GVHD, medication effects, and malignancy may also be confused with infection.

Herpesvirus infections are among the most common in transplant recipients because of their ability to establish lifelong latency after initial infection and reactivate during immunosuppression. Herpesviruses can also be transmitted with the allograft during transplantation.

Cytomegalovirus is the most significant viral infection after transplantation, with risk for infection depending on donor and recipient serostatus (Video: Risk for Cytomegalovirus Infection in Transplant Recipients). After SOT, the risk for cytomegalovirus is as follows:

  • Highest (>50%) for donor-positive/recipient-negative (D+/R−) transplantation
  • Intermediate (15%-20%) for D−/R+ and D+/R+ transplantation
  • Lowest for D−/R− transplantation

Risk is also significantly increased with the use of lymphocyte-depleting agents.

Comparatively, after allogeneic HSCT, the risk for cytomegalovirus is highest for D−/R+ transplantation. Cytomegalovirus is an immunomodulatory virus, and posttransplant infection is associated with increased rates of rejection, GVHD, opportunistic infections, and posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD).

Cytomegalovirus may present as asymptomatic viremia, cytomegalovirus syndrome (a nonspecific viral syndrome with fever and cytopenia) or end-organ disease (

). Cytomegalovirus end-organ disease is the most severe manifestation and can affect various organs. Disease may also be localized to the allograft in SOT. Colitis is the most common manifestation of cytomegalovirus disease after transplantation and can occur with low viral loads or without viremia. Biopsy demonstrating cytopathic effects in tissue with cytomegalovirus-positive stains provides definitive diagnosis of organ disease. Parenteral ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir is first-line therapy for treatment of cytomegalovirus; parenteral ganciclovir is preferred as initial therapy for severe disease or if enteral absorption is a concern. See Human Cytomegalovirus in Infectious Disease for additional information.

EBV is strongly associated with PTLD, which results from clonal B-cell proliferation of EBV-infected cells; PTLD should be suspected in any patient in the middle or late posttransplant period presenting with lymphadenopathy or an extranodal mass, often with fever. Treatment involves rituximab, decreasing immunosuppression, and, often, chemotherapy. Seronegative recipients are at highest risk for PTLD.

Reactivation of herpes simplex virus and VZV is very common in transplant recipients (see Varicella-Zoster Virus in Infectious Disease); therefore, patients should receive prophylaxis with acyclovir or valacyclovir (if not receiving valganciclovir for cytomegalovirus) during periods of high immunosuppression. Human herpesvirus type 6 can cause encephalitis in HSCT recipients. Norovirus infection may cause chronic diarrhea following transplant. Patients with chronic hepatitis B virus can develop reactivation if not receiving preventive therapy (see Hepatitis B in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease). Polyomavirus BK can cause nephropathy after kidney transplantation and hemorrhagic cystitis in HSCT recipients.

Bacteria are the most common cause of infections after SOT and HSCT. Early after transplantation, SOT recipients experience high rates of nosocomial infections (e.g., hospital-acquired pneumonia, catheter-associated urinary tract infections, bloodstream infections, Clostridioides difficile infection) and postoperative infections. HSCT recipients experience high rates of bacteremia because of impaired host defenses.

Opportunistic, reactivated, and community-acquired infections often predominate later in the posttransplant period because SOT immunosuppression and medications for treatment and prevention of GVHD suppress cellular immunity. Nocardia, tuberculosis (see Mycobacterium tuberculosis Infection in Infectious Disease), and nontuberculous mycobacteria (see Nontuberculous Mycobacterial Infections in Infectious Disease) are examples. Donor-derived transmission should be considered in patients without typical exposures for an infection. Encapsulated bacterial infections such as Streptococcus pneumoniae remain common even late after HSCT because of impaired humoral immunity.

Transplant recipients experience higher rates of infections with multidrug-resistant pathogens because of greater exposure in the health care system. These pathogens can include extended-spectrum β-lactamase producing Enterobacterales, drug-resistant Pseudomonas, and vancomycin-resistant enterococci.

Types of fungal infections also vary according to posttransplant timing, level of immunosuppression, and use of antifungal prophylaxis. Candidiasis is most common in the early period following transplantation, particularly in intra-abdominal SOT, and during neutropenia in HSCT. Aspergillosis and other invasive mold infections occur most commonly in HSCT and lung transplant recipients, particularly in the setting of treatment for GVHD or rejection or during neutropenia in HSCT. Without prophylaxis, risk for Pneumocystis pneumonia is very high in the middle posttransplant period and presents as a more acute and severe pneumonitis than that seen in patients with HIV (see Pneumocystis jirovecii in Infectious Disease). Cryptococcosis tends to occur during this period of significant T-cell suppression; it usually presents as subacute meningitis, although other organ involvement may also occur. Lastly, endemic fungal infections, including histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, and coccidioidomycosis may present with severe, disseminated disease. See Fungal Infections in Infectious Disease for additional information.

Posttransplant parasitic infections are often caused by transmission through allograft or reactivation of infection in the recipient. Clinical presentations can vary significantly from syndromes in other populations. For example, Toxoplasma gondii is typically a disease of reactivation and classically presents as encephalitis with multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions on imaging (see Toxoplasma gondii in Infectious Disease). However, after heart transplantation, toxoplasmosis most commonly occurs as a donor-derived infection when seronegative recipients receive a seropositive allograft, and clinical manifestations may include central nervous system, pulmonary, and disseminated infections. Strongyloides can reactivate many years after initial exposure and cause a hyperinfection syndrome, classically with gram-negative bacteremia and meningitis. Donor-derived or reactivation of trypanosomiasis or leishmaniasis can also occur if the recipient or donor was from an endemic area.

Preventive therapies play an important role in decreasing the risk of posttransplant infection. Most immunizations are safe in patients after transplantation except for live virus vaccines, which are contraindicated after SOT and are avoided for at least 2 years after HSCT. The timing and recommended number of doses varies based on the specific vaccine, patient population (SOT or HSCT), whether the series was initiated before transplantation, and serostatus.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is one of the most important prophylactic medications following transplantation. It is used to prevent Pneumocystis; reduce rates of toxoplasmosis, Nocardia (although breakthrough infections have occurred), and Listeria; and decrease the incidence of urinary tract infections in kidney transplant.

Antifungal prophylaxis for candidiasis is indicated during the early months after HSCT and may need to be extended in the setting of GVHD; if high-dose glucocorticoids are used, prophylaxis should cover Candida and Aspergillus, typically with posaconazole (voriconazole is approved only for treatment).

Strategies for preventing cytomegalovirus include prophylaxis or pre-emptive therapy, which involves serial monitoring for cytomegalovirus by quantitative nucleic acid amplification testing and initiation of therapy when significant viremia is detected. For SOT, prophylaxis with valganciclovir is often preferred for patients at high risk (D+/R−, lymphocyte depletion) and is usually given for at least 3 to 6 months. Letermovir is approved for use in D+/R− kidney transplant recipients and can be given instead of valganciclovir. Many HSCT programs used monitoring and pre-emptive therapy to avoid cytopenias caused by valganciclovir, but with the availability of letermovir, primary prophylaxis in HSCT has become more common, especially in high-risk populations (R+, early GVHD, HLA mismatch).

Health Care–Associated Infections

Health care–associated infections (HCAI) have been linked to indwelling medical devices, prosthetic devices and materials, surgery, invasive procedures, transmission of organisms between patients and health care personnel (HCP), and environmental factors. Approximately 3.2% of hospitalized patients acquire at least one HCAI, costing the U.S. health care system an estimated $28 billion to $45 billion annually. The most common HCAIs include pneumonia, gastrointestinal infections, surgical site infections, bloodstream infections (73% associated with central venous catheters), and urinary tract infections (UTIs, 75% associated with catheters). Elimination of HCAIs remains important for the U.S. health care system. Of HCAIs overall, 35% to 55% are considered preventable.

Hand hygiene is the foundation of infection prevention, but an adherence rate of less than 50% has been reported. Hand hygiene should be performed at least before and after every patient contact. The World Health Organization’s five key hand hygiene moments describe opportunities for hand hygiene. Hand hygiene should include all surfaces of the hands up to the wrists, between fingers, and the fingertips. Alcohol-based hand rubs are generally preferred to hand disinfection with soap and water, except when hands are visibly soiled, when personnel have direct contact with blood or body fluids, and after contact with a patient with Clostridioides difficile infection or the infected patient’s environment (because soap and water is more effective than alcohol-based hand sanitizers in removing C. difficile spores).

Standard precautions should be practiced universally to protect HCP from exposure to pathogens. Blood and all body fluids except sweat are potentially infectious, regardless of the patient’s infection status. Personal protective equipment (gloves, gown, mask, and eye protection) are barriers protecting HCP from exposure to blood and body fluids. Protective equipment should be donned and doffed carefully (please refer to Resources for Worker Safety on the CDC website) and followed by hand hygiene. Transmission-based precautions are performed in addition to standard precautions to prevent transmission of epidemiologically significant organisms ( [Table: Table: Transmission-Based Precautions]

).

Additional preventive measures include the following:

  • Careful and judicious device use
  • Safe injection practices (one needle, one syringe, one-time use)
  • Aseptic technique for invasive procedures and surgery
  • Clean environment
  • Clean patient equipment

HCAI prevention “bundles” comprise several evidence-based processes of care that, when performed together, consistently have a greater impact on decreasing HCAIs than individual components performed inconsistently ( [Table: Table: ICU Care Bundles]

). All U.S. health care facilities are required to have an infection prevention program.

Needlestick and sharps injuries increase the risk for HCP acquiring blood-borne infections such as HIV, hepatitis B (HBV), and hepatitis C (HCV). Most injuries occur with hollow-bore needles, which confer a higher risk of blood-borne pathogen transmission. A deep injury, injury from a needle placed in a vein or artery, visible blood on the sharps device, and high viral load in the source patient (i.e., those with HBV, HCV, and HIV) also increase the risk of transmission. Personal protective equipment and practices for sharps safety minimize the risk, as does avoiding workplace fatigue and under-resourcing of work environments. Additionally, all HCP should be immunized against HBV.

Needlestick or sharps injuries should immediately be washed with soap and water and reported. The source patient should be assessed for HBV, HCV, and HIV. The exposed HCP should seek immediate treatment and receive baseline testing for HIV and for HCV with anti-HCV with reflex to HCV RNA within 48 hours of exposure; those with an initial positive result should be referred for treatment of pre-existing infection.

Postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) management for HBV is outlined in [Table: Table: Hepatitis B Postexposure Management for Health Care Personnel]

. See Hepatitis B in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease for additional information regarding HBV treatment.

HCV exposure management involves monitoring and timely diagnosis and treatment. Follow-up testing of HCP is indicated if the source patient is positive for HCV or status is unknown or if HCV RNA testing is unavailable. An HCV RNA test at 3 to 6 weeks following exposure is recommended; if negative, a follow-up anti-HCV with reflex to HCV RNA at 4 to 6 months following exposure is advised. A positive HCV RNA test at any point indicates referral for treatment (see Hepatitis C in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease).

PEP for HIV should be offered to all exposed HCP when the source patient is positive or if the status of the source patient is unknown; therapy can be discontinued if the test returns negative unless acute HIV infection is a concern. PEP should be initiated as soon as possible, preferably within a few hours. The preferred PEP regimen is given for 4 weeks (see Prevention in Infectious Disease). Follow-up HIV testing occurs at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months after exposure; if a fourth-generation antigen-antibody assay is used throughout monitoring, follow-up testing can occur at 6 weeks and 4 months.

Of catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) overall, 17% to 69% may be preventable. Urinary catheters are used in 15% to 25% of hospitalized patients in the United States, compelling efforts to establish appropriateness criteria for catheter use. Adverse outcomes related to CAUTI include pyelonephritis, perinephric abscess, and bacteremia (<5%). The most common CAUTI pathogens are as follows (in descending order):

  • Escherichia coli
  • Klebsiella pneumoniae and Klebsiella oxytoca
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  • Enterococcus species

Antibiotic resistance among these pathogens is increasing.

Colonization with bacteria or yeast occurs within 48 hours of catheterization. Catheter duration is the primary modifiable risk factor for CAUTI; each day increases the risk. Nonadherence to aseptic technique (e.g., opening a closed system) and insertion by a less experienced operator also increase the risk. Patient-related risk factors include female sex, age older than 50 years, diabetes mellitus, severe or nonsurgical underlying illness, and serum creatinine level greater than 2.0 mg/dL (176.8 µmol/L). Appropriate indications for indwelling urinary catheters are listed in [Table: Table: Indications for Indwelling Urinary Catheter Use]

. Management of urinary incontinence using external catheters is preferred when feasible. Care provided in the ICU is not itself an indication for a catheter.

Key prevention strategies ( [Table: Table: Prevention of CAUTI]

) include limiting urinary catheter use to appropriate indications only (see [Table: Table: Indications for Indwelling Urinary Catheter Use]

) and considering other options associated with lower infection risk (intermittent straight catheterization, external catheters) when urine collection is necessary. Most studies have not shown definitive benefit of antimicrobial- or antiseptic-coated catheters for short- (<14 days) or long-term catheterization; these catheters are more expensive and, in some cases (e.g., nitrofurazone-coated catheters), cause more patient discomfort.

CAUTI is diagnosed in patients with an indwelling urethral or suprapubic catheter (or catheter removed in the 48 hours before symptom onset) or with intermittent catheterization who have signs and symptoms compatible with UTI (see Diagnosis of Urinary Tract Infections in Infectious Disease for information), one or more bacterial species in a urine specimen (≥10^3 colony-forming units/mL), and no other identifiable infection source. CAUTI is often a diagnosis of exclusion. Catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria (≥10^5 colony-forming units/mL without urinary tract signs or symptoms) is common and generally does not require treatment. Change in appearance or odor of urine or pyuria without accompanying symptoms does not indicate UTI.

Before initiating antimicrobial treatment, a urinalysis and urine culture should be obtained to guide definitive therapy. CAUTI management includes removing the urinary catheter (and only replacing if still needed). Removal is strongly recommended for catheters in place for 2 or more weeks because biofilm on the catheter makes it difficult to eradicate bacteriuria or funguria, and treatment may lead to antimicrobial resistance. Therapy should always be adjusted to the narrowest coverage spectrum possible based on culture results. Treatment is generally given for 5 to 7 days if symptoms resolve promptly and longer (10-14 days) for patients with delayed response or bacteremia. Candiduria in a patient with a catheter frequently represents colonization and rarely requires treatment. Candida CAUTI is considered when significant candiduria persists despite catheter removal or replacement and the patient is symptomatic. CAUTIs caused by Candida species requiring treatment should be treated for 14 days.

The overall risk of developing a surgical site infection (SSI) is 1% to 3%; however, the risk varies widely by surgery type. Wound class affects the risk of infection:

  • Less than a 2% risk with clean wounds
  • Less than a 10% risk with clean contaminated wounds
  • A 20% risk with contaminated wounds

Most infections occur within 30 days after surgery or within 90 days after surgery with implants; however, infections can manifest beyond these ranges. Risk factors include patient-related, procedure-related, and postoperative factors ( [Table: Table: Surgical Site Infection Risk Factor Mitigation]

). The patient’s skin and gastrointestinal or female genital tracts are major sources of organisms causing infection, depending on the type of surgery. The time during which the surgical site is open represents the period of greatest risk. The following are common SSI pathogens:

  • S. aureus (23%)
  • Coagulase-negative staphylococci (17%)
  • Enterococci (7%)
  • E. coli (5%)
  • P. aeruginosa (5%)

Exogenous sources of organisms (surgical personnel, surgical instruments, environment) are less common causes of SSIs, usually identified when a cluster of infections is present.

Prevention is divided into preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative measures (see [Table: Table: Surgical Site Infection Risk Factor Mitigation]

). Up to 60% of SSIs are preventable, and modifiable host factors should be optimized before surgery. Preoperative screening for S. aureus, followed by decolonization if results are positive, may mitigate SSIs before elective cardiothoracic and orthopedic procedures. If antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated, select the correct agent, dose, and time for administration (60 minutes before incision; 2 hours before incision for vancomycin or fluoroquinolones), and redose during surgery based on surgery duration and antibiotic half-life. Continuing antibiotics postoperatively does not decrease SSI incidence, even with intraoperative spillage of gastrointestinal contents or presence of wound drains.

A combination of clinical features, laboratory and microbiologic findings, and radiographic results is used to diagnose SSIs. Clinical signs and symptoms vary by infection site and type as well as by implicated organism (e.g., some organisms are more likely to cause purulence). Inflammatory changes at the surgical site (pain or tenderness, warmth, swelling, erythema) and purulent drainage suggest a superficial incisional infection. Deep incisional SSIs have more extensive tenderness expanding outside the area of erythema and more systemic signs, such as fever and leukocytosis. Wound dehiscence suggests a deep incisional SSI unless the wound or drainage is culture negative. Organ and deep-space SSIs are associated with more systemic signs and local symptoms related to a deep abscess or infected fluid collection. In cases of suspected organ or deep-space SSIs, CT is helpful to localize the infection and determine the best approach to fluid or abscess drainage for culture and treatment. When an SSI is suspected, drainage or infected tissue should be obtained for culture. Deep-tissue or operative cultures are preferable to superficial wound swab cultures that are likely to reflect skin or wound colonization and do not necessarily yield the causative pathogen.

SSI treatment requires debridement of necrotic tissue, drainage of abscesses or infected fluid, and specific antimicrobial therapy for organ or deep-space and deep incisional infections. Repeat debridement or drainage may be required to control and resolve the infection even with appropriate antimicrobial therapy. When an SSI involves an implant, implant removal is often necessary, followed by a course of antibiotics. Superficial incisional infections can usually be managed with oral antibiotics without tissue debridement. Culture results guide the choice of antimicrobial agent; treatment duration varies by anatomic site and by depth of infection as well as clinical response.

Central line–associated bloodstream infections (CLABSIs), associated with all types of central venous catheters (CVCs), are the most preventable HCAI. CLABSI risk factors include prolonged hospitalization before catheterization, neutropenia, and reduced nurse-to-patient ratio in the ICU. Additional risk factors (modifiable) are shown in [Table: Table: CLABSI Risk Factor Mitigation]

. Pathogens associated with CLABSIs include the following:

  • Coagulase-negative staphylococci (20.5%)
  • S. aureus (12.3%)
  • Enterococcus faecalis (8.8%)
  • Non-albicans Candida species (8.1%)
  • K. pneumoniae or oxytoca (7.9%)
  • Enterococcus faecium (7%)
  • Candida albicans (6.5%)

Antimicrobial resistance is a problem for many of these pathogens. CLABSI complications include endocarditis, septic thrombophlebitis, and metastatic infection.

CVCs should be inserted only by experienced personnel using the insertion bundle:

  • Hand hygiene
  • Chlorhexidine skin antisepsis of the insertion site (using recommended application methods and contact time)
  • Maximal barrier precautions (mask, cap, gown, sterile gloves, large full body sterile drape covering patient
  • Optimal catheter site selection (subclavian site preferred, avoid femoral site)

See [Table: Table: CLABSI Risk Factor Mitigation]

for further modifiable factors to prevent CLABSI. Insertion bundles, checklists, and staff education have significantly reduced CLABSIs. If CLABSI rates remain high despite adherence to these strategies, patient chlorhexidine bathing and antimicrobial-impregnated catheters (silver-sulfadiazine–chlorhexidine, minocycline-rifampin) may be considered. Routine CVC exchange or replacement or administration of systemic antimicrobial prophylaxis at time of insertion or during CVC use should be avoided.

CLABSI is suspected when a patient with a CVC has bacteremia not resulting from infection at another site. Fever is a common clinical manifestation, and inflammation or purulence at the catheter insertion site may be present. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures (20 mL per set) should be obtained from different sites before starting antibiotics. Avoid blood cultures drawn directly from CVCs because they have a higher rate of false positivity and may falsely identify a CLABSI and lead to unnecessary antibiotic therapy.

Infected CVCs should be removed (avoiding guidewire exchange); this removal is particularly important for S. aureus, P. aeruginosa, antimicrobial-resistant gram-negative bacilli, and Candida species infections. Therapy duration for most uncomplicated non–S. aureus CLABSIs is 7 to 14 days ( [Table: Table: CLABSI Management]

). S. aureus CLABSI is usually treated for at least 4 weeks (see Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia in Infectious Disease); however, shorter-term therapy may be considered in select patients who have immediate catheter removal with resolution of fever and bacteremia within 72 hours of starting appropriate therapy and who have no implanted prosthetic devices; no evidence of endocarditis by echocardiography (preferably transesophageal), suppurative thrombophlebitis, or metastatic infection; and neither diabetes mellitus nor immunosuppression. Bacteremia clearance should be confirmed with follow-up blood cultures. If bacteremia persists after CVC removal and appropriate antimicrobial therapy, evaluation for a deeper source of infection, including endocarditis, should be performed (see Endocarditis in Infectious Disease). Infectious Diseases Society of America guidelines state that all patients with candidemia should be evaluated by an ophthalmologist to rule out the presence of Candida endophthalmitis within 1 to 2 weeks (see Systemic Candidiasis in Infectious Disease).

Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) is pneumonia developing more than 48 hours after hospitalization. Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is pneumonia developing 48 hours after endotracheal intubation; it occurs in 10% of patients. Half of patients with HAP develop serious complications, including respiratory failure, pleural effusion, septic shock, empyema, and kidney injury. Nosocomial pneumonia is often precipitated by an aspiration event or series of microaspiration events. Mechanical ventilation increases the risk of pneumonia 6-fold to 21-fold. HAP and VAP risk factors include age older than 70 years, recent abdominal or thoracic surgery, immunosuppression, and underlying chronic lung disease. Modifiable risk factors are listed in [Table: Table: VAP Risk Factor Mitigation]

.

HAP and VAP are often caused by bacteria, but viral and fungal pathogens should be considered in immunocompromised patients. Risk factors for multidrug-resistant pathogens associated with VAP are provided in [Table: Table: Multidrug-Resistant VAP Pathogens]

.

Commonly used ventilator bundles include subglottic suctioning, peptic ulcer disease and deep venous thrombosis prophylaxis, and avoiding gastric overdistention. Use of ventilator bundles has been shown to decrease VAP rates by 71%. Additional interventions are listed in [Table: Table: VAP Risk Factor Mitigation]

.

Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical, radiographic, and microbiologic findings. A new lung infiltrate on imaging plus clinical findings, including new-onset fever (temperature >38.0 °C [100.4 °F]), leukocytosis or leukopenia, purulent sputum, and decline in oxygenation, suggest pneumonia. Noninvasive sampling (endotracheal aspiration) with semiquantitative sputum cultures (heavy, moderate, light, and no growth) are suggested for diagnosing VAP. Clinical findings without radiographic abnormality suggest tracheobronchitis, which does not require antibiotic treatment.

Respiratory sample culture results should guide therapy for suspected HAP and VAP; a specimen from the lower respiratory tract should be obtained before starting antimicrobial therapy. However, inability to obtain a specimen should not delay therapy initiation for VAP, and empiric antimicrobial therapy should be instituted pending results of noninvasive sampling with semiquantitative cultures and based on local VAP antibiograms, if available.

Empiric HAP and VAP regimens should include coverage for S. aureus, P. aeruginosa, and other gram-negative bacilli. An agent active against MRSA (vancomycin, linezolid) should be included for patients with MRSA risk factors or those in a unit with MRSA prevalence greater than 10% to 20% (or unknown) unless a MRSA nasal swab is negative (negative predictive value is approximately 99% in pneumonia). Two antipseudomonal agents of different classes are recommended for empiric regimens only for patients with risk factors for resistance, with structural lung disease (bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis), or in a unit with greater than 10% resistance to an agent being considered for monotherapy.

Despite the pathophysiology of aspiration associated with HAP and VAP, antimicrobial coverage for oral anaerobes is not routinely recommended unless lung abscess or empyema is suspected. Cephalosporins should be avoided as monotherapy in settings where extended-spectrum β-lactamase–producing gram-negative organisms (such as K. pneumoniae) are prevalent; consider a carbapenem instead.

Microbiologic results should be reviewed at 48 to 72 hours, and all patients should be re-evaluated for clinical improvement. Antimicrobial therapy should be de-escalated (to narrow-spectrum or oral therapy) based on microbiologic results and clinical stabilization or discontinued if the diagnosis of pneumonia is in doubt. Patients who do not improve within 72 hours of appropriate therapy should undergo investigation for infectious complications, an alternate diagnosis, or another site of infection. HAP and VAP should be treated for 7 days or less.

Antimicrobial resistance has been noted in nearly all bacterial pathogens. Multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs) are most prevalent in health care settings (highest incidence in long-term acute care hospitals) but are also observed in the community. Almost 50% of S. aureus HCAIs in the United States are methicillin resistant; about 30% of enterococci are vancomycin resistant; 20.7% of Enterobacterales produce extended-spectrum β-lactamase and are resistant to all β-lactam antibiotics; 3.3% of Enterobacterales are resistant to carbapenems; and 14.2% of P. aeruginosa and 43.1% of Acinetobacter species are multidrug resistant (some Acinetobacter are resistant to almost all antibiotics).

Candida auris is an emerging drug-resistant pathogen shed from skin into the environment, where it can survive for weeks and be transmitted to others. It causes severe invasive infections, particularly in immunocompromised patients. See Systemic Candidiasis in Infectious Disease for additional information.

MDRO infections are difficult to treat, with mortality rates up to four times higher than infections caused by antibiotic-sensitive strains. Limiting transmission of MDROs in health care settings requires full adherence to hand hygiene protocols, contact precautions, and cleaning and disinfecting of the environment and patient care equipment. More than 50% of hospitalized patients receive antibiotics, a major risk factor for acquiring an antibiotic-resistant organism and C. difficile infection (see Clostridioides difficile Infection in Infectious Disease). Judicious use of antimicrobial agents is increasingly important to combat the rise of MDROs and emergence of untreatable infections.
