HIV/AIDS

Advances in antiretroviral therapy (ART) have revolutionized HIV management, and the life expectancy of persons with HIV approaches that of the general population. HIV care remains complex, especially as many persons with HIV are aging and are at increased risk for metabolic complications and comorbid conditions. Ending the HIV epidemic remains an overarching goal, and efforts are needed to increase HIV screening rates, link newly diagnosed persons to treatment, and retain persons with HIV in regular follow-up. This chapter will focus on HIV-1 infection. HIV-2 infection is rare in the United States, primarily occurring in parts of Africa; it is generally less progressive and carries a lower risk of immunocompromise and opportunistic infections.

The CDC and American College of Physicians recommend that all persons between the ages of 13 and 64 years be tested for HIV at least once; the U.S. Preventive Service Task Force recommends this screening for persons aged 15 to 65 years. Persons with higher risk of HIV exposure should undergo repeat testing at least annually. Routine HIV testing is also recommended in pregnant persons and in any person diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection.

Acute HIV infection occurs soon after transmission. Acute infection may be asymptomatic or associated with nonspecific symptoms suggesting an acute viral illness ( [Table: Table: Acute HIV Infection Signs and Symptoms]

). A fourth-generation combination antigen/antibody immunoassay, which detects the presence of p24 antigen and HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies, is commonly used for diagnosis. The testing algorithm is outlined in

. The presence of p24 antigen, an HIV structural protein, can be detected as early as day 14 after HIV acquisition. IgM and IgG antibodies to HIV do not develop until approximately day 20 and day 30, respectively, after infection. Patients with a negative antigen/antibody test in whom clinical suspicion for acute HIV is high should undergo HIV RNA polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing. Nucleic acid amplification testing can detect the virus as early as 6 to 8 days after infection.

A few persons with HIV maintain very low or undetectable levels of HIV RNA, accompanied by well-preserved CD4 cell counts, in the absence of antiretroviral therapy; these patients are considered HIV controllers or HIV elite controllers. A confirmatory HIV-1/2 antibody differentiation immunoassay detecting the presence of HIV antibodies and serial quantitative HIV RNA detecting very low or undetectable viral loads confirms the diagnosis.

Initial evaluation should include complete history (including sexual, substance use, and mental health history) and examination for signs and symptoms of opportunistic infections or other comorbid conditions. Patient education and counseling should include information on prevention of HIV transmission to others. Initial laboratory tests include CD4 cell count, HIV viral load, HIV resistance testing, baseline organ function, and evaluation for other infections with higher prevalence in persons with HIV ( [Table: Table: Initial Laboratory Screening in HIV Infection]

).

HIV infection increases the risk for numerous vaccine-preventable infections because of the detrimental effects on cell-mediated immunity and B-cell function. Routine immunization is a key component of preventive care for persons living with HIV; vaccine recommendations are summarized in [Table: Table: Vaccinations for Adults with HIV]

.

Prophylaxis for opportunistic infections depends on the CD4 cell count ( [Table: Table: Opportunistic Infection Prophylaxis]

). Before beginning prophylaxis, active infection should be ruled out to avoid undertreatment and selection for resistance.

All persons with HIV infection should begin ART as soon as possible, ideally within 1 week of diagnosis, regardless of CD4 cell count. Rapid initiation of ART has been shown to improve engagement in care and viral suppression and to reduce the time during which a person newly diagnosed with HIV can transmit the virus to others.

The primary goal of ART is to suppress the HIV viral load below limits of quantification using commercial assays. A durably suppressed viral load is associated with improved immune function, reduced risk of opportunistic infections, and improved quality of life and survival.

Antiretroviral agents used in the United States are shown in [Table: Table: Antiretroviral Agents Used in the United States]

. Recommended initial ART regimens for persons with HIV are shown in [Table: Table: Initial Treatment Regimens for Most Persons with HIV Infection]

and include two or three drugs from two different classes, preferably including an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (bictegravir or dolutegravir). Bictegravir- or dolutegravir-based ART regimens are preferred for their high efficacy, favorable tolerability and safety, high barrier to resistance, low potential for drug interactions, and once-daily dosing formulation to facilitate adherence.

A long-acting injectable antiretroviral regimen consisting of cabotegravir (an integrase strand transfer inhibitor) and rilpivirine (a nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor) is approved to replace daily oral ART in persons with a suppressed viral load. This regimen should be avoided in patients with resistance to either agent or with chronic hepatitis B virus infection (in the absence of additional hepatitis B active medications).

Patients with or at risk for reduced kidney function or osteopenia should avoid tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF). Abacavir is not recommended as initial therapy owing to concerns about its association with cardiovascular disease and the risk of a life-threatening hypersensitivity reaction. Many antiretrovirals interact with other drugs, and drug interactions must be assessed when beginning ART or any new medication. Such assessment is especially necessary when pharmacokinetic boosters (ritonavir or cobicistat) are used specifically to inhibit drug metabolism and raise levels of antiretrovirals.

After ART is initiated, viral load levels and CD4 cell counts are monitored to ensure effectiveness and to determine immune recovery. With optimal therapy, HIV RNA in blood should become undetectable within 8 to 24 weeks of initiating ART. CD4 cell counts may take several months to increase and may never show full recovery, especially in persons who started ART in the setting of advanced HIV/AIDS. CD4 cell count should be monitored every 6 months until it remains greater than 250/µL for at least 1 year; thereafter, as long as viral load remains undetectable, CD4 cell count monitoring can be stopped.

Viral resistance testing should be performed at diagnosis to ensure selection of a fully active regimen and should be repeated if the viral load increases during ART. However, resistance testing should not delay three-drug ART initiation; the regimen can be modified when results are available. Standard genotypic resistance testing in antiretroviral-naive persons assesses for mutations in the reverse transcriptase and protease genes. Patients who acquire HIV while taking cabotegravir for pre-exposure prophylaxis should also undergo genotypic testing to evaluate for integrase inhibitor mutations. Treatment with this class should be avoided until test results exclude resistance.

Virologic failure is defined as failure to achieve or maintain an HIV RNA level less than 200 copies/mL. The most common reason for breakthrough viremia is poor medication adherence, and barriers to taking ART should be discussed. In the event of virologic failure, resistance testing results are used to guide selection of a new regimen. Plasma levels of HIV RNA must generally be greater than 500 copies/mL to provide enough virus for resistance testing. Resistance testing may be unreliable if performed while the patient is not taking an antiretroviral. Laboratory monitoring should be repeated 1 month after switching regimens to assess effectiveness and toxicity.

ART in pregnancy benefits the patient and significantly reduces the risk of perinatal HIV transmission. ART initiation is recommended as soon as possible for pregnant persons with HIV. A three-drug, fixed-dose combination regimen of tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) or TDF with emtricitabine or lamivudine plus dolutegravir is recommended; TAF plus emtricitabine plus bictegravir is also a preferred option. Data are insufficient to recommend continuing a two-drug regimen in the setting of pregnancy but may be pursued with caution if viral load is suppressed. Darunavir with ritonavir is recommended when integrase strand transfer inhibitor resistance is suspected. Atazanavir and raltegravir are not preferred ART agents during pregnancy but are reasonable alternatives if preferred agents cannot be used. Patients taking ART who become pregnant should continue treatment without interruption. Because of limited data on its use in pregnancy, individuals who become pregnant while taking long-acting cabotegravir plus rilpivirine should be switched to a preferred oral triple-drug regimen. Provider and patient may opt to continue, however, with close viral load monitoring.

Metabolic disorders and specific organ diseases have become increasingly recognized among persons with HIV. Weight gain is generally noted within the first year of ART. Weight gain is more common with regimens containing TAF than those with TDF; however, changing the antiretroviral regimen solely because of weight gain is not recommended. Age-associated comorbidities and declines in kidney and liver function may complicate HIV management through drug interactions and increased toxicity.

HIV infection itself and some antiretrovirals, including TAF and certain protease inhibitors, may worsen hyperlipidemia. Boosted protease inhibitors and integrase inhibitors may worsen insulin resistance. Glucose and lipid levels should be assessed at entry into HIV care and after initiating or changing ART; when abnormal, fasting values should be obtained. Hemoglobin A~1c should not be used for diagnosis of diabetes in those taking ART because it may underestimate glycemia in patients with HIV.

Kidney function is abnormal in up to 30% of persons with untreated HIV, and a baseline assessment of creatinine clearance is important to ensure appropriate medication dosing. This should be repeated 1 to 2 months after initiation or change in ART and reassessed every 6 months. Some antiretrovirals may alter creatinine secretion, leading to elevations in the absence of kidney disease. TDF is associated with higher rates of kidney disease than TAF. A urinalysis should be obtained to assess proteinuria at initiation of care and repeated annually.

Bone mineral density is reduced in HIV, and TDF is associated with accelerated bone loss. For this reason, TDF should be avoided in persons with osteoporosis or risk factors for bone loss. Baseline bone densitometry by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry is recommended in men 50 years and older and postmenopausal women with HIV.

Persons with HIV are at increased risk of liver disease because of coinfection with hepatitis B or hepatitis C virus (HBV, HCV), hepatic steatosis, and antiretroviral hepatotoxicity. All patients with HIV should be screened for viral hepatitis; if negative, immunization against hepatitis A and HBV is indicated. HIV is associated with accelerated progression of liver disease, and persons with chronic HBV or HCV should undergo treatment. Persons coinfected with HIV and HBV should be treated with an antiretroviral regimen that includes TDF or TAF plus emtricitabine or lamivudine. Persons with HIV and HCV should receive HCV direct-acting antiviral treatment, although attention must be paid to drug interactions between the antiviral regimens (see Hepatitis C in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease). Elevated liver aminotransferase levels in the absence of viral hepatitis should prompt evaluation for metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease.

Rates of cardiovascular disease (CVD), including myocardial infarction and stroke, are higher in persons with HIV infection, who are also often diagnosed with CVD at a younger age than those without HIV. Factors associated with increased cardiovascular risk in persons with HIV include traditional cardiometabolic risk factors and systemic inflammation associated with HIV, even in the setting of viral suppression. Guidelines from the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association and HIV Medicine Association recommend initiating at least moderate-intensity statin therapy in persons with HIV aged 40 to 75 years with a 10-year atherosclerotic CVD risk estimate of 5% to less than 20%. Moderate-intensity therapy should also be considered in patients with less than 5% risk, especially if other atherosclerotic CVD risk factors are present. High-intensity therapy is recommended for patients with a 10-year risk of 20% or more.

HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders may manifest as impaired memory, attention, executive function, and information processing speed. Neurocognitive decline with aging occurs faster in persons with HIV compared with the general population and is associated with impaired adherence to ART and increased morbidity and mortality. Referral to a neuropsychologist and neurologist for evaluation and management may be warranted. ART initiation and continuation is the main treatment for HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders; it also has a role in prevention and treatment of HIV-associated dementia.

HIV encephalitis is the cause of HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder in later stages of untreated illness. It can also present as CD8 encephalitis, consisting of perivascular inflammation resulting from infiltration of CD8+ lymphocytes, which may occur as part of an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome and, in some cases, is associated with viral escape (low levels of detectable HIV RNA in cerebrospinal fluid [CSF]).

Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) is a disorder associated with worsening of a pre-existing infectious process (paradoxical IRIS) or with revelation of a previously unrecognized pre-existing infection (unmasking IRIS). It has also been reported with noninfectious complications, such as lymphoma. IRIS usually occurs within 1 week to a few months of initiating effective ART in patients with low pretreatment CD4 cell counts (<100/µL). Management includes continuing ART while treating the opportunistic infection. In select patients, NSAIDs or glucocorticoids may be useful in mitigating inflammatory symptoms.

Opportunistic infections are caused by pathogens that do not commonly cause significant disease in immunocompetent persons. Untreated HIV is associated with impaired cell-mediated immunity, which increases the risk of opportunistic infection.

Recommendations for prophylaxis against opportunistic pathogens are outlined in [Table: Table: Opportunistic Infection Prophylaxis]

.

Mucocutaneous Candida infections, including oropharyngeal and esophageal disease, generally occur at CD4 cell counts less than 200/µL. Oral candidiasis usually presents as thrush, with mucosal whitish plaques that can be scraped off the tongue or buccal mucosa (

). Oropharyngeal candidiasis can be treated with a 1- to 2-week course of oral fluconazole or, alternatively, with topical antifungal therapy (e.g., clotrimazole troche). Retrosternal burning or odynophagia suggests esophageal disease, which requires 2 to 3 weeks of systemic treatment. Lack of improvement is an indication for endoscopy.

All persons with HIV, regardless of CD4 cell count, should be screened for exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, preferably with an interferon-γ release assay, unless they have a history of active or latent tuberculosis. Persons with untreated HIV are at increased risk of developing active tuberculosis, with an estimated annual risk of up to 16%. Reactivation can occur at any CD4 cell count although the risk increases with greater immunodeficiency. Tuberculosis in persons with HIV is more likely to manifest at extrapulmonary sites. When treating latent or active tuberculosis in persons with HIV, drug interactions between rifamycins and antiretrovirals must be carefully considered (see Management of Tuberculosis in Infectious Disease).

Tuberculosis treatment in patients with HIV infection may be complicated by IRIS. In persons starting antituberculosis therapy (without meningitis), not yet receiving ART, and with a CD4 cell count less than 50/µL, ART should be initiated within 2 weeks. In persons with CD4 cell counts of 50/µL or greater, ART should be started within 2 to 8 weeks of initiating antituberculosis therapy. For those with tuberculous meningitis, high-dose glucocorticoids should be initiated with tuberculosis treatment, and ART can be started when tuberculous meningitis is under control, after at least 2 weeks of antituberculous therapy.

P. jirovecii pneumonia presents as a subacute illness with fever, dyspnea, and dry cough in persons with a CD4 cell count less than 200/µL. Chest radiographs often show bilateral interstitial infiltrates (

); cavitation or pleural effusion is unusual and suggests another diagnosis. A normal chest radiograph does not exclude the diagnosis, and chest CT is more sensitive, demonstrating patchy “ground-glass” opacities. The organism is not readily cultured, and diagnosis is often made by histopathology or cytopathology. Sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage fluid may demonstrate Pneumocystis cysts on fungal stains. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid or sputum PCR for P. jirovecii may also aid in diagnosis, but a positive result cannot distinguish colonization from active disease. Serum 1,3 β-d-glucan, a component of the cell wall of Pneumocystis cysts, is often elevated and may support the diagnosis, but is not specific. First-line treatment is high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; patients with a partial pressure of oxygen less than 70 mm Hg breathing ambient air or an alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient of 35 mm Hg or greater at diagnosis should be given adjunctive glucocorticoids to prevent worsening that may accompany treatment initiation.

C. neoformans is a ubiquitous environmental fungus and an opportunistic pathogen in persons with HIV and a CD4 cell count less than 100/µL. Infection presents as subacute meningitis with headache, mental status changes, and fever. Lethargy and altered mentation may also occur and are associated with increased intracranial pressure. Serum cryptococcal antigen is a useful diagnostic test that is often diagnostic. Blood cultures, CSF cultures, CSF antigen testing, and CSF PCR are other useful diagnostic tests. Management includes antifungal therapy and attention to increased intracranial pressure (see Cryptococcosis in Infectious Disease). For patients with cryptococcal meningitis who have not yet started ART, this therapy should generally be delayed until 4 to 6 weeks after starting antifungal therapy to mitigate the risk of IRIS. Some experts suggest ART may be initiated as early as 2 weeks after antifungal therapy for cryptococcal meningitis when close laboratory monitoring and observation is feasible. Primary prophylaxis without a positive serum cryptococcal antigen is not recommended considering the overall low prevalence of infection and potential for drug-drug interactions and toxicity.

T. gondii infection in persons with HIV is most commonly a reactivation disease, typically occurring in persons with a CD4 cell count less than 100/µL and seropositivity for T. gondii IgG. Infection manifests as a focal encephalitis with headache, confusion, fever, and motor weakness. Seizures may occur with advanced disease. Imaging by head CT or brain MRI (which is more sensitive) typically reveals multiple ring-enhancing lesions (

). The differential diagnosis includes primary central nervous system lymphoma, which most often appears as a single lesion on imaging, and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, which is usually nonenhancing and disproportionally involves white matter (see Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy in Infectious Disease).

M. avium complex (MAC) infection usually presents as disseminated disease in patients with CD4 cell counts less than 50/µL; symptoms and signs include fever, night sweats, weight loss, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and cytopenias. MAC can also present as localized disease, most commonly as a focal, inflammatory lymphadenitis resulting from IRIS approximately 4 weeks after initiating ART. Blood cultures for acid-fast bacilli will often grow MAC, but the organism may also be seen on lymph node, bone marrow, or liver biopsy.

Cytomegalovirus most commonly presents with CD4 cell counts less than 50/µL. Retinitis, presenting with vision changes or floaters, is the most common cytomegalovirus end-organ disease in persons with HIV. Cytomegalovirus colitis or esophagitis can also occur (see Human Cytomegalovirus in Infectious Disease).

Bartonella species infection is increased in individuals with advanced HIV. Bartonella henselae is associated with cat scratches because of claws contaminated with the feces of infected fleas. In patients with HIV infection, it most commonly causes bacillary angiomatosis presenting with violaceous cutaneous lesions but can also affect other organ systems. Diagnosis of bacillary angiomatosis requires tissue biopsy.

Persons with HIV are at increased risk of malignancy. AIDS-associated malignancies are often linked to coinfection with other oncogenic viruses, including non-Hodgkin lymphoma (associated with Epstein-Barr virus), Kaposi sarcoma (associated with human herpesvirus type 8), and invasive cervical carcinoma (associated with human papillomavirus). Kaposi sarcoma may appear as dark red, brown, or violaceous lesions on the skin or mucous membranes (

). Human herpes virus type 8 can also cause primary effusion lymphoma and Castleman disease (giant lymph node hyperplasia). Human papillomavirus–related malignancies are significantly increased in patients with HIV infection, including cervical and anal cancers, and regular guideline-based screening is important (see [Table: Table: Initial Laboratory Screening in HIV Infection]

).

HIV infection can be associated with hematologic abnormalities, including lymphopenia, neutropenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Possible causes include immune-related conditions (e.g., immune thrombocytopenic purpura, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis), associated malignancy, secondary infection, or HIV itself (because of bone marrow suppression or defective hematopoiesis). Patients who are acutely ill with a low CD4 cell count (<200/µL) should be expeditiously and extensively evaluated for these causes. Bone marrow evaluation may be required in some cases. Empiric treatment for infection or microangiopathies may be needed, and ART and treatment of the underlying cause is essential. In stable patients with a hematologic abnormality as the presenting sign of HIV infection, ART often reverses the cytopenia. Newer antiretroviral medications are less likely to cause cytopenias (e.g., anemia) compared with earlier generation ART.

HIV infection may be acquired through sexual contact, exposure to infected blood or body fluids, or perinatal exposure ( [Table: Table: Risk of HIV-1 Transmission]

). Transmission rates are reduced by barrier contraceptive methods, such as condoms, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), and clean needle programs for persons who inject drugs. Universal blood donor testing has largely eliminated transmission through blood transfusion in the United States.

ART has extraordinary potential to reduce new, incident HIV. Although reducing viral load to an undetectable level in blood does not prove absence of virus in semen or vaginal fluid, the rate of transmission from a sexual partner with an undetectable viral load has been demonstrated to be close to zero (“Undetectable = Untransmissible”, “U=U”). Medical care necessary to achieve sustained viral suppression consists of testing and diagnosing infected persons, linking them to health care for counseling and treatment, and ensuring antiretroviral adherence. Each step along this continuum is a potential obstacle to successful HIV management.

Postexposure prophylaxis has been used successfully for many years to prevent infection after occupational and nonoccupational HIV exposure. Prophylaxis should be started as soon as possible but within 72 hours of sexual, percutaneous, or mucosal exposure to blood or genital secretions from a person with or at high risk for HIV. It is generally not recommended more than 72 hours after exposure and when the HIV risk is negligible. A three-drug regimen is given for 4 weeks; the U.S. Panel of the International Antiviral Society recommends an integrase inhibitor (bictegravir or dolutegravir) plus two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors: TDF or TAF plus emtricitabine or lamivudine. The exposed person should undergo HIV testing at baseline and at 4 to 6 weeks and 3 months after exposure.

The CDC and U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommend PrEP with ART to reduce the risk of infection for persons at high risk of HIV acquisition, including persons at risk through sexual contact and persons who inject drugs ( [Table: Table: Persons Who Should be Considered for PrEP]

). A two-drug oral combination of TDF and emtricitabine, taken once daily, is FDA approved for PrEP; with proven adherence, it has been shown to be more than 90% effective in reducing infection in those at high risk and is recommended across at-risk populations. TAF and emtricitabine, rather than TDF and emtricitabine, should be chosen for persons with a creatinine clearance of 30 to 60 mL/min and may be preferred in persons with osteoporosis. Data are insufficient to support the use of TAF and emtricitabine in persons whose risk factors include receptive vaginal intercourse or injection drug use. Cabotegravir, an integrase strand transfer inhibitor, is a long-acting intramuscular injection that is administered every 2 months after the initial dosing for PrEP; it is approved for use with kidney impairment. However, data are insufficient to recommend cabotegravir as PrEP for persons who inject drugs. Lenacapavir is also approved for prevention of HIV and is dosed by subcutaneous injection every 6 months. Patients should also be counseled on the need to continue barrier precautions to prevent other sexually transmitted infections. Laboratory testing before initiation and during PrEP is outlined in [Table: Table: PrEP Laboratory Testing]

. Persons who acquire HIV while taking PrEP with TDF or TAF plus emtricitabine should have a third drug (either bictegravir or dolutegravir) added to the two-drug PrEP regimen pending results of HIV RNA and viral resistance testing. Integrase inhibitor resistance has been observed in persons who test positive for HIV and are using cabotegravir for PrEP; in this setting, integrase inhibitor resistance testing should be performed before initiating ART with an integrase inhibitor–based regimen.

Three types of influenza viruses primarily infect humans: A, B, and C. Influenza A viruses are divided into subtypes based on two surface proteins, hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). Influenza A viruses can infect animals and humans and produce epidemics and pandemics. Influenza B viruses only affect humans and cause yearly epidemics but not pandemics. Influenza C causes mild illness and does not cause epidemics.

Minor changes in the H and N surface envelope glycoproteins (antigenic drift) of influenza A and B viruses cause yearly epidemics, and major changes (antigenic shift) in influenza A after genetic recombination from animals cause global pandemics. The most recent influenza pandemic occurred in 2009 and was caused by H1N1. Emerging subtypes of importance include H7N9, which circulates among poultry in China and can cause severe illness in humans; H5N1, which infects humans through close contact with infected poultry and can spread from person to person; and variants circulating in pigs that can sporadically infect humans.

Other respiratory viruses that may be documented in adults are outlined in [Table: Table: Select Respiratory Viruses in Adults]

.

Influenza usually causes a self-limiting illness with fever, cough, rhinorrhea, myalgia, and headache in most patients. Those at higher risk for severe primary influenza, complications such as superimposed bacterial pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus (see Microbiology of Community-Acquired Pneumonia in Infectious Disease), and death include the following:

  • Older adults (≥65 years)
  • Pregnant and postpartum persons
  • Immunocompromised patients
  • Patients with chronic medical conditions (especially chronic lung disease)
  • Persons with obesity (BMI ≥40)
  • Persons with neuromuscular disease
  • Residents of extended-care facilities

Less common but severe complications include the following:

  • Asthma exacerbations
  • COPD exacerbations
  • Myocarditis
  • Encephalitis
  • Rhabdomyolysis
  • Myositis
  • Sepsis
  • Multiorgan failure

During the endemic season, patients can be diagnosed using either rapid antigen tests or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of nasopharyngeal swabs. Both tests are highly specific, but PCR has a sensitivity of nearly 100%; the rapid antigen tests have a sensitivity between 59% and 93%. The Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guidelines for seasonal influenza recommend PCR over rapid antigen tests. During seasonal influenza activity, testing for influenza should occur in patients at high risk who present with influenza-like illness, pneumonia, or nonspecific respiratory illness if the testing result will influence clinical management:

  • Decisions on antiviral treatment initiation
  • Impact on other diagnostic testing
  • Antibiotic treatment decisions
  • Infection control practices

Other outpatient candidates for testing include those who present with acute onset of respiratory symptoms and either exacerbation of chronic medical conditions or with known complications of influenza, such as pneumonia. During times of influenza activity, testing for influenza at hospital admission is recommended for all patients with acute respiratory infection and in those with acute worsening of chronic cardiopulmonary disease. Treatment decisions should not be delayed pending confirmatory results.

The IDSA guidelines recommend initiating antiviral treatment as soon as possible for adults with documented or suspected influenza who are hospitalized and for outpatients with severe or progressive illness regardless of illness duration. Treatment should also be initiated as soon as possible for all other patients at high risk for influenza-related complications. Treatment can also be considered for otherwise healthy outpatients if started within 48 hours, household contacts of severely immunosuppressed patients, and health care workers who care for patients at high risk of developing complications from influenza.

Neuraminidase inhibitors are active against influenza A and B and can be given orally (oseltamivir) or intravenously (peramivir) or can be inhaled (zanamivir); however, zanamivir is contraindicated in patients with chronic lung disease. Antiviral therapy should be given for at least 5 days, but a longer duration (up to 10 days) should be considered in severely ill or immunosuppressed patients, particularly those who continue to have detectable viral DNA in a respiratory specimen after 5 days of treatment. Immunosuppressed patients are at risk for neuraminidase inhibitor resistance during or after therapy.

Baloxavir is a polymerase acidic endonuclease inhibitor that can be given as single-dose therapy for uncomplicated influenza. It must be started within 48 hours of symptom onset and appears to be as effective as a 5-day course of oseltamivir. Baloxavir is FDA approved for the treatment of patients at high risk of influenza complications, but it should not be used in hospitalized or immunocompromised patients. Baloxavir use has been associated with the emergence of resistance.

Widespread influenza vaccination is the most important preventive intervention; all persons aged 6 months or older without contraindications and all health care personnel should be vaccinated (see Influenza in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Oral oseltamivir and baloxavir and inhaled zanamivir are FDA approved for chemoprophylaxis (zanamivir is not approved in patients with chronic lung diseases) to contain outbreaks in institutional settings (such as long-term care facilities) and hospitals in conjunction with droplet precautions and vaccination. Chemoprophylaxis should be initiated as soon as possible and no later than 48 hours after exposure; oseltamivir and zanamivir should be continued for 7 days after the most recent exposure; baloxavir is given as a single dose. Good hand hygiene and face masks can prevent secondary infections in households.

Three novel coronaviruses, severe acute respiratory syndrome–coronaviruses (SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2) and Middle East respiratory syndrome–coronavirus (MERS-CoV), can infect animals and cause severe disease and epidemics in humans. SARS-CoV emerged in China in 2002, causing an acute pneumonia epidemic, but no SARS-CoV infections have been reported since 2004. MERS-CoV emerged in 2012 in Saudi Arabia in humans and camels, with most infections occurring in the Arabian Peninsula. MERS-CoV causes pneumonia, diarrhea, and kidney failure with a mortality rate of approximately 40%. SARS-CoV-2, the third novel, deadly coronavirus, causes COVID-19.

Symptomatic disease is characterized by fever, fatigue, dry cough, gastrointestinal symptoms, and loss of taste and smell. Severe respiratory disease leading to death can occur, but most infections are mild or asymptomatic.

Symptomatic patients with suspected infection should be tested. In addition, those who have had close contact with a person infected with SARS-CoV-2 should also be tested when 5 days have passed since the last exposure. SARS-CoV-2 infection is diagnosed using a viral test, either a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) or an antigen test. NAAT has superior sensitivity, but antigen tests are more convenient, less costly, and have a shorter turnaround time. Antigen testing is often used at home; because of inferior sensitivity, negative antigen tests for persons with symptoms or recent exposure warrant confirmation with additional testing. However, antigen tests are preferable for those with recent SARS-CoV-2 infection (i.e., within 3 months) and are indicated for repeat testing because a positive NAAT may represent prolonged viral RNA shedding rather than a new infection. Rarely, multisystem inflammatory syndrome can result from antecedent SARS-CoV-2 infection (see Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Rheumatology).

The mainstay of therapy for inpatients with COVID-19 who are not critically ill is intravenous remdesivir for 5 days; patients requiring oxygen therapy should also receive glucocorticoids. Critically ill patients (i.e., those receiving mechanical ventilation or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation) should receive glucocorticoids without remdesivir; baricitinib or tocilizumab are immunomodulators that can be added within 24 to 48 hours of ICU admission (and within 96 hours of hospitalization). If baricitinib or tocilizumab is not available, alternative immunomodulators, such as abatacept and infliximab, can be considered based on guidelines.

For outpatients with confirmed infection who are at risk for progression to severe disease and have been symptomatic for 5 days or less, guideline-recommended options include nirmatrelvir-ritonavir combination therapy for 5 days, intravenous remdesivir for 3 days, or (if other agents are not available or cannot be used) molnupiravir for 5 days. Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir should not be used in patients with severe kidney impairment; additionally, multiple drug interactions can preclude use in vulnerable populations that are at high risk of progression. Rebound COVID-19 after nirmatrelvir-ritonavir use has been reported. Those with recurrent symptoms should undergo repeat antigen testing and should restart the isolation period if positive; because recurrent symptoms are usually mild, retreatment is not routinely recommended.

Contact and respiratory precautions should be implemented for hospitalized patients with suspected or proven infection. In the outpatient setting, vaccinations, masking, handwashing, and social or physical distancing are effective preventive strategies. The most important preventive strategy is vaccination (see COVID-19 in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Because of emerging variants and changing data on treatment and prevention, readers are encouraged to see updated IDSA guidance or the Annals of Internal Medicine COVID-19 article collection and resources.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) shares many of the virologic and clinical properties of parainfluenza viruses. RSV subtypes A and B can cocirculate during an epidemic. RSV can also cause severe lower respiratory tract infection in adults older than 60 years and those who are immunocompromised, such as in bone marrow transplant recipients and those with underlying heart or lung disease.

RSV is spread by respiratory droplets and contact with fomites on the hands of infected persons. Nosocomial transmission is common and can be prevented by health care personnel adhering to contact isolation procedures; utilizing gowns, gloves, masks, and goggles; handwashing; and cohorting. The incubation period between exposure and illness onset is 3 to 5 days. Cough and nasal congestion can last 2 to 3 weeks, and complications, including bacterial otitis and sinusitis, are common. Pulmonary function abnormalities have been seen in RSV-infected adults for up to 2 months.

RSV is diagnosed by PCR from a nasopharyngeal swab or from a lower respiratory tract sample. Several FDA-approved multiplex PCRs include RSV in their panel. In immunocompetent patients, RSV testing should be pursued if the diagnosis will affect clinical management, for example, identifying RSV and ruling out the presence of other pathogens (such as influenza or SARS-CoV-2) that may benefit from treatment.

RSV infection requiring hospitalization has been associated with childhood asthma, and RSV is a major viral cause of exacerbations of chronic bronchitis and wheezing in adults. Hospitalized patients are routinely treated with supportive measures. Off-label use of ribavirin can be considered in select immunocompromised adults (such as hematopoietic stem cell and lung transplant recipients) with lower respiratory tract infection. Ribavirin has a modest effect on reducing hospital days and length of ICU stay and can reduce the effect of illness on arterial oxygen saturation. Ribavirin can be administered orally or by nebulizer; adverse effects include hemolytic anemia, and it can be teratogenic in pregnancy.

Pregnant individuals, adults aged 75 years or older, and adults aged 60 to 74 years who are at risk for severe disease are eligible for the RSV vaccine (see Respiratory Syncytial Virus in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Human herpesviruses (HHVs) are a group of eight DNA viruses ( [Table: Table: Human Herpesviruses]

. In humans, infection with HHV results in lifelong viral latency with the possibility of reactivation and oncogenesis. HHV can be transmitted by physical or sexual contact during active infection or through asymptomatic shedding of the virus (in saliva, semen, or cervical secretions); other routes include blood transfusion, organ transplantation, or maternofetal transmission. Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) is the only HHV that can be transmitted by the airborne route; it is also the only HHV with a vaccine that produces protective humoral immunity. Antivirals are available for some HHVs, and immunoglobulin therapy is available for cytomegalovirus and VZV.

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) type 1 infection is transmitted by oral-oral or oral-genital contact. HSV typically causes painful, small vesicles on an erythematous base, transitioning to pustules and subsequent crusting of the lesions (

); erosions or ulcers may also develop. It affects approximately 48% of adults. During stress, severe illness, or immunosuppression, patients may experience recurrence of oral stomatitis or esophagitis. The incidence of primary genital infection by HSV-1 is increasing. HSV-1 is among the most common viral causes of encephalitis (see Herpes Simplex Encephalitis in Infectious Disease).

HSV-2 is sexually transmitted and typically causes genital and rectal ulcers with or without proctitis (see Herpes Simplex Virus in Infectious Disease). HSV-2 affects approximately one sixth of adults in the United States; it can cause the following complications:

  • Recurrent benign lymphocytic meningitis (Mollaret meningitis)
  • Myelitis
  • Sacral radiculopathy
  • Neonatal infection or death (maternofetal transmission in primary genital infection)

HSV-1 and HSV-2 can cause herpetic whitlow (typically occurs on a distal finger as a vesicular lesion on an erythematous base), herpes gladiatorum (a skin infection typically associated with contact sports), keratoconjunctivitis, and retinitis and can trigger the occurrence of erythema multiforme.

Patients are treated with the following medications:

  • Oral nucleoside analogues (acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir) for treatment and suppression of HSV-1 and HSV-2 (see [Table: Table: Treatment of Genital Herpes Simplex Virus]

) - Topic antiviral agents (trifluridine and vidarabine) for herpetic keratitis - Intravenous acyclovir for severe mucocutaneous disease, disseminated infections in immunosuppressed persons, esophagitis, and suspected or proven HSV encephalitis

VZV (HHV-3) is transmitted by inhalation of respiratory droplets and colonization of the respiratory tract, with subsequent viremic dissemination to the skin, liver, spleen, and sensory ganglia. After primary varicella infection (chickenpox), the virus remains latent in the dorsal root or cranial ganglia. Reactivation causes herpes zoster (shingles), especially in adults older than 60 years or in immunosuppressed patients. Contact and airborne precautions should be used for all hospitalized patients with varicella, for patients with disseminated herpes zoster, and for those with dermatomal zoster who are immunosuppressed.

Primary varicella infection is an acute illness characterized by fever and an eruption of vesicles on an erythematous base (

). The rash is often pruritic and commonly begins on the face and trunk, then spreads to the extremities; mucocutaneous surfaces (oropharynx, conjunctiva, genitals) may also be affected. Lesions present in various stages of development on any one part of the body and include macules, papules, vesicles, and scabs. Skin lesions may become superinfected with Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus (impetigo). Most children recover without sequelae, but adults may develop pneumonia, encephalitis, hepatitis, and cerebellar infection causing ataxia.

Herpes zoster typically causes a painful vesicular rash that follows a dermatomal distribution that does not cross the midline (

). Prodromal symptoms such as burning, stinging, or tingling often occur in a dermatome, followed by eruption of grouped vesicles or pustules on an erythematous base. The most common dermatomes affected are in the thoracic region. Immunosuppressed patients can have multiple dermatomes affected or disseminated disease.

The risk, severity, and complications of herpes zoster, in particular postherpetic neuralgia (defined as neuropathic pain lasting more than 3 months after resolution of the rash), are increased in older patients, those with greater initial pain and more severe infection, and possibly patients who are immunosuppressed or taking immunosuppressive or immunomodulating medications.

Other complications include the following:

- Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (infection of the first division of the trigeminal nerve) rash may occur over the forehead and upper eyelid, or with nasal tip involvement; patients require ophthalmologic evaluation because blindness can result

(Ramsay Hunt syndrome) manifests with vesicular lesions in the ear canal, peripheral facial nerve paralysis, and auditory/vestibular symptoms - Pneumonia - Hepatitis - Central nervous system complications (see Viral Meningitis in Infectious Disease)

Varicella or herpes zoster can be diagnosed clinically by the typical vesicular rash and confirmed with VZV PCR testing of a swab from the base of a vesicular lesion if the diagnosis is unclear. For unusual cases or when the distinction between HSV and herpes zoster is required, ancillary studies are available ( [Table: Table: Differentiating Between Varicella Zoster and Herpes Simplex Virus]

). Young patients presenting with herpes zoster should be tested for HIV.

Patients are considered infectious until all lesions are dry and crusted.

Antiviral therapy (acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir) speeds recovery and decreases the severity and duration of neuropathic pain if begun within 72 hours of VZV rash onset. Intravenous acyclovir should be used for immunosuppressed or hospitalized patients and those with neurologic involvement. Evidence is insufficient to support the addition of glucocorticoids to reduce the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia.

Immunizing patients 50 years and older and those 19 years and older with immunocompromise with the recombinant subunit vaccine is the most important preventive strategy and is an effective means of decreasing herpes zoster and postherpetic neuralgia occurrence (see Varicella and Herpes Zoster in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

Postexposure prophylaxis should be provided to susceptible persons (VZV IgG negative); postexposure varicella vaccination is appropriate in immunocompetent persons, and varicella-zoster immune globulin should be used in immunocompromised adults and in pregnant persons.

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) (HHV-4) is highly prevalent; serologic studies show evidence of previous EBV infection in almost all adults. It is often transmitted by saliva and is the main cause of infectious mononucleosis in children and adolescents. Patients have the following symptoms:

  • Fever
  • Severe fatigue
  • Exudative pharyngitis
  • Cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy
  • Splenomegaly

Atypical lymphocytosis and aminotransferase level elevations are clues to the diagnosis. Detection of heterophile antibodies (monospot test) or EBV-specific antibodies suggest the diagnosis. Heterophile antibodies have limited sensitivity (especially in the first week of illness) and specificity, as they can be falsely positive in those with other infections or autoimmune disorders. EBV-specific antibodies target several different EBV antigens, and the pattern of positivity can suggest recent or previous infection. Anti-viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgM appears transiently during acute infection; anti-VCA IgG appears shortly thereafter during the acute phase and persists. In contrast, anti-EBV nuclear antigen (EBNA) appears later following infection and remains positive for life. New or recent infection is strongly suggested by the presence of anti-VCA IgM with or without anti-VCA IgG. The presence of anti-EBNA suggests more remote infection. EBV PCR has little use in immunocompetent patients.

Treatment is supportive; glucocorticoids may be given to patients with autoimmune hemolytic anemia, central nervous system involvement, or tonsillar enlargement with a compromised airway. EBV is associated with the development of EBV-positive diffuse large B cell lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and posttransplant lymphoproliferative disease in solid organ transplantation (see Viral Infections in Infectious Disease).

Cytomegalovirus (HHV-5) infections are most commonly asymptomatic but may present with a mononucleosis-like syndrome without pharyngitis and with negative heterophile antibody test results. Cytomegalovirus may be transmitted through various modes:

  • Saliva
  • Blood transfusion
  • Organ transplantation (cytomegalovirus-positive donor to cytomegalovirus-seronegative recipient)
  • Placenta (congenital cytomegalovirus)
  • Breastfeeding

Approximately 60% to 90% of adults have latent cytomegalovirus infection with disease reactivation more common in immunosuppressed persons (those with AIDS, transplant recipients [see Viral Posttransplantation Infections in Infectious Disease], those receiving immunosuppressive therapy). In immunocompromised persons, cytomegalovirus manifests as asymptomatic viremia, cytomegalovirus syndrome, or cytomegalovirus end-organ disease (see

). Immunocompetent patients occasionally also experience colitis.

Because cytomegalovirus can present in numerous ways, a high index of clinical suspicion is important. Diagnosis is commonly confirmed with molecular tests, such as PCR testing of serum, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, or cerebrospinal fluid, or by demonstrating typical cytopathic “owl’s-eye” intracellular inclusions on biopsy specimens (

). Pathologic diagnosis is confirmed by cytomegalovirus immunostains. Serologic assays have a role in the diagnosis of acute cytomegalovirus infection, in which the IgM antibody is positive but the IgG has not yet seroconverted. For other syndromes, serology has limited diagnostic utility because most adults are seropositive; however, serologic assays are performed routinely in pretransplant evaluations to assess the risk of cytomegalovirus reactivation after transplantation and to determine appropriate prophylaxis.

Antiviral therapy with intravenous ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir is used in immunocompromised patients or in immunocompetent patients with severe disease. Oral valganciclovir is also used as prophylaxis or pre-emptive therapy (treat if the PCR serum testing converts to positive) in transplant recipients. Foscarnet and cidofovir can be used in cases of ganciclovir resistance or intolerance. Letermovir is an FDA-approved drug to prevent cytomegalovirus infection in bone marrow transplant recipients and donor-positive/recipient-negative kidney transplant recipients. Maribavir is approved for use in transplant recipients with cytomegalovirus unresponsive to alternative therapies.

Mpox is a zoonotic infection endemic in west and central Africa that caused a global outbreak beginning in May 2022. It is caused by an orthopoxvirus that can spread from human to human by respiratory secretions, by skin-to-skin contact, and by fomites (e.g., contaminated objects). The incubation period ranges from 4 to 21 days. Most infections have been diagnosed in men who have sex with men, but transmission in women and children has also been documented.

The main clinical presentation is development of painful vesicular lesions that can sometimes become umbilicated. Lesions most commonly start on the anogenital regions but can spread throughout the body. Fever, painful lymphadenopathy, and respiratory symptoms can be present.

Mpox is diagnosed by performing PCR testing on a swab of skin lesions for orthopoxvirus DNA.

Treatment is primarily supportive. Antiviral treatment is considered for immunocompromised patients or those with severe disease. Available agents include tecovirimat, vaccinia immune globulin, cidofovir, and brincidofovir. Interim data analysis from a randomized trial in 2024 showed that, although it is safe, tecovirimat monotherapy did not demonstrate efficacy compared with placebo; its role in combination therapy remains understudied.

Prevention involves avoiding skin-to-skin contact with infected individuals. Two vaccines are available for persons at high risk. The main vaccine is a live, nonreplicating modified Ankara vaccine. An alternative is a replication-competent smallpox vaccine, but it should only be used if the first vaccine cannot be used because it carries an increased risk of adverse effects.

Measles has re-emerged in the United States after being eliminated in 2000. This resurgence is owing to low vaccination rates in the population and virus reintroduction from endemic countries. Measles is a highly contagious viral infection that presents with the following symptoms:

  • High fever
  • Rhinorrhea
  • Cough

  • Conjunctivitis

  • Diffuse macular rash

Complications include otitis media, pneumonia, encephalitis, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, and death. Adults, pregnant persons, and immunocompromised persons are at high risk of more severe illness and complications. Real-time PCR detection of viral RNA in respiratory and urine samples and measles-specific IgM in serum confirm the diagnosis. Suspected infection should be reported to the local health department within 24 hours. Treatment is primarily supportive, but antibiotics may be required for treatment of suspected bacterial superinfection such as pneumonia or otitis. The World Health Organization recommends two doses of vitamin A supplementation given 24 hours apart for all children and adults with measles, although the benefit in well-nourished adults is uncertain.

Mumps has also re-emerged because of low vaccination rates. Mumps typically cause parotitis associated with low-grade fever, headache, and malaise. Complications include orchitis, meningitis, pancreatitis, encephalitis, and hearing loss. Real-time PCR of a buccal swab confirms the diagnosis; mumps-specific IgM can also be used.

The measles-mumps-rubella vaccine (see Measles, Mumps, and Rubella in Foundations of Clinical Practice) is the best way to prevent infection, but this vaccine cannot be given to immunosuppressed persons because it contains a live-attenuated virus.

Stewardship and Emerging Resistance

Emergence of antibiotic resistance is potentiated by all antibiotic use. Careful antibiotic use is essential to preserving effective medication options. Approximately 201.9 million outpatient antibiotic prescriptions were dispensed in the United States in 2020, and at least 28% of these were considered unnecessary. Most prescriptions are for acute respiratory infections (usually caused by viruses) and asymptomatic bacteriuria not requiring antibiotic treatment. Approximately 50% of hospitalized patients receive antibiotics, and 50% of these prescriptions are considered unnecessary or inappropriate. The CDC and the World Health Organization developed comprehensive plans outlining urgent actions to combat antibiotic resistance; these include addressing carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) and other highly resistant gram-negative bacteria, developing improved diagnostics, and accelerating research for new antibiotics.

Antibiotic stewardship refers to coordinated interventions to improve antibiotic use and clinical outcomes by promoting optimal antibiotic regimens. Goals include minimizing adverse events (5% risk per antibiotic per patient), risk of Clostridioides difficile infection, and emergence of resistance. A key responsibility of stewardship programs is avoiding antibiotic administration when not indicated. Antibiotic selection, dosing, therapy duration, and route of administration are also considered. Antimicrobial stewardship teams, including an infectious diseases physician and a dedicated pharmacist, can prevent unnecessary combination therapy, avoid redundant double anaerobic coverage, streamline de-escalation, target antibiotics with a high risk of C. difficile infection (e.g., clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, and broad-spectrum antibiotics), monitor pharmacokinetics and adjust doses, convert intravenous to oral agents, and raise awareness of potential adverse effects (e.g., increased risk with fluoroquinolones for QT interval prolongation, aortic aneurysm and dissection, hypoglycemia, and tendinitis and tendon rupture).

Combination antibiotic therapy does not prevent the emergence of resistance. However, it may be considered in specific circumstances, such as empiric therapy regimens, to broaden the spectrum of activity or provide coverage for potential antimicrobial-resistant organisms pending culture and susceptibility results. Antibiotic combination therapy may also provide synergistic activity in limited situations, such as enterococcal endocarditis and CRE bacteremia.

Conversion from an intravenous to an oral antimicrobial agent should be considered for ease of administration and to limit intravenous catheter use. Factors supporting readiness for conversion include a temperature of 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) or less, an improving leukocyte count, clinical stability and improvement of signs and symptoms related to infection, a functioning gastrointestinal tract, no indication for intravenous therapy, and availability of a suitable oral alternative with good oral bioavailability (including fluoroquinolones, metronidazole, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and doxycycline).

An infectious diseases consultation should be considered for infections with antibiotic-resistant organisms because few effective antibiotics are available for these infections. Particularly problematic antibiotic-resistant organisms include the following:

  • Enterococcus faecium
  • Staphylococcus aureus
  • Klebsiella pneumoniae
  • Acinetobacter species
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  • Enterobacter species

This group includes extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)–producing gram-negative bacteria and carbapenemase-producing CRE (K. pneumoniae carbapenemases [KPC] and New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase) that destroy carbapenems. The presence of ESBLs can be inferred by the antibiotic sensitivity pattern (i.e., cefotaxime, ceftazidime, ceftriaxone, or cefepime resistance). Carbapenems are the preferred treatment option for serious infections caused by ESBLs. In addition to several newer antibiotics, tigecycline, ceftazidime-avibactam, and meropenem-vaborbactam remain treatment options for infections caused by KPC-producing gram-negative bacteria. Ceftolozane-tazobactam is an option for multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa infections.

Several older antibiotics retain activity against select antibiotic-resistant organisms. Minocycline has activity against multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter and has been used to treat ventilator-associated pneumonia with an 80% clinical response rate. Minocycline is also useful for treating infections caused by Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, a problematic pathogen with intrinsic antibiotic resistance to many agents. In vitro susceptibility to minocycline can be inferred from susceptibility to tetracycline; however, some tetracycline-resistant strains are sensitive to minocycline.

Fosfomycin is a bactericidal oral antibiotic with gram-negative and gram-positive activity (including methicillin-resistant S. aureus and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus [VRE]). It achieves high concentrations in the urine and may be used to treat uncomplicated cystitis caused by ESBL Escherichia coli. It is not recommended for use with upper urinary tract infections or for treatment of other multidrug-resistant gram-negative pathogens.

Colistin (polymyxin E) is a bactericidal agent, administered intravenously or by nebulized aerosol, used to treat multidrug- and pan-resistant aerobic, gram-negative infections, including P. aeruginosa. Proteus, Providencia, Burkholderia, Morganella, and Serratia species are resistant to colistin. Colistin resistance has been described in some multidrug-resistant gram-negative infections (mostly carbapenemase-producing K. pneumoniae). The most common adverse effect is nephrotoxicity (up to 50% of patients), which is usually reversible.

Outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy (OPAT) is defined as administration of at least two doses of intravenous antibiotics on different days without intervening hospitalization. OPAT allows patients to complete parenteral antibiotic therapy at home or in other outpatient settings when an oral antibiotic is inappropriate or unavailable. Bone and joint infections are those most commonly treated with OPAT; other potentially OPAT-treatable infections include endocarditis, cardiac device infections, abdominal infections, skin and soft tissue infections, central nervous system infections, and antibiotic-resistant infections for which parenteral antibiotics are the only option (such as urinary tract infection).

Patients should be clinically stable and their infection improving before starting OPAT. When considering OPAT, an assessment can help determine if the patient is an appropriate candidate ( [Table: Table: Considerations for OPAT Candidates]

).

Increasingly, OPAT is being started without initial hospitalization after careful medical assessment by a well-established and organized OPAT program. OPAT requires close laboratory monitoring that may include the following:

  • Antibiotic levels (vancomycin, aminoglycosides)
  • Complete blood count
  • Creatinine level
  • Liver chemistry tests
  • Coagulation tests
  • C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate

Patients receiving daptomycin therapy should undergo baseline measurement of kidney function and creatine kinase level, followed by weekly monitoring. Antibiotic doses and timing should be adjusted based on monitoring results. Treatment failure may result from relapse or progression of primary infection (60% and 21%, respectively) or therapeutic complications (19%). Successful OPAT requires patient participation; supervised infectious diseases OPAT programs have been shown to be safe, efficient, and clinically effective.

Allergy and Immunology

Anaphylaxis is an acute, severe systemic reaction that can be life-threatening if not recognized and treated appropriately. This section focuses on evaluating the cause of anaphylaxis and future risk reduction. Diagnosis and emergency treatment of anaphylaxis are discussed in Anaphylaxis in Critical Care Medicine.

Evaluation begins with a detailed history of each event and the preceding 24 hours. It should include assessment for exposures and factors that can cause or contribute to anaphylaxis through IgE-mediated mechanisms or direct mast cell activation, including the following:

  • Dietary intake
  • Medications
  • Recent illnesses
  • Recent substance use, such as alcohol
  • Heat or cold exposure
  • Menstrual cycle
  • Exercise

Tryptase levels indicate mast cell activation and can help establish the diagnosis of anaphylaxis. If levels are elevated during the episode and normal at baseline, anaphylaxis is confirmed, although normal tryptase levels do not rule out anaphylaxis. Guidelines additionally recommend measuring baseline serum tryptase level in patients with recurrent, idiopathic, or severe anaphylaxis; Hymenoptera venom–associated anaphylaxis; or suspected mastocytosis. A tryptase level greater than 8 ng/mL that was not measured during or immediately after an episode of anaphylaxis should prompt evaluation for hereditary or clonal mast cell diseases (see Mastocytosis in Hematology).

All patients with anaphylaxis require referral to an allergist. Identification of the cause (most commonly food, medication, latex, and stinging insect venom) is critical to preventing future episodes and can be done in most cases. When the history suggests a particular trigger, skin prick tests and allergen-specific serum IgE level measurements can help confirm the suspected allergen.

Venom immunotherapy should be given to prevent anaphylaxis from stinging insect venom. Patients who experience anaphylaxis to a necessary medication can undergo desensitization protocols to help them tolerate the drug; however, the allergy may return if the treatment is interrupted or discontinued.

Modification or discontinuation of the use of medications and substances that can interfere with anaphylaxis treatment (β-blockers, ACE inhibitors) or contribute to anaphylaxis severity through direct mast cell activation (opioids, NSAIDs, alcohol) should be considered. Optimizing treatment for asthma, COPD, and cardiovascular disease is also important to reduce the severity of future anaphylactic episodes.

All patients with a history of anaphylaxis should be prescribed epinephrine and educated on its use.

Urticaria (hives) represent localized edema caused by mast cell degranulation. Urticaria are characterized by well-demarcated plaques that appear rapidly and resolve within hours. Individual lesions may be skin-colored, white, violaceous, or pink, sometimes surrounded by a pink flare (see

). Urticaria are extremely pruritic and often appear on areas that undergo repetitive pressure or rubbing, such as the waistline. Although individual urticaria resolve in less than 24 hours, recurrent crops of hives may last for weeks. If individual urticarial lesions persist longer than 24 hours or are accompanied by systemic symptoms, such as joint pain and fever, urticarial vasculitis should be suspected. When the episodes last longer than 6 weeks, the condition is classified as chronic.

Food allergy, viral infection, and medication reaction are the most commonly identified causes of acute urticaria. Infrequent but important causes of urticaria include autoimmune thyroid disease and malignancies, particularly lymphoma. Physical urticaria are induced by stimuli such as sunlight, sweating, pressure, vibration, water, or cold temperatures.

Urticaria is a clinical diagnosis that can be confirmed through physical maneuvers, such as circling lesions with a marker to see whether they resolve within 24 hours and gently scratching uninvolved skin with the end of a tongue depressor to see if urticaria (rather than erythema alone) can be induced, a condition known as dermographism (see

).

The cause of urticaria is investigated primarily by history and physical examination. In most cases, urticaria resolve spontaneously and the cause is never determined. Diagnostic evaluation is not recommended unless the history suggests a specific cause. If symptoms persist, laboratory tests, including a complete blood count, urinalysis, inflammatory markers, thyroid-stimulating hormone level, and liver chemistry tests, can be considered. If urticarial vasculitis is suspected, skin biopsy is indicated.

Nonsedating, long-acting antihistamines (e.g., fexofenadine) are the treatment of choice for urticaria; topical antihistamines are not effective and may lead to allergic contact dermatitis. Dupilumab (a monoclonal interleukin-4 receptor antagonist antibody that blocks the action of interleukin-4 and interleukin-13) or omalizumab (an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody) are options for chronic urticaria not responsive to antihistamines.

Angioedema is characterized by localized swelling caused by fluid extravasation into the interstitial spaces. Such swelling often involves the lips, tongue, mouth, or face but may also affect the gastrointestinal tract, where it can produce recurrent abdominal pain. Angioedema occurs through two main pathways: mast cell–mediated (presenting in isolation, with urticaria, or as part of the systemic reaction in anaphylaxis) and bradykinin-mediated (presenting in isolation without evidence of mast cell activation or urticaria). Because the approach to angioedema with urticaria is identical to that of urticaria alone, and the approach to anaphylaxis with or without angioedema is the same as that of anaphylaxis alone, this section will focus on isolated angioedema.

Isolated angioedema may occur through mast cell–mediated or bradykinin-mediated pathways. Mast-cell mediated causes include allergies, whereas bradykinin-mediated causes include medications (i.e., ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs) and, less commonly, C1 inhibitor deficiency due to hereditary angioedema or acquired inhibitors. Acquired inhibitors are rare and typically associated with malignancy and autoimmune conditions.

A careful history focused on diet, current medications, new exposures, and family history of similar episodes is important in the evaluation.

Diagnostic testing includes a basic chemistry panel, liver enzyme testing, a complete blood count, inflammatory markers, and C4 level. In most angioedema cases, referral to an allergist is indicated.

ACE inhibitor–induced angioedema should be suspected in patients with angioedema taking an ACE inhibitor, regardless of when the medication was started. In addition, ACE-inhibitor–induced angioedema can recur after discontinuing the medication, usually within the first month.

When there is high suspicion of hereditary angioedema or an acquired inhibitor, further testing with quantitative and functional levels of C1 esterase inhibitor and C4 complement levels is available.

When an allergy is suspected, measurement of allergen-specific serum IgE levels or skin prick testing may be considered.

Treatment of angioedema is discussed in further detail in Anaphylaxis in Critical Care Medicine.

Food allergy is an adverse reaction caused by an abnormal immune response that reproducibly occurs after exposure to a specific food. Food allergy may be IgE mediated, non–IgE mediated, or mixed and may result in several clinical syndromes, including urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis, eosinophilic esophagitis, and oral allergy syndrome.

Common food allergens include peanuts, tree nuts, fish, shellfish, milk, eggs, soy, and wheat. Delayed anaphylaxis to mammalian meat due to galactose-α-1,3-galactose (α-gal) allergy is an increasingly recognized cause. Sensitization to this oligosaccharide may occur after a tick bite, most commonly from Amblyomma americanum (the Lone Star tick), which has salivary α-gal. Allergic reactions related to α-gal syndrome may include gastrointestinal disturbance, urticaria, and recurrent anaphylaxis, often occurring 2 to 6 hours after exposure. Because of the timing of evening meals, anaphylaxis from α-gal syndrome is more likely to occur in the middle of the night, which is uncommon in anaphylaxis caused by other triggers.

Diagnosis may be difficult; food allergy is often confused with food intolerance. Food allergy should be suspected in patients who present with anaphylaxis or other allergic symptoms that develop within minutes to hours of food ingestion. A detailed history to identify causative foods is critical in focusing the evaluation. Skin prick testing and targeted allergen-specific serum IgE levels can help identify causative foods; however, neither is diagnostic, and the results must be interpreted along with the clinical history. Ordering extensive IgE or IgG immunoassays during evaluation of a food allergy is not recommended and may result in inappropriate diagnoses. Food elimination diets and/or oral food challenges under the supervision of an allergist may be needed for more definitive diagnosis in some cases.

The primary treatment for food allergies is preventing events by avoiding food allergens. Omalizumab, an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody, may be used to reduce the likelihood of an allergic reaction to foods. Antihistamines are recommended in managing symptoms. Cases of anaphylaxis should be treated emergently with epinephrine.

Hymenoptera is an order of insects that includes wasps, bees, hornets, and yellow jackets. Venom injected during a Hymenoptera sting usually causes a limited local reaction with up to 5 cm of erythema and pain surrounding the site of the sting. Cold compresses are often sufficient treatment, although NSAIDs may help manage pain. Large local reactions may extend up to 10 cm in diameter, and a brief course of oral prednisone may be required to address painful swelling. Routine antibiotic therapy is not indicated, but if a large local reaction does not begin to subside as expected on about day 3, addition of antibiotics for secondary infection may be considered. Systemic allergic reaction may result in anaphylaxis or widespread urticaria without anaphylaxis. Intramuscular injection of epinephrine (into the anterolateral thigh if possible) is first-line treatment for anaphylaxis and may be considered for the treatment of urticaria in adults. All patients who experience a systemic allergic reaction, including those who have urticaria without anaphylaxis, should be supplied with epinephrine for autoinjection and considered for venom immunotherapy.

Serum sickness is a type III (immune complex–mediated) hypersensitivity reaction occurring within 1 to 2 weeks of administration of an inciting agent. Common manifestations include fever, rash (including urticaria), headache, and polyarthritis or polyarthralgia. Common inciting agents associated with serum sickness are immune-modulating medications, such as rituximab and infliximab; vaccines; and venoms and antivenoms. Serum sickness–like reaction presents similarly but is not associated with the formation of immune complexes or kidney involvement; inciting agents include antibiotics (most commonly, penicillins and cefaclor), viral infections, and vaccines.

History should focus on identifying the inciting agent, and a thorough examination can help identify signs of systemic illness and exclude other diagnoses. The pruritic rash of serum sickness is highly variable and may first manifest around the injection site but can also be generalized.

Diagnosis is generally made clinically. Laboratory studies may be helpful when serum sickness is suspected as well as in excluding other diagnoses; tests should include a complete blood count, inflammatory markers, a comprehensive metabolic panel, and urinalysis. Apart from elevated inflammatory markers, laboratory findings vary and may show leukopenia or leukocytosis, elevated serum creatinine level, and proteinuria. Notably, patients who present with serum sickness–like reactions will not exhibit kidney dysfunction. Additional testing to exclude infection and inflammatory conditions is often necessary.

The mainstay of treatment is avoiding the offending agent. Symptoms are self-limited and often resolve within a few weeks. Supportive treatment is indicated for symptom management and may include antihistamines, analgesics, and, in some cases, glucocorticoids.

Primary immunodeficiency disorders often present during childhood, but milder heritable forms may not manifest until adulthood. Primary immunodeficiency should be considered when patients have frequent infections or infections with unusual organisms. The specific microbiology is often a clue to which arm of the immune system is affected (see [Table: Table: Properties of Selected Primary Immunodeficiency Disorders]

). Diagnosis allows directed therapy, targeted immunization, and optimized empiric treatment of secondary infections.

Selective IgA deficiency (SIgAD) is the most common primary antibody deficiency, although most patients remain asymptomatic. IgA provides mucosal immunity; therefore, patients with SIgAD are susceptible to respiratory tract infections and, less frequently, gastrointestinal tract infections. Sinopulmonary infections are the most common presenting manifestation, particularly with encapsulated bacteria ( [Table: Table: Properties of Selected Primary Immunodeficiency Disorders]

). In rare cases, anti-IgA IgE antibodies can lead to anaphylaxis to transfused blood products; however, transfusions can be given with close monitoring.

Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) is a heterogeneous syndrome associated with decreased quantitative immunoglobulin levels and impaired humoral response to antigens. Diagnosis is usually delayed until adolescence or adulthood, although a history of recurrent infection throughout childhood is frequently noted. Indications to screen for primary immunodeficiencies such as CVID include the following:

  • More than three respiratory tract infections (otitis, bronchitis, sinusitis, pneumonia) requiring antibiotics in a year
  • More than one episode of pneumonia in a 3-year period
  • More than one severe bacterial infection, such as osteomyelitis and meningitis
  • Recurrent abscesses
  • Unusual pathogens or location of infection

CVID increases the risk for upper and lower respiratory tract infections caused by encapsulated bacteria, Mycoplasma species, and respiratory viruses. Patients with gastrointestinal infections typically present with acute diarrhea caused by common enteropathogenic viruses or bacteria. Chronic diarrhea with malabsorption suggests giardiasis or chronic infection with norovirus, an increasingly recognized pathogen in this population. Additionally, patients with CVID are at increased risk for autoimmune disease, inflammatory bowel disease, granulomatous disease, bronchiectasis, and malignancy.

Diagnosis is made by measuring immunoglobulin levels. The humoral response can be tested by measuring specific antibody production before and after immunization.

Pooled immune globulin replacement therapy is administered through intravenous infusions or subcutaneous injections and is associated with lower rates of infections and hospitalizations. Immunization is only partially effective because of impaired vaccination response, and live vaccines should be avoided. Prophylactic antibiotics are not typically indicated because they can predispose patients to infections with resistant organisms.

Infections and other antigenic stimuli trigger an inflammatory reaction through the classical, alternative, or lectin pathways of the complement cascade system. The result is formation of the membrane attack complex, which adheres to microbial pathogens to facilitate immune detection and destruction.

Deficiencies in the complement system can be divided into deficiencies in early or activating components (C2, C3, C4) and late or terminal components (C5-C9). Early component complement deficiency, especially of C4, is associated with increased rates of systemic lupus erythematosus and increased risk for infection with encapsulated organisms. Patients with early component complement deficiency present with recurrent sinopulmonary infections, similar to patients with CVID.

Patients with terminal complement protein defects typically present with recurrent infections of Neisseria species, particularly meningococcal meningitis. A personal or family history of recurrent Neisseria infections is an indication to test the total hemolytic complement (CH~50) level because any defect in the classical complement pathway will result in a low total level.

Chronic granulomatous disease is an inherited primary immunodeficiency involving impaired killing of microbes following phagocytosis by leukocytes. This disease is characterized by repeated episodes of cellulitis or skin abscesses, pneumonia, and suppurative lymphadenitis dating to childhood. The most common organisms are Aspergillus, Staphylococcus aureus, Burkholderia cepacia, and Nocardia. Pathology often shows granulomata at sites of infection.

Although diagnosis of primary immunodeficiencies is relatively rare in adults, secondary immunodeficiencies are common. [Table: Table: Medications Causing Secondary Immunodeficiency Disorders^a]
