bodies.insec24002:
Ear, Nose, Mouth, and Throat Disorders

Hearing loss is common, and the prevalence increases with age, affecting 30% to 50% of adults aged 65 years and older. An estimated 13% of adults aged 18 years and older have difficulty hearing even when using a hearing aid. Hearing loss is underrecognized by patients and physicians, can negatively affect relationships, and can lead to social isolation and reduced quality of life. It is associated with higher rates of unemployment, depression, dementia, hospitalization, falls, functional decline, and death.

Simple and effective tests, such as evaluating whether a patient can hear a whispered voice, finger rub, or a single-question screening (for example, “Do you have difficulty with your hearing?”), can be performed in the office (see [Table: Table: Screening Maneuvers to Assess Hearing]

). The American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery recommends that clinicians screen patients aged 50 years and older for hearing loss. The World Health Organization recommends screening for hearing loss every 5 years for patients aged 50 to 64 years and every 1 to 3 years for those older than age 64 years.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, however, found insufficient evidence to support assessing the benefits and harms of screening for hearing loss in asymptomatic adults aged 50 years or older.

In patients with identified hearing loss, physical examination includes otoscopic examination and Weber and Rinne tests to differentiate conductive from sensorineural hearing loss (see [Table: Table: Distinguishing Between Conductive and Sensorineural Hearing Loss]

). Referral for audiometry is indicated when hearing loss is identified. Imaging (typically MRI) is rarely required unless the hearing loss is acute and unilateral or associated with other neurologic changes.

Hearing loss is categorized by whether it affects the outer or middle ear (conductive hearing loss) or inner ear (sensorineural hearing loss), or both (see

) (see [Table: Table: Causes of Hearing Loss]

). Conductive hearing loss is caused by obstruction or pathology that prevents sound transmission and may be associated with pain or ear drainage (see

).

Sensorineural hearing loss is caused by disorders of the cochlea, auditory nerve, or central nervous system and is often accompanied by tinnitus or vertigo. Presbycusis is the most common cause of sensorineural hearing loss. Risk factors associated with sensorineural hearing loss include aging, loud noise exposure, tobacco and alcohol use, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and peripheral neuropathy. Genetics is implicated in 25% to 50% of cases of adult-onset hearing loss. Medications such as antibiotics and chemotherapeutic agents may also cause sensorineural hearing loss ( [Table: Table: Causes of Hearing Loss]

). Although sensorineural hearing loss can also be associated with loop diuretics, high-dose aspirin, and NSAIDs, it is often temporary in the absence of other ototoxic medications.

Treatment options for hearing loss include hearing-assistive devices, hearing aids, and cochlear implants. Use of hearing aids is low because of patient barriers that include cost, stigma, cosmetic appearance, perceived ineffectiveness, and physical discomfort in wearing them.

Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) occurring with an onset of less than 72 hours is considered a medical emergency. Although most cases are idiopathic, specific causes include viral infections, neoplasms, autoimmune disease, and vascular disorders. Ramsay Hunt syndrome is caused by reactivation of the herpes zoster virus in cranial nerve VII. Patients may present with acute hearing loss, ipsilateral facial paralysis, and vesicles in the auditory canal or on the tympanic membrane (see

).

In addition to hearing loss, patients with SSNHL may also present with ear fullness, tinnitus, and/or vertigo. Meniere disease (see Peripheral Vertigo in Common Symptoms) can present with symptoms similar to those of SSNHL; however, in Meniere disease, vertigo is typically the most prominent symptom, and hearing loss tends to be recurrent and episodic; in SSNHL, hearing loss is more abrupt. History and physical examination are essential for diagnosis and include inspection of the ear canal and tympanic membrane (TM) to exclude causes of conductive hearing loss, such as cerumen, effusion, foreign body, otitis, and TM perforation. Cranial nerve testing and Weber and Rinne testing should be completed to confirm sensorineural hearing loss. No routine laboratory testing is recommended.

SSNHL requires urgent referral for audiometry (within 14 days of symptom onset, although some experts suggest 72 hours) and MRI with internal auditory canal protocol with contrast to evaluate for acoustic neuroma. MRI may also reveal other causes, such as cochlear inflammation, demyelination, or small-vessel ischemia. If MRI is contraindicated, high-resolution CT of the temporal bones is an alternative. For patients with idiopathic SSNHL, oral glucocorticoids may be considered within 2 weeks of onset, although strong evidence of efficacy is lacking.

Acoustic neuroma (also known as vestibular schwannoma) is an uncommon cause of hearing loss. It often presents as slowly progressive, unilateral, high-frequency, sensorineural hearing loss. It may be accompanied by unilateral tinnitus and disequilibrium due to involvement of the cochlear nerve and vestibular nerve, respectively. Larger tumors may cause trigeminal and facial nerve dysfunction or headache, nausea, and vomiting from increased intracranial pressure. Most are sporadic and unilateral but when bilateral can be associated with NF2-related schwannomatosis.

Audiometry is needed to confirm sensorineural hearing loss, and MRI is the diagnostic test of choice. Treatment options include surgical resection, radiation therapy, or a combination of both. Observation is an option for small tumors causing minimal symptoms, older patients, or patients who are poor candidates for surgery or radiation therapy. Hearing loss is likely to progress without treatment, necessitating close follow-up with serial MRIs and hearing assessments.

Tinnitus is the conscious perception of sound (most commonly buzzing or ringing) without an external source. It may be unilateral or bilateral and may be intermittent or constant. In patients presenting with tinnitus, the following history should be obtained:

  • Onset
  • Duration
  • Quality (pulsatile nature, pulse synchronous, or asynchronous)
  • Laterality
  • Associated symptoms (hearing loss, vertigo, imbalance, focal neurologic symptoms, depression, or anxiety)
  • Noise and medication exposures
  • Effect on quality of life

Temporary tinnitus (days to weeks) is often caused by exposure to loud noise or medications such as aminoglycosides, cisplatin, aspirin, NSAIDs, and loop diuretics. Chronic tinnitus (more than 6 months) may be due to hearing loss, cerumen impaction, vascular abnormalities, and metabolic disorders (e.g., diabetes mellitus and thyroid disease).

Physical examination should include otoscopy, auscultation over the periauricular region and neck for vascular lesions, and neurologic examination. Performing audiometry is reasonable. Patients with unilateral or pulsatile tinnitus, asymmetric or sudden hearing loss, or focal neurologic symptoms should undergo prompt evaluation with advanced imaging (CT or MRI) and may require referral to an otolaryngologist.

Treatment involves addressing underlying and associated conditions, including insomnia and depression, which can worsen tinnitus. Medications and herbal supplements have not been shown to be beneficial. Hearing aids may help manage tinnitus associated with hearing loss by producing a masking effect. Similarly, sound therapy, which uses external sound generators to mask the tinnitus, may be helpful for persistent, bothersome tinnitus. Cognitive behavioral therapy is an effective therapy for tinnitus but may be limited by availability and lack of reimbursement.

Otalgia is a common reason for medical visits and is divided into primary otalgia (pain originating from the ear) or secondary otalgia (pain from an extra-auricular source). Acute otitis media and externa, eustachian tube dysfunction, and cerumen impaction account for most cases of primary otalgia. Causes of secondary otalgia are broad because of the ear’s complex innervation pattern and proximity to multiple structures. Pain originating from the sinuses, teeth, jaw, temporomandibular joint, salivary glands, nerves, and neck may all cause secondary otalgia. Temporal arteritis and malignancy are uncommon but important causes of ear pain.

Patients with acute otitis media (AOM) usually present with unilateral ear pain and diminished hearing along with bulging or intense erythema of the tympanic membrane (see

). Otitis media with effusion (OME) is often mistaken for AOM in adults; it is characterized by the presence of fluid in the middle ear without acute inflammation or signs of systemic illness (see

). Recurrent OME is often due to dysfunction of the eustachian tube resulting from allergies and upper respiratory tract infections; it usually resolves spontaneously.

Although there are numerous guidelines for the treatment of AOM in children, the condition is rare in adults and management is less clear. Some guidelines recommend initial observation for uncomplicated AOM in adults, whereas others suggest prescribing antibiotics. If antibiotics are prescribed, amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanic acid covers the most common organisms. Fever, posterior ear pain, and facial nerve paralysis are rare but suggest complications, such as mastoiditis, and may require urgent imaging and surgical consultation. Patients with recurrent AOM or persistent hearing loss should be referred to an otolaryngologist.

Acute otitis externa (AOE) (see

) is diffuse inflammation of the external ear canal and may involve the pinna and tragus, with rapid onset within the preceding 3 weeks. The usual cause is bacterial infection, most commonly with Pseudomonas or Staphylococcus aureus. Symptoms include otalgia, pruritus, ear fullness, and ear discharge. Patients should be assessed for history of the following, which may influence treatment choices:

  • Recent swimming
  • Immunocompromising conditions (e.g., diabetes mellitus, HIV infection, chemotherapy)
  • Radiation therapy
  • Tympanostomy tubes or perforation of the tympanic membrane

On physical examination, tenderness upon pushing on the tragus or pulling on the pinna is present. AOE should be differentiated from ear cellulitis (which usually involves the lobule), perichondritis (characterized by sparing of the lobule), and Ramsay Hunt syndrome (distinguished by pain or vesicles in a dermatomal distribution).

For uncomplicated cases, topical treatments, including antibiotics, glucocorticoids, antiseptics (acetic acid), and combination therapies, are first-line management; systemic antibiotics alone are often ineffective and should be avoided. Quinolone drops are preferred in the case of a nonintact tympanic membrane. Patients should be instructed on proper technique for ear drop instillation, including cleaning excess debris before instilling the drops and then lying down with the affected ear facing upward for 3 to 5 minutes.

Malignant otitis externa (MOE) is a deeper infection of the external canal that includes bone involvement of the skull base. It occurs mainly in patients who have diabetes, are immunocompromised, or are older. Patients present with severe unresolving otalgia radiating toward the face with ear discharge, headache, and temporomandibular joint pain. Otoscopy reveals edema and granulation tissue in the external auditory canal. Imaging with CT of the temporal bones and skull base is indicated to confirm bony involvement. Initial treatment requires topical therapy, systemic antipseudomonal antibiotics, and urgent referral to an otolaryngologist. Because MOE may recur, patients require periodic follow-up for a minimum of 1 year.

Cerumen helps to protect, clean, and lubricate the external auditory canal. Its normal expulsion, assisted by jaw movement, may become inadequate, and the resultant cerumen accumulation may cause ear pain, fullness, and itching; tinnitus; or hearing loss. People who wear hearing aids are at higher risk for cerumen impaction and should receive regular ear canal checks and education on hearing aid care.

When symptomatic, cerumen can be removed by topical cerumenolytics, irrigation, or manual removal. Irrigation is performed using a large syringe with a large-gauge intravenous catheter attached (needle removed). Application of a few drops of a cerumenolytic or warm water 15 to 30 minutes before irrigation is recommended to soften cerumen. The syringe should be filled with water close to body temperature (to avoid dizziness from caloric effects), and the catheter should be directed superiorly and posteriorly but not directly at the tympanic membrane with a basin held below the ear to catch the water.

Topical agents and irrigation should be avoided if the tympanic membrane is perforated; mechanical removal is preferred in these instances. Patients should be counseled not to insert any foreign object into the ear canal because it can worsen cerumen impaction by pushing wax deeper into the canal. Doing so can also cause lacerations and perforate the tympanic membrane.

Epistaxis is a common problem affecting up to 60% of the U.S. population, with 6% of those affected requiring medical attention. Ninety percent of epistaxis cases originate in the anterior nasal septum in the Kiesselbach plexus (see

). Posterior bleeding, although less common, is more likely to result in significant hemorrhage. Patients with epistaxis should be assessed for the following history:

  • Timing and frequency of epistaxis
  • Local trauma
  • Nose picking
  • Intranasal medications and anticoagulant/antiplatelet use
  • Arid environments
  • Infection
  • Intranasal drug use (cocaine)
  • Past nasal or sinus surgery or trauma
  • Family and personal history of bleeding disorders

Anterior bleeding can be managed with compression of the alae (lower one third of the nose) for at least 15 minutes while leaning forward. A topical vasoconstrictor such as oxymetazoline can be applied along with compression. If bleeding continues, anterior rhinoscopy should be performed, and if the bleeding site is identified, a topical vasoconstrictor, topical tranexamic acid, or nasal cautery may be useful. If bleeding does not resolve, nasal packing with an inflatable tamponade device or foam polymer tampon may be necessary.

Refractory or recurrent bleeding may rarely require embolization or surgical ligation in consultation with an otolaryngologist. Patients with recurrent unilateral epistaxis should undergo nasal endoscopy to evaluate for nasal masses. Those with a recurrent personal or family history of bilateral nosebleeds should be examined for oral mucosal or nasal telangiectasias, with consideration of referral to an otolaryngologist to rule out hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia.

Posterior bleeding may cause substantial blood loss. Patients with persistent or recurrent bleeding not controlled by nasal cauterization and packing should be evaluated by an otolaryngologist for consideration of arterial ligation or endovascular embolization.

Most upper respiratory tract infections are caused by viruses that infiltrate epithelial cells, leading to activation of inflammatory mechanisms with resultant fever, cough, and congestion. Rhinoviruses are the cause of most cases of the common cold. Virus transmission is through inhalation or direct contact with secretions infected with viral particles; hand hygiene is an effective means of prevention. Symptoms of uncomplicated infection may persist for up to 2 weeks. Antibiotic therapy is ineffective, does not shorten the duration of symptoms, and may lead to increasing antimicrobial resistance and alteration of gut microbiota.

Treatment goals for upper respiratory tract infection are focused on reducing the severity of discomfort caused by coughing, sneezing, and malaise. Analgesics may help with myalgia and headache, whereas nasal symptoms may improve with nasal decongestants, nasal saline irrigations, intranasal ipratropium (improves rhinorrhea and cough), intranasal glucocorticoids (for nasal congestion), or antihistamines. Dextromethorphan and honey may improve cough. There is little evidence to support the use of expectorants or mucolytics. Zinc-containing intranasal products should not be used because of the risk for anosmia.

Pertussis (whooping cough) is suggested by the presence of cough persisting for more than 2 weeks associated with posttussive vomiting, severe cough paroxysms, or an inspiratory whooping sound. A nasopharyngeal swab for Bordetella pertussis culture or polymerase chain reaction testing confirms the diagnosis. Patients with probable or confirmed pertussis are treated with a macrolide antibiotic. Postinfectious cough should be considered in cough (usually dry) persisting for at least 3 weeks following an acute respiratory infection. For more information on the evaluation and management of cough, see Subacute and Chronic Cough in Common Symptoms.

Patients with acute rhinosinusitis present with three cardinal symptoms of less than 4 weeks’ duration: purulent nasal discharge, nasal obstruction (congestion, blockage, or stuffiness), and facial pain/pressure. Most cases are caused by viruses, allergies, or irritants. Acute rhinosinusitis is usually self-limited; therapies that may relieve symptoms include analgesics (e.g., NSAIDs or acetaminophen), saline nasal irrigation, and intranasal glucocorticoids—all targeted to the patient’s specific symptoms. Avoiding unnecessary antibiotics aligns with high-value care.

Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS) presents similarly to acute viral rhinosinusitis; ABRS is diagnosed when either the cardinal symptoms of acute rhinosinusitis are present for at least 10 days or double worsening occurs. Double worsening is defined as worsening of symptoms following a period of initial improvement within 10 days. After the diagnosis of ABRS is made, a 3- to 5-day period of watchful waiting is recommended before starting antibiotics. Indications for antibiotic treatment and regimens are described in [Table: Table: Acute Sinusitis Treatments]

. Patients who are seriously ill, deteriorate despite appropriate antibiotic therapy, or have recurrent episodes should be evaluated radiographically (typically with CT) and may be referred to an otolaryngologist.

Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) manifests with at least 12 weeks of nasal congestion with purulent drainage, diminished sense of smell, or facial pain or pressure. It may be associated with nasal polyposis and asthma. Demonstrating mucosal involvement by nasal endoscopy or imaging is necessary for diagnosis. Nasal polyps should be identified because their presence affects treatment for severe and refractory CRS. Treatment for both CRS with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) and CRS sans (without) nasal polyps (CRSsNP) includes intranasal glucocorticoids and intranasal saline. In severe or refractory CRSwNP, limited courses of oral glucocorticoids may be helpful and are often used preoperatively to reduce polyp burden in patients requiring surgical polyp removal. Biologics such as dupilumab, an inhibitor of interleukin-4 and interleukin-13, may also be used in patients with refractory CRSwNP.

Allergic rhinitis involves sneezing, congestion, and rhinorrhea often linked to a seasonal allergen or other exposure, and patients may present with watery or red eyes. Nonallergic rhinitis occurs in response to nonallergic stimuli, such as hot and spicy foods, drugs, and irritants. First-line treatment of allergic and nonallergic rhinitis consists of avoiding precipitating factors and monotherapy with intranasal glucocorticoids. Combination therapy with an intranasal glucocorticoid and an intranasal antihistamine may be used for more significant symptoms. Adding a nonsedating oral antihistamine is another option.

Intranasal ipratropium is useful in patients with rhinorrhea as their main or sole symptom and may be most effective in vasomotor rhinitis (gustatory, irritant odors, or cold-induced rhinitis). Leukotriene receptor antagonists are less effective and may cause adverse effects. Oral decongestants may be helpful for short-term use.

Rhinitis medicamentosa is chronic rhinitis resulting from prolonged or excessive use of topical nasal decongestants. Treatment involves discontinuing the decongestant and, if needed, adding intranasal glucocorticoids.

Patients with acute pharyngitis present with a sore throat that may worsen with swallowing; symptoms typically last less than 1 week. Most cases are viral in cause; only 5% to 15% of pharyngitis cases are caused by bacteria, most often group A Streptococcus (GAS). Features suggesting viral cause include concomitant cough, conjunctivitis, coryza, hoarseness, and oral ulcers. Patients with viral pharyngitis should be treated conservatively with symptom control (analgesics [NSAIDs or acetaminophen], lozenges or topical sprays, and increased environmental humidity).

In bacterial pharyngitis, antibiotic treatment reduces symptom duration and the likelihood of transmission as well as the risk for rheumatic fever and suppurative complications (such as peritonsillar or retropharyngeal abscess). The modified Centor criteria can help guide the need for testing and treatment of bacterial pharyngitis (see [Table: Table: Modified Centor Criteria]

). Patients with a modified Centor score of 2 or less do not need to be tested for streptococcal disease; those with a score of 3 or greater should be tested with a rapid streptococcal antigen detection test. Antibiotic treatment is reserved for patients with positive test results; penicillin and amoxicillin are first-line therapies. Throat culture should be considered in patients at high risk for complications (immunocompromised state) in the setting of high clinical suspicion but negative results on rapid antigen detection testing. The modified Centor score does not assess risk for less common but important viral causes of pharyngitis, such as COVID-19 and Epstein-Barr virus (infectious mononucleosis), both of which often have prominent systemic symptoms, including fatigue and malaise.

In cases of severe sore throat, the presence of associated drooling, muffled voice, and an enlarged tonsil with uvula deviation suggest a peritonsillar abscess. Similarly, patients with bulging of the oropharynx, stiff neck, cervical crepitus, or signs of respiratory distress may have a retropharyngeal abscess. After ensuring the airway is secure, immediate CT of the neck should be performed if an abscess is suspected.

Patients with small abscesses (<2 cm) and mild symptoms may be considered for medical management without surgical drainage, but most patients require drainage by needle aspiration or incision and drainage. All patients with peritonsillar abscess should receive antibiotics with activity against Streptococcus species and oral anaerobes, even if symptoms improve after drainage. Common antibiotic choices include intravenous (IV) ampicillin/sulbactam, oral amoxicillin/clavulanate, or either IV or oral clindamycin in patients with penicillin allergy; initial IV antibiotics may be transitioned to oral therapy once the patient can tolerate oral medication. A single dose of a glucocorticoid may be provided to reduce swelling and pain.

Fusobacterium necrophorum infection can cause Lemierre syndrome, a rare suppurative complication of pharyngitis caused by local spread of infection with resultant septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein. Lemierre syndrome occurs mostly in healthy young adults. Clinicians should suspect Lemierre syndrome in patients with severe pharyngitis and neck pain and in those who do not respond to appropriate antibiotics. Diagnosis is made with CT of the neck with contrast.

Nonsuppurative complications of GAS pharyngitis include scarlet fever and toxic shock syndrome, which occur with the primary infection, and late complications (developing within weeks), including acute rheumatic fever (ARF), acute (poststreptococcal) glomerulonephritis, and poststreptococcal reactive arthritis.

ARF is primarily a childhood disease, more common in individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, and rare in adults. Clinical manifestations include fever, migratory large-joint polyarthritis, and carditis (usually pancarditis, most commonly presenting as valvular disease). Less common symptoms are chorea, erythema marginatum (annular pink to red, nonpruritic rash with central clearing), and subcutaneous nodules. Rheumatic heart disease is an important sequela of ARF and usually develops 10 to 20 years after the initial ARF. The mitral valve (mitral regurgitation) is the most commonly affected valve, followed by the aortic valve.

The revised Jones criteria (see [Table: Table: Revised Jones Criteria]

) are used to diagnose ARF, which is confirmed if the patient has a recent history of GAS infection in addition to two major criteria or one major and two minor criteria.

Treatment is threefold:

  • Eliminate GAS infection and asymptomatic carriage with a single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin G.
  • Provide supportive treatment of arthritis and arthralgias with NSAIDs.
  • Treat heart failure associated with rheumatic heart disease. Patients with rheumatic heart disease should receive subsequent periodic assessment with echocardiography; valve repair or replacement may be required in some cases.

Primary prevention of ARF can be achieved by timely diagnosis and treatment of GAS infection. Secondary prevention of recurrent GAS infection is indicated for all patients with a history of ARF because subsequent GAS infections are associated with rheumatic heart disease progression. Monthly penicillin administration is a common regimen for secondary prevention; the duration depends on patient age and disease severity.

Disorders of taste (dysgeusia, hypogeusia, and ageusia) and smell (hyposmia, parosmia, and anosmia) can cause significant distress; adversely affect quality of life, nutrition, and safety (e.g., inability to notice gas leaks, burning food, or smoke); and lead to depression and social isolation. Disorders of taste and smell are more common with increased age; they may be an early marker of neurodegenerative diseases (such as Parkinson disease and Alzheimer disease) or result from head trauma or severe sinus disease. Medication-induced alteration of taste and smell is generally reversible, and if resolution does not occur with discontinuation of the offending agent, further investigation into other causes should be pursued.

Burning mouth syndrome often presents with altered or loss of taste in addition to burning and pain of the oral mucosa. The most common causes include sinus disorders, upper respiratory infections (most recently with COVID-19), and medications (antibiotics, terbinafine, ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors/serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, and antineoplastics).

Epiglottitis in adults is a rare, severe inflammatory response to upper respiratory tract infection that can cause partial or complete airway obstruction; it requires emergent identification and intervention. Immunization with Haemophilus influenzae type B vaccine has shifted the causative agents to a broad range of community-acquired respiratory pathogens, including Streptococcus and Staphylococcus. Patients with epiglottitis typically appear seriously ill, presenting with excessive salivation due to difficulty managing oral secretions, severe odynophagia and dysphagia, voice changes, and anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. The classic symptoms seen in children, such as stridor and tripod positioning, are less common in adults because of the larger airway diameter in adults. If airway obstruction seems imminent, airway control supersedes diagnostic evaluation.

Physical examination may reveal severe tenderness to palpation in the region of the larynx and hyoid bone. Lateral neck radiography may reveal an enlarged and edematous epiglottis (the thumbprint sign). CT and ultrasonography can be helpful in making the diagnosis. Although CT is sensitive, it may be difficult to obtain because symptoms may worsen with supine positioning. On endoscopy, the epiglottis and surrounding structures appear hyperemic and engorged, occluding portions of the airway (see

). Hospital admission is recommended, often to an ICU setting and with surgical consultation because intubation or tracheostomy may be required, although rare. Treatment consists of immediate parenteral antibiotic therapy and regular airway reassessment. Parenteral glucocorticoids may help reduce airway inflammation in some cases, but their use is not standardized.

The salivary glands include the major (parotid, submandibular, and sublingual) glands and thousands of minor glands (see

). The parotid gland can be palpated from the earlobe forward to the gumline of the second upper molar, where the Stensen duct opens. The submandibular gland can be felt along the floor of the mouth when palpating from posterior to anterior, terminating with the Wharton duct under the tongue. Disorders of the salivary gland include stones (sialolithiasis), infection (sialadenitis), gland tumors, and sialadenosis.

Sialolithiasis accounts for 50% of salivary gland disease. Patients present with gland swelling. Eighty percent of cases are found in the submandibular gland, 90% of which are in Wharton duct rather than the gland. In contrast, parotid stones are often within the parotid gland itself. Stones may be palpated and are typically tender, small, and hard, which distinguishes them from tumors that are typically firm and nontender. Management of sialolithiasis includes stimulation of saliva production with warm compresses, sialagogues (sour candies or vitamin C lozenges), salivary gland massage, increased fluid intake, and proper oral hygiene. Recurrent sialolithiasis can result in chronic sialadenitis, and chronic obstruction can lead to salivary gland atrophy.

Patients with acute sialadenitis typically present with sudden onset of acute pain and swelling of the affected salivary gland, which may be accompanied by fever, chills, and malaise. Acute bacterial (suppurative) sialadenitis is commonly polymicrobial, often with Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobes. Less common causes of sialadenitis include viral infection (mumps, cytomegalovirus, HIV), mycobacterial infection, and recent radiation therapy. Conditions that decrease salivary flow increase the risk for sialadenitis; these include volume depletion, Sjögren disease, poor oral hygiene, sialolithiasis, malnourishment, past radiation therapy, and use of anticholinergic medications. Physical examination often reveals tenderness and erythema over the affected gland. Palpation may result in pus exuding from the duct’s orifice, although an obstructed duct will not excrete fluid on palpation. Purulent drainage can be cultured to direct antibiotic therapy.

Management of bacterial sialadenitis includes the measures taken for sialolithiasis as well as antibiotics with coverage for S. aureus and anerobic organisms.

Salivary gland tumors most commonly present as a painless salivary gland mass; facial paralysis and lymphadenopathy increase concern for malignancy. Previous radiation therapy, smoking history, and viral infection (Epstein-Barr virus, HIV, human papillomavirus) are risk factors. Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI and tissue biopsy (typically with fine-needle aspiration) are the first steps in evaluation.

Sialadenosis is chronic painless bilateral salivary gland enlargement usually affecting the parotid glands. It is commonly associated with an underlying disorder, most often alcohol use disorder, cirrhosis, bulimia and anorexia nervosa, and diabetes. Imaging with ultrasonography or CT can be done to rule out a neoplastic cause. Management focuses on treating the underlying disease.

Poor oral hygiene is one of most common chronic conditions in the United States and significantly affects overall health and quality of life. Common dental diseases include dental caries and periodontal disease.

Dental caries are caused by bacteria. Certain foods and beverages (especially those containing sugar) create an acidic environment that erodes enamel and dentin, leading to tooth sensitivity, pain, and inflammation. The stained pits and fissures of dental caries can be seen on examination (see

). Pulpitis occurs when the erosion extends down to the pulp cavity, requiring removal of the caries and placement of a filling. If untreated, the erosion can affect the root or cause periodontitis requiring root canal or tooth extraction, or an abscess requiring incision and drainage.

Nearly half of U.S. adults have periodontal disease, which is associated with increased risk for diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Gingivitis (inflammation of the gums) is the initial manifestation of periodontal disease (see

). Gingivitis is reversible with routine dental visits and cleanings, brushing with fluoride toothpaste, flossing, fluoride varnish anticavity treatment, and use of chlorhexidine oral rinses. Periodontitis affects the periodontal ligament and presents with halitosis, inflamed gums that bleed easily, tooth sensitivity, and pain. Treatment is the same as that for gingivitis with the addition of deep cleaning to remove tartar from the surface and roots of the teeth.

Periodontal disease can progress to development of a dental abscess, presenting as severe and persistent pain at the affected tooth, localized swelling, and possible spontaneous drainage of pus. Depending on the abscess location, pain may radiate to the sinuses or jaw. The infection may be complicated by spreading cellulitis, trismus, or systemic symptoms such as fever and tachycardia. The diagnosis is made clinically, but dental evaluation may include dental radiographs. Definitive treatment requires drainage and root canal therapy or dental extraction. While the patient awaits dental treatment, analgesia is appropriate, but antibiotics are not necessary unless there are signs of extraoral spread, such as cellulitis or systemic symptoms.

Ludwig angina is a life-threatening infection of the floor of the mouth and should be suspected in patients with submandibular swelling and edema of the mouth floor, drooling, neck pain, dysphagia, or dysphonia. Ludwig angina often originates from the second and third lower molar teeth and can cause airway obstruction secondary to supraglottic edema. The causative pathogen is usually viridans streptococci. Management includes urgent CT, blood cultures, airway management precautions, broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, and surgical drainage if indicated.

Necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis, formerly called Vincent angina, is characterized by halitosis, oral pain, and ulcerated and necrotic areas of the tonsils and gingiva with red irregular edges that may create a grayish pseudomembrane that bleeds if scraped (see

). Lymph nodes may be enlarged and tender. This condition is usually seen in patients with poor oral hygiene or malnutrition, or those who smoke. Treatment includes oral antibiotics, twice-daily chlorhexidine rinses for 2 weeks, and debridement if the condition is severe.

Dental fracture is an emergency because a tooth becomes nonviable 1 hour after fracture. Patients should handle the tooth by the crown, wash it in cold water, reposition it in the socket, and bite gently on a washcloth to help keep the tooth in place until seen by a dental professional. If immediate repositioning is not possible, the tooth should be placed in cold pasteurized milk while immediate care by a dental professional is sought.

Leukoplakia is a premalignant lesion that presents as white patches on the oral mucosa that cannot be wiped off. It should be differentiated from oral candidiasis (white, curd-like plaques that are easy to wipe off) and oral hairy leukoplakia. Oral hairy leukoplakia (see

) occurs in patients with immunosuppression (most commonly HIV infection) and is caused by the Epstein-Barr virus. It presents as adherent linear white plaques on the lateral surface of the tongue. Erythroplakia, which presents as red mucosal patches, has a higher risk for malignant transformation than leukoplakia. Both leukoplakia and erythroplakia require biopsy to rule out dysplasia. These conditions are seen most frequently in patients who use tobacco and alcohol.

Aphthous ulcers (“canker sores”) are recurrent, round or oval-shaped, painful ulcers with a gray-white pseudomembrane base and an erythematous halo that affect the inner lips, buccal mucosa, and tongue (see

). Ulcers heal spontaneously within 7 to 10 days. The diagnosis is made clinically. Vitamin B~12, vitamin C, folate, iron, and zinc deficiencies may be associated. Severe, recurrent oral ulcers suggest the possibility of infection or a systemic disease such as Behçet syndrome, Crohn disease, HIV infection, or erythema multiforme.

Black hairy tongue is characterized by elongation and defective desquamation of filiform papillae, which manifest as a discolored hairy tongue (see

). It is more common in men and with advancing age, poor oral hygiene, smoking, certain antibiotics (including penicillin, tetracycline, and linezolid), and medications causing dry mouth (e.g., antipsychotics, tricyclic antidepressants). Management includes good oral hygiene and tongue brushing as well as discontinuation of predisposing causes.

Geographic tongue is fairly common and may be sporadic, familial, or associated with psoriasis. These migratory patterned patches of smooth red surfaces and white patches on the dorsal tongue (see

) are usually asymptomatic, but patients may report discomfort and burning, which are exacerbated by hot or spicy foods. About 40% of patients will develop tongue fissures.

Eye Disorders

An understanding of the basic anatomy of the eye (see

) is necessary to accurately diagnose eye disorders.

Although the treatment of many serious ophthalmologic conditions will be done in collaboration with an ophthalmologist, patients often first present to internal medicine physicians with eye and vision concerns. Internal medicine physicians must be able to identify conditions that can cause permanent vision loss and require immediate ophthalmologic evaluation (see [Table: Table: Eye Conditions Requiring Immediate Ophthalmologic Evaluation]

).

Patients with periocular trauma and potential globe injury should undergo visual acuity assessment and anterior eye segment evaluation with either a penlight or slit lamp. Findings that suggest globe rupture include pupil deviation toward the laceration site, anterior chamber depth loss, blood collection (hyphema) (see

), and subconjunctival hemorrhage surrounding the cornea. Patients with possible globe injury should not undergo tonometry or pupil dilation. Instead, an eye shield should be applied, and the patient should be urgently referred to ophthalmology.

Chemical injury to the eyes causes decreased vision, eye pain and burning, foreign body sensation, and tearing. Examination may reveal eyelid swelling, erythema, conjunctival injection, blepharospasm, and corneal defect. Eye irrigation with normal saline or lactated Ringer solution should be initiated immediately, with emergent referral to ophthalmology.

Vision-threatening eye infections requiring immediate antibiotics and ophthalmologic evaluation include endophthalmitis, keratitis, hyperacute bacterial conjunctivitis, infected corneal ulcers, and orbital cellulitis. Orbital cellulitis is characterized by pain, eyelid swelling, and erythema. It is differentiated from preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis, an infection of the anterior portion of the eyelid that rarely leads to serious complications, by the additional presence of proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and pain with eye movement. CT imaging can help differentiate between orbital and preseptal cellulitis. Findings of orbital cellulitis on CT imaging include inflammation of the deeper structures of the eye posterior to the orbital septum (e.g., the extraocular muscles), whereas preseptal cellulitis appears as swelling in the eyelids and superficial soft tissue structures anterior to the orbital septum. Although treatment of orbital cellulitis requires prompt empiric parenteral broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, preseptal cellulitis may be managed with oral antibiotics and close monitoring.

Red eye occurs in several eye conditions (see [Table: Table: Cardinal Features of Eye Conditions That Cause Red Eye]

). Assessment begins by determining unilateral or bilateral involvement, symptom duration, and the presence of associated discharge, pain, photophobia, and visual changes. History should also focus on the presence of antecedent trauma, previous similar episodes, contact lens use, and medical history. Examination should include assessment of visual acuity, pupillary size and light response, and redness pattern and location, as well as palpation of preauricular lymph nodes.

Conjunctivitis is the most common cause of red eye and can be due to infectious or noninfectious causes.

Viral conjunctivitis is commonly spread through direct contact and often occurs concomitantly with an upper respiratory tract infection (see

). Common pathogens include adenovirus, coxsackievirus, and enterovirus. Symptoms typically start in one eye before spreading bilaterally. Pharnygitis (likelihood ratio [LR], 5.4-9.9), preauricular adenopathy (LR, 4.5), and watery discharge (LR, 2.5-5.6) make viral conjunctivitis more likely. Although watery discharge is present in more than two thirds of viral conjunctivitis cases, it is also present in one fourth of bacterial conjunctivitis cases. These numbers are reversed for mucopurulent discharge, with presence in more than two thirds of bacterial conjunctivitis cases and one fifth of viral conjunctivitis cases. Therapy for viral conjunctivitis is supportive and includes cold compresses; antibiotics are not indicated. Viral conjunctivitis is highly contagious, and frequent handwashing is advised. Symptoms are usually mild and resolve within 1 to 2 weeks.

Bacterial conjunctivitis is highly contagious and commonly spreads through direct contact. Gram-positive bacteria are commonly implicated. Cold compresses can be used to relieve symptoms. Topical antibacterial therapy, including trimethoprim–polymyxin B or erythromycin, is associated with earlier clinical and microbiological remission as well as reduced transmissibility compared with placebo. However, 65% of patients improve without antibiotic therapy within 2 to 5 days, and withholding antibiotics is reasonable for patients who are not immunocompromised, do not wear contact lenses, and do not work in health care facilities. Patients who wear contact lenses are at increased risk for keratitis and pseudomonal infection. They should be treated with a topical antibiotic that has pseudomonal activity, such as a fluoroquinolone.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes hyperacute bacterial conjunctivitis, characterized by sudden onset of symptoms with rapid progression to vision loss (see

). Emergent ophthalmology referral, systemic and topical antimicrobials, and possible hospitalization are indicated.

Allergic conjunctivitis can be seasonal or perennial and is characterized by clear watery discharge, bilateral eye pruritus, and redness. It is often accompanied by other allergic symptoms, such as rhinorrhea (see

). Treatment involves removing the offending agent when possible and using topical antihistamines or mast-cell inhibitors.

All forms of suspected conjunctivitis occurring in the context of contact lens use should raise concern for keratitis. Regardless of the cause, contact lens use should be discontinued until redness and discharge resolve completely.

Keratitis is inflammation of the corneal epithelium and superficial stroma most commonly due to bacterial infections (especially Pseudomonas species) in contact lens wearers. Viral infections, such as herpes simplex virus and adenovirus, can also be responsible. Diminished vision and severe eye discomfort with circumferential hyperemia are typical (see

and

). Both bacterial and viral keratitis require immediate ophthalmologic evaluation.

Episcleritis is a self-limited inflammation of the episclera (the layer between the conjunctiva and sclera) that usually resolves within several weeks (see

). Treatment consists of systemic NSAIDs for symptom relief. Patients with recurrent episodes should be evaluated for underlying disease.

Scleritis is an inflammatory disorder of the sclera that causes severe pain and, unlike episcleritis, can threaten vision (see

and

). Scleritis is often associated with underlying inflammatory diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic vasculitis. Diagnosis should prompt immediate referral to an ophthalmologist, and systemic glucocorticoids or immunosuppressive agents are usually required for treatment.

Uveitis is a group of diseases characterized by inflammation of the uvea, which includes the iris, ciliary body, and choroid (

). Anterior uveitis affects the iris and ciliary body and is characterized by the presence of leukocytes in the anterior chamber of the eye. Uveitis affecting the iris alone is termed iritis, whereas involvement of the iris and adjacent ciliary bodies is called iridocyclitis. Posterior uveitis is characterized by the presence of leukocytes in the vitreous humor and can involve the choroid and retina (chorioretinitis).

Uveitis is associated with many systemic infections and inflammatory diseases, including spondyloarthropathies and sarcoidosis (see

). A hypopyon (see

) or purulent material accumulation in the anterior eye chamber may be observed in severe cases. Patients with uveitis require immediate referral to an ophthalmologist.

Endophthalmitis is severe ocular inflammation caused by an infection within the eye (including the aqueous humor, retina, vitreous humor, and optic nerve). Infection, typically with bacteria or fungi, can occur through endogenous spread of systemic infection or exogenously due to trauma or surgery. Retinal damage can result from both infection and the immune response to the infection.

Making the diagnosis is difficult because ocular findings and symptoms are similar to those of other inflammatory eye diseases noted previously. Patients require immediate referral to an ophthalmologist when endophthalmitis is suspected.

Subconjunctival hemorrhages result from ruptured subconjunctival blood vessels due to intense coughing, vomiting, and minor trauma. They are asymptomatic and usually resolve within several weeks (see

). No treatment is necessary.

Blepharitis is eyelid inflammation, which may be posterior or anterior. Posterior blepharitis involves inner eyelid inflammation near the posterior edge of the eyelid (i.e., closer to the eye) and the meibomian glands. Posterior blepharitis can occur in patients with rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis. In anterior blepharitis, inflammation occurs at the eyelid bases, often involving the eyelash follicles and extending from the lid up to the eyebrow or down toward the maxilla (i.e., cutaneously away from the eye). Anterior blepharitis may be associated with eyelid colonization with staphylococcal species, contact dermatitis, and psoriasis.

Findings may include eyelid swelling, redness, and skin flaking; eyelash loss, misdirection, and crusting; and dry eyes or excessive tearing (see

). Corneal erosions and ulcerations can be seen in severe cases. Treating all forms of blepharitis involves warm compresses, eyelid washing and massage, and artificial tears. Refractory cases require referral to an ophthalmologist and consideration of topical glucocorticoids or cyclosporin.

Dry eye (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) is a multifactorial inflammatory disorder resulting from abnormal eye lubrication. Normal tear film consists of an aqueous component formed by lacrimal glands, lipids produced by meibomian glands, and mucins produced by conjunctival goblet cells. Abnormalities in any component of the film can lead to dry eyes. In most cases, ocular surface inflammation also plays a central role. Systemic medications, such as β-blockers, antihistamines, antipsychotics, and antineoplastics, can also cause dry eye. Systemic conditions associated with dry eye include Sjögren syndrome, rosacea, rheumatoid arthritis, peripheral arterial disease, and daily cigarette use.

Symptoms are usually bilateral and include ocular pain, foreign body sensation, light sensitivity, tearing, irritation or redness, and fluctuating visual disturbance. Treatment includes artificial tears and ointments, increased fluid intake and ambient humidity, avoidance of environmental and medication triggers, and protective eyewear. Punctal occlusion or plugs are occasionally necessary. Reducing inflammation, most commonly with topical cyclosporine, and treating eyelid disease with appropriate hygiene are also indicated in some patients.

Chalazia are caused by obstruction of the meibomian (sebaceous) glands, which leads to inflammation and the development of sterile lipogranulomatous material. They tend to be slow growing and painless (or slightly tender) and develop under the eyelid skin. Hordeola (styes) are also caused by obstruction of a sebaceous gland but with normal skin flora, most commonly Staphylococcus aureus, causing more inflammation. Hordeola can be internal (from the meibomian glands) or external (from the glands of Zeis or Moll). They have a faster onset and are more painful than chalazia, and they appear as a large pimple or small abscess of the eyelid.

Both hordeola and chalazia are treated conservatively with warm compresses applied several times daily and gentle massage to promote drainage. Makeup, contact lenses, and eye creams should be avoided until complete resolution. Antibiotic cream or eye drops may help accelerate healing in hordeola. Nonresponding hordeola and chalazia as well as very large hordeola should be referred to an ophthalmologist for incision and drainage or steroid injection. Recurrent hordeola require consistent daily eyelid hygiene with mild soap and warm water.

Corneal abrasions are superficial epithelial defects that result from foreign bodies, contact lens use, mechanical trauma, and chemical burns. Symptoms include a foreign-body sensation, light sensitivity, severe eye pain, and tearing. Fluorescein staining permits visualization of abrasions and should be performed in all patients along with visual acuity assessment. Vision loss requires immediate ophthalmology referral. Otherwise, pain management with acetaminophen or NSAIDs may be sufficient for treating small abrasions. Topical antimicrobials may not be necessary for patients who do not wear contact lenses, but data on this common practice are inconclusive despite a recent Cochrane review. However, in contact lens wearers, topical antibiotics with antipseudomonal activity (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, gentamycin, and tobramycin) should be given to prevent bacterial infection. Eye patches should be avoided in patients with small, uncomplicated corneal abrasions.

Corneal ulcers often result from bacterial infections and extend deeper than abrasions, exposing the underlying stroma. Corneal ulcers warrant immediate referral to an ophthalmologist.

Cataracts (lens opacification) increase with age and frequently cause glare sensitivity and vision impairment, particularly at night and when reading road signs or fine print. Examination reveals lens opacification along with diminished or absent red reflex. Asymptomatic cataracts do not require treatment. Patients with vision-impairing cataracts should be referred to an ophthalmologist for phacoemulsification with intraoperative lens replacement.

Glaucoma is a group of progressive optic neuropathies characterized by atrophy of the neuroretinal rim of the optic nerve, resulting in an increased cup-to-disc ratio (see

). Most but not all affected patients have increased intraocular pressure (IOP). Glaucoma is the second leading cause of blindness in the United States.

Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) accounts for more than 80% of glaucoma cases in the United States. POAG is characterized by decreased aqueous flow with a normal iridocorneal angle (see

). POAG is often asymptomatic until later disease stages. Peripheral visual field loss is the earliest symptom of POAG, but it frequently goes unreported; progression to central vision loss occurs in untreated patients. Once present, vision loss is permanent. Diagnosis is based on peripheral vision loss, optic disc damage (often demonstrated as disc cupping on fundoscopic examination) (

), and increased IOP. Treatment focuses on decreasing IOP with surgery or medications (see [Table: Table: Topical Medications for Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma]

). Prostaglandin analogues are first-line medical therapy in most patients.

In angle-closure glaucoma (ACG), a narrowed iridocorneal angle obstructs aqueous flow (

). ACG may be primary or secondary to a process such as posterior chamber hemorrhage or a tumor causing iridocorneal angle closure. Symptoms can develop acutely or insidiously, depending on the rate of IOP increase. Acute symptoms include severe eye pain, headache, nausea/vomiting, and visualizing halos around lights. Eye dilation should be avoided when ACG is suspected to prevent precipitously increasing IOP. Extremely high IOPs are seen on tonometry. Acute ACG is an ocular emergency, and laser peripheral iridotomy should be performed within 1 hour of presentation. If iridotomy is delayed, IOP-lowering drops should be administered to lower the pressure until iridotomy can be performed.

Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is among the most common retinal disorders seen in primary care (see [Table: Table: Common Retinal Disorders]

); it is a progressive disease involving the central retina that causes painless central vision loss. Initial symptoms include distorted vision (particularly with reading), difficulty with facial recognition, and central scotoma. Vision difficulties may be particularly evident in low-light settings. AMD is classified as either wet (neovascular, exudative) or dry (non-neovascular, atrophic) (see

and

). Both forms are characterized by drusen (lipid deposits) and retinal pigment epithelium defects. Neovascularization and hemorrhage are additionally seen in wet AMD. Wet AMD can progress to blindness in weeks to months, whereas dry AMD typically progresses to blindness over years to decades.

Smoking is the most significant modifiable risk factor for AMD, and cessation is strongly encouraged for all patients. Evidence also suggests an association between genetic factors related to cardiovascular disease and AMD. In addition to quitting smoking, hypertension control and control of lipids are recommended to prevent vision loss due to AMD. Supplementation with vitamin C, vitamin E, β-carotene, zinc, and copper may decrease AMD progression in patients with intermediate AMD, geographic atrophy, or other advanced AMD in at least one eye. In patients who continue to smoke, lutein and zeaxanthin can be used instead of β-carotene to avoid increasing the risk of lung cancer (see Supplements and Herbal Therapies in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Intravitreal injections of vascular endothelial growth factor inhibitors are a cornerstone of advanced disease treatment and may improve vision or delay further deterioration.

Optic neuritis is a demyelinating inflammation of the optic nerve and is most commonly due to multiple sclerosis. It manifests as painful acute monocular vision loss that develops over hours to days. Visual symptoms include blurred or foggy vision, decreased color vision, and central scotoma. Bilateral involvement is rare and may indicate neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. Examination may reveal papillitis (see Optic Neuropathies in Neurology and Presenting Signs and Symptoms of Multiple Sclerosis in Neurology), an afferent pupillary defect, and a central scotoma on visual field testing. Diagnosis is clinical, although MRI may confirm the diagnosis and reveal other lesions. First-line therapy is high-dose intravenous glucocorticoids.

Retinal detachment involves the separation of the retinal neurosensory layer from underlying structures. Symptoms include unilateral flashing lights and floaters. Risk factors include advanced age, myopia, diabetic retinopathy, cataract surgery, and a positive family history. Retinal detachment is an emergency requiring immediate referral to an ophthalmologist (see

).

Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) presents as sudden, painless severe monocular vision loss. Occlusion of smaller branches (branch retinal artery occlusion) leads to less profound visual field defects. CRAO is most commonly due to carotid artery atherosclerosis but can also be caused by cardiogenic embolism, thrombophilia, and (infrequently) giant cell arteritis. Some affected patients have a history of antecedent transient episodes of painless vision loss. Fundoscopic examination may reveal retinal pallor, a “cherry red” fovea, and interrupted blood columns within retinal vessels (see

). CRAO is an ocular emergency requiring urgent referral to an ophthalmologist and evaluation for causes of stroke.

Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) is usually caused by primary thrombus formation, whereas branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) is generally due to compression of a vein by adjacent arterioles. Risk factors for CRVO include advanced age, diabetes mellitus, and hypertension. Patients with CRVO typically present with painless, blurred monocular vision. BRVO may be asymptomatic or cause scotoma or visual field defect. Examination may reveal an afferent pupillary defect (particularly in CRVO), retinal vein congestion, retinal hemorrhage, and cotton-wool spots (see

). The presence of CRVO should prompt immediate referral to an ophthalmologist.

Roth spots are white-centered retinal hemorrhages, likely secondary to retinal capillary rupture. Although historically associated with subacute bacterial endocarditis (see Diagnosis of Endocarditis in Infectious Disease), they occur in many underlying conditions, including HIV retinopathy, leukemia, vasculitis, and hypertensive retinopathy.
