Urologic Conditions

Erectile dysfunction (ED) refers to the inability to achieve or maintain an erection necessary for satisfactory sexual performance. The most common causes are the following:

  • Vascular disease
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Hypertension
  • Dyslipidemia
  • Obesity
  • Neurologic disease, including stroke and postoperative nerve injury
  • Medications
  • Androgen deficiency
  • Prostate cancer therapy
  • Psychological causes

Assessment of ED begins with obtaining a comprehensive history (medical, surgical, sexual, and psychosocial). An accurate medication list should be elicited because many medications are associated with ED (see [Table: Table: Drugs Commonly Associated With Erectile Dysfunction]

). Clinicians should clarify whether the problem is attaining or maintaining erections, whether it occurs with masturbation or with partners, and whether nocturnal and early-morning erections are present. Psychogenic ED, which is ED due to psychological or interpersonal factors, is more common in younger patients and in those with a history of sexual abuse. ED that occurs with preserved ability to achieve nocturnal and early-morning erections should raise suspicion for psychogenic ED.

The International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF-5) is a tool to assess ED symptoms and monitor treatment efficacy [see [Table: Table: The International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF-5)]

)].

Physical examination includes assessment of vital signs and BMI and examination of genitalia and secondary sex characteristics. The American Urological Association (AUA) 2018 ED guideline recommends obtaining a morning total testosterone level for all patients. If hypothyroidism is suspected, a serum thyroid-stimulating hormone level should be obtained. ED is associated with coronary artery disease, and the presence of ED, particularly without clear cause or when felt to be vasculogenic, should prompt screening for cardiovascular risk factors, including diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, as well as assessment of cardiovascular risk using a validated risk assessment model.

Nonpharmacologic treatment options include lifestyle modifications, such as smoking cessation, exercise, and weight optimization. Psychological counseling should be considered in patients with psychogenic ED.

Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitors (avanafil, sildenafil, tadalafil, and vardenafil) are first-line pharmacotherapy for ED and function by increasing the vasodilatory effects of endogenous nitric oxide. They have similar efficacy and should be titrated to optimal dosing. Tadalafil is the longest-acting PDE-5 inhibitor and is approved for treatment of both ED and benign prostatic hyperplasia at lower daily doses. Avanafil has the most rapid onset of action. All PDE-5 inhibitors require sexual stimulation to be effective, and sildenafil and vardenafil should be taken on an empty stomach.

Common adverse effects include dyspepsia, headache, flushing, dizziness, and visual disturbances. PDE-5 inhibitors should not be used concurrently with nitrates due to the possibility of severe hypotension. The fourth Princeton Consensus Conference provides guidelines regarding the safety of ED treatment in patients with known cardiovascular disease or cardiovascular risk factors (see [Table: Table: Treatment of ED in Patients With Cardiovascular Disease]

). Testosterone therapy along with a PDE-5 inhibitor may be more effective for patients with documented androgen deficiency after discussion of risks and benefits.

Options for patients who have contraindications to PDE-5 inhibitors include intraurethral and injected intracavernosal alprostadil as well as vacuum erection devices. Alprostadil causes arterial smooth muscle relaxation, leading to penile vasodilation. Intracavernosal alprostadil is more effective and has fewer adverse effects, although its use is associated with chronic fibrotic changes (4.9% incidence) and injection site pain. Priapism is an adverse effect of both formulations (approximately 1.9% incidence), and patient education is required. Patients can also be offered a vacuum erection device, which has been shown to be safe and effective. Implantation of a penile prosthesis is reserved for patients in whom other management options fail.

Premature ejaculation (PE), or male early ejaculation, is one of the most common sexual disorders in men. It is defined as ejaculation with minimal stimulation that occurs earlier than desired. It is classified as lifelong or acquired and is often associated with psychological distress, low self-esteem, anxiety, and depression. Postinsertion ejaculatory latency time (ELT) is the time for ejaculation to occur after penetrative sex and is used as an objective measure of PE. Generally, a cutoff time of less than 1 minute is considered abnormal when associated with psychological distress. In men who are concerned about PE but do not meet these criteria, there are two additional PE subsets:

  • Natural variable PE, or occasional short ELT that occurs inconsistently
  • Subjective PE, or subjective concern or preoccupation about short ELT within population norms

Therapy is aimed at extending ELT time. Healthy lifestyle changes should be encouraged because PE is associated with metabolic syndrome, alcohol intake, obesity, and sedentary lifestyle. Treatment options include pharmacotherapy, behavioral techniques, or both. The AUA recommends a daily selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), on-demand clomipramine (a tricyclic antidepressant), or topical penile anesthetics as first-line treatment. On-demand SSRI taken 3 to 5 hours before sexual activity is another option but is not as effective as daily use. Tramadol or an α-blocker is an option if first-line therapies fail. Onset of effect differs among therapies. An increase in ELT can be seen shortly after initiation of topical anesthetics. Response to SSRIs is slower but may be seen several days after initiation, with most patients achieving benefit within several weeks. Men with concomitant ED should be treated for ED first.

Treatment for natural variable PE and subjective PE includes reassurance, psychotherapy, and education.

Hematospermia is the presence of blood in ejaculated semen. Although distressing, it is usually benign. Evaluation includes urinalysis, but testing is otherwise based on associated symptoms, including lower urinary tract symptoms, urethritis, and hematuria.

Retrograde ejaculation is a condition in which semen flows retrograde into the bladder. It may be idiopathic or due to bladder neck surgery, medications including SSRIs, or neurologic causes.

Painful ejaculation may be caused by pelvic lesions, previous trauma, infections, or surgery and often coexists with other chronic pelvic pain syndromes. Men presenting with painful ejaculation should undergo evaluation for causes of pelvic pain and lower urinary tract disorders.

Decreased libido is defined as a reduced sexual desire. When associated with concomitant marked personal or interpersonal distress, the condition is termed hypoactive sexual desire disorder. Although commonly experienced as part of normal aging, numerous medical and psychiatric conditions can cause decreased libido, including alcohol use, mood disorders, and systemic illness. Medications associated with ED similarly can decrease libido ( [Table: Table: Drugs Commonly Associated With Erectile Dysfunction]

). Treatment involves addressing the underlying causes. Testosterone treatment can be considered when sexual dysfunction is accompanied by documented androgen deficiency and after a discussion of risks and benefits of treatment with the patient (see Management of Male Hypogonadism in Endocrinology and Metabolism).

Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a histologic diagnosis characterized by smooth muscle and epithelial cell proliferation in the prostate’s periurethral transition zone. BPH may lead to benign prostate enlargement causing direct urethral obstruction at the bladder neck, which, along with increased smooth muscle tone and resistance, can cause lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS).

LUTS can be divided into obstructive voiding or bladder storage (irritative) symptoms. Obstructive voiding symptoms include difficulty initiating urination, weak urinary stream, dribbling, straining to void, urinary hesitancy, and incomplete bladder emptying. Irritative symptoms include nocturia, dysuria, and urinary frequency and urgency. The AUA Symptom Index (AUA-SI), a validated seven-item questionnaire, can be used to objectively assess LUTS severity and evaluate treatment response. The International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) includes the AUA-SI and an additional question on quality of life; guidelines now recommend the use of the IPSS [see [Table: Table: International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)]

)].

The incidence of LUTS increases with age and has many non–BPH-related causes (see [Table: Table: Causes of Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms in Men]

). In the evaluation of LUTS, patients should be asked about previous sexually transmitted infections (STIs), urethral trauma, and urologic procedures. A comprehensive assessment of both prescription and over-the-counter medications should be performed. Anticholinergics (antihistamines and tricyclic antidepressants) can lead to detrusor muscle dysfunction with decreased bladder contractility. Decongestants (sympathomimetics) bind to α-receptors, which can lead to bladder outlet obstruction. Opioid use can also result in urinary retention. Lifestyle factors can contribute to LUTS, and fluid intake and consumption of bladder irritants, including alcohol, caffeine, and acidic and spicy foods, should be determined.

In addition to a directed history and physical examination, a urinalysis should be performed in all patients with LUTS. A prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level can be obtained in those who meet criteria for PSA-based prostate cancer screening (see Prostate Cancer in Oncology) but is not necessary to diagnose or treat BPH except when used as a proxy for prostate size. Otherwise, the evaluation of LUTS is guided by the suspicion of underlying conditions other than BPH ( [Table: Table: Causes of Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms in Men]

).

The goal of treating LUTS secondary to BPH is symptom relief. Lifestyle modifications, including minimizing fluid intake before bedtime and avoiding bladder irritants, such as caffeine and alcohol, should be recommended to all patients. Patients with bladder storage symptoms may benefit from scheduled voiding and pelvic floor muscle strengthening exercises. Active surveillance is recommended for patients who have mild symptoms (IPSS score <8) and those with more severe disease (IPSS score ≥8) who are not bothered by their symptoms. Symptoms should be reassessed annually using the IPSS.

Pharmacotherapy is recommended for patients with bothersome moderate to severe symptoms (IPSS score >8). Patients should be evaluated 4 to 12 weeks after treatment initiation to assess response, which can be monitored using the IPSS. A decrease of 3 or more points represents clinically significant improvement. A postvoid residual may also be helpful because an increasing postvoid residual with treatment may indicate medication failure, need for further evaluation, or consideration of more invasive interventions.

α-Blockers are first-line pharmacotherapy and function by promoting smooth muscle relaxation; they do not affect disease progression. Symptom improvement is generally seen within 48 hours of initiation, with maximal improvement noted within several weeks.

Efficacy among all α-blockers is similar, and selection should be based on minimizing adverse effects. Nonspecific α-blockers (alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin, and terazosin) block both α~1A prostate receptors and α~1B smooth muscle receptors in blood vessels and can be associated with orthostasis and lightheadedness. These agents should be started at low doses and slowly titrated upward. Silodosin and tamsulosin, which are α~1A-specific α-blockers, are less likely to cause orthostasis and do not require dose titration; however, they are more likely to cause retrograde ejaculation. If cataract surgery is planned, α-blocker therapy should be delayed because of possible development of intraoperative floppy iris syndrome, a condition characterized by impaired pupil dilation and increased risk for perioperative complications.

PDE-5 inhibitors can be used as initial therapy in patients with BPH symptoms and concomitant ED. Caution should be exercised in combining PDE-5 and α-blockers because of increased risk for hypotension, especially with nonspecific α-blockers. Although suggested by guidelines as an option, the combination of tadalafil and α-blockers has not been shown to offer advantages over either agent alone.

5α-Reductase inhibitors (dutasteride and finasteride) may be used in BPH-related LUTS with prostatic enlargement, as demonstrated by a prostate volume of over 30 mL on imaging, a PSA level higher than 1.5 ng/mL (1.5 µg/L), or an enlarged prostate on digital rectal examination. 5α-Reductase inhibitors function by preventing the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, inhibiting prostate growth. Over 6 to 12 months, the prostate is reduced in size, which should cause an expected 50% reduction in serum PSA level. In patients with LUTS who have an enlarged prostate, combining a 5α-reductase inhibitor with an α-blocker can be more effective than either agent alone. Adverse effects of 5α-reductase inhibitors include decreased libido, ED, breast tenderness, and gynecomastia. Although several trials have shown reduced incidence of low-grade prostate cancer with 5α-reductase inhibitors, they are associated with a slight increase in high-grade prostate cancer.

Antimuscarinic agents, such as trospium, oxybutynin, and tolterodine, can be used to treat bladder storage symptoms by relaxing bladder detrusor muscles. These are generally not used as monotherapy.

Saw palmetto is frequently used to treat LUTS secondary to BPH but lacks data supporting its efficacy.

Surgical treatments for LUTS secondary to BPH include transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) and several other options, including vaporization of the prostate, prostatic urethral lift, laser enucleation, and water vapor thermal therapy. These options are usually reserved for individuals who do not respond to pharmacotherapy or develop BPH complications, such as urinary retention or persistent gross hematuria.

Evaluation of acute testicular and scrotal pain should begin with a concise history focusing on pain characteristics, associated symptoms, trauma history, previous urologic disorders, and sexual history, followed by a focused genitourinary examination.

Testicular torsion is the most important diagnosis to rule out initially. Although it is most common in younger men, it can occur at any age. Testicular torsion involves twisting of the spermatic cord structures, leading to ischemia and eventual testis infarction. It is most often characterized by acute onset of severe pain in one testis that rapidly progresses in severity over a period of hours and may be accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Examination findings include an exquisitely tender and swollen testis that is elevated with erythema of the overlying scrotal skin. The cremasteric reflex, testicular elevation in response to stroking the inner thigh, is typically absent; however, presence of the cremasteric reflex does not rule out torsion. A negative Prehn sign, when there is no pain relief upon lifting the testicle, also suggests testicular torsion.

Patients with suspected testicular torsion require immediate urologic consultation for exploratory surgery. When the diagnosis is clear, imaging (with Doppler ultrasonography) should not delay immediate exploratory surgery because surgical delay reduces the probability of testicular viability. If the diagnosis is unclear, the Testicular Workup for Ischemia and Suspected Torsion (TWIST) score can be used to assess torsion risk and direct the evaluation (see [Table: Table: Testicular Workup for Ischemia and Suspected Score]

). When torsion is present, surgical detorsion should be performed within 6 hours.

Epididymitis is usually secondary to infection; when infection spreads to the adjacent testis, it is termed epididymo-orchitis. Both conditions typically cause unilateral scrotal pain of gradual onset that worsens over a period of days. Examination reveals tenderness and swelling of involved structures. Pain may be relieved with scrotal elevation (positive Prehn sign). The normal cremasteric reflex is usually present in patients with epididymitis and epididymo-orchitis.

In patients at risk for STI, Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are the most commonly implicated pathogens. In men who are at low risk for STIs (including those with recent prostate biopsy, vasectomy, or urinary tract instrumentation procedures), colonic bacteria, such as Escherichia coli, are the most common pathogens. In men who practice insertive anal sex, enteric organisms, chlamydia, or gonorrhea are all possible pathogens. Urinalysis and culture should be obtained in all patients, and STI testing is indicated for those at risk. Imaging is usually not necessary. Treatment consists of empiric antimicrobial therapy directed toward the most likely pathogen (see [Table: Table: Antimicrobial Therapy for Epididymitis and Epididymo-orchitis]

). Conservative measures include scrotal elevation, NSAIDs, and rest.

Acute pain in the testicles and scrotum can result from other conditions, such as malignancy and inguinal hernia (see [Table: Table: Other Causes of Acute Testicular and Scrotal Pain]

).

Hydroceles form when fluid accumulates within the space between the visceral and parietal layers of the tunica vaginalis (see

). The suspected cause is an imbalance between fluid secretion and reabsorption by the tunica vaginalis. Symptoms include scrotal swelling and pain. On scrotal transillumination, light shines through the scrotum (see

). Ultrasound can be used to confirm the diagnosis but is not usually necessary (see

). Asymptomatic hydroceles require no intervention, whereas patients with bothersome symptoms can be referred for surgical excision of the hydrocele sac. Fluid aspiration is usually ineffective because fluid often reaccumulates.

Varicoceles occur in 15% to 20% of men and are caused by dilation of the pampiniform plexus of the spermatic veins (see

). Symptoms include scrotal swelling and dull and/or aching pain. On examination, the swelling has a “bag of worms” consistency that becomes smaller with scrotal elevation and supine positioning. Accompanying testicular atrophy may be observed. Although most commonly left-sided, varicoceles can also be right-sided or bilateral. Varicoceles may be associated with male infertility. In patients who are minimally symptomatic with no testicular atrophy, conservative measures (such as NSAIDs and scrotal support) are recommended. For patients with bothersome symptoms or testicular atrophy on examination who desire fertility, surgical ligation (preferred) or percutaneous venous embolization is recommended.

Epididymal cysts are soft, rounded structures in the head of the epididymis; when larger than 2 cm, they are termed spermatoceles. Diagnosis is based on the examination, but ultrasonography can be used if there is diagnostic uncertainty. These cysts are usually asymptomatic and require no intervention, but larger painful spermatoceles can be surgically excised.

Patients with acute bacterial prostatitis typically present with acute onset of local symptoms (dysuria; urinary frequency and urgency; and suprapubic, perineal, glans penis, and/or rectal pain) accompanied by fevers, chills, nausea/vomiting, and malaise. Examination focuses on vital sign assessment and abdominal, genital, and digital rectal examinations. Gentle digital rectal examination reveals an enlarged, tender, and often boggy prostate. Prostate massage may lead to bacteremia and should be avoided. Urinalysis and urine culture should be obtained along with blood cultures in patients with evidence of systemic infection.

Empiric antimicrobial therapy should be initiated at the time of diagnosis and modified as appropriate based on urine culture results. Most patients can be managed with oral agents in the outpatient setting, whereas severely ill patients and those with suspected sepsis should be hospitalized and initially treated with parenteral antibiotics (see [Table: Table: Empiric Antimicrobial Therapy for Acute Bacterial Prostatitis]

). Antimicrobial agents are typically continued for 2 to 4 weeks; some experts recommend treatment for up to 6 weeks.

Chronic bacterial prostatitis involves persistent prostate infection lasting longer than 3 months. It commonly manifests as recurrent lower urinary tract infections with the same organism. This diagnosis should be considered in men who have recurrent symptoms after receiving antibiotics for treatment of a urinary tract infection. On digital rectal examination, the prostate may be normal, tender, and/or boggy. In patients with an initially negative urine culture, a repeat urine culture obtained after prostate massage can increase the likelihood of identifying the causative organism. Antimicrobial therapy is similar to that used for acute bacterial prostatitis and should be guided by urine culture results and continued for 4 to 6 weeks.

Chronic prostatitis/pelvic pain syndrome reflects the presence of chronic prostate or pelvic pain without evidence of infection. Symptoms vary widely and include chronic urinary symptoms, pelvic pain, and pain with ejaculation. Although there is no clear first-line treatment, α-blockers, NSAIDs, and daily tadalafil (even in men without erectile dysfunction) are recommended. Medications helpful for neuropathic pain, including gabapentinoids and tricyclic antidepressants, may also be offered. Pharmacotherapy should not be repeated if no improvement is noted after an initial course of appropriate duration. Approximately 30% of patients will improve with or without therapy.

A hernia is a protrusion of tissue through a defect in the surrounding fascia. There are three different types of groin hernias: indirect inguinal, direct inguinal, and femoral hernias. Indirect inguinal hernias, the most common type, originate at the internal inguinal ring, pass through the inguinal canal and external inguinal ring, and may descend into the scrotum in men. Direct inguinal hernias originate near the external inguinal ring and usually do not descend into the scrotum. Femoral hernias result from a protrusion of tissue below the inguinal ligament and medial to the femoral vessels.

Inguinal hernias occur more frequently among men, but femoral hernias, which account for less than 5% of groin hernias, are more common in women. Inguinal hernias may be asymptomatic or present as groin pain and/or a scrotal or inguinal bulge. Examination may reveal a visible or palpable bulge in the groin or scrotum that is accentuated by the Valsalva maneuver, although a visible bulge is less common in women. The diagnosis is often made clinically; imaging studies are rarely needed in men, but ultrasonography, the preferred imaging technique, is often required for diagnosis in women.

In patients with incarcerated hernias, reduction should be attempted by applying pressure to the area with the patient in the Trendelenburg position. If the hernia remains nonreducible, surgical evaluation should occur. Strangulation of a nonreducible hernia occurs when there is vascular compromise of the entrapped hernia. Strangulation should be suspected when a hernia is accompanied by significant tenderness, overlying erythema, or nausea and vomiting. A strangulated hernia is a surgical emergency, and the patient should be referred for immediate surgical evaluation.

Otherwise, in men, small, asymptomatic, or minimally symptomatic indirect and direct inguinal hernias may be observed or surgically repaired. Large or bothersome inguinal hernias are usually repaired surgically. In women, surgical repair is recommended for indirect and direct inguinal hernias. All femoral hernias, which have a greater risk for strangulation, should be repaired regardless of sex. Laparoscopic and open approaches have similar outcomes, but recovery time is shorter for the former.

Although the prevalence of urinary incontinence (UI) increases with age, it affects adults at all ages. More than 10% of adults in their 30s and 40s report urinary incontinence, with rates rising to at least 33% of community-dwelling adults older than 65 years and 66% of nursing home residents. The incidence is also higher in women than in men. The true prevalence is likely much higher, however, because many patients, especially men, do not report symptoms because of embarrassment. Older persons are often not assessed for UI and, when treated, are less likely to receive evidence-based treatment than younger individuals. UI increases the risk for falls, depression, and social isolation. It also reduces quality of life and is a major factor leading to loss of independence and nursing home placement.

Risk factors for UI include many common chronic medical conditions (e.g., diabetes, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, Parkinson disease, osteoarthritis, and dementia) along with the medications used in their treatment. Other risk factors are pelvic surgery, including hysterectomy and prostate surgery; pelvic irradiation; pelvic trauma; and obesity.

There are five main classifications of UI:

  • Stress
  • Urge
  • Overflow
  • Functional
  • Mixed

UI classifications and disorders predisposing patients to specific types of incontinence are presented in [Table: Table: Types of Urinary Incontinence and Commonly Associated Conditions]

. Stress UI and urge UI are most common, although mixed presentations frequently occur.

All pregnant and older patients should be asked about incontinence as part of their routine care because they may hesitate to volunteer information. Some guidelines additionally suggest routinely asking all women and middle-aged men about urinary incontinence. Questions about specific symptoms, precipitating events, duration, and frequency, and interference with quality of life, can be helpful in diagnosing the type of UI. Standardized questionnaires, such as the validated 3 Incontinence Questions (3IQ), are easy to administer in an office setting (see

). A voiding diary may also be helpful.

Evaluation should incorporate a targeted history, including surgeries, instrumentations, and radiation therapy. Female patients should be questioned about pregnancies and gynecologic procedures, and male patients should be asked about symptoms suggestive of prostate enlargement. Fluid intake, including amount, timing, and alcohol and caffeine use, should be assessed. A comprehensive medication history should be obtained, with special attention to the use of diuretics and medications with cholinergic or anticholinergic effects, including over-the-counter medications. Additionally, all patients should be screened for chronic conditions associated with increased risk for incontinence and impact on quality of life ( [Table: Table: Types of Urinary Incontinence and Commonly Associated Conditions]

).

The physical examination should include a neurologic and genitourinary examination, with pelvic examination in women for vaginal atrophy and pelvic prolapse, and prostate examination in men. Urinalysis is reasonable because transient incontinence may be explained by the presence of a urinary tract infection. Additional laboratory investigation or diagnostic testing is usually unnecessary. Postvoid residual assessment, which is performed with ultrasonography after spontaneous voiding, may be considered in patients in whom overflow incontinence is suspected. Urodynamic studies are required only for complex cases in which neurologic disease is suspected and surgical intervention is being considered.

Treatment strategies for UI are listed in [Table: Table: Treatment Strategies for Urinary Incontinence]

. Nonpharmacologic therapy consisting of lifestyle modification and behavioral therapy is the preferred treatment for all types of UI. Lifestyle modification, including weight loss (if appropriate), decreased consumption of alcohol and caffeine, treatment of constipation, and smoking cessation should be trialed for a minimum of 6 weeks. Behavioral therapy is more effective than pharmacologic therapy and should be initiated along with lifestyle modification as first-line therapy.

Pharmacologic therapy may be used as second-line therapy for some types of UI. Patients with continued symptoms and reduced quality of life despite behavioral and pharmacologic therapies should be referred to a specialist to consider third-line treatments, including device therapy, injectable agents, and surgery. Indwelling urinary catheters are not recommended for any type of incontinence because of the unacceptably high risk for infection associated with their use.

First-line behavioral therapy for stress and mixed UI is pelvic floor muscle training (Kegel exercises). Patients should be counseled that symptom improvement may not be noticeable until pelvic floor muscle training is consistently performed for several months. Some studies have demonstrated benefits of concomitant biofeedback therapy, in which a vaginal electromyography probe is used to provide direct confirmation that the patient is contracting the pelvic floor muscles correctly.

Vaginal estrogen formulations (tablets and ovules) increase continence compared with placebo in patients with stress UI, but transdermal patches or implants are not helpful. Systemic estrogen should not be used for stress or mixed UI, especially in patients with breast cancer.

Pessary devices are a low-risk, third-line treatment option for patients with stress UI. Limited high-quality evidence supports cystoscopically guided injection of bulking agents into the urethral mucosa at the bladder neck. In patients who respond, up to 70% require repeat injection. Surgical treatment is reserved for stress UI that does not respond to other therapies and typically consists of sling cystourethropexy for women or an artificial urinary sphincter for men. Intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxin A and midurethral sling surgery are third-line options for patients with mixed (combined stress and urge) urinary incontinence and are of similar efficacy.

Behavioral therapy for urge UI consists of bladder training and timed voiding ( [Table: Table: Treatment Strategies for Urinary Incontinence]

).

If behavioral therapy and lifestyle modification fail to correct urge or mixed UI, several classes of pharmacologic agents are available as second-line therapy ( [Table: Table: Treatment Strategies for Urinary Incontinence]

). Anticholinergic agents are contraindicated in patients with angle-closure glaucoma and severely impaired gastrointestinal motility and should be avoided in patients with tachyarrhythmias. These agents should be used with caution in men with BPH owing to the risk for urinary retention. Older persons are especially susceptible to the central nervous system effects of anticholinergics, and they should be avoided in patients with cognitive impairment.

Third-line therapy includes devices and procedural therapies. Refractory urge UI may be treated with botulinum toxin injections into the detrusor muscle. Adverse effects include urinary retention requiring self-catheterization. In rare cases, surgically implanted sacral nerve root neurostimulation devices may be used in combination with behavioral therapy and pharmacotherapy for refractory urge UI.

Behavioral therapy for overflow UI includes double voiding and triggered voiding. Intermittent catheterization may be used to decrease the need for containment products, such as pads or diapers.

Pharmacologic treatment of overflow UI associated with BPH is discussed in Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia in Interdisciplinary Medicine.

In patients with cognitive impairment–related functional UI, prompted voiding by the caregiver may be helpful. Prompted voiding involves regularly asking the patient to report about incontinence, inquiring whether they need to void and providing assistance, and praising them for maintaining continence.

Urinary retention can be classified based on its cause: obstructive, neurologic, or iatrogenic. It is most common in men, in whom obstruction can be caused by BPH (the most common cause), prostate cancer, phimosis/paraphimosis, or meatal stenosis. In women, acute urinary retention is rare. Obstructive causes in women include pelvic organ prolapse, uterine mass (fibroid or pelvic malignancy), or a gravid uterus. In both sexes, bladder calculi, bladder malignancies, and fecal impaction can result in obstructive urinary retention. Infections, such as prostatitis, urinary tract infections, and STIs, can also result in obstruction.

Neurologic causes of urinary retention often result from impairment of the sensory or motor neural pathways supplying the detrusor muscle, resulting in reduced detrusor activity. These causes include spinal cord injuries, demyelination processes such as multiple sclerosis, stroke, and neuropathies such as diabetic neuropathy.

Medication adverse effect is a frequent cause of urinary retention. Medications with anticholinergic adverse effects block the muscarinic receptors of the detrusor muscle, leading to reduced contractility. Other common causes are α-adrenergic agonists, which can increase prostate and bladder neck tone, and opioids, which inhibit the parasympathetic fibers that convey the sensation of bladder fullness. Postoperative urinary retention depends on the type of anesthesia, surgical procedure, and patient characteristics such as age and comorbidities. The use of α-blockers can reduce this risk.

Acute urinary retention usually presents with bladder distention and accompanying suprapubic pain, feelings of urinary urgency, and even urinary incontinence from overflow. Acute urinary retention requires urgent management with catheterization to decompress the bladder. The duration of catheterization will depend on the underlying cause. If the urinary retention is the result of an acute issue such as an infection or postoperative complication, then a voiding trial should be attempted as soon as possible. For male patients, treatment with α-blockers may increase the success rate of the voiding trial without catheterization.

Chronic urinary retention, generally defined as a postvoid residual of greater than 300 mL that persists over 6 months, can be asymptomatic. Symptomatic patients will generally present with urination difficulty, but unlike acute urinary retention, chronic retention is generally not painful. Management depends on the patient’s symptoms, any complications such as hydronephrosis or kidney injury, and the underlying cause.

Following catheterization, physicians should monitor patients for postobstructive diuresis, which can result in volume depletion, electrolyte abnormalities, and acute kidney injury, especially in patients with chronic urinary retention.

Balanitis is inflammation of the glans penis and is more common in uncircumcised men. The most common cause is accumulation of material such as skin cells and sweat due to poor hygiene, which can result in fungal and bacterial growth leading to inflammation. Patients often present with 3 to 7 days of pain, irritation, and erythema of the glans and foreskin. Proper hygiene is often sufficient for both prevention and management; however, empiric antifungals may also be used if needed.

Complications of balanitis include phimosis and paraphimosis. Phimosis, or the inability to retract the foreskin, is a result of inflammation and swelling of the foreskin. The foreskin can be forcibly dilated if necessary. Definitive treatment is elective circumcision.

Paraphimosis results when the foreskin becomes stuck behind the glans penis, resulting in vascular and lymphatic constriction of the glans. Patients present with erythema of the glans penis and significant pain. Failure to reduce paraphimosis constitutes a urological emergency.

Breast and Gynecologic Conditions

A palpable breast mass warrants evaluation in all patients. Although breast cancer should always be considered, most breast masses, particularly in women younger than 30 years, are benign conditions, such as cysts, fibroadenomas, fat necrosis, infections, or lipomas, or gynecomastia in men. For more information on gynecomastia, see Gynecomastia in Endocrinology and Metabolism.

Evaluation requires consideration of breast cancer risk factors (see [Table: Table: Breast Cancer Risk Factors]

) and a detailed history of the mass, including onset, changes with the menstrual cycle, associated symptoms, and changes in the overlying skin or nipples.

A clinical breast examination (CBE) should be performed in all patients presenting with a breast mass and includes the following:

  • Visual inspection, with attention to any skin changes
  • Palpation of the breast
  • Palpation of the axillary, supraclavicular, and cervical lymph nodes

Findings on CBE may suggest a benign (smooth, mobile, regular) or a malignant (fixed, hard, heterogeneous) process. However, the predictive value of CBE is poor, and all women require further evaluation with imaging and/or biopsy. In men, if symptoms and physical examination are consistent with gynecomastia, further evaluation should be directed toward the cause of the gynecomastia.

Imaging of a breast mass may include diagnostic mammography and targeted ultrasonography of the mass. Mammography is the first test performed in most women aged 30 years or older and men aged 25 years or older. The mammogram may demonstrate a mass, asymmetric density, or abnormal or pleomorphic calcifications potentially indicating breast cancer (see Staging and Prognosis of Breast Cancer in Oncology).

Ultrasonography is the preferred method of evaluation for women younger than 30 years and men younger than 25 years. It is also the test of choice in pregnant patients.

When breast imaging is completed, results are categorized by using the Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) (see [Table: Table: BI-RADS Assessment Categories]

). Biopsy is recommended for category 4 and 5 breast findings. Regardless of the BI-RADS category, however, any suspicious finding or mass detected on CBE should be evaluated by biopsy, even if no mass is identified on imaging. In most cases, if a patient requires a biopsy, an image-guided core-needle biopsy is the most appropriate choice. It is important to always perform imaging before biopsy because a biopsy can distort the tissue.

For cystic lesions, fine-needle aspiration may be appropriate for a simple cyst; however, if imaging suggests a benign process, aspiration may not be necessary. Any complex cyst that is BI-RADS category 4 or higher should be biopsied rather than aspirated.

Management of an abnormal finding requires consultation with a breast surgeon. A surgical biopsy is performed when the core-needle biopsy is technically challenging because of the location of the lesion, when atypical hyperplasia is seen on core-needle biopsy specimens, or when the pathology and imaging findings are discordant. Abnormalities on core needle biopsy, especially ductal carcinoma in situ, may require surgical excision to rule out a missed malignancy in the surrounding tissue (see Ductal Carcinoma in Situ in Oncology).

Breast pain (mastalgia) is common and may be cyclic or noncyclic in relation to the menstrual cycle. Cyclic breast pain is most common in women aged 20 to 39 years. The pain is often diffuse and bilateral, occurs during the premenstrual phase, and frequently resolves with onset of menstruation; it is usually associated with hormonal changes and is typically benign. Noncyclic breast pain is often caused by medication use (contraceptive agents, hormone therapy, psychiatric medications), underlying breast disease (fibrocystic disease, infection, trauma, cancer), or stretching of the Cooper ligaments (connective tissue that maintains breast structural integrity). Nonbreast causes of breast pain include costochondritis, trauma, coronary artery disease, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and intercostal nerve pain.

Evaluation of breast pain includes a detailed history to identify characteristics of the pain and its relationship to menses as well as a CBE. Care should be taken to ensure all women evaluated for breast pain with no obvious abnormal findings are up to date with routine age- and risk-appropriate breast cancer screening. Women with cyclical pain and a normal CBE result do not require additional imaging. Patients with noncyclic focal mastalgia who are younger than 30 years should be evaluated with breast ultrasonography, whereas those older than age 30 years should undergo diagnostic mammography and breast ultrasonography. Any palpable breast mass should be evaluated with diagnostic imaging (see Breast Mass in Interdisciplinary Medicine).

For women with cyclic breast pain and negative clinical findings, conservative management (education, reassurance of the absence of malignancy, advice to wear a supportive and well-fitting brassiere, and topical NSAID therapy) is recommended because cyclic pain usually resolves spontaneously. Medical management, typically with danazol or tamoxifen, is rarely indicated but may be offered for patients with severe pain that persists despite conservative management.

Treatment of noncyclic breast pain depends on the underlying cause.

Mastitis is inflammation of the breast tissue that usually occurs during lactation. Lactational mastitis is secondary to milk stasis and usually occurs within the first 3 months of lactation. It presents with severe pain, redness, warmth, and swelling of the breast. Initial treatment includes NSAIDs, cold compresses, and, most importantly, complete breast emptying through nursing or pumping. Infection may result, and antibiotics should be given if symptoms are severe at presentation or persist after 12 to 24 hours of breast drainage. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause, and cephalexin or dicloxacillin is used in the absence of methicillin-resistant S. aureus risk factors. Therapy may be directed by the results of breast milk culture, and ultrasonography should be performed if abscess is suspected.

Nipple discharge most commonly results from physiologic causes (galactorrhea), but it may also be associated with malignancy. Evaluation is always necessary. Galactorrhea is characterized by discharge that is bilateral, emanates from multiple ductal openings, and may occur with breast movement. Pregnancy is the most common cause, but thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, and the use of certain medications (e.g., antipsychotic and antidepressant agents) may also be causative. Testing includes a pregnancy test, thyroid-stimulating hormone level, and prolactin level.

Nipple discharge that is unilateral or bloody, occurs without breast movement, or occurs in a woman older than 40 years raises concern for a pathologic cause, including intraductal papilloma and breast cancer. Evaluation is guided by patient age. In patients older than 30 years, both mammography and breast ultrasonography should be completed. In patients younger than 30 years, ultrasonography is the first-line test.

Abnormal uterine bleeding is defined as excessive bleeding in terms of flow volume, frequency, or duration. Among nonpregnant women of reproductive age, abnormal uterine bleeding is classified according to cause by using the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics system with the acronym PALM-COEIN, which stands for the following:

  • Polyp
  • Adenomyosis
  • Leiomyoma
  • Malignancy and hyperplasia
  • Coagulopathy
  • Ovulation dysfunction
  • Endometrial
  • Iatrogenic
  • Not yet classified

Abnormal uterine bleeding in this population can be further classified as ovulatory or anovulatory. [Table: Table: Classification of AUB in Nonpregnant Women of Reproductive Age]

describes the characteristics and causes of abnormal uterine bleeding in these patients. Ovulatory bleeding is accentuation of the cyclic menstrual bleeding. In anovulatory bleeding, the lack of ovulation and cyclic progesterone leads to irregular bleeding, endometrial hyperplasia, and an increased risk for endometrial cancer.

Evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding in the premenopausal woman starts with a detailed history, including assessment of menstrual history and medical and gynecologic history. Physical examination should assess for evidence of acute bleeding. Pelvic examination can determine the source of the bleeding, assess for trauma to the genital tract, and look for uterine enlargement or irregularity. Initial laboratory testing includes a pregnancy test, complete blood count, and ferritin level. Additional testing should be based on clinical indications and may include coagulation tests and thyroid-stimulating hormone level. Young women with heavy menses should be screened for bleeding disorders, specifically von Willebrand disease.

Transvaginal ultrasonography may be considered to evaluate for structural abnormalities, particularly if physical examination suggests an enlarged or irregularly contoured uterus. Although transvaginal ultrasonography can be used in postmenopausal women to evaluate the endometrial stripe and risk for endometrial cancer, it is not useful in evaluating for endometrial cancer in premenopausal women.

Endometrial biopsy should be done in premenopausal women aged 45 years or older and those younger than 45 years who are at increased risk for endometrial cancer secondary to tobacco use, a history of unopposed estrogen (polycystic ovary syndrome, obesity); tamoxifen use; Lynch or Cowden syndrome; or reproductive factors, such as early menarche or nulliparity.

Management of abnormal uterine bleeding is aimed at the underlying cause. Structural abnormalities, such as endometrial polyps or submucosal fibroids, may be surgically resected. Treatment of underlying endocrine disorders (thyroid disease, polycystic ovary syndrome) may result in improvement.

For women with heavy ovulatory cycles, treatment is aimed at reducing menstrual blood loss. Hormonal contraception is often the first-line treatment, assuming the woman desires contraception. NSAIDs may also be used because these drugs reduce synthesis of prostaglandins in the endometrium, leading to vasoconstriction and reduced bleeding. Oral tranexamic acid, an antithrombotic agent, stabilizes clots and may be used for treatment of heavy uterine bleeding and in women who cannot tolerate hormonal treatment.

For women with anovulatory cycles, treatment is aimed at providing adequate progestin to maintain endometrial stability. The type of therapy depends on the patient’s plans for contraception. For women who wish to preserve fertility, medroxyprogesterone acetate used for the second half of the menstrual cycle will restore cyclic withdrawal bleeding. For women interested in contraception, oral contraceptive pills containing estrogen and progesterone, a progestin-containing intrauterine device, depot medroxyprogesterone, and other forms of hormonal contraception may be used. Endometrial hyperplasia on biopsy requires treatment with progestins.

For women experiencing acute and severe bleeding, such agents as gonadotropin-releasing hormone or intravenous administration of high-dose estrogens may be used. For women who do not respond to medical therapy, operative procedures, such as endometrial ablation, uterine artery embolization, or hysterectomy, may be performed.

After menopause, women should not experience uterine bleeding. Causes of bleeding include endometrial polyps, endometrial atrophy, and vaginal atrophy as well as endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma. The evaluation of postmenopausal bleeding includes a detailed history and physical examination, including a pelvic examination. Because postmenopausal uterine bleeding is concerning for endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma, all postmenopausal patients with uterine bleeding should undergo endometrial biopsy unless a transvaginal ultrasound reveals an endometrial stripe 4 mm thick or less.

Dysmenorrhea is characterized by cramping lower abdominal and pelvic pain during menstruation; it may also be associated with low back pain, headache, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Dysmenorrhea is classified as primary or secondary. Primary dysmenorrhea occurs during menstrual cycles without an identifiable cause. Secondary dysmenorrhea may result from pelvic conditions, of which endometriosis is the most common.

A detailed history is necessary to assess the timing of pain and the relationship to the menstrual cycle. Sexual history is important to assess infection risk. Primary dysmenorrhea can be treated with NSAIDs or hormonal contraception, including estrogen-progesterone and progesterone-only methods. Secondary dysmenorrhea requires treatment of the underlying condition.

Menopause is the permanent cessation of menses. The average age of menopause in the United States is between 51 and 52 years. It is diagnosed retrospectively 12 months after the final menstrual period. Menopause may be natural; surgical, after bilateral oophorectomy; or medical, as a result of such treatments as chemotherapy. Menopause occurring before age 40 years is considered premature menopause or, more appropriately, primary ovarian insufficiency. Menopause starting between age 40 and 45 years is considered early menopause. Perimenopause refers to the years preceding menopause when ovarian function declines and is often associated with anovulatory cycles, hot flashes, and other symptoms resulting from changing estrogen levels. Perimenopausal symptoms may start as early as the late 30s in healthy women.

Symptoms of menopause include vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, night sweats). Hot flashes generally start in the perimenopausal period and can last for a few years or may be lifelong. Symptomatic genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) occurs in approximately half of all women and is characterized by vaginal burning, irritation, dyspareunia, dysuria, and recurrent urinary tract infections. Pelvic examination findings may include a pale, dry vaginal lining with reduction in rugae (see

). Women may also experience other symptoms, such as depression, anxiety, and irritability, but it is unclear whether these symptoms can be attributed to menopause. Increases in LDL cholesterol, abdominal adiposity, and bone loss may also occur.

Routine laboratory testing for the diagnosis of menopause after age 45 years is not recommended because the diagnosis can be made clinically. Patients with possible primary ovarian insufficiency (onset age <40 years) should have pregnancy ruled out and undergo measurement of follicle-stimulating hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone, prolactin, and estradiol levels. Testing can also be considered in patients with early menopause (age of onset, 40-45 years) (see Evaluation of Amenorrhea in Endocrinology and Metabolism).

It is important to remember that pregnancy is possible in the perimenopausal period, even if menstrual cycles are irregular, and contraception should be discussed if pregnancy is not desired. Estrogen-containing contraception can also treat any vasomotor symptoms present in the perimenopause period.

Systemic estrogen therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and may improve quality of life. Hormone therapy is considered safe for most women before age 60 years or when initiated within 10 years of menopause. The approach to initiating menopausal hormone therapy is outlined in

.

When systemic estrogen therapy is initiated, the lowest dose required to manage symptoms should be used. Women who have an intact uterus also require a progesterone component dosed continuously or cyclically to avoid estrogen-related endometrial proliferation. Continuous dosing does not result in cyclic vaginal bleeding, whereas estrogen with cyclic progesterone will result in withdrawal bleeding.

Common contraindications to hormone therapy include pregnancy, unexplained vaginal bleeding, liver disease, coronary artery disease, stroke, thromboembolic disease, breast cancer, and endometrial cancer. Adverse events associated with estrogen therapy include cardiovascular disease and venous thromboembolism. These risks are greatest when therapy is initiated more than 10 years from menopause. Transdermal estrogen is preferable to oral estrogen because it is associated with less thromboembolic risk.

Combination hormone therapy results in a slight increase in the risk for breast cancer and an elevated cardiovascular risk, especially in women older than 60 years and/or those with increased baseline risk. All women considering hormone therapy should receive individualized risk assessment and counseling. Women without a uterus who are using estrogen alone do not have a clinically significant increased risk for breast cancer. Use of hormone therapy in menopause should be reassessed every year to determine benefits and risks. Treatment duration is based on continued presence of vasomotor symptoms.

For women who prefer not to use or have contraindications to hormone therapy, nonhormonal drugs can help modulate vasomotor symptoms. Antidepressant agents, including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (such as citalopram, escitalopram, and paroxetine), and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (such as venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, and duloxetine) as well as gabapentin and fezolinetant, are effective. Cognitive behavioral therapy and clinical hypnosis are also recommended by the North American Menopause Society’s 2023 position statement on nonhormone therapy. The use of clonidine and pregabalin are not supported by evidence and research on supplements, such as soy, black cohosh, and other phytoestrogens, for treating vasomotor symptoms remains inconclusive.

Management of GSM includes topical low-dose estrogen therapy to relieve symptoms such as vaginal dryness, itching, and irritation. Nonhormonal agents, including as-needed vaginal lubricants for intercourse and vaginal moisturizers, are also available.

Vaginal hormonal preparations include estradiol or conjugated estrogen in tablet, cream, or ring forms. Low-dose vaginal estrogen builds the vaginal epithelium and restores the acidic pH and microenvironment. Moreover, improving the lining of the lower urethra reduces dysuria and recurrent urinary tract infection. For women with breast cancer (current or past), low-dose vaginal hormone therapy may be used in the context of multidisciplinary shared decision making. Vaginal dehydroepiandrosterone is another option for GSM treatment.

The selective estrogen receptor modulator ospemifene is another FDA-approved treatment option for GSM; most experts consider it a second-line option because of adverse effects.

Although the differential diagnosis of acute pelvic pain is broad, clinicians should first consider several critical diagnoses, including ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), ruptured ovarian cyst, ovarian torsion, and appendicitis, when evaluating a woman with acute pelvic pain. See Causes of Abdominal and Pelvic Pain in Common Symptoms.

Medical history taking should elicit characteristics of the pain, past diagnoses and surgeries, and sexual history. Physical examination focuses on vital signs, abdominal/pelvic examination, and bimanual examination. A pregnancy test should be obtained for all women of reproductive age presenting with acute pelvic pain. Any woman with a positive pregnancy test should have ectopic pregnancy ruled out before other diagnoses are considered. Other laboratory testing may include sexually transmitted infection (STI) testing, complete blood cell count, and type and screen depending on the clinical scenario. Transvaginal ultrasonography can help diagnose ectopic pregnancy, ovarian cysts, ovarian torsion, and tubo-ovarian abscess as a complication of PID and is usually the diagnostic test of choice when these diagnoses are a consideration.

The management of acute pelvic pain depends on the diagnosis. Women with ectopic pregnancies should be promptly evaluated by an obstetrician to determine whether surgery or medical management with methotrexate is appropriate. The treatment of PID is covered in Pelvic Inflammatory Disease in Infectious Disease. A gynecologist should be involved in the management of ovarian cysts, particularly for a ruptured hemorrhagic cyst in a patient with unstable vital signs and ovarian torsion, which is considered a surgical emergency. Appendicitis requires surgical consultation.

Chronic pelvic pain (CPP) refers to pelvic pain lasting 6 months or longer; it is often associated with negative behavioral, emotional, sexual, or cognitive consequences. Evaluation and diagnosis of CPP are challenging because the cause is often multifactorial and involves both physiologic and psychological components. Risk factors for CPP include the following:

  • Physical, sexual, and/or emotional abuse
  • Pelvic inflammatory disease
  • History of abdominopelvic surgery
  • Chronic pain syndromes
  • Psychological conditions, such as anxiety or depression

Common causes of CPP can be classified as gynecologic, gastrointestinal, urologic, and musculoskeletal/neurologic as outlined in [Table: Table: Common Causes of Chronic Pelvic Pain]

.

Evaluation includes a detailed history to determine characteristics of the pain, including association with menstrual cycle, urination, or bowel movement, as well as assessment for risk factors and known causes of CPP. The physical examination includes detailed abdominal, neurologic, and gynecologic examinations. Laboratory testing is of limited value unless specific disorders are suggested by the history and clinical examination (such as urinalysis for urinary tract infection or STI testing). Transvaginal ultrasonography is used to identify anatomic pathology, such as a pelvic mass. A normal pelvic examination and normal transvaginal ultrasound are reassuring, and further testing with pelvic MRI or laparoscopy is of limited utility.

Treatment is aimed at the underlying cause and may be challenging if the cause is not identified. An interdisciplinary multimodal approach to treatment is often required. Menstrual suppression with hormonal contraception can help many patients. Pelvic floor physical therapy, cognitive behavioral therapy, and sex therapy are recommended. Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, gabapentin, and pregabalin may be helpful in patients with neuropathic pain. Trigger point injections should be considered in those with myofascial chronic pelvic pain. Acupuncture and yoga may be helpful for some patients. NSAIDs may be helpful for patients with moderate CPP. Routine surgical lysis of adhesions is not indicated. Peripheral nerve block or surgical release can also be used for suspected nerve impingement or entrapment.

Uterine fibroids are the most common pelvic tumor in women. Risk factors include early menarche, obesity, being of African descent, and a family history of uterine fibroids. Although they are asymptomatic in many patients, mass effect may lead to pelvic pain, and impingement on the bladder or bowel may lead to urinary or bowel symptoms. Masses may also result in compromised fertility secondary to changes in uterine shape. Heavy menstrual bleeding is also common, especially with submucosal fibroids.

Diagnosis is often suggested by the presence of an abnormal uterus on physical examination, but transvaginal ultrasonography is diagnostic. Advanced imaging, such as MRI, is rarely necessary, except for planning of surgical therapy.

Treatment is dictated by symptoms. In patients with heavy bleeding, combined oral contraceptives are an effective option. A progestin-based intrauterine device may also be useful in selected patients. In patients with pain secondary to mass effect, surgery may be appropriate with the approach determined by patient preference, including desire for preservation of fertility. Hysterectomy, myomectomy, and uterine artery embolization may be appropriate in selected patients.

Endometriosis is the presence of endometrial tissue external to the uterus. The most common location is the ovaries (endometrioma), but it may occur anywhere in the pelvis, including the fallopian tubes, posterior cul-de-sac, colon, and round ligaments. Endometriosis may be present in 6% to 10% of reproductive-age females, but the clinical presentation is variable. Cyclic pain, dyspareunia, and dysmenorrhea are common; infertility may also be present. The physical examination may reveal localized areas of tenderness or palpable masses in involved areas but can be normal. Although a definitive diagnosis requires laparoscopy with biopsy, a presumptive diagnosis of endometriosis is often made on clinical grounds. Transvaginal ultrasonography may be helpful in identifying endometriomas and other implants.

Treatment is guided by symptoms and extent of disease. Menstrual suppression with the use of continuous combined oral contraceptives or progestins alone is often effective. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists are also effective. Ablative surgery may be necessary for extensive disease, refractory symptoms, or infertility.

Female sexual dysfunction is characterized by persistent or recurrent distressing sexual concerns or difficulties and is common, particularly in menopausal and perimenopausal women. According to the DSM-5, female sexual dysfunction is divided into three categories:

  • Female sexual interest/arousal disorder
  • Female orgasmic disorder
  • Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder

Female sexual interest/arousal disorder is characterized by a lack of or significant decrease in sexual activity, including sexual interest, thoughts, excitement, and pleasure. Female orgasmic disorder is characterized by a significant delay in, infrequency of, or absence of orgasm, or significantly decreased intensity of orgasm during sexual activity.

Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder is characterized by persistent or recurrent difficulty with sexual intercourse, vulvovaginal or pelvic pain during intercourse, fear or anxiety about such pain, and/or involuntary tensing or tightening of pelvic floor muscles during attempted vaginal penetration.

Diagnosis of any of these sexual disorders requires that the symptoms of the disorder occur more than 75% of the time for at least 6 months and cause clinically significant distress.

Beyond the three categories of female sexual dysfunction, women may experience sexual dysfunction related to medical conditions or as adverse effects from medications. Perinatal events, such as cesarean or instrument delivery or perineal tears, may cause pelvic pain. Estrogen levels are lower during breastfeeding, which may result in vaginal dryness. Mental health conditions such as depression may contribute to decreased sexual desire or frequency. Additionally, sexual dysfunction is a common adverse effect of antidepressants. Menopause, GSM, gynecologic surgeries, or treatment for gynecologic malignancies may also affect sexual function.

In assessing sexual function, it is important to realize that sexual functioning involves multiple components, including emotions, relationships, experiences, physiologic responses, overall health, and personal beliefs; therefore, a comprehensive approach is needed to evaluate and treat the condition.

Assessment of female sexual dysfunction includes the following:

  • Detailed questions regarding the patient’s sexual and gender identity
  • Symptom characteristics, including duration, acute or gradual onset, and whether symptoms are associated with a specific partner or are a generalized concern
  • Association with pain
  • Precipitating events
  • Level of distress caused by the symptoms
  • Current life stressors
  • Medical and surgical history
  • Medications
  • History of physical, emotional, and/or sexual abuse

Screening for concurrent depression is indicated. The Female Sexual Function Index or the Female Sexual Distress Scale can be used during the assessment. Pelvic examination is aimed at assessing for specific sites of pain or tenderness, vaginal dryness, or atrophy. Laboratory testing is of limited value and is performed only if an underlying cause is suspected.

Therapy is aimed at the underlying cause of female sexual dysfunction, which is often multifactorial. There are two FDA-approved medications for female sexual dysfunction:

  • Flibanserin, a serotonin receptor agonist/antagonist, is approved for premenopausal women with female sexual interest/arousal disorder without depression. Its use is limited secondary to adverse effects (dizziness, syncope, hypotension, somnolence), the incidence of which is increased when the drug is combined with alcohol or certain medications, such as antidepressants.
  • Bremelanotide is a subcutaneous injection also approved for use in premenopausal women with sexual interest/arousal disorder, but it can only be used eight times per month and is limited by adverse effects (skin darkening, nausea, vomiting).

Off-label use of bupropion may improve sexual functioning, although extensive data are lacking. Bupropion is more commonly chosen when selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor– or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor–associated sexual dysfunction requires consideration of an alternative treatment for depression. Similarly, low-dose testosterone treatment (off-label) increases sexual function scores; however, adverse effects must be discussed and long-term safety data are lacking.

For women whose symptoms are related to vaginal dryness and atrophy, vaginal moisturizers and vaginal estrogen therapy may be helpful. Lubricants can be used as needed for intercourse. Pelvic physical therapy and objects, such as dilators, to increase the diameter of the vagina may be used for patients with vulvovaginal pain. Ospemifene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator approved by the FDA for treatment of dyspareunia associated with vulvovaginal atrophy.

Treatment strategies must also address the psychological and behavioral aspects of female sexual dysfunction. Cognitive behavioral therapy, couples therapy, or sex therapy may be helpful. Treatment of concomitant mental health conditions, such as depression and anxiety, is also important.

Vaginitis describes conditions associated with vulvovaginal symptoms that may include vaginal discharge, burning, itching, or odor. Normal physiologic vaginal discharge is odorless and is not associated with any irritation. The most common causes of vaginitis are infectious and include bacterial vaginosis, candidiasis, and trichomoniasis (see [Table: Table: Presentation, Evaluation, and Management of Vaginitis]

). Other noninfectious causes of vaginitis include irritant vaginitis, allergic vaginitis, and atrophic vaginitis.

History should include details about the vaginal discharge (volume, color, odor), relation to menstruation, use of douches or other products, sexual history, dysuria, and dyspareunia. Physical examination includes assessment of the vulva and vagina for erythema, edema, excoriation, and discharge. However, history and physical examination alone are insufficient for diagnosis, and laboratory testing is necessary to determine the cause before initiating treatment. Diagnostic testing traditionally includes assessment of vaginal pH, amine (whiff) test, and microscopic evaluation with saline and potassium hydroxide (KOH) wet mounts. Although these tests allow for immediate diagnosis at low cost, physician offices may not have the necessary equipment or expertise to perform them. Increasingly, nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) of vaginal discharge are being used to diagnose bacterial vaginosis, candidiasis, and trichomoniasis; they also are useful in detecting cervicitis caused by gonorrhea and chlamydia. The performance of NAATs is far superior to that of traditional tests for vaginitis, with sensitivities and specificities exceeding 90%, but at greater expense. NAATs can be used for initial evaluation or when pH and microscopy testing is inconclusive.

The characteristics of bacterial vaginosis, vulvovaginal candidiasis, and trichomoniasis are presented in [Table: Table: Presentation, Evaluation, and Management of Vaginitis]

.

Bacterial vaginosis is the most common cause of vaginitis. It results from the loss of the normal hydrogen peroxide– and lactic acid–producing lactobacilli in the vagina, with an increase in the vaginal pH that contributes to an overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis and other anaerobes. Anaerobic overgrowth results in the production of amines, causing the characteristically malodorous discharge. Patients with bacterial vaginosis are at increased risk for STIs, including HIV infection, as well as for preterm delivery (see Sexually Transmitted Infections in Infectious Disease).

More than half of patients with bacterial vaginosis are asymptomatic.

For symptomatic patients, the Amsel criteria for a positive diagnosis are fulfilled when three of the four conditions are present:

  • A thin vaginal discharge with a fishy odor
  • Vaginal pH greater than 4.5
  • A positive whiff test result in which application of 10% KOH to vaginal secretions results in a fishy odor; and
  • The presence of clue cells, vaginal epithelial cells that on microscopy have ill-defined cell borders due to adherent coccobacilli (see

).

Although a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) can confirm the diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis, it is not required to make the diagnosis when the Amsel criteria are satisfied.

Asymptomatic bacterial vaginosis does not require treatment. [Table: Table: Presentation, Evaluation, and Management of Vaginitis]

outlines treatment options for symptomatic bacterial vaginosis. Of note, newer data suggest that the treatment of male partners with both oral metronidazole and topical clindamycin reduces the recurrence of bacterial vaginosis in women.

Vulvovaginal candidiasis is the second most common cause of vaginitis; it is usually caused by Candida albicans and less commonly by nonalbicans Candida. Unlike pharyngeal candidiasis, it frequently occurs in immunocompetent women with no risk factors. Factors that may increase the risk for vulvovaginal candidiasis include diabetes mellitus, pregnancy, and use of glucocorticoids or antibiotics. Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis is categorized as infections occurring three or more times per year.

Vulvovaginal candidiasis is typically characterized by vaginal itching, irritation, and discharge and may be associated with dysuria. Examination reveals vulvar edema and excoriation, with thick, white, curdy vaginal discharge. Diagnostic testing involves 10% KOH wet mount of the discharge showing yeast, hyphae, or pseudohyphae (see

) or positive NAAT. For recurrent infections, cultures are important because patients may have an infection with a non-albicans Candida species requiring different treatment.

Asymptomatic patients should not receive treatment. See [Table: Table: Presentation, Evaluation, and Management of Vaginitis]

for treatment options for symptomatic uncomplicated and complicated vulvovaginal candidiasis. Recurrent symptoms after treatment warrant an evaluation for underlying predisposing factors.

Trichomoniasis is a vaginal infection caused by Trichomonas vaginalis, a flagellated protozoan, and is an STI. It is associated with increased risk for preterm labor in pregnancy as well as increased risk for HIV transmission.

Women may be asymptomatic or present with copious vaginal discharge that is malodorous; pale yellow, green, or gray; and frothy. It is often associated with vulvar itching and burning. Vaginal pH is often elevated, but this is not helpful diagnostically. Although microscopy with examination of a wet mount of the vaginal fluid showing motile trichomonads can be diagnostic (see

), the CDC recommends NAAT. When Trichomonas is identified, testing for other STIs should be considered. See [Table: Table: Presentation, Evaluation, and Management of Vaginitis]

for treatment of trichomoniasis. Women should be retested within 3 months of treatment. Treatment of sexual partners is recommended to prevent reinfection.

Vulvar symptoms are often related to diseases and physiologic processes that affect the vagina, including vaginitis and GSM. See Vaginitis in Interdisciplinary Medicine and Menopause in Interdisciplinary Medicine for more information. Vulvar cancer, vulvar lichen planus, vulvar lichen simplex, and vulvar lichen sclerosus may be limited to the vulvar surfaces and are discussed in this section. There is substantial overlap in the clinical presentation of these disorders, and biopsy is often necessary for diagnosis.

Vulvar cancer most frequently develops in patients older than 50 years and is usually squamous cell carcinoma linked to chronic inflammation or human papillomavirus infection. It presents as a mass, nodule, or plaque on the vulva that is often asymptomatic but may be friable and bleed. Evaluation of a suspicious lesion includes colposcopy and biopsy.

Vulvar squamous intraepithelial lesions are raised white or macular lesions on the vulva that are frequently multifocal. Although many do not have malignant potential, high-grade lesions may progress to squamous cell carcinoma, and colposcopy and biopsy should be performed.

Lichen simplex chronicus, lichen sclerosus, and lichen planus often present with significant vulvar pruritus. [Table: Table: Lichen Simplex Chronicus, Lichen Sclerosus, and Lichen Planus Findings]

describes the clinical findings of each condition.

Lichen simplex chronicus is a chronic nonscarring dermatitis of the vulva and is often secondary to atopic dermatitis. The itch and resulting scratching drive further itching and skin breakdown, resulting in thickened and lichenified skin. Diagnosis is clinical, and treatment involves patient education to stop scratching, vulvar hygiene, and topical medium- or high-dose glucocorticoids as needed to control symptoms.

Both lichen sclerosus and lichen planus are scarring inflammatory disorders. The pruritus of lichen sclerosus can be particularly debilitating and have a significant impact on quality of life. Lichen sclerosus is usually limited to the anogenital skin, whereas lichen planus is more typically widespread. Biopsy should be considered in patients with lichen sclerosus and lichen planus to confirm the diagnosis and to assess for malignancy because the chronic inflammation can increase the risk for squamous cell carcinoma. Lichen sclerosus and lichen planus are both treated with high-potency topical glucocorticoids. For more information on lichen planus, see Lichen Planus in Dermatology.
