Clinical Evaluation of Kidney Function

The kidney selectively removes waste while retaining needed substrate, maintains fluid and electrolyte homeostasis, regulates blood pH, maintains bone health, and produces erythropoietin. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) measures total nephron filtration of blood and correlates closely with toxin removal and overall kidney function. Other markers of disordered glomerular function, such as proteinuria and hematuria, are also indicators of kidney disease that may precede any evidence of reduced filtration.

Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) is a product of protein metabolism. Levels increase with reduced GFR and with increased urea reabsorption caused by renal hypoperfusion. BUN is also affected by protein intake and catabolic rate. Lower levels are noted in starvation and in patients with liver disease. BUN will increase with glucocorticoids, hemorrhage, or trauma. BUN may be useful in detecting renal hypoperfusion when elevation of BUN from increased reabsorption is disproportionate to the rise in serum creatinine level.

Although numerous methods for estimating kidney function are available ( [Table: Table: Methods for Estimating Kidney Function]

), serum creatinine and serum cystatin C are the primary biomarkers used to estimate GFR. Estimated GFR (eGFR) has several implications, including staging of chronic kidney disease, drug dosing, and eligibility for clinical trials and kidney transplantation. Early loss of kidney function is difficult to detect because compensation through hypertrophy and hyperfiltration preserve GFR despite nephron loss.

Serum creatinine is the most extensively used measure of kidney function. Creatinine is freely filtered by the glomerulus and is also secreted into the urine by the proximal tubule. The relationship of serum creatinine to GFR is nonlinear; significant losses in kidney function at higher GFR may be masked by only small changes in serum creatinine, whereas small filtration changes at lower GFR are associated with large fluctuations in serum creatinine (

). The contribution of tubular secretion as a proportion of total creatinine excretion increases as GFR declines. Therefore, when urine creatinine clearance is used to estimate GFR, secreted creatinine will contribute to overestimation of true GFR. With complete loss of kidney function (anuria), serum creatinine may increase by up to 1.0 mg/dL (88.4 μmol/L) per day in patients with average muscle mass.

Creatinine is a metabolite of creatine, which is mostly present in skeletal muscle. Persons who have higher muscle mass or take creatine supplements have a higher serum creatinine compared with less muscular persons with the same GFR. Loss of muscle mass that occurs in aging, muscle wasting, malnutrition, or amputation will result in lower serum creatinine despite stable GFR. In persons with decreased muscle mass, serum creatinine therefore tends to overestimate the GFR.

Some medications, including cimetidine, trimethoprim, cobicistat, dolutegravir, and bictegravir, inhibit proximal tubule secretion of creatinine, resulting in elevated serum creatinine without a change in GFR.

Creatinine-based formulas are used to estimate GFR by adjusting for factors that affect serum creatinine and creatinine clearance. These formulas account for the effects of age, sex, and/or muscle mass (estimated by weight) (see [Table: Table: Methods for Estimating Kidney Function]

). Some formulas, such as older versions of the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) creatinine equation and the Modification of Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD) study equation, include race as a variable as well; however, this inclusion may translate into delayed or inequitable care, because race is a social construct, not a biological variable. For example, an older version of the CKD-EPI creatinine equation for a patient identified as Black resulted in an estimated GFR that was 16% higher than any other race. See Race-Based Medicine in Foundations of Clinical Practice for additional information.

The CKD-EPI creatinine equation is the most widely used method for estimating GFR and is the most accurate equation for most persons, particularly in older persons and those with a GFR >60 mL/min/1.73 m^2. To estimate GFR, the National Kidney Foundation and the American Society of Nephrology recommend using the 2021 CKD-EPI creatinine equation, which has been refitted to estimate kidney function without a race variable (see [Table: Table: Methods for Estimating Kidney Function]

). When using CKD-EPI to calculate drug dosages requiring adjustment for GFR, eGFR should be multiplied by body surface area/1.73 m^2, particularly in persons with very high or very low body surface area.

The MDRD study equation does not accurately estimate high GFRs. Clinical laboratories that use the MDRD do not report GFRs >60 mL/min/1.73 m^2; therefore, physicians may not be aware of the presence of kidney disease in its early stages. In this context, an increasing serum creatinine level, proteinuria, or other urine abnormalities should alert the clinician to the presence of kidney disease.

The Cockcroft-Gault equation is the least accurate method. However, it remains in use for drug dosing because it was used in pharmacokinetic studies for most medications.

Creatinine clearance obtained by using 24-hour urine collection may be a more accurate measure of GFR than serum creatinine alone, particularly in patients whose serum creatinine may be an over- or underestimation of their true muscle mass. However, it is not recommended for routine estimation of GFR because it is affected by both the completeness of collection (e.g., an under collection will underestimate creatinine clearance) and by tubular creatinine secretion.

Radionuclide imaging provides the most accurate measurement of GFR and is the gold standard in research. It is useful for accurate determination of GFR during the following:

  • Evaluation of kidney donors
  • Evaluation of recipients for other organs
  • Assessment of the differential GFR of each kidney before nephrectomy

Cystatin C is produced by all nucleated cells, freely filtered by glomeruli, and catabolized by tubules. Compared with serum creatinine, serum cystatin C levels are less affected by age, sex, or muscle mass but may be increased by certain conditions (such as malignancy, hyperthyroidism, inflammation, or HIV infection) as well as glucocorticoids or smoking. Changes in serum cystatin C may identify small decreases in kidney function better than serum creatinine. Formulas using cystatin C to estimate GFR are particularly helpful for patients in whom creatinine-based GFR may be inaccurate (such as in cases of drug-induced reduction of creatinine secretion described earlier, or in those with reduced or increased muscle mass).

Combining filtration markers (creatinine and cystatin C) into the CKD-EPI creatinine-cystatin C equation is more accurate and informs clinical decision making (such as in drug dosing or treatment eligibility) better than either marker alone.

Urine dipstick and urine microscopy are indicated in the evaluation of both acute and chronic kidney disease ( [Table: Table: Findings on Urinalysis]

). Analysis is best performed on a fresh specimen within 30 to 60 minutes of voiding. A clean-catch, early morning midstream collection is preferred.

See [Table: Table: Findings on Urinalysis]

for details on urine dipstick.

Specific gravity reflects hydration status and the kidney’s ability to concentrate urine. A specific gravity of 1.010 indicates isosthenuria because it is of similar specific gravity to plasma.

Low urine pH may occur in persons eating high-protein diets or those with metabolic acidosis and volume depletion. Alkaline urine (pH ≥7.0) may be detected in vegetarians and those with infections caused by urea-splitting organisms (e.g., Proteus). Urine pH may be inappropriately high in some forms of renal tubular acidosis (type 1 distal) and may be appropriately low in others (type 4 distal).

Dipstick reflects pseudoperoxidase activity of erythrocytes and free heme pigments (hemoglobin and myoglobin). Three or more erythrocytes result in a positive test (1+ blood). A positive test in the absence of erythrocytes in the urine sediment may indicate myoglobinuria (due to rhabdomyolysis) or hemoglobinuria (due to intravascular hemolysis following transfusion, or shear stress related to mechanical heart valve and perivalvular leak). False-positive tests may occur with other substances with pseudoperoxidase activity, including peroxidase-expressing bacteria (Enterobacteriaceae, staphylococci) and drugs such as chloroquine. Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) and a high specific gravity can cause a false-negative result. Medications (rifampin, phenytoin) or food (beets) can cause heme-negative, red-colored urine.

Although various proteins may be present in urine, the dipstick preferentially detects albumin. Because dipsticks are dependent on urine concentration, false negatives may result from dilute urine and false positives may result from highly concentrated urine. False-positive tests can also occur with highly alkaline urine specimens (urine pH >7). Because moderately increased albuminuria (formerly known as microalbuminuria) may go undetected by dipstick, direct quantification of albuminuria and/or proteinuria using a random (spot) protein-creatinine ratio or albumin-creatinine ratio or a 24-hour urine collection is required in high-risk patients.

Glucosuria typically occurs when plasma glucose exceeds 180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L). Glucosuria in the absence of hyperglycemia suggests proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome), as seen with myeloma or exposure to drugs (such as tenofovir disoproxil fumarate). Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, such as empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and canagliflozin, cause glucosuria by preventing proximal tubular reabsorption of glucose. Glucosuria may be present in normal pregnancy due to changes in tubular threshold for glucose reabsorption.

Ketonuria most commonly occurs in starvation, diabetic ketoacidosis, and alcoholic ketoacidosis. Urine ketones may also be seen in salicylate toxicity and isopropyl alcohol poisoning. Urine dipstick detects acetone and acetoacetate, but not β-hydroxybutyrate; therefore, in diabetic ketoacidosis and alcoholic ketoacidosis in which β-hydroxybutyrate is the primary ketone, the dipstick underestimates ketone excretion. False-positive tests may occur with drugs containing sulfhydryl groups, such as captopril.

Leukocyte esterase is an enzyme present in leukocytes. A positive test suggests pyuria (≥10 leukocytes/hpf). A false-negative test may occur in the setting of concentrated urine or in the presence of glucosuria, proteinuria, ascorbic acid, tetracycline, cephalexin, or oxalic acid.

A positive nitrite test signifies the presence of gram-negative bacteria (Escherichia coli; Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Citrobacter, and Proteus species) capable of converting urine nitrates into nitrites. The test is falsely negative if there is inadequate contact time for urine nitrates with the bacteria, a low-nitrate diet, the presence of vitamin C, elevated urinary specific gravity, or a pH<6. The nitrite test is negative in urinary tract infection (UTI) caused by nonconverting organisms (Enterococcus, Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, or Haemophilus species).

The presence of both leukocyte esterase and nitrites on urine dipstick is highly predictive of a UTI; conversely, the absence of both has a high negative predictive value for a UTI (see Diagnosis of Urinary Tract Infections in Infectious Disease).

Bilirubin should be absent from the urine when serum levels are normal. Conjugated, water-soluble bilirubin is excreted in the urine in severe liver disease or obstructive hepatobiliary disease.

Gut bacteria produce urobilinogen through metabolism of bilirubin. Urobilinogen is then absorbed through portal circulation and excreted in urine. Increased urobilinogen is associated with hemolytic anemia or parenchymal liver disease. Decreased levels are seen with severe cholestasis and obstructive disease.

Microscopic assessment of urine sediment is indicated for patients with abnormalities on dipstick and in those with acute kidney injury, newly diagnosed chronic kidney disease, or suspected glomerulonephritis (see [Table: Table: Findings on Urinalysis]

).

Erythrocyte morphology may indicate their origin (see

). Isomorphic erythrocytes (round, consistent size) suggest a nonglomerular origin as a result of infection, mass, cyst, or stone. Dysmorphic erythrocytes are fragmented erythrocytes with significant variability. Acanthocytes, a form of dysmorphic erythrocytes characterized by vesicle-shaped protrusions, are most suggestive of a glomerular source of bleeding. The presence of acanthocytes should result in prompt evaluation for glomerulonephritis (

). Urinary conditions (e.g., hypertonicity, blood clots) can cause dysmorphic “crenated” erythrocytes, which have spiky projections and are not specific for glomerular disease. See Clinical Evaluation of Hematuria in Nephrology for more information.

The presence of ≥5 leukocytes in the urine sediment (see

) indicates pyuria, which is most commonly caused by a UTI. Pyuria may also be detected as a result of urine contamination caused by genital secretions. To reduce the likelihood of contamination, patients should be counseled on clean urine collection technique.

Sterile pyuria is the presence of urine leukocytes in the setting of a negative urine culture; common causes include vaginitis and cervicitis, prostatitis, acute interstitial nephritis (AIN), kidney stones, kidney transplant rejection, and, less commonly, UTIs caused by organisms that do not grow by standard culture techniques (Chlamydia species, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Ureaplasma urealyticum).

Urine eosinophils may suggest interstitial nephritis, pyelonephritis, atheroembolic disease, glomerulonephritis, small-vessel vasculitis, UTI, prostatic disease, or parasitic infections. Poor sensitivity and specificity limit the utility of urine eosinophils in the diagnosis of interstitial nephritis.

Renal tubular, transitional, and squamous epithelial cells may be seen on urinalysis (see

).

Renal tubular epithelial cells are round with central nuclei and are 1.5 to 3 times larger than leukocytes (“fried egg” appearance). Their presence in the context of granular or muddy brown casts suggests acute tubular necrosis.

Transitional and squamous epithelial cells generally do not indicate pathology:

  • Transitional epithelial cells are slightly larger than renal tubular epithelial cells and may be binucleate; they originate anywhere from the renal pelvis to the proximal urethra.
  • Squamous epithelial cells are the largest epithelial cells and are flat and irregular with small central nuclei. They are derived from the distal urethra or external genitalia, and their presence in large numbers (>15/hpf) denotes contamination by genital secretions.

Urinary casts are encased in a matrix composed of Tamm-Horsfall protein (uromodulin). These cylindrical casts form in the distal tubular lumen. Any cells or debris in casts must be present in the tubule at the time of cast formation, having originated from a more proximal part of the nephron.

  • Erythrocyte casts are highly suggestive of glomerulonephritis.
  • Leukocyte casts may be present in AIN and infections (pyelonephritis).
  • Pigmented or granular (muddy brown) casts contain tubular cell debris (

) and may be present in acute tubular necrosis; the severity of acute kidney injury correlates with the number of granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells.

See [Table: Table: Urine Casts]

.

Crystalluria results from the supersaturation of solutes in concentrated urine. These solutes are derived from metabolic disorders, inherited diseases, drugs, or toxins. The presence of crystals can assist with identification of stone composition. [Table: Table: Urine Crystals]

describes features of common crystals. Certain drugs can crystallize in concentrated urine and when used in high doses, including sulfadiazine, sulfamethoxazole, intravenous acyclovir, and methotrexate.

Assessment for urine protein is indicated in patients with any suspected kidney disease. Concurrent increased serum creatinine or abnormal findings on urine sediment raises concern for active kidney disease in any patient with proteinuria.

Assays to detect urine protein include the following:

  • Urine dipstick
  • Random (spot) urine protein-creatinine ratio
  • Random (spot) urine albumin-creatinine ratio
  • 24-Hour urine collections

Because of the challenges of 24-hour urine collections, the random urine albumin-creatinine ratio and protein-creatinine ratio have been widely adopted. Both random tests detect albuminuria, but the urine protein-creatinine ratio also detects nonalbumin proteins. Random collections correlate well with timed collections and are sufficiently accurate for screening and monitoring proteinuria despite inaccuracies due to diurnal fluctuations of urine protein and interindividual differences in urine creatinine excretion. For details, see [Table: Table: Definitions of Proteinuria and Albuminuria]

.

Urine albumin, when present at high levels, indicates glomerular injury; conversely, the absence of albuminuria essentially excludes most glomerular diseases. Smaller proteins are filtered at the level of the glomerulus and then reabsorbed by the proximal tubule; their presence in urine generally indicates tubulointerstitial disease. Urine protein electrophoresis can characterize proteins, allowing for classification of the proteinuria as glomerular or tubular. It also detects light chains present at high levels in the urine (such as in monoclonal gammopathy), although it is less sensitive than free light chain assay. Transient, small elevations in urine protein can occur with acute illness or fever, rigorous exercise, and pregnancy. Orthostatic proteinuria is a benign proteinuria that increases when the patient is upright but decreases when the patient is recumbent. This condition is more common in adolescents but should be considered in those up to age 30 years. A split 24-hour urine collection (daytime collection compared against a nighttime collection that includes first morning void) can evaluate this diagnosis.

Screening for proteinuria should be done for high-risk patients, such as those with diabetes or hypertension. Screening for proteinuria or chronic kidney disease in asymptomatic adults without risk factors is not recommended.

In patients with diabetes, urine albumin screening is recommended because of its ability to detect early diabetic kidney disease. The American Diabetes Association recommends yearly assessment, beginning at diagnosis for patients with type 2 diabetes and 5 years after diagnosis for patients with type 1 diabetes. A urine albumin-creatinine ratio is the recommended screening test.

Hematuria is defined as the presence of ≥3 erythrocytes/hpf in the urine sediment and may be microscopic (detectable only on urine testing) or macroscopic (grossly visible). Hematuria is most often of nonglomerular origin. A glomerular origin is suggested by concurrent proteinuria, presence of acanthocytes, increased serum creatinine or decrease in eGFR, or systemic signs and symptoms.

Urinalysis should not be used for urothelial cancer screening in asymptomatic adults. However, a single incidental finding on the urine dipstick of trace blood or higher is sufficient to warrant further investigation. Evaluation should be pursued even in patients with bleeding diatheses or those taking antiplatelet or anticoagulation therapy. If menstruation, viral illness, vigorous exercise, or other benign cause is suspected, urinalysis should be repeated after the cause is resolved; persistent hematuria should prompt additional evaluation. If infection is confirmed, urinalysis should be repeated after treatment to document resolution of hematuria.

In a patient with asymptomatic microhematuria, it is important to evaluate for a glomerular cause. The following should be assessed:

  • Kidney function
  • Erythrocyte morphology
  • Urine protein

The absence of proteinuria generally rules out a glomerular process, with exceptions including very mild glomerular disease (most often IgA nephropathy) or thin glomerular basement membrane disease related to a type IV collagen defect that may present as isolated hematuria. Systemic signs and symptoms raise suspicion for kidney disease, particularly those associated with rheumatologic disorders and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

Macroscopic hematuria should prompt urology referral even if self-limited, with further evaluation of glomerular disease and malignancy as indicated.

If a nonmalignant or gynecologic cause of hematuria is ruled out, hematuria may indicate a malignancy (see Bladder Cancer in Oncology). In cases of suspected medical renal disease, urologic risk–based assessment should occur concurrently. The American Urological Association guidelines recommend stratifying patients as having low/negligible, intermediate, or high risk for an underlying urothelial malignancy, with risk status dictating subsequent management (see [Table: Table: Risk Stratification for Urothelial Malignancy]

). Low-/negligible-risk patients should have a repeat urinalysis within 6 months and require no additional evaluation if normal. If repeat urinalysis continues to show hematuria, these patients are reclassified as intermediate risk (3 to ≤25 erythrocytes/hpf) or high risk (>25 erythrocytes/hpf). Intermediate-risk patients require cystoscopy and kidney ultrasonography. High-risk patients require cystoscopy and CT urography, if there are no contraindications, or MR urography. For intermediate-risk patients who prefer to avoid cystoscopy, obtaining urine cytology or urine-based tumor markers to assist in the decision to pursue cystoscopy could be considered. However, urine cytology or urine-based tumor markers are not recommended in the initial evaluation of hematuria for low-/negligible- or high-risk patients.

Ultrasonography is the most commonly used kidney imaging modality. It is easily available, safe, and relatively inexpensive. Ultrasonography can demonstrate hydronephrosis, kidney size and cortical thickness, echogenicity, and presence of cysts and tumors. In the absence of hydronephrosis or distended bladder, the diagnosis of obstruction is unlikely in most cases. Echogenicity is the ability of a tissue to reflect the ultrasonic waves and is recognized as brighter shades on the sonogram image. Echogenicity is nonspecific and can imply acute or chronic parenchymal disease. Additionally, ultrasonography can measure pre- and postvoid bladder residual for evaluation of bladder dysfunction or outlet obstruction. Ultrasonography is also useful for uncomplicated nephrolithiasis; a positive ultrasound may be adequate for initial diagnosis, particularly for stones >5 mm. Ultrasonography is less useful in evaluating diseases (including stones) of the mid or distal ureter. Doppler ultrasonography may detect renal artery stenosis or renal vein thrombosis but is highly user dependent.

CT is appropriate for patients with a nondiagnostic ultrasound or a more complicated presentation. Noncontrast helical CT is the gold standard for diagnosis of nephrolithiasis and is appropriate for evaluating renal colic. Most stones, including small stones, can be detected on CT as well as those in the distal ureter not detected on ultrasound. CT may provide information regarding stone composition, and, because the entire urinary tract and abdomen are visualized, alternative diagnoses may be suggested.

CT urography, which uses iodine-based contrast and is urinary tract specific, is the imaging test of choice for patients with unexplained hematuria who are at high risk for malignancy and allows characterization of kidney tumors and cysts. CT with contrast is valuable for imaging the renal vasculature.

MRI with gadolinium-based contrast is an alternative for evaluation of kidney masses and cysts when CT cannot be performed. MR angiography for detection of renal artery stenosis and venography for detection of renal vein thrombosis can be performed with or without gadolinium-based contrast, although contrast provides optimal imaging. MR angiography and CT angiography have mostly replaced standard angiography of renal arteries.

Radionuclide imaging provides the most accurate measurement of GFR (see [Table: Table: Methods for Estimating Kidney Function]

).

Clinical and laboratory features are often insufficient for definitive diagnosis of kidney disease. Kidney biopsy may therefore be essential for diagnosis and management. Indications for kidney biopsy include the following:

  • Glomerular hematuria
  • Severely increased albuminuria (formerly known as macroalbuminuria or overt proteinuria)
  • Acute or chronic kidney disease of unclear cause
  • Kidney transplant dysfunction or monitoring

AIN and atheroembolic disease may require biopsy for diagnosis because they frequently present only with increased serum creatinine.

Percutaneous kidney biopsy with ultrasonography or CT guidance is most common. When percutaneous biopsy is not possible, transjugular approach or open or laparoscopic surgical biopsy can be performed in centers with appropriate expertise. Contraindications to percutaneous biopsy include bleeding diatheses (including antiplatelet use or anticoagulation), uncontrolled hypertension, poor kidney visualization, atrophic kidneys, perinephric abscess, UTI, pyelonephritis, and a patient who is unable to tolerate the procedure. Solitary kidney and pregnancy require weighing of risks and benefits.

The most common and concerning risk of biopsy is retroperitoneal bleeding. Perirenal bleeding accompanies every kidney biopsy. Major bleeding complications, including the need for transfusion or angiography with or without embolization, and hemodynamic instability occur in <3% of biopsies. CT with contrast is the most effective noninvasive method to assess for large hematoma or an ongoing bleed. However, angiography provides definitive diagnosis of an ongoing bleed and allows for therapeutic intervention. Minor complications, including pain and hematuria, are more frequent. Arteriovenous malformations, kidney loss, and death are very rare complications.

Electrolyte Disorders

Osmolality refers to the concentration of a solution and is determined by the number of solutes per kilogram of solvent. In serum or plasma, osmolality can be calculated using the following formula:

2 × [Na^+] + Glucose (mg/dL)/18 + Blood Urea Nitrogen (mg/dL)/2.8 + Ethanol (mg/dL)/4.6 if present

Normal serum osmolality is between 275 and 295 mOsm/kg H~2O. The difference between measured osmolality and calculated osmolality (the osmolal gap) should be <10 mOsm/kg H~2O. A greater value suggests the presence of an osmotically active molecule such as an alcohol (see Increased Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis in Nephrology).

Tonicity, or effective osmolality, is determined by extracellular solutes (primarily sodium salts, and to a lesser degree, glucose) that cannot cross the cell membrane; therefore, tonicity regulates water flux between extracellular and intracellular spaces. Because water moves freely between the intracellular and extracellular spaces based on the osmotic gradient, the osmolality of both compartments is virtually identical.

Osmolality is tightly controlled within a narrow range by thirst and antidiuretic hormone (ADH; also known as vasopressin). ADH stimulates reabsorption of water in the collecting duct of the kidney. Increases in tonicity stimulate both thirst and ADH. As long as there is access to water, appropriate thirst, normal control of ADH, and a functioning nephron, serum osmolality should be maintained in the normal range. Disorders of osmolality reflect impaired water homeostasis. Because the body will defend volume status over tonicity, volume depletion will stimulate ADH such that at any given osmolality, volume depletion will result in ADH release with risk for hyponatremia.

Hyponatremia is defined as a serum sodium concentration <135 mEq/L (135 mmol/L).

Evaluation of hyponatremia begins with measurement of serum osmolality. There are three categories of hyponatremia (

):

  • Hypertonic (osmolality >295 mOsm/kg H~2O)
  • Isotonic (osmolality 275-295 mOsm/kg H~2O)
  • Hypotonic (osmolality <275 mOsm/kg H~2O)

Symptoms caused by hyponatremia depend on both the rapidity and degree of decline in serum sodium. Acute hyponatremia in <48 hours provides inadequate time for the brain to adapt. A sudden drop in serum sodium causes water to move into brain cells, producing cerebral edema and possible headaches, seizures, or death. A more chronic decrease in sodium allows cells to regulate their volume by decreasing intracellular electrolytes, and patients may be asymptomatic.

Hypertonic hyponatremia (osmolality >295 mOsm/kg H~2O) results from an increased concentration of effective osmotic solute (typically glucose). The increase in osmolality pulls water out of cells, diluting the sodium. For every 100-mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) increase in glucose, sodium decreases by 1.6 to 2.2 mEq/L (1.6-2.2 mmol/L).

Isotonic hyponatremia (osmolality 275-295 mOsm/kg H~2O) is a laboratory artifact (pseudohyponatremia). Normally, plasma is 93% water (in which solutes are dissolved) and 7% solids (proteins and lipids). Conditions that increase the solid portion of plasma will decrease the water phase and result in a decrease in the overall concentration of sodium in plasma. This can occur in several situations:

  • Severe hypertriglyceridemia, in which case the plasma will appear milky
  • Increased plasma proteins (e.g., multiple myeloma or monoclonal gammopathies)
  • Severe cholestasis in which there are markedly increased levels of lipoprotein X, which can be measured with lipoprotein electrophoresis; unlike hypertriglyceridemia, the plasma is not milky

Quantification of sodium using a direct ion-selective electrode, which measures the sodium directly in the water phase, will prevent this artifact.

Hypotonic hyponatremia (osmolality <275 mOsm/kg H~2O) reflects excess water for the sodium present and is further categorized by volume status into hypovolemic, hypervolemic, or isovolemic (see

).

In hypovolemic hypotonic hyponatremia, volume depletion leads to renal sodium and water reabsorption stimulated by sympathetic outflow, angiotensin, aldosterone, and ADH, resulting in urine sodium concentration <20 mEq/L (20 mmol/L) and urine osmolality >300 mOsm/kg H~2O (except if taking diuretics or if secondary to renal salt wasting).

In hypervolemic hypotonic hyponatremia caused by heart failure or cirrhosis, effective circulating blood volume is inadequate despite total volume overload, resulting in urine chemistries similar to hypovolemic hyponatremia.

Isovolemic hypotonic hyponatremia is secondary either to impaired dilution of urine or to water intake that exceeds the kidney’s ability to excrete dilute urine. Urine osmolality distinguishes between these two entities. Urine osmolality <100 mOsm/kg H~2O indicates excessive water intake, as seen with psychogenic polydipsia or poor solute intake. Because the kidney cannot excrete urine with a solute concentration <50 mOsm/kg H~2O, low solute intake limits the ability to excrete water. Low solute intake combined with high liquid intake (as seen in beer potomania or chronic low food intake) can therefore result in hyponatremia.

Isovolemic hypotonic hyponatremia with urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg H~2O can occur in patients with late-stage chronic kidney disease because of impairment of urine dilution, causing hyponatremia after excessive dietary fluid intake. Urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg H~2O also occurs in isovolemic hypotonic hyponatremia due to the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH). Medications are the most common cause of SIADH, with antidepressants and thiazide diuretics being the most common; other causes are listed in [Table: Table: Causes of SIADH Secretion]

. Athletes who overhydrate during strenuous activity (which stimulates ADH) can acutely lower their sodium. 3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (ecstasy) can also cause hyponatremia. This drug stimulates ADH and, because of the associated fever and dry mouth, induces thirst. A frequent finding in SIADH is a low serum uric acid level (<4.0 mg/dL [0.24 mmol/L]). Cortisol and thyroid hormone are required to suppress ADH; therefore, deficiencies of these hormones should be evaluated.

ADH levels may be elevated postoperatively due to decreases in effective perioperative volume status (e.g., preoperative fasting, intraoperative blood loss) and perioperative stress (pain, nausea, anxiety). Therefore, use of a hypotonic intravenous solution (e.g., lactated Ringer) often results in postoperative hyponatremia. Administration of medications associated with SIADH, such as opioids, may further contribute to hyponatremia, although the pain itself may be the actual trigger.

Treatment of hypotonic hyponatremia is determined by the underlying pathogenesis. In patients with volume overload, treatment is targeted to the underlying disease process along with free water restriction. In hypovolemia, volume expansion with isotonic fluid (e.g., 0.9% saline) will suppress ADH, thereby increasing free water excretion with correction of the hyponatremia.

Treatment of isovolemic hypotonic hyponatremia is determined by the severity of symptoms and the rapidity of the decline.

Symptomatic patients with acute hypotonic hyponatremia (serum sodium typically <120 mEq/L [120 mmol/L]) should be treated with a 100-mL bolus of 3% saline to increase the serum sodium by 2.0 to 3.0 mEq/L (2.0-3.0 mmol/L). If symptoms persist, the bolus can be repeated once or twice at 10-minute intervals as long as the serum sodium can be measured. If the acute decline in sodium is secondary to excess water intake, fluid restriction will rapidly correct the hyponatremia.

Postoperative hyponatremia is usually mild, with sodium levels rarely <130 mEq/L (130 mmol/L). Treatment focuses on volume repletion, avoidance of hypotonic intravenous fluids, and management of pain and nausea. In rare cases when the sodium level drops below 130 mEq/L (130 mmol/L), hypertonic saline can be administered.

In isovolemic hypotonic hyponatremia with a more chronic decline (>48 hours’ presentation) in serum sodium, overly aggressive treatment can result in neuronal damage and osmotic demyelination. Accordingly, unless it is documented that the hyponatremia is acute, all cases should be treated as chronic. The osmotic demyelination syndrome is characterized by varied neurologic manifestations, including paresis, movement disorders, behavioral abnormalities, seizures, and obtundation. Symptoms typically occur 2 to 6 days after overly rapid correction and are often irreversible. Patients at greatest risk have severe hyponatremia (sodium <105 mEq/L [105 mmol/L]) that is chronic and often associated with liver disease, malnutrition, or hypokalemia. The goal of initial therapy is to increase the serum sodium by 4.0 to 6.0 mEq/L (4.0-6.0 mmol/L) in a 24-hour period. If there is significant neurologic impairment (such as seizures or coma), sodium can be acutely increased 2.0 to 4.0 mEq/L (2.0-4.0 mmol/L), but no greater than 6.0 mEq/L (6.0 mmol/L) in 24 hours, using either a bolus or a continuous 30-mL/h infusion of 3% saline, with frequent monitoring of the urine volume and serum sodium. Simultaneous administration of desmopressin makes the rate of correction resulting from 3% saline more predictable and safer for the patient because it prevents unexpected water diuresis and rapid increases in the serum sodium.

In patients with asymptomatic isovolemic hypotonic hyponatremia or with minimal symptoms (headache, lethargy), free water restriction is safe and effective. However, limiting fluid intake to <800 mL/24 h is often intolerable. If water restriction is not adequate, therapy is targeted at blocking ADH activity or increasing water excretion. Loop diuretics increase free water excretion and, along with salt tablets, may successfully increase the sodium. However, a randomized study showed no therapeutic benefit in patients treated with water restriction alone versus water restriction plus furosemide with or without salt supplementation. Oral urea, 15 to 30 g/d, is also effective in increasing water excretion, although its use is often limited because of unpalatable taste. Vaptans are ADH antagonists that are effective and usually well tolerated. However, they may be cost-prohibitive, and their use is limited to 1 month because of potential liver toxicity.

Hypernatremia is defined as a serum sodium concentration >145 mEq/L (145 mmol/L). Although less common than hyponatremia, hypernatremia is often seen in hospitalized patients and is associated with increased mortality in the critically ill.

Hypernatremia can be divided into three broad categories:

  • Inappropriate intake/administration of hypertonic solutions
  • Loss of hypotonic fluids
  • Excessive water loss due to defects in ADH release or action

A detailed history and physical examination combined with measurement of urine electrolytes and osmolality help distinguish the pathogenesis of hypernatremia.

The most common cause of hypernatremia is loss of hypotonic body fluids with inadequate water replacement due to lack of access to water or absence of thirst. Hypotonic losses may result from vomiting, diarrhea, excessive sweating, insensible losses through the respiratory tract (especially in patients on a ventilator), or renal losses from osmotic diuresis (such as with glucosuria). If the losses are nonrenal, urine osmolality will be >600 mOsm/kg H~2O. If the losses are renal (osmotic diuresis), urine osmolality is usually between 300 and 600 mOsm/kg H~2O. Hypotonic losses with inadequate replacement result in intravascular volume depletion with orthostasis or frank hypotension.

Hypernatremia can also occur with administration of excessive quantities of hypertonic saline, sodium bicarbonate, or salt ingestion. The acute increase in extracellular sodium causes water to move out of brain cells, causing shrinkage and neurologic findings. Symptoms can range from lethargy to seizures and coma.

Less commonly, hypernatremia may be secondary to either an inadequate release of ADH (arginine vasopressin deficiency [central diabetes insipidus]) or action of ADH (arginine vasopressin resistance [nephrogenic diabetes insipidus]). As long as there is access to water, the sodium should be in the high-normal range and hypernatremia is unusual. Arginine vasopressin deficiency can result from tumors that invade the hypothalamic-pituitary region, infiltrating diseases (e.g., sarcoidosis), tuberculosis, or surgical destruction. Arginine vasopressin resistance can be caused by drugs such as lithium or conditions including severe hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, or chronic kidney disease. Common symptoms are polydipsia and polyuria. Urine osmolality <300 mOsm/kg H~2O in a patient with polyuria and hypernatremia confirms the diagnosis. An increase in urine osmolality after a dose of desmopressin (ADH analogue) distinguishes between arginine vasopressin deficiency and arginine vasopressin resistance. Because solute loss is not excessive, hypernatremia from water loss is usually associated with minimal symptoms unless the sodium increases acutely. For more information, see Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency (Central Diabetes Insipidus) in Endocrinology and Metabolism.

The management of hypernatremia is determined by the underlying pathogenesis.

When secondary to acute hypertonic gains, treatment needs to rapidly restore normal sodium concentration. Water can be administered as intravenous 5% dextrose. In addition, if volume overload is present, a loop diuretic should be used. The goal is to replace the entire water deficit within 24 hours.

If hypernatremia has occurred for >24 hours, the brain adapts by uptake of electrolytes and other osmotically active solutes. Data regarding the maximum safe rate of correction are lacking, and expert opinions have suggested a correction of no more than 10 to 12 mEq/L (10-12 mmol/L) in 24 hours. However, although rapid correction of sodium could theoretically cause cerebral edema, this does not seem to occur in adults, and decreases as much as 1.0 mEq/h (1.0 mmol/h) appear to be well tolerated.

Water deficit or volume of replacement water required is estimated using the following formula:

(Total Body Water) × [(Current Sodium – Ideal Sodium)/Ideal Sodium]

The change in the serum sodium for each liter of infusate can be calculated using the following formula:

(Infusate Sodium) − (Serum Sodium) ÷ (Total Body Water + 1)

Total body water is usually estimated as 60% and 50% of lean body weight in young men and women, respectively, and approximately 50% and 45% in older men and women, respectively.

If possible, water should be administered orally or by means of a nasogastric tube. Because dextrose-containing solutions may cause glycosuria and increased free water losses, it is important to monitor serum glucose and maintain it below 180 mg/dL (10 mmol/L). In the presence of hemodynamic compromise due to intravascular volume depletion, replacement fluid should be isotonic saline; otherwise, a hypotonic solution (half [0.45%] normal saline) can be used.

Arginine vasopressin deficiency can be treated with intranasal or oral desmopressin. Arginine vasopressin resistance is more difficult to treat. Therapy is aimed at limiting solute intake to decrease the amount of free water that the kidney can excrete and induction of mild volume depletion using a thiazide diuretic to increase salt and water reabsorption proximal to the collecting duct. The polyuria associated with lithium-induced arginine vasopressin resistance can be ameliorated with the addition of amiloride, which reduces lithium uptake by the principal cell of the cortical collecting tubule.

Hypokalemia is defined as a serum potassium level <3.5 mEq/L (3.5 mmol/L). It can be divided into disorders of internal balance (movement of potassium between the intracellular and extracellular compartments) and disorders of external balance (potassium intake and output) (

).

Serum potassium >3.0 mEq/L (3.0 mmol/L) is usually asymptomatic. Because the ratio of intracellular to extracellular potassium is the major determinant of the membrane potential of electrically active tissue, hypokalemia symptoms and signs may include the following:

  • Weakness or paralysis
  • Decreased gastrointestinal motility or ileus
  • Cardiac arrhythmias; ECG manifestations may include ST-segment depression, decreased T-wave amplitude, and increased U-wave amplitude (

) - Severe hypokalemia, which may cause rhabdomyolysis

The cause of hypokalemia can usually be determined from the history and simple laboratory evaluation. Rarely, hypokalemia is spurious, as can occur in leukemia when delayed sample processing allows large numbers of metabolically active leukocytes to take up potassium. In addition to leukocytosis, a clue to pseudohypokalemia is the lack of signs and symptoms associated with hypokalemia.

Hypokalemia can occur secondary to disordered internal balance. Insulin or β~2-agonists shift potassium into cells, causing an acute, transient, and modest hypokalemia that is usually asymptomatic. Ingestion of soluble barium or cesium salts, which block potassium exit from cells, can produce severely symptomatic hypokalemia with levels below 2.0 mEq/L (2.0 mmol/L). Increased cell production after repletion of vitamin B~12 or folate in deficient individuals can also cause hypokalemia. Hypokalemic periodic paralysis, either an inherited autosomal dominant disorder or an acquired disorder rarely seen in patients with hyperthyroidism, may present with severe muscle weakness and paralysis.

Most cases of hypokalemia are due to disordered external balance with total body potassium depletion, usually from increased potassium excretion. Because the kidney can almost cease potassium excretion, only a severely compromised diet can cause hypokalemia. The major determinants of renal potassium secretion are distal tubular flow rate and aldosterone; both increase sodium reabsorption, which increases the electronegativity of the tubule lumen and promotes potassium secretion. Under normal conditions, distal sodium delivery and aldosterone levels are inversely related, thus preventing disruptions in potassium homeostasis by changes in intravascular volume.

The gold standard test to distinguish between renal and extrarenal causes of total body potassium depletion is a 24-hour urine potassium <30 mEq/24 h (30 mmol/d); however, this test is often impractical. The preferred alternative is a spot urine potassium-creatinine ratio. A value <13 mEq/g identifies hypokalemia secondary to lack of intake, transcellular shifts, or gastrointestinal losses.

Gastrointestinal losses are usually caused by diarrhea or laxative misuse. Frequently, a concomitant metabolic acidosis is present. Renal potassium wasting may be caused by numerous factors, including the following:

  • Medications (most commonly diuretics)
  • Delivery of non-reabsorbable anions (such as bicarbonate) to the distal tubule
  • Aldosterone excess
  • Hypomagnesemia
  • Tubular defects (type 2 [proximal] and type 1 [hypokalemia distal] renal tubular acidosis)

Primary aldosteronism is associated with hypertension and a metabolic alkalosis. Renal potassium wasting also occurs in inherited tubular defects, including Liddle, Bartter, and Gitelman syndromes. In Liddle syndrome, increased sodium reabsorption in the distal nephron causes hypertension, metabolic alkalosis, and potassium wasting. Bartter and Gitelman syndromes are caused by mutations in transporters that mimic the effects of diuretics on the tubule (e.g., mimicking loop diuretics in Bartter syndrome and thiazides in Gitelman syndrome). In Bartter syndrome, urinary calcium excretion is normal or increased, whereas in Gitelman syndrome, hypocalciuria occurs.

The total body potassium deficit is difficult to predict and can be up to 200 mEq (200 mmol) for each mEq/L (mmol/L) decrease in plasma potassium. In patients with neuromuscular or cardiac symptoms, it is important to increase the potassium promptly. Because of the risk for inducing phlebitis, concentrations of potassium >10 mEq/L (10 mmol/L) using a peripheral vein should be avoided. Infusion through a central vein can be increased to up to 40 mEq/h (40 mmol/h) with close cardiac monitoring. For mild hypokalemia (2.5-3.5 mEq/L [2.5-3.5 mmol/L]), oral supplementation using potassium chloride or potassium bicarbonate is usually adequate. Concurrent hypomagnesemia must be corrected to prevent ongoing potassium losses. In patients with potassium wasting, potassium-sparing diuretics can be helpful. When significant hypokalemia is secondary to acute transcellular shifts, total body potassium is normal and excessive potassium replacement may cause rebound hyperkalemia.

Hyperkalemia is defined by a serum potassium level >5.0 mEq/L (5.0 mmol/L). Levels >6.0 mEq/L (6.0 mmol/L) can cause fatal arrhythmias. Slow increases in potassium are better tolerated than abrupt increases. Signs and symptoms of hyperkalemia are manifested in electrically active tissue and include muscle weakness and ECG abnormalities.

Initial evaluation of hyperkalemia requires a history and physical examination, review of all medications, assessment of kidney function, and an ECG. Initial ECG manifestations include peaked precordial T waves and a shortened QT interval. With progression of hyperkalemia, lengthening of the PR interval, loss of the P wave, widening of the QRS complex, a sine wave pattern, and asystole may occur (

). However, ECG findings do not always correlate with the serum potassium level and do not necessarily progress in an orderly fashion.

During the clotting process, cells are disrupted with the release of intracellular potassium, and pseudohyperkalemia may occur in serum specimens when there are extreme elevations of leukocytes or platelets. In these cases, a repeat plasma specimen will be normal. A tight tourniquet, an excessively clenched fist during blood draw, and an inadequately processed tube can also cause local potassium release.

Hyperkalemia may be caused by transcellular shifts, as occur in states of insulin deficiency or hypertonicity, or with the use of β~2-adrenergic blockers. Rapid breakdown of cells, such as that seen in rhabdomyolysis or tumor lysis syndrome, can acutely raise serum potassium levels.

Hyperkalemia usually results from increased intake with decreased renal excretion. Hyperkalemia frequently occurs with oliguric acute or chronic kidney disease with a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) <20 mL/min/1.73 m^2. Potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride, triamterene, spironolactone) also commonly cause hyperkalemia through decreased excretion. Other medications that decrease potassium excretion include trimethoprim and pentamidine (by blocking the epithelial sodium channel) and NSAIDs (by decreasing renin). Hypoaldosteronism caused by ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, heparin, type 4 renal tubular acidosis (often seen in diabetic kidney disease), or primary adrenal insufficiency also causes hyperkalemia, especially in the presence of excess potassium intake or volume depletion.

Elevation in the serum potassium level >6.5 mEq/L (6.5 mmol/L), or >6.0 mEq/L (6.0 mmol/L) with ECG changes, should be promptly treated. Treatment is directed at stabilizing the cardiac membrane, shifting potassium into cells, and removing potassium from the body. Intravenous administration of calcium gluconate quickly antagonizes the effects of hyperkalemia on the cardiac membrane. Its duration of action is relatively short and therefore is never definitive therapy. Intravenous administration of insulin alone if serum glucose is >250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L) or with 10% dextrose will drive potassium into cells and is effective for up to 6 hours. Potassium can also be shifted into cells using high-dose nebulized albuterol. Because sodium bicarbonate therapy does not promote redistribution of potassium, it has fallen out of favor as a treatment option.

Definitive treatment of severe hyperkalemia, unrelated to reversible transcellular shift, must include removal of potassium from the body. In patients without severe kidney disease, loop diuretics can be effective. Use of the potassium exchange resin sodium polystyrene sulfonate is controversial; its effectiveness is limited, and it produces adverse gastrointestinal effects, including volume overload and, rarely, bowel necrosis. Patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate bind potassium in the gastrointestinal tract and effectively lower potassium. Hemodialysis is the treatment of choice in patients with severe hyperkalemia and oliguric kidney disease.

Hyperkalemia with a serum potassium level <6.0 mEq/L (6.0 mmol/L) is often overtreated and, in the absence of signs of cardiac toxicity, does not warrant emergent interventions. Limiting potassium intake may be beneficial, and increased sodium intake along with a thiazide or loop diuretic will increase potassium excretion. In hypoaldosteronism, fludrocortisone will normalize the potassium; however, it may cause elevated blood pressure and edema, and long-term effects of fludrocortisone are unknown. All potentially causative medications should be discontinued if possible. However, discontinuing renoprotective medications, such as ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-receptor blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, in patients with chronic kidney disease is associated with adverse outcomes; cessation is warranted only if hyperkalemia persists despite other medical management. If necessary, potassium binders may allow continuation of essential medications.

Phosphate (PO~4) is found primarily within bone and the intracellular space and is required for metabolic pathways involved in energy production, cellular repair, and enzymatic activity. Hypophosphatemia is defined as a serum phosphate level <2.7 mg/dL (0.87 mmol/L). Levels <2.0 mg/dL (0.65 mmol/L) are associated with muscle weakness. Severe hypophosphatemia (<1.0 mg/dL [0.32 mmol/L]) is associated with life-threatening symptoms, including delirium, seizures, coma, heart failure, respiratory failure, rhabdomyolysis, and hemolysis.

Hypophosphatemia results from transcellular shifts, decreased intake, or increased excretion. Movement of phosphorous into cells occurs with respiratory alkalosis, insulin treatment, refeeding syndrome, or, less commonly, as part of the hungry bone syndrome following parathyroidectomy or with prolonged exposure to continuous kidney replacement therapy. Ferric carboxymaltose, an intravenous iron preparation, has been associated with hypophosphatemia by causing renal phosphate wasting. Medications that bind phosphate in the gut (calcium, antacids) can decrease effective intake. Because the kidney can decrease phosphate excretion to very low levels, low dietary phosphate rarely causes hypophosphatemia without coexisting malnutrition. Increased excretion may be caused by diarrhea or renal wasting. Excretion of >100 mg of phosphate in a 24-hour urine collection or a fractional excretion of phosphate (FEpo~4) >5% suggests renal wasting. Renal losses of phosphate occur in hyperparathyroidism and in proximal tubular dysfunction. Patients undergoing partial hepatectomy will frequently develop hypophosphatemia.

Mild hypophosphatemia can be treated with oral sodium or potassium phosphate. Moderate to severe hypophosphatemia (levels <2.0 mg/dL [0.65 mmol/L]) should be treated with intravenous sodium phosphate. Calcitriol is sometimes required to increase intestinal absorption of phosphate.

Hyperphosphatemia is defined by a serum phosphate level >4.5 mg/dL (1.45 mmol/L). Symptoms are usually related to co-occurring hypocalcemia. Acute severe elevations in phosphate can cause precipitation of calcium phosphate in the kidney, resulting in phosphate nephropathy.

Hyperphosphatemia caused by reduced renal excretion does not usually occur unless GFR is severely impaired due to acute kidney injury or severe chronic kidney disease. Hypoparathyroidism decreases excretion through increased phosphate tubular reabsorption; hypocalcemia is often present. Rare defects in the action of fibroblast growth factor 23 (such as in tumoral calcinosis) also increase tubular reabsorption of phosphate.

Because phosphate is primarily an intracellular anion, widespread cellular damage as occurs in rhabdomyolysis and tumor lysis syndrome increases serum phosphate, especially if GFR is decreased. Hyperphosphatemia can also be associated with diabetic ketoacidosis and, less commonly, lactic acidosis. Excessive phosphate intake rarely causes hyperphosphatemia because the kidney rapidly excretes phosphate. However, phosphate-containing cathartics can cause acute elevations in serum phosphate, especially in patients with reduced GFR.

If kidney function is adequate, serum phosphate levels should normalize in 12 to 24 hours. If necessary, phosphate excretion can be increased with intravenous saline. In patients with impaired kidney function, dialysis may be necessary. Because many foods contain phosphate, dietary phosphate restriction is difficult. Therefore, patients with chronic hyperphosphatemia must often use agents that bind phosphate in the gastrointestinal tract to prevent absorption. See Management of Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral and Bone Disorder in Nephrology for more information.

There are approximately 24 grams of magnesium in the body, with 99% residing intracellularly and within bone. Magnesium is essential for protein and nucleic acid synthesis, cell adhesion, enzyme reactions, and modulating channel activity.

Hypomagnesemia is defined by a serum magnesium level <1.7 mg/dL (0.7 mmol/L). Clinical manifestations, which usually do not develop until serum magnesium is <1.2 mg/dL (0.5 mmol/L), include the following:

  • Tremors
  • Fasciculations
  • Muscle weakness
  • Carpopedal spasm
  • Chvostek sign (contraction of the ipsilateral facial muscles by tapping the facial nerve)
  • Trousseau sign (carpopedal spasm after inflation of blood pressure cuff above systolic blood pressure)
  • Seizures

Hypomagnesemia also appears to potentiate cardiac arrhythmogenicity due to hypokalemia, myocardial ischemia, and various drugs. In addition, hypomagnesemia causes hypokalemia due to renal potassium wasting, and it causes hypocalcemia by impeding parathyroid hormone release and action.

Hypomagnesemia results from decreased gastrointestinal absorption or increased renal secretion. History and physical examination often delineate the cause. More than 10 mg of magnesium in a 24-hour urine collection or a fractional excretion of magnesium (FE~Mg) >2% suggests renal wasting in the setting of hypomagnesemia.

Causes of decreased magnesium absorption include severe malnutrition, diarrhea, and malabsorption. Proton pump inhibitors are an important cause of hypomagnesemia, with most reported cases occurring after prolonged use, which rapidly reverses upon discontinuation of the drug.

Hypomagnesemia from renal losses occurs with diuretics, cisplatin, aminoglycosides, or calcineurin inhibitors. Vascular endothelial growth factor inhibitors used in cancer treatment can cause significant magnesium wasting. Other causes of urine losses include volume expansion, alcohol ingestion, and diabetic ketoacidosis.

If significant symptoms are present, 4.0 grams of magnesium sulfate should be infused over 12 hours and repeated if necessary. Importantly, half of acutely infused intravenous magnesium is excreted by the kidney; therefore, slow-release oral magnesium or nasogastric tube delivery may be better to replete mild to moderate hypomagnesemia.

Hypermagnesemia is defined by a serum magnesium level of >2.4 mg/dL (0.99 mmol/L).

Hypermagnesemia occurs infrequently and most commonly results from excessive intake in the setting of decreased kidney function. Antacids and laxatives contain magnesium, and therapeutic infusions of magnesium sulfate for refractory asthma and prevention of eclampsia are potential causes of hypermagnesemia.

Symptoms of hypermagnesemia do not occur until levels are 4.8 mg/dL (1.98 mmol/L). Early symptoms include loss of deep tendon reflexes, progressing to flaccid paralysis at higher levels. Hypermagnesemia also results in hypotension from loss of vascular tone. Laboratory analysis often shows hypocalcemia.

Prevention is the key to management of hypermagnesemia. Hypermagnesemia is usually self-limited; magnesium-containing agents should be limited or avoided in individuals with kidney disease. Magnesium excretion can be enhanced with saline diuresis. For more severe symptoms, intravenous calcium will antagonize the effects of magnesium.
