Acute Kidney Injury

Acute kidney injury (AKI) is characterized by a sudden decrease in kidney function commonly accompanied by decreased urine output, fluid retention, metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, and hyperphosphatemia. The Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Acute Kidney Injury Work Group definitions for AKI are described in [Table: Table: Definition of Acute Kidney Injury]

.

Multiple studies have shown a correlation between more severe stages of AKI and higher mortality and health care utilization. Patients with AKI have an increased risk for developing chronic kidney disease (CKD) and end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). Likewise, patients with preexisting CKD are at an increased risk for AKI, a condition known as acute-on-chronic kidney disease.

The incidence of AKI is estimated to be approximately 20% of all hospital admissions; approximately 10% of these patients require dialysis. AKI affects >50% of patients in the ICU. Mortality varies depending on the severity of AKI, underlying cause, and patient population. Critically ill patients with AKI in the context of multiorgan failure have mortality rates >50% when dialysis is required.

AKI can be divided into prerenal, intrinsic, and postrenal causes and can be due to pharmacologic or nonpharmacologic causes:

  • Prerenal AKI (prerenal azotemia) is caused by decreased renal perfusion. The integrity of renal tissue is preserved, and tubular and glomerular function remains normal.
  • Intrinsic AKI is caused by structural damage to the renal parenchyma.
  • Postrenal AKI refers to AKI caused by urinary tract obstruction.

See [Table: Table: Pharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

and [Table: Table: Nonpharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

.

Prerenal AKI and acute tubular necrosis (ATN), also referred to as acute tubular injury, account for up to 75% of AKI cases in hospitalized patients.

Patients with AKI can be asymptomatic until extreme loss of kidney function occurs but can also present with oliguria (urine output <500 mL/d or <0.3 mL/kg/h) or anuria (urine output <50 mL/d). Severe AKI can lead to symptoms caused by volume overload, electrolyte abnormalities, and uremia. Acute uremic symptoms include nausea, vomiting, anorexia, fatigue, muscle cramps, restless legs, confusion, and pruritus. Physical signs may include asterixis and a pericardial rub. Other manifestations may be bleeding (due to platelet dysfunction), pericarditis, and seizures. Drug or metabolite accumulation and toxicity may complicate the course.

The diagnosis of AKI is based on increased serum creatinine levels from the patient’s baseline or precipitous decline in urinary output. The most reliable way to distinguish AKI from CKD is knowledge of previous serum creatinine levels. Documentation of similarly elevated creatinine levels for ≥3 months suggests that kidney failure is chronic. However, serum creatinine concentration can be increased by several factors independent of kidney function, limiting its specificity for a diagnosis of AKI. Serum creatinine is not a sensitive marker of kidney injury in patients with sepsis, liver disease, muscle wasting, or fluid overload. Moreover, the rise in serum creatinine is delayed 24 to 36 hours after the onset of injury and decline in glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

The history focuses on identifying the following:

  • Vasoactive and potential nephrotoxic medications, including over-the-counter, herbal, and recreational drugs
  • Recent exposure to iodinated contrast agents
  • Other predisposing conditions for AKI
  • Urinary obstructive symptoms

See [Table: Table: Pharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

and [Table: Table: Nonpharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

.

Physical examination focuses on blood pressure, heart rate, and signs of volume status such as jugular venous pressure level and bladder percussion/palpation. Laboratory evaluation includes blood urea nitrogen, serum creatinine, electrolytes (including serum bicarbonate), complete blood count, urinalysis, and microscopic examination of the urine sediment. See [Table: Table: Prerenal Acute Kidney Injury Versus Acute Tubular Necrosis]

and [Table: Table: Urinalysis and Microscopy in Acute Kidney Injury]

. Arterial or venous blood gas may be obtained for the evaluation of acid-base disturbances if clinically indicated.

In patients with oliguria, the fractional excretion of sodium (FE~Na) or urea (FE~Urea) can help distinguish between prerenal AKI and ATN, with some caveats (see [Table: Table: Prerenal Acute Kidney Injury Versus Acute Tubular Necrosis]

).

Ultrasonography of the kidneys (Video: Ultrasound in Acute Kidney Injury) and bladder should be obtained to exclude urinary tract obstruction when the underlying cause of AKI is unclear or obstruction is suspected. Kidney size may help distinguish between AKI and CKD, because small kidneys with increased cortical echogenicity and/or thinning suggests CKD. Kidney size can be normal in patients with CKD caused by infiltrative disorders such as diabetes mellitus, HIV-associated nephropathy, amyloidosis, or multiple myeloma. Kidney biopsy should be considered in patients with AKI from no apparent cause, suspected glomerulonephritis, or unexplained systemic disease.

AKI can be divided into prerenal, intrinsic, and postrenal causes.

See [Table: Table: Pharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

and [Table: Table: Nonpharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

for the causes of prerenal AKI.

Prerenal AKI (prerenal azotemia) is caused by hypoperfusion of the kidney with a subsequent decrease in GFR, which is reversible with appropriate intervention. Renal hypoperfusion can occur due to intravascular volume depletion, decreased effective arterial circulation, renal vasoconstriction, and/or medications. Patients may present with acute hemorrhage, loss of gastrointestinal fluids, heart failure, decompensated liver disease, and sepsis; they may have a history of recent diuretic or NSAID use. Physical signs of hypovolemia include hypotension, tachycardia, and orthostasis. Patients with heart failure or cirrhosis have physical examination findings supporting these conditions.

In prerenal AKI, the kidney responds by reabsorbing urea, sodium, and water. Laboratory values that support a diagnosis of prerenal AKI are listed in [Table: Table: Prerenal Acute Kidney Injury Versus Acute Tubular Necrosis]

. Prerenal AKI due to hypovolemia can be distinguished from ATN by the response to a volume challenge. An increase in urine output (if oliguric) and decrease in serum creatinine level support the diagnosis of a prerenal cause.

Drug-induced prerenal AKI typically results from decreased blood flow to the kidney or intraglomerular hemodynamic alterations. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors or diuretics can cause prerenal AKI from volume depletion. Drugs impairing vasodilatation of the afferent arterioles (such as NSAIDs) or vasoconstriction of the efferent arterioles (such as ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers) can cause prerenal AKI, especially in the setting of volume depletion, decreased effective arterial circulation (i.e., heart failure), or preexisting CKD or cirrhosis. Calcineurin inhibitors such as cyclosporine and tacrolimus can cause prerenal AKI from afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction.

Management includes discontinuing nephrotoxins and increasing renal perfusion by treating the underlying cause, such as correcting volume deficits. If prerenal AKI is not recognized and treated in a timely fashion, prolonged renal hypoperfusion can result in ATN.

Intrinsic AKI occurs from structural damage to the renal tubules, interstitium, glomerulus, or vascular structures or from intratubular obstruction. Sepsis-related AKI is common in patients receiving intensive care and is due to several factors, including hypoperfusion progressing to ATN, nephrotoxic drugs, cytokines, and reactive oxygen species. See [Table: Table: Pharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

and [Table: Table: Nonpharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

.

ATN, also referred to as acute tubular injury, due to ischemia, nephrotoxins, and/or sepsis is the most common cause of AKI in hospitalized patients. A history of sepsis, protracted hypotension, or nephrotoxin exposure along with assessment of hemodynamics and volume status can aid in diagnosis. Laboratory values suggestive of ATN are described in [Table: Table: Prerenal Acute Kidney Injury Versus Acute Tubular Necrosis]

. Urine sediment usually reveals renal tubular epithelial cells and casts, as well as pigmented granular (muddy brown) casts (

).

Unlike prerenal AKI, ATN does not rapidly improve with restoration of intravascular volume and adequate renal perfusion. Treatment is supportive because no efficacious pharmacologic therapies exist. Complete or partial renal recovery can take days to weeks. Nonoliguric ATN portends a better renal prognosis than oliguric ATN. Patients with advanced CKD are less likely to recover kidney function compared with patients with baseline normal kidney function or early CKD. Patients with severe ATN who require acute dialysis often recover kidney function but may progress to dialysis-dependent ESKD.

Severe ischemia due to prolonged hypotension, protracted prerenal state, or sepsis can cause ATN (see [Table: Table: Nonpharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

). The ischemic injury leads to cytokine release, oxygen-free radical and enzyme production, endothelial activation and leukocyte adhesion, activation of coagulation, and apoptosis. GFR declines because of renal vasoconstriction, tubular back leak of filtrate, and tubular obstruction from sloughed cellular debris.

Normotensive ischemic ATN can occur without overt hypotension, but with blood pressure decreased relative to baseline, in conditions with impaired renal autoregulation. These conditions include older age, hypertension, atherosclerotic or renovascular disease, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, liver cirrhosis with portal hypertension, and CKD. Management may involve treating volume deficits and decreasing antihypertensive medications to allow the blood pressure to increase to baseline levels.

Drug-induced ATN can be a consequence of prolonged hemodynamic alterations or direct tubular injury (see [Table: Table: Pharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

). The drugs associated with prerenal AKI can cause ATN from prolonged hypoperfusion. Early recognition and prompt discontinuation of the drug are essential for renal recovery. The risk for drug-induced ATN increases in older persons and in patients with decreased effective arterial circulation, CKD, or concomitant nephrotoxin exposure. Hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and metabolic acidosis may reflect underlying tubular injury.

Osmotic nephrosis is a form of tubular injury due to hyperosmolar substances such as sucrose-containing intravenous immunoglobulin, mannitol, hydroxyethyl starch, dextran, and contrast media (see Contrast-Associated Acute Kidney Injury in Nephrology). It is characterized by vacuolization and swelling of the renal proximal tubular cells with resultant tubular obstruction and damage.

Aminoglycosides (e.g., gentamicin) cause nonoliguric ATN through direct renal tubular cell toxicity, with an increase in serum creatinine occurring 5 to 7 days after initiation of therapy. Cisplatin causes ATN through direct tubular toxicity, renal vasoconstriction, and inflammation. Amphotericin B causes dose-related AKI through both renal vasoconstriction and direct tubular toxicity and may be associated with arginine vasopressin resistance in addition to the aforementioned tubular defects. Lipid-based preparations decrease the risk for nephrotoxicity. Vancomycin nephrotoxicity can occur in the setting of high trough levels (>15 mg/L), high vancomycin dose (≥4 g/d), prolonged duration of therapy, and/or concomitant nephrotoxic drugs, most notably an aminoglycoside or piperacillin-tazobactam. Certain types of synthetic cannabinoids used as recreational drugs have been associated with ATN.

Heme pigment released from myoglobin or hemoglobin can cause AKI through intravascular volume depletion, renal vasoconstriction, direct proximal tubular injury resulting in ATN, and tubular obstruction. Urine heme pigment from myoglobin or hemoglobin causes a positive urine dipstick for blood with the absence of erythrocytes in urinary sediment.

In rhabdomyolysis, myoglobin is released in the circulation from damaged skeletal muscle. Major causes include trauma, acute compartment syndrome, drugs and toxins, seizures, viral infections, metabolic and electrolyte disorders (i.e., severe hypokalemia), endocrinopathies (diabetic ketoacidosis, hyperglycemic hyperosmolar syndrome, hypothyroidism), malignant hyperthermia, and intense exercise, particularly in poorly conditioned individuals. Global warming is associated with increased risk for dehydration, blood hyperosmolality, and heatstroke, increasing the risk for heat-related AKI from rhabdomyolysis or heat-induced inflammatory injury, especially in agricultural or industrial workers in developing countries.

Rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI is more likely to occur with serum creatine kinase levels >5000 U/L. Hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, metabolic acidosis, increased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) concentration, and increased aspartate and alanine aminotransferase levels can occur. Urinary findings include FE~Na <1% due to renal vasoconstriction (though may become >1% if ATN develops), myoglobinuria, and pigmented granular casts.

In addition to correcting the underlying cause, prevention and management of AKI involve aggressive intravenous isotonic fluid infusion aimed at maintaining urine output >200 to 300 mL/h. Although limited studies suggest that alkalinization of the urine with intravenous bicarbonate to increase the urine pH to >6.5 may prevent tubular cast formation, there is no evidence that such alkaline diuresis either prevents rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI or hastens recovery. If urine alkalinization is used, it should be closely monitored; if the patient develops symptomatic hypocalcemia and/or arterial pH >7.5 or if urine pH does not increase to >6.5 after several hours, it should be discontinued. Benefit has not been established for the use of mannitol or loop diuretics, and these may cause harm. However, diuretics may be required for the management of volume overload to avoid dialysis. Dialysis may be necessary for treatment of severe electrolyte and acid-base abnormalities and volume overload in patients with oligoanuria. Most patients have partial or complete renal recovery.

Heme pigment nephropathy due to hemolysis is less common and occurs when large amounts of heme pigment are released into circulation due to intravascular hemolysis. Causes include glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, drug reactions, cardiopulmonary bypass circuits, incompatible blood transfusion, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, malaria, certain poisonings, and snakebites. Laboratory abnormalities include anemia, increased LDH, and decreased haptoglobin. Urinary findings include FE~Na <1%, hemoglobinuria, and pigmented granular casts. Treatment of hemoglobinuria involves treating the underlying cause as well as volume repletion with intravenous isotonic fluids and kidney replacement therapy when necessary.

Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is a common cause of AKI and is characterized by inflammation and edema of the interstitium. The classic clinical presentation of fever, rash, and peripheral eosinophilia occurs in only 10% to 30% of patients with AIN. Urinary findings can include leukocytes, erythrocytes, and leukocyte casts. See [Table: Table: Urinalysis and Microscopy in Acute Kidney Injury]

and see

. Urine eosinophils are neither sensitive nor specific for AIN, and testing for urine eosinophils (Hansel stain) is not recommended for diagnosis.

Drug-induced AIN, especially caused by antibiotics, proton pump inhibitors, or NSAIDs, is the most common cause of AIN and should be considered in any patient with AKI, a characteristic urinalysis, and a history of any drug exposure (see [Table: Table: Pharmacologic Causes of Tubulointerstitial Nephritis]

). Other causes include infections, toxin exposure, and systemic diseases such as autoimmune disorders (see [Table: Table: Nonpharmacologic Causes of Tubulointerstitial Nephritis]

). Tubulointerstitial nephritis with uveitis is a rare systemic inflammatory disease that usually presents with a predominantly anterior uveitis and variable systemic symptoms. Adolescents and young women are typically affected, and presentation may be preceded by infection or the use of specific drugs (e.g., NSAIDs, antibiotics).

In AIN, the serum creatinine level typically increases 7 to 10 days after drug exposure but can increase much sooner following repeat exposure to the same drug. Drug-induced AIN from NSAIDs, including selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors, is usually not associated with fever, rash, or eosinophilia and develops 6 to 12 months after drug exposure. AIN from NSAIDs can be associated with nephrotic syndrome due to minimal change glomerulopathy or membranous nephropathy. The onset of proton pump inhibitor–induced AIN is variable but typically occurs 10 to 13 weeks after exposure. Proton pump inhibitors are thought to be a risk factor for the development of CKD. Chemotherapeutic agents, including ifosfamide, immune checkpoint inhibitors, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and pemetrexed, are an underrecognized cause of AIN.

Renal recovery from drug-induced AIN is usually complete if the drug is stopped immediately after the onset of kidney injury but may take weeks to several months. Irreversible interstitial fibrosis (see Chronic Tubulointerstitial Nephritis in Nephrology) can develop after ≥2 weeks of continued exposure. Kidney biopsy should be considered if there is no improvement in kidney function after 5 to 7 days of drug discontinuation. Early glucocorticoid administration may limit damage associated with drug-induced AIN.

Acute glomerulonephritis with AKI results from immune-mediated damage to glomeruli. Urinary findings include proteinuria, dysmorphic erythrocytes, and erythrocyte casts (see [Table: Table: Urinalysis and Microscopy in Acute Kidney Injury]

and

). Constitutional signs and symptoms are often present. Serologic assays and kidney biopsy identify most causes. Early recognition is extremely important because, without treatment, it can result in irreversible kidney damage or be fatal. See Conditions Associated with the Nephritic Syndrome in Nephrology for more information.

Macrovascular (large and medium vessel) or microvascular (small vessel) disease can cause AKI (see [Table: Table: Nonpharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

).

Acute renal arterial occlusion, most often embolic due to atrial fibrillation or atherosclerotic aortic disease, and acute renal vein thrombosis can cause acute renal infarction and present as abdominal or flank pain, elevated serum LDH levels, and hematuria. A notable risk for renal vein thrombosis accompanies nephrotic syndrome, particularly with membranous nephropathy. Diagnosis may be made by CT angiography, MR venography, or kidney ultrasonography with Doppler. Treatment usually consists of anticoagulation and supportive care.

Patients with atherosclerotic disease who undergo an invasive vascular procedure such as vascular surgery or angiography are at increased risk for atheroemboli-induced AKI (cholesterol emboli). Atheroembolic events can occur spontaneously or several days to weeks after manipulation of arteries. Plaque rupture causes cholesterol embolization to distal small- and medium-sized arteries, resulting in ischemia with end-organ damage. In addition to the kidneys, atheroemboli can affect the arteries in the skin, muscle, gastrointestinal tract, liver, eyes, and central nervous system. Physical examination findings may include the following:

  • Livedo reticularis, a lacy network of bluish-red vessels that is usually seen on the lower extremities (

) - Hollenhorst plaques on funduscopic examination, which appear as a yellow refractile body within arteriole (

) - Ulcerations - Cholesterol emboli causing cyanosis, necrosis, or gangrene of the toes (

)

Laboratory findings can include low serum complements, peripheral eosinophilia, and eosinophiluria; urinalysis may be unremarkable or can reveal proteinuria, hematuria, leukocyturia, or granular, leukocyte, or erythrocyte casts. Treatment of atheroemboli is supportive and consists of risk modification with aspirin, statins, and management of hypertension. Renal prognosis is poor.

AKI can also occur from polyarteritis nodosa causing microaneurysms of medium- and small-sized arteries that subsequently rupture, resulting in hemorrhage, thrombosis, and organ ischemia and infarction. See Polyarteritis Nodosa in Rheumatology for more information.

AKI from microvascular disease can present as thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and glomerular capillary thrombosis (see [Table: Table: Nonpharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

). For more information, see Increased Destruction and Abnormal Distribution in Hematology. Urine may show hematuria, erythrocyte casts, and/or proteinuria. Hypertensive emergency and scleroderma renal crisis can also cause TMA. Treatment is based on the underlying cause.

Intratubular obstruction can cause AKI through precipitation of either protein or crystals within the tubular lumen. Examples include monoclonal light chain deposition in multiple myeloma, calcium oxalate deposition from ethylene glycol ingestion, crystals from drugs, and uric acid from tumor lysis syndrome (see [Table: Table: Pharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

and [Table: Table: Nonpharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

.)

In multiple myeloma, AKI from light chain cast nephropathy is the most common type of kidney disease. Cast nephropathy is due to direct tubular toxicity and obstruction from the precipitation of filtered free light chains. See Myeloma Cast Nephropathy in Nephrology for more information.

Agents associated with crystal-induced AKI are listed in [Table: Table: Pharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

. Ethylene glycol toxicity causes AKI from intratubular precipitation of calcium oxalate crystals. Ethylene glycol should be suspected in a patient with a history of ingestion and whose laboratory studies demonstrate an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis and osmolal gap. Treatment consists of supportive care, the alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor, fomepizole, and hemodialysis if needed. Orlistat, a gastrointestinal lipase inhibitor used to induce clinically significant weight loss by fat malabsorption, has also been associated with intratubular calcium oxalate deposition and AKI. High doses of vitamin C, which is metabolized to oxalate, can also lead to AKI from calcium oxalate precipitation in the tubules. Crystals from protease inhibitors can cause AKI from both intratubular crystal deposition and nephrolithiasis.

Urinary findings include hematuria, leukocyturia, and crystals. AKI is usually reversible after discontinuation of the drug. Predisposing factors include volume depletion, CKD, and changes in urine pH. Correction of volume depletion with intravenous fluids is critical for both the prevention and treatment of crystal-induced AKI. High-dose intravenous acyclovir can cause acyclovir crystal deposition in the tubules, which can be prevented by previous intravenous fluid administration and slow rate of drug infusion. Because crystals from sulfonamide antibiotics and methotrexate are more likely to form in acidic urine, urinary alkalinization can prevent crystal deposition.

Acute phosphate nephropathy is a potentially irreversible cause of AKI due to phosphate-containing bowel preparations. Although many of these agents have been removed from the U.S. market, acute phosphate nephropathy is occasionally seen in patients, particularly those with preexisting CKD, who have taken sodium phosphate retention enemas. A transient severe increase in serum phosphate levels in the setting of volume depletion causes acute and chronic tubular injury from tubular and interstitial precipitation of calcium phosphate crystals. AKI can present days to months after exposure. Predisposing factors include volume depletion, CKD, older age, NSAID use, and hypertension treated with ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, or diuretics.

Postrenal AKI can occur from obstruction anywhere from the renal pelvis to the external urethral meatus (see [Table: Table: Nonpharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

). Upper urinary tract obstruction (at the level of the ureters or renal pelvis) must be bilateral or affect a single functioning kidney to cause AKI. Obstruction of urinary flow leads to hydronephrosis and eventual renal parenchymal damage. If postrenal AKI is not treated promptly, the obstruction can predispose the patient to urinary tract infections and urosepsis, and it can also lead to CKD and ESKD.

Postrenal AKI should be suspected in patients with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia, neurogenic bladder, nephrolithiasis, pelvic malignancies, previous retroperitoneal radiation therapy, abdominal or pelvic surgeries, or retroperitoneal adenopathy. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with anuria, oliguria, or polyuria. Symptoms of lower tract obstruction include abdominal fullness or pain, urinary frequency, urgency, hesitancy, nocturia, overflow incontinence, and incomplete voiding. Acute nephrolithiasis may present with flank pain and hematuria. A distended palpable bladder may be evident in bladder outlet obstruction. Hyperkalemia and features of distal renal tubular acidosis may also be evident.

Lower urinary tract obstruction can be diagnosed by an elevated postvoid bladder residual volume on ultrasound. Hydronephrosis on kidney ultrasound is present in most causes of obstruction, but false-negative results may occur in the early stages or from encasement of the ureter or kidney, as seen in retroperitoneal disease. Noncontrast CT is indicated for suspected nephrolithiasis. Treatment focuses on reversing the cause of the obstruction. Prognosis depends upon the severity and duration of the obstruction. Renal recovery is generally good if obstruction is relieved within 1 to 2 weeks.

Contrast-associated AKI, defined as an increase in serum creatinine levels within 24 to 48 hours of iodinated contrast agent exposure, is a common cause of reversible AKI in the hospital setting.

The major risk factor is a reduced estimated GFR (eGFR) at baseline, especially in patients with AKI or with CKD and an eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m^2. Other risk factors include the following:

  • Conditions of decreased renal perfusion (such as hypovolemia, hypotension, or low effective circulating volume in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction)
  • High contrast dose or repeated administration
  • Intra-arterial contrast administration
  • Advanced age
  • Diabetes, particularly in patients with impaired kidney function

Pathogenesis is thought to involve renal vasoconstriction causing medullary ischemia and direct oxygen free radical–associated renal tubular epithelial cell injury resulting in ATN. AKI tends to be nonoliguric, with FE~Na <1%. The urine sediment may be bland or show granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells or casts if ATN is present.

Preventive strategies for patients at high risk for contrast-associated AKI include the following:

  • Minimizing use and amount of contrast
  • Avoidance of concomitant nephrotoxins
  • Prophylactic volume expansion with intravenous isotonic fluids, such as 0.9% saline or isotonic sodium bicarbonate

If tolerated, intravenous fluids should be administered to all patients who have an eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m^2 and can be considered for patients with an eGFR of 30 to 44 mL/min/1.73 m^2 who have other risk factors for AKI. Withholding diuretics should be considered 24 hours before contrast administration if not clinically contraindicated. Oral acetylcysteine is no longer recommended for prophylaxis based on the results of the PRESERVE trial. There is also no role for hemodialysis or hemofiltration to prevent AKI following contrast exposure. Treatment of contrast-associated AKI is supportive.

Cardiorenal syndrome (CRS) is a disorder of the heart and kidneys whereby acute or long-term dysfunction in one organ induces acute or long-term dysfunction in the other.

CRS is characterized by the following triad:

  • Concomitant decreased kidney function
  • Diuretic-resistant heart failure with congestion
  • Worsening kidney function during heart failure therapy

CRS is seen primarily in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. The decreased kidney function in CRS is thought to be due to neurohumoral activation, venous congestion and increased renal venous pressure, reduced renal perfusion, and right ventricular dysfunction.

Management is challenging because treatment directed toward improving cardiac function (diuretics, ACE inhibitor/angiotensin receptor blocker, vasodilators, and inotropes) can sometimes worsen kidney function. Evidence does not support the use of ultrafiltration over intensive diuretic management. Decreased kidney function in patients with heart failure is an independent risk factor for all-cause mortality.

Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is a potentially reversible functional kidney impairment that occurs in the setting of portal hypertension due to liver cirrhosis, severe alcohol-associated hepatitis, or acute liver failure. HRS is caused by reduced renal blood flow during simultaneous dilation of the splanchnic arterial bed and is characterized by increased renal vasoconstriction. Tubular function is preserved with the absence of significant hematuria and proteinuria, as well as lack of renal histologic changes. Urine sodium concentration is typically <10 mEq/L (10 mmol/L).

HRS is a clinical diagnosis made after exclusion of other causes of kidney dysfunction, characterized by the following:

  • Increase in serum creatinine of at least 0.3 mg/dL (26.5 μmol/L) and/or ≥50% from baseline within 48 hours
  • Bland urinalysis (ensuring that ATN or other intrinsic renal causes are not present)
  • Normal findings on kidney ultrasound (ensuring postrenal cause is not present)
  • Exclusion of other causes of AKI (especially volume depletion)

HRS-AKI, previously referred to as type 1 HRS, is defined as ≥2-fold increase in serum creatinine to a level greater than 2.5 mg/dL (221 µmol/L) in <2 weeks. Patients are often oliguric. Lack of improvement in kidney function after withdrawal of diuretics and 2 days of volume expansion with intravenous albumin (1 g/kg/d divided dosing) supports the diagnosis. A more gradual decline in kidney function, previously referred to as type 2 HRS, is associated with diuretic-resistant ascites.

The ultimate therapy for HRS is treating the underlying liver failure, such as liver transplantation or treatment of acute alcohol-associated or viral hepatitis. General short-term management includes discontinuing diuretics, restricting sodium, restricting water in hyponatremic patients, and evaluating for precipitating factors in the setting of liver cirrhosis. Therapeutic interventions include vasoconstrictors in combination with albumin infusion. The American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases recommends intravenous terlipressin as the preferred vasopressor. An initial trial of albumin with oral midodrine and octreotide can be provided if terlipressin is not available, although efficacy data are limited. For patients who are treated in an intensive care setting in which terlipressin is not available, norepinephrine may be substituted as the vasoconstrictor. Patients with HRS have an overall poor prognosis without liver transplantation. All patients with cirrhosis and AKI should be considered for urgent liver transplantation evaluation given the high short-term mortality even in responders to vasoconstrictors (see Liver Transplantation in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease). Kidney replacement therapy is usually reserved for patients with severe AKI who are liver transplant candidates.

Tumor lysis syndrome caused by massive lysis of tumor cells can occur after chemotherapy or spontaneously in patients with a large tumor burden. AKI can result from catabolism of nucleic acids to uric acid, hyperuricemia, and precipitation of uric acid in the renal tubules, with subsequent renal vasoconstriction and direct tubular injury. Severe hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, and hyperphosphatemia can occur, with calcium phosphate deposition in the renal tubules causing further injury. Preventive and treatment measures include administration of intravenous isotonic fluids and hypouricemic agents such as rasburicase. See Tumor Lysis Syndrome in Oncology for more information.

Abdominal compartment syndrome is defined as a sustained elevated intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) associated with new organ dysfunction. IAP >20 mm Hg is commonly associated with ACS, although the absolute value is not a sufficient criterion. IAP can be measured with a transvesical pressure transducer through an indwelling Foley catheter and is most accurate in patients who are intubated, sedated, and receiving paralytic agents. Abdominal compartment syndrome occurs in the setting of abdominal surgery, trauma, hemoperitoneum, retroperitoneal bleed, ascites, bowel obstruction, ileus, and pancreatitis. It can also occur from capillary leak with concurrent massive fluid resuscitation. Increasing IAP causes hypoperfusion and ischemia of peritoneal and retroperitoneal structures, and can lead to hemodynamic, respiratory, neurologic, and kidney impairment. Renal vein compression and renal artery vasoconstriction can cause oliguric AKI. Management includes supportive therapy, abdominal compartment decompression, and correction of positive fluid balance.

AKI can occur in the setting of hospitalization with COVID-19 infection and was reported to affect a large proportion of those patients who require intensive care and mechanical ventilation. At the time of the pandemic, the most common histologic finding reported in the literature was ATN. Etiology, however, can be multifactorial and can include the following:

  • Prerenal AKI
  • AIN due to antimicrobials
  • Renal vein thrombosis in the setting of a hypercoagulable state
  • CRS
  • Kidney injury caused by complement activation and cytokine release in the setting of severe illness

Cortical necrosis, thrombotic microangiopathy, pigment nephropathy, acute glomerulonephritis, and collapsing glomerulopathy are less commonly reported. Management is primarily supportive. Kidney replacement therapy may be required.

In most cases of AKI, treatment of underlying medical conditions and discontinuation of nephrotoxic medications lead to improvement in kidney function. No specific pharmacologic therapy is effective in established ATN. Supportive measures include the following:

  • Optimizing hemodynamics and renal perfusion
  • Preventing further kidney injury
  • Treating AKI complications
  • Providing appropriate nutrition

Diuretics can be used for volume overload. Bicarbonate can be administered to correct metabolic acidosis. Dietary potassium, magnesium, and phosphate should be restricted. Phosphate binders may be required to prevent severe hyperphosphatemia. Medication dose adjustments for diminished GFR are necessary to avoid toxicities. Patients with AKI should be monitored during follow-up for complete recovery of kidney function and/or emergence of CKD, and patients with preexisting CKD should be evaluated for worsening kidney function.

In some patients with severe AKI, initiation of kidney replacement therapy (KRT) may be necessary to manage urgent complications such as volume overload refractory to diuretics, hyperkalemia or metabolic acidosis refractory to medical management, uremic manifestations, and dialyzable toxins. KRT options include the following:

  • Intermittent hemodialysis (IHD)
  • Continuous KRT (CKRT)
  • Hybrid therapies, such as prolonged intermittent KRT (PIKRT)
  • Peritoneal dialysis (PD)

IHD, CKRT, and PIKRT are extracorporeal therapies that require vascular access in the form of a large-bore, double-lumen central venous catheter; PD requires the placement of an intra-abdominal dialysis catheter and is utilized less frequently for AKI than for ESKD.

IHD, typically delivered three to six times a week for 3 to 5 hours per session, allows for rapid correction of electrolyte disturbances and rapid removal of drugs or toxins. The main disadvantage is the risk for hypotension caused by the rapid solute and volume removal. CKRT, employed using a variety of modalities, is administered 24 hours daily and removes solutes and fluid much more slowly than IHD, resulting in better hemodynamic tolerance. PIKRT removes solutes and fluid more slowly than IHD but more quickly than CKRT and is administered 8 to 12 hours daily. Acute PD is not as effective as the other KRT modalities, especially for urgent clinical scenarios such as hyperkalemia. However, acute PD may be useful when other modalities are unavailable or vascular access cannot be obtained.

Randomized clinical trials have not shown a survival benefit of CKRT over IHD or PIKRT for critically ill patients with AKI. CKRT is preferred in patients with hemodynamic instability or cerebral edema because IHD may worsen neurologic status by compromising cerebral perfusion pressure. IHD is favored in patients who need rapid solute removal, such as those with severe hyperkalemia or drug intoxications. Transitions in therapy are common depending on the changing needs of the patient.

Studies of the timing of KRT initiation in critically ill patients and those with sepsis demonstrate no mortality benefit for early introduction of KRT versus that based on usual clinical criteria. In fact, the latter strategy was sometimes associated with avoiding the need for KRT.

In critically ill patients with a very poor prognosis, establishing goals of care and patient preferences for therapy is imperative. In such cases, shared decision making, a time-limited trial of KRT, and involvement of palliative care services are often appropriate.

Chronic Tubulointerstitial Nephritis

Tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN) involves damage to the renal tubules and interstitium. Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is commonly due to allergic drug reactions, infection, or systemic diseases and can cause acute kidney injury within days to weeks (see Acute Interstitial Nephritis in Nephrology). Inflammation and edema of the kidney interstitium and tubules occur, which generally improve after the offending drug is discontinued or the underlying disease is treated but can progress to chronic TIN (CTIN). CTIN involves interstitial scarring, fibrosis, and tubular atrophy and causes a slow decline in kidney function over months and years. CTIN can also develop in the setting of primary glomerular disease, vascular disease, and ischemia secondary to atherosclerosis and hypertension.

CTIN is often asymptomatic until severe CKD occurs. Patients frequently present with only an elevated serum creatinine, although they may have symptoms such as polyuria and nocturia due to renal-concentrating defects.

A review of medications (prescribed, over the counter, and herbal) and careful history suggesting nonpharmacologic triggers should be performed to determine cause ( [Table: Table: Pharmacologic Causes of Tubulointerstitial Nephritis]

and [Table: Table: Nonpharmacologic Causes of Tubulointerstitial Nephritis]

). A thorough physical examination infrequently provides clues. Patients may be hypertensive. Urinalysis may be normal or demonstrate pyuria and/or proteinuria <1500 mg/24 h. [Table: Table: Laboratory Manifestations of Chronic Tubulointerstitial Nephritis]

lists other laboratory manifestations of CTIN. Kidney ultrasound typically reveals small kidneys if disease is advanced. Kidney biopsy is the gold standard modality and may establish a final diagnosis in difficult cases.

[Table: Table: Pharmacologic Causes of Tubulointerstitial Nephritis]

and [Table: Table: Nonpharmacologic Causes of Tubulointerstitial Nephritis]

detail the causes of TIN.

Kidney involvement in Sjögren disease may include interstitial nephritis, distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis (RTA), and glomerulonephritis (see Clinical Manifestations of Sjögren Disease in Rheumatology). Nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, and progressive kidney disease may occur.

Kidney involvement in sarcoidosis is not uncommon and can manifest as nephrocalcinosis from hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria, obstructive uropathy, and TIN with granuloma formation (see Sarcoidosis in Rheumatology). Kidney recovery is often incomplete.

TIN may occur in systemic lupus erythematosus and is often associated with concurrent glomerular disease but can also be the only manifestation of lupus nephritis. The severity of TIN is a useful predictor of progressive kidney disease. For additional information, see Kidney Involvement in Rheumatology and Lupus Nephritis in Nephrology.

TIN may develop in both ANCA-associated (i.e., granulomatous TIN) and ANCA-negative vasculitis involving the renal medulla. There are also reports of drug-induced AIN associated with ANCA formation against myeloperoxidase, elastase, and lactoferrin.

TIN is the most common renal manifestation of systemic IgG4-related disease and is characterized by abundant IgG4-positive plasma cell interstitial infiltrates. Other features may include hypocomplementemia, peripheral eosinophilia, and renal masses (see IgG4-Related Disease in Rheumatology).

Certain infections such as bacterial, viral, fungal, and parasitic infections can cause CTIN (see [Table: Table: Nonpharmacologic Causes of Tubulointerstitial Nephritis]

). In transplant recipients who are immunosuppressed, BK polyoma virus can cause an interstitial nephritis.

Chronic pyelonephritis or vesicoureteral reflux may cause CTIN. Persistent chronic pyelonephritis can progress to localized xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, characterized by a destructive mass that invades the renal parenchyma.

Lymphoma and acute leukemia can infiltrate the kidney, causing TIN. Presenting features include proteinuria, sterile pyuria, and enlarged kidneys. Multiple myeloma can cause TIN in the form of myeloma cast nephropathy, Fanconi syndrome, or interstitial light chain deposition.

Medication-induced AIN may evolve to CTIN due to protracted exposure to an offending agent (see [Table: Table: Pharmacologic Causes of Tubulointerstitial Nephritis]

). Commonly associated drug classes include antibiotics, NSAIDs, and proton pump inhibitors.

Analgesic nephropathy was first described in patients taking combinations of phenacetin (banned since 1983) with aspirin, caffeine, acetaminophen, or NSAIDs. It can also occur with the individual drugs. When severe, analgesic nephropathy is associated with renal papillary necrosis, manifesting as gross hematuria, flank pain, and, occasionally, obstruction and infection. Affected individuals typically have a history of heavy analgesic use.

The calcineurin inhibitors cyclosporine and tacrolimus can cause CTIN. Longer durations of exposure increase risk for CTIN. Associated thrombotic microangiopathy is uncommon but may contribute to acute or chronic kidney injury.

Lithium exposure can cause a type 1 hypokalemic distal RTA, arginine vasopressin resistance, and CTIN in up to 20% of long-term users. Risk factors include advanced age, cumulative dose, and repeated episodes of lithium toxicity with high serum levels. Kidney dysfunction can progress to end-stage kidney disease even after discontinuation.

Many chemotherapy agents can cause TIN. Immune checkpoint inhibitors and tyrosine kinase inhibitors are the main classes implicated.

Other associated agents include the following:

  • Ifosfamide
  • Pemetrexed
  • Lenalidomide
  • Vemurafenib
  • Nitrosoureas, particularly streptozotocin and semustine

Synthetic cannabinoids, anabolic androgenic steroids, toluene, and cocaine are associated with AIN. The incidence of CTIN with repeated exposure is unknown.

Heavy metals (i.e., lead, arsenic, mercury, cadmium) are divalent cations primarily handled by the proximal tubule and can cause tubular dysfunction, CTIN, and proteinuria. Proteinuria is due to reduced ability of the proximal tubule to reabsorb protein and is usually non-nephrotic with the exception of mercury, which can also cause glomerular injury. Occupational exposure to lead occurs from welding, the battery industry, and mining. Toxicity may also develop after months to years of exposure to lead in water, soil, paint, or food. Gout is common. The diagnosis of lead nephropathy is based on exposure history, kidney dysfunction, and elevated blood lead levels. Levels may be normal if exposure has abated. Cadmium can also lead to hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis, and osteoporosis.

Certain herbal supplements such as some Ayurvedic medicines contain heavy metals. Aristolochic acid or Balkan endemic nephropathy is a cause of CTIN due to exposure to plants and herbal supplements containing aristolochic acid. It can present as AKI, CTIN with progression to end-stage kidney disease, or tubular dysfunction with Fanconi syndrome. Because urothelial cancers can occur even after discontinuation, cystoscopy with CT of the abdomen and pelvis with and without intravenous contrast for urography, also called CT urography, should be considered in patients with aristolochic acid exposure and nonglomerular hematuria.

Other epidemics of unexplained kidney disease, such as Mesoamerican and Sri Lankan nephropathy, have occurred primarily in agricultural communities in Central America and Asia and are referred to as CIN in agricultural communities (CINAC). CINAC commonly affects young to middle-aged men and often progresses to kidney failure.

The cause of CINAC is likely multifactorial and may include the following:

  • Genetic predisposition
  • Heat stress
  • Dehydration
  • Agrochemicals
  • Heavy metals
  • Communicable diseases
  • High sugar consumption

Obstructive uropathy from prostate disease, malignancy, nephrolithiasis, pelvic radiation, medications (e.g., ergot alkaloids and dopamine agonists), and retroperitoneal fibrosis can cause CTIN and progressive kidney dysfunction. RTA, hyperkalemia, and mild proteinuria are common.

Management involves discontinuing the offending drugs or toxins and treating the underlying disease. Treatment of heavy metal toxicity includes chelation (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid or oral succimer for lead; dimercaptosuccinic acid for mercury and arsenic). In patients with progressive chronic kidney disease, management is supportive and includes treatment of hypertension, proteinuria, and metabolic abnormalities (see Complications and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease in Nephrology).
