Chronic Kidney Disease

Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is defined as abnormal kidney structure or function present for at least 3 months. CKD is stratified into stages 1 to 5 based on estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Stage G1 does not have a reduction in eGFR and is defined by the presence of anatomical defects or markers of kidney damage such as albuminuria, hematuria, or electrolyte and other abnormalities caused by tubular disorders. Because albuminuria is associated with increased renal and cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) group further subdivides the eGFR-based kidney stages by degree of albuminuria (

). This dual eGFR and albuminuria algorithm provides a means for predicting which patients are at highest risk for progression of CKD to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), also known as kidney failure requiring replacement therapy, defined as CKD stage G5 treated with chronic dialysis or kidney transplantation.

CKD affects approximately 14% of the U.S. adult population, with 5.1% having stage G3 disease and <1% having advanced CKD (defined by stage G4 or G5). The high burden of CKD-associated mortality is notable: Whereas <10% of patients with CKD stage G3 progress to ESKD, most patients die from cardiovascular disease or infection before progressing to advanced CKD. The highest prevalence of CKD in the United States is among persons aged ≥60 years.

CKD results from various etiologies that cause chronic damage to the glomeruli, tubulointerstitium, or vasculature. Glomerular damage causes albuminuria. Tubulointerstitial damage may manifest as abnormalities in renal-concentrating abilities and low-grade tubular proteinuria. As the underlying structural abnormalities progress, glomerular filtration rate (GFR) falls.

In healthy adults aged >30 years, the average rate of decline of eGFR is approximately 1 mL/min/1.73 m^2 per year; those with risk factors such as increased albuminuria/proteinuria and/or diabetic kidney disease have more rapid progression. The most important predictors of progression to ESKD are baseline eGFR and severity of albuminuria/proteinuria. The eGFR trajectory over time adds prognostic value for ESKD and cardiovascular outcomes.

Controversy exists regarding routine screening of asymptomatic patients for CKD. Screening patients at risk for CKD, including those with diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, previous acute kidney injury, or a family history of kidney disease, is generally recommended. Additional risk factors to consider include, but are not limited to, genitourinary disorders; multisystem diseases and chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus, vasculitis, HIV infection); and occupational and environmental exposures (e.g., lead and pesticides).

CKD is typically asymptomatic except in advanced stages (G4, G5). As eGFR falls below 60 mL/min/1.73 m^2, numerous alterations in metabolic pathways become altered due to the loss of nephron mass and hormone synthesis. Hypertension is a frequent early manifestation of CKD. Advancing CKD results in impaired ability to excrete salt and water, manifesting as edema. Patients with nephrotic-range proteinuria may also develop edema or anasarca.

When CKD progresses to ESKD, uremic symptoms can occur and include the following:

  • Fatigue
  • Nausea
  • Loss of appetite
  • Insomnia
  • Irritability
  • Difficulty concentrating
  • Confusion
  • Pruritus
  • Encephalopathy or seizures (in very advanced stages)

Uremia can also induce pleuritis and pericarditis. Crystalized cutaneous urea and other nitrogenous waste appear as chalky skin deposits, termed uremic frost, and occur rarely as a late manifestation of uremia. A large proportion of patients with CKD stage G5 manifest few or only intermittent uremic symptoms.

eGFR can be established using serum creatinine and the 2021 Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) creatinine equation. If confirmation of GFR is required because of conditions that affect serum creatinine independent of GFR (such as extremes of muscle mass or diet), cystatin C should be measured to employ the CKD-EPI cystatin C or creatinine–cystatin C equation. Initial assessment of albuminuria includes a spot urine albumin-creatinine ratio. Elevated albumin-creatinine ratios should be confirmed by repeat testing. See Estimation of Glomerular Filtration Rate in Nephrology for more information.

Diagnosis of CKD requires an eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m^2 confirmed at least 3 months after initial assessment or persistent proteinuria, albuminuria, or structural kidney disease regardless of eGFR. Kidney biopsy is used to determine the cause of CKD when a glomerular or tubulointerstitial disease is likely and when specific therapy is available to delay or prevent further kidney injury. The complementary role of genetic testing is evolving. Kidney biopsy is not routinely performed in the presence of shrunken kidneys (<9 cm), which indicate chronic irreversible disease. Ultrasound findings of hyperechoic kidneys may be noted, consistent with medical kidney disease, and usually reflect long-standing CKD. There is a lack of evidence regarding the use of urinalysis in routine screening for CKD.

Patients who experience acute kidney injury (AKI) can have slow recovery. Acute reduction in eGFR persisting from 7 to 90 days is termed acute kidney disease. Although diagnosis of CKD requires at least 3 months of persisting abnormalities in structure or function, studies have demonstrated that kidney function can continue to improve for up to 1 year after an initial episode of AKI. AKI is a risk factor for subsequent CKD. Both the severity of AKI and the time required for recovery from AKI influence the likelihood of having CKD after 1 year. A large meta-analysis suggests that the hazard ratio of developing CKD after AKI ranges from 2.3 to 8.0, with higher risk related to worsening degree of AKI. A subset of patients progress to stage G5 or ESKD. Patients with a history of AKI should therefore have their kidney function monitored.

According to KDIGO guidelines, referral to a nephrologist should be considered for evaluation and management of CKD in the presence of the following:

  • Sustained fall in GFR of >20%, or of >30% after starting hemodynamic therapy
  • GFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m^2
  • Albuminuria (≥300 mg/g) in combination with hematuria, or a twofold or greater increase in albuminuria in patients being monitored for significant albuminuria, or an albumin-creatinine ratio that is consistently >700 mg/g
  • Uncertain cause of CKD
  • Erythrocyte casts

  • 20 Erythrocytes/hpf that is sustained and not readily explained

  • Hypertension refractory to treatment with four or more antihypertensive agents
  • Persistent serum potassium abnormalities
  • Presence of CKD complications, such as anemia, acidosis, or bone disease
  • Recurrent or extensive nephrolithiasis
  • Hereditary kidney disease

  • 3% to 5% 5-year risk of requiring KRT

A kidney failure risk equation (KFRE) has been developed and validated. The KFRE uses four variables (age, sex, eGFR, and albuminuria) to predict 2- and 5-year risk for ESKD in patients with CKD stages G3 to G5. The use of this equation is consistent with KDIGO guidelines, which recommend integration of risk prediction in the evaluation and management of CKD, and studies suggest that KFRE usage improves clinical decision making compared with eGFR-based strategies.

Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death among patients with CKD. The risk for cardiovascular-related death in patients with CKD stages G3 and G4 is four to five times higher than the risk for progression to ESKD. Mortality risk increases with decreasing eGFR and increasing albuminuria. Many clinical trials guiding the prevention or treatment of cardiovascular disease did not include patients with advanced CKD. However, most post hoc analyses of randomized controlled trials including participants with CKD demonstrated efficacy regardless of baseline CKD status, including interventions such as percutaneous coronary interventions. Thus, experts recommend against withholding efficacious therapies from those with CKD due to unsubstantiated concerns of lack of efficacy or harm.

Hypertension is both a cause and consequence of CKD. Blood pressure control is an important care component to slow the progression of CKD. For more information, see Secondary Hypertension in Nephrology.

Elevated LDL cholesterol and triglyceride levels with low HDL cholesterol levels are common among patients with CKD. Although statins have not been shown to slow the progression of CKD, they do reduce cardiovascular and all-cause mortality in patients with CKD. However, large trials have failed to demonstrate a mortality benefit for statins in patients with dialysis-dependent ESKD.

KDIGO indications for treatment with a statin include the following:

  • Patients aged ≥50 years with non–dialysis-dependent CKD
  • Patients aged 18 to 49 years with non-dialysis–dependent CKD and any of the following:
    • Coronary artery disease (CAD)
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Previous ischemic stroke

  • 10% estimated risk for coronary death or nonfatal myocardial infarction

  • Adult kidney transplant recipients

The 2018 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline on the management of blood cholesterol indicates that it is reasonable to initiate a moderate-intensity statin with or without ezetimibe in adults 40 to 75 years of age with CKD, an LDL cholesterol measure of 70 to 189 mg/dL (1.8 to 4.9 mmol/L), and a 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk of ≥7.5%. The guideline recommends against initiating statin therapy in patients on dialysis, but it may be reasonable to continue statins in patients beginning dialysis therapy. In persons with diabetes and CKD, a high-intensity statin can be considered.

Dyslipidemia associated with the nephrotic syndrome helps maintain plasma oncotic pressure but, over time, may hasten the progression of glomerular injury. Dyslipidemia in the nephrotic syndrome requires aggressive treatment to prevent atherosclerotic disease. For more information, see The Nephrotic Syndrome in Nephrology.

The prevalence of CAD is significantly increased among patients with CKD. This is partly explained by the high prevalence of shared risk factors/comorbidities, such as diabetes or hypertension. Additionally, CKD is independently associated with CAD. This association intensifies with declining eGFR and rising albuminuria. The alterations in calcium and phosphorous homeostasis associated with CKD correlate with increased risk for vascular calcifications and cardiovascular disease, although clinical outcomes of therapy targeting these biochemical abnormalities remain unclear.

In patients with CKD, serum biomarkers for myocardial ischemia such as cardiac troponins may be chronically elevated due to decreased renal clearance. Serial troponin measurements and other markers such as creatine kinase-MB can help distinguish acute ischemia from chronic elevations.

As kidney function declines, homeostasis of calcium and phosphorus becomes compromised, resulting in alterations of blood levels of calcium, phosphorus, regulatory hormones, bone mineralization, and pathologic calcification. The term chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD) encompasses these changes.

Three hormones are largely responsible for regulating calcium and phosphorus homeostasis:

  • Parathyroid hormone (PTH)
  • Fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF-23)
  • Vitamin D

PTH is the most important regulator of calcium and phosphorus concentrations. PTH has three separate mechanisms to increase serum calcium: stimulation of osteoclasts to resorb bone, hydroxylation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D in the kidneys, and tubular reabsorption of calcium (

). Concurrently, PTH induces renal phosphorus excretion.

FGF-23 is a peptide secreted by osteocytes and osteoblasts. It acts on the kidney to induce phosphaturia and downregulates 1α-hydroxylase to inhibit synthesis of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. FGF-23 rises in stage G3a CKD, preceding PTH elevation. As GFR falls and PTH rises, PTH directly stimulates further FGF-23 production.

As CKD progresses, increased FGF-23 and decreased nephron mass reduce the conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D by renal tubular cells. Reduction in 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels results in lower intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphorus in the gut, mitigating increases in serum phosphorus but also contributing to hypocalcemia. Reduced 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels also increase PTH production by the parathyroid glands, and hypocalcemia is a potent stimulus for further increases in PTH levels.

Increased plasma PTH caused by CKD is referred to as secondary hyperparathyroidism. Increased PTH levels result in reduced calcium excretion, increased calcium absorption from the gut, increased phosphorus excretion by the kidneys, and activation of osteoclast bone resorption. Early in CKD, the increase in renal phosphorus excretion induced by PTH and FGF-23 enables normal phosphorus levels despite reduced renal excretory capacity. However, as CKD progresses, compensation for the increased release of phosphorus from bone is lost, and phosphorus levels rise. This results in a vicious cycle as hyperphosphatemia stimulates PTH production.

If secondary hyperparathyroidism cannot be adequately controlled, tertiary hyperparathyroidism can ensue. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism is the result of prolonged PTH stimulation resulting in severe parathyroid hyperplasia with elevated PTH levels that are no longer suppressible by elevated plasma calcium concentration.

Serum calcium and phosphorus levels typically remain in the normal range until eGFR drops below 30 mL/min/1.73 m^2, at which point the ability of elevated FGF-23 and PTH levels to promote phosphorus excretion becomes overwhelmed, and hyperphosphatemia develops. Progressive decline in 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels results in reduced intestinal calcium absorption, and hyperphosphatemia promotes precipitation of calcium and phosphorus in extraskeletal tissues, leading to hypocalcemia. Patients with CKD also have a higher prevalence of 25-hydroxyvitamin D deficiency.

KDIGO guidelines recommend that patients with CKD be evaluated for 25-hydroxyvitamin D deficiency and PTH levels to aid in the detection and management of secondary hyperparathyroidism and its complications ( [Table: Table: Laboratory Abnormalities in Hyperparathyroidism]

).

An increased prevalence of arterial calcification, including the coronary arteries, has been noted in patients with CKD (

); the burden of calcification is highest in patients with ESKD. Arterial calcification reduces vascular compliance, contributing to the increased prevalence of left ventricular hypertrophy observed in patients with CKD. Arterial calcification is associated with cardiovascular and all-cause mortality; KDIGO guidelines suggest treating patients with CKD and arterial calcification as appropriate for patients in the highest category of cardiovascular risk. However, treatments specifically targeted at reducing vascular calcification have not been shown to improve clinical outcomes.

Renal osteodystrophy refers to alteration of bone morphology with CKD, rendering affected patients at increased risk for bone pain, falls, and fractures. Diagnosis of renal osteodystrophy can be supported by PTH levels monitored over time, but definitive diagnosis requires a bone biopsy. KDIGO guidelines recommend a bone biopsy if it is likely to affect treatment decisions.

Four main types of renal osteodystrophy, categorized by histologic changes, occur:

  • Osteitis fibrosa cystica (high bone turnover)
  • Adynamic bone disease (low bone turnover)
  • Osteomalacia (decreased mineralization)
  • Mixed uremic osteodystrophy (high bone turnover and decreased mineralization)

Osteitis fibrosa cystica is due to abnormally high bone turnover that occurs after prolonged exposure to sustained high levels of PTH. It is associated with increased number and activity of osteoblasts and osteoclasts and expansion of osteoid surfaces. Classic skeletal changes on radiograph include subperiosteal resorption of bone, most prominently at the phalanges of the hands, and radiolucent bone cysts of the long bones (

).

Adynamic bone disease occurs when there is a lack of bone-cell activity and a markedly reduced rate of bone turnover. Histopathologic abnormalities include decreased osteoclast activity and osteoid. Patients have suppressed PTH levels (e.g., caused by medications such as calcitriol or parathyroidectomy) or skeletal resistance to PTH from down-regulation of the bone PTH receptor due to high circulating PTH levels. Bisphosphonates may worsen adynamic bone disease by inhibiting osteoclast activity and should therefore be avoided in patients with adynamic bone disease documented on bone biopsy, as well as in patients with a high clinical suspicion for adynamic bone disease.

Osteomalacia is characterized by decreased mineralization of osteoid at sites of bone turnover. Although patients with CKD are at increased risk for osteomalacia, CKD does not cause osteomalacia per se; vitamin D deficiency caused by coexisting factors such as intestinal malabsorption or restricted access to sunlight are often present.

Mixed uremic osteodystrophy is the term used to describe elements of both high bone turnover (osteitis fibrosa cystica) and decreased mineralization (osteomalacia).

Patients with CKD may also develop osteoporosis. KDIGO guidelines suggest bone mineral density testing to assess fracture risk if results will affect treatment decisions for patients with CKD stages G3a to G5 with evidence of CKD-MBD and/or risk factors for osteoporosis.

Patients with CKD who have osteoporosis and eGFR >30 mL/min/1.73 m^2 can be treated as per the population without CKD, including nonpharmacologic lifestyle interventions and management of secondary hyperparathyroidism. Bisphosphonates are not recommended for patients with eGFR <30 to 35 mL/min/1.73 m^2. Denosumab and raloxifene can be used in CKD, but patients taking denosumab should be monitored for hypocalcemia. Furthermore, the FDA issued a warning that use of denosumab may be associated with severe hypocalcemia leading to hospitalization and death in patients with dialysis-dependent stage G5 CKD (see Other Causes of Hypocalcemia in Endocrinology and Metabolism). Data on use of anabolic bone agents are limited. Data guiding management of osteoporosis for patients with CKD stages G4 to G5 are limited, and comanagement in conjunction with an expert in CKD-MBD should be considered. For additional information, see Pharmacologic Management of Low Bone Mass and Osteoporosis in Endocrinology and Metabolism.

Elevated phosphorus, PTH, and FGF-23 levels are associated with risk for adverse cardiovascular events and mortality among patients with CKD and ESKD. Observational studies suggest a mortality benefit of phosphate binders and vitamin D analogues to lower serum phosphorus and PTH. Unfortunately, prospective randomized trials are lacking in this field.

KDIGO guidelines for treatment of CKD-MBD rely on available data and expert opinion. Treatment is based on serial assessments of serum phosphorus, calcium, and PTH levels. KDIGO guidelines recommend that elevated serum phosphorus levels be lowered toward the normal range. Optimal PTH levels in patients with CKD are not known. KDIGO guidelines recommend avoiding hypercalcemia and calcium loading given concerns that exposure to exogenous calcium contributes to vascular calcification in all stages of CKD.

Treatment options include dietary modifications, phosphate binders, a sodium/hydrogen exchanger 3 inhibitor, activated vitamin D agents, and calcimimetics ( [Table: Table: Treatment of Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral and Bone Disorder]

). The dose of calcium-based phosphate binders should be minimized, or noncalcium-based binders can be used preferentially. Tenapanor can be considered for patients receiving dialysis with refractory hyperphosphatemia despite phosphate binders. Use of calcitriol and vitamin D analogues to lower PTH levels in patients with CKD stages G3a to G5 who are not receiving dialysis should be avoided; these agents are reserved for patients with CKD stages G4 to G5 with severe and progressive hyperparathyroidism. Oral and intravenous calcimimetics are available and approved by the FDA for persons with CKD requiring dialysis who have elevated PTH levels despite phosphate control and activated vitamin D use.

Tertiary hyperparathyroidism does not respond to phosphate binders or calcitriol therapy. Patients often require parathyroidectomy.

There are currently no therapies approved for lowering FGF-23 levels.

Anemia in the setting of CKD is common and increases as CKD progresses into stages G4 and G5. Anemia in CKD is usually normocytic, and the cause is multifactorial. Contributing factors include the following:

  • Relative lack of erythropoietin production
  • Erythropoietin resistance
  • Disordered iron handling with elevated hepcidin, leading to functional iron deficiency as well as true iron deficiency with blood loss
  • Neocytolysis in the uremic milieu

Concern for the development of left ventricular hypertrophy and observational data linking higher hemoglobin levels with better outcomes led to the belief that higher hemoglobin values were beneficial in patients with CKD and ESKD. However, large randomized controlled trials demonstrated either no benefit or an increased risk for cardiovascular events and strokes in groups assigned to higher hemoglobin targets through erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs). Furthermore, these trials revealed only modest improvements in fatigue and no benefit in physical functioning with higher hemoglobin targets. Thus, KDIGO recommendations as well as the American Society of Nephrology (ASN) high-value care tenets suggest considering ESAs only for patients with CKD who have hemoglobin concentrations <10 g/dL (100 g/L).

An FDA boxed warning for use of ESAs includes an increased risk for serious cardiovascular events when ESAs are administered to patients with CKD who have hemoglobin levels >11 g/dL (110 g/L).

Hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors are oral medications that treat anemia by increasing the endogenous production of erythropoietin and increasing hemoglobin levels. Vadadustat has been approved by the FDA for use in patients with ESKD who have been on dialysis for 3 months or longer. It is not approved for patients with CKD who are not on dialysis and carries a boxed warning citing increased risk for thrombotic vascular events.

All patients with CKD and anemia should have iron profiles assessed, including transferrin saturation and ferritin levels. KDIGO suggests maintaining transferrin saturation levels >30% and serum ferritin levels >500 ng/mL (500 μg/L) using either oral or intravenous iron supplementation. Inadequate iron stores contribute to ESA hyporesponsiveness. Blood transfusions should be minimized because of concerns for iron overload and sensitization to HLA antigens, which lead to allosensitization and increased waiting times for kidney transplantation.

Defective acid excretion in CKD frequently leads to metabolic acidosis. Untreated metabolic acidosis causes muscle and bone loss due to increased muscle proteolysis and bone resorption with impaired bone formation, respectively. Patients with early CKD often have a normal anion gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis due to impaired ammoniagenesis, resulting in reduced bicarbonate generation. As GFR declines, organic and inorganic anions are retained, and an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis develops. For more information, see Metabolic Acidosis in Nephrology.

Although robust data supporting alkali therapy are lacking, KDIGO guidelines suggest consideration of alkali therapy when serum bicarbonate is chronically <18 mEq/L (18 mmol/L) to avoid potential complications of metabolic acidosis. Alkali therapy should be titrated to achieve a serum bicarbonate level between 18 mEq/L (18 mmol/L) and the upper limit of the normal range; excessive alkali therapy in the setting of a reduced GFR may induce a metabolic alkalosis, which is associated with increased mortality. An alternative approach is the provision of alkali through a diet rich in fruits and vegetables, which may have equal efficacy in improving serum bicarbonate levels.

Hyperkalemia commonly develops as eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73 m^2. It may occur at higher eGFR levels in patients with diabetes mellitus and hyporenin-hypoaldosterone type 4 renal tubular acidosis pathophysiology; see Type 4 (Hyperkalemic Distal) Renal Tubular Acidosis in Nephrology. Key renoprotective medications, including ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs), contribute to hyperkalemia through their action, blocking aldosterone-mediated potassium excretion in the distal nephron. Monitoring for hyperkalemia allows implementation of interventions to lower serum potassium levels. Interventions such as a low-potassium diet, oral bicarbonate, and oral potassium-binding resins (e.g., sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, patiromer) allow continued administration of renoprotective medications late into the course of CKD. For additional information, see Hyperkalemia in Nephrology.

The severity of proteinuria is strongly associated with adverse clinical outcomes, including progression of CKD, cardiovascular morbidity, and mortality. It is unclear whether proteinuria is a marker of the underlying severity of kidney damage and disease or if proteinuria itself activates inflammatory pathways and contributes to tubulointerstitial fibrosis.

KDIGO recommends use of an ACE inhibitor or an ARB in all patients with CKD and urine albumin excretion >300 mg/24 hr and also suggests use in patients with CKD and a urine albumin excretion ≥30 mg/24 hr. Although renin-angiotensin system blockade will decrease proteinuria, the use of dual therapy combining ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or direct renin inhibitors results in more adverse events (hyperkalemia, hypotension, AKI) without additional cardiovascular or renal benefits.

Two major issues exist regarding drug administration in patients with CKD:

  • Renally excreted drugs require dose adjustment to avoid accumulation and potential adverse effects.
  • Reduced functional nephron mass increases the probability that a potentially nephrotoxic drug will cause nephrotoxicity.

Nephrotoxins may cause AKI or CKD. Several medications, including NSAIDs, calcineurin inhibitors, and ACE inhibitors/ARBs, have effects on glomerular blood flow. Patients with AKI who are taking NSAIDs should discontinue these medications. For patients with CKD, the ASN recommends avoidance of NSAIDs, including cyclooxygenase 2 inhibitors, due to the risk of worsening kidney function. Although ACE inhibitors or ARBs are a cornerstone of treatment for patients with CKD, these drugs increase the risk for AKI during episodes of acute illness and/or volume depletion. Drugs that cause AKI are reviewed in [Table: Table: Pharmacologic Causes of Acute Kidney Injury]

.

Medications or toxin exposures associated with the development and progression of CKD include proton pump inhibitors, NSAIDs, combination-ingredient analgesics, lithium, exposure to lead, and environmental exposure to the carcinogenic plant toxin aristolochic acid. Care for patients with CKD should include avoidance of these medications as well as dose adjustment of renally excreted medications, including antibiotics and direct oral anticoagulants.

Data strongly support the adverse impact of tobacco exposure on kidney function. Risk increases with the duration and amount of smoking exposure and decreases for former smokers as the smoking-free interval lengthens. Smoking increases the risk for cardiovascular disease outcomes for patients with CKD and exacerbates the adverse effects of coexisting risk factors such as albuminuria. Smoking cessation should be encouraged and supported for patients with CKD.

In animal models, protein-restricted diets slow progression of kidney disease by reducing glomerular filtration pressure. However, in the Modification of Diet in Renal Disease study, no definitive benefit was seen in renal outcomes in patients randomly assigned to the low-protein (0.6 g/kg/d) group. High-protein diets may accelerate kidney functional decline. The Kidney Disease Outcomes Quality Initiative nutrition guidelines suggest a low-protein diet with close clinical supervision for patients who are metabolically stable with stages G3 to G5 CKD. These guidelines recommend that a registered dietitian nutritionist collaborate in the medical nutrition therapy for all patients with CKD and ESKD, including kidney transplant recipients.

For many years the armamentarium of medications proven to slow the progress of CKD was limited to ACE inhibitors and ARBs. The expansion of FDA-approved medications, including sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists, and nonsteroidal MRAs with kidney-protective effects, resulted in additional agents that can benefit patients with diabetes. See Treatment and Prognosis of Diabetic Kidney Disease in Nephrology for information on the management of diabetic kidney disease.

Studies have demonstrated reduced adverse kidney and cardiovascular outcomes in patients with CKD and increased proteinuria but without diabetes who are treated with SGLT2 inhibitors. Beneficial outcomes were most pronounced in patients with an albumin-creatinine ratio >300 mg/g. Of note, trial participants were treated with ACE inhibitors or ARBs before starting treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors unless unable to tolerate RAS inhibitors. SGLT2 inhibitors should be considered in patients with CKD and elevated proteinuria without diabetes in addition to renin-angiotensin system inhibition.

Intravenous iodinated contrast has long been associated with AKI and is termed contrast-associated AKI (CA-AKI). Contrast-induced AKI (CI-AKI), a subset of CA-AKI, is directly mediated by the contrast agent. Data show that the frequency of CA-AKI is less than originally believed, because hospitalized patients who require noncontrast imaging develop AKI at the same frequency. However, the risk for CA-AKI and CI-AKI increases with increasing severity of CKD.

The 2023 American College of Radiology Manual on Contrast Media suggests avoidance of iodinated contrast for patients with an eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m^2, although KDIGO guidelines advise caution in withholding contrast in the evaluation or treatment of possibly fatal conditions in these patients. Patients with CKD and an eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m^2 who require iodinated contrast should receive intravenous hydration with 0.9% saline before and after receiving contrast unless a contraindication exists. Prophylactic saline infusion should also be considered in patients with an eGFR of 30 to 44 mL/min/1.73 m^2 who have other risk factors for AKI. Before using contrast, consider discussions with radiologists or interventionalists on using low-osmolality contrast agents and minimizing radiocontrast dose. For more information, see Contrast-Associated Acute Kidney Injury in Nephrology.

Group I gadolinium-based contrast media (GBCM) used in MRI have been associated with nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) in patients with ESKD on dialysis, advanced CKD with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m^2, or AKI. Patients with NSF present with symmetric, fibrotic, indurated papules, plaques, or subcutaneous nodules most commonly located on the legs, mid thighs, and upper arms (

). The American College of Radiology considers group II GBCM to present a very low to nonexistent risk of NSF, and it should be the GBCM type used for patients at risk for NSF who must receive MRI with contrast. There is insufficient data to quantify risk in patients receiving group III GBCM, but it should also be avoided in patients at risk for NSF. A discussion with the radiologist may be warranted when ordering an MRI with contrast in at-risk patients. Additional recommendations include using the lowest volume of contrast adequate for the study and, for patients receiving hemodialysis, scheduling the study temporally close to their next hemodialysis session.

Patients with CKD are at increased risk for infections that can be prevented by vaccination; however, these patients also have impaired immune responses to vaccines. Patients with CKD should receive recommended vaccinations according to CDC guidelines, which state that vaccinations in patients with CKD may be more effective when performed before the need for chronic dialysis or kidney transplantation. Special considerations for patients with CKD include the following:

  • Patients with advanced CKD near dialysis dependence or those with ESKD on hemodialysis not already immune to hepatitis B virus (HBV) should be vaccinated against HBV.
  • Patients with CKD or the nephrotic syndrome should be vaccinated against pneumococcus.
  • The influenza vaccine should be administered annually to all patients with CKD; patients with ESKD should preferentially receive the inactivated influenza vaccine.

For more information on vaccines, see Immunization in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

Patients with advanced CKD may ultimately require kidney replacement therapy (KRT). For patients who choose hemodialysis, timely vascular access creation is essential. Referral to an experienced surgeon many months before hemodialysis is critical because arteriovenous fistula placement, the safest and most enduring option for vascular access, can be technically challenging and may require several months for full maturation. Arteriovenous fistulas have superior clinical outcomes compared with arteriovenous grafts. Tunneled catheters may be used for dialysis promptly after placement, but they are associated with increased risk for bloodstream infection and death.

Protecting the veins of the nondominant arm is paramount and involves limiting phlebotomy and intravenous catheters in that arm. Data demonstrate that peripherally inserted central catheter lines placed before or after initiation of hemodialysis are independently associated with a 15% to 20% lower likelihood of transition to any working fistula or graft. The ASN recommends that peripherally inserted central catheter lines should be avoided in patients with an eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m^2. Avoidance of subclavian venous catheters helps limit subclavian stenosis, which can impair the proper functioning of arteriovenous access used for dialysis.

CKD stages G1 through G3a in older patients (≥65 years) without albuminuria is of minimal clinical importance. For older patients with progressing or severe CKD necessitating discussions about KRT and/or referral for evaluation for kidney transplantation, a patient-centered approach is preferred. Comorbid medical conditions, functional status, expected outcomes, and patient preferences regarding goals of care should be considered. Quality of life increases for older adults who receive kidney transplants but may or may not improve with dialysis. Nutritional status often improves after starting dialysis, but functional status usually declines and risk of falls increases for many older patients after initiation of dialysis.

Pain is a common symptom in patients with CKD. Medications used for treatment of acute and chronic pain must be considered in context of the risk of AKI and altered metabolism with reduced kidney function. Nonpharmacologic interventions should be utilized. Systemic NSAIDS should be avoided in patients with CKD due to the risk of AKI. Topical NSAID preparations should be used with caution given the risk of systemic absorption. If opioid-based pain medications are required, oxycodone, hydromorphone, or tramadol are preferred because of their shorter half-life and hepatic elimination. Tramadol should not be used in patients who are also taking selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) due to the risk of serotonin syndrome. If higher doses or other opioids are required, patients must be monitored closely for adverse effects with accumulation of metabolites.

For neuropathic pain, the use of gabapentin or pregabalin is appropriate with dose reduction based on the degree of CKD. SSRIs and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors may also be used; some medications in these classes require dose reduction in CKD.

Referral to a pain management program is indicated for refractory or difficult-to-manage pain syndromes.

CKD stage G5 is defined as an eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m^2, and ESKD, now also referred to as kidney failure requiring replacement therapy (KFRT), is defined as CKD stage G5 treated with chronic dialysis or kidney transplantation.

Patients with an eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m^2 should be educated about KRT options, including hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, and kidney transplantation. Studies demonstrate no benefit in starting KRT in asymptomatic patients or at a specific eGFR cutoff compared with watchful waiting once eGFR falls below 10 mL/min/1.73 m^2 and initiating KRT for symptoms or metabolic abnormalities that are refractory to medical treatment. Shared decision making about goals of care for patients with advanced CKD is an important high-value care tenet of the ASN.

Kidney transplantation is the preferred treatment for ESKD. It improves life expectancy and quality of life and provides significant cost savings to the health care system compared with dialysis. However, demand far exceeds supply. In the United States, wait times for deceased-donor kidneys range from 3 to more than 5 years.

Patients should be referred to a kidney transplant center for evaluation when the eGFR is 15 to 20 mL/min/1.73 m^2 or when the risk for kidney replacement therapy exceeds 40% over 2 years using a validated risk calculator. Early referral is important because preemptive kidney transplants (transplants before needing dialysis) are associated with improved clinical outcomes compared with receiving a transplant after starting dialysis. Early referral also allows time to identify living donors.

Patients and donors undergo extensive health screening to identify issues that may affect the safety and/or outcome of the transplant. In the potential recipient, these include active malignancy, CAD, or infections. Adequate social support and financial resources are important to ensure medication adherence and long-term survival of the transplanted allograft. Donors are screened for intrinsic kidney disease, hypertension, and diabetes to minimize risk related to reduced renal mass resulting from donation nephrectomy. Donors are at risk for future development of hypertension and proteinuria, with a small number of donors progressing to CKD. Blood pressure and kidney function of donors should be monitored as part of routine medical follow-up.

Patients are generally managed by a transplant nephrologist for the first 6 months posttransplant and are then co-managed with a general nephrologist and/or internal medicine physician.

Immunosuppressive medications are required to prevent allograft rejection. Induction therapy is started perioperatively with polyclonal anti–T-cell antibodies (thymoglobulin) or monoclonal anti–interleukin-2 receptor antibody (basiliximab) in most patients. Calcineurin inhibitors with pulse glucocorticoids are also started.

Long-term maintenance therapy usually includes a combination of calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus or cyclosporine), antimetabolites (mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine), and glucocorticoids. Some patients with well-matched allografts can discontinue glucocorticoids. Doses of these medications are highest immediately posttransplant and are decreased over the next several months to minimize side effects ( [Table: Table: Adverse Effects of Immunosuppression after Kidney Transplantation]

), including long-term nephrotoxicity, while maintaining adequate immunosuppression.

Calcineurin inhibitors are metabolized by the cytochrome P-450 system. Drug-drug interactions may occur, leading to high or low levels of the calcineurin inhibitor and placing patients at risk for calcineurin toxicity or rejection. Care should be taken to check for potential interactions before adding or adjusting medications.

Immediately posttransplant, patients are monitored for acute rejection and postoperative complications. Thereafter, minimizing medication adverse effects and risk for infection becomes the focus while maintaining adequate immunosuppression to prevent rejection.

Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in kidney transplant recipients. Kidney transplantation, despite restoration of kidney function, should be treated as a cardiovascular disease equivalent for purposes of risk factor modification. KDIGO guidelines recommend dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and ARBs as first-line agents for blood pressure control in transplant patients. Care should be taken with calcium channel blocker dose adjustments because they have drug-drug interactions with calcineurin inhibitors. Dyslipidemia is a common adverse effect of calcineurin inhibitors, sirolimus, and glucocorticoids. Treatment with a statin improves cardiac outcomes; however, statins have drug-drug interactions with calcineurin inhibitors and can increase toxicity of both drugs.

Immunosuppression significantly increases the risk for infection. Within the first month after transplantation, the most common infectious complications are similar to other surgeries and include urinary tract infections and wound infections. Afterward, opportunistic infections become more prevalent (see [Table: Table: Common Infections after SOT]

).

Polyoma BK virus uniquely affects kidney transplant recipients, only rarely occurring with other organ transplants or in immunosuppressed states. The most common clinical manifestation is an acute or indolent rise in serum creatinine due to tubulointerstitial nephritis or ureteral stenosis. Treatment requires reduction in the immunosuppression dose, but this must be balanced against the risk of allograft rejection.

For more information, see Infections in Transplant Recipients in Infectious Disease.

Because kidney transplant recipients are at higher risk for developing cancer, it is important to follow age- and sex-appropriate cancer screening guidelines before transplant. In addition, ultrasonography should be used to screen for renal cell carcinoma in patients on long-standing hemodialysis.

Immunosuppressive medications increase the risk for several forms of malignancy, with nonmelanoma skin cancers being the most common. Therefore, transplant recipients should be screened regularly for skin cancer in addition to age- and sex-specific cancers.

Posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders can occur with long-term immunosuppression. These malignancies are caused by uncontrolled B-lymphocyte proliferation associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and impaired T-cell surveillance. Treatment involves reduction in immunosuppression, administration of the anti–B-cell monoclonal antibody rituximab, and chemotherapy. Additionally, calcineurin inhibitors may be switched to sirolimus because of its antiproliferative effects.

Kaposi sarcoma is common and is associated with human herpesvirus 8 infection. Treatment involves reduction in immunosuppression dosing and switching to a sirolimus-based regimen.

After kidney transplantation, the onset or recognition of type 2 diabetes mellitus is common and contributes to cardiovascular risk. Factors for posttransplantation diabetes mellitus (PTDM), previously known as new-onset diabetes after transplant, include medications (glucocorticoids, calcineurin inhibitors, mammalian target of rapamycin inhibitors), weight gain with improved nutrition, increased insulin metabolism with improved kidney function, and concomitant hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. Posttransplant patients should be screened yearly with a hemoglobin A~1c. KDIGO guidelines recommend that patients with PTDM be treated similarly to patients who have both CKD and type 2 diabetes mellitus.

AKI is a common posttransplant complication and can occur immediately posttransplant or at any time thereafter. Acute rejection should always be part of the differential diagnosis because early recognition and treatment are associated with better long-term outcomes. In addition to acute rejection, posttransplant AKI may be caused by the following:

  • Renal vasoconstriction from calcineurin inhibitor toxicity
  • Calcineurin inhibitor–induced thrombotic microangiopathy
  • BK polyomavirus nephropathy
  • Ureteral stenosis
  • Nontransplant-specific AKI cause

Glomerular diseases can recur in the transplant allograft. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is one of the most common forms of glomerular disease to recur. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and thrombotic microangiopathy should be treated aggressively if disease recurrence is seen in the transplanted kidney, because these conditions are associated with high rates of graft failure. Patients with lupus or ANCA vasculitis should have quiescent disease for several months preceding transplantation to reduce risk for disease recurrence. Diabetic kidney disease and IgA nephropathy may also affect allograft function after transplant.

Secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism, common in patients with ESKD, can persist for several months posttransplant; continuation of calcimimetics may be warranted if the patient is hypercalcemic. Additionally, hypophosphatemia is common due to renal phosphorus wasting. Long-term glucocorticoid use can cause osteopenia, osteoporosis, and osteonecrosis. Calcineurin inhibitors may also induce magnesium wasting. See Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral and Bone Disorder in Nephrology for more information.

Most transplant centers do not recommend immunization within the first 3 to 6 months posttransplant because of increased immunosuppression and decreased likelihood of developing long-term immunity from the vaccine. Influenza vaccine, however, may be administered within 1 month of transplant in the setting of an influenza outbreak. Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in transplant recipients. For additional information, see Prevention of Infections in Transplant Recipients in Infectious Disease.

The advent of effective direct-acting antiviral agents for treatment of HCV infection has opened the door to expanding the use of kidneys from HCV-positive donors. Some transplant centers are offering kidneys from HCV-positive donors to HCV-positive and HCV-negative recipients, and then treating the recipient for HCV after transplant.

Clinical trials demonstrate successful cure of HCV infection in previously HCV-negative recipients of kidneys from HCV-positive donors. For more information, see Hepatitis C in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease.

Successful kidney transplantation can be performed in recipients who have HIV infection that is controlled by antiretroviral medication. These patients should be referred to transplant centers with expertise in this area.

Hemodialysis achieves clearance of blood solutes by convection and diffusion with dialysate flowing countercurrent to blood separated by a semipermeable dialyzer membrane. Hemodialysis is most commonly performed three times per week for 3.5- to 4.5-hour treatment sessions at an outpatient dialysis unit. In addition to the inconvenience of time spent in the dialysis unit, patients may have symptomatic hypotension during or following dialysis and/or excessive fatigue following sessions. Frequent and/or longer treatments provide better control of volume status and serum electrolytes with fewer treatment-related symptoms. Home hemodialysis allows increased autonomy with more frequent but shorter treatments.

For patients who are first starting dialysis treatment or who have missed numerous dialysis sessions, dialysis disequilibrium syndrome can be seen during or following dialysis. Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome is thought to arise from osmotically mediated fluid shifts during hemodialysis, causing cerebral edema and a wide variety of neurologic symptoms, ranging from mild symptoms (such as headache, nausea, blurred vision, restlessness, and confusion) to, in rare cases, severe manifestations such as coma and seizures.

Peritoneal dialysis utilizes an indwelling catheter to perform exchanges of dialysate into the peritoneal cavity, which serves as a semipermeable membrane allowing for diffusion of solutes and osmosis of water. Dialysate is exchanged about three to five times per day. Patients can perform exchanges during the day, or a cycler can be used to exchange the fluid overnight while the patient sleeps. Patients can work or perform activities during the day. Clinical outcomes are similar for patients on peritoneal dialysis compared with hemodialysis, although patients starting KRT who have residual kidney function may have better outcomes with peritoneal dialysis.

Peritonitis is a complication associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Repeated infections can cause peritoneal damage, reducing the efficacy of dialysis treatments. Peritoneal dialysis–associated peritonitis is infrequent, with an average of one episode every 2 to 3 years. It is usually caused by gram-positive skin flora and less commonly by gram-negative intestinal flora. Proper aseptic technique when handling the peritoneal dialysis catheter and exit site care are critical in preventing peritonitis.

Some patients with CKD stage G5 or ESKD, especially those who are older or with multiple comorbidities, may not desire intensive dialysis or choose not to initiate KRT ( [Table: Table: Goals of Care in End-Stage Kidney Disease]

). Kidney supportive care applies tenets of palliative care to improving the quality of life for patients with advanced CKD. Treatment is aligned with the patient’s goals through culturally sensitive shared decision making and advance care planning focused on delay of progression, quality of life, and symptom management. Conservative care allows multidisciplinary treatment without use of dialysis. Data are heterogeneous but suggest that, among older patients who select conservative care versus KRT, survival is shorter, but quality of life is similar with fewer hospitalizations. Nephrology palliative care is a growing subspecialty within the field, supporting patients who elect conservative care as well as their primary care providers and general nephrologists. About 20% of patients on KRT decide to discontinue treatment prior to death. For patients who withdraw from KRT, death usually occurs within 2 weeks. Patients who are older or have multiple comorbid conditions are more likely to elect withdrawal.

Sudden cardiac death is the leading cause of death in ESKD. This population is at increased risk due to rapid shifts of serum electrolytes during dialysis, chronic volume overload contributing to left ventricular hypertrophy and cardiac fibrosis, hypertension, and blood pressure variability. Uremic toxins also contribute. Avoiding rapid changes in serum potassium during dialysis may help limit arrhythmias, and adherence to dietary salt and fluid restriction may help limit volume overload. Intradialytic hypotension induced by rapid volume removal during dialysis may cause cardiovascular and central nervous system injury due to organ hypoperfusion. Vascular calcification is accelerated by uremic toxins, chronic inflammation, and calcium-based medications/vitamin D analogues. Limiting medications that raise serum calcium and achieving adequate clearance during dialysis may help delay the progression of atherosclerosis. Although hypertension and blood pressure variability are associated with mortality for patients on KRT, the optimal blood pressure goal is not known.

Infection is the second leading cause of death in ESKD. Patients have a relatively immunosuppressed state from chronic inflammation. Tunneled dialysis catheters increase the risk for bacteremia, and empiric antibiotics should be administered while waiting for blood culture results in patients with suspected bacteremia. Tunneled catheters should be removed for severe sepsis, evidence of metastatic infection, concomitant exit-site or tunnel infection, persistent fever, or bacteremia despite antibiotics. Exchange of the catheter over a guidewire is the best option for clinically stable patients without a tunnel infection or for patients who clear the bacteremia within 72 hours of antibiotic administration. Antibiotic lock therapy, consisting of instillation of an antibiotic solution in the catheter lumen, is an alternative for stable patients with less virulent gram-positive organisms. Prevention of catheter-associated infections is best achieved by minimizing the need for their use through advanced planning to achieve functioning arteriovenous access.

Acquired cystic kidney disease is common among patients with severe CKD and ESKD. Cysts are at increased risk for transformation into renal cell carcinoma, but screening is not recommended for most patients with ESKD to avoid routine cancer screening for patients with limited life expectancy. Screening can be individualized for patients with longer life expectancy, such as potential kidney transplant recipients. A high index of suspicion is warranted for patients with new-onset gross hematuria, unexplained flank pain, or persistently elevated hemoglobin levels. Urology evaluation is indicated for cysts that are suspicious for malignancy.

Calciphylaxis (calcific uremic arteriolopathy), characterized by calcification of the vascular media leading to ischemic skin lesions, is a complication of ESKD (

). Skin changes begin with induration and progress to tender subcutaneous plaques followed by frank necrosis. The lesions are painful and predict poor outcomes, including loss of mobility, hospitalization, sepsis, and death. Risk factors include secondary hyperparathyroidism, longer duration of dialysis, obesity, diabetes, and use of warfarin. There are no FDA-approved treatments. However, interventions employed include the following:

  • Optimization of phosphate control
  • Avoidance of calcium products and vitamin D analogues
  • Initiation of calcimimetics
  • Intravenous and intralesional sodium thiosulfate
  • Vitamin K therapy
  • Use of direct anticoagulants in lieu of warfarin

Multidisciplinary care that includes wound management, dermatology, and plastic surgery is necessary.

Patients with CKD and ESKD are more likely to have depression and anxiety. The prevalence of depression is estimated to be 20% to 30% and is 12% to 52% for anxiety. Contributing factors may include illness burden and psychosocial factors such as diminished social support. Limited data suggest treatment efficacy with behavioral therapy or SSRIs.

Patients with ESKD often have pruritus and sleep disturbance, including restless legs syndrome and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Because these are not life-threatening symptoms, they often receive less focus than other complications. However, they are significant contributors to diminished quality of life. The cause of pruritus is not known but may include inflammation or increased activity of skin opioid receptors. Twenty percent to 80% of patients with ESKD have pruritis. Treatment includes optimizing dialysis clearance, emollients, gabapentin, SSRIs, and the kappa-opioid receptor agonist difelikefalin, which is administered with dialysis.

Sleep disturbance is common among patients with ESKD and can be improved with increased intensity of dialysis, which should be the first-line therapy followed by other therapies used in patients without ESKD. Restless legs syndrome is estimated to affect approximately 20% and OSA up to 50% of patients with ESKD. OSA is associated with increased mortality. Symptoms of OSA in a patient with ESKD should prompt evaluation and treatment.

Patients receiving KRT are often sedentary. Physical activity and exercise should be encouraged and are associated with mortality benefits.

The Kidney in Pregnancy

Pregnancy is a state of volume expansion and vasodilation. Sodium and water retention increase plasma volume, augmenting renal blood flow and increasing glomerular filtration rate (GFR) by up to 50%. With the GFR increase, serum creatinine levels decrease. Therefore, high normal serum creatinine levels may indicate significant kidney impairment. Despite the volume expansion, blood pressure (BP) begins to decrease in the first trimester and reaches the nadir in the second trimester due to peripheral vasodilation.

Proteinuria increases, with the upper limit of normal increasing from 100 mg/24 h in nonpregnant individuals to approximately 200 mg/24 h in pregnant individuals. Values >300 mg/24 h are considered abnormal. Preexisting proteinuria may also worsen during pregnancy, making pregnancy-related changes difficult to distinguish from a flare of an underlying kidney disease or development of preeclampsia.

Because of increased renal vascular and interstitial volume, kidney size may increase by 1 to 1.5 cm. Physiologic hydronephrosis and hydroureter, due in part to external compression of the ureters, are common in pregnancy. These changes increase as pregnancy advances and may take weeks to resolve postpartum. The dilated collecting system can lead to urinary stasis, which increases the risk for urinary tract infections. Therefore, screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria (and treating if present) at least once in early pregnancy is recommended. See Asymptomatic Bacteriuria in Infectious Disease for more information.

Chronic respiratory alkalosis due to progesterone-induced hyperventilation commonly decreases Pco~2 to 27 to 32 mm Hg (3.6-4.3 kPa). Kidney compensation results in decreased serum bicarbonate levels between 18 and 20 mEq/L (18-20 mmol/L), with a serum pH of approximately 7.45.

Changes in antidiuretic hormone response to osmolality (reset osmostat, which is the threshold for which antidiuretic hormone secretion is lowered) cause mild hyponatremia (decrease in serum sodium of 4 to 5 mEq/L [4-5 mmol/L]). No treatment is indicated.

Hypertension is a modifiable risk factor for adverse maternal and fetal outcomes in pregnant persons. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) and the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommend measuring blood pressure at each prenatal visit.

ACOG defines chronic hypertension as a systolic BP ≥140 mm Hg or diastolic BP ≥90 mm Hg starting before pregnancy, diagnosed before 20 weeks’ gestation, or persisting longer than 12 weeks postpartum ( [Table: Table: Hypertension in Pregnancy]

). It is associated with worse maternal and fetal outcomes. The lower BP measurements associated with physiologic changes of pregnancy can mask hypertension during the first trimester.

ACOG recommends treating pregnant individuals with persistent systolic BP ≥140 mm Hg or diastolic BP ≥90 mm Hg and maintaining BP at <140/90 mm Hg. These goals were updated in 2022 based on the results of the Chronic Hypertension and Pregnancy (CHAP) trial, which demonstrated that treatment to a goal BP of <140/90 mm Hg reduced the primary composite outcome of the following:

  • Preeclampsia with severe features occurring within 2 weeks postpartum
  • Medically indicated preterm birth
  • Placental abruption
  • Fetal or neonatal death

Any evidence of end-organ damage requires treatment, regardless of severity of hypertension. Importantly, all antihypertensive medications cross the placenta.

Renin-angiotensin system agents (ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and direct renin inhibitors) are contraindicated, even early in pregnancy, because of teratogenicity and should be discontinued before conception (in those planning pregnancy). If conception has already occurred, these agents should be stopped immediately and the pregnant individual should be counseled regarding possible fetal effects.

First-line therapy includes long-acting nifedipine and labetalol, which have been used safely and extensively in pregnancy. Although no specific agent is preferred due to lack of data supporting one over the other, long-acting nifedipine can be dosed daily and may improve adherence. Methyldopa is also safe to use in pregnancy but may not be as effective, and use is often limited by adverse side effects. The β-blockers metoprolol and pindolol have also been used in pregnancy, although atenolol and propranolol may have adverse fetal effects. Diuretics must be used with caution because they may induce oligohydramnios if started during pregnancy. Spironolactone is not recommended during pregnancy due to the risks for male fetus feminization and growth restriction.

To prevent preeclampsia, ACOG recommends initiating aspirin (81 mg/d) between 12 weeks and 28 weeks of gestation (preferably before 16 weeks) for all pregnant individuals with chronic hypertension. Aspirin should be continued until delivery.

Gestational hypertension first manifests after 20 weeks of pregnancy without proteinuria or other end-organ damage (features of preeclampsia) and resolves within 12 weeks of delivery (see [Table: Table: Hypertension in Pregnancy]

). Preeclampsia occurs in approximately one third of patients with gestational hypertension. Gestational hypertension can recur in subsequent pregnancies and is associated with an approximately fourfold risk for development of chronic hypertension.

Preeclampsia is defined by new-onset hypertension and proteinuria (urine protein ≥300 mg/24 h or urine protein-creatinine ratio ≥300 mg/g) that occur after 20 weeks of pregnancy ( [Table: Table: Diagnostic Criteria for Preeclampsia]

). If proteinuria is not present, diagnostic criteria are met if there is evidence of end-organ damage (e.g., liver/kidney injury, pulmonary edema, cerebral/visual symptoms, thrombocytopenia) in the setting of hypertension. Eclampsia is the presence of seizures in context of preeclampsia without other cause. The HELLP syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) is a life-threatening syndrome present in 10% to 20% of cases of preeclampsia.

To prevent preeclampsia, the USPSTF recommends low-dose aspirin (81 mg/d) after 12 weeks of pregnancy for individuals with one or more high-risk factors and two or more moderate-risk factors ( [Table: Table: Risk Factors for Preeclampsia]

). Antihypertensive medications, when used to treat pregnant individuals with chronic hypertension, can reduce the incidence of preeclampsia with severe features.

Symptoms of preeclampsia include rapid weight gain due to edema, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain (particularly concerning if in the upper right quadrant, signifying possible HELLP syndrome), headaches, altered mental status, and blurred vision. If untreated, preeclampsia ultimately leads to maternal end-organ damage and fetal growth retardation and may cause maternal and/or fetal death.

Definitive treatment of preeclampsia is delivery. Maternal risk for complications diminishes in the hours after delivery, although proteinuria may take months to resolve. Although maternal benefits must be weighed against neonatal risks for a preterm delivery, severe preeclampsia is an indication for immediate delivery regardless of gestational age. Mild preeclampsia may be managed conservatively with maternal and fetal monitoring and hypertension treatment. In the setting of preeclampsia, most experts initiate treatment at BP >150-160/100-110 mm Hg, although there is no consensus. See Acute-Onset Severe Hypertension in Nephrology for more information. In all cases, close attention to hypertension is recommended in the postpartum period.

The 2019 ACOG recommendations define acute-onset severe hypertension as systolic BP ≥160 mm Hg and/or diastolic BP ≥110 mm Hg (see [Table: Table: Hypertension in Pregnancy]

). Acute-onset severe hypertension may occur in the setting of previously controlled chronic hypertension, as a component of preeclampsia, in the HELLP syndrome, or de novo in individuals without these complications. Pregnant patients with acute-onset severe hypertension that persists >15 minutes require emergent therapy, most typically with intravenous labetalol or hydralazine or with immediate-release oral nifedipine.

The target goal of treatment is not normalization of BP but, rather, a target BP of <160/110 mm Hg within 30 to 60 minutes. Maternal and fetal monitoring is advised. Maternal BP should be controlled before delivery. Magnesium sulfate is also advised as emergent therapy for seizure prophylaxis and should be given to women with acute-onset severe hypertension, regardless of other signs of preeclampsia or eclampsia.

Chronic kidney disease and a serum creatinine level >1.4 mg/dL (124 μmol/L) increases the risk for kidney and pregnancy-associated complications. Proteinuria may also increase risk, but an elevated serum creatinine has greater impact. Complications include preeclampsia, acute kidney injury, progression of chronic kidney disease, end-stage kidney disease, preterm delivery, gestational hypertension, intrauterine growth retardation, and fetal loss. Preconception counseling regarding these risks as well as care from a multidisciplinary team, including a maternal-fetal specialist, are essential. Patients receiving immunosuppressant therapies (e.g., mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide) for glomerular diseases may need medications discontinued before conception.

Pregnancy is uncommon in individuals receiving dialysis, which is associated with infertility. Because β-human chorionic gonadotropin levels may increase in nonpregnant individuals receiving dialysis, ultrasonography is usually necessary to confirm pregnancy. Pregnancy in those receiving dialysis is associated with very high risk for preeclampsia and fetal loss, although live birth rates have improved to 60% to 80%. To optimize fetal outcomes, hemodialysis frequency and dose are increased to manage BP and volume status.

After kidney transplantation, hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian function improves and fertility may be restored. Outcomes are improved with better allograft function (serum creatinine <1.5 mg/dL [133 μmol/L]) and stable immunosuppression; patients with kidney transplants should wait at least 1 to 2 years after transplantation with a stable allograft before attempting conception. No immunosuppressive medication has been extensively studied in pregnancy, and all have some associated risk:

  • Mycophenolate mofetil is teratogenic and should be replaced 3 to 6 months before conception with azathioprine, which has an extensive history of use in pregnancy; sirolimus is also teratogenic.
  • Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus and cyclosporine) are generally safe, although case reports of adverse effects have been reported.
  • Glucocorticoids increase the risk for pregnancy-induced hypertension and diabetes.
