Headache and Facial Pain

The International Classification of Headache Disorders, third edition (ICHD-3), identifies three clinical subtypes of headache: primary headaches, secondary headaches, and painful cranial neuralgias ( [Table: Table: Classification of Headache Disorders]

).

Primary headaches are defined by clinical criteria and are the conditions most seen in clinical practice. These include tension-type headache, migraine, cluster headache and the other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (TACs), and less common primary headache syndromes.

Identifying headaches that are caused by another disorder (secondary headaches; see Secondary Headache in Neurology) is a primary goal of the initial evaluation of a patient with headache. Suspicion for a secondary headache is heightened with an acute or progressive headache pattern and the presence of clinical “red flags” ( [Table: Table: Red Flags for Secondary Headaches]

).

A detailed headache history is the most valuable clinical assessment tool for evaluating headaches (Video: Headache History). Neurologic examination with funduscopic testing is essential, and, when red flags are present, brain imaging is the most important diagnostic study. Noncontrast head CT is recommended for acute headache presentations in the setting of trauma or suspected vascular origin. For subacute or chronic headaches with new or progressive features, brain MRI is more appropriate given its greater sensitivity and safety. Contrast administration or vascular imaging may be added in select clinical circumstances. Stable headaches meeting criteria for migraine or tension-type headache usually do not require imaging.

Additional testing is determined on the basis of differential diagnostic considerations and may include erythrocyte sedimentation rate determination, C-reactive protein measurement, lumbar puncture, serum chemistries, or toxicology screens. Electroencephalography is not indicated in the assessment of headache disorders unless seizures are present or suspected.

The most prevalent primary headache condition, tension-type headache is defined by clinical criteria as a headache disorder that, unlike migraine, is mild to moderate in intensity and is not associated with nausea, severe sensory sensitivities, or neurologic symptoms ( [Table: Table: Criteria for Episodic Tension-Type Headache]

). Subclassification is based on monthly headache frequency: infrequent episodic (<1 day), frequent episodic (1-14 days), and chronic (≥15 days). Imaging is not indicated.

Acetaminophen, aspirin, NSAIDs, and caffeine-containing compounds are effective immediate treatments for tension-type headache. Amitriptyline is the only agent shown to be effective in controlled trials for tension-type headache prevention; venlafaxine and mirtazapine have more limited data. Muscle relaxants, benzodiazepines, opioids, and onabotulinum toxin A have no role in managing tension-type headache.

Nonpharmacologic treatment strategies, such as relaxation training and cognitive behavioral therapies, have reasonable scientific support for effectiveness. Recent evidence suggests benefit from acupuncture. Physical therapies have only modest effect, and spinal manipulation has no effect.

The ICHD-3 recognizes several subtypes of migraine, including migraine without aura, migraine with aura, and chronic migraine. Each subtype is characterized by episodes of disabling headache lasting hours to days. Accuracy of diagnosis and management is enhanced by using formal ICHD-3 criteria, although the POUND mnemonic (Pulsatile quality of headache, One-day duration, Unilateral location, Nausea or vomiting, Disabling intensity) is helpful for recalling the symptoms typically associated with migraine.

Because of extensive phenotypic variation, nearly half of migraine presentations are misdiagnosed. Neck pain (75%) and “sinus” symptoms, such as tearing or nasal drainage (50%), are more common in migraine than other features perceived to be characteristic of migraine, such as vomiting or aura.

In the presence of a stable clinical pattern of migraine and a normal neurologic examination, brain imaging is not indicated.

Migraine without aura is the most prevalent migraine subtype ( [Table: Table: Criteria for Migraine Without Aura]

). Although clinicians often emphasize unilateral location or pulsatile characteristics, moderate to severe pain is the most sensitive feature, and worsening by routine physical activity is the most specific element among the pain criteria. Photophobia, phonophobia, and nausea are each reported by approximately 75% of patients with migraine without aura.

Migraine with aura is diagnosed after two discrete aura episodes have occurred ( [Table: Table: Criteria for Migraine With Aura]

).

Aura may occur in 20% to 30% of patients with migraine. It frequently precedes pain but may occur during or without head discomfort. Aura symptoms involve positive and negative neurologic phenomena developing gradually and evolving over a period of 5 to 60 minutes. Resolution is gradual and complete. ICHD-3 criteria recognize several aura subtypes:

  • Typical aura involves any combination of homonymous visual, hemisensory, or language symptoms.
  • Brainstem aura is defined by the presence of two of the following brainstem symptoms: dysarthria, vertigo, tinnitus, hypoacusis, diplopia, ataxia, or decreased level of consciousness.
  • Hemiplegic aura comprises any aura involving motor weakness.
  • Retinal aura involves monocular visual compromise. These auras need to be distinguished from ocular pathologies, such as retinal ischemia or detachment.

Estrogen-containing oral contraceptives should be avoided in migraine with aura of all subtypes because they are associated with an increased risk for stroke.

Chronic migraine is defined as headache for 15 or more days per month ( [Table: Table: Criteria for Chronic Migraine]

). Transformation from acute to chronic migraine occurs at an annual rate of 3%. Older age, female sex, head trauma, major life changes or stressors, obesity, chronic pain, mood and anxiety disorders, and inappropriate acute migraine management (e.g., using a drug that may cause or exacerbate medication overuse headache [MOH]) are risk factors.

Patients with chronic migraine experience more disability and are more likely to report migraine-related comorbidities (mood or anxiety disorders, sleep dysfunction, irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia) than patients with episodic migraine.

Acute migraine treatment aims to eliminate pain and restore function (Video: Acute Migraine Management). Treatment goals involve freedom from pain, nausea, and sensory sensitization within 1 to 2 hours and maintaining such control through at least 24 hours.

Because migraine characteristics show significant interindividual and intraindividual variability, different treatment options and strategies are required ( [Table: Table: Acute Migraine Therapies]

). Guidelines recommend tailoring treatments to the severity and symptomatology of the episode. Because consistency of response to any treatment rarely approaches 100%, most patients benefit from two or more acute migraine therapies. Administering medication at the time of mild pain has been shown to improve therapeutic outcomes when compared with treating moderate to severe headache; therefore, treatment should be started as early as possible in the episode. Migraines awakening a patient from sleep or associated with nausea and vomiting may require medication in parenteral or nasal formulations. Treatment should be limited to fewer than 8 to 10 days per month for triptans, ergot alkaloids, opioids, or combination analgesics and fewer than 15 days for simple analgesics to avoid MOH.

Evidence-based guidelines recommend several simple and combination analgesics as first-line therapies for acute migraine. Acetaminophen has established efficacy only in migraine of mild to moderate intensity; data suggest the response may be enhanced by coadministration with metoclopramide. Aspirin, administered alone or in combination with acetaminophen and caffeine, also has established efficacy in acute migraine. The effectiveness of several NSAIDs is supported by strong evidence. Special formulations of these products have been shown to be more rapidly absorbed and effective than their standard tablet counterparts. These formulations include effervescent aspirin, solubilized ibuprofen and celecoxib, and diclofenac powder for oral solution.

Triptans are selective 5-hydroxytryptamine 1B and 1D receptor agonists that inhibit cerebral vasodilation, neurogenic inflammation, and pain sensitization in patients with migraine. Guidelines recommend adding a triptan to an NSAID in patients with moderate to severe migraine who have not responded to NSAID monotherapy over a series of at least three migraine episodes.

Current evidence suggests that all oral triptans possess nearly similar clinical efficacy. Orally dissolvable tablets are intestinally absorbed; their only advantage is use without the need to drink liquids. Nasal spray options may have a more rapid onset, bypassing the gastrointestinal tract. Outcomes are similar to those of oral agents, but unpleasant taste, nasal congestion, or burning may be limiting factors. Subcutaneous sumatriptan provides the most rapid onset and achieves the highest response rates of all triptan agents and formulations. Local site reactions and more prominent “triptan” sensations characteristic of the class (flushing, chest or throat tightness, paresthesia) may be noted.

Different formulations of one triptan may be used safely within the same day, but the use of a different triptan or an ergot alkaloid should be delayed by 24 hours. Despite labeling precautions, the concurrent use of triptans and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor antidepressants is safe in most cases. Because of vasoconstricting properties, all triptans are contraindicated in the presence of coronary, cerebral, or peripheral vascular disease; uncontrolled hypertension; or migraine with brainstem or hemiplegic auras.

Newer migraine-specific acute therapies have no significant vascular risks because of their different mechanisms of action and are especially useful when triptans are contraindicated. Ditans, such as lasmiditan, are highly selective 5-hydroxytryptamine 1F receptor agonists. The gepants, including ubrogepant, rimegepant, and zavegepant, are calcitonin gene–related peptide (CGRP) antagonists. Both medication classes have favorable safety and tolerability profiles, but they are more expensive and slightly less effective compared with triptans.

Other agents also are effective for managing acute migraine. Parenteral and nasal formulations of dihydroergotamine are the most available and effective options among the ergot alkaloids. Dopamine D~2 receptor antagonists (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) are often used as oral adjuncts to analgesics or triptans and can reduce migraine pain when delivered parenterally. Guidelines recommend against using opioids and butalbital-containing compounds for acute migraine. In addition to the potential for dependence or addiction, these agents have been linked to an increased risk for transformation from episodic to chronic migraine. These agents should be used sparingly and only when more appropriate immediate therapies are contraindicated.

Patients not responding to multiple acute migraine treatments may be candidates for referral. Neuromodulatory devices shown to be effective in acute migraine treatment may be used by specialists in this setting.

Migraine lasting longer than 72 hours is known as status migrainosus. Many patients with this condition can be treated with glucocorticoids for several days. Severe cases of acute migraine or status migrainosus may require emergency department or inpatient management. The cornerstone of care in these settings is an intravenous dopamine antagonist, such as metoclopramide or prochlorperazine. These agents are typically combined with intravenous diphenhydramine (to limit dystonic reactions), intravenous ketorolac, and hydration. Opioids may be associated with prolonged hospital stays and should be avoided. A longer course of treatment involving repetitive intravenous dihydroergotamine with antiemetics over 2 to 3 days is very effective in managing refractory status migrainosus.

Migraine prevention aims to reduce migraine frequency, intensity, and duration. None of the medications used for migraine prevention were designed for this specific purpose. The best agents may reduce migraine frequency by half in approximately half of the patients treated.

Nonpharmacologic preventive measures are required. Identification and avoidance of triggers are often helpful. Stress management techniques, such as relaxation therapy or biofeedback, have established efficacy. Sleep pattern regulation; small, frequent meals; adequate hydration; and daily aerobic exercise are all extremely helpful. Regular work and school schedules should be encouraged. Use of stimulants (e.g., caffeine or nicotine) must be ceased or limited. Diet should be modified to avoid additives or preservatives, such as monosodium glutamate and artificial sweeteners. Evidence supports using certain supplements, such as petasites (butterbur), magnesium, riboflavin, and feverfew.

Pharmacologic prophylaxis of episodic migraine should be considered in patients with high headache frequency (≥4 days/month), including those with chronic migraine, or debilitating headaches despite adequate acute treatment. Data suggest that preventive medication (Video: Migraine Prevention) can reduce migraine frequency and intensity, patient disability, and medical cost. Several weeks or months are often required before maximum benefit is achieved. Once a response occurs, the medications should be continued for 6 to 12 months, at which point dose reduction or drug discontinuation may be considered.

Treatments recommended by evidence-based guidelines for pharmacologic prevention of episodic and chronic migraine can be organized into nonspecific and migraine-specific options ( [Table: Table: Preventive Migraine Therapies]

). Treatment selection is informed by previous therapeutic trials, coexisting medical conditions, cost, and patient preference. Guidelines from the American College of Physicians recommend propranolol, metoprolol, amitriptyline, venlafaxine, and valproate as first-line choices for the prevention of episodic migraine. Because of higher costs, these guidelines recommend integrating migraine-specific agents into migraine prevention after one or two adequate but unsuccessful trials of traditional nonspecific preventive medications. Other guidelines, however, consider migraine-specific agents to be a first-line option. Migraine-specific therapies include monoclonal antibodies targeting CGRP or its receptor (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab) and direct antagonists to the CGRP receptor (atogepant, rimegepant). International Headache Society guidelines also suggest that onabotulinum toxin A injections are indicated in the management of chronic migraine. Due to a relatively unfavorable adverse effect profile, topiramate is typically reserved for use as a third-line agent for prevention of episodic migraine following failure of nonspecific and migraine-specific treatments.

In contrast, topiramate is first-line pharmacologic prophylaxis for chronic migraine. The CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab), the oral CGRP receptor antagonist atogepant, and onabotulinum toxin A are also useful in preventing chronic migraine. No evidence supports using calcium channel blockers, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor antidepressants, or gabapentin for migraine prevention.

Neuromodulatory devices may be helpful in specialized clinical settings.

TACs are the most severe and stereotypic primary headache disorders. Pain is intense, localized to the periorbital or temporal areas, and associated with pronounced ipsilateral cranial autonomic features, such as nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, ptosis, or miosis. TACs do not include trigeminal neuralgia, which is a painful cranial neuralgia (see Painful Cranial Neuralgias in Neurology).

Cluster headache is the most common TAC. The headaches may last 15 to 180 minutes; the shorter duration distinguishes cluster headache from migraine ( [Table: Table: Criteria for Cluster Headache]

). Cluster headaches recur once every other day to eight times daily over a span of weeks to months, with periods of recurrent headache activity interrupted by months to years of headache remission. Many of the episodes are nocturnal, and some may be provoked by alcohol ingestion.

Cluster headache has several acute and preventive treatment options. Oxygen inhalation and subcutaneous sumatriptan are both effective. Less effective alternatives include nasal sumatriptan and zolmitriptan. A 2-week course of glucocorticoids may help reduce headache frequency at the onset of the cycle. Verapamil and galcanezumab have been shown to reduce cluster headache frequency. Noninvasive vagus nerve stimulation has efficacy in acute cluster headache management.

Chronic paroxysmal hemicrania presents with symptoms similar to those of cluster headache, but episodes are shorter (2-30 minutes) and occur at least five times daily. Response to indomethacin is confirmatory.

Short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks with conjunctival injection and tearing (SUNCT) also presents like cluster headache, but episodes are even shorter (1-600 seconds) and may occur dozens or hundreds of times daily. SUNCT is refractory to treatment, but some patients respond to lamotrigine.

Hemicrania continua presents with persistent, side-locked unilateral headache and ipsilateral autonomic features. This condition responds to indomethacin.

Other primary headache syndromes seen occasionally in clinical practice are outlined in [Table: Table: Other Primary Headache Syndromes]

. In two of the most common, primary cough headache and primary stabbing headache, indomethacin is the treatment of choice.

Unlike primary headache syndromes, secondary headaches result from identifiable biological or structural causes. One of the most clinically relevant is posttraumatic headache (see Head Injury in Neurology); other considerations include vascular disorders, infection, and brain tumors (see Clinical Manifestations of Brain Tumors in Neurology).

Thunderclap headache is defined as a severe episode of headache pain developing abruptly and reaching maximum intensity within 1 minute. Although occasionally of primary origin, thunderclap headache is usually due to a secondary cause and is a medical emergency that warrants immediate diagnostic evaluation. Noncontrast head CT should be performed without delay. Lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement, cell counts, and xanthochromia evaluation should be performed if subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is suspected and the head CT is nondiagnostic because CT has only 95% sensitivity for SAH unless performed very early after onset. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI and noninvasive vascular imaging (magnetic resonance angiography [MRA] or CT angiography [CTA]) of cranial and cervical vessels should be considered in patients to further assess the possibility of aneurysmal SAH and other causes, such as reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) and intracranial venous thrombosis.

lists essential considerations in the differential diagnosis.

SAH is discovered in nearly 25% of patients with thunderclap headache, making it the most common cause of this condition. The headache associated with SAH may be described as the worst the patient has ever experienced, although this finding has limited specificity. Mortality is 50%, with an additional 25% of affected patients experiencing significant morbidity. Many patients describe a previous abrupt, severe, global or focal headache consistent with a sentinel leak in the preceding 1 to 2 weeks.

In the presence of a normal neurologic examination, the following features increase the likelihood of a diagnosis of SAH:

  • Age 40 years or older
  • Onset during exertion
  • Witnessed loss of consciousness
  • Concomitant neck pain

Sensitivity of head CT within 6 hours of onset of pain in patients without a new neurologic deficit is excellent but drops to approximately 95% at 12 hours and to 50% at 1 week. Lumbar puncture in SAH typically reveals a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) erythrocyte count greater than 10,000/μL (10,000 × 10^6/L) and an elevated protein level. CSF xanthochromia may take 4 hours or more to develop but is nearly 100% sensitive between 12 hours and 7 days. Urgent neurosurgical consultation is required in confirmed SAH (see Subarachnoid Hemorrhage in Neurology and Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Treatment in Neurology).

RCVS is characterized by recurrent thunderclap headache and multifocal constriction of intracranial vessels normalizing within 3 months of onset (see Other Causes of Ischemic Stroke in Neurology and Subarachnoid Hemorrhage in Neurology). Predisposing factors are listed in [Table: Table: RCVS Predisposing Factors]

. RCVS is the second most frequent cause of thunderclap headache. The headaches may be triggered by exertion, Valsalva maneuvers, emotion, or bathing. RCVS is commonly associated with posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES).

Diagnostic evaluation should include brain imaging as well as noninvasive imaging of brain and neck vessels with MRA or CTA. Areas of ischemia or hemorrhage may be seen in the parenchyma, and subdural or subarachnoid hemorrhages also may be seen in some patients. CTA and/or MRA may reveal multiple areas of segmental intracranial arterial constriction. CSF analysis is necessary only if SAH is suspected and imaging is nondiagnostic. Digital subtraction angiography has been associated with transient neurologic deficits and is typically avoided.

Management begins with resolving predisposing factors, avoiding physical exertion, and managing blood pressure. Verapamil and nimodipine are the drugs of choice for treating vasospasm. Glucocorticoids may worsen the clinical course and should be avoided when RCVS is a diagnostic consideration. Repeat MRA or CTA is necessary at 12 weeks to document vasospasm resolution, at which time medication is tapered. In 90% of patients with RCVS, clinical symptoms and imaging abnormalities resolve within days to weeks. For management of patients with SAH secondary to RCVS, see Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Treatment in Neurology.

PRES is characterized by clinical features of headache, seizures, altered mental status, and visual loss. It may occur in various clinical settings, such as RCVS, eclampsia, uncontrolled hypertension, severe infection, autoimmune and kidney disorders, and in patients taking immunosuppressants and chemotherapy. Brain MRI is more sensitive than CT and often shows areas of white matter edema (parietal and occipital lobes) and occasionally intracranial hemorrhage (

). PRES management is focused on treating the underlying cause.

Headache is the most common symptom and may be the only presenting manifestation in cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT, also called cerebral venous sinus thrombosis). Risk factors include the following:

  • Presence of hypercoagulable states
  • Thrombophilia
  • Pregnancy (and the puerperium)
  • Oral contraceptive use
  • Dehydration

The pain is typically unremitting from onset and may worsen with the Valsalva maneuver. Other symptoms include pulsatile tinnitus, diplopia, and seizures. Examination may reveal papilledema, decreased mentation, and abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI) palsy secondary to increased intracranial pressure. Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a subtype of CVT that usually involves extension of dental or sinus bacterial infection and manifests as acute-onset headache, proptosis, periorbital edema, and ophthalmoplegia.

CVT diagnosis requires neuroimaging. Although brain MRI or CT may be suggestive, MR or CT venography is often necessary to establish the diagnosis.

Anticoagulation is recommended in patients with CVT even if they have hemorrhagic parenchymal lesions (see Intracerebral Hemorrhage Treatment in Neurology). Treatment with low-molecular-weight heparin results in lower hospital mortality than treatment with unfractionated heparin. Anticoagulation with warfarin or dabigatran is generally continued for at least 3 to 6 months. Extended anticoagulation should be considered in patients with severe hypercoagulable states, myeloproliferative disorders, or recurrence and perhaps in patients with idiopathic thrombosis. Treatment of cavernous sinus thrombosis additionally requires immediate antibiotic administration, often coupled with surgical drainage.

Dissections of the cervical arterial vessels often present with acute pain in the head and neck, typically occur in patients younger than 50 years, and may develop spontaneously or because of trauma. Risk factors include the following:

  • Hypertension
  • Migraine
  • Polycystic kidney disease
  • Connective tissue disorders

Carotid artery dissections often present with orbital pain, partial Horner syndrome (ptosis and miosis only), and ipsilateral signs of cerebral or retinal ischemia (see Other Causes of Ischemic Stroke in Neurology). Patients with dissections of the vertebral arteries may describe occipital and neck pain and posterior fossa symptoms, such as dysarthria, dysphagia, ataxia, and hemifield visual loss. Neurologic symptoms may occur hours to days after the inciting event. Brain MRI may show a tapered arterial lumen or increased arterial diameter with an intramural hematoma. Noninvasive vessel imaging with MRA or CTA is typically sufficient (

).

Comparative trials have not documented the superiority of anticoagulation in patients with dissections, and many are treated with aspirin.

Increased intracranial pressure in the absence of any vascular or space-occupying lesion is the hallmark of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) (also known as pseudotumor cerebri). Approximately 90% of affected persons are women of reproductive age with an elevated BMI. IIH is associated with a variety of risk factors ( [Table: Table: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Risk Factors]

).

Headaches, visual symptoms, and intracranial noises (pulsatile tinnitus) are the most common presenting symptoms of IIH. Head pain is nonspecific and may be like that of tension-type headache or migraine. Vision may be blurred, doubled, or periodically dim in brief episodes known as visual obscurations.

Findings on neurologic examination include papilledema and occasionally ophthalmoplegia. Careful visual field testing is essential in the initial and follow-up evaluations of IIH. Although only 25% of patients may report visual symptoms, 90% have some abnormality on visual perimetry. Typical findings include blind spot enlargement and peripheral field reduction.

Enhanced brain MRI may reveal optic nerve sheath widening, an empty sella, or posterior optic globe flattening. MR venography may reveal unilateral or bilateral stenoses of the intracranial transverse sinuses. A CSF opening pressure greater than 250 mm H~2O in the absence of another cause of increased pressure with normal CSF composition confirms the diagnosis.

IIH treatment is aimed primarily at preserving vision. Patients with elevated BMI require a weight-loss program, and bariatric procedures may be helpful, when necessary. Acetazolamide is the drug of choice. Topiramate may be less effective but carries the potential added benefit of weight loss. Surgical procedures may benefit patients with medically refractory IIH. Options include ventriculoperitoneal or lumboperitoneal shunting or, in patients with definable transverse sinus stenosis, endovascular stent placement.

The cardinal feature of intracranial hypotension is a postural headache, typically worsening within 20 seconds of sitting or standing. Tinnitus, diplopia, neck pain, nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia are additional symptoms. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI typically shows diffuse, smooth dural thickening with enhancement (

). Cerebellar tonsillar descent (like that of a Chiari malformation), subdural fluid collections, decreased ventricular size, and pituitary gland engorgement are other possible findings.

The most common source of intracranial hypotension is CSF leakage after a lumbar puncture, often in patients with risk factors ( [Table: Table: Postdural Puncture Headache Risk Factors]

). Postprocedure bed rest does not affect the likelihood of postdural puncture headache. More than 50% of these headaches resolve spontaneously by day 4 after the procedure; more than 75% resolve by day 7. Management begins with bed rest and oral caffeine. An autologous epidural blood patch (EBP) should be considered in patients with headaches refractory to conservative therapy or those with severe neurologic symptoms. Headache remission rates vary, and repeat procedures may be necessary. The use of fibrin glue is considered only when EBP is ineffective or contraindicated.

Spontaneous intracranial hypotension may present with thunderclap or subacute headache. Associated symptoms are similar to those of postdural puncture headaches. No single diagnostic test detects spontaneous intracranial hypotension. The location of CSF leakage, which is typically spinal, may be detected in 50% of patients by spinal MRI or CT myelography. Patients without identifiable sites are empirically treated with nontargeted lumbar EBP procedures, whereas patients with definable locations receive more precise EBP delivery. Repeat procedures may be required, and patients with refractory symptoms may require surgery.

MOH, previously called “rebound” headache, is a highly prevalent condition affecting 1% of adults. This clinical syndrome may result from overtreatment with acute medication in patients with underlying migraine or tension-type headache. Using triptans, ergot alkaloids, opioids, or combination analgesics for 10 or more days per month or simple analgesics for 15 or more days per month constitutes medication overuse. MOH has yet to be demonstrated with the use of ditans or gepants.

Affected patients often report daily or near-daily headache that is refractory to numerous treatment options. MOH is more common in midlife, in women, and in patients with high baseline headache frequency. In patients with migraine, opioids are associated with a 44% increase and butalbital compounds with a 70% increase in the risk for headache progression. These medications should be avoided in patients with recurrent primary headache disorders.

Management of MOH involves discontinuing the overused drug and introducing appropriate preventive medication directed at the primary headache disorder. Immediately initiating preventive therapy combined with simultaneous acute medication withdrawal is superior to protocols delaying either of those components.

Migraine and tension-type headaches are the most common sources of recurrent headache in pregnant patients. Many patients with baseline primary headache disorders will experience reduced headache frequency or intensity, but some develop new or worsening headaches. New or different headache development during pregnancy should provoke concern for a secondary headache disorder, particularly when noted during the third trimester ( [Table: Table: Common Secondary Headache Disorders of Pregnancy]

). Predictors for secondary headache include hypertension, fevers, seizure, and abnormalities on physical examination. Imaging with noncontrast brain MRI and possibly MRA/MR venography helps inform management.

Acetaminophen, low-dose aspirin, diphenhydramine, and metoclopramide are considered relatively safe options for acute headache treatment in pregnancy. The FDA has warned against using NSAIDs at 20 weeks or later in pregnancy. Triptans may be reasonable for patients with more severe migraine. No preventive medications have established safety in pregnancy, and guidelines recommend balancing risks and benefits of using propranolol, metoprolol, amitriptyline, verapamil, and oral magnesium. Lidocaine-containing pericranial nerve blocks can also be considered to reduce headache frequency.

Head or facial pain may develop along the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, glossopharyngeal nerve, and nervus intermedius, in addition to the upper cervical roots via the occipital nerves ( [Table: Table: Cranial Neuralgias]

). These pains remain isolated to the distribution of the affected nerve and present with distinct clinical characteristics. Differentiation from primary headache disorders is often made on clinical grounds because these conditions lack the sensory sensitivities and nausea typical of migraine and the autonomic features found with TACs. MRI of the brain is necessary to exclude underlying secondary pathology.

Trigeminal neuralgia is the most common and intense cranial neuralgia. Incidence increases with advanced age. Multiple sclerosis should be considered in patients with onset before age 50 years. Pain is typically unilateral and localized to the maxillary and mandibular branches of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V). The pains are brief and “shock-like” or electric, lasting seconds to minutes. Paroxysms may be spontaneous or triggered by innocuous stimulation of the face. Refractory periods are common after a series of paroxysms. Ipsilateral autonomic features are rare.

Neurologic examination is typically normal. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI with MRA is the initial imaging test indicated for patients with trigeminal neuralgia. In classic trigeminal neuralgia, brain MRA identifies neurovascular contact between a loop of the superior cerebellar artery and the trigeminal nerve. Contact causing displacement or atrophy of the nerve has been associated with a greater likelihood of symptom development. When contrast-enhanced brain MRI detects nonvascular structural pathology (such as compressing and demyelinating causes), the patient is diagnosed with secondary trigeminal neuralgia. If neither artery impingement on the nerve nor a secondary cause is present, the label of idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia is applied.

Evidence suggests initial treatment with carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine can be helpful. Pain may resolve within a few days, although mild dizziness and drowsiness are common. Other adverse effects of these medications, including hyponatremia and agranulocytosis, are less common but necessitate intermittent monitoring. Alternative drugs are gabapentin, pregabalin, baclofen, and lamotrigine.

Patients unresponsive to two trials of monotherapy or combined therapy should be referred for procedural management. Nonsurgical options are effective in 50% of patients and include percutaneous radiofrequency coagulation, glycerol injection, or focused stereotactic (gamma knife) radiosurgery. Posterior fossa microvascular decompression of the neurovascular contact zone is a more invasive but more effective option. It should be prioritized in patients with low surgical risk.

Occipital neuralgia presents as a posterior headache in the distribution of the occipital nerves. The pain is usually acute, unilateral, and lancinating and often lasts minutes, with frequent recurrences. Mild discomfort may be present between episodes, with more severe pain triggered by movement of the cervical spine or tactile stimuli to the scalp. Examination is typically normal but can reveal tenderness along the occipital nerves or diminished sensation; palpating the nerves may trigger an episode. Relief with an occipital nerve block supports the diagnosis but is nonspecific. MRI of the brain and cervical spine may be necessary to assess for anatomic causes of nerve compression.

Treatment options include conservative measures, such as massage or cool compresses, and occipital nerve injection. Medications such as gabapentin, pregabalin, and tricyclic antidepressants and injections of botulinum toxin (off-label use) are used, but their efficacy is unknown. Surgery or occipital nerve stimulators may be necessary in patients with refractory disease.

bodies.nrsec24002:
Head Injury

Traumatic brain injury (TBI) results from biomechanical forces applied to the head and neck. Damage may be temporary or permanent and may arise from functional or structural alterations in the central nervous system.

Severity is determined primarily by the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) ( [Table: Table: Glasgow Coma Scale]

) and is categorized as mild, moderate, or severe ( [Table: Table: Characteristics of Traumatic Brain Injury by Severity]

). When indicated, noncontrast CT is the imaging modality of choice because of its wide availability, low expense, ability to rapidly diagnose hemorrhage, and high sensitivity for bony injuries.

Mild TBI, also known as concussion, typically causes temporary neurologic impairment without evidence of structural damage on conventional neuroimaging. Symptoms are typically physical (e.g., headache and vomiting), cognitive (e.g., poor concentration and confusion), emotional (e.g., depression and anxiety), or sleep related (e.g., insomnia and fatigue) (see [Table: Table: Characteristics of Traumatic Brain Injury by Severity]

). In most patients, the physical examination is normal and further diagnostic investigation is unnecessary.

[Table: Table: Indications for Head CT in Mild Traumatic Brain Injury]

shows CDC indications for head CT in mild TBI; head CT in patients with TBI with these indications has nearly 100% sensitivity (but low specificity) for identifying abnormalities.

Management of mild TBI is based on expert opinion and is outlined in

. Although traditional management mandated complete physical and cognitive rest, studies show that early symptom-limited activity improves outcomes. Patients should be advised to exercise as tolerated after 1 to 2 days of rest and to escalate mental activities after 3 to 5 days. Patients with mild TBI, a normal neurologic examination, and (when necessary) a normal head CT scan may be safely followed as outpatients; clear instructions to seek help if new symptoms arise or old symptoms worsen are important. Most symptoms resolve spontaneously within 7 to 10 days.

Headache is the most common and disabling symptom and requires systematic identification, evaluation, and treatment. Posttraumatic headaches usually have the characteristics of migraine and tension-type headaches, and episodic and preventive treatment is matched to the headache phenotype. Simple analgesics and triptans are common treatments for acute episodes ( [Table: Table: Acute Migraine Therapies]

). Prevention with amitriptyline or venlafaxine may be used for either phenotype, while propranolol and similar agents are often considered for migraines ( [Table: Table: Preventive Migraine Therapies]

). Opioids and butalbital products should be avoided. See Headache and Facial Pain in Neurology for information on evaluating and treating headaches.

Patients with visual, vestibular, or cognitive symptoms for more than 2 weeks should be referred to a health care professional (such as a physical or occupational therapist or physical medicine and rehabilitation clinician) who is an expert in managing concussions.

Patients with moderate and especially severe TBI have more significant findings (see [Table: Table: Characteristics of Traumatic Brain Injury by Severity]

) and are at high risk for complications and poor outcomes. Periorbital or mastoid bruising (

) and hemotympanum may be present and indicative of basilar skull fracture.

In addition to surgical therapy, if indicated, management focuses on preventing and treating complications. In patients with severe TBI, the incidence of clinical seizures is estimated at 12% and subclinical seizures at 25%. A new-onset seizure within 7 days of TBI has been associated with posttraumatic epilepsy. Data are inconclusive regarding risk reductions in rates of early seizure, late seizure, or mortality with the prophylactic use of antiseizure drugs. When initiated, weak evidence supports the use of levetiracetam rather than phenytoin, for a short duration of use (≤7 days) versus a longer duration of use (>7 days). Risk factors for posttraumatic seizures helpful in informing management decisions are listed in [Table: Table: Risk Factors for Early Posttraumatic Seizures]

.

Current evidence does not support routine monitoring of intracranial pressure in patients with severe TBI. When increased intracranial pressure is present, treatment may include elevation of the head of the bed, mechanical hyperventilation, ventriculostomy, and osmotic therapy with mannitol or hypertonic saline.

Medical management of severe TBI includes normalization of blood oxygenation (arterial Po~2 >60 mm Hg [8.0 kPa]) and blood pressure (systolic >90 mm Hg), deep venous thrombosis prophylaxis, glycemic control, and treatment of infectious or gastrointestinal complications. Feeding patients to attain basal caloric nutrition by day 5 or, at the latest, day 7 after injury decreases mortality. Fever should be controlled aggressively with acetaminophen and cooling blankets. When appropriate, early tracheostomy has been associated with improved outcomes.

Glucocorticoids increase mortality in severe TBI and should be avoided.

For critically ill adults with TBI, survival and functional outcomes are improved with treatment in subspecialized neurocritical care units.

An epidural hematoma usually arises secondary to arterial bleeding with collection of blood between the dura mater and skull. Most epidural hematomas involve a laceration of the middle meningeal artery from a temporal bone fracture. Lateral extension of bleeding is limited by dural attachments at the skull sutures, resulting in a lentiform hematoma (

), and expansion occurs inward toward the brain parenchyma.

Many patients with an epidural hematoma have a “lucid interval” followed by rapid neurologic compromise. Headache, vomiting, and declining mental status may occur early. Stupor or coma with ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III) palsy (Video: Third Nerve Palsy) and contralateral hemiparesis may signal transtentorial (uncal) herniation. Urgent surgical evacuation is recommended for patients with a GCS score lower than 9, anisocoria, or a hematoma greater than 30 mL in volume.

A subdural hematoma (

, Video: Head CT Scan Showing Subdural Hematoma) is a collection of blood between the brain and dura mater, typically caused by rupture of bridging veins. This may occur spontaneously, as a complication of anticoagulation, or after trauma. Because of cerebral atrophy and subsequent tension on the subdural bridging veins, older persons and those with alcohol use disorder are particularly susceptible.

Presentations may be acute, subacute, or chronic. Whereas an acute subdural hematoma typically presents with coma or neurologic compromise, subacute and chronic hematomas (which develop days to weeks after injury) may be associated with nonspecific symptoms—including headache, altered mental status, or somnolence—in addition to focal neurologic findings.

In patients with acute subdural hematomas, a hematoma thickness greater than 10 mm, a GCS score lower than 9, and pupillary asymmetry or fixation are all indications for immediate surgical treatment. In patients with chronic hematomas, a hematoma thickness greater than 10 mm, a midline shift greater than 5 mm, and progressive neurologic symptoms are all indications for neurosurgical drainage.

Any athlete suspected of sustaining a mild TBI should be immediately removed from play and assessed by a clinician trained in evaluating and managing concussion. Guidelines recommend initial screening with a symptom checklist and neurologic examination involving specific cognitive evaluation and balance testing. Specific instruments, such as the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool, fifth edition (also called the SCAT5), are useful for acutely detecting sports-related concussion. Neuropsychological testing provides an objective and more sensitive measure of cognitive function; it should be employed as part of a comprehensive TBI management program for patients with persistent symptoms.

Full return to play should occur only after the patient successfully completes an individualized return-to-play protocol. Most protocols are based on expert opinion and include gradual exercises to reintroduce work or school activities. Additional requirements for return to play include the following:

  • Resolution of symptoms from mild TBI
  • Return to preinjury neurocognitive state
  • No symptoms with physical or cognitive exertion or stress

Traumatic encephalopathy syndrome is increasingly recognized in athletes retired from contact sports. This clinical syndrome is associated with the pathological diagnosis chronic traumatic encephalopathy. See Traumatic Encephalopathy Syndrome in Neurology for more information.

TBI is a common consequence of service in the armed forces, particularly among those deployed to a combat theater; 80% of these TBIs are mild.

The Military Acute Concussion Evaluation and a requisite 24-hour rest period are mandated for military personnel who experience a direct blow to the head, a vehicular collision, or an explosive blast. Return to duty requires complete recovery.

Sequelae of mild TBI in the military include posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, anxiety, insomnia, and cognitive and balance disorders. The prevalence of PTSD is higher in military personnel with mild TBI compared with civilian populations, and both groups are at increased risk for suicide. Specific screening for PTSD and depression is mandatory (see Posttraumatic Stress Disorder in Interdisciplinary Medicine). Sequelae from deployment-related TBI may persist as long as 8 years. Returning service members with any TBI are best managed through a multidisciplinary approach, with referral to mental health specialists frequently indicated.

Evidence of chronic traumatic encephalopathy is infrequently found in brain pathology from military personnel and is more common among those with previous civilian TBI and contact-sports exposures (see Traumatic Encephalopathy Syndrome in Neurology for more information).

Adults older than 75 years are at particular risk for hospitalization and death from TBI. Falls, motor vehicle collisions, and accidental blows to the head are the leading mechanisms of injury in this population. Preventing these events is an essential aspect of geriatric medicine. See Fall Prevention in Foundations of Clinical Practice for more information.

Anticoagulation is associated with an increased risk for intracranial hemorrhage after trauma. Intracranial hemorrhage in patients treated with warfarin has significant morbidity and a mortality rate as high as 50%; immediately correcting the INR limits hematoma expansion. Reversal of direct oral anticoagulants should also be performed (see Anticoagulants in Hematology for more detailed information).

Reinitiating anticoagulation after intracranial hemorrhage is clinically challenging, and little empiric evidence exists to guide decision making. Resuming anticoagulation within 6 days increases the risk for intracranial hemorrhage, whereas delaying treatment beyond 13 days raises the rate of thrombotic complications. For patients with lower risk for hematoma expansion (such as younger patients or those whose hemorrhage is small) and higher risk for thromboembolism (such as those with a mechanical heart valve), the optimal time to resume anticoagulation may be day 7 after trauma.

bodies.nrsec24003:
Seizures and Epilepsy

A seizure is defined as a paroxysmal event of signs/symptoms due to abnormal cerebral neuronal activity. The International League Against Epilepsy defines epilepsy as two or more unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or one unprovoked seizure with a risk for further seizures over the next 10 years that is similar to the risk after two unprovoked seizures (≥60%).

Diagnosis relies on a detailed patient history. Seizures are characteristically stereotyped; symptom variability between events suggests an alternative diagnosis (see Differential Diagnosis of Seizures in Neurology). Epilepsy usually requires antiseizure medication (ASM) therapy, but isolated seizures may not, especially if provoked by reversible or preventable causes. Seizure classification terminology is evolving but is usually divided into focal and generalized categories (

).

Focal seizures may be classified as preserved consciousness (formerly known as simple partial or focal aware) or impaired consciousness (formerly called complex partial or focal unaware/impaired awareness). Focal preserved consciousness seizures are very localized focal seizures with varying manifestations depending on the site of origin ( [Table: Table: Examples of Focal Preserved Consciousness Seizures]

). Focal impaired consciousness seizures, by definition, alter awareness (memory, responsiveness, language, or cognition can be affected). Focal impaired consciousness seizures can present as “staring episodes” and, in such instances, they must be differentiated from absence seizures (see Generalized Seizures in Neurology) ( [Table: Table: Differentiation of Seizure Types Presenting as Staring Episodes]

). In general, focal seizures are less frequent and have a longer duration than absence seizures.

Generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS) have a characteristic tonic phase of whole-body stiffening, wide-open eyes, and a single loud groan (ictal cry), followed by a clonic phase of rhythmic, synchronous limb jerking that is initially fast and gradually slows and ceases. The seizure typically lasts 1 to 3 minutes and is often followed by stertor (deep, slow snoring). A postictal state with confusion, hypersomnolence, and fatigue is common and can persist for hours or even days. The patient loses consciousness through the active seizure and into the postictal period.

GTCS may be preceded by other seizure types, generalized or focal. Auras or automatisms (semi-purposeful repetitive mouth or ipsilateral hand movements) before GTCS and postevent unilateral weakness (Todd paralysis) suggest a focal onset.

Absence seizures are characterized by brief episodes of staring (see [Table: Table: Differentiation of Seizure Types Presenting as Staring Episodes]

). They may occur as the only seizure type in school-aged children and are often confused with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder or focal unaware seizures. Absence seizures can have onset outside of childhood, especially in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME), a common adolescent- and young adult–onset epilepsy.

Myoclonus is a single quick jerk of a limb or the entire body lasting less than a second; it is not always associated with a seizure (see Myoclonus in Neurology). Electroencephalography (EEG) can confirm a diagnosis of myoclonic seizures, with each jerk associated with a generalized spike-and-wave discharge (

). Myoclonic seizures can also occur repetitively and result in falls. Maintained awareness and very short duration differentiate myoclonic seizures from GTCS.

Tonic seizures present as episodes of increased muscle tone, ranging from mild extension of the arms and head to more severe stiffening of the entire body. Atonic seizures present with sudden loss of muscle tone. Both tonic and atonic seizures occur with no warning, last a few seconds, and cause altered awareness, which often leads to falls and physical injuries. The patient does not experience postevent confusion. Prolonged episodes of increased or decreased tone with long duration of loss of consciousness are unlikely to represent seizures (see Differential Diagnosis of Seizures in Neurology).

Epilepsy syndromes represent the constellations of patient characteristics, seizure type, and clinical course that define specific seizure disorders, such as temporal lobe epilepsy and JME.

Temporal lobe epilepsy is the most common adult-onset focal epilepsy. Typical symptoms of a temporal lobe focal seizure may include an aura of déjà vu, fear, or a rising sensation in the stomach; loss of awareness; staring; behavioral arrest; and amnesia. Automatisms may be observed. Speech arrest may be seen with involvement of the dominant hemisphere. Temporal lobe epilepsy is commonly associated with mesial temporal sclerosis with hippocampal atrophy, T2 hyperintensity, and loss of internal architecture (

). Temporal lobe epilepsy can also arise from the neocortical surface and spread to the hippocampus. This distinction in location affects surgical options in drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy.

Other focal epilepsies include frontal, parietal, and occipital lobe epilepsies ( [Table: Table: Examples of Focal Preserved Consciousness Seizures]

, [Table: Table: Differentiation of Seizure Types Presenting as Staring Episodes]

). These diagnoses may also have possible causes shown on MRI, including cavernous malformations, cortical dysplasia (

), traumatic brain injury, stroke, and tumors. In most adults with focal epilepsy, however, brain MRI is normal and the cause is unknown.

EEG may show focal spikes or sharp waves in the corresponding brain region in focal epilepsies, but EEG is often normal between seizures (

).

Idiopathic/genetic epilepsies are not caused by an underlying structural neurologic disorder and often have complex, polygenic inheritance. That is, patients with these epilepsies often have no family history or identifiable single genetic mutation, despite the probable genetic cause.

In adults, JME is the most common form of idiopathic/genetic generalized epilepsy. Seizures in JME are often called “college seizures” because of the age of onset (teens or twenties) and associated triggers (sleep deprivation, substance use, stress).

The presence of myoclonic seizures is required for the diagnosis of JME; patients may report dropping items from their hands (e.g., coffee cup or hairbrush) because myoclonic seizures in JME generally occur in the morning. Most affected patients have GTCS, and approximately 30% of patients have absence seizures. Epilepsy may not be diagnosed until the first GTCS occurs because myoclonic seizures are often not recognized as seizures. Patients are usually otherwise neurologically healthy and can live relatively normal lives because seizures are often controlled with one or two ASMs. Brain MRI is typically normal, and EEG may show generalized spike-and-wave discharges (see

). Lifelong ASM therapy is typically recommended.

For any patient with a possible first seizure, obtaining a detailed history is crucial to distinguish seizures from other episodic conditions. Clarifying actual symptom onset is key; often, the first event that leads to clinical presentation may not be the actual first event. A history of previous staring events or myoclonus is often overlooked; this may help identify epilepsy and should be specifically sought through careful questioning.

Provoking factors, risk factors, and triggers can lead to seizures ( [Table: Table: Clinical Factors Associated With Seizures or Epilepsy]

); these classifications are distinct from one another, and differentiating between them is essential.

Provoking factors can cause seizures in patients with or without epilepsy; avoiding these provocations should prevent further seizures. Medications are a common provoking factor, and drugs that lower seizure threshold should be avoided. Alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal are other common provoking factors.

Risk factors increase the likelihood of developing epilepsy and include a history of brain trauma, meningitis, or stroke; however, an acute seizure (occurring in the first week after such an event) may not necessarily lead to the development of epilepsy.

Triggers lead to seizures in patients with preexisting epilepsy but do not cause epilepsy.

Many episodic disorders mimic seizures but are nonepileptic events. These include the following:

  • Syncope
  • Migraine
  • Movement disorders (tremor, tics)
  • Sleep disorders
  • Stroke
  • Psychogenic nonepileptic spells/events

Seizures usually have positive symptoms, such as jerking, tingling, and visual flashes, whereas strokes have negative symptoms, such as weakness, numbness, and vision loss. Normal mentation with a headache after the episode suggests migraine.

Associated lightheadedness or chest pain may suggest syncope or cardiac disease. Syncope may present with shaking (convulsive syncope) and must be differentiated from GTCS ( [Table: Table: Differentiating GTCS and Syncope]

). In one study, more than 90% of healthy volunteers had nonepileptic myoclonus (generalized or multifocal) when syncope was induced; only a few had classic, motionless syncope. For distinguishing syncope from seizures and psychogenic loss of consciousness, video EEG can be very useful, in combination with tilt-table testing, because there are specific EEG changes diagnostic of syncope.

Psychogenic nonepileptic spells/events (PNES), or functional seizures, were formerly called pseudoseizures. This latter term should be avoided because pseudo implies falseness and seizure is a misnomer. A “nonepileptic seizure” does not meet criteria for a seizure at all; an “epileptic seizure” is simply an organic seizure and can occur whether or not the patient has epilepsy (e.g., a provoked seizure).

PNES are most often related to posttraumatic stress disorder or conversion disorder. Factitious disorder and malingering are rare and far less likely. Patients with PNES often have a history of military experience, sexual or physical abuse, chronic medical illness, or prominent life stressors. PNES often mimic GTCS, but certain features help distinguish the diagnoses ( [Table: Table: Differentiating GTCS and PNES]

). Event capture during video EEG monitoring usually is required to confirm the diagnosis. PNES are commonly associated with lack of pharmacologic treatment benefit from ASMs; management should emphasize early diagnosis with video EEG monitoring.

Returning combat veterans who develop seizures require careful evaluation, often including video EEG monitoring. Many have had head trauma and are at increased risk for epilepsy, but many also have posttraumatic stress disorder and may have PNES. Assuming an epilepsy diagnosis and empirically treating the patient can be detrimental, especially because veterans tend to experience a delay in PNES diagnosis compared with the general population.

Neuroimaging with MRI of the brain is recommended for all patients with a first seizure. CT scan of the head may be obtained initially in patients in whom hemorrhage or stroke is suspected or to rule out increased intracranial pressure before a lumbar puncture. The use of MRI with contrast may be deferred unless infection, tumor, or vascular lesions are suspected. Because temporal lobe epilepsy is common, MRI sequences focusing on the hippocampus and temporal lobes are useful.

Emergent lumbar puncture is recommended in adults only if an infectious cause, such as meningitis or encephalitis, is suspected.

Outpatient EEG is recommended in patients with a first seizure. Because capturing an actual seizure is unlikely, the physician must rely on “epileptiform” abnormalities, such as focal sharp waves (see

) or generalized spike-and-wave discharges (see

). These findings are not diagnostically confirmatory; rather, they may help support the diagnosis in an appropriate clinical context. A single routine EEG is only 40% to 50% sensitive for such findings, so clinical judgment based on history remains critical. Sleep deprivation before EEG and capturing sleep during EEG can increase the yield.

A normal EEG does not rule out epilepsy. Capturing events during continuous video EEG monitoring remains the gold standard in diagnosis; it is usually arranged in dedicated inpatient epilepsy monitoring units (typically elective admissions for diagnostic purposes) or in the ICU (patients who are sedated or confused or have unusual movements) ( [Table: Table: Indications for Immediate Continuous Video EEG Monitoring]

). This type of EEG is essentially the only method of diagnosing nonconvulsive status epilepticus, but diagnosis often requires clinical correlation (see Nonconvulsive Status Epilepticus in Neurology).

Continuous video EEG monitoring in specialized epilepsy monitoring units can also be conducted in parallel with ASM withdrawal under close supervision. Patients who have not responded to two adequately dosed ASMs are considered to have refractory disease (see Drug-Resistant Epilepsy and Epilepsy Surgery in Neurology); they should be referred to an epilepsy center, where continuous video EEG can be done to confirm the epilepsy diagnosis and determine candidacy for epilepsy surgery.

Determining the recurrence risk guides the decision to treat a patient with a seizure. The 2-year recurrence risk after a single unprovoked seizure is approximately 40%. The risk is lower (20%-30%) if the patient has no epilepsy risk factors and the MRI and EEG are normal. A first unprovoked seizure is often not treated; although treatment may reduce the risk for seizures over the next 2 years, it does not change a patient’s long-term prognosis for developing epilepsy. Treatment with ASMs is recommended in the setting of two unprovoked seizures (or one unprovoked seizure with significant EEG or MRI abnormalities, such as trauma or stroke) because the recurrence risk is at least 60%.

Empiric pharmacologic treatment generally is not recommended unless the patient’s history and evaluation are strongly suggestive of epilepsy. An exception is convulsive status epilepticus, which must be treated emergently if clinically suspected. Empiric therapy may also be considered in the setting of acute critical illness, wherein recurrent seizures could have significant negative consequences.

Generally, prophylactic treatment in patients without seizure history is avoided. It may be considered for the first week after moderate to severe head trauma based on assessment of the potential risks and benefits. The role of prophylactic treatment following brain tumor resection is unclear.

Alcohol- or benzodiazepine-withdrawal seizures, which usually occur within 48 hours of cessation of use, typically are not treated with ASMs. Primary and secondary prevention of withdrawal seizures is usually accomplished with temporary use of benzodiazepines or phenobarbital.

Many ASMs are available for patients with epilepsy ( [Table: Table: Spectrum of Use of Antiseizure Medications]

). Older ASMs, such as phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine, and valproate, are typically not preferred. Newer ASMs are not more effective in controlling seizures, but they typically have fewer adverse effects, fewer drug interactions, and less need for laboratory monitoring, although the cost may be higher. Most often, treatment is guided by the seizure type (focal versus generalized), comorbidities, childbearing status, and potential adverse and beneficial side effects rather than ASM mechanism or epilepsy cause. Guidelines suggest generic ASMs are appropriate for most patients.

Common adverse effects and monitoring recommendations are listed in [Table: Table: Adverse Effects and Monitoring of Antiseizure Medications]

. A key dose-dependent adverse effect is hyponatremia, which may occur with oxcarbazepine, carbamazepine, and eslicarbazepine. It is a major concern with these medications in older patients, especially with concomitant diuretic use. Another key dose-related adverse effect is thrombocytopenia secondary to valproate therapy.

ASMs with important effects on kidney and liver metabolism are listed in [Table: Table: Key Pharmacologic Issues With Selected ASMs]

. Inducers of liver enzymes can increase statin and warfarin clearance and necessitate higher doses or alternative options. Other commonly prescribed medications that can interact with enzyme-inducing ASMs include calcium channel blockers, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, antipsychotics, tricyclic antidepressants, hormonal contraceptive therapy, and many anticancer drugs.

Bone mineral density testing and calcium and vitamin D supplementation are recommended with long-term use of valproate or enzyme-inducing ASMs because these agents increase bone catabolism. This precautionary step is recommended even in patients without traditional osteoporosis risk factors.

Phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, and lamotrigine commonly cause rash, which usually resolves with drug discontinuation but sometimes may be severe and life-threatening. For example, rapid titration of lamotrigine has been associated with the development of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome (also known as drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms [DRESS]), and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Expert consensus, however, considers lamotrigine to be a first-line, broad-spectrum ASM with an overall excellent safety and efficacy profile, when titrated slowly.

Gabapentin has a low incidence of rash and has good evidence of efficacy in older adults.

All ASMs carry a warning about worsening depression and suicidality, and all patients must be screened and monitored for these symptoms. Levetiracetam may cause depression, anxiety, anger, or agitation. Perampanel may cause homicidal ideation. Topiramate may cause psychosis. Lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, and valproate, on the other hand, are mood stabilizers.

Measuring certain ASM serum levels (phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate, phenobarbital, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine) is useful, given their known therapeutic windows and predictable dose-related adverse effects. However, in a patient whose epilepsy is well controlled without clinical adverse effects, dose reduction because of high levels usually is unwarranted. An exception is in patients with a low albumin level or kidney dysfunction who are taking highly protein-bound ASMs, such as valproate and phenytoin. In these situations, unbound (free) serum levels should be measured, as this will be more accurate than the standard (total) serum levels.

Well-designed studies have not shown differences in ASM bioequivalence (according to FDA standards) when switching between generic drugs or switching from a brand to a generic drug. Monitoring for ASM toxicity and seizures is advised if any change is made.

In adults who are seizure-free for at least 2 years, the American Academy of Neurology recommends discussing risks and benefits of ASM withdrawal with the patient. Risks include possible seizure recurrence and a small chance that seizures will no longer respond to medications. Shared decision making on ASM withdrawal should also explore individualized quality of life (e.g., impact of seizures on working, education, and driving). The best predictor of seizure freedom is time; although data are imprecise, a period of seizure freedom greater than 2 years probably predicts further seizure freedom. Cautionary factors for ASM weaning include the presence of JME, a history of difficulty controlling seizures, and the presence of significant epilepsy risk factors (see [Table: Table: Clinical Factors Associated With Seizures or Epilepsy]

). It is unknown if EEG or imaging studies helpfully inform the decision to withdraw ASMs. There are no standardized ASM tapering schedules.

All patients who have had a seizure, even a single provoked seizure, must be instructed about activity precautions, including driving restrictions. Patients should be advised to avoid common triggers and provoking factors (see [Table: Table: Clinical Factors Associated With Seizures or Epilepsy]

). Most patients with epilepsy can work, even if they are not completely seizure free. Patients should avoid operating heavy machinery, using firearms, lifting more than 9 kg (20 lb), taking tub baths, swimming in unsupervised locations, and being near open flames or heights (such as rooftops). Most states restrict driving in patients with any episode of altered awareness or motor control. The American Academy of Neurology recommends a minimum seizure-free interval of 3 months before resumption of driving, but this varies by state. Some states require mandatory reporting to the Department of Motor Vehicles. Exceptions include persons with seizures provoked exclusively by correctable secondary factors and those with seizures occurring during medically supervised medication interruptions and transitions as long as effective levels of ASMs have been reintroduced. Driving should also be paused in those undergoing tapering and full discontinuation of ASMs.

Besides the risk for trauma, asphyxia, and death from seizures, patients with epilepsy are at increased risk for unexplained death. This risk is approximately 1 in 1000 and increases to approximately 1 in 100 in patients with drug-resistant seizures, especially those with uncontrolled GTCS and those taking multiple ASMs. Mechanisms are unknown and may involve cardiac, respiratory, and autonomic dysregulation. Studies show that patients prefer to discuss openly the potential for sudden death in epilepsy; doing so can encourage medication adherence and home safety planning (such as using webcams and bed monitors and sharing bedrooms).

Any patient who does not achieve seizure freedom after treatment with two adequately dosed, appropriately chosen ASMs is considered to have drug-resistant epilepsy. Referral to an epilepsy center is indicated to confirm the diagnosis and to evaluate the patient for surgical candidacy, starting with video EEG monitoring.

Because the chance of achieving seizure control from additional medications (a regimen of three or more ASMs) is less than 10%, other treatment options must be considered. In appropriately chosen surgical candidates, especially those with temporal lobe epilepsy, resection can lead to seizure freedom in 60% to 70% of patients.

Implantable cerebral (deep brain stimulation and responsive neurostimulation) and vagus nerve stimulators and the ketogenic diet are available palliative therapies but typically do not result in complete seizure control.

Incidence of new-onset epilepsy is highest in older adults (aged >60 years). Because recurrence after a new-onset seizure in this age group is more likely (50%-60%) than in younger adults, treatment after one seizure is sometimes considered. Major risk factors for seizure recurrence include stroke and dementia.

Older adults usually require lower ASM doses and are at increased risk for drug interactions and adverse effects. Data suggest that levetiracetam, lamotrigine, and gabapentin are better tolerated and as effective as older ASMs (see [Table: Table: Spectrum of Use of Antiseizure Medications]

). Valproate should be used cautiously because it can cause (reversible) parkinsonism and cognitive dysfunction.

Women with epilepsy (WWE) may experience seizures around menstruation or ovulation, known as catamenial seizures. Catamenial seizures are more common with focal seizures than generalized seizures. They are triggered by the cyclical changes in progesterone, estrogen, or ASM levels during the menstrual cycle. Treatment of catamenial seizures focuses on the best ASM regimen for the patient’s epilepsy syndrome. In patients whose seizures are uncontrolled by ASMs, adding progestin-containing oral contraceptives or acetazolamide to the ASM regimen may be helpful, but oophorectomy is not recommended to improve seizure control.

ASM selection in WWE focuses on the general characteristics of the ASMs and the specific considerations in patients who may become or are pregnant ( [Table: Table: Spectrum of Use of Antiseizure Medications]

, [Table: Table: Adverse Effects and Monitoring of Antiseizure Medications]

).

Evidence is contradictory about decreased fertility rates in WWE. Valproate, however, is associated with anovulation and polycystic ovary syndrome. Topiramate, carbamazepine, and other enzyme-inducing ASMs (see [Table: Table: Key Pharmacologic Issues With Selected ASMs]

) are of special concern in patients taking oral contraceptive agents, given their ability to induce metabolism of estrogen-containing contraceptive agents, potentially leading to unexpected pregnancy with concomitant teratogenicity.

Most WWE have normal, healthy children. The rate of major congenital malformations (MCMs) in untreated WWE mirrors that of the general population. All WWE of childbearing potential should receive preconception counseling and folate supplementation. WWE who take ASMs are unlikely to have an increased risk for cesarean section, late-pregnancy bleeding, or premature delivery, unless they smoke; however, they may be at risk for having a small-for-gestational-age child. The best predictor of seizure control during pregnancy is seizure frequency in the previous 9 to 12 months.

Levetiracetam, lamotrigine, and oxcarbazepine are the preferred ASMs because of their lower teratogenicity risk. Patients with difficult-to-control seizures, however, may need to continue teratogenic medications, such as valproate. Pregnancy alone is not reason enough to stop or change ASMs if epilepsy is well controlled. Physicians must balance the risk of teratogenicity with the risk of uncontrolled seizures, particularly GTCS, which can result in fetal anoxia and death.

Valproate, phenobarbital, and phenytoin are associated with MCMs and lower IQ in offspring; these drugs should be avoided if possible. Valproate is also associated with neural tube defects. Topiramate, carbamazepine, and ASM polypharmacy also should be avoided because of an increased risk for MCMs; topiramate is specifically associated with cleft lip and palate.

Serum levels of lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, carbamazepine, phenytoin, and levetiracetam are known to decrease significantly during pregnancy (due to increased volume of distribution, decreased protein binding, and/or increased liver metabolism). For lamotrigine, a dose escalation of approximately 50% is needed to maintain therapeutic levels and prevent seizures; levels should be followed at least monthly during pregnancy. After delivery, the lamotrigine dose should be rapidly decreased to avoid a sudden increase in serum levels and toxicity risk.

Breastfeeding is recommended in most WWE who take ASMs, as the benefits generally outweigh the risks. Infant sedation is a concern, but ASM exposure through breast milk is probably less than that in utero.

Enzyme-inducing ASMs (see [Table: Table: Key Pharmacologic Issues With Selected ASMs]

) increase oral contraceptive metabolism, which increases the chance of pregnancy. Alternative methods of contraception, such as intrauterine devices or barrier methods, are recommended.

Not all seizures require emergent treatment. Most GTCS will cease spontaneously within 2 to 3 minutes. Treatment of prolonged seizures depends on seizure type. Convulsive status epilepticus (CSE) is defined as a GTCS lasting more than 5 minutes or two such episodes within 5 minutes without return to baseline in between. It is a true emergency, analogous to ventricular tachycardia. Nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) refers to prolonged episodes (30 minutes or longer) of electrical seizure activity without clinically obvious seizure activity; it is analogous to atrial fibrillation with or without rapid ventricular response (management varies with symptom severity).

Seizure cause usually determines the outcome in status epilepticus; thus, evaluation for serious causes (meningitis, intracranial hemorrhage) must be conducted in parallel with treatment. If meningitis is suspected in status epilepticus, head CT is usually indicated after convulsions have stopped. Seizure treatment and head CT should occur before lumbar puncture, but no test should delay antibiotic administration, as this has the most impact on mortality and morbidity.

CSE is diagnosed clinically and presents as continuous generalized clonic jerking of the entire body. Unless PNES is strongly suspected, empiric therapy is indicated without awaiting results of EEG, imaging, serum studies, or lumbar puncture because a longer duration of CSE is strongly linked to worse outcomes.

Securing the airway and obtaining intravenous access are the first steps in management (

). If hypoglycemia is present, thiamine should be given, followed by intravenous glucose. First-line treatment is an intravenous benzodiazepine (or intramuscular midazolam). If intravenous access is not available, midazolam may be given intranasally, although absorption is less reliable. Fear of respiratory depression should not limit treatment; counterintuitively, benzodiazepine treatment is associated with lower intubation rates.

Typically, benzodiazepines should be followed by an intravenous ASM (“second-line therapy”) to avoid seizure recurrence. Fosphenytoin is preferred over phenytoin because it can be infused more rapidly and has a lower incidence of skin necrosis (due to drug extravasation). Both fosphenytoin and phenytoin can cause acute bradycardia and hypotension. Alternative second-line intravenous therapies include valproate, levetiracetam, and lacosamide.

If convulsions stop but the patient does not either improve within 10 minutes or return to baseline within 30 minutes, immediate continuous EEG is required to diagnose NCSE. NCSE after CSE is still a medical emergency and should be treated aggressively.

If convulsive seizure activity does not cease, intubation is typically required, and patients are placed in an anesthetically induced coma for 24 to 48 hours by using propofol, midazolam, or pentobarbital (thiopental is also available outside the United States). Intravenous anesthesia carries considerable risk, including prolonged ICU hospitalization and associated morbidity (e.g., infection, deep venous thrombosis). Continuous EEG monitoring is mandatory. Hypotension is most common with pentobarbital, which may accumulate in tissues and require many days for clearance. Midazolam is less morbid but often leads to tolerance and tachyphylaxis.

NCSE should be suspected when a patient has altered mental status of unknown cause. It is equally common in medical, surgical, and neurologic ICUs (15% to 25% of critically ill patients with encephalopathy) and should be considered even when a patient has no known neurologic history. Continuous EEG monitoring is required for diagnosis and should be prompted by certain situations (see [Table: Table: Indications for Immediate Continuous Video EEG Monitoring]

). Shorter duration EEG is typically inadequate because many patients experience intermittent rather than continuous seizures, although certain patterns on initial short studies may predict future seizure risk. At least 24 hours of monitoring is recommended in noncomatose patients, and at least 48 hours is recommended in comatose patients.

Treatment is based on clinical examination, not on EEG alone. If the patient is not comatose, initiating aggressive therapy with intubation and an intravenous anesthetic–induced coma is usually avoided because the risks may outweigh the benefits. Outcomes are typically related to seizure cause, rather than severity of seizures or altered mentation.
