Stroke

The World Health Organization defines stroke as a disease of sudden-onset focal neurologic deficits associated with dysfunction in the brain, retina, or spinal cord due to occlusion or rupture of a cerebral or spinal artery.

Determining the exact subtype of stroke present has important implications for therapeutic interventions, prevention strategies, and prognosis.

Ischemic stroke is caused by infarction that leads to focal neurologic deficits and stems from a vascular occlusion in the brain, spinal cord, or retina. Transient ischemic attack (TIA) is a focal deficit that resolves (usually within minutes) without evidence of infarction on imaging.

Hemorrhagic stroke is less common than ischemic stroke and has higher short-term mortality. It has two subtypes:

  • Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) includes focal or global neurologic dysfunction, including headache and alterations in consciousness, due to bleeding in the brain (intraparenchymal) or ventricles (intraventricular).
  • Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is defined as bleeding in the subarachnoid space and commonly results from aneurysm rupture or trauma. Patients with aneurysmal SAH often, but not always, present with the “worst headache of their life,” associated with sudden-onset neurologic dysfunction.

Although their clinical manifestations often overlap with stroke, subdural and epidural hematomas are not considered to be strokes and are discussed in Subdural Hematoma in Neurology and Epidural Hematoma in Neurology.

Stroke remains primarily a clinical diagnosis supported by imaging; it requires a careful history to determine the nature of the symptoms, onset speed, and medical comorbidities. A neurologic examination is needed to determine if neurologic deficits consistent with abnormalities on imaging are present. In the acute setting, the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS), a validated scale that can be rapidly performed, is universally used ( [Table: Table: National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale]

). The history and examination are also instrumental in determining eligibility for acute stroke therapeutics, as well as the appropriate secondary prevention strategies.

Additionally, results of the physical and neurologic examinations will often suggest the cause of ischemic stroke, such as atrial fibrillation or a carotid stenosis, although further evaluation is required to confirm the cause (

).

Because the neurologic examination cannot reliably distinguish ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke, neuroimaging is required before initiating treatment. In acute ischemic stroke, the initial noncontrast head CT scan is often normal, although some patients with larger deficits can exhibit early findings (

,

). Even 24 hours after onset, a head CT scan may not show evidence of infarction, especially when small or in the brainstem. Video: Head CT Scan Showing Ischemic Stroke shows an example of ischemic stroke on noncontrast CT scan 2 days after symptom onset.

MRI is more sensitive than CT for acute infarction, showing changes on the diffusion-weighted imaging sequence within minutes of symptom onset (

). Because of its longer acquisition time, brain MRI is rarely the initial test of choice in acute suspected stroke; when indicated, it is obtained after the initial head CT scan. MRI is not routinely used in planning immediate therapeutic interventions for ischemic stroke, but it may be useful for such in a narrow set of circumstances.

CT angiography (CTA) of the head and neck and CT perfusion scanning may be performed emergently if endovascular therapy is being considered in ischemic stroke.

Head CT can usually detect hemorrhagic stroke (

). In patients presenting with symptoms suggestive of SAH, including the sudden onset of the “worst headache of their life”, a normal CT scan obtained within 6 hours of symptom onset makes SAH very unlikely and further testing is usually not required. If the symptoms are present for more than 6 hours, a normal head CT scan is insufficiently sensitive to rule out SAH and lumbar puncture must be performed to assess for the presence of cerebrospinal fluid blood or xanthochromia (yellow color stemming from erythrocyte breakdown). In patients with hemorrhagic stroke seen on a CT scan, additional imaging may be indicated. In SAH, catheter-based angiography is required to diagnose, and potentially treat, a cerebral aneurysm.

[Table: Table: Common Neuroimaging Modalities for Stroke]

summarizes the indications and benefits of each imaging modality.

Ischemic stroke can be categorized into several subtypes on the basis of the underlying cause and clinical presentation, including large artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolic disease, lacunar infarcts, and other less common causes. TIAs may occur with any of these subtypes.

shows examples of ischemic stroke subtypes on MRI.

The main mechanism of stroke due to large artery atherosclerosis is plaque rupture with artery-to-artery embolism, rather than just reduction in flow from the presence of stenotic plaque. The infarct pattern on neuroimaging can help distinguish these mechanisms. Intracranial plaque can also occlude perforating arteries that supply blood to the deep structures in the brain, such as the basal ganglia or brainstem (see

and

).

Large artery atherosclerosis is further subdivided by extracranial or intracranial location. A diagnosis of ischemic stroke secondary to large artery atherosclerosis is typically based on stenosis on imaging of greater than 50% in the extracranial internal carotid artery (ICA), and greater than 70% in intracranial arteries.

For extracranial ICA imaging, carotid duplex ultrasonography, CTA, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) are all used in clinical practice. Duplex ultrasonography is the initial test of choice for evaluating ICA stenosis because of its wide availability, low cost, and low risk; if high-grade ICA stenosis is detected and the patient is a candidate for surgery or stenting, confirmatory testing is required before intervention:

  • CTA has very high sensitivity for ICA stenosis and intracranial atherosclerotic disease and is commonly used in the acute stroke setting (Video: CT Angiogram Showing Carotid Stenosis).
  • MRA (see

) is less widely available for emergency use.

Surgical intervention is possible only for extracranial ICA. The intracranial arteries can be imaged noninvasively with CTA or MRA, and the results help guide medical management.

Cerebral infarcts due to a cardioembolic source tend to involve the cerebral cortical surface or cerebellum. These patients have unrevealing vascular imaging and require cardiac testing to determine a possible cardioembolic source. Atrial fibrillation is the most common cause of cardioembolic stroke, and ECG is recommended in all patients with ischemic stroke, with additional cardiac monitoring in those in whom the cause of stroke has not been identified.

Transthoracic echocardiography is the first-line test to evaluate left ventricular function and potential sources of emboli. Injecting agitated saline (bubble study) is indicated when there is suspicion of a patent foramen ovale (PFO) or other right-to-left shunt source of cerebral emboli, particularly in patients younger than 55 years.

The use of transesophageal echocardiography to evaluate for an intracardiac source of stroke is not routinely indicated in patients who are older, given the low yield for findings that require anticoagulation or surgery. Transesophageal echocardiography may be considered on a case-by-case basis in younger patients without stroke risk factors or in whom suspicion for endocarditis or an intracardiac tumor (such as myxoma or fibroelastoma) exists.

The cardiac sources of emboli are characterized as high or low risk based on a threshold of 2% per year risk for stroke.

High-risk sources include the following:

  • Mechanical heart valve
  • Atrial fibrillation or flutter
  • Left atrial or ventricular thrombus
  • Myocardial infarction within 4 weeks
  • Dilated cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction less than 40%
  • Endocarditis
  • Left ventricular regional hypokinesis
  • Atrial myxoma
  • Rheumatic heart disease
  • Mechanical circulatory support

Low-risk sources include the following:

  • PFO
  • Aortic arch atheroma
  • Atrial septal aneurysm
  • Bioprosthetic valve
  • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or left ventricular hypertrophy
  • Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
  • Mitral annular calcification

For further details on anticoagulation criteria in atrial fibrillation, see Anticoagulation in Cardiovascular Medicine. For recommendations regarding percutaneous PFO closure to prevent a secondary stroke, see Patent Foramen Ovale in Cardiovascular Medicine.

Characteristic presentations of lacunar infarcts include pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, ataxic-hemiparesis, and clumsy-hand dysarthria. Imaging reveals infarcts less than 1.5 cm in diameter in deep locations, such as the internal capsule, thalamus, or pons, without corresponding arterial stenosis. The main risk factor is hypertension, which leads to local damage at the level of the penetrating artery with subsequent occlusion.

Patients with an embolic stroke of undetermined source (ESUS) have similar imaging characteristics as patients with cardioembolic stroke but have unrevealing cardiac testing and vascular imaging. When this occurs, the patient’s clinical syndrome, underlying medical comorbidities, and neuroimaging characteristics can inform which additional diagnostic testing to consider, with special attention to hypercoagulable states, including underlying malignancy.

Prolonged outpatient cardiac monitoring with surface electrodes or an implantable monitor is indicated in ESUS and may reveal atrial fibrillation in approximately one third of patients. In patients with an implantable pacemaker, interrogating the device may also reveal episodes consistent with atrial fibrillation.

The leading causes of stroke in younger patients without risk factors are cervicocephalic arterial dissection and PFO. The former is characterized by local symptoms, such as head or neck pain (commonly starting after a rapid head movement), as well as Horner syndrome or other cranial nerve deficits preceding or accompanying typical stroke symptoms (see Patent Foramen Ovale in Cardiovascular Medicine).

In younger patients, an evaluation for autoimmune and hypercoagulable disorders should be considered. Hypercoagulable disorders and other rare cardioembolic causes may present with an infarct pattern similar to that of atrial fibrillation. Cerebral vasculitis is an extremely rare cause of stroke and presents with numerous infarcts affecting multiple arterial distributions.

Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) is characterized by thunderclap headache and is associated with certain medications, such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, sympathomimetic agents, and tacrolimus, or pregnancy; these patients can present initially with surface SAH and develop infarcts later in the disease course (see Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome in Neurology).

TIA is characterized by a transient focal neurologic deficit without infarction on neuroimaging. Symptoms of TIA are like those of stroke ( [Table: Table: Symptoms of Transient Ischemic Attack]

). TIAs have the same subtypes as ischemic stroke and, like minor stroke (typically defined as NIHSS score 1-5), can be associated with a high risk for recurrence even if they last for only seconds to minutes; thus, they should be treated with the same urgency.

The ABCD^2 score ( [Table: Table: ABCD^2 Score]

) can help with risk stratification and has been used in clinical trials to further identify patients with TIA who may benefit most from additional medical therapy, such as dual antiplatelet agents. TIA scoring systems do not identify all patients with high risk.

Patients with high-grade extracranial ICA stenosis who have a TIA in a downstream neurologic territory have the greatest short-term risk for stroke. This risk is highest within 2 weeks of TIA for patients with greater than 70% stenosis; 50% to 70% stenosis also carries significant associated risk. Expedited vascular imaging of the ICA to identify surgical candidates and cardiac evaluation for atrial fibrillation are required for all patients with TIA.

The initial evaluation of patients with stroke requires ruling out a hemorrhagic stroke and, if absent, determining candidacy for acute reperfusion therapy. Reperfusion therapy is based on the principle that there may be salvageable brain tissue (ischemic penumbra) if cerebral blood flow is restored.

Patients presenting within 3 hours of symptom onset without hemorrhage may be eligible for thrombolytic therapy depending on specific inclusion and exclusion criteria ( [Table: Table: Contraindications to Intravenous Thrombolysis]

). Treatment between 3 and 4.5 hours after stroke onset is endorsed in national treatment guidelines, although treatment after 3 hours or with unknown onset time is off label and not FDA approved. Immediate MRI can be used to identify a very select group of patients who may benefit from treatment with thrombolysis when the time of onset is unknown; this practice is weakly endorsed in some national guidelines.

An intravenous recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (either alteplase, which is administered as an infusion, or tenecteplase, which is administered as a single bolus) increases the probability of reduced neurologic disability at 3 months, and the benefit is greater the more quickly it is administered. Because of the associated delays, obtaining advanced imaging or laboratory values before thrombolytic administration should be avoided unless coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia is suspected. Premorbid disability or dementia should not prevent consideration for thrombolysis and endovascular therapy in eligible patients.

Before a thrombolytic is administered, patient blood pressure must be lower than 185/110 mm Hg, whereas after thrombolysis the blood pressure should remain below 180/105 mm Hg to prevent hemorrhage. Intravenous labetalol as a single bolus or intravenous nicardipine infusion is recommended, whereas nitrates should be avoided given the potential to increase intracranial pressure (ICP).

Well-defined clinical monitoring intervals after thrombolytic administration exist for blood pressure, neurologic, and airway checks; all antithrombotic agents should be avoided until 24-hour follow-up neuroimaging shows no hemorrhage.

The most significant complication of thrombolytic administration is symptomatic ICH, defined as a change in neurologic status with intracranial bleeding that can explain the change. Symptomatic hemorrhage should be suspected in patients who develop headache, nausea, altered level of alertness, or worsening of neurologic deficits. In those circumstances, the infusion of thrombolytic agents should be stopped immediately and imaging performed emergently. Thrombolysis-related coagulopathy may be reversed by using an antifibrinolytic agent such as tranexamic acid or aminocaproic acid and cryoprecipitate infusions targeting dysfibrinogenemia.

After 24 hours, antiplatelet agents for stroke prevention and anticoagulant agents for deep venous thrombosis prevention can be started if hemorrhage is absent on follow-up imaging.

Systemic thrombolysis may have lower efficacy in patients who have a large vessel occlusion (LVO) in the terminal carotid artery, middle cerebral artery stem (M1) and proximal branch (superior division M2), and basilar artery, but it should not be withheld. Endovascular therapy in addition to thrombolysis may be indicated in these patients. In patients presenting less than 6 hours from onset in whom an LVO is suspected based on cortical deficits and/or high NIHSS score, emergent CTA or MRA is indicated to determine eligibility for endovascular therapy but should not interfere with time to thrombolysis. CTA or MRA should also be performed in patients presenting within 6 to 24 hours with a clinically suspected LVO, small core infarct, and large penumbra (Video: Thrombectomy Video Series) to identify potential candidates for endovascular therapy. Treatment centers without mechanical thrombectomy capability should pursue immediate transfer of patients with LVO to suitable centers without waiting for completion of thrombolysis. A treatment algorithm for stroke within 24 hours of onset is provided in

.

For patients with acute ischemic stroke who are ineligible for thrombolysis or endovascular therapy, antiplatelet therapy is the mainstay of emergency treatment. When administered within 48 hours of stroke, aspirin reduces the short-term risk for recurrent stroke. Monotherapy with clopidogrel, however, has no established benefit in the acute stroke setting. A dysphagia evaluation is necessary to ensure that the patient can safely swallow aspirin; if not, aspirin should be administered rectally.

Patients with high-risk TIA or minor noncardioembolic ischemic stroke are a unique population because they have a significantly higher short-term risk for recurrence compared with other patients with stroke. Short-term dual antiplatelet agents reduce the risk for recurrent stroke in this population when initiated within 72 hours. In general, trials enrolled patients with an ABCD^2 score of 4 or greater, NIHSS score lower than 6, or evidence of large artery atherosclerosis. The length of treatment with aspirin and clopidogrel combined versus monotherapy varied between the clinical trials, with the two largest studies using 21 days and 90 days. A post hoc analysis of these studies showed less clinical benefit after 30 days and a higher risk for systemic hemorrhage, so guidelines have tended to recommend this duration of treatment. An exception is in patients with intracranial atherosclerosis, for whom data suggest that treatment as long as 90 days with dual antiplatelet agents could be beneficial. Aspirin and ticagrelor also show a benefit compared with aspirin alone when used for 30 days without significantly higher bleeding. Aspirin-ticagrelor was also superior to aspirin-clopidogrel for TIA and minor stroke among patients with cytochrome P450 family 2 subfamily C member 19 (CYP2C19) loss-of-function alleles.

Systemic anticoagulation with heparinoids within 48 hours of symptom onset, even for patients with atrial fibrillation, is not effective at reducing the immediate risk for recurrent stroke for most patients and is instead associated with higher risk for hemorrhagic conversion. When anticoagulation is indicated, the use of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) is usually preferred and delayed for at least 48 hours. The acute use of systemic heparinoids may be considered on a case-by-case basis in patients with mechanical heart valves, left ventricular thrombus, hypercoagulable states, and mechanical circulatory support with small infarcts (less than one third of the middle cerebral artery distribution).

Among patients with atrial fibrillation, the START, TIMING, ELAN, and OPTIMAS trials have demonstrated that that the optimal timing of the initiation or resumption of anticoagulation with DOACs depends on stroke severity. In patients with a minor stroke (defined as infarct size <1.5 cm) or moderate stroke (defined as a stroke in the superficial cortical branch of a cerebral artery), starting a DOAC after 2 to 3 days was associated with a slight reduction in the risk for ischemic stroke without a significant increase in hemorrhage. Similarly, a 2025 meta-analysis demonstrated that initiation of a DOAC within 4 days is beneficial in patients with an acute ischemic stroke with an NIHSS score of 3 to 10. In patients with severe stroke (defined as multiple branches or the whole arterial territory of a cerebral artery), early anticoagulation (started after 6-7 days) was associated with favorable outcomes but some notable increase in hemorrhage; starting anticoagulation within this time period for severe stroke is reasonable depending on the patient.

Management of acute hypertension in ischemic stroke differs when thrombolysis is not involved. Early treatment of hypertension may reduce blood flow to vulnerable ischemic penumbra and cause harm in most patients. In patients with blood pressure of 220/120 mm Hg or greater or whose acute comorbid conditions (such as a concomitant acute coronary event, acute heart failure, aortic dissection, postfibrinolysis intracranial hemorrhage, or preeclampsia/eclampsia) require antihypertensive treatment, cautious lowering by 15% in the first 24 hours after stroke onset is reasonable. Otherwise, blood pressures below this level should not be treated. After 24 to 48 hours, antihypertensive drugs are safe to be started or restarted in patients with blood pressure greater than 140/90 mm Hg and titrated to control blood pressure within a week, although doing so does not clearly affect outcomes. See Secondary Prevention of Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease in Cardiovascular Medicine for other secondary prevention strategies.

Treating hyperglycemia in patients with acute stroke is reasonable; however, in one study, an intensive glycemic control strategy for as long as 72 hours targeting levels of 80 to 130 mg/dL did not improve neurologic outcomes compared with an approach of 80 to 179 mg/dL and led to more episodes of hypoglycemia (see Inpatient Management of Hyperglycemia in Endocrinology and Metabolism).

Healthy Lifestyle Counseling in Foundations of Clinical Practice provides information on treating cardiovascular risk factors related to primary prevention of stroke. Routine screening for asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis is not recommended. Medical treatment with a statin reduces the risk for stroke in persons with asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis and is indicated in all patients. Persons with asymptomatic stenosis of 70% or greater should not undergo routine carotid revascularization, and shared decision making should be used to decide whether revascularization should be added to medical management. Patients with high-risk features, such as rapid progression or high-grade stenosis, silent infarcts on brain MRI, or evidence of impaired vasomotor reactivity of microembolic signals on transcranial Doppler ultrasound, may be considered for revascularization based on perioperative risk analysis. Ongoing clinical trials in patients with greater than 80% stenosis may provide more information on the relative advantages of revascularization and medical therapy.

Patients with stroke benefit from tobacco cessation and diet and exercise changes to maintain cardiometabolic health. Patients with infarcts benefit from blood pressures of less than 130/80 mm Hg; treatment with a thiazide diuretic, ACE inhibitor, or an angiotensin receptor blocker is preferred. High-intensity statin therapy to achieve an LDL cholesterol level below 70 mg/dL (1.81 mmol/L) lowers the risk for stroke among patients with ischemic stroke or TIA presumed to be of atherosclerotic origin. See Secondary Prevention of Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease in Cardiovascular Medicine for more information.

After the acute phase, chronic antiplatelet agents are indicated for patients with noncardioembolic ischemic stroke and TIA. The underlying stroke subtype drives the choice of medication (

). In noncardioembolic stroke, aspirin or clopidogrel is effective at reducing the risk for recurrent stroke; clopidogrel is slightly superior to aspirin for a composite cardiovascular disease outcome, especially in patients with underlying peripheral artery disease. Aspirin-dipyridamole is also more effective than aspirin alone for secondary prevention, whereas there is no difference in stroke reduction with clopidogrel monotherapy versus aspirin-dipyridamole. Clopidogrel may be better tolerated than aspirin-dipyridamole because of its once-daily versus twice-daily dosing and lower incidence of headache. Aspirin remains a reasonable option when considering cost and ease of use.

Ticagrelor, alone or in combination with aspirin, has also been shown to reduce risk for stroke in patients with acute ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA, showing the most efficacy in patients who do not respond to clopidogrel; data on efficacy beyond 90 days, however, are lacking. Prasugrel should be avoided in patients with a previous stroke. The benefit of platelet resistance assays in directing therapy has not been established in long-term stroke prevention.

In a trial of patients with intracranial atherosclerosis, warfarin was associated with increased mortality compared with aspirin and should be avoided.

Patients with atrial fibrillation, ventricular thrombus, a mechanical heart valve, or venous thromboembolism should receive long-term anticoagulation. For a review of anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation–related stroke, see Anticoagulation in Cardiovascular Medicine. In patients with ESUS, however, two trials (RE-SPECT ESUS, NAVIGATE-ESUS) with rivaroxaban and dabigatran did not reduce the risk for recurrent stroke and were associated with risk for systemic bleeding.

Patients with a nondisabling stroke or TIA due to ICA stenosis greater than 70% and some patients with stenosis of 50% to 69% benefit from early revascularization. The choice of endarterectomy or angioplasty with stenting is determined by several patient-specific factors and local surgical experience. Trials have consistently found a higher risk for perioperative stroke with stenting and a higher risk for perioperative myocardial infarction with endarterectomy. Data on 30-day outcomes suggest that the optimal timing for the highest benefit and least risk from carotid endarterectomy is day 3 to 14 after symptom onset. Carotid artery stenting has been suggested as a preferred alternative to carotid endarterectomy in some patients, such as those younger than 70 years or at high risk for cardiovascular complications with general anesthesia. However, the safety of early carotid artery stenting is controversial, and current guidelines from the European Society for Vascular Surgery recommend carotid endarterectomy over carotid stenting in patients who are to undergo revascularization within the first 14 days after symptom onset. Revascularization is not feasible in patients with complete ICA occlusion, and external carotid–to–internal carotid bypass is not effective for stroke prevention. Extracranial vertebral artery stenting is associated with a high risk for stroke recurrence and is not routinely indicated.

Symptomatic intracranial artery stenosis greater than 70% is associated with a high risk for recurrent stroke and should be treated with a high-intensity statin, aggressive blood pressure control, long-term aspirin with consideration of clopidogrel for the first 90 days, and lifestyle modifications; in one study, meeting physical activity targets was very effective. Stenting the affected artery, however, is associated with a high risk for procedural stroke and should be avoided.

Closing a PFO is indicated in younger patients with embolic stroke and a large shunt with no alternative cause or need for anticoagulation. Efficacy in patients older than 60 years has not been established in randomized trials (see Patent Foramen Ovale in Cardiovascular Medicine).

Patients with stroke are at high risk for developing in-hospital and long-term neurologic complications.

Patients with ischemic stroke may develop worsening deficits from hemorrhagic conversion of the infarct, usually within 48 hours. Antiplatelet agents should be held for at least 1 week in most patients with large hemorrhagic conversion. Patients with petechial pattern hemorrhagic conversion with stable imaging can be started on antiplatelet agents within 48 hours of conversion.

Patients with a large hemispheric ischemic stroke are at risk for neurologic deterioration from cerebral edema in the first 24 to 72 hours after a stroke. Patients with significant symptomatic cerebral edema and increased ICP after an ischemic stroke have a survival advantage with decompressive hemicraniectomy, although neurologic compromise may be significant.

Patients with stroke may also show neurologic worsening from seizures and systemic infections; these conditions should be treated aggressively.

ICH can present similarly to ischemic stroke, with headache and impaired consciousness as distinguishing characteristics. A CT scan of the head is the initial imaging because of its high sensitivity for ICH, low cost, and ability to provide useful information on the underlying cause.

, Video: CT Scan Showing Intracerebral Hemorrhage, and Video: CT Scan Showing Pontine Intracerebral Hemorrhage show examples of ICH.

The most common cause of ICH in deep structures of the brain (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum) is hypertension. Lobar hemorrhages near the cortical surface may have various causes, including hypertension, hemorrhagic tumors, arteriovenous malformations, and cortical vein thrombosis. In patients older than 50 years, especially those without hypertension, lobar ICH may be caused by cerebral amyloid angiopathy. In this syndrome, amyloid protein similar to that seen pathologically in Alzheimer disease deposits in cerebral arterioles near the cortical surface, weakening the arterial wall and making it prone to rupture. Recently updated diagnostic criteria for cerebral amyloid angiopathy have been published ( [Table: Table: Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy Criteria]

).

The Glasgow Coma Scale (see [Table: Table: Glasgow Coma Scale]

), patient age, and imaging features (ICH volume, presence of intraventricular hemorrhage, and infratentorial origin of bleed) are needed to calculate the ICH score, which provides prognostic information and is required for regulatory purposes. An ICH score of 1 is associated with a mortality rate of less than 15%, whereas mortality is greater than 95% with scores of 4 to 5.

Indications for further imaging with CTA or MRI include atypical hemorrhage location, immunosuppression, or clinical concern for malignancy. Scoring systems are available to determine if further imaging is required, such as CTA to rule out a vascular malformation, although most patients will not require it.

The mainstay of therapy in ICH is avoiding hematoma expansion, as it leads to neurologic worsening. The main risk factors for hematoma expansion are coagulopathy and hypertension. For more information, see sections on treating bleeding in the setting of anticoagulant use (Anticoagulants in Hematology), thrombocytopenia (Thrombocytopenic Disorders in Hematology), and other acquired bleeding disorders (Acquired Bleeding Disorders in Hematology). Platelet transfusion in the setting of antiplatelet therapy–related ICH does not improve outcomes.

In patients with a systolic blood pressure of 150 to 220 mm Hg, the American Heart Association recommends a treatment target between 130 and less than 140 mm Hg using agents that will lower blood pressure in a sustained manner without fluctuations; this level should be maintained for at least 7 days after ICH to improve functional outcomes. Antihypertensive medications should be held if systolic blood pressure falls below 130 mm Hg. Intravenous drips and monitoring in the ICU are recommended, with oral agents gradually introduced after 24 hours as the patient is transitioned out of the ICU. Intravenous nitrovasodilators, such as nitroglycerin and nitroprusside, should be avoided as they may increase ICP. Early withdrawal of blood pressure therapy is associated with increased mortality, and guidelines caution against terminating care in the first 48 hours.

Close monitoring of plasma glucose is recommended. Treating glucose levels less than 40 to 60 mg/dL (2.2-3.3 mmol/L) and greater than 180 to 200 mg/dL (10.0-11.1 mmol/L) is reasonable to improve outcomes. Although therapeutic hypothermia has no role in ICH treatment, managing elevated temperatures may improve outcomes.

Elevated ICP is a major determinant of morbidity and mortality in ICH. Short-term bolus osmotherapy with mannitol or hypertonic saline may temporarily reduce ICP in patients with ICH; glucocorticoids are ineffective in reducing cerebral edema in ICH and should not be used.

Among patients presenting with intraventricular hemorrhage, the same blood pressure targets should be maintained, but the patient should be monitored closely for signs of hydrocephalus and elevated ICP, such as worsening level of arousal, unilateral dilated unreactive pupils, or cranial nerve VI palsy. Ventricular drainage is preferred over medical therapy when elevated ICP and hydrocephalus result in a decreased level of consciousness.

Seizures are also associated with an acute ICH and should be suspected in patients whose deficit is not well explained by neuroimaging. Electroencephalography should be considered in such settings (see Diagnostic Evaluation of Seizures and Epilepsy in Neurology). In patients with suspected or documented electrographic seizures, antiseizure drugs should be administered to improve neurologic outcomes. When intracranial hemorrhage results from cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, the immediate treatment is anticoagulation.

Surgical procedures may be considered in patients with moderate to severe ICH and intraventricular hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, or an infratentorial hematoma location. Prophylactic decompression is recommended for cerebellar hemorrhage with a diameter greater than 3 cm or volume greater than 15 mL. Certain large supratentorial hematomas may also require surgical intervention.

Patients with SAH present with sudden-onset severe headache, known as thunderclap headache and often described as the worst headache of their life (see Thunderclap Headache in Neurology and

for more information). Examination findings suggestive of SAH include confusion and somnolence, nuchal rigidity, pupillary dilation from oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III) compression by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm, or subhyaloid hemorrhages on funduscopy. Findings on CT scan are often diagnostic (Video: CT Scan Showing Subarachnoid Hemorrhage).

The most common cause of SAH is saccular (berry) aneurysm rupture, which has the highest morbidity and mortality among causes of hemorrhagic stroke. Common saccular aneurysm locations are the anterior and posterior communicating arteries, middle cerebral artery, and basilar artery tip. Saccular aneurysms can often be visualized with CTA or MRA, although the resolution is insufficient to detect smaller aneurysms. Catheter-based angiography is necessary to definitively diagnose aneurysms and other causes of SAH, such as arteriovenous malformations.

Two scales are used to predict prognosis when evaluating aneurysmal SAH and should be used in most patients: the Hunt-Hess scale for predicting mortality based on clinical presentation and the modified Fisher scale for predicting vasospasm risk based on imaging.

Hunt-Hess Scale:

  • 1: Mild headache or no symptoms
  • 2: Moderate to severe headache; the only neurologic deficit is cranial nerve palsy
  • 3: Drowsy or confused; mild deficits
  • 4: Stupor; moderate to severe hemiparesis
  • 5: Deep coma, posturing

Modified Fisher Scale:

  • 0: No subarachnoid or intraventricular hemorrhage; diagnosis with lumbar puncture
  • 1: Minimal SAH and no intraventricular hemorrhage
  • 2: Minimal SAH with bilateral intraventricular hemorrhage
  • 3: Thick SAH without bilateral intraventricular hemorrhage
  • 4: Thick SAH with bilateral intraventricular hemorrhage

A subset of patients who have SAH in the basal cisterns without evidence of an aneurysm are diagnosed with a perimesencephalic SAH, which has a more benign natural history than aneurysmal SAH. SAH can also be seen in isolation in the sulci near the cortical surface (nonaneurysmal SAH) and has several possible causes, including RCVS, dural sinus thrombosis, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, arteriovenous malformations, and mycotic aneurysms. Patient history and examination can help determine which of these underlying causes is likely.

Mycotic aneurysms are uncommon complications of endocarditis. If hemorrhagic stroke has occurred in a patient with endocarditis, vascular imaging is indicated for mycotic aneurysms, although CT angiography may not visualize them because they tend to be small and near the cortical surface. If suspicion for mycotic aneurysm is high but initial imaging is unrevealing, catheter-based angiography is indicated for diagnosis and may provide a therapeutic option for endovascular treatment.

SAH treatment focuses on preventing early (≤48 hours) and late neurologic complications. In the first 48 hours, a major cause of morbidity is aneurysmal rebleeding; early surgical exclusion of the ruptured aneurysm and blood pressure control are required. Elevated systolic blood pressure has been associated with aneurysmal rebleeding, and most guidelines recommend maintaining systolic blood pressure values below 160 mm Hg; short-acting titratable medications such as nicardipine are preferred. Elevated ICP from obstructive hydrocephalus, cerebral edema, seizures, and cerebral vasospasm are other leading causes of poor outcomes.

Elevated ICP from obstructive hydrocephalus or global cerebral edema is a common consequence of SAH and has high mortality without intervention. Examination findings that raise concern for elevated ICP include impaired consciousness, loss of brainstem reflexes, and stereotyped posturing movements to painful stimuli. The presence of hydrocephalus on neuroimaging should prompt neurosurgical placement of an external ventricular drain to measure and relieve elevated ICP.

New-onset seizures after SAH should be treated with antiseizure medications for 7 days. Prophylactic antiseizure treatment should not be routinely used but may be considered in high-risk clinical settings, such as a middle cerebral artery aneurysm, cortical hemorrhage or infarction, or high-grade SAH. Impaired consciousness due to nonconvulsive status epilepticus may also occur and requires electroencephalographic monitoring for diagnosis.

Patients are at risk for developing cerebral vasospasm beginning near day 5, which can lead to delayed cerebral ischemia. The degree of hemorrhage on a head CT scan may predict vasospasm risk (modified Fisher scale, see Subarachnoid Hemorrhage in Neurology), but frequent monitoring with daily transcranial Doppler imaging (or CT angiography and perfusion studies) is recommended in all patients. Prophylactic nimodipine should be started as early as possible to improve neurologic outcomes and continued for 21 days or until hospital discharge. Catheter-based angiography may also be needed to establish vasospasm as the cause of neurologic worsening and has the added benefit of potential endovascular treatment, including use of intra-arterial vasodilators and angioplasty. Another treatment option for vasospasm in patients with a treated aneurysm is induced hypertension, although the exact treatment targets are not well established.

If SAH is caused by a mycotic aneurysm, antibiotics with central nervous system coverage are indicated, and neurosurgical intervention should be considered. In patients with SAH secondary to RCVS, calcium channel blockers such as verapamil or nimodipine may prevent subsequent cerebral ischemia; glucocorticoids should be avoided because they may lead to worse neurologic outcomes.

Medical complications are a significant source of morbidity and mortality in patients with SAH. Patients with impaired consciousness and coma at presentation are at the highest risk for stunned myocardium (with a decrease in left ventricular ejection fraction) and pulmonary edema because of the large sympathetic surge in SAH. Other medical complications include pulmonary and urinary tract infections, dysphagia with aspiration, the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, and cerebral salt wasting. Because of these possible medical and neurologic complications, patients with SAH require care in a specialized ICU with experience in treating SAH.

Hypertension management significantly reduces the risk for all hemorrhagic stroke subtypes. In patients with cerebral amyloid angiopathy (see [Table: Table: Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy Criteria]

), long-term anticoagulation should be avoided given the annual risk of up to 10% for first, and recurrent, ICH.

Management of asymptomatic saccular aneurysms is based on aneurysm location and size, although all patients benefit from hypertension management and tobacco cessation. Conservative treatment and serial imaging is often appropriate for aneurysms smaller than 7 mm, but surgical intervention with either clipping or coiling should be considered for patients with multiple risk factors for rupture (posterior circulation location, tobacco use, hypertension) and in those with larger aneurysms. Other factors associated with a higher risk for rupture include age older than 70 years, Finnish or Japanese ancestry, and previous SAH. In addition to size, a scale (https://www.mdcalc.com/calc/10459/phases-score) can be used for risk stratification for patients with a cerebral aneurysm.

Regardless of size, aneurysms should be followed with annual noninvasive neuroimaging. MRA has the benefit of no radiation or contrast, whereas CTA may provide a slightly better resolution. Catheter-based angiography is not routinely indicated unless endovascular treatment is being considered. Enlarging aneurysms should also be considered for surgical intervention.

As in primary prevention, hypertension management reduces the risk for recurrent hemorrhagic stroke. After the acute in-hospital setting, a target blood pressure of lower than 130/80 mm Hg is advised in patients with ICH; thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, and angiotensin receptor blockers are the preferred therapies if pharmacologic treatment is necessary. Adherence to a low-salt diet and daily exercise are also likely to aid hypertension management and subsequent hemorrhage reduction.

Antiplatelet agents can be considered when there is a clear indication, such as previous myocardial infarction. In patients with hypertensive ICH, resuming antiplatelet agents for secondary cardiovascular disease prevention is safe and can be considered between 2 and 4 weeks. Whether anticoagulation can be safely resumed in hypertensive hemorrhages is the subject of the ongoing ASPIRE trial.

See Secondary Prevention of Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease in Cardiovascular Medicine and Anticoagulation in Cardiovascular Medicine for more information on lipid-lowering therapies and anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation–related stroke, respectively.

In patients with a previous SAH, unruptured aneurysms should be considered for surgical intervention even if smaller than the threshold for primary prevention (7 mm), given the higher risk for recurrence. Surgery is considered on a case-by-case basis in patients with ICH secondary to an arteriovenous malformation.

Patients with SAH and ICH have a very high early mortality due to elevated ICP, extensive neurologic injury, and medical complications (including seizures and systemic infections). Care in a specialized neurologic ICU with access to neurosurgery can reduce in-hospital mortality. In patients with ICH, the degree of neurologic recovery is based on the degree of initial neurologic injury, similar to ischemic stroke. Patients with SAH can often recover levels of consciousness but often have long-term cognitive sequelae in addition to other neurologic deficits.

In-hospital medical complications are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with stroke. Admission to a specialized stroke unit is associated with a reduced long-term risk for all-cause mortality. Specialized stroke units are effective because they use multidisciplinary care teams that follow structured protocols.

Head-of-bed elevation and aggressive oral hygiene can prevent aspiration pneumonia, but nasogastric or percutaneous gastrostomy tubes do not. Prophylactic antibiotics should be avoided, even in patients at high risk for pneumonia. Urinary tract infections are common in stroke patients because of neurologic injury and impaired mobility affecting bladder emptying; care protocols include screening for retention and avoiding or removing indwelling catheters. Early mobilization with specially trained therapists may reduce the risk for medical complications and hasten recovery.

Pulmonary embolism is a leading cause of death in patients with stroke, and pharmacologic prophylaxis should be started for all patients. In patients with ischemic stroke, prophylaxis should start on admission except in patients treated with thrombolysis, in whom a 24-hour neuroimage showing no hemorrhage is required before doing so. In patients with hemorrhagic stroke, subcutaneous heparin or enoxaparin should be started 24 hours after ICH if imaging shows no evidence of expansion and in SAH upon securing the aneurysm.

A 2018 systematic review found that supplemental oxygen in patients with normal oxygen saturation as measured by pulse oximetry increases mortality in patients with stroke and other acute illnesses (see Oxygen Therapy in Critical Care Medicine). Stroke guidelines recommend avoiding supplemental oxygen unless the oxygen saturation as measured by pulse oximetry is 94% or lower.

In-hospital stroke is usually ischemic and frequently observed perioperatively. Patients undergoing cardiac surgery involving cardiopulmonary bypass, particularly multivalve procedures, are at highest risk for stroke in the postoperative setting. The most common cause is atrial fibrillation. Patient comorbidities and acuity of illness may delay recognition of in-hospital stroke, but patients may be eligible for acute stroke therapeutics and should be evaluated with the same urgency as patients presenting in the outpatient setting.

The modifiable preoperative risk factors for in-hospital stroke are similar to those causing stroke in the short term without surgery, including symptomatic stenosis of the extracranial ICA greater than 50%. Patients with a recent stroke secondary to ICA stenosis who are undergoing nonemergent surgery are likely to benefit from revascularization beforehand. Asymptomatic ICA stenosis, however, is not clearly associated with perioperative stroke, and routine prophylactic ICA revascularization is not indicated. See Perioperative Management of Neurologic Disease in Foundations of Clinical Practice for more information on perioperative stroke.

Surgery within 90 days of stroke, regardless of cause, increases the risk for perioperative stroke; elective surgeries should be avoided within this time. Patients with stroke involving a large brain volume or with a recent hemorrhagic stroke are also at risk for cerebral hemorrhage if placed on cardiopulmonary bypass or anticoagulation. If possible, nonemergency major cardiac procedures should be avoided.

In the long term, patients with stroke are at high risk for delayed neurologic complications. Cognitive impairment, vascular cognitive impairment, and seizures may occur. Most patients with stroke exhibit neurologic impairment and disability 1 year after stroke and beyond.

Extensive physical, occupational, and speech therapy improves neurologic recovery, and aerobic exercise may help as well. Fatigue after stroke is common and associated with the development of poststroke sleep-disordered breathing, which, if untreated, may reduce participation in rehabilitation activities and affect recovery. Patients with poststroke fatigue should be screened with polysomnography because screening questionnaires may not be as effective in patients with stroke.

Poststroke depression is a common complication and, when present, should be treated with pharmacotherapy or psychotherapy. The use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors to improve poststroke disability in the absence of depression, however, should be avoided given the lack of efficacy and increased risk for fractures in patients with stroke. Furthermore, antidepressants should not be used to prevent poststroke depression.

Frequent passive stretching in the hospital may reduce the risk for spasticity; if present, spasticity can be treated with botulinum toxin to targeted muscles, but oral agents are not as effective. Task-specific practice and neuromuscular electrical simulation may improve outcomes.

Other medical treatments, such as amphetamines, amantadine, memantine, or bromocriptine, have not been established as effective for promoting recovery.

Adherence to secondary stroke prevention guidelines is inconsistent after hospital discharge. Standardized discharge orders, aligned with recommended core measures for patients with stroke, can reduce the risk for hospital readmission and recurrent stroke.

These standardized orders

  • Ensure that appropriate antiplatelet or anticoagulant agents and high-intensity statin therapy are started at hospital discharge
  • Include essential patient education about diet, exercise, smoking cessation, and other healthy lifestyle choices to reduce the risk for recurrent stroke
  • Allow for stroke-specific education regarding typical stroke symptoms and the importance of rapid return to care if symptoms occur so that acute stroke therapeutics can be initiated

Cognitive Impairment

Cognitive impairment may affect any or all of the five major domains of cognitive function: memory, executive function, attention and concentration, language, and visuospatial perception. Although impairment in one domain may affect another, highlighting the initial and predominant domains of impairment is helpful in both diagnosis and staging.

Memory can be divided into short-term and long-term memory. Short-term memory loss can be assessed by asking whether the patient has greater difficulty with declarative (e.g., orientation to the day of the week and time of day) or episodic (e.g., recalling recent events) memories. Other clinical indications of short-term memory loss include frequently misplacing items or getting lost. Difficulty recognizing close friends and family or recalling autobiographical information is more concerning for long-term memory impairment and suggests a more progressive level of impairment. Semantic memory loss for known facts and common vocabulary is also concerning for more long-term memory impairment.

Executive function often overlaps with impairment of memory as well as attention and concentration. Executive impairment is clinically assessed by asking about new concerns with decision making or judgment (e.g., patient recently experienced a scam), planning, and/or multitasking.

Attention and concentration are the abilities to focus on a task and to sustain focus for some time, respectively. Patients with impairment in this domain are easily distracted and have trouble with other cognitive skills, such as learning or making decisions.

Language impairment can be assessed by inquiring about word-finding difficulty; dysfluency; word substitutions or paraphasic errors; and problems with comprehension, reading, or writing.

Visuospatial perception impairment often presents with reading concerns, or patients may have difficulty writing in a straight line or signing their name. They may mis-reach for items, have difficulty parallel parking, or bump into walls or furniture.

Cognitive impairment is a spectrum of decline in cognition that can have reversible or irreversible causes; identifying the cause helps direct management (

).

Subjective cognitive impairment describes a syndrome of persistent self-perceived cognitive decline that cannot be detected with cognitive testing tools. In one study of more than 1000 community-dwelling adults with subjective cognitive impairment, however, 18% developed mild cognitive impairment (MCI) after a median of 3 years.

MCI is an objective syndrome of diminished cognitive skills, such as memory and visuospatial awareness, with relative preservation of day-to-day function; it is diagnosed using patient or caregiver reports and a validated tool (e.g., Mini–Mental State Examination, the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, Saint Louis University Mental Status examination) that documents clear cognitive deficits. MCI may be reversible with treatment of underlying conditions or remain static; in some patients, it may progress to dementia. Thus, patients with MCI should be assessed periodically for modifiable risk factors and functional impairment.

Dementia is characterized by progressive cognitive impairments that interfere with activities of daily living (ADLs). The stage of dementia is determined by the extent of the patient’s functional impairment and cognitive testing. Evaluation should include assessment of basic and instrumental ADLs and should include the patient and at least one other informant. Basic ADLs include eating, bathing, dressing, grooming, and toileting. Instrumental ADLs include administering medication, managing finances, cleaning, shopping, and cooking.

Patients with some impairments of instrumental ADLs have a mild stage of dementia, whereas patients with impairments of most or all of their instrumental ADLs or who require prompting for basic ADLs have moderate dementia. Patients requiring assistance for both instrumental and basic ADLs are considered to have severe dementia.

Similarly, the DSM-5 uses the term major neurocognitive disorder for dementia; mild neurocognitive disorder describes objective cognitive impairment that does not interfere with the patient’s daily functioning.

The Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) Dementia Staging Instrument is a tool that weighs both functional and cognitive impairment on a numeric scale and is often used to quantify dementia severity. The categories are as follows:

  • No dementia (Global CDR Score = 0)
  • Questionable dementia (Global CDR Score = 0.5)
  • Mild dementia (Global CDR Score = 1)
  • Moderate dementia (Global CDR Score = 2)
  • Severe dementia (Global CDR Score = 3)

A CDR score of 0.5 is consistent with MCI.

The diagnosis of dementia has a significant effect on overall prognosis. The life expectancy of men and women diagnosed at age 65 years is 5.7 years and 8 years, respectively; life expectancy drops to 2.2 and 4.5 years, respectively, when the diagnosis is made at the age of 85 years. Similarly, 35% of patients reside in a nursing home within 3 years of diagnosis, a figure which climbs to 57% at 5 years.

The Mini–Mental State Examination (MMSE), the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), the Eight-item Informant Interview to Differentiate Aging and Dementia (also called AD8), and the Saint Louis University Mental Status (also called SLUMS) examination are the most frequently used tools when obtaining objective data of cognitive impairment. The cognitive examination should be followed by a neurologic examination to detect any deficits that may be attributable to cerebrovascular disease or motor evidence of neurodegenerative disease, such as parkinsonism. More detailed cognitive assessments such as neuropsychological testing are usually not necessary but may be helpful in selected patients with equivocal findings or when a concomitant disorder such as depression is suspected.

The evaluation of a patient with established cognitive impairment focuses on determining the underlying cause. In addition to the standard history, specific attention should be paid to known developmental, learning, or physical disabilities; history of traumatic brain injury; the social history, including highest level of education, current or previous occupation, year of retirement, and recent changes in the patient’s living situation; lifestyle factors and substance use; and the family history of any neurodegenerative diseases. A medication history is crucial because polypharmacy and anticholinergic drugs may cause or contribute to cognitive deficits. It is also important to assess for sleep disturbances; sensory deficits, such as hearing or vision loss; and presence of neuropsychiatric symptoms, including depression, anxiety, hallucinations, or apathy. Additionally, physicians should inquire about new motor symptoms, such as a change in gait, slowed movement, or tremors.
