Importantly, nondegenerative causes of cognitive impairment, including certain infections, electrolyte abnormalities, hypothyroidism, and vitamin B~12 deficiency, are often reversible and must be recognized and addressed early in the clinical course. [Table: Table: Secondary Causes of Cognitive Impairment]

shows common secondary causes, diagnostic tests, and treatments.

Blood testing must, at minimum, include a complete blood count, a comprehensive metabolic profile, and measurement of thyroid-stimulating hormone, serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and serum vitamin B~12 levels. Testing for syphilis is indicated only if suspected from the history; the treponemal antibody test is preferred over the rapid plasma reagin test. Neuroimaging, preferably with brain MRI, should be completed in all patients. Biomarker testing for Alzheimer disease is limited to a select number of patients being considered for antiamyloid therapy and should not be pursued in all patients.

Previous or new behavioral symptoms must also be assessed when evaluating cognitive function. Behavioral and mental health disorders may be a cause of cognitive impairment or may be seen in some forms of dementia. For many patients and caregivers, a behavioral issue may be the chief concern. Specific assessment for the following factors may help in determining the degree and cause of cognitive impairment:

  • Previous psychiatric diagnoses, reports of ongoing mood or anxiety symptoms, and current psychiatric medications. Using screening tools such as the Geriatric Depression Scale, Beck Depression Inventory, PHQ-9, and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 scale (GAD-7) may be helpful.
  • Psychotic features, such as hallucinations, delusions, and paranoia
  • Personality changes, disinhibition or apathy, altered eating habits, or repetitive rituals or obsessions
  • Social isolation, as reflected by degree of engagement in hobbies, social activities, and physical exercise
  • Sleep impairment, which is a contributing factor to both behavioral and cognitive changes

Safety must also be assessed by asking about falls, wandering, leaving the stove on, and difficulty driving. If firearms are present, extra precautions should be taken to ensure that they are safely secured.

The differential diagnosis of cognitive disorders is varied and includes the following:

  • Neurodegenerative disorders, such as Alzheimer disease, frontotemporal dementia, and dementia with Lewy bodies
  • Normal-pressure hydrocephalus
  • Vascular cognitive impairment
  • Autoimmune and paraneoplastic disorders
  • Medication adverse effects
  • Toxic-metabolic processes
  • Psychiatric disorders
  • Structural lesions

Neurodegenerative diseases ( [Table: Table: Degenerative and Vascular Cognitive Disorders]

) are defined by protein accumulation in the brain and irreversible nerve damage resulting in a wide spectrum of cognitive and motor impairments on examination.

Multiple neurologic disorders may cause cognitive symptoms. For example, the Parkinson-plus syndromes, including corticobasal degeneration and progressive supranuclear palsy, are associated with cognitive impairment (see Parkinson-Plus Syndromes in Neurology). Delirium and the diseases listed in [Table: Table: Secondary Causes of Cognitive Impairment]

may also cause cognitive impairment.

NPH presents with cognitive decline, gait disturbance, and urinary incontinence, typically in patients older than 60 years. The cognitive impairment seen in NPH is usually an executive impairment due to increased pressure and compression of the frontal-subcortical circuits. The abnormal gait is classically described as “magnetic” because of the difficulty patients have lifting their feet off the ground, resulting in a wide stance, short stride, and poor heel strike. Impaired bladder control in NPH results from brainstem compression, specifically the pontine micturition center.

NPH is caused by abnormal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) absorption by the arachnoid granulations into the cerebral venous sinuses, causing a reserve of CSF in the ventricles that often leads to disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus (also known as DESH). On brain MRI, disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus is characterized by enlarged sylvian fissure space or dilated sulci, compacted medial subarachnoid spaces or sulci, and ventriculomegaly without evidence of cortical atrophy (

).

Early diagnosis and management are critical for patients diagnosed with NPH; earlier treatment can reverse or significantly improve symptoms, whereas delayed treatment correlates with a lack of benefit. NPH is diagnosed on the basis of clinical history, imaging suggestive of the diagnosis, and a 10-meter gait examination before and at least 30 minutes after a high-volume lumbar puncture in which 30 mL or more of CSF is removed.

Documented improvement in gait (but not cognitive impairment, which is unlikely to improve) after large-volume CSF removal by lumbar puncture confirms the diagnosis of NPH; referral to neurosurgery for ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement is indicated. Patients should be informed that ventriculoperitoneal shunt complications occur in 35% of patients, and co-pathologies consistent with neurodegenerative causes are relatively common.

After Alzheimer disease, cerebrovascular disease is the most common cause of MCI and dementia. Vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) is divided into subcortical ischemic cognitive impairment, poststroke cognitive impairment, and multi-infarct cognitive impairment. Additionally, patients with VCI often have comorbid neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer disease, a combination known as mixed cognitive impairment. Mixed cognitive impairment is more common than isolated vascular cognitive impairment, which accounts for 12% of dementia cases.

Subcortical ischemic cognitive impairment is often caused by underlying arteriolosclerosis or microvascular disease. Arteriolosclerosis is usually secondary to hypertension and affects the smooth muscle of small and penetrating arterioles serving subcortical structures in the brain. Microvascular disease due to impaired capillary ability to deliver nutrients and clear waste in the parenchyma is more often due to type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Because of the disruption of the frontal-subcortical circuits, executive and attention impairments are commonly seen on cognitive examination. White matter subcortical and periventricular hyperintensities are seen on T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences on brain MRI (Video: Brain MRI in Vascular Cognitive Impairment).

Atherosclerosis of large arteries, atrial fibrillation, and cardiac disease are common causes of brain injury in poststroke and multi-infarct cognitive impairment. Clinical cognitive and neurologic examinations for these conditions are heterogeneous and correlate with the anatomic location or locations of brain injury on imaging. Poststroke cognitive impairment is diagnosed when cognitive impairments follow immediately or within 6 months after a stroke, whereas multi-infarct cognitive impairment typically results from multiple cortical infarcts, with correlating cortical signs on neurologic examination.

For mixed cognitive impairment, in addition to brain injury due to a vascular cause, the presence of hippocampal atrophy on brain MRI suggests concomitant Alzheimer disease.

Pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic treatment of modifiable cardiovascular risk factors, including hypertension, dyslipidemia, and diabetes, is recommended for management. Recommended lifestyle changes include 150 minutes per week of physical activity divided into three to five sessions, cognitive and social stimulation, and healthy dietary habits (Mediterranean and Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay [also called MIND] diets).

No medications are FDA approved for VCI. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, such as donepezil or galantamine, are used in mild to moderate stages of vascular cognitive impairment. Combination therapy with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and memantine (an N-methyl-d-aspartate [NMDA] antagonist) has been shown to be clinically effective in moderate to severe stages of disease.

For information on managing behavioral symptoms, see Treatment Approach to Neurobehavioral Symptoms in Neurology.

Alzheimer disease is the most common cause of dementia, with its incidence in the United States projected to rise to more than 130 million adults by 2050. This neurodegenerative disease (see [Table: Table: Degenerative and Vascular Cognitive Disorders]

) is caused by an abnormal aggregation of extracellular β-amyloid protein plaques and intraneuronal phosphorylated tau protein in the brain.

Typical Alzheimer disease usually occurs in patients older than 65 years. Most patients present with an amnesic clinical profile with progressive impairments in episodic memory. The average clinical course involves gradual progression over 7 to 10 years, but this varies widely among patients; some patients with typical and many patients with atypical Alzheimer disease may have a shorter disease course.

Alzheimer disease is also the most common cause of dementia in persons younger than 65 years, and memory loss remains the most common clinical presentation of early-onset Alzheimer disease. Atypical presentations of Alzheimer disease, such as posterior cortical atrophy, logopenic variant primary progressive aphasia, and frontal variant Alzheimer disease, are more likely to present in younger patients but can occur at any age.

Diagnosis is made on the basis of clinical history, cognitive testing, imaging, and laboratory studies. Coronal T1-weighted brain MRI often shows atrophy of the mesial temporal structures, specifically the entorhinal cortex and hippocampi, as well as parietal atrophy (

).

Clinical judgement should be used when ordering biomarker testing for Alzheimer disease in symptomatic persons; such testing is only required in patients with MCI or mild dementia who are considering treatment with antiamyloid drugs. Either CSF analysis or amyloid PET is recommended. A CSF profile of decreased β-amyloid protein (due to consumption in extracellular amyloid plaque formation) and elevated total and phosphorylated tau (due to impaired metabolism) is consistent with Alzheimer disease. Similarly, a positive amyloid PET scan supports an Alzheimer disease diagnosis. The FDA has also approved the phosphorylated tau protein 217/β-amyloid 1-42 plasma ratio for the detection of amyloid plaques associated with Alzheimer disease in patients aged 55 years and older with signs and symptoms of cognitive decline.

Asymptomatic persons, regardless of family history, should not undergo biomarker testing for Alzheimer disease.

Genetic testing, regardless of symptoms, may be considered for persons with a strong family history, but they should be first referred for genetic counseling. The apolipoprotein E (APOE) e4 variant confers an increased risk for Alzheimer disease. APOE genotyping is not routinely recommended. However, patients receiving antiamyloid therapy who are homozygous for the APOE e4 variant also have an increased risk for amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA); therefore, genotyping is indicated in patients preparing to undergo antiamyloid therapy.

Mild to moderate Alzheimer disease may be treated with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, such as donepezil, rivastigmine, or galantamine. In patients with moderate to severe disease, memantine, an NMDA antagonist, can be added or used alone. Memantine may also be used in patients who cannot tolerate acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, regardless of disease stage. Common adverse effects of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors include gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., diarrhea, vomiting, or stomach discomfort) and, less commonly, symptomatic bradycardia or hypotension. Gastrointestinal symptoms are dose related and often resolve with time or dose reduction. If bradycardia or hypotension occurs, the drug should be discontinued. Adverse effects of memantine include confusion, dizziness, and headache, although these are relatively uncommon.

Additionally, lifestyle changes targeting improved sleep hygiene, diet, and exercise (aerobic exercise that increases heart rate for 30 to 50 minutes at least three to five times weekly) as well as social and cognitive stimulation also help with neuroprotection.

Caregiver education and planning for anticipated lifestyle and financial changes should be discussed once a diagnosis is made.

Two disease-modifying therapies for mild Alzheimer disease are available, lecanemab and donanemab. They are monoclonal antibodies that target the amyloid protein, slowing disease progression by 25% to 35% and decreasing the risk for progressing to the next stage of cognitive decline. The most common adverse effects are infusion reactions and ARIA. Most cases of ARIA are asymptomatic, but patients may develop headache, confusion, vision changes, gait impairment, focal neurologic symptoms, and seizures. Referral to a subspecialist for screening and management is recommended to ensure that the benefit of these therapies outweighs the risk for each candidate.

For further information on treating neurobehavioral symptoms, see Treatment Approach to Neurobehavioral Symptoms in Neurology.

Variants of Alzheimer disease include the following:

  • Dysexecutive Alzheimer disease
  • Posterior cortical atrophy (PCA)
  • Logopenic variant primary progressive aphasia (lvPPA; see Primary Progressive Aphasia in Neurology)

Less common variants include frontal-variant Alzheimer disease (also called behavioral-variant Alzheimer disease) and motor-variant Alzheimer disease.

These disorders present with atypical clinical features, but pharmacologic management is identical to that of Alzheimer disease; an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and/or memantine is used depending on the stage of the disease. Additional targeted management is also used for behavioral (dysexecutive Alzheimer disease) and visuospatial impairments (PCA).

Patients with dysexecutive Alzheimer disease develop a predominantly executive impairment rather than the amnesic syndrome of typical Alzheimer disease. Onset is typically before age 65 years, but some patients may present later in life. Unlike typical Alzheimer disease, patients experience difficulty in decision making, planning, and multitasking.

Dysexecutive Alzheimer disease may share some of the behavioral symptoms typically exhibited in frontotemporal dementia (FTD) (see Frontotemporal Dementias in Neurology) but is caused by the same β-amyloid and phosphorylated tau protein seen in late-onset Alzheimer disease. Brain MRI findings are also similar to those in FTD, showing frontotemporal atrophy on T1-weighted coronal and sagittal images in contrast to the expected temporoparietal pattern of typical Alzheimer disease.

PCA is characterized by a clinical profile of predominant visual impairments due to deficits in visuospatial perception. The history is typically consistent with mis-reaching for items, bumping into walls, difficulty reading due to movement of the text, and difficulty writing in a straight line. Balint syndrome is a classic triad that describes a common clinical presentation including simultanagnosia (inability to perceive more than one object at a time), optic ataxia (difficulty reaching for an object with normal motor and cerebellar function), and oculomotor apraxia (difficulty voluntarily moving eyes horizontally). The pattern of atrophy seen on axial T1-weighted brain MRI involves primarily parieto-occipital regions consistent with the clinical profile.

FTD is one of the more common neurodegenerative causes of early-onset dementia, accounting for 10% of dementias diagnosed in patients younger than 65 years. More than half of the patients with FTD have behavioral variant FTD (bvFTD). The remainder of patients with FTD may have one of two variants of primary progressive aphasia (semantic variant or nonfluent variant); these conditions may have pathologic findings similar to those of the frontotemporal lobar degeneration seen in bvFTD (see Primary Progressive Aphasia in Neurology).

BvFTD is characterized by early behavioral changes; the average age of onset is 58 years. Core clinical features include the following:

  • Significant impairment in executive functioning, such as reasoning, judgment, and problem solving
  • Hyperorality/new eating patterns
  • Compulsive/ritualistic behavior
  • Loss of sympathy/empathy
  • Disinhibition
  • Apathy

Cortical atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes is characteristically seen on T1-weighted brain MRI (

).

Diagnostic criteria have been developed for possible FTD (three of the core clinical features) and probable FTD (three core clinical features and frontotemporal atrophy on imaging).

Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (also called FTLD) is the pathologic entity associated with FTD and may be seen in any of the three forms of FTD. Multiple distinct pathologies exist within this group. Several genetic variants are also known, including that involving C9orf72, which may also cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

Care for bvFTD is largely supportive and focused on symptoms. Given the early behavioral changes seen in FTD, an interdisciplinary approach with nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic interventions is needed. Although not FDA approved for this indication, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are first-line therapy for behavioral symptoms in bvFTD. Caregiver support is necessary to avoid burnout, potentially avoidable depression or anxiety, or undue guilt when placement in assisted living environments is needed. Because of the association with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, all patients with bvFTD should be monitored closely for muscle weakness, cramping, or fasciculations.

The typical pharmacologic treatments for cognitive deficits in Alzheimer disease are not effective in patients with bvFTD, unless they have comorbid Alzheimer disease.

Primary progressive aphasia (PPA) is characterized by dementia with predominant language impairment (Video: Expressive Aphasia). Pathology may be consistent with FTLD (nonfluent variant PPA [nfPPA] and semantic variant PPA [svPPA]) or Alzheimer disease (lvPPA).

Because of their association with FTLD, svPPA and nfPPA are often considered variants of FTD, but both clinical syndromes have been observed with other underlying pathologies, albeit less commonly. nfPPA is clinically characterized by dysfluency and grammatical errors (see Video: Expressive Aphasia), whereas svPPA is defined by loss of object or word comprehension and naming with preserved fluency. T1-weighted brain MRIs show a dominant posterior frontal pattern of atrophy for nfPPA and a dominant anterior temporal pattern of atrophy for svPPA (

).

lvPPA is the most common of the three clinical variants and more commonly associated with Alzheimer disease pathology. It is characterized by preserved fluency with frequent word-finding difficulties, circumlocutions, word substitutions, and paraphasia. For right-handed and 50% of left-handed individuals, a left posterior temporal and parietal atrophy pattern is often seen on T1-weighted brain MRI. Unlike typical Alzheimer disease, lvPPA often starts with language impairment, which continues to be the predominant impairment throughout the disease course.

The absence of Alzheimer disease biomarkers in CSF or a negative amyloid PET scan can aid in ruling out Alzheimer disease in patients with PPA. Fluorodeoxyglucose-PET may provide an alternative means of diagnosis. The presence of temporoparietal hypometabolism consistent with Alzheimer disease has a specificity of 97% and is clinically indicated when differentiating between Alzheimer disease and FTLD.

All three subtypes of PPA are primarily managed with targeted symptomatic therapy.

Referral to a speech pathologist early in the disease is recommended to develop compensation techniques. Expectations should be discussed with families and caregivers because these techniques may lose their clinical benefit with cognitive decline later in the disease process.

Patients with PPA may often have preserved insight into their disease process; as such, the inability to communicate effectively is often frustrating, leading to significant levels of neurobehavioral symptoms in this patient population. Pharmacologic management of such symptoms may be preferred to psychotherapy in settings of language compromise.

Management of cognitive deficits in patients with PPA suspected to be caused by Alzheimer disease includes acetylcholinesterase inhibitors for mild to moderate disease; acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and/or memantine can be used for moderate to severe disease. For further information on treating neurobehavioral symptoms, see Treatment Approach to Neurobehavioral Symptoms in Neurology.

Lewy body dementias are neurocognitive disorders characterized by intracytoplasmic inclusions in the brain that contain α-synuclein protein (Lewy bodies). The two most common Lewy body dementias are dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) and Parkinson disease dementia. DLB is the second most common cause of neurodegenerative dementia after Alzheimer disease, accounting for 30% of diagnosed dementias. Parkinson disease dementia is estimated to occur in 30% to 50% of patients who have had a Parkinson disease diagnosis for at least 10 years.

The central, core, and supportive clinical features of DLB are listed in [Table: Table: Degenerative and Vascular Cognitive Disorders]

. Cognitive impairment in DLB occurs before or within a year of the onset of parkinsonian motor symptoms and is characterized by predominant executive and visuospatial dysfunction. The diagnosis of probable DLB is made with the presence of two or more core clinical features, whereas the diagnosis of possible DLB is made with the presence of one core clinical feature.

Indicative studies can help with diagnosis when only one or no core clinical features are present. Such studies include polysomnography consistent with rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder, single-photon emission CT or PET scan with reduced basal ganglia uptake, or low uptake on iodine 123 myocardial scintigraphy. The typical T1-weighted brain MRI pattern of atrophy shows medial temporal lobe preservation.

Other findings that support the diagnosis of DLB include a posterior pattern of hypometabolism with preservation of the posterior cingulate cortex on fluorodeoxyglucose-PET scan (posterior island sign or cingulate island sign) and characteristic quantitative electroencephalographic changes.

Compared with Parkinson disease dementia, cognitive decline in DLB is an early symptom; the average clinical course is estimated to be 5 to 7 years. The behavioral and neuropsychiatric profile of DLB is distressing for many caregivers and is a factor for disease progression and early placement in an assisted living facility.

Parkinson disease dementia differs from DLB in the timing of motor symptom onset as parkinsonian signs present at least 1 year before cognitive symptoms and remain the predominant feature of the disease (see Parkinson Disease in Neurology). The clinical criteria for Parkinson disease dementia require, in addition to earlier onset of parkinsonism, impairment in at least two cognitive domains resulting in functional impairment that is not attributable to motor or autonomic symptoms. An executive pattern of impairment is often a predominant feature.

Although supportive testing, such as single-photon emission CT or PET scan with reduced basal ganglia uptake, may aid in evaluation, Parkinson disease dementia remains a largely clinical diagnosis. MRI findings are generally nonspecific.

Although not yet standard care, α-synuclein seed amplification assays and skin biopsy for phosphorylated α-synuclein may assist on the diagnosis of α-synucleinopathies such as Parkinson disease and DLB.

Management of cognitive symptoms in DLB and Parkinson disease dementia is similar to that in typical Alzheimer disease, with studies suggesting clinical benefit from acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as rivastigmine (off label for DLB but approved for Parkinson disease dementia) or donepezil (off label for DLB and Parkinson disease dementia).

In patients with DLB, antiparkinsonian medications are not absolutely contraindicated, but they may worsen hallucinations; physical therapy is preferred to manage parkinsonian features in these patients. For information on treating parkinsonism in Parkinson disease dementia, see Treatment of Parkinson Disease in Neurology.

Many patients with DLB are extremely sensitive to neuroleptic medications, particularly first-generation agents, and are at high risk for severe worsening of symptoms resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome when exposed to these drugs. For further information on treating neurobehavioral symptoms, see Treatment Approach to Neurobehavioral Symptoms in Neurology.

Traumatic encephalopathy syndrome (TES) is a clinical syndrome of progressive neurodegenerative cognitive impairment following repetitive head trauma. TES is usually seen in patients with a history of participation in contact sports, military combat deployment, or civilian injury. Clinically, behavioral symptoms predominate:

  • Increased irritability
  • Aggressiveness
  • Personality changes
  • Depression
  • Suicidality

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (also called CTE) is a term used to describe the pathology of most patients with TES, which consists of three-repeat and four-repeat tau proteins (see [Table: Table: Degenerative and Vascular Cognitive Disorders]

). A subset of patients with TES may show a pathology more like Lewy body dementia or Alzheimer disease, and epidemiologic studies have reported a strong association between TES and parkinsonism. The neurofibrillary tangles in chronic traumatic encephalopathy are predominately found in a perivascular pattern in the frontal cortex and more diffusely throughout the rest of the cortex and brainstem. Brain MRI commonly shows a slit-like space in the septum pellucidum (cavum septum pellucidum).

Management includes early psychological and/or psychiatric treatment, including SSRIs and/or psychotherapy, for behavioral symptoms as well as interdisciplinary management with social work and occupational and physical therapy for social and motor symptoms (impairment in coordination, swallowing, speech, and parkinsonism), respectively. See Treatment Approach to Neurobehavioral Symptoms in Neurology.

Rapidly progressive dementia describes a clinical syndrome of cognitive impairment that progresses in weeks to months, with complete dependence in 1 to 2 years. While some cases progress inexorably, many are due to causes that are treatable; if the condition is diagnosed and treated early, the resultant cognitive impairment may be reversible. A diligent search for a reversible underlying cause is necessary, with specific testing directed by suggestive features of the history and physical examination ( [Table: Table: Differential Diagnosis of Rapidly Progressive Dementias]

,

).

Autoimmune dementia or autoimmune encephalopathy (see Paraneoplastic (Autoimmune) Neurologic Syndromes in Neurology) can cause rapidly progressive dementia. The presence of early psychosis or seizures, young age of onset, history of cancer or treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors, history of smoking, and family history of cancer or autoimmunity are clues that may suggest an autoimmune process. Evaluation is comprehensive, including brain MRI, electroencephalography, CSF analysis, routine blood work, and neuronal antibody testing. Other labs should be guided by clinical suspicion. Early recognition and diagnosis are important for timely treatment and improving the prognosis.

Wernicke encephalopathy is a common reversible clinical syndrome characterized by cognitive impairment (Wernicke aphasia, Video: Receptive Aphasia), oculomotor dysfunction, and gait ataxia. It arises from thiamine (vitamin B~1) deficiency in the setting of inadequate diet or alcohol use disorder. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome suggests a more progressive stage of the disease that includes damage of the mammillary bodies, leading to anterograde and retrograde memory impairment. Immediate and timely thiamine repletion early in the disease course can prevent irreversible damage.

Prion disease describes a category of rare neurodegenerative diseases caused by prion protein pathology with a rapidly progressive course of dementia. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is a uniformly fatal spongiform encephalopathy that may account for 60% of rapidly progressive dementias. Most patients have sporadic disease, with an average age of onset in the seventh decade. Inherited CJD causes affect 5% to 15% of patients and arise from prion protein (PRNP) gene variants. Variant CJD is uncommon and may be caused by ingesting contaminated meat products.

Clinical diagnostic criteria of CJD typically involve rapidly progressive cognitive impairment with two or more of the following features:

  • Akinetic mutism
  • Myoclonus
  • Extrapyramidal signs
  • Visual compromise
  • Cerebellar dysfunction

The diagnosis also requires detecting abnormal protein in CSF or pathologic specimens. The real-time quaking-induced conversion (also called the RT-QuIC) assay for abnormal prion protein is highly suggestive of the disease, with sensitivity exceeding 90% and specificity approaching 100%. CSF 14-3-3 protein is relatively nonspecific but may add incremental value in establishing the diagnosis of CJD.

Supportive findings on brain MRI include hyperintensity and restricted diffusion of parts of the basal ganglia (caudate and/or putamen), thalamus, and cerebral cortex (known as cortical ribboning) (

). Generalized periodic sharp waves or sharp wave complexes on electroencephalography also support the diagnosis.

There is no effective treatment. Targeted behavioral management and supportive care can be helpful.

Delirium is the most common type of cognitive impairment resulting from a medical condition. It often manifests as acute waxing and waning confusion that lasts for hours to days. The cognitive impairment seen in delirium is clinically heterogeneous and often affects multiple cognitive domains. Most typically, sudden attention and concentration, executive, and behavioral changes are seen in comparison to baseline ( [Table: Table: Causes, Features, and Management of Delirium]

).

Delirium may be described as either hypoactive or hyperactive in nature, and cognitive fluctuations are characteristic of the disease. Patients with dementia are especially susceptible to delirium given their already decreased cognitive reserve and cognitive vulnerability to minor infectious, metabolic, electrolyte, and iatrogenic changes.

Evaluation of delirium should include a careful history and physical examination as well as appropriately directed laboratory and imaging studies to identify provoking factors (see [Table: Table: Causes, Features, and Management of Delirium]

; see also Alcohol in Interdisciplinary Medicine and Toxicology in Hospital and Critical Care Medicine). In addition to treatment of the underlying medical condition, nonpharmacologic behavioral interventions, such as engagement and empowerment of family members, calm redirection, adequate pain management, and promotion of early mobility, should be prioritized (see [Table: Table: Causes, Features, and Management of Delirium]

).

In the setting of delirium management in patients with dementia, typical and atypical antipsychotics have been associated with increased morbidity and mortality and should be avoided. Severe refractory agitation or behavioral symptoms that delay appropriate diagnosis and care may require pharmacologic sedation to prevent self-harm. Brexpiprazole is the only agent approved to treat agitation associated with Alzheimer dementia. See Treatment Approach to Neurobehavioral Symptoms in Neurology for further information on treating neurobehavioral symptoms. It is important to have an informant who is knowledgeable about the patient’s cognitive baseline to ensure that treatment results in a return to baseline. See Delirium in Hospital and Critical Care Medicine for information on ICU delirium.

It is important, especially in a hospital setting, to distinguish delirium from sundowning, a syndrome of restlessness, irritability, confusion, or agitation in patients with or without dementia that typically occurs in the evening hours. Sundowning should be considered once common medical causes of delirium have been ruled out and collateral history from an informant supports the diagnosis. The nonpharmacologic behavioral interventions for sundowning are like those recommended for delirium.

Neurobehavioral symptoms are common in neurocognitive syndromes. In many patients, neuropsychiatric disorders are prodromal to cognitive disorders; in other patients, they are symptoms and manifestations of these same disorders.

Common mood disorders include anxiety and depression, which, for many patients, may be associated with loss of autonomy. Nonpharmacologic behavioral interventions include improved sleep hygiene, dietary recommendations, physical exercise (aerobic exercise with increased heart rate for 30 to 40 minutes at least three to four times weekly), and social and cognitive stimulation. Education and training on evidence-based practices to improve behaviors should be provided to care partners and caregivers. For example, the DICE (Describe, Investigate, Create, and Evaluate) approach aims to identify behavioral triggers in order to properly develop behavioral management tools.

If nonpharmacologic interventions are ineffective, pharmacologic management may be appropriate. The general recommendation for managing patients with concomitant dementia is to “start low and go slow.” SSRIs, such as sertraline and citalopram, and trazodone can be used to manage irritability, including verbal aggression; agitation; and depressive symptoms in patients with dementia.

Psychosis is also a common feature seen in many dementias, including atypical Alzheimer disease, bvFTD, and DLB. Psychotic symptoms often include visual hallucinations, paranoia, and delusions. In caring for such patients, it is important for caregivers and clinicians to cooperate to identify possible triggers and determine whether the symptoms undermine the patient’s safety or interfere with the delivery of basic care needs. When possible, nonpharmacologic behavioral interventions are preferred.

For many patients, neurobehavioral symptoms may include physical aggression toward others, including caregivers. This may be a consequence of confusion, delusions, or fear. If nonpharmacologic behavioral interventions for psychosis and physical aggression are unsuccessful, pharmacologic management can be considered. Brexpiprazole is the only agent approved to treat agitation associated with Alzheimer dementia. Typical and atypical antipsychotics have an FDA boxed warning in dementia because some studies show increased morbidity and mortality in patients with dementia. Patients and caregivers should be informed of this risk before this class of medication is prescribed; however, clinical judgment of the risks and benefits should be made on the basis of the safety of the patient and the caregiver. An ECG should be obtained and the hemoglobin A~1c level should be checked before patients start taking antipsychotics, given the risk for QT prolongation and metabolic syndrome.

Quetiapine is an atypical antipsychotic that is commonly used in clinical practice for patients with psychotic features because of its lower risk for extrapyramidal adverse effects. This is often relevant for patients diagnosed with dementias such as DLB with signs of parkinsonism already present on examination. However, risperidone (maximum dosage of 1 mg/d) has the greatest evidence for managing neurobehavioral and psychotic symptoms in patients with dementia. Risperidone also has the greatest risk for extrapyramidal symptoms; thus, close neurologic monitoring is recommended. Some support exists for using aripiprazole, 2 to 10 mg/d, for management. Use of these antipsychotics in the management of dementia is off label.

Movement Disorders

Movement disorders are characterized by hypokinetic and hyperkinetic patterns of motor output. The most typical hypokinetic pattern, parkinsonism, is characterized by paucity and slowness of movements (bradykinesia). Hyperkinetic disorders are categorized on the basis of the distribution and qualities of the involuntary excessive movements displayed ( [Table: Table: Classification of Movement Disorders]

).

Neurologic examination of movement disorders should include detailed assessment of motor function and gait. The key features in classifying movement disorders are the speed, amplitude, and fatigability of voluntary movements and the rhythmicity, suppressibility, randomness, and directionality of involuntary movements. Muscle tone should be assessed for rigidity, an increase in resistance to passive movements that is independent of the velocity and direction of these movements. Gait examination should consider the base of standing, ambulatory pace, stride length, foot clearance off the ground, postural stability, and arm swing.

Some cases of movement disorders may be challenging to define and may necessitate a second opinion or referral to a neurologist/movement disorder specialist to help guide the diagnostic process.

The most common type of hypokinetic movement disorder is parkinsonism, of which Parkinson disease is the most common form ( [Table: Table: Common Causes of Parkinsonism]

). Parkinson-plus syndromes combine features of parkinsonism with other features found in the patient’s history or physical examination. Parkinsonism may also result from microvascular disease or large strokes, in which case it is characterized predominantly by gait impairment, with the upper extremities relatively spared. Some medications cause parkinsonism. Additionally, patients with normal-pressure hydrocephalus may exhibit parkinsonism accompanied by gait instability, dementia, and urinary incontinence (see Normal-Pressure Hydrocephalus in Neurology).

Parkinson disease is a slowly progressive neurodegenerative disorder involving the gradual loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra. Pathologic findings include Lewy bodies, which are intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions composed of α-synuclein and ubiquitin. Genetic influences and exposure to certain environmental factors, including pesticides, can increase the risk for Parkinson disease. Aging is a major risk factor, and a sharp rise in global incidence is expected over the next 20 years.

Parkinson disease has four cardinal signs:

  • Bradykinesia
  • Resting tremor
  • Rigidity
  • Gait/balance impairment

Bradykinesia is characterized by progressive decrements in the speed and amplitude of repetitive movements. This feature is often associated with reduced facial expression and arm swing. Small handwriting (micrographia) is common, and patients may report difficulty with fine and gross movements. Speech becomes slower and quieter (hypophonic).

Resting tremor is characteristically unilateral at onset and remains asymmetric; it is most commonly noticed in the upper extremities and jaw (Video: Resting Tremor). A resting tremor can re-emerge after a few seconds’ delay after arms are held outstretched and during ambulation.

Rigidity is often asymmetric. It may occur on the same side as tremor and, in such cases, may be “cogwheel,” with intermittent release of the rigidity with passive movement; this results in a jerking or ratcheting movement quality. As many as 30% of patients with Parkinson disease have a tremor-free akinetic rigid syndrome at presentation.

Gait disturbance manifests as a slow, narrow-based, and shuffling gait, with associated reduced arm swings, stooped posture, and imbalance when turning (Video: Parkinsonian Gait). As the disease progresses, severe freezing of gait and postural instability are noted. In contrast, a cerebellar ataxic gait is characterized by a wide base, frequent truncal swaying and veering, and impaired tandem walking in a straight line. The presence of a wide-based, unsteady gait or early prominent postural instability with frequent falls is not typical in Parkinson disease and suggests a Parkinson-plus condition (see Parkinson-Plus Syndromes in Neurology).

Parkinson disease is also associated with various nonmotor symptoms, ranging from autonomic dysfunction to problems with sleep, mood, and cognition ( [Table: Table: Nonmotor Symptoms of Parkinson Disease]

). These symptoms, including hyposmia (diminished sense of smell), constipation, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (see Restless Legs Syndrome and Sleep-Related Movement Disorders in Neurology), may precede the onset of motor symptoms by years.

Cognitive impairment in Parkinson disease is not uncommon and initially involves mild subcortical deficits, especially in processing speed, short-term memory, executive function, and attention. Cortical functions, such as language and declarative memory (memory of facts and events), are relatively spared. Thirty percent to 50% of patients may develop dementia in the later stages of Parkinson disease, but early cognitive impairment is a red flag pointing to other diagnoses, such as dementia with Lewy bodies (see Lewy Body Dementias in Neurology).

The presence of bradykinesia with at least one other cardinal feature and the absence of red flags for atypical forms of parkinsonism ( [Table: Table: Red Flags for Atypical Forms of Parkinsonism]

) are essential for a diagnosis of Parkinson disease; no radiologic or laboratory tests can confirm the diagnosis. A clear therapeutic response to levodopa is highly supportive of the diagnosis. Alternatively, lack of response to increasing dosages from a starting point of 500 mg/d to 1000 mg/d for at least 1 month makes the diagnosis of Parkinson disease highly unlikely.

MRI can rule out stroke or hydrocephalus in select patients but is unnecessary in patients who have classic Parkinson disease with no other neurologic symptoms or signs and good response to levodopa. A dopamine transporter scan, such as a single-photon emission CT scan using ioflupane-123 ligand (

), may be obtained when Parkinson disease cannot be differentiated clinically from essential tremor or drug-induced parkinsonism. The test cannot distinguish Parkinson disease from Parkinson-plus conditions.

Specific biomarkers and tests for Parkinson disease are being studied, including seed amplification assays to measure α-synuclein (in cerebrospinal fluid and serum and on skin biopsy) and functional fluorodeoxyglucose PET. The clinical utility of these methods is under investigation.

Depression and anxiety are common in Parkinson disease and can be detected by using routine clinical mood and anxiety scales, such as the 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale. All patients with Parkinson disease should be screened annually for depression. Treatments include psychotherapy, antidepressants (excluding antipsychotic agents), and dopaminergic medications (when mood symptoms correlate with motor symptoms). Depression should be distinguished from apathy, a state of reduced motivation and goal-directed behavior that is not associated with sad mood and emotional distress.

All patients with Parkinson disease should also be assessed for fall risk at each visit. Falls in patients with Parkinson disease may be related to postural imbalance, impaired stepping, freezing of gait, or orthostatic hypotension. Detecting risk factors for falling and implementing a multidisciplinary management approach—including medication assessment, therapy, supportive devices, and education—can reduce morbidity and costs related to falls. Postural stability can be best assessed by the pull test, in which an examiner throws the patient off balance by pulling backward on the shoulders. A positive test result, characterized by the patient toppling into the examiner’s arms or taking more than two corrective steps, is the most reliable predictor of the risk for backward falls.

No available medication has established efficacy to slow the progression of Parkinson disease. Rigorous daily exercise can improve gait quality and balance and may provide disease-modifying benefits. Experimental therapies, including agents targeting α-synuclein aggregation, are under study.

Symptomatic treatments include medications ( [Table: Table: Medications for Parkinson Disease]

), surgical therapy, and supportive measures. Dopaminergic medications and dopamine agonists are the mainstay in treating motor symptoms. Several other medications can supplement the dopaminergic agents and help reduce the medication-induced complications that may emerge as Parkinson disease progresses.

The American Academy of Neurology recommends levodopa as the initial preferred therapy for motor symptoms of early Parkinson disease. Levodopa should be started when the symptoms begin to impair the patient’s quality of life. Alternatively, dopamine agonists such as pramipexole, ropinirole, and rotigotine may be prescribed as the initial therapy in patients younger than 60 years who are at higher risk for dyskinesia and have very mild and nondisabling parkinsonian symptoms. Patients taking dopamine agonists should be warned about impulse control disorder, which manifests as a tendency to engage in out-of-character impulsive behaviors, such as excessive gambling, overspending, and hypersexuality. Other adverse effects of the dopamine agonists include sleep attacks, dependent edema, nausea, orthostatic hypotension, hallucinations, and confusion.

All patients with Parkinson disease will eventually require levodopa. Carbidopa, a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor that does not cross the blood-brain barrier, blocks the adverse effects of levodopa outside the brain, such as nausea and orthostatic hypotension. It is used in combination with levodopa. Most adverse effects of levodopa are self-limited and are avoided if the dosage is slowly titrated over 1 to 2 weeks. In patients who experience severe peripheral adverse effects of levodopa, higher doses of carbidopa may alleviate these symptoms.

Several formulations of levodopa are commercially available (see [Table: Table: Medications for Parkinson Disease]

). Levodopa should be used at the lowest effective dosage to minimize risk for dyskinesia. Immediate-release formulations of levodopa, which have a rapid peak-dose effect, should be prescribed initially in preference to other formulations.

After a few years of levodopa treatment, as many as 50% of patients may develop motor fluctuations, including the following:

  • “Wearing-off” phenomenon (loss of the beneficial effect of the medication before the next dose is administered)
  • “Sudden off” state (unrelated to timing of the medication)
  • “Early morning off” state

The newer extended-release formulations may offer more sustained symptom control throughout the day, which can reduce wearing off between doses. Wearing off also can be lessened by frequent dosing of levodopa and by adding long-acting dopamine agonists, catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitors, monoamine oxidase B inhibitors, or the adenosine receptor antagonist istradefylline. Apomorphine injections are the mainstay of treatment for sudden off episodes, with sublingual apomorphine or inhaled levodopa as alternatives.

Levodopa-induced dyskinesias may also emerge as a result of dopamine receptor hypersensitization and manifest as involuntary choreiform movements during peak doses of levodopa. Amantadine can be added to the treatment regimen to treat dyskinesia.

Anticholinergic medications can also be added for additional benefit in patients with prominent tremor or dystonia but should be avoided in older patients and patients with dementia. Rasagiline, modafinil, and doxepin may help with fatigue in Parkinson disease, although the level of evidence is weak.

Medication-induced psychosis, especially visual hallucinations, can occur with use of dopaminergic medications. Uncontrolled psychosis is a major risk factor for nursing home placement and contributes to increased mortality in Parkinson disease. Treatment strategies include addressing any systemic trigger and simplifying the medication regimen (e.g., by removing non-levodopa medications or decreasing the levodopa dosage). Although generally contraindicated, antipsychotic agents may be required in patients with refractory symptoms. Pimavanserin, a selective serotonin 5-HT2a receptor inverse agonist, is the only FDA-approved medication for Parkinson psychosis; quetiapine and clozapine are often used as less expensive, albeit off-label, options.

Patients with Parkinson disease who maintain a clear response to levodopa are candidates for device-assisted therapies when motor fluctuations or dyskinesia causes disability or when quality of life decreases despite optimal oral levodopa and adjunctive therapies. Device-assisted therapies include deep brain stimulation (DBS), continuous levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) infusion, continuous subcutaneous levodopa infusion (CSLI), and continuous subcutaneous apomorphine infusion (CSAI) (

). LCIG, CSLI, and CSAI are usually reserved for patients who have frequent motor fluctuations, including those who are not good candidates for DBS because of cognitive issues. DBS, but not LCIG, CSLI, or CSAI, can also be used to treat levodopa-refractory tremor. MRI-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy is an ablative method that can be used as an alternative treatment for refractory tremor. Patients who are candidates for device-assisted therapies should be referred to a specialized center for evaluation by a multidisciplinary team.

Parkinson-plus syndromes typically present with a combination of parkinsonism and additional features that are atypical for idiopathic Parkinson disease (see [Table: Table: Red Flags for Atypical Forms of Parkinsonism]

). These conditions often progress more rapidly than Parkinson disease and are refractory to standard therapies, particularly levodopa. The primary syndromes include progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy, and corticobasal degeneration ( [Table: Table: Parkinson-Plus Syndromes]

). Each of these primary syndromes is associated with specific findings on neuroimaging, such as midbrain atrophy in progressive supranuclear palsy (

).

Several drugs, especially dopamine receptor–blocking antipsychotic agents and antiemetic medications (e.g., metoclopramide), can cause parkinsonism ( [Table: Table: Medications Causing Drug-Induced Parkinsonism]

). Drug-induced parkinsonism is symmetric, lacks nonmotor features, and is reversible after removal of the causative agent. In 10% of patients, parkinsonism persists more than 6 months after the agent is removed, which represents the unmasking of a preclinical neurodegenerative disease.

Dopamine receptor blockers can also cause several other extrapyramidal complications ( [Table: Table: Extrapyramidal Complications of Dopamine Receptor Blockers]

).

Tremor is an involuntary, rhythmic, oscillatory movement of a body part that is classified by its presence at rest or with action ( [Table: Table: Classification of Tremors]

). Many persons have an asymptomatic, barely perceptible physiologic tremor. A tremor becomes a disorder when it impairs a person’s function.

Essential tremor is the most common movement disorder (Video: Essential Tremor). It is defined as an isolated tremor syndrome of at least 3 years’ duration characterized by bilateral action tremor in the upper extremities. It can also involve the voice, head, or legs. It should be differentiated from an enhanced physiologic tremor, which is a normal physiologic tremor whose amplitude has been increased by physical or psychological stress, medications, caffeine, or thyrotoxicosis.

Common features of essential tremor include the following:

  • Positive family history (50% of patients)
  • Slow progression
  • Onset in adolescence or middle age

The tremor may be alleviated by alcohol and may be aggravated by stress, illness, fatigue, or stimulant use. A few affected patients experience substantial progression, leading to marked disability. Essential tremor with mild additional neurologic signs, such as mild ataxia or isolated additional tremor at rest without bradykinesia, is classified as essential tremor plus.

Assessment of any form of action tremor, including suspected essential tremor, should include thyroid and kidney function studies, liver chemistries, measurement of serum electrolytes, and a review of medications ( [Table: Table: Medications Causing Drug-Induced Action Tremor]

). Patients younger than 40 years, especially those with a progressive coarse tremor, parkinsonism, dystonia, or psychiatric or liver disease, should undergo screening for Wilson disease with serum ceruloplasmin and 24-hour urine copper measurements. Slit-lamp ophthalmologic examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings (

) should also be considered. Other rare causes of action tremor include dystonic tremor, rubral tremor, and orthostatic tremor (see [Table: Table: Classification of Tremors]

).

Treatment of essential tremor is based on symptoms. Weighted utensils and wrist weights can help reduce tremor amplitude when eating. The most effective pharmacologic treatments are propranolol, primidone, and topiramate. The use of primidone may be limited by drug-drug interactions. Additional second-line options include atenolol, sotalol, clonazepam, alprazolam, gabapentin, and nimodipine. Botulinum toxin injection can help with some medication-refractory tremors, especially those involving the neck and voice, but its benefit for limb tremor is limited by local weakness. Other medication-refractory tremors can be effectively treated by targeting the ventral intermediate nucleus of the thalamus with DBS (unilaterally or bilaterally) or focused ultrasound thalamotomy (unilaterally).

Dystonia involves sustained or intermittent muscle contractions leading to repetitive twisting and posturing movements of specific body parts. Dystonia is distinguished from chorea by the nonrandom and directional pulling nature of its movements and from myoclonus by its slower speed. The dystonias are characterized by cause ( [Table: Table: Causes of Dystonia]

) and clinical characteristics, especially pattern of involvement. Generalized dystonias involve multiple body parts, always including the trunk, whereas focal and segmental dystonias have a more restricted distribution and usually spare the lower extremities. Hemidystonia is limited to one side of the body.

Generalized dystonias often start at a young age (<25 years) and have inherited, metabolic, or vascular causes. The most common type of generalized dystonia involves a variant in the torsin family 1 member A gene (TOR1A). Patients with primary generalized dystonia should be challenged by a short trial of levodopa to test for dopa-responsive dystonia, a rare but treatable cause of generalized dystonia. Young adults with progressive dystonia should be tested for Wilson disease, especially in the presence of other associated findings (such as tremor and parkinsonism) (see Essential Tremor and Other Tremors in Neurology). Anticholinergic agents are recommended for generalized dystonia; globus pallidus interna DBS can be used in severe or refractory disease.

Focal adult-onset dystonias are often sporadic and include cervical dystonia (spasmodic torticollis), eyelid dystonia (blepharospasm), vocal cord spasmodic dysphonia, and task-specific hand dystonia (writer’s cramp). Cervical dystonia often involves involuntary deviation of the head from the midline, an irregular head tremor that lessens with positional changes (null point), and transient improvement of movements by specific sensory tricks (such as gently touching the face with the hand). For focal or segmental dystonia, botulinum toxin injections can be helpful but must be guided by electromyography and administered by trained individuals because of the risk for weakness.

Chorea manifests as random, nonrepetitive, flowing dance-like movements (Video: Choreoathetosis) and can have various causes ( [Table: Table: Causes of Chorea]

).

Patients with acute and subacute onset of chorea should be assessed for potentially reversible acquired causes such as autoimmune, toxic, or metabolic causes, whereas a more insidious onset is typical of neurodegenerative disorders. The most common neurodegenerative cause of generalized chorea is Huntington disease, an autosomal dominant condition marked by symptoms of progressive parkinsonism, gait impairment, impulsiveness, psychiatric disease, dementia, and premature death. Parkinsonism presents early in patients with juvenile Huntington disease (Westphal variant) or in the terminal stages of adult-onset Huntington disease. MRI often shows caudate atrophy (

).

Symptomatic treatments of chorea include the dopamine depleters valbenazine, deutetrabenazine, and tetrabenazine; antipsychotic agents; clonazepam; and antiseizure drugs.

Myoclonus is a fast, shock-like, jerky movement that can be physiologic (e.g., hypnic jerks at sleep onset) or pathologic (caused by medications, toxins, or systemic or central disease) ( [Table: Table: Causes of Acquired Myoclonus]

). Myoclonus can originate from various parts of the nervous system, including the cortex, subcortical structures, spine, or peripheral nerves. Cortical myoclonus is often epileptic. Negative myoclonus is caused by sudden loss of muscle tone, as seen in asterixis with kidney or liver failure, and in the legs after a prolonged hypoxic episode (Lance-Adams syndrome). Myoclonus management includes addressing the underlying systemic or toxic causes and administering antimyoclonic agents, such as clonazepam, levetiracetam, or valproic acid.

Tics are stereotyped, rapid movements interrupting the flow of normal movements. They may provide transient relief from premonitory uncomfortable sensations and are at least partially suppressible. Tics usually start during childhood and subside during adulthood, but they may persist in some patients. Waxing and waning of tics over time is common.

Tourette syndrome is characterized by childhood-onset motor and phonic tics with a duration of at least 1 year. Phonic tics include vocalizations and, less commonly, echolalia (repeating others’ words) and coprolalia (uttering obscenities). Tic severity may range from minimal to very disruptive. Common comorbidities include attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and mood disorders. Diagnosis is clinical.

Treatment options include reassurance (in mild disease), cognitive behavioral therapy, and addressing psychiatric comorbidities. Anti-tic medications are indicated when tics interfere with daily functioning, education, or work. First-line treatments include aripiprazole, clonidine, guanfacine, topiramate, levetiracetam, and tetrabenazine. Aripiprazole is the preferred agent in severe cases. In refractory disease, other antipsychotic agents (risperidone or pimozide), cannabis-based agents, injections with botulinum toxin (for isolated or simple motor tics), and DBS therapy may be considered.

Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a common movement disorder characterized by an urge to move the legs. Patients report an uncomfortable sensation that is worse at rest and at night and is transiently relieved by movement. RLS can interfere with falling or staying asleep.

Patients with RLS should be screened for iron deficiency because iron supplementation in the presence of low-normal ferritin levels (15-75 ng/mL [15-75 μg/L]) may resolve the symptoms. Supplementation with intravenous ferric carboxymaltose is also likely efficacious in idiopathic RLS without a low ferritin level, whereas efficacy of oral iron supplementation in this situation remains unproven.

Nonpharmacologic management includes improving sleep hygiene; exercising; and avoiding caffeine, alcohol, and antihistaminergic, serotonergic, and antidopaminergic drugs. Use of a peroneal nerve vibrational device may be helpful. First-line pharmacologic treatments include gabapentin, gabapentin enacarbil, and pregabalin. Guidelines recommend against the routine use of levodopa and the dopamine agonists pramipexole, ropinirole, and rotigotine, but these medications may be useful in patients placing a high value on symptom relief with short-term use at the expense of adverse effects with longer-term use. Guidelines also state that clonazepam, valproate, carbamazepine, and bupropion have no role in RLS treatment.

In refractory RLS, opioids (such as prolonged-release oxycodone) may be useful. Opioid therapy is typically restricted to patients with severe symptoms recalcitrant to other therapies and should be dispensed in adherence to guidelines for prescribing opioids (see Acute and Chronic Pain in the Outpatient Setting in Common Symptoms).

Periodic limb movements of sleep are brief triple flexion (ankle, knee, hip) movements of the legs that repeat in 20-second cycles during sleep. This disorder is very common and can occur independently of or in association with RLS, sleep-disordered breathing, or narcolepsy. It is diagnosed by using polysomnography. Treatment is required only if the disorder causes marked sleep fragmentation. Options for therapy include RLS drugs as well as melatonin and clonazepam.

REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is caused by loss of normal atonia (paralysis) during the REM phase of sleep, leading to dream-enactment behavior. Patients with this condition tend to shout, kick, punch, and jump while dreaming. History is often obtained from a bed partner because patients do not recall their dream-enactment behavior. Polysomnography can confirm the diagnosis. The differential diagnosis includes nocturnal epilepsy and non-REM parasomnias. Isolated RBD has a high predictive value as a specific and early marker of future development of synuclein-related neurodegeneration, such as Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, or dementia with Lewy bodies. Patients with RBD would be potential candidates for future disease-modifying interventions to prevent these disorders. RBD responds well to melatonin and clonazepam.

Whereas REM sleep disorder behavior events tend to last for seconds and occur with the patient’s eyes closed, non-REM complex behaviors, such as sleepwalking, tend to last up to several minutes and occur with the patient’s eyes open. Patients typically do not recall the event. Factors predisposing to non-REM complex sleep behaviors include poor sleep quality, medications such as sedative-hypnotics, and fever (see Evaluation of Insomnia in Common Symptoms).

Tardive dyskinesia is an extrapyramidal complication of dopamine receptor–blocking medications (see [Table: Table: Extrapyramidal Complications of Dopamine Receptor Blockers]

). It is associated with characteristic choreiform and dystonic craniofacial movements, which often involve other body parts, such as the neck and trunk. Other movements, such as tremor, myoclonus, and akathisia (restlessness), can be part of a tardive syndrome.

Removing the offending medication is the first step in treatment. Symptoms of dyskinesia, however, can be permanent or take months to resolve. Longer duration and higher doses of the causative medication, older age, and female sex increase the risk for irreversibility. The risk is highest with typical antipsychotic agents, but many atypical antipsychotic and antiemetic agents can also cause tardive dyskinesia. All patients receiving these agents must be warned about the risk for this complication.

If symptoms persist after removing the offending agent, treatment options include the monoamine depleters valbenazine, deutetrabenazine, and tetrabenazine. Other options are amantadine, clonazepam, ginkgo biloba, levetiracetam, and, in refractory disease, DBS.

Functional movement disorders are a form of functional neurologic disorder (also known as conversion disorder; see Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders in Interdisciplinary Medicine) in which patients experience movement disorders that are bizarre, variable, distractible, and incongruous with organic movement disorders. Examples include tremor with variable frequency and amplitude, fixed dystonia, and an acrobatic, uneconomic gait. Like other functional disorders, acute onset, episodic course, and exacerbation with stress are common features.

Management includes education, stress management, and cognitive behavioral therapy.

Cerebellar ataxia is a syndrome characterized by incoordination and imbalance and is caused by dysfunction of the cerebellum and its connecting pathways. Common features include nystagmus, dysarthria, dysrhythmia, and an ataxic gait, which is characterized by a wide base, frequent truncal swaying and veering, and impaired tandem walking in a straight line (Video: Ataxic Gait). The differential diagnosis is broad and includes acute (ischemic, demyelinating, and infectious), subacute (autoimmune, paraneoplastic, and nutritional), and chronic (hereditary, alcohol-related, and idiopathic) causes. Spinocerebellar ataxias are a group of hereditary disorders associated with slowly progressive ataxia, neuropathy, and pyramidal signs.

The evaluation for subacute ataxia includes the following:

  • Brain MRI
  • Anti–tissue transglutaminase, Lyme, and paraneoplastic antibody testing
  • Serum vitamin B~1, vitamin B~12, and vitamin E measurement
  • Systemic malignancy testing
  • Rapid plasma reagin testing
  • HIV testing

Management is based on addressing the underlying cause, if identified, and supportive and rehabilitative therapies.
