Multiple Sclerosis

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disorder of the central nervous system (CNS) that causes inflammatory damage to the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerves. Most of the overt clinical symptoms of MS are caused by functional interruption of critical axonal pathways by inflammatory lesions.

The most common clinical manifestations of MS are optic neuritis, myelitis, and brainstem/cerebellar syndromes.

Patients with optic neuritis typically have subacute visual deficits in one eye that are occasionally associated with pain with eye movement or flashing lights (photopsia). Formal ophthalmologic examination shows reduced visual acuity, a scotoma or visual field deficit, difficulty with color discrimination (specifically red desaturation), and an afferent pupillary defect (formerly known as Marcus Gunn pupil). Papillitis (flared appearance of the optic disc caused by inflammatory changes) (

) can sometimes be seen, although this finding only occurs with involvement of the nerve head. Optic disc pallor is usually seen as a late consequence of optic neuritis and is secondary to atrophy of the optic nerve (

).

Spinal cord involvement, or transverse myelitis, results in sensory or motor symptoms below the affected spinal level. Unlike other spinal cord processes, MS generally causes a partial myelitis, and symptoms of full-cord transection are rare; crossed sensory-motor symptoms may also occur (as in partial Brown-Séquard syndrome). During acute inflammation, some patients experience a tight, band-like sensation around the body involving the affected spinal level (“MS hug”). Lhermitte sign manifests as a shock-like sensation radiating down the spine or limbs with flexion of the neck. Urinary frequency, urgency, hesitancy, or retention may also be seen. Neurologic examination generally reveals focal weakness or reduced sensation below a specific spinal dermatome. Muscle tone may be reduced acutely, whereas spasticity and hyperreflexia often are delayed findings.

Brainstem syndromes often involve pathways for eye movement and result in diplopia. Examination may reveal dysconjugate eye movements, nystagmus, or internuclear ophthalmoplegia (inability to adduct one eye and nystagmus in the abducting eye [Video: Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia]). Disruption of vestibular or cerebellar pathways may result in ataxia and/or vertigo. Neurologic examination reveals appendicular or truncal ataxia, dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing, difficulty with rapid alternating movements, and impaired tandem gait (see Video: Ataxic Gait).

An MS relapse is defined as new or worsening neurologic symptoms lasting more than 24 hours. Symptoms develop over the course of hours to days and often peak in severity over the course of days to weeks. This is typically followed by a period of remission lasting weeks to months. Remyelination and recruitment of other brain regions to substitute functionally for the damaged area may result in clinical improvement during remission, but many patients do not return to their previous baseline.

Relapses must be differentiated from pseudorelapses, which are transient exacerbations of previous neurologic symptoms and signs caused by temporary reduction in neuronal electrical conductance by systemic factors rather than by new inflammatory lesions. Common causes of pseudorelapse include infection (usually urinary or upper respiratory tract), stress, and the Uhthoff phenomenon (worsening symptoms due to increased body temperature from external factors, such as a hot shower or high temperatures, or internal factors, such as fever or exercise). Managing pseudorelapse triggers can help avoid inappropriate changes in disease-modifying therapy or initiation of unnecessary glucocorticoids.

Most patients with MS also develop subtle, chronic symptoms due to more widespread cortical demyelination and nonlesional axonal pathology. At least 50% of patients with MS experience cognitive deficits, typically in the domains of short-term memory, visuospatial function, and processing speed. Many patients with MS also report fatigue, which can manifest as a feeling of exhaustion despite adequate sleep, a feeling of brain fog, and easy physical fatigability.

The McDonald criteria ( [Table: Table: Multiple Sclerosis Diagnostic Criteria]

) integrate symptoms of CNS demyelination resulting from a series of clinical relapses or progression and separated in space and time, physical examination findings, distribution of lesions on MRI, and (if necessary) the presence of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-unique oligoclonal bands and elevated kappa free light chains.

The McDonald criteria were revised in 2024 to include new guidance on diagnostic markers that have been shown to be accurate in MS diagnosis. These new markers include the central vein sign (a small-diameter hypointense mark running through the lesion), paramagnetic rim lesions, and elevated CSF kappa free light chains. The 2024 McDonald criteria revisions also include guidance on diagnosing MS in persons older than 50 years because they are at higher risk for misdiagnosis because of nonspecific T2-intense lesions on MRI (especially in the setting of vascular risk factors such as diabetes mellitus, smoking, or hypertension). In this population, the presence of contrast-enhancing lesions, spinal cord lesions, CSF positivity, or CVS-positive lesions can help differentiate demyelinating from vascular lesions.

Properly applying the diagnostic criteria can prevent unnecessary neurologic testing, referrals, and misdiagnoses.

A standardized brain MRI protocol should be used to evaluate possible MS. Spinal cord imaging also should be performed in patients with symptoms of myelitis, insufficient features on a brain MRI to support the diagnosis, or an age older than 40 years and nonspecific brain MRI findings. Strict adherence to the McDonald MRI criteria for MS-specific lesions is critical because many other disorders (migraine, head trauma, and cerebrovascular disease) can cause brain (but not spinal) lesions on MRI.

shows examples of periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, and spinal lesions that are characteristic of MS. The 2024 McDonald criteria revisions also include the optic nerve as a fifth topology or affected area; therefore, a lesion in the optic nerve can be used as evidence of MS.

Ancillary testing can show objective clinical evidence of a demyelinating lesion. Demyelinating lesions of the optic nerve can be electrophysiologically confirmed with visual evoked potentials. Optical coherence tomography, which uses near-infrared light to quantify the thickness of the retinal nerve fiber layer and macula, can also confirm optic nerve damage in acute or previous optic neuritis. Conductance delay in brainstem auditory evoked potentials and somatosensory evoked potentials can act as surrogate markers of demyelination in brainstem and spinal cord pathways. Despite the usefulness of such testing for determining anatomic localization, however, MRI is the only objective measure that fulfills the diagnostic criteria.

CSF testing is not required for diagnosing MS but can support the diagnosis when the MRI criteria are not otherwise fully met. The normally functioning blood-brain barrier excludes immunoglobulins from the CSF in healthy persons, which results in a blood-to-CSF IgG ratio of 500:1 or greater. Disruption of the blood-brain barrier or intrathecal production of IgG may result in oligoclonal bands, reflecting elevated oligoclonal immunoglobulin concentrations in the CSF. Oligoclonal bands present in the CSF that are absent in the serum occur in 85% to 90% of persons with MS. An elevated IgG CSF-to-blood index and an elevated CSF IgG synthesis rate may also be seen. Additionally, nonspecific mild elevations in the CSF leukocyte count or protein level are sometimes seen. The 2024 McDonald criteria added the kappa free light chain index as a second CSF biomarker that fulfills criteria for dissemination in time. Concordance between the kappa free light chain index and oligoclonal bands is approximately 87%.

Various demyelinating and systemic inflammatory diseases; metabolic, infectious, vascular, neoplastic, and paraneoplastic disorders; and headache syndromes may mimic the clinical signs and symptoms or radiologic changes of MS and should be considered in the differential diagnosis when evaluating a patient with possible MS ( [Table: Table: Differential Diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis]

).

Patients with MS can present and/or progress through four clinical phenotypes defined below and in

.

Approximately 85% of patients with MS experience an initial relapsing-remitting course. Patients with a first demyelinating event that does not meet the definition of clinically definite MS are said to have a clinically isolated syndrome (CIS). Two common forms of CIS are optic neuritis and transverse myelitis.

Disease-modifying therapies reduce the risk for conversion from a CIS to relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS) by approximately 50%, and stratification of risk for conversion can inform treatment decisions. Patients with brain lesions on MRI at the time of their CIS have a 10-year risk for conversion to RRMS of approximately 90%, whereas patients without brain lesions have a much lower risk (10%-20%).

Determining activity status and progression also informs treatment decisions in RRMS (see

). In the first few years of the disease course, significant or complete recovery from relapse is common. Eventually, postrelapse recovery generally diminishes, and permanent disability accumulates. Without treatment, half of patients with RRMS develop secondary progressive MS (SPMS) after a median of 10 to 15 years. In SPMS, relapses become infrequent or cease completely, but slowly progressive neurologic disability continues to accrue in multiple domains. Data now suggest that using disease-modifying therapies can decrease the chance of conversion to SPMS.

Approximately 15% of patients with MS have primary progressive MS (PPMS) at presentation. This phenotype often develops later in life (in the fifth or sixth decade) compared with the younger age of onset (third or fourth decade of life) in typical RRMS.

Patients with a radiologically isolated syndrome have no clinical symptoms of MS but have incidental MRI findings that meet the radiologic criteria for MS. Although an MS diagnosis cannot be made without demyelinating signs and symptoms, patients with a radiologically isolated syndrome are at high risk for later conversion to clinically definite MS and should be monitored with annual MRI.

Although some patients with MS may avoid physical activity because of disability, fatigue, and the Uhthoff phenomenon, repeated studies have shown multiple benefits from both strengthening and aerobic exercise programs. Patients with significant Uhthoff phenomenon induced by exercise should be reassured that neurologic injury will not result from exercise; they can also be counseled on strategies to minimize discomfort, such as heat avoidance or external cooling (cold water, fans, body-cooling devices) during exercise.

Exercise can also help preserve bone health. Patients with MS have a three- to sixfold increased risk for reduced bone mineral density, most likely from a combination of reduced physical activity, repeated use of glucocorticoids, and vitamin D deficiency.

Vitamin D deficiency is common in patients with MS, and reduced serum levels of vitamin D are predictive of MS development and future accumulation of lesions on MRI. The role of vitamin D supplementation is controversial. Some studies have shown a benefit of this vitamin in reducing symptoms of fatigue and MRI activity compared with placebo. However, reductions in relapses or disability progression have not been shown, and meta-analyses suggest that the current evidence is insufficient to suggest a protective role for vitamin D supplementation in MS.

Measures to prevent infection are necessary for patients receiving more aggressive, immunosuppressive MS treatments, especially given the increased risk for MS relapse during a systemic infection. Current MS treatment guidelines recommend maintaining standard immunizations, annual vaccination against influenza (with inactivated vaccine), and COVID-19 immunization. Immunizations should be withheld during MS relapses. All live vaccines are contraindicated in patients receiving immunosuppressive or immunomodulating therapies.

Patients with MS-related bladder dysfunction are at elevated risk for recurrent urinary tract infections; thus, strategies to reduce the frequency of bladder infections are necessary.

Facilitating smoking cessation for all patients with MS should be a priority because cigarette smoking results in a threefold increased risk for conversion from RRMS to SPMS and faster rates of disability accumulation.

Many patients with MS are women in their childbearing years. The estrogenic state of pregnancy has an immunomodulatory effect that tends to reduce MS disease activity during pregnancy, often precluding the need for treatment during this period. Although the risk for relapse increases slightly in the first 3 months postpartum, this does not seem to contribute negatively to prognosis; multiple studies have shown that pregnancy does not result in additional permanent disability and that multiparous patients have better long-term MS outcomes than nulliparous or uniparous patients. See [Table: Table: Disease-Modifying Therapies for Multiple Sclerosis]

for recommendations on treating MS in patients who are pregnant or planning pregnancy. Data on the effect of breastfeeding on MS relapse risk are mixed, with some studies showing a protective effect from exclusive breastfeeding.

Symptoms lasting less than 24 hours should not be considered or treated as a relapse. The possibility of a pseudorelapse should always be considered before initiating treatment or changing disease-modifying therapy; suspicion of this condition should trigger clinical investigation for an underlying cause. The subsequent treatment of any infection or metabolic disturbance often results in improvement in neurologic symptoms; reassurance and counseling are appropriate to manage stress or Uhthoff phenomenon.

The standard treatment for MS relapses is high-dose glucocorticoids, typically intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/d for 3 to 5 days). Multiple trials have shown that bioequivalent dosages of oral glucocorticoids (such as prednisone, 1250 mg/d for 3 to 7 days, with or without taper) are equally effective and well tolerated, with reduced cost.

Adverse effects of high-dose glucocorticoids include insomnia, hyperglycemia, metallic taste, gastritis, fluid retention, irritability, and (rarely) psychosis. These effects are typically short lived, given the brief treatment duration. Frequent or prolonged glucocorticoid treatment should be avoided to minimize the risks for osteopenia and early cataracts.

Patients not benefiting from glucocorticoid treatment may respond to plasmapheresis, administered as five to seven exchanges performed every other day. Intravenous immune globulin has not been shown to be effective for acute relapse treatment.

Preventing MS relapse is vital. Various immunomodulatory or immunosuppressive medications reduce the risk for relapse, disability progression, and new MRI lesion formation; disease-modifying therapies may also reduce mortality and prevent conversion to SPMS.

Many choices of disease-modifying therapy ( [Table: Table: Disease-Modifying Therapies for Multiple Sclerosis]

), with differing routes of administration, mechanisms of action, and potential adverse effects, exist for patients with RRMS.

All of the disease-modifying therapies are now also approved for CIS and active SPMS (see

for definitions of the four phenotypes of MS activity), but no medications have proven efficacy in patients with inactive SPMS. Guidelines suggest stopping disease-modifying therapy in patients with SPMS who have had no new MRI lesions and have been nonambulatory for 2 consecutive years. Ocrelizumab is the only FDA-approved therapy for PPMS.

Whereas traditional treatment paradigms recommended an escalation approach, starting with lower-efficacy and lower-risk therapies, more recent evidence shows that early high-efficacy therapies significantly reduce disability in the long term ( [Table: Table: Relative Efficacy of Disease-Modifying Therapies in RRMS]

). For this reason, patients are no longer initially started on injectables like interferons or glatiramer acetate but are instead offered moderate- to high-efficacy therapies. High-efficacy therapies include ocrelizumab and ofatumumab, which are well-tolerated, with the most common adverse events being infusion or injection reactions. Other highly effective monoclonal antibodies, natalizumab and alemtuzumab, are typically limited to use as second-line agents because of the risk for serious reactions, such as progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and secondary autoimmunity and cytopenia, respectively. For this reason, use of natalizumab and alemtuzumab requires participation in a mandatory monitoring program for risk mitigation. Comorbidities, patient tolerability, risk stratification, and disease activity should be considered when choosing a disease-modifying therapy.

Once patients begin to take a disease-modifying therapy, monitoring for treatment breakthrough (relapses, disability progression, MRI activity) and adverse effects should continue at least annually, and a treatment change should be considered if any such events occur.

Ocrelizumab, ublituximab, and ofatumumab are monoclonal antibodies against the CD20 antigen that cause lysis of circulating B cells. Ocrelizumab is the first medication to show benefit for both patients with RRMS (reductions in relapse rates, MRI disease burden, and disability accumulation) and those with PPMS (reduced chance of disability progression). Safety concerns for these therapies include allergic infusion reactions (for ocrelizumab), injection-related reactions (for ofatumumab), and increased risk for treatment-related infections.

Natalizumab is a monoclonal antibody targeting a cellular adhesion molecule on activated T cells that is required for transmigration into the CNS. Treatment with this medication is highly effective, resulting in a two-thirds reduction in relapse rates, slowing of disability progression by approximately 40%, and a reduction in MRI activity of approximately 90% compared with placebo. Despite this high efficacy, natalizumab is typically limited to use as a second-line agent because of the risk for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), a CNS demyelinating infection caused by reactivation of the JC virus. Treatment duration, JC virus seropositivity, and previous chemotherapy or immunosuppressive exposure increase the risk for PML. PML is uncommon in time-limited treatment in patients without other risk factors. PML presents as mental status changes, ataxia, weakness, and visual changes. If PML is suspected, natalizumab should be immediately discontinued, and brain MRI and polymerase chain reaction testing of the CSF for JC virus should be obtained.

Alemtuzumab is an anti-CD52 monoclonal antibody that causes complement-mediated lysis of circulating lymphocytes. It reduces relapse rates and disability progression by approximately half and reduces new lesions and brain atrophy on MRI compared with interferon beta. Despite high efficacy, use of this drug is limited because of substantial safety concerns, including infection, secondary autoimmunity (e.g., thyroid disease, immune thrombocytopenia, glomerulonephritis), and cytopenia (especially lymphopenia) (see [Table: Table: Disease-Modifying Therapies for Multiple Sclerosis]

). The use of alemtuzumab requires intensive safety monitoring and potential prophylaxis.

Interferon beta (available as interferon beta-1a and interferon beta-1b) is an immunomodulatory cytokine treatment that shifts immune responses away from autoimmunity and increases the integrity of the blood-brain barrier. It reduces relapse rates by approximately one third, compared with placebo, and has positive effects on disability progression and MRI findings. Head-to-head studies show general equivalence of the formulations, although those requiring frequent injections have slightly higher efficacy in some studies. Interferon beta may exacerbate depression; care should be taken when administering it to patients with a history of psychiatric disease.

Glatiramer acetate exerts its immunomodulatory effect by modifying the nonbinding sites of major histocompatibility complex molecules. Structurally similar to myelin basic protein, it may also work through molecular mimicry. Reduction in relapse rates with glatiramer acetate is similar to that with the interferon beta formulations.

The sphingosine-1-phosphate medications (fingolimod, ozanimod, siponimod, and ponesimod) are oral agents that result in sequestration of activated lymphocytes within lymph nodes. These drugs are effective treatments for RRMS, reducing relapse rates, the risk for disability progression, and the development of new MRI lesions. Intensive screening and monitoring are necessary with these medications because of rare adverse effects, including infection and heart block.

The fumaric acid esters (dimethyl fumarate, diroximel fumarate, and monomethyl fumarate) are oral agents that activate the nuclear factor (erythroid-derived 2)-like 2 transcriptional pathway and result in immunomodulation. Dimethyl fumarate reduces relapse rates by slightly less than half and reduces the risk for disability progression and MRI lesion development. Diroximel fumarate, a prodrug that is rapidly converted into dimethyl fumarate, is an alternative, as is monomethyl fumarate. Infectious risks of these drugs correlate with prolonged lymphopenia; frequent blood-count monitoring is required.

Teriflunomide is an oral medication that inhibits a mitochondrial enzyme involved in pyrimidine synthesis in rapidly dividing cells. This drug reduces relapse rates by a third compared with placebo and reduces the risk for disability progression and new MRI lesion development. Dual-method contraception is recommended with teriflunomide because of its teratogenic effects.

Cladribine is an oral purine antimetabolite with a unique dosing strategy (administered in two brief courses over 2 years) that markedly reduces relapse rates and disability progression in patients with RRMS and SPMS with activity. Because of safety concerns (such as malignancy, infection, and hepatotoxicity), it is generally recommended for patients who have had inadequate response to, or are unable to tolerate, alternative treatments.

Mitoxantrone is no longer used because of cardiac toxicity and treatment-related leukemia.

Despite the use of disease-modifying therapies, many patients experience chronic and intermittent neurologic symptoms. Properly managing these symptoms with pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic approaches can increase the quality of life in patients with MS ( [Table: Table: Treatment of Symptoms Related to Multiple Sclerosis]

).

Disorders of the Spinal Cord

Myelopathy (disease of the spinal cord) arises from extrinsic (external compression) and intrinsic (intramedullary) pathologies, such as infection and inflammatory, metabolic, vascular, and genetic conditions. Given the vital anatomy contained in this small-diameter structure, spinal cord injury must be recognized and treated promptly. Rapidly determining the location and cause of dysfunction is crucial to inform decisions about the best neuroimaging methods and treatment options, including the possible need for surgical intervention.

Spinal cord disorders often present with neck or back pain with weakness and sensory changes at or below the level of injury as well as bladder or bowel dysfunction. Squeezing or banding sensations around the chest or abdomen may be reported.

Corticospinal tract injury results in spastic paresis or paralysis, with weakness, hyperreflexia, muscle spasticity, and extensor plantar responses (Video: Extensor Plantar Response). Sensation is often lost at or below the injury site. Involvement of the distal spinal cord and lower roots (cauda equina syndrome) results in decreased lower-extremity muscle tone, areflexia, and loss of perianal sensation. Disruptions in bowel and bladder function and loss of sphincter tone are often noted. Many patients with myelopathy, especially those with chronic disease, also present with an abnormal gait, such as sensory ataxia (see Video: Ataxic Gait), or spasticity.

Compressive myelopathy may be secondary to spinal epidural hematoma, metastatic cancer, spinal epidural abscess, or spinal structural causes, such as disk herniation and spinal stenosis. Specific signs and symptoms can provide clues as to the cause of compression ( [Table: Table: Causes of Compressive Myelopathy]

):

  • Fever with focal back pain and tenderness, especially in patients with recent back instrumentation, a history of intravenous drug use, or bacteremia, may indicate an epidural abscess (see Spinal Epidural Abscess in Infectious Disease for more information on spinal epidural abscesses).
  • A history of neoplasia should raise concern for metastatic disease with possible cord compression (

) or pathologic vertebral fracture. - Anticoagulant use raises the risk for compression from an epidural hematoma, particularly in the setting of recent back instrumentation.

In contrast, acute disk herniation and trauma may cause rapid onset of myelopathic findings in the absence of underlying disease.

Patients with chronic spinal stenosis due to osteoarthritic degenerative spinal disease frequently present with chronic myelopathic symptoms. Degenerative spinal disease often affects the cervical and lumbar regions, but thoracic cord involvement is rare. Most patients report progressive leg weakness, spasticity, distal numbness, and bladder impairment. Compressive myelopathy should thus be considered in older patients with gait dysfunction or weakness. Some patients with lumbar stenosis also describe symptoms similar to vascular claudication (pseudoclaudication), with exertional groin, thigh, or buttock pain and possibly weakness or numbness. The pain of lumbar stenosis may be relieved by sitting or lying down (especially with back flexion) but typically persists longer than the discomfort caused by vascular claudication.

MRI of the spinal cord is the preferred means of diagnosing compressive myelopathy. Imaging should be performed emergently in cord compression thought to be secondary to abscess or malignancy because neurologic compromise can progress rapidly, and the entire spine (cervical, thoracic, and lumbar) should be imaged because multiple areas may be involved.

CT myelography can show compressive myelopathy when MRI is not feasible but often does not reveal the cause of compression. Additionally, myelography may be difficult to arrange emergently and is problematic in patients with contrast dye allergy or impaired kidney function.

Emergent treatment of cord compression is usually indicated to prevent further neurologic decline, but full neurologic function is rarely regained. Surgical decompression is typically required, but medical therapies can complement surgical treatment.

Adjunctive therapy is tailored to the underlying cause; an epidural hematoma may first require managing the bleeding diathesis, and cord compression caused by epidural abscess requires antibiotics. Glucocorticoids are not indicated with hematoma, abscess, or traumatic spinal cord compression. Although initial trials in acute traumatic spinal injury suggested benefit, later studies and reanalysis of initial trial data have suggested a lack of benefit and potential harm from glucocorticoids. In contrast, spinal cord compression from metastatic disease requires emergent use of high-dose glucocorticoids.

Urgent surgical evaluation is mandatory in most patients with compressive myelopathy. A symptomatic spinal epidural hematoma or abscess usually requires surgical drainage. In patients with metastatic disease, trial evidence suggests that surgical decompression followed by radiotherapy is most beneficial for patients younger than 65 years who have a single area of compression, paraplegia for less than 48 hours, and a predicted survival of greater than 6 months. Spinal instability, however, mandates surgical treatment. Radiotherapy without surgery may be preferred in patients not meeting these criteria or with certain radiosensitive tumor types, such as leukemia, lymphoma, myeloma, and germ cell tumors. For more information on spinal cord compression due to metastatic disease, see Spinal Cord Compression in Oncology.

For chronic cervical or lumbar stenosis or acute disk herniation, symptom management may be sufficient in most patients. Surgical decompression may be required for patients with myelopathy refractory to medical management or significant or progressive neurologic deficits. See Treatment of Neck Pain in Common Symptoms and Treatment of Low Back Pain in Common Symptoms for more information about treating neck and back pain, respectively.

Noncompressive myelopathy can be caused by many types of disorders, including infection and inflammatory, metabolic, vascular, and genetic conditions. Inflammatory causes are most common, including transverse myelitis, multiple sclerosis (see Multiple Sclerosis in Neurology), neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), and sarcoidosis (see Sarcoidosis in Pulmonary Medicine and Sarcoidosis in Rheumatology).

Transverse myelitis (TM) may be idiopathic or associated with a heterogeneous group of demyelinating, infectious or parainfectious, and autoimmune disorders, most prominently multiple sclerosis ( [Table: Table: Inflammatory Causes of Noncompressive Myelopathy]

). Affected patients frequently experience subacute weakness, sensory changes, and bladder or bowel dysfunction. Some patients experience an initial prodrome of back pain or a thoracic banding sensation.

Idiopathic TM (ITM) (

) is a monophasic, inflammatory, and demyelinating disorder of the spinal cord. ITM typically affects only one region of the spinal cord. The diagnostic criteria for ITM require the following:

  • Presence of clinical features of the syndrome
  • Evidence of inflammation (either cerebrospinal fluid leukocytosis or contrast enhancement on spinal cord MRI)
  • Exclusion of other potential causes

Patients with the following characteristics are much more likely to have ITM than other disorders causing secondary TM, such as multiple sclerosis:

  • Complete myelitis (symptoms referable to complete rather than partial cord transection)
  • Lack of elevated oligoclonal bands or IgG index in the cerebrospinal fluid
  • No lesions on brain MRI

The distinction between ITM and other disorders, such as multiple sclerosis, is crucial because ITM is not a recurrent disorder and does not require long-term immunomodulatory therapy. Recurrence of symptoms or new symptoms beyond a 30-day period should raise suspicion for multiple sclerosis or other recurrent disorders.

Infectious causes should always be considered when evaluating patients for possible ITM ( [Table: Table: Infectious Causes of Noncompressive Myelopathy]

). Infections that can affect the spinal cord include the following:

  • Herpes simplex virus
  • Varicella-zoster virus
  • West Nile virus
  • Human T-lymphotropic virus
  • Lyme disease
  • Syphilis

Additionally, HIV infection can cause a TM-like syndrome at the time of seroconversion or result in a chronic degenerative vacuolar myelopathy in patients with chronically low CD4 cell counts. Mycobacterium tuberculosis can also infect the meninges and spinal cord and present with a TM-like syndrome.

The consensus-based treatment of ITM is intravenous methylprednisolone, 1 g/d for 3 to 5 days. Increasingly, patients are also given intravenous immune globulin or plasmapheresis as part of first-line therapy. These therapies are intended to stop inflammatory damage to the spinal cord and allow patients to recover neurologic function. Treatment of secondary TM depends on the underlying cause. The addition of glucocorticoids to treat infectious disorders is controversial but may be indicated when the infections are associated with significant spinal cord edema.

The presence of a longitudinally extensive myelopathy (three or more spinal segments) should raise suspicion for NMOSD, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody–associated disease, or sarcoidosis-associated myelopathy (

). However, all these causes can present with short-segment lesions as well. These diseases usually have other manifestations suggesting the diagnosis, such as optic nerve involvement in NMOSD (see [Table: Table: Inflammatory Causes of Noncompressive Myelopathy]

). A serum central nervous system demyelinating disease evaluation panel can be done for NMOSD and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody–associated disease. Further evaluation of sarcoidosis involves chest radiography or CT to look for hilar lymphadenopathy and sometimes PET to determine areas to biopsy. Nodular leptomeningeal enhancement is suggestive of sarcoidosis.

Severe and prolonged vitamin B~12 deficiency can result in subacute combined degeneration, a dysfunction of the corticospinal and dorsal sensory tracts of the spinal cord that manifests as paresthesias, reduced vibration and position sense, and ataxia; spasticity and paraplegia may occur in severe cases. See [Table: Table: Causes of Subacute Combined Degeneration]

for more information on subacute combined degeneration.

MRI can show increased signal in the affected white-matter pathways without associated inflammatory changes. Laboratory study results reveal a low serum vitamin B~12 level and elevated levels of serum methylmalonic acid and homocysteine. Macrocytic anemia may be present, but the neurologic manifestations of vitamin B~12 deficiency may occur first. The clinical symptoms of vitamin B~12 deficiency can sometimes occur with low-normal vitamin B~12 levels; methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels should be measured in this situation when there is a high index of clinical suspicion for vitamin B~12 deficiency.

Vitamin B~12 replacement usually halts progression of the disease but may not reverse existing symptoms. See Vitamin B~12 Deficiency in Hematology for more information on vitamin B~12 deficiency causes, diagnosis, and treatment. See Short Bowel Syndrome in Gastroenterology and Atrophic Gastritis in Gastroenterology for information on potential gastrointestinal causes of vitamin B~12 deficiency.

Nitrous oxide use also can cause a relative vitamin B~12 deficiency that results in subacute combined degeneration. Supplementing vitamin B~12 in this circumstance without stopping use of the nitrous oxide may impede improvement in symptoms.

Copper deficiency (due to malabsorption, nutritional deficiency, or zinc toxicity) can also cause subacute combined degeneration, usually with accompanying anemia and leukopenia. This entity should be considered in patients with suggestive symptoms who have normal vitamin B~12 levels.

Myelopathy from such nutritional deficiencies should also be considered in patients with previous bariatric surgery.

[Table: Table: Vascular Causes of Noncompressive Myelopathy]

summarizes vascular causes of myelopathy.

Hyperacute onset (<12 hours) of paraplegia or quadriplegia should raise suspicion for spinal cord infarct. Infarcts in the territory of the anterior spinal artery typically present as sudden-onset flaccid paralysis with preserved vibration and position sense because of the lack of dorsal column involvement. Thoracic spine presentations in the setting of aortic dissection or surgery are most common. Prolonged hypotension during cardiovascular procedures or complex neurologic surgery can also sometimes result in infarction from lack of perfusion to watershed regions of the spinal cord.

A stroke code should be activated for patients with concern for spinal cord stroke within 3 hours of symptom onset because thrombolysis may be offered in certain circumstances. Diffusion-weighted spinal cord imaging should be performed, but it may not be positive on the first day of symptoms.

Dural arteriovenous fistulas of the spinal vascular supply can either result in chronic myelopathy due to venous congestion or cause infarction of the cord due to altered vascular dynamics or thromboses. Presentation is typically slow in onset. Fistulas are most common in men older than 50 years and in persons with previous spinal surgery. Careful review of spinal MRI often shows abnormal vascular flow voids. Diagnosis is often challenging and typically requires digital subtraction angiography of all radicular vessels along the entire spine.

Although rare, several genetic disorders can result in chronic myelopathy (see [Table: Table: Genetic Causes of Noncompressive Myelopathy]

). Some of these disorders have clear familial inheritance, but others may result from de novo mutations. Genetic counseling is indicated whenever genetic testing is considered.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia comprises disorders that result in chronic, progressive, and ascending weakness and spasticity, often beginning in childhood or adolescence. Genetic testing is available, but no treatment currently exists.

Female carriers of X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy sometimes develop adrenomyeloneuropathy, a degenerative condition of the spinal cord and peripheral nerves. These patients can be diagnosed through alterations in serum very-long-chain fatty acid profiles or genetic testing.

Neuromuscular Disorders

Neuromuscular disorders include motor neuron diseases, peripheral neuropathies, radiculopathies, ganglionopathies, plexopathies, neuromuscular junction disorders, and myopathies ( [Table: Table: Classification of Neuromuscular Disorders]

,

). Peripheral and central nervous system neuromuscular disorders can be differentiated on the basis of patient history and neurologic examination findings as well as neurophysiological studies, such as electromyography (EMG)/nerve conduction studies (NCSs), and MRI ( [Table: Table: Common Symptoms and Signs of Neuromuscular Disorders]

, [Table: Table: PNS Versus CNS Disorders]

). For additional information on the radiculopathies, see Low Back Pain in Common Symptoms and Neck Pain in Common Symptoms.

Peripheral neuropathies present with motor, sensory, and autonomic symptoms (see [Table: Table: PNS Versus CNS Disorders]

) and are classified on the basis of the distribution of sensorimotor findings (

).

Initial laboratory testing for peripheral neuropathy should include the following:

  • Complete blood count
  • Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
  • Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chain assay
  • Thyroid function tests
  • Hemoglobin A~1c and fasting plasma glucose
  • Vitamin B~12

Additional tests can be ordered to diagnose underlying causes based on typical clinical presentations ( [Table: Table: Clinical Findings and Laboratory Testing in Peripheral Neuropathy]

).

Weakness, asymmetry, proximal findings, a rapid course, or atypical features should prompt EMG/NCSs (Video: Electromyography by Needle Electrode), which can differentiate neuropathy from other neuromuscular disorders. EMG measures electrical activity of motor units and their muscle fibers; NCSs evaluate the electrical properties of peripheral nerves. On EMG, the amplitudes of motor unit potentials are high and prolonged in neuropathy and low and brief in myopathy. The velocity of nerve conduction decreases in demyelinating neuropathy and remains unchanged in axonopathy.

Skin biopsy is frequently required in small fiber neuropathies, in which NCS findings are often normal. Nerve biopsy should be considered only in the rare setting of diagnostic uncertainty in which a vasculitic, infectious, or infiltrative neuropathy is suspected. Autonomic tests, including quantitative sudomotor axon reflex and tilt-table tests, can help confirm autonomic neuropathy but are indicated only in rare cases.

Mononeuropathies involve a single nerve and can cause motor and sensory symptoms in the territory of the affected nerve. Multiple nerves may be involved sequentially in mononeuropathy multiplex, a condition most often associated with pain and caused by vasculitis.

Carpal tunnel syndrome results from focal compression of the median nerve at the wrist. Most often, paresthesia and pain are experienced in the first three digits but may radiate to the entire hand or proximally. With milder symptoms, carpal tunnel syndrome can be diagnosed clinically, and treatment is supportive, including neutral positioning, wrist splints, and pain control. Injected or oral glucocorticoids may also improve symptoms. Weakness, thenar atrophy, refractory pain, or active denervation evident on EMG/NCSs should prompt surgical decompression. See Carpal Tunnel Syndrome in Common Symptoms for further information about carpal tunnel syndrome.

Ulnar mononeuropathy presents with paresthesia and numbness in digits 4 and 5 and, in severe cases, with weakness and atrophy of intrinsic hand muscles. The site of compression is commonly at the medial epicondyle because of frequent leaning on the elbow. Management includes education to avoid pressure on the nerve, elbow splinting, and, in patients with persistent pain, weakness, or active denervation on EMG/NCSs, decompression surgery.

Radial mononeuropathy presents as wrist drop and finger extensor weakness caused by compression of the nerve near the axilla as it crosses the humerus. This is often caused by prolonged immobility in patients who are comatose or intoxicated (“Saturday night palsy”); spontaneous recovery is typical.

Peroneal nerve palsy presents as foot drop and is caused by compression of the nerve at the head of the fibula, usually caused by crossing the legs, immobility, obesity, trauma, or compression of the leg against a bed railing. Patients whose condition does not improve within 3 months should be further assessed by EMG/NCSs and lumbosacral imaging because proximal lesions may mimic peroneal palsy.

Bell palsy is idiopathic paralysis of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) that causes unilateral paralysis of upper and lower facial muscles. In contrast, upper facial muscles are spared in central facial weakness (stroke) because of their bilateral central innervation. Patients with Bell palsy often experience eye closure weakness but not ptosis. Periauricular pain, altered taste, and hyperacusis also may occur. Between 70% and 90% of patients with Bell palsy fully recover within a few weeks.

In classic Bell palsy, brain imaging and laboratory testing are not required. Treatment with a 10-day course of oral prednisone, started within 72 hours of onset, is recommended to expedite the rate and speed of full recovery. The utility of adding antiviral treatment to prednisone is controversial, but patients with severe palsy may experience a small benefit. Antiviral monotherapy should be avoided. Use of an eye patch and artificial tears to prevent corneal dryness is recommended. Synkinesis (concomitant movement of perioral and periorbital muscles) may result from aberrant reinnervation after Bell palsy.

Secondary causes of facial nerve palsy include diabetes mellitus, Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, HIV infection, vasculitis, and malignancy. In endemic areas, testing for Lyme disease should be considered (see Lyme Disease in Infectious Disease). Bilateral facial palsy or involvement of other cranial nerves should raise suspicion for potentially serious pathology. If a secondary cause is suspected on the basis of history (subacute onset over days, comorbidities, rash) or clinical examination (deficits unrelated to the facial nerve, such as weakness in extraocular, masticatory, or lingual muscles), additional testing is indicated, and prednisone is typically avoided. Brain MRI with contrast is recommended in patients with lingering or worsening weakness after 2 months.

Plexopathies are conditions that affect the brachial plexus (convergence of cervical roots forming upper extremity nerves) or the lumbosacral plexus (lumbosacral roots merging to form lower extremity nerves). Presentation often involves motor and sensory deficits in the territory of multiple contiguous nerves or dermatomes. Common causes of plexopathy include diabetes, malignancy, radiation, infection, and trauma. Imaging is mandatory to rule out structural lesions and malignancy.

Idiopathic brachial plexitis (also known as neuralgic amyotrophy) presents with subacute unilateral severe scapular pain followed by pronounced weakness and atrophy in shoulder girdle and upper extremity muscles. It is likely immune mediated and is usually preceded by a triggering event, such as infection or surgery, even if the event is not in the region of the brachial plexus. EMG/NCSs can confirm the diagnosis, and imaging can rule out alternative causes. Treatment is supportive. Gradual recovery (90% by 3 years) is common.

Idiopathic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy is immune mediated and very similar in presentation to diabetic lumbosacral radiculoneuropathy (see Neuropathies of Diabetes Mellitus and Impaired Glucose Tolerance in Neurology).

Polyneuropathies arise from various disorders that injure the peripheral nerves (see [Table: Table: Clinical Findings and Laboratory Testing in Peripheral Neuropathy]

). Polyneuropathies may affect large nerve fibers (leading to impaired proprioception, hyporeflexia, and weakness) or small nerve fibers (causing pain, dysesthesia, and dysautonomia). Additionally, polyneuropathies may be primarily axonal or demyelinating. If axonal, the distal axonal segments are affected first, leading to a length-dependent stocking-glove pattern of involvement. For example, a sensory-predominant distal symmetric axonal neuropathy is typically seen with metabolic, toxic, and systemic neuropathies. Demyelinating neuropathies, which result from injury to the peripheral nerve myelin sheath, can cause non–length-dependent weakness and sensory loss.

Diabetes causes various neuropathies in up to 50% of patients ( [Table: Table: Peripheral Nerve Dysfunction in Diabetes Mellitus]

). The most common presentation is symmetric distal neuropathy involving small and large sensory fibers and, to a much lesser extent, distal motor nerves. Clinical examination may reveal length-dependent loss of light touch, pinprick, and vibration sensations; loss of the ankle reflex; and, in advanced disease, distal weakness. Pain and paresthesia may predominate, especially when small fibers are involved. Patients with a pure small fiber variant of symmetric distal neuropathy may have normal distal sensory and reflex findings on examination and normal EMG/NCS results at presentation; this pattern can be seen even in patients with impaired glucose tolerance. Between 11% and 25% of patients with glucose intolerance have evidence of small fiber neuropathy on specialized testing, but few (5%-10%) are symptomatic.

Autonomic diabetic neuropathy can cause orthostatic hypotension, bladder and erectile dysfunction, abnormal hidrosis, and gastroparesis. Diabetic mononeuropathy can involve the cranial nerves and truncal nerve roots (with a dermatomal pattern in the chest or abdomen) and predispose patients to entrapment neuropathies, such as carpal tunnel syndrome.

Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoneuropathy (also called diabetic amyotrophy) is associated with subacute painful involvement of the proximal lumbosacral plexus, followed by resolution of pain and onset of bilateral but markedly asymmetric weakness with atrophy and unintentional weight loss. Spontaneous recovery over 1 to 3 years is typical but may be incomplete.

In rare cases, patients using insulin for diabetes management may experience treatment-induced neuropathy of diabetes (formerly called insulin neuritis), a self-limiting condition that may lead patients to discontinue insulin therapy.

Treatment is determined by the type of neuropathy present (see [Table: Table: Peripheral Nerve Dysfunction in Diabetes Mellitus]

). See Diabetic Neuropathy in Endocrinology and Metabolism for further information about diabetic neuropathy, including neuropathic pain treatment.

Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute autoimmune demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy that presents with rapidly progressive flaccid weakness. Onset is preceded by a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection in one third of patients, triggering a T-cell autoimmune attack against peripheral nerve and root myelin. Campylobacter jejuni, cytomegalovirus, and SARS-CoV-2 infections are considerations. Weakness is ascending, starting in the lower extremities, spreading to the upper limbs and bulbar and respiratory muscles, and reaching its nadir in less than 4 weeks. The weakness may occur first in the proximal muscles. Paresthesia and early low back pain are common. Dysautonomia can be severe and predispose patients to labile blood pressure and arrhythmias. Progressive respiratory and bulbar weakness may lead to rapid respiratory failure; close monitoring of ventilatory reserve, including vital capacity and negative inspiratory force, is mandatory. On examination, diffuse areflexia is a key finding; sensory loss is not marked, although paresthesia is common. The Miller Fisher variant of GBS presents with ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, and antibodies to GQ1b ganglioside protein.

The differential diagnosis of GBS (with distinguishing features) includes the following:

  • Botulism (descending weakness)
  • Myasthenic crisis (without pain and paresthesia)
  • Acute myelopathies (hyperreflexia and other upper motor neuron signs)
  • West Nile virus infection (asymmetric paralysis, fever, and muscle pain)

Lyme disease, HIV seroconversion, and tick paralysis are also considerations.

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis shows a highly elevated protein level with a normal or mildly elevated leukocyte count (albuminocytologic dissociation) in 90% of patients within 7 days of symptom onset. Early normal CSF does not rule out GBS. EMG/NCSs are the confirmatory tests and show a predominantly demyelinating pattern; sensitivity is initially low but increases to 90% by week 5. Treatment initiation should not await EMG/NCS confirmation; a negative early study should be repeated later if the diagnosis remains suspected. Additional studies, such as spinal MRI and serologic testing for Lyme disease, HIV, SARS-CoV-2, West Nile virus, and myasthenia antibodies, may be considered in appropriate clinical settings.

Therapy includes supportive management and immunotherapy. All patients with GBS should be hospitalized for close respiratory and cardiovascular monitoring. Decisions about intubation should be guided by the need for airway protection and serial measurements of forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force rather than hypoxemia, which is a late sign of hypercapnic respiratory failure. Plasmapheresis and intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) have equal efficacy in shortening recovery time and ventilation duration. Serial treatment with IVIG after plasmapheresis is not superior to either treatment alone and does not add significant benefit. Glucocorticoids may worsen outcomes and are contraindicated in GBS. Prognosis is favorable, with 80% of patients resuming ambulation within 6 months after onset. Relapse occurs in 6% of patients with GBS and necessitates repeat treatment.

Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) is an autoimmune neuropathy. It often presents with progressive or relapsing symmetric proximal and distal weakness and sensory symptoms with diffuse areflexia. Its temporal course is subacute or chronic, often progressing beyond 8 weeks after onset. Atypical forms include multifocal asymmetric and distal symmetric variants, but respiratory failure is rare. CIDP may be isolated or comorbid with several other systemic conditions, including diabetes, lymphoma, and HIV infection.

CSF findings are like those of GBS (albuminocytologic dissociation), and a demyelinating pattern on EMG/NCSs is the key to diagnosis. Nerve biopsy is often unnecessary but, in complex presentations, can differentiate CIDP from vasculitis or amyloidosis.

First-line treatments include glucocorticoids, periodic IVIG, or plasmapheresis, which all have similar efficacy. Treatment is typically continued for at least 6 months. Half of patients achieve remission, but the other half relapse and must resume immunotherapy. Second-line therapies, including azathioprine, cyclosporine, or cyclophosphamide, are often used off label to treat refractory disease. Long-term subcutaneous immune globulin therapy may prevent CIDP relapses. Efgartigimod alfa, a neonatal Fc receptor blocker, is another option for reducing relapses; it may be considered in cases refractory to glucocorticoids and immune globulins. A subset of patients may carry antibodies against proteins of the nodes of Ranvier (neurofascin and contactin) and not respond to typical therapies.

Prolonged intensive care treatment, particularly in association with sepsis and multiorgan failure, can lead to diffuse weakness, ventilator dependence, and prolonged posthospitalization disability. Weakness may be secondary to critical illness myopathy, critical illness axonal neuropathy, or a combination of both. Critical illness myopathy is more common and less severe, whereas critical illness neuropathy is associated with a more protracted recovery. EMG/NCSs can differentiate between the two, but often components of both are present simultaneously. The differential diagnosis includes GBS, myasthenia gravis, vasculitis, and central causes of weakness. No definitive treatment is available, but appropriate glycemic control, early mobilization and physical therapy, and minimization of glucocorticoid use improve the prognosis.

Neuropathies associated with monoclonal proteins occur in monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, multiple myeloma, amyloidosis, and other hematologic malignancies (see Immunoglobulin Light-Chain Amyloidosis in Hematology). Paraproteinemic neuropathy frequently presents as a symmetric distal sensory neuropathy, but sensorimotor, multifocal motor, and cranial nerve variants also occur. Therefore, all patients with peripheral neuropathy should be tested for paraproteinemia (see [Table: Table: Clinical Findings and Laboratory Testing in Peripheral Neuropathy]

). Diagnosis depends on the detection of monoclonal proteins, and treatment is based on the underlying condition. A severe CIDP-like polyneuropathy may occur in paraproteinemic neuropathy associated with organomegaly, endocrinopathy, M protein, and skin changes (POEMS syndrome).

Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease consists of more than 70 genetic disorders in which peripheral neuropathy is the only or main clinical manifestation. The most common inherited neuropathy, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1, is an autosomal dominant demyelinating neuropathy presenting with early onset, slowly progressive distal weakness, areflexia, and sensory loss without pain or paresthesia. Foot deformities, such as hammer toes, high arches, and distal leg atrophy, are common (

). EMG/NCSs typically reveal uniform slowing of nerve conduction velocities, and genetic testing is confirmatory.

Autonomic neuropathies manifest as diffuse or focal impairment of the cholinergic or sympathetic autonomic systems. Diabetes, amyloidosis, and HIV infection are common disorders underlying secondary autonomic neuropathy.

Amyloid neuropathy is caused by extracellular deposition of amyloid protein in peripheral nerves and other tissues. Amyloidosis starts with painful small fiber neuropathy and progressively causes major autonomic impairment and weakness and multiorgan involvement. Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome can be seen.

Primary amyloidosis (also called light-chain [AL] amyloidosis) is associated with monoclonal proteins, whereas familial amyloidosis is secondary to a transthyretin gene variant (see Immunoglobulin Light-Chain Amyloidosis in Hematology and Cardiac Amyloidosis in Cardiovascular Medicine). Several classes of medications, including small interfering ribonucleic acids (e.g., patisiran, vutrisiran) and antisense oligonucleotides (e.g., inotersen, eplontersen), are FDA-approved treatments for hereditary transthyretin-related amyloidosis with polyneuropathy.

In contrast, primary autoimmune ganglionopathy is a distinct and potentially treatable cause of autonomic neuropathy that is often associated with antibodies against ganglionic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. The presentation may range from acute pandysautonomia to chronic focal autonomic dysfunction. Antibody testing and skin biopsy help with diagnosis. Response to IVIG, plasmapheresis, or immunosuppression is common.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a neurodegenerative motor neuron disease that causes progressive weakness, atrophy, and early death. ALS often begins as isolated extremity or bulbar weakness (dysphagia, dysarthria [Video: Dysarthria]) but relentlessly spreads to other regions. Upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, spasticity, and extensor plantar response [see Video: Extensor Plantar Response]), lower motor neuron signs (atrophy and fasciculations [see Video: Fasciculations]), and the absence of sensory deficits are characteristic. Frontotemporal dementia occurs in 20% of patients with ALS. Oculomotor palsy, incontinence, and tremor are atypical.

Diagnosis is based on clinical evidence of upper and lower motor neuron signs and EMG/NCS evidence of lower motor neuron signs in at least two (probable ALS) or more (definite ALS) regions. Brain and cervical spinal imaging and laboratory testing must be used to exclude cervical cord compression, vitamin B~12 and copper deficiencies, Lyme disease, HIV infection, hyperparathyroidism, and thyrotoxicosis. Multifocal motor neuropathy, a treatable condition that mimics ALS, is characterized by severe weakness with minimal atrophy, absence of upper motor neuron signs, and EMG/NCS evidence of motor conduction block.

Treatment of ALS is supportive and should involve multidisciplinary care. Riluzole (glutamate release blocker) and edaravone (free radical scavenger) are FDA-approved treatments for ALS; however, they offer only modest benefits in terms of survival and functional decline. Noninvasive ventilation, when indicated, can also improve life expectancy. Nutritional support (including percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy) and treatment of pseudobulbar affect with dextromethorphan-quinidine also have shown some benefit. Prognosis and care goals should be discussed with the patient early in the disease course to avoid unwanted diagnostic and therapeutic measures.

Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disease of the postsynaptic neuromuscular junction associated with antibodies to acetylcholine receptors. Onset most commonly occurs in the third decade of life in women and after age 50 years in men. Fluctuating, painless weakness without sensory loss is typical. Ptosis and diplopia are the first manifestations in two thirds of patients, although only half of these patients eventually develop generalized myasthenia, typically within 2 years. Early bulbar and cervical involvement is seen in 10% of patients. Weakness may be missed on clinical examination unless fatigability is assessed by sustained or repeated muscle activation.

The presence of respiratory symptoms should prompt close monitoring of respiratory variables because of the risk for rapid respiratory failure (myasthenic crisis). This crisis can occur as part of the natural history of bulbar or generalized myasthenia or be triggered by external factors, including infection, surgery, or certain medications (especially aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium, β-blockers, and hydroxychloroquine).

Diagnosis of MG is based on clinical, serologic, and electrodiagnostic findings. Disease-specific antibodies are found in 90% of patients; 85% have typical MG with acetylcholine receptor antibodies, but 5% have anti–muscle-specific tyrosine kinase (MuSK) or anti–lipoprotein receptor–related protein 4 (LRP4) antibodies. MuSK-positive myasthenia is more likely to cause focal or severe bulbar, cervical, or respiratory weakness. The characteristic electrodiagnostic finding of MG is a decremental response to repetitive nerve stimulation testing. Improvement in ptosis 2 minutes after placing an ice pack over a closed eyelid (ice pack test) can support the diagnosis in some patients. Edrophonium testing is no longer used in the United States and many other countries because of poor test characteristics and adverse clinical outcomes. All patients with MG should undergo chest CT to assess for the presence of concomitant thymoma.

Symptomatic treatment of ocular and mild generalized myasthenia usually starts with the cholinesterase inhibitor pyridostigmine. Patients with more advanced disease require immunosuppressive therapy. Oral glucocorticoids often are used as first-line treatment but can cause transient exacerbation at high doses; they should be titrated upward slowly in patients with mild to moderate weakness. In the presence of prominent bulbar or generalized weakness and in myasthenic crisis, treatment with IVIG or plasmapheresis should precede initiation of glucocorticoids because of the risk for triggering respiratory failure with glucocorticoids alone. The immunosuppressants azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine, and eculizumab are effective long-term maintenance therapies; however, these drugs have a delayed onset of action, and bridging therapy with concomitant glucocorticoids, IVIG, or plasmapheresis is usually required. Several new drugs have been approved to treat refractory myasthenia, including the complement inhibitors eculizumab, ravulizumab, and zilucoplan; the neonatal Fc receptor blockers efgartigimod alfa, rozanolixizumab, and nipocalimab; and CD19 B-cell depleter inebilizumab. Among these agents, neonatal Fc receptor blockers may serve as potential first-line agents owing to their rapid action and favorable safety profile.

Thymectomy should be performed in all patients with thymoma; it should also be offered as an early option to minimize immunotherapy and hospitalizations and improve clinical outcomes in patients without thymoma who are aged 18 to 65 years and have acetylcholine receptor antibodies.

MuSK-positive myasthenia responds well to plasmapheresis and glucocorticoids but requires aggressive maintenance immunosuppression. Prolonged remission has been reported with rituximab (off-label use); thymectomy and pyridostigmine are not helpful.

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is an autoimmune disorder of the presynaptic neuromuscular junction associated with antibodies against the voltage-gated calcium channel. This disorder presents similarly to MG, except that weakness improves with exercise, and hyporeflexia and dysautonomia are present. Diagnosis is confirmed by detection of serum anti–voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies (90%) and the EMG/NCS finding of incremental motor response to repetitive nerve stimulation. Malignancy, especially small cell lung cancer, is found in half of patients. Treatment consists of addressing any underlying malignancy or, in nonparaneoplastic disease, immunosuppression, IVIG, or plasmapheresis. Amifampridine and pyridostigmine can provide symptomatic benefit.

Myopathies are classified on the basis of cause (acquired versus inherited) and clinical and pathologic characteristics ( [Table: Table: Classification of Myopathies]

). Most myopathies involve symmetric weakness of the proximal limb muscles. Additional features that can indicate a specific diagnosis include the clinical course; the presence of pain and stiffness; atypical distribution in ocular, bulbar, or distal limb muscles; and episodic symptoms ( [Table: Table: Clinical Features of Myopathies]

).

Diagnosis is based on history and physical examination, muscle-related serum markers (creatine kinase [CK], aldolase), EMG/NCS findings, muscle biopsy, and, in certain patients, genetic testing. A normal sensory and reflex examination and the results of EMG/NCSs differentiate myopathy from neuropathy. The serum CK level is elevated in many forms of myopathy and can be followed to monitor disease activity and treatment response in inflammatory myopathies. Mild elevation of the serum CK level (<5 times normal) is not specific to myopathies and can also occur in ALS, CIDP, muscle trauma, and persistent serum CK elevation without weakness (benign hyperCKemia). Low amplitude, short duration, and polyphasic shape of motor unit potentials on EMG/NCSs can confirm the presence of myopathy. Muscle biopsy is the most helpful test to confirm the diagnosis of myopathy, but genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis of some hereditary myopathies without biopsy.

Polymyositis, dermatomyositis, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, and inclusion body myositis are idiopathic inflammatory myopathies. Polymyositis and dermatomyositis present with acute or subacute proximal muscle weakness. Inclusion body myositis has a slowly progressive course and causes early weakness and atrophy of finger flexors, quadriceps, and bulbar muscles. Muscle biopsy reveals inflammation and characteristic inclusion bodies. Antibodies to cytosolic 5’-nucleotidase 1A have high specificity, but immunosuppression provides limited benefit. See Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathies in Rheumatology for further information on inflammatory myopathy.

Hypothyroid myopathy can cause diffuse myalgia, proximal weakness, and myoedema (muscle mounding after percussion). Hyperthyroidism also can cause myopathy in association with fasciculation (see Video: Fasciculations), ophthalmoplegia, and hyperreflexia. Excess endogenous or exogenous glucocorticoids, parathyroid or pituitary dysfunction, and vitamin D deficiency are other endocrine-related causes of myopathy.

Toxic myopathy can be triggered by the use of statins and other drugs (see [Table: Table: Classification of Myopathies]

).

Statins can cause a spectrum of symptoms, ranging from mild myalgia to myopathy to rare cases of rhabdomyolysis. The risk for myopathy increases with higher dosages, the addition of fenofibrate or gemfibrozil, the addition of cytochrome P450 3A4 isozyme inhibitors, and the use of lipophilic statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin, and lovastatin). Discontinuing the statin should be considered if the serum CK level is elevated (typically, >5-10 times the upper limit of normal) or in patients with weakness or severe pain. Some patients develop a necrotizing myositis that continues to progress after statin therapy is discontinued. These patients have a serum antibody to the hydroxymethylglutaryl–coenzyme A receptor and may respond to immunosuppression. In patients with a strong indication for statin therapy but significant muscle symptoms, retrial with a hydrophilic statin (rosuvastatin or pravastatin) should be considered after muscle symptoms resolve, with continued CK level monitoring.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors can cause a distinct generalized myopathy that may lead to cardiorespiratory failure. Treatment consists of removing the offending agent and initiating immunosuppression.

Inherited myopathies are listed in [Table: Table: Classification of Myopathies]

. Many of these disorders develop early in life, but some present in adulthood. Myotonic dystrophies are systemic diseases associated with myotonia, an impairment of muscle relaxation causing stiffness and a delayed hand-grip release. Myotonic dystrophy type 1 causes distal weakness and is associated with cataracts, frontal balding, cardiac and endocrine disease, and mild cognitive impairment. Progression of weakness is slow, but diagnosis should prompt assessment for cardiac disease with ECG and echocardiography; close monitoring with spirometry for pulmonary disease that can cause premature mortality is also indicated.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a severe muscle wasting disorder with onset in childhood. Although it was historically associated with a shortened lifespan owing to respiratory and cardiac complications, survival has significantly improved in recent years with advances in multidisciplinary care and emerging therapies. These include vamorolone (a glucocorticoid with a favorable adverse effect profile), givinostat (a histone deacetylase inhibitor), and gene- and exon-skipping therapies.

Mitochondrial myopathy presents with significant variability and can cause fatigue, myalgia, ophthalmoplegia, and various extramuscular manifestations involving vision, hearing, and gastrointestinal and cardiac function. Mitochondrial myopathies should be suspected in the presence of multiorgan involvement with a fluctuating course and maternal transmission.

Adult-onset metabolic myopathies may present with isolated exercise-induced weakness, cramps, and myoglobinuria. They include many deficiencies of key metabolic pathways, such as glycogen storage and fatty acid oxidation; the most common types are carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency and McArdle disease.

Acid maltase deficiency (Pompe disease; formerly classified as glycogen storage disease, type 2) has an adult-onset form associated with proximal and respiratory muscle weakness. Diagnosis is based on assessment of α-glucosidase activity and genetic testing. Alglucosidase alfa is FDA approved to prevent progression of weakness.
