Neuro-oncology

Both benign and malignant intracranial tumors can have devastating neurologic consequences because of the space constraints within the skull and potential surgical inaccessibility. [Table: Table: Presenting Symptoms/Findings of Central Nervous System Tumors]

shows the presenting symptoms and findings of intracranial tumors, which are usually associated with a slow, progressive course. Acute symptoms typically occur when tumors cause seizure or hemorrhage.

Seizures and headaches are common symptoms of intracranial tumors. In the presence of elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), the headache may increase with coughing, sneezing, straining, or the Valsalva maneuver and may be associated with nausea, vomiting, blurry vision, papilledema, and an inability to abduct the eyes secondary to a partial abducens nerve palsy. Elevated ICP can lead to life-threatening herniation, syncope, or cerebellar “fits” (episodic limb extension, flexion, and stiffening; loss of consciousness; slowed or irregular respiration; and pupil dilation), which may be confused with seizures.

Head CT without contrast may be useful emergently to assess for hemorrhage or herniation but is not sensitive for detecting a mass lesion, especially in the posterior fossa. Brain MRI is preferred; contrast administration improves diagnostic sensitivity. Management is determined by tumor location and pathology.

Brain metastases are the most common intracranial tumors. The most likely sources are lung, breast, and kidney cancers and melanoma. Metastases can be solitary but are more often multiple. Metastases typically appear as ring-enhancing lesions on postcontrast MRIs, usually at the gray-white (cortical-subcortical) junction. Survival without treatment is generally measured in weeks to months.

Patients with symptomatic brain metastases should be considered for local therapy, including surgery or radiation therapy; most brain metastases are treated with whole-brain or more targeted radiation (stereotactic radiosurgery). Resection may increase survival in younger patients with good baseline function and a single or limited number of metastases and may benefit patients with large tumors and mass effect; it may also be considered when the underlying diagnosis is uncertain. Patients with multiple brain metastases or uncontrolled systemic disease are less likely to benefit from surgery unless the remaining disease is controllable with other measures.

Leptomeningeal metastasis (also known as carcinomatous meningitis) is a rare diagnosis that requires a high index of suspicion; presenting symptoms vary and include head or neck pain, neurologic deficits, and altered mental status. Although it may occur in solid tumors, it is more common in leukemia and lymphoma. MRI typically shows dural thickening with nodular enhancement; in patients with cranial nerve deficits or radiculopathy, nerve root enhancement on postcontrast MRI of the brain and/or spine may be present. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis with cytology and often flow cytometry is required to make the diagnosis; because of limited sensitivity, serial lumbar punctures are sometimes needed. Meningeal involvement typically portends a poor prognosis, as treatment has limited efficacy.

Meningiomas are the most common primary central nervous system (CNS) tumors. Often found incidentally, meningiomas are benign dural-based tumors that typically show homogeneous enhancement on postcontrast MRI. They have a smooth, rounded shape and often a “tail” that tracks along the dura outside the brain parenchyma (

). On noncontrast images, meningiomas may be hypointense or isointense and thus not readily seen.

Because of their characteristic MRI appearance, many meningiomas are followed clinically with serial brain MRIs, without resection or biopsy, unless they are accompanied by severe headaches, drug-resistant seizures, significant neurologic deficits, or peritumoral edema.

Acoustic neuromas (also termed vestibular schwannomas) are benign, slow-growing nerve sheath tumors. Incidence increases with age and varies among studies; it is estimated to be around 1 to 3 persons per 100,000. The most common presentation is unilateral hearing loss, with or without tinnitus, followed by balance dysfunction. Widespread use of imaging studies has led to increased incidental diagnosis in asymptomatic persons. Acoustic neuromas are the most common tumor at the cerebellopontine angle in adults, and for this reason they may also cause sensory deficits, facial palsy, or compression of posterior fossa structures.

Treatment is determined based on the presence of symptoms and tumor size and growth rate. See Acoustic Neuroma in Interdisciplinary Medicine for more information.

Glioblastoma (

) is the most common, highest grade, and most aggressive glioma subtype in adults. Previous exposure to medical therapeutic radiation is the only consistent risk factor for gliomas. No evidence exists that environmental electromagnetic fields, cell phones, or smoking increase the risk for this tumor. Gliomas rarely metastasize, and routine evaluation of patients with glioblastoma by using lumbar puncture or MRI of the spinal cord is generally not recommended.

MRI typically shows a large, space-occupying lesion with central necrosis, mass effect, heterogeneous enhancement, and surrounding edema. Lower-grade gliomas may not enhance. Treatment is usually resection, if possible, followed by radiation and chemotherapy. Temozolomide is considered first-line treatment; a better response is expected in patients with a methylated O-6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) promoter. Bevacizumab is considered for patients with recurrent disease; traditional chemotherapeutic agents have generally not shown benefit in these patients.

Prognosis depends on the pathologic type. Five-year survival rates for glioblastoma are less than 10%, and survival is often measured in months. Prognosis is better in patients who are younger than 45 years, have an excellent functional status, have minimal residual tumor after resection, and receive chemotherapy and radiation after surgery.

Primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL) occurs initially without systemic or lymph node involvement. Signs and symptoms are based on location within the brain. Systemic B symptoms are uncommon. On MRI, PCNSL appears as a single, well-demarcated, deep white matter (periventricular) lesion with minimal mass effect or edema. About 90% of PCNSLs are diffuse large B-cell lymphomas.

Evaluation of possible PCNSL should include HIV testing, lumbar puncture (if not contraindicated because of elevated ICP), and ophthalmologic evaluation with vitreous fluid sampling. The demonstration of lymphomatous cells in vitreous or CSF samples may obviate the need for biopsy. Systemic staging should include bone marrow biopsy, testicular ultrasonography, and whole-body PET or CT. Avoiding empiric treatment with glucocorticoids is very important before biopsy, unless needed for lifesaving treatment of herniation or edema, because this treatment can temporarily suppress lymphoma and prevent or delay a tissue diagnosis.

High-dose intravenous methotrexate is the treatment of choice. Combination with other chemotherapeutic agents may improve response rates. Conflicting data exist regarding intravenous rituximab. Whole-brain radiotherapy may be considered in patients with residual or progressive disease following primary chemotherapy. Despite being chemo- and radiosensitive, PCNSL typically has multiple recurrences and a generally poor prognosis.

Seizures are more common in low-grade than high-grade tumors. Tumors near the cortex, especially the temporal lobe or primary motor cortex, are especially associated with seizures. White matter and posterior fossa tumors, on the other hand, typically do not cause seizures. Gangliogliomas and dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumors cause medication-resistant seizures in more than 90% of patients, and these tumors should be resected, if possible. Seizures may be caused not directly by the CNS tumor but by associated conditions or treatment, such as electrolyte disturbances, infection, chemotherapy, or paraneoplastic encephalitis.

In patients with CNS tumors without seizures, prophylactic antiseizure drugs (ASDs) are not recommended. Evidence is insufficient to support using ASDs to reduce the risk for peri- or postoperative seizures in patients undergoing surgery for CNS tumors.

In patients with seizures, older ASDs (phenobarbital, phenytoin, valproic acid, carbamazepine) should be avoided because of drug interactions and adverse effects. Levetiracetam and lacosamide are preferred because of their lack of drug interactions, intravenous availability, better tolerability, and rapid titration to a therapeutic dose. Patients with unprovoked seizures after resection typically require lifelong ASD treatment.

Cerebral edema can lead to focal neurologic deficits, elevated ICP, or herniation. Symptomatic cerebral edema is treated with glucocorticoids, preferably dexamethasone because of its lack of mineralocorticoid effects. Antiangiogenic agents, such as bevacizumab, can be used as glucocorticoid-sparing agents to treat subacute or chronic edema but take weeks or months to have an effect.

Brain herniation manifests as an abrupt decline in mental status (loss of alertness and responsiveness); unreactive, dilated pupils; and motor weakness with flexor or extensor posturing. This is an absolute emergency that has a high likelihood of imminent death. Emergent intervention includes elevation of the head of the bed to 30 degrees, hyperventilation (usually with mechanical ventilation), infusion of hypertonic saline or mannitol, and administration of glucocorticoids, typically in that order. These treatments can be lifesaving and often are used as a bridge to emergent surgery.

Certain characteristics are associated with an increased risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE) in patients with CNS tumors ( [Table: Table: VTE Risk Factors in Patients with CNS Tumors]

). Despite the risk for intracranial hemorrhage, therapeutic anticoagulation is generally recommended in confirmed thromboembolic disease. Anticoagulation has historically been avoided in melanoma, choriocarcinoma, papillary thyroid carcinoma, and renal carcinoma because of an assumed increased risk for hemorrhage. However, studies have not shown that anticoagulation increases hemorrhage risk in patients with these cancers. Besides the usual contraindications, anticoagulation should be avoided in patients with previous intracranial hemorrhage and a platelet count less than 50,000/μL (50 × 10^9/L). Expert opinion also recommends pre-anticoagulation neuroimaging with head CT to assess for hemorrhage.

Low-molecular-weight heparin is generally preferred over unfractionated heparin. Exceptions include treatment of patients with kidney impairment and situations when rapid reversal may be required. Inferior vena cava filters have high complication rates and should be reserved for patients with an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation. Warfarin or low-molecular-weight heparin may be considered for long-term therapy, although medication interactions between warfarin and chemotherapy or ASDs are a concern. Evidence is insufficient to recommend direct oral anticoagulants for patients with CNS tumors, although their use may be increasingly accepted in clinical practice.

The presence of a CNS tumor is a contraindication for thrombolytic therapy in pulmonary embolism, although exceptions may be made for low-risk tumors, such as meningiomas.

Low-molecular-weight heparin in combination with pneumatic compression stockings is recommended for VTE prophylaxis in hospitalized patients with CNS tumors as soon as possible after resection. Long-term outpatient prophylactic anticoagulation is not recommended.

Headaches are a common symptom in patients with brain tumors. Multiple factors influence the choice of treatment, such as the primary tumor type and the patient’s functional status and prognosis. Headache treatment in patients with brain tumors should follow the general guidelines for treatment of primary and secondary headaches, such as lifestyle changes and adequate sleep (see Headache and Facial Pain in Neurology). Medication choice may also be guided based on headache characteristics.

Neurocutaneous syndromes are genetic disorders characterized by peripheral and CNS tumors that can cause significant morbidity and mortality due to local growth or malignant transformation. Many patients with neurocutaneous syndromes are relatively asymptomatic, although some experience learning disability, vision or hearing loss, cardiovascular complications, or pain.

The two most common neurocutaneous syndromes, neurofibromatosis type 1 and NF2-related schwannomatosis (formerly called neurofibromatosis type 2), are distinct in genetics and presentation. Neurofibromatosis type 1 is the most common type and is usually diagnosed in childhood because of its prominent neurocutaneous manifestations. The tumors commonly occur outside the nervous system, and both the nonneurologic and peripheral neurologic tumors can be malignant; thus, close surveillance is recommended.

Neurofibromas are uncommon in NF2-related schwannomatosis and are not part of the diagnostic criteria. Lesions in this condition are primarily central (not peripheral).

Antibody-mediated neurologic syndromes may occur as primary autoimmune or secondary paraneoplastic disorders. These disorders have become increasingly relevant as recognition, awareness, and diagnostic testing have risen over time. Various syndromes have been described with different neurologic manifestations and findings on serum and CSF studies ( [Table: Table: Common Autoimmune and Paraneoplastic Neurologic Disorders]

).

Limbic encephalitis is one of the most common presentations and manifests as acute or subacute mood and behavioral changes, short-term memory problems, seizures, and cognitive dysfunction; thus, it may appear as a rapidly progressive dementia (see Rapidly Progressive Dementias in Neurology).

“Red flag” findings suggestive of an antibody-mediated neurologic syndrome include the following:

  • New-onset status epilepticus or psychosis in a previously healthy patient
  • Acute movement disorder (ataxia, chorea, myoclonus, tremor)
  • Acute progressive peripheral neuropathy
  • Neurologic findings accompanied by systemic evidence of autoimmune disease (thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes mellitus, vitamin B~12 deficiency) or systemic signs of malignancy (weight loss, lymphadenopathy)

In suspected cases, the patient should be evaluated for an antibody-mediated process and for systemic cancer, which may include surveillance for years after the primary syndrome is diagnosed. Evaluation should include brain MRI with contrast, blood and CSF antibody testing, and malignancy assessment (e.g., full-body CT, body and brain PET, mammography, colonoscopy, and testicular or pelvic ultrasonography) as appropriate for tumor detection.

Treating the symptoms directly (with, for example, ASDs or antipsychotic agents) is typically ineffective without appropriate tumor resection and immunotherapy. Even when the tumor is removed, long-term immunotherapy may be needed. Immediate management with intravenous immune globulin or intravenous methylprednisolone is often helpful. Long-term treatment with azathioprine, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, or rituximab may be considered.

Optic neuropathies are disorders of the optic nerves that cause monocular vision loss. They can occur in isolation or in association with neurologic or systemic findings. [Table: Table: Causes of Optic Neuropathy]

summarizes the differential diagnosis of optic neuropathy. Presentation (acute or subacute) and presence or absence of pain determine the clinical approach ( [Table: Table: Monocular Optic Neuropathies]

). Optic neuropathies must be differentiated from other acute causes of vision changes, such as angle-closure glaucoma and scleritis. These disorders are often associated with pain and findings on eye examination, such as conjunctival or scleral injection (see Eye Disorders in Interdisciplinary Medicine).

Giant cell arteritis is an ophthalmologic emergency and should be excluded in patients aged 50 years or older who present with transient or permanent monocular vision loss, regardless of the presence of pain. Urgent treatment with high-dose glucocorticoids may limit vision loss in giant cell arteritis.

In optic neuritis, intravenous methylprednisolone has been shown to shorten recovery time and reduce the 2-year incidences of recurrence or conversion to multiple sclerosis.

Glucocorticoids are not recommended in nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy or central or branch retinal artery occlusion unless giant cell arteritis is suspected. Retinal artery occlusion can originate from carotid artery stenosis or cardioembolic causes and can be treated with thrombolysis if presenting within 4.5 hours (off-label use after 3 hours).

Nystagmus is a rhythmic, involuntary oscillation of the eyes. It may consist of a slow, drifting phase with a corrective “jerk” in the opposite direction or of slow, pendular oscillations. Nystagmus may be continuous, paroxysmal, or triggered by changes in gaze direction or head positioning. Patients with nystagmus may report blurred or decreased vision, abnormal head positioning, changes in depth perception, and problems with balance and coordination. Patients with nystagmus may also experience vertigo.

Nystagmus may be physiologic, congenital, or a sign of a central nervous system pathology, such as multiple sclerosis, structural brain lesions, medication toxicity, head injury, or metabolic abnormalities. The suspected underlying cause directs evaluation. See Vertigo in Common Symptoms and Multiple Sclerosis in Neurology.

Ocular motility disorders (also termed oculomotor disorders) may result from lesions in the supranuclear pathways (e.g., frontal lobes), the cranial nerve nuclei, or infranuclear structures (cranial nerves, neuromuscular junction, extraocular muscles). Ocular motility disorders may present with gaze palsy (vertical or horizontal), strabismus, and diplopia. Diplopia, however, can also be a manifestation of myasthenia gravis.

Oculomotor nerve palsy affects adduction and vertical movement but spares abduction. Parasympathetic fibers controlling pupillary constriction to light are on the outside layer of the oculomotor nerve, so compressive lesions result in a fixed, dilated pupil; a posterior communicating artery aneurysm should be considered in a patient who is awake, and cerebral herniation should be considered in a patient who is somnolent. Neuroimaging is recommended in both situations. Emergent head CT is recommended for patients with acute-onset oculomotor nerve palsy associated with severe acute headache and meningeal signs to rule out subarachnoid hemorrhage. If head CT scan is negative, a lumbar puncture should be performed unless the CT was performed within 6 hours of symptom onset. CT or MR angiography should be completed urgently in patients without clinical evidence of subarachnoid hemorrhage to assess for a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.

Pupillary sparing oculomotor nerve palsy suggests microvascular disease, and emergent neuroimaging is not required in persons with known vascular disease. Brain MRI with contrast is indicated in patients without vascular risk factors and in those with symptom progression, other focal neurologic signs on examination, or lack of improvement after 6 to 12 weeks.

Internuclear ophthalmoplegia is characterized by impaired adduction of the affected eye accompanied by nystagmus of the abducting contralateral eye during horizontal eye movement. It is frequently associated with multiple sclerosis or stroke (

) (see Presenting Signs and Symptoms of Multiple Sclerosis in Neurology).

Anisocoria is physiologic in as many as 20% of affected patients or may be caused by pharmacologic, traumatic, or other medical conditions ( [Table: Table: Causes of Anisocoria]

). The affected pupil is typically larger in a well-lit room and smaller in a darker environment.

Horner syndrome comprises miosis, anhidrosis, and ptosis resulting from disruption of the sympathetic fibers in the following locations:

  • From the hypothalamus to the cervicothoracic (C8 to T2) spinal cord (first-order neuron)
  • From the sympathetic trunk to the superior cervical ganglion (second-order neuron)
  • From the internal carotid artery through the cavernous sinus to the oculosympathetic fibers in the eye

The presence of central nervous system signs suggests a first-order Horner syndrome, as the second- and third-order neurons run along the sympathetic trunk and blood vessels rather than in the central nervous system. [Table: Table: Causes of Horner Syndrome in Adults]

Evaluation is guided by the patient’s presentation and often includes MRI of the brain and cervical spine and, when an apical lung process is suspected, chest CT.

Issues in Oncology

The field of oncology has its own language and terminology that are often misunderstood. A clear understanding of this terminology is necessary to facilitate informed discussions with patients and develop realistic treatment goals.

The one pure and simple term is cure. Cure means that the cancer is gone, no further treatment is required, and patients can be expected to live out their lives without seeing that cancer again. Cure should not be confused with the term overall survival, which is defined as the duration from the start of treatment until death. Patients often misunderstand overall survival to be synonymous with cure. Similarly, median survival outcomes that are reported in studies are too often offered to patients as an indication of how long they will live. However, it must be understood and explained that medians identify the center of an often-broad, bell-shaped curve and may be meaningful for populations but cannot predict an outcome for an individual patient.

Patient expectations can be further confused by the frequent use of the phrase significant improvement in survival, in which significant refers to the statistical certainty of the finding but is often misinterpreted as a substantial improvement in survival time. Many drugs have been approved with statistically significant improvements in median survival that are limited to less than 2 or 3 months, a quantity that most would agree is not substantial.

Furthermore, one must be cautious about interpreting nonrandomized comparisons of older versus newer survival data. Improved screening and surveillance techniques are leading to more accurate staging and earlier recognition of smaller volumes of cancer. This advancement creates a lead-time bias that may appear to amplify the benefits of a newer treatment when nonrandomly compared with an older one. Therefore, randomized controlled trials are the only reliable means of comparing one treatment with another.

One of the most misrepresented and misunderstood terms is progression-free survival, or the time from when a treatment is started until that treatment is no longer controlling the cancer. The word survival was initially included in the term because the duration of progression-free survival is defined by either growth of the cancer (progression) or patient death, whichever occurs first. Thus, the term has nothing to do with, and is often confused with, overall survival. The term progression-free interval more accurately describes progression-free survival.

Response rate refers to the percentage of patients in a clinical trial whose tumors shrink to a prespecified degree, as indicated on imaging studies such as CT or MRI, with treatment. Response rate has not been shown to correlate with other metrics, such as overall survival, but there is a strong emotional benefit to patients when the tumor is regressing, and in symptomatic patients, such shrinkage is likely to alleviate, prevent, or delay symptoms.

Clear and candid communication between clinician and patient is essential for good oncologic care. When communicating treatment options and recommendations, clinicians must work to establish realistic treatment goals. When cure is not realistically possible, the following goals should be discussed:

  • Lengthening survival
  • Shrinking a tumor
  • Controlling disease growth
  • Palliating or preventing disease-related symptoms
  • Maintaining quality of life at a level acceptable to the patient

The potential benefits of treatment must be weighed and considered against their risks and toxicities. Patients with incurable cancer may face choices regarding aggressive therapy that is designed to prolong their life but is associated with unpleasant and potentially dangerous adverse effects. The gravity of these adverse effects must be weighed against the probability and extent of prolonged survival. Similarly, more aggressive initial therapy may result in prolonged remission or disease-free survival but may not necessarily change overall survival. Each patient will have a unique perspective on how they interpret this equation. For more information on how one might structure the conversation on identifying patient priorities and the importance of training in serious illness communication, see Communicating With Patients About Serious Illness in Foundations of Clinical Practice and

.

More recently, because costs of anticancer treatments have increased astronomically, the concept of financial toxicity has received greater attention. Financial worries are a significant source of anxiety for many patients with cancer, and receiving a cancer diagnosis is a primary factor leading to personal bankruptcy. Inability to meet copays or coinsurance requirements, especially for expensive oral anticancer medications, greatly hinders patients’ access to necessary therapy. In confronting these financial challenges, concerns fall into two basic categories:

  • High-cost drugs that are highly active and offer clear and substantial benefits
  • High-cost drugs that have minimal activity and offer statistically (but arguably not clinically) significant benefits and that are limited in scope

A clear understanding of the goals of care and toxicities, including financial toxicity, is necessary for patients and physicians to make informed choices in treatment options. This concept of financial toxicity goes beyond individual patients in affecting the overall health care economy. Quantifying the overall benefit of extending a patient’s life by relatively short periods (i.e., <2 months’ median benefit) and contrasting that benefit with the financial cost of care requires consideration of complex ethical, economic, and public health issues.

Early-stage cancers often have a high chance of cure. With increasing cancer stage, however, the possibility of cure diminishes. Most metastatic cancers are treatable but not curable. This finding is especially true for patients with poor performance status due to chronic medical comorbidities or those who have not been able to tolerate initial treatment attempts.

For such patients or for those who have exhausted standard treatment options, supportive, comfort-oriented care may be most appropriate. Use of adequate analgesia, as well as care from supportive care specialists, is essential throughout the continuum of care but especially so in patients with pain or symptoms from either disease or therapy. Palliative care, when instituted early in conjunction with anticancer therapy, helps patients better tolerate their cancer treatment and should not be delayed to the point at which no more active cancer therapy is considered. For more information, see Pain Management in Patients With Terminal Illness in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

Society’s most vulnerable members are disproportionately affected by cancer. Even after adjustment for traditional risk factors, socioeconomic status, race, education, social isolation, and access to health insurance and medical care are associated with well-documented disparities in cancer survivorship. Social determinants of health not only place individuals, families, and entire communities at risk for developing cancer, but they also compound the economic impact of screening, preventing, or managing and treating a new cancer diagnosis. Patients from economically disadvantaged communities are less likely to have cancers diagnosed at earlier, more curable stages and are less likely to be able to access, and maintain access, to necessary oncologic care. For more information, see Health Equity in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

To plan a proper treatment strategy, a clinician must first determine the stage, or extent, of the cancer. Early-stage cancers can often be cured by local therapy, such as surgery or radiation therapy, whereas cancers at more advanced stages require a more systemic treatment approach. Staging in a patient with cancer is generally the most accurate indicator of prognosis and largely dictates the therapeutic strategy.

Most solid tumors are staged on a scale of stage I to IV, using the TNM system. In the TNM system, T (T1-T4) refers to the size or extent of local invasion of the primary tumor, N (N0-N3) indicates the extent of locoregional lymph node involvement, and M indicates the absence (M0) or presence (M1) of distant metastases. If the primary tumor, cancer involvement of nearby lymph nodes, or metastasis cannot be measured, this is denoted with X (e.g., TXNXMX). Some hematologic (liquid) tumors have unique tumor-specific staging systems (e.g., the Ann Arbor staging system for lymphomas).

The appropriate staging with imaging techniques depends on the expected behavior pattern of each cancer type and differs from one tumor to the next. Therefore, a proper cancer evaluation requires knowledge of the specific disease entity so that the appropriate tests can be done. Tests with a very low yield should not be ordered without specific directing symptoms. For example, bone and brain imaging is frequently necessary for staging many patients with lung cancer, given the prevalence of bone and brain metastases during the early course of this disease. However, in patients with presumed locoregional colorectal cancer, asymptomatic bone or brain metastases are exceedingly rare, and routine imaging of these sites as part of staging in the absence of specific symptoms is not warranted.

Performance status is a means of quantifying the overall medical fitness of a patient. A good performance status predicts survival in cancer treatment and is often used as an adjustment factor in anticancer therapies. Patients with a poor performance status are much more likely to experience serious or life-threatening toxicity and much less likely to benefit from treatment.

It is important to differentiate patients with a poor performance status who are debilitated due to chronic comorbidities from patients who would otherwise be medically fit but are acutely debilitated by their cancer. The latter situation may warrant an attempt at aggressive treatment because reversing the cancer is the only strategy that will improve the patient’s overall condition. In the former scenario, a patient may only be able to tolerate less aggressive treatment or may need to forego specific anticancer treatment altogether. Cancer drug approvals are based on clinical trials, almost all of which limit participants to patients with good performance status, so the degree to which the results of these trials are relevant to patients with poor performance status is limited.

In addition, age alone should not be regarded as a reason to avoid aggressive treatment. Older patients who are otherwise medically fit and healthy and have a good performance status may tolerate aggressive therapy well, whereas younger patients with several medical comorbidities resulting in a poor performance status may be unable to tolerate aggressive treatment.

The two predominant performance status scales are the Karnofsky Performance Scale and the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group/World Health Organization system (also called the Zubrod score). These are outlined and contrasted in [Table: Table: Oncology Performance Status Systems]

.

The classic cancer treatment modalities are surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy. With recent advances, chemotherapy is now best subdivided into the more classic cytotoxic chemotherapies, targeted or precision therapies, and immunotherapies. Targeted therapy is an approach that exploits information obtained from molecular profiling of individual tumors and uses agents that attack specific mutations, amplifications, or fusions present in the specific tumor. Antibody-drug conjugates are a subset of targeted therapies. In this strategy, an antibody that recognizes a target on the tumor cell is linked to a toxin or drug in order to concentrate the drug delivery to the tumor. In contrast, immunotherapy does not attack the tumor directly but rather enables the patient’s own immune system to attack the cancer. An important new approach that combines targeted therapy and immunotherapy is chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR T-cell) therapy.

Despite these technologic advances, careful clinical evaluation and staging, understanding and communicating realistic goals of care, and recognizing and promoting patient preferences remain central to the practice of oncology. Meaningful progress has been made in many cancers. However, most cancers that metastasize, although treatable with substantial potential for improvements in overall survival and quality of life, are still incurable.

Supportive management of treatment-related adverse effects has also improved; however, adverse effects of cancer chemotherapy remain problematic for many patients, and maintaining a careful balance between sensitivity to the risks versus benefits is crucial when discussing treatment options with patients.

Finally, exercise has been shown in randomized controlled trials to reduce toxicities of cancer treatment, including reducing fatigue and improving cardiorespiratory fitness and strength. Exercise also improves mood and quality of life during active treatment and should be recommended for patients receiving systemic therapy or radiation therapy.

For most solid tumors that are localized, complete surgical resection remains at the center of treatment, although micrometastases that may remain can still cause harm. Neoadjuvant (preoperative) or adjuvant (postoperative) treatment with modalities such as radiation therapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy (alone or in combination) may be used to eradicate residual microscopic disease and increase the chance for cure. Neoadjuvant therapy, which is used for micrometastases of an already-resectable tumor, should be distinguished from conversion therapy, which seeks to convert an unresectable tumor to a resectable one by shrinking it away from critical structures and creating a plane for resection that previously was lacking.

The modality of neoadjuvant and adjuvant treatment, in terms of chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or both, depends on the tumor type and its distinctive spreading pattern. Before initiating neoadjuvant and adjuvant therapy, it is important to acknowledge that some patients undergoing treatment would be cured with surgery alone and are therefore exposed to needless additional toxicity. Randomized trials are crucial in determining whether, for any given population of patients, neoadjuvant or adjuvant therapy improves an important outcome, such as cure or disease-free survival, without unacceptable toxicity.

Balancing therapy efficacy and toxicity has traditionally been based on stage, pathology, and understanding of the overall behavior of that tumor. Currently available imaging and laboratory studies, however, are somewhat limited in terms of their ability to identify which patients will be at risk for cancer recurrence after definitive surgery. Numerous tumor markers, gene panels, and other technologies have become available, but few are definitive.

The preferred assay would be predictive, meaning that it could identify the subset of patients who are at risk for recurrence and who will benefit from an intervention such as adjuvant chemotherapy to delay or prevent such recurrence. An example of this is a commercially available 21-gene recurrence score assay for breast cancer that identifies a patient population who is at risk for recurrence and for whom chemotherapy would lower that risk. Such predictive tools are highly useful because they provide actionable information in terms of whom to treat. Unfortunately, the availability of such predictive assays is limited.

A similar multigene assay in colorectal cancer is prognostic in that it can quantitate a patient’s risk for recurrence but fails to identify which patients, if any, will have their risk lowered by chemotherapy. Therefore, it does not provide information that is definitive for decision making. Predictive tests are of greater value in that they provide clear, actionable information.

Current developments in chemotherapy are centered on creating agents that target specific driver alterations in a particular type of cancer. The goal of this precision medicine is to identify these specific alterations that are driving growth and survival in a particular tumor and to treat them with agents designed to inhibit that aberrant pathway.

Genomic profiling of tumor tissue can be done from fresh biopsy specimens; from archived, paraffin-embedded specimens; or through liquid biopsies, which isolate and analyze tumor DNA that is shed into the bloodstream (circulating tumor DNA [ctDNA]). These precision medicine techniques can guide clinicians in deciding which therapies are and, in some cases, are not appropriate for a particular patient. Markers can be either inclusionary, in that they include a patient in a therapy that otherwise might not be considered, or exclusionary, in that they exclude a patient from a treatment that otherwise might have been used.

Although in theory these agents should be more selective and have fewer toxicities than older, conventional cytotoxic chemotherapies, this has not always been the case. Many of the signaling pathways that are hyperactive in tumor cells remain at least somewhat active in healthy cells, and so disruption of these pathways can produce considerable adverse effects.

An example of an inclusionary marker is the BRAF V600 mutation in melanoma. Specific BRAF inhibitors, such as vemurafenib, dabrafenib, or encorafenib, are appropriate only for use in melanomas harboring this specific mutation, whereas melanomas lacking this mutation are not treated with these agents. Similarly, trastuzumab, a monoclonal antibody against HER2 on the cell surface, is active only in tumors that overexpress HER2. In short, targeted therapy works only if the target is present and clinically relevant.

Examples of exclusionary markers are RAS mutations. The antiepidermal growth factor receptor monoclonal antibodies cetuximab and panitumumab were initially thought to be appropriate for treatment of all colorectal cancers. Subsequent research showed not only that tumors harboring mutations in KRAS or NRAS were highly resistant to these agents, but also that these agents may even accelerate the growth of tumors with RAS genetic mutations. All metastatic colorectal cancers now require tumor genotyping for KRAS, NRAS, and BRAF mutations, and only tumors lacking all three of these mutations can be treated with cetuximab or panitumumab.

ctDNA can often be isolated from the blood of patients with metastatic cancer, and molecular profiling of the tumor can be accomplished with a blood sample. This liquid biopsy may help avoid an unnecessary invasive procedure when archived tumor tissue is not available. Although developing data suggest that ctDNA may also be useful for surveillance after surgery or to identify at-risk patients for adjuvant therapy, studies have not outlined specific actionable results. As such, these assays are prognostic but not predictive, and routine use has not been recommended in any of the major North American or European guidelines at this time.

Immunotherapy agents are drugs that do not attack the cancer directly but rather mobilize the patient’s immune system to do so. This capability has become possible through the identification of immune checkpoints, which normally serve as brakes on the immune system to prevent it from attacking itself and causing autoimmune diseases. Antibodies that block these checkpoints release the brakes on the immune system and allow it to aggressively attack the tumor. Immunotherapy has become the standard monotherapy for treatment of some cancers, although it is insufficiently active in others. Use of immunotherapy concurrently with older cytotoxic chemotherapies has also led to improved outcomes. However, patients with some other cancer types (e.g., common types of colon and pancreatic cancers) have not yet benefited from available immunotherapies.

Adverse effects of immunotherapy are related to resultant autoimmunity from the less regulated immune system and can be severe.

The first immune checkpoint identified was the antigen-4 (A-4) molecule on the surface of the cytotoxic lymphocyte (T cell), hence its designation cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4). Antibodies that block CTLA-4, such as ipilimumab or tremelimumab, have been successful in mobilizing the immune system against melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, and other malignancies. Their current use tends to be mostly in conjunction with the PD-1 inhibitors discussed below.

The other immune checkpoint that has been successfully exploited is the PD-1 receptor. Anti–PD-1 agents, such as nivolumab, pembrolizumab, and dostarlimab have shown substantial and durable activity against melanoma and non−small cell lung cancers, as well as other tumors. Agents against PD-L1, such as atezolizumab or durvalumab, have also shown important clinical activity. Combinations of these agents have shown further effectiveness but with increased toxicity and considerable expense. Many other checkpoints in the immune system are now being explored, and numerous drugs are in development.

Further progress in immunotherapy has occurred in the use of adoptive cellular immunity, particularly the development and commercialization of CAR T cells. In this strategy, the patient’s T cells are harvested, genetically manipulated to express a receptor for an antigen on the tumor cell, expanded, and reinfused into the patient. The chimeric antigen receptor then binds to the tumor cell and activates the T cell to destroy the cancer. This strategy requires a target antigen that is unique to the tumor and is not expressed to a meaningful degree on healthy tissue.

CAR T cells have shown striking activity in selected B-cell leukemias and lymphomas, albeit with substantial clinical and financial toxicity. Thus far, this strategy has been used only in hematologic malignancies, including leukemia, lymphoma, and myeloma; however, numerous investigations of CAR–T-cell studies in almost all tumor types and potential off-the-shelf, allogenic CAR–T-cell products are underway.

Breast Cancer

In the United States, breast cancer is the most common type of cancer, excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer, and is the second leading cause of cancer-related death in women. Approximately 290,000 new invasive breast cancer cases were diagnosed in 2021, and around 43,000 deaths from breast cancer occur yearly in the United States. The lifetime risk for developing invasive breast cancer is 12.4% (1 in 8) for U.S. women.

Breast cancer incidence increases with age. The median age of diagnosis in women is 61 years. Incidence rates are highest in non-Hispanic White women, whereas mortality is highest in Black women. Women account for 99% of breast cancer cases. Characteristics posing an elevated risk for breast cancer are summarized in [Table: Table: Breast Cancer Risk Factors]

.

Several breast cancer subtypes have been identified (see

), including tumors that express estrogen and/or progesterone receptors (hormone receptors) and tumors that overexpress HER2. These receptors play a key role in tumor biology and in the prognosis and treatment of patients with breast cancer.

In the United States, around 80% of patients with breast cancer are diagnosed with early-stage disease (stage I-II), 15% are diagnosed with locally advanced disease (stage III), and 5% to 6% are diagnosed with metastatic disease (stage IV).

Obtaining a family history is critical because patients with possible hereditary breast cancer syndromes should be referred to a genetic counselor for assessment and possible genetic testing. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) and the American Society of Clinical Oncology-Society of Surgical Oncology criteria for genetic testing are outlined in [Table: Table: Breast and Ovarian Cancer Genetic Testing]

.

Notably, there is some discordance between these guidelines, with the American Society of Clinical Oncology-Society of Surgical Oncology recommending testing a larger subset of the population; the main difference between these criteria are in the age at diagnosis and the somewhat less stringent guidelines in terms of family history. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends the use of a brief familial risk assessment tool in women with a personal or family history of breast, ovarian, tubal, or peritoneal cancer or family history suggesting BRCA1/2 pathologic variants. Women with a positive test result on the risk assessment tool should receive genetic counseling and, if indicated after counseling, genetic testing. Cascade testing for family members of affected individuals should be considered. Pathogenic BRCA1 and BRCA2 variants predispose carriers to multiple malignancies; risk reduction strategies are summarized in [Table: Table: Cancer Risk Management for BRCA1/2 Variants]

.

Breast cancer screening for women at average risk is discussed in Screening for Breast Cancer in Oncology. The American Cancer Society recommends screening certain women at high risk using annual mammography and breast MRI ( [Table: Table: MRI Breast Cancer Screening Recommendations]

).

Several tools have been validated to estimate breast cancer risk. The Gail Model Risk Assessment Tool can calculate the 5-year and lifetime risks for breast cancer, and the Tyrer-Cuzick Risk Assessment Calculator can estimate the 10-year and lifetime risk. High risk is defined as a 5-year risk of breast cancer of 1.67% or greater based on the Gail Model Risk Assessment Tool or a lifetime risk of 20% or higher per the Tyrer-Cuzick Risk Assessment Calculator.

Patients with increased risk based on these scores are candidates for enhanced screening (such as earlier initiation of screening or supplemental testing with MRI), and chemoprevention (with endocrine therapy) can be considered, per NCCN guidelines. In contrast to NCCN guidelines, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force advises against using any hard cutoff point to define increased risk. Instead, they recommend prioritizing each patient’s values and preferences when considering the trade-offs between reducing the risk for breast cancer and the potential for adverse effects. Patients with atypical ductal hyperplasia or lobular carcinoma in situ are also candidates for chemoprophylaxis.

Tamoxifen and raloxifene are selective estrogen receptor modifiers that block estrogen uptake in breast tissue. Exemestane, anastrozole, and letrozole are aromatase inhibitors that prevent the conversion of androgens into estrogens. Tamoxifen can be used regardless of the patient’s menopausal status, whereas raloxifene is approved only for postmenopausal women and aromatase inhibitors are used only to treat postmenopausal patients. These agents proportionally decrease the risk for breast cancer and are given for 5 years. [Table: Table: Primary Chemoprevention for Breast Cancer]

summarizes these chemoprophylaxis options.

For women with germline pathogenic or likely pathogenic BRCA1 or BRCA2 variants, breast cancer screening with annual breast MRI should start at age 25 years, with mammography added at age 30 years. If a first-degree relative developed cancer before age 30 years, however, screening should be further individualized. Prophylactic bilateral mastectomy for BRCA1 or BRCA2 variant carriers decreases the risk for breast cancer by greater than 90%. Additionally, prophylactic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy decreases the risk for ovarian, fallopian tube, and primary peritoneal cancers by more than 80% and decreases the risk for all-cause mortality before age 70 years by 77%. Premenopausal prophylactic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, which reduces the risk for breast cancer by 50%, is recommended for patients at high risk upon completion of childbearing.

Breast cancer staging and prognosis are presented in [Table: Table: Staging and Prognosis of Invasive Breast Cancer]

. The prognosis is excellent for patients with localized disease (i.e., small tumors with neither lymph node involvement nor distant metastases). Several other factors have been associated with a favorable prognosis, including but not limited to the presence of hormone receptors and a low tumor grade. American Cancer Society data from 1989 to 2017 show a 40% decrease in deaths from breast cancer. The 5-year relative survival for all invasive breast cancer stages in patients diagnosed from 2010 to 2016 is 91.4%.

For asymptomatic patients with newly diagnosed stage I to II breast cancer, current guidelines recommend against using imaging studies for staging because the incidence of metastases is low. Staging with PET/CT or CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis plus bone scan is recommended for patients with stage III disease or for those with stage I or II disease who have signs, symptoms, or laboratory findings suggesting metastatic disease. Measuring serum markers such as CA15-3, carcinoembryonic antigen, or CA27-29 is not standard of care for early-stage breast cancer.

Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), classified as stage 0 breast cancer, is a noninvasive breast cancer typically detected as calcifications on mammography. Its incidence has increased from 3% of breast cancers before the era of mammographic screening to 20% to 25% of breast cancers today. Patients with DCIS infrequently present with a palpable mass or with Paget disease of the breast.

Because half of local DCIS recurrences are invasive cancers, the goal of treatment is to eradicate the area of DCIS and decrease the risks for local recurrence and death from breast cancer. Local treatment involves either lumpectomy, often followed by radiation therapy, or mastectomy. Postlumpectomy radiation therapy improves disease-free survival but not breast cancer–specific mortality and can be omitted in some cases, especially in patients with small, low-risk DCIS. Gene expression analysis can help with risk stratification.

Around 90% of DCIS express estrogen hormone receptors. In women with estrogen receptor–positive DCIS, 5 years of treatment with tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor decreases the risk for local recurrence and contralateral breast cancers. Tamoxifen is the appropriate treatment in premenopausal women. For postmenopausal women, both tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors are effective options.

Antiestrogen treatment of DCIS, however, has not shown a survival benefit and may be omitted in patients who prefer not to take endocrine therapy or who do not tolerate treatment. Adjuvant endocrine therapy is also not indicated following bilateral mastectomy, or for patients with hormone receptor–negative DCIS. HER2 testing and HER2-targeted therapies are unnecessary in DCIS. Patients with DCIS should undergo annual mammography starting 6 to 12 months after radiation therapy, if given, and follow-up visits every 6 to 12 months for 5 years after diagnosis.

Breast cancer treatments can be divided into local therapies, including surgery and radiation therapy, and systemic therapies (summarized in [Table: Table: Breast Cancer Treatment]

). Systemic therapies can be given in the preoperative (neoadjuvant) or postoperative (adjuvant) settings (see

).

There are two surgical options for invasive breast cancer: breast-conservation therapy and mastectomy. Breast-conservation therapy involves wide excision followed by breast radiation therapy and is typically used in patients with cancers measuring less than 5 cm, without skin involvement, and with clear margins after excision. Mastectomy is recommended for cancers that are too large to be removed with lumpectomy with an acceptable cosmetic outcome, locally advanced cancers such as those with skin involvement, and inflammatory breast cancers.

A sentinel node biopsy has traditionally been done at the time of breast surgery in patients with clinically negative axillary lymph nodes. However, recent randomized trials have shown that sentinel node biopsy can be safely omitted in postmenopausal women with cancers that 2 cm or smaller, grade 1 or 2, hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative, and clinically node negative. In these patients, axillary ultrasonography is recommended to confirm that there are no nodes with abnormal morphology.

In patients undergoing breast-conservation surgery with sentinel node biopsy and who will receive chemotherapy or antiestrogen therapy and whole-breast radiation therapy, axillary dissection is not required if no more than two sentinel nodes are involved. For patients with three or more positive sentinel nodes, axillary node dissection is recommended.

For patients with clinically involved axillary nodes, axillary lymph node dissection is often recommended. However, the tumor receptors and the number of affected lymph nodes play a role in this decision. Sentinel node dissection has a lower risk for lymphedema, sensory loss, and shoulder abduction defects than axillary dissection.

Postmastectomy radiation therapy reduces the risk for local recurrence and distant metastases while improving overall survival. It is generally recommended for patients who have the following:

  • Higher-risk disease, including tumors larger than 5 cm
  • Tumors with positive margins or skin involvement
  • Inflammatory breast cancer
  • Four or more positive axillary nodes
  • One to three positive axillary nodes in the setting of other high-risk features

Most hormone receptor–positive early-stage invasive breast cancers are treated with initial excision followed by radiation therapy and adjuvant systemic therapy. For some patients with large hormone receptor–positive tumors, neoadjuvant chemotherapy or endocrine therapy can be given before surgery to shrink the tumor and facilitate breast conservation. HER2-positive and triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) with larger tumor size and/or lymph node involvement are treated with neoadjuvant therapies. This approach enables assessment of tumor response to therapy; adjuvant treatment could then be tailored based on this response. Patients with these cancer subtypes who have no residual cancer (pathologic complete response) after neoadjuvant therapy have an overall better prognosis.

Patients with stage I to III breast cancer receive adjuvant systemic therapy to eradicate occult microscopic foci of breast cancer and decrease the risk for local and distant recurrence (curative intent). Some are also candidates for neoadjuvant therapy. The type of systemic therapy used depends on the patient’s characteristics, including menopausal status, as well as the breast cancer subtype and stage (see

).

In addition to adjuvant endocrine therapy and chemotherapy as indicated, adjuvant therapy with specific oral or intravenous bisphosphonates should be considered in postmenopausal patients (including those receiving ovarian suppression) with higher-risk disease. This treatment has been shown to decrease the risk for distant recurrence and modestly improve overall survival. It also preserves bone density in patients treated with aromatase inhibitors and/or ovarian suppression.

Most patients with hormone receptor–positive, HER2-negative breast cancer first undergo surgery, followed by adjuvant endocrine therapy; menopausal status is a key factor in the treatment selection. Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator that blocks estrogen uptake by breast cancer cells. It is effective in both premenopausal and postmenopausal women. The aromatase inhibitors letrozole, anastrozole, and exemestane have similar efficacy and prevent the conversion of androgens to estrogen in the adrenal glands and peripheral tissues. However, they do not inhibit estrogen production in the ovaries. They are thus not effective in premenopausal women without concomitant ovarian function suppression (OFS), which is usually accomplished with a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist (e.g., leuprolide, goserelin, triptorelin).

Adverse effects of tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors are shown in [Table: Table: Primary Chemoprevention for Breast Cancer]

. The risk for thromboembolism and endometrial cancer should be discussed with patients before starting tamoxifen. For patients taking tamoxifen, it is important to avoid medications with strong CYP2D6 inhibition, such as bupropion or fluoxetine, because these may decrease tamoxifen activation. Up to one third of women treated with aromatase inhibitors develop aromatase inhibitor–associated symmetric arthralgia, joint stiffness, and bone pain. This musculoskeletal syndrome is managed with NSAIDs or duloxetine, acupuncture, a treatment break, and changing to an alternate aromatase inhibitor or switching to tamoxifen.

Endocrine therapy options for premenopausal women with estrogen receptor–positive breast cancer include tamoxifen alone or with OFS, or an aromatase inhibitor combined with OFS. Treatment with OFS should be used in select patients because it often causes more adverse effects compared with tamoxifen therapy alone (see [Table: Table: Primary Chemoprevention for Breast Cancer]

). For those with low recurrence risk, tamoxifen therapy alone for 5 years may be appropriate. Extended endocrine therapy of up to 10 years is associated with a reduction in recurrence risk (3.7%) and breast cancer mortality (2.8%). Disease-free survival, however, is improved in premenopausal women with higher-risk cancers with the addition of OFS. The selection and duration of treatment are based on the patient’s menopausal status, tumor histopathologic characteristics, stage, and patient goals.

Neoadjuvant endocrine therapy with an aromatase inhibitor can be considered in postmenopausal women in whom treatment increases the surgical options for locoregional control.

Otherwise, 5 years of adjuvant aromatase inhibitor therapy or 2 years of tamoxifen therapy followed by 3 years of aromatase inhibitor therapy is associated with a statistically significant lower recurrence risk and improved survival in postmenopausal women with higher-grade ductal or lobular cancers. Aromatase inhibitors are superior to tamoxifen, with an additional 29% proportional decrease in breast cancer recurrence. Both tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors also decrease the risk for contralateral breast cancer.

Extended endocrine therapy of up to 10 years improves disease-free survival in patients with high-risk features but does not affect overall survival. Decisions regarding extended endocrine therapy should be tailored to patient risk and comorbidities that may affect tolerability, including bone health and history of venous thromboembolic disease.

Some patients with hormone receptor–positive tumors additionally benefit from combination chemotherapy regimens, which are given in the adjuvant setting before endocrine and radiation therapy. Adjuvant chemotherapy is usually given to patients with more than three positive axillary nodes. For patients with zero to three positive axillary nodes, the use of multigene assays (e.g., Oncotype DX, MammaPrint, PAM50) can be used to predict the potential benefit of adding chemotherapy to a patient’s treatment. After chemotherapy, patients receive adjuvant antiestrogen therapy for at least 5 years. Adjuvant tamoxifen leads to a 39% proportional reduction in breast cancer recurrence at 15 years and a 30% proportional reduction in breast cancer mortality.

Acute adverse effects of adjuvant chemotherapy include bone marrow suppression, alopecia, allergic reactions, neuropathy, nausea, and premature menopause and infertility in premenopausal women (see Effects of Cancer Therapy in Oncology). Women of childbearing age who wish to preserve fertility should undergo fertility counseling for consideration of oocyte or embryo banking before chemotherapy. Older patients have a higher risk for cardiotoxicity. For older women with early and advanced breast cancer, considering estimated life expectancy, functional status, and medical comorbidities is important before administering adjuvant chemotherapy.

Targeted agents, such as olaparib, are exclusively used in patients with germline BRCA pathogenic variants. Additionally, both abemaciclib and ribociclib are approved for selected patients with moderate- to high-risk hormone receptor–positive, HER2-negative breast cancer with lymph node involvement.

For patients with HER-positive tumors larger than 2 cm or patients with positive lymph nodes, neoadjuvant therapy with chemotherapy regimens in combination with trastuzumab and pertuzumab is the standard of care. Patients with no residual disease at the time of surgery have an excellent prognosis and often complete 1 year of treatment with trastuzumab with or without pertuzumab. Patients with residual disease following neoadjuvant chemotherapy have a greater recurrence risk, and adjuvant HER2-directed therapy combined with cytotoxic therapy (e.g., an antibody drug conjugate) can reduce recurrence and improve survival.

In patients not receiving neoadjuvant therapy who have HER2-positive cancers that are greater than 5 mm, node positive, or both, adjuvant systemic chemotherapy combined with HER2-targeted treatment (such as the monoclonal antibody trastuzumab or the combination of trastuzumab and pertuzumab) is recommended. The addition of trastuzumab to chemotherapy decreases the risk for cancer recurrence by 53% and the risk for death by 34%. Trastuzumab is generally given for 12 months.

For patients with HER2-positive breast cancers smaller than 2 cm and without lymph node involvement, a de-escalation adjuvant regimen with paclitaxel and trastuzumab is well tolerated, with a 10-year recurrence-free survival rate of 96.3%.

The main toxicities of trastuzumab are infusion reactions, such as fever or chills, and reversible cardiomyopathy. Patients receiving trastuzumab should undergo baseline echocardiography, followed by echocardiography every 3 months during treatment.

Half of the tumors that overexpress HER2 also express hormone receptors. In patients with these cancers, adjuvant endocrine therapy should also be started once cytotoxic chemotherapy is completed.

Patients with TNBC have a 50% proportional reduction in the risk for recurrence and of breast cancer mortality with chemotherapy. The immune checkpoint inhibitor pembrolizumab is approved in the neoadjuvant setting in combination with chemotherapy for patients with tumors larger than 2 cm or patients with positive lymph nodes. If patients have residual cancer after neoadjuvant therapy, they should receive additional oral chemotherapy (capecitabine) and continue pembrolizumab. Patients who achieve a pathologic complete response undergo treatment with pembrolizumab alone for 1 year.

Adjuvant cytotoxic chemotherapy is recommended for patients with triple-negative cancers larger than 5 mm or with positive lymph nodes. Typically, two or three agents are given for four to eight cycles. The most common chemotherapies used for adjuvant treatment are anthracyclines (doxorubicin or epirubicin), cyclophosphamide, and the taxanes (paclitaxel or docetaxel).

Olaparib is approved for patients with a germline pathogenic BRCA variant with residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy.

Locally advanced breast cancer includes a subset of clinical stage IIB cancers and stage IIIA to IIIC cancers. These cancers may have high-risk characteristics, such as skin, chest wall, or extensive lymph node involvement. Locally advanced cancers are usually treated first with neoadjuvant systemic therapy, followed by surgery, and then radiation therapy. In some postmenopausal women, neoadjuvant antiestrogen therapy can be used instead of chemotherapy.

Neoadjuvant therapies may decrease the size of the primary breast cancer to allow for breast-conserving lumpectomy. The amount of residual cancer after neoadjuvant chemotherapy has prognostic significance, particularly in triple-negative or hormone receptor–negative, HER2-positive cancers. Patients with complete pathologic responses have the lowest risk for recurrence, whereas those with residual disease may benefit from intensifying treatment with additional chemotherapy.

Inflammatory breast cancer represents a small subset of locally advanced breast cancer in which patients present with swelling, thickening, or erythema of the skin overlying the breast, classically with a peau d’orange (orange peel) appearance (see

). Patients may present with breast enlargement or swelling, often misdiagnosed as mastitis, with subsequent delay in management. A palpable breast mass may also be present. The skin changes are caused by cancer cells obstructing dermal lymphatic vessels, although biopsy results may not always reveal this pathology. A biopsy should be obtained to confirm the diagnosis as well as hormone receptor and HER2 status.

One third of patients have distant metastases at diagnosis, and nearly all have lymph node involvement. For this reason, these patients should undergo routine staging with either CT and bone scan or PET, even without metastatic disease symptoms. This contrasts with noninflammatory breast cancers where staging scans are necessary only for those with concerning symptoms or stage III disease. Patients are treated with neoadjuvant therapy (selected based on breast cancer subtype), mastectomy, and radiation therapy.

Most patients diagnosed with breast cancer are cured. There are nearly 3 million women alive in the United States with a previous or current breast cancer diagnosis. Following early active therapy (surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy), patients are monitored for recurrence, second primary cancers, and physical and psychosocial long-term effects of breast cancer treatment. Patients with hormone receptor–positive breast cancer continue receiving antiestrogen treatment for 5 to 10 years and require management of menopausal symptoms and other toxicities, including bone loss, during that time. Guidelines recommend that patients be evaluated for a detailed cancer-related history and undergo physical examination every 3 to 6 months for the first 3 years, every 6 to 12 months for the next 2 years, and then annually.

Patients should undergo annual mammography of remaining breast tissue. Screening breast MRIs are needed only if patients meet criteria (see Breast Cancer Chemoprevention and Other Risk Reduction Strategies in Oncology). Patients should not undergo routine blood tests or other routine imaging studies at follow-up visits because these are not helpful for diagnosing recurrences earlier. Laboratory and imaging studies other than breast imaging should be guided by a patient’s symptoms or findings on examination that raise concern for recurrence.

Patients should be evaluated at each visit for changes in family history of cancers and referred for genetic counseling as appropriate. Patients taking tamoxifen should have annual gynecologic examinations and be evaluated by a gynecologist for any abnormal vaginal bleeding because of the increased risk for endometrial cancer. Patients taking aromatase inhibitors should undergo bone density studies and receive osteoporosis treatment, ideally with bisphosphonates, if their T score is –2.5 or lower.

Lymphedema can occur after sentinel lymph node biopsies; however, the risk is higher after axillary lymph node dissection and radiation therapy. This complication can lead to swelling and fibrotic skin changes and is associated with significant morbidity. Prevention and early detection are key to avoiding long-term problems. Management includes complex lymphatic therapy based on manual lymphatic drainage, compression, exercise, skincare, and sequential pumps. Some patients require surgical management.

For patients with breast asymmetry, reconstruction options are often fully covered by insurance. Menopausal symptoms should be managed with nonhormonal options, such as gabapentin for nocturnal hot flushes. Depression, anxiety, and sexual dysfunction are not uncommon in this population and should be appropriately assessed and managed.

Approximately 5% of patients with breast cancer present with de novo metastatic disease, and up to 30% with early-stage disease develop metastases. Metastatic breast cancer is not curable, and the goal of systemic therapy is to improve survival, relieve symptoms, and maintain quality of life. Treatment and prognosis are related to whether visceral metastases are present, the number of sites involved, the interval between initial diagnosis and metastases (those with intervals of <2 years have a poorer prognosis), the patient’s performance status, and tumor biology.

In evaluating a patient with newly diagnosed metastatic breast cancer, it is important to biopsy a distant metastatic site. This step is necessary both to confirm the diagnosis and to assess hormone receptor and HER2 status because there may be treatment-altering discordance in the receptors in the metastatic lesion compared with the previous primary breast cancer in up to 15% of patients. Biomarkers that will influence treatment options, such as PIK3CA or ESR1 pathogenic mutations, PD-L1 status, tumor variant burden, and deficient mismatch repair/microsatellite instability, should be tested on tumor tissue or by testing circulating tumor DNA in plasma. Bone biopsies have limitations in terms of assessing tumor receptor status, and other sites should be preferentially biopsied if possible.

Endocrine-based therapy is usually the initial treatment in postmenopausal women with hormone receptor–positive, HER2-negative breast cancer. Aromatase inhibitors are superior to other agents as first-line treatment. Fulvestrant, which inhibits estrogen receptor function, and tamoxifen are other options. Premenopausal women can receive tamoxifen or ovarian suppression combined with either tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors as initial treatment.

The addition of CDK4/6 inhibitors (abemaciclib, palbociclib, ribociclib) to endocrine therapy improves the response rate and duration of response to hormonal therapy in estrogen receptor–positive tumors. These drugs have been incorporated into routine care for most women with metastatic estrogen receptor–positive, HER2-negative breast cancer. After progression of CDK4/6 inhibitors and endocrine therapy, other endocrine-based targeted agents can be used. Once endocrine agents are exhausted or the tumor stops responding to endocrine-based treatments, chemotherapy, including treatment with antibody-drug conjugates, can be considered.

For patients with HER2-positive advanced breast cancer, treatment should include HER2-directed therapy, such as trastuzumab, given with either chemotherapy or antiestrogen therapy. The latter is recommended only for patients with HER2-positive and hormone receptor–positive disease. First-line treatment with trastuzumab and pertuzumab (dual HER2-targeted therapy) added to docetaxel has been shown to improve overall survival, with median overall survival of 56 months in a phase III clinical trial. Subsequent lines of therapy include fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and antibody-drug conjugates. Continuing HER2-directed therapy throughout the treatment of the disease is crucial.

Advanced TNBC has historically been treated with chemotherapy. The addition of pembrolizumab, a monoclonal antibody that targets PD-L1, alongside chemotherapy, has been shown to improve overall survival for patients with metastatic TNBC with a high PD-L1 score (combined positive score ≥10). TNBC may also respond to platinum agents, particularly in BRCA variant carriers. In patients with germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 pathogenic variants, poly (adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (olaparib, talazoparib) improve progression-free survival relative to single-agent chemotherapy. These agents cause synthetic lethality by producing an increase in double-stranded DNA breaks that would usually be repaired by the BRCA pathway.

For all subtypes of breast cancer with bone metastases, bone-modifying agents such as zoledronic acid or denosumab are recommended to decrease fractures, pain, and the need for radiation therapy. Palliative radiation therapy can be used to treat painful bone metastases and other sites of tumor-related pain or obstruction. Patients with TNBC and HER2-positive cancers have a higher risk for brain metastases, which are treated with surgery, stereotactic radiation therapy, or whole-brain radiation therapy. Palliative care teams can be helpful for managing symptoms of pain, nausea, anorexia, and fatigue. Throughout the course of advanced breast cancer, it is essential to engage in discussions with patients regarding their goals of care, emphasizing their values and preferences as they navigate treatment for an incurable illness.
