Gastroenterologic Malignancies

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is largely preventable through screening (see Colorectal Cancer in Oncology), yet it is the fourth most common cancer and the second leading cause of cancer-related death in the United States. Epidemiology, pathophysiology, risk factors, screening, and clinical manifestations is discussed in Colorectal Neoplasia in Gastroenterology.

CRCs found on the right side of the large intestine (cecum, ascending colon, and proximal two thirds of transverse colon) have substantially different biological characteristics, possibly related to their embryologic origin. These tumors carry a substantially worse prognosis compared to those on the left side (distal one third of transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, and rectum). Symptoms may also differ based on tumor location (see

). Patients with colon cancer at any location may present with hematochezia, pain, or acute clinical signs from perforation or obstruction (see

).

Most CRCs retain the full function of their nuclear mismatch repair (MMR) proteins and are known as MMR proficient (pMMR). However, approximately 12% to 15% of locoregional CRCs and approximately 3% to 4% of metastatic CRCs lack one or more mismatch repair enzymes and are known as MMR deficient (dMMR). MMR deficiency manifests as increased microsatellite instability (MSI) in the cancer cell’s DNA; the terms dMMR and MSI are essentially synonymous from a clinical perspective. Determining the MMR status in all cases of CRC is critical because current immunotherapies are essentially inactive in pMMR CRC but are highly active in dMMR tumors.

Approximately 20% of patients with dMMR tumors will have a germline MMR deficiency known as Lynch syndrome, which is associated with a high lifetime risk for CRC as well as endometrial and other cancers (see Lynch Syndrome in Gastroenterology).

Staging with the TNM system (considering the characteristics of the primary tumor [T], regional lymph node involvement [N], and metastatic disease [M]) is the first step in planning treatment ( [Table: Table: Staging of Colorectal Cancer]

). Evaluation includes measuring serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels in addition to routine laboratory studies; full colonoscopy (if possible); and contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Patients with rectal cancer also require rectal MRI, which offers more precision in assessing tumor penetration and lymph node involvement. PET does not provide greater accuracy in staging and should not be used for preoperative staging or postoperative surveillance unless contrast-enhanced CT and MRI are contraindicated.

The rectum is the most distal 12 to 15 centimeters of the large bowel. Whereas treatment historically has emphasized the use of surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy in most patients, current approaches offer consideration of nonoperative management and emphasis on posttreatment functional outcome.

MMR status should be determined for all rectal cancers before treatment is planned because dMMR rectal cancers have very high rates of durable complete clinical response to immunotherapy with PD-1 inhibitors alone. Therefore, initial treatment with a PD-1 inhibitor is the preferred approach, with radiation therapy and/or surgery reserved for those very few cases with incomplete response or locally recurrent disease.

Rectal cancers without full-thickness penetration of the bowel wall and with no enlarged lymph nodes (stage I disease) may be treated with surgical resection. Alternatively, when stage I tumors are distal enough that surgery would require a permanent colostomy or otherwise result in poor bowel function, neoadjuvant therapy with both radiation therapy and chemotherapy, followed by surveillance without surgery if a complete response is achieved, is an option.

Patients with full-thickness tumors (stage II) and tumors with involved lymph nodes (stage III) traditionally have required radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and surgery. Current data support the use of total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT), in which all planned radiation therapy and/or chemotherapy is given before surgery, in most cases. In patients in whom a complete clinical response to TNT is achieved, nonoperative management with close surveillance may be considered. As seen with stage I tumors, a complete response to TNT might eliminate the need for surgery in distal rectal tumors and preserve anal sphincter function. However, if the mass is not fully eradicated, surgical resection is necessary.

Whether part of adjuvant or neoadjuvant therapy, radiation therapy in rectal cancer has traditionally involved long-course treatment over 5.5 weeks with concurrent intravenous 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) or capecitabine, an oral prodrug that is converted into 5-FU. So-called short-course radiation therapy with higher doses given over 5 days without concurrent chemotherapy is now accepted as an alternative in many cases.

Leucovorin, 5-FU, and oxaliplatin (FOLFOX) or capecitabine plus oxaliplatin (CAPOX) regimens are typically used for the chemotherapy-only portion of treatment. Capecitabine and, to a lesser extent, 5-FU may be associated with erythema and dry palms and soles that may progress to blistering (hand-foot syndrome). Mucositis, diarrhea, and neutropenia may also occur. Oxaliplatin often causes peripheral neuropathy that may be permanent.

Following therapy, patients with rectal cancer should be evaluated at approximately 6-month intervals for up to 5 years with a history, physical examination, and serum CEA assessment. Contrast-enhanced CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis are typically obtained annually for 5 years. Patients who achieve a complete response to nonsurgical therapy and are managed nonoperatively require additional endoscopic and MRI surveillance of the rectum, especially for the first 2 years after radiation therapy.

Most patients with nonmetastatic colon cancers are initially treated with surgical resection. For locally invasive colon cancers that appear potentially challenging to resect fully, neoadjuvant chemotherapy may facilitate excision. In patients who did not receive preoperative chemotherapy, pathologic evaluation determines the need for adjuvant treatment.

Stage I colon cancer is treated with resection alone. Patients with stage II cancer lacking high-risk features, such as poorly differentiated histology, T4 primary tumor, lymphovascular invasion, inadequate lymph node sampling, elevated postoperative CEA, or perforation or obstruction, carry a favorable prognosis and are unlikely to benefit from adjuvant treatment. Patients with one or more of these risk factors should be considered for adjuvant 5-FU or capecitabine. All patients with stage II colon tumors should also be assessed for MSI or dMMR status because such tumors at this stage are at low risk for recurrence and relatively resistant to adjuvant chemotherapy; in most cases, they should not be treated with adjuvant chemotherapy regardless of other risk factors.

Patients with stage III cancer should receive adjuvant chemotherapy. FOLFOX and CAPOX are equally acceptable adjuvant chemotherapy regimens and reduce the risk for cancer recurrence and death. Five-year survival with a 3-month course of CAPOX appears to be virtually the same as with a 6-month course but with substantially less toxicity.

The role of posttreatment surveillance following curative-intent treatment is to identify oligometastatic disease in the liver or lung that may be resectable with curative intent. As with rectal cancer, routine evaluation and serum CEA assessment should be done at approximately 6-month intervals, with annual CT for up to 5 years after therapy.

Patients with metastatic foci confined to the liver or lung should be referred for surgical evaluation. Complete resection of metastatic foci may lead to cure in 25% or more of these patients.

Colonoscopy is recommended 1 year after definitive treatment (3 to 6 months if a complete colonoscopy was not done preoperatively) and then in 3 years, followed by every 5 years, unless abnormalities are found.

All metastatic CRC requires immunohistochemical and molecular analysis for dMMR or MSI determination; KRAS, NRAS, and BRAF gene mutation status; and HER2 amplification status. These tests can be done on either the primary tumor or a metastatic lesion; rebiopsy of metastases for these studies is not needed. Mutational analysis of circulating-tumor DNA can also provide this information.

Patients with dMMR/MSI tumors are likely to respond to immunotherapy with a PD-1 inhibitor with or without a CTLA4 inhibitor. Response rates are high, and up to 10% of patients will achieve a long-term complete response and may be cured.

Patients with metastatic disease limited to the liver should be evaluated for surgical resection with curative intent. Patients with resectable lesions may undergo initial resection or receive neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery.

Unresectable pMMR metastatic CRC is treatable but not curable. Although chemotherapy may be palliative and even extend survival, patients with a poor performance status may not benefit or may have unacceptable toxicity. A careful discussion should be undertaken with the patient to establish goals of care and realistic expectations. 5-FU, often combined with leucovorin, is at the center of most treatment regimens for patients with metastatic pMMR CRC. Capecitabine is an oral alternative to 5-FU. Other cytotoxic agents used in metastatic CRC include irinotecan and oxaliplatin.

Bevacizumab, an anti–vascular endothelial growth factor monoclonal antibody, is often given concurrently with first-line cytotoxic chemotherapy regimens. This agent potentiates other chemotherapies, resulting in a modestly increased progression-free survival and, in some studies, overall survival. Bevacizumab commonly causes hypertension, sometimes requiring antihypertensive medication. It also interferes with wound healing and should be discontinued 6 to 8 weeks before elective surgery and withheld for at least a month after surgery. Very rare but potentially life-threatening adverse effects include gastrointestinal perforations and arterial thrombotic events, such as myocardial infarction and cerebrovascular accidents.

Cetuximab and panitumumab are monoclonal antibodies that block activation of the epidermal growth factor receptor. They are potentially active only in tumors that have nonmutated (wild-type) KRAS, NRAS, and BRAF genes and have a nonamplified HER2 gene. These agents appear to have activity only in tumors derived from the left side of the large intestine. The major adverse effect of these agents is an acneiform rash, which can be painful, pruritic, and socially debilitating. There is a tight correlation between rash and antitumor activity, and patients who have only a mild skin rash are unlikely to be benefitting from these agents.

An exception is patients with metastatic CRC who have a BRAF V600E mutation. In these patients, the combination of a BRAF inhibitor (e.g., encorafenib) and an EGFR inhibitor (cetuximab or panitumumab) is active. This combination can be used either alone as a second-line regimen or concurrently with first-line chemotherapy.

In CRC tumors with high HER2 amplification (3+ amplification by immunohistochemistry) anti-HER2 combination therapies (e.g., trastuzumab plus tucatinib) are active, as is the antibody-drug conjugate fam-trastuzumab-deruxtecan.

Multigene sequencing beyond KRAS, NRAS, and BRAF may open some experimental options, but it rarely yields useful information in terms of standard management options at this time.

Anal cancer is a human papillomavirus (HPV)–associated malignancy. Unlike rectal cancer, which is an adenocarcinoma, anal cancer is a squamous cell carcinoma. Anal cancer is often curable with combined radiation therapy and chemotherapy; surgery is typically not indicated and is used only as a salvage procedure. Mitomycin plus either capecitabine or 5-FU is the standard chemotherapy regimen. Although complete regression may be observed as soon as 8 weeks after radiation therapy, responding tumors may continue to regress for up to 6 months after radiation therapy. If tumor growth is seen after radiation therapy, salvage surgery with a permanent colostomy is indicated.

Distant metastases are less common. When they do develop, chemotherapy with a platinum-containing regimen (oxaliplatin, cisplatin, or carboplatin) is often active. Immunotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors, such as nivolumab or pembrolizumab, has shown modest activity in metastatic disease.

Although HPV vaccination is effective in preventing HPV-related malignancies, there is no evidence that HPV vaccination plays a role in treatment or posttreatment management of patients with anal cancer. See Human Papillomavirus in Foundations of Clinical Practice for further discussion of HPV vaccination.

Approximately 57,000 patients are diagnosed with exocrine pancreatic cancer each year in the United States. Mortality is high, with approximately 46,000 deaths expected annually. Only patients whose disease has not spread to other organs and who can undergo a complete resection have a chance of cure. When disease is confined to the pancreas but locally unresectable because of invasion into the celiac vessels, median survival is approximately 1 year. For those with metastatic disease, median survival is typically about 6 months.

Most pancreatic cancers lack a genetic predisposition, although 5% to 10% of patients have a strong family history of pancreatic cancer, an identifiable variant that confers increased risk, or both. Some rare familial pancreatic cancer syndromes have been recognized, including in patients with BRCA pathogenic variants. Germline testing for BRCA, PALB2, ATM, CHEK2, and other heritable pathogenic variants is now recommended for all patients with pancreatic cancer. In patients without pancreatic cancer who harbor a predisposing germline variant (e.g., BRCA2, ATM, STK11, CDKN2A), annual screening with MRI and/or endoscopic ultrasonography should be considered, especially if a family history of pancreatic cancer is present (see [Table: Table: Cancer Risk Management for BRCA1/2 Variants]

). Less than 1% of pancreatic cancers are dMMR; patients with dMMR should be tested for germline MMR deficiency (Lynch syndrome). Chronic pancreatitis, obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, high red meat consumption, alcohol use, and tobacco use are other risk factors.

Painless jaundice, abdominal pain, weight loss, persistent fevers, or protracted nausea and vomiting may be presenting symptoms. Manifestations of hypercoagulability, including Trousseau syndrome (a migratory superficial thrombophlebitis of the lower extremities), chronic disseminated intravascular coagulation, and venous thromboembolic disease may occur and may be the first sign of underlying pancreatic cancer.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen (or noncontrast chest CT and abdominal MRI) are appropriate for staging and treatment planning. PET has not been shown to add value and is not part of standard management for most patients with pancreatic cancer.

For patients whose disease is confined to the pancreas with or without involved locoregional lymph nodes, resection is the most important consideration. Percutaneous or endoscopic ultrasonography-guided transgastric biopsy can be used to confirm the diagnosis; however, some patients with clinical features strongly suggesting malignancy may not require a preoperative biopsy because false-negative results would not eliminate the need for surgical resection. MRI may also be useful in delineating resectability in borderline patients. Conversion therapy—using radiation and/or chemotherapy to convert locally unresectable disease to resectable disease—may be considered in patients in whom a response might create a plane of resection.

Patients should undergo resection if they appear to have technically resectable disease and no evidence of metastatic disease. Adjuvant chemotherapy can prolong survival in patients who are medically well enough to receive chemotherapy. Treatment options include 5-FU, leucovorin, irinotecan, and oxaliplatin (modified FOLFIRINOX) in patients with good performance status who can tolerate aggressive chemotherapy and gemcitabine plus capecitabine for less fit patients for whom adjuvant chemotherapy is still appropriate. The data for use of adjuvant radiation therapy for patients with pancreatic cancer are controversial, but most recent data do not show a benefit to the routine use of postoperative radiation therapy.

Patients with pancreatic cancer who have BRCA pathogenic variants may also benefit from treatment with poly (adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase inhibitors if they respond to initial FOLFIRINOX treatment.

Patients experience considerable morbidity following resection of pancreatic cancer, with most requiring pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy, and those with the most extensive pancreatic resection need lifelong insulin therapy.

For metastatic disease, FOLFIRINOX or the combination of nab-paclitaxel and gemcitabine has each shown better antitumor activity and modest survival benefits over single-agent gemcitabine in randomized trials; however, the combination regimens have higher toxicity. Liposome-encapsulated irinotecan added to 5-FU has shown modest activity as second-line therapy in patients who have not been previously treated with irinotecan.

Epidemiology, risk factors, and clinical manifestations of esophageal and gastric cancer are additionally discussed in Metaplastic and Neoplastic Disorders of the Esophagus in Gastroenterology and Gastric Adenocarcinoma in Gastroenterology.

Upper gastrointestinal tract cancers are a major cause of cancer deaths worldwide, particularly in Asia and Africa. The incidence has been increasing steadily in North America and other Western countries, albeit with changing histology. With the dramatic rise over the past several decades in the incidence of adenocarcinoma of the distal esophagus and proximal stomach, esophageal cancer and gastric cancer are now considered a single entity (gastroesophageal cancer).

Smoking and alcohol use remain the major risk factors for traditional squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus. Risk factors for the now far more common adenocarcinoma of the esophagus, gastroesophageal junction, and proximal stomach also include smoking along with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and obesity. The development of Barrett esophagus resulting from GERD, especially with dysplastic features, is a further risk for developing adenocarcinoma of the esophagus, and regular surveillance is indicated. See Barrett Esophagus in Gastroenterology for more detailed information on Barrett esophagus and GERD.

Patients may present with pain or difficulty swallowing, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, or persistent dyspepsia. Upper endoscopy and biopsy establish the diagnosis. Endoscopic ultrasonography is routinely used to assess the depth of tumor penetration and presence of involved lymph nodes. Unlike with evaluation of other gastrointestinal tumors, PET-CT is indicated as part of standard preoperative staging and management of gastroesophageal cancer.

Although surgery is the primary treatment of locoregional disease, data have shown a survival benefit for neoadjuvant therapy, both with chemotherapy alone and with chemotherapy plus concurrent radiation therapy. More recent data additionally demonstrate improved outcomes with the use of adjuvant immunotherapy (PD-1 inhibitors), and this is now regarded as standard care, although the benefit is more substantial in squamous cell cancers than in adenocarcinomas.

Treatment of recurrent or metastatic disease is determined by histologic subtype (adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma), whether HER2 is overexpressed, the presence and intensity of PD-L1, and MMR status.

Approximately 25% of gastroesophageal adenocarcinomas overexpress HER2, and recent data have shown that the combination of trastuzumab and the PD-1 inhibitor pembrolizumab added to chemotherapy results in a striking increase in clinical response. Trastuzumab deruxtecan, an antibody-drug conjugate, is an option for second-line treatment of advanced HER2-positive gastroesophageal cancers.

For PD-L1–positive squamous cell and adenocarcinomas, the immune checkpoint inhibitors nivolumab or pembrolizumab are used with chemotherapy; for patients with squamous cell cancer, nivolumab in combination with ipilimumab is also an option.

Data also support the use of PD-1 inhibitors for all metastatic dMMR tumors.

Gastrointestinal neuroendocrine tumors (NETs), formerly called carcinoid tumors, arise from the endocrine cells of the digestive tract. Pancreatic NETs arise from the islets of Langerhans cells and were previously called islet cell tumors. NETs are rare but are typically indolent, and patients frequently survive many years, resulting in a high prevalence relative to the incidence. Patients with inherited syndromes, such as multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN1), are at increased risk for NETs.

Well-differentiated NETs exhibit indolent growth. These range from low-grade (low proliferative index) to intermediate-grade (somewhat higher proliferative index) tumors. As would be expected, intermediate-grade tumors are generally, but not always, more aggressive than low-grade tumors. Poorly differentiated, high-grade NETs are highly aggressive tumors.

Most NETs do not produce hormones and are termed nonfunctional; they are often discovered incidentally. The liver is the most common site of metastases, and metastatic disease may be present asymptomatically for many years before it is identified.

Approximately 25% of gastrointestinal NETs produce a hormone, in which case the hormone-related symptoms are often both the source of presentation and morbidity. They can produce serotonin, which can cause the classic carcinoid syndrome of diarrhea and facial flushing. The clinical features of functional pancreatic NETs, most commonly gastrinomas and insulinomas, are discussed in Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors in Gastroenterology. Although histologically similar, gastrointestinal and pancreatic NETs behave differently and are treated differently, with several drugs showing activity against pancreatic NETs but not gastrointestinal NETs.

Well-differentiated gastrointestinal NETs are predominantly found in the appendix, often incidentally detected after an appendectomy. Metastases from well-differentiated NETs smaller than 2 cm confined to the appendix are extremely uncommon; no further surgery is indicated, and routine follow-up imaging is not recommended.

Given the indolent nature of other well-differentiated NETs, observation and serial imaging are appropriate initially; asymptomatic patients may do well, with minimal growth and no symptoms for years, even with metastatic disease. A follow-up examination and imaging at approximately 3 months is appropriate. In patients whose disease appears stable at the 3-month CT scan, further monitoring with serial imaging at 3- to 6-month intervals is appropriate.

Given their aggressive behavior, poorly differentiated, high-grade NETs are treated with the platinum-based cytotoxic regimens used for small cell lung cancer.

In tumors with somatostatin receptors, the somatostatin analogs octreotide or lanreotide may be used for hormonal control or to stabilize progressing disease. For tumors that progress after treatment with somatostatin analogues, peptide receptor radionuclide therapy is recommended. Hepatic arterial embolization, radiofrequency ablation, or surgical debulking is sometimes used to decrease hormone production or to relieve symptoms of tumor bulk.

Lung Cancer

This section focuses on lung cancer tissue types, staging, treatment, and follow-up. See Lung Cancer in Pulmonary Medicine for discussion of epidemiology, screening, clinical manifestations, and diagnosis of patients with lung cancer.

The two major classes of lung cancer are non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small cell lung cancer (SCLC). Approximately 80% of lung cancer cases are NSCLC, which is divided into adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma. Adenocarcinoma is the most common NSCLC subtype and accounts for almost all lung cancer diagnoses in patients who have no smoking history. It most commonly presents as a solitary nodule or mass located in the periphery of the lung.

Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common subtype of NSCLC. It correlates highly with smoking history and usually originates in the central airways (trachea, main stem bronchi, lobar, and segmental bronchi) (see

). Individuals with squamous cell carcinoma often have cough and hemoptysis caused by central airway involvement. Radiographically, squamous cell carcinoma may manifest as postobstructive pneumonia or lobar collapse. In large cell carcinoma, an undifferentiated carcinoma, patients characteristically exhibit a peripheral mass with prominent necrosis (see

).

In the past decade, the development of targeted therapy for specific genetic alterations has allowed for the individualization of therapy and improved survival. For example, at least 15% of adenocarcinomas will have driver alterations (e.g., EGFR, ALK, ROS, RET, KRAS, HER2/neu), many of which can be specifically targeted. These alterations may also be found in patients with squamous or undifferentiated NSCLC. Knowledge of the alteration pattern for a specific tumor is critical to making therapeutic decisions for most patients. It is essential that all patients with NSCLC undergo appropriate genetic testing, preferably on biopsy specimens.

SCLC accounts for about 20% of all lung cancers. It is most strongly associated with cigarette smoking and typically occurs adjacent to the central airways, often with extensive lymphadenopathy and distant metastasis at diagnosis. Imaging commonly shows a perihilar mass (see

) or a large mediastinal mass that encompasses lymph nodes with an uncertain primary site. Paraneoplastic syndromes are most associated with SCLC. These include the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (rare in other lung tumors), hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (see

), inflammatory myopathies, Cushing syndrome caused by ectopic adrenocorticotropic hormone secretion, and other hematologic and neurologic syndromes.

The initial evaluation of lung cancer includes a full history, physical examination, complete blood count, serum chemistry testing, and CT of the chest. The definitive diagnosis of lung cancer requires tissue histopathology or cytology. Because many techniques are available for tissue diagnosis, the diagnostic strategy depends on the size and location of the tumor, patient characteristics, and local expertise. In general, mediastinal and central lesions are best approached with bronchoscopy, and smaller peripheral lesions are best approached with transthoracic needle aspiration. In patients with radiographic evidence of advanced-stage disease, diagnosis and staging are best accomplished with a single invasive test at a location that will establish both the diagnosis and disease stage.

Definitive staging of lung cancer is essential because it allows for accurate prognostication and serves as a guide for treatment decision making. NSCLC is staged using the TNM staging system, considering the characteristics of the primary tumor (T), regional lymph node involvement (N), and metastatic disease (M).

PET/CT is a standard component of initial staging for all patients with NSCLC and is useful for assessing mediastinal nodes and identifying distant metastatic disease. Brain MRI is indicated for all patients diagnosed with NSCLC except those with very early-stage cancer based on initial imaging. Brain metastases are seen in about 20% of patients at diagnosis and in more than 40% during the course of the disease. Mediastinal node sampling, through either mediastinoscopy or endobronchial ultrasonography–guided biopsy, is also indicated in patients with NSCLC except for those with very early-stage cancers and those with clinically evident distant metastatic disease.

SCLC is generally staged as limited or extensive disease. Limited disease is defined as disease that affects only one hemithorax and regional lymph nodes that can be safely encompassed in a radiotherapy field. The presence of disease outside these locations defines extensive-stage disease.

Patients with SCLC should undergo contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and MRI of the brain with contrast. Alternatively, PET/CT and brain MRI may be preferred in selected patients. Mediastinal node sampling is not routinely performed in the evaluation of SCLC.

Treatment of NSCLC is based largely on disease stage and is divided into early-stage, locally advanced, and metastatic categories.

Early-stage disease refers to lung cancer that is localized and potentially amenable to surgical resection. This category typically encompasses stage I and II cancers, although some patients with stage II cancer are not amenable to resection based on location or extent of the primary tumor. Stages I and II are differentiated by the presence or absence of intrapulmonary or hilar nodal metastatic disease and by the size and invasiveness of the primary tumor into adjacent structures.

Patients deemed potential surgical candidates based on imaging need to undergo a rigorous functional evaluation to predict their anticipated pulmonary reserve after surgery. The initial evaluation consists of FEV~1 and Dlco measurement. If both are greater than 80% of the predicted value, no further evaluation is needed. However, if either is less than 80% of the predicted value, the predicted postoperative FEV~1 and Dlco should be calculated to determine whether resection is feasible.

Lobectomy is the preferred surgical procedure in early-stage disease. Proximal tumors may be less amenable to lobectomy. In these patients, sleeve resection (resection of the involved lobe and a portion of the main stem bronchus) has fewer postoperative complications and is preferable to pneumonectomy. Sublobar resection can be considered in older patients or those with small stage I cancers.

Approximately 50% of patients who have surgically resected stage I, II, or IIIA cancer survive 5 years. Patients with pathologic stage I cancer who undergo surgical resection have a 60% to 70% survival rate at 5 years, and patients with stage II cancer have an approximate 40% survival rate at 5 years.

Primary radiation therapy, most commonly in the form of stereotactic body radiation therapy, is an appropriate treatment option for patients with early-stage NSCLC who cannot undergo surgery. Stereotactic body radiation therapy results in excellent rates of local control and is currently the preferred treatment for patients with lymph node–negative cancer when surgery cannot be done. For patients with lymph node–positive cancers who are not surgical candidates, combined chemotherapy and radiation therapy is used. Patients with localized tumors treated with radiation therapy have a mean survival rate of greater than 3 years.

Platinum-based adjuvant chemotherapy administered after resection of stage II or III lung cancer decreases the risk for death at 5 years by approximately 5% in patients with stage II disease and 10% or more in patients with stage III disease. Adjuvant chemotherapy can also be considered for high-risk patients with lymph node–negative early-stage NSCLC (see [Table: Table: High-Risk Factors in Stage IB to IIB NSCLC]

). Chemotherapy consists of cisplatin with a second agent and is typically given for four cycles.

Patients treated surgically for stage I or II disease who have positive margins benefit from re-resection when possible and, if this is not possible, should be treated with postoperative radiation therapy.

Targeted therapy and immunotherapy also have a role as adjuvant treatment in some patients with early-stage disease. For tumors found to have certain mutations in the EGFR gene, treatment with osimertinib after adjuvant chemotherapy has led to a statistically significant improvement in outcomes and reduction in recurrence risk. For tumors harboring an activating fusion involving the ALK gene, treatment with alectinib instead of chemotherapy significantly improved disease-free survival. In patients without an EGFR or ALK genetic mutation, the addition of immunotherapy, such as atezolizumab or pembrolizumab, after completing chemotherapy further improves outcomes. For patients with resected disease and no contraindications, such as significant autoimmune disease, immunotherapy should be administered for 1 year.

After treatment is completed, patients with early-stage disease remain at risk for both distant and local recurrence. Many patients with smoking histories are also at risk for developing a second primary lung cancer and cancers of the head, neck, and other sites. Recommendations for surveillance include history, physical examination, and chest CT at least every 6 months for the first 2 years and then annually. Smoking cessation decreases the risk for new primary lung cancers by 20% to 90%; the risk steadily declines beginning 5 years after quitting but never reaches the incidence found in persons who have never smoked.

Locally advanced lung cancer (stage III) is defined by clinically detectable lymphadenopathy in the mediastinum or by a primary tumor that invades into local structures, such as the mediastinum, heart, trachea, esophagus, or great vessels.

Stage III disease is extremely heterogeneous, and all patients with stage III disease should be seen by an experienced multidisciplinary team. Patients with limited ipsilateral mediastinal node involvement, a single nodal station, and nonbulky disease can undergo surgical resection. These patients will all generally receive neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy and/or radiation treatment. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy with chemotherapy and immunotherapy in appropriate patients has been shown to be effective and can potentially allow for more limited lung resection. Molecular testing is essential in this setting because patients with EGFR and ALK alterations do not benefit from this approach. Patients with resectable stage III NSCLC with certain EGFR mutations, however, should receive adjuvant osimertinib. Adjuvant alectinib is given to patients who have tumors with an ALK gene fusion.

For patients with more extensive disease (e.g., multistation ipsilateral nodal involvement), concurrent chemotherapy and radiation therapy followed by immunotherapy has curative potential.

Similarly, patients with unresectable disease, typically because of N3 (contralateral mediastinum) nodes or an extensively invasive primary tumor, are treated with combined or sequential platinum-based chemotherapy and radiation therapy. Unfortunately, the risk for recurrence, both locoregional and distant, is very high despite chemoradiation treatment. The use of durvalumab, an immune checkpoint inhibitor that blocks PD-L1, has shown statistically significant improvement in overall survival in this scenario.

Metastatic NSCLC (stage IV) is defined as disease that has spread to distant sites such as the liver, bone, or brain. The presence of one or more tumor nodules in the contralateral lung also qualifies as metastatic disease, but the prognosis in patients with that pattern is notably better than that in patients with distant disease; therefore, it is classified as M1a, with other distant sites given the designation of M1b (single site) or M1c (multiple sites). Patients with only a single site of metastatic disease (most frequently in the brain) are potentially curable after resection or stereotactic radiosurgery.

Treatment options for patients with metastatic NSCLC have dramatically increased in the past several years. This development has led to statistically significant improvements in survival for patients with selected subtypes of metastatic NSCLC. Despite these advances, however, metastatic NSCLC remains an incurable disease for most patients. Early palliative care interventions in this patient population generally improve quality of life even as they continue to receive cancer-directed treatments.

Before selection of the optimal treatment for a patient, it is essential to determine histology, perform broad molecular profiling to check for driver alterations, measure PD-L1 expression in tumor cells, and evaluate performance status. Identifying these alterations, assessing markers for immunotherapy response, and selecting the appropriate therapy can improve prognosis and survival (see

). For patients with a relevant genomic alteration, targeted therapy is frequently the recommended first-line treatment. The list of relevant validated genomic alterations for which targeted therapies are available continues to expand (see [Table: Table: Targeted Therapies for Metastatic Lung Cancer]

). Tissue-based testing is preferred, but if this is not feasible, molecular testing can be done on peripheral blood leukocytes (so-called liquid biopsy). A quantitative measure of PD-L1 on tumor cells is used to determine suitability for immune checkpoint inhibitors that target this pathway; higher expression (especially if >50%) is more predictive of treatment response.

For patients with lung cancer that does not have a driver alteration, initial treatment consists of an immune checkpoint inhibitor either alone or in combination with chemotherapy and/or a second immune checkpoint inhibitor. Combining chemotherapy and immunotherapy has been shown to improve survival regardless of PD-L1 status, although it also increases the risk for adverse effects. In the front-line setting, single-agent pembrolizumab is particularly beneficial if PD-L1 expression is seen on 50% or more of tumor cells. Studies have found steady improvements in 5-year overall survival rates (18%-30%) with newer immunotherapy-based first-line regimens. The PD-1 inhibitor cemiplimab, for example, is approved first-line therapy in combination with platinum-based chemotherapy regardless of PD-L1 expression or histology, or as monotherapy when PD-L1 expression is 50% or higher.

As mentioned, platinum-based chemotherapy is used in the first-line setting in combination with immunotherapy for patients without a driver alteration (or alone in these patients with a contraindication to immunotherapy) or in the subsequent-line setting after targeted therapies or immunotherapy. Cisplatin is slightly more active, but carboplatin is commonly used in the noncurative setting because of its more favorable adverse effect profile. Chemotherapy is administered for four to six cycles.

Bevacizumab, a monoclonal antibody directed against vascular endothelial growth factor, can be added to platinum-based chemotherapy with or without immunotherapy. It only modestly improves progression-free survival and overall survival and carries a risk for thrombosis, stroke, myocardial infarction, and hemoptysis. The squamous subtype is a contraindication to bevacizumab because of increased risk for fatal hemoptysis.

For tumors that respond to initial treatment, it is standard to continue some treatments as maintenance therapy, specifically the targeted therapies, immunotherapies, bevacizumab, and select chemotherapies (pemetrexed, gemcitabine). In patients with very limited residual disease after systemic therapy, stereotactic body radiation therapy can be used to treat residual metastatic sites. This improves progression-free survival compared with maintenance chemotherapy alone. It can also be used to treat isolated or limited areas of disease progression in patients receiving otherwise active systemic therapy.

Targeted therapy or immunotherapy can be used as a subsequent-line treatment for patients who did not receive it as part of their initial therapy. Treatment options for patients who have progression of metastatic disease after targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and platinum-based chemotherapy are limited. Assessment should be performed for driver alterations if not previously done because highly active therapies are available and can benefit patients even in cases of progression after chemotherapy (see [Table: Table: Targeted Therapies for Metastatic Lung Cancer]

). Otherwise, treatment typically consists of single-agent chemotherapy. Long-term outcomes in this setting are poor.

Patients with a poor performance status due to lung cancer that has a treatment-naive driver alteration should be considered for urgent initiation of targeted therapy. If no driver alteration is present or if the patient has irreversible end-organ damage, they are unlikely to benefit from chemotherapy or immunotherapy and should be considered for hospice care.

Treatment recommendations for SCLC are based on whether the patient has limited or extensive disease, as defined previously.

Patients with SCLC usually present with proximal and often large tumors but may occasionally present with a solitary pulmonary nodule, in which case the diagnosis of SCLC may not be made until after surgical resection (see Diagnosis of Lung Cancer in Pulmonary Medicine). After resection, these patients should be treated with adjuvant chemotherapy or chemoradiation. Surgery can also be performed in those few patients presenting with small primary tumors without lymph node spread, although preoperative evaluation should include endobronchial ultrasonography or mediastinoscopy to rule out occult nodal involvement. These patients should also receive adjuvant chemotherapy.

Most patients with limited SCLC will not meet the criteria for primary surgery. Treatment for such patients consists of thoracic radiation therapy combined with four cycles of platinum-based chemotherapy (cisplatin or carboplatin plus etoposide). Consolidation with immunotherapy has been shown to improve outcomes when given after chemotherapy or chemoradiation therapy. Prophylactic cranial irradiation can be considered in patients with responsive disease because it may decrease the rate of subsequent brain metastases and possibly improve overall survival. Prophylactic cranial irradiation increases the risk for cognitive impairment in patients 60 years and older, however, and is not indicated in patients with poor performance status or those with preexisting neurocognitive impairment. Alternatively, patients can undergo surveillance with serial MRI of the brain.

For patients with extensive disease, treatment consists of combination platinum-etoposide chemotherapy and immunotherapy for up to four cycles, continuing immunotherapy as maintenance until progression. Patients with extensive disease who have a favorable response to chemotherapy but persistent involvement in the lung may be treated with radiation therapy. Patients with lower-volume disease that is responsive to treatment and without brain metastases can be considered for prophylactic cranial irradiation, although there is less benefit than for limited-stage disease. It is important to recognize that SCLC differs from NSCLC in that patients with poor performance status who have not been previously treated may exhibit prompt and significant responses to chemotherapy.

Despite treatment response, recurrences are very common, even in patients with limited disease. For patients with recurrent disease who have had a disease-free interval of more than 3 months, re-treatment with the initial platinum-based doublet regimen can be used because the likelihood of response is favorable. Single-agent chemotherapy with topotecan or lurbinectedin is beneficial in patients who maintain good performance status. If immunotherapy was not used as part of the initial treatment, it should be considered in this setting, although the results are not as remarkable as in patients with NSCLC. As with NSCLC, addressing goals of care and aggressive symptom management are important.

Head and Neck Cancer

This section covers squamous cell carcinoma in the oral cavity, oropharynx, nasopharynx, hypopharynx, larynx, paranasal sinuses, thyroid, and salivary glands. Thyroid cancer is discussed in Thyroid Cancer in Endocrinology and Metabolism.

Using smoked or smokeless tobacco is an important risk factor for head and neck cancer. Alcohol use is also a known risk factor, and the combination of alcohol and tobacco synergistically increases the risk.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection spread through oral sex is also a significant cause of head and neck cancer, with most HPV-associated cancers arising in the oropharynx (tonsils or base of the tongue). Although treatment is not altered, the prognosis of HPV-associated oropharynx cancer in patients who do not have a history of tobacco use is better than that of non–HPV-related cancer. The prognosis of HPV-associated oropharynx cancer is also worse in patients who have a history of tobacco use than in those who do not but is better than for non–HPV-related cancer.

Symptoms vary with the cancer’s location, but concerning signs and symptoms include an unexplained neck mass, unilateral hearing loss or ear pain, nasal obstruction, oral pain, nonhealing oral ulcers, dysphagia, odynophagia, and hoarseness. Patients with HPV-related oropharynx cancers most commonly present with a painless neck mass, which may develop quickly, and often appears as a cystic mass on ultrasonography.

Initial evaluation of patients suspected of having head and neck cancer includes history and physical examination. Infection should be suspected in patients with a rapidly developing neck mass, particularly in the setting of upper respiratory symptoms or with typical physical findings of infection (e.g., warmth, tenderness, and erythema). In contrast, malignant neck masses are commonly painless, firm, and/or fixed on examination and are not associated with antecedent infection.

If malignancy is a potential concern, prompt referral to an otolaryngologist for assessment and direct laryngoscopy is essential. Fine-needle aspiration of suspicious neck masses provides accurate diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma. Tumor staining for p16 is standard for oropharynx cancers because p16 is overexpressed in HPV-positive cancers and can be used as a surrogate marker for HPV-related cancer if found in the oropharynx. This test is done only for oropharynx cancers because prognosis only differs for HPV-related cancers originating in the oropharynx.

When a diagnosis of malignancy has been established, imaging is indicated for assessing the extent of local disease and evaluating nodal and distant metastatic disease. MRI is preferred for assessing the primary tumor. PET/CT is useful to evaluate regional nodes and rule out distant metastatic disease, although it is not accurate in nodes smaller than 1 cm.

Stage is the most important determinant of prognosis, but the staging of head and neck cancers is complex because each subsite uses a different staging system. Staging of primary tumors is based on the size and extent of invasion into adjacent structures. Nodal staging is based on the number of positive nodes, size, and the presence or absence of bilateral lymphadenopathy. HPV-related cancer of the oropharynx has a different staging system than non–HPV-related cancer based on statistically significant differences in prognosis. Patients with early-stage head and neck cancers have long-term survival rates of 70% to 90%. Multimodality tumor board discussion is valuable for determining the proper treatment course.

In the one third of patients who present with small tumors without lymph node metastases, treatment is either surgery or radiotherapy. Treatment decisions consider tumor location and potential postoperative complications, including appearance and speech preservation. They also factor in the expected adverse effects of radiation therapy, such as acute mucositis and fatigue, as well as longer-term changes in taste, xerostomia, dental health, and an increased risk for second malignancies. The need for additional dissection of lymph nodes in the neck is determined by the site and stage of the primary tumor, presence of enlarged nodes, and the results of diagnostic imaging.

Radiation therapy and larynx-sparing surgery, consisting of either transoral laser surgery or open partial laryngectomy, offer equivalent survival benefit in patients with early-stage laryngeal cancer. These treatments focus on attaining optimal survival and function of voice, swallowing, and airway mechanics.

Adjuvant radiation therapy after primary surgical resection is recommended for patients with one or more high-risk pathologic features ( [Table: Table: Head and Neck Cancer High-Risk Features]

). Concurrent chemotherapy, typically single-agent cisplatin, and radiation therapy are used for patients at high risk for recurrence, based on nodal extracapsular extension or positive margins. Docetaxel can be substituted for cisplatin in patients who are ineligible for cisplatin treatment. Pembrolizumab, when started before surgery and continued following surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy, has been shown to reduce the risk for developing distant metastatic disease; it is now a standard part of treatment in patients undergoing surgery.

For patients with an unresectable primary tumor, extensive nodal disease, or radiographic evidence of extranodal extension, multimodality treatment with combined chemotherapy and radiation therapy is indicated. As above, cisplatin is the most commonly employed agent, with docetaxel reserved for patients who are ineligible for cisplatin. Pembrolizumab is not used in this setting.

Treatment of nasopharyngeal carcinoma with radiation alone can be used with excellent outcomes in patients with very early-stage disease. For all other patients, however, treatment consists of induction chemotherapy followed by combined chemotherapy and radiation therapy.

After treatment of localized disease, a history and physical examination, including laryngopharyngoscopy, should be conducted every 1 to 3 months for the first year after primary treatment, decreasing in frequency thereafter, with annual evaluation 5 years and beyond. Patients treated with radiotherapy that includes the thyroid bed are at risk for hypothyroidism and thyroid carcinoma. Periodic assessment of thyroid function and a physical examination of the thyroid are indicated, although screening thyroid ultrasonography should not be performed. Similarly, there is no indication for repeated PET/CT or other imaging surveillance after a negative posttreatment scan unless worrisome signs or symptoms are present. Up to 20% of head and neck cancer survivors develop a second primary cancer related to smoking and alcohol use. In addition to lifestyle modification, screening for lung cancer should be implemented in people at increased risk.

Locally recurrent head and neck cancer is curable in some patients, such as those with small, localized lesions and a long disease-free interval. Patients with limited recurrence are treated with surgery and adjuvant therapy as needed. For patients with unresectable local recurrence, treatment with radiation or chemoradiation is appropriate in some cases. Reirradiation can be associated with long-term survival but also with a potentially significant risk for toxicity, including pain, tissue necrosis, infection, and fatal bleeding.

For patients with distant metastatic disease or unresectable persistent local disease not amenable to surgery or radiation therapy, systemic therapy is the mainstay of treatment. The current standard front-line treatment is either a combination of platinum-based chemotherapy and pembrolizumab or, in patients with PD-L1–positive cancer, use of pembrolizumab alone. Patients with distant metastases and unresectable local disease have a poor prognosis, especially if their performance status is declining; treatment decisions should include options for palliative and hospice care.

Genitourinary Cancer

Adenocarcinoma of the prostate is the leading cancer diagnosis among men in the United States. Age serves as a crucial risk factor; prostate cancer is rarely diagnosed before the age of 40 years, with a significant rise in incidence in patients beyond this threshold. Family history and genetics also play an important role in risk. Men with a first-degree relative diagnosed with prostate cancer are at higher risk. Prostate cancer is linked with germline pathogenic variants in multiple genes, such as BRCA1/2, ATM, CHEK2, HOXB13, and Lynch syndrome genes, among others.

Prostate cancer is most frequently diagnosed after identification of an elevated serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level during screening. See Prostate Cancer in Oncology for a discussion of current issues relating to prostate cancer screening.

Although urinary symptoms may be present in patients with prostate cancer, they are usually related to concomitant benign prostatic hyperplasia. In some men with metastatic disease at the time of initial presentation, bone pain or back pain can be the presenting symptom. If the diagnosis is suspected based on an elevated serum PSA level, repeat testing may be indicated depending on the degree of elevation and clinical presentation. Persistent serum PSA elevation should prompt urology referral, as should an abnormal finding in the prostate on digital rectal examination (DRE).

Overdiagnosis (i.e., finding clinically insignificant cancers) is a major obstacle for recommendations of population-based prostate cancer screening. Multiparametric MRI is used to assess for the presence of clinically significant cancers, potentially avoiding biopsy in some patients with an elevated PSA level.

Prostate biopsy is performed using transrectal ultrasonography for guidance, with or without MRI targeting. Multiple core biopsy specimens should be taken from different regions of the gland to provide a sufficient diagnostic yield. The findings of atypical small acinar proliferation and multifocal high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia are both associated with a high risk for underlying cancer and should prompt further evaluation with MRI (if not already completed) and often re-biopsy.

Prognosis and treatment options in localized disease are determined by risk stratification using serum PSA measurement, Grade Group (based on Gleason score), and TNM cancer staging based on biopsy results and DRE (see [Table: Table: Prostate Cancer Risk Stratification]

). Imaging studies need not be done in patients whose risk is low or very low. Imaging should be obtained in others to evaluate for regional lymph node involvement and metastatic disease; options include prostate-specific membrane antigen PET or radionuclide bone scan combined with CT or MRI. Germline genetic testing for gene variants associated with prostate cancer, including BRCA1 and BRCA2, should be done in all men with high-risk disease, including patients with positive lymph nodes or metastatic disease. Other genes strongly recommended in panel testing include EPCAM, HOXB13, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2. Genes with a moderate risk for prostate cancer that are often included in panel testing include ATM, CHEK2, and PALB2. The risk for an underlying variant in patients with metastatic disease is 11.8%.

In addition, somatic tumor mutation testing with next-generation sequencing should be done in all patients with metastatic prostate cancer who are candidates for targeted systemic therapies. Tumor mutation testing can be repeated sequentially when a change in treatment is being considered.

Treatment options for men with newly diagnosed localized prostate cancer include active surveillance, radiation therapy, and radical prostatectomy. For men with limited life expectancy or significant medical comorbidities, observation is most appropriate.

Active surveillance is deferral of curative-intent therapy in lieu of regular monitoring for evidence of disease progression. It is an option for men with low- or very low-risk prostate cancer who have a life expectancy of at least 10 years. Active surveillance should consist of the following:

  • DRE no more than every 12 months
  • Serial serum PSA measurement no more than every 6 months
  • Prostate MRI no more than every 12 months
  • Repeat biopsy no more than every 12 months

Testing is only done more often as clinically indicated, with consideration of active treatment if disease progresses. Fifteen-year metastasis-free survival is as high as 97% in appropriately selected patients.

Active treatment of localized prostate cancer is typically a choice between external beam radiation and radical prostatectomy. Brachytherapy, in which radioactive implants are inserted into the prostate, is also an option for men with low-risk cancer or selected men with low-volume intermediate-risk cancer.

Each of the active treatment options is associated with specific adverse effects. Radiation therapy is associated with short-term risks for enteritis (approximately 20%) and cystitis (approximately 50%). These conditions become long-term complications in a very small percentage of patients. Erectile dysfunction typically increases over time after radiation therapy. By 2 years, approximately 60% to 70% of men have at least moderate erectile dysfunction.

With radical prostatectomy, the main risks are urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction, both of which are relatively common after surgery. The rate of chronic moderate to severe urinary incontinence is approximately 5% to 10%. Erectile dysfunction can persist for several years; approximately 40% of men report erectile dysfunction 2 years after surgery. Notably, in one recent study on patient-reported outcomes in men treated with surgery, radiation therapy, and active surveillance, most treatment-related differences in long-term adverse effects disappeared by 5 years.

In terms of efficacy, a large study showed no difference in survival after 10 years for patients with localized prostate cancer detected through serum PSA screening who were randomized to receive active surveillance, surgery, or radiation therapy. A trend toward improved survival was noted for patients older than 65 years who received either of the active interventions. Patients undergoing surgery or radiation therapy had decreased disease progression and were less likely to develop metastatic disease.

For men with intermediate- or higher-risk localized disease who are treated with radiation therapy, the addition of a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist or antagonist will delay disease progression. This practice has also been shown to improve overall survival after radiation therapy in men with high-risk and very high-risk prostate cancer.

After definitive local treatment, men are monitored for evidence of recurrence with serial serum PSA measurements every 3 to 4 months and DRE yearly; DRE can be omitted from monitoring if PSA level is undetectable.

PSA level should rapidly become undetectable following radical prostatectomy. PSA recurrence after surgery is defined as a detectable PSA level that increases on at least two measurements. However, after radiation treatment, PSA level will fall gradually and reach a nadir but will not necessarily become undetectable. After radiation therapy, PSA recurrence is defined as an increase in PSA level by at least 2 ng/mL (2 µg/L) above the nadir PSA level.

For men with PSA recurrence following treatment for localized disease, evaluating for evidence of clinical local or metastatic disease with imaging studies is indicated. For patients with PSA-only recurrence (also referred to as M0-recurrent prostate cancer), treatment options depend on the initial treatment modality and patient- and disease-specific risk factors, such as life expectancy and PSA doubling time.

Observation is a reasonable consideration depending on these factors. Men with a slow PSA doubling time (>10 months) do not require immediate treatment because it can take several years for clinical metastatic disease to develop in this setting. If the PSA doubling time is rapid (<10 months), treatment is generally recommended.

If treatment is indicated, and the initial treatment was surgery and metastatic disease has not been identified, salvage radiation therapy with or without androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) can be offered. If the initial treatment was with radiation therapy, local therapy (such as surgery or cryotherapy) can be offered, provided a transrectal ultrasound–guided biopsy specimen is positive, and no distant metastatic disease is identified. If the biopsy result is negative, ADT can be considered. In addition, enzalutamide, an androgen pathway inhibitor, has been shown to improve outcomes when added to ADT in men with castration-sensitive M0 prostate cancer. Other androgen pathway inhibitors (darolutamide, apalutamide) have also been shown to improve outcomes and can be used.

Options for providing ADT include orchiectomy, GnRH agonist therapy (with or without antiandrogen therapy), and GnRH antagonist therapy (see [Table: Table: Treatments for Metastatic Prostate Cancer]

). Psychological aversion to orchiectomy has limited its use in the United States, although it is a rapidly acting and cost-effective way to achieve androgen depletion. Intermittent treatment with ADT is an option for some men with M0 disease, especially those with long PSA doubling times. This strategy allows for reduction in ADT-related adverse effects in men who do not require continuous treatment.

ADT results in many short- and long-term adverse effects. Short-term effects include loss of lean body mass, fatigue, gynecomastia, hair loss, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and vasomotor symptoms. Long-term risks include increased risk for cardiovascular disease, venous thromboembolism, and reduction in bone density. All men treated with ADT should receive supplemental calcium and vitamin D. Baseline fracture risk assessment is recommended using a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry, although the impact on outcomes is uncertain.

In men who develop castration-resistant (cancer that progresses despite castration levels of testosterone <50 ng/dL [1.7 nmol/L]) M0 prostate cancer, options include observation and addition of a second- or third-generation antiandrogen medication (see [Table: Table: Treatments for Metastatic Prostate Cancer]

). As previously mentioned, the decision to add antiandrogen therapy depends on the PSA doubling time.

Once distant metastatic disease is diagnosed, the mainstay of therapy is ADT (orchiectomy, GnRH agonist therapy, or GnRH antagonist therapy). In patients who have clinical metastatic disease and are to be treated with a GnRH agonist, short-term antiandrogen therapy should precede or be started at the same time as the GnRH agonist. The combination should be continued for at least 7 days because of the risk for a transient worsening of disease-related symptoms, termed a flare reaction, with unopposed GnRH agonist treatment. Initial concomitant antiandrogen therapy is not necessary if a GnRH antagonist is used. Intermittent ADT is not typically recommended in men with clinical metastatic disease, although it can be offered to mitigate adverse effects.

Response to ADT can be assessed most easily by serial serum PSA measurement, but imaging also plays a role. Serum testosterone level should be less than 50 ng/dL (1.7 nmol/L) in men treated with ADT.

Men with newly diagnosed clinical metastatic disease are considered to have castration-naive prostate cancer. In this population, ADT can be combined with docetaxel alone or with darolutamide; abiraterone/prednisone alone or with docetaxel; enzalutamide; or apalutamide to improve survival. Radiation to the primary tumor can also be considered for men with low-volume metastatic M1 disease.

There are many treatment options for men with castration-resistant prostate cancer (disease that has progressed despite ADT therapy) (see [Table: Table: Treatments for Metastatic Prostate Cancer]

). Osteoclast inhibitors (bisphosphonates or denosumab) will reduce bone pain and lower fracture risk in men with castration-resistant metastatic prostate cancer and should be routinely prescribed for patients with bone metastases. Initial treatment options for castration-resistant prostate cancer additionally include docetaxel with prednisone; abiraterone with prednisone; enzalutamide; and, for symptomatic bone metastases, radium-223. Another radioisotope, lutetium-177, can be offered to men with progressive PSA membrane PET–positive metastatic disease after past treatment with docetaxel and an androgen pathway inhibitor. Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors can be used in patients with BRCA or homologous recombination repair genetic alterations.

For patients who develop progressive disease, a different agent can be used. Cabazitaxel, a chemotherapy agent, can be combined with prednisone for patients who have cancer progression after treatment with docetaxel. Pembrolizumab can be used for patients with cancers that have high levels of microsatellite instability or deficient mismatch repair after progression with front-line therapy and in the absence of an alternative treatment. PARP inhibitors are also a treatment option in patients with an appropriate germline variant or somatic mutation.

Testicular cancer is the most common solid tumor diagnosed in men aged 15 to 35 years, although it accounts for only about 1% of all cancers diagnosed in the United States. It is also one of the most curable forms of cancer, largely because of its sensitivity to chemotherapy.

Patients most commonly present with unilateral testicular swelling or mass. A solid testicular mass should be considered malignant until proven otherwise. This is the case for cisgender males as well as transgender females who were assigned male at birth; the risk for testicular cancer remains even with gender-affirming hormonal treatment.

Patients with localized symptoms should undergo scrotal ultrasonography and measurement of baseline tumor markers, including serum α-fetoprotein, β-human chorionic gonadotropin, and lactate dehydrogenase. Diagnosis is made through radical inguinal orchiectomy. Needle biopsy of a testicular mass is contraindicated because of concern regarding tumor seeding to the scrotum and inguinal nodes. Following diagnosis via orchiectomy, staging is performed using CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and repeat measurement of tumor marker levels. Marker levels fall at predictable rates after surgery, and sufficient time is needed before it can be concluded that these levels remain elevated. It is essential to discuss and offer sperm cryopreservation before initiating additional treatment after orchiectomy.

Management depends on histology, results of staging studies, and the presence or absence of serum tumor marker elevation after orchiectomy. Histologically, testicular cancers are either pure seminomas or nonseminomatous germ cell tumors. Tumors with seminoma pathology but elevated α-fetoprotein levels, a characteristic of nonseminomatous germ cell tumors, are termed mixed germ cell tumors and are managed as nonseminomatous germ cell tumors.

For pure seminoma, active surveillance is preferred after surgery for early-stage disease; adjuvant radiation therapy or chemotherapy with one to two cycles of carboplatin is also appropriate. Stage II seminoma is defined by retroperitoneal lymph node metastases and can be treated with either radiation to the para-aortic lymph nodes and superior ipsilateral pelvis or chemotherapy, depending on the extent of lymph node involvement.

Patients with seminomas and more extensive lymph node involvement should receive chemotherapy. For higher-stage disease, cisplatin-based chemotherapy is used. Following chemotherapy, PET/CT can determine whether residual masses require resection. Residual masses that show negative results on PET scan do not require resection and can be monitored. For residual masses that show positive results on PET scan, biopsy should be considered before removal because of the high false-positive rate with PET in this setting.

Treatment options for patients with early-stage nonseminomatous germ cell tumors after orchiectomy include active surveillance (in selected patients), retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND), or limited chemotherapy. If RPLND is performed and shows nodal involvement, adjuvant chemotherapy is recommended. The persistence of tumor marker elevation after orchiectomy without abnormal imaging findings is also an indication for chemotherapy.

Some patients with clinically metastatic retroperitoneal nodes can be managed with RPLND if markers are negative and nodal metastases are limited and small. Otherwise, chemotherapy is recommended for patients with clinical nodal disease, including those with several positive nodes, large nodes (>2 cm), or elevated markers. Any residual masses after chemotherapy should be resected.

For the first year after treatment, all patients with testicular cancer should undergo clinical evaluation every 2 to 3 months. Additionally, tumor marker measurement and imaging studies should be conducted periodically, with specific intervals determined by histology, stage, and previous treatment. After the first year, evaluations can be performed less often.

Patients with recurrent disease are treated and may be cured with combination chemotherapy or high-dose chemotherapy and autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

Men treated with chemotherapy for testicular cancer are at risk for long-term complications, such as cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, pulmonary toxicity, hypogonadism, infertility, chronic kidney disease, and neurotoxicity. The risk for developing a second solid tumor is approximately twice as high in men with a history of testicular cancer than in those without this history.

Renal cancers typically arise in the cortex of the kidney. The most common histology is clear cell carcinoma, which is also the most responsive to medical treatment. In the past, the most common presenting symptoms of renal cell carcinoma were hematuria, abdominal mass, and weight loss. Currently, most patients are diagnosed incidentally based on imaging studies done for other reasons. Ultrasonography can be used to differentiate benign cysts from complex cysts or solid masses. If a lesion is not clearly a benign cyst, dedicated kidney CT is indicated for further evaluation. If CT findings are pathognomonic for renal cell cancer, a confirmatory kidney biopsy is not needed to establish the diagnosis.

Many different paraneoplastic syndromes can be seen in patients with renal cell carcinoma, including the following:

  • Anemia
  • Hepatic dysfunction in the absence of liver metastases (known as Stauffer syndrome)
  • Fever
  • Hypercalcemia
  • Alterations in glucose metabolism
  • Erythrocytosis
  • AA amyloidosis
  • Thrombocytosis
  • Polymyalgia rheumatica

Many of these conditions can improve with resection of the primary tumor, metastatic sites, or both.

A suspicious solitary renal mass smaller than 4 cm does not necessarily require treatment, and active surveillance can be a reasonable option. If treated, surgery or ablation, most commonly cryoablation, is an option. Larger lesions require surgical treatment consisting of partial or radical nephrectomy, depending on the size and location of the primary tumor.

For patients with pathologic stage I kidney cancer, no adjuvant therapy is recommended. For patients with high-risk stage II or III clear cell carcinoma, 1 year of adjuvant pembrolizumab improves progression-free survival and is FDA approved for this purpose. Although sunitinib has also been approved by the FDA as an adjuvant therapy following surgery, its effect on survival has not been consistently proven, and it is associated with significant toxicity. Postoperative surveillance to detect recurrent disease involves history and physical examination, basic laboratory studies, and chest and abdomen imaging. The frequency of testing depends on the extent of local disease.

Resection or debulking of the primary renal cell cancer in patients with metastatic disease can be considered, but whether this approach improves outcomes in patients treated with modern therapies is unknown. Surgery or other local therapies (such as stereotactic radiation therapy) also have a role in the treatment of isolated or several easily resected areas of metastatic disease.

No specific frontline therapy has been shown to be superior for patients who present with metastatic clear cell or non–clear cell histology. Various agents, including immune checkpoint inhibitors and tyrosine kinase inhibitors, have been shown to be effective. Most frontline regimens combined a targeted therapy agent with an immune checkpoint inhibitor.

Bladder cancer is the most common cancer of the urinary tract, and most patients have transitional cell carcinoma. Common symptoms include hematuria and irritative urinary symptoms.

Any patient with gross hematuria should be referred for urologic evaluation, as should any patient confirmed to have persistent microscopic hematuria after evaluating for benign causes, such as urinary tract infection, nephrolithiasis, or underlying kidney disease with a glomerular source of erythrocytes. Notably, use of anticoagulants does not alter the need for urologic evaluation in patients with hematuria.

The primary modality of initial evaluation is cystoscopy, with biopsy of any visible tumor or mucosal abnormality. Random biopsy is performed if no abnormality is seen. If cancer is confirmed, examination under anesthesia and transurethral resection of the bladder tumor (TURBT) is performed to determine histology and depth of invasion.

Most patients are found to have superficial bladder cancer, or non–muscle-invasive disease. This includes exophytic lesions (Ta, low grade or high grade), carcinoma in situ (Tis, always high grade), or early-stage invasive cancer (T1). Small low-grade Ta tumors are treated with TURBT followed by observation or intravesical chemotherapy. All other noninvasive disease is treated with TURBT followed by either intravesical bacillus Calmette-Guérin therapy or intravesical chemotherapy.

After primary treatment for noninvasive disease, cystoscopy surveillance is indicated because of the risk for recurrent disease. Patients with larger tumors, higher-grade tumors, tumors that invade into the lamina propria, and tumors with multifocal or noninvasive recurrence have a higher risk for muscle-invasive recurrence. Most patients require cystoscopy 3 months after initial therapy, with subsequent cystoscopy at periodic intervals based on risk for recurrence. Cystectomy can be considered for patients at high risk for developing muscle-invasive disease.

If muscle-invasive disease is diagnosed, staging imaging studies for nodal and metastatic disease are indicated. Cystectomy with or without neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy is standard treatment; the addition of neoadjuvant therapy is preferred as it improves overall survival. Partial cystectomy can be considered in very carefully selected patients. For patients with limited disease who are unable or unwilling to undergo cystectomy, maximal TURBT can be combined with concurrent chemoradiotherapy. Adjuvant chemotherapy after surgical resection is an appropriate consideration in patients with high-risk features (e.g., positive nodes and extension beyond the bladder) who have not received neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Adjuvant immunotherapy has been shown to improve outcomes regardless of whether neoadjuvant chemotherapy was given.

Treatment of metastatic disease requires systemic therapy, and treatment outcomes remain poor. Cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy remains the evidence-based choice. Maintenance therapy with avelumab, an immune checkpoint inhibitor, has been shown to improve overall survival. For patients not eligible for cisplatin, either carboplatin-based chemotherapy or an immune checkpoint inhibitor can be used. With further progression, options include chemotherapy, antibody-drug conjugates, and immunotherapy, if not previously used. A targeted drug against fibroblast growth factor can be used if a mutation is present in that gene.
