Gynecologic Cancer

Ovarian cancer is the third most common gynecologic cancer worldwide, after cervical and uterine cancer. In the United States, ovarian cancer is the second most common after uterine cancer and the leading cause of death among the gynecologic cancers. Around 90% of ovarian cancers are malignant epithelial tumors, 75% of which are high-grade serous tumors. This chapter focuses on epithelial cancers. Fallopian tube cancer and primary peritoneal cancer are often considered to be in the same system as ovarian cancer and are treated similarly.

Risk factors for ovarian cancer include the following:

  • Increased age
  • Pathogenic variants of ovarian cancer susceptibility genes
  • Early menarche (before age 12 years) or late menopause (after age 52 years)
  • Nulliparity

Oral contraceptives, one or more births, and breastfeeding all offer protective effects against ovarian cancer.

The most common ovarian cancer susceptibility genes are BRCA1, BRCA2, and the mismatch repair (MMR) genes associated with Lynch syndrome. Approximately 10% to 15% of women with ovarian cancer carry a pathogenic variant in one of these genes. All women with epithelial ovarian cancer, fallopian tube cancer, or primary peritoneal cancer should be offered germline genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 pathogenic variants, ideally as part of a panel that includes other high-risk genes, such as BRIP1, EPCAM, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PALB2, PMS2, RAD51C, and RAD51D. These panels may also include ATM, which is associated with a moderate risk for ovarian cancer.

The cumulative lifetime risk for ovarian cancer is 39% to 58% in BRCA1 carriers and 13% to 29% in BRCA2 carriers (see Breast Cancer Epidemiology and Risk Factors in Oncology). In patients with a personal or family history of other Lynch syndrome cancers (e.g., colorectal cancer, cancer of the endometrium or small bowel, transitional cell carcinoma of the ureter or renal pelvis), MMR pathogenic variant testing is recommended in addition to germline genetic testing.

Ovarian cancer screening is not recommended for patients of average risk. In addition, there is no clear evidence that screening patients at high risk with either transvaginal ultrasonography or serum CA-125 measurement improves cancer-related outcomes.

For women with BRCA1, BRCA2, or MMR gene pathogenic variants, prophylactic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is recommended. The benefit of this procedure diminishes with age. It should be done after the completion of childbearing or by age 35 to 40 years for patients with BRCA1 pathogenic variants and by age 40 to 45 years for patients with BRCA2 pathogenic variants. For BRCA1 or BRCA2 carriers, prophylactic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy decreases the risk for ovarian cancers by more than 80% and decreases all-cause mortality by 77%. Further recommendations for genetic testing for and treatment of breast and ovarian cancer syndromes are discussed in Breast Cancer Epidemiology and Risk Factors in Oncology.

Patients with ovarian cancer usually present at an advanced stage with bloating, abdominal or pelvic pain, constipation, urinary symptoms, or early satiety. The initial evaluation should include the following:

  • Physical examination, including pelvic examination
  • Serum CA-125 measurement, complete blood count, chemistry profile, and liver function testing
  • Transvaginal ultrasonography
  • Additional PET, CT, or MRI as clinically indicated, especially for suspected metastatic or disseminated disease

Patients with a high suspicion for ovarian cancer should be referred to a gynecologic oncologist. Surgical exploration is recommended for diagnosis of early ovarian cancer because removing the cancer intact without rupture improves survival. Conversely, fluid cytology or image-guided biopsy can be done for advanced ovarian cancers with peritoneal masses, ascites, or pleural effusions, particularly if the disease is not initially resectable and neoadjuvant chemotherapy may be used.

Staging and prognosis are shown in [Table: Table: FIGO Ovarian Cancer Staging, Treatment, and Survival]

. Early-stage, low-grade histology, serous histology, minimal to no disease after surgical debulking, and young age are associated with improved survival. Thirty-one percent of patients diagnosed with ovarian cancer survive 10 years, one third of whom have stage III or IV cancer. The 5-year overall survival rate is around 49% and is longer for patients with early-stage disease and favorable histologic subtypes.

Surgical staging includes total hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, peritoneal washings, omentectomy, and pelvic and para-aortic lymph node sampling. Surgical debulking, including resection of metastatic disease, improves prognosis. The volume of residual disease after surgery correlates inversely with survival. Less than 1 cm of residual tumor after surgical resection is associated with improved prognosis.

Patients with stage I ovarian cancer with favorable histology (typically low-grade tumors) may be treated with surgical resection alone. All other patients should receive adjuvant platinum-taxane chemotherapy. There are several options for more advanced disease. In women with stage III disease, the addition of intraperitoneal chemotherapy to systemic therapy has been shown to improve survival in some trials, albeit with more toxicity. In selected high-risk patients (such as those with ascites or pleural effusions at diagnosis), the angiogenesis inhibitor bevacizumab can be added to the initial treatment and then as maintenance therapy. Similarly, the poly (adenosine diphosphate-ribose) polymerase inhibitors olaparib, niraparib, veliparib, and rucaparib can also be used as maintenance for selected patients, particularly in those with BRCA1 or BRCA2 pathogenic variants or tumors with evidence of homologous recombination deficiency. Finally, in patients with initially unresectable disease, neoadjuvant chemotherapy is recommended to shrink the tumor to facilitate surgical debulking.

Posttreatment surveillance consists of physical and pelvic examinations every 2 to 4 months for 2 years, then every 3 to 6 months for the following 3 years, and then annually. Surveillance of CA-125 levels may facilitate early identification of tumor progression but does not affect survival. If desired, surveillance can be initiated if the CA-125 level is elevated at diagnosis.

Despite optimal treatment, 80% to 85% of women with stage III or IV ovarian cancer will relapse. Patients who relapse 6 months or more after initial platinum-containing chemotherapy are considered to have platinum-sensitive disease, have a better prognosis, and are usually treated with platinum-containing combination chemotherapy. Adding bevacizumab to combination chemotherapy improves disease-free survival but increases the risk for serious gastrointestinal and cardiovascular toxicities. For patients with platinum-resistant disease, various single agents can be used.

Cervical cancer remains the second most common cause of mortality from cancer in women worldwide. In the United States, approximately 14,000 new patients are diagnosed with invasive cervical cancer per year, and about 4000 deaths are reported. During the last 30 years, cervical cancer incidence and deaths in developed countries have decreased by more than 50%, primarily because of screening and preventive treatment. Squamous cell carcinoma is the histologic type in 70% of cervical cancers, with adenocarcinoma accounting for 20%; the remaining 10% is divided into other rare histologic types.

The mean age of diagnosis in the United States is 48 years. Risk factors include earlier onset of sexual activity and having several partners or a high-risk partner (e.g., history of sexually transmitted infection, positive for human papillomavirus [HPV]). Immunosuppression, including HIV infection, low socioeconomic status, smoking, and oral contraceptive use are additional risk factors. HPV is the causative agent in most patients and can be detected in 99.7% of cervical cancers. The HPV 16 and 18 variants account for 70% of cases. HPV vaccination markedly decreases the incidence of cervical dysplasia and cervical cancer. HPV vaccination is covered in Human Papillomavirus in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

Patients with early cervical cancer are frequently asymptomatic. The most common symptoms are abnormal or heavy vaginal bleeding or vaginal discharge. Patients with advanced disease may present with pelvic or back pain along with bowel or bladder symptoms. The diagnosis is established by direct biopsy of a visible lesion, colposcopy, or cone biopsy (conization). Current guidelines recommend complete blood count, chemistry profile, liver function testing, and imaging studies for staging moderate- and high-risk cancers. HIV testing should be considered. Cervical cancer staging and treatment are described in [Table: Table: FIGO Cervical Cancer Staging and Treatment]

. For patients with tumors 2 cm in size or smaller that are confined to the cervix with no lymph node involvement, fertility-sparing surgeries such as conization (only for stage IA) or radical trachelectomy, in which the cervix and upper vagina are removed but the uterine corpus is preserved, are options.

The 5-year relative survival rate for all stages of cervical cancer is 67.5%. The anatomic stage is the most important predictor of prognosis. Ninety percent of patients with localized disease survive 5 years. The 5-year survival rate drops to 58% for patients with regional disease and 17% for those with disease extending outside of the true pelvis or involving the bladder or rectum.

Surveillance is recommended to monitor for potentially curable recurrences. Guidelines recommend a history and physical examination every 3 to 6 months for 2 years, every 6 to 12 months during years 3 to 5, and then annually based on the risk for recurrence. Annual vaginal cytology, cervical cytology, or both can be considered but is unlikely to detect asymptomatic recurrences alone. Imaging and laboratory studies are recommended only if indicated based on symptoms or findings on examination that are suspicious for recurrence.

Endometrial (uterine) cancer is the most common gynecologic cancer worldwide, occurring primarily in postmenopausal women. In the United States, approximately 66,000 new cases are diagnosed each year and about 13,000 deaths are reported. Risk factors include Lynch syndrome (lifetime risk, 13%-71%), obesity, tamoxifen use, unopposed estrogen exposure (without progestin), nulliparity, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus. The endometroid histology accounts for 80% of cases, and more than 90% of patients present with abnormal vaginal bleeding (see Evaluation of Abnormal Uterine Bleeding in Nonpregnant Women of Reproductive Age in Interdisciplinary Medicine). Endometrial biopsy is usually diagnostic. All postmenopausal patients with vaginal bleeding should undergo endometrial biopsy unless a transvaginal ultrasound reveals an endometrial stripe 4 mm thick or less. Premenopausal patients older than age 45 years with abnormal uterine bleeding and those younger than 45 years with endometrial cancer risk factors should also undergo biopsy.

Staging should include chest radiograph to rule out lung metastases, whereas abdominal and pelvic CT should be used for higher-risk tumors only. A detailed family history should be obtained, and germline genetic testing should be considered for Lynch and Cowden syndrome (see Lynch Syndrome in Gastroenterology). CA-125 level can be assessed for selected patients.

Endometrial cancer staging and treatment is summarized in [Table: Table: FIGO Endometrial Cancer Staging and Treatment]

. Treatment is primarily surgical, most commonly total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Postoperative chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy can be considered for patients with stage IB to III disease. For patients with metastatic disease, carboplatin and paclitaxel is often the first-line regimen; other chemotherapy-based regimens are also approved options. Finally, targeted therapies for selected patients are appropriate, including pembrolizumab for patients with tumors with high microsatellite instability, which are more common in those with Lynch syndrome. Approximately 96% of patients diagnosed with localized disease, 71% with regional disease, and 20% with distant disease are alive after 5 years.

Lymphoid Malignancies

Approximately 80,000 new cases of lymphoma were diagnosed in 2024 in the United States. The lifetime risk for developing non-Hodgkin lymphoma is 2.1%, whereas the lifetime risk for developing Hodgkin lymphoma is considerably less. Although the incidence of lymphoma has only slightly declined recently, death rates have decreased significantly owing to significant therapeutic advances.

The incidence of non-Hodgkin lymphoma rises with increased age, whereas the incidence of Hodgkin lymphoma shows a bimodal age distribution, with an early peak in the second and third decades of life, then a decline, followed by a sustained increase with older age. Those who are diagnosed later in life with Hodgkin lymphoma have a worse prognosis.

Although most cases of lymphoma seem sporadic, familial clustering can be seen, with an increased relative risk in first-degree relatives. Patients with both congenital and acquired immunosuppression (such as HIV infection, organ transplantation, or inherited immunodeficiencies) are at greater risk.

Various viral infections are also associated with increased risk:

  • Epstein-Barr virus is associated with both Hodgkin lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma, which is a common cause of pediatric and adolescent cancer in endemic areas.
  • Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 is associated with T-cell leukemias and lymphomas, endemic in Japan, West Africa, Central America, the Southeastern United States, and the Caribbean.
  • Hepatitis C virus is associated with an increased risk for lymphoma, particularly splenic marginal zone lymphoma.
  • HIV infection is associated with an increased risk for principally B-cell lymphomas, typically with aggressive histology, more advanced stage, higher incidence of B symptoms (temperature >38.0 °C [>100.4 °F], drenching night sweats, or a weight loss of >10% of body weight over the past 6 months), and higher risk for extranodal and central nervous system involvement.
  • Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus (human herpesvirus 8) is associated with primary effusion lymphoma.

Patients with autoimmune rheumatic disorders, such as Sjögren disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and rheumatoid arthritis, also have an increased risk for non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Lymphadenopathy is the most common sign of lymphoma. There are many causes of lymphadenopathy, and in most patients, it is of benign origin (infectious or inflammatory). Palpable small cervical and inguinal lymph nodes may be noted in otherwise healthy adults and need not be evaluated further. An increase in node size or distribution, along with persistent systemic symptoms, particularly B symptoms, raises concern for lymphoma and should prompt evaluation.

In establishing the diagnosis of lymphoma, an excisional biopsy is often preferred over a core-needle biopsy because it may better determine nodal architecture. Although often acceptable to diagnose carcinoma, fine-needle aspiration cytology is generally inadequate to diagnose lymphoma. Flow cytometry of lymphocytes either in the peripheral blood or from the biopsy specimen can additionally show monoclonality of B-cell or T-cell markers. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis can assess lymph nodes that are not amenable to physical examination but generally should not be done in asymptomatic patients before establishing the lymphoma diagnosis.

Although most patients with lymphoma typically have lymph node involvement, presentation in extranodal sites is not uncommon.

Diagnosis and classification of lymphoma are established not just on the basis of standard cell type and nodal architecture but also on flow cytometry, immunohistochemical stains, and cytogenetic or molecular genetic features. Review by an experienced hematopathologist is essential to obtaining proper classification, and there is overlap among tumor types.

Staging the anatomic extent of spread can be simplified through the Lugano modification of the Ann Arbor staging system (

). Lymphomas are staged as I to IV based on the number of disease sites and extranodal involvement. Staging involves physical examination, CT, and PET in most patients. The use of PET has rendered bone marrow biopsy unnecessary in many patients with Hodgkin lymphoma and large cell lymphoma because marrow involvement is rarely found if it is not suggested by PET or abnormal complete blood count.

Lymphoma stages are also designated as A, B, or E; A indicates no systemic symptoms are present, and B indicates one or more B symptoms (temperature >38.0 °C [100.4 °F], drenching night sweats, or a weight loss of >10% of body weight over the past 6 months). Other symptoms that may occur, such as fatigue, pruritus, and nodal pain following alcohol ingestion, are not considered B symptoms. Extranodal (E) involvement is pertinent for stage I and II disease and signifies non-nodal involvement that is contiguous with nodal disease.

The prognosis of lymphoma varies greatly depending on the subtype, stage, and comorbidities. Immunophenotypic, cytogenetic, and molecular genetic classifications are also commonly used to predict the prognosis. Prognostic indices have been validated for most common types, including the International Prognostic Index for large cell lymphoma, the Follicular Lymphoma International Prognostic Index, and the Mantle Cell International Prognostic Index.

Hodgkin lymphoma represents approximately 10% of lymphomas and is curable in most patients. Ninety percent of patients have classic Hodgkin lymphoma with one of four pathologic subtypes, but 10% have nonclassic disease characterized by nodular lymphocyte predominance on biopsy ( [Table: Table: Mature Hodgkin Lymphoma Subtypes]

). Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma is thought to be a separate entity from Hodgkin lymphoma. It is generally indolent and, in advanced stages, noncurable.

Hodgkin lymphoma is most commonly found in young adults. Presentation with mediastinal, cervical, and supraclavicular involvement is particularly common for those with the nodular sclerosis subtype (

) (

). Patients may also present with B symptoms, although that is more commonly seen in older adults with more advanced disease. Pruritus may also be a presenting symptom.

A lymph node biopsy specimen shows Reed-Sternberg cells (

), malignant cells that originate from germinal center B cells and are seen in an inflammatory infiltrate. The number of Reed-Sternberg cells and variability in the composition of the infiltrate determines the pathologic subtype (see [Table: Table: Mature Hodgkin Lymphoma Subtypes]

). Patients are staged by physical examination and PET/CT. Routine bone marrow biopsy is not necessary unless there are unexplained blood test result abnormalities.

All patients with classic Hodgkin lymphoma, including those with early-stage disease, receive chemotherapy because this has been shown to result in higher cure rates than other treatment modalities. For patients with favorable early-stage disease, treatment can consist of just two courses of chemotherapy and involved-site radiation therapy. Chemotherapy alone for four cycles in patients with good response is also an option. Response to treatment as demonstrated by PET may allow for tailoring of the treatment regimen. For more advanced disease, chemotherapy alone is used.

Doxorubicin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine, with bleomycin, brentuximab vedotin, or nivolumab are the most commonly used regimens in the United States. Brentuximab vedotin is an anti-CD30 monoclonal antibody associated with less pulmonary toxicity and improved efficacy compared with bleomycin. Fertility is also better preserved, and secondary acute leukemia is less common with the brentuximab vedotin-based regimen than with the more intense bleomycin-based regimen. Nivolumab, a PD-1 inhibitor, is also an option in place of bleomycin and brentuximab vedotin. Although these regimens are usually well tolerated, each has a specific profile of adverse effects. Bleomycin has a significant risk for causing permanent lung injury (especially in older patients), and peripheral neuropathy is a common complication of brentuximab vedotin treatment. PD-1 inhibitors have a unique adverse effect profile, including immune-related events (see Toxicities Related to Immune Dysregulation in Oncology).

For patients with relapsed or refractory disease, salvage chemotherapy and autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) may provide curative options. Brentuximab vedotin is effective in treating refractory disease and has also been used for consolidation after autologous HSCT. The PD-1 antibodies (nivolumab as well as pembrolizumab) are also highly active in relapsed or refractory disease.

Nodular lymphocyte–predominant Hodgkin lymphoma is distinct clinically and pathologically from classic Hodgkin lymphoma, and it behaves more indolently. It represents approximately 10% of Hodgkin lymphomas and is more likely to appear with localized disease but is associated with a high rate of late relapse. Early-stage disease may be treated with radiation therapy alone and is potentially curable, whereas advanced-stage disease is not curable. Rituximab alone or combined with chemotherapy may be used for patients with more advanced or relapsed disease.

Approximately 85% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas are B-cell derived and express surface immunoglobulin and B-cell markers, whereas 15% are T-cell derived ( [Table: Table: Mature Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma Subtypes]

).

Indolent lymphomas may be present for many years without symptoms and typically have a favorable response to various sequential therapies when needed, but all have a tendency for continued relapse.

Follicular lymphomas demonstrate lymph node architecture with a follicular morphology. They arise from the germinal center B cells of the lymph node and are characterized by the presence of a t(14;18) translocation that causes an overexpression of the BCL2 oncogene. Follicular lymphomas are classified based on their dominant cell type: predominantly smaller cells (grade 1), a mixture of smaller and larger cells (grade 2), and predominantly large cells (grade 3). For prognostic and treatment purposes, grades 1 and 2 are commonly combined. Grade 3 follicular lymphoma can be divided into 3A and 3B. Grade 3A follicular lymphoma is more akin in behavior and treatment to grades 1 and 2, whereas 3B is usually treated more like diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

Follicular lymphoma is the most common indolent B-cell lymphoma and accounts for approximately 30% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas. A minority of patients present with localized disease and can be treated with radiation therapy and/or systemic rituximab-based therapy with curative intent.

Most patients with follicular lymphoma will present with stage III or IV disease. Many patients are not symptomatic at diagnosis and may not require therapy for many years. Single-agent rituximab is associated with high response rates and durable remissions; although asymptomatic, nonbulky disease is often observed, early treatment with rituximab in patients with stage II to IV disease delays time to initiation of next treatment, including cytotoxic chemotherapy. Although such early treatment does not improve overall survival, it may be suitable for select individuals. Combining rituximab with chemotherapy (such as the alkylating agent bendamustine) or the immune modulator lenalidomide leads to remission in more than 90% of patients. The use of maintenance rituximab after induction of an initial remission is associated with prolonged duration of remission but no clear improvement in overall survival. It is also often associated with infectious complications caused by hypogammaglobulinemia. Patients with relapsing or refractory cases can be treated with other approaches, including alternate chemotherapy regimens as well as bispecific antibodies, chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, and autologous or allogeneic HSCT.

Histologic transformation, most typically to a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, occurs in approximately 30% of patients with follicular lymphomas and is associated with an aggressive course and poor prognosis. Transformation may be suggested by a change in the clinical pattern of disease with new systemic symptoms, rapid progression of a localized area of disease, a rise in serum lactate dehydrogenase level, or markedly higher areas of standardized uptake values on PET scans. A new biopsy is required to establish that transformation has occurred.

Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma is an extranodal marginal zone lymphoma. MALT lymphomas most commonly arise in the gastrointestinal tract, especially the stomach, as well as in the thyroid, orbits, skin, and lung. They generally demonstrate indolent behavior and a low propensity for transformation. Repetitive immune stimulation from underlying chronic infection or an autoimmune process likely plays a role in the pathogenesis of this tumor.

Gastric MALT lymphoma is associated with Helicobacter pylori infection, and early-stage disease may be initially treated with antibiotics and proton pump inhibitors, as this treatment alone can lead to remission in some cases. Systemic therapy or radiation therapy is appropriate in patients who are negative for H. pylori or after failure of therapy with antibiotics and a proton-pump inhibitor in those with H. pylori infection. Other localized MALT lymphomas may be treated with radiation therapy, to which they are quite sensitive. When systemic therapy is required, rituximab alone or in combination with chemotherapy is associated with high response rates.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) are the same disease; the only difference is the primary site where the cancer manifests (blood and bone marrow for CLL and mostly lymph nodes for SLL). CLL is generally readily diagnosed as an increase in absolute lymphocytes on complete blood count. The lymphocytes are predominantly small and mature appearing, although they may be fragile and form smudge cells on the peripheral smear (

). Flow cytometry using peripheral blood is essential in establishing the diagnosis and will reveal B-cell antigens (CD19, 20, and 23), coexpression of CD5 (normally a T-cell marker), and low levels of a monoclonal surface immunoglobulin. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy are not necessary to diagnose and stage most patients with CLL.

Although less common, other lymphomas may appear similar to CLL in peripheral blood smears and must be distinguished by morphology, flow cytometry, and genetic studies. These other disorders include hairy cell leukemia, marginal and mantle zone lymphomas, T-cell lymphoma, and prolymphocytic leukemia.

CLL is typically an indolent disease, and many patients do not require therapy for many years. Prognosis can relate to the extent of cytopenias, organomegaly, and degree of nodal involvement but also to cytogenetic and molecular genetic characteristics. CLL and SLL are treated the same, and CLL is now grouped more with lymphomas than leukemias in many treatment centers.

There have been rapid advances in the number and efficacy of active agents for CLL. Although these therapies are not curative, most patients can now achieve durable remissions once treatment is required. Treatment regimens have shifted away from traditional chemotherapy agents (chlorambucil, cyclophosphamide, bendamustine, fludarabine, cladribine, pentostatin) and now use targeted agents such as Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors (BTKs) (ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib) and B-cell lymphoma 2 inhibitors such as venetoclax.

BTKs are now approved for first-line therapy and are active in a broad spectrum of patients, including those with 17p deletion, an indicator of poor prognosis and resistance to older treatments. Venetoclax is active in the first-line setting as well as in refractory cases and is associated with brisk apoptosis, which can induce tumor lysis syndrome (TLS). Patients require close monitoring and even consideration of hospitalization for intravenous fluids when starting venetoclax (see Tumor Lysis Syndrome in Oncology).

Therapies can also be used in combination. For instance, the monoclonal antibody obinutuzumab can be given with either acalabrutinib or venetoclax as a first-line treatment. Allogeneic HSCT is rarely performed in those with CLL but has been used in refractory cases in selected, younger patients. Anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy has also shown efficacy in select refractory cases.

Patients with CLL are prone to infection, in part related to associated hypogammaglobulinemia. The infection risk increases in more advanced disease, a result of both impaired T-cell–mediated and B-cell–mediated immune response along with treatment-induced immunosuppression. In patients with a history of severe infections and low immunoglobulin levels, generally defined as less than 500 mg/dL (5.0 g/L), regular treatment with intravenous gamma globulin reduces infectious events; prophylactic antibiotics are also a consideration. Patients with CLL and SLL may also develop autoimmune cytopenias, such as immune thrombocytopenic purpura and autoimmune hemolytic anemias. Transformation to large cell lymphoma (Richter transformation) occurs in about 5% of patients with CLL/SLL and is associated with a poor prognosis and refractory disease.

Like CLL, hairy cell leukemia is a low-grade B-cell disorder with characteristic clinical, pathologic, immunophenotypic, and genetic changes. Patients typically present with cytopenias and splenomegaly; lymphadenopathy is typically absent. Circulating “hairy cells,” characterized by cytoplasmic projections, are often identified in the peripheral blood smear (

). When seen on bone marrow biopsy, these cells have a lacunar appearance. Classically, the bone marrow aspirate is a dry tap because of some degree of marrow fibrosis. Flow cytometry shows characteristic surface markers. In addition, the BRAF V600E mutation has been associated with hairy cell leukemia in most patients and represents a diagnostic marker and a therapeutic target.

As with CLL and other low-grade lymphomas, some patients with hairy cell leukemia do not require immediate treatment if not symptomatic. However, the front-line therapy remains purine nucleoside agents, typically pentostatin or cladribine. These agents are highly active, and almost all patients respond, many with durable responses, with only one course of treatment. Relapses can be treated with the alternate purine nucleoside agent, followed by rituximab. The selective BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib has also shown activity in patients experiencing relapse.

The hairy cell leukemia variant is a distinct entity. Patients typically present with a high circulating leukocyte count, as opposed to the leukopenia seen in the classic form. These patients respond less well to cladribine and have shorter durations of response.

Patients with the more aggressive lymphomas, such as diffuse large B-cell and Burkitt lymphoma, are more likely to present with systemic symptoms or signs of rapid tumor progression. These patients have a greater potential for cure with therapy compared with indolent lymphomas.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma represents approximately 30% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas and is the most common lymphoma diagnosed worldwide. These patients often present with symptomatic enlarging lymphadenopathy. Approximately 40% may have symptoms or signs of extranodal disease, and one third have systemic B symptoms. Biopsy specimens show diffuse effacement of normal nodal architecture by large, atypical lymphoid cells with prominent nucleoli and basophilic cytoplasm. Flow cytometry reveals B-cell antigens, and most patients have monoclonal surface immunoglobulin. Patients should also have molecular studies performed to assess for double-hit lymphoma (showing gene rearrangements of MYC in addition to either BCL2 or BCL6), which is associated with worse prognosis.

Patients who present with localized disease can be treated with a short course of chemotherapy with or without consolidative radiation therapy; standard chemotherapy for localized involvement is rituximab plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP).

Most patients have advanced disease (stage III or IV) at diagnosis and require a longer course of chemotherapy. Consolidative radiation therapy may be given to sites of bulky disease. Residual masses, which are often benign, may remain after treatment. PET may help determine if these represent active disease or just scarring. Patients with poor prognostic features, such as elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase level, extensive tumor burden, and poor performance status because of disease burden, may require more aggressive initial therapy. The pola-R-CHP regimen, in which the the anti-CD79B monoclonal antibody polatuzumab-vedotin is substituted for vincristine (O) in R-CHOP, is the only regimen demonstrated to be superior to R-CHOP alone in patients with high-risk disease. It is first-line therapy in higher-risk patients based on International Prognostic Index score.

Autologous HSCT, anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)–T-cell therapy, and bispecific therapies have been shown to be effective in the relapse setting. Both CAR–T-cell therapy and bispecific antibodies have revolutionized outcomes for those who are primarily chemorefractory. These treatments are associated with unique adverse effects, including cytokine release syndrome (fevers, hypoxia, hypotension) as well as neurotoxicity, and are primarily administered at a specialized cancer center.

Double-hit lymphoma is usually treated with aggressive chemotherapeutic regimens other than R-CHOP and has a high propensity for central nervous system involvement or relapse.

Primary mediastinal large cell lymphoma putatively arises from thymic B cells. It is a distinct clinical, morphologic, and genetic lymphoma, often appearing in younger patients. It has a female predilection and a relatively high cure rate, and patients tend to present with bulky but localized disease. Primary mediastinal large cell lymphoma may have significant overlap histologically and genetically with nodular sclerosing Hodgkin lymphoma, and some cases may be difficult to classify as one or the other; these are called mediastinal gray-zone lymphomas.

A relatively rare B-cell lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma is remarkable for its extremely rapid growth. The endemic form occurs primarily in Africa, is a common cause of childhood cancer, and is associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Patients may present with a large jaw mass. The sporadic form is more typically seen in the United States and occurs at an older age; patients are more likely to present with abdominal or pelvic involvement. A third variety of Burkitt lymphoma is the immunodeficiency-associated form and occurs in patients with HIV infection. MYC gene activation is characteristic of all forms of Burkitt lymphoma.

Because of its rapid growth, early signs of TLS are often present in patients with Burkitt lymphoma even before treatment is initiated, and TLS should be anticipated during treatment because the tumor is quite chemosensitive. Prophylaxis for TLS, or treatment if TLS is already present, should be started before initiation of chemotherapy. For a more complete discussion of TLS, see Tumor Lysis Syndrome in Oncology.

Various aggressive multiagent chemotherapy regimens with rituximab are associated with high cure rates. These regimens are more intensive than standard lymphoma therapy and are associated with risk for treatment-related mortality. Treatment of occult central nervous system involvement is included in initial treatment regimens because of the risk for leptomeningeal involvement.

Mantle cell lymphomas represent approximately 3% to 6% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas. Median age at diagnosis is 68 years, and there is a 3:1 male predominance. It is defined by a t(11;14) translocation, which leads to constitutive overexpression of cyclin D1, a cell-cycle gene regulator. Patients can present with nodal or extranodal disease, and the disease is usually widely disseminated at diagnosis. Gastrointestinal involvement with lymphomatoid polyposis is well described, as is involvement of the peripheral blood and bone marrow.

Although mantle cell lymphoma is responsive to various conventional chemotherapy regimens and newer agents, patients will often relapse. A subset of patients with indolent disease may not require therapy for many years. There is no clear consensus on the optimal therapeutic approach, with treatments spanning a spectrum of less aggressive (Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors or bendamustine plus rituximab) to more aggressive (R-CHOP with or without HSCT) regimens.

Notably, as in patients with CLL/SLL, 17p deletion or a TP53 mutation is associated with poor prognosis and suboptimal responses to chemotherapy. However, these patients can be treated using a nonchemotherapy approach (an anti-CD20 antibody in conjunction with a BTK inhibitor and venetoclax) with better outcomes.

T-cell lymphomas, a heterogeneous group of malignancies with distinct clinical features and morphology, represent approximately 10% to 15% of lymphomas in Western countries. They are more common in Asia. Diagnosis relies on routine pathology, flow cytometry, and immunohistochemistry. Monoclonality can be confirmed by findings of clonal rearrangements of the T-cell receptor genes detected by polymerase chain reaction. In general, T-cell lymphomas are more refractory and relapse more quickly following response to therapy than B-cell lymphomas.

Mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome are the two major subtypes of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. The skin findings in mycosis fungoides range from nonspecific maculopapular eruptions or plaques, to more defined skin tumors with ulceration, to diffuse erythroderma (

). There is often a preceding prodromal illness, or “premycotic” period, with milder skin disease that waxes and wanes or that may progress for months or even years with nondiagnostic skin biopsies. Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma is often misdiagnosed, leading to delays in diagnosis, and evaluation in potential cases requires consultation with experienced hematopathologists. A multidisciplinary team approach (oncology, dermatology, pathology, and radiation oncology) with expertise in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma is recommended given the rarity of this disease.

Pruritus is common and can be debilitating. Ultimately, as skin involvement becomes more extensive, the disease often progresses to involve extracutaneous sites, including lymph nodes and organs, such as the lung, liver, and gastrointestinal tract. Infections are more common as a function of underlying immunodeficiency and disruption of the protective skin barrier. Sézary syndrome is a more aggressive form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma in which diffuse erythroderma characterizes the skin involvement, and malignant T cells circulate in the blood.

The staging of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma depends on the extent of skin disease and involvement of lymph nodes and extranodal sites. Early stages of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma are confined to the skin and managed with topical therapy, such as glucocorticoids, retinoids, or ultraviolet light therapy, which may be combined with interferon. Survival is greater than 10 years. More advanced disease is associated with a survival of less than 4 years and requires more aggressive skin treatment with electron-beam radiation therapy and systemic chemotherapy. Patients with Sézary syndrome require systemic chemotherapy. Extracorporeal photopheresis uses psoralens, compounds that enter Sézary cells and sensitize them to injury after activation with ultraviolet light. This treatment is indicated for many patients with Sézary syndrome. Large cell transformation can occur and often requires systemic therapy; however, limited lesions can be treated with radiation therapy.

Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified, is the most common subtype of peripheral T-cell lymphoma. It is typically found in older adults at an advanced stage and has a male predominance; patients generally have a poor clinical outcome compared with those who have B-cell lymphomas.

Various combination chemotherapy regimens have been used. The addition of etoposide or brentuximab vedotin (in patients with CD30-positive tumor cells) to standard combination chemotherapy has improved the efficacy of upfront therapy. The use of HSCT, both autologous and allogeneic, may benefit some patients, although there is controversy as to when and in whom these are best used. Newer therapeutic agents that target the underlying biology of T-cell lymphoma, such as pralatrexate, romidepsin, and duvelisib, lead to significant responses in patients with relapsed disease.

Patients with anaplastic large cell lymphoma can present with nodal as well as extranodal disease, including that of the skin, bone marrow, and bone. Patients commonly have B symptoms. Tumor cells are typically CD30 positive. An important prognostic and potentially therapeutic distinction is the presence or absence of a t(2;5) or mutation ALK gene translocation and protein expression. Patients diagnosed with ALK-positive disease are younger and have a much more favorable prognosis with conventional chemotherapy and may also respond to treatment with crizotinib.

Although still rare, anaplastic large cell lymphoma associated with textured breast implants have been increasingly reported; patients most commonly present with a periprosthetic fluid collection best detected with ultrasonography. Surgical intervention is required, followed by chemotherapy or radiation therapy in rare instances.

Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma was initially thought to be a disease of impaired immune regulation rather than a true malignancy. However, patients with this disease are now recognized to have clonal rearrangement of T-cell receptors, consistent with a T-cell neoplasm. Patients with angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma often present with systemic B symptoms, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and a skin rash. They commonly have polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia along with an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level. Autoimmune manifestations (such as autoimmune hemolytic anemia) may be present. Although in some patients the lymphoma is responsive to glucocorticoids and conventional chemotherapy, it typically has a moderately aggressive clinical course and high risk for relapse. However, the incorporation of brentuximab vedotin to chemotherapy has improved these outcomes in the first-line setting.

Lymphoblastic lymphoma is an aggressive lymphoma that can be of T- or B-cell origin. It is akin to and treated with protocols for acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Presentation with a mediastinal mass, blood or bone marrow involvement, and central nervous system involvement is typical. Treatment usually involves intensive chemotherapy.

Cancer of Unknown Primary Site

Although previous studies have suggested that up to 5% of patients diagnosed with metastatic cancer do not have an identified primary site, improvements in imaging and other diagnostic techniques have steadily decreased that number. Patients without an identified primary site now represent approximately 1% to 2% of all cancers. This heterogeneous group of patients is classified as having cancer of unknown primary (CUP).

On identification of metastatic cancer, evaluation should focus on confirming or excluding the presence of potentially more treatable cancers, histologies, or subtypes of CUP rather than extensive testing just to identify the primary site. A full medical history and physical examination (including pelvic examination in female patients); complete blood count and serum chemistry studies; and contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis should be obtained. In female patients, breast examination and mammography should be done to search for a breast primary cancer, and a gynecologic evaluation should be performed to look for an ovarian primary. Male patients require a testicular examination and, in those with bone metastases, a prostate examination and serum prostate-specific antigen testing to evaluate for prostate cancer.

Specific symptom- or presentation-related evaluations should be pursued, such as upper endoscopy and colonoscopy in patients with gastrointestinal symptoms or evidence of gastrointestinal bleeding. Patients with regional lymphadenopathy require focused evaluation, such as pan-endoscopic evaluation of the head and neck for patients with isolated or dominant cervical lymphadenopathy or anoscopy for those with isolated inguinal lymphadenopathy. In some patients (e.g., those with squamous carcinoma in cervical lymph nodes or those presenting with a single metastasis), PET may suggest the possible primary location, but otherwise, PET is not routinely ordered.

The most accessible tumor mass should be biopsied for histologic evaluation and confirmation of malignancy, and a limited number of immunohistochemical stains are warranted to assess the nature of the tumor and identify or exclude the most treatable histologic types (e.g., lymphoma or germ cell tumor). Given the substantial activity of immunotherapy and targeted therapy for melanoma, immunohistochemical screening to assess for this histology should be considered as well. Next-generation sequencing can be considered for the purpose of identifying actionable targets, especially in tumors likely to be of lung origin. In addition, all tumors of unknown primary should be assayed for mismatch repair protein deficiency because these tumors can be treated with immunotherapy, such as the PD-1 inhibitors pembrolizumab and dostarlimab.

Gene expression arrays designed to identify the putative site of origin have been commercially promoted. However, the clinical utility of these tests to identify more effective therapy has not been established, and a randomized trial did not show a survival benefit for profile-directed therapy over empiric treatment. Because this sort of gene expression profiling adds expense without demonstrated benefit, routine use in the evaluation of CUP is not recommended.

Nonspecific tumor markers, such as serum carcinoembryonic antigen, CA 19-9, CA 15-3, or CA 125, are not routinely recommended because they are not definitive for identifying a specific primary site.

Ultimately, CUP is a diagnosis of exclusion after a reasonable evaluation has failed to identify the primary tumor, which may be too small to be detected or may have been destroyed immunologically and is no longer present. Once the more treatable possibilities have been excluded, specific identification of the site of origin is very unlikely to improve treatment options or clinical outcome. At that point, it should be determined if the metastatic cancer has a favorable or unfavorable prognosis and whether there is a specific, efficacious therapy for that patient.

For patients with CUP, identifying a favorable prognostic subgroup allows selection of specific treatments (surgery, radiation therapy, and/or chemotherapy) to which patients are most likely to respond and on occasion achieve long-term remission and cure.

Poorly differentiated cancers are usually more aggressive than well-differentiated cancers, and those with metastatic poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma have a poor prognosis. However, some patients with poorly differentiated CUP that is not definitively an adenocarcinoma may have specific treatment options.

In particular, young men with poorly differentiated carcinoma that is predominantly in the midline, such as those with large retroperitoneal or mediastinal lymphadenopathy, or both, should be carefully evaluated for the possibility of a germ cell tumor. Serum α-fetoprotein and β-human chorionic gonadotropin levels should be measured, and a testicular examination and ultrasonography should be performed. Even if these evaluations have negative findings, an unrecognized germ cell tumor may still exist, and these patients should be treated for this possibility with a platinum-based chemotherapy regimen.

Patients with poorly differentiated neuroendocrine tumors also warrant careful consideration. These tumors frequently metastasize like small cell lung cancers and respond similarly to platinum-based chemotherapy.

Women with adenocarcinoma detected solely in axillary lymph nodes may represent a subset of patients with CUP who may have a more favorable prognosis.

These patients should be presumptively considered to have locoregional breast cancer. If mammography is unrevealing, breast MRI should be performed. If the MRI results are negative, the patient is still assumed to have presumptive locally advanced breast cancer. These patients should receive treatment consistent with a locally advanced breast cancer diagnosis.

Patients with isolated or dominant cervical lymphadenopathy should undergo full endoscopic examination of the upper aerodigestive tract to evaluate for a head and neck primary. Even if a primary is not identified, treatment along a head and neck paradigm with chemotherapy and radiation therapy is often appropriate. Patients with squamous cell cancer presenting with high cervical lymphadenopathy occasionally achieve cure. Supraclavicular lymphadenopathy or adenocarcinoma makes a head and neck primary far less likely, and therapy is less efficacious.

Isolated inguinal lymphadenopathy should prompt a careful examination of the anal, perineal, and genital regions, including anoscopy. Even in the absence of a defined primary tumor, definitive resection or radiation to inguinal or other isolated solitary or regional lymph nodes may provide long-term tumor control and cures in rare circumstances.

Women who have adenocarcinoma with abdominal carcinomatosis and ascites should be presumptively treated for ovarian cancer. Ovarian cancer paradigms, including initial cytoreductive surgery and ovarian cancer chemotherapy regimens, should be used.

Therapy for CUP that does not fall into a favorable subgroup is empirically directed with chemotherapy and radiation therapy based on the pattern of presentation. Patients with CUP presenting above the diaphragm should be evaluated and managed as if they have metastatic lung cancer. This has become a more favorable subgroup than in the past because targeted immunotherapy options have improved the outcomes for patients with non-small cell lung cancer and molecular profiling may identify a targetable variant or fusion. CUP that is predominantly below the diaphragm should be managed as gastrointestinal cancer.

Chronic medical comorbidities and performance status of the patient greatly influence the range of treatment options. As in patients with other solid tumors, patients with multiple comorbidities and poor performance status are less likely to benefit from aggressive chemotherapy and are far more likely to experience serious or life-threatening toxicity. Palliative and hospice care should be considered in such patients.

Skin Cancer

Melanoma has been increasing in incidence worldwide because of increased sun exposure. Most patients with melanoma present with cutaneous disease, and it is important to note that it can also begin in mucosal and ocular sites. Ocular melanoma is the most common cancer of the eye and has distinct biology and behavior. About half of cutaneous melanomas arise in preexisting nevi. Melanoma can also appear in nodal or visceral sites without a known cutaneous or mucosal primary site. See Melanoma in Dermatology for information on the diagnosis of melanoma.

Advances in systemic therapy during the past decade have resulted in statistically significant improvements in survival for patients with metastatic melanoma. These advances include the use of molecular therapy targeted against specific gene mutations and immunotherapy.

Treatment of melanoma is dependent on the stage of disease involvement, with early-stage and select stage III or IV cases being cured with surgical intervention. The risk for local or distant recurrence is predicted by the depth of invasion (Breslow depth) and the presence of ulceration and nodal involvement. Surgical resection margins for melanomas do not need to be excessive. Melanomas with a thickness of less than 1 mm should be resected with a 1-cm margin, and those with a thickness ranging from 1 to 2 mm should be resected with a 1- to 2-cm margin.

Nodal metastases are uncommon in thin melanomas, and sentinel lymph node biopsy is not usually performed if the melanoma is nonulcerated with a Breslow depth of less than 0.8 mm. Follow-up in these patients should include frequent skin self-examination and full-body skin examinations by a dermatologist every 6 months. Patients with early-stage disease can be assessed clinically and do not need radiographic staging.

As the depth of invasion increases, the risk for nodal and distant metastases increases. Assessing for lymph node metastasis with sentinel lymph node biopsy is recommended for intermediate and thicker melanomas. Patients with confirmed positive results from sentinel lymph node biopsies (stage III) should be considered for adjuvant systemic treatment with targeted therapy and/or immunotherapy if any of the nodal metastases is greater than or equal to 1 mm in size. Otherwise, these patients may be followed by clinical examination and serial ultrasonography of the nodal basin involved to detect nodal recurrences. Lymph node dissection is no longer routinely performed, even if the sentinel node is positive, because it is not associated with improved survival. Those with clinically positive nodes or positive lymph node biopsy results should also undergo imaging to detect metastatic disease with MRI of the brain along with full-body PET/CT or CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis.

Patients with clinical stage III or IV disease who are deemed surgical candidates should also be considered for neoadjuvant pembrolizumab (an immune checkpoint inhibitor) before surgery, followed by adjuvant pembrolizumab.

Patients with melanoma can also present with solitary or oligometastatic disease amenable to resection that is sometimes curable. Following metastasectomy, adjuvant systemic therapy has been shown to improve overall outcome.

For those who are not deemed surgical candidates, systemic therapies have advanced significantly over the past decade. Current treatment includes immune checkpoint inhibitors, targeted therapy against BRAF, NRAS, and MEK mutations, as well as tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy; conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy plays a limited role.

The use of immune checkpoint inhibitors has revolutionized the therapy and prognosis of patients with metastatic melanoma. Monoclonal antibodies against cytotoxic T-lymphocyte–associated protein 4 (ipilimumab) or PD-1 (nivolumab, pembrolizumab) may result in significant tumor responses.

Ipilimumab alone has a relatively low response rate (20%) and is associated with considerable toxicity, with various immune-related adverse effects that can include rash, colitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, myocarditis, and endocrine insufficiency syndromes (see Toxicities Related to Immune Dysregulation in Oncology). Nivolumab and pembrolizumab are associated with a higher response rate (30%-40%). They can cause similar adverse effects to those seen with ipilimumab, but less frequently.

Durable benefit in terms of survival is possible in a substantial fraction of patients with metastatic melanoma treated with combination immunotherapy ( [Table: Table: Treatment of Advanced, Unresectable Melanoma]

). Combining ipilimumab with nivolumab improves response rates compared with either ipilimumab or nivolumab alone but results in significantly more immune-related toxicities.

LAG3 is responsible for inhibiting T-cell proliferation and effector T-cell function and is found to be upregulated in melanoma. The anti-LAG3 monoclonal antibody relatlimab combined with nivolumab has also demonstrated improved outcomes compared with nivolumab alone in patients with unresectable melanoma without a BRAF mutation.

Approximately 40% to 50% of melanomas harbor a BRAF gene mutation (most commonly V600E), and another 20% have an NRAS or MEK mutation; each of these corresponding mutation proteins activate the mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway, representing a therapeutic target. In patients with metastatic disease bearing a BRAF mutation, however, overall survival is superior if they receive first-line therapy with immunotherapy rather than BRAF/MEK oral inhibitors (2-year survival: 72% vs 52%). Patients who do not respond to checkpoint inhibitors may proceed to targeted therapy.

Melanomas with BRAF mutations respond best to oral therapy with BRAF/MEK inhibitor combinations (dabrafenib/trametinib, vemurafenib/cobimetinib, and encorafenib/binimetinib). Compared with BRAF inhibitors alone, these combined BRAF/MEK inhibitors improve the rate and duration of response; this combination also improves tolerability because it suppresses paradoxical activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway.

In addition to their use in metastatic disease, immune checkpoint inhibitors and BRAF/MEK inhibitors have shown survival benefits in the adjuvant setting in patients with resected stage III (nodal) disease.

Treatment with tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, a form of T-cell immunotherapy, has demonstrated effective responses for those whose cancer has progressed after checkpoint inhibition as well as treatment with BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy requires hospitalization with close monitoring because of immunosuppression and the risk for other adverse effects, including fever, cytopenias, hypotension, and hypoxia.

All patients should be encouraged to perform frequent skin self-examinations as well as receive regular skin evaluations by a dermatologist for life every 6 months. Patients with early-stage melanoma need not undergo routine blood testing or imaging studies in the absence of signs or symptoms.

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer and is associated with sun exposure. The incidence of BCC is increasing secondary to improved surveillance methods and increased sun exposure. Patients with BCC usually present with localized disease.

The diagnosis of BCC is made through shave or punch biopsy. (See Basal Cell Carcinoma in Dermatology for more information.) Treatment includes surgical resection, Mohs surgery, electrodesiccation/curettage, cryosurgery, topical chemotherapy, or radiation therapy. After treatment, it is crucial to prioritize consistent dermatologic monitoring and to avoid sun exposure.

Complex BCC includes cancer in anatomically difficult locations (e.g., medial canthus of the eye), multiple BCC, and very large tumors. Metastatic disease is rare. Complex BCC that is not surgically resectable may be managed with targeted therapy using vismodegib or sonidegib, which may reduce the tumor enough to allow definitive therapy with surgery or radiation.

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) mostly involves sun-exposed areas, such as the face, ears, neck, lips, and hands. The prevalence of SCC is increasing because of widespread sun exposure. Cutaneous SCC is also commonly seen in patients who are immunocompromised, such as those who have received organ transplants or have chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Less often, SCC forms in the skin of genital areas and can sometimes arise from actinic keratoses, a precancerous skin condition.

Biopsy is required for confirmation of SCC. (See Squamous Cell Carcinoma and Keratoacanthoma in Dermatology for more information on diagnosis.) Surgical excision is typically the first-line treatment. If surgery is contraindicated, radiation or local cryotherapy is an option. In the case of unresectable or metastatic disease, immunotherapy can be considered. Long-term dermatologic follow-up is required because of risk for recurrence and development of other skin cancers.

Bone and Soft Tissue Tumors

Sarcomas make up only 1% of all human malignancies. Well over 50 histologic subtypes of sarcomas arise from mesodermal tissue, such as bone, cartilage, nerves, fat, muscle, vessels, and connective tissue. Therefore, every sarcoma is a rare tumor that should be referred to and managed by a multidisciplinary team of surgeons, radiation therapists, medical oncologists, and pathologists in a sarcoma center.

Most patients with bone sarcoma present with pain at the affected site, sometimes associated with a palpable mass. Plain radiography and MRI are typically used for evaluation of the primary site. Core-needle biopsy is preferred. Careful planning of the biopsy approach is critical because the biopsy tract must be encompassed within the subsequent surgical resection. Incisional biopsy is recommended only if necessary. Following diagnosis of high-grade bone sarcoma, additional imaging to evaluate for metastatic disease is indicated.

Osteosarcoma is the most common bone sarcoma and can arise in various locations. It is diagnosed in about 1000 patients annually in the United States; most patients are children or young adults, but osteosarcoma can also occur in older adults. It is an aggressive tumor that typically requires treatment with surgery and combination chemotherapy. Metastatic disease is seen in 10% to 20% of patients, and the most common metastatic site is the lungs. Bone metastases can also be seen in some patients. For patients with lung-only metastatic disease, cure is possible with surgical resection. Chemotherapy and targeted therapies can be used to treat disseminated metastatic disease.

Ewing sarcoma is less common than osteosarcoma. It is also largely a pediatric tumor but can be seen in adult patients. Presentation, initial imaging, and biopsy considerations are similar to those seen with osteosarcoma. Ewing sarcoma is very aggressive and requires a combination of local treatment for the primary tumor (with surgery, radiation therapy, or both) and aggressive combination chemotherapy. Unlike with osteosarcoma, even limited metastatic disease is rarely curable. Select patients with limited lung metastases can be offered surgical resection along with systemic chemotherapy. Combination chemotherapy is used to treat distant metastatic disease.

Chondrosarcoma is characterized by formation of cartilage matrix. It comes in different forms and is predominantly a surgical disease. Chondrosarcoma does not typically respond to systemic chemotherapy and is also relatively resistant to radiation.

Patients with soft-tissue sarcoma typically present with either a palpable soft tissue mass or with pain or other symptoms caused by local effects of the growing mass. Initial imaging is with CT or MRI, based on the primary site. The diagnosis is most often confirmed with core-needle biopsy. As with bone sarcoma, incisional biopsy is not recommended unless necessary.

Treatment of soft-tissue sarcoma depends on stage, which is based on size, grade, and depth of invasion. Low-grade tumors are less likely to recur locally than high-grade tumors. Surgery is the primary treatment for nearly all soft-tissue sarcomas. Neoadjuvant or adjuvant radiation therapy is used to treat high-grade tumors because it has shown a statistically significant reduction in the risk for local recurrence. The use of adjuvant chemotherapy depends on the sarcoma subtype.

Metastatic soft-tissue sarcoma can be treated with surgery in patients with limited metastatic disease, with cure possible in some cases. Systemic therapy, most commonly with chemotherapy, is used for treating disseminated metastatic disease. Soft-tissue sarcomas vary greatly in their response to chemotherapy treatment, and survival with metastatic disease is limited in most patients. Use of chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy against MAGEA4 (afamitresgene autoleucel) has resulted in improved responses for relapsed, unresectable, or metastatic synovial sarcoma.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) are sarcomas characterized by an activating variant in the c-kit or PDGF-α proto-oncogene, which leads to constitutive activation of the receptor tyrosine kinase. Histologically, GISTs are identified by overexpression of the KIT gene, the immunohistochemical marker for KIT protein.

Although these tumors may be asymptomatic or incidentally discovered during an endoscopic or imaging procedure, most are associated with nonspecific gastrointestinal symptoms. Some may cause overt bleeding, pain, or signs of obstruction. Most GISTs arise in the stomach, with fewer in the small bowel and fewest in the rectum. GISTs arising in the stomach have a better prognosis than those arising elsewhere. Other prognostic factors include tumor size and mitotic rate.

For patients undergoing a potentially curative resection of a localized GIST, low-risk tumors do not benefit from further treatment. Higher-risk tumors are treated for 3 years with the adjuvant tyrosine kinase inhibitor imatinib. Imatinib is also used to treat unresectable or metastatic disease. Multiple other targeted therapy drugs are available for cancer that worsens despite imatinib treatment.
