Oncologic Urgencies and Emergencies

Obstruction of the superior vena cava (SVC), or SVC syndrome, is usually caused by malignancies with large mediastinal masses. Lung cancer accounts for almost 75% of cases of SVC syndrome, whereas lymphoma and other solid tumors each contribute to approximately 10% of cases. Rarer tumors, such as germ cell tumors, thymoma, or mesothelioma, account for the remaining 5%.

Patients typically present with edema of the head, neck, and arms; cyanosis; plethora; and distended cutaneous collateral vessels. They may also have headaches, cough, dyspnea, hoarseness, and/or syncope. The severity of symptoms depends on the degree of SVC narrowing and the speed of onset, with slower development allowing venous collaterals to develop. Most patients do not require emergency intervention, and deaths due to SVC syndrome are rare. A grading system based on symptoms has been established and can help guide urgency of treatment ( [Table: Table: Grading Superior Vena Cava Syndrome]

). Chest CT with intravenous contrast usually confirms the diagnosis (see

).

The management of SVC syndrome is based on symptom severity and the underlying malignancy. In patients requiring immediate treatment of respiratory distress or cerebral edema, an SVC stent can be placed without tissue diagnosis. However, most patients do not require emergency intervention. In patients who are stable without a known diagnosis of cancer, a tissue biopsy should be obtained first with treatment directed by the type of cancer. Options for obtaining diagnostic tissue include mediastinoscopy, bronchoscopy, thoracentesis (if a pleural effusion is present), or biopsy of a peripheral area of lymphadenopathy.

Cancers that are highly responsive to chemotherapy, such as small cell lung cancer, lymphoma, and germ cell cancers, are treated with initial chemotherapy. Non–small cell lung cancer may be treated with initial chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or both. Initial surgery may be required in thymoma and mesothelioma. Although glucocorticoids and loop diuretics are often used, there is no clear evidence of their effectiveness. Anticoagulation therapy should be added if thrombosis is present.

Treatment of curable malignancies should not be compromised by the presence of SVC syndrome because prognosis is often not otherwise worsened.

Cancer and cancer treatment are risk factors for venous thromboembolism (VTE) (deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism). In one study, VTE occurred in 12.5% of patients with solid tumors during the 12 months after the initiation of chemotherapy. Following death caused by cancer itself, VTE is the second most common cause of death in patients with malignancy. Symptoms such as calf discomfort, pleuritic chest pain, or shortness of breath should prompt evaluation of deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism (see Diagnosis in Hematology). The preferred treatment options for cancer-associated thrombosis include low-molecular weight heparin, fondaparinux, intravenous heparin, and more recently, direct oral anticoagulants.

Elevated intracranial pressure can result from primary brain malignancies or from brain metastases, which occur in 10% to 20% of adult patients with cancer. The most common types of primary cancer that cause brain metastases are lung cancer, breast cancer, kidney cancer, and melanoma. Median survival after diagnosis of brain metastases varies widely; the prognosis of patients with some of these malignancies and brain metastases has improved with the development of new therapeutic agents.

Symptoms of increased intracranial pressure include headache, depressed global consciousness, vomiting, and even features of herniation. Emergent CT or MRI will confirm the diagnosis. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in patients with increased intracranial pressure because of the risk for herniation. When a lumbar puncture is under consideration and there is a concern for increased intracranial pressure, central nervous system imaging should be performed first.

Glucocorticoids decrease vasogenic edema and relieve symptoms in 75% of patients. Patients with severe symptoms are treated with a loading dose of dexamethasone of 10 to 20 mg followed by 4 to 6 mg every 6 hours. The most critically ill patients may require osmotic diuresis with mannitol or hypertonic saline, head elevation, hyperventilation, and possibly decompressive surgery. Antiseizure drugs should be used in the 25% of patients who present with seizures; otherwise, prophylactic antiseizure drugs are not needed. Anticoagulation can usually be safely administered when needed for indications such as concomitant venous thromboembolic disease. See Management of Complications of Central Nervous System Tumors in Neurology for further discussion of management of complications from central nervous system tumors.

Neoplastic epidural spinal cord compression (ESCC) develops in approximately 2.5% of patients with metastatic cancer. The most common types of cancer that cause ESCC in adults are lung, breast, and prostate cancer; myeloma; and lymphoma. Approximately 85% of ESCC cases are due to epidural extension from vertebral body metastases. Lymphomas are more likely to involve a paraspinal mass that extends through the neural foramina to cause cord compression.

As the vertebral mass enlarges, there are typical but not universal signs and symptoms of progression (see [Table: Table: Manifestations of Spinal Cord Compression]

). Pain is usually the first symptom and is initially localized, is worse at night, and then intensifies over a few weeks. As the mass enlarges, it may impinge on the nerve root, causing radicular pain that may worsen with recumbency. Encroachment of the mass on the spinal cord itself may cause motor or sensory deficits. Bowel and bladder dysfunction is a late finding in up to half of patients.

Examination may show motor or sensory deficits. If a sensory level is present, it is typically one to five levels below the actual level of cord compression. However, the absence of neurologic signs should not delay evaluation of back pain and potential ESCC because early recognition is critical to salvage neurologic function.

In patients with neoplastic ESCC, neurologic status when treatment begins is the most important predictor of outcome. Among patients who are able to walk when starting treatment, 80% remain ambulatory. However, fewer than 20% of nonambulatory patients regain the ability to walk. Although data regarding the efficacy of glucocorticoids and the best dosing schedule are sparse, glucocorticoids decrease edema. Patients with suspected ESCC should be treated immediately with moderate- or high-dose glucocorticoids, such as a 10-mg loading dose of intravenous dexamethasone, followed by 4 to 6 mg every 6 hours. Treatment with glucocorticoids should not be delayed while diagnostic evaluation is being completed. Emergent MRI with contrast of the entire thecal sac is the preferred imaging test when ESCC is suspected.

Urgent consultations with neurosurgery and radiation oncology should be initiated as soon as the diagnosis is established. Definitive treatment with surgery, radiation therapy, or both depends on whether the patient has a known cancer diagnosis, the stability of the spine, the sensitivity of the cancer to radiation or drug therapy, and the patient’s overall prognosis. For patients who are acceptable surgical candidates with an expected survival of at least 3 to 6 months, initial decompressive surgery followed by radiation therapy increases the likelihood of ambulation compared with radiation therapy alone. See Compressive Myelopathy in Neurology for further discussion of spinal cord compression.

The types of cancer that most commonly cause malignant pleural effusions include carcinomas of the breast, lung, gastrointestinal tract, and ovaries; lymphomas; and mesotheliomas. Patients present with progressive dyspnea and may or may not have concomitant chest pain. See Pleural Effusion in Pulmonary Medicine for further discussion of pleural effusions. Chest radiography is the initial diagnostic study, often followed by CT, which provides more precise anatomic detail.

Thoracentesis is the initial treatment of symptomatic effusions. Further management depends on the rate of reaccumulation, the severity of symptoms, and the patient’s prognosis. Recurrent effusions are common unless the tumor is responsive to systemic therapy. Repeat therapeutic thoracentesis is appropriate for slowly recurring effusions. For effusions with more rapid reaccumulation, the best options for management are placement of an indwelling pleural catheter or pleurodesis. Both methods offer similar symptom relief.

Malignancy accounts for 13% to 23% of pericardial effusions and may be the first sign of the disease. Lung, breast, and esophageal cancers; melanoma; lymphoma; and leukemia are the most common malignancies that cause pericardial effusions. Cardiac tamponade results when the pericardial fluid pressure impairs filling of one or both ventricles, leading to decreased cardiac output. Patients present with dyspnea, chest discomfort, or fatigue. Symptoms from progressive cardiac tamponade may be inappropriately attributed to nonspecific systemic signs of cancer or heart failure until cardiac filling and cardiac output are emergently compromised. Patients usually have elevated jugular venous distention and may have hypotension, pulsus paradoxus, and peripheral edema.

Echocardiography usually establishes the diagnosis of a pericardial effusion. See Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Cardiac Tamponade in Cardiovascular Medicine in Cardiovascular Medicine for further discussion of cardiac tamponade. Treatment of symptomatic pericardial effusion involves percutaneous pericardiocentesis or drainage during surgical placement of a pericardial window.

Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is caused when tumor cells release their contents into the bloodstream, either spontaneously or secondary to treatment, leading to hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia (see

). These electrolyte abnormalities can lead to acute kidney injury, cardiac arrhythmias, seizures, and death. TLS is seen most often in highly proliferative hematologic malignancies, such as acute leukemia and high-grade lymphomas, but can develop in other cancers, including chemosensitive solid tumors.

The risk for TLS can be categorized based on the tumor burden; the cell-lysis potential of the cancer type; and patient characteristics, including preexisting kidney failure, volume depletion, acidosis, hypotension, or nephrotoxin exposure.

Patients at intermediate risk for TLS can be managed with monitoring of laboratory values, ensuring adequate hydration, and xanthine oxidase inhibitors (allopurinol or febuxostat, which prevent the formation of uric acid). Those at high risk should additionally receive intravenous fluids before chemotherapy as well as rasburicase instead of a xanthine oxidase inhibitor; rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase that catalyzes the oxidation of uric acid to the more water-soluble compound allantoin, facilitating its excretion. It is contraindicated in patients with G6PD deficiency, and testing should be considered if time allows. There is no clear benefit of alkalinization to increase uric acid excretion or prevent uric acid nephropathy, particularly given the availability of rasburicase. Alkalinization additionally increases the risk for hyperphosphatemia and precipitation of calcium phosphate crystals.

The Cairo-Bishop definition defines TLS as two or more of the following serum chemistry abnormalities or changes within 3 days before to 7 days after the start of cytotoxic therapy:

  • Serum urate level greater than 8 mg/dL (0.47 mmol/L), or a 25% increase from baseline
  • Serum potassium level greater than 6 mEq/L (6 mmol/L), or a 25% increase from baseline
  • Serum phosphorus level greater than 4.5 mg/dL (1.5 mmol/L), or a 25% increase from baseline
  • Serum calcium level less than 7 mg/dL (1.7 mmol/L), or a 25% decrease from baseline

Patients who develop TLS require continuous cardiac monitoring; serum measurement of serum electrolyte, creatinine, and urate levels every 4 to 6 hours; and correction of electrolyte abnormalities. Depending on the severity, rasburicase should be given to most patients. If kidney function allows, patients should also receive aggressive intravenous fluids with the use of a loop diuretic if needed to maintain urinary output. Patients may require kidney replacement therapy for severe oliguria or anuria, persistent hyperkalemia, symptomatic hypocalcemia, or a calcium-phosphate product greater than or equal to 70 mg^2/dL^2.

Hypercalcemia of malignancy occurs in 20% to 30% of patients with advanced cancer. It is most frequent in patients with myeloma and lung, breast, kidney, and head and neck cancers. The incidence of hypercalcemia in patients with breast cancer and myeloma, however, may be decreasing with the prophylactic use of bisphosphonates. Osteolytic bone metastases are usually the cause of hypercalcemia of malignancy. Paraneoplastic production of parathyroid hormone–related protein may occur in localized tumors without widespread bone metastases and is more commonly seen in patients with lung cancer. Lymphomas can cause hypercalcemia by overproduction of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.

Patients may present with nausea, vomiting, constipation, fatigue, polyuria, polydipsia, altered mental status, or muscle weakness. Volume depletion and acute kidney injury are common. Symptoms depend on both the serum calcium level (more severe symptoms with calcium >14 mg/dL [3.5 mmol/L]) and the rate of rise. ECG findings include a short QT interval; in severe cases, various arrhythmias may occur, including ventricular fibrillation.

Initial management is based on the severity of hypercalcemia (see Management of Hypercalcemia in Endocrinology and Metabolism). Treatment options include vigorous intravenous saline administration, calcitonin, and bisphosphonates or denosumab. Patients with severe or symptomatic hypercalcemia should immediately receive isotonic saline volume expansion. Calcitonin can decrease calcium within several hours in responsive patients by increasing kidney excretion of calcium and decreasing bone resorption; it is useful as a temporizing measure while waiting for more definitive treatments to take effect. Loop diuretics can be considered to manage volume overload but are otherwise not necessary. Hemodialysis may be necessary in patients with severe kidney or cardiac dysfunction.

Treatment with an intravenous bisphosphonate or with denosumab, a receptor activator of nuclear factor κB ligand, is recommended to treat severe hypercalcemia of malignancy (serum calcium >14 mg/dL [3.5 mmol/L]). Bisphosphonates, such as zoledronic acid, inhibit bone resorption and can lower calcium levels to normal in 50% of patients in 4 days and in 88% of patients in 10 days. The Endocrine Society suggests denosumab as primary therapy, although the evidence supporting this recommendation is of low certainty. Effective treatment of the underlying malignancy remains the most appropriate long-term means of controlling hypercalcemia.

Effects of Cancer Therapy and Survivorship

Myelosuppression remains the major toxicity of many traditional chemotherapies. Neutropenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia are common issues in patients receiving cytotoxic chemotherapy.

Febrile neutropenia is defined as neutropenia accompanied by a single temperature of 38.3 °C (101.0 °F) or sustained (for ≥1 hour) temperature of 38.0 °C (100.4 °F). It typically occurs 5 to 15 days after chemotherapy. Serious infectious complications are more likely with increasing severity (absolute neutrophil count <500/µL [0.5 × 10^9/L]) and longer duration of neutropenia. Prompt evaluation of neutropenic fever is critical and should include assessment for a source, including obtaining appropriate cultures, followed immediately by administration of empiric, broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy.

Antibiotic monotherapy with an intravenous antipseudomonal β-lactam agent, such as cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam, is usually appropriate. Other antimicrobials, such as fluoroquinolones or vancomycin, can be added if antimicrobial resistance is suspected or if shock is present. Vancomycin may also be added for suspected catheter-associated infection, skin or soft-tissue infection, or pneumonia. Specific anaerobic therapy (clindamycin or metronidazole) is generally not needed unless an anaerobic source is suspected.

Selected patients without significant comorbidities who are stable and adherent, and in whom a short duration of neutropenia is anticipated, can be treated on an outpatient basis with intravenous or oral antibiotics. In these patients, guidelines recommend a fluoroquinolone plus amoxicillin-clavulanate as first-line therapy.

Persistent fever in the setting of prolonged neutropenia and adequate antibiotic coverage should prompt concern for a potential invasive fungal infection. The incidence of fungal infection (especially candidiasis or aspergillosis) increases in patients who experience more than 7 days of neutropenic fever. Fungal markers (serum galactomannan, β-d-glucan) as well as fungal cultures can help confirm fungal infection. High-resolution CT of the chest to evaluate for pulmonary nodules followed by bronchoscopy can investigate a possible diagnosis of fungal pneumonia.

The prophylactic use of myeloid growth factor (e.g., granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) reduces the risk for febrile neutropenia. These medications may be administered to patients receiving regimens associated with a high risk for this complication or as secondary prophylaxis in patients with a previous episode of neutropenic fever.

Growth factors are not routinely initiated for the treatment of neutropenic fever but can be considered in patients at high risk. Risk factors for complications include the following:

  • Expected prolonged (>10 days) and profound (absolute neutrophil count <100/µL [<0.1 × 10^9/L]) neutropenia
  • Age 65 years and older
  • Uncontrolled primary cancer
  • Comorbidities such as hypotension, pneumonia, or sepsis
  • Invasive fungal infection
  • Hospitalization at the time of fever development

To prevent infectious complications, prophylactic antimicrobial, antiviral, and antifungal drugs may additionally be recommended based on the chemotherapy regimen and the duration and severity of neutropenia; prophylaxis applies mainly to patients undergoing treatment for acute leukemia or allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation. There is no established role for myeloid growth factors in the treatment of patients with neutropenia without fever.

Anemia in patients with cancer may be related to chronic inflammation, tumor infiltration of bone marrow, chemotherapy, myelophthisis, blood loss, and nutritional deficiencies (especially iron). Red blood cell transfusions and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents are sometimes required. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents have been associated in some studies with more rapid cancer progression and increased risk for venous thromboembolism but can be considered under special circumstances (e.g., incurable cancer that is being treated with myelosuppressive treatments and palliative intent, moderate to severe chronic kidney disease, or patients who decline blood transfusions).

Thrombocytopenia is generally managed with platelet transfusions, when needed, and appropriate chemotherapy dose reductions and delays. Romiplostim (a thrombopoietin growth receptor agonist) can be used to treat chemotherapy-related thrombocytopenia, although its best role is undefined.

Although nausea and vomiting are common adverse effects of chemotherapy, their incidence and severity have been markedly reduced by antiemetic medications (see Nausea in Foundations of Clinical Practice). Nausea and vomiting can be classified as acute (within 24 hours of chemotherapy), delayed (>24 hours after chemotherapy), and anticipatory (before a new cycle of chemotherapy).

Antiemetic prophylaxis should be scheduled for the first 3 to 4 days after each cycle, and short-acting antiemetics should be provided as needed for breakthrough nausea. For patients receiving a moderately emetogenic regimen, prophylaxis should include high-dose glucocorticoids and a serotonin receptor antagonist (ondansetron or palonosetron). For a highly emetogenic regimen, a neurokinin-1 receptor antagonist (aprepitant, fosaprepitant, or netupitant) and olanzapine should be added. Olanzapine can be continued for the first 3 days after highly emetogenic chemotherapy. Excellent control of nausea and vomiting during the first few cycles of chemotherapy can prevent anticipatory symptoms. Behavioral therapy or benzodiazepines can be prescribed for patients who experience anticipatory symptoms.

Diarrhea is a common effect of cancer chemotherapy, especially with tyrosine kinase inhibitors, 5-fluorouracil, and checkpoint inhibitors. Infectious causes should be ruled out when diarrhea occurs; otherwise, treatment is focused on maintaining hydration, electrolyte repletion, and antimotility agents such as loperamide. Patients experiencing diarrhea caused by checkpoint inhibitors should be treated promptly and may require glucocorticoids or infliximab.

The gastrointestinal tract is also susceptible to damage resulting from radiation administered to the abdomen. Acute and chronic radiation colitis are both common, affecting as many as 20% of patients. Acute radiation colitis appears during or soon after radiation exposure and patients usually present with diarrhea and abdominal discomfort. It is usually self-limited, and symptomatic treatment is often sufficient.

Chronic radiation colitis appears at least 3 months after radiation exposure and results from an obliterative vasculopathy of the intestines. Diarrhea, abdominal pain, bleeding, and strictures may occur in addition to bacterial overgrowth. Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion and is based on history and endoscopic findings, although imaging may be necessary in complicated disease. Endoscopy reveals mucosal changes including erythema, telangiectasias, and atrophy. Treatment is supportive. Antimotility agents or bile salt sequestrants may help alleviate diarrhea. Recurrent bleeding often requires endoscopic intervention, including thermal coagulation therapy. Surgery is avoided because postoperative complication rates are high, secondary to poor wound healing.

Acute radiation proctitis occurs during or within 6 weeks of radiation therapy. Chronic radiation proctitis can occur after 6 weeks of radiation therapy. Symptoms vary from painless rectal bleeding to rectal pain and fecal urgency. Sucralfate enemas are an effective treatment.

Alopecia is the most common cutaneous adverse effect, especially with traditional cytotoxic chemotherapies. Scalp cooling can reduce hair loss due to chemotherapies and is FDA approved for use in patients with solid tumors. Fluoropyrimidines (5-fluorouracil and capecitabine) are associated with palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (hand-foot syndrome), characterized by redness, peeling, and tenderness of the palms and soles. Dermatologic symptoms are the most common immune-related adverse events caused by immune checkpoint inhibitors. Patients typically present with a maculopapular rash, generalized pruritus, or a psoriasiform rash. Treatment usually includes topical or systemic glucocorticoids.

Bleomycin, nitrosoureas, and gemcitabine have the strongest associations with pulmonary toxicity, but many other chemotherapies have toxicity potential. Additionally, targeted therapies (e.g., rituximab, trastuzumab, cetuximab, and osimertinib) and immune checkpoint inhibitors can be associated with acute pulmonary toxicity that can be permanent in some cases.

Radiation therapy can be associated with pneumonitis, typically occurring within 1 to 3 months of treatment, and may lead to radiation fibrosis. See Radiation Pneumonitis in Pulmonary Medicine for further discussion of disorders of pulmonary function related to cancer therapies.

Doxorubicin and other anthracyclines can cause irreversible cardiomyopathy; the risk increases with cumulative dosing. Trastuzumab can also induce dose-independent cardiomyopathy that is usually reversible; the risk increases when trastuzumab is combined with anthracyclines. Fluoropyrimidines have been associated with coronary spasm and ischemia during administration.

The tyrosine kinase inhibitors nilotinib and ponatinib are associated with coronary disease, and dasatinib is associated with pulmonary hypertension. Ibrutinib and other Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors, used commonly in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, increase the risk for atrial fibrillation. The anti–vascular endothelial growth factor antibody bevacizumab is associated with hypertension and an increased risk for coronary and other vascular events. Antiandrogen therapy for prostate cancer increases the risk for cardiovascular events. Thoracic radiation therapy may cause significant damage to the heart, including the pericardium, myocardium, valves, coronary vasculature, and conduction system. Clinical disease usually presents two to three decades after treatment.

Monitoring for and management of cardiac complications in cancer survivors is discussed in Cardiovascular Disease in Cancer Survivors in Cardiovascular Medicine.

Cisplatin is the most common type of chemotherapy affecting kidney function and is associated with acute tubular necrosis; the risk is reduced with aggressive hydration. High-dose methotrexate can induce acute kidney injury; urine alkalinization and leucovorin rescue are used to mitigate this toxicity. Both ifosfamide and cyclophosphamide, in high doses, may cause hemorrhagic cystitis. Hemolytic uremic syndrome is most associated with mitomycin-C and gemcitabine.

Peripheral neuropathy is a frequent toxicity of platinum agents, taxanes, vinca alkaloids, and proteasome inhibitors. Both compression and cryotherapy are being studied as strategies to decrease chemotherapy-related neuropathy. Oxaliplatin causes transient hypersensitivity to cold and a non–temperature-dependent persistent peripheral neuropathy. Patients should minimize eating, drinking, or even touching cold items for several days after receiving oxaliplatin.

Rituximab, along with other immunosuppressive agents, has rarely been associated with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. 5-Fluorouracil and high-dose cytarabine are associated with cerebellar toxicity. The posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome has been linked to chemotherapy that targets vascular endothelial growth factor, such as bevacizumab or sunitinib.

Because whole-brain radiation therapy can cause long-term impairment of cognitive function, focused high-dose radiation therapy (i.e., stereotactic radiosurgery) has become the preferred treatment for patients with limited brain metastases.

With the widespread use of checkpoint inhibitors, patients with cancer are at risk for toxicities associated with the induction of autoimmunity (see [Table: Table: Immune Toxicities of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors]

). Antibodies such as ipilimumab; pembrolizumab and nivolumab; and atezolizumab, durvalumab, and avelumab are associated with immune-related colitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis, dermatitis, endocrinopathies (hypophysitis, thyroiditis, and adrenalitis), and neuritis. These toxicities require prompt recognition and sometimes temporary or permanent cessation of immunotherapy. Moderate or severe toxicity requires treatment with glucocorticoid therapy, and high doses may be required in severe cases (see [Table: Table: Treatment of Moderate to Severe ICI Toxicity]

). Endocrinopathies such as thyroid and adrenal insufficiency are treated with hormone replacement.

After treatment ends, survivorship care becomes crucial. This care includes screening for recurrence and secondary malignancies; monitoring for late-organ dysfunction; and providing support for psychological, sexual, vocational, and other effects of treatment. An initial treatment plan for cancer may be based not only on providing the highest probability of cure but also on a strategy to reduce the risk for long-term complications.

Bone loss occurs at an increased rate in the following patient groups:

  • Cancer survivors who have received long-term glucocorticoid therapy
  • Patients who have undergone premature menopause induced by surgery (e.g., oophorectomy), medications, radiation, or chemotherapy
  • Patients treated for breast cancer with aromatase inhibitors
  • Patients treated for prostate cancer with androgen-deprivation therapy (increased risk for osteoporosis)
  • Patients with multiple myeloma (may cause generalized bone loss as well as lytic bone disease)

Assessment of bone density and treatment or prophylaxis should be considered to reduce the risk for fracture in each of these patient groups. Treatment commonly includes routine supplements of vitamin D and calcium (while monitoring serum calcium levels) and bisphosphonates or denosumab. Vigilance is required to detect bisphosphonate complications, such as osteonecrosis of the jaw (see

) and atypical subtrochanteric spiral fractures of the femur.

Surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy may all affect sexual function and fertility of both men and women. Multiple factors may decrease libido, including altered body image after breast surgery and the generalized fatigue associated with radiation therapy or chemotherapy. Anxiety and depression further diminish interest in sex. Counseling, support groups, and treatment of underlying mood disorders are helpful.

In women, premature menopause and infertility can result from pelvic radiotherapy and chemotherapy, particularly with alkylating agents. Estrogen is the most effective therapy for vasomotor symptoms related to premature menopause. For women with an intact uterus, estrogen should be combined with progestin. Estrogen replacement therapy is contraindicated in patients with breast and endometrial cancer. Tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors, and ovarian suppression may also cause menopausal symptoms, decreased libido, and vaginal dryness.

Men commonly experience erectile dysfunction after prostate surgery or irradiation, and androgen-deprivation therapy suppresses libido.

Risk factors for infertility relate to the dose and duration of chemotherapy as well as patient age. Consultation with fertility experts should be offered before starting chemotherapy in women and men who plan to have children in the future; egg, embryo, and semen cryopreservation may be options. Female patients should also a receive gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist during chemotherapy to preserve ovarian function. Fertility evaluations can often be done on an emergency basis, so delay in the initiation of definitive cancer treatment is minimized.

Short- and long-term declines in cognitive function can occur after cancer therapy. It remains unclear whether cancer and its treatment unmask preexisting cognitive impairment, whether the decline represents a sign of more rapid aging, or whether there is a more specific neurotoxic effect.

Childhood, adolescent, and young adult cancer survivors treated with cranial radiotherapy are at increased risk for subsequent central nervous system neoplasms. Surveillance consists of history and neurologic examinations every 1 to 5 years that focus on suggestive symptoms, such as new or worsening headaches; worsening nausea and vomiting; and new-onset cognitive, motor, sensory, or behavioral changes and other focal neurologic deficits. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether routine MRI surveillance reduces morbidity and mortality in this group of patients.

Oncologists play a critical role in providing patients with a survivorship plan. At the end of treatment, patients should receive details regarding long-term follow-up. This information can be crucial to the patient and primary care physician to ensure optimal care is provided after treatment is completed. Recommendations can include surveillance for cancer recurrence, healthy lifestyle modification, and strategies to reduce or prevent the late effects of cancer treatment. Some institutions are incorporating a survivorship visit after completion of treatment.

Cancer survivors should, at a minimum, have age- and gender-appropriate cancer screening. Secondary malignancies may develop in cancer survivors owing to a preexisting genetic predisposition, a “field” effect from previous carcinogen exposure, or late effects of previous cancer treatments.

Patients with identified genetic variants with an increased risk for additional malignancies should have genetic counseling and referral to a high-risk genetic clinic. Patients with smoking-related head and neck cancer are prone to second head and neck cancers, as well as lung and esophageal cancers. Patients exposed to chemotherapy with alkylating agents have an increased risk for myelodysplastic syndromes and acute leukemia. Radiation to the neck can be associated with hypothyroidism and thyroid cancer years later. Women receiving radiation to the mediastinum for Hodgkin lymphoma and other cancers have a marked increase of breast cancer, particularly if they were treated in adolescence and early adulthood, with the increased risk beginning about 8 years after treatment. For women who receive chest radiation before age 30 years, annual breast cancer screening with breast MRI and mammography is recommended to begin 8 years after therapy, starting no sooner than age 25 years.

Screening for Cancer

This section discusses cancer screening in asymptomatic, average-risk persons. Screening for cancer in patients at high risk is covered in the respective subspecialty sections of ACP MKSAP.

The balance of benefits and harms of screening mammography in average-risk women has shifted with the advent of increasingly effective breast cancer treatments, which improve outcomes even in the absence of early detection, as well as emerging information about overdiagnosis. Women at average risk include those without a personal history of breast cancer or a high-risk breast lesion, genetic variants conferring elevated risk for breast cancer, or a history of radiation to the chest as a child.

In average-risk women aged 50 to 74 years, there is a clear benefit to screening mammography, and all breast cancer guidelines recommend screening mammography in this age-group. Specific screening recommendations, however, vary by specialty society ( [Table: Table: Breast Cancer Screening in Women at Average Risk]

and Video: Recommendations for Breast Cancer Screening). In women younger than 50 years or older than 74 years, the balance of benefits and harms is less clear, and screening recommendations vary. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends biennial screening mammography, which imparts most benefits of annual mammography with fewer harms (most notably, a reduction in overdiagnosis) in average-risk women (cisgender women and persons assigned female at birth) aged 40 to 74 years. The USPSTF also concludes that both digital mammography and digital breast tomosynthesis, or “3D mammography,” are effective mammographic screening modalities. Breast cancer screening with clinical breast examination is not recommended.

Both transgender men and women may need screening for breast cancer, depending on age, gender-affirming treatment received, and personal risk factors. The American College of Radiology has developed a set of recommendations to inform clinical decision making.

Shared decision making with consideration of the patient’s level of risk, values, and preferences guides the screening decision. Potential harms of screening include false-positive results and overdiagnosis, which may result in unnecessary biopsies and substantial patient anxiety. For example, modeling data for the 2024 USPSTF recommendations estimate that biennial screening for women aged 40 to 74 years would result in 1376 false-positive results per 1000 women screened over a lifetime of screening, as well as 14 cases of overdiagnosis.

Approximately 50% of women have dense breasts on mammography, resulting in decreased sensitivity of mammography for breast cancer (more so with film than digital mammography). Increased breast density is associated with an increased risk for breast cancer, but patients with dense breasts should not be considered at high risk for breast cancer on the basis of dense breasts alone. For women in whom increased breast density is the sole risk factor for breast cancer, there is no evidence that adding MRI or ultrasonography to mammography affects breast cancer mortality, and most guidelines conclude that evidence is insufficient to recommend adjunctive screening. The American College of Radiology, however, notes that ultrasonography may be considered in this circumstance. Furthermore, some states have legislated that women be informed when dense breasts are noted on imaging and that this finding may increase the risk for breast cancer. Women with dense breasts should undergo further risk stratification; for those at high risk, additional screening may be considered (see Breast Cancer Chemoprevention and Other Risk Reduction Strategies in Oncology).

Radiologists use the Breast Imaging-Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) to categorize mammography findings, assess breast density, and make recommendations for further evaluation based on results of mammography (see Breast Mass in Interdisciplinary Medicine).

Screening for prostate cancer in asymptomatic, average-risk men has been controversial, and recommendations among U.S. professional organizations continue to evolve ( [Table: Table: Recommendations for Prostate Cancer Screening]

). In general, a strategy of shared decision making is recommended for average-risk men between the ages of 50 and 69 years. As an example, for men aged 55 to 69 years, the USPSTF recommends that clinicians engage in a discussion of the potential benefits versus harms of screening for prostate cancer before ordering prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing and that clinicians not screen men unless they express a preference for screening. The USPSTF recommends against routine PSA-based screening for prostate cancer in men aged 70 years or older.

Benefits of screening for men aged 55 to 69 years include prevention of one prostate cancer–related death for every 1000 men screened for 10 years (number needed to screen is 1000). Risks include overdiagnosis, overtreatment, and false-positive results that trigger unnecessary biopsies and patient anxiety. Estimated rates of overdiagnosis and overtreatment vary widely.

If the decision is made to proceed with screening, the American Urological Association (AUA) recommends choosing less frequent screening intervals (2-4 years), which may reduce overdiagnosis and the number of false-positive results while preserving most of the screening benefit. The AUA also recommends that the interval for rescreening and the decision to discontinue screening may be personalized based on patient preference, life expectancy, and general health. Screening is not recommended for men with a life expectancy of less than 10 to 15 years.

Patients with certain germline variants, such as BRCA1/2, are at increased risk for prostate cancer; for recommendations for screening in these patients, see [Table: Table: Cancer Risk Management for BRCA1/2 Variants]

.

For men who elect screening and who have elevated PSA levels, further evaluation is recommended (see Diagnosis and Staging of Prostate Cancer in Oncology).

There is significant variation in colorectal cancer screening guidelines. The American College of Physicians (ACP) recommends screening for colorectal cancer in asymptomatic adults aged 50 to 75 years (grade A); although the ACP recommends that clinicians consider not screening adults aged 45 to 49 years, it does recommend having a discussion with the patient regarding the benefits and harms of screening. In contrast, many professional societies, including the USPSTF, the U.S. Multi-Society Task Force on Colorectal Cancer (MSTF, an initiative of U.S. gastroenterology societies), and the American Cancer Society (ACS), recommend initiation of screening for colorectal cancer at age 45 years. The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that screening for colorectal cancer in adults aged 45 to 49 years has moderate net benefit (grade B). According to the USPSTF, screening decisions in patients aged 76 to 85 years should be individualized according to life expectancy and ability to tolerate treatment of colorectal cancer if diagnosed. Screening history should also be considered before screening patients in this age-group, because patients who have not yet undergone screening are the most likely to benefit (grade C). The USPSTF suggests that screening may be discontinued in patients older than 85 years, whereas the ACP suggests discontinuing screening in average-risk patients older than 75 years or when life expectancy is less than 10 years.

There is little head-to-head comparative evidence that any one recommended screening modality provides a greater benefit than the others ( [Table: Table: USPSTF Estimated Benefits of Colorectal Cancer Screening]

). In addition, despite unequivocal evidence that colon cancer screening reduces mortality, an estimated one in three U.S. adults who are eligible for colon cancer screening has not been screened. Therefore, the USPSTF supports using the test that is most likely to result in completion of screening. Understanding a patient’s values and preferences and selecting a test to which the patient is most likely to adhere may improve screening rates. The ACP suggests a similar screening strategy. Clinicians should be familiar with the characteristics of each screening strategy to facilitate effective discussion with patients ( [Table: Table: USPSTF Recommendations for Colorectal Cancer Screening]

).

The ACP suggests colonoscopy every 10 years, flexible sigmoidoscopy every 10 years plus fecal immunochemical testing (FIT) every 2 years, or FIT or high-sensitivity guaiac-based fecal occult blood testing every 2 years as acceptable screening regimens. In contrast, the MSTF has ranked colorectal cancer screening tests in tiers based on the available evidence, cost-effectiveness, test availability, and several other factors. The MSTF recommends colonoscopy every 10 years or annual FIT as first-tier tests; CT colonography every 5 years, FIT-DNA testing every 3 years, or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 to 10 years as second-tier tests; and capsule colonography every 5 years as a third-tier test. The serum circulating methylated SEPT9 DNA test is an FDA-approved screening strategy. However, this test’s sensitivity for detecting colorectal cancer is only 48%, and the MSTF does not recommend its use.

For more information, including information on screening in higher risk patients, see Colorectal Neoplasia in Gastroenterology and Colorectal Cancer in Oncology.

The USPSTF recommends screening women aged 21 to 65 years every 3 years with cervical cytology (a Pap test); in women aged 30 to 65 years who want to lengthen the screening interval, primary human papillomavirus (HPV) testing (HPV testing alone) or HPV cotesting (HPV testing with cervical cytology) every 5 years can be performed. The USPSTF recommends against screening women younger than 21 years regardless of sexual history because screening has not been shown to reduce cervical cancer incidence or mortality compared with starting screening at age 21 years. The USPSTF guidelines are endorsed by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. Comparison between the USPSTF and ACS guidelines is presented in [Table: Table: Comparison of Cervical Cancer Screening Recommendations]

.

Screening can be discontinued at age 65 years in non–high-risk women with adequate past screening, defined as three consecutive negative Pap smears or two consecutive negative HPV cotesting results in the past 10 years, with the most recent test occurring within 5 years. In women older than 65 years with life expectancy of at least 10 years and risk factors for cervical cancer (history of abnormal Pap smears, history of a high-grade precancerous lesion, in utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol, immunocompromise, previous HPV infection), continued screening should be considered.

Women who have never been screened have the highest incidence of and mortality from cervical cancer. The mortality reduction from screening in women who have not been previously screened may be as high as 74%. Women older than 65 years who have never been screened or in whom adequacy of previous screening cannot be confirmed should undergo Pap testing every 3 years, primary HPV testing every 5 years, or HPV cotesting every 5 years until the criteria for adequate screening have been fulfilled.

Screening should not be performed in women who have had a hysterectomy with removal of the cervix unless a high-grade precancerous lesion (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia 2 or 3) was present, in which case screening should be continued for at least 20 years after hysterectomy.

Transgender men who have a cervix should be screened according to the aforementioned guidelines. Cervical cancer screening should not be used as a requirement for testosterone therapy.

Interpretation of screening results is complex and takes into account several variables, including the presence of HPV and cytology results, if done. The need for treatment or further testing, often colposcopy or repeat screening, depends on the likelihood of the presence of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3 (CIN3), adenocarcinoma in situ, or cancer (collectively known as CIN3+ disease). Factors that increase the likelihood of CIN3+ disease include increasing age, presence of HPV, HPV subtypes 16 and 18, and immunocompromise. Previous screening results also affect the likelihood of CIN3+ disease. A management application from the American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology provides individualized management guidance based on the screening results (https://app.asccp.org/).

For more information, see Cervical Cancer in Oncology.

Although lung cancer screening with chest radiography is not recommended, annual screening with low-dose CT in patients with heavy cigarette use results in a 20% to 24% reduction in lung cancer mortality (number needed to screen is 265 with 3 to 5 screens performed and 10 years of follow-up). The USPSTF recommends lung cancer screening with annual low-dose CT for persons aged 50 years to 80 years with a 20-pack-year smoking history; screening should be discontinued in patients who have not smoked for 15 years The ACS also advises lung cancer screening with annual low-dose CT for persons aged 50 to 80 years with at least a 20-pack-year smoking history; however, in contrast to the USPSTF guidelines, the ACS recommends screening all persons who formerly smoked who meet these criteria regardless of when they last smoked (see Lung Cancer Screening in Pulmonary Medicine for additional information).

Genetic or familial syndromes may be associated with many types of cancer, including breast, colon, ovarian, and pancreatic. The USPSTF recommends using a brief familial risk assessment tool, such as the Ontario Family History Assessment Tool, to screen for BRCA1/2 gene variant risk in patients with a personal or family history of breast, ovarian, tubal, or peritoneal cancer or who have an ancestry associated with the variants. Patients identified as being at risk for familial or genetic syndromes should be referred to genetic counseling for consideration of genetic testing (see Genetic Tests and Testing Strategies in Foundations of Clinical Practice).

The USPSTF, the Society of Gynecologic Oncology, and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommend against screening for ovarian cancer with serum CA-125 testing or ultrasonography in patients at average risk.

According to the USPSTF, evidence is insufficient to determine the balance of benefits and harms of screening for skin cancer with a visual skin examination (I statement). However, the USPSTF recommends that persons younger than 24 years who have fair skin receive counseling to minimize exposure to ultraviolet radiation to reduce their risk for skin cancer (grade B) and recommends offering selective counseling to adults older than 24 years with fair skin types (grade C). The USPSTF also concludes that there is insufficient evidence to assess the balance of benefits and harms of counseling adults about skin self-examination for skin cancer prevention (I statement).

The USPSTF recommends against screening for pancreatic cancer in asymptomatic adults (grade D). For screening recommendations for patients with elevated risk, see Hereditary Pancreatic Cancer and Surveillance in Gastroenterology and [Table: Table: Cancer Risk Management for BRCA1/2 Variants]

.

Evidence is insufficient to recommend routine anal cancer screening in average-risk populations, but the International Anal Neoplasia Society consensus guideline suggests screening high-risk patients, including persons living with HIV, men who have sex with men and transgender women without HIV, persons born female with a history of abnormal cervical cytology, solid organ transplant recipients, and other patients with immunocompromise. For more specific information, see [Table: Table: Initial Laboratory Screening in HIV Infection]

.

Routine screening for bladder cancer, testicular cancer, and thyroid cancer is not recommended by any expert group.

Pulmonary Diagnostic Tests

Pulmonary function testing assesses airflow, lung volume, and gas transfer and aids in recognizing patterns of altered respiratory physiology. Such testing can include spirometry, response to bronchodilators, bronchial challenge testing, lung volume testing, and measurement of Dlco.

Findings are compared with the normal distribution in a healthy population that takes age, sex, height, and other factors into consideration. Deviation from the predicted result is represented as a z-score (defined as the number of standard deviations from the predicted value), which is based on 2022 European Respiratory Society/American Thoracic Society guidelines. This score reduces bias due to age, sex, and other factors ( [Table: Table: Pulmonary Function Test Results and Associated Impairment]

). Some laboratories still use percent predicted as their cutoff, typically corresponding to 80% of the predicted value.

Spirometry measures the maximal volume and flow of air during a best-effort forced exhalation. Reported values include FEV~1, FVC, and the FEV~1/FVC ratio.

Spirometry correlates with home peak expiratory flow meter measurements but is more reliable and provides more data. Although spirometry is easily performed in the outpatient setting, technical test validation is needed, and patient factors, including poor effort, coughing, and failure to exhale for a minimum of 6 seconds, may result in suboptimal test performance and misinterpretation. If spirometry is unable to be performed, peak flow measurement can help in the diagnosis of asthma.

Bronchial challenge testing is used to identify bronchial hyperresponsiveness. This test is particularly helpful in patients whose symptoms suggest asthma in whom initial spirometry is normal.

As part of the test, patients inhale increasing doses of a substance known to induce bronchospasm, such as methacholine, in a stepwise fashion. This is followed by repeat measurement of FEV~1; the test is positive if FEV~1 falls by 20% or more from the baseline value at a methacholine dose of 8 mg or less.

Bronchial challenge testing has a high negative predictive value for ruling out asthma; however, a positive test can occur in other conditions, including the following:

  • COPD
  • Tobacco use
  • Upper respiratory infections
  • Allergic rhinitis
  • Bronchiectasis
  • Cystic fibrosis

Lung volumes can be measured by body plethysmography or nitrogen diffusion. Measures include the following:

  • Total lung capacity
  • Vital capacity
  • Functional residual capacity
  • Expiratory reserve volume
  • Residual volume

Dlco measurement estimates the amount of gas transfer through the alveolar-capillary unit and is proportional to the surface area of functional lung. Dlco is measured by inhalation of a gas mixture containing carbon monoxide and helium; the resulting value is corrected for hemoglobin level, if available.

Pulmonary function testing interpretation classifies abnormal results as obstructive, restrictive, or mixed obstructive/restrictive and assesses the severity of impairment.

A reduced FEV~1/FVC ratio is consistent with obstruction. Severity of obstruction is determined according to the measured FEV~1 as a percentage of the predicted value (see [Table: Table: Pulmonary Function Test Results and Associated Impairment]

). The American Thoracic Society and the European Respiratory Society define a reduced FEV~1/FVC ratio as below the lower limit of normal, whereas the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease defines a reduced FEV~1/FVC ratio as below 0.70 on a postbronchodilator test. In their 2021 technical standard, the American Thoracic Society and European Respiratory Society changed the criteria for bronchodilator responsiveness to an increase from baseline in FEV~1, FVC, or both of at least 10% relative to the predicted value. These new criteria have not been universally implemented, and many laboratories still use the former thresholds (12% and 200 mL) for a significant bronchodilator response. Measurement of lung volumes may help in assessing obstructive lung disease but is not necessary for diagnosis. Elevation of total lung capacity (TLC) and residual volume (120% or greater of predicted) can be observed and generally indicates hyperinflation and air trapping, a common pattern in severe COPD.

If FEV~1 or FVC is reduced and the FEV~1/FVC ratio is 0.70 or greater, then the pattern may be interpreted as restrictive; however, measurement of TLC is needed to confirm the presence of restrictive disease. If TLC is less than 80% of predicted (or the lower limit of normal), a restrictive pattern is present.

Some patients present with coexisting restrictive and obstructive pulmonary disorders, such as combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema. In these cases, both a low TLC (restrictive) and low FEV~1/FVC ratio (obstructive) are present.

Obesity can alter respiratory physiology and function, often resulting in reduced lung volumes (FEV~1 and FVC). Patients with obesity will typically have a preserved FEV~1/FVC ratio and may have a modest reduction in TLC and expiratory reserve volume.

Dlco is reduced in conditions in which functioning alveolar-capillary units are destroyed (COPD), infiltrated (diffuse parenchymal lung disease), or removed (lung resection) and in which their function is compromised (pulmonary parenchymal and vascular disorders). Conditions that increase pulmonary capillary blood volume, such as pulmonary alveolar hemorrhage, left-to-right shunt, or asthma, can cause an elevation in Dlco.

The flow-volume loop is a graphic representation of maximally forced inspiratory and expiratory flow (on the Y-axis) against volume (on the X-axis). The shape of the spirometric flow-volume loop can help differentiate obstructive from restrictive patterns and suggest the anatomic location of airway obstruction (

).

The 6-minute walk test provides a valid and reliable measurement of exercise capacity in patients with lung disease. Patients walk at their own pace along a course for 6 minutes, and the total distance walked is recorded.

Shorter distances on the 6-minute walk test correlate with increased mortality in several lung diseases, including COPD, diffuse parenchymal lung disease, and pulmonary arterial hypertension. Serial 6-minute walk testing can also help assess response to therapy in patients with chronic respiratory disorders, especially pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Oximeters calculate the difference between absorption of infrared light by oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. A normal hemoglobin saturation measured by pulse oximetry is 95% to 100%, and values below 90% indicate hypoxemia.

Several factors can affect the accuracy of pulse oximetry readings. Erroneous readings may result from the following patient factors:

  • Cool extremities
  • Poor circulation
  • Nail polish
  • Motion artifact
  • Skin pigmentation

Less commonly, the substances in the blood that absorb infrared light may result in erroneous readings, including carboxyhemoglobin (present in carbon monoxide poisoning) and methemoglobin (caused by medications such as nitrates, some topical anesthetics, and dapsone).

In these cases, alternative methods of measuring oxygenation (e.g., arterial blood gas analysis) are needed.

Measurement of fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) in an expiratory breath sample provides a noninvasive way to quantify eosinophilic airway inflammation and serves as a complementary tool in the management of lung diseases, particularly asthma.

More than half of patients with asthma have eosinophilic (type 2) airway inflammation, and elevated FeNO levels correlate modestly with blood and sputum eosinophilia. In these patients, FeNO levels may help predict glucocorticoid responsiveness and monitor response and adherence to anti-inflammatory therapy. The American Thoracic Society guidelines suggest that FeNO levels above 50 ppb indicate glucocorticoid-sensitive airway inflammation. Patients with levels below 25 ppb are less likely to have eosinophilic inflammation and glucocorticoid responsiveness.

FeNO testing is recommended as an adjunct in asthma evaluation for patients aged 5 years and older. It can also help evaluate chronic cough; levels may be high in nonasthmatic eosinophilic bronchitis, a condition involving inflammation without bronchospasm (spirometry is normal).

In addition, FeNO measurement may be useful for diagnosis of asthma when spirometry cannot be performed or if diagnosis remains uncertain after standard evaluation. It can also help guide treatment decisions in persistent allergic asthma.

Several imaging modalities can be helpful in the evaluation of pulmonary disease. [Table: Table: Characteristics of Pulmonary Imaging Modalities]

provides information on these modalities and their characteristics. [Table: Table: Initial Testing Suggested for Various Indications]

shows suggested initial imaging methods for specific indications.

Conventional chest radiography is indicated as the initial imaging procedure for most patients with significant respiratory symptoms. Posteroanterior and lateral views should be obtained.

Advantages of chest radiography are the availability of testing and the low dose of radiation exposure for the patient. Limitations include the need for deep inspiration and breath holding, relatively low image resolution, and the 2D images produced.

CT of the chest allows detailed, high-resolution imaging of the lungs and options for both static and dynamic imaging techniques. Helical scanners allow rapid scanning but may require patients to hold their breath at full inspiration for 30 seconds or more.

Reconstruction can include sagittal and coronal images and results in 3D representation of the extent and distribution of disease. More specialized techniques reformat the data to highlight specific structures, such as the vasculature (maximum-intensity projection) and the airways (minimum-intensity projection).

Additional variables in CT imaging include the use of contrast and slice thickness and interval. The choice of examination technique depends on the clinical context and information sought.

Noncontrast CT of the chest is often preferred because contrast makes assessing the lung parenchyma more difficult. Use of intravenous contrast dye helps delineate mediastinal structures and is particularly useful in patients with suspected lymphadenopathy or vascular pathology. CT angiography is used for detection of pulmonary embolism and uses a rapid, timed bolus of intravenous contrast.

For most patients, routine (slice thickness of 2 or 2.5 mm) noncontrast CT provides the needed information. For patients with suspected diffuse parenchymal lung disease, a high-resolution (slice thickness of 1 mm) CT should be ordered. Expiratory high-resolution CT can evaluate for air trapping and further inform the diagnosis of small airways disease. However, because the slice interval (the distance between individual slices) is larger with high-resolution CT than with conventional CT, this technique “skips” interval sections of the lung and should not be used to evaluate lung nodules.

CT exposes the patient to a much higher dose of radiation than traditional chest radiography and is currently the primary source of imaging radiation exposure. Low-dose CT is now recommended for lung cancer screening in the United States (see Lung Cancer Screening in Pulmonary Medicine).

Point-of-care thoracic ultrasonography provides a noninvasive means of rapidly assessing the lungs, pleura, and diaphragm. It is particularly helpful in critically ill patients because of its accessibility.

Thoracic ultrasonography shows the presence, characteristics, and volume of pleural effusions more accurately than chest radiography. In addition, performing pleural drainage procedures, such as thoracentesis or thoracostomy tube placement, with ultrasound guidance reduces risks for complications, including pneumothorax.

Ultrasonography is helpful in assessing the presence of pneumothorax. Demonstration of movement of the visceral pleura against the parietal pleura (Video: Lung Sliding Sign or Video: Lung Pulse Sign) excludes a pneumothorax at the area scanned.

Thoracic ultrasonography assesses diaphragm function more accurately than fluoroscopy. Ultrasonography of the lung parenchyma can also identify pulmonary edema (Video: Pulmonary Edema on Ultrasound) and areas of lung consolidation (Video: Lung Consolidation on Ultrasound).

Factors limiting ultrasound usefulness include obesity and significant soft tissue edema or musculature, which can degrade image quality. In addition, complex or high-density pleural collections (empyema, hemothorax) may be too echogenic for accurate detection or identification of adjacent tissue structures (

).

PET uses the radionuclide 18-fluoro-2-deoxyglucose, which accumulates within highly metabolically active cells, such as cancer cells, and appears as discrete areas of uptake. Integrated PET/CT allows improved localization of the metabolic activity. PET is widely used to evaluate the likelihood of malignancy in lung nodules, to stage known thoracic tumors, and to evaluate for metastatic disease from other nonthoracic malignancies.

False-positive PET scans can occur in the setting of other hypermetabolic conditions in which cells accumulate fluorodeoxyglucose, such as infection or inflammation. False negatives can occur in the setting of tumors with low rates of metabolic activity, such as carcinoid tumors; adenocarcinoma in situ; and, rarely, metastatic kidney, prostate, or testicular cancer. PET is also not reliable for the determination of malignant potential in lung nodules less than 8 mm.

Bronchoscopy is a diagnostic ( [Table: Table: Diagnostic Bronchoscopic Procedures]

) and therapeutic ( [Table: Table: Therapeutic Bronchoscopic Procedures]

) tool for patients with lung disorders. It is used for the diagnosis of localized and diffuse pulmonary diseases and is important in the diagnostic evaluation of pulmonary infections, particularly in immunocompromised patients. Early diagnosis and directed treatment are keys to management of these patients, and invasive testing such as bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage is often necessary, particularly in patients who cannot produce sputum.

Endobronchial ultrasonography is the initial procedure of choice for obtaining tissue from mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes in the diagnosis and staging of patients with known or suspected thoracic malignancy.

Common complications of bronchoscopy include hypoxia and bleeding, both of which are typically self-limited.
