Airways Disease

Asthma is an inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by cough, wheezing, chest tightness, dyspnea, and variable airflow obstruction. Approximately 8% of the U.S. population has a diagnosis of asthma, and prevalence is increased among patients older than age 65 years, women, and persons living below the poverty level.

Asthma is a major health burden throughout the world and accounts for nearly 10 million office visits per year. It can be life threatening and caused 9.9 deaths per million Americans in 2017; mortality is higher among older adults. Asthma disproportionately affects Black and Hispanic patients.

The onset of asthma can occur at any age, and the natural history varies with respect to the duration and severity of symptoms, sex, and response to therapy. Children often have a family history of atopy or exposure to sensitizing allergens, such as dust mites or cockroaches. Childhood asthma may improve or resolve during adolescence or adulthood, particularly in males. Adults with new-onset asthma may have occupational exposures known to induce bronchial hyperreactivity.

Patients with severe symptoms generally have a more sustained course, lower pulmonary function, and increased risk for persistent airway obstruction. Diagnosis and treatment of asthma in older adults is often challenged by symptom overlap with other conditions (COPD, heart failure) and the normal effects of aging on pulmonary physiology.

The pathophysiologic mechanisms of asthma include chronic airway inflammation; airway narrowing resulting from edema, subepithelial fibrosis, smooth muscle hypertrophy, and mucus hypersecretion; and airway smooth muscle constriction resulting from bronchial hyperreactivity in response to various stimuli.

The airway cellular inflammatory profile in patients with asthma is variable; includes eosinophils, T lymphocytes, mast cells, and neutrophils; and persists even in the absence of symptoms. Type 2 inflammation with eosinophilia is commonly recognized in allergic asthma; however, other cellular profiles exist, and neutrophilic inflammation is increasingly recognized in older patients.

Bronchial hyperreactivity causing airway obstruction is typically episodic and triggered by stimuli that would not induce symptoms in healthy people. Common triggers include allergens, dust, fumes, exercise, extremes of temperature, and respiratory infections.

Risk factors for asthma include both host and environmental factors. Although genes predisposing to atopy, bronchial hyperreactivity, and airway inflammation have been identified, a genetic predisposition likely interacts with additional factors to produce disease. These include the following:

  • Exposure to indoor allergens (mites, furred animals, cockroaches, molds)
  • Exposure to outdoor allergens (pollens, molds)
  • Tobacco smoke exposure
  • Occupational sensitizers and allergens
  • Viral respiratory infections
  • Air pollution
  • Obesity

Although asthma is heterogeneous, distinct phenotypes are recognized and have implications for underlying mechanisms, treatment, and outcomes. Commonly described specific phenotypes are not yet broadly accepted, but these subsets tend to have different cellular compositions of airway inflammation and may respond variably to anti-inflammatory therapies.

Common symptoms of asthma are cough, wheezing, chest tightness, and dyspnea. They occur intermittently and often in response to various stimuli, including allergens, infections, dust, fumes, and exercise. Symptoms often have a diurnal variation, worsening in the evening and early morning. Viral respiratory infections are a particularly robust trigger for most patients. Variability of symptoms—both improvement and worsening of symptoms over time—is a key diagnostic feature of asthma.

History taking should establish whether the patient has ever smoked tobacco or other substances; has pets; or has had environmental exposures to dust, fumes, or particulate matter known to cause bronchial hyperreactivity. A personal or family history of atopy or allergic sinus disease may be present. In particular, the presence of nasal polyps, sensitivity to aspirin, and wheezing is known as the asthmatic triad. The physical examination may demonstrate wheezing, reduced airflow, or a prolonged expiratory phase; however, some patients with asthma may have normal respiratory findings, particularly when they are asymptomatic.

Confirmation of reversible airflow obstruction is the cornerstone of asthma diagnosis. This can be achieved with measurement of FEV~1, FVC, and the FEV~1/FVC ratio on spirometry or with serial measurement of peak expiratory flow rates. Airway obstruction that improves with bronchodilators, on subsequent measurements, or after 4 weeks of anti-inflammatory treatment supports a diagnosis of asthma. For adults, a change in FEV~1 or FVC after the administration of bronchodilator therapy is deemed significant if the difference between the postbronchodilator value and the prebronchodilator value is more than 10% of the predicted value. (Note that these criteria, introduced in the 2021 American Thoracic Society/European Respiratory Society technical standard, have not been universally implemented. Many laboratories still use the former thresholds [12% and 200 mL] for a significant bronchodilator response.)

If asthma is suspected but no airflow obstruction is present during the initial evaluation, bronchial challenge testing is indicated. This test is usually performed with inhaled methacholine, although other stimuli (exercise, mannitol) have been validated. If a bronchial challenge test is negative, asthma is unlikely. A positive challenge test confirms bronchial hyperreactivity but does not confirm asthma because other disorders may also demonstrate this finding; therefore, clinical correlation with symptoms and other testing is needed.

Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) and blood eosinophil testing can be considered as adjuncts in asthma evaluation for patients aged 6 years and older. Elevated FeNO (>50 ppb) and/or elevated blood eosinophil count (level greater than predicted) can indicate type 2 inflammation and direct targeted biologic therapy. Biomarker evaluation is also recommended for the diagnosis of asthma if spirometry or peak flow testing is not available. The absence of biomarker elevation, however, does not exclude asthma as a cause of symptoms.

Chest radiography is helpful in many patients to assess the likelihood of other diagnoses, such as COPD, heart failure, parenchymal lung disorders, central airway obstruction, and bronchiectasis. This assessment is especially important in older adults, for whom asthma is often underrecognized and undertreated.

Subtypes (phenotypes) of asthma and other closely related conditions exist that may require specific considerations in diagnosis and testing. These include allergic asthma, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, cough-variant asthma, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, reactive airways dysfunction syndrome, occupational asthma, and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.

The presence of atopy can identify an allergic asthma phenotype in a patient with respiratory symptoms. The key constituents of the atopic response (activated eosinophils and IgE) are generated by pathways involving cytokines secreted mainly by Th2 cells. This class of asthmatic airway inflammation is referred to as type 2 inflammation and is present in at least half of all patients with asthma. Biomarker evaluation in these patients often demonstrates serum eosinophilia, high IgE levels, and an elevated FeNO level. In patients with severe disease, elevated levels of IgE and eosinophils are therapeutic targets for biologic therapies.

Other common tests to identify atopy include allergy skin-prick tests and laboratory measurement of allergen-specific IgE in serum. Results of each method are generally concordant. Skin testing is more sensitive but subject to errors related to administration, whereas serum tests are more specific but have higher costs. A normal level of total serum IgE does not preclude clinical allergies.

Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease is the syndrome of asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis accompanied by sensitivity to aspirin and other NSAIDs that inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX)-1. Clinical characteristics of this disease include adult onset; airway and peripheral eosinophilia; inflammatory sinusitis with polyposis; and persistent, often severe, asthma. Ingestion of triggering COX-1 inhibitors can cause life-threatening bronchospasm within minutes to hours, sometimes accompanied by rhinorrhea, conjunctival injection, and flushing.

Long-term management, in addition to the usual stepped asthma care, includes discontinuation of all aspirin and nonselective NSAIDs and use of leukotriene-receptor antagonists that target the increased leukotriene production in this form of asthma. Aspirin desensitization can often improve control but requires specialized expertise. The selective COX-2 inhibitor celecoxib, which does not inhibit COX-1, is a safe anti-inflammatory agent in patients with aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.

Patients with asthma whose primary symptom is chronic cough without other symptoms are considered to have cough-variant asthma. Diagnosis often requires documentation of bronchial hyperreactivity with a methacholine challenge test because most patients will have normal baseline spirometry.

Recommended therapies are the same as those for other types of asthma. Other causes of chronic cough that should be investigated include gastroesophageal reflux and upper airway cough syndrome resulting from rhinitis. Frequently, these causes coexist and require concomitant therapy (see Subacute and Chronic Cough in Common Symptoms).

Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) refers to acute, measurable airway obstruction that occurs in response to exercise. EIB is one of the most common symptoms in patients with asthma but also occurs in patients without asthma, typically elite athletes, during periods of high-intensity exercise. Environmental factors play a key role in precipitating symptoms. Exercise in cold, dry air, such as during winter or in indoor ice rinks; exposure to high levels of trichloramines in swimming pools; and inhalation of airborne particulates and ozone have all been implicated.

Other disorders, such as inducible laryngeal obstruction and cardiac disorders, can mimic EIB; therefore, establishing the presence of bronchial hyperreactivity is crucial for accurate diagnosis. For most patients, this assessment entails bronchial challenge testing with inhaled agents or, ideally, with exercise.

Recommended therapy for EIB is either an inhaled glucocorticoid plus short-acting β~2-agonist (SABA) or low-dose inhaled glucocorticoid-formoterol as needed or before exercise. Guidelines from the Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) no longer recommend treatment of asthma with a SABA alone because of safety concerns, although the National Asthma Education and Prevention Program (NAEPP) endorses this practice. Potentially effective nonpharmacologic measures include pre-exercise warm-up and warming cold air before inhalation, such as with a mask or scarf.

An estimated 15% of adult asthma is work related; therefore, a careful occupational history is an essential part of asthma evaluation. Occupational asthma includes asthma that is directly caused by or exacerbated by exposure to sensitizing substances or irritants in the workplace.

Typical sensitizing agents are high-molecular-weight substances, such as proteins, that induce an IgE-mediated immunologic response. Examples include animal and plant allergens, latex, grains, and the diisocyanates used in processing polyurethane products. Once sensitized, patients may subsequently react to very low levels of exposure. Those at risk include farmers and animal workers, health care workers, latex glove users, bakers, and manufacturers of polyurethane products.

A key clinical indicator is the relationship of symptoms to work exposures; symptoms often improve during time away from work. Spirometry before and after workplace exposure is a cost-effective way to confirm a suspected diagnosis of occupational asthma. Alternatively, demonstration of bronchial hyperreactivity through bronchial challenge testing or serial peak flow measurements can be used.

In addition to providing pharmacologic therapy, treatment consists of reducing exposure to the offending agent through workplace modifications or removing patients from the workplace entirely. The overriding principle of treatment is prevention, which includes workplace interventions to avoid exposures and monitoring for early identification of disease.

A well-described subset of irritant-induced occupational asthma, reactive airways dysfunction syndrome occurs in patients without preexisting asthma after a single, high-level exposure to fumes, gases, or vapors. Symptoms are usually severe enough to prompt immediate medical evaluation. The diagnosis requires evidence of asthmatic symptoms for at least 3 months after the exposure and is confirmed by demonstration of airway obstruction or bronchial hyperreactivity on spirometry.

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is an ongoing immunologic response to inhaled Aspergillus species that leads to persistent eosinophilic airway inflammation, increased IgE levels (both total and on Aspergillus-specific testing), and eventual tissue damage with airway remodeling.

Patients present with difficult-to-control asthma, productive cough, and expectoration of mucus plugs. Radiographs may demonstrate pulmonary infiltrates and bronchiectasis. Diagnostic criteria are debated but include the presence of asthma, elevated IgE levels (≥500 U/mL [≥500 kU/L]), elevated blood eosinophil count (≥500/µL [0.5 × 10^9/L]), positive skin tests to Aspergillus antigens, increased IgE and IgG levels on Aspergillus-specific testing, and either central bronchiectasis or infiltrates.

Management should involve specialist care and is aimed at suppressing the enhanced immunologic response with systemic glucocorticoids and/or reducing the fungal antigenic burden with antifungal agents. Treatment duration is typically several months, and biologic therapy can be considered in patients with refractory symptoms and dependence on systemic glucocorticoids. Omalizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to free serum IgE and improves asthma control in patients with ABPA, including reducing the need for systemic glucocorticoids. Other biologic agents used in the management of severe asthma, as well as nebulized antifungal therapy, are proposed alternative options.

Asthma and COPD overlap is not a single disease entity but rather a heterogenous condition that includes features of both asthma and COPD. Risk factors include childhood asthma, cigarette use, and air pollution. It is characterized by a greater symptom burden, more frequent exacerbations, a worse quality of life, and a higher mortality than with either asthma or COPD alone.

Diagnostic criteria vary, but clinical findings include fixed airflow obstruction with some degree of bronchodilator reversibility together with atopy, elevated IgE levels, an elevated FeNO level, and elevated blood eosinophil levels.

Treatment is similar to that for asthma, with an emphasis on inhaled glucocorticoids. Long-acting muscarinic antagonists are also helpful. More research on this patient population is needed, both to better define the phenotype and to develop targeted therapy.

Goals of longitudinal asthma management are to control chronic asthma symptoms, prevent exacerbations, and minimize risk for persistent airway obstruction. These goals should be accomplished in a stepwise approach by assessing asthma severity, controlling symptoms on an ongoing basis, and then modifying therapies appropriately. The 2020 NAEPP guidelines and the 2025 GINA guidelines ( [Table: Table: GINA Asthma Treatment Guidelines]

) offer similar but distinct stepwise approaches. Overall, the GINA guidelines preferentially emphasize the use of inhaled glucocorticoid–long-acting β~2-agonist (LABA) combination therapy in all patients, including as rescue therapy.

Long-term management of asthma includes the following three essential components:

  • Assessment of symptom control and risk. Standardized, validated questionnaires that can discriminate between well-controlled and inadequately controlled asthma on the basis of patient symptoms include the Asthma Control Test and the Asthma Control Questionnaire. Patients with daytime symptoms occurring less than twice weekly and nocturnal symptoms occurring less than twice monthly during the preceding 4 weeks are considered to have well-controlled asthma. Risk is based on measured lung function and the potential for future exacerbations, which is related to the presence of comorbidities and historical features known to predict future exacerbations. Comorbidities such as gastroesophageal reflux disease, sinus disease, obstructive sleep apnea, vocal cord dysfunction, and obesity are common and should be actively managed to reduce symptoms and potentially improve asthma control ( [Table: Table: Common Asthma Comorbidities]

). - Treatment. Once symptoms and risk are assessed, therapy should be initiated. All patients with asthma should be provided with quick-relief (rescue) medication to use as needed for symptoms. In addition, controller medications are used as maintenance therapy to control symptoms and prevent exacerbations. A critical component of therapy is teaching and assessing proper inhaler technique; patients require training to effectively use these devices. Use of a spacer can be helpful with compatible inhaler devices. - Review response and adjust therapy. Control of asthma and tolerance of asthma therapies should be assessed several months after medication initiation. Controller medications can be stepped up or down to maintain symptom control while minimizing medication exposure.

All patients with asthma require access to quick-relief (rescue) therapy. SABAs have traditionally been the preferred medications to quickly reverse bronchospasm and relieve acute asthma symptoms; however, new information suggests that they may be safest when used in combination with inhaled glucocorticoids ( [Table: Table: Asthma Medications]

).

SABAs have a rapid onset of action and deliver medications directly through the airways, reducing systemic adverse effects. Their main mechanism of action is induction of airway smooth muscle relaxation using stimulation of β~2-agonist receptors. SABAs are generally not administered on a scheduled basis nor as the sole agent. Albuterol is the most commonly used SABA in the United States.

Although the NAEPP continues to recommend as-needed SABA as a quick-relief medication, the GINA guidelines recommend the use of an inhaled glucocorticoid-formoterol combination over a SABA or an inhaled glucocorticoid-SABA combination as rescue therapy. Similarly, the NAEPP recommends an as-needed SABA for intermittent asthma, whereas GINA prefers the inhaled glucocorticoid-formoterol combination.

Short-acting inhaled anticholinergics are less effective than SABAs at relieving acute bronchospasm; however, they may be used as adjunctive therapy to SABA treatment in the management of acute exacerbations in the emergency department. This combination has been shown to reduce hospitalization rates in this setting.

Controller medications are used to provide ongoing symptom relief and to prevent asthma exacerbations. Several classes of controllers target different mechanisms of the asthma profile; therefore, combining medications can achieve good control. The choice of therapy generally depends on the assessment of risk and is adjusted on the basis of symptom response and patient tolerance (see [Table: Table: Asthma Medications]

and [Table: Table: GINA Asthma Treatment Guidelines]

).

Inhaled glucocorticoids are the most effective class of asthma controller medications. These agents alleviate several pathologic processes of the asthmatic response, including airway mucosal edema, mucus hypersecretion, and airway inflammation. In active smokers, the effectiveness of these medications is diminished and the required doses may be higher than those for nonsmokers.

Adverse effects are related to dosage and vary by steroid formulation. The effects relate to local deposition (oral candidiasis, dysphonia) but can sometimes be generalized resulting from some degree of systemic absorption. Systemic adverse effects, such as adrenocortical suppression, reduced bone mineral density, and cataracts, generally do not occur at dosages below 400 μg/d of inhaled budesonide or equivalent dosages of other inhaled glucocorticoid formulations. The rate of pneumonia is increased with high-dose and high-potency formulations. Despite these risks, the benefits of inhaled glucocorticoids outweigh the potential adverse effects.

Although oral glucocorticoids are a cornerstone of therapy for the treatment of acute asthma exacerbations, long-term use should be avoided because it exposes patients to the common adverse effects of these agents (see [Table: Table: Asthma Medications]

).

Inhaled LABAs that provide sustained airway dilation with once- or twice-daily dosing are an important tool for asthma treatment. When added to an inhaled glucocorticoid, they provide improved control and decrease the risk for exacerbation. Administration in a single inhaler is preferred because of greater adherence and reduced cost compared with administration of each drug in a separate inhaler. Single-agent use of LABAs is not recommended because of the increased risk for asthma-related death when used without another controller medication. However, five large clinical trials showed that LABAs, when used with inhaled glucocorticoids, did not significantly increase the risk for asthma-related hospitalization, intubation, or death compared with inhaled glucocorticoids alone and resulted in significantly fewer asthma exacerbations.

Leukotriene-receptor antagonists have a modest bronchodilation effect, and patients with aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease often respond well to these agents.

Long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMAs) provide sustained airway dilation. Tiotropium has been shown to improve lung function and reduce exacerbations when added to therapy in patients with asthma not controlled with an inhaled glucocorticoid plus a LABA. For patients with excessive adverse effects from LABAs, a LAMA can reasonably be substituted; however, no substantial evidence suggests that LAMAs versus LABAs should be the first choice for long-acting airway dilation.

Newer therapies directed against specific mediators of the asthmatic response have altered the treatment paradigm for patients with severe asthma not adequately controlled on standard therapy. Several types of biologic therapies are now available for use in these patients, with more in development. The currently available agents are primarily directed against type 2 inflammation, which is estimated to affect at least half of patients with asthma, and target the pathways involved in the activation of eosinophils and IgE production ( [Table: Table: Biologics Indicated to Treat Severe Asthma]

). A process known as phenotyping combines clinically recognizable characteristics, such as atopy, allergen sensitization, and seasonal variation, with biomarkers such as IgE and eosinophil levels to determine whether patients have type 2 inflammation and could benefit from specific biologic treatments.

If patients have high total IgE levels and atopy, as documented by skin testing or elevated serum allergen-specific IgE, the anti-IgE biologic omalizumab may provide benefit. Omalizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds IgE and has been shown to reduce exacerbations in patients with severe persistent asthma despite therapy with a high-dose inhaled glucocorticoid plus LABA and, often, additional pharmacologic therapies. Omalizumab reduces emergency department visits and may be cost effective in eligible patients with moderate to severe atopic asthma that is not well controlled with other therapies.

Patients with eosinophilia can benefit from inhibitors of interleukins involved in eosinophilic recruitment and maturation. These agents include mepolizumab, reslizumab, and benralizumab, which target interleukin (IL)-5, and dupilumab, an inhibitor of IL-4 and IL-13. The level of blood eosinophilia that predicts efficacy varies for each agent and ranges from an absolute eosinophil count of 150/μL (0.15 × 10^9/L) to 400/μL (0.4 × 10^9/L), regardless of IgE level. Tezepelumab is the newest biologic therapy for severe asthma and has a broader indication; its use is not limited to a specific asthma phenotype.

Both anti-IgE and anti-IL therapies reduce symptoms, need for oral glucocorticoids, and exacerbations in eligible patients with moderate or severe persistent asthma. These treatments are expensive and should only be considered after verifying patient adherence to asthma medications, assessing inhaler technique, and addressing any comorbidities.

Comprehensive, nonpharmacologic asthma care strategies include the following:

  • Avoidance of triggers with allergen management (mold abatement, pest control, air filters)
  • Reduced exposure to environmental tobacco smoke
  • A healthy diet and exercise program to promote weight loss

In addition, bronchial thermoplasty is a radiofrequency airway treatment administered using bronchoscopy that can reduce exacerbations and improve quality of life. Candidates are patients with an FEV~1 higher than 60% of predicted and severe asthma that is poorly controlled despite high-dose inhaled glucocorticoid–LABA combination therapy.

An asthma exacerbation is an acute worsening of symptoms or lung function from baseline that necessitates a step-up in therapy. Prompt recognition and treatment of asthma exacerbations are needed to relieve symptoms and prevent hospitalizations. All patients with asthma should have a written asthma management plan that helps them recognize the symptoms of an exacerbation and begin self-treatment.

Self-treatment of an exacerbation consists of the following:

  • Frequent use of reliever medications
  • Increased dose, frequency, or both of controller medications
  • Addition of a short course of oral glucocorticoids (typically 5-7 days of prednisone, 40-50 mg/d)

Patients who do not improve with self-treatment or who have signs that indicate a severe attack ( [Table: Table: Signs of a Severe Asthma Exacerbation]

) should be evaluated in an acute care facility, where management should include the following:

  • Close monitoring of dyspnea, work of breathing, and vital signs
  • Frequent inhaled SABA administration
  • Prompt glucocorticoid therapy
  • Administration of supplemental oxygen to maintain oxygen saturation above 93%

For further discussion of severe asthma exacerbations, see Obstructive Lung Diseases (COPD and Asthma) in Critical Care Medicine.

Clinicians should screen for patient factors that contribute to an increased risk for death from asthma and then counsel patients appropriately ( [Table: Table: Severe Asthma Exacerbation Risk Factors]

).

Severe refractory asthma is present in patients who require high doses of an inhaled glucocorticoid plus a second controller or oral glucocorticoids to prevent worsening and in those who experience two or more exacerbations requiring an emergency department visit or a hospitalization within 1 year. This group of patients consumes the most asthma-related health care resources.

It is important to verify the diagnosis in these patients and to document medication adherence and correct inhaler technique before considering additional therapies. In addition, comorbidities should be aggressively managed. Treatment guided by specific phenotypes, such as biologic agents for patients with high IgE or eosinophil levels and leukotriene-receptor antagonists for patients with aspirin sensitivity, can be helpful in this group. Referral to a team of subspecialists is often indicated.

Pregnancy can lead to either worsened or improved asthma control. Patients should be closely monitored for exacerbation, which occurs most frequently during the second trimester. Pregnant patients should be advised that the advantages of asthma treatment outweigh the potential risk to the fetus from asthma therapies. Inhaled glucocorticoids, oral glucocorticoids, SABAs, leukotriene-receptor antagonists (montelukast, zafirlukast), and LABAs have all been used extensively during pregnancy without data to suggest fetal harm.

COPD is a chronic lung disease defined by chronic respiratory symptoms due to airway abnormalities that cause persistent airflow obstruction. It currently affects more than 6% of the U.S. population and 10% of the global population. COPD is associated with high morbidity and mortality and is the sixth leading cause of death in the United States. The World Health Organization predicts that by 2030, COPD will become the world’s fifth most prevalent disorder and the third leading cause of death.

COPD is an inflammatory condition. Cigarette smoke and other irritants activate both macrophages and epithelial cells within the respiratory tract. The epithelial cells then release several neutrophil chemotactic factors, and the macrophages and recruited neutrophils release proteases that cause destruction of lung parenchyma. Proteases are typically inactivated by antiproteases, such as α~1-antitrypsin, but protease levels are increased in COPD. Oxidative stress from irritants and inflammatory cells may also lead to additional inflammation and tissue destruction.

Ultimately, patients develop fibrosis of the small airways and reduced elastic recoil of the lungs, leading to static hyperinflation; in addition, mucin concentrations are abnormally elevated. As the degree of inflammation increases, airflow obstruction worsens and the ability to fully exhale decreases. Inhalation is initiated before exhalation is completed, resulting in dynamic hyperinflation (air trapping). Hyperinflation appears as an increased anteroposterior diameter of the chest and flattening of the diaphragm on chest radiographs. The diaphragmatic flattening further limits the ability to increase breath volume during exertion. Compensatory use of accessory muscles to increase tidal volume and increased respiration rate augment minute ventilation. These changes increase the work of breathing and contribute to the sensation of dyspnea in patients with COPD.

Exposure to cigarette smoke—including secondhand exposure—is the most important risk factor for COPD in the United States, whereas nonsmoking risk factors contribute to more than 50% of the global COPD burden. Genetic predisposition may explain some of the variation in susceptibility to developing COPD when exposed to cigarette smoke.

COPD can also result from long-term exposure to other irritants, such as air pollution (both indoor and outdoor) and occupational chemicals and dusts. An example of indoor air pollution is biomass fuel used for cooking inside the home, which is a common risk factor for COPD in some parts of the world. A family history of COPD is also a risk factor for the disease, as is α~1-antitrypsin deficiency. For further discussion on α~1-antitrypsin deficiency, see α1-Antitrypsin Deficiency in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease.

COPD is a heterogeneous condition, with some patients presenting predominately with a chronic productive cough because of mucus hypersecretion and others presenting with progressive dyspnea because of hyperinflation. Other variable symptoms include nonproductive cough, chest tightness, wheezing, and fatigue.

The heterogeneity extends beyond clinical symptoms. Phenotypic heterogeneity has been characterized on the basis of clinical, physiologic, molecular, and radiographic variables. For example, eosinophilia has been associated with increased responsiveness to glucocorticoids. In addition, a subgroup of patients appears to be more prone to developing acute exacerbations. Understanding such variables may improve prognostic accuracy and help individualize patient care.

Because of the heterogeneity of COPD, tools have been developed to aid in prognosis and treatment decisions, and several staging assessments are available. For example, the BODE index uses the variables of BMI, airflow Obstruction, Dyspnea, and Exercise capacity to predict outcomes and response to therapy. Airflow obstruction is determined using the postbronchodilator FEV~1 as a percentage of the predicted value. The BODE index provides better prognostic information than the FEV~1 alone and has been used to approximate 4-year survival and risk for hospitalization for COPD. Perceived dyspnea is graded using the modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) Dyspnea Scale questionnaire ( [Table: Table: Modified Medical Research Council Dyspnea Scale]

). Exercise capacity is determined by the walking distance on a 6-minute walk test.

Patients with COPD often have comorbid conditions that further increase morbidity and mortality. Although some conditions, such as cardiovascular disease and lung cancer, share common risk factors, others seem to be independently associated with COPD or consequences of its treatment. These conditions include sarcopenia, weight loss, osteoporosis, and depression.

The possibility of COPD should be considered and spirometry performed in patients with progressive dyspnea, chronic cough with or without sputum production, or recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, particularly in the presence of known risk factors for COPD, such as smoking. The role of screening spirometry in asymptomatic individuals with risk factors is controversial. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends against screening for COPD in asymptomatic adults, whereas the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) report suggests performing screening spirometry in individuals with risk factors for COPD.

In the appropriate clinical context, COPD is diagnosed using spirometry to document airflow obstruction. COPD is confirmed by a postbronchodilator FEV~1/FVC ratio of less than 0.70 (GOLD guideline) or less than the lower limit of normal. This fixed airflow obstruction differs from the finding in patients with asthma, whose airflow obstruction is reversible with bronchodilator therapy. Measuring lung volumes and diffusing capacity is not required to diagnose COPD but may help to determine disease severity. Clinicians should rule out other causes of chronic respiratory symptoms, including heart failure, bronchiectasis, obliterative bronchiolitis, tuberculosis, and diffuse panbronchiolitis.

Disease assessment entails determining severity of symptoms and risk of acute exacerbation. Several validated tools are available to assess symptom severity, including the [Table: Table: COPD Assessment Test (CAT)]

, the mMRC scale, the St. George’s Respiratory Questionnaire, and the Clinical COPD Questionnaire. The Clinical COPD Questionnaire is also often used to screen patients for COPD symptoms.

Factors that predict a high risk for recurrent acute exacerbations include the following:

  • FEV~1 of less than 50% of predicted
  • Two or more acute exacerbations within the past year
  • History of hospitalization for an acute exacerbation

A structured assessment of disease severity to help guide treatment decisions can be obtained using the GOLD model ( [Table: Table: GOLD Model for Classifying Severity of Disease in COPD]

), which is determined by the combination of symptoms using the COPD Assessment Test or mMRC scale (see [Table: Table: COPD Assessment Test (CAT)]

and [Table: Table: Modified Medical Research Council Dyspnea Scale]

) and the history of acute exacerbations. The total COPD Assessment Test score ranges from 0 to 40, with higher scores indicating greater symptom severity. The degree of airflow obstruction as measured by spirometry ( [Table: Table: GOLD Patient Severity Categories in COPD by Spirometry]

) and presence of comorbid conditions are additional markers of disease severity.

Clinicians should also determine whether the patient has any of the common comorbidities associated with COPD that indicate a higher morbidity and mortality and then treat appropriately.

Pulse oximetry at rest and with exertion should be used to determine the need for supplemental oxygen. Arterial blood gases can be measured to assess for underlying hypercapnia in patients with a low FEV~1, change in mental status, acute exacerbation, elevated serum bicarbonate level, or oxygen saturation of less than 92% on pulse oximetry.

An α~1-antitrypsin level should be obtained once in all patients with COPD. A pattern of basilar emphysema, associated liver disease or panniculitis, or a strong family history of emphysema in patients with COPD suggests possible α~1-antitrypsin deficiency; however, none of these features is sufficiently sensitive to rule out the condition without testing.

A management plan for COPD should include the identification and reversal of risk factors, especially ongoing exposure to cigarette smoke. The severity of a patient’s COPD disease should guide the choice of therapy ( [Table: Table: Recommended Therapy for COPD by GOLD Patient Group]

). Patients should be monitored for evidence of disease progression that may guide additional therapy. Goals of therapy include the following:

  • Reduce symptoms
  • Improve exercise tolerance
  • Improve quality of life
  • Prevent and treat exacerbations
  • Prevent disease progression
  • Decrease mortality

Smoking cessation is essential in the management of COPD because it can slow the decline of FEV~1. Clinicians should encourage patients to quit smoking and be aware that success rates for smoking cessation increase when counseling is combined with medication therapy. All smokers without contraindications should receive at least one FDA-approved treatment for smoking cessation (see Tobacco in Interdisciplinary Medicine).

Pharmacologic therapies ( [Table: Table: Therapeutic Agents Used in COPD]

) help reduce COPD symptoms, improve quality of life, and reduce the frequency and severity of exacerbations. Bronchodilators are the mainstay of therapy for COPD irrespective of the severity of the disease. Each time that bronchodilators or other inhalers are prescribed, the clinician should ensure that the patient receives education on proper inhaler technique. Recommended initial management is outlined in [Table: Table: Recommended Therapy for COPD by GOLD Patient Group]

.

Inhaled bronchodilators include β~2-agonists and anticholinergics/antimuscarinic agents. Both are available as short- and long-acting inhalers and improve symptoms and expiratory airflow. SABAs and short-acting muscarinic antagonists result in similar bronchodilation, and either can be used as monotherapy; however, dual treatment results in greater bronchodilation and expiratory airflow, which may lead to symptom benefit in select patients.

If short-acting bronchodilators are insufficient to control symptoms in patients with more severe disease, a long-acting bronchodilator (LABA or LAMA) can be added. Choosing the appropriate long-acting bronchodilator inhaler requires consideration of patient and physician preference, potential adverse effects, and cost. If symptoms persist on monotherapy, the addition of a second long-acting bronchodilator from the alternate bronchodilator class may result in clinical improvement. Long-acting bronchodilators alone should not be used in patients with a history or diagnosis of asthma unless an inhaled glucocorticoid is also prescribed because of the potential for increased mortality risk in this patient population when a LABA is used without an inhaled glucocorticoid.

Inhaled glucocorticoids are typically used only in combination with a long-acting bronchodilator for treatment of COPD (see [Table: Table: Recommended Therapy for COPD by GOLD Patient Group]

). Inhaled glucocorticoids are not used alone unless a patient is not able to use long-acting bronchodilators. Although inhaled glucocorticoids are associated with an increased risk of pneumonia, they improve lung function and reduce symptoms and exacerbations in patients with moderate to severe COPD. Furthermore, in patients with severe COPD, triple inhaler therapy with a LABA, a LAMA, and an inhaled glucocorticoid may provide additional symptom benefit, reduce exacerbations and, when combined into a single inhaler, decrease mortality. Guidelines recommend adding inhaled glucocorticoids to long-acting bronchodilator therapy if the eosinophil count exceeds a threshold of 150 to 300/µL (0.2-0.3 × 10^9/L) or if the patient has significant asthmatic features together with COPD.

Oral glucocorticoids are recommended for short-duration treatment of acute exacerbations of COPD (see Therapeutic Management of COPD Exacerbation in Pulmonary Medicine). However, long-term use of oral glucocorticoids should be avoided because of the risk for adverse effects, including diabetes and osteoporosis.

The methylxanthines (aminophylline and theophylline) are now rarely used to treat COPD. Theophylline has been shown to improve functional capacity and reduce the number of exacerbations; however, it has a narrow therapeutic window and is only used for patients with advanced COPD who have refractory symptoms not controlled by standard therapy. Studies have shown no benefit of the use of either aminophylline or theophylline during acute exacerbations.

Roflumilast is a selective phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor that is used to reduce the frequency of exacerbations in patients with severe COPD (FEV~1 <50% of predicted) who primarily have symptoms of chronic bronchitis. It should be considered in such patients with at least two exacerbations or one exacerbation requiring hospitalization within the past year.

Antiproteases, including α~1-antitrypsin, typically inactivate proteases that may lead to permanent lung injury. In patients with α~1-antitrypsin deficiency, α~1-antitrypsin augmentation therapy may slow the progression of related emphysema; however, this therapy is costly and has not been definitively shown to decrease exacerbations or the rate of FEV~1 decline. It is not effective for the treatment of patients whose COPD is not caused by α~1-antitrypsin deficiency.

Macrolide antibiotics have anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial effects. Long-term macrolide therapy may reduce the frequency of exacerbations when prescribed for patients with severe COPD and a history of frequent exacerbations. Mucolytics and antitussives are not routinely used for management of COPD but may provide some symptomatic relief in patients with significant sputum production.

Biologic agents have some focused indications for treatment of patients with COPD. Dupilumab, for example, can be added to the regimen of long-acting bronchodilators and inhaled glucocorticoids for patients with chronic bronchitis and high eosinophil count.

Ensifentrine is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor that improves lung function and may decrease exacerbation frequency but has not been shown to improve patient quality of life; its role in therapy is unclear.

Immunizations can prevent infections in patients with COPD. Because infections are the most common trigger of acute exacerbations, routine immunizations are recommended for all patients with COPD, including annual influenza vaccination; COVID-19 vaccination; respiratory syncytial virus vaccination (for patients older than 50 years); tetanus, diphtheria, and acellular pertussis vaccination (if not vaccinated in childhood); zoster vaccination (for patients older than 50 years); and pneumococcal vaccination. For further discussion on immunizations, see Immunization in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

Pulmonary rehabilitation is a comprehensive program that combines exercise training, nutritional support, education, and social support for patients with chronic lung conditions. It has been shown to relieve symptoms, improve quality of life, and decrease frequency of hospitalizations in patients with COPD. Clinicians should consider adding pulmonary rehabilitation to appropriate medical therapy in select patients, particularly those recently hospitalized after an exacerbation and those in GOLD severity group B or E.

The use of supplemental oxygen has been shown to improve quality of life and decrease mortality in patients with COPD and resting hypoxemia with an arterial Po~2 of 55 mm Hg or less or an oxygen saturation (as measured by pulse oximetry) of 88% or less. Patients with cor pulmonale, heart failure, or erythrocytosis should also be offered the use of supplemental oxygen if their Po~2 is 59 mm Hg or less or oxygen saturation is 89% or less. Some patients may not qualify for oxygen at rest but may desaturate during sleep, exertion, or air travel. Although supplemental oxygen is typically prescribed if the oxygen saturation falls below 89% in these situations, the benefits in these patients are less defined.

Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (PPV), also termed noninvasive mechanical ventilation, can be used for acute and chronic respiratory failure. For patients with a COPD exacerbation and acute hypercapnic respiratory failure with acidosis, noninvasive PPV improves symptoms and reduces intubation rates, length of hospital stay, and mortality. Noninvasive PPV may also be beneficial for palliative care and helpful with discontinuing mechanical ventilation in patients with COPD and pneumonia; however, it does not replace intubation and mechanical ventilation in patients who are critically ill, are comatose, or have had a cardiac arrest. Adding home noninvasive PPV to oxygen therapy in patients with chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure (Pco~2 of 52 mm Hg [6.9 kPa] or higher) after an acute exacerbation of COPD additionally prolongs the time to readmission and death. Noninvasive PPV is generally well tolerated, and improvement of the pH and Pco~2 within 1 to 2 hours predicts success.

The National Emphysema Treatment Trial demonstrated improved quality of life, exercise tolerance, pulmonary function, and survival with lung volume reduction surgery in patients with upper lobe–predominant emphysema and significant exercise limitations that persisted after pulmonary rehabilitation. Patient selection was critical to success; patients with any of the following have high operative mortality and should not be offered this surgery:

  • FEV~1 of less than 20% of predicted
  • Diffusing capacity of less than 20% of predicted
  • Non-upper-lobe-predominant disease

Nonsurgical lung volume reduction procedures, including bronchoscopic placement of endobronchial valves or plugs and thermal ablation of the airway, are being studied for treatment of emphysematous changes in patients with COPD. Early results suggest that patients with severe air trapping and hyperinflation may derive the most benefit from these techniques. Patient selection criteria for endoscopic techniques are complex and vary according to the specific procedure.

Referral for lung transplantation can be considered in patients with severe COPD. Transplantation improves quality of life, and the median life expectancy is 5.9 years. The decision to refer should be based on the patient’s life expectancy, quality of life, and preferences. In general, candidates are patients at high risk for dying in less than 2 years who have a high probability of 90-day postoperative survival. Patients with any of the following may be referred for evaluation for lung transplantation:

  • Elevated BODE index (5 or 6)
  • Resting hypoxemia
  • Hypercapnia
  • FEV~1 of less than 25% of predicted
  • Significant exercise limitation despite medical therapy, smoking cessation, and participation in a pulmonary rehabilitation program

To classify the severity of disease, the current GOLD initiative recommends considering the degree of airflow limitation using the postbronchodilator FEV~1, the number of exacerbations, and the patient’s symptoms. This approach can guide escalation or de-escalation of medical therapies as appropriate (see [Table: Table: GOLD Patient Severity Categories in COPD by Spirometry]

, [Table: Table: GOLD Model for Classifying Severity of Disease in COPD]

, and [Table: Table: Recommended Therapy for COPD by GOLD Patient Group]

).

To approximate 4-year survival, clinicians can use the BODE index ( [Table: Table: COPD Prognosis Estimation Tool]

) as a prognostic indicator in patients with COPD.

In patients with severe disease and an overall poor prognosis, referral for palliative care or hospice can help improve symptom burden. Palliative care can help manage symptoms such as dyspnea, anxiety, and depression in patients with COPD at any stage of disease. Opioids are commonly used to treat dyspnea that persists despite medical therapy. Guidelines suggest considering hospice care in patients with severe COPD, which is defined by the following:

  • Disabling symptoms despite medical therapy
  • Progression of disease as evidenced by increasing emergency department evaluations or hospitalizations
  • Hypoxemia or hypercapnia

An acute exacerbation of COPD is a worsening of a patient’s typical symptoms over the course of fewer than 14 days that is often accompanied by local or systemic inflammation. Most commonly, exacerbations involve worsening dyspnea, an increase in the severity or frequency of cough, and an increase in the amount of or a change in the character of sputum produced. Most exacerbations are triggered by a respiratory infection (either viral or bacterial), smoking, and environmental exposures. An exacerbation can be triggered by other causes, and in some cases no trigger is identified. Studies suggest that exacerbations are underreported by patients and result in adverse outcomes.

Acute exacerbations of COPD may decrease quality of life, increase health care costs, accelerate the decline in lung function, and increase mortality; therefore, it is important to prevent exacerbations whenever possible. Strategies to prevent exacerbations include the following:

  • Smoking cessation
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation when appropriate
  • Recommended immunizations
  • Proper inhaler technique and use of medications

Long-term use of azithromycin or roflumilast has also been shown to prevent future exacerbations in select patients with severe COPD and a history of frequent exacerbations.

The first steps in managing a presumed COPD exacerbation are to confirm the diagnosis and determine the severity of the exacerbation. A mild exacerbation is one that can be managed solely by short-acting bronchodilators. A moderate exacerbation requires treatment with antibiotics, glucocorticoids, or both. A severe exacerbation is defined by the need for an evaluation in the emergency department or hospitalization.

Patients with mild symptoms may not require any additional testing. Patients who should be hospitalized are those with respiratory distress or who are at risk for developing respiratory distress; additional testing, including chest radiography, ECG, complete blood count, and basic metabolic panel, should be obtained to rule out other causes or comorbidities contributing to the acute presentation. Oxygen saturation should be measured by pulse oximetry. Arterial blood gas measurement is recommended for patients with severe exacerbations to determine the presence of hypercapnia or hypoxemia. A sputum culture is not routinely used to assess COPD exacerbations because it rarely affects management. In addition, because the prevalence of pulmonary embolism is higher in patients with COPD, a thromboembolic event should be considered as a potential trigger, especially if patients do not improve with typical therapies for a COPD exacerbation.

The management goals during an acute COPD exacerbation are to relieve acute symptoms and to prevent future exacerbations.

Supplemental oxygen should be used to maintain oxygen saturation between 88% and 92%. Noninvasive PPV may be required if adequate oxygenation or ventilation cannot be maintained. Patients may require intubation and mechanical ventilation if they cannot tolerate noninvasive PPV, have an altered mental status, or have worsening hypercapnic or hypoxemic respiratory failure despite the use of noninvasive PPV. For further discussion of respiratory management in critically ill patients with COPD, see Obstructive Lung Diseases (COPD and Asthma) in Critical Care Medicine and Noninvasive Mechanical Ventilation in Critical Care Medicine.

SABAs with or without anticholinergic agents should be used to relieve acute symptoms of an exacerbation. The use of oral glucocorticoids during acute exacerbations has been shown to decrease the frequency of treatment failure, length of stay, and the risk of early relapse while improving FEV~1 and hypoxemia. Glucocorticoids have also been shown to decrease the need for hospitalization if used early. Randomized trials have demonstrated that short courses of lower-dose oral prednisone (40 mg for 5 days) are usually equivalent to longer courses, higher doses, and intravenous glucocorticoid administration.

Although viruses are the most common infectious triggers of COPD exacerbations, bacterial causes include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Antibiotics should be prescribed for 5 to 7 days in patients with exacerbations requiring invasive or noninvasive mechanical ventilation and in patients who have all three of the symptoms of an exacerbation (dyspnea, increase in sputum volume, and increase in sputum purulence) or two of these three symptoms if an increase in sputum purulence is present. A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis showed that for mild to severe COPD exacerbations, the combination of antibiotics and oral glucocorticoids reduced treatment failure.

If the patient is still smoking, treatment should also focus on smoking cessation because this change can prevent future exacerbations.

Bronchiectasis is a chronic suppurative lung disease associated with irreversible enlargement of the airways resulting from destruction of airway architecture. An injury to the lung typically results in prolonged airway inflammation, which leads to localized injury with subsequent mucus stasis. This state can lead to further airway obstruction, chronic infection, and inflammation with worsening bronchiectasis.

The most common causes of bronchiectasis include cystic fibrosis (CF), aspiration, immunodeficiencies, and connective tissue diseases ( [Table: Table: Causes of Bronchiectasis]

). In many cases of bronchiectasis, an underlying cause is not identified.

Bronchiectasis should be considered in the differential diagnosis for any patient with a chronic cough, especially with a history of frequent respiratory infections or if the cough is productive. Other possible symptoms include hemoptysis, wheezing, and chest pain.

Other features that should alert the clinician to consider bronchiectasis, especially without significant smoking history, include clubbing and previous sputum cultures growing uncommon pathogens, such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Aspergillus, or nontuberculous mycobacteria. Patients with bronchiectasis may also present with extrapulmonary symptoms, especially fatigue.

Initial evaluation should include a comprehensive medical history, including childhood diseases and family history, and careful exclusion of known causes of bronchiectasis. Bronchiectasis is diagnosed by high-resolution chest CT; diagnostic criteria include an airway diameter greater than that of its accompanying vessel and a lack of distal airway tapering (

). Bronchial wall thickening or cysts may be present.

Every patient diagnosed with bronchiectasis requires evaluation for a treatable underlying cause. This evaluation may involve testing for chronic bacterial or mycobacterial infections, which can identify potential causes of disease progression and help determine targeted antimicrobial therapy for exacerbations. Patients should also be evaluated for the presence of connective tissue disease and immune dysfunction, including immunoglobulin deficiencies. In select patients, testing for CF, ciliary dysfunction, or α~1-antitrypsin deficiency may be appropriate; however, even with rigorous evaluation, more than half of all cases are labeled idiopathic.

Chronic symptoms of cough and sputum production typically indicate irreversible airway dilation; therefore, treatment of the underlying cause may not lead to improvement in current symptoms but could prevent further progression. Otherwise, treatment of bronchiectasis focuses on the following:

  • Airway clearance
  • Exacerbation prevention
  • Infection treatment

The goal of airway clearance is to improve mucous clearance and thereby prevent chronic or recurrent infections. Bronchodilators, inhaled glucocorticoids, and combination inhalers have been shown to decrease symptoms but have no effect on the decline of lung function or frequency of exacerbations. Patients should be encouraged to exercise, which can improve airway clearance and symptoms. Airway clearance can be otherwise achieved in several ways, most commonly through positive expiratory pressure devices, but also with postural drainage and manual techniques. In addition, the use of nebulized hypertonic saline (3% and 7%) can work as a mucolytic to improve airway clearance.

Studies suggest that long-term use of macrolide antibiotics may prevent future exacerbations because of their anti-inflammatory effects. When deciding whether to use macrolide antibiotics, the risk for future exacerbations should be weighed against the possibility of developing macrolide resistance. These agents are typically reserved for patients with frequent exacerbations (two or more per year). Antibiotics may also be used in the management of chronic non–CF bronchiectasis to eradicate organisms such as P. aeruginosa or methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. If eradication is not successful in patients with Pseudomonas infection, suppressive therapy with inhaled antibiotics may provide some symptomatic benefit.

Brensocatib, an oral dipeptidyl peptidase 1 inhibitor, can help decrease neutrophilic inflammation and has been shown to decrease the rate of pulmonary exacerbations and FEV~1 decline; it may be helpful in patients with recurrent exacerbations despite appropriate therapy.

Surgical resection may be considered in patients who have localized disease with persistent symptoms despite therapy.

Exacerbations of bronchiectasis may be difficult to differentiate from baseline symptoms; however, the following are considered evidence of an exacerbation:

  • Changes in sputum volume, viscosity, or purulence
  • Increased cough
  • Wheezing
  • Dyspnea
  • Hemoptysis
  • Decline in lung function

Therapy for an exacerbation is ideally guided by routine sputum and acid-fast bacilli culture results to identify a possible predominant organism for treatment. Empiric antibiotic therapy is recommended and may be based on previous culture data until the results of the current sputum culture become available. If previous data are not available, a fluoroquinolone may be started to ensure Pseudomonas coverage until sputum culture results are available.

Treatment is generally continued for 14 days; however, shorter and longer courses have not been adequately compared. Longer courses can be considered for patients whose symptoms have improved but not returned to baseline. For patients who do not experience improvement with oral antibiotics or who do not have susceptibility to oral antibiotics, intravenous antibiotics may be required, either at home or in the hospital. There is no role for oral glucocorticoids in bronchiectasis exacerbations without concomitant glucocorticoid-sensitive respiratory disease.

CF is an autosomal recessive disease affecting the CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene. It is diagnosed in approximately 1 of 2000 to 3000 live births, with a predominance in individuals of European descent. Although the most common genetic variant resulting in disease is ΔF508, there are at least 1500 other genetic variants.

The pathogenesis of the clinical manifestations of CF remains incompletely understood; however, the abnormal homozygous CFTR genotype results in unusually thick secretions that are difficult to clear. The changes in respiratory secretions lead to bacterial colonization of airways and chronic bacterial infection, resulting in chronic inflammation and, ultimately, bronchiectasis. Further tissue destruction results from insufficient lung antiproteases to counteract the effect of elastase released from neutrophils. This ongoing inflammatory process also results in large amounts of free DNA and matrix protein deposition within areas of tissue destruction, which further drives increased viscosity of lung secretions.

Thickened secretions in the gastrointestinal tract impair flow of bile and pancreatic secretions, leading to pancreatic exocrine and endocrine deficiency, liver disease, and the development of malabsorption and maldigestion. The secretions increase the risk for bowel obstruction (distal ileal obstructive syndrome, intussusception, and rectal prolapse). Therefore, individuals with CF often present with malnutrition and weight loss. Sinus disease, often requiring surgical intervention, is also common.

Most patients with CF are diagnosed as children. Adults diagnosed with CF most often present with pulmonary or gastrointestinal symptoms. Pulmonary manifestations often include chronic productive cough, recurrent sinusitis, and recurrent pulmonary infections requiring several courses of antibiotics. For those with gastrointestinal symptoms, loose and frequent stools with abdominal pain are most common. Pancreatic insufficiency (either endocrine or exocrine) may occur but is less common. More than 95% of men with CF are infertile, most commonly secondary to absence of vas deferens.

Failure to include CF in the differential diagnosis is often the greatest challenge in diagnosis. In addition to persistent pulmonary or gastrointestinal symptoms requiring repetitive treatment, a family history of CF should raise suspicion for the disease. Radiographic findings include hyperinflation followed by bronchiectasis and cyst formation with disease progression, often beginning in the upper lobes.

Because of an increased concentration of chloride in sweat gland secretions, sweat chloride testing is a primary diagnostic tool for CF. Abnormal results on repeat testing are diagnostic of CF. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis and helps with prognosis. Sweat chloride testing, however, is less sensitive in adults than children. A negative sweat chloride test in an adult patient does not rule out CF; if clinical suspicion remains high after negative repeat sweat chloride testing, consideration for referral to a center with expertise in CF or genetic testing is appropriate.

The primary objectives of CF treatment are maintaining lung health and controlling or minimizing disease in organs affected by CF. The pillars of CF management include the following:

  • Airway clearance
  • Antibiotic therapy
  • Nutritional support
  • Psychosocial support

The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation practice guidelines recommend long-term use of medications to improve lung function and reduce exacerbations. These agents include mucolytics, hydrating agents, inhaled antibiotics, oral macrolide antibiotics, and CFTR modulators. Several CFTR modulators are available to treat patients with eligible variants; the most advanced are elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor combination therapy and ivacaftor monotherapy, which can be prescribed to patients with CF and at least one ΔF508 variant. The treatment of CF lung disease is rapidly evolving, and management involves a multidisciplinary approach best provided at a CF care center.

Pulmonary CF exacerbations are identified by either an increase in pulmonary symptoms or a decline in the patient’s baseline FEV~1. Management is similar to that of bronchiectasis and consists of the following:

  • Increasing airway clearance
  • Treating with oral or intravenous antibiotics
  • Ensuring adequate nutrition, hydration, and bowel movements

Antibiotics should be tailored to prior sputum culture results while awaiting an updated sputum culture. Double coverage of Pseudomonas infection should be considered in patients whose cultures show Pseudomonas that is resistant to at least one common antipseudomonal antibiotic and in patients who are likely to require multiple courses of antibiotics throughout their lives. Antibiotics are typically prescribed for 14 days; however, some patients may require shorter or longer courses to recover to their baseline.

Hemoptysis is common in patients with CF, most often presenting as streaks of blood mixed with sputum. Most cases can be managed by briefly stopping irritating inhaled agents (including dornase alfa, hypertonic saline, and inhaled antibiotics) and treating underlying infection with antibiotics. In patients with massive hemoptysis and CF, CT angiography of the chest is indicated because hemoptysis is often caused by tortuous vessels; angiography with embolism is usually more effective than bronchoscopy in diagnosing and treating the bleeding.

Central airway obstruction of the trachea or mainstem bronchi may present as dyspnea, cough, wheezing, and hemoptysis. The presence of stridor should be considered a life-threatening emergency. Localized wheezing may be present on examination.

Malignancy is a common cause of central airway obstruction. Other causes include inducible laryngeal obstruction, tracheal stricture, tracheomalacia, goiter, vascular rings and aneurysms, mediastinal masses, excessive dynamic airway collapse, and foreign body aspiration.

Pulmonary function tests may help identify the cause of obstruction; flow-volume loops can localize anatomic sites of airway obstruction (see

). A flattened expiratory flow limb suggests a variable intrathoracic obstruction such as intrathoracic tumors and tracheomalacia, whereas a flattened inspiratory flow-limb suggests a variable extrathoracic obstruction such as tracheomalacia, tumors, inducible laryngeal obstruction, and vocal fold paralysis. Flattening of both flow limbs results from a fixed obstruction such as from tracheal stenosis. In addition to obtaining flow-volume loops, chest CT should be performed in any patient with focal wheezing to rule out an endobronchial lesion, and bronchoscopy may be necessary for both diagnosing and managing intraluminal obstruction.

Inducible laryngeal obstruction (previously termed “vocal cord dysfunction”) is a transient inappropriate narrowing of the larynx in response to triggers that may include asthma, exercise, reflux, inhaled irritants, and stress. The most common symptom is dyspnea; throat tightness, cough, and dysphagia are also common. Although patients often describe their symptoms as wheezing, stridor may be heard on examination (Video: Intermittent Laryngeal Obstruction). Spirometry may show flattening of the inspiratory loop of the flow-volume curve but is often normal (see

). Inducible laryngeal obstruction is diagnosed by flexible laryngoscopy. Treatment includes speech-behavioral therapy consisting of therapeutic breathing maneuvers and vocal cord relaxation techniques together with minimization of triggers such as asthma, postnasal drip, and acid reflux. Onabotulinumtoxin A injections are also used in some cases of spasmodic dysphonia related to inducible laryngeal obstruction.
