Diffuse Parenchymal Lung Disease

Diffuse parenchymal lung diseases (DPLDs), also called interstitial lung diseases (ILDs), form a diverse group of nonmalignant disorders resulting in the inflammation and scarring of alveolar structures. These disorders tend to mimic each other clinically and radiographically.

The estimated prevalence of DPLDs is approximately 70 per 100,000 persons. Typically, DPLDs are classified into those with a known cause and those that are idiopathic ( [Table: Table: Classification of DPLD]

). This classification has implications for management strategies and prognosis.

The most common presentation of a DPLD is subacute to chronic exertional dyspnea and nonproductive cough. History should include a review of the following:

  • Potential exposures, including occupational, SARS-CoV-2 infection, home environment, animals, hobbies, and current and past medications
  • Over-the-counter supplements
  • History of radiation therapy
  • Family history of lung disease or connective tissue disease (CTD)
  • Symptoms suggestive of CTD

Lung examination findings can range from a normal auscultatory examination to the presence of inspiratory Velcro-like crackles or an inspiratory squeak suggestive of fibrosis. Extrapulmonary examination findings of associated CTD, such as joint deformities or Gottron papules, may suggest an underlying cause of DPLD. Advanced disease may be complicated by pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale, with findings of jugular venous distention, peripheral edema, and a pronounced pulmonic component of S~2.

Patients with DPLD often have normal resting pulse oximetry. Desaturation of greater than 4% with ambulation is consistent with a diffusion limitation, which is a hallmark of DPLD.

Typically, bilateral diffuse reticular and reticulonodular patterns on chest radiography suggest DPLD. The presence of consolidation, pleural effusions, pleural calcification, bronchiectasis, or lymphadenopathy may provide clues to discrete causes of DPLD. Chest radiographs can be normal in patients with minimal disease, and a normal chest radiograph does not rule out DPLD. Imaging with high-resolution CT is indicated in patients with a high suspicion of disease but normal radiographs.

Patients with clinical suspicion of DPLD should undergo complete pulmonary function testing, including lung volume testing with plethysmography or nitrogen diffusion and Dlco measurement. Most DPLDs have restrictive physiology with decreased FEV~1 and FVC, preserved FEV~1/FVC ratio, and decreased total lung capacity (less than 80% of predicted). The Dlco is also typically decreased (see Pulmonary Function Testing Interpretation in Pulmonary Medicine). Some forms of DPLD, however, may exhibit obstructive or mixed obstructive and restrictive deficits.

Noncontrast high-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest is the imaging modality of choice for evaluation of DPLD and should be performed in all patients. Distribution of disease and pattern of pulmonary parenchymal involvement may suggest the underlying diagnosis ( [Table: Table: Characteristics of DPLDs]

).

The addition of expiratory images to accentuate air trapping may reveal small airways disease. Images with the patient in the prone position may be helpful to distinguish subpleural reticular opacities and septal thickening from dependent atelectasis.

For patients with newly detected DPLD of apparently unknown cause and clinical suspicion of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), American Thoracic Society guidelines recommend serologic testing to exclude CTD-associated DPLD. Routine testing with the following is recommended:

  • C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate
  • Antinuclear antibodies
  • Rheumatoid factor and anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies
  • Myositis panel
  • ANCA

See Autoantibody Tests in Rheumatology for further discussion of testing for CTD.

When pulmonary function tests, serologies, and HRCT are insufficient for making the diagnosis of DPLD, diagnostic options include bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage, transbronchial biopsy, transbronchial cryobiopsy, and surgical lung biopsy. Careful assessment of risk factors, possible diagnostic strategies, and effect of the results of lung biopsy on treatment should be discussed within a multidisciplinary team, including a thoracic radiologist, thoracic surgeon, and pulmonary specialist with expertise in DPLD.

DPLDs that occur almost exclusively in individuals who currently smoke include the following:

  • Respiratory bronchiolitis–associated interstitial lung disease (RB-ILD)
  • Desquamative interstitial pneumonia
  • Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis (PLCH)
  • Smoking-related interstitial fibrosis (SRIF)

Smoking, in conjunction with other endogenous or exogenous factors, may also contribute to IPF, as well as combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema.

RB-ILD typically demonstrates upper zone–predominant ground-glass opacities with fine centrilobular nodules on HRCT. Pulmonary function tests may show a combined restrictive and obstructive pattern together with the decreased Dlco present in all forms of smoking-related DPLD.

Desquamative interstitial pneumonia, a more severe form of smoking-related DPLD, usually shows diffuse ground-glass opacification with lower-zone predominance on HRCT. Physiologic testing shows pure restrictive disease.

PLCH often occurs in younger patients and frequently causes pneumothorax. HRCT shows diffuse thin-walled cysts and nodular lesions in upper lung and midlung zones. PLCH often produces restrictive disease, but affected patients may have preserved total lung capacity and evidence of obstruction when significant cystic disease is present. Demonstrating abnormal numbers of Langerhans cells with S100, CD207, or CD1a staining on tissue obtained by either transbronchial or open lung biopsy confirms the diagnosis.

SRIF occurs in younger patients and has a less severe course compared with IPF. Radiologically, SRIF may mimic RB-ILD; however, SRIF is pathologically distinct, with deposition of hyalinized collagen in alveolar septa and minimal inflammation. Like RB-ILD, combined restriction and obstruction may be present on physiologic testing in SRIF.

COPD is a common comorbidity that may add an obstructive component to testing in any patient who smokes.

For all smoking-related DPLDs, the primary management is smoking cessation, which may lead to disease regression. Glucocorticoids may be considered in patients with severe disease or refractory symptoms.

Immune-mediated injury from underlying CTD can result in CTD-related interstitial lung disease (CTD-ILD). Lung disease typically manifests in patients with an established CTD but occasionally arises before extrapulmonary findings develop. Younger patients who present with DPLD have a higher prevalence of underlying CTD. Patients with CTD treated with methotrexate are also at risk for drug-induced DPLD.

CTD-ILDs encompass all major HRCT patterns of DPLD ( [Table: Table: DPLD-Associated Connective Tissue Diseases]

). Unlike in patients without CTD, nonspecific interstitial pneumonia is more common than usual interstitial pneumonia in patients with CTD.

One form of CTD–ILD that warrants particular attention is the antisynthetase syndrome. This syndrome presents as polymyositis or dermatomyositis with radiographic evidence of ILD in combination with one or more anti–aminoacyl-transfer RNA synthetase antibodies. Patients may not have overt signs of systemic disease; however, ILD may be severe and rapidly progressive. See Antisynthetase Syndrome in Rheumatology for further discussion of the antisynthetase syndrome.

Immunosuppressive therapy, in consultation with rheumatology and pulmonary specialists, is recommended for patients with CTD-ILD. Specialty care is recommended because of the many nuances of treatment; for example, glucocorticoids are not recommended for patients with DPLD who have systemic sclerosis. The agent of choice will vary on the basis of the underlying CTD. Possible choices include mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, rituximab, and tocilizumab. Antifibrotic therapy with nintedanib (tyrosine kinase inhibitor) or pirfenidone (growth factor inhibitor) may slow the decline of lung function in patients with progressive fibrotic CTD-ILD. Initial therapy is often a combination of glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive therapy; glucocorticoids are not intended for long-term use because of the adverse effect profile.

Repetitive inhalation of specific antigens in a sensitized patient can result in hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP). This immunologic response results in noncaseating granulomas and peribronchial mononuclear and giant cell inflammation. The antigens are typically complex proteins that can come from several sources, including agricultural dust, thermophilic fungi, and bacteria, but they can also be low-molecular-weight organic compounds.

Symptoms are nonspecific and may include the following:

  • Dyspnea
  • Cough
  • Chest tightness
  • Constitutional symptoms including fever
  • Weight loss

A careful history is vital to identify potential antigens. Serologic testing is often limited, is not standardized, and may not include antibodies to the responsible antigen.

Historically, HP was classified on the basis of duration with acute, subacute, and chronic forms, each with different presentations. Recognizing the impact of fibrosis on prognosis in HP, recent guidelines recommend classifying patients as fibrotic or nonfibrotic HP on the basis of radiologic and/or histopathologic features.

In patients with nonfibrotic HP, HRCT typically shows diffuse parenchymal infiltration (ground-glass opacities, mosaic attenuation) and small airway disease (centrilobular nodules, air trapping) (

). In contrast, signs of fibrotic HP include a combination of reticular abnormalities and/or ground-glass opacity with architectural distortion (traction bronchiectasis, volume loss, and honeycombing). Coexistent lung fibrosis and signs of bronchiolar obstruction are additionally highly suggestive of fibrotic HP. Diagnosis of HP, even in patients with an identified culprit exposure, can be challenging and often requires multidisciplinary discussion based on clinical, radiologic, and, in some cases, findings on bronchoalveolar lavage. If a confident diagnosis cannot be obtained on the basis of available data despite a clinical suspicion of HP, histopathology, typically with transbronchial lung biopsies, can ascertain the diagnosis in both nonfibrotic and fibrotic variants but is often not necessary.

Removal of exposure to the offending antigen is essential in the treatment of HP. Management decisions are otherwise driven by symptoms, the degree of compromise in respiratory function, and radiographic findings.

Patients with mild disease may be monitored for response to removal of the inciting antigen. Immunosuppressive therapy with glucocorticoids and other immunosuppressants is frequently used for those with more severe symptoms, although data for this practice are not robust. Antifibrotic therapy can be considered in patients with fibrosis on imaging.

Many medications have been implicated in the development of DPLD ( [Table: Table: Selected Drug-Induced DPLDs]

). The time from exposure to disease onset can vary, even for the same agent. Prompt treatment by removal of the offending agent is important for symptom resolution. For patients with more severe symptoms, glucocorticoids may have some benefit, although data are anecdotal.

Radiation pneumonitis typically occurs 4 to 12 weeks after radiation exposure. Patients present with cough, dyspnea, and radiographic infiltrates. Fever, pleuritic chest pain, fatigue, and weight loss are accompanying nonspecific symptoms. Differential diagnosis often includes infection and drug-induced lung injury.

On imaging, a well-defined nonanatomic demarcation between normal and abnormal lung consistent with the radiation field is pathognomonic but not always present. Other lung abnormalities, such as organizing pneumonia, also may be observed outside the field of exposure.

Observation may be appropriate for patients with mild disease. Glucocorticoids are used for those with severe symptoms or hypoxemia. From 6 to 12 months after radiation exposure, additional findings on HRCT may develop, including septal thickening, traction bronchiectasis, and volume loss consistent with chronic fibrosis.

Individuals exposed to radiation are also at risk for radiation recall pneumonitis. This condition can occur when lung tissue is subsequently exposed to certain immune checkpoint inhibitors and chemotherapy agents, including doxorubicin, etoposide, gemcitabine, paclitaxel, and pemetrexed, which trigger pathologic changes in the lung tissue previously exposed to radiation.

Patients who have experienced COVID-19 pneumonia may develop a range of chronic respiratory symptoms, functional limitations, and imaging abnormalities, including reticulation, parenchymal bands, bronchial dilation, and architectural distortion. Collectively and liberally referred to as post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis, these changes typically occur in patients with severe pneumonia. Ongoing research is exploring the natural history of post-COVID fibrosis, as well as the potential role of immunomodulatory and antifibrotic therapies.

IPF, which is associated with the histopathologic pattern of usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP), is the most common idiopathic form of DPLD. Thought to reflect dysregulated fibrosis in response to alveolar epithelial injury, IPF typically presents with chronic cough and dyspnea in patients between ages 50 and 70 years. Although most cases are idiopathic, risk factors include smoking, genetic factors, and male sex. Given that IPF often occurs in older patients who smoke, patients are often treated for COPD without improvement before the diagnosis is made.

Lung examination is notable for bibasilar Velcro-like inspiratory crackles. Clubbing is present in up to 50% of patients.

Chest radiographs may demonstrate bibasilar reticular changes. Characteristic abnormalities on HRCT include bilateral, subpleural, and basal predominant reticular changes. Advanced cases may develop traction bronchiectasis with honeycombing (

). When HRCT findings are classic for UIP, lung biopsy is not necessary for diagnosis.

IPF is progressive, with a median survival of 3 to 5 years after diagnosis. Patients may experience acute exacerbations with rapidly worsening symptoms and development of bilateral ground-glass opacities superimposed on areas of background fibrosis. These events may represent an acceleration of the disease. Although glucocorticoids and antibiotics are frequently used, there are no proven therapies for acute exacerbations of IPF.

Management of IPF should include consideration of antifibrotic therapies and oxygen supplementation for hypoxemia. Nintedanib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, and pirfenidone, an antifibrotic agent, are approved for use in patients with IPF. Although the mechanisms of these two medications differ, the clinical response is similar, with both demonstrating a decline in the rate of disease progression. Although these medications delay IPF progression, they are not curative. Referral to a pulmonologist or an ILD center is appropriate before initiating such treatment.

Given the progressive and unpredictable clinical course of IPF, early referral to a lung transplantation center is strongly recommended, especially if the patient does not respond to medical therapy. Palliative care consultation to establish advanced care plans should be considered for patients with IPF who are not candidates for lung transplantation.

Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) occurs as both a common variant in CTD-ILD and as idiopathic NSIP, which is a distinct clinical entity. Idiopathic NSIP is the second most common form of idiopathic ILD to IPF. It typically affects a younger population and has a more favorable prognosis than IPF. Differentiation of idiopathic NSIP from IPF is critical because the two diseases have distinct treatment algorithms.

The HRCT scan typically demonstrates bilateral lower lobe reticular changes and scattered ground-glass opacities (

). Although NSIP can progress to fibrosis, honeycombing, which is a classic feature for UIP, is rarely seen in NSIP. Biopsy is frequently warranted to confirm the diagnosis and to exclude alternate abnormalities; it may reveal inflammation and fibrosis.

Cellular and fibrotic forms of NSIP are described on the basis of the extent of inflammation and fibrosis. Patients with the cellular form have a better prognosis and typically respond to immunosuppressive treatments. As with IPF, select patients, especially those who develop the progressive fibrotic phenotype, may benefit from antifibrotic therapy and consideration for lung transplantation.

Organizing pneumonia is defined by histopathologic findings of patchy proliferation of granulation tissue that affects the terminal bronchioles and alveolar ducts and spaces and is associated with surrounding inflammation. This pattern is nonspecific and often follows or is associated with various types of injury to the lung, including acute infection, radiation exposure, drug-induced pneumonitis, and autoimmune diseases. When no cause is identified, the diagnosis is termed cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP).

Patients with COP typically have a subacute presentation with cough, dyspnea, fever, and malaise over weeks to months. Because chest radiographs typically demonstrate patchy opacities that mimic pneumonia, patients are often initially misdiagnosed with pneumonia and treated with antibiotics (

); however, nonresolving symptoms and failure to respond to antibiotics should raise suspicion for organizing pneumonia or COP.

HRCT findings can range from ground-glass opacities to areas of alveolar consolidation resembling infectious pneumonia. The diagnosis may not require lung biopsy if the clinical presentation and HRCT findings are consistent with COP. For cases with atypical presentation, lung biopsy helps make the diagnosis.

Patients with COP respond well to glucocorticoid therapy. Relapses of COP with tapering of glucocorticoids are common; such cases warrant consideration of glucocorticoid-sparing therapies.

Acute interstitial pneumonia develops rapidly over days to weeks, resulting in acute respiratory failure with bilateral alveolar opacities on HRCT of the chest. The pathologic findings on open lung biopsy are those of diffuse alveolar damage. This process is clinically, radiographically, and pathologically indistinguishable from acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). In the absence of known risk factors for ARDS, the syndrome suggests a diagnosis of acute interstitial pneumonia.

As with ARDS, management includes ventilatory support and critical care. Mortality remains high (approximately 50%), and patients who recover from the initial illness often have complications, are at risk for chronic lung disease, and may relapse. Patients are often treated with high-dose glucocorticoids, despite a lack of strong evidence to support their use.

Combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema (CPFE) is a distinct clinical entity wherein fibrotic lung disease, similar to IPF, coexists with emphysematous changes in the same patient (

). Even with advanced architectural changes, the competing effects of fibrosis and emphysema often result in mixed findings on pulmonary function testing. Higher lung volumes than those in patients with pulmonary fibrosis alone may occur, and a preserved FEV~1/FVC ratio may be present despite emphysema. Marked impairment in gas exchange manifesting as reduced diffusing capacity is typical for CPFE.

Treatment is guided by the underlying illness, including treatment for emphysema/COPD (see Management of COPD in Pulmonary Medicine) and consideration of antifibrotic agents. The presence of pulmonary hypertension in patients with CPFE portends a poor prognosis, and treatment for pulmonary hypertension should be initiated when indicated. Lung transplantation is the only curative therapy.

Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous disease of unknown cause that can affect any organ system. The prevalence of sarcoidosis is approximately 10 to 20 per 100,000 individuals. More than 90% of patients with sarcoidosis have lung involvement. Many patients are asymptomatic, with lung involvement incidentally found when chest radiography is performed for other reasons (

).

CT scan can show pulmonary parenchymal disease or intrathoracic lymphadenopathy, either alone or in combination. The presence of nodules along bronchovascular bundles on HRCT suggests sarcoidosis. Findings on chest radiograph can help predict the probability of spontaneous resolution ( [Table: Table: Chest Radiograph Staging of Pulmonary Sarcoidosis]

).

Pulmonary function testing is typically abnormal, and findings can be obstructive, restrictive, or both. Sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of exclusion. Diagnosis, with a few exceptions ( [Table: Table: Sarcoidosis Syndromes That Do Not Require Biopsy]

), typically requires bronchoscopic biopsy, with tissue obtained from a lymph node or from the pulmonary parenchyma. The diagnosis is made by the finding of noncaseating granulomas, with exclusion of potential mimicking infections (e.g., mycobacteria, fungi), exclusion of other systemic granulomatous diseases, and, ideally, involvement of more than one organ system.

Many patients with sarcoidosis do not need to be treated. Spontaneous resolution without treatment is common and is related to the radiographic stage of disease (see [Table: Table: Chest Radiograph Staging of Pulmonary Sarcoidosis]

). The decision to treat and assessment of response to treatment should be based on symptoms and organ dysfunction, not radiographic findings. For patients without symptoms or organ dysfunction, observation is appropriate. If treatment is required, glucocorticoid therapy is appropriate. Although not recommended in guidelines, methotrexate is noninferior to prednisone for initial treatment and has similar rates of adverse effects in clinical trials. The decision of which initial therapy to pursue should be based on discussion of costs, tolerance, and adverse effects on an individual basis. For patients with more severe or prolonged symptoms, adverse effects from long-term glucocorticoids should be considered. In this setting, glucocorticoid-sparing therapies are often used.

Development of pulmonary hypertension in patients with sarcoidosis is a poor prognostic indicator, with a median survival of approximately 3 years.

Pulmonary consultation should be considered for management of persistent disease. For patients with pulmonary hypertension or severe disease with significant activity limitation resulting from lung impairment, evaluation for lung transplantation is appropriate.

For information on nonpulmonary manifestations of sarcoidosis, see Sarcoidosis in Rheumatology.

Occupational Lung Disease

Occupational lung disease can affect any part of the respiratory tract, including the sinuses, airways, lung parenchyma, and surrounding pleura. As a result, diseases associated with occupational exposure include the following:

  • Rhinitis
  • Asthma
  • Reactive airways dysfunction syndrome (see Reactive Airways Dysfunction Syndrome in Pulmonary Medicine)
  • COPD
  • Pleural disease
  • Diffuse parenchymal lung disease
  • Malignancy

Occupational lung disease can present acutely, subacutely, or chronically after many years of exposure; therefore, diagnosis requires a careful employment history that includes occupational exposures ( [Table: Table: Occupational Lung Disease Screening Questionnaire]

). Although clinical presentations related to silica and asbestos exposures are well characterized and recognized, new agents that may lead to respiratory diseases are frequently introduced in various industries.

Factors suggesting an underlying occupational lung disease include patient concerns about an exposure, a temporal association with an exposure, unexplained signs or symptoms, and evidence of coworkers with similar symptoms. In addition, patients may experience relief of symptoms when away from the work environment and recurrence of symptoms upon their return to work. As with diffuse parenchymal lung disease, cough and dyspnea on exertion are common symptoms of occupational lung disease.

The time course from exposure to the development of signs and symptoms of occupational lung disease is highly variable. Exposures within the same industry can also vary according to use of best protective practices and the type of workplace. For example, coal worker’s pneumoconiosis in the United States has substantially decreased since the institution of federal safety standards.

Adequate determination of exposure requires a clear description of job duties and assessment of the extent of exposure. In addition, clinicians should obtain a history of additional exposures from hobbies and the home environment (see [Table: Table: Occupational Lung Disease Screening Questionnaire]

). Key features of the more frequently encountered occupational lung diseases are summarized in [Table: Table: Key Features of Occupational Lung Diseases]

, and common diagnostic testing is shown in [Table: Table: Common Diagnostic Tests for Occupational Lung Diseases]

.

When an occupational lung disease is suspected, the clinician should request a Safety Data Sheet from the patient’s employer; the Safety Data Sheet details chemical properties and known health risks associated with substances within the workplace. The U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration requires that employers make this information available upon request for employees who work with potentially harmful materials.

For individuals who have undiagnosed disorders, persistent unexplained symptoms, or permanent impairment possibly due to an occupational lung disease, referral to an occupational or environmental lung disease specialist is appropriate.

The key to management of occupational lung disease is either removal of the offending agent from the workplace or preventing worker contact with the offending agent. Further investigation of the workplace to ensure the identification of all affected individuals is also essential.

Other treatment approaches will depend on the underlying disease. These may include inhaled glucocorticoids for occupational asthma, immunosuppressive or anti-fibrotic treatment for diffuse parenchymal lung diseases, and lung transplantation for advanced end-stage fibrotic lung disease.

Workers’ compensation and determination of disability related to the impairment attributed to occupational exposure may require referral to a specialist with expertise in occupational lung disease.

Pleural Disease

The pleural space is the area between the visceral and parietal pleura, which cover the lung and the chest wall, respectively. The physiologic function of this space is not well understood, but it may help maintain negative intrapleural pressure, which prevents atelectasis. The two main abnormalities affecting the pleura result from the presence of either excess fluid (pleural effusion) or excess air (pneumothorax) in the pleural space.

Normally, the pleural space contains only a small amount of fluid (<15 mL). Pleural effusions result from conditions that affect the rate of fluid entry from pleural capillaries and the ability of lymphatics to absorb the fluid. More than 1.5 million new cases of pleural effusion are diagnosed each year in the United States. Heart failure, pneumonia, and malignancy are the most common causes of pleural effusion in the United States; malignancy causes approximately 15% of pleural effusions.

Patient history and physical examination often suggest the cause of a pleural effusion. Symptoms typically include dyspnea, cough, and pleuritic chest pain. Older adults often present with atypical symptoms, such as fatigue and failure to thrive.

Key points for history taking include the following:

  • Severity and duration of symptoms
  • Constitutional symptoms (e.g., fevers, night sweats, weight loss)
  • Occupation
  • Exposures (e.g., asbestos)
  • Recent illness, injury, or travel
  • Medical history (e.g., heart failure, previous surgeries, medications)

The chest examination may reveal dullness to percussion and diminished or absent fremitus and breath sounds if the effusion is larger than 300 mL. Several other key physical examination findings may suggest the cause of the effusion ( [Table: Table: Key Physical Examination Findings of Pleural Effusion]

).

Chest radiography should be the first test performed to evaluate a possible pleural effusion. Although radiographic findings vary, abnormalities may be detected with as little as 200 mL of pleural fluid on the posterior-anterior chest radiograph or 50 mL on the lateral view (

).

Thoracic point-of-care ultrasonography is a helpful addition to chest radiography for identification of small effusions, particularly in semirecumbent or supine patients, such as those who are critically ill (

). Ultrasonography also allows estimation of the quantity of the fluid present and determination of whether the effusion is free-flowing or loculated (i.e., with septations) (

). In addition, using ultrasound guidance for pleural procedures (e.g., thoracentesis) decreases the rate of complications.

CT of the chest with contrast is another test that is useful in the evaluation of pleural effusions. Advantages of CT include the following:

  • Ability to detect small amounts of pleural fluid
  • Assessment of coexisting intrathoracic abnormalities, such as pulmonary and pleural masses
  • Identification of an empyema (suggested by scan enhancement of the pleura around the fluid, creating a lenticular-shaped opacity) (

)

Once a pleural effusion is identified, the next diagnostic test to consider is thoracentesis.

Indications for thoracentesis include diagnosing a pleural effusion of unknown cause and removing fluid in patients with significant symptoms (e.g., dyspnea). Clinical features that should prompt evaluation include fever, pleurisy, lack of resolution after treatment for heart failure, or concern for malignancy. Thoracentesis should be performed with ultrasonography guidance because this approach allows for both a greater success rate and a reduced risk for solid organ puncture and iatrogenic pneumothorax.

Complications after ultrasound-guided thoracentesis are rare but include pneumothorax, bleeding, pain, cough, dyspnea, and re-expansion pulmonary edema.

After thoracentesis, the ipsilateral chest wall should be examined with ultrasound at several rib interspaces to assess for the amount of remaining fluid as well as lung sliding. The presence of lung slide effectively rules out a pneumothorax at that site. If there is loss of lung slide after a procedure, chest radiograph should be obtained. Chest radiograph otherwise does not typically need to be obtained in an asymptomatic, nonventilated patient.

Intraprocedural factors that should prompt closer follow-up (e.g., urgent chest radiography) include the following:

  • Aspiration of air during the procedure
  • Multiple needle passes
  • Poor ultrasound imaging
  • Development of increased chest pain or dyspnea.

Re-expansion pulmonary edema is an uncommon complication after thoracentesis. It occurs in less than 2% of cases and may be symptomatic or asymptomatic; when present, symptoms usually occur quickly but may be delayed up to 24 hours after the procedure. Risk factors include prolonged lung compression, rapid re-expansion of the lung, and poor performance status. The removal of larger volumes of pleural fluid may also increase the risk.

Pleural fluid analysis begins with assessing the appearance ( [Table: Table: Pleural Fluid Characteristics and Diagnostic Considerations]

;

) and determining whether the effusion is exudative or transudative. Exudative and transudative effusions have a wide range of causes ( [Table: Table: Causes of Transudates and Exudates]

). Exudates result from inflammation, which causes increased capillary permeability, impaired drainage by lymphatics, or both. Transudates are the result of an imbalance between hydrostatic and oncotic pressures, most commonly the result of heart failure and cirrhosis.

Differentiation between exudates and transudates is commonly based on Light’s criteria ( [Table: Table: Criteria for Exudative Pleural Effusion]

). Checking pleural fluid cholesterol can also help classify an effusion as an exudate, particularly when combined with measurement of pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level. Many of these criteria are sensitive for exudates; however, they are less specific, and up to 25% of transudates are misclassified as exudates.

Other tests of pleural fluid are often performed on the basis of clinical suspicion. If infection is suspected, analysis of pH and glucose, cell count, Gram stain, and aerobic and anaerobic cultures should be performed; culture bottles should be inoculated at the bedside to increase yield. If malignancy is suspected, cytologic analysis of fluid should be performed. A pleural N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide level can help identify heart failure as a cause of effusion, and a pleural creatinine level should be checked if urinothorax is suspected. A pleural fluid amylase level can help identify a pancreatic effusion or esophageal rupture, whereas triglyceride level is helpful if chylothorax is suspected.

Cell counts can help determine the cause of a pleural effusion; however, they are not disease specific. Neutrophil-predominant effusions are usually secondary to an acute process, such as a parapneumonic effusion in the setting of pneumonia.

Lymphocyte predominance (>50%) is common in chronic effusions. The most common causes worldwide of lymphocyte-predominant effusions are tuberculosis and cancer. A lymphocyte count greater than 85% should prompt consideration of tuberculosis or lymphoma.

Greater than 10% eosinophils in an effusion is a nonspecific finding and is most commonly caused by malignancy, followed by idiopathic and parapneumonic causes ( [Table: Table: Pleural Cell Counts and Clinical Conditions]

).

Pleural fluid acidosis (pH <7.3) is nonspecific and occurs in the following conditions:

  • Malignant effusions
  • Complicated parapneumonic effusions
  • Esophageal rupture
  • Inflammatory conditions, such as rheumatoid and lupus pleuritis
  • Urinothorax

A pH less than 7.2 in a parapneumonic effusion indicates that a complicated pleural effusion is present and that tube thoracostomy drainage is needed.

Glucose normally diffuses freely across the pleural membrane. A pleural glucose level less than 60 mg/dL (3.33 mmol/L) narrows the differential substantially and suggests that the effusion is the result of rheumatoid pleurisy, complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema, esophageal rupture, malignancy, lupus, or tuberculosis.

In patients with underlying heart failure who are receiving diuretics, a serum or pleural N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide level greater than 1500 pg/mL (1500 ng/L) suggests a cardiac cause of the effusion.

Pleural fluid amylase level greater than the upper limit of normal for serum amylase or a pleural fluid-to-serum amylase ratio greater than 1.0 suggest pancreatitis or esophageal rupture.

A pleural fluid triglyceride level elevated above 110 mg/dL (1.24 mmol/L) supports the diagnosis of chylothorax. A triglyceride level of 50 to 110 mg/dL (0.57-1.24 mmol/L) suggests the presence of pleural chylomicrons; a high chylomicron level confirms the diagnosis of chylothorax. A true chylothorax results from a disruption of the thoracic duct and is usually caused by thoracic surgery or trauma. Other causes include malignancy (lymphoma), chylous ascites, tuberculosis, and lymphatic malformations.

A pleural fluid-to-serum creatinine ratio greater than 1.0 suggests the presence of a urinothorax.

Tuberculosis should be considered in a patient with a lymphocyte-predominant exudative effusion of unclear cause; however, confirming the diagnosis may be challenging. An acid-fast smear of pleural fluid has a sensitivity of less than 5%, and mycobacterial culture has a sensitivity of approximately 30% because of the low mycobacterial load.

Adenosine deaminase, an enzyme present in lymphocytes, is elevated in most tuberculous pleural effusions (sensitivity, 90%). In countries with a low incidence of tuberculosis, testing for adenosine deaminase can be useful because a negative test result helps to exclude tuberculosis. Pleural biopsy is useful for histology and is also the most likely source to yield a positive mycobacterial culture (sensitivity, 50%). Rapid nucleic acid amplification tests on pleural fluid samples are increasingly used to detect pleural tuberculosis.

Cytologic examination of pleural fluid has an average sensitivity of 60%. Sensitivity is higher in adenocarcinoma (84%) and lower in lymphoma (40%), squamous cell carcinoma (24%), and mesothelioma (29%). Obtaining and sending more than two fluid samples for cytology when malignancy is suspected offers minimal benefit.

If cytology results are negative and malignancy is still suspected, pleural biopsy is indicated. Biopsy under direct visualization with thoracoscopy has a diagnostic sensitivity for malignant disease of greater than 90%. In cases of pleural nodularity or thickening, image-guided closed pleural biopsy (with ultrasound or CT) may be attempted before thoracoscopy. Closed pleural biopsy without image guidance provides only a random sample of pleural tissue and does not permit visualization of pleural abnormalities. It is less sensitive than fluid cytology and has been replaced by image-guided biopsy and thoracoscopy in the diagnostic evaluation of pleural malignancy.

A parapneumonic effusion is a pleural effusion associated with bacterial pneumonia. It can be uncomplicated (sterile and free flowing) or complicated (infected or loculated). Uncomplicated effusions are typically small and resolve with treatment of the pneumonia. They are associated with a pleural pH greater than 7.2 (often >7.4), a glucose level greater than 60 mg/dL (3.3 mmol/L), and an LDH level less than 900 U/L.

Complicated parapneumonic effusions occur with substantial inflammation or bacterial invasion of the pleural space. Pleural fluid analysis typically shows a low pH, a low glucose level, and a high LDH level. An empyema is defined as a bacterial infection of the pleural space, which results in purulent fluid or a positive Gram stain. Pleural fluid cultures, however, identify pathogens in only 56% of cases.

Complicated parapneumonic effusions and empyema usually require drainage. Criteria for drainage include the presence of frank pus, a positive Gram stain or culture, or a pH of less than 7.2. Drainage may also be considered for an effusion with a pH of 7.2 to 7.4 if the pleural LDH is greater than 900 U/L. Options for drainage include video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery and thoracostomy tube drainage, generally with the combined use of intrapleural fibrinolytics (e.g., tissue plasminogen activator) and a mucolytic agent (deoxyribonuclease). Early intervention improves outcomes, and a multidisciplinary team approach will help inform treatment decisions.

The bacteriology of pleural space infection differs depending on whether the infection is community acquired or hospital acquired. In the community, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus anginosus group are the organisms typically associated with pleural infection. Methicillin-resistant S. aureus and Enterobacteriaceae organisms are more prevalent in nosocomial empyema. Anaerobic bacteria are cultured in more than 20% of all pleural space infections and may be a result of the common association with aspiration or the anaerobic environment of the pleural space. Polymicrobial infections are common, and empiric antibiotic regimens administered before culture results are available should include coverage for anaerobes.

The diagnosis of a malignant pleural effusion signifies advanced disease and overall poor prognosis (usually 4-7 months from diagnosis). In these cases, the goal of management is to relieve symptoms.

Several therapeutic options exist, and treatment decisions should be based on symptoms, prognosis, degree of anticipated lung reexpansion, and patient performance status. Repeat therapeutic thoracentesis is appropriate for patients with poor prognosis (<3 months) and slow reaccumulation of fluid. Patients with rapid reaccumulation of fluid and dyspnea should be offered more definitive management.

Indwelling pleural catheters with intermittent outpatient drainage provide substantial symptom relief, and approximately 50% of patients achieve spontaneous pleurodesis after 6 to 8 weeks. Chemical pleurodesis refers to obliteration of the pleural space with a sclerosing agent (typically talc). Talc can be introduced through thoracostomy tube (talc slurry) or during thoracoscopy (talc poudrage). Talc pleurodesis has a success rate of 60% to 90%, depending on the degree of lung reexpansion. Pleurodesis is less likely to be effective in patients with incomplete lung reexpansion following thoracentesis.

Recurrent benign pleural effusions portend a poor prognosis because they indicate worsening of the underlying disease. One-year mortality rates are up to 50% in patients with effusions secondary to heart failure and kidney disease and 25% in those with liver failure. Therefore, refractory benign effusions also deserve prompt attention.

If diagnostic uncertainty persists, additional evaluation with imaging (chest CT with contrast) and thoracoscopy should be considered. Options for management include tunneled pleural catheters, pleurodesis, or both after careful discussion with a multidisciplinary team.

See Ascites in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease for further discussion of pleural effusions in patients with ascites (hepatic hydrothorax).

Pneumothorax is defined as air in the pleural space, which can occur spontaneously or result from trauma or a procedural complication. A primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) occurs in a patient without known underlying lung disease, whereas a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP) occurs in a patient with a known underlying lung disease, such as COPD. Risk for recurrence is 23% to 50% over 1 to 5 years in patients with PSP and is greater than 50% over 1 to 3 years in those with SSP. Risk factors for primary and secondary spontaneous pneumothorax are listed in [Table: Table: Risk Factors for Pneumothorax]

.

Symptoms include sudden onset of dyspnea and sharp pleuritic chest pain and are typically more severe in SSP because patients have less respiratory reserve. Physical examination findings can be subtle but usually reveal reduced lung expansion, hyperresonance to percussion, and diminished breath sounds on the side of the pneumothorax. Tension pneumothorax should be suspected in patients presenting with significant cardiorespiratory distress (worsening dyspnea, hypotension, absent breath sounds on one side, tracheal deviation, and distended neck veins).

Chest radiography is an appropriate initial test in most patients because it can confirm the diagnosis and determine the size of the pneumothorax. A lung margin greater than 2 cm away from the chest wall at the level of the hilum is considered a large pneumothorax (

). CT is the most sensitive imaging modality for small pneumothoraces and is particularly useful in patients with bullous emphysema. Ultrasonography can also be helpful for diagnosis; the presence of lung sliding ( Video: Lung Sliding Sign) indicates no pneumothorax at that specific location, and the presence of a lung point (Video: Lung Point Sign) confirms the edge of a pneumothorax. Ultrasonography is indicated when patients are unstable and concern is present for tension physiology.

Clinical symptoms drive the management of pneumothorax ( [Table: Table: Management of Pneumothorax]

). Tension pneumothorax (large and hemodynamically compromising) should be managed by emergent needle thoracostomy followed by thoracostomy tube placement and hospitalization. Observation alone is safe for small and moderate to large pneumothoraces in otherwise healthy patients with minimal symptoms. Patients should be encouraged to stop smoking; among men, the lifetime incidence of PSP is much higher in lifelong heavy smokers (12%) versus those who have never smoked (0.1%).

Recurrence prevention is recommended after the second episode of pneumothorax on the ipsilateral side in PSP and after the first occurrence of SSP. Intervention to prevent recurrence includes both chemical and mechanical pleurodesis. Endobronchial valves, which allow air to leave but not to enter the damaged area of the lung, and autologous blood patches serve as a second-line therapy when a persistent air leak is present. Patients should avoid air travel until the pneumothorax completely resolves, and scuba diving is generally not recommended after spontaneous pneumothorax.

Pulmonary Vascular Disease

Updated guidelines in 2022 suggested new hemodynamic parameters to define pulmonary hypertension (PH) ( [Table: Table: Updated Hemodynamic Parameters to Define PH]

). These changes were based on a growing body of evidence showing that normal resting mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) is approximately 14 mm Hg and rarely exceeds 20 mm Hg. The new diagnostic threshold for PH is an mPAP of 20 mm Hg, replacing the former diagnostic threshold of 25 mm Hg. This change is important because mortality risk increases when resting mPAP exceeds 20 mm Hg.

The current classification system of PH identifies five groups on the basis of mechanism, histologic profile, hemodynamics, and clinical presentation ( [Table: Table: Classification Groups of Pulmonary Hypertension]

). The term pulmonary hypertension encompasses all groups of PH, whereas pulmonary arterial hypertension refers solely to group 1 disease.

Symptoms in PH occur as the result of progressive changes in the pulmonary circulation and right ventricle (RV). Pulmonary vascular remodeling, a process of structural change in the pulmonary arteries, is the key inciting pathophysiologic process in PH. As pulmonary vascular remodeling progresses, pulmonary artery (PA) pressures rise. RV remodeling and compensation initially allow for maintenance of a normal cardiac output. With disease progression, the RV compensation becomes inadequate and patients begin to experience classic symptoms of RV failure associated with PH: exertional dyspnea, lower extremity edema, abdominal edema or early satiety, chest pain, palpitations, and, in advanced cases, syncope. Because these symptoms are nonspecific, the time from symptom onset to diagnosis frequently exceeds 2 years.

Findings on physical examination may include an accentuated or persistently split S~2 and tricuspid regurgitant (TR) murmur. Jugular venous distention, RV heave, hepatomegaly, ascites, and peripheral edema can occur with progressive RV failure.

If PH is suspected, transthoracic echocardiography should be performed (

). Echocardiographic features of PH are indicative of elevated pressure within the pulmonary circulation and maladaptive right heart changes and include elevated TR jet velocity, right heart enlargement, interventricular septal flattening or leftward bowing, and eventually decreased RV function (

). Echocardiography is used to estimate pulmonary artery pressure; however, these values are only estimates and cannot confirm the diagnosis of PH. If the echocardiogram suggests intermediate or high probability of PH, the patient should undergo further evaluation, including consideration of right heart catheterization.

In addition to echocardiography, the initial evaluation of patients with suspected PH should include noninvasive assessment of alternative or contributory heart or lung disease (including chest imaging, ECG, pulmonary function testing, blood gas testing, and N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide/B-type natriuretic peptide). Those with suspected PH should also undergo testing to rule out pulmonary arterial obstruction by chronic thromboembolic disease (i.e., ventilation-perfusion scan). Reproducible measurement of exercise capacity with the 6-minute walk test provides prognostic information and a baseline for assessment of therapeutic response. Additional advanced testing may be considered in select cases.

Not all patients with PH fit exclusively into one category of disease. For example, patients with predominant pulmonary arterial hypertension can have concomitant comorbidities, such as left-sided heart disease or chronic lung disease, that contribute to PH. Therefore, evaluation must identify and assess pertinent comorbidities.

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is defined by elevated pulmonary vascular resistance predominantly in the distal pulmonary arterioles. Abnormal vascular tone and aberrant endothelial and smooth muscle cellular growth lead to vascular narrowing with resultant hypertension.

There are several subclassifications of group 1 PAH based on cause of disease (see [Table: Table: Classification Groups of Pulmonary Hypertension]

). Idiopathic PAH (previously referred to as primary PAH) occurs typically in middle-aged adults, particularly women. Heritable forms account for up to 10% of cases, with most cases attributable to autosomal-dominant variants in bone morphogenetic protein receptor type 2 (BMPR2).

PAH can also occur in association with the following:

  • Connective tissue diseases (most commonly systemic sclerosis in North America and Europe)
  • Portal hypertension
  • Congenital heart disease
  • HIV infection
  • Drug or toxin exposure
  • Schistosomiasis
  • Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease

Approximately 10% of patients with systemic sclerosis develop PAH; those with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis are at highest risk for PAH. Disease in these patients is often refractory to PAH treatment, and outcomes are worse than in those with PAH from other causes. Rarely, PAH occurs in those with rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, mixed connective tissue disease, or overlap syndromes. In patients with connective tissue disease, glucocorticoids and other immunomodulator therapies are not indicated to treat PAH; instead, treatment with pulmonary vasodilator therapy is indicated.

Portopulmonary hypertension can affect patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension (see Portopulmonary Hypertension in Hepatology and Biliary Tract Disease). Although the mechanism remains unclear, it may be related to the inability of the diseased liver to metabolize vasoactive substances.

PAH in patients with HIV infection is not common; however, HIV-infected patients have a disproportionately higher risk for developing PAH compared with patients without HIV infection. Both viral and host factors have been implicated, and disease can occur in the absence of AIDS-related complications.

The drugs and toxins most strongly associated with PAH are listed in [Table: Table: Drugs and Toxins Associated With PAH]

.

The diagnosis of PAH is confirmed hemodynamically by right heart catheterization (demonstrating precapillary PH) (see [Table: Table: Updated Hemodynamic Parameters to Define PH]

) with exclusion of significant left-sided heart disease, CTEPH, and lung disease.

The European Society of Cardiology-European Respiratory Society 2022 guidelines recommend using a pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) threshold of 160 dynes (2 Wood units [WU]) to diagnose PAH. This recommendation is based on observational data suggesting increased mortality in patients with PAH and a PVR of greater than 2 WU; however, current therapies have not been evaluated in patients with a PVR less than 3 WU, leading to inconsistent adoption of the lower PVR threshold.

Identifying the cause of a patient’s PAH should be attempted. Serologic tests for underlying connective tissue disease, hepatitis, and HIV are advised. Pulmonary function testing is recommended; spirometry is usually normal, but Dlco may be reduced. Genetic testing is recommended for all patients with idiopathic PAH, pulmonary veno-occlusive disease, and pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis, as well as patients with PAH associated with anorexigenic drugs and those with a family history of PAH.

Therapy for PAH is directed at reducing vasoconstriction and interrupting the pathways mediating cellular proliferation within the pulmonary circulation. Initial therapy should be determined on the basis of disease severity ( [Table: Table: Pharmacologic Therapy for Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension]

). Risk assessment with validated risk calculators at the time of diagnosis and subsequent follow-up is critical to establish and define a goal-oriented treatment approach. Risk calculators incorporate several patient variables (e.g., 6-minute walk distance, natriuretic peptide elevation, functional status) to estimate short- and long-term mortality. Therapy should be adjusted with a goal to achieve low-risk status (<5% risk for disease progression over 1-5 years) within 12 months of treatment initiation.

In most patients, a combination of PAH-specific therapies targeting separate pathways within the pulmonary circulation is associated with superior outcomes compared with single-agent therapy. Combination therapy with an endothelin-1 receptor antagonist (such as ambrisentan or macitentan) and a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor (such as tadalafil or sildenafil) is the recommended first-line therapy. In selected high-risk patients, a parenteral (intravenous or subcutaneous) infusion of a prostacyclin analogue (such as treprostinil or epoprostenol) is recommended in addition to first-line therapy.

The addition of subcutaneous sotatercept, a novel biologic therapy, to standard therapies has been shown to improve hemodynamic and functional parameters and reduce clinical worsening. Sotatercept should be considered for patients with PAH who do not achieve low-risk status during follow-up despite optimization of initial combination therapy.

Rarely, high-dose calcium channel blockers are effective. Calcium channel blockers should be reserved for vasoreactive patients who demonstrate marked improvement in mPAP on vasoreactivity testing (decrease in mPAP ≥10 mm Hg to reach an absolute value ≤40 mm Hg, without a decrease in cardiac output with use of nitric oxide or epoprostenol during right heart catheterization). Although survival among vasoreactive patients is greater than that of other patients with PAH, close follow-up is required because many lose this response over time and require conventional PAH therapy. Importantly, the absence of vasoreactivity during right heart catheterization does not suggest that a patient will not benefit from appropriate PAH therapy.

Additional supportive treatments include oxygen supplementation and diuretic therapy when indicated. Patients of reproductive age who have PAH should be counseled on the risks of pregnancy and advised against becoming pregnant. In addition, because of the teratogenicity of certain medication classes (endothelin receptor antagonists and soluble guanylate cyclase inhibitors), females of reproductive age should be counseled regarding the use of two forms of highly reliable contraception, with regular pregnancy testing. In patients with atrial fibrillation, restoring normal sinus rhythm should be attempted because persistent atrial fibrillation in patients with PAH is associated with increased mortality. Supervised exercise training improves functional capacity.

Given the physical, emotional, and psychosocial consequences of life with PAH, palliative care should be considered and can improve function and quality of life. In patients for whom optimal drug therapy is unsuccessful in mitigating risk status, prompt referral for lung transplantation should be considered.

Patients with CTEPH have organized, chronic thrombi within the pulmonary arterial system. They demonstrate both mechanical obstruction of pulmonary arteries and disordered pulmonary angiogenesis, fibrinolysis, and vascular remodeling. These changes manifest as precapillary PH.

Untreated CTEPH can lead to RV failure and death. Although it is likely that fewer than 5% of patients who experience an acute pulmonary embolism (PE) develop CTEPH, more than 1 in 5 patients diagnosed with CTEPH do not have a documented history of PE. For further discussion of acute PE, see Deep Venous Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism in Hematology.

Because previous PE is not always evident in patients diagnosed with CTEPH, it remains an underrecognized cause of PH and requires a high index of suspicion. In patients diagnosed with precapillary PH, evaluation for CTEPH is warranted, even when a history of acute PE is absent. Although CT scanner technology and imaging techniques are rapidly improving, guidelines recommend V/Q scanning over pulmonary CT angiography (CTA) to rule out CTEPH in all patients with PH without an obvious cause. In the absence of parenchymal lung disease, a normal V/Q scan excludes CTEPH with a negative predictive value of 98%.

In patients with known prior VTE, treatment with thrombolytic therapy or mechanical thrombectomy does not necessarily reduce a patient’s risk for subsequent CTEPH. Although guidelines do not recommend follow-up CTEPH screening for all patients who present with acute PE, the diagnosis should be considered in any patient who remains symptomatic or develops symptoms consistent with PH after 3 months of anticoagulation. Echocardiography is the initial test of choice in evaluating these patients for possible PH, followed by V/Q scan, if indicated.

When V/Q scan identifies a perfusion defect (i.e., abnormal perfusion despite normal ventilation), additional imaging to characterize arterial obstruction and vascular anatomy is indicated. Digital subtraction angiography has long been the gold standard; however, advances in pulmonary CTA have led many experts to prefer pulmonary CTA because it is less invasive than digital subtraction angiography and, in many cases, offers excellent resolution and identification of pertinent vascular anomalies due to chronic pulmonary embolism, such as webs, intimal irregularities, and luminal narrowing. Pulmonary CTA may be less sensitive for more distal lesions. Additional imaging and multidisciplinary review are also key to rule out alternative diseases that may cause relative pulmonary vascular obstruction and mimic chronic pulmonary embolism (including pulmonary artery tumors, pulmonary vasculitis, peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis, and pulmonary vein stenosis). In addition, current guidelines recommend screening for antiphospholipid syndrome in patients with CTEPH. Screening for other thrombophilic disorders is generally not recommended.

Anticoagulation and evaluation for pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE; also known as pulmonary endarterectomy) are fundamental for CTEPH. Lifelong anticoagulant therapy is indicated in all patients to help prevent further thromboembolism. In patients with CTEPH and antiphospholipid syndrome, anticoagulation with vitamin K antagonists is recommended as first-line therapy.

The only potentially curative therapy for CTEPH is PTE, which involves surgical resection of organized thrombotic material. PTE can normalize pulmonary artery pressures in many patients with low operative mortality and excellent long-term outcomes. About half of patients with CTEPH will be eligible for surgery, and about one third of patients who undergo surgery will have normalization of pulmonary hemodynamics.

In patients deemed inoperable (because of anatomy or surgical contraindications) and those who have persistent PH despite PTE, medical therapy and/or balloon pulmonary angioplasty should be considered. Riociguat, a pulmonary vasodilator that acts on the nitric oxide pathway, is FDA approved for symptomatic patients with inoperable CTEPH or persistent/recurrent PH after PTE. Balloon pulmonary angioplasty has recently emerged as an alternative option in these patients; however, in operable patients, it is not recommended as a substitute for PTE, given insufficient data to suggest equivalent outcomes between the two procedures.

Most cases (60%-80%) of PH are attributable to left-sided heart disease (group 2) and lung disease (group 3). Group 2 PH, commonly due to heart failure (with preserved or reduced ejection fraction) or significant left-sided valvular heart disease, presents with elevations in left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures. It is often diagnosed on the basis of abnormalities identified on echocardiogram and a hemodynamic profile that demonstrates features of postcapillary PH (see [Table: Table: Updated Hemodynamic Parameters to Define PH]

). Treatment focuses on medical and, in some cases, surgical treatment of the underlying cardiac disease. No clear evidence suggests that pulmonary vasodilators improve outcomes in patients with PH related to left-sided heart disease.

In group 3 PH, chronic hypoxia and distortion of the vascular bed are major contributors to pulmonary vascular remodeling. Patients with group 3 PH demonstrate precapillary PH during right heart catheterization. Therapy largely focuses on treatment of the underlying lung disease, supportive supplemental oxygen when indicated, and pulmonary rehabilitation. In patients with PH due to diffuse parenchymal lung disease, inhaled treprostinil can be considered because it improves 6-minute walk distance, N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide, and time to clinical worsening. In contrast, pulmonary vasodilators have not been demonstrated to improve outcomes in patients with PH related to COPD or other causes of chronic lung disease.

Because PH increases the risk for death in patients with left-sided heart or lung disease, these patients should be referred early for potential lung and/or heart transplantation.

Chronic nocturnal hypoxia associated with sleep-disordered breathing is also associated with PH. Studies show that the prevalence of nocturnal hypoxia in patients with PH is as high as 89%. Guidelines suggest considering an evaluation for sleep-disordered breathing or nocturnal hypoxemia with polysomnography or home sleep study in patients with PH. In patients with PH related to alveolar hypoventilation syndromes, noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation can dramatically improve or even normalize PH.

Some PH cases are caused by diseases that do not share any particular clinical or pathologic similarities or in which the mechanisms of pulmonary vascular disease are poorly understood (group 5). This classification includes such diseases as sarcoidosis, sickle cell disease, multiple myeloma, and myeloproliferative neoplasms. As with group 2 and 3, treatment of the underlying process is the focus of therapy.

Acute RV failure occurs in conditions that disrupt either RV contractility or loading conditions (preload or afterload). Signs and symptoms are similar to those seen in PH but may also include those associated with diminished cardiac output, such as hypotension and resting hypoxia. Diagnosis is often confirmed with serum biomarkers, echocardiography, and right heart catheterization.

Management of acute RV failure depends on the underlying cause. Patients with RV infarction secondary to acute coronary syndrome should undergo urgent coronary intervention if indicated, whereas patients with PE should be considered for reperfusion therapy. Supplemental oxygen therapy can mitigate hypoxic vasoconstriction. Volume management depends on the underlying cause and ranges from diuretic therapy (with early consideration of ultrafiltration) to cautious volume administration in PE and cardiac tamponade. Patients may require vasopressor or inotropic support, although the optimal approach to therapy in this situation is unclear.

Chronic RV failure is a common complication of PH. Management includes supplemental oxygen for hypoxemia, diuretic therapy for volume overload, and treatment of the underlying disease. Care must be taken to avoid volume depletion to prevent hemodynamic decompensation or, especially in patients with underlying left-sided heart disease, development of cardiorenal syndrome.

Lung Tumors

The finding of a pulmonary nodule discovered incidentally is increasingly common because of the frequency of CT performed for other reasons. Principles of pulmonary nodule evaluation include reviewing imaging history, estimating the probability of malignancy, and discussing management preferences with the patient. Nodules found during lung cancer screening are generally higher risk because of patient risk factors and are separately managed and classified using the American College of Radiology Lung CT Screening Reporting and Data System.

On imaging, pulmonary nodules appear as small opacities (<3 cm) surrounded by normal lung parenchyma; they are asymptomatic. In contrast, a focal pulmonary opacity larger than 3 cm is considered a lung mass and is presumed malignant until proved otherwise.

Management of these lesions can be complicated and often requires subspecialty referral. Guidelines recommend management based on nodule size and characteristics. When more than one nodule is present, follow-up is determined by the size and characteristics of the largest lesion. Shared decision making is an integral part of the evaluation and management of pulmonary nodules.

Certain nodule characteristics suggest a benign cause. A well-demarcated and fully or centrally calcified nodule typically represents a previous infectious granuloma and is benign. The most common causes of such granulomas are endemic fungi (e.g., histoplasmosis) and mycobacteria (e.g., tuberculosis or nontuberculous infection).

The first step in evaluating a solid nodule larger than 8 mm is estimating the probability of malignancy. This estimate is important because of the wide variation in risk for malignancy and the diagnostic options for nodules between 8 and 30 mm.

Several quantitative predictive models are available, including the Brock model, which has moderate sensitivity (60% to 86%) for malignancy but excellent negative predictive value (99%). Criteria specified in the models vary and include age, sex, smoking history, nodule size, location within the lung, and presence of spiculated or lobular border. Lung cancer risk calculators, including the Brock model as well as the Mayo Clinic and Herder models, can be accessed on the Society of Thoracic Surgeons website.

Solid nodules with moderate probability of malignancy should be characterized further with PET/CT. If the scan is negative for metabolic activity, continued surveillance is warranted. A nodule with moderate or intense uptake suggests malignancy and requires referral for further evaluation.

If the probability of malignancy is initially high, the next step is staging with PET/CT, followed by definitive management with surgical resection or chemotherapy and radiation.

Solid indeterminate nodules of 8 mm or smaller are usually detected incidentally. The first step, as with larger nodules, is estimating the likelihood of malignancy.

Nodules of 8 mm or smaller have a lower probability of being malignant, are difficult to biopsy, and are not reliably characterized by PET. As a result, follow-up of these small nodules is usually by serial CT. The recommended frequency and duration of follow-up are based on guidelines from the Fleischner Society and are endorsed by other professional societies ( [Table: Table: Recommendations for Single Pulmonary Nodule Follow-Up]

).

A subsolid nodule is a focal rounded opacity either with an appearance of pure ground glass (focal density with underlying lung architecture still preserved) or with a solid component (part solid) but still more than 50% ground glass in appearance (

).

These nodules often represent premalignant disease, such as adenocarcinoma in situ, and can be very slow growing. Observed doubling times can range between 400 and 800 days, which has implications for both the frequency and the duration of follow-up.

Subsolid nodules are not reliably characterized by PET, and nonsurgical biopsies also have limited sensitivity. Development of a solid component in a pure ground-glass nodule or enlargement of the solid component suggests malignancy (see

). Follow-up recommendations are based on imaging findings and nodule size ( [Table: Table: Recommendations for Solitary Subsolid Lung Nodule Follow-Up]

).

Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide. In the United States, it is estimated that more than 230,000 new cases will be diagnosed and more than 130,000 lung cancer-associated deaths occur annually. The earlier the stage at which the cancer is diagnosed, the better the prognosis. Although overall 5-year survival rates are low, recent improvements in the survival rate have occurred largely secondary to advances in targeted therapy and immunotherapy.

Two major types of lung cancer are non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small cell lung cancer (SCLC). Approximately 80% of lung cancer cases are NSCLC, which is classified as adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma. SCLC accounts for about 15% of all lung cancers.

For more details on the types of lung cancer, see Lung Cancer Types in Oncology.

The main risk factor for lung cancer is exposure to tobacco smoke (including secondhand exposure). The risk for lung cancer increases with an increasing number of smoking pack-years and other carcinogenic exposures. An overall reduction of cigarette smoking would result in a significant reduction in lung cancer mortality.

Other risk factors associated with lung cancer include the following:

  • Previous radiation therapy
  • Exposure to environmental toxins (asbestos, radon, metals, and diesel fumes)
  • Pulmonary fibrosis
  • HIV infection
  • Family history of lung cancer
  • Alcohol use disorder

Until 2013, screening for lung cancer was not widely performed because previous studies had not shown that early detection resulted in any mortality benefit for lung cancer. The National Lung Screening Trial, however, demonstrated a 20% reduction in lung cancer mortality in patients with a pack-year history of at least 30 years who were screened annually for 3 years. As a result, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends annual lung cancer screening with low-dose CT in high-risk patients (grade B recommendation).

Screening should be performed in patients aged 50 through 80 years who have no symptoms of lung cancer and at least a 20-pack-year smoking history. The USPSTF recommends cessation of screening once a patient has not smoked for 15 years, in patients with limited life expectancy, and in those who are not candidates for or willing to undergo surgery. In contrast to the USPSTF recommendation, the American Cancer Society recommends screening all patients with a smoking history who meet the criteria regardless of when they last smoked.

Evaluation for possible lung cancer should determine the cell type and stage of the lung nodule or mass. Initial evaluation begins with the following:

  • Complete history
  • Physical examination
  • Complete blood count
  • Serum chemistries
  • CT of the chest

Most lung cancers present at a late stage. NSCLC and SCLC present with similar symptoms resulting from the local effects of the tumor, metastatic spread involving other organs, or paraneoplastic syndromes. The most common symptoms at presentation include cough, dyspnea, chest pain, weight loss, and hemoptysis. Similarly, the presence of findings on physical examination (consolidation, effusion, bone tenderness, neurologic findings) usually indicates advanced disease. CT findings can assist with diagnosis ( [Table: Table: CT Findings Suggestive of Lung Malignancy]

).

PET/CT can be helpful in the initial evaluation of potential lung cancer. Several studies have demonstrated that PET/CT identifies unsuspected mediastinal involvement, distant disease, or both, which informs staging biopsy strategy and reduces futile (noncurative) surgery. The mass of the nodule and its metabolic rate affect the sensitivity of PET/CT to detect lung cancer; false-negative results are more likely for cancers smaller than 1 cm and slow-growing cancers, such as carcinoid tumors.

The definitive diagnosis of lung cancer requires tissue histopathology. In patients with radiographic evidence of advanced-stage disease, diagnosis and staging are best accomplished with a single invasive test at a location that will establish both the diagnosis and the disease stage. Many techniques are available for tissue diagnosis, and the strategy will depend on the size and location of the tumor, patient characteristics, and local expertise. In general, mediastinal and central lesions are best approached with bronchoscopy, and smaller peripheral lesions are best approached with a transthoracic needle. The introduction of navigational bronchoscopy is slowly changing this paradigm as recent evidence demonstrates similar diagnostic sensitivity for peripheral nodules and fewer procedural complications. Sputum cytology has poor sensitivity in detecting lung cancer and is rarely used.

Staging and treatment of lung cancer is discussed in Lung Cancer in Oncology.

Carcinoid tumors are low-grade neoplasms comprised of neuroendocrine cells; they account for 1% to 2% of all lung cancers. Smoking is not clearly a risk factor. Arising in the proximal airways, the predominant symptoms or signs are those of an obstructing mass (cough, dyspnea, monophonic wheezing) or bleeding. Bronchial obstruction may cause lobar atelectasis and recurrent episodes of pneumonia in the same pulmonary segment or lobe (

). Carcinoid tumors may initially be misdiagnosed as asthma or pneumonia, leading to a delay in diagnosis. Lung carcinoid tumors are rarely associated with carcinoid syndrome. Surgical resection is often curative, and 10-year survival rates exceed 90%.

Adenoid cystic carcinoma is a salivary gland tumor that occurs in the lower respiratory tract and accounts for less than 1% of all lung cancers. Surgical resection is the preferred treatment.

Hamartomas are the most common benign lung neoplasm. These rare lesions are a combination of cartilage, connective tissue, smooth muscle, fat, and respiratory epithelium. On imaging, they tend to appear as smooth-bordered nodules, which may have “popcorn” calcification or contain fat.

The lung is a frequent site for metastatic disease from other malignancies, which include head and neck, colon, kidney, breast, and thyroid cancers and melanoma. Metastatic disease can present as solitary or multiple nodules; lymphangitic spread; and endobronchial, pleural, or embolic lesions. Surgical resection may be appropriate when a solitary pulmonary metastasis is identified without evidence of other metastatic disease.

Malignant pleural mesothelioma is a rare neoplasm that originates from the cells lining the pleural cavity (mesothelium). It can present as small nodules, plaque-like masses, or confluent sheets that can encase the lung.

Malignant pleural mesothelioma is associated with inhalational exposure to asbestos fibers and has a latency of 20 to 40 years. In addition to malignant pleural mesothelioma and lung cancer, asbestos exposure has been linked to a spectrum of nonmalignant pleuropulmonary diseases ( [Table: Table: Nonmalignant Asbestos-Related Pleural and Pulmonary Diseases]

). Because of environmental control of asbestos, the rate of mesothelioma in the United States has been declining since 2000.

Patients with malignant pleural mesothelioma usually present with advanced disease. Symptoms include chest pain, dyspnea, cough, hoarseness, night sweats, or dysphagia. Clinical suspicion for malignant pleural mesothelioma should arise in the setting of pleural thickening or recurrent exudative pleural effusion and a history of asbestos exposure.

The sensitivity of pleural fluid cytology is 29%, and diagnosis often requires a pleural biopsy. Medical or surgical thoracoscopy has a greater than 90% sensitivity for malignancy.

Treatment options depend on the extent of disease and patient factors and preferences and may include surgery, radiation therapy, systemic chemotherapy, and immunotherapy. Prognosis of malignant pleural mesothelioma remains poor, with an overall survival of 9 to 17 months after diagnosis.

The mediastinum is anatomically near the center of the thoracic cavity and is bound by the sternum anteriorly, the lungs and pleura laterally, and the vertebral column posteriorly. Tumors in the mediastinum can be either benign or malignant, and symptoms vary depending on size (mass effect) and systemic effects of the tumor. Dividing the mediastinum into compartments can be useful in developing a differential diagnosis when a mediastinal mass is discovered (

). CT of the chest is usually the first step in evaluation of a potential mediastinal mass. This imaging can define the anatomic position of the mass, and in some cases, the diagnosis can be made radiographically. CT can also help with planning of a biopsy, if indicated.

The anterior mediastinal compartment lies between the posterior sternum and the great vessels and heart. It is the most common mediastinal location of malignant tumors. Masses in this location are usually remembered as the “terrible Ts”: Thymoma, Teratoma/germ cell tumor, “Terrible” lymphoma, and Thyroid. The most common masses are thymic lesions, which are associated with various paraneoplastic syndromes, such as pure red cell aplasia and myasthenia gravis. Patients with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) and Down syndrome are at increased risk for germ cell tumors.

Masses in the middle mediastinum are common and are usually caused by lymphadenopathy, cysts, esophageal disorders, or vascular lesions (aneurysm). Lymphadenopathy is most common and can be the result of lymphoma, sarcoid, lung cancer, or metastatic disease.

Masses in the posterior mediastinum include neurogenic tumors, meningoceles, and spine lesions. Neurogenic neoplasms are most common and are classified on the basis of their neural origin.
