Sleep Medicine

Sleep disorders are grouped into the following six classifications:

  • Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders
  • Sleep-related breathing disorders
  • Central disorders of hypersomnolence
  • Sleep-related movement disorders (including restless legs syndrome)
  • Insomnia
  • Parasomnias

For a discussion on sleep-related movement disorders, see Restless Legs Syndrome and Sleep-Related Movement Disorders in Neurology.

For a discussion on insomnia, see Insomnia in Common Symptoms.

Excessive daytime sleepiness refers to difficulty staying awake and alert during daytime hours. Lack of self-recognition is common and poses a safety hazard if sleepiness occurs while driving or operating machinery.

Sleepiness, a cardinal symptom of many sleep disorders, differs from fatigue, which is a lack of energy or sense of exhaustion that prevents mental or physical activity at the desired intensity or pace. Fatigue is unlikely to be solely attributable to a sleep disorder and is more likely to occur in other medical conditions.

The cause of excessive daytime sleepiness can be categorized as disease related or circumstantial ( [Table: Table: Causes of Excessive Daytime Sleepiness]

).

Sleepiness can occur acutely when a person is deprived of the 7 to 8 hours of sleep that most adults require. Functional impairment resulting from an inadequate amount of sleep is termed “insufficient sleep syndrome.” It is likely the most common cause of excessive daytime sleepiness and is associated with cardiovascular disease and metabolic disorders, such as glucose intolerance and obesity.

The initial evaluation of excessive daytime sleepiness should include a thorough history to assess sleep duration and time available for sleeping before additional testing is pursued. Physicians should also ask about sleep hygiene, sleep times, sleep environment, napping, caffeine use, the effect of sleepiness on activities, and duration of symptoms. In addition, they should probe for symptoms of specific sleep disorders (snoring, apneas, leg discomfort, and sleep attacks).

A simple tool that promotes self-realization of suboptimal sleep habits is a 1- or 2-week diary of the sleep-wake schedule. A more objective assessment of sleep and wakefulness can be obtained with a wrist actigraph, a device that measures movement and ambient light during a period of 1 or 2 weeks. Wrist-worn consumer fitness products using similar technology may provide useful feedback. Questionnaires such as the Epworth Sleepiness Scale can quantify sleepiness and help gauge the patient’s response to treatment.

Objective sleep testing through either in-laboratory or at-home multichannel recordings is often indicated when the history and physical examination suggest a primary sleep disorder. In certain cases, a multiple sleep latency test—a sleep laboratory–based study that measures the time to sleep during a series of daytime nap opportunities after a normal night of sleep—provides an objective measure of sleepiness and is key to establishing the diagnoses of narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia.

All patients with excessive daytime sleepiness should be counseled about the dangers of drowsy driving and the need to maintain a routine sleep-wake schedule that allows for 7 to 8 hours of sleep per night. Specific treatment depends on the underlying condition. Short-term management of the occasional bout of acute sleepiness may include strategically timed naps or caffeine.

Jet lag results when the internal circadian clock is out of phase with the local time after air travel across multiple (typically more than three) time zones. Symptoms occur within 1 to 2 days after travel and may include insomnia, daytime sleepiness, and neuropsychiatric impairment. Eastward travel is more difficult to adapt to than westward travel.

For short trips (1-2 days), remaining on origin time might be preferable, if feasible. For longer trips, adjusting to the destination time may alleviate jet lag. Ways to promote adjustment include avoidance of sleep deprivation and dehydration, as well as bright light therapy starting up to 3 days before travel with the intention of aligning the circadian phase to the destination time. In-flight hypnotic medications pose a risk for parasomnias (e.g., walking while asleep), particularly if alcohol is consumed. Post-arrival measures include timed bright light exposure, timed melatonin, caffeine intake, and naps.

As much as one fifth of the American workforce maintains a job schedule outside the usual day shift hours. Although some people acclimate well to this schedule, many experience excessive sleepiness, mood perturbations, and neurocognitive dysfunction. Symptoms persisting for at least 3 months meet the criteria for shift work sleep disorder.

Management should first include counseling that takes into consideration eliminating shift work through a change in work schedule. If this change is not feasible, then education about symptom management should be provided.

Interventions to improve daytime sleep may include bright light avoidance in the morning, maintaining a structured sleep-wake pattern (even during nonwork weeks), and use of melatonin, which is of modest benefit in shifting the physiologic sleep cycle. Hypnotic medications are of varying effectiveness and pose the risk for carryover effects into the nighttime work period. Interventions to promote nighttime wakefulness include bright light treatment in the evening before the night shift, caffeinated beverages, planned napping during work breaks, and wake-promoting stimulants.

Modafinil and armodafinil are stimulant medications with FDA approval for use in shift work sleep disorder to promote wakefulness during the overnight work period. They are administered just before or early in the night shift to prevent interference with sleep onset the next morning. Access can be limited by cost, and adverse effects include headache, nausea, anxiety, and (rarely) serious skin reactions.

Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is defined by sleep interruption resulting from repetitive upper airway narrowing or collapse. These disordered breathing events, captured during polysomnography or home sleep apnea testing (HSAT), are classified as either apneas (complete cessation of airflow for ≥10 seconds) or hypopneas (reductions in airflow). The apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) is determined by division of the number of these events by total sleep time.

Although AHI does not incorporate every important OSA outcome (e.g., oxyhemoglobin desaturations), this frequency-based measure is the best composite metric of disease severity. An AHI of 5 to 14 events per hour indicates mild OSA, 15 to 30 per hour indicates moderate OSA, and more than 30 per hour indicates severe OSA. The degree of sleepiness, however, does not always correlate with the AHI.

With sleep onset, the pharyngeal muscles that maintain upper airway patency relax, resulting in redundancy of the airway soft tissues and airway narrowing. Snoring is often a result of this process. The supine position promotes posterior displacement of the tongue, further compromising the airway lumen. This narrowing is additionally compounded during rapid eye movement (REM), a stage of sleep characterized by atonia of nearly all muscles except for the extraocular muscles and respiratory diaphragm. As a result, pharyngeal obstruction and disordered breathing events are most prominent during the REM stage. Airway obstruction is terminated with a brief awakening from sleep (microarousal), during which upper airway patency is restored and ventilation resumes, typically followed by resumption of sleep and repetition of the process throughout the nightly sleep period.

Repetitive arousals and disruption of the sleep architecture contribute to the development of excessive daytime sleepiness and the neurocognitive symptoms of OSA. Oxyhemoglobin desaturations can be profound, particularly during REM and in patients with underlying cardiopulmonary disease.

Current evidence suggests a causal link between OSA and systemic hypertension; however, relationships with mortality and other disorders such as heart failure, cardiac arrhythmias, and type 2 diabetes mellitus are merely associative.

The most important risk factor for OSA is obesity, particularly in those with prominence of adipose tissue in the trunk and neck, which may explain in part why men have a higher prevalence than women, although the risk increases in women after menopause. The prevalence of OSA also increases with age.

In addition, the following can contribute to upper airway narrowing:

  • Tonsillar hypertrophy
  • Macroglossia
  • Retrognathia and micrognathia
  • Upper airway mass lesions

Finally, alcohol and sedative drugs can exacerbate OSA.

Sleep-related choking or gasping, often first noticed by the bed partner, is probably the most sensitive pretest indicator of OSA. This indicator, together with loud snoring, daytime sleepiness, and hypertension, is suggestive of at least moderate sleep apnea. Other symptoms include overnight awakenings, nocturia, and unrefreshing sleep. Morning headaches can occur but are not common. OSA may also be initially recognized after a procedure that entails general anesthesia and/or opioids, manifesting as repeated episodes of postoperative hypoxemia or frank respiratory failure. Similarly, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine suggests screening inpatients for OSA and arranging for expedited evaluation of those in whom OSA is suspected.

The most important established consequence of OSA is excessive daytime sleepiness. Collateral history from a family member and questionnaires (e.g., Epworth Sleepiness Scale) can help identify excessive daytime sleepiness. In addition, neuropsychiatric symptoms are common and may include mood alterations, difficulty concentrating, and problems completing tasks at school or work.

Objective testing is required for a diagnosis of OSA. Physical examination findings (crowded oropharynx, neck circumference) and questionnaires might increase pretest probability and guide decision making about testing; however, they are insufficiently sensitive or specific to establish the diagnosis. Overnight pulse oximetry is also poorly discriminative and does not have a proven role in diagnosis.

HSAT has surged in popularity because of pressures from third-party payers compounded by resource constraints related to the COVID-19 pandemic. Rather than measuring electroencephalographic sleep as in polysomnography, HSAT uses the following components for diagnosis:

  • A combination of respiratory instruments
  • Noninvasive measurements of vascular tone
  • Pulse oximetry
  • An accelerometer to detect posture

HSAT is highly sensitive in diagnosing OSA in patients with a pretest likelihood of moderate to severe disease as suggested by daytime sleepiness associated with at least two of the following findings: sleep-related choking or gasping, loud snoring, and hypertension. HSAT is less sensitive in those with milder sleep apnea; in-laboratory polysomnography may be the preferred diagnostic test in these patients. Polysomnography is also preferred over HSAT in patients with comorbid conditions in which diagnostic and treatment algorithms are more complex (e.g., heart failure, neuromuscular disease, advanced pulmonary disease).

The strongest indication for treatment of OSA is excessive daytime sleepiness, which improves with effective therapy in most patients. Neurocognitive and mood symptoms are also likely indications for treatment. In patients who perform mission-critical work (e.g., truck drivers, pilots), the threshold for treatment may be lower than that for others. The role of treatment in otherwise healthy or asymptomatic individuals is unclear.

Several treatment options exist for OSA, the efficacy of which is generally based on the ability to reduce, if not abolish, apneas and hypopneas. Positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy typically reduces the AHI toward zero by splinting open the upper airway. However, because the AHI does not always correlate with important outcomes in OSA, other treatments may adequately manage OSA for a given patient, even if residual sleep apnea persists.

Although PAP has been shown to modestly reduce blood pressure in some patients with OSA and hypertension, its role remains unproven as an adjunct in the management of comorbid cardiovascular diseases, such as heart failure and atrial fibrillation, particularly in context of the large percentage of this population without OSA-related symptoms (e.g., daytime sleepiness). Because large clinical trials of PAP therapy that measure important cardiovascular outcomes, including mortality risk, are methodologically challenging, benefit may be difficult to prove.

Patient education is recommended for newly diagnosed patients with OSA. Weight loss should be recommended to all patients with OSA who are overweight or obese. In minimally symptomatic patients with mild OSA, weight loss might be the preferred therapy. Additional measures for mild OSA include reducing alcohol intake before bedtime, avoiding sedating medications, and avoiding a supine posture if OSA is position dependent. Referral to a bariatric surgeon should be considered for patients with BMI of 35 or greater who have not benefited from or are intolerant of PAP therapy. Results from trials of obesity medications, such as glucagon-like peptide-1 agonists, showing benefit in OSA and its sequelae are now emerging. As a result, tirzepatide, which is taken for glycemic control in type 2 diabetes and weight loss, has been approved by the FDA for treatment of OSA.

PAP remains the most effective therapy for preventing disordered breathing events, alleviating symptoms, and improving sleep-related quality of life in patients with OSA. PAP works by pressurizing the upper airway to maintain luminal patency.

Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is titrated by a technologist during in-laboratory polysomnography. In contrast, diagnosis by HSAT is often coupled with treatment with auto-adjusting PAP, which uses a computer algorithm to detect and overcome upper airway resistance in real time. CPAP and auto-adjusting PAP are considered therapeutic equivalents in terms of adherence to treatment, reducing the AHI, and improving OSA symptoms. Bilevel positive airway pressure (BPAP), which delivers separate inspiratory and expiratory pressures to augment alveolar ventilation, has no proven role in OSA without a concomitant hypoventilation syndrome.

The effectiveness of PAP therapy hinges on patient adherence. Educational programs can help, as can direct-to-patient reports wirelessly transmitted from the device to a smartphone or computer. Adverse effects, such as xerostomia and nasal dryness and congestion, can be ameliorated by in-line humidification. Intranasal glucocorticoids or anticholinergics may be useful for recalcitrant nasal congestion or rhinitis. Modified pressure profiles that vary pressure over a respiratory cycle may enhance comfort. An increasing array of interfaces (“masks”) is available to promote comfort and provide a cushion seal to mitigate air leak.

When patients with OSA treated with PAP are hospitalized, PAP should be continued in the inpatient setting, provided it does not interfere with medical care.

Oral appliances increase upper airway caliber primarily by exerting traction to advance the mandible. They do not reduce the AHI or increase oxygen levels as reliably as PAP, and they are generally not indicated in more severe cases of OSA. Relative contraindications to oral appliance therapy include temporomandibular joint dysfunction and tooth loss that precludes anchoring of the hardware. However, these appliances may result in good control of mild to moderate OSA and improvement in symptoms such as daytime sleepiness. Oral appliances may have a higher rate of adherence than CPAP.

Although surgical procedures are generally not first-line therapy for OSA, they can be a reasonable alternative for some patients; however, criteria to determine optimal candidacy are unclear. In general, a higher BMI reduces efficacy of surgical treatments; society guidelines suggest referral only of patients with a BMI less than 40 for consideration of sleep surgery, when indicated.

Maxillomandibular advancement has been shown to significantly improve the AHI, even in severe disease, and can be considered for patients who do not benefit from or tolerate PAP therapy. Soft palatal procedures such as uvulopalatopharyngoplasty are of limited efficacy in reducing AHI but may be an option in select patients, particularly as surgical approaches are refined over time. Although tonsillectomy may be considered in some cases, it is rarely effective as a standalone treatment for OSA in adults. Tracheotomy is an effective treatment for OSA; however, because of limitations in patient acceptance and aesthetics, it is rarely utilized beyond patients who have concomitant chronic respiratory failure and need for mechanical ventilation.

A hypoglossal nerve stimulator has been shown to improve the AHI in some patients. Implanted in the chest wall, it synchronizes with the respiratory cycle to contract the tongue muscles during inspiration. Noninvasive (intra-oral) neurostimulator devices are also now available for use in patients with mild OSA.

Although medications (other than those targeting weight loss) do not yet have an indication as a treatment for OSA, a recent phase III clinical trial of a combination drug that enhances muscle tone of the upper airway showed a 50% reduction in AHI and improved oxygenation for up to 12 months. In addition, emerging data show that oral carbonic anhydrase inhibition may improve AHI, oxygenation, and sleep quality in OSA.

Small trials of upper airway exercises, also known as myofunctional therapy, have also shown reductions in snoring and improvements in AHI.

Supplemental oxygen is not recommended as primary therapy for OSA.

Central sleep apnea (CSA) syndromes are defined by pauses in airflow caused by loss of output from the central respiratory generators in the brainstem to the respiratory muscles, resulting in lack of respiratory effort.

Under normal circumstances, a steady state exists in which ventilation maintains arterial Pco~2 in the normal range. In CSA syndromes, the response to arterial Pco~2 is exaggerated, resulting in ventilatory overshoot, hyperventilation, and reduction of the arterial Pco~2 to a level at which respiratory efforts cease. This central apnea further destabilizes ventilation and perpetuates the process. On polysomnography, CSA is identified by the absence of respiratory effort associated with loss of airflow for at least 10 seconds.

Primary or idiopathic CSA, in which no risk factors are identified, is uncommon. Comorbid illnesses that predispose to instability of the ventilatory control system are the most common risk factors for CSA. The most prevalent association is between CSA and heart failure, which manifests as Cheyne-Stokes breathing, characterized by a crescendo-decrescendo pattern of ventilation. Atrial fibrillation, both in the setting of heart failure and in those with normal left ventricular systolic function, is an additional risk factor for CSA.

Opioid analgesics—known for their respiratory depressant effects in high doses— are also associated with CSA. Opioids have destabilizing effects on ventilation, resulting in CSA and a chaotic breathing rhythm.

Approximately 10% of patients with OSA treated with PAP exhibit “treatment-emergent CSA,” the significance of which is a matter of debate. In many cases, CSA dissipates as the patient acclimates to PAP therapy.

Other risk factors for CSA include stroke, brainstem lesions, and possibly kidney injury. High-altitude periodic breathing is a form of CSA.

It can be difficult to determine which symptoms are specific to CSA and which are secondary to comorbid conditions. In-laboratory polysomnography is required to accurately diagnose CSA. In addition, although the AHI is traditionally used to describe the severity of CSA, it has not been validated as a predictor of important clinical outcomes in CSA. Finally, abnormal oximetry does not reliably discriminate between OSA and CSA.

Sleep-related symptoms (awakenings/interrupted sleep, gasping, daytime sleepiness) likely represent an indication for treatment of CSA. Initial management should target modifiable risk factors. For example, reduction or elimination of opioids improves CSA, and medical optimization of heart failure has been shown to improve CSA and Cheyne-Stokes breathing. CPAP may occasionally be useful, especially in patients with overlapping OSA. Adaptive servo-ventilation (ASV) is a form of BPAP therapy that effectively suppresses CSA.

Whether CSA is an independent risk factor for worsened prognosis in patients with heart failure remains a matter of debate, and the evidence is insufficient to support that CSA should be targeted for treatment to improve cardiovascular outcomes. Two large trials of ASV treatment in patients with CSA and heart failure showed no improvements in important cardiovascular outcomes despite good control of breathing events. An unexpected increase in mortality was observed in one trial in patients with reduced ejection fraction treated with ASV. Because the first of these trials in 2015 showed an unexpected increased risk of death in patients with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) less than 45%, ASV has been avoided in such patients. However, as the technology has evolved and the second trial, published in 2024, did not show a signal of increased mortality risk, the use of ASV in this population is being reconsidered. Expert opinion supports use of ASV in selected patients with reduced LVEF under the care of an experienced center.

Unlike OSA, oxygen during sleep may be indicated for patients with CSA who have hypoxemia during sleep, as well as for those who cannot use or tolerate CPAP. The impact of supplemental oxygen on sleep-related outcomes in CSA, however, is not well studied.

An implanted phrenic nerve stimulator is available for treatment of CSA, but as an invasive and costly intervention that requires more study, it is not a first-line option.

Sleep-related hypoventilation syndromes are associated with advanced COPD, obesity, restrictive lung diseases, neuromuscular disorders, and other diseases ( [Table: Table: Causes of Sleep-Related Hypoventilation Syndromes]

). These conditions are defined by impaired gas exchange during wakefulness that are further compromised with sleep, especially during the muscle atonia of REM.

Capnometry (measurement of either transcutaneous or end-tidal carbon dioxide levels) is increasingly used to confirm hypoventilation during sleep, although oxygenation criteria are also used to diagnose sleep-related hypoventilation syndromes. Sustained reductions in oxyhemoglobin saturation in the setting of a compatible medical condition signify a hypoventilation syndrome. OSA may or may not be an associated feature.

In patients with severe COPD, supplemental oxygen is often used. The noninvasive pressure support of BPAP can also be used if hypercapnia is confirmed (see Noninvasive Positive-Pressure Ventilation in Pulmonary Medicine). In the overlap syndrome in which OSA is superimposed on COPD, CPAP therapy has been shown to decrease mortality rates.

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) results from a combination of the mechanical load on the respiratory pump and blunting of the ventilatory response to carbon dioxide. Persons with a BMI of 30 or higher are considered at risk for OHS; it is estimated that more than half of patients with a BMI of 50 or more have OHS. The hallmark of OHS is daytime hypercapnia, defined as a Pco~2 greater than 45 mm Hg (6.0 kPa). A clue to the diagnosis is a serum bicarbonate level greater than 27 mEq/L (27 mmol/L).

Many patients with OHS present when chronic hypercapnia and hypoxia lead to polycythemia, right-sided heart failure, and pulmonary hypertension. Other causes of hypercapnia and hypoventilation, including COPD and OSA, should be excluded before making the diagnosis of OHS.

Some patients can be diagnosed and subsequently managed with home sleep apnea testing, but in-laboratory polysomnography is often required. OSA is usually but not always superimposed on OHS. Gas exchange impairment beyond the typical repetitive desaturations of the sleep apnea syndromes is often encountered during sleep testing when OHS is present.

Weight loss is essential, and consideration can be given to bariatric surgery. PAP therapy is indicated; the American Thoracic Society recommends CPAP as initial therapy for stable ambulatory patients diagnosed with OHS. Some patients may require BPAP.

For hospitalized patients with suspected OHS-related respiratory failure, the American Thoracic Society recommends either BPAP, with or without a backup respiratory rate, or volume-targeted pressure support. This therapy should be continued after hospital discharge until the patient can be evaluated with polysomnography and titrated with the appropriate positive-pressure support. Supplemental oxygen may also be necessary but should not be administered as the only treatment for OHS.

Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation devices are often prescribed to alleviate sleep-related symptoms and support blood oxygen levels in patients with neuromuscular disorders ( [Table: Table: Positive Airway Pressure Modes]

). BPAP or volume-assured devices (average volume-assured pressure support), either with or without supplemental oxygen, are indicated in the setting of daytime hypercapnia suggesting chronic respiratory failure. Polysomnography may aid in optimizing machine and oxygen settings and in assessing concomitant sleep disorders but is not always needed.

Tracheostomy and home mechanical ventilation are effective and may be appropriate for some patients. Supplemental oxygen may further depress ventilation in patients with respiratory muscle weakness and should generally not be prescribed without adjunctive ventilatory support.

High Altitude–Related Illnesses

An ascent to altitude is associated with decreased barometric pressure. This decrease reduces the amount of ambient oxygen available for gas exchange, resulting in hypobaric hypoxia. Physiologic responses to this condition mechanistically underlie the disorders collectively referred to as high altitude–related illnesses ( [Table: Table: Spectrum of High Altitude–Related Illness Syndromes]

).

Susceptibility to high altitude–related illness is individualized and difficult to predict. Although these illnesses can occur at any age regardless of fitness level, patients with a history of high altitude–related illness are at risk for recurrence. Other risk factors include rapid ascent (>3500 m [11,500 ft] in <2 d or >500 m/d [1600 ft/d] above altitudes of 3000 m [10,000 ft]) and medical comorbidities that impair oxygenation, such as diffuse parenchymal lung disease, COPD, and pulmonary hypertension. Gradual ascent to altitude as well as acetazolamide, dexamethasone, and nifedipine can be prophylactic in patients at high risk for high altitude–related illnesses.

Acute mountain sickness is the most common high altitude–related illness and is estimated to affect as many as 25% of visitors to an altitude of 2000 m (6500 ft), an elevation below that of most major western U.S. ski areas. Cerebral blood flow and oxygen delivery to the brain are altered by the hypoxia and hypocapnia associated with an ascent to altitude. In the resultant high-altitude periodic breathing, chemoreceptors that are sensitive to hypoxia increase ventilation. This increase drives arterial Pco~2 toward the apneic threshold and results in a pause in breathing (central apnea) when the threshold is crossed. With this pause, arterial Pco~2 eventually rises enough to again stimulate breathing. The cycle of ventilatory overshoot, hypocapnia, and central apneas repeats frequently at night.

Symptoms of acute mountain sickness are nonspecific and include headache, fatigue, nausea, and vomiting; high-altitude periodic breathing can result in interrupted sleep, insomnia and paroxysms of dyspnea that awaken patients. Heavy exertion and dehydration tend to amplify symptoms, which typically resolve within 24 to 48 hours in absence of further ascent. Alcohol ingestion, which promotes dehydration, can intensify the sequelae of high-altitude periodic breathing. Treatment and prevention approaches are shown in [Table: Table: Spectrum of High Altitude–Related Illness Syndromes]

.

Severe, life-threatening cerebral edema can occur if the cerebral compensatory pathways are overwhelmed. High-altitude cerebral edema is a feared manifestation of acute mountain sickness that tends to occur at higher elevations (>3000 m [10,000 ft]). It is characterized by altered mental status and ataxia progressing to coma. Recognition of cerebral edema mandates immediate intervention. Definitive treatment is immediate descent from altitude, particularly while the patient is still ambulatory, because incapacitation at high altitude exponentially complicates evacuation. Dexamethasone, supplemental oxygen, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy, if available, are also indicated.

The pulmonary vasculature constricts in response to hypoxia, resulting in increases in pulmonary vascular resistance. An exaggerated increase in pulmonary artery pressure and increased capillary permeability contributes to the development of high-altitude pulmonary edema, which is noncardiogenic.

Although high-altitude pulmonary edema is uncommon, it can be life threatening. Patients are often tachypneic and tachycardic, and lung examination may reveal crackles or wheezing. Pink, frothy sputum or frank hemoptysis may occur, indicating worsening gas exchange and respiratory failure. Treatment includes supplemental oxygen and rest, which acutely reduce pulmonary artery pressures. Descent from altitude is also indicated. See [Table: Table: Spectrum of High Altitude–Related Illness Syndromes]

for other adjunctive therapies.

The principles of hypobaric hypoxia also apply to commercial air travel. Airline cabins are pressurized to the equivalent of 1500 to 2500 m (approximately 5000-8000 ft) in altitude, resulting in an inspired oxygen tension between 110 and 120 mm Hg (about 70% of that at sea level). Although the resultant arterial Po~2 of approximately 60 mm Hg (8.0 kPa) is adequate for healthy individuals, those with underlying pulmonary disease are at risk for hypoxemia during flight ( [Table: Table: Risk Factors for Air Travel in Pulmonary Disease]

). For patients with chronic lung disease, especially if associated with resting hypoxemia, preflight evaluation with hypoxia altitude simulation testing to determine recommended oxygen use is helpful ( [Table: Table: Preflight Screening in Chronic Lung Disease]

). In-flight oxygen supplementation is advised if significant hypoxemia is noted during testing (defined by PO~2 <50 mm Hg [6.7 kPa] or oxygen saturation <84%).

The risk for pneumothorax during air travel is low because cabins are pressurized. In patients with chronic lung disease, such as asthma or COPD, signs or symptoms indicative of a pneumothorax (acute chest pain, dyspnea) should prompt the in-flight administration of supplemental oxygen, which may promote resorption of pleural air.

After cardiothoracic surgery, a delay of 3 to 4 weeks before air travel is reasonable. An existing pneumothorax in this setting has traditionally been considered a contraindication to flight because of the potential risk for expansion and tension physiology; however, air travel may be safe in the presence of a small postoperative pneumothorax that has been radiographically stable in carefully selected patients.

Approach to the Patient With Rheumatologic Disease

Rheumatology addresses the diagnosis and treatment of diseases of the joints, muscles, and connective tissues, and the autoimmune and inflammatory processes that affect the musculoskeletal as well as all other organ systems. A patient’s history and physical examination are critical to achieving an accurate diagnosis and formulating an effective treatment plan.

Although joint pain and limitation are frequently presenting symptoms, many rheumatologic conditions are systemic and may involve multiple organ systems. It is critical to define the following:

  • The number of structures and/or organs affected
  • The pattern of involvement (e.g., which joints) and which systems are affected (e.g., musculoskeletal, skin, vascular, renal, cardiac)
  • The timing of onset
  • Whether the condition presents in an additive, waxing and waning, or migratory pattern

Because rheumatologic conditions may also have a genetic component, obtaining a thorough family history is essential.

Most rheumatologic conditions include, as a primary or secondary finding, involvement of the musculoskeletal system. Therefore, differentiating between inflammatory and noninflammatory signs and symptoms is central to the evaluation of patients with musculoskeletal pain. Autoimmune conditions typically present with inflammation, whereas mechanical, degenerative, and central sensitization disorders are characteristically noninflammatory. The cardinal signs of inflammation are pain, erythema, swelling, and warmth; noninflammatory conditions typically lack these features, except for pain. Patients may simultaneously experience more than one type of joint problem and, therefore, more than one type of pain (e.g., inflammatory and noninflammatory). See [Table: Table: Inflammatory Versus Noninflammatory Arthritis]

for a comparison of the two types.

An accurate history and a thorough musculoskeletal physical examination are essential to differentiate inflammatory and noninflammatory arthritis and can help lead to a diagnosis and avoid unnecessary testing. Musculoskeletal pain may be articular, periarticular, or referred. Pain only upon active range of motion indicates a problem with tendons or muscles (i.e., periarticular pain, which occurs only when the patient activates the motive structures). Pain upon both passive and active range of motion suggests an intrinsic articular problem.

See Upper Extremity Musculoskeletal Pain in Common Symptoms and Lower Extremity Musculoskeletal Pain in Common Symptoms for more information.

Monoarthritis involves a single joint and is classified as acute or chronic.

Acute monoarthritis can be noninflammatory (e.g., caused by trauma, hemarthrosis, or internal derangement) or inflammatory (e.g., crystal-induced, infectious, or autoimmune). Evaluation for acute infectious arthritis should be guided by the clinical presentation and physical examination, but suspicion should always be high. Joint aspiration is usually the most effective means of diagnosing the underlying cause.

Chronic inflammatory monoarthritis (≥6 weeks in duration) can be caused by chronic infection (e.g., mycobacterial, fungal, or Borrelia burgdorferi) or by autoimmune rheumatologic disease. Assessment for systemic disease (complete history; physical examination; and laboratory studies, including serologic testing) may be indicated.

Chronic noninflammatory monoarthritis is usually caused by osteoarthritis.

Joint aspiration is the most effective means of distinguishing inflammatory from noninflammatory processes (e.g., high versus low leukocyte count) and can frequently help diagnose the underlying cause. Joint aspiration must be performed to evaluate for infection. Synovial biopsy may be necessary to identify some processes (e.g., tuberculosis; fungal infection; and, rarely, tumor).

Oligoarthritis involves two to four joints, typically in an asymmetric pattern.

Acute inflammatory oligoarthritis may be caused by infection (characteristically with Neisseria gonorrheae, but potentially with any organism) or rheumatic fever or may be a result of crystal-induced arthritis. Chronic inflammatory oligoarthritis can be caused by autoimmune conditions, such as seronegative spondyloarthritis (e.g., psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, enteropathic arthritis, or ankylosing spondylitis). Chronic inflammatory oligoarthritis is rarely caused by rheumatoid arthritis (RA) or systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

Chronic noninflammatory oligoarthritis is usually caused by osteoarthritis.

Polyarthritis involves five or more joints and often involves the small joints of the hands and/or feet.

Acute inflammatory polyarthritis (<6 weeks in duration) can result from the following:

  • Viral infections (e.g., parvovirus B19, HIV, hepatitis viruses, rubella, or chikungunya)
  • Immune reaction to exogenous proteins (e.g., serum sickness or serum sickness–like illnesses)
  • Early manifestation of chronic inflammatory polyarthritis

Chronic inflammatory polyarthritis includes RA, SLE, and psoriatic arthritis. Chronic noninflammatory polyarthritis is commonly due to osteoarthritis.

Common nonarticular sources of musculoskeletal pain include the soft tissues (tendons, ligaments, and bursae) around or away from the joints. Isolated tendon and/or ligament involvement usually suggests noninflammatory disorders, such as mechanical injury/irritation, overuse, or degeneration (e.g., rotator cuff disorders or elbow tendinopathy, such as lateral epicondylitis or “tennis elbow”). Crystal deposition disease may affect tendons. Disorders of widespread musculoskeletal pain (e.g., fibromyalgia) also cause symptoms localizing to these structures, but without inflammation or evidence of structural abnormality.

The enthesis is a complex structure at the site of the insertion of a tendon or ligament onto bone. Severe persistent inflammation of the enthesis (enthesitis) is a characteristic feature of spondyloarthritis, especially when multiple entheses are affected. When the inflammation extends along the associated tendon and local ligaments, it results in diffuse swelling known as dactylitis (“sausage digits”)—another characteristic feature of spondyloarthritis, particularly psoriatic arthritis (see

). When a single enthesis is painful and tender, a noninflammatory enthesopathy may be responsible, particularly in the setting of overuse or trauma.

See Upper Extremity Musculoskeletal Pain in Common Symptoms and Lower Extremity Musculoskeletal Pain in Common Symptoms for more information.

Many rheumatologic diseases, particularly those that are inflammatory or autoimmune in nature, are characterized or accompanied by specific or widespread extra-articular involvement.

Fever, morning stiffness, and fatigue occur in numerous rheumatologic conditions. Fever is usually low grade but may be high and spiking in some conditions (e.g., autoinflammatory diseases). Morning stiffness lasting more than 60 minutes is common in most forms of inflammatory arthritis. Significant and even disabling fatigue is common and is a particularly prominent feature of fibromyalgia.

Skin involvement is common in rheumatologic conditions and may go unnoticed by the patient. Different rheumatologic diseases are associated with a wide spectrum of rashes (see [Table: Table: Dermatologic Manifestations of Rheumatologic Disease]

). Skin involvement can also be an adverse effect of medications used to treat rheumatologic conditions, including rashes and skin infections secondary to immunosuppressive therapy.

Eye involvement in rheumatologic diseases usually follows disease-specific patterns, and the location and type of involvement can help narrow the differential diagnosis (see [Table: Table: Ocular Manifestations of Systemic Inflammatory Disease]

). If not quickly recognized and treated, certain forms of eye involvement can have devastating consequences, including permanent loss of vision. See Red Eye in Interdisciplinary Medicine for additional information on ocular manifestations of rheumatologic disease.

Rheumatologic diseases frequently affect internal organs, with different diseases tending to follow characteristic patterns (see [Table: Table: Internal Organ Involvement in Rheumatologic Disease]

). Chronic inflammatory rheumatologic conditions are associated with an increased risk for premature cardiovascular disease.

Laboratory studies are useful for diagnosing rheumatologic diseases, identifying the extent/severity of involvement, evaluating disease activity, and monitoring therapeutic responses. Because of limited specificity, results of these tests should always be interpreted in the context of the clinical history and physical examination and should be applied with great caution, if at all, in the setting of low pretest probability (see Likelihood Ratios in Foundations of Clinical Practice for discussion of pretest probabilities).

The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) measures the fall of erythrocytes (in millimeters per hour) through anticoagulated blood. Normal erythrocytes have negatively charged surfaces, leading to mutual repulsion and slowing sedimentation. In inflammatory conditions, elevated concentrations of serum fibrinogen and other acute phase reactants and/or hypergammaglobulinemia (polyclonal or monoclonal) neutralize the erythrocytes’ surface charges, leading them to settle at a faster rate. The ESR increases normally with age; a well-accepted rule of thumb is to adjust the upper limit of normal as (age in years)/2 for men and (age in years + 10)/2 for women.

ESRs are elevated in many rheumatologic diseases, as well as in chronic infections and malignancies. The ESR can also be elevated in pregnancy, diabetes mellitus, obesity, and end-stage kidney disease. Because of rheostatic properties, some forms of anemia and macrocytosis are also associated with an increased ESR. Conversely, ESR can be abnormally low in low-fibrinogen states, such as liver or heart failure, and in conditions of excessive cellularity (e.g., polycythemia vera). Sickle cell disease and microcytosis (including spherocytosis) may also decrease ESR.

A markedly elevated ESR (>100 mm/h) should alert physicians to conditions such as giant cell arteritis, multiple myeloma, metastatic cancer, or other overwhelming inflammatory states (infection or autoimmune disease). A very high ESR with a normal c-reactive protein (CRP) level is suggestive of a paraproteinemia.

CRP is produced by the liver, mainly in response to interleukin-6 generated by macrophages. CRP levels and ESR usually follow a common pattern, but CRP more rapidly responds to changes in inflammation. In many rheumatologic conditions, CRP is elevated 2 to 10 times the normal level; higher levels (especially >10 mg/dL [100 mg/L]) do not exclude rheumatologic disease but should prompt consideration of alternative diagnoses, such as infection. CRP is considered a better marker than ESR for measuring inflammation in spondyloarthritis. In contrast, in some patients with SLE, CRP may remain normal despite active disease; infection should be considered for an elevated CRP level in a patient with SLE. Like ESR, CRP level can be elevated in the setting of obesity and suppressed in patients with liver disease (reduced synthetic capacity).

The complement system is an essential part of the immune response, promoting vasodilation, attracting leukocytes, and assisting in the lysis of opsonized bacteria during humoral immunity.

Complement components are acute phase reactants that are synthesized mainly in the liver and are increased in many inflammatory states. However, in response to diseases that lead to immune complex formation (SLE; cryoglobulinemic and urticarial vasculitis) and other conditions, such as infections (subacute bacterial endocarditis, sepsis, viremia) and glomerulonephritis, complement cascades are activated, and complement levels may fall because of excessive consumption. Paradoxically, genetic deficiency of early complement components may increase the risk for lupus-like autoimmune diseases, presumably because of an impaired ability to clear immune complexes.

C3 and C4 are the most commonly measured complement components. The CH~50 assay should not be performed routinely because of cost and limited utility but can be especially useful if there is a suspected complement deficiency.

Rheumatoid factor is an IgM antibody directed against the Fc hinge portion of IgG. Although characteristically associated with RA, rheumatoid factor is present in approximately 70% of patients with RA and is common in several other diseases, such as bacterial endocarditis and hepatitis C virus infection. In the appropriate setting, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) autoantibodies are more specific than rheumatoid factor for RA (95%) but less sensitive (67%). The presence of both autoantibodies together increases the likelihood of RA. Patients with RA who have anti-CCP antibodies are more likely to experience rapid joint damage from erosive disease. Patients with hepatitis C virus infection alone are typically positive for rheumatoid factor but negative for anti-CCP antibodies.

Antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) are directed against a variety of nuclear antigens and are almost universally present in SLE (>95% of patients). However, up to one third of the healthy population has a low ANA titer (1:40), and up to 5% has a titer of 1:160 or more. ANAs are also common in several other autoimmune conditions, infection, and malignancy and may be drug-induced. Higher ANA titers are more strongly associated with an underlying rheumatologic disease. However, ANA titer does not correlate with disease activity and should not be used for activity assessment. ANA testing should not be performed in a patient with nonspecific symptoms and normal findings on clinical examination (low pretest probability); in that setting, it does not establish the diagnosis of a connective tissue disease.

Extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) antibody testing (i.e., testing for antibodies to specific nuclear components, such as DNA or centromeres) should be reserved for patients positive for ANA and with a clinical syndrome suggesting a specific underlying connective tissue disease. ENA testing should not be routinely performed, even in the setting of a positive ANA result, without a strong clinical suspicion of an underlying connective tissue disease. Many laboratories offer a reflexive panel and will automatically test for ENA antibodies if ANA testing is positive.

[Table: Table: Autoantibodies in Rheumatologic Disease]

provides details on these and other autoantibodies and their associations with specific conditions.

Radiography is essential for evaluating many rheumatologic diseases and can assess and differentiate various kinds of inflammatory arthritis, osteoarthritis, and crystal arthropathies ( [Table: Table: Radiographic Findings of Rheumatologic Diseases]

). Radiography has limitations because it gives a two-dimensional picture of three-dimensional structures, is limited in its ability to visualize soft tissues, and may not detect early or small erosive changes. Nonetheless, radiography is usually the first imaging test ordered to evaluate arthritis because it is readily available, is inexpensive, requires only a low level of ionizing radiation, is relatively operator independent, and is useful in monitoring disease progression.

CT provides multiple views and orientations from a single study but is more useful for bony abnormalities than for soft-tissue inflammation or fluid collections. CT is more sensitive than radiography or MRI for detecting bone erosions. However, CT is more expensive than radiography and exposes the patient to more radiation. It is mainly used in acute trauma or when a patient cannot undergo MRI.

Dual-energy CT can detect and quantitate tissue urate deposits (see

). Although not indicated in routine testing, dual-energy CT is more sensitive than plain radiography and can be useful to identify urate deposition when the diagnosis of gout is uncertain. It may also be useful for determining the extent of ongoing urate deposition after extended urate-lowering therapy in some patients.

MRI is the most sensitive radiologic technique for detecting soft-tissue abnormalities, inflammation, and fluid collections but is less effective than CT for demonstrating bony abnormalities or erosions. MRI is sensitive for detecting early spine and sacroiliac joint inflammation and may be indicated for evaluating suspected spondyloarthritis if radiographs are negative. MRI is also indicated in the evaluation of osteonecrosis and osteomyelitis if plain radiographs are normal and suspicion is high. MRI does not expose patients to radiation but is associated with high cost; limited availability; and possible patient intolerance due to claustrophobia, body habitus, or some metallic implants. The American College of Rheumatology Choosing Wisely list recommends against routine MRI of the peripheral joints to monitor RA because of inadequate data supporting its use. MRI is the imaging modality of choice for evaluating the central nervous system in autoimmune disease.

The use of ultrasonography to evaluate rheumatologic diseases has expanded dramatically. Ultrasonography is relatively inexpensive, can scan across three-dimensional structures, and can provide real-time data in the clinic without exposure to ionizing radiation. It can be used to accomplish the following:

  • Demonstrate soft-tissue abnormalities, including synovitis, tendonitis, bursitis, crystal deposition, and effusions
  • Identify and define bony erosions
  • Assess synovial inflammation using Doppler technology
  • Assist with tendon or joint injections
  • Assess joint and soft-tissue structures during dynamic motion
  • Assess for temporal artery inflammation

Ultrasonography is also operator dependent, however, and training and practice are needed to achieve competence.

Angiography involves injecting a dye or contrast material into the vasculature to visualize the dimensions of the vascular lumen. Angiography may be directly performed using a catheter to deliver dye to the imaging area or by injecting the dye into a vein and allowing it to circulate. The latter procedure is less invasive and is typically done with CT or MRI, but it may have lower resolution than the classic invasive approach. Angiography can help define the nature of vascular narrowing and the pattern of organ involvement, and it can be useful in defining vascular involvement in many rheumatologic diseases, including primary central nervous system vasculitis and polyarteritis nodosa. It is less useful for small-vessel vasculitis and does not image the vessel wall.

PET can provide information on abnormal metabolic activity of tissues, aid in diagnosis of certain systemic rheumatologic diseases, and help assess disease activity. PET is also useful in diagnosis and monitoring the activity of large-vessel vasculitides and cardiac sarcoidosis but is not widely available.

Joint aspiration and synovial fluid analysis can discriminate between inflammatory and noninflammatory effusions and are essential for distinguishing between infectious arthritis and acute crystal arthropathies. Joint aspiration must be performed when evaluating monoarthritis to diagnose or exclude infection. Aspirated synovial fluid should be sent for leukocyte count, Gram stain, and cultures, as well as evaluation for crystals under polarized light. See [Table: Table: Synovial Fluid Analysis for Arthritic Conditions]

for more information.

There is no absolute cutoff of synovial fluid leukocyte counts for ruling out infectious arthritis; however, counts greater than 50,000/μL (50 × 10^9/L) with polymorphonuclear cell predominance have a high likelihood of infection. Counts less than 2000/μL (2.0 × 10^9/L) are usually associated with noninflammatory causes. Notably, crystals can coexist with infection, and their presence does not rule out infection if suspicion is high.

A patient’s nailfolds can be visualized in the office using an ophthalmoscope or a dermatoscope with a small amount of clear gel placed on the nailfolds. This technique is especially useful for evaluating patients with Raynaud phenomenon. In patients with Raynaud phenomenon, nailfold capillary abnormalities are associated with increased likelihood of an underlying disease and should prompt evaluation for a rheumatologic cause of secondary Raynaud phenomenon (e.g., systemic sclerosis [see

], dermatomyositis, mixed connective tissue disease, undifferentiated connective tissue disease, lupus, Sjögren disease).

When appropriate, tissue biopsy of involved organs can be helpful in diagnosing numerous rheumatologic conditions:

  • Vasculitis (lung, kidney, or temporal artery biopsy)
  • SLE (kidney or skin biopsy)
  • Dermatomyositis (muscle or skin biopsy)
  • Sarcoidosis (lung or lymph node biopsy)

Tissue biopsy may also help assess disease activity (e.g., kidney biopsy in SLE). The benefits should be appropriately balanced with possible risks of the procedure.

Patients with arthritis frequently experience mental distress and have higher rates of depression than the general population. Concurrent depression in chronic conditions, such as arthritis, is associated with reduced adherence to medical treatment recommendations. Among patients with RA, for example, anxiety and depression are associated with reduced response to treatment and poorer quality of life. Patients with some rheumatologic diseases (e.g., SLE) may also have central nervous system involvement that can manifest as mental health disorders. Screening for depression, recommended for all adults, is therefore of still greater importance in individuals with rheumatologic diseases and may improve outcomes. Actively engaging adults with arthritis in evidence-based self-management programs is helpful not only for arthritis but also for reducing depression and improving self-efficacy.

Persons from specific racial, ethnic, or economic groups may be more prone to developing or have worse outcomes from rheumatologic diseases. Although some differences may reflect genetics, many disparities in rheumatologic disease are likely to reflect differences in access to care and treatment, medical literacy, language skills, and other social determinants. For example, disease activity among patients with RA has been shown to vary by race in some but not all clinical settings. In one meta-analysis, Black patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty were more likely to have worse pain, worse function, and less satisfaction than White patients 6 months to 2 years after surgery. In addition, health care disparities have an impact on the severity and outcome of diseases like SLE, increasing the likelihood of organ damage and mortality. Physicians should be aware of health inequities and work to resolve disparities in rheumatologic diseases. For additional information, see Health Equity in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

Principles of Therapeutics

This section reviews the indications for use, mechanisms of action, major toxicities, and monitoring requirements of medications used in the management of rheumatologic disease. For a discussion of urate-lowering therapy, see Urate-Lowering Therapy in Rheumatology. Drug applications in specific disease states are discussed in their respective sections.

Glucocorticoids are a broadly effective and sometimes lifesaving treatment for many inflammatory diseases, including systemic vasculitis, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), acute crystal arthropathy, polymyalgia rheumatica, inflammatory myopathies, and autoinflammatory diseases. Rapid onset, ease of use, low cost, multiple routes of administration, and universal availability make glucocorticoids appealing in the acute setting. Adverse effects depend on dose and duration and may affect multiple organ systems ( [Table: Table: Adverse Effects of Glucocorticoids]

). See Screening and Case Detection for Osteoporosis in Endocrinology and Metabolism for a discussion of screening for osteoporosis in patients receiving long-term glucocorticoid therapy.

Systemic glucocorticoids are used as part of initial treatment strategies or for disease flares. These agents generally should be used at the lowest dose and shortest duration effective. Intra-articular, topical, or intralesional glucocorticoids are typically used for localized inflammatory manifestations.

NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin production by inhibiting the two isoforms of cyclooxygenase, COX-1 and COX-2. COX-2 is an inducible enzyme typically expressed in inflammatory milieus, whereas COX-1 is constitutively expressed and helps maintain homeostasis. Most COX inhibitors are nonselective and inhibit both isoforms, resulting in downregulation of prostaglandin production in inflammatory states and prostanoid function interference (e.g., renal blood flow and maintenance of gut mucosal integrity) ( [Table: Table: Potential Toxicities of NSAID Use]

). Nonselective COX inhibitors also inhibit thromboxane A~2, thereby inhibiting platelet function. Celecoxib is the only COX-2 selective agent currently available in the United States.

Although they alleviate symptoms, NSAIDs are not usually disease modifying. NSAIDs increase the risk for gastrointestinal bleeding and adverse cardiovascular events; thus, they should be prescribed at the lowest dose for the shortest time possible. NSAIDs should be avoided in patients receiving anticoagulation.

NSAIDs vary in their kinetics, COX-1/2 selectivity, and other features, and they carry somewhat different degrees of gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, and other risks ( [Table: Table: Features of Selected NSAIDs]

).

Topical NSAIDs (diclofenac) pose a lower risk for systemic adverse effects than oral NSAIDs. They are strongly recommended for patients with knee osteoarthritis and conditionally recommended for patients with hand osteoarthritis. Topical diclofenac may also be preferred for patients at high risk for toxicity from oral NSAIDs or those age 75 years or older.

Colchicine inhibits microtubules, impairs neutrophil function, and inhibits inflammasome-mediated interleukin-1 activation. It is often used for gout treatment and flare prophylaxis. Other indications include the following:

  • Acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis (pseudogout)
  • Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis (also called hypersensitivity vasculitis)
  • Oral and genital ulcers from Behçet syndrome
  • Familial Mediterranean fever

Gastrointestinal adverse effects, particularly diarrhea, are common but reversible with dose adjustment or discontinuation. Rare but severe adverse effects include severe myelosuppression, especially with overdose, and neuromuscular toxicity after prolonged use. Dosing must be adjusted for kidney disease. Colchicine coadministration with strong cytochrome P-450 3A4 inhibitors (e.g., clarithromycin), which reduce hepatic catabolism of colchicine, should be avoided.

Pain is a central symptom for patients with inflammatory arthritis and osteoarthritis; a patient-centered approach is important for pain management. In addition to pharmacologic interventions, treatment should include patient education and consideration of nonpharmacologic therapy.

The efficacy of acetaminophen for osteoarthritis and low back pain has been questioned. Controlled trials and meta-analyses have shown no benefit from the drug, even at high doses. However, because of its favorable safety profile, it may be empirically tried for short-term or add-on therapy. The daily dosage should not exceed 3000 mg/d. American College of Rheumatology (ACR) guidelines conditionally recommend acetaminophen for patients with knee, hip, or hand osteoarthritis and limited pharmacologic options.

Duloxetine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) approved by the FDA for the management of chronic musculoskeletal pain and fibromyalgia, provides modest pain relief for knee osteoarthritis, chronic low back pain, and fibromyalgia. Milnacipran, another SNRI, is also approved for fibromyalgia. To avoid withdrawal symptoms, SNRI doses should be tapered slowly when the drug is discontinued.

Gabapentinoids (gabapentin and pregabalin) inhibit voltage-gated calcium channels, thereby reducing pain signaling from the periphery to the central nervous system. Pregabalin is FDA-approved for fibromyalgia. Common adverse effects (dizziness, disequilibrium, somnolence, weight gain, peripheral edema, and cognitive difficulties) may limit its utility. The FDA has issued a safety alert stating that serious breathing difficulties may occur in patients using gabapentin or pregabalin who have respiratory risk factors (e.g., older persons, patients with COPD, and patients receiving opioids and other drugs that depress the central nervous system).

Traditional opioids should generally be avoided in the treatment of rheumatologic diseases because of limited efficacy, high toxicity, and high potential for dependence.

Tramadol is a mixed opioid analgesic and weak SNRI with a lower potential for addiction than traditional opioids. It is conditionally recommended for osteoarthritis pain management when NSAIDs are contraindicated and other treatment modalities are ineffective.

[Table: Table: Conventional Synthetic DMARDs]

summarizes the mechanisms of action, indications, and common monitoring parameters of various conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs).

Hydroxychloroquine is an immunomodulator widely used to treat SLE, in which it decreases mortality and the likelihood of nephritis. It is rarely sufficient as single-drug therapy for RA but is useful as an adjunctive therapy. Adverse effects are uncommon but include risk for retinal toxicity.

Methotrexate is a first-line medication for RA and other autoimmune diseases, given once weekly at 10 to 25 mg orally or subcutaneously, and can be used alone or in combination with other therapies.

Potential adverse effects include headaches, fatigue, and nausea (particularly around the time of weekly dosing). Hepatotoxicity and cytopenia can occur (especially macrocytic anemia); dose adjustment is required with kidney disease. Methotrexate should be avoided in patients with significant hepatic or kidney disease and is absolutely contraindicated around pregnancy. Avoiding or limiting alcohol consumption is recommended during methotrexate use.

Folic acid supplementation minimizes toxicity while preserving efficacy. For patients who continue to have adverse effects despite folic acid therapy, increasing the dose of folic acid, splitting the dose of oral methotrexate over 24 hours (one dose in the morning and one dose in the evening), or changing to a weekly subcutaneous route of administration may help.

Sulfasalazine is used to treat RA, often as part of combination DMARD therapy, nonaxial psoriatic arthritis, and peripheral-predominant ankylosing spondylitis. Serious adverse effects include blood dyscrasias, hepatitis, and hypersensitivity reactions. Because of the benefit of its salicylate moiety for inflammatory bowel disease, sulfasalazine may be effective for patients with enteropathic arthritis.

Leflunomide is FDA-approved for RA and psoriatic arthritis, with efficacy similar to that of methotrexate. Patients must be monitored for hepatotoxicity and myelosuppression. Other common adverse effects include nausea, headaches, rash, diarrhea, and elevated serum aminotransferase levels. Peripheral neuropathy is an uncommon adverse effect that is usually self-limited if the drug is discontinued. Leflunomide is highly teratogenic and absolutely contraindicated around pregnancy.

Azathioprine is used to treat various inflammatory diseases. Its primary toxicity is myelosuppression, especially in patients with a decreased or absent thiopurine methyltransferase enzyme. Concomitant use with xanthine oxidase inhibitors (allopurinol, febuxostat) is relatively contraindicated because of increased risk for myelosuppression.

Mycophenolate mofetil is a first-line agent for lupus nephritis and is effective for interstitial lung disease associated with systemic rheumatologic disease. It is commonly used as a glucocorticoid-sparing agent for idiopathic inflammatory myositis. Gastrointestinal adverse effects, including diarrhea, are common. Myelosuppression may occur.

Cyclophosphamide has a rapid onset of action (days to weeks) and is used to treat severe vasculitis, life-threatening complications of SLE, and interstitial lung disease. Cyclophosphamide has largely been displaced by safer drugs for first-line treatment of ANCA-associated vasculitis (rituximab) but is still used in severe cases or when these agents fail. Serious potential adverse effects include severe immunosuppression, leukopenia, hemorrhagic cystitis, and ovarian failure, as well as long-term risk for bladder cancer, leukemia, and lymphoma.

Calcineurin inhibitors include cyclosporine, tacrolimus, and voclosporin. Cyclosporine is now rarely used for rheumatologic conditions because of renal adverse effects, hypertension, hyperuricemia (often presenting as gout), and need for frequent drug level monitoring. Tacrolimus may be considered as alternative or additive therapy for some patients with lupus nephritis. Voclosporin, a next-generation calcineurin inhibitor with higher potency and an improved adverse-effect profile, is FDA-approved for lupus nephritis. Topical forms of calcineurin inhibitors are used for inflammatory skin conditions, including psoriasis and lupus rashes.

Biologic DMARDs are highly specific, parenterally administered, protein-based agents with extracellular targets (cytokines, cytokine receptors, or cell surface molecules on immune cells) (

). Nomenclature for biologic agents includes a suffix used to identify the type of agent, such as the following:

  • -mab has historically indicated a monoclonal antibody, but newer monoclonal agent nomenclature developed in 2021 includes different suffixes (-tug; -bart; -mig; -ment)
  • -kin indicates an interleukin-type substance
  • -ra indicates a receptor antagonist
  • -cept indicates the presence of a receptor-based molecule

[Table: Table: Biologic DMARDs]

summarizes the structures, targets, indications, and common monitoring parameters of biologic DMARDs. For information on these drugs in pregnancy, see Medications and Pregnancy in Rheumatology. Biologic DMARDs increase the risk for infection to varying degrees. Targeted screening is therefore necessary before initiation (see Vaccination and Screening in Immunosuppression in Rheumatology).

The cost of biologic agents is significant and may be a barrier to access.

Biosimilar agents are “copycat” versions of brand-name biologic medications. These medications are not exact replicas and must undergo phase III testing to prove efficacy equivalent to that of the parent biologic. In the United States, biosimilars are distinguished from their originator molecules by a four-character alphabetic suffix (e.g., infliximab-dyyb). Biosimilars hold promise for decreasing cost and improving access, but those benefits have rarely been realized because of regulatory and market factors.

Targeted synthetic DMARDs are a newer category of immunomodulating medications composed of kinase and phosphodiesterase inhibitors (see [Table: Table: Targeted Synthetic DMARDs]

). Unlike biologic agents, they can be administered orally. However, the cost, efficacy, and safety profile of these agents are more similar to those of biologic DMARDs than conventional synthetic DMARDs. This medication class is rapidly changing, with several medications and indications having been approved.

Tofacitinib, baricitinib, and upadacitinib are oral agents that inhibit Janus kinase (JAK) signaling, with variable potency against JAK1, JAK2, and JAK3; upadacitinib is the most selective for JAK1. JAK inhibitors are now approved for RA, psoriatic arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis, with efficacy noninferior to that of biologic DMARDs. Deucravacitinib inhibits tyrosine kinase 2, a related JAK. It is approved for psoriasis, is likely to be effective for psoriatic arthritis and other rheumatologic disorders, and may have a better safety profile than other JAK inhibitors.

The FDA warns that tofacitinib and possibly other JAK inhibitors are associated with an increased risk for myocardial infarction or stroke, cancer, blood clots, and death. Other risks include dyslipidemia, hepatotoxicity, leukopenia, and reactivation of herpes zoster at a rate higher than seen with biologic DMARDs.

Apremilast is a phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor approved for psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. It does not cause immunosuppression or myelosuppression but is less efficacious than biologic DMARDs, has a slow onset of action, and has unknown effects on progression of erosive damage. Risks include gastrointestinal adverse effects (mainly nausea and diarrhea) and weight loss. It should be used with caution in patients with a history of depression. Apremilast is also FDA-approved for treatment of oral ulcers in Behçet syndrome.

Avacopan is an oral small-molecule medication that selectively blocks the C5a receptor, reducing neutrophil chemoattraction and activation. In ANCA-associated vasculitis treated with typical induction therapy, adding avacopan has been shown to be a safe approach to reducing glucocorticoid doses and toxicity and may improve sustained remission.

Intravenous immune globulin, composed of IgG concentrates purified from pooled human plasma, is approved for treatment of dermatomyositis. Potential adverse effects include headache, fever, nausea, aseptic meningitis, and thromboembolic events.

Patients with autoimmune diseases should be assessed for immunization status at diagnosis and/or initiation of treatments. The 2022 ACR vaccination guidelines outline recommendations for vaccination of patients with rheumatologic diseases and advise when to hold vaccines or medications to optimize efficacy and safety. Whenever possible, patients should receive recommended vaccinations at least 2 to 4 weeks before initiating immunosuppressive regimens. The ACR conditionally recommends that patients treated with DMARDs may defer receipt of live-attenuated vaccines or hold DMARD therapy for a period of time before (the timing depends on the specific DMARD therapy) and 4 weeks after vaccine administration to mitigate the risk for active infection. Before a DMARD is held, the risk for potentially exacerbating the underlying rheumatologic disease should be carefully considered. Patients can safely receive nonlive vaccines (e.g., inactivated influenza, pneumococcal, recombinant zoster, and COVID-19 vaccines). Vaccine response may be diminished during immunosuppressive treatment, particularly with high-dose glucocorticoids or B-cell–depleting therapy; thus, timing of vaccine administration should be carefully considered. (See Immunization in Foundations of Clinical Practice for more information.)

Patients with latent or active tuberculosis, active hepatitis B virus infection, or untreated hepatitis C virus infection or HIV infection require initiation of appropriate therapy before beginning immunosuppressive treatment. Screening for these conditions should also be performed before the start of therapy. Patients with risk factors for tuberculosis exposure should have annual tuberculosis screening.

Nonpharmacologic measures are often used to address pain not eliminated by pharmacologic therapy for rheumatologic diseases. These measures include physical therapy, occupational therapy, surgery, weight reduction, psychosocial support, and self-management programs. Many patients also use complementary and alternative medicine as adjuncts to traditional medical interventions.

Physical therapists can assess aerobic fitness, conditioning, and ability to carry out activities of daily living. Pain and functional limitation can be mitigated through manual therapy, assistive devices, joint protection techniques, and thermal treatments. Physical therapists can recommend a targeted exercise program with adaptation for home exercises. Physical therapy referral is appropriate for tendinitis, bursitis, many forms of arthritis, and chronic soft tissue pain due to overuse, injury, and chronic pain syndromes (e.g., fibromyalgia).

Occupational therapists assess upper extremity functioning, including the ability to perform self-care and job-related tasks. Braces and splints may be provided for painful or unstable joints. An ergonomic evaluation of the workstation may accompany instruction in improved body mechanics and avoidance of repetitive trauma.

Nontraditional options for symptom management are used by up to 90% of patients with chronic pain, including those with rheumatologic diseases. Commonly used over-the-counter supplements include turmeric, fish oil, vitamins, glucosamine, and chondroitin. Some supplements are associated with significant drug interactions and adverse reactions, so a careful medication history should be obtained. See Nonopioid Pharmacologic Therapy in Common Symptoms for a discussion of cannabis for pain management.

Mind-body interventions, such as tai chi, meditation, and yoga, can improve psychological well-being, strength, balance, and pain level. Chiropractic and osteopathic manipulation and massage remain popular. Randomized controlled trials support the use of tai chi for arthritis; smaller trials suggest benefit from meditation techniques, yoga, massage, acupuncture, and manipulative medicine for various musculoskeletal problems.

Surgical procedures, such as carpal tunnel release or rotator cuff tendon repair, can address conditions that arise from repetitive trauma, injury, and degenerative changes in the soft tissue. Synovectomy of inflammatory pannus is occasionally used when a single or limited number of joints in patients with inflammatory arthritis do not respond to other treatment. Total joint arthroplasty, particularly of the knee or hip, can reduce or eliminate pain and restore function in patients with an inadequate response to medication and physical or occupational therapy.
