Rheumatoid Arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic autoimmune disease typically characterized by chronic inflammatory polyarthritis affecting both small and large joints, with a predilection for the joints of the hands and feet. Cervical spine involvement is also relatively common, especially in patients with long-standing disease. The prevalence of RA in the general population is 0.5% to 1%; its incidence is highest in the third through fifth decades, and it is two to three times more common in women than men.

Genes account for 60% of the risk for RA. The most important association is the (HLA) DRB1 gene, which includes alleles coding for the “shared epitope,” a five–amino acid sequence that preferentially binds and presents citrullinated peptide antigens. Citrulline is not a native amino acid in humans; instead, it is formed by the action of the enzyme peptidylarginine deiminase (PADI), which is expressed in sites of inflammation. Citrullinated proteins are immunogenic, especially in people who have the shared epitope. The development of antibodies to these citrullinated protein antibodies represents a break in tolerance that may progress to clinical disease over time.

Many of the other genes associated with RA also affect immune pathways.

Environmental factors, particularly smoking, are synergistic with genetic risk for RA. In smokers with a genetic predisposition, the risk for developing RA may be as high as 20 times that for nonsmokers. The presence of the shared epitope markedly increases the risk for RA among persons who smoke, likely because of increased immune response to inflammation-induced protein citrullination in lung tissue. Patients with RA, especially those with a family history of the disease, should be counseled about smoking cessation.

Although no single microbe is implicated in RA development, there are associations with altered mucosal microbiota in the lung, mouth, and intestines. Porphyromonas gingivalis, a bacterium associated with periodontitis, expresses its own PADI enzyme and provides a potential link to formation of citrullinated peptide. Intestinal and sputum dysbioses have also been associated with RA development.

Women are two to three times as likely as men to develop RA. The role of estrogen and other sex-specific factors is incompletely understood, and estrogen and other sex hormones have both stimulatory and inhibitory effects on the immune system. Estrogen receptors are present on synovial fibroblasts and may drive the production of cartilage-damaging metalloproteinases. Stimulation of estrogen receptors on macrophages can increase production of tumor necrosis factor (TNF), a key RA inflammatory cytokine.

The 2010 ACR (American College of Rheumatology)/EULAR (at the time called the European League Against Rheumatism and now called the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology) classification criteria for RA are sensitive and emphasize early diagnosis and treatment to prevent permanent consequences of chronic inflammation ( [Table: Table: Classification Criteria for Rheumatoid Arthritis]

).

RA is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory disorder, and symptom onset is usually gradual. Patients with RA typically report joint pain and inflammatory symptoms, including swelling and morning stiffness lasting at least 30 minutes to several hours. Stiffness is also worse following rest and is alleviated by ongoing activity. Synovitis is palpable on joint examination, manifesting as fullness or bogginess of the affected joint. Gently squeezing the joints may also elicit tenderness; as part of the screening examination, the metacarpophalangeal and/or metatarsophalangeal joints can be squeezed together. Another sign of early RA is the inability to make a fist, which is due to flexor tenosynovitis.

The pattern of joint involvement is useful for diagnosing RA. RA most characteristically affects the metacarpophalangeal joints, metatarsophalangeal joints, and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints of the hands and feet but spares the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of both the upper and lower extremities (see

and

). Uncontrolled disease activity can lead to various joint deformities. Swan neck deformity refers to DIP flexion and PIP hyperextension. Boutonniere deformity involves DIP hyperextension and PIP flexion (

). Wrists, elbows, shoulders, hips, knees, and ankles can also be involved. RA tends to affect joints symmetrically (i.e., joints on both sides of the body are generally involved), but severity may be asymmetric. RA may rarely present as persistent involvement in a single joint. RA spares the thoracic and lumbar spine but affects the cervical spine, especially the C1-C2 (atlantoaxial) articulation. See [Table: Table: Inflammation Consequences on Joints, Supporting Structures]

for more information.

The most useful laboratory studies to aid in the diagnosis of RA are rheumatoid factor and anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibodies. Rheumatoid factor is an immunoglobulin, usually IgM, directed against the Fc hinge portion of IgG. Rheumatoid factor occurs in approximately 70% of patients with RA. Because rheumatoid factor can be associated with other diseases (e.g., viral hepatitis, endocarditis) and its presence increases with age, the specificity of rheumatoid factor is limited at about 85%. Anti-CCP antibodies are also present in approximately 70% of patients with RA but have a specificity of 95% in patients presenting with joint inflammation. The importance of rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies in asymptomatic patients is less clear; both antibodies may predate the onset of clinical disease. In patients with RA, anti-CCP antibodies are more predictive than rheumatoid factor for erosive disease.

Approximately 10% to 20% of patients diagnosed with RA are seronegative (i.e., positive for neither rheumatoid factor nor anti-CCP antibodies). These patients are more clinically heterogeneous, have different genetics and risk factors, and generally have a better prognosis than those with seropositive RA.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level are elevated in 75% of patients with RA and can be used, along with symptoms and examination findings, to monitor treatment response. The systemic inflammation inherent to RA may also lead to anemia of inflammation and modest thrombocytosis.

Plain radiography of the hands and/or feet is the standard imaging study for RA and can aid in diagnosis and assessing progression. Radiographs obtained early in the disease may be normal or reveal soft-tissue swelling only. Later radiographic changes include periarticular osteopenia, marginal erosions, and joint-space narrowing (see

and

). Radiography of the cervical spine with flexion/extension views is appropriate if C1-C2 subluxation is suspected.

Ultrasonography and MRI are more sensitive than plain radiography for detecting abnormalities in joints and soft tissues. Ultrasonography is useful for detecting joint fluid (effusion), synovial tissue thickening and increased vascularity, tenosynovitis, and early erosions. MRI can be used to assess bone marrow edema, synovitis, and erosions but in clinical practice is generally reserved for assessment of soft-tissue derangements, such as tendon ruptures. MRI of the cervical spine is specifically indicated if atlantoaxial involvement is suspected.

RA must be differentiated from other conditions that cause joint swelling. Osteoarthritis, psoriatic arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, crystal-induced arthritis, and polymyalgia rheumatica can be differentiated from RA by their different patterns of joint involvement, laboratory associations, and radiographic findings. Viral infections such as parvovirus B19, chikungunya, and acute hepatitis B virus infection can cause polyarticular arthritis and may mimic RA. Rheumatoid factor may also be positive in acute hepatitis B virus infection.

Palindromic rheumatism is a syndrome characterized by recurrent episodes of inflammatory mono- or oligoarthritis. Symptoms last hours to days and may be migratory or nonmigratory, with interval symptom-free periods lasting days to months. Affected joints recover without permanent damage. However, roughly half of patients will develop another rheumatologic disease, most commonly RA and sometimes systemic lupus erythematosus.

RS3PE (remitting seronegative symmetric synovitis with pitting edema) syndrome is associated with swollen hands and peripheral pitting edema. Unlike with RA, the onset of symptoms is often sudden. The syndrome may be associated with polymyalgia rheumatica and rarely with malignancy.

RA joint damage is a consequence of synovitis within the joint. The synovial lining, normally only a few cells thick, becomes expanded through proliferation of resident fibroblast-like synoviocytes and immune system cells (T cells, B cells, macrophages), facilitated by angiogenesis. Cytokines (TNF, interleukins), often signaling through Janus kinases, and cartilage-damaging metalloproteinases contribute to inflammation and damage. Receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa B ligand (RANKL), produced by inflammatory cells, activates osteoclasts to erode bone. The metalloproteinases and activated osteoclasts result in various irreversible changes to the joints (see [Table: Table: Inflammation Consequences on Joints, Supporting Structures]

).

The most common RA skin changes are rheumatoid nodules (

), present in up to 30% of patients. Nodules typically occur in the olecranon region and can be confused with gouty tophi, but they can also occur over the hand and foot joints and even in the lungs. Patients with rheumatoid nodules are at increased risk for severe joint disease and cardiovascular and respiratory involvement. Some patients with RA who are treated with methotrexate may have a noticeable increase in the size and number of rheumatoid nodules, a condition referred to as accelerated nodulosis.

Patients with RA are also at an increased risk for neutrophilic dermatoses, such as pyoderma gangrenosum and Sweet syndrome (see Sweet Syndrome in Dermatology). Palpable purpura and skin ulcers may result from small-vessel cutaneous vasculitis.

The most common eye manifestation in RA is dry eye (keratoconjunctivitis sicca). It occurs in 10% to 15% of patients and can be severe. Most of these patients also have dry mouth and are classified as having secondary Sjögren disease (see Sjögren Disease in Rheumatology).

Less common (1%) are episcleritis (inflammation of superficial scleral vessels) and scleritis (inflammation of deep scleral vessels). RA is one of the most common diseases associated with scleritis, which can be intensely painful and vision threatening and can lead to thinning of the sclera and perforation. Keratitis (corneal inflammation) is ulcerative and occurs at the periphery of the cornea. Severe keratitis is known as corneal melt. Both scleritis and keratitis require immediate referral to an ophthalmologist (see Red Eye in Interdisciplinary Medicine).

Lung inflammation may precede joint symptoms in patients with RA, although these patients may be asymptomatic.

Interstitial lung disease (ILD) may develop in 50% of patients with RA; clinically significant disease is seen in 10% of patients and contributes to excess mortality. Smoking is a significant risk factor for ILD in patients with RA. ILD is characterized by dyspnea, dry cough, a restrictive pattern and decreased diffusing capacity on pulmonary function testing, and diffuse parenchymal changes on high-resolution chest CT.

Bronchiectasis and bronchiolitis also occur in RA, and bronchiolitis can be obliterative and/or constrictive.

Pleural disease occurs in up to 5% of patients; pleural effusions are exudative and can be large. RA pleural effusions are characterized by low glucose and pH (mimicking bacterial or tubercular infection and malignancy) and low complement levels, as well as elevated levels of total protein, rheumatoid factor, and lactate dehydrogenase. Inflammatory cells in the RA effusion are characteristically mononuclear; a neutrophil-predominant effusion suggests infection.

Upper airway involvement from cricoarytenoid arthritis occurs rarely; symptoms include hoarseness, sore throat, dysphagia, and stridor. Cricoarytenoid arthritis can pose problems for endotracheal intubation.

Cardiovascular disease, especially coronary artery disease, remains the major cause of excess death in patients with RA. Systemic inflammation leads to accelerated atherosclerosis and, subsequently, coronary artery disease. More recent data suggest that risk for cardiovascular disease may be decreasing toward that of the general population in patients with well-controlled RA. For purposes of perioperative evaluation, patients with RA should be considered at high cardiovascular risk. Mitigation of cardiovascular risk includes optimal management of RA, as well as addressing cardiovascular disease risk factors, such as hypertension and dyslipidemia, as per guidelines for the general population (see Management of Primary Hypertension in Nephrology and Management of Dyslipidemias in Cardiovascular Medicine).

Clinically significant pericarditis is rare. Granulomatous myocarditis, valvular disease (mainly mitral), conduction block, and aortitis can occur but are very rare.

Anemia of inflammation is the most common RA hematologic abnormality. Felty syndrome is a rare condition consisting of neutropenia and splenomegaly; it occurs in patients with long-standing, severe, seropositive RA. Patients with Felty syndrome are at risk for serious bacterial infections, lower extremity ulceration, lymphoma, and vasculitis. Patients with RA can also have large granular lymphocyte syndrome, which can progress to large granular lymphocyte leukemia. Findings overlap with those of Felty syndrome and include neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly, and recurrent infections. Patients with RA are at increased risk for lymphomas (particularly large B-cell lymphomas), and risk is correlated with disease activity.

Small-vessel cutaneous vasculitis occurs in a small percentage of patients with RA, leading to palpable purpura or periungual infarcts. A larger-vessel vasculitis similar to polyarteritis nodosa can affect multiple organ systems but is rare given current therapeutic options. Patients with rheumatoid vasculitis typically are seropositive and have long-standing and untreated erosive joint disease.

See Principles of Therapeutics in Rheumatology for details on the uses, mechanisms of action, major toxicities, and/or monitoring requirements of the medications used in RA.

The 2021 ACR RA treatment guidelines advocate for early diagnosis and aggressive early disease-modifying treatment to prevent irreversible joint damage and to minimize use of NSAIDs, glucocorticoids, and opioids.

A key treatment goal is to treat to target, with the target being achievement of low disease activity or remission. Disease activity assessment involves making a measured determination using the following:

  • Combinations of the patient’s and physician’s impressions of disease activity
  • Numbers of tender and swollen joints (typically by using 28 joints that exclude the feet)
  • In some activity scoring systems, measurement of erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein

These parameters are combined into a composite score, which can then be categorized as remission or low, moderate, or high disease activity. The Clinical Disease Activity Index (CDAI) and Disease Activity Score 28 (DAS28) are two commonly used instruments to assess disease activity and response to treatment. Treating to target in RA reduces radiographic damage and cardiovascular risk and increases work productivity.

The 2021 ACR RA treatment guidelines can assist in initial treatment decisions in early RA. Treatment is typically advanced at 12-week intervals, with the goal of reaching remission or low disease activity as rapidly as possible. Patients who remain in remission or a state of low disease activity for 6 months or longer may be able to reduce treatment intensity, although they rarely tolerate discontinuation. Treatment decisions for established RA are more complex. An approach to the treatment of both early and established RA is outlined in

.

Additional ACR guidelines from 2022 support an integrative management approach for patients with RA and strongly recommend engagement in various forms of exercise. Rehabilitation techniques, a healthy diet, and self-management techniques are recommended as adjunctive therapies.

Methotrexate is the anchor drug in RA, used as monotherapy and as a component of combination therapy. The target doses of methotrexate should be at least 15 mg weekly but can be titrated to doses as high as 25 mg weekly in partial responders; the treating physician should generally maximize methotrexate dosing before adding other agents. At doses greater than 15 mg weekly, methotrexate oral absorption approaches its effective limit; a split dose of oral methotrexate over 24 hours (one dose in the morning and one dose in the evening) or switching to subcutaneous administration allows for higher serum drug levels. Folic acid supplements minimize toxicity without diminishing efficacy. Among patients with RA taking methotrexate alone, 30% to 50% achieve remission or low disease activity. See Methotrexate in Rheumatology for further information on the adverse effects of methotrexate.

Leflunomide may be a useful alternative for patients who cannot tolerate methotrexate. In patients with low disease activity, hydroxychloroquine monotherapy is conditionally recommended over other synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs). Both hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine can be used in combination with methotrexate as triple therapy. Data suggest that triple therapy is similar in efficacy to methotrexate combined with TNF inhibitors but may be inferior in prevention of radiographic progression and in patient experience. The addition of a biologic DMARD or targeted synthetic DMARD to methotrexate is conditionally recommended over triple therapy for patients taking maximally tolerated doses of methotrexate that are not at target.

Biologic DMARDs can be used as monotherapy but are typically added to methotrexate when moderate to high disease activity persists. The combination of methotrexate and a biologic DMARD slows the rate of radiographic damage to cartilage and bone, even in the setting of continued clinical disease activity. TNF inhibitors are the most frequently used biologic DMARDs (see [Table: Table: Biologic DMARDs]

). Other biologic DMARDs used in RA include abatacept (a selective T-cell costimulation modulator), tocilizumab or sarilumab (anti–interleukin-6 receptor antibodies), and rituximab (an anti–B-cell antibody).

Tofacitinib, baricitinib, and upadacitinib constitute a class of FDA-approved oral small-molecule Janus kinase inhibitors, or targeted synthetic DMARDs (see [Table: Table: Targeted Synthetic DMARDs]

), whose efficacy in RA, cost, and safety profiles are similar to those of biologic DMARDs.

Until better data are available to guide therapeutic decisions, the choice of a biologic or targeted synthetic DMARD remains empiric and based largely on patient characteristics, including consideration of patient comorbidities.

NSAIDs may help to control symptoms but are not disease modifying in RA and do not prevent joint damage. Thus, they should be used sparingly and along with DMARD therapy. Topical NSAIDs may be effective for some patients and cause less toxicity.

Unlike NSAIDs, glucocorticoids can have a disease-modifying effect, in addition to their efficacy in symptom management. Low-dose prednisone (5-15 mg/d) can be used to rapidly improve RA symptoms until long-term medications become effective, or they can be used short term for disease flares. The 2021 ACR RA treatment guidelines conditionally recommend initiating conventional synthetic DMARDs without short-term glucocorticoids in DMARD-naive patients. Although glucocorticoid use is associated with a reduction in radiographic progression, long-term therapy with glucocorticoids has substantial potential adverse effects, including osteoporosis, diabetes mellitus, infection, and increased cardiovascular risks.

Surgical therapy has become less common in RA because of current treatment strategies. However, some patients may benefit from synovectomy for a single persistently swollen joint, carpal tunnel release, repair of a ruptured tendon, total joint replacement (shoulder, metacarpophalangeal joints, hip, knee), or joint fusion for a painful damaged joint.

For a discussion of antirheumatic medication use in the perioperative period, see Perioperative Management of Rheumatic Disease in Foundations of Clinical Practice.

The risk for RA increases in the first year after a first pregnancy. Breastfeeding may decrease this risk. Among patients with established RA at the time of conception, two thirds will go into remission or a state of low disease activity during pregnancy, and one third will not improve or will get worse. Medication management is an important concern, and pregnancy plans should be discussed with any patient of childbearing age who will be prescribed therapy. See Medications and Pregnancy in Rheumatology for further discussion.

Osteoarthritis

Osteoarthritis (OA) is a chronic progressive multifactorial disorder of maladaptive cellular repair to joint stress. Previously deemed a “wear and tear” disease and an inevitable consequence of aging, OA is now recognized as a disorder driven by a complex interplay of genetics; biomechanics; cell stress; biochemical change in cartilage and extracellular matrix components; and degradation and inflammation, which is usually subclinical. It affects all tissues of the joint and is characterized by cartilage and meniscal degradation, subchondral bone changes (bone marrow lesions, subchondral sclerosis), and osteophyte formation. OA is accompanied by low-grade synovitis and is driven by imbalanced anabolic and catabolic processes that represent aberrant joint responses and result in joint tissue degeneration.

OA is the most common form of arthritis worldwide and is a leading cause of pain and disability, affecting approximately 30 million U.S. adults. OA is the leading cause of lower extremity disability among older adults, with an estimated lifetime risk for knee OA approaching 50%. Prevalence is projected to more than double by 2030, largely because of increasing rates of obesity and the aging of the population. Incidence and prevalence vary by joint and depend on whether a clinical or a radiographic definition of OA is being applied.

Epidemiologic risk factors for OA include the following:

  • Age older than 55 years
  • Female sex
  • BMI of 25 or greater
  • Genetics
  • Occupations that involve repetitive motions or physical labor

Obesity is the most important modifiable risk factor, especially for knee OA. Increased body weight is also a risk factor for hand OA, perhaps underscoring the systemic nature and effect of obesity and the metabolic and/or inflammatory mechanisms in the pathogenesis of hand OA. Single inherited conditions rarely predispose to OA; however, variants in genes involved in bone or articular cartilage structure or metabolism are possible risk factors.

Risk factors involving the joint itself include abnormal loading, injury, malalignment, and intrinsic cartilage or bone tissue defects. Injury may be acute (e.g., anterior cruciate ligament tear) or accumulate over time (e.g., physical labor or overuse); regardless of cause, injuries have been linked with the future development of OA at various sites. Hip dislocation, congenital dysplasia, femoroacetabular impingement, and knee malalignment are also associated with incident OA.

Given the multifactorial causes, OA may develop as a consequence of one or more risk factors; how the interaction of these risk factors culminates in OA is complex and not fully understood.

In most cases, no identifiable proximal cause of OA is recognized. Although the term primary OA is commonly used for this category, a complex interplay of genetics, age, sex, biomechanics, biochemistry, and inflammation is implicit in its development. Primary OA may affect almost any joint, but clinically significant presentations occur in the small joints of the hands and feet, spine, hips, and knees. One or more of these areas might be affected and symptomatic in a given individual.

Erosive (inflammatory) OA is a subset of primary hand OA. Erosive OA prominently affects the distal interphalangeal (DIP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints, leads to more joint erythema and swelling than other forms of primary hand OA, and is more common in women. Radiographs reveal diagnosis-defining central erosions with a “seagull” or “gull-wing” appearance in these interphalangeal joints (see

); joint ankylosis (bony fusion) may also occur. Whether erosive OA comprises a separate disease entity or is part of the continuum of OA remains controversial.

Secondary OA is historically defined by the presence of a predisposing disorder; however, an increasing number of risk factors for primary OA are being identified, thus blurring the line between the primary and secondary forms. Pathologic changes, clinical presentations, symptoms, and management are indistinguishable between primary and secondary OA. When OA occurs in a joint not typically affected by primary OA, or when it presents at a younger age, secondary causes of OA should be considered. Commonly recognized causes of secondary OA include the following:

  • A history of joint damage, such as trauma, infection, or surgical repair (e.g., anterior cruciate ligament repair or meniscectomy)
  • Congenitally abnormal joints (e.g., hip dysplasia) and/or malalignment
  • Systemic metabolic, endocrine, microcrystalline, and neuropathic disorders, particularly those that affect cartilage (e.g., hemochromatosis and chondrocalcinosis)
  • Underlying inflammatory arthritis with accompanying damage (e.g., rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis)

See [Table: Table: Secondary Causes of Osteoarthritis]

for a description of typical joint involvement in secondary OA.

The diagnosis of OA is based on history and physical examination; radiography is confirmatory but may be unnecessary. In early OA, clinical findings may not be accompanied by radiographic changes; conversely, some patients with prominent radiographic changes may have minimal or no symptoms. Patients with OA are typically older than 50 years; diagnosis at an earlier age should prompt inquiry into a history of joint damage, endocrine or metabolic disorders, or a genetic proclivity for early disease.

Joints most commonly affected are the hands (DIP, PIP, and first carpometacarpal joints), feet (especially the first metatarsophalangeal and mid-foot joints), knees, hips, and spine (cervical and lumbar regions), but the distribution varies. When OA affects a single joint, it more often results from injury or joint asymmetry and often occurs in weight-bearing joints (hip or knee). Generalized OA, which affects multiple joint groups, often symmetrically, may result from a combination of genetic and environmental factors.

Patients with OA usually describe an insidious onset of intermittent symptoms, which become more persistent and severe over time. The most common symptom is joint pain exacerbated by activity and alleviated with rest. Patients also describe self-limited morning stiffness usually lasting less than 30 minutes, in contrast to the prolonged morning stiffness of inflammatory arthritis. A single joint may initially be involved, with eventual involvement of multiple joints.

Joint examination may show the following:

  • Joint-line tenderness
  • Crepitus
  • Decreased range of motion
  • Bony enlargement without synovitis
  • Effusion (most commonly in the knees)

Patients with long-standing hand OA may have Heberden and Bouchard nodes (bony enlargement of the DIP and PIP joints, respectively; see

) and squaring of the first carpometacarpal joint. Hip involvement typically manifests as anterior groin pain and decreased range of motion, especially internal rotation. Knee symptoms include pain on walking and climbing stairs and difficulty transferring from a seated to a standing position. OA affecting the spine (spondylosis) can affect the vertebral bodies, facet joints, and neural foramina and may lead to spinal stenosis and radiculopathy (see Low Back Pain in Common Symptoms for further discussion).

Patients with OA generally lack systemic or constitutional features. Pain and structural changes, however, ultimately result in functional impairment, disability, psychosocial isolation, and reduced quality of life. Inability to exercise regularly may have adverse consequences for general health.

Laboratory testing is not necessary to establish a diagnosis of OA but is helpful if other causes of arthritis are being considered, such as crystal arthropathy, rheumatoid arthritis (RA), psoriatic arthritis, or hemochromatosis (all of which can coexist with OA). Acute phase reactant levels are not elevated in OA. Routine laboratory tests (complete blood count, kidney and liver chemistries) are not necessary for diagnosing OA but may be important to help define the safety of pharmacologic therapy, especially in older persons and patients with comorbidities.

If a joint effusion is present, evaluation for concurrent crystal arthropathy, infection, or other inflammatory cause should be considered, ideally by synovial fluid analysis. OA synovial fluid is typically clear and noninflammatory, with a leukocyte count of 2000/μL (2.0 × 10^9/L) or less.

Although imaging is not necessary to diagnose OA, it can be helpful to confirm the diagnosis, establish baseline severity and/or monitor progressive severity, and exclude other diagnoses. Radiographic features of OA include asymmetric joint-space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis (or eburnation), osteophytes, and bone cysts (

); however, these changes may not be present in early disease. Even in established OA, symptoms may correlate poorly with imaging findings. Although MRI and ultrasonography can detect subtle OA changes, they are not needed for routine OA diagnosis.

Diagnosing OA can be challenging when OA is present in atypical joints, an accurate history is difficult to obtain, or a concurrent inflammatory arthropathy may be present. Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, gout, RA, and psoriatic arthritis may coexist with OA or mimic OA (see [Table: Table: Differential Diagnosis of Osteoarthritis]

). Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease may occur in joints also typically affected by OA (hands or knees) but is associated with intermittent “flares,” and radiographs often show cartilage calcification (chondrocalcinosis). Gout and OA commonly co-associate, particularly in the DIP joints. Rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis can be differentiated from OA by prolonged morning stiffness, signs and symptoms of chronic and persistent inflammation, and elevated inflammatory markers on laboratory testing. Unlike OA, RA typically spares the DIP joints, and the presence of rheumatoid factor and/or anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies favors the diagnosis of RA. Psoriatic arthritis can involve the DIP joints, but dactylitis and a history of psoriasis help differentiate it from OA. In older patients with psoriasis and insidious-onset arthritis, OA may be a more likely diagnosis than psoriatic arthritis. Synovial fluid analysis can also help distinguish between OA and these inflammatory joint disorders.

Other conditions to consider in evaluating a patient for OA include nonarticular sources of pain, such as bursitis and tendinitis. Hip pain that is not in the anterior groin but instead around the lateral hip and buttock may indicate trochanteric bursitis or lumbosacral radiculopathy. Similarly, knee pain may be secondary to pes anserine bursitis or iliotibial band syndrome rather than intra-articular pathology and may present with medial or lateral knee pain, respectively. See Lower Extremity Musculoskeletal Pain in Common Symptoms for further discussion of nonarticular pain conditions.

To date, the FDA has approved no agents to prevent, delay, or remit the structural progression of OA. Instead, current treatment is directed to the management of pain and disability. Evidence-based guidelines for OA management are available from the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) and Arthritis Foundation, the Osteoarthritis Research Society International, the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology, and other organizations. There is considerable consensus among these guidelines, particularly that optimal OA management requires a comprehensive plan that may include educational, psychological, and physical management, along with pharmacologic interventions. The recommendations are usually specific to the anatomic area affected.

Patients with OA should receive individualized, often multidisciplinary, treatment that considers patient expectations, functional and activity levels, occupational and vocational needs, joints affected, severity of disease, and coexisting medical conditions. Instead of a single algorithm, the practitioner should consider the patient’s clinical state and institute treatment, which may include single or multiple modalities that may be cycled in and out as needed (

).

The nonpharmacologic approach to OA starts with assessment of physical status, activities of daily living, health education, motivation, beliefs, and other biopsychosocial factors. An individualized management plan includes the following:

  • Education on OA and joint protection
  • Exercise regimen
  • Weight loss (especially if lower extremity joint involvement is present)
  • Assistive devices as appropriate

Data suggest that participation in self-efficacy and self-management programs that use a format based on multidisciplinary groups is associated with improvement in OA symptoms. Physical activity includes graduated aerobic exercise and strength training, with attention paid to strengthening periarticular structures and minimizing injury. Tai chi has also been shown to be as beneficial as physical therapy for knee OA pain and is strongly recommended by the ACR for knee and hip OA. The combination of diet and exercise is more effective at decreasing OA-related knee pain and dysfunction than is diet or exercise alone; no evidence supports following a specific diet to decrease OA symptoms. Weight loss provides meaningful improvement in symptoms; larger benefit accrues with greater loss of weight. Knee braces and/or canes are recommended for patients with impaired ambulation, joint instability, or pain, whereas shoe inserts are not recommended. The ACR also conditionally recommends cognitive behavioral therapy, acupuncture, and thermal interventions (locally applied heat or cold) for knee, hip, and hand OA. Balance exercises are conditionally recommended for knee and hip OA, and yoga is recommended for knee OA.

In the absence of disease-modifying OA drugs, pharmacologic treatment is considered when symptoms are bothersome to the patient and are inadequately or incompletely addressed by nonpharmacologic interventions. Pharmacologic therapy for OA includes oral, topical, and intra-articular medications. Choice of treatment depends on individualized assessment, with particular attention to comorbidities, concomitant medications, and, especially, adverse treatment effects. See Principles of Therapeutics in Rheumatology for details on the medications used in OA.

Oral agents for OA include NSAIDs, acetaminophen, duloxetine, and tramadol. NSAIDs are efficacious in OA, regardless of anatomic location, and are the initial oral treatment of choice. However, their adverse-effect profiles make sustained use problematic, especially in older persons and patients with comorbidities. A proton pump inhibitor (and/or other gastroprotective agent) may improve tolerance and minimize risk; the proper choice of an NSAID should consider drug pharmacokinetics and adverse gastrointestinal, kidney, and cardiovascular effects. For OA, NSAIDs should be used in the lowest possible dose and for the shortest possible time. Nonetheless, NSAIDs remain the mainstay of OA treatment.

Topical NSAIDs are safe, associated with the least systemic exposure, and effective for treating knee and hand OA. For knee and hand OA, topical NSAIDs are preferable and should be considered before use of oral NSAIDs. They are not effective for hip OA and have limited efficacy in OA at other sites. Other topical agents, such as capsaicin, lidocaine, and methyl salicylate preparations, may also be used as adjunctive measures, especially when NSAIDs are ineffective or are not tolerated.

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses suggest that acetaminophen provides no benefit for hip or knee OA but may be considered as an add-on therapy, as well as for short-term and episodic use. ACR guidelines conditionally recommend acetaminophen for knee, hip, and hand OA in patients with limited pharmacologic options.

Duloxetine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor with central nervous system activity, has shown efficacy for pain from knee OA. This suggests a role for central sensitization in OA pain modulation.

Opioids for OA should be avoided because evidence shows only slight benefit and a high risk for toxicity and dependence. Opioid use should be considered in limited circumstances and for refractory therapy only when symptoms are intolerable or no alternatives exist. Tramadol, a partial opioid with fewer adverse effects and less addictive potential than pure opioids, may be considered in some patients in whom other analgesics have not relieved pain. Nonetheless, concerns about the potential for adverse effects of tramadol continue.

Patients with OA frequently use glucosamine, an oral dietary supplement. Although glucosamine appears to be safe, substantial evidence suggests that it lacks efficacy. ACR guidelines strongly recommend against glucosamine in patients with knee, hip, and/or hand OA. Chondroitin sulfate is strongly recommended against in patients with knee and/or hip OA, as are combination products that include both glucosamine and chondroitin sulfate. However, chondroitin is conditionally recommended for patients with hand OA.

Patients with knee or hip OA who experience inefficacy of, intolerance of, or contraindication to oral and topical therapies may benefit from intra-articular glucocorticoid injections. Despite the lack of formal evidence for the utility of this therapy in joints other than the knee and hip, there may be a possible benefit in other joints, such as the first carpometacarpal joint. The ACR strongly recommends using ultrasound guidance for hip-joint glucocorticoid injections.

Long-term harm from intra-articular glucocorticoids has not been consistently demonstrated; however, benefit is usually short term and wanes within 3 months. Injections can be administered repeatedly but are not usually given more often than every 3 months. At least one study has suggested that knee joints undergoing repeated injections may be more likely to experience cartilage loss, but the effect size was small and the clinical significance remains controversial.

Major guidelines recommend against the routine use of intra-articular hyaluronic acid injections. The quality of trials assessing efficacy of intra-articular hyaluronic acid varies, and the degree of benefit is low.

Intra-articular stem cells, platelet-rich plasma, biologics, and botulinum toxin are not efficacious and are not recommended.

Surgery for OA is considered when nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic approaches fail to control pain or improve functional limitation. Multiple high-quality studies have shown that arthroscopic surgery for knee OA provides no better outcomes than conservative management unless the patient has joint buckling, instability, or locking or a concomitant and symptomatic mechanical disorder.

In contrast, total joint replacement is a “curative” option for patients in whom conservative therapies have failed; it relieves pain and improves function. In appropriate patients, total joint replacement should not be delayed for a continued trial of conservative measures. Overall, long-term outcomes are excellent, although hardware loosening and infection may occur.

Recent studies suggest that for patients with class III obesity and knee OA, bariatric surgery may significantly improve pain and function even without further OA management.

Fibromyalgia

Fibromyalgia is characterized by widespread chronic pain, fatigue, disturbed sleep, and mental fogginess. This common condition (prevalence, 2%-3%) is more prevalent in women than men, and age at onset is usually between the third and sixth decades.

Fibromyalgia appears to be a disorder of pain perception and processing. Its pathophysiology is not well understood. However, it is thought to relate to central sensitization, characterized by amplification of pain signaling within the central nervous system. Brain neuroimaging of patients with fibromyalgia shows abnormalities within structures responsible for pain transmission and interpretation. Accruing data suggest that genetics may also play a role.

The characteristic clinical features of fibromyalgia include widespread chronic pain; fatigue; sleep disorders (both disrupted and nonrestorative sleep); and cognitive symptoms, often termed “fibrofog.” See [Table: Table: Clinical Features of Fibromyalgia]

for additional features. Patients frequently have other coexistent painful conditions, including chronic headaches, temporomandibular joint disorder, irritable bowel syndrome, interstitial cystitis, and chronic pelvic pain. Two instruments are available to aid in the diagnosis of fibromyalgia: one issued jointly by the American Pain Society (APS) and the FDA, called the Analgesic, Anesthetic, and Addiction Clinical Trial Translations Innovations Opportunities and Networks (ACTTION)-APS Pain Taxonomy, and a 2016 revision of the 2010 American College of Rheumatology Preliminary Diagnostic Criteria (see [Table: Table: Diagnostic Criteria for Fibromyalgia]

and

). A diagnosis of fibromyalgia obtained by using these tools is valid irrespective of other diagnoses and does not exclude other clinically important illnesses.

Notably, these diagnostic tools are based entirely on patient reporting of symptoms and no longer incorporate the assessment of tender points on physical examination. Although tender points may be characteristic of fibromyalgia, the finding of specific tender points on physical examination has multiple shortcomings in practice.

Extensive laboratory studies (e.g., antinuclear antibody [ANA] testing) should not be performed unless other specific diagnoses are suspected. Positive ANA test results, particularly at low titers, are nonspecific and have a low positive predictive value. In addition to ANA positivity driving unnecessary additional testing, patients with fibromyalgia and positive ANA results are often incorrectly diagnosed with a connective tissue disease and given inappropriate and potentially harmful therapy. For example, studies have shown that many patients with fibromyalgia and a positive ANA result are unnecessarily treated with high-dose glucocorticoids. Imaging studies are also not indicated.

Diagnoses that are associated with fibromyalgia and diagnoses that may present with similar symptoms (e.g., hypothyroidism, polymyalgia rheumatica, inflammatory myositis, psychiatric disorders, primary sleep disorders) should be evaluated for when suspected.

Multiple rheumatologic conditions (Sjögren disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis) are also associated with a higher risk for coexistent fibromyalgia (20%-30%) than observed in the general population. In patients with autoimmune disease and comorbid fibromyalgia, it is crucial to recognize when comorbid fibromyalgia is the primary driver of musculoskeletal symptoms to avoid overtreatment with immunosuppressive agents.

Optimal management of fibromyalgia requires a holistic approach, including education, exercise, and psychosocial support. Pharmacotherapy is often warranted, although nonpharmacologic measures remain a cornerstone of treatment.

Patients should be educated regarding their condition, with validation that their symptoms are real and reassurance that their pain is not due to tissue injury and will not lead to permanent disability. Aerobic exercise can improve well-being and function as well as reduce pain. Because patients initially experience postexercise pain and thus may be unwilling to continue, exercise must be introduced gradually and supported encouragingly. Although evidence supporting their use is modest, mind-body and low-impact modalities (tai chi, water aerobics, and acupuncture) can be helpful. Stress management, sleep hygiene, and weight reduction (in patients with obesity) are also important in improving function and quality of life.

Patients with fibromyalgia and coexisting psychiatric illness should be referred for psychological support, although access to practitioners with experience treating chronic pain conditions is often a barrier. Cognitive behavioral therapy has shown modest benefit in reducing pain, negative mood, poor sleep, and disability.

Choice of pharmacologic therapy is based on symptom profile, patient comorbidities, and medication adverse effects because no trials have directly compared the efficacy of medications.

The antiepileptic agents gabapentin and pregabalin, the latter of which is FDA-approved for fibromyalgia, improve quality of life and decrease pain in the short term. In principle, these agents act by reducing pain signals from the dorsal root ganglia to the thalamus. Adverse effects, including sedation, disequilibrium, weight gain, and peripheral edema, are frequent. In older patients, gabapentinoid doses should initially be low and then be slowly titrated, as appropriate.

Tricyclic antidepressants, such as amitriptyline, raise norepinephrine and serotonin levels and have mild benefit, although efficacy may wane with time. These agents induce drowsiness, with potential benefit for disordered sleep, and should be taken just before bedtime. Anticholinergic and antihistaminic adverse effects may be limiting; low doses are recommended (e.g., 10-25 mg of amitriptyline).

Two serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), duloxetine and milnacipran, are FDA approved for fibromyalgia and have modest effects on pain and fatigue. They may be particularly appropriate in patients with concomitant depression. Some practitioners report that the administration of a tricyclic antidepressant at bedtime, combined with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (e.g., sertraline) in the morning, may mimic the aggregate effect of the SNRIs while helping normalize the sleep-wake pattern.

Tramadol has a dual effect as both an agonist of mu-opioid receptors and an SNRI. Although studies have shown tramadol is helpful, it is classified as an opioid, with associated concerns of class adverse effects, including tolerance and addiction. These concerns are less extreme than with other opioids, which are contraindicated for the long-term management of fibromyalgia. Evidence for the efficacy of opioids in patients with fibromyalgia is lacking, and patients receiving opioids have poorer outcomes than those treated without opioids.

Evidence does not support NSAIDs or acetaminophen for treating fibromyalgia.

The patient and physician should understand that fibromyalgia is a chronic illness. The benefit of treatment will likely be partial and usually temporary, often requiring a rotating sequence of treatments, or a combination of drug therapies in patients not responding to monotherapy. Nevertheless, treatment can help patients manage and cope with their symptoms as well as maintain function and autonomy. In patients who do not respond to monotherapy, specialty referral or assessment and care in a specialized multidisciplinary program may be useful.

Spondyloarthritis

Spondyloarthritis comprises arthritic disorders classified together by common genetic and environmental risk factors and clinical manifestations. Spondyloarthritis is a spectrum of disorders that includes axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis and nonradiographic axial spondyloarthritis), psoriatic arthritis (PsA), reactive arthritis, and enteropathic arthritis. Their common feature is enthesitis (inflammation at entheses, the points where tendons, ligaments, and joint capsules insert into bone). Clinically, enthesitis manifests as inflammation, pain, and new bone formation in and around peripheral joints; dactylitis (diffuse digital swelling [“sausage digits”] including the joint capsule, tendons, and ligaments) (

); and, in many cases, ossification at the spinal entheses. The term spondyloarthritis reflects the fact that most of these conditions also tend to involve the spine.

Genetics as well as immunologic, biomechanical, and environmental factors contribute to spondyloarthritis pathogenesis. The exact mechanisms of these processes remain incompletely understood.

Genetic factors account for approximately 90% of the pathogenesis of spondyloarthritis. Inheriting HLA-B27 significantly increases the odds ratio of developing ankylosing spondylitis in many patient populations. Although HLA-B27 is the most important gene, it accounts for only 30% of the genetic risk. Additionally, HLA-B27 alone is insufficient to cause ankylosing spondylitis; HLA-B27 is prevalent in 6.1% of the general population, and less than 1% of these patients will develop ankylosing spondylitis. Other important genes include ERAP-1 and genes involved in the interleukin (IL)-17/IL-23 immune inflammatory axis. Women with ankylosing spondylitis tend to have less radiographic progression than men, indicating that sex-specific factors may be important.

IL-17A/IL-23 cytokine pathway dysregulation plays a key role in pathogenesis. Patients with ankylosing spondylitis have increased T helper (Th)-17 cells. IL-23 and IL-17 mediate the inflammatory stress response to injury and are implicated in new bone formation. Genetic studies and the success of anti–IL-17 antibody therapy suggest that IL-17 is a key cytokine in the inflammatory process.

Entheses are major sites of the disease process in spondyloarthritis. Mechanical stress and microinjury at the entheses induce activation of local immune cells (e.g., T cells, resident macrophages, and innate lymphoid cells), inflammatory cytokine release, and proinflammatory cell recruitment. Pathologic repair response to injury leads to new bone formation.

Environmental factors, such as infections and gut microbiota, have been implicated in the pathogenesis of spondyloarthritis disorders. Intestinal dysbiosis or a proinflammatory microbiome is common in spondyloarthritis and may contribute to this observation. Intestinal inflammation is thought to lead to a permeable gut, allowing exposure of dysbiotic bacteria (especially flagellated bacteria) to the intestinal immune system. Terminal ileitis, similar to that seen in Crohn disease, occurs in up to 60% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis. Dysbiosis also contributes to PsA pathogenesis. Reactive arthritis has a well-established association with intestinal and urogenital pathogens.

Spondyloarthritis comprises four distinct but overlapping diseases ( [Table: Table: Clinical Features of Spondyloarthritis]

):

  • Axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis and nonradiographic axial spondyloarthritis)
  • Psoriatic arthritis
  • Enteropathic arthritis
  • Reactive arthritis

Some taxonomies include a fifth, undifferentiated category for patients who have spondyloarthritis features but manifestations that are insufficient to permit classification into one of the four categories. For example, a patient with episodic dactylitis and a history of uveitis would not fit neatly into one of the standard categories but would be classified as having peripheral spondyloarthritis by criteria discussed below.

Emphasizing the relatedness of all four categories, the Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society (ASAS) developed classification criteria that eschew individual diseases and instead divide patients into those with axial involvement ( [Table: Table: ASAS Classification Criteria for Axial Spondyloarthritis]

) and those with only peripheral joint involvement ( [Table: Table: ASAS Classification Criteria for Peripheral Spondyloarthritis]

). Although these criteria were designed for study enrollment rather than clinical practice, they demonstrate the common clinical features that are part of the spondyloarthritis family.

Axial spondyloarthritis is further categorized as radiographic (r-axSpA; also known as ankylosing spondylitis), which demonstrates definite evidence of sacroiliitis on plain radiographs, or nonradiographic (nr-axSpA), which demonstrates minimal or no evidence of sacroiliitis on plain radiographs. However, patients with nr-axSpA may have findings of sacroiliitis on MRI.

Ankylosing spondylitis (radiographic axial spondyloarthritis) is a chronic inflammatory disease affecting the axial skeleton (including sacroiliac joints), entheses, and peripheral joints. Prevalence is 0.32% in North America but only 0.07% in Africa, largely following the population prevalence of HLA-B27. Although ankylosing spondylitis was historically believed to be more frequent in men, a cohort study from 2023 demonstrated similar incidence in men and women. The risk is increased in the relatives of an affected patient. The disorder usually begins in the third to fourth decades (typically before age 45 years). It can occur as early as adolescence and as late as the 60s in rare cases.

Ankylosing spondylitis initially presents with subacute onset of inflammatory low back pain, including pain and stiffness of the low back and/or buttocks at night and in the morning that improve with activity. The synovial facet joints are also involved, and back extension may be painful and an early manifestation of the disease. Over time, the thoracic and cervical spine can become involved.

The disease has three phases: inflammation; fibrosis; and ossification, which can drastically limit range of spinal motion. If untreated, patients can assume a kyphotic stance and may only be able to look down as they walk. Fibrosis and ossification of the spine occur at the vertebral entheses and are visible radiographically as syndesmophytes and ossification of the spinal ligaments, eventually leading to complete spinal fusion (“bamboo spine”). After 2 years, 20% to 45% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis have radiologic progression that is expected to continue. Risk factors for progression include the following:

  • Male sex
  • HLA-B27 positivity
  • Presence of baseline radiographic changes
  • Disease and symptom duration
  • Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) levels
  • High disease activity
  • Smoking status
  • Alcohol consumption

Enthesitis is most commonly appreciated in the feet at the plantar fascia and where the Achilles tendon inserts into the heel (

). Enthesitis of the costovertebral joints can also affect chest wall expansion, leading to pain at night and in the morning that improves with movement.

Peripheral joint involvement may include the hips (

), shoulders, knees, and, less commonly, other joints.

Acute anterior uveitis occurs in up to one third of patients with ankylosing spondylitis. It is episodic, unilateral, and typically self-limited. It uncommonly causes permanent visual damage.

Fibrosis affecting the upper lobes of the lung, visualized by high-resolution CT, is reported in 7% of patients with early disease and 21% of patients after 10 years of disease. Involvement of the thoracic spine, costochondral junctions, and sternomanubrial joint can affect chest expansion, contributing to restrictive lung disease.

Renal amyloidosis is a rare manifestation that occurs in patients with long-standing, poorly controlled disease. AA amyloid deposition can lead to proteinuria and eventually kidney failure and is associated with increased mortality. In patients with poorly controlled disease, AA amyloidosis is the most common cause of kidney disease. IgA nephropathy can also occur, presenting as hematuria and proteinuria.

Cardiac involvement in ankylosing spondylitis includes aortitis of the subaortic valve region (an area of high fibrocartilage content), leading to aortic dilatation and aortic valve regurgitation. Atrioventricular block and myocardial infarction occur more commonly in patients with ankylosing spondylitis than in the general population. The increased myocardial infarction rate is thought to be due to chronic inflammation hastening the development of atherosclerosis.

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), often subclinical, is evident in up to 60% of patients. Ten percent of patients have coexisting psoriasis.

Osteopenia and osteoporosis are more common in patients with ankylosing spondylitis. Vertebral fractures can occur, often after only minor or minimal trauma because of low bone mass and spinal rigidity. CT or MRI should be performed to detect fracture if there is a high level of suspicion because plain radiographs can appear normal. Fractures can occur through the vertebral body or through a disk space that has become fixed because of syndesmophyte formation; either can lead to nerve injury or myelopathy. Another rare neurologic manifestation is cauda equina syndrome, manifested by saddle anesthesia and bowel and bladder incontinence.

Patients with nr-axSpA present with clinical features similar to those of ankylosing spondylitis (r-axSpA), including inflammatory back pain, peripheral inflammatory symptoms, and extra-articular features. Diagnosis is made by suggestive clinical features, HLA-B27 positivity, and/or definitive MRI findings of sacroiliac joint inflammation. Patients with nr-axSpA have a lower prevalence of HLA-B27 than patients with ankylosing spondylitis, and CRP levels may be normal. Between 5% and 30% of disease in these patients progresses to r-axSpA over the span of 2 to 30 years. Risk factors for disease progression include the following:

  • Male sex
  • Tobacco use
  • Elevated CRP level
  • High-grade sacroiliac joint inflammation

PsA is an inflammatory joint disease associated with psoriasis. Psoriasis affects approximately 3% of the U.S. population, and PsA may develop in up to 30% of patients with psoriasis. An estimated 15% of patients with psoriasis who are monitored by dermatologists have unrecognized PsA. Conversely, some patients considered to have psoriatic arthritis because of concurrent psoriasis and joint pain have an unrelated joint condition, most commonly osteoarthritis. Hyperuricemia and gout are comorbidities associated with psoriasis and PsA.

In most cases, PsA develops years after psoriasis, but 15% of patients may develop PsA concurrently with or even before psoriasis. Risk factors for PsA include obesity; metabolic syndrome; severe psoriasis; psoriasis involving the nails, scalp, or genitals; or inverse psoriasis. Psoriatic nail changes are present in more than 80% of patients with PsA.

The genetics of PsA are complex. HLA-B08, -B27, -B38, and -B39 are seen in PsA, and the HLA type can influence clinical expression. HLA-C06 is seen less frequently in patients with PsA than in those with psoriasis alone. In part because of HLA expression, PsA is rare in individuals of Asian and African descent.

Five clinical subtypes of PsA are described:

  • Asymmetric oligoarthritis involving four or fewer, typically large, joints.
  • Polyarticular arthritis affecting multiple joints of the hands, which may be symmetric and resemble rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Distal interphalangeal joint–predominant variety, which may occur with the preceding subtypes or in isolation (

). Notably, distal interphalangeal joint involvement is also common in osteoarthritis and is occasionally seen in gout. - Arthritis mutilans, a more aggressive form of PsA involving the hands. Telescoping of the digits from substantial joint destruction may occur. Arthritis mutilans is probably a progressive form of the preceding three subtypes. - Spondyloarthritis with sacroiliitis and spine involvement. This may occur in isolation or in conjunction with other subtypes. It occurs in up to 50% of patients with PsA, more commonly among patients with HLA-B27. Axial PsA involvement may be distinguished radiographically from ankylosing spondylitis by asymmetry, skip lesions, and bulkier syndesmophytes.

Enthesitis is common in PsA and indicates more severe disease. The severity of nail involvement also correlates with severity of skin and joint disease. Dactylitis of the fingers or toes develops in 40% to 50% of patients with PsA. Enthesitis of the plantar fascia or Achilles tendon occurs in up to 50% of patients.

Eye involvement also develops in PsA. Conjunctivitis is more common than uveitis or iritis. Uveitis occurs in up to 8% of patients with PsA.

Patients with psoriasis and PsA have an increased prevalence of many comorbidities, including atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, metabolic dysfunction–associated liver disease, anxiety, and depression.

Spondyloarthritis, isolated sacroiliitis, and peripheral arthritis can occur in patients with Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, and unspecified IBD. Spondyloarthritis is the most common extra-articular manifestation of IBD. Dactylitis and enthesitis can also occur with enteropathic arthritis.

There are two types of peripheral arthritis in IBD. Type I peripheral arthritis characteristics include the following:

  • Pauciarticular (fewer than five joints) involvement in medium to large joints, especially in the lower extremities
  • Asymmetric disease pattern
  • Parallel with IBD activity

Type II peripheral arthritis characteristics include the following:

  • Polyarticular (five or more joints) involvement in a wide range of joints, sometimes including the upper extremities
  • Symmetric disease pattern
  • Persistence and independence from IBD activity

Both type I and type II peripheral arthritis are nonerosive. The prevalence of peripheral arthritis is highest in younger patients (up to 25%) and much lower in patients older than 50 years (2%). Male and female patients are equally affected. Up to 30% to 40% of patients may first present with arthritis before gastrointestinal manifestations are apparent.

The risk for IBD in patients with established spondyloarthritis is as high as 14% and is highest in patients with ankylosing spondylitis. As noted previously, 60% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis have evidence of asymptomatic bowel inflammation, and most patients with ankylosing spondylitis who develop IBD are in this group. Patients with ankylosing spondylitis should be asked about bowel symptoms on follow-up visits. Elevated serum and fecal calprotectin levels can be used to identify patients with ankylosing spondylitis who have more active bowel inflammation and may help predict IBD development.

Other clinical manifestations of enteropathic arthritis are outlined in [Table: Table: Clinical Features of Spondyloarthritis]

.

Reactive arthritis is a rare spondyloarthritis that occurs after specific bacterial infections. The most common organism responsible for reactive arthritis is Chlamydia trachomatis; 4% to 8% of infected patients develop reactive arthritis. Gastrointestinal pathogens include several species of Salmonella and Shigella, Campylobacter jejuni, and Yersinia species; reactive arthritis occurs in approximately 1% of infected individuals. Respiratory pathogens, including Chlamydia pneumoniae and Mycoplasma pneumoniae, are also known causes of reactive arthritis. Clostridioides difficile is an uncommon, but important, cause of reactive arthritis given its frequency in hospitalized patients. Approximately 1.4% of patients with C. difficile colitis will develop reactive arthritis. An inciting organism is identified in only about 50% of patients. Women develop reactive arthritis more commonly than men (relative risk, 1.5). HLA-B27 is found in 50% to 80% of patients with reactive arthritis; the highest frequency (90%) is seen in those who develop reactive arthritis from Yersinia infection.

Reactive arthritis develops 2 to 3 weeks after genitourinary and gastrointestinal infections. Synovial fluid leukocyte counts can be elevated, often around 50,000/μL (50 × 10^9/L) with a predominance of neutrophils. Synovial fluid in reactive arthritis can also demonstrate rice bodies; these small pieces of hypertrophic synovial tissue are sloughed and accumulate in the joint and may require a large-bore needle to aspirate.

Reactive arthritis is typically pauciarticular and involves larger joints. Enthesitis of the Achilles tendon or plantar fascia is common; enthesitis may also occur in the knee, a joint with multiple entheses. Dactylitis of fingers and toes is also common in reactive arthritis. Sacroiliac joint and spine inflammation and pain are less common than peripheral manifestations.

Mucocutaneous manifestations include genitourinary disease (such as urethritis, cervicitis, cystitis, or prostatitis). Patients can have painless oral ulcers, typically affecting the hard palate. Conjunctivitis is the most common eye finding, but anterior uveitis and even keratitis can occur. Keratoderma blennorrhagicum, a psoriasiform skin rash, occurs on the palms and soles but occasionally can become generalized (

). The lesions begin as discrete plaques and then enlarge and coalesce. Circinate balanitis is a similar psoriasiform lesion on the glans penis in men. Erythema nodosum is rare.

Important differential diagnostic considerations include infectious arthritis, disseminated gonococcal infection, Whipple disease, IBD, and Behçet syndrome.

The typical course of a reactive arthritis flare is 6 weeks to 6 months. Manifestations can last 1 year. Episodes may recur in some patients; approximately 25% of patients will have chronic persistent disease.

Diagnosing spondyloarthritis subtypes can be challenging given the absence of specific diagnostic laboratory tests and because some imaging findings (such as sacroiliac changes on MRI) can be seen even in healthy patients. A spondyloarthritis diagnosis is based on the combination of clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings.

Except for those who have incidental overlap with other conditions, patients with spondyloarthritis are negative for rheumatoid factor, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide, and antinuclear antibodies. Serologic testing should be performed only if an alternative diagnosis is being considered.

HLA-B27 antigen testing is never diagnostic but can help determine risk for spondyloarthritis in uncertain situations. For patients with inflammatory low back pain but normal or nondiagnostic plain radiographs of the spine and sacroiliac joints, a positive result on a test for HLA-B27 antigen can be useful for deciding whether to pursue advanced imaging. Conversely, a patient with inflammatory low back pain, uveitis, and radiographic evidence of bilateral sacroiliitis does not need HLA-B27 antigen testing because the diagnosis is clear. Risk for spondyloarthritis in offspring is about 20% if the child inherits the gene and markedly less if results of HLA-B27 antigen testing are negative.

Patients with spondyloarthritis may have anemia of inflammation as a result of chronic inflammation. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and CRP can help support an inflammatory process and can be monitored during therapy. However, these values are not always elevated, particularly in ankylosing spondylitis. All patients with chronic spondyloarthritis should be monitored for standard cardiovascular disease risk factors.

Radiography of the sacroiliac joints is an initial test for patients suspected of having ankylosing spondylitis. Anteroposterior radiography of the pelvis or a Ferguson view of the pelvis (in which the x-ray beam is directed 20 degrees cephalad to show all sacroiliac joints in one plane) can depict the changes of sacroiliitis (

). The radiologic changes are initially more intense on the iliac side of the joint, with sclerosis and erosions (

). Erosive changes lead to a pseudo-widening appearance of the sacroiliac joints; in advanced cases, ankylosis of the sacroiliac joints can occur. Involvement of sacroiliac joints is symmetric and bilateral in ankylosing spondylitis and enteropathic arthritis. However, sacroiliac joint involvement is more asymmetric and unilateral in PsA and reactive arthritis.

Radiographs of the spine in ankylosing spondylitis can show the following:

  • Squaring of the vertebrae anteriorly (due to erosion at the insertion of entheses)
  • Sclerosis at the anterior edges of the vertebrae (“shiny corner” sign [

]) - Syndesmophytes (delicate bony bridging between vertebrae that can result in a “bamboo” appearance of the spine in advanced ankylosing spondylitis [

]) - Sclerosis at the facet joints - Ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament (in more advanced cases)

Patients with PsA or reactive arthritis with spondylitis can also have syndesmophytes; these tend to be bulkier and more asymmetrically placed than syndesmophytes in ankylosing spondylitis. Whiskering (the result of new bone formation at the insertion of the hamstrings into the pelvis) is also seen on radiography in patients with spondyloarthritis. Bony proliferation can occur in other entheses, such as the Achilles tendon or plantar fascia insertion into the heel.

Low-dose CT and MRI of the sacroiliac joints can be done if necessary. Low-dose CT is more specific and is useful to clarify ambiguous changes seen on plain radiographs, whereas MRI is more sensitive and can identify sacroiliac inflammation, such as bone marrow edema, even in the absence of radiographic changes. However, 25% of healthy individuals can have MRI changes that meet ASAS criteria for sacroiliitis, and up to 41% of persons who regularly participate in impact-loading athletics may have similar MRI changes. The extent of involvement and presence of erosions on MRI increase the specificity of the result. The presence of MRI changes also aids in the diagnosis of nr-axSpA.

Peripheral joint changes in spondyloarthritis include erosions and new bone formation. In PsA in particular, radiographic findings classically take the form of erosions of the distal head of the proximal joint and juxta-articular new bone formation at the proximal head of the distal joint, leading to a “pencil-in-cup” appearance across the joint (

).

Spondyloarthritis treatment goals include control of inflammation as well as prevention of radiologic progression. Early institution of therapy with close monitoring to target disease remission is vital, particularly in high-risk individuals whose disease is likely to progress. Patient education, exercises to maintain range of motion and control weight, and modification of diet and lifestyle habits (e.g., smoking cessation) to prevent cardiovascular disease are important components of care.

See

for details on therapy.

NSAIDs are recommended as initial therapy for most patients with ankylosing spondylitis because they relieve pain and improve stiffness. There is ongoing debate regarding whether NSAIDs are effective in inhibiting new bone formation. The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) conditionally recommends continuous NSAID use (rather than on-demand use) for patients with active disease, whereas the more recent ASAS-European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) guidelines recommend continuous NSAIDs only if needed to control symptoms. A dose of a longer-acting NSAID taken in the evening can improve comfort throughout the night and into the morning. Per the ASAS-EULAR recommendation, at least two NSAIDs at maximum dose should be tried for 4 weeks before NSAID therapy is considered a failure.

For patients with severe peripheral-predominant arthritis, sulfasalazine is recommended over methotrexate. However, these agents have little or no effect on axial disease.

According to the 2022 ASAS-EULAR recommendations, tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors, IL-17 inhibitors, or Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors should be considered in patients with persistently high disease activity despite conventional treatments, such as NSAIDs. TNF inhibitors and IL-17 inhibitors are preferred over JAK inhibitors given long-term experience and the cardiovascular risk associated with JAK inhibitors. An elevated CRP level and the presence of inflammation on MRI of sacroiliac joints are the best predictors of response to treatment with TNF inhibitors. Numerous randomized controlled trials have shown improvements in clinical, radiographic, and MRI outcomes in patients with active ankylosing spondylitis receiving TNF inhibitors. IL-17 inhibitors and JAK inhibitors are associated with improved clinical and MRI outcomes. Long-term data on radiologic outcomes on IL-17 and JAK inhibitors are lacking. Routine serial spine radiography for monitoring is not recommended.

Uveitis is generally treated with topical glucocorticoids. For severe or frequent recurrences, TNF inhibitors (e.g., adalimumab or infliximab) are preferred. Similarly, TNF inhibitors are recommended for treating patients with ankylosing spondylitis and coexisting IBD.

Physical therapy to maintain general range of motion is essential. Patients with damage to hip or shoulder joints may require total joint arthroplasty, which may dramatically improve function and quality of life.

Treatment for nr-axSpA is similar to that for ankylosing spondylitis. A TNF inhibitor, certolizumab pegol; IL-17 inhibitors; and the JAK inhibitor upadacitinib have been approved for nr-axSpA. Conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) have no role in treating nr-axSpA.

Overall, treatment of PsA should consider the category of musculoskeletal manifestations (e.g., peripheral arthritis, enthesitis, axial arthritis) as well as accompanying nonmusculoskeletal manifestations (e.g., skin disease, uveitis, IBD) because available agents are not equally effective in different domains. The general principle is to use an agent to cover as many active domains as possible.

For limited disease, such as a single digit with dactylitis or mono- or oligoarthritis, an oral or topical NSAID or a local injection of glucocorticoids may suffice. High-dose oral glucocorticoids should be avoided because eventual tapering of the dosage increases the risk for erythrodermic psoriasis.

For more active disease, stepwise initiation of pharmacotherapy is recommended (see

). For peripheral arthritis, conventional synthetic DMARDs (preferably methotrexate, especially in patients with significant skin involvement) can be used. Sulfasalazine and leflunomide are also options for peripheral arthritis but are not as effective for treating skin conditions. Notably, initiation of a biologic agent without a trial of a conventional synthetic DMARD may also be appropriate in some patients, such as those with concomitant inflammatory bowel disease or uveitis. In patients who do not respond to a conventional synthetic DMARD, a biologic DMARD can be trialed. Among biologic agents, IL-23 inhibitors and IL-17 inhibitors have better efficacy for skin conditions than TNF inhibitors but are equally efficacious for treating peripheral PsA. TNF inhibitors, IL-17 inhibitors, and JAK inhibitors are preferred in patients with axial involvement. Combination DMARD therapy does not have the same effect in PsA as in rheumatoid arthritis. Surgery may be indicated for severe damage to larger joints.

Enteropathic arthritis is best addressed by managing bowel inflammation; treatment decisions should occur in conjunction with a gastroenterologist. For spondyloarthritis associated with bowel involvement, medications to address both peripheral arthritis and bowel inflammation include sulfasalazine, azathioprine, methotrexate, and glucocorticoids. TNF inhibitors (such as adalimumab and infliximab) are especially useful for bowel and joint symptoms, including spine disease. Although etanercept is reported to be effective for arthritis and spinal involvement in patients with IBD, it is not effective in treating IBD. IL-17 inhibitors may cause IBD to flare and are not preferred agents in these patients. NSAIDs should be avoided if possible because of the potential for IBD flare. An IL-12/23 inhibitor (ustekinumab), IL-23 inhibitor (e.g., risankizumab), and JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib and upadacitinib) are therapeutic options in patients who have not responded to TNF inhibitors. These agents are also approved for treating IBD.

Patients with acute C. trachomatis genitourinary tract infection should receive appropriate antibiotic therapy (see Chlamydia trachomatis Infection in Infectious Disease). Because of a lack of benefit, antibiotic treatment of reactive arthritis due to enteric organisms is not usually warranted unless there is ongoing infection or the patient is a potential carrier.

For mild arthritic disease, NSAIDs or joint injections with glucocorticoids or a short course of systemic glucocorticoids may be sufficient until the disease self-resolves. For more persistent or severe disease, sulfasalazine (preferred) or methotrexate may be required. There are few data from controlled studies for either agent, but case series and reports suggest efficacy. TNF inhibitors may also be needed if these agents fail, but again data are scant. Given the monophasic nature of reactive arthritis in many patients, a trial off therapy is warranted 3 to 6 months after remission.

Topical glucocorticoids can be used to help address skin manifestations, and topical ocular glucocorticoids are useful for uveitis.
