Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a multisystem autoimmune disease characterized by a heterogeneous constellation of organ involvement and the presence of antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and other autoantibodies. These include anti–double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith antibodies, which are specific for SLE.

Approximately 90% of adult patients with SLE are female, but disease activity is frequently more severe in males. Incidence increases at puberty and peaks in the third decade. The risk for SLE is higher in patients with a family history of SLE; however, genetics account for only 24% of this risk, which suggests environmental exposures are strongly associated with SLE development.

In SLE, a complex and varying interaction of genes, environment, and random events leads to a breakdown of self-tolerance and autoimmunity. Defects in cellular apoptosis result in inadequate clearance of intracellular proteins, especially nuclear antigens, promoting the generation of self-directed T and B cells and the initiation/propagation of autoimmunity. Cytokine generation supports autoreactivity, with type 1 interferons playing a major role. Autoantibodies may directly induce tissue damage or promote the formation of immune complexes that lead to complement activation and tissue inflammation.

SLE flares may be associated with infections (e.g., influenza), pregnancy, sunlight exposure in patients who are photosensitive, and nonadherence to immunosuppressant therapy.

Skin disease occurs in most patients with SLE and is classified as acute, subacute, or chronic.

Acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (ACLE) can be localized or generalized. ACLE is a photosensitive, nonscarring, erythematous, macular, patchy eruption, sometimes with desquamation. The facial eruption of ACLE (the classic malar or butterfly rash) is characterized by erythema and edema over the cheeks and bridge of the nose, sparing the nasolabial folds (

); the neck, upper chest, and dorsum of the arms and hands can also be involved in generalized ACLE.

Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) is a photosensitive rash occurring especially on the arms, neck, and upper trunk, usually sparing the central face (

). It consists of erythematous annular/polycyclic or patchy papulosquamous lesions, often with a fine scale, that may leave postinflammatory hypo- or hyperpigmentation. SCLE is associated with anti-Ro/SSA autoantibodies (prevalence >75%) and can occur in isolation as a result of drug-induced SCLE or as a manifestation of underlying SLE. Features that may favor a diagnosis of drug-induced SCLE are widespread disease, including lesions outside of photo-exposed areas, bullous or erythema multiforme–like lesions, and vasculitic-appearing lesions.

Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) is the most common manifestation of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus and can cause scarring, atrophy, and permanent alopecia (

and

). DLE can also be localized or generalized. DLE presents as hypo- or hyperpigmented patches or plaques, with erythema during active disease, which may be variably atrophic or hyperkeratotic in more chronic lesions. DLE more commonly occurs in isolation, with 5% to 25% of patients with DLE having coexisting SLE. Generalized DLE is more likely to progress to SLE. Other, less common manifestations of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus include tumid lupus erythematosus and lupus panniculitis (see [Table: Table: Dermatologic Manifestations of Rheumatologic Disease]

).

Painless oral or nasopharyngeal ulcerations occur in 5% of patients. Hard palate involvement is characteristic. Nonscarring alopecia is a common feature of active SLE and occurs in 50% of patients. Hair regrowth is a sign of disease control.

Raynaud phenomenon is seen in 20% to 40% of patients with SLE. Patients with SLE may also demonstrate nailfold capillary changes. Livedo reticularis, when present, may suggest the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies. Some patients with SLE may develop cutaneous vasculitis in the distal extremities.

Joints are affected in up to 90% of patients with SLE. Joint involvement may manifest as nonerosive small-joint polyarthralgia or arthritis; Jaccoud arthropathy (nonerosive polyarthritis that leads to reducible deformities); or rhupus, in which patients have both SLE and rheumatoid arthritis. Osteonecrosis is a serious complication of SLE that most commonly affects the hips but can also involve other large joints. See [Table: Table: Musculoskeletal Manifestations of SLE]

for additional details regarding these joint manifestations.

Myositis and myopathy occur rarely, resulting from active SLE or medications, such as glucocorticoids and hydroxychloroquine.

Fibromyalgia is a common comorbidity in SLE.

Kidney disease occurs frequently among patients with SLE and remains an important source of morbidity. Up to 20% of patients with lupus nephritis progress to end-stage kidney disease. Lupus nephritis occurs in patients manifesting anti–double-stranded DNA or anti-Smith antibodies and can present with the following:

  • Minimal laboratory abnormalities (nonnephrotic proteinuria, hematuria)
  • Nephritis (hypertension, edema, active urine sediment, and elevated serum creatinine level)
  • Nephrosis (nephrotic-range proteinuria, edema, hypoalbuminemia, hypercholesterolemia, and, in some cases, thrombosis)

All patients with SLE should be regularly evaluated for kidney involvement through assessment of serum creatinine, urinary protein, and microscopic evaluation of urine. Active kidney disease should be suspected when there is active urine sediment or proteinuria greater than 500 mg/24 h (or a spot urine protein-to-creatine ratio >500 mg/g). Elevated or rising anti–double-stranded DNA antibody titers or decreased C3 and C4 complement levels are biomarkers associated with active kidney disease. Kidney biopsy should be performed in most patients with evidence of kidney involvement (e.g., abnormal proteinuria, active urinary sediment, and/or elevated creatinine level) to define the type and extent of disease.

See Lupus Nephritis in Nephrology for information on the classes and management of lupus nephritis.

Neuropsychiatric SLE (NPSLE) may involve the central and/or peripheral nervous systems. NPSLE prevalence is high (75%), and the most commonly reported manifestations (headache, mild cognitive dysfunction, mood disorder) are also common in the general population. More serious manifestations of NPSLE include seizures, psychosis, movement disorders, aseptic meningitis, autonomic disorders, myasthenia gravis, and various forms of peripheral neuropathy.

Patients suspected of having serious central NPSLE should undergo central nervous system imaging (CT, MRI, or PET) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis as appropriate. In some patients with severe disease, CSF analysis and serology for NPSLE-associated autoantibodies (antineuronal, anti–N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor, anti–ribosomal P, and others) may be useful. Neuropsychologic testing may help define and distinguish cognitive changes in certain patients. For patients suspected of having peripheral neuropathies, electrophysiology studies should be performed.

Asymptomatic pericarditis is the most frequent cardiac manifestation of acute SLE (40%). Symptomatic pericarditis is less common; features include chest pain, exudative effusion, and, rarely, tamponade or chronic constriction. Myocarditis occurs in 5% to 10% of patients with SLE and presents as acute to subacute heart failure. Cardiac MRI is more sensitive and specific than echocardiography for diagnosing myocarditis, but gadolinium use may have restrictions in a patient with SLE and kidney disease.

Valvular abnormalities occurring in SLE include those associated with antiphospholipid syndrome (nonspecific thickening of the mitral and aortic valve leaflets, vegetations, regurgitation, and stenosis). Libman-Sacks endocarditis (noninfectious verrucous vegetations) preferentially affects the mitral valve and can cause embolic complications. Patients with SLE also have an increased risk for accelerated atherosclerosis leading to coronary heart disease and should undergo appropriate testing and management if presenting with cardiac symptoms.

Pleural disease is the most common pulmonary manifestation of SLE, occurring in 45% to 60% of patients with SLE. Parenchymal lung involvement occurs in less than 10% of patients, whereas pulmonary artery hypertension is rare (occurring in approximately 5% of patients). Two rare but serious manifestations include acute lupus pneumonitis and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. Early recognition, rapid evaluation (CT and/or bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage or biopsy), and aggressive respiratory support combined with high-dose glucocorticoids and immunosuppression are required.

Shrinking lung syndrome is a rare condition most commonly seen in SLE and occasionally in other autoimmune diseases, such as Sjögren disease. It is characterized by dyspnea, episodes of pleuritic chest pain, a progressive decrease in lung volumes, and no evidence of interstitial lung disease or significant pleural disease on chest CT.

See [Table: Table: Pulmonary Manifestations of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus]

for more details.

In patients with SLE, normocytic, normochromic anemia of inflammation is common; autoimmune hemolytic anemia occurs in approximately 10% of cases and correlates with SLE activity. Lymphopenia and leukopenia are also common but usually mild. Thrombocytopenia occurs in 30% to 50% of cases, and approximately 10% of patients develop severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count <50,000/μL [50 × 10^9/L]) in isolation or in conjunction with hemolytic anemia. SLE-associated cytopenias are secondary to active disease, organ dysfunction, or medications, and it is usually difficult to determine the underlying cause.

Antiphospholipid antibodies and lupus anticoagulant are present in approximately 40% of patients with SLE, and thrombotic events occur in approximately 30% to 40% of patients. These events include venous and arterial thrombosis, miscarriage, stillbirth, livedo reticularis, and cardiac valve thickening/vegetations. The risk for thrombosis is highest in the presence of triple positivity for lupus anticoagulant, anti–β~2-glycoprotein, and anticardiolipin antibodies. Patients with SLE are at increased risk for thrombotic events even in the absence of antiphospholipid antibodies. See Antiphospholipid Antibody Syndrome in Hematology for more information.

Gastrointestinal involvement is a common (40%) and underrecognized SLE manifestation. Esophageal reflux and dysmotility occur in 10% to 50% of patients and are more common in those with Raynaud phenomenon. Peritoneal serositis presents as abdominal pain and improves with immunosuppression. Mesenteric vasculitis, inflammation of the small and large bowel, pancreatitis, and protein-losing enteropathy are uncommon but may be severe.

Elevated liver function test results are seen in 25% to 50% of patients and are not usually associated with symptoms. Frank SLE hepatitis is observed in 9% of patients and is associated with the presence of anti–ribosomal P antibodies. SLE hepatitis generally responds to glucocorticoids and rarely progresses to end-stage liver disease.

Medications used to treat SLE (NSAIDs, prednisone, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine) also frequently affect the gastrointestinal system and may cause esophagitis, gastritis, pancreatitis, and hepatitis.

Patients with SLE are at increased risk for infection, particularly pneumonia, tuberculosis, and herpes zoster. Infection should always be considered in a patient with SLE who has an atypical presentation or whose condition worsens despite appropriate immunosuppression. Pulmonary infiltrates are typically treated as infection and active SLE until the diagnosis is clear.

Risk for malignancies is also higher among patients with SLE than in the general population:

  • Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma: 3 times higher
  • Myeloma and liver cancer: 2 times higher
  • Cervical, lung, bladder, and thyroid cancer: 1.5 times higher

Malignancy risk in SLE results from chronic immune stimulation, genetics, and environmental factors. The latter includes such medications as cyclophosphamide (bladder cancer) and azathioprine (myeloproliferative disease).

Patients with SLE have a 2- to 10-fold increased prevalence of coronary artery disease. It is the most common cause of death among patients with long-standing SLE. A history of high SLE disease activity (especially nephritis) and prednisone dosages greater than 10 mg/d are independent risk factors for coronary artery disease.

The diagnosis of SLE should be considered in patients, especially young women, with any objective manifestations typical of SLE.

The 2019 SLE classification criteria from the European League Against Rheumatism (now called the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology)/American College of Rheumatology were developed to recruit homogeneous populations for research studies and may help the clinician document disease manifestations and help suggest a clinical diagnosis of SLE. The 2019 criteria include the requirement for a positive ANA result greater than or equal to 1:80 at least once, with the addition of clinical and/or immunologic criteria totaling at least 10 points on a weighted scale ( [Table: Table: EULAR/ACR Classification Criteria for SLE]

). These criteria compare favorably to previous published criteria, with a sensitivity of about 96% and specificity of about 93%.

Initial evaluation for SLE includes routine laboratory testing to establish organ-specific involvement, including complete blood count, chemistry panel, and urinalysis with microscopy.

ANA should be obtained to screen for nuclear-directed autoantibodies. The most appropriate method for testing ANA is the indirect immunofluorescence assay, which is highly sensitive (>95%) for SLE but not specific. ANA test results should be interpreted in the context of the probability of disease because ANA may be present in patients with other autoimmune diseases as well as in healthy individuals. Low-titer ANA (<1:80) is considered a negative result; even ANA at an elevated titer in the absence of specific features of SLE may be noninformative.

If the ANA result is positive and the clinical context supportive, antibodies to extractable nuclear antigens, including anti–double-stranded DNA, anti-Smith, anti–U1-ribonucleoprotein, anti-Ro/SSA, and anti-La/SSB, as well as tests for other autoimmune diseases under consideration, should be obtained to further characterize the disease ( [Table: Table: Common Autoantibodies in SLE]

).

Disease activity markers, including C3 and C4 complement, should be assessed initially and regularly thereafter. Complement levels are typically reduced during SLE activity, reflecting immune complex formation and complement consumption. Rising titers of anti–double-stranded DNA antibody levels may be concordant with SLE disease activity. Other SLE autoantibodies, including ANA, do not reflect disease activity and do not need to be repeated. Serial measurements of erythrocyte sedimentation rate can be used to monitor disease status. C-reactive protein levels are normal or minimally elevated during SLE flares, except in the setting of serositis or infection.

The differential diagnosis of SLE includes the following:

  • Multisystem autoimmune diseases
  • Acute and chronic infections
  • Medication effect
  • Malignancies (particularly hematologic)
  • Neurologic diseases (e.g., multiple sclerosis)

Patients with a positive ANA titer and objective SLE manifestations that do not meet the criteria for SLE are considered to have undifferentiated SLE, connective tissue disease, or incomplete SLE. With time, more manifestations may develop, thereby permitting classification as SLE.

Certain medications can cause drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DILE) (see [Table: Table: Medications Commonly Associated With DILE]

). The syndrome is usually milder; malaise, fever, arthritis, and rash are associated with transient positivity for ANA and antihistone antibodies. Kidney and central nervous system disease can occur but are uncommon. Symptoms usually resolve after discontinuation of the offending agent. Patients with SLE are at no more risk for DILE than the general population, and medications associated with DILE are not contraindicated in patients with SLE.

SLE most often follows a relapsing-remitting pattern (70% of cases) with periods of inactive disease, although some patients may have a monophasic or persistently active pattern. The most commonly used instrument for monitoring disease activity is the SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI), which incorporates both clinical and laboratory measures but is typically used in research studies. Most patients have a profile of clinical manifestations and laboratory abnormalities that can help determine disease activity. Typical goals of therapy are clinical remission or low disease activity.

Pharmacologic therapy is almost always required; the choice of agents should reflect disease activity and specific organ involvement ( [Table: Table: Medications Commonly Used to Treat SLE]

). Management requires frequent disease assessment and adjustment of treatment to reflect changing conditions.

Hydroxychloroquine is a mainstay of treatment in SLE because it reduces disease-associated damage, prevents disease flares, and improves kidney and overall survival. In addition, hydroxychloroquine may reduce the risk for thrombosis, liver disease, and myocardial infarction; improve lipid profiles; and improve outcomes in high-risk pregnancies. Almost all patients with SLE without contraindications should receive hydroxychloroquine, 5 mg/kg/d or less. Patients should undergo a baseline eye examination and then annual monitoring by an ophthalmologist after 5 years of treatment to reduce the risk for retinal toxicity. Hydroxychloroquine can be used alone for mild disease (especially skin and joints) and in combination with other agents in severe disease.

Glucocorticoids are also used in most patients with SLE, particularly in acute disease. The glucocorticoid dose should be determined by disease activity and organ systems threatened. For severe disease activity (profound cytopenia, class III/IV nephritis, and NPSLE), high-dose glucocorticoids are recommended. For life- or organ-threatening disease (such as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis or seizures), high-dose intravenous glucocorticoids are given, typically followed by daily oral glucocorticoids. After disease stabilizes, glucocorticoids should be tapered to the lowest effective dosage, preferably to no more than 7.5 mg/d within 4 to 6 months. Glucocorticoids should be discontinued entirely if possible.

For moderate or severe disease, immunosuppressive therapy should be initiated concurrently with glucocorticoids to achieve and maintain disease control and to allow tapering of glucocorticoids. The choice of medication should be determined by the organs involved and disease severity. Intravenous cyclophosphamide is used as induction therapy for severe or refractory disease (e.g., acute central nervous system lupus, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, or myocarditis), followed by maintenance therapy with mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine. See Treatment and Prognosis of Lupus Nephritis in Nephrology for details on therapy for lupus nephritis.

The biologic agent belimumab is FDA approved for patients with incomplete response to conventional treatments and is useful for skin and/or joint involvement and moderate or severe disease. Anifrolumab, a monoclonal antibody against the type 1 interferon receptor, has been FDA approved for the treatment of patients with moderate to severe SLE but without severe lupus nephritis or NPSLE. Anifrolumab appears to be of particular benefit in patients with skin and joint involvement, but this is still being defined.

Less commonly used medications include quinacrine, methotrexate, leflunomide, calcineurin inhibitors, and rituximab. NSAIDs can be prescribed to treat arthritis and pleuropericarditis. Statins and antihypertensive agents are often used to reduce cardiovascular risks. Renin-angiotensin system inhibitors should be considered in patients with proteinuria. Adequate vitamin D intake is important in patients with SLE. Bone health should be monitored, with treatment for appropriate patients, especially those receiving glucocorticoids. Sun avoidance and regular use of sunscreen that blocks both ultraviolet-A and -B should be recommended for all patients with SLE.

See Principles of Therapeutics in Rheumatology for information on SLE medication toxicities, monitoring parameters, and more.

SLE activity and medications can affect menstrual regularity and thus may affect conception and fertility. The preferred method for contraception is an intrauterine device or a progesterone-only contraceptive. Cyclophosphamide may cause premature menopause, especially when administered to women older than 30 years.

Pregnancy can be considered when SLE is quiescent, and conception should be planned after at least 6 months of adequate disease control. This will also allow for medication modification if needed.

Pregnant patients with SLE have a five- to eightfold increased risk for miscarriage, stillbirth, premature delivery, and intrauterine growth retardation. Outcomes are worse in patients with active disease, nephritis, or anti-Ro/SSA or antiphospholipid antibodies.

Proteinuria may increase during pregnancy in patients with SLE, making the distinction between SLE and preeclampsia a challenge. Increased anti–double-stranded DNA antibody titers, decreasing complement levels, or the development of active urine sediment suggests SLE as the cause. In contrast, serum urate levels are increased in preeclampsia but not during SLE flares.

Fetuses of women who have anti-Ro/SSA or anti-La/SSB antibodies are at risk for neonatal lupus erythematosus, which is characterized by rash and/or congenital heart block. The risk for congenital heart block in the offspring of an anti-Ro/SSA–positive woman is only 2%, but the risk increases to 20% with subsequent pregnancies if a child is born with heart block. Hydroxychloroquine may reduce the overall risk. Women with SLE who have concurrent antiphospholipid syndrome may require low-molecular-weight heparin or low-dose aspirin to achieve a successful pregnancy.

Management of SLE medications during pregnancy is complicated. Hydroxychloroquine and low-dose glucocorticoids can be started during or continued throughout the pregnancy. Higher-dose glucocorticoids can be used to treat flares or end-organ involvement. The preferred immunosuppressive agent for SLE during pregnancy is azathioprine, but tacrolimus can also be used. Cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, and mycophenolate mofetil should be avoided because of risks for teratogenicity. See Medications and Pregnancy in Rheumatology for additional information.

The prognosis in SLE has improved significantly. The 5-year survival rate is 90%, although mortality remains high compared with that in age-matched controls. Early mortality is usually related to SLE disease and infections, and late mortality is related to cardiovascular disease. Factors adversely affecting survival include myocarditis, nephritis, low socioeconomic status, male sex, and age older than 50 years at diagnosis.

Sjögren Disease

Sjögren disease is a systemic autoimmune disorder primarily affecting salivary and lacrimal glands. Females are predominantly affected, with a female-to-male ratio between 6 and 9 to 1. Sjögren disease commonly presents in the fifth and sixth decades of life, but patients of any age may be affected. Primary Sjögren disease occurs in isolation; secondary Sjögren disease develops with other autoimmune diseases, most commonly rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus. Whereas the primary form is uncommon (ranging from 0.5 to 5 patients/1000), secondary Sjögren disease is often observed (10% to 30%) among populations with existing rheumatologic conditions.

Sjögren disease is thought to result from activation of mucosal epithelial cells by unknown stimuli. This leads to activation of both the innate and adaptive immune systems, including extensive influx of lymphocytes into exocrine glands, autoreactive B-cell stimulation, and autoantibody production. The resulting chronic inflammation and damage impair the ability of lacrimal and salivary glands to produce or deliver secretions. Although the role of viruses has been suggested in the pathogenesis of Sjögren disease, no single virus has been implicated.

The most common presentation of Sjögren disease is sicca, consisting of ocular and oral dryness. Patients report gritty eyes or a foreign body sensation. Oral dryness can cause difficulty eating unmoistened food and increases the risk for dental caries. Symmetric parotid and lacrimal swelling can occur. Other exocrine glands can be involved, leading to skin and vaginal dryness. Exocrine gland involvement in the upper respiratory tract may lead to symptoms related to the nose, sinuses, and posterior pharynx.

Extraglandular manifestations may occur in some patients ( [Table: Table: Extraglandular Clinical Manifestations of Sjögren Disease]

). Common extraglandular manifestations include arthralgia, fibromyalgia, fatigue, and Raynaud phenomenon. Both peripheral and central nervous systems may be involved, although the former is more common. The typical peripheral nervous system manifestation is axonal polyneuropathy. Cutaneous manifestations include xerosis and palpable purpura. Pulmonary manifestations include cystic lung disease and different types of interstitial lung diseases (nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis, usual interstitial pneumonia, lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia, and cryptogenic organizing pneumonia). Patients with primary Sjögren disease should be clinically screened for cough and dyspnea; if these are present, further evaluation with high-resolution CT and pulmonary function testing is indicated.

Patients with Sjögren disease are at increased risk for non-Hodgkin lymphoma compared with the general population. Estimates suggest as much as a 44-fold increased risk for mucosal-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma; this increase presumably results from an elevated risk for lymphomatous transformation due to chronic activation of tissue lymphocytes. Features conferring a higher risk for lymphoma include the following:

  • Lymphadenopathy
  • Persistent gland swelling
  • Cutaneous vasculitis
  • Glomerulonephritis
  • Low serum C3 and C4 complement levels
  • Mixed cryoglobulinemia
  • Rheumatoid factor positivity
  • High focus score (number of mononuclear cell infiltrates containing >50 inflammatory cells per 4-mm^2 glandular section) on labial salivary gland biopsy specimens

About 5% of patients with Sjögren disease develop lymphoma over time, usually within the first decade after diagnosis.

An evaluation for Sjögren disease is typically performed in the setting of persistent ocular or oral dryness, an increase in dental caries, or parotid swelling. The diagnosis requires objective confirmation of exocrinopathy along with demonstration of autoimmunity ( [Table: Table: Classification Criteria for Primary Sjögren Disease]

). Ophthalmic dryness can be assessed with the Schirmer test, in which a strip of filter paper is placed under the lower eyelid and wetting is measured; less than 5 mm of wetting in 5 minutes indicates dryness. More formally, dryness and corneal damage are ascertained with slit-lamp examination by an ophthalmologist. Topical staining may be used to identify injury and fissures in the cornea. Dry mouth is assessed by direct examination, with dental caries and a lack of saliva suggesting the diagnosis. Sialometry objectively measures the rate of saliva production. However, this is rarely done because it requires special equipment that is not available in most settings. Other forms of imaging (e.g., CT, MRI, or ultrasonography) may be useful in defining structural abnormalities in the appropriate clinical setting.

Multiple autoantibodies may be found in patients with Sjögren disease. Antinuclear antibodies and/or rheumatoid factor are often present. The presence of anti-Ro/SSA autoantibodies is specific in primary Sjögren disease but less so in secondary Sjögren disease because these antibodies are also common in systemic lupus erythematosus. Anti-La/SSB autoantibodies can be seen in Sjögren disease; however, they are not included in formal classification criteria and are not sufficient for diagnosis when present in isolation.

When initial evaluation is uninformative, a lip (minor salivary gland) biopsy is recommended. Characteristic histologic features include a focal periductal aggregate of lymphocytes (defined using the focus score as described above), collectively termed focal lymphocytic sialadenitis.

The differential diagnosis of Sjögren disease typically relates to the presence of sicca and/or parotid and lacrimal enlargement. Sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, lymphoma, amyloidosis, and infection (e.g., mumps, hepatitis C virus infection, HIV infection) may be associated with similar findings. Salivary gland biopsy is relevant to exclude these conditions in patients with glandular enlargement. Ocular and oral dryness may also occur with aging or as an adverse effect of medications or treatment (such as antidepressants and antihistamines or radiation of the head and neck). Unilateral or single enlargement of a gland should raise concern for obstruction or malignancy.

Management of sicca centers on preserving moisture and relieving symptoms. Medications that may worsen symptoms of dryness include antidepressants, antihistamines, anticholinergics, diuretics, and neuroleptics. Alternative agents should be used whenever possible. Eye dryness is treated with over-the-counter artificial tears, gels, and ointments; for refractory or more severe symptoms, topical cyclosporine or a small-molecule integrin antagonist may be added. Plugging the lacrimal ducts to promote tear retention is performed in severe cases. For oral dryness, first-line treatment should be nonpharmacologic salivary stimulation, both with gustatory stimulants (e.g., sugar-free candy) and mechanical stimulants (e.g., sugar-free gum), along with preventive dental care and smoking cessation, if applicable. Meticulous dental care is essential to prevent gingivitis and dental decay, regardless of symptom severity. Artificial saliva may be used, but its effects are transient. Pharmacologic therapies should be reserved for moderate or severe oral dryness. These include the muscarinic agonists pilocarpine and cevimeline, which are contraindicated in narrow-angle glaucoma. Vaginal dryness may be treated with topical lubricants or estrogen.

Patients with Sjögren disease are at increased risk for complications from surgery requiring general anesthesia that are related to the use of anticholinergic drugs and the low-humidity environment in the operating room. Management may include use of ocular lubricants, humidified oxygen, and chest physiotherapy to mobilize secretions.

Active extraglandular disease should be treated with systemic therapies. In most cases, glucocorticoids may be considered as a first-line option, but only at the minimum dose and length of time necessary to control the active disease. Immunomodulatory (e.g., hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide) and biologic (e.g., anti–B-cell therapy with rituximab or belimumab) agents should be considered based on the severity and type of organ dysfunction, or for glucocorticoid sparing. Musculoskeletal pain is common in Sjögren disease but should not be treated with immunomodulatory or biologic therapy unless there is objective evidence of active inflammatory arthritis.

The prognosis of primary Sjögren disease is favorable, with no overall increase in mortality. Management of sicca reduces the risk for corneal damage or tooth loss. In rare instances, end-organ involvement can be life-threatening. Secondary Sjögren disease may be associated with significant morbidity from the primary condition. Patients with anti-Ro/SSA or anti-La/SSB antibodies who are trying to conceive or are pregnant should establish care with a perinatologist because these antibodies confer an increased risk for congenital heart block in the fetus. Pregnant patients with positivity for anti-Ro/SSA or anti-La/SSB antibodies should undergo echocardiography of the fetus to evaluate for cardiac abnormalities.

Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathies

Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIMs) are characterized by progressive muscle weakness, elevated serum muscle enzyme levels, and evidence of inflammation on muscle biopsy. The major categories include polymyositis, dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis, and immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.

The differential diagnosis of muscle disease is broad and includes hereditary, environmental, infectious, and acquired conditions ( [Table: Table: Differential Diagnosis of Myopathy]

). IIMs often present with symmetric proximal muscle weakness without substantial muscle pain or tenderness. An elevated serum creatine kinase level is a common finding that suggests muscle damage. The presence of pain or tenderness should prompt consideration of alternative causes, such as infectious, endocrine (thyroid), or drug-induced myopathies. Medications are common causes of muscle pain and weakness and should also be considered in the differential diagnosis of the inflammatory myopathies ( [Table: Table: Drug-Induced Myopathies]

). See Myopathies in Neurology for additional information.

Muscle weakness must be differentiated from generalized fatigue, which is common and caused by such conditions as cardiopulmonary disease, malignancy, depression, and deconditioning. Primary neurologic disorders (e.g., spinal muscle atrophies, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and myasthenia gravis) may cause muscle weakness but are distinguished by involvement of nonproximal muscle groups and/or nerve involvement on electromyography. An elevated serum creatine kinase level is uncommon with these neurologic disorders; if the creatine kinase level in one of these disorders is elevated, it may not be as high as in patients with IIM. Exercise-induced weakness may point to a metabolic or mitochondrial cause rather than an IIM.

IIMs are an uncommon and heterogeneous group of diseases. The annual incidence is between 2 and 10 cases per million. The prevalence is estimated to be 5 to 22 per 100,000. Two peaks of onset occur: the first in childhood and the second in adulthood. The peak incidence is between ages 40 and 50 years. Female adult predominance is seen (approximately 2:1), except for inclusion body myositis, which preferentially affects men.

Like many other autoimmune diseases, IIMs probably result from interactions between genetic and environmental factors. The clearest genetic association is with HLA alleles, including HLA-DRB103:01 with polymyositis and juvenile dermatomyositis and HLA-DRB08:01 with dermatomyositis. Distinct HLA alleles have also been associated with different IIM subgroups, as defined by myositis-specific antibodies. However, because HLA associations in IIM vary by ethnic groups around the world, their utility in diagnosis and categorization is limited.

Environmental factors may activate or modify gene expression and likely influence disease progression and severity as well as onset. Associations with infections, medications, occupational exposures, ultraviolet light, and other factors have been reported. The clearest associations have been with medications, including statins, cytokine-targeted therapies (interferons and tumor necrosis factor inhibitors), and checkpoint inhibitors.

Immune mechanisms that contribute to IIM vary among subtypes and include the presence of T- and B-lymphocytic infiltrates, as well as increased cytokine and chemokine levels in muscle tissue. Autoantibodies are expressed in many but not all patients; specific autoantibodies and differing histologic patterns are associated with distinct clinical characteristics, suggesting that pathogenic mechanisms vary across subsets. In addition to adaptive immunity, innate immunity (e.g., interferon pathways) may contribute to the pathogenesis of inflammatory myositis. The type I interferon pathway is active in dermatomyositis, and the type II interferon pathway is active in antisynthetase syndrome and inclusion body myositis. Non–immune-mediated mechanisms are also important, especially for the progression to atrophy, fibrosis, and structural damage to muscle tissue.

Most patients with IIM present with symmetric weakness affecting the proximal muscles. Neck flexors and shoulder and hip girdle muscles are commonly involved. Patients may have difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs. Symptoms usually progress over months, except in inclusion body myositis, which progresses over years. Respiratory muscles can be affected, and some patients have difficulty swallowing (dysphagia or dysmotility) related to involvement of the upper gastrointestinal tract. Cardiac muscle can be involved in some subsets of IIM.

Interstitial lung disease (ILD), most commonly nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis, occurs in both polymyositis and dermatomyositis. It is an important cause of morbidity and mortality, particularly in patients with the antisynthetase syndrome and anti–melanoma differentiation–associated gene 5 (anti-MDA5) subtype (see Dermatomyositis in Rheumatology). Muscle weakness of the chest wall can also cause breathing difficulties. Pulmonary involvement is not typically seen in inclusion body myositis.

Pathognomonic skin findings are associated with dermatomyositis but not polymyositis. Mechanic’s hands (see Dermatomyositis in Rheumatology) can occur in patients with the antisynthetase syndrome associated with polymyositis or dermatomyositis.

In addition to cardiac muscle involvement, other reported cardiac conditions include arrhythmias, atrioventricular block, and pericarditis. Patients with myositis are at higher risk for heart failure and myocardial infarction.

There is a clear association between malignancy and IIM; patients with dermatomyositis have a 3- to 12-fold higher risk for malignancy than age-matched populations. The association between malignancy and polymyositis is smaller. The risk for malignancy peaks in the 3 years after diagnosis of dermatomyositis or polymyositis. Commonly associated cancers include ovarian, lung, breast, pancreas, stomach, and colon cancers and lymphoma. Higher risk for malignancy is associated with the following:

  • Older age at onset
  • Severe cutaneous disease
  • Dysphagia
  • Resistance to therapy
  • Presence of anti–transcription intermediary factor 1-gamma antibodies or anti–nuclear matrix protein 2 antibodies (see [Table: Table: IIM-Specific Antibodies]

)

Age- and sex-appropriate cancer screening is indicated at the time of diagnosis of dermatomyositis or polymyositis and regularly for several years thereafter. Many experts advocate CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, particularly in patients with dermatomyositis.

Although the categories of dermatomyositis, polymyositis, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, and inclusion body myositis are clinically useful, they do not fully account for the varying features within each group, and there are now subcategories within each group. Some patients with dermatomyositis or polymyositis may further demonstrate the antisynthetase syndrome. In addition, overlap syndromes may have features of inflammatory myopathy along with other rheumatologic diseases, such as systemic sclerosis, mixed connective tissue disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus.

In addition to muscle involvement, patients with dermatomyositis usually have characteristic skin findings ( [Table: Table: Cutaneous Manifestations of Dermatomyositis]

), such as the following:

  • Heliotrope rash (

) - Gottron papules (

) - Gottron sign - Periungual erythema - Mechanic’s hand (

) - Facial erythema or photodistributed poikiloderma (shawl and V signs) (

) - Calcinosis cutis

Although skin and muscle biopsies can be helpful for diagnosis and prognosis, some cases of dermatomyositis can be diagnosed on the basis of characteristic skin findings without a muscle biopsy.

A small subset of patients with dermatomyositis never develop muscle involvement (amyopathic dermatomyositis); these patients can be diagnosed with skin biopsy in the setting of at least 6 months without muscle involvement. A subset of patients with amyopathic dermatomyositis and positivity for anti-MDA5 antibody have cutaneous ulceration, painful palmar macules, and papules. These patients are at high risk for ILD and should be screened for ILD on diagnosis.

Patients with polymyositis have proximal muscle weakness without the skin involvement of dermatomyositis. Because patients with polymyositis lack pathognomonic clinical features, a muscle biopsy is recommended to confirm the diagnosis and differentiate this subgroup from those with other forms of myositis. In general, patients with polymyositis have a lower risk for pulmonary or other extramuscular disease features than those with dermatomyositis.

The antisynthetase syndrome occurs in approximately 30% of patients with dermatomyositis or polymyositis. The syndrome is associated with antibodies to aminoacyl-transfer RNA (tRNA) synthetases (most commonly anti–Jo-1, directed at histidyl-tRNA synthetase) and is characterized by a high risk for and greater severity of ILD. Other features include arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, and mechanic’s hand (

).

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) is characterized by the following:

  • Rapidly progressive, severe muscle weakness
  • Increased likelihood of muscle pain
  • High serum creatine kinase levels
  • Muscle biopsy specimens demonstrating prominent myonecrosis with only limited inflammation

An immune-mediated mechanism is suggested by the presence of antibodies to signal recognition particle or 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase in about two thirds of patients ( [Table: Table: IIM-Specific Antibodies]

). HMG-CoA is the clinical target of action of statins in lipid lowering, and statin exposure may result in antibodies to HMG-CoA reductase, which can sometimes lead to IMNM. However, statins more commonly induce muscle disease through direct rather than autoimmune myotoxicity (see Toxic Myopathy in Neurology). In patients with statin-triggered IMNM, weakness may persist or progress even after statins are discontinued. Notably, some patients with anti–HMG-CoA reductase antibodies may never have had statin exposure.

Inclusion body myositis is an insidious condition affecting older adults. It is distinguishable from other forms of myositis by its slow progression and different pattern of muscle involvement. Patients report a history of weakness for an average of 5 years before seeking care. Both proximal and distal muscle involvement occur; finger flexor and quadriceps weakness and atrophy are hallmark features. Muscle involvement is usually asymmetric. Up to half of patients with inclusion body myositis have cricopharyngeal muscle involvement, leading to dysphagia and increased risk for aspiration.

Serum creatine kinase levels are elevated to a lesser extent than seen in other forms of IIM. Autoantibodies are less often present, but the anti–cytosolic 5′-nucleotidase 1A autoantibody is found in up to half of patients and rarely in controls (see [Table: Table: IIM-Specific Antibodies]

).

Other systemic rheumatic diseases (e.g., systemic sclerosis, mixed connective tissue disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and, less commonly, rheumatoid arthritis and Sjögren disease) may include myositis as a clinical feature but typically have other prominent clinical features and different antibody associations.

IIM should be considered in any patient who has progressive proximal muscle weakness without another explanation and has abnormalities on testing as outlined below.

Elevated serum muscle enzymes are useful in differentiating intrinsic muscle disease from neurologic causes of weakness. Elevated serum creatine kinase levels are a sensitive indicator of muscle pathology and are generally a reliable marker of disease activity and severity. Therefore, creatine kinase levels can be used to monitor response to treatment and detect relapses in myositis. Aldolase levels may be elevated when serum creatine kinase levels are normal. Serum aminotransferase and lactate dehydrogenase levels may also be elevated but are nonspecific. Troponins can be used to screen for cardiac muscle involvement.

Only about half of patients with IIM have identifiable autoantibodies. Some autoantibodies, such as antinuclear antibodies, lack specificity. The myositis-specific antibodies have more diagnostic and prognostic value and can be useful for identifying risk for specific features or subsets (see [Table: Table: IIM-Specific Antibodies]

).

Although not required to diagnose IIMs, MRI is useful in identifying regions of active muscle inflammation and in guiding muscle biopsy. MRI can also assess the extent and severity of muscle involvement and therapeutic efficacy.

High-resolution CT (along with pulmonary function testing) should be used to assess ILD in high-risk patients.

Electromyography (EMG) is most helpful in differentiating myopathy from neuropathic causes of weakness (e.g., polyneuropathy, motor neuron disease). The following EMG findings may suggest myositis:

  • Increased insertional activity
  • Fibrillations
  • Positive waves
  • Early recruitment of short-duration, small-amplitude polyphasic motor unit action potentials

However, these findings are not specific and may be observed in other causes of myopathy. EMG can be helpful in identifying muscle involvement with mild and subclinical weakness. Muscles that have undergone recent EMG should not be subjected to muscle biopsy because of the potential for a false-positive result.

Muscle biopsy is valuable for diagnosing and distinguishing IIMs and for excluding metabolic myopathies, mitochondrial disease, and infection.

Polymyositis and dermatomyositis share common histopathologic features, including inflammatory cell infiltrates, muscle fiber necrosis, degeneration, and regeneration, but differ in the types and locations of the cell infiltrates. Perifascicular atrophy and fibrosis, as well as perimysial inflammatory infiltrates, are observed in dermatomyositis. In polymyositis, the inflammatory cells are localized in the endomysium and there is increased expression of the major histocompatibility complex class I molecule. Muscle biopsy findings in inclusion body myositis include mononuclear cell infiltrates, “rimmed” vacuoles, and a lack of muscle cell necrosis. Electron microscopy can show characteristic inclusion bodies. In the absence of vacuoles and inclusion bodies, inclusion body myositis is often misdiagnosed as polymyositis. Muscle biopsy in IMNM shows prominent necrosis with minimal inflammatory cells.

Skin biopsy can be useful in the diagnosis of dermatomyositis. Typical findings include a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, vacuolar changes at the dermal-epidermal junction, and increased dermal mucin.

The 2017 classification criteria for IIMs from the European League Against Rheumatism (now called the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology)/American College of Rheumatology have been an advancement in standardizing definitions. Although intended for research studies, classification criteria can also help support a clinical diagnosis. These criteria allow classification of IIM without a muscle biopsy. The criteria first define the probability of IIM and then apply the classification tree for subgroups of IIMs (

). Limitations include the fact that there are too few patients with IMNM or antisynthetase syndrome to characterize these subsets, along with lack of inclusion of MRI findings or most myositis-specific antibodies.

Glucocorticoids are the cornerstone of therapy for rapid and effective control of most forms of IIMs. Starting dose varies by severity and organ involvement but is typically high (up to 1 mg/kg of prednisone) and should be tapered over 6 months. Intravenous methylprednisolone may be considered in cases with gastrointestinal malabsorption and as pulse dosing in severe or refractory cases.

Prolonged exposure to high-dose glucocorticoids, particularly in older patients, can lead to glucocorticoid-induced myopathy, resulting in proximal muscle weakness and diagnostic confusion in a patient with IIM who had previously been improving. Chronic glucocorticoid-induced myopathy manifests after weeks to months of prolonged glucocorticoid exposure, is associated with normal or near-normal creatine kinase levels, and may be associated with cushingoid features on examination. Worsening myopathy after prolonged glucocorticoid exposure, despite declining creatine kinase levels, suggests glucocorticoid-induced myopathy; this condition should prompt reduction in the glucocorticoid dose in favor of glucocorticoid-sparing immunomodulatory agents. Reduction or elimination of glucocorticoids results in clinical improvement within several weeks.

Immunomodulatory agents are used as glucocorticoid-sparing agents; methotrexate and azathioprine are the preferred initial therapy. Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) can be used in addition to or as an alternative to traditional agents or in cases refractory to conventional agents. Evidence for IVIG is strongest for dermatomyositis and IMNM. Second-line therapy includes mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, cyclosporine, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, or JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib (for dermatomyositis).

IMNM is often acute and severe and should be treated aggressively with combinations of glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive agents. IVIG is effective for anti–HMG-CoA reductase antibody–positive IMNM. Rituximab can be used to treat anti–signal recognition particle (SRP) antibody–positive IMNM. Statins should be avoided in patients with IMNM who are positive for anti–HMG-CoA reductase antibody.

Inclusion body myositis usually does not respond to immunosuppression, and any therapeutic trials should be discontinued if benefit is not appreciated. An initial response to empiric glucocorticoids should indicate an alternative diagnosis. Reports suggest that IVIG may be helpful in managing dysphagia.

Physical therapy can help maintain muscle function and should be universally recommended. Because dysphagia and aspiration are common causes of morbidity and mortality in patients with inclusion body myositis, speech therapy should be consulted for advice regarding aspiration risks and precautions.

The prognosis in IIM varies from resolution to severe, treatment-resistant disease with functional impairment and early mortality. The degree of serum creatine kinase elevation at diagnosis does not predict outcome. Poor prognosis is associated with the following:

  • Prolonged disease activity before treatment
  • Greater weakness at presentation
  • Extensive multisystem disease
  • Co-occurrence of malignancy
  • Certain myositis-specific antibodies or histologic features

Patients with anti-SRP antibodies often have severe disease that is difficult to control. Patients with anti-MDA5 antibodies often have a poor prognosis given this antibody’s association with rapidly progressive and often fatal ILD; in contrast, patients with anti–Mi-2 antibodies have a favorable prognosis with a lower risk for ILD, and patients with dermatomyositis with this autoantibody are quite responsive to treatment.

Given the lack of effective treatment, patients with inclusion body myositis typically demonstrate a slow and gradual loss of function, with progression to wheelchair dependence within 10 to 15 years of symptom development. However, life expectancy does not appear to be affected.

Systemic Sclerosis

Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a multiorgan disease characterized by fibrosis and vasculopathy. The skin is the most apparent target, but internal organs are also affected. SSc is relatively rare, with a prevalence of 275 cases per million and an annual incidence of 19 cases per million. The peak incidence occurs in patients aged 20 to 50 years, and it is more common among women.

Vascular injury, vascular and visceral fibrosis, and innate and adaptive immune activation with autoantibody production play interactive roles in SSc. Genome-wide association studies have identified up to 28 risk loci for SSc. One of the earliest SSc manifestations is Raynaud phenomenon, suggesting that vascular injury precedes the fibrotic reaction. With vascular damage, several cytokines are released: Vascular endothelial growth factor contributes to disordered angiogenesis, transforming growth factor-β is a key fibrogenic cytokine, and endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor that also induces vascular smooth muscle proliferation and fibroblast activation. B cells are also activated and produce interleukin-6, which further stimulates fibroblasts and leads to autoantibody production. These processes result in progressive obliterative vasculopathy.

The 2013 Classification Criteria for SSc were developed by a joint committee of the American College of Rheumatology and the European League Against Rheumatism (now called the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology) and provided a case definition of SSc for research studies; they are also useful for the clinician to review ( [Table: Table: Classification Criteria for Systemic Sclerosis]

).

SSc is divided into three subtypes based on the extent of skin involvement:

  • Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (DcSSc)
  • Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (LcSSc)
  • Systemic sclerosis sine scleroderma

See [Table: Table: Manifestations/Features of Scleroderma Spectrum Disorders]

for characteristics of these subtypes. Specific long-term complications may be more likely in one subtype than another; however, overlap is common. LcSSc is formerly known as CREST (calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia) syndrome. However, most patients with LcSSc do not have all CREST features. LcSSC is less commonly accompanied by fibrosis of internal organs than is DcSSc but is associated with pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Various disorders may present with skin thickening and other manifestations that mimic SSc and should be considered in the differential diagnosis ( [Table: Table: Manifestations/Features of Scleroderma Spectrum Disorders]

). These conditions are not typically associated with Raynaud phenomenon, and the absence of Raynaud phenomenon in a patient with skin thickening makes SSc less likely. In contrast, Raynaud phenomenon is so prevalent in SSc that any patient presenting with features of autoimmune-associated (secondary) Raynaud phenomenon (such as onset after 40 years of age, telangiectasias, digital pitting, or nailfold capillary abnormalities) should be tested for antinuclear antibody positivity and associated autoantibodies.

The diagnosis of SSc depends on the presence of specific clinical findings ( [Table: Table: Manifestations/Features of Scleroderma Spectrum Disorders]

) and autoantibodies ( [Table: Table: Autoantibodies in Systemic Sclerosis]

), which are present in 90% to 95% of patients.

The skin is the organ most commonly involved in SSc, with the hands being universally affected. In LcSSc, the skin over the face, neck, hands, and feet is affected. In DcSSc, skin involvement is more extensive and additionally includes the arms, trunk, and lower extremities.

The earliest skin manifestations in DcSSc are often diffusely swollen fingers/hands. This will later give way to thickened, bound-down, atrophic skin. Skin thickening in LcSSc may be more subtle than in DcSSc, and the inability to tent the skin over the fingers (sclerodactyly) may be an important clue. The skin changes can lead to joint contractures (

). Small mat-like telangiectasias are common in LcSSc and occasionally occur in DcSSc. They are primarily found on the hands and face and can also be seen on the oral mucosal side of the lips and upper trunk; these lesions blanch with light pressure. Poikiloderma (areas of hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation, telangiectasias, and atrophy) can occur in areas of fibrosis. Facial skin involvement can lead to limitation of the oral aperture and difficulty eating. The face may be devoid of wrinkles.

Pruritus, common in other autoimmune skin diseases, can be severe in patients with progressive skin disease in SSc. Pruritus may lead to psychological distress and can be difficult to treat.

Calcinosis occurs in approximately 25% of patients with SSc, typically in the hands, forearms, elbows, gluteal region, and iliac crest (

). These deposits can be seen or felt and are easily detected on radiographs.

Joint involvement occurs in up to 60% of patients. It is mainly polyarticular and in some patients can be erosive, involving the small joints of the hands (including the metacarpophalangeal joints and the wrists); the distal interphalangeal joints are generally not affected. Between 1% and 5% of patients have rheumatoid arthritis–SSc overlap, with positivity for anti–cyclic citrullinated antibodies and classic rheumatoid arthritis manifestations along with SSc features.

Patients with more severe SSc may develop acro-osteolysis, or resorption of the terminal bony tuft of the fingers and, less commonly, the toes (

). This manifestation is typically seen in patients with significant distal vascular involvement, including ulceration, ischemia, and calcinosis.

Tendon rubs can be felt or heard with a stethoscope because inflammation/fibrosis affects tendons or tendon sheaths. Tendon rubs occur in about 10% of patients with DcSSc and are a marker for active disease.

SSc-associated myositis occurs in 10% to 15% of patients. Serum creatine kinase and/or serum aldolase levels are elevated, and electromyogram demonstrates myopathic changes. There is a strong association between SSc-associated myositis and myocardial involvement. The presence of anti–PM-Scl as well as anti-Ku antibodies identifies patients with an overlap between myositis and SSc.

Raynaud phenomenon occurs in approximately 95% of patients with SSc; it is the most common early manifestation of SSc, typically occurring years before recognizable SSc. Raynaud phenomenon is initially episodic, but with vascular fibrosis, the blood supply becomes permanently restricted. SSc will develop in approximately 80% of patients with the combination of Raynaud phenomenon, an SSc-associated autoantibody, and nailfold capillary abnormalities (

).

Digital ulcers occur in about 15% of patients with SSc, typically on the extensor surfaces and tips of the fingers and toes but also on the dorsum of hands and feet and the lower extremities (

).

Myocardial fibrosis is a consequence of microvascular disease and a cause of early death. It results from repetitive ischemia-reperfusion injury of the myocardium. Myocardial involvement may lead to heart failure, intraventricular conduction block, and arrhythmias. Diastolic dysfunction is more common than systolic dysfunction, and a right bundle branch block is a predictor of early mortality in SSc.

Symptoms of esophageal dysmotility and reflux are common in all forms of SSc and may be an early disease manifestation. Approximately 80% of patients with SSc have involvement of the lower two thirds (smooth muscle portion) of the esophagus, with symptoms resulting from dysmotility and/or gastroesophageal reflux disease. Evaluation using manometry and 24-hour pH monitoring can confirm involvement and severity. Risks for Barrett esophagus and adenocarcinoma are increased in affected patients. A dilated esophagus (patulous esophagus) on chest imaging indicates advanced esophageal involvement.

Gastric symptoms generally result from dysmotility. Patients describe early satiety, may report nausea and vomiting from delayed gastric emptying, and can be evaluated using gastric scintigraphy. Gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE; also known as “watermelon stomach”) is most common in patients with DcSSc and those with anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies. Bleeding ectasias can cause significant blood loss and are treated using endoscopic therapies.

Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth is common and can cause malabsorption and diarrhea. The diarrhea is described as explosive and typically follows a meal. Diagnosis is established via a carbohydrate substrate–based breath test, although an empiric trial of rotating antibiotics is often used. Small intestine dysmotility can result in pseudo-obstruction. Large intestine dysmotility may lead to constipation, and anorectal involvement may cause fecal incontinence.

Primary biliary cholangitis can be seen in patients with SSc, especially those who are anticentromere antibody positive. An alkaline phosphatase level at least 1.5 times the upper limit of normal and a positive result on an antimitochondrial test support the diagnosis.

Scleroderma renal crisis affects 5% of patients with DcSSc and 2% of patients with LcSSc. Risk factors include the following:

  • DcSSc, especially recent-onset, rapidly progressive skin disease
  • Disease-associated heart failure or pericardial disease
  • Tendon friction rubs
  • Use of glucocorticoids (>15 mg/d)
  • Presence of anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies (associated with renal crisis prevalence as high as 20%-25%)

Scleroderma renal crisis occurs within 4 years of SSc onset in 75% of cases. Patients characteristically present with manifestations of hypertensive emergency, including headache, encephalopathy, seizures, and hypertensive retinopathy. Rarely, a normotensive form of scleroderma renal crisis can occur. Risk factors for a poor prognosis include male sex, older age, and heart failure. Close blood pressure monitoring is important because changes in blood pressure from ambulatory baseline measurements may alert physicians to an impending renal crisis.

Laboratory findings include microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and proteinuria. The serum creatinine level is typically elevated and may remain so for some time after blood pressure is controlled. Abnormalities in the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and in endothelin-1 are thought to contribute to the pathophysiology. Although ACE inhibitors, especially captopril (due to greater clinical experience with this agent and because its rapid onset and short duration of action permit rapid dose escalation), have dramatically improved the outcome of patients with scleroderma renal crisis, prophylactic use of ACE inhibitors may worsen scleroderma renal crisis outcomes and is not recommended even in high-risk patients.

Lung involvement in SSc includes pleuritis, interstitial lung disease (ILD), and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Restrictive disease can occur with extensive skin involvement of the trunk in DcSSc. Patients with SSc are at increased risk for cancer in general and for lung cancer in particular.

ILD occurs in 30% to 40% of patients with SSc overall and in 85% of patients with anti–Scl-70 (antitopoisomerase-1) antibodies. ILD is the main cause of disease-associated death. Men are more likely to develop ILD. The most common high-resolution CT pattern is nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis, followed by usual interstitial pneumonitis. An abnormal FVC early in the disease course (within the first 5 years) is highly predictive of progressive disease. There is a strong association between ILD and gastroesophageal reflux disease, but the contribution of refluxed material to ILD is uncertain. All patients should undergo pulmonary function testing and high-resolution CT at initial SSc diagnosis, and yearly rescreening with pulmonary function testing should be considered thereafter. The 2023 American College of Rheumatology/American College of Chest Physicians guidelines recommend that patients with SSc-related ILD undergo pulmonary function testing with Dlco every 3 to 6 months for the first year and less frequently thereafter, along with ambulatory desaturation testing (e.g., via a 6-minute walk test ). A 10% decline in FVC or 15% decline in Dlco within 12 months should raise concern for progression. High-resolution CT can be done as needed for follow-up.

The prevalence of PAH in SSc is 10%. Patients with PAH initially present with exertional dyspnea; in advanced disease, chest pain and lower extremity edema occur as the right heart fails. Telangiectasis may be a marker for pulmonary vascular disease in SSc. A Dlco less than 55% of predicted and an FVC/Dlco ratio of 1.6 or greater on pulmonary function tests suggest the presence of PAH. Two-dimensional transthoracic echocardiography and Doppler echocardiography provide noninvasive assessments of pulmonary artery pressures and should be performed in patients who have symptoms of or are at substantially increased risk for PAH. Many screening algorithms for PAH are available and can help determine whether the patient should proceed to right heart catheterization, the gold standard for evaluating PAH. A mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg is considered elevated. Severe PAH is typically progressive and can lead to cor pulmonale and right-sided heart failure. See Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (Group 1) in Pulmonary Medicine for further discussion of diagnosis and treatment of PAH.

Treatment options for SSc are mainly symptomatic and organ system specific ( [Table: Table: Treatments of Common Manifestations of Systemic Sclerosis]

).

ACE inhibitors (typically captopril) can be lifesaving in patients with scleroderma renal crisis and should be titrated to control blood pressure. Dialysis support may be needed temporarily. ACE inhibitor therapy should be continued in scleroderma renal crisis even in the presence of a rising serum creatinine level and the need for dialysis because late improvement may occur. The addition of plasma exchange to ACE inhibitors in patients with scleroderma renal crisis and microangiopathic features has been suggested; angiotensin receptor blockers should be considered only when ACE inhibitors are not tolerated.

The American College of Rheumatology/American College of Chest Physicians 2023 guidelines and guidelines from the American Thoracic Society recommend mycophenolate mofetil as the preferred agent for the treatment of ILD in SSc. Alternative preferred options include tocilizumab or rituximab; additional options include cyclophosphamide, nintedanib, and azathioprine. The American College of Rheumatology/American College of Chest Physicians guidelines also recommend against using glucocorticoids for treating ILD because of potential risk for renal crisis.

Autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation has been studied for several years in patients with rapidly progressive, severe SSc; lung function, skin thickening, and antibody status significantly improved in one third to one half of studied patients. Current guidelines recommend referral for stem cell transplantation and/or lung transplantation in patients who have progression of ILD while receiving medical therapy.

The use of chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR T-cell) therapy for treating patients with significant, progressive disease is currently under investigation. Early data suggests benefit, with some patients achieving an immune reset.

Studies have shown that compared with healthy control patients, pregnant patients with SSc experience an increase in first-trimester miscarriage, preeclampsia, preterm delivery, and low birth weight. A meta-analysis of pregnancies in patients with SSc suggested that although disease manifestations, including digital ulcers, may improve, 14% of patients may develop new manifestations or worsening of disease during pregnancy; in another 10%, disease will worsen in the first 6 months postpartum. Contraindications to pregnancy in patients with SSc include PAH and severe restrictive lung disease (FVC <1 L).

Data from a French SSc cohort and meta-analysis indicate that the 5-year survival rate is 85%, but the 15-year survival rate is only 53%. Risk factors associated with increased mortality include age at disease onset, DcSSc, male sex, African ancestry, anti–Scl-70 antibodies, kidney disease or crisis, ILD, cardiac involvement, pulmonary hypertension, and cancer.

Patients with SSc have an elevated risk for cancer, especially those who are RNA polymerase III antibody positive. In these patients, the presence of RNA polymerase antibodies has been estimated to increase the risk for malignancy by 48%. Anticentromere antibodies appear to be protective. Some types of cancer present at rates three times higher than those seen in the general population ( [Table: Table: Cancers in Systemic Sclerosis]

). Patients should undergo age-, sex-, and risk factor–appropriate cancer screening.

Mixed Connective Tissue Disease and Undifferentiated Connective Tissue Disease

Autoimmune diseases are complex, and some patients have clinical features of more than one of the classic systemic autoimmune diseases simultaneously or sequentially. These conditions are classified as overlap syndromes. Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) is a specific variant of overlap syndrome that includes clinical manifestations meeting a dual or triple diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), autoimmune myositis, systemic sclerosis, and, in some patients, rheumatoid arthritis. MCTD is rare, and 80% of patients are women. MCTD is associated with positivity for anti–U1-ribonucleoprotein (RNP) antibodies and a high antinuclear antibody titer with a speckled pattern.

Other patients present with signs and symptoms that are autoimmune in nature (often including Raynaud phenomenon) but do not rise to the level of a specific rheumatologic condition; such patients have undifferentiated connective tissue disease (UCTD), also referred to as undifferentiated systemic rheumatologic disease.

See [Table: Table: Comparison of MCTD and UCTD]

.

Raynaud phenomenon and pulmonary involvement are common features; puffy hands and inflammatory arthritis are also observed. Pericarditis is the most common clinical manifestation of cardiac involvement, reported in up to 40% of patients. Pulmonary arterial hypertension is the major cause of death. Severe kidney and neurologic diseases are uncommon.

Although antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, and anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies are often present, the presence of anti–double-stranded DNA, anti-Smith, or anti-Ro/SSA antibodies makes primary SLE a more likely diagnosis.

Treatment for MCTD is directed at the specific organ system involved in the individual patient and is guided by the management of these manifestations as would occur in the “parent” condition (see [Table: Table: Comparison of MCTD and UCTD]

).

Prognosis of MCTD depends on the spectrum and severity of organ involvement. Patients with initially mild disease may develop new and more severe manifestations over decades, including interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension. Patients with MCTD are at increased risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

UCTD usually remains mild and stable; however, in a minority of patients, UCTD may evolve into a more specific autoimmune disorder, most commonly SLE. Most patients with UCTD who develop a more specific disease do so within the first 2 to 5 years after presentation. A definite disease is more likely to develop in patients with the following:

  • Cytopenias
  • Hypocomplementemia
  • Presence of certain antibodies (e.g., anti–double-stranded DNA, anti-Smith, anti–Scl-70, anticentromere, anti-Ro/SSA, or antiphospholipid antibodies)
  • Serositis
  • Kidney disease
  • Puffy fingers
  • Abnormal nailfold capillaries
