Crystal Arthropathies

Gout is characterized by episodic flares of painful inflammatory arthritis in response to monosodium urate crystals formed in joints due to excessive serum levels of urate. Gout is increasingly common, with a current prevalence of approximately 4% in the United States. Factors contributing to increased prevalence include dietary trends, obesity rates, and an aging population. Nearly all patients with gout experience comorbidities, including hypertension, coronary artery disease, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Some comorbidities (e.g., CKD) contribute to hyperuricemia; many comorbidities complicate treatment by posing relative contraindications for appropriate therapeutics (e.g., NSAIDs in patients with CKD).

In men, serum urate levels rise after puberty, whereas premenopausal women are generally protected from hyperuricemia by estrogenic effects. Men typically have their first gout flare in the third to fifth decade; women are more likely to experience serum urate elevations and their first flare after menopause.

Uric acid is the product of purine metabolism. Approximately two thirds of urate production derives from turnover of intracellular nucleic acids; the remainder comes from dietary purine intake. A small proportion of patients overproduce uric acid as a consequence of an inherited metabolic or enzymatic disorder. Unlike most mammals, humans do not express the enzyme uricase, which converts urate into highly soluble allantoin. Urate therefore accumulates and can precipitate as crystals in joints and other tissues if serum concentrations exceed the saturation point. At normal body temperature and pH, the saturation point of urate is 6.8 mg/dL (0.40 mmol/L).

Approximately two-thirds of the daily excretion of uric acid occurs in the kidneys, and the remaining uric acid is eliminated by the gut. In the kidneys, almost all serum urate is filtered at the glomerulus, but approximately 90% is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule; in most patients with gout, hereditary underexcretion of uric acid is the primary cause of hyperuricemia ( [Table: Table: Causes of Hyperuricemia]

). The factors that lead to the progression from hyperuricemia to gout are unclear; an elevated serum urate level is predictive, but not all patients with hyperuricemia develop gout. A serum urate level greater than 10 mg/dL (0.59 mmol/L) is associated with a 50% likelihood of an initial gout flare within 15 years.

A gout flare (acute gouty arthritis) is triggered when resident synovial macrophages ingest monosodium urate crystals, leading to activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and generation of interleukin (IL)-1β. IL-1β causes local vasodilation, triggers production of other inflammatory cytokines, and recruits and activates neutrophils. Complement activation on the surface of monosodium urate crystals also promotes neutrophil recruitment.

Early acute gout flares are typically monoarticular, and at least 50% of first flares in men involve the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint of the great toe (podagra) (

). Inflammatory states, such as infection, surgery, and myocardial infarction, can provoke gout flares. The hallmarks of a flare are pain, tenderness, swelling, redness, and warmth. Flares typically begin at night and peak within 12 to 24 hours. If untreated, most gout flares self-resolve within days to a few weeks, although with long-standing disease, flares can persist for months. In men with established disease, flares eventually affect the proximal feet, ankles, and knees, and later almost any joint, including the spine. Postmenopausal women may present differently, with initial flares often involving the knees or finger joints affected by osteoarthritis. For patients with more severe or long-standing disease, polyarticular flares may occur. Soft tissue can also be involved, manifesting as acute bursitis (e.g., olecranon and prepatellar), periarthritis, and gouty panniculitis and cellulitis, the last of which can be misdiagnosed as a refractory bacterial soft-tissue infection.

Intercritical gout is the asymptomatic period between gout flares. Early in the disease course, the intercritical period can be years. As the disease progresses, the intercritical period may progressively shorten. Even during intercritical periods, urate crystals still reside within joints and soft tissues, and subclinical systemic inflammation persists.

If gout is not treated properly, gout flares tend to become increasingly frequent, more severe, and commonly polyarticular. These flares may eventually coalesce into persistent inflammatory arthritis (chronic gouty arthritis), with intermittent exacerbations superimposed on the baseline persistent disease.

Some patients develop tophi. Tophi are chalky masses of monosodium urate, surrounded by inflammatory cells and a rind of fibrous tissue. Tophi are usually located around joints and in soft tissues, with a predilection for the extensor surfaces of the elbows, distal Achilles tendon, fingers (proximal and distal interphalangeal joints) (

), and helices of the ears. Tophi are deforming, can interfere with function, and directly erode bone. The presence of tophi has been associated with greater risk for comorbidities, including cardiovascular and kidney disease. Ulceration of overlying skin can predispose to infection, which can be difficult to treat because tophi are avascular.

A diagnosis of gout (the chronic disease state) should be considered in any patient who has had or is experiencing one or more episodes of acute monoarticular or oligoarticular inflammatory arthritis that may represent a gout flare. Although designed primarily for research, gout classification criteria are available, including as an online calculator, and are 92% sensitive and 89% specific.

See [Table: Table: Differential Diagnosis of Acute Gout Flare]

.

The gold standard for diagnosing a gout flare is identification of negatively birefringent, needle-like monosodium urate crystals, along with neutrophils, in synovial fluid (see

). Crystals within neutrophils are usually also seen. (“Negatively birefringent” means that under polarized light, the crystals appear yellow when parallel to and blue when perpendicular to the polarizing axis of an optical filter.) Arthrocentesis is not always performed when gout flare is suspected, but when infection is a concern, joint aspiration for Gram stain and culture is mandatory.

In any acute arthritis in an adult, gout flare should be considered. The following findings support a gout flare diagnosis when arthrocentesis is not feasible:

  • Onset of severe pain and swelling over several hours
  • Involvement of the first MTP joint or midfoot/ankle
  • Presence of erythema
  • Previous similar acute arthritis episodes
  • Male sex
  • Associated cardiovascular disease

The involved joints are warm, red, swollen, and tender. Low-grade fever may be present, particularly during polyarticular flares; therefore, joint aspiration is important for excluding infection.

Serum urate measured at time of flare may not be helpful because levels can decrease during acute systemic inflammation. Thus, although an elevated serum urate level supports the possibility of gout, hyperuricemia alone does not establish the diagnosis, and lack of hyperuricemia at time of acute arthritis does not definitively rule out gout. A serum urate level 2 weeks after gout flare resolution more accurately measures baseline level. C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate are elevated during gout flare but are nonspecific. Joint fluid has an inflammatory leukocyte count (>2000/μL [2.0 × 10^9/L] and occasionally >100,000/μL [100 × 10^9/L]) with neutrophil predominance. Importantly, the presence of intracellular crystals and leukocytes in synovial fluid defines gout flare but does not definitively rule out a concomitant infection.

Radiographs may be normal early in the gout disease course or reflect only soft-tissue swelling during a flare. However, the characteristic radiographic changes of established disease may help confirm a history of previously unrecognized gout and support a diagnosis of current gout flare (

). Musculoskeletal ultrasonography and dual-energy CT can demonstrate monosodium urate deposition in joints and can contribute to the diagnosis. Ultrasonography can identify unsuspected tophi or a “double-contour” sign at cartilage surfaces (

), which is highly specific for urate deposition. Dual-energy CT can be performed to identify urate deposition when the diagnosis of gout is uncertain and may also be useful in determining the extent of ongoing urate deposition after extended urate-lowering therapy in established disease (

). The double-contour sign on ultrasonography, identification of monosodium urate crystal deposition on dual-energy CT, and gout-related joint damage on radiography are included in gout classification criteria.

Treatment of acute gout flares focuses on anti-inflammatory therapy; colchicine, NSAIDs, and glucocorticoids are all reasonable options (see Anti-Inflammatory Agents in Rheumatology). Treatment choice should be determined by potential drug interactions and patient preferences and comorbidities. The simplest approach is colchicine, 1.2 mg at the first symptoms of a gout flare, followed 1 hour later by a 0.6-mg dose. Colchicine is most effective when given within 24 hours of symptom onset and can be continued at a dose of 0.6 mg once or twice daily until the flare resolves. High-dose NSAIDs (e.g., naproxen, 500 mg twice daily) administered until a few days after symptom resolution are effective, as are glucocorticoids in any form: intra-articular injection, intramuscular injection (e.g., depo-methylprednisolone, 40-80 mg), or an oral “burst” of prednisone (e.g., a dose in the range of 0.5 mg/kg/d for 5-14 days, based on speed of flare resolution). Glucocorticoid treatments should be individualized; for example, intra-articular injection may be favored in patients with a single joint affected and may minimize systemic exposure in patients with diabetes or other relative contraindications. Treatment with adrenocorticotropic hormone, although effective, is discouraged because of its high cost. Topical ice reduces the duration of flares and may be considered as adjunctive therapy.

Most gout flares respond to therapy lasting 1 week or less, although more severe flares may require longer treatment. For patients with severe and refractory flares, or with contraindications to other treatments, use of IL-1β inhibitors (e.g., canakinumab or off-label use of anakinra) is effective and can be considered.

Guidelines conflict as to whether patients with gout should receive dietary counseling to reduce serum urate levels. If this is suggested, patients may limit intake of shellfish, oily fish, red meat, high-fructose foods, and alcohol. However, overly strict diets that are unlikely to be adhered to are not helpful. Healthy diets, such as the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet, may lower urate as much as strict low-purine diets and be more likely to have high adherence rates. Notably, dietary restrictions alone are rarely sufficient for treating gout. Weight loss (among patients who are overweight) and increased low-fat dairy intake may also reduce serum urate levels. In treating patients with gout for hypertension, agents other than thiazide diuretics (which increase serum urate levels) can be considered; losartan and calcium channel blockers both have urate-lowering effects.

The 2020 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) and 2016 European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR; now known as the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology) recommendations support a “treat to target” approach, reducing the serum urate level to less than 6.0 mg/dL (0.35 mmol/L) and, in the EULAR guidelines, to less than 5.0 mg/dL (0.30 mmol/L) in patients with tophi.

The ACR strongly recommends initiating urate-lowering therapy for patients with gout and any of the following:

  • One or more subcutaneous tophi
  • Radiographic damage (any modality) attributable to gout
  • Two or more gout flares annually

For patients who are experiencing their first flare and have CKD stage G3 or greater, a serum urate level exceeding 9.0 mg/dL (0.53 mmol/L), or urolithiasis, the ACR conditionally recommends initiating urate-lowering therapy. These guidelines strongly recommend that patients receiving urate-lowering therapy continue it indefinitely to achieve and maintain a serum urate target less than 6.0 mg/dL (0.35 mmol/L). Evidence also suggests that achieving and maintaining this urate target might lower cardiovascular risk in patients with gout.

In contrast to the ACR and EULAR guidelines, a 2017 guideline issued by the American College of Physicians endorses a “treat to avoid symptoms” approach. This approach may include short- or long-term anti-inflammatory agents as well as urate lowering, but it is guided by the clinical picture rather than the serum urate level. A clinical trial comparing these two approaches is underway.

Current recommendations support initiating urate-lowering therapy during an acute flare, but only if adequate anti-inflammatory therapy is concurrently started; doing so may improve long-term adherence. If the patient is already receiving urate-lowering therapy, dosing should not be stopped or modified during the flare.

The three classes of urate-lowering therapy are xanthine oxidase inhibitors (which reduce urate production), uricosuric agents (which decrease renal urate resorption), and pegloticase (which enzymatically digests urate).

Allopurinol is the recommended first-line therapy for most patients and is FDA approved. According to ACR guidelines, allopurinol should be initiated at 100 mg/d and titrated in 100-mg increments every few weeks until a serum urate level less than 6.0 mg/dL (0.35 mmol/L) is achieved (or lower as needed to control flares or resolve tophi). For patients with CKD stage G4 or G5, allopurinol should be initiated at 50 mg/d and the dosage titrated in 50- to 100-mg increments until the serum urate target is achieved. The maximum allopurinol dosage is 800 mg/d.

An uncommon but serious complication of allopurinol is a hypersensitivity reaction indicated by a rash that may progress to DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms) syndrome (DRESS syndrome is also increasingly being referred to as drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome [DIHS] because eosinophilia is not always present). Allopurinol should therefore be discontinued in patients who develop a rash. Risk factors for DRESS syndrome include CKD, diuretic use, and presence of the HLA-B58:01 allele. The 2020 ACR gout guidelines conditionally recommend genetic testing for HLA-B58:01 before initiation of allopurinol therapy in all patients of southeast Asian or African descent, given the high prevalence (4%-10%) of the allele in those populations. Patients who are HLA-B*58:01 positive should usually receive alternative treatment.

Febuxostat is as efficacious as allopurinol, but it is less likely to cause hypersensitivity reactions and is FDA approved in mild to moderate CKD. Elevated aminotransferase levels can rarely occur, and liver enzymes should be monitored. In February 2019, the FDA issued a boxed warning regarding cardiovascular risk with febuxostat, limiting its approved use to patients who are unresponsive to or cannot tolerate allopurinol. However, subsequent studies have not observed a similar cardiovascular risk.

Xanthine oxidase inhibitors should generally not be coadministered with purine analogues, such as azathioprine, because the combination can result in myelosuppression.

The uricosuric agent probenecid is infrequently used as a single agent because it is less effective than xanthine oxidase inhibitors; it should be avoided in patients with CKD (estimated glomerular filtration rate <50 mL/min/1.73 m^2) or nephrolithiasis. Combination therapy with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor and probenecid may occasionally be more effective than a xanthine oxidase inhibitor alone; however, this approach is rarely necessary because of the success in titrating doses of xanthine oxidase inhibitors to achieve the desired effect.

Pegloticase, a recombinant form of uricase, is an option for patients with severe recurrent and/or tophaceous gout who cannot tolerate or are resistant to standard therapies. Infused every 2 weeks, pegloticase lowers serum urate to nearly zero. When pegloticase is used alone, 40% of patients develop antibodies to the drug, rendering it ineffective and increasing the likelihood of infusion reactions. Pretreatment and coadministration of methotrexate can suppress tachyphylaxis, thereby reducing infusion reactions, and permit successful pegloticase use in roughly 80% of patients. This strategy is FDA approved. Nonetheless, pegloticase should be discontinued in any patient for whom it ceases to work; serum urate level should be checked before each infusion, and pegloticase should be discontinued if the serum urate level exceeds 6.0 mg/dL (0.35 mmol/L) on two consecutive assessments (indicating antidrug antibody formation). Moreover, pegloticase should never be used concurrently with oral urate-lowering agents because these agents can obscure the ability to determine whether pegloticase is ceasing to work based on serum urate level. Pegloticase is contraindicated in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.

Whenever urate-lowering therapy is initiated for gout, mobilization of monosodium urate crystals from joints and soft tissues can provoke flares. Accordingly, patients starting urate-lowering therapy during intercritical periods should be prescribed anti-inflammatory prophylaxis. The ACR strongly recommends continuing prophylaxis for 3 to 6 months, with ongoing evaluation and continued prophylaxis as needed if flares continue. Most patients tolerate colchicine, 0.6 mg once or twice daily; for those who do not, low-dose NSAIDs or glucocorticoids are appropriate substitutes.

Calcium pyrophosphate (CPP) crystals can deposit in cartilage, leading to several different kinds of joint problems. The following are the four phenotypes of calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD):

  • Asymptomatic CPPD
  • Acute CPP crystal arthritis
  • Chronic CPP crystal inflammatory arthritis
  • Osteoarthritis with CPPD

CPPD primarily affects older patients. The risk for cartilage calcification (chondrocalcinosis) doubles every decade past 60 years, and nearly half of individuals in their late 80s have CPP visible on plain radiographs. For younger patients with CPPD, laboratory evaluation for contributory metabolic diseases (hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypophosphatasia, hypomagnesemia) is warranted.

The pathophysiology of CPPD is incompletely understood. Pyrophosphate produced by chondrocytes likely precipitates with extracellular calcium to form CPP crystals, which then deposit and can activate inflammatory pathways, resulting in an acute arthritic flare. Osteoarthritis may drive chondrocyte injury to promote pyrophosphate secretion. Conversely, CPPD may drive osteoarthritis by causing mechanical damage and inducing proinflammatory activity within cartilage and synovium.

Asymptomatic CPPD occurs as radiographic changes in the absence of clinical symptoms. Cartilage calcification (chondrocalcinosis) appears as a linear opacity below the surface of articular cartilage (

) and can also be detected using musculoskeletal ultrasonography. It most commonly occurs in the knees, wrists (triangular fibrocartilage), pelvis (symphysis pubis), and metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, in descending order. Asymptomatic CPPD is common in older patients and in typical osteoarthritic joints, where it may be a consequence of osteoarthritis-related cartilage dysfunction.

Acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout) typically presents as monoarticular inflammatory arthritis, characterized by sudden onset of swelling, pain, loss of function, tenderness, and warmth of the affected joint (commonly a knee or wrist). Like gout flares, CPP flares may be provoked by systemic insults, such as major surgery or acute illness. Flares are typically milder than gout flares and less commonly affect the MTP joint, but if untreated, they can persist for weeks or months.

Definitive diagnosis requires identifying CPP crystals (along with neutrophils) in synovial fluid; in contrast to urate crystals, CPP crystals are rhomboid-shaped and exhibit weakly positive birefringence (blue when parallel to and yellow when perpendicular to the polarizing axis of an optical filter). As in gout flares, joint infection may coexist with acute CPP arthritis, and synovial fluid Gram stain and culture are usually warranted. Radiographic evidence of cartilage calcification in older patients with acute monoarticular arthritis suggests, but is not diagnostic of, acute CPP crystal arthritis.

The crowned dens syndrome is a rare presentation of acute CPP crystal arthritis involving the C2 vertebra. Radiographically it may present as calcification of the cartilage over the dens. Patients present with acute neck pain, fever, and headache, mimicking meningitis.

Chronic CPP arthropathy may present in one of two patterns: (1) chronic CPP crystal inflammatory arthritis or (2) osteoarthritis with CPPD. Chronic CPP crystal inflammatory arthritis is a chronic, symmetric, deforming polyarthritis often involving the wrists and MCP joints (“pseudo–rheumatoid arthritis”); it is rare and difficult to treat. CPPD-associated osteoarthritis manifests as typical osteoarthritic findings in joints not commonly associated with osteoarthritis (such as shoulders or MCP joints); slowly progressive joint destruction occurs in the absence of clinical signs of inflammation. Radiographic CPPD often precedes osteoarthritis onset, suggesting a causal role for CPP.

For patients with CPPD related to hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypophosphatasia, or hypomagnesemia, clinical manifestations include those of the coexisting metabolic disorder. Hooked “beak” osteophytes of the second and third MCP joints are particularly characteristic of coexisting hemochromatosis, and evaluation with HFE genetic testing is warranted.

In contrast to gout, there is no known mechanism for dissolving articular CPP crystals or preventing their formation. Instead, treatment aims at reducing the inflammatory manifestations of the disease ( [Table: Table: Management of Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition]

). Associated metabolic conditions should be treated, but this treatment rarely results in CPPD disease remission.

Basic calcium phosphate (BCP) deposition occurs in older persons and targets both articular cartilage and periarticular tendons and ligaments. BCP deposition is rarely associated with inflammatory arthritis and periarthritis, most classically manifesting in older women as “Milwaukee shoulder,” an inflammatory state that causes progressive destruction of the rotator cuff and glenohumeral joint. Diagnosis is usually clinical; radiographs show calcium deposition in the affected tissues. Visualization of BCP crystals requires special stains and/or electron microscopy and is rarely performed.

Systemic Vasculitis

Vasculitis is inflammation of blood vessels, including capillaries, arteries, and veins, that leads to downstream ischemia and tissue damage. Clinical manifestations are based on the size and location of affected blood vessels. Vasculitis can be primary, secondary to another underlying autoimmune disease, or triggered by other causes ( [Table: Table: Causes of Secondary Vasculitis]

). Vasculitis mimics must be considered in the differential diagnosis ( [Table: Table: Differential Diagnosis of Vasculitis]

).

Vasculitis encompasses many diseases with variable clinical presentations and pathophysiology. A well-established classification scheme focuses on size of the involved vessels. Vessel size can provide insight into processes and presentations, but conditions and vessel sizes may overlap (see

).

Primary autoimmune vasculitis disorders are discussed in this section. For a discussion of Behçet syndrome, see Behçet Syndrome in Rheumatology.

Giant cell arteritis (GCA; also called temporal arteritis) is the most commonly diagnosed vasculitis. It usually affects patients older than 50 years (peak incidence, 70-80 years). The female-to-male ratio is about 3:1.

Histologically, GCA is characterized by granulomatous inflammation of large and medium-sized arteries, with infiltration of CD4-positive lymphocytes, macrophages, and multinucleated giant cells. Inflammatory disruption of the internal elastic lamina is common. Involved vessels include the aorta; its major branches off the arch; and secondary branch vessels, including the external carotid, subclavian, axillary, temporal, ophthalmic, ciliary, occipital, and vertebral arteries. The vessel involved dictates the clinical symptoms.

Common GCA symptoms include headache (typically temporal but occasionally more diffuse), constitutional symptoms, concomitant polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR), and scalp tenderness over the temporal artery. Headache and scalp tenderness can be unilateral or bilateral. Jaw aching and fatigue with chewing indicate ischemia (claudication) of the muscles of mastication. The most feared complication of GCA is ischemic optic neuropathy due to occlusion of the posterior ciliary artery, or occasionally the ophthalmic artery, which can cause irreversible blindness. Early recognition and treatment of any vision change (e.g., reversible diplopia or visual defect) are critical. Intracranial ischemic strokes are rare.

Extracranial disease involving great vessels in the chest and arms occurs in up to 50% of patients but can be subclinical; it also can result in upper or lower extremity claudication. Severe but uncommon complications include aortic aneurysm and dissection. Up to 50% of patients with GCA have PMR, which may occur before, concurrent with, or after diagnosis of GCA (see Polymyalgia Rheumatica in Rheumatology). GCA may also occur while glucocorticoids for PMR are being tapered.

Physical examination may reveal scalp or temporal artery tenderness, nodularity, and induration. Large-vessel involvement can manifest as reduced peripheral pulses; discrepant blood pressures; and bruits over the aorta and carotid, subclavian, and femoral vessels.

Laboratory studies almost always show elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C-reactive protein (CRP) level. Rarely, however, the inflammatory markers may be normal. Nonspecific evidence of inflammation may include anemia, elevated serum ferritin level, and thrombocytosis. Serologic testing reveals no specific autoantibodies (although low antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor levels are common in older patients).

GCA is suspected on the basis of clinical presentation; new or atypical headache, jaw claudication, or visual changes in a patient older than 50 years, especially with concurrent PMR, should raise suspicion. The diagnosis should be confirmed, when possible, by temporal artery biopsy, temporal artery ultrasonography, and/or imaging of the great vessels. Preferred imaging modalities include arterial ultrasonography, magnetic resonance angiography, CT angiography, and fluorodeoxyglucose PET. Ideally, imaging should be performed before or within 3 days of beginning glucocorticoid treatment. However, treatment should not be delayed for testing.

Temporal artery biopsy is diagnostic, but false-negative results are common because of skip lesions; adequate biopsy sampling (>1-cm length of temporal artery) is crucial. Although bilateral temporal artery biopsy can slightly increase the yield, unilateral biopsy is recommended. Temporal artery biopsy findings can remain abnormal for at least 1 month after initiation of glucocorticoids; however, biopsy should be performed as soon as possible. Given the risk for blindness, treatment should be initiated as soon as the diagnosis is suspected and should not be delayed for biopsy. If the pretest likelihood of disease is high, treatment may be continued even in the presence of a negative biopsy result.

Suspected GCA should be treated immediately to prevent vision loss. Beginning high-dose prednisone (1 mg/kg/d, up to 80 mg) is recommended. Intravenous pulse methylprednisolone for 3 days is recommended for acute vision loss; however, data on this approach are limited, and established blindness is usually irreversible. Prednisone plus the interleukin-6 inhibitor tocilizumab is conditionally recommended as initial therapy once GCA is diagnosed because the combination has improved efficacy compared with prednisone alone and typically permits faster glucocorticoid taper. Upadacitinib, a Janus kinase inhibitor, is also an effective treatment for GCA and can be used as a glucocorticoid-sparing agent. Symptoms and inflammatory markers usually respond rapidly to treatment; lack of response should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis. High-dose prednisone is maintained for 2 to 4 weeks. At treatment initiation, all patients should undergo bone densitometry to stratify risk for glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis and receive prophylaxis as needed.

After symptoms resolve, prednisone is tapered as tolerated. Glucocorticoids should be discontinued, if possible, within 6 months, but longer treatment may be warranted as dictated by disease activity. Patients should be monitored for symptom recurrence, and new or recurrent symptoms should prompt noninvasive reevaluation for active disease, which may include imaging. ESR and CRP should be monitored monthly but should not be the sole indication for adjusting glucocorticoid dose. Mild flares can be managed with modest increases in prednisone and slower tapering. The addition of low-dose methotrexate may facilitate glucocorticoid tapering and may be considered in patients with significant glucocorticoid contraindications, although data are limited.

GCA is self-limited in some patients (lasting 2-6 years) and chronic in others. Patients with GCA have a higher risk for aortic aneurysms and dissections, and patients with large-vessel involvement should undergo periodic monitoring on an individualized basis.

Although not a vasculitis, PMR is an inflammatory disorder that frequently (in up to 50% of cases) accompanies GCA. PMR and GCA likely reflect a clinical spectrum with similar patient demographic characteristics, although PMR occurs 3 to 10 times more frequently. Patients presenting with PMR should be asked about arteritis symptoms because 10% to 20% have or will develop concomitant GCA.

PMR classically presents with pain and stiffness of the shoulder and hip girdles, but in approximately 20% of cases, patients may also have peripheral inflammatory arthritis affecting the small joints of the hand. Symptoms may affect some or all of these areas; symmetric presentation and abrupt symptom onset are classic. Pain and stiffness are most pronounced in the morning. Subdeltoid and subacromial bursitis and biceps tenosynovitis are common features of PMR. Mild synovitis in the wrists and metacarpophalangeal joints can be seen in about half of patients. Inflammatory markers are usually highly elevated, although ESR is normal in some cases. PMR is diagnosed clinically. Temporal artery biopsy should be performed only if GCA is suspected.

Unlike GCA, PMR responds dramatically to moderate-dose prednisone (12.5-20 mg/d); lack of a significant improvement within a few days should prompt consideration of alternate diagnoses. Prednisone taper is initiated 4 weeks after symptoms resolve, although the overall tapering regimen can last months to years.

Methotrexate can be used in select cases as a weak glucocorticoid-sparing agent. Sarilumab, an interleukin-6 inhibitor, has been approved by the FDA to treat PMR in patients with inadequate response to glucocorticoids or intolerance to glucocorticoid taper.

Prognosis of PMR is good, although periodic recurrences are common. Monitoring of recurrence is managed similarly to the approach used for GCA. For relapses, guidelines for the management of PMR (developed by the American College of Rheumatology and the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology [formerly called the European League Against Rheumatism]) recommend increasing the prednisone dose to the last prerelapse dose at which the patient was doing well, followed by a gradual reduction within 4 to 8 weeks to the relapse dose.

Takayasu arteritis (TA) causes inflammation of the large vessels, most commonly the aorta, followed by the subclavian, common carotid, and renal arteries; the pulmonary arteries may also be involved. TA is rare, with a prevalence of 40 per million in Japan and up to 8 per million elsewhere. Although vascular involvement and clinical features overlap somewhat with GCA, TA predominantly affects women younger than 40 years. Arterial lesions are often stenotic (“pulseless disease”), and one third of lesions are aneurysmal. Histopathology is similar to that of GCA.

TA manifestations include new-onset hypertension, lightheadedness, constitutional symptoms, limb claudication, tenderness over the carotid arteries, reduced pulses, arterial bruits, and blood pressure discrepancies between the extremities. Heart failure related to aortic insufficiency or coronary artery disease may occur. Neurologic complications include vertigo, transient ischemic attack, and stroke.

As with GCA, laboratory studies are nonspecific and reveal anemia as well as elevated ESR and CRP level. Vessel imaging using magnetic resonance angiography (preferred), fluorodeoxyglucose PET, and CT angiography is recommended and frequently diagnostic. Large-vessel imaging may demonstrate arterial stenosis or aneurysm (

).

Primary treatment of TA is high-dose oral glucocorticoids (1 mg/kg/d, up to 80 mg/d) with a slow taper. Guidelines conditionally recommend adjunctive treatment with nonbiologic immunosuppressive medications (e.g., methotrexate, azathioprine) to mitigate glucocorticoid exposure. For refractory disease, adding a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor is preferred over adding tocilizumab. Endovascular or reconstructive vascular procedures are sometimes required; if possible, these should be performed during periods of inactive disease.

The leading cause of death is heart failure; stroke and cardiovascular disease also contribute to morbidity. The 10-year survival rate is 90%.

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a rare systemic necrotizing vasculitis that affects medium-sized and sometimes small arteries. Prevalence is approximately 31 per million but is declining. Average age at onset is 50 years.

Historically, PAN has been strongly associated with hepatitis B virus (HBV). Because HBV prevalence has declined with the advent of the HBV vaccine and antiviral treatment, the proportion of patients with HBV-associated PAN has declined from 36% to less than 5% of all PAN cases. PAN may also occur in association with hepatitis C virus. However, most contemporary PAN cases are idiopathic. Pathophysiology is not well understood.

PAN most commonly affects the skin, peripheral nervous system, gastrointestinal tract, and kidneys; the disease does not involve the lungs. See [Table: Table: Features of Polyarteritis Nodosa]

for the clinical and laboratory findings. When present, kidney involvement is renovascular rather than glomerular and often leads to hypertension. Cutaneous PAN is a variant confined to the skin. Cutaneous features include the following:

  • Livedo reticularis (

) - Retiform purpura (

) - Painful deep ulcers with skin necrosis due to ischemic infarction

Because of the intense inflammation of medium-sized vessels, subcutaneous nodules may be palpable.

Diagnosis is often confirmed via angiography of the mesenteric and/or renal vasculature, which demonstrates saccular microaneurysms and areas of narrowing in medium-sized vessels. The gold standard for diagnosing PAN is histologic identification of focal segmental panmural necrotizing inflammation of a medium-sized vessel, obtained on biopsy of involved, easily accessible tissue (e.g., skin or a superficial nerve).

Intravenous pulse glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide are indicated for severe organ-threatening disease; glucocorticoids and disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs are used for milder disease. HBV-associated PAN is treated with short-term glucocorticoids, antiviral medication, and plasmapheresis if necessary.

The 5-year survival rate for treated PAN is 80%, and the relapse rate is 10% to 20%.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS) is a rare small- and medium-vessel vasculitis; it affects the brain parenchyma, spinal cord, and leptomeninges. Incidence is 2.4 per 100,000. Median age at onset is 50 years, and the male-to-female ratio is 2:1. The three histologic presentations have a patchy distribution:

  • Granulomatous (most common)
  • Lymphocytic
  • Necrotizing

Patients with PACNS usually present with gradual and progressive symptoms of headache, cognitive impairment, and neurologic deficits as well as transient ischemic attacks and strokes.

Laboratory findings are normal. Cerebrospinal fluid is abnormal but nonspecific in 80% to 90% of patients, with elevated protein levels, lymphocytic pleocytosis, and occasional oligoclonal bands. Inflammatory markers, such as ESR, are rarely elevated (in contrast to other systemic vasculitides).

MRI shows nonspecific white and gray matter changes and infarcts. Magnetic resonance angiography and CT angiography have limited usefulness because of poor resolution. Visualization of the vasculature with conventional cerebral angiography is a common part of the evaluation when PACNS is suspected, based on the clinical presentation and MRI findings. It may demonstrate vessel “beading” (alternating dilations and stenoses) but has limited sensitivity and specificity. Brain biopsy should be performed in any patient in whom the diagnosis is seriously considered; however, the patchy distribution of findings results in a 50% false-negative rate.

Evaluation also focuses on excluding other conditions, including infection, malignancy (e.g., intravascular central nervous system lymphoma), and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome.

PACNS is treated with high-dose glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide. Patients often have permanent disability from neurologic damage, and the recurrence rate is 27%.

Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis and the most common type of vasculitis in children. It presents with fever, rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, conjunctival congestion, and mucositis.

The most feared complication is coronary artery aneurysm, which can lead to coronary occlusion and ischemia. Although Kawasaki disease almost never develops in adulthood, adults who had Kawasaki disease as a child may have residual coronary aneurysms that require monitoring and management.

A Kawasaki-like syndrome (multisystem inflammatory syndrome) has been identified in patients who have been infected with COVID-19 (see Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Rheumatology).

ANCA-associated vasculitis includes three diseases characterized by pauci-immune small blood vessel inflammation ( [Table: Table: Features of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis]

):

  • Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
  • Microscopic polyangiitis
  • Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis

The presence of ANCA can be detected on serologic testing and helps to define the diseases.

The two types of vasculitis-associated ANCA are p-ANCA (perinuclear, directed against myeloperoxidase) and c-ANCA (cytoplasmic, directed against proteinase 3 [PR3]). Perinuclear and cytoplasmic refer to patterns of immunofluorescent staining; enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays against myeloperoxidase and PR3 are used to confirm antibody positivity.

ANCA may play a direct role in disease propagation by activating primed endothelial cells and neutrophils, leading to vessel damage. The granulomatous inflammation in some forms of ANCA-associated vasculitis suggests a role for cell-mediated immunity. There is increasing recognition that the alternative complement pathway is involved in the pathogenesis of ANCA-associated vasculitis. Although most cases of ANCA-associated vasculitis are idiopathic, a few are drug induced (e.g., by propylthiouracil or levamisole, an adulterant often found in cocaine).

See ANCA-Associated Glomerulonephritis in Nephrology for details on ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is the most common ANCA-associated vasculitis, with an annual incidence of 10 to 20 per million.

GPA affects the small vessels of the upper and lower airways (sinuses, lungs), kidneys, eyes (scleritis), skin, and peripheral nerves (see [Table: Table: Features of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis]

). At least 50% of patients have constitutional symptoms. Most patients (>95%) are ANCA positive, with antibodies against PR3/c-ANCA.

GPA presents as systemic or localized disease. The systemic form is more common and involves major organs. Patients with localized disease are more likely to be younger and female; have mainly ear, nose, and throat involvement; and are less likely to be PR3 positive.

In the setting of a classic clinical presentation and positivity for anti-PR3/c-ANCA antibodies, diagnosis of GPA is straightforward. However, because of the significant risks associated with treatment, biopsy of involved tissue is usually recommended if possible. Histopathology of most tissues demonstrates pauci-immune necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis.

To induce remission in organ-threatening or life-threatening disease, treatment of GPA typically consists of glucocorticoids plus either rituximab or cyclophosphamide; selected patients may benefit from plasma exchange. For patients without organ-threatening disease, glucocorticoids and rituximab are recommended for induction therapy; methotrexate or mycophenolate mofetil are alternatives to rituximab. Avacopan can be used during induction to decrease glucocorticoid exposure and toxicity.

Once remission is achieved, patients should receive maintenance therapy with rituximab, azathioprine, or methotrexate; rituximab appears to be most effective for preventing relapse and is preferred. Maintenance therapy is recommended for 24 to 48 months. Glucocorticoids alone are insufficient to control GPA and should be tapered during the first year after diagnosis given their known adverse effects. With use of these treatments, GPA mortality has declined from 90% to around 10%. Kidney failure and infection remain the main causes of death.

The annual incidence of microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) is estimated at 3.6 per million, with the highest predominance in Asian countries. Average age at onset is 50 to 60 years, with a predilection for men over women (1.8:1). ANCAs are less prevalent in MPA than in GPA (50%-75%) and are usually directed against myeloperoxidase.

Like GPA, MPA characteristically affects the lungs and kidneys, along with other organ systems. In contrast to GPA, MPA tends to spare the upper airways, and lung involvement is not granulomatous on biopsy. See [Table: Table: Features of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis]

for the characteristics of MPA.

Diagnosis is suspected on the basis of typical clinical findings and is supported by positivity for myeloperoxidase ANCA. The diagnostic gold standard is a biopsy specimen demonstrating necrotizing pauci-immune vasculitis of small vessels in any affected tissue. In general, the absence of granulomas distinguishes MPA from GPA. However, kidney biopsy specimens from patients with GPA often lack granulomas; in such cases, other clinical features and serologic tests help to differentiate between GPA and MPA.

Treatment of MPA is similar to that of GPA.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is the rarest ANCA-associated vasculitis, with an annual incidence of 0.11 to 2.66 per million. Eosinophil activation, infiltration, and degranulation participate in disease pathogenesis.

The typical patient with EGPA has a prodromal history of difficult-to-treat or glucocorticoid-dependent asthma (96%-100%), rhinitis, and/or atopy. This prodrome is followed by increased peripheral and tissue eosinophilia, with migratory pulmonary infiltrates and, less commonly, endomyocardial infiltration and gastrointestinal disease. The acute vasculitic phase includes the following:

  • Mononeuritis multiplex or peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy (≤75%)
  • Kidney involvement (25%)
  • Skin involvement (60%)

See [Table: Table: Features of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis]

for the characteristics of EGPA.

Laboratory findings show peripheral eosinophilia (eosinophil count >10% or >1500/μL [1.5 × 10^9/L]). Only about 40% to 60% of patients have positivity for ANCA, which is usually directed against myeloperoxidase.

Diagnosis is based on typical clinical findings, eosinophilia, and biopsy specimens demonstrating fibrinoid necrosis and eosinophilic infiltration of vessel walls, as well as extravascular granuloma formation. Because cardiac disease is the leading cause of death in patients with EGPA, the ACR conditionally recommends that all patients diagnosed with EGPA undergo baseline screening echocardiography.

In EGPA, glucocorticoids alone may be sufficient for mild disease, such as asthma and allergic symptoms. Mepolizumab, a monoclonal antibody that binds interleukin-5, is FDA approved for EGPA and has a favorable safety profile; it can be used for initial treatment in nonsevere disease or maintenance therapy. For kidney, gastrointestinal, cardiac, or neurologic involvement, induction therapy includes the combination of glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide; rituximab is an alternative to cyclophosphamide. Options for maintenance therapy in severe disease include methotrexate, azathioprine, mepolizumab, or rituximab.

EGPA has the lowest mortality rate among all forms of ANCA-associated vasculitis. The 5-year survival rate is 97%, and the relapse rate is 28%.

Immune complexes develop from cross-linking of multiple antigens and antibodies. Immune complexes can deposit in small vessels, leading to complement and neutrophil activation, with consequent inflammation and tissue damage. Although any tissue or organ may be affected, the classic finding is invariably in the skin. Inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation from damaged vessels result in nonblanching palpable purpura, usually in dependent areas (

). The various immune complex–mediated vasculitides are distinguished by the antigen that drives them, the class of antibody generated, and differences in clinical presentations.

Cryoglobulins cause an immune complex–mediated small-vessel vasculitis primarily affecting the skin, peripheral nervous system, and kidneys. Central nervous system involvement may rarely occur. In addition to their ability to form immune complexes, all cryoglobulins demonstrate the unique feature of precipitating in the cold. See Cryoglobulinemia in Hematology for further details on cryoglobulins.

Mixed cryoglobulinemia, which accounts for 75% to 90% of all cases of cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, is rare, with an estimated prevalence of 1 in 100,000. Mixed cryoglobulinemias are usually associated with infections (such as with hepatitis C virus), autoimmune diseases (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjögren disease), and, rarely, lymphoproliferative disorders.

Cutaneous symptoms (palpable purpura, digital ischemia, ulcers, necrosis, and livedo reticularis) are seen in about 90% of patients. Other common manifestations include peripheral neuropathy, arthralgia without arthritis, and glomerulonephritis (usually membranoproliferative). Pulmonary and/or gastrointestinal involvement is rare.

Testing for cryoglobulins requires that a sample of blood be maintained at 37.0 °C (98.6 °F) until clotting is complete to avoid incorporation of the cryoglobulins into the clot. Incorrect sample collection can result in false-negative cryoglobulin results. In addition to detection of cryoglobulins, laboratory abnormalities frequently include depressed C4 complement, low CH~50 levels, and elevated rheumatoid factor levels.

Treatment of cryoglobulinemia requires first addressing the underlying cause (e.g., antiviral therapy for hepatitis C virus–related cryoglobulinemia). When the manifestations of the cryoglobulinemia are severe (e.g., glomerulonephritis, ulcerating cutaneous lesions, digital gangrene), the vasculitis itself must also be treated. Standard first-line therapy is glucocorticoids and rituximab in combination.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) is a common vasculitis of childhood that rarely occurs in adults. Onset is usually preceded by upper respiratory tract infection, often with streptococcal bacteria.

Patients with IgA vasculitis typically present with palpable purpura in dependent areas. Other common findings include arthritis and arthralgia (60%); abdominal pain or gastrointestinal bleeding (50%); and glomerulonephritis, which is more common in adults (30%) than children.

Kidney involvement confers a worse prognosis. Identification of kidney involvement is critical because although IgA vasculitis without nephritis can generally be managed conservatively, glomerular disease may require immunosuppressive therapy in severe cases. Urinalysis findings in IgA vasculitis with nephritis may include hematuria, erythrocyte casts, and proteinuria. See IgA Vasculitis in Nephrology for further information on kidney involvement in IgA vasculitis.

There are no specific laboratory tests for diagnosis, but adults suspected of having IgA vasculitis (characteristic rash, abdominal pain or bleeding, and arthritis or arthralgia) should be evaluated for kidney involvement via urinalysis with microscopy and measurement of urine protein. Diagnosis is confirmed by histology. Skin biopsy demonstrates leukocytoclastic vasculitis with heavy deposits of IgA and complement. When characteristic skin histology accompanies the typical clinical syndrome of IgA vasculitis, kidney biopsy is rarely necessary. If a kidney biopsy is performed, histology shows IgA deposition within the mesangium.

Although IgA vasculitis in children tends to be self-limited, adults are more likely to develop persistent nephropathy and may require treatment, depending on the clinical manifestation. This treatment includes NSAIDs for pain and glucocorticoids or other immunomodulating agents.

Hypersensitivity vasculitis (also known as cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis, cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis, or cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis) is mediated by immune complex deposition confined to the skin. It may be triggered by an antigen, such as a drug or infection; in 50% of cases, the antigen is unknown. The condition affects male and female persons of all ages.

The most common presentation of hypersensitivity vasculitis is palpable purpura in dependent regions, often developing 7 to 10 days after exposure to a triggering antigen. Lesions appear in “crops” and resolve over a few weeks after the antigen is removed. Internal organs are unaffected.

Skin biopsy demonstrates leukocytoclastic vasculitis without immunofluorescent deposits. Evaluation should be guided by clinical signs and symptoms and may require only a complete blood count, basic chemistries, and urinalysis.

Removal of the antigen (if identified) and supportive care are usually sufficient. Resolution within a month is the rule. If symptoms persist or recur, anti-inflammatory agents, topical or low-dose systemic glucocorticoids, colchicine, or dapsone may be helpful.

Miscellaneous Systemic Inflammatory Diseases

Multisystem inflammatory syndrome (MIS) is an uncommon, severe immune-mediated disorder that follows an antecedent SARS-CoV-2 illness. It is recognized both in children and adolescents (MIS-C) and among adults (MIS-A). The adult form frequently results in inflammation affecting the heart, gastrointestinal tract, skin, and brain. MIS may arise in previously healthy persons and may develop after both asymptomatic and severe acute illness induced by SARS-CoV-2.

Consequently, MIS may occur as a distinct illness, days to weeks after the apparent resolution of the primary acute stage of COVID-19. Moreover, MIS may be so severe, in and of itself, to result in shock, multiorgan failure, and heightened risk for death.

The following is the CDC case definition of MIS-A: a patient aged 21 years or older who has been hospitalized for at least 24 hours, or with an illness resulting in death; who meets the criteria outlined in [Table: Table: Case Definition for MIS in Adults]

; and for whom there is no other more likely alternative diagnosis for the illness.

Although anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive agents are often used to manage severe MIS-A (including intravenous immune globulin and high-dose glucocorticoids), the optimal management remains uncertain.

The epidemiology of Behçet syndrome, a systemic vasculitis, varies widely. Endemic areas are along the historic Silk Route from East Asia to the Mediterranean. Prevalence is highest in Turkey (20-600/100,000). Outside of endemic areas, Behçet syndrome tends to be less severe.

The main genetic risk factor is the major histocompatibility complex I antigen HLA-B51. Many experts believe that the condition represents mixed mechanisms involving both autoimmunity and autoinflammation.

Behçet syndrome consists of a constellation of characteristic signs and symptoms, most commonly including mucocutaneous ulcers, skin lesions, and inflammatory eye disease. Most patients with Behçet syndrome present with painful oral and/or genital ulcers (

). Genital ulcers typically occur on the scrotum and vulva and tend to scar. Cutaneous manifestations include pustular lesions, skin ulcers, acneiform nodules, and erythema nodosum. Eye disease includes panuveitis, optic neuritis, and retinal vasculitis.

Behçet syndrome has several other possible clinical manifestations. Gastrointestinal involvement may be present, making the distinction between Behçet syndrome and inflammatory bowel disease challenging. Arthritis and enthesitis may be present. Vascular involvement is seen in both the arterial and venous systems. In the arterial bed, both aneurysms and thrombosis may be seen; the pulmonary bed may be affected. The most common form of venous disease is thrombosis, which occurs in the lower extremities but may also occur in the cerebral and cardiac circulations. Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis) can also occur. Central nervous system disease may include parenchymal brain involvement, especially in the brainstem, as well as aseptic meningitis. Pyramidal, motor, and behavioral changes may occur.

Diagnosis of Behçet syndrome is based on the presence of characteristic signs and symptoms ( [Table: Table: International Criteria for Behçet Syndrome]

). Pathergy—accumulation of a pustular neutrophilic infiltrate after puncture of the skin with a sterile needle—strongly suggests Behçet syndrome (

). However, results of pathergy tests are often negative, particularly in nonendemic areas. Imaging may define typical, but nonpathognomonic, patterns of vascular involvement.

Management involves selecting agents appropriate to the type and severity of clinical involvement. For oral ulcers, topical and systemic glucocorticoids may be used. Apremilast, a phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor, is FDA approved for oral ulcers in Behçet syndrome. Thalidomide and colchicine are both accepted treatments; colchicine may be better for arthritis than for oral ulcers. However, these two oral agents are not FDA approved for Behçet syndrome. Topical and/or oral 5-aminosalicylic acid derivatives may be used for gastrointestinal involvement. For resistant severe ulcers or for vascular, ophthalmologic, or central nervous system involvement, oral disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as azathioprine and cyclosporine, may be considered. Tumor necrosis factor inhibitors, particularly infliximab and adalimumab, are frequently effective. In severe cases of vascular or neurologic involvement, cyclophosphamide may be an option. Acute thrombosis should be treated with immunosuppressives, in addition to appropriate use of anticoagulants, because the cause of the thrombosis is inflammatory rather than thrombotic.

Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) is a noninflammatory condition characterized by calcification and ossification of spinal ligaments (especially the anterior longitudinal ligament) and entheses (tendon and ligament attachments to bone). DISH is more common in men and usually presents with back pain and stiffness, with the thoracic spine most often involved. Although spinal ligamentous ossification is also seen in ankylosing spondylitis, the spinal calcifications in DISH demonstrate confluent (“flowing”) ossification and are less vertically oriented than those seen with ankylosing spondylitis. Notably, DISH also lacks involvement of the sacroiliac joints.

Radiographic changes characteristic of DISH include confluent ossification of at least four contiguous vertebral levels, usually on the right side of the spine (

). It has been suggested that the aorta may serve as a mechanical barrier to the production of bony hyperostosis on the left side of the spine.

Relapsing polychondritis is a rare condition (annual incidence, 3.5 cases/1 million) characterized by inflammation and destruction of cartilaginous structures.

The pathophysiology of relapsing polychondritis is poorly understood. An association with HLA-DR4 supports an autoimmune cause, and laboratory studies sometimes show antibodies to various cartilage components.

Cartilaginous structures most characteristically involved include the ear (especially the helix and antihelix of the external ear), nose, and throat. The initial presentation is frequently redness and swelling of the external ear, but it may progress to structural collapse and a floppy appearance (

). Middle or inner ear involvement may cause hearing loss. Other cartilaginous structures that can be affected include the bridge of the nose and articular cartilage, leading to saddle nose deformity and inflammatory arthritis, respectively. Involvement of the tracheal rings can cause airway obstruction (including subglottic and tracheal stenosis), requiring surgical intervention. Inflammatory eye disease is common during the course of the disease.

Diagnosis is made clinically; biopsies are rarely necessary but, if done, will reveal a polymorphic inflammatory cell infiltrate. Tracheobronchial involvement mandates an aggressive evaluation, including imaging (typically CT), pulmonary function testing, and, in some cases, tracheobronchoscopy.

In 30% of cases, relapsing polychondritis may be associated with other autoimmune diseases, including ANCA-associated vasculitis. The MAGIC (mouth and genital ulcerations with inflamed cartilage) syndrome appears to represent a confluence of relapsing polychondritis and Behçet syndrome. Persons with an overlap of these two disorders are reported to have a higher prevalence of aortitis, Raynaud phenomenon, and elevated anti–collagen II antibody titers.

Management of relapsing polychondritis depends on severity. For mild symptoms, NSAIDs and dapsone may be considered. For acute and/or severe involvement, high-dose glucocorticoids are the initial treatment. Oral immunosuppressants (e.g., methotrexate) may be added. The tumor necrosis factor inhibitors infliximab and adalimumab have been used to good effect. The anti–interleukin-6 agent tocilizumab may also be effective.

Autoinflammatory diseases are monogenic conditions in which innate immune pathways are activated independently of any specific known antigen. The result is periodic or chronic inflammation, fever, and multiorgan involvement. The best-studied of these conditions result from variants that cause enhanced function of inflammasomes, multimolecular complexes that raise the levels of activated interleukin-1β.

In familial Mediterranean fever, variants of pyrin (a protein expressed in neutrophils, eosinophils, monocytes, and dendritic cells) lead to inflammasome activation, causing fever, arthritis, rash, and sterile peritonitis. Renal amyloidosis may ensue. The cryopyrin-associated periodic fever syndromes result from activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome. In the pediatric version (neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease), inflammation leads to permanent joint deformity, encephalitis, and, if not treated, early death; adult versions of cryopyrin-associated periodic fever syndromes are milder and may be triggered by cold. In TRAPS (tumor necrosis factor receptor–associated periodic fever syndrome), variants in the tumor necrosis factor receptor result in persistent activation of the receptor on inflammatory cells. Patients present with fever, chills, and severe muscle pain lasting more than 1 week. Other genetic variants can also lead to periodic fevers, such as through the activation of the signaling molecule nuclear factor-kappa B or through the unstimulated production of interferons.

To the extent possible, treatments address the involved signaling pathway. See [Table: Table: Select Autoinflammatory Diseases]

for features and treatment of these diseases.

The VEXAS (vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, autoinflammatory, somatic) syndrome is a newly recognized adult-onset autoinflammatory disorder caused by variants in UBA1, a gene encoding the ubiquitin-activating enzyme 1. VEXAS syndrome has an estimated prevalence of 1 in 13,591 adults and occurs almost exclusively in men, with disease prevalence rising with advancing age (1 in 4269 men older than age 50 years). Manifestations include the following:

  • Fever
  • Cytopenias
  • Characteristic vacuoles in myeloid and erythroid precursors
  • Dysplastic bone marrow
  • Neutrophilic cutaneous and pulmonary inflammation
  • Ocular involvement
  • Chondritis
  • Vasculitis
  • Venous thrombosis

Diagnosis is based on genetic testing. High-dose glucocorticoids and other immunosuppressive agents that target inflammatory pathways, such as Janus kinase inhibitors and IL-6 inhibitors, can be effective. Prognosis may be poor, including heightened risk for death.

Adult-onset Still disease is a rare systemic condition (prevalence, 1-10 cases/1 million) characterized by fever with daily evening spikes, evanescent salmon-colored macular or maculopapular rashes that peak with the fever, arthralgia, and elevated leukocyte counts. Adult-onset Still disease is thought to represent an overexpression of interleukin-1β and other inflammatory cytokines, and as such it is sometimes conceptualized as a polygenic autoinflammatory syndrome. Adult-onset Still disease may present as a single episode; may recur; or, most commonly, may be chronic and progressive (35%-67% of affected patients). Recent expert consensus indicates that adult-onset Still disease and systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis are the same disease and should be treated similarly. Both disorders may be complicated by macrophage activation syndrome.

The Yamaguchi criteria for adult-onset Still disease consist of four major and five minor criteria ( [Table: Table: Yamaguchi Criteria for Adult-Onset Still Disease]

). Diagnosis requires the presence of at least five criteria, including at least two major criteria. The presence of infection, malignancy, or another rheumatologic disorder known to mimic adult-onset Still disease precludes the diagnosis. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein levels are elevated; ferritin levels are often extremely high.

Past treatment options, including glucocorticoids and methotrexate, were frequently inadequate. Interleukin-1β–directed biologic therapies (e.g., anakinra, canakinumab) as well as anti–interleukin-6 receptor therapy (e.g., tocilizumab) have shown promise and should be used as early as possible in conjunction with short-term glucocorticoids (low or high dose based on the severity of the clinical presentation).

Sarcoidosis is a multisystem inflammatory disease characterized by formation of noncaseating granulomas in multiple organs and tissues. Although sarcoidosis most commonly affects the lungs (see Sarcoidosis in Pulmonary Medicine), approximately 50% of patients have extrapulmonary involvement and 2% have only extrapulmonary involvement.

Rheumatologic manifestations of sarcoidosis include arthritis, which can affect multiple joints and possibly lead to erosive damage, Jaccoud arthropathy (nonerosive joint deformity), and dactylitis. Myopathy may also occur. Bone involvement, reported in up to 15% of patients, is associated with a chronic course and poorer prognosis (

). Liver involvement is common but frequently asymptomatic; more serious involvement includes central nervous system, eye, and cardiac disease. Central nervous system sarcoidosis most commonly presents as brainstem involvement with cranial nerve deficits, but any part of the brain may be involved. Silent cardiac involvement occurs in at least 25% of cases; cardiac sarcoidosis may also cause symptomatic arrhythmias (including complete heart block) or heart failure.

Cutaneous sarcoidosis is seen in approximately 30% of patients. The spectrum of skin involvement is broad, including asymptomatic or pruritic plaques or papules, often violaceous, anywhere on the body. Lupus pernio is a specific form of sarcoidosis that manifests as violaceous infiltrative subcutaneous plaques or nodules on the nasal tip and central face (

).

A definitive diagnostic test for diagnosis does not exist. Diagnosis usually requires compatible clinical and radiographic manifestations, exclusion of other diseases that may have a similar presentation, and tissue biopsy specimens showing noncaseating granulomas. All patients with sarcoidosis should undergo ECG; further evaluation of systemic sarcoidosis should be defined by apparent signs and symptoms. Laboratory studies should include inflammatory markers, calcium, and vitamin D. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme levels are frequently elevated and may support the diagnosis, but they are nonspecific. Cardiac assessment may involve echocardiography, advanced cardiac imaging, and/or electrophysiologic monitoring.

Management of symptomatic extrapulmonary sarcoidosis almost always requires high-dose glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone, 40-60 mg/d). If glucocorticoids are ineffective or contraindicated or dose tapering leads to heightened disease activity, patients may be treated with thalidomide, methotrexate, or azathioprine. Cyclophosphamide or tumor necrosis factor inhibitors may be warranted in severe cases or when essential organs are at risk. Asymptomatic extrapulmonary sarcoidosis does not always require treatment. Sarcoidosis limited to the skin may respond to topical or intralesional agents or hydroxychloroquine, or it may require more aggressive systemic treatment.

Löfgren syndrome is a form of systemic sarcoidosis characterized by bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum (

), and migratory polyarthralgia, usually accompanied by fever. Ankle arthritis is a common site of joint involvement with Löfgren syndrome. It is more common in younger patients, women, and European persons of Scandinavian descent. Presence of all three parts of the triad is 95% specific for sarcoidosis, obviating the need for biopsy. Because Löfgren syndrome is usually self-limited, treatment focuses on symptom management, often with an NSAID, until the condition resolves.

IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is characterized by tumefactive infiltration of IgG4-bearing plasma cells and other lymphocytes, along with storiform fibrosis, into one or multiple organs, with resultant organ inflammation, enlargement, fibrosis, and dysfunction. Although initial reports of IgG4-RD concerned involvement of the pancreas (see Autoimmune Pancreatitis and IgG4 Disease in Gastroenterology), additional organs may be involved ( [Table: Table: Conditions Associated With IgG4-Related Disease]

). In 70% of cases, serum levels of IgG4 antibodies are elevated. The signs and symptoms of IgG4-RD depend on the organ or organs affected. Pathogenesis remains inconclusive, with uncertainty about whether the lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate is a cause or a consequence of the disease.

The American College of Rheumatology/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (formerly known as the European League Against Rheumatism) classification process for identifying IgG4-RD involves the following:

  • Identifying characteristic clinical or radiologic organ involvement and/or a suspicious biopsy specimen
  • Excluding alternative diseases
  • Confirming the diagnosis on the basis of characteristic pathologic findings, usually including IgG4 expression on biopsy tissue or an elevation in serum IgG4 level

Initial management of IgG4-RD includes moderate- to high-dose glucocorticoids, which are tapered over 2 months. Azathioprine is preferentially used as a glucocorticoid-sparing agent, and rituximab has been reported to have significant efficacy. In some cases, surgical intervention may be needed (e.g., to address an infiltrative mass jeopardizing a particular organ).

Variants in genes encoding for collagen, fibrillin, and other components of connective tissue can lead to skin and joint laxity, skeletal fractures, and cardiovascular complications related to involvement of the aorta and cardiac valves. The three most common syndromes are Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, and osteogenesis imperfecta. [Table: Table: Genetic Diseases of Connective Tissue]

summarizes clinical findings and management of these syndromes. Distinct from these three processes is the hypermobility spectrum disorder, which consists of symptomatic hypermobility that does not fulfill the criteria for the hypermobile variant of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or other connective tissue disorder.

Vascular monitoring is necessary in patients with Marfan syndrome and several types of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Patients with Marfan syndrome should undergo echocardiography to assess the aortic root and ascending aorta at the time of diagnosis and 6 months later to ensure structural stability. Follow-up studies should be completed at least annually; MRI and CT are often used to further delineate risk. Patients with Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome should undergo cardiology or cardiac surgery consultation. See Screening for and Surveillance of Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm in Cardiovascular Medicine for more information.

Table: CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Adults

CDC Case Definition for Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Adults

Case Definition

Patient aged ≥21 years who has been hospitalized for ≥24 hours or hospitalized for any length of time with an illness resulting in death

AND

Subjective or documented fever (temperature ≥38.0 °C [100.4 °F]) for ≥24 hours before hospitalization or within the first 3 days of hospitalization

AND

Fulfillment of the following clinical and laboratory criteria:

Clinical Criteria

≥3 of the following before hospitalization or within the first 3 days of hospitalization (at least 1 must be a primary criterion) without a more likely alternative diagnosis:

Primary

  1. Severe cardiac illness^a

  2. Rash and nonpurulent conjunctivitis

Secondary

  1. New-onset neurologic signs and symptoms^b

  2. Shock or hypotension not attributable to medical therapy (e.g., sedation, kidney replacement therapy)

  3. Abdominal pain, vomiting, or diarrhea

  4. Thrombocytopenia (platelet count <150,000/μL [150 × 10^9/L])

Laboratory Criteria

  1. Positive result on SARS-CoV-2 nucleic acid amplification, serology, or antigen testing AND

  2. Elevated levels of at least two of the following: C-reactive protein, ferritin, interleukin-6, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, procalcitonin
